## Summary of the Privilege.

This present work has been printed with Imperial Privilege: <note>original: "Cæſareo Priuilegio"</note> which the Most Serene Prince, <note>This likely refers to Prince Philip, later Philip II of Spain, acting on behalf of Emperor Charles V.</note> by the advice of the Court at Madrid, in the present year 1553, on the 27th of May, has graciously granted to the Author for a period of ten years: namely, that no one without his permission may either print or sell this work, under penalty of the confiscation of the books and the tools of the trade, as well as a fine of thirty thousand <term>maravedís<gloss>The Latin text uses "dupondiorum" to refer to this small Spanish copper coin, which was the standard unit for legal fines and price fixings.</gloss></term>. Indeed, the price of each individual sheet <note>original: "diplomata," referring here to the printed gatherings or leaves.</note> has been assessed at the price of three maravedís. Therefore, let no one plead ignorance of this matter.

<meta>This page is the formal dedication of Domingo de Soto’s "On Justice and Right" (1553). It follows the legal privilege and establishes the pedagogical intent of the work. Soto addresses the young Prince Don Carlos, son of Philip II, framing the legal treatise as a manual for a future ruler.</meta>

# TO CARLOS THE GREAT, <note>original: "CAROLO MAGNO". This refers to the young Prince Don Carlos (1545–1568), then only eight years old. Soto uses the name "Magnus" (Great) to honor both the boy’s grandfather, Emperor Charles V, and the boy's own potential.</note>
## FIRST-BORN SON OF THE MOST SERENE PHILIP THE SECOND,
### Prince of the Spains,
->his own Friar, <note>Soto was a member of the Dominican Order (Order of Preachers), whose members are called Friars.</note> Domingo de Soto,<-
->[wishes] happiness.<-

---

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'O' begins the text. Inside the letter, a figure—likely representing a scholar or the author—sits in a contemplative landscape with classical-style buildings and hills in the background.</image-desc>

**THIS WORK, CARLOS THE GREAT, WHICH IS TITLED** *On Justice and Right*, and which I am now allowing to go forth into the public eye almost against my will, gave me no reason to hesitate for long as to whom I should most especially dedicate it: for your Highness was immediately present at the very beginning of my thoughts. For since God and the nature of things brought you forth into the use of this light from such a long lineage of Kings and Emperors <note>original: "Caesarum"</note>, so that He might betroth to you this heaven-born Virgin—Justice, I mean—whom from the whole world would I more wisely choose than your Serenity to dedicate her image? Truly, so that you might know by her face right from the cradle that virtue which you are to holily cultivate throughout the entire course of your life; that you might look upon her again and again, and entice yourself with her beauty and delight in her embraces; that you might grow intimately accustomed to her character and drink in her most wise warnings with your whole heart. Finally, so that you might imbue that "whiteness of your wool" <note>An ancient metaphor, common in Latin literature, comparing a young person's mind to undyed wool that is ready to take on the "color" of its education.</note>, while it is still white in the tenderness of your age, with her colors.

I remember that I was ordered by those holy fathers at the Council of Trent <note>original: "Tridentina Synodo". Soto was a prominent theologian at this major ecclesiastical council.</note> to deliver a sermon concerning your birth; for then that happy and auspicious day dawned for us. I promised much concerning you, and that holy Church, offering vows to God for your health, safety, and happiness, placed great hope in you. For why would anyone hesitate to promise great things of you, Illustrious Prince, for whom such a numerous line of your grandfathers and great-grandfathers stands as surety, through their innumerable, most famous, and most religious deeds? 

But indeed, we pray to Eternal God that you may in fact fulfill not only my own faith, which I as a private man have pledged for you, but also your public faith, which you hold obligated to so many kingdoms and nations. Therefore, begin to learn from this, your burgeoning age, over how many nations you shall sit as judge; to whom, as to "Justice itself living" <note>original: "iustum ipsum vivens." A reference to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, where the judge is described as personified justice.</note>—as that Philosopher of great name says—there will be a gathering from almost the whole world. Thus, when you realize how much human safety is at risk in the formation of your Imperial character, you may understand how much ease and accessibility your modesty must provide, so that you may be adorned both with other gifts of virtue and especially with Justice, which we have here vividly depicted in her own colors according to our ability. 

Xenophon wrote the *Education of Cyrus* <note>original: "Cyropaediam"</note>, Aristotle instructed Alexander, Seneca instructed Nero, and Plutarch instructed Trajan, as others have done for others. As for me, although you enjoy such an education from wise men that you lack no service from my smallness, I have nevertheless not feared to offer this *Education of Carlos* <note>original: "Carolopædiam." Soto coins this term modeled on Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*.</note> to your Brightness in the meantime: where, as I began to say, you may contemplate the beauty of Justice, and likewise the countenance of a most happy Prince. For here, as the light and power of reason grows within you, you will perceive above all else how much a King differs from a Tyrant—a name which your ancestors have always held as most accursed. Specifically, while the tyrant turns all public matters toward his own private lust, the King, on the contrary, looks continually to the one common good: for the sake of that alone he establishes laws, creates magistrates, exacts tributes, sets rewards, decrees punishments, wages wars, and settles peace—

<summary>In this dedication to the young Prince Don Carlos, Domingo de Soto presents his treatise on law as a moral and political guidebook, contrasting the virtues of a true King with the vices of a Tyrant.</summary>
<keywords>Don Carlos, Philip II, Council of Trent, Justice, King vs Tyrant, Carolopaedia, political philosophy, Spanish Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to Prince Don Carlos. The opening syllable "nat" completes the word *destinatum* (destined) from the previous page, referring to the Prince being destined by nature and God to embrace the "Virgin Justice."</meta>

[desti]ned: in short, he should never consider anything in his mind, nor perform anything in his actions regarding himself, except that which is directed toward this goal. For this reason, you will also be taught here repeatedly that God—through whom all kings rule and by whose wisdom they decree just things—has certainly not conferred such great power upon kings so that they might either violate His laws or inflict injury upon any mortal. 

Rather, it is so that they themselves may repel injuries, resist them being inflicted, and reverse those already committed: clearly understanding that, just as they are the most absolute <note>The author uses the term "absolutissimi," referring to the legal principle that a King is "absolutus" (released) from human legal coercion, though still bound by divine law.</note> from all human coercion, it is fitting for them to live most bound both to reason and especially to the laws of God. Furthermore, here your Serenity will discover by how holy a bond justice and mercy (which are commonly thought to be at odds) are married in an excellent prince. For he ought to possess a severity that does not verge into cruelty, and a clemency that does not degenerate into sloth: a face that is grave but not grim; mild and placid in his speech, yet terrible in his zeal for justice. He should show himself to be cherished through love and fear, not so much by the clashing of arms as by the integrity of his character. He should be, in short, what that famous poet sang: **A SHEPHERD OF THE PEOPLE** <note>original Greek: "ΠΟΙΜΕΝΑ ΛΑΩΝ" (poimena laon). This is a classical title for a king used frequently by Homer in the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*.</note>. That is to say, one who does not consider himself to be hunting wild beasts, but leading a flock.

Finally, what you must gaze upon most thoughtfully and considerately in this model of justice, O best of Princes, is how holily you ought to look up to, adore, and cherish religion. Specifically, you must not mix the sacred with the profane, but you must hold the most holy Church—for whose faith God created Kings, and men, and the world itself—in the highest esteem above all secular matters, and attend to her with all veneration and reverence. For secular happiness, unless it is directed toward that eternal happiness, is established in vain; it is far from being able to prosper in any way. No gem decorates a Christian crown more brightly than the sign of the Cross. What images of virtues—to note them all briefly—would this "mirror of justice" not reflect back to you, if you were to grow accustomed to its gaze? 

But I fear both exceeding the length of a letter and burdening your not-yet-mature age with premature warnings. There will be a time, God willing—as the safety of your Kingdoms is greatly at stake—when you will frequently consult, attentively hear, and value wise men (especially those of proven life) as highly as it concerns a Prince to have eyes. In the meantime, we pray for this for your Highness: that you may respond in character to the prayers of your father and your grandfather the Emperor <note>original: "Cæsaris." This refers to Carlos's grandfather, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>. Indeed, I know intimately how anxiously he desires that God the Greatest might enrich you with as great a store of virtues as it concerns us all that you be most rich in them.

<summary>Soto explains that a King's power is granted by God not for self-interest, but to protect the people from injury and uphold the Church. He characterizes the ideal Prince as a "Shepherd of the People" who balances severity with mercy and places religious devotion above secular concerns.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the formal treatise after the introductory dedication. The author transitions from addressing the Prince to providing the theological and philosophical justification for his work on Law and Justice. He explains his decision to return to teaching and publishing due to the evolving nature of financial crimes and the requests of his students at the University of Salamanca.</meta>

# By Brother Domingo de Soto of Segovia, Theo-
# logian, of the Order of Preachers, Confessor to his
# Imperial Majesty, and Professor at Salamanca,
## Ten Books on Justice and Right.

### P R E F A C E.

<margin>
Praise of Justice.
</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'I' begins the text. The letter is set within a square frame featuring a woodcut illustration of a landscape with trees and a building in the distance. The body of the 'I' is decorated with leafy flourishes.</image-desc>
**J**ustice is a most illustrious virtue, the legitimate offspring of our Faith, the strength of hope, the handmaid of charity, and the brightest beam of all other virtues. Both secular and, especially, Divine oracles exalt her above the heavens. She is the one who gathers humanity—a <term>social animal<note>original: "ciuile animal," a reference to the Aristotelian concept that humans are naturally meant to live in a community or *polis*.</note></term>—into unity, protects them from injuries, unites them in love, maintains them in peace, adorns them with virtues, and finally, by divine gift, raises them to eternal happiness. This, I say, is the virtue that we have resolved to clarify in the present Work and to treat according to the modest measure of our talent. But since it is the duty of this most brilliant star (as the Laws themselves teach us) to render to each person their <term>right<note>original: "ius." In Latin, *ius* can mean both a "right" belonging to a person and the "body of law" itself.</note></term> according to the norms of the laws, I have deemed it appropriate to entitle the Work, *On Justice and Law*. For my 
<margin>
The author’s purpose.
</margin>
mind intends to amplify the majestic dignity of this virtue, to establish its foundations, and to examine its laws, parts, types, and as many iniquities, frauds, and acts of violence as oppose it. I will do this to the extent that divine strength supports me, surveying these matters in their widest scope and depicting each in its proper place. For although I am well aware of the dignity and abundance with which many Theologians and Jurists have enriched this subject, nevertheless, through the wickedness of the times, human lust has given birth to—and continues to bring forth daily—new forms of fraud. By these means, everyone satisfies their insatiable greed against what is right and divine law. Therefore, it must be considered nothing less than worthwhile if the many new types of unfair contracts, agreements, currency exchanges, usury, and simony have induced us to publish new volumes on an ancient subject. Furthermore, the more that has been discovered by our predecessors in any matter, the richer the "forest" of material they provide for those who follow to devise new insights, if they possess any talent. Add to this that no one has ever treated Scholastic matters—which are complex by nature—so successfully that they cannot, through more vigilant diligence (I am not 

<column-break/>

speaking of my own), be established more firmly and precisely, arranged more orderly, and polished more elegantly. For this reason, I—who, after many years spent in these University Chairs, had been distracted by other public business and had bid farewell to this province, and who, after being untangled from those affairs, had dedicated myself to sacred letters—have now been called back to this same task by the wishes of the students, though I was thinking of nothing less. The <term>Conscript Fathers<note>original: "Patres Conscripti." A prestigious title borrowed from the Roman Senate, here referring to the senior faculty or governing body of the University of Salamanca.</note></term> summoned me despite my total resistance, and my superiors compelled me against my will. Subsequently, when by public vote this lectureship on Justice fell to me, they began to demand most insistently that I commit what I had dictated in the Schools to the press. This was so that those present might be relieved of the labor of writing, and those absent might enjoy the fruit of our toil. I agreed most gladly, for I myself had been laboring to give birth to this work for a long time; such was the persistence of those who frequently approached me with various moral dilemmas and consultations regarding the new types of contracts appearing daily. Indeed, there is no reason to find fault with Theologians for taking up this task, which might seem more suited to Jurists. After all, Canon laws emerged from the very heart of Theology, while Civil laws came from the midst of moral Philosophy. It is therefore the role of the Theologian to weigh the decrees of Canon law against the Gospel norm, and the role of the philosopher to examine Civil laws based on the principles of philosophy. Hence <margin>Cicero.</margin> **Cicero**, in the first book of *On Laws*, judges that the discipline of law must be drawn not from a praetor’s edict, nor from the Twelve Tables, but from the very depths of philosophy. Indeed, he says, a litigious reckoning of laws is an ignorance of right rather than a science. And the Jurist says (in the first law of the *Digest* section "On Justice and Law") that we strive for a true philosophy, not a simulated one. Yet, although my established practice in the schools is to clarify the <term>Master of Sentences<note>referring to Peter Lombard, whose *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note></term> and Saint Thomas Aquinas with commentaries, I have nevertheless decided it is more prudent to change my method of writing slightly. This is not because I am attempting a doctrine different from that of this divine author [Thomas Aquinas] among the Saints—whom all the Schools universally adore as a most brilliant star, both for all other subjects and especially for these moral disciplines—but because, although he and others provide...

<summary>Domingo de Soto introduces his treatise on Justice and Law, explaining that he was compelled by the University of Salamanca to publish his lectures to address new forms of economic fraud and usury. He argues that theologians have a rightful role in analyzing law through the lens of moral philosophy and the Gospel.</summary>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues from the author's preface, moving from the dedication to the structural outline of the entire work. Soto transitions into the first book, which focuses on the nature of Law, following the scholastic method typical of the University of Salamanca.</meta>

<header>Brother D. Soto, On Justice and Right,</header>

<margin>Division of the work.</margin>
Imbued with [the study of] the mind, I have commented on many other things; however, I thought it more fitting to forge a new work in which I would arrange everything more orderly, rather than writing my own notes separately around [the text of Thomas Aquinas]. ¶ I have divided the work into ten books: the first two are about Right, that is, about laws, which are the supreme rule of Justice. The third is about Right, insofar as it is the object of Justice, and about the substance of this virtue and its related parts, up to distributive justice <note>Distributive justice concerns how a community shares resources and honors among its members based on merit.</note>. The fourth is on the preambles to commutative justice <note>Commutative justice governs private transactions and the equal exchange of goods between individuals.</note>: namely, on ownership and restitution. The fifth is on injustice arising from injurious action: namely, on homicide and the rest. The sixth is on usury and contracts. The seventh is on currency exchanges. Then the eighth is on vows. The ninth is on tithes and <term>simony<note>The act of buying or selling sacred things or ecclesiastical offices.</note></term>. Finally, the tenth is on the status and residency of Prelates <note>High-ranking clergy such as bishops.</note>. Thus, the work on Justice, which is primarily contained in the ten commandments of the <term>Decalogue<note>The Ten Commandments.</note></term>, is also completed in a "Decade" of ten books. I will ensure that each individual book is divided into Questions and Articles in the Scholastic style, so that I may depart as rarely as possible—except for the sake of expanding on matters—from the order of Saint Thomas [Aquinas]. Nevertheless, let all my assertions undergo the censure of the Holy Mother Church, and the subsequent refinement of those who judge sincerely. May God the Greatest therefore breathe upon our efforts for His own glory.

<margin>Title of the work.</margin>
<margin>The name "Right" is used in two ways.</margin>
<margin>Isidore, book 5, chapter 3.</margin>
¶ As I begin, with God’s help, a discussion on Justice and Right, I must start with Right. For this name is used in two ways: in one way, for that which is "law"—just as <term>Isidore<note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and archbishop whose "Etymologies" was a standard reference in the Middle Ages.</note></term> says in the fifth book of his *Etymologies* (referenced in the Decrees, distinction 1), where he says that "Right" (*Ius*) is a general name, while "Law" (*Lex*) is a specific type of Right. In the other way, it is taken as the "object" of justice: namely, for the equity that justice establishes in things. And whichever way you take it, a notion of "Right" is required to understand Justice. But because every virtue must be measured by its own rules, it is fitting to post those rules before the doors of the work, and thus to speak of laws before all else in the first two books.

<margin>The first book on laws.</margin>
In the first part, I will speak of the eternal, natural, and human law; and in the latter part, of Divine law. The first book will be completed in seven questions. And since (as Cicero, often cited in his work *On Duties*, is the authority) every orderly instruction must begin from the substance of the thing, which is grasped by its definition: the first question raised is about law in general.

<column-break/>

# QUESTION ONE,
## On law in general.

->Saint Thomas [Aquinas], Part 1 of Part 2, Question 90.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether any of the definitions of law established by the Doctors is legitimate.<-

<margin>Various definitions of law.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'C' showing a robed figure seated at a desk within a circular medallion, surrounded by a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>
ALTHOUGH MANY and various definitions are found among Orators as well as among Theologians and Jurists, I find none (or hardly any) that fits law as a universal category, except that which Saint Thomas [Aquinas] (1. 2. q. 90. art. 4.) gathers, if it is refined a little more. For
<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
that definition of Cicero in the second book of *On the Laws*—"Law is a certain eternal
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
thing, which rules the entire world by the wisdom of commanding and forbidding"—is specific to the eternal law of God. But that which he proposed in the first book—"Law is the highest reason implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the opposite"—does not extend beyond natural laws. However, that definition in the <term>Digest<note>Original: "ff. de leg. & sena. consul. l. 1." This refers to the *Pandects* or *Digest* of the Roman Emperor Justinian, the foundational text of Roman Law.</note></term> regarding laws and senatorial decrees—"Law is a common precept, the counsel of prudent men, etc."—is ascribed only to human law. Just as that definition of Aristotle
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
in the *Rhetoric to Alexander* (in the chapter on the deliberative genus): "Law is the common consent of a city which prescribes in writing how each thing must be done." To which Isidore alludes in his fifth book:
<margin>Isidore.</margin>
"Law is a written constitution." Therefore, if you look at its vast breadth, as far as it extends, Law is nothing other than a certain
<margin>Definition of law.</margin>
ordinance of reason and a precept for the common good, promulgated by him who has care for the community. In this statement, the "genus" (category) of law is expressed, along with its purpose, its cause, and the form of its establishment.
¶ But for the explanation of this same definition, it is necessary to dispute in order about each of the four parts from which it is constructed. This question, therefore, requires four articles. The first of these will be about the "genus" of the definition,
<margin>The first article of the question.</margin>
namely, to examine in which power law exists: whether it is an act of the intellect or of the will. For I seemed to assert that it is a work of the intellect when I said that it is an "ordinance and precept of reason." However, there are some arguments to the contrary.

<meta>The catchword "Pri-" indicates the start of the word "Primus" (First) on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Domingo de Soto outlines the ten-book structure of his treatise and begins Book One by defining "Law." He synthesizes definitions from Cicero, Aristotle, and Roman Law into a single universal definition: law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, promulgated by a legitimate authority.</summary>
<keywords>Law, Justice, Right (Ius), Thomas Aquinas, Cicero, Aristotle, Common Good, Natural Law, Eternal Law, Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general plan of the work to the specific inquiry of Book One. It establishes the foundational question: What is the nature of law, and where does it reside—in the human mind (intellect) or the human will?</meta>

# First Book: Question 1

<margin>Argument 1.</margin> ¶ First: Since in the intellect there is nothing but "habit" <note>A stable disposition or learned quality of the mind.</note> and "act," it does not appear which of these might be law.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second: It belongs to law to move subjects, for a King moves his people through laws. However, it belongs to the *will* to move; for an animal is not moved except by something it desires under some aspect of "the good," as Aristotle, the author of *On the Soul*, states in book 3, text 49. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> The "good," however, is the object of the will, not the intellect.

<margin>Third argument.</margin> ¶ Added to this in the third place is the authority of certain recent authors of no small reputation, who define the substance of law as follows: "Law is the right will of the person who represents the people," etc. These authors certainly seem to find support in <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine, who says in book 4 of *The City of God* that in ancient times the judgments of Princes stood for laws. Furthermore, the Jurist in the Digest <note>The *Digest* (or *Pandects*) is a massive compilation of Roman legal opinions commissioned by Emperor Justinian.</note>, in the section "On the Constitutions of Princes," law 1 (which is also cited in the *Institutes* "On Natural Law and the Law of Nations"), says: "What has pleased the Prince has the force of law." <note>original: "quod Principi placuit legis habet vigorem"</note>

¶ Fourth: Paul also seems to object in Romans 7, where he says: "I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind." Indeed, the law that is in the "members" <note>The physical body or lower impulses.</note> is not only absent from the intellect but also lacks reason entirely.

¶ On the contrary, however, stands the power of law, which is to command, as stated in the law "The Power of Law" in the Digest section "On Laws." This is the task of prudence and consequently of the intellect.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'A' depicting a seated scholar or saint in a study, wearing a cap and robes, with a book or desk visible.</image-desc>

To this question, a response is given in two conclusions. The first is: law resides in the intellect as its own proper work. Here, however, concerning the name, <margin>The name 'Law' is derived in various ways by writers.</margin> it must be noted immediately that the name "Law" <note>Latin: *Lex*</note> is derived differently by different people because of the various powers and qualities of the thing itself. <margin>Isidore.</margin> For Isidore, in book 5 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, derives it from "reading" <note>original: "a legendo"</note> because it is brought forth in writing so that it may be read by all.

But since this is accidental to it, <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> Saint Thomas and the school of theologians more appropriately believe it is called from "binding" <note>original: "a ligando"</note>, inasmuch as it possesses the power of obligating. Although <margin>Cicero.</margin> Cicero, in book 1 of *On Laws*, felt it was derived from "reading," in the sense of "choosing" <note>original: "eligere"</note>. Indeed, he says that although the Greeks call law after "distributing" (for what we call "law," they call *nomos* from *nemein*, which is "to distribute," <note>Greek: νόμος (nomos) from νέμειν (nemein).</note> because it distributes to each what is his own), I, however, name it from "reading"—that is, "selecting" <note>original: "deligendo"</note>. And he adds: "For as they place the power of law in equity, so we—that is, the Latins—place it in choice; and yet both are proper to law." Thus he speaks. Therefore, since all these qualities belong to law, it matters little from which of them you derive the name. However, even if I do not at all repudiate the theologians’

<column-break/>

etymology, Cicero’s opinion is very pleasing to me: that law should be the same as a rule for "reading"—that is, for choosing. For a rule teaches how to choose by directing. <margin>The etymology of law passed down by Cicero is more approved.</margin> From wherever the name is drawn, it is very clear that in reality, law is a thing of the intellect. This is demonstrated by both of its powers: it is both a rule and an obligatory command.

Therefore, although Saint Thomas puts only one of these in his definition, we have combined both in the definition of its category: namely, "ordering" and "commanding." For law does not simply order or direct, like someone who merely shows the way, but it commands by ordering and orders by commanding.

<margin>First argument for the conclusion.</margin> ¶ From the first part, then, it is argued: Law is the rule of equity and iniquity and the measure of action; for so it is generally held in the Digest "On Laws," where law is called the rule of what is just and unjust. Now, the rule and measure of our actions is reason; for the rule of actions is that which directs toward an end, which is the task of "sighted" reason alone. It is to this end that reason leads the will, which is a "blind power." Therefore, it is the function of reason to establish law.

Add that just as in natural things, that which is first is the measure of the rest—like "one" in numbers, or the motion of the "prime mover" in respect to lower motions— <margin>Confirmation.</margin> so because the "end" <note>The goal or purpose.</note> (as the Philosopher teaches in *Physics* book 2) is the starting principle of human actions, it follows that the action of reason, which orders means toward an end, is the measure and thus the law.

<margin>Second argument.</margin> ¶ From the second part it is argued secondly as follows: The task of law is to command and forbid, as held in the Law "The Power of Law" in the Digest "On Laws and Senatorial Decrees," and as the very form of the law shows: "Worship one God," "Do not swear in vain by Him." Indeed, this is so widely accepted and admitted by all that for this reason we call laws "precepts" and "commands." But to command belongs to reason; therefore, law is elicited from reason and thus consists in the intellect.

Saint Thomas teaches that the "minor premise" of this syllogism—namely, that commanding is an act of the intellect through the virtue of prudence— <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> in the *Summa Theologiae* [1. 2. question 17, article 1, and question 57, article 6]. It is the mark of those who consider little to attack this opinion as if it were only Saint Thomas’s; for they fail to see that it is not his invention, but the clearest and most constant opinion of <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle. In book 6 of the *Ethics*, chapter 10, he distinguishes three virtues of the practical intellect: namely, *euboulia* <note>Greek: εὐβουλία; the virtue of deliberating or consulting well.</note>, which is the virtue of consulting well—that is, investigating the means suitable to the end. For there is no deliberation about the end, because all things by their own nature...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right

...seek their own happiness: and **sagacity** <note>original: "synefin," a Latinization of the Greek *synesis*, meaning intuitive understanding or insight</note>, which the Latins call "shrewdness," which is the virtue of judging rightly. For there are some who are sharp-witted in searching for the means to an end, yet they are not so strong in judgment that, once those means are found, they can think rightly about the best course of action. But beyond these, the final act of **prudence** is required, which is **command** <note>original: "imperium," the specific directive act of the mind</note>. In this, practical reason differs from speculative reason. For because speculative reason is not ordered toward performing a task, it has precisely two acts: discourse and judgment. Practical reason, however, additionally requires command for the work, toward which the preceding two acts are ordered. And therefore **Aristotle** says that among all acts, this is the highest and most perfect, from which prudence is most especially named a virtue.

<margin>To command is an act of the intellect.</margin>
Nor indeed is this only the opinion of Aristotle; rather, it is the opinion of all the philosophers who either preceded or followed him.

<margin>This is supported by simple reasoning.</margin>
Indeed, the very nature of things and human custom teaches us this truth plainly. For it is clear that to command is to speak—namely: "do this," or "do not do that." Speaking, however, is the business of the intellect, since its concepts are expressed through voice and writing; therefore, it belongs to the intellect to command. For when God commands the angels, or when one of them commands another, this is surely achieved through the speech of the intellect, not the will. By the same law, therefore, if a command exists within our internal powers (which cannot be denied), it belongs to the intellect, certainly not to the will.

And this reasoning is confirmed: When someone prays to God in their mind: 
> *Thy will be done: Give us this day our daily bread:* 
it is plain that they are speaking not with the will but with the intellect. Therefore, if any power commands the others, that power is surely the intellect through similar words.

<margin>Third principal argument.</margin>
Third, it is argued from human usage that law is the proper work of the intellect, not the will. Willing and "nilling" <note>the act of "not-willing" or rejection</note>, which are the only acts in the will, bring no command with them. For indeed, although I may know for certain that my superior most earnestly desires that I should preach or do something else, I am nevertheless not bound to obey until he, speaking to me, commands it. Moreover, speech is the sign of concepts. And from this, an analogy is drawn for our internal works. For although someone may choose a good work after the judgment of reason, we nonetheless experience that after such a choice, men can be faint-hearted and sluggish in entering upon that same work. For many have chosen in their minds to lead a very holy life, yet 

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
because of the sluggishness of the "command" of prudence, they are most slow to set about it. 

¶ Furthermore, it is argued:

<column-break/>

Men are bound to conform themselves and be obedient to the eternal law of God, as is widely disputed in book 1 of the *Sentences*, distinction 45. However, we are not bound to conform to His "will of good pleasure" <note>original: "voluntas beneplaciti," referring to God's secret or ultimate will regarding specific outcomes</note>. For even if I know that God wills the death of my father, it is permissible for me—and even honorable—to be saddened by it. And conversely, He commanded **Abraham** to sacrifice his son, to which law that Patriarch was bound to comply; and yet God did not have the "will of good pleasure" that he should actually carry it out. Therefore, the law of God is not in His will, but in the intellect of the one commanding or forbidding.

<margin>The error of the contrary opinion is revealed.</margin>
By these points, the fiction of the contrary opinion is also refuted—the one where they say that the will is not the handmaid of the intellect, but the queen, and the intellect is the servant. Indeed, the matter is quite the opposite. For to rule is the function 

<margin>First reason.</margin>
of that which illuminates and directs; light, however, exists not in the will (which is a blind power) but in the intellect. For it is not called the light of the will, but of the intellect. Concerning this, **David** says:

<margin>Psalm 90.</margin> <note>Modern Bibles cite this as Psalm 4:6.</note>
> *The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.* 

Wherefore **Aristotle** in *Politics*, Book 1, Chapter 3, 

<margin>Aristotle, Politics 1.3.</margin>
expressly says that the mind commands the appetite (under which name he includes the will)—though not with "despotic" command, as the soul rules the body, but with "political" command, as a King commands citizens. Hence **Plato** says wisely in book 3 of *The Laws*:

<margin>Plato.</margin>
> *We must not pray or strive that all things should follow our will, but that our will should follow our prudence.*

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
To this: "King" <note>Latin: *Rex*</note> is named from "ruling" <note>Latin: *regendo*</note>, which is an act of prudence; therefore, it is the function of this virtue to establish laws. For this is the primary duty of the one who sits at the helm of the kingdom's government. Wherefore **Cicero**, in book 1 of *On Laws*, 

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
after that definition of law cited above (namely, "Law is reason implanted in nature"), adds: "And so they think that prudence is law, whose force is such that it orders us to do right and forbids us to stray." And **Aristotle** in *Ethics*, Book 10, Chapter 9, says: "Law 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
has compelling force; which is indeed a speech proceeding from some prudence and mind." 

Who then could ever doubt that law is a work of prudence, and consequently of the intellect, which everyone calls a "practical dictate"? And this is the legitimate sense of that verse in **Proverbs 8**: "By me Kings reign, and the 

<margin>Proverbs 8.</margin>
framers of laws decree just things." For in saying "they reign," the power of kings is designated; since all power is from the Lord God, as the Apostle reports in Romans 13. However, in what follows—"and the framers of laws," etc.—the *use* of that same power is understood. Whence he says, "By me," that is, through the virtue of prudence, which flows from my fountain...

<summary>Soto argues that law is an act of the intellect rather than the will, identifying it specifically with "command" (imperium). He refutes the idea of the will as "queen," asserting that the intellect must provide the light and direction necessary for any true law or government.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of law, specifically arguing that law is an act of the intellect rather than the will. Having established that "commanding" is a mental act, Soto now moves to his second major conclusion, defining law as a stable "habit" of practical reason and addressing the objections of contemporary thinkers (the "Moderns") regarding the mechanics of human action.</meta>

### Book One, Question 1. ###
->a 5<-

...flows from you, Kings establish right laws, and use them properly.

<margin>Second Conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: law is a universal proposition and a dictate of practical reason <note>original: "dictamen rationis practicæ"</note> that exists within the mind as a habit. This conclusion is an assertion made by Saint Thomas Aquinas in the *Summa Theologiae* (First part of the second part, question 90). Understand this explanation: within the intellect, there are both simple propositions of understanding and others that involve judgment. Law, however, is not merely an understanding; it is a precept that follows a judgment—not just any judgment, but one concerning morals. Indeed, they call that a "practical judgment." First, through the first virtue of **prudence**, namely **good deliberation** <note>original: "eubouliam," from the Greek *euboulia*</note>, those things which are useful are sought out; next, through **insight** <note>original: "synesin," from the Greek *synesis*</note>, which is the second virtue, they are approved by judgment; third, they are chosen by the **will**; and subsequently follows the **command of prudence**. This command is not a proposition in the "indicative" mood (stating a fact), but certainly in the "imperative" mood: "this must be done," or "this must be avoided." For if these words only had the force of a noun—for instance, "it is worthy to be done" or "it is an unworthy deed"—they would be "speculative" propositions and would not yet possess the force of law. However, when they have the force of a future participle ("to-be-done"), then they are considered practical dictates. And if these are in the Mind of the Prince and are promulgated to the people, then they exist as laws. Furthermore, it is required that they exist as a **habit**: that is, they must be fixed and permanently enduring. For temporary precepts that pass away as single acts—because they are not universal but are fitted to a specific person, place, and time (such as "do this" or "do not do that")—are not considered laws, but are rather applications of laws, as will be seen in the next article.

<margin>The arguments are resolved.</margin>
Through this conclusion, the first argument presented before the question is answered: specifically, it was asserted that law is a proposition inherent as a habit. For even if a law is enacted as a specific act, it remains impressed and written in the mind as a habit.

<margin>The fallacy of the Moderns.</margin>
¶ And from this, the fallacy of certain **Moderns** <note>original: "Neotericorum," referring to contemporary 16th-century scholastic rivals</note> is revealed. They contend against Saint Thomas that no command of the intellect is necessary for action, failing to notice that they openly contradict not just Thomas, but **Aristotle**. For a certain author argues in his *Commentary on the Ethics* (chapter 2, on prudence) in this way: if a command is a proposition of the intellect, it is either an act of apprehension or of judgment. Apprehension alone is not enough for work; but if it is a judgment, that judgment is sufficient by itself without any other command. For as soon as someone judges that it is good to do this or that, they can immediately choose it—and in that choice, there is already

<column-break/>

<margin>The first point of the Moderns is resolved.</margin>
merit. Thus, one can immediately act without any other power of commanding. Therefore, either the choice of the will itself is the "command," or there is no command at all. And he adds (I know not what moved him to say it) that this is the common opinion; yet I do not remember having seen any authors of great value who hold it. By a double error, he shows he has not consulted Aristotle on this matter. First, we deny that a command is a proposition that is simply either apprehensive or judicial. Those are categories of the "indicative" mood; whereas a "commanding" proposition is not a judgment, but rather something that *requires* a prior judgment. And from this, their other fallacy is uncovered. For a **command** <note>original: "imperium"</note> (as Aristotle plainly teaches) is not that judgment which precedes the choice, but the **bidding** <note>original: "iussio"</note> which follows the choice. We concede, therefore, that judgment—which is the act of insight <note>original: "synesis"</note>—is sufficient for choice, in which some merit may reside; yet choice is not enough for the actual use and performance of the work unless a command follows it.

<margin>Another argument by the same author.</margin>
¶ But nevertheless, a third argument arises from this same author: if an intellectual command follows the choice, it follows either by necessity or freely. Not by necessity: for then no virtue of prudence would be needed to command, which is against Aristotle and the truth. But if it follows freely, then it seems to follow that the choice of the will alone is not enough to move the intellect, but requires another act besides; yet neither Aristotle, nor Saint Thomas, nor any of the philosophers ever posited such an act. On the contrary, all confess that the command follows the choice. This argument twisted us more than was right <note>referring to a previous discussion in Soto's commentary on the *Summa*, 1-2, question 17, article 3</note>.

<margin>The previous reasoning is cleared up.</margin>
However, I now find it easy to clear this up, responding that the command follows neither necessarily from the choice, nor does it require another act in the will besides that same choice. But it must be noted that for one power to be moved by another, it is necessary that both be well-disposed. Consequently, unless the choice is sufficiently rooted and the intellect is well-prepared through prudence, the command will not follow from the choice. Therefore, where the choice is solid and valid, and the intellect is sufficiently obedient through prudence, the command will follow immediately upon the choice; otherwise, it will follow either slowly or not at all.

<margin>Solution to the third principal argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument: while granting that it belongs to the King to move [the state], it is also granted that the will is the mover of both the intellect and the other powers. However, it does not follow from this that the will is the "queen" or that the intellect is a "slave."

<summary>Soto defines law as a "dictate of practical reason" that functions as a permanent mental habit, rather than a fleeting act of will. He defends the Aristotelian-Thomistic view that the intellect must issue a "command" (imperium) following a choice of the will to initiate action, countering contemporary thinkers who merged command and choice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Soto’s analysis of the relationship between the will and the intellect in the formation of law. He has previously argued that law is essentially an act of the intellect (a command), but here he clarifies the vital role the will plays in "moving" the intellect to act, while addressing famous definitions of law from Roman legal tradition and Scripture.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right, #

...slave. For the will does not move as a directing and knowing power, which would be required for it to be called "queen." Indeed, the very name "queen" sounds this way to our ears; but the will moves by impelling and applying the other powers to their duties. It is for this reason that human actions are called "voluntary"—that is, stemming from the will. For example: once a goal is intended (such as "I want to be rich"), the will applies the intellect to the task of investigating the means to achieve it. After the intellect judges these means, the will then chooses them, and subsequently, through that choice, moves the intellect again to issue a command, in which the very essence of ruling consists. This clearly alludes to the words of the second law in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de legib." — the Digest is a massive compendium of Roman law compiled under Emperor Justinian</note> regarding laws—a law which Marcianus did not blush to borrow from the Stoic Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus was a foundational Greek philosopher of the Stoic school</note>: where he says that **law is the queen of all divine and human things.**

<margin>The last objection is resolved with confirmations.</margin>
¶ I believe, therefore, that enough has been said to satisfy those who claim that law is the will of the one who acts on behalf of the people: for, as we showed above, no will of a Prince is binding unless it has been prescribed by an edict. It is in this manner that we must understand the words of the law cited above regarding the constitutions of princes: **What pleased the Prince has the force of law.** <note>original: "Quod Principi placuit legis habet vigorem" — a famous maxim of Roman law often used to justify absolute royal power; Soto is here re-interpreting it to limit that power</note> For this merely suggests that no law exists in the intellect unless a choice in the will precedes it; nevertheless, the will itself is not the law. Rather, if that which pleases the Prince is first conceived in the mind and then commanded by voice, *that* is the law. The meaning, therefore, is this: "What the prince has pleased to proclaim as an edict has the force of law." In this way, the same law immediately explains itself in these words: "Whatever the Emperor has established by letter or signature, or decreed upon inquiry, or spoke formally, or prescribed by edict, is established as law."

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
For this reason, there was no need to summon Cicero from the first book of *On the Laws* to prove that law resides in the will, simply because, according to him, law <note>original: "lex"</note> is named from "choosing" <note>original: "eligendo"</note>. For he does not think that the choice itself is the law, but rather that the law follows the choice of the Prince and teaches the subjects to choose between the fair and the unfair. Whence he immediately adds that "law is the mind and reason of a prudent man, and the rule of right and wrong."

<margin>The passage from Paul is explained.</margin>
<margin>Chapter 7 of the Epistle to the Romans, on those words: "I see another law," etc.</margin>
¶ The fourth argument, however, belongs to a different matter. For Paul calls the "law of the members" by a far different meaning. He distinguishes, I say, four laws: namely, the **law of sin** fighting against the law of God, and the **law of the members** opposing the **law of the mind**.

<margin>See the Author on [Romans] 7.</margin>
And although it might seem to some that the law of sin and the law of the members are the same (just as the law of God and the law of the mind might seem so), it appeared to us in our Commentaries that they differ somewhat. For the **law of the mind** is the effect of God's law and its impression upon our mind, just as a footprint in the dust is the effect of a foot. The **law of the members**, however, is the natural inclination of our sensuality toward its objects, according to the full weight and impetus of nature. This is an effect of the loss of "original justice," by which that same sensuality was held restrained in obedience to reason. The **law of sin**, meanwhile, is either the effect of that same inclination (such as acting against God's will), or it was the first transgression of our first parents through which the members were loosened—from which dissolution sins proceed. Therefore, the "law of the members" is not a true law: because it does not incline us toward the good, but is called a law through a metaphor; it is nature destitute of original justice, and thus an oblique rule turning us away from the right path.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But you argue: If it is a rule, how can it exist outside of the intellect?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that law exists primarily and essentially in the intellect as the thing that "rules and measures"; nevertheless, it is said to exist "by participation" in the powers and members which it moves, as the thing that is "ruled." Just as the Sun is said to be in a hall because of its effect (light), or as art is said to be in a statue. In a similar way, the law of sin is in the members.

## ARTICLE II. ##

### Whether Law always has an order toward the common good. ###

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' showing two figures in a rustic landscape: one figure appears to be resting or seated on the ground while the other stands or approaches.</image-desc>The second article follows, in which the second part of the definition—which designated the *end* <note>the goal or purpose</note> of law—must be explained. For there are arguments suggesting that it is not necessary for law to be ordered toward the common good.

<margin>Argument 1. Isidore.</margin>
¶ First, as Isidore says in Book 5 of the *Etymologies*: "If law consists of reason, then everything that consists of reason will be law." Now, not only that which is directed toward the common good consists of reason, but also that which refers to a particular good. Therefore, nothing is detracted from the reason of a law if it is not ordered toward the common good.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: Precepts (as was said above) have the force of law, insofar as the power of law is to command and prohibit. But precepts are also given concerning individual actions in which our morals are established; therefore, it is sufficient for laws to be ordered toward a particular good.

¶ On the contrary, however, is the same Isidore in that same fifth book, where he says that "law is written for no private benefit, but for the common utility of the citizens."

<summary>Soto explains that while the will initiates action, law itself is an intellectual command. He also interprets St. Paul's "law of the members" as a metaphor for human nature after the Fall, concluding with a new inquiry into whether all laws must serve the common good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Soto’s inquiry into the nature of law. Having established that law is a command of the intellect, he now addresses the essential purpose of law: the "common good." He draws on both classical philosophy (Aristotle and Plato) and Roman law to argue that any decree serving only a private interest fails to be a true law.</meta>

# Question I of the First Book #

**Column 1:**

<margin>A responsive conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with a single conclusion: Every law, so that it may be solid and firm, must promote the subjects toward the **common good.** This conclusion is affirmed by a twofold reason, depending on whether the "common good" is used to mean **natural happiness** <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "happiness" (eudaimonia) refers to the flourishing and well-ordered life of a community.</note> which we attain in this age—namely, the quiet, tranquil, and peaceful state of the commonwealth—or for that **supernatural happiness** which awaits us in the next life as our supreme end, toward which every worldly good is directed by its very nature. Indeed, if you look at the first reason regarding the common good, the conclusion is demonstrated in this way:

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
Every part is directed toward its whole by the natural order, just as the imperfect is directed toward the perfect. Since all citizens are parts of the city, the law prescribed for them must establish them in the common good of the entire city, just as the parts of a single body are ordered toward the service of the whole.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle agrees with this reasoning in the *Ethics*, Book 5 <note>The Latin text cites Book 9, but Soto likely refers to the famous discussion of legal justice in Book 5 of the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, where he says: **Legal justice**—that is, civil laws—are the "productive and preservative factors of happiness and its components."

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato also says this in the first dialogue on *Laws*, where he states: "A legislator must establish all laws for the sake of public peace." For this reason, he refutes the custom of the Spartans, who directed all their laws toward the goal of waging war as vigorously as possible; for they would have acted more prudently had they sought peace.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Cicero</margin>
Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, Book 10: "We wage war so that we may live in peace." And Cicero says in the second book of *On Laws*: "It is certain, indeed, that laws were established for the safety of citizens, the preservation of states, and the quiet and blessed life of all."

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ If we look higher toward the supreme blessedness, which is God, we can attach a second and equally excellent reason. Law (as we were saying recently) is the primary rule of our actions; but the function of a rule—and especially a primary one—is to direct things toward their supreme end and goal. Therefore, it follows that both the legislator’s intention and the law itself must be aimed at the common good.

<margin>Third reason of the Philosopher.</margin>
¶ A third reason is taken from another condition of law. For the "Philosopher" <note>Aristotle is frequently referred to simply as "the Philosopher" in Scholastic writing.</note> says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, that every law is **universal**—that is, it is established for all people in general and concerns every virtue. We are taught the same by that cited law: "Law is a common precept" <note>original: "Lex est commune præceptum." — a citation from the Digest of Justinian (ff. de legib.).</note>. Laws are established not for individual persons, but for general application. It follows, therefore, that law must be directed toward the supreme end, which is common to all, and not tailored to private interests. He correctly says in the same

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

book, chapter 1: "The laws themselves dictate concerning all things,
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
aiming at either the common utility of all, or of the best citizens, or of the Princes." Here he suggests three types of commonwealths: namely, democracy, aristocracy, and the kingdom. From this, it follows that **legal justice** <note>The virtue of behaving in accordance with the law for the sake of the community.</note> encompasses all the virtues.

<margin>Final reason.</margin>
¶ I wish to add a final reason. The source and origin of all laws is the **eternal law** of the divine mind. God, however, has ordered and referred all things back to Himself. Therefore, all universal laws must be so regulated by that law that they tend toward the same goal. This did not escape the divine Plato in his first dialogue on *Laws*, where he says it is necessary for the legislator to follow this order: that human things are everywhere referred to divine things.

<margin>Plato</margin>
<margin>First corollary.</margin>
¶ From these points, it follows first that when a legislator establishes laws for his own private advantage, he should understand himself to be a **tyrant**.

<margin>Second corollary.</margin>
¶ It follows next that in every commonwealth—for example, in an entire kingdom—all laws must be referred to the end of the whole. This does not mean that particular laws should not be permitted for individual cities according to their condition, but that all cities ought to help one another like members of one body. However, different kingdoms, even if they are under one king, should not be governed in such a way that the property, wealth, and policy of one are unequally dragged away for the benefit of another; rather, each should be administered for its own advantage.
**For example:** If overseas kingdoms <note>Soto is almost certainly referring to the Spanish colonies in the Americas.</note> were acquired for no other reason than that all their goods should come to Spain, and we twisted their laws for our own benefit—treating them, for instance, as if they were our slaves—the beauty of **equity** would not be preserved. It would be otherwise if they served one another’s needs through commerce. These points concern the end of laws; for regarding its effects (which are to make citizens good) and other matters concerning happiness itself, we shall speak in the third question.

<margin>To the first.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is answered that although a law might happen to be ordered toward the particular good of an individual, its stability rests on the fact that that particular good is referred to the common good. Just as in theoretical matters, no truth of a particular conclusion is solid unless it is resolved into first principles.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ And by the same reasoning, the second argument is resolved: namely, that precepts regarding individual goods have the force of law because those individuals are ordered toward the common good. Nevertheless, precepts of this kind are not strictly called "laws"...

# Francisco Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law #

**Column 1:**

...are to be considered; rather, they are applications of laws to particular cases. For laws (as has been stated and demonstrated by the legal codes) must be universal. For example: A law is "Worship one God," which prescribes neither a specific time nor a place, nor does it address a single specific person. It would be a **precept**, however, if a prelate today ordered someone for a just reason to perform a sacred rite, or compelled a city to pour out prayers. Likewise, it is a law that "dear parents should be honored," and that "parents should nourish their children." But it is a **precept** when a judge orders you to provide alimony to either a parent or a child in a specific state of necessity. Therefore, since a law commands generally regarding our actions, which concern specific things, it follows that precepts are the applications of laws to those specific things. Because of this, even if one law explains another more specifically, it does not immediately cease to be a law, provided it remains universal. For it is a law that we rest from work on the Lord's days and the feast days of the Apostles, even though this is an explanation of that more general law, "You shall keep the Sabbaths holy" <note>original: "Sabbatha sanctifices"</note>.

### ARTICLE III.

->*Whether the reason of any person whatsoever is the maker of law.*<-

<margin>Concerning the authors of laws.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring a landscape with a building and a tree.</image-desc>
The third article will take up the third part of the definition, which concerned the **authors of laws**. For it is argued that it is appropriate for any private individual to establish laws in their own order.

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
First, from the saying of the Apostle in Romans 2: "The Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature those things which are of the law: for they are a law unto themselves." However, he asserts this concerning every individual mortal, insofar as each person, led by the light of nature, knows how to discern good and evil for themselves.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued: The intention of the legislator is to lead his citizens to virtue; but anyone can lead another to virtue; therefore, the reason of any person can carry the weight of law.

<margin>The third argument. Aristotle.</margin>
And in the third place comes the opinion of the same Aristotle in the *Ethics*, Book 10, near the end, where he compares the **father of a family** <note>Latin: "patrem familias"</note> in his own home to a Prince in his republic: just as the latter governs the city, so the former governs the home. Therefore, just as a Prince can set laws for a city, so a father is able to set laws for his own household.

<margin>Isidore.</margin>
On the contrary is Isidore in the same Book 5 of the *Etymologies* (cited in Distinction 2), where he says: "Law is a constitution of the people, according to which the elders, together with the commoners, have sanctioned something." By these words, he seems to teach that it is not for just anyone to write laws.

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

<margin>Solution of the proposition.</margin>
The present question, like the one above, is resolved by a single conclusion. Establishing laws belongs not to just anyone, but to the **commonwealth** <note>Latin: "reipublicae"</note> and to those who represent it or have care over it. This conclusion is easily gathered from the conclusion established just before in this way:

<margin>The conclusion is deduced from the preceding point.</margin>
A law is a rule directing toward the **common good**; however, directing toward the common good is the proper role of the commonwealth, for which such a good is the immediate end. Therefore, the power of making laws lies only with the commonwealth itself and with the one who has care of it.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
You may easily understand the minor premise through the teaching of Aristotle in the *Ethics*, Book 1. For efficient causes have a proportion to their final ends: such that as the efficient cause is higher, its end is also more sublime. For the immediate end of a soldier is to defend a specific place; but the end of a General is victory; and the end of a King is peace. Therefore, it pertains to the King to order all inferior things toward that supreme end. For the same reason, because the end of the bridle-making art is referred to the equestrian art, it follows that the equestrian art directs the operation of the bridle-making art. Therefore, because the common good is the peculiar end of the commonwealth, and laws lead us there, it is the proper right of the commonwealth to establish those laws by which it leads us to that same end.

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Hence Plato, in the *Dialogue on Kingship*, says: "It is the duty of the King to establish laws."

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle establishes the same in the *Ethics*, Book 10; and in the law "If the Imperial" <note>Refers to a specific section of the Code of Justinian regarding imperial constitutions.</note> in the *Code on Laws and Constitutions*, it is read that it is granted to the Emperor alone both to establish laws and even to interpret them.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
A second reason is also added: for law has a **coercive power**, as Aristotle is the authority in the *Ethics*, Book 10, and Papinian in the first book *On Laws*, where he calls law a "coercion." This power and vigor exists only in the commonwealth and the Prince, just as it is the power of the whole animal to move its limbs.

<margin>A beautiful consideration.</margin>
However, one must discern by consideration between those who can **enact** laws and those by whose **counsel** they are enacted. For legal experts (Jurists) draw out laws from the heart of natural philosophy by reason and judgment; yet no one is able to grant them firmness and the vigor of coercion except the one who possesses jurisdiction. Hence, just as the consultations of the prudent do not have the weight of laws by themselves, so neither should a Prince proclaim laws without their mature counsel.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
An argument against this conclusion, however, quickly presents itself. God is the Prince of all legislators, and yet He is neither a commonwealth nor a representative of one, since He certainly did not beg His authority from a commonwealth.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The response, however, is: It is not asserted in the present sense that every governor represents the commonwealth as if he were its vicar...

...exists from him; rather, it is sufficient to have the care of it, either as a vicar <note>A deputy or representative acting in the name of a superior.</note> or as its author and lord to whom the public governance is entrusted. In a similar way, we must think of Christ, even insofar as he was a man, since as the Redeemer and King of the kingdom of heaven, he was the founder of our laws. And consequently, his vicar is the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note>. For he does not act on behalf of the Church as if he received authority from it, but rather as the vicar of Christ, whose place he takes. From Christ alone, even if he is elected through the Church, **he receives his authority**. The same judgment applies to the bishops and prelates established by him. However, secular kings and monarchs are in a different position. For they were not created by God immediately and directly—as they say—except for Saul and David, and their lineage, to whom God himself committed the scepter. But as held in the legal principle "What pleases the prince" <note>original: "l. quod placuit. ff. de consti prin." — a reference to the Roman Digest, stating the ruler's will has the force of law because the people conferred their power upon him.</note>, kings and princes are created by the people, into whom the people transferred their own empire and power. This will be made clearer later in Question 6 and more extensively in Book 3, Question 4. Hence, that word of the Wise Man from Proverbs 8 cited above, "Through me kings reign" <note>original: "Per me reges regnant"</note>, is not to be understood otherwise than that it was granted to mortals by God himself, as the author of natural law, that every commonwealth should have the judgment to rule itself; and consequently, where reason—which is also the breath of the divine spirit—demands it, it may transfer its power to another, by whose laws it may be more providently governed.

¶ Regarding the first legislators, secular histories report various accounts. For Pliny, in Book 7 of his *Natural History*, chapter 56, says that Ceres was the first of all to give laws; though others have thought it was Rhadamanthus. But in truth, Josephus, in his work *Against Apion*, shows the truth most clearly and eloquently: namely, that among mortals, Moses was the first to promulgate sacred laws as they were delivered to him by God. For those legislators whom Isidore mentions at the beginning of Book 5 existed much later. Phoroneus, he says, was the first king to establish laws for the Greeks; Hermes Trismegistus for the Egyptians; Solon for the Athenians; Lycurgus for the Spartans; and finally, Numa Pompilius, who succeeded Romulus, for the Romans.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book 1, Question 1, from the previous page. Having established who has the authority to make laws, Soto now moves to Article 4: whether the public proclamation (promulgation) of a law is necessary for it to be binding.</meta>

## F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right ##

...promulgation is further necessary. ¶ On the contrary, we read in the legal collections <note>original: "distinctio. 4. cap. in istis." — a reference to Gratian’s Decree, a foundational collection of Canon Law.</note> that laws are instituted only when they are promulgated.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The question is answered with two conclusions. First: No law has any force as law before its promulgation; rather (as the cited decree asserts), it is only then instituted when it is proclaimed. Therefore, this conclusion permits no exception (as some might think). This is proven by the very nature of law. For a law is a <term>rule and measure</term> of our actions; however, a rule is useless unless it is applied to those performing the actions. It cannot be applied except through knowledge of it, for whoever uses a rule must be able to look upon it. It follows, therefore, that before the promulgation by which it becomes known to the subjects, it does not bind them by obligation, but is only then commanded when it is proclaimed. Hence, in the Code of Justinian <note>original: "l. leges. C. de legib. & consti."</note> it is said: "The most sacred laws, which constrain the lives of men, ought to be understood by men." And in the New Constitutions <note>original: "Aucten. vt factæ nouæ constit." — refers to the *Novellae*, or new laws, of Emperor Justinian.</note>, laws are ordered to be valid only when they have been made manifest to the public. The same is held in Canon Law <note>original: "iure canonico"</note> in the chapters *Ad hæc* and *Cognoscentes*.

<margin>A small doubt.</margin> You may doubt, however, what should be understood by the term "promulgation." Should a law not be considered promulgated until the knowledge of it has been spread to every single person? The reasoning just provided would seem to suggest so.

<margin>Reason for hesitation.</margin> Truly, if a law applies itself through knowledge of it, then it follows that until it is known to all, it does not bind; and thus, it would not be considered promulgated. And <margin>Confirmation.</margin> this is confirmed by the fact that he who is unaware of the law is excused by ignorance, which would not happen if he were bound by the chain of the law. ¶ For the sake of this argument, a second conclusion is established. <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> For a law to be considered promulgated, it does not require that it reach the knowledge of every individual; rather, it is promulgated when it is solemnly declared in the prince’s court, or in a province by the first herald, or by another legitimate way. This is held in the cited chapter of the law. And the reason is this: a law is promulgated at the moment it is established under the form of a command. A command is made as soon as it is first publicly declared; therefore, as soon as it is first solemnly made manifest, it is considered promulgated and takes on the force of a command. ¶ However, there remains <margin>A scruple.</margin> a "scruple" <note>A small doubt or difficulty in reasoning.</note>: whether, as soon as a law is—for ex-

<column-break/>

ample—promulgated in the Emperor’s Court, all the inhabitants of the kingdom are bound by it? This seems contrary to reason; for then even those in the most remote areas, whom the news could not yet have reached, would not be excused by ignorance, which is a wicked thing to assert. Regarding this, although it seems to pertain to the definition of the word, the doctors of both Civil and Canon law <note>original: "iuris vtriusque doctores"</note> seem to speak differently than reason teaches. <margin>Panormitanus.</margin> For Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> and others on the chapter *Cognoscentes*, and Johannes Andreae <note>A renowned 14th-century canonist.</note> on that word "Given at Rome," <margin>Baldus.</margin> and Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis, a highly influential 14th-century jurist.</note> on the law "Most sacred laws" cited above, although they admit that a law is promulgated when it is solemnly declared, they nevertheless think no one is bound by it before they have heard it, unless the person is accused of "crass and culpable" <note>Willful or negligent ignorance.</note> ignorance. Their reason is that they think being excused by ignorance is the same thing as not being bound by the law. <margin>Third conclusion against the authors.</margin> ¶ Against these authors, however, a third conclusion is established: As soon as a law is solemnly promulgated in the Court or in the Metropolis of the kingdom, it binds everyone; even though those who are ignorant without fault are excused from sin. <margin>First proof.</margin> Both parts of the conclusion are proven. For the law is promulgated to the whole world. Indeed, it does not say, "We command the citizens of this city," but, "to all those living under our jurisdiction"; therefore, it then binds everyone. <margin>Second proof.</margin> Secondly, it is argued that when a preacher, for example, or another private person warns me of a law that has been placed, from then on ignorance would no longer excuse me, and yet that messenger did not bind me; therefore, the solemn promulgation that preceded it had already bound me. <margin>Third proof.</margin> And thirdly, it is argued: If everyone were not bound by the law immediately upon its solemn promulgation, it would follow that the ignorant could not properly be said to be "excused"; for an excuse is a release from an obligation that one has, but according to the contrary opinion, the ignorant are not yet bound. Therefore, both must be said, as our conclusion asserts: namely, that the law immediately binds everyone, both those hearing it and those absent, though those unaware are nonetheless excused from its bond <note>That is, they are bound by the law's authority, but not guilty of a moral fault for breaking it unknowingly.</note>. <margin>Incidental question.</margin> ¶ But perhaps someone might inquire more closely whether it is enough for a law to be solemnly promulgated in one place so that everyone in that jurisdiction is immediately subject to the law. For example: If the Emperor, being the lord of many kingdoms, promulgated a law in Toledo that included Belgians, Flemings, Italians, and Indians. Or if the Pope in Rome, or a General Council, solemnly brought forth a law, whether it would then immediately bind everyone. And because of the doubt...

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that for a law to be valid, it must be promulgated (publicly announced). He maintains that once a law is solemnly proclaimed in a central location, it legally binds all subjects immediately, although individuals who have not yet heard the news are morally excused from guilt for not following it.</summary>
