St. Thomas responds very learnedly that we speak of the divine will in two ways: in one way, according to its own nature in which it exists: and thus it is not so much "rational" in the strict sense as it is **reason itself by its very essence**. For "rational" implies a participation <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "participation" refers to a being having a quality (like reason or life) that it received from a higher source, rather than being the source itself.</note> in reason. In the other way, it is spoken of in regard to those things which He disposes concerning us: and in relation to such effects, it is granted to be rational: because He dispenses and administers all things according to the order of His own reason.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: all irrational, insensible, and lifeless creatures—which arise and perish in a continuous flow of changeability—are governed by the eternal law of God.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas clarifies this by the gap between human and divine law, which you should understand as follows:

<margin>St. Thomas’s reasoning explained.</margin>
Irrational creatures, because they do not act through a **knowledge of the end** <note>The "end" (*finis*) refers to the purpose or goal of an action.</note>, in no way move themselves toward it; rather, they are driven by another. For this reason, since a human does not set a law for subjects except by imprinting a rule upon their minds through which they might move themselves, it follows that human laws do not extend except to men who participate in reason. As for other things, man moves and governs them through his own human actions—namely, with bridle and spurs—and other inanimate things through different instruments. For it would be ridiculous for someone to prescribe a law to beasts of burden regarding when and how they should eat, sleep, plow, or run. And a person would be even more foolish to command herbs to grow, or trees to bear fruit, or a stone to place itself in a building in a certain way. Furthermore, even if tamed animals, like dogs and monkeys, are accustomed to tricks through a sort of "law," God does not only imprint a rule upon the minds of rational and intellectual creatures by which they move themselves, but He has also implanted **impulses and instincts** in the whole universe of things. By these, they are driven toward their individual ends: like the bee to making honey, the swallow to building a nest, and the earth to bringing forth crops—and the rest to their own powers of acting. It is regarding this instinct and power of all things that the Psalm says:

<margin>Psalm 148.</margin>
*He set a decree and it shall not pass away.* <note>original: "Præceptum posuit & non præteribit."</note> From this it follows that God does not administer and dispose all things in the same way, but governs the actions of men and angels through rules by which they move themselves toward an end; the rest, however, He governs through powers and instincts by which they are moved. In these latter categories, even men are to be counted regarding their natural actions: such as nutrition, growth, and the like.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: Human actions—namely,

<column-break/>

all free actions—are subject to the eternal law, and are comprehended under its order far better and more perfectly than other things of a lower rank. This conclusion is more easily accepted than the previous ones. For human actions 

<margin>Proof.</margin>
are those which proceed from a knowledge of the end and are directed toward it. On both sides—that is, both in terms of knowledge and impulse—they are placed under the eternal law; therefore, they are subject to it more perfectly than others. The second premise is proven: All truth (as we were saying above) is a certain participation in the eternal divine truth, and consequently so is any knowledge of an end. Furthermore, just as an inclination and "weight" toward their own 

<margin>Another reason.</margin>
ends is given to other things, so to man—indeed, more excellently—there is implanted by nature (which is the work of God) a certain inclination and weight toward that which accords with the eternal law. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For we are (as **Aristotle** taught in the second book of the *Ethics*) born for virtues. This, I say, is innate to the rational creature: to live according to reason. Therefore, both according to knowledge and according to the propensity for the good—both of which are necessary for free movements—human actions are placed under the eternal law. 

<margin>How the righteous and the wicked are under the yoke of eternal law.</margin>
¶ There is, however, a difference between the just and the wicked: in that in evil and depraved men, both principles are corrupt and debased. For the "star" of natural knowledge is darkened by earthly affections, and the natural affection for the good is crushed and weakened by corrupt habits. Nevertheless, neither is entirely extinguished. In the good and the just, however—since no one is worthy of this name unless he acts in the grace of God—both are increased and nourished. For a ray of faith is added to the natural light, and special help from God is added to the natural inclination. Thus, as far as action is concerned, the just are subject to the eternal law far more perfectly and excellently than the unjust. 

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas, however, noted this considerately: that to the extent they fail to submit themselves to the sovereign eternal law through **action**, they are subjected to that same law through **passion** <note>In this context, "passion" refers to being the recipient of an action, specifically punishment or suffering.</note> more harshly as an avenger. For as much as they neglected to do in merits, so much do they suffer more bitterly in torments. 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Hence **Augustine** says in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*: "God," he says, "from the just misery of the souls who desert Him, knows how to order the lower parts of His creation with the most fitting laws."

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>

by their own nature they can neither fail nor deviate, this is a restraint and a coercion of the eternal law. Indeed, this is much more powerful than the restraint of the human will, which is prone to wandering away from such law.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ The conclusion of the second argument is granted: namely, that in divine matters nothing is subject to law; rather, all things are that same law by their very essence.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is answered that for brute animals and inanimate things, the eternal law is promulgated <note>To "promulgate" a law means to formally proclaim or make it known so that it is binding.</note> regarding their natural operations through the "stamping" of instincts and powers for acting. This is similar to how the natural law is promulgated to us through the "stamping" of light within our minds. For even if irrational creatures do not participate in human reason so as to be able to obey human laws, they nonetheless participate in divine reason, which is more wide-reaching. Hence, just as the limbs obey the soul with a "despotic" <note>In Aristotelian terms, "despotic" rule refers to the soul's absolute control over the body, whereas "political" rule refers to the mind's more persuasive control over the passions.</note> mastery, as the author states in the *Politics*.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>

A thing is called a "monster" in respect to a particular cause that intended a complete and perfect thing; and it is called "chance" in respect to a human, to whom it happens unexpectedly while they are unaware or not intending it. However, the very causes of monsters and chance events are fully foreseen by divine reason. Therefore, to God, nothing is accidental or fortuitous.

<margin>To the fifth.</margin>
¶ To the fifth, the answer is that the actions of all men, both the just and the wicked, are subject to the divine law. Regarding the citation that "those who are led by the Spirit of God are not under the law," <note>original: "Qui spiritu Dei aguntur eos non esse sub lege" – A reference to Romans 8:14 and Galatians 5:18.</note> it must be read in this sense: that they are not weighed down by the burden of the law. Because they listen to the dictates of the law out of a "filial" <note>Child-like or loving fear, as opposed to "servile" fear based only on punishment.</note> rather than a servile fear, they live by the guidance of the Holy Spirit rather than by the compulsion of the law, as if they were free from the law. Hence that saying: "The law is not laid down for the just," <note>original: "Iusto non est lex posita" – 1 Timothy 1:9.</note> and that in 2 Corinthians 3: "Where the spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." Regarding the other point about the "wisdom of the flesh," it is likewise granted that the wicked are not subject to the commanding divine law in their actions, yet through their sufferings they fall back under the same law as it carries out justice.

<margin>To the final argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the sixth, it is answered that things are moved toward their end and preserved within that end by the same causes. 

<column-break/>

Consequently, not only in this life of the "church militant," <note>A traditional term for Christians currently living on earth, struggling against sin.</note> but also in the next life, all live under the same divine law. Specifically, the blessed—whether you consider humans or angels—enjoy that eternal happiness by divine decree; while the damned—both demons and humans—endure the decree of divine justice within those prisons.

# QUESTION FOUR on the natural law.

->St. Thomas, Part 1-2, Question 94.<-

## ARTICLE I.

->Whether the natural law is a habit existing within us.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate floral vine work and a central scroll motif within a square frame.</image-desc>
AFTER the eternal law, it follows that we should speak of the others which are derived from it. And first, in this fourth question, concerning the law of nature. And in this first article, concerning its substance: whether it is a "habit" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a *habitus* (habit) is a stable quality or disposition of the soul that allows a person to act easily and consistently in a certain way.</note> inherent in us.

<margin>First argument: the negative side.</margin>
It is argued, therefore, against what is supposed: The eternal law, according to Augustine in Book 1 of *On Free Choice of the Will*, is that by which it is just that all things be perfectly ordered. Therefore, by that law, man is sufficiently and abundantly governed. Since nature does not overflow with superfluous things, there is no need for us to have any other law besides the eternal one.

<margin>The second.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Man tends toward his goal differently than brutes do, for he moves himself toward the goal freely through his knowledge of it, guided by reason. Brutes, however, do not act by any reason, but are driven by natural instinct. Therefore, man is not moved by the law of nature, but only brutes are.

<margin>The third.</margin>
¶ On the affirmative side of the question, it is argued thirdly that it is a habit. There are three things in our soul (as the Philosopher <note>A standard title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> states in Book 2 of the *Ethics*): namely, power, habit, and passion. Now, the natural law is clearly neither a power nor a passion, because both power and passion are "indifferent" to opposites—that is, to good and evil—whereas the law is a dictate of what is good. Therefore, it is a habit.
¶ On the contrary, however, is what we showed above in the first question: law is a dictate of reason. This implies an *act*, namely, "this or that must be done." <note>The author is contrasting a "habit" (a potential or readiness to act) with an "act" (the actual command or thought of the mind).</note>

# Question IV of the First Book

**Column 1**

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
This question is answered with three conclusions. First: The natural law is engraved and imprinted upon our minds.
<margin>The conclusion is argued.</margin>
It is proven thus: Law (as has been said) exists as the rule and norm of our actions, and (as we were saying) has a twofold subject. For it exists both in the one who rules and in the one who is ruled: in the former as the mover, and in the latter as the thing moved. Furthermore, human actions (as defined in the previous question) are subject to the eternal law. Therefore, God, who disposes all things sweetly, has, as the author of nature, imprinted a light upon our minds. Through this light, we participate in His eternal law and direct our actions toward their proper end, toward which they are carried by their very nature. Regarding this light, when people asked who would show them good things, David turned toward God and 
<margin>Psalm 90 <note>The author cites Psalm 90, though this famous verse "The light of your countenance is signed upon us" is found in Psalm 4:6 in the Vulgate.</note></margin>
responded: *The light of your countenance is signed upon us.* <note>original: "Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui."</note> Indeed, the "face of God" is a most significant term for the light of His wisdom and the "aspect" of His reason, through which He is known, just as a man is known by his face. Moreover, this natural imprinting is called the "natural law," according to the words of Paul in Romans 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
chapter 2: *The Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature 
<margin>Gloss.</margin>
the things that are of the law.* <note>original: "Gentes quæ legem non habent, naturaliter quæ legis sunt faciunt."</note> On this passage, the <term>gloss</term> <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria" was a standard collection of medieval biblical commentaries.</note> says: if they do not have the written law, they nevertheless have the natural law, by which everyone understands and is conscious of what is good and what is evil.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: The natural law is neither a power nor a passion, nor is it a <term>habit</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition or quality that allows a person to act readily and easily, like a skill or a virtue.</note> according to its substance. This is the conclusion of Saint Thomas in the *Summa Theologiae* 1. 2. q.
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
94, which few believe because few take the care to perceive it correctly.
<margin>The opinion of the moderns.</margin>
For the more recent philosophers commonly judge intellectual "habits" to be habitual propositions and judgments; they believe this because frequent acts of assent leave behind a habitual assent, from which actual judgments are later produced. But in truth, this philosophy is not pure: for a "habit" is not a judgment itself, but a certain quality and virtue for drawing forth judgments. From this truth, our 
<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
conclusion is proven: Law is a <term>dictate</term> <note>Latin: "dictamen." A formal command or rule issued by reason to guide behavior.</note> (as said above) that reason establishes concerning things to be done: such as "Thou shalt not steal," "Thou shalt not commit adultery," etc. Just as speculative judgments are the work of the intellect, a "habit" (as we said) is neither a judgment nor a proposition, but the power to produce such things. Therefore, the law is not a habit by its essence, but a dictate that has the form of a precept.
<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From this, it follows that the law of nature is not the same thing as <term>synderesis</term>. <note>Synderesis is the innate "spark" of conscience or the natural capacity of the human mind to recognize basic moral principles (e.g., "do good, avoid evil").</note> For the same
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Holy Doctor taught in part 1, question 79, that synderesis is a habit—namely, the virtue of the mind that inclines us to assent to practical principles, just as

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

the habit of the intellect is the propensity and impulse to assent to theoretical principles. And for this reason, synderesis is said to urge us toward the good and to murmur against the evil. In short, just as the habit of the intellect is not a collection of principles but the virtue of assenting to them, so synderesis is not the natural law, but the virtue of assenting to those principles and practical dictates which *are* the natural law. Hence, wherever one reads that synderesis is the "law of our intellect" (as in the writings of Basil), it must be understood not by essence, but because synderesis is the habit containing the natural law; for it is by its power that we judge those principles. I say these things for the sake of those devoted to the study of physical <note>Here, "physics" refers to the broader study of nature and the soul's operations.</note> meditation.
<margin>Second conclusion. <note>The author repeats the label "Second Conclusion," here applying it to the way the law exists in us as a disposition.</note></margin>
¶ Second conclusion: The natural law exists in us by way of a habit.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
Natural precepts are not only considered by reason in the moment when one is actively commanding or listening to a precept; they exist "by way of a habit," that is, in a permanent manner even in the absence of the act. Therefore, just as Sacred Scripture is called "our faith" because it is a collection of all those things to which we assent through the habit of faith, so the collection of principles for acting is called a "habit," because we provide assent to them by the power of synderesis.
<margin>An incidental question.</margin>
¶ But if you ask: what is this thing that remains by way of a habit besides synderesis?
<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is: they are the "species" <note>In this context, "species" are mental representations or concepts stored in the memory.</note> left behind in the memory.
<margin>Objection.</margin>
However, a student of philosophy might rise up against this: The natural law is bestowed upon our nature at the very moment of its conception; but at that time, no "species" of things are generated; rather, we acquire them later with the help of the senses.
<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that the law of nature is said to be bestowed and imprinted upon us by nature because, once the terms of "good" and "evil" are apprehended, the intellect—by the power of synderesis—immediately forms these judgments and dictates: "Good is to be embraced, and evil is to be rejected," and similar truths which become known by the light of that same intellect. Therefore, there was no need for an infusion of "species" [at birth]; rather, they are acquired afterward with no difficulty.
<margin>Another objection.</margin>
¶ Nonetheless, another argument emerges against this imprinting of synderesis. For a habit (as Augustine states in the book *On the Good of Marriage*) is that by which 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
something is done when there is a need; but synderesis is not of this kind, since small children before the use of reason, and indeed the damned, cannot use natural principles.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that Augustine only draws out the nature of a habit,

nature, where it is not hindered. Nevertheless, when reason is bound—as it is in those who are sleeping—this habit is unable to perform its function. ¶ Regarding this **good judgment** <note>original: "synesi." This refers to the intellectual virtue of judging well according to common laws.</note> and the habit of the intellect toward self-evident theoretical principles, I am often swayed by this argument: that they are not qualities distinct from the intellect itself. This is because habits are usually employed so that when a power is indifferent toward two contraries, it may be determined and directed toward one of them by that habit. In this way, the **desiring appetite** <note>original: "appetitus concupiscibilis." The faculty of the soul that seeks basic sensory goods.</note> is determined toward the good of virtue through temperance. However, the intellect is already determined by its own nature toward those things known by the natural light; it embraces such truths by its very nature. Therefore, it has no need to be "clothed" in some additional quality, but perhaps these natural inclinations themselves are what we call "implanted habits." But if someone finds the opposite view more proven, let them consider another reason. For now, we are sinking deeper into **Metaphysics** than is necessary.

<margin>To the first principal argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded: although we are governed by the eternal law, this happens through the natural law, which is a participation in it. Just as the light of the Sun illuminates us through the light radiated upon us, so because the natural law is not entirely distinct from the eternal law, but is its participation, it is by no means redundant.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second: even if we grant the premise—namely, that we move freely while animals move naturally—the conclusion is denied when it is inferred that man is not moved by natural law. For the freedom of our actions is founded upon a certain natural principle: for man desires nothing except under the aspect of "the good." Indeed, he relies on that natural principle: *Good is to be pursued.* However, when a good according to reason is proposed on one side, and a sensory good on the other, he can freely choose to prefer one over the other. Furthermore (as we said in the previous question), the natural law in us takes on the character of a "law" (unlike the instinct of animals) precisely because we are led by reason, whereas animals are driven by external impulse.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is responded that **Aristotle**, in that passage of the *Ethics*, Book 2, did not list everything that exists in the soul. He mentioned nothing of the acts of the intellect or will, nor of mental images; he only enumerated the principles by whose power the intellect operates. But the natural law is not such a power, but the work itself—namely, the dictate of reason—which exists in us in the manner of a habit, as explained above.

### ARTICLE II.
#### Whether the natural law contains multiple precepts.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a figure in a garden landscape with a tree and architectural elements.</image-desc>
Consequently, in the second article, **St. Thomas** asks whether the natural law contains multiple precepts. Anyone who hears this title carelessly will judge the question to be ridiculous; for since the **Decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> and many other annexed precepts take their origin from the law of nature, who could doubt that there are very many precepts of natural right? But in truth, St. Thomas everywhere speaks deliberately according to **Philosophy**. For those things are called "precepts of the law of nature" in an absolute sense which are proper to it insofar as they are distinguished from human and divine law: namely, those principles which require no discourse of logic, but are known by the natural light in and of themselves. These are clearly the ones just defined as being "congenital" to our nature. Regarding these, then, it is not vain to ask if there are several.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
¶ For it is argued that there is only one. Law (as said above) is categorized under the "genus" of a precept. If, therefore, there are multiple precepts of nature, there are multiple laws of nature—yet we commonly hold there to be only one law of nature.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Human nature is one, and the reason of the human race is one; therefore, its first precept is one. If you say that precepts are multiplied according to the number of "natures" from which a human is composed—so that there is one natural precept insofar as he is a "being," another insofar as he is an "animal," and another insofar as he is a "man"—it would then follow that even those things which happen to us from the inclination of the desiring appetite belong to the law of nature. Since these are not contained within the bounds of reason, this seems absurd.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued against the name "precept." No law binds except by the reason that it is enacted by a superior. But nature is neither our superior nor our judge; only God and His ministers (men) are. Therefore, the law of nature, unless divine or human law were present, would have no binding force such that its transgression would be a sin.

¶ On the contrary is the fact that these precepts of natural law relate to the **principles of action** <note>original: "principia agibilia." The starting points for moral reasoning.</note> just as principles do in **theoretical matters** <note>original: "speculabilibus." Theoretical or scientific knowledge.</note>. But the latter are many; therefore, so are the former.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Question IV of Book I, regarding the Nature of Natural Law. On the previous page, the author was debating whether natural law is an "implanted habit" of the mind and how the light of reason functions when a person is sleeping or otherwise hindered. ### First Book, Question IV.

<margin>Two types of self-evident propositions.</margin>
Regarding the precepts of the natural law—not just any precepts, but those specific to it, such as those that require no complex reasoning (like human law) or higher revelation (like divine law), but are known through themselves—it must be noted that a proposition is called "self-evident" in two ways: in one way, according to itself; and in the other, in relation to us. A proposition is self-evident in the first way when the predicate is part of the very essence of the subject: for example, "God exists," or "Man is a rational being." Indeed, anyone who truly grasped the nature of the subject would need no middle step to perceive the truth of the proposition. However, in relation to us, such propositions are not always self-evident, because we do not fully perceive the nature of the extremes <note>original: "extremorum." In logic, "extremes" refers to the subject and the predicate of a statement.</note>.

<margin>Boethius.</margin>
Hence, according to the opinion of Boethius in his book *On the Hebdomads*, some propositions are simply self-evident to everyone because their terms are obvious to all: such as "the whole is greater than its part." Other propositions, however, are self-evident only to the wise who truly perceive the terms, such as "An Angel is not circumscribed by a place." For to one who understands that an Angel is not a physical body, it immediately becomes clear that it is not confined to a physical location. Descending to our main point: just as the first thing offered to speculative reason is **being** <note>original: "ens." This is the most basic concept in philosophy: the fact that something "is."</note> (for this is what we first perceive about all things), so the first thing offered to practical reason regarding things to be desired and done is **the good**. For just as the first object of the intellect is being, so the first object of the will is the good. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> wisely began his *Ethics* with this principle: "The good is what all things desire."

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Having established these two points, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: The specific precepts of natural law—that is, the first self-evident principles—are multiple.

<margin>Argument for the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven: natural principles (as the name suggests to the ear) are those which nature has imprinted upon us. However, human nature consists of several partial levels. First, man is a **being**, a nature he shares with all created things. Next, he is a **living being** along with plants; then, an **animal** among animals; and finally, he is a **human**. Therefore, according to all these levels of nature, he possesses specific primary precepts.

<margin>The first practical principle, which is general and applies to man insofar as he exists.</margin>
For example, insofar as he is a "being," this is the most general of all precepts: "Good is to be sought and pursued, and evil is to be rejected and avoided." This precept is common to all things in the world; it is the end of all desirable things into which all pleasant things are reduced as if to a first principle—just as in the world of 

<column-break/>

theoretical thought, every thing must either be or not be, as Aristotle teaches in the 4th book of the *Metaphysics*, text 9.

<margin>The second common practical principle.</margin>
Next, because the first of natural goods is existence, another more specific principle immediately follows: "One’s own existence must be preserved." For all things desire to preserve themselves and to resist what would destroy them. The reason for this is general: because existence is a "good" for each thing, while destruction is an "evil." No other cause need be sought, since this (as we were just saying) is the first principle into which all desires are resolved. Whatever a human—or any thing in the world—desires, they desire it under the aspect of a good, whether it is a true good or only an apparent one. And yet, in this desire, I see that man—though he is the most perfect of all things under heaven—is in a certain way lower than the others, because he consists of two different natures. For all other things desire only that good which is truly good for them; but man also desires that which, though it feels good to the senses, is actually an evil to his reason, which is his true nature.

<margin>The reason why man seeks not only the true good but the appearance of good, whereas it is found to be otherwise in other things.</margin>
¶ Then, descending further, another principle of the law of nature is derived: the precept of man insofar as he is an animal, which pertains to the union of male and female.

<margin>The third principle of man insofar as he is an animal.</margin>
For here exists a specific way for animals to preserve their species. For although in trees, like Palms and Laurels, and in certain herbs, a kind of image of "male" and "female" can be detected, nevertheless, true male fertilization was recognized by Philosophy only in animals.

<margin>The last and specific principle of man.</margin>
¶ From these, finally, is drawn another principle of man insofar as he is **rational**. By this reason, he has an inclination toward the knowledge of God and the good of virtue. From this, in turn, comes his desire for society and civil life. Hence the rule: "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you," and "Do not do that which you would not want done to yourself." In short: that most general principle—that good is to be sought and evil rejected—becomes a specific principle of the natural law in man: namely, that the moral good of virtue is to be desired and embraced, and the contrary evil of vice is to be rejected, so that happiness may be attained.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: The natural law is nonetheless one.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven because the unity of a law is derived from its "end" or goal. Just as these precepts have one source, which is reason, so they have one end and scope, which (as we said) is "the good" in general.

<margin>Some laws are explained.</margin>
¶ Through these points, therefore, both Canon Law and Civil Law—which speak of natural right—become clear.

<summary>This page explains that natural law is composed of multiple precepts based on the different levels of human nature (existence, animal life, and rationality), all unified by the single goal of seeking "the good." It establishes the foundational principle that "good is to be done and evil avoided" as the basis for all ethics and self-preservation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question IV from the previous page, specifically focusing on the fourth article: whether the natural law consists of many precepts or just one. Soto is currently addressing objections regarding the definitions of natural law provided by legal and theological authorities like Isidore of Seville and the Roman Jurists.</meta>

->F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law<-

<margin>Civil and canon laws.</margin>
...civil and canon laws follow. Indeed, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar whose *Etymologies* helped define law for the Middle Ages.</note> (as found in Distinction 1, "natural law") makes no mention of that most general category which is common to all living things. Instead, he speaks only of that which is common to all nations, such as the union of man and woman. However, the Civil Law <note>Referring to the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundation of Roman law.</note> expresses this more precisely in the *Institutes* (on natural law) and the *Digest* (on justice and law): specifically, "Natural Law is what nature has taught all animals." For he calls "teaching" that natural instinct implanted by nature. Otherwise, "to teach" properly denotes a discourse of <term>reason</term>, which belongs specifically to the <term>Law of Nations</term> <note>original: "ius gentium." The laws common to all human civilizations based on shared reason.</note> and Civil Law.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**TO** the first argument, then, it is answered that a "precept" and a "law" are not exactly the same thing. For we have said that "law" is something more universal; therefore, by reason of a single end and principle, a collection and order of many precepts belong to one law—just as the whole of Holy Scripture belongs to one faith.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it is granted that all inclinations, even those of the sensory appetite, belong to the natural law, yet in different ways. For insofar as they are considered not as obedient to reason, but as tending toward their own sensory objects, they are called "natural precepts" in the same way they exist in brute animals. But insofar as they are governed by reason, they are the specific precepts of man. From this it follows that in man, just as there are two different natures <note>the animal and the rational</note>, so there are two laws. But because the sensual is taken from the "genus" of animal (which acts as the "matter" in man) while the rational nature is his "form" (which defines his species), it follows that all sins—because they are contrary to reason, even if they align with sensual nature—are called "simply against the nature of man," as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> testifies in Chapter 4 of *On the Divine Names*.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, which is the most important, the answer is given through a distinction. Truly, in wicked behaviors, although both are in reality connected, two things are considered: namely, the nature of "evil" and the nature of "guilt" <note>original: "ratio mali & ratio culpae."</note>. Regarding the nature of natural evil: even if we were to imagine, through an impossible thought, that neither God nor any other superior existed, the perverse order of reason itself would still be the cause for murder, theft, and similar acts to be moral evils—just as a limp is a "natural evil" because it is a deviation from the rule of walking. However, the nature of "guilt"—which implies enmity [with God] and the deserving of punishment—is not understood except where there is a Superior whom we are bound to obey. Hence, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note> most excellently defines sin as being "against the law of God." The response to the argument, therefore, is

<column-break/>

that nature alone would indeed bind us so that a transgression would be "evil," even if it were not "guilt." Yet, because nature is the effect of God, and natural law is a derivation of the divine <term>eternal law</term>, it happens that the precepts of nature bind us so that their transgression is not only an evil, but a true guilt.

---

## ARTICLE III.

### Whether all acts of virtue belong to the natural law.

To the two conclusions of the previous article, it is worthwhile to add two others. This is so we may examine, first, how all the virtues flow from those natural principles like conclusions; and second, how there is one natural law, and that same law exists among all people. It is asked, therefore, in this third article: Whether all virtues belong to the natural law. The argument is made from the negative side.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
The Eternal Law, already established above, is the origin and source of all laws. Since virtues are directed by some law, all virtues must take their origin from there. But natural law is different from the eternal law; therefore, the acts of the virtues do not all belong to the natural law, but to the eternal law.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: those things that are "according to nature" suit everyone, since the nature of all is one. However, not all virtues suit all people. For abstinence and fasting, which for one person is the moderation of temperance, is contrary to that same virtue in another who is weaker. Therefore, not all virtues are the offspring of the same law. This is especially true because every law (as has been said) is ordered toward the common good, while certain virtues, like temperance, are ordered only toward the particular good of the individual person.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, duties performed according to civil laws are true virtues. But civil laws are not the same for everyone; for every excellent republic is fortified by its own peculiar laws. Therefore, those virtues belong not to the natural law (which is one for all), but to human law.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, it is argued: Divine Law, such as the Gospel, does not descend from natural law, since it is higher. Therefore, virtues conforming to it—such as the receiving of baptism and sacramental confession—can in no way be said to belong to the natural law.

<margin>Fifth.</margin>
¶ Fifthly, if all human virtues were streams and conclusions of natural law, it would immediately follow that all vices are against nature; but...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "autem" (but/however), leading into the continuation of the fifth objection on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Soto distinguishes between "evil" as a deviation from reason and "guilt" as disobedience to God, arguing that natural law derives its moral weight from the Eternal Law. He then begins investigating whether all virtues are inherently part of the natural law or if some are purely products of civil or divine law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question IV, which investigates the nature and scope of the Natural Law. On the preceding page, the author addressed whether the natural law consists of one or many precepts, concluding that while it has many commands, they are unified by a single principle of reason. This page moves to Article 9: whether all acts of virtue belong to the natural law.</meta>

->First Book, Question IV<-

...however, there are certain things which are specifically judged to be against nature; therefore, not all actions are performed according to the law of nature.

<margin>John of Damascus</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the opinion of John of Damascus <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749) was a Syrian monk and theologian whose work "On the Orthodox Faith" was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 2, where he says that all virtues are according to nature, while all vices are entirely against nature.

<margin>In what sense the proposed question is discussed.</margin>
In the same way as it was defined above—that all laws are derived from the <term>eternal law</term> <note>The plan of divine wisdom by which God governs the universe.</note> and that human actions are consequently subject to it—we now debate whether all human virtues are performed according to the norm of the natural law. This question serves to explain the root of the distinction between the virtues belonging to the natural law, human law, and divine law. Therefore, according to the requirements of the arguments, a distinction is necessary here. For virtue can be considered both according to its general definition and form, and according to its particular object. I say that virtue receives its general form and name from the fact that it is a work performed according to <term>reason</term>. And based on this consideration, the first conclusion is established here:

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ All human virtues are according to human nature. This is proven: Virtue is nothing other than an operative habit <note>A "habit" in this context is a stable disposition or quality of the mind that allows a person to act well with ease.</note> according to the norm of reason; however, it is proper to the nature of man, insofar as he is a rational animal, to tend toward acting according to reason. For since the "form" from which a thing receives its species grants it a natural inclination, it follows that—just as it is the nature of a heavy object, according to its form, to fall toward the center, and the nature of fire to ascend upward—so it is the nature of an animal whose soul is rational to live according to reason.

<margin>Cicero</margin>
Thus Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman and philosopher whose writings on law and duty deeply influenced Christian thinkers.</note> says in Book 2 of *On Invention*: "Virtue is a habit of the soul, consistent with reason in the manner of nature" <note>original: "Virtus est animæ habitus, naturæ modo... cõsentaneus rationi."</note> (that is, according to the mode of nature). And in Book 3 of *On Duties*, he says: "Virtue—for instance, courtesy, justice, and liberality—is more according to nature than pleasure, than life itself, or than riches." Finally, virtue can be defined in no more significant a way (as Cicero himself says in Book 1 of *On the Laws*) than as "nature perfected and brought to its highest point."

<margin>Second conclusion. First reason.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: If you contemplate the acts of the virtues according to their subject matter and specific types, not all of them belong to the law of nature. The first reason for this conclusion is this: Human law is distinguished from natural law by the consensus of all; however, in a general sense, all virtues belong to the law of nature, as is clear from the first conclusion. Therefore, it is necessary that the virtues of human law and those of the natural law be distinguished by the specific objects from which they receive their classification.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
This is proven secondly, so that the legitimate

<column-break/>

cause may be revealed. Those virtues are said to belong to the law of nature toward which nature inclines us immediately: not only as if to first principles, but also as if to conclusions blossoming from those same principles without the need for human discourse. On the other hand, those virtues are human which are performed according to laws discovered by human reason to suit the variety of times, places, and affairs. Examples are easy to find. The precepts of the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> belong to the natural law. For from that principle that "good is to be loved," and from the other that "every thing loves its own being and life," the precepts of the "first table" <note>The first three commandments, which concern man's relationship with God.</note> emerge immediately without a long discourse of reasoning: namely, that we should love God, the Best and Greatest, by whose benefit we have been granted both this earthly life and the expectation of eternity, and that we should not despise Him by the abuse of oaths, but rather worship and venerate Him on holy days. Furthermore, from the principle "Do to others what you wish to be done to you, and do not do what you do not desire," all the mandates of the "second table" <note>The remaining commandments, which concern duties toward other people.</note> are deduced, all of which are rooted in the duties of justice. Wherefore (as we shall say below), no dispensation can be granted regarding these, nor can any excuse be offered through ignorance. But these points must be weighed more precisely further on. Beyond these, however, human reason has devised various laws according to different circumstances. For instance, after nature became corrupt <note>A reference to the Fall of Man in theology, necessitating more complex legal structures.</note>, the <term>Law of Nations</term> <note>original: "ius gentium." The universal laws practiced by all civilized peoples, like property rights.</note> established the division of property; and every individual commonwealth instituted its own laws according to the quality of its people and place—such as laws regarding prescription, sales, and other human contracts—toward which "naked nature" did not initially incline.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC).</note> skillfully distinguished these two in Book 5 of the *Ethics* <note>original: "Ethi. 7." Soto likely refers to Book 5, chapter 7 of the Nicomachean Ethics.</note>, where he distinguishes between natural justice and "legal" (that is, human or civil) justice. Specifically, natural justice is that which has the same force everywhere, not because it "seems so" or "does not seem so"—that is, not because human reason argues so from circumstances. Civil justice, however, is that which at the beginning makes no difference whether it is one way or another, but once it has been established, it *does* matter: such as that a prisoner be redeemed for a <term>mina</term> <note>A unit of currency in ancient Greece.</note>, or that a goat be sacrificed to the gods, but not two sheep. The same applies to ecclesiastical laws, such as the choice of foods or the observance of this or that day as a festival. Nevertheless, divine law laid the roots for these institutions. Let these things be said in general, to be further targeted in the next and subsequent questions.

<margin>To the first.</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is answered that it is not at all contradictory for all laws to flow from the eternal law, and yet for human virtues to belong to natural law only insofar as every virtue is in harmony with reason: for the natural law...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...natural law is not separate from the eternal law, but is a <term>participation</term> <note>original: "participatio"; in Scholastic philosophy, this describes how a created being shares in the perfection or likeness of God—here, how human reason shares in God's eternal plan.</note> in it.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second point, however, it is replied that although different virtues suit different persons <note>For example, the virtues required of a soldier differ from those of a priest.</note>, they are nonetheless all performed according to reason when the circumstances are weighed; and for this general cause, they are considered to belong to the law of nature. Nor is it an obstacle that some are ordained for the good of the individual person: for the universal good of nature is preserved within individuals. For through the right use of food and sexual union, nature is sustained. And furthermore, through particular virtues, progress is made toward the common happiness.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is replied: That although the virtues of human laws, according to their general kind—namely, because they are performed according to reason—are said to be of the law of nature, they are nevertheless simply called "of human law" because everything is named after its own specific <term>form</term> <note>original: "atoma specie"; literally "indivisible species," referring to the specific category that defines a thing's identity.</note>.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ And in almost the same way, it is replied to the fourth. For the virtues that conform to divine law are not simply called "of the law of nature," but rather "supernatural"; although in a certain way, according to their general kind, they may also be called "of natural law." This is not in the same way as human laws, because divine law is in no way derived from the natural law as human law is; rather, it is because natural reason, illustrated by divine light, also inclines in some way toward the divine virtues. For assuming that man is created for supernatural happiness, it is agreeable to reason that he should also be exercised in the duties of the supernatural law.

<margin>To the fifth.</margin>
¶ To the fifth, it is replied according to the doctrine of the superiors. For since there is a double nature in man—one proper to him, which is to live according to reason; the other generic, namely, common to all animals, which is to propagate the species through the union of male and female—it follows that just as all virtues are according to our proper nature (that is, according to reason), so too all vices are against nature (that is, against the prescription of reason). Nevertheless, those things which are perpetrated not only against the reason proper to us, but also against the generic nature of animals, are called "against nature" by <term>antonomasia</term> <note>A rhetorical term meaning to use a title or epithet in place of a proper name; here, it refers to certain acts that specifically claim the title "unnatural."</note>. Thus, simple fornication is against nature, that is, against reason—which dictates that children should be acknowledged by their parents so that they may be properly raised and instructed in morals, which is proper to man—but the "unspeakable crime" <note>original: "nefandum crimen"; a common historical euphemism for sodomy or non-procreative sexual acts.</note> is so called because, in addition, it is directed against the very foundation of generation common to all living creatures.

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether the law of nature is one for all<-
->mortals.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<margin>Gratian:</margin>
IT IS NOT enough to have established that the natural law is one in each individual, as was said in Article 2, unless we explore whether it is the same among all people. For it is argued that it is not the same in the whole human race. For <term>Gratian</term> <note>The 12th-century jurist who compiled the "Decretum," the foundational collection of Canon Law.</note> says at the very beginning of the *Decretum* that natural law is that which is contained in the Law <note>The Old Testament/Torah.</note> and the Gospel. But not everyone obeys the Gospel, as Paul says in Romans 10; therefore, the natural law is not the same among all.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Law is that according to which something is said to be just. However, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher, often called "The Philosopher" by Scholastic authors.</note> says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 7, that no natural justice is so natural that it is not in some way variable among different people; for even the right hand is by nature stronger than the left, and yet in some people this is not the case.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, whatever good nature inclines toward belongs to the law of nature; however, the inclinations and propensities of nature differ among men with vast variety. For some are born for honors, others for pleasures, and others for other things; therefore, the law of nature is not the same among all.

<margin>Isidore.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is <term>Isidore</term> <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential encyclopedist of the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 5, whose decree is found in Distinction 1: "Natural law is common to all nations." For what is written in the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "ff."; a standard abbreviation for the Digest of Justinian's Roman Law.</note> on Justice and Law, Law 1—namely, "Natural law is what nature has taught all animals"—is understood not only regarding the law proper to humans, but generally regarding the union of male and female.

FOR the unravelling of this question, the earlier distinction between natural principles and their conclusions must be recalled; for according to this distinction, the response is easily given in two conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ The first is: The natural law, insofar as it extends only to principles, is the same among all mortals; not only regarding the truth of its rightness, but also regarding knowledge of it. For the principles of <term>practical reason</term> <note>The use of reason to decide how to act, as opposed to "speculative reason" used for theoretical knowledge.</note> are similar in this respect to the principles of speculative things, which everywhere prevail with unshakable truth and shine clearly by natural light. For nowhere can there be any mortal so wild or barbarian, provided he is of sound mind, to whom truths of this kind are not accessible: "Good is to be sought, and evil avoided," "Do unto others..." etc., and the rest, which in the second article...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the universality of Natural Law. Having previously established that the primary principles of Natural Law (such as "do good and avoid evil") are known to all, the author now addresses the "secondary conclusions"—the specific rules derived from those principles—and why they might not be followed or known by everyone.</meta>

### Book One, Question IV.
C 2
<meta>catchword: excu-</meta>

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The secondary conclusion: Natural Law, regarding its conclusions, although it is for the most part the same among all people both in its correctness and in how it is known, nevertheless falls short of the former <note>The "former" refers to the primary, self-evident principles of natural law mentioned on previous pages.</note> due to specific obstacles in certain cases, and falls short of the latter <note>The "latter" refers to universal knowledge of the law.</note> because of the clouds of reason by which it is blinded due to evil customs.

<margin>Demonstration.</margin>
The proof of this conclusion is taken from the distinction between <term>practical reason</term> <note>original: "rationem practicam"; the use of logic to determine how one should act.</note> and <term>speculative reason</term> <note>original: "speculatiuam"; the use of logic to understand theoretical truths or facts, like mathematics.</note>. For although both use principles that are self-evident, they do not proceed with the same kind of reasoning. Indeed, speculative reason—because it deals mostly and primarily with "necessary" things (namely, those things that cannot be otherwise)—discovers the truth in its conclusions just as surely as it sees it in its principles, without any failure.

<margin>The difference between practical and speculative reason.</margin>
In practical reason, however, because it proceeds from necessary principles toward "contingent" things <note>Things that depend on circumstances and can change.</note> in which human actions consist, it is necessary that failures sometimes occur. These failures are more frequent the further one descends into specific details. From these points, our conclusion is deduced: namely, that although in the conclusions of speculative demonstrations the correctness of truth is the same for everyone, in the conclusions regarding actions, a failure sometimes occurs.

<margin>The reasoning is explained with examples.</margin>
The examples are clear. From that self-evident principle, *Do to others what you would wish to be done to you*, practical reason draws this law: *A deposit <note>Property or money held in trust for someone else.</note> must be returned as soon as it is requested.* This law is mostly true; however, it fails when the timing or the rightness of the request fails—for instance, when someone who left weapons in your care, having been seized by madness, demands them back in order to commit a murder. In the same way, from that principle, *Men must live in peace and tranquility* (which is most known to everyone as a good in itself), this law follows: *One must abstain from the noise of arms.* Yet it fails when an enemy invades the commonwealth. Similarly, from the same principle, the law is gathered that *Everyone should keep their promises.* Yet it fails when a cause emerges because of which fulfilling the promise would be shameful.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ But you might perhaps ask whether, regarding the *knowledge* of these same conclusions, there is any difference between practical and speculative reason. For nothing appears by which they differ: for just as practical conclusions are not equally known to all, neither are speculative ones. I say that the conclusion, *Every triangle has three angles equal

<column-break/>

to two right angles*, is just as true as the principle, *Where two lines meet, they form an angle*; yet it is not equally known to everyone.

<margin>Response.</margin>
I respond. Thus far there is no difference; however, it differs in that ignorance of necessary speculative truths happens because of a lack of teaching—that is, because you have not learned it. But ignorance in practical matters happens (as has been said) from evil custom darkening the reason. From these things, the final part of the conclusion follows: namely, that the more practical conclusions are fitted to specific details, the less they are known. This is clear by example. From that principle: *Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself*, that commandment of the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, *You shall not commit adultery*, is immediately inferred; for that cannot be done without injury to a spouse. If, however, you define the matter more narrowly—namely, *You shall not commit simple fornication*—although this is likewise prohibited there, nevertheless, because it does not have a connected injury <note>Meaning it does not necessarily involve breaking a marriage contract or harming a third party like a spouse.</note>, it is not so universally known but that it could be ignored among unrefined nations, even if they are not the most evilly established. Indeed, I do not know whether among some barbarians unaware of our faith, such ignorance could be entirely excusable. Similarly, from the same principle it clearly follows: *You shall not bear false witness*; since this forbids an injury, it is most well-known to all. But if you press it more strictly, *Do not utter any lie*, it is not so well known. Indeed, you will find among the common people those who think a "jocose" or "officious" lie <note>Types of lies categorized by Scholastic thinkers: a "jocose" lie is told in jest; an "officious" lie is told to help someone or prevent harm.</note> carries no fault. And this is the reason why all the prohibitions of the "second table" <note>The commandments regarding one's neighbor (the last seven).</note>, so that they might be more obvious, are expressly about those crimes by which an injury is inflicted on neighbors. Nevertheless, just as all harm is forbidden under the name of murder, so all filthiness is forbidden under the name of adultery, and every lie under the name of false witness. But ignorance of the commandments of the Decalogue could never be excused for any mortal, even if they smeared their crimes with some pretense—like those who, for the sake of religion and contrary to the prohibition of murder, thought to appease and worship their gods with human slaughter. Concerning whom the Psalmist says: *They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons.*

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
And <term>Cicero</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and philosopher.</note> mentions in a certain speech that in his age the Gallic nations were never polluted by such a rite; and that same monstrosity of wildness is said to be common to the peoples of the **New World**. For the demons, enemies of the human race, drive men mad with that blindness so that they might satisfy their envy with human blood.

<margin>Caesar.</margin>
And **Julius Caesar**, in Book 6 of the *Gallic War*, relates that formerly among the Germans, robberies had no infamy if they were committed outside the borders of each city. But they offered as a pretext for the crime that the young men used that exercise to drive away laziness and sluggishness...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...might shake them off, and prepare themselves for waging wars. But enough of these matters for the present.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, the response is that the words of <term>Gratian</term> <note>original: "Gratiani"; the 12th-century monk who founded the study of canon law.</note> should not be read in such a truncated way: "natural law is that which is contained in the Law and in the Gospel." It is not as if he were teaching that *everything* in the Gospel belongs to natural law. Rather, they must be read together with the following words: "Natural law is that by which everyone is commanded to do to others what they want done to themselves," etc., which is contained in the Gospel. Thus, these words are a parenthesis, teaching that natural law is fully contained in the Gospel—yet not only natural law, but also divine law in addition.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, which is from Aristotle, a response has already been given. It is not indeed the principles of nature that fail, but the conclusions that sometimes do.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Regarding the third argument, it is conceded that the natural inclinations belonging to man, insofar as he is a "sensible animal" <note>An animal capable of perception and feeling.</note>, pertain to the law of the <term>fomes</term> <note>original: "fomitis"; literally "tinder," a theological term for the leftover inclination toward sin or irrational desire following the loss of original innocence.</note>. This refers to the sensory appetite when it is deprived of <term>original justice</term> <note>The state of perfect harmony and innocence humans were believed to have possessed before the Fall.</note>. However, if these inclinations are considered insofar as they are properly human, then they are subject to the law of nature—that is, to reason, the moderator of all other powers, which ought to keep all emotions within their proper boundaries.

### ARTICLE V.

->Whether the law of nature can be changed or abolished.<-

After these points, it is easy to see in this fifth article what the corollaries of the preceding ones are: namely, whether the law of nature is either changeable or capable of being uprooted from the human mind.

<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
It is argued, then, that it is changeable. For we read in <term>Ecclesiasticus 17</term> <note>A book of the Bible, also known as Sirach.</note>: "He added to them discipline, and the law of life." Here the <term>gloss</term> <note>A standard medieval commentary written in the margins of texts.</note> notes: "the law of the letter, specifically for the correction of natural law."

<margin>Second argument. Isidore.</margin>
¶ And <term>Isidore</term> <note>St. Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar.</note> in Book 5 (which is in Distinction 1, chapter "natural right") says that common possession of all things and liberty belong to natural right; yet now, by the <term>law of nations</term> <note>original: "iure gentium"; a set of laws shared by all civilized peoples, often distinguished from both natural law and specific civil laws.</note>, both the division of property and even slavery have been introduced into the world; therefore, the law of nature is changeable.

<margin>Third. The other part of the question is tested by two arguments.</margin>
Furthermore, it is argued that it can be torn from our hearts, first from what has already been said. For there have been many nations so dull and wasted by every kind of depravity that they issued laws contrary to nature. Hence, regarding that passage in <term>Romans 2</term> <note>A letter by St. Paul in the New Testament.</note>, "When the nations who do not have the law," etc., the gloss says that in the "inner man" renewed by grace, the law of justice is inscribed, which sin had erased.

<margin>Gloss. Fourth argument.</margin>
And fourth, it is argued: The law of grace is more ef-

<column-break/>

-fective than the law of nature; but grace is erased by sin; therefore, the law of nature can be erased much more easily.

<margin>Gratian. Augustine.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the decree of Gratian, Distinction 5, chapter 1: "Natural law does not vary by time, but remains always immutable." And the opinion of Augustine in Book 2 of the *Confessions*: "Your law is written in the hearts of men, which indeed no iniquity erases."

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
To this question, the response is very easy by making a distinction: having assumed the gap that lies between principles and their conclusions, the law of nature can be considered changeable in two ways. One way is by addition, which might be made to it; and the other is by subtraction <note>original: "distractionem"; in this context, taking something away or diminishing it.</note>.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ The first conclusion is established: Nothing forbids the law of nature from being changeable in the first way (by addition). For divine law, both the Old and the New, was added to it for two chief benefits. First, because it had already been obscured in the minds of mortals and covered with a mist, so that it might be renewed. Specifically, so that it would be clear that not only external acts, but also internal ones, must be composed according to the norm of the law; and that natural rights are owed not only to friends, but also to enemies. The second benefit was so that those counsels which it lacked might be supplied. And this is what the gloss on Ecclesiasticus 17, cited in the first argument, calls the "correction" of the law of nature, which was accomplished through the written law.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: The law of nature is not changeable in the second way (by subtraction) regarding its primary principles—meaning that what was previously part of the law of nature should cease to be such a right. However, regarding the "secondary precepts," which are like the immediate conclusions, although it is for the most part immutable, it can nevertheless sometimes (but rarely) be changed due to human obstacles, as was explained in the previous article. For even regarding the necessary conclusions of "speculative things" <note>Theoretical or mathematical truths.</note>, it happens that one may sometimes hallucinate due to a "bleariness of the mind." Therefore, this change does not happen so much in the law itself as in the things themselves. For the truth of that general precept, "A deposit must be returned," or "A promise must be kept," does not change unless the circumstances change—from which change a contrary truth arises. For example, the law "Eating meat and drinking wine is healthy for men" changes in a particular case because a man is seized by a fever, for whom such a diet becomes harmful. Hence <term>Aristotle</term> in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 7, says: "Natural right is immutable, just as fire burns everywhere," which he understands as referring to the first principles; but regarding the conclusions, he adds that they can be changed.

<summary>This page explores the immutability of Natural Law, arguing that while its core principles are eternal and unchangeable, its specific applications (conclusions) can appear to change when human circumstances or "distractions" shift. Soto explains that Divine Law was given to "correct" and clarify Natural Law after it was obscured by human sin and social decay.</summary>

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>

It can, however—though not frequently, but rarely—be erased in some men as far as its conclusions and secondary precepts are concerned.

<margin>The conclusion is argued.</margin>
The conclusion needs no other evidence than what is sought from the points above. For <term>Barbarians</term> <note>A term used by Renaissance writers for non-European peoples, often those without written laws.</note> can be so perverted by such great viciousness of customs and clouded by perversities of errors, that they do not consider as sins those things which the law of nature forbids. And this occurs not only in conclusions that are far removed from the principles—such as a "helpful lie" or simple fornication—but even in those which are closer and consequently more luminous. For there have been found (as we have learned from trustworthy sources) among those mortals of the **New World** those who not only permitted unspeakable depravity against nature with impunity, but even denoted it with no fault. By which reasoning, certainly, it is possible for republics and princes to institute laws against nature, according to the word of Isaiah: *Woe to those who establish unjust laws.* <note>original: "Væ qui condunt leges iniquas." Isaiah 10:1.</note> And according to this, that gloss on Romans 2 is to be understood, which says that guilt has erased the law of justice from the hearts of the unfaithful.

<margin>To the third principal argument.</margin>
¶ There remain, therefore, two of the earlier arguments to be resolved. To the third, it is responded that although grace is more sublime and more effective than nature, it is nonetheless not innate or inborn to us, and thus not so deeply fixed; and therefore it is more easily uprooted through our fault than is the law of nature.

The third kind of laws is those of humans, concerning which greater reasons for disputing exist. It is asked first, therefore, whether human laws are necessary in addition to the natural law. And it is argued from the negative side: First,
<margin>First argument for the negative side. Augustine.</margin>
because (as <term>Augustine</term> says, whom we cited from Book 1 of *On Free Will* in the previous question) through the eternal law all things are most sufficiently ordered; but that law is communicated to us abundantly enough through the natural law; therefore, human laws are redundant.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second, law is a measure (as we said above) of our actions. But reason is not the measure of things; rather, it is the nature of things itself that reason inspects, as <term>Aristotle</term> is the authority in Book 10 of the *Metaphysics*. Therefore, since human laws proceed from reason, they do not have the legitimate nature of laws.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third, a measure, such as a law is, ought to be (as Aristotle teaches in the same place) most certain. But certainty cannot belong to human reason concerning things to be done, which are singular and changeable, according to that passage in Wisdom 9: *The thoughts of mortals are timid, and our foresight uncertain.* <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:14.</note> Therefore, no law proceeds from human reason.

<margin>Fourth argument.</margin>
¶ Fourth, he argues by another way. Even if human reason could be a certain rule of our actions, it would be much more convenient for the republic to be governed by the living voice of men than by established laws. For indeed, since a judge (as Aristotle is the authority in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, Chapter 4) is a "living justice," recourse to him would be made more easily and fittingly than to a deaf and dumb law. For since actions consist in the use of singular instances, human law (as we shall see in the following question) cannot provide for all things, nor look forward to singular circumstances, as a judge would do by his own prudence.

<margin>Isidore.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is **Isidore**, Book 5 of the *Etymologies*, Chapter 20 (and it is cited among the *Decreta*, Distinction 4), where he says that laws were made so that through fear of them human audacity might be restrained, and innocence might be safe among the wicked...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of human law as an extension of natural law.
