->### Fra Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law<-

...justice: and that in the wicked themselves, through the dread of punishment, their audacity and ability to do harm may be restrained.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The solution to this question is easily gathered from the very nature of things and the human condition. It is answered, therefore, with two conclusions. The first is: It was absolutely necessary that, in addition to the law of nature, other human laws be established to account for the variety of things and the emerging cases and affairs.

<margin>First reason</margin>
This conclusion rests on two roots: namely, our discursive <note>original: "discursivo"; referring to the step-by-step process of human reasoning, moving from one premise to a conclusion.</note> intellect and the needs of things. Indeed, just as in theoretical matters, so too in practical ones, a power is innate within us to deduce conclusions from universal and self-evident principles; and these are of two different kinds. For some we demonstrate as necessary, as in Mathematics; but others, because the consequence is not as evident, we gather as matters of opinion, according to the quality of each science. In the same way, in practical matters, we express the precepts of the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> from first principles (as has been said) as if they were necessary conclusions; and therefore they belong to the law of nature. Nevertheless, because our actions are concerned with individual cases, it is necessary to descend from those same principles to particulars, observing the circumstances of place and time. Therefore, those rules established in this manner—because they do not spring necessarily from natural principles alone but are established with the aid of reason—are called human laws. Such are the laws that have been established for sales and other exchanges of goods, without which our species would be unable to live its life.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But perhaps someone might rise up here against the providence of God and nature. Would it not have been more providently arranged for us if the law of nature itself taught us all things down to the smallest detail? For it is argued that this would have been more beneficial because reason is often obscured by passions, while the law of nature is always clear.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is that all things are arranged according to our nature. For it is the character and nature of reason to move through discourse; and therefore, a wise God and sagacious nature placed only the seeds within us, which were to reach fruit through the cultivation of reason. This is true both in theoretical and practical matters: that is, in the arts as well as in morals.

<margin>Second reason for the conclusion.</margin>
From this, our conclusion is gathered a second time. For just as the created intellect was endowed with the light of principles regarding the sciences—from which it might reason toward various branches of knowledge and opinions, and devise through meditation various arts in stone, wood, wool, and other materials useful to us—

<column-break/>

—namely, those things by which we are clothed, sheltered, nourished, and delighted. In the same way (as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose works formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance legal theory.</note> states at the beginning of the second book of the *Ethics*), He cast the seeds of moral virtues into us, which, when cultivated by our discipline and habit, would whiten toward the harvest. Now, the most powerful and effective discipline of morals is the establishment of human laws. Therefore, besides the law of nature, which acts as the seed, human laws are necessary so that the crops may grow more abundantly.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Thirdly, the same conclusion is proven. Although the law of nature is a universal rule of morals, it does not employ compulsory punishments, which are nevertheless necessary for human beings in the <term>state of fallen nature</term> <note>original: "statu naturæ lapsæ"; the theological concept that human nature is corrupted by sin and requires external restraint to behave well.</note>. Therefore, besides the law of nature, it is worthwhile to employ penal laws.

<margin>Aristot.</margin>
This is the teaching of Aristotle in the tenth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 9, where he says that some become good by nature, others by habit, and others by discipline.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Nature, indeed, is not in our power, but by some gift of God, people are born such as the "choir of virtues" <note>An allegorical way of saying "the virtuous character."</note> seems to have produced. Others, however, become good through habit right from infancy. But yet, not everyone can be sufficiently instructed by discipline, except only those who have been "softened" by habit. Just as a <term>fallow field</term> <note>original: "novale"; land being prepared for crops.</note>, before it receives seeds, has need of the curved plow; so, against those who are prone to evil but hard and defiant toward good—who, namely, cannot be led for the sake of what is honorable—fear is necessary so that they may be restrained from evil by force. Thus, they may leave a quiet life for others, and their own restless mind may be commanded by fear to take heed. For man is (as Aristotle states in the first book of the *Politics*, chapter 2), when his perfection is received, the best of all animals; but if he becomes estranged from law and judgments, he is the worst of all. For injustice is most cruel when it holds weapons. But man holds weapons through his innate prudence, which must therefore be directed by laws and coerced by fear. And for this reason (as we said in Question 1), no one can establish laws except either the commonwealth or the one who exercises its authority. By the same logic, nature fathered man as a "civil animal" <note>original: "ciuile animal"; a translation of the Greek *zoon politikon*, meaning a creature naturally suited for organized society.</note>; namely, so that he might live in society, hedged in by laws.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is answered that although the law of nature is a participation in the eternal law, human reason cannot grasp the entire power of natural principles except—as is its nature—by reasoning. For it does not see those things which lie hidden in universal principles with a simple intuition, as an intellectual angel sees; but by reasoning, it deduces one thing from another. For this reason, just as it is in theoretical matters by the eternal light, so also...

### Book One, Question Five

So too in practical matters are we illuminated by the eternal law in a twofold way. First, by receiving general principles; second, so that by reasoning from those same principles, we may derive other particular laws. Since these exist preeminently within that same eternal law, they are not sufficiently unfolded through natural law alone. This much concerns the directive power of laws. But regarding their coercive power, the reasoning is nearly the same. For the law of nature irritates, gnaws at, and strikes the consciences of evildoers; and as <margin>Paul.</margin> *Paul* says to the Romans: it accuses them enough in their thoughts <note>referring to Romans 2:15</note>, so that sensible men, struck by that fear and deterred by the horror of their own shame, might be sufficiently corrected. For as <margin>Augustine.</margin> *Augustine* says in the first book of the *Confessions*: "You have commanded, O Lord, and so it is, that every disordered mind should be its own punishment." <note>original: "iussisti Domine & sic est, vt pœna sua sibi sit omnis inordinatus animus"</note> But because there are others so deeply submerged in the whirlpool of the senses that they fear nothing except what is placed before their eyes, physical punishments had to be added through human laws. <margin>Paul.</margin> For this reason, *Paul* says that the law is not laid down for the just man: because the law of nature, illuminated by the ray of faith, is enough for him to be pulled back from evil and enticed toward the good. ¶ And from this, <margin>Solution to the second argument.</margin> the solution to the second argument is clearly gathered. For we grant that reason is not the primary rule, but rather the natural law, which is the image of the eternal law; nevertheless, reason, looking upon that exemplar, expresses human laws. <margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ Regarding the third point, however, we cannot deny that human laws do not flourish with that same certainty as theoretical conclusions. This is because they are not established concerning necessary things, but concerning singular, contingent matters subject to variety. Nor is it necessary for every measure to possess infallible certainty; it is enough that each be faithful according to the nature of its subject matter. And this is the reason why human laws are not, like natural laws, <margin>To the fourth.</margin> immobile. ¶ The fourth argument is of heavier weight. For it is a question which <margin>Aristotle.</margin> *Aristotle* touched upon in the third book of the *Politics*, chapter 11: namely, whether a republic is better governed by the best man or by the best law. He defines it as better for the law to rule than a man. This is something he also mentioned in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, <margin>First reason why it is better for law to rule than man.</margin> chapter 6. Namely, because it is easier to find one or a few wise makers of laws than a multitude of judges. Indeed, a few men in a single century are enough to make laws; but to judge the law, a great many are necessary. Secondly, because laws are <margin>Second reason.</margin> made after long consideration of time, whereas judgments are thought out very briefly; and therefore an error happens more easily <margin>Third reason.</margin> here than there. Furthermore, and most importantly, since laws are established concerning universals and the future,

<column-break/>

and do not touch individuals specifically, they are not founded out of respect for persons. But a senator or a judge, because he deals with individual persons, can be struck by hatred or love, and most especially corrupted by greed. Therefore, it is better that as much as possible all things be explained by laws, and that only the smallest matters, which cannot be determined by law, be left to the judges. Whence he says that those who command the law to preside, command God to preside and the laws (as if they flow from Him); but he who commands a man to preside, adds a savage beast. This is because lust and anger drive even the best men off course when they are in power. Judges, therefore, should not be the laws themselves, but (as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> *Aristotle* says in the fifth book of the *Ethics*) they ought to be the faithful guardians of the laws. ¶ And through these points, a response is given to a certain argument that *Aristotle* <margin>Aristotle’s argument as above.</margin> poses to himself in the same place concerning craftsmen. For it seems more conducive to the health of the body, he says, for a doctor to heal the sick by his own prudence rather than being bound by the prescriptions of books. For he will have a much better perspective on the particular circumstances of the disease; therefore, by the same reasoning, the republic could be governed more healthily by the singular prudence of men, informed by particular events, than by prescribed laws. I say the response is twofold. First, <margin>Solution to the first.</margin> it is denied that a doctor’s prudence has any power unless it has been instructed by the medical art; for healing happens more certainly through the art than without it. Second, it <margin>Second solution.</margin> cannot happen so frequently to doctors that they have a heart corrupted toward killing the sick, as it happens to judges regarding the delivery of a sentence, either in favor of one party or to the ruin of another. And therefore it is more dangerous to permit judgments to the whim of a judge than to a doctor. Nevertheless, when the faith of a doctor is feared—namely, when he comes under suspicion of being corrupted by a price or of plotting against the health of the sick out of hatred—he must be watched more sharply so that he preserves the prescriptions of the art exactly <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for perfect precision.</note>. Indeed, I would add that it is most dangerous and rash for doctors to prefer their <margin>It is dangerous and rash for a doctor to prefer his own opinions and estimates over the art.</margin> own opinions and estimates over science and art. ¶ But let us return to the judges: Added to this is a fourth point (as the same Philosopher says in the tenth book of the *Ethics*): while the law commands uprightness, even if it restrains a man from pleasures, it is troublesome or hateful to no one; whereas a judge easily comes under suspicion of whether he has been infected by hatred or some other emotion. For which reason <margin>Fourth reason.</margin> (as I gather from this), the tutors and counselors of princes ought to use this caution: when they themselves do not dare to rebuke their patrons, they should offer laws of virtues and histories to be read, which do not generate envy and which do instruct morals.

¶ Responding to the remaining difficulty of the argument, we admit that those smaller details, which cannot be encompassed by laws, must be left to the discretion of the judge, as established in the *Digest* under "On Laws" (*l. non possunt*) <note>original: "ff. de legib. l. non possunt." Refers to the *Digest* of Justinian, Book 1, Title 3, Law 12, which argues that laws cannot cover every individual case.</note>. This is because, while we cannot embrace everything within laws, we must neglect some things so that we do not lose everything; just as those who, when a storm threatens, throw certain things into the raging waters so that they may save the rest of the ship. For this reason, a judge requires supreme knowledge and prudence, in addition to uprightness of soul, so that he may skillfully adapt the universal principles of the laws to the outcomes of specific events.

## ARTICLE II.

### *Whether every human law is derived from the natural law.*

<margin>
First argument from the negative side.
Aristotle.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a landscape with a bridge and a face integrated into the upper flourish of the letter.</image-desc> The second article is whether every human law derives from the natural law. For it is argued first from the negative side: Civil justice (as Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 7) is that which, from the beginning, makes no difference whether it is done one way or another. However, that which flows from the law of nature was already mandatory even before human law existed. Therefore, not every human law is derived from the natural law.

<margin>
Second argument.
Aristotle.
Isidore.
</margin>
Secondly, positive law (as Aristotle says in the same place and Isidore in Book 5) is divided in opposition to natural law. However, those things which descend from the natural law are not divided against natural law; rather, they are its offspring. Therefore, human laws are by no means derived from the natural law.

<margin>
Third argument.
</margin>
Thirdly, the law of nature (as Aristotle says in the same place) has the same force among all people. Human laws, however, do not; rather, each republic is supported by its own specific laws. Therefore, not all laws arise from the law of nature.

<margin>
Fourth argument.
</margin>
Fourthly, a natural reason can be provided for everything that flows from the law of nature. However, a reason cannot be given for everything established by our ancestors, as Julian says in the *Digest* under "On Laws" (*l. non omnium*). Therefore, not all human laws are derived from the natural law.

<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, are the words of Cicero in the second book of *On Invention*: Fear and religion have sanctioned things that proceeded from nature and were approved by custom.

<margin>
First conclusion.
Augustine.
</margin>
The question is answered with four conclusions. One is: Every human law that has been established as "right," if it is indeed correct, derives from the law of nature. Indeed, it possesses the rectitude and reason of law only to the extent that it receives them from the law of nature. For a law (as will be more broadly apparent in the next article) is not a law unless it is just. Indeed, (as Augustine says in the first book of *On Free Choice of the Will* <note>original: "1. de lib. ar. Augu."</note>), it has the power of law only insofar

<column-break/>

<margin>
Argument for the conclusion.
</margin>
as it participates in the reason of justice. From this it is argued: what is just and right in human affairs must be judged according to the rule of reason. Now, the rule of reason (as we were just saying) is the nature of things, which reason ought to look upon as a model in all its actions. Therefore, human laws, as they are fabricated by reason itself, are all born from the natural. Nor indeed (as we said above) does it prevent human laws from being measured by two rules: namely, the eternal and the natural, the latter being a participation in the former. For just as an architect draws lines on stone or wood based on a conceived form of a house—which serve as a rule for the workman, who must follow them while hewing and forging—so God has imprinted his eternal law upon us, which serves as a certain sign of that law. Therefore, while we imitate the law of nature, we hold to the eternal law. Hence Cicero says in the second book of *On Laws*: Law is the 
<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>
distinction between the just and the unjust, expressed according to that most ancient and principal nature of things, toward which the laws of men are directed—laws which punish the wicked and defend and rouse the good.

<margin>
Second conclusion.
</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: A thing is derived from the law of nature in two ways. In one way, like a conclusion deduced from principles; and in the other way, as a specific determination of some common genus. For from that principle, "What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to anyone else," follow these conclusions: "You shall not kill," "You shall not commit theft," and so on. But from the principle that "Every virtue is worthy of reward, and every vice worthy of punishment," human law has sanctioned 
<margin>
The conclusion is explained.
</margin>
that the assassin and the thief should be hanged, and the heretic burned. In this case, it draws a general type of punishment down to a specific one. Just as a craftsman adapts the form of a house conceived in general to particular structures, so that this one is built one way, and that one another. And the wide distinction between these modes of derivation is clear. For the former happens by way of a syllogism <term>syllogism: a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term>. In that case, both premises are naturally known: namely, "What you do not want for yourself, do not do to another"; you do not wish to be killed, nor to be despoiled of your goods, nor to suffer injury regarding your wife; therefore, you shall not commit homicide, nor theft, nor adultery. The latter mode, however, does not happen in this way. For from the fact that "Every evil person must be punished," a syllogism is correctly constructed: "if this person is evil, let this person be punished." However, this universal—that is, taken with its distribution—is not what is determined by positive law in the second way; rather, it is a universal genus which is applied to its own species. For example, if the wicked person is to be struck with a penalty, let such a person—namely a thief—be punished with such a penalty. This does not follow by a similar syllogism...

<summary>De Soto argues that all valid human laws must derive from natural law, either as direct logical deductions from universal moral principles (like the prohibition of theft) or as specific legal determinations of general rules (like setting specific punishments for crimes).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Question Five, Article Two, regarding how human laws are derived from the natural law. The previous page established that while some laws are direct conclusions of natural principles, others require human "determination" to be specific.</meta>

->Book One, Question V.<-

not through a syllogism, but through human estimation by which we measure out the punishment for a fault. For the reasoning works like this: Every evil person must be punished; however, the fitting punishment for a thief is hanging, and for a heretic, burning <note>original: "latroni autem congruens supplicium est suspendium, hæreticoque incendium." This reflects the severe penal practices of the 16th century, which the author is using as an example of how general principles are applied specifically by human choice.</note>. Therefore, they are to be punished in this way. Yet, the second part of this reasoning is not a natural realization, but a matter of human judgment.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ From this, a third conclusion follows: The derivation of human law from the natural law that occurs by way of a *conclusion* is not a new creation of a virtuous act, but rather an explanation of a virtue that was previously hidden within natural principles.

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
For indeed, "You shall not commit adultery," "Return what has been deposited," and the Ten Commandments <note>original: "Decalogus"</note> were virtues even before human reasoning addressed them, though they were hidden in natural principles. They were, however, explicitly set down so that no one could use ignorance as an excuse. But the second type of derivation <note>the "determination" or specific application</note> is a new creation of an act into the category of virtue. For by the law of nature, it was not a virtue to kill a thief or a heretic; the law of nature only said they should be punished. It was human law that made their execution a virtuous act of justice. In the same way, the law of nature is like a general principle: one must live temperately and frugally so that the body can more readily serve the soul. From this, it does not obviously follow that one must abstain from meat or eat only once a day; nevertheless, human law, by judging the matter, derived from that principle what kind of temperance ought to exist. Therefore, human law established the abstinence from meat under the virtue of temperance, where it was not specifically required before. In the same way, the command "Keep holy the Sabbath" was determined to this or that specific feast to be observed and to the hearing of sacred rites.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thus, as St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 95, a. 2.</note> says, human laws of the first kind have their vigor from the natural law; but those of the latter order do not.

<margin>The absolute reason for the conclusion.</margin>
If you search for the highest reason for this, it is, I believe, that conclusions are actually contained within their principles; however, a specific species is only contained within its genus potentially. This is clear from the *Predicables* <note>A reference to Porphyry’s introduction to Aristotle’s logic.</note>. For "Animal" does not actually contain every species; otherwise, any individual animal would belong to every species at once. Because of this, those laws established by narrowing a genus down to a specific species have no power except in that specific determination which human reason has established. For example: "One must live temperately; now, for this time and this people, this specific temperance is fitting; therefore, during Lent <note>original: "Quadragesima," the forty-day period of fasting before Easter.</note> one must abstain from meat."

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The first argument is therefore resolved by this most recent opinion.

<column-break/>

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the *Ethics*, Book 5, called "legal justice" that which is purely civil—that is, what is derived in the second way from the natural law. Because of this, before it was established, it was not a virtue, and subsequently, it did not matter whether it was done this way or that. It is different for the other mode of derivation. Hence, through this distinction, in the fourth article, we shall divide human law into the "law of nations" and "civil law."

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ In the same way, the response to the second argument is that human law—not just any, but civil law which is derived in the second way from the natural law—is distinguished from natural law.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, the response is that the natural law, which Aristotle says has the same power everywhere, consists in principles. For he himself acknowledged in the same place that conclusions, and especially specific determinations, vary among various nations.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, the response is that the legal expert in the cited law does not deny that a reason can be given for those things elicited from the law of nature by way of conclusions. However, for those things derived in the second way—because they were established through the consultation of elders through experience and prudence, much like specific determinations of universals—a reason is not always to be demanded. Rather, one must have faith in their experience and prudence, as Aristotle is the authority in the *Ethics*, Book 6.
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

->ARTICLE III.<-

### Whether the qualities of human law are correctly described by Isidore.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
Concerning the other types of law—namely eternal, natural, and divine law—there is no need to investigate the qualities in which their rectitude is placed. For those are, by their very nature, inherently good and right. But regarding human law, because our reason is prone to delusion, it is necessary to explore with what conditions a law ought to be adorned so that it may be good.
<margin>Isidore.</margin>
Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), whose "Etymologies" was a standard medieval textbook.</note> places these in the following order in Book 5, Chapter 21: "A law," he says, "shall be honorable, just, possible, according to nature, according to the custom of the country, suitable to the place and time, necessary, useful, and also clear, lest it contain anything deceptive through obscurity; written for no private benefit, but for the common utility of the citizens." <margin>Responsive Conclusion</margin>
The question is answered with a single conclusion: Isidore most excellently described the goodness of law in all its parts—first briefly, and then more explicitly. For there are two things to consider in a law by which the conditions of a good law must be measured and examined. For law is both a prescribed form that leads human actions toward their due end, and furthermore, it is a measure and rule set down according to the model of eternal and natural law. If it is considered as a form leading to an end, it must be of such a kind as is conducive to that 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
end, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was commonly referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance scholarship.</note> in Book 2 of the *Physics*. For a saw must have a form necessary for what is most suitable for sawing. If it is considered as a rule and measure, it must be modeled after the eternal and natural law. The goal of human law is human utility (as stated in the Digest <note>A part of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundational body of Roman law.</note> "on laws"): that is, their salvation and the training of their morals so that they may live calmly and happily. The first condition of a good law, therefore, regards the eternal law, which is the fountain of all rectitude. And this is what Isidore means by "consistent with religion" <note>original: "religioni congruens"</note>: namely, that by which God is worshiped, who must be established as the primary end of our actions. 

<margin>Plato</margin>
For Plato himself recognized this in Book 1 of *The Laws*. The second quality attributed to human law is in relation to the natural law, which is its other model. And this is what he adds there, saying, "it should fit with discipline" <note>original: "disciplinæ conueniat"</note>. 

<margin>Plato</margin>
For discipline (as Plato teaches in the second dialogue of *The Laws*) 

<column-break/>

is the education of children and the training of our morals. Therefore, to "fit with discipline" is the same as being a rule applied to the composing of morals. Indeed, this discipline must be handed down to men according to their nature. There remains, then, the third aspect regarding the end: that the law should "profit the safety and well-being of men." For here, "safety" <note>The Latin *salus* can mean both health/safety and eternal salvation.</note> is called the best disposition of the soul, by which we are preserved unharmed from the attacking passions and diseases that are our calamity. For so says Paul: "For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed" <note>A reference to the New Testament, Romans 13:11.</note>. 

<margin>All law qualities are reduced to three.</margin>
<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
¶ According to St. Thomas, the number of other qualities is reduced to these three. 

<margin>The conditions of laws are explained individually.</margin>
Nevertheless, the figure and beauty of the law is depicted more explicitly in the manner of orators. Truly, since it is a rule of virtues whose reward is honor, nothing is more ancient to the law than that it be **honorable**. And because the true honor of virtue is to be sought from God, he excellently explained what he had called "consistent with religion" using the word "honorable." Yet this is also taught by the same word so that the law may not be **shameful**: namely, something that offends the eyes and ears, as were the rituals and laws of their temples among those wretched pagans. Such was the law of the Bacchanalia <note>Ancient Roman festivals of Bacchus/Dionysus, notorious for their wild and unrestrained behavior.</note>, which were celebrated with drunkenness and the obscene nudity of men. Furthermore, a law would be dishonorable if it punished noble and illustrious magnates with the same infamous execution as common thieves. Next, to declare what he had called "fitting with discipline," which we said pertains to the law of nature, he adds: **Just, possible**, etc. 

<margin>A just and possible law.</margin>
For human discipline is placed in three things. First, that it be equal to reason, 

<margin>Argument</margin>
holding its line in all things; in this consists the essence of justice. But if you argue that nothing is honorable that is not also just, and therefore the 

<margin>Solution</margin>
repetition of "honorable and just" is redundant, the answer is: if you take "just" universally for every virtue, it is the same as honorable; however, **justice** as a specific virtue is a part—that is, one 

<margin>Cicero</margin>
of the four species of the honorable, as Cicero says in Book 1 of *On Duties* following Aristotle. For "honorable" is the same as moral virtue, which is divided into the four cardinal virtues <note>Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>. To say "honorable and just," therefore, is a specification of the genus by the species. ### First Book, Question V.

<margin>The Answer.</margin>
The answer is that even if the previous point is granted, it was necessary to explain what the "possibility" of a law consists of. Namely, it must be drawn from the character and condition of the citizens. Therefore, "possible" in this context is understood as that which is not difficult. 
<margin>Aristotle. A twofold understanding of "impossible."</margin>
For the Philosopher <note>Aristotle is traditionally referred to as "the Philosopher" in scholastic texts.</note> says in Book 1 of *On the Heavens* that "impossible" is understood in two ways: one way simply, and the other for that which is not well or not easily doable. The reasoning for "possibility" ought to be weighed according to the quality of the persons, which Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose works defined medieval law.</note> calls "nature." For the same exercises and burdens of labor should not be commanded for children and those not yet firm in age, or those worn out by old age, as for others who are firmer and stronger. Nor are as many fasts or spiritual duties to be demanded by law from secular people as from religious monks. Third, it is required for proper discipline that the law be "clothed" in all its circumstances. 
<margin>Law ought to be suitable to the place and time.</margin>
The circumstances are time and place. And therefore he says: "according to the custom of the country, suitable to the place and time." For since the nature of things cannot be changed—which in different regions brings about different human dispositions, customs, and diseases—laws ought to be adapted to the customs of the region. For Germans (to use them as an example) are less afraid of death, and more fierce and grim; and therefore among them, some types of crimes are punished with the most atrocious punishments, which are not suitable for Spaniards because of their excessive horror of such things. The other things that follow to the end of the law regard human 
<margin>Law, necessary and useful.</margin>
salvation. For the law ought to both pull men back from evil and promote them toward good.
Because of the first, it is called "necessary"—namely, to avoid inconveniences and harms by which we are subverted. Because of the second, it is called "useful." For "useful" in this context is the same as a "means" <term>medium: the instrument or path toward a goal</term>; it is not used in a simple sense, but differs from "necessary" in that they regard different effects. From this, lawmakers should especially consider that they should not overwhelm subjects with a multitude of 
<margin>A multitude of laws is faulty.</margin>
laws, but should be content only with those that are strictly necessary; for the multitude itself immediately becomes "impossible" to follow. From there, they are immediately made like spiders' webs, by which flies are caught, but not lions. I say an immoderate crowd of laws provides only this: that the good and mild, who do not need laws, live hedged in; while the stubborn and untamed have more laws to trample underfoot to satisfy their lusts. ¶ But for the same purpose of the law, it is extremely fitting that it be wrapped in no obscurity,

<column-break/>

lest it become a mousetrap for catching the ignorant; but it should be so manifest that no one among the transgressors could fail to have understood it. Hence, under the same title "On Laws and Constitutions," we read: "The most sacred laws, which constrain the lives of men, ought to be understood by men; so that everyone, having more clearly recognized their command, may either avoid forbidden things or pursue permitted ones." ¶ Finally, so that Isidore might openly 
<margin>Isidore.</margin>
indicate the same goal of laws, he concluded with a summary of everything, saying: "Written for no private advantage, but for the common utility of the citizens." For as there is a difference between a king and a tyrant only in this reasoning—that the former refers everything to the common good, while the latter refers it to his own private interest—so there is this same gap between a good and a bad law. But truly, since laws can be established for private advantage in other ways and respects, it would be the worst and most pestilential of all if they were founded for the sake of profit. Namely, so that the treasury <note>original: "ærarium," the public treasury.</note> of the lawmakers might grow rich, or the wealth of courtiers increase, through the fines of transgressors or the frequency of dispensations <note>A dispensation is an exemption from a law granted by an authority.</note>. Most excellently, therefore, 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine says in Book 1 of *On Free Will* that an unjust law is not a law. And elegantly, Cicero in Book 2 of *On the Laws* [says]: "It is certainly established that laws were founded for the safety of citizens, the preservation of cities, and the quiet and blessed life of men; and that those who first enacted such decrees for peoples showed that they would write and pass things by which, once those writings were received, people would live honorably and blessedly; and such things thus composed and established, they named 'laws.' From which it is right to understand that those who drafted destructive and unjust orders for peoples, since they did the opposite of what they promised and professed, passed anything rather than 'laws'; so that it may be clear that in the very interpretation of the name 'law' there is the force and sense of justice and of cultivating right." But what need is there for witnesses? Law is a rule; and unless a rule is straight <note>original: "recta," meaning both physically straight and morally right.</note>, it does not retain its nature. An unjust law, however, is crooked; therefore, it is nothing less than a law.

Therefore, the first and third arguments we raised above are clearly resolved.

Yet it differs from the law which is written by the consent of the commonwealth. However, a law ought to be established that does not conflict with the custom of the country, unless the custom is worthy of being discarded. ¶ To the

<meta>This page continues the "Response" section of Book 1, Question 5, regarding the definition and qualities of law. # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

human affairs are subject to such great variety that laws can never be established with such certainty that they do not sometimes need to be interpreted based on equity and goodness <note>original: "ex æquo & bono"</note>. For even the natural law regarding the return of a deposit fails when it is demanded by someone who intends to do harm. In the same way, the law that punishes a murderer with death fails when a man kills a wife caught in the act of adultery. For this reason (as <margin>Aristotle</margin> says in the cited passage), such defects are not in the law itself, but in human affairs, whose occurrences <margin>The law is like a Lesbian rule.</margin> cannot be more certainly grasped. For this very reason, the law is most appropriately compared to a "Lesbian rule." For there was an island where the stones, because of their unmanageable hardness, could not be squared by carving to fit a standard rule. Therefore, conversely, the rule—which for this reason was not made of iron but of lead—was bent so that it could adapt to the bumpiness of the stone: so that, according to the curve of the rule, the placement in the wall could be determined, or the spot leveled where it might fit more aptly. From this it follows that when a law is accommodated to things out of necessity based on equity and goodness, Aristotle attributed that "crookedness" not to a fault, but to a merit, because of the instability of human affairs. Nevertheless, outside of such necessity, a "Lesbian rule" deservedly has a bad reputation. This occurs when the law is bent to the will of princes, or for other reasons where morals are not aligned with the law, but the law is twisted to match the corruption of morals.

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether Isidore and those who follow him divide civil laws and human right appropriately.<-

<margin>First reason from the negative side.</margin> Finally, in this last article of the question, we must see whether the divisions of human right are appropriately made. And it is argued from the negative side: Both Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose writings were foundational for medieval legal theory.</note> and the civil laws divide human right into the "law of nations" and "civil law," as is clear in Distinction 1 and the *Digest* regarding Justice and Right <note>original: "ff. de Iust. & Iure." Soto is citing the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Roman Law.</note>. There, after natural right (which is contrasted with human right), the law of nations and civil law are subdivided. However, the law of nations seems to pertain to natural law rather than civil law; for it is a conclusion of natural right. Therefore, Isidore himself, who said that natural right is common to all nations, adds that the law of nations is so named because nearly all nations use it: therefore, the division is inept. ¶ Second-

<column-break/>

ly, it is argued: Another division of laws is made into the laws of <margin>Second reason.</margin> priests and soldiers, which is indeed taken from different offices. Therefore, since the offices and trades of a commonwealth are almost innumerable, that division would have to be extended to infinity. ¶ Thirdly, <margin>Third reason.</margin> it is argued: civil law is divided into Senate decrees, plebeian decrees, and other things of that kind. But these seem to differ only materially—namely, as laws established by many or few—and not by a formal reason of commanding. Now, a material division does not fall under the rules of art, because it can proceed to infinity, just as if you were to speak of the laws of the Athenians, or the Spartans, or the Romans: therefore, that is by no means an artful division. And in the same way, another partition is challenged, by which laws are divided into the Cornelian, Julian, Sempronian, and others which receive different names only from their authors. For since authors are without number, such a division is made without art. ¶ On the contrary stands <margin>Isidore.</margin> both the authority of Isidore and that of the experts of the law.

<margin>The concluding response.</margin> The present question is resolved by a single conclusion, which is this: Human right, insofar as it is the same as human law, is divided artfully in a fourfold way. For every <margin>The conclusion is shown.</margin> genus is divided by itself according to that which is contained in its definition, and (as they say) formally; but not according to that which happens to it from the outside. Just as "animal," because it contains a soul within itself which by intrinsic reason is either rational or irrational, is divided by itself into rational and irrational—but not into white and black, like something colored. Now, four elements are included by themselves in the definition of human law: therefore, it can be divided into species in just as many ways. For the first thing that belongs to human law by its nature is to be derived (as we said in Article 2) from divine right. This happens in two ways: namely, by the way of a natural inference, and by the way of an arbitrary determination. Therefore, according to these differences, human right is first of all distributed into the law of nations and civil law. For whatever mortals have reasoned out from natural principles by way of a conclusion is called the "law of nations" <term>Ius gentium: The "law of nations," or universal principles of justice recognized by all civilized peoples through reason.</term>. The examples are manifest. Let us establish this natural principle: Human life must be sustained and cherished in peace and tranquility. From this, assuming the second premise—that human nature is corrupted and, living in common, would neither cultivate the fields diligently nor live in peace—the nations inferred that possessions ought to be divided. # Book One, Question 5.

Initially, they derived the **law of servitude** <note>original: "servitutis legem"; referring to the historical legal justification for slavery—that it was more merciful to enslave a prisoner of war than to execute them</note>; for otherwise, an enemy could not have been spared in war. Again, from this same principle, another premise was added: namely, that humans—being **social animals** <note>original: "civile animal"; a reference to the Aristotelian idea that humans are naturally meant to live in communities</note>—cannot sustain themselves unless they help one another through mutual services. From this, they derived all the laws of **sale, hiring, pledging**, and other forms of exchange, pacts, and agreements, as found in the first book of the Digest <note>original: "ff. de Iust. & Iure. l. 1. Ex hoc iure"</note>, by which human society is bound together and sustained. However, whatever is established as a specific instance of a general category is called **civil law**. For each city or republic has enacted its own particular decrees. For example, from the natural principle that "God must be worshipped with sacrifices," various specific sacrifices were instituted—namely of oxen or goats. As <margin>Aristotle, Ethics, Book 5, ch. 7</margin> Aristotle says in the 5th book of his *Ethics*, chapter 7: "One should sacrifice a goat to the gods, but not two sheep." <note>This illustrates that while the impulse to worship is natural, the specific ritual is a human, "civil" decision.</note> Indeed, the sacrifices of the **Old Law** were divinely instituted, as was our most holy **Eucharist** by the Redeemer himself, who became a victim and sacrifice for us. Laws regarding punishments—by which different penalties are decreed for various types of crimes—also belong to civil law. <margin>The distinction between natural law, the law of nations, and civil law.</margin> Therefore, **natural law** is written in our minds without any reasoning process. The **law of nations** <note>original: "ius gentium"</note>, however, is derived from natural reasoning without a formal assembly of men or long deliberation. But **civil law** is established by the decision of men coming together in a single council. <margin>Isidore.</margin> Hence, Isidore says in Book 5, chapter 5: "Civil law is that which each people or city establishes as its own for divine and human reasons." <margin>A doubt.</margin> However, one doubt <note>original: "scrupulus"</note> arises here that is worthy of an answer. It seems to follow from this that the precepts of the **Decalogue** (the Ten Commandments) belong to the law of nations, since (as seen above) they are derived from natural principles like conclusions. Yet this conclusion is false; for regarding their root, they are considered part of the **natural law**; but regarding their explanation and establishment, they belong to **Divine Law**, both the Old and the Gospel Law. <margin>The solution.</margin> To this, however, it is replied that by reason of their origin, every law of nations is said to be of natural law, although by reason of how it is inferred and established, it is called the law of nations. For this reason, nothing prevents the Decalogue from being considered, in the latter sense, part of the law of nations before the written law existed. Nevertheless, because the inference is so obvious, perhaps it would only be given the name of natural law. For the Decalogue is so clear that it is very close to the principles of natural law. But because the

<column-break/>

minds of mortals were becoming clouded <note>original: "caligante"; a common theological metaphor for the darkening of human intellect due to sin, necessitating written law</note>, those precepts were carved onto tablets by the finger of God and thus obtained the name of **Divine Law**. This is not because they are above natural things, but because they were set forth with God as the author. <margin>To the first argument.</margin> By this, the first argument is solved. For the law of nations is not denied to be natural in a certain way, yet it is considered to differ from it because it requires an inference—especially when the conclusion is further removed from the principles. <margin>The second condition of human law.</margin> The second condition of human law is its **orientation toward the common good**. According to this order, it is divided with respect to different offices and ministers who perform excellent works for the common good: such as the law of **priests**, who are consecrated to religion and worship; the laws of **soldiers**, who are the public guardians; and the laws of **magistrates**, who are appointed to administer justice. However, it does not follow from this (as was argued earlier) that this division must be multiplied to the number of all the craftsmen in the republic. <margin>The second argument is solved.</margin> For others are not public ministers appointed for the common good, but rather serve particular needs. <margin>Third: From where human law takes its division.</margin> Third, it is fitting for human law to be instituted by those who handle the public administration of the republic. But of the types of republics (as we said above, following Aristotle’s *Politics*), there are many species. One is an **Aristocracy**, <margin>First: Aristocracy.</margin> which is the rule of the best men; therefore, the laws issued by them are called **Senate decrees** <note>original: "Senatusconsulta"</note>, "responses of the wise," and so on. The second species of government is an <margin>Second: Oligarchy.</margin> **Oligarchy**, which is the rule of a few wealthy and powerful men. According to this, we have **Praetorian law**, which is also called "honorary law." The third regime <margin>Third: Democracy.</margin> is a **Democracy**, that is, popular power, whose laws are called **plebiscites**. Another regime is distinguished as **Tyranny**, but because of its corruption, no legal name is taken from this species. But the fourth form of government <margin>Fourth species of government.</margin> is a **Kingdom**. According to this, we take the species of laws called **constitutions of princes**. Regarding these, there is a title in the first book of the Digest: the first law of which states, "What pleases the Prince has the force of law." <margin>Aristotle.</margin> However, Aristotle seems to suggest something else from these, which he perhaps judged to be the best. And from this <margin>Isidore.</margin> (as Isidore records), laws were born which the elders enacted together with the common people. <margin>To the third argument.</margin> And by these points, the third argument is satisfied. For the differences between these laws are not discerned solely by the number of legislators, but rather by the different species of government.

Furthermore, the same reasoning does not apply to the division of laws into Roman, Athenian, Spartan, and so on. This distinction is not based on the specific nature of the laws themselves, but simply on their numerical distribution among different peoples.

<margin>The fourth condition of human law.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, what human law includes by its very nature is the organization of human morals and the restraint of various impulses of the soul. From this perspective, we derive the division of laws into the **Julian law on adultery**, the **Cornelian law on assassins** <note>original: "de Sica."; referring to the *Lex Cornelia de Sicariis et Veneficiis*, a Roman law against assassins and poisoners</note>, the **Aquilian law** <note>original: "Aquili."; the *Lex Aquilia*, which provided compensation to owners of property injured by someone's fault</note>, and others. Although these laws took their names from their authors, they do not differ solely for that reason (as was argued in the fourth objection <margin>To the fourth.</margin>); rather, they differ because of the distinct nature of the actions for which they were enacted. Thus, all the arguments are now resolved. ### QUESTION SIX,
#### On the power of human law.
##### Saint Thomas Aquinas, Part 1-2, Question 96.

### ARTICLE I.
#### Whether human law should be established in general terms.

Following the necessity, quality, and divisions of human law, we must now consider its power and efficacy. Beginning with its general nature, we first ask whether law should be established in general terms <note>original: "in communi"; meaning whether laws should apply to broad categories of people and actions rather than specific individuals</note>.

<margin>Argument for the negative side.</margin>
¶ The argument for the negative side is as follows. First, from the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the 5th book of his *Ethics*, chapter 7, where he says: "laws are also commanded concerning individual matters, such as performing sacrifices to **Brasidas**" <margin>Aristotle</margin> <note>Brasidas was a Spartan general; after his death, specific laws were passed to establish rituals in his honor</note>; he distinguishes this from things instituted by public decrees. From this, it is gathered that laws are placed not only in general terms, but also in specific instances. <margin>Argument 2</margin> ¶ Second, laws concern our actions, which occur in specific, individual circumstances; <margin>Argument 3</margin> therefore, they ought to be enacted for specific cases. ¶ Third, law is the measure of our actions; and a measure, as taught in the 1st book of the *Metaphysics*, must be extremely certain. However, our actions are slippery and uncertain; therefore, it would be more fitting for laws to be decreed for individual cases rather than in general terms. <margin>Pomponius</margin> ¶ To the contrary is **Pomponius the Jurist** in the Digest, in the section on laws, where he says: "It is necessary that laws be established for those things which happen frequently, that is, for those things

<column-break/>

which usually occur in practice; but not for those things which happen contrary to expectation or unexpectedly." This point is emphasized in the three laws that follow it.

<margin>Single conclusion responding to the question.</margin>
The response is easily established through a single conclusion. **Law must be established in general terms.** This means it should not command, "If this or that specific person kills," or "for this specific reason," or "with this specific circumstance, let them be executed." Rather, it should speak in general: "**Whoever kills.**" For those accidental circumstances cannot be encompassed by law, but must later be weighed through **prudence** <note>original: "prudentiam"; the practical wisdom used by a judge or ruler to apply a general law to a specific case</note>. Indeed, just as in theoretical matters—as **Plato** commanded—one must rest in the "species" <note>general categories</note>, because there is no true science of individual things (which are fleeting), but only experience; so too in practical matters, there can be no law concerning the individual things that happen by chance, but only prudence. Furthermore, the conclusion is proven <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> both from the purpose of the law and from other things connected to it. For it was already asserted in the previous question that a law must be enacted for the **common utility** of the citizens. It follows, then, that such a law must be created as is expedient for the common good. Now, the common good consists of many things, regarding both persons and the variety of affairs. There are, I say, those who are compelled to obey the laws: the old and the young, the powerful and the weak, the wise and the ignorant—to whom many situations can occur. Therefore, the lawgiver must provide for all of these; which cannot be done otherwise than by placing the law in general terms. Furthermore, a law is established (as **Augustine** says in the 1st book of *The City of God*) not to last for a short time, <margin>Augustine</margin> but for long ages. For the republic suffers heavy damage from the frequent changing of laws; but if law were placed concerning individual cases, it would have to be changed immediately whenever those cases changed. From the present conclusion, that axiom is derived: **Law does not look at those things which happen rarely, but at those which occur for the most part.** This is what the Jurist [Pomponius] pronounces in the words cited.

<margin>The first sin of those who help individual cases with peculiar laws.</margin>
¶ Therefore, those who strive to meet individual cases with specific laws sin gravely against this nature of laws. There exists (to give an example) a law concerning **bribery** <note>original: "ambitu"; referring to the illegal canvassing or bribery for political or academic office</note>; namely, by which candidates are prohibited from soliciting and grasping for office. But to make this wall firmer, it is fortified by another law: namely, that no one may go to their houses, that they themselves may not walk about, that no one may speak with another. If a student acts against this, let him be deprived of his right to vote; if the candidate himself does so, let him also lose the right to seek the **Chair** <note>original: "Cathedram"; a professorship or high academic position</note>. In truth, this is more than is just; it is to entangle human souls.

<margin>The second sin of these people.</margin>
Secondly, they likewise offend against this same doctrine, who

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence on the word "who" (qui), which is also the catchword for the following page.</meta>

<summary>Soto argues that human laws must be written as general principles (in communi) rather than for specific individuals or rare events, as the law serves the common good over long periods. He criticizes over-regulation, such as excessive rules against bribery, which he believes "entangle human souls" unnecessarily.</summary>

# Question VI of the First Book

<margin>
Those who, in establishing laws, look only to what is currently present.
</margin>
...those who, in establishing laws, do not look toward future times any further than what is presently before them. There are those, I say, who—considering only a small number of people burning with <term>charity</term><note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to intense religious devotion or love for God, often found in the early stages of a religious movement.</note>—burden religious families with a heavy weight of laws. When later generations are unable to bear these, they shake them from their necks. Therefore, the truest doctrine is that laws ought to be established in a general sense, so that they can be adapted over many different times to the qualities of various persons and circumstances.

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>
Regarding the first argument, the response is that three levels of human <term>precepts</term><note>Commands or rules of conduct.</note> and prohibitions are distinguished at present. 
<margin>The first level.</margin>
The first is entirely general: namely, when statutes are created not for the sake of any specific individual, but for the good of the entire <term>republic</term><note>The "commonwealth" or the community as a whole.</note>. These are properly called "laws," such as: *He who commits murder shall be punished by death*; *Magistrates shall not be appointed for a price*; *Judges shall not sell their judgments for a price*. These are laws in the strict sense.
<margin>The second level.</margin>
The second level consists of things granted for the sake of an individual person. These are not called "laws" so much as <term>privileges</term> or <term>dispensations</term><note>A "privilege" is a "private law" for one person; a "dispensation" is an exemption from a general law.</note>. An example is when a king grants the rights of nobility to a soldier who has fought bravely in war, or when the Pope imparts true privileges to those giving alms to support the war against the Turks. However, this must be understood clearly.
<margin>
A true law can be established for a specific person.
</margin>
A "true law" can indeed be established for the sake of an individual person, such as the laws regarding Feast Days which we celebrate solemnly in honor of the Holy Virgin or any other Saint; for these are proclaimed in common to the entire people. Privileges, however, do not carry such an appearance of universality; otherwise, they would take on the form of a law. An example [of a general law] is one that exempts the entire nobility from paying taxes, or the general rule that *He who has served as a soldier for so many years shall be a retired veteran.* 
<margin>The last level.</margin>
In the final level are the sentences of judges (which, as said above) are not laws, but rather the applications of laws to specific cases.
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The response to the second argument is very simple. For since a law is a "measure," there should not be as many laws as there are actions. Just as a craftsman uses a single ruler to arrange many stones, and we measure many quantities with the same yardstick, so we regulate many actions with one common law.
<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Regarding the third argument, we admit that human laws cannot possess as much certainty as exists in <term>natural law</term><note>Universal moral principles thought to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note>. However, the same degree of certainty is not to be demanded in all things, as
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle says in the first book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, it is enough for human laws if they are right in the majority of cases, even if they occasionally fail.

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE II.

### Whether it belongs to human law to restrain all vices.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or authority figure, in a classical architectural setting.</image-desc>

Now that we have seen that the general form of law is that it should be established for the community, it follows that we should look at its "latitude"—that is, whether all vices should be prohibited by human laws. An affirmative reason stands right at the threshold.
<margin>The first reason.</margin>
Truly, if laws (as Isidore taught above) were established by humans for this purpose:
<margin>Isidore.</margin>
that the audacity of the wicked might be restrained by fear of them, and since they cannot be restrained unless all vices are prohibited, it follows that all things ought to be forbidden by human laws.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ Secondly, since we have already heard from Aristotle that the purpose of the legislator is to make citizens good and studious—and this cannot happen unless men are restrained from all vices—it follows that laws should suppress all vices.
<margin>The third reason.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, human law (as has also been seen) is derived from natural law. All vices are contrary to natural law; therefore, all vices should be guarded against by human laws.
¶ On the contrary is Augustine in the first book of *On Free Choice of the Will*, where he says that human law permits many things and leaves them unpunished which are instead punished by Divine Providence.
<margin>Augustine.</margin>

The response to this question is very clear from custom and practice, and it consists of two conclusions.
<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The first is: Human laws do not prohibit all vices.
<margin>
The conclusion is supported by natural reason.
</margin>
It is supported by this natural reason: Law (as we repeatedly state) is a measure of human actions. A measure (as the Philosopher <note>A common medieval title for Aristotle.</note> testifies in the 10th book of the *Metaphysics*) must be "homogeneous"—that is, of the same nature as the things we are measuring. Indeed, we measure continuous quantities with a yardstick, a foot, or a span, which are themselves continuous quantities. We measure liquids and grains by the bushel, but weights by the pound; we observe this in every category. It follows, then, that the laws of men must be adapted to the human condition. This is what Isidore advised when he commanded that law ought to be "possible according to nature and according to the custom of the country." The human condition demands that laws not be punishers of vices with the utmost rigor; therefore, they should be established as such. Understand that our condition and character require this because laws [are given] to the whole multitude...

<summary>This page discusses why laws must be general rather than tailored to individuals and argues that human law should not attempt to prohibit every single vice, as it must be adapted to the limitations of the human condition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Question 6, specifically focusing on the scope of human law—what it should prohibit and what it should command. # Francisco Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

...the multitude are placed: for in a multitude, there are far more who are not imbued with the habits of virtue, but who struggle with depraved and corrupt passions, and who are therefore not strong enough to achieve the excellent works of the virtues. For those who are studious possess habits by which we acquire the faculty of acting diligently. Therefore, just as the same laws are not to be given to children as to men, nor to laypeople as to the religious, so too those things from which the whole multitude cannot abstain due to human fragility are not to be prohibited under the threat of punishment. Instead, only those things which the majority are able to avoid should be forbidden.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The latter conclusion: Human laws ought primarily to prohibit those vices, outrages, and crimes that disturb the republic's peace and quiet. Such are crimes that involve an injury to others: for instance, those against <term>commutative justice</term><note>Justice governing private transactions and the restoration of equality between individuals, such as paying back a debt or compensating for a loss.</note>, such as homicides, thefts, adulteries, frauds, snares, and other things of that kind.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Indeed, this tranquility and serenity of the republic is the target and goal of all who establish laws. In fact, other things are permitted to go unpunished so that these [worse crimes] may be avoided: namely, <term>meretricious acts</term><note>Prostitution; many medieval and early modern legal theorists argued for its tolerance as a "lesser evil" to prevent adultery or the rape of "honest" women.</note> are permitted to prevent adultery, and <term>usury</term><note>The practice of lending money at interest, which was often legally restricted or prohibited in this era.</note> to prevent thefts.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
Hence it follows that crimes and outrages are not punished more harshly in the republic because they are graver before God, but because they are more hostile to peace. For perjuries, which are worse than thefts, and blasphemies, which exceed homicides in their monstrosity, are not prohibited by capital punishment but are reserved for God’s chastisement. Nevertheless, those things which shake the substance of religion, such as <term>heresy</term><note>Holding beliefs contrary to official Church doctrine.</note> and <term>apostasy</term><note>The complete abandonment or renunciation of a religious faith.</note>, as well as those things which infect the ears by their foulness—even if they are not injurious to men—are nonetheless to be punished more sharply.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ To the first argument it is replied that while <term>Isidore</term><note>original: "Isidorus." Referring to St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar whose "Etymologiae" was a standard reference for law and definitions.</note> says that the audacity of men must be restrained by fear of laws, he explains himself: that injuries which impure and audacious men inflict against the justice of the republic ought to be prohibited by laws. However, he does not judge it necessary that all faults into which the weakness of the human race falls must be punished by the force of those same laws.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument it is replied that men are to be enticed and promoted toward virtue in their own way—namely, so that by moving from their imperfection toward perfection step by step, they may be advanced. For this reason, those excellent duties which are possible only for upright men who have progressed in virtue ought not to be instituted by laws which must be common to everyone. Rather...

<column-break/>

...only those things which even the imperfect can approach and endure should be instituted, so that once they are imbued with these easier matters, they may be strong enough to ascend to other difficult things of their own accord. And it should not happen that, while they are hedged in by the excessive narrowness of laws, they break out into worse behaviors.

<margin>Proverbs 30.</margin>
For (as is read in Proverbs 30) *he who wrings the nose too hard brings forth blood.*

<margin>Matthew 9.</margin>
And in Matthew 9: *If new wine*—that is, difficult commands burning with heat—*is put into old wineskins*—that is, into impure men torn by corrupt passions—*the wine is poured out.* This means the precepts are held in contempt, and out of that contempt, the wicked break out into worse things.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument it is replied that although human law is derived from natural law, it does not have to match it perfectly in every detail. Therefore (as <term>Augustine</term><note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), a central figure in Western theology and philosophy.</note> says in the place cited), because it does not forbid all things, the things it does forbid and command are not to be disapproved of.

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether human law commands the acts of all virtues.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a seated scholar or figure within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>
AS we have looked at the prohibition of evils, so too must we see how far human law extends regarding the command of virtues—namely, whether it ought to command the acts of all virtues.

<margin>Argument for the negative side.</margin>
And it is argued on the negative side: The duties of virtues and the works of vices are opposites. Human law does not prohibit all vices; therefore, it does not command all studious actions.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, the work of virtue proceeds from virtue. But virtue is the *end* of the law; for as we said, the legislator's goal is to make citizens good and studious. The precepts of the law, however, are not the end, but the means to achieving that end. Therefore, the works of virtues do not fall under the precept of the law.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ In the opposite direction is the authority of the <term>Philosopher</term><note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle.</note> in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 1, where he says: laws dictate concerning all things for the common utility of all. Wherefore, he says, the law commands both to do those things which belong to a brave man, and likewise those which belong to temperance, and those which belong to a mild man, and similarly in the other virtues and vices, commanding some things and forbidding others.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ TO the present question, just as to the preceding one, the response is given in two conclusions. The first is: There is no species of virtue concerning whose acts human law does not command some.

<margin>Aristotle. Plato on laws.</margin>
This is the conclusion not only of Aristotle in the place cited, but also of Plato in Dialogue 1 of *Laws*.

<summary>Soto argues that human law should only prohibit vices that harm the peace of the republic and command only those virtues achievable by the average person, rather than imposing a standard of perfection that would lead to rebellion. He also establishes that while law doesn't command every act of virtue, every type of virtue has at least some acts that fall under legal jurisdiction for the common good.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question 6, "On Human Law," specifically investigating the extent to which human law can and should command acts of virtue. It follows the previous discussion on which vices the law ought to prohibit.</meta>

-> # Book One, Question VI. <-

...concerning laws. Where he <note>Referring to Plato in his work *The Laws*.</note> says those who discuss the divine republic should be thought to have looked not at a small part of virtue—and especially not the lower part—but at universal virtue itself, and to have sought laws through <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> each of its species. The reason that nature teaches us, and which Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto's scholastic framework.</note> clarifies, is this: The species of virtues are distinguished by the nature of their objects. However, there is no object of virtue that cannot be referred to the common good, although very often the same thing also refers to a private good. For instance, things belonging to <term>fortitude</term><note>The virtue of courage, especially in the face of danger.</note> can be applied both to the protection of one's own person or a friend, and again to the defense of the republic. And things belonging to <term>temperance</term><note>The virtue of moderation, particularly regarding physical pleasures.</note> relate to the good health of a private man, and again so that the citizen might become more fit for the contemplation of those things which lead to the public good. It is similar in the rest. Since, therefore, every human law (as has been said) is established for the common utility of mortals, it follows that there is no species of virtue about whose actions human law does not command. But if faith perhaps suggests some private matter, it will be answered to you below. 

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The latter conclusion: Human laws do not command concerning every single act of every single virtue. Thus, they command concerning some acts of individual virtues, yet not concerning every act of all of them. 

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
As if, for example, we said: in the matter of fortitude, human law commands defending the republic, even with the danger of death; but it does not command so defending a friend; rather, it leaves this to the law of nature. In the matter of temperance, the Church commands fasts on certain days; but it does not command eating moderately during the rest of the year, which the law of nature does. In the matter of religion, it commands dedicating certain days to the Saints and attending sacred rites; but not concerning other free thoughts. In the matter of justice and liberality, it commands in grave necessity both that parents nourish children according to their status, and sometimes children vice versa for parents. Outside of those cases, it remits the rest to the law of nature and divine law concerning the honor to be deferred to parents. In sum, human law commands only those duties which are referred to the common good: either by themselves and directly, such as putting on arms for a public war; or indirectly (as they say), such as those which pertain to good discipline through which citizens are instructed toward the good of justice and peace. 

<margin>Question.</margin>
You ask, therefore: what if there were some species of virtue which could in no way be referred to the public 

<column-break/>

good? It is answered that there is <margin>Solution.</margin> absolutely none of which at least some act cannot at some time be referred to that same good. Nor does this general conclusion embrace only the moral virtues, but truly the intellectual virtues as well. For by human laws, both arts are commanded in the republic and the contemplations of the sciences. 

<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ But truly, if the matter stands so that the conclusion also encompasses the intellectual virtues, an argument immediately emerges that it is not universally true. For the object of the supreme intellectual virtue in which our happiness is placed—since it is God Himself by His essence—is referable to no other common good. 

<margin>Response.</margin>
It is answered, however, that although God is referred to no other end in Himself—because He is the universal end of all things and the supreme end—nevertheless, insofar as He is reached and possessed by us through the <term>facial vision</term><note>original: "faciali visione"; this refers to the "Beatific Vision," the direct seeing of God "face to face" in the afterlife.</note>, it is indeed referred both to our happiness and beatitude, and also to His own glory, which becomes more illustrious in the blessed through that same vision.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is answered that just as human law does not prohibit every single vicious act, so it does not command every single virtuous act. But there is a difference: as far as virtues are concerned, there is no species of which it does not command some act; however, as far as vices are concerned, nothing prevents there being some species of which it prohibits no act. And for that reason, in the preceding article, it was answered negatively regarding universality, but in the present article, affirmatively. For it prohibits no "joking" lie or "helpful" lie, nor any simple fornication, unless it has a circumstance that changes its species in the genus of morality, such as adultery or incest. 

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is answered that an act of virtue is spoken of in two ways: in one way, regarding its substance—because, namely, it is according to the norm of reason, whether it proceeds from a <term>habit</term><note>original: "habitus"; in scholastic philosophy, a habit is a stable disposition that allows a person to act with ease and pleasure.</note> or is done by one who is not endowed with the habit. In the other way, because it proceeds from a habit, and thus is done promptly and with delight. Law, therefore, commands nothing concerning habits, but concerning acts, which are the means for acquiring a habit. It commands, I say, to fight for the republic, caring nothing whether it is done from habit; acting from habit, however, is not a precept of the law, but the goal. For by commanding us to work, the lawmaker intends to engender habits in us by which we are made studious <note>In this context, "studious" means one who is habitually virtuous or diligent in goodness.</note>.

<summary>Soto argues that human law can command acts from any category of virtue (moral or intellectual) provided they serve the common good, though it does not command every possible virtuous act. He distinguishes between the outward substance of a virtuous deed, which the law requires, and the internal habit of virtue, which is the law's ultimate goal but not its direct command.</summary>
