### ARTICLE IV.

*Whether human law imposes a necessity upon subjects in the court of conscience.*

<note>The "court of conscience" (forum conscientiæ) refers to a person’s internal moral standing before God, rather than their external standing before a human judge.</note>

HAVING seen the extent of human law’s reach, it remains to see its power: specifically, whether it reaches as far as the conscience, and whether it has the power to bind it. <margin>Argument 1.</margin> An argument for the negative side is immediately obvious. The power of an inferior does not reach as far as the court of a superior where it might bind his judgment. Human law-making power is inferior to divine power; therefore, it cannot bind consciences in the <margin>Argument 2.</margin> divine court. ¶ Second, it is argued that if this were true, it would follow that a father of a household could likewise decree laws for his children that would bind their consciences in the court of God. For just as we are commanded to obey superiors, so too must we honor our parents, which includes obedience. However, this seems contrary to what was said above: namely, that laws cannot be established without the power of coercion, which a father <margin>Argument 3.</margin> does not possess. ¶ Third, the judgment of conscience depends on divine mandates, which are the signs and evidence of the divine will. However, it happens that human laws conflict with divine ones, according to <margin>Matthew</margin> that passage in Matthew 15: <note>original: "irritum fecistis mandatum Dei propter traditiones vestras"</note> "You have made the commandment of God void for the sake of your traditions." Therefore, not every <margin>Argument 4.</margin> human law binds in the court of conscience. ¶ Indeed, a fourth argument is made. The sentence of a judge (as we said above) is a certain application of the law; however, such a sentence does not always bind, even if it is just in the external court—for instance, when a judge condemns an innocent person based on the evidence presented and proven, though it is contrary to the truth. In fact, sometimes the condemned person cannot obey the sentence at all: as in the case of a man who secretly married one woman and publicly married another. In such a case, he is justly and legally ordered to render his marriage debt to the second, and yet he ought to die rather than comply; for it would be fornication. Therefore, even a just law does not bind in <margin>Argument 5.</margin> conscience. ¶ Fifth, human laws often tend to inflict false accusations and, subsequently, injury upon men, according to <margin>Isaiah</margin> that passage in Isaiah 10: "Woe to those who decree unrighteous laws, and the writers who have written injustice, to oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the humble of my people." It is lawful for anyone to repel the oppression <margin>Peter</margin> of tyranny. ¶ On the contrary is the Apostle Peter in his first Letter, chapter 2. Where, after he warned all Christian families to be subject to their

<column-break/>

masters, not only the good ones but also the difficult ones, because such was the will of God, he adds: "For this is grace, if for the sake of conscience toward God a man endures sorrows, suffering unjustly." By saying "for the sake of conscience toward God," he implies that the conscience is bound by civil laws.

This is a question in which there is somewhat more doubt and difficulty than in those preceding. To understand it, one must distinguish between just and unjust laws. Therefore, the question is answered with three conclusions. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> First: Human law, whether civil or canon <note>Canon law is the internal legal system of the Catholic Church.</note>, if it be just, thrives with authority and is powerful in its ability to bind the <margin>Proof.</margin> consciences of subjects. This is proven. All human law (as has been said) is derived from the eternal law through the natural law, according to that passage in Proverbs 8: <note>original: "Per me Reges regnant, & legum conditores iusta decernunt"</note> "Through me kings reign, and the makers of laws decree just things." Here (as we noted above when making distinctions), the first part designates the power of reigning granted to princes by God, according to <margin>Paul</margin> Paul: "All power is from the Lord God." The second part designates the wisdom through which they establish laws and put them into execution. Therefore, from that same eternal law, the power is subsequently derived to these same laws, so that they are binding in conscience before God Himself. <margin>All its causes must coincide for the justice of a law.</margin> The justice of a law is judged based on all its "causes": namely, the final, efficient, material, and formal causes. By "final," I mean that it is established for the common good; for the same difference (as we have said) that exists between a tyrant and a king is also recognized between laws. Namely, <margin><insert>Alfonso de Castro, Book 1, On the power of penal law, 542.</insert></margin> that which is passed for the common utility is held to be just; but that which is for a private interest is tyrannical. <margin><insert>Law concerning... in ecclesiastical matters... on restitution... on judgments.</insert></margin> Second, from the side of the agent: specifically, that he who passed it did not exceed his own authority. Third, from the side of the matter: Because, just as things that are good for the time and place ought not to be prohibited, so also evil works are not the proper subject matter of a command. Fourth, from the side of the form: For <margin><insert>The law for the proposed... elegantly... on the immunity of churches.</insert></margin> since law is a rule, it ought to shine with such rectitude and equity that it maintains such a proportion toward the citizens in both honors and burdens as they themselves have to the body of the republic. For they are like parts in a whole; and for this reason, just as duties are divided by nature among the parts, so also burdens are to be commanded of each according to the proportion of the citizens' means, and honors are to be bestowed according to the proportion of their dignity. Therefore, a law that is perfect in these points will be binding. <margin>Second Conclusion.</margin> ¶ Second conclusion: An unjust human law does not bind in the court of conscience. This conclusion is well known from what precedes. For an unjust law, since...

<summary>Soto explores whether human laws have moral authority over the soul. He concludes that "just" laws—those serving the common good and issued by proper authority—bind a person’s conscience because they derive their power from God’s eternal law.</summary>

-> # Book One: Question VI <-

<margin>From what source the injustice of a law is to be weighed.</margin>
Since a law is not right, it cannot be a rule, and therefore it is not truly a law; moreover, that which is not a law binds no one. The injustice of a law is weighed in two ways. First, if it is contrary to the human good: for instance, if for some reason it opposes the four causes previously mentioned—namely, through a defect of its proper end, its author <note>the "agent"</note>, its matter, or its form. In the second way, a law is unjust if it is contrary to the divine good. And although nothing can be contrary to God except by reason of the matter or the other aforementioned causes, this distinction is nevertheless noted so that a path may be cleared for the third conclusion, which is as follows.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Those laws which oppose only the human good, although they do not bind in conscience of their own accord, they sometimes bind by reason of **scandal** <note>In this context, "scandal" refers to an action that might lead others into spiritual ruin or cause civil disorder and rebellion.</note>: however, those which impiously repugn the divine good bind in no way whatsoever; rather, they must be openly resisted. The first part is clear: for in matters that do not display manifest tyranny, it is not possible to resist the powerful without scandal; and therefore they are to be tolerated for a time until they may be led to a sounder mind through a gentler path. For the Christian counsel in Matthew 5 pertains to this.

<margin>Matthew.</margin>
"Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him another two: and if anyone takes away your tunic, give him your cloak as well." But truly, if tyrants were to lead us by their laws toward idolatry, or bar us from our sacraments, or drive us toward other customs or rites contrary to the faith, no scandal should be feared; rather, it would be most grave if we did not resist them immediately, even at the cost of our lives. For this is the legitimate meaning of that passage in Acts 5.

<margin>Acts 5.</margin>
"We must obey God rather than men." For so Peter responded to the high priest who commanded that they should not preach in the name of Christ. By these formulas of injustice, arranged according to the art <note>referring to legal science</note>, all those cases are encompassed which the interpreters of the law multiply into twelve or more; as can be seen both among other compilers of "Summas" and in the work of Sylvester under the word "law," section 9.

<margin>Sylvester. Question.</margin>
<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ However, so that these matters may be more accurately aimed, we must first examine the first conclusion to see at what level of certainty it is held. To this it is answered that the conclusion is not established with as sublime or firm a degree of certainty regarding civil laws as it is regarding ecclesiastical laws; for this reason, the fourth conclusion is applied specifically to ecclesiastical laws—most especially those of the Pope and the Councils.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ It must be confessed as a matter of Catholic faith that ecclesiastical and holy laws bind in the court of conscience, by their very nature, under the penalty of mortal sin <note>original: "reatu mortalis maculæ," literally the "guilt of a mortal stain."</note>.

<margin>Waldensians.</margin>
For there crept in long ago the error of the Waldensians <note>A medieval spiritual movement later declared heretical for rejecting church hierarchy.</note>, and after that the error of John Wycliffe, and finally that of their legitimate heir, Luther: namely, that there is no power in either the Supreme Pontiff or the whole Church to establish either articles of faith or laws of conduct.

<column-break/>

<margin>John Wycliffe. Luther.</margin>
For so his twenty-seventh article holds among those presented to Pope Leo: "Therefore (as they say) only those mandates bind in conscience which are explicitly set forth in the Gospel."

<margin>Heretics are refuted by the oracles of Scripture.</margin>
There exist, however, most clear testimonies by which these men are refuted. Such as that in Luke 10: "He who hears you, hears me: and he who despises you, despises me."

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
And Matthew 18: "If he sins... tell the Church; if he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector."

<margin>Matthew 18.</margin>
Where it is most certain that the jurisdiction of the Church is designated. Likewise: "Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven." And John 20: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth: as the living Father sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained."

<margin>John 20.</margin>
<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
What is more evident than that (as Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence.</note> says) the power which Christ himself had brought from the Father was there conferred upon the Apostles and subsequently upon the Church? Especially since "retaining sins" is the function of one who has the power to bind.

<margin>Deuteronomy 17.</margin>
And in Deuteronomy 17, a law exists stating that he who would not obey the priest should die the death; yet no one is punished with death except for a grave mortal sin. Therefore, by even stronger reasoning under the New Law, which Christ instituted and the Holy Spirit governs, the same authority must be confessed. And those words in Acts 15 openly show this.

<margin>Acts 15.</margin>
"It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than these necessary things." In truth, since the Church understands its laws to bind us under the penalty of mortal guilt, and since Christ promised His care and the governance of the Holy Spirit (whom He promised to send from the Father for this very purpose, so that the Church might not be deceived in such arduous matters), it is gathered with most certain faith that the Church is not deserted in this, but prevails with a certain authority to bind.

<margin>Reasoning against the heretics.</margin>
¶ Finally, this is proven by the reasoning of the **end** <note>the purpose or goal of the law</note>. For truly, since the status of mortals is never fixed, but varies shiftily according to the diversity of times and places, Christ would not have sufficiently provided for the Church in perpetuity through the laws He personally established, unless He had left power in the Church to establish new ones according to the time, which would be able to bind in His own divine court.

<margin>Council of Vienne.</margin>
This heresy was already justly condemned in the Council of Vienne (as is found in the Clementines under *ad nostram* regarding heretics), in the Council of Constance, and thereafter by Leo X.

<margin>Council of Constance.</margin>
<margin>Leo X.</margin>
¶ But truly, regarding civil power, it is not so—

<summary>This page argues that unjust laws do not bind the conscience unless resisting them would cause "scandal" (social harm), while asserting that Church laws possess a divine authority to bind the conscience under penalty of mortal sin, contrary to the claims of Wycliffe and Luther.</summary>

### F. D. Soto, *On Justice and Law*

This conclusion is supported by strong evidence, yet there are several arguments to the contrary.
<margin>Argument 1</margin>
First, binding someone to "guilt" in the court of conscience—since it wounds the soul—seems to be a spiritual power, such as that which exists in the Church, rather than a power belonging to civil authority.
<margin>Argument 2</margin>
Second, civil power does not extend so far as to be able to remit <note>forgive or take away</note> sins; it follows, therefore, that it should not be able to cast someone into sin. It might be deemed unfair that one who lacks the power to "loosen" (forgive) should have the power to "bind" (condemn), whereas the Church has the power to do both.
<margin>Argument 3</margin>
Third, the immediate goal of civil power is the temporary state of the republic; therefore, it does not extend its reach to eternal punishments.
<margin>Argument 4</margin>
Fourth, a power that cannot punish a guilty person with eternal pain in the court of conscience cannot bind them under the weight of such guilt. Civil power can impose no penalty in the court of conscience, unlike spiritual power, which decrees those penalties in the Sacraments which, if not paid here, will be suffered in the next life.
<margin>Final argument</margin>
Lastly, it is argued to uncover the very nerve and core of the matter: either the obligation to sin rests on the will of the Prince who passes the law, or it follows from the very nature of the law regardless of his will. If you grant the first, it would mean a civil law never binds under the weight of sin, because there is no law that explicitly states such a condition. If, however, you grant the second—that the obligation follows the nature of the law—it would follow that a Prince could create no law that does *not* bind under the weight of sin. This is hard to believe, especially since in religious orders—particularly our own <note>the Dominicans</note>—there are many rules that do not bind us under the weight of sin.

<margin>Civil laws bind in conscience.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, despite these objections, the conclusion put forward in the first place according to the mind of St. Thomas retains its unshakable truth even in civil laws: namely, that they bind unto guilt, and by their nature, unto **mortal** <term>mortal sin: a grave sin that causes the death of the soul and separation from God</term> guilt.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
Truly, just as it was for the ecclesiastical community, so too for the civil community: the power of self-governance was necessary by reason of its goal, including the power to establish laws for the variety of times and regions. Although this power (as will be discussed more fully in Book 4 under the title of "Dominion") flows from God differently than ecclesiastical power does. For Christ conferred the latter upon the Church through Himself by divine law; but the former descends through the law of nature, by which any republic has the authority to administer itself, which it can then confer upon kings. Therefore, because the civil republic is also the family of God, it follows that just as one who harms a neighbor against these laws is held guilty before the neighbor's tribunal, so also is one who is helpful to neighbors according to those same laws

<column-break/>

deemed worthy of reward. Thus, the same applies to those who either violate or observe human laws established through the power granted by God. And this is what it means to "bind in conscience."
<margin>Confirmation of the same conclusion.</margin>
The same conclusion is further confirmed: to act against the law of the Prince is a moral evil; therefore, it is a sin before God. The premise is well-known: if a law is just, it stands as a rule of reason; to overstep the line of reason is a deviation <note>obliquitas</note>, and consequently a sin. The logic is clear because whatever is morally evil is a sin, as St. Thomas excellently argued in the *Summa Theologica* (Part 1-2, Question 21).
<margin>Another reason for the same.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, human law is derived from natural law (as has been said), which establishes a general virtue in a specific form—for example, the general idea of "peace" is applied to the specific rule of "not using weapons at night." Therefore, human laws bind in the court of conscience.
<margin>Final argument.</margin>
Finally, a concluding argument is applied specifically to civil law. Although the Prince's immediate goal is the peaceful state of the republic, the supreme goal is eternal happiness, toward which that temporal goal tends. Therefore, he can bind in that supreme court through his laws, by the virtue granted to him from heaven. Let us conclude, then, that while it is not manifest heresy to deny this authority and vigor to civil laws (as it would be for ecclesiastical laws), it would certainly be reckless and against the consensus of the most renowned doctors.
<margin>The opinion of Jean Gerson.</margin>
¶ However, Jean Gerson <note>a famous 14th-century French theologian and reformer</note>, a man otherwise of great renown, forces us back into a dispute over whether human laws of this kind bind through themselves insofar as they are human—that is, insofar as they are established by power granted to men—or whether they bind only insofar as they are reinforced by divine law. In his treatise *On the Spiritual Life of the Soul* (Lecture 4), he maintains a singular opinion on this matter: namely, that no law, neither civil nor ecclesiastical, nor even natural law, has the power to bind in conscience unto guilt, but only divine law binds. Human law binds only insofar as it is an interpreter of the divine. This opinion differs from the common view not only in name (as some think), but certainly in a very wide sense. I say he does not merely mean that human laws bind because such powers are granted to men by God (for we admit this); rather, he says that no created power granted by God has the power to bind under the weight of sin, but only to explain and declare divine right. Thus, according to him, the Pope, in commanding annual confession, does not bind by his own power, but merely declares divine right; because, he says, even before the Pope’s decree, the law of God required confessing once a year.

<summary>This page discusses whether civil (secular) laws have the moral authority to bind a person's conscience, concluding that breaking a just law is a sin before God because civil authority derives from natural law. It also introduces and critiquies the dissenting view of Jean Gerson, who argued that only divine law can truly bind the soul.</summary>

### First Book, Question VI. 53

...but because it was unknown to us, ignorance excused us. In the same way, he says, unless fasting during Lent <note>Quadragesima</note> were already divine law, the Pope's precept would not be binding unto guilt; but because such a law existed, the fact that it was declared through the Pope binds us. And by a much more forceful reason (as he judges), the laws of princes, unless they are declarations of divine law previously unknown, in no way bind a person to guilt <note>original: "ad culpam", meaning the state of having committed a sin</note>. 

Just as the instruction of a doctor who orders a bedridden man to abstain from harmful food is not binding unto guilt in itself; rather, the sick man incurs guilt because he transgresses the divine prohibition against homicide <note>self-harm or suicide</note>, which the doctor merely "declares" is being perpetrated by the eating of such food. And in this order, he [Gerson] infers as many as fourteen "wonderful" corollaries. In short, he maintains that just as the Church cannot create new articles of faith—but only explain those that lay hidden in Holy Scripture—so too it cannot create new laws. Indeed, he even says the natural law does not bind in any way except by explaining divine law. 

Behold the opinion of Gerson, understood by very few, and therefore believed by some. <margin>Gerson's motive.</margin> His reasoning is this: because just as no one but God alone can bestow grace, so no one can take it away; and therefore, no one can bind a person to the guilt through which grace is removed. <margin>Another reason for the same.</margin> Likewise, just as the Church cannot make laws concerning internal acts—because it cannot punish them—so because it cannot inflict the eternal punishment owed to guilt, it follows that it lacks the power to bind a person to guilt. And for this reason, he says, Augustine defined sin as being "a word or deed, etc., against the law of God," <note>original: "contra legem Dei"</note> namely, because it does not happen that one sins against any other law.

<margin>Gerson's position differs little from the Lutheran heresy.</margin> Yet, if it is permissible to speak thus of a Catholic Doctor, his view differs very little from the Lutheran heresy recently challenged, which takes all power of making laws away from the Church. Indeed, the Lutherans hold up Gerson as their patron against Catholics, although Gerson phrases this more mildly by saying the Pope can "declare" divine laws. <margin>First argument against Gerson.</margin> Furthermore, to say that before Ecclesiastical sanctions, annual confession and Lenten abstinence were matters of divine law is certainly a baseless assertion, even a rash one, because it is in no way persuasive. <margin>Second argument.</margin> There was indeed a commandment of confession, but the prescription of the specific time was entrusted to the wisdom of the Church. Regarding this, when the Church commands this or that under penalty of excommunication—for instance, to appear in court and similar things—who would dare say that was already divine law, except for the fact that such power of compulsion was given to the Pope by God? <margin>Third argument.</margin> Likewise, in John 20, Christ first said: "All power is given to me," <margin>Final argument.</margin> so that in adding, "Receive the Holy Spirit," it would be understood that he was conferring that same power upon the Church. And finally, how 

<column-break/>

could the Pope be the Vicar of Christ unless he could establish laws for his household and urgent precepts? 

It is therefore more certain than certainty itself that there exists in the Church a power not only for *declaring* divine law, but for *founding* human law. It is called "human" because it proceeds from human power, even though that power was received from God. For just as trees and animals receive the power of generation from God, yet nonetheless the creatures themselves generate and act through their own power; likewise, men through their own power establish laws which did not bind before. They bind specifically because they were established by men, as Aristotle says in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 7. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Now truly, who would deny that the law of nature binds of itself?

<margin>Almain.</margin> Jacques Almain, in his *Question on the Power of the Church*, chapter 12, concedes that Ecclesiastical power can bind to mortal sin because the Pope is the Vicar of Christ; however, he denies this for civil power, except in Gerson’s manner <note>i.e., only when the civil law mirrors a divine law</note>. Nevertheless, it is also most true regarding civil power, as has been explained and demonstrated above.

<margin>To Gerson's first argument.</margin> Hence, it is easy to respond to Gerson's arguments and those we have added. For although God alone bestows grace, He Himself does not take it away, but we do through our crimes; and therefore, nothing prevents men from establishing laws by their own institution, the transgressors of which fall from His grace because they did not obey His ministers. For that reason, though men cannot inflict eternal punishment, He Himself, as the supreme judge of all, inflicts it.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin> Nor does it stand in the way that civil power does not extend to the remission of sins: for there are different ministries of God, as Paul says. Where Augustine said sin is against the law of God, he implied the "eternal law," from which all laws are derived, even human ones; he thus encompassed all laws under one very broad name. <margin>To the final argument.</margin> To understand the other argument—namely, how the laws of princes bind to guilt, whether by their own will or by the nature of the law—the distinction between Ecclesiastical and Civil power must be noted. <margin>Distinction between Ecclesiastical and Civil power.</margin> For Ecclesiastical Prelates, because they are judges of spiritual matters, can establish laws: not only by determining works into specific types of virtue or vice, but also by discerning between venial and mortal sin, and even decreeing the transgression of their law to be a mortal crime. Secular princes, however, are unable to define that—namely, whether their laws are to be kept under penalty of venial or mortal guilt—but they only establish works as being in the category of virtue or vice. Whether the transgression or omission [of a secular law] brings mortal stain upon the transgressor...

### F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right

<margin>Question.</margin>
...whether it weighs upon the transgressor must be examined from the nature of the matter. Let us say, for example: The King commands that in a time of famine, grain is not to be exported from the kingdom, or in a time of imminent war, that arms be taken up. He has established those works specifically under the virtue of obedience: and the second specifically under the virtue of fortitude. And because these matters are of great importance, it is a mortal sin <note>original: "mortale", a grave sin that separates the soul from God</note> not to comply at that time. However, if he commands that one should not ride mules, or not wear silk—which from that point begins to be a virtue of temperance—or not to carry arms—which is then a virtue of peace—if these matters are of little importance, the disobedience will be no more than a venial sin <note>original: "venialis", a lesser sin that does not destroy the relationship with God</note>. ¶ But another superior objection remains to be solved: namely, that in such a case a Prince could not make laws that do not bind unto guilt <note>original: "ad culpam", meaning the state of sin</note>; which is false, since such laws are in use in religious orders. However, the logical consequence is denied. But you may now ask for the sign by which one must distinguish which law binds 
<margin>The opinion of the legal experts.</margin>
unto guilt, and which does not. There are some among the interpreters of the law who say that laws to which a penalty is attached do not bind unto guilt; this, however, will be rejected immediately in the next article.
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Furthermore, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas</note>, in the matter regarding fasting, says it is not sufficiently clear that the law of fasting binds unto mortal sin: because it was not enacted with that specific addition "under the penalty of mortal guilt." Here he suggests that a law which does not explain this does not bind unto guilt.
<margin>The error of Cajetan.</margin>
Furthermore (unless I am mistaken), he is most seriously deceived in this. For laws are never customarily issued with such an addition as, "We command this under the penalty of mortal or venial guilt." Instead, that must be weighed from the nature and gravity of the act. Therefore, the most faithful rule is:
<margin>A beautiful rule.</margin>
Every law which is issued absolutely—that is, which does not explain the contrary—binds unto guilt, either venial or mortal, according to the 
<margin>The reason for the rule.</margin>
value of the act. And the reason is clear: because the law brings with it a precept of obedience; and obedience is a virtue in itself, and disobedience is a sin. From this it follows that whoever wishes to enact a law, whether they be secular Princes or Ecclesiastical superiors, which does not bind unto guilt, they must explain that fact. No other sign can be established. Proof of this is found in our own constitutions <note>Soto refers to the Constitutions of the Dominican Order</note>: in the heading of which it is stated: "Our Rule and constitutions do not bind us to guilt but to punishment <note>original: "non obligant nos ad culpam sed ad poenam"</note>, except on account of a command or contempt." This is indeed proof that, unless that addition were made, 
<margin>A final doubt.</margin>
the law could not fail to bind unto guilt. ¶ However, a final doubt remains at the end of the question. Whether human laws are able to bind under the penalty of a lethal stain <note>mortal sin</note> to such an extent that 

<column-break/>

death must even be undergone before the law is violated, whether by omission or transgression. It 
<margin>The reason for doubting.</margin>
appears that such power does not reside in human legislators, since they are not the masters of life 
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
and death. Cajetan (on the *Prima Secundae*, question 96, article 4) established the rule that every human law which binds unto mortal sin consequently binds one to suffer death for its observation, unless some case is excepted by the benevolence of the laws. 
<margin>The foundation of Cajetan's view.</margin>
His reason is that the death of the soul is to be avoided above all before the death of the body; and because of this, when a human law binds unto mortal sin, one must sooner succumb to the sword than run counter to the law. Indeed, he says, it is the same to say that a human law cannot bind to death for its observation as it is to say it cannot establish an act as a mortal sin. He then attaches some examples. For a man ought rather to die than to contract a marriage with a blood relative. And in the chapter *Sacris* regarding those things done through force or fear, Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV, a significant canon lawyer</note> says that since one should incur mortal sin for no fear, it is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons, no matter the fear. ¶ I 
<margin>In what sense Cajetan's opinion is true.</margin>
think, however, it is true that a human law is able to bind with such great rigor, and yet Cajetan’s response is in need of some correction. Therefore, first of all, it is certain that what is commanded can be of such great importance to the commonwealth that the law binds even unto death for its observation. For when a Prince in war commands a soldier to hold his post, from which an immediate danger to the commonwealth exists, he ought to desert his life rather than his post. Indeed, whenever he commands something under penalty of death, the danger of death must be undergone for the keeping of the law. For even if the Prince is not the absolute master of life as God is, nevertheless, when a cause arises, he can expose his subjects to death, just as the whole can expose its parts. Nevertheless, Cajetan's 
<margin>Cajetan's rule is not universal. Cajetan's reasoning is resolved.</margin>
rule is not so universal. Nor is it the same thing to bind unto mortal sin and to bind despite the danger of death. For the law of fasting undoubtedly binds under the penalty of mortal sin; and yet, if a tyrant threatened someone with death unless they broke the fast, there would be no guilt in breaking it—unless the tyrant compelled it in contempt of the law <note>i.e., as a way to force the person to renounce their faith or the authority of the Church</note>: for then the Christian would be bound to die rather. Truly, although one should rather die than sin, nevertheless, a law is not always presumed to compel so rigidly. And therefore, whether a law binds to seeking death or not must be examined from the gravity of the act. In fact, not even divine law binds us everywhere with such sharpness.

### Question VI of the First Book

<columns>
<margin>Church laws do not bind under the threat of death.</margin>
For no one is bound to baptize himself or his son at the risk of death, nor to receive other sacraments <note>original: "sacramenta"</note>. Indeed, I would believe that Ecclesiastical laws never bind with such compelling force, unless either contempt for that same law is involved, or an injury to the faith.

<margin>The reason for this statement.</margin>
And the reason is this: he who acts against the law out of fear of death does not transgress out of disobedience, but out of fear. Just as one who breaks a fast because of hunger does not formally sin against obedience, but against temperance <note>the virtue of moderation</note>.

<margin>Answering other arguments of Cajetan.</margin>
However, the fact that no amount of fear allows one to contract marriage with a blood relative is because such a person is not the "matter" of marriage <note>meaning the union is legally and spiritually impossible</note>, nor can it be made valid through fear; rather, such a union would be fornication. Furthermore, regarding that chapter titled *Sacris* <note>a reference to a specific section of Canon Law</note>, everyone understands it to refer to participation in sacred rites where scandal is involved. For if, while a priest celebrates in the presence of those known to be excommunicated, the common people were to take scandal—suspecting that the Church's laws have no value or that the priest is a manifest rebel—in such a case, he ought to die rather than do it. Otherwise, communicating with excommunicated persons to flee the danger of death would not be a lethal crime <note>original: "lethale crimen", a mortal sin</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
It remains, therefore, to respond to the arguments proposed at the head of the question. The first has already been solved thus: namely, that although a human being does not have power in the "court of God" <note>original: "in foro Dei", referring to the internal conscience</note> by his own right, nevertheless, acting as God's minister, he can command it. He who resists such a command resists God's ordinance, and brings damnation upon himself, according to Paul in Romans 13.

<margin>Paul. To the second argument.</margin>
Regarding the second argument, it is granted that the head of a household can bind his children to a mortal sin. For instance, if he were to command them most justly and severely regarding a matter of great weight. For their power also comes from the Lord God, who indeed commands children to honor their parents.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Hence Augustine says on Psalm 70: "Where a father commands what is not against the Lord, he is to be heard just as God is." And Solomon in Proverbs 6 says:

<margin>Solomon. Paul.</margin>
"My son, keep the commands of your father." And the Apostle <note>Paul</note> in Romans 1 numbers "disobeying parents" among other grave crimes.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
Upon these words, Ambrose says: "With what great insolence are they seized, that they would not even acknowledge their parents, who are the authors of their birth? For this is to be without understanding—namely, without the love of God." Now, a sin against the love of God is a mortal sin. And in Deuteronomy 21, the penalty of death was decreed for a son who was stubborn and defiant, who would not listen to the command of his father or mother, and who, though corrected, scorned to obey. These

<column-break/>

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
are the words of the law. Indeed, among all natural forms of obedience (as Aristotle teaches in the first book of the *Politics*), this is the first: that which is owed to parents. Furthermore, a wife might sometimes be bound under such guilt to obey her husband, even if his commands, because they lack coercive power, do not have the full force of laws. However, whether a master exercises the same authority over servants and the rest of the household, I would not easily believe.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
To the third, the answer was given in the third conclusion: that laws opposing divine laws do not have the strength of laws, but are rather to be trampled upon.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
And the answer to the fourth is much the same: sentences that are entirely "just" only according to the external court <note>legal systems based on evidence</note> but are founded on a false presumption do not bind in conscience. Since they are contrary to the truth, natural and divine law contain something else. Yet they are considered in different ways. For as long as a sentence is not entirely contrary to divine law, then the condemned person—provided he can remove himself from the judgment without scandal or violence against the judge—may nonetheless obey it. This happens when an innocent person is condemned. But when the divine law is entirely contrary—as when someone is forced to acknowledge a woman as his wife who truly is not—he ought sooner to die than obey.

<margin>To the fifth.</margin>
And the fifth is answered in a similar way. For when human laws are unjust toward subjects, if it can be done without scandal, they are not to be obeyed in conscience; it is otherwise if such scandal would arise.

->ARTICLE V.<-

->*Whether every penal law binds unto guilt.*<-

It is worthwhile here to apply two articles concerning penal law <note>a law that specifies a punishment for an act</note>, in which there lies some singular ambiguity. And first, it is asked whether a human law that binds one to a penalty <note>original: "poena"</note> likewise binds one to guilt <note>original: "culpa", meaning moral fault or sin</note>.

<margin>The first reason.</margin>
And the argument is made from the negative side. First of all, laws containing the penalty of "irregularity" <note>a canonical status that bars someone from the priesthood or church office</note> do not all bind unto guilt. For a judge who is justly the cause of a death sentence becomes "irregular," as is clear in the title on voluntary homicide and the Canon *aliquantos*. Similarly, a man who marries twice becomes irregular, as is clear in distinction 34; yet there is no sin in these cases. For this perhaps is the one cause for which the rule of law made an exception: "Without guilt (unless there be a cause), no one is to be punished." From this is collected the axiom: "Even if a penalty cannot be inflicted without cause, it can nevertheless be inflicted without..."

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
without fault. ¶ Second, in religious orders (as was already mentioned above regarding our own order), there are laws that bind one to a penalty without fault: therefore, whenever a prince attaches a penalty to a law, he should not be thought to bind the person to a fault <note>meaning moral guilt or sin</note>, but rather to be satisfied with the penalty. <margin>Nahum.</margin> This is so that he does not go against the oracle of the Prophet Nahum in chapter 1: *Double tribulation shall not rise up* <note>original: "Non consurget duplex tribulatio." This theological principle suggests a person should not be punished twice—by both guilt and a penalty—for the same act in certain legal contexts.</note>. <margin>Third reason</margin> ¶ Third, there are innumerable laws, both divine and human, which do not take the form of a command, but only of a penalty; such as that in Exodus 22: *If anyone steals an ox or a sheep... he shall restore five oxen for one ox, and four sheep for one sheep.* And in the Decree of Gratian <note>Canon Law</note>, 2. q. 3: *He who fails to prove what he has charged should suffer the penalty he himself would have inflicted.* And in the section on punishments in the Civil Law <note>original: "l. capitali. ff. de pœnis"</note>. Thus the laws state: *arsonists are punished by the head* <note>the death penalty</note>. *Usurers are to be punished by the head.* There are many similar laws in which nothing is explicitly commanded or forbidden, but only a penalty is established. Therefore, these do not bind one to a fault, but strictly to a penalty. ¶ On the contrary, there is Canon Law: Canon *Satis peruersum*, distinction 56, where it is held to be quite perverse <note>original: "satis peruersum"</note> that anyone should be deprived of their duties whom their own fault or crime does not cast down from their rank. The same is noted in the civil law regarding the *Lex Aquilia* <note>a Roman law on damages</note>.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
If the nature of punishment were sufficiently weighed, there would be no reason for this question to be called into doubt; the matter is so clear in itself. But because the common people—by I know not what colorful reasoning—say that a law binding to a penalty does not bind to fault, it is necessary to strike down this error. ¶ It is therefore answered with a single general conclusion: There is no penal law whatsoever (if it is to be legitimately called "penal") that does not bind to a fault, unless the legislator has expressed a contrary intention by saying, "we do not intend to bind to fault," or something similar, as was explained in the previous question. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> This conclusion belongs to St. Thomas Aquinas in the *Summa Theologiae* <note>II-II, question 108, article 4</note>, where he elucidates it—as he does almost everything—with great clarity. And it is very well known by the light of natural reason. <margin>Reason for the question.</margin> For punishment <note>original: "pœna"</note>, as its very name testifies, has such a kindred connection to fault <note>original: "culpa"</note> that it has neither the substance nor the just name of "punishment" unless it is imposed for a fault. For we are speaking here of "punishment" in the legal sense, as it pertains to vengeance and retribution. For "punishment" is also used in a physical sense for the torment one suffers from a fever or any other disease that brings pain. Furthermore, no other proof is needed beyond the meaning of the name. For to avenge, to take vengeance, to demand an execution, and thus to inflict a punishment, is by no means lawful except on account of a fault. Therefore, unless a fault is present, the term is used improperly and outside the meaning of the words. For through punishment a just

<column-break/>

recompense for fault is made. Namely, so that he who sinned by following his own will (for according to Augustine: *where there is no will, there is no sin*) should suffer something against that same will of his. <margin>Second reason.</margin> ¶ Second, this is proved thus: If human laws (as established in the previous article) are set down absolutely without the threat of a penalty, they bind to fault; but the threat of a penalty added to a law is not a sign of the contrary; therefore, even then, the same obligation to fault remains. The minor premise <note>the second part of the logic</note> is proved because the threat of a penalty by its nature looks toward this: that the law may be observed more carefully. For that reason, in the article on the acts of the law, it was said that one act is to punish; just as in theoretical matters conclusions are drawn from principles, so in practical matters the observation of a precept is drawn out by the threat of a penalty. Therefore, not only is a penalty not an indication that fault has been removed, but on the contrary, it is an open testimony to the gravity of the fault contracted by the transgression and omission of the law. <margin>Third reason</margin> ¶ Third, it is argued that no other cause can be given for why a larger, smaller, or maximum penalty is attached to a law than the proportion of the fault; according to that passage in Deuteronomy 25: *According to the measure of the sin, so shall the number of stripes be.* Similar to this is the chapter *Exiuit* regarding those things done by a majority, and the chapter *Fœlicis* in Book 6 of the Decretals. Therefore, every punishment is a testimony of a fault. <margin>Fourth reason.</margin> ¶ Fourth, the divine example is added. For in that law which God first gave to our parents in the state of innocence, because its violation was so exceedingly grave and enormous, he threatened a most cruel penalty, saying: *In whatever hour you eat of it, you shall die the death.* Thus it happened that death, diseases, and other calamities and hardships—which would not be punishments but natural to us if we were created in a purely natural state—are now, because of the fault of Adam, both called and are punishments. This is because we have been stripped of original justice, which would have kept us safe from these things. Therefore, we sinned in a certain way by the will of that parent. Thus no one is punished except on account of a fault, whether their own personal fault or that of their parents, of whom they are in some way a part. Hence that passage in Exodus 20: *I am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation.* I confess that we are indeed sometimes scourged by God, not only for past offenses, but so that we may live more cautiously in the future. <margin>The conclusion is strengthened from Holy Scripture.</margin> Those scourges, however, are not so much punishments as they are preventative medicines. Moreover, all things are ultimately traced back to the fault of our origin <note>Original Sin</note>. Finally, the same conclusion is confirmed by other examples from God, specifically in Exodus 21 and Leviticus 20. <margin>Leviticus 20.</margin>

# First Book, Question VI.

[God] established punishments according to the gravity of the crimes: *He who curses his father or mother, let him die the death* <note>original: "morte moriatur," a phrasing from Exodus 21:17</note>. *If any man commits adultery with the wife of another, let him die the death,* etc. For this reason, even if no penalty is attached to the commandments of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> in the Gospel, they have nevertheless been applied through human laws. This ensures that the murderer, the thief, and other wicked and impure men are restrained from violating those laws by the fear of death. And it is surely a sophistical <term>cavillous diversion<gloss>a deceptive or trivial legal argument used to avoid the truth</gloss></term> to say that things are different in divine laws than in human ones, when human laws ought rather to be imitators of the divine. ¶ Furthermore, who could doubt that when a King, having threatened the penalty of death, orders a soldier not to desert his post, it is a mortal <term>fault<gloss>a serious moral sin, or "culpa" in Latin</gloss></term> to retreat from there? For it is an infallible rule that a prince cannot decree a penalty of death, mutilation, exile, or the confiscation of all goods against anyone, except for a transgression or omission of a law that constitutes a lethal fault. Truly, I do not see from where this more-than-common opinion could have arisen—the idea that laws binding one to a penalty do not bind one to a fault. For punishment is, by its very nature, both the natural effect and the clear judgment of a fault. However, those who introduced this idea are not those who philosophize about the nature of things.
<margin>*The opinion of others.*</margin>
¶ But indeed, other Doctors, more learned in this area, although they do not entirely deny our conclusion, nevertheless moderate it 
<margin>*Henry.*</margin>
with this distinction, which they take from Henry of Ghent <note>A prominent 13th-century philosopher and theologian</note> in his *Quodlibet* 3, question 22. For he was perhaps the one who provided the handle for the common opinion we were just attacking. Nevertheless, he himself held a more moderate view. His distinction is this: of penal laws, some are those that explain a command or a prohibition to which they attach the threat of a penalty. Those who defend him call these "mixed" penal laws—that is, laws binding to a fault as well as a penalty. But there are others that express neither a command nor a prohibition, but only a penalty under a certain condition, the form of which we proposed in the third argument. And these they call "purely" penal laws. They say, therefore, that those mixed laws bind to a fault, but these 
<margin>*The former opinion is rejected.*</margin>
pure ones do not. Nevertheless (to say this without disparaging the reputation of those authors, who are worthy of esteem), I do not think I grasp the force of this distinction. On the contrary, I consider the universal truth of our conclusion to be unshaken: namely, that nothing can have the nature of a punishment except where a fault underlies it, for the reasons already given. But in the absence of a fault, that which bears the image

<column-break/>

of a punishment will instead be a price, or a contract, or something else, as will immediately become clear in the solution to the third argument.

<margin>*To the first argument.*</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is answered that <term>irregularity<gloss>a canonical status that prevents a person from being ordained or performing priestly duties</gloss></term>, when it is not imposed for a crime (for the matter is different regarding those), in no way takes on the nature of a punishment. Rather, it is a type of "indecency" or lack of fitness which renders a man unsuitable for holy orders and sacred functions. For who would say that if a judge most justly sentences a man to death, it is a "punishment" for him that he cannot be promoted to holy orders? Who, I ask, ever opposed a penalty to excellent virtue? But it is unbecoming and indecent (as we shall say in Book 5, Question 1) that he who is contaminated by blood should dispense the sacraments of the most innocent Lamb <note>referring to Christ and the Eucharist</note>. For by the same reasoning, a <term>bigamist<gloss>in this historical context, a man who had been married twice, even if sequentially after a death</gloss></term> becomes "irregular" not as a punishment, but because of what it signifies: since Christ took for himself only one Church as his bride. Just as relatives are unsuitable and unfit for contracting marriage, certainly not as a punishment, but because of the absurdity of the thing. Therefore, the rule of law contains a universal truth: that no one is to be punished without a fault. For the parenthetical phrase "unless a cause underlies it," if you listen to the <term>gloss<gloss>the standard commentary on the law</gloss></term>, only teaches that when a cause occurs without a fault, it can happen that a man is kept away from some dignity because of "indecency," which they call "irregularity." Although the same parenthesis is understood differently by Saint Thomas [Aquinas] in the place cited than by the commentator: namely, concerning the divine scourges already mentioned, which are inflicted not so much as a punishment for crimes committed, but as medicine for the future. ¶ To the second
<margin>*To the second argument.*</margin>
response, it is sufficient that where a law has expressed its intention of not binding to a fault, the matter will be safe. However, it does not follow from this that where a penalty is added without such an expression, the fault is thereby removed. For the word of the Prophet Nahum has nothing to do with the matter: for "double tribulation" there does not mean the same thing as fault and punishment. Rather, that sentence designates the mercy of God, who, once the penalty has been paid in full to the Just One, never demands another. 
<margin>*To the third.*</margin>
¶ Regarding the third argument: those who defend the distinction of Henry [of Ghent] contend that those laws mentioned do not bind to a fault. Nor do any of those that appear in Leviticus 20: *If anyone commits adultery with the wife of another, let the adulterer and the adulteress die the death,* etc. In short, [they say] no law, whether Canonical or civil...

...which is posed under this conditional form, they believe binds only to the penalty: but specifically those laws which, by commanding, explain that something is to be done or not done under the threat of a penalty. An example is the decree *Every person of either sex* <note>original: "Omnis utriusque sexus," a famous canon from the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215</note> concerning penance and remission. By this decree, it is commanded that everyone should confess their sins at least once a year and receive the sacrament of the Eucharist at least on Easter Sunday; otherwise, while living they shall be barred from entering the church, and when dying they shall be deprived of a church burial.

<margin>
Two things to be noted.
The first.
</margin>
Here, however, I would note two things. First, that even if this opinion is true, it detracts nothing from the truth of our conclusion: because those penalties are not established except for **faults** <term>faults<gloss>Latin: "culpae," referring here to moral sins or transgressions of conscience</gloss></term>, which are forbidden either by those laws or by others.

<margin>The second.</margin>
The second point is that I would not dare to deny that those penal laws—whether divine, canon, or civil—which decree punishments for crimes, bind a person to a fault. For even if those crimes were not prohibited by other mandates, it is certainly expressed clearly enough in these laws that those punishments (and especially capital ones) are instituted to restrain the faults suggested therein; therefore, those faults are virtually prohibited by the law.

<margin>A distinction.</margin>
Therefore, I think we must use this distinction: When a punishment is applied to a fault, as in the laws mentioned, the obligation is under the guilt of a fault. However, when a law has the form of a **concession** or a **dispensation** <note>Meaning a permit or an exception granted by authority</note>, then such a law does not bind to a fault. Nevertheless, that which is added under the guise of a punishment does not have the true nature of a penalty, but rather of a price or an agreement. Let us provide examples. This law—*whoever carries grain out of the kingdom shall lose it or pay such a penalty*—truly binds to a fault.

<margin><unclear>Consensus humana</unclear> <note>Likely intended as "Human Concession"</note></margin>
However, if the King's intention was not to prohibit the distribution of grain, but to collect money by that means, then the law would not bind to a fault. But in that case, the added condition would not be a punishment, but a concession and a price, so that whoever wished to export it would contribute that much. Just as a state can pass a law by forbidding, saying: *Whoever cuts wood in the forest shall be struck by such a penalty*; and again, it can allow it for a price: *Whoever cuts wood shall pay so much.* In the same way: *If anyone rides a mule, let him lose it*; surely (as I see it) this binds to a fault. But if, after the law was passed, the citizens procured a dispensation and wished to redeem it for a price, then this law—*Whoever rides a mule shall pay so much*—is not penal: because it is not prohibitory, but rather concessive.

<margin>An objection.</margin>
¶ But what if our own institutions, and those of other religious orders, are objected against us, in which it is stated: *We do not wish to bind to a fault <note>sin</note> but to a penalty*?

<column-break/>

<margin>Response.</margin>
Where a penalty is named without a fault, the response is that such things are not properly and legitimately "penalties," but are instead like agreements and pacts: because monks wish to bind themselves by such a vow that if they do these things, they will suffer those consequences. They are called penalties not ineptly, however, because they are demanded and paid back on account of forbidden things. Just as in our little book *On Avoiding the Abuse of Oaths*, we said that without an obligation to a new fault, anyone can bind himself so that as often as he abuses an oath, he must pay a certain amount.

<margin>
Another objection.
Section 10.
</margin>
Perhaps someone might also cite against us some civil laws that establish penalties where no fault appears to be present. Such as those regarding prison-breakers <note>original: "effractoribus carcerum"</note> who flee (Digest, *concerning prison-breakers*, law *on those*, etc., and *concerning custody and producing defendants*, law *against them*), even though it is permitted for any prisoner to do so without fault.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
But we shall respond to these in Book 5, Question 6: that either there is a fault there, or a fault is presumed.

<margin>

<margin>Second.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the sixth question of the first book, where Soto argues that penal laws (those imposing punishments) can bind a person’s conscience even before a judge has issued a formal sentence. He provides several historical and legal examples to prove that certain penalties apply automatically ("ipso facto") when an act is committed.</meta>

# Question VI of the First Book

For in ancient times, the law of Leviticus 15 stated that whoever touched a woman defiled by a flow of blood should be unclean until evening; this uncleanness was certainly contracted without any judicial sentence. Almost identical laws existed regarding lepers and other infected people, who by the very fact of their condition <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> were required to keep themselves away from the company of others. Likewise, regarding the sacrifices commanded to be offered to expiate sins, the offenders were bound in conscience to present themselves to the priests. In the same way, the Church today can establish penalties for certain sins, just as it has mandated the Lenten fast: we are rightly bound to undergo these as penances. Therefore, the law binds the conscience. To these is added the law of Christ in Matthew 19: "He who dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery." This implies that it is permissible in conscience to dismiss an adulterous spouse—at least regarding the separation of the bed—before the case is brought to trial, and the spouse is bound to endure that penalty.

<margin>Fourth argument.</margin>
¶ Fourth, the argument is made from many human laws. First, a deceased person can bequeath the use and profit <term>usufruct<gloss>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property belonging to another</gloss></term> of an estate to his wife on the condition that she lives modestly, or does not enter into a second marriage; therefore, as soon as she breaks that condition, she is bound in conscience to return the legacy to the heir. By the same logic, someone who establishes a college from his own wealth can make laws stating that whichever colleague commits this or that crime shall be deprived of his rights in the college or must restore what he received from it. These laws certainly bind in conscience without any other judge's sentence. Furthermore, a King can, by such a law, appoint judges and ministers of justice to public office with the condition that whoever sells a judgment or accepts bribes shall, by that very fact and without waiting for a sentence, be subject to this or that penalty. Such laws certainly exist in Spain and other well-ordered provinces. These laws truly constrain the conscience. And in our University, it is decreed that a scholar who uses bribery or improper solicitation <note>original: "subornare," referring to "ambitioning" or campaigning for a professor's chair</note> while seeking a Chair is, by the fact itself, deprived of his right to vote.

<margin>Fifth argument.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, fifth: when a King sets the price of grain or any other merchandise by law, adding a penalty for the transgressor, he binds the person to that penalty in conscience. And there exist among all people laws of prescription <note>original: "præscriptionis," the legal method of acquiring property by long-term possession, similar to adverse possession</note>, by virtue of which a "good faith" possessor acquires ownership of movable goods in ten years, and in forty years for immovable

<column-break/>

property, without any sentence from a judge. This is widely evident in both Civil and Canon Law under the same titles regarding prescription. This law is indeed penal: for because of the negligence of the owner who ignored his property for such a long interval, he is deprived of its ownership. Therefore, a penal law binds the conscience before a judge’s sentence.

<margin>Sixth argument.</margin>
¶ Sixth, it is argued from the chapter *Si qui* in the *Liber Sextus* <note>A collection of Canon Law published in 1298</note>, where two ways are distinguished by which someone can be deprived of possessed things: namely, either by a sentence or by the law itself <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>. Indeed, unless the law itself fined the guilty party before a judge’s sentence, that distinction would be pointless, because only one method of punishing would remain: namely, by sentence.

<margin>Seventh.</margin>
¶ Seventh, penal laws are established in legal codes under different forms. Some are those that explain a sentence is *to be* passed; these are merely "monitory" or warning laws, as held in the commentary <note>original: "gloss."</note> on the chapter *Unico* regarding arrows <note>original: "de sagitta," a reference to a canon prohibiting the use of crossbows against Christians</note>. This occurs whenever it is said, "We command under penalty" or "under threat of excommunication, or anathema, or suspension." Hence, concerning that word in the chapter *Dolentis* on the celebration of the Mass—"we strictly forbid under penalty of suspension"—the commentators read it such that they understand it only to threaten a sentence that is to be delivered later. This is stated more expressly in the chapter *Relatum* on the right of patronage: after the words "you should take care to prohibit it under threat of anathema," it is immediately added: "If, however, anyone should be a contemner of your prohibition, you shall subject him to excommunication." But other laws exist that are more urgent: namely, those that do not warn of a penalty but inflict it as a punishment. Of these, four are found in the chapter *Cum secundum leges* in the *Liber Sextus*. First: that those contracting incestuous or unnatural marriages—that is, polluting themselves with shameful acts against nature—shall, by that very fact, lose ownership of their property. Second: that an abducted woman who marries her abductor against the will of her parents shall lose all her goods by the law itself. Third: that even those who transport weapons or goods to the enemies of the faith shall, by this very fact, be deprived of the ownership of those goods. And above all, fourth: that heretics, by the fact itself, are deprived of their goods, which are to be awarded to the state treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>. These deprivations occur "by the fact itself" (as cited there) according to civil laws. To these, a fifth case is added in the crime of high treason <term>Lese-majesty<gloss>From "laesa maiestas," a crime against the dignity of the sovereign or state</gloss></term>. And a sixth in Canon Law against those who either strike or capture a Cardinal of the Roman Church, as is clear in the chapter *Felicis* on penalties in the *Liber Sextus*; for these people are considered to have injured the majesty of the Church. And the seventh is the law...

# F[ray] D[omingo de] Soto, On Justice and Law

...a similar law exists against those who mutilate or wound pilgrims going to Rome or Jerusalem: as is clear from the Roman custom where, during the Mass of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "cœna Domini". Soto refers to the famous papal bull "In Coena Domini," which listed offenses resulting in automatic excommunication.</note>, all such individuals are declared excommunicate and deprived of their goods. I say that for all such criminals, it is decreed by law that they are fined of their property by the very fact of the deed <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>. From this it follows that laws bind one to the penalty in the "court of conscience" <note>The internal moral judgment of the individual before God, as opposed to a legal court.</note>; otherwise, no gap would remain between these types of laws and those that are merely advisory. This reasoning is confirmed: because the penalty of excommunication, suspension, and "irregularity" <term>irregularity<gloss>A canonical impediment that prevents someone from receiving or exercising Holy Orders</gloss></term> is incurred by the deed itself <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> even before a judge’s sentence.

<margin>Eighth argument.</margin>
¶ Eighth, a much more urgent argument is made from the chapter *Pro humani* regarding voluntary homicide in Book 6. There, against those who kill someone via assassins, the sentence is issued that they are excommunicated and deprived of every honor, rank, office, and benefice by the very fact of the act <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, and these things may be freely granted to others. Thus, once the crime is established by probable arguments, no further sentence is required. These are the words of the law.

<margin>Paul the Second.</margin>
To this is added, with even greater force, the Decretal *Extrauagans, Ambitiosae* of Paul II <note>Pope Paul II, reigned 1464–1471.</note>, in which a more severe censure is denounced against those who alienate ecclesiastical property: namely, that by the very fact of the act <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> and without any further declaration, they are deprived of their benefices and dignities.

¶ On the contrary, however, stands what is said in the same chapter *Cum secundum leges*, after the words: "We decree the goods of heretics confiscated by the law itself" <note>original: "ipso iure"</note>. It is then added: "However, the execution of such confiscation, or the seizure of the goods themselves, must not be carried out by princes or other temporal lords (according to the declaration of our predecessor Pope Gregory) before a sentence regarding the same crime has been promulgated by the local Bishop or another ecclesiastical person who has authority over this matter."

I will take care to discuss the present question at greater length than perhaps seems necessary, because exceptionally learned men disagree on it. Among them is Alfonso de Castro <note>A Spanish Franciscan theologian (1495–1558) and contemporary of Soto, famous for his work on penal law.</note>, a Franciscan who is certainly well-deserving in letters and religion, and whom I must respect accordingly. For although in other matters, and perhaps even in this one, he may have hit upon the truth more surely than I, I nevertheless seem to feel somewhat differently. I will therefore respond to the question in our usual manner with five conclusions, and I will labor to the best of my ability to respond to the reasons and testimonies brought against me. I would not have made such a great dispute of this

<column-break/>

were it not so important for the Christian family that their consciences be informed on this matter. However, so that the speech may be clear and lucid, among the many things debated concerning penal law, it is most relevant to the matter to know only this.

<margin>The title of the question is made clear.</margin>
Whether by the very fact that someone transgresses a law—one which deprives the transgressor of his goods by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>—he is bound in conscience to hand over those same goods to the treasury <term>fisc<gloss>The public treasury or government funds</gloss></term>; or whether he can retain them without guilt until the judge’s sentence—either because he retains ownership until then, or because he enjoys the right of possession or grant. For this question, which asks about the cause, is a new one.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let the first conclusion be this: A penal law, simply because it says "by the fact itself" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> or "by the law itself" <note>original: "ipso iure"</note> or something similar, does not bind one to the penalty before a sentence is passed by a judge, in such a way that the guilty person is bound in conscience to strip themselves of their goods immediately upon committing the fault. But if any law binds in such a way, it must be judged from other factors.

<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
We therefore place this conclusion in direct opposition to Abbot Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a leading authority on Canon Law.</note>, notwithstanding his authority. His rule is that he whose goods are confiscated by the law itself <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> cannot retain them with a good conscience, because, he says, they are immediately acquired by the treasury. His words are found in the aforementioned chapter *Canonum*.

<margin>Natural reasons support the aforementioned conclusion.</margin>
And since testimonies are illuminated by natural reasons, I will begin with such reasons. Especially since the supporters of the contrary opinion rely on the principle that no law (as they say), whether human, divine, or natural, supports our opinion; yet, even if no law, human or divine, says this expressly, natural reasons are the interpreters of natural law. Therefore, that same religious author [Alfonso de Castro] wisely took care to warn theologians not to be satisfied with mere citations of Doctors.

<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ The first reason is this: Punishment (as the name itself sounds) is so called because it is a "passion" <note>Soto uses the word in the Aristotelian sense: a "passion" is something one undergoes or suffers, while an "action" is something one does.</note>. Nature, however, shrinks from the idea of the same person being both the actor and the sufferer. Therefore, a law that would make me the minister and executor of my own punishment would not be in conformity with nature; and since (as was said above) human laws are derived from natural law, no such law is binding in that way. But because this reason appears quite weak to the supporters of the contrary opinion, let us weigh how much weight it actually has.

<margin>The previous reason is explained.</margin>
Law is the inanimate rule of our actions, which must be applied to subjects through the ministers of justice. Therefore, it belongs to the ministers to compel their subjects to the observation of the law; and compulsion is done through the infliction of punishment. Therefore, such...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of penal laws.
