### First Book, Question VI.

<margin>Aristotle</margin> ...such an observation belongs to the judge: and it is against nature for a defendant to be forced to act against himself. For this reason, Aristotle, in the 5th book of his *Ethics*, called the judge "living justice" <note>original: "iustum animatum". This refers to the idea that a judge is the personification of the law's intent.</note>, who must act against the defendant according to the law. Therefore, if I am judging correctly, a penal law <term>penal law<gloss>A law that imposes a punishment, such as a fine or imprisonment, for a specific offense.</gloss></term> speaks to two different parties through its two parts. When it commands that no one should do a certain thing, it addresses the subjects; but when it adds that whoever does the opposite "by that very fact" <note>original: "eo ipso"</note> loses ownership of their things, or loses their goods by the law itself, or that their goods are confiscated, it is not speaking so much to the subjects as to the judges—the executors of justice—to whom it commands such a punishment.

<margin>Second argument.</margin> ¶ Second (which is a pressing argument for me): however much a law threatens a punishment, it nevertheless keeps the most equitable right of nature unharmed: which is that the offender must be heard. From this source has flowed that most established and firm ruling of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory, cited in Canon Law regarding legal possession.</note>: <margin>Gregory</margin> "We can define nothing against a party that has not been heard." He does not merely say, "we do not wish to," but "we are not able to": because nature itself forbids it. Indeed, since the law (as shown above) is passed in general terms and could not foresee the unique circumstances of every event, this task is delegated to the judge so that, having looked into these circumstances, he may deliver a sentence. For a defendant can allege either ignorance, or weakness, or a most overwhelming occasion, or perhaps that he did not strike against the law so severely as to be worthy of the bitterness of the full punishment. Therefore, even in the crime of heresy—which is the most impious and accursed of all—a heretic is heard in whatever way he wishes to excuse his deed. And it happens very often that the offense is so slight that he is not prosecuted with the full rigor of the law, and thus is not stripped of all his goods. By the same reasoning—indeed, by an even fairer one—in the crime of high treason <note>original: "læsæ Maiestatis"</note> and in any others whatsoever, the cause must be weighed in its particulars, and judged according to its gravity or lightness: even if the law says a thousand times "by the law itself" <note>original: "ipso iure"</note> and "by the fact itself" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> and "by that very act" <note>original: "eo ipso"</note>. This is because <term>equity<gloss>The Greek term "epieikeia," meaning the correction of a law where it is defective owing to its universality.</gloss></term> can never be banished from the courts by any law. Therefore, when the law says "by the fact itself," it is the same as saying "from the nature and type of the deed": which does not prevent the punishment from being weighed again regarding the quantity and manner of the deed, just as the lawmaker himself would do if he were present. And from there another most holy law has flowed: that no one is to be condemned unless they have confessed or been convicted, as held in the Canons "Nos in quenquam" and "Iudex" <note>Citations from the Decretals of Canon Law emphasizing the necessity of proof.</note>. If this reasoning is accepted, see into what distress you would throw a wretched offender if he were bound (as the opposing opinion holds) to hand over his own goods to the treasury before a judge's sentence. Truly, you not only force him to be the executor of the law against himself—which nature does not tolerate—but you also appoint him as judge: namely, so that he himself may weigh whether his offense deserves such a great punishment. Take, for example, a man who, knowingly and deliberately, conceived a slight heresy within himself and spoke it aloud, which lasted for only a day or a single hour in private: should you immediately force him in conscience to offer up his vast substance to the treasury, even while he is very wealthy, despite the fact that, having come to his senses, he is now firm in the faith? In truth, this would be a most atrocious judgment; no judge, whether secular or ecclesiastical, would have pronounced such a sentence, much less should he be forced to do so privately in his conscience. And yet, if the opposing opinion were true—especially the opinion of those who hold that one incurs the legal penalty even for a hidden crime <note>original: "occulto crimine"</note> that can in no way be proven—he would be forced to do it, since he who can pretend no ignorance is truly a heretic. Indeed, to take another argument from common practice: what priest has ever driven a <margin>Another argument.</margin> penitent into such distress as to make him make his goods public before a condemnation?

<margin>Third reason</margin> ¶ Added to this, thirdly, is that human laws (as we were taught above by Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville, whose definitions of law were foundational to medieval and Renaissance legal thought.</note>) ought to be tolerable and adapted to human weakness: laws that even those who are not so advanced in virtue can bear. If, however, the law so constrained men that they had to strip themselves of their substance, however rich, of their own accord, it would be intolerable, and far unlike the sweet and light yoke of Christ. Nor does the reasoning of the adversaries hold weight, when they say <margin>The adversaries' weak reason</margin> that laws are observed more cautiously this way: for such caution in guarding a law must be applied so that the dispute does not become impossible to observe.

<margin>Fourth argument.</margin> ¶ But since we have touched upon the hidden heretic for whom there is no witness, let us take from there a fourth argument, which is this Dilemma: Either you want the hidden heretic—namely, one who uttered heresy outwardly without any witness—to incur the civil penalties of the law (for no one doubts the excommunication), or you do not. The former is surely a very harsh opinion; yet if he does not incur them unless he speaks before witnesses, a manifest argument is taken from this: that he is not bound to pay the penalties before a condemnation. For since witnesses are in no way necessary except for a trial, he who denies the sentence...

<summary>Soto argues that "ipso facto" penalties do not require self-punishment before a legal trial, as natural law guarantees the right to be heard and requires a judge to apply equity to specific circumstances.</summary>

## Francisco de Soto, on Justice and Right.

...that the sentence of a judge is necessary for the deprivation of goods, he freely grants that witnesses are necessary for a heretic to be liable to the penalty of the law. Although the aforementioned author did not make this argument explicitly, he looked ahead with clear eyes when, in Question 15 of his second book, he agreed with his colleague Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as Panormitanus.</note> that a secret heretic incurs the penalty of the law: for if

<margin>The foundation of the aforementioned assertion is not very solid.</margin>
witnesses are superfluous. However, the foundation that he laid for this assertion of his not only seems unsolid, but rather supports the contrary opinion. The foundation is taken from the chapter *Accusatus* <note>A specific chapter in the *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law.</note> regarding heretics in Book 6, where the Pope commands that the confiscation of goods be carried out against a deceased heretic whose heresy had not yet become known while he was alive. Yet, from that very source, it is more clearly gathered that his heresy was not truly "secret," since witnesses appeared after his death. And in truth, to condemn a man for a crime that is simply secret would seem to be contrary not only to the chapter *Secundum leges* <note>Latin: "According to the laws."</note>, which forbids confiscation before a judge's sentence, but also to the entire order of Law. It is ordained by this order that no one is to be punished except by way of investigation, denunciation, or accusation: because the laws have always considered that which cannot be proven to be outside their jurisdiction—excepting the censure of excommunication <term>excommunication<gloss>A spiritual penalty that excludes a person from the sacraments and community of the Church.</gloss></term>, which by its nature does not require a formal hearing of the case, but only the prior warning of the law itself.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
¶ But let me apply a fifth specific argument here to understand the words of the aforementioned doctor. In the second of his books, in which he argued excellently concerning the *Just Punishment of Heretics* (Chapter 6), he said that not everyone uttering heresy incurs the penalty of the law, but only a "heretic": as is held in the said chapter *Secundum leges*. For instance, one who is obstinate in their heresy. Now, he either calls "obstinate" the one who is rebellious against the law alone—namely, one who deliberately denies what he knows to be against Scripture or against the Holy Church—or he does not yet consider him obstinate until he has been warned in a trial and still clings stubbornly to his heresy. If he meant the former, I do not understand why he added in that Chapter 6 that those who, upon being warned, immediately recant and condemn their error, are to be punished not by the legal penalty, but by a discretionary one. For there, he is openly speaking of a warning not from the law, but from a judge. But if he understood there (as he plainly seems to have understood) that a heretic does not incur the legal penalty except at that moment when, having been warned in court, he does not repent, then his whole argument collapses. For first, it is false that a secret heretic—against whom no

<column-break/>

proof can be had—is deprived of his goods. Indeed, it follows openly that no one is deprived by the law itself or by the act itself <note>original: "ipso iure & facto"</note> until they are brought into court, where they may be condemned not only for heresy but for obstinacy <term>pertinacia<gloss>The legal concept of "pertinacity" or stubborn persistence in error, which was required to prove the crime of heresy.</gloss></term>.

<margin>Another reason.</margin>
Furthermore, the entire practice of the Inquisitors is denied. For whoever has affirmed a manifest heresy to himself without witnesses is considered a heretic (unless excused by ignorance)—that is, excommunicated as one who is obstinate against the warning of the law. And therefore, even if he was never warned by a man, if he were later convicted in court, all his goods could by law be confiscated, and they are confiscated, unless some part is returned to him due to the lightness of the heresy. Nevertheless, while he seeks pardon, he is not "released" from the penalty but "reconciled" to the Church. It is different for one who is only *suspected* of heresy, against whom the legal penalty does not apply, but rather a discretionary one. I have said these things not to defeat the author, but to confirm through his own words that a secret heretic is not bound to surrender his goods until he has been convicted of the crime in court.

<margin>Sixth argument.</margin>
¶ This is further confirmed by a sixth point: if someone, with no one knowing, deliberately spoke a heresy to himself, and without any denunciation, offers himself voluntarily to the fathers of the Holy Tribunal <note>The Inquisition.</note>, even though he is excommunicated by the act itself, he is not usually fined all his goods nor publicly shamed. Truly, I do not know how one could respond to this otherwise.

<margin>Seventh argument. Chrysostom.</margin>
¶ In the seventh place comes that famous sentiment of Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father.</note> in his commentary on the *Epistle to the Hebrews*, which is cited in the laws on penance: "I do not say that you should betray yourself." From this, it follows that no one is bound to betray himself, unless someone is betrayed by infamy, or evidence, or accusation, being compelled by the authority of a judge. If, however, a secret defendant were bound to offer his goods to the treasury <note>original: "fisco"</note>, he would be forced to betray himself repeatedly; for if he were a person of high rank, how else could he surrender them?

<margin>Triple evasion.</margin>
¶ But our opponents strive to weaken this reasoning in three ways. First, by turning it back against us. For similarly, they say, it would follow that a thief who secretly plundered the treasury would not be bound to make restitution lest he betray himself. Second, they say that they must then make restitution secretly through a third party. And third, they say that if it cannot be done without infamy, the necessity of restitution ceases.

<margin>The reasons of the opponents are refuted.</margin>
However, the first response is an escape rather than a solution. For there is a wide difference between a penalty <term>poena</term> and restitution <term>restitutio</term>. For what Chrysostom says (with the whole body of law agreeing) is that no defendant is bound to betray himself for the purpose of being punished. This is for the reason that...

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

<summary>The author argues that a "secret heretic" is not legally required to surrender their property or face confiscation until they have been formally convicted in a court of law. He emphasizes the distinction between spiritual excommunication and the legal punishment of losing one's goods, asserting that natural law protects a person from being forced to betray themselves.</summary>

### First Book, Question VI.

-> That no one is bound to be both the actor and the sufferer. <-

However, what you have stolen from another, you are bound to restore not as a punishment, but by reason of **commutative justice** <note>original: "iustitiæ commutatiue"; this refers to the justice governing private exchanges and the requirement to return what belongs to another to maintain equality.</note>. This is true even if it becomes necessary to expose yourself to some degree of infamy, provided you cannot do so secretly. Indeed, that rule—that no one is bound to restore money at the cost of their own reputation—which appears in Book 4 under the title *On Restitution*, will be shown to be fallacious, intolerable, and even pernicious if understood universally as it stands, without moderation or exceptions. For certainly, one who had plundered the **treasury** <note>original: "fiscum"; the public or state treasury.</note> or a great sum of money would be bound to restore it, even with the loss of their reputation. It is different regarding the danger of one's life. To the point, then: if no one is bound to betray themselves in order to undergo a punishment, it follows that they do not owe that punishment in their conscience either. To this is added an argument from the law *Aut facta* in the **Digest on Penalties** <note>original: "ff. de poen."; 'ff' is a standard abbreviation for the Digest, a massive collection of Roman legal rulings.</note>, in the section *Nonnunquam*, where it is held that punishments are increased whenever it is necessary to set an example for many. Punishments, therefore, ought to be exemplary and public, not hidden.

<margin>The opponents' solution.</margin>
Finally, an eighth argument is made. The law—to persist with the chapter *According to the laws* <note>original: "c. Secundū leges."</note>—permits a defendant to possess their own goods until condemnation; indeed, it even forbids those goods from being snatched away. Therefore, the defendant possesses them in **good faith**. I know that the supporters of the contrary opinion consider this argument weak. They heap up many fallacies against this logic, such as: "A judge of the treasury cannot demand the defendant's goods; therefore, the defendant is not bound to hand them over of his own accord." For as it is held in the **Digest on Gambling** <note>original: "ff. de alea"</note>, law 1, a person who steals in a house where gambling is publicly practiced is indeed bound to restore the stolen items to the owner; however, the owner is not given a legal action in court for the penalty because he was hosting gamblers. From this, they infer that a defendant condemned by the law itself is permitted to possess their goods—not by a permission that removes the fault, but by one that does not demand the punishment, just as prostitutes are permitted.

<margin>Rebuttal.</margin>
Yet, the fallacies they bring forward first cannot deceive the force of the argument. For the nature of the "permission" must be weighed according to the subject matter. Since everyone is the legitimate owner and possessor of their goods before committing a crime, and since the law, immediately after stating the penalty of deprivation, adds that confiscation should not be carried out before the judge's sentence, it clearly seems to grant the defendant the use of their own goods. It is different if you steal. Nor is there a need to bring in another law or reason for this kind of concession so that the defendant may possess in good faith. By this same reasoning, as held in the title *On Prescription* in Book 6, the heirs of the deceased **prescribe** <note>Prescription is a legal method of acquiring ownership of property through long-term possession.</note> their goods. Although

<column-break/>

I see well enough that this point carries very little weight. For even if heretics did not possess their goods in good faith, their heirs could still have that good faith for the purpose of prescription, owing to their ignorance of the crime. Just as can happen with the heirs of a thief. Truly, though I am not so much a lover of my own judgment, nevertheless these reasons—where neither Holy Scripture nor an express text of law stands in my way, as indeed they do not—would persuade me of the matter more effectively than a long **phalanx of Doctors** <note>A "phalanx of Doctors" refers to a long list of academic authorities and legal scholars.</note> who skim through the simple assertions of others without any real insight. Even so, the testimonies of the most approved authors are not lacking to us.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
For there is, first of all, **St. Thomas** in the *Summa Theologica* <note>original: "2.2. q.62.arti.3."</note>, who expressly says that no one is bound to a punishment before condemnation by a judge.
<margin>Conrad</margin>

Nor indeed, as some think, did he hold the opposite view in Book 4, where he discusses the question of things acquired through gambling. For there he says only this: that he who has lost and paid what was prohibited by the law of games can recover it before the judge's sentence if he can. The reason for this is far different, because the law of games is not penal; rather, Adrian thinks it hinders the transfer of ownership.

First, because it does not belong to them to judge regarding the **court of conscience**. <note>original: "foro conscientiæ"; the internal spiritual judgment of a person's soul before God, as opposed to a public legal court.</note> Second, because among the ancients, this was the opinion of **Panormitanus** alone. For **Felinus** and others embrace it for no other reason than that he said it. Therefore, there is no need to cite more: for by naming one, you have counted them all. And by this also is revealed the weakness of the argument made against us: namely, that if only a sentence is required as a declaration of the crime, why must the defendant—to whom the crime is perfectly well known—wait for the sentence before being bound to return his goods? For these people are always stuck in the same **pitfall** <note>original: "falebra"; a trap or obstacle.</note>. # Question VI of the First Book

<margin>Johannes Andreae</margin>
...the nation of the Church. This is the assertion of Johannes Andreae <note>Johannes Andreae (c. 1270–1348) was a celebrated Italian canonist, often called the "fountain and trumpet of canon law."</note> in the section *According to the laws*. But there is no
<margin>Proof.</margin>

I say this if the heretic sold or donated, etc. For if he bought food and clothing without fraud, such payments are not reclaimed from the sellers, because by **natural law** <note>original: "iure naturæ"; the moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> he was allowed to sustain his own life. Their dilemma is therefore this: either the heretic was deprived of the **ownership** <note>original: "dominio"; legal title or control.</note> of his goods from the moment of the committed crime, or he was not. If you grant the former, then he was deprived of it **by the act itself** <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> before the judge’s sentence. But if he was truly the owner until the sentence, it could not be brought about by the sentence that he *had not been* the owner, because there is no power over the past. If the sentence cannot do that, it follows that it could not render those contracts void which were celebrated by the free will of the heretic while he was the owner; for they were confirmed in good faith by the will of the true owner. Therefore, it cannot rescind contracts in such a way that buyers are defrauded of their price. For one who buys from a legal possessor has no reason to lose his payment. But certainly, this argument is not of as much weight as its authors estimate.

For example, the holder of an entailed estate, or a minor before the legal age, or a college or a convent of monks—although they are owners of their goods, they are nevertheless bound by law so that they cannot alienate them. If they do so, the contracts are not valid and are considered void.

# Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

...according to the divine <note>original: "divos"; a traditional Roman title for deceased emperors.</note> **Severus** and **Antoninus**. He can neither manumit <note>to legally grant a slave their freedom.</note> slaves from another's property, nor are debtors bound to pay him. ¶ One thing must be noted and warned of here: that where a judge interrogates some wrongdoer who is either marked by infamy, or suggested by evidence, or by a previous half-full proof <note>original: "semiplena probatione"; a legal term for evidence that is suggestive of guilt but not sufficient for conviction on its own.</note>, and that person denies it—since they were already bound then to confess, and therefore impeded the judgment through injustice—they would then become guilty of the penalty for which they ought to have been justly condemned. However, if a treasury official <note>original: "fiscalis"; an officer of the state or church treasury.</note>—while he alone knew of a crime that he could not prove, and the person was not yet marked by infamy—were to secretly seize the heretic’s goods (which is another argument of the opposing side), he would certainly act against the law and be held to **restitution**.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ But lest this be missed in the present discussion, let us also apply the same general conclusion concerning the sentence of the judge. Whenever a judge, by a just and lawful sentence, condemns a defendant to a penalty that does not involve death or the infliction of bodily injury, the defendant is bound to obey, even if he must perform some act: such as paying money, or going into exile, or remaining in prison, even perpetually. It is different, however, if he is sentenced to **corporal punishment**. For then he is only bound to endure it; he is not at all bound to perform the act of punishment himself.

<margin>Proof of the first part.</margin>
The first part is clear from the fact that everyone owes obedience to the powers that be, unless excused by some divine or natural law; but in that case, there is no excuse. Therefore, no other executor of the law is required than the judge himself pronouncing the sentence: for that, where it does not involve corporal punishment, is the legitimate execution.

<margin>Proof of the other part.</margin>
The latter part is proved by the contrary reasoning. For the **law of nature** granted to us to protect our own life holds us excused, so that no obedience can compel us to lay vengeful hands upon ourselves.

<margin>Cajetan is defended.</margin>
Nor will I neglect here to defend **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note>, to whom it is falsely attributed that he denied in article 3, question 60 of the *Secunda Secundae* that after someone has been condemned by a judge to a monetary fine, they are bound to pay it. Indeed, he never denied that, but rather that no one can be condemned to this by the law *ipso facto* <note>original: "ipso facto"; by the very fact itself, or automatically.</note>, nor absolutely to that which requires his own action. Therefore, he in no way contradicts himself when in question 69, article 4, he says that one who is condemned to either go into exile or pay a fine is bound to sincerely comply.

<margin>A false reason for the preceding conclusion.</margin>
¶ Nor do I think this should be passed over in silence: that the reason why no one can be condemned to either kill himself or inflict other punishment upon himself is not because "no one is the master of his own life." For it would be ridiculous if you raised this reason to a judge while he was ordering you to do it. For he would have this response ready:

<column-break/>

"I do not command you to kill yourself because you are the master of your life, but because **I have the power and judgment over it**." For an executioner has no more mastery over a defendant than the defendant has over himself; and yet, by the judge's authority, he kills him.

<margin>The true reason for the same conclusion.</margin>
The reason, therefore, why no one can be so bound is that he cannot be deprived of that **natural benefit** which a human has to protect his own life. For this reason, although no one may violently resist in such a case, he cannot be prevented from guarding against death either by fleeing or by some other way. Because of this, when a punishment is of the kind that people are accustomed to take upon themselves for the sake of religion and penance, it would oppose no law; even if a superior in a religious order commanded a monk, or a Bishop a priest, that he should take it up with his own hands: for example, that he should be struck by a whip by his own hand.

¶ It remains, therefore, to respond to the series of arguments, which is both long and entangled with difficult knots.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The first has already been resolved. For even if the law binds as much to punishment as to fault, it does so in different ways. Since it is a rule, by the very fact that someone deviates from it, they sin: for **fault** <note>original: "culpa"; moral guilt or sin.</note> is nothing other than a deviation from the law which is derived from the eternal and divine law. But the law binds to punishment by establishing it: and in this sense, the power of the law is said to punish. However, applying the punishment belongs to the judge.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is answered that although the obligation to punishment does not emerge before the judge's sentence, it does not follow that the judge has greater power than the law: both because the judge works as a **minister of the law** through its power, and most especially because the law of itself binds to fault. But it only follows that the punitive power of the law does not reach the defendant except through the mystery of its minister. For this reason, the judge is called by **Aristotle** "living justice." <note>original: "iustum animatum"; literally "animated justice," referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> As for what is added at the end of the argument regarding each person's will, through which a man can transfer ownership of his goods, it is irrelevant. For everyone has free faculty over their own things so that they can bind themselves of their own accord; the state, however, cannot do so except through prescribed forms and methods—namely, so that when you stand as a rebel against the law, you can be compelled by a judge.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the divine laws brought forward in the third argument, no valid argument is built against us. For the woman who suffered from a flow of blood <note>A reference to the biblical story in the Gospels.</note> was bound by the law of nature to abstain from her husband lest she infect him with disease, even though the flow was not a fault...
unclean...

He clarifies that judges act as the "living voice" or ministers of the law, not as powers superior to it.</summary>

### Book One, Question VI.

Legal impurity <note>original: "immundities legalis"; referring to the ritual "uncleanness" described in the Old Testament which required specific purification rituals.</note>, however, for those who recognized it, was contracted through the fault itself. Therefore, just as someone who sins today is defiled by that very act and is bound to make satisfaction through the fruits of penance, so it was for those defiled in ancient times. For those physical things were symbols <note>original: "figura"; a "figure" or foreshadowing of a spiritual reality.</note> of our spiritual states. <margin>Toward confirmations of the same argument.</margin> ¶ From this, the response to the divine laws—which established various ceremonies of sacrifice and purification for various sins—becomes clear. For God, against whom the offense is committed, can demand whatever satisfaction He wishes; the sinner is then bound to pay it without any other judgment. By the same reasoning, the Church today can institute fasts, almsgiving, and prayers, through which each person is bound to expiate their own sins. As for what was added regarding lepers, it is irrelevant: for by the law of nature, those with deadly diseases are bound to withdraw from the company of others so as not to infect them with contagion, even though the disease is not a fault and such withdrawal is not a punishment.

¶ Nor does the Gospel's permission for a husband to separate his bed from an adulteress weigh against us. That separation is not to be regarded strictly as a punishment, but rather as a contractual license arising from the spouse's broken faith. For there is a pact between spouses, with faith given and accepted by both, that each shall keep the other’s bed unstained. Therefore, when one has broken their faith, the other is free from the bond of paying the marital debt <note>the traditional obligation of spouses to be sexually available to one another.</note> to them. Just as if I promised you my labor on the condition that you pledged yours to me: if you fail your word, I am no longer bound to stand by mine. <margin>To the fourth argument and its parts.</margin> ¶ And in almost the same way, one responds to all parts of the fourth argument. First, regarding the man who left a legacy to his wife under a certain condition: this is far from our current purpose. There was no need for <margin>Cajetan.</margin> **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> in his *Summary* under the word "punishment" <note>original: "Summa verb. pœna".</note> to make such an exception, since a condition of that sort is by no means a penal law. For the deceased, if he was a private person, could not establish a law; rather, it is a conditional contract of the type "I give so that you may do" <note>original: "Do ut facias"; a standard legal formula for a reciprocal agreement.</note>. Because of this, if you do not fulfill the condition, you are bound to restore to me what is mine.

¶ The response to the second part is similar. Truly, a person who establishes a college with his own wealth <margin>Founders of colleges.</margin> could make statutes stating that if any of the members stayed out overnight, or married, or did anything else, they would by that very fact <note>original: "ipso facto".</note> lose their rights in the college in their own conscience. Such a law would indeed have force in the conscience, because the founder was able, if he pleased, to bestow his goods under that condition. 

<column-break/>

Though, truth be told, I would advise no one to establish such laws, for they are snares for consciences. This is, as the saying goes, to "draw blood by squeezing the nose too hard" <note>original: "nimium emungendo sanguinem elicere"; a proverb meaning to push a rule so far it becomes harmful or cruel.</note>. For the welfare of the community is sufficiently cared for if these particular laws are established like general ones—namely, that offenders are punished when they are caught through the normal course of justice. But because the negligence of superiors is often presumed, this kind of rigor is permitted.

¶ Furthermore, a similar response applies to the <margin>To the third part.</margin> third part regarding the laws by which Kings are accustomed to "bind the hands" of justice officials so that they do not take bribes. Indeed, since the King chooses them of his own free will as his own ministers, and decrees salaries for them from his own treasury, and pays them their rights by his own mandate, he can choose them on the condition that they are bound in conscience to pay the penalties for their own crimes. Therefore, if they choose to accept the condition, they are bound to fulfill it. And for that reason, they are bound by an oath, because otherwise the law itself could not compel them to punishment before a condemnation. 

However, as for that phrase "that they are bound in conscience to pay," I confess I cannot approve of it, because no example of it is found in common law. Secular princes should not judge matters of conscience. Nor indeed, in that "golden authority" <note>original: "aureo auct."; likely referring to a specific decree in the Justinian Code or the Novellae regarding judicial integrity.</note> stating that judges should be appointed without any bribery—which most sharply forbids the greed of judges—is there any mention of conscience. Nevertheless, where their corruption is so shameless, I would not altogether reject such legal rigor.

¶ Regarding the penal laws of our University <margin>The author's judgment on the penal laws of the University of Salamanca.</margin> <note>The University of Salamanca, where Soto taught.</note>, by which presenters and canvassers <note>original: "ambitores"; those who seek office or influence through illicit means or bribery.</note> or suborners are immediately <note>original: "ipso facto".</note> deprived of their right to vote, I have always judged that these do not bind in conscience to that penalty before a condemnation. The exception is the person who is already notorious <note>original: "infamia laborans"; suffering from a loss of legal standing or reputation.</note> for the matter and denies the truth when legally questioned. For in this case, I would judge them just as if they had been condemned, as was said above regarding the heretic. And I judge the same for other electors in Churches and colleges. In addition to the reasons declared above, there is another specific one here: otherwise, hardly any election would be safe, which would be most ruinous for the state. Therefore, if such laws claimed to bind the conscience before condemnation, they should not be tolerated, as they are dangerous.

¶ To the fifth argument, the response is that one <margin>To the fifth argument.</margin> must look closely at a law to see what truly has the nature of a penalty, and what has the nature of a price or some other thing. Indeed, when a law sets a price for grain or other merchandise, and adds a penalty for anyone who sells it more dearly, the person is bound in conscience by that very fact to restore the excess amount...

<margin>Regarding the other part of the same argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other part of the argument concerning the laws of prescription <note>original: "præscriptionis"; a legal principle where a right or liability is created or extinguished by the passage of time, such as gaining ownership of land by living on it for many years.</note>, the response is that such laws are not purely penal. Although it is a penalty for one who is negligent with their property to lose their right to it, these laws were primarily established for the sake of peace and to ensure that the paths to endless lawsuits are closed. For this reason, the prince has the power to transfer ownership. Therefore, the passing of the legal timeframe itself makes the good-faith possessor the owner of the thing without any judicial sentence. Consequently, no conclusion follows from this that a purely penal law expects a defendant to strip themselves of their own goods before the case has been heard.

<margin>Regarding the sixth argument.</margin>
¶ To the sixth argument, the response is that the distinction in that cited chapter between a penalty "by law" and a penalty "by man" is clear. A penalty "by law" <note>original: "pœna iuris"</note> is one which the law itself establishes and which a judge is bound to inflict unless there is a very obvious reason for mercy based on equity and goodness. A penalty "by man" <note>original: "pœna ab homine"</note>, however, is one which the judge imposes at his own discretion, either through his mandates or upon the defendant after a crime has been committed.

<margin>Regarding the seventh.</margin>
¶ To the seventh argument, it is answered that this is the difference between "monitory" laws <note>original: "leges monitorias"; laws that serve as a warning or notice</note> and others: the former say that "by the very fact" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> an emerald-colored disobedient person must not only be declared to have committed a crime, but must also be condemned to the penalty. When, however, someone has struck against the second type of law, it is enough if they are condemned for having transgressed them. For then, without any further explanation of a sentence, they are considered bound to the penalty.

¶ Regarding excommunication <note>original: "excommunicatione"; a church penalty excluding someone from the sacraments</note>, it has already been explained why it binds "by the very fact." However, suspension and "irregularity" <note>term: irregularity; a canonical impediment that prevents a person from receiving or exercising Holy Orders, often due to a "stain" like being involved in a death</term>—because they are nothing more than a certain contamination, defilement, and subsequent unworthiness (as we said in the previous article) for handling sacred things—are contracted by the very act of the fault. Indeed, they are sometimes contracted even without a fault, as is clear in the case of a judge who is the unintentional cause of a death. Therefore, these require no sentence from a judge.

<margin>Regarding the eighth.</margin>
¶ But regarding the laws cited in the eighth argument, I admit they apply a more stinging point. Nevertheless, the response is that in the cited chapter on homicide in Book 6 <note>original: "de homicid. li. 6."; referring to the *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law</note>, it is not simply held that he who incurs the crime of the Assassins <note>note: "Assassins" here refers to a specific legal category of professional or treacherous murderers mentioned in medieval law.</note> is bound to pay the penalty before a sentence, beyond the excommunication he suffers by the very fact. Rather, it says that after the crime has been established by probable arguments, no further sentence of excommunication or even deposition <note>original: "depositionis"; removal from office</note> is required. It is not denied, therefore, that

<column-break/>

a sentence is required regarding the crime itself. In fact, it is for this reason that the phrase is added: "after it has been established by probable arguments," that is, arguments by which the matter can be proven in a trial. For no private person can judge whether arguments are "probable" except for a judge alone.

<margin>Therefore, the "gloss" (interpretation) of those who say no other sentence is required is "sinister" (clumsy/wrong). Rather, the Archdeacon (as Sylvester says) more "dexterously" (correctly) judges that even then a declaratory sentence of the fact is required.</margin>
<margin>Archdeacon. Sylvester.</margin>
For this reason, the interpretation of those who say no other sentence is required is clumsy. Rather, the Archdeacon <note>original: "Archidia."; refers to the famous canonist Guido de Baysio</note> (as Sylvester <note>note: Sylvester Prierias, a prominent theologian and legal commentator.</note> notes) more correctly judges that even then a "declaratory sentence of the fact" is required. The text itself only says that a sentence regarding the penalty is not required. I am clearly convinced that this was the author's mind. The penalty for Assassins is also such that anyone may freely kill them; but truly, if this were permitted to a private individual before they were condemned for the crime, it would give anyone the opportunity to pretend this person or that person was an Assassin so that he might kill whomever he wished. Such license would be disastrous. Therefore, it is most certain that this is not permitted to anyone before a judge's sentence. Consequently, it is not lawful to strip them of their goods, or others who use their service, before that same sentence.

<margin>A final scruple.</margin>
¶ There remains, then, a final doubt from the "Extravagant" <note>note: *Extravagantes* were Papal decrees that "circulated outside" the standard early collections of Canon Law.</note> *Ambitiosae* of Paul II. There, it is held that a cleric who merely alienates <note>original: "alienauerit"; sells or transfers to someone else</note> the property of the Church is, by that very fact, deprived of his ecclesiastical benefices <note>term: benefice; a church office, like a parish, that provides an income to the priest</term>, and those offices are considered vacant without any declaration.

<margin>First resolution.</margin>
But in truth, a very strong argument for our side stands first from these words. For the Supreme Pontiff, by expressing that a declaration is not necessary in this case, openly shows that if he had not added this word, it would not have been enough for him to say "by the very fact" for the defendant to be bound in conscience to leave his benefices before a sentence. This is what we have been striving to establish up to this point.

<margin>Second resolution.</margin>
Secondly, it is answered in the same way we spoke concerning a prince: he is able to deprive whomever he chooses if that person acts against a condition he agreed upon. For example, if he accepted gifts. Indeed, since the Supreme Pontiff is the grantor and dispenser of benefices, he declares through that decree that every priest receives the church's priesthood under that law and tacit condition: that if he should alienate its goods, he is considered deprived of those same priesthoods. Nevertheless, I do not know whether even then some declaration regarding the crime should be required for the sake of quieting consciences. However, regarding this, I refer to ecclesiastical practice.

# Book One, Question VI. #

### ARTICLE VII. ###
### Whether everyone is subject to the law. ###

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
As we continue to examine the authority and power of the law, it remains to be asked in this seventh place whether everyone is subject to the law. The argument for the negative side is drawn <margin>Paul.</margin> from the Apostle in 1 Timothy 1: "The law is not laid down for the righteous." <margin>Urban.</margin> This is confirmed by Pope Urban in the legal collections <note>original: "19. q. 2. Canon. Duæ sunt"; referring to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of canon law.</note>, where he says that for one who is led by a "private law" (namely, that of the Holy Spirit), no reason requires him to be constrained by "public law"—that is, human law, which is established for the community. Therefore, not everyone is bound by the law. ¶ <margin>Second argument.</margin> Secondly, the civil law itself supports this in the section regarding the status of the ruler <note>original: "lex, princeps. ff. de legū."; a reference to the Digest of Justinian, specifically the famous dictum "Princeps legibus solutus est."</note> <margin>Ulpian.</margin> where the legal expert Ulpian says that "the prince is released from the laws." <margin>Paul.</margin> ¶ On the contrary is what the Apostle says in Romans 13: "Let every soul be subject to the higher powers." But no one is subject to a power unless they are subject to its laws.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The present question will be satisfied by three conclusions based on the two powers of the law. For it has already been shown above that the law is both a rule for directing actions <term>directive power (vis directiva)</term> and a force for compelling obedience <term>coercive power (vis coërciva)</term>. A person can be submitted to the law in both ways. Therefore, let the first conclusion be: All who are subject to a power are consequently subject to its laws; indeed, even the prince is subject to the law in regards to its directing power. <margin>The conclusion is proven.</margin> The matter is clear: for to be subject to another is the same as obeying their commands, and consequently their laws. We will speak of the prince shortly. I say "all subjects" because those who are foreigners are not included under someone's law. Indeed, the law of the French has nothing to do with the Spaniards. Furthermore, if any are exempted from a lower authority by the privilege of a higher one, they are not submitted to the lower authority's command insofar as that privilege extends. <margin>Corollary.</margin> For this reason, clerics are not subject to secular laws, especially when the law decrees matters concerning Church affairs which are not subject to princes (as is clear in the chapter "Ecclesia" on constitutions), or if the law was established out of hatred for the Clergy, or if it does not apply to Clerics with equal right. For example, a prohibition on wearing silk does not prevent them from wearing such fabrics during sacred rites. And a prohibition against citizens riding mules (intended to make them into warriors) has nothing to do with priests. However, laws regarding the pri-

<column-break/>

-ces of goods, and ensuring that merchandise is not diverted from the kingdom, and others of that kind, bind Clerics and secular people equally. On this matter, consult the summary writers under the entries for "law" and "Cleric." <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ Second conclusion: Regarding the coercive power of the law, the righteous who are led by the habits of virtue are not subject to the law, because they perform nothing by force in matters of virtue, but rather <margin>Proof.</margin> do everything of their own accord. Indeed, as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle testifies in the 2nd book of the *Ethics*, virtue causes a studious person to act promptly and with delight. ¶ <margin>Third conclusion.</margin> To this, we add a third conclusion similar to it: The prince is not subject to the law regarding its coercive power. <margin>Proof.</margin> The conclusion is obvious: because coercion cannot be directed by the same person toward themselves. It is not intellectually possible for someone to apply force to themselves, and thus to compel themselves by their own law. For this reason, the meaning of that Royal word—"Against you only have I sinned" <note>A quote from Psalm 51, attributed to King David.</note>—is a single and significant one: that he recognized God alone as his superior there. It is as if he had said: "On earth I have no one to whom I owe an account for my errors, and therefore I have sinned against you alone." (Though there is also another genuine meaning: that no evil would be a sin, except that it is against the law of God). <margin>Reason for the difference between the second and third conclusions.</margin> Therefore, the reasoning for these similar conclusions is different. For the fact that a righteous man is not subject to the law is taken from the man himself, who certainly does not need coercion. This conclusion is understood not to refer to just any righteous people, but to those of perfected virtue. For as long as the struggle with our passions persists, the fear of punishment lasts alongside it, and thus some reason for coercion remains. This second conclusion is so supported by the testimony of Paul that it did not escape the notice of the Philosophers. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle says in the 10th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 9, that laws are entirely necessary throughout life for this reason: the multitude obeys necessity and punishments rather than honor. Therefore, legislators ought to encourage people toward virtue for the sake of honor; for those who are good will obey primarily because of habit. Against the disobedient and those of duller wit, however, they must institute corrections and punishments. And in the 5th book of the *Politics*, chapter 9, he says: "Those excellent in virtue and power are not to be bound by laws." This can refer to both the second and third conclusions: namely, that virtue refers to moral goodness, while power refers to the leadership. "But they," he says, "are themselves the law, and for that reason should be esteemed as Gods among men." <margin>Reason for the third conclusion.</margin> However, the fact that the law does not compel its own prince does not come from the idea that he does not need it, but that the law naturally...

...by his own nature. But indeed, princes ought not to consider this exemption among their privileges; rather, it is an unfair condition for them. For subjects, who are not only guided by the light of the law but also spurred on by its punishments, make use of two aids toward virtue. The prince, however, is destitute of one of these, since there is no one who can compel him or dare to rebuke him; indeed, there is hardly anyone who might teach him the truth. For this reason, <margin>A beautiful interpretation of a sacred passage.</margin> that passage in Proverbs 21: *Just as the divisions of waters, so is the heart of the King in the hand of the Lord*, has this correct sense: that while the hearts of private citizens are in the hand of God in such a way that He governs and compels them through His ministers of justice, the heart of the King is placed in the divine hands alone. <margin>An appropriate comparison.</margin> Just as God alone could divert a huge and rapid river, contrary to its nature, in a direction other than where its channel leads, so only He can hold back the King—who is a slave to his own will—or turn his mind toward another path.

<margin>Wholesome counsel.</margin> Therefore, the **King**, to the extent that God has made him more free and more exempt from the compulsion of the laws, ought himself to be all the more vigilant toward reason and obedient to the divine will. He should, as a result, listen to the laws he sets for others, lest he stumble into that reproach of Christ: *They who say and do not do, and who lay heavy burdens on others but will not move them with even a finger* <note>original: "Qui dicunt & non faciunt... Matth. 23." Referring to Jesus's criticism of the Pharisees in Matthew 23:3-4.</note>. Hence, in the section on constitutions <note>original: "extra, de cõsti. c. ¶ But the whole difficulty of the matter is not yet exhausted. For we have established our first conclusion generally, so that it includes both the righteous and the prince himself, who, like the rest, are bound by the **directive force** <term>directive force: the power of a law to guide the conscience and reason of a person, as opposed to "coercive force," which is the power to punish.</term> of the laws. Truly, although the prince is not a subject to himself, nothing prevents him from submitting himself to his own law; for while he enlightens others, he also provides light for himself. Yet this is not <margin>A doubt.</margin> without doubt regarding how it is understood. For it seems to contradict itself that a prince should be subject to the law without being compelled by the law. The Pope makes laws concerning fasting, hearing the sacred rites, and annual confession, and these under penalty of excommunication. And the Emperor likewise forbids anyone from committing perjury under a certain penalty. You argue therefore as follows: <margin>First reason for doubting.</margin> If the prince is subject to the law as far as its directive force is concerned, it follows that when he transgresses it, he sins; therefore, it binds him. But an obligation is a <margin>Second reason.</margin> **coercive force**. ¶ Secondly, if you exclude the coercive force from the law, you have removed the very nature of law. For

<column-break/>

(as was defined above) laws can be established by the person acting on behalf of the commonwealth precisely because they are not laws without coercive force. Therefore, if the prince is not subject to the coercion of the law, he is not subject to the law at all. Instead, he might follow it as if it were the opinion of some wise man—say, Plato or Seneca—which does not bind one to guilt; or just as his law might bind foreigners who are not under his jurisdiction, and we might choose to listen to the decrees of the French. ¶ Thirdly, it is asked <margin>Third reason.</margin> by whom the prince is bound when he establishes a law. It is not by God, because that law is not divine; nor is it by himself, because the law itself is not a vow, by which men are usually bound. And to make the argument stronger, let us suppose he does not wish to be bound by his own law.

¶ Although these arguments attack the conclusion, they do not defeat it. <margin>The recent doubt is dissolved.</margin> For it must first be considered that the prince is not outside the commonwealth, but a member <margin>First lesson.</margin> of it—specifically, the head. Secondly, it should be recalled from what was said earlier that human law binds <margin>The first principal conclusion is proven again.</margin> in conscience because it is derived from the eternal law through the natural law. From these points, the obligatory force can be immediately deduced. Specifically, from that natural principle: *The right you do not wish for yourself, do not establish for another.* <note>A variation of the Golden Rule: "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you."</note> For Christ rebukes the opposite, saying: *They impose burdens on others which they themselves do not touch.* Because the prince establishes a law, he is submitted to it by natural law.

But perhaps it is more clearly deduced this way: A **legislator** (as has been said), in creating a law, constitutes an act within a certain species of virtue. For example, when the Pope brings forth a law of fasting, he establishes that act as the obligatory virtue of abstinence; and when he commands the keeping of some feast, he places it within the virtue of religion. Once the work of virtue is established, the whole commonwealth, and thus the head itself, is bound to act according to it. If you should ask why <margin>A question.</margin> punishment does not then <margin>The solution.</margin> compel the prince, notice the wide distinction. Because the law is a rule, it follows that a deflection from it is a fault (a sin) even without any further execution or application of the law. Punishment, however, is applied to the law for the sake of its observation, and therefore requires execution and application. But the executor is the prince himself, and it is contradictory for him to compel himself—though he can pay the penalty if he wishes. ¶ When we establish that the prince is subject to his own laws, we mean those laws that apply equally to him as to his subjects. If the King commands that no one walk about girt with a sword or dressed in silk, there is no equal reason why he should abstain from these. But if the Pope ordains a fast or the solemnity of a feast, the same equity applies to him, unless for a just cause he...

He supports this using the natural law principle of equity: a ruler should not impose burdens on others that he is unwilling to bear himself.</summary>

### ARTICLE VIII.
#### *Whether it is lawful for a subject to act beyond the words of the law.*

Postremus articulus virtutis legis est, vtrū omnis epieikeia sit subditis interdicta, an verò liceat subdito contra verba legis agere. Et arguitur quòd nemini subditorum id liceat. Ait enim Augusti.
The final article regarding the power of the law is whether all <term>epieikeia</term><note>A Greek term (ἐπιείκεια) meaning "equity" or "reasonableness"—the idea that one should follow the intent of a law when the literal words would cause an injustice.</note> is forbidden to subjects, or whether it is lawful for a subject to act against the literal words of the law. <margin>*The first argument. Augustine.*</margin>

However, he who disregards the words of the law, thinking he is serving the legislator's intention, seems to be judging the law; therefore, this is not permitted to subjects. ¶ Secondly: The role of 
<margin>*The second argument.*</margin>
interpreting the laws belongs entirely to the one who is their founder. But only the prince can found laws; therefore, it is free for no one else to interpret them, but only to act according to them. ¶ Thirdly: Those who founded the laws 
<margin>*The third argument.*</margin>
must be considered to have been enlightened by the light of wisdom, of which Proverbs 8 says: "By me kings reign and the founders of laws decree just things." Therefore, it is not permitted to judge the intention of the legislator in any way other than through the words of the law. ¶ On the contrary, however, is Hilary in Book 13 *On the Trinity*: <note>original: "Intelligentia dictorum ex causis est assumenda dicendi: quia non sermoni res, sed rei debet esse sermo subiectus."</note> "The understanding of things said must be derived from the reasons for saying them: because the matter should not be subject to the speech, but the speech to the matter." From these words, it is gathered that it is more prudent to attend to the cause that moved the legislators than to the mere words of the law.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Article VIII, focusing on the interpretation of the law's spirit (equity) versus its literal wording. It builds on the previous page's refutation of Luther's absolute freedom by establishing a structured legal framework for when a citizen may—or may not—disregard the literal text of a law in favor of its intended purpose.</meta>

->## On Justice and Right, by Domingo de Soto<-

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
...nevertheless, in a case where the law is known to oppose the common welfare, it is not to be observed. The example given by <term>St. Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto and the School of Salamanca.</note> is this: during the siege of a city, it is beneficial for the common safety that a law forbids the gates to be opened. Nonetheless, if citizens whose lives are vital to the safety of the commonwealth are fleeing enemies and wish to be received into the city, the gates must be opened to them despite the literal words of the law. This is because such is the "mind" or intent of the law; if the lawmaker were present, he would surely allow it. This conclusion follows directly from the first.

<margin>A conclusion is drawn from the previous one.</margin>
Indeed, as was stated above, the law is established for the general good because it cannot sufficiently foresee every particular case. This is held in the civil laws <note>original: "l. Neque leges. & .l. Non possunt. ff. de legib." Refers to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law.</note> "Neither laws" and "They cannot." It follows, then, that whenever a case occurs which the lawmaker would have judged as an exception had he foreseen it, the law should not be observed.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The third conclusion.** Notwithstanding these two assertions, the practice of <term>epieikeia</term><note>A Greek term (ἐπιείκεια) usually translated as "equity." it refers to the interpretation of a law according to its spirit and the common good when the literal application would be unjust.</note> (equity) in such a law belongs by custom and order to the Prince alone, except in those cases where a sudden danger is so pressing that if one had to wait to consult the Prince or his representative, damage would be feared in the meantime. In such a case, it is permitted for a subject to act against the words of the law. Truly, that is "necessity, which has no law."

<margin>Doubt concerning the second conclusion.</margin>
¶ However, while nothing doubtful hides in the first conclusion, there is some doubt in the second. For St. Thomas seems to constrain it too much when he says that only in that specific case where the observation of the law would lead to the destruction of the "common safety" should it not be observed—for it should also not be followed if it leads to private destruction.

<margin>The reason for hesitating.</margin>
For anyone to whom it was clear that observing the law would be fatal to himself, and it was certain from the nature of the law that it was not the lawmaker's intent to drive subjects into such danger, that person is in no way bound to keep the law. For example, if it were certain to me that enemies had prepared an ambush for me on the road, I am not bound to go to Mass on a holy day.

<margin>St. Thomas is explained. The solution.</margin>
The response is that St. Thomas does not deny this, but he is speaking of the danger to the commonwealth. For a besieged city is not bound to open its gates to every single fleeing citizen if it brings danger to itself; therefore, it is not lawful for the gatekeeper to open them. Indeed, even if there were persons very useful for defending the city, if it were certain that a troop of enemies would rush in with them and capture the city, they are not bound to open the gates. It is otherwise where there is not such great danger; for then, in the face of imminent peril, the gatekeeper himself could open them.

<margin>Objection to the third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion, however, is not quite so clear. For while it asserts that a subject may act against the law without consulting a magistrate when danger is suddenly imminent, some argue that he must still seek recourse. This applies whether the subject is unsure of the law's intent, or whether he is absolutely certain. It does not apply when he remains in doubt; for then (as Thomas says in the solution to the second point) he must follow the words of the law without any interpretation.

<column-break/>

However, when he is entirely certain, even if there is no danger in delay, he is not bound to consult a <term>Prelate</term><note>A high-ranking religious superior or administrative official.</note>. For someone who, on a fast day, has no other food available but meat, may eat it without any consultation of a superior so that he does not perish from hunger—even if he could approach the superior without danger.

<margin>The solution. Cajetan.</margin>
¶ To understand this matter, although <term>Cajetan</term><note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> distinguishes four parts here, a three-part division would be more perceptive.

<margin>Three-part division.</margin>
Either it is clearly evident to the subject (for it is of the subject we speak) in the occurring case that it is not the mind of the law that it be observed, and

<margin>The first part.</margin>
then no further subdivision is needed: whether the danger is sudden or there is time enough to go to the prefect, it is permitted to act against the law without his counsel at all, as is clear from the cases we just explained.

<margin>The second part.</margin>
Or, on the other extreme, such a subject remains in equal doubt on both sides. Thus, he has the assent of neither side as to whether it is lawful to act against the law or not. In that case, if there is time to have recourse to a superior, he must do so; but if sudden danger does not permit it, the law must be followed to the letter. This is the case St. Thomas describes in the second solution, because a subject is not permitted to interpret the law in such a case.

<margin>The third part.</margin>
But if he holds a middle path, such that he is neither entirely certain nor entirely doubtful, but leans toward the side that he can act against the law—meaning he holds that opinion but with a fear of the opposite—then if a delay is granted by which he can consult the magistrate, he is bound to do so. But if it is not permitted due to sudden danger, he can safely act against the law. This is the case of the third conclusion.

<margin>An incidental question.</margin>
¶ Now, if you ask whether it is a sufficient reason for equity (epieikeia) that a subject acts against the law simply because the "reason" for the law fails in his particular person and case:

<margin>The response.</margin>
The response is that if the reason fails only in the particular, it is not enough. However, if the cause has ceased for the entire category or class of things, then the law also ought to cease. Nevertheless, until the Prince or custom abrogates it, it does not lose its force. For example, the law cautions that no one should carry weapons at night. Therefore, no matter how peaceful you are and though no danger of a fight is feared from you, you cannot act against the law. However, because...

Soto provides a three-part framework for navigating cases of certainty and doubt regarding legal interpretation.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on equity (Article VIII of the previous question) and begins Question VII regarding the mutability of human laws. It transitions from how to interpret the spirit of a law to whether the laws themselves should be periodically updated.</meta>

<header>Book One, Question VII.</header>
<sig>e 5</sig>

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
The <term>Holy Doctor</term><note>A title for St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), whose *Summa Theologiae* serves as the basis for this commentary.</note> discusses <term>equity</term><note>original: "epieikeia"</note> elsewhere, specifically in the *Secunda Secundae*, Question 102; we would be "dancing outside the choir" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to wander off-topic or speak out of turn.</note> if a longer discussion delayed us here. 

<margin>First thing to be noted.</margin>
However, these points are specifically to be noted here. First: although it is sometimes permitted, because of equity, to act against the literal words of the law in favor of its intent, conversely, outside of such cases, to observe the mere "shell" of the words while the intent of the law is corrupted is a betrayal of the law. For so the law holds in the <term>Digest</term><note>original: "ff. de legi." Refers to the *Pandects* or *Digest*, a massive collection of Roman juristic writings compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> regarding laws: "One acts in fraud of the law who, while preserving the words of the law, evades its meaning." And in the following law: "Fraud is committed against the law when that which the law did not want to happen is done, yet the law did not specifically forbid it." 

<margin>Example.</margin>
The law prohibits an adulterer from appointing an illegitimate son as his heir; therefore, to grant the inheritance to another person who then gives it to the son is to observe the words of the law, but not its intent. Another law prohibits a priest from resigning a <term>benefice</term><note>An ecclesiastical office that provided a steady income.</note> in favor of his own son; but if one confers it upon the son of another so that the other may repay the favor for his own son, this is an iniquity directly opposed to equity.

Through these points, the solutions to the arguments become clear. 

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first, it is answered that he who acts against the words of the law in that final case of necessity does not judge the law itself, but the singular case, in which he perceives the law is not to be observed. 

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And in like manner, it is answered to the second. For in this case, the subject does not interpret the law in a general sense, but in a specific case where it is manifest that the lawmaker intended otherwise; it is different if he hesitates in doubt, as was said regarding the second case. 

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is answered that no matter how great the wisdom of lawmakers, it is never enough for them to foresee all occurring cases.

# QUESTION SEVEN, on the change and variety of human law.
### St. Thomas, *Prima Secundae*, Question 97.
## ARTICLE I.

->Whether human law ought to be changed in any way.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing floral and scrolling foliate motifs.</image-desc>

THE FINAL QUESTION regarding human law is to explain how firm and fixed it ought to be. Therefore, we first ask whether it should be changed in any way. 

<margin>First reason for the negative side.</margin>
It appears that this is by no means permitted: for human law

<column-break/>

(as we said above) is derived from the natural law; the natural law is immutable; therefore, so is human law. 

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Secondly, this is gathered from the nature of a rule, which is what a law is; according to Aristotle in the <term>Ethics</term><note>original: "5. Ethico. cap. 5." Referring to Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note>, a rule 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
ought to be solid and standing; law is a rule, therefore it is immobile. 

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, law must be just and right; but what is once just remains so forever. 

<margin>Confirmation. Pope Nicholas.</margin>
¶ There is also the testimony of Pope Nicholas, <term>Distinction 12</term><note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the foundation of medieval Canon Law.</note>: "It is ridiculous and a quite abominable disgrace that we should allow the traditions which we received from the fathers of old to be broken." 

<margin>First argument for the negative.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, the arguments are no fewer. Reason seems to demand that whenever something better is discovered, the human law should be changed accordingly. Indeed, human laws, like other arts, were thought out and invented by human reason; but other arts are changed when something better occurs; therefore, the same should be observed in laws. 

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, the reasoning of the past should be taken into account as a precaution for the future; however, it happens that ancient laws are cruder and less refined than is suitable for succeeding customs; therefore, unless old laws were updated whenever better inventions occurred, it would be an inconvenience. 

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, because human laws deal with the slippery flow of individual circumstances, they cannot be exactly established except through the experience of time. For experience (as 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle is the author in Book 2 of the *Ethics*) requires time; therefore, whenever the passage of time brings something better, it is expedient for laws to be changed. 

<margin>Final argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, there is the addition of Augustine in Book 1 of *On Free Will*, where he says: "Temporal law, although it is just, can nevertheless be justly changed over time."

The arguments of the present question pull the matter toward two different extremes. For those of the first order contend that human law is entirely immutable. The others, through the opposite extreme, argue that they should be changed wherever something better occurs. Therefore, the answer must be given in two conclusions, by which we may moderate both extremes. 

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ The first is: it is sometimes lawful, fitting, and holy for human law to be changed. The truth of this conclusion 

<margin>The conclusion is argued in two ways.</margin>
arises from two roots: namely, from the nature of the human reason by which laws are established, and from the nature of our actions regarding which they are decreed. 

<margin>First reason.</margin>
For since our nature is rational—that is, discursive and a seeker of truth by a certain progression—it cannot, like an intellectual angel who
