<meta>Continuity: This page continues Question VII on the mutability of human laws, moving from the philosophical justification for changing laws to the prudential reasons for maintaining legal stability.</meta>

...knows all natural things at once, and suddenly penetrates the depths of truth. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Thus, just as in the study of sciences, over the passage of time, philosophers advanced from the imperfect to the perfect—as evidenced by Aristotle in the first book of the *Physics*, the first book of *On the Soul*, and other books—so too does practical reason operate in the composition of morals. Therefore, just as Thales of Miletus and the other <term>Seven Sages</term><note>A group of 6th-century BC Greek philosophers and statesmen famous for their foundational wisdom.</note> of that age began to polish the sciences (which until then were crude and unrefined) and which Plato and Aristotle later perfected, so too did Lycurgus, Solon, and among the Romans, <term>Numa Pompilius</term><note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious and political institutions.</note>, establish their republics—previously barbaric and rustic—with more refined laws. These laws were thereafter cultivated more precisely, accurately, and cleanly as time progressed.

<margin>Second reason.</margin> There is a second reason based on the condition of our actions: these are so subject to the diversity of regions and times that they never remain in the same state. <margin>Augustine</margin> An example is found in Augustine, Book 1 of *On Free Choice of the Will*, where he says that if a people is well-moderated, grave, and a most diligent guardian of the common utility, a law is rightly passed allowing such a people to create their own magistrates through whom the republic may be administered. Furthermore, if that people gradually becomes depraved and sells its votes, committing the government to shameful and wicked men, such power to grant honors is rightly taken away from the people and returns to the judgment of a few good men. 

<margin>Second Conclusion. St. Thomas.</margin> The second conclusion, which <term>St. Thomas</term><note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text.</note> established most holistically and which ought to be most clearly understood by legislators, is: A law must not be changed for just any cause that offers some improvement, but only when the improvement is so excellent that it compensates for the damages and losses that the changing of a law naturally brings.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> The reasoning for the conclusion is as follows. Since human laws are established for the common utility and safety (as has been said), they must be changed for the exact same reason: namely, when the change results in an increase of the common good. However, a change, by its very nature, brings harm; for when the custom of observing a law has, in a sense, turned into nature—since custom is a "second nature"—the very change of the law is a kind of change of nature. Thus it happens that things done against custom are considered serious, even when they are minor. For the same reason, the venerable "gray hair" of the law holds human minds through love; when this is extinguished, the novelty of another law brings with it a certain degree of resentment. Therefore, when the change of a law is being considered,

<column-break/>

these things must be weighed in the balance: namely, that it should not be changed unless such a great cause weighs in from that side as to be able to compensate for these evils. This occurs entirely when either the greatest and most evident utility comes from the new law, or a massive necessity compels the abolishing of a customary law because of its manifest injustice. Hence, in the <term>Digest</term><note>A collection of Roman juristic writings; the specific citation is *ff. de const. prin. l. 2*.</note>, in the section *Concerning the Constitutions of Princes*, law 2, Ulpian says: "In establishing new things, the utility ought to be evident so that one may depart from that law which has long seemed equitable."

<margin>The rule should be observed both in the secular and in the Ecclesiastical republic.</margin> This rule, therefore, ought to be most strictly observed both in the secular republic and especially in the Ecclesiastical one, particularly in matters pertaining to sacred things. Namely, the method of performing the <term>Office</term><note>The Daily Office or Liturgy of the Hours: the official set of prayers (psalms, hymns, readings) recited at fixed times by clergy and monastics.</note> to which the clergy are accustomed should not be changed for just any reason, even if it seems excellent. And much less should the method of sacred rites be changed in matters concerning divine worship, upon which the people have their eyes fixed and their hearts set. For this could hardly be done without loss and scandal. One must not murmur against the novelty of the <term>Breviary</term><note>The book containing the text of the Divine Office. De Soto refers to 16th-century debates over liturgical reform.</note> since the most holy Pope permits it; however, the purpose for which the change was made—namely, so that those paying the fixed hours might learn the <term>Psalter</term> by heart—is not the one the Holy Fathers prescribed for the saying of the <term>Canonical Hours</term>.

<margin>Ecclesiastical chant was instituted not for the sake of study, but only for divine praises.</margin> Ecclesiastical chants were instituted not for the sake of study, but only for divine praise, so that the melody of the <term>Church Militant</term><note>The Christian church on earth, struggling against sin.</note> might be established in the likeness of the <term>Church Triumphant</term><note>The church in heaven.</note>. There, they do not cease to cry out daily, "Holy, Holy," etc. <note>original: "Sanctus, Sanctus, &c."</note> And toward this goal, the Fathers measured the Antiphons, Responsories, and Psalmody. Indeed (as is found in the histories of the ancients), it is even said that angels brought them down from heaven. 

Furthermore, to permit priests to pay their duty at home differently than they do in Church is to offer them a manifest occasion not to sing with others in Church, but to earn their wages like mutes. Add to this the danger that the same method of hours might be introduced publicly into the Church, which would gravely offend the ears of the people. 

<margin>The author's judgment on the plurality of Breviaries.</margin> These things have come to my mind for the present because, to the best of my small ability, I ardently desire that there might be a single form of the Breviary in all of Christendom. For the variety of the Church—which sits as a queen "clothed in variety" at the right hand of the bridegroom—shines sufficiently in the variety of religious orders and other ceremonies of the Christian family. However, that such a great diversity has prevailed regarding the canonical hours in the Latin language is perhaps, if it is permissible to say so, no honor.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Question VII regarding whether human laws can and should be changed. The previous page established that while natural law is fixed, human reason evolves and circumstances change, necessitating legal updates. This page addresses the limits of a legislator's power to change laws and the weight of established custom.</meta>

# Question VII of the First Book

<margin>Argument for the negative side.</margin>
It is not without reason that a doubt arises here: whether a legislator has the power to change laws at his own whim without any intervening cause. On the negative side, the argument appears to be that laws may not be changed in any way other than they are established. If they were not established for the common benefit, they would not be laws; therefore, if they are changed for any other reason, that change will not be valid. ¶ However, in the response, there are many parts.

<margin>First assertion, which partly satisfies the proposed doubt.</margin>
First, if a legislator who holds supreme power were to abolish a law without cause, the act would stand: that is, it would thereafter have no force as a <term>statute law</term><note>The author distinguishes between 'lex' (positive or human-made law) and 'ius' (the underlying concept of right or natural law).</note>, except insofar as it retained the force of law through natural or divine right. Nevertheless, as long as the law was beneficial to the state, he would be committing a serious crime by removing it.

<margin>Proof of the aforementioned assertion.</margin>
For instance, if the Pope were to abolish the requirement for annual confession, only the divine right of confession would remain; and if the Emperor were to repeal the law for hanging thieves, there would remain only the natural right that they should at least be punished. The matter is clear: because a law is not a law unless it has coercive force, and it receives this force from the Prince or the state. Therefore, just as a state would have no laws if it did not enact them—even if it needed them—likewise, if the state abolished a law, it would no longer be a law.

<margin>Second assertion.</margin>
The second part is this: a new law that a legislator establishes, or one into which he changes another, would not have the force of law if it were not for the common good or if it were intolerable.

<margin>Reason.</margin>
Indeed, although a law he repeals would truly be repealed, he does not have so much power in lawmaking that whatever he carries out is immediately firm and valid, unless (as has been said) it is just. ¶ These things are said regarding all power, both secular and ecclesiastical; however, we add a third specific part regarding ecclesiastical power.

<margin>Third assertion regarding Ecclesiastical power.</margin>
Namely, that neither the Pope nor a Council can err in the positioning and changing of those laws which are necessary for the Christian family, inasmuch as they are governed by the Holy Spirit. Specifically, it will never be permitted by divine providence for a Pope to either abolish all laws of fasting or to extend the law of confession to once every ten years, because such laws are of the greatest importance to the state. Nor, on the other hand, will it be permitted to command that as soon as anyone is conscious of a mortal sin, they must fly to the ears of a priest to confess, because such a law would be intolerable.

<margin>To the first argument of those put forward in the first order.</margin>
It remains to respond to both series of arguments. To the first of the first order, it is answered that natural law, which is a certain participation in the <term>eternal law</term><note>In Scholastic philosophy, the 'Eternal Law' is God's rational governance of the universe.</note>,

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument (continued).</margin>
remains immovable, because it is derived from that eternal law through the divine reason that established it—which divine reason is indeed also immovable. However, human law is derived from natural law through human reason, moving from the general category to the specific instance. And because human reason does not sufficiently foresee all future things, for this reason, the law itself becomes mutable. It is added, furthermore, that natural law contains universal principles that are abstracted from singular cases; human laws, however, rely on particular foundations situated in actions that are contingent and fleeting.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And by this, it is answered to the second argument that a measure ought to be immutable only as far as the nature of the material allows; but the measurement of mutable things does not allow for a more solid permanency.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The response to the third is made in almost the same way: that "rectitude" in physical quantities is not defined relatively in order to another thing, but is absolutely straight in itself because its ends do not deviate from the middle. However, the rectitude of human law is not absolute, but is taken in relation to the common good, to which things do not always have the same proportion. Therefore, when those circumstances change, the rectitude and justice of the law also change.

<margin>To the final argument.</margin>
¶ The authority of the law in <term>Distinction 12</term><note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law; 'Distinction 12' deals with the authority of custom versus written law.</note> only warns, in favor of the second conclusion, that it is ridiculous to break the decrees of the fathers without a most urgent cause; it is otherwise when a legitimate cause is present.

<margin>To the arguments of the second order.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, the remaining arguments to the contrary must be tempered and weakened insofar as they fight against the second conclusion.

<margin>To the first, St. Thomas.</margin>
To the first, <term>St. Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text's legal philosophy.</note> responds most deliberately that the nature of the arts is one thing, but that of laws is another. For the arts have vigor and efficacy from reason alone, and therefore, as often as something better occurs to the intellect, they ought to be changed; for there is no danger in changing for the better, since the whole business is contained within the intellect.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Laws, however, obtain their greatest force from <term>custom</term><note>Latin: *consuetudo*. The author argues that laws rely on habit and public acceptance, not just logic.</note>, as the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus", referring to Aristotle.</note> says in Book 2 of the *Politics*. So much so that long-standing custom (as <term>Ulpian</term><note>A famous 3rd-century Roman jurist whose writings make up a large part of the Digest of Justinian.</note> says in the laws) is to be held as law. Because of this, one must weigh not only the good that a new law brings but also the detriment that the custom of the old law suffers.

<margin>Easy solution to the other arguments.</margin>
The remaining two arguments, following the opinion of <term>Augustine</term><note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western legal thought.</note>, only prove that it is permitted to change laws; they do not prove that it can be done for just any reason, even if something else seems somewhat more suitable.

<summary>This page discusses the limits of a ruler's power to change laws, concluding that while a ruler can technically repeal a law, doing so without cause is a moral crime and that new laws must serve the common good to be valid. It also highlights the importance of custom, noting that unlike science or art, law relies on social habit and should not be changed lightly.</summary>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether custom is able to obtain the force of law.<-

<margin>Argument 1 from the negative side.</margin>
**I**t is not irrelevant to the discussion on the changing of laws to weave in an article about custom, through which laws are also typically changed. The question is asked, therefore, whether custom can obtain the force of law. There are several arguments on the negative side. First: human law is derived from eternal law through natural law; however, no custom can prevail against those higher laws. Therefore, no custom has the power to change human laws <note>The author is arguing that if human law is a "daughter" of unchanging natural law, it should also be unchangeable by mere habit.</note>.

<margin>Argument 2: Saint Thomas. <unclear>in 1. 2. q 97 ar. 3. & c. v. tal in vto. iter.</unclear></margin>
¶ Second, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential theologian whose work Soto is commenting upon.</note> argues excellently: no good can be fashioned out of multiplied evils; indeed, the more an evil is multiplied, the worse it becomes. He who first begins to act against the law does evil; therefore, nothing good can be produced by a heap of similar acts. Law, however, since it is the rule of our actions, is an outstanding good; therefore, no custom can transition into the nature of law.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: To establish laws is the duty of public power alone; custom, however, gains strength through the private acts of citizens. Therefore, no custom can annul the authority of law.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ To the contrary is Augustine in his letter to Casulanus, where he says: The custom of the people of God and the institutions of the ancestors are to be held as law; and just as transgressors of divine laws must be restrained, so must those who hold ecclesiastical customs in contempt.

---

<margin>The question is satisfied by a single three-part conclusion.</margin>
**T**he present question is satisfied by a single, yet three-part conclusion. The conclusion is this: Custom is endowed with a triple power: namely, that it may interpret an old law, change it, and subsequently obtain the force of a new one.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proven thus: The reason and will of the legislator, once promulgated, is not only the interpreter of the law, but also the repeal of the old and the constitution of the new. Moreover, the promulgation of such reason and will is customarily done not only by word, but also by deed; for what someone performs outwardly by action, they are judged to approve inwardly in the mind. When a prince allows his subjects (whom he is able to restrain) to act in a certain way repeatedly over a long interval of time, he reveals his reason and will by that permission. Therefore, just as he establishes an edict by verbal promulgation, so by such permission he considers the custom of the citizens as law, which then becomes either an interpreter or a total abolition of the old law. ¶ For

<column-break/>

<margin>What comes under the name of custom.</margin>
<margin>Isidore.</margin>
a fuller understanding of the matter, it will be worthwhile to know what is implied by the name "custom." Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose Etymologies served as a standard encyclopedia for the Middle Ages.</note> appears somewhat obscure in the 5th book of his *Etymologies* (which is cited in the *Decrees*, distinction 1), where he says: "Usage <note>original: "Mos"</note> is a long custom drawn only from morals <note>original: "moribus"</note>." He seems to commit the error of repetition in his definition: "Usage from morals." Note, therefore, that the word *mos* (usage/manner) is used in three ways. First, it is taken for a single human act, specifically a free one; for the actions of brute animals are not called "morals" <note>original: "mores"</note> except by metaphor. And from this usage, it is called "moral philosophy"—that is, the study of human acts.

<margin>It is used in three ways.</margin>
<margin>First usage.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, it is taken for a habit born from the frequency of similar acts, just as we say a man is well- or ill-mannered <note>original: "morigeratum"</note>. These first two usages are not relevant to the current matter.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Third, it is taken as being the same as "custom" <note>original: "consuetudo"</note>; and in this way, it is nothing other than a frequency of similar acts over a long time in some community—for instance, in a kingdom, a city, or a college. Thus, Isidore said nothing foolish. For in saying that "usage" is a "custom drawn from morals," he used the word in the third sense in the first instance, and in the first sense in the latter.

<margin>Isidore.</margin>
<margin>What the difference is between usage and custom.</margin>
Custom, therefore, when it is in harmony with reason and granted by the prince, has the force of law. Indeed, it differs from law only in this: that law is handed down in writing, whereas custom is handed down by use. For so says Isidore: "Law is a written constitution; usage, however, is long custom." And he adds: "Custom is a certain right <note>original: "ius"</note> established by morals, which is accepted as law where law is lacking." And in the law *Diuturna* (in the *Digest*, "On Laws"), it says: "Custom is usually observed as right and law in those matters which do not descend from writing." And further down, the jurist Paulus says: "Indeed, this right is held to be of great authority, having been so thoroughly approved that there was no need to include it in writing."

<margin>A doctrine to be committed to memory.</margin>
¶ This, therefore, must be committed to memory: that custom does not have the force of law of itself, but only insofar as it flows from the consent of the prince. Thus, even if the opinions of Aristotle or Plato or any other philosopher—or indeed the most healthy opinions of all the jurists—were present, they would never have the force of law unless they were stabilized by the consent of the prince. In the same way, custom would not otherwise obtain that same power. For example, the opinion of Baldo <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous professor of civil law.</note> that a thief should be hanged for a third theft could never have obtained the force of law unless the prince sanctioned it in writing or approved it through custom. For this reason, where a law might expressly state that no custom shall prevail against the law, such a decree [prevents] custom...

<summary>This page explains how repeated public custom can acquire the status of law through the implied consent of a ruler. Soto defines the various meanings of 'usage' and argues that custom serves to interpret, change, or replace written statutes.</summary>

### Book One, Question VII.

...[the Prince] invalidates it, so that through that [declaration] the law is never repealed; for in that case, custom accomplishes nothing, because it is never an indication of the Prince's will. Nevertheless, a custom can be so long-standing to the contrary—especially across the reigns of different princes—that it might overcome even that invalidating decree. But it must furthermore be noted that custom not only binds as a sign of the proclamation of a new law, but sometimes it is a sign and testimony that such a law <unclear>existed</unclear> <note>original: "extiterit"</note> in the past, even if it is not found in writing. ¶ How long a time must be observed for a custom before it obtains the force of law is not certain by right. In some cases (as they say) two acts are sufficient, in others three, <margin>The Rule.</margin> in others ten. But in truth, there can be no wiser rule than that which was established in the chapter *Cum tanto* regarding customs <note>original: "c. cùm tanto. de consue." This refers to a specific section of Canon Law in the Decretals of Gregory IX which discusses when a custom becomes "reasonable" and "legitimately prescribed."</note>: where it is held that custom ought never to create a prejudice against positive law unless it has been reasonable and legitimately prescribed. Regarding the word "reasonable," it must be noted that for a custom to gain the strength of law, it must possess the conditions of a good law, as established above. And secondly, regarding the word "prescribed," it should be considered that custom then acquires the force of law when, by the common judgment and will of men, it would be a sin <margin>A healthy warning.</margin> to act against it. ¶ For this reason, I will not fail to warn here how much danger is created when something is permitted once or twice in any republic. Indeed, to persuade someone of a new request, the argument is brought forward that a single act can do no harm; but afterward, by the likeness of that first act, a second is persuaded, and subsequently the custom gains strength. The same danger exists among powerful men. For instance, if vassals, for the sake of politeness and goodwill, once offered small gifts to their lord and patron, immediately that politeness is snatched into custom, and a favor <margin>Question.</margin> becomes a required right. ¶ But does every <margin>Reason.</margin> ancient custom abrogate the law? For reason seems to persuade us so: since while the Prince ignores the behavior, he is thought to be interpreting <margin>Solution.</margin> his own will. It is answered, nevertheless, that this is not the case at all. Rather, as long as a usage contrary to the law arises from nothing other than the negligence of the prince, or from the fact that he is not powerful enough to take vengeance upon wrongdoers, it never prescribes against the law. It only does so when he is both powerful enough to restrain the abuse and permits it, not out of cowardice, but with an "eyes-open" tolerance <note>original: "oculata dissimulatione"</note>. Nor indeed can it happen before a long-standing habit gains authority: for

<column-break/>

since law ought to be established with prudence and judgment, and judgment requires time, it happens that a custom does not grow strong enough to reach the force of law in a short time. For perhaps by this reasoning <margin>Custom of the Gauls.</margin> the habit grew in the lands of the Gauls <note>Referring to the French.</note> of eating meat on Saturdays between the Nativity of the Lord and the Purification of the Virgin <note>Christmas and Candlemas (February 2nd). Soto is highlighting regional variations in Lenten or fasting disciplines.</note>; and in the Spains <note>The various kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula.</note> the eating of animal intestines. When, however, we say that the tolerance of a Prelate is the cause for a custom becoming law, this is understood to refer to that Prelate who is the legislator. For even if a Judge in the city, or a Prelate of a convent or a province, ignores the transgressions of laws, a custom of that kind never attains the strength of law, because it is not a sign of the will of the supreme Prelate, who is the legislator. ¶ Furthermore, anyone might wonder whether every usage <margin>Another question.</margin> turned into a custom constitutes a binding law. For it is common for men to begin, for the sake of piety, either to observe a feast day or to keep a fast: not indeed as a commandment, but out of the piety of the soul and (as they say) out of devotion. For example, if in some province they began to abstain from meat on Wednesdays <note>original: "feria quarta"</note>, would it therefore afterward become a commandment? <margin>Solution.</margin> It is answered that one must weigh how such a religious practice was observed. For if it was only out of free devotion, it is never turned into a commandment, unless afterward the religious practice begins to be repeated as if it were a commandment. For a suspicion has always held me that the custom of reciting the Office of Our Lady <note>The "Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary," a cycle of prayers modeled on the Divine Office.</note> at stated hours did not have the force of a commandment in the beginning, nor did it obtain that force before four hundred years ago. Otherwise, in our Order <note>Soto was a member of the Dominican Order (Order of Preachers).</note>, it would not have been commanded of us to recite it while rising in the dormitory. Nevertheless, afterward the religious practice grew so strong that there is now scarcely anyone who would dare to deny it is a commandment.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> To the first of the arguments at the front of the question, therefore, it is answered that the nature of natural and divine laws is far different from that of human laws. For the former were established by the divine will, which no human will or custom is able to resist. Indeed, the more ancient a custom against divine and natural law is, the cause of a more grievous sin it becomes; so far is it from custom detracting any strength from those laws. ¶ To the second argument, however, it is answered <margin>To the second argument.</margin> that since, as has often been said, human laws fail in certain cases, a custom can be initiated against the law through lawful acts; which repeated acts, indeed, obtain the force [of law]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Question VII, Article II regarding how custom (habitual practice) interacts with established law. It specifically addresses whether a custom that begins through illegal or "unlawful" acts can eventually gain the force of law, and then transitions to Article III regarding the power of rulers to grant dispensations.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,

...they will fail the law: because through those instances it is shown that the ancient law was useless. For as long as the reason for the law persists, no custom will be able to overcome it; for in that case, the custom will not be reasonable, but the law will instead always be the victor—unless perhaps the custom shows that the law, while not useless, is nevertheless not suited to the nature of the country. This alone is sufficient to abolish the law.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
But in truth, St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> seems to have answered briefly. For he taught how a custom can be initiated through lawful acts, yet he did not answer what happens if it is initiated through unlawful acts.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a prominent commentator on Aquinas</note> responds that even when it begins through unlawful acts, it can obtain authority through the passage of time.

<margin>The author's critique.</margin>
<margin>A distinction.</margin>
However, I think it is worthwhile to make a distinction. Regarding the effect of making an old law obsolete, a custom—even one that had an unlawful origin—can obtain force among later generations, though not among the same men who started it. For example, suppose our ancestors began to act wrongly against some law; we, in our own age, find that the law has been abolished by custom. We are not bound to scrutinize what kind of beginnings that custom had, but we are free from that same law. But regarding the other effect, which is the power to bind or obligate, a custom will not obtain the force of law as long as it grew through unlawful acts, for the reason already stated: because a law must be fair and just.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
To the third argument, it is answered that the multitude of private individuals who introduce a custom can be of two conditions. For either they constitute a free republic <note>original: "respublicam"</note> that governs itself without a prince—and then the custom of the people will be the constitution of the law—or, if they live under a king or another prince, then (as has been said) custom is not law by itself, but only insofar as it is an interpretation of the prince's will.

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether the rulers of a multitude can grant dispensations from laws.<-

After it was defined at the end of the previous question that subjects are not permitted to use <term>equity <note>original: "epieikeia," the principle of following the spirit of the law when the letter is harmful</note></term> except in sudden danger, it now remains to be seen whether at least the governors of the multitude can grant a <term>dispensation <note>an exemption from a law in a specific case</note></term> from the law in those cases where they judge it to be expedient. And the argument

<column-break/>

is made from the negative side.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Law (as was shown above from Isidore) is enacted for the common good. However, the common good must not be interrupted for a private benefit; for indeed (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies in the 1st book of the *Ethics*), the good of the nation is more divine than the good of one man. Therefore, it is not permitted to grant a dispensation to someone so that they may act against the law.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, in Deuteronomy 1, this instruction is given to leaders: "You shall hear the small as well as the great; you shall not respect any man's person, for the judgment is God's." But to grant to one person what is denied to the whole republic is "respect of persons" <note>favoritism or partiality</note>; therefore, this is by no means permitted.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third, no dispensation falls upon divine or natural law. Human law, however, must be conformed to those, seeing as it is derived from them; therefore, dispensation does not apply to human law either.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 9: "A dispensation has been committed to me."

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
For the understanding of this question, it should be noted with St. Thomas that "dispensation" properly implies the measurement of something common in relation to individuals. For this reason, the head of a household is called a "dispenser" <note>original: "dispensator"</note>, because he commands the tasks of each person with a certain weight and measure, and distributes necessary things from the common storehouse. In the same way, a person in a republic is called a "dispenser" when it falls to him to arrange, with order and reason, how the common law is to be observed by individuals.

¶ Therefore, the question is answered with two conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first is: He who is charged with the government of the multitude has the power of dispensing from human law in certain cases and for certain persons.

<margin>Persuasion for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is gathered from that principle often repeated before: because human law is established for the general case, it cannot encompass all singular cases. Because of this, it can happen that what is fitting in general and in most cases may fail in a specific person and case—namely, because its observance might be an obstacle to a better good or an occasion for some evil. Therefore, since he who carries the care of the republic must look out for the safety of each person, effective reason dictates that he should then provide the faculty for such a person to act against the law.

<margin>Second Conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: When a cause does not run consistent with reason and is not directed toward the common good, then for a Prelate <note>a high-ranking official or ruler</note> to grant a dispensation according to his own whim is a sin, either of infidelity or of imprudence. It is "infidelity" <note>breach of trust</note> insofar as he does not look out for the common good, but for his own or that of another private person; and "imprudence" if...

### Book One, Question VII.

<margin>The fallacy of some who confuse equity with dispensation.</margin>
...if prudence does not adorn the zeal with which one is moved for the public good, lest he dispense against the law before he has thoroughly explored and perceived the cause. For this reason, Christ our redeemer, as written in Luke 12, judged it difficult for both virtues to be joined in a steward. For he said: "Who then, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the lord has set over his household?" <note>original: "Quis putas est fidelis dispensator & prudens quem constituit dominus super familiam suam?"</note> ¶ However, so that these matters may become clearer, several things must be considered here. First of all, a fallacy suggests itself here that conquers many. Namely, that a dispensation is the same thing as equity <note>original: "epieikeia"</note>: because to them, a steward seems to do nothing other than interpret the law in such a case according to what is fair and good. But in truth, the matter is otherwise. For these four things differ in meaning with respect to the law: Invalidating, abrogating, interpreting through equity, and dispensing.

<margin>What invalidating is.</margin>
For to **invalidate** <note>original: "irritare"</note> is to impede and cancel a law or a vow so that it does not obtain the power of binding. For example, if a King did not approve or confirm a law established by citizens, but canceled it. Just as a father can invalidate the vow of a son; over which, if it were already solid and binding, he could not dispense.

<margin>What abrogation is.</margin>
But to **abrogate** a law is to remove it entirely after it already has force. Although, if it were placed only for a predefined time, then it is not so much said to be removed as to be fulfilled. In which sense, among others, Christ said: "I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfill it." <note>original: "Non veni legem solvere, sed adimplere"</note>

<margin>What the interpretation of law is.</margin>
To **interpret** through equity <term>epieikeia: a Greek concept in legal philosophy where the literal letter of the law is set aside to follow the "spirit" or "intention" of the lawmaker in specific, unforeseen circumstances</term> is to declare that the law itself has no place in such a case.

<margin>What dispensation is.</margin>
But in truth, to **dispense** is to exempt someone among the subjects from the law: granting them a license and faculty without which they would be liable to the law. The distinction is therefore clear: equity is not exempting a subject by license in a case where they were bound, but rather explaining that in that case they were *not* bound; dispensation, however, is the granting of a license. Therefore, equity is appropriate not only for Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note> but also for subjects (as has been said); but dispensation is for Prelates alone.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you argue to the contrary: if a Prelate cannot dispense without a cause, then a dispensation is nothing other than a declaration of the cause for which the reason of the law fails in such a case. This conclusion is denied. For even if the reason for the law fails in this person, they are not therefore immediately untied from the bond of the law. For it is one thing for the observation of a human law to be contrary to reason (where equity has a place); but it is another thing for the reason of the law to fail in this person, where a dispensation is nevertheless necessary. Let there be examples. If not eating meat on a forbidden day 

<margin>Solution.</margin>

<column-break/>

were to cause me to die of hunger, I can eat by using equity; however, even if I did not need the "taming of the flesh" for which fasting was ordained—indeed, if abstinence and lack of food were some hindrance to my study—I do not therefore become free from the law. Rather, there is a cause for the Prelate to dispense with me: not indeed by interpreting that the law does not then include me, but even if it *does* include me, by providing me the license for the sake of a greater benefit, so that it is not a fault for me not to fast. Likewise, while a law might forbid low-born and infamous men from mounting horses, if a case occurred for one of them where he would fall into the hands of enemies unless he escaped on a horse, then equity teaches him that he is not bound by the law in that case. But in truth, even if it happened that some man of that class was useful for war, he would not immediately be allowed to use a horse; yet, a reason for a dispensation would emerge. And one must speak in a similar way regarding a vow.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From which it follows that to dispense is not only to change one obligation into another, but it can also be done through remission and relaxation, at least in part. Otherwise, it would not be a dispensation, but a mere commutation <note>The substitution of one form of penalty or obligation for another</note>. You vowed a difficult pilgrimage to Jerusalem: but a public cause of the Church occurs in whose aid there is a need for alms: the Pope can commute that vow into some money, even an amount less than the expenses of the journey would have been.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ But you ask, perhaps, whether the duty of dispensing is situated in the power of the Prince and Lawmaker alone.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
For there is this argument for the affirmative side: that the dispensation of a law is a certain particular abrogation of it; but to abrogate a law is the function of the same person whose role it is to establish it.

<margin>Response.</margin>
It is responded nonetheless that such power over laws—although full power belongs to the lawmaker alone—is nevertheless, as the aforementioned reason persuades, situated in the hands of lower governors as well in several cases. First, by power delegated from a superior: which either the laws grant to inferiors, or custom interprets. As in dispensing a simple vow, with three exceptions. Next, by ordinary faculty, both in their own proper laws and also in the laws of a superior. A Bishop, I say, can dispense in the laws of the Pope, either by grant of law or by custom. Furthermore, in a threefold order of things: namely, if either the matter is light, or the case is frequent, or the law regards the proper good of his own city or diocese. This is the opinion of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Catholic theologian and commentator on Aquinas</note> on 1.2. question 97, article 4, which I believe is seasoned with his own wit...

<summary>This page defines and distinguishes four legal concepts: invalidation, abrogation, equity (epieikeia), and dispensation, clarifying that dispensation is a specific grant of license by a superior. It also explores whether lower officials, such as Bishops, have the authority to grant dispensations in laws established by higher authorities like the Pope.</summary>

# Dominic Soto, on Justice and Law,

I believe this to be true. For this reason, Saint
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thomas did not ask strictly whether a prince or legislator could grant dispensations, but more broadly whether the **leaders of a community** <note>original: "rectores multitudinis"</note> could dispense from human laws. For leaders are not only princes, but also those who sit at the helm of any community. Furthermore, those matters are considered "light" <note>minor or trivial matters</note> which are not established by a command properly speaking—that is, one binding under pain of mortal sin—but by a statute. By this reasoning, even our local Priors can dispense from the prohibition of eating meat, the wearing of linen, and other matters of that kind. Next, the frequency of cases is a reason why a Bishop can dispense. For example, regarding fasts: although this is a law of a superior <note>meaning a law from the Pope or a General Council</note>, it would be a very heavy burden to approach the Pope every time someone needed a dispensation from a fast. I would, however, qualify this:
<margin>A qualification of the previous assertion.</margin>
A Bishop may dispense from such laws for a day or a short time when a cause is present; however, whether he can do so for an entire lifetime, I do not know. By the same reasoning, he may dispense if one of a married couple becomes unable to demand the "marital debt" <note>the right to sexual intimacy in marriage</note> due to incest with the other’s relative. This is especially true when access to Rome is not possible, either due to the poverty of the person or some other reason. It is different if the impediment preceded the marriage and would thus prevent it from being contracted in the first place: in such a case, only the Pope can dispense. Furthermore, if a specific city law exists forbidding the import of wine or grain from outside so that the city’s own produce may be sold, I believe the Governor <note>original: "Prætor"</note> could dispense; yet it is different for a Bishop regarding marriages and holy orders, which pertain to the public good.
<margin>Legitimate causes for dispensation.</margin>
¶ The holy Decrees <note>referring to Canon Law</note> explain the causes by which a dispenser ought to be moved to grant a dispensation: namely, **time, utility, person, and quality.** In short, to encompass them all, a dispensation should not be granted unless it results in the **common good**, for which every law is established. Indeed, the current state of the Church of God serves as a very clear witness to how much danger is stirred up for the commonwealth when the dispensation of laws begins to be granted for private interests or for reasons that should be kept silent. For if laws bring no other benefit to the commonwealth than being profitable to the prince, they are a destruction and a undermining of the public good rather than a benefit. The result is that only the poor are coerced by laws, while those who lack for nothing are subject to none. Let it be far from us (as we said before) that laws should be made to serve as a private fund <note>original: "peculium"</note> for the legislator. But as soon as the reason for which they were passed ceases to exist,

<column-break/>

the laws ought to be repealed, lest citizens be forced to buy a dispensation for a price.
<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ But if you ask whether the fact that a person who made a vow cannot fulfill it without great difficulty and trouble is a sufficiently suitable cause for dispensing—for this is the reason most frequently offered as a pretext—
<margin>The Resolution.</margin>
it is answered that if the difficulty is inherent in the thing itself—for example, if someone with imprudent and poorly weighed judgment vowed a long fast on bread and water, or a pilgrimage on foot that their legs could not handle—that very rashness is a cause for dispensing. However, when the difficulty arises not from the nature of the thing, but from the **corrupt habit** of the one who vowed, it is different. Since the very difficulty of abstaining from an evil custom was the reason for making the vow, that difficulty should not be brought back as a reason for a dispensation. If, however, after you have made a vow (for example) of a pilgrimage to Jerusalem or even of entering religious life, you suffer a permanent illness or weakness that acts as a legal impediment, you are released from the vow. We have, however, established a specific discussion regarding the dispensation of vows in the eighth book.
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
<margin>A final doubt.</margin>
¶ A final doubt remains: whether a person who is granted a dispensation without a cause remains safe in their conscience.
<margin>The solution of the Jurists.</margin>
The Jurists answer, as gathered from Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV, a famous legal commentator</note> in the chapter *Cum ad monasterium* concerning the statutes of monks,
<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
and from Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis, an influential canon lawyer</note> in the chapter *non est voti* regarding vows, that if someone inferior to the Supreme Pontiff dispenses without cause, the dispensation does not hold; because the faculty of dispensing was granted to them under this limit. If, however, the Pope dispenses, then a distinction must be made: for in those matters that depend on **divine law**, such as a vow or an oath, if he dispenses without cause, the dispensation does not hold. It is otherwise in those matters which are purely of **positive law** <note>man-made laws, such as fasts or legal formalities</note>, because these depend entirely on his own will.
<margin>The aforementioned authors are refuted.</margin>
And indeed, the first distinction perhaps does not possess great truth: for regarding laws that depend purely on his own ordinary power, there is no reason why a Bishop should not exercise the same faculty that a Pope does over his own.
<margin>The latter distinction of the Jurists is proven.</margin>
The second distinction, however, is exceedingly probable. Therefore, in matters that depend on divine law, not only does the one dispensing sin, but the dispensation itself is to be dreaded as void and of no value before God. For this reason, when a dispensation is granted for a **plurality of benefices** <note>the practice of one person holding multiple church offices and their incomes</note>, or when an infant or child is allowed to have the care of souls, or a layman is placed over monks as an Abbot, or a person who has taken solemn vows (as Panormitanus notes) is called back to a more relaxed order—especially one that has only the name of an order—it is to be feared...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence as per the catchword "est ra-" (it is to be feared...). This page highlights Soto's concern with the moral integrity of legal exceptions, arguing that dispensations must serve the public good rather than being sold for profit or granted for personal convenience.</meta>

[It] is not ratified or valid before God. Therefore, both those who procure such dispensations for others and those who seek them for themselves sin gravely. Indeed, even if a dispensation granted without cause were legally valid, it is still a grave sin not only to grant the dispensation but also to seek and procure it. In those matters that are of purely **positive law** <term>positive law: laws specifically enacted by human authorities, such as the state or the church, rather than being inherent in nature</term>, a dispensation without cause is not excused from sin, although the dispensation remains valid. Nevertheless, 
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan, in the place cited and in his *Summa* under the word "dispensation," does not consider the consciences of those who are dispensed without cause to be at peace. His reasoning is that although the positive law is removed, the force of the **natural law** remains, which dictates that no one should withdraw themselves from the 
<margin>Cajetan’s opinion is not sufficiently certain.</margin>
burdens of the community without cause. However, I have not yet determined for myself how much weight this argument holds. Truly, if my relief were the burdening of others—as when someone procures a privilege to exempt themselves from paying taxes without cause, which results in the aggravation of others—it would be a **mortal sin** <note>a grave sin that, in Catholic theology, destroys the relationship with God</note>. Regarding fasts, however, it is not so clear: unless the exempt person causes a **scandal** <note>an action that leads others into sin or spiritual confusion</note>. If scandal is absent, perhaps the fault would be no worse than a **venial sin** <note>a lesser sin that does not break one's relationship with God</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, to the **first argument**, the answer has already been given: a dispensation granted to a private person does not oppose the law, even if the law was passed for the common good. This is because such a dispensation

<column-break/>

ought not to be granted if it harms the common good; rather, it should result in its increase. 
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the **second argument**, it is replied that there is no "respecter of persons" <note>partiality or favoritism</note> involved, even though equal things are not always commanded of unequal persons. Indeed, nothing is more unjust than equality where the persons are not equal. 
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the **third argument**, an answer has already been given above regarding the changing of laws. For the natural law, regarding its common and general precepts, can have no failure; therefore, these are indispensable <note>meaning they cannot be set aside by any human authority</note>. However, regarding natural conclusions, **equity** <term>epieikeia: the virtue of following the spirit of a law when following the literal letter would be harmful</term> has power. By the virtue of this equity, a person who holds weapons in deposit for a master does not return them to him if the master has gone mad. Moreover, dispensing from these natural laws belongs to God alone, who dispensed in ancient times so that one man might be joined to several wives in marriage. In **divine positive laws** <note>laws given directly by God in scripture that are not necessarily part of human nature</note> which are not of the natural law, He Himself can also dispense, or someone to whom He has specifically committed that power. I say "specifically" because the Pope, although he is the Vicar of Christ, cannot dispense from divine law by his **ordinary power** <note>the standard legal power inherent in his office</note>. The Apostles, however, by His special commission, dispensed in the form of baptism so that it might be done in His name. And in Acts 15, they tolerated that Christians abstain from "strangled meat and blood," even though Christ—who is our salvation and redemption, blessed forever—had abolished those rites by divine law.

# BOOK TWO
## On Justice and Right.

### PREFACE.

<margin>Subject of the second book.</margin>
The argument we have established regarding laws is not only necessarily lengthy, but it will be more distinct if we divide it into two books. Therefore, since in the first book we have sufficiently discussed (according to our capacity) natural and human law derived from eternal law—through which man is ordered toward his natural end—it follows that in this second book we should discuss **divine law**, through which we are promoted to supernatural happiness. For although St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose *Summa Theologiae* Soto is commenting upon here.</note> (as he usually does with all things) enriched this material magnificently—especially regarding the **Old Law** <term>Old Law: the Mosaic law found in the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament</term>—our work will not be entirely superfluous, if God permits.

### QUESTION ONE,
#### On the Old Law.
->St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* 1-2, question 98.<-

### ARTICLE I.
->*Whether, besides the natural and human law which are derived from the eternal, a divine law was necessary for men.*<-

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
FIRST, therefore, it is asked in general whether any supernatural divine law was necessary for men. St. Thomas disputed this question in Question 91; however, we have placed it here where we begin to speak of divine law. The argument is made for the negative side. Natural law is, as has been said, a certain participation in the eternal law; moreover, eternal law is divine; therefore, besides the natural law, there was no need for another divine law.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Second: God, as read in Ecclesiasticus 15, "left man in the hand of his own counsel," which is an act of reason; therefore, he had no need for a law that was superior to his reason, but could be sufficiently governed by human laws established through reason.

<column-break/>

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
Especially because human nature, since it is more excellent than irrational beings, is more self-sufficient than brutes are to themselves; but irrational creatures do not need a law higher than the natural one implanted in them; therefore, neither do humans.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third, it is argued: Even if we needed a divine law, one was enough; both because the kingdom of heaven is one, and of one king, according to that Psalm: "God is King of all the earth" <note>Psalm 47:7</note>; and the intention of the law is one. For through it, God wills (as the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 2) that "all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth." And for this reason especially, since natural law descending from the eternal is one, divine law—the closer it is to the eternal—should be even more unified.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 118.</margin>
<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is that Davidic petition: "Set a law for me, O Lord, the way of your justifications" <note>Psalm 119:33 (numbered 118 in the Vulgate)</note>. Here David indicated human unworthiness, which, since it is not sufficient for itself with natural law, longs for something higher. And also that it was bipartite <note>consisting of two parts: the Old and New Laws</note>, as Paul says in Hebrews 7: "The priesthood being translated, it is necessary that a translation of the law also be made."

<margin>Division of the divine law.</margin>
TO understand the question, it must be recalled from what was said above how divine law is recognized as twofold: namely, **eternal** and **positive**. For the eternal law belongs to His own essence; it is the fountain and abyss of light from which all knowledge and law flow; but divine **positive law** is a participation in that essence, given further to us and written in our hearts, as Paul says to the Corinthians. And the present question is established concerning this.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ To which it is answered with two conclusions. The first is: besides natural and human law, it was necessary that another, higher one be set for us (as David says), which is therefore called "positive"; and it would be more significantly called "placed" <note>original: "posita" - a play on words, as "positive law" refers to law "posed" or "placed" by an authority rather than arising from nature.</note>.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas founded this conclusion on four reasons, which he brilliantly elicited from that Davidic oracle in Psalm 118: "The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, providing wisdom to the little ones."

<margin>First reason.</margin>
The first reason is taken from the end of man. For indeed, if our nature had not been elevated higher than to a natural end—which does not exceed its powers—it would not have needed any other higher speculative knowledge or law. However, since with it <note>This sentence continues on the next page.</note>

# BOOK TWO
## Question I.

...with the fact that God created us in his own image, and thus made us capable of possessing him through the vision of himself—a goal that we cannot reach by our own natural strength. Therefore, it was necessary for us to have, first, in the speculative intellect <note>speculative intellect: the part of the mind concerned with knowing truth for its own sake, rather than for practical action.</note>, the knowledge of faith. This faith shows us that goal and the goods to be hoped for (as Paul says), toward which our life must be directed. Just as an archer must look at the mark he prepares to hit, so too in the practical intellect <note>practical intellect: the part of the mind that applies knowledge to action or behavior.</note> there was a need for a law higher than the natural one, which would be for us a rule of duties by which we might attain that same happiness. Furthermore, in the will, a more special and unique help was needed than that by which the nature of things is governed, through which we would be able to direct and advance our affections toward that end. The Psalm <note>Soto is quoting Psalm 18 in the Vulgate (Psalm 19 in modern Bibles), which praises the perfection of God's law.</note> touched upon this intention in its final clause: *Giving wisdom to little ones.* For man, considered in his own nature, is "little" and too weak to reach that finish line unless supernatural wisdom were supplied to us from above. ¶

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
The second reason for this conclusion is taken from the necessity of informing human judgments. Since our actions deal with singular, contingent matters which are slippery and deceptive, and which subsequently produce various judgments in different minds, there arises from this a diversity of human laws among different nations. Thus, the law of the Athenians was one thing, that of the Romans another, and it is yet another for the Spanish and another for the French. Therefore, it was necessary for a law to shine upon us from God, which would be the most faithful and certain norm to which all human laws would be required to align and aim. And through this, a person could know for certain what was fitting for them and what was harmful. Such is the Decalogue <term>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments</term>, carved by God into tablets, and the Gospel, imprinted on our minds. For this reason, David called the law a *faithful testimony.* Indeed, no human law exists that is so certain and stable. ¶ Third, this

<margin>Third reason</margin>
same law was necessary for us because of our absolute justice. For this justice is not placed so much in external duties as it is within the
<margin>Matthew 15.</margin>
soul. For from the heart, as Christ says, come evil thoughts, and from there [evil] works: such as adulteries, homicides, etc. Men, however, because they cannot inspect the hidden recesses of others' hearts, are not able to cleanse internal acts by their laws. It was therefore necessary for there to be a law of God, which would prohibit not only the hand but also the soul—inasmuch as it would restrain not only theft and adultery, but also the 

<column-break/>

lust for them. And this is signified by that second clause of David’s sentiment: *converting souls.* Namely, that divine law not only restrains the wickedness of works but also thoroughly cleanses the inner chambers of hearts. ¶ Finally, the fourth cause of divine
<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
law was that—as Augustine is the author in Book 1 of *On Free Will*—human laws cannot restrain all vices, even external ones; indeed, they ought not. For if they busied themselves with coercing everything with punishments, then they would both hinder many good things and push citizens into worse crimes. For instance, if they punished all lies with severe penalty, there would be no one who would dare to speak; and if they drove away prostitutes, they would provide the occasion for worse things <note>A common medieval argument: that legalizing certain smaller vices (like prostitution) prevents greater social evils (like rape or the breakdown of marriage).</note>. It was therefore necessary for a law to exist that forbade everything before the tribunal of God, since there is no danger in Him punishing all things; rather, it is the most equitable justice. And this is what the first word of the same Psalm sounds like: *The law of the Lord is immaculate*; that is, not admitting even the smallest stains of baseness, but wiping away all of them. ¶ The final conclusion: that this 
<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
divine law is divided into two parts—which are not entirely two different species, but differ as the imperfect and the perfect of the same species—was most fitting and most worthy of divine wisdom. 
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason for the conclusion—although St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> passed over it—is clearly gathered both from the height of the law and from the dullness of our nature. Truly, since divine law so far exceeds the smallness of our intellect, and our race has, as it were, grown up through all the ages, such high mysteries should not have been entrusted to the human race while it was acting out its childhood; for it would not have grasped them then. Instead, it was worthwhile to be imbued through the oracles of the Prophets, the figures of things to come, and finally the meanings of ceremonies, as if under a pedagogue <term>pedagogue: historically, a servant who led children to school and supervised their conduct; here, a metaphor for the Old Law guiding humanity toward Christ</term>, until, having become accustomed to them, it might reach the proper age that would recognize God made man (hoped for after such a long expectation), and would fitly hear Him preaching about the secrets of the Trinity, and finally receive Him as one formerly promised. It was therefore expedient that that shadowy law <note>The Old Law</note> precede the truth of the New [Law]. And this is the doctrine of the Apostle to the Galatians, Chapter 3: 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
*Therefore the law was our pedagogue in Christ.* But where faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue; for you are all sons of God through faith. And in Chapter 4: *When we were little ones, we were serving under the elements of this world; but when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son,* etc.

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

Here, however, the progression from the imperfect to the perfect is weighed from three main headings: namely, from the **end** toward which the law leads; from the **order of justice** which it establishes; and from the **mode** by which it compels its subjects. From the "end," I say, because that law proposed a sensible and earthly good as a prize. But concerning this distinction, we shall speak more clearly in the next question, article 3. ¶ The second distance by which that law was separated from our own—the Law of those enjoying the Gospel—as if it were a <term>pedagogy</term> <note>pedagogy: Here used in the ancient sense of a "tutor" or servant who escorted children to school and supervised their basic behavior before they reached maturity.</note> for children and servants, is that it did not explain the internal justice of hearts as ours does. Not that it had not restrained evil desires; for it was in the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>Decalogue: The Ten Commandments.</note>: *You shall not covet your neighbor's goods, nor his wife,* etc. But the Gospel more explicitly blunts the depravity of thoughts: *Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart.* And: *Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.* Because of this, He says: *Unless your justice exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.* ¶ The third interval is in the mode of compelling. For that law urged subjects mostly through the fear of punishments, like children and servants; but ours allures us through the love which Christ pours into our hearts. However, regarding this point as well, a more convenient place for speaking will be given in the cited article of the following question.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it has already been answered how this positive law of God differs from the <term>eternal law</term> <note>eternal law: God's rational purpose for the universe, which exists in His mind from all eternity.</note>, and for what reason it is necessary for us beyond the natural law. Namely, that the natural law, which does not exceed the capacity of our nature, directs us toward a natural end; but the divine law, through which the eternal law is shared with us in a higher way, raises us to the supernatural.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And likewise, it is answered to the second argument that although a "plan" or "counsel" is a work of reason, it is nevertheless necessary to be informed by a supernatural law. And in this, it has been done more gloriously and excellently with us than with irrational animals. For they have an order only toward a natural end, which is humble; even if they attain it by their own powers, it is nothing extraordinary. But we were created for supernatural happiness—indeed, we owe this unspeakable benefit to God above all bodily creatures. Therefore, our nature cannot reach it by itself. But nevertheless, since (according to Aristotle) <note>original: "Aristotele authore"</note> what we can do through friends we can, in a certain way, do through ourselves, the excellence of man is revealed here: that God is so most-

<column-break/>

-ready to bring us help that he is never lacking to us except by our own fault.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The third argument proves precisely this: that it would have been incongruous for two laws to flow from one God if they were as utterly distinct as the laws of different nations are. Nevertheless, it was expedient and fitting that one God should set down some precepts for imperfect men to whom it was suitable to spend their "childhood" as if under a tutor, and other precepts for those advanced to a mature age. This is especially true because our salvation, which is the end of the law, was to come to us through Christ, for whom it was therefore fitting to establish a perfect law. But nonetheless, it was necessary for the world to be prepared for his reception through the other law (as has been said). The natural law, however, because it contains universal precepts and those common to all mortals of whatever condition, cannot be anything but one.

### ARTICLE II.
->*Whether the old law was good.*<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'Q' featuring a seated scholar holding a book, surrounded by leafy patterns.</image-desc>
Since human nature is usually weakened to such an extent that there has been no lack of a <term>Manichaean</term> <note>Manichaeans: A dualistic religious group that believed the material world was created by an evil deity and thus rejected the Old Testament as the work of an "evil God."</note> crowd who barked against the Old Law as if it were evil and established by an evil God, the question is asked whether it was good.

<margin>First reason from the negative side.</margin>
And it is argued from the negative side. Many things are written in the Old Law that are repugnant to the New; such as the very first word: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* The contrary of which is asserted in John 1: *The world was made through him* (namely, the Word), *and without him nothing was made.* Soon after, it is read there that God rested on the seventh day from all the work he had performed; and yet in John 5, Christ says, *My Father is working until now, and I am working.*

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Second, God himself confesses in Ezekiel 20, saying: *I gave them precepts that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live.* Now, a law is judged by the quality of its precepts; therefore, that law was not good.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
¶ Third, for the goodness of a law, two things are especially required, as <term>Isidore</term> <note>Isidore: St. Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar whose definitions of law were foundational for medieval legal theory.</note> taught us above. First, that it consults the common salvation of souls; next, that it be not difficult to observe and accommodated to human custom. Neither of these was in that law.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
For as to the first, Paul says in Romans 5: *The law entered in so that sin might abound.* And in chapter 7: *Without the law, sin was dead; but I was once alive without the law; but when the commandment came...*

---

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> TO the question, the answer is given in three conclusions. First: The Old Law (as Paul says) was holy, and just, and good, and most fitting in all its causes. Though it was not in every way absolute and perfect. This conclusion <margin>Proof.</margin> is asserted and confirmed through every category of cause. First, from the nature of both objects: namely, both the matter about which it commanded, and the form and figure of the commanding itself. For it was both a composer of morals and a <term>shadow of things to come</term> <note>shadow of things to come: A common theological term meaning the Old Testament laws were symbols or "previews" of the truths to be fully revealed in the New Testament.</note>, and was good in both respects. Truly, since there is a twofold reason in us, just as the truth of speculative sciences is weighed by being in harmony with speculative reason, so also the goodness of a law is found in its being in accord with practical reason. The Old Law, in the part where it was a rule of morals, excellently drove away both the depravity of works and the desires struggling against reason. For that Decalogue which God carved for Moses on the tablets was a compendium, the substance, and the flower of the entire natural law:

<column-break/>

indeed, as will be more broadly apparent in Question 3, it both directed man toward God and bound him together with other men. It restrained not only the hand, but even the heart by that commandment: *You shall not covet your neighbor’s goods, nor his wife,* etc. Hence Paul says in Romans 7: <margin>Paul.</margin> *I agree with the law, that it is good.* And again: *I delight in the law of God according to the inner man.* By which word he surely shows the power of the law was such that it resisted the sensual desires which harass the outer man—that is, the sensual man. But truly, since the holiness of a law is measured by its order toward its end, and the end of divine law is not like that of human law (which is the temporal tranquility and peace of the commonwealth), but rather eternal happiness, which is placed in the vision of God: that law is considered perfect which leads all the way to that end. That other law, however—good indeed, but not simply <margin>The difference between the Old and the New Law.</margin> absolute—is one which, although it leads by directing toward that end, does not actually bring one all the way there. It was by this distinction that the Old Law differed from our own. Indeed, since that end exceeds the powers of nature, the works of no law suffice to carry anyone there unless grace is helping from above, according to Romans 6: <margin>Paul.</margin> *The grace of God is eternal life.* And since grace was bestowed upon the whole world through the redemption of Christ, who was the Lawgiver of the Gospel, the Old Law (which did not contain this grace in itself) was good insofar as it commanded the duties of the virtues, yet it was not perfect like ours, which through the same grace of our Lawgiver leads us to its end. Hence Paul says in Titus 3: <margin>Paul.</margin> *When the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, not by the works of justice which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out upon us abundantly.* And in John 1: *The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Christ.* And the same applies to what he says in Hebrews 7: *The law brought nothing to perfection.* ¶ We have already said that this difference must be repeated by us in Question 7. In the meantime, however, lest the reader be left hanging in suspense, let us open the matter. For it is not easy to understand. Indeed, here is an <margin>Objection against the handed-down distinction.</margin> argument to the contrary. In the <term>circumcision</term> <note>circumcision: The primary ritual sign of the covenant in the Old Law, which Soto argues functioned somewhat like a sacrament.</note> of the ancient law, grace was conferred by the power of faith in Christ there professed, by which grace original sin was remitted, just as in our law through baptism by the power of the same Christ. Again, those who fulfilled the works of the law through that same grace then deserved eternal life just as we do. And just as they, when fulfilling the law without grace...
