<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The Law only provided works that were morally good; it did not, however, provide the merits required for eternal happiness <note>original: "beatitudinis merita." In scholastic theology, "merit" refers to an action that God rewards with eternal life; Soto argues the Old Law by itself lacked the grace to earn this.</note>. This is the same for us. What difference then remains between their Law and ours? The answer is not found in the works themselves, but in something else. Specifically, the cause of that grace by which those people were received into the friendship of God was not granted except through Christ, the giver of our Law. For that cause was his unique
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Passion, according to what Paul says in Colossians 1: *Now through his death and blood he has reconciled you, when you were once alienated and his enemies.* Therefore, as it is said among theologians regarding a contrite person: although they may be absolved of their sins through the grace of Christ before they make a confession, it is nonetheless by the power of the intended confession—which is the sacrament of his Passion—that this contrition works. Thus, when they approach the feet of the confessor, they are then truly absolved. The same must be thought regarding the whole body of the righteous who preceded Christ’s Passion. Namely, they were like a "deposit" <note>original: "in deposito." This suggests they were held in a state of waiting (often called the Limbo of the Fathers) until the debt of sin was paid.</note> until Christ should come, who, by paying the price of redemption, would expiate all their sins. And for this reason, the gates of heaven were closed to them, as if they were not worthy to be admitted into the possession of the children
<margin>Paul.</margin>
of God. And this is what Paul says in Romans 3: *God set forth Christ as a propitiator in his own blood to demonstrate his justice for the remission of preceding sins through the forbearance of God, to demonstrate his justice in this time.* Behold how the fountain of all grace was the Passion of Christ, even with respect to those who came before. There is therefore this difference:
<margin>In what sense the proposed difference is maintained.</margin>
that they were not saved through the works of the law, but through faith in the Jesus Christ who was to come, upon whose Passion the merits of the righteous rested. ¶ Soon, however, we are saved through faith in that same Christ who is present in our Law; specifically, he who earned grace for us at that moment in time by which we might fulfill the law suitably and worthily—at the moment when his law began to bind us. And this is the perfection by which our law excels the old one regarding moral precepts. ¶ Next, the 
<margin>The goodness of the divine law is shown by its final cause.</margin>
goodness of the same law is shown by reason of its <term>final cause</term> <note>The "final cause" is the intended purpose or goal for which something is created.</note>. For it was established to prepare and pave the way on earth for the coming Messiah. Moreover, this preparation consisted of two things. First, it was to be a proclamation and a foreshadowing of future things; and second, it was like a beginning of the Gospel. It was a proclamation through the oracles of the Prophets; hence Christ says in the last chapter of Luke: *It is necessary that everything written about me in the law, and in the
<margin>John 5.</margin>
Psalms, and the Prophets be fulfilled.* And in John 5: *If you believed Moses, you would also believe me.* Truly, it was a foreshadowing through the ceremonies, which were shadows of things to come,

<column-break/>

<margin>Paul.</margin>
according to what is said in 1 Corinthians 10: *All our fathers were baptized in Moses, and in the cloud, and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink.* For all these things were done as a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic precursor to something in the New Testament.</note> of us. It was, furthermore, like a beginning of the Gospel, insofar as under that law a specific people was set apart from the rest of the world and restrained from the worship of idols, and devoted to the worship of the one God. Hence Paul in Galatians 3:
<margin>Paul.</margin>
*Before faith came, we were kept under the same law, enclosed for that faith which was to be revealed.* And this concludes the first point. ¶ But so that the goodness of the same law may also be strengthened by the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The "efficient cause" refers to the agent or author who brings something into being.</note>, a second conclusion is added. God
<margin>Second Conclusion.</margin>
was the author of the same law: as is evident in Matthew 15: *You have made the commandment of God void because of your traditions.* For at that time, he was speaking about the
commandment: *Honor your father and your mother,* which was written in the law. And the reason is gathered
<margin>Reason for the question.</margin>
from what was said above: that law, as has been stated, was a preparation for the Gospel. Furthermore, not even the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>The Manichaeans were followers of a dualistic religion who believed the Old Testament was the work of an evil deity, distinct from the God of the New Testament. Soto is refuting this view.</note> could deny that God was the author of the Gospel. Therefore, since it belongs to the same person to propose the end and to arrange the means, the same God brought that law through himself and his ministers. For the Devil would never—as the Manichaean blasphemed with a devilish mouth—have established that law by which Christ was foreshadowed and worshiped, by whom the Devil himself was to be conquered and expelled. And the Redeemer himself showed this sense in Matthew 12: *If Satan casts out Satan, his kingdom is divided.* However, the assertion of this conclusion must be noted, for it not only strikes down the blasphemy of the Manichaeans (who, raving and lying, claimed it was the work of the prince of darkness), but also teaches that it was not the law of some angel or man, as human laws are, but just like the New Law, it was brought by God and should therefore be considered divine. For it says everywhere: *The Lord spoke to Moses, saying.* And in Exodus 24: after Moses reported the law to the people, they responded: *Everything that God has spoken to us, we will do.* And further on, while he established the same law with the sprinkling of blood as a testament in the figure of Christ (who was to confirm the new one with his own blood), he says: *This is the blood of the covenant which God has made with you.* This is also what Paul recounted in Hebrews 9. Therefore, when John says: *The law was given through Moses,* he does not mean that it was Moses's own law, but that it was promulgated through his ministry: just as the Gospel law was not the Apostles', but Christ's, made known by their preaching.

<meta>This page continues the discussion by Francisco de Soto regarding the divine origin and nature of the Old Law (the Mosaic Law). The previous page established that while the Old Law did not confer the grace of Christ directly, it was a necessary stage in salvation history. Here, Soto addresses the "Third Conclusion" regarding the delivery of the Law through angels and begins a systematic refutation of the Manichaean heresy, which claimed the Old Testament was the work of an evil deity.</meta>

# Question I of the Second Book

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Indeed, so that no part of the defense of that Law is overlooked, a third conclusion is put forward.
<margin>Paul.</margin>
That Law was established by God through the ministry of angels, according to the words of Paul in Galatians 3: *The Law was given through angels by the hand of a mediator.* To this, Stephen also bears witness in Acts 7 <note>The text says "Actuũ. 17," which is likely an error in the original manuscript or transcription for Acts 7, where Stephen's speech occurs.</note>, saying: *You received the law as delivered by angels.*
<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
And Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> in the fourth chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy* teaches that it is fitting for the secrets of divine things to be brought to men through the service of angels. However, this reasoning would not apply uniquely to the ancient Law, but also to our Law [the Gospel]; yet our Law was not brought through angels, but through Christ himself.
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
And therefore, St. Thomas [Aquinas] applies a specific analogy of that same providence, which he borrows from architects. For the architect of a ship does not hew and prepare the timber by his own hand, but through his assistants; yet he himself joins the structure of the ship together. The same is seen in the architect of a house. It was therefore fitting that God should send ahead the Law—which smoothed the way for the perfection of the Gospel—through his heavenly servants; but that He, having become man, should personally establish the Gospel and consecrate it with His own blood.
<margin>Paul.</margin>
The Apostle distinguished this interval in Hebrews 1, where he commends the excellence of the Gospel because through it, God has spoken to us in His Son: who is better than the angels, whom He made spirits and His ministers, sent into service for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation.

<margin>The Manichaeans.</margin>
The arguments raised to the contrary were the weapons of the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement that viewed the material world as evil and the Old Testament God as a lesser or evil being.</note>; among their other heresies was this: they tore the Old Law apart with insults and rejected it as if it had been established by the prince of darkness.
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine mentions this heresy in his book *On Heresies*, chapter 46, and wrote twenty-three books *Against Faustus* to refute it, among others.
<margin>Cerdo.</margin>
Although Cerdo <note>A Gnostic teacher in the 2nd century.</note> is said to be the first author of this heresy and the teacher of Marcion, he was succeeded a hundred years later by Manichaeus. For these men, not understanding that evil in itself has no cause but is rather a privation of good, and that the good God is not the creator of evils, collapsed into that madness of asserting two equal principles of things: namely, a prince of light, the author of good things; and a prince of darkness, the inventor of evils. And from there, since they placed the Old Law in the category of evil things, they said it was the invention of that prince of darkness.
<margin>Arguments of the Manichaeans against the Old Law.</margin>
The main points of the arguments they devised against the Law are roughly these:

<column-break/>

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
First, regarding the "end" <note>In philosophy, the "end" or *finis* is the ultimate purpose or goal of a thing.</note>—which is the first of all causes—they disapproved of it because it promised nothing but earthly things.
<margin>Faustus.</margin>
Hence, Faustus <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean bishop who debated Augustine.</note> says in Book 4 that he does not accept the Old Testament because the inheritance is not in it as it is in the New. For this reason, he denied that both laws belonged to the same God.
<margin>The Solution.</margin>
However, this has already been answered above: God promised them earthly things as if to children <note>Soto uses a common pedagogical argument: God treated the ancient Israelites like children who needed tangible rewards before they could understand spiritual ones.</note>; both so that He might outline future things through them, and so that He might make it publicly known how faithful a keeper of His promises He is.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
The second category of their arguments was that in many sayings, that Law conflicted with the Gospel, as we touched upon in our first argument.
<margin>Augustine’s Solution.</margin>
To this, Augustine responds very extensively in his books *Against Adimantus*, namely by reconciling those things which could seem to be in conflict.
<margin>The principal point.</margin>
For it is not at all contradictory that all things were made by God (as Moses says, *God created* <note>original: "Creauit Deus"</note>) and yet that He established those things through the Word, as if through His own art (as John says, *Through him all things were made* <note>original: "Per ipsum facta sunt"</note>).
<margin>Regarding the confirmations.</margin>
Nor does it stand in the way that man was made in the image of God according to nature, as is held there [in Genesis], and yet according to the malice of their behavior, Christ said to the Jews in John 8: *You are of your father the devil.* Nor is it a contradiction that He rested on the Sabbath day from the work of creating the world, and yet He always works by preserving and governing it.
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
Thirdly, they blamed the Law, as we suggested in the second argument, because it contained "evil" precepts. Chiefly cruel ones, such as: *An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth* <note>original: "Oculum pro oculo: dentem pro dente"</note>. For this reason, Christ rejected it in Matthew 5 as if it were unjust, saying: *But I say to you, love your enemies.* Soon they also cited things contrary to charity, such as the bill of divorce and the permission of usury; for in Deuteronomy 23, it was permitted to lend at interest to foreigners. And that which is cited in Matthew 5: *You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.* These things are allegedly evidence that both laws were not enacted by the same God. To these points, the answer is given in much the same way: namely, that since those people were so tenacious in their injuries, so thirsty for wealth, and so hardened against charity, God permitted them that vengeance of "like for like" <note>term: "talionis vindictam" — the Lex Talionis or law of retaliation.</note>, the divorcing of wives, and a limit on usury, so that He might restrain them from even more monstrous acts. But when the law of grace arrived, Christ built higher levels of charity upon it. Furthermore, that phrase, *You shall hate your enemy*, did not actually exist in the [Old] Law, as is clear from Leviticus 19, but was an interpretation of the Pharisees. Where-

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "Quare" (Wherefore), which is also the catchword at the bottom of the page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological defense of the Mosaic Law against the criticisms of the Manichaeans and the interpretations of contemporary scholars like Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples. # F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law

<margin>The annotation of Faber is not at all safe.</margin>

The annotation of Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Fabri Stapulensis" — a leading French humanist and theologian who sometimes clashed with traditional scholastic views.</note> regarding that same passage of the Gospel is not at all safe. <margin>Sacred testimonies against Faber.</margin> For he claims that it was clearly understood from the Old Scriptures that they everywhere called down evil upon enemies, as in Psalm 53: *Turn back evils upon my enemies,* and Psalm 82: *Let them be ashamed and troubled forever and ever.* <margin>Solution to the argument.</margin> It is a godless error to brand the Law with this mark—that it commanded the hatred of enemies. For the fact that the Israelites were commanded to destroy the Canaanites and Jebusites was not a command of hatred, but an execution of justice. On the contrary, Proverbs 25 commanded: *If your enemy is hungry, feed him.* Furthermore, those phrases in the Psalms, according to the consistent interpretation of Augustine, are not imprecations of evil—as if David had wished for bad things to happen to his enemies—but rather prophecies of the future. It is as if he had said: *You will turn back evils upon my enemies.*

<margin>Regarding the second argument.</margin>

Therefore, the response to the second argument is that when God confesses to have given them "precepts that were not good," he is referring to the ceremonies. He did not call them "evil," but "not good": that is, not perfect, nor sufficient in themselves for life. This is because they did not bestow the grace that washes away sins; rather, the people confessed their sins through those very ceremonies. Indeed, grace in the rite of circumcision flowed from faith alone. And therefore he added: *and judgments in which they shall not live,* namely, the life of grace. And later: *And I polluted them in their own gifts*: that is, through those gifts which they offered for their sins, it was shown that they were polluted. Finally, fourthly, the same Manichaeans <note>A dualist religious movement that viewed the material world as evil and rejected the Old Testament as the work of a lesser, evil deity.</note> reproached the Law above all for two reasons: first, that it was difficult to observe, and second, that it was the cause of sins. This is the point addressed by our third argument.

<margin>Regarding the third argument. The author in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans.</margin>

Truly, however, regarding those same passages cited from Paul in Romans 5 and 7, we have sufficiently explained that the Law was not the "effective" or "positive" cause for sin to live and for man to die to grace. <margin>Paul.</margin> On the contrary, Paul himself wipes this stain from the Law by saying that it was "holy." And in 1 Timothy 1: *But we know that the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully.* But because it forbade evil and taught what sin was, it served two roles: first, it took away the excuse of ignorance; second, because (as the Lyric poet <note>The Roman poet Horace: "Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusque negata" — we always strive for the forbidden and desire what is denied.</note> says) *we strive for the forbidden*, men took occasion from the Law to be carried into evil with even greater force. Because the Law did not bestow grace, it was a "negative" cause of sin: that is, it did not provide enough help to avoid it. Hence Paul does not say "an occasion being given," but *an occasion being taken*: that is, one which the Law did not provide, but which men took from it—namely, original sin,

<column-break/>

the "kindling" <note>original: "fomes" — a theological term for the lingering inclination toward sin in human nature.</note> of the flesh left in us, worked in me all concupiscence through the commandment. Therefore, in chapter 5, where he had said sin entered *so that* [vt] transgression might abound, the particle "so that" does not indicate the purpose or cause. For it was not the will of God, the giver of the Law, to incite men to evil through it; rather, it describes the consequence. For it followed from the weakness of men that, once the Law was given, sins were piled up.

<margin>Regarding the fourth argument.</margin>

The fourth argument has been sufficiently answered where we explained the reason for both the imperfection of the Law and its eventual cessation. Since it was a "figure" <note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as prefiguring something in the New Testament.</note> of the Law of Grace, nothing prevents it from having been established by God while still lacking absolute perfection. It was a preparation for the Messiah, the author of grace, who is the perfection of the Law; therefore, it followed both that it would not reach its perfection until his coming, and that it would be made obsolete by the presence of that same God.

<margin>Regarding the fifth argument. A double doubt. The first.</margin>

In the fifth argument, however, more than one doubt is sought to be resolved. One concerns those ancient utterances in which God was said to speak to Moses: specifically, whether he spoke by himself, or whether it was an angel speaking in his name. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine, in *On the Trinity* Book 2, chapters 12 and 13, and in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* chapter 27, leans toward the view that one of the angels, through a divine dispensation, bore the person of his Lord. This is just as a scribe, while delivering a sentence in the name of a judge, says: "We command, etc." Or in the same way a priest says in the place of Christ: *This is my body.* <margin>Augustine's opinion is strengthened.</margin> And the manner of speaking in Scripture supports his assertion. Indeed, in Exodus 3, where we read that the Lord appeared to Moses from the bush in a flame of fire, the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says the *Angel* of the Lord appeared. Augustine reads it this way. Nevertheless, he who appeared said: *I am the God of your father.* And in Genesis 32, he who wrestled with Jacob said to him: *Why do you ask my name, which is wonderful?* <margin>Reason for the previous assertion.</margin> Therefore, the angel was speaking in the person of God. The reason is this: since those voices were perceptible to the senses, it is clear they were produced in "beaten air" <note>original: "aëre verberato" — a traditional scholastic explanation of how spirits or God produced sound waves.</note> which men hear, and thus they thundered through the ministry of angels, whom God employs. For this reason, the Angel is considered to speak in the person of God. Although regarding that word of the Father in John 3 <note>The author likely means the baptism or transfiguration accounts in the Synoptic Gospels (e.g., Matthew 3:17), as this quote does not appear in John 3.</note>: *This is my beloved Son*, we have not hesitated to say that the voice was God's own, attributed to the Father: namely, that either God himself "beat the air," or that he performed it through angelic service as if using an instrument, just as we use...

He also discusses the scholastic theory that God spoke to Old Testament figures through the mediation of angels.</summary>

# Second Book, Question I.

<margin>Second question. Solution.</margin>
...we use the tongue. For this reason, it is said that the law was given through angels, or through the "arrangement of angels" <note>original: "dispositionem angelorum" — a reference to Acts 7:53</note>, because while God spoke to Moses on the mountain, that voice resounded in his ears through the work of angels. ¶But yet, a second question arises here because Exodus 33 asserts that the Lord spoke to Moses "face to face." It is answered, however, according to Augustine in the cited passages, that this should be understood according to the common opinion of the people <note>The "common opinion" refers to the human perception of a direct encounter, rather than a literal seeing of the divine essence</note>. For a little later, he most earnestly pleaded with God, saying: *Show me your glory*: surely that which he had not yet seen. Therefore, whether he saw God's face afterward, as Paul did in his rapture, or only the "back parts" <note>original: "posteriora" — see Exodus 33:23, where God allows Moses to see His back but not His face</note>, that is, something in which His glory shone upon him, is still under debate. Nevertheless, when he received the law on the mountain, God spoke to him with a voice fashioned through angels.

<margin>Another objection. Resolution.</margin>
What then is it that John says, *The Law was given through Moses*: for which reason it is surely called "Mosaic"? The answer is that just as Christ himself revealed the law to the Apostles, which they were to proclaim to the world, so God delivered it to Moses through angels, so that he himself might announce it to the people. And therefore it is called "Moses's law," as that of the proclaimer.

---

### ARTICLE III.

#### Whether that law ought to have been established for the people of Israel alone, and whether it ought to bind only them.

<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
After enough has been said by us regarding the goodness and causes of the ancient law, it follows that we should turn our discourse to its subjects. The question is asked, therefore, whether it was fitting for it to be established specifically for the people of Israel, and to bind only them. And it is argued from the negative side. That law, as has been said, was a figure and preparation for the Gospel: but a figure and a path ought to correspond to its end in likeness. However, the evangelical law was to be for the salvation not only of the Jews, but also of all the Gentiles, according to that oracle of Isaiah 49 prophesied concerning Christ: *It is a small thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to convert the dregs of Israel* <note>original: "faeces Israël" — the Vulgate's term for the "remnant" or "preserved" of Israel</note>: *I have given you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation even to the end of the earth.* Therefore, the old law also should have been promulgated to the entire world. This is especially so because it is read in Acts 10: *God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation, whoever fears Him and works justice is accepted by Him.*

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶Secondly, if that law bound the Jews alone,

<column-break/>

their condition would have been the worst and most burdensome among all mortals. For they could not obtain salvation without the observation of the law. For it is stated in Deuteronomy 27: *Cursed is everyone who has not remained in the words of this law, nor fulfilled them in work*: but the rest of the multitude of Gentiles, outside that law, could be saved by the law of nature alone <note>The "law of nature" refers to the innate moral sense common to all humans</note>; therefore, a wider path to salvation lay open to the Gentiles than to the Jews.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶On the contrary, however, is the opinion of Paul in Romans 3: *What advantage then has the Jew? Much in every way. Chiefly because the words of God were entrusted to them.* And David says <note>referring to Psalm 147:20</note>: *He has not done so for every nation: and his judgments he has not manifested to them.*

<margin>A double question clear in the proposed inquiry. First. Second.</margin>
The question, as was suggested during the arguing, seeks two things. First, whether it was appropriate for that law to be enacted for that singular people. Second, whether it bound only them. For someone might think that although it was promulgated to the Jews, nevertheless, since it was the Law of God—who is King of the whole world—whomever the fame of it reached would be bound to receive it. The response will consist of five conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion which satisfies the first question. First proof of the conclusion.</margin>
First: it was fitting for the law to be given to that people alone. This conclusion is gathered from what precedes. For since it was a work of God, whose supreme wisdom *reaches from end to end, and disposes all things sweetly* <note>original: "attingit à fine vsq; ad finem, & disponit omnia suauiter" — Wisdom 8:1</note>, no doubt remains that it was most well-advised and appropriate. Nevertheless, because this reason is too general, another must be explored from the end of the things themselves, in which the mind may find rest: namely, one that reflects the reason of divine wisdom. For it is one thing to ask why a certain people was selected to whom that law should be given, and not rather published to the whole world; and another thing to ask why that people was the Hebrews.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶Let there be, therefore, a second conclusion. The reason why a choice of some people was made from among all mortals is taken from the end of the same law, which was the coming of the Messiah. From this, a two-fold reason is received.

<margin>Double reason for the conclusion.</margin>
One is that since the whole world could not grasp the sublimity of such an exalted mystery—inasmuch as there were so many human minds in it, clouded both by natural dullness and by perversity of character—He condescended so that a certain small people would be particularly selected, to whom such high and hidden mysteries would be entrusted in the beginning. For if they had been spread immediately throughout the world, they would sooner have been held in ridicule than believed. For thus they are accustomed...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into why God chose the Hebrew people specifically to receive the Mosaic Law and the mysteries of faith, rather than revealing them to all nations at once.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

Wise and prudent men are not accustomed to publicizing their secrets recklessly, but rather they choose those to whose loyalty they may commit them. This is according to that passage in Ecclesiasticus 6: *Let many be at peace with you, but let one in a thousand be your counselor.* Indeed, you do not dare to broadcast news of a very grave matter to the common crowd at the beginning, lest you appear ridiculous; instead, you first whisper it into the ears of a few, until the rumor gains strength. God certainly could have made human minds such that everyone would understand at once, but nevertheless, He disposes all things gently, according to the way of nature. For fifteen hundred years of experience has taught us—I will not say how difficult the mysteries of our faith are to grasp—but how slow the human mind is, and how unteachable it is in laying hold of the best things; for only the smallest corner of the world retains the faith, and even that is torn in so many parts.

<margin>Second reason</margin>
The second reason is likewise taken from the same end: that it was fitting for there to be a chosen lineage from which Christ would draw His descent. For just as the Roman and Athenian nations, to give an example, celebrated their own names, so it was fitting for the ancestry and genealogy of Christ to have been illustrious in the world. And for both reasons, that people was marked with the character of circumcision so that they might be distinguished from the rest of the world. And that sign was commanded in that specific member <note>A reference to the reproductive organ</note> so that His lineage might be signified, who, along with the rest of our sins, was going to wipe away the stain contracted through generation. And just as there were more illustrious families among the Romans—such as the Caesars, the Camilli, the Scipiones, and so on—so also from that people the stock of David was chosen, from which the divine flower might bud. Therefore, as we recall from the first chapter of Romans, Christ was named the Son of David.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Regarding the other proposed part of the question—namely, why the Hebrew people in particular were chosen—the **Third Conclusion** is established: The reason for this kind of choice neither can nor should be sought in any cause or merit of that people, but must be attributed to the mere mercy of God.

<margin>Two reasons that are not quite apt.</margin>
For you might devise two causes fitting for that people. One of these would be that, while the rest of the nations of the world were immersed in the impiety of idolatry, the offspring of Abraham persisted in the true worship of the one God; thus, it was just for them to be uniquely chosen as God's special possession.

<margin>The first is refuted.</margin>
But yet, this reason is not convincing. For after receiving the law, they rushed into that same idolatry, which was much more wicked and absurd for them than for the Gentiles. Hence Exodus 33 and Amos 5 say: 

<column-break/>

*Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me in the desert for forty years, O house of Israel? And you carried the tabernacles of your god Moloch, and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves.* <note>original: "Nunquid hostias & sacrificium..." — Soto quotes the Vulgate version of Amos 5:25-26</note> Therefore, someone might perhaps devise a second reason: that although they were later idolaters, nevertheless they flourished in some duties of justice either before or after the law, by whose merit the law was given to them.

<margin>The second cause is rejected</margin>
However, it is plainly read in Deuteronomy 9: *Know that the Lord your God did not give you this land as a possession because of your justice, since you are a stiff-necked people.*

<margin>The true reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, the immediate reason was the promise made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, as is read in the same chapter.

<margin>The stated reason is explained.</margin>
Here it should be noted that Abraham preceded the Law and Moses by five hundred years. To him, as read in Genesis 12 and 22, the land of the Canaanites was promised, along with the future Messiah. And since the law was a foreshadowing, as we have said, and a preparation for that same Messiah, the law to be promulgated to his offspring was included in that same promise. Because of this, in the cited place in Deuteronomy, it says: *Not because of your justice and the equity of your heart do you enter to possess their lands*—meaning those of the Gentiles—*but because they acted wickedly, they were destroyed as you entered, and so that the Lord might fulfill His word which He promised under oath to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.* Thus, the expulsion of the Gentiles was because of their sins, but nevertheless, the introduction of the Jews and even the granting of the law was because of the promises of God.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
The Apostle, teaching this in Galatians 3, says: *The promises were spoken to Abraham and his seed.* And he does not say "to seeds," as if in many, but as if in one: *And to your seed, who is Christ.* Therefore, the law was given to that people because of the promises. Moreover, those promises were made so that the people from whom Christ was to put on flesh might surpass the rest of the world in holiness; according to that passage in Leviticus 19: *You shall be holy, because I am holy.*

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Nevertheless, although this was the immediate cause, the mind does not yet rest in it. For it remains to be answered: why did God choose Abraham and his progeny to reveal the mysteries of Christ and promise that He would be born of his blood, rather than any other mortal? Were his merits the cause? In truth, not at all; but, as the conclusion asserts, it was the mercy of God.

<margin>The merits of Abraham were by no means the cause.</margin>
For this is primarily supported by that oracle of Isaiah 41: *Who raised up the just man from the East, and called him to follow him?* For he was called from the land of the Chaldeans, as is read in Genesis 11.

# Question 1 of the Second Book

<columns>
1

<margin>
That people was selected above others as the lineage from which Christ would take His origin; but this itself must be attributed to mercy. The reasoning for the aforementioned assertion.
</margin>
...is read; which region was indeed in the eastern part of the promised land. Soon, reason also demonstrates the same point. For since the grace by which we are made pleasing to God does not fall under human merit <note>In theology, "merit" refers to a work that entitles a person to a reward; Soto argues here that no human action could "earn" the coming of Christ.</note>, it follows that no creature could earn its beginning and head. Christ was that beginning; therefore, not even the stainless Virgin was able to merit His coming—much less any of the ancient fathers. And since the Law was a figure of Christ, neither Abraham, nor his ancestors, nor his descendants merited it. Therefore, it was pure divine clemency that he and his lineage were chosen among all mortals. No human cause can be designated for this; rather, such an election must be traced back to the root of predestination, which has no cause other than the will of God, according to that 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
famous axiom of Augustine in his commentary on John:
> Why He draws this person and not that one, do not seek to judge, if you do not wish to err. <note>original: "Quare hunc trahat, & illum non trahat, noli velle iudicare, si non vis errare."</note>

Nevertheless, what we confess regarding the Virgin Mother of God, and also regarding Abraham, must be judged according to their respective ranks. For although the Virgin did not "earn" the incarnation of Christ in a legal sense, yet, once that divine purpose was fixed, God made her worthy to conceive Him—according to what the Church sings: 
> Who merited to carry the Lord of all. <note>From the Marian antiphon "Alma Redemptoris Mater."</note>

And in a similar way, in his own lower rank, God made Abraham worthy among mortals, so that He might choose his blood for His Son who was to be born.

<margin>The election of Abraham is designated in the sacred Canon.</margin>
¶ This election is first designated in the sacred Canon <note>The "Canon" refers to the Holy Scriptures.</note> in Genesis 10. There, when the text reaches the description of the lineage of Shem, the son of Noah, the Scripture says:
> To Shem also, the father of all the children of Heber, children were born.

Saint Augustine meditated on this word most carefully in the 16th book of *The City of God*.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
For the children of Heber were called Hebrews. Because of this, although he was not the firstborn of Shem, he was named first because of this dignity. Therefore, the name "Hebrew" is not derived from Abraham (as if they were "Abrahaites"), as some of the Jews imagine, but they drew their name from Heber. For that patriarch lived during the age of Nimrod <note>The biblical figure associated with the building of the Tower of Babel.</note> when the division of languages occurred; for that reason, he called the name of his son Peleg, as is read in the same place, which means "division," because in his days the earth was divided. Therefore, Heber was divinely separated from the rest who had conspired with Nimrod against God Himself. Abraham was the sixth descendant from this Heber, whom God commanded (as read in Genesis 12) to depart from his own land and his kindred. ¶ And this concludes the first part of the question. Regarding the second part—namely, whether the obligation of the Law extended to the Gentiles—two other conclusions are subjoined.

<column-break/>

2

<margin>Distinction of the precepts of the ancient law.</margin>
The following distinction is first set forth: In the Law, there were certain precepts belonging to the natural law, such as the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> and other moral rules. But there were others added to that same natural law, such as the ceremonial and legal requirements. Therefore, let this be the fourth conclusion in order.

<margin>The fourth conclusion in two parts.</margin>
All mortals were bound to keep those things which belong to the natural law—not indeed because of the bond of the Mosaic Law, but because nature herself commands it. However, the observance of the remaining requirements <note>The ceremonial and judicial laws specific to the Jews.</note> was not necessary for salvation for anyone outside of that chosen people.

<margin>Proof of the first part.</margin>
The first part is very well known; since even before the coming of the Law, the entire human race was bound to keep everything that nature taught, being illuminated by the "light of the divine countenance" <note>A reference to human reason as a reflection of God's light.</note>—both regarding divine worship and human society. The written Law exempted no one from this kind of yoke. Regarding these natural precepts included in the Law, Paul says in Romans 2:

<margin>Paul</margin>
> The Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law.

<margin>Proof of the second part.</margin>
The second part is clearly gathered from what has been said. For those who are assumed into a more sublime order of religion are bound by more rules than the rest who live a more relaxed life, as can be seen in the case of clerics and monks. That people was selected for a more excellent degree of holiness, as was fitting for the people from whom Christ was to be born, and who carried the figure of Christ Himself. Therefore, that people alone was obligated to those peculiar institutions added to the natural law. Hence, Deuteronomy 18 says:
> You shall be perfect and without blemish before the Lord your God.

For this reason, a certain image of a religious profession was enjoined upon them, as if they were practitioners of a stricter religion, according to chapter 26 of the same book:
> I profess today before the Lord your God, etc.

<margin>The fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ From this, finally, the fifth conclusion is gathered. Both while that Law was running and before it, men were able to obtain salvation under the natural law. I say "in the natural law," yet not through the powers of nature alone. For the grace of God is a supernatural thing; therefore, no one was ever able to attain it without some faith of the intellect and the subsequent moving help of the divine will. And in this sense, Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian theologian.</note> is understood in the 9th chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, where he says that many Gentiles

# Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

...If you wish to investigate whether they <note>The "Gentiles" or ancient pagans who lived before Christ.</note> entered the path of salvation, you must first consider whether they committed any vices so clearly at odds with natural reason <term>Natural reason: The basic human capacity to distinguish right from wrong, common to all people regardless of religion.</term> that they could not hide behind any shield of ignorance. For those whom you find to be such, it would be an impiety to suspect they were saved. Therefore, none of the idol-worshippers could be excused. Nor those who were "ignorant" of the sins of adultery, theft, and worse atrocities. It is different regarding simple fornication: it is probable that some of the heathens could be excused by ignorance of this before the written Law was given.

Similarly, although Socrates drank the poison—which in truth is not permitted—he could nonetheless be excused by ignorance, surely believing that the law by which he was condemned was a good one. A similar thing must be said of Seneca, who was given the choice of death by a tyrant. But neither Cato, nor any of the others who brought death upon themselves <note>Soto is distinguishing between those forced to die by the state (Socrates/Seneca) and those who chose suicide (Cato).</note>, are excused by legitimate ignorance; for the light of nature clearly teaches that it is permitted to no one to take their own life.

<margin>*Augustine*</margin>
Furthermore, Augustine, in his book *On True Religion*, commends Plato with praise because he maintained perpetual abstinence. <margin>*It is likely that Plato was in God's grace.*</margin> And it is certainly very likely that he was received into God's grace. However, these matters, which are based on conjecture, ought not to delay us.

<margin>*To the first argument.*</margin>
Therefore, in response to the first argument of this chapter's question: it was not necessary for the Law—which was a "figure" <note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of our Law—to correspond to it with such similarity as to be equally universal. Rather, for the reason already stated, it was fitting for it to be prescribed to a particular people from whom Christ would be born. This is according to Romans 9: <margin>*Paul.*</margin> "To them," namely the Jews, "belongs the adoption as sons of God, the covenant, and the giving of the law; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh." <note>original: "Quorum... est adoptio filiorum Dei, & testamentum, & legislatio: quorum patres, ex quibus Christus est secundùm carnem."</note> Consequently, God was not a "respecter of persons." For since He is a debtor to no one, He has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills. Hence Augustine says <margin>*Augustine.*</margin> in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*: "All whom God teaches, He teaches out of mercy; but those whom He does not teach, He does not teach out of judgment." For this [lack of teaching] comes from the condemnation of the human race for the sin of our first parent <note>Adam.</note>. However, once we assume our merits—which sprout from His grace—He renders to each according to his works without favoritism, as Paul says.

<margin>*To the second.*</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it is denied that the condition of the Jews was worse than that of the Gentiles. On the contrary, that people was more excellent the more strictly they were bound to God's law and worship. Just as among Christians, the more

<column-break/>

tightly men bind themselves by religious vows, the more happily they live. Hence Deuteronomy 4 asks: "What other nation is so renowned that it has ceremonies and just judgments?" Therefore, as it is written in Exodus 12, whichever of the Gentiles wished to migrate into the family of the Jews and enroll his name under that Law, he was admitted once circumcised. This is similar to the practice now for those who profess religious orders. 

<margin>*A hesitation.*</margin> 
But if someone should hesitate here as to whether any of the Gentiles could receive a small part of the Law without professing the whole; and especially whether they could be circumcised while living outside the Law. <margin>*The affirmative side is argued.*</margin> For reason seems to persuade us toward the affirmative side. For between Abraham and Moses, circumcision lasted for five hundred years without the [Mosaic] Law. <margin>*The Response.*</margin> It is answered that nothing forbade the Gentiles from borrowing certain ceremonies from the Jews that pleased them. Just as the Romans received some laws from foreign nations. Nevertheless, unless they professed the Law, it would not properly be "divine" to them. In fact, I believe that after the Law was given, circumcision led no one to salvation unless they professed the whole Law. For it was, just as Baptism is for us, a profession of the law. Paul teaches this clearly in Galatians 5 with these words: <margin>*Paul.*</margin> "I testify to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is a debtor to perform the entire law." <note>original: "Testificor omni homini circumcidenti se, quoniam debitor est universæ legis faciēdę."</note>

### ARTICLE IV.

For it was a preparation for salvation, which was to be conferred through Christ; but as soon as man fell, he stood in need of the remedy of salvation: therefore, it ought to have been brought forth immediately at the world's beginning. <margin>*The second.*</margin> ¶ Secondly: It was given for the sanctification of those from whom Christ was to be born. Therefore, just as circumcision was commanded to him, so also the Law ought to have been placed upon him. <margin>*The third.*</margin> ¶ Thirdly: As we were just saying, just as Abraham was selected from the whole world as the one from whom Christ would take His origin...

# Book Two, Question I

...might draw his origin; so afterwards from that people David, from whom he might lead a particular lineage; for which reason he was called the son of David: therefore, under David, who was born more than four hundred years after Moses, it <note>The "it" refers to the giving of the Old Law.</note> would have been more appropriately brought forth.
<margin>Paul.</margin>
On the contrary, however, it is gathered from Paul in Galatians 3, where he says the Law was ordained by Angels in the hand of a mediator: for the order of God also denotes the opportuneness of time.

The question is resolved with very little effort if the reason is sought from the will of God alone. For since that will has no prior cause nor owes anything to the human race, He gave the law when He knew it was fitting through His wisdom. Nevertheless, there remains to be explored the cause on the part of men, <margin>Conclusion answering the question.</margin> for whose salvation it was given. And therefore, an affirmative conclusion is established: It was given at that point in time because it was most beneficial to the human race. For indeed, it was established as a remedy for the wicked to soften their hardness and tame their pride; and as an aid for the good, to promote their salvation. And from these two roots, two reasons for the conclusion are drawn. <margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin> Indeed, if you look at the former, human pride is puffed up by two things: namely, natural wisdom and power—that which the crafty serpent placed in his suggestion when he attacked Eve. "For you shall be," he said, "like gods, knowing good and evil." <note>Genesis 3:5</note> For the same storm <note>The "storm" of pride.</note> had also driven him <note>Lucifer/The Serpent</note> from heaven. It was therefore for the benefit of the human race that God left it to its own favor for long centuries; furthermore, that it might learn by long experience how ignorant it was by its own nature both for knowing what was expedient for itself and how lazy it was for acting. For this reason, therefore, He left mortals for two entire ages, namely, one for <margin>First age of the world.</margin> one thousand five hundred years and more before the flood, in which He submerged the world, pestilential with the stench of crimes and outrages. Yet truly He did not so completely abandon it that He did not distinguish some with remarkable holiness in the line that led to the genealogy of Christ: such as Abel, Enoch, and finally Noah, in whose righteousness and that of his family the seed of the world was preserved. And from there, as if granting a new truce, He waited for man in the second age of almost five hundred years until Abraham, <margin>Second age.</margin> whom the wicked Nimrod <note>Nimrod was traditionally considered the builder of the Tower of Babel and the first tyrant.</note>, rebelling against God, preceded by one hundred and fifty years; and Ninus of Babylon <note>A legendary king of Assyria, often credited in the Renaissance with the invention of idols.</note>, through whom idolatry crept into the world, by fifty years. And because sin against nature is the punishment for idolatry and infidelity, as Paul clearly taught in Romans 1, <margin>Paul.</margin> a little later the unspeakable 

<column-break/>

foulness of the Sodomites infected the air; at which time indeed God sent Angels to Abraham, as the history in Genesis 18 relates, who might promise Christ to him in his own name for the salvation of the human race. Here one must not overlook that <margin>Mystery.</margin> mystery: namely, that the very Angels who came to set those cities on fire as if with hellfire, simultaneously brought the news of future salvation. Therefore, the cry and smoke of Sodom ascending to heaven both provoked God to justice, so that He might take vengeance on those unspeakable things, and at the same time moved Him to mercy, so that He might provide for men in the future. Whence, so that the same messengers of God might reveal to the world how much more the Lord is inclined toward mercy than toward justice, they promised pardon to those most corrupt cities on account of ten righteous men they might find. For on account of eight souls whom He found righteous at the time of the flood, He had not utterly destroyed the whole world. Then, however, having sealed the family of Abraham with the character <term>Character: Here meaning a permanent mark or seal, specifically circumcision.</term> of circumcision, <margin>Third age.</margin> He accustomed a third age of another five hundred years, so that it might be more ready to receive the law. It was of such great danger to entrust those divine precepts to the world immediately. For indeed, since the promise was made only to him and his offspring—whereas the law ought to be handed down not to one family, but to a sufficient number of men who would constitute a people—He waited until that same progeny increased into a people. And furthermore, lest they might not easily accept a suddenly received law as if it were a new thing: behold the delays by which God waited to bring the law until <margin>The old law was brought forth at the beginning of the fourth age.</margin> the beginning of the fourth age under Moses, in the year 2,458 from the creation of the world. Then, therefore, the law was given to blunt human pride in that part which is born from natural wisdom. For even then the natural light <note>The innate human ability to reason.</note> was so greatly darkened that men could scarcely distinguish between good and evil, but called (as the Prophet says) evil good, and good evil. Therefore, the office of the law was to teach this by explaining the principles of nature. Whence Paul in Romans 5: "Through the law is the knowledge of sin." <margin>Paul.</margin>
But truly it remained to teach those same men that even the knowledge of sin was not enough for overcoming and conquering it, unless strength were supplied from heaven for acting. And for this reason, <margin>The world was under the written law for three ages.</margin> God left the world under the written law for three other ages: namely, one thousand five hundred years until Christ, so that by long experience of affairs they might learn their own same infirmity and weakness, so that they might receive Him more desirably.

For the end of the moral precepts was to compose behavior; but the end of the ceremonial precepts was the coming Christ, the author of grace: both of which are required for the true salvation of the soul, which is the sole end of the law. <margin>Another confirmation.</margin>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
SINCE the specific questions regarding each kind of precept must be revisited individually below, we shall respond to the present general question with four brief conclusions. The first is: it was necessary for the moral precepts to be explained in that Old Law, as is proven by Exodus 20, where the Decalogue is found written, and other places where other things are written.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
Indeed, just as the chief intention of human law is to bind men together in mutual benevolence, so also is it God's purpose through His laws to join them to Himself in the closest friendship. Therefore, His intention is not merely to make us good in a human fashion, but to make us pleasing to Himself. Since similarity is the source of mutual love—according to Ecclesiasticus 13: "Every animal loves its like"—it follows that no one can be pleasing and acceptable to the most high God unless they are similar to Him in goodness according to their own degree. And since,
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
according to Aristotle in book 2 of the *Ethics*, virtue is that which makes its possessor good and his work good, the intention of the divine law is to imbue men with virtues pleasing to Himself and to decorate them with the ornament of good character. This, however, does not happen except through moral precepts—for that is why they are called "moral." Therefore, they were necessary in the Law. <margin>A clear sense of the divine warnings by which mortals are drawn to the imitation of divine virtues.</margin> And from this arises a clear sense of those warnings by which God, who loves us most dearly, allures us toward virtues that imitate the divine. As in Leviticus 19: "You shall be holy, because I am holy." And in the Gospel, Christ says: "Be merciful, as your Father is merciful," in Luke 6. And in Matthew 5: "Be you therefore perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." It is as if He said: "You cannot be dear to Him in any other way, unless you are made like Him through imitative virtue." ¶ But if you argue against the number of these precepts on the grounds that it was not sufficient—because, as is clear in the Decalogue, they are strictly precepts of justice (which concerns our relationship to others), while there are other virtues a man has in relation to himself, such as courage, temperance, and many others of that kind—the answer will shine forth for you in the following question, where other precepts will be made clear; all of which, however,
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
are reduced to the Decalogue. ¶ The second conclusion: In addition to the moral ones, it was fitting and necessary that the Old Law explain the precepts of ceremonies. For the name "ceremony" <note>original: "ceremōnia"</note> is said to derive either from Ceres—whom they worshipped as the goddess of grain—to which Cicero seems to agree in his first speech against Verres with these words: "The sacred rites of Ceres, the most...

### Book Two, Question II.

...our ancestors wished to be bound by religion and ceremony. 
<margin>Valerius.</margin>
Whether (as Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus, a 1st-century Roman author who wrote on religious rites.</note> more willingly accepts) the word "ceremony" comes from the town of Caere, where the sacred objects of religion were hidden when Rome was plundered by the Gauls, it nevertheless signifies those rites which pertain to divine worship. However, divine 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
worship—as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> skillfully taught in this place—is instituted by divine laws in a different and more profound way than by human ones. For since human law, as we were saying just now, consults only human affairs (we define nothing regarding Church matters for the present), it does not institute a higher worship of God than what it judges conducive to the common temporary good. But God, drawing men to himself, teaches his own worship through his own laws, so that men, having set aside earthly things, might be lifted up in their minds to him. And since we profess ourselves his servants not only through internal acts of believing, hoping, and loving, but also through external protestations, it was necessary for those 
<margin>First doubt.</margin>

<margin>Second doubt.</margin>
God through their ceremonies, as if through other moral behaviors. The second doubt is that we seem to approve as just the custom of human laws that direct divine worship toward their own civil end, even though this appears to be a perversion where we "use what should be enjoyed." <note>original: "fruendis vtimur." A reference to Augustine's distinction where God is to be "enjoyed" for His own sake, while the world is to be "used" to reach Him. Reversing this is a moral error.</note> ¶ Regarding the first 
<margin>The distinction between moral, ceremonial, and judicial [precepts].</margin>
doubt, it must be said that ceremonial precepts are not so different from moral ones that they are entirely distinct species; rather, they differ as the specific determination of a general category. You may easily perceive this if you recall the distinction we established in Book 1, Question 5, between those things that are purely positive law and those that are natural law. For although every law and precept is derived from natural principles—otherwise, as we showed there, it would have neither the force of law nor of a precept—the derivation is different. For from the same universal principles, some things are derived by way of conclusions (just as in the speculative sciences), while others are derived by way of determining a universal form into a specific one. In this way, moral and ceremonial 

<column-break/>

commands differ: namely, that the former [moral] are derived in the first way, while the latter [ceremonial] are derived in the second. For example: "Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself" is a self-evident principle. Soon, the fact that you do not wish to be killed by another, or your property to be plundered, or your marriage bed defiled, becomes clear by that same natural light. From these, moral precepts are gathered by natural consequence: *You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not commit adultery.* And we shall speak below in almost this same way about other things outside the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, for there are several degrees. However, human law and all positive law determines the general category into a specific form not by natural deduction, but by human judgment. For example: That God is to be worshipped is a natural principle. But *how*—in this or that way—nature does not teach; rather, it is sanctioned by the Gospel Church through human laws (such as canons derived from the apostles). For instance, that we shall keep such-and-such feasts, and profess our religion with these or those rites. But whereas Christ entrusted the business of the Church—which had already progressed in holiness—to the Church itself, God personally provided this for that unrefined people [the Israelites] whom he wished to be distinguished from the whole world. I say he sketched everything out for them as if for children. Therefore, he explained that same natural principle of worship specifically through those animal sacrifices and other rites which nature did not clearly teach. And these are the ceremonial precepts. Although this was unique to that law: that since it was a shadow of the future Messiah, who was to be the true God, it was fitting to command such sacrifices and ceremonies by which, under a cloud and figure, his worshippers might profess that same Messiah. 
<margin>To the second doubt.</margin>
¶ To the second doubt, the answer is that it happens in two ways that divine worship is referred to a civil and human end. In one way, the human end is considered supreme. This would be the perversion of using what should be enjoyed, and enjoying what should be used. However, to refer divine worship to a temporal end, not as the supreme end, but as one that is in turn referred back to God, is no perversion. Indeed, through this, we profess that everything comes to us from the divine. For this reason, the Church pours out prayers and offers sacrifices and the solemnities of Masses for temporal goods. Human law, therefore, refers divine worship to its own end in this way. Although Canonical and Ecclesiastical laws, following divine ones, ought to provide this for civil affairs: that they move the minds of men, detached from earthly things, toward God. ¶ The superstitious religion of the Gentiles, however, is to be blamed insofar as their rites in...

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...they first dedicated their own rites to false gods. Soon after, they were seduced by demonic illusions and struggled to foreknow the future through the inspection of animal entrails <note>The practice of extispicy or haruspicy, common in Roman religion</note> and other superstitious auguries. Third, they made use of filthy ceremonies. And finally, by placing their happiness in earthly prosperity, they seemed to worship the gods for no other reason than that they lacked their help. For this reason, they worshipped one goddess for crops, another for wine, and another for wars; when they were in need of these things, they took particular care to appease them.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion.** Besides these two kinds of precepts <note>Moral and ceremonial</note>, a third kind, the **judicial**, was again necessary. The reasoning for this is similar to what we have explained regarding the ceremonial ones. Since divine law establishes men first in relation to God, and then in mutual friendship and peace with one another—both of which the natural law commands in a general sense—it followed that God should explain both in specific detail. Thus, just as He established ceremonial precepts specifically regarding divine worship, so too He ought to have established judicial ones, by which goodwill and peace among men might be maintained.

<margin>The first distinction between the three kinds of precepts: namely moral, ceremonial, and judicial. St. Thomas.</margin>
Observe, therefore, the difference between these three kinds of instructions: the other two are derived from the moral precepts, which are the dictates of the natural law. Specifically, the ceremonial precepts relate to divine worship, while the judicial ones relate to human tranquility. Therefore, as **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica I-II, q. 99</note> teaches in his first solution, the Old Law added something above the natural law, in the same way that human laws are additions to that natural right. For even under the New Law, we have ceremonials, as has been said: such as the singing of Psalms, processions, the burning of incense, and other things of this kind. We also have judicial matters, such as excommunications, suspensions, and irregularities <note>Legal impediments in Canon Law</note>, as well as the ancient penances of the Canons. Similarly, in civil law, we find judicial punishments decreed for wrongdoers. However, for the reason stated above, Christ did not express these in the Gospel but committed them to the Church and the civil commonwealth. God, however, explained everything in the Old Law.

<margin>Second distinction.</margin>
¶ From this follows a second distinction. Namely, that **moral precepts** belong simply to natural law—that is, they are commanded because they are good, or prohibited because they are evil. The others, however, belong to positive divine law (just as our ceremonies and judicial rulings belong to positive human law): they are good because they are commanded, or evil because they are prohibited.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Just as **Aristotle** distinguishes in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 7, between **natural justice** <note>original: "iustum naturale"</note>—that which is such by its own nature—and **legal justice** <note>original: "iustum legitimum"</note>, which before it was established

<column-break/>

mattered not at all, but matters once it has been established. And perhaps **Paul** alluded to these three types in Romans 7, <margin>Paul.</margin> saying that "the law is holy" <note>original: "lex est sancta"</note> regarding the ceremonial (since that which is dedicated to God is holy); "the commandment is just" <note>original: "mandatum iustum"</note> regarding the judicial; and "good" (that is, honorable) regarding the moral.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Finally, a **fourth conclusion** is added to these. Although other names are found in the Old Law—namely, **commands**, **testimonies**, and **justifications**—all of them are nevertheless reduced to these three types.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason for the conclusion is as follows. Certain things exist in the law which are proclaimed as precepts of things to be done. Others, however, are applied as a strength for their preservation. Of the former, there are the three types already established; of the latter, there are another three. For that which leads to the observation of the law is, first, the authority of the legislator, and second, the utility of the law—which is either the attainment of a reward or the caution of a punishment.

Therefore, those things by which the authority and majesty of the legislator are commended are called **testimonies**. As in Deuteronomy 17: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one." And the beginning of the Law, where He is pronounced the creator of heaven and earth. And in the Psalms: "You are terrible; and who shall resist you?" and "Almighty is His name," and similar phrases.

But those things by which either rewards or punishments are brought forward are called **justifications**. As in Deuteronomy 18: "If you hear the voice of the Lord your God, He will make you higher than all nations." And Isaiah 1: "If you be willing and hearken to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you will not, and will provoke me to wrath, the sword shall devour you." For through these, divine justice is commended.

A **command** <note>original: "mandatum"</note> is perhaps the same as a precept. But since they seem to be distinguished from one another in the passage cited, perhaps **precepts** refer to those things necessary for salvation, while **commands** refer to those things performed out of charity beyond what is required <note>term: "supererogation" — doing more than duty requires</note>, of which kind are the Evangelical counsels. And that passage from Exodus 2: "If you take your neighbor's garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun sets." Or perhaps precepts are those which God wrote on the tablets (the Decalogue), while commands are those He revealed to Moses to proclaim to the people. Nevertheless, the justifications themselves are also testimonies of divine justice. All of them, however, are reduced to the three primary general types. For the others (as has been said) are not so much precepts as they are things pertaining to their safekeeping.

### Question II of the Second Book

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Having established these points in this manner, we respond to the first argument to the contrary by stating that although moral precepts are nothing other than what the law of nature dictates and clear reason can teach, it was nonetheless worthwhile for God to bring aid to them with such prudence, not only in supernatural matters but also in natural ones. For although the *synderesis* <term>Synderesis: the innate spark of conscience or the habitual knowledge of the primary principles of moral law which, according to scholastic theology, can never be fully extinguished.</term> of reason can never be so extinguished that the first principles of natural law do not shine within it, it can nevertheless be covered by such a fog <note>original: "caligine"</note> that it hallucinates and wanders concerning their conclusions. This occurs not only in theoretical matters <note>original: "speculabilibus"</note>, but also in morals. It is indeed wondrous to say how many ravings of ancient wise men concerning theoretical matters have been recorded. And in morals, they considered not only simple fornication but even graver matters as permissible. And it is believable that this cloud of the mind darkened mortals especially at the time when the Law was given. For the same reason, supernatural faith teaches us not only about supernatural articles [of faith], but also about others that nature teaches—such as that God is one and the cause of all things, that the soul is immortal, and similar truths.

<margin>To the confirmation of the same argument.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding the point added in that same argument—namely, that it is the "letter of the law" that kills—we deny that this does not apply to moral precepts. <margin>Augustine</margin> On the contrary, as Augustine is the authority in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 14, and as we, instructed by him, have treated at length in our commentary <margin>The author in the 3rd chapter of the Epistle to the Romans.</margin> on the third chapter of Romans, it is the very precepts of the Decalogue <term>The Ten Commandments</term> of which Paul says "the letter kills" <note>original: "literam occidere"</note> and "works wrath" <note>2 Corinthians 3:6 and Romans 4:15</note>. This was not because the law did this by its direct intention (as has already been said), but because by revealing the works of sins, these precepts stripped subjects of any excuse; and yet that law did not confer the grace [to fulfill them]. However, those who, being justified by faith in the coming Christ, fulfilled those laws, increased their righteousness before God. And for that reason, David called those same works "justifications."

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
The second argument was also resolved when we explained how ceremonial matters also pertain to morals and merits. Nonetheless, because they are not drawn from the dictate of nature by natural light alone, but rather by human or divine judgment, they are distinguished from moral ones. Thus, to worship God is a moral principle; but to do so by this or that rite is ceremonial. <margin>To the confirmation. Dionysius.</margin> To the other point added there, it is responded that even if words are more convenient for signifying truths, it is nonetheless natural for humans to understand spiritual things through sensible likenesses of things, as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian who wrote on the "Celestial Hierarchy."</note> is the authority in his first chapter. For this reason, it was fitting that such ceremonies be commanded to that people, by which they might profess the coming Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the third argument.</margin> Likewise to the third, as with the ceremonial ones, it is responded that even if acts of justice in general pertain to moral precepts, nevertheless these or those specific precepts of judgments are called "judicial." Just as "every evildoer must be punished" is a moral precept; but "a thief must be hanged" and "a heretic burned" are judicial. Since judicial matters partly agree with moral ones—namely, that they are derived from reason and pertain to morals—and partly with ceremonial ones—namely, in that both are specific determinations of general precepts—it follows that they are sometimes counted among the moral ones. For example, in Deuteronomy 5: "Hear, O Israel, the ceremonies and judgments." At other times they are counted among the ceremonial, as in Leviticus 18: "You shall do my judgments and keep my precepts." In the former place, moral things are understood by the name of "judgments"; and in the latter, ceremonial things. <margin>To the fourth argument.</margin> The fourth was indeed resolved above, except for that small part concerning moral virtues distinct from justice. It will certainly be established in the very next question how their precepts are reduced to justice, because a "precept" always expresses the nature of a "debt" <note>The idea that all moral duties are a form of "debt" or obligation owed to God or neighbor.</note>.

#### Whether the Old Law ought to have induced its subjects to its observance through temporal promises and threats.

After the precepts of the Old Law, it follows in the third article that we speak of its rewards and punishments, by which its followers were both enticed to obedience and deterred from transgression. However, temporal desire leads souls far away from God; according to Augustine in his book *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 36: <margin>Augustine</margin> "The poison of charity is cupidity" <note>original: "venenum charitatis est cupiditas"</note>. Therefore, those enticements and terrors were least fitting for a divine law. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> Second, human laws appear more lowly from the fact that [per...]
