# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law

...through these slippery and perishing temporal matters, they promote citizens toward the good. Therefore, the divine law, which leads mortals toward immortal happiness, ought not to use similar little gifts <note>original: "munusculis"</note> and deterrents. This is especially true because temporal prosperity is common to both the unjust and the just, and adversity hits the just as well as the unjust, according to Ecclesiastes 9: "All these temporal things happen to the just and the wicked: to the good and the bad; to the clean and the unclean; to him who offers victims, and him who despises sacrifices." <note>Ecclesiastes 9:2</note> Therefore, temporal goods or evils are inappropriately established as rewards or punishments for the mandates of divine law.

¶ To the contrary, however, is that which was recently cited from Isaiah 1: "If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you." <note>Isaiah 1:19-20</note>

<margin>The meaning of the proposed question.</margin>
First, the title of the question must be noted. For it is not called into doubt whether the guardians of that law, through faith and the grace of Jesus Christ, would obtain eternal rewards, and whether transgressors would be afflicted with perpetual punishments, just as happens to those who profess the Gospel. For the light of the other life had shone upon those ancients, as is clear from Genesis 37: "I will go down to my son in the underworld <note>original: "in infernum," referring here to Sheol or the place of the dead</note> mourning." For that is how they named the departure from this present life, because the heavenly gates were not yet open to them; for which reason even the just descended to Limbo <term>Limbo: specifically the *Limbus Patrum* (Limbo of the Fathers), where the souls of the Old Testament righteous waited for Christ to open the gates of Heaven.</term>. And in Ezekiel 37, a prophecy of the future resurrection stands open in that field which he saw prophetically full of bones. For it was said to him, "Do you think these bones shall live?" And it follows: "Behold, I will send spirit into you and you shall live." And Job 19: "I believe that my Redeemer lives." And in Acts 23, mention is made of the opinion of the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect of the time that denied the resurrection, the existence of spirits, and oral tradition.</note> who denied the resurrection of the dead, contrary to the faith which the rest of the people upheld. And David in Psalm 101: "The just shall be in eternal memory." And Wisdom 5: "Then shall the just stand with great constancy against those who afflicted them." And regarding the wretched suffering punishments, it is added: "Seeing this, they shall be troubled with horrible fear," etc. Therefore, what is proposed in the question is not why those fathers were not rewarded or punished except temporally, but why—since the same eternal rewards and punishments awaited them as await us—only temporal ones were recorded in the written law.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
¶ It is answered, therefore, with a single conclusion: It was fitting and most appropriate for that people to be led by those promises and threats of temporal things. Now, 

<column-break/>

<margin>First proof of the conclusion.</margin>
it was already shown in the previous book that laws draw men toward their observation through the fear of punishments and the hope of rewards, in the manner of the theoretical sciences, which move one toward the assent of conclusions through the knowledge of principles. For this reason, the prudence of a legislator ought to be such that he establishes both rewards and punishments according to the dispositions of the citizens. Now, as we recalled in the preceding question, Paul in Galatians compares that people to a child while he is being educated under a tutor <term>Pedagogue/Tutor: from the Greek *paidagogos*, a slave who supervised a child's conduct and led them to school; Soto uses this to show the Old Law's role as a supervisor for the "immature" faith of the Israelites.</term>. But it is the natural disposition of children to be enticed only by those little gifts which are before their eyes, for they cannot perceive with the mind those things which are absent. By the same logic, they are deterred by the fear of present things. It was therefore most expedient that the law—which, as has been said, was preparing that nation for the perfection of the Gospel as a kind of imperfection—should use that lowest kind of rewards and punishments.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Therefore, Paul in Philippians 3 reminds the family of the Gospel—as children already advanced by the love of God and sent into their inheritance—by his own example, saying: "Forgetting those things which are behind, and stretching myself forth to those things which are before, I press toward the mark, for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded," etc. <note>Philippians 3:13-15</note> See, therefore, why in Exodus 3, where God appeared to Moses (whom he would delegate to the elders of the people in Egypt, to whom he was going to give the law), he promises them only this: that he will lead them into the kingdom of the Canaanites, a land indeed flowing with milk and honey. Christ, however, the bringer of the New Law in Matthew 4, proposes to us no kingdom lower than that of heaven. There, the goods of the earth are promised; but in the Gospel, eternal life. And Deuteronomy 28 says: "If thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God... the Lord thy God will set thee on high above all nations of the earth: and all these blessings shall come on thee... Blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field," etc. <note>Deuteronomy 28:1-3</note> In Matthew 5, however: "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land." <note>Matthew 5:3-4</note> Not, certainly, the lowly land of the Canaanites flowing with milk and honey, but the heavenly land of the Angels, overflowing with divine nectar.

<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ And to this, which is the canonical reason, let us subjoin another very close to it, budding from the same root. Since those things which Christ was going to promise to the world could scarcely be believed by men on account of their loftiness—because they had not even entered into the hearts of men—God deliberately wished to declare his faithfulness in those temporal things, so that he might claim a more certain

<summary>Soto explains that the Old Law used temporal rewards (like the land of Canaan) and punishments because the Israelites were in a "spiritual childhood" and needed tangible incentives. He contrasts this with the New Law of Christ, which promises the eternal Kingdom of Heaven.</summary>

### Question II of the Second Book

...He might claim our trust among us when He later promised invisible things. For this reason, He allowed that people to go into Egyptian exile, so that from there He might afterwards recall them into the promised land in the best of faith, with such great signs and portents. Namely, so that in those events He might both depict the future promises of heavenly things, and also persuade the human race of how faithful He is in His promises.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
And for this reason, as I believe, Augustine in the fourth book of *Against Faustus* calls that the "Old Testament" and this the "New." To be sure, this is not only because that one preceded this one, but also because its promises were for things that grow old with time; in our Testament, however, those things are promised which remain forever. <note>Augustine argues that "Old" refers to the perishable nature of the earthly rewards given to the Israelites, whereas "New" refers to eternal life.</note>

¶ There is a similar distinction between the punishments of that law and our law. For it is evident both elsewhere and frequently, and most clearly in Leviticus 26, where after the temporal rewards—namely, "If you walk in my precepts," etc., "I will give you rain in its season so the earth may sprout its seed," and many things of that kind—He adds: "But if you will not hear me, I will visit you quickly with poverty and burning heat which shall waste your eyes and consume your souls. You shall sow your seed in vain, which shall be devoured by your enemies." <note>Leviticus 26:3-16</note> Yet one must not be so mistaken about this interval as to believe that no one there performed works except through fear of punishment. For those holy fathers, such as Moses, Abraham, and the prophets, revered God with **filial fear**. <note><term>filial fear</term>: A respectful, loving fear of God as a father, rather than a "servile fear" which is merely the dread of a slave for a master.</note> And conversely, in the Gospel, many are drawn along by **servile fear**.

<margin>Paul</margin>
Indeed, as the Apostle [Paul] warns us in Romans 1, Christ has much more openly threatened us in the Gospel with the wrath of God revealed from heaven: namely, the torments of hell. But the difference is that there, God did not threaten anything except temporal punishments; but to us He threatens eternal ones. For God says through Isaiah: "If you listen, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you." <note>Isaiah 1:19-20</note> But Christ says: "And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life." <note>Matthew 25:46</note> Furthermore, that law was full of fear, which is why it was given on the mountain with thunder and lightning; explaining this in Exodus 20, Moses says: "God came to prove you, and so that his terror might be in you." But our law shone forth in the fire of love on the day of Pentecost.

<margin>Paul</margin>
Paul explains this distinction in Hebrews 12. For this reason, those sinning against that law were immediately snatched away to punishment—as is clear in the forging of the [golden] calf—or were handed over to the Philistines, or Babylonians, or other enemies, whom an angry God used as His avengers.

<column-break/>

Hence David says in Psalm 77: "When he slew them, they sought him and returned." <note>Psalm 78:34 in modern numbering.</note> But for us (which is worth noting), Christ threatened no temporal punishment in the Gospel; instead, all things await us in the next age. For this reason, we ought to dread much more bitter things than they did. But regarding the distinction between both laws, we shall have a more accurate discussion in Question 7, and a clearer discourse where it remains for us to speak about the Evangelical Law.

---

<margin>To the first argument</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that there are three ranks of men distinguished by their desire for temporal things. One is of the **perfect**, who do not cast even one eye toward these sorts of fleeting goods, but having cast them aside entirely, they are fixed on God. That people [the Israelites] was not in this rank, although certain very rare individuals reached this level; 
<margin>Paul</margin>
of whom Paul says in Hebrews that "the world was not worthy." Another is the extreme rank of the **perverse**, who place their end in these sorts of slippery goods. 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine asserts that the desire of these people is the "poison of charity"; for them, a law that promised temporal things would be dangerous. But the third is the middle rank of the **imperfect**, who desire temporal goods in such a way that they judge them a path toward the enjoyment of eternal things. Therefore, it is beneficial for these people to be enticed toward the love of God through these temporal things. For as it says in the Psalm: "He will acknowledge you when you do good to him." <note>Psalm 49:19 in the Vulgate.</note>

<margin>To the second argument</margin>
¶ To the second it is responded that the excellence of divine law over human law is perceived from the fact that human law proposes rewards to be conferred by men, but God proposes those things which He Himself is going to bestow. And for that reason, with the best judgment, He grants those things to the just and withdraws them from the unjust—unless at times reason demands the contrary. Hence, if you survey the histories of the Old Testament <note>original: "veteris instrumenti"</note>, as long as that people obeyed God and the law, they abounded in temporal prosperity; and conversely, while they fell away from His grace, they then experienced the adversity of the heavens and of enemies.

<margin>Paul</margin>
But if He exercised some just people with such adversities—those whom Paul says in Hebrews were "distressed and afflicted"—He did this so that it might yield for them a greater crown. Although He also allowed some who observed the law externally, while keeping an internal heart fixed on temporal things, to enjoy them for the accumulation of their condemnation—according to that passage in Isaiah 29: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me."

# QUESTION THREE,
## Concerning Moral Precepts.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* I-II, question 100.<- <note>Soto is following the structure of Thomas Aquinas’s most famous work, specifically the section on the Old Law.</note>

### ARTICLE I.

#### Whether all moral precepts belong to the law of nature.

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
HITHERTO WE HAVE DISCUSSED the precepts of the law in general; we must therefore now descend to the individual species. Among these, the moral precepts hold the first and primary place. Regarding these, we are preparing two questions: namely, this one concerning all of them in general, and another specifically concerning each one. First, therefore, it is asked whether all [moral] precepts belong to the law of nature. And it is argued on the negative side. First, from Ecclesiasticus 17 <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach.</note>: Moral precepts are called "discipline," for it is said of them, "He added discipline to them, and he gave them the law of life as an inheritance." Discipline, however, since it is acquired through teaching, is distinguished from the law of nature; for the latter is not learned, but perceived by natural instinct. Therefore, not all moral precepts are of the law of nature.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: Divine law is more perfect than human law. However, human law adds many instructions for good works to the natural law. From this it follows that while the law of nature is the same among all people, human institutions of customs vary among different peoples. Therefore, it was much more fitting that the divine law should add something further beyond the natural.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: Not only natural reason, but also faith contributes to the institution of morals. Whence Paul says to the Galatians 5: "Faith works through love." <note>original: "Fidem ait per dilectionem operari"</note> Faith, however, is not included under the law of nature, since it is raised above natural reason. Therefore, not all moral precepts of the divine law pertain to the law of nature.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is that statement of the Apostle to the Romans 2: "The Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature those things which are of the law," where he was designating the moral precepts.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
The present question is raised not only regarding the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, but universally regarding all things which by their nature pertain to morals.

<column-break/>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To which it is responded with two conclusions. The first is: All moral precepts—not only those written in the Old Testament, but any others that may exist—are of the law of nature.

<margin>The Proof.</margin>
The conclusion is proved: Moral precepts, as they have been defined, differ from ceremonial and judicial ones because they pertain to morals *per se*—that is, by their very nature—excluding any <term>positive law</term> <note>Positive law refers to laws specifically "posited" or decreed by a lawgiver, like a King or God, rather than laws inherent in the nature of things.</note>. For ceremonial and judicial rules pertain to morals not by themselves, but because they were established by an arbitrary law. However, the uprightness of morals must be judged by its relation to natural reason, which is the proper principle of human actions. Just as the straightness of a stone or wood is measured by a standard rule. Namely, so that those customs are called—and are—upright which accord with reason, while those which deviate from it are rejected. Moreover, the judgment of reason, both practical and speculative, proceeds from principles to conclusions; for this is the very act of reasoning. It follows, therefore, that all moral precepts, whether they are principles or conclusions, belong to the law of nature; for <term>law</term> <note>Soto uses the word "ius," which can mean both "law" and "right."</note> is nothing other than a rule.

<margin>Second Conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: Moral precepts of this kind exist in a threefold grade. For some moral precepts are of the law of nature according to three different ways in which they descend from those same first principles of nature.

<margin>The three ways they descend from natural principles.</margin>
For some are conclusions which are approved or rejected through those same universal principles immediately, with almost no effort, but by any sort of consideration. And these are in the first grade.

<margin>First.</margin>
Such as: "Honor your father and your mother," "You shall not kill," "You shall not steal," and things of this kind. For from that principle, "Do to others what you wish to be done to yourself," <note>The Golden Rule.</note> and assuming this further point, also naturally known by itself, that you would wish to be honored by your children, it follows that you also ought to honor your parents. Unless you prefer to deduce it from the principle that he who receives a benefit owes a benefit; for the greatest of temporal benefits is that which we receive from our parents. Again, from that principle, "Do not do to others what you do not wish to be done to yourself," by immediately assuming that you would not want to be harmed by another either in your person or in your goods, it is gathered: "You shall not kill," "You shall not steal," "You shall not commit adultery."

<margin>Second.</margin>
But there are others which everyone’s reason does not immediately gather from the same principles, unless assisted by the support of the wise, whose role it is to meditate more deeply on things. Such as that in Leviticus 19: "Rise up before the hoary head, and honor the person of the aged man." For this is not as well known as the debt...

<meta>The text ends with the catchword "debitum" (debt), indicating the first word of the next page.</meta>

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that all moral laws, including the Ten Commandments, are rooted in natural reason rather than just being arbitrary divine decrees. He categorizes these laws into three levels, explaining that basic moral rules like "do not kill" are immediately obvious conclusions from the Golden Rule, while others require the wisdom of experts to understand.</summary>

# BOOK TWO, QUESTION III.

...the duty of honoring parents. And that passage of the Gospel: *Do not say to your brother, "Racha"* <note>Matthew 5:22. "Raca" is an Aramaic term of contempt roughly meaning "empty-headed."</note>: which is not as manifest as the prohibition against killing.

<margin>The third degree.</margin>
But there are other things which, although they are consistent with natural reason, reason cannot reach by itself unless it is divinely illuminated. Of this order are many things pertaining to divine worship: *You shall not make a graven image* and *You shall not take the name of your God in vain.* For natural reason does not intimately grasp <note>original: "medullitùs callet," literally "to know into the marrow."</note> these and similar things unless it is irradiated by divine splendor.

<margin>An objection against the aforementioned truth.</margin>
¶ In order that these matters may receive a little more light, it is first argued to the contrary.

<margin>The first reason.</margin>
Moral and judicial precepts, as was said in the previous question, are also derived from the law of nature: for they are also congruent with reason; otherwise they would not have the character of law, as we showed in the previous book. They should therefore be placed in some degree of the law of nature.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> are considered either universal principles of the law of nature, or conclusions. The first cannot be said: because, as St. Thomas teaches, they are nothing but conclusions sprouting directly from those principles. If, therefore, they are conclusions, how are they placed in the first degree?

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
Likewise, those things which God teaches us above nature are not of the law of nature: why then do we establish a third degree there?

<margin>To the first objection.</margin>
¶ To the first, the response is gathered from what was said above. For even if ceremonial and judicial laws descend from the law of nature, they do not do so by natural consequence and inference—like conclusions from principles—but through the "determination" <note>A technical legal term meaning the specific application of a general principle to a particular case, such as deciding exactly how a thief should be punished.</note> of a genus to a species, at the discretion of the legislator. And therefore, they are placed in a different order, removed from the law of nature, rather than being placed in its direct line. For this reason, these did not remain under the Gospel law as the moral precepts did, but were abolished.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
<margin>Scotus.</margin>
¶ Regarding the matter of the second argument, the Doctors <note>Highly respected theologians of the Church.</note> hold varying opinions. For in the *Sentences* (Book 3, Distinction 37), Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note> and several of the Scholastics establish the universal principles of nature as the first degree, and the conclusions of both the second table of the Decalogue and others in the second. Regarding their opinion, we must dispute more closely below in Article 8. In the meantime, however, the opinion of St. Thomas must be carefully observed so that no one is deceived into thinking that the Decalogue is placed among the universal principles just because he places it in the first degree. Indeed, the primary principles that are "self-evident" do not constitute a degree, but are the root and source. For a "degree" is the same as a "step" <note>original: "gradus enim idem est quod gressus."</note>; just as in a line of blood-relation the trunk and root are not a degree, but the brothers are; and those

<column-break/>

falling immediately from there are in the first degree. Thus, in the law of nature, the principles are not the "degrees," but the consequences that descend from them. And the other degrees are discerned by their distance from those same principles. Therefore, since there are two tables in the Decalogue, the seven later commandments found in the second table are placed in the first degree. In the second degree are those things outside the Decalogue, such as the precepts of honoring elders, and other things that do not pertain to justice. But the precepts of the first table consist in the third degree. They are not placed in the third order because they are not the most worthy of all; rather, they are judged as more distant from the principles of nature because, due to their sublimity, our reason does not fully elicit them unless divinely aided. Just as in those of the second degree, the training of wise men is needed. One order of dignity, therefore, is recognized among these, and another order of knowledge. For what is more closely in accord with nature, or what is more worthy, than the precepts of the first table, seeing as they regard the worship of the one God? And yet, because they are further removed from human knowledge, no crime among the Pagans spread so widely as the impiety of idolatry. For regarding the other precepts of the second table, there was very little error. And regarding those in the second degree, there was less error than regarding the first table. And this is the order of knowledge which St. Thomas most skillfully distributed through degrees.

<margin>A Question.</margin>
<margin>The Solution.</margin>
¶ Perhaps the reader here asks whether all those degrees of kinship prohibited in Leviticus 18 <note>This chapter lists prohibited sexual relations, including incest.</note> were of the law of nature. It is answered that those which ascended through the direct line were prohibited by the law of nature: such as, "you shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother." And likewise with a daughter and a granddaughter; and furthermore with a stepmother and a sister. But other relations placed to the side, such as with the sister of one’s mother or father, or with a brother’s wife, were not prohibited because they were inherently evil; rather, they were evil because they were prohibited by positive divine law. For this reason, the former were "moral" [natural] precepts, while the latter were "judicial." And consequently, these later degrees are not prohibited in the Gospel; they would be permitted by the law of nature if the Church had not forbidden them by human law on account of the impropriety they present. But more on these in Article 8 when dealing with dispensations.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
By these things, the solutions to the arguments are clear. For the moral precepts are called "discipline" because they are not the first universal principles known by themselves, but are those which require some clarification.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ And to the second...

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

...secondly it is answered that, just as human laws add certain things to the law of nature, so too has divine law added ceremonial and judicial matters. And 
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
to the third argument, it is answered that although faith is a supernatural light, it is nonetheless necessary for clarifying certain natural precepts. Although these precepts can be gathered from the law of nature, due to their loftiness they require a supernatural ray to become clear to all mortals. For this reason, faith counts the article of the existence of one God among others—a truth which had nonetheless become known to wise men through natural light. From this, it follows that in the assertion made above—namely, that moral precepts are those which pertain *by themselves* to good morals—the phrase "by themselves" does not exclude supernatural light, but only excludes other positive laws, as has been explained. Therefore, even if there were no positive law, natural law would still command that one God be worshiped, along with the other commands of the first tablet <note>The first tablet of the Ten Commandments focuses on duties toward God.</note>; yet, unless the light of faith had shone upon mortals, not everyone would have clearly perceived them.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether the moral precepts of the law concern all acts of the virtues.<-

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or saint, at a desk with a book.</image-desc>IT FOLLOWS in the second article that we should weigh the sufficiency of these same precepts. And it is argued that they do not concern the acts of all virtues. The observation of these precepts is called "justification," according to that verse of the Psalm [119:8]: *I will keep your justifications*; but justification is an act of justice; therefore, all these things dwell in this virtue alone.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, the same is argued from the very name of "precept," which signifies the nature of a debt. For a debt <note>original: "debitum," referring to what is owed or required by law.</note> pertains to no other virtue than justice, through which every person is rendered their right.
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ And thirdly, there is the fact that law (as was said above) is established for the common good; which, as 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle is the authority in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, is the object of justice.
<margin>Augustine</margin>
¶ To the contrary is what Augustine says: that sin is nothing other than a word, deed, or desire against the law of God.
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
And Ambrose says that transgression is a violation of divine law and disobedience to heavenly mandates. But sins are opposed to all the virtues; therefore, the moral precepts of the law extend to all virtues.

The present article is brought into question not only so that it may be clear how wide-

<column-break/>

-ly the power of divine law extends—which commands regarding all virtues—but so that its excellence may become known by comparison with human laws. It is therefore resolved by three conclusions.
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First: human laws command concerning only the acts of justice by their primary intention; but concerning the other virtues, they command only insofar as they are referred to justice. This conclusion was demonstrated by its own natural reasoning in the previous book, Question 6; yet it is to be revisited here for the sake of divine law.
<margin>The conclusion is supported.</margin>
The precepts of any law (as shown above) have an order toward the common good. For this reason (as Aristotle teaches in Book 3 of the *Politics*), different laws are established according to different forms of government: some for a democracy, others for an aristocracy, and others for a kingdom. This is because they propose the common good to themselves in different ways. However, it has already been shown above how divine and human law differ. For human law only proposes the human good, which regards peace and friendship among men. Men maintain the bonds of friendship only through those external duties that belong to the virtue of justice—namely, the virtue through which each person is given what is their own. Therefore, human law attends to the virtue of justice as its primary purpose. And if it commands anything else regarding courage <note>original: "fortitudine"</note> or temperance, it is only insofar as they relate to its common good. It commands courage, I say, not that which is necessary for you to repel your own injuries, but that which is necessary for military affairs—for instance, that you do not desert your post in the battle line. Likewise, it commands the moderation of temperance, not so that you are not intemperate with yourself or your own wife, but so that you do not commit adultery. This is the opinion of Aristotle in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, Chapter 1, where he says that laws dictate concerning all things, aiming either at the common utility of all, or of the best men, or of the leaders, where he distinguishes three types of government.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: Divine law establishes precepts not only regarding acts of justice, but equally regarding the works of all the virtues.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is proven by the opposite reasoning: the end of divine laws is not that benevolence which exists between men, but the friendship of men with God, and subsequently their familiarity, both in the present age and finally in the future eternity. A person, however, becomes dear to God not only through the duties of the specific virtue of justice, but also through all diligent actions by which a person lives rightly with themselves—not only externally, but also in the internal mind in which God has impressed His image. Therefore, divine law commands acts of courage, temperance, gentleness, and so on.

<summary>This page discusses how divine law clarifies natural laws through faith and argues that while human law primarily concerns external justice for the sake of social peace, divine law encompasses all virtues (like courage and temperance) to foster a person's internal and external friendship with God.</summary>

## Second Book, Question III.

...not only in relation to justice among men, but furthermore in how they adorn the divine image within man himself. For this reason, with equal and primary intention, the law commands both the intellectual virtues, which are the lights of reason, and the moral virtues, which subject the appetite to that same reason. Specifically, it commands the three primary Theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity—and soon after the four moral virtues, according to the assertion in Wisdom 8 <note>Wisdom of Solomon 8:7</note> concerning that same divine law and wisdom: *She teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and virtue; than which nothing is more useful in life for men.* <note>original: "Sobrietatem & sapientiã docet, & iustitiam, & virtutem: quibus vtilius nihil est in vita hominibus." Note that "virtue" here often refers to "fortitude" or "strength."</note>

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion.** The law does not propose all works of the virtues with the same rigor of compulsion. Rather, those which belong to the necessary order of reason it commands under the penalty of guilt; but the rest, which pertain to a more abundant perfection and adornment of the virtues, it advises under the form of counsel. Such are those matters pertaining to the love of enemies, as in Proverbs 25: *If your enemy is hungry, feed him.* And the other precepts of mercy, as in chapter 3: *From the firstfruits of all your produce, give to the poor.*

<margin>A double doubt.</margin>
<margin>First reason for doubting.</margin>
¶ A double doubt, though a small one, remains from these points. The first concerns the difference established between human law and divine law. For it appears to the contrary that the divine law, just like the human, directs its primary intention toward justice. For it chiefly requires obedience, which is a form of justice. Furthermore, whatever it commands, it directs either toward preserving <term>particular justice</term> <note>Special or particular justice refers to fairness in specific dealings between individuals, like contracts or punishments.</note> among men, or toward that justice by which the appetite is submitted to reason. Therefore, it never departs from the paths of justice.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
<margin>To the first doubt.</margin>
¶ To this, however, it is easily answered that the distinction lies in this: human law has as its goal "special justice," the specific virtue by which human society and trust are maintained. Divine law, however, simply seeks the perfection of each individual. For the obedience that belongs to <term>legal justice</term> <note>Legal justice refers to the individual's duty to the common good and the law.</note> is not the end of the law, but is the virtue that subjects citizens to the prince; for the end of the law is to make good citizens through obedience. Moreover, that subjection of the appetite to reason, even if it belongs to the end of the law because human perfection consists in it, does not properly have the character of justice because it does not order a man toward another, but toward himself. Rather, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, it is called justice only <margin>Aristot.</margin> metaphorically, insofar as the appetite and the reason of the same subject are considered as two distinct parts.

<margin>Second doubt.</margin>
<margin>Reason for hesitating.</margin>
¶ The second doubt is that the Old Law does not seem to have instituted all the virtues. For (as read in Matthew 5 <note>The OCR says Matth. 6, but the quote "You have heard it said..." is from the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5.</note>), Christ, having made a comparison between both laws, said: *You have heard 

<column-break/>

that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not kill": but I say to you, whoever is angry with his brother,* etc. And for this reason, he stated before: *Unless your justice abounds more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.*

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered that whatever Christ expressed that has the true character of a precept was already enclosed in the Old Law; but it was the Pharisees who had obscured it. For if Christ prohibited the hatred of enemies, the same was also prohibited in Leviticus 19, where it is read: *You shall not hate your brother in your heart.* And if Christ restrained the concupiscence of the heart, the same was written in Exodus 20: *You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.*

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first of the arguments, therefore, it is answered that where divine mandates are called "justifications," the name is not drawn from justice as a special virtue between men, but from justice as it ought to be between man and God, which is a legal and general virtue. That is to say, we must always have our own wills conformed to reason and likewise to His divine commands, by which means we persist in His friendship.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And in the same way, it is answered to the second. For even if every precept carries the character of a "debt," it is not the debt of special justice, but the debt of the will to reason, and of man to God. For whatever is owed to reason is also owed to God, who is the author of reason. And this is general obedience.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, the third is now resolved. For even if every law is directed toward the common good, human law looks after the common good in one way, and divine law in another.

### ARTICLE III.

->*Whether all moral precepts of the Old Law are reduced to the ten of the Decalogue.*<-

<margin>Argumen. 1.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a scene with human figures in a landscape.</image-desc>
SINCE it has been determined that the Old Law commanded concerning the acts of all virtues, and yet in the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> there are only ten precepts of justice, it remained to be asked whether the remaining acts of other virtues are reduced to these ten. And it is argued from the negative side. The first heads of all, as we read in Matthew 22, are: *You shall love the Lord your God* and *You shall love your neighbor.* However, these are neither placed in the Decalogue, nor does it seem possible for them to be reduced to it; therefore not all are reduced...

<sig>g 5</sig>

<summary>This page explores the scope of divine law, arguing that it encompasses all virtues (theological and moral) to perfect the individual, not just social justice. # Fra Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
...are directed toward Him. ¶ Secondly, it is argued: The third commandment, *Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day* <note>original: "Memento vt diem Sabbathi sanctifices"</note>, appears to be ceremonial. However, moral matters are not reduced to ceremonial ones, but rather the other way around: since moral matters are conclusions of natural law, and ceremonial ones are certainly not. Therefore, not all things are reduced to the Decalogue.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: moral precepts do not only concern acts of justice, but also extend to the remaining virtues that pertain to conduct. In the Decalogue, however, there are only precepts of justice. Therefore, not all things are reduced to that source.

<margin>Gloss.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, there is the <term>Gloss</term> <note>A "Gloss" is a standard medieval or early modern commentary printed in the margins or between the lines of a text, often the Bible or Law codes.</note> on that passage of Matthew 5: *Blessed are you when men revile you* <note>original: "Beati estis cùm vos maledixerint homines"</note>, stating that Moses, in proposing the ten precepts, later explained them in parts.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
This question will appear more clearly below in Article 11, where the number of other precepts is related in detail. For now, it will be resolved in general by two conclusions. ¶ The first is that the primary distinction between the Decalogue and the remaining precepts is that God, by the ministry of Angels (as has been said), engraved those ten on the tables of Moses; the others, however, He gave through Moses. Therefore, one must meditatively observe the difference: that man was taught the Decalogue by God alone, but the rest were taught by men.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
It was most consistent with reason that God, as the author of nature, should teach by Himself only those things which either natural reason elicits from the first principles of nature with very little consideration, or which become known immediately through infused faith. Of these, the latter are in the first table <note>Referring to the first three/four commandments regarding God.</note>, and the former in the second <note>Referring to the remaining commandments regarding neighbor.</note>, as will be shown below. And since justice is the most expansive among all the virtues, the entire Decalogue is occupied with explaining this virtue. For this reason, He omitted two types of precepts: namely, those which He had sealed in our minds as self-evident principles—for these required no further publication, such as: *Do unto others as you would have them do unto you*—and also those which require the more vigilant investigation of wise men. These latter He left to be taught by Moses and other wise men later on.

<margin>Second Conclusion.</margin>
¶ From this, the latter conclusion is gathered: namely, that all things are reduced to the Decalogue. For those general principles are contained in the Decalogue just as principles are contained in their closest conclusions; since *Thou shalt not kill* and *Thou shalt not steal* <note>original: "Non occides, Non furtum facies"</note> are nothing other than: *Do not do to others what you do not wish to be done to yourself.*

<column-break/>

The rest, indeed, are contained in the same Decalogue just as conclusions are in their principles. For example, that passage in Leviticus 19: *Rise up before the hoary head* <note>original: "Coram cano capite consurge" - a command to respect the elderly.</note> is contained by virtue in the commandment *Honor your parents*. And *Thou shalt not commit fornication* is reduced to *Thou shalt not commit adultery*; and *Thou shalt not give at interest* <note>original: "Non fœnori dabis" - referring to usury or lending for profit.</note> is reduced to *Thou shalt not steal*. Nevertheless, because these things must be explained more copiously and clearly in Article 11, the rest must wait until then.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that those principles concerning the love of God and neighbor were not expressly placed in the Decalogue because they had no need of publication, given that they are self-evident; rather, the Decalogue was an explanation of them. For the first is immediately known through faith, as will become more evident in the next article. For whoever confesses that God exists, by that same confession, holds it as most certain that He is to be loved. Nor can anything be more clearly consistent with natural reason. However, because the *manner* of loving—since it is a supernatural matter—is not known to all mortals, He expressed it in the precepts of the first table, to which those principles are reduced as a principle is contained in its conclusions. And in like manner, the second principle regarding the love of neighbor is reduced to the precepts of the second table.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it has already been said above that the precept of sanctifying the feast in a general sense—for instance, that we should offer some time to divine meditations—is not ceremonial, but moral; but in its specific details, it is ceremonial.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The response to the third argument has likewise been explained. Truly, since the Decalogue contains only those precepts which God brought forth by Himself, it was fitting for it to express only the manifest conclusions of nature. And since every precept carries with it the character of a "debt" (or duty), which is more apparent in the virtue of justice but more hidden in the rest, it follows that the Decalogue embraces only those precepts which pertain to justice. The rest, concerning fortitude and temperance and others, are reduced to the same Decalogue in that part where they include the character of a debt.

### Book Two, Question III. 107

<margin>*The first argument for the negative side.*</margin>
After the three previous articles discussing moral precepts in general, we must now descend specifically to the **Decalogue**. Four points are considered regarding their arrangement: namely, their distinction, number, order, and the manner of their delivery. The question is therefore asked whether the precepts of the Decalogue, as they appear in Exodus 26 <note>The text cites Exodus 26, though the Ten Commandments are famously found in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5; this may be a citation of a specific commentary or a historical printing error.</note>, are appropriately divided into **three** on the first table and **seven** on the second. The argument begins from the negative side. Faith, which is an intellectual habit, and *latria* <note>term: latria; The highest form of worship and adoration, which according to Catholic theology is offered to God alone.</note>, which is the adoration of religion, are two distinct virtues; therefore, the precepts of faith and *latria* are distinct. Thus, the command, *You shall have no foreign gods before me* <note>original: "Non habebis deos alienos coram me"</note>, pertains to faith, while what follows, *You shall not make a carved image* <note>original: "Non facias sculptile"</note>, pertains to *latria*. From this, it would follow that there are four commandments on the first table.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
<margin><insert>or four others</insert></margin>
¶ Secondly: That first statement, *I am the Lord your God* <note>original: "Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus"</note>, is affirmative; however, what follows, *You shall have no foreign gods before me*, is negative. Since affirmative precepts are distinguished from negative ones, they must be two separate commandments; and thus, the first table would result in four, by adding the other two: *Do not swear by His name in vain*, and *Sanctify the Sabbaths*.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: The Apostle Paul, in Romans 7, posits only one type of concupiscence <note>term: concupiscence; In this context, the internal desire or "coveting" of something forbidden.</note> when he says, *I would not have known concupiscence unless the law said: You shall not covet* <note>original: "Concupiscentiam nesciebam nisi lex diceret, Non concupisces"</note>. Therefore, there is only a single prohibition against coveting, and so it should not be divided into one regarding another’s wife and another regarding other property.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is the authority of **Augustine** on this same passage of Exodus, who distinguishes three precepts on the first table and seven on the second.

<margin>A double assertion upon which everyone agrees.</margin>
Regarding the precepts of the Decalogue, no one can deny that there are **ten**, as the very name "Decalogue" <note>From the Greek *deka* (ten) and *logos* (words/statements).</note> clearly proclaims it. For this reason, there is a single, harmonious opinion among all on this point. Likewise, by the same consensus, they affirm that the first table contained the written precepts pertaining to the love and worship of God, while the second table contained those which explicitly involve the love of neighbor. However, as to exactly how many there are in each group, there is no unanimous agreement.

<margin>A threefold opinion.</margin>
<margin>The first: Hesychius.</margin>
There are three opinions. The first is that of **Hesychius** <note>Hesychius of Jerusalem, a 5th-century biblical exegete.</note> on that passage of Leviticus 26: *So that ten women shall bake bread in one oven*. He places four on the first table and six on the second. He considers the first to be the affirmative statement: *I am the Lord your God*; and the second: *You shall have no foreign gods before me*.

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
Furthermore, **Jerome** on Hosea 10, regarding the phrase *When they are punished

<column-break/>

for their two iniquities*, separated these two in the same way. Hesychius places as the third commandment, *You shall not make for yourself a carved image*, and the fourth, *You shall not take the name of God in vain*. As for the observation of the **Sabbath** inserted there, he does not think it should be counted among the precepts, nor should it be understood literally. This is because, since it was changed among Christians to the Lord's Day (Sunday), he does not count it among the permanent moral precepts, which remain unchanged. Instead, he says it is to be understood according to the Spirit: that we should never do any work of this world. In the precepts of the second table, however, he compresses the ninth and tenth into one. Thus, he makes only six.

<margin>The second opinion: Origen.</margin>
¶ The second opinion is that of **Origen** in the same place, who likewise distinguishes four on the first table, though slightly differently from Hesychius. For he does not make *I am the Lord your God* a distinct precept, but considers it the same as the following, *You shall have no foreign gods*. He considers the second to be *You shall not make a carved image*; the third, *You shall not take the name of God in vain*; and finally, the fourth, *Remember to keep holy the Sabbath day*. He is then forced, like Hesychius, to count the remaining ones as six.

<margin>The third conclusion: Augustine.</margin>
¶ Despite these conflicting views, a certain conclusion is established, which is the **Third opinion of Augustine** in the same place: The precepts of the Decalogue are distinguished into **three** on the first table and **seven** on the second.

<margin>The first evidence.</margin>
For a clear understanding of these matters, it must be noted that the first mention of the two tables is found in Exodus 31, where, after the precepts God gave to Moses on the mountain are recounted, it is added: *The Lord also gave to Moses, when the words of this kind were completed on Mount Sinai, two stone tables written by the finger of God.* In that passage, they are neither named "first" and "second," nor is it recorded what was written on either one. However, it is the confession of the Hebrews that five precepts were engraved on each. This is indeed the opinion of **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>, most learned in the law, in the third book of *Antiquities*, chapter 6.

<margin>Josephus.</margin>
There, I say, he states that five "words" were written on each: on one, specifically four concerning the love of God—for he separates into two *I am the Lord your God* and *You shall not make a carved image* (from which Origen and later Jerome drank their opinion). And on that same first table, he places the fifth commandment concerning the honor to be shown to parents. Perhaps he does this because, since God is the one from whom all fatherhood is derived, He willed that we should honor our parents as His likeness. Yet, it is very likely that the precepts were distributed equally because the tables...

And it is no slight conjecture that on the second table there existed only five negative commands: *You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, You shall not covet.* For Paul, in Romans 13, deliberately enumerates these concisely <margin>Paul.</margin> where he says: "All these are summed up in that word, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.'" As for what he adds—"And if there is any other commandment"—he only included this because of those which wander outside the Decalogue. But truly, since those two orders are resolved into two headings concerning the love of God and neighbor, other Church Fathers, looking not so much at the number as to the mystery, call those which refer to the love of God the "first table," and those concerning the love of neighbor the <margin>Another lesson.</margin> "second." <margin>Proof of the first part of the stated conclusion.</margin> ¶ Having established these things, because the asserted conclusion has two parts, it is first proven that there are only three precepts in the first table. To begin with, <margin>Hesychius. The first reason against Hesychius.</margin> Hesychius <note>Hesychius of Jerusalem (d. c. 450 AD), a biblical exegete.</note> too violently cut off the precept of observing the Sabbath from the number of the Decalogue. First, because while the rest were written there in the literal sense as pertaining to morals, it is absurd to say that this one alone was mixed in for a purely spiritual sense, especially since they are all <margin>Second reason. 110.</margin> arranged in the same sequence. Furthermore, since that was an explanation of natural law, and there were no mortals who did not set aside fixed days for their gods, it was necessary that God explain a feast day for His own household <margin>Fourth reason. 110.</margin> and the reason for it. To this we add that the spiritual sense of abstaining from sins was of little relevance there; this is discussed more broadly in Question 7. The argument <margin>The foundation of the aforementioned author is refuted.</margin> to the contrary was resolved above in a similar case. For indeed, while the precept of divine worship is moral, the particular rites are ceremonial; thus, it happens that keeping *one* feast is moral, but that it be this or that day belongs to Ecclesiastical law.

<margin>Augustine's argument against Origen.</margin> ¶ Against the opinion of Origen <note>Origen (c. 184–253 AD), an early Christian scholar. He argued that the prohibition of idols was a separate commandment from the prohibition of other gods.</note>, however, Augustine argues that it is the same thing to worship one God and to have no foreign gods. For, since no one can serve two masters, "worship one God" is understood exclusively. As for what is added—"You shall not make for yourself a carved image"—it explains more perfectly

<column-break/>

what he had said: "You shall have no foreign gods." For making a carved image is not forbidden except insofar as it is the impiety of idolatry. For in Exodus 25, images of Seraphim were commanded to be placed in the temple. Therefore, since all of that is one; and the second is, "You shall not take His name in vain"; and the third, "Remember the Sabbath day": it follows that, according to the Trinity of Persons, there are also three precepts of that table. Again, he rightly argues that the prohibition of <margin>Another reason from the same author.</margin> coveting another's wife is distinct from the reason for coveting another's things. For according to the Peripatetic <note>term: Peripatetic; Referring to the philosophy of Aristotle, who taught that human actions are categorized and defined by their "objects" or goals.</note> principle, acts are distinguished by their objects: and it is clear that a woman’s use is a different object from the possession of things; wherefore one pertains to lust, and the other to greed.

NEVERTHELESS, these things being established, the arguments proposed at the beginning of the question raise a doubt. For the first is in favor of those saying there are two [separate] precepts: *You shall have no foreign gods*, and, *You shall not make a carved image.* For the former appears to belong to faith, while the latter belongs to *latria* <note>term: latria; Adoration or worship offered to God alone, as opposed to honor given to saints.</note>. To this, <margin>To the first argument of St. Thomas.</margin> St. Thomas does not respond very clearly. He says, indeed, that it was not necessary for a precept of faith to be expressed in the Decalogue, for that is presupposed as a principle. Just as was said in the preceding article regarding the general precept of love. Whence Paul says in Hebrews 11: "He who comes to God must believe that He is." Therefore, it did not need a new promulgation; but nonetheless, it was necessary to add a precept of *latria*, which is the protestation of faith. But he does not explain which of those two is to be held as the precept of the first table. Nor does he explain whether that precept is negative or affirmative. And <margin>The solution of St. Thomas seems incomplete.</margin> for this reason, his solution certainly seems incomplete. For below in article seven, regarding the first point, he recognizes only one affirmative precept among the commandments of the first table—concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath—insinuating that the two prior ones are negative; and yet in the common form of the Church, the first precept is: "Worship one God." Thus, then, let the mind of the same Holy Doctor be understood, which <margin>The thought of St. Thomas.</margin> I think is most true. Out of those three members of the first precept, I say that the one at the head—"The Lord your God is one"—is not a moral precept, but a truth of faith, which everyone who approaches Him is bound to confess. Wherefore, since those who receive the law of God already profess themselves His subjects, they ought to presuppose the confession of faith, as Paul says.

# ARTICLE V.

->*Whether the number of the precepts of the Decalogue is fitting.*<-

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
In the preceding article, the distinction between the precepts of the first and second tables was defined. It follows immediately to dispute the number: namely, whether the number ten is fitting. And the argument is made for the negative side. Sin, as was shown above from the definitions of both Ambrose and Augustine, is a transgression of the divine law. Sins, however, are threefold: namely, those by which one sins

<column-break/>

either against God, or against one's neighbor, or against oneself. Since, therefore, there is no precept of the third kind in the Decalogue—for instance, one by which a person is ordered within themselves—it is incomplete.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: in the third precept of the first table, it appears short, since out of so many solemnities and sacrifices by which God was worshipped, it made mention of only one Sabbath. And the same argument is made against the second precept, where care is only taken that *the name of God not be taken in vain*, even though, besides perjury, blasphemies and false doctrines frequently arise by which God is dishonored by men. And a similar objection is raised against the fourth precept. For everyone, by a natural bond, owes love not only to parents, but also to children and others, whether joined by blood or any other necessity. Therefore, since according to Paul <note>1 Timothy 1</note>, *the end of the precept is charity*, individual precepts should have been written about each of these. ¶ Third,
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
it is argued: Every kind of sin is committed in the heart before it is committed in deed. For as Christ says, *Out of the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, etc.* But regarding adultery and theft, the sins of the heart are explained separately after the prohibitions of the acts (*You shall not commit adultery*, *You shall not steal*): *You shall not covet your neighbor's goods* and *You shall not covet your neighbor's wife*. Therefore, the same rule should have been observed in the rest. ¶ And fourth and finally, it is argued:
<margin>Final argument.</margin>
The <term>sensitive appetite</term> <note>The faculty of the soul that responds to sensory perceptions.</note> is divided into the <term>irascible</term> <note>The "spirited" part of the soul concerned with overcoming obstacles or anger.</note> and the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>The part of the soul concerned with desiring basic needs or pleasures.</note>. Both parts are the seat of corrupt affection; therefore, just as the concupiscible part was restrained by specific precepts, so too should the irascible have been curbed. ¶ To the contrary is that passage in Deuteronomy 4: *He showed you His covenant which He commanded you to perform... And behold the words which I wrote on two stone tablets.* These are exactly ten.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
The question is very easy, having been raised only so that the doubts of the arguments might be clarified. Therefore, the conclusion is that the number of the Decalogue is most fitting. This is evident not only by the general reason that the works of God are perfect, but also by specific reasons drawn from the end of the law. For it has been said that the end of the divine law is to establish man first in relation to God, and then in relation to neighbors. We owe fidelity to God above all, which consists in this: that we give His honor to no one besides Himself. This, therefore, is provided for in the first precept: *You shall have no foreign gods.*

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...foreign [gods]. Next, we owe Him reverence, which consists in this: that we cast no injury against Him. This is provided for by the second commandment: *You shall not take the name of your God in vain.* Furthermore, because of the benefits He has so abundantly bestowed upon us, we owe Him obedience and service. Specifically, we must set aside certain times to give to meditation upon Him; we are reminded of this by the third commandment. And since among these benefits the first was the work of creation, the Sabbath day was designated, on which God rested after that work was completed. 

Now, the order of man to man is either specific or general. The specific debt, and the most illustrious of all, is that by which children are bound to obey their parents, from whom, under God, they received life, which is the foundation of all goods. Therefore, immediately after the third commandment concerning the service owed to God, the fourth follows concerning the honor to be deferred to parents. Indeed, as we were saying a little earlier, it is not unlikely that this was inscribed on the first table <note>Soto is discussing the traditional division of the two stone tablets; usually, the first table contains duties to God and the second contains duties to neighbors. Some traditions place the commandment to honor parents on the first table as parents are seen as God's representatives.</note>.

Man has a general order toward the rest of the human community, to whom he is a companion by natural law, and to whom he owes this: that he be harmful to no one, whether in deed, word, or heart. First, one inflicts harm on another in deed against their own person by taking their life, which is the greatest of all temporal goods. This is prohibited by the fifth commandment: *You shall not kill*, where every bodily injury is forbidden. Second, harm is done to a person joined to them <note>Referring to a spouse.</note>, which is prohibited by the sixth: *You shall not commit adultery*. Third, harm is done to external goods, which is inhibited by the seventh: *You shall not steal*. In word, one does harm by damaging a citizen's reputation, which is everywhere forbidden by the eighth commandment: *You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor*. 

Finally, one is injurious in heart against anyone through concupiscence <note>Inordinate desire or lust.</note>: whether pertaining to luxury, which is restrained by the ninth commandment (corresponding to the sixth): *You shall not covet your neighbor's wife*; or according to avarice, which is finally checked by the tenth commandment: *You shall not covet your neighbor's goods.* For such desires are injurious, inasmuch as they are the roots of external works, according to the word of Christ: *Out of the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, etc.* <note>Matthew 15:19</note>

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
And as St. Thomas skillfully noted, these three orders are distinguished in the commandments of the first table. For the first—*You shall not make for yourself a carved image*—prohibits an external work; *You shall not take the name of your God in vain* prohibits the impudence of the mouth; but *Remember the

<column-break/>

Sabbath day* has as its end the internal contemplation of the mind. And since we must see immediately in Article II how other precepts are reduced to these ten, and since in the following question a more explicit discussion of each must be resumed, it will suffice for the present to have summarized everything almost in the words of St. Thomas.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, which questioned why in the Decalogue no commandment was applied concerning the virtues that specifically order a man within himself <note>Such as temperance or fortitude.</note>, but only those which pertain to justice (by which human society is maintained) were expressed there. <margin>First solution of St. Thomas.</margin> The first response of St. Thomas is two-fold: since all commandments are related to love, it was necessary to express those which dim reason did not clearly perceive. However, self-love has never been unknown to any mortal; it is so ingrained in nature that every thing loves itself and preserves itself entirely. Or perhaps because, since in the Decalogue man is commanded to love God and neighbor, one's own love is quite clearly commanded there. For the right love of a man for himself is to maintain the proper order toward God and toward his neighbor. For he who loves God extinguishes in himself all passions—whether of the concupiscible or irascible appetite <note>The "concupiscible" appetite seeks simple pleasures; the "irascible" appetite deals with obstacles and anger.</note>—by which the reason that keeps us subject to God is disturbed.

<margin>Another solution.</margin>
But the latter response is more plausible. Namely, that the Decalogue, as we said above, differs from other precepts in this: that God taught it to us by Himself, according to that passage in Deuteronomy 10: *He wrote on the tablets according to what He had written before, the ten words which the Lord spoke to you.* It was fitting for God, as the author of nature, to command us by Himself those things which immediately shine forth to the human mind by natural light, where that same light is not obscured by darkness. Since every commandment has the character of a debt, and the character of a debt belongs to justice (which is of a man either toward God or toward another man, for justice is directed toward another), it was most appropriate that God should express to us in the Decalogue only the precepts of justice, which are the primary conclusions of nature. For the character of a debt of a man toward himself does not shine so clearly by natural light. At first glance, it may appear to anyone that he has free power in those things which pertain to himself; for this reason, the virtues of fortitude and temperance, which instruct a man in his morals with respect to himself, [were left for later instruction].

<summary>Domingo de Soto explains the logical arrangement of the Ten Commandments, categorizing them by how they prevent harm in deed, word, and heart, and addresses why the Decalogue focuses on justice toward others rather than personal self-regulating virtues.</summary>

### Question III of the Second Book

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
He entrusted to Moses and the rest of the wise men the tasks of teaching mortals. By instructing them in these matters, they taught what each person specifically owes to themselves. Regarding the second point, all other observances of solemnities are referred back to the Sabbath. For all of them were instituted both in memory of some past benefit and as a figure of something in the future. Among past benefits, the chief was the creation of the world, which was recalled to memory through the Sabbaths. Among future things, the most excellent is the rest of the mind in God <note>This refers to 'spiritual rest,' a common theological theme where the Sabbath symbolizes the soul finding peace in the Creator.</note>, which occurs in the present age through grace and in the future through glory; according to that passage of Isaiah 58: *If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, you shall be called the delightful Sabbath of the Lord, and the glorious holy one of the Lord.* These things were prefigured by the rest of the Sabbath. The remaining feasts, such as the celebration of the Passover <note>original: "Phasæ", from the Hebrew *Pesach*</note>—which was a commemoration of the benefit of the people’s liberation from Egypt and a shadow of the future passion of Christ—and all things of that kind were referred to this same order. Similarly, it is responded to the other part of the argument that in the prohibition of taking the Divine name in vain, all other vices are included, whether they be false doctrines or blasphemies. And in a like manner, it is subsequently responded to the third part of the same argument: that all other duties of love are contained in a certain way within the fourth commandment. For it has been explained why only those precepts that represent a clear reason for a debt are contained in the Decalogue <note>The "Decalogue" is the formal name for the Ten Commandments.</note>. Now, that a person should harm no one is a manifest debt; and therefore, harms are universally prohibited by six commandments: namely, so that no one may inflict them upon anyone. However, that someone should bestow something upon another as a debt is not so clearly known by the light of natural reason. The only exception is that which children owe to their parents by the law of their birth and by reason of their upbringing and instruction. Therefore, God expressed that in the Decalogue. But the other benefits that are owed because of other relationships and natural connections, He left to be explained by Moses and the other wise men, as was said above. For instance, what parents owe to their children; the reason for this debt is not as if the parents received something from them, but because children are something of the parents themselves, and by loving themselves, they love their own offspring, as Aristotle is the author in Book 8 of the *Ethics*. But regarding these reductions of other precepts into the Decalogue, see Article 11.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
To the third, it is responded that although a work may be condemned by any prohibition, and its affection [the desire for it] is forbidden at the same time, there is nonetheless a difference. In those things which nature itself shrinks from, such as murder and falsehood, because the desire for them is not attractive in itself but is sought for the sake of other passions (such as for revenge or greed), it was enough for the deed itself to be inhibited. But in those things that are pleasing to the senses, such as sexual matters and the abundance of things [wealth], since the appetite for them is delightful in itself, it was fitting not only that the deeds be prohibited, but the appetites separately—as it is in overcoming these that there is a peculiar difficulty. But we shall discuss this again in the next question.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
Finally, to the fourth, it is responded that since those passions in the "irascible" appetite result from the passions of the "concupiscible" appetite <note>In medieval psychology, the "concupiscible" appetite is the drive toward simple pleasures/away from pain, while the "irascible" appetite is the drive to overcome obstacles to get those pleasures or avoid those pains (like anger or courage).</note>—for from the love of that which delights is born the repelling of opposites—once the concupiscible is settled, there was no need for a further prohibition of the irascible.

### ARTICLE VI.

->Whether the commandments of the Decalogue are arranged in the proper order.<-

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'P' featuring intertwining vines and floral patterns.</image-desc>
**P**ollowing the distinction and numbering of the commandments, it follows to meditate upon their order, to see if it was clear. The argument is therefore made from the negative side.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
First, since our knowledge begins from the senses, and the love of neighbor is more exposed to the senses than the love of God—according to that passage in 1 John 3: *He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?*—the second table, which pertains to the love of neighbor, should have preceded in place the first table, which pertains to the love of God.

<margin>Argument 2</margin>
Next, since evil things are prohibited by negative commandments, while good things are established by affirmative ones, and by the way of nature (as Boethius is the author in the commentary on the *Categories*),

<margin>Boethius.</margin>
vices must first be extirpated before virtues are implanted; according to that verse of the Psalm: *Turn away from evil and do good.* And that in Isaiah 1: *Cease to act perversely, learn to do well.* Whence also the Lyric poet <note>Likely referring to the Roman poet Horace: "To flee vice is the beginning of virtue."</note> says: *To flee vice is the primary virtue.* It follows that negative commandments should go before affirmative ones.

<margin>Argument 3</margin>
And likewise, those precepts inhibiting the thoughts of the heart should precede those that restrain the hands from works, seeing as the heart is the root of all works. ¶ On the contrary is the fact that the order of the Decalogue was the disposition of God; whose works, as the Apostle says in Romans 13, are "ordered."

<margin>Paul.</margin>
