Fray Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*,

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin>
This question is quite simple, yet it is worthy of knowledge, and it is answered with four conclusions. The first is: The order of the Commandments required that humans be instructed first in their relationship to God before their relationship to one another. This is proven from the previously established foundation: namely, that the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> ought to contain those commands that shine forth by the light of nature. From this, it follows immediately that they should be arranged in a series according to how close they are to reason, and how much their opposites conflict with reason. Now, the supreme end <note>The "end" or *finis* in scholastic thought refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of an action.</note> of our actions presents itself first of all to reason, and a sin against that end is more serious than a sin regarding the means to it. It follows, therefore, that the commandments by which we are most closely subjected to God—who is our ultimate end—rightfully hold the first place. Such, indeed, are the three commandments of the first table.
<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
This is confirmed by an analogy taken from the army. Soldiers must be instructed in their duty to their commander before their duty to one another; for it is a more serious offense against the commander than if a soldier commits a wrong against a fellow soldier.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Among the commandments of the first table, that which pertains to *latria* <note>original: "latriam"; the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note>—that is, the worship of the one God—ought to be first; the second is that by which reverence is shown to Him; and the third is that by which service is paid to Him.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
For the first foundation and basis of military service is that the oath given by a soldier, and confirmed by a sacred vow, should be for the commander alone, abjuring every pact and agreement with enemies. Therefore, it is the gravest of all crimes if, by breaking such faith, one deserts to the enemy. For this reason, the first commandment is that we should not have foreign gods. Next to this is the commandment concerning the reverence due to God alone, and third is the service to be rendered to Him. For he who dishonors the prince sins more gravely against the prince's honor than he who merely fails to obey him. Therefore, the second commandment is that the name of God should not be used in vain; and finally, the third is that we should celebrate His Sabbaths.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: Of the commandments by which humans are bound together in friendship, the first ought to be that by which they are commanded to show honor to their parents.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason has already been touched upon above. Namely, that although no one should harm anyone else, one is not obligated to confer a benefit upon everyone, but specifically upon one's parents. Therefore, the nature of "debt" <note>The legal or moral obligation one owes to another.</note> which is present in every commandment is more evident in respect to parents; thus, that commandment ought to be placed before the other negative ones.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
<margin>The sequence of negative commandments.</margin>
¶ The fourth conclusion: In the series of negative commandments <note>Commandments that forbid actions, such as "Thou shalt not..."</note>, that order ought to be preserved which exists among the gravity of the evils they prohibit. A person is harmed more seriously by deed than by word, and by word more than by heart. Furthermore, one is harmed most by deed when deprived of life, which is the greatest of all temporal goods. Next, if one is harmed in the person of their spouse, which destroys the certainty of offspring; and thirdly, if one suffers the loss of property. For this reason, the fifth commandment forbids murder, the sixth adultery, the seventh theft, and the eighth false testimony. The ninth forbids the coveting of another's marriage bed, and the tenth the greed for other things. We shall speak of these individually in the next question.

---

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, in response to the first of the arguments for the question, it is said that although the love of neighbor is more noticeable to our senses than the love of God, nevertheless, the latter is the reason and cause of the former; and the series of commandments ought to follow the order of dignity.
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ In the same way, it is responded to the second argument that although, regarding the same subject matter, one must cease from vices before acting virtuously in practice—nor can a virtuous habit be formed unless the vice is driven out—nevertheless, in the intention of the legislator, the virtue for which vices are expelled comes first. Thus, by the order of dignity, even in the same subject matter, the commandments of virtues ought to be placed before the prohibitions of the contrary vices. Furthermore, when commandments are established in different subject matters, the more excellent must be preferred. The commandment about honoring parents concerns a different and more excellent subject matter than those subject to negative commandments, and thus it is rightfully preferred.
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is responded that although the sins of the heart are the cause of deeds, and thus prior in execution, nevertheless, because deeds offend more gravely, their prohibition occurs more quickly to reason.

In every matter, a vice is opposed to a virtue; therefore, in every instance, affirmative and negative commands should have been paired together. Specifically, we should not only be commanded not to kill, but also to look out for the life of our
<margin>Argument 2.</margin> neighbor, and so on in other cases. ¶ Second: since every law is based on reason, there was no cause for the reasoning behind the command to be added only to the first and third commandments; rather, it should have been

<margin>Argument 4.</margin> first and fourth. ¶ Fourth: and as has been said, punishment is a cause for observing the law—especially among the ancients, since that Testament was a law of fear. Therefore, a mention of punishment should have been 
<margin>Argument 5.</margin> applied to all of them, yet it was applied only to the first and second. ¶ And finally, a fifth argument: All divine commandments are to be retained in the deepest part of the memory, according to that passage in Proverbs 3: *Write them on the tablets of your heart.* <note>original: "Describe ea in tabulis cordis tui."</note> One must therefore answer why only the third commandment, among all the others, was singularly commended to everlasting memory. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that God—as we read in Wisdom 11 <note>The text cites Wisdom 2, but the quote "number, weight, and measure" is from Wisdom 11:20.</note>—made all things in number, weight, and measure. Therefore, this must be believed especially regarding His commandments.

The present question is no less obscure than the preceding one, and therefore it is answered with this 
<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> definitive conclusion: The Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> is delivered in a most brilliant form, just as it is arranged with the most fitting distinction, number, and order. For the greatest wisdom shines forth in the commandments of the divine law, according to that passage in Deuteronomy 4: *This is your wisdom and understanding before the peoples.* <note>original: "Hæc est vestra sapientia & intellectus coram populis."</note> It is the mark of a wise person to arrange all things in the light of order and to adapt them to a fitting form. These things (as is clear from what has preceded) are brilliantly observed in the Decalogue. But indeed, this question was raised so that the inquiries of the arguments, which are five in number, might be answered.

<margin>Difficulty touched upon in the first argument.</margin> In the first argument, therefore, it is asked: since a vice is opposed to each virtue, why was a negative commandment not paired with its affirmative counterpart in
<margin>Solution.</margin> every subject matter? The answer is that every affirmation includes a negation. For it follows that if something is white, it is not black, because opposites cannot exist together. Conversely, however, not every negation implies an affirmation.

<column-break/>

For it is not the case that what is not black is immediately white, because there are intermediate states between opposites. For the same reason and in the same way, we are not necessarily bound by the law of justice to do good to everyone whom we are bound not to harm. For the prohibition of evils is broader than the command of good things. And for this reason, no affirmative commandment is attached to the six prohibitions of the second table <note>The "second table" refers to the commandments regarding duties toward other people (Commandments 5-10 in many traditions).</note>. We are bound, I say, to kill no one and to rob no one of their goods, yet we are not bound to preserve the life or goods of everyone else—unless an urgent necessity arises, which is not covered by the law of justice, but by the law of mercy. These commandments, because they are not so obvious to the light of nature, were entrusted to the wise to be taught. However, those to whom we owe obedience, service, and honor are God and parents, from whom we received our being in their respective degrees. And therefore, after two negative commandments regarding God—which caution us not to transfer the faith we owe to Him alone to false gods, and not to obscure the reverence due to Him with empty oaths—a third affirmative commandment is added concerning the keeping of the Sabbath day, by which we show our service to God; and a fourth concerning the honoring of parents. For these, there was no need to add contrary negations, because the affirmation of serving and honoring implies the negation of dishonoring and rebelling. ¶ Here, however, many doubts would occupy us if they did not find a more suitable place to be disputed in the next question.
<margin>First doubt.</margin> Indeed, while St. Thomas <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas</note> recognizes only one affirmative commandment in the first table, he
<margin>Solution.</margin> teaches that the first two are negative. Yet we have already touched upon this above, and we shall see more clearly later, how the first—namely, *You shall have no strange gods*—includes the affirmation of worshipping the one God. Likewise, a doubt emerges here regarding the third commandment, which is asserted to be affirmative; yet if you exclude the Church's decree <note>original: "Ecclesiasticam sanctionem"</note> regarding hearing the Mass, it does not seem to be anything other than negative as far as divine law is concerned, namely that we are forbidden from servile work <term>servile work: manual labor traditionally prohibited on the Sabbath and holy days</term>. But concerning these and similar matters, we shall speak in the following question. ¶ Regarding the second argument,

->Whether the commandments of the Decalogue are<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' at the beginning of the article.</image-desc>

AFTER these things, it remains to examine the force of the Decalogue: namely, whether a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A 'dispensation' is a formal exemption from a law granted by a higher authority.</note> is possible regarding any of its commandments. And the argument is made from the

<margin>Paul.</margin>

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>

Subsequently, arguments are built regarding fornication and theft. <margin>Argument 4.</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from discussing the specific reasons behind individual commandments (like the Sabbath or honoring parents) to a broader theological and legal debate: whether the Ten Commandments are absolute or if exceptions—dispensations—can be granted by any authority, including God Himself. The author begins by refuting the radical voluntarism of William of Ockham.</meta>

# Question III of the Second Book
h 2
<meta>catchword: tia est</meta>

<margin>Argument 5.</margin>
¶ Finally, a fifth argument is made: The observation of the Sabbath is one of the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, and it was the most sacred to the Jews; but in former times, a dispensation <note>A legal exemption from a rule</note> was granted regarding this for the Maccabees. For we read in the first book [of Maccabees], chapter 2: "And they thought on that day, saying: Whoever comes against us in battle on the Sabbath day, let us fight against him." Therefore, the precepts of the Decalogue are dispensable.

<margin>Isaiah.</margin>
¶ A contrary testimony is provided by Isaiah, chapter 24, where certain people are rebuked because they "changed the law and broke the everlasting covenant." This is understood primarily to refer to that law contained in the Decalogue.

<margin>The sense of the question.</margin>
This question is among those disputed concerning the Decalogue that is worthy of being known, as it establishes the extent of its authority. For its meaning is not merely whether any human has the authority to grant a dispensation from these sorts of precepts; that meaning can fall into doubt for no one. Indeed, since it is a matter of public confession, even the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> does not possess such ordinary power. This is because an inferior cannot change the laws of a superior, and much less natural laws, which are impressed upon our hearts. But the doubt is whether they are simply so indispensable that not even God Himself, through His absolute power, could grant such a dispensation. Here, from the final article of the previous book, we must recall the distinction between these three things: interpreting the law, and dispensing the law—which is nothing other than relaxing the law in a particular case and for certain persons while its general reason and force remain.

<margin>Three opinions on the question.</margin>
¶ Regarding this understanding of the question, three opinions are usually debated, as is often the case: namely, two extremes and one middle view.

<margin>First opinion: Ockham.</margin>
The first opinion, representing one extreme, is that of Ockham <note>William of Ockham, a 14th-century philosopher known for his "nominalist" views</note> in the *Sentences*, Book 2, distinction 19. There he says not only are all the precepts of the Decalogue dispensable, but that God could even command the opposite. He claims that if God were to command the opposite, it would be praiseworthy and meritorious to act against those original commandments. Indeed, he even says that God, by His power alone, could produce hatred of Himself within our will, and also command us to pursue Him with hatred. In both ways, he admits that such hatred would be praiseworthy.

<margin>Ockham’s common reason.</margin>
Nor has he persuaded himself of such remarkable dogmas by any other means than his "familiar Achilles" <note>In scholastic logic, an "Achilles" refers to a person's strongest, supposedly unshakeable argument</note>: namely, *Whatever does not involve a contradiction, God can do.* This is according to the words of the Angel in Luke 1: "With God, nothing shall be impossible." <note>original: "Non erit impossibile apud Deum omne verbum."</note> These things, however,

<column-break/>

he says, involve no contradiction. But in truth, this opinion presents itself as so openly contrary to reason and consequently so absurd that it is very easy to reject.

<margin>The Parisian Article. Article 54.</margin>
In the first place, the Parisian Article <note>A reference to the Condemnations of 1277 in Paris, which sought to curb certain philosophical and theological errors</note> condemns those who would affirm that anyone could merit anything through hatred of God. Nor does such an article admit the gloss <note>interpretive note</note> that it should be understood as referring to God’s ordinary power. For there could never have been a controversy about that; an article is only defined to settle some dispute.

<margin>First reason against the former opinion.</margin>
¶ But besides the article, it is argued: That primary axiom of the Nominalists <note>The school of thought associated with Ockham</note>—*Whatever does not involve a contradiction, God can do*—is wrongly defended by some of them. For if it is understood that God can do anything that does not openly entail two contradictory statements, it is false. For these same men deny that two contradictories can be gathered from the statement "A man is a horse," and yet God cannot do that. Nor was the Angelic meaning anything other than that whatever God promises, or whatever is "doable," God can perform. For this is called the "word of God" <note>original: "Dei verbum"</note>, as He is one who acts by speaking.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Something is truly said to involve a contradiction which, assuming the nature of one side of the contradiction, necessarily infers the other from what has been granted. And because the nature of a rational animal is immutable, it is not possible for it to be "un-rational"; if it were granted that God could make a man be a horse, he would be "un-rational" and not "un-rational" <note>A logical absurdity</note>. To the point, then: To have hatred for God is as evil by its intrinsic reason—that is, as discordant with His eternal law—as it is intrinsic for a man to be rational. Therefore, it is as repugnant <note>logically inconsistent</note> for that to be licit as it is for a man to be, and at the same time be irrational. And thus, it is repugnant for God to either effect or command hatred of Himself.

¶ But so that the matter may be more clearly perceived, suppose, for example, that a just man by the command of God hates Him: it would then follow that he is simultaneously in His grace and in His enmity; no clearer contradiction than this can exist. For that he remains in His friendship is obvious, since he is doing nothing other than obeying His will; but that he is equally an enemy is shown by his hatred, with which he pursues God. For to deny this is to deny the nature of the act itself, since friendship is defined by love.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Likewise, God cannot hate Himself. For what intellect could grasp the contrary? And yet the whole reason for the repugnance is that hatred of God has such an innate malice that it could not be desired by any right will; therefore, a similar repugnance exists...

Soto argues that certain moral laws are intrinsically tied to reason and God's nature, making them logically and theologically indispensable.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,
### Page 116

...[the senten]ce is that God might command the same thing to another. For it would be to command that another act according to His rule and will, and at the same time act against it. For what can be more contrary to the divine rule than for the Supreme Good to be hated? It is therefore denied that this does not involve a contradiction.

<margin>
*The second opinion of Scotus.*
</margin>
¶ There is, therefore, a second opinion belonging to Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher</note> in his *Sentences* <note>original: "3. Sententiar. distinct. 37"</note>, which is not so extreme, but walks a middle path. He says, indeed, that something belongs to the law of nature in two ways. In one way, as a practical principle known from its very terms <note>Self-evident truths</note>, or a conclusion that is a necessary consequence of such a principle. Other scholars in his school distinguish these into two degrees: but their teacher considers both as the same regarding the reason for a dispensation. And in such things, he says, which are of the strictest natural law, no dispensation can exist. But there are other things which are neither necessary principles nor conclusions necessarily drawn from them; and thus they do not have a necessary connection to the attainment of the ultimate goal. His second assertion is: The precepts of the second table <note>The commandments regarding duties to fellow humans (4 through 10)</note> are of this second order, and for that reason, they are dispensable through divine authority; but the precepts of the first table <note>The commandments regarding duties to God (1 through 3)</note> are of the first order, and therefore cannot be dispensed even by God Himself.

<margin>
*The third opinion of St. Thomas and William of Auxerre.*
</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, a third opinion is that of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in this present passage; and the same was held by William of Auxerre <note>original: "Altissiod."</note> in his third book, and by the ancients; according to which two conclusions are established by which the question is resolved.

<margin>
*The first conclusion.*
</margin>
The first is: All the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, of both the second and the first table, are entirely indispensable—to such an extent that not even God can grant a dispensation from them. For this is the clear mind of Saint Thomas, as is evident both in the whole article and clearly in the solution to the second argument. Otherwise, the question would not be worthy of such great dispute.

<margin>
*The second conclusion.*
</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Regarding other precepts that wander outside the Decalogue and are not implicitly contained within it, even if they are of the law of nature, nothing prevents them from being dispensable. In short, neither any principles, nor indeed the conclusions of the first, second, or third degree, which were designated above in the first article, admit any dispensation. But those precepts which do not intrinsically contain the very essence of justice, but rather special modes of observing it, can be dispensed: for example, those which are neither explicitly nor implicitly in the Decalogue, as will become clearer below. There is a fourth opinion, if you wish, that of Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334)</note> in his *Sentences*, who holds that only the fourth and fifth commandments are

<column-break/>

dispensable. We shall refute his delusion <note>original: "hallucinationem"</note> below. Both conclusions of Saint Thomas are therefore proven by this two-part reasoning:

<margin>
*The first proof of both conclusions.*
</margin>
In those precepts, as we showed in the last article of the first book, a dispensation can be made when, if they were observed literally in a certain case, the intention of the legislator would be thwarted. But by no precept of the Decalogue can the intention of God be thwarted in any case or for any reason; on the contrary, whenever one acts against the precept, one contradicts that same intention. Therefore, a dispensation from them is in no way lawful. The major premise is so well known that it is not doubted even by the adversaries; but the minor premise, which is the point of controversy, is proven thus: The intention of the legislator is primarily directed toward the common good as its end, for this is inseparable from his intention. Next, it regards the order of justice and virtue, which are the means of attaining and keeping that same end. Therefore, when the precepts themselves intrinsically contain that very essence and preservation of the common good, or the order of justice toward that same good, those same precepts contain the legislator's intention by their very intrinsic nature in such a way that it cannot be removed from them; and thus they are not dispensable, because it can never happen that acting against them does not oppose the intention of the legislator.

Examples make the matter clear: if the command of the law of the commonwealth were this, "Let no one be a destroyer or subverter of the commonwealth," or this, "Let no one act unjustly." Truly, a dispensation would be repugnant to the intrinsic reason and nature of such laws; for it is a contradiction in terms <note>original: "implicatio enim est contradictionis"</note> to say it is lawful for someone to act unjustly, or to attack the common good, to whose protection all laws are directed. However, if the law said, "Let no one open the city gates (while it is under siege)," because this is not the safety of the commonwealth itself but a mode of preserving it, there would be no contradiction if a dispensation were made for some reason—for instance, if a fleeing general wished to retreat there. But the precepts of the Decalogue are of the first order. For the precepts of the first table have an innate order toward the common good, which is God; but the precepts of the second table are toward the common good of men—namely, so that no injury is done to anyone, but each person's right is preserved. Though this is not as perfect, it is nonetheless just as intrinsically good as that which is owed to God; indeed, since it expressly contains the very essence of justice, it refers intimately to God Himself. For he who says, "You shall not steal," says the same thing as, "You shall not act unjustly, or unlawfully, or wickedly." For so, as...

### Question III of the Second Book
# Page 117

...precepts of the Decalogue are to be understood, as St. Thomas says. And in this matter—saving his high reputation—the Subtle Doctor <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308)</note> has wandered into error by distinguishing, in this regard, between the precepts of the first and second tables <note>The "first table" refers to the first three commandments regarding duties to God; the "second table" refers to the remaining seven regarding duties to neighbors</note>.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ Second, so that the force of reason may be more clearly displayed, it is argued thus: the acts of committing adultery (which is in the Decalogue) and lying or fornicating (which are implicitly hidden there, for the prior conclusion applies to both) are as intrinsically evil—just as we recently argued regarding the hatred of God—as it is for a human being to be rational. Therefore, they are repugnant to the justice and integrity of human nature. Since God cannot grant a dispensation except where there is some reason of equity and goodness, He cannot grant a dispensation in these matters; or, to speak more moderately, they are not "dispensable," just as a human cannot be made to be irrational. This is what St. Thomas was thinking when he said that precepts of this kind contain in themselves the very essence of the common good, and thus the intention of the legislator. For it is natural to God to will nothing but what is good; and it is natural to these acts—theft or lying—to be evil.

<margin>Peculiar proof of the second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, so that opposites may shine more brightly when placed side by side, the second conclusion is proved thus: those precepts which do not contain the common good (the goal of the law) in themselves, but rather serve as a medium or means—for instance, the order of justice used to achieve that good—can sometimes fail to meet the intention of that same common good. Therefore, in such cases, a dispensation from them would not harm that goal, and they would consequently be dispensable. For example: the law for preserving the good of faithfulness requires that a deposit be returned; nevertheless, when you deny a mad owner his own sword, you are certainly not acting against that goal <note>A classic legal example: returning a weapon to a person who has lost their mind would cause harm, violating the higher purpose of the law</note>, as is clear in the recently cited example of opening a besieged city contrary to the literal words of the law. Likewise, if the law requires citizens to take turns standing guard, granting a dispensation to someone for a just cause is not against the common good.

<margin>Another reason for the same point.</margin>
¶ Moreover, the same conclusion is supported by an argument from Scotus himself, which he does not truly resolve: according to Paul in Romans 13, all the precepts of the second table are included in that principle: *You shall love your neighbor as yourself.*

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Now, the love of neighbor follows from the commandment to love God. For as John says: *If you do not love the human you see, how can you love the God you do not see?* <note>1 John 4:20</note> Since the commandment to love God is indispensable (as Scotus admits), it follows that the commandment to love one's neighbor—and thus the precepts of the second table—must also be indispensable. In response to this argument, omitting 

<column-break/>

<margin>Scotus's solution.</margin>
other solutions, Scotus replies by making a distinction regarding the love of neighbor. This love by which we are bound to wish that our neighbor loves God, he says, follows from the love of God. For whoever truly loves God must wish that all others love Him as well; and thus, this form of neighborly love is indispensable. However, he claims the love by which I wish my neighbor temporal life, honor, worldly goods, an uncorrupted marriage bed, and family, does not necessarily follow from the love of God, nor does it have a necessary connection to the attainment of the ultimate goal. Therefore, God can grant me a dispensation so that I do not sin by killing, stealing, or dishonoring parents, etc.; indeed, I would still attain the ultimate goal. 

<margin>Against the solution.</margin>
¶ However, there is an argument against this solution arising from contrary principles. For the love of neighbor which belongs to the law of nature is that which follows from the love of God, who is the author and institutor of nature. This is not only the love by which we wish him to love God (for that is more a part of the love of God itself), but also that by which we desire for him the natural goods that belong to mutual and reciprocal love. For who would say that nature—and God Himself—commanded nothing else but that we should love Him? On the contrary, since we are all God's handiwork, He has so joined us together that we should maintain justice and faith among ourselves. Whence John says: *He who sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?*

<margin>Response to Scotus.</margin>
¶ Therefore, it is answered to Scotus that this love of neighbor possesses an inseparable justice. Consequently, as a necessary consequence of the love of God, it has a necessary connection to the attainment of the ultimate goal. Therefore, for God to grant a dispensation for homicide or theft would be the same as if He granted a dispensation for justice itself to be justly disturbed—which is a logical contradiction.

<margin>Solution to another of Scotus's arguments.</margin>
¶ And by the same reasoning, another of Scotus’s arguments is solved: namely, that if the precepts of the second table were not dispensable, it would follow that God necessarily willed something outside of Himself, such that He could not will the contrary (for instance, honoring parents, or that no one should steal another's goods). 

<margin>God wills something outside Himself.</margin>
I answer this by means of a distinction: that God "wills something outside of Himself" can be understood in two ways. In one way, that He wills the *existence* of that thing; and in this way, He wills nothing outside Himself necessarily, because He created all things freely, and likewise sustains and preserves them. In another way, it means He wills a *necessary connection* between extremes. And in this way, it must necessarily be confessed...

He maintains that acts like murder and theft are intrinsically evil and that violating them would be a logical contradiction of divine justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of whether God can grant exceptions (dispensations) to the Ten Commandments. Having critiqued Duns Scotus on the previous page, Soto now addresses specific counter-arguments and begins to examine the views of other major theologians like Cardinal Cajetan and Durandus of Saint-Pourçain.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...philosophers must maintain that some things are willed by necessity: specifically, all those things which are of eternal truth. For instance, that a human being is a rational animal, and—as Augustine says—that four and three are seven. These truths would remain even if the world had never been made and no physical things existed. In this same way, "thou shalt not kill," "thou shalt not steal," "thou shalt not commit adultery," and so on, are necessary objects of the divine will because they are of eternal truth. Therefore, God can neither command nor permit their opposites to be done justly. Even Scotus himself, compelled by necessity, has to concede this regarding the first principles of nature which he acknowledged to be indispensable—such as the rule that one should do to others what he wishes done to himself—and regarding the love with which humans love God (which is a created act). From this love follow the precepts of the "first table" <note>The first three commandments concerning duties to God</note>, which Scotus himself admits are indispensable.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
And by these points, the arguments to the contrary are resolved. For to the first, the response is that Aristotle, in the passage cited <note>referring to the Nicomachean Ethics</note>, is speaking of natural justice in a way that does not include the ultimate goal and order of justice itself, but rather the specific method of observing it. For example: that a citizen must keep their word is so intrinsically good that no exception can be granted for it. However, *how* that word is kept in this or that specific way can vary and be subject to an exception. For this reason, a sword should not be returned to a madman <note>A classic ethical dilemma: if you promised to return a weapon, but the owner has since lost his mind, justice requires you to break the specific promise to preserve the higher good of safety</note>. By doing so, human faith and trust are not subverted but preserved.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, the response is that there is a wide difference between a human lawmaker and God. Human laws do not possess an intrinsic justice born from nature itself; rather, they are "good" because they were established by law, and "evil" because they were forbidden. For that reason, even if they are relaxed in a particular case, the ultimate goal of the law is not subverted. For example, if you do not fast on a day forbidden by the Church, or if a thief—for a just cause—is not hanged. Similarly, God can grant exceptions in His *positive laws* <note><term>Positive laws</term> are laws established by a specific authority or decree, as opposed to "natural laws" which are inherent in the fabric of reality</note>. He can indeed release anyone from the requirement of baptism or the requirements of the other sacraments. He could likewise grant exceptions regarding all the ancient ceremonial and judicial laws. Nevertheless, regarding the *natural* precepts which have an innate justice, an exception is impossible from the very nature of the thing. Therefore, because God is justice itself, if He were to grant an exception to these, He would be denying Himself by subverting the order of justice. Yet, as Paul says in 2 Timothy 2: "God is faithful, and He cannot deny Himself."

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The third argument, however, is the one that presses the matter more closely: it seems

<column-break/>

indeed that God commanded the homicide of Isaac by Abraham, ordered the children of Israel to plunder the Egyptians, and commanded the prophet Hosea to commit fornication. Furthermore, a judge commands that a criminal be killed. To these points, <margin>Cajetan's solution.</margin> Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas</note> responds with a distinction: namely, that the precepts of the Decalogue are indispensable according to the "order of justice" they contain. However, they are "dispensable" by God according to their application to a specific individual act. Nevertheless, he says that this exception is not a "relaxation" of the command, but rather God acting so that this specific act is *not* murder. Specifically, when He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, He did not relax the law of nature (in the way a Pope might relax the law of fasting in a specific case). Instead, He made it so that the act was not murder, precisely because it was commanded by the Supreme Authority, without whom it would have been murder. For "homicide" does not signify just any killing, but specifically *unjust* killing.

<margin>Cajetan's solution is obscure.</margin>
¶ However, this response is obscure and slippery, and it seems to repeatedly "beg the question" <note><term>Begging the question</term> (petitio principii) is a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</note>. First, to say that a command is not dispensable insofar as it includes the order of justice sounds like saying nothing more than: "It is not dispensable to remain in a state against justice." Or as Durandus says in the cited passage, speaking of things in a "composite sense" <note>A logical term referring to things considered together rather than in isolation</note>: God cannot command or permit evil things to be done justly while they are still evil. Since this is in no way doubtful, it is irrelevant to the matter at hand. The only real doubt is whether this—taking another's property against the owner's will or killing a person—could become lawful by God's permission, given that nature forbids it. To answer that it is "dispensable by application to a singular act" is to beg the question unless it is explained more clearly. So that we do not cloud the matter in further darkness, this one distinction must be carefully considered; I believe no one who understood it—not even Scotus himself—could deny our position. I say that God has two powers over the whole world: one is that He is the Lord <margin>God has two powers.</margin> by right of creation. He is the Master not only of all external goods, but also of bodies and even human life itself, and of the Angels, whom He could return to nothingness as His own handiwork. The other power is that He is the Legislator and thus the universal Judge of all. For the sake of clarity, it is necessary to consider one separately from the other. This being established, we say that if He were not the Master of all things, but only the Legislator and Judge, He could in no way grant an exception for someone to take another's property...

<meta>The catchword "invito" at the bottom indicates the next page begins with the phrase "against the will [of the owner]."</meta>

<summary>Soto argues that the moral laws of the Decalogue are rooted in eternal, necessary truths and cannot be set aside by God. He critiques Cajetan’s explanation of divine exceptions, proposing instead that God can command actions like the sacrifice of Isaac because He is the sovereign Creator and Owner of all life, not just a Lawmaker.</summary>

--- Page 123 ---
<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s investigation into whether the Ten Commandments can be subject to "dispensation"—that is, whether God can grant a legal exception to their rules. On the previous page, Soto argued against Duns Scotus, maintaining that the Commandments are based on eternal, necessary truths. Here, he explains that famous biblical examples of "divine exceptions" (like the Israelites taking Egyptian gold or Abraham being told to kill Isaac) are not actually exceptions to the laws against theft or murder, but are instead exercises of God's supreme authority as the ultimate owner of all property and life.</meta>

# Book Two, Question III.

...against the owner's will, if he were innocent, one could lawfully take it: because this is so intrinsically wicked that it cannot be done justly. But truly, because God is the Lord, he can hand over anyone's property to another even against the owner's will. This, however, does not have the nature of a dispensation. For when you give your own property to someone else, you are not "dispensing" from the law against theft; rather, the person taking it is not stealing. If a father were to give his young son's clothing to a friend against the child's will, he does not grant a dispensation for theft—even if the little son is stripped against his will—because the father is the true owner. In the same way, my superior would not be granting a dispensation for theft if, without my knowledge or against my will, he gave someone else the power to take my books.

<margin>The Egyptians.</margin>
Therefore, in like manner, although God handed over the vessels of the Egyptians to the Hebrews as their Lord, and later promised them the Promised Land, he by no means dispensed with the law against theft. Nor was that act theft; for although the specific owners were deprived against their will, the gift was made by the supreme Lord. This is confirmed by the fact that even if—to assume the impossible—God were not the lawgiver and held no power over the laws, that seizure of property would still have been legitimate. This is proof that no dispensation <note>An official exception to a law</note> was involved there.

<margin>God used the legitimate authority of a judge in handing over the Egyptians' vessels to the Hebrews.</margin>
However, I have spoken here conditionally: for in those transfers, God did not use his absolute power as Lord, but rather his legitimate authority as a judge. For since the Hebrews had received no wages for the labors they performed for the Egyptians, God paid them through a just judgment. And, as is read in Deuteronomy 9, because of the abominable crimes of the Canaanites, he drove them from their lands and brought the Israelites into them. When a judge deprives a criminal of his goods, even against his will, he is by no means "dispensing" from the law against theft; for the prohibition against stealing only forbids what the law of nature prohibits. Namely, it forbids stripping an innocent person of their goods against their will by private authority, as will be shown in Book 5, Question 3.

In the same way, God—as the Lord of bodies, rather than just as a lawgiver—could grant Hosea the use of a prostitute's person, so that he might use her even against her will. 

<margin>Hosea.</margin>
For although individual consent is required for marriage under ordinary law, yet where God joins two who refuse, the union would be just as legitimate—indeed, much more so than if they had consented themselves. 

<margin>The author believes God reconciled the minds of Hosea and the promiscuous woman so that they would consent to marriage.</margin>
Nevertheless, we should not believe God used absolute power there; rather, since he "disposes all things sweetly," <note>original: "omnia disponat suauiter," a reference to the Book of Wisdom 8:1</note> he perhaps reconciled the minds of both so that they consented to the marriage. In this sense, Hosea was commanded to "make children of fornication" <note>Referencing Hosea 1:2</note> because he was commanded to take the offspring of one who was then a prostitute. For even if no other

<column-break/>

<margin>...to marriage.</margin>
marriage had been created through individual consent, God’s grant—since he is the Lord of bodies—would be enough to ensure that the union was not fornication.

<margin>Abraham.</margin>
Similarly, therefore, one must speak of the story of Abraham: for when God commanded him to sacrifice his son, he by no means granted a dispensation for murder. If God were only a lawgiver, he could never have done this; but because he is the Lord of life, he could hand that life over to Abraham’s power, just as the owner of a beast can grant its life to whomever he wishes. For this reason, it was not murder; for, as was said regarding the prohibition of theft, the ban on homicide only forbids what the natural law finds abhorrent. Therefore, when a judge hands a guilty man over to the executioner, he does not "dispense" from the law against murder; for the prohibition does not extend to that killing—rather, the law commands it. Just as it is not a dispensation for someone to kill an attacker in self-defense <term>blameless defense</term> <note>original: "inculpata tutela"</note>, because nature does not forbid it. Thus, if a man were the Lord of his own life as he is of his beast, he could grant someone the power to kill him without any dispensation. And because God is the Lord in this way, he could hand the son to the father to be slaughtered without a dispensation.

Indeed, as St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> very perceptively touched upon the matter,

<margin>St. Thomas’s very perceptive opinion.</margin>
God can kill one who is innocent of actual fault not only as Lord, but as a judge. For by reason of the transgression of Adam, we have all incurred the penalty of death; which God therefore demands from us daily through diseases and accidental events. Nevertheless, divine mercy is also praised in this case: that he did not wish for Abraham to carry out that grim execution of an innocent person.

<margin>The difference between St. Thomas and Scotus.</margin>
The difference, therefore, between St. Thomas and Scotus is this: Scotus thinks that theft—remaining defined as theft—can be lawfully done by divine dispensation, just like the breaking of a fast. But St. Thomas denies this. He concedes, however, that as Lord, God can make the taking of a thing (which was not yours before) *not* be theft.

<margin>The error of Durandus.</margin>
Through these points, the error <term>deception</term> <note>original: "deceptio"</note> of Durandus is clearly exposed. He denies that a dispensation for theft was made by God for the Hebrews in the despoiling of the Egyptians, or for Hosea in his fornication; yet he concedes that God dispensed Abraham from the law against the murder of his son. He was deceived, I say, because he did not see that just as God could hand over the goods of the Egyptians as Lord, so too could he hand over the life of a son to a father. Thus, just as the former was not theft, the latter was not murder—which is forbidden by nature and implies an evil act.

<sig>h 4</sig>

<summary>Soto argues that God's commands to the Israelites, Hosea, and Abraham were not "exceptions" to moral laws, but rather exercises of His supreme ownership and judicial authority over all property and life. He reconciles these biblical events with the idea that the Ten Commandments are unchangeable by redefining the acts so they no longer count as theft or murder.</summary>

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>Durandus is mistaken in thinking a dispensation can apply to the fourth commandment.</margin> ¶ Nor indeed was he <note>Referring to the theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain</note> seized by any less a "blindness of mind" when he granted that a dispensation could apply to the fourth commandment <note>In the Catholic numbering used here, the Fourth Commandment is "Honor thy father and mother."</note>, judging that there was not as intrinsic a reason for justice in that mandate as in the others. Yet the truth stands to the contrary. For it is deeply rooted in nature that you owe honor to those from whom you received your existence: therefore, the contrary of this can no more be done justly than can theft.

<margin>Regarding Samson.</margin> ¶ But truly, regarding Samson, one must either say that as a brave man he was able—without any specific revelation or dispensation—to expose himself to extreme danger to destroy his enemies; or, as I would more willingly assert following Augustine, he did this by a revelation from God. Indeed, his strength was not natural but supernatural, hidden in his hair; and as his history relates, he sought that strength from God again for that final assault.

<margin>Regarding Eleazar.</margin> Regarding Eleazar <note>A hero from the Book of Maccabees who died stabbing a war elephant from below.</note>, however, I will easily admit that like a strenuous soldier he attacked the elephant, disregarding his own safety.

<margin>It is more probable that Abraham and Sarah were siblings than cousins.</margin> ¶ It is no wonder if the fourth argument is held to be of greater weight by some. First, concerning Abraham and Sarah, it seems far more probable to me, as it does to Cajetan and certain others, that they were brother and sister rather than cousins. First, because not only in Genesis chapter 12, but also in chapter 20, the husband called his spouse "sister"—whereas to avoid danger, it would have been sufficient to persuade her to say she was his cousin. Furthermore, in the second place, the Hebrew text says: "she is truly my sister." And although cousins were also called "brothers," just as James is called the "brother of the Lord," nevertheless, "truly sister" has greater emphasis. But the strongest argument is that if he had only wanted to signify she was his brother's daughter, he would not have used such an explicit explanation of words, saying: "The daughter of my father, and not the daughter of my mother." For it is a stretch to use "daughter of my father" for "granddaughter of my grandfather." This is especially so when he so significantly adds, "And not the daughter of my mother." For this whole phrase seems placed there to explain the reason why she was his sister. For perhaps when a sister was not from the same womb, but only from the same father, marriage was not forbidden.

<margin>Josephus.</margin> Nevertheless, Josephus—perhaps because he had not understood this—was the first who said in Book 2, Chapter 15 of his *Antiquities* that Sarah was the daughter of Haran and the sister of Lot, and consequently Abraham's niece.

<margin>Augustine.</margin> Saint Augustine followed this author in his commentary on Genesis, and others did thereafter. But this is not the place to discuss this more closely or define it more certainly. For as far as the present matter is concerned, it is enough that the children of Adam contracted marriages among

<column-break/>

themselves as siblings, which is certain beyond certainty; and thus a dispensation was granted for this natural prohibition. It is answered, therefore, that Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> only denies that a dispensation can be made either regarding the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> itself, or regarding any of the precepts implied therein which contain the very essence of justice or injustice—such as honoring elders, avoiding fornication, and so on. However, the prohibition of marriage between siblings is not because of an injustice or injury that one of them would suffer, but because of a natural indecency. In this case, for the sake of a natural end—namely, the propagation of the human race, as was the case with Adam’s children—or for another reason, a dispensation could be granted without any absurdity. For even the second degree of consanguinity <note>Relationship by blood, such as first cousins.</note> carries a certain natural impropriety for contracting marriage, which is why it is forbidden by the Church; and yet it admits of dispensation.

<margin>It could happen that even a father and daughter, or a son and mother, could lawfully be joined in marriage.</margin> But for a father to be joined in marriage to a daughter, or a son to a mother, is so foul that it is not subject to dispensation. Although, if it could happen that the entire human race survived only in a father and daughter, it is not entirely lacking in probability that they could be joined in marriage.

<margin>To the fifth argument.</margin> ¶ Finally, to the fifth argument, Saint Thomas responds nothing other than that the Maccabees' thought regarding fighting on the Sabbath was not a dispensation but <term>epieikeia</term> <note>original: "epieikeia"; a Greek term for "equity"—the principle that a law should not be followed to the letter if doing so violates the spirit of the law or causes grave harm.</note>, which we spoke of above. For we are not bound to keep a feast day at the risk of death, as Christ taught us in Matthew 12: namely, that works of charity do not violate a feast day. However, this does not seem to fully satisfy the matter. For whatever is contained in this precept—namely, to cease from servile work and hear the sacred rites—receives dispensation; not only that which is done by God, but even that which the Church can do. For this reason, as we saw above, Hesychius does not count this in the Decalogue as natural law. But concerning this, see the next question, article 3.

<meta>This page continues the inquiry into the nature of law and obligation. # Book Two, Question III.

...that passage from Deuteronomy 16: <note>original: "Iustè quę iusta sunt exequêris"</note> *You shall justly follow what is just.* By the same reasoning, one should perform acts of courage strenuously and bravely, and acts of temperance temperately. Now, to act "justly" and "strenuously" does not happen without the habit of virtue; therefore, this manner of acting falls under the requirement of the law.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly: nothing pertains more to the force of a command than the intention of the legislator. As Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> says in the second book of the *Ethics*, the legislator intends to make the citizens virtuous. <note>The Latin *studiosos* here refers to people who are diligent in virtue, or "good citizens."</note> But no one is truly virtuous until they have formed a habit; therefore, acting from a habit falls under the command of the law.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: the manner of virtue is to perform the duties of virtue with a prompt and joyful soul. We are commanded to do this in Psalm 99: *Serve the Lord in gladness.* And in 2 Corinthians 9: *Not out of sadness: for God loves a cheerful giver.* Therefore, all these manners of acting fall under the command. ¶ On the contrary is the argument that a virtuous person (as we were just saying) cannot worthily fulfill the duties of the virtues unless they are imbued with the habit. For this reason, if this "manner of virtue" were required by the command, whoever fulfilled the law without such a habit would be judged a transgressor and would consequently be liable to the law’s penalty. However, the consequence is clearly false, because the law threatens punishment so that it may be kept through fear, and thus citizens may generate a habit through the custom of acting.

<margin>The sense of the question is explained.</margin>
To understand this question, we must first distinguish the "manner of virtue" discussed here from the "manner of charity," which will be discussed in the following article. For charity is an "infused habit," <note>In scholastic theology, an "infused habit" is a gift directly from God, like grace, whereas an "acquired habit" is developed through practice.</note> the inseparable companion of "sanctifying grace." A habit of virtue, however, can be "acquired" and "unformed" <note>An "unformed" (informis) habit is a disposition to do good that lacks the supernatural motivation of divine love.</note>. Therefore, we are not asking here whether the habit of grace is required to satisfy the command, but whether it is required that a person operate from a habit—at least an unformed one.

<margin>Three conditions required in a virtuous person, from Aristotle.</margin>
Secondly, one must remember the three conditions that Aristotle requires of a virtuous person in the second book of the *Ethics*, chapter 4. These are: first, that he acts knowingly; second, choosing the action for its own sake (that is, by choice in relation to the end); and third, that he chooses it with a firm and unchanging soul. Some unlearned people split "choosing" and "for its own sake" into two parts, but without a conjunction, it is a single condition: to choose for the sake of the end of virtue. And these three together are not three separate "manners," but one single manner of virtue; for if one is missing, the manner is lost. ¶ Having established these points, it must be noted that just as this manner of virtue has three parts, it is considered in a three-fold difference by divine and human law. For part of it is considered by both,

<column-break/>

part by divine law alone and not human, and part by both of them in another way. Therefore, the question is answered with three conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first is that both human and divine law regard and judge knowledge, which is the first part of the manner of virtue. For what someone does in ignorance, they do not do simply by their will. Therefore, in both divine and human judgment, ignorance excuses a fault either entirely or in part.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: that second condition—that the work be done by choice for the sake of the end—is not considered by human law, but it is considered by divine law.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The root of this distinction is the distance between human and divine knowledge. Truly, as was said above and as Aristotle mentions in the tenth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 9, any law urges its own preservation through the fear of punishment. But a legislator cannot demand punishment from anyone except regarding a matter that can come to his knowledge. For he is not able to judge other things. Men, however, as we read in 1 Kings 16, see only those things that are apparent; they cannot judge the secrets of the heart. Instead, as it says in the Psalms: *God alone searches the hearts and the reins.* <note>The "reins" is an archaic term for the kidneys, once thought to be the seat of emotions and hidden desires.</note> From this it becomes clear that human law can judge neither a man’s intention nor his will, and thus cannot bind him to perform works with a specific intention or will. Divine law, however, weighs that above all else in its scales, and decrees rewards and punishments accordingly. Human law, I say, cannot punish internal anger, even if it produces a firm proposal to do harm; divine law, however, can. Indeed, Christ says in Matthew 5: *Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment*; and, *Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.* By the same reasoning, someone who returns owed money or a sword to a creditor with a corrupt intention—namely, to practice usury or to commit a murder—is not a violator of human law; nevertheless, he will pay the penalty to God.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: That third requirement for the manner of virtue—namely, to operate with a firm and stable soul, which properly pertains to the "habit," and which is the main point of this present question—is not included under the command of either human or divine law. I say that someone who pays the honor due to parents satisfies human law, even if he does not possess the "habit of piety." And unless the act is corrupted by some other circumstance, he similarly satisfies divine law so as to avoid sin. ¶ From these points, certain conclusions emerge...

He concludes that while God judges internal intent, neither human nor divine law requires a person to already possess a perfect virtuous habit to fulfill a specific command.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

... we fulfill those out of charity. For the mode of charity is to do the commands of God or His Son: or by an act through which we are established as His children.
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin> ¶ And **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority Soto follows</note>, reciting two contrary opinions and reconciling them, responds with two conclusions, which become clear through this distinction.
<margin>Distinction.</margin> The act of charity is considered in two ways. In one way, as it is a certain unique act of the specific virtue of loving: just as there is one act of hoping and another of believing: namely, that whose formal contrary is to hate. And according to this way, the first conclusion is established.
<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The act of charity falls under a specific command. Namely, under this one: **You shall love the Lord your God, and your neighbor as yourself.** But in another sense, it is considered not as belonging to a specific object, but as a universal condition and "mode" <note>original: "modus": the internal manner or spirit in which an action is performed</note> of all virtues. For we explained a little earlier that not having strange gods, not swearing falsely, and sanctifying the Sabbath are nothing else than loving God: just as honoring parents, not stealing, and not killing are nothing else than loving one's neighbor—not indeed formally, as they say, but materially <note>original: "non quidem formaliter... sed materialiter": In Scholastic thought, to do something "materially" is to perform the outward action; to do it "formally" is to do it with the specific internal intention or virtue required</note>. An example is found in the virtue of justice: for there is one specific "commutative" justice <term>commutative justice: the fairness required in private dealings and exchanges between individuals</term>, and another "general" justice, which is the mode of universal obedience common to every virtue: and therefore it is called "legal" [justice]: because through every virtue we obey the law. Therefore, regarding this sense of charity, the second conclusion is established.
<margin>Second Conclusion.</margin> Such a mode of charity does not fall under the command: which is to say, in this command, **Honor father and mother**, it is not included that parents must be honored out of the charity of God: but rather that outward reverence be shown to them. Therefore, although you provide it while in a state of mortal sin <note>the state of being separated from God's friendship through serious wrongdoing</note>, you do not thereby become a transgressor of the command.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> The conclusion is proven. The charity of God is the general mode of all virtues because it is the "end" <note>the ultimate goal or purpose</note> toward which the divine law directs [us], according to that which was cited above from
<margin>Paul.</margin> 1 Timothy 1: **The end of the commandment is charity.** And Romans 13: **Love is the fulfillment of the law.** Now, it has already been defined that the *end* does not fall under the command of the law, but rather the *actions* by which one tends toward it. Therefore, St. Thomas rightly says that the intention of the end is a formal mode of a higher order. Which is to say, it is not included in the substance of the commands. And in this way he reconciles the stated opinions: namely, that the one affirming that the mode of charity falls under the command should be understood as referring to the specific command of love; while the one denying it should be interpreted as referring to the others. ¶ But since this question teems with many ambiguities, it requires a more accurate and thus slightly

<column-break/>

broader discussion. And so that we may first dispatch the easier points, besides the two opinions which St. Thomas recites here, there exists a third which cannot be drawn into agreement with them.
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin> For there are those who reject the second conclusion of **St. Thomas**, saying that every single command of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and all divine commands include the mode of charity. Thus, unless the duties of the law are performed in a state of grace <term>grace: the supernatural life of the soul and friendship with God</term>, they are not only not meritorious, but are actually sins: namely, as transgressions of those same commands. --This opinion, I say, is not only held by the **Lutherans** <note>Followers of Martin Luther, whose theology Soto is refuting in the context of the Counter-Reformation</note>, as we noted in Book 3 of *On Nature and Grace*, and shall repeat here in Book 8; but it was also formerly the opinion of the otherwise famous doctor **Dionysius the Cistercian** <note>A 14th-century theologian known for his rigorist views</note> in his [commentary on the] 2nd [book] of the *Sentences*, distinction 17.
<margin>Dionysius the Cistercian.</margin> For he was deceived by that fallacious reasoning:
<margin>Dionysius's reason.</margin> "By whatever commands God intends to draw us to the love of Himself: therefore we are bound to perform all things out of that same love." And he brings forward in his favor that [word] of Peter the Apostle, **Let all your works be done in charity**; and another from **Bernard** [of Clairvaux]: **Everything that is commanded is established in charity alone**; and similar sayings from **Augustine**. ¶ However, this opinion is not only false, but is very close to error, having been condemned by the **Council of Trent** <note>The major 16th-century council that defined Catholic doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation</note>, canon 7, against the Lutherans: namely, that all works performed outside the grace of God are sins. Against which error we
<margin>Author of the book *On Nature and Grace*.</margin> fought in Book 1 of *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 19, and the four following. For even if we set aside those works which are evil by their object and circumstances, the rest are either commands, or counsels <term>counsels: recommendations for spiritual perfection, such as voluntary poverty, that are not strictly required for salvation</term>, or indifferent things: such as eating and walking, which can be done well or poorly. If, therefore, all acts of obedience to the commands outside of
<margin>First reason against Dionysius.</margin> grace were sins, then those things which fall under "counsel" would also be sins. For if God binds us to fulfill the commands out of charity, He seems to have commanded the same regarding counsels as well; and even regarding other natural works which are rightfully permitted to us for living our lives. For all things are established by God as the Parent of nature. And so, all works performed in sin would be sins. ¶ Then it is argued: if we
<margin>Second reason.</margin> were bound to perform the duties of all the commandments out of charity, this would be either because of their common obligation, or because of the specific command of charity. Not indeed because of the general obligation of all of them; for through those, nothing is commanded or forbidden to us except [outward] works: such as honoring a father, and abstaining from injuries by which friendship is violated. But if some charity is included in the honoring of parents, certainly that will be enough...

<margin>
To the last argument.
</margin>

<margin>
The opinion of Saint Thomas.
</margin>
For first of all, the law of charity binds (if you trust the faith of Saint Thomas <note>original: "diuo Thomae"</note>) when someone first enters the path of reason, to refer himself and his affairs to God. When first, I say—not at that exact moment in time, but when a person begins to deliberate fully and recognizes that there is one primary parent of all things. And certainly, he asserted this not without reason.

<margin>
The reasoning of Saint Thomas.
</margin>
For since God led us to be created for this, and natural reason shows Him to us as the one first cause of all, it becomes most consistent with reason that then a person ought to propose to withdraw from evil out of love for Him, and to act for the good. For this is to love God above all things at that moment. Therefore, with His special help present then, a person would receive faith and grace, by which he would be cleansed from original sin. Whatever the case may be regarding this, I believe that when a person capable of reason is dipped in baptism, he ought to refer his life to God: for just as he is then bound by the precept of faith to believe, so too he is bound to hope for what he believes, and to love Him from whom he hopes for those things: as we showed in Book 2 of *On Nature and Grace* <note>original: "de natu. & gra."</note>, chapter 12 and following: like someone who gives their name to a prince in military service. And consequently, I would believe that whoever did not dispose himself to grace then would sin specifically against charity: just as he would against faith if he did not believe.

<margin>
When the commandment of love for God binds.
</margin>
And not only in these cases, but perhaps as often as we begin some distinguished work, or a cause for undergoing martyrdom is offered to us, or we receive some illustrious benefit from God—such as when He has rescued us from a most present danger of death—it would not be rash to assert, but rather a matter of prudence, that we are bound by the same precept to love God: even as to the *mode* <note>In Scholastic theology, the "mode" (modus) refers to the way an action is performed—specifically, performing an act *out of love for God* rather than just doing the outward action itself.</note>: that is, to prepare ourselves as much as is within us to enter into grace with God.

<margin>
Instruction.
</margin>
¶ However, it is necessary to note here that, like the rest, the specific commandment of charity can also be fulfilled regarding the substance of the work without its *mode*.

<margin>

Therefore, this commandment does not universally bind to its own *mode*, but only when the occasion for internal loving arises: for in this mentioned case, there is only a necessity for external protection. <margin>

<margin>
To the second.

<margin>
St. Thomas.
</margin>

For he says that he who does not honor parents out of the charity of God is not a transgressor of the commandment about honoring parents: although he is a transgressor of the commandment which is about the act of charity, for which transgression he deserves punishment. For from these words, some of our people infer this to be the mind of Saint Thomas: that wherever the matter of other commandments occurs, the mandate of charity runs parallel, against which one then sins if the rest are not fulfilled out of charity. However, this understanding is contrary to the holy Thomas. Indeed, he who defines that the *mode* of charity is not included in other commandments teaches that it does not always run with them: but, since it is affirmative <note>Affirmative commands (thou shalt) do not require constant, every-second compliance, unlike negative commands (thou shalt not).</note>, it has its own defined times, as he teaches more clearly in the solution to the second point. His mind, therefore, is that if at that time when the commandment of charity and its *mode* binds, any of the others happens to occur, then that other thing must be fulfilled out of charity: not because of its own obligation, but because of the bond of the former [charity].

<meta>This page continues the resolution of Question III, focusing on how the "commandment of charity" (the requirement to act out of love for God) relates to the other Ten Commandments. Soto is concluding the specific objections regarding whether a person can fulfill the law's "substance" without the "mode" of grace.</meta>

### Book Second. Question III. ###

<margin>To the first principal argument.</margin>
It remains for us to provide the responses to the arguments proposed at the beginning of the question. Therefore, it is answered to the first that since one of the commandments is that of charity <note>The theological virtue of supernatural love for God</note> itself and its manner, whoever keeps all the commandments is necessarily in a state of grace.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you argue to the contrary: It is possible for a man living in sin never to encounter a specific time when the commandment of love is required; in that case, he would be able to keep all the other commandments regarding the substance of the work <note>The physical act of the commandment, such as not stealing, regardless of the internal motivation</note>, and yet he would not enter into life. Because of this argument, there are those who claim that for one existing in sin, there is a commandment to be converted to God; because the sinner does not fulfill this, he does not enter life. However, although this is a debated point, I have never been persuaded that a man is bound by more commandments precisely because he has fallen into sin than he is bound by while he exists in grace. Rather, it is necessary for him to be converted by the necessity of the end <note>The ultimate goal of salvation</note>, if he wishes to have eternal life. Whatever you hold concerning this matter, the present argument does not prevail.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response, therefore, is that the word of Christ is understood to refer to those who are in grace. For if such a person keeps all the commandments, he will be saved. But he who falls from grace through a single transgression has not "kept the commandments." And therefore, it is not enough for him thereafter to keep the rest until he repents for the one he violated.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, the response is that this requirement—to refer all things to God—belongs to the specific commandment of charity. For this reason, whenever the time for that same commandment occurs, we are bound to refer all things we are then doing to God as to a supernatural end. Therefore, at that specific moment in time, someone who obeys his parents while outside of a state of charity, although he would not be a violator of the fourth commandment <note>Honor thy father and mother</note>, would nevertheless be a transgressor of the commandment of charity.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> further adds that since these are two affirmative commandments not binding "at all times" <note>original: "non obligantia ad semper"—meaning they don't have to be performed every second of every day</note>, they can bind at different times. Thus, it can happen that someone fulfilling the commandment of love is not at that moment transgressing the commandment regarding the "mode" of charity. Here he clarifies most plainly what we recently noted regarding the nearby words at the end of the question. In his view, then, it is not a sin to fail to refer that work to the glory of God as a supernatural end. Therefore, the word of Paul <note>likely 1 Corinthians 10:31, "Do all for the glory of God"</note> can exhibit a double sense: namely, that of a commandment and that of counsel. If it is a commandment, it does not bind at all times; if, however, it is counsel, the sense is that we should always strive to maintain ourselves in God's grace through the fulfillment of all the commandments. Nevertheless, even he who, while in sin,

<column-break/>

performs works that are morally good, does the same for the glory of God in a natural way. Therefore, a third sense of those same words is that we should set no other end for any work than God: but rather perform all things for that end for which they were created. This commandment, at least regarding the substance of the work, is fulfilled even outside of grace.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, the response is that since no one is able to complete the commandments unless he also fulfills the commandment of charity when it occurs, and this cannot be perfected without grace, it follows that without grace we cannot fulfill them all.

<margin>The solution of St. Thomas is extended.</margin>
But truly, although Saint Thomas was content with this solution here, where he was treating the "mode" of charity, nonetheless, a man after the fall of nature through the sin of Adam cannot fulfill all the other commandments without a special gift from God. For we are like the infirm, who can walk a few steps, but cannot progress very far. And therefore, although we can perform one or another morally good act by our own natural power, we are not able to stand for long without falling.

<margin>The author in the book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 22. Augustine. Council of Milevis.</margin>
We have established this most extensively in Book 1 of *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 22, from the sayings of Augustine and the Councils of Milevis <note>A 416 AD council against Pelagianism</note> and Orange <note>original: "Arauicani"—the 529 AD council on grace and free will</note>, and we explained it through the doctrine of the same Holy Doctor <note>Aquinas</note> in the *Summa Theologica* I-II, question 109.

# ARTICLE XI.

->*Whether other moral precepts that*<-
->*wander outside the Decalogue are appropriately*<-
->*both distinguished and reduced to the same Decalogue.*<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral scrollwork and a bird perched on a branch within the letterform.</image-desc>

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
THIS article has often been desired and hinted at in the preceding sections, so that the sufficiency of the number of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and the moral precepts annexed to it might be explained. It is argued, therefore, that no other moral precepts were necessary besides those ten. For "all the law and the prophets," as Christ asserted in Matthew 22, "hang upon these two": the love of God and of neighbor. The first of these is abundantly explained by the first table <note>The first three commandments concerning God</note>, and the second by the second table <note>The remaining seven concerning neighbor</note>; therefore, no others are necessary in addition.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If there had been a need for other precepts, this would be either as general principles or as specific determinations of the commandments themselves. Not as general principles, certainly, because those two greatest commandments were not explicitly necessary; but they are, as we were saying, prior to the Decalogue...
