<meta>This page continues the resolution of Question III, where Soto is investigating the nature of the Old Law and its sufficiency. Having previously discussed the "mode" of charity, he now addresses whether the Ten Commandments (the Decalogue) adequately cover all aspects of human morality and virtue.</meta>

### Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right ###

preceding principles: all general conclusions, however, are found in the Decalogue. Indeed, there was no need for other moral precepts to serve as general specifications: for, as shown before, the specifications of moral precepts belong to the ceremonial and judicial laws. <note>Scholastic theologians divided the Law of Moses into three parts: Moral (timeless ethics like the Ten Commandments), Ceremonial (religious rituals), and Judicial (civil laws for ancient Israel).</note>

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, an argument is made against the sufficiency of these same commandments. Moral precepts (as established above) ought to be instituted concerning all acts of virtue: therefore, just as there exist in the Law, beyond the Decalogue, precepts pertaining to liberality, mercy, chastity, and worship <note>original: "latria," the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</note>: so also should precepts be applied concerning fortitude, temperance, and those types of virtues which concern a man's relationship to himself: and yet they are not found: therefore, the Old Law did not sufficiently provide for all things.

<margin>Psalm 18.</margin>
¶ On the contrary stands that testimony of David: *The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls.* <note>Psalm 19:7 in modern Bibles, Psalm 18:8 in the Vulgate. Original Latin: "Lex Domini immaculata conuertens animas."</note> By which we are taught that it prohibited all evils by which the soul is stained, and commanded all goods by which it is converted: therefore, since all these are not explicitly in the Decalogue, it must be that they are held scattered in other places, which are then reduced back to the Decalogue itself.

¶ The beginning of the resolution of this question must be taken from what was said above. First, we must assume the distinction of ceremonial and judicial laws from moral ones. Namely, that ceremonial and judicial laws have their force solely from divine institution: just as human laws do in a commonwealth. For they are not among those things that are "just because they are good" or "prohibited because they are evil": but rather concern those things that mattered not at all before they were commanded or prohibited.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
But (as Aristotle says in the 5th book of the *Ethics*) because they have been established, they do matter. That is, they are good because they are commanded, and evil because they are prohibited. Therefore, no discussion is held concerning them at present. Moral laws, however, have their force and binding energy not from institution alone, but from the dictate of natural reason, even setting aside any other law.

<margin>The threefold order of moral laws. The first order.</margin>
These exist in a threefold order. For some are the most common and thus most obvious principles, which therefore need no formal publication: such as the mandates concerning the love of God and neighbor; and that rule, *Do unto others as you would have them do unto you*, and similar things. These, therefore, are not in the Decalogue: but are, as it were, its goal.

<margin>The second order.</margin>
Others are indeed universal, but are conclusions of those same principles: which anyone, even a common person, can easily perceive for themselves. Nevertheless, because of the perversity of morals and the clouding of reason, their judgment can sometimes 

<column-break/>

be perverted, and so they require formal publication. All the precepts of the Decalogue belong to this second order. Although those of the second table <note>The commandments regarding duties to other people (honor parents, do not kill, etc.)</note>—because they require no light of faith—were placed above in the first degree of conclusions; while the precepts of the first table <note>The commandments regarding duties to God</note>—because they do require that light—are in the third degree.

<margin>The third order.</margin>
But the third order consists of those things which not everyone can so easily perceive by the light of reason, but which require the support of the wise. These we have therefore placed in Article 1 under the second degree of conclusions. And these are the things outside the Decalogue added by Moses and Aaron through divine suggestion.

<margin>All precepts of the third order are reduced back to the Decalogue.</margin>
But since those things which are less known become known through those which are most obvious, precepts of this third order are reduced to the Decalogue, in which they are implied: with specific ones corresponding to specific commandments. The examples are clear.

<margin>First commandment.</margin>
For since the worship of foreign gods is proscribed and condemned by the first commandment of the Decalogue, all things that look toward idolatrous superstition are referred back to it. Such is that passage in Deuteronomy 18: *Let there not be found among you anyone who purifies his son or daughter by leading them through fire: nor let there be a sorcerer, or an enchanter, nor one who consults spirits or diviners, or who seeks the truth from the dead.*

<margin>Second commandment.</margin>
Again, because perjury is guarded against by the second commandment, the prohibition of blasphemy is reduced to it; this appears in Leviticus 24, where the blasphemer was ordered to be overwhelmed with stones. Also, the prohibition of false doctrine, mentioned in Deuteronomy 18, where false prophets are ordered to be refuted.

<margin>Third commandment.</margin>
To the third precept, concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath, all the institutions of ceremonies are reduced.

<margin>Fourth commandment.</margin>
Just as to the fourth, concerning the honor to be deferred to parents, all things are applied by which we are commanded to honor elders and teachers. Such is that in Leviticus 19: *Rise up before the hoary head: and, honor the person of the aged.*

<margin>Fifth commandment.</margin>
By the same right, the fifth commandment, by which murder is condemned, encompasses all laws by which any bodily injury to a neighbor is forbidden; and indeed, even internal hatred. Such are those in the same chapter: *You shall not stand against the blood of your neighbor.* And again: *Do not hate your brother in your heart.*

<margin>Sixth commandment.</margin>
In the same manner, in the sixth commandment—the prohibition of adultery—every kind of lust is implied. First, simple fornication, and the unspeakable crime <note>A common euphemism for sodomy</note>, and bestiality: according to Deuteronomy 24: *There shall not be a harlot from the daughters of Israel, nor a fornicator from the sons of Israel.* And Leviticus 18: *You shall not lie with a male: you shall not have intercourse with any beast.*
And...

### Question III of the Second Book ###

And by the same logic, another command is related to the seventh precept <note>The Seventh Commandment: "You shall not steal."</note>, which condemns theft; this is found in Deuteronomy 23 <note>The text incorrectly cites Deuteronomy 18.</note>, where usury is prohibited: *You shall not lend to your brother for interest.* <note>original: "Non fœnerabis fratri tuo ad usuram."</note> There is also the prohibition of fraud, according to that passage in Deuteronomy 25: <margin>The eighth.</margin> *You shall not have different weights in your bag.* This likewise covers all types of schemes and false accusations. Finally, in the same way, the prohibition of false judgment and every kind of lying and slander is joined to the eighth precept <note>The Eighth Commandment: "You shall not bear false witness."</note>, which is the prohibition of false testimony. For it is read in Exodus 23: *Neither shall you follow the crowd in judgment to go astray from the truth.* And further down: *You shall flee from a lie.* And in Leviticus 19: *You shall not be a slanderer or a whisperer among the people.* <margin>The ninth and tenth.</margin> Regarding the last two, however, since they restrain all improper desire, there remains no other precept to be added to them. <margin>A single minor doubt.</margin> ¶ Regarding these matters, only a single simple doubt remains. For in this series of "reductions," many more serious sins are categorized under lighter ones: for instance, blasphemy is reduced to perjury; and unspeakable and bestial shames are reduced to adultery; and finally, robbery <term>rapina (robbery)|Taking by force, whereas theft (furtum) is taking in secret.</term> is reduced to theft. Yet, reason would seem to suggest that lighter matters should be reduced to the more severe ones. <margin>Cajetan's reasoning.</margin> To this, Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), known as Cajetan, a major Dominican commentator on Aquinas.</note> adds this reason: that since those lighter sins are "more common" (as he says) and more frequently in use, the other sins which occur more rarely are referred back to them. But truly, this reason does not seem to fully dissolve the doubt. For by that logic, simple fornication, which spreads more widely among men, ought to be the primary prohibition in the Decalogue to which adultery would be reduced. Therefore, the reason is none other than what we have noted above many times. Namely, that since those things which are most obvious ought to be written in the Decalogue—and among all virtues, justice is most known, and among all iniquities, injury to others is most known—those things which are clearly owed to God were placed on the first tablet. On the second tablet, however, only those things which involve an injury to a neighbor were placed. Such is the case with adultery. For the "unspeakable crime" <note>A common euphemism for sodomy or bestiality.</note> and bestiality, even if they are most foul and consequently more serious, are nonetheless not sins against justice <note>Justice, in this legal sense, refers specifically to the rights of another person.</note>, but against one's own body. Nevertheless, in the case of theft and robbery, it is true that by cautioning against the lesser, the greater is prohibited.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> ¶ Through these points, therefore, the arguments are easily resolved. To the first, it is answered that although the whole law depends on those two commands <note>The "Greatest Commandment": Love God and love your neighbor.</note>, nonetheless some things are inferred more evidently from them; and these are compiled in the Decalogue. Other things, however, are less evident, and these are left to the teaching of the wise.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, it is answered that the ceremonial and judicial laws, as has been said, are determinations of general principles—not by way of logical inference, but by way of judgment by which generalities are specifically determined. For this reason, those are not "reduced" to the Decalogue; rather, only those things which wise men elicit from there by reasoning through the power of natural instinct are so reduced.

<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third argument, the answer is given through what has often been said: namely, that in the Decalogue only those things are prohibited which cause a manifest injury—either to a person present, like murder; or to future offspring, like adultery. But the remaining things which order a man in relation to himself, such as fortitude and temperance—because their opposites are not such manifest crimes—are left to others to teach. For example, to leaders in war, who teach that one must not flee, as in Deuteronomy 20: *Do not be afraid; do not retreat.* And to heads of households, who should instruct their own to live temperately, as in the same book, chapter 21: *He scorns to hear our warnings; he gives himself to feasting and luxury and banquets.* For this is the rebuke and correction which parents ought to use with their children.

This question, although it was sufficiently discussed in the time of Saint Thomas against the Pelagians <note>The Pelagians were a 5th-century group who argued that humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace; Augustine was their primary opponent.</note>—both by others and especially by Augustine—has nevertheless become more famous after the Lutherans <note>Followers of Martin Luther, who emphasized "justification by faith alone."</note> attempted to attribute justification to faith to such an extent that they denied all power of justice to works. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
that this article in the writings of Saint Thomas is more concise and complicated than his usual brilliance of mind; because the matter was so well-established in his time, he did not think it necessary to fully unravel it in this place. Therefore, to open up both Saint Thomas and the matter itself, it must be noted that just as justice is twofold—namely, *infused* and *acquired*—so too is justification: one happens before God, and the other before men. Therefore, we must speak first of that which is before God, which is justice in the simplest sense, and then of the other, which is only called "human justice."

<margin>Author of the book "On Nature and Grace."</margin>
Justification, therefore (as we said in chapter 6 of the second book cited), if you take the name properly and according to its first meaning, is the same as "the making of justice"—that is, the work by which someone is made just from being unjust. Just as "heating" <note>original: "calefactio"</note> is the action by which a cold thing becomes hot. For names of this kind signify a change between two extremes. Nevertheless, it is accepted a little more broadly for the "increase" and—as the Physicists say—the "intensification" of that same justice. For in forms that have a range of degrees, not only the beginning but also the progress receives the same name. For water is said to be "heated" for as long as it becomes hotter. Regarding the first meaning,

<column-break/>

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Paul says in Romans 4: *To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly*—that is, makes him just from being unjust. And in chapter 6: *He who has died is justified from sin.* Justification in this first way is therefore nothing other than the remission of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to that passage in Corinthians: *You are justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the spirit of our God.* For this reason, justification in this context is not derived from "particular justice" (the virtue by which each person gives another their right), but rather as it implies the "rectitude" of the whole man in respect to God. Indeed, just as in physical things something is said to be "justified" to another when it is made equal to it (like a stone to a mason's rule), so too is a man justified before God when, being subject to His will, he measures his works according to God's law and rule. Regarding the second mode of justification, however, John says in Revelation 22: *Let him who is just be justified still.* And Ecclesiasticus 18: *Do not fear to be justified even unto death.* And James 2: *You see that a man is justified by works, and not by faith alone.* In these words, James would have opposed Paul (who says: *We consider that a man is justified by faith and not by works*) unless Paul were speaking of the *infusion* of divine grace, while James was speaking of its *increase*. Thus it happens that in both of the aforementioned ways, since justification is a supernatural work, it does not happen except through the grace of God and through infused justice.

<margin>The difference between children and adults regarding the infusion of justice.</margin>
But there is a difference: the first infusion of justice in children happens through the sacrament alone <note>Meaning the Sacrament of Baptism.</note>; in adults, however, it happens through their own "dispositions." These might be the voluntary receiving of baptism, or through contrition—which, although it is not a "merit" of grace (otherwise, as Paul says, it would not be grace), is nonetheless a preparation without which God grants it to no one. Therefore, for conversion, the first required disposition is faith; for Paul says, *He who comes to God must believe that He exists.* Next, hope is required, according to Romans 8: *By hope we are saved.* Finally, a movement of charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) means divine love or selfless love for God and neighbor.</note> is required, according to that passage of John: *We have been moved from death to life, because we love the brothers.* And according to the Savior’s word: *He who loves me will be loved by my Father.* But truly, after we have been made just by divine power and established as children of God, we perform works through the virtues infused by Him along with grace and through His divine favor—that is, the merits of life—by increasing justice. The first justification is therefore the acquisition or attainment...

<margin>Acquired justice among men.</margin>
¶ However, **acquired justice** as it exists among men is one thing according to the truth of the matter: namely, when a person truly performs the "works of the law," which Paul calls the *law of works* in Romans 3. And it is called the **justice of works**, as we have noted in that place, because it is a human rectitude established in moral behavior through natural faculty according to the standard of the laws. It differs from the **justice of faith** in that such rectitude, although it makes the substance of the works morally good, does not justify the *person* through the remission of past sins. True justice, however, which is founded in faith—and is therefore called the **justice of faith**—justifies the person first from past transgressions through grace, so that they may then carry out just works that are pleasing to God. 

But there is also **human justification** in the external forum <note>The "external forum" refers to public, human legal courts, as opposed to the "internal forum" of a person's conscience or God's judgment.</note>, when a judge acquits a defendant based on evidence and testimony. In this sense, the Wise Man says in Proverbs 17: *He who justifies the wicked and condemns the just is an abomination to God.* <note>original: "Qui iustificat impium, & condemnat iuſtum, abominabilis eſt vterque apud Deum."</note> However, this specific meaning is not relevant for the present discussion. Therefore, even regarding acquired justice among men, "justification" is used in one way for the acquisition and attainment of the habit of justice (that is, of any virtue, for justice is used here as a general name), and in another way for the execution and practice of virtuous works.

¶ Having reflected on these matters, and descending to the literal text of Saint Thomas <note>Refers to Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose work Soto is commenting upon.</note>, let us answer the question with five conclusions. For he specifically raises the question regarding the moral precepts of the Old Law, because they are the particular subject of this inquiry: namely, whether they "justified"—that is, whether they made a person just before God and worthy of eternal life.

<margin>Assumption for the decision of the question.</margin>
For the decision of this matter, he assumes that just as the word "healthy" is properly used for an animal that is formally healthy in its health, but secondarily for a sign or cause of health (just as we call urine "healthy" or medicine "healthy"), so **justification** is properly and formally used for the reception and keeping of justice, which is the remission of sins; but secondarily for the disposition toward and the signaling of that same justice.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ With this assumed, the **first conclusion** is established: The precepts of the law justified in the secondary and improper way, both in so far as they disposed men toward the grace

<column-break/>

of Christ which justifies, and in so far as they signified that same future mercy of Christ. For as Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin> says in *Against Faustus*, the life of those people was prophetic and a figure of Christ, according to that passage in 1 Corinthians 10: *All these things happened to them in figure.* <note>original: "Omnia in figura contingebant illis." This refers to the idea that Old Testament events were "types" or "previews" of Christian truths.</note>

You may ask, however, whether this was unique to the precepts of that Law and singular to its moral rules. For our own works are also preparations for grace. It is answered that there is no difference in this regard between the works of that law and our own concerning the justification of each person. Indeed, just as our works outside of grace can be morally good and thus, with special divine help, a disposition toward grace, so it was with their works—whether ceremonial, judicial, or moral. But there is this difference: since grace and mercy come to us only through Christ, the people were disposed by the works of that Law to receive that same Messiah and his Gospel law, which even the ceremonies signified. Because of this, the conclusion encompasses all works of the Law. Our works of the law, however, do not dispose us to receive or signify a Christ yet to come; rather, through them, we worship the Christ whom we have already received.

¶ If, however, we speak of **justification** properly so called—that is, the reception and cultivation of justice—then, as we warned a little earlier, a distinction must be made. For "justification" is used either for the acquisition and attainment of justice, or for the execution of that which has been acquired (that is, for the practice of the works of a just man). But among the virtues, some are **acquired** and others are **infused**. The former are generated by the use and habit of our own works, according to Aristotle in the second book of the *Ethics*. <margin>Aristotle</margin> The latter are infused by God along with grace. In these latter virtues consists that simply true justice which is before God—namely, the remission of sins—according to that word of Paul in Romans 4: <margin>Paul</margin> *If Abraham was justified by the works of the law, he has glory,* <note>original: "Si Abraham ex operibus legis iuſtificatus eſt, habet gloriam."</note> meaning in the eyes of men, but not before God. It is regarding this true justification that we are presently inquiring.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
Regarding this, therefore, the **second conclusion** is established as a negative and general one: The moral precepts by which human acts are instituted could in no way effect that kind of justice then, nor can they do so in us now. This conclusion should not be understood as referring uniquely to the precepts of the Old Law, but to all moral precepts in general, even those of our own time. And this is the argument...

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> He established, I say, that salvation never befell anyone except through faith in Jesus Christ. Here it is not denied that grace was then accustomed to be conferred in circumcision; however, it was not conferred by the power of the sacrament, but through the faith which that people professed through that ceremony. And the reason for the difference is that then, since the Passion [of Christ] had not yet been offered, it was applied through faith only by intention, as a future goal. Therefore, those ceremonies were not an instrument of the Passion, but strictly a testimony of it. But indeed, since through the Gospel we profess the Passion already offered, our sacraments are considered not only testimonies of it, but also instruments, in whose application there lies a hidden power that effects grace.
<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin> ¶ Therefore, to return to the matter: if "justification" is used for the exercise and execution of justice, a fifth conclusion is added: All the precepts of the law justified. For apart from grace, they were morally good, justifying one before men. In those, however, who obtained justice before God through His grace, these works were true merits worthy of eternal happiness. Nor in this was there any gap between our works and theirs.
Saint Thomas acknowledges, however, some difference between the ceremonial precepts and the rest—whether moral or judicial: that the ceremonial ones, he says, justified (that is, were meritorious) because they contained justice in itself in a general sense; namely because through them worship was offered to God—just as we now worship God through the use of incense and other ecclesiastical ceremonies. But in a specific sense—that is, by the proper nature of the action—they did not contain justice in themselves, except by the sole determination of divine law. Which is to say: to sacrifice certain animals (namely calves, or goats, or little lambs, or sparrows) in a set number, and to smear the horns of the altar with blood, and other things of that kind, contained no justice according to their own nature—no more than killing dogs or certainly mice. They contained justice, however, from the determination of the divine law; further, because they were divinely instituted. And therefore, he says regarding precepts of this kind that they did not justify, except from the devotion and obedience of those performing them. <margin>To the first argument.</margin> **Through** these points, therefore, the solutions to the arguments become clear. For the word of Paul in Romans 2, that "the doers of the law will be justified," is understood according to the sense of the fifth conclusion regarding the execution of justice: namely, that those fulfilling the law outside of grace were performing works that were morally good; but within grace, they were performing works that were meritorious *of worthiness* <note>original: "de condigno"; a Scholastic term referring to merit that deserves a reward based on a certain equality of value, made possible by divine grace.</note>. <margin>To the second.</margin> Moreover, that other passage in Leviticus 18—namely, that the man who performs the judgments of the law "shall live in them"—is not understood to mean that the works themselves grant spiritual life. Rather, it means that he who kept the law would not incur the penalty of death, which the law always threatened. Although he would also live spiritually in them for this reason: that a just man, by keeping the law, would preserve the friendship of God. <margin>Third.</margin> The third argument only proves that the works of human laws justify by an "acquired justice" <note>Justice developed through habit and social standing in a human community.</note> which exists among men. But the second conclusion, which is the principal point of this article, denies that any works *by themselves* justify one before God.

# QUESTION FOUR #
->On the Precepts of the Decalogue Individually<-
->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, q. 122<-

## ARTICLE 1 ##
->Whether the precepts of the Decalogue are precepts of justice.<-

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial "Q" with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
**W**e have thought it necessary to subjoin this fourth question—concerning each of the precepts in particular—to the preceding question, in which the commandments of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> were discussed in general, so that

<column-break/>

nothing more may be desired for their understanding. For species and individuals become clearer once they are placed under their proper genus <note>Soto uses the logical language of "genus" (general category) and "species" (specific types) to organize his legal theory.</note>. For this reason, we have summoned here the same question from Saint Thomas, II-II, question 122, which is the final section on justice. For the Decalogue, insofar as it is part of the Old Law, pertains to the treatise on laws in general, which Saint Thomas placed in the I-II <note>The First Part of the Second Part of the *Summa Theologiae*.</note>; but insofar as it regards justice, it is treated specifically in the II-II. We, however, because of the innate affinity between the species and the genus, have joined both together. Therefore, although this was sufficiently instilled in the previous question, nevertheless, because this is the proper place for it, it is first asked whether all the precepts of the Decalogue are parts and species of justice. 
<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin> And the argument is made from the negative side. The purpose of the legislator, as Aristotle testifies in the 2nd and 5th books of the *Ethics*, is directed toward making the citizens good. However, he cannot accomplish this unless he imbues them with the duties of all the virtues. For this reason, it is said that he commands concerning all virtues. Therefore, the Decalogue, which embraces the whole law, ought not to have contained only the precepts of justice. ¶ <margin>Second.</margin> Secondly, the law also handed down judicial and ceremonial precepts, and finally others concerning acts of justice pertaining to the common good—for instance, concerning public magistrates, such as how the priests of the temple and the judges of the people were to be chosen. Therefore, these also ought to have been reduced into the numbering, and not only those ten which establish private virtues. ¶ <margin>Third.</margin> Thirdly, the two tables of the Decalogue are resolved into the <margin>Third.</margin> love of God and neighbor, as was said above. Therefore, they are contained under charity rather than under justice. ¶ To the contrary is the fact that justice is the only virtue (or those annexed to it) through which one person is ordered toward another. But the precepts of the Decalogue, if you inspect them, all have respect for the relation of one person to another. Therefore, they all pertain to justice.

---

<margin>The sole conclusion.</margin> **The** question is very easy and has been more than sufficiently resolved. It is therefore answered with a single conclusion: It was necessary that all the precepts of the Decalogue pertain to justice. It is proven thus: <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> The Decalogue ought to contain nothing except the first principles of the law. For the multitude of "conclusions" <note>Specific legal applications derived from general principles.</note> is so numerous that they cannot be grasped in a fixed number. But it is fitting for principles to have such a manifest reasoning of "debt"—for a "precept" implies the reasoning of a debt <note>In Latin, *debitum* means both "debt" and "that which is owed" or "duty." Justice is defined as giving to each their due/debt.</note>—that with the easiest effort, a person—

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the Old Law. Having established that the Law of Moses contains moral, ceremonial, and judicial precepts, Soto now transitions into a detailed examination of the Ten Commandments (the Decalogue) under the framework of Justice.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right #

...let each see this: the nature of debt appears most clearly in the logic of justice alone, for debt openly brings a relationship to another person. For since everyone is the master of himself and his own things, it is not well-established that a man can owe something to himself <note>Soto is following the Aristotelian idea that justice strictly requires two distinct parties; you cannot "owe" yourself in a legal sense</note>; let it follow then that it was fitting for all these matters to pertain to justice. Therefore, the precepts of the first table <note>The "Tables of the Law" refer to the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments; the first table traditionally contains duties toward God, the second duties toward neighbor.</note> pertain to the **religion** of God, which is the most powerful part of justice; the fourth precept pertains to **piety** <note>original: "pietatem"; here referring specifically to filial duty toward parents and country</note>, which is closest to it; but the subsequent ones pertain to the justice which exists among equals.

<margin>A doubt arising from the doctrine of St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Nothing remains to be noted here that was not defined in the previous question, unless someone perchance doubted this: that Saint Thomas seems contrary to himself. For in the first article of the previous question, he did not say that the precepts of the Decalogue are "first principles," but rather "proximate conclusions." For that reason, he placed the precepts of the second table in the first rank because they are approved by a small amount of consideration through those common first principles—namely, "Do unto others as you would have them do unto you," and so on. Yet here, he says they *are* first principles.

<margin>Reconciling the passages of St. Thomas.</margin>
But truly, there is no contradiction. For he does not say here that the precepts of the Decalogue are "first principles" in an absolute sense, but with a restriction: they are the "first principles *of the law*." That is, they are intrinsic to the law. For a "Law" is a collection of precepts that have been published and established. However, the precepts that are established are drawn from the first principles of nature by way of a conclusion. Because of this, there is no conflict in saying the mandates of the Decalogue are conclusions of the first principles of nature—which are extrinsic to the law, acting as its fountain and origin—and yet these same precepts are the first ones carried out through the law, from which other things outside the Decalogue are deduced. Thus, just as in speculative matters the knowledge of first principles is called **understanding** <note>original: "intellectus"</note>, while the knowledge of conclusions is called **science** <note>original: "scientia"</note> (pertaining to the discourse of reason), so too the universal principles of morality require no discourse of reason; they are written in a simple understanding and seen by a simple act. The Decalogue, however, requires some work of the reason. For this reason, Saint Thomas does not say that the intellect immediately assents to the precepts of the Decalogue, but rather the *reason* which gathers them from the first principles.

¶ Again, where he says that religion is the most powerful part of justice, he understands this because of the excellent dignity of the object [God]; even if this falls short of justice in that we do not return an "equal" amount through it. For this defect is rather 

<column-break/>

an excellence. For because of the most eminent excellence of God and the exuberance of the benefits we receive from Him, we are unable to return an equal debt to Him.

<margin>To the first.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that although God's intention was to make men good, He executed this in a certain order: He gave us the mandates of the Decalogue Himself, as the heads of the law; however, He committed to the wise the task of instructing us concerning other matters.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, regarding judicial and ceremonial matters: it was already stated in the first article of the previous question why they do not belong to the Decalogue. Specifically, because they are not drawn out like conclusions from the first principles of nature; indeed, they are not even drawn from the Decalogue itself. Therefore, they are not reduced to the Decalogue, but are "determinations" of generalities pertaining to **positive law** <note>Human-made or divinely-decreed laws that specify details, such as specific punishments or ritual steps.</note>. Ceremonial laws pertain to divine worship, and judicial laws to civil customs. Furthermore, there was no need for matters concerning public magistrates to be explained in the Decalogue because they do not pertain to everyone, but only to certain states of men; thus they are more aptly listed in the register of judicial laws.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Third: regarding the third argument, it only proves that the precepts of the Decalogue are referred to **charity** as if to their end; nevertheless, they are properly concerning the works of justice.

---

### ARTICLE II. ###
#### Whether the first precept of the Decalogue was handed down in a suitable manner. ####

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap initial C depicting a scholar at a desk writing in a book.</image-desc>
**Having** established the Decalogue under the virtue of justice, its individual precepts must be explored and weighed in order. It is asked of the first, therefore, whether it was suitably handed down. And the argument is made for the negative side.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
A human is held by a tighter bond to God than to a father according to the flesh, according to the 12th chapter of Hebrews: "How much more shall we obey the Father of spirits and live?" But the precept of paternal **piety** <note>The duty to parents</note> is established affirmatively: namely, "Honor your father and your mother." Therefore, the first precept of religion, by which we worship God, should also have been placed affirmatively; especially since affirmation is prior to negation.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second: the first precept of the Decalogue looks to religion. Since this is one virtue, it has one act; therefore, it should have been [expressed] as a single act and not...

<meta>catchword: and not</meta>

### Book Two, Question IV ###

<margin>Thirdly.</margin>
...and that it is designated by that triple word: *You shall have no other gods before me; You shall not make for yourself a carved image; You shall not adore them, nor worship them.* <note>original: "Non habebis Deos alienos coram me : Non facies tibi sculptile: Non adorabis ea, neq; coles."</note> ¶ Thirdly, through this precept—as Augustine testifies in his book *On the Ten Strings*—the vice of superstition is excluded. However, there are many more perversities of superstition beyond mere idolatry; therefore, that form of the same precept was truncated. ¶ On the contrary is the authority of Scripture in Exodus 20.

<margin>A single conclusion.</margin>
To the question, a single conclusion is given in response. The form of the first precept was most appropriately expressed through a triple negation: namely, *You shall have no other gods; You shall not make for yourself a carved image; You shall not adore them, nor worship them.* The conclusion is proven if we first lay down what has been very often asserted: namely, that the end of the legislator is to make citizens good. For this progress of goodness ought to imitate the natural order of generation. In the order of generation, two things must be observed. First, that the part which is the beginning of life be established first. For if you consult nature, the first part that lives in the soul is the heart; if you consult art, the first foundation for building a house is laid. In the course of morals, however, the first foundation is the right intention of the will toward the end; for from this, all actions regarding the means obtain their goodness. Since, therefore, our supreme end is God, the first foundation in our instruction ought to be laid in **religion**, by which we worship God.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Secondly, it must be noted in the order of generation that naturally, impediments must be removed before the seeds of virtue are sown; just as farmers first clear the field before they sow, according to that word in Jeremiah 4: *Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns and briers.* <note>original: "Nouate vobis nouale & nolite serere super spinas & tribulos."</note> From these two points, it follows that the first of all the precepts of the law ought to have been that by which the impediment to religion was removed. Since this impediment is primarily the devotion to false gods, the first precept was most appropriately placed under the form of a triple negation. ¶ Here, therefore, the error of the common people must first be rejected. For the common folk think the first commandment is that greatest commandment of love—namely, that the one God be loved—when nevertheless, as was said above, this is not included within the **Decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments</note>. Rather, it is presupposed before the Decalogue as the end and foundation of everything on the first table, which are certainly nothing other than certain explanations of that love;

<column-break/>

just as the six commandments of the second table are explanations of the other commandment regarding the love of neighbor. Furthermore, it is not a precept of faith. For this too is premised to the whole law, according to the word of Paul: *He who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder.* <note>Hebrews 11:6</note> Wherefore, as we noted above in article four, in the head of the Decalogue in Exodus 20 it is held: *I am the Lord your God: You shall have no other gods,* etc. The first word of which does not have the form of a precept, but of an admonition. It is as if He had said: "Let him who approaches my law be admonished that I am the Lord his God." With this confession of faith prefixed, He then begins the law, adding: *You shall have no other gods,* etc. Therefore, as Saint Thomas taught in article four of the previous question, the first precept of the Decalogue concerns **latria** <note>original: "latriæ"; the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</note>, that is, divine worship. This is the first head not only of the Christian religion, but also of natural law. For this reason, there was never a nation so barbarian among the heathens that did not place the first foundation and base of its laws in the worship of God. This worship consists in this: that God alone is believed in, held, adored, and venerated. Thus, the impiety of idolatry is set directly opposite to this first precept. For that reason, it is placed under a negative form: *You shall have no other gods.* Since it is clearer than the midday sun to all mortals that God exists, there was no need to state it affirmatively, but rather negatively: namely, that there are not more than one. From this, it follows that the form of this precept is negative, as we noted according to Saint Thomas in the previous question, articles 4 and 7, and as he expressly teaches here.

<margin>A doubt arising from the Ecclesiastical Catechism.</margin>
<margin>Solution to the doubt from St. Thomas and Bonaventure.</margin>
¶ However, the **Ecclesiastical Catechism** <note>Instructional handbooks used by the Church to teach the faith to the laity</note> might seem to wish to contradict this doctrine, since in several churches it is explained affirmatively: *Worship one God; Do not swear by him in vain,* etc. To this, Saint Thomas responded in the same cited article 4 that this negative precept includes the affirmation of one God. Hence, Saint Bonaventure says in Book 3, Distinction 37, that although it is negative according to its form, it is nevertheless affirmative according to the reality of the matter. This is made known by the logic we just established. Therefore, having presupposed by the **natural light** <note>The human capacity for reason and moral intuition without special revelation</note> that God exists, the negation of many gods is the affirmation of one. It is as if He said, *You shall have no other gods,* which is just as valid as if He had said: "You shall have only one God as your own and domestic God."

<summary>Soto explains that the First Commandment is phrased negatively to clear away the "thorns" of idolatry before establishing true worship. He distinguishes the Commandment itself from the foundational act of faith and the "Great Commandment" of love, which are presupposed by the Law.</summary>

# Friar Dominic de Soto, On Justice and Right #

<margin>To the first.</margin> To the first argument, therefore, it is answered that although there is one affirmative commandment in the second tablet <note>The second "tablet" refers to the commandments regarding our duties to other people, such as "Honor your father and mother."</note>, as there is in the first regarding the religion of God, the order is nevertheless reversed. For in the second tablet, following the order of dignity—where affirmation is superior to negation—the affirmative commandment is placed before the others. In the first tablet, however, the order of execution is followed, where negation precedes affirmation. Wherefore, the soul is purged by the first two commandments: namely, from infidelity, so that it acknowledges no other gods; and from irreverence, so that it does not use God's name unworthily. Finally, in the third place, the affirmative commandment of the Sabbath is added, by which the service due to God is established. ¶ And there are those who meditate on the order of these three commandments according to the attributes of the Divine Persons. Specifically, that the first corresponds to the Father, to whom the majesty of unity is attributed. For He is the principle without a principle; because of this majesty, faith is owed to Him, so that no other God is admitted alongside Him. The second corresponds to the Son, to whom truth is attributed, and thus it is owed to Him that no false witness be produced <note>The author links "taking the name in vain" to the attribute of Truth found in Christ.</note>. The third corresponds to the Holy Spirit, to whom goodness and holiness are attributed, and thus sanctification is owed through service. But if one wishes to look at our three duties, the first corresponds to the fidelity of the heart; the second to the truth of the mouth; and the third to the probity of deeds. 

<margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, it is answered that although the act of religion is truly one, its violation occurs not in one way but in several. For there were those among the nations who worshiped creatures as gods in their minds without any sculpted image. 

<margin>Varro.</margin> Indeed, Marcus Varro <note>A Roman scholar and writer (116–27 BC).</note> records that the Romans worshiped the gods for some time without statues. Of these, Paul says in Romans 1 that they "devolved divine honors upon birds, serpents, and stones." <note>original: "Diuinos honores ad volucres, serpẽtes, & lapides deuoluiſſe."</note> And against these it is said: *You shall have no other gods.* Others, however, placed images in their shrines which they adored; against these it is added: *You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor shall you worship them.* 

<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third argument, it is finally answered that all the fictions of superstition are understood to be driven away and exploded by this same commandment. 

<margin>A doubt concerning images.</margin> ¶ Concerning the second member of this commandment—*You shall not make for yourself a carved image*—a doubt is usually treated regarding images: whether they are foreign to true religion. For they seem here to be forbidden as the very material of idolatry. And in Deuteronomy 4, it is said most explicitly: where Moses says, *You saw no likeness on the day the Lord spoke to you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire: lest perhaps, being deceived, you should make for yourselves*

<column-break/>

*a carved likeness or an image of male or female, etc.* <note>original: "Non vidiſtis aliquam ſimilitudinem in die qua loquutus est vobis Dominus in Oreb de medio ignis: nè fortè decepti faciatis vobis ſculptam ſimilitudinem aut imaginem maſculi vel foeminæ &c."</note> where it was most holily forbidden for that people to fashion any likeness of the stars or other things of heaven or earth to be adored. Therefore, on the occasion of these and similar oracles of Holy Scripture, there have not been wanting heretics who contended that the religious use of images should be banished and proscribed from the Christian family. Indeed, this heresy was so ancient that it is not quite clear who its first parent was. 

<margin>Platina.</margin> For what Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina (1421–1481), a papal historian.</note> calls the "Felician heresy" in his *Life of Hadrian I* cannot be understood as if Felix of that time was its first author; for previously there had been the Emperor Leo III, the destroyer of images; and much earlier, John of Damascus 

<margin>Damascenus.</margin> was a refuter of the same heresy. The first, therefore, whom I have read regarding this matter is the very ancient Epiphanius, from before the age of Jerome. For in his second volume, book 3, regarding the heresy of the Collyridians, he sharply lashes out against human statues and images and their adoration; he attacks them again in his letter to John of Jerusalem. However, perhaps because he is excused by ignorance—since he wrote this against idolaters—he is not numbered among the heretics. But John of Damascus, close to that age, in book 4, chapter 17, attacks this error as heretical. Nearly three hundred years after that age, specifically in the year 720, the Roman Emperor Leo III revived the same heresy, excluding all images from temples with the great rigor of his edicts. This error was then condemned by Pope Gregory III in a Roman Council of ninety-three bishops, as Sigebert reports. 

<margin>Gregory III.</margin> And afterwards, a second Council <note>The Second Council of Nicaea, 787 AD.</note> was called regarding the same matter under Empress Irene, where the same heresy was slain by the sword-point of anathema by three hundred bishops. Later, it was exploded by Hadrian (as Platina reports) in the Council of Frankfurt against Felix; and then in the Sixth Synod of Constantinople (as reported in the *Decretals* on Consecration, distinction 3, canon "Venerabiles"), it was decreed that venerable images are to be cherished. Hadrian accepted this Synod, as is evident in the same place, canon "Sextam Synodum." 

<margin>John Wycliffe.</margin> After many centuries, however, that most pestilential John Wycliffe, condemned in the Council of Constance, attempted to reintroduce the same heresy. Against him, the solemn author Thomas Netter of Walden <note>A 15th-century English theologian who defended the Church against Wycliffe.</note> amassed much evidence in volume 5 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 150...

# Question IV of the Second Book #

witnesses. Finally, in our own times, 
<margin>Luther</margin> 
the Lutherans—as we have seen with great anguish and sorrow of heart—have stripped their temples of all images.
<margin>A threefold consideration of images.</margin>
¶ Therefore, a threefold consideration must be held regarding the adoration of images. The first is if they are adored with the worship of <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latriæ"; the highest form of worship, which the Church teaches is reserved for God alone</note>: that is, with the cult due to God, as if a divine power resided within the objects themselves. This is the impiety of idolatry, which is forbidden here and in the cited passage of the Law as an unspeakable crime, contrary to the first commandment. For this reason, it is commanded: *You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor shall you adore them*; that is, you shall not make them so that you adore them as if they were God.
<margin>An interpretation of the text of Gregory.</margin>
And in this way, we must understand the text of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD)</note> to Serenus, the Bishop of Marseille, which is recorded in the *De Consecratione*, distinction 3, canon *Perlatum*. There, he praises Serenus for forbidding the adoration of images, but he accuses him of breaking them. For they were being adored as if they were gods; therefore, it was the bishop's duty to teach that they should not be adored in that way, but by no means should he have broken them. Secondly, this kind of adoration is considered in terms of the danger of exposure to idolatry. For this reason, God saw fit to most vehemently deter the ancient people from such images, as he knew them to be most prone to that vice. This was not only because they were fickle and devoted to the senses—and thus to physical idols—but also because they had been raised in Egypt, where the stars of heaven and the lowest animals of the earth were worshipped, and because they lived among the Canaanites, Jebusites, and other idolaters. Likewise, because at that time God had not yet appeared in human form as He has to us, no physical likeness could be expressed then, as John of Damascus noted in Book 4, Chapter 17. Therefore, no image of sacred things was permitted then, except those by which the divine majesty was presented to the sight of that sensory-driven people with terror. Indeed, for this purpose, those Cherubim in Exodus 25 were commanded to be fashioned on both sides of the oracle: not, I say, so that they might be looked upon as images of angels are now adored by us as our advocates, but so that the fearsome divine majesty might be made more venerable to them. Finally, the third consideration of images is insofar as God Himself and the saints are represented in them. For they are, as it were, the "scriptures of the common people," bringing the holy ones to our memory, so that we may both venerate them for their glorious deeds and shape our own lives by their examples. And for this reason, it is nothing other than a duty and a good part of religion to adore images—especially for us

<column-break/>

who worship and profess God Himself made man. Indeed, after He appeared to us in a physical form, it is right to express the holy ones themselves in physical images. Nor is there any fear that they will be adored by us as gods, as the Holy Synod says in the previously cited Canon *Venerabiles*. ¶ But indeed, it must not be kept silent at present that they do not serve us merely as "scriptures" by bringing the holy ones to our memory. For we do not adore the scriptures or the names of the saints, but rather God and the saints who are represented through them. Regarding images, however, we must think far differently. For they do not merely elevate us to adore the holy ones—for no heretic has denied the use of images for this purpose—but we ought to adore the images themselves. Indeed, the Church does not only say, "We adore You, O Christ," but also, "We adore Your cross." And to that same cross she says, "Hail, O Cross, our only hope." They are not, however, adored insofar as they are stones, or wood, or any other material, but insofar as the forms of God or the saints exist in them. From this it follows that each image is to be adored with the same cult as the reality itself: thus, the image of God and of Christ with the worship of <term>latria</term> <note>Worship due to God</note>, but the image of the Virgin or any other Saint with the worship of <term>dulia</term> <note>original: "duliæ"; the honor or veneration given to saints as servants of God</note>.

### ARTICLE III.
### Whether the second commandment is placed in a suitable form.

The second place is held by the commandment by which the taking of the divine name in vain is prohibited. And it is argued that it is not placed in a suitable way.
<margin>The first negative argument.</margin>
The *Gloss* on Exodus 22 explains that commandment otherwise: namely, "do not think a creature to be the Son of God." By this gloss, errors regarding faith are prohibited. But in Deuteronomy 5, it is phrased differently: *You shall not take the name of your God in vain*, that is, by attributing the name of God to wood and stone. By this, a false confession—which is an act of infidelity—is prohibited. Faith, however, is more excellent than religion, since it is its foundation; and infidelity comes before superstition. Therefore, according to those explanations, this should have been established in the first place, not the second.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: in the same place in Exodus 20, the same word is explained, *You shall not take the name of God in vain*, that is, for nothing. In that sense, it seems only to guard against vain swearing—that is, swearing which is done without judgment and prudence;

<sig>i 5</sig>
<meta>prudence;</meta>

# Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law #

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
...prudence: but perjury is much more serious—that is, a false oath which lacks truth—as is an unjust oath, which lacks justice. Therefore, the phrasing of that prohibition <note>The Second Commandment: "Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain."</note> was insufficient. ¶ Thirdly: Blasphemy is a more wicked and more enormous impiety than a vain oath; therefore, it ought to have been more expressly forbidden than a "vain" oath. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the authority of Holy Scripture.

---

<margin>Single conclusion.</margin>
Let a single conclusion be given in response to the question: This commandment is placed in the best possible manner and location. <margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin> Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> explains this conclusion with beautiful reasoning. For indeed, as we have already stated, it was fitting that the obstacles to true religion be excluded before its affirmative commands were issued. Therefore, the negative commandments had to be arranged according to the number of things that obstruct religion. There are two such impediments. One is by way of "excess": as when you share the worship due to the one true God with false ones. The other is, as it were, by way of "defect": as when you do not revere the God whom you alone adore according to His dignity. By the first commandment, the former vice was excluded: namely, that we should not worship many gods. For he who worships a false god alongside the true one does not truly worship Him who is true. Hence, from Isaiah 28: *The bed has been narrowed*—namely, the bed of the gods—*so that one or the other must fall out*—namely, from the heart of man: either the true or the false. *And the short cloak*—that is, just religion—*cannot cover both.* <note>original: "Coangustatum est stratum... et pallium breve"; Soto uses the imagery of Isaiah 28:20 to argue that the human heart cannot hold both true worship and idolatry simultaneously.</note> It remained, therefore, that by the second commandment, the irreverence should be guarded against by which the acknowledged true God is dishonored, as far as lies within our power. For it is prior to undertake the worship of one God than it is to avoid dishonoring Him.

<margin>On the use and abuse of swearing.</margin>
¶ Regarding the use and abuse of swearing, besides our commentaries on that passage of Matthew—*Do not swear at all*—we have published a small book in which we discussed almost everything pertaining to this matter. Nevertheless, it is necessary to satisfy the exposition of the present text.

<margin>The second commandment is not entirely negative.</margin>
First of all, it must be observed here that this second commandment is not so strictly negative that it is in no way permitted to use the divine name as a testimony to truth, but rather that we should not take it "in vain" <note>original: "in vanum"; meaning "emptily" or "without purpose."</note>. Indeed, just as the first commandment embraces two contrary parts—namely, the express negation of idolatry, which includes the affirmation of true worship, as was explained—so also this commandment excludes the abuse of swearing in such a way that it simultaneously implies the "religion" <note>In this context, "religion" is the technical term for the virtue of giving God His proper due through acts of worship and reverence.</note> of swearing. Wherefore, just as a person who swears falsely transgresses this prohibition, so also 

<column-break/>

a person who swears legitimately exercises a virtue, which is reduced to this commandment. For it is clear from Deuteronomy 6 that legitimate swearing is an act of religion: *You shall fear the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve, and you shall swear by His name.* And in Jeremiah 5, God does not complain that the children of Israel had sworn, but that they had sworn by those who were not gods. Let us conclude, therefore, that swearing, if done legitimately, is not just any virtue, but truly a virtue of religion; for by it we profess God to be the supreme source of truth, by whose testimony all truth is certainly established.

¶ However, you will object to us the word of Christ in Matthew 5, where, citing the ancient law, he seems to have either entirely rejected or amended it, saying: *You have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not swear falsely"* (for so it was written in Leviticus 19), *but you shall perform your oaths to the Most High* (which was indeed the sense of Deuteronomy 6: *And you shall swear by His name*). *But I say to you, Do not swear at all.* In this, He seems to condemn every oath whatsoever. <margin>Jerome.</margin> Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the biblical scholar and translator.</note> responds that He did not prohibit swearing entirely, but rather swearing by creatures in the manner of idolaters, who thought a divine power resided within them. But in truth, as we have sufficiently discussed in that aforementioned book (Chapter 3), the sense is simply as it lies: that we should swear neither by God nor by creatures, except where natural reason and religion demand it. This is clear from the words of James 5: *Above all, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor any other oath*; that is, neither by God nor by a creature. For the understanding of Christ’s mandate, therefore, we must recall what we touched upon above: namely, that all the commandments of the Decalogue and all the moral truths implied in them are nothing other than explanations of natural law. Therefore, they must be illustrated by the light of nature. For example, He commanded: *Thou shalt not kill.* In that place, nothing is prohibited except homicide, which nature forbids. Hence, when a judge fixes a criminal to the gallows, or when someone kills an aggressor while defending themselves with legitimate protection—since the law of nature commands the one and permits the other—there is no exception made to the commandment at that time, because the commandment did not forbid those cases. In like manner, when Christ says *Do not swear at all*, He in no way forbade us anything except the abuse of oaths. For where reason requires an oath, nature is the interpreter of the mandate. Moreover, He added the word "at all" <note>original: "omnino"</note> to wipe away ignorance, lest anyone falsely believe that swearing by creatures, even in vain, was not perjury. Thus, that little word "at all" did not exclude all cases of swearing, but...

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that the Second Commandment is perfectly ordered to ensure reverence for God, and that Christ’s prohibition of swearing in the Gospels refers to the abuse of oaths, not their legitimate use as acts of religious virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Second Commandment regarding the prohibition of taking God’s name in vain. Having established that this commandment is perfectly placed within the Decalogue, the author now begins to define what constitutes a "vain" oath and the necessary conditions for a lawful one, drawing on St. Thomas Aquinas, St. Augustine, and the Prophet Jeremiah.</meta>

# Question IV of the Second Book #

...all the various ways of swearing in vain. This is exactly what Christ himself explained through the following exposition: "neither by heaven, nor by earth," etc. <note>Matthew 5:34-35</note>

<margin>The duty of swearing is not a virtue in its own right. St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Next, it must be observed that the duty of swearing is not a virtue in its own right—in the way that charity and justice are—but rather, necessity places it within the bounds of virtue. An oath is to be understood as honorable and right only according to its specific "companions": namely, truth, justice, and necessity. Indeed, if that state of innocence from which our first parent cast us out had endured, there would have been no virtue in swearing; for in that state, no fraud could have existed, and holy faith <note>original: "fides"; here meaning trust or reliability</note> would have reigned among men. But because man was cast down from there, and "every man has become a liar," <note>Psalm 116:11</note> human trust has subsequently been so weakened that it is not enough on its own to reassure the mind of a believer. Therefore, by the grace of God, the oath was granted to us as a necessary means to strengthen that same trust of ours.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence, when Christ says, "Let your speech be 'yes, yes,'" <note>Matthew 5:37</note> he does not simply mean "affirm what is true and deny what is false"; rather, he points to the sincerity in which God created our nature, and which we ought always to imitate. However, when he adds, "whatever is more than this comes from evil," according to the interpretation of Augustine, this does not signify the "evil of fault" <note>original: "malum culpae"; meaning a moral sin</note>—as if it were never permitted to swear without committing a crime—but rather the "evil of punishment" <note>original: "malum poenae"</note>. This means the oath descends from that original stain of sin through which men lost their own authority, such that full trust is not given to them without an oath. Therefore, as Augustine says, the word for oath <note>original: "iuramentum"</note> is derived from the word for "law" or "right" <note>original: "iure"</note>. For he who swears, Augustine says, "renders the right of truth to God."

<margin>The word for oath is derived from "right" (ius).</margin>
Or perhaps, in a way that alludes more closely to the name, the term for "sworn right" <note>original: "iusiurandum"</note> is derived from the fact that what is sworn must be held as a law; it must be kept as sacredly as a right <note>original: "ius"</note> because you have appointed God himself as the witness to the truth. Thus, an injury is done to God himself if, after an oath, you seek out some other testimony. <margin>Paul.</margin> Hence Paul says in Hebrews 6: "An oath is the end of all controversy for confirmation." For this reason, the Legal Consultant says in the opening chapter of the title *On Oaths* <note>original: "de iureiurando"; referring to the Digest of Roman Law (ff.)</note>: "The religious practice of the oath came into use as the greatest remedy for expediting lawsuits." <margin>Cicero.</margin> And in his book *On Duties*, Cicero says: "Our ancestors intended that no bond should be tighter for binding trust than a sworn oath." ¶ We have, therefore, the sense of this precept: it is negative in such a way that it still permits the legitimate religious use of swearing. It remains, then, to explain the "companions" who keep an oath 

<column-break/>

<margin>The three companions of an oath according to Jerome.</margin>
within the boundaries of virtue and honesty. For these are three in number, which Jeremiah, inspired by God, brought forth in Chapter 4: "And thou shalt swear, 'The Lord liveth,' in truth, and in judgment, and in righteousness." Regarding this, Jerome says it must be noted that a sworn oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and justice. Because of this, wherever any one of these is missing, it is perjury—though for different reasons. Indeed, a sworn oath that lacks *truth* is most properly called perjury. One that lacks *justice*, however, is wicked, even if it happens to be true. It is subsequently considered perjury because he who promises something unjust under oath swears to do what he ought not to fulfill; he becomes a perjurer by the same logic whether he later fulfills it or not. Nevertheless, an oath made without discretion and *judgment*, although it may be true and regarding a just matter, is nonetheless "rash"; because of the danger of swearing falsely, it also earns the name of perjury.

<margin>Three degrees of vanity.</margin>
¶ To come closer to the point: where the vain taking of the divine name is forbidden, three degrees of "vanity" are noted in a specific order. For a thing is "vain" if it is done to no purpose—that is, if it lacks its proper end. A false oath, therefore, is in the first degree of vanity; for it lacks *truth*, which is the marrow and substance of an oath. Indeed, it is as vain as a hazelnut shell that is empty of its kernel. An unjust oath, however—such as when you swear you will perform unjust deeds like murder or theft—is "vain" because it lacks the ornament of *justice*. For this reason, it not only fails to bind the person, but it is actually a sin to fulfill it. Therefore, its entire wickedness must be weighed by the quality of the justice (or lack thereof) in the object of the oath. For example, if you swore to commit a mortal sin, the oath is mortal, whether you carry it out or not. But if you swore to tell a joke-lie, the oath is venial, because fulfilling it is no worse than a venial sin.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But you might argue: "If someone does not fulfill the oath, they have sworn falsely; but to swear falsely in any individual case is a mortal sin; therefore, an oath regarding a venial matter <margin>Solution.</margin> will be a mortal sin." The Minor premise is denied. For failing to fulfill a *promissory* oath is only a sin when the oath is obligatory. When it does not bind, even if the person who does not fulfill it then shows and makes it so that the oath was "false," the malice of the oath is not to be weighed from that failure (since he did not sin in that moment), but from the act of swearing itself. If the object of that act is a venial sin, the oath will be no worse than venial. But a rash oath, on the other hand...

<summary>This page defines the nature of a lawful oath, arguing that swearing is a necessary tool for human trust following the Fall. It identifies the three essential "companions" of a valid oath—truth, justice, and judgment—and explains how the absence of any of these leads to various degrees of perjury or vanity.</summary>
<keywords>oath, perjury, truth, justice, judgment, St. Augustine, St. Jerome, St. Thomas Aquinas, vanity, mortal sin, venial sin, Roman Law, Cicero</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s commentary on the Decalogue (the Ten Commandments). The previous page established that an oath is only virtuous when accompanied by truth, justice, and necessity. Here, Soto categorizes the gravity of different types of perjury and concludes the discussion on the Second Commandment before transitioning to the Third Commandment regarding the Sabbath.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right #

...vain, namely that which is both true and concerning a just matter, but lacks judgment and prudence; for that reason it is vain because it lacks the necessity that makes an oath a virtue. But it is called "perjury" for this reason alone: that he who swears vainly is in danger of swearing falsely.

<margin>The sequence and order of the gravity of various perjuries.</margin>
¶ Through this, we can see the gravity of the guilt of these three types of perjury. First, perjury of the first kind—that is, an **assertory oath** <note>An oath where one "asserts" that a past or present fact is true.</note> regarding a falsehood—is a lethal crime, not only by its general nature and the reason of its object, but in every individual instance. For while that which is mortal by its nature is common to the other commandments of the Decalogue (since all pertain to justice, which is necessary for the commonwealth, so that the observance of all is necessary for salvation), the fact that it is mortal in every single instance is a unique quality among them all. For example, although theft is a mortal sin by its nature, it can become a venial sin through the lightness of the matter—such as if you were to steal a single penny. However, to swear falsely, even in the smallest matter—such as if you perjure yourself saying you are not touching the pen <note>original: "calamum," a reed-pen</note> you hold in your hand—and even if you do it for any great necessity, such as for the salvation of the whole world, it is nonetheless a mortal sin. For it is just as false that you are not touching the pen as if you had sworn some other very grave thing that was false. To bring God in as a witness to a lie is a mortal act of irreverence. Regarding the gravity of a **promissory oath**, we have just recently said that it must be weighed according to its object. However, a **rash oath**—that is, one which has no other vanity than that it is made without necessity and circumspection—is not mortal by its nature, but only venial. For example, if you were to affirm with an oath that it is raining while it is raining in everyone’s sight; or when the matter is very trivial, where it matters nothing whether it is believed or not; or when another person would have believed you even without an oath. ¶ In the frequency of oaths, however, there lies the most immediate danger of perjury. For this reason, this "monstrous beast" <note>Soto uses this metaphor to describe the habit of constant swearing.</note> must be avoided with all care and vigilance. Furthermore, to swear by false gods, regardless of how much truth or human justice is involved, is the sin of idolatry. However, to make use of an oath sworn by infidels is permitted in a case of necessity, as **Augustine** says in his letter to Publicola.

<margin>Response to the first argument.</margin>
TO the first argument, therefore, it is responded that those interlinear expositions are not literal, but mystical. Hence, out of hatred for the **Arians**, <note>A fourth-century heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ.</note> it was explained that the name of God is usurped in vain when the **Word incarnate**, 

<column-break/>

which is by substance the name of God, is asserted to be a creature. The other exposition on Deuteronomy 5 refers to infidels, whose impiety is struck down because they swear by stones and wood as if they were gods.

<margin>Response to the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second it has already been answered: the name of God is not only taken for nothing when one swears rashly without judgment and prudence, but even worse, when one perjures oneself falsely or unjustly.

<margin>Response to the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, finally, **St. Thomas** responds that just as common and trivial lessons are first presented to one who is first being educated in some science, so too order required that common things and those more frequent in use should be prohibited immediately, so that through them men might understand that they are forbidden from more serious things. Indeed, I believe that God did not express the horrifying forms of blasphemy for this reason: that by remaining silent, He expressed more clearly that they are so abominable that they ought not even be named in the Law. For he who does not know the true God, it is no wonder if he is turned toward false ones; yet, that he who worships the true God should dishonor Him with blasphemies is so wicked that it is evident even without any written law. Furthermore, consider this in the words of this precept: to emphasize the majesty of the divine name, it is not only prohibited to perjure oneself by it, but even to take it into one's mouth in vain. Therefore, not only in the form of swearing, but even in trivial conversations, one must not speak of God vainly, nor bring forth His name without cause. And although there are many divine names, because all are of the same power, it was said in the singular number: *Thou shalt not take the **name** of God in vain.* However, the Hebrews extract another meaning from this precept: namely, that the name most celebrated in the Law, **Adonai**, was to be worshipped but not spoken aloud. For this reason, they called it in Greek the **Tetragrammaton**, <note>original: "Tetragrãmaton," meaning "four letters," referring to the Hebrew name YHWH.</note> that is, the name of four letters.

And it is argued from the negative side. It is understood either according to the spiritual sense, or according to the literal sense: according to the spiritual...
