<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the Ten Commandments. Having concluded the Second Commandment regarding oaths and perjury, Soto now begins "Question 4," which transitions to the Third Commandment: the sanctification of the Sabbath. He discusses whether this commandment is moral (universal) or ceremonial (specific to the Jewish Law).</meta>

# Book Two, Question 4 #

...it is not a specific rule, but a general principle for all.
<margin>Ambrose</margin> For Ambrose says in [his commentary on] Luke 13, regarding the leader of the synagogue who was indignant that Christ healed on the Sabbath: "The Law on the Sabbath does not prohibit healing a man, but rather servile works"—that is, being burdened by sins, which are prohibited by every precept. However, according to the literal sense, it is ceremonial. For we read in Exodus 31: "See that you keep my Sabbath, because it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations"; that is, a remembrance of the world created by me. However, the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> are not general or ceremonial, but specific and moral; therefore, this precept is least suited to the Decalogue.

<margin>Argument 2</margin> ¶ Secondly: All precepts of the Decalogue, being of the law of nature, are also observed in the Gospel law. But we followers of the Gospel neither keep the Sabbath nor the Lord’s day in the Jewish manner; for indeed we prepare food and perform other such tasks that were not permitted to them. Therefore, this precept does not properly belong to the Decalogue.

<margin>Argument 3</margin> ¶ Thirdly: The transgression of any precept of the Decalogue is, by its nature, a mortal sin <note>original: "piaculum," a grave sin requiring expiation</note>. However, in the old law, it was permissible to violate the Sabbath without offending God: for they were circumcised on the eighth day, even if it fell on a Sabbath. And Elijah, while he completed his forty-day journey, did not stop on the Sabbaths. Other things of that kind were done lawfully; therefore, it is not a precept of the Decalogue. ¶ On the contrary, however, stands the testimony of Holy Scripture.

<margin>First conclusion</margin> The question is answered with three conclusions. The first is: The precept of the sanctification of the Sabbath is appropriately placed in the third position, and it is affirmative.

<margin>Proof</margin> It is proven. In the establishment of religion, as has been said, the obstacles to true religion first had to be rooted out by negative precepts. These obstacles are indeed idolatry and irreverence. Once these were uprooted, it followed that a precept of religious service <note>original: "famulatus," the service or devotion a servant owes a master</note> should be applied. This, then, is the precept of sanctifying the Sabbath; therefore, it is placed in an appropriate spot.

<margin>Second conclusion</margin> ¶ Second conclusion: In this same third commandment, external worship of God is commanded—namely, physical rest for the purpose of serving God.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion</margin> It is proven. Divine worship is as much internal, such as meditation and mental prayer, as it is external, such as the offering of sacrifices. However, the internal is presented to us, who are sensory beings, under the likeness of external things: just as we are instructed by the ceremony of burning incense how the mind of the one praying must be elevated toward God;

<column-break/>

according to that [verse] of the Psalm: "Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight." Therefore, it was also fitting for external worship to be signaled to us in a similar way through some sign.

<margin>Third conclusion</margin> ¶ Third conclusion: The same third precept is most aptly proposed to us under a sign commemorating the creation of the world; namely, that just as the Lord rested on the seventh day from the work he had performed, so we, ceasing from servile works every seventh day, shall set aside time to be dedicated to recollecting divine blessings.

<margin>The conclusion is demonstrated</margin> It is proven. For since "being" is the foundation of all goods, it follows that the first of blessings—from which all other things come to us—was our formation and the construction of the world, created for our sake. Therefore, the memory of that same blessing opens a path for us to commemorate the rest. Hence, in Exodus 20, having first given the precept concerning the sanctification of the Sabbath, the reason is added: "Because in six days God made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested."

<margin>Reason against the first conclusion</margin> ¶ Nevertheless, there are arguments for doubting each of these conclusions. For against the first, insofar as it asserts this precept is affirmative, the very form of the precept is offered, which seems not affirmative but negative: through it, in the literal sense, nothing else is meant but to cease from servile work. To cease, however, is to abstain from work—that is, *not* to work—just as to fast is to abstain from food, which is *not* to eat.

<margin>Solution</margin> But to this it is answered that the precept is affirmative: namely, to sanctify the day, which means to dedicate it to holy service. Hence, in Exodus 20, it is phrased affirmatively: "Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day." But the *form* of sanctifying is added: "You shall do no work in it"—meaning servile work—so that you may be free for divine matters. And this is confirmed by the institution of the Church, which specifically expressed that general way of sanctifying, commanding that we hear the Mass <note>original: "sacra," literally "the sacred rites," but contextually refers to the liturgy of the Mass</note> on feast days.

<margin>First doubt</margin> ¶ However, the second conclusion offers us more difficult occasions for doubt. For the first doubt of all is whether this precept commands only external worship for us, or indeed internal work at the same time.

<margin>Scotus</margin> For there is [Duns] Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), an influential Franciscan theologian and philosopher</note>, who in Book 3, distinction 37, seems to feel that by this precept one is commanded to have a good act of the mind regarding God on feast days: namely, love for Him. This he had asserted more explicitly in the same book, distinction 27, saying that the specific time for fulfilling the precept of the love of God is contained within this precept; namely, that at such a time one should remain...

<summary>This page discusses the theological justification for the Third Commandment (keeping the Sabbath), arguing that it is both an affirmative call to worship and a necessary external sign of God's creation. Soto addresses scholastic counter-arguments regarding whether the Sabbath is merely a ceremonial relic or a fundamental moral law.</summary>
<keywords>Sabbath, Third Commandment, Decalogue, servile works, creation, Duns Scotus, St. Ambrose, external worship, internal prayer</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s analysis of the Third Commandment (Sanctify the Sabbath). Having previously debated whether the commandment is purely ceremonial or moral, Soto now examines a specific theological opinion: whether the "rest" commanded on holy days applies primarily to the soul’s rest from sin, and whether sinning on a feast day constitutes a "double sin."</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law, #

...everyone ought to search within themselves, gathering their thoughts and ascending to their God. From this, it follows that everyone is then bound to feel <term>contrition</term> <note>Sincere sorrow for sins</note> so that they may also maintain the manner of charity. It follows immediately, according to this opinion, that under the name of "servile work" from which one must rest, we should not only understand mechanical works and other such things by which one human serves another, but most especially the sins by which a human becomes a slave to the devil. For "he who commits sin is a slave to sin" <note>John 8:34</note>. This was the opinion of <term>Hesychius</term> <note>A 5th-century theologian from Jerusalem</note> which we challenged in the previous article—that this precept only has a spiritual meaning regarding the cessation from sin. These thinkers, while not believing it *only* means that, nevertheless believe that to be its primary meaning. Therefore, he who sins on a feast day, in addition to the guilt he would contract on any other ordinary day, sins again by contaminating the feast. Thus, he is stained by a double mark of sin, and consequently is bound to confess both, just like one who commits a murder in a church, or one who violates a nun <note>Because the sacredness of the location or the person adds a second layer of sacrilege to the crime</note>.

<margin>Alexander of Hales</margin>
This is the opinion of Alexander of Hales in the third part, question 32, member 5, article 2, where he expressly says in his answer to the fourth point that fornication on a feast day carries a double malice. And indeed, his students were taught this opinion by that distinguished doctor.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
Indeed, the same appears to be the opinion of Saint Thomas in this article, during his resolution of the third argument: where he distinguishes a threefold type of <term>servile work</term> <note>Activities traditionally forbidden on the Sabbath</note>: namely, that by which a human serves sin, that by which they serve another human according to the body, and that by which they serve God. He adds that servile works in the first and second ways are contrary to the observance of the Sabbath, insofar as they hinder a person's application to divine things. And he concludes that because a person is more hindered from divine things by the work of sin than by a bodily work that is otherwise lawful, he who sins on a feast day acts more against this precept than he who performs another lawful bodily work.

Furthermore, <margin>Ambrose</margin> Ambrose clearly seems to support this opinion in the place cited in the first argument regarding Luke. <margin>Augustine</margin> And Augustine in his book *On the Ten Strings* <note>original: "de decem chordis," a treatise on the Ten Commandments</note>: where he says, "A Jew would do better to do something useful in his field than to be a rioter in the theater. And their women would do better to spin wool on the Sabbath day than to dance immodestly all day during their new moon festivals." And, pressing the matter more vehemently, he adds: "But to you," that is, the Christian, "it is said that you should observe the Sabbath spiritually in the hope of future rest which the Lord promises you: however, this hope does not exist except through internal love."

<column-break/>

<margin>First reason</margin>
And certainly, reason seems to favor this same opinion quite strongly. First, since it is an affirmative command (as has been said) pertaining to service, and since the service most pleasing to God is that which is performed within the mind, it seems to bind us most especially to this. <margin>Second reason</margin> Add to this that since, by divine law, it commands some "sanctification" (as the name implies), it is necessary to define that sanctification even apart from the Church’s regulations; yet no other sanctification can be more fittingly defined than divine love, through which the righteous person is made holy.

<margin>Solution to the previous doubt</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, notwithstanding these points, the legitimate response to this doubt is that the force of this precept extends not to internal love or contrition, but to external worship, as we established in the second conclusion (which is that of St. Thomas). <margin>The aforementioned assertion is proved</margin> It is proved thus: All the other precepts of the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, except the eighth and ninth in which the name of "concupiscence" <note>Strong desire or lust</note> is expressed, command and prohibit only external works; therefore, this one does as well. For there is no reason why you should exempt this from the general rule, since no mention is made here of internal movement.

<margin>Another reason for the same assertion</margin>
¶ Secondly, this is clearly shown by the Church’s institution, by which the worship commanded in this precept is determined: which is to hear Mass, as is clear from the decree on consecration, distinction 1, the canon "Masses." This precept indeed took its origin from tradition and the Canon of the Apostles, as is clear in the same place, the canon "All the faithful." Therefore, since the Church expressed the worship included in this precept by its own statute—just as it determined the time for the divine precept of confession to be once a year—and since this precept of hers binds us only to external worship, it is obvious that no other content exists there by divine law. Otherwise, unless the Church explained it, she would not have been a faithful interpreter of divine law. I would say: "to external worship only," yet in such a way that I do not exclude that internal act from which the external one proceeds—namely, the will to hear Mass with becoming reverence and attention, so that it becomes a human act. However, it does not compel us to any other love or contrition. <margin>Confirmation</margin> And this reason is confirmed because, as the most accepted usage of the Church holds, besides the cessation from servile work, there is no worship commanded on feast days except that which the Church expresses. Therefore, it is rash to add another obligation on top.

<margin>Argument 3</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued: The commandment to love God, as was said above, is not included within the Decalogue, but is fixed outside at the front as the end <note>The ultimate goal or purpose</note> of all the commandments. Therefore, the precepts of the Decalogue are entirely distinct from the commandment of love.

¶ Fourthly...

<summary>Soto discusses whether the Sabbath command requires internal holiness and whether sinning on a holy day is a "double sin." He ultimately concludes that while internal devotion is good, the specific legal requirement of the commandment focuses on external acts of worship like attending Mass.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the Third Commandment. Having previously discussed whether "rest" refers to physical or spiritual states, he now presents several formal arguments against the idea that sinning on a feast day constitutes a special, additional sin (sacrilege) or that the commandment strictly requires an internal state of grace.</meta>

### Book Two, Question IV ###

<margin>Argument 4</margin> ¶ Fourth, it is argued: The goal of a command, as shown above, does not fall under the command itself. This is because commands are only given concerning the means to an end. For example, the command to fast does not bind a person to the mortification of the flesh <note>The physical "wearing down" of the body</note> specifically, but rather to the manner of abstinence prescribed by the Church, even though that mortification is the ultimate goal. Since, therefore, the goal of the commandments of the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments</note> is divine love, it follows that this love is not strictly required by any single one of those specific commands.

<margin>Argument 5</margin> ¶ Fifth, the same conclusion is confirmed: these types of commands do not bind us to the "mode of charity" <note>The internal state of being in God's grace while performing an act</note>. Rather, regarding the "substance of the work" <note>The external physical act required by the law</note>, they can be fulfilled even without charity in order to avoid sin. Therefore, it is without reason—indeed, it is contrary to reason—to single out this one commandment and claim it cannot be observed without the mode of charity. Yet, the opposing opinion contends exactly that, asserting that on a feast day, a person is bound to dispose themselves toward grace.

<margin>Argument 6</margin> ¶ Sixth, it is argued that this commandment does not bind one to <term>contrition</term> <note>Sincere, heart-felt sorrow for sin</note>. It is beyond controversy a mandate of "religion" <note>The specific virtue of giving God His due worship</note>. Contrition, however, is not an act of religion, but of "penance," which is a distinct virtue annexed to justice.

<margin>Argument 7</margin> ¶ Seventh, a truly massive argument occurs to me against this opposing opinion: if this commandment bound us to contrition and to the true love of God, how dangerously burdensome it would be for the Church to multiply feast days! This would be to ensnare the souls of Christians and cast them into the narrowest of straits, namely, that they would so frequently be bound to such a difficult task.

<margin>Argument 8</margin> ¶ Eighth, it is argued that this commandment does not bind one to "not sinning" on a feast day as an obligation added to the other mandates. All moral precepts are to be understood not in a spiritual or metaphorical sense, but according to the plain letter of the text, as is most widely confessed. The style of establishing morals should not be figurative, but plain. Sins are not called "servile works" in the literal sense, but through a metaphor. Therefore, when we are commanded to cease from "servile work," we are only restrained from those works which the common people call servile—namely, those by which men serve other men.

<margin>Confirmation</margin> This is confirmed by the fact that, regarding divine law, the substance of this commandment is the same for us now as it once was for the Hebrews. They were bound to no interior act, but only to those external rituals. Therefore, neither are we bound to anything except our own external rituals.

<margin>Evasion</margin> ¶ But you might say: "Because a feast day is sacred time, it is contaminated by any sin whatsoever, just like a sacred place." Against this, however,

<column-break/>

there is a manifest argument: <term>sacrilege</term> <note>The violation of something sacred</note> is not committed except either against a person by reason of a vow (for instance, if a monk or a priest commits fornication), or by reason of an Ecclesiastical statute (for instance, if blood or seed is shed in a sacred place). Regarding *time*, however, no such law exists. Furthermore, even a sacred place is not contaminated by *every* sin, but only in those two ways mentioned. For even if you blaspheme or commit perjury in a church, you do not technically commit sacrilege <note>In the strict legal sense used by theologians here</note>. Why then would you do so if you committed it on a feast day? Let us conclude, therefore, that a sin committed on a feast day is not sacrilege, and thus confessing the "circumstance of the feast" is not strictly necessary—though it may accidentally aggravate the sin, and it is therefore advisable to confess it. Nor does such a precept bind one to any interior act other than that which is necessary for the exterior one: namely, truly hearing Mass with enough attention for it to be a human act. Nevertheless, since internal love and meditation on divine things are the *goal* of this commandment, Christians should be greatly encouraged and enticed toward these things on feast days, and warned to beware of sins.

¶ There are some here who, for the sake of clarity (as they see it), distinguish two goals of this precept: one is the "immediate" goal, which is hearing Mass (to which we are bound); the other is the "mediate" goal, which is the elevation of the mind through charity (to which we are not bound). For my part, although the dispute seems to be over words, I would not call the former a "goal," but rather the "substance" of the precept. For the precept has two members: one negative, which is to cease from servile work; the other affirmative, which is the worship prescribed by the Church. And this second part is the goal, not so much of the commandment itself, but of its first member.

¶ Therefore, <margin>St. Thomas</margin> in response to the authority of St. Thomas: when he says that sins oppose the observance of the Sabbath, he does not mean regarding the substance of the precept, but regarding its goal. For this precept refers to being "vacant" for God <note>Free from other business to focus on the divine</note> and for divine things; sin opposes this goal more sharply than servile work does. For this reason, it is worse to commit fornication on a feast day than to dig <note>original: "peius est fornicari in die festo quàm cauare"</note>. This is not because the feast is violated by the fornication, but because the sin is worse in itself and more repugnant to God's intention. This is exactly what Augustine says. Furthermore, when he adds in the same place that the Sabbath must be observed "spiritually" by Christians, he does not say this as if that were the substance of the precept (such that he who does not observe it thus would be a transgressor), but rather that such a manner is required if it is to be kept according to the intention of the one...

<summary>Soto argues that the Third Commandment strictly requires external observance (refraining from labor and attending Mass) rather than an internal state of grace. He contends that sinning on a feast day is morally wrong but does not constitute the specific additional sin of sacrilege.</summary>

...wisdom so that it may be preserved in the hope of future rest, which the Lord promises us. And that this is the meaning is manifestly clear: because he compares the Christian there with the Jew, saying that the Jew kept it as a figure <note>original: *in figura*; meaning as a symbolic foreshadowing</note>, but we ought to keep it in spirit. Nevertheless, as for the substance of the precept, they were bound in the same way as we are; therefore, it follows that the spiritual sense is not part of the substance of the precept. Regarding the words of Ambrose, the response will be clear in its place, where the mind of St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> will also become clearer. The first reason we submitted to the contrary opinion only proves that internal service through charity <note>Divine love</note> is the goal of the commandment; however, it does not follow from this that it falls strictly under the legal requirement of the commandment itself. To the latter argument, it is denied that any other worship is contained under this commandment than that which the Church has determined.

<margin>The third commandment of the Decalogue is partly moral, partly ceremonial.</margin>
¶ Regarding the third conclusion, it must only be noted that this commandment is partly moral and partly ceremonial. It was already said above that a moral precept is derived as a conclusion from <term>natural law</term> <note>Universal moral principles discoverable by reason</note>. Since all mortals are bound by that same law to worship God, it follows that they must cut away some time from other business and dedicate it to that same duty. For according to the Wise Man, for every thing, by natural law, its own time is owed: as for refreshment, sleep, and other duties. Come now, consider the sweetness and gentleness of God’s commandments. Even if no law of worshiping God had proclaimed a rest for certain days, the very reason of nature—which assigned light for labor and darkness for rest—would demand that we take holidays for some days, in which we might recreate our souls by interrupting our labors. To what business, then, could we better have devoted those days than to worshiping our God? And therefore, regarding this, there can be no <term>dispensation</term> <note>A legal exemption from a rule</note> from the Church. I say the Church—which established feast days by <term>positive law</term> <note>Laws created by human or ecclesiastical authority rather than nature</note>—can, as we said above, either remove or change them all; at least the act would hold legally, even if the Holy Spirit did not permit it because it would be destructive. However, no dispensation can ever be made so that a man is not bound to spend some time—whether days or hours—deputed for divine worship. But that these specific days or others become feast days is "ceremonial": over which the Church subsequently has authority. Every ceremony, moreover, is a figure, either commemorative or prefigurative. Therefore, this commandment signified in the <term>literal sense</term> the benefit of creation, as a memorial of it. But in the <term>allegorical sense</term> it pre-

<column-break/>

signified the rest of Christ in the tomb: which day was also the Sabbath, as if He then rested from the work of redemption. But also in the <term>tropological sense</term> <note>The moral interpretation of scripture</note>—which pertains to behavior through metaphor—it signifies the cessation from the works of sin. Wherefore, according to that sense, it was not a special commandment, but it referred to the general reason for all things by which we are barred from this slavery of sin. And finally, in the <term>anagogical sense</term> <note>The interpretation dealing with the afterlife and eternity</note>, it signified the everlasting rest that awaits us in heaven. It is therefore established in the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments</note> according to the literal and moral sense. Hence, because of this many-sided significance of the Sabbath, although there were many other solemnities of feasts in the law, mention was made of this one alone in the Decalogue, by which the rest are included. For each of the others was instituted for a particular benefit, but that of creation was universal. Regarding the feasts of that law, and how our individual feasts respond to each of theirs, we shall see in the next question.

<margin>The reason for the abolition of the Sabbath and its change into the Lord's Day.</margin>
¶ And yet through these things, the reason is clear why it was changed by the Catholic Church, from the age of the Apostles until now, into the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>. For that literal reason of commemorating the benefit of creation was changed into a higher one: the benefit of "re-creation" <note>original: *recreationis*; referring to the restoration of humanity through Christ</note>, which was accomplished by Christ through grace. For He completed this benefit by rising on the Lord’s Day, which was the first light in the state of grace—infinitely more excellent than that of which God then said, "Let there be light." 
<margin>Another reason</margin>
Besides the fact that even that first day of the world's creation was the Lord's Day, since the seventh was the Sabbath. The allegorical figure of Christ resting in the tomb ceased with the arrival of the truth. But the anagogical sense of perpetual heavenly rest fits the Lord's Day much more aptly. For the volatility of this world is signified by the cycle of the week, but the eternity of immutable happiness is more significantly expressed by the Lord's Day.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the first argument, therefore, which proceeded from the authority of Ambrose, it is answered that that Father, a lover of mystical senses, objected that kind of understanding to the Jews because they did not permit works of mercy to be done on the Sabbath. And therefore, when he said that the works of sin are prohibited by that commandment, he did not mean it in the literal sense—in which the substance of the special precept is placed—but in the tropological sense, which is the general virtue of all commandments. <margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second [it is] respon-

He also details the four levels of scriptural interpretation—literal, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—as they apply to the Sabbath.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 144 regarding the nature of the Third Commandment. Soto is now moving from the theoretical definition of the Sabbath to practical applications: specifically, what constitutes "servile work" and what activities are permitted for Christians on Sundays and feast days compared to the stricter requirements of the Old Testament Jewish law.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<columns>2</columns>
<header>Book Two, Question IIII.</header>
<page-num>145</page-num>

It is granted that the observation of the Sabbath among the Jews was symbolic; and for that reason, they observed it with a stricter religious discipline, to the point that they could not even prepare food with fire, as is clear from Exodus 16 and 35. This was surely so that they might express to the life <note>original: *ad vivum*; meaning "vividly" or "exactly"</note> that cessation of God from the making of the world. For a figure, since it is a sign of a thing, ought to reflect the truth most faithfully even down to the smallest details. We, however, do not keep holidays because of that symbolic ritual, but by the institution of the Church, both for the Lord’s days <note>Sundays</note> and other feast days. Therefore, we observe such feasts more in keeping with <term>natural law</term> <note>Moral principles considered inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</note>: namely, so that we may also prepare what is necessary for food in a natural manner. And it is more easily dispensed for us regarding other things that serve the necessity of nature.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ In the third argument, therefore, a most vast field is opened regarding those things which are both lawfully permitted to us on feast days and granted by dispensation. For they are so many that they can hardly be grasped by number; therefore, only their main headings can be held in memory. And first, since in this precept there is something negative, as has been said—that is, to cease from <term>servile work</term> <note>Manual labor traditionally performed by servants or slaves, forbidden on holy days</note>—and another part affirmative, which is to hear the sacred [office]. Concerning both, those things must be weighed by which the precept is violated without injury. Wherefore, first of all, that distinction of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> touched upon above must be presupposed.

<margin>A distinction.</margin>
Namely, that of servile works, some are sins, by which the devil is served. And these are forbidden throughout all the commandments, but are signified here in this singular moral metaphorical sense. Others, however, are those by which a man serves another man according to the body, such as the mechanical arts. And these are forbidden by this precept according to the letter. But there are others besides, by which we serve God, namely those which pertain to His worship. And these are so far from being rejected by this precept that they are greatly conducive to its end. For in this, we abstain from other servile works so that we may serve God.

<margin>Six headings from which you may distinguish what is permitted on feast days.</margin>
¶ There are therefore six headings through which we can judge those things which are permitted on the Sabbath. The first is what we have just said: namely, if it pertains to the worship of God. Among these, however, there are degrees.

<margin>The first.</margin>
Spiritual things hold the first place, which are given to us supernaturally by the uncreated Spirit, such as the administration of the sacraments, by which grace is conferred, in which the spiritual life consists. For this reason, even the ancients administered circumcision on the Sabbath if the eighth day fell then. Whence Christ says in John 7: *A man receives circumcision on the Sabbath, so that the law of Moses may not be broken.* <note>original: "Circuncisionem homo accipit in Sabbatho, vt nō soluatur lex Moysi."</note> And we also 

<column-break/>

administer all the sacraments. And furthermore, we perform those things which pertain to the ministry of the altar: namely, we preach, we pray, and we read those things which contribute to meditation and the reflection of the soul. In the second degree are those bodily things in which worship itself also consists: such as, for the ancients, carrying the Ark of the Covenant, and for us, carrying the statues of saints, the cross, and similar things in processions. To these are added playing the organ and other instruments; concerning which works it is understood in Matthew 12: *The priests in the temple violate the Sabbath* <note>original: "Sacerdotes in templo Sabbathum violāt"</note>—that is, they perform bodily labors—*and are without guilt.* In the third degree are placed those things which are preparatory to sacred rites. But these are threefold. For some are so close to worship that it cannot happen without them: as anciently the priests slaughtered and roasted the animals which were offered to God, and now the bells are rung. Others, however, are things that could be done on the preceding day; and these should not be done on a feast day without cause, but prepared beforehand: such as cooking hosts <note>The bread used for the Eucharist</note> and constructing the apparatus for monuments—unless perhaps a continuation of feasts requires that they be made on the feast day itself. Yet there are others, not indeed through themselves, but accidentally looking toward divine worship, such as cultivating the fields of a poor Church or hospital, or transporting stones for its construction. And these ought not to be done on a feast day without necessity, nor without the permission of the Prelate <note>A high-ranking cleric such as a Bishop</note>; since they are truly servile works, therefore, although the law of mercy is a cause for dispensing, they nevertheless ought not to be done without the bishop's dispensation, or at least the Parish priest's, where custom so holds.

<margin>The second kind of works which are permitted on a feast day.</margin>
¶ The second kind of works which are permitted on a feast day consists of spiritual actions which proceed from our spirit: such as teaching, counseling, and other things of that kind. For a "servile work" is the same as a "bodily work." For it is the body which serves the soul; wherefore those things which pertain to the soul are not counted among servile works. Nevertheless, it is not inferred from this that the exercise of the mechanical arts is permitted on a feast day, even if those arts are also intellectual. For the nature of spiritual things must be weighed not only by their origin, but also by their end. Therefore, sciences whose end is to enlighten the intellect are spiritual; but those whose end is placed in a manufactured work which is completed by hands, and for that reason are called mechanical, are held to be servile. But indeed, there are some spiritual things which the Church, for good cause, has forbidden on feast days, such as administering the law, arguing court cases, and solemnly swearing an oath in judgment unless for the sake of peace, as is clear in the extra-decretals, concerning holidays, chapter...

He categorizes permissible acts into those serving God (sacraments, processions, preparation for rites) and spiritual actions of the mind (teaching), while maintaining that purely manual "servile" labor remains prohibited.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Vitoria’s student and successor Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the Third Commandment ("Remember the Sabbath day"). He is detailing specific exceptions where the prohibition against work on holy days does not apply, moving from judicial actions to the distinction between "servile" and "liberal" arts.</meta>

<page-num>146</page-num>
<header>F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,</header>

the chapters *Every day* <note>original: *omnes dies*</note> and *The complaint* <note>original: *conquestus*</note> in Canon Law. Nevertheless, these rules also admit a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A formal exemption from a church law</note> in the face of an imminent, atrocious, and extraordinary crime. For example, if a public thief or one guilty of <term>treason</term> <note>original: *maiestatis laesor*; literally "one who harms majesty"</note> were captured on a feast day, it would be permitted to haul him immediately to punishment. And for the sake of religion, heretics are usually moved to the fire on a solemn feast.

<margin>The third category.</margin>
¶ The third category and heading of such permitted works is that which, although they are physical, are not strictly "servile." For among physical acts, some are servile by their nature, an example of which is found in the <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>Manual labors like carpentry or smithing, traditionally performed by servants or laborers</note>. Others, however, are by their nature "free," such as the works of the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>Subjects like music, logic, and geometry, considered "free" (Latin: *liber*) because they were studied for their own sake</note>. This includes music and drawing geometric figures on a tablet <note>original: *abaco*</note>; it is certain that these are permitted on feast days. However, some things are common to both free people and servants, about which there is doubt whether they are permitted: such as writing, traveling, hunting, and so on. Indeed, if writing is reduced only to that which is speaking with those who are absent—such as writing letters, or orations to be delivered to the people, or lectures to be read—it is clear that it is permitted. But if it leans toward servile work, such as transcribing for a fixed wage or earning a living with the pen in another way, that is not at all lawful. Regarding traveling after hearing Mass, the custom of certain provinces permits it, especially for those who are already on a journey. But to go hunting for the sake of recreation is clearly not a servile work.

<margin>The fourth cause.</margin>
¶ The fourth cause for which it is not a sin to work on a feast day is added: necessity. First, regarding those things that pertain to daily sustenance—that is, seasoning and preparing food with fire. This includes the work of cooks, those who stuff pastries, and butchers and meat-sellers. Bakers and oven-keepers, however, are not excused, as bread can be made the day before the feast—unless there were such a cluster of feast days that it required it. Second, by the necessity of bodily health, doctors, pharmacists, and bloodletters are excused. This also includes those who flee personal danger, following the example of Elijah who fled on the Sabbath from the face of Jezebel. Whence Christ says in John 7: "Are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the Sabbath?" Yet pharmacists are not excused except according to the necessity of the current day. For it is a servile art which only necessity makes lawful on a feast day. Third, the necessity of the common safety of the commonwealth excuses soldiers in war, those who build ramparts and walls there, and those who endure any other labors. For this reason, as read in 1 Maccabees 2, the Maccabees wisely decreed to repel hostile battle on the Sabbaths. Furthermore, because of particular necessities, works are permitted on a feast day. Whence Deuteronomy 22 says: "You shall not see your brother's sheep

<column-break/>

or ox wandering and pass by, but you shall lead them back to your brother." Christ alluded to this in Matthew 12: "Which of you will there be, who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will he not take hold and lift it out?" And by this we are excused while we combat conflagrations and floods. Indeed, in harvest time, if the breeze is blowing, grain may be justly winnowed. Moreover, where inclement weather is feared, the threshing floors may be worked; and even—though this should not be so easily permitted—the crops may be reaped. Although in these cases, where it is doubted whether the necessity is urgent, it is more advisable to go to the Bishop or at least the parish priest, through whom these things may be permitted. And under this heading are also excused those who perform duties necessary for the commonwealth which cannot be interrupted on all feast days without heavy loss. Such duties are performed by sailors, couriers, mule-drivers, and those who serve them, such as farriers <note>original: *mareschalci veterinarii*</note> who shoe beasts with iron shoes, and those who light the furnaces for smelting glass. There are those who grant the same faculty to those who bake bricks and lime, but in these I do not see as much necessity. Add that for the sake of the <term>ornament of the commonwealth</term> <note>The honor or public display of the state</note>, it is permitted for craftsmen to work on feast days, such as for tournaments. Nevertheless, it is always healthier to procure a dispensation. Just as necessity makes one immune from the transgression of the common law, so it does for a particular law. For it is permitted for lawyers to inform judges on a feast day, and in the case of pressing necessity, even for scribes to perform certain acts.

<margin>The fifth cause.</margin>
¶ The fifth cause that exempts workers from the transgression of the feast day is the concession of the Church. For Pope Alexander III indulges in the chapter *it is permitted* <note>original: *licèt*</note> concerning holidays, that fishermen may catch herring on feast days. And the same applies to tuna and other fish that are caught only at one time of the year, and that a short one.

¶ Finally, the sixth heading of excuse is custom. In the said chapter *Every day* concerning holidays, it is forbidden to hold markets on a feast day. But now it is a very frequent custom for fairs <note>original: *nundinas*</note> to be celebrated on a feast day. Customs, however, then free one from fault when they are consistent with reason, introduced by the consent of the prelates, and received through antiquity.

<margin>For what reasons one may, without sin, not attend the sacred rites on a feast day.</margin>
¶ Behold the negative part of this precept, which is to cease from servile work. The affirmative part, however, which is to hear the Mass <note>original: *sacrum*</note>, must be observed more reverently and not omitted for any cause unless it be very urgent: such as if there be a cause of fleeing the danger of death, or of serving the sick who cannot be left alone without danger, or if the abduction of a girl were feared, and similar things. Although in this too, custom can prevail. For where it is the custom for marriageable girls not to go out in public, they contract no fault by not proceeding to the church.

It also notes that local customs and Church concessions (such as for seasonal fishing) can justify activities normally forbidden on the Sabbath.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s discussion of the Third Commandment, specifically addressing whether receiving payment for work on a feast day changes its legal status from "permitted" to "forbidden." It then transitions into Question 5 regarding the Fourth Commandment (Honoring Parents).</meta>

<page-num>147</page-num>
<header>Second Book, Question IV.</header>

Indeed, if a mother fears for her daughter’s safety in any way, she may remain at home as her guardian. Furthermore, if a husband, burning with jealousy, restrains his wife from going out to a sacred service, she is bound to obey him. Likewise, servants and household attendants must obey when their master commands a journey or some other business, even if they do not hear the sacred rites <note>original: *sacrum non audiant*; referring to attending Mass</note>. However, the guilt will be shifted onto the master himself if he hinders the servant from hearing Mass without a just cause.
<margin>The scruples of some.</margin>
¶ Now, that which currently offers some people an occasion for hesitation is whether all those things said to be permitted on a feast day become illicit simply because they are performed for a wage <note>original: *mercede*</note>. For you will find some captured by the opinion that those who work on a feast day with the primary intention of receiving payment are transgressors of the day; but if they perform their duty chiefly because of necessity, they may receive a supplementary stipend. Indeed, others judge that a wealthy person is bound to perform works of mercy on a feast day for free.
<margin>The reason for doubting.</margin>
The "scruple" <note>A small doubt or hesitation</note> of these men has this foundation, if it has any at all: that "servile work" is that which is done in service to another. He who works for a wage serves another like a servant; therefore, that work becomes servile. For when necessity is the reason why works are permitted on a feast day, it is because those works are then common to both free people and servants. If, therefore, they are made servile by a contracted wage, they would subsequently become illicit.
<margin>The Solution. Cajetan.</margin>
¶ But in truth, without any scruple—as <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note> also acknowledged in the present article—any work that is permitted on a feast day, whether because of necessity, custom, or any of the causes we have just reviewed, remains equally just, even if it is done solely for the sake of payment. For the hope of profit does not make a work "servile." Indeed, the works of free men—such as commerce, music, hunting, military service, and the like—all have a proposed reward for themselves. Conversely, servile work is often performed for free, such as <term>mechanical work</term> <note>Manual labor or crafts</note>. Nor does the act of serving another constitute "servile work." For the works of free men are also usually done in service to another. And conversely, servile works can be done in service to the craftsman himself.
<margin>The first reason.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is argued: household servants receive stipends for their service even when performed on a feast day. Indeed, musicians especially serve on feast days and in churches for a wage.
<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ After this, it is argued: although works on a feast day may be necessary,

<column-break/>

nevertheless, craftsmen and artisans are not bound to provide them for free. This is because they are not "necessary" due to the poverty of the persons involved, but from the nature of the situation, as is clear in the previous examples. Therefore, they can licitly perform them solely for a wage, as they would not do them otherwise. And they may likewise bargain for the price. Therefore, by no means should we judge what is a "servile work" and what is not based on a wage or reward, but rather by the primary categories mentioned a little earlier. Thus, if teaching a science is permitted in itself on a feast day, it will also be permitted to demand a fee for the labor. The same applies to an advocate if he provides legal counsel on a feast day. Judge the same for physicians and other attendants of the sick.
¶ From this it follows that studying on a feast day for the sake of profit is not illicit. For otherwise, even students would violate the law if they devoted themselves to letters on a feast day, for most do so in the hope of gain. And it makes no difference whether you expect the profit after a long time or receive it in the present. Nor does it matter whether the teacher or advocate is rich or poor. Nevertheless, the advice given to the wealthy is to dedicate feast days either to divine matters or to the causes of the poor out of generosity.

***

->Whether the fourth commandment regarding honoring parents is appropriately delivered.<-

THE preceding questions have delayed us for quite a long time. This one regarding the fourth commandment, however, is very easy to dispatch.
<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
It is nevertheless argued, according to custom, that it was not appropriately placed. So far as this commandment pertains to <term>piety</term> <note>In the Roman and Scholastic sense, *pietas* refers to duty and devotion to parents, family, and country</note>—which is a part of justice—it is not a direct species of justice, but a "potential" part. There are many other similar parts of justice,
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
as you find in Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, Second Part of the Second Part (2.2), Question 80</note>, such as observance, gratitude, truth, etc. Therefore, not only this affirmative commandment should have been placed here, but others for similar virtues as well.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, not only honor is owed to parents, but also sustenance. Therefore, it was also deficient in this regard, as it expressed only honor.
<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, neither was the cause subjoined to it...

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
One very brief conclusion is sufficient for the question. Most appropriately, the fourth commandment regarding the honoring of parents is placed immediately after the three commandments concerning the love of God. 

<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proven thus: The commandments of the first table <note>The "Tables of the Law" refer to the two divisions of the Ten Commandments: those regarding God and those regarding man.</note> commend the love of God, as has been said, and the commandments of the second table commend the love of neighbor. Among neighbors, parents are the most "neighborly" <note>The Latin *proximi* means both "neighbors" and "those closest to us."</note>, for we owe what we are to them, second only to God. For they are the *particular* source of our existence, just as God is the *universal* source of all things. Therefore, the place due to this commandment is next to the place for loving God. Indeed, the <term>piety</term> <note>original: *pietas*; in a Roman and Scholastic sense, this refers to the dutiful respect and love owed to God, parents, and homeland.</note> owed to parents is so closely related to that which is owed to God that Aristotle, in the 8th book of the *Ethics*,

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
aptly said that no one can ever repay an equal amount to the Gods and to one's parents. And Cicero, in his

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
*Speech After His Return*, says: "We ought to hold our parents most dear, because from them life, patrimony, liberty, and citizenship have been handed down to us. But above all, we must cherish God, by whose benefit we hold all these things."

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the matter of the first argument, one must notice what we explained more clearly at the start of the eighth book: namely, that some parts of justice are "specific," such as <term>distributive</term> and <term>commutative</term> justice <note>Distributive justice concerns how a community shares goods; commutative justice concerns fair exchange between individuals.</note>, while others are "potential" parts—that is, annexed to it. These potential parts do not have the full, perfect nature of justice and are not directly governed by it, yet they are categorized under it because of something they share in common. For the nature of justice is to be "toward another" to whom an equal debt is repaid. Thus, religion aligns with justice because it is "toward another"—namely, toward God—to whom, however, we cannot return an equal amount. In this, it falls short of perfect justice. The commandments of the first table belong to religion, which is a virtue annexed to justice. By the same logic, piety toward parents—to whom we cannot return an equal amount—is a potential part of justice. Similarly, <term>observance</term>—which is the reverence shown to men because of their virtue—is also included. For no equal 

<column-break/>

reward can be returned by men to virtue, as Aristotle notes in the 2nd book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, this virtue is categorized under the fourth commandment, just as we noted above regarding that phrase in Leviticus 19: "Rise up before the gray head" <note>A command to respect the elderly.</note>. <term>Liberality</term> <note>Generosity</note>, however, "limps on a different foot" <note>A metaphorical way of saying it fails to meet the criteria for justice in a different way.</note> to avoid being strictly justice: specifically, it is concerned with bestowing benefits that are not strictly owed; likewise <term>grace</term> <note>gratitude</note>, which repays benefits not by the logic of a legal debt, but by the logic of moral honesty. All these virtues are therefore reduced to this commandment. For it was already stated in the previous question that the Decalogue should precisely contain those things that reason could draw from natural principles without the help of wise men (unless one's reason were clouded). However, these matters require some support from the wise to be fully understood. Furthermore, the debt children owe to parents is common to all mortals, while other debts are specialized; and specialized debts serve under the general ones.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The response to the second argument is much the same: the reason why we are debtors to our homeland, our blood relations, and our other kin is because of our parents, who fathered us in such a place and such a lineage. Therefore, since the commandments of the Decalogue are the first principles of the Law, "parents" are named as a sufficient stand-in for all such relations.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The solution to the third argument follows the same path: namely, that honor is owed to parents by all children in and of itself, whether the parents are wealthy or poor. Financial support <note>original: *sustentatio*</note>, however, happens to be owed only when the parents are in need. Those things that occur by chance are categorized under those things that are essential.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, in response to the fourth argument: it was most fitting, as we explained in the previous question, that the reward of a long life was proposed for this mandate, and for the transgressor, the punishment of a short one. Hence Paul says in 1 Timothy 4: "Piety is useful for all things, having the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come." Since we received life from our parents under God, he who is grateful to them deserves not only to possess eternal life, but also to have his temporal life increased; but he who is ungrateful deserves to be deprived of it. For this reason, Solon—as Cicero relates in *Pro Sexto Amerino*—established no punishment for <term>parricide</term> <note>The murder of a parent.</note>. When asked why, he replied that he thought no one would ever do such a thing. ### ARTICLE VI.

*Whether the six remaining commandments are handed down in an appropriate order and manner.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a scholar or saintly figure seated in a landscape with a tree.</image-desc>
<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
Enough has been said above concerning the remaining six commandments: but lest we exclude them from the order, it is argued that they have not been sufficiently handed down. First, thus: There are other wrongs besides murder, adultery, theft, and false witness that are inflicted upon citizens: therefore, the number was incomplete.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
<margin>movement.</margin>
Second: <term>Concupiscence</term> <note>original: *concupiscentia*; in this context, it refers to disordered desire or "coveting."</note> in the ninth and tenth commandments is either understood as the movement of sensuality—according to that saying of James 4: "Where do wars and quarrels among you come from? Do they not come from your concupiscences, which war in your members?"—or it is understood as the consent of the will, where the nature of sin is perfected, and likewise the nature of virtue and merit, according to that saying of Wisdom 6: "The desire for wisdom leads to an everlasting kingdom." But the former movement could not be forbidden, because it is natural for a corrupted nature to fight against reason; according to the words of Paul: "I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind" <note>Romans 7:23</note>. Otherwise, the stirrings of sensuality would be mortal sins, which is false. Regarding the second (consent of the will), it is already forbidden by each individual commandment. For he who forbids murder simultaneously forbids the will to murder: therefore, there was no need for a peculiar mandate.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Third and finally: Murder excels adultery and theft in gravity: yet its desire was not separately forbidden. Therefore, there was no

<column-break/>

reason why the concupiscence of others should be separately inhibited. ¶ On the opposite side stands the authority of the Law itself.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
After those things explained above, the response to the question is very easy, and is contained in a single conclusion. The six commandments were set down with a proper rationale in the tenor of their prohibition.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proven thus. There are two parts of justice: to do good, and to turn away from evil. Now, the first (doing good) is not owed to all people indiscriminately in itself, but to certain persons: and the one to whom it is chiefly owed is God, and after Him, parents. However, to not harm others by injuries or violence is owed to everyone. For this reason, after the first table and the fourth commandment—in which those things owed to God and parents are prescribed—the harms regarding all people in general are most excellently forbidden. Regarding the distinction, number, order, and tradition of these, and the gravity of each, it has been discussed more than enough in the previous question.

<margin>Scruple.</margin>
But if you still hesitate regarding the number, because many things are owed to others besides parents and kinsmen—according to the word of Paul: "Render to all their dues: to whom tribute is due, tribute," etc. <note>Romans 13:7</note>—other affirmative commandments ought to have been added.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that since the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> contains only the first principles of the Law, it was not fitting that anything be handed down in it except those things which are owed to all mortals by common reason: and such is the honor we owe to parents. But regarding others, debts are contracted not by one reason, but by various reasons, and therefore there was no need for a special commandment for them: rather, general justice was sufficient, which commands that each be given his own right. ¶ And through this teaching, that which we noted in Question 3 against <term>Burgensis</term> <note>Paul of Burgos (c. 1351–1435), a Jewish convert to Christianity and influential biblical commentator.</note> on Leviticus 19 becomes clear. He, contrary to Saint Thomas—and indeed, contrary to the plain truth—denies that the commandment of love of neighbor is common and most well-known to all: specifically because friendship was not discovered by the philosophers in respect to everyone, but only in respect to the virtuous. For the mind of Saint Thomas and the truth of the matter is that since the commandment of love of neighbor includes both doing good and not doing evil, the former is most well-known—not indeed in respect to all neighbors, but in respect to a certain kind, namely parents—while the latter is known in respect to everyone. And therefore, from that same principle, only the fourth is elicited...

To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that since the harms and injuries by which one person harms another could not be collected into a certain fixed number, it was practical—and likewise fitting—to set down only the main headings, to which other related parts are connected. For whatever damage you inflict on another, you either strike at their person—and that category of things is reduced to homicide—or at a person joined to them by way of lust—and these are referred to adultery. Damage caused to property, however, whether through usury <note>The practice of lending money at interest, which was heavily regulated or forbidden in medieval law.</note> or through some other deception, all tend toward theft. Likewise, all injuries committed through words—such as lies, detractions, and verbal insults—fall under false testimony.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ To the second, it is replied that the name of "concupiscence" <term>concupiscence: an intense, often disordered desire or "inclination" toward something, usually sensual pleasure.</term> does not forbid the impulses and charms of the senses themselves, but rather the consent of the will, where sin resides, according to the word of Christ: *He who has looked at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.* And although in any one precept both the act and the desire for it are forbidden, a singular necessity nonetheless demanded that the desire for another's wife and another's goods be expressed specifically. This is for the reason we declared in the fifth article of the previous question: namely, because the objects of other sins do not, in themselves, entice one toward desire; rather, they are desired because of other emotions. For example, homicide is desired for the sake of vengeance, which is born of hatred and anger. Therefore, in those cases, it is enough that the acts themselves are forbidden. However, those things which pertain to the concupiscence of the flesh and of the eyes <note>A reference to 1 John 2:16, a common framework for understanding sin in the 16th century.</note> entice the soul by their very nature. Thus, there is not only a difficulty in abstaining from those acts, but also a new difficulty in restraining the desire; for that reason, besides the act itself, it was practical for the desires to be forbidden by specific prohibitions.

# QUESTION FIVE,

->On the ceremonial precepts.<-

->St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, question 101, articles 2 & 3.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether the ceremonial precepts were fourfold: namely, sacrifices, sacraments, sacred things, and observances.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure at a desk within a room, likely representing a scholar or the author himself.</image-desc>
ALTHOUGH OUR TASK has been to expand upon Saint Thomas [Aquinas] by explaining him, our approach will be different in these questions regarding ceremonial and judicial laws. For he himself explained everything so abundantly and eloquently that his teaching can neither be further extended nor further clarified. Therefore, to provide a brief summary, we first ask whether the ceremonies are divided by a fourfold partition: namely, into sacrifices, sacraments, sacred things, and observances.

<margin>First argument.</margin> And it is argued from the negative side: If they were distributed in this way, it would be primarily because the ceremonies pertained to divine worship, as the names "sacrifices" and "sacred things" themselves designate. However, there were some ceremonies that seemed to have nothing to do with the worship of God, such as the abstinence from certain foods that was commanded in <margin>Leviticus 11.</margin> Leviticus 11, and the abstinence from certain garments—specifically, that no one should wear a garment woven of two materials, that is, of wool and linen—as was <margin>Leviticus 19.</margin> cautioned in Leviticus 19. Therefore, not all ceremonies served the purpose of worship.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly, if those sacrifices, sacraments, and observances were suited for some use, it was primarily so that they might be figures <note>In theology, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament event or law that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of certain things, according to the word of <margin>Paul:</margin> Paul, *all things happened to them in figures.* However, that was by no means appropriate for a law; for as <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine argues in Book 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*, and as the previously cited Isidore of Seville claims, a law ought to be manifest and accessible to all. Since those things which are hidden in the mysteries of figures present a theatrical and enigmatic representation rather than the clarity of law, it was not fitting for them to be figurative.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Thirdly, the sincerity of law is a lover of simple precepts and an expeller of many. Indeed, a multitude of precepts is a burden and an occasion for ruin rather than a support for virtue, according to...

...according to that saying of Peter in Acts 15: "Why do you now try to place a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither we nor our fathers <margin>Argument 4</margin> could bear?" Therefore, that multitude of ceremonies should have been avoided. ¶ Fourth, those ceremonies were a shadow and a foretelling <note>original: "vmbra & prognoosticum"</note> of Christ. Sacrifices, moreover, abundantly prefigured Christ, who, according to the Apostle in Ephesians 5, offered himself as a sacrifice, an offering, and a victim. In the New Law, however, the sacrifice of the altar is at once both a sacrifice and a sacrament; it is the most significant of all, and is itself called "sacred." Since all sacrifices and sacraments are types of observances, there is no need for that fourfold distinction. Otherwise, even more members would have to be added, such as solemnities, offerings, and many things of that kind. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that the Law mentions all of these.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> To the question, a response is given in four conclusions, following the number of arguments. The first is: All those ceremonial matters pertained to the worship of God. For as we distinguished the three orders of precepts in Question 2, moral precepts are drawn from the principles of nature as conclusions. Ceremonial and judicial precepts, however, are not conclusions, but specific determinations <term>determinations: the specific "filling in" of a general natural law (e.g., nature says to worship God, but divine law "determines" that it should be done with a specific sacrifice).</term> of general precepts, which are established by a certain judgment. Ceremonial matters concern religion, which orders us toward God; judicial matters concern the peace and tranquility of citizens according to the love of one's neighbor. For it is a natural precept that God should be worshiped. However, that he be worshiped in this or that way is a matter of human or divine judgment. As <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle says in Book 5 of the *Ethics*: to offer sacrifice <note>original: "Litare"</note> with these or those animals matters nothing by its own nature, except because it has been established by law. <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion: It was fitting for that divine worship in the Old Law to have displayed a foretelling figure of Christ and his Gospel Law. <margin>Proof.</margin> This is proven. Just as a human being consists of both soul and body, so also worship is both interior and exterior, according to that Psalm: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God." And just as the body is related to the soul, so too is exterior worship related to the interior. The worship of the soul consists in being joined to its God; for this reason, it is fitting that the external worship be different according to the different ways of that union. Thus it happens that in the state of eternal happiness, where the soul possesses God as present according to its intellect and affection, there is no need

<column-break/>

for shadowy and figurative worship, but all things are perfected in praise, according to that saying of Isaiah 51: "Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise." But in the state of the present life, where we live as exiles absent from that sight, we find it necessary to be enlightened by the rays of that same divine truth under sensible figures, <margin>Dionysius.</margin> as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher who wrote "The Celestial Hierarchy."</note> teaches in Chapter 1 of *The Celestial Hierarchy*. Yet this happens in different ways according to the different states of the human condition. For us who live under the Gospel Law—because even if the truth itself does not shine forth directly, the way is already open and revealed through Christ—it is worthwhile to have no other figures than those of that eternal happiness which still awaits us in the future. However, for the ancient people, to whom not only the divine truth itself but even the "way" (which was the Christ to come, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 7) had not yet been made manifest, it was most fitting to be occupied in that exterior worship. This was not only to be a figure of the eternal truth to be contemplated in the fatherland <note>i.e., Heaven</note>, but also of Christ, who was to be the way, the truth, and the life. Specifically, through such long-lasting and celebrated use of these things, that people, being accustomed and reminded, might most readily receive the truth when it later arrived. Hence, <margin>Paul.</margin> Paul, in Hebrews 10, in order to suggest the difference between the Ancient Law and ours, says that the Law (the Old) had a "shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things"—namely, the kind of image that we have. For a shadow is further removed from the truth than an image, which expresses the truth more closely. <margin>Tertia conclusio.</margin> ¶ The third conclusion: It was also fitting that the people should be occupied not by just one ceremony, but by a manifold variety of them, and devoted to divine worship. The appropriateness of this is weighed both from the necessity of the wicked and from that of the righteous. For those who were prone to idolatry—since the superstitions of the idolaters were many-sided—needed to be instructed, by contrast, with a multitude of ceremonies, so that being occupied with them, they would not seek out those things they saw among the Pagans. But the good also, who were inclined toward the contemplation of divine things, were no less to be imbued with doubled ceremonies: both so that by that diligence they might persist in divine contemplation and be refreshed by the variety, and also so that they might repeatedly look forward to the manifold mysteries of Christ through a multi-layered worship of ceremonies. <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> ¶ The fourth conclusion: Although the ceremonies of the ancients were various and manifold, they are nevertheless reduced to four heads, which are sacrifi...

# Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>
The reason for the conclusion.
</margin>
...rites, sacraments, sacred things, and observances. For in the matter of worship, three things are to be considered. First, that in which the substance of worship is placed: namely, the sacrifice which is offered in reverence to God. Second, the instruments: such as the temple, the vessels, and other things of this sort. These are called **sacred things**, which are "anathemas" <note>original: "anathemata" — here used in the Greek sense of things set apart or dedicated to a deity, rather than a curse</note>: that is, things handed over and consecrated to divine worship. Third, the worshipers themselves, in whom two things are distinguished: namely, the consecration either of the whole people or of individual ministers. And these are the **sacraments**, by which either the people are sanctified or the ministers are consecrated. Finally, there is their particular way of life and service, by which they are distinguished from outsiders who are not of the same religion, both regarding food and regarding clothing. These are called **observances**. Therefore, these four species are included under the single category of "ceremonies."

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>
And through these points, the solution to the arguments becomes clear. For to the first, it is responded that the abstinence from certain foods and the manner of clothing did contribute to divine worship. They did so not primarily in themselves like sacrifices, but as preparatory ornaments; for this reason, they are also contained under the category of ceremonies. <margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ To the second, it is responded that the secrets of divine things are not to be broadcast to everyone. For this reason, mysteries are so named from "muttering" <note>original: "mussitando" — Soto is referencing a traditional etymology of 'mystery' relating to keeping the mouth closed or whispering</note> and from the compression of the lips. Otherwise, as Christ warned, it would be to "cast pearls before swine" <note>Matthew 7:6</note>. For what a person does not understand, they immediately despise. Because of this, the use of figurative schemes and types of things is not out of place in Holy Scripture. Indeed, just as in theaters men see through sensory representation what they cannot grasp with the naked intellect, <margin>To the third argument.</margin> so it is also worthwhile in Scripture. ¶ To the third, it is responded that just as when one medicine does not suffice for a sick body, another and then another is applied; so it was necessary in those ceremonies, which, as we said above, did not justify by themselves, but were "weak and beggarly elements" <note>Galatians 4:9</note>. And therefore, like a wise legislator, God thought it more prudent to permit the transgressions of a multitude of ceremonies than to let that people fall into idolatry if they were to remain idle. <margin>To the fourth argument.</margin> ¶ Finally, to the fourth, the reason for the distinction of those four has already been given. For our sacrifice <note>the Eucharist</note> contains Christ himself, which is therefore a sacrament; however, the sacrifices of the Old Law were not so. Therefore, the sacraments—by which the

<column-break/>

people were purged and expiated according to their degree—were one thing, and the sacrifices were another. Likewise, solemnities pertained in a certain way to sacred things, just as the temples were sacred. For sacrifices were offered at fixed times, just as they were offered in a certain place.

### ARTICLE II.

-> Whether legitimate causes can be assigned <-
-> to each of these types of ceremonies. <-

<margin>
First argument.
</margin>
IT FOLLOWS IN
the second article that we should speak, at least briefly, about the causes of the ceremonies. It is asked, therefore, whether they <margin>Gloss.</margin> had any causes at all. And the argument is made from the negative side. Regarding that passage in Ephesians 2: "voiding the law of commandments by decrees," the **gloss** <note>The Glossa Ordinaria, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> says that the observances of the ancient law were voided by the Evangelical decrees because they were "out of reason" <note>original: "ex ratione" — meaning they lacked a basis in natural reason</note>; therefore, by the opposite sense, they lacked reason. Especially because if they were strong in reason, they would have been moral laws. For whatever consists of reason is deduced from the principles of nature, from which moral precepts arise. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second, it is argued that they at least had no **literal** cause. Truly, if all ceremonies had no meaning except as signs and figures, then no other reason existed in them than to prefigure future things through those objects, and thus they had no cause that existed according to the primary meaning of the letter. And this is confirmed by the very words of the Law. For if there were any ceremony that had a literal cause, it would most likely be either circumcision or the Passover <note>original: "Phase Paschæ"</note>. Regarding the first, we read in Genesis 17: "That it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you." Regarding the second, in Exodus 13: "It shall be as a sign in your hand, and as a memorial before your eyes." Therefore, other things had even less of a literal cause. <margin>Paul.</margin> ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that not only did the sacraments and sacrifices carry the figure of Christ, but even the histories themselves did: such as the crossing of the Red Sea, the wandering in the desert, and others of that kind. Concerning these, Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10: "All these things happened to them in figure." But in the histories, besides the mystical understanding, there was also a literal one; therefore, the ceremonies also had a literal cause.
