# Question V of the Second Book

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>The conclusion is argued.</margin>
<margin>The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>.</margin>
<margin>Paul.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
The question is answered with two conclusions. The first: the entire system of ceremonies in the Mosaic law derived its causes from a proper and intended purpose. This conclusion is evident to anyone who believes that this law was the work of God, a point already established above against the Manichaeans <note>A dualist sect that rejected the Old Testament as the work of an evil deity</note>. For since God governs all things by His wisdom, and since it is the role of a wise person—according to the Philosopher in the first book of the *Metaphysics*—to set things in order, it follows that whatever proceeds from God is ordered, as the Apostle says in Romans 13. Now, the order of any thing requires two conditions: first, that it be instituted for a proper purpose. For those things that are done not seriously, but in jest, or not deliberately, but happening outside the intention of a goal, are called disordered and rashly done because they lack a connection to an end. Second, it is also necessary that whatever is directed toward a goal must have a proper proportion to it. Just as Aristotle says in the second book of the *Physics* that the shape of a serrated saw <note>original: "ferræ dentatæ"</note> is determined by its purpose <note>i.e., cutting</note>, so in practical matters the logic of the means is derived from the goal. Therefore, since the Law is a work of divine wisdom, it must possess both types of rational order. For this reason, the author of the Law himself says in Deuteronomy 4: "This is your wisdom and understanding in the sight of the nations."

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
<margin>The difference between the literal and mystical sense.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: It is not credible that there was any ceremony of the ancient law that did not have both a sense and a cause: namely, both literal and mystical. To understand this, we must note—as we explained more fully in the introductory remarks on Matthew—that the literal and mystical senses differ in this way: the **literal sense** is that by which the words themselves signify things, whether by their original institution or through a metaphor. The **mystical sense**, however, is that which the *things* signified by the words signify in turn. Let us look at some examples. The history in Genesis stating that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman, narrates actual events in the literal sense. However, those historical events, interpreted by Paul in Galatians, signified the two testaments through allegory. Again, that passage in Isaiah 7, "Behold, a Virgin shall conceive," etc., foretold in the proper literal sense the conception of the Virgin Mother of God. Meanwhile, the passage in chapter 11, "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root," signified the same birth of the Virgin in a literal sense, yet an improper one—that is, through a metaphor. But the rod of Aaron, which blossomed as recorded in Numbers 17, was a type and figure of the same thing in the mystical and allegorical sense. With this interpretation established, the conclusion is proven. The worship of the ancient law,

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>

<column-break/>

as stated above, differed from ours in that our worship is not "shadowy" <note>original: "vmbratilis" — referring to a symbolic foreshadowing</note>, even though it carries an image of the Church Triumphant. The ancient worship was instituted for two ends: namely, both to offer due honor to God and to foretell the future Messiah. For just as the oracles of the prophets were proclamations of future events, so the entire history of that Law appeared to be nothing other than a kind of theater where a drama of the future <note>original: "futurorum comœdia"</note> was performed. From this it follows that the entire apparatus of ceremonies had both a cause and a literal sense—either to avoid the impiety of idolatry or to commemorate some benefit, such as the observation of the Sabbath—and additionally a figurative sense. Just as the eating of the lamb was both a foreshadowing and a shadow of the benefit of the liberation from Egypt, and a figure of the slaying of Christ.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, to the first argument, it is responded that those ceremonies, when compared with ours, are considered to have lacked "reason" only in the sense that they signified nothing by their own nature. For it was inherently indifferent <note>original: "impertinens"</note> whether this or that animal was slaughtered, or that a garment not be woven of both linen and wool; rather, they had their entire cause from their divine institution. Our Law, however, because it is based on the duties of charity, derives its reason from the nature of things themselves. For this reason, those ancient rites are not called "moral": not because they had no reason, but because their goodness and merit were not drawn from the nature of things.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
<margin>The double literal cause of the sacrifices of the ancient Law.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that just as a metaphorical sense is no less literal than a proper sense (since both are signified by the words), so the fact that things were instituted to commemorate a benefit does not take away the literal sense. Therefore, nothing prevents the literal cause of circumcision from being a monument to the covenant made with Abraham, and the cause of eating the lamb from being a memory of the people's liberation, even if they additionally demonstrated something future in our law through allegory. Thus, Saint Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> most learnedly and richly explains the causes of both kinds specifically for each ceremony in *Summa Theologiae* I-II, question 102, article 3, and the three following; he moves through the four orders of ceremonies arranged above. For the literal cause of the sacrifices was twofold: namely, so that through them the human mind might be raised to God to reflect on the benefits received from His bounty; and therefore almost every kind of foodstuff was offered—namely, animals, bread, wine, oil, and honey. Furthermore, incense and salt were offered, with which God feeds us; according to...

<summary>This page argues that all Mosaic ceremonies had a rational purpose, functioning on both a literal level (to prevent idolatry or commemorate history) and a mystical level (to foreshadow Christ). It distinguishes between the "shadowy" nature of Old Testament law and the nature-based charity of the New Testament.</summary>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

<note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of 1 Chronicles 29:14</note> "All things are yours, and what we have received from your hand, we have given to you." But because the greatest of all gifts was Christ—for as it says in John <note>John 3:16</note>, "God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him might not perish, but have eternal life"—the mystical <note>symbolic or spiritual</note> cause of those ancient sacrifices was this same Christ. Hence, in Hebrews 10, it is noted that the priest of the Old Law offered the same sacrifices which could never take away sins; Christ, however, offered one sacrifice for sins forever. 

There were three species of four-legged animals offered: namely, sheep, cattle, and goats. Among the birds, the turtledove and the pigeon were offered. However, among fish, none were considered suitable for sacrifice because they cannot live outside of the water. These animals were killed as a figure <note>a symbolic preview</note> of Christ, who was to be immolated on the cross. For this reason, even the manner of killing them was prescribed, so that they might differ from the practices of the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish pagans</note>. They were offered both as "holocausts" <note>burnt offerings</note> in honor of God, and also to expiate <note>atone for</note> sins, and to pacify and appease Him. Thus, some were called "peace offerings," and others "sin offerings."

<margin>The literal and mystical reason for the sacred things of the temple.</margin>
The causes for the sacred objects—namely the temple, the vessels, and the solemnities in which sacrifices were offered—are assigned two reasons: the literal and the mystical. For that people, while they wandered through the desert, had a portable tabernacle <note>a tent-sanctuary</note>; but later, once they were brought into possession of the Promised Land, they had a temple. Literally speaking, a wandering people could not have a fixed temple, nor was it fitting for a settled people to have a changeable tabernacle. But regarding the figure <note>symbolism</note>, the tabernacle signified the Church of those struggling and journeying through this world, while the temple signified the eternal assembly of the heavenly host. There, just as in the construction of the temple no sound of a hammer or axe was heard, there will be no mourning, nor crying, nor noise; instead, just as in this earthly struggle each person exercises themselves through the favors of God in duties of charity and justice and the fruits of penance—hewing and polishing themselves—so all shall be placed together by divine arrangement.

<margin>Another reason for the temple according to Chrysostom.</margin>
Regarding the fact that only a single temple was granted to them, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> assigns the reason that by abstaining from the various locations and altars of the various gods worshiped by the pagans, they might profess one true God. However, another reason must not be kept silent, which Chrysostom <note>Saint John Chrysostom</note> meditated upon eloquently in his homily against the Jews. For they were prohibited from celebrating the Passover and festivals except in Jerusalem and in one temple,

<column-break/>

<margin>Josephus.</margin>
as is evident in Deuteronomy 16 and in the writings of Josephus, Book 3, Chapter 13. This was done, among other reasons, so that after the temple was later destroyed by Titus and Vespasian <note>Roman commanders who destroyed the Temple in 70 AD</note> and never rebuilt thereafter, it would become openly clear that the Law had ceased. For this reason, while the Hebrews were held captive in Babylon and were asked to celebrate their feasts, they replied: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?" <note>Psalm 137:4</note> as if to say: "It is a sin for us to perform our solemnities anywhere other than Jerusalem." Therefore, if the Jews would reflect on this now, they would easily be led to believe that their Law has been abolished, seeing that its sacrifices have been rendered obsolete by the removal of the temple.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Regarding the vessels, the lampstands, and the rest, see the writings of Saint Thomas, and subsequently regarding the solemnities. Aside from the daily feast in which a lamb was sacrificed in the morning and evening (as read in Numbers 28 and 29), there were seven: namely, the Sabbath every single week.

<margin>Sabbath.</margin>
And the New Moons at the beginning of each month;

<margin>New Moon.</margin>
and the most solemn celebration of the Paschal lamb <note>Passover</note>, which was done in memory of the liberation from Egypt.

And on the fiftieth day thereafter, Pentecost, in memory of the giving of the Law.

<margin>Feast of Trumpets.</margin>
And fifth, the Feast of Trumpets in the seventh month, namely September. (For March was the first month.) This was in memory of the liberation of Isaac through the ram which Abraham saw caught by its horns among the briars, as read in Genesis 22; those horns were represented by those trumpets.

<margin>Feast of Tabernacles.</margin>
And the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "scenopegiæ"</note>: that is, of the booths, to commemorate the benefit of divine protection through the desert.

<margin>Feast of Ingathering.</margin>
And finally, the seventh feast, the Feast of Ingathering; specifically when the funds necessary for divine worship were collected.

<margin>Causes of the sacraments.</margin>
In the third place, it is easy to assign both causes <note>literal and mystical</note> for the sacraments as well. For through circumcision, the whole people was cleansed from original sin and initiated into the worship of God. Therefore, what Baptism is to us, Circumcision was to them: namely, the profession of the Law. Soon followed the eating of the paschal lamb, which signified our Sacrament of Refreshment <note>the Eucharist</note>. Additionally, there was the offering of victims and the bread of proposition <note>showbread</note>, which was the peculiar worship of the priests. And as figures of the other sacraments we possess, there were purifications and washings.

<margin>Causes of the observances.</margin>
Finally, even the "observances"—namely the choice of foods and the clothing of both the people and the priests—did not lack their own causes, whether you consider the literal or the mystical. Saint Thomas, in the place cited, explains all these things with excellent mental focus and the most vigilant diligence and explanation. Wherefore—

### ARTICLE III.

### *Whether the ceremonies of the ancient law existed before the Law, or whether they provided justification under the Law.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape with figures and buildings.</image-desc>
It follows that we should add to the previous discussions a consideration of both the timing and the power of the ceremonies. For it is argued that ceremonies existed before the Law <note>The "Law" here refers to the Mosaic Law given at Mount Sinai</note>. First, because as we read in Genesis 4, Cain and Abel offered gifts to the Lord; this was a type of sacrifice and burnt offering in honor of God. Likewise Noah, as read in Genesis 8, and Abraham, as held in chapter 22 of the same book. And regarding sacred objects, Abraham in Genesis 13 and Jacob in Genesis 28 built altars. ¶ Also, thirdly: 
<margin>The third argument.</margin>
Circumcision, which was the highest of the sacraments before the Law was given, was commanded to Abraham in Genesis 17; and Melchizedek, under the law of nature, as read in chapter 14 <note>The text mistakenly cites chapter 13</note>, was a priest of the most high God. ¶ Furthermore, that those ceremonies justified <note>i.e., made a person righteous or "right with God"</note> under the Law seems to be gathered from that passage 
<margin>The fourth argument.</margin>
in Leviticus 10: <note>original: "Quomodò potui placere Domino in ceremonijs mente lugubri?"</note> "How could I have pleased the Lord in ceremonies with a mournful mind?" Here Aaron excused himself to Moses, saying that because of his grief over his slain sons, he could not please God with his sacrifice. From this, the opposite sense is gathered: that at other times, he did please God. He who pleases God is justified before Him. Added to this is the word of David: <note>original: "Lex Domini immaculata conuertens animas."</note> "The law of the Lord is perfect, converting souls" <note>Psalm 19:7</note>. ¶ To the contrary, however, is the Apostle in Galatians 2: "If a law had been given that could justify, then Christ died for nothing"—that is, without cause. To concede this would be blasphemous.

To this question, we respond with four conclusions, provided that we distinguish between two times before the Law: namely, the time that preceded Abraham, and the time that followed from him until Moses. For those two ages that flowed from the creation of the world until the Flood, and from then until Abraham, contained the purely natural state of the nations; for with Abraham, God began to deal particularly with the salvation of the human race. Let the first conclusion be: There were never any mortals who

<column-break/>

did not have their own ceremonies and rites of divine worship. I do not mean ceremonies established by the authority of a divinely placed law from above, but by natural reason acting as a teacher. For since nature teaches our race that God is to be worshipped, the various
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
nations established various forms of worship according to the reasoning of their faith which they conceived regarding Him. Just as they are drawn by an instinct toward a peaceful state of the republic, they also establish judgments by laws. For as has already been said often above, ceremonial and judicial matters are not concluded from the first principles of nature in the same way as moral laws are, but are established by human judgment <note>original: "arbitramento humano"</note>. And from this it happens that while the law of nature and the law of nations <note>term: "jus gentium" — the shared laws common to all civilized peoples</note> are the same among all, ceremonial and judicial laws are nonetheless varied. And since worship is not administered or dispensed except through priests, according to the word of Paul in Hebrews 8: <note>original: "Omnis pontifex ad offerendum munera & hostias constituitur"</note> "Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices," there was likewise no nation that did not have its own priests. This priesthood succeeded either by the right of the firstborn <note>term: "primogeniture" — the right of the eldest son to inherit the family's leadership and religious duties</note>: as is said of Melchizedek, who was Shem, the firstborn of Noah; and as noted in the history of Jacob, who bought the birthright from the firstborn Esau for this reason—because God had granted the priesthood to him, even though he was the younger; according to that passage in Malachi 1: <note>original: "Iacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui"</note> "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." Indeed, it would not be a futile thought if we were to meditate on this as the cause of Cain’s indignation toward his brother: that although he himself was the elder, and therefore the legitimate priest, his brother's offering was nevertheless held as more pleasing to God than his own. Among the Romans, however, it is not so certain that priests succeeded by the right of the firstborn, for they were created by the people. And regarding the priests of the Egyptians, sacred history reported in Genesis 41. Furthermore, what we affirm regarding worship, we understand regarding the four subsequent types of ceremonies. For every nation had its own sacrifices by which they professed divine honor; and its own altars, and shrines, and groves consecrated for those same sacrifices. Additionally, they had sacraments: at least that common one by which they cleansed themselves and their children from original sin. I do not say "common" in the sense that it was one and the same for all nations; for since that was neither divinely revealed to the whole world, nor inferred from the principles of nature—since the stain of our origin <note>original sin</note>, as we said in Book 1 on Nature and Grace, was not naturally known—but was ceremonial, it follows that it was not the same among all. But where natural reason obtained its own light, the offerings were insti-

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>

<margin>Paul.</margin> 
Because of this, Paul calls them "justifications of the flesh" <note>original: "iustitias carnis"</note> in Hebrews 9, which were imposed until the time of reformation. "For if the blood of goats and bulls," he says, "and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh." The second part of this conclusion was touched upon in the final article of the third question. For there we showed the reason why the moral precepts of that law did not justify: in which our precepts agree with theirs. That is, they did not by themselves remit the sins of the sinner, since they are natural works, whereas the remission of sins happens through the grace of God above nature. However, the sacraments of that law and our law differ in this: since Christ had not yet suffered—and his death is the perennial fountain of all grace—those sacraments were not instruments through which the actual Passion was applied. Instead, it was applied through faith by way of the "end" <note>Meaning the ultimate goal or purpose toward which the rituals pointed.</note>, toward which all their works were directed. On account of this, it was not circumcision, but 

<column-break/>

faith, testified through it, that sanctified. Neither was it the offering of victims, but that same faith, according to Leviticus 4 and 5, where, while mention is made of those same offerings, it is added: "The priest shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him." It is as if the guilt were pardoned not by the power of the sacrifices, but through faith and the grace of God. And therefore, in Galatians, Paul called those sacraments "weak and 
<margin>Paul.</margin> 
beggarly elements" <note>original: "infirma egenáque elementa"</note>. Clearly, it was not they but faith that justified. And this is what Paul seems to me to have taught with that word: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." He shows, I say, how the righteousness of that law did not rely on circumcision, which was commanded to Abraham, but on the faith professed through it. For us, however, the Passion already performed is applied through the sacraments, by which, as if by its instruments, we are justified. Yet those who were justified then, just like us, earned merit through all the works of the laws, whether they were ceremonial, moral, or judicial. 
<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> 
¶ Fourth conclusion: That cleansing of the sacraments of that time from the plague of bodily filth, even if it had some natural reasoning, was nevertheless most powerfully situated in the mystery of our [salvation]. The literal reason, I say, in the case of lepers and others who were infected with poisonous diseases, was so that their contagion might be avoided. For this reason they were driven from the camp, and were not received back unless they were clean by the judgment of the priests. Those, however, who touched a carcass, although they were not cast out of the camp, were nevertheless not admitted into the temple because of the horror [of death], unless they were washed. Yet the principal cause was certainly to foreshadow the cleansing from the decay of sins that would come through Christ, as the 
<margin>Paul.</margin> 
Apostle discusses at length in Hebrews 7 through 10. For one may observe many 
<margin>Many things in the ritual of the old law which, unless [symbolic], would be considered miraculous.</margin> 
things in that ritual which, unless they were a figure of our own, would be considered miraculous <note>or "prodigious"—things that defy natural explanation.</note>. First, the frequency of lepers and others suffering from contagion, such as does not exist among us. Then, the divine care and the expensive caution used in driving them away and avoiding them. Thirdly, that the judgment of them was committed to the priests, without whose sentence they were not admitted into the temple. Christ held this so sacred that he nevertheless sent those whom he himself healed to the priests. This is despite the fact that such business seemed to be the duty of doctors rather than priests—and especially so because those ceremonies had no natural power to cure leprosy or a flow of blood. Indeed, they were not even applied until the leper was already judged to be clean. For so we must hear the word of 
<margin>Levit.</margin> 
Leviticus.

<summary>This page argues that the rituals of the Old Testament (like circumcision and cleansing from leprosy) did not possess inherent power to forgive sins, but rather functioned as symbolic acts of faith pointing toward Christ. The author explains that while these ceremonies managed physical purity and public health, true spiritual righteousness always came from faith in God's grace.</summary>

# Question V of the Second Book

Leviticus 14 says: "This is the rite of the leper when he is to be cleansed," that is, when he is to be judged as being clean. For it follows: "When the priest, having gone out of the camp, finds that the leprosy is cleansed, he shall command him who is being purified"—that is, the one pronounced to be healthy—"to offer," etc. <note>original: "Hic est ritus leprosi quando mundandus est..."</note> Therefore, the priests were not appointed as doctors to heal, but as judges to deliver a sentence regarding health. In this matter, they are believed to have used the testimony of medical doctors. Consequently, lepers were only healed through natural means and medical effort. Healing by miracle happened very rarely, as is read concerning Miriam, the sister of Moses, in Numbers 12, who was covered in leprosy as white as snow for seven days. For the common opinion—that when priests erred by judging someone not to be a leper, that person was miraculously healed by God's favor even if not by the power of the offering—is apocryphal <note>Meaning it is of doubtful authenticity or not supported by scripture.</note>. That rite of the sacraments was therefore instituted to signify the duty of the Christian priesthood in expiating <term>piacula</term> <note>A term for sins or crimes requiring atonement through ritual purification.</note>.

<margin>To the final argument.</margin>
¶ Therefore, in response to the final argument, it is said that if the works of the law were done out of grace, they converted souls as things pleasing to God; however, the legal ceremonies were applied neither for the cleansing of bodies nor for the purification of souls.

### ARTICLE IV.

-> Whether the ceremonies of the Old Law so <-
-> ceased at the death of Christ that <-
-> they cannot be observed from then on <-
-> without mortal sin. <-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The fourth article follows concerning the abolition of the ceremonies. It is argued that those ceremonies ought not to have ceased at the death of Christ, such that they could not be observed from then on without committing a mortal sin. One reads in Baruch 4 <note>The text cites Baruch 5, but this passage is traditionally located in Baruch 4:1.</note>: "This is the book of the commandments of God, and the law that is forever"; in which the ceremonies of the laws were also included. This is likewise proven by the example of Christ, who, even while preaching the New Law, sent the cleansed leper to the legal priests (as we just said), as if approving of the ancient ceremonies. Furthermore, the ancient ceremonies, as has been said, had not only mystical causes but also literal ones; therefore, for 그 reason, they were intended to remain.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued that after the Gospel itself, it is permitted to 

<column-break/>

keep them. It is not to be believed that the Apostles sinned after the confirmation of the Holy Spirit from on high, yet they observed the ancient legal customs. For, as is read in Acts 16, Paul circumcised Timothy. And as is held in chapter 21, listening to the counsel of James, he was purified along with the men he had taken. And Peter, as the same Paul reports in Galatians 2, withdrew himself from the company of the Gentiles; regarding which Paul does not fear to affirm that he rebuked him as being blameworthy. Indeed, as is recorded in Acts 15, the council of the Apostles imposed on the Church that they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled <note>referring to animals killed without draining the blood</note>, which were held among the ceremonies of that law; therefore, it is not a sin for Christians to observe ceremonies of that kind.

¶ On the contrary, however, is the admonition of the Apostle in Galatians 5: "If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing." <note>original: "Si circumdimini, Christus nihil vobis proderit."</note> But to place an obstacle to Christian redemption cannot be anything other than a deadly sin; therefore, to be circumcised and to perform other ceremonies thereafter following the passion of Christ is a sin, and a grave one at that, as it is an insult to Christ.

Regarding the previous articles—both because they required a lengthy discourse and especially because in the works of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential 13th-century theologian.</note> they were excellent, bathed in light, and enriched with expansion—we have touched upon them only briefly and perfunctorily. Here, however, a fuller scholastic disputation is required, and we will therefore devote more diligent effort to explaining it. For a full answer to the question, four conclusions are necessary. First: The Law of Moses ought to have ceased through the Law of Christ, and thus it has altogether ceased.

<margin>First conclusion. Paul.</margin>
Paul asserted this conclusion in many places; God especially entrusted to him among the Apostles the task of interpreting the Old Law. As in Hebrews 7: "The priesthood being translated, it is necessary that a translation of the law also be made." And in chapter 8: "In saying a new [testament], he hath made the former old." And in Ephesians 2: "Abolishing the law of commandments contained in ordinances." But there is no need to multiply testimonies in a matter of faith. We began to reveal the reason for this already above in Article 2, while giving the reason why that law had to be figurative.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Since exterior worship was instituted for the sake of declaring and professing internal worship, worship is threefold according to a threefold state. For in the fatherland <note>A theological term for Heaven, the final home of the soul.</note>, where nothing is hoped for in the future, there is no need for worship that predicts the future. But for the law of the Gospel, to which Christ is present—who has paved the way for us to that place—only that worship is suitable which is an image of that triumphant state.

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right [De Iustitia & Iure]

of the Church, toward which we strive through faith and hope. But for the ancients, to whom the Messiah was not present but promised, that worship was appropriate which served as a shadow of Him, through whom they were to be moved toward that same promised happiness. By being accustomed to these rituals, they would be fit and ready to receive Him. Therefore, just as faith and hope will entirely cease when the heavenly truth is present—and thus our figurative worship will cease—so too, when the Sun of Truth, namely Christ, is present, it was necessary for His shadow to be abolished. Indeed, that law was not established forever, but until the fullness of time should come, as <margin>Paul.</margin> Paul testifies in Galatians. Therefore, as we said in Book 1, Question 1, that is one of the senses of Christ's words in that verse: *I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it* <note>original: "Non veni soluere legem sed adimplere"</note>: that is, I have not come to abrogate, break, or remove it as if it were meant to be perpetual; but to fulfill it—that is, to complete the time for which it was established and to perfect the truths of which it bore the shadows, so that it might be known to have faded away. 

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Second conclusion.** Not only did the law cease regarding ceremonial and legal matters, but if you look at its obligatory force, it was entirely antiquated at that time. Indeed, without any exception, Christ says that once the priesthood was transferred, the law was transferred; and the New Testament made the first one old. And Christ said simply, *It is finished.* I would add this second conclusion here so that the understanding of that common axiom might become clear: "The Law ceased regarding ceremonial and judicial matters, but not regarding moral matters." For if you take this to mean that we are bound by the obligatory force of the ancient law to keep the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> or any other moral precept, it is completely false. For that law was established only for that specific people, from whose bond <margin>Paul.</margin> Christ has freed us, as the Apostle taught in Romans 7, using the example of a widow who, upon the death of her husband, is free from the law of marriage. There, he makes no exception for moral laws. Therefore, the meaning of that common assertion is that the moral laws did not cease because they were part of the **natural law** <note>original: "iure naturae"</note>, which binds all mortals; even the Gentiles were formerly bound by these, though not by the power of the Mosaic law. Thus, no testimony of the Old Law can be brought against a Christian regarding its power to bind, but only as a testimony of our own law. For this reason, we revere and venerate the Old Testament in the sacred canon.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion:** It is now in no way permitted to observe the ceremonies of the Old Law after the promulgation of the Gospel; rather, it would 

<column-break/>

be a mortal sin, and even heresy, to do so. <margin>The conclusion is gathered from the above.</margin> This conclusion is gathered by a clear inference from the preceding points. For ceremonies, as we have said, were certain professions of the coming Messiah. For the confession of faith is made not only with words, but also with signifying deeds. Now, the faith we confess concerning Christ is exactly the same as that which the ancients professed; not only because it concerns the same Christ, but because both peoples confess the same truths—namely His birth, passion, resurrection, etc.—yet through declarations of different times. For they confessed that truth of Isaiah: *Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son.* We, however, confess the similar Gospel truth: *that she has conceived and has borne.* Therefore, just as one who now claimed that Christ *was going to be* born, suffer, and rise again would be impious toward the faith (since he would be affirming a falsehood contrary to the faith), so too would he who asserted the same through the performance of ceremonies. Hence, <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine says against Faustus: "Already He is not promised as one to be born, to suffer, and to rise again—which those sacraments in a certain way sounded forth—but it is announced that He *has been* born, *has* suffered, and *has* risen; which these sacraments performed by Christians now sound forth." 

¶ But truly, many things must be considered regarding this cessation of legal matters, about which there is no complete agreement among either the ancient Fathers or the Scholastics. <margin>First doubt.</margin> For there is a dispute as to the exact point in time when the Old Law was abolished and the Gospel Law gained its force. <margin>Second.</margin> Again, whether the legal rituals, as soon as they were "dead," were likewise "deadly" <note>This refers to the "Mortua et Mortifera" debate: whether the Old Law ceremonies were merely "dead" (no longer required) or "deadly" (sinful to perform).</note>. <margin>Third.</margin> And whether our law existed in counsel before it obtained the power of binding obligation. <margin>Disagreement of Augustine and Jerome.</margin> For Augustine, as can be seen in Epistle 19, challenged Jerome to a dispute on this matter. Between them, this difference is observed: Jerome recognized only two periods of the ancient law. One, which flowed up to the moment of the Passion, in which all legalities had life and retained their power of binding. The other, running from that same moment of the Passion until the end of the age, in which they were both dead and deadly. Therefore, as soon as they were extinguished, they began to be lethal. For this reason, he denied that any of the Apostles observed legal rituals after Christ's ascension; he asserts they only pretended to do so. Augustine, however, distinguishes three periods: The first, in which he agrees with Jerome, namely that before the Passion they were living and likewise binding. The second, however, in which they were dead, but nevertheless not deadly;

<meta>catchword: deadly [fera:]</meta>

But indeed, after the sufficient proclamation of the gospel—which according to Augustine is the third period, lasting until the end of the world—they are both dead and deadly <note>Theologians distinguished between "dead" (no longer having spiritual power) and "deadly" (sinful to practice).</note>. Rather, he says that from its institution until the gospel was proclaimed, it remained a counsel. Thus, at the moment of the passion, nothing was changed regarding baptism, but it began to be a command only after proclamation. **Second**, he differs regarding the legal rituals. For what we say—that they lasted in their obligatory force until the passion, and were then "dead" both in power and obligation—he denies. He says instead that circumcision did not bind except until the institution of baptism, and from then on it ran alongside baptism as a counsel until the proclamation of the gospel. Therefore, any Jew hearing the gospel could either circumcise his son or baptize him, and either would suffice for him. ### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...for some time. Thus, the Jews were bound everywhere to observe the <term>legal ceremonies</term> <note>Latin: *legalia*. The ritual laws of the Old Testament, such as dietary restrictions and animal sacrifices.</note> until the proclamation of the Gospel resounded to them. In short, since the ancient law, according to him, was not antiquated until the promulgation of the Gospel, the New Law did not begin to be a commandment until that time.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ These things having been narrated, our fourth conclusion is this: The boundary of the laws, by which the Old Law ceased and the New began, was the time of the Passion <note>The suffering and death of Jesus Christ.</note>. However, this conclusion must be understood with its attachments—namely, with the other assertions that we have closely defined around it.

<margin>Proof of the first conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is proven. The legal ceremonies were figures and a shadow of the future redemption through Christ. Now, a shadow—if we may seek a lesson from visible things—does not last except until the light of truth appears. But the truth of redemption was perfected in the death and resurrection of Christ; therefore, at that time, those shadows of the legal ceremonies expired in their power when Christ said, <note>original: "Consummatum est"</note> "It is finished," and they breathed out their binding force. Indeed, this applies to the whole Law, as we were saying a little while ago. For according to all commentators, that passage in John 19, "It is finished," refers to this, as does the veil being torn in two, as read in Matthew 27. Everyone, I say, recognizes there the boundary of both Testaments: namely, the abolition of one and the obligation of the other. For it was unbecoming and inconsistent with divine providence for the world to endure for any time without any obligation to a law; and thus, if the bond of the ancient law was broken in the death of Christ, the New Law began to bind then, or at the resurrection.

<margin>Second. Paul.</margin>
¶ Second, the force of the argument is strengthened from the inference of Paul in Romans 7, where from the fact that we have been liberated from sin, he infers that we are likewise exempt from the yoke of the law. Since, therefore, we were made free from sin in the death of Christ, it follows that we were then also free from the law.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ In the third place, his example in that same passage is added. For he says that just as a woman becomes free from the law of marriage upon the death of her husband, so also the <term>Synagogue</term> <note>In scholastic theology, "Synagogue" represents the religious community and legal order of the Old Covenant, personified here as a wife.</note> was freed from the obligation of the law in the death of Christ.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
¶ Fourth, this is finally confirmed by the word of the same Apostle cited above: *When the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law take place,* where he denoted the logical consequence of things. But Christ, in his death, transferred the Mosaic priesthood into the Gospel priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, as Paul explains in the same place; teaching how Christ, appearing as the high priest of future good things, entered once into the holy place, having found eternal redemption. Indeed, he offered this sacrifice on the altar of the cross; therefore, the transfer of the law took place then. By these points, therefore, all three

<column-break/>

<margin>The assertions of Scotus are refuted.</margin>
members of the opinion of <term>Scotus</term> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian who often disagreed with the Thomistic school to which Soto belonged.</note> are undermined: namely (to begin from the second), that circumcision did not bind except until the institution of baptism, which institution he himself admits preceded the Passion. For if the Law was not extinguished until the Passion, and thus all other legal ceremonies bound until then, it is false that circumcision did not retain that same power up to that point. This is furthermore confirmed by the word of Christ, <note>original: "Non veni soluere legem sed adimplere."</note> "I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it." For since he did not fulfill it until his death, if he had broken the bond of circumcision before then, he would have broken the law before he fulfilled it. And by the same reasoning, his third saying is rejected: namely, that the same circumcision and Law bound the Jews who were ignorant of the Gospel after the Passion of Christ. For the whole Law was finished in the Passion and Resurrection.

<margin>First reason against Scotus.</margin>
Likewise, his first assertion is refuted: namely, that baptism after the Passion was only a "counsel" <note>In theology, a "counsel" is a recommended good act (like a vow of poverty), whereas a "precept" is a mandatory command.</note>. For where the obligation of the prior law ceased, the obligation of the subsequent one began. Otherwise, the world would be so free from divine positive law that it would be bound by none.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is argued toward the same point. Although Augustine and Jerome disagree on other matters, they are nevertheless unanimous in this: that the Old Law first died in the Passion of Christ, both in its power and its obligation, and that then the New Law began to bind. To affirm, therefore, that circumcision ceased to bind before the Passion, yet bound those ignorant of the law after the Passion, and to deny that baptism bound immediately from the Passion of Christ, is clearly to go to war with both of the Holy Fathers. Hear the words of Augustine in the cited epistle, where he says: *When the faith came, which was previously announced by those observations and revealed after the death and resurrection of the Lord, those old sacraments lost the life of their office.* And in this, he gladly admits that he adheres to Jerome.

<margin>Gloss.</margin>
Add also the <term>gloss</term> <note>A standard marginal or interlinear commentary on the Bible used by medieval scholars.</note> upon that passage in Hebrews 8: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire," which says, *You did not desire them,* namely, from the time of the Passion. For they began to be displeasing then, when the truth of which they were figures was completed, as Augustine himself says on Psalm 39.

<margin>First reason against the foundation of Scotus.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is argued against that very foundation of Scotus. For he thinks that the obligation of a law begins when it comes to the notice of the subjects; which is surely false. Rather, it begins to bind as soon as it is established by the prince through a public edict. Indeed, the preaching of the Apostles was not the *establishment* of the law, because they themselves were not the legislators of the Gospel, but the proclaimers of Christ—though they could, as individuals, establish other laws. Whence...

### Book Two, Question 5

<margin>Second [proof]</margin>
Secondly, on the feast of Pentecost, the Law was not given to the world, but rather the power and faculty were given to the Apostles to proclaim it. For Christ had said before: <note>original: "Ite prædicate Evangelium: docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos."</note> "Go, preach the Gospel: teach all nations, baptizing them." This is a sign that the obligation of baptism already applied even then.

<margin>Third [proof]</margin>
¶ Likewise, it is argued for the same point: If the law bound no one until they heard the law, it would be improper to say that ignorance excuses them. An excuse only exists regarding something a person is actually required to do. Therefore, if ignorance excuses a person, it is a sign that the bond of the law already extends to everyone; yet ignorance protects the person from the guilt of breaking it.

¶ And thirdly, it is argued for the same point: It would follow that if someone has not yet heard the law, they are not bound; nor would they be bound even when their ignorance became <term>vincible</term> <note>Vincible ignorance refers to a lack of knowledge that a person could and should have overcome through reasonable effort.</note>, such that it was their own fault they did not hear it. For I ask: when did the obligation begin? Surely, one cannot answer anything except: "When the law was given."

<margin>Fourth [proof]</margin>
¶ And fourthly, from that same way of thinking, it would follow that after someone was released from the Old Law and bound to the New, it could happen—without any change in the New Law itself—that they would again be released from the New and held to the Old. For instance, if a Jew living far from Jerusalem after Pentecost had heard that the Law of Christ was binding—to which he gave faith, though not lightly, before seeing sufficient signs, as could happen—he would then be bound to the New Law and not the ancient one. But if later, false prophets told him the opposite, using false signs and testimonies so that he returned to his prior faith without personal fault, he would again be exempt from the obligation of the New Law and become subject to the Old.

¶ And by this, the argument is dissolved where Scotus says: "No one stands in a different relation to any law than they did before, unless it is promulgated to them differently." But before the Passion, people were not bound to baptism; therefore, they were not bound until it was promulgated to them.

<margin>Solution to Scotus's argument</margin>
For the first premise is distinguished: if he means that no one stands in a different relation to the law regarding the *bond* of obligation before it is proclaimed, that must be denied. Indeed, as soon as a law is solemnly enacted by a ruler, it binds. But if he means that no one is held to be in *guilt* before they know the law, we certainly admit that—with the qualification, however, that it was not their own fault that they failed to hear it.

<margin>A most urgent reason against another Scotic assertion</margin>
¶ But against another assertion of Scotus—namely, that from the Passion until sufficient proclamation, both <term>circumcision</term> and baptism coexisted as <term>counsels</term> <note>A "counsel" in this context is a recommendation or optional good work, rather than a strictly binding command.</note>, so that a Jew had the choice of which he preferred to receive—it is argued most urgently (as I judge). For either he

<column-break/>

understands this regarding a Jew who is ignorant of the Gospel, or one who has heard it and was bound to receive it. It cannot be said of the former, for that person was clearly still bound by circumcision—especially according to Scotus himself, who says the Old Law bound until the New was proclaimed. But if he means the latter, reason demonstrates the opposite. For since that person would no longer be excused by ignorance, they were bound to profess the Christian religion. Now, the profession of Christianity occurs in baptism; therefore, they were bound to be baptized, and likewise to baptize their small children just as Christians are bound now. Otherwise, it clearly follows that no Jew, even if they accepted the faith two years later, would ever be bound to be baptized, nor to baptize their offspring—which would be a most absurd thing to grant. Truly, I confess I do not grasp Scotus’s opinion in this matter.

<margin>Scotus's first argument</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, there are arguments against these asserted truths, not only from Scotus but others worthy of resolution. To proceed in the order of the succession of time, Scotus argues that before the Passion, as soon as baptism began to be a counsel, the obligation of circumcision likewise became a counsel. He says that the commandment of baptism totally removes circumcision, rendering it entirely useless and harmful; therefore, the counsel of that same baptism removes the necessity of circumcision, leaving it as a counsel as well. He proves this consequence by stating that if the commandment of one thing is the prohibition of another, then the counsel of that same thing at least removes the necessity of the other.

<margin>Solution</margin>
However, this consequence is most fallacious. It only holds in cases where those things are in conflict with each other, as is clear with virginity and marriage. For whoever is commanded to maintain virginity is entirely forbidden from marriage. Therefore, the counsel of virginity removes the commandment of marriage. But where both things can coexist, the consequence is not valid. For the counsel of prayer during Lent does not remove the commandment of fasting. Since the Law was established to last until the truth of redemption arrived, there is no reason why circumcision specifically should be said to have lost its binding force simply because baptism was offered as a counsel.

<margin>Scotus's second argument</margin>
¶ Secondly, he argues for the same point: if a Jew, having been imbued with our faith before the Passion, baptized his small child but did not circumcise him, that child would fly to heaven; therefore, circumcision was not a commandment. But neither is this consequence valid, because the father himself would sin by not likewise circumcising. Not indeed because of the necessity...

<summary>Soto argues that the Old Law's binding power ended at Christ's Passion, refuting Duns Scotus's claim that it continued until personal proclamation. He maintains that while ignorance might excuse guilt, the legal obligation itself changes the moment a law is enacted.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

...the necessity of conferring grace upon a son, but because of the necessity of fulfilling the law. As even **Scotus** himself rightly concedes: although a Hebrew boy might obtain grace through a "natural sacrifice" <note>A simple prayer or offering used before formal laws were established.</note> used in a danger of death before the eighth day, he was nevertheless bound by the law to be circumcised if he survived until the eighth day. Similarly, even if someone is now flooded with the Holy Spirit through the "baptism of fire" <note>Also known as 'baptism of desire,' referring to the grace received by a person who intends to be baptized but cannot reach water.</note>, they are nonetheless bound to be washed with water if it is available.

<margin>Another argument.</margin>
¶ But an argument remains against our assertion that baptism before the Passion was merely a matter of "counsel" <note>In theology, a 'counsel' is a spiritual recommendation, whereas a 'precept' is a mandatory command.</note>. A Jew at that time, having witnessed sufficient miracles and the power of Christ's words, would be bound to take up His law. For He says: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin." <note>original: "si non venissem, & locutus eis non fuissem, peccatum non haberent." John 15:22</note> However, people could not become Christians except through baptism; therefore, they were bound to be baptized, and thus baptism was already a command at that time, and subsequently, circumcision had altogether ceased.

<margin>The Response.</margin>
To this argument, the answer is: the premise—that a Jew could not then receive the Gospel law without baptism—is rejected, since the law was not to be received until the time following the Passion. Therefore, all Jews who had previously accepted the [Old] Law were bound to be baptized immediately after the Resurrection at the preaching of the Apostles.

<margin>A Reply.</margin>
¶ But you argue: therefore, if Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people.</note> were converted before the Passion, they were not bound to be washed by baptism immediately.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The logical consequence is denied. Indeed, since they could not be circumcised, they were bound to be baptized. Furthermore, it should undoubtedly be believed that Jews converted before the Passion were also immediately dipped in the sacred font so that they might be marked with the Christian "character" <note>A theological term for an indelible spiritual mark left by a sacrament.</note>. This is proven by the Gospel testimony cited above, which states that Christ's Apostles baptized while the Master was still living. ¶ As for the other arguments of **Scotus** intended to prove that the Old Law lasted after the Passion until the proclamation of the Gospel, they retain no force after what has been said. For if you argue that a Jew after...

<margin>An Argument.</margin>
...the Passion, suffering from "inculpable ignorance" <note>Ignorance that is not one's fault because there was no way to know the truth.</note> of the Gospel, was bound to circumcise his children: therefore, circumcision, and thus the entire law, was still binding.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The first part of that logic is denied, if you weigh the strictness of the obligation. For since he could simply fail to circumcise without fault (for instance, if he had heard the Gospel), he should not be considered simply bound. But if it is not pleasing to speak with such strict rigor, another response is provided: that he was bound, not by the power of a command, but because of the ignorance from which he suffered—

<column-break/>

—just as someone who today believed it was Friday would be bound to abstain from meat, even if it were actually Monday.

<margin>Clarification of the previous solution.</margin>
¶ This response is explained more clearly. If the law—at the time God commanded circumcision to Abraham—had been ordered this way: "All your descendants shall be circumcised until the exact moment when the Messiah has suffered and risen," then surely no one could assert that the law was binding after that point in time. Nevertheless, those who were ignorant of that turning point would still have to be circumcised afterward because of their ignorance. I have framed the case under a condition which, in truth, happened in essence. For the Old Law was established only until that moment in time when Christ said: "It is finished," <note>original: "Consummatum est." John 19:30</note> and rose again.

<margin>A Reply.</margin>
¶ But if you argue more urgently: If a Jew after the Passion—moved either by a slight inkling or out of malice—believing the Old Law to be abolished, refused to circumcise his infant, he would indeed sin; and if not against his conscience, then against the law by which he was bound.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
It is answered that he would sin against the conscience which he was bound to have before the sufficient proclamation of the Gospel.

<margin>Another reason.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, even if the obligation of circumcision were extinguished immediately from the Passion, it seems to have retained the power of holiness. For if a Jew, ignorant of the Gospel, circumcised a son, that infant would be saved.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
It is answered that he would be saved not by the power of circumcision—which was now empty—but by the faith of the parents. Thus, circumcision at that time was worth nothing more than a sign by which a declaration of holy faith was made under the "Law of Nature" <note>The moral laws inherent in human nature, even without written scripture.</note>; the same sign that Jews used for children before the eighth day.

¶ However, a doubt that presses more troublesome here is: If a Jew at that time had heard the preaching of the Gospel and witnessed the power of miracles (and therefore "culpable ignorance" <note>Ignorance that is the person's own fault because they ignored clear evidence.</note> would not excuse him), but persisted nonetheless in his "perfidy" <note>In this historical context, 'perfidy' refers to a stubborn refusal to accept the Christian faith despite evidence.</note> and circumcised the boy, would that boy be cleansed of the stain of original sin? One side argues "yes," because if the same sacrament were applied by another person who was "invincibly ignorant," the boy would obtain salvation (as we just said); and the wickedness of the one performing the circumcision is no reason to harm the wretched infant. For if someone were to baptize a child today, intending to do what Christians perform, even if they did not believe in baptism at all, it profits the child. Nevertheless, it is answered that such a circumcision would in no way profit the boy. The reason is plain: for circumcision itself no longer provided any benefit except through the faith of the one applying it...

He distinguishes between the inherent power of Christian baptism and the faith-dependent nature of the now-expired Jewish rituals.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the transition between the Old Law of Moses and the New Law of the Gospel. ### Book Two, Question V.

...[necessi]ties: <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the necessity of faith</note> he, however, who was bound to believe the Gospel, was applying faith wrongly. Otherwise, it would have to be granted that even now Jews circumcising their children benefit them for salvation; to grant this would be a most absurd heresy. But he who, in **invincible ignorance** <term>invincible ignorance: a state where a person is unaware of a truth through no fault of their own, making them not morally responsible for the error</term>, used that sacrament, was rightly applying his faith. Therefore, it is denied that in such a case the wickedness of the one circumcising would not harm the boy. It is different, however, with our baptism, which contains the power of sanctifying within itself, by whomever it may be applied.

¶ But truly, besides these reasons, another remains of greater energy. Christ, during his passion, brought no law; therefore, the evangelical law did not begin to obligate then. 

<margin>Response.</margin>
The legitimate response to this is that while He lived among mortals, He brought the law for that specific moment in time when He would perfect the mystery of salvation and rise again into the other, immortal life. 

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
But nevertheless, a doubt remains whether the law began to obligate from the same point at which He, dying, abolished the old one. 

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
For if you grant this, you will seem to contradict the Gospel, since after the resurrection He commanded the Apostles: *Go, preach... baptizing them.* <note>original: "Ite prædicate... baptizantes eos." Matthew 28:19</note> Here it seems He brought the law as if it began to obligate from that time. Likewise, reason does not seem to permit the law to begin obligating immediately from the moment of the passion. For the mystery of salvation, which has two boundaries—namely, **dying to sin** and **rising to a new life**—was not finished at the point of the passion, but in the resurrection, according to that word of Paul in Romans 4: *He was delivered up for our sins and rose again for our justification.* <note>original: "traditus est propter delicta nostra, & resurrexit propter iustificationem nostram." Romans 4:25</note> As we have explained there. 

If, however, we grant that the old law ceased when Christ said, *It is finished* <note>original: "Consummatum est." John 19:30</note>, yet the new law did not begin until after the resurrection, we fall into this pitfall: that for some time the world was without any obligation of law except the natural law, as it was before the written law. This seems most harsh to me; indeed, it seems openly repugnant to the nature of both testaments. For just as in natural things "the corruption of one is the generation of another" <note>A common philosophical maxim of the time: when one thing ceases to exist, another must immediately take its place.</note>, so also the old was not abolished except through the obligation of the new, just as a shadow is abolished by the presence of the sun. This example is very famous among all interpreters of Scripture. 

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Indeed, Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapters 7, 9, and 10, seems to establish this expressly. 

<margin>Response.</margin>
Therefore, it is answered that the saints, and indeed the Apostle, did not establish the moment of the cessation of one law and the obligation of the other at a single point, but regarded the whole three-day period <term>triduum: the three days Christ was in the tomb</term> as one single event.

<column-break/>

But truly, to speak with rigor, first it must be held for certain—due to the reason just given—that the obligation of one shook off the other. Therefore, if the one ceased when Christ said, *It is finished*, then the new began from that point; for then the price of redemption was paid, and the kingdom of heaven was opened. For immediately the Fathers <note>The "Holy Fathers" or righteous souls waiting in Limbo (the Limbo of the Patriarchs).</note> saw the divinity of Christ. 

But because the old law prefigured not only that, but also the resurrection into a new life, we can best say that it did not cease until the resurrection, and the new began from there. Whence **Saint Thomas** [Aquinas], in the 3rd part, question 66, article 2, says: *Baptism,* he says, *received its power when Christ was baptized. But the necessity of using this sacrament was enjoined upon men after the passion and resurrection.* This is both because the figurative sacraments, which baptism and the other sacraments of the new law succeed, were terminated in the passion of Christ, and also because through baptism a man is configured to the passion and resurrection of Christ, insofar as he dies to sin and begins a new life of justice. And therefore it was necessary for Christ first to suffer and rise again before the necessity of configuring oneself to His passion and resurrection was enjoined upon men. 

Whence, the fact that Christ said after the resurrection, *Go, preach*, etc., is not a sign of a law being brought then, but He then commanded the Apostles to promulgate to the whole world that law which **already obligated**, as Saint Thomas says in the 4th book of the *Sentences*, distinction 3, article 5. Indeed, Christ signifies this very thing, adding: *Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.* <note>Matthew 28:20</note> Thus, Christ established the law before the passion, which would obligate after His death; but after the resurrection He commanded the Apostles to spread it abroad, and at Pentecost He sent them power from on high which was necessary for that same function.

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
¶ These things being thus established, we must respond to another doubt that the opinion of **Augustine** brings with it. For truly, if immediately after the passion or resurrection the law was dead, it follows that it was immediately **deadly** <note>In this theological context, "deadly" (mortifera) means that practicing the rituals was now a mortal sin.</note>; therefore it would not be permitted to keep it by any means. The consequence is proven by the reason by which we proved the third conclusion, which is that of Saint Thomas: those ceremonies were from that time forward lies; therefore, whoever kept them would be lying by that very act, just as someone who asserted that Christ was *about to be born*, *about to suffer*, or *about to rise again*. A lie is always a sin. And when it is pernicious, like this one, it becomes lethal. And so the opinion of **Jerome** is to be preferred: that it was not permitted to keep them. But nevertheless...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,

We must stand with Augustine, to whom the Council of Florence (as has been stated) subscribed: and the answer must be that the ceremonies were not then observed as signs of things to come, but in honor of the "burial of the synagogue." <note>This refers to the theological concept that the Old Law should be "buried" with dignity rather than discarded like paganism.</note> If you should ask what the cause of that honor was, the response is that it was so a distinction could be made between the Old Law and **Gentility** <term>Gentility: here meaning paganism or the state of non-Jewish nations who never had the Law of Moses</term>. For if the Old Law had been cast out as suddenly as paganism was, it would have fallen under the suspicion that it was no more holy than paganism. And this was so appropriate that, in my opinion, God for a time concealed from the Apostles themselves the mystery that the legal ceremonies were to be driven out by the Gospel, namely, so that they might observe them more securely. That fact is attested by the history in **Acts 10**, which narrates that Peter, after being shown a linen vessel sent down from heaven full of "common" animals and being commanded to eat, replied: "Far be it, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean." <note>original: "Absit Domine, quia nunquam manducaui omne cōmune & immundum."</note> However, once that cause for honoring the synagogue ceased, it was no longer permitted to observe those same ceremonies. If you ask how much time the "sufficient promulgation of the Gospel" lasted—during which it was permitted to observe those royal rites—the answer is that it certainly began to be promulgated from **Pentecost**. But at what exact point in time the Law was altogether extinguished and became deadly is not certain. Perhaps, as **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus, a major medieval philosopher</note> says, it lasted until the destruction of Jerusalem, which happened nearly forty years after Christ's passion. For I would believe that the Apostles themselves, while living, began to preach the total abolition of the Law. Whatever the point of time may be, it is certain that it had entirely ceased long before the time of Augustine, as he himself teaches in the same **Epistle 19** against Jerome. Therefore, from that time on, it is a crime to return to those ceremonies. 

In this matter, I certainly cannot agree with the contrary opinion of <margin>The opinion of Cajetan.</margin> **Cajetan**, who in Part 3, Question 37, did not refuse to approve the custom of the **Indians** <note>Refers to the indigenous peoples of the Americas or "the Indies"</note> who, though baptized, circumcise themselves—not as if observing an ancient rite, but so that by that religion they might imitate Christ. Truly, the Fathers never dared to <margin>First reason against Cajetan.</margin> concede this after the Passion, except for the reason <margin>Second.</margin> given by Augustine. And the Council of Florence <margin>Third.</margin> simply denies that it is permitted. And Paul says simply: "If you are circumcised, Christ profits you <margin>Last.</margin> nothing." And to imitate Christ in this is to imitate the Law, for the sake of which He Himself suffered it. Nor can it be excused from having the **appearance of evil**. <note>original: "speciem mali"</note> Nor does Cajetan respond adequately to these points. It is a different matter, however, if someone removes that skin for the sake of health. <note>Soto clarifies that medical circumcision is not what he is condemning.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
It remains, therefore, to respond to the arguments posed at the head of the question. Indeed, the authority of the Prophet **Baruch** only means that the Law would be eternal according to its moral precepts, which endure of themselves; but according to its ceremonial ones, it would endure only through the future truths which they prefigured. ¶ Furthermore, the act of Christ, who sent the lepers he had cleansed to the priests, does not prove that the Law was to remain after the Passion, but only that it would endure until then. Indeed, while Christ was preaching before the Passion, the Law ran alongside the Gospel, as we have already asserted above. 

<margin>To the third part of the same argument.</margin>
¶ And to the third part of the same argument, the response is that the literal reasons for the ceremonies were directed toward divine worship; however, that worship was to be transformed into another following the Passion of Christ. Hence, **Circumcision** was changed into **Baptism**, and the **Sabbath** (as was said) into the **Lord's Day**; and the feast of the **Paschal Lamb** into the feast of the **Resurrection**. The feast of **Pentecost**, however, remained. For the Law was given to us in a certain way on that same day—that is, the power of promulgating it was conferred upon the Apostles, just as the ancient Law was given to Moses.

<margin>To the two parts of the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the first two parts of the second argument, a response has been given through the opinion of Augustine explained above. For by that reasoning, it was permitted for Paul to circumcise **Timothy** (who was Jewish on his mother's side) and to purify himself; namely, so that he would not seem to throw away and bury the Law in the same contemptuous way as paganism. And also so that he would not offer a scandal to the tender converts who were not yet sufficiently instructed. 

¶ Regarding the <margin>To the third part: Paul.</margin> third part—namely, the dispute which Paul mentions in **Galatians 2** that occurred between him and Peter—those leaders, as we have said, were in disagreement. The history of Saint Jerome and Augustine on this is very well known and solemn. It happened at **Antioch**, where Peter was communicating with the new Christian converts from the Gentiles—not only in speech, for the Jews would find no occasion for scandal in that, but even at the table, eating with them pork and other common foods forbidden by the Law. He had already learned this was permitted from the vision of the linen sheet shown to him. But when certain recent Jewish Christians arrived there, whom James had sent to him, Peter withdrew from the company of the Gentiles to avoid offending them, and he abstained from those "unlawful" foods. When Paul happened to arrive there and learned of the turmoil of the Gentile Christians—who concluded from Peter's action that legal ceremonies must be kept in Christianity—he rebuked him in the sight of all; because, he says, "he was to be blamed." <note>original: "reprehensibilis erat"</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "death" of the Old Law ceremonies. Having established that there was a transitional period where Jewish rites were permissible but not mandatory, the text now examines a famous dispute between Saint Augustine and Saint Jerome regarding a specific incident in the New Testament (Galatians 2) involving the Apostles Peter and Paul.</meta>

### Question 5 of the Second Book

<margin>Jerome</margin>
**Jerome**, therefore, was of the opinion that the legal ceremonies became "deadly" <note>meaning sinful to perform</note> immediately after the Passion of Christ. He denies that **Peter** actually observed them; rather, he says that Peter only *simulated* <note>original: "simulasse"; here meaning to pretend or act for the sake of appearances</note> keeping them. Consequently, he says that **Paul** did not rebuke Peter in truth, but only in a simulated way for the benefit of the Gentiles.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Saint Augustine**, however, protests against Jerome's opinion on both points. First, he asserts that Peter could licitly <note>lawfully</note> have observed the legal ceremonies, and indeed did observe them. Second, he argues that Peter was truly reprehensible <note>deserving of criticism</note> and was therefore truly rebuked. There are those, however, who take up the defense of Jerome, among whom is <margin>Hadrian</margin> **Hadrian** <note>likely referring to Pope Hadrian VI, a noted theologian</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 1). To support Jerome, they bring forward what Paul himself said: namely, that the Jews and Barnabas "consented to Peter’s simulation." By using this word, it seems to be implied that Peter’s observance was not a true one.

<margin>Double simulation</margin>
Wherefore, they say, a **double simulation** occurs in practice. One type is when a person pretends something is being done which is not actually being done—such as in stage plays—or if someone were to pretend to circumcise himself but did not actually do so. If this is done with the intention of deceiving, it is a sin because it is a lie. But another type of simulation happens when the act is truly performed, yet not for the reason others believe. For example, if someone were to cut away a piece of skin for the sake of health, while those standing around believed it was being cut for the Jewish religion. In this way, they say, **Paul** "simulated" when he circumcised **Timothy** to avoid a scandal, and Peter "simulated" when he abstained from common <note>non-kosher</note> foods.

<margin>Augustine poorly understood by Hadrian</margin>
Hadrian also remarks that Augustine would never have disagreed with Jerome if he had understood him. I, however, would say that Augustine was understood less by this doctor <note>Hadrian</note> than Augustine himself understood Jerome. For Augustine did not believe that Peter’s fault was a lie—namely, that he simulated what he did not do. Rather, Augustine believed that Peter could truly observe the legal rites without simulation, and did observe them in the manner explained above, but that he observed them *more than was right*. It works in Augustine’s favor that Paul did not accuse Peter of *observing* the legal rites, but of *forcing the Gentiles to Judaize* <term>Judaize: to adopt Jewish customs and laws as if they were necessary for salvation under the New Covenant</term>. This means that Peter applied such excessive diligence in their observance that he led converts from the Gentiles into the opinion that the rites had to be kept in the same way and for the same purpose as under the Old Law, as if they had not ceased.

And first, it is proven that observing the legal rites was no crime; otherwise, Paul would never have truly circumcised Timothy merely to avoid scandal, nor would he have purified himself at the persuasion of James. Indeed, he would have instead taught that it was

<column-break/>

not permitted. Furthermore, the fact that Peter was truly reprehensible cannot be denied without doing a very grave <margin>No one can deny that Peter was reprehensible without doing injury to the scripture.</margin> injury to the Scripture. Indeed, if Paul had simply rebuked him in a general sense, one might somehow interpret it as having been done for show; but when he said with such emphasis, "I resisted him to his face, because he was reprehensible" <note>original: "In faciem ei restiti, reprehensibilis erat" (Galatians 2:11)</note>, to deny that he was truly reprehensible, and thus truly rebuked, is to contradict Holy Scripture.

For what <margin>John Mair's quibble</margin> **John Mair** <note>original: "Ioannes Maio."; a prominent Scottish philosopher and theologian</note> says (in Book 4, Distinction 3, Question 1)—that the Scripture does not state that Peter *was* reprehensible, but only that *Paul said* this—is a quibble no less injurious to Scripture than denying it altogether. For since <margin>Argument against Mair</margin> the Catholic faith compels us to confess that whatever the Apostles affirmed is a divine oracle, it follows that it is as true that Peter was reprehensible as it is that Paul affirmed it. Otherwise, if it were permitted (as <margin>Augustine</margin> **Augustine** says) to deny the sense of Scripture which is clearly literal, its entire authority would immediately perish.

<margin>Objection</margin>
If anyone should then infer that Peter’s fault was a "mortal sin" <note>a grave sin that severs one's relationship with God</note>—for leading others into such a false opinion was a serious sin against the faith, which the Apostles supposedly could not commit after being "confirmed" <note>strengthened by the Holy Spirit at Pentecost</note>—<margin>Solution</margin> it is answered that Peter did not think such a great scandal would arise. Therefore, that lack of consideration was a "venial sin" <note>a lesser, pardonable sin</note>.

Finally, how shall we respond to the argument brought forward for Jerome: that Paul called Peter’s action a "simulation"? <margin>Regarding the argument previously suggested for Jerome</margin> It is answered that he did not call it that because it was not a true Jewish act, but because it was not done with a Jewish intention or end—as if it were still a sign of things to come retaining its own power. One must distinguish between the effect Peter had on converts from Judaism and those from the Gentiles. He led the Jews and **Barnabas** to "consent to his simulation"—that is, to withdraw themselves along with him from the company of the Gentiles. But he "forced the Gentiles to Judaize"—that is, to believe they themselves were bound to abstain from pork and other common foods. For this reason, for the sake of emphasis, Paul said that he had even led Barnabas away with him. For since Barnabas had been set apart to preach to the Gentiles, it was less permissible for him to withdraw from the fellowship of the Gentiles.

There yet remains one <margin>Doubt</margin> doubt <note>original: "scrupulus"; literally a small pebble or source of unease</note>: that in Distinction 15, in the canon *Sancta Romana*, Jerome is honorably received, and his doctrines are approved which were written against...
