### Friar Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Law*

He defined Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus, a monk and theologian who was a contemporary and eventually a rival of Jerome</note> and others. How then is **Augustine** preferred over Jerome in this matter, even by the judgment of the Council of Florence? <margin>Response.</margin> It is answered that these views do not conflict at all. Indeed, in the Canon, "The Holy Roman Church," the "palm" <note>symbol of victory or excellence</note> was most deservedly given to **Jerome** against those whom he had defeated as wanderers from the faith. And for that reason, he is received as a solemn Doctor of the Church. However, Augustine was not placed above him in all the things he disputed there, even though his teaching is looked upon with similar honor. <margin>To the last part of the second main argument.</margin> <margin>Triple solution of Saint Thomas.</margin> ¶ Regarding the last part of that same second argument, which seeks the meaning of the Apostolic Council in Acts chapter 15, **Saint Thomas [Aquinas]** brought forward three solutions. <margin>Vain interpretation of those who understand the sanctions of the apostolic Council spiritually.</margin> The first is of certain people who thought those decrees of the Council were by no means to be understood in the literal sense, but in the spiritual: namely, that in the prohibition of "blood," murder is understood to be forbidden; in the prohibition of "strangled meat," violence and robbery are inhibited; but in the prohibition of "meat sacrificed to idols," idolatry is meant. However, this way of interpreting is vain <note>original: "vanus"; meaning empty or without substance</note>. For since those crimes were considered illicit even among the Gentiles, and were also explicit in the Decalogue <note>the Ten Commandments</note>, there was no reason why a Council should be assembled again regarding them. <margin>The second explanation is rejected.</margin> The second was the opinion of others: that these things were forbidden in the literal sense, not for the observance of the Law, but to restrain gluttony. But truly, since there were other greater inducements to gluttony of which no mention was made there, it is not to be believed that gluttony was the cause of the prohibition. For what enticement to gluttony is found in strangled meats or things sacrificed to idols? <margin>The true interpretation drawn from history.</margin> Therefore, history itself teaches us the legitimate solution. For indeed, when converts from Judaism—and especially the Pharisees—contended fiercely to retain circumcision and the rest of the ceremonies along with the Gospel, the Apostles, meeting in Council about that matter, decreed that circumcision and the legal observances <note>term: "legalia"; the specific rituals and dietary laws of the Old Testament</note> were not to be observed by the Gentiles, nor was the honor of a "synagogue burial" <note>a metaphor for showing respectful transition away from Jewish rites</note> to be granted to them. But nevertheless, on account of the stubbornness of the Jews, they forbade those four things to the same Gentiles: not as if the observance of the Old Law were necessary, but so that commerce <note>social interaction and fellowship</note> could be entered into between the Christians of both peoples. It was therefore forbidden to them to abstain from meats sacrificed to idols, namely, lest they come under suspicion of idolatry among the converts from Judaism. For this reason, some have falsely thought that "idolatry" was what was forbidden there; for it was well known to all

<column-break/>

that idolatry was execrable <note>detestable</note> to the Gospel. Nevertheless, because the priests of the Gentiles held a market for meat sacrificed to idols, Christians were forbidden from using those foods. Second, they were forbidden to eat blood and strangled meat: things which the Jews so abhorred that it would cause them nausea if anyone used such feasts in their sight. Furthermore, **fornication** was specifically forbidden to them: not because it was not already forbidden by natural law, but because the Gentiles, covered by the darkness of the mind, recognized no fault in "free love" <note>original: "libera Venere"; referring to casual sexual acts which Greeks and Romans often did not consider sinful</note>, nor was it explicitly clear in the Decalogue <note>Soto notes that while "adultery" is in the Ten Commandments, the status of sex between unmarried people was less clear to the Gentiles</note>. <margin>First argument against the previous solution.</margin> ¶ However, arguments exist against this solution. First, if those things were not forbidden for the sake of observing the Law, it did not satisfy the question of the Jews, who contended that the legal rituals should run alongside the Gospel. <margin>Second.</margin> Second, because it is held in the Council itself: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than these *necessary* things." If, therefore, it was "necessary," the necessity proceeded from the Law. <margin>Third.</margin> Third, because if blood and strangled meat were forbidden for that reason, then the eating of swine’s flesh and other common foods ought to have been forbidden equally. <margin>To the arguments made.</margin> To these things it is answered that the Apostles did not respond to the Pharisees according to the Pharisees' own mind; rather, they granted those prohibitions to pacify their sedition and tumult; and for this end, they judged them to be "necessary." They forbade those two—namely, blood and strangled meat—which were more hated by the Jews; but they did not forbid swine's flesh or other types of game and fish because it would be extremely bothersome for the Gentiles to be deprived of their use on account of the Jews. And therefore the holy Council said: "to impose no further burden upon you than these necessary things." But all of this doctrine is easily gathered from the words of **Paul** in 1 Corinthians 8, where he teaches that the eating of meat sacrificed to idols is not illicit in itself, but because of the scandal <note>original: "scandalum"; an obstacle to the faith of others</note> of the weak; in this way, he declared the Council's decree. He teaches the same in Romans 14, where he says all foods are clean except on account of scandal or conscience. And in Matthew 15, **Christ** says: "Not what enters through the mouth defiles a man." <margin>Corollary.</margin> ¶ And from these things, it follows that the prohibition was not made forever, but for a time—and a very short time at that—while the Christian people were coalescing, until the Jewish people could set aside that horror of those foods. Therefore, the force of that Council expired either in the age of the Apostles itself or shortly thereafter. <margin>Argument: The Council of Gangra.</margin> ¶ Nevertheless, a Canon of the **Council of Gangra** <note>a 4th-century provincial council</note>, "If anyone" (Distinction 30), seems to oppose this opinion, where it is held...

# QUESTION SIX.
## Regarding the judicial mandates.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* I-II, Questions 104 and 105.<-

### ARTICLE I.
#### *Whether judicial precepts are correctly distinguished from ceremonial ones.*

<margin>First argument.</margin> <image-desc>The letter T is decorated with an architectural scene.</image-desc>The third genus of precepts, as we established in the previous sections, is that of the <term>judicial precepts</term> <note>these are the laws in the Old Testament governing civil life, property, and punishments, distinct from religious rituals or universal moral laws</note>. Regarding these, it is first asked in what ways they are distinguished from the <term>ceremonial precepts</term> <note>laws governing religious rituals, sacrifices, and purity</note>. And first, it is argued that they do not differ in the way stated above—namely, that ceremonial laws pertain to divine worship while judicial laws pertain to the peaceful coexistence among citizens. This is argued because judicial laws, as the name implies, are those handled in the court before a judge, and yet outside the court there are other things that contribute to that same peaceful state. Furthermore, just as among the ceremonial laws there were some that ordered a person toward himself—such as the choice of foods and clothing—so too it was fitting that among the judicial laws there should be some precept-

<column-break/>

ion that pertained to the individual person specifically; therefore, not all judicial laws pertained to justice, which is the relationship of one citizen to another. ¶ <margin>Second</margin> Secondly, it is argued against another difference that is usually established between these precepts: namely, that ceremonial laws were established to be signs, figures, and shadows of things to come, whereas judicial laws were not. For the commentators on the judicial laws in Exodus 21 and 22 interpret all of them allegorically and morally as well. ¶ <margin>Third.</margin> And from this, a third argument is gathered against the third difference that is customarily applied: namely, that it is no longer permitted to observe the ceremonial laws, but it is different for the judicial ones. For if the judicial laws were signs of future things, they ought to have ceased in the same way as the ceremonial ones. Hence the Apostle [Paul] says generally in Hebrews 7: <margin>Paul.</margin> "When the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law take place." ¶ To the contrary, however, is the fact that interpreters of the Law are accustomed to distinguish these three differences among such precepts.

ALMOST all of these matters have been discussed and defined in the previous sections; but so that a summary of them may be placed before the eyes, they are repeated. Let us therefore assume the distinction, explained more than once in the preceding pages, between <term>moral precepts</term> on one side and the other two genera on the other. For we have already said that moral precepts are those gathered from natural principles by way of logical inference. Ceremonial and judicial precepts, however, are those established only by a certain <term>determination</term> <note>original: "arbitramento," referring to the specific application of a general principle to a concrete rule</note> from a general precept by way of specification. For example, if we say: "God is to be worshipped," therefore, He is to be worshipped in this or that way. "A wrongdoer is to be punished," therefore, by this or that punishment. ¶ To the question, therefore, it is answered with three conclusions expressing the triple distinction between ceremonial and judicial laws. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> **First conclusion.** The logic of the judicial precepts consists in two things: first, that it is not inferred from the principles of nature as a direct conclusion (and in this they differ from moral laws and agree with ceremonial laws). Second, that they look toward the coexistence of men with one another (and in this they move away from the ceremonial). Indeed, just as from the principle that God is to be worshipped, these or those sacrifices were instituted by divine choice—which in their own nature had no reference to morality—so too from the principle that peace must be guarded in the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "respublica"</note> according to one's strength, the judicial laws were gathered: such as that he who steals one sheep should pay back four, and that a night-thief might be killed in the act, but a day-thief by no means, and so on. These things, however...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
This conclusion has been so commonly addressed up to now that it would be tedious to linger on it as if stuck in a rut. ¶ **The second conclusion.** Judicial precepts <note>original: "præcepta iudicialia"; these are the civil and legal statutes of the Old Testament, such as property laws</note> are distinguished from ceremonial ones in a second way: ceremonial laws were established as a figure and shadow of things to come, whereas judicial laws were only so as a consequence.
<margin>The conclusion is derived from the previous one.</margin>
For this distinction takes its origin from the first conclusion. Indeed, since the worship practiced by the ancient fathers pertained to the sanctity of the people—a sanctity which depended on Christ the mediator—it was fitting and necessary, as explained above, that they profess his future coming through those same ceremonies. However, since judicial laws were established not for divine worship, but for fostering justice and equity among citizens, reason did not require them to be prognostications of the same future Messiah. Nevertheless, because the entire status of that people was in expectation of the same coming God, those same judicial laws, as a consequence, offered some shadow of him, according to the word of Paul in 1 Corinthians 10: *All these things happened to them as a figure.* <note>Soto is quoting the Vulgate version of 1 Corinthians 10:11, where "figura" implies a symbolic precursor.</note> **Examples:** The payment of tithes signified the perfection—designated by the final unit of ten—that was to be attributed to Christ. And that passage in Exodus 21, stating that a Hebrew servant should be free in the seventh year after six years of service, prefigured the heavenly freedom that will follow the struggle of this world, which will be the perfect Sabbath. For this reason, the judgments of the Gentiles, such as those of the Greeks and Romans, contained no hidden mystery like the laws of the Hebrews.
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The third conclusion.** Although the judicial precepts have been so entirely emptied and extinguished that they are in no way obligatory after the resurrection of Christ, they differ in a third way from ceremonial laws: while it is no longer permitted to observe ceremonial laws in any way, it is nevertheless permitted to re-establish judicial laws.
<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The first part of this conclusion has already been sufficiently demonstrated above, where we showed that the entire law has ceased regarding its Mosaic authority. The second part, however, is gathered from the second conclusion, just as the second was from the first. For the reason why it is not permitted to revive ceremonies now is the one assigned above: since they were prognostic signs of future things, now that the truth is present, they have become false lies. Since this reason is not found in judicial laws—because they were not established primarily

<column-break/>

to signify something—there is no danger if they are established again under the New Law. For this reason, tithes were established by the Church, which were judicial in terms of their specific portion <note>original: "quota"; referring to the specific 10% amount</note>; laws of retaliation <note>original: "talionis"; the 'eye for an eye' principle</note> have occasionally been established, as has the requirement to return fourfold for a simple theft, and similar things. All these are very easy to understand and clear from what has been said before.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**To the first argument**, therefore, it is answered: although "judicial laws" are named after "judgment" because it belongs to the prince (who holds the power of judging) to organize the commonwealth, it nonetheless falls to the same prince not only to resolve disputes, but also to deliberately enact laws regarding voluntary contracts. Thus, not only those matters handled in court, but also those in the home and in the commerce of citizens, are called "judicial."
<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ **To the second part** of the same argument, it is answered that the nature of ceremonial and judicial laws is different. For since worship pertains to God, toward whom man is ordered as his own proper end, it follows that man refers himself to that same worship by regulating himself in food and clothing; for this reason, there was a ceremonial precept regarding this. However, man is not ordered toward his neighbor as toward an end, but they are like two members of a whole. Therefore, there was no need for a judicial precept regarding a man’s relationship to himself; rather, all such laws ordered him toward another. The solutions to other arguments are sufficiently clear from the preceding text.

### ARTICLE II.

->*Whether the judicial precepts are appropriately divided into four kinds.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'P' depicting two figures in classical dress engaged in a conversation within an architectural setting.</image-desc>
**After** the distinction of the judicial from the ceremonial, it follows that we should speak of their division among themselves: namely, whether they were distributed in a fourfold way. Specifically: some that instructed princes in relation to subjects; others regarding subjects toward one another; a third kind that organized the people in relation to foreign nations; and finally others that fostered domestic harmony within the family.

# Book Two, Question VI. 169

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The first argument is as follows: The supreme power of a commonwealth consists of the high priest and those assisting him in spiritual matters, and the king in temporal matters. <margin>Aristotle</margin> For according to Aristotle in the 7th book of his *Politics*, this is the best form of government, as it is most effectively unified and thus bears the most distinct resemblance to divine governance. Therefore, fitting laws should have been established for these two powers above all else; however, we do not read that this was the case in the Old Law. For just as God chose Aaron himself, as is clear in Exodus 28, and commanded that tithes be paid to the Levites for their support (as written in the final chapter of Leviticus), He ought also to have created the king Himself. Yet He did not do this, but left it to the people. For it says in Deuteronomy 17 <note>original: "Deuter. 27"; the text cites chapter 27, but the law for kings is in chapter 17</note>: *When you say, "I will set a king over me," then you shall set him whom the Lord your God chooses.* Nor did He designate salaries for kings. Furthermore, from the time of Moses until Saul—a period of four hundred years—the people remained with priests but without a king; God only permitted a king then for the people's own misfortune, as recorded in 1 Samuel 8 <note>original: "2. Reg. 8"; in older Bibles, 1 & 2 Samuel were called 1 & 2 Kings</note>.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued that the judicial statutes regarding the social life of citizens among themselves were not fittingly established. For it was commanded in Numbers 27 that if a man died without a son, his inheritance should pass to his daughter; and yet <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle, in the 2nd book of his *Politics*, chapter 7, says that kingdoms and possessions will be ruined if they pass to women. Furthermore, in Leviticus 25 <note>original: "Leuit. 22"</note>, it was held that in the Year of Jubilee <note>a sacred year every 50 years when debts were forgiven and land returned to original owners</note> all sold possessions should return to their original owners. This seemed to stand in the way of the stability of contracts, without which mortals cannot live together. Also, in Exodus 21, the law of retaliation <note>term: lex talionis; the principle of "an eye for an eye"</note> was established, so that the guilty party should give an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth—the excessive harshness of which Christ pointed out in Matthew 5. There were also other legal sanctions among that people which seemed absurd.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, those judgments found therein regarding foreign nations seem unsuitable. For it is written in Deuteronomy 23: *The Ammonites and Moabites, even after the tenth generation, shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord forever.* And yet, conversely, it is added: *You shall not abhor the Edomite.* This certainly seems to involve a "respect of persons" <note>favoritism based on identity rather than merit</note>, which, as stated in Acts 10, does not exist with God. Also, in Exodus 22 <note>original: "Exod. 20"</note>, it is cautioned: *You shall not wrong a stranger, nor afflict him.* Nevertheless, in Deuteronomy 23, that same people was permitted to lend money to foreigners at interest <note>term: usura; the practice of charging interest on loans, which was forbidden between fellow Israelites</note>; these two precepts seem to contradict each other.

<column-break/>

<margin>Argument 4</margin>
¶ Fourthly, the judicial precepts regarding household members do not seem sufficiently consistent with reason. First, regarding servants, we read in Exodus 21: *If someone strikes his male or female servant with a rod, and they survive for a day or two, he shall not be subject to punishment, because they are his money.* Nature itself recoils at leaving a killer unpunished; for this reason, human laws punish masters who kill their servants quite severely. Regarding children, that law in Deuteronomy 21 seems harsh: namely, that a father should bring his own son to the elders of the city to be punished <note>referring to the law regarding a rebellious son</note>. Finally, regarding wives, the law which permitted a bill of divorce (as found in Deuteronomy 24) seems destructive to the nature of marriage, which ought to be permanent for the sake of raising children.

¶ On the contrary is what Divine Wisdom says in Proverbs 8: *All my words are righteous; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them.* And David says: *The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.*

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], Summa Theologiae, 1-2, q. 105.</margin>
<margin>Responding conclusion.</margin>
Do not think that we have brought up this question so that we might discuss it as extensively as it reaches; for St. Thomas, as is universally acknowledged, completed that task with nearly divine genius in Question 105 of the *Prima Secundae*. However, so that we do not break the thread of our own discourse, it is fitting for us to pass through these points in summary.

We have decided, therefore, to respond with a single conclusion. It was necessary to distribute the judicial precepts of the Old Law into four members. Indeed, since the prudence of making laws is a most illustrious art, and art shines through order and arrangement, it was appropriate that the number of judicial laws by which the commonwealth was established be arranged according to the notable parts and ranks of that same commonwealth.

<margin>The fourfold order among the parts of the commonwealth: namely, the Prince to the subjects, the subjects among themselves, the whole commonwealth to foreigners, and the components of the household.</margin>
These ranks are four in number: namely, the Prince to the subjects, the subjects among themselves, the whole commonwealth to foreigners, and the parts of the parts—that is, the members of a single family. Therefore, laws were divinely enacted regarding princes: how they were to be chosen, how they should conduct themselves toward the people, and subsequently, how they in turn should be honored by the people.

Next, laws were enacted regarding the citizens concerning buying and selling, and other contracts that are freely made among men; and likewise, judgments were decreed against wrongdoers who would violate those rights.

Then, laws were applied regarding how the people should conduct themselves toward foreign nations, both in waging war and in receiving travelers.

And finally, regarding the domestic family...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, it is therefore answered that in the governance of a commonwealth, two considerations must be maintained. The first is that all citizens should participate in the selection of magistrates and the management of public affairs. For by this logic, as Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> writes in the second book of his *Politics*, equity is established, and peace follows within the commonwealth. The second consideration is that the best form of rule should be chosen. According to the same Philosopher in the third book of the *Politics*, out of the three species of government—namely Aristocracy, Democracy, and Monarchy—this last one is the most excellent. Through His divine wisdom, God preserved all these elements regarding the leaders of His people. First, because He took special care of that people—according to Deuteronomy 7: *The Lord your God has chosen you to be a special people to Himself* <note>original: "Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, vt sis ei populus peculiaris"</note>—He reserved the election of the king for Himself. Thus, just as He Himself created the high priest, so also He says of the king in the cited place of Deuteronomy: *When you say, "I will set a king over me," you shall set him whom the Lord your God chooses from among your brothers.* <note>original: "Cùm dixeris, constituam super me regem, eum constitues quem Dominus Deus tuus elegerit de numero fratrum tuorum." See Deuteronomy 17:15.</note> For this reason, kings were anointed by the Prophets by divine command. However, since a monarchy is the best government when the king excels in suitable virtues, so it becomes the most poisonous when it corrupts into tyranny. Because that people was both cruel and greedy and lustful—vices by which a king is most easily corrupted—God delayed giving them a king with full power for four hundred years. Nevertheless, He governed the people in the likeness of a monarchy through a single individual, such as through Moses and his successors, the judges, until the people—as if shaking off divine rule—wished to create a king for themselves. Hence, in 1 Samuel 8, God says to Samuel: *They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.* <note>original: "Non te abiecerunt, sed me, nè regnem super eos"</note> Behold how diligent God was in maintaining the best government of a kingdom. Therefore, the outcome of the matter itself shows how much an absolute royal power was introduced against His will. For immediately under Rehoboam <note>The son of Solomon whose harsh rule led to the rebellion of the ten northern tribes.</note>, the divided kingdom brought about the cause of its own desolation, according to the word of Christ: *Every kingdom divided against itself will be brought to desolation.* <note>original: "Omne regnum in seipsum diuisum desolabitur"</note> ¶ Regarding Aristocracy, which is the power of the best men, He ordered seventy men to be chosen from the elders of Israel, as is clear in Numbers 11; hence Deuteronomy 1: *I took the wise and noble men from your tribes and appointed them as leaders.* As for Democracy, which is popular power, He willed it to be preserved to the extent 

<column-break/>

that the whole people would create the magistrates and they would be chosen from all the tribes. Hence Exodus 18: *Provide wise men from all the people.* And Deuteronomy 1: *Choose wise men from among you,* etc. Furthermore, the reason why tithes were awarded to the priests and not to the princes was that it was fitting for priests to be established from one singular tribe so they would be held in greater reverence, and therefore they had to be supported by the others. Secular princes, however, were chosen indiscriminately from all tribes, for whom land possessions were decreed. Moreover, their stipends increased according to the needs of wars, and then nature itself taught that the contributions from the people should be increased for them. <margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ Regarding the subject of the second argument, it should be noted that judicial laws—which serve the quiet of human citizens—are divided into two orders, following the two types of communication and exchange of things that exist among a people. For one type of communication is done by the public authority of the prince, and another by the private will of each person. Indeed, men are subjects to the prince, but possessions belong to the domain of private individuals. Therefore, judgments by which men are compelled to observe rights, and punishments by which crimes are avenged, are instituted by the authority of the prince; however, the giving and exchanging of things are celebrated by the private will of each individual. God ordained the best judicial laws for both orders for the ancient people. For He established, regarding the first, judges and masters, as is clear in Deuteronomy 16, as well as the number of witnesses and various punishments for various crimes. And regarding the second, so that peace might be more firmly established among them, He divided the land of promise for them. Hence Numbers 34: *I have given you the land for a possession, which you shall divide among yourselves by lot; to the more you shall give a larger inheritance, and to the fewer a smaller one.* But regarding its use, He willed the fruits to be in some way common, according to that passage in Deuteronomy 23: *When you enter your neighbor's vineyard, eat as many grapes as you please.* Many other things He thereafter established most beautifully, as can be seen in the works of St. Thomas [Aquinas]. <margin>To the form of the argument.</margin> ¶ To the form of the argument, therefore, it is answered that God preserved the law of nature in the succession of inheritance to the extent that He did not want women to enter into the right of inheritance unless a male heir was lacking. For the succession of a patrimony ought to follow the nature of generation, through which the species is propagated; however, the power of generation resides in the loins of the man, to whom the woman is, as it were, naturally subordinate. ### Question VI of the Second Book

<margin>The most powerful reason why the right of masculine primogeniture is passed down.</margin>
...the male offspring, into whom the generative power is transferred, the inheritance passes, which he transmits with his blood to his descendants. And I judge this to be the first of all natural causes why the rights of primogeniture in well-ordered commonwealths are transferred through the male line, and women are not admitted except in the absence of males. To this is added a second reason: that the prudence of a man excels that of a woman, both in other matters and also in increasing the family estate. As <margin>Aristotle</margin> says in the third book of the *Politics*, chapter 3: "It is the man’s role to acquire, and the woman’s to preserve." <note>original: "viri inquit est acquirere, mulieris autem feruare"</note> For this reason, in the second book of the *Ethics*, he had judged that kingdoms perish in the hands of a woman. There is a third reason: since the administration of the estate belongs to the man, when an inheritance falls to a daughter, the son-in-law is then not as diligent in increasing the father-in-law's estate and magnifying his name as a son would be. Therefore, while the property that passes to a daughter subsequently passes to a son-in-law, it is in a sense considered to migrate into foreign blood. In the Old Law, however, this was necessary so that the partition of possessions made among the tribes would not be confused. Although in such an event, care was taken that a female heir should not marry anyone other than a man of her own tribe. <note>This refers to the case of the daughters of Zelophehad in Numbers 36.</note> Truly, among Christians, daughters ought not to be cast so far out of succession that they are not admitted even when sons are lacking. For by this reasoning, primogenitures are usually alienated further than if women <margin>Reason for the law of the Jubilee year.</margin> succeeded. ¶ By the same reasoning, another law was added regarding the year of Jubilee: for if sales were made in perpetuity, the division of possessions among the tribes would not have been permanent. Indeed, natural reason certainly does not shrink from this: for by that reasoning—as Aristotle warns in the place recently cited—namely, if possessions are divided in perpetuity, wealth tends to be <margin>Reason for the law of retaliation.</margin> heaped up in one place and leaves others poor. ¶ Moreover, the law of retaliation <note>The *lex talionis*, or "eye for an eye."</note> was not at all inappropriate for that vengeful nation: so that through it, though it seemed somewhat harsh, they might be restrained from avenging themselves too sharply against enemies; although Christ taught that such things do not suit Christian kindness. Regarding other matters, see the works of Saint <margin>To the third argument.</margin> Thomas Aquinas. ¶ Regarding the third argument, it must likewise be noted that a commonwealth can conduct itself in two ways toward foreigners: namely, either by the law of peace, if it weaves commerce with them, or by the law of war, if they are enemies. And by the law of peace, foreign nations approached the Jewish people in three ways. First, as those making a transit like travelers: regarding whom the law stood in Exodus 23: *You shall not wrong a stranger.* <note>original: "Peregrino molestus non eris."</note> In the second way, so that

<column-break/>

they might live among them as sojourners: regarding whom it was also stated in chapter 20, *You shall not distress a stranger.* <note>original: "Aduenam nō contristabis."</note> In the third way, because they wished to be admitted entirely into their rite and fellowship. Among these, an order was distinguished according to natural reason. For the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> warns in the third book of the *Politics* that foreigners are not to be rashly received into the commonwealth unless they are descended from a grandfather or great-great-grandfather; otherwise, many dangers would threaten the commonwealth from them. For this reason, because the Edomites descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob, and the Israelites themselves had lived as strangers among the Egyptians for more than two hundred years, they were commanded to receive them peacefully, and to mark proselytes who wished to profess their religion with the sign of circumcision. But truly, because the Amalekites were their perpetual enemies—according to that passage in Exodus 27: *The war of God was against Amalek from generation to generation* <note>original: "bellū Dei erat cōtra Amalech à generatiōe in generationē." See Exodus 17:16.</note>—and likewise the Ammonites and Moabites had been expelled from the land of promise, God could drive them away from His commonwealth without respect of persons. ¶ But also regarding war against enemies, whether initiating or sustaining it, a most holy law was written in Deuteronomy 20: first, that they should offer them peace. Second, that they should cast their trust upon God Himself. Third, that they should send home those who were unfit or who might be an impediment. Fourth, finally, that they should use victory modestly: <margin>To the fourth argument.</margin> sparing women and children. ¶ Finally, to the fourth argument, it is answered that since the family consists of three orders—namely, husband to wife, parent to children, and master to servants—God saw to <margin>Laws of servants.</margin> it that excellent laws were enacted concerning all three. And first regarding servants (slaves), which pertained to mitigating their labors, it was commanded in Deuteronomy 5 that they should rest on the Sabbath day just as their masters did. Likewise, in memory of the liberation from Egypt, where they themselves had served, and as a foreshadowing of Christian liberty, and especially for the sake of brotherly charity, it was cautioned in Exodus 21 that no one from the sons of Israel should be a servant perpetually: but in the seventh year he should go out free, with all that they had brought with them, having been provided with travel supplies besides, as read in Deuteronomy 15. Nor was God negligent regarding their protection: indeed, in the same chapter 21, He established that a master who mutilated a servant should let him go free, as well as a maidservant whom he had taken as a wife. However, that which was objected in the argument—namely, that the killer of a servant escapes unpunished—was understood to apply when he had struck with a rod for the sake of correction, not with the intention of wounding; nor was it certain afterward whether...

# QUESTION SEVEN,
->On the Gospel law regarding its substance.<-

->St. Thomas, Part 1-2, Question 106.<-

## ARTICLE I.
->Whether the new law is a written law, or rather one instilled in hearts.<-

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'Q' with floral and classical architectural motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
WE HAVE DISTINCTLY SHOWN four types of laws near the beginning of the previous book: namely, the eternal, the natural, and the human (which were discussed in Book 1), and finally the divine law, which we have undertaken to elucidate in this book. This divine law we have divided into the Old and the New. Since the former has been discussed up to this point, it follows that we should weave together a discourse on the New Law, which is the Gospel Law. This law (if you except the eternal law) is the "law of laws," for whose sake the world was created, for the delivery of which God himself descended from heaven, and which is written by the finger of that same God in our hearts. It is through this law alone that the gates of hell are closed to the whole world, and souls are directed toward the eternal happiness of heaven. Therefore, so that we may weigh this celestial law in all its parts and dignities: It is first asked whether it should be called a "written law," like human laws and the old divine law, or whether, like the natural law is impressed by nature, so this law is supernaturally impressed upon our minds.

<column-break/>

For there are several arguments that it is a written law. First: this law is the <margin>First argument.</margin> Gospel itself; yet concerning this, John says in chapter 20: "But these things are written, so that you may believe." <note>original: "Hæc autem ſcripta ſunt, vt credatis"</note> <margin>Argument 2.</margin> Second: If this law were not written but instilled, it would not differ at all from natural law; for of the natural law the Prophet says: "The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us." <note>original: "Signatum eſt ſuper nos lumen vultus tui Domine," Psalm 4:6</note> <margin>Argument 3.</margin> Third: The Gospel law is proper to Christians, whereas the instilled law is open to all nations in common. For we read in Wisdom 7 that divine wisdom transfers itself through the nations into holy souls and constitutes them friends of God and Prophets; therefore, the New Law is not an instilled law. <margin>Jeremiah.</margin> On the contrary, however, the prophecy of Jeremiah in chapter 31 bears witness: where God, designating our law, says: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will consummate a new covenant upon the house of Israel and upon the house of Jacob." Explaining this covenant, he adds: "I will give my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their hearts." <margin>Paul.</margin> And Paul, in Hebrews 8, alleges this for this very purpose, and in 2 Corinthians 3, he discusses it more extensively.

This question, arising from these recently cited testimonies of Scripture among Catholic doctors, serves to commend the primary excellence of our law. Let us therefore establish the conclusion which is most widely accepted by all Catholics: Our law differs from the old in this, <margin>Catholic conclusion.</margin> that while the old was written on stone tablets, ours is inscribed in hearts. However, to reveal the full meaning of this conclusion is not entirely straightforward. For <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine, in his book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 21, considers it to pertain only to this: that the charity of God—which according to Paul is both the fullness and the end of the law—is "poured out into our hearts," as the same Apostle says, through the Holy Spirit. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> Following him, St. Thomas interprets the conclusion thus: Every thing, he says (as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle is the author in Book 9 of the *Ethics*), seems to be that which is most principal in it. In the law of the New Testament, this principal element is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is given through faith in Christ and is the power to fulfill the law; according to Romans 8: "The law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death." Since this grace is infused within our hearts by God, it follows that the law itself is principally fixed in our hearts. Nevertheless, those things which are to be believed and done are proposed to us in the sacred pages. By this reasoning, it can be called "written" in a secondary sense. However, there is a need to discuss these things more fully...

# Book Two, Question VII.

<margin>First argument against the previous statements.</margin>
...to be [more] fully explained: since arguments will immediately be offered from the opposite side. First, that the virtue of law is to instruct and direct the intellect, and to illuminate minds: however, this virtue is made clear through scripture in the Gospel, just as it was to the ancients in their own canon <note>The "canon" here refers to the body of Old Testament law.</note>: therefore, there is no reason why our law should not be called "written" just as theirs was.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
The second argument is that both charity and grace were divinely infused into the hearts of the ancients as much as into ours, by whose virtue they observed the law: therefore, there is no reason why that law should be called "instilled" any less than ours.

<margin>Two virtues of law.</margin>
¶ For a fuller understanding of this, two virtues of law must be distinguished: one is directive, by which the intellect is illuminated so that it may know what is right; and the other is affective and motive of the will for acting. And according to both, the Gospel law <term>lex Euangelica</term> <note>The "New Law" of the New Testament, contrasted with the Mosaic Law of the Old.</note> is singularly inscribed within the mind. For a person can be taught the law in two ways. One way is by reading scripture, and the other by hearing a living voice. And this is the more excellent way: since hearing, as 

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Sense and the Sensible*.</margin>
the Philosopher <note>A standard title for Aristotle in this period.</note> says in his book *On the Sense and the Sensible*, is the sense of learning. And indeed, the law was given to the ancients in the first way: namely, written on stone tablets, which the subjects there looking upon might follow. But God did not send ours to us written in such a way from heaven, but he himself, having descended from there, published it by his living voice into the ears of mortals, and impressed it upon the mind: that is, he persuaded them by the energy of his speech and the power of miracles. Nor indeed does he daily engrave it in us merely in a human manner, but he also supernaturally generates within us the assent of faith, which things from above reveal to us. Thus, since the generation of faith requires two things—namely, that the things to be believed be proposed, and that the intellect grant them its assent—Christ accomplished both for us without writing. Although for that first duty he joined ministers to himself: namely, the Apostles and their successors, who were his helpers in preaching the same faith and law. 

<margin>Paul.</margin>
And this is what the Apostle <note>St. Paul.</note> says in 2 Corinthians 3: *You are our letter, written in our hearts*: that is, fixed in our hearts through charity. But explaining how they were a letter, he adds: *You are shown to be a letter of Christ, ministered by us*. That is: Although we proposed the things to be believed to you, Christ is nonetheless the one who engraved the assent of faith in you. Therefore, as much as pertains to the illumination of the intellect, which is the first virtue of law, our law is primarily written in our mind through its own power, because the assent of faith is the work of God. But because those things which are proposed to the intellect in the ab-

<column-break/>

sence of Christ and the Apostles might slip from memory, it is written "by accident" <term>per accidens</term> <note>Meaning writing is a secondary necessity caused by human weakness, rather than being the essential form of the Gospel.</note>. For if the voice of the Lord always sounded in our ears, we would have no need for scripture. Wherefore, as Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> is the authority in his prologue to Matthew, we ought to use the grace of the Holy Spirit in place of books: but because we have cast that grace aside, letters were invented. For Christ handed nothing down to the Apostles in writing. ¶ But also as much as pertains to the other virtue of law, which is to affect and move the will to action, it is likewise written within: since we cannot fulfill the law to the end intended by the one commanding it except through the grace and favor of God. For the law only shows what we ought to do: immediately taking away, as we said above, any excuse: for which reason Paul says "the letter kills": but the power of acting is supplied to us through grace and charity. For which reason he adds, "the Holy Spirit gives life." And this is what John says: *The law was given through Moses*—that is, written on tablets in which there was no power to act—*but grace and truth* (for purifying hearts, which is the end of the law) *came through Jesus Christ*.

**These** things being established, the solutions to the arguments are very easy. 

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
For to the first it is answered that in both the Old and New Law those things are written which pertain to the faith and grace of the Holy Spirit: namely, both those things which lead to knowing the divinity of God and the humanity of Christ, as well as those things to be done by which charity is preserved. This faith and charity were given to them in their hearts under that testament just as they are impressed under ours. However, since both there and here that impression was made by the virtue of one mediator, the difference is that in the Old Law, that mediator was not yet present—he had not yet preached by himself, nor had the sacraments of that law yet received the power of his passion (which had not yet occurred) to confer grace. But our law was handed down to us by Christ himself, and the Holy Spirit declared it to the Apostles; accordingly, the sacraments infuse that same charity and grace into us. Thus, our law is deservedly judged as "innate in hearts" compared to the old, just as the old was "on tablets." Whence Paul does not simply say "in hearts," but "in fleshy hearts": so that he might allude to the stone tablets, signifying the hardness of the hearts of that people, whereas through the charity of the new law, hearts, being "fleshy," are softened.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument it is answered that the natural law is instilled...

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
...was instilled in hearts by a natural path; but the law of grace was instilled supernaturally. ¶ And to the third argument, the answer has now been given: that not only under the written law, but not even under the Law of Nature <note>The moral law discoverable by human reason alone, prior to the laws of Moses.</note>, did anyone ever receive the grace of the Holy Spirit except through faith in Christ. And therefore, although the same wisdom of faith justified all who were righteous from the time of Adam until now, it is nevertheless uniquely considered "inscribed in hearts" because of the presence of that very Author of grace <note>Referring to Jesus Christ as the source of grace.</note>.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether the New Law justifies.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' containing an illustration of a seated figure (likely a saint or scholar) at a writing desk.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
THE SECOND excellence of our law is sought from its effect; and therefore it is asked whether it possesses the power of justifying. For it is argued on the negative side: No one is made righteous except through obedience to the divine law, according to the passage in Hebrews 5: *Christ became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him.* However, the Gospel does not universally ensure that it is obeyed, as Paul testifies in Romans 10: *Not all obey the Gospel.* Therefore, the New Law has no more power to justify than the Old Law did.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, Paul proves in Romans that the Old Law did not justify because, when that law arrived, transgression increased. For he says in Chapter 4: *The law works wrath. For where there is no law, there is no transgression.* But the New Law aggravates transgression much more severely, because a person who sins after the New Law—which makes the divine will known more clearly—is worthy of a greater penalty. This is according to Hebrews 10: *Anyone who set aside the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses; how much worse punishment do you think he deserves who has trampled the Son of God underfoot?* Therefore, the New Law justifies even less than the Old.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third, to justify is a task peculiar to God, according to the word of Paul in Romans 8: *It is God who justifies.* But the Old Law, just like the New, was brought forth with God as its author; therefore, there is no reason why the New should justify more essentially than the Old.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is that same Apostle in Romans 1: *I am not ashamed of the Gospel: for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.* Here he recognized something unique in the Gospel. Since salvation and justification are the same thing, it must be that the power of the Gospel Law is to justify, and likewise to save those who believe.

<column-break/>

THIS question has been more richly and clearly explained in Question 3, the final article, the solution of which is contained in three conclusions. For in the Law, according to what we were just saying, two things must be considered: namely, the teachings themselves and the commands written externally for believing and acting; and furthermore, the internal grace and favor of the Holy Spirit for carrying out the works of that same law and for attaining its end.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
With this established, the first conclusion is: The Gospel Law, if you consider only the pure teachings, commands, and the substance of the works, does not justify by itself any more than the Old Law or the Law of Nature itself. For we have already explained in the place cited how the word of Paul—*Not from works, but from faith and grace is man justified*—is understood not only of the works of the Old Law, but also of our own. This is similar to his saying, *The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life,* which, according to the interpretation of <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine in his book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, is to be understood even of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> itself. For regarding the very concupiscence <note>Unordered or sinful desire.</note> prohibited in the Decalogue, <margin>Paul.</margin> Paul adds: *I did not know concupiscence was sin, unless the law said, "You shall not covet."*

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
For the law provides nothing other than to teach what sin is; but to cleanse from sin—because it is a supernatural power—is ascribed to grace alone through faith in Christ.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: The Gospel Law, if you meditate upon its internal power, justifies man. But because this same power justified not only those under the Gospel, but also the ancient fathers and those who lived justly under the Law of Nature, a third point is added.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Third conclusion: The Gospel Law is judged to justify above all others because the Author of grace Himself—by whose faith salvation was achieved in the past—was the bringer of our law, which He confirmed with His own blood. Through the price of that blood, we obtain saving grace through His sacraments. These things have now been sufficiently explained above.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, regarding the first objection, it is granted that salvation comes to no one except through obedience to the Gospel; yet from this, it is only gathered that the New Law—in terms of the substance of works and external commands and teachings—does not justify by itself, just as the Old Law did not, as we granted in the first conclusion.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The answer to the second argument is similar. For the grace of the Gospel justifies its subjects, yet it does not confirm them so strongly that they are unable to sin. Indeed, whoever violates the law against that same grace is guilty of a greater punishment...

# Book Two, Question VII.

**Left Column:**

...of punishment <note>Original Latin fragment: "plicij". Likely part of "supplicii," referring to the degree of punishment based on knowledge.</note> by which he more clearly knew the will of his master. Nevertheless, this is worthy of note: that the word of Paul, namely, *the Law works wrath* <note>original: "Lex iram operatur"; Romans 4:15</note>, does not apply to the Gospel in the same way it does to the Mosaic Law. For the Old Law, in its common name, signifies not grace but the mere letter: which only shows what sin is, and thus becomes an occasion for sinning, from which the wrath of God arises. The Evangelical Law, however, includes not only the letter but grace and its sacraments. Therefore, it is not a law of wrath, but of kindness and mercy.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ And subsequently, the third argument is answered in almost the same vein. Namely, that although the same God was the author of both laws, he was so in different ways. For he wrote that former law only on tablets; but ours, in the manner already explained,
<margin>Paul.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
as Paul says, he wrote on "fleshy hearts" <note>2 Corinthians 3:3</note>. Therefore, as Augustine explains in his book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, the same Apostle calls that law written outside of man the "ministry of death and damnation" <note>original: "ministrationem mortis & damnationis"</note>; but ours, the "ministry of the spirit and of justice."

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether the new law should have been given from the beginning of the world.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' with ornate floral and scrolling leaf patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>
IT FOLLOWS that just as we disputed concerning the Old Law, so we should investigate concerning the Gospel Law, why it was not immediately established at the very beginning of the world. For it is argued that this would have been most fitting. God, as held in Romans 2, is not a respecter of persons; and yet, as held immediately in chapter 3, "All men have sinned and lack the glory of God" <note>original: "egent gratia Dei"; Romans 3:23</note>: therefore, He ought to have flooded the world with the Gospel light immediately upon man's fall, so that all might enter the way of salvation.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued: it is no less fitting for the Gospel Law to have been universal in terms of time as it is in terms of place. For God wants all men to be saved; and He willed it for this reason—as is clear in the final chapters of Matthew and Mark—that the Gospel be preached in the whole world; therefore, He ought to have made it known to all ages.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third and finally, it is argued: it would have been more prudent to provide for man those things necessary for the spiritual and eternal life, which is more excellent, than for the corporal life, which is temporal. But from the beginning, He provided most providently for man in temporal matters, handing over to him all that He had created into his dominion, as is clear in Genesis 1. Therefore, He should have

**Right Column:**

also instituted mortals in the Gospel Law, which was most necessary for spiritual salvation, right from the beginning of the world.

¶ On the contrary stand the Apostolic testimonies: "Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is natural" <note>original: "animale"; 1 Corinthians 15:46</note>. And in
<margin>Paul.</margin>

<margin>A responsive conclusion.</margin>
THE question is answered with a very easy "no." It was not fitting for the Gospel Law to shine upon mortals immediately from the beginning of the world, but it was much more prudent for it to be deferred through so many ages. To understand this conclusion, however, it must be noted beforehand that there is a 
<margin>Dual sense of the question.</margin>
double sense to the question. One is, assuming it ought not to be given except through Christ, by the shedding of whose blood it was to be confirmed. And then the question is the same as asking whether Christ ought to have taken on flesh at the very start of the world. However, it is not the place of the present discussion to debate this sense. For it is disputed by Saint Thomas in Part 3, Question 1. And we, in the final article of this book, will bring forward reasons for such a delay in time.

<margin>Triple reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The other sense is whether it was fitting for the Gospel Law to be given before Christ's advent, or before his redemption. And in this sense, the response is that it would not have been expedient. For this, 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Saint Thomas assigns three reasons. The first is: the New Law, as we were just saying, is primarily the grace of the Holy Spirit; which, as Paul says, the Holy Spirit has poured out abundantly upon us. But the abundance of grace ought not to be poured out until the impediment that stands in its way through sin was removed; hence John 7: "The Spirit was not yet given" (namely, in its overflowing) "because Jesus was not yet glorified." That impediment was removed through the death of Christ; therefore, until He suffered, it was not fitting for the law of
<margin>Paul.</margin>
grace to be given. And Paul explains this reason in Romans 8, where he says: God, sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, on account of sin, condemned sin in the flesh—that is, in the flesh which, though not in its own Person <note>original: "supposito"; referring to Christ's divine personhood which is sinless</note>, was nevertheless infected with sin—so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us. For there is that wonderful antithesis through which the divine power is made manifest: namely, that God did not condemn sin in just any way, but through the very flesh in whose nature sin had been committed and was creeping into all. Therefore, the law of grace, such as the Gospel is, ought to take its vigor from the death of Christ.

## ARTICLE I.

### Whether the New Law is the completion of the Old.

<margin>First argument.</margin>

AND this question was also touched upon in the preceding sections and largely defined. But so that fresh reasons may be applied, it will be resolved by three conclusions corresponding to the number of arguments.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> 
First: The Gospel Law is neither entirely different from the ancient Law, nor is it altogether the same; rather, it is distinct from it in the way that the perfect is distinct from the imperfect.

<margin>Proof.</margin> 
All parts of this are proven. Since every single law has a specific goal, laws that tend toward different goals are entirely different—just as the laws of a state administered by a King would be different from the laws of one governed by an Aristocracy, or those of one ruled by a Democracy. However, those laws that are directed toward the same goal, but where one reaches that goal more closely than the other, do not differ more widely than the perfect from the imperfect under that same goal. This is like the laws established for mature and perfect men compared to those by which children are instructed. An example is found in natural motions: a movement upward is different from a movement forward; yet a more intense heating is not an entirely different kind of motion from a weaker heating.

To the point, then: since the New and Old Law tend toward the same goal—for the God of both Testaments is the same—He educated the ancients like children under a <term>pedagogue</term><note>In the Roman world, a 'pedagogue' was a guardian/tutor who supervised a child's behavior until they reached adulthood.</note> for the sake of eternal life, while He has established us as grown men for that same blessedness. Conversely, in our time, some are drawn by fear; for Christ also threatened us with eternal fire.

Therefore, the distinction is not to be taken from the condition of individual persons, but from the condition of the "states" of both laws in general. For that was the state of children, who are restrained from evil by fear rather than led to good by reason; but our state is that of free children, whom Christ has liberated from law and death (as held in Romans 8). Since free children are led by filial love rather than servile fear, ours is called the law of love, and that one the law of fear.

Nor, conversely, should it be denied that our law contains works—both moral, according to that saying in Matthew 5: "Do good to those who hate you," as well as <term>ceremonial</term><note>Rituals and religious observations distinctive to a specific faith community.</note>: such as the sacraments, according to that saying in Luke 20: "Do this in memory of me." But nevertheless, because that law was placed mostly and primarily in those "works"—namely in ceremonies which did not <term>justify</term><note>The process by which a person is made righteous or "right" in the eyes of God.</note> as our sacraments do—and because the works of the moral laws did not bring salvation, but rather faith in Christ alone did; and because our law consists primarily, as has been explained, in internal faith and grace, which the Holy Spirit has poured out abundantly upon us; that law was called the "law of works," while ours is called, by <term>antonomasia</term><note>A rhetorical figure where a title or descriptive phrase is used instead of a proper name; here, calling the New Law "The" Law of Faith.</note>, the law of faith and grace.

<margin>The reason why the old law is called the law of works, and the new law the law of faith.</margin>

->Second conclusion.<-

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>

Our law was the completion of the ancient one. For everything that is perfect completes that which is imperfect by supplying its defects. This manner of "supplying" was explained at length in the discussion at the end of Romans chapter 3, on that verse: "Do we then destroy the law through faith? Far from it: but we establish the law." <note>original: "Legem ergò destruimus per fidem? Absit: sed legem statuimus"</note> For in the law, there are two things to consider: namely, both the end goal and the precepts. The goal of that law was twofold. One was common to both that law and ours, which is to lead one to eternal life through justice; the other, however, was peculiar to it, namely to prefigure future truths. The precepts, truly, were of a threefold kind: namely, moral, ceremonial, and judicial. And regarding all these things, our law most perfectly completed the old one. First of all, regarding that supreme goal—which is to justify—our law completed the old by perfecting what the old was not able to do. For since those works did not justify of themselves except through faith in Christ, all those who died a just life were held in <term>limbo</term><note>Specifically 'Limbo of the Fathers' (Limbus Patrum), a place where the souls of the righteous were said to wait until Christ's resurrection opened the gates of heaven.</note>, as if kept in a storehouse, awaiting His arrival who would open the way to the kingdom for them. And the Giver of our law exhibited that benefit which they were expecting; thus, our law rightly completed the old in this way. Whence Paul says in Romans 8: "What was impossible for the law, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh: so that the justification of the law (that is,

<margin>See the author on chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Romans.</margin>

<margin>In how many ways the new law was the completion of the old.</margin>

<margin>Paul.</margin>

<column-break/>

that which the law sought) might be fulfilled in us." Next, it also fulfilled the other goal of the same law, namely to signify/foreshadow, which was the proper function of the ceremonial laws; it did this by showing the light of the truths of which that law bore the shadow. Whence in Colossians 2, Paul says those ceremonies were a shadow of things to come, but the "body" is of Christ: that is, the truth of those things belongs to Christ. Because of this, that law was called the law of shadow and figure, while our law is the law of truth. Second, Christ also perfected and completed the precepts themselves with the New Law, both in deed and in word. In deed, namely, by keeping the law: for He was both circumcised and presented in the temple, and performed other legal requirements, according to Galatians 4: "Made under the law." In word, however, He fulfilled (that is, perfected) the precepts in three ways. First, by bringing forth their legitimate understanding: as with murder and adultery, whose meaning the Pharisees had corrupted, teaching that only the hand was forbidden there, not the mind. For Christ taught that the affections of the mind are also restrained there. Second, He applied safeguards to keep them more securely: such as not swearing at all, nor by heaven, etc., unless necessity intervenes. And third, by adding <term>counsels</term><note>Advice for spiritual perfection (like voluntary poverty) that goes beyond the mandatory commandments.</note>: as is clear in Matthew 19, where to the young man asserting he had kept the precepts, He counseled that if he wished to be perfect, he should sell what he had and follow Him. Since, therefore, Christ fulfilled the law in these ways, He rightly perfected it, and subsequently showed through the Gospel that the Old Law was excluded—not, however, destroyed, as Paul says, because it remains as a testimony to our law.

<margin>Paul.</margin>

->Third conclusion.<-

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>

The New Law was contained in the Old; not indeed "actually," like a thing placed in a location, but "virtually," as the perfect is contained in the imperfect—for instance, an animal in an embryo, an action in a potentiality, a species in a genus, or a tree in a seed. The conclusion is plainly manifest from what has been said. In this sense, that passage in Ezekiel 1 is understood: "There was a wheel within a wheel," <note>original: "Rota erat in rota"</note> which is, according to Gregory’s interpretation, the New Testament in the Old. Whence Chrysostom, explaining that passage in Mark 4, "The earth brings forth fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear," <note>original: "Vltrò terra fructificat, primùm herbam, deinde spicam, deinde plenum frumentum in spica"</note> adapts it to three kinds of laws. For the Law of Nature was only able to grow like grass; the Law of Moses brought forth the ears; and the Law of the Gospel completed it with the full grain.

Moreover, all things commanded to be done, although they seem more lofty than those which appear openly there, were almost all stored away there in their substance. But because they were not understood by everyone, they have been explained more clearly and more abundantly through Christ.

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
FINALLY, our law must be compared to the old one in terms of its "gravity" or weight. It is argued that it is heavier, both because it prohibits not only external acts but also internal ones—and there is great anguish and labor in suppressing these—and also because the old law promised temporal prosperity to those approaching God, whereas ours promises tribulations, ac-

On the contrary, however, is the testimony of Christ in Matthew 11: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened"—namely, according to the exposition of <margin>Hilary.</margin> **Hilary**, burdened by the weights of the [Old] Law, which **Peter** mentions in Acts 15. Whence He also adds: "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light."

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
To this question, a distinction is proposed, and it is answered with two conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
In the law, there are two types of difficulty and labor to consider: namely, that which comes from the object <note>The specific actions or "matter" required by the law.</note> and that which comes from the manner of acting. Let this be the first conclusion: If the difficulty is weighed in terms of the object, the ancient law was much heavier than the new. For it imposed upon the shoulders of that people not only the **Decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> but also a most numerous and "unbearable" (as Peter says) pack of ceremonies and judgments. Indeed, it was fitting to keep that wild nation, which was prone to seeking novelties, occupied, lest leisure offer them an opportunity for evil. Our law, however, besides the very law of nature, has commanded nothing except the sacraments, and even these are for our own good.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: If you judge the difficulty by the manner of acting, and you consider those things which Christ expressed, our law is in a certain way heavier—specifically for those who are not yet imbued with the habits of virtue. For He expressed to us that we must also compose the movements of our minds; and as <margin>Proof of the conclusion. For he says that to perform just acts is easy; but to perform them *justly*—that is, with promptness and alacrity of mind—is very difficult until the virtues become sweet through ingrained habits. Whence **Chrysostom**, commenting on the passage in Matthew 5 regarding the least of the commandments, says: The commandments <margin>Chrysostom.</margin> of Moses are easy in the doing, such as "You shall not kill" or "You shall not commit adultery"; but the commandments of Christ, namely "You shall not be angry" and "You shall not lust," are difficult in the doing. They are not heavy, he says, to one who loves, <margin>A beautiful admonition for the Christian people to take up.</margin> but they are heavy to one who does not love.

# F. D. Soto, On Justice & Right #

### Second Book, Question 8, Article II ###

Nonetheless, Bishops <note>original: "Antistites"; referring to high-ranking church officials or prelates</note> must use this power as temperately and moderately as possible, lest they make the yoke of the Master—which He himself willed to be light and sweet—troublesome and bitter. Therefore, first of all, in establishing these laws, they must hold this most sacred principle in view: that no law should be established except that which they deem necessary for the safer guarding of the Gospel. For the Gospel is the "Wall of Zion," which the Church ought to surround with an outwork <note>original: "antemurali"; a secondary defensive wall or rampart</note>. Next, care must be taken lest a multitude of laws expose the laws themselves to contempt, and thus become the reason why they are not fulfilled by deeds, but rather redeemed by a price <note>A critique of the practice of paying for dispensations from church laws rather than following them</note>, and subsequently the wall is shaken once the outwork is destroyed.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence Augustine, in his *Inquiries of Januarius* regarding such a multiplication of laws, says: "Our very religion, which the mercy of God willed to be free with the most manifest and very few celebrations of sacraments, they oppress with servile burdens, to the point that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable, for they are subject to legal sacraments and not to human presumptions."

<margin>The latter conclusion is illustrated.</margin>
¶ Regarding the latter conclusion, note here also that we did not assert that our law is simply more difficult even in its manner of acting, but rather in its expression compared to the ancient law; for that law also, when rightly understood, restrained the internal mind. For while it prohibited murder and adultery, it also warned that the affections for them were to be torn from the soul. Furthermore, one who allows disordered and corrupt motions of the mind finds it much more difficult to abstain from wicked deeds. Hence, although the prohibition of internal motion may seem rigid, it is nonetheless sweeter for avoiding the outward deed.

<margin>The Law of Christ is light and sweet.</margin>
In short, see how the law of Christ was light and sweet. It contains only three things: namely, moral precepts, sacraments, and counsels <term>counsels</term><note>Evangelical counsels, such as voluntary poverty or celibacy, which are recommended for perfection but not commanded for all.</note>. And He commanded the moral precepts for the reason that, since they are of the law of nature, He could not *not* command them. The sacraments, however, although they seem to be additions, were commanded to us for this purpose: that through the grace they confer, they might help us in fulfilling the law, which we are otherwise unable to fulfill by ourselves. Therefore, in this also our law is lighter than the old: since to lift the burden of the law, He provided us with sacraments, whereas for the ancients, those ceremonies were burdens. But as for the counsels, Christ taught us that they are most healthful for us, yet He did not wish them to have the necessity of a command.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the argument made.</margin>
Therefore, in response to the contrary argument, the adversities and anguishes which the New Law offers to those who love God become sweet through both the hope of the Kingdom now open to us and through filial love.

<margin>Epilogue of the differences between the Old and New Law.</margin>
¶ It is therefore worthwhile, at the end of the present question which was organized around the differences between the Old and New Law, to collect an Epilogue of them all to the best of our ability; they are twelve in number.

<margin>First.</margin>
The first difference is taken from the dignity of the legislator and the minister of the law. For the Old was given through Moses; the New, however, was brought and proclaimed by God Himself made man. Thus, that one is called the Law of Moses; this one, the Law of Christ.

<margin>Second.</margin>
The second is observed by reason of the subject. For that one, as we said just now, was written outside of man on tablets; this one, however, is inside the soul. Wherefore that one is called corporeal and written; this one, spiritual and indwelling.

<margin>Third.</margin>
The third is considered by reason of time. For that one was temporal—that is, intended to last for a certain time; ours, however, lasts until the end of the world. Therefore, that one is called temporal; ours, perpetual.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
The fourth, by reason of universality. For that one was given to one peculiar people; ours, however, to the whole world. Wherefore that one can be called particular; ours, universal.

<margin>Fifth.</margin>
The fifth difference is evident by reason of figure. Since that one was a shadow and figure of ours; ours, however, is the truth of that one. For which reason that one was shadowy; ours, manifest.

<margin>Sixth.</margin>
The sixth, by reason of signification: for even if the same faith was necessary for them and for us for salvation, nonetheless, those things which they believed implicitly as future events, we now explicitly confess as deeds already done.

<margin>Seventh.</margin>
The seventh distinction, and indeed the most important, is weighed on the part of perfection and effect. For although neither our works nor those of the ancients justify without grace, nonetheless, because the Passion had not yet been presented to them, nor did their sacraments confer grace as ours do, the Gospel law justifies—which the other could not provide by itself. Therefore, that one is called the law of works; ours, the law of faith and grace.

<margin>Eighth.</margin>
Hence, the eighth difference is taken from the nature of the precepts. For that one was heavier; ours, truly, is lighter and sweeter.

<margin>Ninth.</margin>
The ninth difference: our law contains more explicit and thus more extensive precepts than that one; for instance, it more expressly prohibits interior acts.

<margin>Tenth.</margin>
And the tenth, that it adds the perfection of the counsels to those things.

<margin>Eleventh.</margin>
The eleventh, that that law promised temporal things and threatened with temporal punishments; for which reason it is called...
