# QUESTION NINE,
## Concerning those things which are contained in the New Law.

### Saint Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, 1st part of the 2nd part, question 108.

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether the New Law established external acts in a sufficient order.*<-

[A decorative woodcut drop-cap initial 'P' depicting a landscape with several buildings, a tower, and rolling hills under a cloudy sky.]

THE FINAL QUESTION regarding the New Law, and indeed regarding the whole subject of laws, is raised concerning those things established by this same Evangelical law. These consist of three kinds: namely, precepts, sacraments, and counsels <note>Precepts are commands one must follow; sacraments are ritual channels of grace; and counsels (like voluntary poverty or celibacy) are recommendations for spiritual perfection but are not strictly mandatory for all Christians.</note>. By these, we are instructed both in our external works and in the internal movements of the soul. It is asked first, therefore, whether it properly established external actions.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
The argument for the negative side is that the Gospel ought to have established nothing regarding such actions. The Evangelical law is the law of the Kingdom of Heaven, as is clear from the preaching of Christ: "The kingdom of heaven has drawn near." And in Matthew 24: "This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached." However, a kingdom of this kind does not consist of external works but of internal ones, according to Luke 17: "The kingdom of God is within you." And in Romans 14: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but justice, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit." For this reason, the difference established above between the Old Law and our own is recognized: that the former restrained the hand, while the latter restrains the soul <note>The Latin "cohibebat manum, hæc verò animū" refers to the idea that the Old Law punished outward crimes, while the New Law judges the intent of the heart.</note>. Additionally, in Romans 8, it is called the "law of the spirit." And in 2 Corinthians 3: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." There is no liberty

<column-break/>

where a person is obligated to perform or avoid external works; therefore, it [the New Law] should have decreed nothing concerning external duties.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, the main argument is made in the opposite direction: that the New Law was lacking and insufficient regarding such external works. For the Evangelical law pertains to faith, which "works through love," according to Galatians 5: "In Christ Jesus, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but faith which works through love." Regarding faith, however, there are many more things to be explicitly believed than were explicit in the Old Law; therefore, it should have also added more moral mandates regarding love. Yet it did not do this, because it only commanded the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> to us, just as the Old Law did. Likewise, regarding the ceremonies pertaining to divine worship, it seems narrower and shorter, because it only handed down the sacraments to us; it left the remaining worship of the Church to be established later. Similarly, while God spoke many judicial laws <note>Laws regarding civil government and legal disputes specific to the ancient nation of Israel.</note> there by Himself, He handed down none to us, but permitted this to the commonwealth, both civil and ecclesiastical. It is, therefore, less sufficient and less provident regarding external matters than the ancient law. ¶ To the contrary is that of Matthew 7: "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be likened to a wise man who built his house upon a rock." A wise builder omits nothing that is conducive to the construction.

<margin>The Foundation.</margin>
IN this question, one must meditate upon the highest prudence and kindness of God in founding the Evangelical law. First of all, therefore, from the previous discussions, this foundation must be recalled: that the Evangelical law is not only higher than human law—since it instructs us not merely toward a natural end, but toward a supernatural one—but it is also more excellent than the Mosaic law. This is because it provides the faith and grace which that law prefigured, through the passion of Christ; and through this grace, we are introduced into the kingdom of heaven. From this foundation, it is gathered that the same law establishes nothing concerning our works except those which are ordered and referred toward that same grace. And it prohibits or counsels each thing in the same degree and order by which it contributes toward that grace.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ With this pre-established, the question is answered with four conclusions. The first is: In external works, the Evangelical law, as a foundation, most providently effects the seven sacraments. For there are three kinds of works...

The conclusion is proven as follows: Grace, in which the substance of the Law consists, is considered in two ways: namely, regarding its generation and acquisition, and again regarding its use and exercise. Now, its generation and infusion is a supernatural gift that God communicates to us through a mediator—that is, through His Son made man. Therefore, Christ Himself, according to His humanity, was first full of grace without measure; subsequently, through that same humanity, He imparts it to us in weight and measure, according to that passage in the first chapter of John: *The Word was made flesh* <note>original: "Verbum Caro factum est"</note>. And: *We saw him full of grace and truth*. And: *From his fullness we have all received*. And since God arranges supernatural things with such sweetness that they are shared with us in a manner suited to our nature, and since our knowledge begins with the senses, it was fitting for that same grace to be supplied to us through external signs. Through these, we are both made certain of our salvation according to our capacity, and our souls are stirred toward divine worship. These are the seven sacraments, the sufficiency of which is not for this present place to discuss. For that people, as we have noted repeatedly from the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul’s letters, such as Galatians, where the Old Law is described as a tutor for children.</note>, was as if in a childhood age under a tutor, not yet endowed with manly prudence. Furthermore, they bore figures and shadows of future truths. For both reasons, it was appropriate that God Himself should instruct them by His laws concerning even the smallest details, rather than committing the institutions of the state to them. But the Christian family—being more advanced in age and prudence, and thus fit to receive the inheritance—and who, through their ceremonies, no longer

We distinguished three levels of these in Question 3. The conclusion is manifest: for the prudence of a legislator must not fail in matters of necessity. ¶ The fourth conclusion: In

Instead, just as was said concerning ceremonial matters, He committed <term>judicial matters</term> <note>Judicial laws are the specific civil or legal regulations used to govern a society, such as punishments for crimes or rules for contracts.</note> to the state, both civil and ecclesiastical. For it has already been said often that ceremonial and judicial laws differ from moral ones because they are not derived from the principles of nature, but rather narrow down a general precept to a specific one by a certain judgment. And just as ceremonial matters pertain to divine worship, so judicial matters pertain to the peaceful state of the commonwealth.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, for the reason just assigned—namely, that the Gospel people have progressed in prudence and are admitted as free people to the inheritance—they were to be left to their own commonwealth in these judicial matters. Thus, the laws of contracts and the punishments of wrongdoers, which God Himself established in the former Law, were to be decreed by the leaders of the Gospel and secular Princes at their own discretion.
<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
There is also another reason for this: that the former Law was given to one and the same small people, whereas ours is given to the whole world. That people, therefore, could observe all those rules; but for Christians, judgments must be established according to the diversity of times, regions, and men. For which reason Chri-

<summary>Soto explains that while Christ personally established the sacraments and essential moral laws (the Ten Commandments) necessary for salvation, He left specific ceremonial details and civil judicial laws to the discretion of the Church and secular rulers, reflecting the "maturity" and global nature of the Christian people compared to the ancient Israelites.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question 9, Article 1, concerning the external acts prescribed by the New Law (the Gospel). It addresses how Christ’s teachings differ from the Old Law by emphasizing spiritual freedom and internal grace while leaving specific ceremonial details to the Church.</meta>

->Book Second, Question IX.<-

In reality, Christ threatened us with nothing and promised us nothing except for the depths of hell, the heights of heaven, and the sufficiency of life. For this is the meaning of: *You shall receive a hundredfold, and you shall possess eternal life* <note>original: "Centuplum accipietis, & vitam æternam possidebitis" from Matthew 19:29</note>. Truly, as for other works of supererogation <note>Acts done beyond what is strictly required by God’s commandments</note>, he neither commanded them, nor did he intend for all of them to be commanded by the Church. However, he did want some to be established, such as the fasts of Lent and certain feast days. The rest he recommended as counsel and left to the choice of each individual, as we shall see in Article 3.

<margin>Three reasons why the Gospel law is called the law of liberty.</margin>
From these points, therefore, we gather a triple reason why James in Chapter 1 called our law the "law of perfect liberty." First, because he handed over the possession of our inheritance to us as adult sons who are already graduating from their early tutelage. Second, because Christ did not restrict us to ceremonial or judicial rules as he did the ancients; rather, he freely left those to be established by leaders and magistrates according to the conditions of places and times. But thirdly, because he did not want us to fulfill those rules like slaves out of fear, but from a habit of grace, like free-born children.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that although the kingdom of God consists chiefly in the inner reaches of the heart—namely, in justice, peace, and spiritual joy—nevertheless, external works also belong to that kingdom as a consequence. These are either works that flow outward from internal movements, such as the worship of God and honoring one's parents, or works without which those same spiritual virtues cannot be preserved, such as the prohibition of murder, theft, and so on. Therefore, even if our law chiefly restrains the soul, it must nonetheless restrain the soul from those actions that disturb it. Just as, conversely, by prohibiting the "hand" <note>the outward action</note> to the ancients, he consequently prohibited the "soul" <note>the inward intent</note>. Truly, the Gospel law does not, by itself, establish those things which do not have a necessary connection to grace, as the Old Law did. Such things include food and drink, of which Paul speaks—for instance, the choice of foods and fasts—which Christ did not decree, but which the Church enacted by his authority.

<margin>To the other part of the same argument.</margin>
To the other part of the same argument, a sufficient response has been given where we explained why the Gospel law is called the law of perfect liberty.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
To the second main argument, the response is that the nature of faith is different from that of moral precepts. For since faith surpasses natural reason—which we therefore cannot grasp except through grace—it was necessary for the law of more abundant grace to reveal the mysteries of that same faith to us more fully and expressly. Moral precepts, however, belong to the natural law;

<column-break/>

therefore, once the foundations were laid in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, the Christian commonwealth was able to understand them.

<margin>To the other part of the second argument.</margin>
To the other part of the same argument, it is responded that since the sacraments of the New Law confer grace, it was necessary for the author of grace himself to institute them. However, regarding the rites of the sacraments and ecclesiastical ceremonies—because they are not strictly necessary for grace—Christ committed them to the Church, for the reasons we cited above.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you should object that the Redeemer himself handed down certain ceremonies to the Apostles, as is clear in Luke 9 and 10: *Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts* <note>original: "Nolite possidere aurum, neq; argentum, neq; pecuniam in zonis vestris"</note>.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that those instructions do not pertain to ceremonies; rather, they were either permissions or instructions necessary for the Apostles for that specific time.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
I say they were "permissions" according to the exposition of Augustine in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*. For since the Apostles and preachers of the word have a right to demand sustenance, that phrase, "Without a pouch, without money, etc.," does not so much have the form of a command, according to Augustine, as it does a concession. That is to say: "There is no need for you to provide travel expenses, since you have the right to seek food." Hence he adds: *For the laborer is worthy of his food*. Other saints, however, say these were commands—not ceremonial ones, but moral. For it was necessary then that those who were fresh in Christ’s discipleship and not yet sufficiently accustomed to poverty should be trained in that same state of begging. Thus, to those who were already more advanced, the same Redeemer says in Luke 22: *When I sent you without a money bag, and pouch, and shoes, did you lack anything?* And when they responded "nothing," he added: *But now, he who has a money bag, let him take it, and likewise a pouch.* It was as if they had by then entered a state of perfect liberty, when they were now to be left to live by their own judgment.

<margin>Fifth.</margin> ¶Fifth and finally, it is argued that since judgment is an act of justice—according to that Psalm, *Until justice be turned into judgment* <note>original: "Quoufq; iuftitia conuertatur in iudiciū" from Psalm 94:15</note>—there was no reason why he should so greatly deter us from judging.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> To the question, what other conclusion should I respond with than that in that Sermon—by which Christ brought laws to the whole world—he most perfectly shaped all human morals, both within and "at the core" <note>original: "intùs & in cute," a Latin idiom meaning "thoroughly" or "inside and out"</note>. Each individual word, however, would require individual chapters to be explained. 

<column-break/>

But since their explanation is so widely available in the writings of the Saints—to which we, according to the small measure of our talent, have appended our meditations in their commentaries—we shall pass over them here in a cursory and brief manner. 

<margin>The conclusion explained.</margin> For the Lord there, like a most wise architect, laid the first foundation of the entire Christian structure, which in moral matters is the "end" <term>finis: the ultimate goal or purpose of an action</term> toward which all customs are directed. Now, the end of our morals is beatitude and happiness; therefore, he established this first of all against the vain opinion of the philosophers. *Blessed are the poor in spirit*: this is against those who, as Aristotle says in the first book of the *Ethics*, placed happiness in riches. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin> *Blessed are the meek*: against those who had established it in honors. *Blessed are those who mourn*: against those who had placed it in [material] riches. Soon, once the end was established, he instructed the hearts of the Apostles, whom he had placed over the world, so that as leaders and lights of the world they might be as detached from all earthly affections as was necessary for those who, as the salt of the earth and the light of the world, ought both to preserve the whole world from the infection of temporal things and to lead it to the heavenly fatherland. 

Next, he instructed our souls within—from where the root of our works proceeds in order to themselves—regarding two things that are necessary for virtue. First, on the part of the object: namely, that we should not only abstain from evil works, such as homicide, adultery, and the like, but also be thoroughly cleansed from the affections for them. *Whoever is angry with his brother*, and *Whoever sees a woman [to lust after her]*, etc. For God, the searcher of hearts, holds the internal heart as pleasing above all works. 

Furthermore, he rectified the intention of the end, from which the praise or blame of a work chiefly emanates; namely, by commanding us to take care lest we do anything for the sake of petty human glory, so that we do not lose our reward by waiting for it from men, when he himself desires to bestow a most abundant reward upon us. 

Furthermore, he descended to imbuing men with the duties they owe toward their neighbor. First, that we should not judge his hidden deeds, thereby usurping the office of God; for such judgment, since it offers us a reason for either hating or despising our neighbor, is injurious and harmful. Next, so that we are not negligent to the injury of sacred things, which pertain to God; namely, that we do not commit them to the unfit and the unworthy, as if to swine. And above all, he took care to expand our charity so far that it reached even to our enemies. Finally, he taught how without...

### Book Two, Question IX ###

Through divine favor, we are unable to fulfill the mandates of the most holy law [by our own strength]. Hence He says, *Ask and you shall receive; knock and it will be opened to you.* <note>original: "Petite & accipietis: pulsate & aperiet vobis" from Matthew 7:7</note> He also urged caution, that we should strive to enter through the narrow gate: for the path of virtue, since it sits in the middle between two extremes, is narrow; however, the field of straying is vast. 
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Hence, Aristotle says that the target can be hit in only one way, but missed in infinite ways. For this reason, He also ordered us to beware of false prophets who divert us from the right path. Finally, many other mandates shine forth in that place, which the narrowness of the present space does not allow to be fully explained.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, then, let it be answered that Christ specifically explained those three precepts because the Pharisees were interpreting them wrongly to the people. For they judged that guilt resided only in the outward work, but not in the internal disposition <term>affectu: the internal state or intention of the soul</term>. This was (as Saint Thomas Aquinas says) because it appeared to them that the movements of anger and lust <note>original: "Veneris" - referring to Venus, the goddess of love, used here for sexual desire</note> were natural. Furthermore, perhaps (as I believe) because they did not see any damage inflicted upon a neighbor through internal commotions of the soul that do not break out into an action, they recognized no injustice in them. Christ, however, taught that those internal states are wicked—not only because they are the cause of outward works, but because they are injurious in themselves. For to hold a neighbor in hatred is an injury. To the prohibition of perjury, He also added a bridle on swearing; perhaps because they thought that to swear to the truth was no sin, even if it were done rashly and without judgment. Indeed, some blasphemers now argue that swearing pertains to the reverence of God, saying that he who swears "well"—meaning frequently—believes well.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, a response is given in a similar way, assuming that distinction established earlier between ceremonial and judicial laws: namely, that the New Law did not reject judicial laws so completely that they could never be instituted again; but it put the ceremonial laws to rest in such a way that they can in no way be revived. For this reason, Christ corrected the judicial laws, but did not correct the ceremonial ones at all, instead dismissing them. 
<margin>Double error of the Pharisees concerning judicial matters.</margin>
Moreover, the Pharisees were hallucinating in two ways regarding judicial matters. First, they thought that some things which were merely permissions were, in themselves, just and commanded: such as the divorce of a wife and the scraping together of usury from foreigners. Therefore, He untaught them both. Regarding divorce, He declared it was not a commandment because it was "right," but was 

<column-break/>

permitted because of their hardness of heart, as a lesser evil. He also prohibited the exaction of usury in Luke 6, saying: *Lend, hoping for nothing in return.* <note>original: "Date mutuum: nihil inde sperantes" from Luke 6:35</note> However, we shall explain this passage more refinedly in Book 6. In the second way they erred by thinking that certain things the law had established to be done for the sake of justice should be carried out either out of a desire for vengeance, or greed for temporal things, or hatred of enemies. Therefore, Christ thought it worthwhile to explain three precepts in the opposite sense. For they thought that the judicial law of retaliation <term>talio: the "eye for an eye" principle</term>, which was given so that justice might be preserved, should be executed for the sake of vengeance. The Lord, therefore, tore this error from their souls, teaching that our minds ought to be ready, whenever charity demands it, not to return evil for evil, but to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes us. In the same way, another judgment of repaying four sheep for one provoked their minds to greed; and therefore He taught that we should be ready in spirit to permit even our cloak to the one wishing to contend with us in judgment for our tunic. Finally, thirdly, from those laws which commanded them to wage war against the Canaanites and Jebusites, they gathered that hatred toward enemies was a commandment. Therefore, He taught that those laws had now ceased, but rather that enemies ought to be loved. Concerning ceremonial laws, however, for the reason already stated, He mentioned nothing; instead, He pierced them all with a single word. For when He said to the Samaritan woman in John 4: *The hour comes when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem... but true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth,* <note>original: "Venit hora quando neque in monte hoc neque in Hierosolymis adorabitis patrem... sed veri adoratores adorabunt patrem in spiritu & veritate" from John 4:21-23</note> teaching that the temple was to be destroyed, He likewise taught that all those temporal obstacles of sacrifices would pass away into spiritual worship.

<margin>To the third</margin>
¶ To the third, a response of this kind is subjoined. All things that mortals can desire in the world are reduced to those three which John noted in the second chapter [of his first epistle], saying: *All that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh*—that is, bodily delights and pleasures; *the concupiscence of the eyes*—namely, the greed for riches; *and the pride of life*—namely, the ambition for honor and the desire for glory. In the ancient law, however, delights were not promised; indeed, the people were kept away from them. Therefore, Christ had no need to deter the people from them. Nevertheless, height of honor and an exuberance of riches were promised. For it is read in Deuteronomy 28: *If you will hear the voice of the Lord your God, He will make you higher than all nations.* And further down: *He will make you abound in all...*

to all good people. Therefore, it was Christ's plan to correct these two things: for this reason, he expelled vainglory from three types of works, into which all duties are reduced. For whatever a person does, they perform either for their own sake—and this is signified by the name of fasting, by which a person subdues their own pleasures—or out of love for their neighbor, which is the category of almsgiving; or for the sake of divine worship, such as prayer. From these three, because they are works of supererogation <term>supererogation: performing more than what is strictly required by duty or law</term>, men are accustomed to seek the favor of the world. <margin>To the fourth.</margin>
To the fourth argument, it is responded that God did not forbid us necessary concern, but rather superfluous anxiety. This consists of four things: namely, when someone establishes their end in temporal things, serving God for the sake of temporal gain, or valuing them more than God Himself. And therefore He says, *Do not store up for yourselves.* For he who stores up treasures establishes his end in that treasure; for this reason He adds, *Where your treasure is, there your heart is also* <note>original: "Vbi est thesaurus tuus, ibi est cor tuum" from Matthew 6:21</note>—that is, your intention, which is the act concerning the end. Secondly, [He forbids] being so anxious about temporal things that we distrust divine help, for God cares for us even in temporal matters. Therefore He added: *For your Father knows what you need before you ask him.* <note>original: "Scit enim Pater vester quid opus sit vobis antequàm petatis eum" from Matthew 6:8</note> Thirdly, lest a man be so anxious as if relying on himself; for this reason He says that no one can add anything to their stature. Fourthly, lest anxiety regarding the future preoccupy and distress us more than is just. Because of this He says, *Do not be anxious about tomorrow.* <note>original: "Nolite soliciti esse in crastinum" from Matthew 6:34</note> In a similar way, He did not prohibit public judgment, without which men cannot conduct their lives, but rather rash judgment: that is, lest one should judge impulsively regarding hidden matters without cause.

### ARTICLE III.

->*Whether the evangelical law suitably added certain counsels to us.*<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The last thing that remains to be considered in the evangelical law is the order of counsels, by which Christ has raised us above all nations of the world to the height of blessedness. It is asked, therefore, whether counsels were suitably applied to us through the evangelical law. And it is argued first that there are no works of counsel. For everything that a person can return to God, they already owe to Him by virtue of the precept of love, 

<column-break/>

by which one is bound to love Him above all things. This is because He created us from nothing; by which reasoning, whatever we are, and consequently whatever we are capable of, we owe to Him. Hence, in 1 Chronicles 29, the Wise Man says: *All things are yours, and we have given to you from the things we received from your hand.* <note>original: "Tua sunt... omnia: & de his quæ de manu tua accepimus dedimus tibi" from 1 Chronicles 29:14</note> Therefore, no work of supererogation remains that could be considered a counsel.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued: If counsels were for the benefit of mortals, there was no reason why God should not have handed them down to the ancients just as He did to us. However, we do not read of such counsels in the Old Law; therefore, Christ ought not to have added them.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Thirdly: Counsels are given concerning those things which are expedient for reaching an end. However, not all things are expedient for all people. Therefore, our Lord ought not to have determined specific counsels, but should have left them either to each person's judgment or to the wisdom of the learned, who, knowing who is fit, would advise them on works of counsel.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
Fourthly: If there were any counsels, they would especially be those pertaining to the perfection of life. However, Christ placed those among the precepts in Matthew 5, such as the love of enemies and offering the other cheek to one who strikes you.

On the contrary is that saying from Proverbs 27: *The heart is delighted by ointment and various perfumes: and the soul is sweetened by the good counsels of a friend.* <note>original: "Vnguento & varijs odoribus delectatur cor: & bonis amici consilijs anima dulcoratur" from Proverbs 27:9</note> Christ, however, as He is the wisest, is also our greatest friend; therefore His counsels bring us the greatest weight of benefit.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The solution to the question is contained in three conclusions. The first is: Many counsels belong to natural law, which were always duties of virtue, not only under the written law but even before it.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven: for to assist the wretched, even outside a case of grave necessity, has always been a duty; as has using the pleasures of the world more sparingly than the law permits for some good cause. In short, the wise have always considered it a counsel to renounce those things which a person could lawfully do.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: Most suitably, in the New Law, not only were those natural counsels made explicit, but others were recently added which were not in the Old. This is proven: The difference between works of counsel and those which are in precept is that works of precept are necessary for salvation, while works of counsel are duties of supererogation, through which the perfection of charity is reached more expeditiously. Since, therefore, there was this gap between the Old Law and the New—that the former was a law of servitude...

He argues that while some counsels exist in natural law, Christ's New Law formalizes them to help believers reach spiritual perfection more effectively than the Old Law.</summary>

# Question IX of the Second Book

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
and of fear: ours, however, is the law of liberty: it follows that it was appropriate for the former [the Old Law] not to impose anything except precepts; and for ours [the New Law] to add counsels, which anyone might freely carry out. ¶ **Third conclusion.** The evangelical counsels <term>evangelical counsels: recommendations for spiritual perfection in the New Testament, such as voluntary poverty, which are encouraged but not strictly commanded for salvation</term> and indeed all natural goods are reduced to three kinds: namely, poverty, continence, and obedience. This is proven. Counsels, as asserted in the previous conclusion, are those things through which a person proceeds more expeditiously toward the perfection of charity. Now, a person is positioned between spiritual goods, by which charity is acquired, and temporal goods, by which the path of that same charity is hindered; thus, the closer one approaches the former, the further one is from the temporal—and vice versa. Of temporal things, as we noted very recently, there are three kinds: namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. <note>original: "concupiscentia carnis, concupiscentia oculorum, & superbia vitæ," a reference to 1 John 2:16</note> Therefore, whoever establishes their end in these things so as to set their rules of life according to the affection for them, would be entirely devoid of charity. For this reason, we are instructed through precepts to use them duly and justly according to what is prescribed; however, to uproot the soul from them entirely is not possible for everyone—indeed, not even for many in this age. Therefore, under counsel, Christ left this to whoever could take it: *He who can take it, let him take it.* <note>original: "qui capere posset, caperet" from Matthew 19:12</note> Through poverty, we renounce the lust of the eyes—that is, resources and riches; through continence, the lust of the flesh—that is, the delights of touch; but through obedience, the pride of life <note>The text here says "oculorum superbiam" (pride of the eyes), likely a variation or scribal slip for "superbia vitae" (pride of life) mentioned just above</note>—that is, honors and the vanities of the world. Therefore, Christ proposed those three at the very beginning of His laws: namely,

<margin>The conclusion is urged.</margin>
->*Blessed are the poor in spirit, Blessed are the meek, Blessed are those who mourn.*<- <note>original: "Beati pauperes spiritu, Beati mites, Beati qui lugent" from the Beatitudes in Matthew 5</note>

These were indeed necessary for the Apostles by reason of their status, as we have written concerning those same words; however, for the rest, they were left as counsel. Whence, as read in Matthew 19, Peter says:

->*Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then will there be for us?*<- <note>original: "Ecce nos reliquimus omnia & secuti sumus te, quid ergo erit nobis?"</note>

For this reason, apostolic men—that is, those who strive to imitate the apostolic way of life—take these three vows: according to the teaching of Christ to the young man,

->*If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have and give to the poor, and follow me.*<- <note>original: "Si vis perfectus esse, vade & vende omnia quæ habes & da pauperibus, & sequere me"</note>

Where, by the word "follow," He expressed obedience, which is the highest of the vows and the end of the others. For we bid farewell to the world for this reason: that we may follow Christ more expeditiously. These, therefore, are placed simply under counsel, to which heads all things are reduced. For giving

<column-break/>

alms beyond what is required by necessity belongs to the counsel of poverty; and abstaining from lawful pleasures belongs to the counsel of continence; and sometimes for a person not to follow their own will where it would have been permitted belongs, in a way, to the counsel of obedience—such as forgiving an offense for which you could have demanded vengeance.
<margin>Question.</margin>
<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ But if you ask what are those new things that were added in the New Law? First of all, virginity is not read to have been a counsel until the Virgin Mother of God. And furthermore, that a person should leave all things entirely with a confirmed vow; when Christ offered this to the young man, he was stunned as if at a new thing. To this Peter's statement also alludes: *What then will there be for us?* <note>original: "Quid ergo erit nobis?"</note> as if to say, we who have done what no one has done until now. Although even in the law of nature—though not for the sake of religion, but for the sake of philosophizing—histories relate that Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the Greek Cynic philosopher famous for living in a tub and rejecting all material possessions</note> and many of the Pythagoreans <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras who practiced communal ownership and asceticism</note> cast away wealth and human splendor. # BOOK THREE
# On Justice and Right.

# QUESTION ONE,
## Concerning Right.
### St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, Question 57.
## ARTICLE I.
### Whether Right is the object of justice.

<margin>Twofold meaning of Right.</margin>
Right <term>Right: translated from the Latin "ius," which refers to the objective "just thing" or the legal framework</term> pertains to Justice, the virtue which is the subject of our present work; for this reason, we have titled this section "On Justice and Right." As we stated at the beginning of the first book, "Right" is used in two ways: first, as a rule of reason and a dictate of prudence, which serves as the standard by which we weigh the equity of justice (such as laws); and second, for equity itself, which is the object of justice—namely, that which justice establishes in actual affairs. Therefore, since we have so far completed two books concerning Right in the first sense (that is, concerning Laws), it follows that as we approach the definition of Justice more closely, we must speak of "Right" in the second sense of the name, seeing as the definition of justice itself must be established through it.

<margin>Division of the book.</margin>
For this present book, the third in order, contains a treatise on justice in general, and its divisions into legal and particular justice, and into distributive and commutative justice. It also covers the first species, distributive justice, where we discuss the "respect of persons" <term>respect of persons: the unfair bias or favoritism shown to individuals based on their status rather than merit</term>. St. Thomas explains this matter in the *Summa Theologiae* II-II, Question 57 and following.

<margin>St. Thomas. First argument for the negative side.</margin>
¶ It is first asked, therefore, whether Right is the object of justice? One argues for the negative side based on the words of Celsus the Jurist in the first book of the *Digest* "On Justice and Right": "Right is the art of the good and the fair" <note>original: "Ius est ars boni & æqui"</note>. An "art" is not the object of the virtue of justice (which resides in the will), but is in itself an intellectual virtue, as Aristotle <margin>Aristotle.</margin> attests in the sixth book of the *Ethics*.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second, Justice primarily subjects us to God, according to that saying of Augustine in his book *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*: "Justice is love serving God alone, and for this reason, ruling well over all other things which are <margin>Augustine.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>Isidore.</margin>
subject to man" <note>original: "Iustitia est amor tantũ Deo seruiẽs"</note>. However, "Right" does not pertain to divine matters, but to human ones. For Isidore, in his fifth book, chapter 2, distinguishes between "Divine Law" <term>fas: divine or natural law</term> and "Human Right" <term>ius: human-made law or rights</term>, stating that *fas* is divine law, while *ius* is human law. Therefore, Right is not the object of justice.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, are both the same Isidore and the Philosopher <note>"The Philosopher" is the standard scholastic title for Aristotle</note>. For Isidore says in the same place that "Right" (*ius*) is so named because it is "just" (*iustum*). This is also recorded in the legal decrees (Distinction 1, canon *ius*). And the Philosopher, at the beginning of the fifth book of the *Ethics*, says: "All men wish to call justice that habit from which they become performers of just actions."

<margin>Division of justice.</margin>
<margin>Philosopher.</margin>
In the very doorway of this question, it must first of all be presupposed that "Justice" is accepted in one way as a general name for every virtue. For the Philosopher, in the first chapter of the fifth book of the *Ethics*, calls this "total virtue." Hence, a "just man" is the same as a "virtuous man," no matter which virtue he is distinguished by. The reason for this very broad meaning is that in every virtue there exists the character of obedience owed to the law. Whatever includes the character of "debt" or "duty" takes on the form of justice. It was certainly in this sense that Christ used the name of justice in Matthew 5 and 6: *Unless your justice abounds, etc.* and *Take care not to perform your justice before men.* Also Paul, in 1 Timothy 1: *The law is not set for the just man.* <margin>Paul.</margin> Yet we are not treating justice in this sense here; in that sense, it does not have a specific object, but rather that which is "lawful" is proper to each individual virtue. Instead, it is accepted here as a "particular" moral virtue and one of the four cardinal virtues <term>cardinal virtues: the four principal moral virtues—Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance</term>, whose office is to do what is just.

<margin>Solution to a hidden objection.</margin>
Second, lest anyone reproach us for an "inversion of order"—suggesting that we should have spoken of justice before speaking of Right—let them know that it is the teaching of Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* (text 33) that whoever is about to treat a power or a habit must begin from the object. It is from the object that the habit receives its specific kind and through which it must be described. For example, one who begins a discussion on the senses must first discuss the "sensible" <term>sensible: the object perceived by the senses, like color or sound</term>. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> For the eye is not properly defined by being an organ composed in this or that way, but by being the sense for perceiving colors; and likewise, the hearing is the sense for perceiving sound; and a saw is an instrument for cutting wood; and temperance is the habit by which we rightly use the pleasures of touch. In the same way, in the cited place of the fifth book of the *Ethics*, Aristotle defines justice

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>A responsive conclusion.</margin>
...justice through the just: namely, that it is the habit by which we will the just and perform the just. And Ulpian <note>Ulpian (c. 170–223 AD) was a celebrated Roman jurist whose writings formed a large part of the Digest of Justinian.</note> in the *Digest*, under the title "On Justice and Right" <note>original: "ff. de iustit. & iur." — a standard legal citation for the Digest of Justinian.</note>, says: "Justice is a constant and perpetual will, rendering to each their own right." Since, therefore, justice is defined through "right," we must rightly begin our investigation from the concept of right.

<margin>The reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ Having established these points, the question is answered with a single conclusion: **Right is the object of justice.** This conclusion is sufficiently clear from the authorities of Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar and encyclopedist.</note>, the Philosopher <note>Standard reference to Aristotle.</note>, and the Jurist <note>Referring back to Ulpian.</note> just cited, who call "right" that "just thing" which justice establishes in actual affairs. Nevertheless, it is further demonstrated by a reason taken from the ways justice differs from the other virtues. There are three differences in order.

<margin>The first distinction of justice, uniquely stated, from the other virtues.</margin>
The first is that, while it is proper to all virtues to produce a right work, the "rightness" of the other virtues is measured in relation to the agent himself; but the rightness of justice is measured in relation to another person. The reason is that justice is the virtue that orients the one who possesses it toward someone else, while the other virtues orient the person toward themselves. For example, **Temperance** is concerned with the right use of the pleasures of touch; therefore, it establishes a middle ground between the two internal feelings of the temperate person—namely, so that in the use of food or sexual pleasures they do not stray from reason, nor take less than what the sustaining of life requires. Similarly, **Fortitude** establishes a measure between fear and boldness. **Justice**, however, creates an equality between the one who owes and the other to whom something is owed. For instance, if both of us had five, but you lent me one, because of which you only have four while I have six, justice requires that I return one to you so that each of us has five, which is the middle point between four and six. In the same way, if you have hired out your labor to me, justice demands that my payment equals that labor. Wherefore, two things are said to be <margin>justified</margin> or "adjusted" when they are made equal: for instance, when an architect "justifies" a stone to a ruler <note>original: "ad normam," referring to a builder's square or standard of measurement.</note>, or a shoemaker "justifies" a shoe to a foot.

<margin>The second difference.</margin>
The second difference arises from this: in the matter of the other virtues, nothing is judged truly and legitimately "right" except with respect to the agent's intent. For example, if a greedy person eats a meager meal, not to live temperately but to avoid spending money, that work is not judged "right," nor measured by virtue. If, however, a debtor pays a creditor exactly as much money as is owed, but with a sinister intention—namely, so that the creditor might squander it—or if someone returns a sword held in deposit to its owner, knowing it is being reclaimed for an evil use, then such a 

<column-break/>

work is judged "just" in a simple sense, because it is equal to what was owed, even though it is not a "work of virtue," nor is the one who pays it being virtuous <term>virtuous: translated from "studiosus," meaning one who is diligent in practicing virtue</term>.

<margin>The third difference.</margin>
¶ And from this, in turn, a third difference arises: namely, that the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to established theological authorities, particularly the Scholastics.</note> rightly ascribe an object to the virtue of justice which they call "Right" and "the Just," but they do not do so for any of the others. This is because in the virtue of justice, the "just" itself is established by the nature of the thing; in the others, however, it is established only by the right intention of the agent. For this reason, Saint <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> Thomas (which must be considered deliberately) does not begin his treatises on other virtues—such as fortitude or temperance—with their objects, but with the virtues themselves which create rightness in the work. He begins the treatise on justice, however, with the object, which consists in the things themselves. Indeed, in other virtues, it is not so much called an "object" as the "matter" with which the virtue is concerned: for instance, the matter of fortitude is the danger of war, and the matter of temperance is the pleasures of touch, in which virtue establishes a middle point between two emotions. But the virtue of justice properly has an object: the very equality of things toward which the virtue tends, just as sight tends toward colors. We have, therefore, the conclusion that Right is the object of justice.

<margin>Buridan</margin>
¶ However, there are some who, seeing this distinction only on the surface, attack it. I refer to Buridan <note>Jean Buridan (c. 1300–1361), a French philosopher and influential commentator on Aristotle.</note>. In his commentary on Book 5 of the *Ethics*, Question 1, he rises against this doctrine as follows. <margin>Buridan’s argument against St. Thomas.</margin> He says: Either Saint Thomas is speaking of the rightness of a work insofar as it is the rightness of a virtue, or he is speaking of its rightness absolutely, even if it is not done by virtue. If the first way, then just like the duties of other virtues, the work of justice is not right except in relation to the agent. For Aristotle <margin>Aristotle.</margin> teaches in the *Ethics*, Book 2, Chapter 4, that no work is an act of virtue unless it is done by choice for a legitimate end; therefore, as we just said, someone who returns a sword to the true owner so that he may commit a murder is not being virtuous. If, however, he speaks of the rightness of the work absolutely, not insofar as it proceeds from virtue, then in the matter of other virtues such rightness is also found without relation to the agent: for example, if someone observes the law of fasting out of hypocrisy, or behaves bravely in war for the sake of vain glory. It is answered, <margin>Solution to the argument.</margin> nevertheless, that the difference is established in "rightness" considered absolutely. It is this: since the rightness of justice is by its nature discoverable in the things themselves, one who pays a debt equal to what is owed with a bad intention and end does indeed perform a just work—since he renders to another his right—even though he himself is not "just" (that is, virtuous), because he does not act when...

### Question 1 of the Third Book

...when, where, and how it is necessary. In the other virtues, however, if you take away any single circumstance of the virtue, no moral rectitude remains: that is to say, that fasting will not be a work of temperance, nor will an attack in war be a work of courage, because such works have no other rectitude except in relation to the habit of the virtue.

<margin>Regarding the first argument. Buridan.</margin>
Therefore, to respond to the principal objections concerning the matter of the first argument, the same Jean Buridan <note>Jean Buridan (c. 1300–1361) was a French priest and influential philosopher who developed the theory of impetus.</note> and several others who are less skilled in understanding the meaning of terms deny that the name **Right** (*ius*) is taken for the object of justice. Instead, they say it is the same thing as **Law** (*lex*), according to the word of Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose Etymologies served as a standard reference for medieval definitions.</note> which is cited in Distinction 1: "Right is a general name, but Law is a species of Right."

<margin>Buridan is refuted.</margin>
But truly, those who deny this are opposed by truth itself, armed with the authority of all. For indeed, what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> called "the just" when he said that justice is the habit that produces just things, the Jurist <note>The Roman jurist Ulpian.</note> clearly named **Right** (*ius*), saying: "Justice is the virtue of giving each their own right." If, therefore, justice creates right and the just, who would deny that **Right** is the object of justice? On the contrary, I would believe that through <term>apocope</term> <note>A linguistic term for the loss of one or more sounds or syllables at the end of a word.</note> (that is, by the cutting off of the final syllable of the word), *iustum* (the just) was shortened to *ius* (right), just as we say *potes* for that which is *potestis*. Hence in Greek, <term>Dikaion</term> <note>original: Δίκαιον</note> signifies the same thing indiscriminately: both "the just" and "right." For this reason, Isidore himself in that same passage immediately adds that it is called "just" because it is right. Consequently, law itself is called "just" precisely because it establishes "the just" in affairs. But because the names of crafts and finished works are also transferred to signify the arts themselves—just as the name of "medicine," which is a thing composed through art, is applied to the art itself—the name of **Right** was derived: first to signify the art of knowing what is just, and from there again to signify

<margin>Law and the art of the good and fair are not the same.</margin>
the law. For you must be careful not to think that the "art of the good and fair" and "law" are the same thing. For the art is not a command, but rather a moral science, such as exists in jurists for investigating what is fair to sanction by law. Law, however, is a rule of prudence, or a practical command established from that science: for example, "do this" or "do not do that." This indeed resides in the sovereign, as we declared in Book 1, Question 1.

<margin>The intent of Isidore.</margin>
Wherefore, when Isidore says that law is a species of right, he does not mean "species" as something directly subordinate to a genus (as "man" is to "animal"), since he adds that "right" is that which is just. Rather, he means it is a written rule and precept of right. For one kind of Right is natural, implanted in our minds, and another is written; and according to Isidore, Law is a written

<column-break/>

constitution.

<margin>The error of Accursius.</margin>
¶ And through this, the sense of Celsus's words is revealed: "Right is the art of the fair and the good."
<margin>Budé.</margin>
Where the confused Accursius <note>Accursius (c. 1182–1263) was a famous Italian jurist known for his "Great Gloss" on Roman law.</note> says that "the fair" is not the same as "the good," inventing some sort of distinction between those parts. Nevertheless, as the learned Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French humanist scholar who applied philological methods to Roman law.</note> noted there, and as we declared above in Book 1, Question 6, the phrase "the fair and the good" is taken as a single name for that which is <term>epieikeia</term> <note>The Greek term for "equity" or "fairness"—the principle of interpreting the spirit of the law when the letter of the law would be unjust.</note>. This is the interpretation of the law in a case where it is clear that the legislator, if he were present, would not have wanted the law to be observed according to the rigor of the text. For laws cannot provide for every individual case. Hence it happens that when the Jurist says Right is the art of the good and fair, "Right" is taken not for the written word, but for the natural. Inasmuch as equity, acting against the words of the written right, keeps its intent unharmed, in which it preserves natural right. Therefore, the art of the fair and the good is the same as the art of protecting natural right where the written word appears iniquitous. For it is held in the *Institutes*: "By the Edict of the Praetor, this iniquity of the law was amended." And Ulpian says: "If anyone obtains an iniquitous right against another, let him be subjected to that same right himself." From this also emanated that axiom: <term>The height of right is the height of injury</term> <note>original: "Summū ius, summa iniuria" — meaning that a law applied too strictly without equity becomes an injustice.</note>.

<margin>The sense of Ulpian. Right.</margin>
¶ Yet from these very things that have been said, we gather the understanding of Ulpian in that same law, where he says: "**Right** (*ius*) is named after **Justice** (*iustitia*)." Indeed, if you take "Right" as the object of justice, as was said, it is actually false. For justice is rather named after "Right," since a habit derives its species from its object. Furthermore, by the rule of grammar, the longer word is derived from the shorter. Therefore, the Jurist takes "Right" for the art and science of judging concerning natural right. That art arises from justice for this reason: that only he who is just flourishes in prudence for judging rightly about things to be done, as Aristotle says in the 6th book of the *Ethics*.

<margin>Summary of the aforementioned.</margin>
¶ So that we may make a summary of what has been said: **Right** exists in things; but the **art of the fair and good** is in the intellect, teaching how to work the just, like the art of a smith. But **Law** is the rule of the practical intellect established through prudence, and is thus the "reason" of the just—that is, the factor that makes and constitutes the just. Finally, **Justice** is the virtue of the will which, according to the law, establishes the just in things.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thus it happens that when it is said that "right is rendered" to someone, it is taken in no other way than as the object of justice. Albeit Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> distinguishes somewhat: namely, that "rendering right" may be to pronounce a sentence in favor of someone, whether according to the truth of the matter, or accor...

### ARTICLE II.

### Whether the division of Right into natural and positive is appropriate for its category.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' at the beginning of the article.</image-desc>

<margin>The first argument.</margin> AFTER having seen what "Right" is, we must follow with its division: whether this category, "Right," is appropriately divided into these two species, namely, the natural and the positive. And it is argued from the negative side. There is no such thing as natural Right among humans; therefore, the division assumes something false. The premise is proven: Natural Right is immutable and the same among all people, as is held in Distinction 1, the canon "Natural Right" <note>Refers to the Decretum of Gratian, the foundation of medieval Canon Law.</note>. However, in human affairs, nothing is immutable, because all human things fail in certain cases; therefore, there is no natural Right.

<margin>The second.</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is argued: There is no positive Right; for positive Right is that which is established by human will and judgment, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 7. Isidore says the same in the same Distinction, where he says that civil Right is what each people has established for itself. However, from the fact that it is established by human will, it does not follow that it is "right" or "straight," and thus, it does not follow that it is "Right"; therefore, there is no positive Right.
<margin>Aristotle. Isidore.</margin>

<margin>The third.</margin> ¶ Thirdly, divine Right is neither positive, since it does not rest on human authority; nor is it truly na-

<column-break/>

-tural, because it exceeds nature; therefore, the division is not sufficient.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin> ¶ On the contrary, however, is the authority of the Philosopher in the cited place, *Ethics* Book 5, Chapter 7, where he divides political Right—specifically civil right—into natural and positive, which he calls "legal."

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' at the start of the first point.</image-desc>

<margin>The first foundation.</margin> HERE it must first of all be known that "Right" is distributed by these same divisions, whether you take it as "Law" <note>original: "lex"</note>, or as "the just" <note>original: "iustum"</note>, which is the object of justice. For from the "Right" which is the object of justice, justice has the character of a virtue, and law has the character of a rule. Therefore, all things that were said in Book 1, Question 5, concerning the divisions of "Right" taken as "Law," also apply to this place, and accordingly, the discussion here will be shorter.

<margin>The second.</margin> Secondly, it must also be carefully observed here that "Right" is not immediately to be divided into three parts—namely, into natural Right, the law of nations <note>original: "ius gentium"</note>, and civil Right—as the school of legal experts almost universally thinks. This is so even though Isidore seems to judge it so, as will be clear in the following article. Nor should it be divided into four, as others think: namely, into these three and divine Right. But if you consult the art of dividing, "Right"—as it is common to both the divine and the human—is divided into two: namely, natural and positive. Divine Right is divided similarly; and then human positive Right is divided into the law of nations and civil Right.

<margin>Conclusion-response.</margin> Therefore, a single conclusion responds to the question: Right is primarily divided into natural and positive.

<margin>The proof.</margin> The conclusion is proven. Right, or "the just," is the same as the equal and the adequate. But this can happen in only one of two ways: namely, either from the nature of things, or from the agreement of human will (for let us set aside divine law for a moment, about which we must judge similarly). For example: that he who received something on credit should restore just as much, the nature of things teaches; and therefore, it is natural Right. Similarly, it is natural Right that a woman be joined to a man for the sake of procreation. However, that a measure of grain should be sold for five shekels <note>original: "siclis"</note> was certainly not made by nature, but by human agreement: namely, the consensus of the commonwealth or the prince. For since the coercive power is required for the character of a law, not every agreement obtains the force of law, but only that which belongs to the commonwealth. Hence, what passes privately between citizens is not a law, but a pact. In the same way, that relatives in the fourth degree may enter into marriage was not forbidden by nature, but by human will. Since, therefore, the "equal" and the "just" can only come into use in these two ways, it follows that these two members complete the category of Right itself. Therefore, when you hear that natural Right is that which is from nature, understand it in two ways: namely, from nature teaching it...

### Book Three, Question I.

...prompted and instigated by nature itself toward that very end. Hence Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a Roman jurist whose writings make up a large part of the Digest</note> says in the first book of the Digest on Justice and Right: "Natural law," he says, "is common to all: for it is held everywhere by the instinct of nature, not by any constitution." Here, by contrasting natural instinct and constitution, he suggests our two-part division. <margin>Cicero.</margin> To this same point refers the division by Cicero in his book *On Invention*, saying: "Natural right is that which is brought to us not by opinion, but by a certain innate power." All these definitions, therefore, are established through their "efficient cause" <note>The efficient cause is the agent or force that brings something into being; here, nature is the agent</note>. But truly Aristotle, in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, in the chapter already <margin>Aristotle.</margin> cited, defines it through its "formal cause" <note>The formal cause is the essence or definition of what a thing is</note> in the philosophical manner, saying: "Natural right is that which everywhere has the same force, and not because it seems so"—that is, it is necessary everywhere by its very nature, and not because it is placed there by human judgment and choice. For indeed, that one who receives ten should return as many is not just because men think it so, but by its own nature, just as fire is hot. However, that grain should be sold for so much, or wine for so much, and that this vice should be punished with such a penalty, or this or that sacrifice be offered, and similar things—not nature, but human will has made these just. Wherefore the Philosopher <note>Standard scholastic title for Aristotle</note> says there that "legal justice" <note>original: "iustũ legitimum"</note> was of no consequence before it was established, but it matters after it has been established. In short, this present division coincides with that which the Doctors <note>Theologians and legal scholars</note> distinguish: some things are either commanded because they are good, or prohibited because they are evil <note>Natural Law</note>; while other things are either good because they are commanded, or evil because they are prohibited <note>Positive Law</note>.

<margin>The first objection against the definition of natural law.</margin> ¶ Nevertheless, some ambiguity presents itself concerning that definition of natural law through its efficient cause: For if natural right is what nature teaches, no one could be ignorant of it; and yet there are many things concerning natural law which barbarian nations are ignorant of—as we noted regarding simple fornication from the Apostolic Council in Acts 15—which was prohibited to converted Gentiles so that <margin>Second.</margin> they would not be excused through ignorance. Again: if natural right is that to which nature instigates us, it follows that all natural law is necessary; yet this seems to be false, since, as we said above, a dispensation can be granted regarding some of it. ¶ To the <margin>To the first objection.</margin> first of these, it is responded that not everything nature teaches is grasped by everyone, but only by those who have clear reason and are free from every cloud. For those who are immersed in vices and have obscured their reason with darkness do not sufficiently perceive the rays of nature. The second doubt was touched upon during the arguments at the beginning of the question.

<margin>To the first main argument.</margin> It is therefore responded to the first argument where the same doubt was raised, by conceding that all natural right is simply necessary by its own nature. For this reason, in the preceding book, Question 3, we said it is "indispensable" <note>Meaning it cannot be set aside by human authority</note>. Indeed, although Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Franciscan theologian</note> himself considers the precepts of the "second table" <note>The commandments regarding relations with neighbors, such as "thou shalt not kill"</note> to be dispensable, he should not deny that they are necessary by their nature. But perhaps he would say that God, being superior to nature, could grant a dispensation over them; just as angels and the heavens, although they are things necessary by their nature, can be supernaturally annihilated. However, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that even this is not possible regarding those same precepts—since it is utterly repugnant to their nature for them to be lawful, just as it is for a man to be irrational. But truly, that which is necessary by its nature can be changed when circumstances change. For the necessity of each thing must be weighed according to its nature. If the nature of a thing is immutable, then its right will also be simply immutable: for instance, because the heaven is an immutable thing, its motion is immutable; but because water is a mutable thing, although it is simply natural for it to cool, it nevertheless heats when it is hot. In the same way, that a deposit <note>Property held in trust for another</note> must be returned to its owner is simply necessary when considered in itself; but because man is mutable, if the owner is in a depraved state and seeks his sword to commit murder, it must not be returned to him. For just as it would be right to return it if he were sane, so when he becomes insane, it is right not to return it. In the same way, it is a simply necessary right in itself that you must pay whatever you owe; but when you are unable to pay, the law does not bind you. Therefore, this change does not happen so much in the "Right" itself as in the men themselves. And from this root, at the end of the first book, we derived the reason why it is expedient for human laws to be changed sometimes: namely, because things change. And in Book 2, Question 3, we demonstrated that a "dispensation" cannot apply to those laws which contain the very reason of justice and its end; but it can apply to those which do not bring the end with them, but rather the means. For this is the kind of natural thing that Aristotle, in the place cited, says can change. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> For although the right hand is naturally stronger, sometimes it fails, and the left arm is the robust one. ¶ To the second, it is responded <margin>To the second.</margin> by conceding that it is not a general rule that whatever the will establishes immediately becomes just. For if it establishes anything against natural law, it will never obtain the force of law, as was said above, with the prophet Isaiah 10 crying out:
> Woe to those who decree iniquitous laws. 
But when a thing is not only not repugnant to nature but is actually appropriate for the place and time: then human will, if it possesses public authority, can establish it. Because it has been established, it becomes just; and, as Aristotle says, what was not...

# Brother Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>To the third point.</margin>
...it did not refer to it, it now does. ¶ Finally, in response to the third point, as we have suggested above: divine law is not divided against natural and positive law by the same kind of division. Rather, it is divided in a similar way. ¶ Thus, to make the division clear, first of all, law is divided into divine and human; then, each branch is subdivided by exactly the same method: so that one part of divine law is natural, and the other is positive. For the whole of natural law is divine, because God is the author of nature and consequently of every law derived from it. But <term>divine positive law</term><note>Law that is specifically "posited" or decreed by God's will through revelation, rather than discovered through reason alone.</note> is that which is established by God above nature, such as the laws of the Sacraments for the Christian family, or the ceremonial and judicial laws of the Old Law <note>The laws given to the Israelites in the Hebrew Bible.</note>. However, the commandments of the first table of the Decalogue <note>The first three of the Ten Commandments, which concern duties toward God.</note> are not called divine positive law in a simple sense—even though, as stated above, they are made explicit through faith—because they spring from the very nature of things, even if they are not recognized by everyone without the assistance of faith.

-> Whether the Law of Nations is the same as <-

<margin>First argument.</margin>

This refers to laws that are common to almost all human societies, such as the use of money or the protection of ambassadors.</note>: in which of those branches should it be included? It is argued that it is contained under natural law. For that law in which all men agree cannot be anything but natural, which (as we were just saying) is common to all. By the Law of Nations, all nations agree, according to Ulpian in the first book of the Digest on Justice and Right: "The Law of Nations is that which the human nations use." And the Institutes on natural law say: "The Law of Nations is common to the whole human race." Therefore, the Law of Nations and natural law are the same.

-re itself taught the same law, and thus it is natural.

<margin>Isidore.</margin>

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with a single conclusion: The Law of Nations is both distinguished from natural law and included under positive law. Although Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> does not explicitly state this conclusion here, nevertheless his arguments at the beginning of the question—where he argues the Law of Nations is natural—suggest that his intent is to deny that and to affirm instead that it is positive law. Moreover, <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> in the *Summa Theologiae* Part I-II, Question 95, Article 4, he states this plainly, where he divides positive law into the Law of Nations and civil law; a point we explained in Book I, Question 5. And the reasoning he brings forward here makes the same thing clear. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> The conclusion is thus proven: Natural law (as we said in the previous article) is that which is adjusted and commensurate to another by the very nature of the thing. This happens in two ways. One way is according to the absolute consideration of things; just as male and female by their absolute nature are fitted together for the task of procreation, and a father is naturally inclined to nourish his son. In another way, something is commensurate to another not according to its absolute nature, but considered in relation to a certain end and through certain circumstances. For example: That this field should be possessed by this specific master, and another by someone else. Nature, considered absolutely, no more requires this than that all things should be possessed in common. However, if the same field is considered as needing to be cultivated to bear fruit and possessed in peace—and given the state of <term>corrupt nature</term><note>The theological concept of humanity's fallen state after original sin.</note> in which men are more sluggish about spending their own labor for the common good and are greedy for the things of others—reason immediately concludes that it is entirely beneficial for divisions of possessions to be made. As the Philosopher <margin>The Philosopher.</margin> teaches in the second book of the *Politics*, and as we shall show in our fourth book in the question on the division of things. From this distinction, therefore, the reason for the conclusion is drawn. For to apprehend a thing absolutely is common not only to humans but also to other living creatures by natural instinct; and therefore, the law which is simply natural, such as the union of male and female and the nurturing of offspring, is common to all animals. But truly, to judge concerning things in relation to an end and under certain circumstances does not belong to all animals, but specifically to man by the power of reason, whose function it is...
