### Third Book, Question I.

...to compare one thing to another. Therefore, that law which is established through such comparative reason is called the <term>Law of Nations</term><note>Latin: *ius gentium*. In the sixteenth century, this referred to laws that all human civilizations naturally agree upon, such as the rules of trade or diplomacy.</note>, that is, the law which all nations, insofar as they are rational, have established for themselves.

<margin>The various words of the Jurists are elucidated.</margin>
¶ Through the understanding of these points, the words of the <term>Jurists</term><note>The legal scholars of ancient Rome, such as Ulpian and Gaius, whose writings formed the basis of European law.</note> become clear, the explanation of which falls to the moral philosopher. For Ulpian says in the first book of the <term>Digest</term><note>Latin: *ff.*, a standard abbreviation for the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Roman law commissioned by Emperor Justinian.</note> on justice and law, that the Law of Nations departs from natural law; he says this can be easily understood because natural law is common to all animals, while the Law of Nations is common only to humans among themselves. And Gaius, in the law "All Peoples," says: "That which natural reason has established among all men is observed equally among all, and is called the Law of Nations." He does not say "That which the simple light of nature [establishes]," but "That which reason—which is proper to humans—establishes," that is, "posits."

<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
And from this, another argument for the conclusion is taken. For <term>Natural Law</term><note>Latin: *ius naturale*. Principles of right and wrong inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> is simply necessary—that is, it does not depend on human consent. However, the Law of Nations binds because it is "seen" to be so—that is, because it is so judged by men. For the possessions of things would never be divided unless men agreed that some should possess these things and others should possess those. Therefore, the Law of Nations is not simply natural, but <term>positive</term><note>Law that is "posited" or created by human decision rather than existing automatically in nature.</note>.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But if you should shake our conclusion with the argument that it would follow that the Law of Nations is the same as <term>Civil Law</term><note>Latin: *ius civile*. The specific laws of a particular city or state, like the laws of the United States or the United Kingdom today.</note>, listen to the difference between these types of law so that the answer may become clearer to you.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
First of all, both the Law of Nations and Civil Law differ from Natural Law in that Natural Law is simply necessary according to the absolute consideration of things, as has been said, and is therefore common to all living creatures. But both the Law of Nations and Civil Law are "posited" by human reason. However, the Law of Nations and Civil Law differ primarily by this fundamental distinction, which we drew from the mind of St. Thomas Aquinas in Book 1, Question 95, Article 4.

<margin>The first distinction between Civil Law and the Law of Nations.</margin>
Specifically, the Law of Nations is elicited from the natural principles of things considered in relation to a certain end and circumstances by way of *conclusion*. For example, if you say: "Fields must be cultivated," and "Men are more negligent toward common property than toward their own," it follows: "Therefore, property should be possessed privately." <note>This was a standard argument for private property: people take better care of things they own than things shared by everyone.</note> Civil Law, however, is gathered from one natural principle and another premise established by human choice; therefore, it is not gathered by way of a logical deduction, but by the <term>determination</term><note>A specific application of a general rule. For example, "Murder is wrong" is a principle; "The penalty for murder is 20 years in prison" is a determination.</note> of a general principle into a special law, as has been said repeatedly regarding ceremonial and judicial laws. For example, if you say: "Things should be sold at a just price," but "The just price of wheat according to the conditions of the present place and time is five shekels." The second part is not from the law of nature. Similarly: "An evildoer must be punished," therefore "A thief should be hanged." From this 

<column-break/>

first difference, a second follows: that to 

<margin>The second difference.</margin>
establish the Law of Nations, an assembly of men in one place is not required, because reason teaches this to each person by itself. But to establish Civil Law, a council of the commonwealth or the authority of a prince is required, so that it may be established after counsel has been taken on both sides. And from this follows a third difference: namely, that the Law of Nations is common to all nations, as was said; but Civil Law is, as Isidore of Seville says, that which each people or city establishes as its own. Therefore, the law of the Athenians is one thing, and the law of the Romans is another, etc., as is held in the <term>Institutes</term><note>A textbook of Roman law for students.</note> on natural law and the law of nations, in the paragraph "But the Law."

<margin>Almost all contracts were introduced by the Law of Nations.</margin>
Furthermore, almost all contracts were introduced by the Law of Nations, such as buying and selling, leasing, etc., without which human society cannot stand, as is clear in the same Institutes, in the paragraph "Moreover, Law," and in the Digest on justice and law, in the law "From this Law." Isidore, because he knew that the Law of Nations differs from both Natural and Civil law, distinguished law into these three branches so as not to make too many divisions. It is more skillfully divided, therefore, into Natural and Positive law; and then human Positive law into the Law of Nations and Civil Law.

¶ But a warning is needed lest anyone be deceived by Aristotle's division in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 7, where he divides <term>Political Law</term><note>Latin: *ius politicum*. The laws governing a community or "polis."</note> into natural and legal. For he does not use "political" in the exact same way that jurists use "civil"; for natural law is not a species of civil law, but is placed in opposition to it. Therefore, he called "political law" in a general sense all law which a city uses, which includes Natural Law as well as the Law of Nations and Civil Law.

¶ However, not all the doubts that grow out of this conclusion have been extinguished; for there seem to be laws to the contrary. For Pomponius says in the law "Just as" in the Digest on justice and law, that religion toward God, and that we should obey our parents and country, belong to the Law of Nations. 

<margin>The first argument against the aforementioned things.</margin>
And Florentinus says in the law "That violence," that the Law of Nations looks to repelling injuries; yet all these things are of Natural Law. For the commandment of religion and of honoring parents are in the <term>Decalogue</term><note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, which, as we have sufficiently demonstrated above, is a sprout of natural law. And repelling injuries is a conclusion of that principle: "Every thing seeks to preserve itself." Therefore, the Law of Nations is the same as Natural Law.

¶ And secondly, the same thing is argued. In the last book, we often repeated this difference between 

<margin>The second [argument].</margin>
moral precepts on one hand, and ceremonial, judicial, and civil law on the other: that moral precepts are inferred from the principles of nature by way of conclusion, but the others are not, as we were just declaring. For which reason we said...

# Brother Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

...that the <term>Decalogue</term><note>The Ten Commandments.</note> belongs to <term>Natural Law</term><note>Latin: *ius naturae*. Moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note>. Therefore, if the <term>Law of Nations</term><note>Latin: *ius gentium*. Rules of conduct that all civilized peoples naturally follow, such as trade and diplomacy.</note> is derived from these same principles by way of a conclusion, it follows that it would likewise belong to natural law.

<margin>To the first [argument].</margin>
¶ To the first argument, it is answered that the <term>Jurists</term><note>The ancient Roman legal experts whose writings formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance law.</note> extend the Law of Nations too far. For they believe that this name encompasses whatever is common to all mortals, and that natural law is only that which humans share with the <term>brutes</term><note>Non-human animals.</note>. However, there are many natural laws that belong specifically to human nature and not to animals—such as the Decalogue and what is implied therein. Therefore, the difference is not what they say, but what we have proposed: namely, that those things derived from the absolute nature of things by a necessary consequence belong to natural law; whereas those things derived not from absolute consideration, but (as explained) in relation to a specific goal, belong to the Law of Nations. Therefore, the Decalogue does not belong to the Law of Nations, but to Natural Law.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ And from this, the solution to the second argument is drawn out. For when we said the Law of Nations is drawn from the principles of nature by way of inference, it is not understood that the inference is entirely necessary [in a logical sense], but rather that it is fitting for the nature of the thing in relation to a specific goal. For the division of property does not follow from the necessity of tilling the fields or their peaceful possession as necessarily as "Thou shalt not kill" follows from the principle "Do not do to others what you would not have them do to you." Rather, the division of property is established because it is most congruent and expedient for that goal.

<margin>The final doubt.</margin>
¶ From this, however, a final doubt arises: whether an <term>exemption</term><note>Latin: *dispensatio*. A formal release from a legal obligation.</note> can occur within the Law of Nations, or whether it is indispensable just like natural law.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
It is answered with a distinction: some things in the Law of Nations are so conducive to human society that it is in no way lawful for an exemption to be granted regarding them; indeed, perhaps an exemption would be void—such as the division of property we just mentioned. For, except among those in <term>religious orders</term><note>Monks or friars who take vows of poverty and hold all things in common.</note>, the common possession of goods would be intolerable. However, there are other things in that same law that can be exempted for a cause. For example, <term>slavery</term><note>Latin: *servitus*. Soto is writing at a time of intense debate regarding the rights of indigenous peoples in the Americas and the nature of bondage.</note> belongs to the Law of Nations, and yet an exception has been made so that Christians captured in war are not held as slaves. Also, some civil contracts, even those belonging to the Law of Nations, can be subject to exemptions. It is part of the Law of Nations to keep faith with enemies, such as protecting <term>ambassadors</term><note>Latin: *legatos*. Envoys or diplomats during wartime.</note> in war; yet if the cause of the faith demanded the opposite, it would not have to be kept. Indeed, if they were spreading corrupt dogmas, they ought to be <term>burned</term><note>A reference to the historical practice of the Inquisition and the execution of heretics; the "corrupt dogmas" refers to religious teachings deemed heretical by the Church.</note>, and no exemption would be necessary.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first.</margin>
Therefore, the first main argument has now been resolved; for it is denied that everything in which all nations agree is natural law.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ And to the second, it is answered that when <term>The Philosopher</term><note>Aristotle.</note> says men are slaves by natural law, he does not mean natural law in the absolute sense. For if human nature is considered absolutely, there is no reason why one should serve more than another. But it is so if considered in relation to a goal: for example, so that one may be taught by another, or so that one might be saved in war. And therefore, it belongs more to the Law of Nations, although the servitude of one who is more unrefined, so that he may be imbued with morals by one who is wiser, is not contrary to liberty (as we shall say in the fourth book in its proper question). Thus, it is more "natural" in the sense of being congruent to the nature of the individual.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is likewise answered that although the Law of Nations requires the consensus of men, it does not require a formal assembly as <term>Civil Law</term><note>The specific laws of a particular city or state.</note> does; for all nations, though dispersed, are taught that law by natural reason.

### ARTICLE IV.

->*Whether paternal and masterly right, and political justice, are distinguished from each other by any reasoning.*<-

---

REgarding what remains from the previous sections, a doubt exists concerning certain types of right, such as <term>paternal right</term><note>The rights of a father over his children.</note> and <term>masterly right</term><note>The rights of a master over a slave or servant.</note>, which do not seem to be fully included under the definitions above. It is asked, therefore, whether paternal and masterly right are distinguished both from <term>political justice</term><note>The justice governing a city or state of free citizens.</note> and from each other.

<margin>The first argument for the negative side.</margin>
And the argument is made, as is our custom, from the negative side. It belongs to justice in general to "render to each his own." Since, therefore, right is the object of justice, it follows that it should regard everyone equally. Therefore, no distinction should be made between father and son, or between master and slave.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Second: The Law which (as we said in Article 1) is the reason and constitutive rule of what is just, looks to the <term>common good</term> of the whole city, not to the private good of any person. But the father and son, and master and slave, belong to a private family; therefore, paternal and masterly right are not distinguished from political right.

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
¶ Third: If these types of right were to be distinguished, for the same reason many other types ought to be recognized according to the various ranks among citizens: such as military right, the right of priests, and so on.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the authority of...

### Book Three, Question I.

...the authority of the <term>Philosopher</term><note>Aristotle (384–322 BC), whose works on ethics and politics formed the foundation of medieval law.</note> in the *Ethics*, Book 5, chapter 6, who distinguishes <term>paternal justice</term><note>Latin: *ius paternum*.</note> and <term>masterly justice</term><note>Latin: *ius dominativum*. The rights of a master over a servant.</note> from <term>political justice</term><note>Latin: *ius politicum*. The laws governing equal citizens.</note>.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
This article is presented solely to explain the passage cited from Aristotle. It is answered with three very brief conclusions which summarize Aristotle's view. The first is: Between a father and a son, there is no <term>absolute political justice</term><note>Latin: *simpliciter iustum politicum*. Justice in its fullest, most equal sense between independent citizens.</note>, but only justice in a certain respect. And remember, we are not using "political" here to mean "civil law" as distinguished from natural law or the law of nations, but—as we were just saying—to mean the justice maintained between citizens. For Aristotle uses it this way so that it also encompasses natural law.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is thus proven. Justice, as we have said until now, is the same as that which is adequate and commensurate to another. For justice only exists between two or more people. However, one person is "other" than another in two ways: in one way because they are simply distinguished from them, like any citizen from another citizen; in another way "in a certain respect," namely because they are in some way "other" (as a separate person) but in another way "the same" (as a part of the other). A son is not simply "other" than his father, but only in a certain respect, insofar as he is a part of him—as held in Book 8 of the *Ethics*—specifically as <term>seed</term><note>Aristotle argued that children were physically derived from the father's substance, making them "parts" of him until they reached maturity.</note> separated from him. Therefore, between father and son there is no absolute justice, but only justice in a certain respect, which is specifically called "paternal justice."

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ By the same reasoning, the second conclusion is established. Between a master and a servant, there is no absolute justice. For as the Philosopher says in Book 1 of the *Politics*, a servant is not simply something "other" than the master; indeed, whatever he is, he belongs to the master as an <term>instrument</term><note>In the Aristotelian view, a servant was considered an "animate tool" of the master.</note>. Therefore, just as there is no proper sense of justice between a tool and a craftsman, nor does a craftsman do an injustice to the tool if he uses it according to his whim, so it is between master and servant; it is justice only in a certain respect, which is called "masterly justice."

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion. Between a husband and a wife, there is a greater degree of justice than between a father and a son, or between a master and a servant. This conclusion is added to the above to reconcile the Philosopher with the <term>Apostle</term><note>Saint Paul the Apostle.</note>. For if you listen to the Apostle 

<margin>Paul.</margin>
saying in Ephesians 5 that a husband and wife belong to the same body—according to that passage in Genesis 2, "They shall be two in one flesh"—you might easily conclude from this that there is less justice between husband and wife than between father and son, because they 

<column-break/>

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
seem to be "less" two distinct people. Nevertheless, Aristotle, in the passage cited, recognized more justice between them. The reason is that both, though not on equal footing, nevertheless share an order toward the common management of the family. For this reason, both children and servants are bound to obey the <term>head of the household</term><note>Latin: *patrifamilias*.</note> by almost the same right as they obey a father. For although a wife is bound to obey her husband, to whom she is joined for the generation of offspring—and for that reason is said to be in some way the "same body," that is, the same bodily principle, which is why the first woman was formed from the rib of the man—nevertheless, no individual woman is a "part" of her husband in the way a son is of his father. Rather, if it were permitted to speak this way, she is his "partner" <note>Latin: *compars*.</note>; for both are parts of "one flesh," and for that reason they are called "two in one flesh." And she stands in relation to the man much less as a servant. For this reason, in Book 1 of the *Politics*, Aristotle 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
attributes it to <term>barbarism</term><note>Aristotle argued that only "barbarian" cultures treated women as equivalent to slaves.</note> when a woman and a servant are held in the same rank; and therefore, between a husband and wife, there is <term>domestic justice</term><note>Latin: *oeconomicum iustum*. Justice pertaining to the management of a household (*oikos*).</note>.

<margin>Explanation of the first conclusion.</margin>
¶ Regarding the first conclusion, it must first be noted that when it is asserted that between father and son there is no absolute justice, but only justice in a certain respect, that "certain respect," although it diminishes the strict definition of justice, does not diminish the nature of <term>debt</term><note>The moral obligation or "what is owed."</note> or natural virtue; rather, it increases it. For since justice is both "toward another," implies a "debt," and establishes "equality," it fails to meet the definition of justice by a defect in any of those three conditions. Between a father and son, it fails by the first condition: because the son is not "simply" another person. Furthermore, it fails by the third condition: because we cannot return an equal amount to our parents. It does not, however, fail by the second condition: for we owe more to our fathers than to anyone else. Therefore, beware of thinking that paternal right has less of the "nature of law" than political right; on the contrary, it is more natural, even if it has less of the formal structure of justice. Moreover, these conditions apply much more justly to us in respect to God. First, because we are in some way something belonging to Him—not indeed parts, but certainly effects—and therefore we are much less capable of returning an equal amount to Him than to our parents. <term>Liberality</term><note>Generosity.</note>, however, fails the definition of justice because it does not concern a debt. It follows from these things that the justice "in a certain respect" that exists from a father to a son is something more excellent than simple justice: namely, <term>piety</term><note>Latin: *pietas*. In the classical sense, this refers to the duty and devotion one owes to parents, ancestors, and the divine.</note>.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ You will perhaps ask, however, whether when we said there is no absolute justice between father and son, this is understood from both sides: namely, the father toward the son as well as the son toward the father. It is answer...

<margin>Solution.</margin>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>First argument.</margin>
...it is understood on both sides, although not by an equal measure. For the relationship of a son to a father is not <term>simply just</term><note>Latin: *iustum simpliciter*. This refers to justice in its most complete and perfect form, occurring between two independent and equal individuals.</note>: not only because the son is a "part" of the father, but because he cannot return an equal benefit for what he has received. The father's relationship to the son is also not "simply just," but for the first reason: namely, because he relates to the son as a whole relates to its part. Therefore, just as there is no proper category of justice between a man and his own limbs—because they are not "simply two" distinct things—so it is between a father and a son. For whatever a father bestows upon his son, he bestows in a way upon himself; the prosperity or adversity of the son affects the father himself. For this reason, <term>Seleucus</term><note>Seleucus I Nicator (c. 358–281 BC), a successor of Alexander the Great. The story illustrates the "oneness" of the family unit.</note>, the monarch of the Locrians, when both of his son’s eyes were to be put out as punishment, divided the penalty equally so that one eye was taken from each of them, as if they were one single man. ¶ However, someone might perhaps raise the following argument against this truth.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
Even if it were true that a son is "something belonging to the father" as long as he is under parental care, once he is <term>emancipated</term><note>Released from the father's legal control (*patria potestas*).</note>, he then lives on his own and becomes a citizen just like his father. From that point on, he is equally eligible for public magistracies. Indeed, he is sometimes superior to his father—for instance, if he becomes a praetor, a consul, or a leader in war. Likewise, contracts of buying, selling, and others can then be celebrated between father and son, in which the weight of the law hangs from an equal balance on both sides. Therefore, a <term>perfect form of justice</term><note>Latin: *perfecta ratio iusti*.</note> can indeed intervene between father and son.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
And indeed, <term>St. Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note> seems to agree with this in his solution to the second argument, where he says that a father and son, or a master and servant, can be considered in two ways: as they are individual men, and as one is "something belonging" to the other. Therefore, certain laws are even given to fathers regarding how they should behave toward their sons.

<margin>Cajetan's solution.</margin>
<term>Cajetan</term><note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> contends that regardless of how sons are considered, there is no <term>absolute justice</term><note>Latin: *ius simpliciter*.</note> between them and their parents, but only justice <term>in a certain respect</term><note>Latin: *secundum quid*. A logical term meaning something is true only under certain conditions or in a limited sense.</note>. For the "right" that exists between them as humans, he says, is modified by the fact that one is a part of the other. Thus, it becomes justice in a certain respect—namely, "paternal justice."

<margin>The Author's response.</margin>
But truly, if my judgment is of any weight, I would rather distinguish the matter thus: regarding <term>natural rights</term>, paternal right always remains between sons (even emancipated ones) and parents—for example, regarding the honors to be paid to them, and regarding certain services and assistance when they have need of their children’s help. But regarding <term>civil matters</term>, there is "absolute justice" and what is "simply just" between them.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the first argument, then, he concedes that it belongs to justice to render to each what is his own, provided that it belongs to one person

<column-break/>

<term>simply</term> in relation to another. For when someone gives himself something that is due to him—for instance, food or clothing—he does not perform an act of "absolute justice"; and it is the same when a father nourishes his son.

<margin>To the second [argument].</margin>
¶ The response to the second argument is also drawn from what was said above. For although justice looks toward the common good, that does not prevent it from lacking a "perfect character" between father and son. However, because the parts of a household are also related to the common good, justice also establishes laws both for fathers regarding their children and for masters regarding their servants.

<margin>To the third [argument].</margin>
¶ Regarding the third, it is not denied that even in a republic, military law and the law of priests are distinguished, as was conceded and declared in Book 1 during the explanation of the divisions of laws. However, those laws do not fall short of perfect justice in any way, as paternal justice does, because they concern one person <term>simply</term> in relation to another. For all members of the republic have an immediate order toward the common good. Therefore, justice between a prince and a citizen, or between any magistrate and a subject, is just as "absolute" as it is between other citizens; but those rights differ according to their various offices, as was declared in the place cited.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of justice. Having previously discussed whether justice can exist in domestic relationships (like father and son), the author now moves to Question II: the formal definition of justice itself, engaging with the classic legal definition provided by the Roman jurist Ulpian and reconciling it with the philosophical frameworks of Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

# Book Three, Question II.

<margin>A responsive conclusion.
Proof. Aristotle.</margin>
The question is answered with a single affirmative conclusion. That definition <note>The author is referring to the famous definition by the Roman jurist Ulpian: "Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each his due."</note> is certainly good when correctly understood. Indeed, since every virtue is a "habit of choosing," as **Aristotle** says in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, and a habit takes its specific nature from the act (just as the act takes its nature from the object), the best definition of any virtue is one that expresses the nature of the thing through its proper act and object. For just as the rational soul is the "form" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that makes a thing what it is.</note> of a human being, so the act is the form of the habit. Justice, however—as has often been said above and shall be demonstrated below—is the virtue that orders the one who possesses it toward another person, establishing equality between them in what is given and received. Therefore, the proper act of justice is to render to each his own right <note>original: "ius suum"</note>.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Furthermore, there are three conditions common to every virtue, which **Aristotle** declares in Book 2 of the *Ethics*: namely, that one acts with **knowledge**; second, that one **chooses** the action for the sake of the proper end; and thirdly, that one acts **perpetually and constantly** in all actions as is fitting. For one or two acts of virtue do not make a person "studious" <note>In this context, "studious" (Latin: *studiosum*) refers to someone who is diligently virtuous or excellent.</note>, just as "one swallow does not make a spring." Therefore, where the **Jurist** <note>Referring again to Ulpian in the *Digest* of Roman law.</note> says, "Justice is the *will*," he does not use the word for the soul's power, but for its act. For the name of a power is sometimes given to its act, just as the knowledge of first principles is called "understanding." Nor is this an "identical predication" <note>A logical term meaning a statement where the subject and predicate are exactly the same thing (A = A).</note>, but a "causal" one: for justice is the habit by which a voluntary act is produced. It is in this way that **Augustine** says in his commentary on John, "Faith is to believe what you do not see"—that is, faith is the *habit* of believing. Thus, "will" is placed here in the position of the *genus* <note>The broad category to which a definition belongs.</note>. The jurisconsult used the word "will" in an oratorical manner to express, first and foremost, the proper subject of the virtue, which (as we are about to say) is the will. Secondly, it expresses the work of virtue, which must proceed spontaneously from one who knows and chooses; for what is done through ignorance or by force is not a "duty," because it is not voluntary.

<margin>Anselm.</margin>
By the same reasoning, when **Anselm** said in his book *On Truth* that justice is "rectitude" <note>rightness or straightness</note>, he did not make what is called an identical proposition—for only the Divine Will is its own rectitude—but he used a causal proposition, because justice produces rectitude in the work performed. Furthermore, what **Ulpian** added—"perpetual"—serves to bring out the third condition of virtue.

<margin>Two modes of perpetuity.</margin>
"Perpetual" is understood in two ways: In one way, by reason of the **act**, which is never interrupted; this kind of perpetuity belongs to God alone. In the other way, by reason of the **object**: namely, that a person resolves to act dutifully and according to the law in every possible event.

<column-break/>

And this condition is necessary for every virtue. Yet he wisely added the word **constant**, which is not the same as "perpetual." For "perpetual" only describes the resolution and intention of always acting in such a way; but "constant" adds the **firmness** of that same resolution. It ensures that a person does not waver or vacillate in their purpose, but holds it fixed. Indeed, this constancy is achieved by no one until they have attained full virtue: specifically, so that they do not turn away from the rectitude of justice because of greed, fear, any pleasure, or any other emotion. Hence, "constant" is the same as standing "square on all sides like a die" <note>Latin: *tessera quadratus*. A reference to Aristotle's description of the virtuous person as a cube or die, which remains upright no matter how it is thrown.</note>. For how many people do you find who have the intention of always acting excellently, but who, because they are not supported by the firm roots of virtue, repeatedly slip away? Thus far, the *genus* of the virtue of justice has been defined. The fact that he added "of rendering to each his own right" serves as the *difference* <note>The specific characteristic that distinguishes a species from others in the same category.</note>, setting justice apart from all other virtues and thus completing the definition of its type.

<margin>Buridan’s error.</margin>
From this it follows that **Buridan** <note>Jean Buridan (c. 1300–1360), a French priest and influential philosopher.</note> is unreasonable when, in his commentary on Book 5 of the *Ethics*, he denies that the aforementioned definition fits justice in all its acts. For the Jurist adds in that same passage: "The precepts of the law are these: to live honorably, not to harm another, and to render to each his own." Buridan therefore claims that the definition of justice applies only to the third part of these precepts. However, this is false; rather, the definition expresses the whole substance of justice. Its proper function is to render to each his right, and consequently to harm no one. For the commandments "You shall not kill" and "You shall not steal" explain the various aspects of justice. But the first part of the Jurist’s list—"to live honorably"—is not an act peculiar to justice alone, but is a general act of all virtues. For it has already been stated that every virtue has a general character of justice, as we will explain more fully later. Therefore, that part is not included in the definition assigned to "particular justice" <note>Justice as a specific virtue concerning fairness between individuals, rather than "legal justice" which encompasses all virtue.</note>. The Jurist's definition is therefore excellent—indeed, it is more explicit than **Aristotle's**, which states: "Justice is a habit by which men act justly." Aristotle's version does not explain the specific nature of the "just," which is to render a right to another. If you wish to reconcile both definitions and explain them more clearly, you may conclude with **Saint Thomas** that:

<margin>Absolute definition of Justice.</margin>
**Justice is a habit by which each person, with a perpetual and constant will, renders to each his own right.**

<margin>Objection. Solution.</margin>
Nor is it an objection that this definition also applies to the prince and the judge. For the prince renders right by commanding and directing as a guardian of the just; the virtue, how-

### ARTICLE II.

### Whether Justice is a Virtue that orders the one who possesses it toward another.

<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
Having established the definition of justice, it follows that we should explore its substance and innate qualities one by one: and this by examining each part of the definition. We ask, therefore, about its final distinguishing characteristic—which is to grant to each their own right—whether justice is properly "toward another" <note>original: "ad alterum"; this is the core philosophical question of whether you can be "just" to yourself, or if justice requires a second person.</note>. And it is argued from the negative side, using that passage from the Apostle in Romans 3: *The justice of God is through faith in Jesus Christ.* For faith is not spoken of as a comparison of one person to another.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly, the justice of God is eternal; and yet from eternity He had no other beside Himself to whom that justice could be referred. Therefore, justice is not necessarily "toward another."

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Thirdly, even if the duties of justice are toward another, they nonetheless require moderation and correction in relation to the one performing the action. For a greedy man is reluctant to give up the money he holds that belongs to another. Therefore, as it says in Proverbs 11: *the justice of the simple shall direct his way.* Thus, justice is not only concerned with things involving another, but also with moderating the inner feelings of the person who possesses the virtue.

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
On the contrary is **Cicero** in the first book of *On Duties*, saying that justice is that principle by which the society of men among themselves and the community of life is maintained. Furthermore, by this description, an ordering and respect of one person toward another is implied.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is very easy, and contained within two conclusions. The first is: Justice, properly so called, requires two distinct subjects <note>original: "supposita"</note> between which it establishes equality.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
This is the conclusion of the **Philosopher** <note>In this period, "The Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle.</note> in the last chapter of Book 5 of the *Ethics*.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Furthermore, this is clearly evident from the meaning of the name itself. For "justice" is the same as "equality" or the "habit of equality." Now, things are not called "equal" except abusively or by metaphor unless there are two of them, as is clear in physical quantities adjusted to the same standard. Again, "to act justly," if applied to morals, is only appropriate for human actions. But actions—as the **Philosopher** is the author in Book 2 of *On the

<column-break/>

Soul*—do not belong to a nature or to parts, but only to the whole subject <term>Subject (suppositum)</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "suppositum" is an individual, self-subsisting being. For example, a hand doesn't "act," the whole person acts using the hand.</note>. For "humanity," he says, does not spin wool, nor do the fingers or the hand, but the woman does. Nor does the hand properly strike an injury, nor does it pay a debt through justice, but the man does; unless perhaps we speak by a likeness, or as if they were joined instruments. Consequently, it follows that justice performs its duties not just between any two distinct things, but between two distinct persons.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: Nothing prevents justice, when spoken of metaphorically, from existing between the parts of the same subject. And the **Philosopher** also adds this conclusion in the same place. An example is evident between two parts of a

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
man. For first, there is a kind of justice between the limbs: namely, while the eyes lead the feet with their light, and in turn the feet carry the eyes by their effort. Moreover, the sensory part—for instance, the "spirited" and "desiring" faculties—when they obey reason with a "despotic" obedience <note>This refers to the classical idea that the mind should rule the body and emotions like a master rules a servant.</note>, are said to "keep justice"; and when they rebel, they are said to "disturb justice."

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence **Augustine** says in the book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*: "It pertains to justice that, because one serves God, he rules well over the other things that are subject to man." Now, the appetite is subject to reason, according to that passage in Genesis 4: *Its appetite*—namely, of sin—*shall be toward you, and you shall master it.*

<margin>The Question.</margin>
This is a very easy matter that needs no further expansion, unless perhaps someone asks whether the logic of "justice" between these parts of the same man is as great as that between a father

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
and a son. For it appears to be so: because since a son is "something of the father," we have said that "the just" is found between them only in a qualified sense.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
It is responded, however, that the logic is different. For since the father and the son are two distinct persons, the logic of justice is truly and properly established between them, even if it is somewhat diminished within the breadth of that same logic. But between reason and appetite, because they are not two distinct persons, there is no justice except metaphorically.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that when **Paul** says justice is through faith, he does not take "justice" as it is a species of moral virtue that performs a "just work"—that is, one made equal to another man—but as it frees the man himself from sin by rectifying his appetite so that it is obedient to reason. And according to this logic, it is metaphorical justice. Although, as we said above, it equally justifies a man in respect to God by rendering him subject, pleasing, and acceptable to Him, and to His will...

# Book Three, Question II.

...measured to the will. And according to this, it can also properly be called justice. <margin>Response to the second argument.</margin> ¶ Regarding the second argument, the response is that God’s justice is eternal according to His purpose, in which His very substance consists; however, according to its effect, He did not have anyone from eternity upon whom He might exercise that justice, but began to do so <margin>Response to the third argument.</margin> after He created the world. ¶ Finally, regarding the third point, the response will appear more clearly in Article 4. In the meantime, the response is that the passions which resist the works of justice are restrained by other virtues; once these passions are mitigated, a right choice is made through justice, as will be elucidated in the place cited.

### ARTICLE III.

### Whether Justice is a Virtue.

<margin>Argument 1.</margin> <note>The text begins with a decorative drop cap 'C' featuring floral motifs.</note> CONCERNING the category of the definition—which was stated to be a "habit of acting justly"—it is asked whether justice is a virtue. And it is argued from the negative side. Christ says: *When you have done all things that are commanded of you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which we ought to do* <note>original: "Serui inutiles sumus: quod debuimus facere fecimus"; Luke 17:10</note>. But a work of virtue <margin>Ambrose.</margin> is not "unprofitable" (or useless). For Ambrose says in Book 2 of *On Offices* that we do not call "utility" the estimation of monetary gain, but the acquisition of piety. Therefore, doing what one is obligated to do—in which justice consists—is not a work of virtue. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly, that which is done out of necessity is not meritorious. But to render to each his own, which is the work of justice, is a necessity. Therefore, it is not meritorious, and consequently, it is not a virtue, since we earn merit through all virtues by God's favor. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Thirdly, every moral virtue is concerned with <term>agibilia</term> (things to be done or actions); however, those things which are established externally are not <term>agibilia</term> but <term>factibilia</term> (things to be made), such as the <margin>Aristotle.</margin> tasks of the arts, as Aristotle is the author in Book 9 of the *Metaphysics*. Since, therefore, the duty of justice is to complete an external just work, it follows that it is not a virtue. <margin>Gregory.</margin> ¶ On the contrary is Gregory in Book 2 of the *Morals*, where he distinguishes four cardinal virtues: namely, temperance, prudence, fortitude, and justice. Furthermore, Wisdom itself, as appears in chapter 8, proclaims that it teaches these same virtues.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> TO the question, it is responded with a single conclusion. ¶ Justice is a moral virtue. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> It is proven: According to Aristotle in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, a virtue is that which makes its possessor good and his work good. Justice is of this kind; therefore,

<column-break/>

it is a virtue. The "Minor" premise is proven: The good of man is to operate according to the rule of reason; for since man is by his nature rational, our actions are judged as upright according to reason. The duty of justice itself is specifically to establish equity between two people according to the line of reason. It follows, therefore, that it is a virtue. And as Aristotle says, it is <margin>Aristotle.</margin> not just any virtue, but one as much more radiant than the others as <term>Hesperus</term> (the Evening Star) excels the other stars of the firmament in brightness. This Cicero also repeats in Book 1 of *On Offices*, where <margin>Cicero.</margin> he says that the splendor of virtue is greatest in the habit of justice, from which "good men" receive their name.

<margin>A doubt or hesitation.</margin> ¶ One might hesitate at this point whether "good men" are named so because of the virtue of justice in a different way than from any of the other virtues. For any virtue makes a man "good" in a simple sense. A skill in painting makes a "good painter," and the medical art makes a "good doctor," yet neither makes a "good man." An intellectual virtue, such as knowledge, produces a "learned man," yet it does not reach the point of establishing a "good man." Only moral virtue, which makes a man (whose nature is rational) live according to reason, establishes a "good man." But beyond this definition, "goodness" is also used as a synonym for "benignity" or "fertility," by which a man is beneficial to another—just as land is called "benign" and "good" because it is fertile. One might therefore assert that justice names a man "good" for both reasons: because the just are not only studious, but also good and useful to others. But truly, the matter inspected at its core is not so. For "goodness" in the sense of benignity and fertility is not just to give in any way, but to give what is not owed, which belongs to liberality and magnificence. Indeed, Aristotle does not fear to call even a "prodigal" (a wasteful spender) "good"—that is, benign and generous—because he pours out his own goods. But justice does not so much "give" as "render" (or pay back). Hence Cicero, in the same place, attributes this second kind of goodness <margin>Cicero.</margin> not to justice, but to beneficence. For he says: "And to this (justice) is joined beneficence, which may also be called benignity or liberality." <margin>The true solution to the proposed doubt.</margin> Thus, justice only makes the possessor good, and his work good, with goodness of the same kind as the other virtues. And therefore, where Cicero says good men are named from justice, he took "justice" as a general name for all virtues; although justice holds the summit among the cardinal virtues for this reason: that it orders a man toward others, and thus cannot help but exert itself immediately in public.

<summary>This page defines justice as a cardinal moral virtue that aligns human actions with reason, specifically in relation to others. It distinguishes justice from mere generosity or skill, arguing that it makes a person "good" by fulfilling moral obligations and maintaining social equity.</summary>

...come forth into the public. And in truth, he who is just, so as to most promptly return to each what is his own, is very close to being beneficent and liberal.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the first argument, therefore, St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Scholastic theologians like Soto.</note> responds excellently: he who does what he owes brings no "utility" in the sense that he adds no profit to the one to whom the debt is paid; rather, he merely keeps his hands from causing that person loss. However, he is useful to himself, insofar as by doing what he owes of his own accord, he merits a reward from God. In relation to God, therefore, we are not like slaves in relation to mortal masters. Indeed, slaves, whatever they are, belong to their masters; therefore, whatever work they perform accrues to the master as profit. For this reason, they are "useful," for the useful is a good for the sake of something else. But the services we pay to God accumulate no profit for Him, because He has no need of our goods. Instead, the utility overflows back onto us; for God, there is nothing but glory. And therefore we are called "unprofitable servants" <note>original: "serui inutiles"; from Luke 17:10</note>, which means we add nothing to God, because we do nothing except that which we owe out of justice. Nevertheless, because that which we owe is the virtue of justice, which God has commanded us, it happens that by doing what we owe, we merit a reward from Him.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it is responded that there are two kinds of necessity. One is the necessity of coercion; this removes merit and praise, as well as blame, as Aristotle says at the end of Book 5 of the *Ethics*. The other is the necessity of a precept or an end, which we cannot attain without such a means. This does not drive out the nature of virtue, insofar as a man does what he owes by his own will, from which the nature of praise arises. It does, however, exclude the merit of "supererogation" <note>The performance of more work than is required by duty or law.</note>, such as exists in works of counsel. 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Hence Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9: *If I preach the Gospel, I have no glory.* <note>original: "Si Euangelizauero, non est mihi gloria."</note>

<margin>To the third argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, St. Thomas responds that justice does not consist in external things regarding the act of *making* them (which belongs to art), but regarding their *use*, which is owed to another. Some people struggle so much to clarify these words that they rather obscure them; for the matter is clear. I say that justice is not the art of "makeable things" <note>term: "factibilium" refers to the Aristotelian category of *poiesis* (making/craft) as opposed to *praxis* (doing/moral action).</note>, because its function is not to mint money or build a house, but to use money by paying it to a debtor. Hence, when an architect builds a house after receiving payment, even if he constructs it through art as he should, it is nonetheless justice that applies him to the task of building so that he may pay his debt.

### ARTICLE IV.
### Whether Justice Resides in the Will.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap 'C' containing a seated figure, likely a scholar or judge.</image-desc>

But justice does not rectify the act of the intellect or any other cognitive power. For we are not called "just" because we *know* what is just—since that is common even to the wicked—but because we *work* and *will* just things, as Aristotle says. 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

For justice, as has been said, implies an order toward another; but no sense knows an order of this kind, which the sensory appetite follows. It is gathered therefore from this induction that no power remains in which justice can reside except the will. ¶ Concerning this conclusion, no one...

### Book Three, Question II.

<margin>A famous question.</margin>
No one disagrees on this point; however, there is a dispute among the Doctors <term>Doctors</term><note>The "Doctors" refers to the authoritative teachers of the Church and the university, such as St. Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus.</note> as to whether it is proper to justice, among the cardinal virtues, to be located in the will; I mean justice and the other virtues annexed to it, such as religion, liberality, and similar virtues.

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
<margin>Buridanus.</margin>
For *Scotus* (as we remember touching upon in previous sections) in his commentary on the *Sentences*, Book 3, distinction 33, and *Ockham* in Question 10—whom many of the moderns follow, and especially *Buridan* in the last question of Book 1 of the *Ethics*—stubbornly hold that not only justice, but also fortitude and temperance, reside in the will.

<margin>The most powerful argument of Scotus and Buridan.</margin>
Their most powerful reason is this: since the proper work of virtue is to make a choice right concerning the end, as *Aristotle* teaches in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, chapter 4,

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
it ought to reside in that power whose property it is to make a choice. This, however, is the will, from which the praise or blame of a work proceeds; therefore, the will is the seat of all virtues.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ But truly, although this dispute in *St. Thomas* is found not here, but in the *Summa Theologiae* I-II, question 56, yet as far as the present matter is concerned, the doctrine of those men stands in diametric opposition to Aristotle. He indeed, in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, chapter 3, tries to demonstrate professionally <note>original: "ex professo"; meaning openly or as a matter of expertise.</note> that the moral virtues—namely fortitude and temperance—are concerned with restraining pleasures, pains, and sorrows. His foundation is the opposite of the one they use.

<margin>The aforementioned opinion is diametrically opposed to Aristotle.</margin>
For indeed, since the will is the proper appetite <term>appetite</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, "appetite" (appetitus) refers to the soul’s natural inclination or "reaching out" toward a perceived good.</note> of a human being, and the appetite of any thing is by its nature inclined toward the good of that thing (unless hindered from elsewhere), and acting rightly according to fortitude and temperance is the proper good of the human being himself, the will needs no habit <term>habit</term><note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition of the soul that makes it easy to perform certain acts well.</note> of virtue at all for these things. But since virtue is concerned with what is difficult, it is necessary for that power from which the disturbances of the mind arise that resist the choice of virtue. These disturbances the power itself is not sufficient to restrain on its own; for that reason, it needs a habit to help it. Since, therefore, the whole difficulty of rightly attacking and enduring in war arises from fear and excessive boldness, it is the "irascible" power <note>The "irascible" faculty deals with difficult obstacles (like anger or fear), while the "concupiscible" deals with basic desires (like pleasure or food).</note> that needs virtue. And likewise, the "concupiscible" power needs it to restrain pleasures, so that once these passions are calmed, the will may make a right choice.

<margin>To the argument of the aforementioned opinion.</margin>
Therefore, their "major premise" is denied—namely, that virtue must be in that power which makes the right choice. For when a power can do this by itself, it does not need a virtue; rather, virtue is necessary where the difficulty and obstacle to choosing and subsequently acting rightly is born. Thus, it follows that *Scotus* denied without reason that the habits of the sensory appetite deserve the name of virtues properly speaking, since they are cardinal virtues. For through that repression of sensory affections, they are truly the principles and causes of right choice.

<margin>To another argument of Buridan.</margin>
¶ And by this, the fallacies of all the arguments that *Buridan* piles up are exposed, one of which is: "The will is often inclined toward the appetite, and cannot consent to reason without difficulty; therefore, it needs a habit inclining it toward reason." Indeed, the antecedent <note>The "antecedent" is the first part of a logical "if-then" statement.</note> is denied: for by itself the will does not incline toward the [sensory] appetite, but is most disposed toward the good of the person, which is the good of reason. If it sometimes follows the appetite, it is because it is pulled away by an appetite that is badly affected; therefore, it does not need a habit in itself, but in the appetite, to drive out the affection by which it is overcome.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ But this opinion is tested by this argument: The intellect is by its nature inclined toward the truth, and yet it still requires the habits of the sciences.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is responded, however, that the reasoning is different. For our proposition is understood when a power is inclined toward the good in the manner of an appetite—that is, in the manner of an active power, because it is carried toward it. In that case, because it leans toward its object by its own nature with no one prodding it, it needs no habit. But the cognitive power is not active in the sense of being carried toward the object; rather, it is passive—that is, suited to receive the image of the object within itself. For that reason, just as it cannot know the thing except through the "species" <term>species</term><note>In scholastic philosophy, "species" are the mental representations or forms of objects that allow the mind to perceive them.</note> shed by the object, so it cannot judge rightly except through habits that demonstrate the truth of the thing and thus apply the intellect to judging.

¶ Regarding justice, however, the reason is different, as we said above: for by its nature, the will is not as inclined toward the good of another as it is toward its own good. For that reason, even if it suffered no violence from the passions, it nevertheless needs a habit inclining it to render to another what is theirs. Therefore, a little further below, we shall show that justice is not concerned with the passions.

<margin>Another reason.</margin>
¶ If you argue that granting what is right to another is the "proper good" of the one granting it—for virtue is the good of the studious man, since it makes its possessor good—therefore the will does not need a habit for this either. It is responded that although justice is formally the good of the one possessing it, its object is the good of another: for it is concerned with this, which is to return to another what is theirs. And in this lies the difference from the other virtues.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is responded that justice is not truth in the sense of the correspondence of a thing to knowledge, but as it signifies righteousness, which reason, which...

truth

### ARTICLE V.

->Whether Justice is a General Virtue.<-

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial N with floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>
IT IS NOT enough to have established that justice is a virtue unless it is examined whether it is a special virtue or a general one. And it is argued that there is no such thing as general justice. Justice is one of the <term>cardinal virtues</term> <note>The four "hinge" virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>, as is clear from Wisdom 8: "She teaches temperance and justice, prudence and virtue" (that is, fortitude). A general thing, however, is not divided into its own species.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And it is confirmed: because temperance, by the very fact that it is a cardinal virtue, is not general but special.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Justice is toward another, but fortitude and temperance organize a man in relation to himself. These are different principles; therefore, justice is not "general" in such a way that it extends to temperance and fortitude.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued: If justice were a general virtue, it would be essentially the same as all others, which Aristotle seems to suggest in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 1, where he says that justice is "the whole of virtue"—that is, the same as every virtue. But this is false: for then justice would be divided into fortitude and temperance, and would be predicated of them just as "animal" is predicated of "man" and "horse." Yet this is absurd to say: because the definition of justice—which is to be "toward another"—cannot essentially be the <term>genus</term> <note>The overarching category.</note> of all virtues that are *not* toward another. Therefore, it would be a most absurd division to split justice into

<column-break/>

other cardinal virtues as if they were its species.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, it is argued: In the virtues, seeing as they proceed from the inclination of nature, nothing is superfluous, just as it is not in other works of nature. If, therefore, "general justice" sufficiently directs a man toward the common good, "particular justice" would be superfluous. This is especially true because "the one" and "the many" do not change the species: to establish a man in relation to the common good is to establish him in relation to many; to establish him in relation to a particular person is to order him toward one. There is, therefore, no reason why we should distinguish two species of justice on this basis. Otherwise, we should have to invent a third, "middle" justice, which would establish the members of the same family toward the good of the home, since that is halfway between the common and the private.

¶ On the contrary, however, is the word of Aristotle already cited, namely: "Justice is the whole of virtue," which is to say, "Every virtue is a certain kind of justice." To this opinion agrees not only common speech, but also the Gospel: "Unless your justice abounds..." <note>Matthew 5:20: "For I tell you, unless your righteousness [justice] exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven."</note> where every virtue is reckoned under the name of justice. From this, it follows that every studious person is called "just."

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
For a full response to this question, five conclusions are necessary. For we have judged that three of Saint Thomas’s articles can be decided more clearly and conveniently under this single heading.

**First Conclusion.** Most excellently, justice is first of all divided into "general" and "particular" justice.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
The conclusion is proved: Justice (which must be repeated time and again) is a man's virtue by comparison to another. This comparison can be made in two ways. For a man is compared either to another considered as an individual citizen, or to another considered as one endowed with public authority, by which he administers the common good. For the commonwealth, and the prince administering it, has a relationship to all citizens, and each individual has a relationship to the commonwealth. Just as in the human body one limb is compared both to another limb and to the whole (to which the parts themselves are ordered), so too do citizens stand in the commonwealth. Therefore, the definition of justice can be taken from both comparisons. Wherefore, the justice that orders citizen to citizen, as one part to another, is **particular justice**—under which fall all contracts of buying, hiring, restitution of loans, payment of wages, etc. The other, however, which orders citizens toward the common good, is **general justice**, which is indeed so named,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Article V from the previous page, examining whether justice is a general virtue that encompasses others or a distinct, specific virtue. It maintains continuity by further explaining how justice relates to the "common good" and the "legal" framework of a state.</meta>

# Question II of the Third Book.
<meta>catchword: If however</meta>

it is determined, both by its object and its end: for the common good is the general good of all. It is also determined by its effect and its specific duty: namely, that it directs all virtues toward such a common good. For example, it ensures that a brave man acts vigorously in war for the sake of the common good, and a temperate man abstains from another's bed for the preservation of that same common good. And since this ordering of parts toward the common good is achieved through laws by which a prince instructs everyone toward that same good, this same justice is also called **legal justice**.

<margin>*A Doubt.*</margin>
¶ There remains, however, a doubt that was sought in the third argument: namely, whether this general virtue is essentially the same as each individual virtue. Is it the case that, just as "animal" is a <term>genus</term> <note>A general category in logic</note> that is essentially predicated of every species, so also prudence and fortitude are essentially "justice"? For this reason, a second conclusion is added.

<margin>*Second conclusion, which satisfies the doubt just posed.*</margin>
¶ Legal and general justice is not essentially the same as each individual virtue, but is a specific virtue, directing all others through its own command toward the common good.

<margin>*Clarification of the conclusion.*</margin>
The clarification of this conclusion demonstrates it abundantly. For a thing is called "general" in two ways: In one way, by predication, just as "animal" is the genus for its species; and what is general in this way belongs to the essence of those things for which it is general. Therefore, it is essentially predicated of each one, for the genus belongs to the essence of the species. In another way, something is called general according to its power (or virtue): namely, because it is a cause influencing lower things, just as the sun is in respect to all lower causes. And what is general in this way is not essentially the same as the particular things, nor is it predicated of them. For fire is not the sun.

<margin>*Reason for the conclusion.*</margin>
From this division, the reasoning for the conclusion is gathered. General or legal justice is in no way a genus in respect to the other virtues; rather, it possesses only this power: to direct all things toward the common good. Therefore, it is not essentially the same as them, but is a certain special virtue commanding the others. A most fitting example for us shines forth from **charity**. For charity is a special virtue, distinct from faith and hope according to its own proper definition; nevertheless, through its command, it refers all the works of the other virtues to God as to a supernatural end. For when someone either acts vigorously in war or uses tangible pleasures with moderation for the sake of natural honesty, that work is performed by those virtues alone. But if he performs those same works for the sake of God, that relationship is created by charity. Just as when someone steals for the sake of <term>fornication</term> <note>sexual immorality</note>, the theft 

<column-break/>

is carried out by injustice, but it is commanded by lust. In a similar way, therefore, if someone exercises themselves in the duties of particular virtues for the sake of their specific ends, those duties do not exceed the limits of those virtues. But when they perform those same duties for the sake of the protection and cultivation of the common good, and so that they may obey public laws, that relationship is created by legal justice, which is therefore called "general." If you ask what it means for one virtue to command others: the answer is that it is nothing other than moving them to work as a universal cause, and concurring with them in that same work.

<margin>*Third conclusion.*</margin>
¶ Third conclusion. This general and legal justice resides primarily in the prince <term>architectonically</term> <note>original: "architectonicè"; meaning in the manner of a master-builder who directs the whole project</note>, and subsequently in the subjects, by which they are rightly disposed to promptly obey the laws and the prince.

<margin>*The conclusion is proven.*</margin>
Indeed, just as an architect arranges all the stones and wood as is necessary for the building, so must a prince instruct and direct all citizens toward the common good.

<margin>*Fourth conclusion.*</margin>
¶ Fourth conclusion. Each of the virtues, considered as it is commanded by legal justice, can receive a denomination so as to be called "legal." Just as every virtue, by the reason that it is commanded by charity, can be called "charity" in a certain way. This conclusion was added to interpret **Aristotle**. For when he says that "Justice is the whole of virtue," he offers this sense: that any virtue commanded by legal justice is, in a certain way, legal justice.

<margin>*Fifth conclusion.*</margin>
¶ Fifth conclusion. Besides legal justice, which is general in the manner explained, **particular justice** is required. It is proven thus:

<margin>*Proof of the conclusion.*</margin>
Virtues, as has often been said, are distinguished by their objects. But besides the definition of the object of legal justice—which is to direct the works of the other virtues toward the common good—there is another particular definition of "rendering to each what is his own." Therefore, for this purpose, particular justice is necessary.

<margin>*Confirmation.*</margin>
And this reasoning is confirmed: besides legal justice, other particular virtues are required, namely fortitude and temperance, to carry out acts concerning their particular objects; notwithstanding that those same acts may be directed by legal justice toward the common good. Therefore, by equal right, particular justice is required, from which a work concerning its own object may be elicited—an act which is sometimes commanded by legal justice, and sometimes not at all. For someone can return a loan or pay a wage to a worker, not out of obedience to the law, nor for the common good (for which he has no love), but to keep his own faith for its own sake. In that case, such an act emanates from particular justice alone.

<summary>This page distinguishes between "Legal Justice," which directs all virtues toward the common good like an architect, and "Particular Justice," which focuses on specific duties like paying debts. It uses the analogy of charity to explain how one virtue can "command" others without being essentially the same as them.</summary>

Regarding the second conclusion, however, 

<margin>The opinion of the Moderns.</margin>

Therefore, another specific virtue to which this duty is assigned is unnecessary. He seems to gather his second 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

Furthermore, every virtue perfects the one who possesses it, so that he may always act when, where, and how he ought. But it often happens that one must act for the sake of the common good and in obedience to the law; therefore, any virtue at that time, if

Therefore, particular virtues possess the character of general justice, and thus another specific virtue is not necessary. ¶ But truly, these arguments are not as strong as those thinkers believe. Indeed, reason first and foremost, and then the teachings of Aristotle, stand in opposition to them. For first, they accept this postulate with us: that the character of legal and general justice is to act for the sake of the common good and for obedience to the law. From this very point, a 

<margin>First argument against Buridan.</margin>
manifest reason emerges against them. For it is possible for someone to be well-disposed by virtue to act for a particular end, but not for the common end—and vice versa. Where there are different difficulties in acting, there is a need for different virtues; therefore, legal justice is distinct from particular virtue. The premise is proven by experience. For you may see an abstinent man who lives frugally for the sake of a particular moral good, and yet he is moved by no respect for the law. Indeed, perhaps he holds it in hatred because he hates the ruler. Because of this, if the work had no other reason for its moral goodness, he would never perform it for the sake of the law. Again, to do a work of virtue for the sake of obedience has a different 

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
character than doing it for another honorable end. Just as breaking a fast because of hunger or out of contempt for the law are different vices, so too are obedience and temperance different virtues. There are also the

to a private person. Just as in a ship, the virtue of a rower is one thing—namely, to row industriously, even if he thinks nothing of the ship’s safety—while the virtue of the pilot is another, as he is the one looking after that very safety. Therefore, legal justice <note>Justice that looks toward the law and the common good</note> does not only imply a general category of all virtues, but is a specific virtue.

<margin>Response to Buridan's first argument.</margin>
¶ Hence, in response to Buridan’s first argument, it is denied that a particular virtue <note>such as honesty or courage in a single act</note> directs its work toward the common good by its own nature; rather, legal justice provides this direction for it. This is just as a particular virtue is not "charity" except insofar as it is directed toward God by the virtue of charity.

<margin>Response to another point from Aristotle.</margin>
And to the earlier authority of Aristotle, it is replied that he does not affirm that magnificence <note>The virtue of spending large sums of money for noble purposes</note> operates for the sake of the common good, but says it is useful to the multitude. Neither does fortitude <note>courage</note> incline toward the common good by its own nature. For it is one thing that war should not be declared or undertaken by a prince except for the common good; it is quite another thing that the fortitude of each individual soldier should refer itself to that same good.

<margin>Response to the first main argument.</margin>
From these points, the transition to the solutions for the principal arguments becomes easy. To the first, it is replied that the justice placed in the number of cardinal virtues is not legal and general justice, but particular justice. As for why we do not divide any of the other virtues—such as temperance or fortitude—into "general" and "particular," the reason is that they are, as we said above, located in the sensitive appetite <note>The part of the soul dealing with physical senses and emotions</note>. This appetite does not extend to the common good but is concerned with particular things. Justice, however, which is in the will following intellectual knowledge, extends toward that same common good.

<margin>Response to the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is replied that because the peculiar good of each person can be referred to the common and public good, it happens that legal justice commands all individual virtues. Consequently, the works of all virtues are called "equities" <note>just acts</note>, just as all vices are called "iniquities" <note>unjust acts</note>, according to 1 John 3: "All sin is iniquity" <note>original: "Omne peccatum est iniquitas"</note>.

<margin>Response to the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ To the tripartite fourth argument, it is replied that although legal justice is abundantly sufficient through its command to refer all works of the virtues to the common good, particular justice is nonetheless required to bring forth an act regarding its own specific object—just as other particular virtues are required. Nor do the common good and the private good differ only by the logic of "one" and "many"; rather, the nature of the common good is one thing, and that of the individual good is another—just as the nature of the whole is one thing and that of the part is another. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For this reason, Aristotle, in Book 1 of the *Politics*, mocks those who thought a city differed from a household in no other way

than the difference between "much" and "little." Nevertheless, because there is no proper nature of "the just" between members of the same family (as was said above), a third species of justice is not distinguished.

## ARTICLE VI.
### Whether Justice has a specific subject matter, or whether it is concerned with the passions and subject matters of other virtues.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
