<columns>2</columns>

...commands, and those things which belong to the temperate man, and those of the mild man, and so on. But the question at hand concerns particular justice <note>Justice regarding the relationships between specific individuals, rather than the state as a whole</note>.

<margin>**First conclusion.**</margin>
Concerning this, two conclusions are established. The first is: Justice is not concerned with the entire subject matter of all the virtues, but only with external actions and things.

<margin>**Proof of the conclusion.**</margin>
It is proved thus: The entire "forest" of things that fall under our choice and can be corrected according to the norm of reason constitutes the subject matter of the moral virtues. For a virtue is called "moral" <note>original: *moralis*</note> precisely because it is the composer and cultivator of morals <note>original: *morum*, referring to customs and character</note>. Now, there are three types of things subject to our will: namely, the affections of the mind <note>passions or emotions</note>, external actions, and finally the physical things themselves which we use. However, a human being is ordered toward another person only through actions and things; for the moderation and softening of passions belongs properly to a person’s internal rectitude within themselves. Since, therefore, justice differs from the other virtues in this—that the others settle a person within themselves, while justice establishes equity between multiple people—it follows that the proper matter of justice consists of operations and things: for example, showing the honor due to another, abstaining from insults, and returning money or any other thing owed to a creditor.

<margin>**Final conclusion.**</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Justice is not concerned with the passions and internal affections of the mind. This is gathered from the reasoning of the previous conclusion, but is further explained by two others.

<margin>**First reason for the conclusion.**</margin>
First, from the perspective of its subject, which is the will. Indeed, the actions of the will have neither the nature nor the name of "passions," as seen in St. Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae* <note>1a 2ae, question 22, article 3</note>. From that passage, St. Thomas reasons that a passion brings with it a physical change in the body, which properly exists only in the sensitive appetite <note>The faculty of the soul that deals with physical desires and emotions</note>. Since, therefore, justice exists only in the will, it is not concerned with passions.

<margin>**Second.**</margin>
Likewise, because the matter of justice, as we just said, is located in that which is toward another; since hidden passions are not directly ordered toward another, it follows that this virtue is not about passions.

¶ These conclusions are found not only in St. Thomas, but also clearly in Aristotle’s *Ethics*, Book 5. Therefore, among those who have studied their doctrine with care, there is no one who denies them. Nonetheless, some of the Nominalists <note>A school of philosophy that often disagreed with the "Realism" of Aquinas</note>, such as Buridan <note>Jean Buridan, a 14th-century logician and philosopher</note> in his commentary on the *Ethics*, Book 5, Question 1, wonder why St. Thomas establishes such a difference between the matter of justice and other virtues. 

"Indeed," Buridan says, "just as all virtues are in the will, so too all of them—and justice equally—must restrain the passions that hinder each person’s choice." And conversely, he argues that the other virtues are also concerned with operations and things. Regarding this doctor [Buridan], however, it is more to be wondered at that he read Aristotle so superficially.

<column-break/>

Indeed, the whole crowd of his arguments is resolved into that principle whose falsity we have already exposed above. 

<margin>**Buridan’s Reasoning.**</margin>
The principle is this: To whichever virtue it belongs to make a right choice regarding its object, there are many passions that disturb justice so that it does not return what is due to each: such as love, hatred, greed, foul desire, and the like. Therefore, it is the duty of justice to restrain these passions. Thus, justice is concerned with passions. 

And vice versa, he argues that fortitude and temperance are concerned not only with passions, but also with external actions themselves and physical things. For eating and drinking when and where it is appropriate are external operations, and yet they belong to the virtue of temperance. And thus, food and drink are the things with which that same virtue is concerned. Therefore, temperance does not only perform its duty regarding internal allurements, but also regarding external actions. In the same way, to fight bravely is an external operation which nevertheless proceeds from fortitude <note>courage</note>. Therefore, the matter of justice and other virtues is mixed; and so it cannot be defended that justice is concerned with external operations, while the others are concerned only with passions.

<margin>**Another reason against St. Thomas.**</margin>
¶ And furthermore, an argument is made in favor of these men against the foundation of St. Thomas. If justice is said not to concern passions because through them a person is not ordered to another, this is false: because anger and the lusting after another's wife are injurious to one's neighbor, as we said above. Therefore, restraining these internal feelings belongs to justice. 

A similar argument runs regarding temperance and fortitude. For if those virtues were not concerned with external operations, it would be because those actions do not affect how a person stands in relation to himself. But this is false: because using food and drink according to the command of virtue adorns and improves a man in respect to himself. Therefore, temperance is indeed concerned with those external operations.

¶ From this, these thinkers conclude that every single virtue must be split in two: namely, that one "justice" should exist in the appetite to restrain passions, and another in the will to make the choice. By the same logic, one temperance exists in the concupiscible appetite <note>the part of the soul that desires pleasure</note> and another in the will; and similarly, one fortitude exists in the irascible appetite <note>the part of the soul that deals with anger or difficult challenges</note> and another in the will. 

But as to how aggressively these men oppose Aristotle, let anyone with eyes to see be the judge.

<margin>**Aristotle.**</margin>
For in the second book of the *Ethics*, Aristotle ascribes no subject to temperance and fortitude except the sensitive appetite; and in book 3, chapter 10...

<margin>An effective argument against the aforementioned opinion.</margin> 
But even if Aristotle had not taught this, the argument itself is effective, as we have already declared above. For indeed, **temperance** is sufficient to restrain all the affections of the <term>concupiscible appetite<note>The part of the soul driven by desires for pleasure, such as food or sex.</note></term>, however you consider them: whether as obstacles to temperance itself, or to justice, or to any other virtue. In Book 5 of the *Ethics*, he says the "mean" of justice is not a "mean of reason" among the emotions, but an **objective mean** <note>original: *medium rei*; a balance found in the things themselves, like paying exactly what is owed, rather than an internal emotional balance.</note>, as we are about to say.

<margin>Another argument for the same point.</margin>
Likewise, a most manifest argument is made against those opponents. Just as the affections of the concupiscible appetite are an impediment to the virtue of justice, so too they are sometimes an impediment to the virtue of fortitude. Therefore, if by that reasoning justice must be placed in the concupiscible appetite, by the same right fortitude should also be placed there—and by equal reasoning, temperance in the irascible. This would be an unlearned muddle of all the seats of the virtues. Thus, to turn their own "Achilles" <note>The term for an opponent's strongest or "invincible" argument.</note> back against them: nothing superfluous should be admitted in the order of the virtues. Since temperance suffices in the concupiscible and fortitude in the irascible, there is no need for a virtue of justice in those parts. Furthermore, once the passions of the sensory appetite are calmed, the will makes the right choice on its own, because it is inclined by its nature toward a good work. Therefore, there is no need in the will for either temperance or fortitude for this task, but only for **justice** with respect to another person's good.

¶ But truly, so that no doubt remains for you: when it is said that no passions belong "through themselves" <note>essentially or directly</note> to justice, this is understood as its "matter" <note>the raw material it works on</note>. For as its *effect* and in a certain way its *end* <note>goal</note>, it is certain that joy follows justice, just as sadness follows injustice. Indeed, Aristotle says in Book 5 of the *Ethics*: "He is not just who does not rejoice in just operations." And in Book 8: "Delight," he says, "is the end of virtue, for the sake of which the studious work"; just as those who act wickedly are immediately weighed down by sadness. From this comes that point in Book 2 of the *Ethics* which our adversaries hurl against us—namely, that moral virtue is concerned with pleasures and pains. If this is understood as being about its *matter*, it applies only to the virtues of the sensory

<column-break/>

appetite. If, however, it is understood to mean that there is no moral virtue that does not generate joy and drive away sorrow, then it is also common to justice.

**In order** that the solutions to the arguments of the contrary opinion may become clear, we shall respond to them all in order. To the first argument, therefore, 
<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
placed at the start of the question, the response is: although particular justice belongs essentially to one part of the soul—namely, to the **will** in which it is located—nevertheless, because the will moves the other parts and applies them to their duties, it happens that justice is poured out into all parts, not indeed directly, but through a certain "overflowing." This explains the <gloss>gloss regarding the Euphrates</gloss> <note>A traditional allegory where the four rivers of Paradise represent the four cardinal virtues; the Euphrates, meaning "fruitful," was often linked to Justice because it flows out to benefit everyone.</note>, which compares justice to a river flowing out to all things. For Augustine, 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
in the place cited, distinguishes those four virtues of the soul differently according to the understanding of Saint Thomas. For the **cardinal virtues** are used in two ways: in one way as they are *special* virtues, distinct by their objects; in another way as they designate four *modes* <note>characteristics or styles of action</note> belonging to every virtue. For he says that **prudence** is the knowledge of things to be sought and avoided; **temperance** is the reframing of desire from things that provide temporary delight; **fortitude** is the strength of the mind against things that are temporarily troublesome; and **justice** is that which is diffused through the others: the love of God and neighbor.

¶ The response to the second argument 
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
clarifies the matter brilliantly. Indeed, among internal affections, external actions, and the things themselves, the order is such that actions are in the middle ground between the affections (which are their principles) and the things (which are their matter). Therefore, the passions—namely, anger, desire, greed, etc.—through themselves neither help nor harm one’s neighbor, and thus, considered as such, they have nothing to do with justice. For this reason, we said that the mitigation of such affections through themselves pertains to the person possessing them within themselves. However, they harm or help a neighbor through **external operations**. But the fact that someone is harmful or injurious to another usually arises from a double defect: namely, either from a wickedness of the will, or from a depraved affection of the sensory appetite. For example: someone can steal something from another or cause damage, not indeed from a desire for possessing it, but from a will to do harm. Indeed, someone could violate another’s marriage bed in this way, not for the sake of fleshly pleasure, but only to cause injury. And conversely,

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law

<columns>

Conversely, as is very often the case, someone may seize the property of another, not out of an inherent wickedness of soul—for they might prefer not to cause harm—but out of greed. Distinguish, therefore, the duties of the virtues, and assign to each its own. The correction and rectification of an action, insofar as they bring about fairness toward another, is the function of **justice**. However, insofar as unfairness arises from a corrupted emotion, it belongs to other virtues: such as to **generosity**, which moderates avarice; and to **temperance**, which restrains greed, and so forth. Nevertheless, since external actions do not take their essential character from internal motives but from the things themselves, it happens that these same actions are the "matter" of justice rather than of the other virtues.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
If you should then ask why it was necessary to group actions and things together (for since the object is understood within the action, and the action is designated by the object, it was enough to posit one or the other):

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that this was not said idly. For there are some actions that are not properly concerned with "things"—that is, with physical possessions—such as honoring and dishonoring, gossiping, praising, and so on; while others consist in the use of things, such as the giving or taking of money, and the **restitution** <note>The act of returning something to its rightful owner.</note> of any objects whatsoever. All of these are the subject matter of justice.

### ARTICLE VII.

->*Whether the mean of justice is an objective mean: and its act, to give each their own right.*<-

<note>original: "Vtrùm medium iustitiæ sit medium rei: eiusq; actus, ius vnicuique suum tribuere." The "objective mean" or "mean of the thing" refers to a balance found in the object itself (like a debt of $10 requiring exactly $10), rather than a balance relative to the person's feelings.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a central flower/fruit motif surrounded by scrolling foliage and vines within a square frame.</image-desc>
SINCE it has been defined that **justice** is a virtue, and every virtue consists in a **mean** <note>The "golden mean" or middle ground between two extremes.</note> which it establishes by its act, it follows that we must examine whether the mean of justice is an **objective mean** <note>original: "medium rei"</note> and whether its act is to give each person their own right.

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
The argument is made for the negative side. The definition of a "genus" (specifically, a moral virtue) applies equally to all its "species." However, **Aristotle**, in the *Ethics* Book 2, chapter 6, defines virtue as a habit of choice consisting in a mean relative to us, defined by reason. And he adds that this mean consists between two vices—namely, between two emotions, one of which is excessive and the other deficient. Therefore, the mean of justice must also be established between passions <note>Internal emotions or impulses.</note>.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued: In those things that are "simply good," one does not find "too much" or "too little," and thus no mean. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle gives an example of this in Book 2 of the *Ethics*

<column-break/>

regarding the virtues: for the greater a virtue is, the better it is. But justice, as held in the *Ethics* Book 5, chapter 1, concerns that which is "simply good"—that is, things absolutely good in themselves, such as honors and riches. Therefore, such an object of justice does not consist in a mean.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Thirdly: in the aforementioned definition of virtue, Aristotle said that virtue is a habit consisting in a mean "as reason defines it in relation to us," because the mean is not the same for all men. For what is a lot of food for one person is a little for another. This discrepancy likewise applies to justice: for he who lays hands on a prince is not punished with the same penalty as he who wounds a commoner. Therefore, the mean of justice is not "objective" <note>original: "rei"</note>, but "rational" <note>original: "rationis"; subjective or relative to the situation.</note>.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
Fourthly and finally, it is argued: If the mean of justice were an objective mean, it would be primarily because its act is to return to each person what is theirs. But this is not universally true. For **Augustine**, in *On the Trinity* Book 14, attributes to justice the duty of succoring the miserable. 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
And **Cicero**, cited above in *On Duties* Book 1, says that 

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
beneficence and generosity belong to justice. Yet through mercy and generosity, one does not grant a "right" <note>original: "ius"; a legal or strict moral entitlement</note>, but rather bestows a favor.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
The **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> teaches the opposite in the *Ethics* Book 5, chapters 3 and 4.

This question is quite easy and is resolved very briefly by two conclusions, which are clearly gathered from what was just said.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion is: The mean which is the object of justice is not a "mean of reason" as in other virtues, but an **objective mean**. For we are speaking here of **particular justice**; 

<margin>The title of the question is explained.</margin>
for "general justice" is not narrowed specifically to this object, but spreads widely across the subject matter of all virtues, as has been said. However, it is necessary first to understand the terms. There are some who, at present, distinguish "things" against "passions": namely, that the other virtues moderate passions, while justice establishes a mean in things. 

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
Nevertheless, even if it matters very little to the case, it is only distinguished in contrast to "reason," as will become clear through the proof. The conclusion is proved from what has been said. For this distinction is established between justice and the remaining passions: that those virtues are concerned with passions, whereas justice is concerned with actions and things. Among the passions, the mean of virtue is not established by the nature of the things themselves, but by the judgment of reason. For example: **Temperance** consists in a moderation of the passions: namely, so that you do not take more or less than...

# Book Three, Question II.

take more than is appropriate. However, this "more or less" is not measured by the nature of the things themselves—as if everyone should eat exactly one pound or at a specific hour—but rather according to what is beneficial for each person's health, depending on the place and time. Therefore, what was a lot for the very frugal Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic (c. 412–323 BC), a philosopher famous for his extreme asceticism and for living in a ceramic jar.</note> was too little for the voracious Milo <note>Milo of Croton, a legendary Greek wrestler famous for his immense strength and appetite; tales said he could eat an entire bull in a day.</note>. However, the **mean of justice** <note>The "mean" refers to the virtuous middle point between extremes.</note>—because it consists in the equality of things in relation to another person—is not measured by that subjective plumb line of reason and individual judgment, but is taken from the very nature of things. You buy a house, for example, or hire someone else's labor: the price must be equal to the things themselves. Just as two quantities are, by their nature, equal. Finally, justice is not said to establish an "objective mean" (as a thing is distinguished against reason) because such a mean is inconsistent with reason; on the contrary, it is highly rational. For reason teaches nothing more clearly than that you should return to a creditor an amount equal to what is owed. But because reason depends here on the nature of things, that which is established as equal in things is what conforms to reason. Nor is the mean of other virtues called a "mean of reason" because it is not established in things (on the contrary, it is established between the desire to take much and the desire to take little); rather, it is because, conversely, such a mean depends on reason as its cause. For eating a pound of bread is not a "mean" for me unless the reason of **prudence**, having weighed my nature and condition, judges that this is suitable for me. See, therefore, with what skill Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s theological work.</note> treats the matter in an almost mathematical manner. For it might have seemed—as it did to his critics—that he ineptly established a distinction by saying other virtues are concerned with passions, while justice is concerned with actions and things. And yet, this was necessary to support the way of demonstrating the difference between the mean of justice and the mean of other virtues.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ Yet one of the beginners in theology <note>original: "Theologiæ tyronibus."</note> might think of one objection against this argument. It seems that **temperance** sometimes establishes an objective mean in the manner described: namely, when a spouse devotes effort to their children when and where it is appropriate—that is, by using their own spouse and not another’s. For in this, they keep the faith they owe, and by using another, they inflict an injury by breaking that same faith.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
From what has been said above, however, the response is easy: when someone refrains from another's bed by restraining their lust, this belongs to temperance; but when they do so to preserve the right of the spouse, it belongs to justice. This "middle path" of justice will be explained more widely in the fifth question, and therefore

<column-break/>

we must pause here. For there, we will clarify how this objective mean is established differently in **distributive justice** and differently in **commutative justice** <note>Distributive justice concerns how a community shares goods among its members; commutative justice concerns private exchanges and contracts between individuals.</note>. For the former follows a **geometric proportion**, while the latter follows an **arithmetic** one.

<margin>His second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The latter conclusion of the present article concerns the act of justice. Its proper act, I say, is to render to each what is their own. This conclusion is connected to and a "sibling" of the one above.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
For if the object of justice is to establish a mean in things by which equality among men is maintained—and equality is the same as the "just," and the "just" (as we said above) is exactly the same as "right" or "law" <note>original: "ius"</note>—it follows most clearly that the act of justice is to grant each person their right, as the Legal Scholar <note>Likely referring to Ulpian, a Roman jurist whose definitions formed the basis of the Corpus Iuris Civilis.</note> affirmed in the definition posed above.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
With this, Ambrose also harmonizes in Book 1 of *On Duties* <note>original: "1. de Offic." referring to St. Ambrose’s *De officiis ministrorum*.</note>, where he says: "Justice is that which renders to each what is their own, does not claim what belongs to another, and neglects its own utility so that it may safeguard common equity." This, as will be clear in the following sections, applies to both types of particular justice: namely, both distributive and commutative. For general justice, as we said above, has a much broader duty, since it does not have one specific object; and thus its act is not only this, but (as has been said) to direct all virtues toward the common good. ¶ Moreover, in what we say—giving each their right—is also included this: to harm no one, which Ambrose calls "not claiming what belongs to another." For although justice primarily applies to voluntary exchanges in which both parties grant something to the other, it is also derived to involuntary acts, where one person takes something from another against their will.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first of the principal arguments, therefore, let it be answered that since the objective mean, as explained, is also in accord with reason, the definition of a moral virtue is preserved in justice as well.

In this way, the greater the good is, the more excellent it is. Therefore, just as the way to love God is to love Him without limit, because He is loved as the final end, so also these goods are to be desired and procured. ### ARTICLE VIII.

### Whether Justice is the most eminent among the moral Virtues.

---

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring a landscape or floral background with a figure.</image-desc>
FINALLY, in this last article of the question, justice must be compared with the remaining moral virtues, and we must ask whether it is indeed the most excellent of them all. <margin>First argument.</margin> And the argument is made for the negative side. For a person to give from his own what he owes to no one is more excellent and more rare than to return what he is a debtor for; both because where there is less obligation,

<column-break/>

the power of virtue to bestow is greater; and also because in this we are most likened to God, who confers not out of debt, but out of bounty. Therefore, liberality is more excellent than justice, and especially "magnificence" <note>A virtue concerning the spending of large sums of money for great and noble public causes.</note>, which, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in the 4th book of his *Ethics*, is the ornament of all virtues and likewise of justice. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is argued that justice is not even the most illustrious of the <term>cardinal virtues</term> <note>The four "hinge" virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>. For Prudence is one of the four cardinal virtues, and yet it is more excellent than justice; which is weighed on the part of the object, and also on the part of the subject. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> For Aristotle teaches professionally in the 10th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 7, that the intellect is the most excellent of all powers, and thus higher than the will, because the "true" is a worthier object than the "good"—namely, more universal and subsequently more abstracted from matter. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Thirdly, it is argued: Temperance, which is one of the cardinal virtues, is much more useful to us than justice; therefore, it is also more eminent. The premise is proven: for it brings us more advantages—specifically, health of the body, tranquility of the mind, and freedom of the will. For intemperance corrupts all these things in us; and yet these three advantages are the foundations of all virtues: namely, the intellectual virtues for contemplation, justice for obeying the laws, and all others which are exhibited through the exercise of the body. <margin>Argument 4.</margin> ¶ Fourthly, an argument is also made regarding Fortitude (Courage). For the proper character of virtue, as the Philosopher is the author in the 2nd book of the *Ethics*, is to strive toward the difficult and the good. However, Fortitude is concerned with something more difficult than justice: namely, the dangers of death, which is the most terrible of all things; therefore, Fortitude stands above justice. <margin>Cicero.</margin> ¶ On the contrary, however, is Cicero in the cited place, where he says: "In justice, the splendor of virtue is greatest, from which men are named 'good'."

### Question II of the Third Book

<margin>Subdivision.</margin> regarding the object. However, among natural virtues, some are intellectual and others are moral. The multitude of moral virtues is reduced to the four cardinal ones <note>The cardinal virtues are Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>. Therefore, the question requires four conclusions for its clarification. The first 

<margin>First conclusion. St. Thomas. First reason.</margin> is this: Intellectual virtues surpass moral virtues in dignity. This is the conclusion of St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Part 1-2, Question 66, Article 3.</note>. It is proven first by the nature of the subject. For since it is the property of virtue to direct rational actions, that virtue which resides in a power that is rational by its very essence is more excellent than that whose subject is rational only by participation. The intellect is the very essence of reason; the will, however, is rational only insofar as it participates in reason by obeying it, 

<margin>Aristotle. Second reason.</margin> as Aristotle clearly teaches in the first book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, the intellectual virtues are more excellent. Second, this is evident from the object. For that the "True" is more excellent than the "Good" is clear from the fact that the True abstracts from the existence of things. The intellect is sufficiently perfected through the knowledge of truth whether the things exist or whether none exist at all. However, no one desires the "Good" unless it brings existence with it. Now, existence is a material condition; for a nature is received into an individual subject <note>original: "supposito"—a technical scholastic term for an individual substance or person.</note> when it begins to be. The more something is refined and purified from matter, the more excellent it is. Since, therefore, the True is the object of the intellectual virtues, and the Good is the object of the moral virtues, it follows that the intellectual virtues are higher in dignity. 

<margin>The preceding reason is elucidated.</margin> Yet, because few understand this reason, few believe it. For we do not deny that the intellect can also know singular things and the existence of things; nor do we deny, conversely, that the will can also desire the good in general. But the distinction lies in this: since the intellect is an apprehensive and judicial power, it is perfected in knowing what is true. The appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the Will.</note>, however, because it is carried toward the object, desires nothing unless it may enjoy and possess it. 

<margin>Argument</margin> Therefore, the argument is fallacious if you argue: "Better" is the comparative of "Good"; since the Good is the object of the will, it follows that its object is 

<margin>Solution.</margin> better than the True. This, I say, is a fallacious piece of false reasoning <note>original: "paralogismus"—a logical fallacy.</note> because the True itself is a certain kind of Good, and indeed the most excellent of all. For this reason, in our heavenly homeland <note>original: "in patria"—referring to the state of being in Heaven after death.</note>, our happiness is placed in that intuition of God, who is the abyss of all truths. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin> Added to this is the doctrine of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in the 10th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 10, where he establishes by six reasons that supreme happiness consists in the contemplation of things. For though he was only dreaming, he "caught the scent" of true 

<column-break/>

blessedness, even if he did not hit the mark exactly. He proves, I say, that happiness consists in intellectual fruition because, first, intellectual virtues are in a nobler power and have a nobler object. Second, because intellectual operation is more continuous; for the moral virtues, which are occupied with bodily things, cannot endure. Third, because contemplation delights with a sweeter softness than the exercise of moral virtues. Likewise, because contemplation will remain forever in our heavenly homeland, but moral virtue will not. 

Added to this, moreover, is that for the same reasons the contemplative life surpasses the active life and is much more beautiful—just as Rachel was more beautiful than Leah <note>A common medieval allegory based on Genesis 29: Rachel represents the contemplative life and Leah the active life.</note>—and is thus more constant and fruitful, requiring fewer things. Mary, sitting at the feet of the Lord, was the example of this, while Martha was disturbed by many things <note>A reference to Luke 10:38–42.</note>. I have endeavored to confirm this conclusion with so many arguments because I cannot sufficiently wonder at those who grant more dignity to the moral virtues than to the intellectual ones. 

Those people were given an opportunity by the opinion which 

<margin>Scotus's opinion</margin> Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a famous Franciscan theologian who often disagreed with the Thomist/Dominican view.</note> attempts to assert in his commentary on the *Sentences*: namely, that the Will is a power more excellent than the Intellect. From this they infer not only that moral virtues are to be preferred (from which it clearly follows that the contemplative life does not surpass the active, nor does happiness consist in contemplation), but they further infer from the moral virtues that justice is of a higher grade than prudence. 

Nevertheless, the corollary of our conclusion is that prudence holds the first place among the moral virtues, 

<margin>Prudence holds the first place among all moral virtues. St. Thomas.</margin> as St. Thomas affirms in the same Question 66, Article 1. And indeed, beyond the general reasoning of the other intellectual virtues, prudence is more precious than the others even if it is considered in that part where it is moral. For a moral virtue derives its uprightness from reason as if from its original root. 

<margin>Reason of St. Thomas.</margin> Since, therefore, prudence perfects reason itself, while the others perfect the appetite, it is the best of all. Second, prudence is the leader and commander of all the others. For although the other virtues produce a right intention of the end—such as acting bravely, temperately, and justly—nevertheless, they attain that same end only by the office of prudence, which disposes the means, as Aristotle is the author in the 6th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 12. It excels the others, therefore, by a similar reasoning to how a general commands the other soldiers. Indeed, the others are so connected to it that without it, none can obtain the rank of virtue. 

<margin>First argument.</margin> Before we proceed from here, it is worthwhile to test this conclusion with arguments that are by no means unsuitable.

First... <meta>catchword: Primùm (First)</meta>

<meta>Continuity with page 215: Soto continues his exploration of the nature of virtues, specifically comparing the dignity of intellectual virtues (like science and wisdom) against moral virtues (like justice and temperance).</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

First, the proper nature of virtue, as is understood from its very name, is to apply a power to its use. This, however, does not belong to the intellectual virtues, but to the moral ones. For intellectual virtue only provides the faculty of acting—namely, knowledge—as the Holy Doctor <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> wisely taught in the *Summa*, 1st part of the 2nd part, Question 57, Article 1. Virtue, however, which resides in the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the faculty of the will or desire.</note>, applies knowledge to use, both in contemplation and in operation. Now, a habit <note>term: habit <note>original: "habitus"—a stable disposition or quality of the mind or soul.</note></note> exists for the sake of its use; for without use, it is idle and redundant. Therefore, intellectual virtue exists for the sake of moral virtue, and thus moral virtue, as that which has the nature of an end <note>The "end" refers to the purpose or goal.</note>, is more excellent.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Second, a moral virtue is, as Aristotle says in the 2nd book of the *Ethics*, that which makes its possessor good. Wherefore, as we said above, neither arts nor sciences simply <note>original: "simpliciter"—absolutely or in a general sense.</note> make a person good, but only moral virtue does. For this reason, it is worthy of greater praise, as it is through this that we earn merit before God and make our way toward blessedness <note>original: "beatitudinem"—heavenly happiness.</note>. Since intellectual virtues can exist without being used and are common to both the upright and the wicked, moral virtue is therefore more perfect than intellectual virtue.

<margin>To the argument.</margin>
<margin>The distinction of St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ These arguments greatly move those who touch the matter only on the surface <note>original: "in cortice summis labijs attingunt"—literally "touch the bark with the tips of their lips."</note>. However, there is an excellent distinction by St. Thomas cited in the same question, through which they are easily refuted. For he says that nothing prevents that which is "simply" better from being "in a certain respect" <note>original: "secundum quid"—relatively or in a particular case.</note> not as good for someone because of necessity. For instance, to philosophize is "simply" better than to be wealthy; but for one in need, it is better to be wealthy. By the same reasoning, although intellectual virtues are better by reason of their object—through which their excellence of rank is simply measured—moral virtues nevertheless participate more in the general definition of virtue, which consists in the order toward action and use. This is because they reside in the appetite, whose role is to move and drive the other powers to work. Hence, in the *Summa*, 2nd part of the 2nd part, Question 47, Article 4, he concluded that Prudence is more excellent by this reasoning than the other intellectual virtues: namely, because it does not only consider the truth (which is the object of the intellect) but orders it toward the good under the aspect of the good—that is, toward the use of works, by which a person becomes good.

<margin>Another argument.</margin>
<margin>The solution of some.</margin>
¶ But someone might perhaps argue: if moral virtue has more of the "nature of virtue," it follows that it is the nobler virtue. Deceived by this enthymeme <note>A logical syllogism where one premise is implied.</note>, some disciples of St. Thomas think his mind was that intellectual virtues are nobler beings and nobler habits, but that moral virtues are nevertheless nobler virtues.

<margin>The previous solution is refuted.</margin>
However, this sense clearly struggles against his actual mind; for he says that intellectual virtues are *simply* the nobler virtues, as he was speaking about the substance and nature of virtues. And the reason is clear: because if they are nobler habits, since

<column-break/>

they are habits of virtue, it follows that they are also nobler virtues. It is answered, therefore, that this consequence is invalid: "The general definition of virtue applies more to the moral ones, therefore they are simply nobler virtues." This is because the nobility of a virtue is not measured simply from the definition of virtue, but from the nature of the object. Let this be your example: Aristotle teaches us in the 1st book of *On the Soul* that the science of the soul is nobler than others because it concerns a nobler object; and yet the definition of science, which is evidence, is more brilliant in mathematics. Therefore, mathematics are not "simply" nobler sciences, but only "in a certain respect." By the same reasoning, Theology is a "simply" nobler science than music.

<margin>To the argument.</margin>
¶ The arguments made, therefore, conclude only this: that moral virtues have more of the "nature of virtue," and thus they make the possessor simply good, and they are more useful, and consequently of more abundant praise, etc.

<margin>Reply.</margin>
¶ But on the other hand: The dignity of a virtue should be measured "simply" by its order toward supreme happiness. Now, moral virtues move us more closely toward that; therefore, they are more worthy.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The major premise being granted with the minor, the conclusion is denied. For although virtues are to be valued in relation to happiness, those in which happiness *consists* are worthier than those through which we *strive* toward it. And although we progress there through moral virtues, we nevertheless enjoy God through contemplation. Thus, in this life, the intellectual virtues exist for the sake of the moral ones (for knowing is for the sake of doing); but "simply" speaking, the moral virtues are the means by which we progress toward supreme contemplation. For that reason, even if the moral virtues are more "praiseworthy," the intellectual virtues are "honorable" above them. For praise is owed to useful means, but honor to the end itself.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From which it follows that when we prefer intellectual virtues to moral ones, it must be understood by comparing genus to genus, and the supreme intellectual act (namely the vision of God) to the supreme moral act (namely love). But if the comparison is made in an individual case, charity—and indeed justice—is more precious than any single natural science.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: General and legal justice is the most illustrious of all those moral virtues that reside in the appetite. I have added this so that Prudence may keep its own honor.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
It is proven from that sentence of Aristotle in the 1st book of the *Ethics*: "The common good is more divine than the particular." For legal justice, as was said above, refers all the virtues that instruct a person toward particular goods to the common good. It is therefore an architectonic virtue, governing all others just as an architect governs the workers, a general the army, and a prince the republic.

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
Wherefore Cicero speaks of it when he says...

He concludes that Legal Justice is the highest moral virtue because it directs all other virtues toward the common good.</summary>

# Book III: On Justice and Right

...placed anything above justice. And in the civil republic, no punishments are decreed for any vices so great or so bitter as those for crimes of injustice, provided you except heresy and unspeakable wickedness.

<margin>A small doubt.</margin>
¶ However, one small doubt <note>original: "scrupulus" — literally a small sharp stone; figuratively a source of anxiety or a technical objection.</note> can arise from these points: namely, whether we should establish that justice is so much more perfect than the other moral virtues that any of its acts is more excellent than any act of the others. <margin>The opinion of some. Reasoning for the previous opinion.</margin> For many of our colleagues hold this view without hesitation. But this can certainly be defended with no probability. For who would say that selling small fish at a just price, or paltry vegetables, because it is an act of justice, is of greater praise and merit than the greatest act of fortitude or temperance? Such a person would most deservedly be considered ridiculous. Therefore, when we compare one virtue to another, the comparison is only made, as we were saying just now, between genus and genus: or between the greatest act of one and the greatest act of the other. Yet nothing prevents that which is superior in its general kind from being inferior in a specific instance due to the triviality of the matter. <margin>Fourth conclusion. St. Thomas. Proof of the conclusion.</margin> ¶ Fourth conclusion: Of the other two moral virtues, fortitude is more outstanding than temperance. This is the conclusion of St. Thomas in the place cited <note>referring to the *Summa Theologiae*, Second Part of the Second Part (2.2), question 66, article 4.</note>. This is first proven by the reasoning of the object and the subject. For temperance is concerned with the delights of touch, which is the most material of all the senses, seeing as it is the foundation of all. Furthermore, from the perspective of the act: fortitude is concerned with the dangers of life in war, from which all temporal goods flow; temperance, however, is concerned with those things upon which life indeed depends, either of the individual (regarding food) or of the species (regarding sexual matters). But nonetheless, because in those things a present and horrendous danger of death does not loom so closely, there is not as much difficulty, nor as much virtue, which is concerned with what is difficult.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
St. Thomas dissolves the first argument with a three-part response. For even granted that liberality <term>liberality: the virtue of being generous with one's own wealth</term> exceeds justice in this—that the liberal person grants what he does not owe—nonetheless, justice approaches more closely to the common good. For it grants to each what is his own, by which public peace is preserved, for which liberality is not as necessary; rather, it looks to the private good, which is shared out of itself. Second: Justice is extended more widely, for it is necessary in respect to all people, which does not apply to liberality. Likewise, because the foundation of liberality is justice. For no one deserves the name of liberality by bestowing what he does not owe, unless he is first just by paying

<column-break/>

what he does owe. And the same is true of magnanimity <term>magnanimity: "greatness of soul," the virtue of aspiring to great honors justly</term>.
<margin>A doubt concerning mercy.</margin>
¶ A doubt remains here concerning mercy <note>original: "misericordia"</note>: which, although it is a moral virtue, nonetheless appears more noble than justice, as the holy Doctor <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> himself confesses (2.2. q. 30. art. 3), because it is a virtue proper to God. <margin>The solution.</margin> To this, however, it is responded that if mercy is taken as that which moderates the sadness felt for another's misery, it is lower than justice, since it resides in the concupiscible appetite <term>concupiscible appetite: the faculty of the soul that seeks basic sensory goods and flees sensory evils</term>. But if it is taken not as referring to a sensory affection (such as compassion), but only as the will to lift others out of misery, it is much more noble than justice, because it is a virtue divine by its very nature. For to will and to be able to help all miseries and defects, both public and private, supposes a subject that cannot be liable to any calamity or defect—which can only suit the inaccessible majesty of God. For this reason, its effect is also the most noble of all: namely, to relieve and utterly remove needs without any debt. For if we made liberality inferior to justice, the reason was that it is founded upon justice, and does not approach the common good as closely, nor extend to all; mercy, however, at its peak (as it exists in God), does not presuppose justice. On the contrary, God produced things through mercy before He owed them anything, and it regards the public good and extends to the entire commonwealth. And therefore, since it is a divine virtue, the comparison of justice does not extend to it. <margin>Objection.</margin> If you should object that justice is also a divine virtue, and therefore is not exceeded by mercy: <margin>Response.</margin> the conclusion is denied. For justice is divine in such a way that, according to its own proper definition (namely, to pay a debt), it can be human. Mercy, however, insofar as it suffers no misery in itself because it removes all misery, is most proper to God, and thus in Him it is more illustrious and shining than justice. <margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, its conclusion is granted: namely, that prudence is superior in dignity. For we are only comparing justice to the moral virtues which are in the appetite. <margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third, regarding temperance, it is responded that although it brings us benefits—for which reason Aristotle <margin>Aristotle.</margin> in the 7th book of the *Politics*, chapter 15, equates it with justice by such reasoning: where he says that temperance, just like justice, is necessary in times of war and peace—simply speaking, however, for the reasons brought forward above, justice is to be preferred. <margin>Regarding the aforementioned fourth argument.</margin> ¶ Concerning the fourth argument: regarding fortitude, which was contended in the fourth argument to be placed before justice, the major [premise] etc.

He also concludes that fortitude is superior to temperance because it involves the greater difficulty of facing death.</summary>

### Book III: Question II

<margin>First reason for doubting.</margin>
There remains a reason for doubt. For this vigorous and noble virtue <note>original: "virtus" — here referring specifically to Fortitude</note> has many arguments advocating for itself in this cause. First, if you begin its praise from its name, fortitude seems to hold the name of "virtue" by way of excellence. For so it is read in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 8: "She teaches sobriety and justice, prudence and virtue," <margin>Secunda.</margin> that is, fortitude. And the very essence of virtue—which is to apply the mind to its proper use—shines with an exceptional brilliance in fortitude: namely, in that it exposes a man to the most present and most horrific death of all. <margin>Third.</margin> And thirdly, its excellence is commended by the splendor it holds within the republic. For the high-ranking and those of the most illustrious blood are heaped with the greatest wealth and looked upon with honors for this reason: that they protect the republic through the virtue of fortitude. Because of this, lineages have never been accustomed to being ennobled by a shorter path in the republic than through military fortitude. This is something that the histories of the Gentiles—namely the Spartans, Romans, and Greeks—have handed down to perpetual memory. For this virtue—leaving aside Hercules, Theseus, and those whom the poets invent—made the Alexanders, Caesars, Scipios, and others of that kind world-famous.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, to set aside profane matters, we ought to weigh the majesty of virtue (as we were saying a little earlier) by its greatest act: now, the best act of fortitude, such as **martyrdom**, is more excellent in both praise and merit than the supreme act of justice. For "no man has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends," and most especially for God as a testimony of faith; therefore, fortitude holds the pinnacle among the moral virtues. <margin>Fifth reason.</margin> In addition, since man's highest natural good is liberty, that virtue will be the greatest of all through which liberty is especially reclaimed: and this is fortitude. For as Aristotle says in Book 7 of the *Politics*, those who do not overcome the dangers of war become slaves. Add to this that the most precious thing is that which is rarest: and this is fortitude, for you will find men endowed with it more rarely than with other virtues. <margin>Last.</margin> In short, the nature and power of fortitude is to conquer others and provide for oneself, which most closely reflects the virtue and power of God; whence all men fear the brave and those of robust spirit, and everyone venerates and reveres them. <margin>Solution to the proposed conclusion.</margin> ¶ Nevertheless, notwithstanding these points, one must persist unhesitatingly in the opinion <note>that justice is the highest virtue</note>. For it will be enough praise for fortitude to have called justice into a legal dispute over precedence. For even if we were silent regarding the other reasons

<column-break/>

commemorated above, this one thing is enough for the victory of justice: that fortitude is in no way necessary except for the protection and guardianship of justice. For most wisely, as recorded in <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Plutarch, Agesilaus <note>A famous king of Sparta known for his military leadership and modest lifestyle.</note>—when asked as if he were a judge this very question, namely which of these two virtues was superior to the other—responded: "**We would have no need of fortitude if we were all just.**" Truly, unless justice were violated, there would be no occasion for wars in which fortitude serves the republic. Therefore, it is responded <margin>To the first argument.</margin> to the main argument that although fortitude is concerned with what is more difficult, justice is concerned with what is better. For it is more noble that the peace and tranquility of the human race be preserved through justice than the life of a private man. Therefore, justice (as we have said) shines in both times of peace and war. Nor is fortitude necessary for peace, unless justice has been overthrown. In the same way, it is responded to the objection regarding the name. <margin>To the second.</margin> For fortitude claimed the name of "virtue" for itself not simply by excellence, but because that quality and force of virtue which makes the mind robust and constant excels in it. To the other point <margin>To the third.</margin> regarding the splendor of nobles, for whom fortitude made their names famous: It is responded that if fortitude bore them such honors, it did so only as the **soldier and servant of justice**; for it cannot achieve the essence of virtue except insofar as it is the guardian and champion of justice. Truly, since honor is owed to virtue alone (as Aristotle says in Book 1 of the *Ethics*), and most especially to justice, when men exercise strength of spirit in any way other than by defending justice, they are no more "brave" than fierce bulls, savage bears, and monstrous tigers. Therefore, the republic established the high-ranking and illustrious so that they might strenuously protect the sacred virtue of justice with their fortitude; namely, not so that they might offer injury to others by their power, but so that they might repel it from all sides. ¶ To the other point <margin>To the fourth.</margin> which was objected with greater probability regarding the fortitude of martyrs, it is responded that although the act of martyrdom (which is most noble in the eyes of God) is elicited from the virtue of fortitude, it does not derive all its praise from there; rather, it is because it is commanded by the supreme effort of charity <note>In this context, "charity" means divine love or selfless love (*caritas*).</note>, than which "no one has greater than to lay down his life for his God." Wherefore the virtue of religion, which is more outstanding than justice, performs its functions there. Hence it is that laying down one's life for any other friend would not equal the supreme act of justice. To the other <margin>To the fifth.</margin> it is denied that it is the most specific property of fortitude to...

### QUESTION THREE
### concerning injustice.

->St. Thomas, Summa Theologica II-II, question 59.<-

### ARTICLE I.
### Whether injustice is a special vice.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'C' showing a landscape or architecture within the letter frame.</image-desc>

Since the study of opposites is the same—as Aristotle teaches in the first book of the *Topics*—this work of ours, which we have titled *On Justice and Right*, will deal in the following sections not only with the virtue of justice but very much with the vices of injustice. For this reason, after explaining the nature of justice, it is necessary to provide the next discourse on its opposite, injustice. The question is asked, therefore, whether injustice is a special vice. And the argument is made, according to our custom, from the negative side. Every sin, as is held in 1 John 3, is "iniquity"; <note>1 John 3:4: "Everyone who sins breaks the law; in fact, sin is lawlessness (iniquity)."</note> and iniquity is the same as injustice—namely, inequality. Therefore, injustice does not describe a special vice, but a general condition of all sins.

¶ Second, it is argued: no special sin is opposed to all virtues. However, injustice is opposed to all virtues; for the injustice that is committed in adultery

<column-break/>

is opposed to chastity; and that which is committed in homicide is opposed to gentleness; and that which is committed in insult is opposed to politeness, and so on. Therefore, it is not a special vice.

<margin>Third.</margin>

¶ Third: Injustice is opposed to justice, which resides in the will; but every sin, on the authority of Augustine, is voluntary. Therefore, every sin is an injustice. ¶ On the contrary is the fact that injustice is the direct opposite of justice; since justice is a special virtue, it follows that injustice is a special vice.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'Q' with floral or vine patterns.</image-desc>

The question is quite easy to answer. For by the rule of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle’s "Topics" provides logical rules for definitions and opposites.</note>, in as many ways as one of a pair of contraries is spoken of, so is the other. It follows that just as one type of justice is a general and "legal" virtue, while another is a special virtue, so too is one type of injustice general and another special. Therefore, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first: **Illegal injustice**, which is directly opposed to legal justice, is a vice that is indeed special in its essence, but general in its intent and command. Both parts of this are clear by the same reasoning used to demonstrate the nature of justice. For just as legal justice <note>term: "legal justice" — the virtue that directs a person’s actions toward the common good of the community.</note> has the common good as its object and is therefore a special virtue by essence—yet it nonetheless commands all other virtues and refers them to its own end—the same must be judged of injustice. For illegal injustice is the disobedience of laws and a contempt for the common good, and therefore it is a special vice. Nevertheless, it ranges through all other vices. For one can commit adultery, kill, or steal out of contempt for the law.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>To the first argument.</margin>

¶ The second conclusion: **Injustice** which perverts equality (which is toward another person) and turns it into inequality—for instance, when a man wants to have more of goods or honors, and less of evils, such as by selling too dearly or buying too cheaply—is a special vice. This is evident from the fact that it has a special subject matter and object. Both conclusions were expressly established by Aristotle in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 1 <note>The text says "6th Ethic," but justice is discussed in Book 5 of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.</note>, where he says a person is "unjust" in two ways: namely, those who overstep the laws, and those who take more than their share and are unfair. Likewise, a "just" person is two-fold: he who acts lawfully (that is, obeys the laws and looks to the common good), and he who is fair (that is, who gives to each what is theirs).

The response to the first argument will further clarify the matter. For the answer is that just as legal justice is spoken of in relation to the common human good, so...

<summary>This page concludes a comparison between justice and fortitude, arguing that justice is rarer and more essential for peace. It then begins a new inquiry into injustice, defining it as both a general disobedience of law (illegal injustice) and a specific vice of unfairness or greed (particular injustice).</summary>

# Question III of the Third Book

...and divine justice is spoken of in relation to the divine good; since every sin is repugnant to this good, sin is rightly defined in a general sense as a word or deed against the law of God. And by this reasoning, every sin is an iniquity <note>original: "iniquitas" — a lack of equity or fairness, often used interchangeably with sin in a legal-theological sense</note>.

<margin>The doubt.</margin>
¶ You may doubt, however, whether the formal reasoning of "illegal iniquity" applies to all sins. For it appears to be so, given that no sin exists unless it is committed against the laws.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
The response, nonetheless, is that although common sin is *materially* <note>meaning the outward action itself violates a rule</note> an illegal iniquity, it does not apply to all of them *formally* <note>meaning the specific intent of the sinner is to break the law</note>. Examples have already been frequently given above. Indeed, if you commit a theft, not because you hold God’s laws in contempt, but to satisfy your greed; or if you commit a homicide, not to disturb the common good, but because you are unable to restrain your anger: you are *materially* illegal because you are a transgressor of divine law, but not *formally* so, because that was not your intention. You are nonetheless inequitable and unjust against a particular form of justice. However, if you committed these crimes in contempt of the law and against the common good, then you would be an illegal and perverse citizen.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it is responded that injustice—because it is concerned with all actions—is nonetheless involved in a peculiar way; not directly, but indirectly and materially, it opposes all virtues. This is because it violates the rights of another through various corrupt affections.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third, it is responded that although the will, like reason, extends itself to the matter of all virtues, justice nonetheless has its own peculiar reasoning; therefore, not every sin is injustice.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether whoever does an unjust act is immediately considered an unjust person.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'C' containing a miniature woodcut scene of a landscape with trees and a building.</image-desc>
SINCE virtue, according to Aristotle, is that which makes its possessor good, it is appropriate to investigate whether, conversely, whoever does an unjust thing should immediately be considered an unjust and wicked person.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The argument for the affirmative side is as follows: Habits <note>term: "habitus" — a settled disposition or character trait acquired through repeated action</note> receive their specific nature from their objects. The proper object of justice is the just; and the proper object of injustice is the unjust. Therefore, just as one is considered just because they do a just thing, so too is one considered unjust because they do an unjust thing.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second, it is ar-

<column-break/>

-gued: Every virtue relates to its own proper act in the same way. The same reasoning, therefore, will apply to all vices. Whoever does something intemperate is an intemperate person; therefore, whoever does an unjust thing will be an unjust person.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third: Whoever does an unjust thing sins mortally by the very nature of the act. For they act against equity, either by killing, or committing adultery, or stealing, etc., all of which are mortal sins by their nature. A mortal sin, however, renders a person unjust before God, just as grace renders them just. Therefore, whoever does an unjust thing is unjust.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is the opinion of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 8, where he discusses how it may happen that someone does an unjust thing who, nevertheless, does not immediately become an unjust person.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' with intricate floral and scrollwork designs inside and around the letter.</image-desc>
THIS question is raised for the sake of Aristotle; namely, so that his passage just cited may be explained. His doctrine can be summarized in a single two-part conclusion. To this, we will add another so that we may simultaneously resolve the fourth article of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, which is closely related to this one.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Let this be the first conclusion: Not everyone who does an unjust thing is to be called "unjust" in themselves immediately—for instance, if they do it out of ignorance or passion—but only that person who dares to do it from habit and from choice.

<margin>Foundation.</margin>
So that even a young student <note>original: "tyrunculus" — a little recruit or beginner</note> may perceive the sense of this conclusion, let them remember that the nature of virtue requires that one acts knowingly and by choice, for the sake of what is honorable, and persistently, as was cited above from Book 2 of the *Ethics*. Therefore, if someone, either by chance or by some sudden emotion, performs a single act of virtue, they are not immediately "studious" <note>meaning virtuous or diligent in character</note>, because they do the good not in themselves, but by accident. Aristotle, therefore, thought it necessary to teach this same principle regarding vices.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
For a person to be called "unjust," it is required not only that they do an unjust thing, but that they do it from a sickness of the soul; for instance, from the corruption of a habit. Saint Thomas clarifies this reasoning in this way: Just as the object of justice is the just, so the object of injustice is the unjust—namely, the unequal. The proper root, however, from which the unjust arises, is the habit by which the power of the soul is inclined toward the object. Therefore, he who operates from choice and habit is properly unjust.

<margin>Two ways it can happen that someone commits an unjust act and yet is not an unjust person.</margin>
It can happen in two ways that someone, while performing an unjust act, is not an unjust person. First, because of a lack of connection between the act and the object: specifically, because the one acting does not intend it. For an act becomes spontaneous, and subsequently "human" <note>meaning a deliberate act for which a human is morally responsible</note>, through intention. Thus, if someone does not act of their own will for any reason, they are excused from being "unjust"; and since the voluntary...

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

...ignorance and force remove responsibility. For Aristotle says that if someone does something unjust through ignorance or is compelled by force, he is injurious to no one. For example, if someone moves your hand so that you strike another: in that case, neither the mind nor the action is truly directed or applied to the injustice; rather, it becomes an injustice by accident <note>original: "per accidens" — an incidental occurrence rather than an essential or intended one</note>. Therefore, there is no blame, just as you would gain no praise if you did something just in that same accidental manner.

In the second way, it happens that one who does an unjust thing is not himself an "unjust man" due to a lack of connection between the act and his habit <note>original: "habitus" — in Scholastic philosophy, this refers to a stable disposition or character trait, rather than a repetitive behavior</note>. That is to say: although the object of the action is voluntary and intended—and thus the operation is directed toward that object—the action does not spring from a settled habit.

For instance, if a man who is otherwise mild and upright should wound another in a sudden storm of anger, he does not then act from choice <note>original: "ex electione" — deliberate choice following reflection</note>, since it is necessary for deliberation to come first. Thus, he does not act from habit. From these points, our conclusion is gathered: namely, for someone to be deservedly named "unjust," it is required that they perform an injustice in itself <note>original: "per se"</note>. For where one does it by accident, he will not be an unjust man. And since a habit is linked to its object through action, two types of connection and application are necessary for a person to act unjustly "in themselves" and thus become an unjust person: namely, that the operation be linked to the object through intention (meaning the object is willed), and furthermore, that the same operation be linked to a habit through choice (meaning it proceeds not from a fleeting passion, but from a settled character).

Here, no ambiguity remains if only the Aristotelian mind is laid open. For indeed, that one who admits to something either ignorantly or under compulsion is neither just nor unjust carries the evidence of reason: because an action that is not spontaneous is not a human act at all.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
Yet, it appears false that someone who—knowingly and prudently—transgresses out of a sickness of the soul (such as anger or another passion) is not "unjust." For a threefold genus of sins is distinguished: namely, from vincible ignorance <note>ignorance that could and should have been overcome</note>, which does not entirely excuse; from passion, which is worse; and from malice, which is by design and choice, and is the worst of its kind. Therefore, Aristotle is wrong not to admit this third degree.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that a Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> judges a "just" or "unjust" man differently than he is judged before God. For God weighs the acts, not just the habits; and therefore whoever transgresses, however just he may otherwise be, becomes and is held as unjust in God's sight. Just as whoever does well in a single act—even if he is endowed with no habit of virtue—deserves well of Him. Nor does Aristotle deny that an act

<column-break/>

proceeding from passion is to be blamed; he only holds that these names, "just" and "unjust," connote nothing except settled habits. Wherefore he says that what happens outside of reason—that is, through ignorance—is a misfortune; but the evil which proceeds from knowledge, yet without vice (that is, without a settled habit), he calls a "sin." Vice, however, is the name for a habit, not a single act. And indeed, we speak this way in common speech. For just as "one swallow does not make a summer," so a person is not called "studious" or "depraved" by one or two acts; but only when he operates from a habit, and likewise from design and choice. For this reason, the schools of Theologians, when evaluating this, consider it "sinning from malice"; and thus, strictly speaking, only such a person is held and said to be "evil."

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
From these points, the final conclusion is gathered.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Whoever, knowingly and prudently, does an injustice—that is, not through ignorance that is the total cause of the work—even if he does it from passion without a habit, sins mortally by the nature of the act. The conclusion is very clear. For whatever is opposed to charity <note>divine love and the bond of community</note> is a mortal sin; and the sin of injustice, because it slaughters the virtue necessary for the peace of the republic, is by its nature resistant to charity. It is therefore mortal by its own character. I should say: if it does not proceed from ignorance that is the total cause of the work—that is, which completely removes the fault. For ignorance of the law would not remove it, nor would every ignorance of fact, though it might be worthy of pardon, as stated in Book 5 of the *Ethics*.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle is the authority for this. Indeed, Paul says: "I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly" <note>1 Timothy 1:13</note>. I would add the phrase "by its nature" both to differentiate it from prodigality, gluttony, and other sins which are not mortal by their nature unless by circumstances, and also to denote that it can happen that one sins venially <note>a "lesser" sin that does not break the relationship with God</note> against justice due to the insignificance of the matter <note>e.g., stealing a single penny</note>.

The examination of these things, however, belongs to another place.

<margin>Interpretation of Aristotle.</margin>
And through these things which have been said, one must understand what Aristotle says in Chapter 9: namely, that the opinion of those who think it is in a man's power to "be unjust" immediately is false. That is to say, to do so from deliberate choice. They also think a just man can do an injustice no less than an unjust man—specifically, "in himself." They err, he says, because one who is imbued with the best habits, even if he wants to, cannot easily choose injustice; even though he might do something unjust through ignorance or a sudden movement of emotion. From this arose the axiom: "No one becomes extremely wicked suddenly" <note>original: "Nemo repente pessimus"</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that habits and acts are sorted into species based on their objects...

### Third Book, Question III.

...toward objects intended formally—as they say—and for their own sake <note>original: "per se"</note>. However, when it is done materially and by accident <note>original: "materialiter ac per accidens"</note>—that is, stemming from accidental ignorance or passion—the act is not sufficient to label a man as "just" or "unjust" in the idiom of the philosophers.

<margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, it is answered that there is a wide difference between "the just," which is the object of justice, and "the temperate" or "the brave," which are the objects of other virtues. Because "just" and "unjust" are found within the things themselves <note>Soto means that justice concerns external distribution and external objects, regardless of one's internal state</note>, even if an act occurs by accident, it is still called just or unjust. For this reason, Aristotle ingeniously established that in this specific virtue, someone can do an unjust deed even if they are not an "unjust man." However, the object of temperance is not found in things according to their own nature, but rather in relation to the person acting; therefore, when a temperate act occurs by accident, it can in no way be called "temperate." Because of this, no such distinction was needed for that virtue: whoever performs a temperate act *is* temperate, because an act will not be temperate unless it is intended for its own sake. Thus, if someone abstains from something by mere chance, just as he is not temperate, he likewise does not perform a "temperate act," since he does not do it when, where, and how it is required. By the same reasoning, when Lot, for example, knew his daughters because of his drunkenness <note>Referring to the biblical story of Lot in Genesis 19</note>, just as he was not an intemperate man, he likewise did not perform an "intemperate act." In short, this distinction between material and formal "just" or "unjust" has no place in the objects of temperance or fortitude.

<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ The third argument is sufficiently resolved where we showed that although God’s grace is lost by any act of injustice—and so before God, that man becomes "unjust" (that is, a sinner)—it does not follow that among moral philosophers, for whom formal labels are weighed not by a single act but by habit, every sinner is called "unjust" or "wicked."
