### ARTICLE III.

->Whether one can suffer injustice willingly.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin> After looking at the one who *commits* an injustice, it follows that we should speak of the one who *suffers* it: namely, whether anyone can suffer injustice willingly. The argument for the affirmative side is as follows: Injustice is the same as inequality. However, anyone who harms himself of his own accord departs from equality just as much as if

<column-break/>

he were harming another. Therefore, even a willing person can suffer what is unjust, and thus suffer an injury.

<margin>Second.</margin> ¶ Second: No one is punished with a penalty except on account of injustice. However, those who commit suicide are punished civilly. For Aristotle says in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, final chapter, <margin>Aristotle</margin> that a certain ignominy was established against them—namely, that they were forbidden burial. Therefore, one can suffer injustice willingly.

<margin>Third.</margin> ¶ Third: Doing and suffering injustice are relative terms; thus, no one does an injustice unless another suffers an injustice. But it happens that someone does an injustice to one who is willing to suffer it—for example, if one sells something for more than the just price or lends money under usury <note>original: "sub foenore" — charging interest on a loan, which was traditionally considered an act of injustice/sin</note>. Therefore, someone can suffer injustice willingly. 

¶ On the contrary is the fact that suffering injustice is the opposite of doing injustice. But as was defined in the preceding article, no one does an injustice except willingly; therefore, no one suffers it except unwillingly.

AND this article is also employed for the sake of interpreting Aristotle, who in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 9 and following, established that no one suffers an injustice or an injury while suffering it of his own accord. His doctrine is made clear through two conclusions. The first is:

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> Speaking in itself and formally <note>original: "per se & formaliter"</note>, no one can do an injustice except willingly, nor suffer one except unwillingly.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> This conclusion is supported by this clear, natural reason: Just as it is of the intrinsic nature of an *action* that it proceeds from the agent, so it is of the intrinsic nature of a *passion* <note>original: "passio" — here meaning the state of being acted upon or "suffering" an effect</note> that it is done by another, without the one suffering it contributing force. From this, Aristotle (in the 3rd and 8th books of the *Physics*) <margin>Aristotle</margin> concludes that the agent and the sufferer cannot be entirely the same thing; rather, everything that is moved is moved by another. Now, the principle of acting proper to human beings is the will. Thus, a man is properly said to "do" that which issues from his will; and conversely, he "suffers" that which happens to him against the refusal of his will. For to suffer is to be conquered and overcome. But where someone suffers willingly, he contributes force and cause to it, and consequently is said to "act" rather than to "suffer." It follows, therefore, that speaking formally and in itself, no one suffers anything except unwillingly. Indeed, this very thing is what "suffering" is: to be subject to violence.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion: Nothing prevents anyone, speaking accidentally and materially <note>original: "per accidens ac materialiter"</note>, from suffering an injustice willingly; just as someone can, by accident, do what is just unwillingly.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> The conclusion is proven: For instance, if someone, being ignorant of what is happening, consents to that which is bad for him—as when the drunk Lot, deceived by his daughters, committed incest; and Jacob, being ignorant, committed a shameful act <note>Referring to Jacob being deceived into marrying Leah instead of Rachel</note>; or when someone, compelled by necessity, receives a loan under usury.

<summary>Soto explains that while "doing" injustice requires intent, "suffering" injustice is defined by the victim's lack of will; therefore, one cannot "formally" be a victim of injustice if they desire the outcome. He clarifies that external acts like usury or suicide might involve a willing participant "materially," but they do not meet the philosophical definition of suffering an injury.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

¶ Concerning these conclusions, I should first of all note that although "right" <note>original: "ius"</note> and "the just" <note>original: "iustum"</note> are essentially the same, nevertheless in the common way of speaking, "suffering an injury" <note>original: "iniuriam pati"</note> does not seem to carry the same distinction as "suffering something unjust" <note>original: "iniustum pati"</note>. I mean to say that one is not as properly said to suffer an injury materially as to suffer something unjust. Indeed, suffering an injury seems always to be used for what is suffering something unjust *in itself* <note>original: "per se"</note>: namely, while being unwilling and refusing. And from here arose that legal axiom: **To one who is knowing and willing, no injury is done.** <note>original: "Scienti & volenti non fit iniuria"—a fundamental principle in Roman and Canon law suggesting that if someone consents to an act, they cannot later claim it was a legal injury against them.</note> Likewise, no one is said to inflict an injury unless they act knowingly and prudently in doing what is unjust.

<margin>Argument.</margin> ¶ Against this conclusion, an argument immediately presents itself: if no willing person could be affected by injury, it would follow that no one, even if consenting to some pact out of fear, could complain of injury—which is clearly false. For marriages contracted through consent arising from the fear of death are dissolved by the laws because of the injury involved.

<margin>Solution.</margin> If anyone intends to repel the force of this argument by saying that he who consents through fear does not "will" it under that condition, Aristotle seems to stand against him, who says in the 3rd book of the *Ethics*:

<margin>Reply.</margin> He who would not will something in general, yet wills it in a particular circumstance, is said to "will" it simply <note>Soto uses "simply" or "absolutely" here to mean the final choice made in a specific moment, even if it is a choice between two evils.</note>; just as one who throws merchandise overboard in a shipwreck, although he would not wish to do so in a general sense, nevertheless wills it simply in that moment to save the ship.

<margin>Response.</margin> ¶ It is responded that this condition, which the Scholastics call **unwillingness** <note>original: "nolleitas"—a technical term for a "would-rather-not" state of mind.</note>, is sufficient for someone to be considered as having suffered an injury, even if they "will" it simply—provided that consent is extorted against the law. For to suffer an injury is the same as being deprived of one's own right. Therefore, when someone is led to execution by law, however much they are unwilling, they suffer no injury. And if an option were then offered to them—for instance, that if they wished to marry a prostitute or be sentenced to the galleys, their life would be spared—no injury would be done to them, even if they would prefer to escape death without that condition. From this it follows again that he who is led into an unjust situation by cunning and fraud suffers an injury in itself, just as if he consented by force, because he does not act of his own free will.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> TO the first argument, therefore, it is responded that no one, by bestowing their own goods voluntarily when they do not owe them, commits any injustice or inequality; for since a person is the master of their own things by their own will, they can by that same will both give them away and allow themselves to be despoiled.

<margin>Reply.</margin> But you argue: if someone squanders their goods—namely, if having a family to support, they prodigally pour out their substance—those who receive them seem to

<column-break/>

inflict an injury upon him; and yet he himself bestows it with the most absolute will. <margin>Solution.</margin> It is responded that although that spendthrift <note>original: "prodigus"</note> sins, nevertheless the one receiving does him no injury, but perhaps does so to the family to whom those goods in some way belonged. However, this is not the appropriate place for treating these matters more closely.

<margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ The common response to the second argument is that an individual person can be considered in two ways: first, according to themselves absolutely. In this way, certainly, they can do no injustice to themselves. For when someone either defames, mutilates, or kills themselves, they indeed act against charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the moral obligation to love and care for oneself as a creation of God.</note> (by which they are bound to love themselves), but not at all against justice. This is both because justice is only toward another <note>original: "ad alterum"</note>, and because they suffer it knowingly and willingly. In the second way, a person can be considered insofar as they are a member of the commonwealth, and a creation and image of God. And in this way, he who kills himself inflicts an injury both upon the city and especially upon God. And therefore he pays the penalty under both civil and divine law. This is the opinion of Aristotle in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 11. However, it should not be inferred from this that the commonwealth has dominion over life and death just as God does; for it cannot kill anyone as a "master," just as any individual can slaughter his own herd or beast without cause; rather, it acts as a judge on account of a fault. This is discussed more broadly in the next book under the title **On Dominion**, and again in Book 5 under the title **On Homicide**. In the same way, he who kills another, even if that person desires it and begs for it—of which you have an example in the armor-bearer who killed Saul at his command <note>A reference to the biblical account in 1 Samuel 31, where King Saul asks his armor-bearer to kill him.</note>—also commits an injury, not against the one who commanded it, but against God, who is the master of life, and the commonwealth, which is the guardian of life.

<margin>A small question.</margin> But could that King command another to kill him, since he possesses supreme power? <margin>Solution.</margin> It is responded that a prince has no power whatsoever to kill an innocent person, and much less to command his own homicide; if, however, he had exercised such great tyranny, he could appoint a judge over himself to put him to death by law.

<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third argument, finally, it is responded that doing and suffering injustice, if taken materially, always follow each other as relatives. For no one can do an unjust act except to someone who suffers it; nor truly suffer it, except from someone who does it. But if the speech is formal: because this must be weighed by the will of the agent and the resistance of the sufferer, it can happen that someone is injurious to another, and yet the other suffers no injury...

Soto also clarifies that consent given under extreme fear or fraud still constitutes an injury because it lacks true free will.</summary>

### ARTICLE I.
### *Whether judgment is an act of justice.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial Q featuring a seated figure in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
Since we have already spoken of the habit <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "habit" is a stable disposition or quality of character.</note> of justice, and of its contrary, injustice; and since a habit exists for the sake of its exercise, it follows that we must speak of its most powerful act, which is "to judge," and whether this is an act of justice. He [Thomas Aquinas] argues from the negative side. Everyone, he says, 
<margin>First argument.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
judges well the things they know (Aristotle, Book 1 of the *Ethics*): therefore, judgment belongs to the cognitive power. Now, the cognitive power in moral matters is perfected through prudence; therefore, judgment is a function of the intellectual virtue of prudence rather than of justice, which resides in the will. ¶ Se-
<margin>Second.</margin>
condly, the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 2): "The spiritual man judges all things." But a man becomes spiritual through charity <note>Divine love or "caritas."</note>, which, poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, purges them from the affection for earthly things; therefore, judgment is a duty of charity rather than justice. 
<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: it is proper to every virtue to perfect right judgment in its own specific matter. 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was frequently referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in this era.</note> says in Book 3 of the *Ethics*, chapter 4, every virtuous man is the rule and measure of those things which are to be done. For those things, he says, are called just and temperate which are such as the just and temperate man performs. Therefore, judging is not unique to justice. 
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, judging seems to belong only to judges and princes; but universal justice is common even to subjects; therefore, judgment is not the proper task of justice. ¶ On the contrary is that Psalm: "Until justice be turned into judgment."

<column-break/>

This single question is resolved by the following conclusion.
<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
Judgment is the act most especially proper to justice. The conclusion becomes manifest from the very sound and composition of the name. For "judgment" <note>original: "iudicium"</note> is the 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
same as the "proclamation of the right" <note>original: "iuris dictio"</note>, and "to judge" <note>original: "iudicare"</note> is the same as "to speak the right" <note>original: "ius dicere"</note>, and "judge" <note>original: "iudex"</note> is the same as "one who speaks the right" <note>original: "ius dicens"</note>. From this it follows that to judge is the proper act regarding "the right" <note>original: "ius"</note>. Now "the right," as was said above, is the object of justice—namely, that just thing which is established in reality through justice. Therefore, "to judge," according to its primary and natural meaning, is the same as to decree and define that which is just and right. To correctly assess and define any matter proceeds from a right affection and habit by which one relates to that same matter. For 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
as the Philosopher says in Book 3 of the *Ethics*, chapter 5, as each person is, so the end seems to him. For instance, he who is chaste judges well regarding abstinence from sexual pleasures, and he who is sober judges well regarding abstinence from food. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the proper act of justice is right judgment—that is, the right determination of what is just. Hence Aristotle, in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 4, says that everyone flees to the judge as if to a "living justice." For a judge is, as it were, justice living and speaking.

There is no reason for doubt hidden in the conclusion except for those sought by the arguments already made. First, therefore, the "sciolists" <note>Pretentious or superficial students.</note> and those just emerging from their studies of Logic might be deceived; for to those who have only looked at the surface of the matter, it might appear that 
<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
judgment, according to its genuine meaning, is an act of reason rather than justice. This is because "to judge" is the same as "to speak the right," and "to speak" is a function of the intellect, not the will; for words are signs of concepts, and thus the intellect first forms the speech that is uttered by the voice. But the matter, when inspected more deeply, stands differently. Indeed, since the name "judgment" descends from "right" <note>original: "ius"</note>, it was first applied to signify the right definition of just things. But then it was derived to signify, in a universal sense, the right definition of other virtues regarding their own objects, in both speculative and practical matters. For example, the right definition in the matter of temperance and fortitude, etc. And likewise in the sciences, it refers to that which expresses the correspondence of the object to the intellect. In all these things, however, two 
<margin>Two virtues are required for right judgment.</margin>
virtues are required for right judgment: namely, the one which pronounces the judgment, and the one which disposes the power of the judge so that it is fit and suited for the rectitude of the judgment. The former is proper...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law,

<columns>2</columns>

belongs to reason, whose function it is to speak <note>In scholastic philosophy, "speaking" or "pronouncing" refers to the cognitive act of forming a definitive statement or conclusion.</note>, as we were just showing: but the latter part properly belongs to a habit <note>A "habit" (habitus) is a stable quality or disposition of character that makes it easy to act in a certain way.</note> that correctly disposes a power toward its object. Such a habit regarding theoretical things is speculative and resides in the intellect; however, in practical matters, it is a habit that disposes the appetite <note>The "appetite" here refers to the faculty of desire or will that moves a person toward a perceived good.</note>. Specifically, in matters of temperance, it is the habit of temperance; in matters of courage, the habit of courage. For no one will judge most correctly that it is good to attack when one ought to, unless he is brave; nor will he judge it better to use food with moderation than to be submerged in it, unless he is temperate. Therefore, by the same logic, judgment is a work of justice insofar as it inclines a person toward a right judgment, but it is a work of prudence insofar as it pronounces that judgment. But indeed, so that they may be right, the moral virtues prepare the disposition <note>original: "affectum"</note>.

<margin>Question.</margin>
<margin>Solution.</margin>
But if you should ask again: which of these virtues does the duty of judging more properly belong to? The answer is that it belongs more closely to reason and prudence, by which it is pronounced; and yet, it belongs most essentially to justice, from which it derives its rightness. Wherefore,

<margin>The Philosopher.</margin>
The Philosopher <note>A standard title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> says in Book 6 of the *Ethics*, chapter 12: "Moral virtue is that which makes the purpose itself right, while prudence is that which deals with the means."

<margin>The reason why all virtues are connected to prudence.</margin>
¶ And through this, the reason is clear why all virtues are connected to prudence. For since it is the role of prudence to pronounce right judgments in every moral matter—a rectitude which it receives from moral virtue—one cannot be prudent unless one is endowed with all the virtues. Nor, conversely, will any moral virtue have the status of a virtue without prudence, since without it, the virtue cannot carry out its purpose.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ The second argument proves this: that it belongs to charity <note>Divine love.</note> to judge rightly concerning divine things, toward which it disposes the appetite, so that through the gift of wisdom a right judgment is made. Justice, however, disposes the will toward what is natural and humanly right, so that the just person, through prudence, may also pronounce a fit judgment concerning those things.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is answered that although it is common to all virtues to prepare the disposition for a right judgment regarding their own proper objects, there is nevertheless a difference. While the other virtues, as has often been said, order a person toward himself, justice orders a person toward another. And every person is the master of their own affairs, but not of those things which involve another. Thus, in the other virtues, no judgment is required except the private judgment of the virtuous person himself; but in the matter of justice, there is additionally a need for

<column-break/>

a superior, who may judge between two litigants. For this reason, judgment is more uniquely ascribed to the virtue of justice than to any of the others.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ And likewise, it is answered to the fourth that although it may also be appropriate for subjects who excel in justice to judge privately, nevertheless, because this virtue presides in an architectonic <term>architectonic: a "master-building" virtue that directs and organizes the actions of others toward a common goal</term> manner in the prince and in his ministers, the most powerful act of this same virtue—which is to judge and to declare the law <note>original: "iusque dicere"</note>—properly belongs to them.

### ARTICLE II.
#### Whether it is lawful to judge.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'C' featuring a figure in a landscape with a tree and a small building.</image-desc>
Having established to which virtue judgment belongs, it follows that we should investigate whether it is lawful. And it is argued from the negative side. Punishment is not inflicted except for a fault; however, for those who judge, the punishment is decreed that they themselves shall be judged, according to that passage in Matthew 7: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged." Therefore, judging is unlawful.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second: It is not lawful for a sinner to judge, according to that passage in Romans 2: "You are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judges; for in whatever you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things that you judge." But no one is free from sin. For as John says, "If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves." Therefore, it is lawful for no one to judge.
¶ On the contrary, however, we are encouraged by that passage in Deuteronomy 16: "You shall appoint judges and masters in all your gates, that they may judge the people with a just judgment."

Since it was determined in the previous article that judgment is an act of justice, it follows from that that judging is lawful. But this present article is not redundant for that reason; indeed, it is employed not so much to demonstrate that fact as to describe and establish the conditions that are required for a judgment to be right. Therefore, the conclusion does not correspond to the title in its form so much as to the equity of right judgment.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is this: In order for any judgment to be right, three things are required: namely, that it proceed from the authority of the judge, from the disposition of justice, and from the rectitude of prudence. If any of these is lacking, the judgment will be flawed, and consequently unlawful.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is proven. Judgment, as has been said, is right and likewise lawful to the extent that it is an act of justice. But for it to be an act of justice, these three aforementioned things

It also establishes the three conditions for a lawful judgment: authority, a just intent, and prudent reasoning.</summary>

### Book Three, Question IV.

customs are required: therefore, these same things are entirely necessary for a right judgment. The latter premise is proved as follows: for the proper power of justice is coercive <note>The power to enforce a law or sentence by force.</note>; however, no one can coerce another unless that person is subject to him. This is clear from the example of natural things. For an agent does not overcome a passive object unless it is subject to it within the sphere <note>original: "periodum"</note> of its activity. Therefore, the authority of a prince and a judge is required. Hence Paul says in Romans 14:
<margin>Paul.</margin>
"Who are you who judges another’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls." <note>original: "Tu quis es qui iudicas alienum feruum? domino suo stat aut cadit."</note> And so, since God is the universal Lord of all, no one among mortals is a legitimate judge unless he has received the authority to judge from God Himself. Wherefore, in Romans 13, he says: "There is no power except from God" <note>original: "Non est potestas nisi à Deo"</note> and, "he who resists the power, resists the ordinance of God." And further down, he says that any judge is a "minister of God, an avenger to execute wrath upon him who does evil." How this power is derived from God to men through the law of nature will be elucidated in the next book under the title *On Dominion*.

The second requirement, as we were saying just now, for the rectitude of judgment is that it must proceed from an affection and inclination for justice. This needs no other proof than that judgment is the proper act of this virtue, as it affects the soul toward what is just. Wherefore, if a judge takes away anything from the right of one party to give it to the other, he subverts the very substance of justice.

The third thing that the rectitude of judgment demands is the duty of prudence <note>Prudence, or "practical wisdom," is the intellectual virtue of applying general principles to specific situations.</note>; its task is to pronounce the judgment. Therefore, if a person speaks the law and determines what is just between litigants, yet does not do so when, where, and how the laws require, he destroys the virtue of justice in this regard. Hence, a judgment that lacks the authority of a presiding official is called "usurped." One that lacks the substance of justice is called "iniquitous." But one that is without prudence—if the legal order is missing—is considered "suspect"; if, however, it is pronounced out of levity and without legitimate proofs, it is "rash" <note>Temerarium: a judgment made too quickly without sufficient evidence.</note>.
<margin>Instruction.</margin>
¶ Concerning each of these conditions, first note this: a defect in any of them, by its very nature, constitutes a mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a serious offense that severs one's relationship with God, as opposed to a "venial sin" which is a lesser offense.</note>. I say that a judge who, having no authority or usurping another's, judges someone not subject to him, sins mortally. For example, if a secular judge involves himself in the cases of clerics <note>In the 16th century, the clergy were generally exempt from secular courts, a privilege known as "benefit of clergy."</note>: even if he were not excommunicated by law, he would by that very act be stained with mortal guilt, just as if he were a private person. Indeed, it is all the more grave because he does this under the pretext of

<column-break/>

public authority. And if he were to deprive a cleric of his goods, he would truly be a thief; and if he were to kill him, he would truly be a murderer.
<margin>Another thing to be noted.</margin>
The second condition must also be carefully weighed. For the assertion that judgment must proceed from an affection and inclination for justice is ambiguous <note>original: "amphibolum"</note> and can have a threefold meaning. The first is that it must not be done against justice. This is the mandatory sense: namely, that what is one's own is sincerely granted to each. A defect here renders the judgment iniquitous. The second meaning is that the judgment should proceed from a *feeling* of justice. Yet a defect in this is never a mortal sin. Indeed, if a judge delivers a just sentence, even if he does not do this out of a habit or love of justice because he is a wicked man, he does not sin mortally, though it would be a venial fault. For since a judge is the guardian of justice, he ought always to judge with a feeling for it. The third sense, finally, is that the judgment must not be delivered out of some other wicked affection: namely, hatred, love, or greed. A defect in this will be a sin according to the affection from which it proceeds. For example: if a judge sentences a man who is truly a thief and has been legitimately proven so to the gallows out of hatred, he does not indeed sin against justice, but he does sin against charity. And if he does it out of greed for money, he is not indeed iniquitous, but he is greedy; and if out of a desire for empty glory, then he is vain and sins venially. Wherefore, although he kills out of hatred, he will not be considered a murderer in the way a private person would be, since he has the legal right to kill.

¶ A defect of the third condition will also be a mortal sin: for instance, if he should neglect the rules and circumstances of the law, or when a private person judges hidden matters lightly and rashly. However, it can become venial due to the lightness of the matter: as when a judge skips some minor legal terms, or if someone judges another lightly regarding a trivial thing, as we shall say in the next article.
<margin>To the first argument. Augustine.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, the holy fathers respond in various ways. For Augustine, in his *Sermon on the Mount*, says that rash judgment is forbidden there: which consists of judging the intention of hearts, or uncertain and hidden things. Concerning this rashness, the discussion must begin in the next article.
<margin>Hilary.</margin>
Hilary, however, says that the judgment of divine things is forbidden: since these exceed our grasp, they are not to be judged by us using human rules, but simply...

¶ To the second argument, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto’s school of thought.</note> responds by making a distinction: namely, that a judge who is in a state of grave public sin cannot judge others who are guilty of similar or lesser offenses, especially when those sins are public. And he cites Chrysostom in support, who exhorts on the passage from Matthew 7: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged." <note>original: "Nolite iudicare, & non iudicabimini."</note> If, however, the judge’s sins are hidden, he can indeed condemn similar sinners if he does so with humility. This is confirmed by the opinion of Augustine, who in his book *On the Sermon on the Mount*, says: "If we find that we are in the same vice, let us groan together and invite one another to struggle together." <note>original: "Si inuenerimus nos in eodem vitio esse, congemiscamus & ad pariter conandum nos inuitemus."</note>

This is also supported by the chapter *Quaesitum* <note>A specific legal decree in Canon Law.</note> in the section *On the times for ordaining*, where we seem to be warned by this reasoning. This opinion was once so celebrated that even Saint Thomas sometimes subscribed to it, namely in his commentary on the *Sentences* <note>original: "4. distinct. 19. q. 2. articu. 2."</note>, where he asserts without distinction—whether the judge's sin be public or hidden—that it is a mortal sin to solemnly condemn another sinner. For this reason, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas.</note> also disputed this matter in his *Quodlibets*. Nevertheless, despite these arguments, Saint Thomas rightly corrected his opinion in the *Summa* <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's mature masterwork.</note>—both here and in the cited place in the Third Part—so that he does not judge a hidden sinner who is a judge to be sinning mortally by judging.

<margin>First proposition in the mind of St. Thomas.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the aforementioned assertion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, we summarize the opinion in these propositions. First: It is lawful for a judge who is entangled in a hidden crime, no matter how grave, provided he is not excommunicated or suspended, to condemn subjects, whether for the same crime or for a different one. The reason is that such a judge nonetheless possesses the legal title to judge. To deny this is heresy. Likewise, he can possess prudence and the intent to preserve for each person their right; therefore, nothing is lacking for him to use the power of judgment. It would be different if he were a heretic who, by reason of excommunication, cannot sit as a judge. Nor is it the same as a priest who administers the sacraments in sin; for that office requires the power of holy orders, in the conferring of which grace is given, through which he is made worthy and fit to administer the sacraments, through which grace is bestowed. And therefore, he ought to flourish in sanctity, as they say, which he provides to others. And this was precisely decreed in the chapter *Quaesitum*. However, the power of jurisdiction must be judged differently.

<margin>Solution to the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ The remaining arguments only prove that there is a certain decency <note>A moral appropriateness or fittingness.</note> that he who judges others should behave in the way he wishes his subjects whom he condemns to be. And therefore, it will perhaps be a venial <note>A lesser, pardonable sin.</note> sin when a sinner condemns a sinner. For, as we said above, to do what is just not out of the "habit" of justice is not a sin, if it is done out of an affection for the same virtue and through its act. And although a sinner lacks "infused" justice <note>Justice given directly by God's grace.</note>, he can nonetheless have "acquired" justice <note>Justice developed through human habit and practice.</note>. But it will be a venial sin because when someone judges another, he professes himself to be clean of the crime; and therefore, if he is not so, he is in a way a hypocrite, whom Christ rebukes there: "Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not see the beam in your own eye?" <note>original: "Quid vides festucā in oculo fratris tui, & trabē in oculo tuo nō vides?"</note>

<margin>The final proposition.</margin>
¶ The final proposition of Saint Thomas is that a public sinner who condemns others sins mortally because of the scandal caused; for then justice falls into contempt among the people. Indeed, the person who sees it perceives that the law does not have the same force over the judge as that which the judge exercises over his subjects.

<margin>The reasoning.</margin>
But truly, although by its nature this sin is mortal, it can nonetheless become venial due to the lightness of the matter. And for this reason, Saint Thomas added: "if it be regarding more serious crimes," and especially if it be regarding similar ones—for instance, if the judge were himself a public thief, yet he nevertheless prosecuted petty thieves; or if he committed public acts of adultery, yet he nonetheless weighed down other adulterers with judgment. For if he were, for example, a fornicator, but he avenged robberies and homicides, it would not be a mortal scandal; indeed, when the crime is not infamous, there would be no scandal at all—as in the case where, out of greed, he was not as charitable with alms as he ought to be.

### ARTICLE III.

-> Whether rash judgment—namely, <-
-> that which proceeds from suspicion—is lawful. <-

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
<note>The source includes a decorative drop cap 'I' with floral and architectural motifs.</note>
In the preceding articles, we disputed the judgment of a judge and how it is rendered lawful. In this article, it follows that we must speak concerning unjust judgment, which is accustomed to happen everywhere not only to a public judge but also to all private individuals: namely, whether it is illicit when it proceeds rashly from suspicion. For the arguments for the negative side stand as follows. First: Suspicion seems to be an uncertain opinion regarding some evil.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the 6th book of the *Ethics* that suspicion can relate to both the true and the false. Regarding singular and contingent things <note>events that may or may not happen</note>, we can have no opinion except an uncertain one. Therefore, since human judgment concerning singular and contingent human acts is conceived in this way, if no judgment arising from suspicion were permitted, it would be impossible to judge at all.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
¶ Second: Through every il-

<column-break/>

licit judgment, an injury is inflicted upon another. For since a right judgment is an act of justice, it follows that a corrupt judgment is an act of injustice. However, through a suspicion that remains hidden within the mind, no injury is inflicted upon one's neighbor; therefore, it is not illicit.

<margin>The third argument.</margin>
¶ Third: If judgment based on suspicion were illicit—and thus, as we were just saying, an act of injustice—since injustice is by its nature a mortal sin, it would follow that every rash judgment would be, by its nature, a lethal crime.

<margin>The Gloss.</margin>
Yet the consequence is false; for as the Gloss of Augustine <note>A standard medieval commentary featuring Saint Augustine’s views</note> holds regarding that passage in 1 Corinthians 4, "Judge not before the time": we cannot avoid suspicions. Therefore, judgment based on suspicion is not illicit.

<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, the Doctors unanimously confess along with Chrysostom, regarding that passage in Matthew 7, "Judge not," etc., where he says: the Lord by this command does not forbid Christians from correcting others out of benevolence, but rather that Christians should not despise other Christians through the boasting of their own righteousness, hating and condemning others based for the most part only on suspicions.

<margin>A useful foundation for resolving the question.</margin>
This question is of primary importance and necessary for human understanding and practice. Therefore, in order to define it clearly, it must be observed that "rash judgment" is to be evaluated in many ways. First, concerning its own substance: namely, whether you merely doubt the evil of another, or whether you suspect it through an uncertain opinion, or perhaps you deliver a certain sentence. Second, concerning the causes by which you are moved to judge thus. Third, from the conjectures that draw you into such suspicion. And fourth, finally, from the object: namely, from the magnitude of that evil which you attribute to the person being judged. Therefore, to unfold these matters lucidly, let us begin the matter from the very substance of judgment. Thus, although Saint Thomas distinguishes only three, it is worthwhile to discern four degrees of rash judgment so that the discourse may be more clear:

<margin>Four degrees of rash judgment.</margin>
that is, if you include doubt among them. The first is **doubt**, namely when the mind is hanging in balance, giving assent to neither side of the contradiction. For example, if you remain uncertain whether your neighbor is stained by some crime, yet you offer no assent either to the affirmative or the negative. Therefore, this degree does not reach the point of being a rash judgment, since it carries no judgment within itself. The second degree is **suspicion**, which is the assent of one side...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of judgment, specifically transitioning from the character of the judge to the psychological and moral nature of "suspicion" (suspicio) and how it leads to rash judgment.</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>What the name "suspicion" designates.</margin>
...of one side of a contradiction with the fear of the other: what the Dialecticians <note>Logicians who use formal reasoning.</note>, following the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> in the 6th book of the *Ethics*, call "opinion." However, at present, the name "suspicion" implies three things. First, as has been said, an assent with fear; that is, that you agree with one side in such a way that you are not entirely firm, but waver regarding the other. Second, it implies the quality of the object. For although an "opinion" may be indifferent to good or evil, the word "suspicion" in Latin carries a negative connotation. For a person is said to "fall into suspicion" or "suffer from suspicion" when a sinister opinion is conceived or held about them. Indeed, if it concerns something good, it is instead called "good estimation." Third, it implies that this opinion is born from slight causes: for instance, when we have thin conjectures about the secrets of hearts or hidden matters, which cannot generate suspicion by themselves except due to our own flightiness or a tainted mind. Therefore, this enters into the category of <term>rash judgment</term> <note>A judgment made without sufficient evidence, often driven by personal bias.</note>. For rashness is opposed to prudence; and for that reason, it is the same as a judgment conceived thoughtlessly without a legitimate cause.

<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
But truly, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto’s theological legal theory.</note> included these two degrees without distinction under the first category. For he discerns, as we began to say, only three degrees of suspicion. The first of these, he says, is when a man begins to doubt the goodness of someone based on slight evidence. And this, he says, is a <term>venial sin</term> <note>A lesser sin that does not break one's relationship with God, as opposed to a mortal sin.</note>. Nevertheless, there is surely no small gap between "doubting" and "suspecting": for to doubt is to have a suspended mind without any assent; but to suspect, if you listen to the Philosopher in the 6th book of the *Ethics*, is to assent to one side of a contradiction while fearing the other. For we may doubt the certain number of the stars, but we do not "suspect" it. Therefore, Saint Thomas did not observe the rigor of the words so anxiously because, since neither is a mortal sin, the moral judgment of both is the same. And so, whether no assent is held or a fearful one is, he denoted both by the name of doubt and suspicion. Therefore, the third degree, which is held as the second by Saint Thomas, is when someone estimates the malice of another as certain based on slight evidence. And this degree, although Saint Thomas calls it by the general name of "suspicion," is actually more than suspicion. Finally, the fourth degree, which is his third, pertains specifically to the public judge: namely, when from such suspicion, without legitimate witnesses...

<margin>degree.</margin>
<margin>degree.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
...he brings forth a sentence of condemnation against someone. ¶ These things having been established, he answers the question with three conclusions, so that we do not stray from the text of Saint Thomas. First: Suspicion of the first and second kind—joining "doubt" under the name of "suspicion" for the sake of brevity with Saint Thomas—is a sin by its nature; yet it is no worse than venial, unless it proceeds to a mortal sin due to its causes or other factors.

<margin>First proof.</margin>
Indeed, that it is a sin is evident from the fact that everyone enjoys this natural right: that they ought to have a good reputation among all people until legitimate evidence betrays their crimes. Therefore, suspicion of this kind, since it violates such a right to some extent (that is, under doubt), contains some degree of injury—even when you doubt without full assent, as will become more evident below. Add to this that it is also harmful in a way: both because it is the cause of you valuing your neighbor less than is fitting—and there is a danger that you will follow contempt with hatred—and also because it is dangerous in that you might defame him. We will add other causes below.

<margin>Second.</margin>
However, that it is not mortal by its nature is clear from these points: first, because by its nature it does not expel charity; and next, because it pertains to human temptation, without which our life is not led. As the cited <gloss>gloss</gloss> <note>A marginal or interlinear commentary on a text.</note> says regarding 1 Corinthians 4: "Judge not before the time." From which Augustine infers that we can hardly avoid suspicions of this kind. Therefore, it is a lighter fault to hesitate without assent than to suspect through it. ¶ Moreover, that it can become mortal because of its causes is proven as follows.

<margin>The triple root from which all suspicions arise.</margin>
For suspicions of this kind, which legitimate conjectures do not generate, arise in a man for a threefold cause. First, from his own wickedness. For as each person is himself, so does he bring judgment upon others—estimating others, of course, from his own conscience. According to Ecclesiastes 10: "A fool walking on the way, since he is himself unwise, estimates all men to be fools." <note>original: "In via stultus ambulans, cum ipse sit insipiens, omnes stultos aestimat."</note> The second root of such suspicion can be the hatred someone has for another. For there is a huge force by which the will acts upon the intellect to weaken it. For anyone toward whom you are affected by hatred, anger, or envy, you immediately despise; and contempt is a very ready cause for you to easily believe anything sinister about them.

<margin>The Philosopher.</margin>
Finally, the third cause of suspecting in this way is long experience. By which reasoning the Philosopher in the 2nd book of the *Rhetoric* says that old men are exceedingly suspicious because they have many times experienced the defects of men. And although this third cause does not hold as much guilt, because experience...

# Book Three, Question 4
### P 4.

...knowledge increases certainty, which is contrary to the nature of suspicion; nevertheless, it is not free from at least a light fault <note>original: "leui saltem culpa." In Catholic theology, a "light fault" refers to a venial sin, which does not break one's relationship with God but is still a moral error.</note>. However, both of the other prior degrees contain a manifest perversity. And so, the second degree especially often makes suspicion a mortal sin, such as the hatred, envy, or anger that provided its fuel. Whether it can also reach the level of a mortal fault due to the gravity of the object will be disputed immediately.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The Second Conclusion.** Suspicion of the third degree, which Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a Dominican friar and immensely influential philosopher and theologian.</note> placed in the second position, is by its very nature a mortal sin if it concerns a grave matter. This is proven because such a certain assent, if it is rash—that is, emanating from slight evidence—brings no small injury. For as much as someone judges another to be evil with certainty, he cannot help but despise him

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
and consequently hate him. And it is confirmed to be a mortal crime by the fact that suspicion of the first kind is a temptation that we can hardly shake off; yet we can easily avoid the firmness of assent when the conjectures are not very pressing. Hence, Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most important Church Fathers.</note> says in the recorded gloss: "Even if we cannot avoid suspicions because we are human, we must nevertheless restrain our judgments—that is, our definitive and firm opinions." For this reason, such a judgment by its very nature opposes charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the theological virtue of selfless love for one's neighbor.</note>, in which the essence of a mortal crime consists; and it carries, moreover, a certain amount of

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
hidden injustice. ¶ **The Third Conclusion.** Suspicion of the third degree is a most open mortal sin of injustice, and it is all the more grave to the extent that it is more wicked for a judge, who is the guardian of justice, to condemn anyone except by legitimate testimonies.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Concerning these conclusions, although they are true, there is nevertheless a primary doubt: whether they are sufficiently and clearly corroborated by the testimony of the Gospel.

<margin>Reason for the doubt.</margin>
For most of the Doctors <note>High-ranking theological authorities.</note> bring forward for this opinion that passage from Matthew 7: *Judge not, and you will not be judged* <note>original: "Nolite iudicare, & non iudicabimini."</note>. However, this passage is not so very clear for condemning the internal rash judgment that we are currently discussing. For there, the Lord seems only to mark those who, while they themselves are entangled in greater crimes, rebuke their neighbors for smaller ones. For it follows immediately: *Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, and do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the speck out of your brother's eye.* <note>Matthew 7:3-5.</note> He therefore defames there the hypocrisy of those who, by reproaching others, profess themselves to be rich in virtues which they do not possess. Hence,

<column-break/>

<margin>Jerome</margin>
Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for his translation of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says: "He speaks of those who, while they themselves are liable to a mortal crime, do not grant smaller sins to their brothers: straining out a gnat, but swallowing a camel." <note>original: "culicem quidem liquantes, camelum verò deglutientes." A metaphor for focusing on trivialities while ignoring massive errors.</note> Truly, if you survey the opinions of the Doctors, they all recognize this meaning. Nevertheless, our conclusions against rash judgments apply not only to that sense, but also to this one: that to judge concerning hidden things is a sin in general, even for those who are not

<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
hypocrites, but otherwise upright. Indeed, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an early Church Father known for his preaching. "Opere imperfecto" refers to a commentary once attributed to him but now considered "Pseudo-Chrysostom."</note> in the *Incomplete Work* (if it was that Saint's) says that in that place of the Gospel, "to judge" is taken to mean "to avenge injuries." He asserted this not without reason, if you listen attentively to the words: *Judge not, and you will not be judged.* For these words propose a reward to the one not judging: that he will not be judged. Indeed, if "to judge" were used there, as we wish, for "not to suspect," then the reward would not cohere: namely, that no suspicion will be held against us. For Christ seems to promise something remarkable there: namely, that if we forgive our own injuries, our own will also be forgiven to us. Hence, in Luke they are placed together: *Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven.* <note>Luke 6:37.</note>

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, the conclusion is not only most true, even outside of hypocrisy, but it is asserted in the same place.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
For although Augustine allows other interpretations, nevertheless, as the expositor in Book 2 of *The Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*, he also gladly admits this one. For he says that it is commanded there that we should interpret those deeds which are doubtful as to what spirit they were done in the better part <note>original: "in meliorem partem." This is a legal and moral principle: when an action is ambiguous, one should assume the best possible intention.</note>. Moreover, the words themselves—*Judge not, and you will not be judged*—show this. For to judge includes condemnation. Therefore, Christ exhorts us that we should condemn no one, lest we ourselves be condemned in the final judgment. Indeed, if we abstain from this judgment, we may earn mercy.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
And that passage in Romans 14 is added: *Let not him who does not eat judge him who eats.* <note>original: "Qui non manducat, manducantem non iudicet." Romans 14:3.</note> Where not only hypocrites who are in greater crimes, but also everyone who is otherwise upright is prohibited from judging; for that is what "let him who does not eat not judge" sounds like. And so that he might denote the connection of these things, which are "to judge" and "to despise," he first said: *Let him who eats not despise him who does not eat*; and finally he added: *And let him who does not eat not judge him who eats.* Although not without cause did he say "despise" in the first place, and "judge" in the second, as I noted in that place...

F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right <note>original: *de Iustitia & Iure*. Francisco de Soto was a Spanish Dominican theologian of the School of Salamanca.</note>

...us. <meta>translator note: the word finishes a thought on judging others, likely "despismus" or similar, regarding despising others.</meta> Finally, the same sense is found in 1 Corinthians 4: *Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:5</note> Where he designates the reason why you should not judge: not just because you yourself may be a sinner, but because those things you take as certain and clear are actually uncertain and obscure. Therefore, the conclusion is supported not only by the reasons we have drawn from the nature of things, but also by the divine oracles.

<margin>Three things are required for a rash judgment to be a mortal sin</margin>
¶ There remain, however, minor doubts regarding each conclusion. First, concerning the second conclusion, which asserted that rash judgment is by its nature a mortal sin, it must be noted that three things are required for this. First, that it be certain; second, that it be gathered from slight conjectures; and third, that it concerns a grave matter. Now, "certain judgment" implies only one condition in theoretical matters: namely, that it has absolutely no mixture of fear or ambiguity, which pertains to science and both human and divine faith. In moral matters, however, a small doubt is considered as nothing. Therefore, when you are so firm in your opinion that you hardly doubt at all, you are considered to judge as if with certainty, and for that reason, you sin mortally—provided, however, that such a judgment is not a sudden impulse, which must certainly be weighed even in moral conduct. Indeed, if when you see a young man talking with a girl without witnesses, you are suddenly seized by a judgment, there is no reason to fear mortal guilt; it is when you confirm the same opinion through deliberation with a calmed mind and after reflection. Regarding the "slightness" of causes that make the guilt mortal, no certain rule can be established.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
And indeed, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s School of Salamanca.</note> in his response to the first point seems to approve no other causes excusing judgment from guilt except when someone is proven evil through suitable witnesses; for then, he says, one can lawfully judge another to be evil. But this must be understood in respect to a judge <note>Meaning a formal official in a court of law.</note>, who ought not to wait for absolute evidence of the fact, but for human certainty, which is held through suitable witnesses; without this, however, he must by no means rush to a sentence. Nevertheless, even without such testimonies, anyone—whether a judge or a private person—can be excused from guilt even while forming a certain judgment in his own mind. For it is attributed to the praise of Solomon in 3 Kings 3 <note>1 Kings 3 in modern Bibles.</note> that from the words of the women—one of whom agreed to have the child cut in half, while the other refused—he drew out a judgment as to which of them

<column-break/>

had given birth to the boy. Yet, he did not punish the other woman on account of such a judgment, but rather handed the child over to the true mother. Therefore, no rule can be given more certain than this: those conjectures and signs excuse one from guilt which would lead a prudent and honest man to judge in such a way. If I see a man climbing through windows with a ladder at night, I can certainly judge him to be evil without any guilt. If you see a youth and a girl petulantly embracing in a secret and dark place, there is no guilt in forming an unfavorable judgment about them.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For as Aristotle is the authority in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle’s *De Anima*.</note>: We can think when we want, but we cannot "opine" <note>In this context, to *opinari* means to form a belief based on evidence; Soto argues that once the evidence is seen, the mind is naturally drawn to a conclusion.</note> at will; that is, abstaining from judgment is not always in our power. Although a judge, even if he may conceive such a judgment as a private man without guilt, ought not to proceed to punishment based on it—just as Solomon did not proceed to punishment. However, a prince or a prelate may abstain from appointing such a suspect person to a magistracy or the administration of the Church. Thus, the lighter the conjectures are, all else being equal, the more the sin increases; and the weightier they are, the more the sin is diminished. And from this, it follows again that sometimes it cannot be certainly defined whether a judgment is mortal or venial.

<margin>The rule of the Summists is not universal.</margin>
¶ In the same way, one must judge the gravity of that evil which you inflict upon another by judging him. For the "Summists" <note>Authors of *Summae Casuum*, practical handbooks for confessors to determine the severity of sins in confession.</note> consider a judgment to be about a grave evil only when someone judges another to be in mortal sin. But although this rule is mostly true, it is not entirely certain; rather, one must look to the "infamy" <note>Infamia: the social and legal loss of reputation.</note>. For from that, the gravity of the judgment is weighed. Therefore, where a sin would not be so infamous, judging someone to be in it would not be mortal; for example, if you easily and certainly judged courtiers or other profligate youths to be carrying on shameful affairs with loose women, or that a soldier had killed another in a duel. For they are in no way ashamed of having committed these things. Conversely, although that evil might not be a sin, but something natural, a judgment could nonetheless be a crime—for instance, if you certainly judged, for a slight reason, that a man of eminent rank and reputation was born of "infamous blood" <note>Meaning of low-status or socially stigmatized ancestry.</note>. For in this, you would also gravely injure him. Therefore, no certain rule can be established for this either, but one must consider whether the evil is such that the other would be more distressed to hear it said of himself than if it were a mortal sin.

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
¶ From these points, let us then take a step back

For St. Thomas seems to feel this way, and Cajetan feels so as well, saying that no judgment short of certainty is anything but a minor fault <note>original: "veniale," or venial sin.</note>. Furthermore, however, reason seems to persuade us of the contrary: for although that should deservedly be held as a rule, an exception must nonetheless be made when you suspect a most serious evil regarding a most honorable person. For moral rules are not to be weighed with
<margin>The Solution.</margin>
metaphysical rigor, but according to the magnitude of the injury. And in truth, if you consult the judgment of prudent men, you inflict more injury upon Peter if you think with dread that he is incestuous with his mother, daughter, or sister, than if you certainly believed him to be an ordinary fornicator. You would despise him much more vilely if he came under suspicion of heretical depravity, or treason against the state, or some other monstrous crime, than someone whom you certainly believed to be ensnared in lesser crimes.

<margin>
The final doubt.
</margin>
¶ Finally, the last doubt concerns the person who doubts another's goodness without giving full assent—a situation we included under the category of minor sin in the first conclusion. For no reason for this opinion is apparent, since that person delivers no judgment of evil. On the contrary, it should rather be attributed to virtue that someone keeps their mind suspended when certain conjectures point to a neighbor's guilt.
<margin>The Response.</margin>
The response is nonetheless that, although it is not as great a fault as suspecting, and indeed often—where conjectures lean toward a bad judgment—it is praiseworthy to suspend judgment: nevertheless, the reasons can be so slight that even that suspension of the mind is a fault. For, as we said above, everyone has a right not only that no sinister suspicion be held about them, but that everyone holds a good opinion of them. And this is confirmed by the fact that surely if you were to take away the good opinion from Peter, who already holds a good opinion of John, you would be doing wrong; therefore, it is an evil for you also to hold yourself merely negatively toward your neighbor for a very slight cause. Indeed, it could sometimes be a serious sin. For who would doubt that if, seeing the holiness and most upright life of John the Baptist or the most holy Virgin—to say nothing of God's son—people were to doubt their goodness, they would commit a grave sin? In truth, this should not be called into doubt.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to the first argument, it has already been answered that although human judg-

<column-break/>

ment cannot be entirely certain about individual matters, everyone can nonetheless, in a human fashion—that is, while there are suitable testimonies—judge poorly of another without committing an injury. ¶ To the second,

<margin>A small question regarding the matter of the second argument.</margin>
matter may be more clearly open, let us examine the causes of the malice of such internal judgment: whether, when it is certain in its kind, it is a serious sin in itself. For the negative side seems
<margin>The negative side is argued.</margin>
true because, since the neighbor suffers no detriment through it, neither in his person nor in his affairs, there is no reason why it should be condemned with such a mark.
<margin>The solution of some.</margin>
You may find those responding that it is enough for it to be a serious sin that it is prohibited by God, who by His freedom could prohibit whatever He wished.
<margin>A refutation.</margin>
But these people do not consider that this is not an evil because it is prohibited; rather, it is prohibited because it is an evil. For it is among those things that are against natural law, which Christ only commanded us in the Gospel beyond the sacraments pertaining to religion. Nor is it enough if you respond that the judgment is evil because it relates to external harm, such as defamation. For since it is speculative <note>meaning internal or theoretical</note>, it does not have an immediate relation to action. And therefore it is answered that
<margin>The true solution.</margin>
even if it never went outside, it is a serious sin in itself in its hidden places. First, as we said, because it is a cause of contempt and hatred. Second, it is clear because by it you defame your neighbor within yourself, since you conceive a bad opinion of him. From which follows a third argument for this: for if the sinister suspicion I have of Peter were never a serious sin for me, it would follow that it would not be a sin to spread it into the minds of others, as long as no other damage followed; for if mental suspicion is not a sin for me, neither would their own be for them, and thus it would not be a sin for me to sow it. Which, however, is false. Furthermore, there is the argument that judging hidden things is to usurp what is God’s own, according to that word of Paul: *Who are you to judge another’s servant?* <note>Romans 14:4</note>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether internal suspicion constitutes a mortal sin. ...[if justice] concerns external operations, then suspicious judgment pertains directly to injustice when it proceeds to an external act: and then, he says, it is a mortal sin <note>original: "peccatum mortale," a grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace in Catholic theology.</note>. He adds, however, that internal judgment pertains to injustice insofar as it is compared to external judgment, just as an internal act relates to an external one: for example, as lust relates to fornication, and anger to homicide. Therefore, this text remains obscure and consequently doubtful, because he does not clearly state that a judgment which does not proceed to external actions is a mortal sin. Nevertheless, it must undoubtedly be held that such a judgment is, by its nature, a mortal sin, and that against justice.

<margin>St. Thomas is explained.</margin>
St. Thomas distinguishes those two parts: that the commanding judgment of an external act—namely, of defaming or condemning—is directly against justice, as expressed in the third conclusion. Just as an effective will to kill is reduced to homicide, so a speculative judgment <note>A judgment made in the mind without the immediate intent to act upon it.</note> by which no external work is commanded does not pertain directly to external injustice. And in these lies the difference: namely, "directly" and "indirectly." But it is nonetheless a mortal sin, as was said in the second conclusion. Just as anger or lust for another's wife with consent to the pleasure is mortal, even if it does not proceed to the act. Indeed, not only is the effective will to kill mortal, but also the internal desire for a neighbor's death or serious harm, even if you do not wish to cause those damages yourself.

# ARTICLE IV.

->Whether doubts should be interpreted in the<-
->better part.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a detailed landscape scene with a stone bridge over a river, buildings, and trees under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>
<margin>The first argument from the negative side.</margin>
It is not enough to know that rash judgment is iniquitous; rather, we must explore whether we ought always to interpret doubts in the better part <note>That is, to assume the best about someone's intentions or actions when they are unclear.</note>. And the argument is made from the negative side. Since judgment is a work of reason, the perfection of which consists in truth, it ought rather to be passed on those things which happen most often, so that we are less frequently deceived. But it happens more often that men act wickedly than rightly: for since the senses of man are prone to evil from his youth, as read in Genesis 8, it follows that, as held in Ecclesiastes 1, the number of fools is infinite. Therefore, it is more advisable to interpret doubts for the worse than for the better.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: He lives piously and justly, according to Au-

<column-break/>

gustine, who is an impartial judge <note>original: "integer æstimator," one who evaluates things fairly without bias.</note> of things, leaning toward neither side. But he who decides a doubtful matter in the healthier part <note>The more favorable interpretation.</note> leans toward one side: therefore, this is by no means permitted.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: A man ought to love his neighbor in the same way he loves himself. But concerning oneself, it is healthier to judge doubts for the worse, according to that saying in Job 9: *I feared all my works*. Therefore, we ought to conduct ourselves toward our neighbor in the same way.

¶ On the contrary, however, is that which is said in Romans 14: <margin>Paul.</margin> *Let him who does not eat not judge him who eats*; the commentary <note>original: "glossa," referring to the standard medieval biblical commentary, the Glossa Ordinaria.</note> on which says that doubts are to be interpreted in the better part.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
This article is so closely connected to the previous one that it is largely understood through it. Therefore, the answer is given in a single conclusion gathered from the preceding points. Wherever manifest signs do not appear which indicate the neighbor's evil, we must have a good estimation of everyone, and thus interpret that which is doubtful in the better part.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion, I say, is gathered from the preceding. Everyone has a right to have a good estimation held of them everywhere, until their crimes legitimately betray them. Therefore, he who conceives a sinister opinion of another without fit testimony is injurious to that person, and thus we are bound to decide ambiguous signs in the better part.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ The conclusion requires no dispute beyond the previous one, unless you perhaps inquire whether we are bound to interpret doubts in the better part *positively*—that is, to assent to the better part—or if it is enough *negatively*—that is, simply not to judge poorly. Indeed, when some external ambiguous signs of another's vice appear, it is surely difficult to have a contrary assent. But if you say it is enough to suspend the mind, a counter-argument immediately emerges: that it is also difficult to restrain the intellect.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
¶ Cajetan here thinks it is enough that we hold a negative position. Nevertheless, I would not dare to advise anyone of this. Indeed, a certain rule can hardly be established, but one must flee to prudence <note>original: "prudentia," the virtue of practical wisdom or right judgment.</note>.

<margin>Solution of the proof.</margin>
I say we must first distinguish whether you previously knew the one whose doubtful signs
<margin>of the doubt.</margin>
appear, or if he is unknown to you. For if he is held in good estimation by you, it would be a sin to change that on account of those doubtful signs—either a greater or lesser sin according to the nature of the signs. But if you do not know him, then Cajetan argues here that it is not prudent in such a case to conceive an assent to the better part, because those neutral signs by their nature do not generate such an assent: and therefore, he says, there is none...

### Book Three, Question IV.

<margin>Refutation of Cajetan.</margin>
...there is an obligation to give a good assent. For this reason, he [Cajetan] says that Christ deliberately spoke in the negative, saying: "Do not judge" <note>original: "Nolite iudicare," from Matthew 7:1.</note>, and did not say, "always judge well." However, I would sooner believe the contrary, and I would respond to him that even if such conjectures do not produce a "good assent" <note>A firm belief based on evidence.</note>, the law of nature nevertheless compels us not only to avoid thinking ill of any man because of doubtful signs, but even to think well of everyone, notwithstanding ambiguous indicators. Therefore, the conclusion must be understood positively—unless in a case where the evidence so strongly points toward the darker side that it would be enough to avoid assenting to either side. In that case, the counsel is to move the mind away from such thoughts. When, however, the signs are no longer doubtful but are so effective that they would move a prudent and upright man, there is no obligation to interpret them in a better light. Christ, therefore, did not speak negatively because it is enough merely to suspend judgment, but because the good reputation which we are bound by natural law to hold of everyone ought not to be extinguished in us for trivial reasons.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, St. Thomas responds that even if the person who interprets doubts in a better light is more frequently deceived, it is nevertheless better to be deceived more frequently by having a good opinion of some bad man, than to be deceived more rarely by having a bad opinion of some good man: because from the latter, an injury is born; whereas from the former,
<margin>Reply.</margin>
none. But on the contrary: Falsehood is an evil of the intellect—inasmuch as the intellect is born to judge the truths of all things. No one, however, is bound to either procure or incur an evil personal to themselves in order to avoid an evil to their neighbor. Therefore, it seems more advisable to turn one's judgment toward the darker side. 
<margin>Cajetan's solution.</margin>
Cajetan thinks he responds sufficiently to this by saying that St. Thomas does not say absolutely that he who inclines toward the healthier side in judging is deceived in most cases; but rather that he is deceived *more* often than if he leaned toward the darker side. This allows for the possibility that he is not actually deceived "frequently" when judging well. 
<margin>Cajetan is refuted.</margin>
I, however, do not understand this solution. For the force of the argument is satisfied by what he himself concedes with St. Thomas: namely, that we are deceived more often by judging well than we would be by judging poorly. And therefore
<margin>The author’s solution.</margin>
the response is that the good of the moral virtues is not to be weighed according to the good of the intellect simply, but in relation to acting, the immediate principle of which is the "appetite" <note>In this context, the "appetite" refers to the faculty of the will or desire that leads to action.</note>. For a man, as we said above, is not called "good" because of his intellectual virtues considered absolutely,

<column-break/>

but because of his moral virtues, which are concerned with actions. From this it follows that sometimes a false speculative judgment <note>An abstract belief about a fact that happens to be wrong.</note> produces a true practical dictate <note>A correct decision on how to behave morally.</note>. For instance, Jacob, from that false premise—"This is Rachel"—inferred that true conclusion: "This woman is to be known by me" <note>Referring to the biblical story where Jacob is tricked into marrying Leah instead of Rachel. Though he was factually wrong about who his bride was, his intent to fulfill his marital duty was morally correct.</note>. This was indeed true because of "invincible ignorance" <note>A legal and theological term for ignorance that a person cannot overcome by reasonable diligence, thus removing their guilt.</note>. Therefore, while I judge Peter to be good, even if I am deceived speculatively, nevertheless, because the judgment is conformed to a righteous appetite, it results in being morally—and thus simply—good. For this reason, when a man informs the judgment of the intellect according to a moral rule, he does not choose an "evil" in an absolute sense, but only in a qualified sense <note>original: "secundum quid," meaning in one specific respect (factually), but not in the most important respect (morally).</note>; in an absolute sense, he chooses the "good." For this cause, we said above that judgment is an act of justice (which disposes the soul well toward one's neighbor) rather than an act of the reason which utters it. Wherefore, that response of Cajetan and others does not appear worthy enough to me—namely, that because the lesser of two evils is to be chosen, even if a false opinion is a personal evil, it is nonetheless to be chosen because it is smaller. I say it is not true that it is a "lesser evil" in an absolute sense. For the good of the intellect—namely, intellectual virtue, as we demonstrated above—is absolutely better than the good of the will. But nevertheless, as far as morals are concerned, to form a judgment with the risk of falsehood in order to avoid an injury is not only a "lesser evil"; rather, it is not an evil at all in an absolute sense, but only in a qualified sense: namely, a speculative evil. This is especially true because an error regarding "contingent singulars" <note>Individual, specific facts that could be otherwise, as opposed to universal truths like "2+2=4."</note> is not an absolute evil of the intellect, just as it does not pertain to its perfection to know their truths in an absolute sense, but rather the truths of universals, which cannot be subject to falsehood—as St. Thomas says immediately in his solution to the second point. Add to this that such an evil is not even "chosen." For when judgments are clear, it is not prudence to form a "good" judgment; but when they are doubtful, it is only true that the intellect is *exposed* to the danger of falsehood. 
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
To the second argument, it is responded that the reasoning for judging *things* is different from the reasoning for judging *persons*. For when we judge things speculatively, no harm threatens our neighbor; for that reason, truth is then to be investigated simply, which is the good of the intellect. And likewise, in doubtful matters, judgment must be suspended, lest you throw the intellect into the precipice of falsehood. And of this, 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine speaks. When, however, the judgment is about persons, then—because the "good" and "evil" are weighed according to the person being judged—namely, regarding their honor...
