or contempt, we ought to be more attentive to avoid injury quickly. This is especially true because an error regarding particulars <note>Specific, individual cases or circumstances.</note>, as we were just saying, is not directly opposed to the good of the intellect in its simple sense. From these points, gather the prudence by which you discern that a purely speculative judgment of a matter is not a moral sin, unless you apply it to a specific person. For instance, while you might see the corpse of a slain man and judge that it was a mortal sin to kill him, or when you hear a proposition that is heretical and judge that it was a sin to assert it from the heart, you commit no sin yourself. You only commit a sin when, without a legitimate cause, you judge *this specific man* to have been either a murderer or a heretic.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The third argument demands a very excellent rule by which it may be answered. To interpret something in a worse light—namely, by suspecting it based on slight evidence—happens in two ways: either definitively or by way of supposition. The first way is what we say is illicit. The second way, however, does not involve defining a final sentence, but acting on a supposition, "if by chance it is so." This is done not to cause harm, but to meet a danger to oneself or one’s neighbor; this is a work of prudence, not injustice. You see a man whose clothing suggests he is a thief; although you ought not to believe this with a definitive judgment, nor suspect him for the purpose of doing him harm, it is nevertheless permitted to you not to trust him with your house. Similarly, when you have a virgin daughter, it is permitted for you to drive young men away from speaking with her. And in the same way regarding one’s own affairs: while your own works may seem bright in the sight of God—an opinion which is always dangerous—you ought to fear them lest they be infected by some stain. Conversely, to judge the works of others as good offers us no danger.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From these points it follows that even if you suspect ill of someone who is currently being considered for election to some dignity, you could oppose him by keeping your suspicion to yourself. However, to spread that suspicion into the ears of others to splash the man with infamy is by no means lawful, unless the suspicion was certain to you for legitimate reasons and you saw that such an election would lead to the ruin of the commonwealth. In that case, unless it were a secret of sacramental confession, it would be permitted to impede it. And vice versa, your suspicion can be so slight that it ought not even to restrain you from electing him if he is otherwise suitable.

# ARTICLE V.
## *Whether it is always necessary to judge according to written laws.*

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Since judgment, as has been said, is an act of justice, and the rules of justice are the laws, it is rightly asked whether it is always necessary to judge according to written laws. The argument is made for the negative side. Unjust judgment must everywhere be guarded against and avoided, but sometimes written laws contain iniquity; according to Isaiah 10 <note>original: "Væ qui cōdunt leges iniquas..." from Isaiah 10:1.</note>: "Woe to those who decree wicked laws, and the writers who have registered injustices." Therefore, one must not always judge according to written laws.

<margin>Argument 2. Aristotle.</margin>
¶ Second: Judgment must concern individual events. However, a written law, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> testifies in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 10, cannot encompass every individual case. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary to act against the words of the law.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: A law is written so that the mind of the legislator may be made manifest to the subjects. Sometimes, however, it happens that if the legislator were present, he would judge otherwise. Therefore, in such a case, it is permitted to follow the mind of the legislator against the written text.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
¶ On the contrary is the opinion of Augustine in his book *On True Religion* <note>original: "lib. de ver. relig."</note>, where he says: "In these temporal laws, although men judge regarding them when they establish them, once they have been established and confirmed, it will not be permitted for judges to judge them" <note>Meaning judges must apply the law, not sit in judgment of the law itself.</note>.

---

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
We discussed this question fully in Book 1, Question 6, Article 8. But because St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> moves it again appropriately in this present place, it is necessary to respond to the same point, as there will be no lack of things that can be noted here beyond what was defined there. The response is therefore given through a distinction in two conclusions. For it must first be presupposed that judgment is nothing other than a certain definition and constitution of what is just. Now, "the just" is twofold, as has often been said above and as Aristotle teaches in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 7: namely, one is natural, which springs from the nature of things considered absolutely. The other is positive, which the Philosopher calls "legal," namely, that which is established by human agreement and choice.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Let this be the first conclusion: When the written law contains natural right <note>original: "ius naturale".</note>, it is in no way permitted for either the prince or the subjects to act against it, but it is always necessary to judge according to it.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Article 5 of Question 4, regarding whether a judge must always render judgment according to written laws. ### Question 4 of the Third Book

laws of this kind are not constitutive of that justice, but are only <term>declarative<note>A declarative law simply explains or puts into words a principle that is already naturally right (like "do not kill"), whereas a constitutive law creates a new rule for the sake of order (like "drive on the right side of the road").</note></term>. Therefore, the justice of these laws derives its full strength not from the laws themselves, but from the nature of the things themselves. This is evident in the precepts of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and in those things which are implied there by necessary consequence. For this reason, they are so holy and firm that not even God, in his capacity as legislator, can grant a dispensation from them, as we discussed in Book 1, Question 3. However, for this very reason, the question here is not simply whether one must always judge according to laws in general. For concerning natural laws, the light of which God has imprinted on our minds, there is no room for doubt: one must always judge according to them. Instead, the question specifically concerns written laws, among which human laws are numbered.

<margin>The final conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the following conclusion is added. When a written law is human, it is nonetheless necessary for both the prince <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> and the subject to judge according to it, provided it does not conflict with natural law. This is proven because, although such laws are not declarative of natural justice, they are nonetheless <term>constitutive<note>Meaning they establish what is "just" in a specific society by agreement or decree.</note></term> of a justice that has been deemed expedient by human agreement according to the conditions of different regions and times. And so, Aristotle says <note>original: "Arist." referencing the *Nicomachean Ethics*</note> that although before these laws were established it mattered not at all, once they have been established, it does matter.

<margin>Explanation of the above conclusions.</margin>
¶ These conclusions encompass not only lower judges but also the prince himself. He is indeed bound to judge according to the laws—not only the natural ones but also those which he and his ancestors have enacted—as long as no cause arises for them to be changed. However, there is a distinction: lower judges can neither grant dispensations from the laws nor interpret them. Yet, this is within the power of the prince. Thus, in a case where he can grant a dispensation from the law, he can also judge against the letter of the law. For example, if someone condemned to death were extremely useful to the commonwealth, the prince could grant him his life for the sake of that public benefit. All these matters were sufficiently discussed and defined in Book 1, to the best of our ability.

<margin>A theological doubt.</margin>
¶ However, a theological doubt remains to be settled here in its proper place: whether an unjust sentence—that is, one delivered contrary to the laws—is binding in <term>conscience<note>The internal moral judgment of an individual before God.</note></term>. In other words, does it truly absolve a defendant or strip a plaintiff of his right? <margin>The reason for doubting.</margin> There is an argument for the negative side: since the judge is the guardian of justice—to whom, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, people flock as if to a living and speaking justice—and since all these things which are performed in the

<column-break/>

external forum are directed toward the peace of the commonwealth and the quieting of consciences, it seems to follow that a formal sentence by one who holds public authority should render those consciences safe and settled. This is especially true because human law often binds in conscience even where the mere law of nature would not, as is seen in the law of <term>prescription<note>The legal principle where ownership of property is gained by long-term possession, even if the original transfer was flawed.</note></term>, by which ownership is transferred to the possessor.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, the answer is that no sentence delivered against just laws is binding in conscience. This conclusion is manifest and is also admitted by the doctors of law, as can be seen in the writings of Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV, a major canon lawyer</note> and Panormitanus <note>Nicolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century jurist</note> on the chapter "Quia plerique" regarding the immunity of the church. Because a sentence has no strength except insofar as it is a declaration of the law, where it is not an interpreter of right law, it has no standing in conscience. I am speaking of an unjust sentence contrary to the laws—namely, one that takes from one man what was truly his and gives it to another to whom it did not belong. For if something is adjudicated to someone that was truly theirs, even if the other party was deprived of it while the entire legal order was bypassed, the person will possess what was adjudicated to them in good conscience, since it was indeed theirs. The bypassing of the legal order, although it is a sin for the judge and injurious to the party, does not place the person who possesses what is truly theirs in "bad conscience." This is clear from a very simple example: if you either steal back what is yours by fraud or take it by force from a possessor, you may perhaps commit a mortal sin by executing with private authority what you should have done with public authority, but you are not bound to the restitution of what you took.

Let us return, then, to the principal assertion: that an unjust sentence neither takes away nor confers a right. It follows from this that even if you acted in good faith while litigating, as soon as you certainly discover that the sentence delivered in your favor was not just, you are bound to restore what was adjudicated to you. However, you may not be bound to restore the legal expenses if you litigated in good faith, whether you were the defendant or the plaintiff. And I say "unjust" in terms of the truth of the matter, even if the judge decided correctly based on the evidence and proofs presented in the external forum <note>The public court of law</note>.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ But what if the injured party does not appeal? For by that very act, they seem to have consented and thus sent away their own right; therefore, they are not admitted back into court to claim it again.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that even if they did not appeal, they are not deemed to have renounced their right. Rather, they simply suffer the fact that they will no longer be heard in the external forum if they try to claim it again. This truth is confirmed not only by natural reason but also from the law...

# Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>A true argument.</margin> From Julius <note>A reference to the Roman jurist Julius Paulus</note> regarding the **recovery of payments not owed**, it is gathered that those who do not appeal within the prescribed time are thereafter barred from the tribunal. Some say the reason for this is as a penalty for their negligence. I, however, believe it is not only for that reason, but more importantly to put an end to lawsuits; the most holy laws have always been attentive to this goal. But if someone has acquired property through an unjust sentence—whether for themselves or their ancestors—and has held it in good faith for the legally required time through **prescription** <note>Prescription is the legal process by which a person gains ownership of something simply because they have possessed it for a long time without challenge.</note>, they may possess it with a clear conscience from then on. This is because they have a legitimate title—that is, a title presumed by the law.

<margin>Another doubt regarding Ecclesiastical benefits.</margin> ¶ However, a more troublesome doubt arises concerning ecclesiastical **benefices** <note>A "benefice" was a church office, like a priesthood or parish, that provided an income to the holder.</note>: namely, when someone is stripped of a priesthood through an unjust sentence and it is conferred upon another, whether the new possessor may thereafter hold it with a safe conscience. Among others, the legal interpreters Panormitanus <note>The nickname for Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous expert in Church law.</note> (in Chapter 1, <margin>Panormitanus. Innocent. Solution to the doubt.</margin> on the establishment of prebends) and Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV, who was also a major legal scholar.</note> (in the chapter *Because most*, on Church immunity) treat this knowledgeably. We must, therefore, distinguish between types of sentences. One is **declarative**: this is when there is litigation between parties over a right, some other matter, or a prebend, and the sentence declares which of them it belongs to. In such a case, without a doubt—just as in other secular matters—the sentence does not bind the conscience <note>Meaning it does not make an unjust thing "right" in the eyes of God.</note>. Therefore, if the possessor knows it was not just, they are bound to renounce it. The other type is a **privative** sentence: this is when a superior punishes someone with the loss of their priesthood because of a crime and confers it on another. In this case, the aforementioned doctors judge that if the accused does not appeal—because by that very act they seem to consent—the other may possess it with a safe conscience. It is otherwise if the accused does appeal; for then, even if they were unjustly denied a hearing, they are not deemed to have consented. I, however, with all due respect to their reputation, would not believe this so absolutely, but rather with a distinction. If the prelate, I say, knowingly and deliberately condemned the man unfairly, I judge that the sentence does not hold. Therefore, whenever the possessor understands this, they are bound to renounce it, and the prelate is bound to restore it to the other. But if the prelate condemned him in good faith according to **what was alleged and proven** <note>original: "secundùm allegata & probata" — a legal principle that a judge must rule based only on the evidence presented in court, even if they suspect the truth is otherwise.</note>, even if the person was falsely accused, the sentence holds, and thus the other may safely possess it—unless, however, the possessor was the very slanderer who falsely accused him. For in that case, all doctors of Canon Law rightly hold that he is unfit to possess it. Furthermore, I would believe this only regarding ecclesiastical benefices which are conferred by the authority of Prelates. For in other matters, even if the sentence is just according to what was alleged and proved, if it proceeded from a false presumption, it does not bind the conscience, as

<column-break/>

Innocent properly noted in that same chapter *Because most*. It follows that if someone is falsely reported for the name of **heresy** and is deprived of his goods: as soon as the **treasury** <note>original: "fiscus" — the state or royal treasury.</note> learns that he was reported and condemned through **calumny** <note>False and malicious accusation.</note>, it is bound to restore him to the possession of his property. Let these things, therefore, suffice for this matter.

---

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> TO the first argument, therefore, it is responded that just as written law provides no strength to **natural law**—on the contrary, it receives its own force from it—so too it cannot diminish the strength of natural law in any way. For the men who wrote those laws are not the masters of nature. Thus, when a written law opposes natural law, it has no force, and one should not judge according to it. In such cases, they are not considered laws, but **corruptions of laws**. But when a written law is permitted by natural law (namely, because it does not stand in its way), then one must judge according to the laws, even if perhaps it would have been better for the law to have been established differently. This is especially to be noted, as we explained in the place cited above: namely, that it is not necessary for the validity of a written law that what it decrees be "better" than its opposite. This should be weighed and debated when the law is being made; but once it is established and confirmed by use, subjects ought not to judge it, but rather act according to it, until the prince or the republic changes it. Indeed, laws are not to be changed for just any reason that offers a "better" logic. For example, a law is established so that goods are not exported out of the kingdom; perhaps the reason it was established no longer exists. Even so, though it is the prince's duty to change it, it is not permitted for subjects to act against it as long as natural law permits it—unless it begins to be against nature or against religion (for example, if it were to oppose Church laws). ¶ To the second <margin>To the second argument.</margin> argument, a response is given in like manner: that just as a law can sometimes conflict with natural law (and then it is not to be kept), so too, although it may be rightly established, if in particular circumstances it goes against natural law, it is permitted to act against it. For, as **Modestinus** <note>A 3rd-century Roman jurist.</note> says in the Digest (on laws and decrees): no principle of law or kindness of **equity** <note>Equity refers to fairness and justice that looks beyond the strict "letter of the law" to the "spirit of the law."</note> allows us to turn those things which were introduced healthily for the benefit of men into severity through a harsh interpretation. For in such a case, the legislator, if he were present, would judge differently than what he wrote. And by this, the third argument is dissolved.

<summary>This page discusses when human and church laws bind a person's conscience, arguing that while laws should generally be followed for social order, they lose their authority if they directly contradict natural law or are based on malicious false accusations.</summary>

# Book Three, Question IV.

### ARTICLE VI.
### Whether a usurped judgment is always perverse.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' at the start of the section 'TRIA'.</image-desc>

WE HAVE STATED ABOVE that three things are required for a right judgment: namely, the authority of the judge, the equity of justice, and the order of prudence. Regarding this third requirement—that is, the order and process of the law—it is of no concern to the Theologian, but is a matter for the lawyers. Therefore, since the second requirement was discussed in the preceding articles, it follows that we should dispute the first: Whether a usurped judgment—that is, one delivered by someone who <margin>First argument.</margin> is not a judge—is in every case perverse. And it is argued from the negative side. Justice is a certain rectitude of things to be done; however, nothing is lost to the truth regardless of who pronounces it, but truth is to be embraced from whoever speaks it. Therefore, a sentence does not obstruct justice regardless of <margin>Argument 2.</margin> who proferred it. ¶ Second: A good part of judgment is to punish sins. Yet, several private individuals are mentioned with praise who took vengeance for the sins of others: such as *Moses* who, as we read in *Exodus 2*, slew the Egyptian; and *Phineas* the son of *Eleazar* who killed *Zimri*, as written in *Numbers 25*. This, as held in *Psalm 105* <note>The source text says Psalm 115, but this is likely a typographical error in the original for Psalm 106/105:31.</note>, was credited to him as righteousness. Therefore, it is lawful for private persons to judge without public authority. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third: Spiritual power, which is distinguished from temporal power, sometimes interposes itself to judge secular persons. Therefore, a usurped <margin>Paul.</margin> judgment is not everywhere wicked. ¶ To the contrary is that saying in *Romans 14*: "Who are you to judge another man’s servant?"

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> TO the question, it is answered with a single conclusion. A usurped judgment—that is, one proferred without legitimate authority over the person against whom it is delivered—is not only <margin>Proof.</margin> perverse, but also void. It is proven thus: Judgment is the application of the law to persons with coercive force. However, this cannot happen without public authority. Therefore, if it is done otherwise, it is flawed and null. The minor premise is proven: It belongs to the same person to establish the law as it does to interpret and declare it. But the application of the law to persons is a type of interpretation—that is, a declaration—that such a person in such a case is bound. Therefore, just as the law can only be established by one who possesses public authority to compel the citizens, so also is it the right of that person alone, or one holding their authority, to declare the law. The conclu-

<column-break/>

-sion is clear, and was decided in the first book, question 1.
¶ However, it must be noted here that among those things required for a right public judgment, the first is the authority of the judge. For even if other things are lacking—namely, prudence and justice—sometimes the sentence holds, at least while it is delivered according to what is alleged and proven (as we were just saying), and it is always to be feared. And yet, if it emanates from someone who is not a judge, it is so utterly void that it is not even to be feared. Hence <margin>Gregory.</margin> *Gregory* <note>Pope Gregory I, the Great.</note> says skillfully: "The sentence of the pastor, whether just or unjust, is to be feared" (Question 11, Case 3). For he posits two conditions for it to be feared even if it is unjust: namely, that it is the sentence "of a pastor," and that it is a "sentence"—that is, one that does not contain a manifest and intolerable error. ¶ From this it follows first that one who <margin>First corollary.</margin> has occupied a kingdom through tyranny can neither establish any law nor declare the law in any way that binds the citizens in conscience, unless perhaps they eventually become legitimate princes through prescription <term>prescription: the legal gaining of a right or title through long-term use or possession</term> or the consent of the commonwealth, as we read regarding the Franks among the Gauls, and the Goths among the Spaniards. ¶ Second, it <margin>Second.</margin> follows that once a person has legitimately obtained a magistracy, even if they later commit a crime for which they deserve to be deposed, nevertheless their sentence binds until they are deprived of office by the order of law, unless they are excommunicated *ipso facto* <note>Latin: "by the very fact."</note>. For example, although a magistrate may have committed the crime of treason, for which he ought to be expelled from his office by right, his sentence nonetheless holds until he is juridically deprived. It is otherwise if he were a heretic; for then he is excommunicated by the very fact, and thus, although not deprived of the office itself, he is suspended from its function.
<margin>Doubt concerning arbitrary judges.</margin> ¶ Perhaps someone might doubt regarding arbitrators: for their judgment binds both in the external court and in conscience. Yet they seem to possess no public authority, because they have only what they received from the parties—which, however, was only private power. <margin>Solution.</margin> It is answered that they have public authority in a certain way. For since everyone is bound to keep faith with another, it is established by the law of nations <term>law of nations: "ius gentium," the customary laws common to all people</term> that those who have been appointed as mediators by parties have the power to bind through their sentence, although the execution of it belongs to the prince and his ministers, who possess coercive force.

For it is read that when he had seen an Egyptian striking one of the Hebrews, he killed him. Wherefore, since he caught that Egyptian in the very act of the crime, he could have killed him by way of defense: for everyone has the right to repel force with force, not only for <margin>Ambrose.</margin> oneself, but for one's brother. And in this way, Ambrose, in his book *On Duties*, excuses Moses from fault. But if he had already ceased striking the Hebrew, or if the killing was not necessary for defense, it must be said that he killed him for vengeance. And indeed, the history seems to favor this latter view more gracefully. But in that case, since he did not have public authority, he cannot be excused from fault: unless it is said that he did it by divine revelation. And this reasoning seems to be approved by that passage in Acts 7: that by striking the Egyptian, Moses thought his brothers would understand that the Lord through his hand would give salvation to Israel. And although it is not expressly said that God commanded that striking, but rather that Moses thought he would save the people in that way, nevertheless, the striking certainly seems to be excused there; therefore, either of these solutions can be very well defended. But truly, St. <margin>St. Thomas. Augustine.</margin> Thomas—a most faithful follower of Augustine—seems more willingly to embrace him, who in his *Questions on Exodus* does not excuse Moses from fault, but rather compares him to a most fertile fallow field, which when it is first tilled, is praised for its luxuriance and the fertility of its useless weeds, because of the hope it promises of a future harvest. <note>Augustine’s metaphor suggests that Moses' early violent zeal, while technically a "weed" (a sin), showed that his spirit was "fertile soil" ready for God's future work.</note> And thus he interprets that passage in Acts 7: that since his soul was full of desire to liberate the people, he judged by that reasoning that he would accomplish the task. ¶ Finally, in response to the third <margin>To the third argument.</margin> argument, it is said that since spiritual power stands above secular power, an ecclesiastical prelate can compel secular persons by judgment in those things which pertain to grace and to glory.

# QUESTION FIVE,
## On the division of Justice.

->St. Thomas [Summa Theologica] II-II, question 61.<-

### ARTICLE I.

*Whether particular Justice is correctly divided into distributive and commutative.*

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate foliate patterns and scrolls.</image-desc>
AFTER WE HAVE DISCOURSED on Justice in general, and on its contrary, injustice, and on its related matters—namely right and judgment—as much as the subject required, it remains for us to descend to that most famous division of it, by which it is divided into distributive and commutative justice. <note>Distributive justice concerns how a community divides goods among its members; commutative justice concerns fair dealings and exchanges between individuals.</note> This is therefore the fifth question in the order of this book: whether particular justice is correctly divided into distributive and commutative. This question will be settled in four articles. The first of these teaches the reason for the division; the second, the "mean" or middle ground of each; the third, the diversity of their subject matter; and finally, the fourth, their form. From the negative side of the question, <margin>First argument.</margin> it is argued first: Since there are three orders of the state—namely of the whole to the parts, of the parts to the whole, and of the parts among themselves—it would be more beautiful and closer to the art of the subject if there were an equal three-part division: namely into "legal" justice, which establishes the first order; and "distributive," which looks to the second; and "commutative," which concerns the third. Therefore, a two-part division is ineptly made. ¶ Second, it is argued: If there were <margin>Argument 2.</margin> any reason for this division, it would either arise from the fact that they have distinct subjects: namely, that distributive justice is in the prince, upon whom it is incumbent to distribute public goods, while commutative is in the subjects, whose peace and tranquility are maintained by this reason—that each person preserves the right of others. For this distinction seems at first glance to be suggested by this division. But in truth, every species of justice is as much in the subjects as in the prince—specifically in the prince for the purpose of governing, and in the subjects so that they may be governed, as was said in Question 1 regarding legal justice. For commutative justice is in everyone by the same reasoning; therefore, the reason for the division cannot be taken from this difference. But if you say the difference is taken from the fact that distributive justice is weighed in relation to the many, for whom...

### Book Three, Question V

<margin>Argument 3.</margin> distribution must be made among many, whereas commutative justice is from one person to another. On the contrary, it is argued that one and many do not change the species of an action. For a single human being is of the same species whether compared to two or to three others. ¶ Then, it is argued thirdly that the division is incomplete. For vindictive justice <note>Vindictive justice refers to "punitive justice"—the legal system of punishing crimes.</note> seems to be included under neither distributive nor commutative justice. For if you answer that it is contained under distributive because a prince decrees punishments for the wicked just as he decrees rewards for the upright, the opposite is true: both because a private person can lawfully seek vengeance, and also because vengeance ought to be carried out according to the equality of the crime, which is the duty of commutative justice. But if, overcome by this reasoning, you say it belongs to commutative justice, this reasoning seems to protest that it is the duty of the prince alone to exact punishments for faults, which carries the appearance of distributive justice.

<margin>Aristotle</margin> ¶ On the contrary is the authority of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, distinguishing two species of justice, one of which directs distributions, and the other commutations <note>Commutations refer to exchanges, contracts, and dealings between individuals.</note>.

<margin>Responsive Conclusion.</margin> So that the answer to the question may become clearer, let us proceed from the exposition of the terms. Since justice in general, according to Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, is the virtue by which each person is called "just," it follows that according to their names, distributive justice is called that particular justice by which a person is just in the distribution of common goods. Commutative justice, likewise, is that particular justice by which each person is just in exchanges. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> These things being easily understood, the answer is given with the following affirmative conclusion. Particular justice is by its own nature dissected into these two members, differing in species, which are commutative and distributive. This is the conclusion of Aristotle in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 2, and is therefore supported by his authority. It is proved nonetheless by reason. The distinction of habits <note>A "habit" in scholastic philosophy is a settled disposition or character trait, like a virtue.</note>, if it is specific, is derived from the nature of the objects: for habits are distinguished by their acts, and acts by their objects. Now, in a republic <note>original: "republica". Here meaning any organized political community or state.</note> in which justice establishes equity, there is a two-fold order, which is both particular and diverse: namely, that of the whole to the parts, and that of the parts among themselves. Therefore, through these two orders, two species of justice are also discerned. That which is of the whole to the parts—for example, that which distributes common goods well among the citizens—is called distributive. The other, which preserves equity between the parts, is named commutative. They are therefore two distinct species. But although this conclusion is the clear confession not only of St. Thomas but also of Aristotle, there are not lacking interpreters of Aristotle who <margin>Buridan's opinion.</margin> think the opposite. For Buridan <note>Jean Buridan (c. 1300–1361), a French priest and influential philosopher.</note>, in

<column-break/>

the same passage (Ethics, Question 7), does not think these virtues differ in species. Nor does he use any argument at all except that the reasons for the opposite side, he says, are not sufficiently valid. However, this line of argument ought not to move any philosophical person against Aristotle, unless he himself relied on stronger ones. Furthermore, this reasoning shown here abundantly demonstrates the point in moral philosophy, from which a mathematical demonstration is not to be expected, as Aristotle taught immediately at the beginning of the *Ethics*.

<margin>Second reason against Buridan.</margin> ¶ It is argued secondly for the same conclusion. The duty of justice is to render to each what is owed (*debitum*). Now, the nature of what is "owed" is different in distributive justice from that which is in commutative justice; therefore, the virtues themselves differ in species. The minor premise is clear. A thing is said to belong to a person in two ways. In one way, simply, because it is his own private possession. In the other way, "in a certain respect" <note>original: "secundum quid"</note>, as they say: namely, because it is not his own private property, except insofar as it belongs to the whole of which the person is a part. For indeed, those things that belong to the whole belong in a certain way to the parts. And from these arises a different reason for the debt: one reason, because the thing was the creditor's own property; another reason, because it belonged to the whole republic. Therefore, since commutative justice is concerned with a debt of the latter kind, and distributive justice with the former, it follows that they are different virtues.

<margin>Third reason for the same.</margin> ¶ And from this second argument, a third is formed. There is a need for a distinct species of virtue where the difficulty of acting is also distinct in species. But we experience one level of difficulty in pouring out common goods, which a prince has in his power and which never belonged to the citizens, and another in paying back those things we have received from others. Therefore, distinct virtues are required. The minor premise is clear: for that each should return what he received from another, reason and natural inclination immediately plead: "It was not yours, but another gave it to you; you would be the worst of men if you did not return it." However, when a prince or the dispensers of common goods have those goods in their possession, they can only be brought with the greatest difficulty to distribute them if they can usurp them for themselves. Furthermore, long experience teaches us this in princes and <margin>Confirmation.</margin> officials. And this reasoning is confirmed by the authority of Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> in the 2nd book of the *Politics*, saying that men are more prone to be affected toward their own goods than toward common ones. Therefore, distributive justice is one virtue, and commutative is another.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book Three, Question V, regarding the classification of justice. The previous page established the primary division of justice by Aristotle. # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

Since justice is a good, and it is primarily divided into common and particular, it follows that justice is first of all divided by Aristotle into legal justice—which is universal—and particular justice. Thus, legal justice is that which regards the order of the parts to the whole, directing citizens toward the common good; whereas particular justice is concerned with particular goods. And it is this particular justice which is further divided 
<margin>A scruple <note>original: "Scrupulus"; a scholastic term for a lingering doubt or minor difficulty in an argument.</note>.</margin>
into distributive and commutative. But does distributive justice not also deal with the common good? 
<margin>The solution.</margin>
The answer is that although it deals with the common good, it does not have it as its object in the same way as legal justice, which seeks to increase it. Rather, the matter of distributive justice is to distribute and spread those goods among individual citizens. And because a habit is named after the end toward which it tends <note>original: "habitus denominatur à termino ad quẽ"</note>—just as heating is named for the heat that is produced, not the cold that is expelled—distributive justice is considered "particular," insofar as it makes common goods particular. Legal justice, conversely, directs particular things toward the common good. Furthermore, just as legal justice exists not only in the prince for the sake of ruling, but also in the subjects for the sake of obeying; so too distributive justice exists among the citizens, so that they may be content without complaining. Besides this, it can also happen that a private person, such as the head of a large family, might use it to distribute his own goods among his household. 
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second argument, which sought the root of the difference between these species, it has been sufficiently answered by what has been said. For this difference is gathered neither from the perspective of the subject, nor from the perspective of number; rather, one must examine it both from the different order, as was said, and from the different nature of the debt: because commutative justice restores that which is simply a debt, while distributive justice restores that which is in a certain sense a debt <note>meaning a proportional or merit-based claim rather than a strict one-to-one legal debt.</note>. 
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, the answer is that punitive justice <note>original: "iustitiam vindicatiuam"</note> can be viewed in two ways: in one way, as it pertains to public justice, which directs citizens toward the common good. In this sense, the act is elicited by commutative justice, but commanded by legal justice, which resides in the prince and his ministers. For a judge punishes crimes not only when a defendant is accused, but from his own office (as they say) <note>original: "ex proprio officio"</note> for the sake of the tranquility of the republic. I say, however, that this is a duty of commutative justice because no distribution of goods occurs there, nor properly of evils (since evils are not "stored up" to be distributed); rather, a restoration is made to the equality of the crime by inflicting a punishment. This form belongs to commutative justice, as we shall soon see, although 

<column-break/>

it carries the image of distributive justice insofar as the more wicked are punished more severely. It is commanded, however, by legal justice, whose role it is to administer the republic through laws, the granting of benefits, and the infliction of punishments, and to use particular virtues by commanding them for this end. But if punishment is considered with respect to a particular person to remove the harm they suffered—in which sense punishment is found not only in the prince, but also in a particular citizen affected by injury, who is permitted by custom and order to seek vengeance—not to return evil for evil, but so that compensation may be made to them (though they cannot execute this except through public power); then punishment is not an act of justice, but of a special virtue in itself, which is reduced to commutative justice. This is the doctrine of Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 108, article 2. ¶ But you may ask: why is punishment for the common good considered commutative justice (whether in the prince or the citizen), while punishment that refers to the good of a particular person is considered a special virtue? The answer is: because the republic, through a penalty equal to the crime, both returns to the evildoer something equal in a certain sense and recovers its own honor, which is a true commutation <note>an exchange or restoration of balance</note> of justice. However, when a particular person is avenged, they receive nothing for their lost honor or reputation; instead, the other person suffers just as they themselves had suffered. Therefore, it does not reach the boundaries of commutative justice, as it would if their honor were repaired by the virtue of restitution, or if another favor or money were paid in its place. Hence, Saint Thomas compares this virtue to another special virtue: that of gratitude for a benefit received. For that is neither simple liberality (because some image of a debt underlies it) nor is it simple justice (because it is not a legal debt, but a moral one). For this reason, it is a special virtue that adheres to justice. ¶ Finally, it should be noted by princes regarding distributive justice that since it is a virtue between two extremes, it is constrained on both sides. Therefore, it does not allow such an outpouring of goods as to exhaust the public treasury—which is of the utmost necessity—nor does it allow the prince to be so stingy in distributing goods that he finds no favor among the citizens, whom he must very often rely upon. But this above all must be guarded everywhere: that public taxes and revenues, which are established for public uses and decreed for the people, should not be alienated <note>transferred to private ownership or misused</note>. For from that, not only is the republic gravely endangered, but the poor people are most distressingly burdened and oppressed; because that is the cause for taxes being demanded at increased rates day by day. But this will be discussed more broadly at the end of the following question.

Having defined the types of justice on the previous page, Soto now moves to Article II to compare the mathematical foundations of distributive and commutative justice.</meta>

# Book Three, Question V.

### ARTICLE II.
->Whether the mean of distributive and commutative<-
->justice is the same.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
**I**t follows in this second article to investigate the mean of these virtues: namely, whether it is understood in the same way in both. For there is an argument for the affirmative side: since the mean of the moral virtues is limited by reason between two extremes, as is seen in fortitude and prudence, and since justice is the most powerful among them, it seems to follow that the mean is designated in the same manner in all justice. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Furthermore, since both distributive and commutative justice are "particular" justice, insofar as they refer to and terminate in particular persons, it appears that the mean in both is taken according to the equality of thing to thing—for instance, in distributive justice the equality of merit to reward, and in commutative justice the equality of the thing returned to that which was received. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Thirdly and finally, it is argued: the distribution of common goods seems to be the same duty as compensating for services and labor that citizens expend upon the republic with bestowed benefits; but this is the task of commutative justice, as the Divine Doctor <note>Referring to St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> asserts in the same place (2. 2. question 108), because it ought to be done according to the equality of thing to thing, just as is the infliction of punishments, even if both occur through the command of legal justice. Therefore, nothing remains by which distributive justice differs from commutative. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> ¶ On the contrary is the opinion of Aristotle, who in the same place establishes the mean in distributive justice according to <term>Geometric proportion</term> <note>A proportion based on ratios (e.g., 4 is to 2 as 10 is to 5).</note>, and in commutative justice according to <term>Arithmetic proportion</term> <note>A proportion based on equal differences between numbers (e.g., the difference between 2 and 4 is the same as the difference between 4 and 6).</note>.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
**T**his question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: The mean of both distributive and commutative justice is established according to an equality that exists in external things. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> This is the conclusion of Aristotle in the *Ethics*, Book 5, chapters 3 and 4. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> Indeed, we meditated upon this difference in the first question of this book between the other moral virtues and justice according to their nature: that while the rest compose the character of a man in relation to himself, justice is in relation to another. The mean of other virtues is found between two extreme affections, which the virtue moderates and rectifies. For example, fortitude is between fears and audacities, and temperance is between exorbitant desires and the sorrows that arise from the absence of 

<column-break/>

pleasures of touch. Justice, however, because it resides in the will—where there are no passions—is not their moderator; rather, it is solely incumbent upon justice to set a mean in the things that are owed to others. For although greed and avarice are sometimes an impediment to the duties of justice, it does not belong to justice itself to repress that avarice, but rather to liberality, which is concerned with such affections. <margin>Final conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion is from the same Aristotle in the same place: The equality which is the mean of distributive justice is not of the same nature as that in commutative justice; rather, in distributive it is Geometric, and in commutative it is Arithmetic. For Arithmetic equality is taken according to the equality of the excesses of numbers <note>The "excess" refers to the mathematical difference between terms.</note>, and it is taken at minimum in three terms, of which the middle term is repeated twice. It has a twofold respect. For just as the arithmetic proportion of two to four is such as four is to six (since the excesses are equal <note>4 minus 2 = 2; 6 minus 4 = 2.</note>), even though the Geometric proportion of four to two is greater than six to four—for the former is double, while the latter is <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialtera"; a ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2.</note>. And it is called Arithmetic proportion because it is between numbers as if between its nearest and proper terms (for *arithmos* <note>original: "arithmos"; Greek for number.</note> is number), although it is equally found among continuous quantities. Geometric equality, however, is observed through the equality of ratios: as the proportion between eight and four is equal to that which exists between four and two, because each is double, even though the excesses are unequal. But because the middle term is taken twice, Aristotle says this relationship of proportions consists at minimum of four terms: as the proportion of *a* is to *b*, such is *c* to *d*. For an Arithmetic proportion occurs between only two terms, such as between one and two, although proportionality—that is, the equality of proportions, as has been said—requires three. Hence, in commutations <note>Exchange of goods or services.</note>, two persons are made equal through the equality of two things. <margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin> The conclusion is thus made clear in this way: When a prince decrees to distribute ten <term>talents</term> <note>A large unit of currency or weight in antiquity.</note> to the citizens, he ought to divide them into as many parts as there are citizens, but in such a ratio that as the proportion of Peter's merits is to Paul's merits, such is the proportion of the reward of the former to the reward of the latter. For if Peter's merits are as six and Paul's as three—which is a double proportion—and a reward as two is conferred upon Paul, then a double reward is owed to Peter, namely as four. For then it will be that just as the proportion of Peter’s merit to his reward is, for instance, sesquialter, such is also the merit of Paul to his own reward.

<summary>This page discusses the mathematical definition of the "mean" in justice, distinguishing between the Geometric proportion used in distributing rewards based on merit and the Arithmetic proportion used in fair exchanges of goods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the "mean" in justice. Following the introduction of the topic on page 243, Soto here explains the mathematical difference between distributive justice (which uses geometric proportion) and commutative justice (which uses arithmetic proportion), responding to potential objections regarding how rewards and punishments are calculated based on a person’s status.</meta>

its reward from a permuted proportion. Namely, if A is to B as C is to D, then as A is to C, so will B be to D. Let A and B be merits, and C and D be rewards. And this <margin>Objection.</margin> is finding the geometric mean <note>Geometric proportion in this context refers to a ratio-based equality (e.g., if one person has double the merit of another, they receive double the reward) rather than an equal amount for everyone.</note>. But you may ask why we do not set such examples where the reward <margin>Solution.</margin> would be equal to the merit? We respond that we have done this deliberately: since it is incidental to distributive justice and, as they say, irrelevant for the reward to be exactly equal to the merit. Otherwise, for this reason, it would not differ from commutative justice. Indeed, an equal sum of goods is not always distributed to citizens, even if they always had equal merits; for the human republic sometimes has more goods, sometimes fewer. For now, for example, it distributes thirty talents <note>original: "talenta." A talent was a massive unit of weight or currency in the ancient world.</note> which it seized as plunder from the enemy; at another time twenty, and at another ten. And therefore an equal reward for his merit cannot always fall to the soldier. The same is found in public fruits, which sometimes come forth more generously and sometimes more sparingly. And in the Agrarian Law <note>Roman laws governing the distribution of public lands among the citizens.</note> regarding the division of lands. Therefore, regard should only be had for geometric equality. 

But in the distribution of divine goods which will be performed by Christ on the day of judgment, because those goods are infinite and cannot be exhausted, the distribution will be made not only according to geometric proportion—so that by as much as someone's merits exceed another's, they also exceed in reward—but also according to Arithmetic proportion, so that each receives as much in reward as they had in merits, which proceeded from divine grace.

¶ So much for distributive justice. In commutative justice, however, a different logic must be held: namely, that there be equality between the thing received and that which is returned. For example: Before two merchants entered into a partnership, each had five. But Peter, through a contract or a loan or however else, gave Paul one; Paul then has two more than Peter. This is an arithmetic proportion <note>Arithmetic proportion here refers to simple addition and subtraction to restore a balance of quantities.</note>: consider the four that Peter has compared to the five they both had, and the five compared to the six Paul now has; the mean of these is five. Therefore, through commutative justice, restitution must be made such that Paul also returns one to Peter, by which logic both may be at the mean, without any regard for the quality or condition of the persons. Indeed, whether contracts and agreements are celebrated by custom and law between a magnate and a commoner, or between an honest man and a scoundrel, or between friends or enemies, the nature of commutative justice does not vary. ¶ With this

<column-break/>

declaration having been set forth, the conclusion is proven. <margin>Conclusion.</margin> The mean of justice, whose duty is to render to each their due, must be attended to and weighed through the formal logic of "debt," from which the virtue derives its character. It has been shown that the logic of debt in distributive and commutative justice is different; therefore, the mean varies according to that difference. 

This variety is this: that which is owed in distributive justice is not owed because it was a citizen's own possession, but because that person is a part of the republic; and what belongs to the whole belongs, in a certain way, to the part. Therefore, the more important a part someone is, by that same proportion they ought to receive more goods. Nature provides us an example in the stomach, which is a common organ of the body; for it does not supply the same nourishment to the feet as it does to the eyes, nor the same to the liver as to the spleen, but to each according to its nature and dignity. 

But debt in commutative justice arises from the fact that a thing was the possession of another; therefore, with no regard held for the merits of the persons, as much must be returned to each as they themselves had contributed. <margin>Argument.</margin> ¶ But if you argue to the contrary: In commutative justice, just as in distributive, the condition and dignity of persons is sometimes weighed. For just as one who strikes a prince with a slap is punished with a greater penalty through vindictive justice than if he struck a common man—as Aristotle <margin>Aristotle</margin> also noted in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 5—so while compensation is made through restitution, he who beats an honorable and noble citizen owes more than one who harms a commoner with a similar blow. Therefore, in this respect, these forms of justice do not differ. 

<margin>Response.</margin> It is answered that the quality of the person is seen in both forms of justice; however, in distributive justice, it is considered in itself—so that by the increase of the person’s status, the proportion to another is increased; for courtesy and humility have more merit in a noble man than in a man of lower station. Yet in commutative justice, the person is only considered insofar as the quantity of the injury is increased thereby, which must be repaired to achieve equality.

**THROUGH** these points, therefore, the solution to the previous arguments becomes clear. <margin>To the first argument.</margin> For the first was answered in the previous conclusion according to the difference of justice from the other virtues. And likewise, the second is solved by the later <margin>To the second argument.</margin> conclusion. For we concede that the mean of both types of justice is established according to equality in things which are arranged between two or more persons; however, it is done in different ways: because the mean in distributive justice is attended to according to the equality between two proportions, namely...

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, however, it is responded that the granting of benefits is only for services and labors received; for that reason, it has a certain character of a wage, and thus is a duty of commutative justice <note>Commutative justice governs private transactions and the "fair price" or direct exchange between individuals.</note>. For such a person, even if no specific stipend had been established for such acts, is worthy of having just benefits conferred upon him in exchange for his service. But the distribution of common goods is not a compensation, but a simple attribution of those things which belong to the whole body to its parts. For this reason, the merits of the parts are not estimated in the same way in all republics, as Aristotle mentions in the place cited. For where the republic is governed by Democracy, that is, by popular power, no other merits are weighed except liberty; so that because all enjoy equal liberty, they may receive equal things. Unless perhaps less falls to the freedmen, who were once slaves; while more falls to those who are more distinguished by their free birth. But in an Oligarchy <margin>Oligarchy</margin>, that is, the power of the few, the estimation is made according to the quantity of wealth: so that the more someone has, the more they receive—which is the most unjust distribution of all. But in an Aristocracy, that is, the power of the best, the use of distribution is according to the merits of virtues. And such a distribution ought to be seen in a kingdom, which a most excellent king rules. For since honor nourishes the arts, no incentive or fuel for virtues is more powerful among mortals than to confer honors upon each according to their merits. Indeed, those who are kindled toward their duties by the love of virtue alone, looking toward the future age, are exceedingly rare. For this reason, Cato was accustomed to admonish the Conscript Fathers <note>original: "Patres Conscriptos." This was the formal title for the Roman Senators.</note> that they should consult well on which virtues they placed rewards; since the youth could not pursue anything other than those things through which they could attain the honors established for them.

### ARTICLE III.
*Whether the matter of distributive and commutative justice is the same.*

<note>Decorative drop cap 'D' within a square floral frame.</note>
CONCERNING the matter of these species, it is asked in this third article whether it is the same for both types of justice, which is divided only into these most specific categories. For it appears at first that the matter is the same:

<column-break/>

otherwise the virtues themselves would be so diverse that they would not be contained under the single cardinal virtue of justice. For the diversity of the matter of temperance and fortitude establishes two cardinal virtues in themselves. However, the consequence is false and contrary to the opinion of Aristotle and of everyone who discerns only four cardinal virtues. Next, it is argued against what the question also asks implicitly. Commutative justice is divided into many species: therefore these are not the most specific and indivisible categories. The premise is clear. Aristotle enumerates different matters, or rather forms, of commutative justice: one is voluntary exchange, and the other is involuntary. The latter is again divided into involuntary by force, and involuntary by fraud; therefore, neither is a most specific <margin>Aristotle.</margin> species. ¶ On the contrary is Aristotle in that place where he says that distributive justice directs distributions, while commutative justice directs exchanges; yet he distinguishes no species of this commutative justice.

THE question has two parts, to which it is worthwhile to respond with two conclusions. 
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first is this: The matter which they call "remote" is the same for both types of justice; but the "proximate" matter is different <note>In scholastic philosophy, "remote matter" refers to the objects themselves (like money), while "proximate matter" refers to the specific human action or relationship involving those objects.</note>. 
<margin>The first part of the conclusion is proved.</margin>
The first part is shown thus: The remote matters of these virtues are both the persons between whom, and the things in which, the distribution and exchange occur. And these are the same: for both distribution and exchange involve external things, namely grain, wine, oil, and money among the same citizens. 
<margin>Proof of the second part.</margin>
The second part of the conclusion is also clear. The proximate matter is the use of those things. It is established that distributive justice directs that use which is to adjudicate things to citizens by reason of what is owed—not because it was the private property of individuals, but because it belonged to the whole republic. For this function (as we said), a different reasoning is required and a different difficulty exists than in commutative justice <margin>To the first argument.</margin>. However, the faculty of commutative justice is to moderate the use of things in returning the specific debts of individuals. ¶ From this, the response to the first argument becomes clear: for this diversity of uses, although it establishes a diversity of the species of virtue, it is not so great as to prevent both from being contained under the species of "particular justice" <term>particular justice: the virtue governing relationships between individuals or between the community and an individual, rather than general legal justice</term>, which deals with extrinsic things and their uses regarding particular persons. It is different, however, for temperance and fortitude: for one of these deals with the delights of touch—those sensible things that lure and draw us to themselves—while the other deals with objects...

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion is this: The variety of matters subject to commutative justice <note>Justice governing the private interactions and exchanges between individuals, ensuring that what is given is equal to what is received.</note> does not at all split the same virtue into several species; rather, it is one and the same, indivisible. We can indeed track the truth of this conclusion through this series of divisions. For the first division is taken from the diversity of exchanges in relation to the will.

<margin>Double exchange.</margin>
For one type of exchange is voluntary, while the other is involuntary. An involuntary exchange occurs when someone usurps something belonging to another—whether a person, property, or work—against the owner's will, as in theft. A voluntary exchange occurs when someone receives a thing from a willing and consenting owner, as in a loan. Here it must be noted immediately that the name "exchange" does not denote simple giving or receiving; for where a thing is given freely and received as a gift, there is no exchange. Rather, giving is properly called an exchange (as the name proclaims) when one gives in order to receive, and the other receives in order to return—as is evident in loans, deposits, sales, leases, and other civil contracts of that kind.

<margin>voluntary</margin>
Therefore, an exchange signifies a certain spontaneous and voluntary action on both sides: namely, of both the giver and the receiver. By contrast, an involuntary exchange assumes an involuntary action, both on the part of the sufferer and the part of the taker. For in theft, the owner does not give in order to receive, nor does the thief take in order to return; instead, the former suffers against his will, while the latter freely takes what he would never wish to pay back. Yet, when he later makes restitution, it matters not whether he returns it voluntarily led by repentance or compelled by public authority. For an exchange is called involuntary or voluntary from the primary root of the taking—that is, from the involuntary removal. For even where the taking was voluntary, the return can be involuntary, such as when a dishonest buyer is forced by power to pay the price.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding gifts, however, there is a doubt whether the assent of both parties is required—namely, not only of the giver but also of the receiver. That is, if Peter, in his mind or by word, gave something to an unaware Paul, would he be bound by that gift before the other accepted it? And it seems he would be bound, because when someone vows something to God within himself,

<column-break/>

he is immediately bound; likewise, therefore, the one who gave seems to be tied.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is responded, however, that since giving implies a relation to a receiver, an obligation does not seem to arise before the other accepts. And therefore, it can perhaps be revoked, even without any just cause. It is otherwise concerning a vow made to God, because He, if it is just, always accepts. But if a gift is made solemnly before witnesses to an absent person, then one must stand by civil law. For I believe that without the recipient's consent or a legitimate cause, the laws do not allow revocation. If this is so, then conscience does not permit it either.

<margin>Manifold types of exchanges.</margin>
¶ But because Aristotle teaches in the third book of the *Ethics* that the involuntary occurs for two reasons—either through force and fear, or through ignorance—he subdivides involuntary exchanges in the fifth book into two types: those done secretly and without the owner's knowledge through fraud, and those done through manifest violence.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Aristotle describes both there, and Saint Thomas even more fully in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 61, article 3 <note>Soto is referencing the *Summa Theologiae* of Thomas Aquinas, the foundational text for his school of thought.</note>. For both can fall upon your property, or your person, or your kin—that is, those joined to you by some necessity. Your things, then, are either stolen from you craftily and secretly, which is called theft; or manifestly, and that is called robbery. Against the substance of your person, murder or other injury can be committed, either secretly, as through poisoning or traps, or manifestly, through open force. And again, the dignity of the person can be attacked either secretly, such as through false testimony and hidden detractions by which reputation and esteem are worn away and corroded, or manifestly, either through slander in court or through insults by which honor is diminished. In a person joined to oneself, an injury can be done to someone, either in a wife through secret adultery, or in a servant who is seduced to flee. In these cases, one can also be burdened by manifest injuries. Nevertheless, what was said regarding a servant has the character of robbery or theft.

## ARTICLE IV.
### Whether the form of both types of justice is the same.

<note>The text begins with a decorative drop cap 'S'.</note>
It remains finally that we explore in the fourth place whether the form of justice, just like its remote matter, is the same in both virtues. We ask this primarily for the sake of Aristotle, who, in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 5, disputes whether the form of justice is a certain retaliation <note>original: "repassio"; the concept of "suffering back" or *lex talionis* (an eye for an eye)</note>. And it is argued from the affirmative side based on the final judgment, from which the rule should especially be taken.

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
For there (as Paul says), each one ought to receive according as he has done in the body <note>2 Corinthians 5:10</note>; and Christ says in Matthew 7: "In the judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and in the measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you." From these words, it is gathered that everyone is to be punished by retaliation according to the quantity of the actions by which they acted wickedly.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Likewise, it is argued in the second place. In

<column-break/>

both types of justice, a certain recompense <note>original: "repensio"</note> is observed: namely, in distributive justice, of a reward to the merit and dignity of the person; and in commutative justice, of thing for thing, whether some injury intervened or none at all, as we were saying above. Now, retaliation seems to be the same thing as recompense—whether of good or evil—for that which each person receives, whether they took it by force or by the will of the owner. Therefore, the form of each justice consists in retaliation; or what is said less elegantly in Latin, in "counter-suffering" <note>original: "contrapassione"</note>.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ Aristotle is to the contrary in the same Book 5 of the *Ethics*, asserting against Rhadamanthus <note>A mythical judge of the underworld known for inflexible, literal justice</note> that not every just thing consists in simple retaliation.

SO THAT the response to this question may be more clearly established, the meaning of the word "retaliation"—or as he says, "counter-suffering"—must be considered beforehand with St. Thomas.

<margin>What retaliation signifies.</margin>
For the primary meaning of this word is adapted only to that which someone suffers against their will. For "to suffer" <note>original: "pati"</note> implies violence; and something is violent, according to Aristotle in *Ethics* Book 3, to which the one suffering contributes no force.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For this reason, in moral matters, it signifies an injury which someone receives unwillingly. Therefore, to "suffer back" <note>original: "repati"</note> is the same as to suffer just as much as one inflicted on another by force or fraud; whether it be done to the person, which is most proper, or in things, which also has its own character on account of being involuntary. This was just in both ways according to the ancient law, following that of Exodus 21: "He shall give life for life, eye for eye," etc. And in the following chapter: "If anyone steals an ox or a sheep and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox, and four sheep for one sheep." Therefore, the retaliation of the thief was not to return the single amount—for simple restitution required that—but to pay a penalty for the injury. From this proper meaning, the name descended to voluntary exchanges, in which the name "suffering" <note>original: "passio"</note> does not preserve its exact meaning, but is a certain misuse of terms, nonetheless accepted by custom for the sake of discussion.

<margin>Responsive conclusion according to the mind of Aristotle.</margin>
These points having been lightly touched upon, Aristotle responds with a single conclusion by which he denies that justice is universally preserved under the form of retaliation.

<margin>Another conclusion.</margin>

For even if the citizens had contributed nothing to the commonwealth, except that they are upright men, a reward is conferred on each according to the proportion of their merits (as has been explained), with no quality weighed between thing and thing.
