<meta>This page continues the discussion of commutative justice and the concept of "repassio" (reciprocity or suffering in return). Soto is examining whether justice consists merely of returning the exact same action or value that was received.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
...though justice would always consist of a just reciprocity <note>original: "repassio"; a technical term for suffering the same thing one has inflicted, similar to the law of retaliation</note> where the defendant suffers precisely what the author of the deed had inflicted upon him, it can nevertheless be made just once the status and quality of both parties are weighed. This is the conclusion of **Aristotle** where he corrects the opinion of **Rhadamanthus**. <note>Rhadamanthus was a mythical judge of the underworld in Greek mythology, famous for his inflexible and literal interpretation of "an eye for an eye."</note> For he used to say:
> If what he did, he also suffers himself:
> The judgment shall be straight, and the outcome equal.

<margin>Aristotle's reason for this conclusion.</margin>
However, Aristotle refutes him, for if someone holding a **magistracy** strikes another, or if even a **king** wounds a citizen against justice, it is not consistent with reason that he should receive the exact same wound in return. Conversely, where a private man lays rash hands upon a king, he would not pay enough of a penalty if an equal blow were struck against him; rather, he who, for example, cut off the hand of a king, ought to be punished with his life. And if he himself were to behead someone, he should not therefore be mutilated in any specific member of his body. Therefore, the "just" of commutative justice does not consist in the exact compensation of the same act. Yet, perhaps Rhadamanthus would not deny this equity. For indeed, the very thing that is taken away receives an increase or decrease in value based on the **status of the person**. In truth, just as an injury inflicted upon a prince is more atrocious, so it is lighter in the eyes of men when he inflicts it. For this reason, since justice consists in equality, the punishment must be increased for one who strikes a prince, and the penalty diminished for the prince himself. Nor should this be the case only in bodily injuries, but also in external goods. For he who has forcefully inconvenienced another in his property does not make satisfaction by simply returning the same amount, as if he had received those things by the owner's will; rather, he must be prosecuted by law for the injury, as is done in the legal code.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The **third conclusion**. In voluntary exchanges (in the sense that we use the term "reciprocity" there), justice will not be preserved if someone, contributing his own property or his own workmanship, receives from another simply that which he himself has, or what he can provide by his own art. <margin>The conclusion is demonstrated.</margin> This is also a conclusion of **Aristotle**, for it can happen that the goods of different citizens and craftsmen are not of equal price. For example: A **shoemaker** needs a house which another craftsman builds for him; it is not enough for the construction of the house that he returns one or two pairs of shoes, but he ought to pile up as many as the construction of the house was worth. In the same way: one **farmer**, who abounds in grain, needs the wine or oil of another. It does not always happen that a measure of grain is of the same value as a measure of wine; therefore, those things which are of lower value must be made equal through multiplication to the thing which is more excellent.

<column-break/>

And by this reasoning, justice can consist in reciprocity; otherwise, not at all. ¶ From these things, therefore, says **Aristotle**, the necessity of **coins** arose. <margin>The origin of coins.</margin> For a coin or "numisma" is, as it were, that which is a law and a norm; for *nomisma* <note>original: "νόμισμα"</note> in Greek is the same as "rule" and "law" <note>original: "lex"; Soto is connecting the Greek word for money to *nomos*, meaning law or custom</note>. There are, therefore, two uses for coinage: the first is <margin>The double use of money.</margin> that it serves as a **measure**, making all things equal. The construction of a single house could not be estimated precisely in shoes or boots or other handiworks; therefore, the shoemaker sells as many shoes as are needed to acquire the money with which he can buy the house. Furthermore, he who perhaps does not need another's goods right now may need other things, or will need them in the future, or in another place; therefore, the coin is for him like a **pledge** <term>vades<gloss>A legal guarantor or surety</gloss></term> that stands as security for him. For wherever and whenever you present such a coin, you will have something suited to your needs. For this reason, it is also called *moneta* (money), as if it were a "warning law" <note>original: "monitoria lex"; a play on the word *monere*, to warn or advise</note>; <margin>Why it is called money.</margin> and *pecunia* (wealth) from *pecus* (cattle), which the Romans, according to **Pliny** in Book 33, marked with the sign of cattle, because all things (as the Wise Man says) obey money; and in the beginnings of the world, movable and exchangeable goods were mostly sheep, cattle, and herds. From these points, it follows again that the value of a coin (as the Philosopher says in the same place) is not to be estimated entirely from the **nature of the material**, whether it be copper, silver, or gold, but by the **statute and seal** of the commonwealth or the prince, who has engraved his authority on such a coin as a guarantor for all. Whence, in a time of necessity, it can be struck or engraved on any material, even the cheapest, such as iron or leather. Nevertheless, according to the nature and resources of a region, that metal ought to be chosen for this duty which is more solid and possesses a certain permanence. For this reason, **Pliny** in the same book asserts that **gold** was selected <margin>Pliny.</margin> among the metals: not indeed by reason of its color, which he says is brighter and more like daylight in silver; nor by reason of its weight or ease of material, since it yields to lead in both; but because it is the only thing that loses nothing in fire, the material remaining safe even in blazes and funeral pyres. These are his words. Indeed, since fire is the most active of all things, devouring and consuming objects, gold is the more excellent the more it is safe from this danger. It also follows (which **Aristotle** wisely noted there) <margin>Aristotle.</margin> that although the valuation of coins can be increased or decreased when any necessity looms, <margin>The valuation of coins ought to be fixed and firm in the manner of a law.</margin> it is nevertheless right that this should happen very rarely. Indeed, for this reason, money ought to imitate the nature of **law**, so that it is always fixed and firm. For truly, since through the coin (as we have said) the commonwealth and the prince act as a guarantor to all, the faith of that same prince and commonwealth is not a little worn away when citizens are defrauded by such changes without great necessity.

### BOOK THREE, QUESTION VI.

<margin>To the first argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
Regarding the first argument made concerning the final judgment, **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theologian cited here.</note> responds in article 4 of question 61 that it will occur according to the logic of **commutative justice** <note>original: "commutatiuæ iustitiæ"; the justice of fair exchange, often compared to a business transaction where one thing is given for another of equal value</note>, specifically as it repays rewards for merits and punishments for sins.

<margin>Cajetan's objection against St. Thomas.</margin>
However, **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas who often challenged specific points of his logic.</note> raises an "argument against the man" <note>original: "argumentum ad hominem"</note>—namely, that in other parts of his work, Thomas denies that **commutative justice** exists in God. Cajetan responds that both punishment and reward are carried out there according to <margin>Cajetan’s solution.</margin> **distributive justice** <note>original: "iustitiam distributiuam"; the justice used to share out honors or resources among members of a community based on their standing or merit</note>. For, as we read concerning Judas in the first chapter of Acts: *Each person there will be sent to his own place.* He says, however, that it maintains a certain form of commutative justice insofar as one thing is given for another: specifically, a reward for merit and a punishment for an offense.

<margin>Cajetan’s response is rejected.</margin>
Nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, I do not think the same conclusion should be reached regarding the rewarding of the good and the punishing of the wicked, neither according to **St. Thomas** nor according to the truth of the matter. For the granting of rewards is undoubtedly a function of distributive justice. Even so, as we said in article 2, the logic of commutative justice is seen there because, since divine goods are infinite, they are returned to everyone according to a **geometric proportion** <note>a fairness based on a ratio—those with more merit get a proportionally larger reward—rather than everyone getting the exact same amount</note> of merit. In this way, the reward is matched perfectly to the merit, something that cannot always be observed in a human republic where resources are sometimes scarce. But the same is not true for **punitive justice** <note>original: "iustitia vindicatiua"</note> against delinquents. Such justice by no means belongs to distributive justice. This is something **St. Thomas** <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> expressly affirms. For vengeance is drawn from commutative justice, though it is commanded by **legal justice** <note>the justice that looks to the common good of the whole law</note>, as we noted above in the first article of this question. Punishment is not like the distribution of goods. Distributive justice does not look at what citizens have contributed in order to pay them back, but rather at what each person deserves in themselves. Punishment, however, looks fundamentally at what injury someone has inflicted so that they may be struck with an equal penalty. Therefore, it does not first look at the proportion of crimes, but at the quantity of each specific act—which is the duty of commutative justice. Consequently, the same proportion that existed in the crimes is preserved in the punishments. Thus, retribution (as St. Thomas says in the cited passage) does not correspond to the distribution of goods, but to the repayment for services rendered, an action which is likewise part of commutative justice, though commanded by the law. Therefore, the logic of reward is different from the logic of punishment: the former inherently preserves a geometric proportion between the ratio of 

<column-break/>

merits and the ratio of rewards. But as a consequence, where there is an abundance of goods (as in God), an equality of "thing to thing" is maintained: namely, the reward to the merit. Punishment, on the other hand, everywhere looks first to the equality of the penalty to the crime, and as a result, it preserves the geometric relationship of proportions. This is consistent with what **Paul** says: <margin>Paul.</margin> *For the rest, there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the just judge will render to me on that day.* This is rendered through legal justice, which, being a general virtue, commands the others—both commutative and distributive justice alike. Indeed, St. Thomas rightly denies that commutative justice is properly in God when considering its formal definition, because He himself receives nothing from us that could add anything to Him. For as **John** <note>referring to the Apostle or the general scriptural sentiment in Romans 11:35</note> says: *Who has first given to him, that it should be repaid to him?* Nor can we properly take anything away from Him who is immutable. Rather, if we are good, we are good for our own benefit and for our own gain, directed toward the glory of God.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, a sufficiently clear response has been given through the conclusions. The first conclusion explained how in distributive justice there is no **reciprocity** <note>original: "repassio"; the principle of "an eye for an eye" or suffering exactly what one has done</note>, because there is no consideration of whether the citizen has provided or done something for which he should receive an equal return. In exchanges (commutative justice), however, the form of reciprocity can be preserved in the manner already explained.

***

### Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

...assigns to individual citizens, is more excellent than **commutative justice** <note>The justice of fair exchange, like a business transaction.</note>. For this reason, we have departed from the order established by **St. Thomas**. This question will consist of seven articles.

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
The first and primary article concerns this form of injustice which is called **"respect of persons"** <note>original: "acceptionem personarum"; this refers to favoritism or partiality—treating someone better or worse based on their status rather than the facts of a case.</note>, and whether it is by its nature a **mortal sin** <note>A grave sin that separates a person from God's grace.</note>. First of all, to begin with divine law—which is the source and pattern for our own—God seems to "respect persons" when dispensing grace and glory. This is because "respect of persons" occurs when no regard is given to merits. Yet God receives no one into His grace based on our own merits, as the **Pelagian** <note>A follower of Pelagius, a 5th-century monk who argued humans could achieve salvation through their own will without divine grace—a view declared heretical.</note> impiety suggests. Hence, in Matthew 24: *Two shall be in a bed; one shall be taken, and the other left.* Therefore, it should not be considered a vice among men to respect persons.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued: the poor widow who contributed two small coins to the treasury was preferred by the mouth of Christ over others who gave more, though she was socially "unworthy." Furthermore, a person holding public office, especially a spiritual one, who commits the same crime as a commoner is worthy of harsher punishment because of their high status. Therefore, the "respect of persons" should not be condemned as if it were inherently unfair.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
On the contrary is the judgment of God in Deuteronomy 10: *God is great, mighty, and terrible... who does not respect persons nor take bribes.* And **Paul** in Romans 2 says: *There is no respect of persons with God.* For this reason, God Himself (as seen in the same book of Deuteronomy, chapter 1) wished for men to be equally cautious, saying: *There shall be no difference of persons. You shall hear the small as well as the great; neither shall you respect any man's person.*

This term, "respect of persons," although not frequently used by **Cicero** or the ancient Latin authors, has nonetheless been adopted into Latin by the interpreters of Holy Scripture. Nor is it foreign to Greek composition; for in Greek it is *prosopolēpsia* <note>original: "προσωποληψία", from "prosōpon" (face/mask) and "lambanō" (to take/receive)</note>, which means "receiving the face." Hence, in Galatians 2: *God does not accept the person of man*, where the same Greek word is used. However, since it carries the same weight—especially in composition—as "looking upon," it is very well called the "respect of persons," where "person" is understood as "face." It is, therefore, a fitting **metaphor** <note>A figure of speech where one thing is used to describe another.</note> when a judge is forbidden from "looking at the face of persons" in judgment, as we noted regarding Paul in Romans 2: namely, that he should not allow his mind to be affected in judgment by race, sex, age, or other qualities of that kind. To this same point, Leviticus 19 alludes: *Do not consider the person...*

<column-break/>

*...of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful.*

<margin>Lucian.</margin>
And **Lucian** <note>A 2nd-century Syrian-Greek satirist.</note> reports in *Hermotimus* that the **Areopagites** <note>Judges of the high court of Athens.</note> were accustomed to judge at night and in the dark for this very reason: so that they could not look at the speakers, but only at what was being said. And it is attributed to **Socrates** as the height of equity that he refused to bring his wife or children into court to stir up the compassion of the judges.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
And **Aristotle** in the first book of his *Rhetoric* condemns that part of Oratory which is designed to stir the emotions. He commends the Athenian Areopagus primarily for the reason that they had banished that practice from their judgments.

<margin>Definition of "respect of persons."</margin>
From these notes on the name, a description of "respect of persons" can be gathered. It is the crime of injustice by which, in the distribution of honors or goods, one takes account not of the cause pertaining to the matter, but of the person and their other qualities.

<margin>The Gloss.</margin>
The **Gloss** <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," a standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> alludes to this regarding Ephesians 6: *Respect of persons is not with God.* God is a just judge; He discerns causes, not persons. The reason for the name is that while **distributive justice** <note>The fairness with which a community distributes rewards and status.</note> weighs the bare and sincere importance of merits in its scales, and merits are those things which proceed from a rightly ordered will, anything that adds nothing to this heap of merits is considered to belong to the innate conditions of the person. Thus, by the name "person," we understand nature as distinct from the right will, and likewise other actions that are outside the specific cause being judged.

<margin>Responsive conclusion. Proof.</margin>
Let the conclusion of the question be this: **Respect of persons is by its nature a mortal sin.** It is proved thus: Whatever opposes justice is by its nature a lethal crime, as was defined above in Question 34 of this book following **St. Thomas**. For since justice is a necessary virtue, whatever stands in its way is contrary to **charity** <note>The love of God and neighbor, considered the highest virtue.</note>, and is therefore mortal by its nature. Respect of persons stands in the way of justice, as it prevents the legitimate logic of "what is due" from being observed; therefore, it is mortal.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
For this reason, although St. Thomas in Question 63, Article 1, only asserted that "respect of persons" is a sin, he had already established in Question 59, Article 4, that the sin of injustice is counted among the class of mortal sins. Nevertheless, in matters of small importance, it may happen to be only **venial** <note>A lesser sin that does not fully break one's relationship with God.</note>; for instance, if someone were to prefer a less worthy friend over a more excellent one in an election to an office that matters little to the common good. For a person who steals a tiny amount of money would not immediately be guilty of a mortal crime. It is for this reason that we used the qualification "by its nature."

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
From this it follows that all causes and qualities which have no bearing on the dignity of that matter...

## Book Three, Question VI.

For the same reason can be legitimately observed in one distribution, which in the distribution of another thing is not allowed to carry any weight at all. For he who gives or leaves something of his own goods to kinsmen by reason of their family line is not a "respecter of persons" <note>A "respecter of persons" (favoritism) is someone who shows partiality based on status rather than merit or law.</note>; but he who for that same reason would confer a priesthood upon a kinsman would fall into such a crime. In the same way, if one were to prefer an outstandingly learned man—who was not, however, of a particularly well-ordered character—over a holy man who was nevertheless ignorant, in the choice for a Chair <note>original: "Cathedram"; refers to a professorship or a high teaching position.</note>, he would not be considered a "respecter of persons." This is similar to preferring the learned man in another election where a person of conspicuous integrity was required. But we shall speak more precisely <note>original: "emunctiùs," literally "more cleanly wiped," a scholastic term for speaking with greater clarity or sharpness.</note> about these kinds of merits in the following articles.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> Through these points, the response to the first argument is clear. For in God's distributions, one type of consideration must be held when He first receives a man into His grace (whether we contemplate him in his pure natural state or as one stained by the blot of sin); but another consideration is held when we weigh the duties of the virtues in one already admitted to that grace. In the first way, since there is no reason of "debt" <note>God does not "owe" grace to anyone; it is a free gift.</note>, distributive justice has no place, for distributive justice (as has been said) presupposes debt in some fashion. Therefore, "respect of persons" cannot be noted there; rather, it is a mere gift of liberality, just as if a prince were to impart his own private goods to whomever he pleased. For "no one," as John says, "first gave to God that it might be repaid to him." Hence in the Gospel parable in Matthew 20: *Is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Take what is yours and go.* Paul refers to this as the height of the incomprehensible riches of the knowledge of God. In the second way, however, distributive justice shines forth; concerning this, Paul says: <margin>Paul.</margin> *Who will render to each according to his works.* And elsewhere: *We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive the proper things of the body according as he has done, whether good or evil.* For those who have become His members through the grace of Christ subsequently merit well from God. Wherefore, in that instance, God is not a respecter of persons, but renders to each according to the value of the merits which flow from divine grace. <margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, it is answered that when the quality of a person increases the merit or the crime, then it is not "respect of persons" to include that quality among the causes of re-

<column-break/>

ward <note>original: "præmij"</note>. For the poverty of that Gospel widow was the reason why her tiny alms were of greater value than if a rich man had bestowed the same amount; for that reason, she was worthy of a more abundant reward. And conversely, since the pre-eminence and status of a delinquent aggravates the fault of the crime, it follows that the consideration of that dignity does nothing to hinder the vengeance of God's justice if He punishes him more sharply.

### ARTICLE II.

->*Whether the respect of persons can occur in the dispensation of spiritual things.*<-

Having set forth the nature and quality of the "respect of persons"—which, since it is contrary to justice, is a mortal sin—it follows that we should see in what matters it is involved. And first, in this second article, we ask whether it has a place in the dispensation of spiritual things. From the negative side, one argues: Priesthoods and spiritual prefectures are not so much under distributive justice as under commutative justice <note>Commutative justice governs private exchanges and contracts (like a fair wage for work), whereas distributive justice governs how a community shares its common resources.</note>. <margin>The first argument.</margin> "Respect of persons," as was said, is opposed to distributive justice; therefore, it has no place in spiritual matters of this kind. The first premise is proven: for these priesthoods, ecclesiastical prebends <note>A portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman.</note>, and what they call "personates" <note>original: "personatus"; high-ranking ecclesiastical offices that usually did not involve the direct "care of souls" (parish work) but carried great dignity.</note> do not have the precise character of common goods (like the revenues of a republic, which, because they belong to the whole, belong in a way to the parts). Instead, they are stipends of the people established for the ministers of the churches. Therefore, they are owed to worthy persons not for their own sake, but because such persons are owed to the churches. That is, they are dispensed to persons as a reward for service, according to that justice by which "the laborer is worthy of his hire." This justice is not distributive, but clearly commutative. ¶ Secondly, it is argued: Christ our Redeemer seemed <margin>Second.</margin> in the choice of His Apostles—which related most especially to the spiritual life—to have "respected" and "accepted" persons. For, weighing none of their merits, He called them from fishing, money-changing <note>original: "campsoria"; the business of a banker or money-changer.</note>, and other lowly arts of that kind, like the "weak and despised things of this world," as Paul says. Furthermore, He appeared to be a respecter of persons in this: that He took only Galileans from His own country, and His own kinsmen. For, as one reads in Acts 1, the crowds were amazed that those speaking in various tongues were all...

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued: even in **Canon Law**, "respect of persons" <note>original: "personarum acceptio"; the act of showing favoritism based on status or relationship rather than merit.</note> seems not only permitted but commanded in elections. This is evident in the same title, in the chapter *Cum nobis olim*, where an election is approved even though the person elected was not of eminent learning. And in the chapter *Cum dilectus*, an election is likewise approved even though there were (as is read there) others "more worthy" (*digniores*) in the same church.

<margin>Fourth argument.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, it is argued: it is also sanctioned by ecclesiastical decrees that an election should not be made except from persons of the same church, provided a worthy person is found there—even if "more worthy" people are found elsewhere. This is clear in *Distinction 61, chapter Nullus* and *chapter Obitum*, and *Distinction 63, chapter Metropolitano*. Indeed, as the Gloss <note>The "Gloss" refers to the standard medieval commentary on Canon Law.</note> says in the chapter *Cum inter canonicos* regarding elections, a petition for someone from a foreign church is not valid unless two-thirds of the electors consent. Moreover, it must be done by the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note>, as is widely clear in the title concerning the "petition of prelates." Therefore, the "more worthy" are not always to be sought out, even if they could easily be found in other churches. Furthermore, ecclesiastical custom makes this plain to us.

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
For we see in the elections of Bishops that consideration is given not so much to merits as to persons, or lineage, or power. Add to this that in the supreme election of the Supreme Pontiff, a custom has long since grown that no one is chosen unless he is from among the most reverend Cardinals; yet sometimes others could be sought outside that order whose election might perhaps be more pleasing and acceptable to God.

<margin>Fifth argument.</margin>
¶ Fifthly and finally, it is argued: The Pope, as they say, is the master of the benefits and goods of the Church; therefore, he is not restricted to choosing the "more worthy," but can bestow those same goods on whomever he pleases. ¶ On the contrary, however, is James the Apostle in the second chapter of his Canonical Epistle:

> Do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons.

**I**n response to this question, ten conclusions are offered. If, however, we first note what I understand here by the name of "spiritual things"? This will be clarified in the book under the title regarding **Simony** <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling sacred things, named after Simon Magus.</note>. For we do not mean everything that is in the intellect—for knowledge and the arts can be taught for a price—but we mean those things which are given to us freely by God: not only specifically for the benefit of the recipients, but for the common utility. Of these, Christ says: *Freely you have received, freely give* <note>Matthew 10:8; original: "Gratis accepistis, gratis date."</note>. Such are priesthoods, priestly orders, and the use of sacred things. First, therefore, regarding the matter of the first argument, it is necessary to know beforehand that these ecclesiastical

<column-break/>

priesthoods must be weighed not only by the reason of **distributive justice**, but they enter into the line of **commutative justice** <note>Soto is distinguishing between justice that distributes rewards based on merit (distributive) and justice that involves a fair exchange or contractual obligation (commutative).</note>.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let this be the first conclusion: It should not be denied that priesthoods and church prefectures bear the mark of distributive justice, because more honorable and "fatter" <note>original: "pinguiora"; referring to more lucrative or resource-rich positions.</note> posts are owed to those who possess more outstanding merits. Therefore, in the ninth conclusion, we must maintain that in elections of this kind, the more worthy person is to be preferred to the others.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, to this conclusion the second is woven: Regarding ecclesiastical benefits, priestly duties, and dignities which pertain to the service of the churches, judgment must be made chiefly by the rules of commutative justice.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
It is proved thus: The tithes which the Christian people pay are not contributed so that they might be rewards for the merits of persons—like the goods that exist in a public treasury—but were instituted either solely or chiefly for this purpose: to be the stipends of the ministers of the Church. Thus, the Christian religion, unless it had necessary churches, would never compel Christians to contribute tithes. We shall say the same thing below concerning secular taxes, between which and priesthoods only this difference stands: the former are stipends for secular administrations of justice, while the latter are for the spiritual functions of the churches. From this, it follows that the logic of distributive justice found in these dispensations is ordered toward the commutative justice that exists between the pontiffs (both the Supreme Pontiff and the other dispensers and providers of church goods) on one side, and the churches on the other. Indeed, because citizens pay tithes so that the sacraments may be administered to them, the Word of God explained, and ecclesiastical justice preserved: by commutative justice, they are owed suitable administrators of these duties, just like workers in the Lord's vineyard. Nor does it stand in the way that tithes (I do not say the specific amount) are of divine law. For I believe this should be judged like a prince who establishes certain perpetual stipends for the servants and ministers of his house, commanding that they be dispensed to the "more worthy" who can be found. Here, surely, more commutative justice underlies the matter than distributive. Just as, once the collation of a benefit is made, the same justice is established between the minister and his church. Thus, to speak for the sake of explanation, the logic of distributive justice in these matters stands materially toward the logic of commutative justice. For electors are bound to distribute priesthoods according to the merits of persons, not because...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether choosing a less worthy candidate for a church office constitutes the sin of "respect of persons" (favoritism). Soto is arguing that church offices (benefices) are not personal rewards for being a good person, but are "wages" for a specific job. Therefore, justice requires choosing the person best suited for the work, rather than simply the most virtuous person in an absolute sense.</meta>

### Book Three, Question VI.

...are rewards for their own merits, but because the electors owe such ministers to the churches, and the ministers owe such services to those same churches, in exchange for the stipend <note>A fixed payment or salary.</note> paid to them.

<margin>The conclusion is supported by the testimony of Holy Scripture.</margin>
¶ This conclusion, explained in this way, is proven not only by reason (which is manifest), but also by the sacred oracles <note>Holy Scripture.</note>. First, to begin with the Old Law, tithes were decreed for the Levites for a similar reason. For so it is read in Numbers 18: *I have given to the sons of Levi all the tithes in possession for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant.* And a little further down regarding tithes it is added: *Because it is the price for the ministry by which you serve in the tabernacle of testimony.* And in Luke 10, when Christ sent out the Apostles as laborers and harvesters into the world, he added: *Stay in the same house, eating and drinking what they have: for the laborer is worthy of his hire.* Now, "hire" or wages is rendered through **commutative justice** <note>original: "iustitiam commutatiuam"; this refers to the justice of fair exchange, like a contract where one person works and the other pays a fair wage.</note>. And the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 9 says, following the same sentiment, *No one ever serves as a soldier at his own expense,* citing that passage from Deuteronomy 25: *You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain.* He says this was written for our sake, from which he adds: *If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?* By these words, he implied commutative justice. And in 1 Timothy 5, he says: *The priests who rule well are worthy of double honor.* He does not say "those who are good," lest anyone be deceived into thinking that honors and **benefices** <note>original: "præbendæ"; a church office that provides an income.</note> are owed to the persons themselves through justice solely for their own merits. Rather, he says *those who rule well*, so that we may learn that the benefit is given chiefly because of the office—as if by the rule of commutative justice. This follows the word of the same author in the same place: *He who works in the sanctuary eats the things of the sanctuary, and those who serve the altar participate with the altar.*

<margin>First confirmation.</margin>
¶ And this is confirmed by **Canon Law**. For in the chapter *Secundum Apostolum* regarding benefices, Pope Innocent III, citing these very words of Paul, says: *Since according to the Apostle, those who serve the altar ought to live from the altar, and he who is chosen for the burden ought not to be rejected from the reward,* it is clear by analogy that clerics ought to live from the patrimony <note>Inheritance or property.</note> of Jesus Christ, to whose service they are assigned. Added to this is the phrase now most solemn in all of law: *A benefice is not given except for the office.* (From the title on Rescripts, final chapter). Therefore, the goods of the church are not established in view of persons as rewards for their virtues and learning—as if they were to be assigned to them through mere **distributive justice** <note>original: "distributiuam iustitiam"; justice concerned with distributing honors or resources based on merit or status.</note>—but in truth as the

<column-break/>

ministers' wages for the service rendered to the churches. From this, we shall later infer that the quality of those to be chosen and the weight of their merits are to be weighed not absolutely, but in relation to their province and function.

<margin>Second confirmation.</margin>
¶ To this is closely added that Christ gave to the church (as held in Ephesians 4) some as Apostles, others as Pastors and Teachers, etc., *for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.* Therefore, ecclesiastics receive support and stipends from the people as ministers. However, this conclusion must be revisited when, in the following book under the title "On Restitution," we bring into dispute whether a person who offers a priesthood to someone while bypassing more worthy or worthy candidates (through "respect of persons") owes restitution for the damage—and whether to the churches or to the bypassed persons themselves.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion regarding the title of the question: **Respect of persons** <note>Favoritism or partiality.</note> in spiritual matters is, by its very nature, a **mortal sin**; and it is more serious and pestilent the more spiritual things excel over temporal things. This conclusion is too clear to need many testimonies. For under the name of spiritual things are counted ecclesiastical priesthoods, by which the Christian commonwealth is promoted toward eternal happiness. Indeed, through the ministry of priests, Christians are initiated into the sacred mysteries, through which they both enter into and recover divine grace, and by their help and aid they cultivate that same grace. Therefore, since nothing concerns us so much as being promoted toward the glory of God through that same grace, nothing can be more present for our destruction than that crime by which we are either hindered or delayed in this progress—which is exactly what "respect of persons" is in the choosing of such priests and ministers.

¶ Nevertheless, since it is not enough to condemn this kind of favoritism unless the merits of those to be chosen are explained:

<margin>Instruction of St. Thomas.</margin>
It must be noted with **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the highly influential Catholic theologian.</note> that the merits and excellence of anyone’s dignity can be considered in two ways: namely, either absolutely and simply according to the individual person (just as **Aristotle** in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 3, considers the "good man");

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Or in a second way, just as he considers the "good citizen" there: for instance, if you contemplate a person in relation to that duty, magistracy, and function to which they are being admitted.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, let the fourth conclusion be: The dignity of a person must be weighed and required in relation to the specific end <note>The goal or purpose.</note> which is the target of the election. This is most clear, because the rationale for the means must be taken from the end; and in 1 Corinthians 12, the Apostle says, *To each is given the manifestation*...

<summary>Soto argues that church offices are "wages" for service rather than rewards for personal holiness, meaning candidates must be chosen based on their fitness for the specific role. He concludes that showing favoritism in spiritual appointments is a mortal sin because it endangers the eternal salvation of the community.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...manifestation of the spirit for the common benefit: namely, for the advantage of the Christian commonwealth.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ To this is added the fifth conclusion. The first and most important quality to be evaluated in one who is to be placed in charge of the people in spiritual matters is the composure of their character and the ornament of their virtues. We will establish this same conclusion regarding other civil magistrates in the following sections, for it is common to all; however, it holds its primary strength regarding ecclesiastical prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops.</note>,

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
the reason for which is most evident. Indeed, the immediate goal of civil magistrates is only natural: namely, to preserve the commonwealth in a state of tranquility and peace, although that goal is also ordered toward divine happiness. However, the immediate goal and aim of spiritual prelates is eternal happiness,

<margin>Paul.</margin>
and consequently, their duty is to be auxiliary ministers of Christ, according to the word of Paul: *Let a man so account of us as the ministers of Christ.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:1.</note> Therefore, they ought to have one care: to honor the blood of Christ, to promote His redemption, to provoke their subjects to divine love, and to refer all things to the charity of God. They should think of none of those things that perish with the world, but of those eternal things that await us in heaven. No one can care for these things and administer them with dignity unless the same blood of Christ glows within him, and the same love burns.

<margin>Sixth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Sixth conclusion. Besides charity and honesty of character, there is immediately required knowledge of sacred things, prudence, and skill, along with other strengths of mind and gifts necessary for governing—according to the word of the Lord: *Who, thinkest thou, is a faithful and wise servant?* <note>Matthew 24:45.</note> So much so that it is sometimes permissible, and even expedient for this reason, to pass over one who is simply superior in character and choose another of lower life, provided, however, that the person is not wicked or of corrupt morals. For if a man's life is contradictory to his office, no other reason is sufficient to make it lawful to move him to the helm of the church.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
This is clearly established. For it is the primary duty of a prelate to teach sacred things, and through their teaching and examples, to entice and promote their subjects toward the love of divine things. Furthermore, because governance is a work of prudence—as Aristotle states in the sixth book of his *Ethics*—and as he adds there, since all virtues are connected with prudence, a leader ought to excel in all such gifts. Indeed, just as nothing can give heat unless it is itself ignited, so no one can shine for others or stir the heat of virtue unless they burn with charity. ¶ But since a primary doubt is left in this place regarding these matters, namely whether,

<column-break/>

in order to avoid this crime of **respect of persons** <term>favoritism based on personal feelings rather than merit</term>, it is necessary to always choose the more outstanding and more worthy candidate,

<margin>Seventh conclusion.</margin>
the seventh conclusion is established. The "respect of persons" brings about a manifest crime when an unworthy person is chosen while a fit person is passed over. For then an impudent sin is committed against the church contrary to **commutative justice** <term>justice involving fair exchange or contracts</term>, and against the worthy candidate contrary to **distributive justice** <term>the fair allocation of rewards or honors</term>.

<margin>The conclusion is proven.</margin>
This conclusion is admitted by all without controversy. Thus, regarding the section on church prebends, in the chapter *Graue* <note>original: "cap. graue." A reference to a decree by Pope Alexander III.</note>, Alexander III says in council: *It is too grave and absurd that some prelates of churches, when they could promote fit men to ecclesiastical benefices, do not fear to take up the unworthy—those whom neither honesty of character nor knowledge of letters supports. They follow carnal affection rather than the judgment of reason; everyone of sound mind knows what great damage results for the churches from this.*

<margin>Eighth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The eighth conclusion is then woven in. For an election to be held as canonical, solid, and valid according to the external law of the court, it is enough to choose a worthy person. This conclusion is confirmed by the Canons cited in the third argument before this question; and for their reasoning,

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas and the Doctors give this explanation: otherwise, every single election would suffer from false accusations. For in such a court, the weights and moments of merit cannot be easily weighed in a balance to determine who is the absolute best. Therefore, when a King or anyone else by right of patronage chooses a worthy person against whom the laws do not speak, neither the Pope nor a lower prelate can destroy the election in favor of a "more worthy" candidate. I would add here that he who chooses a worthy person will not be held to **restitution** <term>the obligation to compensate for a loss or injury</term> either to the more worthy person or to the church, as we shall see in the following book under the title *On Restitution*.

<margin>Ninth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Ninth conclusion. Regarding guilt, in the **court of conscience** <term>the internal moral forum before God</term> and the court of heaven, it is commanded to choose the *more* worthy person. And first, let no one think this is the opinion of

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas alone, who asserts it unhesitatingly as a most settled matter in the *Summa Theologiae* <note>2. 2. question 63, article 2.</note> and in his *Quodlibetal Questions* <note>q. 6 and 8.</note>, whom his followers follow.

<margin>Alexander, part 2.</margin>
It was also the opinion of Alexander of Hales in part 2, question 136, section 2, and of Nicholas of Lyra on John 21. And not only of the two Mendicant orders, but also of

<margin>Nicholas of Lyra and Godefroid.</margin>
Henry and Godefroid in their *Quodlibetal Questions*.

<margin>Hadrian.</margin>
And it was the opinion of Hadrian, later Pope, in the matter of restitution, and from the

<margin>Henry.</margin>
doctors of Canon Law,

<margin>The Archdeacon.</margin>
the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous canonist.</note> and others.

<margin>Major.</margin>
Finally, John Mair <note>original: "Maioris"</note> followed these in book 4, distinction 24, question 8 and following. However, the patrons of the contrary opinion—if indeed they truly defend a contrary view—

<margin>Hugo, patron of the contrary opinion.</margin>
are Hugo <note>Hugo de Sancto Victore.</note> and the *Apparatus* <note>Standard legal glosses on the decretals.</note> on the chapter *Licet ergo* <note>8. q. 1.</note> and the chapter *Monasterium* <note>16. q. 7.</note>, whom Hadrian mentions...

<summary>Soto argues that while a "worthy" candidate is legally sufficient for a church office to avoid litigation, moral duty (the court of conscience) requires selecting the "most worthy" person based on both character and skill. He emphasizes that spiritual leadership requires both burning charity and practical prudence.</summary>

### Question VI of the Third Book

<margin>Johannes Andreas</margin>
Johannes Andreas <note>original: "Ioãnes Andreas"; a famous 14th-century expert in Canon Law.</note> joined the opinion of Hadrian. I would say that if they hold the contrary view, it is perhaps because they only contend that in the **external forum** <note>The public legal court of the Church.</note>, an election is not to be overturned; for they ought to have decided nothing concerning the **internal forum** <note>The "court of conscience," or one's standing before God.</note>. But if the opinion of Saint Thomas [Aquinas] is true, it cannot be abolished by any disuse or contrary custom. For it belongs to **divine law**, against which no length of time can offer a legal defense <note>original: "praescribit"; referring to the legal concept of prescription, where a right is gained or lost over time.</note>; indeed, the longer an abuse of it has lasted, the more grievous the crime becomes. In these matters, it is not enough to simply count the number of authors or to say, "The Canonists hold this, but the Theologians hold that." Rather, the authorities of the sacred writings must be heard and the reasons must be examined.

<margin>First reason in favor of the first opinion.</margin>
¶ First, the argument is made from **natural law**. Ecclesiastical benefices (as we asserted in the second conclusion) were instituted from the common goods of the people as stipends, and offered to the ministers of the church. Therefore, on this part, whoever does not provide the best minister for the church, without fraud or deceit, breaks faith with the people and the church in a way that violates **commutative justice** <note>The justice governing fair exchange between parties.</note>. Furthermore, he also sins against **distributive justice** <note>The justice governing how a society distributes honors or goods based on merit.</note>. The same virtue that commands one to maintain a proportion in rewards based on merit also advises that the best person who can be found through reasonable diligence should be preferred over others.

<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
¶ Second, it follows that prelates <note>High-ranking church officials.</note> are bound to confer benefices freely (*gratis*). However, he who passes over the better person to confer a post on one less worthy is certainly moved by some other human cause; otherwise, he would not do it. Thus, he neither gives it freely, nor remains free from the **respect of persons** <note>original: "acceptione personarũ"; favoritism or partiality based on personal bias rather than merit.</note>.

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
¶ To this, whoever confers a richer priesthood on the less worthy of two priests clearly violates distributive justice through the "respect of persons." For they could not do this unless they were looking at the person—that is, some quality outside the merits of the case. Therefore, the same stain would contaminate one who adjudicates even a single benefice to an unsuitable person.

<margin>Fourth [reason].</margin>
¶ Furthermore, the givers of these gifts are **stewards** <note>original: "dispensatores".</note>, as Paul says in 
<margin>Paul, 1 Corinthians 4.</margin>
the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 4: "ministers of the mysteries of God." In these, as he adds there, sincere faith is required according to the quoted word of the Lord: *Who, think you, is the faithful and wise steward?* A prince’s treasurer or steward who did not recruit the best possible servants for the same salary into his master’s service would surely be guilty of either a breach of faith or a neglect of prudence.

¶ Indeed, it is **divine law** that builds a firmer faith in this conclusion. First and foremost is the example of Christ in John 21, in the choosing of Peter, which reveals the matter abundantly. Truly He, who could do no injury to anyone—since He was not a mere steward but the Lord of all things—

<column-break/>

did not select anyone else to succeed Him as His **vicar** <note>A representative or deputy.</note> except the best of all the Apostles at that time. Nor did He think it enough to appoint him whom He Himself knew to be the most outstanding; rather, He willed that this be made known to everyone beforehand. For this reason only, as I believe, He publicly asked Peter three times whether he loved Him more than the others (a number that is solemn in judicial warnings), so that it might be clear to all that He was choosing the best by right and order. He did this to teach them to keep the same law most holily in similar elections.

¶ For this reason, I am accustomed to assert without any hesitation that at that moment in time when Peter was chosen as Christ’s vicar, he was the best of all the Apostles. I do not think it safe to deny this. For it is clear that only the **Charity of God** <note>Divine love/grace.</note> is the standard by which one may judge degrees of goodness before God. Furthermore, it cannot be denied that a person is loved by God to the same degree that they love God. If, therefore, Peter loved Christ more than the other Apostles then, he was also loved more by Him, and thus he was the best. That he loved Christ more than the others at that time cannot be doubted, since Christ’s questioning did not arise from doubt (as He Himself was not bound by it), but was like an assertion. And although Peter could not answer the comparison without rashness (since he was the weigher of neither his own merits nor those of others), Christ nevertheless accepted his response, "You know that I love you," as a comparative answer following His own question. Therefore, immediately after the third response, He added, "Feed my lambs." I say he stood as the "best" simply at that time; for nothing prevents John from being loved more tenderly, or perhaps at another time he might have been better. As for the **immaculate Virgin**, it would be a sin to hesitate: she far surpassed all the Apostles in merit.

<margin>Second passage on the same point.</margin>
¶ In the second place, the Apostolic testimony is added from 1 Timothy 3: *He who desires the office of a bishop, desires a good work.* This means he should see to it carefully how much of a burden he imposes on himself, because it is the best of all duties in the church, and therefore the most difficult to govern. Hence he adds: *A Bishop then must be blameless, etc.* Here he requires such an ample and rich store of virtues from a Bishop that, although he makes no explicit comparison, those virtues could hardly be heaped together except in one who is most excellent. Therefore, further down in chapter 5, he warns the same disciple to "lay hands suddenly on no man." Where furthermore...

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

He teaches how much examination ought to precede the distribution of priesthoods of this kind: as much as possible, for the sake of human fragility, it should imitate that final judgment <note>The Last Judgment by God at the end of time.</note> where everyone is measured by the most just scale of their merits.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
¶ In the third place, Canon Law and the decrees of the holy fathers are added. First among these is Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> on Leviticus, chapter 8, which is cited in the Church law <note>original: "8. q. 1. cap. licet ergo"</note>. For he recounts there the history of the Levites: that when Aaron was anointed as priest by God's command, the entire crowd was gathered before the doors of the tabernacle. Regarding these words, Jerome says that although the Lord had commanded the appointment of the leader and had specifically chosen him, the Congregation was still called together. Therefore, he says, the presence of the people is required in the ordaining of a priest, so that everyone may know and be certain that the one who is chosen for the priesthood is the most outstanding among all the people, the most learned, the most holy, and the most eminent in every virtue. This is done with the people as witnesses, according to the words of Paul: "Moreover, he must also have a good testimony from those who are outside" <note>1 Timothy 3:7</note>. These are Jerome's words. And this is an allusion to the example of Christ, who bore witness to the excellence of Peter in the presence of the Apostles. However, despite this insistence of Jerome’s words, Hugo tempers his opinion there—indeed, he denies it—saying it is enough to choose a worthy person. The *Apparatus* <note>A standard legal commentary on the Decretals.</note> adheres to this. Nevertheless, unless they understand this to apply only to the external court <note>term: <term>external forum</term> — the public legal system of the Church, as opposed to the internal court of conscience before God.</note>, they should not be listened to against the text.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
There are also the very harsh words of Augustine on the cited word of James, saying: "It is not to be thought a light sin to hold the faith of the Lord of glory with partiality toward persons." For who could endure a rich man being chosen for the seat of honor in the glory of the church, while a poor man who is more learned and more holy is despised? Listen to that phrase: "to the seat of honor in the glory of the church."

<margin>Pope Leo</margin>
Pope Leo also agrees in the canon "Metropolitano," distinction 63, where he teaches that the best man <note>original: "optimus"</note> is the one to be chosen.

<margin>Chrysostom</margin>
But there is the opinion of Chrysostom in book 2 of *On the Priesthood*, which is most of all to be meditated upon. For he admonishes ecclesiastical pastors by their very name, that they ought to stand before their flock with as great a distance in merit as the excellence of a shepherd stands before his cattle.

<margin>Bernard</margin>
In line with this opinion, Bernard in *On Consideration* to Pope Eugene piles up many such excellent points.

<margin>dimi.</margin>
To these is joined a single and illustrious chapter, *Extra, ut ecclesiastica benef. licet di. conf.* <note>A reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding church benefices.</note>, where, in a rebuke of a Bishop, it is stated that he ought to have distributed ecclesiastical benefices to the more suitable person, not out of carnal affection, but by strict judgment.

<column-break/>

<margin>Council of Basel</margin>
Furthermore, in the pragmatic acts of the Council of Basel, the following form of the oath for electors is found:

> I, [Name], swear and promise to Almighty God and to the Saint in whose name this church is dedicated, to choose the one whom I believe to be better in both spiritual and temporal matters.

And not only Canon Law, but also Imperial Law <note>The civil laws of the Roman/Byzantine Empire, specifically the Code of Justinian.</note> warns of the same thing most holily, as can be seen in the *Authenticum* regarding monks. Indeed, the Emperor commands that he who first appears to be the best among the monks should be placed in charge as pastor. If the best monk is to be appointed, surely the same rule must be observed much more holily regarding bishops, whose order is made more excellent than the institution of monks. But if these arguments held their force even in the early days of the church, when it was strong with illustrious people, how much greater is their force now, when we suffer from such a scarcity of people that choice is hardly permitted? Indeed, one can barely find a worthy man except for the most worthy. In the time of Augustine, Ambrose, Martin, Nicholas, and that breed of mortals, it might not have been a monstrous crime not to seek out the more worthy; but now, so that you might grant it to a worthy man, you must seek out the most worthy, so much has everything fallen into decay.

<margin>Final reason.</margin>
¶ And even if no arguments existed from what has been done, this point proves the matter inescapably: that as long as an exact account of merits is not maintained in the distribution of benefices, there is no one who will pursue the study of letters, and no one who will be imbued with any other character than what is most suited to the Curia <note>The papal court and administration in Rome.</note>. Hence, the great losses that have grown for the church of Christ, founded by his blood, and the plagues of heresies and the neglect of souls bear witness most openly.

<margin>First limitation of the conclusion.</margin>
¶ But before we establish my conclusion, it is worthwhile to clear up several small doubts that emerge from this. First, we do not contend to cast fearful souls into such narrow straits that when the change of office for which a person is chosen is of little consequence, it should be considered a mortal sin to pass over the more worthy candidate. Likewise, such a sin is not to be feared even in matters of greater importance when the excess of merits is not so great that it seems to matter much to the business; for just as stealing a tiny coin is not a mortal sin, God does not compel us to explore people so anxiously, but rather according to prudence, in proportion to the quality and condition of the matter.

<margin>Second [limitation].</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is especially to be noted that we should not look to causes of "metaphysical possibility," but, as moral matter requires, to that which is hoped for in the future according to prudence.

# Book Three, Question VI.

...indeed, even if a man appears who is most distinguished in letters and conspicuous in prudence, yet he is sluggish or entangled in other business, there is not as much hope that he will preach or govern according to his talents. Or perhaps even if he is of excellent character, he is nonetheless unfit for public business. Such men should certainly be passed over for one who, though not as powerful in these gifts, is expected to be more solicitous in care and to apply diligence to executing his office. The outcomes of the matter which follow beyond the hope of the electors do not invalidate the election; for instance, if one who was believed to be diligent is later found to be negligent.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
¶ An argument against this ninth conclusion emerges from the above. It was said that <term>distributive justice</term> <note>Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of honors and resources within a community based on merit.</note> in these priesthoods is referred to <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Commutative justice concerns the fairness of exchanges or fulfilling specific duties/debts between individuals.</note>. When a prelate grants a parish or other ministry to a worthy person in proportion to their tithes <note>The tenth of income paid to the church.</note>, because they have meager subsidies, he satisfies commutative justice through that person. Therefore, he is not then bound to choose another who possesses more abundant merits.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
Two things are answered. First, the logic of distributive justice would not then be preserved, unless perhaps a richer <term>prebend</term> <note>A portion of church revenue granted to a member of the clergy.</note> were expected shortly for that more worthy person. Second, as for commutative justice, since the dignity of a person does not have a fixed, prescribed measure, it happens that where another is more worthy, an inferior person is hardly to be considered "worthy" at all. Moreover, the faith of a dispenser of Christ’s ministries demands that he assign the best minister to any church from those who can be had for that stipend. For if the church could speak, she would choose such a person. Although this fault is not so great as to require restitution <note>The legal or moral obligation to pay back or compensate for a loss or error.</note> if a person who is estimated as "worthy" is chosen, as we said above.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ From here a second argument arises against the same ninth conclusion, which would follow from it: that an elector would sometimes be "perplexed" <note>In scholastic philosophy, "perplexed" refers to a moral dilemma where any choice seems to lead to an error.</note>. For example: with two vacant <term>benefices</term> <note>A church office that provides an income.</note>, the wealthier and "fatter" one having no care of souls attached to it, while the other, though barren in income, has it attached, or has more parishioners under it who are in greater need of teaching. For instance, when the Church of Toledo <note>Toledo was the wealthiest and most prestigious see in Spain.</note>—which is most opulent—is vacant, and at the same time the Church of Granada <note>Granada was a poorer diocese but had many "neophytes" or "New Christians"—former Muslims recently converted to Christianity who required intense instruction.</note> is vacant, which although poorer, has many new converts from Muhammadanism <note>original: "Mahometiſmo" (Islam)</note>, then both the Pope and the King would be perplexed. For if you look at distributive justice, the one which is richer ought to be attributed to the more worthy person; but if you look at the public necessity of the Church, the greater care of souls ought rather to be entrusted to him.

<margin>Response.</margin>
To this it is answered that the account of public necessity must always be held in higher regard, to which the charity of Christ

<column-break/>

binds us more strictly. And therefore the care of souls is to be commended to the more worthy person, and he is not considered to suffer loss to his dignity thereby. For even if presbyters who rule well are, on Paul's authority, worthy of "double honor" <note>1 Timothy 5:17</note>, nonetheless that honor which awaits us before God must be valued first of all—most especially because (as was said) these priesthoods were instituted for the benefit of the churches. Whether that more worthy person would be bound to accept it is a matter of another dispute. Yet the necessity could be so great that he would be bound.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ But from this, another doubt arises: whether this law of choosing the more worthy extends even to those who are already placed in their churches. Namely, when a most "fat" <note>A "fat" (pinguiśśimū) benefice is one that provides a very high income.</note> benefice or bishopric is vacant, should the King and the Pope move people from their current places so that everyone is elevated by degrees? For this seems to agree with the ninth conclusion.

<margin>Dilution.</margin>
It is answered that no certain rule can be established concerning this matter. Indeed, these changes and "ascents" which might be made must be especially guarded against: first, because they provide fuel for ambition. For they cause the minds of bishops to always be hanging in suspense, and—like primary matter <note>A philosophical concept: matter that has no form of its own and is always seeking to become something else.</note>—never content with their own form. For this reason, they can neither hold their "bride" <note>A common metaphor for the relationship between a bishop and his diocese.</note> dear, nor have just care for her. Second, because a pastor's age should not be spent in getting to know and then changing new flocks over and over. But on the other hand, this must not be avoided too excessively, since it is sometimes expedient and fitting for a bishop to migrate to another see. For the title "Concerning the Postulation of Prelates" <note>original: "de postula. prælat." - a section of Canon Law governing the transfer of bishops.</note> is not in vain.

<margin>Another doubt concerning elections.</margin>
¶ After these things follows a doubt about elections, whether when religious <note>Members of monastic orders.</note> and Canons elect a prelate, or when scholars elect a public lecturer for a Chair <note>A university teaching position.</note>: whether each person is always bound to elect the better candidate, even if he sees that he will accomplish nothing with his vote. To this it is answered that in elections, one must always keep in mind that a "vain work" <note>A useless or empty action.</note> is not a work of charity; and therefore all laws must be applied to morals by the judgment of prudence.

<margin>Response.</margin>
Let this be the first response. No one ought to give their vote <note>original: "calculo" - literally a pebble used for voting.</note> to an unworthy person, even if it is clear that he is desired by all the rest; because such a person is only thrust forward through wickedness, and he must be favored with no pretense, nor should he be assented to. If, however, the one who is hoped to be elected is worthy, then it is permitted and fitting to pass over the "most worthy" who cannot be elected, so that a "worthier" one may be elected. Suppose there are three: Peter is the most worthy, Paul is in the middle, and John is at the bottom. If I persist in Peter, and he himself...

# Friar Dominic de Soto, On Justice and Right,

neither Paul nor John will be chosen: but if I side with Paul, he himself will win. Therefore, I ought to follow this plan, even if I have bound myself by an oath to choose the more worthy <note>Latin: *digniorem*</note>. For an oath is understood to apply among those choices that are possible. However, in this and similar cases where such a conflict does not exist, the more worthy candidate must always be chosen. For besides the fact that honor must be preserved for him and dignity for the law, it is also useful so that the elected man may be reminded that the electors were fair to him. In this way, he will become more cautious in his governance.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, an argument immediately presents itself against these points: if the more worthy person were always to be chosen, it would follow that if a less worthy person accepted the election, he would sin just as much as the grantor <note>The *collator*, or the official who bestows the office.</note>, since he appears to be the cause of an illicit act.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this, however, it is answered that the reasoning is not equal. For the burden of care in granting the office does not rest upon the recipient; for that reason, he is not considered the cause of an unfair grant in the same way as the one who bestows it. This is especially true if he is indeed worthy <note>He may be "worthy" even if he is not the "most worthy" of all possible candidates.</note>. In fact, in a doubtful matter, he is not bound to examine himself, but rather the one who bestows the office must do so. Therefore, although it is a crime to solicit a bishopric <note>The term used is *ambire*, referring to the sin of "ambition" or campaigning for high office.</note>, an office that is offered may be accepted without fault. Indeed, although someone might give alms while ignoring the proper order of charity—not to a needy father, but to a stranger, or by squandering it on actors while passing by the poor, and thus commits a sin—those who receive the money are not ensnared in that same sin.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Next, an argument is made by another path from the chapter *Monasterium* (16, question 7), which states that where a lord has established an Oratory or a Chaplaincy, he may give it to any priest. Therefore, it is argued: a person can establish a priesthood under the law that it should fall forever only to his own relatives or to another designated lineage. Since any owner of any goods can dispense them according to his own will, in such a case it is not necessary—indeed, it is not permitted—to seek out the more worthy candidate.

<margin>Solution of some.</margin>
¶ There are those who say that even in such a case, more worthy candidates ought to be sought outside that family if necessary.

<margin>Rejection.</margin>
However, both custom and reason cry out to the contrary. For it is sufficient to choose the more excellent person from among those designated and called, unless there is only one, such as the person named as the closest relative. Since the founder and institutor is not bound to make a distribution as part of his public duty and office, and since those are his own goods, he is not strictly bound to take account of the more worthy candidate in the wider sense.

<margin>Hostiensis and the Abbot.</margin>
Yet there was no reason why Hostiensis <note>Henry of Susa (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canon lawyer.</note> and the Abbot <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), also known as Panormitanus, a famous commentator on the Decretals.</note> should draw a forced argument from this very different text regarding the distribution of the common goods of the church—

<column-break/>

namely, that it is always enough to choose a worthy person.

<margin>Two qualifications of the cited text.</margin>
Two qualifications of that text must be kept in mind here. First, if the person who has been designated is entirely unworthy, another must be substituted. This is because no one, not even from his own substance, can create a priesthood contrary to natural and divine law. The second is that if that institution has some <term>care of souls</term> <note>Latin: *cura animarum*, referring to pastoral responsibilities like hearing confessions or preaching.</note> or governance attached to it, then the rule is most unjust and not to be tolerated insofar as it prevents a more worthy person from being chosen. For example, if someone were to found a monastery with his own income under the condition that the Prior or Abbess could only be created from his own kin or homeland, that law should not be observed to the insult of the Gospel.

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, a doubt arises here concerning patrimonial benefits, to which only citizens or those born in that place are admitted. This seems to detract from the opinion of the ninth conclusion, since more excellent candidates could sometimes be summoned from elsewhere.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that those laws are most equitable. I wish the Church would sanction them everywhere, at least regarding parochial benefits to which the care of souls is attached—just as was being deliberated, in my presence, at the <term>Council of Trent</term> <note>The great reforming council of the Catholic Church (1545–1563). Soto was a major theological advisor there.</note> with the highest consensus of everyone. For it would be in conformity with those decrees summoned in the fourth argument, which decreed that the election should be made from the same church. For as I was just saying, the innate love that everyone has for their native soil is of no small value. Above all, although more excellent outsiders could sometimes be found in terms of merit, it would be much more conducive for the church to avoid the most troublesome and pestilential ambitions and lawsuits; furthermore, it would encourage the inhabitants, through that hope, to educate their children in both letters and morals.

<margin>A commonplace question.</margin>
¶ These doubts having been resolved, let us descend to the tenth conclusion, by which we may answer that common question: which faculty should be preferred over the other in choosing a bishop—namely, <term>Canon Law</term> or <term>Theology</term>? Truly, there was no reason why this assertion should be called into controversy; but Hostiensis, whom the Abbot of Palermo followed in the chapter on consanguinity and affinity, was the one who, by what right I know not, contested this dispute. For they say that where heresies are sprouting, a Theologian is to be preferred to a Jurist; but elsewhere, it is the other way around. And although my own profession <note>Soto was a Dominican Theologian.</note> might lead me into suspicion on this matter, the truth of the thing must not be hidden, especially in these times. For I am not at all unaware of how much I myself lack such merits. ¶ Primarily, if my opinion were that of...
