### Book Three, Question VI.

...were of such weight that it ought to be admitted into counsel, I would prefer that, after moral integrity, a man's prudence, strength of mind marked by gentleness, and dexterity in active affairs be weighed more than eminence in knowledge: provided that he possesses that moderate level of learning which would add the weight of authority to him. Therefore, the person is to be valued above all, not this or that faculty of knowledge. Even though he in whom all these things were illustrated by excellence of learning would by greater right be raised upon the lampstand of the Church. 

<margin>The tenth conclusion.</margin>
¶ But nevertheless, all other things being equal, that Theology is the peculiar science of a Bishop—which we here make the **tenth conclusion**—I do not know who would doubt. For to begin from the very name of "pastor" <note>Latin: *pastor*, meaning shepherd.</note>, which is proper to a Bishop, who could doubt that the chief duty of a shepherd is to reflect upon and meditate by revolving the sacred utterances, from which he may provide the fodder of doctrine to the flock. 

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
This is the opinion of Jerome in his commentary on Leviticus (and in the Decrees, Distinction 36, canon "si quis"), where he says: "There are two works of a pontiff: to learn from God by reading the divine scriptures and by frequent meditation, and to teach the people." And in Distinction 38, canon "omnes," the Prelate <term>Antistes</term> <note>A high-ranking priest or bishop.</note> is admonished to have the law at the ready: namely, both the sacred Canons and the holy Gospel, as well as the divine book of the Apostles and all divine scripture. That is, the Canons of the Councils, 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
as is immediately added in the chapter "placuit." Whence Augustine, in his 59th epistle to Paulinus, regarding that passage of Paul to the Ephesians ("And he gave some as pastors and teachers"), treats them as the same: namely, that Bishops are pastors for the very reason that they are teachers. And why not? Are they not the successors of the Apostles? Therefore, it is their proper duty to teach the people the faith which they themselves first spread, to compose their morals according to evangelical norms, and, like dogs, to bark tirelessly against vices. But why do we use unnecessary witnesses in a matter that is not in doubt?

<margin>First reason for the conclusion. Richard of Middleton. Sylvester Prierias.</margin>
In the past, when they were being marked with the mitre <term>infula</term> <note>The headband or ritual head-covering symbolizing the office.</note>, they were not asked whether they knew both laws <note>The *ius utrumque*, meaning both Canon Law and Civil Law.</note>, but whether they knew both Testaments: as Richard of Middleton and Sylvester Prierias have noted. Although now that things have collapsed, they are only asked if they wish to accommodate themselves to the senses of Divine Scripture and to teach the people what they have drawn from it. As a sign of this, the Gospel is conferred upon them, which they are admonished to preach to the people committed to them.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Add to this that among the ancient bishops, you will find none who was not a theologian. For theologians enacted the canon laws in the councils, and the Supreme Pontiffs collected them from the sacred oracles. Therefore, if you look at the etymology of the name, which Augustine (as cited in Case 8, Question 1, chapter "qui episcopatum") interpreted: namely,

<column-break/>

that "bishop" is the same as "superintendent": in this also he ought to superintend the canon law, even if he does not hold it all in his memory. Indeed, since ecclesiastical law flowed from Theology, the legitimate senses of the canons ought to be examined through that same faculty. Especially since those laws which relate to any episcopal duty ought to be understood more clearly and sharply by Theologians, provided they are powerful in the knowledge that matches their name. But if they are less skilled in law, it is much more worthy of a bishop—as one reads of Moses in Exodus 18—to appoint suitable men to hear secular cases, so that he himself may devote himself to sacred meditation and Christian doctrine, rather than, conversely, being torn away from the sweetness of Scripture to become entangled in secular affairs. 

¶ See, therefore, how far they wander from the mark who think the duty of a bishop is nothing else than to extirpate heresies: since there are other things besides those much more peculiar to them than hearing court cases. This is especially true because, if they are necessary when heresies are sprouting, it follows that they are always necessary so that such things are never brought forth. There are surgeons and lawyers who, since they live off litigation, would not want the causes of quarrels to be cut short. But the episcopal care ought to be far different: namely, that the people were always so instructed in faith and composed in morals that they left no handle for either heresies or lawsuits. 

Therefore, not only where heresies sprout, but where lawsuits creep in through sloth, a theologian-bishop would be more desirable there, or certainly a man marked by integrity, who would settle and cut short lawsuits without the long-winded technicalities of the law. For I see, alas, more lawsuits fostered in the ecclesiastical court than in the civil: whereas the whole effort of a bishop ought to be to mend the internal consciences of men, to pull up the weeds of discord, and not to extend his care so far as to strike with the death-blow of excommunication boys stealing apples and figs from gardens (because this is the "beech-mast" <note>Latin: *fagina*. This refers to the trivial "food" or "pickings" that low-level officials profit from through fines and fees.</note> of officials). This is so absurd that ecclesiastical judges now have no excuse for such a purpose, except to claim they do not intend the excommunication to be binding.

<margin>Final reason.</margin>
But for this reason also they ought to be Theologians, so that they might know how much greater account they must hold lest they strike the people with the crime of disobedience through excommunication: for although the person who does not know it nonetheless wounds his conscience when he does not obey even a feigned excommunication. But enough of this for the present. For I see even Theologian-bishops going down the same path.

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,

to have a regard for churches, rather than a distributive one <note>This refers to "distributive justice," which governs how a community divides honors or wealth among its members based on merit.</note>.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ A response was given to the second point during the proof of the ninth conclusion: there we demonstrated that Christ was so far from the "acceptance of persons" <note>Latin: *personarum acceptio*, meaning partiality or favoritism.</note> that he chose Peter, who was then the best of the Apostles and most suited for governance. Furthermore, he rejected the mother of the sons of Zebedee when she asked for seats at his right and left for her sons. As for why he summoned common men, unlearned in letters, to the evangelical function, there was a two-fold cause. First, because he himself could both teach them and make them into the kind of men suitable for the task. Human electors, however, because they cannot make those they choose worthy, must seek out for election those whom they find already worthy. Next, because it was expedient that the supernatural faith not be promulgated by men who were illustrious in human doctrine, lest it fall under the suspicion of proceeding from human science. For this reason, they were commanded not to think about how or what they should speak before kings and governors, but to broadcast those things which the Holy Spirit suggested. Moreover, that he preferred Galileans to other mortals was a mystery about which Isaiah had prophesied; Matthew (chapter 4) cited his prophecy: *The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, etc., Galilee of the Gentiles. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.* And David said: *The princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali* (for these were part of <margin>To the third.</margin> Galilee) *are their leaders.* ¶ To the third point, which seemed intended against the ninth conclusion, satisfaction was likewise given when we conceded that according to the "external forum" <note>The public realm of Church law and social appearance.</note> it is enough for an office to be conferred upon a worthy person to cut off slanders; but it is otherwise in the "internal forum" <note>The realm of conscience and God’s direct judgment.</note>. 

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, he responds that the laws have decreed that dignities and prebends <term>prebends</term> <note>A portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church, granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note> be granted to persons of the same church for this <margin>Celestine.</margin> reason (as Pope Celestine says in chapter *nullus*, distinction 61): so that each person may have the fruit of his service in the church in which he has spent his age through all the offices. To this, <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> St. Thomas joins another reason, which I find most approved: namely, that every person has a much more inclined mind toward his own city and the church in which he was nourished; by which reasoning he will surely be more useful. Hence, Deuteronomy 17 says: *You may not make a man of another nation king, who is not your brother.* And therefore, even if a stranger might be more worthy, a compensation is made through these factors.

<margin>To the fifth argument.</margin>
¶ However, the fifth argument shakes everything that has been said. For if the opinion of certain people is true—not to call it flattery, which the most holy Pope should never be believed to have assented to—namely, that he is the "Lord" <note>Latin: *dominus*, implying absolute ownership.</note> of benefits, a most forceful argument is constructed from this: that he is not bound to choose the more worthy; indeed, that he can

<column-break/>

grant dispensations regarding this with inferior prelates. The response, therefore, is none other than that he is in no way the "Lord." Otherwise, truly, just as it is said of one who creates a priesthood out of his own private goods, it would be free for him, as a true owner, to confer it upon whomsoever he preferred—which no one would dare to assert. But no argument is needed where the Apostolic trumpet sounds: *Thus let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.* (1 Corinthians 4). Indeed, Christ says in Luke 12: *Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward, whom the Lord has set over his household?* 

¶ Nor do the sacred Canons deviate a fingernail's breadth from this Gospel, because they cannot deviate. Therefore, it will not be tedious to hear the words of the law here. Regarding prebends (*Liber Sextus*, Book 3, Title 4, Chapter 2), it is held thus: *Although the full disposal of churches, personages, dignities, and other ecclesiastical benefits is known to belong to the Roman Pontiff.* It does not say "lordship" <note>Latin: *dominium*.</note>, but "full disposal" <note>Latin: *plenaria dispositio*, the power to manage or arrange.</note>. And in the *Clementines* (concerning litigation, chapter *si duobus*): *Saving, however, in all the premises, the power of the Roman Pontiff, to whom the full and free disposal of churches, personages, dignities, and other ecclesiastical benefits is known to belong from the fullness of his power.* See, therefore, how far the "fullness of the pontifical power" reaches: certainly not so that he is the owner, but so that he has the full management. For, when it says "free," this only signifies that he recognizes no superior on earth. The same is clear from the points above. For we have left it demonstrated that these ecclesiastical goods are the stipends of the people for their ministers, of which the Pope is therefore the mere steward. 

¶ Indeed, I believe those who call him the "Lord of benefits" are ignorant of their own words. For if he is the Lord, he can retain them for himself, and convert them to his own private uses, and use them at his whim; which, however, no one of sound mind will admit. If, however, he cannot use them at his whim, but is bound by reason to distribute them, he is not <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> the Lord. Wherefore St. Thomas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 63, article 2), where he says the ecclesiastical prelate is not the owner but the steward, includes even the Supreme Pontiff; as <margin>Cajetan.</margin> Cardinal Cajetan, the Pope's personal advisor, skillfully noted. But alas, what great evils the Church daily suffers from the contrary and false principle! Since, however, the most holy Pope excels others in honor and dignity in the Church of God, he is bound by a stronger bond to [choose] the more worthy...

# Book Three. Question VI.

to always desire the best. Unless perhaps—to respond to the conclusion of the fourth argument—the Cardinals are bound by a more sacred obligation in the election of the Pope, due to the supreme dignity of the Vicar of Christ, to choose the absolute best candidate. 

<margin>It is false that a Pope cannot be elected if he is outside the College of Cardinals.</margin> 
For this reason, I could never convince myself of that rumor: namely, that it is a fixed rule among them that they cannot choose anyone from outside their own circle. And indeed, I have heard from the Lord Cardinals themselves that this is false. To be sure, there was a most fitting reason for the Church to grant the active votes <note>Latin: *activas voces*; the legal right to cast a vote in an election.</note> to the sacred senate [the College of Cardinals]. This is seen in the Canon Law decree *In Nomine Domini* ("In the Name of the Lord") and the chapter *Licet* in the Decretals regarding elections; namely, to prevent such a large assembly of bishops from being forced to travel to Rome from the most distant regions for every election. However, since it is of such great importance to elevate the best bishop in the world to the highest seat, the idea that the election should be restricted to within a few paces of the city [Rome]—though it is believable that a worthy man will never be lacking among the Cardinals—is certainly not permitted by evangelical sincerity. Hence, in that chapter *In Nomine Domini*, it is commanded that if a suitable person is not found within the Roman church, one should be taken from another.

¶ Therefore, the ninth conclusion remains firmly rooted: that the rule of choosing the best must be kept sacredly, not only in appointing bishops but also in dispensing other priesthoods to which the care of souls <term>cura animarum; the spiritual responsibility for a congregation</term> is attached. For in other positions that lack such care, although a sin against distributive justice <note>The principle of dividing honors and resources based on merit rather than favoritism.</note> is committed by passing over worthier candidates, there is not as much danger. Indeed, for that reason, a mortal sin is either never or very rarely committed in those cases, provided the positions are not granted to the completely unworthy.

<margin>The first doubt concerning annual pensions.</margin>
¶ From this defined conclusion, several doubts seem to arise, which must be examined in order. The first depends on the words just mentioned regarding benefices <term>beneficium; a church office, like a parish or cathedral post, that provides an income or "living"</term> that lack the care of souls: namely, whether the annual pensions that have become common in the Church over the last fifty years can be safely imposed on benefices and received by those to whom they are granted. To this, it is first answered that pensions of this kind do not have ecclesiastical "titles" attached to them. This is because the pensioner does not become the owner of the benefice; rather, a burden of payment is simply imposed upon the person who does hold the office. This payment can be imposed either on the person for as long as they hold the office, or—as is much more frequent in practice—upon the very fruits <note>The "fruits" (fructus) refer to the annual income or revenue generated by the church property or tithes.</note> of the benefices. For this reason, these pensions have neither a spiritual care attached to them, nor a formal duty to perform the liturgy. On this basis, such incomes are considered very "safe" from a legal standpoint,

<column-break/>

precisely because they are not burdened with the care of souls. 
<margin>The author’s refinement of the proposed question.</margin>
I, however, although I have no doubt about the Pope’s full power in dispensing benefices, have always thought these are the most dangerous of all ecclesiastical incomes. I believe this for the very same reason others think they are the safest. For if it is true, as we were trying to show a little earlier, that the Supreme Pontiff is not the owner but the dispenser <note>Latin: *dispensator*; a steward or manager of property that belongs to another (God/the Church).</note> of benefices (which are the wages of the churches), it follows that he cannot award them except for the "ministry of the altar" (as the Apostle Paul says). They should be a reward for some service to the Church, even if it is not purely spiritual—for example, to a leader or soldier who defends the Church in a time of necessity (which is why a third of the tithes were granted to the King of Spain). And they could more fittingly be granted to those who conduct the business of the Church in a council, or at court, or elsewhere; just as it was once the custom to share a portion of the revenues with those who assisted the prelates <note>High-ranking clergy like bishops or abbots.</note>. Furthermore, when a legal dispute over a priesthood cannot be resolved otherwise, it is permissible to grant a portion to the party who steps down for the sake of peace. This is the only type of pension for which there is a specific text in the whole of Law (*Nisi essent* regarding prebends). But that outside of this case, without any title or obligation, the goods of the Church can be spent in this way—it is not clear how this stays within the limits of proper stewardship. Indeed, the novelty of this practice brings it under heavy suspicion.

<margin>The second doubt.</margin>
¶ The second doubt concerns those who neither elect nor confer benefices, but are nevertheless the cause of them being given to people of lesser merit or the completely unworthy. Is this a sin for them? A specific question is asked about "resigners." A person resigns his priesthood into the hands of a Prelate, but only in favor of a relative or another specific unworthy person, and not otherwise. It might seem that the one resigning is without fault, since it is the Prelate who actually performs the appointment.
<margin>Response.</margin>
However, it is answered that the Prelate's crime does not excuse the one resigning, since the resigner is the true cause of the unjust appointment.

<margin>Benefices should by no means be conferred on children.</margin>
¶ At this point, I will not omit a most serious warning: namely, how much care must be taken so that benefices are not given to children. For even if it happens that they have an excellent natural character, not only Canon Law but even Natural Law does not consider them worthy. For "dignity" refers not to hope [potential], but to the thing itself [actual merit]. Yet it very often happens that those who showed great promise as children—and who would have brought forth rich fruit if they had remained without ecclesiastical wealth—reach a...

### ARTICLE III.

#### Whether a plurality of benefices is permitted by law.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Linked to the previous article, we must dispute in this third article regarding the plurality of benefices <note>A "benefice" was a church office, such as a parish or a cathedral post, that came with a guaranteed income or "living."</note>, and whether it is permitted by law in any way. For many Canons <note>Church laws or decrees.</note>, both from Councils and from the Holy Fathers, fight against it from the negative side. First, there is the decree of the Seventh Synod of Constantinople, as reported in the Law (21. q. 1. cap. *clericus*): "From this moment forward, a cleric shall not be numbered in two churches; for this is characteristic of business dealings and base gain for personal advantage, and is foreign to the custom of the church." Here, the word of the Lord is cited: *No man can serve two masters* <note>Matthew 6:24</note>. And in Distinction 70, in the chapter *Sanctorum*, Pope Urban says: "It is absolutely not permitted to entitle anyone in two churches, but each person should be considered a canon <note>A member of the clergy serving a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> only in the one in which he is entitled." Hence, in the Decretals (*de præben. cap. quia*), it is stated that a multitude of prebends <note>The portion of church revenue granted to a canon.</note> is "inimical to the canons."

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
Secondly, the sayings of the saints are alleged by Saint Thomas [Aquinas] in his *Quodlibets* (9. art. 15). 
<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
For Chrysostom says: "That which the darkness blushed at, let the light blush at; what was not granted to the figure [the Old Testament], I believe to be illicit for the reality [the New Testament]." Now, regarding the "figure"—that is, the Old Law—it was not granted among the Levites that one who received his portion in Bethlehem should also receive one in Jerusalem. Since we, therefore, ought to be more perfect, let him who receives in Tyre not receive in Damascus. These are the words of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching.</note>. 
<margin>Bernard.</margin>
And Bernard [of Clairvaux] says: "He who is in multiple benefices will not be in one, but in multiple punishments."

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
Likewise, this practice seems to be against reason, natural law, and the divine law just cited: *No man can serve two masters.* To this is further added the oath by which, under ancient law, everyone binds their faith to serve the specific church to which they have committed themselves. ¶ On the contrary side are the laws which indulge several benefices to the same person, as shown in various places and frequently in the Canons (21. q. 1).

<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
Saint Thomas Aquinas discusses this question in the cited *Quodlibet* 9, article 15. But because the abuse of this matter has crept in too far to the ruin of the 

<column-break/>

Church, it will not be superfluous to examine the matter again and diligently. For since (as Saint Thomas says there) natural, divine, and human law are all entwined here, the definition of this matter belongs to the Theologians—although regarding the third part [human law], it pertains to the Jurists. Therefore, that distinction of Saint Thomas serves as our first foundation: There is a threefold order of actions. First, those which have an inseparable deformity, such as a lie. Second, those which are indifferent, such as taking a walk. Third, those which, although considered purely and absolutely in themselves, represent a certain deformity, yet when "clothed" in specific circumstances, they can be done lawfully—such as killing a man, which is permitted to a judge or to one defending himself.

¶ Having established these points, the question is answered with seven conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
**First.** To hold several prebends is not a matter of the first order [inherently evil]. 
<margin>Support for the conclusion.</margin>
This conclusion becomes clear because the sacred laws grant dispensations <note>Official exemptions from a rule or law.</note> for this in many cases, as will soon be evident.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
**Second.** Neither is it of the second order [indifferent]. 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
For it is not as indifferent as having several suits of clothes; for having clothes, considered absolutely, involves no wickedness or indecency. However, to hold several prebends, if viewed plainly, immediately suggests certain perversions of order. First, because reason teaches that for every ministry, its own proper minister should be appointed; otherwise, one person takes on the roles of many. Second, divine worship suffers detriment. Third, since these goods (as we have said) are the "stipends" of the churches, the churches are defrauded of their right. Use and experience prove this: indeed, with many prebends concentrated in a few people, hardly any church remains that is worthily served in proportion to its tithes. Fourth, from this follows a violation of distributive justice <note>The principle that social goods and offices should be distributed fairly based on merit.</note>: namely, that many worthy people are in need while others overflow. Fifth, it provides food and fuel for ambition; for if the accumulation of prebends were forbidden, priests would not thirst so greedily to be enriched by church goods. Sixth, it is the cause for which the study of literature lies neglected; for on both sides, the hope for reward is weakened—both because merit is not considered, and because the greedy avarice of the wealthy prevents the poor from being promoted. Indeed, seventh, it is a certain transgression of that Pauline rule... <note>Likely referring to the Apostle Paul's teachings on the focused duties of a minister or the laborer being worthy of his hire.</note>

<summary>This page debates the practice of "plurality"—clergymen holding multiple church offices and incomes simultaneously. Soto argues that while not inherently evil in all circumstances, it generally leads to the neglect of religious duties, greed, and a lack of opportunities for deserving but poor scholars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book Three, Question VI, regarding the legality and morality of "plurality"—the holding of multiple church offices (benefices) by a single person. The previous page established that while certain laws forbid holding multiple positions to prevent greed, the author is now exploring the specific legal exceptions and the moral nuances of this practice.</meta>

...of the apostolic precept: *Each one should remain in the calling in which he was called* <note>1 Corinthians 7:20</note>. And also that of Romans 12: *Just as in one body we have many members*, which Gregory cited for this purpose in Distinction 89, chapter *Singula*, where he says: "We command that the individual duties of ecclesiastical law be committed to individual persons separately." For just as in one body we have many members, yet all members do not have the same function, so in the body of the Church there are many members: and therefore the duties ought to be distinct, and churches should be entrusted to different persons; otherwise the whole body would be an eye, or the whole would be hearing, or one eye would serve many bodies.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
**Third conclusion.** To hold several prebends <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend for their service.</note> is a matter of the third order: that is, although considered in itself and in isolation it sounds like an evil (as the previous arguments proved), it can nonetheless be adorned with such circumstances that it becomes lawful.

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
For a clear understanding of this, it is worthwhile to distinguish between types of benefices. For some have residency attached to them; others are more free, such as simple priesthoods which are commonly called *praestameræ* <note>A term for minor church stipends that did not require the holder to live on-site or perform specific pastoral duties.</note>. And of those to which residency is attached, some have the care of souls <term>cura animarum</term> <note>The spiritual responsibility for the salvation of a congregation, typically involving the administration of sacraments like baptism and confession.</note> immediately joined to them, such as bishoprics and parishes; others, however, are immune from this burden. Therefore, I do not believe they should be judged by the same rule.

<margin>Six cases.</margin>
With this established, six cases are noted in the *Summa* of the jurists (21. q. 1) in which two prebends can lawfully be held together in the same person.

**The first** is by reason of poverty <note>Original: *tenuitatis*, referring to the "thinness" or insufficiency of the income.</note>: because the individual offices cannot support individual priests, as held in 10. q. 3. *unio*. This case is true even in those priesthoods subject to the care of souls. Indeed, the same could be permitted for bishops. They could, I say, be so poor (as they often are in Italy) that neither bishopric could support a bishop according to his dignity; and they could be so close together that they could be administered by the same person. There is a text in 21. q. 1. chapter *illud*, where it is granted that the same man be the Archbishop of Tarragona and the Bishop of Fondi.

<margin>Second.</margin>
**The second case** is when one church is dependent on another, as read in the chapter *eam te* under the section "On age, quality, and the appointment of subordinates." How the union of churches is made is clear in the section "On religious houses," chapter *quia monasterium*. Nor should anyone be deceived by thinking this falls into the same case as the first; for the first is understood even where churches are not united. Indeed, the Pope can, without a formal union, adjudicate

<column-break/>

two churches to one priest because of poverty, even with the title of both.

<margin>Annotation.</margin>
However, it must be carefully noted here that in considering this poverty, respect should not be paid to the person, but to the common utility of the Church, to which all these things must be referred. For if a person strives to maintain an ample household and a splendid lifestyle beyond his dignity and condition, that insufficiency of income is not to be judged by that standard; rather, one must look to what benefits the Church. Furthermore, one must be extremely careful lest the union of prebends be made for the favor of the person and to the fraud of the Church. There is some illustrious man, weighed down by a plurality of benefices, who, to remove a scruple of conscience, procures through annexation the joining of all into one. Truly, in my judgment, while he thinks to fascinate the eyes of God with this sophistry, he sins more gravely and shamefully than if he had kept the form of many; for the union of churches ought to be made for their own benefit without malicious deceit if it is to be legitimate.

<margin>Third case.</margin>
**The third case** is on account of the scarcity of clerics, as noted in 21. q. 1. chapter *clericus*. Although it is only said there "on account of the shortage of men," which can refer to the rarity of inhabitants. Nevertheless, the rarity of priests also induces the necessity of entrusting several churches to one man. And indeed, scarcity is to be judged when worthy men are rare. For this reason, I would not forbid one man being assigned to several churches, even with the care of souls, in provinces destitute of the integrity and learning of priests; for this would turn out more happily for the matter of the Church than to appoint entirely unfit priests over the Christian people.

<margin>Fourth case.</margin>
**A fourth case** excusing plurality occurs when someone has one prebend by title and another by commendation <note>A "commendation" (*in commendam*) was a way of holding a church office "in trust," often used as a legal loophole to collect the income of a second office without technically holding the "title."</note>, as found in the same cause and question, chapter *qui plures*.

<margin>How this case should be understood.</margin>
One must be warned, however, about the interpretation of this text. Truly, the legal experts, who focus entirely on the judicial court, perhaps think the conscience of anyone possessing two prebends in this way is safe; but those who look more deeply into divine judgment will judge otherwise. For the same causes—indeed, as I believe, more just ones—must converge so that one may worthily enjoy a second prebend in the sight of God under commendation as if he held both by title. I speak, of course, of perpetual commendations, which are in use in this age. There is a law prohibiting Cardinals who reside in Rome from becoming Bishops; and lest there be a transgression of this law, churches are commended to them...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...fixed perpetually, in no way differently than if the title were inscribed to them. Truly, if it were permitted to speak thus, this pretext of "commendation" <note>A "commendation" was a legal loophole where a person was given the "care" of a church revenue without being officially appointed as its leader, often to bypass laws against holding multiple titles.</note> is a prevarication of the law, even if it is masked; and perhaps it is more criminal for being done in fraud of the law. For he acts in fraud of the law who, while keeping the words of the law, circumvents its intent. <note>original Latin: "l. contra. ff. de legibus. & .C. eodem titul." These are references to the Digest and the Codex, the foundations of Roman and Canon law.</note> There is no doubt that he commits an offense against the law who, having embraced the words of the law, strives against the will of the law. <note>original: "l. non dubium."</note> For if the reason for passing the law was the necessary residency of a Bishop in his own church, what does it matter, I ask, whether it is a "commendatory" who is absent or a true Bishop? For the reason that makes a commendation just and legitimate ought to be this: that at that time no person can be found to whom the office can be legitimately assigned under a title—not, however, to enrich the commendatory.

I would certainly not deny that a Bishop can be summoned to Rome by the Supreme Pontiff for public reasons; yet, that he should remain there perpetually, I do not murmur against—but I do not doubt that a Cardinal Bishop <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy who serves as an advisor to the Pope while technically holding a bishopric elsewhere.</note> is bound by a much holier faith and divine mandate to be present at his own church than at Rome. This is because bishops were instituted by divine law, while Cardinals were created after the age of the Apostles.

<margin>Fifth case.</margin>
¶ The fifth case is when the Pope grants a plurality, as held in the same question in the chapter *Relatio*. And the sixth is if a bishop grants a dispensation, as held in Distinction 70, the canon *Sanctorum*. However, these two cases are to be understood according to the norm of the fourth case just explained: namely, that as far as the "outer forum" <note>The "outer forum" refers to human law and church courts, whereas the "inner forum" refers to the individual's conscience before God.</note> is concerned, they are judged to possess them legitimately; yet, for the dispensation to be accepted by God, it must be surrounded by legitimate causes. Although it is no longer in use for a bishop to be able to dispense regarding a plurality of prebends—since the chapter *Dudum ecclesiastica* in the *Extra* <note>The *Decretals of Gregory IX*, a major collection of Canon Law.</note> regarding elections seems to have abrogated the ancient law—now the Pope alone dispenses, as Panormitanus <note>Nicholò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), one of the most famous commentators on Canon Law.</note> noted there. Yet this should be understood regarding a title to both; for a bishop can well commend a church out of necessity when access to the Roman court is not open.

<margin>Seventh case.</margin>
¶ The seventh case is added as an extraordinary one on account of "sublime and literate persons" who are to be honored with greater benefices, to use the words of the chapter *De multa* regarding prebends. For "sublime" (as they say) refers to blood <note>Meaning persons of noble or royal birth.</note>. Yet that should not be referred to the convenience of the illustrious, but to the splendor of the Church. For the

<column-break/>

Church, while it was crying in its cradle and was being pressed by secular power, had need to be supported by the strength of the illustrious; for which reason it was indulged that they might receive somewhat more in stipends. But now at this age, if it is permitted to tell the truth, I do not know if that same cause for dispensation remains so legitimate. Furthermore, since practical experience openly teaches that the power of the "sublime" has so trampled upon ecclesiastical priesthoods, this has been no small cause of the ruin in which the Church now lies. Although I will never deny that if the well-born and those of noble birth are first of all of good character and then adorned with learning, they bring the greatest splendor and strength to the ecclesiastical commonwealth.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Finally, there follows here a reason for doubting: whether, besides these cases, it is lawful for the Pope to dispense and make several prebends and dignities "compatible" <note>Meaning one person is legally allowed to hold both at the same time.</note>. I bring this into discussion because of the many and varied things affirmed by the Doctors of Canon Law, as anyone can see in Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), an influential Dominican theologian.</note> under the word "benefice," section 4.

<margin>Sylvester. The Archdeacon.</margin>
For first, the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio (c. 1250–1313), a famous canonist often cited simply as "the Archdeacon."</note> says these above cases should be restricted to prebends that are without the "care of souls" <note>Pastoral duties like hearing confessions or preaching.</note>. But truly, this is proved by no reasoning; indeed, even bishoprics for a cause (as we cited above, question 21, case 1, chapter *Illud*) can be permitted to the same person, let alone parishes if they are nearby and poor—though it would then be more decent for them to be united into one. Others say that outside of these cases, it is permitted to no one to have several prebends.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
This is to be understood, however, as being "without a legitimate dispensation." Otherwise, it cannot be doubted that the same power which dispensed in the previous cases can dispense if other cases occur that were not yet thought of, provided they are fair and just. Consult, if you please, Sylvester and other authors of Summaries on this matter.

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
¶ Two doubts, however, remain here. First: whether without a dispensation two benefices can be possessed by the same person. Second: whether in cases where a dispensation is required, he who obtained the dispensation without a legitimate cause has a safe conscience.

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
Regarding the first doubt, a distinction must be made between benefices in terms of residency and care of souls. With this distinction held in advance, a conclusion is established which is the fourth in the order of this article (for we have already sent three ahead).

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
In "simple benefices"—namely, those having neither the care of souls nor requiring residency, such as *prestamerae* <note>A Spanish term for minor church stipends that did not require the holder to live on-site or perform pastoral duties.</note>—no dispensation is necessary for the same person to obtain several. I know that the glosses of the sacred Canons have many...

# Book Three, Question VI.

...many argue the opposite: but nevertheless, not only is the practice now accepted, but our reasoning teaches this conclusion. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> For we must note the foundation we took above from Saint Thomas: namely, that in these matters we must look to a threefold law—divine, natural, and human. This last one is abolished through the disuse of the law or a contrary custom. However, for someone to hold two simple benefices <note>A "simple benefice" is a church office that provides income but does not require the holder to perform spiritual duties or reside in a specific place.</note> is not so contrary to natural and divine law that custom cannot abolish the restriction. This is clear: because although we must keep an eye on distributive justice <note>Justice regarding the fair allocation of resources and honors within a community.</note> in these matters, we must look primarily to commutative justice <note>Justice regarding fair exchange; in this case, ensuring the church receives its required ministry in exchange for the salary provided.</note>, through which churches must be provided with ministers. Where residency is not required, the church is not harmed by a person holding multiple prebends <note>A "prebend" is the specific portion of a cathedral or collegiate church's revenue granted to a member of the clergy.</note>. It is true that Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a Dutch theologian and pope who was a contemporary of the author.</note> softens the wording, saying this is not strictly an "abrogation" <note>A total repeal of a law.</note> but a "derogation" <note>A partial repeal or a sidestepping of a law in a specific case.</note>: because such a provision cannot be made without any cause at all, but only when some cause is present.

Indeed, even if no reason is found now, they are conferred by lower prelates without any dispensation. <margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin> **Fifth proposition.** In those offices that require residency but do not involve the "care of souls" <note>Latin: *cura animarum*, the spiritual responsibility for a parish or congregation.</note>, such as canonries, the law has not yet been abolished: the practice remains that they should not be accumulated by the same person without a dispensation. However, a dispensation can be more easily obtained and granted in these cases than in those involving the care of souls. Indeed, in benefices smaller than canonries which are also bound to the service of attending sacred rites, there is no custom of dispensing.

<margin>Sixth conclusion.</margin> **I would add a sixth conclusion**: that such accumulations of benefices, whether they occur through dispensation or otherwise, cannot be free of fault—sometimes even mortal sin and grave scandal—to the detriment of the churches. This is especially true where they are excessively accumulated and assigned to unworthy persons. This conclusion was established while proving the second conclusion. For now, no <margin>Against the abuse in seeking benefices.</margin> merits are considered or desired, but they are sought, exchanged, sold, inherited, reclaimed, profaned, and squandered just as shamefully and impudently as secular and worldly goods.

<margin>Seventh conclusion.</margin> **Seventh conclusion.** Parishes and similar priesthoods established for the care of souls cannot be held by the same person without a legitimate dispensation; so much so that if the dispensation is not legitimate, they cannot be safely held in the "court of conscience" <note>The "internal forum," referring to a person's standing and guilt before God, regardless of what earthly laws or permits allow.</note> before God. Not on-

<column-break/>

<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
<margin>Adrian.</margin>
-ly is this the opinion of Saint Thomas in the work cited, and of Adrian in *On the Plurality of Benefices*, but the sacred Canons also suggest it, and their interpreters openly declare it. Indeed, the doctors of law do not limit this conclusion to those alone, but apply it to all (which is most true) who need a dispensation to possess them. However, the enormity is more shameful in those offices that involve the care of souls. Thus, even the Pope, if he grants a dispensation without a legitimate cause, sins gravely; and his sin does not free the seeker, the taker, or the holder from guilt. <margin>The Pope sins when dispensing without cause.</margin> <margin>Paul.</margin> First, that the Pope sins is the opinion of the Apostle [Paul] cited above: *Let a man so consider us as ministers of Christ and dispensers of the mysteries of God.* And he adds: *Here now it is required among dispensers that a man be found faithful.* <note>1 Corinthians 4:1-2.</note> Indeed, Christ says in Luke 12: *Who do you think is the faithful and wise steward?* <note>Luke 12:42.</note> And truly, nowhere is such great faithfulness required as in committing and entrusting souls—redeemed by the blood of Christ—to the care of one who should always be present to look after his flock. Hence, Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a mystic and influential church leader.</note> <margin>Bernard.</margin> in *On Consideration* to Eugenius, Book 2, chapter 6, says that rather the Supreme Pontiff—who is spiritual, judging all and judged by none—ought not to use his own will as law, but must imitate Christ above all, who came not to do his own will, but the will of his Father; so that he dispenses everything not for his own benefit, but for the common good. Otherwise, he must be considered a "dissipator" <note>A wordplay on *dispensator* (steward). A dissipator is one who scatters, wastes, or destroys.</note>. For al- <margin>The meaning of the phrase that the Pope has full power to dispense.</margin> though the laws cited above grant him full power of dispensing, they understand it this way because he has no superior on earth by whom he can be judged (we set aside a Council in the case of heresy). Nevertheless, he is held to answer most strictly before God if he breaks faith in his dispensing. Therefore, the reason for the conclusion is this: <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> Priesthoods that have the "care of souls" attached cannot be rightly administered without presence. Such is the vigilance necessary for caring for and looking after souls; however, no one can reside in multiple churches at the same time. Therefore, without a very urgent and necessary cause for that church, one cannot be dispensed from this without a terrible fault. But perhaps the one who received the <margin>A vain objection.</margin> dispensation says: "The Pope granted it; it's his responsibility; I am immune." Yet this quibble makes many feel secure, but it makes no one safe. For the Pope is not the owner (as has been said repeatedly), but the steward; and therefore, he who seeks an unjust dispensation is the cause of the injustice; and he who uses it is always entangled in that same injustice. Added to this is the law of the Lateran Council...

In these places, it is by no means permitted for two parish churches to be held at the same time. <margin>Hostiensis. Panormitanus.</margin> And Hostiensis and Panormitanus <note>Famous medieval canon lawyers often cited as authorities on church law.</note>, along with others commenting on the chapter *Extirpandae* regarding prebends, undoubtedly agree that the residency of such caretakers cannot be fulfilled through a vicar <note>A substitute or representative.</note>. <margin>Second reason for the conclusion.</margin> And the reason is that since a benefice is conferred *intuitu personae* <note>original: "intuitu personae"; meaning "in consideration of the specific person" because of their individual qualities or dignity.</note>, that dignity cannot be replaced by a poor hired hand, who is for the most part unworthy. And even if he were worthy enough to serve as a hired hand, it would not be in proportion to the income of the benefice. The Church pays a just salary for a learned and serious man who, if he were present, could look after and serve his flock with his own charity, counsel, favor, and authority; therefore, these things cannot be accomplished by a hired hand. It is a wonder that a caretaker is allowed—solely for the sake of that care and burden which he has delegated to a substitute as cheaply as he could—to receive such a large portion of the fruits. <margin>Paul. 2 Timothy 3. He who works through another should eat through another.</margin> Paul cries out: *He who does not work, let him not eat* <note>Original: "Qui non laborat, nō manducet." Truly, if only he who works ought to eat, it follows that he who does not work by himself, but through another, should not eat himself, but should be content if that other person eats in his place. Perhaps the parishioner or the holder of the benefice says: "it is enough to substitute this vicar for this church." To which the Church would respond, if she knew how to speak: "Then this reward you give him is enough for this work; why then do you steal the rest from me without providing any service?" This discussion was leading toward the residency of Bishops, but that subject is so vast that we filled almost the entire ninth book with it. <margin>The author's opinion on the residency of Bishops.</margin> In the meantime, let them hear their Supreme Pastor <note>Jesus Christ.</note>, who gave his life for his sheep, warning them how the hireling—who is not the pastor and does not own the sheep—sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees.

<margin>To the arguments.</margin>

### ARTICLE IV.

### *Whether the crime of partiality <note>original: "acceptionis personarum"; literally "respect of persons," meaning unfair bias or favoritism.</note> can exist in the appointment of secular magistrates.*

After these things which have been said concerning ecclesiastical goods, a similar dispute immediately presents itself in this fourth article regarding secular magistrates and public offices and duties, which are customarily established in a commonwealth for the administration of justice: namely, whether in conferring and dispensing these, the crime of partiality can also occur. <margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin> For it is argued first from the negative side. These goods (as we said of ecclesiastical goods) are salaries established and fixed for the ministers of the commonwealth, each of whom provides his services for that pay. Therefore, they do not pertain to distributive justice <note>The fair distribution of benefits and burdens among members of a community based on merit.</note>. Rather, the commonwealth, or the king into whom public power has been transferred, can bestow them as his own property on whomever he pleases, just like hiring workers; and consequently, it follows that partiality has no place there. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> Indeed, it is argued more clearly from the same root in the second place. The commonwealth, and likewise the king, establishes not only those public salaries but also the fees which everyone pays to the ministers of justice according to his own pleasure. Therefore, no reason seems to forbid him from selling the magistracies themselves and the positions of officials; far be it that he could sin in providing for them out of respect for persons. In the contrary, the voice of the people cries out.

The question of this article is very easily defined by what was said in the previous one. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> For the first conclusion is very similar to the second one above. These secular goods of the ministers of justice, although they carry some image and nature of distributive justice, are nonetheless not to be judged solely by that standard, but rather as the matter of commutative justice <note>Justice concerning fair exchange and contracts, such as a salary in exchange for labor.</note>. Truly, they are not to be weighed as if they were the goods of the commonwealth to be applied to citizens only because they are public revenues, or as if they were rewards offered to honest, upright, and wise men for their virtues and the labors exhausted through the study of letters. Rather, they are like salaries decreed for public ministers of justice for the services they render to the commonwealth. This conclusion is even more evident than the one asserted concerning ecclesiastical goods. For unless the administration of justice were necessary...

### Book Three, Question VI.

...administration, would never have been contributed by the people or paid from the king’s treasury merely as a reward for virtues or scholarship. Therefore, the king, through **commutative justice** <note>original: "iustitia commutativa"; this refers to the justice of fair exchange, like a contract where one party provides taxes and the other provides services.</note>, owes such ministers to the kingdom in exchange for the taxes the people pay him. For he owes his citizens protection from foreign enemies and, following that, the preservation of justice against internal wrongdoers.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
From this, the second conclusion follows. Although in the conferring of such magistracies and offices, the face of **distributive justice** <note>original: "distributiva iustitia"; justice concerned with the fair distribution of honors and rewards based on merit.</note> must be observed—so that greater things are given to the worthier—it is additionally necessary to observe commutative justice. This ensures that as much salary is paid to each as their labor, care, and the quality of their function is worth. This conclusion is made more certain by the one above, so that it needs no further testimony.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
The third conclusion is related to the previous ones. The merits of the persons to whom public administrations and duties are entrusted are not to be weighed precisely as they are in distributive justice—according to their absolute standing in themselves—but rather in respect to the end and the function for which they are chosen. That is, whether they are suited to the subjects and fit to carry out that magistracy. From this, it follows that if an unworthy group of men is chosen, the injury to be weighed is not so much the one done to the worthier candidates who were passed over, but the injury done to the city or nation over which such a person is placed, or to the entire kingdom, if they are members of the Royal Court, whether they be presidents or assistants.

<margin>Magistrates were instituted for the necessity of the people.</margin>
For (as I shall repeatedly emphasize) those honors were instituted and the stipends that come with them were decreed solely because of the people’s necessity, and not for the sake of the persons themselves to whom they are granted—unlike the goods that are shared through distributive justice.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
From this, therefore, the fourth conclusion follows. When the worthy do not obtain these honors and stipends, the crime of **partiality** <term>Acceptance of persons (acceptio personarum): the sin of showing favoritism or bias in a professional or legal judgment.</term> is committed, and a bond of restitution arises from it. However, this restitution is not necessarily owed to those who ought to have obtained the office, but certainly to the people who suffered loss and inconvenience. This conclusion, I say, is clearly evident from the above: because a sin is then committed against the people regarding commutative justice, which operates under the legal and universal justice of the prince. Although it cannot be denied that an injury is also done to the worthier candidates against distributive justice; furthermore, those who sweat over letters and virtues with that goal in mind are, in a certain way, defrauded.

<margin>Solon. Democritus.</margin>
For both Solon and Democritus wisely and deliberately said that these two divine powers govern all things: namely, reward and punishment, by which every republic is held together.

<column-break/>

<margin>Ulpian.</margin>
Following these philosophers, Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist whose writings form a large part of the Digest of Justinian.</note> says in the first book of *On Justice and Right*: "We desire," he says, "to make men good, not only through fear of punishments, but also by the encouragement of rewards." <note>original: "Bonos... non solù metu pœnarū, verū etiā p̄miorū quoq; exhortatione efficere cupimus."</note> Nevertheless, that personal right of whatever kind does not create a bond of restitution that must be made to those individuals. Nonetheless (as I was saying), the "acceptance of persons" still takes place in such distributions. For example, if a King were to summon only the people of Salamanca to public duties or other appointments, solely for the reason that they are from Salamanca. It would be different, however, if he used this as a method to investigate their merits. But someone might ask: what merits should be weighed and sought, both in public magistrates and in other lower-order ministers, such as scribes and others of this class? Is it only their integrity? We have deemed this question very necessary here, and for its sake, we append this somewhat lengthy meditation.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
The fifth conclusion is therefore established. No one who is of wicked character, no matter how much they may excel in knowledge or prudence—which in a depraved man is rather **cunning**—should be promoted to such provinces.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Indeed, a wicked man can certainly practice the arts that rely solely on the intellect, such as playing the lute sweetly, painting beautifully, or sculpting skillfully. But that practical skill which is placed in the administration of justice, no one can execute justly unless they are endowed with a universality of virtues.

<margin>This conclusion is illustrated. Aristotle.</margin>
The reason for this is ready at hand, because (as Aristotle stands as the author in the 6th book of the *Ethics*) to rule and command is a task of **prudence**. Prudence, however, has all the virtues connected to itself, and most especially the prudence of a judge. For he is (as taught in the 5th book of the *Ethics*) the guardian of justice. Yet he cannot investigate all the inequities of the republic and punish them according to the laws unless he is adorned with the grace of all the virtues. For as each person is, so does the end seem to him; and for this reason, one cannot judge well concerning duties if one is maliciously inclined toward them. Indeed (as is clear from the use and experience of things), a corrupt soul cannot help but undermine the equity of justice. For which reason,

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle, in the 3rd book of the *Politics*, after arguing that being a good citizen is not the same as being a good man, immediately adds an exception: namely, that the citizen who is a presiding officer or a prince requires all the virtues of a good man. Furthermore, for this reason, he asserted in the 5th book of the *Ethics* that "the magistracy shows the man," <note>A famous Greek proverb (*magistratus virum ostendit*) suggesting that power reveals a person's true character.</note> because while the other virtues [benefit] a man in himself...

<summary>This page argues that public offices are not rewards for individuals but services owed to the people in exchange for taxes. It emphasizes that a magistrate's character is paramount, as a corrupt person cannot administer justice regardless of their intellectual skill.</summary>

### Fr. Dominicus Soto, On Justice and Law

It is easier to cultivate the remaining virtues than justice: for this reason, the virtue and dignity of a person are not considered sufficiently tested until they enter into a magistracy <note>Soto is referencing a famous Greek proverb often attributed to Bias of Priene: "Office shows the man."</note>. Furthermore, since the ministers of justice are the members of the prince, he ought to exhibit his own beauty to the eyes of the citizens through them. Nor is anything else more strictly enjoined upon him—whether you look to divine, natural, or human law—than that he safeguard justice. Justice is preserved, protected, and nourished not so much by the force of laws as by the prudence of ministers, and especially by their charity and probity. For what could be more unjust and perverse than to abuse that very authority, which was divinely created for the protection of justice, for its destruction and slaughter? How prudently
<margin>Aristotle</margin>

Therefore, though the laws themselves may be most holy, without an upright judge they are but the corpses of departed reason. Furthermore, when the subject population sees the guardian of justice delinquent with impunity, they not only hold justice in contempt and find an excuse for their own wrongdoing, but they are drawn into a hatred of the virtues which they see thus going to ruin.

<margin>Greed holds the first place among the crimes of judges.</margin>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
By these points, the earlier argument remains resolved. For it is granted that the public salaries of the ministers of justice belong to the republic where it governs itself, and likewise to the king where there is a kingdom: nevertheless, the king owes the republic fit ministers through **commutative justice** <note>The justice of fair exchange or contracts.</note> because of the taxes they contribute to him. If he does not provide them, he is bound to make restitution for the damages.

<margin>Doubt regarding the second argument.</margin>
<margin>Argument from the negative side.</margin>

<margin>St. Thomas questioned by the Duchess of Brabant.</margin>

But because the solution to this question is pulled in opposite directions—some thinking the sale is illicit by its very nature, as if those salaries and rights of officials were their own private property acquired or to be acquired by hereditary right; while others, relaxing the matter too much, think these same offices are for sale just like the fruit of estates—I shall take care to establish a middle opinion (unless I am mistaken), which will be clear from the following conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>

### Book Three, Question VI.

<margin>Principal argument for the author.</margin>
...are spiritual, and therefore, like ecclesiastical benefits <note>original: "ecclesiastica beneficia," referring to church offices like being a priest or bishop which, under Canon Law, cannot be sold (simony).</note>, they must be conferred for free. However, it is clear that this restriction has no place in the present discussion, as these positions are purely secular. Alternatively, one might argue they are "communal goods"—like prizes for those who excel in learning and integrity—and are thus owed to those individuals for their own sake, much like the revenues of a state, or the rewards given to the good on Judgment Day. But this has already been excluded: we have demonstrated that these are nothing other than stipends and wages for the services and obedience of those who serve the state. No other reason for the "iniquity" of such a sale is apparent, provided no other circumstances are considered; therefore, it is inherently lawful.

Secondly, for the sake of greater clarity, it is argued: Let us imagine a republic that governs itself, for example, through consuls. That state has the power and discretion to establish stipends from its own treasury for each magistrate and official, in whatever amount it chooses. Therefore, when it assigns any person to this or that office—since that person has no pre-existing acquired right to it—the state can either increase or decrease the stipend. By that same logic, it could impose a tax on a portion of that stipend to be paid back to the republic. And by the same logic, it can set a price on that portion, and thus sell the office.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Someone might deny our conclusion in this way: The Republic ought to establish fair fees for citizens to pay officials. For example, so much for a specific document, so much for a seal, so much for a signature, etc. If the price exceeds the quality of the office, the state should command lower fees for the citizens; therefore, it cannot take anything away from that stipend, let alone sell it, but should instead grant the relief to the citizens.

<margin>Refutation of the objection.</margin>
Furthermore, this exception and response does not weaken our argument. Indeed, it may happen that it is expedient and proper to impose high fees on litigants to prune away lawsuits and keep citizens away from the tribunals <note>A common early modern argument that high legal costs deterred "frivolous" or "vexatious" litigation.</note>; or because it is a just tax for the republic. Supposing this, it may happen that the income of the scribes (for example, of a judge) grows too much, becoming excessive for the status of the person. In that case, I do not see why the republic cannot turn a portion of those stipends to its own use, and thus either lease the office or sell it. An example is clear in our own schools. The fees for the scribe are large, and as the University has grown, it is right that they be paid; however, it happened that

<column-break/>

the office became excessively profitable. For this reason, the University decided to take those fees for itself and assign a fixed amount of money to the courier. Truly, I do not see, when an office is provided, what injury there is in receiving a minister on that condition: "If you want this much, take it; if not, leave; another will take it." If this is lawful, it was also lawful to either lease or sell the entire office with its full scope. 

<margin>Another objection.</margin>
Perhaps someone else might raise another exception: Granted a republic that governs itself could do this, a King nevertheless could not, since he is a mere **dispenser** <note>original: "dispensator," an administrator who manages property that belongs to another rather than owning it himself.</note> of offices. Therefore, he cannot sell them as if they were his own, but is bound to distribute offices as the business of the republic. 

<margin>The doubt is resolved.</margin>
However, this objection, unless I am mistaken, in no way overthrows our conclusion. For the King is not considered as a mere dispenser, but as the republic itself. Indeed, he is not to be judged as a "vicar" <note>A deputy or representative acting on behalf of a superior.</note> of the republic—like the **Doge of Venice** <note>original: "Venetorum Dux," whom Soto views as a constitutional official dependent on the state council, unlike an absolute monarch.</note>, who is always dependent on the republic—but as one holding the fullest power of the state, namely the same power that the state itself possessed. For that famous Law explicitly states, *Regarding the Prince*: <note>Soto is citing the *Digest* (1.4.1), the foundation of Roman Law concerning the power of the Roman Emperor.</note> "What pleases the prince has the force of law" <note>original: "Quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem."</note>; for by the **Royal Law** <note>original: "Lege regia," the legendary law by which the Roman people supposedly transferred their sovereignty to the Emperor.</note> passed concerning his authority, the people conferred all their own command and power upon him. By this law and for this reason, they cannot remove him by any means, nor strip his sons of their hereditary right to rule once it has been conferred, unless he should destroy the kingdom by open tyranny. And even then, it is only by the benefit of natural law, which allows one to repel force with force. Thus, the kingdom is his just as each citizen’s house is his own. Consequently, whatever faculty and right the republic had is in his hands—though the republic was not created for him, but he for the republic; and therefore he must direct all things toward the public good. From this it follows that the magnates and lords under royal jurisdiction do not, by the nature of the matter, have the same power to sell offices; because a **Duchy**, for instance, or a **Marquisate** <note>original: "Ducatus," "Marchionatus."</note>, are not considered republics in themselves; nor does the right to establish the fees that subjects pay belong to them absolutely, but depends on the king.

<margin>Who can sell these offices.</margin>
But they are bound to hire ministers of justice at a decent wage. It is true that the towns and **vassals** <note>Subordinates who hold land or office in exchange for service or loyalty.</note> are their true possession; and therefore, if it were expedient for the common good of their people to take a portion from those offices, it would be no iniquity.

<margin>The distinction between the King and other nobles of the republic.</margin>
But there is a difference between the King and those lords, in that whatever the King receives or takes from those offices is reputed to be for the public good; since...

<summary>Soto argues that secular public offices can be sold or taxed by a sovereign or republic because they are wages for service rather than sacred spiritual gifts. He distinguishes the absolute power of a King—who embodies the state’s sovereignty—from subordinate lords or administrators like the Doge of Venice.</summary>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...since it is incumbent upon him to protect the kingdom as if he himself were the republic. The case is different, however, for lower lords; for whatever they might usurp for themselves from such offices would not be considered to result in the public good, unless they themselves applied it to such a good—for instance, to the repair of walls or bridges, and so forth. Therefore, I can find no injustice in the matter if, while we look at the thing purely in the abstract, the king were to sell the rights of officials for the public good. For example, he might grant a praetorship <note>original: "praeturam," a high-ranking judicial or administrative office</note> or the office of a scribe <note>original: "scribæ officium"</note> to his courtiers, who could then appoint substitutes from whom they might expect some portion of the proceeds, if the abundance of the fruits of that office allowed for it—provided that all inconveniences were avoided in good faith. That is to say, those who administered the office must be worthy, and they must commit neither fraud nor robbery to scrape together the price they had paid.

<margin>
Second conclusion.
</margin>

¶ **Second conclusion.** If this matter is considered not so much speculatively, but practically—through its application to common usage and the absurdity of the effects that almost necessarily follow from it—it is not only never expedient or becoming, but according to moral prudence, it is not even permitted.

<margin>
The conclusion is demonstrated.
</margin>

This conclusion is demonstrated in many ways. First, by the very fact that the office is a saleable thing, the person to whom it is sold is not weighed by their merits, but by their money; nothing can be more iniquitous than this. For then, magistracies most often fall to men corrupted by ambition and greed, of the lowest character, and lacking in prudence and learning—and nothing is more pestilential to a republic than this. Furthermore, magistracies are cheapened as a result. Soon, this path is also paved for the plundering of the citizens' goods, for by this same cause, the vice of greed is masked. Indeed, those who received their office for free, unless they are remarkably impudent, do not dare to demand more for their service than is their right. But those who have bought it have an excuse, however feigned, for saying that they can rightfully sell what they previously bought to redeem their own costs. Though in truth they have no excuse. For since the legal fees are fixed, it is their own fault if they buy an office from which they cannot legitimately recover both the price and their livelihood. But if such officials and ministers of justice become a burden to the people through the extortion of money and goods, which they wring out contrary to the law, how will the injured party dare to approach the prince or lord to complain? Indeed, how would the lord not blush to rebuke a minister from whom he himself had previously squeezed the money that the official is now plundering from the common people? Furthermore, there is another harm that these sales bring:

<column-break/>

moreover, it diverts men from other arts they could practice, so that they may live more splendidly off of plunder. ¶ Furthermore, the laws themselves and rights are violated and go to ruin by this reasoning. For a scribe, or a praetor, or any other official who must extort the price of his purchased office from the wretched citizens—in what way, do you think, will he not violate his oath? What injury will he not threaten in order to milk the money of the miserable? ¶ Beyond all this, finally, even if all these evils were to cease, since the prince and the lower lords are bound to administer justice in return for the stipends they receive from the people, to act in such a way that they not only fail to administer it for free, but are not even content with the contributions of the litigants to pay for the ministers—extracting for themselves a new profit from the administration of justice—is a thing that truly cannot be free from the absurdity of fault.

<margin>
The golden "Authenticum" of Justinian.
</margin>

¶ The most holy Emperor Justinian discussed all these matters most clearly in that golden *Authenticum* <note>The "Authenticum" refers to a collection of the "Novels" or new laws of Emperor Justinian</note> titled *That judges be made without any payment* <note>original: "Vt iudices sine quoquo suffragio fiant," Novel 8 of the Justinian Code</note>, by which both of our conclusions are greatly strengthened. For there, he most holily commands that the persons assigned to public offices should receive each thing without reward, giving nothing at all, even on the occasion of votes. These are the words of the *Authenticum*. Yet he does not argue that those offices are not saleable by their nature, but rather says: "It is manifest to all; since he who gives gold and thus buys his administration, adds not only this, but another amount from external sources on the occasion of profit." And thus, once one illicit principle is granted, many robberies follow. Furthermore, the same prohibition is read in the common law <note>original: "iure communi," referring here to the Roman civil law</note> in the law *haec lex* in the Digest under the Julian law on bribery <note>original: "ad. l. Iuli. de ambi."</note>. Therefore, according to the common law, the Catholic 

<margin>
The Catholic Kings.
</margin>

And that same *Pragmatica* was confirmed by the authority of the most Invincible Caesar <note>A title for Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain</note>.

<margin>
Caesar.
Third conclusion.
</margin>

¶ **Third conclusion.** This would be more pestilential than all else, more foully offending the dignity of the republic, and even scandalous, if judgeships were sold, or the seats of those who belong to the King's public councils. I have heard this happens in a certain province outside of Spain. For from this would arise the most immediate danger of the "slaughtering" and betrayal of all laws.

<margin>
Which offices are more foully sold.
</margin>
