# Question VI of the Third Book

...those who perform public duties and manage other affairs, and who are sometimes called into the counsel of justice, it cannot but be inappropriate if they are chosen not by an assessment of their merits but by their price.

¶ However, it must be primarily considered here that even if necessity—which knows no law—should sometimes compel a prince to sell such positions, neither the buyers nor anyone else has the right to sell them further. To do so would be to usurp the duty of choosing a senator, a power which the king commits to no one. Therefore, unless permission is obtained from the king, to whom the right of election belongs, no one is permitted—regardless of the price they paid—to transfer the office to another, whether for a high price or for free. Nor would such a transfer be of any value unless it were ratified by the king’s consent afterward. Furthermore, if someone seeks the king’s permission to transfer their position without explaining that it is a sale, I believe they sin by selling it in such a way that they are bound to the restitution of the price, because it is lawful for no one to sell except the king. Where the king grants that same permission, the obligation for restitution ceases; however, the reason for the sin does not, since the sale is not made for the public good.

¶ I would add, moreover, a fourth conclusion: City senators, to whom it is granted to choose the functions of scribes <note>original: "scribarum functiones," referring to administrative or legal clerks</note>, are unable by any pact to sell their votes for a price. This is not only because of the disadvantages expressed in the second and third conclusions but also because it is repugnant to the very nature and condition of their function.

<margin>Royal Decree <note>original: "Pragmatica regni," a reference to the Pragmatic Sanction or specific royal ordinances governing Spanish administration</note></margin>
Therefore, even if it were perhaps occasionally permitted to the king according to the tenor of the first conclusion, it is by no means lawful for those senators to receive a price. The reason is that they are not the ones into whom the republic has transferred public power, as it has into the king; rather, they are mere dispensers <note>original: "dispensatores," those who manage or distribute on behalf of another</note> and, by privilege, simply electors. For this reason, that cited Royal Decree of the kingdom specifically restrains such audacity. From this, it follows that they cannot divide the salaries and rights of scribes by way of a pension, or compel a scribe to pay a certain amount to another. For it is customary among those senators to agree: "Let us choose your man, provided he pays something back to mine." In truth, I would not dare to assert that the consciences of such men are safe; for this is to value a vote by its price. Therefore, the entire sum of money must be restored to the elected scribe, as if it had been extorted through inequity.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let our fifth and final conclusion be this: Among all these, ecclesiastical Prelates <note>original: "Antistites," high-ranking church officials like bishops</note> sell these kinds of duties most unjustly and foully. For besides the absurdities listed above, they offend Christian eyes with scandal. For "freely they have received, freely let them give"—not only 

<column-break/>

spiritual things, but also the secular things that were instituted for the protection of spiritual matters. It does not escape me, nor would I deny, that certain rights and duties may come to Prelates which have been established in good faith by very ancient custom, as noted in the chapter *statutum* of the *Clementines* on elections <note>original: "cap. statutum. Clem. de electio," referring to a specific decree in the Clementine Constitutions of Canon Law</note>:
<margin><unclear>chapter statutum. on elect.</unclear></margin>
where it is held that whatever profit comes to a bishop from the jurisdiction and the seal of the Ecclesiastical or secular court must be faithfully reserved for his future successor. Nor should it be denied that it is perhaps fair to command some very small fees from litigants, even in an ecclesiastical court, to prevent frivolous lawsuits. However, this must be done much more moderately than in a secular forum. For it cannot happen without scandal—and perhaps not even without injury—that the proceeds from seals and signatures are so immoderate. Since bishops enjoy the large fruits of their bishoprics, they ought to provide those testimonies to their subjects for free. Indeed, the argument mentioned above applies much more forcefully to them: since they ought to administer justice for free, they should be content to extort only a small amount of money from litigants for the ministers, without increasing any other profit for themselves therefrom. Finally, at the end of this inquiry, I would add this last word: that to either impose higher fees on litigants, or to ignore and permit them with the intent that the office might be sold for more, would be a most wicked crime of injustice.

¶ From these points, the second argument remains resolved.
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>

### ARTICLE V.

->*Whether the acceptance of persons can occur in the delivery of judgments.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a figure amidst scrollwork and architectural motifs.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
AFTER these things which have been said concerning magistrates, other duties of the republic, and the establishing and dispensing of judgeships, it follows in this fifth article that we examine whether the crime of acceptance of persons <note>original: "acceptionis personarum," the vice of partiality or favoritism based on who a person is rather than the merits of the case</note> also happens to be committed in the delivery of judgments. For it seems to have no place there. For it has been said that this vice is contrary to distributive justice <term>Distributive justice: the fair allocation of honors or rewards based on merit</term>; however, the pronouncing of the law pertains to commutative justice <term>Commutative justice: the restoration of equality through fair exchange or punishment</term>, whether you look at that part where equity is preserved between private persons (so that each recovers what he contributed) or the other part which vindicates evils (which punishes evils to restore equality), as we declared above in the previous question.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on justice and law by Fray Domingo de Soto. ### Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *Ethics*, <note>original: "Arist. 5. Ethi." referring to the Nicomachean Ethics</note> teaches that injuries committed against magistrates should be punished with a sharper correction than those committed against persons of a lower class. Furthermore, in the book of Sirach, it is commanded: "In judging, be merciful to orphans." <note>original: "Eccl. 4. iubetur, In iudicando esto pupillis misericors."</note> Both of these instructions seem to take the status of the person into account; therefore, in such matters, the "respect of persons" <note>The term "respect of persons" (acceptio personarum) refers to favoritism or partiality based on a person’s status rather than the facts of a case.</note> is not considered a vice.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, if the respect of persons could be considered a vice in legal judgments, then nothing concerning grace or favor should ever be admitted there. For certainly, when a judge grants something freely to one of the parties, he seems to do so out of respect for the person. Yet the consequence of this seems false. First, reason appears to demand that when a judge discovers an innocent person is being accused through malicious deceit, he should be able to grant many indulgences and overlook certain things in that person's favor, which he could not lawfully do in favor of a guilty person. Add to this that, even outside of this case, it appears to be within the judge's discretion to sometimes extend or narrow the limits of the law within its broad range, and in these and other ways favor one party over another in matters not forbidden by law. And thirdly, a supreme prince can sometimes grant life to one guilty person while denying it to another in a similar situation, even if both were condemned to death.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourthly and finally, it is argued that a doubtful point of law sometimes arises about which learned doctors hold various opinions. In such a case, the judge seems to have the power, for the sake of friendship, to deliver a sentence according to one opinion now, and later deliver a contrary sentence according to the other opinion, based on his regard for the person. Therefore, the respect of persons is not always illicit in legal judgments. ¶ To the contrary, however, is that which is written in Proverbs 18: "To respect the person in judgment is not good." <note>original: "Accipere personam in iudicio non est bonum."</note>

<margin>Single conclusion.</margin>
This question is easily dispatched; furthermore, it is resolved by a single conclusion: The respect of persons in the delivery of judgments is frequently committed, and it is both a wickedness and a monstrous crime.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven as follows: Judgment is the right deciding of what is just and unjust—namely, that by which an equality is established between crimes and punishments, as well as between persons who held unequal shares through giving and receiving, once the causes of the matter have been weighed with sincere and honest reason.

<margin>What judgment is.</margin>
However, this judgment is accustomed to being corrupted whenever the eye is cast not toward the cause, but toward the person, or their prayers, or a bribe, or toward hatred or favor. But this is what it means to "accept" or "respect" the person. Therefore, such a vice can creep into judgments of this kind.

<column-break/>

Wherefore, the word "prejudice" <note>original: "præiudiciū"</note> derives its name from the fact that a judgment is rushed before a lawful knowledge of the causes has been obtained.

<margin>The enormity of this crime.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
The enormity of this crime is revealed by the fact that the judge—as Aristotle testifies in the fifth book of his *Ethics*, from which Cicero drew in his book *On Laws*—is the guardian of what is just. Indeed, he is so much the guardian of justice that Aristotle called the judge "animated justice" itself <note>original: "iustitiam ipsam appellauerit animatam," meaning justice come to life in a human person</note>. No perversion can be more monstrous than for justice to be corrupted by a judge. For it is as if justice itself were to tear itself apart with its own hands, or certainly as if reason itself were to act against itself. For a judge ought to rule—as Cicero says in the same place—not as a man, but as reason itself. He is the one to whom people flock as if to living reason, and thus to a speaking rule of equity. For this reason (as we said in the first article, citing the same Aristotle), neither should the method of stirring the judge’s mind with emotions be admitted into court, nor should he judge except with his physical eyes closed, lest the sight of the persons move him. He is so far from being allowed to open his ears to prayers or his hands to bribes. Therefore, there is no well-ordered commonwealth in which the harshest penalties have not been decreed against judges who allow themselves to be tainted and corrupted by bribes.

<margin>To the first argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded with St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> that judgment, if you look at the matter being judged, is common to the logic of both types of justice <note>Soto is referring to "distributive" and "commutative" justice.</note>. For it can be determined by judgment both how the restitution of common goods should be made, and in what manner each person should repay what belongs to another. Nevertheless, if you consider the form, even "commutative" justice <note>Justice concerning private transactions and restitution.</note> carries a certain image of distribution, insofar as the judge takes from one what he grants to the other; and therefore, the respect of persons can hide there.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The second argument has already been dissolved above. For a harsher punishment for an injury inflicted upon princes or magistrates has nothing in common with the respect of persons. Rather, since the dignity of the person increases the magnitude of the injury, it is equitable that the punishment be more substantial. As for the passage from Sirach, it must be tempered by another from Exodus 23. For compassion for the poor ought to move a judge somewhat, but only within the limits of justice: namely, that there be enough mercy toward the poor person to protect him from the power of the rich. But because compassion can also go out of bounds, we are warned in Exodus 23: "Neither shalt thou favor a poor man in judgment." <note>original: "Pauperis quoq; non misereberis in iudicio."</note>

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The solution to the third argument requires [further] meditation...

<summary>In this passage, Domingo de Soto argues that judicial partiality (respect of persons) is a grave crime that corrupts the very nature of justice. He refutes arguments that suggest judges should show favoritism based on status or mercy, asserting that a judge must act as "living reason" and "animated justice."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the "respect of persons" (partiality) within the legal system. ### Third Book, Question VI.

requires consideration: for there is no doubt that the "respect of persons" <note>original: "acceptio personarum"; this refers to partiality or showing favoritism based on a person's status rather than the facts.</note> can sometimes creep even into discretionary acts. We call those things "discretionary" which are legally permitted to a judge. These are of a certain kind: namely, those which, since they are not determined by law, are left to the judge's own judgment.

<margin>Regarding the first part.</margin>
Therefore, in response to the first part designated there, it is first answered that when a matter is in doubt, one should not 

<margin>First proposition.</margin>
lean toward favor against the tenor of the law: both because otherwise the judge would expose himself to the danger of erring, and also because it would provide an opening for judges to judge according to their own whim, and subsequently to craftily weave together a fraud. However, where the innocence of a person is plain to him, he not only will be able to, but indeed it will be fitting to show favor to the innocent as much as possible—at least in discretionary matters that are not restrained by law—provided it is done without causing scandal. Nevertheless, he will not be free to omit or ignore the necessary requirements of the law; because, since he is the guardian of the laws, he must deliver judgment "according to what is alleged and proved." <note>original: "secundùm allegata & probata"; a legal principle that a judge must only consider evidence officially presented in court.</note>

<margin>Second proposition.</margin>
¶ However, I would add a second proposition to this: that by omitting or violating the laws in favor of one who is clearly innocent, although the judge commits a fault—and sometimes a mortal one—both by prevaricating against his office and the law, and also because of the scandal; nevertheless, he is by no means bound to make restitution <term>restitution: the legal and moral obligation to give back or compensate for what was taken</term> to the accuser, because he took nothing that belonged to the accuser.

<margin>Third proposition.</margin>
¶ Third proposition. It is never permitted for a judge to lean against an innocent person, even in discretionary matters; for this would be to nourish iniquity. But truly, where justice is doubtful on both sides, then it is not an open vice to prefer one of the parties over the other in those things which are purely discretionary, provided it is done without scandal and without damage to the other. For if, in favor of a friend, he should prolong the time for proof or other deadlines so that the other party incurs greater expenses or, worn out by the length of time, leaves the lawsuit, it is an injustice. But if he sells a discretionary favor of this kind for money, this indeed, besides being always iniquitous, is remarkably foul. Indeed, I would add that unless that which is granted by law is done with the greatest moderation, it immediately tends toward the "respect of persons."

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you argue to the contrary, that this kind of vice does not exist except when it is against 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
justice: that is denied. On the contrary, it is also committed against equity; and it does not lack iniquity when all discretionary favors are heaped upon one party. Restitution, however, has no place 

<margin>Regarding the third part.</margin>
except where the law is shaken. ¶ Finally, in response to the third part, it is said that it is not always free from the "respect of persons" when a prince graciously 

<column-break/>

grants life or remits some other punishment to certain condemned men, while denying it to similar ones. For indeed, although the rigor of justice is not violated, equity is nonetheless violated. This must be more carefully observed by ecclesiastical prelates and superiors, and especially in religious orders, lest in the dispensations of laws—even those which are legally permitted to them—or in the relaxing of punishments, they be "accepters of persons" <note>partial or biased</note>; for surely this fault is also accustomed to creep into these matters.

<margin>Regarding the fourth part.</margin>
¶ The fourth argument is answered in almost the same way: for there is no doubt that even that practice can strike against the "respect of persons." Therefore, it is always necessary above all 

<margin>Prior proposition.</margin>
to sign a sentence according to the "more probable" opinion, even if the other is "probable." <note>In scholasticism, a "probable" opinion is one supported by good reasons or authorities. A "more probable" opinion has stronger support.</note> For in the theoretical disputes of the schools, no danger is stirred up if someone defends less probable things for the sake of intellectual exercise; but in practical matters which concern the rights of others, it is a sin for a judge to follow the weaker opinion. This is the same for a doctor in practice, upon whom the health of the sick depends, and much more so for a Theologian in those things which pertain to faith. Indeed, a judge doing otherwise would become liable for restitution. From this it follows that judges, and also doctors, consult very poorly for themselves and the common good when, after they have once imbibed one opinion, they can be moved from it by no reason; whereas, lest they intend injury to others, they would be bound to set aside their own honor and migrate to the other opinion as soon as it appeared more probable.

<margin>Latter proposition.</margin>
¶ Let the second proposition be: Where it happens that the opinions are entirely equal, it is not an open crime to embrace now one and now the other opinion; yet it can hardly be without scandal. In all these things, one must watchfully take care lest either friendship or any other affection cast a mist over the intellect, so that the judge deems that opinion more probable which he would prefer according to his own whim.

# Francisco de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

...partiality might arise. <note>original: "personarum acceptio"; this refers to showing favoritism or "respect of persons" based on external status rather than merit.</note> Indeed, since this vice is an enemy only of justice, it seems it should not extend to gratuitous acts, such as the politeness and courtesy shown in mutual honors. For if someone offers honor to those who deserve it, he does no one an injury—provided that he shows the same signs of honor and titles even toward those who are unworthy for the sake of politeness. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is argued: although honor—as all philosophy proclaims—is owed to virtue alone, there are many wicked people to whom honor is granted by law, such as prelates, parents, elders, and the illustrious, even if they possess corrupt morals. ¶ Against these things, nevertheless, James 2 instructs us in his General Epistle with these words: "If a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothing also comes in, and you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing," etc.

We have set aside this question primarily because of this passage in James, so that we may explore what kind of sin it is to show honor to unworthy persons for human and secular reasons. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> ¶ Let this be the first conclusion: Although honor is the reverence shown to anyone because of their excellence, the thing to which honor is properly and uniquely owed is virtue. Aristotle is the author <margin>Aristotle.</margin> of this opinion in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 4, Chapter 3, where he consequently added that honor is the greatest of external goods, of which only the good man is truly worthy. And for the same reason, in Book 1, he taught that refined men seek honor from upright men as a testimony of their virtue. Because of this, the word "honor" descends from "the honorable" <note>original: "honestum"</note>; and honorableness is the fitting companion of virtue. For this reason, the Roman <margin>Marcus Marcellus.</margin> Marcus Marcellus built a temple to Honor in the middle of the city with the law that no one could enter it except through the temple of Virtue. And of Christ, the royal Psalmist sang: "Lord, you have crowned him with glory and honor." And Paul <margin>Paul.</margin> in 1 Timothy 1: "To the King of ages, immortal," etc., "honor and glory." And with these same two parts in Romans 2, he expressed the quality of that eternal happiness, saying: "To those who, according to patience in good work, seek glory and honor." <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ Second conclusion: Nevertheless, besides virtue, there are also other excellences for which honors are owed to mortals in this age; namely, first, because of divine representation—such as to princes and magistrates who represent the person of God. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Hence Aristotle, in the same place in *Ethics*, Book 4, Chapter 3, considers those who are established in power to be worthy of honor. And in Book 5, Chapter 6: "Honor is the reward and prize of the magistrate."

<column-break/>

And servants owe the same to their masters, according to the word of Paul <margin>Paul.</margin> in 1 Timothy 6: "Let all who are under the yoke as servants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor." Next, honor is owed as a testimony to another's virtue. By this reasoning, we honor the illustrious and those of noble blood; for we assume their ancestors reached a high place through degrees of virtue. And much more justly is it owed to parents who sired us, and to the elderly. For in Leviticus 19, it is commanded: "Rise up before the gray head and honor the person of the old man." Even though we read in Wisdom 4: "Venerable old age is not that which stands in length of time, nor is it measured by the number of years. But the understanding of a man is gray hairs, and a spotless life is old age." To offer honor to these, then, even if they lack virtue, is not "partiality," because the cause for honor is not lacking. Wherefore, Proverbs <margin>A most elegant explanation of the passage in Proverbs 26.</margin> 26: "As he who puts stones in Mercury's heap, so is he who gives honor to a fool." <note>This refers to the Vulgate translation of Proverbs 26:8. In antiquity, travelers would add a stone to a "Herm" or heap of stones dedicated to Mercury (Hermes). The text is using this to explain how social status is assigned.</note> This is how not only Saint Thomas but also other distinguished authors of his order interpret it: that "Mercury’s heap" is considered a pile of pebbles which merchants use in calculating accounts of what is given and received—because Mercury was considered the god of such business. In these types of calculations, at one's whim or even by chance as it comes to hand, a pebble that is worth one is set as a ten, and then as a hundred or a thousand. Thus, although someone might be raised to a magistracy without merits, the office itself makes him worthy of honor. Yet, according to the Hebrew reading, the sense is far different. For <margin>Another equally elegant explanation.</margin> among the Hebrews, it is held: "As one who puts a stone in the pocket of a sling"—evidently to cast it upward by force against its nature—"so is he who gives honor to a fool," that is, to one void of merits. <margin>Third conclusion.</margin> ¶ Third conclusion, which acts as an interpreter of James's mind: Although it is a duty to honor the wealthy by reason of the high place they hold in the commonwealth, nevertheless, to offer them honor solely out of regard for their riches is the sin of partiality. The first part <margin>The first part is proven.</margin> is gathered both from what was said above and is also the <margin>Aristotle.</margin> assertion of Aristotle in *Ethics*, Book 4, Chapter 3, where he affirms together that those who are in power and the wealthy are considered worthy of honor. The second part, <margin>The second part is proven by Saint Thomas.</margin> however, is asserted by Saint Thomas in the *Summa Theologiae* (II-II, Question 63, Article 3), where he added no other reason than what he seems to draw from the words of James, though in his *Quodlibetal* (Book 10, Article 12) he explains it more precisely. But in truth, a natural reason is not lacking to support it. Indeed, riches considered separately...

# Book Three, Question VI.

<margin>
Aristotle.
In what way the praiseworthy and the honorable differ.
</margin>
...perceived as such, they show no excellence worthy of honor. For the honorable and the praiseworthy—as Aristotle discusses in the *Ethics*, Book 1, Chapter 12—differ in this: only those things which are good in themselves (which are called "honest" or virtuous) are worthy of honor. Useful things, however, are those which are good not in themselves but only in relation to something else; therefore, they can indeed be praised, but not honored in the same way. Riches, moreover, possess no good except for their use.

<margin>
A softening of the latter part of the conclusion.
</margin>
¶ But indeed, it is expedient to soften the harshness of this conclusion. It should be understood as referring not to just any external signs of honor, but to true honors. For legitimate honor exists when these external signs—such as uncovering the head <note>The custom of removing one's hat as a sign of respect.</note> and bowing—are offered as testimonies of internal esteem. This truly would be partiality <term>acceptio personarum: the sin of favoritism based on status rather than merit</term>: namely, if we held a rich man, void of all other merits, in such high honor in our hearts. And this is what James condemns. Hence he adds: *Do you not judge within yourselves*—namely, when you prefer the rich to the poor—*and have you not become judges of wicked thoughts?* <note>James 2:4</note> Behold, therefore, the sin: to judge a rich man, because of his riches, as superior in true dignity to the poor. However, to show the rich such external signs without an internal judgment—such as giving up a seat, uncovering the head, or inviting them to sit—carries no weight of fault. Instead, it is a concession to common politeness <note>original: "triviali vrbanitati"; refers to standard social etiquette.</note>. Unless you did this, you would be considered insolent.

<margin>
Augustine.
He clearly explains the passage from Saint James.
</margin>
Hence Augustine’s gloss on that same passage: "If we refer this distinction of sitting and standing to Ecclesiastical honors—so that the rich are preferred to the poor in the conferring of priesthoods—it is not," he says, "to be thought a light sin." And further: "But if he speaks of daily social seating, who does not commit this fault? Yet it is not a sin unless one judges so within himself that the person seems better to him simply because he is richer." For this is what he seems to have signified by adding: *Do you not judge within yourselves?* etc. These things are from the gloss.

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>
**T**o the first argument, it is answered first that in "gratuitous" matters <note>Acts of favor or social grace that are not strictly required by law.</note>, one should not hold, but rather interpret as against justice, the idea that someone should mentally repute the rich (or any others in whom no virtue or legitimate excellence exists) as superior in truth to those who excel in virtue or other marks of dignity. Second, it must also be considered in the mind that partiality can occur even in these gratuitous honors. For to broadcast and diminish those titles of honor which are owed to the worthy, so that they are also ascribed to the unworthy, is not without injury to the worthy.

<column-break/>

Indeed, since honor consists in excellence, when you make the name of "honor" common to everyone equally, you then cause it to no longer be a name of honor, and consequently you deprive the worthy of their right. For example: if you were to greet simple priests with the same title as a Bishop <note>original: "Antistite"; a high-ranking prelate or bishop.</note>; or treated a commoner like a magnate, a disciple like a master, or the ignoble like the noble.

<margin>
To the second argument.
</margin>
¶ The second conclusion abundantly dissolves the second argument. Whether a king is permitted to impart honors among citizens at his pleasure was declared in the fourth article, and the following article will do so more fully.

### ARTICLE VII.

**I**t remains finally in this seventh article to add a word concerning taxes: whether partiality can also occur in them. # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>Four names for taxes. Census.</margin>
...We begin here. The first is the *census* <note>original: "census"</note>, which is derived from "assessing" <note>original: "censendo"</note>: for this reason, resources must be reviewed so that taxes may be paid in proportion to them, as is held in the Law *Forma* regarding censuses. But so that it may be a peculiar name distinct from others, it specifically signifies that payment which citizens pay individually, head by head, to the prince. For this
<margin>Which tax it was that the Jews desired to be free from.</margin>
is the tax about which the Jews questioned Christ, when they asked whether it was lawful to pay the census to Caesar. For they did not refuse the tributes which were commanded for the defense and governance of the commonwealth; but they refused that which designated the yoke of subjection, from which they judged themselves to be free as the children of Abraham. Whence it is said elsewhere: "We are the children of Abraham, and have never served anyone." However, this kind of census is not frequently in use among Christian princes, because it pertains more to the swelling of pride and the thirst of avarice than to the necessity of public expenses. For citizens sufficiently profess themselves subjects when they take up other commands. Therefore, it was for that reason that the Caesars ordered the world to be enrolled.
<margin>David.</margin>
Thus David (as recorded in 2 Kings 24) paid such bitter penalties for numbering the people. And it was to this that Christ referred when he asked, "Whose image is this?" <note>Matthew 22:20</note>—namely, of the coin—as if it were paid only as a sign of subjection and adoration of Caesar. <margin>Tribute.</margin> ¶ Tribute <note>original: "tributum"</note>, however, (as the name itself sounds) is said to come from "giving" <note>original: "tribuendo"</note> or "contributing" <note>original: "contribuendo"</note>, because everyone gives a contribution. And since in ancient times that contribution was not made except to feed the public soldier, the word "stipend" <note>original: "stipendium"</note> was also derived from it. Both are found in the law *Ager* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de verb. & rer. signif."</note>. <margin>Difference between tribute and census.</margin> Therefore, tribute differs from census both by reason of its matter and its purpose. For tribute is contributed from the fruits of the earth for the support of the king or the commonwealth; whereas the census is from the head to profess subjection. <margin>Vectigal. The interval between vectigal, census, and tribute.</margin> ¶ The third kind of payment is the *vectigal* <note>a toll or customs duty</note>, differing from both in its purpose and its matter. For it is paid on merchandise that is carried <note>original: "vehuntur"</note> for the sake of trade, for the repair of walls, bridges, and other public works of that kind. <margin>Vectigal is named from carrying.</margin> It is therefore called *vectigal* from "carrying" <note>original: "vehendo"</note>, and likewise it is called *portorium* from the "port" <note>original: "portu"</note>, because it is paid to the gatekeeper <note>original: "portitori"</note>. Therefore, in his speech on the consular provinces, Cicero joins both: *vectigal* and *portorium*; and from this comes
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
the Spanish *Portazgo* <note>a gate-toll</note>. <margin>Pedage.</margin> ¶ The fourth tax is *pedagium* <note>pedage or way-toll</note>, which is the same in matter as the *vectigal* because it is paid from merchandise, yet it differs in its purpose: for it is dedicated to the guarding of roads that are blocked by robbers or enemies. ¶ Concerning all these,

<column-break/>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
let this be the first conclusion: All these kinds of payments, if they are imposed for the aforementioned causes, are just, and are owed to princes by citizens in conscience, according to the word of Paul in Romans 13: *Therefore be subject of necessity, not only because of wrath, but also for the sake of conscience. For this is why you pay tributes: for they are God’s ministers.* <margin>Paul.</margin> *Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom.* And this is referred to in the decree of Augustine <margin>Augustine.</margin> regarding censuses. Paul therefore added that they are "God’s ministers" so that we might understand that the law of paying taxes to support princes is derived from His divine power. But indeed (as Saint Thomas <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> well noted in that place), they ought to seek nothing as a reward, but only for the sustenance of their status and necessary expenses. For (as Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Chapter 6) the proper reward of a prince is honor, and he who is not content with this is a tyrant. Christians, however, ought to refer that honor not to human honor, which is vain, but to the divine honor which awaits us in heaven. ¶ The second <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> conclusion is: If the burdens of taxes are not exacted in proportion to each person's means and substance, or in proportion to transport or trade, or some other legitimate cause, but are instead demanded in view of something else that does not pertain to the matter, it is "respect of persons" <term>acceptio personarum: the sin of partiality</term>. This is something that cannot happen to the prince as frequently as it does to city tax-collectors and senators, who are therefore bound to make restitution if they use any fraud or force. For another danger threatens the prince: namely, demanding more than is required by the necessity of the kingdom. For this must always be weighed, so that when the cause of the tax ceases, the tax also ceases. ¶ But so that we may show some specimen of a legitimate form of taxes, let this be the third conclusion. Taxes <margin>Third conclusion.</margin> should be imposed on means, possessions, and businesses rather than on persons: namely, so that he who abounds more richly in goods, or gains more, pays more—not he who is more in need. ¶ For the sake of explaining this <margin>The tax which is called Alcauala among the Spaniards.</margin> conclusion, let me explain that kind of tax which is currently in use among us in Spain, and in other provinces as well. Our people call it the *Alcauala* <note>A sales tax on all commercial transactions</note>. For this form of tax had its origin among us a little more than a hundred years ago, and for a just cause: namely, while King Alfonso <margin>King Alfonso.</margin> was seeking the Kingdom of Granada through war. But afterwards, not only did the evils of wars endure, but they increased, and so it became permanent. And it does indeed have some image of a *vectigal* <note>customs duty</note> because it is also paid on merchandise.

<summary>This page defines and distinguishes between four types of taxation—census, tribute, tolls, and pedage—grounding their legitimacy in both biblical authority and civil necessity. Soto concludes that taxes must be applied proportionally to wealth rather than personhood to avoid the sin of partiality.</summary>

### Third Book: Question VI.

<margin>There is a difference between this kind of tribute and a customs duty.</margin>
...is paid. However, it differs in its broader scope: for it is collected not only from those goods transported from place to place, but from every single thing sold. Furthermore, the nobility are not exempt from its payment. It even differs in its purpose. For it is not merely assigned for the repair of walls and bridges, but for the general public expenses of the king. Yet, it should not be condemned as an injustice simply because it is a new practice. For when other tributes imposed on the wealth and business dealings of citizens are insufficient to support the king and sustain the commonwealth, it is necessary to provide for this by another way. Nor should it be argued as an injustice because it also includes the nobility. Indeed, since the rest of the common people are unable to bear such immoderate expenses, it is only <margin>The injustice of this tribute.</margin> equitable that they be lightened by the help of the nobles. Nevertheless, this tax displays a certain sign of injustice, which the law *Universi* <note>original: "lex, Vniuerſi. C. de vectiga." referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 4, Title 61</note> commands us to guard against in matters of tribute: namely, that taxes should not be exacted for those things which pertain to one’s own personal use. Indeed, it is entirely consistent with reason that merchants, who buy in order to resell, should pay a quota of the sale. For to them, this is the same as profit, just as produce is to farmers. But for someone who, out of necessity, sells his own home or some other item to meet a personal need, both that law and reason seem to cry out against him being forced to pay tribute. For in that case, it is not the one who has more or gains more who pays, but the one who is in greater need who pays more. ¶ Furthermore, in truth, unless the necessity of wars had been the cause for the revenues of this tribute to be sold off <note>The author is referring to "tax farming," where the right to collect taxes was sold to private individuals</note>, it would have been a very ready way of sustaining the kingdom and the king's treasury. However, it cannot help but appear as a monster that citizens pay tribute to fellow citizens—especially a tax that is paid to the king for the common good. To this is joined another disadvantage: namely, that the poor citizens, upon whom services are commanded, are more heavily oppressed because of it. For however much is sold, they themselves are forced to replenish it. Truly, as the necessity of expenses for the king increases day by day, it is inevitable that the people are harassed by many kinds of troubles daily. Add to this that the lords to whom this kind of tribute is sold demand it with such rigor that they exact every tenth coin <note>original: "decimum quenque nummum" — a reference to the 10% sales tax known as the alcabala</note> most precisely, even though the king himself would hardly ever receive a twentieth. And certainly, although a tenth has been assigned to the king, it would be too heavy to demand this tribute with such rigor unless an urgent necessity of the kingdom required it. The king, piously observing this, is accustomed to negotiate and make a pact with the kingdom regarding this quota, so that the payment becomes more relaxed and tolerable; however, the lesser lords do not do this. To this is added another harm: that while the laws for exacting this tribute would be tolerable if only the royal tax-collectors <term>quaestores</term> <note>In this context, the officials or "quaestors" responsible for the treasury and tax collection</note> existed,

<column-break/>

nevertheless, the remaining crowd of collectors abuses those laws to defraud the people, so that through that harassment they extort not just a tenth, but more than an eighth. I murmur nothing against the necessity of kings, which has no law and can compel even their just minds; I am only explaining the nature of the matter, so that if it were possible to provide for public necessity by other ways, such alienations of the public treasury might be avoided. <margin>A very apt analogy.</margin> For a well is meant to be drawn from for the benefit of the work; yet the law of nature does not allow one to cut off the veins of the springs themselves. But if anyone should ask more insistently whether these tributes are so owed in conscience that <margin>A doubt.</margin> an individual is bound to offer them voluntarily even when not sought out by a collector or a customs officer: <margin>The solution.</margin> It is answered, first, that it is not lawful for anyone to secretly elude the collector, except where the injustice of the tax is entirely obvious. The second part of the response is that while these taxes are exacted with great rigor, it is enough that each person pays obediently when the tribute is requested. Especially when the debt is not of great importance. ¶ The fourth conclusion. There is no "respect of persons" <note>Partiality or unfair favoritism</note> if nobles and the high-born are exempt from the <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> payment of tributes: both on account of the famous lineages of their ancestors' deeds, and because they are designated for the defense of the commonwealth. Indeed, I would even add to this assertion that the king, in the face of urgent necessity for the kingdom, can sell honors of this kind—provided two things are guarded against. First, that they do not have a function of justice, or any other administration or governance attached to them, as we said in Article 4 regarding senators. Second, that it is not done to the injury of others. I say that when such necessity presses, he can grant freedom from tributes to peasants and those of humble birth for a price. For no injustice is contracted from this. And the laws *Hoc iure* and *Si pollicitus* <note>Citations from the Digest of Justinian regarding donations and public promises</note> seem to favor this, as they permit a promise made for the sake of obtaining a public honor. However, care must be taken that the tribute from which one person is relieved does not burden the remaining townsmen; rather, it should be subtracted from the total sum that the town pays.

BY THESE means, therefore, the first argument proposed at the beginning of the question is resolved. <margin>To the first argument.</margin> For indeed, just as in distributions, so too in contributions there can exist a "respect of persons." And subsequently, the remaining two arguments are diluted: since the equity of mercy protects the blind and the <margin>To the other two arguments.</margin> maimed, lest affliction be added to the miserable. And regarding the nobles, the fourth conclusion has provided the answer.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book IV. Following the discussion in Book III regarding the general principles of law and distributive justice (how the state allocates honors and burdens), Soto now transitions to "commutative justice," which governs private transactions and restitution. He begins by establishing the legal and moral foundation of all transactions: the nature of ownership itself.</meta>

F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

# BOOK FOUR
## On Justice and Law.

### PREFACE.

<margin>The division of the book.</margin>
As we begin our discussion of the other type of justice, which is set directly opposite to distributive justice—namely, **commutative justice** <note>Commutative justice governs private dealings between individuals, such as buying, selling, and contracts, ensuring an equal exchange of value.</note>—it is worthwhile to first discuss its two precursors in this fourth book: first, the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of things, and then their **restitution**. Indeed, ownership of this kind, and the division of things, is the base and foundation of all contracts, agreements, and pacts celebrated through commutative justice. Accordingly, all the vices that oppose this virtue are various violations and corruptions of ownership and the possession of things. These types of injuries and the debts contracted from them must subsequently be compensated through the benefit of restitution. Therefore, it is appropriate to dispute five questions regarding the ownership of things. The first concerns the thing itself and its subject. The second concerns its object: namely, how many types there are and of what things. The third concerns the division of ownership and its legitimate transfer. Following these, a fourth dispute will be added regarding the specific ownership of certain individuals. And finally, a fifth regarding the transfers of ownership. Let the first title of the question, therefore, be:

### QUESTION ONE,
### On ownership in general.

### ARTICLE I.
### Whether ownership is the same as the right and power over things.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The present question requires being cut into two articles: one to establish the definition of ownership, and the other to establish its subject. It is asked, therefore, whether ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> is the same as the **right** <note>original: "ius"</note> and power over things. The argument is made from the affirmative side: A "right" is the same as the power of disposing of things and using them freely;

<column-break/>

furthermore, ownership seems to be exactly the same thing. ¶ Second, because **mendicant monks** <note>Members of religious orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans who took vows of poverty. A major medieval debate focused on whether they "owned" the food they ate or merely "used" it.</note> have the right to use food, clothing, and other utensils until the items themselves are consumed, they are said to be the owners of those same things, as Pope John XXII seems to conclude for himself in the <margin>Argument 2. John XXII in "Ad conditorem."</margin> *Extravagantes* <note>A collection of canon laws; specifically the decree "Ad conditorem canonum" (1322) where the Pope argued against Franciscan claims of "pure use" without ownership.</note> *Ad conditorem*. Therefore, no reason for a distinction remains between right and ownership. ¶ To the contrary, however, is the fact that **master** and **slave** <note>original: "dominus & seruus"</note> are correlatives. In the *Institutes* <note>A foundational textbook of Roman law by Emperor Justinian.</note> regarding the law of persons, humans are distinguished into the free and the enslaved; therefore, it is denoted there that he who presides over free people, although he has the right of commanding them, does not however have ownership over them.

<margin>Ownership vs. Domination</margin>
The two proposed arguments designate two branches for us to follow. It must be noted immediately at the entrance of the question that this word, *dominium* (ownership), is not as frequent in use among the orators and ancient Latins as *dominatus* or *dominatio* (domination/rule); these two words are used more frequently by them in a bad sense than a good one. For they signify a certain image of **tyranny**: namely, when someone misuses his subjects for his own personal gain. <margin>Cicero.</margin> Hence Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5, says of Dionysius: "while," he says, "at twenty-two years of age, he had seized domination <note>original: "dominatum"</note>," etc. And in Book 2 of *On the Orator*: "Brutus freed the Roman people from kingly domination." For those things of which men are masters are called in Latin *facultates* (resources), *substantiae* (estates), and *possessiones* (possessions). But it is the **jurists** <note>Legal scholars and experts in Roman and Canon law.</note> who use this word *dominium* to signify what they likewise call the **property** of things, which is distinguished from the possession of them, and from their use and "usufruct" <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of property owned by another.</note>. Nor should this word, according to this meaning, be considered barbaric or unusual. For it is used among illustrious Latin authors, such as in Varro's *On Agriculture*, <margin>Varro.</margin> Book 2: "In trading, and in purchases and handovers, they change ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note>." And it is found in the Holy Scriptures, such as in Tobit 8: "He made this writing so that the half part that remained should come under the ownership of Tobias." And in 1 Maccabees 11: "King Ptolemy obtained ownership of the cities." In law, however, it is a most frequently used word.

<summary>This page introduces the study of commutative justice by defining 'dominium' (ownership). Soto distinguishes between the legal concept of property and the political concept of 'domination' or tyranny, citing both classical Roman authors and Scripture.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of "dominium" (ownership or dominion). Having introduced the topic on the previous page as the foundation of commutative justice, Soto now engages with the definitions provided by later medieval theologians like Gerson and Summenhart, specifically debating whether ownership is synonymous with "right" (ius) or "power" (potestas).</meta>

<page-num>279</page-num>
<header>Question I of the Fourth Book.</header>

It is established. Indeed, they stand out in the *New Digest*, book 3, <note>The *Digest* is a massive 6th-century compilation of Roman law. The "New Digest" (Digestum Novum) refers to the third part of this collection used in medieval universities.</note> distinct titles, regarding the acquisition of ownership of things, and regarding the acquisition or loss of possession.

<margin>What ownership is.</margin>
<margin>Gerson.</margin>
¶ But truly, concerning the description of the word, the later scholars <note>original: "iuniores"</note> expend more labor than is necessary: as for example Gerson in *On Ecclesiastical Power*, consideration 13, and in the treatise *On the Spiritual Life*, lesson 3. <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429) was a prominent French theologian and chancellor of the University of Paris.</note>

<margin>Conrad.</margin>
In this, Conrad is a great supporter, in treatise 1 *On Contracts*, as are several others in distinction 15 of book 4. First of all, these men say that **right** <note>original: "ius"</note> is understood in two ways. First, for the **law**: in which sense we say, "Civil Law" and "Canon Law." Second, for **legitimate power**, by which someone acts upon some person or thing.

<margin>The definition of ownership given by others is challenged.</margin>
Next, they say that ownership is exactly the same as "right" taken in the second sense. Therefore, they say ownership is the immediate power or faculty of taking other things into one's own capacity or lawful use according to reasonably established laws. This is how they speak of ownership; let us weigh whether they do so properly. First, the words themselves truly struggle to accept that the name of "right" and "ownership" should be used for the same thing. For **right** (as seen above) is the same thing (as Isidore says in book 5) as **the just**. <note>original: "iustum." Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636) provided many of the definitions used in medieval law.</note> For it is the object of justice: namely, the equity which justice establishes among men. **Ownership**, however, is the faculty of a master <note>original: "domini"</note> (as the name sounds) over servants or over things which he uses at his own discretion and for his own benefit. It follows, therefore, that "right" is not interchangeable with "ownership," but is superior to it and broader in its scope.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
For a wife has a certain **right** in her husband, according to that saying of Paul in 1 Corinthians 7: *The husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife does.* And a son has a right in his parents, who are bound to have care for their own; and servants in their masters, by whom they ought to be fed and sustained. And by the same reasoning, a subject has a right in a prelate by whom he is to be instructed and governed; and yet none of these, however much you extend the name, is the "owner" <note>original: "dominus"</note> or can be called the owner of his superior.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But Conrad says: At least it should not be denied that any right of a superior over an inferior ought properly to be considered ownership, so that ownership adds the quality of a superior precisely beyond the concept of a right.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
But truly, I would not easily grant this to them either. For indeed, a father has a right in his sons, but not, if we are to speak properly, ownership. It is, I say, equitable and just—and thus a **right**—that a father commands his sons for their own good, whom he loves, instructs, and educates for their own sake.

<margin>The proper definition of ownership.</margin>
Ownership, however, does not signify just any right and power, but certainly that which is over a thing which we can use at our pleasure for our own utility, and which we love for 

<column-break/>

our own sake. This is what the name itself clearly presents to the ears. For the relative term of "owner" is "servant"; <note>The Latin *dominus* (owner/master) and *servus* (slave/servant) are linguistic pairs.</note> who, whatever he is, belongs entirely to the owner, just like a beast. Except that a servant cannot be killed, because God alone is the owner of life.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Hence Aristotle, in book 1 of the *Politics*, chapter 3, distinguishes between civil or royal rule and **despotic** rule, which is ownership-based rule. He says the soul has a master-like (*dominicum*) sovereignty over the body, but the mind has only a civil and royal rule over the appetite—which is not ownership. And in book 5 of the *Ethics*, chapter 6, he distinguishes between the right of a master and the right of a father. For a father possesses a son before the age of majority not as a master possesses a servant, but as a part of himself; and therefore that right is not ownership. A master, however, possesses a servant as an instrument which he uses.

<margin>Richard objects.</margin>
¶ Richard, however, argues to the contrary. <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302), a Franciscan theologian.</note> If someone were to snatch a son from a father, or a wife from a husband, he would be called a **thief**; but **theft** <note>original: "furtum"</note> is not committed except against the will of the owner; therefore both the father is the owner of the son, and the husband of the wife.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this, however, it will be answered in the following book, in the question on theft, that the snatching of sons or a wife is not properly theft, but "captivity" or another species of injury. But to steal a servant is properly theft. Furthermore, it is sufficient for the definition of theft that it be done either against the will of the owner, or against the will of him to whom the thing belongs, even if he is not the owner but possesses it by some other right. For this reason, in the *Institutes* regarding the law of persons, <note>The *Institutes* of Justinian, an introductory legal textbook for Roman law students.</note> men are immediately distinguished into the free and the enslaved: since the right over the free is not properly called ownership, but the right over the enslaved is. For a Prince, although he may be the owner of cities and possessions, is not to be called the owner of the citizens, but rather their King or Duke, etc. Indeed, when he acts with ownership over his subjects—namely, by using them for his own utility—he becomes a **tyrant**. Therefore, neither a judge nor a prelate, even if he has a right over subjects, is properly called their owner. And Christ noted this in Matthew 20: *The princes of the gentiles lord it over them... it shall not be so among you.*

<margin>Ownership.</margin>
For (as we may now say in sum) ownership is only the right which one uses for one's own benefit; "right," however, does not signify this alone, but embraces even the right by which a superior and official makes use of the affairs and good of the subjects for their own sake. Wherefore, "right" must be placed in the definition of ownership as the broader category <note>original: "superius genus"</note>; so far is it from being said that they are interchangeable.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Concerning the husband in respect to the wife, however, that passage in Genesis 3 might perhaps move someone: *You shall be under the power of the husband, and he shall rule over you.*

<margin>Solution.</margin>
Yet this is by no means to be referred to civil ownership...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom "ferendum" connects to the next page's first word, "referendum" (to be referred).</meta>

<summary>Soto defines ownership (dominium) strictly as the right to use something for one's own benefit, distinguishing it from general rights (ius). He argues that while fathers, husbands, and kings have authority and rights, they are not "owners" of their subjects because their rule should be for the subjects' benefit, not their own private utility.</summary>
<keywords>ownership, dominion, right, law, power, Aristotle, Gerson, Conrad Summenhart, justice, theft, slavery, tyranny</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of "dominium" (ownership or dominion). Having introduced the topic on the previous page as the foundation of commutative justice, Soto now engages with the definitions provided by later medieval theologians like Gerson and Summenhart, specifically debating whether ownership is synonymous with "right" (ius) or "power" (potestas).</meta>

<page-num>280</page-num>
<header>F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,</header>

must be endured. Indeed, Aristotle, in the place cited, says that the right of a husband over a wife is "unnamed" <note>original: "innominatum"</note>. But he is said to rule, first, regarding conjugal use: because while nature in its integrity would have been without any shame or the hardship of labor, after the fall, because the woman was to give birth in pain, she was said to be under the husband’s power. Furthermore, because if innocence had survived there would be no place for ignorance—which followed after sin—the husband is therefore said to rule the wife regarding governance, for he ought to teach her: just as we shall say below that the more refined rule over the unrefined. This is not indeed by "legal dominion," <note>Soto distinguishes between 'legal dominion' (where a master rules a slave for the master's own benefit) and 'civil/urban dominion' (where a leader rules for the benefit of the subject).</note> for the masters' own good, but by "civil dominion," for the sake of those themselves who stand in need of discipline.

¶ From this it follows that neither is the definition these men ascribe to ownership legitimate, nor is it exactly constructed. And because (as Aristotle is the author in *On the Soul*, text 85) we know the straight by the straight itself and the crooked, let us establish a "straight" definition according to our grasp, by which we may judge the other.

<margin>The definition of ownership is established and declared.</margin>
Ownership, therefore, if you describe it according to the art, is the specific faculty and right of each person over any thing, which he can use for his own advantage in any use permitted by law.

<margin>From where "faculty" is derived</margin>
Therefore, in the place of the "genus" <note>In logic, the 'genus' is the broad category a thing belongs to.</note>, "faculty" <note>original: "facultas"</note> is placed rather than "power" <note>original: "potestas"</note>. This is certainly not for the reason Jean Gerson gives in chapter 3 of *On the Spiritual Life*—namely, because "faculty" is said to come from *fas* <note>divine law</note>, and therefore a robber's power to use another’s thing is not a "faculty." For "faculty" is not derived from *fas*, but from *facile* <note>easy or ease</note>: so that it is, as it were, "facilitiness." Indeed, "faculty" and "difficulty" are opposites. Because of this, "power" is a genus comprehending more than "faculty." For a tyrant is able to abuse the goods of citizens, yet he does not have the "faculty"—that is, the "ease"—because he cannot do so without the license and faculty of the owner or an intervening just cause. Wherefore there is very little need to add the word "proximate," for "faculty" sounds this way of itself. Indeed, a remote "power" to use another's thing is not a "faculty." I would add, however, the word "specific" <note>original: "propria"</note>, so that ownership may be distinguished from mere possession, use, and usufruct <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it.</note>. For he who has only the use or the usufruct does not have a "specific faculty," but one depending on the true owner or on a judge permitting it. Therefore, since not only the barbarians but also the most Latinate legal experts now use the word "property" <note>original: "proprietatem"</note> by custom, it is more "Latinly" called a "specific faculty." Nor is there need to add, with Gerson, "of taking other things." For even a human being, through his own will (which is the mover of all powers), also uses his own members, over which (as was just recently

<column-break/>

cited from Aristotle) the soul has "dominical command." However, it was added to the definition that ownership is a faculty "for the specific advantage of the user," to differentiate it from other types of right by which a superior governs inferiors for their own good. But it was then said universally, "for any use whatever," so that ownership may be distinguished from "use" and "usufruct." For ownership is the faculty not only of using and enjoying a thing, but also of alienating, giving, selling, or neglecting it, etc. Yet, a "mode" was applied: that the use must be "permitted by law," to resolve an objection by which someone might try to weaken the definition.

<margin>An objection with its resolution.</margin>
For truly, a ward <note>original: "pupillus"; a minor under guardianship.</note> before the legitimate age possesses ownership of his things, yet he does not have the free faculty of acting regarding them, since he can neither give nor sell such goods, because he is prohibited by human law from squandering them. For since ownership is founded in freedom, although he is truly an owner before the use of reason (because he is truly free and not a slave), the "use" of ownership is nevertheless forbidden to him for his own good until the light of reason shines upon him. Whence, as Paul says, as long as the heir is a little child, he differs nothing from a slave <note>See Galatians 4:1.</note>—not indeed regarding ownership, but regarding use—and therefore he is under tutors. And a similar argument is made concerning one whose goods are bound by the bond of primogeniture <note>Entailed estates passed to the firstborn that cannot be sold.</note>: who, though he is truly their owner, cannot alienate them for any reason because he is prohibited by civil law. For that he is truly the owner is clear from the fact that otherwise those goods would lack an owner. Furthermore, when a King, granting someone's petition, binds to the bond of primogeniture goods which were previously free, he takes away no ownership from him; nor afterwards, when he grants the possessor the faculty of alienating, does he confer a new property or ownership upon him. Therefore, he is always the owner, though prohibited just like a ward.

¶ Let us refrain here from mentioning those trifles: whether ownership is the thing itself which is possessed, or the owner, or rather a "relation." However, I will not omit to warn that philosophers should beware those "barbarous" expressions of the Terminists <note>The 'Terminists' were Nominalist philosophers who focused on how words (terms) refer to things, often using technical jargon Soto disliked.</note>. For who could bear to hear that "the ownership of a horse" is either the horse or the rider? For ownership is that condition of things between the possessor and the possessed: namely, the faculty of the possessor over the thing possessed. Because of this, it is defined through its act—which is indeed the peculiar way of defining "powers." For just as sight is the power of sensing colors, and hearing is the power of sensing sounds, so ownership is the faculty of using, enjoying a thing, etc.

<margin>The title differs from ownership in every way.</margin>
¶ In addition to these points, it must be noted that the "title" of ownership is a different thing from ownership itself; a point which certain [scholars] somewhat negligently...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition of "dominium" (ownership or dominion). Having discussed the nature of rule within a household, Soto now moves to define the "title" or legal basis of ownership and explores the distinctions between ownership, use, and usufruct, particularly concerning the poverty of the Franciscan Order.</meta>

# Question I of the Fourth Book.

<margin>What a title is.</margin>
The scholars of Paris <note>Likely referring to the theologians at the University of Paris.</note> consider this: they judge that along with their Chancellor, the same faculty which is "dominion" (ownership) is also "title." In truth, a title is the base of ownership, or the root from which it sprouts. Now, the title of ownership is either nature, law, contract, or election, and so forth. For example: the title of natural ownership which a man has over the things born of the earth is natural life, which cannot be preserved without them; by reason of this, God and nature gave to man—along with the appetite for self-preservation—the right even to use necessary food. Similarly, the title of right (I will not say ownership) which parents have over their offspring is natural procreation. However, the title by which each person possesses private things is the "law of nations" <note>original: "ius gentium," the customary laws common to all peoples.</note>, by which the division of things was made. The title of a bishop, truly, is election. And the title by which one possesses a house is either native inheritance, or purchase, or prescription <note>legal ownership gained through long-term, uninterrupted possession.</note>, etc.

<margin>The distinction between ownership, use, and usufruct.</margin>
¶ From this established definition of ownership, the difference between it, use, and usufruct is gathered. For ownership is the power over the substance of a thing; usufruct, however, is only over its qualities and accidents. I say "over the substance of a thing" because if it is consumable by use, such as food and clothing, the owner can consume it; if not, he can give it away or sell it, like a house and a slave—indeed, he can even kill it, like a beast of burden.

<margin>Usufruct</margin>
But usufruct is the right of using and enjoying the things of others, while preserving their substance <note>Soto is quoting a standard definition from Roman law.</note>: as found in the Digest, *on usufruct* <note>original: "ff. de usu fruct."</note>, and in the Institutes under the same title. For he who has the usufruct of a field or gardens can not only eat the fruits, but also sell them—indeed, he may even lease the field to another.

<margin>Naked use.</margin>
"Naked use" <note>Simple use without the right to the profits or "fruits" of the thing.</note>, however, is the right of using the things of others while preserving their substance, yet without "enjoyment" (the right to the fruits). Wherefore, as held in the Institutes, *on use and habitation*, there is less right in "use" than in "usufruct." For he "enjoys" a thing who has full power over the fruits, which he can not only eat, but also alienate in any way whatever; but he "uses" it who is only permitted to feed upon them, or to nourish his own herds, yet not to sell them off in any other way. For instance, he who has the naked use of a field can enter it, eat the apples, and graze his beasts and cattle on the hay; however, he may not sell the fruits or lease the land. Therefore, in both definitions, it is said "of others' things," because a true owner is not called a "user" or "usufructuary," but rather he who has strictly use or usufruct.

<margin>The Emphyteuta</margin>
Even if the *emphyteuta* <note>A tenant who holds a long-term or perpetual lease of land in exchange for an annual rent and improvements to the property.</note> is said to have "beneficial ownership" <note>original: "dominium utile"</note>, this is in distinction to "direct ownership" <note>original: "dominio directi"</note>, which is ownership in its simple sense. These matters, however, are not our concern at the moment.

<column-break/>

<margin>A serious question.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, because we profess the religion of the mendicants <note>The Dominican Order, to which Soto belonged.</note>, our institution warns us to dispute somewhat concerning this established definition: whether in things consumable by use, "use" can be distinguished from "ownership."

<margin>In consumable things.</margin>
Things not consumable by use are those whose use is not their destruction, such as a farm, a house, and the like. Things consumable by use are those whose use is nothing other than the disposal or consumption of the thing, such as money (the use of which is to transfer it into the ownership of another) and bread (the use of which is to eat it). Regarding those things which are consumed in a single act (where the doubt becomes more serious), this is our present discourse. For in the case of clothing, although it is worn down by use, because it does not perish in a single act of wear, use could somehow be discerned from ownership. We raise this doubt chiefly because of the rule of those who live under the Holy Rule of Saint Francis, and those of our own order who persevere in the same institution. For the Minors <note>The Franciscans.</note> say they have abdicated all ownership, so much so that they do not enjoy ownership of money, nor bread, nor the food they eat, so that they might not be called "proprietors" (if I may use their own word). Truly, this controversy is not only contested among theologians, but various sentences have also been pronounced regarding this by the Supreme Pontiffs. For there exists the Constitution <margin>Nicholas III</margin> of Nicholas III in the chapter *Exiit qui seminat* <note>A famous 1279 papal bull defining Franciscan poverty.</note>, under the title "on the meaning of words" in the sixth book [of the Decretals]. There, by declaring the words of Gregory and other Pontiffs, he clearly affirms and confirms with many added words that the Friars Minor have no ownership—neither in common nor in particular—of tools or victuals, but are mere "users." The ownership of money always remains with the donors, and that of food and tools remains with the Supreme Pontiff. Almost the same sentence exists <margin>Clement V</margin> from Clement V in the decree *Exivi de paradiso* under the same title. However, <margin>John XXII</margin> John XXII opposed a contrary sentence to these in the "Extravagantes" <note>A collection of canon laws.</note>, in the decrees *Ad conditorem*, *Cum inter nonnullos*, and *Quia quorundam*. There he asserts without doubt that in things consumable by use, use is not at all distinguished from ownership, nor can it be separated from it by any agreement. This is certainly a difficult matter. And first, to take our starting point from the nature of things <margin>First argument from the affirmative side.</margin> for the sake of arguing the contrary, it appears that since the use of such things is their consumption, no one can use a thing except as a true owner. For true ownership, if you look back at the definition established above, consists in this—

And yet, if the use of this kind of thing were separated from ownership, it would clearly follow that the use could be leased at a price distinct from the value of the thing itself—as if someone were to charge me a certain amount just for the act of eating, and then on top of that, the full value of the capon <note>A roasted rooster; Soto uses this as a common example of a consumable good.</note>. ¶ <margin>Second argument.</margin> In the second place, it is argued by the authority of law: for in the Digest <note>original: "ff.", the standard abbreviation for the Pandects or Digest of Roman Civil Law.</note> regarding the usufruct <term>usufruct: the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying its substance</term> of things which are consumed by use (Book 2), a provision is made that the usufruct of money cannot be bequeathed without the money itself, nor of other things like wine and oil which are consumed by use. Because of this, as much as can be sincerely gathered from that legal title, the usufruct of these things pertains to a kind of "loan for consumption" <term>loan for consumption: original Latin "mutuatio," a loan where the specific item is used up and an equivalent is returned later</term>. For he to whom the usufruct of money or grain is bequeathed is bound to give security that he will restore the whole thing to the legitimate heir. And in the Digest, regarding usufruct and how one may use it (the law "of all things," section "it is established"), a perpetual usufruct is prohibited, lest ownership become useless; for the ownership of a thing which one was never allowed to use would be in vain. From these points, therefore, an argument is drawn: if the use of the bread and wine of the Mendicants belongs to them, and it is a use of such a kind that they are never required to restore the thing, let it be most clearly established that the ownership also rests with them. The "use of law" is a grant of the law, and in these consumable things, it is not separated from ownership; this, however, they say the Mendicants lack. The "use of fact" is the act itself of eating and drinking, and this alone is granted to them. So says Pope Nicholas in that same chapter *Exiit*. But truly, this distinction is not as easy to understand as it is to say. For "use of law" is understood to be nothing other than what the law permits from the will of the owner. If someone bequeathed the usufruct of money to me, it follows that the use is legitimate for me. If it is legitimate, it is therefore granted by law. In the same way, if you give bread to a beggar, why should that use by the beggar not be considered legal? Added to this is what the Pope says in the same place: that he grants them use just as if they were truly the owners. Indeed, John XXII <margin>John XXII.</margin> openly and frankly confesses that he holds no

But the Minorites <note>The Friars Minor, or Franciscans.</note> cannot use their things in such ways, even when joined as a community. On the contrary, those who bestow money upon them can, as the true owners, take it away at will whenever they please. As for other utensils and food, the <margin>A very appropriate analogy.</margin> Pope declares himself the owner. Therefore, just as when someone receives friends at a banquet, he does not make them owners of the food and drink with which the table is spread—because he does not give them the power to steal those things away to carry into their own homes, but only that they may eat them while sitting there—in almost the same way, the Pope invites the brothers daily, giving them only the power of eating, drinking, clothing themselves, etc. Therefore, even if he took those things away from them, he would do them no injury, nor should he be considered a thief or a robber, but rather an owner reclaiming his own. This is supported by Acts 2, where it is held that all the believers had all things in common. This is to be understood regarding those who lived in Jerusalem: all things, even down to their food, were common to them, and they conducted themselves like guests at the table of a host. <margin>Second reason for the conclusion.</margin> ¶ Furthermore, I myself would support the same point by this reasoning. For the attackers of this kind of poverty confess that monks can have property in common, even though no individual monk has it in particular. Let us use their own confession: I, as an individual monk, can eat from the common goods even though I am not their individual owner; therefore, in the same way, the entire community and the whole Order can use them, even if it lacks all ownership. Nor should the word of John XXII greatly move us when he says he abdicated such ownership. First, because he did not do so legitimately, and—if it is permitted to say—perhaps not even justly; certainly, it was perhaps done out of hatred for Ockham <note>William of Ockham, a Franciscan philosopher who was a fierce opponent of Pope John XXII.</note> and others of his Order who were most hostile to him. Secondly, because his renunciation...
