# Book Four, Question I.

...his successors in the same See <note>The Papacy or the Holy See.</note> have not yet approved; but following the example of their predecessors, they retain the same ownership. ¶ This same conclusion is corroborated by the Law in Deuteronomy 23, where those entering a neighbor's vineyard were permitted the use of the grapes without ownership. For it says: *Having entered your neighbor's vineyard, eat as many grapes as you please, but do not carry any out with you.* <note>Deuteronomy 23:24. This was a biblical precedent for "use" without "ownership."</note> Therefore, it did not make him the owner of the grapes so that he could sell them or exchange them for something else, but rather so that he might be fed like a guest. Likewise, in the *Institutes* regarding Use and Habitation: to one who has the bare use of a field, nothing further is granted than to use the herbs, fruits, flowers, etc., for daily use; it seems, therefore, that use is there distinguished from ownership. To the same point belongs the fact that one who suffers in extreme necessity may help himself with another's bread, yet not so that he may sell it; wherefore, indeed, ownership does not seem to be transferred there, but rather a legitimate use of another's property. Although, where someone suffers a lack of bread, he could take another thing which he might exchange for bread.

<margin>In extreme necessity, ownership is not transferred.</margin>
And the conjecture that ownership is not transferred in extreme necessity is taken from the fact that otherwise, he who did not help the wretched person under that circumstance would remain liable for restitution; for if he were bound to transfer ownership to the other, it would be just as if he were retaining another's property. ¶ These points certainly make the matter very probable, through which the statement of Pope Nicholas <note>Pope Nicholas III, who in 1279 issued a decree defending the Franciscan concept of poverty.</note> becomes clear in some way: 

<margin>Use in fact; use in law.</margin>
namely, that the [Friars] Minor have the **use in fact**, and not **in law**; that is, use in the act, and not in the habit <note>In legal terms, a "habit" refers to a permanent right or standing, whereas "act" refers only to the moment of use.</note>. For "use in law" or "in habit" exists when such use cannot be prevented by the owner; which is not the case among the Mendicants, but only while they are actually eating. However, the matter is different with money: for since such use is to alienate <term>alienate: to legally transfer the ownership of a thing to another</term> it, it is taken for every use; and thus no one uses it legitimately 

<margin>To the first reason.</margin>
unless they are the true owner. ¶ And through these points, a response is given to the reasons to the contrary. For to the first, it must be said that even if no other use remains after the consumption of these things, it does not immediately follow that they are taken for every use: 

<margin>Objection.</margin>
which the nature of ownership requires. ¶ But you argue more insistently: If the Mendicants cannot alienate those things, it is because they are prohibited by law, like wards <note>Minors under legal guardianship.</note> or firstborn sons; therefore, it does not prevent 

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
those fictional owners from being true owners. The antecedent is denied: because no civil law prohibits them from selling or giving those things away, etc. But rather because 

<margin>To the second reason and to St. Thomas.</margin>
the true owner does not permit that kind of power to them. To the laws alleged above, and to the authority of St. Thomas [Aquinas], who denies...

<column-break/>

...that in these things use and ownership can be calculated separately, it is responded that those laws only establish that a price cannot be taken for the use separately from the price of the thing. They do not, however, deny that an owner can restrict the use so that another may use it only in that manner, and not in all the ways required for true ownership.

<margin>To the first main argument.</margin>
The arguments objected at the head of the question are sufficiently clearly resolved. For the second premise of the first argument is false: namely, that ownership and right are equivalent; on the contrary, the nature of ownership entails more than the nature of a right, and thus, "right" is a more general term. And likewise, the response was given to the other: namely, that the right of the Mendicants to food and utensils is not sufficient for them to be their owners.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Of the second, however, both premises are true, as the second conclusion shows: namely, that the Mendicants consume food and clothing of which they are not the owners; yet it does not follow from this that our definition is not legitimate. On the contrary, by that same definition, it is taught that they are not the owners of those things, since they cannot alienate them.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether ownership of things belongs only to God,<-
->and to intellectual and<-
->rational creatures.<-

<margin>First argument of the opposing side.</margin>
Therefore, having fixed the definition of ownership, it follows in the second article to explore its subject: namely, to inquire to whom ownership of things properly belongs—whether, after God, it belongs only to angels and men. For it is argued that ownership, in its own order, is fitting for brute animals; for example, of herbs, which, as is read in Genesis 1, were granted to them for fodder. Indeed, it seems the leader of the bees holds dominion over its swarm; and among cranes, that one which leads the line appears to be the queen of the others. And among wild beasts, the most ferocious lion seems to dominate the remaining beasts, and the hawk likewise carries out dominion over wretched birds.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued to the same point regarding the inanimate heavens, which dominate this sublunary world: inasmuch as they flow heat and power into it, by which it is nourished and grows. 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Wherefore Aristotle, in Book 1 of the *Meteorology*: *It is necessary that this lower world be subject to the superior motions, so that its power may be governed from there.* Wherefore in Genesis 1, the sun is read to have been created to preside over the day, and the moon to preside over the night.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of "use" versus "ownership." The previous page concluded with legal and biblical examples of people using goods (like eating grapes in a neighbor's vineyard) without becoming the legal owners of the source. Here, Soto shifts to a theological and philosophical definition of ownership (dominium) itself.</meta>

# Friar Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Law*,

...to the night. ¶ On the contrary, however, is what is stated in the same place in Genesis 1: that ownership of the world is granted to humans alone. It says: *“Let us make man in our image and likeness: and let him rule over the fish,”* etc. <note>original: "Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostrā: & præfit piscibus, &c." from Genesis 1:26.</note>

<margin>Jean Gerson</margin>
Concerning this question, the modern thinkers <term>Neoterici</term> <note>Soto uses this term to refer to relatively recent Scholastic authors, specifically the followers of the 15th-century French theologian Jean Gerson.</note>, following Gerson as their leader, devise many things that are not very consistent with reason. For he, an otherwise serious author, multiplied several species of ownership in the places cited above. Among these, he attributed many forms of ownership to brute animals, and even to insentient things, as was explained in the arguments formed above. But whether these things (if I may be excused for saying so) were discovered by reason and judgment, or asserted at will, must be examined. Indeed, to those consulting the nature of things, it will immediately become clear that the concept of ownership does not extend so widely. 

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let this, therefore, be the first conclusion: The nature of ruling—and thus having ownership of things—belongs only to those who possess intellect and free will. Specifically, it belongs first to God, then to the intellectual nature of angels, and finally to rational 

<margin>Of which things God has ownership.</margin>
human beings. God, I say—to whom (as the Psalm says) *“the earth belongs, and the fullness thereof”* <note>Psalm 24:1.</note>—holds ownership and sovereignty over all things he created by right of creation. As that confession of the Wise Man states: *“You are the Lord of all things.”* <note>original: "Dominus vniuersorũ tu es." See Wisdom 11:27.</note> He was indeed Lord in power from eternity, yet since the world was founded, he is Lord in use and in act. For before then, there were no things to obey him. It is even a sacrilege to abuse the name of "ownership" so far (as some are not ashamed to do) as to apply it among the Divine Persons; for nothing in God is inferior to God himself, but whatever is there exists as infinite. Nor is the Son in any way subject to the Father, being perfectly equal to Him. Because of this, the entire Trinity has equal ownership—and the same absolute ownership—of creatures: not only regarding their use, but also regarding their natures. For He is one who may not only use all things at his will, but may also create their natures, annihilate them, and alter them beyond the laws of nature—such as preventing fire from heating, heating water without fire, and, as the lord of life and death, depriving not only other animals but also humans of life. 

<margin>Over which things the Angels rule.</margin>
Angels, however, have ownership only over their own natural actions, but not over this world in the same way as humans do. For this world was by no means created for them, who need no body, but only for humans, for whom the angels are ministering 

<column-break/>

spirits. <note>See Hebrews 1:14.</note> Although their Hierarchies are distributed through their Principalities and Dominations, and some indeed command others, this pertains very little to our present subject. 

<margin>The conclusion is demonstrated.</margin>
Let us descend, therefore, to our own species, to whom alone we shall demonstrate that ownership of sublunary <term>sublunariũ</term> <note>In the Aristotelian worldview, the "sublunary" sphere refers to the Earth and everything below the orbit of the moon, which is subject to change and decay.</note> things belongs. First: a "lord," unless we are abusing the word most inappropriately, is only one in whose power it lies to use a thing in this or that way for his own benefit. Now, this suits no one except through intellect and will; therefore, only humans on earth shine with the quality of ownership. 

¶ But so that the matter may shine more clearly, it is argued secondly: Ownership of external things belongs to no one except for the reason that he is himself the master of his own actions. For the ownership that each person has over his own acts is the cause and the root of the ownership he has over other things. However, only man is the master of his own actions <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> (as Saint Thomas is the authority in Part 1-2, Question 1 <note>A reference to the *Summa Theologiae* of Thomas Aquinas.</note>) through intellect and will. Therefore, by the same reasoning, the right to be the master of other things belongs to him alone. Beyond St. Thomas, the very usage of human speech demonstrates the secondary point of this argument. For when someone is seized in the mind <note>i.e., becomes insane or loses mental capacity.</note>, he is said not to be master of himself, but "incapable of himself" <note>original: "sui impotens."</note>. The primary point, however, is based on natural reason. For he who is not master of himself cannot be master of others. 

¶ Moreover, by the testimony of Holy Scripture cited above, which is the interpreter of nature, the same conclusion is proven a third time. <margin>Third reason for the conclusion.</margin> For God said in Genesis 1: *“Let us make man in our image and likeness: and let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and the beasts,”* etc. That is, "in this let us make him in our image: so that he may be established as the lord over the rest of the universe of creatures, which lacks our image." Now, for a human to be made in the image and likeness of God is to be made free in intellect and will; for this is the "face" of God. In the rest of creatures, only a "trace" <note>original: "vestigium." A theological term meaning a faint mark of the creator, whereas humans have the "image."</note> of Him is left, just as the footprint of a human foot is left in the dust, by which the face of that same person cannot be recognized. Therefore, because these two powers—intellect and will—were shared with humans, they were created in the image of God; and from that, they consequently obtained the right of ruling over the other living creatures that lack reason. Indeed, I am not unaware that some distinguish between "royal" and "natural" ownership, saying that freedom is required for the first kind but not for the second. Nevertheless, this is stated without proof; for by nature itself, no one is the owner of things unless he is the master of his own actions...

<summary>Soto argues that true ownership (dominium) requires intellect and free will, meaning it belongs only to God, angels, and humans. He rejects the idea that animals or inanimate objects can "own" anything and roots human property rights in the biblical concept of being made in the Image of God.</summary>

# Question II of the Fourth Book
<meta>catchword: according</meta>

<margin>Fourth reason for the conclusion.</margin>
...of their own, and therefore neither of things. ¶ Fourthly, it is argued: To exercise ownership over a thing (as we showed above) is to use it. However, brute animals are in no way able to "use" things <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "use" (*usus*) is a technical term involving a deliberate act of the will to apply a means to an end.</note>; therefore, they have no ownership. The minor premise is from 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I-II, Question 16, where he taught that use does not belong to brutes, according to that saying of Augustine in his *Book of 83 Different Questions*: 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
"No animal can use a thing unless it participates in reason." <note>original: "Vti aliquod non potest animal, nisi rationis particeps."</note> And the reason is that "to use" is to order a thing toward an end, since the will is directed toward the end, while use concerns the means to that end. Beasts do nothing for the sake of an end, as they do not know the end; rather, they are driven by natural instinct. ¶ And this is further confirmed by a similar reasoning: It belongs to a master to command. This is the same as ordering a thing toward another end, which is entirely foreign to brutes, as 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
the same St. Thomas demonstrated in the following Question 17. ¶ Fifthly, it is argued for the same conclusion: Whoever has ownership of any thing is affected by an injury when it is taken away. 
<margin>Brute animals.</margin>
But brute animals are capable neither of justice, nor of injury, nor of the happiness which they do not know, as 
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle states in the *Ethics*, Book 10, Chapter 8. The reason for this is that since they are not free, they are not <term>sui iuris</term> <note>Latin for "of their own right"; a legal term for an individual who is not under the power of another, such as a master or guardian.</note>; instead, whatever they are belongs to man, for whose sake the world was created. And therefore, he who takes away the fodder or the life from a beast of burden or a herd has committed no injury against the animal, but against its owner. Similarly, one who yields his place to the King's horse offers no honor to the horse, but to the King. Therefore, cattle have no ownership nor right to the grass, but only a natural appetite and also power. If, then, no ownership can belong to brutes, it clearly follows that it can much less belong to the heavens or inanimate things. Man is, for this reason, the middle ground between God and the brutes. For an irrational animal has no ownership. God, however, has supreme ownership: namely, both as to the use and as to the nature of things. But man has ownership as to the use; yet, as to their nature, he has none at all, insofar as he cannot change their natures except by applying active forces to passive ones.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, the response is made by denying the entire preceding statement. For brutes have no ownership of the grass, which is proven by the same authority from Genesis cited to the contrary. For we do not read there that the plants were granted to the cattle and beasts of burden, but to humans alone. "Behold," He says, "I have given to you every herb bearing seed upon the earth," etc., "that they may be for food for you and for all the 

<column-break/>

living creatures of the earth." <note>A reference to Genesis 1:29-30. Soto argues that God gave plants to humans *for* the animals that serve them, rather than giving the animals legal rights.</note> Therefore, the right to the plants was not granted to the brutes, but to us for the sake of those who serve us. Nor is there a "king" among bees except metaphorically; for the king does not order the swarm toward an end, but rather one goes first by natural instinct, and the rest of the army follows. Much less do wild beasts or birds of prey "rule" over others, even though they use them as food. ¶ Next, the response to the second argument is likewise: the heavens possess ownership far less properly in that sense in which we use the name at present. Rather, they are said to "predominate" because by their influence these lower things are nourished, cherished, altered, and changed. Just as in individual elements, that quality is said to "predominate" which stands out over the others.

# SECOND QUESTION, concerning the things of which man is master.

### ARTICLE I.
-> Whether man is master of all things in the world by some right. <-

After we have established that ownership of things among corporal creatures is fitting for man alone, it follows that we should discuss how many kinds of ownership he enjoys and over which things. This question will have two articles. The first will be general; the second will specifically address two types of ownership. ¶ On the negative side, it is argued that man is not the master of absolutely everything created in the world. For this would belong to him either by natural right, divine right, or human right. Not by natural right: because universal ownership was granted to him by God at his creation. Nor by divine right: since then man would be master of whatever he needed by the right of charity; and if that charity were lost <note>In this context, "charity" refers to being in a state of grace with God.</note>, he would fall from that same right; for God allows His goods to be bestowed only upon His friends. But the consequence is false and contrary to human custom, even that of Christians, among whom many just people are pressed by a lack of things, deprived of ownership of all; while many, on the contrary, who are wicked and depraved, abound in the goods of this world, according to...

<summary>Soto argues that ownership requires reason and the ability to direct things toward a goal, meaning animals and nature cannot "own" property. He then begins investigating whether humans possess a right to all things in the world, questioning if such a right is based on nature, grace, or law.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law
<meta>catchword: but</meta>

...according to laws which do not deviate from the divine rule, they possess them. However, it is clear that man is not a master by purely human law; for before human laws existed, God had granted our race mastery over things, which is the foundation of human law by which the ownership of those things was divided. ¶ Secondly, it is argued: Man is not the master of the elements nor of the heavens, because those are not named in Genesis 1 where man was established as the master of things. ¶ To the contrary is the fact that all things were made for the sake of man, as Aristotle is the author in Book 1 of the *Politics*. And David in Psalm 8: "You have subjected all things under his feet."

In this question, those more recent Teachers whom we mentioned in the previous question heap together many kinds of ownership. For Jean Gerson <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429) was a prominent French theologian and Chancellor of the University of Paris.</note> enumerated six; others truly counted up to nine. But it pleased Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart (c. 1440–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts and property.</note> in treatise 1, question 6, to review twenty-three. For they say there is one "beatific" ownership, which the blessed enjoy in glory; and another "gratific" <note>From the Latin *gratificum*, referring to a state of being in God's grace. This theory suggested that only the righteous could truly own property.</note> ownership, which the just have over all created things, so that they may use them by the right of charity, according to that passage in Romans 8: "To those who love God, all things work together for good." And another is natural, and another evangelical, etc. But these men (if I may say so without damaging their reputation) multiply these kinds of ownership for two misguided reasons. First, because they persist in believing that "ownership" (*dominium*) and "right" (*ius*) are the same thing; and next, because they carve up ownership based on the material objects owned. This sort of division, because it lacks systematic art, could go on forever. Indeed, they ought to be distinguished only according to the titles from which they arise.

<margin>First conclusion. Ownership is only fourfold: namely natural, divine, and human (which is itself twofold).</margin>
Let this, therefore, be the first conclusion of this matter: Ownership is only fourfold: namely natural, divine, and human—the latter being divided into two, namely that which arises from the law of nations (*ius gentium*), and the other which is acquired by civil law. This conclusion appears firmer on its own than needing to be confirmed by many arguments. For ownerships were introduced by some law; but law (as was seen in both previous books) is nothing other than natural, of nations, and civil—to which is added divine positive law. This is that which does not belong to man by the debt of his nature, but is added to his nature by divine gift. This is called "divine positive" as distinct from "natural," of which God is also the author. Therefore, that there are no more than these kinds of ownership is clear from the fact that by no right 

<column-break/>

besides these can anyone obtain any ownership. Therefore, no reason permits us to distinguish "original" ownership, and "beatific," etc. For the right by which Adam, now deceased, held the tree of life—which those men call "original"—was divine positive law; that is, it was granted above his nature. Nevertheless, it was in a certain way natural to that state, namely so that men might be able not to die. However, with much weaker justification is a new species of "gratific" ownership invented. For we do not have ownership of the works of grace, because we perform them not through ourselves, but by the supernatural favor of God. And the same applies to the right of the blessed. For first, although they have the right to enjoy glory, that is not properly ownership, but a mere right granted by God, who is the master of glory. Otherwise, since glory consists in the vision of God, one could with equal ease say that the blessed person is the master of God. Secondly, even that right, if it were permitted to be called ownership, is divine positive law. For divine right of this kind exists chiefly in supernatural things, such as what has just been said, and the "evangelical right," by which ministers of the church have the power of absolving from sins, conferring other sacraments, and teaching the faith. This is in truth foolishly called "ownership"; it is rather the right of the ministers of God. For who among mortals could be said to "master" the sacraments? This divine positive right is also extended to natural things. Such is the right to tithes, which the same priests have—namely, the "reaping of temporal things for the sowing of spiritual things," <note>original: "metendi temporalia pro spiritualiũ seminatione." A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:11.</note> as Paul says. Although even this right rests on a natural foundation, for "the laborer is worthy of his hire." Indeed, for that reason, the Apostle brought forward the example of the ox treading out the grain. Likewise, the right and ownership that David had over the kingdom was also divine positive law, since he was chosen by God, unlike other kings who are chosen by the commonwealth. And so too the ownership by which the people of Israel possessed the promised land. Indeed, there are even those who think we exercise ownership over the angels, because of the assertion of Paul in Hebrews 1: "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation?" <note>original: "Nōne omnes sunt administratorij spiritus, in ministeriũ missi propter eos qui hæreditatem capient salutis?"</note> But in truth, it would be an abuse of the word to call men "masters of angels," which is proper to the one man, Christ. Rather, they perform this part by the ministry of God, just as the demons of the lower world are not so much "masters" of the souls they torture as they are executors of divine justice through punishments which they themselves also endure.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion. Man has a natural ownership, not only over all the fruits of the earth, but...

### Question II of the Fourth Book

but also in a certain way over the elements and the celestial spheres, which are like the roof of his own dwelling. Regarding the mastery of earthly things, Genesis 1 is clear: *Let us make man that he may rule over,* <note>original: "Faciamus hominem vt præſit"</note> etc. And again: *Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it: and rule over the fishes of the sea,* etc. For that mastery is not considered a positive divine right, but a natural one. For these rights and types of mastery do not differ by reason of their author—for in that case, all masteries would be called "divine," since all power comes from the Lord God—but they differ because a natural right is something owed to nature, while the other is something applied above nature. Mastery of things fits man in the first way. For insofar as man is a corporeal being, those things necessary for his life are owed to him. Indeed, Aristotle concluded by this reasoning that all corporeal things were made for the sake of man. Therefore, just as God may have created men through a miracle, nevertheless the limbs and natural powers are owed to his nature; so too that granting of mastery over things was a certain explanation of natural law, like a debt owed to human nature, assuming its existence, which He had freely bestowed upon it through creation.

And by equal reasoning, he has mastery in a certain way over the heavens, which are like the roofs of his houses; and over the elements, and over the sun's heat and the light which he uses; and over other influences; and over the rain and snow which serve him by natural right to preserve his life, and to prepare earthly food by their help. It was said, however, with moderation, that we have mastery over the heavens and elements: because we cannot either consume them like the fruits of the earth, or use them as we do animals.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: Even by human law—which in the previous book was divided into the law of nations <term>ius gentium; the common laws shared by all peoples</term> and civil law—man abounds in many masteries. For by the law of nations (as we shall say shortly), private masteries were divided so that "mine" and "thine" might be heard in the world. Moreover, by civil law—that is, the specific law of each city or kingdom—mortals possess many things: such as by the right of prescription <term>legal ownership gained through long-term use</term>, by hereditary right, by the right of primogeniture <term>the right of the firstborn to inherit</term>, etc. All these things are clear and evident.

<margin>Gerson's opinion is attacked.</margin>
¶ However, that which Gerson <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a prominent French theologian.</note> and more extensively Richard <note>Likely Richard FitzRalph (c. 1300–1360), also known as Armachanus, who argued that "dominion is founded in grace."</note> discuss in Question 2 regarding "gratific mastery" <term>dominium gratificum; ownership based on being in God's state of grace</term>, requires careful attention. For it is possible to err in this matter in two ways and through either extreme. Indeed, these named authors say that those who are received into the friendship of God through His

<column-break/>

grace enjoy mastery over things that are not possessed by them by any other title: namely, over all the things of any possessor, because by the right of charity <term>caritas; the theological virtue of love</term> they may use all things.

¶ Against these, however, the fourth conclusion is established.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
One who is in the grace of God has no more mastery or right of using another's property than one who is in sin: for both, in extreme necessity, can use the things necessary for them, regardless of who the possessor is; yet neither can do so outside of that necessity. Furthermore, the contrary of this is both false and dangerous to assert. Indeed, the title

<margin>Charity is not the title for possessed things.</margin>
by which mortals are gifted with the mastery of things is not charity, as Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), whose views on dominion and grace were condemned by the Church.</note> and, in Book 10, Armachanus falsely thought; but rather (as we have said) natural or human law. For God makes His sun to rise upon the evil and the good, and rains upon the just and the unjust: and therefore, no matter how much anyone excels in charity, he nevertheless acquires no new right over these fleeting and slippery things, but rather over the kingdom of heaven; of whose inheritance alone Paul says, *If children, then heirs through Christ.* <note>Romans 8:17</note> Nor does the custom and use of the Christian commonwealth permit that anyone, by the title of charity, should be able to seize the things of others; on the contrary, through this, he would fall away from that very virtue of charity. Even more, Christ commanded us to despise all these things. Nor does Paul concede to the holy preachers of the Gospel any other title to reap temporal things than as a wage for their labor, because they sow spiritual things.

¶ However, that which they bring forward for themselves—*To those who love God, all things work together for good*—protects them with no color of truth: because Paul intended nothing else than that those who love God are not overcome by the turbulent incursions of this world, but use all things as aids to their virtues. And as for what they add, that "among friends all things are common": this only proves that for the friends of God, His eternal goods are common. For these temporal things are not worthy to be bestowed by Him as a reward to His dear ones. Although (as the Psalmist says) He does not abandon the just in their necessities. However, He provides for this through alms or another legitimate way. For if He gave anyone a right to usurp the things of others by the title of charity, He would then place a stumbling block to the peace and tranquility of the commonwealth. For the titles of these temporal things ought to be evident in the external forum <term>the public legal sphere</term>: so that everyone may openly know what is sought from them by right, and what by injustice. Charity, however, lies hidden in the heart. Truly, this opinion is not far removed from that of

of the Lutherans, which we challenged in Chapter 4 on the Epistle to the Romans: indeed, those who extract from that word of Paul concerning "just Abraham and his seed, that he might be the heir of the world," <note>original: "iusto Abraham & semine eius, vt hæres esset mũdi"</note> the meaning that it is permitted for the righteous to enjoy any food, clothing, adornment, and delights of the world. But regarding this falsehood, it is not relevant to the present place. ¶ From the same root—namely, that charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to being in a state of divine grace or friendship with God.</note> is the title for possessed things—the Wycliffites <note>Followers of John Wycliffe, whose views on "dominion founded in grace" were highly controversial.</note> (against whom, as we said, Armachanus <note>Richard FitzRalph (c. 1300–1360), Archbishop of Armagh, who argued against the mendicant orders.</note> stumbled in Book 10, Chapter 4) extract the meaning that no one outside of charity retains any right to spiritual things or lordship over temporal things. This is a foolish heresy, condemned again and again. For although a wicked man is not worthy of the bread he eats, nor of the life by which he lives by way of merit (as Augustine and the other Saints say), nevertheless the right of nature persists in him, so that he may enjoy the sun, which God makes to rise even over the evil. For Holy Scripture celebrates many kings, even while they were in sin; not only those of the Gentiles, such as Nebuchadnezzar and others of both the Chaldeans and Persians, but also of the Hebrews, such as Saul, Solomon, and even David himself. Furthermore, we set aside how much a cloud of uncertainty this madness would cast over the Church, throwing everything into confusion. For such an assault is not for this present place. However, Gerson <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a prominent French scholar and reformer.</note> and Richard should not be branded with the same mark by which heretics are denoted; because according to them, although he who falls from the grace of God may lose the "right of charity" to enjoy the things of others, he nevertheless retains the "right of nature" by which he possesses his own property, and other rights, whether ecclesiastical or civil.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, the arguments require no other new response. For that consequence of the first argument has already been denied: namely, "The lordship of things was granted to man by God; therefore it is not natural to him." This is denied because it was granted not as something applied to nature, but as something owed to nature.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ And a response is also made to the second: that although man is not the lord of the substance of the heavens such that he could alter them, he is nevertheless their lord because he uses them as a dwelling and for other natural comforts. And he is much better a lord of the elements: such as the air for breathing, the sea for navigation, the earth for cultivation, and likewise fire for the impressions of the atmosphere. <note>original: "meteorâs impressiones" — likely referring to weather phenomena or the upper atmosphere.</note>

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether a man can be a lord over another man.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' with floral scrollwork and architectural frame.</image-desc>
It follows in this second article to speak singularly about this species of lordship: namely, whether a man can be the lord of another man. ¶ And it is argued against the affirmative side. No right can deviate from natural right; but by natural right all men are born free: this is plainly confessed by the law-givers themselves in the *Institutes* regarding the law of persons, and in the *Digest* regarding the status of men, in the law titled "Liberty," <note>original: "l. libertas" — referring to specific sections of Roman Civil Law.</note> stating that slavery is that by which someone is subjected to the lordship of another *against nature*. And Gregory asserts the same where he says it is against nature for men to rule over men. Reason also shows the same: for man excels over other living creatures in that he flourishes with reason and the freedom of choice; therefore, by no right could slavery be thrust upon our race. For God made man upright, as is held in Ecclesiasticus 15, and placed him in the hand of his own counsel. And for this reason, when man was first created, he was set above the other creatures by the mouth of God, but not above other men. ¶ Secondly, this is especially confirmed among Christians. For it is hardly fitting that those whom Christ, adopting as sons of God, endowed with liberty, should be permitted to be slaves: for as the Lord himself inferred in Matthew 17, "The children are free." <note>original: "Liberi sunt filij"</note> ¶ The laws in the titles cited regarding the status of men and in the *Institutes* decree the contrary, as does Aristotle in the first book of the *Politics*, in which places multiple species of slavery are distinguished and approved.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
This question is answered with four conclusions. The first is: A man, both by the law of nature and the law of nations, <term>Ius Gentium<gloss>The "Law of Nations," a body of laws traditionally considered common to all human societies.</gloss></term> can be the lord of another man.

<margin>Double servitude according to Aristotle.</margin>
For Aristotle skillfully distinguished a double servitude in the first book of the *Politics*. One is indeed natural, the other legal. Natural servitude is that by which men of more elegant intellect rule over the rest who are dull and unrefined. Indeed, just as in the same man the soul rules the body, so too in the whole human race, one man (as the Comic poet says) <note>Likely referring to Terence or another classical playwright.</note> far excels another. Wherefore, wise nature herself endowed some men with the talent for commanding, but strengthened others with bodily sinews and limbs for serving. And that this natural lordship is right is proved: for the nature of man is that he should live according to reason, and thus obey the same.

### Book Four, Question II

...perfection: therefore, just as the perfection of the sensitive appetite in man is to obey reason, so among men, the perfection of those who are rustic and unlearned in knowledge is to be subject to the governance of the wise.

<margin>Legal servitude is twofold</margin>
¶ The other type is legal servitude. This is twofold, as reported in the *Institutes* <note>The *Institutes* of Justinian, a foundational textbook for Roman Law.</note> regarding the law of persons. For some are slaves who, having exceeded the age of twenty, freely sell themselves for the sake of sharing in the purchase price. The use of this kind of servitude was present in the Old Law. For we read in Exodus 21: *If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years, but in the seventh he shall go out free.* And in Leviticus 25: *If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, do not oppress him with the service of slaves.* And further down: *The male and female slaves who are around you—that is, from the Gentiles—these you shall have as servants and shall transmit to your descendants by hereditary right, and you shall possess them forever. But your brothers, the children of Israel, you shall not oppress through power.* A distinction was therefore established: slaves from the Gentiles could be perpetual, whereas Hebrews could not; they were only temporary.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Regarding this servitude, a second conclusion is set down. Such servitude is lawful. For although men were made free by God, the desire and right to preserve one's life is so innate to all living creatures that, for the sake of survival, the wretched may drive themselves into servitude. For although

> Liberty is not well sold for all the gold in the world <note>original: "Non bene pro toto libertas vendit̃ auro"</note>

nevertheless, it is lawful to sell it for one's life, which is more precious than all gold. Indeed, even parents, compelled by extreme want, were permitted by ancient law to sell their children, as recorded in the same passage of Leviticus 25, and in the chapter concerning fathers who sold their children (Law 2), and in the *Institutes* regarding paternal power (in the gloss); although among Christians, laws of this sort are no longer in use. ¶ They say, however, that among the Ethiopians <note>A term often used in the 16th century to refer to various peoples of sub-Saharan Africa.</note> the same custom still flourishes, and the Portuguese sail there for trade. If they are sold freely, there is no reason why that commerce should be marked by any crime. However, if the rumor that has now become widespread is true, a different judgment must be rendered. For there are those who claim that this unfortunate race is led astray by fraud and deceit, enticed by I know not what trinkets, and lured by craft toward the port, and sometimes even compelled by force; and thus, neither being aware nor suspecting what is to become of them, they are sent here to us and sold. If this story is true, neither those who capture them, nor those who buy them from the captors, nor those who possess them can ever have a clear conscience until they set them free—even if they cannot recover the price paid. For if someone

<column-break/>

possesses another’s property, even if they acquired it through trade or another just title, as soon as they discover it belongs to someone else, they are bound to return it to the owner, even at a loss of the price paid. How much more is one bound to restore to his liberty a man born free who was captured through injustice? If anyone thinks to offer the excuse that it goes excellently for them because we repay their servitude with the benefit of Christianity, let him know he is doing an injustice to the Faith, which ought to be taught and persuaded with the utmost freedom. God is far from accepting such an excuse.

¶ The third species of servitude is also legal. From this (as we are taught in the law cited and in the *Digest* <note>The *Digest* or *Pandects*, a massive compilation of Roman juristic writings.</note> on the status of men, the law "Liberty"), the very name of servitude <note>original: "seruitutis"</note> is derived. Specifically, it comes from the fact that Emperors were accustomed to sell those captured in war rather than kill them; they would "save" <note>Soto is playing on the Latin etymology: *servus* (slave) was thought to come from *servare* (to preserve/save).</note> them. And these are called *mancipia* <note>A Roman legal term for property/slaves.</note> because the victors, whom they could have pierced with a sword, take them by hand <note>original: "manu capiunt" - the etymological root of *mancipia*.</note> in order to preserve them.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ And regarding this servitude, a third conclusion is added. Not only is it lawful, but it actually proceeds from mercy. For if someone can deprive himself of liberty for the sake of sustaining life, everyone ought to consider it better to be delivered to servitude than to death.

¶ There is, however, a wide gap between these types of servitude. For that kind of natural lordship and servitude does not fully reach the reality that the name implies, according to what was explained in the preceding question. For a slave of the second or third species, because he is not free, whatever he is, belongs to the master. The master does not use him for the slave's own good, but for the master’s own utility, just like a beast of burden. Hence, in the *Institutes* (on the title *Through which persons we acquire*), and in the law *Even against their will* regarding the acquisition of ownership of things, whatever a slave acquires is adjudged to the master. Although, between these two species of slaves, I seem to see no difference. For those who, pressed by poverty, handed themselves over to servitude—because they freely sold themselves for a price—cannot lawfully flee, just as they could not steal a horse they had sold. However, I would not dare to force slaves captured in war into such narrow constraints.

<margin>When it is permitted for slaves to flee.</margin>
There is indeed a gloss on the chapter "Law of Nations" <note>original: "ius gentiū"</note> which says slaves are also drawn from the chapter "If any slave" (17, question 4). But nevertheless, that chapter only prohibits anyone from soliciting a slave to leave, which can be understood as referring to those who were purchased. Nor (as I believe) is there a discrepancy between Christians and non-believers, since the Law of Nations is equal for all nations. However, it is more fitting that Christian captives held by other Christians should be allowed to flee, unless someone, having promised not to flee, has pledged his word—which...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

### Book Four, Question II

<margin>Concerning those things that slaves may use as their own, and which slaves may do so.</margin>
Furthermore, a slave is bound to serve. Similarly, it seems to me that we should truly and legitimately distinguish between these types of slaves regarding the extent to which they are bound to serve their masters. For Christians captured in war by other Christians are not bound to serve as <term>mancipia</term> <note>A term for chattel slaves who were considered the legal property of their masters.</note>; nor do their goods belong to their masters, except for those things which were taken as plunder during the war itself. Indeed, even regarding those slaves whom Christians seize from non-believers by the right of war, I do not think that everything they own belongs to their masters in such a way that they are bound in conscience to hand over what they have received as a gift, or by right of inheritance, or won through lawful games. Since they did not fall into that condition of their own free will, their misery should not be constrained by such great affliction. This is because, as stated in the **Rules of Law**, favors are to be expanded, but punishments are to be restricted. However, regarding those who have sold themselves, the reasoning is somewhat more apparent: that whatever they are, they belong to the master according to the prescription of the laws we recently cited. Nevertheless, concerning the judgment of all these matters, one must defer to those learned in the law.

¶ However, concerning the first type of servitude—natural servitude—we must speculate quite differently. For he who is a master by nature cannot, by nature, use slaves as possessed things for his own benefit; rather, he must use them as free men under their own right, for their own purpose and good: namely, by teaching them and instructing them in morals. Therefore, they are not bound to serve them as chattel slaves, but out of a certain natural equity and honesty, except in cases where they have been hired for wages.

¶ And through these points, satisfaction should be given to those who inquire whether we Christians, by the right of natural dominion, may attack non-believers with arms because they seem to be natural slaves due to the "rudeness" of their customs <note>Soto uses "rudeness" to mean a lack of European-style education or civil structure.</note>. For we acquire no right from that to subjugate them by force. This is because that natural servitude does not take away liberty, unlike the condition of those who have either sold themselves or were captured in war. And since the foundation of ownership is liberty, they lose no right over their own things. For Aristotle did not only establish that servitude between one nation and another, but also between persons of the same city and the same house. For there are natural slaves in the very same city of Christians, who nonetheless cannot be despoiled of their property, even if they refuse to obey their natural masters. Regarding what Aristotle also says in the same first book of the *Politics*, chapter 3—namely, that just as we hunt wild beasts, so we can wage war against those men who are born to obey—he is to be listened to only insofar as we may use force to drive away, subdue, and bring into order those who wander about like wild beasts,

<column-break/>

observing no treaties of nations, but seeking the property of others wherever they roam. But regarding this, we have written more extensively in our small book *On the Reason for Promulgating the Gospel*, where a wider space for discussion will open regarding the dominion and right which the Catholic Kings exercise in the **New World** across the ocean.

<margin>Response to the argument.</margin>
To the argument to the contrary, therefore, it is responded that servitude is not contrary to, nor does it properly derogate from, natural law. For the law of nature does not prohibit servitude as if it were a sin; otherwise, it would never be lawful. But (as Saint Thomas is the author in the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 36), a thing is intended by nature in two ways. In one way, <margin>Distinction of intentions.</margin> according to the **primary intention**, just as nature intends generation as the preserver of corruptible nature. In the other way, regarding the **secondary intention**, just as nature intends corruption so that it may generate. Hence, Aristotle in the second book of *On the Heavens*, text 37, says that old age is "beyond nature." By similar reasoning, the laws say that servitude is "against nature"—namely, against the primary intention of nature, which desires all men to be diligent according to reason. However, when that intention fails, punishment follows from fault, which is conformed to corrupted nature. And among the types of punishments, one is legal servitude. For from original sin followed poverty and the turmoil of wars, which drive men into servitude.

¶ Therefore, such servitude is not repugnant to Christians. For Christ made us free only from the law of sin and death, as Paul says in Romans 8. He did not, however, exempt us from the Law of Nations <note>The *ius gentium*, or universal laws recognized by all civilized peoples.</note>. Indeed, in Titus 3, he admonishes slaves to obey their masters; and Peter adds, even the "harsh" <note>original: "dyscolis"—referring to difficult or morally crooked masters</note>, namely the non-believers who wander outside the Church. And in 1 Corinthians 7, he warns that he who is called as a slave should remain a slave. It is true, however, that for the sake of the decency of Christian liberty, custom has long since prevailed that Christians captured in war should not serve in the manner of chattel slaves, as Bartolus noted on the law *Hostes*. Natural servitude would not have occurred in the state of innocence as it exists now, because no one would have been unrefined or ignorant, even if infants and children did not know everything that adults did. Nor would all have been born with the same sharpness of intellect. Therefore, servitude entered through the same sin through which (as Paul says) death entered. As for what Ambrose says (as cited in Distinction 35, Canon *Sexto die*), that servitude crept in through drunkenness...

He clarifies that while servitude is "against nature's first intention," it is a legitimate legal consequence of the fallen state of humanity (original sin).</summary>

# Book Four, Question II.

...servitude into the world, I confess I do not understand it: unless he calls a drunkard a slave, who, having been deprived of the use of reason, becomes like a beast of burden <note>original: "iumētum"</note>. ¶ However, the laws cited above might seem to conflict with one another. On one hand, they assert that servitude was established by the **Law of Nations** <note>The "ius gentium," or Law of Nations, refers to legal principles considered common to all "civilized" peoples, often distinguished from "natural law."</note>; on the other, they claim it is a sanction of the Emperors. Yet, there is no contradiction. For servitude exists by the Law of Nations, as the Canon of Gregory expressly states in the chapter *Cum Redemptor* (12.q.2), where he says: "Men, whom nature brought forth free from the beginning, the Law of Nations has subjected to the yoke of servitude." It is called the Law of Nations because natural reason taught that law to all nations. But it is also called an imperial constitution because the Emperors both ratified it and confirmed it through custom and usage.

### ARTICLE III.
#### Whether a human being is the master of his own life and reputation.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial R featuring floral patterns and a small figure</image-desc> It remains in this third article to add a brief discussion concerning the mastery <note>The Latin "dominium" implies both ownership and the right to control or dispose of something.</note> of one’s own life and reputation. Specifically, whether a human being enjoys mastery over their own life and, consequently, over their honor and reputation. It is argued that each person is the master of their life based on that passage from **Ecclesiasticus 15**: "God made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel." To be left in the hand of one's own counsel appears to be nothing other than making him the master of himself, and thus of his own life. ¶ Secondly: Whatever is the cause for which a thing is such, that cause is even more so (as stated in the **Posterior Analytics** <note>A reference to Aristotle's logic; if life makes other goods valuable, life itself must be the most valuable "property."</note>). A human is the master of other goods for the sake of life; therefore, he is more excellently the master of life itself. ¶ Thirdly, regarding reputation <note>original: "fama"</note>, it is argued from the negative side—that a human is not the master of their own reputation—based on that precept of the Wise Man in **Ecclesiasticus 41**: "Have care for a good name." Here we seem to be appointed as guardians of our reputation, not masters, as we are of money. To this, **Proverbs 22** harmonizes: "A good name is better than great riches." ¶ Fourthly, it is argued by the authority of **Augustine** in *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 20, which is cited in 11. q. 3. in the chapter *Non sunt audiendi*. There, in rebuking those who neglect their own reputation, he adds: "Because our life is necessary for us, but our reputation is necessary for others." By these words, he seems to suggest that the mastery of our reputation does not belong to us, but to the community. Likewise, in Book 1 of **The City of God**, chapter 20, he says that by the commandment "Thou shalt not bear false witness," everyone is prohibited from testifying falsely against

<column-break/>

themselves, just as against a neighbor. Similarly, by the other commandment, "Thou shalt not kill," both the murder of a neighbor and of oneself are prohibited. From this, it is argued: both these commandments equally prohibit testimony against one's own reputation and the killing of oneself. And from the latter, it is concluded that a man is not the master of his life; therefore, from the former, it is equally elicited that no one is the master of his own reputation. ¶ Conversely, against the affirmative part of the first point stands that passage in **Wisdom 16**: "Lord, You are the one who has power over life and death; You lead down to the gates of death and bring back again." Here, God alone is suggested as the master of life. Regarding reputation, on the contrary, it is argued that reputation and honor are counted among "acquired goods" <note>original: "bonis proprijs acquisitis"</note> which we use for happiness. Therefore, just as anyone can use their resources and possessions so long as they do no injury to anyone else in transferring them, so too can one use their honor and reputation; and thus, in a similar way, a human is the master of such goods.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> Although these two questions are resolved by contrary answers, we have joined them both under one dispute so that their opposing reasons, placed side-by-side, might more clearly illuminate both matters. Therefore, the question is answered with four conclusions. The first is: **A human being is not the master of his own life.** This is proved first by the authority of the Book of Wisdom just cited, and from **Deuteronomy 32**: "I will kill, and I will make to live." In these places, it is proved that God has reserved the mastery of our life for Himself. Next, it is proved by the effect, through reasoning gathered from the definition of mastery <note>original: "dominij"</note> explained above. The master of any thing is the one who, without doing injury to anyone, can use it as he pleases, even to the point of its wasting away and consumption. A human, however, cannot kill himself, as the law of justice forbids it; therefore, no one is the master of his own life. I should keep in mind the "law of justice" <note>Soto distinguishes between the law of justice (obligations to others/God) and the law of charity (care for oneself).</note>, lest someone object that the law also prohibits one from squandering their external goods without any fruit, despite being their master. Indeed, although the law of charity—by which everyone is bound to love themselves and their own things—prohibits this, no law of justice does; and therefore, without injury, a true master can pour out such goods. Furthermore, a ward <note>original: "pupillus"</note> is forbidden from transferring goods of which he is the master; yet this is not by the law of justice (as one is forbidden from stealing another's things), but so that he may guard his own. It is different, however, regarding

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

life: for by the law of justice, a human being is forbidden from killing themselves, just as they are forbidden from killing others: because one is no more the master <term>dominus; the legal owner or one with absolute authority</term> of their own life than they are of another's. But you may say, this is to "beg the question" <note>original: *principium petere*; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</note>. For how is it proven that the precept forbidding a person from killing themselves is a precept of justice—which forbids taking what belongs to another? Someone could argue it is merely a command of charity, similar to the command forbidding us from wasting our own goods through extravagance. ¶ Therefore, a second argument is made so that it is not seen as begging the question. If a human being were granted mastery over their own life, it would mean they could occasionally spend it or give it away, just as they can with other goods for just causes: for a power or faculty that can never be put into action is useless. However, a human being cannot deprive themselves of life for any reason, no matter what just pretext is given: therefore, it is a sign that they are not the master of it. ¶ Third, it is argued from the prior and legitimate cause. If a human being were the master of life by some right, it would be by natural, divine, or human right. It is not by natural right: because the first of all natural desires—and indeed the greatest of all temporal ones—is that by which every thing seeks to preserve itself in being. This is in accordance with the saying of the devil (which was nevertheless true) in the book of Job: "Skin for skin, and all that a person has, they will give for their soul." For this reason, nature has granted no thing qualities or instruments that would lead to its own destruction, but rather those by which it might be preserved: such as heat for fire, and coldness for water, and to all living creatures their necessary qualities. Therefore, the law of nature in no way permits a human being to kill themselves, and thus does not grant them mastery over life. Since the law of nature is the work and gift of God, it follows that such a faculty is not granted by positive divine law either. Regarding human law, the matter is clear. Especially since not a single word from either divine or human law can be found on this matter. For in Genesis 1, where a human being was made master of all things—even the animals, which they may therefore slaughter for their own use—the power over their own life was not handed over at the same time. Behold the origin of the conclusion: since life is the foundation of all temporal goods—a life which a human being does not acquire for themselves but receives by the grace of God and the work of parents—it was not fitting for mastery over it to be granted to them. Instead, God as its author retained it, so that it would be unlawful for a human being to depart from a life into which they did not enter by their own power without His command. This was also known by the light of natural reason. For as the Lyric poet <note>Likely referring to Horace or a similar classical authority</note> says: "No one must depart from life without the command of the King" <note>original: *Nemini iniussu Regis de vita exeundum*</note>. But regarding this, we shall speak again in the following book, under the title "On Homicide."

<column-break/>

Therefore, by natural and divine law, a human being is established as the guardian of their own life—which they are bound to sustain—but not its master. ¶ If, on the other hand, you object that a person can, even by private authority, expose their life for their friends, or even to defend their own goods; and that they can cut off a limb for the sake of health, even though limbs are part of life—all of which seem to testify that mastery over one's own life belongs to the person. It is answered that this by no way follows: for it is not permitted to cut off limbs except for the protection of life; and exposing one's life for a friend or for temporal goods does not amount to a person killing themselves. Indeed, that is not the intention there; rather, the intention is to endure death so that one does not abandon the duties of virtue: which both divine and natural law approve.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Not only does an individual not have mastery, but neither the state <term>respublica; the political community or commonwealth</term> nor a prince has absolute mastery over the lives of their subjects; only God does.
<margin>God alone is master of life.</margin>
This is evident because a prince cannot kill the innocent for any reason, but only the guilty—or those proven to be such by legitimate testimony for the punishment of crimes. This does not prove the prince is the master of life, but rather the judge of wrongdoers. Furthermore, in war, the prince can expose citizens to the danger of death for the defense of the state; but neither is this a sign of mastery over life, but rather that he is the guardian of the state. Therefore, whenever you hear that one who kills themselves or another does an injury to the state—as Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 11—do not take this to mean that mastery of life belongs to the state, but rather that the state has been entrusted with the protection and guardianship of the lives of its citizens, and it alone can punish men with the loss of life.
<margin>The state is only the guardian of life.</margin>
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: God is the absolute master of life, because not only as a judge by punishing, or as a guardian by defending, but absolutely as the author of human life, He can deliver men to death, just as any person might their own beast of burden <note>original: *iumentum*</note>. Yet His mercy is so unspeakable that He has never used this absolute power of mastery, neither over our lives nor over our other goods. For if He commanded the Hebrews to despoil the Egyptians, He did so by a just judgment: because the Egyptians owed them wages for their service in mortar and brick. And if He commanded Hosea to take children by a harlot—which He could do as master of bodies—it is nonetheless believable that the Prophet first took her as a wife, so that he might also know her by human law. And if He commanded Abraham, as the master of life, to offer his son as a sacrifice, He nevertheless did not permit it afterward. And if in Exodus 32 He commanded through Moses that each man should kill his brother, He commanded this as the avenger of the [sin of] the molten calf. See then that against na-

### Question II of the Fourth Book

...monstrosity (if the rumors are true) of the Turk and certain barbarian princes. <margin>Wild blindness</margin> They are in such blindness that they think themselves the masters <term>dominus; a legal owner with absolute power of disposal</term> of their subjects' lives: so much so that they can slaughter them without any fault or cause, just as if they were cattle. ¶ Regarding reputation, however—since we have treated the secret of covering and uncovering it more extensively in our formal lecture <note>Soto refers to his *Relectio de ratione tegendi et detegendi secretum*, a specific university discourse on the ethics of secrets</note>—it is enough to respond here with a single conclusion, which is the fourth in order, contrary to that which was asserted about life. <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> A human being obtains mastery of their honor and reputation: specifically, so that they may use them as if they were money, although they are to be valued at a higher price. I know indeed that many, even among our own school, such as Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note> in his commentary on the *Summa Theologiae* (II-II, q. 73) and in his own *Summa*, follow a different opinion: yet this one has always appealed to me more. For the understanding of this conclusion, the contrary opinion must be brought to judgment, so that opposites placed next to each other may shine more brightly. There are three kinds of our goods: First is life, the last are temporal goods <note>material wealth and possessions</note>, and the middle are honor and reputation. And indeed, concerning the extremes there is no dispute, for it is the confession of all that no one is master of their own life, such that they might kill themselves for any cause without committing an injury: rather, it is a crime of injustice. On the other hand, regarding the opposite extreme, all confess that every person is the master of their exterior goods: which one can certainly give away or spend without injury to anyone. <margin>Cajetan's Opinion.</margin> The opinion contrary to ours, therefore, places honor and reputation in the same category as life: we, however, place them in the category of exterior goods. <margin>The author's opinion.</margin> ¶ And our first reason is contrary to the one above. A human being is truly and legitimately the master of all their goods, so that they can spend or neglect them, and use them, without doing an injury to anyone—which is properly an act against justice; honor and reputation are a human being's own goods, granted to them by natural law and acquired and increased by their own effort: nor does any law of justice prohibit a private person from spending them: therefore they do no injury to anyone if they reject them: and thus they are truly their master. I said "no law of justice," by which word the whole matter is revealed. For we are prohibited by the law of charity <term>charitas; the moral obligation to love oneself and neighbor properly</term>, by which we are bound to love ourselves and what is ours, from being wasteful with honor and reputation (just as with external resources) lest we neglect them without cause, as is clear in the scriptures: "Have care for a good name" [Sirach 41:12]. Yet there is no law of justice that forbids us from spending these as if they were someone else's property. And this is what we intend to prove. For indeed, regarding life it stands (as we were just saying), Deuteronomy 32: "I will kill, and I will make to live." and Wisdom 16: "You are the Lord, who has power over life and death." From which it is gathered that we are by no means the masters of our life. And—

<column-break/>

—to these is added natural reason. For life is the foundation of all temporal goods, which man himself does not acquire: but receives by divine benefit and the work of parents. Regarding honor and reputation, however, nowhere is such a thing read. Indeed, natural reason seems to teach the contrary. For honor and reputation, as we just said, we ourselves acquire and obtain after receiving life. Add that honor, as Aristotle says in Books 1 and 10 of the *Ethics*, is the "reward of virtue" <note>original: *praemium virtutis*</note>: virtue, however—at least natural virtue—is our own proper work, through the general help of God: just as supernatural virtue is also, in a way, ours through His singular assistance. Likewise honor and reputation, as Aristotle says in the same place, are part of happiness <term>fœlicitas; human flourishing or well-being</term>: happiness, however, is our own proper good: we are therefore masters of them, so that if we wish to cast them away, we do injury to no one. Unless the person were a public figure <note>Public officials have a duty to maintain their reputation for the sake of their office</note>. For we speak according to the nature of the thing, stripped of all specific circumstances. <margin>Thomas Aquinas, Summa II-II, q. 64, art. 5.</margin> ¶ And this our opinion is confirmed by the authority of Saint Thomas in the *Summa*, II-II, q. 64, art. 5, where he says that one who kills himself not only acts against charity, but against justice with respect to the republic <note>the state or common good</note>, to which the life of a human being belongs. Regarding reputation, however, he adds no such thing. <margin>Response to the 3rd argument.</margin> Rather, in the solution to the third contrary argument, he seems to feel the same about it. For he says that a human being can lawfully dispose of himself as far as pertains to those things that belong to this life, which is ruled by man's free will: but the transition from this life to another, happier one is not subject to man's free will, but to divine power: and therefore it is not permitted for anyone to seek death. It seems, therefore, that he subjected all of a human being's goods to their own mastery, except for life. <margin>In the same place.</margin> ¶ Second, this conclusion is more clearly proven from these recent words of Saint Thomas: If we were not masters of reputation and honor in a different way than we are of life, it would follow that for no end—not even for the sake of spiritual life itself, to avoid sins and attain eternal life—could we postpone or cast away honor and reputation: which is plainly absurd. The consequence is clear, because (as Saint Thomas is the authority in the place just cited, and Saint Augustine in Book 1 of *The City of God*, chapter 20) even for the sake of enjoying eternal happiness, it is not permitted for a human being to inflict death upon themselves: and thus even one who knew that temporal life was ruinous to them for the salvation of the soul and a manifest cause of hell, could not deprive themselves of it. Yet it is far otherwise regarding honor and reputation. For who would doubt that if a private person realized that reputation and honor were for them...

<sig>t 3</sig>

<summary>Soto argues that unlike life, which belongs to God, honor and reputation are goods that individuals "own" and acquire through virtue. Therefore, while suicide is always an act of injustice, a person may lawfully sacrifice their reputation for the sake of their spiritual salvation.</summary>
