<margin>Ambrose's deed is doubtful.</margin>
Now this same point is confirmed by the testimony of the divine Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church</note>: if the story is true, we read that he shut women in his chamber so that through that infamy he might escape being elected as a prelate <note>original: "antistitem"; a high-ranking cleric or bishop</note>. And Augustine reveals many of his own sins; and Anselm lamentably deplores his lost virginity. This would certainly be a crime for them unless they were the masters of their own reputations.

¶ Thirdly, the same is clear because no one can permit their life to be taken from them when they are attacked—at least where they could preserve it without harm to another, such as by fleeing or some similar way. Yet anyone, provided they are a private person, can leave their reputation behind; when it is offered, they can refuse it, and when it is taken away, they can abandon it, even where they might be able to defend it.

<margin>A private person can relinquish reputation and can defend it.</margin>
<margin>2.2.q.73. article 4.</margin>
This is the opinion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto’s school of thought</note> in the *Summa*, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 73, Article 4, in the response to the first objection, where he says that it is within anyone's judgment to suffer the loss of their own reputation, unless this results in danger to others. He certainly could not have stated more clearly that a human being has mastery <term>dominium; the legal right to use or dispose of a thing at will</term> over their reputation.

¶ Fourthly, it is argued: even if reputation and honor are more excellent goods than money, nevertheless a huge heap of money is valued more in human usage than a slender honor and reputation. For this reason, compensation for honor and reputation can be made through money: therefore, if a man is the master of his money, he is also master of his reputation.

¶ Fifthly, this is confirmed by the authority of the Redeemer, who warned us to hold the splendor of all temporal goods—namely honors and human glory—in contempt. Surely He meant for us to flee honors, the first seats, and worldly pride; He was far from obligating us to preserve them in the same way as life.

¶ We have deemed it worthwhile to apply this article to the matter of mastery, as it serves as the foundation for several other places in our work. For from here, in Question 6, we must draw the answer to that inquiry: whether a man is free to waive the restitution <note>Restitution is the act of restoring something to its rightful owner; here, Soto asks if a victim of slander can choose not to demand their reputation back</note> of his reputation, which we shall grant, contrary to the opposing opinion. Likewise, in the following book concerning the matter of detraction <note>Detraction is the sin of revealing another person's real faults to someone who has no right to know, thereby damaging their reputation</note>, we shall examine through this principle what kind of crime and how great a crime one commits who defames himself, and whether that is sometimes permissible. Indeed, to taste these matters briefly for the present: when a private person, by the disclosure of their own crime, defames 

<column-break/>

themselves, they in no way sin against justice, nor do they inflict an injury upon anyone. Therefore, in its own kind, it is nothing but a venial sin <note>A lesser, pardonable sin that does not break one's relationship with God</note> against charity toward oneself—though more serious than squandering money, because reputation is a more precious good. It can, however, become a mortal sin <note>A grave sin that destroys the divine life in the soul</note> if one does it by boasting of their own foulness. Whence David says, *Why do you glory in malice?* etc. And in Isaiah chapter 3, those who *proclaim their sins like Sodom* are rebuked. Likewise, if it is a public person, who holds their reputation and good standing in obligation for the good of their subjects, they would sin mortally against justice. However, one who reveals such a secret crime of theirs not in vain, but for a good cause—as if a thief were to do so to escape the severity of tortures—certainly would commit no fault; indeed, perhaps he would be acting rightly. Nay, truly, if he defamed himself by lying, although he would admit the fault of a lie, it would not be "pernicious" <note>In legal/moral theology, a "pernicious lie" is one told specifically to harm someone; Soto argues self-defamation via lying is not necessarily mortal because it lacks this harm to another</note>, and thus not a mortal sin in its own kind.

Nevertheless, we always exclude public persons; furthermore, we exclude the most absurd and unspeakable outrages that make the ears shudder: for to defame oneself regarding those could hardly be excused from lethal crime.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**T**o the first authority from Ecclesiasticus <note>A book of the Bible also known as Sirach</note>, then, it is responded that the sense is that God made man the master of his own actions: for this is what it means to be "left in the hand of his own counsel." However, it does not follow from this that he is the master of his life.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, that axiom of the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>—*That on account of which every thing is such, etc.* <note>original: "Propter quod vnumquodq; tale"; a logical principle meaning if X causes Y to have a quality, X has that quality even more so. Here, if things exist to sustain life, life must be the higher "possession"</note>—is denied to be aptly accommodated to the present matter. For our being masters of things for the sake of sustaining life only proves that we are the *guardians* of life, not the masters. For we are masters of our actions for the sake of obtaining the friendship of God; yet we are not masters of that same divine grace and friendship of the Lord.

¶ Furthermore, the authority of Ecclesiasticus cited in the third place concerning reputation proves precisely this: that we are bound by the precept of charity to have care for ourselves, for honor, and for reputation. It does not prove, however, that the contrary offense in a private person is an injury against justice, as it would be if someone killed themselves—by which crime, certainly, one would be injurious toward God, in whose power is the mastery of life, and subsequently toward the state, which is the guardian of the same.

<margin>The best way of seeking honor.</margin>
Add that the best way of procuring a good name is to have a thorough care for cultivating the virtues, which honor and reputation follow like a shadow. And therefore, for the sake of the good of virtue, we can spend those things if necessary, as the true masters of them.

¶ The prior authority of the argument, however, has nothing to do with...

# Book Four, Question III.

...attacks us: for if you were to contend from that second part—that our reputation is necessary to others—that dominion over it resides not with us but with the commonwealth, you would likewise infer from the first part (where he says our life is necessary to us) that dominion over our life resides with us, a point which Augustine would not concede. Therefore, he precisely warns us that we should not be negligent of our own reputation, through which we can serve the commonwealth, lest we despise it without a legitimate cause. This is especially true when we cannot cast it away without causing scandal. For he was speaking to certain women who, although they were held in a high place of holiness among the people, were attempting under the pretext of humility to generate a sinister suspicion about themselves so that they might be more cheaply esteemed: by which act they were causing scandal <note>In this context, "scandal" refers to an act that leads others into spiritual doubt or sin.</note>.

<margin>To the latter part of the argument.</margin>
¶ Truly, the latter authority from his work *The City of God* (Book 1), which is a bit more pressing, convinces us only of this: that by the commandment "Thou shalt not bear false witness," we are forbidden from giving testimony against ourselves. This is because such an act is against charity (love of neighbor and self), as his following words teach. However, it does not follow from this that it is a sin of injustice in the same way as if you killed yourself, or brought false testimony against a neighbor, or revealed a secret crime. Therefore, from that precise form of the commandment "Thou shalt not kill," it is not gathered that a specific suicide is against justice, but rather that it is a sin. For other reasons instruct us (which we have set forth above) that we are not the masters of our own lives; from these reasons, we conclude that suicide is against justice <note>Soto is distinguishing between "sin" (a moral failing) and "injustice" (a violation of a specific right or property). He argues we don't "own" our lives—God does—so taking one's life is a theft of God's property.</note>.

# QUESTION III
### On the Division of Things.

### ARTICLE I.

-> Whether by human law the ownership of things was once divided. <-

After establishing both the subject and the object of ownership, order demands that we discuss their division in the third place. And, according to our usual custom, the argument begins from the negative side, as we did above regarding servitude <note>Soto follows the Scholastic method: first stating the arguments against his own position (the "negative side") before providing his resolution.</note>. No human law can counteract natural law; however, that the goods of this world 

<column-break/>

should be possessed in common is a constitution of natural law. This is evident in Genesis 1, where the possession of things was granted to humanity in common. Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential encyclopedist and archbishop.</note> affirms the same in Book 5, which is cited in Distinction 1, chapter "Natural Law" <note>original: "ius naturale"</note>. Nor was this only the case when nature was pure, but also afterward when it was already corrupted; we read something similar in Genesis 9, spoken to Noah and his sons: "Increase and multiply, and go upon the earth, and fill it." Here, God seems to have intended for nothing to be divided. 

¶ Secondly, the opinion of Clement in his fourth epistle more clearly confirms this, which is cited in Question 1, canon "Dilectissimis." There it is read: "The common use of all things that are in this world ought to have been for all men; but through iniquity, one said this is mine, and another said that; and thus division was made among mortals." Now, iniquity is contrary to the equity of law. 

¶ In the third place, the reason of charity <note>Divine or brotherly love.</note> is added. For if all things were possessed in common, the bond of love among mortals would be much firmer. Since where your treasure is, there your heart is also, if they had nothing divided, nothing would remain for which their minds might be divided. Hence, in the early days of the church in Jerusalem, so that the love of all might coalesce more fervently (as is recounted in the Acts of the Apostles), they lived in common; and the lives of monks were instituted after this example. Therefore, Augustine says in his Rule: "Let there be one soul and one heart in God for you, and do not say anything is your own: but let all things be common to you." He implies that the unity of hearts cannot be nourished otherwise than by banishing "mine" and "thine." This did not escape that Christian Poet, who said:

> If you take these two pronouns from our affairs,
> Battles would cease, and peace would be without strife.

And for this reason, that most celebrated axiom has always been: "Among friends, all things are common." Indeed, by this reasoning, the holy fathers always speak in that idiom, saying that all things are common; as Augustine does in his Commentary on John (Tract 6), found in Distinction 8, canon "By What Law." And Ambrose says (Distinction 47, "Sicut hi"): "Let no one call what is common 'private' <note>original: "proprium"</note>." Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), noted for his preaching on wealth and poverty.</note> on Luke, chapter 6: "We have received all things from God; however, what we say—'mine' and 'thine'—are words of lies." Therefore, it was by no means permitted to make a division of things.

¶ The opinion of Christ our Redeemer is contrary to this, in Matthew 22: "Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s."

This question was also fought over among the philosophers in the past. To be sure, Pla...

# Friar Dominic de Soto, on Justice and Right

<margin>Plato wished for wives and children to be held in common in the republic. Aristotle attributes this to him in Book 1 of the *Politics*.</margin>
to <note>This is a continuation of a word from the previous page: "Socrates."</note> whom Aristotle attributes this republic at the very beginning. The same Plato also mentions this kind of republic in his 5th dialogue on the Republic. They attempted to persuade others of this excessive commonality of things for the same reason we just formulated: namely, so that they might most greatly unite and bind the hearts of all into one. However, these men were not worthy of being heard, because they were contemplating our nature in that total sincerity of innocence in which it was created by God through mercy—not knowing that it had been driven out from there by our first parent through injustice <note>Soto is referring to the "Fall of Man" in Genesis, arguing that Plato's idealism only works for a sinless world.</note>. Therefore, the answer to this question consists of five conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion is this: Just as the possession of things in common was in harmony with the state of innocence (except for wives), a form of possession which the law of nature taught; so too the division of ownership is so fitting to the condition of corrupt nature that, short of a miracle, the human race could in no way endure for a long age otherwise. The first part is clear in itself. For at that time, the earth, even untilled, would have brought forth its fruits of its own accord; or it would have required very little cultivation, which no one would have refused. Thus we understand Genesis 2: "God took the man and placed him in the Paradise of pleasure, to work it and keep it." Furthermore, greed for things would have troubled no one then. For it was said after the sin, "In the labor of your face you shall eat your bread." Indeed, that ethnic poet <note>Ovid, in his *Metamorphoses*.</note> caught the scent of that flower of the age when he wrote:

> The earth itself, likewise immune, untouched by the rake, 
> nor wounded by any plowshares, gave all things of its own accord: 
> and they were content with the foods created without anyone's compulsion.
> <note>original: "Ipfa quoq; imunis, raftroq; itacta, nec vllis Saucia vomerib⁹, per fe dabat omnia tell⁹: Contentiq; cibis, nullo cogente, creatis."</note>

Wherefore, no danger would have existed either that the fruits of the earth would fail, or that any discord would arise among those happy people. ¶ The second part, however, is proven from two contrary roots. It is not necessary to spend much effort here shaking that Socratic or Platonic commonality of wives and children for its absurdity to appear. First, the very charity <note>In this context, "charity" means social love and bond.</note> which was intended to be supported by it is instead undermined by it. For those philosophers said that then all men would call any woman "my wife," and all boys "my sons," and the youths would call any older man "my fa-

<column-break/>

ther." But Aristotle refuted this most excellently. For if they understood the word "all" collectively, it would be true; for taken as a group, all the old men would be the fathers of those children. However, that would contribute very little to charity. For the love in the whole commonwealth would then be thin and weak, like a tiny bit of honey in a great deal of water, which it would be unable to sweeten. On the contrary, love would more quickly wither away because no one would recognize his own property, whether a son or a father. But if they understood it distributively regarding individuals—namely, that every individual was the son of every individual—that would certainly contribute greatly to love, but it is nonetheless impossible. For one person cannot be the son except of one mother, and perhaps except of one father. Moreover, a neglect of children would result, because one would rarely recognize his own. To this is added that a child is often recognized as belonging to a specific father by the features of the face; because of this, it would then be impossible for that man’s heart not to be more inclined toward his own children than toward those of others. Thus, nature itself cried out against that confused commonality. Furthermore, after nature had fallen, it would be impossible for quarrels not to arise among men; and subsequently, among uncertain fathers and children, both impious murders and unspeakable loves and sexual unions would be entered into. In short, the distinction of wives and children is so natural that even in uncorrupted nature, where no place lay open for those depraved affections, that absurd mixing of wives would not have been introduced, but each man would have had his own. "For they shall be," it says, "two in one flesh." For it was expedient even then that each should know by what necessity and bond of blood he was joined to others. And although the ancient law, for the sake of propagating God's peculiar people, dispensed with this in some cases <note>A reference to polygamy in the Old Testament.</note>, it was never permitted for one wife to marry two men, precisely so that an uncertain crowd of offspring might be avoided. ¶ Therefore, having set aside this delirious commonality, we return to demonstrating how fitting the division of possessions is to corrupt nature. This is shown from two "corrupt roots": namely, from human negligence and from greed. For while the earth on one hand, rebelling against man because of man’s rebellion, began to bear thorns and thistles and to require the sweat of the human face to nourish man himself; and man on the other hand, after eating the forbidden tree, was filled with so many greeds—the possession of things became necessary as a means to most conveniently serve both needs: both the cultivating of the land so that fruits would not fail, and the repressing of human ava- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, "avarice."</note>

<summary>Soto refutes Plato's idea of communal wives and property, arguing that while common ownership suited the sinless Garden of Eden, private property and family structures are essential for maintaining order and productivity in a fallen world.</summary>

### Question III of the Fourth Book

<margin>He attacks the threefold commonality of things.</margin>
...of a greed that can hardly be satisfied: such possession could not have been in common; therefore, division was necessary. This last premise is proven. For (as Aristotle says in the cited passage <note>Aristotle, *Politics*, Book II</note>), we can understand this possession in common in a threefold way: namely, that either the lands were private but the fruits were common; or conversely, that the fields were common but the fruits were later divided; or that both the fields and the fruits were common. 

If you grant the first, you provide an opening for discord: because then the labors would be unequal. For he who possessed more soil would labor more, yet the fruits would fall equally to everyone according to each person's need; and yet no one would bear it with a level mind that they did not receive more fruit in proportion to how much more labor they had exhausted. 

If, however, they wanted the fields to be common, men would find there an occasion for laziness and sloth: for it is inexpressible how burning is the love for one’s own things, and how sluggish and faint it is toward common things. It is just as when there are many servants: the service is performed worse because each expects others to do what he himself was supposed to do. Indeed, in this manner, it would happen in such a republic that the fruits would be produced poorly. The same disadvantage would follow if both the fruits and the lands were common. And subsequently, because of the human thirst for things, each person would then strive for himself to grab as much of the fruits as he could. By this path, it was inevitable that the peace and tranquility of the citizens—and the friendship which those philosophers cherished—would be disturbed.

¶ The second reason is taken from the debt of order in the republic, which otherwise could not be preserved with dignity. Indeed, diverse orders and diverse classes of men are necessary, as Socrates himself acknowledged.

<margin>Three orders of men are necessary according to Socrates.</margin>
For he established three orders: namely, the farmers, with whom the craftsmen are to be counted; and the guardians, namely the soldiers and nobles, assigned to the protection of the republic; and thirdly, the legal experts, who pronounce the law and answer regarding doubtful matters. From this, therefore, it is argued: if all things were common, everyone would refuse the burden of the farmers and would long to be a soldier. But when war was imminent, unless there were established private rewards, everyone would withdraw from danger; finally, as many as were able would crave to be at the helm of government. Soon, since those of the highest class would require more things, it would follow that greater burdens would be assigned to some, and greater honors to others. Which, unless ownership were divided, could not fail to violently disturb the republic.

¶ Thirdly, the same conclusion is evident. Just as by granting the community of wives, 

<column-break/>

the virtue of temperance is removed (by which one abstains from another’s bed), so by granting the community of possessions, the virtue of liberality <term>liberality: the virtue of being generous with one's own wealth</term> is also removed—which is no small light of the republic. For he who has nothing of his own cannot be generous; and he who possesses everything does not need the generosity of another. And thus the virtue of receiving guests and strangers, and of succoring the miserable, would perish; and subsequently, the gratitude of souls for benefits received would vanish.

<margin>It is heresy to deny the division of things.</margin>
Therefore, the assertion of the division of things is certain to such a degree that its denial is heretical, as Augustine says in his book *On Heresies*. There, in the 40th place, he records the heresy of the "Apostolics" <note>The *Apostolici* were a sect that claimed to lead a perfectly apostolic life by rejecting marriage and private property</note>, who boasted of that name because they did not receive into their communion those who used wives or those who possessed private property. And in the Council of Constance <note>Held 1414–1418; it condemned several reformers</note>, Jan Hus <note>original: "Ioannes Hus"</note> was also condemned for this, as he denied that clerics could possess anything of their own.

¶ Now, if you argue that the division of things has not sufficiently countered these types of evils and disadvantages for the republic—for even now there are uncultivated lands due to human laziness, and men, through ambition and a thirst for things, intrude upon the rights of others, and other evils of that kind—the answer is that it is not necessary for the equity of a law to perfectly achieve its end. It is indeed enough that it establishes, according to its capacity, those things which are accommodated to that end; for the unbridled freedom of men can be entirely restrained by no reins.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Although it is fitting for things to be possessed separately as far as ownership and dominion <term>dominium: legal right of ownership and control</term> are concerned—so that each may know his own by the law of justice and keep his hands from another’s—nevertheless, as far as use is concerned, things ought to be common through the kindness of mercy and liberality. Thus, he who abounds should give to the needy, and he who lacks should return thanks to him. For by this reasoning, the friendship of mortals coalesces more easily than if everything were possessed in common ownership. For from this is derived that axiom: *All things are common among friends.* <note>original: "Amicorum omnia sunt communia"</note>

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: The first division of external things was made by the law of nations <term>ius gentium: the common law of all civilized peoples</term>, although afterward many more were added by civil law. For already in Book 1, Question 5, human law was divided into these two. The conclusion is evident by this reasoning.

<margin>Dominion began at the beginning of the world.</margin>
Furthermore, dominion began at the creation of the world (as we said above). For then God first began to have those whom He might rule, and likewise then both angels and humans, by their own nature and right, began to be masters of their own actions, so that they might serve the Creator with that freedom.

<margin>The division of ownership is consistent with natural law.</margin>
From which it follows that some division of ownership was made by natural law: namely, this division of actions...

### F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law

<columns>
...man has for his own honor and reputation. For this was made each person's own property not by the law of nations, but by natural law. Regarding possessions, however (as the first conclusion taught), the distribution was not made before sin, but immediately after: for from that point (as we have said) the reason for division arose. Wherefore, we immediately read that private property was divided between the two brothers <note>Cain and Abel, the sons of Adam and Eve</note>: indeed, Cain offered from the fruits of the earth, and Abel from the best of his flock. But if these things were not each man's own, neither would Abel deserve praise, nor Cain deserve blame. ¶ Moreover, the division is said to have been made by law—not by natural law, but by the law of nations <note>Original: *ius gentium*. In the 16th century, this referred to a set of universal laws that all civilized peoples naturally agree upon through reason, distinct from "natural law" which is inherent to all living things</note>: because natural law requires no reasoning but is written in hearts, such as the union of male 

<margin>What the law of nations is.</margin>
and female. But the law of nations is that which the reason of every person infers by comparing principles. And therefore it is called the law of "nations"—that is, of "humans"—for whom it is characteristic to reason. Indeed, from the principles of a corrupted nature, the family of Adam was immediately taught, and thereafter all nations in general, that each should possess his own. ¶ But if you ask who first made a division of this kind: there are those who answer that Adam was the first divider. However, others argue against this, saying he did not have royal power or the coercive authority of a state, but was merely a father of a household <note>Original: *patremfamiliâs*</note>, who could not distribute to his sons anything except his own private holdings. Nevertheless, this argument is not very forceful: both because perhaps (though it is nowhere written) he held the authority of a prince by the very fact that he was the first and only parent of the human race. 

<margin>Adam as prince by that very right as the first parent: and indeed lord of the whole world.</margin>
For it is not likely that the world was at any time without a human prince who could avenge wrongdoings. Also, even by paternal right, he could distribute to his sons his resources, which flowed in great abundance. Indeed, it would not even be absurd to say he was the lord of the whole world, since the world was made for man, and then he himself was alone. Nor was the world so crowded with people that he could not rule them through his ministers. But truly, as for the division according to the law of nations, it is not necessary for us to be confined by these difficulties. For those things which are established by such law require neither a prince nor any assembly of a state. For the law of nations differs from civil law in this way: namely, that reason itself teaches it to individuals separately. Therefore, by agreement, each of the brothers, and thereafter their grandsons and great-grandsons, could occupy individual plots and fields and increase their holdings, as reason itself taught that things 

<column-break/>

ignorant of owners <note>Original: *dominorum nesciæ*, or ownerless property</note> should go to the first occupant, and others should abstain from them. As is held in the *Institutes* <note>A textbook of Roman Law</note> regarding the division of things, under the section on wild animals. For it says: 
<gloss>relinquished things</gloss>
that which previously belonged to no one is granted to the occupant by natural reason. And in saying "by natural reason," he means the law of nations, which is for those gathering conclusions from natural principles. Thus we read that Cain built a city, and in Genesis 10, that the offspring of Noah were dispersed to different regions and islands of the world. Likewise, in chapter 11, the progeny of Nimrod were scattered, along with the multitude of those who had conspired with him to build a tower <note>The Tower of Babel</note>. So also in Genesis 13, we read of the division made by a pact between Abraham and Lot: "Behold, the whole land is before you: depart from me, I pray: if you go to the left, I will take the right; if you choose the right, I will go to the left." From this, it follows that not only the division in general, but also the fact that these nations possess this region and others another, is a matter of the law of nations. Against this view, Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> held a different opinion. For because Saint Thomas says in his reply to the first point that the division of things pertains to "positive law," and yet in Question 57 he said it was of the "law of nations," Cajetan, thinking these statements were contradictory, inferred that division in general is from the law of nations, but appropriation in particular is from political law (that is, civil law). However, Saint Thomas extends "positive law" to all human law, so as to include the law of nations. ¶ Moreover, regarding the second part of the conclusion—namely, that many particular domains were later adjudicated by "civil law" (that is, the law of individual cities and kingdoms)—this is very clear. For from that point, with the passage of time, republics transferred their power and the domains of their kingdoms to kings, as is held in the law: *What pleased the prince* <note>Original: *Quod principi placuit*. A famous maxim of Roman Law stating the Emperor's will has the force of law</note>. And from there, common fields were divided by Agrarian law <note>Laws regarding the distribution of public land</note>; and by divine positive law (as we said above), the region of the Canaanites was promised and given to the Israelites, and the kingdom to Saul and David. And later, tithes were given to the Levites, and now to those of the Church. ¶ **Fourth conclusion.** Many things remained 

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
common by the law of nature, the domains of which the law of nations could not divide: for instance, a place (as Aristotle says there), namely a city, roads, and so forth. And (as reported in the same *Institutes*), the elements: namely the air, water, shores, and ports, fish, wild beasts, birds, and so forth. For by natural law, and the permission of the law of nations, fishing and hunting are common—although later civil laws, perhaps not so much by equity as by license and custom, have 

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
interdicted them far too much. ¶ **The fifth conclusion** is the same and is easy.

</columns>

<summary>This page discusses how private property emerged from a state of nature through the Law of Nations (ius gentium), arguing that while some things like air and water remain common, the division of land was a necessary outcome of human reason and biblical precedent following the Fall of Man.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Question III of Book Four, focusing on how property rights are transferred and the reconciliation of private ownership with the philosophical concept of "natural law," which originally suggested communal living.</meta>

### Book Four, Question III

The transfer of ownership can be done by every form of law. First, assuming that specific ownership and possessions have been established through the division of goods, a person—by the natural right of liberty, by which a human is free—transfers ownership of his own things to another. This happens both through spontaneous donation and through any other free exchange, such as selling, bartering, and so on, as we noted in the immediately preceding book and will expand upon more fully in the following sections. Furthermore, I believe that the hereditary succession of children to their father’s goods was established by the **law of nations** <note>original: *iure gentium*. This refers to a set of laws held in common by all civilized peoples, derived from human reason rather than divine revelation or specific local statutes</note>. For regarding this, natural reason immediately instructed the whole of humanity: namely, that the father’s substance, name, and right to honors should remain, in a sense, in his children. Next, the **civil law** <note>original: *ius civile*. This refers to the specific laws of a particular city or kingdom</note> of individual regions applied the rights of primogeniture <note>the right of the firstborn child to inherit the entire estate</note>, prescription <note><term>prescription: the acquisition of a legal right or title through long-term undisturbed possession</term></note>, and other means by which ownership is transferred. Moreover, ownership is transferred against the will of the owner as a punishment and vengeance for crimes. For men are deprived of their goods because of the impiety of heresy, because of the crime of high treason, and because of many other things of that kind. Likewise, for the sake of ending lawsuits, as occurs in prescription.

<margin>*To the first argument.*</margin>
Regarding the first argument, various ways of responding exist. For there are those who understand that axiom—*By natural law all things are common*—not universally, but strictly: namely, either in extreme necessity or among friends. However, neither the facts of the matter nor the legal experts applaud this interpretation. For they understand it to refer to that general community of goods which was later divided by the law of nations, as is clear from the passage cited in Isi-

<margin>*Scotus.*</margin>
dore <note>Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar whose "Etymologies" was a standard reference for law and logic</note>, and in Distinction 8 of the chapter "Different" in Gratian <note>the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of canon law</note>. Furthermore, **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus, a major medieval Franciscan theologian</note> in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 2, skillfully receiving this as a universal truth, says that after human nature was corrupted <note>referring to the "Fall of Man" in theology</note>, this same natural law was set aside. But truly, with all due respect to the Doctor's authority, this appears

<margin>*Isidorus.*</margin>
less consistent with reason. First, because natural law is immobile and unchanging, as is clear from Isidore in Distinction 6. It is not a sin. It is thus. For he concludes from this that the commandments of the Decalogue <note>the Ten Commandments</note> are immutable because they are of natural law. ¶ Likewise, either there was a precept of natural law that things should be held in common, or there was no such precept. If you grant the first part, then either that precept was universal for every state of existence—and no one of sound mind will admit this, for it would be an error to dictate that the same mode of possession should persist in a fallen nature—or it was specific to the state of innocence. In that case, no setting aside of the law has occurred; for the fact that a division is made in our current state does not detract from that equi-

<column-break/>

ty, just as common possession would have lasted as long as innocence lasted. Therefore, the legitimate response is found in **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, Question 66, Article 2, although it will be answered more precisely through a distinction. For in things, one must consider both ownership and use. As for ownership, natural law never prohibited the division of things by a command that would then have to be revoked by a contrary law. Rather, common possession is said to be "of natural law" in a negative sense: that natural law never commanded such a division, but permitted things to be possessed in this or that way, whichever method was more convenient and expedient for the different states of mankind. Therefore, natural law has not changed, but the circumstances have. This is the opinion of **Augustine** in Book 1 of his *Confessions*, which he clarifies with an excellent example. There is, he says, a medicinal rule that wine is suitable for men; yet this is not at all revoked when wine is forbidden to a sick person. Instead, the change occurs in the man, for whom that perpetual rule is no longer fitting. But truly, as for use, it can in a way be affirmed that natural law commands all things to be common in times of necessity.

<margin>*To the second argument.*</margin>
¶ Regarding the second argument, which was made from the words of Clement in the canon *Dilectissimis*, there is a wonderful explanation in the commentary of Joannes Teutonicus. The text says that *the use of all things should have been common to everyone, but through iniquity one person said this is mine, and another said that is his.* But the commentary says "through iniquity" means through the custom of the law of nations, which is contrary to natural equity. Certainly, if the law of nations were iniquity, it would by no means be considered worthy of the name of "law." Therefore, the plain sense is that "through iniquity" means that which came through original sin, by which shattered liberty could not be contained unless

<margin>*To the third argument.*</margin>
a division of goods was made. ¶ Regarding the third argument, it is denied that, once nature was corrupted, the bond of love among mortals would have been firmer if things were possessed in common—as is sufficiently clear from the sequence of our conclusions. For a small number of monks, enclosed within the cloisters of monasteries, can indeed live peacefully in common; however, the vast republics of mortals, whose citizens pant so greedily for secular things, cannot do the same. As for the poet’s saying that two pronouns—***mine and thine*** <note>original: *meum ac tuum*</note>—are the seeds and fuel of lawsuits and battles, we frankly admit it; yet far more would arise if all things were possessed in common. The Saints, however, speak of the use of things when poor neighbors are in need: for then, as has already been said, use ought to be common to the extent that it suffices to relieve the poverty of the miserable.

<summary>Soto argues that private property is a necessary adaptation to human nature after the Fall, explaining that natural law did not forbid private ownership but rather left it to be established by the Law of Nations for the sake of peace and order.</summary>

# QUESTION FOUR
## Concerning the specific lordship of certain individuals.
### ARTICLE I.
*Whether any human being is the lord of the entire world.*

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'P' featuring architectural elements and floral patterns.</image-desc>

After our discussion regarding lordship <note>original: "dominio"; the right of ownership or sovereign control</note> in a general sense, it follows that we should discuss the specific lordships of certain individuals. First, we can argue on the affirmative side regarding Christ our Savior. For the authority of John stands in Revelation 19 <note>The OCR reads "9," but this refers to Revelation 19:16</note>: He who saw, written upon his garment and upon the thigh of him sitting upon a white horse—that is, upon his most innocent and purest humanity, by whose power, as if from a thigh, he fathered the children who are heirs of the heavenly kingdom—"King of kings, and Lord of lords." <note>original: "Rex regum, ac Dominus dominantium"</note> Soon after, it appears the same must be felt regarding the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note>: inasmuch as the same Redeemer substituted him as his vicar on earth to exercise his power. <margin>Ecclesiasticus 15.</margin> Yet, because a specific dispute is presently being raised regarding the Emperor, it is first argued that there is no such thing as a legitimate king. God (as cited from Ecclesiasticus) left man in the hand of his own counsel, which is to say, free: whom he certainly appointed from the beginning as master of things, but subject to no one. Therefore, no one can legitimately be the prince of others. Next, those who follow this line of reasoning argue: neither before the flood, nor at any time afterward, is there any memory of a prince until Nimrod, who through tyranny and force thrust the power of reigning upon the world. Therefore, there is no legitimate way of reigning. For this reason, the Roman Annals extol with praise those who expelled the Kings from Rome, and those who killed Julius Caesar. ¶ It is added, they say, that besides Saul and David, whom God created as kings, and David’s successors, no one is read to have been admitted into a kingdom by divine command; therefore, all others have been intruded against the law. Finally, they add in their own defense, specifically regarding Christians, that saying of Christ in Matthew 17: "From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or taxes?" For when Peter answered, "From foreigners," the Lord concluded: "Therefore the children are free." ¶ On the contrary, however, is Paul in Romans 13: "All power is from the Lord God."

<column-break/>

IN this question, we must discuss the three named persons: namely, Christ our Redeemer, his vicar the Supreme Pontiff, and finally the Emperor. <margin>Whether Christ was the lord of the entire world.</margin> Truly, regarding Christ, those who think of the matter only on the surface do not dare to deny that he was, inasmuch as he was a man, the lord of the world in temporal <note>earthly or political</note> matters. Nor are they moved by any other reason than that he was God. So holds Johannes Faber, an excellent authority on the law "All Peoples" <note>original: "Cunctos populos," a famous law in the Code of Justinian</note>, and Burgos in his third addition to the first chapter of Matthew. From this principle, many doctors of Canon Law attribute the same lordship of temporal things and the fullest power to the Supreme Pontiff; adding further that the Emperor himself receives his imperial power from him, and subsequently kings receive all their royal power. However, we shall not dispute here concerning Christ, nor concerning his vicar, because in our own commentaries on Matthew, we have (I believe) settled these same questions according to our small capacity. Namely, regarding Christ on chapter 1, and regarding the Supreme Pontiff on chapter 20. At present, however, we have set out to discuss not those spiritual questions, which are more aptly suited to commentaries on the Gospel, but rather secular matters. ¶ But if you wish to hear a summary of our judgment, which we revealed there more abundantly and fully: we contended there to persuade the reader of the negative side of both questions—that is, regarding both Christ and the Pope. <margin>Neither Christ nor the Pope is the lord of the entire world.</margin> First, I say that Christ, insofar as he is God, is lord not only of the earth and its fullness, in both spiritual and temporal matters, but also of the heavens and the heavenly spirits: by that right by which he created all things from nothing, and can reduce them back to nothing. <margin>It is explained how Christ was king insofar as he was man.</margin> Then, as for his humanity, we likewise acknowledge according to the same Catholic faith that he, as a man, by the right of redemption <note>original: "iure redemptionis"</note>, was the sole king of the kingdom of heaven. For it was his duty to dispense, administer, and arrange all things that pertain to the eternal inheritance: namely, to found the Church, to institute the sacraments, to create ecclesiastical magistrates, to establish laws, and finally to judge all people and decree eternal rewards and punishments for each according to their merits. Consequently, he could compel all kings to obey his laws, and abrogate their laws wherever they opposed his own; and finally, he could take all temporal things for his own use whenever it was necessary for his spiritual end.

This was not because he lacked the ability—for he was indeed God—but because it was neither fitting for him, nor did he subsequently desire it. Indeed, since he did not come into the world (as the Catholic confession holds) except as a **Redeemer** <note>original: "Redemptor"</note> for the sake of us men and for our salvation, he assumed no power of this world except that which would serve that specific mission. For these futile and slippery kingdoms could add no honor to him who was already God; rather, he despised all such things and cast them aside as worthless. 

¶ Furthermore, regarding the hereditary kingdom that some attribute to him as descending through the lineage of David: that was a particular rule over the tribes of Israel, and it had already utterly ceased with Jehoiakim the son of Jeconiah, or with his uncle Zedekiah, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah 22. From then on, the scepter of Judah remained not with kings, but with priests and the Maccabees until the time of Christ. For this reason (as we mentioned elsewhere), the prophecy of Jacob was fulfilled: *The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader...* (he says "leader," not "king") *...until he who is to be sent comes.* <note>Genesis 49:10</note> It is clear, moreover, that he never exercised any such power in practice, as even our opponents admit; therefore, he would have assumed it in vain. And so it is said in Psalm 2: *I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain*—that is, over the Church—*preaching his commandment.* And in Matthew 28: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth. Hence, before Pilate, he did not deny being a king, yet he confessed that he was not a king in the manner of the kings of this world. For he said, *My kingdom is not of this world.* <note>John 18:36</note> He taught (as Isaiah 9 had foretold) that his kingdom would endure forever and (as in the Psalms) that it is a kingdom for all ages; therefore, he possessed no falling or temporal kingdom. Nevertheless, he was (as John says) the **King of kings and Lord of lords** <note>original: "Rex regum, & Dominus dominantium"</note> because his spiritual purpose stands above the temporal goals of all kings, and therefore he was able to use all things toward that spiritual end. 

¶ If Christ himself did not assume such a temporal kingdom, it is beyond controversy and absolutely certain that he did not leave such a thing to his vicar, the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note>. Instead, he committed to him that same power which he himself exercised: namely, that whenever it should be necessary for that spiritual end, he might command kings, correct their laws, and finally make use of all temporal matters.

<margin>Spiritual and secular</margin>
Nevertheless, the spiritual and secular powers are

<column-break/>

<margin>powers are entirely distinct, although they coexist.</margin>
so distinct that secular power is not derived from the spiritual. Rather, it depends on the spiritual power only in a precise sense: if the secular power should wander out of line through rebellion, it can be restrained so that it does not violate divine or ecclesiastical laws—a point that will be clarified shortly. This is the plain opinion of the Supreme Pontiff himself in the chapter *Solitae*, where he says that he is the Sun, which presides over the day of spiritual things, while the Emperor is the Moon, which presides over the night of secular things. <note>A famous 1210 decretal by Pope Innocent III using the sun/moon allegory to describe the relationship between Church and State.</note> For this reason, he asserts he is superior in spiritual matters, while confessing that the Emperor excels in temporal matters. The same is found in the 96th Distinction, in the canon *Duo sunt*. <note>The "Two Swords" or "Two Powers" doctrine of Pope Gelasius I (494 AD), which argues that the world is ruled by the sacred authority of priests and the royal power of kings.</note> Whoever wishes may see the foundations of all these things firmly and extensively corroborated in our aforementioned commentaries on Matthew. 

¶ Having established these points elsewhere to the best of our ability rather than passing over them here, this question will be resolved in two articles. The first is whether civil power—meaning both Imperial and Royal power—is divinely instituted; in the second, we shall explore whether the Emperor has universal lordship over the entire world.

<margin>Article I.</margin>
Regarding the first point, there are two extremely different opinions among thinkers, which we need not dispute at length here. There are those who attribute to the Emperor not only jurisdiction over the world but also the ownership and property of all goods, even calling him the **proprietary lord** <note>original: "proprietarium dominum"; an owner with absolute rights of disposal</note>. Indeed, **Hostiensis** <note>Henry of Segusio (c. 1200–1271), an influential canon lawyer.</note> in the title on prescriptions makes all princes owners in this way. They cite in their favor the phrase from the law *Bene à Zenone* in the Code: *All things belong to the Prince.* <note>Codex Justinianus 7.37.3. Legal absolutists often used this to claim the monarch owned all private property.</note> And another in the *Authenticum*: *The Empire can at any time take something from venerable houses whenever it wishes.* This is, however, an incredible opinion. Therefore, as **Johannes Fabrus** <note>Jean Faure (c. 1300–1340), a French jurist.</note> well noted on that same law of the Code, the common opinion is to the contrary.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
And let this be our first conclusion here: Neither the Emperor nor any prince is a proprietor in this manner. For it is the **Turk** <note>The Ottoman Sultan, often used in 16th-century European legal texts as a symbol of "oriental despotism" where the ruler supposedly owns all land and property.</note> who, as it is reported, rules by such tyranny that he possesses all the substances of his subjects as his own property, believing he can usurp everything for himself at his whim. However, by the **law of nature**, even if the commonwealth has transferred its power, empire, and jurisdiction to the prince, it has not transferred its private property. Therefore, the prince cannot use those private resources unless it is necessary for the protection and administration of that same commonwealth. As for what the law says,

he says, all things belong to the prince: this is understood to mean those things which fall to the treasury or public exchequer. ¶ Furthermore, there is an opinion held by other Christians at the opposite extreme, claiming that all princes obtain their commonwealths <note>original: "respublicas"; here meaning the state or organized political community</note> through tyranny. They argue this using those clever reasons which we raised on the negative side of the question. ¶ However, this is not merely an opinion, but a manifest error and a perversion of the entire commonwealth. Indeed, the contrary truth is as clear as the midday sun, which we therefore establish here as our second conclusion.

<margin>Second conclusion against the second opinion.</margin>
Namely, that royal and imperial power, and the authority of other princes, is not a human invention, but a most holy ordinance of God—though it is distinct from spiritual power. For Christ himself immediately instituted spiritual power through himself, over which he placed his Vicar as the head, and subsequently bestowed his own power upon that same Vicar, to endure forever in the church. Therefore, that spiritual power was neither created by the commonwealth, nor derived through the commonwealth, but comes from Christ alone through himself.

<margin>It is best proven that civil power is established by natural law.</margin>
However, God ordained civil power through natural law, which is a participation in his own eternal law. This is evident as follows: God, through nature, gave to individual things the faculty of preserving themselves and resisting those things contrary to them—not only regarding the safety of temporal health, but also, through his grace, regarding spiritual prosperity. Since men, when scattered, were unable to exercise this faculty conveniently, he added to them an instinct for living in groups, so that being united, they might provide for one another. But once gathered, a commonwealth <note>term: "respublica"; the organized body of citizens</note> could by no means govern itself, repel enemies, or restrain the audacity of evildoers unless it chose magistrates to whom it might grant its own faculty of power. Otherwise, the entire congregation, being without order or a head, would neither represent a single body nor be able to provide for those things which were necessary. Therefore, by this same reasoning, commonwealths taught and instructed by God have instituted for themselves various forms: some chose annual Consuls, while others chose other forms of public administration. And by that same right, any community could and should—where it was recognized as beneficial—transfer its entire power and command to a single king (which, according to Aristotle, is the best kind of leadership). Thus, as is sanctioned by the frequently cited law, *What has pleased the prince has the force of law* <note>original: "Quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem"; a famous Roman Law maxim</note>, the supreme authority over affairs rests with him. Behold how public civil power is an ordinance of God. This is not because the commonwealth did not create the princes, but because it did so having been divinely instructed. Hence that passage from Wisdom 14: *Your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning*; this must be understood as referring to natural laws,

<column-break/>

both those which he implanted in irrational things, such as the sea and the winds, and those which he placed within men. And for this reason, Paul, in Romans 13, refers the authority of princes not merely to the commonwealth, but to God himself. *Let every soul,* he says, *be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power except from God: and those that exist are ordained by God. Therefore, he who resists the power resists the ordinance of God.* And in Titus 3: *Admonish them to be subject to princes and powers, and to be obedient to their word.* Nor indeed is this true only of the powers of Christian princes; rather, even those powers held by non-believers are from the Lord God. This is because faith does not destroy nature, but perfects it <note>original: "fides naturam non destruxit, sed perfecit"</note>. Through those powers, they can govern the common people in matters concerning natural law. Thus, in Daniel 2, it is read that the God of heaven gave the kingdom and empire to Nebuchadnezzar. Likewise, Christ said to Pilate: *You would have no power against me at all, unless it were given to you from above.* Hence, although in the early days of the Church almost all princes were held by unbelief, Peter nevertheless commands Christians in 1 Peter 2 to be subject to every human creature <note>note: "human creature" here refers to human institutions or ordinances</note> for the Lord’s sake; *whether to the king,* he says, *as supreme,* etc. And further down: *servants, be subject to your masters in all fear; not only to the good and modest, but also to the difficult.* And from this it follows, as we were saying in Book 1, Question 6, that the prince exercises the power of making laws by which he may restrain the commonwealth. Furthermore, it follows that he is not only superior to the individual members of the commonwealth, but is also the head of the whole body collectively; and thus he is so eminent over the whole that he even has the power to punish the whole body at once.

<margin>The commonwealth cannot strip the king of his kingdom except on account of tyranny.</margin>
Therefore, a King cannot be stripped of his right to the kingdom by the commonwealth unless he has been corrupted into a tyrant. ¶ Through these points, finally, that which we said above becomes clear: namely, that civil power does not depend on spiritual power in such a way that it is instituted by it or receives its faculty from it. Nor can a king be removed, compelled, or corrected by the spiritual power, except when he rebels against divine laws and the spiritual end. For although both proceed from God, they do not do so through one another, but in different ways: the former [spiritual] comes from God immediately; the latter [civil], however, comes by means of the law of nature through the civil commonwealth. And in this manner we must understand the word in the *Authenticum* <note>term: "Authenticum"; a collection of Justinian's legal decrees (Novels)</note> concerning instruments, cautions, and trusts, collection 6: *God established Empire from heaven.* And another in the *Authenticum* regarding how bishops ought to be, etc., where it is read that the priesthood and the empire are gifts of God bestowed by heavenly mercy. These things, therefore, were not noticed by those who

# Book Four, Question IV.

...who say that the civil commonwealth begs its authority from the spiritual power, namely from the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note>. Among these is Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists</note> in his commentary on the *Extravagantes* <note>A collection of canon laws</note>, specifically the decree *Ad reprimendum*.

<margin>Before the flood, there was also some form of leadership.</margin>
The arguments to the contrary, therefore, carry no weight. For even if humans were created free by nature, they nonetheless—by the instinct of that same nature, as social animals—appoint Kings and Princes over themselves for their own preservation, so that by obeying them they may live more safely and happily. And although one does not read of any prince in the Bible before the Flood, it is nonetheless very likely that those Patriarchs listed there lived as monarchs; as Augustine says in Book 15 of *The City of God* regarding Cain, who founded a city, or that those nations possessed an Aristocracy or some other form of government. As for what is added concerning Nimrod, we admit that commonwealths have indeed been invaded by tyrants. For even if the power of princes is an ordinance of God, the usurpation of such power—when it occurs by violating the law—is not by God’s command, but is rather permitted by Him as a punishment for the subjects. Regarding such rulers, God says through Hosea in chapter 4: "They have reigned, but not by me; they have become princes, and I did not know them." <note>Hosea 8:4 is the likely intended reference</note>. And Job 34: "Who makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people." And Proverbs 28: "Because of the sins of the land, its princes are many." Just as the use of power, when exercised legitimately, is by the inspiration of God. For it is regarding this legitimate use that Proverbs 8 is specifically understood: "By me Kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." For concerning the others (as we cited in Book 1), Isaiah laments in chapter 10, where he says: "Woe to those who make wicked laws." These are truly established not with God as the author, but with Him merely permitting them. ¶ Regarding the other point about Saul and David, it is granted that although God instituted them only by divine positive law <note>Specific laws revealed by God, as opposed to natural laws inherent in reason</note>, He nonetheless ordained by natural law that others should be chosen by the commonwealth. As for what they assert regarding Christ—who declared that the sons are free—this can by no means be understood to mean that he freed all Christians from the power of princes. Since his Apostles took care to admonish us to be obedient to them, that statement applies specifically to priests; it has no bearing on the present business.

## ARTICLE II.

->Whether the Emperor is the lord of the world.<-

<column-break/>

After we have briefly laid the foundations of the civil commonwealth, it follows in this second article that we descend to the question we proposed concerning the Emperor: namely, whether he is the lord of the whole world. Arguments are first made for the affirmative side. ¶ In the first place (as found in the *Decretals* <note>A collection of papal letters forming part of Canon Law</note> on majorities and obedience, the chapter *Solitæ*), the Supreme Pontiff and the Emperor are the "two great lights" in the world. But the Supreme Pontiff is one for the whole world in spiritual matters, because it was fitting for the entire body of the Church to have one head; therefore, by the same logic, it was fitting that there be one head in temporal matters—and one cannot imagine this being anyone other than the Emperor. ¶ To this is added the weight of both canon and civil law. For there is a text from Jerome in the *Decretum* <note>The Decretum Gratiani, a cornerstone of medieval canon law</note>, Case 7, Question 1, in the canon *In apibus*, where he says that just as among bees there is one leader, and among cranes one guide, so too there is one Emperor. And 
<margin>The Code, on goods.</margin>
in the Code <note>The Codex of Justinian, part of Roman Law</note>, Book 8, chapter 1, the law *Cum multa*: "Imperial fortune towers above all others." And regarding the Rhodian law on jettison, in the law *Deprecatio*, Antoninus <note>The Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius</note> says: "I am the lord of the world." And in the *Extravagantes*, the decree *Ad reprimendum*, concerning the crime of treason, etc., the Emperor Henry says: "The order of the whole world rests in the tranquility of the Roman Empire." ¶ On the contrary side, however, stands the law *Cunctos populos* in the Code, on the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith, where Justinian says: "All the peoples whom the Empire of our clemency rules." By these words, he circumscribes his Empire within specific limits.

The doctors of both laws <note>Both Civil (Roman) and Canon (Church) law</note> are divided on this question. For Hostiensis and Joannes Andreas, and (as it is said) the Italian jurists, maintain the opinion that he is the universal lord of the world. Specifically Baldus on the cited law *Cunctos populos*. And Bartolus on the law *Hostes* in the Digest, regarding captives. There he adds that perhaps whoever denies this incurs heresy, because in Luke 2 it is read that an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. And at the front of his treatise on the *Extravagantes*, the decree *Ad reprimendum*, he repeats this as if it were an article of faith. But Faber, commenting on the same law of the Code, and the "Ultramontanes" <note>Scholars "beyond the mountains," referring to French and Northern European jurists</note>, defend the opposite opinion. Nevertheless, because they dispute this matter only by citing laws that speak in ambiguous words, it is necessary to extract their meaning through reason. ¶ Therefore, the conclusion of this article is: Although the imperial 
<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
majesty is a gift and institution of God, it is nonetheless in no way credible that he shines with the empire of the whole world. The first part was sufficiently confirmed above; it remains, therefore, to demonstrate the latter. And lest the meaning of the word keep us in doubt, we call the "world"...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<columns>2</columns>

...the entire globe and circumference of lands and waters: for the Romans called that portion of the earth known to them, which they had subjected to their Empire, "the world" <note>original: *orbem*</note>. Regarding this, there is another question: but in the sense that the words convey, the conclusion is proved. And we speak (as we said above) concerning the **dominion of jurisdiction** <note>original: *dominio iurisdictionis*; this refers to the legal right to govern and judge, rather than the private ownership of land</note>: for regarding the **ownership of property** <note>original: *rerum proprietate*</note>, that was already denied in the previous conclusion of the preceding article. Therefore, although it is not the burden of the one denying this infinity of empire to prove his opinion, but rather the duty of the one asserting it to demonstrate such a right: nevertheless, the following argument is made for the stated conclusion. If the Emperor were the lord of the universe: this would belong to him either by divine law, or natural law, or human law (namely, of nations or civil law). However, it is by none of these: therefore, he is not. First, let us argue concerning positive divine law as distinguished from natural law. The sacred oracles relate that kingdoms were granted to Saul and David and their descendants, for God Himself instituted them by His own mouth; besides these, to no one else. Furthermore, the law of nature, considered purely, preferred no mortal over the rest in dominion. For all are born free, as has already been shown.

¶ This truth is confirmed as follows. If men lived wandering and dispersed, none would be the master of the others: therefore, when they gathered themselves into cities and towns, no one by natural law was superior to the rest by legal dominion, by which he could compel others by laws. Rather, there was only natural dominion, by which those outstanding in intellect rule over the unrefined: which (as has been said) does not possess **coercive force** <note>original: *vi... coërciua*; the power to physically enforce laws</note>. Therefore, if anyone is the lord of the world, he was created by the authority and grant of the commonwealth: in which manner it is said that civil power is divinely ordained. However, it is proved that he was not created in this way.

¶ For a commonwealth to institute a King or Emperor for itself, into whom it transfers its power, a public assembly is required, or at least that the majority should consent in such an election. However, the entire circumference of lands never held such an assembly, nor indeed even a tenth part, if you survey with the mind's eye the **Antipodes** <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe</note> and all the nations in their circuit: therefore, there never existed a single lord of the world. Nor did the name and fame of the Roman Caesars ever penetrate as far as the Antipodes and the islanders recently discovered by us.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: even granted that all the nations of the world could either meet in one place or be reached by letters to elect one Monarch; nevertheless, this was by no means expedient by natural law. For Aristotle, in the *Politics*, Book 7, chapter 4,

<column-break/>

<margin>
A Prince rules and commands only those whom he can conveniently administer.
</margin>
taught that a commonwealth is not better because it is larger: but only as large a one ought to act under one prince as he can conveniently administer by himself or through his own officials. Just as a ship smaller than the proper size is not fit for navigation, nor could one two **stadia** <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 600 feet; here used to illustrate an absurdly oversized and unmanageable vessel</note> long be conveniently steered. And Augustine, in Book 4 of *The City of God*, chapter 15, says: "Iniquity," he says, "has made kingdoms larger." And to expand a kingdom by subduing nations seems a felicity to the wicked, but a necessity to the good: namely, because the iniquity of enemies compels that they be suppressed by war and added to our Empire. These are nearly his words. For the King is the soul of the kingdom: hence just as according to the same Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the second book *On the Soul*, not just any soul can animate and give life to any body regardless of size—but there is a predefined method and measure for all things consisting in nature—because an ant cannot be increased to the height of a man, nor a man to that which belongs to an elephant; so neither can a prince, by his own warmth, nourish a whole commonwealth of nations and regions so vastly dispersed. He cannot know, amend, correct, and arrange what is happening in every province: for one man cannot receive messengers from everywhere in the world in a short time, nor can he dispatch his **magistrates** <note>original: *praetores*</note> and other ministers to every nation to punish what occurs everywhere. Indeed, even the fear of him cannot reach across such vast expanses of space. Therefore, since power exists for the sake of its use, if the use of this most ample power is not possible, it follows that such an institution would be in vain: and God and nature do nothing in vain.

¶ But let someone rise up against this. Christ most providently instituted a universal vicar for the world, as we said in the first argument: why therefore could not the same world be governed by one person in temporal matters, just as in spiritual ones?

<margin>
A distinction to be noted between the governance of the Church and Civil governance.
</margin>
The response is that the reasoning is very different. For Christ was the universal Redeemer, and subsequently the sole King of the Kingdom of Heaven diffused throughout the whole world: who disposes all things by His infinite power. And therefore, He instituted ordinary Patriarchs, Archbishops, and other prelates and priests to administer spiritual matters by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit: concerning which matters it is not necessary for all to assemble so frequently into one universal Council, but it is enough for His decrees to be sent everywhere. However, because Kings receive power from their own kingdoms, there is no reason why all should depend on one man in the whole world.

¶ Thirdly, it is argued. If the world is one...

He highlights the distinction between the universal spiritual authority of the Church and the localized, consent-based nature of civil power.</summary>

### Fourth Book, Question IV.

<columns>2</columns>

...is a universal monarch in temporal <note>worldly or secular</note> matters, either this was introduced by natural law before Christianity, or by the law of the Gospel. It was not the first, because before the birth of Christ, those three monarchies flourished: namely, those of the Chaldeans, the Persians, and the Greeks. The fourth, the Roman, succeeded them at nearly the same time as Christ. Indeed, Daniel had seen these in that statue, as read in chapter 2 of his prophecy. Yet none of those was mistress of the whole world, but only of nations enclosed within certain limits. Moreover, Christ in the Gospel did not arrange or change anything regarding civil monarchs; therefore, he did not commit this to the Pope either, except for the reason mentioned above: insofar as the purpose of spiritual matters requires it.

<margin>*No one is superior to a king in temporal matters.*</margin>
I take for myself a strong argument from the chapter *Through the venerable* <note>original: "Per venerabilem"; a famous decree by Pope Innocent III regarding the independence of the French King</note> in the section "who are legitimate sons." There, Innocent III confesses that a King recognizes no superior whatsoever in temporal matters. Although the commentary <note>original: "gloss."</note> understands this as a matter of fact, rather than a matter of law, it certainly does not prove it; for the head <note>legal source</note> it cites, *In the bees* <note>original: "In apibus"; a reference to hierarchical order in nature</note>, does not conclude this, as will immediately become clear. And although interpreters understand the word specifically regarding the King of France, the text does not allow this limit; for it speaks absolutely of the king insofar as he is a king.

<margin>*How the Emperor is superior to Christian kings.*</margin>
I would certainly not deny that the Emperor is superior to Christian kings. For he is the protector and champion of the faith, crowned for this purpose by the Pontiff; and therefore, in causes of faith—namely, both to ward off and drive away the enemies of the cross, as well as to quench schisms—he can convoke Christian Kings. However, that an appeal might be made to him in ordinary legal cases is not in use, except in imperial cities, nations, and provinces.

<margin>*From where some infer that the Emperor is lord of the world by divine law.*</margin>
There exists an argument which is considered more pressing than the others against this truth (as I judge it); and it is taken from Augustine’s fifth book of *The City of God*, chapters 12 and 15. From this, many think it is elicited that by divine law, the Emperor is the lord of the world. For he says that since the kingdoms of the East had long been illustrious, God willed that such a one of the West should be made, which would be later in time, but more illustrious in the breadth and magnitude of its Empire; and He conferred this upon the Romans, who were good according to their own fashion. God, therefore, gave the Empire to them (as Saint Thomas also says in the third book of his work *On the Governance of Princes*) namely, on account of their moral virtues, even though they had not earned eternal happiness by them.

<margin>*The qualities of the Romans.*</margin>
Chiefly on account of their love of country, their zeal for justice, and their civic benevolence. Moreover, as if

<column-break/>

the strength of this opinion, it is added that neither did Pope Sylvester cast any doubt upon the most Christian Constantine, nor did Ambrose upon Theodosius, such that they would have abdicated the Empire.

To this, however, one does not respond in only one way. In the first place, I have often noted how poorly Augustine has been commonly understood in this passage; for he did not intend to assert that God awarded the Empire to the Romans as if it were a reward for their virtues. For in both chapters cited, he purposefully strives to show that whatever they did, they performed for the sake of worldly glory and the expanding of their own name. Therefore, he judges that either no one, or perhaps only one or two, were truly studious of virtue; for that appetite for glory was a sin, or at least a venial one. For this reason, he says that although the virtue of Cato was closer to true virtue than the virtue of Caesar, neither was properly a virtue; and God repays no reward for sin. Rather, he says that God permitted that Empire by a just judgment, in the same way that Christ says those who perform their justice before men have "received their reward" <note>Matthew 6:2</note>: namely, from men, with God permitting it and disposing things by the natural course. Hence, after the words cited at the end of chapter 12, he says: "Because for this one vice—that is, the love of praise—they suppressed the desire for money and many other vices, God granted them that Empire." If, therefore, it was granted "for a vice," it is not understood to have been granted otherwise than by permission. Finally, regarding the same point in chapter 15, he concludes: "There is no reason for them to complain about the justice of the highest and true God: because they have received their reward." He is, of course, alluding to the Gospel regarding those who work for the sake of vain glory. Therefore, God did not make them lords in the way He made Saul or David kings; but they became so either by the law of war, or through their own tyranny with Him permitting it.

Furthermore, even if Augustine were understood incorrectly on this—as if he meant that God conferred the Empire on the Romans as a reward for legitimate virtues—he was not speaking of any Empire other than that which had previously been the Eastern one, namely among the Chaldeans, Persians, and Greeks. That empire was never universal to the whole world, but only to certain regions. And for that reason, he adds that the Empire of the Romans was more extensive, but not over the entire globe. I know that Bartolus <note>A famous 14th-century legal commentator</note>, in that treatise cited above, *To repress* <note>original: "Ad reprimendum"</note>, holds the contrary opinion: namely, that King Nebuchadnezzar was the universal king of the world, citing that passage of Daniel 2: "You, O king..."

<summary>Soto argues that neither the Pope nor the Emperor holds a divine right to universal worldly rule, refuting common interpretations of St. Augustine and legal precedents. He contends that the Roman Empire's power was a result of human action and divine permission rather than a divinely instituted office like the biblical kingship of David.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological debate regarding the extent of the Emperor’s power.
