# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

"you are the king of kings. The God of heaven has given you the kingdom, and strength, and power, and glory." <note>original: "rex regum es... gloriam dedit tibi"; a reference to Daniel 2:37 addressed to Nebuchadnezzar</note> However, this only signifies that he was the greatest of the kings known at that time, as Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus de Lyra, a famous medieval biblical commentator</note> says. It does not mean, however, that he held lordship and power over the entire world. Indeed, if the foundation of the Christian Empire were no firmer than what the Easterners <note>the Greeks/Byzantines</note> and subsequently the Romans usurped in the world, it would be too meager and weak to be able to make the consciences of the Emperors secure.

<margin>The right of the ancient Emperors was primarily based on arms.</margin>
For no one can doubt that they held their right primarily through arms; and thus they subdued nations terrified by power rather than by law. For even if some nations are read to have been attacked in war by them due to broken treaties, those treaties had nevertheless been extorted, and it was not a sin to break them. For what right did they have over the most remote nations? And—to pass over others—what of the land of Israel? This was the land God had promised and granted to them, and for whom He had prohibited by law (as read in Deuteronomy 17) that they should make a foreigner their king.

<margin>Christ did not approve of lordship over the Jews.</margin>
Nor indeed does the word of Christ, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's," <note>Matthew 22:21</note> fight against this with any sting: for there He did not approve of Caesar’s lordship. Instead, wishing to exempt Himself from that judgment, He referred only to the law of nature: "If you owe anything to Caesar, pay it; but primarily to God, what is due to Him." But this is what many do not notice: namely, that although God had perhaps permitted those nations to come under the yoke of the Romans because of their sins, they infer that the Romans subdued them by right—when in truth there is no force of logic in that conclusion. For God often delivered the people of Israel into the hands of the Philistines and Chaldeans; and yet it would be the most obvious error to affirm that a right was created for them to war against that people and reduce them to captivity.

<margin>Julius Caesar ruled through injustice.</margin>
To this, Julius Caesar seized the republic by private authority, and subsequently maintained his lordship through injustice, for which he suffered the penalty of death <note>referring to his assassination</note>.

<margin>The right of the Christian Empire.</margin>
The legitimate right of the Christian Empire, therefore, is this: the republic consented either to Augustus (as is said) or to the Christian successors afterward, such as Constantine; by whose grant the Christian Emperor is legitimate.

<margin>The election of the Emperor is transferred from the Greeks to the Germans.</margin>
This Emperor, therefore, was previously chosen by the Greeks; but later, in the year of our Lord 706 <note>Soto likely refers to the era of the 'Translatio Imperii,' though the coronation of Charlemagne was 800 AD</note>, the election was transferred to the Germans by papal authority, as is written for perpetual memory in the chapter *Through the venerable* <note>original: "cap. venerabilem"; a famous canon law decree</note> regarding elections. Therefore, to conclude the matter briefly, the one Christian Emperor exists by the best right, most happy and unconquered. However, that he is the lord of the entire world is supported by neither reason nor law; for the part that consented was very small in respect to the whole world. Therefore, with the law of nature protesting, that part could not place an Emperor over the Antipodes <note>people living on the opposite side of the globe</note> and the remaining regions. The Pope, however, because (as we said in the previous article) he is not a king in temporal matters by the authority of Christ except insofar as they are necessary for a spiritual end, is nowhere read to have enlarged such an Empire.

<margin>To the arguments of Baldus.</margin>
## To the arguments to the contrary,
that we may begin to respond to the Doctors <note>learned legal scholars</note>, in truth Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis, a 14th-century jurist</note> (if you look at what has been said) attempted in vain to found the contrary opinion in the law of nature; nor indeed is this surprising, since it does not pertain to jurists to weigh the law of nature. But much more absurdly (if I may say so with all due respect), Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, perhaps the most influential medieval jurist</note> stepped beyond his faculty into Gospel law: where he judged it a heresy to deny, on account of the word of Luke, that the Emperor is lord of the world. For the Evangelist only plainly reported this history: that an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled; yet he in no way affirms that that edict proceeded by legitimate right. It is just as if you were to infer: "The Royal Psalmist affirmed, 'The fool said in his heart, there is no God'; therefore he affirmed that there is no God." On the contrary, if you meditate on the mystery, the Evangelist seems to have condemned that edict more clearly. For he appears to have recorded that frothy insolence of Augustus so that he might warn that not he (as he boasted), but He who was being born, is the Lord of the world: He who indeed bound the universe with laws, and is finally going to call it into judgment. Furthermore, the "whole world" there does not mean the entire globe. For Augustus would not have been so out of his mind that he would order the Antipodes and other nations to be enrolled, which were many thousands of miles distant from him and unheard of; rather, they called "the whole world" their entire dominion, which was very widely extended. In this same idiom, we also call the islands and the continent lying across vast spaces the "New World" and the "New World." For it was a frequent use among the Latins to call a portion of the world "the world": as Lucan says in Book 3: "You Arabs have come into a world unknown to you." <note>original: "Ignotū vobis, Arabes, veništis in orbē"</note> But worse, in the aforementioned *Extravagantes* <note>a collection of canon law</note> in the section *To repress* <note>original: "Ad reprimēdū"</note>, the same Bartolus runs into Paul. For the Apostle says in Romans 13 nothing other than: "Let every soul be subject to higher powers." He, however, reports that those who are not [subject] to the Roman Empire...

### Fourth Book, Question V.

...they do not obey, they tear down divine commands: for they are commanded, "Let every soul be subject to the Roman prince." <note>original: "Omnis anima Romanorum principi sit subiecta." A variation of Romans 13:1, where the author notes a specific (and perhaps biased) addition of "Roman" to the scripture.</note> For Paul was not speaking specifically about a Roman prince, but generally about all powers, so that individuals should obey their own superiors. Therefore, that addition was a perversion of the sacred scripture. ¶ Regarding that point cited at the start of the question—the chapter *Solitae*—it has now been sufficiently answered. There, we explain how spiritual and civil power are two luminaries: yet the Sun <note>Representing spiritual power.</note> shines upon the whole world, arising immediately from Christ by divine positive law. The Moon, however, <note>Representing civil/political power.</note> flows from the same God mediately by natural law through the commonwealth. Yet, the commonwealth could not choose one ruler for the entire world, but only for Christendom. Furthermore, that saying of Jerome—the canon regarding bees—teaches only that there should be one Emperor for one commonwealth. <note>original: "in apibus"; referring to the natural order where a beehive has a single leader.</note> It does not, however, affirm that the entire world lives under one Emperor in temporal matters: but that there is one in all of Christendom, to whom even the Empires of the Turks and the kingdoms of the Saracens—which were once under Christian law—pertain. For even among bees, there is not a single leader for all the bees in the world, but one for each hive. As for the citation from the law *Cum multa*, which states that the Imperial fortune excels all others, we freely admit this: because it is the most excellent of all. However, it does not follow from this that a single man rules everyone in the entire world. For the royal dignity is more excellent than all Duchies and Marquisates; yet a single King does not preside over all the dukes of the world, but only those who live within his own kingdom. Regarding the word of Antoninus <note>Emperor Caracalla, in the legal text "deprecatio".</note> in the law *Deprecatio*, it cannot be denied that it reeks of arrogance: for who could say, without such a stain, "I am the lord of the world"? For that title belongs to God alone. And therefore, his assertion carries no weight. For Justinian, cited to the contrary, speaks far more modestly: "All the peoples whom the Empire of our clemency rules." <note>original: "Cunctos populos quos clementiæ nostræ regit Imperium"</note> Whatever glosses the interpreters may devise, the sincere sense is that he wished to circumscribe his Empire within boundaries, not only by law but in fact. And in the law *In nomine Domini*, concerning the office of the African prefect, he also names the boundaries of his regions. And in the *Institutes* regarding how parental power is dissolved, in the section *If by enemies*, the "threshold of the empire" <note>term: <term>Postliminium</term> (the legal right of a person captured in war to return to their previous status upon crossing back into imperial territory).</note> is placed, from which the name *postliminium* is derived. Also, the law *Mercatores* distinguishes between his subjects and those of the King of the Persians. And in the Clementine decree *Pastoralis*, the Pope seems to prescribe the limits of the Empire. Therefore, those who respond that certain people are exempt either by prescription or by

<column-break/>

privilege, ought first to establish his universal lordship over the whole world, so that they might then infer that whoever now acts outside the Empire is exempt by a particular law. Regarding another law cited in the *Extravagantes*, titled *To repress*, Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential medieval jurists.</note> invents many things: asserting that the Emperor is the universal lord of the World, and this by the institution of the Supreme Pontiff. This is something that surely no Caesar ever admitted, nor does reason teach it: for, as was said above, civil power descends through the election of the civil commonwealth. But this "whole world" must be understood in the same way as was said before: namely, the vastness of that portion of the world known at that time, which was subject to the Roman Empire. Or perhaps Caesar wishes to say that through the regularity of the Roman Empire, not only were his subjects in tranquility, but even foreign kings remained quiet, deterred by fear of him. For Bartolus did not look with a sharp enough eye at how civil power descends from God through natural law, and therefore through the constitution of a commonwealth; and thus, neither before the coming of Christ was there one monarch of the whole world, nor indeed did our Savior change the law of nations <note>term: <term>Ius gentium</term> (the "law of nations," a set of laws thought to be common to all mankind).</note> in this regard. The sequence of topics seemed to demand here that a question be applied concerning the singular lordship which the Catholic Sovereigns have held over those Western infidels discovered fifty years ago; <note>A reference to the Spanish discovery and colonization of the Americas (the "Indies").</note> however, it would have been too long. Therefore, we have set it aside to be disputed in the small book *On the Method of Preaching the Gospel*, which we have ready.

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right, #

...ownership depends. It is therefore asked first whether anyone, by their own natural will, has the power to transfer the ownership of their property to another. And it is argued first from the negative side.
<margin>First argument.</margin>
If everyone could transmit ownership according to their own will, it would follow that they could do so by a single internal act of the mind alone: for a mental concept is a true form of speech, of which spoken words are merely signs, according to Aristotle in the first book of *On Interpretation*. <note>Aristotle's *Perihermeneias* (On Interpretation) explores the relationship between thoughts, words, and reality.</note> By this same reasoning, a vow made to God in the mind is valid. Therefore, if someone can give property by voice, it should follow that they can do so by the mind; however, the consequence seems false. For matrimonial consent, through which each spouse hands themselves over to the other, is not legally binding unless it is expressed outwardly by voice or by gestures.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: if natural law granted every individual the right to be the sole judge of their own will in transferring the ownership of their things, it would follow that such a will could in no way be restrained by civil law. For human laws, as shown in Books 1 and 3, possess no force against natural law. However, the frequent practice of every well-ordered commonwealth shows this to be false. For minors under the age of twenty-five are prohibited from alienating their goods, as is clear in the *Digest* under the same title, Law 1. <note>The *Digest* (or *Pandects*) was a massive compilation of Roman legal opinions commissioned by Emperor Justinian. "ff." is the traditional abbreviation for it.</note> Likewise, by the particular laws of certain kingdoms, the rights of "majorats" <term>entailed estates (mayorazgos)</term> are established so that their possessors cannot spend or sell the goods bound to the estate. Similarly, neither a Prelate nor a Cathedral Chapter can alienate Church property at will, except for certain causes and in certain prescribed ways, as is clear from the decree of Leo and the entire title regarding the non-alienation of Church property.
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: If anyone could alienate their property at their own whim, it would follow that the same person could likewise transfer the ownership of a price or reward to another for a shameful or wicked act. Yet the consequence is false. For he who gives anything to corrupt a judge, or to an assassin to kill a man, or through usury, or through Simony <term>the buying or selling of sacred things or church offices</term>—even if he does so of his own accord—does not transfer legal ownership, as the sacred laws decree. Therefore, it is not a right of nature that anyone can freely give away their things. Indeed, there are those who feel the same regarding a prostitute, who by the merit of her body can receive the ownership of no reward.
<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourth, it is argued: several particular laws in Spain and in certain other kingdoms restrain the intention of parents, and especially of priests, lest they bestow any of their goods upon their "spurious" <note>original: "spurijs"; usually referring to children born of illicit or sacrilegious unions, such as those of the clergy.</note> children. And yet, if natural law granted the liberty to anyone to sell or give away their substance,

<column-break/>

those laws would be protected by no equity. Therefore, free alienation is not a matter of natural law.
¶ To the contrary is the authority of the law, in the *Institutes* under "On the division of things," the section *Per traditionem* <note>original: "By delivery"</note> and in the *Digest* under "On acquiring ownership of things," the law *Qua ratione* in the section *Literae*. There it is held that nothing is so agreeable to natural equity as that the will of an owner, wishing to transfer his property to another, should be held as valid.

<margin>Ownership is transferred by the will of the owner or by law; otherwise, it is acquired anew by other titles.</margin>
The question, as we were saying, is extremely necessary to know for the subject not only of restitution <note>Restitution is the act of restoring property or rights to their rightful owner.</note> but of all commutative justice <term>justice governing exchanges between individuals</term>. To understand this, it is first of all worthwhile to know that ownership can be transferred in only two ways: namely, either by the will of the owner or by the law. I say "only two" because I am speaking not of any acquisition of ownership whatsoever, but specifically of its *transfer* (translation). For ownership passes from one to another not only through transfer, but also by the law of nations through division and through discovery, as is clear in the titles just cited from the *Digest* and the *Institutes*. Indeed, things which are granted to the first person to occupy them are not acquired through transfer. Therefore, we shall make no mention here of found things—into whose ownership they might fall—but we must defer that until the fifth book, under the title of "Theft."
<margin>Definition of the transfer of ownership.</margin>
The transfer (translation) of ownership is the transmission of a thing from the one who previously possessed it legitimately to another, who likewise begins to be the owner. This, therefore, does not happen except by the will of the legitimate owner or by the law having power over him.
¶ Second, it should be noted that law—not only divine but also human—has a double power in the transfer of ownership. For it can impede transfer, both by restraining the owner's will so that he does not give, and by taking away the capacity of the other so that he does not receive. And secondly, the law can effect a transfer against the owner's will, both as a punishment for a crime and for the support of the public good (the commonwealth). We must therefore speak of these three parts in the present question: namely, voluntary transfer, legal impediment, and legal transfer.
¶ These things being established, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first:
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Every mortal has a natural right of giving and in any way alienating things of which he is the true and legitimate owner. This conclusion is drawn from what has been said above. For we have said that the natural and divine foundation of the ownership of things is human reason and liberty...

### Question V of the Fourth Book ###

...and liberty. For truly, because God created man in His own image—that is, rational and free—it is through this reason and will that man has dominion over his own actions. From this, he was made master of things, according to Genesis 1: *Let us make man in our image and likeness, that he may rule over the fish of the sea,* etc. <note>Genesis 1:26. This is a foundational text for "dominion theology," the idea that human rights over nature are divinely granted through the faculty of reason.</note> For this very reason, we have demonstrated that among all creatures beneath the moon, only man is fit to be the master of any thing. If, therefore, a man is established as a master through his will, he can, through that same will, renounce whatever dominion he holds. ¶ Second, this is proven by the fact that all things were created for the sake of man; thus, he may use the things he possesses as he pleases. Indeed, as seen in the definition of ownership provided above, ownership is nothing other than the faculty and right to use a thing in any manner permitted by law: namely, giving, selling, consuming, and alienating <term>alienation: the legal transfer of property to another</term> it in any way. This matter is most clear. Furthermore, a person can sell not only his possessions but even himself, as asserted previously. For although no one is so much a master of himself that he may rightfully deprive himself of life, he is nonetheless its guardian, such that he may sell himself in order to preserve his life.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: notwithstanding this same natural law, the civil law can both restrain the will of an owner and deprive him of the ownership of his goods even against his will. This conclusion is gathered from the principles of nature no less clearly than the previous one. For man is by nature a social animal; however, the life of mortals cannot coalesce into one unless they are kept in peace by public authority. This authority is both the guardian of the commonwealth and the judge of justice.

<margin>Why the commonwealth restrains citizens in the proper use of things.</margin>
For legitimate guardianship, it is first necessary for the commonwealth to look out for its citizens, lest they squander their goods before their liberty is guided by a full judgment of reason. For this reason, wards <note>original: "pupilli," referring to minors under legal guardianship</note> are prohibited from disposing of their goods, such that any transfer they make is void and of no effect. Second, it is also necessary to collect from the citizens the funds required for the same commonwealth’s expenses. For by the law of nature, the parts exist for the sake of the whole. And finally, as the judge and guardian of what is just, it belongs to the commonwealth to punish crimes. Therefore, just as it can take a life, so too can it strip any citizen of his goods. See, then, how these two conclusions, which at first glance seem to fight one another, are both children of the same parent: natural law. It is natural law, I say, that everyone can dispose of their goods by their own will. But yet—

<column-break/>

—only when that will, guided by reason, is able to avoid error. Wherefore, in the same Law 1, *On Minors*, <note>A reference to the *Digest* of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law.</note> the Prætor <note>A high-ranking Roman magistrate responsible for the administration of justice.</note> says: *following natural equity...* etc., he provided that children, whose judgment is weak and exposed to the snares of many, should not distribute their own substance. Therefore, although Ulpian <note>Domitius Ulpianus (c. 170–223 AD), one of the most cited Roman jurists.</note> in Law 1, *On Agreements*, also called it natural equity that the faith of contracts be preserved—adding, *For what is so congruent with human trust as to observe those things which have been agreed upon among men?*—he did not fear to also call it natural equity that those who enter into agreements regarding their affairs at a tender age should not be bound to stand by their word.

**BUT** truly, although both conclusions are clearly established, the arguments to the contrary are not without ambiguity.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
And indeed, there is a doubt by which someone might perhaps be moved: whether ownership can be transferred through an internal act of the mind. This will be examined more thoroughly in Book 8 under the title *On Vows*, where Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose *Summa Theologiae* is being commented upon here.</note> says that a promise is not made among men except through external acts.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Meanwhile, however, the argument is answered through these statements. First, transfer is of two kinds. One is that which occurs through a transaction and contract, whereby (as the Jurist Labeo says in Law 2 of the *Digest*, *On the Signification of Words*) an obligation is born on both sides. Regarding this, there is no doubt for anyone that it cannot occur without an external sign, since in that case there is not a simple giving, but a hypothetical one: namely, a mutual one, "I give so that you may give" <note>original: "do ut des"</note>—as is evident in buying and selling, and the like. This is especially true in the marriage contract, the consent for which is null unless it is expressed outwardly. The other kind is a simple transfer, such as a gift, which requires no obligation from the other party. And regarding this, there is a doubt. For if I, with a firm consent in my mind, give or promise something, after that is a true assertion, it seems to bind the man. Therefore, the argument of certain authors is invalid (among whom is Almain <note>Jacques Almain (c. 1480–1515), a French theologian known for his work on power and authority.</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences*, Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 2), who infer from the fact that matrimonial consent requires external expression that no ownership can be transferred to another through a mental gift. ¶ But you argue: "To give" is the relative term of "to receive"; therefore, until the other receives it, no transfer occurs. It is answered that this argument concludes most truly; however, this is the very thing we are debating: whether someone who has said to himself in his mind, "I give to such a poor girl this dowry as alms..." <note>The Latin text ends on a partial word "eleemosynam" (alms), which is completed by the catchword "mofynam."</note>

<margin>On primogeniture.</margin>
¶ But nor is a natural reason lacking regarding <term>primogeniture: the right of the firstborn child to inherit the entire estate</term>, as to why they were bound by that bond so they could not be dispersed. For although on one hand the argument is not weak that it opposes the law of nature—because all children of the same parents are born with an equal lot, and therefore ought to be nourished and educated with equal right—for which reason many republics do not increase the rights of primogeniture so much that the firstborn succeeds to the entire paternal substance; yet on the other hand, this yields not only to the dignity of the commonwealth, but also to its benefit and stability.

<margin>The reason for the institution of entailed estates.</margin>
Therefore, the great nobles should not think that <term>maioratus: entailed estates or "mayorazgos" that pass undivided to a single heir</term> were established for their own sake—namely, so that their lineages might endure forever—but for the good of the commonwealth. For it is expedient that its common body have bones and nerves by which it is supported. For this reason, it was decreed that certain illustrious houses should persist as the strengths of the commonwealth, both to serve as advisors and also to be its supports in time of war. And since, as the Lyric poet says,

<margin>Horace, Satires, Book 2, Satire 5</margin>
> *Lineage and virtue, without wealth, are more worthless than seaweed:* <note>original: "Et genus & virtus, nisi cū re, vilior alga est"</note>

it rightly seemed to kings to provide for the perpetuity of houses in such a way that the house would descend to the firstborn, while the remaining offspring would be content with their own maintenance. For the wisdom of farmers is similar; they prune the smaller branches all around a tree or vine so that the main shoot may grow into a sturdy trunk. Thus it happens that both the firstborn and those who have not entered the legitimate age are so rightly and deservedly restrained from <term>alienating: the legal transfer of property to another</term> their goods that the alienation is void and null, as no ownership is transferred through it.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third [argument], a slightly different response is given: For just as the Prince, because he is the guardian of the commonwealth, can compel citizens to contribute where it is necessary; so too, because he is the judge of justice, he can both deprive owners of their goods on account of crimes and make others incapable of receiving them. And for this reason, he who offers money to corrupt a judge or to an assassin is punished with the same fine; and those to whom it is offered most deservedly become incapable of acquiring ownership of it. A more detailed discussion of this matter will be held in the seventh question. Moreover, concerning the profit of a prostitute, we must speak in that same seventh question, and that for a different reason.

Then there are *spurii* who are raised from a specific concubine. But a *nothus*, as Quintilian says in Book 3, is one who is born from an illegitimate wife, namely from adultery. Since we do not have a Latin name, we use a foreign one. For the Greeks call whatever is illegitimate—that is, does not observe the law—a *nothus*; just as they call a "nothe" fever one that does not observe a legitimate period and limit. At present, however, *manzeres* and *spurii* are considered in the same degree as far as the succession of inheritance is concerned. Indeed, such

### Book Four, Question V ###

**Illegitimate children** <note>The Latin *spurii* refers specifically to children born of an uncertain father or an illegal union.</note> do not succeed to an inheritance from either the father or the mother if there are legitimate children. For a testator is not seen to prefer the successions of outsiders to those of their own family. This is found in the law <term>cum acutissimi</term> <note>original: "l. cùm acutissimi. ff. de fide cōmif." — a reference to the Roman Digest regarding trusts</note>, from which Law 9 of the **Laws of Toro** <note>A 1505 Spanish legal code</note> took its origin, which repels illegitimate children from inheritance. However, a mother can appoint them as heirs from a **fifth part** <note>The "quinto" was the portion of an estate over which a testator had free disposal under Spanish law</note> of the whole estate. But if the mother lacks legitimate offspring, they succeed her <term>ab intestato</term> <note>Inheriting when someone dies without leaving a valid will</note>; however, they do not succeed the father, because he is not legally certain. If, however, they are born of a condemned union on the mother’s side—such as from incest, or debauchery, and especially from adultery—they succeed neither by will nor without one. Yet it is not forbidden for either the mother or the father to leave them that same fifth part. These matters are beyond any controversy.

¶ However, what we call into question here is whether a father or mother, outside of a will, can in good conscience leave them anything contrary to the legal prohibition, or entrust it to the faith of a friend who might later deliver it to them. Regarding both, we must answer whether it is a mortal sin—for the father, the friend, and even the son receiving it—and whether such goods must be restored, and to whom. In such cases, one must distinguish <margin>What a father can do by natural law with illegitimate children.</margin> **natural law** from **civil law**. For if we look to pure natural law, there is no doubt that a father can give his goods to an illegitimate son just as to anyone else without fault; and the other can also possess them without fault, unless perhaps he has other children whom this act would drive into poverty (which is not relevant to the present business). But the doubt is whether civil law has made such illegitimate children so <term>incapable</term> <note>original: "inhabiles"</note> of enjoying paternal goods that they can in no way acquire ownership, or whether it merely deprives them of such goods by way of a penalty. This matters greatly: for if they are made incapable—just as a minor is for giving, or a person guilty of <term>simony</term> <note>The buying or selling of spiritual things or church offices</note> is for receiving—they are bound to restore those things even before a legal sentence is passed. If, however, the law is merely **penal**, then (as we argued at great length in Book 1), before a sentence is handed down in court, the son can possess those goods in good conscience.

¶ And so as not to prolong the dispute further, I believe we must answer by making a distinction between the illegitimate children of laypeople and the children of clerics or those in religious orders. Indeed, in common law, nothing explicit is found by which parents are prohibited from giving them something outside of a will, either while living or leaving it upon death. But there are particular laws of the kingdom that bring the matter into doubt. In the laws of the kingdom, nothing is found decreed more strictly against the illegitimate children of laypeople than what is defined in Law

<column-break/>

<margin>What civil law decrees concerning the illegitimate children of laypeople.</margin> 3, Title 15, Part 4 <note>Refers to the *Siete Partidas*, the 13th-century Spanish statutory code</note>. Namely, that they cannot succeed by hereditary right to paternal goods. And Law 1 of the *Fuero Real* <note>original: "l. 1. fori"</note> under the title of hereditary succession likewise prohibits them from succeeding in an inheritance; which is also confirmed by the cited Law 9 of Toro. Regarding these children, therefore, I would assert that if a father entrusts something to the faith of a friend to give to his son born of adultery, that friend is bound to observe the law of nature—that is, to give it to the son—and the son can receive it just as if he were a stranger. Thus, a father can give all his goods to him if he has no legitimate children; if, however, he has legitimate ones, he cannot disinherit them, except for up to a fifth part. Nor do I believe any sin intervenes. When the treasury claims the goods, one must stand by the external law. I am persuaded of this conclusion because that law, since it is to the detriment of the children, must not be expanded further than it sounds: it prohibits nothing except being "heirs." Therefore, a father giving his goods outside of a will does not act against the rigor of the law, nor in fraud of it, because a penal law binds only to what it explicitly states.

<margin>On the children of clerics and those in religious orders.</margin> ¶ However, a more intricate doubt remains regarding the children of clerics—that is, those initiated into holy orders—and the children of those in religious orders. For concerning these, although not in common law, much more significant and strict words are found in the particular law of the kingdom. There exists Law 22, Book 1, Title 3, and Law 2, Title 3, Book 5 of the **Royal Ordinance** in this form: "So that no occasion be offered for any woman to be given to the concubinage of clerics, if the children of clerics were to succeed to their goods by hereditary right, we decree and command that the children of such clerics (and Law 9 of Toro extends this likewise to the children of monks) shall neither have, nor inherit, nor be able to inherit the goods of their parents, nor of other blood relatives." And it follows: "Nor may they receive." For this is what the Spanish word means, **let them not have** <note>original: "Ni ayan"</note>; nor may they be able to get possession of any legacy, or donation, or other grant made to them. These words indeed not only exclude them from being heirs, but even seem to make them legally **incapable and incompetent** to possess paternal goods in any way, except by a special concession from the King. And it is not to be doubted that the King can make such a strict law: for as was decided in Book 1, human laws bind in the forum of conscience when they are just; and such a hatred for the offspring of clerics is equitable. Wherefore, it is truly probable to me that this law is not only penal, but also prevents the transfer of **ownership** <note>original: "dominij"</note>, just as if a minor were to give, or a person guilty of simony or an assassin were to receive. Nevertheless—

# Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

The father is bound to nourish and educate the child as long as he lives, because that right of nature is not revocable. He can even give the child gifts while alive from which they may sustain their life. ¶ Therefore, to respond to the most common cases—namely, when a priest or a cleric in holy orders entrusts his goods to the faith of a friend <note>This refers to a "fideicommissum," a trust based on a "handshake deal" or honor rather than a formal legal contract.</note> so that the friend may give them to the cleric’s son—first, as far as guilt is concerned, the cleric perhaps sins mortally against the law by binding himself to such a strict obligation. Second, in my opinion, I would judge that this **trustee** <term>fideicommissarius</term> <note>original: "fideicommiffarium"; a person who receives property on the condition that they pass it to another.</note> is in no way bound to award those same goods to the cleric’s son, even if he promised to do so. For the law of nature does not compel one to keep a faith pledged against civil law. ¶ It is asked, therefore, regarding **restitution** <note>The act of returning something to its rightful owner or the state.</note>, what should be done with those goods? The answer is that, if my judgment is of any weight, if the cleric gives to the friend not on the condition that he return it to the son, but absolutely; and if the other does not receive it on the condition of holding it in the son’s place, but as his own—even if the cleric has conceived a certain hope that the friend would hand it over to the son, and would not otherwise leave it to him—nevertheless, that friend can safely in good conscience possess those goods as his own. And our reasoning is that even if the law made the son incapable of receiving things he did not yet possess, it could not deprive the cleric of his own goods except as a penalty, which does not bind before a judge’s condemnation, as was said in Book 1. Therefore, the donation made to the friend holds until such time as he is deprived of it through a sentence. Indeed, he cannot even be condemned by the **treasury** <term>fiscus</term> <note>original: "fiscum"; the public or royal treasury.</note> unless the presumption is proved that he received it specifically to return it to the cleric’s son. If, at that point, the friend wishes to give those goods to that same son as his own property, the donation will still hold. If, however, the cleric gave to the friend not absolutely, but under the condition that he give to the son, and the friend did not receive them except under that condition, then the donation made to the friend did not hold. For that reason, he himself cannot retain them, nor can he give them to the cleric's son. I believe, therefore, that concerning those goods, before a condemnation occurs, it should be judged in conscience as if they were left **without a will** <term>ab intestato</term> <note>original: "ab intestato"; a situation where someone dies without leaving a valid legal will.</note>; for the treasury has no right until a condemnation is made. And so, if the cleric left a legitimate heir through the laws of intestacy, the goods are theirs; if not, they should be distributed for pious uses—provided that the trustee is safe and that the matter will never come to the notice of the treasury. For if he feared that, it would be more advisable to reveal it to the treasury. I have expressed these points at such length because advice is very frequently sought regarding this matter.

<column-break/>

# ARTICLE 2.

## Whether ownership is transferred through gambling.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the beginning of the text section.</image-desc>

CONCERNING this part of civil power, by which it can invalidate the transfer of ownership, we must next dispute those things which are acquired by gambling. For it seems that no ownership of those things is acquired, but rather they are liable for **restitution** without any need for a court sentence. For gambling—especially with dice—and consequently anyone subject to that kind of luck, is prohibited for clerics by both laws: namely, by **Canon Law** <note>Church law.</note>, as is clear in the chapter *Clerici* 2, and Distinction 35, canon *Episcopus*, where even a layman is ordered either to desist from games or be deprived of communion; and in the *Authentica* concerning most holy bishops, in the section *Interdicimus*. And it is likewise prohibited for laypeople by **Civil Law** <note>State or Roman law.</note>, as can be seen in the Law of the Use of Dice in the Code on Religion, and the law *Solent* in the Digest on Gamblers. And furthermore, it is forbidden by the particular laws of the kingdom. This prohibition, moreover, is argued to be of the same kind by which minors <note>original: "pupilli"</note> are forbidden from alienating their goods, and by which, as we were saying in the previous article, the children of clerics are rendered incapable of entering into inheritances. For those laws were enacted similarly out of a hatred for gambling. ¶ Secondly, this is confirmed: in gambling, so many types of vices meet that the transfer of ownership through it ought rightly to be forbidden. Since, as is held in that same Law on Dice, although it is an ancient practice, it nevertheless leads in time to tears; for some who do not know how to play have lost their own livelihoods, and consequently, out of this disorder, they attempt to blaspheme. And besides those things commemorated there, the one who gambles is as lavish and prodigal with his own goods as he is most greedily desirous of others'; for gambling generates an insatiable thirst for winning, which pertains so much to avarice that it seems to verge on theft. Whence **Aristotle** in Book 4 of the *Ethics*, chapter 1, compares gamblers with thieves and brands them with the infamy of avarice and illiberal behavior, since they snatch from friends what they ought rather to bestow upon them. ¶ Finally, thirdly, it is argued from the words of the cited law on dice in the Code on Religion, where it is held that if something is done to the contrary—that is, if someone has gained anything by gambling—no condemnation should follow by which the loser is forced to pay; but if he has paid, what was paid should be returned. ¶ On the contrary, however, is...

### Book Four, Question Five

that by natural law anyone can transfer their own goods to another through a game. Therefore, civil prohibition should not be extended further than reason suggests, the words of the law state, and the custom of the courts holds. These laws do not seem to contend anything other than that the person who lost has a right to **reclaim** <note>original: "repetitionem"; a legal term for a lawsuit to recover property or money paid.</note> it in court, as will be shown immediately. Because of this, as long as the loser does not reclaim it, the winner possesses it legitimately and even has true ownership.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To this question, about which you might find more controversy among the Doctors of Law than is perhaps necessary, he responds with four conclusions. The first: Play, if you take the name in its general sense, implies something permitted by the law of nature; indeed, it can even be a virtue, as Saint Thomas is the authority in the *Summa Theologiae* (2. 2. question 168). For truly, although man is born to labor and must "eat his bread in the sweat of his brow," he cannot, being a fragile creature, endure in labor unless the recreation of the soul sometimes interrupts the work and wipes away the sweat. It is permitted, therefore, to play sometimes for the sake of lightening the mind, provided that moderation is not lacking. Thus, just as it is permitted to procure other recreations of the soul at a moderate price according to one's social status—such as hunting and similar things—so it is sometimes permitted, and can even be a virtue, to play for money. This is clear because just as it is permitted to spend money on honorable foods to refresh the body, so since both the mind and the body are refreshed by games, there is no reason why one should not be allowed to spend something on them, provided you do not take it away from a greater necessity. Hence Aristotle, in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, chapter 6, establishes a middle ground for jesting as he does for other virtues, which he calls **eutrapelia** <term>wittiness</term> <note>original: "eutrapeliam"; a virtue involving pleasantness in conversation and play.</note>; we might call it "playfulness." Therefore, he also judges that men sometimes fail by lacking play, and these he calls "boorish." And Cicero says in Book 1 of *On Duties* that it is permitted to use play and jesting, but only as we use sleep and rest: which are not necessary for their own sake, but so that we may rise up refreshed and more vigorous for labor.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Just as play is made honorable by many **circumstances** <note>original: "accidentibus"; in Scholastic philosophy, these are the conditions (who, what, where, why) that change the moral nature of an act.</note>, so it is corrupted by many others. The first part is proved: First, to set aside those things permitted in Church solemnities—such as the feast of the most holy Body of Christ, like David dancing before the Ark of the Lord as read in 1 Kings 6 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 6.</note>—the laws themselves also testify to this. For the cited law, *Solent*, by which playing for money is prohibited, nevertheless permits jousting, wrestling, and other mock battles and rehearsals for war. This is because, the law says, they are done for the sake of exercising virtue—that is,

<column-break/>

courage. These exercises are referred to again by Greek names in the law regarding dice. Therefore, no republic has ever prohibited playing ball. Indeed, it is a credit to nobles for the strengthening of the sinews and the agility of the limbs it provides. However, these points are not relevant to the current matter.

<margin>Things that dishonor play.</margin>
¶ The circumstances that make games illicit are many. First is danger: for which reason tournaments and the art of archers were forbidden under the threat of **excommunication** <term>anathema</term> by Canon Law. Second, play is dishonored especially by gestures or words that display foulness, which were especially in use among the pagans. For this reason, games are spoken of poorly in Holy Scripture. Hence Tobit 3: "I never mixed myself with those who play," and Jeremiah 15: "I did not sit in counsel with those who play." Therefore, you may read reproaches everywhere among the saints with which they disparage games. To such an extent that Chrysostom, in his 6th Homily on Matthew, broke out in these words: "God does not grant us play, but the devil: for the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Third, it happens that a game is a sin because of the **scandal** <note>A "scandal" in this theological sense is an action that leads others into sin or diminishes the dignity of one's office.</note> of the person: for which reason dice games are forbidden to clerics for the sake of their honor; for they ought to be lights to you rather than given to excessive joys. However, let us pass over these and similar circumstances—such as the place (if they occur in a church) or the time—as they relate little to the present case.

¶ But the matter we now bring into controversy is only to examine things acquired through play, to see what legal right they carry. Therefore, another circumstance that makes games wicked is that it makes men both squander their own property and covet that of others. From this, many other evils arise; and this occurs most of all where there is no skill or exercise involved, but much laziness and, according to human judgment, a great deal of luck.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Concerning this type of game, let our third conclusion be: To play at dice and other games prohibited by law—provided the law is accepted by the people and not abolished by custom—is a sin. The conclusion is proved: for a just law, as we said in Book 1, can prohibit nothing except what is judged to be fitting. Therefore, what the law prohibits, it makes illicit, and thus it creates a fault to which the civil law can undoubtedly bind. Such games are prohibited because they are judged harmful to the commonwealth.

### Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

Therefore, it is a sin to violate laws of this kind. Nor does the fact that penalties are set for transgressors stand in the way: indeed, as we have demonstrated abundantly elsewhere, I believe, a penalty—if it truly deserves that name—cannot be imposed except for a fault <note>The author argues that legal punishments imply a moral or "fault-based" transgression (culpa).</note>. And although games of cards are not forbidden under common law, they are nevertheless prohibited by the law of the kingdom, as is clear under the title concerning colluders. ¶ Whether gambling is a mortal sin <note>A "mortal sin" is a grave offense that, in Catholic theology, destroys the relationship with God, as opposed to a "venial sin" which is less serious.</note> by its very nature, I would not easily decide. For this must be weighed by the nature and gravity of the act, as we said in the same book. And indeed, if you strip such games of all their corrupt qualities, since they are not by their nature against either charity or justice, they do not appear to be marked with a mortal character. On the contrary, to play at banquets—as held in the law *quod in convivio* under the title on dice—or to play for a small amount of money, can even be a virtue. Yet, when a large amount of money is put at risk, they can hardly be practiced without corruption: namely, without lawsuits, perjuries, and blasphemies. Besides the fact that this is the readiest way of all for squandering one's goods and demolishing illustrious houses. Whence the Lyric poet <note>The "Lyric poet" refers to Horace (Epistles 1.18.21).</note> says:

> He whom ruinous Lust or headlong dice strip bare.

For this reason, those who host gamblers have contracted such ill-will and hatred in the republic that, in former times, those who harmed them—whether by word, blow, or other damage—were permitted to do so with impunity, as is held in the law *praetor* under the title on gamblers. For priests, however, it is hardly permitted to use forbidden games without it being a mortal sin; and especially for monks and bishops: because gambling is prohibited to them not for the same reason it is to secular people, but because it is contrary to the dignity of their office. ¶ Moreover, so that both points may clarify each other, the fourth conclusion is added.
<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
Those things which are acquired through gaming pass into the ownership of the winner: for which reason, until the person who loses seeks to reclaim them, they are not bound by the obligation of restitution. For the clarity of this conclusion, natural law <note>Natural law refers to universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> must first be consulted, so that from there one may descend to civil law.
<margin>By natural law, one can transfer his own goods to another through play.</margin>
Indeed, that by natural law anyone can transfer his own goods into the ownership of another by way of a game can fall into doubt for no one. For as we said above, there is no transfer of ownership more natural than that which is done by the free will of the owner. ¶ But secondly, this is proven more explicitly. If such a transfer of ownership were forbidden by natural law, it would be so primarily either because of its form, its object, its effect, or from some other source. First, it is not corrupted by natural law because of its form: for besides the fact that both players

<column-break/>

could give a gift for free, this is not a simple donation: but a kind of pact, "I give that you may give" <note>original: "Do ut des"; a standard legal formula for a reciprocal contract where both parties perform an action.</note>. Specifically, I expose my money to risk, so that you in turn may expose yours. And the risk of one is valued as much as the risk of the other. Nor truly is it to be condemned because a matter is committed to uncertain fortune—that is, to an outcome whose cause is known only to God: for in this way, the name of "fortune" sounds nothing absurd among Christians. Indeed, many other human businesses are lawful which are committed to that doubtful variety.
<margin>Dividing by lot is lawful.</margin>
First, there are "divisory lots," namely when those who cannot agree on how to divide any property commit the matter to a lot: which Saint Thomas, following the opinion of Augustine (2. 2. question 95), deems lawful. Next are "depositions," namely while those disputing over a thing make a deposit, so that it falls to the one on whose side the truth stood. And another kind of lot occurs when the money of many is gathered to buy jewelry, which is then distributed by a lot drawn among them. And (about which we shall speak in Book 6) the contract of insurance
<margin>The contract of insurance is lawful according to all.</margin>
for maritime goods is held as lawful by the consensus of all the Doctors: in which, nevertheless, fortune (in the human way of speaking) dominates greatly. Nor does it stand in the way that the one who loses in a game receives no benefit for his money. For, as we said, he gave that of his own accord for the "hope" of winning, should the dice fall in his favor.
¶ That which makes the matter more doubtful for some, however, is avarice: namely, an immense greed for another's property. But neither is this in itself a cause of mortal sin: it is so far from subjecting the winner to the burden of restitution. For avarice,
<margin>Two types of avarice.</margin>
as Saint Thomas (2. 2. question 118) learnedly advised, is twofold. One is that which is opposed to justice: namely, when someone desires what belongs to another contrary to right. And this is a mortal sin by its nature. But the other is that which is opposed to liberality <note>Liberality is the virtue of being generous and sensible with money.</note>, and in Latin is called "illiberality" (stinginess): namely, the burning desire of one who nevertheless does not wish to receive anything contrary to right: and this is not a mortal sin by its nature, unless it occupies the mind so much that it hinders necessary works of charity. Regarding the proposal, therefore, that a fellow player desires to win, there is no sin, not only because victory is sweet to the one who strives, but also out of love for gain. Nor, even if he desires it most ardently, as long as
<margin>Greed for gain is not mortal if it is without fraud and the other is of sound mind.</margin>

### Book Four, Question V

...as long as they remain within the boundaries of justice, so that it is not a lethal crime <note>A "lethal crime" or mortal sin is a grave offense that, in this theological context, would separate a person from God’s grace.</note> by its nature. Although the excessive litigation over temporal goods is in itself a venial sin <note>A "venial sin" is a lesser offense that does not break one's relationship with God but is still morally wrong.</note>. Nor, in truth, is the extravagance of those who gamble a mortal sin by its nature, unless those things are squandered which are necessary for the support of a family or for fulfilling the commandments of God.

<margin>According to natural law, gambling is neither a mortal sin nor creates an obligation for restitution.</margin>
¶ Therefore, according to pure natural law, it is neither a mortal sin to gamble, nor does any obligation of restitution arise from it. For this reason, laypeople—if there are any exempt from imperial laws—do not sin by gambling. For, as Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s theological arguments.</note> says in the same place when speaking of this very matter, the civil law does not bind everyone; nor does it bind those among whom laws of this kind have been abolished through contrary custom. From this it follows that if any sin or bond of restitution intervenes, this depends on civil law, whether common or particular. We must therefore see how these laws prohibit gambling. For if they forbid the transfer of ownership <term>dominium: the legal right to fully own and control property</term>, it is clear that the one who wins—just like a usurer, without waiting for a judicial sentence—is held by the law of restitution. If, however, the winner is only deprived of the gain by way of a penalty, or for the recovery of it by another, then he is held to no prior restitution, because he truly acquires ownership. And indeed, regarding whether the prohibition suggests the former meaning, I find this single word of the law to be hinted at in the cited Law on Games of Chance <note>original: "l. alearum"</note>, which we mentioned during the argument: namely, if something is done to the contrary, no condemnation should follow—meaning the loser is not forced to pay—but what has been paid should be returned. If, therefore, it must be returned, it seems ownership is not transferred.

¶ Nevertheless, despite this word, I certainly believe the law's rigor is not so great. First, because what it says—"let it be returned if paid"—the Emperor immediately explains, adding: "and let it be recovered by competent actions from those who gave it." It must therefore be returned if it is sought; otherwise, the one who lost transferred true ownership. And reason certainly persuades one of this excellently. For since no force or fraud intervenes there, but a free agreement, there is no reason why the minds of those playing together should be restrained from being able to transfer ownership to one another. For it is sufficient that a period of grace is given to the loser for recovery.

<margin>The opinion of Paludanus regarding the restitution of gain.</margin>
Likewise, if the winner were held to restitution, he would be held either to the owner who lost or to the poor. Paludanus <note>original: "Paludanus" - referring to Petrus de Palude, a 14th-century Dominican theologian and jurist.</note>, in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 3, asserts that he must restore it to the poor before he is condemned by a judge. For he says that by natural law he is bound to the poor, and by civil law alone to the one seeking recovery. Therefore, if he has already given to the poor, he can

<column-break/>

afterward, when called into court, plead before the judge that he has already fulfilled natural law. However, his claim that one is bound by natural law to the unworthy <note>In this context, "the unworthy" refers to those who obtain money through illicit games.</note> is something he himself attempts to prove: because those playing together are engaged in an illicit thing, and therefore the one who lost has lost ownership, and the other has not acquired it. Nevertheless, this opinion has absolutely no probability. Indeed, by natural law, no one is prohibited from alienating their goods in that way entirely. Therefore, the winner would be held to restore to no one. And if he were held, he ought to do it for the true owner; for beggars do not succeed by natural law, except where there is no supply of the owner <note>Soto argues that charity to the poor is a secondary obligation that only applies if the original owner cannot be found or reimbursed.</note>.
<margin>When ownership of a thing is acquired for the poor.</margin>
Since, therefore, he gave it of his own accord, no obligation of restitution remains, unless the same person seeks recovery by civil law.

¶ Finally, all these things are clearly confirmed, both by the particular law of the kingdom and also by custom. For there exist laws in Title 10 of the Royal Ordinances, which concerns colluders:
<margin>The laws that exist concerning colluders.</margin>
namely, the first law concerning soldiers while they are acting under their banners: that whoever wins anything from them at that time is held to restore it to them immediately. Here, certainly, it is suggested that the transfer of ownership is hindered, which does not seem far from equity in favor of a soldier acting in war. Regarding others, however, there follows generally the second law of John II <note>King Juan II of Castile (1405–1454).</note>, differing in words from the former in this form: "We command that whoever loses anything in a game can recover it from the same person who won, provided that he does so within the term of eight days; but if he has not sought it within that term, anyone else may seek it; and if another is lacking, the judge and magistrate himself shall recover it by virtue of his office." And this is the law that is held by usage. From this it follows that if it is not sought back, the one who won can possess it perfectly well, and is not held to restore it.

<margin>A doubt arising from the words of Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ There remains here, however, some ambiguity from the words of Saint Thomas in the place already twice cited (Second part of the Second part, Question 32, Article 7). For he says that concerning those things acquired through dice, something is illicit by divine and natural law: namely, that someone wins from those who cannot alienate their property, such as minors and the insane; and that someone draws another to the game out of greed for winning; and that he wins from him fraudulently. And in these cases, he says, the winner is held to restitution.

¶ It must be noted here, however, first regarding minors and wards: because it often happens in practice with students <note>original: "Scholaribus"</note> that those whom their fathers support in study or at court, it is believable that they can sometimes gamble a small amount relative to their status. For example, if someone who spends a hundred ducats annually squanders four or five in a game, it is very likely that the father...

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right

...that their father has ratified it: for they well know that young men can hardly live without those expenses.

¶ But truly, can a Scholasticus <note>A scholasticus was a schoolmaster or university official charged with oversight and discipline of students.</note>—who is the guardian not only of the university’s constitutions but of all laws—restrict this matter more tightly? For instance, if he forbids anyone from losing more than two silver pieces in a game, does this rule bind the conscience? To this, the response is not simple, but multifaceted. First, such an official possesses no inherent power to establish laws, as this belongs solely to the University as a whole. Rather, he holds only the legal right to ensure that the laws—both of the University and others—are observed by the scholars. Consequently, he cannot personally create a new law regarding gambling; namely, he cannot forbid a scholar who is legally independent <note>original: "sui iuris"</note> from transferring ownership <term>dominium: the legal right to own and control property</term> by gambling beyond what he himself prescribes.

Indeed, if it is permitted by common law and the law of the realm, the transfer of ownership will take place despite his personal rule, even if the student gambles away all his goods. However, the student will have the right to claim them back <note>original: "repetitionem," a legal action to recover property.</note>. Yet, the official can, through his own rule, apply new penalties—such as excommunications or fines—to the existing laws of the University and elsewhere so they are more carefully observed. Therefore, if someone gambles beyond his prescription, he is bound only to the penalty if he is condemned; although he also incurs some fault of disobedience. This is indeed a mortal sin if the penalty of excommunication is applied. Nevertheless, the one who wins—no matter how large the amount—is bound to no restitution unless a claim for recovery is made, or unless the loser was a son under paternal authority <term>filiusfamilias: a son who, regardless of age, remains under the legal power of his father and technically cannot own property of his own.</term>

¶ Another doubt is whether, if a son under paternal authority wins something from another that exceeds what he himself was permitted to lose, is he bound by that very fact to make restitution? It appears he is not bound, for no injury is done to one who is willing and knows the circumstances. Since the person playing with him knew well that he could not legally win anything from a son under paternal authority, and yet chose to play anyway, he is seen as making a voluntary gift of whatever he might lose. Thus, perhaps the matter can be sustained. Nevertheless, it is more probable that, unless it is truly clear that he made a gift separate from the conditions of the game, the son does not acquire ownership of what he wins. For the condition of both players ought to be equal; therefore, there is no equity in a son being able to win more in conscience than he is able to lose.

<margin>Adrian, Book 4, on the matter of restitution. The third opinion of Adrian, or rather of Saint Thomas, on the opposite side.</margin>
¶ Regarding the one who draws <note>original: "trahit," meaning to entice or lure someone into a game.</note> another into gambling, there is a justified doubt as to whether he is bound to make restitution, even though Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent authority for Soto’s arguments.</note> affirms it. Thus, in the chapter "Because in the above," he has agreed with us thus far: namely, that the winner is not bound—

<column-break/>

—to restitution; however, in this specific point, he defers to Saint Thomas. For he who entices another does nothing against justice.

<margin>He explains the opinion of Saint Thomas.</margin>
The response is that Saint Thomas does not hold this opinion regarding every kind of enticement. For simply because someone invites another, or to some extent moves them toward a game, he burdens himself with no obligation of restitution, provided the other comes of his own accord—as someone who was otherwise prepared to play or was led to it by a simple request. But by the word "drawing" or "enticing," he means when someone draws another who is unwilling: namely, by using force or ensnaring them with fraud. In such cases, it is clear that he is bound to restitution, because he wins from one who is unwilling. Nor should one be considered "drawn unwillingly" only if they play under simple physical force; it also includes one who is instigated by such relentless pleading and words that, unless they played, they would be overcome with shame and regarded as unrefined or ignoble. For example, if there is an honorable man of the highest reputation, living with a certain splendor of life, whom another person shames with relentless words until he plays—even though he had firmly resolved not to—then that "enticer" is surely bound to restitution. For gambling ought to be entirely free, so that the one who loses is seen to truly intend the transfer of ownership.

¶ However, another phrase that Saint Thomas adds there—namely, that those who are bound by civil laws are held to restitution—seems contrary to our fourth conclusion. Yet, he either means cases where the civil law explicitly states that ownership is not transferred, or he means that one should restore it if it is claimed back. Otherwise, it would truly be an excessively harsh saying.

<margin>A doubt concerning those who gamble on credit, pledging their word.</margin>
¶ One thing must not be passed over in silence at the end: namely, whether one who gambles not for present cash, but for money not present and on credit, pledging his word <note>original: "impignorata fide," literally "pawned faith" or an oath of honor.</note>, is bound to pay. It appears the affirmative part is true by natural law, since he has made a promise and is not forbidden by civil law from giving. It is responded, nonetheless, that as long as he has only made a simple promise, he is not to be thought of as renouncing his right (which he holds by benefit of civil law) to refuse payment or seek recovery. Therefore, just as he could have sued to get it back if he had paid, so too the one who promised can in good conscience defend himself in a trial so as not to pay. Nor does he act against natural law, even though among nobles it might be held against him as a disgrace. If, however, he expressly promised that he would not use the benefit of the law to recover it, I believe he could voluntarily depart from his right; at the very least, if he swore an oath, he is bound to stand by his oath—unless the loss of goods is so great that he might seek a dispensation <note>A formal release from a religious or legal obligation.</note>.

### Question V of Book Four

<margin>A doubt to be noted.</margin>
Finally, there is one last point to consider: suppose someone has lost a large sum of money through gambling, but is afraid to seek its return through a public trial. Could he then secretly steal it back from the winner, or perhaps keep money he owes that person as a form of self-compensation <note>original: "recompensationem," a legal concept where one cancels a debt by offsetting it against what is owed to them</note>? In the passage cited earlier, Adrian <note>Adrianus: Likely referring to Pope Hadrian VI, a Dutch theologian who taught at Leuven and was a significant authority for Soto.</note> judges that this is permitted. He argues that since the loser has the right to seek the money through a public trial, he may also recover it through other means. However, with all due respect to such a great man, I am not sure this is as certain as he believes. For once a true transfer of <term>dominium: the legal right to own and control property</term> has occurred, one cannot recover it except by using the benefit of the law—specifically within the time frame prescribed by the law, such as within eight days in Spain. The old gambling law stating that these claims do not expire for forty years is no longer in use anywhere. Furthermore, perhaps the loser *must* seek it through a court; otherwise, the winner is not bound in conscience to return it, because the laws decree nothing more than that a legal action is granted to the loser. Yet, I am not entirely certain about this: if the loser asks for the money back privately within the legal time limit, the winner is likely bound to return it, though I tend to lean toward the opposite view.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the first argument—namely, concerning the laws—enough has already been said about how they prohibit gambling. Neither clerics, if they win, nor others who win from them, seem to be bound to restitution any differently than laypeople. For although they may sin more gravely due to the scandal and the requirements of their holy office, the obligation to return the money is the same as it is among the laity.

<margin>Priests and even Bishops can gamble, just like others.</margin>
For when priests lose money by gambling, they have the legal capacity to lose it; even Bishops do, as will be shown in Book 9. They are the masters of their own property. The case is different for members of religious orders <note>Religiosis: Monks or friars who have taken a vow of poverty and do not own personal property.</note>. Therefore, it is denied that the laws prohibiting gambling prevent the transfer of ownership in the same way they do for orphans or those committing <term>simony: the illegal buying or selling of spiritual things or church offices</term>.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
To the second argument, the response is that although the vices mixed into gambling can be mortal sins, no obligation for restitution arises from them except in the manner already explained. Indeed, although wastefulness is a sin, a wasteful person nonetheless transfers ownership of his goods. To the word of Aristotle, who grouped gamblers with thieves, the response is that he did not do this because the logic of the two is the same, but because gamblers are "illiberal"—they act against the laws of friendship. A man ought

<column-break/>

to play with friends, to whom he should rather give his own goods than scrape away theirs.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
Finally, the third argument has also been answered where we explained that legal phrase: "let him return what was paid"—that is, if it is demanded back.

### ARTICLE III.
->Whether ownership is transferred by a contract that is void under civil law.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a scene with figures and architectural details.</image-desc>Regarding the same branch of civil power by which the will of an owner is restrained from transferring ownership, we must examine whether a contract that is void in civil law is also void in the conscience, such that it truly prevents the transfer of ownership. The argument for the negative side is as follows: When the purpose of a civil law ceases, the law itself loses its force, and thus one must stand by natural law. The purpose of laws requiring legal formalities <note>solennitatem: the specific words, witnesses, or documents required by law to make a contract "official."</note> in contracts is to prevent fraud and deceit. Therefore, where it is clear that no fraud has occurred, the contract should hold firm in the conscience. ¶ Second, to clarify this premise, it is argued that even Divine law does not bind when its purpose ceases; therefore, human law, being inferior, binds even less. This is proven by the precept of "fraternal correction": when there is no hope of the person being corrected (which is the goal of the correction), the command does not bind. As Augustine says: *if I knew it would not benefit you, I would not frighten you, I would not warn you.* In the same way, for example, if a will <note>testamento: a last will and testament</note> lacks the civil formalities but the testator's will is clear, one should follow natural law rather than civil law, so that the person's will is fulfilled. ¶ Third, it is argued that if civil law were observed with such rigor, it would often happen that a person close to death could never fulfill their final wishes—for instance, if legal witnesses could not be found. This seems like an absurd conclusion to allow. ¶ On the contrary, however, it is argued that civil laws (as stated in Book 1) do bind in the court of conscience. These laws absolutely establish the formalities of contracts with such strictness of language that a contract is otherwise considered as if it never happened, as is clear regarding wills in the law *Hac Consultissima* <note>A specific law in the Code of Justinian regarding the requirements for making a valid will.</note>.

<summary>Soto discusses whether a gambling loser can secretly recover their losses and begins a new debate on whether contracts that lack legal formalities are still morally binding in the 'court of conscience.'</summary>
