<meta>This page continues Soto's exploration of whether civil laws regarding contracts and wills bind a person's conscience. Having discussed gambling in the previous section, he now addresses whether a contract that is legally "void" due to a lack of formal requirements is also void in the eyes of God and moral conscience.</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

<margin>
The opinion of Innocent in the chapter "Quia."
</margin>
The present question has not been greatly debated among the Doctors <note>learned legal and theological scholars</note>; however, Innocent IV <note>A 13th-century Pope and influential canon lawyer.</note> in the chapter *quia plerique* regarding the immunity of the church, says one thing in passing: namely, that he who possesses something through a contract which lacks the **legal solemnity** <note>original: "solennitas iuris," meaning the specific formal procedures required by law for a contract to be valid.</note> is bound to make restitution. In this, he teaches that a contract lacking the required formalities is null and void in the court of conscience. He then provides an example of a contract made by the will of a **minor** <note>original: "pupillus," a child under guardianship.</note> without the consent of a tutor.

<margin>
The opinion of Panormitanus, which is contrary to Innocent and is the common view.
</margin>
Panormitanus, however, in his commentary on the same chapter, following Antonius de Butrio, embraced the contrary opinion: namely, that where fraud and deceit are absent, one must stand by **natural law**, so that the contract holds firm regardless of the civil law. Sylvester Prierias subscribed to this view under the headings "Alienation" (§.12) and "Testament" (i. §. 5). Later, Adrian VI <note>Pope and theologian who taught at Leuven; a major authority for Soto.</note> agreed in his *Quodlibets* (6. art. 1) for the reasons we recently recited at the start of this question. Indeed, Antonius de Butrio asserts that he gave counsel that the legacies of an "illegal" testament should nonetheless be honored. Consequently, he adds in his treatise on the Franciscans <note>original: "tractatu Minoritano."</note> that a legacy made by a Franciscan friar—even if he is legally incapable of receiving it under human law—must nonetheless be paid in conscience. This, therefore, is the **common opinion**.

¶ There are, however, certainly many arguments to the contrary, and these are not weak; they confirm the opposite view with greater probability. I have heard for a long time in our schools here that this contrary opinion—or rather, the much more probable one—is defended: namely, that a contract void under civil law is also void in conscience. Yet, I do not dare to assert this opinion so absolutely when such cases come before me. Instead, I embrace a **middle path** tempered from both sides, as far as my understanding goes.

<margin>
The author's instruction.
</margin>
To explain this, it must be noted that the state and the secular Prince can hinder the transfer of ownership in two ways. One way is **absolutely**: examples of this we have already produced regarding a minor before the legal age and the possessor of an entailed estate <note>original: "maioratus," property that must pass to the eldest son.</note>; through these, ownership is undoubtedly not transferred. The second way is not simple and absolute, but by prescribing the **form of the contract** to prevent fraud: just as the civil state commands the formalities of testaments, and the Church commands the forms of contracts by which church property is alienated. Regarding these, the question is answered with this conclusion.

<margin>
The author's opinion.
</margin>
¶ A contract which lacks an essential legal formality, although it is not *ipso facto* <note>by the very fact</note>

<column-break/>

simply void in conscience—unlike one made by a minor under the legal age—is nonetheless void to the extent that anyone can, in good conscience, use the **benefit of the law** in such a case. The conclusion is explained thus: Suppose my brother dies childless and makes an "informal" testament—that is, one lacking the legal formalities, by the defect of which it would rightly be declared void in court (for a testament lacking minor formalities should still be considered legitimate). Suppose, I say, my brother, whose heir I am by law since he died without a valid will <note>original: "ab intestato."</note>, named a stranger as his heir in such a testament. I can, with a safe conscience, enter upon the inheritance and defend myself by the nullity of the testament, even though I know my brother intended otherwise and there was no fraud. And therefore, while the inheritance is awarded to me in the external court, I can possess it in **good faith**. In the same way, if my father made legacies through such a testament (putting aside pious works for the moment <note>The Church often required that "pious" legacies, like those to the poor or the church, be honored even if the will was legally flawed.</note>), I am not bound in conscience to fulfill those legacies.

Why I have moderated the conclusion in this way—that the transfer of ownership in these events is not entirely voided and annulled *ipso facto*—I will explain at the end of the proofs for this conclusion. Nor do I dare to assert this conclusion so strongly as to think the contrary view is entirely improbable; for where I do not find my assertion held by others, I am usually a little more hesitant to proclaim it. Nevertheless, I will submit the arguments which make this opinion, in my view, much more probable than the contrary. And if I had any authority among theologians, I would say that the judgment of **natural law**, and especially of **conscience**, should be deferred to none other than the **Theologians**.

Let us, therefore, assume the tenor of the civil laws. In a **nuncupative testament** <note>An oral will declared before witnesses.</note>, for example—where the heir and witnesses are named by word of mouth without the signature of a notary—seven witnesses are required, as found in the *Institutes* regarding testaments (§. final).

<margin>
The formality of testaments is described.
</margin>
And likewise in a written testament that is closed and sealed, as found in the cited law *Hac consultissima* (Code, on testaments) and the specific law of the realm, **Law 3 of Toro** <note>The *Leyes de Toro* (1505) were a landmark set of Spanish laws clarifying the application of Roman and customary law.</note>. Although in an open written testament, three witnesses with a notary suffice, or five without one. However, under ancient law, sometimes more were required, sometimes fewer: as in the testament of an Emperor, or a soldier, or a blind person, etc., as is noted extensively by the Doctors in the commentaries on those same titles in the *Institutes*, the *Code*, and the *Digest*. Legally qualified witnesses are also required: meaning neither a woman, nor a deaf person, nor a mute...

<summary>Soto argues that while a contract or will lacking legal formalities might not be automatically void in the eyes of God, a person may morally use the law's technicalities to claim an inheritance in good faith. He contrasts his "middle path" with the views of earlier legal scholars like Panormitanus, grounding his argument in the role of the state to prevent fraud through mandated procedures.</summary>
<keywords>solemnity of law, contracts, testaments, inheritance, conscience, natural law, civil law, Law of Toro, Innocent IV, Adrian VI, legal formalities, restitution</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Question 5 of Book Four, where Soto debates whether legal "solemnities"—the formal requirements like witnesses or signatures—are necessary for a contract or will to be valid in the eyes of God (the "court of conscience"). He is currently weighing the opinions of legal giants like Innocent IV and Panormitanus.</meta>

### Book Four, Question V.

<column-break/>

a mute person, nor an "infamous" person <note>original: "infamis"; in Roman law, someone who lost their legal standing due to certain crimes or shameful professions</note>, may be admitted as a witness, as is cautioned in the same *Institutes* in the section on witnesses. However, we define nothing on this point here, but rather defer it to the secular judgment. Similarly, in Pontifical law <note>Canon law</note>, it is most carefully provided that the property of the Church should not be sold without three specific contracts, as noted by the Doctors <note>learned legal commentators</note> in the Decrees and the chapters on not alienating church property. Therefore, the **contrary opinion** <note>the view of Panormitanus mentioned on the previous page</note> asserts that even if a will is pronounced null in the **external forum** <note>original: "foro exteriori"; the public legal system</note>, one must still abide by the will of the deceased in the **court of conscience**, provided that no fraud was involved. The same would apply when the legal formalities of contracts are missing in the sale of church property.

¶ However, we [Soto] put forward the following arguments to the contrary:

<margin>
The author’s opinion is clear.
</margin>

First, I shall assume from Book 1 that civil laws bind us in conscience, a point on which Panormitanus himself in that same place most clearly agrees with Innocent. If that is so, I argue as follows: Such laws make no exceptions whatsoever, but state absolutely that wherever such formal ceremony is lacking, the contract is null. For this is the conclusion of the law in the Code titled *Hac consultissima*: where a will has not been signed, it is appropriate that it be held **as if it were never done** <note>original: "pro infecto"; a legal term meaning the act has no legal existence</note>. And again: "We do not wish the will of the deceased to hold from an imperfect testament," unless it is between parents and children regarding the division of an inheritance. As the **Gloss** <note>standard medieval commentary on law</note> says, and as Justinian states in the *Institutes* on how wills are invalidated: "An imperfect testament is without doubt null." He later says he wishes to live by those same laws. Furthermore, in the law of the kingdom cited as the **Third Law of Toro** <note>original: "3. tauri"; the Laws of Toro (1505) were fundamental to Spanish civil law</note>, it is held that where the number of witnesses is not correct, the will shall have no standing, neither in court nor outside of it. And in the cited canon *sine exceptione*, it is held that the unauthorized sale of church property is void. Since, therefore, the law has the same power as the words it speaks, it follows that it must be obeyed without any creative interpretation. But you may say, "The laws do not use the phrase 'in conscience.'" This is merely a **quibble** <note>original: "cavillus"</note>; for it is not the custom of legislators to add such words, yet the obligation in conscience follows from the very nature of laws.

¶ But so that the point of the matter may become more evident, it is argued secondly as follows:

<margin>
Second reason.
</margin>

It is a most established axiom among the Doctors that "The law does not look at accidental cases," but rather at those things which happen most frequently. For as Pomponius says in the *Digest* concerning laws, they ought to be established regarding those things which happen and can occur in common use, but not regarding those things which happen **contrary to expectation** and by surprise.

<column-break/>

Therefore, although the reason for these laws was to prevent fraud and deceit, the law nevertheless retains its force even if, in some specific case, that particular goal is not lacking. Examples of this are very frequent and obvious, and it is a wonder that Panormitanus and his followers did not see them.

The law prohibits—as we said in Article 1—**minors** <note>original: "pueros"; children or those under guardianship</note> from selling their own property of their own accord; the purpose of this is surely so that their goods are not squandered through their imprudence. Yet it happens that there is a boy of ten or twelve years who can wisely manage his affairs and dispose of his goods to his own advantage; will the contract he made without a tutor therefore hold in conscience? Certainly it will not. Likewise, the purpose of the law of **fasting** is the "taming of the body"; if someone does not need that taming, is he thereby exempt from the law? **Not at all** <note>original: "minimè gentium"; a strong Latin negation</note>. The law also prohibits carrying weapons at night; can someone who is peaceful carry them? By no means.

In the same way, therefore, in the matter at hand: although in some specific case no fraud was present, the force of the law is nonetheless not extinguished. And the reason for this is most evident: because otherwise, laws would cast **scruples** <note>anxious doubts about sin</note> into the consciences of the simple-hearted. For it would often be obscure and ambiguous whether a fraud was great enough to require obeying the civil law, or so small that one should lean toward **natural law**. Therefore, the legislator did not want the citizens to be the judges of these matters, but rather that they should sincerely listen to the law as long as it is not contrary to nature.

¶ But you say: "It is against natural law that if someone wished to dispose of their goods, their will is not fulfilled simply because of a lack of formal ceremony."

Actually, it is not. In fact, it is highly consistent with that same nature: namely, so that the frauds and deceptions which human fallacy might build against the deceased are removed. For this reason, it was said in Article 1 that the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "respublica"</note> can restrain the natural will of citizens in distributing their things, and thus prescribe a method for them. Indeed, I believe that if frauds became frequent due to secret ways of paying debts, a Prince could enact laws stating that a payment made without witnesses would be invalid; so much so that in conscience, what was paid against the laws could be demanded a second time. But whatever the truth of that may be, there should be no doubt that an **illegal contract** can be held as void in conscience, even if fraud was not involved, because of the risk that was present. If that is possible, I do not see what could have been made more effective by the meaning of words...

<summary>Soto argues that legal formalities (like witnesses and signatures) are morally binding in conscience. He contends that laws are made for the general good to prevent fraud, and individuals cannot exempt themselves from these rules even if they feel their specific case is honest.</summary>

# Book Four, Question V.

...than that of these laws: Let the will be null; let it be held as if it were never made. And if it should be imperfect, it shall not uphold the deceased's wish; it becomes void and shall carry no authority, neither in court nor out of it. 

<margin>Third reason</margin>
¶ Thirdly, he argues: Whoever leaves behind an illegitimate will <note>original: "testamentum illegitimum"; a will that fails to meet the strict legal requirements of the time</note> dies just as if they had died without any will at all, since by law that document is a nullity. Therefore, such a deceased person must be judged exactly as if they had died **intestate** <note>original: "intestatus"; dying without a valid legal will</note>. If someone had left legacies or named an heir without any will, the legal heir would certainly not be bound in conscience to fulfill those wishes, even if no fraud were involved; therefore, the same applies where a will is not legally valid. For example: if someone dying without children said in the presence of his brother, "I appoint such-and-all stranger as my heir," or "I leave such-and-all legacy," (assuming this was not a gift given during life), but the brother did not promise to uphold it—or even refused—and no notary or witnesses could be found to draft the will according to the law; surely that brother, the legitimate heir, even if he knew the deceased’s wishes perfectly well and knew no fraud was involved, would not be bound in conscience to yield to the other heir or fulfill the legacies. This is despite the law of nature. Specifically, this is because the law, in order to justly avoid fraud, decreed that the deceased’s will is nothing unless it is established through a formal testament. Indeed, the law could justly do this as a penalty for the testator's negligence, as we shall soon say regarding **prescription** <note>original: "præscriptione"; a legal term for acquiring or losing rights through the passage of time</note>. Therefore, where a will is not legally valid, the judgment is the same.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, it is argued: The judgment in the **court of conscience** <note>original: "foro conscientiæ"; the internal spiritual realm where one is judged by God</note> is exactly the same as in the **public court** <note>original: "foro exteriori"</note> whenever the facts of the case are clear, provided the public judgment does not proceed from a false presumption. If someone dies intestate, even if the legal heir admits in court that the deceased intended to appoint another heir or leave certain legacies, but no witnesses were present, that legal heir would not be compelled to hand over the inheritance or fulfill the legacies. Therefore, the judge must pronounce the same even when a will is "illegitimate," since by law it is null. Thus, the legal heir remains safe in conscience, given that the sentence did not stem from a false assumption. I know well that judges have sometimes disagreed on this, specifically when the heir confesses the deceased’s intent; but I truly believe it should be pronounced just as if the deceased had arranged nothing at all. But you may say: such sentences only

<column-break/>

hold in the public court, but not in the court of conscience. Quite the contrary: if they did not bind in conscience, then those laws would be "snares for consciences" <note>original: "conscientiarum essent illaqueatrices"; laws that trap people in sin</note>, and they should not be tolerated by the Church. According to that saying in the chapter *Quoniam* regarding prescriptions: "That which cannot be observed without mortal sin must be struck down." Truly, if a judge—proceeding not from a false assumption but according to the confession of the person who is the defendant—acquits him, and yet that person is not safe in conscience, the law is unjust. However, since these laws are rightly not abolished but approved, they must hold in conscience.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
¶ Fifthly, it is argued: From the opinion opposite to ours, it would follow that someone, through no fault of their own and without any outside force, but solely by the wording of the law, could not avoid mortal sin without suffering the most grievous loss of their own goods. For example, imagine a **ward** <note>original: "pupillus"; an orphan or minor under legal guardianship</note> is the legal heir of a deceased person who, via an illegitimate will, named a stranger as heir. In this case, if the **guardian** <note>original: "tutor"</note> does not claim the inheritance for his ward, he himself becomes liable in court; he will be condemned for negligence and forced to pay the ward back for what was lost through his fault. But if he *does* claim it, he clearly sins according to the opinion opposed to ours, because he knowingly and intentionally claims what does not belong to the ward. We are assuming, after all, that he knows no fraud was involved. Such a dilemma should not be allowed.

<margin>Final reason.</margin>
¶ Sixthly and finally, it is argued: Unless laws of this kind bound the conscience, the purpose for which they were established would not be sufficiently provided for. For instance, the Church provided that its property should not be alienated <note>sold or given away</note> without such formality and caution. If, therefore, clerics and religious could not in good conscience reclaim property from someone who bought it without those formalities, the legal safeguard would be useless.

¶ Now, therefore, it is necessary to explain why we said that the transfer of **ownership** <note>original: "dominij"; lordship or legal title</note> is not entirely blocked by such informal contracts. The reason is that if the named heir happens to possess the inheritance through an invalid will, he ought to restore it to the legal heir without any court judgment or petition. Likewise, if a legatee possesses a legacy, he should immediately return it to that same heir. To understand the laws otherwise would be to interpret them with excessive rigor. I would believe, therefore, that one who possesses a thing acquired through a "less-than-formal" contract—provided all fraud, force, and deceit were absent—is not bound to restore it unless he is summoned to court and condemned. And in the same way, if someone buys the property of the Church at a fair price without...

He reasons that if these laws didn't apply to the conscience, they would create impossible moral traps for guardians and legal heirs.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Soto’s exploration of whether legal formalities, such as the number of witnesses required for a will, bind a person’s conscience. He is specifically addressing counter-arguments from famous legal authorities like Panormitanus and Pope Innocent IV regarding the tension between natural law (which requires fewer formalities) and human/civil law (which requires more).</meta>

# Book Four, Question V. 321

Without deceit or fraud, even if the legal formalities <note>original: "solennitas contractus"; the specific rituals or requirements needed to make a contract legally binding</note> of the contract had not been observed, one can justly possess the property while the Church remains silent; however, the Church also has the power, in good conscience, to reclaim it. My reasoning is that human laws intend nothing more than for such contracts to be held as null in a court of law; they do not mean that the transfer is immediately void by the very act itself. Therefore, even if the person who has the right to reclaim the property does not seek it due to ignorance—specifically because they do not know the testament or contract was not legitimate—the possessor, though they know the truth, is not bound to reveal it to them. 

If, for example (a case on which I myself was consulted), a deceased person named a stranger as heir through an illegitimate testament, and neither that stranger nor the brother (who would succeed as heir if there were no will <note>original: "ab intestato"</note>) has yet taken possession, but both are of such integrity that they do not wish to take possession unless the law favors them: in this case, the named heir must undoubtedly step aside and be placed second, and the legal heir should obtain the inheritance. While I do not consider these points fully proven, I believe them to be most true. If anyone holds a contrary opinion, let them either reject this one or follow their own; for anyone who acts against their conscience is wicked, according to the saying: "Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin" <note>original: "Quod non est ex fide, peccatum est"; Romans 14:23</note>. 

¶ Nevertheless, someone might raise a bit of doubt against our assertion. 
<margin>Argument against the author's opinion.</margin>
First, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century jurist</note> brings up a rule by the same Pope Innocent against himself, from the chapter *quod sicut* concerning elections. There he says that an election which agrees with natural law holds firm, even if legal formalities are not observed. But truly—saving the reputation of the distinguished Abbot [Panormitanus] and his followers—Innocent’s rule was not understood sincerely or clearly by them, nor was it cited correctly. For Innocent himself is not speaking about a case where an election is null by positive law <note>man-made, written law</note>, but where it would be invalidated if it were brought to judgment. He adds an example: if one of the electors was not called out of contempt. In that case, if the election is made by the majority (counting that person), it holds by both human and natural law. Although that contempt could be used to invalidate the election. In such a case, I say, he says the elected person is safe in conscience until the election is set aside. This opinion is so far from being against us that it actually supports us: for though Innocent admits that by natural law the election is valid, he says it can be invalidated by human law. Therefore, Innocent should not be believed to have contradicted himself. 

¶ Nor does another rule by the same Panormitanus do anything against us at present: namely, that when

<column-break/>

civil law mandates something against natural law, one must stand by natural law. For this legal provision is not against natural law, but is its moderation and restriction for the sake of peace. 
<margin>Third, from the chapter "When you were" regarding wills.</margin>
¶ What seems to fight most vehemently against us is the chapter *cũ esses* <note>original: "cum esses"; a reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX</note> regarding wills, where Alexander III seems to decree the opposite. He was asked about a custom in the bishopric of Ostia, where no will was admitted unless it followed human laws—for instance, signed by seven or five witnesses. He replied that such laws are alien to divine law, the institutes of the holy fathers, and the general custom of the Church. Therefore, against those laws, one must stand by natural law, according to which: "In the mouth of two or three, every word is established" <note>original: "In ore duorum vel trium stat omne verbum"; Matthew 18:16</note>. And so, he decreed that where any parishioner makes a will before his priest and two or three other witnesses, it shall be valid. 

¶ But indeed, to respond to the text with due reverence: although it is natural law that two or three witnesses suffice—for if humans lived with natural sincerity, that number would be enough—
<margin>Explanation of "In the mouth of two or three," etc.</margin>
nevertheless, it cannot be denied that when human fraudulence creeps into the state, and trust is no longer safe, it is a most holy thing to increase the number of witnesses by law. 
<margin>Response to the chapter "When you were."</margin>
For natural law is not "prohibitive"—meaning it does not forbid requiring more witnesses—but rather "expressive" of human sincerity: namely, that even three are enough. While this number usually suffices in both civil and ecclesiastical cases, more are rightly required in some instances, as we shall discuss in our fifth book. For the Church itself wishes (as seen in Question 5, Canon "Præsul") for more witnesses to be necessary in certain causes—namely, for condemning distinguished persons of the Court, such as Cardinals, priests, etc. Therefore, since the same Holy Church, out of respect for the dignity of persons whose crimes are not easily believed, 
<margin>Persons established in dignity are not easily marked for crimes.</margin>
wished the number of witnesses to be increased, there is no reason for her to reject laws intended to confirm the will of the deceased. The deceased, if his will is challenged, cannot speak for himself; thus the law requires a larger number. This is especially true where wills are either not signed or are sealed; for in open wills, the natural law of three witnesses with a notary is observed. Therefore, the Supreme Pontiff should not be believed to have abolished such laws there, because he has no authority over the laws of princes except insofar as they are against divine law, as the Pope himself admits (Canons "When to the truth" and "There are two"). Nor are they abolished...

<summary>Soto argues that human laws requiring extra witnesses for wills do not violate natural law, but rather protect society from fraud. He harmonizes conflicting legal opinions, asserting that while natural law suggests two witnesses are enough, the Church and State can require more for the sake of peace and the protection of the deceased's true intent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Soto’s discussion on whether human laws—specifically those regarding the formalities of wills and contracts—bind a person's conscience. # Book Four, Question V. 322

<margin>
Other solutions from the chapter "Since you were."
</margin>
The word "abrogation" is used there; however, such an abrogation was never actually accepted by secular rulers. Therefore, although the Gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," a standard collection of legal commentaries used by medieval and Renaissance scholars.</note> interprets that text in two other ways, it is enough for us to respond in one of two ways. First, that the rule should be restricted to <term>pious legacies</term> <note>original: "pia legata"; bequests left for religious or charitable purposes, which usually required fewer legal formalities than standard wills</note>, as explained in the very next chapter; such legacies certainly require less formality. Or, perhaps better, since the Bishopric of Ostia was within the territory of the Church, the Pope was able to command that civil laws need not be observed there. For indeed, a legacy from an "illegitimate" testament is not accepted everywhere, even in pious causes—even if heirs are taught that it is a matter of integrity to fulfill it.

<margin>
To the first main argument at the beginning of the conclusion.
</margin>
The arguments raised at the start of this question carry no weight. In response to the first, the "end" or purpose of a law can cease in two ways: either generally for the whole commonwealth, or in a specific individual case. When it ceases in the first way, the law itself ceases; but when it ceases only in a particular case, the law does not cease, as has been explained at length. What Pope Adrian <note>Adrian VI, a contemporary of Soto and a former professor at Leuven.</note> adds regarding <term>fraternal correction</term> <note>original: "correptio fraterna"; the Christian duty to privately correct a neighbor's sin</note> does not fit by way of analogy. For the commandment of fraternal correction does not have the common good as its end, but rather the specific amendment of an individual brother; thus, when that individual end ceases, the correction would be pointless. However, the end of laws that nullify illegitimate contracts is the common good, which never ceases. Furthermore, the commandment of fraternal correction is "affirmative"—it only binds when and where it is appropriate—whereas those laws are general rules.

<margin>
To the third argument.
</margin>
Finally, to the third argument, it is responded that there is no inconsistency in a person being barred from disposing of their goods due to a chance event—even without their own fault or negligence—so that peace may be kept secure in the commonwealth. For laws are not able to provide for every single individual circumstance.

### ARTICLE IV.

#### Whether prescription transfers ownership to the possessor.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring floral motifs and a central figure within an architectural frame.</image-desc>
We have cleared the first branch of public authority: that which can restrain a legitimate owner so that they may not spend their goods as they please. Now follows the second branch, which concerns the taking away of those same goods from citizens. Specifically, we will

<column-break/>

dispute this in the matter of <term>prescription</term> <note>original: "praescriptio"; a legal principle similar to "adverse possession" or "usucapion," where one gains legal title to property by holding it for a long period of time.</note>. The question is whether prescription takes ownership away from an unwilling owner and confers it upon the possessor. Arguments are made, as is the custom, for the negative side:

First: Unless the state itself is in need, it cannot strip any citizen of their property against their will, except by reason of a crime. Yet it can happen that someone possesses another’s property for thirty or forty years without any fault or negligence on the part of the original owner. Therefore, in such a case, there is no reason why the possessor should acquire ownership.

Second: If prescription had such great power, it would follow that a <term>bad-faith possessor</term> <note>original: "possessor malae fidei"; someone who knows the property they hold actually belongs to someone else</note> could also gain ownership through prescription. For if the purpose of the law was to punish the owner for negligence, the owner is no less deserving of punishment when the possessor holds the property in bad faith than when they hold it in good faith.

Third: If bad faith during the period of prescription creates an obligation to return the property, it follows that even when a possessor merely *doubts* whether the thing they possess belongs to someone else, the right of prescription should be blocked. This consequence, however, seems to contradict Saint Augustine (Case 34, Question 1, Canon "If a virgin"), where he says that anyone is most rightly called a "good-faith possessor" as long as they are unaware they possess what belongs to another.

On the contrary is the authority of Pope Gelasius (Case 16, Question 3, Canons "Of the Prelates," "Whosoever," and "It Pleased"), by which he decrees that a prescription of thirty years holds power even between bishops and churches.

<margin>
By what titles the commonwealth can take goods from unwilling citizens.
</margin>
This is the second part of human power, by which a ruler of the commonwealth—whether ecclesiastical or civil—can both take goods from the unwilling and transfer ownership to others. First, they can exercise this power for the reason of aiding the commonwealth, as was said in Article 1: namely, when the ruler needs the support of the citizens, they may compel them to contribute. For we are, as Paul says in Romans 12, "members of one body," and therefore we are bound to help our own body. Second, they can fine wrongdoers of their goods by reason of a crime. We have already rejected as heretical the idea that a person is deprived of their goods automatically by any mortal sin. Regarding other ways a ruler exercises this power, they are not relevant here; our only question is about prescription.

<margin>
Definition of prescription.
</margin>
Therefore, "prescription" is a legal term. It means exactly the same as "acquiring ownership of a thing through possession extended for a time prescribed by law." And although it is customary to distinguish between "prescription" and "usucapion" <note>In Roman law, usucapion applied to movable goods and shorter terms, while prescription applied to immovable property and longer terms.</note>—not only among Doctors but sometimes within the text of the law itself for the sake of explanation—

# Book Four, Question V. 323

<column-break/>

<term>prescription</term> <note>original: "praescriptio"; a legal method where a right or title is acquired or a debt is cancelled through the passage of time</note> and <term>usucaption</term> <note>original: "usucapio"; the Roman law process of gaining ownership of property through continuous possession</note>, stating that prescription applies to immovable property <note>such as land or buildings</note>, while usucaption applies to movables <note>personal belongings</note>. Nevertheless, the laws frequently use both terms interchangeably. Indeed, to "usucapt" is nothing other than to claim by use: that is, to acquire ownership of a thing through possession continued for the legally required time, as read in the <note>Digest of Justinian</note> regarding usucaption. And this is exactly the same as "prescribing." We should, however, speak like the many, but think like the few; and therefore there is no reason why we should not use the same distinction. Thus, usucaption differs from prescription in two ways: namely, by reason of the subject matter, as we have just said, and by reason of time, as we are about to explain.

<margin>
In what amount of time usucaption occurs.
</margin>
¶ Therefore, since we are here only disputing the <term>forum of conscience</term> <note>the internal moral realm of the soul rather than a public courtroom</note>, let us assume the laws of both Emperors and Popes. For usucaption of movable things occurs in three or four years, as held in the <note>Institutes of Justinian</note> and the Code in the law regarding actions.

<margin>
Prescription of long time and longest time.
</margin>
Prescription, however, is of two kinds: one of "long time" and the other of "longest time." Prescription of a long time occurs over ten years among those who are present <note>living in the same province</note>, and over twenty years among those who are absent: as follows in the same Institutes and the Code regarding the prescription of a long time. For reason demands that the negligence of those present—namely, those residing in the same province or city—be punished in a shorter time than that of the absent, to whom knowledge of the facts could not penetrate so quickly. Prescription of the longest time, however, is thirty years among those present, and forty among those absent: which is necessary in ecclesiastical matters. Regarding this, many chapters exist in the <note>Decretum of Gratian</note>, Case 16, Question 3. And in the cited law, although ten-year and twenty-year prescription may suffice in secular matters, a thirty-year and forty-year period applies to religious matters.

<margin>
That only a forty-year prescription holds place in church matters.
</margin>
Usucaption occurs in three years among those present, or four years among those absent. And it is in this specific place that usucaption is distinguished from prescription. The Roman Church, however, as is added there, ought to enjoy a time of one hundred years; thus, one cannot prescribe against her in any shorter time.

<margin>
Prescription against the Roman Church requires one hundred years.
</margin>
Wherefore, even if the Emperor had granted this hundred-year period to all churches in the preceding law, "As between," nevertheless now only the Roman Church enjoys it, according to the tenor of the same authentic law, "Which actions," as found in Case 16, Question 3, in the chapter "No one."

¶ Having noted these points, our question is whether, in conscience, someone who has possessed a thing for the prescribed times—even if they later find out it belongs to someone else—possesses it safely. Regarding this matter, there are three different opin-

<column-break/>

<margin>
Two extreme opinions.
</margin>
-ions. There are two extremes: one of which holds that one must always judge according to the laws granting prescription even with <term>bad faith</term> <note>original: "mala fide"; knowledge that the property actually belongs to someone else</note>. This is the "Gloss" <note>the standard legal commentary</note> on the final chapter regarding prescriptions. The other opinion holds that even if someone possesses a thing in <term>good faith</term> <note>original: "bona fide"; believing the property is rightfully theirs</note> for the entire duration of the law, as soon as they discover it belongs to another—even if the possessed thing is awarded to them in an external court—they are never safe in conscience until they restore it. This is the opinion of the *Summa Rosella* <note>a popular 15th-century manual for confessors</note> under the word "prescription."

<margin>
First conclusion.
</margin>
¶ Therefore, walking a middle path between these, we respond to the question with two conclusions. The first is: **No one prescribes with a healthy conscience by the benefit of human law, unless they possess it in good faith for the entire time of the prescription.** This conclusion is expressly asserted in that rule of Law: *A possessor in bad faith does not prescribe.* It must be remembered, however, that according to ancient civil laws, the thing possessed used to be awarded even to possessors in bad faith, as Gratian noted in Case 16, Question 3.

<margin>
Formerly, a bad-faith possessor prescribed according to the laws.
</margin>
And it is expressly held in the chapter "Watchfully" regarding prescription, where it is reported that the legislator of Ephesus—in order to avoid the laziness of the wretched and the error and confusion of a long time—first of all enacted a thirty or forty-year prescription by law.

<margin>
The ancient law is corrected.
</margin>
However, Alexander III, in the same chapter, either refutes or at least moderates those same laws, insofar as they do not favor possessors in bad faith; and Innocent III confirmed the same revocation or moderation in the Lateran Council <note>The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215</note> in the final chapter of the same title.

<margin>
Who is a bad-faith possessor.
</margin>
And this is proven by reason. A bad-faith possessor is said to be one who is conscious or doubtful that the thing they possess is not their own. For here, "faith" is taken for "conscience," according to that saying of Paul: *Whatever is not from faith*—that is, in accord with conscience—*is sin.* <note>Romans 14:23</note> Whoever possesses the property of another against their conscience continues in sin; and whoever doubts is bound to search for the truth. Sin, however, supports no one; therefore, no civil law protects a possessor of that kind. And Innocent assigns this very reason for this conclusion in the same chapter. For which reason, the "Gloss" which says that it does not believe the Pope could have revoked those laws is truly of no probability. For even if Imperial power is distinct from Pontifical power—and is not, as those we refuted above say, simply and absolutely subject to it in all things—nevertheless, because in regard to the government of souls, the spiritual power [governs] the temporal divinely...

### Book Four, Question 5. ###

because where the negligence of the true owner reaches the level of a mortal sin, then the person who has <term>prescribed</term> <note>original: "praescripsit"; acquired ownership through long-term possession</note> the property is safe in <term>conscience</term> <note>original: "conscientia"; the internal moral standing before God</note>, even if they later realize the item belongs to someone else. This legal theory rests on the foundation that the Emperor is the master of the world: and therefore, he has the power to transfer <term>dominion</term> <note>original: "dominium"; legal ownership or right of control</note> from one person to another. However, if the owner was not mortally negligent, then although the property is awarded to the possessor in the <term>external court</term> <note>original: "foro exteriori"; the public legal system</note>, they are nonetheless bound in conscience to restore it. The reason for this view is that poorly understood axiom: "When the cause of a law ceases, its binding power immediately ceases as well." Since the law of prescription was established because of the owner's fault in neglecting their property, if that fault is absent, the cause for the prescription ceases to exist.

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, the conclusion is absolutely asserted: that anyone who has prescribed property in <term>good faith</term> <note>original: "bona fide"; acting with a sincere belief that the property was theirs</note> remains safe in conscience, whether the owner was negligent or not—even if, after the time for prescription has passed, they discover that what they possess belongs to another. This conclusion is proven not only by the authority of Saint Thomas, Scotus, and the theologians, as we were just saying, but also by the sacred <term>Canons</term> <note>church laws</note> of Gelasius and the 16th Council of Toledo, Question 3; and by Augustine in the place cited, the canon "If a virgin," 14th Question; and regarding prescription, the canon "Of the Saints," and many others. Furthermore, a very solid argument that these laws are approved by the Popes—not only in the external court but also in the court of conscience—is taken from the chapters *Vigilanti* and *Sina* regarding prescription. For after those most learned Popes invalidated only those prescriptions made in <term>bad faith</term> <note>original: "malae fidei"; knowing the property is not yours</note>, by the opposite sense they confirm those which are supported by good faith.

<margin>Response to Adrian.</margin>
¶ But when we descend to the specific reasons, that argument of <note>original: "Adriani"; Pope Adrian VI, a contemporary theologian-pope</note> Adrian's is invalid: namely, that the Emperor is the master of the world. First, because that is false, as we have demonstrated above; and second, because even if he were the master of the world's kingdoms, he does not have such dominion over private property that he may seize the things of others at his whim, as was also shown above. Furthermore, it is not only the Emperor, but also kings and lower princes who can make laws concerning the transfer of ownership, even if they are not the owners of the items themselves. The reason, therefore, is the one we declared in the first argument: namely, that the prince of the commonwealth, as the guardian of peace, has the power to fine criminals by taking their goods, and so too can he translate the ownership of property from unwilling owners to others for the sake of the public peace. This is done by law, as we said above, which is binding in the <term>heavenly court</term> <note>original: "foro poli"; the court of heaven or conscience</note>, thereby setting the possessor's conscience at rest. Otherwise, as we argued above,

<column-break/>

if such laws did not quiet the conscience of the possessor, they would be both useless and unjust: for they would award property to someone who nevertheless could not possess it with a safe conscience. This would happen through a legal sentence that proceeded not from a false presumption, but from certain knowledge. Those who deny such a power to princes in the realm of conscience value these external goods so highly that they think they are the supreme goal of the commonwealth. Yet Christ took great care to warn us otherwise: so that to "redeem the time," we should leave even our cloak to those contending with us for our tunic. This holy meditation sat deeper in the hearts of the ancient lawmakers than it does in judges today; and it was for this reason that they established such laws of prescription.

<margin>The opinion of Adrian is refuted by four arguments.</margin>
¶ From here, let us take a step against Adrian. His opinion—namely, that if the owner was not mortally negligent, they do not lose ownership—is refuted by four arguments among others. First: because no such exception is read in the law; yet the holy Popes, who were the consultants of men's consciences, would not have omitted it. Second: although the negligent fault of the owner is the commonly cited reason for prescription, if you consult the laws and logic, this is not the most important reason. Rather, it is certainly the **public good**: specifically, so that ownership might be certain, that long-term errors may be removed, and that the possession of things might be peaceful. Listen to the first law of the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "ff."; the Pandects or Digest of Roman Civil Law</note> regarding <term>usucaption</term> <note>original: "vsucapio"; a form of prescription for movable property</note>: "Usucaption was introduced for the public good, so that the ownership of certain things should not be uncertain for a long time or nearly forever, since the span of the established time was sufficient for owners to seek out their property." And in the chapter *Vigilanti* regarding prescription, it says: "The legislator of Ephesus, solely to avoid the sluggishness of the wretched and the error and confusion of long periods of time, was the first to impose the force of law on thirty-year and forty-year prescriptions." Therefore, the law was not intended to punish another's fault, but to provide for the common good. And thus, the latter, not the former, was the primary goal. Consequently, even if the owner's fault ceases, the law of prescription nonetheless grants a right in conscience. ¶ Third, an argument is made in support of this: if the owner's fault had been the purpose of the law, it would surely be either unjust or would very rarely achieve its effect. This is because—a point which those people do not notice—the negligence of an owner regarding their goods is very rarely a mortal sin. Indeed, as is admitted by everyone, prodigality <note>wastefulness or lack of care with resources</note> is not by its nature a mortal sin. On that account, neither...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law, #

whoever neglects his own goods never sins mortally, except accidentally: namely, in a case of grave necessity for his family or the poor whom he is bound to support. Therefore, the justice of <term>prescription</term> <note>original: "praescriptio"; the process of gaining legal ownership through long-term use or possession</note> would rarely occur because of that fault of negligence; thus, that was not the primary cause of the law. ¶ Fourthly and finally, as we argued above, even if that [punishing negligence] had been the purpose of the law, the vigor of the law does not expire immediately just because that purpose ceases in a particular instance—as long as the purpose holds true in general. Therefore, a person who prescribes property legitimately is safe in <term>conscience</term> <note>original: "conscientia"; the internal moral state before God</note>, even if it later becomes known to them that they possess something that belonged to another. ¶ It remains, then, finally to examine the point we left in dispute above. Truly, however, the <term>gloss</term> <note>original: "gloss."; a standard scholarly commentary on legal texts</note> on the final chapter of the section "on prescription" feels otherwise.

<margin>The opinion that one who doubts by law whether a thing is theirs still possesses it in good faith.</margin>
Namely, that one who doubts—even if they have a just cause for doubting—is nonetheless in good faith. He cites in his favor the paragraph "of good faith" in the law "he who knows" under the title "on usury." <term>Panormitanus</term> <note>original: "Panormitan."; Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century expert in Canon Law</note> tends toward the same view, stating it is proven literally from the chapter "if a virgin" cited above, in the 34th Question: where <term>Augustine</term> <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 4th-century theologian</note> says anyone is most rightly called a possessor in good faith as long as they are ignorant that they possess another's property; but when they know, then they are in bad faith. For he who doubts, as Panormitanus judges, is "ignorant." ¶ And it is argued further in favor of this opinion: He who doubts whether the thing he possesses is his own can defend it with a good conscience in court until it is <term>evicted</term> <note>original: "evincatur"; legally recovered by the true owner through a court judgment</note> from him—that is, removed by a legal ruling. Therefore, he remains always in good faith.

<margin>The contrary opinion of the author.</margin>
¶ But truly, without doubt, I would believe the contrary opinion: namely, that the time during which someone—not indeed by a slight hesitation, but by probable suspicion—doubts the thing is theirs, is not counted toward the time required for prescription; indeed, it interrupts the legal timeframe. And the reason is that such a person already has a "wound of conscience," and thus his faith is not "good." For "good" is the same as "healthy and quiet" [peaceful]. Thus, he is no longer truly "ignorant" that the thing belongs to another, as Augustine intends. In truth, Panormitanus—as <term>Hadrian</term> <note>original: "Adrian."; likely referring to the theologian Adriaan Florensz Boeyens, who became Pope Adrian VI</note> properly says in the fourth book of his questions on prescription—did not observe this attentively because he was not a <term>dialectician</term> <note>a specialist in logic and formal reasoning</note>. For ignorance is of two kinds: one is "pure negation," which is a simple lack of knowledge that can coexist with doubt; the other is "depraved disposition," which is a wrong judgment. Augustine, therefore, is not speaking of this latter kind, as Panormitanus thinks, but of the former. I say he does not mean a possessor remains in good faith as long as he is ignorant—that is, as long as he does not certainly judge

<column-break/>

or hold the opinion that the thing belongs to another—but rather as long as he is "ignorant" in the sense that he has no probability or suspicion otherwise, but certainly believes it is his own. For that is what "good faith" sounds like: an uninjured conscience.

<margin>Regarding the argument for his own opinion.</margin>
Nor does that cited paragraph from the laws on usury suggest the contrary. For there it is only held that if someone buys a farm in good faith from a <term>usurer</term> <note>someone who lends money at interest, often seen as a sinful or legal gray area</note>, but before gathering the harvest recognizes it belongs to another—meaning he has probable suspicions—he can indeed keep the harvest until the farm is "evicted," that is, taken away by public judgment. However, it is not held that such a state of conscience allows the time for legal prescription to continue. ¶ To the reason we added, Hadrian responds that it is permitted to no one to possess a thing which he doubts is his own, except for the amount of time granted to him to inquire into the truth.

<margin>Hadrian's Rule.</margin>
Indeed, he adds a rule a little further down: namely, that just as one unjustly takes a thing about which he doubts whether it is his own, so also he unjustly holds and possesses it.

<margin>The rule is challenged.</margin>
But truly, this rule is fundamentally false and contrary to the whole of the law. For since the "condition of the possessor is better" <note>a legal maxim: *in pari causa possessor potior haberi debet*—the person currently holding the item has the stronger legal position</note>, not as much certainty is required to retain what you already possess as is required to take something you do not possess by your own private authority. Therefore, under a state of doubt, I can protect the possession I already have of a thing, whereas under that same doubt, I could not take it from another. When, therefore, I have a thing about which I doubt—that is, I judge with some fear that it belongs to another—if no one asks for it from me, I am bound to investigate the truth. If I can by no means find the truth, I am not therefore bound to give it all up; but according to the degree of my doubt, I should either divide it with the person I suspect is the owner or give a portion to the poor.

<margin>Why doubt destroys good faith.</margin>
The reason, therefore, why doubt destroys good faith is not because I cannot defend the thing in court or use it while doubting; but because, as we said, a "wounded conscience" then does not deserve the name of "good faith" required for prescription.

<margin>Hadrian's opinion on the rendering of the debt.</margin>
¶ After these points, however, we must not pass over in silence the opinion which Hadrian draws for himself from these matters: namely, that a wife who hesitates whether the man to whom she is joined is truly and legitimately her husband is not only forbidden from demanding the <term>marital debt</term> <note>original: "officium debitum"; the moral and legal obligation for sexual intimacy in marriage</note> from him, but is also forbidden from returning it when he demands it. Regarding the chapter "The Lord" on second marriages, where it is commanded to return the debt, he responds that this is to be understood in the <term>external court</term> <note>original: "foro exteriori"; the public legal system and its requirements</note>: for she will be forced to live with him, yet it is not permitted for her to join with him in marital embrace...

<summary>Soto argues that moral ownership through "prescription" requires a clear, "healthy" conscience. He contends that even a probable doubt regarding ownership halts the legal timer for acquiring a property right, contradicting some earlier legal scholars like Panormitanus.</summary>

<margin>The opinion of Adrian is challenged.</margin> <note>original: "Adri."; refers to Pope Hadrian VI, a significant theologian of the era.</note> Indeed, the reasoning for this falls into the same error. For he thinks that if, as one who is doubtful of his property, he cannot possess it; so too that woman, being in doubt, cannot go to her husband. This conclusion, as well as the reasoning, is certainly false, and it is plainly contrary to the chapter *Dominus*. For in that place, the doubt does not concern the external court <note>the public, legal realm</note>, but rather the conscience. For that reason, a distinction is made between "rendering the debt" and "demanding" it. <note>original: "debitum reddere & postulare"; in canon law, the "marital debt" refers to the obligation of spouses to provide sexual intimacy to one another upon request.</note> And the reason is plain: for the husband has legitimate possession of the wife; therefore, the wife cannot despoil him of it through her own doubt until she is certain. Just as I cannot steal his goods from another simply because I doubt they might be mine. Therefore, that legitimate possession excuses the wife from fornication while she renders the debt. 

This is expressly held in the chapter *Laudabilem* under the heading "lest while the suit is pending," and far more clearly in the chapter *Inquisitioni* under the heading "on the sentence of excommunication." From these chapters, Adrian—turning every which way—is by no means able to extricate himself. For it is clearly gathered from the chapter *Inquisitioni* concerning the settling of consciences that there is a three-fold division: namely, that he who is certain that the marriage is not legitimate should humbly endure the sentence of excommunication rather than render or demand the debt; but he who believes this with a light and rash credulity, obeying his confessor and casting aside the <term>scruple</term> <note>original: "scrupulo"; a nagging moral doubt or hesitation</note>, should both render and demand it. But he who labors under a probable belief should not render it, but may demand it. 

¶ However, this truly causes me a greater scruple: that in those chapters, *Dominus* and *Inquisitioni*, the one who is in doubt is restrained from demanding it. From which it follows immediately that if both are hesitating, neither can demand the debt. And the reason for my scruple is that if the one who doubts has applied sufficient diligence to investigating the truth, yet cannot attain it, there is no reason why he should be barred from demanding it. Otherwise, he would remain always bound through no fault of his own, such that he could neither use his present spouse nor move on to another. This would be hard to grant. And therefore I judge the said chapters to be understood thus: that he who probably doubts, as long as he does not make a diligent inquiry, can indeed render the debt but not demand it, because he is in <term>bad faith</term>. However, once that inquiry has been made—I judge, under the censure of others—he may also demand it, because he is now in <term>good faith</term>. For then it is vain to hold a positive assent that 

<column-break/>

the man is not her own. 

<margin>Regarding the arguments at the beginning of the conclusion.</margin> ¶ Therefore, all the arguments in the asserted conclusions are plainly resolved. For the antecedent of the first is denied: namely, that the state cannot deprive anyone of his goods except because of a crime; on the contrary, it can do so for the sake of peace. And as for the second, it has now been sufficiently explained how a possessor in bad faith does not <term>prescribe</term> <note>gain ownership through long-term use</note>. And regarding the third, likewise, how doubt interrupts even good faith.

# SIXTH QUESTION
### On the substance of restitution.
->St. Thomas, Summa Theologiae, II-II, question 62.<-

### ARTICLE I.
#### Whether restitution is an act of commutative justice.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a central letter surrounded by elaborate vine-like flourishes and floral motifs.</image-desc> Another preamble which everyone ought to know beforehand for the purpose of examining the vices contrary to <term>commutative justice</term> <note>original: "iustitiæ commutatiuæ"; justice governing private exchanges and contracts between individuals</note> is the necessity of restitution, and the manner and form of its laws. Namely, so that those things which I shall show in the following books to have been either taken away by injury or retained, it may be established by what law they must be restored. 

The first question, therefore, is concerning the substance of restitution. In its first article, it is asked whether restitution is an act of commutative justice. For the first thing sought for the purpose of investigating a definition is the "genus" or category. 

¶ The argument is made from the negative side: First, thus. Restitution differs in no way from <term>satisfaction</term>; for we use both names interchangeably. Indeed, the laws even seem to accept both as the same, as in the section "on injuries and damage caused," chapter *Si culpa*. There, when it is commanded that satisfaction be made both for damage caused and for injury, both are included under the same name—namely, both the restitution of damage and the satisfaction for injury. However, satisfaction is a part of <term>penance</term> <note>the sacrament of confession</note> for an offense committed against God. Between God and us, there is no relationship of commutative justice because (as Aristotle is the author in Book 5 of the *Ethics*) we are not able to render an equal return to the gods and to parents. Therefore, restitution does not properly belong to commutative justice. 

¶ Secondly, it is argued: Restitution has a place not only in exchanges <note>commutative justice</note>, but also in distributions <note>distributive justice</note>: as when someone does not distribute rewards according to

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...the weight of merits, they are bound to return <note>original: "refundere"</note> it to the one who received less than was just: therefore, it is an act not only of commutative, but also of distributive justice. ¶ On the contrary, restitution is the opposite of "taking away." However, the taking away of another's property is a sin of injustice regarding exchanges <note>original: "commutationes"</note>. Therefore, restitution is an act of that same justice which is concerned with directing exchanges.

<margin>The etymology of "restitution."</margin>
For the solution of this question, it must be noted that "to restore" <note>original: "restituere"</note>—as the composition of the word suggests—is the same as placing someone back into their own place and right again. Indeed, such word-allusions and etymologies are not to be disregarded; since names are the signs of concepts, the founders of languages ought to take care to instill such names into things so that the nature of the things may be explained. First, they imitate our parent <note>Adam</note>, who observed the same, according to Genesis 2: *Whatever Adam called every living creature, that was its name.* Furthermore, "restitution" is a word frequently used by the Latins. For everyone is said to be restored to their place, dignity, and right, just as his goods are restored to a man. Hence, in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de verb. & rer. signific. l. plus est."; a reference to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note>, it is held that there is more in "restitution" than in "exhibition" <note>the act of presenting an object in court</note>. For to exhibit is merely to provide the presence of the object; to restore is also to make one the possessor, to return the fruits <note>the profits or produce of a property</note>, and so on. For example, if someone is taken by force, or unjustly thrust into prison and stripped of his goods, he is not "restored" even if he is "exhibited"—that is, freely permitted to return to his own hearth—unless he is placed back into his original state.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
¶ From this, the conclusion of this question is gathered: Restitution is an act of <term>commutative justice</term> <note>the form of justice concerned with private dealings and ensuring an equal exchange of value, such as in buying or selling</note>. It is proven thus: Opposites belong to the same category, as Aristotle teaches in the *Categories* (chapter 8). Now, to take away another's property against the owner's will is a vice of injustice regarding exchanges; restitution is the opposite compensation; therefore, it belongs to the same category of justice. <margin>How commutative and distributive justice differ.</margin> Secondly: Restitution, to be legitimate, must be done according to the equality of the thing that was taken away, whether it was taken through injury (such as theft and robbery) or by the owner’s will (such as a loan and other contracts). But the equality of things—as Aristotle teaches in Book 5 of the *Ethics*—is established through commutative justice. For it differs from <term>distributive justice</term> <note>the justice concerned with how a community divides honors or wealth based on merit</note> in this way: the latter does not establish equality except between the proportions of merits and the proportions of rewards. Therefore, restitution is an act of commutative justice.

<margin>Restitution does not exist where no debt was owed.</margin>
From this, it follows that restitution, properly speaking, has no place unless the logic of debt intervenes. For if someone gave me a gift of one hundred, and after-

<column-break/>

ward I, in order to return the favor to him, give back just as much, this "returning of the favor" <note>original: "gratiæ relatio"</note> is not to be considered by the name of "restitution." For although it may have a certain "material" similarity to restitution (as they say), because the same thing is returned, it nevertheless lacks the "form" of restitution—namely, the obligation from which restitution takes both its type and its name. Because of this, that gift-giving does not pertain to commutative justice, but rather to liberality. Nor is it necessary for the nature of restitution that the same thing (in number or kind) that was received be returned—even if its original meaning seems to suggest this to the ear—but it is enough that it be of equal value. Indeed, just as the name "exchange" <note>original: "commutationis"</note>, which properly occurs in physical things (like exchanging wine for oil, or goods for money), has been transferred by custom and usage to actions and experiences, so too the name of "restitution" has been extended. For example, if someone was injurious to me with an insulting word, and I later beat him with a club, a certain compensation of exchange can occur. And by the same logic, he who inflicted an injury can repair it with money.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The arguments offered to the contrary present some difficulty. To the first, then, it is responded that although these two names, "satisfaction" and "restitution," are sometimes confused in usage (specifically when the objects themselves are not in dispute), the actions themselves differ by a long distance. But those things which are shown to differ must first be shown in what way they agree; for (as was cited from Aristotle's *Ethics* at the beginning) the more similar equivocal things are, the more their ambiguity remains hidden. Therefore, let our first assertion be: Satisfaction, just like restitution, pertains to commutative justice. For each is done according to the equality of thing to thing, in which commutative justice is distinguished from distributive justice (by which rewards are distributed according to the dignity of persons). Indeed, he who has harmed another by injury must make <term>satisfaction</term> <note>the act of making amends for a wrong or a sin</note> to him according to the measure of equality. <margin>The opinion of Scotus on penance.</margin> I know indeed that <insert>Duns</insert> Scotus <note>a famous 13th-century theologian</note> places penance under "vindicative justice," which he thinks is a species of distributive justice. He considers the penitent not only as a guilty person, but as a minister of God's justice who takes punishment upon himself. Therefore, since satisfaction is a part of penance, he would consequently grant that it pertains to the same justice—as when someone afflicts himself with fasts and vigils. And Saint Thomas <note>Aquinas</note> seems to have embraced this opinion in his commentary on the *Sentences*. Nevertheless, perhaps much more suitably, the penitent...

<summary>Domingo de Soto defines restitution as an act of commutative justice, arguing that it requires restoring a person to their original state of equality rather than simply returning an object. He distinguishes this from distributive justice and addresses scholastic debates regarding whether penance and satisfaction fall under commutative or vindicative justice.</summary>

### Book Four, Question VI.

<margin>
The opinion of Saint Thomas on penance, different from the opinion of Scotus.
</margin>
The penitent is not considered as a minister of vindictive justice <term>vindictive justice: justice concerned with punishment and correcting wrongs</term>, but rather as an offender who accuses himself of the injury brought about and makes satisfaction for it to the one against whom he committed the offense: namely, to God, or to a man, so that he might escape the judge’s vengeance. For this reason, the same Holy Doctor <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas</note> in the *Summa Theologiae* (Part 3, Question 85, Article 3) places penance under commutative justice <term>commutative justice: the virtue governing fair exchange between individuals</term>, even regarding satisfaction, if the article is examined closely. For to affect anyone with an injury amounts to the same thing as if you had taken something from them; and therefore, to make satisfaction for an offense belongs to the same type of justice as if you were paying back a thing taken away. But truly, since we cannot give anything bodily to God after a contrite soul that is more pleasing than the chastisement of the body, there appears in satisfaction regarding Him a certain form of punishment, according to that famous definition by Augustine: *Penance is a certain vengeance of one grieving, always punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed.* ¶ Therefore, for this reason—whereby restitution and satisfaction agree—seven differences are established between these two virtues. The first is taken from the nature of the matter, a difference which Saint Thomas establishes in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 1, Article 5). For inequality, which is contrary to commutative justice, occurs in two ways. One involves external things, such as when someone occupies another's property; the other involves injurious actions and passions, such as when someone violently strikes a citizen or showers them with insults.

<margin>
Seven differences between restitution and satisfaction.
</margin>
<margin>
Concerning what restitution and satisfaction deal with.
</margin>
The former mode requires restitution, by which equality is established in the things taken away; the latter requires satisfaction, namely, so that compensation is made to one's neighbor for the fault committed. Thus, satisfaction does not exist unless an injurious crime was present; but restitution exists even where there was no fault in the taking. This distinction is known even from the words themselves. For "to restore" <note>original: "Restituere"</note> is to give back what was taken; but "satisfaction" <note>original: "satisfactio"</note>, because it is a part of penance, is to repair an injury. It follows, therefore, from this proposition that there is such a divergence between satisfaction and restitution that, although they sometimes concur, one can nevertheless be found without the other. Take an example: robbers and thieves who have plundered another's house by force or theft are bound first to the restitution of those things which they seized, and furthermore to make satisfaction for the injury inflicted—for instance, by asking for pardon or by another way. But truly, when someone has stolen nothing, yet has caused injury by insult or by laying on of hands <note>i.e., physical assault</note>, he can make satisfaction through humble submission or through other pleasing services without restitution. And,

<column-break/>

conversely, one who owes money to a creditor which he borrowed from him is indeed bound to make restitution; but he is not likewise bound to make satisfaction, because he committed no crime as long as he is not in default of payment.

<margin>
Second difference.
</margin>
<margin>
To whom restitution is made, and to whom satisfaction is made.
</margin>
¶ The second difference arises from this first one, regarding those to whom satisfaction and restitution are made. For the former is made not only to men, but also to God—and primarily to Him; but restitution is properly made only to men. The first part is certain. Although it happens that one also sins against neighbors (whom we are bound to love as ourselves, and thus some manner of satisfaction is owed to them), properly speaking, sin is committed against God alone. As Augustine says: *Sin is a word or deed, etc., against the law of God.* And the royal Prophet <note>King David</note> confesses: *Against you alone have I sinned.* <note>original: "Tibi soli peccaui"; Psalm 51:4</note> For indeed, the harms done to neighbors would not be crimes unless they were forbidden by God’s authority.

<margin>
Properly, sin is committed only against God.
</margin>
<margin>
Every obligation of laws has God as its author.
</margin>
For even if the law of nature <term>law of nature: the moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</term> creates an obligation, that obligation also flows from God as the author, just as human law does. For Wisdom says in Proverbs 8: *Through me kings reign, and the framers of laws decree what is just.* From this it follows that satisfaction is properly owed to Him according to what is just, which must be paid either here or in purgatory. Hence, in Leviticus 6, it was provided that he who had extorted something by force, or committed a slander, or anything similar, should first restore everything in full, and then offer a spotless ram to God for his sin. Therefore, satisfaction is properly made to God. It should not be denied, as some contend, that it is also made to men in its own degree; but nevertheless, it is made most of all to God. Restitution, however, is not made to Him, but only to men. And the reason is at hand: because we take nothing properly from God, nor can it be taken in any way—though by analogy to ourselves, we say His honor is taken away through sin, as Paul says in Romans 2: *You then, though you are a Jew, do you dishonor God?* Furthermore, we cannot give back anything to Him that would add to Him. For because He is God, He does not need our goods. Nevertheless, by the same analogy, the satisfaction made to Him is said to be a restitution of honor.

<margin>
Third difference.
</margin>
¶ From these things, in turn, follows the third difference between these virtues, perceived from the diversity of their effects. Through restitution, sin is not remitted <note>original: "remittitur"; forgiven/canceled</note>, but one merely stops sinning; through satisfaction, however, the punishment is remitted, the fault having been forgiven, because it is the payment for the debt of sin. But satisfaction obtains this effect by virtue of the passion of Christ. Therefore, it is lacking if it is done outside of His grace. Restitution

<margin>
Outside of grace through sa-
