<margin>In satisfaction, no punishment is remitted.</margin>
Moreover, satisfaction can be legitimately carried out between men outside of God's grace, and even outside of human friendship—something which is contrary to the nature of satisfaction <note>original: "satisfactioni repugnat"</note>. And <margin>Fourth difference.</margin> this is the fourth difference. For indeed, he who returns in full to an enemy what he had received from him as a loan makes a perfect restitution, even if he does not receive that person back into his friendship. However, satisfaction is not made to one who has been affected by an injury except through the reconciliation of friendship, unless perhaps the failure to reconcile lies with the injured party. These things must be weighed according to the different roots of the debts. I say that the debt of restitution does not arise from an injury, as the debt of satisfaction does. And therefore, although restitution does not have friendship as its goal, satisfaction is not legitimately made unless that grace which was lost is recovered. But truly, even if through the satisfaction made to God the punishment is pardoned by Him for the sinner, it is still not properly to be considered restitution, as Richard <note>Richard of Middleton, a 13th-century Franciscan theologian</note> argues in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 15, Article 5). For he considers that the sinner "restores" what he owes to God. This is an abuse of the word <note>a "misuse of the term"</note> because, as we have said, we neither take anything away from God, nor is anything acquired by Him in the remission of fault that we <margin>Fifth difference.</margin> offer to Him. Rather, it is a remission of debt. ¶ Therefore, to this fourth point is joined a fifth gap: namely, that restitution is not a part of penance in the way satisfaction is. Instead, it is merely a preamble so that one may desist from sin. For if someone has contracted a debt to another and retains it against the owner's will while he is able to pay, or refuses to wash away an injury he inflicted, he cannot worthily approach penance unless he is uprooted from that crime through restitution. Thus, restitution precedes contrition <term>contrition: sincere sorrow for sin</term>, which is the first part of penance in order; whereas satisfaction follows even confession, which is the second part. ¶ From which, finally, <margin>Sixth difference.</margin> a sixth distinction is gathered. Satisfaction is determined by the judgment of priests by virtue of the "keys" <note>the "Power of the Keys" refers to the Church's authority to forgive or retain sins</note>, and it consists of those three kinds: namely, prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. Restitution, however, each person is bound to make of his own accord to achieve equality, or to obey the sentence of a judge. ¶ Furthermore, if you please, take this seventh interval. <margin>Seventh difference.</margin> In purgatory, no restitution is made, nor is it expected to be made; rather, only satisfaction, or rather <margin>No restitution to be made here delays a man in Purgatory.</margin> the payment of punishment occurs. I say this to dispel a common error of the people, who think that the deceased are delayed in purgatory until the restitutions which they commanded here to their heirs are carried out. For this is ridiculous. Indeed, a law would hardly be worthy of God if it decreed that someone should suffer for a fault that is no longer within his power to fix. Otherwise, if the heirs never

<column-break/>

restored the goods, that wretched soul would never leave those purgatorial prisons; by which reasoning Purgatory would be turned into Hell. Let each person see to it for himself how he commands restitution in this world. For if he has been negligent, even if the fault is forgiven, he will pay the penalties in purgatory, even if the restitution is made immediately after his death. Once those penalties are paid, he will be freed even if restitution is never made. For that saying of Augustine, which we shall hear in the very next article, is most ineptly brought forward to the contrary (though I have heard it with my own ears): *The sin is not forgiven unless the stolen thing is restored.* <note>original: "Non dimittitur peccatum nisi restituatur ablatum"</note> For that is understood regarding the remission of fault in this world; because he who does not restore remains always guilty of the fault. Behold by how great a gap satisfaction and restitution differ. From this, the solution to the previous argument is gathered. ¶ To the <margin>To the argument.</margin> latter point, however, Saint Thomas responds rightly: that the restitution of that which was omitted in the context of distributive justice <term>distributive justice: the fair allocation of goods or honors by a leader to members of a community</term> belongs to commutative justice <term>commutative justice: the fair exchange of goods between individuals</term>. For although that thing was never possessed by the one to whom it should have been given, it was nevertheless owed, and therefore in a certain way taken away; and subsequently, it is the function of commutative justice to pay back the same. From which it follows (as Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note> skillfully concludes) that if a prince or lord has for some years skipped a distribution which he was bound to make among registered citizens, and later, led by penance, decides to restore it, he ought not make the restitution to the citizens currently present, but to the heirs of those deceased persons to whom it was owed while they were living.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether it is necessary for salvation that restitution of a thing taken away be made.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring a figure in classical dress within a square frame of swirling vines and foliage.</image-desc>
In the second article (which is the first in Saint Thomas's text), having established the interpretation of restitution, we must answer regarding its necessity: namely, whether the restitution of what was taken is necessary for salvation. And the argument is made for the negative side. For the salvation of the soul—that is, to attain eternal life—it is enough to keep the commandments, according to the word of the Lord in Matthew 19: *If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.* But if someone has fallen into sin, it is enough that he washes his conscience through penance, which is the "second plank after shipwreck" <note>a traditional theological metaphor meaning that if the "ship" of baptismal innocence is lost, penance is the plank that saves the soul from drowning</note>. Restitution, however, is neither...

### Question VI of the Fourth Book

...is not counted among the commandments nor among the parts of penance, as was stated above; therefore, it is not necessary for men. ¶ Second, it is argued: If restitution were necessary, it would be commanded by some specific precept. However, no such precept exists in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> except for "Thou shalt not steal," but this is a negative commandment. A precept of restitution, however, ought to be affirmative, as the name itself implies. Therefore, there is no such precept. ¶ To the contrary is Augustine in his letter to Macedonius, which is cited in the Church law <note>original: "14. q. 6"</note>: "If the property of another, because of which the sin was committed, can be returned and is not returned, penance is not performed but merely feigned. If, however, it is performed truly, the sin is not forgiven unless the taken thing is restored."

This question can be a matter of doubt to no one. It is therefore resolved by a single conclusion.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
The restitution of stolen things is so necessary that without it, no one could remain in the grace of God or recover it. But indeed, for the sake of clarity, the terms of Saint Thomas Aquinas must be explained, because this second article seems somewhat obscure, and even truncated to some.

<margin>Saint Thomas is explained.</margin>
For he says that that which is unjustly taken is subject to restitution, but that which is taken justly is not.
However, since both a loan—which one took up justly—and the price of a thing bought on credit must also be restored, it should be noted how Saint Thomas taught us the proper ways of speaking about things. For regarding that which someone received either as a loan or through any civil contract, he is not properly "compelled to restitution" <note>original: "ad restitutionē cōuincitur"</note> until he is in default and at fault. For it is not necessary to return a loan or a price before the appointed time. And when it is returned on time, it is not properly called "restitution,"

<margin>When someone returns what he owes on time, it is not called "restoring."</margin>
because since the creditor lacked that thing of his own free will until then, he was not yet considered to have less than what was just, nor to have been cast down from his right and status. Instead, it is called either a "simple repayment" <note>original: "simplex redditio"</note> of a loan or the "payment of a price," although in a broad sense it may be called restitution.

<margin>Restitution only takes place in things unjustly taken or withheld.</margin>
Therefore, the name "restitution" strictly has a place only in things taken away—namely, those that were snatched away through injury, or if they were received justly, they are nonetheless unjustly withheld beyond the appointed time. And for this reason, Augustine says that the sin is not forgiven unless the taken thing is restored. Moreover, when Saint Thomas says that what is taken justly is to be "restored into equality," you should not understand this as being about a loan, or the price of a thing sold for future money, or similar things which are received justly but with the intent that they be returned. Rather, he means that which someone received because it was already his own: such as his own deposit, or the wages for his labor, or a thing given as a gift, or something similar.

<margin>He now proves the conclusion.</margin>
With these things established, the conclusion is proven. Commutative justice <term>Commutative justice: The branch of justice governing fair exchange between individuals, ensuring that what is given and received remains equal.</term> is necessary to observe for salvation; but restitution implies the return-

<column-break/>

-ing of that thing which is either unjustly taken or withheld. This return is indeed a work of commutative justice; therefore, it is necessary. From this it follows as a consequence that a precept of restitution exists, and that it binds under the guilt of a mortal sin. Otherwise, it would not be simply necessary for salvation. For he who detains the property of another against the owner's will violates both justice and, consequently, the love of one's neighbor. ¶ But for a more exact examination of this same conclusion, let us understand first with what degree of certainty it must be held: namely, whether it should be considered a Catholic truth. I ask this because Guido the Carmelite <note>Guido Terreni, a 14th-century theologian</note> counts this among other heresies of the Greeks: that their priests commanded no restitution for thieves and robbers for manifest plunder, but instead absolved them by anointing them with simple oil.

<margin>The madness of the Greeks according to Guido.</margin>
The only penance enjoined was that they should share a portion of the thefts with the priests themselves. I do not know, however, by what insanity those men were seized who would be so foolish. For the Lutherans (as can be seen in Luther’s 5th article to Pope Leo) deny "satisfaction" <note>satisfaction: the act of making amends for sin through penance</note>;

<margin>The Lutherans deny satisfaction.</margin>
they do this under the pretext that Christ abundantly satisfied for the sins of the whole world—not knowing how to distinguish between satisfaction in terms of its "sufficiency" and in terms of its "efficacy." <note>This is a common theological distinction: Christ's death was enough to save everyone (sufficiency), but it only applies to those who perform the necessary acts of faith and penance (efficacy).</note> However, to say that restitution is not necessary is not only a heresy but a frenzy. ¶ Here, I will not fail to warn the reader that if he comes across the annotations of Erasmus (up to the fourth edition), he should beware of that note which he added to Luke 11 regarding the words, "As for what remains, give alms." He added the following: "It should be noted that while he has just made mention of plunder, he makes no mention of restitution as a remedy; he only promises that by giving alms, all things will be clean." In that passage, he seemed to either weaken or deny the necessity of restitution. Later, however, in the fifth edition, he scraped away this mark which he had burned into himself.

<margin>The teaching of Erasmus is rejected; he himself rejected it.</margin>
To return to the matter, therefore, I rightly said that a heresy of this kind falls into frenzy. For it is cautioned in the Decalogue: "Thou shalt not steal." He who withholds the property of another against the owner's will acts exactly as if he were committing a theft; for stealing the property of another and withholding it amount to the same thing. Thus Paul says in Romans 13: "Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due," etc. And so that he might embrace everything with more expressive emphasis, he adds negatively: "Owe no one anything, except to love one another." Regarding this little word "except" <note>Latin: "nisi"</note>, we favor the sense that it is not meant to exclude something, but rather to explain it. For when you withhold another's property...

to usurp what belongs to another would oppose the love of one's neighbor, he admonishes us that we should "owe nothing," <note>original: "nihil debeamus" – a reference to Romans 13:8</note> namely, that we should love sincerely. It is as if he had admonished us that we should always owe love; for however much the debt of love is paid, it never ceases. Likewise, Christ says in Matthew 22: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." <note>original: "Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari: & quæ sunt Dei, Deo"</note> Indeed, one who has not stolen a thing but possesses it in good faith is bound by natural reason to return it to the owner as soon as it is established to belong to another. Hence Tobias, as his history relates in chapter 2, when he heard the voice of a bleating kid that his wife had brought home, said: "See that it is not perhaps stolen; return it to its owners: because it is not lawful for us either to eat anything from a theft or to touch it." In short, God in Ezekiel 33 promises pardon to none of the penitent unless they first return the pledge and the stolen property. Add to this that by the same law, whoever knows a thing has been taken by theft is bound to indicate this to the owner. For this is how the word of Jerome should be understood regarding that passage in Proverbs 29, which is cited elsewhere <note>original: "extrà, de furtis. c. qui cum fure"</note> regarding thefts: "he who shares with a thief"—or according to another reading, "participates," namely, in the crime—"kills his own soul." Therefore, not only the thief but also he is held guilty who, being aware of the theft, does not reveal it when the possessor inquires. However, he is not bound to betray a hidden thief, but rather to reveal the theft.

<margin>To the argument</margin>
# THROUGH these points, therefore, the first argument against the question is answered, granting the first premise: namely, that it is sufficient for salvation if one lives innocently through the fulfillment of the commandments; but the latter part is refuted. For he who, by committing theft or inflicting injury, has fallen into guilt, will never rise from it except by prior restitution. For otherwise, he will always be held guilty of theft or of the injury inflicted, which is against the prohibition of the Decalogue. <note>The Ten Commandments</note> ¶ However, there is no lack of arguments against this solution.

<margin>An argument against the solution.</margin>
¶ For the first one stands immediately at the threshold in this manner: No one is guilty of theft or of other detention to which it is clear the legitimate owner consents, or ought to consent. But the law of charity <note>The Christian principle of selfless love</note> seems to bind mortals, and especially Christians, with this bond: that each should postpone these corporal and temporal things to the spiritual salvation of his neighbor. Therefore, everyone is bound to consent that another should possess his goods, lest by retaining them unjustly, the other should kill his own 

<column-break/>

soul. There are those who think this argument is of some weight, though in fact it is of none at all. For Adrian <note>Likely referring to Pope Adrian VI, a significant theologian of the period</note> responds that even if the owner of the thing perhaps consents, this is not clear to the one who possesses it unjustly; and therefore he retains it against conscience. But this solution would not weaken the force of the argument if it had any; for it would be enough that it were clear to him that the owner *ought* to consent. It is therefore answered very easily that although everyone is bound by the order of charity to prefer the salvation of a neighbor's soul to his own goods of body and even temporal life (as St. Thomas is the author in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 26, Article 5), nevertheless, this order of charity only obliges one to expose corporal goods for the sake of protecting a neighbor's soul when such goods are simply necessary to that neighbor, or when one has the care of that soul by his own office. Otherwise, this pertains only to the perfection of charity. Hence, since he who unjustly usurps another's property does not do so because he suffers extreme necessity for those goods, but out of his own lust and corrupted will, the owner is not bound to consent to that unjust possession. It is similar at the point of death when someone attacks another with the intent to kill. For some who are overly merciful say that the one attacked ought rather to permit his own killing than to kill the other who is sinning mortally, so that by his own temporal death he might avoid eternal death in his neighbor. But in truth, no reason can prove this: because the life of the one who is attacked is not necessary to the attacker; and therefore, because he seeks it unjustly, the other can defend it, even if he knows the other will die in sin. But whether it is a "counsel" <note>A recommended but not strictly mandatory religious act</note> to permit one's own death for the salvation of another is not a matter for the present dispute; for "greater love has no man than this, that he lay down his life for his friends." <note>original: "animā suam ponat pro amicis suis"</note>

<margin>To the second argument. A doubt whether theft is prohibited and restitution is commanded by the same precept.</margin>
¶ By the second argument, a solution to a doubt is sought, which perhaps pertains not so much to the matter itself as to the name: namely, whether the precepts by which theft is prohibited and by which restitution is commanded are different. For the first argument that they are the same is that they seem to have the same force: "Thou shalt not steal" and "Thou shalt not withhold another's property." For thus Paul says negatively, "owe nothing to anyone." And St. Thomas in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 66, Article 3, says that to detain that which is owed to another has the same character of harm as unjust taking. And therefore, under unjust taking, unjust detention is also understood. Next, it is argued: that if the precept of resti-

# Question VI of the Fourth Book

<margin>Solution to the doubt.</margin>
If the obligation of restitution were unique, it could only exist as an affirmative command. However, an affirmative precept <note>An "affirmative precept" is a religious or moral law that commands a specific action (e.g., "Honor your father"), whereas a negative precept forbids an action (e.g., "Do not steal").</note> does not bind "for always" (meaning at every single moment); yet, restitution must be made without delay. For as long as someone remains in debt against the will of the owner, they are regarded as a thief. From this, it follows that one is held to make restitution always and for all time. Nevertheless, it is a more precise way of speaking to say that there are, in a sense, two precepts: the first is the command to abstain from theft, which is purely negative; the second is that of restitution, which is affirmative but carries within it a negative—namely, that we are forbidden from withholding the property of another. St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s Scholastic theology</note> is the author of this view in the *Summa Theologiae* (Part 2-2, Question 62, Article 8). This is evident from the diversity of the objects of these laws: bad actions are forbidden by negative precepts, while good actions are mandated by affirmative ones. Stealing is an evil; restoring, however, is a good. The same is clear from the model of Christ: *Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.* <note>original: "Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari."</note> This is why Paul joined the two together, saying: *Render to all their dues,* and, *Owe no man anything.* <note>A reference to Romans 13:7-8</note> It is therefore false to say that the object or the precept is the same as the former; nevertheless, this is traced back to that commandment of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>: *Thou shalt not steal.* And through this, the main argument is answered. 

Regarding what we just added about affirmative precepts, the response is that although the mandate to restore is affirmative, it nonetheless lacks a defined timeframe (unlike others) because of the negative it includes. Rather, its very substance requires that it be done immediately and without delay. This "delay" <note>original: "mora" – a technical legal term for a failure to perform a duty on time</note> must be understood according to civil custom. One is said to be "in delay" when, having found the opportunity for the matter, he does not act immediately. For this reason (as is to be repeated in the final article of this book), the obligation of this precept regarding the interior act of the soul is this: as soon as it is clear to anyone that they possess another's property, they should purpose in their mind to return it. However, they are not in a state of fault if they do not return it instantly, until—having both access to the creditor and the opportunity to pay—they further delay the payment. Whether the guilt grows for as long as one remains in delay, and whether the same guilt is sometimes renewed, belongs to the final article of this book to answer satisfactorily.

---

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether everything in the universe that someone has either taken from another or retains against the owner's will, he is bound to restore.<-

<column-break/>

After discussing the substance and necessity of restitution, it remains to see in the third place the very broad universality of its obligation. The question is therefore asked whether a person is bound to restore everything in the universe that has been taken and withheld. The argument is made for the negative side:

First, there are two kinds of goods in which one can harm another: namely, spiritual and temporal. Restitution of spiritual goods is not necessary; therefore, since they are more excellent than temporal goods, it follows that restitution of temporal goods is not necessary either. The minor premise <note>The second part of a logical syllogism</note> is shown by example: indeed, he who induced another to sin is not bound to restore anything to him, both because the other acted freely and because he can restore himself to his original state through repentance. 

Second, if someone either restrained or withdrew another from the profession of monkhood <note>original: "monachatus" – the state of being a monk</note>, for the very same reasons just brought forward, he is not compelled to restore anything to him; therefore, in this case, making restitution is not worthwhile. 

Third, among temporal goods, life is the greatest. But he who has taken the life or a limb of another remains liable to no restitution, because no one is bound to the impossible—and it is impossible to restore a life or a limb. 

Fourth, no one is bound to sin. But sometimes restitution cannot be made without a fault—for instance, when someone has blackened another's reputation by revealing a secret crime. Therefore, such restitution is by no means necessary. 

Fifth, the honor that someone defiles with insults to another can in no way be restored, because there is no power over the past. Therefore, the bond of restitution has no place there. 

Sixth, when someone is an obstacle to another attaining some spiritual priesthood, he is judged to have taken it from him; for (as Aristotle testifies in the 2nd book of *Physics*, text 56) that which is but a little distance from a thing seems to be no distance at all. And yet, he is bound by no knot of restitution, because a prebend <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend</note> ought not to be taken from one to be conferred on the first person. Therefore, the restitution of everything in the universe is not necessary.

On the contrary is the divine sentence in Ezekiel 33: *If the wicked does penance for his sin, and does judgment and justice, and restores the pledge, and returns what he robbed, etc., he shall surely live.* In this passage, the necessary restitution of all things is implied.

---

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion of this question is stated in the affirmative. Regarding everything in the universe that someone has either unjustly removed or retains having received it through some just civil contract, it is a precept that restitution be made. Nor is there a need for new te— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "testificatione" or "testimoniis," meaning "testimony" or "evidence."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether the obligation of restitution is a mortal sin and begins a new section categorizing the types of "goods" (spiritual, physical, and external) for which restitution might be owed. # Question VI of the Fourth Book

...is established by the testimonies or reasons of what was said in the previous article. For indeed, just as the prohibition of theft is general, so too is the command of restitution, encompassing all things. And therefore, unless an excuse occurs for some reason, or there is a lessening of the fault, its transgression is always a mortal sin <note>A "mortal sin" in Catholic theology is a grave offense that destroys the relationship with God, as opposed to a "venial" or lesser sin.</note>. An excuse, however, occurs either through ignorance or through impossibility; whereas absolution from the obligation occurs through the will of the owner who forgives it. But a lessening of the fault happens by reason of the smallness of the matter <note>original: "tenuitatis materiæ." This is the legal and theological principle that stealing something of very little value, like a single grape or a pin, is not a grave sin.</note>. For he who retains very little seems to retain nothing; and therefore, he is touched only by a light fault.

<margin>The three goods of humans.</margin>
But in truth, the arguments that have been raised require no small consideration. And since there are three types of goods for mortals (as Aristotle mentions in the *Politics*, Book 7, Chapter 1), namely those of the soul, the body, and those faculties possessed externally, we have thought it fitting to follow the order of speaking according to their dignity.

<margin>The goods of the soul are subdivided.</margin>
Furthermore, among the goods of the soul, some are natural, such as the intellect; others are acquired but nonetheless temporal, such as knowledge; and finally, others are simply spiritual, such as virtue and grace. Regarding the former, no specific special dispute is necessary, for they are simply temporal goods. Therefore, if someone (to use an example) were to drive a person mad through illusions or some other way, or divert them from the study of letters through force or fraud, they would be bound to repair the loss at the judgment of prudent men, just as in the case of other temporal goods. It remains, then, for us to begin with spiritual goods, such as grace and the virtues by which it is nourished. It is concerning these that the first argument was proposed.

<margin>To the first argument. Scotus.</margin>
To this, Duns Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian and philosopher.</note> (Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 3, Article 1) and Richard [of Middleton] (same distinction, Article 4, Question 2), whom Paludanus follows in the same place—and Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), who wrote extensively on ethics before becoming Pope.</note> in the matter of restitution—respond by affirming that whoever is the cause of sin for another, specifically by inducing them to it, is bound to restitution. This means they are held to recall that person to God's grace by the most convenient way possible, by persuading them to repent, by praying for them, and by helping them according to their power.

<margin>Adrian.</margin>
Indeed, Adrian adds that no one can forgive the restitution of their own spiritual goods as they can with physical ones, since no one but God is the master of them. And certainly, if you look only at the loss a person suffers when they fall from divine grace, it is most certain that he who deliberately harms his neighbor in such goods does so much more fatally and destructively than if he were to harm him in the body,

<column-break/>

inasmuch as the soul is more precious than the body, and the grace of God more than the entire world. Hence Gregory [the Great] says (as reported in Decree 6, Question 1, Chapter "Ex Merito"): "Those who corrupt the life and morals of good people are worse than those who seize the property and lands of others." <note>original: "Deteriores sunt qui vitam, moresque bonorum corrumpunt..."</note> ¶ However, although others may perhaps judge more wisely than I, I nonetheless seem to see no reason that confirms this opinion affirmed by the aforementioned doctors. And first of all, regarding the guilt: he who, by deliberate effort and out of hatred, strives to drive his neighbor from the grace of God and cast him into His enmity, sins more enormously than if he were to plot against his temporal life, because he intends a far more harmful evil. But in truth, he whose purpose is not to harm his neighbor so enormously in spiritual matters, but rather to pursue his own advantage or fulfill his own pleasure, does not transgress with such gravity as if he were to seize the neighbor's temporal goods. For who would assert that he who solicits a free woman to be corrupted, without any force or fraud—even if he urges her with prayers or a price—is entangled in as grave a crime as if he were to plunder her abundance of goods? In truth, there is no appearance of reason in such an assertion.

<margin>He who harms more does not always sin more gravely.</margin>
Therefore, the argument is a fallacy: "It harms more; therefore, it is a graver sin." For other things are not always equal. Indeed, those who steal the goods of others do so against the will of the owner; whence the injury, and subsequently the fault, receives an increase. But he who entices another to evil applies no force or necessity, and thus brings no injury <note>In legal terms, Soto is arguing that because the person chose to sin, they weren't "robbed" of their virtue in the same way property is taken from an unwilling victim.</note>.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let the second conclusion, therefore, be explanatory of the above. He who casts another into crime by force or fraud is bound to make restitution to them to the extent that he must teach the truth to the one he seduced; and if he used force, he must leave them free to return to a good mind. Suppose someone perhaps deceived a person, teaching that there was no fault where there was—for instance, that a certain contract was not usurious <note>Usury, the lending of money at interest, was a major legal and moral concern in the 16th century.</note> when it actually was—and because of this deception, the person engages in that contract. In such a case, that deceptive man is held to teach the other the truth, lest the deceived person continue to act wrongly. For this reason, a heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> who has sown heresies is bound to recant his errors <note>original: "recantare palinodiam" — to sing a palinode, or a poem retracting a previous one.</note> and, as much as lies within him, uproot the wicked seeds. By the same right, if I have induced someone to hold enmities against my enemy, and he carries them out for my sake, I am held to leave him free so that I am not a cause of evil for him. This conclusion is manifest: since I am the cause not only for why he sinned, but for why he persists in the sin.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion.

<meta>This page continues Question VI of the Fourth Book, specifically addressing whether a person who induces another into sin is obligated to provide restitution under the laws of justice, or if their obligation falls under the duty of charity.</meta>

# Question VI of the Fourth Book

Conclusion: If someone, without force or fraud, has induced another into sin, even if they did so deliberately and with intent, yet the other person knows they are in sin and is free to leave it whenever they wish: then the inducer is not bound by a specific precept of **commutative justice** <note>Commutative justice is the legal principle governing fair exchange and the restoration of what belongs to another.</note> to make restitution, but by the general
<margin>correction</margin>
precept of **fraternal correction** <note>The duty of a Christian to correct a neighbor’s faults out of love (charity), rather than a legal debt.</note> just like anyone else. The first part is proved. First, this inducer, properly speaking, took nothing from the other: for no one takes anything except from one who is unwilling. However, one who sins knowingly and prudently—no matter how much they succumb to the prayers of another—does not do so against their will. Otherwise, they would not sin, as **Augustine** says in *Of True Religion* and in the first book of the *Retractions*: "Sin is so voluntary that if it were not voluntary, it would not be sin." (See also Decree 15, Question 1, Chapter "What however"). **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval philosopher and theologian.</note> and his followers respond, however, that although such an inducer is not the *entire* cause of the sin, they nonetheless exist as a part of the cause and the occasion, and therefore remain in some way liable for restitution. Yet there is an argument against this. When I, by the persistence of my prayers, extort some gift from a friend without force or fraud, I am in no way bound to restore it to him by the force of justice, unless by my own generosity I should decide to be grateful. By equal right, therefore, one who has expressed a woman’s consent to evil—whether by prayer or price—is free from the obligation of restitution after she has voluntarily consented. For "no injury is done to one who knows and consents," according to the **Rules of Law** in the *Sext* <note>The "Liber Sextus Decretalium," a collection of Catholic canon law.</note>. The text in the same title, chapter "None," and in the **Digest** <note>The "Digest" or "Pandects," a major part of the Body of Civil Law (Corpus Iuris Civilis) compiled under Justinian.</note> under the title "Of Advice" (law: *consilii*), also supports this, teaching that no one is bound to restitution for advice that is not fraudulent. ¶ Secondly, the same is proven in another way. No one is bound to make restitution to someone if it is not in their power for restitution to be made. But **God alone** is the author of grace; therefore, man is released from that same bond. If you urge that at least they are bound to what they *can* do, the argument is made otherwise: No one is constrained to restore to someone who voluntarily pardons what was taken from them. But he who does not wish to repent of his sin virtually pardons what was taken from him. Since it is placed in his own power through the help of God's grace alone to recover that divine grace, if he does not recover it, he seems to neglect it by his own fault. And thus, the other is freed from the debt, because he does not withhold what belongs to another. For if I have stolen a weight of gold which I then leave exposed and manifest to the owner, so that he may take it whenever he pleases without my help or that of anyone else, surely if he does not take it, he is deemed to refuse it; and thus I am no longer bound to act. For I am neither bound to warn him to take it, nor to ask: "Look, here is what is yours: either

<column-break/>

take it, or go away." Regarding our proposal: Where, I ask, am I bound to bring the wicked person back to a good mind, if he himself, while able to do so without my work, has no desire to be reformed? ¶ Other minor arguments are added: for according to the authors of the contrary opinion, it would first follow that if someone induced a woman who was living in filth to a filthy act, he would be bound to reform her; which no reason suggests. Likewise, that one who cannot bring back the person he corrupted to the right path would be bound to satisfy them with money as far as possible, even though divine grace cannot be measured by any price. For this is how it is done with honors, yet it is nowhere observed in spiritual matters; for no confessors enjoin such restitutions. Thirdly, it would follow that he who sinned publicly would be bound to make restitution to every single person for whom he was the occasion of ruin. And indeed (as **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Mazzolini (1456–1523), known as Prierias, author of the *Summa Sylvestrina*.</note> says under the word "restitution") there is a strong argument in favor of this opinion: that since **St. Thomas**, the most skillful searcher of all things, made no mention anywhere of this kind of restitution, he judged it to be in no way necessary. ¶ Regarding the second point, such a person is bound by the bond of **fraternal correction**, which is of charity, to correct his brother—and perhaps with a tighter bond than others, all things being equal. For otherwise, I am bound to correct more quickly the person I see in greater danger. And especially the one whom a person compelled into sin by force; as for instance, if someone offered a virgin the shame of rape by threat of death. But this bond does not exceed the lines of fraternal correction. It does not, I say, enter the limits of justice. Hence, in **Exodus 22**, it is only enacted that he who sleeps with a virgin shall provide her dowry and take her as a wife; but that he should ensure her reformation is not added. These things are said not so that we may loosen the reins for lost men; for it is an enormous crime to deprave the morals of another as a teacher of iniquity and a servant of the demon. For even if so much care were applied afterward that it brought the wanderer back to the path, the sin itself and the time in which one remains in sin can hardly be repaired. But nonetheless, these are reminders so that everyone may understand how far the Law of Restitution reaches in its obligation.
<margin>Regarding the second argument.</margin>
In the second argument, another doubt related to this is touched upon concerning the one who has withdrawn someone from a religious profession or dragged them from it. For concerning this, by the same right (as it appears to them), the authors cited above pronounce their judgment. For **Paludanus** <note>Peter de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a French theologian and Bishop of Palestrina.</note>, in the same place cited, does not fear to assert that he who so dissuaded another from the purpose of religion that he persuaded him not to enter,

<meta>The catchword "deret" at the bottom of the page completes the word "persuaderet" (persuaded).</meta>

<summary>This page argues that inducing someone to sin through persuasion rather than force does not create a legal debt of restitution under commutative justice, because sin is a voluntary act and only God can restore lost grace. The author clarifies that while this is a grave moral crime requiring "fraternal correction" out of charity, it does not carry the same legal obligations as theft or fraud.</summary>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

...if someone should lead another away or withdraw them from the monastic life by some other means, they are bound to **full restitution** <note>restitutio in integrum: the legal requirement to restore a situation to its original state</note>: namely, either by persuading them to enter again, or by substituting another in their place; or, if neither of these paths is open, he says the person himself is bound to enter the order. **Antoninus of Florence** <note>A 15th-century Dominican theologian and Archbishop of Florence</note> subscribes to the same opinion in the second part, title 2, chapter 2. And lest this opinion be thought peculiar only to monks, **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a Dutch theologian</note> follows it in his commentary on the fourth book, in the same cited question on restoring the goods of the soul. Furthermore, **Major** <note>John Major (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher and theologian</note> in question 17 brings forward the example of **Raymond** <note>Raymond of Penyafort (c. 1175–1275), a famous General of the Dominican Order</note>, the most celebrated general of our order, who put on our habit for this very reason. These authors hunt for an argument from the chapter *If a Slave* (distinction 54), where a bishop who ordains a slave without the master's knowledge is ordered to **repay the master double** <note>original: "duplum eidem reddere"</note>. From this, by a stronger reason (as they believe), they conclude that the obligation of restitution to a religious order arises in one who has withdrawn a monk from that order. It is true, however, that Adrian and others mitigate this opinion, saying it is only true when someone does it either out of hatred for religion or some other evil intent; but it is otherwise if he is led to it by friendship or compassion for parents. For in those cases, even if a sin is committed, the law of restitution does not bind him.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ However, this opinion does not have much probability. Let the **first conclusion** therefore be according to Adrian’s moderation: He who, with good intention, is an obstacle to one wishing to take up the monastic life, does no injury to the religious order; for the order had not yet acquired any right to that person. To this is added that although the profession of monkhood in general is an **Evangelical counsel** <note>Evangelical counsels are voluntary practices (poverty, chastity, obedience) advised by Jesus but not commanded as laws</note> so great that no other particular work is needed, nevertheless, the fact that a person takes up such an institute here and now and with other circumstances is a matter that can be brought into consultation without doing any wrong.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let the **second conclusion** be this: No one who dissuades another from monkhood, even with an unfair spirit, or opposes them in some other way from becoming a monk, is thereafter liable for restitution to be made either to the person or to the convent by the rigor of justice; but he is bound only by the law of charity and **fraternal correction** <note>The duty to correct a neighbor’s faults out of love rather than legal obligation</note>. This conclusion is demonstrated just like the one above, but indeed more firmly. For first, no restitution is owed to the one who was pulled back from religion: because he was neither constrained by force nor seduced by fraud, and thus suffered no injustice. For where there is no involuntary act but a spontaneous consent, no injustice underlies it; and thus justice does not enjoin restitution. But there can only be 

<column-break/>

a sin against **charity** <note>charitas: the Christian virtue of selfless love for God and neighbor</note>; and therefore charity subsequently advises that a fraternal correction be made. Indeed, whatever root the sin had—whether against charity or against justice—such is the virtue to which the amendment belongs. The second argument is similar to the one above: he who is hindered from religion has it within his own free power to carry out his previous proposal; if he does not wish to, then the one who led him away is exonerated from the burden of restitution. And these arguments are stronger because it is more ruinous to lead a man into a sin against the law than to lead him back from a counsel of religion.

¶ Nor, truly, must restitution necessarily be made to the religious order. For the argument that the order or religion had some right, or at least a near right, is in no way compelling. Indeed, that always depended on the will of the person who was able to go back on his proposal. But if he changed his mind of his own accord, no obligation of restitution remains. Moreover, by the same reasoning, I would add that even if someone led away a **neophyte** <note>A person newly converted or newly entered into training (a novice)</note> from profession—for instance, one who has put on the habit and is a **catechumen** <note>Someone receiving basic instruction in the faith</note>—without force or fraud, although he commits a grave sin, nevertheless, since it is only against charity, no justice binds him to restitution. For if I were to divert this person, who was already preparing to enter this religious order, toward another one, I am not a debtor to the first convent; therefore, it had no right that would bind me even if I had simply pulled him out. Indeed, even for one who persuaded a **professed** <note>One who has taken formal, permanent vows</note> monk to leave with a most wicked spirit, I do not clearly see by what right he is bound to restitution.

<margin>To the argument of others.</margin>
Nor does the argument derived from the likeness of a slave completely force the opposite conclusion. For whatever happens regarding a slave—concerning whom the judgment in conscience will be the same as it is according to civil laws—the same reasoning does not appear to apply to a monk. For a master possesses a slave for his own personal utility, just as he does his horse; but a monk is not to be judged so. For those who have enslaved themselves to divine service, even if they are most strictly bound by a religious vow, are not possessed like slaves for the temporal advantage of the **Prelates** <note>High-ranking church officials or heads of religious houses</note>, but for their own spiritual advantage. Therefore, that servitude is full of liberty. Although a monk may abuse this liberty by casting off his habit, he is only bound by the law of obedience to return, so that he may be made worthy of the kingdom of heaven. And therefore, if he leaves of his own accord, no civil obligation to restitution arises from it.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The **third conclusion** is: If someone, by force, or threats, or fraud, has either pulled back...

### Book Four, Question VI.

...[persuaded] or extracted someone from the monastic life—for instance, by saying it is not a good life—he has acted against justice by moving a person against their will. I admit that once the fraud is uncovered, he is bound to teach the truth and remove the pressure so the person may freely return. He is also perhaps bound, on account of the injury inflicted, to ensure the person is received back into the convent. However, if the person does not return, no further bond of restitution remains.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> ¶ **The fourth conclusion.** Although someone may have hindered, led away, or forcibly expelled a person from a monastery (even one who had already **professed** <note>Taken permanent vows</note>), he is not bound to substitute another in his place, nor is he bound to enter the order himself. Beyond the reasons given above, I am especially persuaded by this: no one is bound to follow a religious counsel <note>A "counsel of perfection," like poverty or chastity, which is encouraged but not strictly required for all Christians</note> except with total liberty. Indeed, the religious life is extremely difficult, as it is a life in which a person abdicates their own liberty; for this reason, a full year of **probation** <note>The novitiate, a trial period before final vows</note> has been holily decreed by law. Therefore, no one can be thrust into a religious order through fear or as a penalty for a crime, even if someone were to corrupt many monks into leaving. Nor can any circumstance change that word of the Lord, where He says: *If you wish to be perfect, go...* <note>original: "Si vis perfectus esse, vade." Matthew 19:21</note>; rather, this must be left entirely to the free will of each individual. No one is admitted to the faith unless they come voluntarily; by what law, then, can we compel an unwilling person to perform works of counsel? Furthermore, the **canonical laws** <note>Church laws</note> teach us the opposite: though they may shut up adults, or heretics, or other great criminals within the walls of monasteries and in the narrowest cells, they nevertheless compel no one to make a religious profession. Therefore, those who think they are favoring monastic institutions by such arguments are perhaps doing an injustice to religious vows, which ought to be most free; by forcing men into them, they make these vows hateful. Added to this is the fact that the religious life might not be suitable for the person who withdrew another, nor might it be beneficial for the convent. For this very reason, a year of profession was established; thus, if before entering he knows it is not healthy for him, he is in no way bound to enter.

¶ Furthermore, a powerful argument fights against those opponents. It would follow from their opinion that anyone who removes a professed monk from a monastery would be forced to profess himself. Yet this consequence is against the law that grants a year of probation, so that whoever finds after trial that such an institution is not for him may freely depart. Additionally, there is not always an equality between persons. Is an illustrious or exceptionally learned man bound to enslave himself to a religious order simply because he removed someone who was of little <margin>Excellent explanation</margin> or no use to the order? Then there is the argument

<column-break/>

that restitution in the **forum of conscience** <note>The internal "court" of a person's relationship with God and morality, rather than a legal court</note> <margin>The author explains when one is bound to restitution in conscience.</margin> does not obligate except in those cases where, if the truth were publicly known, an obligation would arise in the **exterior forum** <note>The public legal system of the Church or State</note> according to the laws. But in truth, neither the Pope nor any Prelate would compel such a defendant to make restitution in that manner; therefore, there is no obligation in conscience.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin> ¶ **The fifth conclusion** must nonetheless be applied. He who has stripped a convent or a religious order of a person who was "fruitful" to the order (for there can be no concern regarding useless people) might perhaps be held liable for the **damage caused** <note>damnum dato: legal term for specific financial or material loss</note>. This would not be for full restoration, but according to the judgment of prudent men. For example, someone who by fraud deceives or by force compels a Professor of a Chair to leave is held liable for the loss of the resulting income. However, I would not state this as something absolutely certain to me. Rather, I think we should stand by the exterior forum; for (as I said) the reasoning here is not exactly the same as it is regarding a slave. Let these points be debated concerning justice; for concerning **counsel**, it is another matter. Indeed, **Raymond** <note>Raymond of Penyafort, who joined the Dominicans as an act of moral compensation</note> acted most excellently by compensating for the damage he had done to the order through his own entry.

<margin>Regarding the third argument.</margin> ¶ The **third argument** now leads us into the consideration of restoring **temporal goods**. These are divided into three differences. <margin>Three types of goods.</margin> Some belong to the body, others are exterior resources, and the third are between these two, namely honor and fame. As **John** said in his Epistle: *All that is in the world is either the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, or the pride of life.* <note>1 John 2:16</note> Among these, however, those pertaining to the body are more deeply innate to us, more natural, and thus more important. The first among these is **life**, which is taken away through **homicide**. Concerning this matter, **Saint Thomas Aquinas** and the theologians respond with the greatest consensus that in such a case, <margin>What kind of compensation should be made for a life taken.</margin> because an equivalent restoration cannot be made, it is sufficient that a **possible compensation** be made. Just as we are unable to repay God and our parents according to strict justice, since it is from them we received life, it is enough to give back to them as much as we can.

¶ But it is worthwhile to explain this more closely. In the first place, it must be recalled from the previous sections that a murderer is necessary both to make restitution for the damage caused and to make **satisfaction** <note>A moral act to repair an insult or injury</note> for the injustice. Therefore, there is a question about both in the forum of conscience. In the exterior forum, the penalty of **retaliation** <note>talionis: the law of "an eye for an eye"</note> is established: so that according to the word of the Lord, *He who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword.* This, however, is not our concern here; we are only instructing **confessors** on how to enjoin penances. Let us speak first, therefore, of the damage caused. Regarding this, the conclusion of all is that if the slain man had a family...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

...nourished them by his own sweat, then the **killer** is bound to compensate for that loss by supporting that same family. The reasoning for this is found in the nature of **commutative justice** <note>Justice regarding the private exchange of goods and services between individuals</note>. He forcibly took away the nourishment of the widow and the orphans: therefore, let him return it. For so it was decreed in the final chapter of the section on injuries and damages: *If a loss was caused by your fault, you are required by law to provide satisfaction for it.* <note>original: "Si tua culpa datum est damnum, iure super his satisfacere te oportet." This is a standard rule of Canon Law.</note> However, these universal statements are more true than they are 
<margin>A doubt.</margin> useful. For it is necessary to answer whether *any* killer, and regardless of how large the deceased's family was, must support them forever. 
<margin>Opinion of Major.</margin> **Major** <note>John Major (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher and theologian</note> in Book 4, distinction 15, question 19, in the final doubt, says that the killer is bound only to return to the heirs of the deceased as much as the man himself would have earned throughout his entire life according to the judgment of prudent men, after deducting the costs of his labor. Because, he says, as much is not owed to a man at rest as to one at work. 
<margin>Opposition.</margin> But this is to say nothing at all: since if you take away the labor from one who lives by his own hands, you leave him with nothing; for if he stops working, he would earn nothing. Furthermore, there is a most urgent argument against this: if someone prevents another from working and laboring, he is bound for the full amount of the loss just as if the person were working, for the man was prepared to work. If you, therefore, stand in his way, you are bound to refund to him what he himself would have earned. 
<margin>Scotus.</margin> And so **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus, a medieval Franciscan theologian</note> in distinction 15, question 3, says such a killer is bound to the support of the family of the deceased: not only the wife and children, but if he also nourished his mother and relatives, the killer is compelled to feed them all as well. **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI</note> follows him in the same distinction, and cites **Speculator** <note>Guillaume Durand, a 13th-century jurist</note> and **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer</note> in support of the same opinion, saying that each of the heirs can sue for the works of the deceased which he could have performed during the entire 
<margin>Disproval.</margin> time of his life. This rule, however, is not perfectly exact; rather, it is very harsh on the consciences of the prudent. For it would follow that a killer, even before being condemned by a judge, ought to be reduced to extreme poverty, and a confessor ought to impose such a penance. Hence, if the killer is a poor man who earns only as much as the deceased earned, he would be bound to give everything and leave nothing for himself. What if, by chance, the man killed was a merchant who had vast revenues, and the killer is likewise a merchant? He would be bound to refund just as much to the heirs. Adrian seems to grant this; Major, however, denies it. For Major says that once the family has a living from elsewhere, the killer is not bound to provide it for them. But in truth, this is irrelevant: for if you consider naked commutative justice, it makes no difference whether 

<column-break/>

the heirs are rich or poor. For (as we were saying in the question of the previous book), justice does not look at this: but it commands that as much as was taken away be returned, provided that he who took it is able to pay. Therefore, setting these things aside, the most certain 
<margin>The author's conclusion.</margin> **conclusion** that can be established here is this: In those things which cannot be restored according to their physical kind, restitution must be made according to the judgment of prudent men. Nor does **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> answer anything more specific; doubtless understanding that nothing more certain can be determined. In this judgment, however, account must be taken of the persons—both the one killed and the killer, as well as the heirs. For (as we were just debating), none of the other rules are solid. Therefore, this is the one used by prudent men. And so, the opinion of the prudent is more helpful here than the science of the theologians or the lawyers. For when a killer is mighty in wealth, a greater restitution is to be enjoined upon him than if he were in want. And if the deceased was useless to his own people, the restitution is less than if he were industrious. Moreover, in these injuries, it must be considered that the quality of the deceased is not only to be weighed by his utility and the need of his family, but also by the **value and dignity** of the person. For he who kills a noble man, or one distinguished in letters or by some other reason, is bound to a much greater restitution than if he were to slaughter a person of a lower class. Therefore, those are deceived who think that because the deceased did not leave a family in poverty, restitution is not necessary: because such a person was worth much more than another. Furthermore, the manner of killing must be considered—whether the homicide was perpetrated by ambush, or by fraud, or by remarkable atrocity. All these things, I say, must come into the deliberation so that restitution may be made lawfully, provided the injurious party can pay all this, even with a grave detriment to his own goods. Although, to respond to an earlier point, no one should be cast into extreme or grave necessity on account of restitution in the **forum of conscience** <note>The internal "court" of the soul/confession, as opposed to a civil court</note>. But there also remains something else to be noticed in such cases: that which is only in hope is not equal to that which is in reality; for the deceased could have died quickly, or have fallen ill, so that he could not support the family. Exactly the same is to be said regarding the **mutilation of a limb**: such as he who cuts off the hand of another is bound to pay the doctor's fees, and the damages, and the lost wages in full: yet according to the judgment of wise men. But if anyone should object to this opinion that passage from Exodus 21, which even in Canon Law concerning...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the obligations of a killer toward the survivors of the deceased, specifically focusing on the legal and moral limits of restitution for bodily harm and the differing opinions on whether a killer must offer their own life or spiritual service as compensation.</meta>

### Book Four, Question VI.

In the section on injuries and damages <note>original: "iniur. & dam. dat." referring to a chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding legal liability</note>, in the chapter "If they brawled" <note>original: "cap. fi rixati"</note>, it was accepted as law: namely, that if one person strikes his neighbor with a stone or a fist, and that person does not die, the one who struck him must restore his lost wages and pay his medical expenses; otherwise, he shall be considered innocent. The response is that he will be innocent in respect to homicide; and if the person who was injured fully recovers, then the striker also escapes completely free. $\mathbb{C}$ From this it follows that the price of such injuries ought not to be estimated at the whim of the one who received the damage. Suppose someone cut off the hand of another, or plucked out an eye: would he be bound to pay as much as the victim himself would ask if, before the mutilation, he had wanted to sell his own limb? Not in the least. There is many a commoner who would not wish to be deprived of an eye for a thousand gold coins; and yet, after it has been torn out, the one who plucked it out is not bound to pay that much. For the same logic is not to be applied here as in the case of recoverable objects. If I have stolen a horse by theft, I must either return the horse itself or simply its value; but because limbs cannot be restored in the same way, they ought not to be valued at as much as men value them when they still possess them. Nevertheless, the deformity that remains in the mutilated person must also be compensated. But finally, it should be noted that among illustrious persons, these financial restitutions are not sought. For they easily forgive the material damages; but the injuries <note>Here "injuries" refers to the "iniuria" or the moral insult and affront to honor, rather than just physical harm.</note> are such that they never allow them to be forgotten.

<margin>Besides damages given, the injury must be compensated. Scotus.</margin>
$\mathbb{C}$ Second, in addition to the damages given, the wrongdoer is bound to make satisfaction for the injury: but on this point also, various opinions are debated. There is, I say, the grave and severe opinion of **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian and philosopher</note> in the place cited. He says, I say, that where the law of retaliation <note>term: "lex talionis" — the "eye for an eye" principle of justice.</note> is sanctioned by law, that law is holy and legitimate; and therefore he says the murderer ought justly and patiently to pay that penalty there. If he means that while he is captured and destined for punishment he ought to endure it patiently, this is most true. However, if he means that the man ought to offer himself up to the judge, this can certainly be supported by no probability:

<margin>No one is bound to be both the accused and the Accuser.</margin>
Since no one is bound to be the accused and at the same time the accuser, such that he would voluntarily cast himself upon the gallows: for this would be against the law of nature, which does not admit such cruel laws and precepts. Yet it is hardly credible that such a grave doctor felt this way. This is conjectured from the words immediately subjoined. For he adds that where the law of retaliation has not been established, the guilty person is not bound to inflict it upon himself, because no one ought to be his own murderer. For from this it is gathered that even where it has been established, the guilty person is not bound to present himself to the judge. For this would amount to the same thing as if

<column-break/>

he were to inflict it upon himself. Nevertheless, he adds that it is then expedient for such a murderer to expose his life in a just cause, such as in a war against the enemies of the Church, for the sake of making restitution to the one whose life he took. And he adds that if he does not wish to make even that much restitution, he cannot be entirely immune from restitution. This is a sufficiently severe and rigid judgment, which he seems to corroborate for himself by the word of Christ: *He who kills with the sword shall perish by the sword.* <note>Matthew 26:52</note>

<margin>Disapproval</margin>
And **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), known for his strict moral theology</note> agrees with him. But I truly confess that I could not so bind anyone. For Christ was speaking of the avenging sword of the commonwealth, by which evildoers perish. Indeed, for a good man who, inflamed by anger, committed a single homicide, it would not subsequently be wise for that reason to commit himself to war; it would be otherwise if he were of such ruined character as to be like a public plague.

<margin>How satisfaction for injury is to be made.</margin>
Satisfaction for the injury is therefore to be made in another way, namely by humbly seeking pardon, or by arbitrary penance. $\mathbb{C}$ When, however, no other way of restoring is open, a convenient restitution is for the killer to help his deceased victim before God with orations and prayers. And this is a salutary thing to be enjoined in sacramental confession in place of penance. Although, to tell the truth, I do not clearly see the obligation of justice regarding this kind of spiritual restitution. Nor does **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto's school of thought</note> mention it, even though Scotus, in the place cited, deems it necessary. Truly, in the judicial court, compulsion is not made except regarding the temporal damage given and the compensation for the injury. But it is nonetheless most healthy counsel when the slain person is in need. For if he had lived as one estranged from the Catholic faith, such restitution would be ridiculous.

<margin>A doubt as to whom restitution ought to be made.</margin>
$\mathbb{C}$ There remains, however, some doubt as to who those heirs are to whom restitution must be made of necessity. For Scotus says that if the deceased supported his parents and other kinsmen and relatives, the killer is bound to sustain them all equally. And Adrian and others follow him.

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
However, the response is given through a tempering of this opinion. For some are "necessary heirs": namely, those who have such a right that they cannot be excluded entirely from the inheritance, such as the wife and husband, parents and children; for the father was bound to sustain these if they were in need. Therefore, this order of heirs succeeds to the right of the deceased; and for that reason, restitution must be made to them out of justice. And the reason is that a human being is a certain good, not only his own, but his wife's, his children's, and his parents'. And therefore, he who took the man away with the sword, took him away from them. But others are heirs...

### Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right,

...only heirs through intestacy <note>Inheritors who receive property when there is no will.</note> who are not "necessary" heirs, such as brothers and more distant relatives. In the internal court of conscience, the killer is not bound by the strictness of justice to these people. For although the deceased might have supported them out of his own generosity, that obligation does not pass to the killer. Otherwise, he would be equally bound to support the deceased's friends, servants, and anyone else he had taken into his home. It is true, however, that in the external court <note>original: "foro exteriori"; the public legal system as opposed to the internal moral forum of confession.</note>, money is usually paid to brothers and other paternal relatives so that they might drop the legal charges for the injury, since they have the right to sue; yet this is not because the killer owes them anything for a "loss given."

<margin>A doubt: does the obligation of restitution pass to the heirs?</margin>
¶ If you should ask whether the heirs of the killer are bound in conscience for the damage if the killer himself did not provide satisfaction while alive, the answer is that they are bound if the deceased left them property; otherwise, not at all. However, they are not similarly compelled to compensate for the personal injury itself, unless the killer had been condemned while alive and the case had reached a final judgment <note>original: "rem iudicatam"; a matter already decided by a court.</note> requiring him to pay specifically for the injury.

<margin>Regarding the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ It follows now to discuss the fourth argument regarding damage to reputation and honor, and how they ought to be restored. How reputation and honor differ will be explained in the following book, question 9, where their treatment has its proper place. For now, it is enough to know that reputation—which is the good estimation of a person held publicly—is darkened by <term>detraction</term> <note>The sin of revealing another's hidden faults to someone who has no right to know them.</note>. For this reason, the defamer is bound to restore and repair it in the most suitable and fitting way possible. Indeed, among temporal goods, it is the most precious after life itself. Nor is it like a life that has been taken, which is irrecoverable; for reputation can be restored to its wholeness.

<margin>A rule for restoring reputation.</margin>
However, a rule must be established right at the outset: damaged reputation does not necessarily have to be restored for the sake of salvation <note>Meaning it is not always a "mortal sin" preventing one from going to heaven.</note> unless it was taken away contrary to justice. This is a universal rule for all goods. Hence, when Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian.</note> assigns three ways of defaming someone, he says the first is when someone speaks the truth and does so justly; this does not bind one to restitution. ¶ But because various opinions are circulated regarding this matter, we shall open the subject with the following notable points, lest we cloud our style with too many citations of authors.

<margin>The first notable point.</margin>
First, for an obligation to restore reputation to arise, it is required that the reputation truly be taken away or darkened. Sometimes, based on the subject matter, it appears to be taken away, when in truth it is not.

<margin>This can happen in four ways. First, if the person defamed is such that, according to human reputation, the act is not considered a disgrace for him.</margin>
This can happen in four ways. First, if the person being defamed is the sort of man for whom, according to human social standing, the claim is not an infamy. For instance, if you said a courtier <note>original: "aulicum"</note> was "serving," as they say, a lady of the court: even if a suspicion

<column-break/>

might arise from this, provided you did not defame the woman in any way, you are certainly not bound to restitution toward the man. Nor if you said he had entered into a duel with another, even if this were a secret and perhaps a lie; for among that class of men, no infamy, or only a very slight one, arises from such things. Second, reputation is not taken away when the person was already publicly infamous. If you lied, for example, saying a prostitute admitted a pimp on a certain night when she had not, it would truly not be a mortal sin to fail to restore her reputation, because she contracted no new stain from it. Third, if the defamation concerns a very trivial matter. For example, if someone defamed another by saying he was negligent in his studies, or that he did not fast for the whole of Lent <note>original: "Quadragesimam"</note>, even if it were a lie; if that person is an ordinary commoner, he considers it as nothing. Fourth, if the defamer is either not credible or appears to have spoken in jest. Since no faith is given to such a person, even if he commits a fault, because he generates no actual infamy, he does not entangle himself in the bond of restitution.

<margin>The second notable point.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is required that the person darken another's reputation through a crime of injustice. For he who reveals a true crime according to custom and law takes nothing away for which he is bound to restore. For example, if you rightly accused someone in a trial; or if, through <term>fraternal correction</term> <note>The Christian practice of privately admonishing a sinner to help them improve.</note>, you prudently summoned several witnesses to whom you revealed your neighbor's fault for his greater amendment; or if, looking out for the good of your friend who was preparing to receive a criminal or untrustworthy servant into his household, you warned him not to do so. None of these cases places a man under the yoke of restitution. Furthermore, if someone defames another against charity but without violating justice, he is likewise not bound by the necessity of restitution. For example, you brought a criminal to court who was truly worthy of punishment and could be convicted by witnesses, yet you did so not looking toward the good, but with an evil mind—say, out of hatred or greed, so that you might ambitiously succeed him in his rank. You have indeed failed against charity and liberality, but you are not proven to owe restitution, because you did not act against justice. For the same reason, if a prelate <note>A high-ranking church official.</note> betrayed a guilty person whom he had lawfully condemned, revealing it to those who did not know of it, he strikes against the laws of charity, yet he is not bound to restore the reputation. Nor is he who speaks of a person lawfully defamed in one place in another place where the matter had not yet been heard.

<margin>The third notable point.</margin>
¶ In addition, it is required thirdly that the injured person has not recovered his reputation through some other way; for then the defamer becomes free...
