Having established that reputation is a possession as valuable as property, the author now examines the specific conditions under which a slanderer is required to restore that good name.</meta>

### Question VI of the Fourth Book 341

...he who defamed is released from the duty of restitution: certainly when the other person has already recovered what they had lost. For instance, if I accused someone of **concubinage** <note>The state of a man and woman living together as husband and wife without being legally married.</note>, but they cleared their name so effectively that no credit is given to my words anymore, I am freed from the burden of making restitution. Here, therefore, are the three conditions from which the obligation to make restitution is forged: namely, that you take away a reputation, that you do so against justice, and that the other person has not already been **restored to their original standing** <note>original: "in integrum reparavit"; a legal term meaning to return someone to their prior legal or social status.</note>.

<margin>There are two ways someone is defamed against justice.</margin>
¶ Having established this, as we descend into the specifics, it remains to be said that (as **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Catholic theology in this period.</note> says) defamation occurs against justice in two ways: first, when someone charges another with a false crime and does so unjustly; second, when—

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
—he charges them with a true crime, but does so unjustly. But is it ever possible for the charging of a false crime to be anything other than unjust? Why then was it necessary to add "unjustly" after "false"?

<margin>The solution.</margin>
The answer is that it was necessary: for (as we shall see in the 4th Question of the following book) a judge, before whose tribunal someone is legitimately proven guilty whom the judge himself knows to be innocent, is bound to sentence him to punishment. In such a case, the judge affirms that false crime by his very act, yet he does so **justly** <note>In the legal theory of the time, a judge had to act on the public evidence ("the world of the court") rather than his private knowledge.</note>; and therefore he is not compelled to make any restitution. However, neither a judge outside of that specific case, nor any private person who knowingly and deliberately constructs a false crime against another, can do so without injustice. In that case, the person will not have made adequate restitution until they assert that they lied—unless perhaps they reach an agreement that the victim will be satisfied with some other form of compensation. We will discuss this further in a moment.

<margin>A noteworthy lesson in the restitution of reputation.</margin>
¶ Indeed, this lesson must also be observed: it is not enough to assert that you lied only in the presence of those to whom you told the lie. Rather, you are bound to create a belief contrary to the one you fostered. Because humans are more **inclined to believe** evil than good, you must show that you spoke falsely—using an oath if necessary and bringing in witnesses—so that the person who was splashed with infamy by your fault may emerge cleansed by your diligence.

<margin>The second mode.</margin>
¶ In the second mode, the darkening of another's reputation happens against justice when someone reveals a **true crime**, yet does so against the necessary order of the law. For example, if someone made a secret crime public outside of court, or brought it into court as an accusation but was unable to prove it. However, when someone merely omits minor details of procedure, they do not immediately become liable for restitution: such as if they made the accusation on a feast day, or in an unsuitable place, or without observing other ceremonies that do not change the substance of the matter.
¶ Nevertheless, this case of restitution is very

<column-break/>

difficult, if it is to be done rightly and correctly. Indeed, it is certain that it is not permissible for that defamer to say they lied; for that would itself be a lie, which should never be told even for the salvation of the entire world. Yet, what **St. Thomas**, **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note>, and most of the Doctors say—namely, that the person should then say they spoke wrongly and unjustly defamed their neighbor, and that they should not be believed—contributes so little to restitution that it often causes more harm than good. Other more recent authors say the defamer should then use **amphibologies** <note>Ambiguous phrases or double-meanings that allow the speaker to avoid a direct lie while changing the listener's mind.</note> so that they do not lie themselves, but others may think they had lied. But in truth, besides the fact that this would be a kind of lie, it would offer no benefit. For this reason, it has always seemed better to me (as **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), known as Cajetan, a leading commentator on Aquinas.</note> also says here) that such a detractor should no longer speak of the matter before those same people. Instead, they should spread a good opinion of the person everywhere, to the extent that they can without lying. And although some might conclude that the person spoke the truth because they did not retract it, the defamer can do no more than that. However, they are bound to the one whose reputation they wounded for the **damages given**: specifically, if because of that injury the victim suffered any loss of their property. Yet this is not a full restoration as it would be if they had defamed them through a lie, but rather according to the judgment of wise and prudent men.

¶ Nevertheless, in making these restitutions, the possibility of the thing must be weighed. For who could make restitution if they were an obstacle to the person they defamed, preventing them from obtaining a **bishopric**, an excellent **university chair**, or a high dignity? Therefore, in these cases, the counsel of wise men must be followed.

<margin>The third mode of defaming unjustly.</margin>
¶ The third mode of unjust defamation, which is added by **Scotus**, **Richard** <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302), a Scholastic theologian.</note>, and others, occurs when someone denies their own hidden crime which another has unjustly revealed, whether in court or outside of it. For example, when a secret concubinary or a thief is reported against the law, and says the reporter lied. For it is a doubt whether he is bound to restore the reputation he wounded by calling that person an unjust informer. And indeed **Cajetan**—

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
—here and in his *Summa*, under the word "restitution," says that both are bound to make restitution to the other: sometimes they are mutually injurious to one another, and no one, as he judges, can give up their own right to their reputation.

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
But **Scotus** and **Richard** respond more mildly: namely, that the man living in concubinage is not bound to make restitution to the reporter in this way...

### Brother Domingo Soto, on Justice and Law, 342

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
...restore his reputation, so that he may confess his own secret crime: but by excusing him with other words: namely, by saying that he was led by good intention and zeal. ¶ I would believe, however, if my judgment is to be heard, that although what **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian and philosopher known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note> advises is healthy counsel, nevertheless, according to the rigor of justice, he who was unjustly defamed is in no way bound to restore the reputation of the denouncer or accuser. This holds even if he denied his own crime, and from that denial it is gathered that the other person either lied or spoke falsely. This is a point that **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), an influential Dominican theologian who wrote a famous manual for confessors.</note> also built upon before us, under the word "restitution," section 3, paragraph 3. For he who uses his own right does no injury to anyone, and thus by the rigor of justice is not compelled to restore anything to that person; and he who, in such a case, conceals his own crime, is using his own right. But if you argue that he lies while denying the crime he committed—and if he denies it with an oath, he sins mortally—from which it appears to follow that he is bound to make restitution to the other. It is answered first: that he can conceal it by remaining silent, namely by neither affirming nor denying. Second, it is answered that even if he sins by denying without an oath, it is not a mortal sin because he does not lie perniciously <note>A "pernicious lie" is one intended to cause harm; Soto argues lying to protect a secret one has a right to keep is less severe.</note>, since he has a right to conceal the truth. And although one swearing falsely sins mortally against God, he does not commit an injustice against the one who revealed the secret. Nor, indeed, as Scotus thinks, is it against the commonwealth; because as long as he has the right to cover his own crime, he is not disobedient to the judge, and therefore is not compelled to make restitution. For that rule mentioned above must be kept deep in the mind: **No sin binds one to restitution unless it be against justice.** <note>original: "Nullum peccatum ad restitutionem obligat nisi sit contra iustitiam." A fundamental principle of Catholic moral theology: only sins that violate another's rights (justice) require physical or social repayment.</note>

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Wherefore, this "metaphysical distinction" of **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican cardinal and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>—namely, that the accuser can be considered either as an unjust accuser (and then the other, by denying the crime, does him no injury) or as a human being (and then an injury is done to him)—this metaphysical distinction, I say, truly has no relevance to morals. For since it is the very same man who accuses, he who protects himself from him by his own right inflicts no injury upon him. Furthermore, that method of mutual restitution is useless. For if the one who accused cannot say that he accused falsely (because he would be lying), but only that he accused "unjustly," he does not repair the other's reputation by this; rather, he confirms that he affirmed a true thing. Likewise, since the other is not bound to confess his secret crime, if he were to say (as Cajetan wishes) that the other was not a slanderer,

<column-break/>

that would be almost like a confession of his own crime. Therefore, the defamed person is not bound to make restitution to the accuser; but if either is bound, it is rather the accuser, who brought the first injury, who is bound to the accused. ¶ Besides these points, when both would be bound, it is certain—contrary to what Cajetan thinks—that **compensation** <note>term: compensation; in a legal sense, the canceling out of one debt or injury by an equal one from the opposing side.</note> takes place: namely, so that injury would be forgiven for injury. For anyone can both forgive and exchange his own reputation, as we shall see shortly. ¶ Finally, the fourth

<margin>The fourth way of unjustly defaming.</margin>
way of unjustly defaming is as much more ruinous as it is more common and less esteemed. Namely, when someone reports what they have heard. You heard, for example, that your neighbor was receiving a "friend" <note>A euphemism for a lover or an illicit visitor.</note>; then, as is the nature of men, you immediately whisper into the ears of the neighborhood in these words: "I heard this or that; I certainly don't believe it, but I'm reporting what was heard." This is indeed an ingenious but pestilent way of slandering. For the more holily you justify yourself, the more credibility you claim for yourself, and therefore you defame more grievously. For thus, as the poet says, **rumor acquires strength as it goes.** <note>original: "fama... vires acquirit eundo"; a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid describing the spread of Rumor.</note> Therefore, although Scotus (in the place cited, distinction 15, question 4) and Cajetan (on the *Secunda Secundae*, question 73, article 2) think that this is not "direct" defamation because by its nature it does not take away reputation, and they do not think it binds one to restitution except by reason of **scandal** <note>term: scandal; in theology, an action that leads another person into sin or spiritual ruin.</note>, I certainly would not dare to make consciences so safe in that way. On the contrary, he who defames in this way—although he is not bound to say he lied, since he did indeed hear it—is nevertheless bound not only to say that he spoke lightly, but also to labor so that he may take away the [bad] opinion that others have conceived. Unless, perhaps, the matter is so public that it has crept in by another path. Therefore, one must be extremely careful of whispers of this kind. ¶ Besides these things, however, the doctors debate many doubts regarding this restitution of reputation, which must be discussed in order. The first is whether

<margin>The first doubt.</margin>
another's reputation must be restored at the cost of one's own reputation. For it appears that this is not necessary: both because everyone ought to look after his own reputation rather than another's, and also because the reputation I took from another did not increase my own. I must, I say, restore the money I have stolen because it increased my wealth; but because I obscured the reputation of another, my own was not made any brighter. ¶ It is answered: nevertheless, without a doubt, we are bound to repair the reputation we have torn apart, even with the loss of our own reputation. For although we ought to look out for our own more carefully than another's, it is not permitted for anyone—

<summary>Soto argues that those who spread gossip or hide secret crimes are not always bound by the same rules of restitution as direct slanderers, though he warns that "ingenious" gossip is especially destructive. He concludes that one must restore a damaged reputation even if it ruins one's own name in the process.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral obligations of restitution. Having previously established that an accuser is not strictly bound to restore the reputation of the accused if the accused merely exercised their right to remain silent, the author now pivots to broader questions of what one must sacrifice—money, honor, or even life—to make amends for an injury.</meta>

### Book Four, Question 6.

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
It is permissible to look out for oneself even if it causes injury to another. This is not unlike other temporal goods. For if you have destroyed another person’s house by fire, or forced a man to cast his merchandise into the waves, even if you gained nothing from it, you are nonetheless bound to make restitution. Hence, **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristot. 5. Ethicorum." Referring to Book 5 of the Nicomachean Ethics, where Aristotle discusses justice and "gain" in a legal sense.</note> very acutely taught that in injuries of this kind, though there is no literal profit, there is a metaphorical profit: namely, that by fulfilling your own will, you have overcome another. For this reason, you are just as bound to make restitution as if what you took had been added to your own wealth. ¶ This doubt, however, gives birth to another: whether this is so true that it admits no exception. For it is a very heavy burden if a **prelate** <note>original: "Antistes," a high-ranking cleric or bishop.</note> or another person of excellent reputation has stained the name of a private citizen, that he should be bound to repair the other’s reputation at the cost of his own, by saying he lied or something similar. It is answered that these moral laws are not to be followed with such [unbending] rigor, but rather as any very wise person would judge after weighing the quality of the persons involved. Therefore, it is enough for an illustrious person to compensate the reputation of another which he has darkened through money or some other means. But if the other person is unwilling to accept this, the defamer is not bound to do more. For even in the case of money, if I owe ten coins which I cannot pay except with a loss of a thousand, I can certainly postpone the payment or seek another way of paying.

<margin>The third doubt.</margin>
¶ A more serious doubt, related to this one, is whether a reputation must be restored at the cost of one's own life. For **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> (2nd part of the 2nd part, Question 62, Article 6), whom some younger writers follow,

<margin>Distinction of goods. Cajetan's Rule.</margin>
distinguishes three orders of things: namely, money; honor and reputation together; and thirdly, life. Concerning these, he established this rule: No one is bound to restore a thing of a lower order at the cost of a thing of a higher order. For example, one is not bound to restore money at the cost of reputation or honor; nor reputation or honor at the cost of life. However, one is bound to restore a thing of any order at the cost of a thing of that same order. ¶ But Cajetan has adapted these kinds of rules, drawn from the depths of **metaphysics** <note>The branch of philosophy dealing with the fundamental nature of reality; Soto suggests Cajetan is being too abstract for practical morality.</note>, much more than is proper for moral philosophy; which

<margin>Refutation</margin>
is why they cannot help but be deceptive. Indeed, there is no reason to doubt that money must sometimes be restored at the cost of one’s reputation. First, because it is lawful for no one to protect their own honor and reputation through the loss and injury of another; nor is the one who was harmed bound to give up his own right (even a monetary one) so that the person who caused the injury may protect his reputation. You have stolen, for example, a 

<column-break/>

large amount of money: there is no doubt that you ought to use all diligence to restore it secretly. If, however, you cannot do so without danger to your reputation and honor, the other person should not be stripped of his substance for that reason—especially when his loss is heavy. For we do not deny that respect should be shown to reputation and money; but nonetheless, all things being equal, the right of the innocent person who was unjustly harmed by you is greater. Secondly, even if we wish to enter into a metaphysical calculation, and granted that reputation is by its nature more excellent than money, yet so much wealth can be accumulated that the pile is far more precious than your reputation. Gold is indeed more precious by its nature than silver, but there can be such a weight of silver that it is valued much higher than a small amount of gold. Furthermore, therefore, that rule [of Cajetan's] is very harmful to the commonwealth; for which reason, let no one believe it who strives to consult his own conscience.

<margin>Whether one is bound to restore at the risk of life.</margin>
¶ Regarding life, however, whether one is bound to perform any restitution at the risk of it, is a more pressing doubt. For since, as we said above, no one is the master of his own life, and since no one is bound to offer himself to death for any crime (as we shall say in the next book), or to bring upon himself the death to which he has been condemned, it appears to follow that no one is bound to make restitution at the risk of his life. It is answered, therefore, that according to the common order and custom of laws, no one is bound to make restitution at the risk of death—not only for money or reputation, but not even for the life which he took from another, even if he killed a distinguished man. And in this, the aforementioned rule [of Cajetan's] also fails: namely, the idea that a thing must always be restored even at the risk of a thing of the same order. Secondly, nonetheless, saving better judgment, I would believe that a singular event could occur in which someone is bound to make restitution at the risk of his own life—not only for reputation and honor, but perhaps even for a monetary matter. For example: if someone had falsely defamed an illustrious family of **heresy** or the crime of **high treason** <note>original: "læsæ maiestatis," the Roman legal concept of "injured majesty," usually meaning treason against the state or ruler.</note>, so that unless the lie were retracted, that same lineage would remain stained by that perpetual blot; he ought indeed to use all diligence to keep his own life safe while fulfilling his testimony. But even if he could not do so without the risk of his life, I believe he would nonetheless be bound to do it. However, one must prudently discern whether the crime and the damage have already passed, or whether...

# Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

...is truly always dependent. You killed a man, as I was saying, whom you cannot now restore to the light [of life]; you are not bound to expose yourself to the danger of death to pay money for him; nor if you have blackened a reputation which the defamed person cannot recover. But yet I am speaking of that case when the reputation actually depends on you so that it can be recovered. I would judge the same regarding life: for example, if through your false testimony alone someone is bound and sentenced to death:
<margin>A distinction to be noted.</margin>
surely you would be bound, even at the risk of your own life, to snatch him from the death into which you are driving him. It is otherwise if you committed a crime for which he is falsely condemned. Indeed, if you did not frame him <note>original: "non imposuisti," literally "did not impose it upon him."</note>, it is no business of yours: and therefore no law compels you then to betray yourself. ¶ But what when one cannot restore a reputation?
<margin>St. Thomas and Scotus.</margin>
**Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s school of thought.</note> says one ought to make compensation in another way; and **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note> says the same in his writings on the 4th book of the *Sentences*, distinction 15, according to the sense of that little gloss on the chapter *Ecclesia* [under the title] *while a suit is pending, nothing should be changed* <note>original: "ut lite pend. nih. innoue." A standard principle in Canon Law to prevent legal "facts on the ground" from changing while a case is being decided.</note>. When a thing cannot be restored, restitution ought to be made in something else of equal value.
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
**Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian known for his "Summa Sylvestrina."</note> truly, under the word "detraction," section 4, dares to affirm the contrary: led, no doubt, by this comparison: that just as a debtor of money is not bound to compensate by offering honor or reputation when he cannot pay; so too, he who cannot restore reputation is not bound to satisfy through money. And this has some probability. For otherwise, he who cannot restore even through money would have to repay it through prayers or some other way.
<margin>The author’s opinion.</margin>
Nevertheless, one must not depart from the standard authoritative opinion <note>original: "opinio regia," literally "the royal opinion," meaning the most certain or dominant view among scholars.</note>. For since money is the price of all things, both honor and reputation are valued by it. And therefore, through money or something else appraisable by money, restitution of these must be made. But when that is lacking, there is no reason why it should be restored through prayers or honors, because these are not the prices of things. ¶ Regarding all these matters, the most important question being debated here is whether it is lawful for anyone to waive the restitution of their own reputation.
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
**Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> certainly defends the negative side of this in his *Summa*, under the word "detraction"; he does not lack other more recent followers. And his basis is that a man is no more the master of his reputation and honor than of his life; and so, just as he cannot kill himself, nor grant that power to another, so he cannot waive the restitution of his reputation. But yet this question need not give us much trouble here: since we laid the contrary foundation above in Question 3,

<column-break/>

and as I believe, we firmly established it: namely, that a man is the master of his honor and reputation just as he is of his money. Although in the same order [of value] it is to be held of more account than money: according to that passage in **Proverbs 22**: "A good name is better than many riches." <note>original: "Melius est bonum nomen, quàm diuitiæ multæ."</note>
<margin>Solution to the doubt.</margin>
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
From which contrary foundation we now elicit a contrary conclusion: namely, that to waive the restitution of reputation and honor is not a mortal sin in its kind—unless because of a circumstance of the person, such as being placed in a public dignity or office, or perhaps some other reason makes it mortal. <note>A mortal sin is a "death-dealing" sin that separates the soul from God, whereas a venial sin is a lesser offense.</note> But if someone waives it without any cause, or does not take serious offense at being defamed, it will be a venial sin for him: just like the prodigality <note>Wastefulness.</note> of money, which is not mortal in its kind; or at least it is a little more unseemly in the same category. And the reason is: because no logic of injustice intervenes concerning the same person toward himself in those things of which a man is master; but it will be a sin against the charity by which everyone is bound to love himself and his own things—which, in temporal matters, does not reach the level of a mortal sin.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ From which conclusion a second is inferred: namely, that if someone, for some good and honest cause, spares the one who defamed him without requiring any restitution—perhaps to look out for the honor of that person, who is otherwise upright, or for some other reason of piety—not only will he contract no guilt, but he will also perform a duty of charity. For we are always speaking without the circumstance of a public person. This conclusion is not only ours, but also that of **Hadrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), who was a respected theologian before his papacy.</note>, an author of no small note; and even explicitly that of Saint Thomas, whatever Cajetan may attempt to the contrary. For he says that man is established as the master of himself through free will, and therefore can lawfully dispose of himself as far as pertains to those things belonging to this life. Nor does he except anything besides the passage of this life to the next—where he openly asserts that man is the master of everything except life alone. And in question 73, article 4, he says most clearly without any riddle that it is placed in the judgment of a man to suffer the loss of his reputation, unless this turns into a danger for others, such as if he is a public person; according to that [saying] of **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> in his 9th homily on Ezekiel:
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
"Just as we ought not to provoke the tongues of detractors by our own effort, lest they themselves perish; so we ought to endure with equanimity those provoked by their own malice, so that our merit may increase." Indeed, [this is clear] not only from the doctors, but from the Gospel...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding whether an individual possesses "dominion" (rightful ownership) over their own reputation. Soto argues that while we are masters of our own fame and can sacrifice it for humility, there are specific limits concerning public office and religious integrity.</meta>

# Questions on the Fourth Book, Question VI. 345

From the Gospel, this is not difficult to infer. For Christ did not entrust us with such a great concern for honor and fame as to suggest that we do not have mastery <note>original: "dominium," a legal term for absolute ownership.</note> over them. On the contrary, in Matthew 5 and frequently elsewhere, He warns us with great urgency to cast away all honors along with the splendors of this world. And elsewhere, he tells us not to desire the first seats. Regarding fame, Paul says that to be judged by men is a "very small thing" <note>original: "pro minimo." See 1 Corinthians 4:3.</note>. He does not say it is "nothing," but "a very small thing," because fame is a certain kind of good, though not among the most important. To this we added, in the place cited, the examples of the saints: namely Ambrose, Augustine, and Anselm, who defamed themselves in their own writings for the sake of humility. They certainly would not have done this unless it were permitted to them within the bounds of virtue.

But if we have sufficiently demonstrated the foundation there—as I believe I have—namely, that a man is the master of his own reputation, there is no reason for us to linger here in confirming these conclusions, which are clearly gathered from that principle. 

However, when the infamy <note>original: "infamia," referring to a formal loss of legal standing or public disgrace.</note> involves heresy or apostasy, which fight directly against faith and religion, such disgrace is not to be endured but must be entirely repelled and wiped away as much as possible. This follows the example of Christ, who, as read in Matthew 4, although he had calmly endured other insults brought against him by the devil, used sharpness against him when he tempted him regarding idolatry. These conclusions will be explained even more clearly in the next book, Question 10, where we have gathered from the same foundation that it is not permitted for a man to allow himself to be disgraced against justice—indeed, it is sometimes a virtue to resist it. In truth, the opinion contrary to ours shamefully detracts from the rights of friendship. For if I can risk my life for a friend, even though I am not the master of my life, why should I not be able to risk my fame and honor?

<margin>Arguments against the conclusion.</margin>
¶ However, there are several objections to the contrary. The first is drawn from the book of Wisdom: "Have a care for a good name; for a good name is better than many riches." <note>original: "Curam habe de bono nomine." See Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 41:12.</note> Nevertheless, it is answered that the care we must have for a good name is the same care that is incumbent upon us for virtue—since a good name is the reward of virtue. We must, therefore, procure a good name by pursuing virtue.

<margin>Virtue must be cherished, and honor follows it.</margin>
For honor is its shadow. Therefore, just as a shadow follows him who walks straight toward the sun, so honor follows him who cherishes virtue. But because, as Aristotle says, honor is not in the power of the one being honored but in the one who gives honor, one should not value a good name too highly for its own sake.

<column-break/>

Because of this, Paul said it was a very small thing to be judged by men. And Augustine, in the 11th Question, Canon 3, says to Secundinus the Manichaean:

> Think of Augustine whatever you please; only let my conscience not accuse me in the eyes of God.

Indeed, he who seeks a good name except through virtue never attains it; just as he who turns his back on the sun never catches the shadow he pursues. ¶ But what if we object using the same Augustine, who says in the 11th Question, Canon 3, that men "cruelly" despise their own reputation? For, he says, "our life is necessary for ourselves, but our reputation is necessary for others." The answer is that Augustine did not imply that the ownership of our fame does not rest with ourselves. Indeed, he should rather have asserted that regarding life, of which we are not the masters—yet he says that life is necessary for us. He only means that although fame is our own property, just like our money, when the commonwealth <note>original: "reipublicae," referring generally to the public good or the state.</note> has need of it, we ought to serve it through our good reputation, just as a rich man serves with his money. 

Consequently, it follows only that a man placed in high dignity, or one necessary to the commonwealth, has his own reputation bound and obligated to his function, as he cannot govern his subjects without it; therefore, he cannot neglect it. Yet it does not follow from this that a private man is bound to preserve his fame, any more than his other temporal goods. Furthermore, Augustine was speaking to certain women who, deliberately putting on a show of humility, were defaming themselves by admitting men into their company—which was certainly not permitted.

<margin>A prelate neglecting his reputation sins mortally.</margin>
¶ From here, let us proceed to those in authority <note>original: "praefectos."</note>. Regarding them, let our first assertion be that a prelate <note>A "praelatus" is any high-ranking official or superior in a religious or legal hierarchy.</note>, as long as he is a prelate, would sin mortally against justice if he neglected his reputation in a matter of primary importance; because, as I just said, he has his reputation bound to his office. Nevertheless, if he were not a person so exceptionally useful to the commonwealth and wished to resign his magistracy, he would be no more bound to keep his fame than a private person—though it is otherwise if he wishes to persist in his public position.

<margin>The opinion of some.</margin>
¶ From these points, many conclude that he who shreds the reputation of a prelate is not only bound to make restitution to him, but also to the body of his subjects. For fame, they say, is not his alone, but also belongs to the community <note>original: "collegij."</note>. But truly, without a moderating distinction, I would not believe this. For the fame of a prelate is his own property, as if he were a private person, even though he needs it for his function. For that reason, while the infamy concerns only the prelate...

<summary>Soto argues that individuals generally have the right to sacrifice their own reputation for humility, but public officials (prelates) have a moral duty to maintain their standing to ensure effective governance.</summary>

The previous page established that while individuals have a right to their own fame, certain crimes like heresy must be defended to protect the faith. This page moves into the mechanics of restitution—how to "pay back" stolen honor or a damaged reputation.</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>
<header>F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law,</header>

...if a rumor is spread—for example, that a superior has a mistress, or some other crime in which his subordinates do not share—it is sufficient for restitution to be made to him alone. This is true even though the obligation to make restitution is greater for a public official than for a private person. However, if the official himself absolves the slanderer from making restitution, I would certainly believe that even if the official acts wrongly in doing so, the slanderer remains safe nonetheless. Furthermore, the slanderer owes nothing more to the college <note>original: "collegio," referring to a formal body or corporation of people, such as a religious chapter or a faculty.</note>; it is just as if the official squandered his own money which he was supposed to distribute to the poor. For he is the master of his own reputation, even if he manages it poorly. It is different if the crime reflects upon the whole group: for instance, if he were slandered for simony <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical privileges or offices.</note> or for heresy, whereby the subordinates would contract the infamy of association. In that case, restitution is indeed owed to the collective body. ¶ From what has been said, another small doubt is resolved: namely, whether "compensation" can occur regarding reputation. It is clearly gathered that it can. For example, if you have picked away at my name regarding some matter, and I in turn have done the same to yours, we can not only agree that each remains with his own wound (if we are private persons), but it will also be permitted for me to refuse to restore yours unless you make the same payment to me. This is proven because, as we have said, reputation can be weighed against money; and therefore, just as with coins, this kind of exchange takes place in matters of reputation.

<margin>It is permitted to repel force with force by defaming.</margin>
However, a person who has been defamed cannot harm the slanderer’s name by way of revenge. He may do so only to "repel force with force" <note>original: "vim vi repellere," a standard legal principle in Roman and Canon law regarding self-defense.</note>: specifically, by revealing some true crime of the slanderer when it is necessary to weaken that person’s testimony against him.

<margin>Concerning the fifth argument.</margin>
¶ The fifth argument, where the inquiry concerns the restoration of honor, is not of such great ambiguity.

<margin>The difference between reputation and honor.</margin>
Honor and reputation differ, as we have discussed more broadly in Question 9. Good reputation is the good estimation and opinion held of a man, which is darkened by detraction—either by the imposition of a false crime or the revealing of a true one. Honor, however, is the reverence shown to another because of some excellence, whether of virtue, birth, office, learning, etc. This honor is worn down and taken away through insults or "contumely" <note>original: "contumeliam," meaning insulting language or treatment intended to humiliate.</note>. For this reason, honor can be restored more easily than reputation: specifically, through a contrary act of reverence.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But regarding this reverence, it is often hesitated whether asking for forgiveness is sufficient to repay the honor.

<margin>The opinion of Cajetan.</margin>
On this point, Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> in the cited question (22. q. 72. art. 3) considers that asking for forgiveness is irrelevant to the restoration of honor. I would not dare to utter such an absolute word; rather, the response should be approached through these points of guidance. First,

<column-break/>

<margin>First guidance.</margin>
asking for forgiveness is the most decent and most appropriate way of restoring honor. Since restitution ought to be made through an "antidote"—that is, through the opposite—and since insult and contumely are signs of contempt (whereby the insulter behaves as a superior, subduing the other), the proper antidote is a contrary humiliation, even a bowing of the body.

<margin>Second guidance.</margin>
The second assertion is that this is neither always sufficient nor always required, but there is a need for prudent judgment. It is clear that it is not always sufficient: for sometimes the insult is so great that an apology is not enough, and another compensation is required. That it is not always required is clear from the rule of Blessed Augustine, who says it is not fitting for prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> to ask forgiveness from their subordinates. Therefore, a common man should not, by right reason, demand such a great humiliation from an illustrious man; restitution could be made in another way. Furthermore, since it is not the custom among nobles and illustrious persons to ask for such forgiveness, they should not be forced to do so by their confessors; rather, they should make such restitutions in their own manner, provided it does not deviate from the Gospel.

<margin>Concerning those who have suffered injuries.</margin>
¶ In addition to this, there is also a need for a distinction regarding those who have suffered insults, as to how their conscience should be bound to forgive the injury. For they are bound not to have a mind for seeking vengeance by private authority. As it is written in Deuteronomy 32 and Romans 12: "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay." Yet, they are not bound to forgo the loss they accepted or the injury, provided they pursue it in the proper manner and order through public authority.

---

<margin>To the sixth argument.</margin>
To the sixth argument, concerning one who acts as an obstacle to another so that they do not obtain a "benefice" <note>original: "beneficium," a church office that provides an income.</note>, Saint Thomas responds with three statements. First: If someone justly—for instance, intending the honor of God or the advantage of the Church—blocks a less worthy person so that the priesthood may be conferred on a more worthy one, no obligation of restitution arises from this, because no fault intervened. The second statement is: If someone unjustly blocks a worthy and fit candidate out of hatred, through counsel, or some other way, before the prelate or electors have firmly decided to confer it on him, he is bound to make some compensation. This should be weighed according to the status of the persons and the proximity the candidate had to obtaining it, according to the judgment of a wise man. He is not, however, bound to the whole value, because that provision could have been blocked in other ways.

<margin>Third guidance.</margin>
The third assertion...

### Question VI of the Fourth Book

...offered. However, if someone should prevent a person from obtaining a <term>benefice</term> <note>An ecclesiastical office, like a parish or bishopric, that provided the holder with a living income from land or tithes.</note> to which a superior had already firmly decided to appoint them in full, then by the Aristotelian rule cited in the argument: *That which is but a small distance from the thing seems to be no distance at all* <note>original: "Quod parùm distat à re, nihil distare videtur." This is a legal maxim suggesting that if an outcome is nearly certain, it should be treated as if it has already occurred.</note>; yet this must be judged according to the actual capacity of the person involved.

<margin>Whether one who does not confer a benefice on a more worthy or even a worthy person is bound to make restitution.</margin>
¶ Before we descend to the examination of those who hinder such appointments, we must investigate the one who confers the office. We must ask: if he does not confer the office upon the more worthy person, or at least upon a worthy one, is he bound to make restitution? And to whom must that restitution be made? This is a point where the <term>Angelic Doctor</term> <note>A traditional title for Saint Thomas Aquinas.</note> is found wanting here, even though the entire matter depends upon it.

<margin>The opinion of Cajetan.</margin>
Indeed, <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Aquinas.</note> here, in his third doubt on Article 2, takes it as an undisputed fact that one who does not confer a benefice upon the more worthy candidate is bound to make restitution to that candidate. For, he says, such a person sins against <term>distributive justice</term> <note>Justice regarding how a community distributes honors or goods among its members based on their merit.</note>. It is certain that this kind of injustice gives rise to an obligation of restitution; for a distributor is bound to apply that which belongs to the whole community to its individual parts. Therefore, if he does not confer it upon someone according to their merit, distributive justice is thereafter transformed into <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Justice governing private exchanges between individuals, requiring an exact "tit-for-tat" equality.</note>, according to which he is bound to restore it to the person—as Saint Thomas clearly taught in the third solution to Article 1 of this question. And certainly, if Cajetan’s foundation were the genuine truth, his conclusion would be beyond doubt.

<margin>Cajetan's foundation.</margin>
For he believes that ecclesiastical goods are to be treated exactly like the goods of a republic, which are owed to citizens by distributive justice alone, seeing as they were established for their benefit. But we have refuted this foundation to the best of our ability in the last question of the previous book. There, through both sacred oracles and sound reasoning, we established the contrary: namely, that although we cannot deny that the conferring of benefices ought to be done *in the likeness* of distributive justice, its ultimate end is to establish the equality of commutative justice. This is because <term>tithes</term> <note>A ten-percent tax on agricultural produce paid to the church.</note> were not instituted as a reward for individuals because they happen to be outstanding in letters or morals. If churches were not necessary, tithes would never have been commanded of Christians. They are, therefore, mere stipends for the church, established for ministers in exchange for their ministry. They are given to them not because they are good priests, as we noted there, but because they preside well; according to the word of Christ: *The laborer is worthy of his wages* <note>original: "Dignus est operarius mercede sua." Luke 10:7.</note>. And that word of Paul: *If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?* <note>original: "Si nos vobis spiritualia seminamus, non est magnum si carnalia vestra metamus." 1 Corinthians 9:11.</note> For the same reason, they were once commanded for the Levites. Since we have already explained all these matters sufficiently there, they do not need to be repeated. 

<column-break/>

Therefore, what must be meditated upon here is primarily <term>commutative justice</term>, through which popes and the electors of church ministers owe suitable ministers to those same churches, in proportion to the stipends that each church pays them. For we must look upon Christ as the founder of the Christian family, who instituted the ministries of the church and proposed the reward of tithes for the ministers, and committed it to the faithfulness and prudence of his stewards to provide suitable ministers for his churches.

¶ From these points, unless I am mistaken, two conclusions are plainly gathered.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
First: A provider is bound by commutative justice to provide a worthy person to the church. Therefore, he who does not do this, but rejects a worthy man to prefer an unworthy one, is bound to make restitution—not to the man he passed over, but to the church.

<margin>Adrian.</margin>
Indeed, <term>Adrian</term> <note>Pope Adrian VI (reigned 1522–1523), a Dutch scholar and reformer.</note> later held this same view in that question of restitution regarding the conferring of benefices, although he did not discuss the matter at such length. The conclusion is notable: for he does not sin against commutative justice except against the church that pays the stipends. For the "worthy" man has no <term>acquired right</term> <note>A legal term for a right that is already vested in a person, rather than a mere expectation.</note>, nor were tithes instituted primarily for his sake.

¶ This is confirmed by the analogy already suggested. If a head of a household sent his hired steward to bring in workers, and the steward intentionally hired those who were not fit for the labor, he would certainly be bound to make restitution—not to the fit workers he passed over, but to the master whom he harmed. Furthermore, the common sense of mankind applauds this opinion. For if a King or a Pope were to "marry" an unsuitable and unworthy man to some church, the consensus of the people would not hold that he is bound to make restitution to the one he did not give it to, but in truth to the church itself. For that reason, he ought to provide another assistant to the bishop, or look to it in some other way so that the harm done to the church—to the detriment of souls—might be alleviated.

<margin>The second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion is that where the priesthood is conferred upon a worthy man, even if a *more* worthy man was passed over, although the elector or provider sins gravely, there is no reason why he should be condemned to restitution by the rigor of justice. The first part of this has already been sufficiently demonstrated by us elsewhere, where we brought forth the crowd of evils that spring from the fact that the more worthy are not chosen. Yet the second part derives its truth from the fact that, in such a case, there is no sin against commutative justice. For we call a man "worthy" in proportion to the <term>prebend</term> <note>The portion of the church's income granted to a specific cleric.</note> he receives. If, therefore, a minister is applied to a church in proportion to the quantity of his stipend, no injury is done to it against the rigor of commutative justice, such that it would owe...

The author argues that restitution is owed to the Church itself (for providing an unfit minister) rather than to the passed-over candidate, as the office is a duty of service rather than a personal reward.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 347 regarding whether a person who fails to appoint the most worthy candidate to a church office (a "benefice") is required to make restitution. Soto is navigating the complex legal and moral distinctions between the "rights" of a candidate and the "duties" of the person making the appointment.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right

restitution is owed to him. I would argue against such rigor: because some injury against the duty of faithfulness is always committed against him, since another more worthy person could have been provided for him. ¶ Against this, however, is an argument that the common people might raise against us: for those who long for these <term>priesthoods</term> <note>Ecclesiastical offices or roles.</note> think, along with Cajetan, that restitution must be made to them because a sin is committed against <term>distributive justice</term> <note>The virtue of distributing shared honors or resources fairly based on merit.</note>. But one should not respond to them by denying that distributive justice obligates one to make restitution to those to whom things are poorly distributed. However, that is understood to be the case when it is "pure" distributive justice—namely, that by which goods are distributed that were established for the sake of the citizens themselves. But this type of justice is not what we are discussing here, as has been explained: for although priesthoods and <term>prebends</term> <note>The portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> are owed to the worthy, and the richer ones to the more worthy, this is not for their own sake, but for the sake of the churches to whom the ministry is owed.

<margin>How a prelate sins when a more worthy person is passed over.</margin>
Yet it cannot be denied that, because distributive justice has been violated, a prelate who has passed over a more worthy person must take a more careful account of it when another election occurs. ¶ I would assert this even more affirmatively and clearly regarding the conferring of secular <term>magistracies</term> <note>Government or judicial offices.</note> which serve the administration of justice. These are indeed owed to the more worthy by distributive justice; but nevertheless, if they are passed over, restitution is not to be made to the ones passed over, but to the people who contribute the salaries, and who suffer the loss and the injury. ¶ But immediately an argument arises against this: namely, that if these things are true, it clearly follows that neither would someone who injuriously prevented another from obtaining a benefice be bound to make restitution to him; yet Saint Thomas and all theologians teach the contrary. The answer is that there is no such logical consequence. For even if he who chooses poorly violates <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Justice concerning private dealings and the restoration of specific rights or property.</note> against the church, nonetheless, he who is capable of the priesthood and fit for it has a "particular right" to seek and procure it, and, if it is granted to him, to possess it. Therefore, he who hinders someone attempting to obtain it against this right does an injustice to him and must make restitution.

<margin>The rule of Gerald is false.</margin>
Wherefore, that rule of <term>Gerald Odonis</term> <note>A 14th-century Franciscan theologian.</note> is false and misleading, which <term>Hadrian</term> <note>Likely referring to Pope Adrian VI in his theological writings.</note> recites in that chapter on restitution: "Consequently, I ask whether one who hinders someone from that which was not yet his by right, but depended on the mere will of another, becomes liable to him for restitution." I say it is false: for although it may be in the discretion

<column-break/>

of the prelate to give it to this person or that one, nonetheless, the other person is despoiled of the "particular right" he has to seek it. Just as one who hinders a poor man by force or fraud from seeking alms is bound to make restitution to him. For although others may grant them freely, he nonetheless has the right of seeking.

<margin>He explains the text of Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ Having considered these things, let us descend to the literal text of Saint Thomas. But regarding his first assertion—namely, that he who is a hindrance to a more worthy person being given an office is not bound by the "cord of restitution":
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
you may perhaps doubt whether the same should be understood regarding one who stands in the way of a worthy person, so that it might be given to another worthy person. The answer is that the judgment is the same: because since both have the right to seek, I may favor whom I wish. Especially since in that case, distributive justice is not violated.

<margin>A Rule.</margin>
¶ In all these matters, however, this rule must be especially kept in mind: that neither force nor fraud should intervene. For if I use force or fraud against a worthy person so that he does not obtain it, there is no doubt that I have inflicted an injury upon him; and so I am bound to make restitution to him—although if I did it for the sake of another worthy person, perhaps I am not bound to the full amount. ¶ Nor does it matter whether you hinder one so that it is given to another worthy person, or so that it is given to yourself, provided you are also worthy. For anyone has the right to seek for himself those things of which he is worthy. And although procuring benefices that have the <term>care of souls</term> <note>A "cure of souls" refers to the spiritual responsibility for a parish.</note> attached is often a sin, it does not for that reason impose the bond of restitution.

<margin>The opinion of Scotus and Richard.</margin>
¶ However, that opinion of <term>Scotus</term> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308).</note> in the 4th book, distinction 15, and of <term>Richard</term> <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302).</note in the same place, must not be passed over here without examination. For they say that if someone procures a prebend for himself or another and is an obstacle to someone else obtaining it—and does this not to harm the other, but to benefit himself or a friend—he is bound to no restitution. But if he does it specifically seeking the harm of the other, then he is bound.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan also seems to subscribe to this opinion in his second doubt here. And in support of this same opinion they cite the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "l. 2. ff. de aqua pluuia arcend." This refers to the Digest of Justinian, a massive collection of Roman law.</note> in the law on "restraining rainwater," in the paragraph "The same Labeo, 2," where it is held that one who breaks a water pipe passing through his own land to a neighbor's property—not with the intent of harming, but for his own use—is not acting injuriously. But if he does it not to benefit himself but to harm his neighbor, he is being injurious to him. But truly, that rule of law has been poorly understood by those authors. For the "intent to harm" can indeed be a sin against charity; but nevertheless, it cannot obligate one to make restitution, as we have often said above, unless it was against justice. Therefore, it must be seen, as far as the matter of restitution is concerned,

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into when a person who interferes with an ecclesiastical appointment (a prebend) is required to make restitution. Soto is currently examining the opinions of St. Thomas Aquinas and the commentary of Cajetan regarding the distinction between acting out of malice and acting unjustly.</meta>

### Book Four, Question VI.

...it remains; not by what intention you do it, but by what right. And this is how the law is to be understood: for he who blocks a neighbor's water, not to benefit himself, is seen as not acting by his own right, and therefore can be restrained in court. However, if he wishes to lay the foundation of a wall through a watercourse that passes through his own land, and by doing so breaks the veins of the water, even if he does it out of hatred for his enemy and violates the duty of charity, he nevertheless owes him no restitution. Therefore, regarding our proposal: he who, using his own right, procures a <term>prebend</term> <note>An income-generating position within a cathedral or church.</note> for himself or a friend without force or fraud—even if he does so out of hatred for another and sins against charity—is bound to no restitution.

<margin>He explains the second saying of St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ And through this, the reasoning of the second saying of Saint Thomas becomes clear: namely, that he who hinders someone who was "on the path" to obtaining a position, if he does so unjustly, is bound to restitution. For example, because he intends the person's harm out of hatred or vengeance. For acting out of hatred or vengeance does not, by itself, weigh you down with the burden of restitution, but acting unjustly does: that is, acting with no right of your own, but by violating another's. Nevertheless, acting out of hatred is a certain sign that you are using no right of your own.

<margin>The third saying is explained.</margin>
¶ In explaining the third saying, <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> puts in much work: namely, to explain that rule from Aristotle's *Physics*, Book 2, text 56: <note>original: "Quod parum distat à re, nihil distare videtur."</note> "That which is a small distance from a thing seems to be no distance at all." For he raises many exceptions in moral matters. For he who is "almost" about to sin does not, because of that, sin. And much less is he who was "almost" about to kill a man punished as a murderer, nor is he bound to restitution. Just as he who was "almost" about to steal is not a thief, but only he who actually steals. Likewise, if a king "almost" fell into an ambush, though he himself was fortunate, those who had laid the traps are not bound to make restitution to him. By these objections, unless I am mistaken, Cajetan—plainly in error—opposes the mind of Saint Thomas, undeservedly rejecting his rule. He could have excused all these exceptions if he had looked at the mind of the divine Thomas for a little while longer. For he struggled with an <term>amphibology</term> <note>An ambiguity in grammatical structure or meaning.</note>. It is a far different thing to be "almost" about to cause damage, than to cause damage to a thing that is "almost" realized. And the divine Thomas did not dream that he who is "almost" about to cause damage is bound to restitution, as Cajetan thinks; but rather he who has actually caused damage to a thing that is "almost" possessed. For example: there is a vineyard or there are crops whose fruit is just now ripening. If a hunter with his company, running around them, was "almost" about to trample them, he is bound to no restitution, because he caused no damage. But if he trampled them while crossing through the middle, he is bound for the whole amount, because he caused damage to fruit that was very nearly ready. Similarly in the case proposed: if you were "almost" about to hinder a man from a prebend, certainly you would be liable for no restitution, because you caused no damage. If, however, you were an actual hindrance to why he did not obtain it, you caused damage to a thing that he "almost" had; and thus, according to your ability, you are bound for the whole amount. However, the divine Thomas wisely added these words, "according to his ability," because certainly in these kinds of hindrances, it can hardly happen that full restitution can be made.

<column-break/>

<margin><unclear>In [this matter]</unclear></margin>
¶ But truly, since these things can come into practical use, do not be annoyed if we express the matter more urgently. When Saint Thomas says the hinderer is bound for the whole amount when the mind of the <term>elector</term> <note>The person or official with the power to grant the office.</note> was "firmly set" on giving it to this person, he either means when he had *already* given it—and this would not be hindering, but taking away—or he means when he had not yet given it. And then it appears that it is not quite the same as if he had given it, such that the hinderer would be bound for the whole; for the elector could have changed his mind. Indeed, he could have done so justly, if another more worthy or equally worthy person appeared later. The response is that it is not to be understood as when he had already given it. For the divine Thomas discerns three degrees. The first is when the elector had not yet decided in his mind to give it to this person, but the person was nevertheless "on the path"; and then restitution must be made according to the judgment of a prudent person. The third is when he has already conferred it, and of this he makes no mention, because this would not be hindering, but taking away. Therefore, if anyone, after the conferral was made, unjustly hindered possession, it is manifest that he is bound for the whole. The middle case, however, is that of which Saint Thomas speaks: namely, when the prelate had already decided to give it to him.

<margin>Cajetan's exposition.</margin>
And then Cajetan says in the fourth doubt, that the hinderer is bound for the whole because the elector was already "bound" to give it to him.

<margin>Rejection [of Cajetan].</margin>
However, I do not know where he inferred this from Saint Thomas, nor is it according to the truth. For the divine Thomas does not place the root of restitution there—in the idea that the elector was "bound" to give it—but in the fact that he had *already decided* to give it. Therefore, even if that person were not the "more worthy" candidate, but merely a "worthy" one: if the hinderer, through force or fraud, changed the mind of the grantor, he is certainly bound for the whole. For although the grantor might have conferred it of his own accord, and was not "bound" to give it to that man, nevertheless the hinderer took from him through fraud what he already almost possessed. And the divine Thomas signifies this when he says, "unjustly and for an undue cause." From which I infer that if the hinderer did not do it through force or fraud, but by making known through prayers...

# Dominic de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

<margin>Second corollary.</margin>
...giving the truth: even if he changed his will in favor of another worthy person, he would not be bound to restitution. ¶ And from this, it is inferred secondly that the same should be judged regarding legacies in wills. For <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> and several others establish a distinction between someone who prevents another from obtaining a benefit and someone who prevents a legatee from having a testator make a legacy to them. They say that the one who hinders the legatee is in no way bound to restitution. To me, however—unless I am mistaken—a different line of reasoning is more appealing. I believe we must use the distinction already established: namely, whether you hinder the person through force and fraud, or through mere entreaties. For if you use force or fraud so that the one who was ready to leave his goods to Peter does not do so, you are bound to make restitution. For although the testator acted of his own free will, you nevertheless took away by injury the right he had of receiving—that is, the faculty, capacity, and immediate fitness. However, if you neither brought force nor created fraud, you are not bound, even if you did it through entreaties.

<margin>On students providing votes.</margin>
¶ Finally, for the sake of our own Schools <note>Soto is referring to the University of Salamanca, where student voting for professors was a standard practice.</note>, it is worthwhile to add a word regarding current affairs. Specifically, how students who provide votes, or others who in various ways hinder someone from attaining a <term>Cathedra</term> <note>A "Chair" or professorship.</note>, are bound to restitution. To arrive at this answer, one must first of all not doubt that students providing votes are not "witnesses," as some believe, but are truly "electors." Indeed, if they were witnesses, there would be no need to summon the entire student body; it would be enough to inquire of a fair number. Nor would it be necessary to stand by the number of votes, nor to ask for opinions through secret ballots. In short, not only the form of voting but the logic itself shows they are electors, since the Rector is entirely bound to abide by their votes. Thus, they cannot be compelled to vote as if they were witnesses, but they can renounce their right to elect—unless the Rector and his advisors see a reason to compel them, either due to a low turnout or to prevent other frauds. This being established, we must judge them exactly as we did regarding <term>prebends</term> <note>Income-producing church offices.</note>: namely, that he who passes over the more worthy and elects a worthy person, though he may sin mortally against <term>distributive justice</term> <note>Justice concerning how honors and resources are shared within a community.</note>, is nevertheless not entangled in the bond of restitution. This is because he gives the University what he owes it by the rigor of <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Justice regarding private exchanges and debts.</note>. But if, passing over the worthy, he elects an unworthy person—and these things I believe are true 

<column-break/>

which we said above—he is bound to restitution. This is not to the one who was passed over, but to the University, if it were possible to restore it. For the University's stipends are not established for the sake of the individuals themselves, but are mere salaries which the University pays to its servants. Hence, just as a King who does not appoint a worthy minister to the commonwealth owes nothing to the person passed over, but rather to the commonwealth, so he who elects an unworthy person causes damage only to the commonwealth which pays the salary. Therefore, although the elector owes the Chair to the more worthy person, this is not for the candidate’s sake, but because by commutative justice he owes the Schools such a servant. I would not deny, however, that he does the candidate some injury; and therefore he would be bound, all other things being equal, to favor him for another Chair. Regarding those who hinder others, the reasoning is different. For he who through force or fraud hinders someone from obtaining a Chair—I do not mean by giving his vote to another, but by physically blocking him from seeking the Chair which he was otherwise certain to obtain, or by deceiving the electors so they do not choose him—is bound to him either in part or in full, in proportion to the fraud or force, because he despoils the candidate of the right he has to seek the position. ¶ Regarding the disqualification of voters, we touched on this in Book 1, and now we repeat it more fully. For students commit injustice in voting in two ways. 

<margin>A distinction to be noted.</margin>
In one way, when they sneak in, though they are not listeners <note>original: "auditores"; registered students of that specific lecture course.</note> of that same Chair; and these, if they cause damage, are immediately bound to restitution because they truly have no right to vote. In the second way, because they are listeners, yet they are to be deprived of the right to vote due to a crime—for example, <term>ambitus</term> <note>Bribery or unlawful canvassing for office.</note> or what they call "subornation." In that case, before they are condemned, they can indeed vote. Therefore, if the Rector does not question them about the crime, they are not acting wickedly by voting. If, however, they are questioned, they are bound to speak the truth, especially if they are under suspicion; and if condemned, they are bound to obey. For if they labor under no infamy or evidence, the interrogation is injurious; and thus, as long as they can do so without lying, they may remain silent. But if, when justly questioned, they conceal the truth, then they act most wickedly—just as if they were condemned—and they act against justice if they provide a vote, since they have escaped a rightful judgment through their own wrongdoing. The same should be judged of those who are not inscribed on the student roll. For they do not lose the right to vote "by the very fact" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> if they are truly regular listeners. And therefore, unless through a sen-

# Fourth Book, Question VI.

...they may even be deprived, they can use the same right.
¶ Regarding those things acquired through gambling—how they are subject to the obligation of restitution if they are demanded, or if force or fraud intervened—enough was said in the preceding question. Regarding found items, however, we must speak in the following book in the question on theft.

### ARTICLE IV.

->**Whether it is sufficient to restore only the simple value**<-
->**of what was unjustly taken.**<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' at the beginning of the article.</image-desc>
It is not enough to have defined that all things taken are burdened with the weight of restitution, but we must also investigate whether it is always sufficient to restore the simple amount <note>The "simple amount" (Latin: *simplum*) refers to the base value of the item or money stolen, without added penalties.</note>. And it is argued from the negative side. For it is read in Exodus 22: "If someone steals a sheep or an ox and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep." That, however, was a judicial law; in the likeness of which similar laws have been established under the law of grace <note>The "law of grace" refers to the Christian era or the Gospel, as opposed to the Old Testament "law of works."</note> by princes. For Zacchaeus said something similar to commend himself to Christ in Luke 19: "If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold." And the practice of the external forum <note>The "external forum" refers to the public legal system (civil or ecclesiastical courts), as opposed to the "internal forum" of confession and conscience.</note> is similar; for a thief is not condemned only to the simple amount, but to return it multiplied, or to suffer punishment. Since, therefore, civil laws bind in conscience, it follows that it is not always enough to restore the simple amount. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that the object of restitution is nothing other than to recall to justice that inequality which was created by the taking; this is achieved if you return exactly as much as you took.

<margin>Two things to be considered in the taking of a thing.</margin>
To the question he responds with two conclusions, according to the two members of this distinction. For there are two things to consider in the taking of another's property. First, the substance of the taking itself, from which the inequality results, so that the person from whom the thing was taken has less, while the one who took it has more. And this is common to both just and unjust takings. For whether you receive a thing by loan, or take it by theft, or buy it on credit: the other has as much less as you have more. The second thing considered in the taking is the manner of taking itself: for instance, if someone takes or tries to take something by fraud or force. And this always involves an injustice, whether he actually takes the thing or takes nothing: like one who failed in his attempt where he could not prevail.

<column-break/>

¶ Let this, then, be the first conclusion. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> As far as the nature and purpose of restitution are concerned, it is generally sufficient to restore the simple amount of what you took, whether you did it by right or by wrong. For indeed, the name "restitution" refers precisely to an office of <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Commutative justice governs private transactions and the exchange of goods between individuals, requiring strict equality between what is given and what is received.</note>, having nothing to do with <term>vindicative justice</term> <note>Vindicative (or retributive) justice is concerned with the punishment of crimes and offenses.</note>. Because of this, it does not matter to the obligation of restitution whether the taking was just or unjust; its only role is to establish equality. You received four, whether through a loan or through theft; therefore, you owe that same amount by way of restitution. If, however, you attempted to commit a theft but were unable to steal anything, you owe nothing by way of restitution. From which it follows that the obligation of restitution, when the debt is certain, does not wait for a judge's sentence but arises from the law itself. Regarding this "augmented" restitution—namely, whether someone should sometimes restore more according to conscience than they took—the discussion will return in the following book under the title of theft. <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion: Regarding the penalty owed by reason of an unjust taking, no one is bound before a legal condemnation, but only when the condemnation has been made. This conclusion would send us into a very wide field of debate here, were it not that it was treated by us in a long and accurate discussion in Book 2, Question 6. For there we established its truth with a long line of reasons, where we declared how, if the sentence is a fine, it must be paid immediately by the defendant; if, however, it is a corporal punishment, he is not bound to offer himself up, but it is enough if he endures it without causing injury to the ministers of justice. Therefore, we should add no word here regarding this second conclusion, lest we be annoying in our repetition. Let anyone interested look there. But no doubt remains regarding the first conclusion after what has been said so far. <margin>A distinction to be noted.</margin> ¶ As for what pertains to this article, it is only that you learn to discern when a matter pertains to mere restitution and when it pertains to a legal penalty. For the former is immediately subject to the burden of restitution without waiting for any sentence; the latter, however, only after the sentence has been passed. Let one example serve for many. For we said there that when a price is established by law for grain, or wine, or any other merchandise, then the one who sells it for more is immediately bound like a thief to the restitution of the excess over the just price; but to the penalty only when condemned. In the same way, one who steals a sheep or an ox is immediately bound to restore the value of the animal. But the fourfold or sevenfold penalty is required only when condemned. By which certainly is satisfied...
