# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

the first part of the main argument has been satisfied. Therefore, consider the rest in the same way. One must investigate, I say, whether the laws are **penal**; <note>A "penal law" in this context is one that does not bind the person's conscience to the act itself, but only obliges them to submit to the penalty if they are caught and sentenced.</note> in which case they do not bind the conscience except after a sentence has been passed. It is otherwise, however, if the laws are of a different kind.
<margin>Tax laws bind in conscience.</margin>
Thus it follows that the laws regarding customs duties and taxes, which are contributed publicly to the king as stipends, bind the conscience to payment even before a legal sentence is given, because they are not merely penal laws. I say this provided that the taxes are just. However, where the matter is doubtful, the judgment does not belong to the subjects; rather, one must turn to the prince, and in the meantime, the laws must be observed, unless they display the most obvious tyranny. ¶ Regarding that tribute which our people call the <term>Alcabala</term> <note>original: "Alcaualam"; a historic sales tax in Spain and its colonies.</note>, we have already disputed this at the end of the previous book, where we spoke of how much justice it possesses according to our understanding. For it is, if demanded with moderation, equitable and just. We said, however, among other things, that it is perhaps permissible in conscience to use this moderation: that while items of no great price are being sold, the sellers are not bound to seek out the tax collectors to pay; for it is enough to pay when it is requested by them. This is provided that in the sale, they do not use fraud or trickery to hide themselves. ¶ However, laws by which the transport of merchandise out of the kingdom is prohibited are penal. Therefore, if you carry out grain, horses, or gold, you are not bound to pay the penalty unless you are caught. Although, as we touched upon in the preceding sections, it is a mortal sin to export such things that are forbidden for the benefit of the realm. Nor does the contrary argument hold weight—that tax collectors, who buy the rights to these fiscal penalties with their own money, have a right to receive them, and therefore he who does not pay causes them loss. This, I say, does not hold: because they ought to understand that they buy those same fiscal penalties on the condition that they extort them precisely from those whom they catch. Indeed,
<margin>Note.</margin>
I would add this in passing for the present: that in the borders of kingdoms which belong to the same king, these prohibitions on the extraction of merchandise and commerce ought not to exist; for they seem to be prohibited not so much for the good of the kingdoms as for profit. But I do not wish to bark against public laws.
<margin>A doubt concerning those cutting wood in others' forests.</margin>
¶ A specific doubt arises here concerning those who stealthily cut wood in others' forests, or stealthily graze their animals in others' pastures. For the common people think that because those who are caught are fined money, which is decreed by a penal law, those who escape are bound to no restitution. This, however, is manifestly false; rather, the same rule must be

<column-break/>

used: namely, that you must distinguish the penalty from the price of the thing taken by theft. For I am accustomed to use this reasoning for the sake of clarity, according to my understanding.
<margin>A distinction.</margin>
For either the <term>coppice</term> <note>original: "caedua sylua"; a forest managed by periodic cutting.</note> is the property of the same city or castle of which those who cut the wood are citizens or inhabitants. In that case, I judge that unless they cause significant destruction, they are bound to no restitution, neither of the penalty nor of the price, unless they are caught. Regarding the penalty, the matter is certain; but also regarding the price, I am persuaded of this because the town seems to distribute wood to its townsmen under that law: that he who is caught pays the penalty, but he who escapes acquires the prey for himself for free. And I would judge the same if each of two neighboring towns has forests; for then they also seem to grant each other wood by that law. Therefore, they are not bound to restitution unless they commit some significant depredation, as we were saying; but if they are caught, they are bound to undergo the penalty. It happens otherwise, however, when carrying wood stealthily from forests that are entirely foreign. Namely, those which belong neither to your town nor to another neighbor whose townsmen share in the forests of your town in turn, as we just said—perhaps because your castle possesses no forest. And this is what is at issue in the question. For there are those who, having embraced that rule—that where
<margin>The rule of some.</margin>
the law applies a penalty, it does not bind under the guilt of sin—render the consciences of those who steal wood secure, so that unless they are caught, they are not subject to restitution. This, however, as we discussed extensively in Book 1, is a deceptive rule. Rather, the law imposes a penalty precisely because a fault underlies it. For a penalty cannot be imposed except for a fault; and for that reason, those who plunder wood from such forests are absolutely bound to the restitution of the price of the wood. For they truly commit the sin of theft, which is mortal in its nature. And the same must be judged regarding pastures. As for the penalty, however, they are not bound unless they are caught and condemned. It would be otherwise if, by chance, the one who forbids the forest explained his will—that he wishes to give the wood under that law and condition; but I have never heard of this happening. ¶ However, some warnings are necessary for the present.
<margin>First notable point.</margin>
First, it is lawful for the cutting of a forest to be forbidden for the good of the commonwealth: namely, lest it be dissipated to its ruin.
<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, it is to be noted that lords to whom the king grants towns with forests cannot guard them in any other way than the king would have done. For he does not grant them any other right than he himself has. And therefore, if the forests allow it, they are not to be forbidden to the townsmen for necessary uses. Indeed, even if the forests are private...

<meta>This page continues Dominic de Soto’s exploration of the "penal" nature of laws regarding natural resources. # Question VI of the Fourth Book

...are the lord’s property, they should not be forbidden with such rigor that physical punishment is inflicted, nor indeed a heavy fine. For truly, trees and wood which the earth produced without cultivation ought to be common by the **law of nations** (*ius gentium*). <note>The "law of nations" refers to a body of customary law thought to be common to all people, based on natural reason rather than specific statutes.</note> Human life cannot be carried out without the daily use of wood. For this reason, their theft is not to be weighed on the same scale as if someone were to steal money from your chest or furniture from your house. Therefore, those who cut wood are nowhere among the nations branded with the infamy of robbers or thieves. It is sufficient, then, to demand moderate penalties. And in truth, where lords keep wretched subjects away from the forests with such bitter punishment that they suffer extreme poverty, they could perhaps, without mortal sin, steal those logs that are necessary for their daily use, at least for their hearths.

¶ In almost the same way, one must judge concerning **hunting**. For hunting is first of all common by the law of nations: namely, that the wild beast or bird which had not been caught by anyone before passes into the right of the one who catches it, as is clear in the *Institutes* and the *Digest* regarding the "division of things." <note>The *Institutes* and *Digest* are parts of the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundational body of Roman Law.</note> <margin>Aristotle</margin> Hence Aristotle, in the first book of his *Politics*, chapter 5, argues that the art of hunting is a part of the art of war. And this right is founded in that dominion given to men in Genesis 1 over all the animals of the earth, the birds of the air, and the swimmers of the waters. <margin>On hunting: for what reasons it may be forbidden.</margin> Nevertheless, hunting is forbidden by law for a threefold reason. <margin>The First.</margin> First, even if the place of hunting is common to the city or town, it can be lawfully forbidden by the prince and the lord by way of governance; for wild beasts and fish are not only an ornament and grace to the republic, but they also serve necessity. For that reason, hunting must not be left to the recklessness of the common people, but must be done by order and law, lest it [the wildlife] perish. <margin>The Second.</margin> Second, the prince can also dedicate some common places of the republic to his own use; nor for this, as some think, is the consent of the people required. It is just that for his own dignity, for the sake of recreating the mind, he should have hunting ready. Moreover, because it is not fitting for boars, stags, and that kind of beast to be hunted by commoners; rather, they should be reserved for the high-born, who may practice the "images of battles" against them. <note>Hunting was often seen as a necessary training for the nobility to maintain their military skills in peacetime.</note>

¶ However, this must not be passed over here without a warning: that the reasoning is not the same for great nobles to preserve and forbid hunting for their own sake as it is for the prince, even if it was granted to them with their rights. For a King can, for example, reserve ten or twelve places for himself in the whole kingdom,

<column-break/>

and perhaps he could not reserve two or three hundred. If, however, the individual nobles had several guarded places in their own towns or territories, the burden on the kingdom would become more intolerable. For wild beasts, birds, and fish are common by the law of nations, as cited in the passages of the *Institutes* and *Digest* on the division of things; and therefore the people are not to be restrained too much from hunting, since they also have the liberty in that way both to recreate the mind and to seek a living.

<margin>The Third.</margin> ¶ But in a third way, which pertains to the matter, hunting is guarded: namely, because it is in a place that is not common to the town, but the private property of the lord himself, in which he guards his hunting. For, as is held in the places recently cited regarding the division of things, the lord of the land can prohibit anyone from entering it for the sake of hunting. But indeed, in all these things, first of all, as we were saying about the woods, care must be taken lest bitter punishments be established; because that is not considered theft or robbery in the same way as when houses or purses are plundered. Therefore, it is certainly cruel to punish with corporal penalty those entering forbidden places for the sake of hunting; but it is enough if they pay double or triple [the value], and lose their traps and tools. <margin>Those who guard wild beasts are bound to pay for damages caused.</margin> Furthermore, this must be most solemnly advised: that those who guard wild beasts should pay in full for damages caused [by the animals to neighbors' crops], which happens very rarely. ¶ But at last, having set aside the penalties—which without doubt are not owed before a legal sentence—let us descend to the **restitution** of the value of the small beast or the catch. It must be said that where hunting is preserved in a common place, and he who hunts is a citizen, I judge him to be bound to no restitution, even if perhaps there is some fault in acting against the law; since that hunting belongs to the whole republic, the law is not presumed to bind one to restitution, but to a penalty if he is condemned. For that is indeed more just than what we said about wood. But when the place is the lord's private property, if you enter the place itself, it is a species of theft—and then most especially when it is surrounded by a wall—and therefore you are bound to the restitution of the damage. I would say this if the place were walled, because if it were open, I do not see why an obligation of restitution arises. For truly, even if the lord of the land has that right of hunting there, so that he can shut others out from it, it does not therefore follow that he has ownership of the wild beasts that are nourished there, just as he does of the trees or the things growing from the earth. First, because the earth does not bear wild beasts like other fruits, but they, as living beings, produce themselves; then also because the same animals are wandering and free to roam wherever they wish. If, therefore, the lord of the land is not the lord of the wild animals, it follows that if someone kills them, he does not [necessarily commit theft]...

And this is most consistent with Law 16, Title 28 of the Third **Partida**, <note>The *Siete Partidas* was a major 13th-century Spanish legal code that remained influential in Soto's time.</note> which decrees that whoever hunts on another’s land without being pre-warned by the lord of the estate may acquire what he captures for himself. This would certainly be unjust if the animal were already under the lord's ownership. However, he who captures a small beast after being warned should not keep it for himself, but it should go to the lord of the estate: namely, as a penalty because he entered another’s land. Therefore, perhaps before a legal condemnation, he is held to nothing. 

But if you pierce a wild animal or catch it in a snare outside the lord’s property, it is certain that you are not held to restitution: especially if you were hunting it on your own estate; and much less so if you found a wild animal causing you damage. Unless, perhaps, there was an agreement between the townsfolk and the lord for a fixed price—established by the lord—that they should not harm the game anywhere, but should renounce their right of hunting, which belongs to the **law of nations**. <note>original: *iuri gentium*. This refers to the concept that certain rights, like hunting wild animals, belong to all people by nature.</note> This happens perhaps because the lord pays for damages in good faith and grants them some remission of taxes so that they renounce that same right.

¶ Birds, however, fall into three categories: for some are purely wild, and to forbid the fowling of these, even on one’s own land, is an injustice; since they stay nowhere except by way of passage. An exception might be if they were very precious, such as hawks: about which there would be a bit more doubt. But even so, I would not dare to oblige hunters to such restitution. Others are at the opposite extreme, being tame and domestic. To steal these, without any controversy, is theft. But others are <margin>About pigeons</margin> in the middle: such as pigeons: which are neither entirely domestic nor entirely wild. And regarding these, I have no doubt that one must stand by the municipal laws, just as with beehives: namely, if a period or distance is prescribed by law—for instance, that no one may catch them within so many paces—it must be judged that they are domestic up to that line. Therefore, anyone can catch them outside that limit, provided it is done in ways permitted by law. 

For the King can also forbid them from being ensnared by certain traps or nets; in that case, however, an obligation of restitution does not arise, but rather a penalty after condemnation. But if they are caught within the space prescribed by law, perhaps the captors are not immune from restitution; since up to that limit, the pigeons are made domestic. However, they are not to be pressed with the utmost rigor as if they were stealing them from the dovecote itself. But where no civil laws exist, if you consult only **natural law**, it appears that it is permitted to build a dovecote, provided there is no protest from those who

<column-break/>

have farms nearby and are going to suffer damages. Indeed, if you listen to **Cajetan** in his *Summa*, <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), was a leading Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> it is a mortal sin to raise pigeons to the ruin of others. But while that might perhaps be true when the detriment is immense, if the lords provide sufficient fodder for the number of pigeons in the dovecote, I do not recognize such a great crime. For this kind of bird is useful to the commonwealth, not only for food, but by reason of its **manure**; <note>original: *stercorationis*. In the 16th century, pigeon guano was a highly valued fertilizer for agriculture.</note> therefore there is no reason why they should be driven out of the civil commonwealth entirely.

The arguments, therefore, raised at the head of the question do not require a solution, but rather an attention to what has been said. For that law of fourfold or fivefold repayment was judicial; and therefore it was enough for a thief, regarding restitution, to return the base amount: but once condemned, he ought to pay the penalty. **Zacchaeus**, however, placed this among other works of **supererogation**: <note>Zacchaeus is a biblical figure (Luke 19:8) who promised to repay fourfold anyone he had cheated. "Supererogation" refers to doing more than what is strictly required by moral duty.</note> that he would spontaneously return fourfold if he had stolen anything: not because he was obligated to do so before condemnation. To the third part, the conclusion is denied: for a judge justly condemns a defendant to something he was not held to before, as a matter of punishment.

# Book Four, Question VI.

...where equality is established between what is received and what is given: therefore, if someone were held to pay back more than they had received, that restitution would deviate from justice.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The response to the question consists of three very simple conclusions. The first is essentially a repetition of what was said above: Everyone is held to restore the damage they have caused another to a just level. This is proven because to cause damage to someone is the same as taking something from them, whether it be money or another good that can be valued in money. For to "suffer damage," as Aristotle says in Book 5, Chapter 4 of the *Ethics*, <note>original: "5. Ethi. c. 4. Arist." Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics is a foundational text for medieval and Renaissance legal and moral philosophy.</note> is nothing other than to have less than what one ought to have. Therefore, whoever has taken something from another is compelled by the virtue of justice to return exactly that much, neither more nor less.

<margin>A distinction.</margin>
However, there are two ways in which one might take something from another: namely, either that which they already possessed in <term>actuality</term> <note>original: *actu*. In Scholastic philosophy, "actuality" refers to something that already exists or has been fully realized.</note>, or that which they possessed in <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: *potentia*. "Potentiality" refers to the capacity for something to happen or be produced in the future, like a seed becoming a harvest.</note>. Hence the second conclusion.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
Whoever takes from another that which they already had in actuality is held to restore the equivalent in value. For example, if you took a house, you are held to its just price; and if you took honor and reputation, you must restore it, as has been said, according to your ability. This matter is already clear from the preceding sections.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Third conclusion: Whoever causes damage to another regarding something they did not yet have in actuality, but only in potentiality, is not held to restore it to the same level of equality as if they had possessed it in actuality. Rather, they must restore it according to the value of that potentiality—specifically, after considering how close it was to being realized and weighing the conditions of the persons and the business involved. For example, if your horses trampled and dug up newly sown seeds, the potential must be weighed relative to the eventual harvest. However, if you destroyed crops that were already whitening for harvest, you owe that much more, as the fruits were closer to reality. This conclusion is proven because a thing that is not yet actual, but only "on the way" and existing in its capacity, is not valued as highly as if it were already actual. Therefore, if it had to be paid back according to its value as a finished product, it would not be a simple restoration, but an increase beyond justice, to which justice certainly does not obligate.

<margin>Argument against the third conclusion.</margin>
Regarding the first two conclusions, there is nothing that can be called into doubt. Furthermore, a quite strong argument immediately presents itself against the third conclusion. Indeed, if someone who possesses a thing in "hope" <note>Referring to "hope" (*spes*) as the legal/economic expectation of a future good.</note> does not wish to sell it based on hope alone, but prefers to wait through all risks until the thing is realized, and then someone snatches it away against their will—then that person would seem to be held to restore not just what it was worth as a hope, but, as it appears, what the thing itself was going to be worth. Therefore, the conclusion is false. Take these examples of the premise: there is a 

<column-break/>

poor farmer who has entrusted his seeds to the earth and prefers to undergo all the risks of heaven and earth and wait for the outcome, rather than suffer the loss of his seed for a fixed price. And rightly so. For as it says in Ecclesiastes 11: "He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap." <note>The author uses this biblical quote to emphasize that the farmer accepts the inherent risks of nature in exchange for the potential reward.</note> Therefore, if you destroy his crops against his will, reason certainly seems to suggest that you are held to the whole value. For instance, take an entire town or castle: if all their seeds were dug up, or rooted out while they were still sprouting, they could not help but suffer grave want later on. If they were not destroyed, they would reap the most abundant harvests, and the townsfolk want to wait through the risks; why then should they be deprived of their expectation against their will? Likewise, if someone has a very tender young colt that shows great promise: at the moment it is only valued at ten, but it will be worth a hundred. In truth, it does not seem consistent with justice that the matter should then be compensated only according to its potential and not according to its future actual value.

<margin>Explanation of St. Thomas's conclusion.</margin>
The response is that the conclusion of St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the most influential medieval theologian for Soto.</note> is to be understood, first, when the damage is caused by chance, and not deliberately through injury against the owner's refusal. For in that case, the expenses that the owner was going to incur must first be deducted, since those were not taken from him but remain in his possession. Secondly, any risks must be weighed according to the judgment of prudent men who judge in good faith. However, when damage is caused through injury against the owner's refusal, a much higher estimation must be made—especially when the damage is grave, such as if you were to destroy a very large vineyard or a vast field of crops, so that a province or a city suffered a serious loss.

Through these points, the solution to the first argument is clear.

<margin>Regarding the second argument.</margin>
Regarding the second argument, the doctrine of Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan, was a leading commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> presents us with a doubt. For St. Thomas says that whoever is late in repaying a loan, or is a debtor for another reason, is held not only to refund what he received but also the damage the creditor suffers from the delayed payment, and the <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: *lucrum cessans*. This is a legal concept referring to the profit that would have been made if the money had been returned on time.</note> that ceases for him. Justice certainly commands this after the whole amount is taken from another against his will.

<margin>Cajetan's opinion on the restitution of lost profit.</margin>
Cajetan, however, infers from this that for the same reason, the lender and the borrower can agree from the beginning about the "lost profit."

<margin>The author's distinction.</margin>
This is perhaps a good inference, provided he understands it to apply from the moment they begin to be in "delay." <note>original: *mora*. A legal term for a failure to pay a debt on time.</note> For example, I lend you ten until the Feast of St. John; if you do not pay then...

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of restitution, distinguishing between things held in "actuality" and those held in "potentiality." Soto argues that while accidental damage to potential goods (like seeds) is compensated based on their current speculative value, deliberate injury requires a much higher restitution reflecting the eventual loss.</summary>

356 F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...you shall pay, because from then on you will be holding it against my will, and I am a merchant whose profit will cease because of your fault: therefore, you shall give me that much. But if he understands that <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucrum cessans." A legal concept where a person is compensated not just for what was taken, but for the potential profit they would have made with that money/asset.</note> must be paid immediately from the time of the loan, truly there is no logical inference. For the whole reason why a merchant can demand lost profit from someone who is in delay is not precisely because the merchant's money is worth more in potential than if it were not exposed to trade: but this is joined with another cause, namely that it is retained against the merchant's own will.

<margin>Why it is permitted to demand lost profit.</margin>
Therefore, while he himself voluntarily lets go of his money, it is harmful to grant that he can demand lost profit. We will discuss this more extensively in Book 6. And so, enough about this for now.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ The solution to the third argument is an exposition of that Gospel passage: *You knew that I reap where I do not sow, and gather where I have not scattered.* <note>Matthew 25:24–26, from the Parable of the Talents. Soto is addressing an argument that if God expects a return on what He didn't personally "labor" over, perhaps merchants can too.</note> There is a twofold exposition of this. First, the Catholic faith teaches us most certainly that the root of all our merits is the grace of God, through which they are accepted by Him: and therefore, whatever merits we offer to Him, He Himself first sowed in us. Hence elsewhere, He compared Himself to one sowing his seed. And therefore, the first exposition is that the word of Christ is not understood according to the truth, but according to the estimation of that wicked servant, who out of hatred thought God was seeking what He had not sown: and therefore Christ says that He judges him out of his own mouth: as if not from the truth of the matter. But the second solution is that He requires something from us besides the grace which He Himself confers on us, namely our assent so that we may allow ourselves to be moved by Him: and furthermore the use of that same grace, by which grace is increased through the growth of merits. Furthermore, the first solution appears more sound. For He Himself moves us to assent: and He Himself sowed the fruits of our merits in us through grace.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Whence Paul: *I planted* (namely, by preaching), *and Apollo watered: but God gave the increase.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:6.</note>

¶ One must beware here of that Lutheran dogma, which we refuted in Book 3 of *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 8.

<margin>The Lutheran Dogma</margin>
For they say that our works are not our merits, but that God merits through us. Nothing more foolish could be said than this falsehood. For merit is only spoken of as belonging to one person in relation to another. Therefore, since meriting is only concerning God and toward Him, He Himself cannot merit. They are deceived by a false understanding of a word of Augustine in *On Grace and Free Will*, where he says God "crowns His own gifts in us." <note>A famous quote from St. Augustine often cited in debates about Free Will: "When God crowns our merits, He crowns nothing but His own gifts."</note> Where Augustine does not say that

<column-break/>

our works are God's merits, but that they are God's gifts: and both are true at once, that they are both God's gifts and our merits. For because they are not merits except insofar as they sprout from the root of God's grace, they are called and are His gifts. But because they occur insofar as they come from the free consent of our will moved by God, they are our merits. God therefore crowns our merits insofar as they are His gifts: and therefore in a certain way we give to Him what we did not receive—namely, the increase of what we received in the root—but yet we give nothing that He Himself did not sow and give growth to.

# QUESTION SEVEN, on the circumstances of restitution.

<margin>St. Thomas. 2. 2. q. 62. art. 5.</margin>
### ARTICLE I.
### Whether it is always necessary for restitution to be made to the one from whom the thing was taken.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a seated scholar or saint writing at a desk within a circular frame.</image-desc>

Since the preceding question revealed to us the substance of restitution, it is fitting that in this seventh one we explore its circumstances. Namely: to whom, by whom, how, and when one ought to restore. This is therefore the first article (which is the fifth in St. Thomas): whether restitution must always be made to the person from whom the thing was taken. For it appears that this is not always necessary. First, because restitution should not be harmful to the one to whom it is made, nor injurious to another. But if it were always to be restored to the one whose thing it is, it would sometimes happen that it would be to his ruin or that of others; as, for example, if a sword were returned to its owner who was asking for it in order to commit a murder: therefore, restitution is not always to be made to the true owner.

¶ Second: what anyone gives unjustly and for an evil purpose, he becomes unworthy to receive back. Now men are accustomed to give something through <term>simony</term> <note>The act of buying or selling ecclesiastical privileges, such as pardons or benefices.</note>, or to corrupt a judge, or to kill a man; which gifts are indeed wicked: therefore, restitution is not to be made to them.

¶ Third. No one is compelled to that which is impossible: sometimes, however, restitution is not [possible] to be made...

### Book Four, Question VII

...it is made possible, if it ought to be done for the one from whom the thing was taken: namely, either because he has departed this life, or has set out on a journey, or is entirely unknown: therefore, it is then not necessary that restitution be made to him. ¶ **Fourth.** A man is more justly compelled to repay a benefit to the one from whom he received more than to the one from whom he received less: therefore, if the poverty of parents occurs at the same time that the time for restoring to another arrives, if both are not possible at once, the benefit should be repaid to the parents sooner than the debt should be restored to the stranger. ¶ **Fifth.** It would be useless and equally vain to restore that which would have to return again into the possession of the one restoring it: but when a prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot, who manages church assets.</note> owes something to the church, if it is restored to the same church, it goes out into his own power: since he himself is the administrator and guardian of the church's goods: therefore, it is not then fitting for restitution to be made to the church. And so, restitution does not always have to be made to the one from whom the thing was taken.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, Paul, having been admonished, took care to tell us in Romans 13: *Render to all their dues: to whom tribute, tribute: to whom taxes, taxes, etc.* <note>Romans 13:7. Soto uses this to ground the legal and moral obligation of restitution in Scripture.</note>

<margin>The opinion of others.</margin>
The main question of this article is on the matter of restitution: to which many of the Doctors respond with a multitude of conclusions: namely, that the goods of the deceased are restored to the heir; and what is owed to an unknown person is restored to the poor; and let it be done similarly for others. But truly, although perhaps it does not differ so much in substance, yet if you observe the propriety of speech, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note> responds much more purely and closer to the point with a single conclusion: which is this universal one:

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
**It is necessary everywhere and always for restitution to be made to the same person from whom the thing was taken.** Indeed, heirs represent the person of the deceased, and therefore what is conferred on them is given to the deceased: and what you restore to the poor, you return to the true owner: for they acquire no <term>ownership</term> <note>original: "dominium." The legal right to own and control property.</note> by themselves except because they are substituted in the place of the true owner. The conclusion is therefore proven: Restitution, as we have said above, is an act of <term>commutative justice</term> <note>original: "commutatiue iustitiæ." The branch of justice governing private exchanges and contracts between individuals, aiming for arithmetic equality.</note>, through which equality is established between persons who have unequal things: but this equalization of things cannot be legitimately established unless you return the very thing you took from him: since he is the one who has less because of your taking: therefore, restitution must always be made to the true owner.

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
¶ However, before we descend to the solution of the arguments, the conclusion must be explained. It was deliberately

<column-break/>

stated that restitution must be made to the true owner. For if you have taken a thing from one who was not its true owner, such as from a thief, it is not to be returned to him, but to the owner from whom he himself had snatched it: and likewise a thing acquired by a <term>son under authority</term> <note>original: "filiofamiliās." In Roman law, a son still under the legal power of his father, meaning he cannot technically own property independently.</note> to his father; and what you have snatched from a monk, to his superior. Indeed, as we are about to say in the next article, the obligation of restitution arises from a twofold source: namely, both by reason of the taking, and by reason of the thing taken. Because of this, in these cases, even if you have received nothing from such owners, nonetheless, because their things are in your possession, you are bound to hand them over into their power.

<margin>Three things to be observed in restitution.</margin>
It is worthwhile to observe three things in such restitutions.

<margin>The first.</margin>
**First**, that it be established for you without any doubt that the thing you snatched from Peter is not his, but Paul's. For while the matter is doubtful to you, then since the condition of the one possessing it is better, you ought to return it to him: so that he himself may see whose it is. Since in a judicial court, unless you clearly prove the thing is not his, you will be compelled to return it to the same one from whom you took it. And I have said deliberately, "is not his," for instance because he never had ownership of it, but snatched it through injury. For if the one from whom you took it owes that thing to another by reason of a loan or other legitimate contract, you cannot by private authority return it to the other, but you must return it to him who has ownership.

<margin>The second.</margin>
**Second**, that you are bound to give to the owner, it is required that you can do so without great detriment to yourself. Because if you fear the thief, or the son under authority, from whom you will receive a beating unless you return it to them, or you will receive some grave damage, you are not bound to return it to anyone but them at your own disadvantage.

<margin>The third.</margin>
**And third**, when you restore to the true owner, you are bound to warn both the thief and the owner: the former, of course, lest afterwards, led by repentance, he restores again what has already been restored once; and the latter, lest he procure to recover it by another way.

<margin>Argument against the second moderation.</margin>

He who took a thing from a thief is bound to restore it to the true owner, not only by the law of charity, but also by the rigor of justice: therefore, such restitution ought to be made not only without detriment, but even with it. The antecedent is first proven. For he who has another's property against the owner's will, the thing itself that was received, as we were just saying, is the cause for restitution to be made by the bond of justice. <meta>This page continues the legal and ethical analysis of restitution, specifically focusing on whether the obligation to return property arises from "justice" (a legal duty) or "charity" (a moral duty), and under what circumstances one should withhold property from its owner.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice & Right

...but would compel the possessor in a judicial forum to hand it over to him: therefore, he was bound by justice. For we cannot be forced in court to do that to which we are bound by charity alone. Likewise, because, as we shall say in the next article, even someone who bought a stolen item from a thief would be bound to restore it to the owner: therefore, in whatever way he receives it. Moreover, the first consequence is proved by the fact that justice obliges one to restore property even at a loss to oneself: as we have said above.

<margin>
To the argument.
</margin>
To this, it is responded that not only charity, but justice obliges one to return property to the true owner, in whatever way you have received it from an unjust possessor. However, the logical consequence—that restitution must be completed even at a loss—is denied. For when you are bound by reason of the *act* of receiving—namely, either because you wrongfully snatched it from the owner or received it as a loan—then you are compelled to restore it even with some loss, as we said, though not at the risk of your life. But when you are bound not by the act of receiving, but only by reason of the *thing* received <note>This is the distinction between *ex datione* (from the act of giving/taking) and *ex re* (from the thing itself). Soto is arguing that if you just happen to have someone's property, your duty is different than if you actively stole it or borrowed it.</note>, then you are not compelled to undergo any danger—if the danger is truly of some significance—but it is enough then that you return it to the same person from whom you received it, while warning the true owner if you can. Sometimes, however, you will perform an excellent service to a friend if you expose yourself to danger to save his property. We will speak of this again more explicitly in the next article.

<margin>
To the first principal argument.
</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for Soto’s work.</note> responds that in a case where restitution gravely harms the person to whom it is made, or results in the harm of another, it should not be made to him at that time, because restitution is meant for the benefit of the person to whom it is owed. Instead, it ought to be delayed until a fitting time, or the item should be deposited with another person who may guard it more safely. This response, however, gives rise to several small doubts.

<margin>
A doubt.
</margin>
And to lay a foundation for all of them, it is asked by what right a depositary <note>A person with whom property is left for safekeeping.</note> is bound in such a case to keep the deposit and deny it to the owner: is it by charity or by justice? For it matters greatly. If justice compels him to keep it, it follows that if he returns it, he would be liable for the restitution of the damages he caused; but if he is bound only by the bond of charity, he is not liable for any restitution thereafter.

<margin>
Response with a distinction.
</margin>
The response is placed in a distinction. For either the one who seeks it wants to abuse his property to the injury of himself or others, and then I am bound by justice to deny it to him—for example, if a madman asks me for his sword to kill himself or another—provided, however, that I can do this without inconvenience to myself.

<column-break/>

For I am not bound to undergo a danger that he presents to me if I do not return it, just as I am not bound to expose myself to danger to defend the life of my neighbor. And that he who can do so without danger is bound by justice to deny it is evident from this: both because by returning it he provides a cause for injury, and because if he does return it, he will be condemned in judgment, though not for the whole amount. Let us always set aside ignorance here, which can excuse men. And for the same reason—indeed, a greater one—I ought to deny it when it is sought to the prejudice of the republic: as when one who owes a large sum of money to a tyrant, which the tyrant seeks so that he may arm an army for the destruction of the commonwealth, is bound at that time by justice to deny it to him.

<margin>
The second part of the distinction.
</margin>
If, however, the owner seeks his property for some abuse that does not have an injury attached to it—as if he demands back from me money I owe him so that he can spend it on prostitutes or squander it—then I am not bound by justice not to return it, since by returning it I am the cause of no injury; rather, he seeks it using his own right. I am, however, bound by charity to look out for my neighbor’s property, and thus, if I can, to delay restitution to another time.

<margin>
Argument against the second part of the distinction.
</margin>
But an argument emerges from the opposite side. No one has a right to sin: therefore, in whatever way he seeks it for the purpose of sinning, even without injury to others, it must be denied to him as a matter of justice.

<margin>
Response of Cajetan.
</margin>
But if you respond that it is lawful for him to give money to a prostitute for an illicit thing, and therefore to seek it so he may use his right, let the argument be framed concerning a gift that is intrinsically a sin—for example, if he seeks it to practice simony <note>The act of buying or selling sacred things or church offices, considered a grave sin.</note>, which is a gift that is intrinsically evil. Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> here frankly admits that even then it is not lawful to give it to him. For he says it is not lawful to return deposited money to the owner so that he may buy a Cardinalate, and much less to lend him money for such a use. But in truth, whatever the case may be regarding a loan (in which there seems to be a greater reason for fault, because the lender, being less compelled, seems more to be the cause), returning a deposit then seems to bring about no injustice. For he seeks what is his own, not to inflict injury on any third party, nor on himself, but only to sin: just as if he were to ask for it so that he might give it to a mistress for a bad cause. And therefore, others wish to evade the argument through a flaw in the phrasing. For it does not follow that "no one has a right to sin" and "this man seeks his money to sin" implies "therefore he does not seek to use his right," because he seeks it for the purpose of giving, to which he has a right, even if not for the fault which...

->### Question VII of the Fourth Book<-

is joined to reason. But truly, in that way in which one has no right to sin, one also has no right to give, if the act of giving itself is a sin. It is otherwise regarding a prostitute’s pay: because the act of giving is not a sin, even though the fornication itself is a sin.

<margin>The first solution.</margin>
Therefore, there are two ways to respond more appropriately. First, whatever the use might be for which someone seeks their money from me, they are nevertheless exercising their own right in seeking it, because they are seeking what is theirs. But you say: "Yet they seek it so that they may use it against the law."

<margin>The second solution.</margin>
It is responded, secondly, that "using one's own right" is understood in two ways. For if "right" is taken to mean the law, no one has a right to sin, since the law permits no one to sin. If, however, the "right" of an individual is taken for that which is his own—namely, that which he uses without doing injury to others—then he who gives money <term>simoniacally</term> <note>Simony is the act of buying or selling sacred things or church offices.</note>, or to corrupt a judge, is using his own right. That is, he gives what is his own; and thus he does no injury to any person, but rather to the law. I, who hold his deposit, am not bound to prevent him from violating that law.

<margin>To the second [argument]. A twofold illegality.</margin>
To the second argument, <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose work Soto is commenting upon.</note> responds with a distinction. For it happens in two ways that someone gives something illicitly. In one way, because the act of giving itself is against the law, such as a simoniacal gift; and then, because the giver deserves to lose ownership (which the receiver does not acquire either), restitution must be made—not to the giver, but to the poor. If, however, the giving itself is not illicit, but rather the *cause* for which it is given—such as the wages of a prostitute—then restitution is not owed.

And indeed, the second part is so clear that it would require no examination, were it not for a certain very recent author from <term>Alcalá</term> <note>The "author from Complutensis" refers to Juan Medina, a professor at the University of Alcalá de Henares (Complutum).</note> who denied this opinion of Saint Thomas, which is held by almost all theologians.

<margin>The opinion of Juan Medina.</margin>
For he says that a prostitute can receive nothing as a price or wage for her wickedness, but only by way of a gift. Therefore, if she received it as a price, she would be bound to restore it. But, with all due respect to the distinguished Doctor, his reasoning is as weak as his conclusion is false. For he says there are two kinds of things which, for different reasons, cannot be valued with a price: namely, spiritual things, which are not valued because they exceed all price; and works which are crimes, which on account of their worthlessness are worthy of no price.

<margin>Medina is refuted.</margin>
Furthermore, both parts of his argument are false. For spiritual things are not unjustly sold for that reason. For even if they are supernatural, men would nonetheless buy them for whatever price they could, insofar as they pertain to human uses. For life exceeds every

<column-break/>

price; and yet a murderer is condemned to restore the life he took according to the judgment of prudent men <note>In legal terms, this refers to paying a settlement or "blood price" to the victim's family, as the life itself cannot be physically restored.</note>. Moreover, spiritual things that have temporal fruits attached to them—such as priesthoods—could then be bought for that reason.

<margin>Why spiritual things are not for sale.</margin>
The reason, therefore, why spiritual things are not for sale is only because they are granted freely by God. And therefore, the dispensers of those things—since they received them not for their own private benefit, but for the common good—ought to give freely what they received freely, as will be more fully evident in Book Nine. For this reason, knowledge which a person acquires by his own effort is sellable. But regarding sins: although by reason of their guilt they are not only worthless and worthy of no price, but even abhorrent and execrable; nonetheless, by reason of the consent of the one who hires out their labor, and by reason of the pleasure of the one who hires them—insofar as these accommodate human uses—they can be purchased for a wage and a price. Wherefore a woman who provides the use of her body can receive a wage for the pleasure the man seeks, just as she might so that she might bear a child for him.

<margin>A man can receive a price from a woman.</margin>
Indeed, for either reason, a male could also receive a price from a female; and even more justly, because he provides more.

<margin>Alexander and the Amazon.</margin>
Just as <term>Alexander</term> <note>Alexander the Great.</note> by natural law was able to receive a price from that Amazonian leader who visited him for the sake of conceiving a child; which, it is said, she obtained through both prayer and payment. For it was the custom of that race of women to summon men by price to come to them. But because women possess greater shame, and for that reason those who devote themselves to such wickedness are rarer than men, they themselves receive a price more justly.

Likewise, if someone for the sake of health needed that release, he could purchase that embrace for a price, notwithstanding that the act has an innate disgrace. And that they can receive this not only by way of a gift, but in the place of a price, is clearly proved: because the state not only permits those wretched women, but even sets a price for them. The very name of "prostitute" <note>original: *meretricis*</note> reminds us of this. For it is derived from "to earn" <note>original: *merendo*</note>. And anyone who did not pay them the established price would be compelled to do so in a judicial court; which would not happen if it were a gift. And the law "the same if for the sake of debauchery" <note>original: *l. idem si ob stuprum. ff. de cond. ob turp. caus.* This refers to a specific law in the Roman Digest regarding "contracts for a shameful cause."</note> confirms this: for it says that a prostitute justly receives that which she takes for an unjust act. For a prostitute, it says, acts shamefully because she is a prostitute; however, she does not take the money shamefully, since she is a prostitute. Likewise, it argues against the assertion of this Doctor [Medina], where he says: if a prostitute takes something with the intention of receiving a price...

In that case, the one who gives can demand it back, because the other person was already bound to do that for free. This is found in the law *ut puta* <note>original: "l. ut puta. ff. de cond. ob tur. cauſ." — This refers to the Digest of Justinian, regarding recovery of property given for an immoral purpose.</note>. From this, the <term>Gloss<note>Standard marginal commentaries used by legal scholars.</note></term>—which the <term>Summists<note>Theological and legal writers who compiled "Summas" or summaries of knowledge.</note></term> follow—infers that the one who receives it is held to restitution. <margin>A distinction to be noted.</margin>
Either the vice from which I am trying to restrain that person with my gift is harmful to someone else, or it has no attached injury. For if it is injurious and harmful—for instance, when I offer a gift to a friend so that he does not commit murder or theft—then I will later be granted the right to demand it back. And indeed, this is the only example given in the law. Nonetheless, if I do not demand it back, I would believe that he is held to no restitution. For even if he were bound to abstain for free, nevertheless, because he abstains for my sake (when he would otherwise have done those evil things), he can, by the law of nature and by his own will, receive a price from me. Therefore, the law does not prohibit the transfer of ownership, but it grants the right of recovery; just as we said regarding gambling. This is done out of hatred for that crime, so that men do not sell the injuries they plan against others for a price. But when the vice is not against justice—as if I were to give something to a friend so that he would not engage in debauchery—then not only can he receive it and is not bound to restitution, but I believe I would not even be granted the right to demand it back. This is because that penal law must be restricted to its own example, which it only provides
<margin>The second mode.</margin>
in cases of vices that have an injury attached to them.

For example, if a litigant offered gifts to a judge, a clerk, or a witness to corrupt them; or to an assassin to kill a man. For then both commit a sin, and therefore both the giver and the receiver are punished by the law with the same price; and consequently, that gift is assigned by right to the <term>fisc<note>The public treasury.</note></term>, as is clear in the law *Mulcta* <note>original: "l. <summary>Soto categorizes illicit payments into those where only the receiver is at fault and those where both parties are at fault. He argues that while natural law might recognize a transfer of ownership, civil law often denies it to discourage crimes like bribery and murder, requiring the money to be returned or forfeited.</summary>

For since everyone is an unjust judge in their own cause, it appears to everyone that they have a certain right, and thus they seek to "buy off" their own harassment. This is the greatest destruction in lawsuits: namely, while each of the litigants seeks to redeem their own harassment, they forestall the other by harassing them first, giving the other a reason to redeem their own as well. And I wish this practice did not proceed even to the point of cloaking the discords of princes.

<margin>Third mode of illicit giving.</margin>
¶ In the third way, it happens that the giving is illicit even on the part of both the giver and the recipient. However, the reason is not like the one noted in the previous section—namely, that the action being bought is harmful—but because the thing is not estimable by a price, such as <term>simoniacal<note>Relating to Simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred things, church offices, or spiritual benefits.</note></term> giving. For if a priesthood is given to me for a price when I am worthy of it, it is not an injury to another person; nevertheless, because the thing being bought cannot be valued in money (since <term>Bishops<note>Original: "Antistites." Literally "those who stand before," used here for high-ranking church officials.</note></term> received their office freely so that they might dispense it freely), it follows that he who receives a price for a spiritual thing acquires no true ownership of that money. For that reason, he is bound to relinquish it immediately, even before a court sentence is passed.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But whether he is then bound to restore it to the poor, or to the one who had given it, is a doubt. On the one hand, the laws command that <term>restitution<note>The act of returning something to its rightful owner or making amends for a wrong.</note></term> be made to "pious causes" (charitable or religious works), as is cautioned in the canon *Qui habetis* (14.q.5) and the canon *De hoc* regarding simony. In a secular court, the judgment would be the same, because the one who gave the money deserves to be deprived of his ownership—indeed, more justly than one who gave money to corrupt a judge. But on the other hand, there is the argument that no one should be despoiled of their property except by a judge's sentence. Therefore, we must discuss this matter in its proper place in Book 9. Meanwhile, however, based on <term>natural law<note>A system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than from the rules of society.</note></term>, it must be said that before a legal condemnation, restitution must be made to the one who gave the money. Yet, let the one restoring it be careful, lest later, when the matter comes to the knowledge of the Church, he be condemned to pay it again.

<margin>Regarding the third argument.</margin>
The solution to the third argument has three parts. For either the creditor to whom restitution is owed is deceased, or absent, or entirely unknown. In the case of the deceased, heirs are substituted in their place.

<margin>Heirs are of three types.</margin>
These heirs fall into three categories. Some are "necessary" heirs: for example, those whom the <term>testator<note>The person who has made a will.</note></term> cannot disinherit except for the rarest and most legitimate reasons. These are the children of parents, and the parents of children. Others succeed "intestate" (when there is no will), such as brothers and kinsmen. Others succeed by the will, such as strangers. In whatever way someone is another's heir, restitution must be made to them. Indeed, as we were saying, restitution to the heir is the same as restitution to the deceased—

<column-break/>

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
—person themselves. ¶ Now, it may prick a person's conscience to wonder if someone who, after searching for heirs and finding none, gives the restitution to "pious uses" (charity), still owes that restitution to an heir who is discovered later. It appears that reason would demand it, since that heir should not be deprived of their right without their knowledge and against their will. To this, it is answered that when the restitution is of significant value and the heir is not found, one must exercise due diligence before the public authority and deposit the debt with them. If, by that authority’s command, the money is spent on the poor or on pious uses, then the one making restitution remains safe, both in conscience and in the eyes of the law. In matters of minor importance, however, such an anxious investigation is not necessary.

<margin>On making restitution to an absent person.</margin>
¶ When the creditor is absent, the restitution should be sent to him in whatever way is most convenient. But what if the transmission cannot be done without great expense?

<margin>Scotus and Richard.</margin>
<term>Scotus<note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), an influential Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note></term> and <term>Richard<note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302), a Scholastic theologian.</note></term> say in Book 4, Distinction 15, that when huge expenses are required, the debtor is not bound to pay them; instead, he may distribute the amount he owes to the poor. However, <term>St. Thomas<note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s work.</note></term> makes no mention of expenses, and he stayed silent on the matter deliberately because he could not establish a simple, universal rule.

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
Therefore, <term>discretion<note>The ability to judge what is right and fair in a specific circumstance.</note></term> is necessary. One must weigh whether you retained what you owe through an "injury" (a wrongful act like theft) or through a lawful contract, such as a sale or a loan. If the thing came into your possession through a lawful contract and the creditor departed before the time of payment, you are not bound to pay the costs of sending the money, because you do not owe more than you received. If you cannot send it without those expenses, you must either keep it safe or deposit it with a judge. It is not permitted to spend it on pious uses unless you have waited for a very long time. However, if you owe the debt because of an injury—for example, if you stole it—or if you received it justly but acted in <term>bad faith<note>Original: "in mala es fide." Knowingly acting dishonestly or unfairly.</note></term> by going abroad before paying, you are undoubtedly bound to send the restitution at your own expense. This is because you are required to keep the creditor "harmless" (without loss), since he lacks his rightful property through no fault of his own.

<margin>A doubt when the creditor is unknown.</margin>
¶ Regarding a creditor who is entirely unknown, the doubt is more serious and more common. This point applies to <term>monopolists<note>Original: "coemptores." Those who buy up all of a certain commodity to manipulate the price.</note></term>, merchants, and counterfeiters who defraud and fleece many people in small amounts; it also applies to those who have plundered a city in an unjust war. Furthermore, it applies to those who have found treasures, which we shall discuss under the title *On Theft*. For the creditors of such debtors are unknown. First of all, therefore, one must be warned...

### Book Four, Question VII.

These people must be warned as to who is truly called "unknown." For someone is by no means to be considered unknown to a debtor just because they are not currently in his knowledge or memory; rather, it is one who, after the facts of the debt have been investigated with skillful diligence, could not be found. Therefore, before this investigation is made, it is not permitted to distribute the funds to be restored for pious uses, nor to make a composition under the authority of the 
<margin>The Crusade Bull.</margin> 
**Crusade Bull** <note>The *Bulla Cruciata* was a papal decree that allowed individuals to contribute to the defense of the faith in exchange for spiritual benefits or the legal settling of financial irregularities, such as "uncertain debts."</note>. For those are precisely called "uncertain debts" whose owners cannot be found after a vigilant search made in good faith. Indeed, those who contracted a debt through an unjust taking are bound to carry out this investigation at their own expense. 

Therefore, where it is found through doubt that something is certainly owed to this person or that—for example, when two people have come to your shop and you are certain you defrauded one of them, even if you cannot know which one—you are nonetheless bound to divide the debt between them or their heirs; since in that case, the creditor is not entirely unknown. By the same reasoning, there are those who think that if a person is certain of which city the man to whom he owes restitution belonged, but neither the man nor his heirs can be found, he owes the restitution to the poor of that same place. But no necessary reason for this appears; rather, it is perhaps 
<margin>A Distinction.</margin> 
worthwhile to make a distinction. For when an army has plundered a city in a collective capacity, then perhaps if the owners are unknown, restitution must be made to the city so that the state <note>Original: "respublica." In this context, it refers to the organized political community or commonwealth.</note> itself may distribute it. However, when the debt was not contracted through an injury brought upon the whole state in that manner, but through injury to individual citizens, it is not necessary for the restitution to be made in that same town. 

Therefore, the conclusion of all the Doctors is that when the owner is unknown, restitution must be made to the poor—or rather, to Christ himself in the person of the poor, as we were saying above. 

¶ Nevertheless, so that this mode of 
<margin>A Doubt.</margin> 
restoring might be understood from its root, it is asked by what law things owed to unknown owners are to be bestowed upon the poor. Is it natural law, divine law, or human law? Who, I ask, made the poor the heirs of such creditors? 

The argument is as follows: The obligation of restoring by natural law binds all mortals, whether they are Christians or living by the law of nature alone; but nature does not teach that when an owner is unknown, the debt is owed to the poor. On the contrary, it seems then that the thing passes into the right of the current possessor. For it is held in the *Institutes* <note>Refers to the *Institutes* of Justinian, a foundational Roman law textbook.</note> "On the Division of Things," that a thing which has no owner is granted to the one who occupies it; and when an owner does not appear, it is the same as if he did not exist. Furthermore, that restitution should be made to the poor was introduced by canon law alone, as is clear in the chapter *Cum tu*

<column-break/>

regarding usury, and the canons *Non sane* and *Qui habetis* (14. q. 5). Moreover, the Popes could not, against the will of the owners, assign uncertain debts to the use of the poor contrary to natural law. For before those holy decrees, it does not appear that this mode of restoring was necessary. 

¶ To this, it is 
<margin>Response.</margin> 
answered first of all that such uncertain debts, if you only consult natural law, fall to the common uses of the state. For since all things (as was said in the preceding book) were handed over into common human ownership, the division of which was made by the law of nations (*ius gentium*), it happens that when the owner does not appear after the expected legitimate time, they return again into public use. 

But since the Vicar of Christ <note>The Pope.</note> manages the care of the poor for the entire Christian commonwealth, he could by right and merit apply these goods—as if they were common property of the state—to the poor, who are the needy members of that same state. And Alexander III <note>Pope from 1159–1181.</note>, in the year of our Lord 1170, ordered the Archbishop of Salerno to do this, as is clear in the said chapter *Cum tu* regarding usury. He was not, however, the first author of this practice; he was led by the example of the most ancient saints, namely Augustine (as is established in the cited canons) and others. Indeed, he was taught by both natural law and the Gospel. For what remains over for anyone <note>Referencing the concept of "superfluous" wealth.</note> must be distributed to the poor, and such goods are considered to "overflow" back into the community. 

¶ From this, it follows first that the ownership of these things does not pass to the poor as if they were the heirs of the creditors; rather, when it is given to them, it is paid as if to the creditors themselves. And then, through the act of giving itself, they acquire true ownership, as if the Pope were then granting it to them in the name of the owners. 

It follows secondly that when the state needs those debts for other pious uses, the right of distributing them to the poor then ceases, and the state can consume them for such uses. For positive law <note>Man-made law (civil or canon law) as opposed to natural law.</note> could not override natural law. For this reason, a secular prince might perhaps then demand those uncertain debts and make a composition—for example, remit the remainder in exchange for a certain portion, as the Pope does, as we shall say shortly.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin> 
private person can distribute what he owes to the poor as he pleases: **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin> 
stated nothing here on this matter; yet in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, dist. 15, q. 1, art. 5), he says that restitution ought to be made according to the judgment of the Bishop or those to whom the care of the city belongs. There, he seems to insinuate that the state itself has such authority.

### Friar Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

However, I would not assert this as a matter of necessity for salvation.

<margin>*A Doubt.*</margin>
Nor did **Saint Thomas Aquinas** teach otherwise, especially since he remained silent on this matter in his *Summa*. ¶ A more useful question, however, is whether the person who holds money belonging to an unknown owner could take a portion for himself, provided he is poor, or bestow it upon his relatives and household members.

<margin>*Cajetan.*</margin>
**Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> indeed affirms this absolutely; but I would not dare to do so without qualification. For if you grant this license to anyone at all, they will immediately invent a state of poverty for themselves and their kin "proportionate to their status," as they say. Therefore, where the necessity is not most manifest and clear, no one can safely claim for themselves what they ought to restore, although they may be able to delay the restitution. But if one thinks to take it for himself, he must do so by the authority of the bishop, or his parish priest, or his confessor, if that person is prudent and wise. This will be permissible only when other, more grievous miseries of the poor do not present themselves to his eyes. When, however, by the authority of a prelate, some of what he owed is applied to him as alms, he truly becomes its owner; nor, should he come into a wealthier fortune, is he bound to restore it further.

¶ You also ask about these **compositions** <note>original: "compositionibus"—legal settlements where a debtor pays a portion of a debt to the Church or State to be cleared of the whole, often used when the original creditor was unknown.</note> which we mentioned just now—whether they are lawful, as the form of the **Crusade Bull** <note>A papal decree that allowed financial settlements to fund defense against the Ottoman Empire in exchange for spiritual and legal benefits.</note> holds: namely, that he who has contracted an uncertain debt may be made free from the remainder of the debt by paying a certain portion. In answering this question, one must always take care in the best of faith that no one deceives himself by thinking something is "uncertain" before a diligent search is conducted to find the creditor. Once this is assumed, there seems to be no reason to doubt that, if a legitimate cause is present, the **Supreme Pontiff** (the Pope) can make such compositions. This is because, by natural law as has been said, those goods belong to the commonwealth, which at that time needs them for such uses. Indeed, as I was just suggesting, when the necessity of the commonwealth is most obvious, perhaps a King could also do this. Nevertheless, because the Supreme Pontiff is a more just judge of alms, and the cause is not always so evident, he is the one who should be approached so that it may be done by his authority. If anyone argues that the unknown creditors perhaps do not consent, this is denied; indeed, they seem to consent, because they regard those things as lost. Anyone would more freely and gratefully contribute a hundred [coins] which he considers entirely lost than four which he has in his purse. And even if

<column-break/>

they did not consent, the commonwealth has the power to do this. But you argue again: even if the Pope can collect those funds, what power does he have to remit a portion of them? The answer is that, as the legitimate administrator of the goods at that time, on account of an encroaching and pressing public necessity, he can forgive a part so that the remainder may be paid more easily and quickly.

¶ Thus far concerning the law (*de iure*). Regarding the facts (*de facto*) and the manner of execution, we say nothing. For the **equity** <note>The principle of fairness that looks at the spirit of the law rather than just the letter.</note> of this law is that through such compositions, so much public money should be collected that it might excuse other taxes or a good part of them. It should be done in such a way that no handle of iniquity is offered to the wicked. Yet, to collect only two silver pieces from one hundred and fifty owed to the commonwealth and the poor, and to remit the rest, offers more harm to the poor (of whom the Pope is the father and the King the patron) than it confers benefit to the public good. Furthermore, a most present danger is created for these **forestallers** <note>original: "coēmptoribus"—those who buy up goods to create monopolies or engage in predatory trade.</note> and plunderers, so that, trusting in this, they may think nothing of defrauding anyone and everyone. This same danger becomes more present because they are certain that every three years such indulgences will be issued. But truly, the frequency of wars which press upon us daily (and not only from the infidels) are, among other things, the cause of this evil, so that the search for subsidies everywhere allows for no moderation. Therefore, we do not speak out against anyone, for our authority is not so great, nor our boldness. But nevertheless, having approved the law, we are occasionally compelled to warn these public defrauders—I mean the forestallers and merchants—lest, relying on the hope of such immoderate remission, they continue to contract debts through fraud. If they do so, let them not delay in restoring them. For he who has no intention of restoring until the indulgence arrives should know that he persists in **mortal sin**; since, once the opportunity to restore is available, it is not permitted for any length of time to withhold what belongs to another.

<margin>*To the fourth argument.*</margin>
To the fourth argument, the response is that each person is more strictly bound to help their parents from what is their own than to help others. However, things that belong to others ought to be repaid to those others rather than bestowed upon one's parents—unless perhaps, as Saint Thomas says, in a case of extreme necessity, in which anyone could and should even take the goods of another to help his father. ¶ Regarding this last word about the time of extreme necessity, several doubts arise.
