->### Question VII of the Fourth Book<-

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
To begin where the reasoning for doubt is most evident, it is asked: when both a debtor and a creditor are forced into a state of extreme necessity <note>A technical term in medieval law meaning a life-or-death situation, such as imminent starvation.</note>, is the debtor bound to help the creditor before himself, or should he rather look to his own needs while neglecting the creditor?

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
**Duns Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan priest and philosopher.</note> in his *Commentary on the Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 2) uses this distinction: If the creditor falls into necessity first, the debtor is then bound to pay him; if, however, the debtor falls into it first, he is bound to provide for himself. Both of these points are so certain that no one could doubt either. For even if you owed nothing to someone suffering extreme need, you would be compelled to help them; and when you yourself are strangled by that same necessity, even if no one else owed you anything, they would be bound to help you. However, when the same necessity seizes both at once, Scotus says that the debtor, setting aside his own life, must return what belongs to the creditor; therefore, he says, the debtor would be a murderer if he usurped the property for himself at that time. There are others, among whom is **Richard of Middleton**, who subscribe to this opinion. His reasoning is this: since both are equal in their need, the creditor surpasses the debtor in right because the necessary thing—namely the food or money the debtor holds—is his own, that is, the creditor's. And he could further bolster his opinion by the fact that in such necessity, neither could snatch from the other what was necessary for him. From this, it seems to follow as a consequence that the debtor could not then retain what belongs to another. For it seems to be the same as if he were snatching it from him.

<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, the contrary opinion is not only much more probable, but beyond 

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
doubt should be embraced. First, **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, although he does not assert it expressly, seems to suggest it; for he says without any exception that in a case of extreme necessity, a debtor should sooner be a protection to his parents—and by 

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
stronger reasoning, to himself. Therefore, **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan, a 16th-century commentator on Aquinas.</note> embraced the same opinion. The reasoning, however, is this, and it differs from that of Scotus: Both are equal in need, but the condition of the possessor, which is always better, favors the debtor more than the fact that the thing was owed favored the creditor. Therefore, the debtor ought to look to himself sooner—or at least, he can—than to the creditor. Truly, that most general desire for all things is so deeply innate in man, and consequently the right of preserving oneself, that he then owes nothing to anyone more than to himself. Wherefore, whether he received it from another through a lawful contract, or through theft or robbery; whether he is late in paying or not; in short, however he may owe it to the other, nature itself grants him the right of retaining it for himself. In such 

<column-break/>

a case, all other debts cease. Therefore, even if you had bound yourself by an oath to pay on that day, it was understood by the law of nature that an exception was made for extreme necessity. ¶ And this opinion is confirmed by a reason that is, unless I am mistaken, manifest: By **natural law**, as has been said, all things are common, but by the **law of nations** <note>Latin: *ius gentium*, referring to the customary laws shared by all civilized peoples, such as private property rights.</note>, the ownership of things was divided. However, the law of nations cannot prejudice extreme necessity; and thus, when such necessity is present, as far as use is concerned, all the force of private ownership—and consequently of debts—ceases. Wherefore, even if the owner had first run into that extreme necessity, for which reason I would have been held under the guilt of homicide to pay him what I owed; if, however, I did not pay, and afterwards I fell into the same necessity, I am no longer bound.

<margin>To the argument.</margin>
¶ It is answered, therefore, to the argument we were making, that the reasoning is different whether you possess the thing when you are suffering extremely, or another who suffers similarly possesses it. For if the other possesses it, you could not snatch it from him; because to snatch it then would be to kill him, as it would be a true action by which you directly take the life of another, just as if you were to strangle a man. But when you possess it—that is, you have the thing in your power, however you obtained it—you do not act, but merely cease to help when you are able. But not helping when you are able is not directly killing; nor is it killing even by accident, except when you are bound to help; and in such a case, you are not bound. For this is how the word of 

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
**Saint Ambrose** <note>Theologian and Bishop of Milan (c. 340–397).</note> must be understood: *Feed the one who is dying of hunger; if you have not fed him, you have killed him.* <note>original: "Quem pascere potuisti, si non pauisti, occidisti."</note> For it is understood to apply when no other right excused you.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But as to whether you are bound more to your parent than to your creditor when both are cast into the same extreme necessity, I think this is a 

<margin>Problem.</margin>
problem <note>In scholastic terms, a *problema* is a question with probable arguments on both sides.</note> that is probable in either direction. Whoever says the creditor will be defending it with good reason: for only that right which everyone has of preserving himself seems in such a case to claim the use of another's property for the debtor. But whoever believes it should rather be the parent can also shield himself with the duty of piety <note>Piety here refers to *pietas*, the natural duty and love owed to family and country.</note>. For it is almost the same thing to preserve the life of a father as your own. But then I would believe the same regarding a wife and a son. For it would be by no means permitted to extend the same right to brothers.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ It remains to decide whether someone suppressed by extreme poverty who consumes a thing which he either owed to another previously or seized at that time is absolved of the debt; or whether, when he later becomes wealthier, he is nonetheless obligated to pay. For there is an argument that he should be entirely absolved: because if he had snatched it from another then, he would not be held liable.

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
To this, Scotus, in the place cited, skillfully responds through this distin... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "distinction" at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>This page debates the ethical priority in life-or-death situations, arguing that a debtor may prioritize their own survival or that of their parents over paying a debt to a creditor, as private property rights are suspended by the natural law of self-preservation in "extreme necessity."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the debate from the previous page concerning the obligations of a debtor in "extreme necessity." Domingo de Soto is evaluating whether someone who survives a life-threatening crisis by using another's property is legally or morally bound to pay it back once they are no longer in danger.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

<note>original: "F. D. Soto, de Iustitia & Iure"</note>

he responded to the distinction. If that person owed the item by virtue of another contract before the state of extreme necessity <note>A legal and theological term for a situation where a person will die without immediate access to resources like food or medicine.</note> arose, he is not immune from the duty of restitution. However, if he takes the item only at that time of crisis, he does not become liable for restitution. The reason is readily apparent: since in a state of extreme necessity all things are held in common, the one who takes does not contract a debt. Nevertheless, if a debt had already been contracted beforehand, there is no reason for that preceding bond to be dissolved; therefore, it shall remain.

<margin>Adrian.</margin>
¶ But in truth, **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a prominent theologian before his papacy.</note>, in his writings on restitution, does not admit this kind of distinction. Instead, he holds absolutely that one who, being subject to extreme necessity, takes the property of another, is bound to restitution once a more favorable fortune smiles upon him. He does not lack followers for this view; indeed, they reinforce his opinion. The weight of their arguments leans toward this: that in extreme necessity, all things are not common in terms of ownership <term>dominium; the legal right to possess and control property</term>. For if it were otherwise, someone who did not help a person in need at that time would later be bound to restitution; this is truly not to be believed, because the commandment to help is a matter of charity, not of justice. Therefore, things are common only in terms of their use; from which it seems to follow that once the use has passed, you are bound to restore the item.

¶ Second, he argues: a person in extreme need is abundantly helped by a thing being lent <note>original: "rem mutuatam"</note>; therefore, no one is bound simply to give it away. And thus, he who consumes the thing remains subject to restitution.

¶ And third: a physician is not bound to provide his services for free to someone in extreme need, nor is a pharmacist bound to give away his medicines for nothing. For it is enough if they wait for payment. This is supported by the text of the canon "If anyone" <note>original: "si quis. de furt." referring to a specific decree in Canon Law regarding theft</note> concerning theft. There it is held that he who occupies the property of another because of the necessity of hunger or nakedness, if he later returns what was taken, he should not be forced to fast. From the opposite sense, it is gathered that if he does not return it, he should be forced to perform the penance of fasting.

<margin>The opinion of Scotus is explained</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, one must persist in the former opinion <note>That the poor man does not owe restitution for what he ate to survive.</note>, provided it is correctly explained. First, when the matter is of little value, everyone confesses that no obligation of restitution remains. But if the thing which the person in extreme need requires is of greater value, one must consider whether he is "simply indigent"—namely, someone who has no means anywhere from which he could pay—or whether, although he does not have it here, he perhaps has it elsewhere, or it is owed to him. In the latter case, he is not to be judged "simply indigent," and therefore it is enough if someone lends to him on credit so that he may meet his necessity. For only absolute necessity creates the right to take the property of another in such a case. If, however, he is simply indigent, it ought to be beyond controversy that he 

<column-break/>

remains liable to no restitution if he consumed the thing he needed. Indeed, although it may be that all things are then common only in terms of use, nevertheless, in the case of those things which are consumed by use, the ownership <term>dominium</term> follows the use by the law of nature—as for example, if it be food, or drink, or money. He who takes it becomes the owner. And in this, if we are not mistaken, the contrary opinion deceives its own followers. For "all things being common in regard to use" means that the person in need can then consume the property of another as if it were his own. And thus, he is not bound to receive it on credit, but the other is bound to give it for free. If, however, the item were something not consumed by use, then once the necessity ceases, he is bound to return it—for instance, if someone used another’s horse to escape the danger of death, or if he needed a bed during a time of sickness.

<margin>Concerning the Physician and the Pharmacist.</margin>
Through this, the argument concerning the Physician and the Pharmacist is answered. For furthermore, if another were in extreme need of his labor or his medicine, he would be bound under pain of mortal sin to provide it; although those standing by would nonetheless be bound by the same bond to contribute if the item were very costly. Nevertheless, in the withholding of these medicines, guilt does not occur as frequently as it does with food and other things, because they are not usually as necessary; nor does the bond of mercy oblige that a very expensive medicine, or such great skill of a physician, be provided to meet the death of a poor man.

¶ As for what was brought forward from the chapter "If anyone" concerning theft, it truly pertains nothing to the matter. For it is plain that no mention is made there of "extreme necessity," as the commentary <note>original: "gloss."</note> rightly says, but of a lighter necessity. For the text says: "If anyone has occupied [property] because of necessity, etc., let him repent for three weeks." And it is clear that since occupying another's property in extreme necessity is no fault, no penance would be imposed.

<margin>Concerning the fifth argument.</margin>
The solution to the fifth argument would send us from here into a long dispute concerning the restitution of the goods of the clergy <note>original: "clericorum"</note>, which are not properly dispensed but are squandered on evil uses; unless we were to have a very wide-ranging discussion of this in Books 9 and 10, which for the present we must therefore refrain from. As it pertains to the present matter, a prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, like a bishop.</note> usurps the property of the church in three ways.

<margin>A prelate can occupy the property of the church in three ways.</margin>
In one way, if that property is not assigned to him, but to another—for example, to the cathedral chapter. And then, whoever receives those things from that official, whether as a gift or for a price, is bound by reason of the thing received to restore them to the owner. If, however, he has alienated property of the church which is under his own administration—for example, in the building fund or in other areas—to his relatives...

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that a person in life-threatening "extreme necessity" who consumes another's property (like food) is not required to pay it back, because the law of nature makes such goods common property in that moment. He distinguishes this from non-consumable goods, like a horse or a bed, which must be returned once the danger has passed.</summary>

### ARTICLE II.

*Whether one who has received something is always bound to make restitution.*

After the circumstance of *to whom*, there follows *by whom*: about which there are two minor questions. The first of this second article is whether everyone who has received something, whoever he may have been, is bound to restore it. And the argument is made for the negative side. Restitution (as we repeat again and again) is the establishment of equality: by which, specifically, something is taken away from him who has more, and given to him who has less. However, it often happens that he who took the thing is deprived of it through no fault of his own: as when someone else steals it from him. Therefore, in that case, he shall not be bound to restore the same. ¶ Second. No one is bound to betray his own crime: according to that saying of **Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Church Father</note>: *I do not tell you to betray yourself.* But it sometimes happens that a debtor cannot make restitution without bringing infamy upon himself; therefore, he is then released from the yoke of restitution. ¶ Third. One thing is satisfied by one simple restitution: yet it sometimes happens that though many have stolen a thing, one restores it in full; therefore, the others are then bound to no further restitution; and thus, not everyone who took the thing is obligated to restitution. ¶ On the contrary side is the fact that he who sins is bound to make satisfaction for the fault: but the fault, as **Augustine** says <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430)</note>, *is not forgiven unless that which was taken is restored*; therefore, the duty lies upon him to make restitution.

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
This question holds a distinguished place in the matter of restitution. For that reason, after a distinction is laid down, it is answered with four conclusions. For in the person who occupies the property of another, there are two things to consider: namely, both the action by which he received it, and the thing
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
itself. Therefore, the first conclusion is: Whoever has in his possession the property of another is bound, by reason of the thing itself which was received, to restore the same to the true owner. It is proved thus: Whoever has more than what is his own 

<column-break/>

ought to return it to him to whom it belongs: for the logic of **commutative justice** <term>justice governing private transactions and the equal exchange of goods</term> demands this. Indeed, its duty is to establish equality between him who has less and him who has more.

<margin>Triple taking.</margin>
¶ But in truth, the "taking" itself is usually threefold. For sometimes it is injurious: namely, that which is done against the will of the owner: such as theft and robbery; regarding this branch, the second conclusion is established.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
Whoever has received a thing through injury is bound to restore the same by reason of the taking: even if he no longer has it in his possession, but perhaps it was stolen from him. It is proved thus: Whoever has brought injury upon another is bound to repair it: even if no gain has come to him from it—namely, because he took away the other's reputation or honor. Therefore, by the same logic, he who has unjustly snatched a thing, since he caused a loss in that thing, is compelled by right to restore it. ¶ In the second way: that action of taking without a gift could be just, and for the use and benefit of the one who received it: as when someone receives a thing on loan, or bought on credit; concerning this, the third conclusion is added, similar to the one above.
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Whoever has received a thing in this way is bound to restore it or its price: not only by reason of the thing received if it remains with him, but also by reason of the taking: even if he has lost it in any way whatsoever. The conclusion is clear: for he who has justly taken another's property for his own use (without it being a gift) is obligated to keep the owner harmless <note>original: "indemnem seruare"; to ensure the owner suffers no loss</note>, not only because of the benefit received, but out of justice.
¶ In the third way: The taking can also be just by the will of the owner, yet not for the benefit of the recipient, but for the sake of the person who gave it. Regarding this, the fourth
<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
and two-part conclusion is applied. No one who keeps another's property as a **depositary** <term>someone with whom property is left in trust or for safekeeping</term> is bound to restore it by reason of the taking; but rather by reason of the thing which he has received. Therefore, if he loses it through no fault of his own, he remains subject to no restitution; but it is otherwise if he loses it through his own great fault. The first part is proved in the opposite way to the third. He who receives a thing in that manner—unless he receives a fee for the guarding, or has otherwise bound himself to keep it safe—does not become the guardian of that thing by reason of justice, but out of grace and benevolence; and therefore, if the thing is lost without his fault, it has perished not to him, but to the owner. But the proof of the second part is: That by natural law (as the rule of law holds), he who provides the cause of the loss is seen to have caused the loss. Therefore, if your grave fault was the cause...

<margin>A rule to be noted.</margin>
¶ In order for these conclusions to be examined in their proper order, this principle must be gathered first from the two prior rules. Every obligation of restitution arises from one of two headings: namely, either by reason of the act of taking <note>original: "acceptionis"</note>, even if you no longer possess the object; or by reason of the object received <note>original: "rei acceptae"</note> which you currently have, even if you were not the one who took it. Therefore, if you both took the object and still have it, you are bound by both cords. Under the term "taking," any action is understood through which you caused a loss or inflicted an injury, even if you gained nothing from it: for example, if you set fire to another’s house or committed an insult. ¶ From this it follows that in whatever way a thing has come into your power—whether justly or unjustly, for a price or for free—as soon as you discover it belongs to another, you are bound to return it to the owner: not only by the law of charity, but also by the law of justice. For instance, if you received it from an illegitimate possessor—*for example*, from a bandit—whether by theft, gift, loan, or as a deposit, or if you bought it for a price, once the true owner is found you are bound to hand it over to him, unless the law of prescription <term>prescription: a legal principle where one gains ownership of property after holding it for a certain period of time under specific conditions</term> happens to favor you. This conclusion is proven. In Question 5, we said a thing is legitimately possessed by only two means: either by the owner's will or by permission of the law. However, in whatever way you received a thing from an illegitimate possessor, neither of those causes was present: because the true owner did not agree, nor did the law grant it. Therefore, you have in no way acquired ownership, and thus you are compelled to return it to the owner. If you do not do so when you could perform it without great detriment to yourself (as we said above), but instead return it to the illegitimate possessor, you remain liable for restitution, since you were bound by justice.

<margin>Who is excused from restitution.</margin>
Nevertheless, I would believe that in these matters of restitution, an ignorance of the law can occur; if such ignorance excuses one from guilt, it shall subsequently excuse one from restitution. For every common person is not expected to know these subtleties of the law. Therefore, one who, being ignorant, received something from a bandit and returned it to him in good faith is not to be compelled in conscience to make restitution. Furthermore, I would except the law of prescription: since after you have possessed a thing in good faith for the legal amount of time under a title of purchase or gift (which is legitimate), you are immune from restitution even if it later becomes known to you that it belonged to another. It is otherwise if you took it by theft: because you always lacked a title, and therefore you never established prescription.

<margin>A doubt: what is understood by the name of the "thing."</margin>
¶ However, a reason for doubt arises here: namely, what is to be understood by the name of the "thing"? Specifically, whether it is the object itself precisely, or also its "fruits" <note>in legal terms, "fruits" refers to the profits, products, or benefits derived from property, such as crops from a field or rent from a house</note>. And let us speak, for example, of the one who is bound not by

<column-break/>

reason of the act of taking, but only by reason of the thing received. Suppose I bought a field from a bandit which produced "fruits" for me: am I bound to restore the fruits as well? To this, it is answered through a rule that is solemn and most celebrated in law.

<margin>A rule to be noted.</margin>
Whoever is subject to restitution solely by reason of the thing received is bound to restore the object, or that which he has of it, and whatever made him richer through it; however, he is not bound to restore that which he consumed in good faith, through which he was not made wealthier. This is a rule of law <note>Soto cites the "Digest" of Roman Law here: Digest 5.3.25.11 and 5.3.25.16</note>, of which the gloss <note>a standard medieval commentary on legal texts</note> says no rule is truer. For example, you are bound to restore the fruits of another's field: not only those you still have, but those you consumed for uses in which, had you not had those fruits, you would have spent other funds. However, expenses and labor are to be deducted. If, however, you consumed them because, *for example*, the field was given to you as a gift, and led by that gift you changed your status and lived more grandly: then surely you are not bound except for that which you would have otherwise spent. In the same way, if you bought a silk garment cheaply from a bandit and wore it out through use, when otherwise you would not have worn silk: you are not bound except for the value of the garment you were accustomed to wearing. Similarly, if you used a horse given to you by a bandit in non-necessary cases for which you would neither have bought nor hired a horse: you are bound to restore nothing for the use, because you were not made wealthier. It is otherwise, however, if you rented out its services, by which you were made richer: for then, after deducting expenses, you are bound for the remainder. In the same way, if you were invited by a bandit and consumed stolen food in good faith, you are afterwards bound for nothing, unless you were going to spend something on food at home. From this it follows that if you lost that thing which you received in good faith from an illegitimate possessor without great fault of your own, you remain subject to no restitution. Conversely, if you sold a stolen thing which you had received as a gift, you are afterwards bound to restore the price, insofar as you were made richer by it. Understand this, however, if you were made wealthier from the thing itself: for if that increase came to you through your own industry <note>meaning through your own hard work or business skill</note>, you are not constrained to restore that. For instance, if you increased your substance by trading with another’s money, you are bound only for the original capital. From these examples, therefore, judge the rest.

<margin>On one who wrongfully retains another's property.</margin>
¶ Regarding the person who retains another's property through injury <note>meaning with wrongful intent or bad faith</note>, the reasoning is different: he is indeed bound for the emerging loss <term>emerging loss: "damnum emergens," the actual loss or damage sustained</term> and for the ceasing profit <term>ceasing profit: "lucrum cessans," the profit the owner would have made if they hadn't lost the property</term>, as will be seen again under the titles on theft and usury; and he is bound for all fruits, in whatever way he may have consumed them. However, he is not bound for that profit which was gained through his own...

<margin>Argument against.</margin>
¶ Against this decision, however, there is an argument that he who buys a thing from a thief in good faith is not bound to return it for free to the true owner. For it was said in the preceding article that by reason of the thing received, no one is bound to restitution with great detriment to himself: therefore, no one is bound according to conscience to suffer the loss of the price he spent without any fault of his own. If, I say, he received it by theft, or by loan, or as a gift, it is well and good; but for a buyer, there seems to be another reason. Because of this, perhaps, there will not be lacking someone who thinks it is then permitted for the buyer to return the thing to the thief so that he may recover his price: nonetheless, that is false. It is indeed permitted for him, if it can be done, to summon the thief and seize him from whom he may extort the price; however, to expose the thing to danger so that it does not come into the hands of the owner is not permitted. For the thing itself, in whosoever’s power it may be, makes him responsible for returning it to the legitimate owner: and if he does not do so, he is bound to restitution: as was said above. And this truth is confirmed. For if the thief had disappeared, so that he could not appear, then he who bought the thing would be the debtor to the owner: and in a judicial court, he would be compelled to produce the thing with the loss of the price: which, as we said above, is a sign that he is bound by justice. Moreover, because the thief can be found, the same owner has lost no right: therefore, he is also then bound to the owner. And it is confirmed: for if it were discovered in a judicial court that the buyer, after he certainly knew the thing belonged to another owner, had delivered it to the thief, he would be convicted to pay the owner. Wherefore, when we said that the possessor of another’s property is not bound to restore it with his own detriment by reason only of the thing received, it is understood to be regarding that detriment which he fears from another—namely, by which the act of restoring itself is hindered—but not regarding the loss which he himself made by buying. For whoever buys should look out for himself: knowing that he buys at that risk, so that if the thing belongs to another, 

<margin>A doubt concerning the sale in good faith of a thing bought from a thief.</margin>
he loses the price. ¶ What, however, is the law if he who purchased a thing from a thief sold it to another in good faith? Whether, knowing later that it belongs to another, he is bound to rescind the contract, and return the price to his buyer and the thing to the owner. For it appears he is not bound, since he is not bound by reason of the taking <note>original: "acceptionis"</note>: since he neither took the thing himself, nor sold it fraudulently; nor by reason of the thing received: since he neither has it, nor has he been made richer by it. For let us suppose he sold it for as much 

<column-break/>

as he had bought it. For if he sold it for more, there is no doubt but that he is bound to return that excess of the price to the owner: because that part of the thing remains with him. This is indeed an argument that could deceive many. For if that thing, as we said above, had been taken from the first buyer by theft without his fault, or consumed in good faith, such that he was not made richer, he would be bound for nothing: therefore, since he sold it in good faith, the same judgment appears to hold. 

<margin>Solution to the doubt.</margin>
Nonetheless, it is answered that although he may not remain obligated to the owner of that same thing (as the argument seems to prove), he is nevertheless bound to keep his buyer harmless <note>original: "indemnem"; to ensure the buyer suffers no financial loss</note>. And therefore, since he knows that he transferred no ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> to him, but that the buyer is endangered by the law of restitution, he is compelled by law to restore his price to him. Just as if he had bought glass for a precious gem from a thief, and sold it again for the same price in good faith: for knowing then afterward the falsity of the thing, he would be bound to rescind the contract. ¶ From which it follows that if that second buyer should not appear, and there is no fear that the thing is to be demanded from him, then he who had sold it to him in good faith, although he then knows it was another’s, is bound to no restitution: since he is free from the owner of the thing, after he neither has the thing nor was made richer by it; and he gave no loss to the other.

<margin>Plunder from an unjust war.</margin>
¶ Similar to these is the case of one who has plundered goods in an unjust war, yet in good faith, because he thought it was just. For then, knowing later that it was not just, he is bound to restore those things by which he was made richer: but not the houses which he burned, or the animals which he killed. ¶ Concerning merchants, however, who have made frequent contracts which they judged to be legitimate, but afterward understand were usurious <term>usury: the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender, often involving interest</term>: whether it is enough for them to restore that precise money which they gained through usury, or also that which they acquired again through the business of the same money, some are in doubt. For it appears to them that usurious money must be restored along with the profits: led by the similar point that another's property must be restored with its fruits <note>original: "fructibus"; products or profits naturally arising from property, like crops or offspring</note>. But without doubt, it is enough if they restore the usurious money. For since money of itself is not fruitful, but only through the industry of the merchant, no similarity can be drawn from things which bear fruit by themselves. Concerning this, however, we shall speak again in Book 6. And thus far concerning the first two conclusions.

¶ In the third indeed, a small doubt lies hidden. It was designated...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of restitution. Having previously discussed the obligations of a buyer in good faith, Soto now transitions to the distinctions between different types of legal loans and deposits, and how the degree of "fault" (negligence) determines who must pay for a loss.</meta>

->F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,<-
->Page 370<-

For the second species of "takings" <note>original: "acceptionum"; referring to ways one comes into possession of another's property</note> occurs when someone rightfully receives something for their own particular advantage and use, such as a loan. It has been asserted that in such a case, by reason of the taking, restitution is necessary even if the thing is lost through no fault of the person. ¶ However, the opposite appears to be true in the single chapter on loans for use <note>original: "cap. vnicum de commod." referring to a specific point in Canon or Civil law</note>, where it is held that he who loses a loaned item without his own fault is bound to nothing. Yet, the resolution is very easy.

<margin>The difference between a loan for use and a loan for consumption.</margin>
Indeed, a loan for use <term>commodatum<gloss>a loan of a specific object to be returned intact, like a horse</gloss></term> and a loan for consumption <term>mutuatum<gloss>a loan of fungible goods to be replaced by an equivalent amount, like grain or money</gloss></term> differ, if we look at the names of the types. The former must be restored in its specific form—for instance, if you received a horse or a vase as a loan for use, which are not consumed by use. In a loan for consumption, however, it is not necessary to restore the exact same item: if you received money, wine, or grain, which are consumed by use, it is sufficient to return the value or an equal amount.

<margin>Another difference.</margin>
The real distinction, however, is that ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of the thing loaned for use is not transferred, whereas it is transferred in a loan for consumption. Through this, the spirit of the law is revealed. For you do not owe the thing loaned for use to you simply by reason of taking it, since you were not made its owner. Because of this, when it perishes without your fault, it perishes not for you, but for the owner—just as if it had perished while in his own possession. But indeed, by the law of the loan, you are held liable even for a **slight fault** <note>original: "leui culpa"; minor negligence</note>, as the text itself says. Not necessarily for the whole value, but in part, according to the degree of fault. And what we say regarding a loan for use, understand also regarding a rental. For if you rented a house or a horse to me, although it resulted in the common benefit of both parties, if the thing is lost without my fault, I owe nothing. For the lessor subjects himself to that risk. I am, however, held liable for slight fault in part, and for **grave fault** <note>gross negligence</note> in full. But when a thing is loaned to you for consumption, because you are established as its owner, you are made a debtor of restitution by the very reason of the taking. Therefore, even if it perishes without your fault, it perishes for you, who are the owner, and thus you are not released from the burden of restitution.

<margin>Concerning the fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ And from here, a convenient transition is made to the fourth conclusion regarding a **deposit** <note>property left in another's care for safekeeping</note>. Namely, that a depository is not bound to restore the thing if he loses it without great fault on his part. So the laws hold in chapters 1 and 2 regarding deposits. Thus, the difference between a loan for use and a deposit is that the borrower for use is held liable for slight fault, because he sought the thing for his own advantage, and thus was bound by justice to guard it. But the depository is held liable only for "great fault," because he was not guarding it for his own benefit; and therefore, he was bound to keep it solely by the benefit of charity. It must

<column-break/>

be understood, therefore, that a "depository" (as we said above) is one who is purely a depository—that is, one who did not bind himself to guard the item for a price. For a guardian of this sort, even if he loses the thing without his fault, is bound by justice to restitution, just like one who undergoes the risk of goods through a contract of insurance. The reason that **gross fault** <note>original: "magna culpa"</note> obligates him is that he provides the cause of the damage; and therefore Jurists call it "broad fault" <note>original: "latam culpam"</note> and say that such a person is held liable as if for fraud <note>original: "de dolo"</note>.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ A doubt arises, however, as to what should be called "slight fault" and what should be called "grave fault." Indeed, at first glance, slight fault seems to be judged as that which is a venial sin before God, and grave fault as that which is lethal <note>mortal sin</note> before Him. But in truth, this difference is not to be weighed in the manner of a Theologian, but in a juridical manner, according to human judgment. For I would believe that in the "court of conscience," the slight fault of a borrower does not obligate him to restitution unless it is mortal before God; for a man can hardly be free from venial sins. Therefore, a man should not be punished or fined with such a great penalty on account of them. Rather, it is called "slight" by human and juridical judgment in respect to the other kind of fault, which is required more abundantly in a depository for him to be condemned. All these things, however, are to be estimated according to the judicial court, whose sentence must be stood by in conscience.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, the response is that he who is bound by reason of the taking is not only bound to create equality because he himself has more, but because the other has less. Therefore, even if he loses the thing in whatever way, he nonetheless remains a debtor.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The second argument inquired how restitution is to be made by someone who has usurped another’s property through a secret crime; for he is not bound to betray himself.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
To which **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> responded nothing more than that it must then be carried out secretly through a confessor. If, however, it cannot be done in a secret way, he does not answer what remains to be done.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
**Cajetan**, however, judges that restitution is never necessary if it involves the danger of one’s reputation. But I judge that this universal rule of his was clearly and fully refuted in the previous question; indeed, **prudent discretion** must be used, so that you compare the value of reputation with the injury and damage that was given, and judge accordingly whether some loss of reputation must be made so that restitution may occur—especially when the matter is pending and (as they say) "in the making" <note>original: "in fieri"</note> so that it can be recovered.

# Book Four: Question VII

Whether an adulteress <note>original: "adultera"</note> who has substituted a bastard son <note>original: "nothum filium"</note> for her husband is bound to reveal herself so as not to defraud the legitimate heirs of their inheritance. Many things are commented upon regarding this various matter, both by the doctoral teachers of theology (on the 4th book, 15th Distinction) and by the interpreters of the law. There is an existing case in the chapter *Officium* regarding penance and remission <note>original: "c. officij. de pœniten. & remiss."; a reference to Canon Law</note>. To hunt for the truth from more certain grounds, it is worthwhile to make a distinction. For either that woman possesses a dowry or other property of her own, which is free for her use and with which she can compensate the true heir for the damage; in that case, the common consensus is that she is by no means bound to defame herself <note>original: "infamare"; to ruin her public reputation</note>, but it is sufficient to make restitution by another path. If, however, she has nothing from which
<margin>A distinction.</margin>
to make restitution, then a sub-distinction must be made. Either she believes that by revealing the truth she will be helpful, or she does not. If no benefit is expected from her revelation, it is most certain that she is in no way bound: for it is a vain work, and neither a work of charity nor of justice. Therefore, that defamation would be reckless because it is useless; in such a case, the woman is to be regarded as a debtor who is unable to pay.
<margin>Scotus.</margin>
Nevertheless, *Duns Scotus* says in the same distinction, question 2, that she must then do as much as she can so that the inheritance does not fall to the illegitimate son: such as by advising him to enter a religious order <note>original: "religionis ingressum"; becoming a monk or friar, which would often involve renouncing an inheritance</note>. Yet, according to justice, there is no reason she is bound to do this. If, however, she thinks she will be helpful because the bastard son, trusting her word, will refuse the inheritance, or perhaps she can prove it in such a way that it gains credit in court: then, if she can do this without any detriment to her life or reputation, it is most firm that she is bound to do so. But if she cannot do it without danger to her reputation
<margin>Scotus, Cajetan, Adrian.</margin>
and honor, *Scotus* then leans toward the view that she is not bound. *Cajetan*, persisting in his own rule, was accustomed to asserting this certainly. *Adrian* <note>Pope Adrian VI</note>, however, in the first question on restitution, judges the opposite: namely, that she is bound even with the loss of her reputation. ¶ Nevertheless, in my judgment
<margin>The author's opinion.</margin>
(if it carries any weight), the reputation of the adulteress must be weighed with prudence against the loss that the true heir suffers. For if the reputation of the woman—who might otherwise be noble and honest—is much more precious than the inheritance, which is perhaps small, she should be advised to remain silent. If, however, the inheritance is conversely estimated to be of greater value—namely, if it is an illustrious entailed estate <term>maioratus<gloss>an inheritance that must pass to the eldest legitimate son to keep a noble house intact</gloss></term>, and she is not of such great name—she is bound to reveal herself: at least at the point of death, so that she does not undergo the danger of homicide <note>referring to the risk of being killed by her husband if she confesses while he is alive</note>. All other things being equal, the condition of the legitimate heir is better. However, I think this is contrary to what *Adrian* judges. For he says that one should never despair that the adulteress might be helpful by revealing the matter; and therefore, one should lean very much toward this side, that she should reveal herself. I,

<column-break/>

on the other hand, would believe the opposite according to my meager understanding: namely, that a disclosure of this kind is never of any use, except when it is evident that the husband was absent at the time of conception, or when it can be proven in another way that she was not known by him then: as is held in the *Law "Filium," Digest, on those who are of their own or another's right* <note>original: "l. filium. ff. de his qui sunt sui vel ali. iur."; a reference to Roman Civil Law</note>. For a bastard is not bound to give any credit to his mother, no matter how much she swears; rather, in court, he is to be considered legitimate, as is commanded by the same law. Nor is any credit due to one alleging her own disgrace; and for that reason, a necessity can hardly be presented that she should be bound to defame herself. For in the aforementioned evident case, her confession is not needed; and in others, it is of no use. ¶ Although this also
<margin>Note.</margin>

<margin>When an adulteress abdicates an inheritance.</margin>

Nor does the argument to the contrary press us: that if someone had bequeathed a hundred to me, believing me to be his son—having been deceived by his own fickleness, or by another without my fault—I can possess those things by the best right. From this, it seems to be gathered by analogy that although I know I am a bastard by the report of my mother, if the father leaves me his goods, I can possess them. I say that the argument does not press solidly, nor does it bring a similar case: because in that cited case, I was not the cause of that ignorance through an injustice. In our present case, however, the father did not appoint me heir of his own free will, but compelled by the law, surely thinking that I am legitimate. And therefore, what acts by the force of law does not support me, knowing that I am not legitimate.

# Book Four: Question VII (Continued)

...her conscience could be at peace if it were certain that her testimony would be entirely helpful to the true heir, unless she would betray herself even at the risk of her life; provided that first every stone was turned to avoid such danger. For she is not bound to avoid her husband's sin <note>The "sin" here refers to the husband's potentially wrongful distribution of property if he knew the truth, or the general moral mess created by the adultery.</note> with such great injury to the true heir. ¶ Therefore, the cited chapter *Officium* <note>original: "Capitulum... officij"; a reference to the Decretals of Pope Innocent III in Canon Law</note> supports what has been said. Indeed, a case was brought there to the Pope regarding a certain sterile woman who, fearing her husband's inheritance would pass to strangers, feigned pregnancy and substituted another's son for her husband's legitimate son. When Innocent was consulted as to whether she should enjoy the benefit of absolution <note>The formal forgiveness of sins in the Sacrament of Penance.</note> before she revealed the fraud, he responded in the affirmative—that she should indeed be absolved. And an example of an adulteress is added, with whom one must act similarly. For the Pope thought either that she would be of no help by revealing the truth, or that perhaps the danger of death loomed over her, or that it was not such an exceptional case that she should defame herself <note>original: "infamare"; to destroy her social standing and reputation</note> for the sake of the inheritance. This was especially so because, since the husband lacked legitimate offspring, there was not such a great danger if a feigned son succeeded. Nevertheless, she is ordered that a competent satisfaction be enjoined upon her by the confessor.

<margin>A doubt concerning the adulterer himself.</margin>
But the reasoning for doubting concerning the adulterer has always been more troublesome and pressing for me in these matters: namely, concerning the man who fathered offspring from another man’s wife, whether he is bound both to restore to her husband what he spent in feeding and educating the substituted son, and also to the legitimate heir the inheritance of which he is defrauded. On the affirmative side, the reason argues that he himself provided a cause for that loss. On the negative side, however, it is argued that he himself did not substitute the son to the husband. For let us suppose he never persuaded the woman to deceive her husband about the matter by saying the child was his.

<margin>Response</margin>
To this, therefore, we respond according to our understanding, that an adulterer of this sort is not bound by as great a bond of restitution as the adulteress, about whom we have spoken; especially if she consented to the adultery of her own accord. But to start the matter from the first line: if an unmarried woman associates with two men, neither of them is bound to believe she conceived from him. Indeed, even if Peter believes the child is his, and Paul receives, nourishes, and enriches him, Peter is not bound to reveal the matter, since the other was deceived either by his own lightness or by the woman's deception, and he himself did not deceive him. Therefore, by almost the same right, an adulterer can defend himself from being led to believe

<column-break/>

the child is his son. For he hardly knows whether she admitted another man besides himself; for she who receives one can be believed to admit another without injustice. Wherefore, as it is written in the law *Lucius* <note>original: "ff. de conditionibus & demonstrationibus"; a reference to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law</note>, "no one can sufficiently prove whose father's son he is." This, therefore, is the first reason why the adulterer is not so bound to make restitution as the adulteress. The second reason is the one we made just before: for even if it is clear to him from the child's face or by another way that the offspring is his, nevertheless he himself did not substitute the child to the husband. Indeed, even if he was a remote cause because he committed adultery, she herself should have seen to what was to be done about the child she had conceived, since she was an adulteress of her own accord. Therefore, if the husband raises the child at home, let it be imputed to her. In truth, I do not clearly see why an adulterer is bound to any restitution out of strict justice. Nevertheless, I would add that while it is most certain he fathered the son, and he is able to make some compensation to either the husband or the heir, or to nourish the son without danger and scandal, he is bound to do so out of honesty and decency.

<margin>Concerning the third argument. Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ In the third argument, a rule for the manner of restitution is requested when several people have conspired in the same theft. Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas</note> only responds that when one person restores the stolen goods, the others are not bound to the owner, but rather to the one who made the restitution for their shared portion. This, however, needs a fuller explanation and response, since it is not a simple matter but a complex one. However, because this same material will return in the next article, it will be decided more exactly there.

# Book Four: Question VII.

...restitution would become greater than what is right. Furthermore, it is often the case that several people assist the one who received the property through either advice or favor; because of this, restitution would have to be made multiple times by different people. Also, they sometimes strive to cause a loss which, in reality, they are unable to bring about. Therefore, if restitution were necessary in such a case, something would be given to another person that had never actually been taken from them. ¶ Third: if someone who did not receive the property were liable for restitution simply because they provided some cause for the act, then by that same logic, a person who does not stand in the way of an injurious taking when they are able to do so would also be forced to make restitution. However, this is false, because no one is bound to put themselves in danger for the sake of saving someone else's property; yet a person would often be exposing themselves to danger if they shouted out against bandits or physically opposed them. ¶ On the contrary, however, is that passage from Romans 1: "They are worthy of death, not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them." <note>A reference to Romans 1:32. The author uses this biblical authority to argue that moral guilt—and thus the duty to make things right—extends beyond the primary actor.</note> Indeed, if those who consent are worthy of punishment, so too are others who assist in any way whatsoever.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with four conclusions. Let the first be the general foundation for the rest: Whoever is the cause of an unjust taking is bound to make restitution by reason of that same taking, even if they did not share in the taken property in any way. This conclusion has already been proven above, where we showed that the obligation to restore arises from a double root: namely, by reason of the taking itself and by reason of the thing taken. He who is the cause of the taking becomes guilty of the act.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: It can happen in nine ways that someone is the cause of a taking. These are usually explained in this verse:
> Command, counsel, consent, flattery, harboring,
> Participating, silence, not opposing, not disclosing.
<note>original: "Iussio, cōsilium, cōsensu, palpo, recursus, Participās, mutus, nō obstās, nō manifestās." This was a common medieval mnemonic used by confessors and lawyers to remember the nine ways one could be an accomplice to a crime.</note>

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
Indeed, this number is gathered by the following distinctions. A person can be the cause of another person acting or taking something in two ways: namely, directly and indirectly. Directly, this happens in three ways. First, on the part of the taking itself: specifically by moving someone toward it in one of four ways: namely by commanding, advising, consenting, or praising the deed. The second way is on the part of the taker: namely, because someone shelters the person who has recourse to them, or supports and protects them in another way; this is signified by the single word "harboring." The third way occurs on the part of the thing taken: namely, while one becomes a participant in the same theft or robbery, or a partner in the crime; and this is signified by the word "participating." Indirectly, a person is said to be the cause when they do not pre-

<column-break/>

vent someone whom they can and ought to prevent. And this happens in three ways: because they fail to issue a command, or fail to advise against the act, or because they withdraw the help with which they could have resisted, or because they hide the deed.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: Of these nine ways, five by their very nature oblige one to restitution. The first and most important is "commanding." Indeed, he who commands is the "prince of causes" <note>The primary instigator or the one with authority who initiates the chain of events.</note> and consequently submits himself primarily to the law of restitution. In the second place is the "consent" of one without whom the act would not have happened—for example, if a guard of a house lets a thief inside. Third is "harboring": for he who is a receiver, supporter, and protector of bandits provides a great cause for loss, since bandits, relying chiefly on such people, nourish their own audacity. And fourth, he who participates either in the crime or in the loot. And finally, fifth, he who does not oppose the act when he ought to: such as a prince or his official; certainly, those who receive taxes and wages for this purpose, so that they may purge the republic of wrongdoers. This conclusion, in all its parts, rests on a single reason: that all these people, according to the tenor of the first conclusion, are truly causes of the action.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The fourth conclusion: A bond of restitution does not always emerge from the other four listed cases, because they do not always count as causes of the action in the same way as the ones above. For he who provides "counsel" is not always the cause of the action, nor is he who "flatters" or "praises." Therefore, unless they have truly acted as a cause, they do not become debtors bound to restore. And the same should be felt regarding the "silent" person who does not cry out while the act is happening, and the person "not disclosing" after the fact; for they are not always bound to reveal it.

<margin>Concerning the first conclusion.</margin>
¶ Descending now to a more accurate examination of these conclusions, let us first explore—concerning the foundational first conclusion—who exactly should be considered a "cause of action."

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
And because this happens in two ways—namely directly and indirectly—let us speak of both modes, starting with "participants," in which the matter is clearer.

<margin>Adrian. Sylvester.</margin>
For Adrian <note>Likely Pope Adrian VI, a noted theologian before his papacy.</note>, in that little question about those who cooperate with a thief—to which Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian famous for his "Summa Sylvestrina," a manual for confessors.</note> alludes under the word *restitutio* (restitution), section 3, along with certain legal experts commenting on the chapter *Sicut dignum* <note>original: "cap. sicut dignum. de homicidio"; a chapter in Canon Law regarding homicide and responsibility.</note>—is convinced of this rule: that only he becomes a cause of the taking without whom it would not have happened. From this, they infer that if a thief was going to commit the theft anyway without any partner, then the person who joined him is not bound for the whole amount (*in solidum*), but only for the portion that came to him, because he was not the "cause" of the theft for the other person. However, their interpreter Adrian adds that if the other person was only going to do it with some partner, even if he would have done it with someone else...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...another: nevertheless, that companion is held **liable in full** <note>original: *in solidum*. This refers to a legal obligation where an individual can be held responsible for the entire debt or penalty, not just a portion of it.</note> because he is truly a cause. But certainly, such people cannot defend themselves with any degree of probability; this is something **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), an influential Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> recognized before us here. For, first of all, it would follow by the same reasoning that if someone had many servants who were most ready to obey his every nod, and he ordered one of them to commit a murder or a theft—which the servant was already most ready to do on his own—or if a servant, seeing his master already preparing a crime, had preempted him of his own accord, then that perpetrator of the crime would not be held liable in full, nor even in part, because the master would have done it by himself anyway. Such a concession would be utterly absurd. Moreover, it is clear that this logical consequence must be granted. For it is the same whether you do for another what he himself was already about to do, or whether you join him in such an event: therefore, if the one joining in is not held liable, certainly the one doing it is not either. Thus, whether the other person with whom Peter joined would have done it without him or with someone else (because he would not have done it without a companion), or whether he would have done it entirely without any partner at all: nevertheless, if Peter joins in, he is held liable in full.

Therefore, in these types of moral outcomes, it is not required that the person held to restitution must have been the **indispensable cause** <note>original: *causa sine qua non*. A cause without which the event would not have occurred.</note> for the thing to happen. For this reason, no rule should be taken from such denials—as in, "he would have done it without a partner"—but one must look only to the affirmation: namely, that whoever joins with another as an effective cause so that they produce a single cause, is considered a cause such that he is held liable in full. Indeed, natural reason shows this. For while two fires are applied to the same object, although each by itself would burn it up, nevertheless, while they act together, each is a cause. This is chiefly confirmed by the fact that in a court of law, no such exception is heard as to whether the other person would have done it or not; rather, both are condemned in full. Since, therefore, the laws bind in the **court of conscience**, it follows that judgment regarding the security of one's conscience must be made according to them. Furthermore, these conditional "what ifs" have nothing to do with morality: that is, they neither increase virtues nor diminish sins. Perhaps the house you tore down was about to fall immediately, and the crops you destroyed were about to be uprooted by a passing whirlwind; nevertheless, nothing frees you from restitution. And the passage in **Matthew 18** <note>Matthew 18:7</note> pertains to this: "It is necessary that scandals come, but woe to the man through whom the scandal comes." That is, although the scandal was going to come through someone else, the person through whom it actually comes is alone in the fault.

<margin>When someone is an aid to another.</margin>
The reasoning, therefore, by which one must perceive whether someone is an auxiliary cause to another is this alone: if he did some-

<column-break/>

-thing that was of some importance to the outcome. Suppose you encountered thieves at night, and as they were moving a ladder to a wall, you also touched it: yet nothing depended on you, for they were already doing it. In that case, according to conscience, you are not to be judged a cause. Just as the servant of a **usurer** <note>A person who lends money at unreasonably high interest rates.</note> is not a cause simply by touching or keeping the money, because, speaking morally, that has nothing to do with the matter. However, those who are their agents—that is, those who execute the contracts and handle the business—are truly causes, as will be clear in Book 6.

¶ I should say this applies when both or many join together into one cause. For if they stole separately—for example, one stole one **crown** <note>original: *scutum*. A gold or silver coin used in Europe.</note> and another stole another later, and thus they plundered the treasury—no one would be held for the whole, as is held in the **"Common Law"** <note>original: *l. Vulgaris*. A reference to a specific law in the Roman Digest (D. 47. 2. 21. 9).</note> regarding theft.

<margin>An argument to the contrary.</margin>
¶ However, opponents may object to this opinion using the words of the same law in the section "on theft," which are also found in the law "thus wounded" regarding the **Aquilian Law** <note>The *Lex Aquilia* was a Roman law providing compensation to owners of property injured by another's fault.</note>. Namely, that if two or more people together carry away the same beam, or timber, or any other heavy stolen object that individuals could not carry alone, then each and every one is held liable in full by an action for theft. From the opposite sense of this, it seems it should be inferred that if each could carry the whole, no one would be held except for a portion—namely, because no one seems to have wanted to take the whole, but only a part. The answer is that this is not the intent of the text; indeed, it is the opposite. For the **Jurist** <note>A writer or expert on law.</note> was careful to answer a silent objection. For indeed, since individuals cannot carry the weight, they are not causes individually but collectively; lest anyone should then infer that they are not held individually, but all together proportionately for restitution, the Jurist steps in, warning that individuals are nevertheless held liable in full. Therefore, even if each could carry it by himself, each would be held by a tighter bond to liability in full.

¶ Behold, therefore, how a participant in a crime is a cause and is held to make restitution in full. For if he participates not in the crime, but only in the loot in **good faith**, it has already been said above that he is not held except by reason of the thing received—for what he has and by which he has been made richer. And by this, one should judge regarding **soldiers** who plunder a house together in an unjust war. For even if individuals would have done it by themselves—indeed, each would rather attack the house alone, or with two or three, because they do not need more helpers—nevertheless, however many (or even a single troop) despoil it, they are held in...

# Book Four, Question VII.

...held liable in full <note>original: *in solidum*; a legal term meaning one is responsible for the entire debt or penalty, rather than just a portion.</note>. Nor is the contrary assertion safe, regardless of what others might say.
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ However, a doubt remains regarding those who caused a great loss not simultaneously as a single cause, but separately: how do they contract the stain of guilt and the obligation of restitution if they stole in such small amounts that none of their individual actions would have been a sin? For example: Individual passers-by on different days near a vineyard each took two or three clusters of grapes. In the end, they harvested the entire vineyard prematurely in that manner. Are they each held to full restitution afterward? It seems they are so held: because if restitution is then commanded under penalty of excommunication, they are bound to it under the guilt of mortal sin <note>A "mortal sin" is a grave offense in Catholic theology that separates a person from God's grace.</note>. Yet, if no one is held except for their own part, no one would sin mortally by not making restitution, because stealing such a small thing is not a mortal sin. It is answered that such "little thefts" were not mortal sins. Nor did the action of anyone become mortal because of the huge damage that emerged later. Nevertheless, when restitution is later commanded under penalty of excommunication by reason of the enormous harm, whoever is bound under penalty of mortal sin is held either to answer for it or to pay only what they took. Therefore, one who has paid their share is not held to turn themselves in. If you argue that the threat of excommunication is not lawful except for a mortal sin, the answer is that this is true in itself by reason of guilt; however, it is otherwise by reason of the emerging damage when it becomes grave.
¶ Thus far regarding the direct cause. But for someone to be an indirect cause—which they also call a cause "by accident"—three things are required. First, that you do not oppose the evil; second, that you are able to oppose it; and third, that you are obligated to oppose it. Saint Thomas [Aquinas], along with Aristotle, taught this in the *Summa Theologiae* <note>original: *1.2. quæst.6. articu.3.*</note>. For another's action to become indirectly voluntary for me, it is required that I do not hinder it when I ought to. Indeed, the pilot of a ship is the cause of its sinking while he is able to save it, since it is under his care. However, if another ship which was not entrusted to him should sink, even if he could have come to its aid, he is not considered the cause of that shipwreck. Furthermore, add that it is not enough that you *ought* to restrain the evil you do not restrain to be entangled in the bond of restitution: rather, it is required that justice obliges you to do so. For the precept of charity alone—as we have often warned in the preceding sections—does not oblige one to restitution.
¶ These things having been established, it remains to examine the distinction which the third and fourth

<column-break/>

conclusion has laid down: namely, that five types of causes oblige one to restitution, while the remaining four do not.
<margin>On the one commanding and the one consenting.</margin>
For it seems that neither the one who commands nor the one who consents should always be forced to restitution, because they are not always an "effective cause." It is answered, therefore, through the aforementioned conclusions, that Saint Thomas established that distinction only regarding what is "in itself" <note>original: *per se*</note>. Therefore, it does not prevent those types from occasionally not being obligatory. For example, it was said that a participant in a crime—that is, one concurring with another—is held liable "in itself." Nevertheless, when they are not an effective cause, they are not held. Similarly, one who commands is indeed a motivating cause "in itself"—indeed, the most powerful of all—applying the servant to the work. Nevertheless, it could sometimes happen that the one commanding contributes nothing to the matter. First, when no damage follows. For in all these things, this infallible rule must be observed: that where the command, the counsel, and the other causes do not actually achieve an effect, although a sin is committed, no obligation of restitution arises. Likewise, when the other person is so certain to do the thing, and is so ready for the work, that they could not be hindered.
<margin>A rule to be noted.</margin>
In that case, someone who said, "Go then and do it," would not be an effective cause that obliges restitution. It would be otherwise if they moved the person by commanding. For this must be weighed by prudence. For even if my wicked servant were certain to commit a murder, if I, who could have hindered him, commanded it, or in some way moved him by commanding, I am not free from restitution. In like manner, "harboring" [a criminal] suggests a cause in itself. Nor does it prevent it from truly being a cause, even if another would have harbored him, as was said. But yet, if that harboring were not an effective cause—because I only receive the thief out of hospitality, and I do not move him (indeed, I dissuade him), nor do I participate in any of the theft, and there are many other inns nearby ready to receive him—I am not to be condemned in the secret court of conscience <note>The "internal forum" or "court of conscience" refers to the moral standing of a person before God, often handled in the sacrament of confession, as opposed to a public legal court.</note>.
<margin>On those who are silent and those who do not resist.</margin>
¶ The same is to be judged regarding those who consent, those who do not resist, and those who remain silent. If they cannot resist, or are not bound by justice to do so, they are not a cause. Therefore, for someone upon whom a duty is incumbent—such as a prince or a judge—consenting to evil and not resisting always makes them a cause, and they are held to restitution. Likewise, a servant who is the guard of a house—whether the one from which a thief goes out to steal, or the one he enters—if he consents, whether that one might go out or the other might enter, he is truly a cause: for he is bound by justice to resist. But if a thief [robs] a neighbor's house—

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

...you see [neighbors] blocked by robbers, or their homes being broken into by thieves; even if you do not resist them while you are able, you certainly sin gravely against charity. However, according to your conscience, you do not subject yourself to the yoke of restitution. But if someone should do this with a wicked intent—namely, because he holds his neighbor in hatred, and therefore the harm to that neighbor is pleasing to him—<margin>Richard of Middleton.</margin> Richard and certain other authors of Summaries believe such a man is held to restitution. <margin>Duns Scotus.</margin> However, Scotus and others more correctly deny this. For we must persist in that rule cited above: that the violation of charity alone, unless justice is also violated, does not induce the necessity of restitution. <margin>Note.</margin> Indeed, I would even judge that if a robber, while in the very act of the crime <note>original: *in flagranti delicto*</note>, were to offer a gift to a neighbor—who is not bound by justice to cry out—so that he would keep silent, that neighbor would not be guilty of restitution according to his conscience. This is true even if he might be condemned in an external court due to the presumption of guilt. I say he is not guilty in conscience if he received not the stolen money itself, but some other payment. The reason is this: because he does not act against justice, but only against charity. Furthermore, even if he is later questioned privately by the one who suffered the loss as to whether he had seen or heard the robbers, he is not bound by justice to answer. It is otherwise if he is questioned by a judge; for then, if he denies it, he is held to restitution, as we shall discuss in the following book under the title "On Witnesses." ¶ To this order of restitution are reduced those by whose fault either damage is given or an injury is inflicted, as is commanded in the legal chapter on injuries and damage. Hence, in Exodus 21, if someone opens a cistern <note>A large underground tank for storing water.</note> into which an ox or a donkey falls, he becomes liable for the damage. This is consistent with the law "On Pits" in the Digest regarding the Aquilian Law <note>The *Lex Aquilia* was a Roman law that provided compensation to the owners of property injured by another's fault.</note>. And in Exodus 22: "If a fire breaks out and catches in thorns," etc., he who started the fire shall make restitution for the damage. <margin>On one who praises.</margin> <margin>St. Thomas Aquinas.</margin> ¶ But regarding other types of causes—namely, concerning one who praises a wrongdoer, or another who gives advice—Saint Thomas says they do not always obligate one to restitution, because they are not always effective causes of the harm. <margin>On one who advises a person wanting to do a greater harm to do a lesser one instead.</margin> ¶ Nevertheless, a doubt presents itself regarding an advisor that should not be ignored: namely, whether one who advises a lesser evil to avoid that which is more harmful is entangled in the snare of restitution. Suppose you see a robber stealing a precious horse, whom you are in no way able to restrain; you advise him to be content with another scrawny horse of lesser value. Are you held to restore that horse? Regarding the law and the fault—that is, whether any fault occurs in advising a lesser evil when it is indicated as a necessary means to encounter a weightier evil—

<column-break/>

we shall dispute this in the sixth book, under the title "On Usury." We will tend toward the side that says there is no fault; indeed, it is sometimes a virtue. For now, however, whatever the case may be regarding fault, I believe it must be said regarding restitution that the advisor is held to none at all. <margin>Adrian VI.</margin> This is what Adrian rightly thinks; for to advise a lesser evil is not to advise evil simply, but rather that comparison which has the character of a good. Nor is the intention then directed toward the evil which is lesser, but toward the prevention of that which is greater. Therefore, it is not only not harmful, but it is actually beneficial. And this is certainly clear from common human intuition. For who would obligate such a man to restitution? Indeed, even the owner of the property would not receive such restitution, since his business was managed in the best possible way. This response is to be understood when both the item of lesser value and the item of greater value belong to the same owner; for then, without injury to any other, you save his property. However, if to avoid a loss being given to Peter, you advise that a smaller one be given to Paul, you are undoubtedly held to restitution, since you have harmed the latter. ¶ Concerning this whole matter, one might wonder whether it should have been disputed here how thieves or witnesses are held to reveal secret debts when it is commanded under the threat of general excommunication. But a broader discussion of this is to be held in the next book, questions 6 and 7.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, the first argument has now been sufficiently resolved. For it is not only he who is the leader in a crime who offends, but also whoever moves him by command, or helps him by consent, or advice, or any other aid; and therefore, such men are folded into the same knot of restitution. <margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ Regarding the solution of the second argument, it must be noted that while many concur in the same damage or injury, he especially and above all who was the leader and moved the others is obligated to make restitution. I say "especially" regarding the fault; that is, he sins more gravely if he does not restore it, whether he was the commander or moving the others in any other way. Nonetheless, if he does not restore it, each individual, as has been said, is held for the whole amount <note>original: *in solidum*; legal liability where any individual participant can be held responsible for the entire debt.</note>. However, if he or any other person restores it, the rest are no longer held toward the true owner, but toward the one who paid. ¶ Nevertheless, as we suggested above, this requires a fuller explanation. Here it must be noted that the other accomplices are not held to the first person making restitution in the same way they were all held before...
