# Book Four, Question VII.

...previously they were held accountable to the owner: for they were debtors, not only by reason of the thing received <note>original: *ratione rei acceptae*</note>, but also by reason of the act of taking <note>original: *ratione acceptionis*</note>, even if they no longer possessed the item. However, they owe nothing to the one who restores it by reason of the taking—since they received nothing from him—but they do owe by reason of the thing received, specifically for that portion which each one enjoyed. Let us say, for example, there are three robbers, the first of whom, led by repentance, restores the whole amount. In that case, it is clear that in conscience the others owe nothing to the owner, since that which was taken has been returned to him; and they are not held to punishment unless they have been legally condemned. 

Whether the others are held to pay their share to the one who restored the whole must be distinguished. For if any of them enjoyed a portion of the loot, without doubt they are each held to pay precisely for their own share. It follows that if the one who restored the whole had actually consumed the entire amount himself, the others owe him nothing. But if he himself had perceived no fruit from the theft, while another or others did, the one who consumed it owes him the whole amount by reason of the thing received. 

But what if none of them gained any profit from the damage caused—for instance, because they tore down a house, or threw the loot they had snatched into a river to avoid being caught? In that case, one must discern whether the one who restored the whole had so influenced the others that they would not have done it without his persuasion. If so, I would agree with 
<margin>Cajetan.</margin> 
what <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> says here: that the others owe him nothing. This is because they owe nothing by reason of the thing received (since they gained no profit), nor by reason of the taking (since he was the entire cause of the act). Nevertheless, it must not be denied that if he would not have attempted the deed without the company of his associates, they may be held to him for some portion. Finally, if all of them offered themselves to the crime of their own accord, then each owes the first restorer a third of the total.

<margin>Another doubt is resolved.</margin> 
¶ From what has been said, the solution to another small doubt is gathered: whether, when two people who committed a theft are <term>jointly and severally liable</term> <note>original: *in solidum obligatis*—meaning each is responsible for the full debt</note>, the owner can forgive one and demand the whole from the other. It is clear that he cannot do this to the prejudice of the one making restitution. For if he extorts the whole from one, he cannot prevent that person from holding the other liable for their share in the manner explained. Therefore, if he wished to gift a portion to one, he ought to have extracted that much less from the other.

<margin>Regarding the third point.</margin> 
¶ To the third point, finally, it is answered that one who is bound to resist a wrongdoer or report him—not out of justice, but out of charity—is not bound, as we said, to throw himself into danger. Nor, if he fails to resist, is he compelled to make restitution. It is otherwise, however, 

<column-break/>

for those upon whom the duty was incumbent by virtue of their office, as has already been explained. 

<margin>A doubt.</margin> 
¶ Regarding these officials, however, you may perhaps ask whether they are bound to this even at the risk of death. For instance, if a <term>praetor</term> <note>A Roman magistrate or, in this context, a high-ranking city official or judge.</note> encounters robbers invading a house at night, is he bound to attack them even if his life is endangered by the attack itself? It seems that reason would demand it, since the duty of guarding is incumbent upon them by office. But nevertheless, the answer is that the damage must be weighed and compared with the danger. For a magistrate is not always bound in every case to cast his life toward death; 
<margin>Whether one is bound to face death for the state in this matter.</margin> 
but only where the harm to the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: *reipublicae*</note> demands it, and where he receives a just wage for the risk, and where he can resist without being reckless.

### ARTICLE IV.

->*Whether one who owes is bound to restore immediately.*<-

<margin>Whether a thief is bound to restore immediately.</margin> 
The final circumstance of restitution is time: concerning which it is asked whether everyone is bound to restore immediately. The argument for the negative side is as follows. First, "affirmative precepts" <note>Moral commands that tell you what *to do* (like "honor your parents") rather than what *not* to do. They generally do not require action at every single second.</note> do not bind at every moment, as they say; but the command to restore is an affirmative precept: therefore it only binds when the circumstance of time is appropriate, and thus not always. ¶ Second: no one is bound to the impossible; but it happens that one who owes is not able to restore immediately: therefore he is not bound then. ¶ Third: restitution is an act of virtue; time is one of the circumstances that are the "ornaments of virtues." Thus, just as the other circumstances are not designated by law but are left to be determined by prudence, so too there should be no law that restitution happen immediately, but only as it is defined everywhere by prudence. ¶ On the contrary is the fact that the logic of the whole category of restitution is the same as that of its specific types. But the wages of a laborer must be paid immediately, according to 
Leviticus 19: *The wages of a hired man shall not remain with you until morning.* <note>Soto translates the Vulgate of Leviticus 19:13.</note> Therefore, all restitution in general must be made on the spot.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin> 
**T**O the question, it is answered with a single conclusion. Everyone is bound, as soon as it is possible for them, either to restore or to request an extension of time from the person who is concerned...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

...to demand. The conclusion is proven. Just as stealing another's property is a sin against justice, so also is it a sin to withhold it against the owner's will. For in the same way, the owner is hindered from its use, which is the very purpose of ownership. It is not lawful to remain in a state of sin even for the smallest moment; indeed, to say it is permissible to be in a state of sin is a contradiction in terms. Hence, in <note>The Book of Sirach, also known as Ben Sira</note> *Ecclesiasticus 21*: "Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent." Therefore, someone else’s property must be restored as soon as the possibility arises.

<margin>The command to restore is not entirely affirmative.</margin>
¶ We have already explained above, in the preceding question, article 2, how the command of restitution—though it takes an affirmative form, as Saint *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says here in the solution to the first point—nevertheless includes a negation: "not to withhold." This is reduced to the commandment, "Thou shalt not steal." For this reason, it does not behave like other affirmative commandments (such as "honor your parents") which involve specific circumstances of time—namely, that they be done when appropriate. On the contrary, like other negative commandments, it excludes all time; and consequently, it allows no delay. This is why *Paul* joined the two together: "Give to all what is owed" and "Owe no one anything." <note>original: *Reddite omnibus debita: & nemini quicquam debeatis* — Romans 13:7-8</note> Look back there if you wish to review.

<margin>Explaining how one must restore immediately.</margin>
¶ From this it follows that what has been said—"immediately"—is to be understood one way regarding the internal act of the mind, and another way regarding the external work. As for the internal intent <note>original: *propositum*</note>, as soon as it comes into anyone's mind that they are in debt of another's property, they must intend to restore it when the opportunity arises. Since, according to the teacher *Augustine*, "sin is not forgiven unless that which was taken is restored," there can be no true repentance without such an intent. In the external act, however, the word "immediately" is not to be judged mathematically, as if in an indivisible point in time, but rather morally and civilly. For while you are lying in bed or reclining at the table and it occurs to you that you owe something, you are not strictly bound by law to get up instantly; rather, you can wait for an opportunity without fraud or deceit. Once that opportunity has passed, you begin to be in delay <note term="mora">In legal terms, 'mora' is a failure to perform an obligation on time, which can incur additional penalties or guilt.</note>, and subsequently in fault.

¶ But if you argue: therefore this command has a circumstance of time, just like other affirmative ones; the conclusion is denied. For the matter of honoring parents or hearing Mass does not always present itself; and the same happens in acts of courage and commands of mercy. Therefore, they do not bind "for always" <note>original: *pro semper*</note>; instead, the circumstance of time in those cases must be judged according to prudence. But in the matter of restoring, the necessity established by law always exists. However, because it requires an action that cannot be done instantly, 

<column-break/>

one is permitted to wait for the opportunity.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ For a clearer evidence of the matter, it is asked in what sense it should be understood that restitution is "immediately" necessary. It could be two-fold: namely, either that it is necessary to escape from the prior sin, or that it is necessary under the penalty of a new sin. In the first sense, there is no controversy that it is immediately necessary, as we were just saying, regarding the intent. Indeed, just as someone who persisted in the intent of stealing would always be in sin, so too would someone who, knowing they have another’s property, did not immediately intend to restore it. This is also confirmed by the fact that if the owner asked for it immediately, you would be bound to return it immediately. Furthermore, if you were not bound to return it immediately, by that same reasoning you would not be bound tomorrow, nor the day after. Regarding this sense, then, no doubt remains.

<margin>Whether he who does not restore when he could commits a new sin.</margin>
¶ However, there is a doubt regarding the second sense. And it is argued that a thief, for example, besides the sin he committed by snatching the item, commits a fresh sin at every moment in which he does not intend to restore it. For we said in the preceding question that the command of restoring is distinct from the prohibition of stealing; this is clear both from its object and its form. For the prohibition of theft is a prohibition of an evil, but the command to restore is an ordering of a good; for it is a good thing to restore, just as it is to make satisfaction. Therefore, *Christ* spoke affirmatively: "Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's" <note>Matthew 22:21</note>; and *Paul*: "Give to all what is owed."

<margin>Paul.</margin>
From this, it is argued: This command is affirmative, the condition of which is "immediately"; therefore, at every moment, one is bound to intend this or to continue such an intent. Otherwise, there will always be a new sin of omission. To this, having granted that it is a distinct command as explained in the place cited, the first response is: besides the sin of theft while it is being committed, a new sin of omission is not committed on the spot if restitution is not made; however, that very sin grows continuously when the delay in restoring is greater. For it is clear, first, that a sin of omission is not immediately committed, because a person is not bound—even morally speaking—to constantly attend to the sin; and also because even if they do attend to it, if they continue the old intent of withholding, that prevents the contrary intent of restoring. Thus, there is no other new sin of omission of a good intent than that which is the continuation of the old one. And this is confirmed: because a man is not even bound to God to make satisfaction through penance immediately under the penalty of a new mortal sin...

### Fourth Book: Question VII

...but one remains in the prior state of guilt. That the sin increases is clear, both because a sin is worse the longer it lasts, and because the damage to the owner grows every day as they are kept from the use of their property for a longer time. Indeed, the delay in restoring can be so great that it becomes a matter of necessity for confession. For although a continued sin does not change its "species" <note>In scholastic theology, "species" refers to the specific category of a sin—for example, whether it is theft or murder.</note> in its physical nature, it is nonetheless significantly increased in the moral order, just as it can increase based on the value of the object. A person who has stolen ten thousand Ducats does not make a legitimate confession unless they express the quantity. However, this increase in gravity does not happen at every single moment. It matters very little if you withhold a thing for two or three hours, or even days, unless the owner is in

<margin>Paludanus. Book 4, distinction 15, question 2, says,</margin>
grave necessity. ¶ Peter de Palude <note>A prominent 14th-century Dominican theologian and jurist.</note> says in Book 4, distinction 15, question 2, that one who retains another's property for a year sins more gravely (even if it is one hardened sin) than if he stole it multiple times and repeatedly throughout the year through several different actions. For in the first case, he is always in a state of sin, while in the latter, he occasionally ceases. Nevertheless, although this view does not lack probability, the contrary view is more probable. First because, as I was just saying, not every hourly or daily continuation of a habit increases the fault by a notable amount; and also because those repeated and multiplied efforts to steal seem worse than the continuation of a habit, which can often happen out of laziness and negligence. ¶ Secondly, I would nonetheless add that a new sin is sometimes committed against the command to restore, insofar as it is an "affirmative" command. <note>An affirmative command is one that requires an action (like "honor your father"), whereas a negative command forbids an action (like "do not kill").</note> This happens first whenever you resolve not to restore the item, for that act of will is wicked. Next, it happens whenever the creditor legitimately asks for it. Indeed, it happens even while you see him being pressed by grave

<margin>Whether it is permitted to delay restitution.</margin>
necessity. In these cases, I say, it is a new sin not to restore. ¶ Following these points, it comes next for us to see whether it is sometimes permitted to delay restitution. Concerning this matter,

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
you will find various opinions among the Doctors. Many things must be weighed here before such a thing is permitted. Indeed, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a hugely influential medieval philosopher.</note> in Book 4, distinction 15, along with most others, holds as a rule that where a debtor cannot restore without enormous loss to himself, he may delay it. But truly, 

<margin>Cajetan’s excellent distinction.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a leading 16th-century theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> seems to me to distinguish wisely regarding three types of "detriment" or loss. For if you call it a detriment that a huge amount of wealth must be restored, this helps not at all in justifying a delay. Otherwise, the

<column-break/>

condition of those who have contracted a larger debt through wrongdoing would be better than those who owe less. The second kind of detriment is the profit that will cease for the debtor if he pays the item back. <note>This refers to *lucrum cessans*, or the potential money a person stops making because they no longer have the capital.</note> And in truth, even this does not excuse him from making restitution immediately. For no one has a right to make a profit using another's money against the owner's will. Therefore, the third order of detriments is "emerging damage": <note>Known as *damnum emergens*, this refers to an actual loss or cost incurred, rather than just a missed opportunity for profit.</note> namely, if someone who owes a hundred cannot restore it without incurring an additional loss of much more—such as if he must sell his goods prematurely at a very low price, or sell the house or land from which he lives, and does so with a greater loss than the debt he owes to the other. And it is by reason of this, if it is ever lawful, that one may delay restitution. And the reason, says Scotus, is because the owner ought to prefer that the debtor avoid a huge loss rather than have the debt restored to himself. But truly, this reason does not entirely prove the point, because no one is bound to yield their own right to avoid another's damage, except in cases of extreme necessity, or a necessity so grave that one would be obliged to offer up what they have. Therefore, the grave detriment of the debtor does not by right compel the creditor to wait

<margin>The reason for protracting restitution.</margin>
for payment. Thus, if there is any reason for delaying restitution at that time, it must be taken from elsewhere: namely, from the fact that the debtor, for that specific moment, is simply unable to pay. This is because, morally speaking, what cannot be done except with such great damage

<margin>Circumstances of this postponement.</margin>
is not considered "possible." ¶ However, such a postponement must be clothed in several circumstances to be just. First, one must consider the initial taking: was it unjust or just? For if the debt was incurred through robbery, or through usury, or other injuries, that debtor is bound to restore it immediately, regardless of what damage he suffers (short of extreme necessity), even if he loses his social standing. For this is not "falling" from his status, but rather descending to his true status from one that was not his own. If, however, he contracted the debts through a just transaction, then one must also consider how he fell into poverty. For if he was stripped of his goods by some stroke of bad fortune without any fault of his own, a postponement of restitution is more easily granted to him. And finally, it must be weighed whether the creditor can bear the delay, or whether he himself is suffering from want. For short of extreme necessity, the condition of the creditor is much better than that of the debtor. ¶ One thing 

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>The Director.</margin>
I say that in judging such cases, deference should be given to the confessor. He affirms this by following the opinion of the *Director* <note>Likely referring to the *Directorium Confessariorum*, a manual for confessors.</note>: namely, if a creditor does not wish to wait for restitution, and the debtor cannot be persuaded to restore it immediately, then the priest can absolve him if he takes a guarantee <note>original: *cautionem*; a formal promise or security</note> that he will pay after a certain time. And the reason, he says, is because the priest is then usefully managing the creditor's business <term>useful management (negotiorum gestio): a legal concept where someone acts on behalf of another without their direct authorization to prevent loss</term>. For if the penitent were not absolved, perhaps that creditor would never recover his debt. He cites the law "on paying" from the Digest <note>original: *l. soluendo. ff. de nego. geft.*, referring to the Roman law Pandects</note> and some others I know not which.

<margin>Sylvester is challenged.</margin>
However, this rule—that the creditor's business is being usefully managed—though it may help in an external court, is worth nothing in the court of conscience. For a priest is not a mediator between a creditor and a debtor, nor is he the creditor's agent; rather, he is the purifier of consciences in the name of God. And therefore, in this matter, he must be intent only on weighing whether the debtor is capable of paying or not, according to the causes and merits we were just explaining. For if he is capable of paying, he is by no means to be absolved against the creditor's will unless he restores what is owed—even if there is a looming danger that restitution might never be made. For the penitent must look out for himself. It can happen, however, that he satisfies the debt if he restores it in installments at set times. On the contrary, in cases that are complicated and where the law is doubtful, it is not necessary for the penitent always to obey the confessor unless the confessor is distinguished in learning.

<margin>The danger facing those who procrastinate on restitution.</margin>
¶ From these points, you may easily gather in what open danger they stand—indeed, in what manifest sin they lie—who procrastinate on restitution until the moment of death. For first, it is certain that whoever knows for a fact that they are weighed down by another's debt, and has no intention of restoring it until death (even if they have a very firm intention of restoring it then, or of ordering the restitution in their will), remains in mortal sin. Such a person is not to be granted the benefit of absolution. And the reason is that, once the opportunity is available, it is not permitted for any length of time to keep what belongs to another against the owner's will. Therefore, if such a person is snatched by sudden death, as often happens to men of this sort, he departs in a state of damnation. And the same must be judged regarding those who, being uncertain whether what they possess is owed to another, refuse to decide the matter by judgment while they are alive, but think it sufficient if they propose to leave the matter to their heir in their will. And the same must be judged entirely of those who, at the point of death, refuse to make restitution themselves when they are able to do so, thinking

<column-break/>

it is enough to command their heirs to do it. For they do not truly have a sincere and honest mind for restitution. Those who do not restore then provide clear evidence that they would not have restored even if they had lived. Thus, their intention to restore is only conditional—"if they die"—which certainly does not suffice for true repentance. And this danger especially threatens great men <note>High-ranking nobles or officials</note>, whose heirs never, or hardly ever, fulfill their wills. Instead, the heir thinks it enough to do what his grandfather ordered his father, and his father ordered him: he simply commands his son to handle the same debt, now burdened with new ones, and the son later leaves it to the grandson. I do not know, then, if this is the legitimate sense of that Gospel word: *It is impossible for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.* <note>Matthew 19:24. Soto suggests the difficulty isn't just wealth, but the cycle of unpaid debts passed through generations.</note>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The first argument is therefore sufficiently settled where we explained that the command of restitution includes a negative <note>i.e., "Thou shalt not withhold what belongs to another."</note>; by reason of which, restitution cannot be delayed.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ And the third is solved in the same way. For the circumstance of time is not determined in the same way for restitution as it is in other affirmative commands <note>Affirmative commands, like "Honor thy father," are ongoing, whereas negative commands, like "Do not steal," apply at every moment.</note>.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The second argument is one that brings several ambiguities with it. For it is granted that no one is bound to the impossible; therefore, he who cannot pay now has the right to delay, and he who cannot pay at all is entirely absolved.

<margin>St. Thomas. Objection against St. Thomas.</margin>
However, Saint Thomas adds that the debtor must nevertheless either ask the creditor for a delay or for a total remission <note>Forgiveness of the debt.</note>. Against this, an argument immediately presents itself: that such a needy person is in no way bound to do this, for impossibility absolves him in conscience. Therefore, even if the creditor refuses to remit the debt, the debtor is not bound to do anything further; thus, that ceremony of asking seems superfluous.

<margin>Clarification.</margin>
It is answered that Saint Thomas does not feel this is necessary when the impossibility is obvious. But because it is so very rarely that clear, it is healthy advice to use that remedy wherever any

<margin>Question.</margin>
doubt remains. ¶ You ask, then, what caution is necessary so that he who entreats for remission may remain safe in conscience.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered with a single, very brief word: in such a way that the remission is truly free. Thus, it is not required that it be "freest" <note>i.e., perfectly voluntary without any social pressure</note>, nor is it enough if it is coerced. Caution must be taken that neither force nor fraud is involved. For if you deceive the creditor, or persuade him that you owe less than you do, or that you did not fall into those debts through such fair dealings, or that you are in much greater poverty...

<summary>Soto argues that restitution must be made immediately if possible, warning that delaying payment until death—often leaving the burden to heirs who ignore it—constitutes a mortal sin. He clarifies that while impossibility excuses a debtor from immediate payment, they should still seek the creditor's forgiveness to ensure their conscience is clear.</summary>

# Question VII of the Fourth Book

If you are compressed by authority more than you are truly persuaded, a donation is not free. Or, if you threaten something unless the person remits the debt to you—or even if you do not threaten, but merely hint at it—it is likewise coerced. Great lords must take the greatest care in this when seeking a remission of debt from their subjects. However, that caution which some scrupulous people think necessary—namely, that the debtor must first place the money into the creditor's power before asking for remission—is excessive. For besides the fact that it rarely happens that a debtor <margin>Cajetan.</margin> actually has the money (as Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> rightly noted), the presence of gold tends to fascinate the eyes and change minds on the spot. Therefore, the circumstances of the matter must be weighed so that the remission is truly free.

<margin>A point of doubt.</margin> ¶ Finally, there remains a final doubt regarding this impossibility: namely, when should restitution be judged impossible? This is to ask whether a man ought to be driven to restore his debt in any necessity short of the extreme. For there is no one who doubts that no one should be cast into extreme necessity <note>In scholastic ethics, "extreme necessity" refers to a life-threatening situation where one lacks the basic requirements for survival (food, clothing, shelter).</note>; because (as we said above) in such a state of necessity, every debt ceases. There are, however, those who assert that a debtor must descend into any state short of that extreme one in order to pay. Thus, even a nobleman ought to work with his hands, and if necessary, even beg. Because just as it is not lawful for anyone to seize another’s property short of extreme necessity, so too <margin>Removal of the doubt.</margin> is it unlawful to retain what belongs to another. ¶ Nevertheless, because these are moral matters, they must be judged in a civil manner. I say we must first look at what I mentioned just recently: by what means and arts the debts were contracted. For he who incurred them through wrongdoing—namely through robbery or fraud—ought indeed to be reduced to poverty. But he who was handling business in good faith, and did not squander his goods on gluttony, gambling, or immoderate displays, but became unable to pay because fortune blew against him, is not to be so rigidly compelled. Nor, if he is a nobleman, must he perform manual labor or beg. It is enough that he live more cheaply and humbly—miserably, even—and lay aside all pomp. For although in such necessity he could not seize the property of others, it does not follow that he cannot retain a small portion of what he acquired in good faith in order to live. ¶ The last remedy for the wretched, which the laws call "pitiable and mournful," 

<column-break/>

is to yield one's goods <term>yielding of goods (cedere bonis): a legal process where a debtor surrenders all their assets to creditors to avoid imprisonment, similar to filing for bankruptcy</term>. Regarding this, someone might ask <margin>When yielding goods is lawful.</margin> whether anyone can yield their goods with a safe conscience, and whether the state should permit it. To this, one must respond with the exact same distinction. For those who enter into or conduct business dealings deceitfully and craftily should not, in truth, be permitted to do so. For there are those who, though they have no assets, scrape together credit from every side to claim some standing for themselves, or what they call "credit." Not content with that fraud, they continue to live sumptuously and more so every day. By this reasoning, they blow up a huge debt <note>original: *aes alienum*; literally "another's copper," the common term for debt</note>, and when later pressed by it, they flee into sanctuary <note>Taking refuge in a church to avoid legal arrest.</note>. This is surely the most pestilential kind of robbery; nor should such people be tolerated by the state (as we shall say again in Book 6), but should be punished like thieves. But those who trade in good faith but are cast into poverty by calamity may use the benefit of the laws with an excellent conscience, so that they are not consumed in prisons. For it was for this benefit that the ceremony of yielding goods was instituted (as found in Law 1 of the Code, "On those who can yield goods" <note>original: *l. 1. C. qui bon. ced. poss.*</note>). Consequently, they may lawfully retain those things which the laws permit them: such as the tools of their trade, and their daily, monthly, and annual food (as found in the law "On yielding goods" in the Digest <note>original: *l. qui bonis. ff. eod. tit.*</note>). For consideration must be had so they do not starve (as is holily cautioned in the law "On condemnation" in the Rules of Law <note>original: *l. in condemnatione. ff. de regu. iur.*</note>). Therefore, even if they later earn some goods that are necessary for their daily living, they may retain them, since that same law, *Qui bonis*, commands that such things are not to be sold. ¶ But you perhaps doubt whether one who comes <margin>When those who yielded goods are bound to restore.</margin> into a "fatter fortune" <note>meaning: significantly greater wealth</note> is bound in conscience to restore the debt. For it appears that through that public disgrace, he has satisfied the law and, by extension, the creditors. But the laws themselves wipe away this doubt, decreeing that he is entirely bound then. For that benefit (as has been said) only supports them so far as to prevent them from being thrust into prison. Whence the cited Law 1 in the Code says that those who have yielded goods are not liberated unless the creditor has received the full amount. And the law "Since even sons" in the same title says that if anything "fatter" should later come to them, this may again be legally plucked away by the creditors up to the amount of the debt. The same is sanctioned in the second law of "He who yielded goods" in the Digest.

The sixth and subsequently the seventh books will follow, concerning the injustice that usually occurs in free and voluntary contracts. Now, an injury is inflicted upon a person whenever harm is brought against them contrary to right; and this occurs either by deed—whether against their person, or one joined to them, or their property—or, finally, by word. ### Book Five: Question I.

"everything that moves and lives shall be food for you" <note>original: "quod mouetur & viuit, erit vobis in cibum"</note>: this is an explanation of natural law, just as that other passage in Genesis 1: "Behold, I have given you every herb and all fruit-bearing trees to be food for you." For meat is as much our natural food as the fruits of the earth. This conclusion is so certain that it is a most true confession of the Catholic faith. <margin>Manicheans.</margin> The heresy of the Manicheans <note>The Manicheans were followers of a dualistic religion who believed that material things, including flesh, were evil.</note> was so contrary to this that, as <margin>Augustine</margin> *Augustine records in Book 1 of The City of God, chapter 20, and explains in Book 6 against Faustus the Manichean.* <margin>The madness of the Manicheans.</margin> For those madmen claimed that the souls of animals were members of God, and therefore it was an impiety to feed upon their flesh. Therefore, <margin>Augustine.</margin> *Augustine* argues to the contrary in the same *Book 1 of The City of God, chapter 20: "When we hear 'Thou shalt not kill,' do we think it is a sin to pull up a shrub? And do we most insanely agree with the error of the Manicheans?" And further on: "We do not apply that commandment to bushes, nor to irrational animals. For by the most just ordinance of the Creator, both their life and their death are subject to our uses."* This heresy is therefore condemned in the passage cited, *Genesis 9: "Everything that moves shall be food for you."* Yet this error had already arisen in the time of the <margin>Paul.</margin> Apostles. For *Paul in 1 Timothy 4 said that they 'forbid marriage and command to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving.' And in Acts 10, when Peter was afraid to eat the animals shown to him in the sheet, the response came from heaven: 'What God has cleansed, you must not call common.'* Thus, no one is permitted to doubt this conclusion.

¶ However, <margin>A doubt.</margin> this may be called into question: whether the eating of meat was in use before the Flood. For it seems the negative side can be gathered from that passage in *Genesis 9*. Since God then granted "everything that moves and lives" for nourishment to Noah as he emerged from the Flood, it is a strong argument that this had not yet been granted before then. This is especially so because in *Genesis 1* we read that only herbs and the things growing from the earth were granted to men and cattle alike. Next comes a conjecture from the same *chapter 9*. For after the words quoted, it immediately adds: *"Just as I gave you the green herbs, I have now given you everything."* It is as if He said, "Even if until now I permitted only vegetables to you for food, from now on, just like the permitted vegetables, I hand over living creatures to you for eating." There is also the added word: *"Except that you shall not eat meat with its lifeblood."* Indeed, if the diet of meat was already a custom, they either devoured it with the blood, or they did not. If you say the former, tell me, I pray, why that horrid act was not prohibited during those sixteen hundred

<column-break/>

years? But if you grant the latter: why, I ask, was there then a need for such a warning? Thus, the conjecture is made that previously there was no use of meat: for that reason, God then first taught men, by this grant, how to use them without blood—that is, boiled or roasted, and not raw like wild beasts. For it was also a solemn custom among the pagan nations <margin>Pythagoras.</margin> imbued with the *Pythagorean* doctrine to abstain from blood, because they thought it was the seat of souls; and it has always been a horror to all mortals to drink blood. 

Then it is argued by reason. For before the Flood, there was a vigor in herbs to nourish, enliven, and strengthen the bodies of mortals, because the earth had not yet been stagnated by that inundation. Therefore, the use of meat was not necessary then, as it was afterward. And this appears to be the reason why they were granted at that time, just as wine was: because neither the herbs nor the waters retained their former vigor, and human bodies had begun to languish and move toward a shorter life. Wherefore <margin>Ovid.</margin> *Naso* <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso).</note> says of that first age of all:
-> Contented with foods created with no one forcing them. <-
¶ Furthermore, the eating of meat seemed to suggest to the ancients some kind of cruelty and ferocity of mind. Whence the same poet in *Book 15 of his Metamorphoses*:
> Spare, O mortals, to defile your bodies with unspeakable feasts:
> There are fruits, etc. And further on:
> With meat, wild beasts satisfy their hunger: yet not all:
> For the horse and the flocks and herds live on grass. And below:
> Oh, what a crime it is for entrails to be buried in entrails!
> And for a greedy body to grow fat on a body crammed within it!
> And for one living creature to live by the death of another!

The common opinion, therefore, is almost entirely that before the Flood there was no use of any meat in meals. Although Saint <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> *Thomas, in the 1st part of the 2nd part, question 102, article 6,* spoke hesitantly: "It seems the eating of meat was introduced after the Flood." But Nicholas of <margin>Lyranus.</margin> *Lyra, on Genesis 9,* asserts it without <margin>Abulensis.</margin> hesitation. And *Abulensis* <note>Alonso Tostado, Bishop of Avila.</note> *on Genesis 1* not only says this, but further suggests such nourishment was prohibited then. For he says God assigned herbs to everyone for food. <margin>Cajetan.</margin> *Cajetan, however, in the same place on Genesis 9,* places himself in the middle, saying that it was neither prohibited <margin>The author's opinion by which the doubt is resolved.</margin> to eat meat, nor was it yet in use.
¶ I, however, (asserting this under the judgment of others) seem to persuade myself of this, which becomes [the resolution] of this article...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the legality of killing animals and eating meat. The author, Dominicus de Soto, is now specifically addressing whether humans ate meat before the Great Flood, distinguishing between the "state of innocence" in Eden and the "fallen state" of humanity afterward.</meta>

# Fr. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion of this article: Before the flood, not only was it not forbidden to eat meat, but it is highly probable that meat was used for human food immediately after the fall of human nature <note>original: "post naturam lapsam"</note>. Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whom Soto is commenting upon.</note> neither mentions a prohibition nor firmly denies its use. I specify, however, *after the fall of nature*: for in the state of innocence <note>The theological state of humanity before the original sin of Adam and Eve.</note>, it is easy to believe that no matter how many centuries it had lasted, meat would never have been used for food. The reason is that the fruits of paradise would have been most abundant, and most potent in their power to nourish and sustain human life. Furthermore, since in that state of happiness there was no room for corrupted desires, no one would have used anything superfluous; they would have been content with what was necessary. This is especially true because eating from the Tree of Life was able to keep them healthy so that they might not die. ¶ Nevertheless, our conclusion is proven regarding the state of corrupted nature. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> The eating of meat is most natural to human life and its preservation after the fall of nature—so much so that physicians find nothing healthier among foods, both for maintaining good health and for the strength of one's forces. Meat possessed this quality immediately from its creation. Therefore, it is argued: if those ancient mortals never tasted meat, it was either because it was forbidden to them, or because its healthfulness and flavor were never known to them, or because it was not necessary. However, no written prohibition is found in scripture, nor could such a thing be taught by natural reason; indeed (as I have just said), nature teaches the opposite. It is not at all credible that in sixteen hundred years <note>The approximate time between Creation and the Flood according to traditional biblical chronology.</note> they never recognized through observation nor discovered through experience that the nature of meat is highly suited for food. This is even less credible given that those people near the dawn of the human race likely excelled their descendants in genius and sagacity. If you say that such food was not necessary because of the abundance, power, and healthfulness of fruits and roots, I would grant that this sufficiently proves that meat would never have been used if the state of innocence had lasted, owing to human frugality and modesty at that time. Yet, in corrupted nature, it is no argument to say that if meat was not "necessary," it was therefore not used. For "all flesh had corrupted its way" <note>original: "corruperat enim omnis caro viam suam"; a quote from Genesis 6:12.</note>. Therefore, since those men were prone to evil and immersed themselves in worse pleasures, it becomes extremely probable that they gave themselves over to such foods and the delights of luxury. This was especially true just before the flood when (as Josephus says in Book 1 of his *Antiquities* <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note>) no

<column-break/>

vice or disgrace was spared. ¶ Next, it is argued: All animals were made for the sake of man. However, there are many that could not have been of use to those men in any other way than by being eaten, such as fish, partridges, chickens, and others of that kind. Especially since hunting (as Aristotle says in Book 1 of the *Politics*) is natural to man, there is no doubt it was practiced by those ancient people. ¶ Thirdly, it is argued: Animal sacrifices were then offered to God, as we read concerning Abel. For this reason, Noah is said to have enclosed clean animals in the Ark by sevens. Sacrifices were not made of useless things that could be of no use to the priests; therefore, they were taken as food. For what praise would Abel have earned for sacrificing the best and fattest of his flock to God if only the skins and wool were useful to the priests, and not the meat? Furthermore, it is credible that those men used milk; why then not meat? Since they stripped the bodies of so many animals daily to be clothed in leather and wool, it is not credible that they threw the meat to the dogs and birds. Indeed, it is most likely that they eventually brought it to the fire to taste it, for they prepared both bread and vegetable foods with fire. ¶ Truly, it is not difficult to answer the passage in Genesis 9 <note>Genesis 9:3, where God explicitly tells Noah "Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you."</note>. Rather, it should be said that in Genesis 1, only herbs were declared by God for food because of the trees of paradise in which God had placed man, which were sufficient for that state. But after nature was corrupted, the human race used meat as food by natural right. Perhaps near the time of the flood, human ferocity had reached such a point that they used raw meat with the blood still in it. To those who emerged from the danger of the flood, God granted—as a natural right—that they might eat fish and meat, except for the blood. That is, they should understand that meat prepared by fire, not raw, is suitable for human food. For this reason, the Hebrews drained the blood from meat excessively. It was a horror to them to taste blood even in sausages or other dishes, though this was common among the Gentiles. Therefore, for the sake of the Gentiles' harmony with them, abstinence from blood and strangled meat was commanded in Acts 15 <note>The Council of Jerusalem, where early church leaders set rules for Gentile converts.</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The arguments to the contrary are very easily solved. To the first, the answer is that although life is common to us and the rest of the animals, it is not by equal right; rather, their life exists for the sake of ours. And therefore, neither he who <meta>catchword: his</meta>

### ARTICLE II.

-> Whether it is lawful to kill wrongdoers. <-

<margin>The first argument for the negative side.</margin>
**A**fter discussing brute beasts, the first step in this second article concerns wicked men who, degenerating from their own nature, fall away into the nature of draft animals—as the testimony of David <note>A reference to Psalm 49:20, "Man... is like the beasts that perish."</note> affirms. It is therefore asked whether it is lawful to cut them off from the assembly of the living by death. For it seems to be a sin to punish a man with death, no matter how wicked he may be. Indeed, we must embrace the examples of Christ: but he forbade the Apostles, as we read in Matthew 13, from uprooting the tares <note>original: "zizania"; weeds that look like wheat.</note>—that is, the sons of wickedness—lest the wheat be pulled up along with them. Therefore, we should consider this a commandment for us.
<margin>The second argument.</margin>
¶ Second. God (as He Himself testifies through the mouth of Ezekiel) does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live. Therefore, following His example, we ought to extinguish no one among those who sin, but rather encourage them toward repentance—especially since it is certain that such a punishment creates the danger of eternal perdition for them.
<margin>The third argument.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
¶ Added in the third place is that which is evil by its very nature cannot be done well for any reason, as Aristotle says in the second book of the *Ethics*. From this, Augustine, in the book *Against Lying*, proves that it is never lawful. To kill a man is an evil in itself—so much so that, as we said in Book 2, it is entirely indispensable <note>meaning no human authority can grant a "dispensation" or exception to the moral law against it</note>. Therefore, it is never lawful. This is especially true because Christian charity extends not only to friends, but also to enemies and the wicked.
¶ To the contrary, however, is cited that passage from Exodus 22: "You shall not suffer wrongdoers to live." And Exodus 21: "If anyone kills his neighbor through injury and by ambush, you shall pluck him from my altar so that he may die," which is cited in Chapter 1 concerning homicide.
<margin>The difficulty. The resolution.</margin>
The present question might perhaps seem to some to require that the prohibition of homicide be discussed immediately at the outset. But one must 

<column-break/>

take notice that we are not entering into a treatise on the precepts of justice here—for that was completed in Book 2, where we interpreted the Ten Commandments <note>original: "Decalogum"</note>—but rather we are dealing with the vices contrary to justice. To the question, therefore, an affirmative conclusion is given without controversy.
<margin>The sole conclusion.</margin>
It is just to kill wrongdoers.
<margin>The reasoning for the conclusion by St. Thomas.</margin>
Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> beautifully derived the reason for this from the previous article. For it was defined there that brute animals are lawfully slaughtered because they are ordered for our use, just as the imperfect exists for the sake of that which is more perfect. By the same logic, since every part is made by nature for the sake of the whole body, it follows that where it is necessary for a man's health, a rotting limb is cut away so that the others, and finally the whole, are not lost through contagion. Since individual citizens are parts of the entire republic <note>original: "reipublicæ"</note>, it follows that when it is expedient for the safety of the republic, the state itself has the right to cut off a citizen by death, lest he infect the whole. For as Paul says in 1 Corinthians: "A little leaven corrupts the whole lump."
<margin>Paul. Objection.</margin>
¶ However, this argument can occur to anyone against this truthful assertion: This prohibition, "Thou shalt not kill," is divine and likewise general; it forbids all mortals, with no one excepted, from killing. But no subordinate has the faculty of dispensing with the law of a superior. Therefore, by no human law can it be established that a man, no matter how much a sinner, may be killed.
<margin>Scotus slipped in his explanation of this precept, "Thou shalt not kill."</margin>
Persuaded by this argument, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a 13th-century Franciscan philosopher often in dialogue/disagreement with Aquinas.</note> in Book 4, distinction 15, question 3, asserted four things. First: That the precept is general. For in Exodus 20, it is stated absolutely. And in Matthew 5, it is repeated in the same form: "Thou shalt not kill." Second: From this he infers that it is not lawful to kill any harmful man by either private or public authority, except in those cases specifically excepted by God in the Old Law. Nor can human law punish any other crime with death. He proves this by the same argument: since this is a divine command, men cannot grant dispensations regarding it. Third: He infers that it is not lawful to kill a daytime thief—that is, one who steals secretly. He proves this because, as is clear from Exodus 21 where crimes and sins to be punished by the head are listed, this case is not counted among them. Indeed, in the following chapter 22, it is expressed that a night thief caught in the act of the crime may be struck down with death, but a daytime thief not at all. And "concerning this exception," he says, "we have heard nothing else." Fourth and finally, he infers that it is not lawful even among Christians to kill an adulteress; for although it was once commanded in Leviticus 20, nevertheless in John 8, Christ [repealed?] the same command...

<meta>This page continues the critique of Duns Scotus’s interpretation of the Fifth Commandment. # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

recalled: where he dismissed the adulteress unpunished <note>A reference to John 8:1–11, where Jesus declines to sentence the woman caught in adultery to death.</note>. Therefore, according to Scotus, laws that command the contrary are not just.

<margin>Scotus is refuted.</margin>
But truly, with all due respect to such a celebrated author, he could not help but draw false conclusions from a false foundation. It is false, I say, to understand that precept, *Thou shalt not kill* <note>original: "Non occides"</note>, in such a general way that it encompasses every single instance of human killing. First, to strike down an attacker in blameless self-defense <note>original: "inculpata tutela"; a legal term for using proportional force to protect one's life</note> is in no way prohibited by that precept; otherwise, since it was not listed as an exception in the Old Law, it would not be permitted under his rule. Nor is the response legitimate which claims that the one attacked does not intend to kill the other, but only to defend himself. For even if the higher goal is defense, he nevertheless chooses to kill the aggressor as a means to that end; for he who defends himself can, with a righteous intention, seek the throat of his enemy. Furthermore, the response of others is not solid: that he kills not by private authority, but by public or divine authority. For indeed, he does not kill by any other right than that private right by which anyone can eat to preserve his life; by that same right, he may slay an attacker. Thus, he who says an attacker is killed by public authority ought to say that a man also eats by public authority.

Secondly, it is argued against what he infers next: namely, that it is not lawful for the state to kill any others except those who were exempted in the Old Law. For first, if that precept, *Thou shalt not kill*, was so general, there was no reason why God should grant dispensations over it in so many cases. On the contrary, since it was a commandment of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, and a negative one at that, God could not even grant a dispensation for it, as we showed in Book 2.

Next, it is argued: either those precepts for killing evildoers were merely legal statutes <note>specific to the Jewish Law</note>, or they were natural. If they were merely legal, they have entirely ceased; therefore, it would no longer be lawful to kill murderers, nor any of the others who are subject to capital punishment there. But if they were, as they truly were, interpretations of natural law, then those cases were excepted from that precept *Thou shalt not kill* by the natural light of reason itself—or rather, they were never included within it.

And this is confirmed by a reason which it is a wonder Scotus did not notice.

<margin>Scotus is too blind on this matter.</margin>
Before the written law, the governments of nations rightly and deservedly avenged crimes with the penalty of death; and yet they did not do this because those cases were excepted by the written law, which did not yet exist. In fact, in that age, they were not bound by the written law; and nevertheless, by public authority, they punished crimes with death, and did so most justly. Therefore, the reason why this is permitted to the state is not an exception in the written law, but

<column-break/>

nature's law itself. This is finally made clear by this most manifest reason: it is just as natural that guilty men and those who are a plague upon the state be cut off, as it is that the innocent should not be killed. Therefore, this power of the state does not depend on that exception from the ancient law, but is granted to it by the right of nature.

In addition to this, if the civil state did not now have the natural faculty to kill any wrongdoers other than those who were excepted in the Old Law, it would not be lawful to kill them by other devised forms of death, nor to afflict others with any corporal punishment—such as whipping thieves with lashes—nor to prohibit other enormous crimes with the threat of death. Yet the consequence of this is most absurd and against the tenor of the Law of Capital Crimes <note>original: "Legis, capitalium. ff. de pœnis"; a reference to the Digest of Justinian, the Roman civil law code regarding punishments</note>, where the death penalty is decreed for arsonists and others; and parricides <note>those who kill their parents</note> are enclosed in a sack and drowned; and heretics are burned; and those who commit treason <note>original: "læsores maiestatis"</note> are most deservedly torn apart; and others are beaten with whips; and others are sent into exile—punishments which were not set down there in the Old Law.

Therefore, lest I prolong the explanation of this matter any further: this precept, *Thou shalt not kill*, like all those of the Decalogue (as shown in Book 2, and which even Scotus cannot deny), is a precept of natural law. It is elicited, of course, from that principle: *Do not do to others what you would not have done to you*, etc. Wherefore, natural reason teaches us its legitimate meaning; and it is general only insofar as nature wishes to preserve human life.

<margin>A most elegant explanation of that precept, "Thou shalt not kill."</margin>
In whatever case natural reason either commands or permits the killing of a man, that same case is not included in the same precept. From this it follows that the killing of an attacker is not an "exception" to this precept, because such a homicide is not forbidden by nature, and consequently could not be forbidden by the law. And by the same, or rather by a fairer reason, the execution of wrongdoers which is done by public authority is not an exception to the same precept, because it was never included within it. Indeed, nature itself commands this no less than the safety of the innocent. For by the same right that each person can defend himself by the death of an enemy, and by which he can amputate a limb to remain safe himself, the state can preserve itself unharmed through the death of a citizen.

It follows next, secondly, that those cases in the ancient law were not all merely legal, but were interpretations of natural law.

Although it was suitable to the character of that nation...

# Book Five. Question I.

...so that some harsher legal measures were then applied: as was the penalty of retaliation <note>original: "talionis pœna"; the principle of "an eye for an eye."</note>, 
<margin>The penalty of retaliation.</margin>
the stoning of the adulteress, and other such things that do not persist in the entire Christian family.
¶ Third, it follows that besides those punishments, every prince, instructed by just reason, was always able—and is still able—to make new laws that inflict death. This is because that precept, *Thou shalt not kill*, does not bind the hands of the commonwealth insofar as it is guided by reason.
<margin><unclear>Blasphemy.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>Homicide.</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>The worst [criminals].</unclear></margin>
¶ Regarding the third assertion of Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan medieval philosopher.</note>—namely, whether it is lawful to kill thieves—we will more conveniently dispute this in Question 3 under the title of theft.
¶ Truly, as for the fourth point he asserts concerning the adulteress—namely that Christ revoked the law of killing her—I do not see by what consequence this can be gathered from the Gospel. For the Redeemer did not take on the role of a judge in that instance; indeed, he seemed to deny that such secular judgment belonged to him as a man. Instead, as a minister and king of the kingdom of heaven, he ensured those accusers were warned that if they themselves were in any crime, they should repent—understanding that everyone’s judgment must begin with oneself. For this was the purpose of the king of the kingdom of heaven: not to judge secular causes. We will discuss the adulteress again in the next article.
¶ Through these points, the second opinion of others is finally refuted. For there are those who, opposing Scotus, lean to the other extreme. They say the aforementioned precept is not only not general, but is specific in this way: *Thou shalt not kill the innocent.* For although in Exodus 22 it is stated absolutely, immediately in chapter 23 it is added: *The innocent and the just thou shalt not kill.* But truly, this way of speaking is not safe either; for whoever kills a guilty and wicked man by private authority also sins against this same precept, as will be clear in the next article. Indeed, even public authority, if it kills that same man while bypassing the order of the law, similarly sins against the precept. Therefore, there is no need to burden that precept with qualifications; if they had been necessary, they would have been expressed in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>. Nor is it necessary to explain it under the form: *Thou shalt not kill, except where there is a just cause.* For this form would appear to be a "begging of the question" <note>A logical fallacy where the premise assumes the truth of the conclusion.</note>. Rather, it is to be understood absolutely as it stands, yet insofar as natural reason explains it.
<margin>The sense of the negative precepts of the Decalogue.</margin>
For the entire Decalogue presents a similar image: *Do not swear at all* <note>original: "Nolite iurare omninò"</note>; and yet it is understood "unless natural reason requires the contrary." And we will interpret *Thou shalt not steal* in the same way. And this is what

<column-break/>

Saint Thomas teaches <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s school of thought.</note> in Part I-II, Question 100, Article 8, where
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
he says that homicide, which is prohibited in the Decalogue, has the character of being "undue" or "wrongful" <note>original: "rationem indebiti"</note>. Nor is this a begging of the question. For the meaning is that what is prohibited is that which is wrongful by the law of nature—namely, that which is evil by its very nature. But nevertheless, by some cause, it can happen that it becomes good. Such causes are to be explained when someone defends himself in "blameless self-defense" <note>original: "inculpata tutela"</note>, and when a judge acts by law against a wrongdoer. Hence, since "homicide" implies a thing that is intrinsically evil, those legal killings of men are not to be called "homicides."
It remains, nonetheless, to dissolve arguments that are not entirely free of ambiguity. Saint Thomas responds to the first argument along with the holy interpreters. 
<margin>To the first argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
Their first solution is that where the wicked cannot be killed without danger to the good, one must abstain. That, however, can happen in two ways. First, if the wicked are so mixed with the just that they cannot be distinguished. Therefore, if it were established that the greater part of a city were infected with heresy, it would not be lawful to burn the whole city to punish the crime. It is different in the assault of an enemy city: for then it is permitted to attack it with sulfurous fire <note>original: "sulphuris iactibus"; likely referring to early gunpowder artillery or incendiary weapons.</note> despite the danger to the innocent. Second, if the guilty cannot be punished without a great commotion of the innocent—namely, those joined to them by blood or other necessity. And this is the exposition of Augustine
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
against Parmenianus. Indeed, the Redeemer gave us another lesson: that we should rather spare the wicked for the sake of the good (just as the angels promised Abraham that if they found ten just men in Sodom, they would spare the whole nation) rather than harm the good for the sake of the wicked. Nevertheless, this rule must be prudently accommodated to human capacity. For a human prince does not flourish with such absolute authority as God. God reserves all things for the final judgment; but a prince is not permitted to spare delinquents for just any cause. This would result in the ruin of the commonwealth. Therefore, although many might take offense, if the punishment can be carried out conveniently, he ought not to cease from punishing the wicked. For this reason, as Paul says, 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
he carries the sword <note>A reference to Romans 13:4, regarding the state’s authority to punish.</note>, so that he may quiet tumults and seditions that stand in the way of the execution of justice—and where necessary, even crush them.
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And...

He qualifies this by citing Aquinas and Augustine, noting that the state should avoid punishing the wicked if it would cause disproportionate harm to the innocent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's legal and theological analysis of the Fifth Commandment. Having discussed the state's general authority to execute justice, Soto now addresses the tension between divine mercy and human law, the moral status of a criminal, and whether private citizens have any right to take a life for the sake of the public good.</meta>

In a similar manner <note>original: "riformi modo," likely a transcription error for "conformi modo."</note>, the second argument is answered.

<margin>Paul. St. Thomas.</margin>
For God, the searcher of the secrets of hearts and eager for human salvation, leads the wicked to repentance through long-suffering patience, as Paul says. Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s Dominican order.</note> advises that human justice ought to imitate this as much as possible. Yet he says "as much as possible" because this applies when sins are not public or tending toward the ruin of others. For otherwise, as we have said, the human judge does not have as broad a faculty as God. I mention this to counter the questions of the common people.

<margin>Dispelling common excuses.</margin>
For someone might doubt whether a judge or prince—when he suspects from the evidence that if he punishes the guilty party with death, the man will be lost to hell, but if he pardons him, the man will change his mind and advance along the path of salvation—ought to spare him. Reason seems to suggest this because bodily life must always be subordinated to spiritual life in the order of charity; and justice is certainly not an enemy of such charity. The first response is that judges, insofar as they make laws, ought to be much more inclined toward mercy than toward the rigor of justice. Nonetheless, even if it were established through revelation that the punishment would cause the eternal damnation of the guilty man, he must not be indulged. Otherwise, it would be easy for anyone to use such trickery <note>original: "vafricie"; meaning craftiness or a legal loophole.</note> to feign impenitence.

<margin>Punishment is ordered toward the public good.</margin>
The reason is that public punishment is not directed toward the reform or the personal good of the one being punished, but toward the public good, so that others may be deterred. Since the public good is more excellent than the individual good, it must be loved above it in the order of charity. Indeed, by this path, the spiritual health of the commonwealth <note>original: "respublica"; the organized political community.</note> is also provided for.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third argument, it is answered that killing a man is not intrinsically evil in the same way lying is—that is, in such a general sense. Rather, it is evil when it is against nature. However, it is against nature only when a man preserves his dignity—that is, when he lives according to reason. For through reason, a man is free and exists for his own sake. But when he falls away from that, he degenerates into the vileness and slavery of the brute animals, according to the Psalm: *Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he is compared to the beasts.* <note>Psalm 49:20 (Vulgate 48:21). This was a standard medieval justification for stripping criminals of certain rights.</note> On that account, it is permitted to kill him just like a beast.

<margin>Aristotle. A wicked man is worse than a wild beast.</margin>
For a corrupt man, as Aristotle says in Book 7 of the *Politics* and Book 1 of the *Ethics*, is as much worse and more harmful than a wild beast as he possesses more ways of doing harm through his intellect and will.

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether it is lawful for any private person to kill a wicked man.<-

<margin>First argument for the affirmative. Second argument. Third argument.</margin>
It is not enough to have defined that it is lawful to kill wicked men unless we also explore the method—namely, whether it is lawful for any private citizen to do so. First, the affirmative side argues from that Mosaic mandate in Exodus 32: *Let every man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.* ¶ Second, it is argued from the fact that in the previous article we compared a corrupt and lost man to beasts; yet it is free for anyone to kill a wild beast, especially if it is harmful; therefore, by the same reasoning, one may kill a man who has become like a brute. ¶ Third, it is worthy of praise for a man to do privately that which is for the common benefit. The killing of evildoers is useful to the commonwealth; therefore, even if done privately, it is just and holy.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
¶ On the contrary stand those words of Augustine in Book 1 of *The City of God*: "He who kills an evildoer without any public administration shall be judged as a murderer." And he is all the more so because he did not fear to usurp a power not granted to him by God.

<margin>The sole conclusion.</margin>
The question is easy and is resolved by this single negative conclusion: It is lawful only for the commonwealth, the prince, and the public magistrate to kill evildoers. This conclusion is primarily drawn from the words of Paul in Romans 13, where he calls only the public judge "God's minister" in this matter, and for the same reason says he "bears the sword" to be an avenger in wrath against him who does evil. He proves this by reason: The killing of harmful men is not good in itself, but only insofar as it relates to the public good. Therefore, the task falls chiefly to him who has been entrusted with the care and guardianship of the common good—just as the amputation of a limb, which is beneficial to the body, falls chiefly to the physician to whom the care of the sick is committed, so that it may be done by judgment according to medical laws. Since the care of the common good is committed only to princes and their ministers (except where the commonwealth governs itself), it follows that only they are permitted to kill evildoers.

¶ Here, first of all, we must more accurately meditate on the reason why it is not right for any private person to kill another, not even in revenge for himself—to answer the common people who can hardly be persuaded of this. For you may hear everywhere not only loudmouths...

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's exploration of the Fifth Commandment, specifically the prohibition of killing. On the previous page, Soto argued that human justice must prioritize the common good over individual mercy, even if a criminal's soul is at stake. Here, he moves into the limits of private vengeance and the highly contentious theological debate over tyrannicide—whether it is ever lawful for a private citizen to kill a ruler.</meta>

### Question I of the Fifth Book

...[there are] certain people, including even some of noble birth, who place so much value on protecting their own honor that they think it is unjust for men to be restrained from avenging their own injuries. I remember hearing a certain <margin>The blasphemy of a most shameful man.</margin> blasphemy from a most shameful man: that not even God could forbid such a thing. Yet, even if God had not forbidden it, the very law of nature would prohibit it. Indeed, the divine prohibition is an explanation of natural law. The reason is readily apparent: for if nature had entrusted vengeance to the very person who suffered the injury, there is no one who would not avenge himself beyond what is just. For the pain of an inflicted injury both clouds the reason and inflames the passions into a rage, and thus no one would avenge himself as justly as he ought, but as <margin>The ruinous abuse of the nobility in avenging injuries.</margin> greatly as he could. We have manifest proof of this in the ruinous abuse of the nobility, who pursue the ceremonies of honor so superstitiously that they challenge men to their deaths for the slightest injury <note>Soto is likely referring to the practice of dueling, which was a major social issue in 16th-century Europe and frequently condemned by the Church.</note>. Therefore, since the most excellent virtue of justice ought to be carried out not with a disturbed mind but with sound judgment—according to that divine oracle in Deuteronomy 16: "You shall execute justly that which is just"—it was exceedingly necessary that injuries be avenged not by the injured party, but by a public person free from all passion. Indeed, this task ought not to be entrusted to men at all, as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle says in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 6, but rather to reason instructed by the laws. Anyone who does not fully grasp this true sentiment should not judge this matter while he himself is suffering from an injury and dominated by anger, but rather when he himself has inflicted the same on another and his reason is free to judge. For then he would not think it just that the limit of vengeance be left to his enemy. For this reason, not even for the sake of correction is it permitted for fathers or masters to kill or even mutilate their children or servants, as <margin>Particular doubts. The first doubt.</margin> we shall discuss in Question 3. ¶ But despite this conclusion, particular doubts nonetheless arise. The first concerns a tyrant: whether it is lawful for any citizen to kill him privately. For it appears, with nature as our teacher, to be legitimate; for the right of <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> self-defense is granted to everyone. Regarding this, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> discusses the matter excellently in his commentary on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 44, question 2, article 2, and in his work *On the Government of Princes*, book 1, chapter 6. The summary of the dispute, according to certain of his interpreters and other <margin>Two types of tyrants.</margin> Doctors, is this: there are two ways a person happens to be a tyrant, namely either by the acquisition of power [usurpation], or solely by the administration of power which he obtained justly. In this second case, the common consensus is that it is not permitted

<column-break/>

for anyone to kill him privately. The reason is that since he has a right to the kingdom, he is not to be stripped of it except by a public judgment, so that he may be heard. But once a sentence has been passed against him, anyone can be appointed as the minister of its execution. Furthermore, if he attacks any citizen individually to slaughter him or seize his goods, that citizen can kill him by repelling force with force—provided it is absolutely certain that he is a tyrant. For if a prince who is otherwise good begins such an act in a sudden impulse, he should not be subjected to the danger of death as if he were a private person. Therefore, to return to the <margin>A two-fold response to the doubt.</margin> point, when a prince exercises tyranny in the second manner [mismanagement], then the admonition of Peter holds true: that even harsh masters <note>original: "dyscolis dominis," a reference to 1 Peter 2:18, where "dyscolos" implies those who are difficult or crooked.</note> must be obeyed. For "this is a grace," he says, "if for the sake of conscience toward God a man endures sorrows, suffering unjustly." Therefore, if the republic has a superior [such as an Emperor or Pope], he must be approached so that he may provide a remedy; but if not, the republic itself can take up arms against him. However, when the republic is not powerful enough, then God must be prayed to, in whose hand the heart of the King exists, and who sometimes permits a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people. And in this <margin>The Council of Constance explained.</margin> case, the decree of the Council of Constance <note>The Council of Constance (1414–1418) famously condemned the proposition that any tyrant could be lawfully killed by any vassal or subject.</note>, Session 15, must be understood, where the error of those who affirmed that it was lawful for anyone to kill a tyrant was condemned as heresy. If, however, someone has seized the republic by an invaded tyranny and the republic has never consented, then everyone has the right to destroy him; for it is lawful to repel force with force. And as long as he holds the republic in this way, he wages a perpetual <margin>Ehud.</margin> war against it. The example of Ehud is brought forward from Judges 3, who hid a dagger in the belly of the tyrant Eglon. <margin>Cicero. St. Thomas.</margin> For the same reason, Tully [Cicero] in his book *On Duties*—whom Saint Thomas follows in the place cited—commends the killers of Caesar with praise, as Caesar had obtained his dominion through tyranny. <margin>Decimus Brutus.</margin> And likewise, Decimus Brutus is commended, who drove out the kings after Tarquinius was killed. <margin>Limitation of this opinion.</margin> ¶ But even if this might be permitted by the extreme rigor of the law, it is not always advisable—unless there is no other way open for the republic, and it is in extreme necessity, and especially if it has a plan ready so that it might be liberated once he is destroyed. For otherwise, killings of this kind do not usually have prosperous outcomes. Indeed, when killers carry this out by private authority, they usually rage through the republic in a worse and more pestilential way than the previous tyrant did. For this reason, <margin>The old woman of Syracuse.</margin> that old woman of Syracuse [prayed] for Dionysius to remain safe... <note>Soto is referring to a famous anecdote where an old woman prayed for the life of the tyrant Dionysius; when asked why, she said she had seen many tyrants, and each one was worse than the last, so she feared his successor would be even worse.</note>

<summary>Soto argues that private vengeance is contrary to natural law and the common good, moving into a nuanced discussion on tyrannicide. He distinguishes between legitimate rulers who govern poorly (who cannot be killed by private citizens) and usurpers (who may be resisted as invaders), while warning that the violent overthrow of a tyrant often leads to even greater suffering.</summary>
