### F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

<margin>Mucius Scaevola.</margin>
...[he] hoped that, just as he himself had succeeded a harsher tyrant, a third, even more monstrous one, would not succeed him. Examples of this are written frequently throughout history. And in truth, the biblical story of Ehud <note>original: "Aiod." See Judges 3:15-30. Ehud assassinated Eglon, King of Moab, to liberate the Israelites.</note> is of little relevance to the matter: both because he was divinely chosen for that deed, and because he had also been sent by the people for that purpose. Furthermore, that tyrant was not merely a governor, but an active enemy. For this reason, Mucius Scaevola <note>A legendary Roman hero who attempted to assassinate the Etruscan king Porsena during a siege of Rome.</note> is worthy of praise insofar as he attempted the destruction of Porsena; however, the fact that he placed his arm into the flames was not a work of virtue, but, as Augustine says, a desire for "empty glory."

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
<margin>Andabatae.</margin>
Therefore, to the first argument, one responds following Augustine in the first book of *The City of God* (which is also the doctrine of Dionysius in the 12th chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*): that when someone performs a task through the ministry they owe to the one commanding them, they are not properly the one doing the deed, but rather the person who commands it. Thus, when Moses was the legitimate judge in God’s place to avenge that monstrous idolatry of the molten calf, and such a great slaughter had to be carried out—namely, of twenty-three thousand—he found it necessary to appoint several ministers as executioners. Therefore, what he said—"let every man kill his brother," etc.—is not to be understood as every single person killing anyone they pleased in a rash and haphazard way. That would have been the savage fight of the **Andabatae** <note>original: "Andabatarum pugna." The Andabatae were Roman gladiators who fought blindfolded; Soto uses the term here to describe a chaotic, lawless brawl where no one can see who they are hitting.</note>. Instead, once those who were in the wrong had been condemned, he designated a large number of ministers. It was therefore necessary for these ministers to kill friend or brother if they were among the condemned. Moreover, they were called "brothers" not only if they were born of the same parent, but also because they were all members of the same people.

<margin>Second doubt.</margin>
<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ From this solution, however, a doubt arises: whether a prince can grant to any private person the power to kill evildoers. The response is that this is not permissible, except under certain regulations. First, he could not grant a general power to citizens so that anyone could kill any guilty person they met without a prior conviction. For it is against natural law for a sentence to be passed against a party who has not been heard and whose case has not been argued; rather, anyone, no matter how dangerous, must be heard, as is held in Acts 25 <note>referring to the Roman legal principle mentioned by Festus: "It is not the Roman custom to hand over any man before he has faced his accusers."</note>. An exception might be if someone were a public invader of the republic or the King; for then it would be lawful for anyone to repel that force against the state.
¶ Second assertion. After a sentence has been passed, it is permissible to appoint any ministers. First,

<column-break/>

against public robbers and the most open enemies of the state who cannot be captured by other means. Regarding these, see the chapter *pro humani* under the title of voluntary homicide, Book 6 <note>A reference to Canon Law (Liber Sextus Decretalium).</note>. Furthermore, the ministry of killing the murderer of a father or brother is often granted to sons and brothers. However, an inferior judge does not have the power to grant this authority; only the prince does. Indeed, this should not be done commonly, but as rarely as possible and in extraordinary cases. For besides the fact that such executioners can scarcely cleanse their consciences of hatred and anger—and thus, while they set traps for the condemned, they accumulate other sins—it often happens in practice that the criminals are killed without the sacrament of confession.

<margin>The custom of the Venetians is not approved.</margin>
¶ For this reason, the custom of the Venetians is certainly not approved by everyone. Since they have many exiles condemned by their country, they grant a power to individuals such that whoever kills one of those exiles is granted his own life and freedom.

<margin>Nicholas.</margin>
¶ Next follows the case of a man who kills his wife caught in the act of adultery <note>original: "in flagranti adulterio."</note>. Regarding this, no theologian or jurist doubts that he sins mortally against the prohibition of homicide for the reason already stated: because no one is to be adjudged to death before they are judged. In this case, the Canon of Pope Nicholas, *Interfectores* (33, q. 2), is to be understood, where such men are considered murderers. Yet, they are not punished by the law because of the severity of the grief, which is extremely difficult to bear at that moment: as held in the law *Gracchus* (Code, *ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis*) and the law *Marito* (Digest, same title) <note>Soto is distinguishing between the "sin" (which the Church condemns) and the "legal penalty" (which the civil law waives due to the husband's temporary insanity or extreme provocation).</note>.

<margin>Third doubt.</margin>
¶ A more serious doubt, however, is whether it is lawful for a husband to kill a wife handed over to him by a judge. There are those who deny this, because that permission is not a command, such as that by which an executioner is compelled to carry out justice. Added to this is the cited canon, *Interfectores*, which considers them murderers without exception. And the very next canon, *Inter haec*, expressly explains that although it may be lawful for a husband to kill his wife according to worldly law, the holy church is not bound by those same laws. Here, the gloss <note>The standard legal commentary on the text.</note> seems to agree that it is always a sin.

<margin>Double question.</margin>
¶ There are two questions involved here. The first is about the law itself: whether it is licit. In ancient times, it was lawful for a father to kill a daughter caught in adultery, as is clear in the law *patri* and the law *neque in ea* (Digest, *ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis*) and the law *castitati* (Code, same title). Later, however, the law was changed, as is clear in the Code under the same title in the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's legal reforms (Novels).</note> *sed hodie*, so that, after being whipped, she would be shut away in a monastery. And this law is now in use in France, and in many other provinces regarding the husband; for that of the father...

### Book Five, Question I. 391
**Bb 4**

<margin>Resolution of both questions.</margin>
...[The law] has now faded from use. Nevertheless, the law of the Spanish kingdoms follows the ancient custom: not indeed with such rigor that an adulteress is necessarily condemned to death, but she is handed over to the husband, to whom the power is given if he wishes to kill her. And there is no reason to doubt that this law is just. For besides the fact that such a crime seems to deserve it, surely it could hardly be otherwise given the temperament <note>original: "ingenio"</note> of the Spanish people regarding this matter. Nor, as we were saying a little while ago when responding to Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a major medieval theologian.</note>, did Christ revoke that law. The second sense of the question is whether, given the same liberty granted to the husband, it is lawful for him to pursue it according to his conscience: and in truth, there is even less reason for doubt regarding this. For although he is not appointed as a necessary minister of justice, he is nevertheless appointed as a free one; therefore, the right is given to him to kill her. Consequently, although it might be a work of mercy to spare her, nevertheless he violates justice neither before men nor before God. Furthermore, there is a powerful argument: if it were not lawful for a husband to kill her without sin, it would be a sin for the prince and the judge to grant that power to him. Nor is the solution valid if someone says that uxoricide <note>The act of killing one's wife.</note> is not permitted to him then, but only that he does so with impunity; for he already enjoyed that privilege even if he killed her without a trial in the very act <note>original: "in flagranti delicto"</note> of the crime. Therefore, when she is handed over to him after being condemned by the solemn form of a trial, it is open testimony that the right of killing is granted to him as a minister of justice. ¶ To the second principal

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
argument, the response is that although men who degenerate from their nature are compared to beasts, they differ nonetheless because beasts are such by their nature: therefore, anyone kills wild animals without injustice, and domestic ones without injury to the animals themselves (though an injury might be done to their owners). A sinner, however, because he is not a beast by nature, ought not to be killed unless condemned by the public judgment of the one whose duty it is. ¶ The solution to the third argument

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
is a most wholesome teaching. For wherever one can benefit a neighbor without harm or injury to another, it is a praiseworthy duty to look after his advantage; however, where the harm of another presents itself—such as the death of a sinner—it ought not to be attempted except by the judgment of the one to whom that function belongs.

### ARTICLE IV.

#### Whether it is also permitted for clerics to kill evildoers.

<column-break/>

<margin>First argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
After the decision that it is not only lawful but even holy for public power to root out evildoers, it follows that we see whether the same is lawful for ecclesiastical leaders. For an argument exists for the affirmative side: according to Paul in 1 Corinthians 4, we ought to be imitators of him and likewise of the saints, just as they were of Christ. But God is accustomed to kill evildoers, according to that Psalm: "Who struck Egypt with their firstborn." And Phineas, although a priest, killed the Israelite cohabiting with the Midianite woman, as we read in Numbers 25. And Samuel the Prophet killed Agag, king of the Amalekites. And Elijah killed the priests of Baal. Finally, Peter killed Ananias and Sapphira.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly: Since spiritual power is superior to temporal power and more closely joined to God, there is no reason why it should have less power to kill those evildoers who are subject to it than the secular power has. ¶ On the contrary is that in 1 Timothy 3: "A Bishop must be without crime, not violent, not a striker," etc.

<margin>The single conclusion.</margin>
The question is easy to solve, and is decided negatively by this single conclusion: It is in no way lawful for clerics, in whatever ecclesiastical power they may be established, to sentence any person, however criminal, to death or to mutilate them.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This is proved by two main points. First, because of representation. For he is consecrated for the ministry of the altar, where the perpetual memory of the Passion of Christ is made. When Christ was killed on the altar of the cross, being struck (as Peter says), He did not strike back; therefore, in imitation of Him, they ought not to be strikers. For as Sirach 10 <note>The book of Ecclesiasticus or Ben Sira.</note> reminds us: "As the judge of the people is, so also are his ministers." Second, this is confirmed because in the Gospel, of which clerics are ministers, no capital punishment or mutilation of a limb is decreed for avenging any crime. ¶ Here, first of all, it must be observed by what law clerics are forbidden from the shedding of blood. For this prohibition is not of natural law. Indeed, if you consider that alone, nothing stands in the way of a bishop being able to judge his subjects to the gallows. However, it is doubtful whether it is by divine law.

<margin>The response of some.</margin>
For there are those who respond by making a distinction. They say, I mean, that a precept can be considered to be of divine law in two ways. In one way, because it is written in the sacred pages; in the other way, because it was established by God Himself...

<summary>Soto argues that while Spanish law permits a husband to kill an unfaithful wife as an act of state-sanctioned justice, members of the clergy are strictly forbidden from exercising capital punishment because they represent the non-violent Christ at the altar.</summary>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice & Right, 392

...as if concerning a supernatural matter: such as the mandates of the sacraments. For so the Apostle distinguishes in 1 Corinthians 7, saying that a wife should not depart from her husband is a commandment of God; but that a believer should not depart from an unbelieving wife who consents to live with him, "I say, not the Lord." <note>Soto is distinguishing between "Divine Law" revealed by God and "Apostolic advice."</note> Therefore, the prohibition against clerics shedding blood, though not in the latter way, yet in the former way, these [authors] say, is divine: because it appears in Paul in the cited place, 1 Timothy 3.

<margin>Paul.</margin>

<margin>Objection.</margin> But if you hesitate whether whatever Paul ordered is to be held as a commandment of God? Since whatever the Apostles spoke as apostles, they brought forth as divine instruments.

<margin>Solution.</margin> It is answered that in the assertion of faith they were moved by immediate revelation. Wherefore their enunciations are held as divine faith; nevertheless, in establishing some laws, although the Holy Spirit assisted them, just as now He assists the church, nonetheless such laws are not properly of <term>divine right|ius divinum: Law believed to be ordained by God, which cannot be changed by human authority</term>, just as the commands of the Pope and Councils are not so now. Whence in Acts 15, Peter says, "It seemed good," not only to the Holy Spirit, but "to the Holy Spirit and to us": because then in the Council they did not use immediate revelation, but human consultation, with the Holy Spirit assisting so they would not err. It is otherwise in putting forth the faith: regarding which they were warned not to think how or what they should speak, but should use revelation alone.

<margin>That response to the doubt is excluded.</margin> ¶ But truly, although this distinction is clearly made from the matter itself, I do not know if it can be applied conveniently enough to the proposal. For that word of Paul, carefully examined, does not seem to look toward this, so as to inhibit clerics from killing evildoers as public authorities: but rather that they should not be <note>original: "percussores"</note> "strikers" as private persons. For he composed a list of qualities: sober, prudent, etc., not violent, not a striker, but modest, not litigious, not greedy. Besides that, his speech there was only with bishops. Nor did he exclude secular judges there from being admitted into the priestly order: which, however, the church does. Therefore, if you insist only on this passage, certainly this prohibition is not of divine law in either of the two ways mentioned above.

<margin>Sophistry.</margin> ¶ But another stronger argument could be brought to the proposal: namely that Christ, as we recalled in the preceding book, question 4, did not assume secular power of judging, but the spiritual power of the kingdom of heaven. Whence it seems to follow that clerics could not exercise it either. However, neither does this argument demonstrate the matter: but only this, that ecclesiastical power, insofar as it is spiritual, does not extend itself to carrying out secular judgments: except insofar as they have an order toward a spiritual end.

<column-break/>

<margin>Solution.</margin> To this, however, it is in no way repugnant that clerics could be ministers of secular princes, to shed the blood of the guilty in their name. Indeed, it is not even repugnant that bishops could strike with the sword those who would disturb that spiritual end.

<margin>The true solution to the doubt.</margin> ¶ From these things, therefore, it follows (as I would certainly believe) that this prohibition is only of purely <term>positive ecclesiastical law|ius ecclesiasticum: Laws created by the Church hierarchy rather than found in scripture</term>.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin> Nor did Saint Thomas bring forth the apostolic word as if it were to be held as law, lest clerics sit as judges in a case of blood <note>A "case of blood" refers to a trial where the penalty is death or mutilation.</note>, but only by way of consequence and example: namely that after they are warned not to be "strikers," the church rightly took care that they should abstain from all striking. And in the same sense Gratian <note>Gratian was the 12th-century jurist who compiled the "Decretum," the foundational text of Canon Law.</note> cites the same word at the beginning of Distinction 45, where in the chapter "Neminem" and the canon "Episcopum" the same prohibition is held. And expressly in the chapter "Sententiam," lest clerics or monks [do so]. And in the title "On clerics who strike." The reason for this ecclesiastical sanction was nothing other than decency and a double honor, which was brought to the conclusion. And furthermore, the purity that ought to be not only in priests, but even in the sacred vessels. Therefore, those who are initiated into sacred orders, just as they take a vow not to pollute themselves with women, so they are prohibited by law from being contaminated by blood. Which two species of filth, if they are shed in the temple, also leave it polluted and, in its own way, "irregular."

<margin>Whom this sanction covers.</margin> ¶ In the name of "clerics" in such a prohibition, all are included indiscriminately, both those in minor orders <note>Minor orders included roles like acolytes or lectors; they were not yet priests.</note> and those initiated into sacred ones. Although regarding the degree of fault, there is not the same rationale for all. For one established in minor orders who exercised secular judgment even to the shedding of blood would not sin mortally: because those orders are not properly "sacred": yet he who was in sacred orders would be infected with lethal sin, whether he bloodied himself as a judge or as a minister of justice. But truly, even in minor orders, there would be some sin. For the shedding of blood is forbidden to all.

<margin>When irregularity is incurred.</margin> ¶ But concerning <term>irregularity|irregularitas: A legal status in Canon Law that prevents a man from being ordained or performing the duties of a priest</term> it is most clear in the law that killers and mutilators all become irregular, whether they did it after receiving orders or before: as is clear in the canon "Episcopum," distinction 45, and distinction 51, the canon "Aliquotantos," and 23, question 8, canon 1, and the canon "Clerici," and the canon "Quicunque," and in the title "On voluntary homicide," the canon "De cetero," and 

can. <note>Catchword for the next page's first word.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "irregularity"—a legal status in the Church that prevents someone from being ordained or performing priestly duties. Soto is specifically looking at whether the shedding of blood automatically triggers this status, and whether the Pope has the authority to grant exceptions (dispensations) to these rules.</meta>

### Book Five, Question 1

...in the chapters "To the hearing" <note>original: "ad audientiam"</note> and in many other places. 

<margin>Sylvester: The mere shedding of blood is not a cause of irregularity.</margin> 

Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a prominent Dominican theologian and legal expert.</note> treats this extensively under the entry "Homicide," section 3. 

¶ It must be noted, however, that although the cited laws <note>The "canons" or Church decrees.</note> decree that all who strike others—and even those who take up arms—are <term>irregular|Irregularity is a canonical "stumbling block" or impediment. It is not necessarily a punishment for a sin, but a status that makes a person "unfit" for the dignity of the priesthood, often due to a connection with death or violence.</term>, the legal experts understand this to apply only to those who have actually killed or maimed someone. For this reason, Panormitanus <note>A famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> says regarding the chapter "Those who [are] clerics or [have] vowed": "The mere shedding of blood does not induce irregularity." This is also expressly stated in the commentary on the <term>Clementines|A collection of Church laws issued by Pope Clement V in the early 14th century.</term> under the single chapter on homicide, following the text's logic: "He kills or maims." Nevertheless, on this point, one must abide by ecclesiastical custom.

¶ However, be careful not to confuse the censures of excommunication with irregularity. Up to this point, we have been speaking of a cleric who strikes someone or a layperson. Conversely, whoever "lays violent hands upon a cleric" <note>Referencing the famous canon "Si quis suadente," which automatically excommunicated anyone who attacked a member of the clergy.</note> incurs the sentence of excommunication, even if he neither maims him nor sheds blood. If that person is a priest and continues to celebrate Mass while excommunicated, he then becomes irregular. Likewise, anyone who sheds semen or blood in a sacred place becomes irregular, provided the shedding was "notable," as they say. For instance, boys who punch each other and get a little blood from their noses are not immediately excommunicated.

¶ Homicide, however, makes the killer irregular even without the shedding of blood <note>For example, by strangulation or poisoning.</note>. Furthermore, it is not required that such actions be sinful for them to cause irregularity. Indeed, even if the actions are virtuous—so long as they are performed freely—they still have this effect. For example, a judge and his officers who justly execute a wicked man become irregular for receiving holy orders, as do all ministers of justice. The commentary notes this regarding the law "Some." 

¶ I say "so long as the actions are free and voluntary" because, as we shall discuss in Article 8, no irregularity is incurred through accidental homicide or other actions that happen against a person's will. Indeed, even when someone kills another or causes their death while defending themselves or their property with "blameless defense," they do not become irregular, as held in the Clementines and in the sixth book of the Decretals. 

¶ From this it follows that <margin>Irregularity is not a fault.</margin> irregularity is not a "fault" (a sin); indeed, it is not even properly a "punishment," as we noted in Book 1, Question 6. Where there is no fault, nothing truly has the nature of a punishment. Rather, it is a certain "incapacity" and "unbecomingness" for the administration of sacred things due to a symbolic impurity. Therefore, when Papal Bulls grant the faculty to absolve from "any sins and censures," the term "censure" does not include irregularity. 

¶ If someone

<column-break/>

perhaps doubts whether the <term>Supreme Pontiff|The Pope.</term> can grant a dispensation from this law—regarding both the fault and the irregularity—the affirmative answer is easily gathered from what was said above. Truly, since this law is "purely positive" <note>Human-made law or Church policy, rather than a direct, unchangeable command from God.</note>—not only because (as we said) Paul’s words do not carry that specific meaning, but also because even if they did, it would not be the kind of Divine law that falls outside the Pope's power to dispense—it is concluded that the Pope can, for a just cause, grant a dispensation so that a priest might be a secular judge or a soldier in war: functions to which the shedding of blood is attached.

After these points, there remains no difficulty in responding to the arguments of the question. 

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> 

The response to the first is that God is to be imitated by each person according to what is fitting for them. Truly, it would not be permitted for us to punish an entire city as He punished Sodom, nor (as we said above) to spare everyone whom He waits for in repentance. Instead, each must act according to the law prescribed for them, which in this matter was fittingly established for the clerics of the Law of Grace <note>The New Testament era.</note>. For the priests of the Old Testament did not handle spiritual matters as ours do, nor the ministries of the most innocent Christ who was slain. Rather, they were ministers of a Law by which physical punishments, even death, were decreed for evildoers. As for what was brought up regarding Peter <note>The story in Acts 5 where Ananias and Sapphira fall dead after Peter speaks to them.</note>, it is irrelevant; for he did not kill those spouses himself, nor were they killed by his command. Rather, he proclaimed the sentence as if by the mouth of God, and upon hearing it, they fell down dead. 

<margin>To the second argument.</margin> 

To the second, it is answered that the spiritual power of clerics should not excel the power of princes by killing bodies, but by looking to the salvation of souls. In this way, they are truly called "princes of the earth." 

<margin>To the third argument.</margin> 

And by this, the third argument is resolved.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
...the definition of justice: hence, since justice is only in relation to another, it follows (as Aristotle shows in the 5th book of the *Ethics*) that no one does an injustice to himself, even if he kills himself.
<margin>Argument 2</margin>
¶ And secondly, it is argued that when a judge, who has the power to put others to death, is himself worthy of the same death for which he would justly condemn others, it appears that he can then inflict the same upon himself.
<margin>Argument 3</margin>

<margin>Single conclusion.</margin>
**T**he question is answered with a single conclusion: It is lawful for no one to kill himself; and whoever does so becomes guilty of a most grave mortal sin. This is proven by three reasons.
<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
First, if a man is considered in himself, he acts against his own natural inclination and the love which he naturally owes himself when he takes away his own life.
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Secondly, if he is considered as a part of the whole <term>commonwealth|The 'respublica' or organized political community.</term>, he is ordered toward the good of the whole; and thus, as Aristotle says in the final chapter of the 5th book of the *Ethics*, he who kills himself inflicts an injury upon the commonwealth.
<margin>Third reason</margin>
Thirdly, if he is considered as a creation of God, human life is a divine gift, depending thereafter upon God as His possession. For this reason, he who destroys himself sins against God, whose servant he is, just as one would who usurps another's property. For to Him alone belongs the judgment of life and death, according to Deuteronomy 32: 
> I will kill, and I will make to live. <note>original: "Ego occidam, & ego viuere faciam."</note>

¶ No one can doubt this conclusion: it is so far against universal nature for anyone to bring death upon himself, by which he is deprived of life, which is the foundation of all goods. However, concerning the reasoning,

<column-break/>

a distinction must first be weighed: that if you consider man absolutely in himself, it is not properly against justice for him to kill himself, but rather against the love by which every thing loves itself. But if he is considered as the handiwork of God and a member of the commonwealth—then, because he has an ordering toward others, he who kills himself becomes unjust in respect to them. 
<margin>Objection against the first reason.</margin>
¶ However, a doubt exists regarding that same first reason: for the inference does not seem effective enough—that if homicide is committed against one's own natural inclination, it is immediately a mortal sin. For not every natural inclination is good; indeed, it is sometimes a duty to act against it. Truly, the human inclination toward a pleasurable good is natural, and even good in its kind. For the animal appetite is carried by its own nature toward that which is pleasurable. For this very reason, nature mixed pleasure into the necessary duties of preservation—both of the individual and the species—so that they might be desirable. Nevertheless, that same inclination is often evil, and thus resisting it is good. Therefore, the virtues of temperance and fortitude, according to Aristotle, serve us for moderating and repressing natural affections; for this reason, the work of virtue is laborious and difficult, namely because by its efforts we fight against natural inclination, which is difficult to overcome. Add to this that <term>original justice|In Catholic theology, the state of perfect harmony and grace in which Adam and Eve were created before the Fall.</term> was given to our first parents to restrain these same affections of nature. For that reason—namely because those affections were natural—that justice itself was supernatural. It is for this reason that Paul in Romans 7 complained that he felt another law in his members fighting against the law of his mind. What kind of argument is it, then: "it happens against natural inclination, therefore it is a sin"? If you mean that the inclination is good, that remains for you to prove; since its goodness is not proven simply by the fact that it is natural. 
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
¶ I remember that I have already spoken to this elsewhere. For man has two inclinations, both of them natural:
<margin>Natural inclination is twofold: one material, the other formal. Man possesses them from this point.</margin>
one by reason of his <term>genus|His biological nature as an animal.</term>, and the other by reason of his <term>species|His rational nature as a human being.</term>. Of these, the former is "material," while the second is "formal." And man thereafter possesses this unique quality among all bodily creatures: that after <term>nature was corrupted|The doctrine of Original Sin, which suggests human nature was damaged by the Fall of Man.</term>, these inclinations are contrary to each other. For as Paul says, 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
> The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. <note>original: "concupiscit aduersus spiritum : & spiritus aduersus carnem."</note>

But since that which is natural to a thing in an absolute sense is what agrees with it formally and according to its species; while that which belongs to it materially belongs...
<margin>What is meant by the absolute natural inclination of man.</margin>

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that suicide is a mortal sin because it violates a person's natural duty of self-love, harms the community, and usurps God’s sole authority over life and death. He also explores the tension between human biological urges and rational nature, explaining why resisting some "natural" inclinations is actually a virtuous necessity.</summary>

# Book Five, Question 1

->**On the Injustice of Suicide**<-

...seeks in a certain respect: that acting according to reason against a material—that is, a sensual—inclination pertains to the perfection of man. Therefore, when it is said that the natural inclination is directed toward the preservation of life, and that the love of life is natural, this is understood as being in accordance with reason. For this reason, to act against that inclination is a sin; it is not only inhuman, but truly against the entire foundation of nature. For it is clear that living is a rational inclination, because it is the nature of a rational being to attain happiness through the works of reason—and these works cannot be performed except by one who is living. ¶ After this, regarding the other two arguments, it should be explained how a man is not the master of his own life, unless this conclusion was sufficiently demonstrated by us in the previous book, Question 3. It is necessary, however, to recall what we also took care to demonstrate there: namely, that the state <note>original: "respublica"</note> does not properly possess dominion over the lives of its citizens in the same way God does. For a prince cannot, at his whim, drive an innocent person to death as God can—which would be necessary for the definition of absolute dominion. Rather, he acts only as the champion of the state and the guardian of justice, as was sufficiently explained there. Furthermore, the example of the "whole" in respect to its "parts" supports this. For a man does not exercise absolute dominion over his limbs such that he may cut them off whenever he pleases; rather, as a guardian of his life, he may put them at risk to defend the whole body, and likewise, when they are decaying, he may cut them away.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Thus, Aristotle is to be understood in the *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 11, where he says that a self-murderer <note>original: "homicidam sui"</note> inflicts an injury upon the state. A long dispute arises here as to whether it is permissible to condemn someone to kill himself—for instance, to drink poison, or to perish by hunger, or to not flee from prison. However, these matters have their proper place below in Question 6, where we must dispute extensively in Article 4 regarding the remedies a defendant may use.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
It remains, therefore, to resolve the remaining minor questions attached to this main one while addressing the arguments. To the first argument, the answer has already been given: namely, that homicide is a sin both against justice and against <term>charity|In this theological context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the supernatural love for God and self that orders a person toward their ultimate good.</term>. Therefore, he who brings death upon himself does not act against justice in respect to himself, but against charity; yet in respect to the state and to God, he acts against justice.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, which adds that a judge might simultaneously be worthy of death: The response is that no one is appointed as his own judge,

<column-break/>

because no one can judge himself rightly. Therefore, just as the cure of a sick doctor is not to be committed to himself, so neither should a criminal judge condemn himself.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
¶ To the third argument, St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s school of thought.</note> responds with what we remember citing in the preceding book: namely, that although man, being constituted through <term>free will|liberum arbitrium</term>, is the master of himself (that is, of his actions), he can dispose of all things that are subject to that same free will—but not of his life, which is subject only to the power of God, from whom he received it. And therefore, for no reason whatsoever is it permissible for anyone to take his own life.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
This is an argument that Augustine discusses most richly in *The City of God*, Book 1, from chapters 17 to 26.
<margin>Paul</margin>
Therefore, not even one who burns with that desire of Paul "to be dissolved and be with Christ" <note>A reference to Philippians 1:23.</note> can kill himself for that cause. Nor may we do so to escape the extreme calamities of this world.
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
For since, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the *Ethics*, Book 3, death is the ultimate of temporal evils, he who would deprive himself of life to lack other evils would then be choosing a greater evil against nature to avoid a lesser one. Neither can someone, struck by the greatest regret for a most monstrous crime, lay wicked hands upon himself to consume himself. Nor, indeed, is it permitted for the purpose of avoiding a most atrocious crime.
<margin>Lucretia</margin>
For this reason, it was not permissible for Lucretia <note>A legendary Roman figure who committed suicide after being raped by the son of the king; her story was a standard case study in medieval ethics.</note> to avoid adultery through the death she brought upon herself—and much less, after she suffered that injury, to cover her ignominy with death, as Livy reports in Book 1.
<margin>Augustine</margin>
As Augustine argues in that place: if by resisting she had freed herself from guilt, she was not worthy of killing herself; and if she had consented to the guilt, she was not her own judge. She therefore killed herself out of "faint-heartedness" <note>original: "pusillanimitate"</note>, because she could not bear the infamy;
<margin>Cato</margin>
just like Cato, who was not able to endure the rule of Caesar.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ But if you ask here in passing: what ought a modest girl endure before she consents to being ravished?
<margin>Solution.</margin>
In truth, any kind of death.
<margin>Another question.</margin>
But truly, if she does not fight back against it with all her strength and resist with her limbs, but remains motionless and does nothing, is she considered to have consented?
<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is: In the "external forum" <note>The public legal system or human courts.</note>, if she remained motionless and silent, she would be judged guilty of the debauchery. For so it was commanded in Deuteronomy 22: that a girl who was pressured in the city, because she remained silent, should be overwhelmed with stones. However, in the <term>forum of conscience|The internal "court" of a person's relationship with God, dealing with actual moral guilt rather than legal appearances.</term>, she is only bound not to consent, nor to accommodate herself to the crime. Therefore, if she is silent out of fear, she does not sin mortally, provided she offers no consent. Nor is she bound to lay hands upon the other. Nevertheless, she who is honorable and noble-minded...

Soto draws on the examples of biblical figures and early Christian martyrs to distinguish between sinful self-destruction and acts performed under divine inspiration or for the sake of virtue.</meta>

F. D. Soto, *On Justice and Right*,

...should not do as much as she *should*, but as much as she *can*. Moreover, what she suffers against her will, she does not lose her virginity; for, as Saint Lucy <note>Saint Lucy of Syracuse (d. 304), a martyr who famously argued that the soul’s purity remains intact if the body is violated without consent.</note> used to say, the body is not defiled except by the consent of the mind. Hence, a woman who would kill herself to avoid rape would be committing a greater sin to avoid a lesser one.

<margin>To the fourth argument: Samson.</margin>
¶ Regarding the fourth argument about Samson, there are those who respond that through the virtue of fortitude, it was permitted for him to gird himself for the destruction of his enemies at his own peril. However, to this we have already responded in Book 2, Question 3, Article 8, that since that deed was not human but supernatural—because his hair, which he had dedicated to God, had already grown back—it must be said instead, with Augustine, that he did it by divine revelation. This is testified by his prayer, in which he sought help from heaven.

<margin>Eleazar.</margin>
Regarding Eleazar, however, of whom we read in 1 Maccabees 6, that he was crushed by an elephant while killing it <note>Eleazar Avaran died during the Maccabean Revolt by stabbing an elephant he believed carried the enemy king, knowing the beast would fall and crush him.</note>, I would easily believe (as I said there) that he undertook this through the virtue and strength of his soul.

<margin>Razias. St. Thomas.</margin>
There is no reason to excuse Razias <note>A Jewish elder who committed a grisly suicide to avoid capture by Nicanor (2 Maccabees 14).</note>, as St. Thomas rightly says; for it was a softness and weakness of mind to prefer to die by his own sword rather than be defeated. This is also blamed in Saul and Cato. Therefore, when the history adds that "he chose to die nobly" (etc.), this is not said according to the truth of the matter, but according to his own estimation.

<margin>Apollonia. Augustine.</margin>
But regarding Apollonia, whose history recounts that she leaped into the flames, anticipating the work of the executioners, Augustine is not entirely certain. If, however, it were true, one must say either that she was already so close to the pyre that she was almost thrown in, or that since she was a woman and ignorant of the subtleties of the law, she is to be excused through invincible ignorance <note>term: "invincible ignorance" (Latin: *ignorantia invincibilis*)—a theological concept describing a lack of knowledge for which a person is not morally responsible.</note>; or, with the same Augustine, we must fall back on the explanation that she did it by divine instinct.

### ARTICLE VI.
#### *Whether it is permissible to expose one's life in defense of a friend or of any virtue.*

<margin>First argument on the negative side.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring stylized foliage and vine motifs.</image-desc>
After the immediately preceding article, we deemed it worthwhile to add this sixth one, even though St. Thomas passed over it here in silence. For they are very closely related and like siblings. It is asked, therefore, whether it is permissible to offer one's own life to death for a friend or for any virtue. For the argument is made on the negative side. To expose one's life to the danger of death amounts to the same thing as if one were to kill oneself; for a pilot not saving a ship when he can is the same as if he were sinking it. But no one is permitted to kill himself, since he is not the master of his life, but its guardian; therefore, neither may he expose his life for another.

<margin>Arg. 2. Augustine.</margin>
¶ Second: in the order of charity, everyone is bound to love himself more than another; at least it is not permitted to love another *more*, since God commands us to love our neighbors as ourselves. But whoever exposes his own life for the life of a friend loves the other more than himself, as Augustine argues in his book *On Lying* <note>original: "lib. de mend. cap. 6." refers to *De mendacio*.</note>, chapter 6. Therefore, this is not permitted, as he concludes in the same place.

<margin>Arg. 3.</margin>
¶ Third: just as spiritual life relates to spiritual life, so temporal life relates to temporal life. But no one is permitted to lose his own spiritual life for the spiritual life of the whole world; therefore, neither should one lose his own temporal life for the temporal life of a friend.

¶ On the contrary is the word of Christ in John 15: "No one has greater love than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
**T**his is an excellent question, worthy not only of philosophers but also of theologians, though I have not seen it formally disputed according to its importance. I have decided, therefore, that it should be resolved with three conclusions. The first is: Catholic faith commands one to lay down his life for God and in testimony of his faith; the opposite assertion of which is manifest heresy. This is clear from the testimony of the Church, which so honors the order of martyrs (as the most prominent among two orders) for this principal virtue, that it considers all sins to be forgiven through the act of martyrdom. It does not pertain to the present place to dispute this. But we add to this same conclusion that it is likewise permissible for the protection of any virtue. For this reason, John the Baptist is included in the catalog of martyrs, because he rebuked the incestuous Herod for his iniquity. And not only in defense of the commandments, but even to defend the truth of the counsels would it be praiseworthy—for instance, if someone were to defend the fact that taking religious vows is a counsel <note>term: "counsel" (Latin: *consilium*)—in Catholic theology, a "counsel of perfection" (like poverty or chastity) is a recommendation rather than a strict commandment.</note>. For all these things relate to the guardianship and defense of the faith. Nor is there anyone who can deny that it is permissible to undergo the danger of death for the republic <note>original: "respublica" - meaning the state or the common good.</note>; since, as we have often said before, the republic can compel its citizens to this, just as the whole can compel its members for its own defense. Therefore, let these foundations be laid without dispute.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ But so that we may reconcile the other extreme, which is also very obvious, with this very point, the second conclusion follows...

<summary>Soto analyzes the "suicides" of biblical and historical figures like Samson and Razias, arguing that true sacrifice requires divine inspiration or a virtuous cause. He then introduces the question of whether a person may licitly risk their life for a friend or the common good, concluding that laying down one's life for God or the state is a high virtue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ethics of self-sacrifice. Having previously discussed whether one can take their own life to avoid sin or shame (using the examples of Samson and Eleazar), Soto now moves to the hierarchy of values: comparing the preservation of one’s own soul (spiritual life) against the physical and spiritual needs of others.</meta>

### Book Five, Question 1.

**The second conclusion.** It is in no way permitted either to lose spiritual life—that is, the grace of God—or to suffer even the slightest loss of it, even for the spiritual salvation of the entire world. Indeed, if—pardon the blasphemy of the word—such a case could impossibly occur, it would not be permitted even to defend the glory of the saints. I remember that some have called this into doubt; nonetheless, the conclusion is so self-evident that the contrary involves a manifest contradiction. For truly, to wish to fall from God’s grace so that others may persist in it is to choose to be in the hatred of God; but to claim that this is a virtue is a contradiction in terms. For if something is a virtue, it is lawful; but through that which is lawful, grace is not lost. Likewise, to desire the hatred of God is to desire that which is <term>intrinsically evil</term> <note>Something that is wrong by its very nature, regardless of the circumstances or intent.</note>. Indeed, even to admit the smallest <term>venial sin</term> <note>In Catholic theology, a "venial" sin is a minor offense that does not break one’s relationship with God, as opposed to a "mortal" sin.</note> for the spiritual salvation of the whole world involves a contradiction. Furthermore, it cannot be lawful to wish to be loved less by God so that others may be loved more; for he who is loved less, loves less. To wish to love less is to wish for something against the very nature of <term>charity</term> <note>Original: *charitas*. In this context, it refers to the theological virtue of selfless, divine love.</note>; and thus, to claim that such an act is a work of charity is a contradiction.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, an argument is made against this truth. It would seem to follow that it is not lawful to put one's spiritual life at risk for the salvation of souls; for if it is never lawful to lose it, it seems to follow that one should not undergo the danger of losing it. Yet the consequence is false: for the "prudent charity" of servants sometimes encourages a man to approach and speak with fallen women to convert them, despite some risk to himself, or to go somewhere to preach where he will face a greater danger to his spiritual life than if he kept himself within the cloisters of a monastery.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is that the first consequence is of no value. For to suffer the loss of grace is a detriment to charity itself; but to expose it to danger is so far from being a weakening of charity that it actually proceeds from the great fervor of it.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let the third conclusion, for the exploration of which the present question is moved, be this: It is lawful, and very often a duty, to expose one's physical life, not only for the spiritual life of a friend, but even for their temporal life; indeed, even for their honor, their reputation, and their temporal goods. On this question, however, the Divine

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine has spoken in various ways. In the place cited during the argument, he seemed to lean toward the negative side. However, in his book *On Friendship*, chapter 10, he expressly says that the life of the body must be laid down for a friend, as, he says, divine author-

<column-break/>

ity has decreed. Doubtless he is alluding to the word of Christ cited by us:
> "Greater love has no man than this." etc.
<margin>"Greater love has no man than this." etc.</margin>
And in truth, it could never come into doubt for me, but that I certainly believed this to be the highest praise of friendship, and consequently a duty of virtue. First, the authority of Christ, if weighed meditatively, clearly carries this sense; even if there are those who, quibbling, say our Savior taught only that it is lawful to expose physical life for the *spiritual* life of a friend, just as He himself did. Indeed, although He cited it for that purpose, that saying was nonetheless commonly circulated among the philosophers, teaching everywhere that:
> "A friend is another self." <note>original: *Amicus est alter ego.* A famous classical definition of friendship often attributed to Pythagoras or Aristotle.</note>
Therefore, their meaning did not refer to spiritual life, but to the fact that the law of friendship allows one to defend the good of a friend—even temporal goods—at the risk of one's own life. Wherefore Christ, alleging a common axiom, approved the same sense: namely, that while it is charity to suffer the loss of other goods for a friend’s sake, the pinnacle is that you would even lay down your life.

<margin>Christ for our life.</margin>
¶ Add that Christ laid down His own life for our temporal life. For just as through sin, as Paul says, death entered the world, so too it was the office of the Redeemer, by liberating us from sin, to liberate us also from temporal death by giving us immortal bodies. For this reason, in the same chapter 5, Paul concludes: just as sin reigned unto death, so also grace reigns through justice unto eternal life. And in chapter 8: "The law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death."

¶ Furthermore, by that word, Christ wished to win the friendship of mortals to Himself as much as possible. For that reason, He cited it absolutely and without exception: namely, that charity is shown most in this, that one lays down his life for his friends. For He does not say "for this or that good" of the friend, but "for the friend," whenever your own life is required.

¶ But to descend to natural reasons, the one that is usually brought forward is not firm enough. For they argue that it is lawful to expose one's life for a friend because it is just to lay it down for virtue and true praise, and laying down one's life for a friend is a virtue. But this reason <term>begs the question</term> <note>A logical fallacy where the premise assumes the truth of the conclusion it is trying to prove.</note>, for this is exactly what is in controversy. Friendship, after all, is not itself a virtue, but is "close to virtue," as is said in Book 8 of the *Ethics*.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
The Philosopher <note>A common medieval and Renaissance title for Aristotle.</note> says:
> "For I am a friend to another because he is virtuous."
But the question is this: whether the law of friendship permits you to expose a life of which you are not the master for the sake of another. Especially since life is the greatest of all temporal goods, and friendship...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "citia," the end of "amicitia" (friendship).</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the hierarchy of sacrifice, concluding that while one must never sin or lose God's grace to save another, it is a virtuous duty to risk or sacrifice one's physical life for the sake of a friend's well-being, following the example of Christ and the principles of classical friendship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether it is lawful for a person to sacrifice their own physical life for the sake of another, building on the distinction between spiritual and temporal goods.</meta>

### Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>An effective reasoning for the conclusion.</margin>
Since friendship is only a temporal good, it might seem that life should not be exchanged for it. Therefore, the reasoning for the conclusion is formed in this way: Our life is higher than any particular temporal good, for it is not the supreme end in which our happiness consists, but is only a means to attain and preserve it. However, it is lawful to expose a useful good in defense of another good that is a part of our happiness, even if, considered by itself, it were of lesser value. For anyone may, by the best right, place their life in danger to defend their temporal goods, because those goods are themselves ordered toward the preservation of that same life and toward its happy state. Now, the life of my friend is my own proper good, pertaining also to my happiness; therefore, by the same reasoning, it will be permitted to me—indeed, it is much more becoming—to lay down my own life for it. For I rightly value that life more than my own external goods, since through my friend I preserve a happy state with myself. Indeed, by the same reasoning, it follows that I can expose my life to protect a friend’s honor and temporal goods, provided they are sufficiently great. ¶ Second, this is argued by the example of Christ. For it is certain that his life, even the temporal one, was more excellent than our spiritual life—for it was the life of God <note>original: *vita Dei*</note>, through which a man was truly God—and yet, because our eternal life redounded to his glory, he spent his life as the price for ours. ¶ Third, it is argued that by the law of nature, we are all mortal members of the same body. Therefore, just as one member of the same body is exposed for another so that they may mutually guard each other, so it is lawful among men. ¶ Fourth, just as it is a duty to lay down one's life for the republic because we are its parts—which we are therefore bound to preserve—so too a part can expose itself to the danger of another part, since the safety of the republic consists in the safety of its parts. ¶ Add to this that to deny that a son ought to protect his father's life at the risk of his own would surely be a form of ferocity and barbarism, since we received this very life from our parents. Therefore, once it is granted that this is lawful by the right of <term>charity</term> <note>Christian love or *caritas*, which seeks the good of the other.</note>, it is not a difficult step to conclude that it is also lawful for a wife, for a son, for a father, and even for a friend. For regarding a king, no one doubts it.

<margin>The memorable deed of Pylades and Orestes.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, there is no philosopher or wise student of nature who does not praise the deed of Pylades and Orestes <note>In Greek mythology, Pylades and Orestes were famous friends; when one was sentenced to death, the other tried to take his place.</note>, whether the story be historical or a fable, as Cicero suggests in his book *On Friendship*. Although to lie so that one might be taken for the other was not a virtue, the sacrifice itself was. ¶ But why do we linger

<column-break/>

<margin>The voice of the people is the voice of nature.</margin>
on a matter that is not in doubt? The voice of the people is the voice of nature <note>original: *vox populi, vox naturae*</note>. And yet there has been no nation, whether barbarian or holy—even if you mean a Christian one—in which it was not, and is not, given extraordinary praise that someone who sees a person cast into the danger of death should offer themselves to the same danger to snatch away the neighbor's life, as long as it appears possible. "As long as it appears possible," I say, for otherwise, it would be rashness. For example: someone who watches people attacking each other with swords, and being able to settle the quarrel with some danger to himself, does not interpose himself (even if he is not strictly bound to do so), is surely regarded as cowardly and infamous. It is so far from being judged that he acted wrongly if he did intervene. And the judgment is almost the same regarding the protection of a friend's honor and other great goods by which his life and honor are sustained. In short, whoever denies that this is an outstanding duty of friendship surely removes its chief ornament from the midst of the republic.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is denied that laying down one’s life for a friend is the same as killing oneself. For we have already said above that the killing of oneself happens in two ways.

<margin>Killing oneself happens in two ways.</margin>
In one way, directly and by itself <note>original: *directè & per se*</note>: and this is never permitted, neither for a friend nor for virtue itself. For a martyr could not strangle himself for the faith. In the other way, it happens <term>accidentally</term> <note>original: *per accidens*; an indirect consequence of an action intended for another purpose.</note>: namely, when someone does not preserve their own life when they are able to preserve it. This is not considered homicide except insofar as one is bound to preserve it.

<margin>How we are held to preserve life.</margin>
And although man is not the master of his own life, but its guardian, he is nonetheless not bound to preserve it by every possible means. Indeed, as we have said, he can expose it not only for virtue but also for temporal goods. Furthermore, he can even choose not to use the best food and regimen, or the best medicine, to preserve it. By the same reasoning, therefore, he can expose it for a friend. But he would sin if he were to squander it—that is, if he were to spend it for no good end or for a trivial one, such as if he were to object it to danger to defend the value of a single coin.

<margin>A scruple.</margin>
¶ From this solution, however, a <term>scruple</term> <note>A point of moral doubt or difficulty.</note> arises: whether in a shipwreck, where there is only one plank that cannot save two people, it is lawful for one to yield to the other. And suppose it is a son and a father. From the conclusion, it seems to follow that it is lawful; however, from this solution, the opposite appears to be gathered. For he who would abandon the plank would be doing the same as if he threw himself into the sea, which is to kill oneself directly. Truly, the matter is doubtful. It is answered...

# Book Five, Question I.

Therefore, the response is that before the son takes hold of the plank <note>The "Plank of Carneades" is a classic ethical dilemma where two shipwrecked men find a plank that can only support one; here, the author discusses a son giving it up for his father.</note>, he may leave it for his father. This is because doing so is not "positively" killing himself, but rather "permitting" himself to die. However, once he is already seated upon it, it does not truly seem lawful for him to cast himself into the waves. <margin>Response to the second argument.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, the response is that the "order of charity"—by which a person is bound to love their neighbor no more than themselves—must be understood in terms of the spiritual life. For the sake of spiritual life, a person ought not to suffer harm even for the sake of the whole world. However, regarding temporal matters <note>Physical life and worldly goods.</note>, that order is not strictly necessary, since temporal things do not, in themselves, belong to perfect happiness but are merely means, as we have said. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> Hence, St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 26, Article 5.</note>, in the solution to the first point, says that since each thing is defined by what is primary within it, the neighbor is to be loved more regarding spiritual matters than one's own body. For example, if our own physical life were simply necessary for the neighbor's spiritual salvation, then it should be spent for them. Here, he explains the order that exists by the necessity of the commandment. Yet later, in the solution to the third point, he says that although it is not a "necessity" of charity for a man to expose his own body for the salvation of his neighbor (unless he is specifically bound to provide for their safety), nevertheless, if someone offers themselves for this spontaneously, it pertains to the "perfection" of charity. In this passage, he does not distinguish between spiritual and corporal salvation, but seems to include both. <margin>Response to the third argument.</margin> ¶ Finally, the last argument was resolved when we demonstrated that the reasoning for spiritual and temporal salvation is not the same. Therefore, it is false to claim that the relationship between one spiritual good and another is the same as the relationship between one temporal good and another.

### ARTICLE VII.

->*Whether it is lawful in any case to kill an innocent person.*<-

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter P containing a woodcut illustration of a person seated at a desk within a room.</image-desc>
AFTER the discussion of the homicide of the guilty, which we described as being performed according to the law, there follows in this seventh article (which is the sixth in the writings of St. Thomas) a dispute over whether it is lawful in any case to kill an innocent person. For arguments are made for the affirmative side. Abraham is praised among other things for the fact that he had destined his innocent little son for the altar. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second: if that which brings a greater harm is permitted, then that which brings a lesser harm will also be permitted; for the gravity of a sin is judged by the harm inflicted.

<column-break/>

Now, it is permitted to kill a sinner, even if they are sometimes exposed to the danger of eternal damnation, as was said above. Therefore, it should also be permitted to kill an innocent person, who is believed with more certainty to fly toward eternal happiness once released from the miseries of this world. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third: that which is done according to the order of justice is no sin. But sometimes a judge, according to the evidence presented and proven, is compelled to sentence an innocent person to death, knowing they were accused by false testimony; and likewise, the executioner who is bound to obey his command. Therefore, it is sometimes lawful to kill an innocent person. ¶ On the contrary, however, is that which is written in Exodus 23: "The innocent and the just you shall not kill."

<margin>The title of the question is illustrated.</margin>
<margin>Two types of innocent persons.</margin>
<margin>A single conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Proof.</margin>
THE title of the question can be understood as referring to two types of innocent persons. First, one who is not only innocent in reality, but also legally, because they have not been proven guilty; it is about this person that the present inquiry is understood. The other is one who, although innocent in reality, is legally proven guilty; concerning this person—since the reason for doubting is weightier and more obscure—a specific question will be raised later in Question 4, Article 2. This current matter is very easily settled by a single conclusion: It is in no way lawful to kill an innocent person against whom there is no unfavorable opinion. The proof is straightforward. For a man, as is clear from what has been said, is considered both in himself and furthermore in relation to the common good. Regarding the first consideration—namely, insofar as he is of a rational nature—it is lawful to kill no one. For even the nature of the most wicked sinner, insofar as it is a creation of God, must be loved. Therefore, a sinner is killed only for the sake of the common good. In the case of an innocent person, however, there is no reason why the state should have the right to kill them, since they are a primary part of the state and contribute most especially to its welfare. <margin>Demosthenes.</margin> ¶ There is no reason why you should doubt much regarding this conclusion; nevertheless, some reasons for doubt, though slight, are offered. The first is when an innocent citizen is in a city besieged by a tyrant, and that tyrant demands his head, perhaps because the citizen is his adversary. There is a history concerning Demosthenes <note>The famous Athenian orator who opposed Philip II of Macedon.</note> who, while the city of Athens was oppressed by siege, the enemy general sought only him, promising to leave the city unharmed. Then Demosthenes related to the senate that fable of the wolves who demanded the dogs from the sheep, using that trickery so that they could later rush upon the unarmed and trembling flock. The doubt, therefore, is whether it would have then been lawful, for the safety of the entire state, to hand over the innocent man into the hands of the enemy to be destroyed...

...to be handed over. For it appears to have been lawful. First, because the state <note>original: "respublica"</note> has the right to expose citizens to certain death for the safety of the whole: as is evident in war: just as the whole has rights over its parts. Then, because the person who is then innocent, by whose death the safety of the entire city is at stake, is bound to surrender himself to the enemy: therefore the state can compel him to do so. Nevertheless, it is answered that this is by no means lawful then.

<margin>The Solution. St. Thomas.</margin>
Wherefore St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto's commentary.</note> established a general conclusion. For, to respond to the first argument, the state can then expose a citizen when he is necessary for fighting and resisting the enemy: because then he is a necessary means in himself <note>A direct participant in the common defense.</note>: but not when he is only "necessary" due to the malice of another. Since homicide is not good in its own right, it is never lawful except for an end for which it is a necessary means in itself. And the death of an innocent is never necessary for the state in this way. Wherefore, just as we mentioned a little earlier, it is not lawful for you—at the command of a tyrant—to pluck out one of your own eyes to save the other: so too it is not then lawful for the state to hand over an innocent to death. For, as was said above, the state is not the absolute master of the lives of citizens, as God is: and therefore God alone has power over the life of an innocent person. ¶ There are those who, although they disagree that the state can kill him at the tyrant's command, nevertheless confess that it can hand him over to be killed. Furthermore, both are exactly the same: and thus neither is lawful. It could, nonetheless, in that case, not defend him: because the state is not bound to defend a private citizen at its own peril.

<margin>Objection by similarity.</margin>
¶ But if you argue to the contrary by similarity: If someone threatened me with death unless I offered my hand or tongue to be cut off, I could hand over the limb to save my life: even though that means is not necessary except through the malice of another: therefore, similarly, the state could hand over its citizen.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
The consequence is denied: because a limb does not have an existence distinct from the existence of the whole: nor is it in any way for its own sake, but for the sake of the whole: nor is it capable of rights or injury in itself. A human being, however, although he is a part of the state, is nonetheless also an individual being <note>original: "suppositum," a technical term for a distinct, self-subsisting individual.</note> existing for his own sake, and thus capable of injury in himself, which the state cannot inflict upon him.

<margin>The arguments raised to the contrary are resolved.</margin>
¶ Whence, in response to the second argument raised above, it is answered that although he himself may then be bound to offer himself to danger to protect the public: nevertheless, he cannot be legally compelled to it: because he is bound not by justice, but by charity. Just as it stands that I am bound in grave necessity to give alms, to which I cannot be compelled.

<column-break/>

<margin>A second scruple.</margin>
¶ Another case of doubt is in war: and indeed in a general assault, where the innocent are mixed with the guilty: there is no doubt that it is lawful to attack the enemies, even with danger to the innocent. But the doubt is in singular combat. I see a soldier rushing at me whom I know to be innocent: for instance, one who certainly believes he is waging a just war against me. Reason seems to suggest that I cannot then kill him. For a war cannot be just on both sides. If therefore he fights justly against me, I cannot justly defend myself.

<margin>The doubt is removed.</margin>
It is answered that it is nonetheless lawful. First, because we can both fight justly out of ignorance, when each thinks he is defending a just cause. Furthermore, although it might then be clear to one of the soldiers in the conflict that justice stands on the other's side, he can defend himself: because he is not bound to suffer that death. Wherefore, not only then out of false presumption (as some say)—namely, because each thinks the other is guilty—but even if he knows he is innocent, he may then fight. He could not, however, kill the other except in his own defense.

<margin>A third scruple.</margin>
But you ask whether a soldier can attack another whom he knows to be innocent. It is answered that if he believes in good faith that he is waging a just war, even if he thinks the other is innocent—for instance, because he either believes this himself or is held in the army against his will—he can attack him: both because the attack itself in war is defense, and also because one prince has the right to attack another. But a soldier who believes he is waging an unjust war could not attack.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument to the contrary, a sufficient answer was given in Book 2, Question 3, Article 8. For God—not as a legislator, as Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a 13th-century theologian who often debated the nature of divine law.</note> thinks—is able to grant a dispensation over homicide: but as the universal master of life, He can grant anyone the power to kill another: just as He did for Abraham: whose obedience was therefore worthy of praise. Although, in His mercy, He did not allow it to be carried out. No mortal, however, uses this absolute mastery over life.

<margin>To the second argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ The solution to the second argument should be noted in St. Thomas: namely, that the gravity of sins is to be considered primarily in themselves, not according to the harm inflicted, but according to the object. Therefore, the killing of an innocent person is more wicked and worthy of greater punishment than the killing of an impure and lost man. First, because a killer of this kind harms a more excellent good, which is more to be loved for its own sake:

Second, because an injury is done to one who was less deserving of it; and thus, it violates justice more wickedly. And third, because it deprives the republic <note>original: "rempublicam"</note> of a greater good, and consequently is more poisonous to the common good. ### ARTICLE VIII.

->Whether it is a right proper to every individual to kill an attacker in their own defense.<-

Since it was defined above that no one is permitted by private authority to kill a wrongdoer, it remains to be investigated whether it is at least permitted to kill an aggressor by way of defense. For there are several authorities among the Saints <note>Refers to the Church Fathers, specifically Augustine.</note> who seem to forbid this.

<margin>
The first argument from the negative side.
2114.
Indeed, Augustine says to Publicola: "Regarding the killing of men so that one is not killed by them, the idea does not please me, unless perhaps one is a soldier or held by a public office, so that he does this not for himself, but for others, having received legitimate power." Here he seems to deny that it is permitted for anyone to kill privately to avoid being killed.
</margin>
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ And in Book 1 of *On Free Will*: "How," he says, "are they free from sin in the eyes of divine providence who are defiled by human slaughter for the sake of those things which ought to be held in contempt?" And he considers all those things which men can lose against their will to be held in contempt, among which is life.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ And Pope Nicholas, in the canon regarding those clerics <note>Distinction 50.</note>, says: "Regarding those clerics about whom you consulted, namely those who had killed a pagan <note>original: "paganum"</note> while defending themselves—whether they can later return to their former status or ascend to a higher one through penance—know that we give no occasion, nor do we grant any license to them to kill any man in any way." Since this law pertains to morals, it seems that laypeople are also subject to it.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourth. Homicide is more serious than simple fornication: but it is permitted to no one to commit fornication to preserve their life: therefore, neither is it permitted to commit homicide.

<margin>Argument 5.</margin>
¶ Finally. If a tree is

<column-break/>

bad, then so is the fruit, as is held in Matthew 7. But defense itself seems illicit according to that admonition of Paul to the Romans, chapter 12: "Do not defend yourselves, most beloved" <note>original: "Non vos defendentes chariffimi"</note>: therefore, the killing of an attacker was even worse.

¶ On the contrary, however, is that passage in Exodus 22: "If a thief is found breaking in or digging under, and dies from a wound received, the striker shall not be guilty of blood." It is therefore permitted, by even more equitable reasoning, to defend one's own life even to the death of the invader.

To the question, a response is given in three conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First. It is permitted to no one to kill an attacker unless it was a necessary means: namely, if he cannot defend himself in any other way.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second. Where that means was necessary, it is lawful—repelling force with force according to the law, with the moderation of blameless defense <term>inculpatæ tutelę: a legal standard requiring that the force used in self-defense must be proportional and only as much as is necessary to stop the threat.</term>—to kill him. Both conclusions are proved at once. For their proof, it is presupposed that it can happen that two effects exist from one action: one of which is produced from the intention of the agent, while the other happens outside of his intention. Just as when someone, digging to plant a vine, finds a treasure. Moreover, moral acts derive their classification <note>original: "speciem"</note> from that which existed in the intention and purpose of the agent; but from that which is accidental, they receive no praise or blame. For instance, if a hunter, intending to direct an arrow at a wild beast, should pierce a man, he is not to be judged a murderer. To our purpose, therefore: where someone defends himself, two effects are to be considered, namely the preservation of one's own life and the destruction of another's. The former was intended, but the latter was accidental. That effect which is primary <note>original: "per se"</note>, from which the action derives its classification, has no character of an illicit thing; for since this is a natural right proper to everyone, the action is in no way corrupted by it. Furthermore, it cannot be corrupted by the accidental effect which followed from that end, except where that means did not have a legitimate proportion to the end—that is, it was not necessary. Therefore, both conclusions follow from the same syllogism: namely, that where that means was not necessary, the killing was unjust; but where it was necessary, it was nothing but lawful. For since everyone is more bound to care for their own life than for another's, no one is bound to yield their right so as to prefer another's life to their own.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion. No one is permitted by private authority to kill a man *intentionally*, so as [to save] their own...
