preserves life: but that task belongs only to **public power**, which directs such a killing toward the public good; this is evident in a prince declaring war on another, or in an officer capturing a wrongdoer. This is proven because killing another *by intention* is reserved for public power alone for the sake of preserving the common good.

¶ Here, it must first be noted that the **second conclusion**, which is the primary focus of this question, lies at the heart of **natural law**. Hence, in the first distinction of the *Decretum* <note>A collection of canon law</note>, under the heading of natural law, the "repelling of violence by force" is included. This is also clear in the *Digest* <note>A compendium of Roman law</note> under the title "On Force and Armed Force," and "On Justice and Law," where the jurist Florentinus says: "By this law, it occurs that whatever anyone does for the protection of their own body is deemed to have been done lawfully." Also, in the section "On Injuries," it is stated that the execution of the law does not constitute an injury. Therefore, since everyone has the right to defend themselves, they commit no injury to anyone in doing so. In summary, in the chapters *Significasti* and *Si vero* <note>References to specific legal rulings in the Decretals</note>, it is said: "Laws and all rights permit one to repel force with force." And in the *Digest* regarding the Aquilian Law, it is expressly held that someone who kills another who is attacking them with a blade is not seen to have killed unjustly. Indeed, it is so natural for any thing to exist that it immediately reacts against whatever might harm it.

<margin>Several conclusions are declared. St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ However, the explanation of these conclusions requires us to begin with the **third** one. For a doubt immediately arises: what did **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> mean when he said that it is permitted to no one to kill a man *by intention* in order to defend oneself? It seems he is denying that this means is lawful, and thus he would seem to contradict himself. For if he means this when killing is *not* necessary, he had already taught that in the first conclusion, making this a useless repetition. But if he means when it *is* necessary, he had said the opposite in the second conclusion.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
¶ The solution to this offered by **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio, a 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note>, unless explained further, presents a certain "metaphysical obscurity." He says that it is permitted for anyone to kill an enemy to defend themselves, but not so that the killing is chosen as the *means*, in the same way a doctor intentionally provides a medicine to achieve health. And this is what is asserted in the third conclusion. Instead, the killing should be an *effect* of the defense: just as the weakness of a sick person is not in the doctor's intention, but is an effect of the cure that follows beyond his intention.

<margin>Cajetan is challenged.</margin>
¶ However, unless this rule is read acutely, many will be deceived. For it is argued to the contrary: it is lawful for the person being invaded, when they see they cannot otherwise escape the hands of the attacker, to aim a spear directly at the attacker's throat *by intention* so that they might strike them down first. Therefore, the rule is false. The premise is clear.

<column-break/>

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For **Aristotle** teaches in the 6th book of the *Ethics* that for an effective will of the "end" <note>the goal</note>, the choice of the "means" (which is judged necessary) follows just as surely as a conclusion follows from premises in logic. Now, a person can lawfully desire that end <note>self-preservation</note>, which they rightly judge they cannot otherwise attain; therefore, they may also choose that means. You may find some even among our own thinkers who deny all this before they will grant that in a conflict, the person being attacked may choose the death of the other. But surely, if the defense is lawful and that means is judged necessary, I do not know why it would not be lawful to direct one's sword straight at the enemy's throat. Indeed, one who sees an enemy heading straight for them with a drawn sword, and fears they cannot defend themselves in hand-to-hand combat, may strike them down with an arrow shot from a distance, or with a bullet <note>original: "globulo"</note>. For this is defense with the **moderation of blameless protection** <term>inculpatae tutelae: a legal standard meaning one used only the force necessary for safety</term>.

<margin>The mind of St. Thomas is clear.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the meaning of **St. Thomas** is clear and entirely physical: he judges that a homicide is done "by intention" for the sake of defense only when someone attacks another by striking first—either to avenge a past injury or to prevent a future one. And for this reason, he says perfectly in the third conclusion that such a thing is only permitted to **public power**, either through war regarding external enemies, or through the execution of justice regarding dangerous citizens, through whose punishment the republic defends itself. In those cases, it is properly considered choosing a "means" to that "end," which is indeed not permitted to a private person. 

But truly, when someone is being attacked, then in whatever way they kill the attacker in blameless defense—suppose because they see they cannot otherwise escape their hands—even if they aim an arrow or another missile directly at the throat or the heart, they are considered not to "intend" the death, but only their own defense. 

<margin>St. Thomas is always consistent with himself.</margin>
And in this sense, it can well be maintained that the killing is not the *means*, but the *effect* of preservation. Although in common speech it is also rightly called a "means," and St. Thomas uses that same name in the first and second conclusions.

<margin>Blameless protection.</margin>
¶ However, regarding the "moderation of protection," one might also doubt what exactly is required for it to be "blameless." For there are those who say that the person being attacked must use the highest judgment to see if they can defend themselves in any way other than by inflicting death—namely, either by fleeing, or by pleading for peace, or by striking the enemy lightly, before it is permitted to pierce them through. But truly, although it is true that these things should be taken into account if it can be done conveniently, yet no reason commands that we bind a person struggling in a life-and-death conflict to such a difficult obligation; primarily because the condition of the person [being attacked] is better...

<margin>Objection against the third conclusion.</margin>
Nevertheless, there exists an argument against the third ambiguous conclusion. It appears, I say, that it is permissible for a private person to kill an enemy, even by choosing it as a means: namely, by anticipating and attacking him. This was denied in the third conclusion. Let us imagine, for instance, a person who is harassed by enemies and is shut up in some small town from which he cannot possibly escape, or in the same house where his enemy is. It is absolutely certain, without any doubt, that this enemy has decreed to kill him, but is waiting for the right hour, or for his companions, or for some other imminent opportunity. It appears that such a wretched person could anticipate the other and, while the enemy is off-guard, overpower him. Or suppose an innocent woman lying in the same bed with her husband knows clearly that he has hidden a sword under the pillow to slit her throat while she sleeps; no other escape is open to the poor woman. Could she not secretly seize the same sword and "finish the story" first? Truly, this is a doubtful matter.

<margin>Resolution.</margin>
To this, no other answer can be given than that as long as that act is "aggression," it is in no way permitted. If, however, it is "defense," there is no reason for it to be condemned. Whether it is one or the other is not to be defined by law or science, but must be judged by the decision of a prudent person in whatever case arises. This serves to quiet consciences after the deed. However, this license should not be preached in public, lest the unrefined masses, who do not know how to discern when it is aggression and when it is truly defense, expand it through abuse.

<margin>Argument against the second conclusion.</margin>
But indeed, against the second conclusion, an argument of this sort exists. The necessary **order of charity** <note>A theological concept (Latin: *ordo charitatis*) describing the priority of whom and what we should love; usually, the soul's salvation is ranked above physical life.</note> requires, as we were just saying, that one prefer the spiritual life of a neighbor to one's own physical life. Since the spiritual is not only more perfect, but is the very end to which temporal life is directed. Whoever attacks another with force by private authority is in mortal sin, because that is permitted to no one. Therefore, the same order of charity binds the other to permit himself to be killed sooner than to thrust the attacker into hell; and thus, it is in no way permitted to kill him. This is an argument that compels not only many amateur scholars to believe its conclusion, but even Gerson,

<column-break/>

<margin>Gerson.</margin>
an otherwise serious author <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a famous French theologian and reformer.</note>, who in his treatise *On the Eucharist* treats this as an established fact. But truly, this would be not only to pervert natural law, but also to make Christ’s yoke—which is sweet and light—bitter and unbearable. For what justice would there be in a law that forced subjects to give the life that mortals value so much as a gift to anyone’s recklessness and audacity? If a tyrant urged me toward evil, I ought to lay down my life for the sake of virtue; but that I should be forced to permit anyone who wishes to kill me most unjustly to do so would be an intolerable thing. Indeed, I am not only not forced to give him my life, but neither my honor, nor my reputation, nor my goods. Suppose, for example, there is an impure and stubborn man who swears that unless I give him a weight of gold, he will commit some grave crime; am I therefore bound to grant him his request? Not in the least.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>When the law of charity obliges.</margin>
Regarding the argument, therefore, it is granted that by the order of charity, the spiritual salvation of a neighbor is to be loved more than our temporal life. However, this law of charity only obliges us when my temporal life is **absolutely necessary** for that spiritual salvation; in such a case, I ought to offer it to danger. For example: if a certain city or person suffers from a "conquerable ignorance" <note>Ignorance that can be corrected with effort or instruction.</note> which I alone can remove, I certainly ought, by the order of charity, to reveal the truth even at the risk of my life. Likewise, if it falls to me by office. For in a time of plague, a prelate is bound, and in a time of war, a prince is bound, not to desert the people: because in this second case, not only charity but also justice concurs. But where my life is not necessary, but they themselves know they are acting wickedly and can stop, and by their own fault do not stop: I am not bound. Though, at times, it might pertain to the "perfection of charity."

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
And this is expressly taught by Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> in the place most recently cited, in the solution to the 3rd point, and in question 25, article 8. He says that although love of the enemy is necessary "in the preparation of the soul" <note>original: *in præparatione animi*; meaning one must always be willing to love them if the situation requires it</note> when necessity occurs, nevertheless, outside of such necessity, loving an enemy is only a matter of the perfection of charity. To descend to the point at hand, therefore: he who attacks me privately with armed force does so by his own fault; therefore, my life is not "necessary" for him, and thus I am not bound to succumb to him. Otherwise, an occasion would be provided for wicked men to attack the just, precisely because they would be certain that they would not be killed by them. With similar audacity, the enemies of the **Maccabees** <note>Jewish rebels in the 2nd century BCE who were initially slaughtered because they refused to fight on the Sabbath.</note> attacked them on the Sabbaths,

<summary>This page discusses the morality of preemptive self-defense and refutes the argument that the "order of charity" requires a victim to allow themselves to be killed to save the attacker's soul from damnation. Soto concludes that while one must value souls, one is not legally or morally obligated to sacrifice their own life for an aggressor who chooses to sin.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

...they were being slaughtered, believing that they could not fight at that time. <margin>1 Maccabees, chapter 2.</margin>Therefore, as we read in 1 Maccabees chapter 2, they decreed even on those holy days to defend themselves with arms. It does not follow, then, that because "I am bound to love the spiritual salvation of my neighbor more than my own physical safety," I am therefore bound to preserve his life more than my own outside of a case of absolute necessity. For to every person is mandated the care of their own life and their own goods, but not the care of others', even if those others are more precious. Just as a father is bound to save his own son more than a stranger who is far better. <margin>When it becomes necessary to kill an aggressor.</margin>

¶ So far we have spoken concerning the freedom a person has to defend themselves. Regarding the necessity, however—that is, whether everyone is *bound* to do so—it is doubted by some. Indeed, there are those who assert it based on what we just stated. This doubt was decided in Article 6: namely, it was demonstrated that it is licit to lay down one's life for a friend. <margin>Three ranks of aggression.</margin>From this, it clearly follows that the one attacked can permit himself to be killed so that he does not kill. Yet truly, sometimes he is bound to defend himself. Therefore, I judge that three ranks should be established regarding this matter for the present. For there is one rank where the person attacked is bound, as I believe, to suffer death rather than kill the attacker, even where the aggression is unjust. For instance, if the aggressor were a King, or a General, or another person who is greatly necessary to the **commonwealth** <note>The "res publica" or the collective good of the state and its people</note>; and the person attacked were a common person whose life mattered nothing to the common good: truly, I would believe that then the one attacked is compelled by **charity** <note>In this context, charity refers to the theological virtue of selfless love for God and neighbor</note> to suffer death rather than inflict it on the other. 

On the other extreme, a case might occur where the person attacked would be bound under pain of mortal sin to defend himself: as if, conversely, a Prince or any other person highly useful to the commonwealth were attacked by some impure and wicked man. Then, without doubt, it would be a **prodigality of life** <note>A reckless wasting of a valuable life that belongs to the service of the state</note> not to defend himself when unjustly provoked, even when it were necessary to kill the attacker. In the remaining middle cases, every person attacked has the right to defend himself; and nonetheless, he is free to renounce that right for the sake of charity. <margin>A doubt.</margin>

¶ But what if someone were to provoke me unjustly, not with weapons, but by some other force or fraud? For example, if I knew a judge had decreed to lead me to death through iniquity, or witnesses through false testimony; and this was absolutely certain to me, and the matter was already imminent—could I not kill them, knowing that I could not otherwise escape death? For it appears to be the same right as if they were attacking me with swords. <margin>Resolution.</margin>The answer is that it is by no means permitted, nor is the right the same:

<column-break/>

since it is only permitted to **repel force with force** <note>original: "vim vi repellere"—a standard legal principle in Roman and Canon law allowing immediate self-defense</note>: and force does not exist except in a present aggression. Otherwise (as we said above), if you were to strike first, you would be the one who is the aggressor. Therefore, in that case, you must seek other legal remedies. 

If, however, a magistrate or other **ministers of justice** <note>Police, guards, or court officials</note> wished to lay hands on me, and it were clear to me that they did so out of iniquity, it would certainly be permitted for me to repel force with force just as if they were private persons. It is otherwise, however, if they attempted it in good faith and by law: namely, because there are clues or some legitimate accusation. For then, even though I were innocent, it would not be permitted for me to wound the ministers in order to escape, as we shall say again below in Question 4. <margin>Another doubt.</margin>

¶ Regarding **temporal goods** <note>Physical property and money, as opposed to spiritual or bodily health</note>, however, there is a doubt whether it is permitted to kill even a thief in their defense. For it appears that this is not permitted: because these temporal goods, which are fleeting and therefore necessarily destined to perish, are not to be valued so highly that a man should be punished with death for their sake. This is especially true because all these things were granted to mortals for the support of human life. And the authority of <margin>Augustine.</margin>Augustine from the second book of *On Free Choice* supports this, as cited in the second argument. 

Indeed, there is also that passage in Exodus 22 which is cited in Chapter 1 concerning homicide regarding the night thief, with the added **gloss** <note>A standard commentary or explanation added to a legal or biblical text</note> of Augustine which is cited in the chapter "If a man digging through" <note>original: "si perfodiens"</note> regarding homicide. For the gloss is that it is permitted to kill a night thief in the very act of the crime, but not once the sun has risen, because at night it cannot be discerned whether he has come for theft or for murder, as can be perceived in the light of the sun. Whereby Augustine signifies that it is only permitted to kill a thief out of fear of death, but not out of fear of losing goods. <margin>Solution.</margin>The answer is that it is nonetheless permitted beyond doubt to kill even a daytime thief in defense of temporal goods if they cannot otherwise be snatched from him. And the reason is that my goods are the means for the sustenance of life, status, and honor. Therefore, just as life is the foundation of all goods, so it is also their protector. <margin>Augustine explained.</margin>Regarding Augustine, however, it is answered either that he was perhaps of the opinion that one may not take a thief's life for temporal goods alone, or better, that he spoke as a moral philosopher: because it hardly ever happens that goods can be snatched from a daytime thief without his death. And when that could be done, it would certainly be unjust to kill him. For so it is held in the law "A Thief" <note>original: "l. furem"</note> in the **Cornelian Law on Assassins** <note>original: "ad. l. Corn. de sica."—referring to the Lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis</note>: "if anyone kills a night thief, he shall only go unpunished if he could not spare him without danger to himself."

### Book Five, Question I. 405

...namely, by recovering his property. According to the **Digest**, in the section on the **Aquilian Law**, <note>original: "ff. ad . l. Aquil."; the Lex Aquilia was a Roman law providing compensation for damage to property.</note> if someone preferred to kill a thief when he could have apprehended him, he is seen to have committed a wrong. From this, legal experts conclude that even while there is hope of a legal way to recover stolen goods, it is not permitted to kill the thief. And certainly, if there were a very certain hope that the goods could be recovered with the easiest effort, this appears true. However, where the matter is doubtful, the owner may be free to exercise his right. Hence, in the same chapter *Interfecisti*, it is added: "If, however, without a desire for hatred, you killed such limbs of the devil <note>original: "diaboli membra"; a common medieval term for those committing grave sins or crimes.</note> while freeing yourself and your property, it is good for you if you wish to fast." It is as if to say, you are not strictly bound to do so. <margin>How long the time for defense lasts.</margin> Furthermore, you might perhaps doubt how long the "time of defense" lasts. Specifically, whether it is only permitted to resist as long as the thief has not yet seized the item, or whether, while he is fleeing burdened with your things, you may pursue him with arms; and if he cannot be caught otherwise, whether you may strike him down by throwing a weapon. The answer is that throughout that entire time of the **flagrant crime**, <note>original: "flagrantis delicti"; being caught in the act or "red-handed."</note> it is permitted to repel force with force, even while he flees. However, after he has already withdrawn to some place of safety, it is not permitted to attack him with force, but rather to hold him until a judge can seize him. Yet, when we assert that these things are permitted—namely, striking down a thief with a weapon—we understand this to be if the goods are of significant value. For a cheap thing—for instance, the value of two or three ducats—just as it would be a sin to expose one's own life to danger for it, so too would it be to kill another. For although you have the right to defend yourself and your property, the damage you prevent for yourself must be weighed against the damage you inflict. <margin>Another doubt.</margin> Though the condition of the innocent person is better. ¶ It remains to be seen regarding **honor**, whether it is permitted to kill an aggressor in its defense. Suppose, for example, there is a noble or illustrious man who sees an enemy approaching him with a sword; if he could save his life by fleeing, is he bound to flee with his own disgrace so as not to expose himself or his enemy to the danger of death? For it appears, according to what has been said, that he could by no means wait; since the **standard of blameless defense** <term>moderamen inculpatæ tutelæ</term> <note>A legal principle requiring that the force used in self-defense be proportionate and necessary to the threat.</note> requires that the death of the enemy be necessary to preserve life, which is not the case here. <margin>The solution.</margin> The answer is that he is nonetheless not bound to take to his heels, because this moderation must be applied without significant detriment to honor. Therefore, priests and monks would be entirely bound to flee in such a case, as it is not their "honor" to wait for such a conflict—indeed, the use of arms does not befit them except in extreme necessity. And the same applies to 

<column-break/>

a commoner of the lowest sort, who would suffer no loss of honor at all by fleeing. ¶ If anyone should argue against us from this that it is therefore also permitted for one who has been provoked and challenged to a **duel** to go out and fight, because he cannot do otherwise without loss of honor: <margin>Removal of the quibble.</margin> it is answered that there is no logical consequence. For in that case, no force is being inflicted, as there is when the enemy is present. Therefore, he who goes out to a duel does not "repel force with force," but rather cooperates in the injustice with which the other person provoked him. Especially since, according to the truth of the matter and the judgment of wise men, not going out is not a disgrace. For where virtue is not being defended, there is no honor, since honor is the reward of virtue. Because of this, since going out to kill by private authority is not a virtue, it follows that it is not truly honor, except in the eyes of the **common crowd**. And by "common crowd" we mean whoever judges things not according to the nature of the reality, but according to popular opinion. But enough on this for now. <margin>Another sophism is excluded.</margin> ¶ However, someone here might perhaps meditate on a sophism. For it seems permitted to a nobleman who received a wound in a conflict to strike back at an enemy who now wishes to stop—not indeed in defense of his life, but of the honor that was taken from him. For if it is permitted to take back property by force from a fleeing thief, why not also take back honor? The answer is that the reasoning is different. For the thief carries away your actual goods which you take back from him; but in the present case, the one who dishonored you does not carry your honor away with him. Therefore, you cannot vindicate it now except through **vengeance**, which is permitted only to the public authority. ¶ From what has been said above, it follows <gloss>that</gloss> if someone were to approach another to strike him very lightly with a stick, the other could repel this even by killing the enemy in the process—especially in **Spain**, where such an injury is considered so atrocious. <note>In 16th-century Spanish culture, being struck with a cane or stick was a supreme insult to a man's "honra" (honor), often viewed as worse than a sword wound.</note> ¶ Whether the same reasoning applies to clerics as to the laity: the answer is that regarding the **law of nature**, it is exactly the same, except that regarding the defense of honor, the reasoning is not equal, as they do not possess honor through arms. Regarding **Ecclesiastical Law**, more shortly.

...found at fault, as is evident in the case of a judge; thus it is that a cleric, even if he kills someone while defending himself, becomes <term>irregular</term> <note>original: "irregularis"; in canon law, an "irregularity" is a status that prevents a person from being ordained or performing the duties of a priest, often incurred through involvement in bloodshed, even if legal.</note>. However, he [St. Thomas] is speaking according to the law that was in use in his own century. For later, in the *Clementines* <note>original: "Clemen. vnica de homi."; a specific decree in the collection of canon law known as the Clementines.</note>, it was providently cautioned that anyone who kills or mutilates his attacker because he cannot otherwise avoid death shall incur no irregularity. Beyond this, in the mentioned chapter *De His*, nothing else is held except that a cleric who killed a pagan while defending himself was strongly advised to withdraw from the priestly office, as if it were not strictly necessary [to do so]. Add to this that perhaps he is speaking as in the preceding chapter, *Clericum*, concerning one who, while in military service—specifically trapped in a siege—had killed a pagan; for he ought not to have remained in the siege. Hence, in the canon *Interfecisti* <note>A legal decree regarding voluntary homicide.</note>, a priest who kills an attacker while defending himself and his property is not deposed from office, but is urged to do penance—perhaps for the sake of setting an example, or because of some presumed fault. But we shall deal more closely with irregularity in the next chapter, where these words of St. Thomas will be more refinedly examined.

The fourth argument carries no weight: for neither fornication nor adultery are means for defense in the way that homicide is.

### ARTICLE IX.

->Whether one who has killed another by accident<-
->is guilty of homicide.<-

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
After voluntary homicide follows a discussion of accidental <note>original: "casuali"; homicide occurring by chance or accident.</note> homicide: whether it makes one guilty of being a murderer. For there are testimonies, both from the Sacred Scriptures and from the holy Fathers, in favor of the affirmative side.

<margin>Lamech.</margin>
For we read in Genesis 4 concerning Lamech, that he killed a man to his own wounding. And the story, according to the holy interpreters, was that while he was hunting and believed he was killing a beast, he killed a man; nevertheless, homicide was imputed to him.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly, we read in Exodus 21: If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and she suffers a miscarriage: if her death follows

<column-break/>

from it, he shall give a life for a life. However, that miscarriage could happen beyond the intention of the one striking; therefore, accidental homicide is not without fault.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Thirdly, in Distinction 50 and in the section of the Decretals on homicide, there are many canons by which clerics who have committed accidental homicides are held to be irregular. Now, where irregularity is imposed as a punishment, it is not incurred except on account of a fault.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
On the other hand, the opposite is met in Augustine’s letter to Publicola, where he says: "Far be it that those things which we do for a good or lawful purpose should be imputed to us, if anything evil happens because of them against our will." Accidental homicide occurs when an evil effect happens to someone who intends something good.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with three conclusions. The first is two-part, and is the basis and root of the others. Nothing accidental is a sin insofar as it happens by accident; but insofar as it contains something voluntary, to that extent it will be a sin. This conclusion is proven according to Augustine against Faustus: a sin is nothing unless it is voluntary. Now, accident <note>original: "casus"</note>, according to Aristotle in the second book of the *Physics*, is a cause beyond intention, and thus beyond the will of the agent. Therefore, accidental things, according to that reasoning, carry no guilt with them.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
Second conclusion: No one who is engaged in a lawful task, and has no malicious intention, incurs the guilt of homicide if someone dies from his action—provided that he applied the required diligence to avoid doing harm. This conclusion is an appendix and corollary to the previous one. For homicide of this kind has nothing of the will in it, but is simply accidental.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Third conclusion: If someone is engaged in an unlawful task, or if, while engaged in a lawful task, he does not apply the required diligence, he is not immune from the guilt of homicide that follows from such an action. The conclusion is proven: it happens that something which is not willed or intended in itself by the act, is willed and intended *per accidens* <note>By accident or indirectly.</note>, insofar as one does not prevent what he both could and should have prevented. For a cause that removes an obstacle is called an accidental cause. Thus it happens that someone who does not remove or prevent a cause or action which he ought to have stopped is held guilty if homicide follows. This happens in two ways: in one way, when he devotes himself to unlawful things which he ought to have avoided; in the other way, when he is occupied with lawful things but does not apply diligence. From this contrary negligence, homicide follows. And this is our asserted conclusion.

<summary>This page clarifies that clerics are generally exempt from canonical 'irregularity' if they kill in necessary self-defense and introduces the moral criteria for accidental homicide. Soto concludes that accidental death only carries moral guilt if the person was doing something illegal or failed to exercise proper caution (negligence).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of homicide. ### Book Five, Question I.

<margin>The conclusion is illustrated.</margin>
For a clear understanding of the matter, we must remember that a thing can be voluntary in two ways.

In one way, it is direct because it was intended; this is termed "simply voluntary" <note>original: "simpliciter... voluntarium"</note> and is the opposite of something "simply accidental," where there is no will involved. In the other way, something happens to be voluntary "by accident" <note>original: "per accidens"</note> because it was not prevented; this occupies a middle ground between the purely voluntary and the purely accidental. Nevertheless, due to the lack of direct intention, it is called "casual" or accidental.

<margin>Three conditions required for accidental homicide to be blamed.</margin>
Therefore, for a death to be considered accidental homicide, it is required: first, that it was not intended; second, for it to be blamed <note>original: "imputetur"</note> on the person, it must truly follow from an action that ought to have been stopped—as held in the chapters *Ad Audientiam* <note>original: "cap. ad audientiam de homi."; a chapter in canon law regarding homicide.</note> and *Presbyterum*. For if the death follows from another source, it is in no way blamed on the person acting, as seen in the chapter *Joannes*. For example, if you were disciplining someone carelessly or incautiously and you wounded them, and death either did not follow, or did not follow from the wound but from poor medical care or some other accident, you are not guilty of homicide in your conscience, but only of the incautious striking. Third, it is required that you not only *could* have avoided such an action, but that you *ought* to have. For although a hunter could avoid hunting, and thus avoid the shot of the arrow by which a homicide was committed beyond his intention, he contracts no guilt from it [if the hunting was lawful]. Similarly, as we were saying a little earlier: while a robber demands money from you, threatening that if you do not give it, he will commit a theft elsewhere—even if you do not give it and he commits the theft, there is no reason why that theft should be blamed on you, because you were not bound to give it.

<margin>A doubt is removed.</margin>
<margin>What kind of sin accidental homicide is.</margin>
From this follows the solution to a small question usually raised today. For it is doubted whether accidental homicide, which is voluntary only "by accident," is always a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a grave action that destroys the relationship with God, whereas a "venial sin" is a lesser offense.</note>. For it appears to be so because of its object [death]. Nevertheless, it is answered that such homicides have no more guilt than was present in the cause—whether the cause was engaging in an illicit activity, or negligence in a lawful one. For example: a cleric is forbidden from riding a horse; if he mounts one in a situation where it was only a venial sin, and he accidentally knocks a man down and kills him, it would only be a venial sin, as held in the chapter *Dilectus*. Likewise, if someone engaging in a lawful activity—like a soldier or a hunter—kills a man out of negligence because he did not look around enough: if that negligence was only venial, the homicide will only be venial. For it is not always necessary to apply the maximum possible diligence, but only as much as is appropriate for the nature of the business. But if the cause involved a mortal sin, even if it was lighter

<column-break/>

than homicide is by its own nature, the guilt in the homicide itself will not be any heavier.
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
This is the opinion of Augustine in the 22nd book of *Against Faustus*: where he says that Lot, who committed incest while drunk, was not guilty of incest, because that crime held no more guilt than was already present in his getting drunk.

<margin>The first part of the second condition is challenged.</margin>
But there is a doubt regarding <term>irregularity</term> <note>An "irregularity" is a legal penalty in the Church that prevents someone from performing the duties of a priest.</note>; and first, there is an argument against the second condition placed above. For it was said that if someone strikes another fatally through incaution and grave negligence, but the victim escapes death through excellent medical care or perhaps a miracle, then the striker is not guilty of homicide. But the counter-argument is: if he had wounded him that seriously with the *intention* of killing him, he would be stained with the same guilt as if he were a murderer; therefore, the same should apply if he did it while being incautious and negligent. The first response is that the irregularity established for murderers is not incurred unless death actually follows. Therefore, even if the escape from death is miraculous, it is enough that the striker is not considered "irregular." Furthermore, regarding the guilt, there is a difference. For he who struck a man with the intention to kill him is immediately guilty of homicide before God, whatever follows; but he who wounded another not by intention, but by a lack of caution, does not become guilty of a greater sin than was in the cause, as we were just saying.

But an argument is made against the other part of the same conclusion, which stated that even if a death follows, it is not blamed if it came not from the wound but from elsewhere.

<margin>The second part is challenged.</margin>
If the wound was truly grave, even if the sick person did not take enough care of himself, or if that treatment which would have saved him was not applied—nonetheless, when he dies, he truly dies from the wound. Therefore, even if the negligence of the sick person or the doctor was also a cause, the striker is nonetheless guilty of homicide. And this is confirmed by the fact that neither is the sick person bound to take such extreme care of himself, nor to seek out the best doctor, nor is the doctor bound to apply such skillful treatment. Therefore, even if death follows not simply from the wound but with other negligences joined to it, it is nonetheless blamed on the striker who provided the cause through an injurious act. Add to this that perhaps a supply of surgeons could not be had, nor anyone else to stop the flow of blood, because of which he died: in that case, since no one besides the striker was at fault, he will be truly guilty.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered to this that when a homicide follows, one must abide by the judgment of doctors, as in the chapter *Significas* <note>original: "cap. significas"; a reference to a specific legal decree.</note>.

<summary>This page analyzes the moral and legal responsibility for accidental homicide, arguing that the level of guilt depends on the original intent or negligence of the actor, rather than the death itself. It also clarifies that in Church law, certain penalties like "irregularity" only apply if the victim actually dies, regardless of how close they came to death.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

### Book Five, Title II.

It is advised to consider whether a wound was truly lethal—the kind from which men usually die. In such a case, regardless of any negligence on the part of the sick person, the homicide is blamed <note>original: "imputatur"</note> on the one who inflicted the wound. If, however, the wound was not of that lethal kind, then the striker's guilt is not affected by the accidental outcome, since he was fully responsible for the initial action. However, regarding <term>irregularity</term> <note>A legal status in the Catholic Church that bars a person from being ordained or performing the duties of a priest.</note>, if death followed without any other person's fault, the homicide is imputed to him. But if the death occurred due to the fault of either the sick person or the physician, the striker is excused. For once a person has received a wound, they are bound by the law of nature to vigilantly look after their own health, and the surgeon is likewise bound by the duty of his office to care for them.

<margin>Those who incur the mark of irregularity.</margin>
¶ Having established these points, we must now move to the modes of irregularity. First, many texts—such as the chapters *Lator*, *Dilectus filius*, *Significasti*, *Joannes*, and *Ex literis* in the section on homicide <note>These are specific chapters within the Decretals of Gregory IX, a primary source of medieval Canon Law.</note>—state that anyone who, following our second conclusion, performs a lawful act and applies prudent diligence but nonetheless kills someone, is not stained by any mark of irregularity. This is because in such a case, there is not only no fault, but the killing was not voluntary. From this conclusion, you may gather that those who care for the sick, while moving a patient in bed to better provide food or help them lie more quietly, incur no irregularity even if death is slightly accelerated by it; this is because they are performing a lawful act. This holds unless their negligence or the tossing of the patient was so immoderate that, in the judgment of prudent men, it was considered a killing and therefore a mortal recklessness.

<margin>A ridiculous incident.</margin>
I heard of a confessor who, while accompanying a condemned man to the gallows, accidentally bumped the beast the man was riding. He later felt a "scruple" <note>A religious or moral doubt or anxiety over a small matter.</note> of irregularity, fearing that he had caused the man to meet his death more hastily. But truly, such concerns are ridiculous.

<margin>The third conclusion is explained.</margin>
¶ In the third conclusion, we proposed two causes of irregularity, the first of which was when someone performs an illicit act. Indeed, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Italian theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> and Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), author of the "Summa Sylvestrina," a popular handbook for confessors.</note> (under the word *homicide*, section 2) and the doctors of Canon Law lay down a universal rule: anyone performing an illicit act is made irregular regardless of how the homicide follows from that act. However, this rule is not primarily found in the written law; rather, the interpreters infer it from the opposite sense—namely, from the aforementioned chapters where those performing lawful acts are excused. It is drawn especially from the chapters *Ex literis 2* and *Dilectus filius*, which state that one who does not perform an illicit act is not irregular if he is not negligent.

<column-break/>

For this reason, others—and even Saint Thomas—hold the view that those who occupy themselves with illicit things become irregular from any resulting homicide. Therefore, the rule must be tempered by certain moderations if it is to be held as universally true.

<margin>When one should be considered irregular who performs an illicit act.</margin>
First, if a cleric caught in adultery is attacked and kills the attacker while defending himself within the limits of blameless defense, he should not be considered irregular, even though he was engaged in an illicit act. This is because that homicide was not voluntary at the time. For although the adultery was voluntary, it was not the cause of the homicide in itself; rather, the cause was the act of wounding, which was not intended. Furthermore, in the mentioned chapter *Ex literis*, a monk is excused from irregularity who, while taking down a bell from a bell tower, dropped a piece of wood that crushed a boy. Suppose that work was "servile" <note>Manual labor forbidden on Sundays or feast days.</note> and perhaps he sinned by doing it on a feast day or against the command of his superior; would he be irregular for that reason? Certainly, it is not to be believed. Likewise, in the chapter *Dilectus*, a cleric is excused who, while riding a horse for his health, unexpectedly killed someone; if that riding had been harmful to the cleric and he had sinned by doing it against a doctor's orders, would he be irregular for that reason? There is certainly no reason to believe so. For the sin that was the cause did not, by its nature, relate to the homicide. But you may say: the "Summists" <note>Authors of "Summae," or encyclopedic summaries of moral and legal cases.</note> do not say this. On the contrary, Sylvester asserts it (under the word *homicide*, section 2, question 18): namely, that if someone cutting down a tree that was his own took great care to see that he did not crush anyone, he is not irregular even if the falling tree happens to crush a passerby. However, if the tree was not his own, he becomes irregular because he was engaged in theft. By the same logic, they would say that if a secular nobleman hunts in his own woods and kills a man purely by accident, he does not become irregular for receiving Holy Orders; yet he would become irregular if the woods belonged to another and he was taking game there against the owner's will.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
¶ These things, however, are truly not to be believed. Rather, the "act" one is performing must be understood as something which, by its very nature, is a common cause of homicide. For example, if a cleric engages in warfare: even if he kills someone unintentionally and without knowing it, he is irregular. The same applies if he practices tournaments or other simulated battles which are forbidden to clerics. Therefore, for an accidental homicide occurring during an illicit act to cause irregularity, it is required that the work he was deliberately doing be dangerous by its very nature. When, however, those acts are not prohibited to clerics because they are dangerous, but for some other reason, then a homicide that is purely accidental is not a cause of any irregularity.

<summary>This page discusses the canonical concept of 'irregularity' resulting from accidental homicide, arguing that a cleric only becomes irregular if the unintended death occurred during a naturally dangerous or lethal activity, rather than any minor illicit act.</summary>

# Question 1 of the Fifth Book

Therefore, I do not know if the opinion of <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> is entirely true when he says that a cleric who commits accidental homicide while hunting is excused in the same way as a layman. For if the hunting is of a type not forbidden to clerics because it is not dangerous, then he is right. If, however, it is prohibited because of danger—such as hunting wild boars with weapons, spears, and fierce dogs—then the cleric would certainly become irregular, whereas a layman would not.

<margin>Many chapters regarding homicide are explained.</margin>
¶ And by this decision, I believe all the chapters that can be cited regarding a person engaged in an "unlawful act" <note>original: "rei illicitæ"</note> are explained. First, in the chapter *Continebatur* <note>Chapters in Canon Law were often named after their first word.</note> concerning homicide, from which they derive their rule: a deacon is judged irregular not because he was doing something unlawful—for throwing sticks to ease the burden of labor was neither forbidden to clerics nor dangerous—but because when someone else leaped upon him, he ought to have been careful not to wound him with the scythe he was carrying. Similarly, in the chapter *Lator*, a cleric who threw another to the ground—an act which seems more unlawful in itself—is not condemned with the penalty of irregularity because his knife fell into the other person not out of his own negligence. In the case of the chapter *Suscepimus*, that monk became irregular not because he killed robbers in defense of his own life, but because he had bound them to protect temporal goods—which monks should not be so greedy for—and thus provided the cause for the homicide. But the case of the chapter *Tua nos* also supports our assertion: for there it is decreed that a cleric who had performed surgery out of <gloss>mercy</gloss> to care for a certain woman, and she died contrary to his intention, was not irregular. From the opposite sense, it is gathered that if he had done it for the sake of <gloss>profit</gloss>, he would have been irregular; namely, because clerics are barred from that art because it is inherently dangerous. 

<margin>When irregularity is incurred due to negligence.</margin> 
¶ The second way accidental homicide is imputed is through negligence. If this negligence is without any fault, there is no cause for irregularity, as held in the chapters cited above, with which we support the second conclusion of <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note>. For even if irregularity is incurred without personal guilt—as is clear in the case of a secular judge <note>A judge who sentences someone to death is "irregular" even if the sentence was just.</note>—it must nonetheless be "voluntary," as we have said. Where negligence is entirely without fault, the effect is not considered voluntary. For an act is only involuntary in "accidental causes" when a person fails to do what he ought to have done. Therefore, as we said above, it was prudently cautioned in the <term>Clementine</term> decrees <note>A collection of Canon Law issued by Pope Clement V.</note>...

<column-break/>

...the only one regarding homicide, that he who kills or maims an attacker because he could not otherwise escape death shall be free from irregularity. By the same law, even clerics and priests seeking the correction of wrongdoers in a secular court and the restitution of things stolen from them are immune from irregularity, provided they protest that they do not do this for vengeance nor for the shedding of blood, even if those criminals are assigned to the gallows. This is found in the sixth book, the chapter *Prælatis*, regarding voluntary homicide.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ You may perhaps ask whether irregularity is incurred in a case where the cause involved only a <term>venial sin</term> <note>A minor sin that does not break one's relationship with God, as opposed to a "mortal" or deadly sin.</note>.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan currently leans toward the affirmative side. Indeed, he says that accidental homicide is always imputed to one performing an unlawful act, both regarding the penalty of irregularity and some degree of fault, but not always regarding mortal sin. He teaches that irregularity is incurred for some fault less than a mortal sin.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
However, although this carries some probability because the homicide is then "voluntary" to some degree, I do not know if it is entirely true. For it is difficult to believe that irregularity, which is imposed as a penalty because of a fault, should be incurred from a venial sin alone. Therefore, I can hardly believe it. For example, the recently cited *Clementine* decree decides that a cleric who kills an enemy in self-defense is not irregular. I do not know who would believe, then, that someone who caused a homicide through the slightest venial fault—perhaps because he did not perfectly discern whether he could defend himself without killing—should become irregular.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The first argument, then, concerned Lamech, who in Genesis 4 confesses to having "killed a man to his wounding." Indeed, as all interpreters hold, while hunting he shot an arrow into Cain, who was hiding, thinking he was killing a wild beast. To this, it is answered that he did not look around sufficiently; or, as others say, since his eyes were already dimming, he did it carelessly while being led by a boy. It was that ignorance which cast him into fault.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is answered that he who strikes a pregnant woman undergoes the same judgment as a homicide where there is a danger of abortion. Namely, if he does it intentionally, he sins mortally; and if by accident, he is as guilty as the cause was. If the fetus was already "animated" <note>In medieval thought, the point at which the fetus receives a soul, usually 40 or 90 days after conception.</note>, he becomes a true murderer, and thus irregular.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the canons cited in the third argument, enough and more has been answered. For no one [incurs] the sentence of irregularity...

### SECOND QUESTION,
### regarding the mutilation of limbs.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 65.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether it is lawful for anyone to
mutilate their own limb.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' containing a circular illustration of a man sitting at a table with a globe and compass, suggesting a geographer or scholar.</image-desc>

Since the life of an animal consists of that which is in the limbs, after the discussion of homicide <note>The previous "Question" in this text dealt with the ethics of killing.</note>, there follows the question of the mutilation of limbs: whether it is lawful in any case. The argument begins with the negative side.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
A sin is committed, as <term>Damascene</term> <note>St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an influential Syrian monk and theologian.</note> says in Book 2, whenever one departs from what is according to nature and moves toward what is against nature. However, according to nature, by God’s design, it is fitting for the body to be whole in its limbs; therefore, it is against nature to mutilate it.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second. Just as the soul relates to the whole body, so do the parts of the soul relate to the parts of the body, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The ancient Greek philosopher, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> teaches in Book 2 of *On the Soul*. But it is not lawful to deprive a man of his soul—that is, to kill him—except by public authority; therefore, it will not be lawful to rob particular limbs of their soul-parts—that is, their powers—except by that same public authority.
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Third. The health of the soul is to be preferred to the health of the body. Yet no one is allowed to cut off a limb for the sake of the soul’s health; for, according to the ancient statutes of the <term>Council of Nicaea</term> <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established early Church laws, including a ban on self-castration.</note>, those who castrated themselves for the sake of preserving chastity are punished. Therefore, the amputation of any limb is not lawful for any other reason.
<margin>Council of Nicaea.</margin>

¶ On the contrary is what is commanded in Exodus 21: <note>original: "Oculum pro oculo ; dentem pro dente, ac manū pro manureddi."</note> *An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, and a hand for a hand shall be given.*

<margin>The sense of the question.</margin>
This question must be decided in two senses: to what extent the amputation of a limb can be done either by public authority or by anyone’s private authority. For the cause of the cutting may be a spiritual "disease"—namely, a voluntary crime—or a natural defect of the body. It is therefore answered with three conclusions. The first:

<column-break/>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First. Just as someone can be lawfully deprived of life by public authority for a serious crime, so too can they be deprived of a limb for a lesser crime. This is proven as follows: Just as the parts of the same human body are its limbs, and are thus created for its service and support, so too individual citizens are members of the whole <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "reipublicæ." Soto uses the analogy of the "Body Politic" where the state is a body and citizens are its limbs.</note>, related and ordered toward it. Therefore, just as one must dispose of the limbs of the same body in a way that is most conducive to the health of the whole body, so it is with individual citizens regarding what is most expedient for the health of the state. Now, a healthy limb cannot be cut off without harm to the body because it is useful to the whole, except when, being infected, it causes harm. Therefore, if a citizen has brought harm to the state, just as the state could extinguish him entirely when the crime deserves it, so too, when the sin is not so grave, it can mutilate him—even if the limb to be cut off were physically healthy and useful to the person.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion. Furthermore, when some limb has been corrupted by a natural disease, it can be cut off with the consent of the sick person themselves to save their life. This is proven because everyone has the right to preserve their own life; therefore, when the amputation of a limb is necessary, anyone can choose it for themselves, just like any other type of medicine. For this reason, it can be done by the authority of a parent or another person taking care of them, even without public permission.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion. Outside of these two cases, mutilation is not lawful for anyone, neither by public authority nor by the consent of a private person. This is proven because the life of the whole consists of the limbs. Therefore, just as homicide is lawful to no one, so neither is mutilation.

<margin>A distinction to be noted.</margin>
¶ Therefore, a distinction is to be noted: because of a spiritual vice <note>i.e., a crime or sin.</note>, it is indeed lawful for the state to mutilate a man, but not for the private person himself. Conversely, because of a physical disease, it is lawful for the sick person to permit a limb to be cut off on the advice of a doctor, yet it is not the state’s duty to be able to compel him to do so. The reason is that everyone is the guardian of their own life, while the state is the guardian of the common good. Thus, while homicide can only occur because of a fault <note>original: "culpam."</note>, mutilation is lawful even for the sake of physical health.

<margin>A petition/enquiry.</margin>
¶ But can the state, or a father, or a <term>prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking religious superior.</note> not compel a son or a subject to permit a limb to be cut off when it is necessary for his health?

<margin>The solution.</margin>
The answer is that the state has no right in this matter. A prelate, however, could compel a subject on account of particular...

Soto distinguishes between the state's power to punish and the individual's right to seek medical treatment, using the analogy of the body and the commonwealth.</summary>

Indeed, even a deformity, if it is severe in the eye, even if it is a defect from birth, prohibits promotion to the priesthood. However, those who are operated upon by the advice of doctors for the sake of health are not thereby rendered unfit for the priesthood: as is held in the same distinction, in the canon <term>If anyone for sickness</term> <note>original: "si quis pro ægritudine"</note>, and in both chapters of the title <term>On the Mutilation of the Body</term>, in the section <term>From the part</term> <note>original: "ex parte"</note>. Nor does only the cutting off of a principal member, such as a hand, induce "irregularity" <note>A legal status in the Church preventing someone from becoming or acting as a priest.</note>: as is held in the chapter <term>You have explained</term> <note>original: "exposuisti"</note> in the same title; rather, it even applies if someone cuts off part of a finger: as the canon <term>He who a part</term> <note>original: "qui partem"</note> holds in the 55th distinction. But this is understood to mean that the loss is so great that he cannot touch the most holy Sacrament without scandal: as is explained in <term>On the Mutilation of the Body</term>, chapter 1 and the last chapter. And perhaps a lighter cause is required for the person who performs the mutilation to become "irregular" than for the one who is mutilated. For in the case of the one performing the mutilation, cutting off a finger is perhaps enough, as we have said, because he "kills" a limb; but in the case of the one who has been mutilated, it is required that there be a notable deformity, whether it comes from an accident or from birth.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
### To the first main argument, therefore, it is responded that what is against a particular nature can be done according to the universal nature: just as the rising of water to fill a vacuum stands as a witness to us. Therefore, although the amputation of a limb is a deformity to the body, it can nevertheless be consistent both with the person's safety and even with the common good. It is true, however, that a well-ordered state abstains from such punishments as much as possible. First, so that they do not demand the "law of retaliation" <note>The *lex talionis*, or "an eye for an eye."</note> from wrongdoers in the ancient manner: namely, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Second, so that they do not cut off right hands, as such a truncation renders a man useless. However, for blasphemers, the tongue is cut off by the best right, and for false witnesses, the teeth are pulled out.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
### To the second, it is responded that since life is not ordered toward another end belonging to the living person themselves, but only to the public good, a person can in no way deprive themselves of it; only the state has that power. However, limbs are ordered toward life, and therefore the person themselves, who is the guardian of their own life, can cut away a limb for the sake of preserving life.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
### Finally, to the third, it is responded that the cutting off of a bodily limb is lawful precisely because it is usually necessary

<column-break/>

for preserving life. But truly, it is never necessary for spiritual salvation. For sin, through which the soul dies, always and everywhere lies under the power of the will; otherwise, it would not be sin. And a faithful God, as Paul says, does not permit a greater temptation to a man than what he himself can overcome through God's grace. Therefore, that word, *If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out; and if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off*: was not said because it could ever be literally necessary, but it is either a hyperbole, or it carries another moral sense about cutting off the occasions of sin, as the saints interpret it; and we also have left an explanation there according to our modest ability. Hence, regarding that passage in Matthew 19: *There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven*: <margin>Chrysostom</margin> John Chrysostom says: Not through the cutting off of limbs, but through the slaughter of evil thoughts.

### ARTICLE II.
### Whether it is lawful for a father to beat his sons, or for masters to beat their servants.

<margin>First argument for the negative side from Aristotle.</margin>
After the discussion of mutilation, it follows to speak of other beatings related to it. And because there is no doubt that this is lawful for the state, it is asked whether it is lawful for fathers to beat their sons. For the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the 10th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 11, that a father's command has no strength, nor the necessity of compulsion, nor does the command of any man at all unless he be a prince; but beating is a species of compulsion: therefore, it is not fitting for fathers, nor indeed for masters.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued: If this were lawful for parents and masters, since it pertains to "fraternal correction" <note>The Christian duty to correct a neighbor's sins.</note>, the same right would support every person, so that anyone could beat anyone else while correcting them.

¶ On the contrary is that passage from Proverbs 13: *He who spares the rod hates his son.* And later in chapter 23: *Do not withhold discipline from a child.* And Ecclesiasticus 13: *For a wicked servant, torture and fetters.*

<margin>Single conclusion.</margin>
### The question is answered with a single conclusion. Only fathers and masters, or those performing paternal care—such as teachers and tutors—are allowed to beat and whip their subordinates; however, they may by no means mutilate them. Each part of the conclusion is proven by this reason. Between mutilation and beating there is this difference: that mutilation is so much a greater

It also establishes that while fathers and masters have a right to use corporal punishment for discipline, they lack the state's authority to permanently mutilate or kill.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the limits of punishment, moving from self-inflicted injury to the authority of parents and masters over their subjects. ### Question II of the Fifth Book

Injury from beating is not the same as mutilation, for the latter is irreparable. Beating, by contrast, is not irreparable, as it only inflicts pain upon the senses. Therefore, since the life of the whole consists of the life of its members, it follows that lawful mutilation—based on the nature of a crime—belongs precisely to the same authority that holds power over life itself. This function belongs solely to the commonwealth <note>The state or public government</note>. Beating, however, is intended for easier discipline and more immediate correction. Nevertheless, even this requires a certain authority which the one beating exercises over the one being struck. A father possesses this authority primarily over his children, then a master over his subjects, and finally a teacher or tutor over his pupils. Regarding prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note>, there can be no doubt, as they flourish with public power. ¶ This matter is quite simple. Yet, although we spoke regarding paternal power <note>original: "patria potestas"</note>—specifically how much power a father has over his children—immediately in the first question of the first book, a diligent student might still ask by what right the negative part of this conclusion is supported.

<margin>Objection against the conclusion.</margin>
For it appears by the law of nature <note>original: "iure naturae"</note> that fathers are free not only to beat their children, but also to punish them with mutilation and, if necessary, even death. For by that same law, the duty to educate and instruct children in morals is incumbent upon them; and such instruction very often demands the punishment of mutilation or death.

<margin>A second reason</margin>
Secondly, it is argued that in the very beginnings of the world, there was no other commonwealth but the domestic one—namely, when the family of Adam alone possessed the world. At that time, since the public punishment of crimes was necessary, it follows that this duty fell to the father. Indeed, Cain was worthy of capital punishment unless God had spared him; the guilty man himself testified to this in his great fear, saying: "Whoever finds me will kill me." Therefore, no one could have inflicted that punishment upon him except his father. Furthermore, if there were some mortals living so dispersed that they lived under no prince, but every house lived separately, then reason itself seems to teach that the father or grandfather could sentence those who deserved death to that same punishment.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, the response is that the law of nature itself forbids parents from taking such vengeance and grants it solely to public power. This is confirmed by the law of nations <note>original: "iure gentium," referring to laws common to all civilizations</note>. For human life must not be extinguished without the most deliberate judgment and legal order; thus, it should not be committed to such a vast multitude as there are parents, who neither know the laws nor are all able to weigh the merits of cases.

<column-break/>

For this reason, nature granted parents the right to educate their children in such a way that it nevertheless prescribed a line where their own capacity ends and public authority begins; as is cautioned in the law <term>If a son</term> <note>original: "l.1. si filius"</note> in the Code <note>The Code of Justinian</note> under the title <term>On paternal power</term>, and in the law <term>The Praetor</term> in the Digest, in the section <term>Furthermore</term>. And to the second argument, we have already responded in the cited place (Book 1, Question 1) that Adam possessed public power by right of his lordship over the world, which was in his hands at that time. But as the human race increased and the world was distributed into families by the law of nations, each family had its own prince. Therefore, as we respond to the other point, those who would live wandering today, separately and privately without a commonwealth, would be living a life contrary to human nature; for man is by his very nature a civil and social animal. Therefore, no solid argument can be taken from such cases against the present truth.

<margin>What kind of power parents have over children.</margin>
¶ It is therefore not permitted for parents to mutilate, nor for any mortal except by public power; but they may strike with a rod or a cane. For this is granted to them by the law of nature. For a man is instructed toward virtue in three ways: he is led by reason, compelled by fear, and enticed by reward. Therefore, before the star of reason shines forth, nature provided that a boy should be both compelled by fear and affected by small gifts. Therefore, paternal instruction, which is the first of all, uses these two. But when reason already enjoys its own light, he then begins to live by law and reason, and thus falls under public power.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ But even the beating administered by parents is not permitted to be excessively cruel, as is held in the cited laws of the Code and Digest. Therefore Paul, in Ephesians 6, says: "You, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger." And below: "And you, masters, do the same to your servants, forbearing threats." Here both parents and masters are warned: first, not to terrify their own with harsh threats; and especially that, while they threaten harsh things when seized by bile <note>Anger or ill-temper</note>, they should not consider themselves bound to carry them out, but rather, they should forgive when calmed what they threatened while their minds were disturbed.

¶ From this, it follows that a father can sin mortally while correcting his son: namely, if anger is not the soldier of his reason, but its leader—providing the reason for the punishment and provoking the son to that same anger. Indeed, if he punishes out of hatred for his son, he sins more severely in this regard than a stranger would.

<margin>The difference between a father and a judge.</margin>
For the difference between a father and a judge must be carefully noted. Public power, as was said above, does not look so much to the reform of the guilty person as it does to the common good through vengeance; but to a father and a master...

<summary>This page discusses why the power of life, death, and mutilation belongs exclusively to the state (the commonwealth) rather than to parents. While fathers have a natural right to use corporal punishment for correction, the author argues that humans are naturally social beings meant to live under public laws, which protect against the emotional impulses of private discipline.</summary>

# Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*,

...master and tutor, it is not lawful to beat their own charges for any other reason than that which more healthily provides for their correction. Therefore, the boy is to be corrected according to his age, condition, and disposition. <margin>Quintilian</margin> Indeed, both Quintilian and those who have written on the education of children do not advise that parents attack their offspring with excessive rigor. For if they are well-born <note>Meaning naturally inclined toward virtue</note>, such rigor usually makes them lazy and fearful; but if they are of a hard disposition, it makes them harder still.

<margin>Solution to the second doubt mentioned above.</margin> ¶ From these things follows, secondly, the solution to the small doubt of whether it is lawful for parents to wound children or masters their servants. For there are four types of injuries: namely, killing, mutilation, beating, and wounding—that is, the infliction of a wound. This can be done with a club or a sword, through a "dyscrasia" <note>An imbalance or injury to the body's humors or physical composition</note> and a breaking of the limb short of mutilation; therefore, it belongs to atrocious beating, which is lawful neither for parents nor for masters.

<margin>Another question.</margin> ¶ After these things, you ask whether it is lawful for these same domestic authorities to beat sons or students even if they are clerics, and whether such a person incurs the penalty of the canon <note>Specifically the canon *Si quis suadente*, which decreed excommunication for anyone who struck a member of the clergy</note>. <margin>Sylvester</margin> Sylvester speaks of this under the word "excommunication," part 6, section 4. <margin>Panormitanus</margin> And indeed Panormitanus, commenting on the chapter *Cum voluntate* regarding the sentence of excommunication, distinguishes that if they are in minor orders <note>Lower levels of the clergy, such as acolytes or lectors</note>, it is lawful to beat them for the sake of correction. And this seems to be gathered from the same chapter, in the section *Si vero*. For it is said that senior clerics, out of a zeal for devotion, may lightly strike youths in minor orders who disturb the divine office. However, immediately and without distinction, it is added that they may also strike subject scholars by virtue of their office of prelate or master. And expressly in the chapter *Ex tenore*, it is held that it is lawful for a Prelate to beat an inferior, even if he is a subdeacon. From this, Sylvester infers that if it is lawful for a prelate, it should be lawful by the same right for a father. And thus the jurists are divided concerning those subjects who are in holy orders. For concerning those in minor orders, no one doubts that they can be beaten.

<margin>Legitimate solution to the proposed question.</margin> ¶ Yet, notwithstanding these things concerning the prelate, it can in no way be doubted that he can strike his subjects—even priests—with lashes in the customary manner, as is clear in the *Decretals* <note>The collected laws of the Church</note>, distinction 45, throughout. Whether, however, he could strike them with a club seized in a fit of rage <note>original: "ex bili," literally "from bile" or anger</note>, I do not know if it would be lawful; because since the manner is not customary, it appears less as correction and more as an injurious assault. But the inference from prelates to parents is not as clear as Sylvester thinks. For prelates possess public power and jurisdiction with coercive force, whereas parents

<column-break/>

and the rest have only domestic <note>original: "oeconomicam," referring to the governance of a household</note> power. Nevertheless, it should not be entirely condemned if masters were also to beat their students with a rod <note>original: "ferula"</note>, even if they were in holy orders. But on this matter, one must abide by custom and the ecclesiastical court.

<margin>A scruple.</margin> ¶ But if you doubt whether, while exceeding the limit in correcting, either a prelate or a father incurs the sentence of the canon: <margin>Response.</margin> The answer is that although he may exceed it in some way, even to the shedding of blood, provided that this happens beyond his intention, he is not to be judged as having incurred the penalty, since he is engaged in a lawful act. Nor can a man be so attentive as to never cross the boundary of virtue. However, when the excess is so enormous that it serves as evidence of hatred, then by shedding blood, he would incur the canon. Therefore, by the same distinction in the canons *Cum Beatus Paulus* and *Disciplina*, prelates are warned toward leniency: namely, that they should instruct their subjects with wholesome words rather than immoderate beatings.

¶ Regarding the husband, however, whether he has the right to beat his wife, the answer is that it should not be denied to them, since the man, as Paul says, is the head of the wife; yet to use that right is a disgrace, and indeed a sin <note>original: "nefas"</note>, unless a most grave necessity arises. <margin>Aristotle</margin> For they are barbarians who use their wives like slaves, as Aristotle is the authority in the first book of the *Politics*. For since two are in one flesh, it is fitting they be joined in a certain equality.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> **TO** the first argument, then, it is answered that although, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, a father does not have coercive force because a household is not a perfect commonwealth like a city, it only follows from this that he cannot kill, or mutilate, or inflict other irreparable harm; however, he is not forbidden from using lighter beatings. <margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second, it is answered that although it is lawful for anyone to instruct others in discipline and to advise them with fraternal correction if they wish to listen of their own accord, nevertheless no one can compel them to it except one who has charge of the other. Such are parents, masters, and tutors; therefore, to them alone belongs the task of punishing with beatings. Add that even by their command, their servant may do the same; but beyond this, it is lawful for no one. Therefore, even if you catch a thief in the act <note>original: "in flagranti delicto"</note> of plundering your goods, you are only allowed to strike him in resistance, but not while he is fleeing as a means of vengeance—unless the beating were so light as to be considered nothing.

<summary>This page discusses the legal and moral limits of corporal punishment within the domestic and ecclesiastical spheres, arguing that while parents and masters may use moderate force for correction, they lack the state's power to kill or mutilate. Soto also addresses the complexities of striking clerics and the ethical boundaries of a husband's authority over his wife.</summary>
