<meta>This page continues the discussion on physical punishments and injuries within the framework of justice. Having previously addressed killing, mutilation, and beating, the author now transitions to the legality of imprisonment and the social impact of injuries.</meta>

# Question II of the Fifth Book

## ARTICLE III

### Whether it is lawful for anyone to commit someone to prison.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
After the topics of slaughter, wounds, and lashings, it follows that we must also speak of prison—whether it is lawful to shut a human being inside one. The argument begins from the negative side. Man is free by his very nature, according to Ecclesiasticus 15: "God left man in the hand of his own counsel" <note>Ecclesiasticus/Sirach 15:14. This is a common scholastic proof-text for the existence of free will</note>. However, imprisonment opposes liberty; therefore, it is repugnant to human nature, and thus it is permitted to no one.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, if it were lawful to restrain a person by prison, it would primarily be to keep them from doing evil. But if it were lawful for that purpose, that same right would belong to everyone, for anyone is allowed to restrain their neighbor from evil. Yet the logical consequence of this is false, for imprisonment is counted among other injuries <note>In a legal sense, an *iniuria* is a violation of a person's rights or dignity</note>. These injuries are indeed more serious when inflicted upon a person who has many others connected to them; for then the injury which touches one person reaches many. Therefore, it is not at all permitted. ¶ On the contrary is the history in Leviticus 24, where a certain man is read to have been thrust into prison for the sin of blasphemy.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: It is lawful for the public authority, and for that authority alone, to shut subjects in prison, whether that authority be ecclesiastical or civil.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Both parts of the conclusion are proven. Among the "goods of the body," three things are considered in order. First, its integrity, which is harmed through killing and mutilation. Second, sensory delight and pleasure, which is hindered by beating. Third, the use of the limbs, which is restrained by prisons and by any other kind of bonds. Now, the first type of harm, because of its gravity, is reserved solely to the state <note>original: *reipublicæ*</note>, as has been said. The second type, because it is lighter, is permitted to parents and masters. Regarding the third, then—since it is not only a path toward the first but even a kind of beginning of it (for a defendant is committed to prison either so that he may eventually be sentenced to a hearing for capital punishment or to pay the penalty for a lighter crime)—it is fitting that this be assigned to the state alone, in whose hands is the power of life and death. Therefore, this is permitted neither to parents nor to masters.

<margin>The double use of prisons in the state.</margin>
¶ From this it follows that there is a twofold use for prisons in the state. For they serve both for the guarding

<column-break/>

of wrongdoers while their cases are being discussed and decided, and furthermore as a punishment. This latter use is one the ecclesiastical power employs most often, since it cannot proceed to lashings <note>The Church was traditionally prohibited from shedding blood or inflicting severe corporal punishment, often using "perpetual" or temporary imprisonment as a medicinal or punitive alternative</note>. And what has been said regarding prisons should also be judged regarding exile.

<margin>Exile.</margin>
For exile is equally opposed to liberty. Indeed, just as life imprisonment is, so too is exile equated by law to death. Consequently, parents cannot send their children into exile, although they may distance them from a place that is infectious to their morals.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Those who inflict such injurious harms, outside the order of law, upon persons who have others connected to them, commit a more serious offense—by the very nature of the matter, all else being equal—than if they had inflicted them on others who lack kinsmen and associates. However, the sin can also be aggravated by other factors, namely the status of the person. At present, we call "connected persons" primarily blood relatives and in-laws, such as a father, son, son-in-law, brother-in-law <note>original: *leuirum*</note>, etc., or those joined by other household necessities, such as a husband, wife, patron, and the like. This even extends outside the home to friends and other close associates <note>original: *necessarios*</note>.

<margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is clear. For the more an injury and detriment spreads to more people, the more serious it is; and all those connected to a person represent, in a certain way, that same person. For a son is something of the father, and a wife is something of the husband; indeed, a friend is "another self." Therefore, he who harms one is injurious to all. Add to this that even when you do not inflict an injury upon the person with whom you commit a sin, you can still harm the connected person. For while a wife consents to adultery of her own will, or a girl to her defilement, although you do not do an injury to those who are willing, you nevertheless inflict one upon the husband and the father. Furthermore, it is clear that the gravity can be increased by other factors. First, from the dignity of the person: as if you provoke a prince, or a very good man, or a widow, or an orphan with an injury, you sin more gravely for that reason. Hence Ecclesiasticus 35: "You shall not despise the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow if she pours out her complaint of groaning."

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Here, however, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, whom Soto is commenting upon</note> makes no mention at present of one who is injurious to someone connected to himself—as if you were to kill your father or brother (for these crimes change the specific type of sin). Rather, he is speaking of persons connected to the victim, where the species of the crime is not changed, but the fault increases by circumstance <note>original: *per accidens*</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the legal authority required to imprison individuals, reserving that right solely to the state or church rather than private masters. It also explores how the severity of a crime increases when the victim has family or social ties, as the injury affects the entire connected group.</summary>

<keywords>imprisonment, public authority, exile, family law, injury, Thomas Aquinas, Ecclesiasticus, legal jurisdiction, moral theology</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the legal discussion on imprisonment from the previous page and begins a new major section on theft (Question 3). De Soto transitions from injuries against the person (killing, imprisonment) to injuries against property, justifying his organizational structure based on the "deeds versus words" distinction used by Thomas Aquinas.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is answered that although man is free by his own nature, nevertheless, when he commits a crime through the abuse of that same will, he loses the right <note>Latin: *ius*</note> that he has to the use of his limbs; and therefore, he is deservedly committed to prison. This follows the example of God, who, although He made man free, sometimes restrains him, according to that passage in Job 5: "He who scatters the thoughts of the wicked so that their hands cannot fulfill what they had begun," <note>Job 5:12</note> even though He sometimes permits them to indulge the sicknesses of their own minds. In the same way, the republic does not hold a defendant in prison for every fault, but only for the more serious ones.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is answered that only parents may keep their children confined, and masters their servants, for a short time—both as a punishment and to restrain them—for that type of inclusion does not have the formal character of a "prison." This is not permitted to other private citizens. For even if anyone can restrain a brother by "fraternal correction" <note>A standard theological term for private, loving rebukes meant to steer someone away from sin</note> to keep him from evil, it is by no means permitted by the use of force. Indeed, private prisons are judged as an enormous crime and are punished in the republic; rather, it is only permitted for anyone to detain for an hour a criminal who has inflicted an injury upon them, until they can hand them over to the ministers of justice.

## QUESTION THREE,
### regarding theft.

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether the definition of theft is good.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial S depicting a seated classical or biblical figure in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>
According to the order of things—if you estimate their value and dignity—after homicide, by which the greatest of temporal goods is taken away, one should immediately speak of detraction and whispering <note>Backbiting or gossip</note>, by which honor and reputation are harmed. For these are held to be worth more than external goods. "For a good name," says the Wise Man, "is better than many riches." <note>Proverbs 22:1</note> However, the arrangement will become clearer if we follow not this order, but another used by Saint Thomas: namely, if we first dispatch those injuries which are committed by *deed*, and then move on to others which are committed by *word*. For by reason of the act itself, a more criminal

<column-break/>

injury exists in a deed than in a word. Furthermore, Saint Thomas in Question 66 places two articles about ownership <term>dominium; the right of possession and control</term> at the beginning, which we already set forth in the previous book as the first foundation of the matter of justice and "commutative injustice" <note>Injustice regarding private exchanges and property rights</note>; there, we led the matter of ownership through all its various points. For the first article of the divine Thomas is about the possession of things in general, which was granted by God to man immediately upon his creation. Disputing this matter in our first Question, we established that supreme ownership of things belongs to God alone by right of creation—not only regarding their use, but also regarding their very natures, which He can certainly create, annihilate, and alter beyond the laws of nature. Among corporal creatures, however, we showed that man alone is the master of things, specifically by the reasoning that he has freedom and mastery over his own actions; a brute animal, however, has none at all, and much less does any inanimate thing. Regarding the second article, Saint Thomas added the division of ownership, which we showed in Question 3 was made by the "law of nations" <term>ius gentium; the legal commonalities shared by all civilized peoples</term>; we also provided extensive reasons why such a division is appropriate for a fallen nature subject to depraved affections. Since we have left these things so copiously discussed there, there is no reason for us to say another word about those articles here. ¶ Therefore, the first article of the present question concerns the name and definition of theft, which in the works of Saint Thomas is the third article.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
And the argument is made from the negative side: that the definition of theft which Saint Thomas and the theologians establish is short and incomplete; namely: "Theft is the secret taking of another's property." Theft consists not only in the *taking*, but in the *retention*; for as long as you do not restore what you have stolen, you are held guilty of theft; therefore, it is not enough to say "taking."

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Secondly, a person can secretly take not only someone else's property, but even their own property which they had deposited with another or pledged as collateral; if they hide this from the other person, they inflict an injury upon them. Therefore, the "taking of another's property" is not required for the formal definition of theft.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, that which diminishes a sin does not constitute the formal reason for the fault. But to sin secretly diminishes the sin—both because it is a sign of shame and because scandal is avoided by that means. ¶ On the contrary is the fact that a definition ought to be a brief and concise statement; but the nature of theft is sufficiently drawn out by those three words <note>The three words are: *occulta* (secret), *acceptio* (taking), and *rei alienae* (of another's property)</note>; therefore, a definition burdened with more would be redundant.

<summary>De Soto concludes the discussion on imprisonment, arguing that while humans are naturally free, criminal acts forfeit the right to physical liberty. He then transitions to the definition of theft, prioritizing injuries of "deed" over "word" and justifying the legal division of property through the law of nations.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded a discussion on imprisonment and the limitations of private citizens' power to detain others. This page begins the third question of Book Five, shifting the focus from injuries against the person to crimes against property, specifically theft.</meta>

### Book Five, Question III.

->**On the origin and definition of the name of theft.**<-

<margin>The opinion of Isidore on the origin of the name.</margin>
Regarding both the name and the definition of theft <note>original: "furti"</note>, you will find a certain variety among the Doctors. For Isidore, in Book 10, because theft is a secret taking, thinks that "thief" <note>original: "fur"</note> is derived from "dark" <note>original: "furvo," meaning dusky or black</note>: namely, because he makes use of the night time. 
<margin>Varro.</margin>
Varro says the same in *On Agriculture*, Book 14. Nor indeed did the Jurist in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de furtis. l. 1." referring to the Roman law Digest</note> reject this etymology, although he also suggests another: namely, that it is named from "carrying" <note>original: "ferendo"</note> or "carrying away" <note>original: "auferendo"</note>. For the Greeks also call thieves *phoras* <note>Greek: φῶρας</note> from "to carry" <note>Greek: φῶρ</note>. However, this matters very little. Yet, regarding the definition, the interpreters of law disagree more significantly with the philosophers. For 
<margin>Definition of theft according to the Jurists.</margin>
Paulus says in the same law: "Theft is the fraudulent handling <note>term: <term>contrectatio</term>—a technical legal term for physical contact or 'meddling' with property</note> of a thing for the sake of making a gain, whether of the thing itself, or even its use or possession, which is prohibited by natural law to commit." And others add that it is the handling of a *movable* thing, because in the *Institutes* <note>original: "Institu. de usucapio. §. quod autem"</note> it is held that theft cannot be committed of a place or a plot of land; and finally they add, "against the owner's will." 
<margin>The fault of the Jurists in defining.</margin>
It is the custom of the Doctors of Law, when they define a certain genus, to note all its species within the definition. Philosophers, however, express the nature of a thing with a summary, which they later unfold more explicitly through divisions. Therefore, according to Aristotle, a definition ought to be a very brief statement explaining the nature of the thing in summary, such as this: "Theft is the secret taking of another's property." 
<margin>The previous definition is rejected.</margin>
In the first place, since "handling" signifies only the touch of a thing, it is more appropriately called "taking" <note>original: "acceptio"</note>, that is, "usurpation." Next, with the broad name of "another's property," we more fully encompass all things captured by theft than if you were to say "a movable thing." For not only movable things, but also immovable things are captured by theft when they are possessed deceitfully. Therefore, there is no need to specify "of the thing or its use," for whoever uses another's property against the owner's will takes that property in a certain way. By saying "secretly" <note>original: "occulta"</note>, "fraud" is sufficiently signified, for he who takes a thing secretly from the owner weaves a fraud. And by the same word, it is designated that the taking happens "against the owner's will," for ignorance is a cause of the involuntary. As for that which is added—"for the sake of making a gain"—it is not only superfluous but also falsely applied. For he who takes another's property to throw it into a river or hand it over to fire is guilty of theft, even if while doing so he is not greedy for gain, but does it to inflict an injury. Therefore, for the nature

<column-break/>

<margin>Three requirements for the nature of theft.</margin>
of theft, three things are required. First, that it has the character of injustice, in which genus it is situated. This is expressed when we say "taking." For it is understood to be "against the owner's will," which is contrary to justice, which gives to each what is his own; and this extends even to detention. The second is that it differs from other species of injustice. This is specifically designated when it is said, "of another's property"—namely, possessed by one who is truly its owner. For he who cuts off another’s limb, or carries off a daughter or a wife to abuse them, is not a thief, but a mutilator, an abductor, or an adulterer. The third is what completes the specific nature of theft and distinguishes it from robbery <note>original: "rapina," usually implying violent theft</note> and banditry: namely, that it is done "secretly" <note>original: "clanculò"</note>. Therefore, the statement explaining these three is the genuine definition of theft: namely, "The secret taking of another's property." ¶ Hence it happens that theft is ineptly divided into "fraudulent and secret taking" and "robbery." 
<margin>Theft is not a genus to robbery, but a species opposite to it.</margin>
Theft is indeed not a genus to robbery, but a species opposite to it. Thus, "injurious taking of another's property" is what is first divided into theft and robbery or banditry, as will be clear in the next article. Both species, however, are subdivided into four based on the object. For if what is taken by theft is a sacred thing, it is called sacrilege. If it is the property of the republic, it is called embezzlement <note>original: <term>peculatus</term></note>. Regarding both, one may read in the *Decretum* <note>original: "23. q. 4. cano. quid ergo," referring to Canon Law</note>. If theft is committed from a scattered herd, it is called cattle-rustling <note>original: <term>abigeatus</term></note>. And he who thus drives away beasts or herds is called a rustler <note>original: <term>abigeus</term></note>. Regarding these, there exists a title in Book 47 of the Digest. Finally, the fourth species is kidnapping <note>original: <term>plagiarium</term> or <term>plagium</term></note>: namely, the theft of a person to be sold. Regarding this, there also exists a title under the Flavian Law on kidnapping. For he who takes a male or female slave from their master is truly a thief, for a slave is possessed like a beast. Unless he were to take a female slave for a time for the sake of shameful acts; for then he would be a fornicator, not a thief. Just as he is an abductor who for that reason carries off a virgin. But what if someone were to carry off another's children or wife to sell them? Is it theft? It has already been answered in the previous book that since a father is not truly the owner of his children or wife, that is not theft, but kidnapping or captivity. ¶ Against these things, 
<margin>Objection.</margin>
perhaps someone might argue: when a son secretly takes something from his father, or a wife from her husband without him knowing, they take another's property; and yet neither is judged 
<margin>Solution.</margin>
a thief. I respond that when the thing is not of such great value, the taking by a child is not judged to be theft, because it is not done "against the owner's will." For by the right of parents, every child is presumed, according to their condition and status, to be...

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**T**hrough these points, the responses to the arguments become clear. To the first, it is answered that the concealment of a sin can be either its cause or a circumstance. It is the cause, for instance, when the delinquent uses concealment so that he may sin more safely, as is evident in fraud and deceit. In that case, it does not diminish the sin, but constitutes its own species, namely theft (as has been said), as distinguished from robbery. However, concealment is a circumstance when the one who has decided to sin hides in the shadows out of shame or to avoid scandal while fulfilling his lust; in that case, it diminishes the character of the sin.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, the Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> responds that detaining another’s property against the owner’s will has the same character of harm as an unjust taking, and is therefore reduced to the character of theft. Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas</note> comments extensively on this response. But since this was sufficiently discussed by us twice in the preceding book (namely, Question 6, Article 1, and Question 7, the last article), there is no need to add more here. But remember, the command of restitution is affirmative, commanding a good work; yet it includes the negation of "retaining," which is the prohibition of an evil. For this reason, it has an affinity with theft. Therefore, this act of detaining does not add a new sin to the act of taking, but is a continuation of it—one that is graver (as we said there) the longer it lasts. However, if a new positive act is added—for example, if you resolve not to return it, or if you use the other's property for consumption without intending to pay for the loss—those acts are multiplied offenses against that same negation of "not retaining" included in the same commandment. Furthermore, a fresh sin is committed against the affirmation of "restoring" whenever the one retaining the property of another either sees the owner in need or hears him asking for it; for 

<column-break/>

then he is bound to restore it by a new merit of right.

<margin>
To the third.
St. Thomas.
</margin>
¶ To the third argument, the same Holy Doctor <note>Aquinas</note> responds somewhat obscurely. His meaning, however, is that he who secretly seizes his own property which is in the possession of another—namely, in the possession of one who either robbed him or is keeping it as a deposit—is to be judged a thief for this reason: although it is his property in an absolute sense, it belongs to the other in a qualified sense <note>original: "secundum quid"</note>, specifically regarding its guardianship or its detention. However, this solution seems to involve several falsehoods.

<margin>
First objection against St. Thomas’s solution.
</margin>
First, a stolen thing in no way belongs to the robber; for a thing is said to belong only to the one who possesses it by right, which does not apply to a thief; indeed, he sins mortally by detaining it.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, this line of reasoning in the solution is false: namely, that he who takes his own property commits theft. For not only is he not considered a thief in common speech unless he takes what belongs to another, but even the laws decree this. This is evident in the Digest <note>original: "l. si is qui rem. 1. ff. de furtis," referring to Roman civil law</note>, where it is held that he who secretly takes back a thing he had loaned is not a thief. Therefore, if after someone has taken something from me, I immediately extort it from him by force, 

<margin>solution.</margin>
I shall not be guilty of theft. It is responded that the intention of Saint Thomas is legitimate, which he himself makes clear immediately in Article 5 of the same question. For if I have deposited my property with someone, or if he has snatched it from me, and I take it secretly from him, I am judged a thief for this reason: because he, not knowing that I have taken it, is bound in conscience to restore it to me; and by the same reasoning, if I take it from the robber without his knowledge. For this reason, Aquinas says that the object is in some way the property of the one keeping the deposit—namely, regarding the right of guarding it—and even of the one who robbed it, because he must keep it in order to restore it. Therefore, I cannot take it by private authority through force or fraud.

# ARTICLE II.

## *Whether theft and robbery differ in kind.*

**F**rom the preceding article, the solution to this small question may be easily gathered; however, for the sake of greater clarity, the difference is asked after once more. Namely, whether there is a specific difference <note>original: "specifica differentia"—a technical term in logic and scholasticism meaning a difference that creates a new category or "species" of action</note> between theft and robbery.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
An argument is made for the negative side. First, because they do not seem to differ except as "hidden" and "manifest"; and these qualities in other kinds of sins do not change the species;

<meta>catchword: vt (as)</meta>

<summary>This page discusses whether taking property from family members or taking back one's own property from a thief constitutes "theft." Soto analyzes the views of St. Thomas Aquinas and Roman law, concluding that while taking back one's own property isn't theft in the strictest sense, it is wrong to do so by private authority because of the responsibilities the current holder (even a thief) has toward the object.</summary>

--- Page 423 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous discussion on page 417, which examined the nuances of theft within family dynamics and the requirements for restitution, the text now transitions into a scholastic debate on the essential differences between theft and robbery.</meta>

...as if you perjure yourself in public or in secret.
<margin>Second Point.</margin> ¶ Secondly, because the specific difference of an act is derived from its goal and its "formal object" <note>In scholastic philosophy, the "formal object" is the specific aspect of a thing that an action targets—in this case, the property rights of another.</note>, which in theft and robbery seems to be the same: namely, the seizure of another's property.
<margin>Third Point.</margin> ¶ Thirdly, just as money is seized to be used, so also a girl is seized to be abused. However, the abduction of a girl <note>original: "raptus puellæ"—this term covers both kidnapping and sexual assault in medieval law.</note>, whether it occurs publicly or secretly, does not change its classification; therefore, neither should the seizure of money.
<margin>Aristotle</margin> ¶ On the contrary is the Philosopher <note>A common title for Aristotle in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 2, where he establishes theft and robbery as distinct species of sin.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> **T**o the question, a very brief conclusion is given in response. Theft and robbery differ in their very nature.
<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> It is proved as follows: The specific difference between acts is observed according to the formal and most immediate difference of their objects. In the case of theft and robbery, this difference is specific; therefore, these crimes differ in kind. The minor premise is proved: Both of these vices agree in that they are contrary to "commutative justice" <note>The form of justice governing private transactions and the restoration of balance between individuals.</note>, insofar as an injustice is committed through either of these takings because another’s right is violated. Moreover, as Aristotle holds in that same work, no one suffers an injustice except unwillingly, against their own will. These actions are injurious, therefore, because they are done against the will of the owner, who thus suffers an "involuntary" act. But indeed, as 
<margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle teaches in the 3rd book of the *Ethics*, an act becomes involuntary in two ways: namely, either through ignorance or through violence. Theft, by its very definition, implies a taking while the owner is ignorant [unaware]; robbery, however, implies a taking while the owner is aware and suffering force. Therefore, theft and robbery differ in kind. Thus, one must not look at the nature of the "other’s property," which is the "material object" <note>The physical item being stolen.</note>, but at the nature of the involuntary act. ¶ This is a distinction recognized not only by moral philosophers but also by the Jurists who derived their laws from that same philosophy, as is evident in the law "sed novo iure" in the Code <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, part of the body of Roman law.</note> concerning fugitive slaves, and in Ulpian’s law "fur" in the Digest concerning thefts. This must be considered carefully so that no one is deceived. For someone might think the difference consists in theft being done in the dark, as is found in Exodus 22, while robbery is done in the light of day. Or that theft is committed in the owner's absence, and robbery in his presence. Yet the distinction consists in neither of these reasons. Rather, the difference is that theft occurs without violence, whereas robbery and banditry occur violently. For as we shall see in the final article, the guilt of robbery increases 

<column-break/>

beyond the guilt found in theft. From this it follows that theft can occur in the owner's presence, just as robbery can occur in his absence. For example, if an impure man rushes into a house while the master is present and either overwhelms him while he resists, or ties him up so he cannot resist, or shuts him in a room, or strikes such fear into him that he remains silent—even if the attacker is unarmed—he is considered a robber and a bandit because he uses force. If, however, the master does not consent but remains silent out of his own restraint, sparing either the reputation or the life of the thief, it will not be robbery, but theft. By the same logic, if someone attacks a house with force, even if no one is inside, it will be robbery. Thus, the bandits who occupy public roads are not merely thieves, but also robbers. Furthermore, the distinction found in the second law concerning thefts, where two kinds of theft are distinguished—one "hidden" and the other "manifest"—is irrelevant here. For "manifest" is not used there to mean robbery, but for the case where a thief is caught in the act (*flagrante delicto*), as is immediately explained in the third law.

Therefore, all arguments remain resolved. 
<margin>To the first argument.</margin> To the first, it is answered that other sins (apart from injustices) do not have the involuntary nature of another person as their object, as theft and robbery do; therefore, they do not vary in kind based on the different types of involuntary will, as these do.
<margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ And through this, the second is also answered: although they deal with the same material and remote object—namely, another's property—the formal and immediate object is not the same.
<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third, it is answered that the abduction of a girl, no matter how secretly it is done with respect to others, is always known to the girl herself; and because she is always presumed to have resisted, it is called abduction [robbery].

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
To the question, a single conclusion is given in response. Theft, and by even stronger reasoning robbery, is a sin, and specifically one that is mortal by its nature. It is proved: A mortal crime, as we have often been accustomed to say, is weighed by the fact that it extinguishes charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the theological virtue of love for God and neighbor, which scholastics believed was the "life" of the soul; its loss meant spiritual death.</note>, which is the life of the soul: theft is of this kind; therefore, it is mortal. The minor premise is proved: That crime which opposes the virtue necessary for the commonwealth, through which its peace and quiet are preserved, extinguishes charity: theft, however, opposes justice, in which the whole trust of mortals and human society stands secure. For through theft, citizens are deprived of their rights, and thus the peace of the city is disturbed: it is therefore against charity. Yet robbery is so much more grave as violence is worse than fraud. It was said, however,

<summary>Soto argues that fornication is inherently more sinful than theft because it violates the "potential life" of a child and the natural order of the family, even though theft is more socially shameful or more clearly condemned in the Ten Commandments. He concludes that while sexual sins are generally worse by nature, specific instances of theft (like stealing massive wealth) can be more damaging in practice.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

in its own category, it is the least of the sins of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>.

Among the arguments against this conclusion, Saint Thomas first raises the point regarding the theft committed by the children of Israel in Egypt, which was no sin; but it has already been sufficiently stated in Book 2 that this action did not have the character of theft. For beyond the fact that God, as the Lord of all things, could grant them those goods without any special dispensation, He, as a righteous judge, paid them the wages for the labor they spent in mud and brick. <margin>A Scruple <note>A "scruple" here refers to a difficult moral or legal question that troubles the conscience.</note>.</margin> ¶ But truly, is it permissible for princes to imitate God in this regard by secretly commanding something that their ministers are bound to execute without public outcry? For example: if a prince were to command a courtier to privately strip someone of their goods or their life, would <margin>The Solution.</margin> that person be bound to carry it out? The answer is that if he does this because a cause has been stated and a sentence of condemnation has been passed, he must undoubtedly be obeyed; for it is sometimes expedient for such executions to be secret. In that case, it would not be theft, but the execution of a penalty. However, if he commands it without the form and order of a trial, it is a crime, and he must not be obeyed; for even a prince is bound to proceed by judicial order. Indeed, he is not God, who cannot err. Unless perhaps—which happens very rarely—in a specific case where the justice was most evident, and it could permit neither delays nor public noise. But when war is publicly declared, then, unless the injustice of the cause is manifest, the command of the prince should <margin>Augustine, 23, question 1, canon "What fault." <note>A reference to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of canon law, citing St. Augustine on the duties of soldiers.</note></margin> clear the consciences of the soldiers, as Augustine says in the 23rd book, question 1. <margin>To the first argument.</margin> ¶ Regarding the other argument which we placed first, concerning the person who either steals or forcibly seizes their own property, it has been partly addressed in the first article, and the rest remains to be said now. For a doubt remains, overlooked there, as to whether it is permissible for anyone by <margin>Saint Thomas.</margin> private authority to recover what is owed to them. To this, Saint Thomas responds in the negative: for if you had deposited that thing with him and you steal it without his knowledge, you burden him, so that he remains bound to restore it to you, unaware of the theft. But if he had usurped it against the law, you sin in that you transgress the laws of right by privately usurping the judgment that belongs to public power; which is indeed a mortal crime and most strictly prohibited by civil law. <margin>A Doubt.</margin> ¶ Yet it is worthwhile to explain this more fully. For what shall a poor man do who can in no way recover his property through the path of the law? For it is among the rules of the law in Book 6 that "no one ought to be enriched by another’s property." It is answered 

<column-break/>

therefore, regarding both the fault and the restitution. For it is permissible for anyone to take their own property by private authority, provided these conditions are present. <margin>Conditions that must be met for it to be lawful for anyone to recover property by private authority.</margin> First, that he is certain beyond all doubt that the thing is owed to him; for where there is any doubt, it is by no means permitted to bypass the order of the law. For this reason, servants—whether of princes or of lower masters—can by no right secretly snatch anything from their masters under the pretext that they have not been sufficiently compensated for their service and attendance. For they are very often accustomed to claim this for themselves before their confessors. To them, however, it must be answered that if they cannot extort the price agreed upon between them by any other way, they may indeed take it secretly. But as for that additional pay which the servants themselves think ought to be added further, they may not take it at all—unless they were forced by their masters through fraud to serve. For no injury is done to one who is willing. And therefore, if you do not wish to serve for that price, leave. The second condition is that, having tried everything, you are certain that you cannot recover your property through a legal path. For otherwise, you would be doing an injury to public authority. But in such a case, a distinction is needed. For either that impossibility arises because you lack witnesses and documents by which you can prove your right: and then it is by no means permitted to snatch your property by force; for no one is permitted to use force privately, except to repel force with force in the heat of the crime. Therefore, if you cannot acquire your property by another way, no remedy remains for you: for one must rather consult the public peace than your private advantage. Therefore, let everyone look out for themselves with what caution they alienate their goods. If, however, you can snatch such a debt owed to you in a hidden way without scandal, or make compensation to yourself, it will indeed be permitted; provided you guard against the danger that your debtor might make the restitution a second time <note>i.e., you must ensure the person doesn't pay you back again later, thinking they still owe you.</note>. And this much regarding the excuse of fault. For as far as restitution is concerned, provided it is clearly established to you that the thing is yours, even if you snatch it from the debtor by violence, you are not bound to restore anything. Nor can you be compelled to answer to censures of excommunication; but you must only undergo the penalties if condemned. In a second way, it can happen that the path of recovering one's property is closed off, not because the proofs are not legitimate, but because of the iniquity of the judge who refuses to decide the case: in that case, reason seems to more clearly prove that it is permissible for anyone, even by force, to take their property.

### Question III of the Fifth Book

to take his own: for a ruler can, for this reason, declare war on another: namely, because he has no other judge who might render him his right. Nonetheless, it is answered that even then it is not lawful to proceed by force openly. But if it cannot be recovered by a hidden path, either a superior must be approached, or if no other remedy remains, the loss of goods is rather to be endured than to disturb the commonwealth by force: as **Saint Thomas** seems to teach in this question, article 8 <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, q. 66, a. 8.</note>. However, where a commonwealth is so barbaric or oppressed by such great tyranny that no one could obtain his right: then, if he could restore himself to his right without the clashing of arms, even with some violence, it would not be entirely unjust. I say this regarding the right to external goods <note>Property or material wealth.</note>. For it would be permitted in no case to avenge oneself. As in, if you have suffered an injury, even if you cannot obtain justice, it is in no way permitted for you to avenge it privately. Nor is it the same for rulers. For he in whose hands the sovereignty of the commonwealth rests is not only its judge, but also the judge of external enemies, not only for repelling injuries but also for avenging them.

<margin>
Regarding the second argument.
**Saint Thomas**.
A twofold nature of things found.
</margin>
The second argument, however, touches upon the matter of "things found": to which **Saint Thomas** responds with this distinction. There are certain things found that were never anyone's property: such as the small stones and gems produced by the seashore. And the finders of such things are subject to no restitution: because that which was never anyone's is granted to the one who takes possession of it. See the *Institutes* on the division of things, the paragraph "Wild animals" <note>original: "§. feræ." — a reference to Justinian’s *Institutes*, 2.1.12.</note> and the *Digest* under the same title. And the same reasoning applies to the discovery of ancient treasure: namely, that of which no memory of an owner can exist. For by then, that treasure is regarded in the same way as a gold mine which the earth nourishes. Except that, by civil laws, half is added to the owner of the field, just as if it were the fruit of his land.

<margin>
Ancient.
</margin>
Indeed, the Gospel Parable regarding the finder of treasure in another’s field shows that this civil law is very ancient <note>Matthew 13:44. Soto notes that the man in the parable buys the field first to ensure the treasure is legally his.</note>, where it is attributed to his prudence that he bought it before revealing the treasure, so that it might fall to him in its entirety. But there are other things found on the surface of the earth, or recently lost elsewhere, or deposited, of which the owners or surviving heirs are therefore presumed to exist. And these, says **Saint Thomas**, cannot be taken with the intention

<column-break/>

of keeping them, unless it is established that the owner cast them away as abandoned, according to the word of **Augustine** <note>14. q. 5.</note>: "If you found something and did not return it, you stole it."

<margin>
**Augustine**.
</margin>
¶ However, as we explain these things, we must run through the specifics. And first, that pebbles found on the shore of the sea belong to the finder is an express definition of the law (*Institutes* on the division of things, paragraph "Pebbles," and the *Digest* under the same title, the law "Likewise pebbles" <note>original: "l. item lapilli."</note>). And the reason is that the shores remained common by the **Law of Nations** <term>jus gentium: a set of laws considered common to all mankind, based on natural reason</term>. And the judgment of natural law is the same concerning veins of gold and other metals that are in the bowels of the earth.

<margin>
Reason for doubting.
</margin>
For it appears to be permitted to everyone for the same reason, since by the **Law of Nations**, these resources have not been divided.

<margin>
The Response.
</margin>
It is responded, however, that by this law alone it is not entirely permitted, unless the inhabitants themselves consent: or if they held the same treasures as abandoned. For regions were divided by the **Law of Nations**: and therefore, although those things are common to the people of that region, nevertheless, foreigners cannot usurp those same things against the will of the inhabitants. For a Frenchman is not empowered to penetrate our lands for this cause, nor are we to theirs against their will: but this is for another place to dispute.

</margin>

Therefore, taking those treasures has no character of theft: as held in the law "False" <note>original: ".l. falsus." — Digest 47.2.43.4.</note> (*On thefts*). And the reason for the same law is that it is not theft unless there is someone from whom it is stolen. ¶ Therefore, he who finds such a treasure in his own ground—it is granted to the finder: as held in the *Institutes* on the division of things, the paragraph "Treasures," and the *Code*, book 10, on treasures, the only law. But truly, if someone finds it in another's field by deliberate effort and by searching for it without consulting the owner, by civil law (as held in the laws just cited), the whole treasure belongs to the owner of the ground: because the finder is considered a thief. If, however, he should find it by chance while doing something else, the law says he shall retain half and give the other half to the owner. And this is perhaps to preserve peace. And the law is the same for him who finds a treasure of the same kind in a house he has bought: although there are those who deny it. # Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Law,

...if he should buy a house, using the same prudence that Christ praised in the Gospel <note>A reference to the Parable of the Hidden Treasure in Matthew 13:44, where a man sells all he has to buy a field containing treasure.</note>. It is otherwise, however, if he should find money or anything else in the wall of the house, or in its inner chambers, which a former owner had placed there and left behind through forgetfulness: for then it belongs to that same owner or his heirs, as held in the law *a tutore* in the Digest regarding the recovery of property <note>original: "l. à tutore. ff. de rei vendicatio." The Digest (or Pandects) is a major part of the Body of Civil Law compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note>.

<margin>Paludanus.</margin> 
From this, it follows that the opinion of Paludanus <note>Pierre de la Palud (c. 1275–1342), a prominent French theologian and archbishop.</note>—who says in his commentary on the *Sentences* that by custom all treasures, wherever they are found, belong to the princes—is not to be listened to. As 
<margin>Sylvester.</margin> 
Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), an Italian theologian known for his "Summa Sylvestrina."</note> well says regarding the word "discovery" [**inuentum**], section 13: such a custom has not been introduced in a well-ordered republic. For in Spain, these cited laws are observed to the letter. Therefore, if a contrary custom has taken hold elsewhere, it is by force, and against the law of nature and the law of nations. For it is held in the *Institutes* and the cited law that 
**Hadrian** <note>The Roman Emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138 AD) established a famous legal compromise: treasure found on one's own land stayed with the finder; found on another's land, it was split 50/50 with the landowner.</note>, following natural equity, granted it to the one who found the treasure. And that law of the Code regarding treasures says: "We grant free faculty to the finder, lest an envious calumny further pursue a benefit from God."

<margin>Question.</margin> 
Whether the prince is able to exact any portion from the finder, one might perhaps doubt. 
<margin>Solution.</margin> 
It is answered, however, that no justice appears in such an exaction; and therefore it is not in use in Spain. Nor, where it might be in use, would I believe it to bind the conscience; rather, according to common law, the finder can possess it in good conscience. For the said title of the *Institutes* mentions nothing of the prince: but where it says that he who finds it in another's place gives half to the owner, it adds by the same reasoning that if he finds it in the Emperor’s place, he gives half to Caesar; and if in a fiscal or public place, he also gives half to the treasury. This same thing is read in the law *non intelligitur* in the Digest regarding the right of the treasury. These laws only speak of where the places are the property of the prince or the city. Therefore, the prince as lord cannot exact anything when the treasure is buried in the place of a citizen—unless perhaps, due to an urgent and grave public necessity, he could seek that kind of tribute as a governor; though I do not know if I would sufficiently approve of that.

<margin>Regarding veins of metals.</margin> 
Regarding veins of metals [minerals], however, the custom has now obtained that a fifth part <note>The "Quinto Real" or Royal Fifth, a tax levied by the Spanish crown on precious metals mined in its colonies and territories.</note> goes to the prince, because those veins are natural things which, in a way, produce metals for the public good.

There is, however, a much greater doubt concerning found things that are not treasures, but are presumed to have owners. Indeed,

<column-break/>

there is almost a single consensus of both theologians and jurists (as the compilers of legal summaries say under the word "discovery" [**inuentum**]) that these must be restored to the poor.

<margin>Common opinion regarding found things that are not treasures.</margin> 
First, let us take it as a given in this matter that the finder is strictly bound to search for the owner in good faith, through public announcements and other means appropriate to the value of the item; otherwise, he will be held guilty of theft. However, once that investigation has been performed—although I do not dare to assert anything firmly against the common opinion—there are nonetheless very weighty arguments to me that the finder can retain it for himself in conscience.

It is proved thus: By the law of nature and the law of nations, those things belong to 
<margin>The author’s first reason for the following opinion.</margin> 
the finder. And there is no law, whether Evangelical or ecclesiastical, that assigns them either to the poor or to anyone else; therefore, the finder can take them for himself. The first premise is proved: As was said in Book 3, the law of nature did not divide things, but permitted them to be possessed in common. However, the law of nations permits that thing whose owner does not exist to belong to the first occupant. Truly, that thing whose owner does not appear after legitimate diligence is treated just as if it belonged to no one. Therefore, he who finds it acquires the right to it just as if it were ancient treasure. Indeed, antiquity provides nothing other than evidence that the thing lacks an owner; this fact—that the owner is not found—is the reason in the same way that no injury is done to anyone, because it does not appear against whom a theft might be committed.

Furthermore, that there is no positive law <note>Man-made law (civil or canon) as opposed to natural law.</note> which grants these things to the poor is proven. For the legal experts assert none except the chapter *Tua* regarding usury and similar laws, by which money from usury or simony <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred things or ecclesiastical offices.</note> is adjudged to the poor. But laws of this kind only speak of things evilly acquired and obtained, as held in the canon *Non sane* (14, question 5). Discovery, however, is not an inequitable acquisition, but a lawful one; nor is it a clear debt such as what you received by loan or credit.

<margin>Second reason.</margin> 
Secondly, it is argued: Before the law of the Gospel, it is most probable that by the law of nature, found things belonged to the finder, just like ancient treasures. For the laws make no other distinction than this: if a thing is found which is presumed to have owners, it should not be taken except with the intention of returning it to the owners. This law only compels the finder to search diligently. For this is the sense of the law *falsus* in the Digest regarding theft, which says that he who takes a found item with the intention of not returning it is guilty of theft...

# Book Five, Question III.

...if he does not know the owner: namely, because he is bound to search for him. If, however, the owner is not found, nothing is said [in the law] about the poor. Therefore, there is no reason why, under the Law of the Gospel, it should become a debt of justice to bestow these things upon them. ¶ But you may say that such things fall under the common right of the commonwealth, and therefore should be applied to its poor. This, however, is certainly not sufficiently proven. For we showed above that this is only true where it is clear that someone owes something to an unknown owner—specifically because he received it unjustly or under the promise of returning it. A discovery, however, is not of this kind; rather, it is a "benefit of God," as the law says, to find something. Indeed, if such things fell to the common right of the commonwealth or the poor, I do not see why ancient treasures should not as well. Nor does it stand in your way if you say that the person who <margin>lost.</margin> lost it does not lose his right, but would wish for it to be given to the poor so that it might result in his spiritual benefit. For if no injury is done to him by the very fact that he cannot be found, by that same fact he lacks the ability to execute his right of seeking it. Likewise, if it is clear to me that the one who lost it is a Turk <note>In the 16th century, "Turk" was often used as a general term for a non-Christian or an enemy of the faith.</note>, how will it benefit him for it to be given to the poor? Therefore, the right does not pass to the poor because of the good of the loser (for he could even be a wicked man), but from another source—namely, because these are "redundant" goods in the commonwealth. Yet this is not sufficiently <margin>Another reason for the same point.</margin> proven, since it is not proven that they are owed. Furthermore, it is a great argument for me that Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto.</note> mentions nothing here about the poor; he says only that a finder who believes in good faith that things are held as abandoned [**pro derelictis**] does not commit theft by keeping them for himself. Certainly, once due diligence is done, they are considered abandoned. For he is speaking then not of ancient treasures, but of those things which recently had an owner. The arguments brought from Augustine and Jerome in the 14th Question, 5th Article, prove nothing. Augustine says, "I say, if you found something and did not return it, you have snatched it away." And Jerome says in the canon *Multi*: "It is a sin similar to robbery if someone does not return what was found." However, they clearly mean when the owner can be found and the finder <margin>The author's opinion.</margin> does not inquire in good faith. ¶ Let us conclude, therefore, first: that where the finder is indigent, he can safely take either the whole find or a part for his own necessity. This is something that even the supporters of the opposite opinion admit, as is clear in the same Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a prominent legal-theologian cited on the previous page.</note> in the place cited, provided he does this on the advice of a prelate or a confessor—though perhaps even that is not strictly necessary. Second: if the one who finds it is rich, the most wholesome counsel is that found items whose owners cannot be found should be distributed to the poor or 

<column-break/>

for public and pious uses. For as Gregory says: <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> "It is the mark of a God-fearing soul to acknowledge a fault where there is no fault." <note>original: "Timorati animi est, ibi culpā agnoscere, vbi culpa non est." This means a sensitive conscience worries about sin even in permissible acts.</note> But as to whether this is a mandatory command, I would not quite dare to affirm it. However, whoever would maintain this will defend his opinion by the fact that, by natural law, those things which are "redundant" [surplus] in the commonwealth belong to the needy, as we shall say in the very next article. That these things are redundant appears in a way from the fact that they have no certain owners; yet they are presumed to have had some owners, which does not apply to ancient treasures.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin> TO the third argument, it is responded that theft is judged not to be a great fault in two ways. First, on the part of the subject: because it is mitigated by the necessity of the one stealing. Furthermore, because as we just said, in its kind [**genere suo**], it is the least compared to other mortal sins. Hence it is added in the same place: "A thief, when caught, shall restore sevenfold; but he who is an adulterer shall lose his own soul." <note>A paraphrase combining elements of Proverbs 6:30-32.</note> ¶ Regarding the second part, it is responded that a theft can happen that is so slight and so meager that it is not a mortal sin; for this reason, it was said to be mortal "in its kind" <note>A technical scholastic distinction: an act might be "mortally sinful" by its nature (like stealing), but "venial" in practice if the matter is trivial (like stealing a grape).</note>. However, a reason for doubt arises here: how <margin>Doubt.</margin> should the quantity of a theft be weighed so that it carries only a venial fault? Should it be weighed relatively or absolutely? Indeed, since the gravity of theft must be weighed by the damage caused, and <margin>The reason for the hesitation.</margin> you might harm a needy person more, for example, by stealing a single farthing [**quadrantem**] than you would a very rich man from whom you snatched a gold ducat, it seems to follow that it should be estimated relatively. On the contrary, however, it is argued that if this were true, it would follow that stealing a hundred gold coins from the Emperor would never be a mortal crime, since he receives far less damage from it than a poor old woman from whom you might snatch two small coins [**minuta**]. For even in the Gospel, the almsgiving of that old woman was more abundantly commended for the reason that she put more into the treasury relative to her means. <note>Referring to the "Widow's Mite" in Mark 12:41–44.</note> ¶ This <margin>A distinction.</margin> dispute, however, is settled by a distinction. For there is some quantity of money so great that by itself, without any respect to the person, it is the cause of mortal sin in theft. For instance, if we say two or three gold ducats; therefore, even if they are stolen from the Emperor, although he himself may value them at a straw, it is nonetheless a crime. But there is another sum so small that it does not have so much fault in itself, yet it would become mortal due to the poverty of the owner: as if you were to steal a silver coin or a double-coin from a wretched man. For such a sense, as he thinks, is contrary to reason; rather, he says Thomas meant only that he who has the intent of 
<margin>The mind of St. Thomas.</margin>

But indeed, even if the mind of St. Thomas is not so clear, I would believe the opposite of what Cajetan refutes to be true. For if I know the character of a faint-hearted man who is greatly offended and disturbed in mind and afflicted by minimal things, and is perhaps stirred to anger, surely if I had the intent of harming him through those minimal things, I would violate charity and friendship; for because of this, he would be my enemy, and thus I would fail mortally. And this is true not only by harming him in deed, but even in word and gesture. I say "minimal things" by which narrow-minded men are accustomed to be vehemently offended; for they could be so small that someone who considered himself offended by them would be held up to mockery: and then an injury of that kind would not be a fault. ¶ 
<margin>Another objection.</margin>

<column-break/>

For then a transition from one category to another <note>original: "transitus de genere in genus"</note> would occur. Yet the consequence is false. <margin>Reply.</margin>
studious reader rising up against this solution in this way. It would follow at least that if the same thief did not commit such thefts from the same persons, but from different ones—so that he took a penny <note>original: "obolum"</note> from one and then another, and subsequently a farthing or another small coin from another—he would never sin mortally. This is proven: because he gives a grave loss to no one. Nor indeed is there any rebuttal in the fact that he himself receives a great gain: for theft is not to be estimated from the gain accruing to the thief, but from the damage given. If, however, you grant the consequence with its resulting parts, you admit that a thief can be enriched by another’s substance without mortal sin; and thus you would provide patronage to those public buyers who defraud various people in small amounts. For according to your opinion, they would not sin mortally. ### Question III of Book Five

Whether that [punishment] is deserved is another question: for since external goods are not to be held in such high regard, especially among Christians—whom Christ admonished to leave behind both cloak and tunic to one who asks <note>A reference to Matthew 5:40: "And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also."</note>—there appears no reason for a life to be taken for a theft. Common law <term>ius commune; the legal system based on Roman and Canon law used in Europe during this period</term> also supports this. For although that penalty once existed in the ancient laws, it was later seen as cruel. Therefore, care was taken that no one should be punished by death for a simple theft, as held in the law *But by the new law* <note>original: "l. sed nouo iure." C. de seruis fugit.</note> and in the *Authenticum* titled *That no judge be allowed to have...* <note>original: "Authē. vt nulli iudici liceat habere."</note> collection 9. Only public robbers <term>latrones; specifically those who use violence or highway robbery, as opposed to "fures" or secret thieves</term> are deemed worthy of such a death. And indeed, in the time of Saint Thomas, it was not the practice to hang simple thieves, but only robbers, from the gallows. For he says that punishment should not be inflicted for every mortal sin, but only for that by which irreparable damage is done—which theft is not. Indeed, in Spain, this law was formerly observed, as is clear in Part 7, Title 14, Law 18; only the sacrilegious who plundered sacred things and others of that kind were hanged. Later, however, as the audacity of lost men grew, the penalties were increased.

<margin>The opinion of Baldus.</margin>
¶ And I believe that Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential Italian jurist.</note> was the cause of this punishment; who, concerning that same law, *But by the new law*, asserted two things. First, that even if a thief is not worthy of death for a simple or a double theft, a third offense is already considered robbery. Second, he infers from this that when one theft is massive, it is then equivalent to three. 

<margin>First objection against the opinion of Baldus.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, though I would not murmur against the laws, nevertheless Baldus’s reasoning is null. For first, robbers are not to be judged solely by the frequency of their acts, but by the manner: namely, because they use force and disturb the commonwealth with plunder, and they alone are designated for death by law. A thief, however, though he may sin repeatedly, if he always does so secretly—such that he neither blockades public roads, nor makes a break-in into homes, nor offers slaughter—is not considered a robber. Therefore, he ought to enjoy ecclesiastical privilege <note>The right of sanctuary within a church to avoid secular punishment.</note> if he retreats into a sacred place. 

<margin>Second [objection].</margin>
And thus his second assertion has much less probability: that because a massive theft is equivalent to three, it is worthy of death. For although it may be equivalent in quantity, it is not so in the manner, such that it should be considered robbery—although, on account of notable audacity, it bears a resemblance to it. However, what he finally brings forward as the reason for his assertion—namely, that it is permissible to transgress the laws on account of an enormous crime—is unworthy of a legal expert. For to transgress the laws is a sin, and a sin cannot be permissible. But perhaps he calls it a "transgression" when something is done against the words of the law, yet not against its intent.

<column-break/>

Nevertheless, it must be noted further here <gloss>that</gloss> the assertion of Baldus or any other doctor <term>doctor; a high-ranking legal or theological scholar</term> can in no way be held as law; indeed, not even the dictates of the Jurists themselves, unless their teachings have been received as laws either by the authority of the prince or by the custom and practice of the commonwealth. For, as was demonstrated in Book 1, only public authority has the power to establish a law that has coercive force. 

<margin>Practice now follows even Baldus.</margin>
¶ It is therefore now most widely accepted that thieves, for a simple or double theft, if it is not large, are either beaten with whips, or have their ears cut off, or are branded with iron and banished. But for a third offense or for one enormous theft, they are hanged from the gallows. This law is also the custom among the Spanish, as is clear in Book 4 of the *Royal Forum* <note>original: "regalis for." referring to the Fuero Real, a 13th-century Spanish legal code.</note>, Title 15, Law 6: he who has stolen 40 *dipondia* <note>An ancient Roman unit of currency; Soto is comparing historical currency to contemporary values.</note> must pay nine times as much. But if he commits a similar theft a second time, he shall be killed. Nevertheless, that same law is not in use now under that level of rigor, such that someone would be hanged for a tenth part of one ducat. For that amount was perhaps valued more highly then than double a ducat is now.

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether it is lawful for one who is pressed by poverty to steal.<-

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
After the injustice of theft has been shown under such strict law, it is fitting to dispute whether any case should be excepted from it—at least where extreme necessity strikes. And it is argued first for the negative side, from that chapter cited above, *If anyone* <note>original: "si quis."</note> in the *Extravagantes* <note>Collections of Canon Law not included in the original Decrees.</note> regarding theft: where it is held that if someone, because of the necessity of hunger, has stolen clothing, food, or cattle, he should do penance for three weeks. This would not be ordered unless theft were then unlawful. 

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, the same is argued from Aristotle’s *Ethics*, Book 2, where he says certain things are immediately entangled with malice as soon as they are named; and he adds the example of theft. This signifies that it is intrinsically evil, and therefore can be made lawful for no end and for no cause; in which it is similar to a lie. 

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: a man ought to love his neighbor as himself. But it is not lawful for anyone to steal in order to help a neighbor through alms, as Augustine warns in his book *Against Lying*; therefore, it is not lawful to do so to help oneself.

¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that in necessity—as the common axiom goes—all things are common.

### Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A responsive conclusion. Ambrose.</margin> **T**he question is answered with three conclusions. The first: Goods that are surplus to a person are owed, by the law of nature, to the support of the poor. This is the authority of Ambrose, which is recorded among the decrees, distinction 47: "The bread you withhold belongs to the hungry; the clothing you lock away belongs to the naked; the money you bury in the earth is the redemption and release of the wretched." <note>original: "esurientium panis est, quem tu detines : nudorum indumentum est, quod tu recludis: miserorum redemptio & absolutio est, pecunia quam tu in terra defodis."</note> The natural reasoning is gathered as follows: No law of nations <term>ius gentium; the laws shared by all civilized peoples</term> or human law can detract from natural or divine law, since these are superior. By the law of nature and divine providence, it was established that lower things should serve the necessity of humans, for whose sake they were created. Therefore, where such surplus goods do not serve their possessor, they could not be forbidden by any human law from being put to the use of the needy.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion: Notwithstanding this, no one outside of extreme necessity can snatch away the goods of one who has plenty. This is proven because, even if that wealthy man is bound to distribute those same goods, there are many needy people appearing at different times and places; therefore, it is proper for that charitable distribution to be carried out by the possessor.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin> ¶ The third conclusion: In extreme necessity—that is, where it is evident and urgent—then that person in distress may lawfully use the property of others to help himself, whether those things are taken secretly or openly. This conclusion has already been asserted by us many times: for the right of preserving oneself is so innate to man that all other things yield to it.

<margin>Declaration of the first conclusion.</margin> ¶ You should not understand the first of these conclusions to sound like an obligation of justice, but only of mercy, as we noted in Book 4, Question 2, concerning the division of things. For after things were divided, each person is the master of his own. Nevertheless, the common natural right persists to the extent that one who has plenty ought to be beneficial to the needy. By this reasoning, the truth of the second conclusion arises: namely, that no one, however much they are suffering, may steal from a rich man. Nor is the following argument valid: "The rich man in such a case (namely, grave necessity) is bound to give to the needy," according to the words of John in his canonical letter: "He who sees his brother in need and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God abide in him?" <note>1 John 3:17</note> Therefore, [it is argued] that the needy person may seize it by his own authority. This is not valid because that obligation is not of justice, but of charity, to which no one can be compelled against their will. But indeed, this matter of the obligation of almsgiving is not for this present place. For Saint Thomas treats it in the *Secunda Secundae*, Question 32. ¶ Concerning the third conclusion, however, which pertains to the present matter:

<column-break/>

<margin>What should be called extreme necessity.</margin> There is a doubt as to what kind of necessity should be judged as "extreme." Is it only when someone is already being strangled by hunger, or consumed by cold or some other calamity? For the name itself, "extreme," seems to designate that. <margin>Response.</margin> It is responded, however, that one should not wait for that moment, as the common people believe. For there are those who call that "extreme necessity" for which a remedy is then impossible. That point is therefore considered the moment of extreme necessity when you see a brother approaching the danger of an incurable sickness, or another misery that usually consumes men—when, I say, the greatest misery can still be prevented and avoided. Indeed, a necessity that places a person in danger of losing their honor, although it is not considered "extreme," is nevertheless certainly "grave"; it binds the one who has the means to bring aid under the guilt of mortal sin. ¶ But what if a girl is in danger of losing her modesty <term>pudor; referring to her chastity or virtue</term> due to a lack of food? For it seems that this too should be considered extreme, since not only honor but even the salvation of the soul is endangered. It is responded, nonetheless, that although it is an illustrious duty of mercy to help such wretched people endangered in their orphanhood, it is not considered "extreme" such that the girl may seize another's property. For there is no necessity that can compel her to make herself available to another <note>meaning, to resort to prostitution</note>; otherwise, that consent would not be a sin; but she ought to perish rather than commit a crime. Furthermore, there are civil laws by which it is ordered that one suffering extremely should resort to a public magistrate before taking another's property privately. This, however, is to be understood as being when it can be done conveniently. <margin>Objection against the response.</margin> ¶ But indeed, perhaps someone will rise up against us in the present case. For we have said both elsewhere many times and just a moment ago, that no one can be compelled to that which he is bound by charity alone, but only to that to which he is obligated by justice. No one is bound to help in extreme necessity except out of charity—for if the obligation were of justice, he who did not help then would be bound to restitution <term>restitutio; the legal and moral act of making good on a loss or returning stolen property</term>, which he does not concede. Therefore, neither can public power then rightfully compel anyone, nor can the one who is in danger privately take anything of another's. <margin>Solution.</margin> It is responded that it matters little whether you say some reasoning of justice intervenes in such necessity; strictly speaking, however, it is nothing but mercy, yet binding most strictly. That coercion then has a place is because of the unique right that belongs to everyone to preserve their own life. ¶ Things to be weighed...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is "Appendenda," indicating the next page will continue the list of points to be weighed or considered.</meta>

<summary>Soto explores the moral limits of private property, concluding that while surplus goods are owed to the poor by natural law, individuals may only take from others without permission in cases of "extreme necessity" to preserve life. He distinguishes between the obligations of charity (mercy) and legal justice, arguing that the right to life is the highest natural right.</summary>

# Book Five, Question III.

The debate should have been weighed here as to whether someone who, in a moment of necessity, seizes another's property is bound to restore it if they later happen upon better fortune. However, this discussion was already sufficiently completed in the preceding book under the title concerning restitution.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, regarding the Canon cited in the first argument, the response there was that it refers to a necessity which is not "extreme" <note>In scholastic law, "extreme necessity" is a life-or-death situation where property laws are suspended.</note>; in such a case, it is indeed a fault to steal.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, we frankly concede that theft is an action that is intrinsically evil; indeed, as we said in Book 2, it is of such a nature that God, as the author of the law of nature, cannot grant a dispensation for it. But just as we said regarding the prohibition of homicide—that in the general command, "Thou shalt not kill," <note>original: "Non occides"</note> because it is a natural precept, those cases which nature itself cannot include are not encompassed—nor in the command, "Do not swear at all" <note>original: "Non iurare omnino"</note>—so too the prohibition of theft could not forbid the taking of another’s property which nature itself has granted to humanity in dire need. Therefore, such a taking is not theft, but the acceptance of a thing granted by nature.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third, the response is that everyone has an equal right in the same necessity to seize another's property to help the needy. But outside of that necessity, Augustine forbids alms to be made from "rapine" <note>rapine: taking property by force or pillage.</note>.
