### ARTICLE V.
### Whether robbery can in any way be done without sin.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' within a square frame featuring floral scrollwork.</image-desc> **A**lthough theft may be permitted in extreme necessity, nevertheless, because robbery (*rapina*) is a more atrocious crime, it remains to be seen whether it too is sometimes permitted. The argument is made for the affirmative side. Plunder is carried out by force, which has the character of robbery; yet, Ambrose, in his book *On the Patriarchs*, judged it permitted to take plunder from enemies. There he says: "When the plunder is in the power of the victors, it befits military discipline that everything be reserved for the king," specifically for the expenses of war as well as for the rewards of the soldiers. Therefore, robbery is permitted in some cases.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: The princes of lands extort many things from their subjects against their will, which carries the appearance of robbery, and yet it is a serious matter to judge them as wrongdoers. Therefore, robbery is not everywhere a mortal crime.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued: That which does not belong to the possessor may be licitly taken from him. However, unbelievers are unjust 

<column-break/>

possessors of their goods, according to that saying of Augustine in his letter to Vincent the Donatist: "You falsely call things yours, which you neither possess justly, and which you have been ordered to lose according to the laws of earthly rulers." <note>original: "Res falso appellatis vestras, quas neque iuste possidetis, & secundum leges terrenarum legum amittere iussi estis"</note> Therefore, it appears licit to snatch these same things from them.

> ¶ To the contrary is the fact that, as a thing unjustly acquired, a sacrifice or offering is forbidden to be made from robbery, according to Isaiah 61: "For I the Lord love justice, and I hate robbery in a burnt offering." <note>original: "Ego Dominus diligens iudicium, & odiens rapinam in holocaustum."</note>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with three conclusions. First: Robbery is in no way permitted, neither to private nor to public power. Thus, just as theft is never permitted—and where the taking of another’s property is permitted, it does not have the character of theft—so, by an even stronger reasoning, must it be judged regarding robbery. It is proved: whatever by its very name has an innate character of injustice is so intrinsically evil that it cannot be done well. Robbery, however, means the same thing as a violent taking against justice, just as theft means a fraudulent one. Therefore, robbery can in no way be permitted.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ But for a greater explanation of this, two other conclusions are added. The second conclusion is: Only the state <term>respublica; the commonwealth or organized political community</term> and the prince who acts in its place can, through violence, extort something from its citizens without injury. Whoever, however, by private authority seizes something through violence is a robber and a thief, and is thus guilty of this iniquity. Both parts of this are proved at once. To apply violence is a duty proper to public authority, for violence is the same as coercion; but coercive power <term>vis coactiva; the legal right to use force</term> resides only in the state and in the prince who represents it, just as only the whole animal can compel its members. For this power was granted by nature itself to restrain men from evil and lead them to good. This grant, as we said above, was not expedient to be given to private individuals, because it ought to be carried out through mature judgment. From this it follows that violence in a prince, if done by the proper way and order, does not have the character of robbery—namely, if he uses it either against external enemies or against internal evildoers according to the prescription of the law. In a private person, however, such violence always has the character of robbery. And for this reason, in the third article, even for someone who is certain that a thing possessed by another is his own, and can legally prove it, but cannot obtain it because of the injustice of a judge, we denied that he could seize the thing by force.

<summary>Soto distinguishes between "theft" (secret taking) and "robbery" (taking by force), arguing that while extreme necessity may justify taking property, only the state holds the legitimate authority to use force. Private acts of violence to reclaim property are condemned as robbery, as the right to coercion belongs solely to the public authority for the common good.</summary>

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right
### Page 430

...to attack. But if you should object that at least the person who suffers extreme need is an exception, I believe that by the very law of nature he is exempt from this law. For the preservation of life holds such a high place in natural law that a taking under such duress should not be marked with the character of robbery <note>Soto uses the term "rapina" for robbery, which in scholastic law implies taking by force or violence, as opposed to "furtum" or secret theft.</note>.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: If a prince, or a judge, or any other magistrate abuses his power to seize anything from citizens by force, he commits the notorious crime of robbery, and he is bound to make restitution. Indeed, such powerful figures sin all the more shamelessly and wickedly because they ought to keep justice—of which they are the appointed guardians—immaculate toward everyone with the most sacred faith.

<margin>Saint Thomas responds to the first argument.</margin>
Regarding these conclusions, there is no ambiguity except for those points hinted at through the proposed arguments. Indeed, to the first argument concerning war booty, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> responds that in a just war, booty is lawful and does not carry an obligation of restitution. Nevertheless, the sin of greed against charity <note>Charity here refers to "caritas," the Christian love of neighbor.</note> can still be committed even then:

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
as Augustine says in his book *On the Words of the Lord*: to serve as a soldier for the sake of booty is a sin. But if the war is unjust, robbery is committed.

<margin>Unjust war stems from three sources.</margin>
¶ Now, an unjust war, as we said in Book 3 concerning judgment, occurs for three main reasons.

<margin>The first.</margin>
First, from a defect of authority: for only princes possessing sovereign authority <term>merum imperium; the highest legal power to command and punish</term> have the right either to declare or to wage war. Other magnates and powers subject to kings do not; they may only use force against wrongdoers who are their own subjects. Therefore, if they attack foreigners by force of arms, they must be judged as private persons and they commit robbery, even if they otherwise had a just cause.

<margin>The second.</margin>
Next, the justice of a war requires a cause—not just any cause, but one worthy enough to undergo such enormous dangers and to stir up such calamitous and destructive disturbances in the commonwealth. For in the tumults of war, not only are all secular things endangered, but also the spiritual health of the commonwealth, all sacred things, and faith itself.

<margin>The third.</margin>
Thirdly, the form of law is required, and this must be followed even more exactly than in private judgments, as the stakes involve the ultimate public good. Specifically, war should not be declared unless all methods of peace have first been offered, nor should it be carried further than equity allows. But more on this elsewhere. Therefore, booty from a just war is lawful, not only to repair damages but also to be distributed among the soldiers. And although the primary duty falls upon the prince to weigh the merits of the justice 

<column-break/>

of the war—and in this respect, even if he himself provokes an unjust war, the soldiers are sometimes excused—the injustice could nevertheless be so blatant that it would strip even the subjects of any excuse.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument concerning princes and magnates, the conclusions themselves respond sufficiently: namely, that if they use force to extort what contributes to the common good, it is not the crime of robbery. However, if they squeeze out anything beyond what is right, they are not free from crime. In fact, they offend all the more wickedly because there is no one who can resist their power. Hence Augustine says in Book 4 of *The City of God*: "If justice is removed, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies but small kingdoms?" <note>original: "Remota iustitia, quid sunt regna nisi magna latrocinia? quia latrocinia quid sunt nisi parua regna?"</note> And Ezekiel 22 says: "Her princes in her midst are like wolves seizing prey." <note>original: "Principes eius in medio eius quasi lupi rapientes prædam"</note> Thus it follows that they are also bound to make restitution.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ The third argument offered a very broad and, in these times—I know not whether I should say—necessary dispute concerning the right of waging war against non-believers, on account of that Western World <note>A reference to the Americas and the ongoing debates in Spain regarding the rights of Indigenous peoples.</note> which our people discovered in our century. But for good reason, as we said in the preceding book under the title concerning dominion, we have refrained from such a dispute in this work. However, God willing, we shall produce a small book *On the Method of Promulgating the Gospel*, where we intend to treat these matters according to our capacity, if not according to the dignity of the subject.

<margin>Three ranks of non-believers.</margin>
In the meantime, however, it will suffice for interpreting Augustine to note that there are three ranks of non-believers.

<margin>The first.</margin>
Some are those who, by right and in fact, live their lives under the jurisdiction of Christian princes; such were once the Saracens <note>Muslims</note> and Hebrews in Spain, and the Jews who continue to live in Italy and Germany today. Regarding these, no one doubts that Christian princes are able to act against them by law and even deprive them of their goods. This truth is widely evident, both in the *Decretals* under the title "Concerning Jews and Saracens," as well as in the *Decrees*, distinction 54. Closely following these are the heretics who, as John says, "went out from us." <note>1 John 2:19</note> It was specifically about these that Augustine was speaking. For his discourse was against the Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa during late antiquity.</note>; it is most clear in both canon and civil law that heretics in general were to be punished by the loss of their goods, as appears in the chapter *Cum tu* in the sixth book of the *Decretals*.

<margin>The second.</margin>
¶ Others are non-believers who, although not in fact, are nonetheless subject to Christian princes by right—at least regarding the possession of their kingdoms. Namely, those who possess lands by force which were once under our jurisdiction, such as the Africans, the Saracens, and the Turks [who occupy] Greece...

<summary>Soto defines the crime of "rapina" (robbery by force), arguing that magistrates who abuse their power or leaders who wage unjust wars are guilty of this crime and must make restitution. He also begins categorizing non-believers (infidels) to determine when a Christian state has the legal right to seize their property or territory.</summary>

# Book Five, Question III.

...holding Greece by tyranny <note>Soto is referring to the Ottoman Turks, who had conquered the former Byzantine (Greek) Empire.</note>. Regarding these, it is also certain that they can be provoked by us in war, and even be stripped of those same regions. Nevertheless, by private authority, no one among us who is traveling through their lands has the power to either plunder or snatch away their goods. This is partly because, beyond the regions themselves, the domestic goods which they earn by their own industry are their own; and it is chiefly because public authority is required to subjugate them. Therefore, no one can be a nuisance to them unless by the power and grant of the prince.

<margin>Third order.</margin>
¶ However, there is a third order of infidels: those who are subject to us neither by law nor by fact, nor indeed are they hostile to us. Such are those who have either not heard the Christian name, or—what amounts to the same thing—are excused through a forgetfulness that surpasses all memory. Strictly speaking, however, no one is excused: for since the whole world is bound to receive the faith once they have heard its preaching, if they had rightly observed the <term>law of nature</term> <note>The "lex naturae" refers to basic moral principles known to all humans through reason, such as "do good and avoid evil."</note>, Christ would have illuminated them with faith in some way of His own. Yet they are said to be "excused" in the sense that, as long as they hear nothing of the faith, their lack of belief is not a sin. Regarding these, a dispute is often contested as to whether it is lawful for us to attack them in war.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Indeed, *Cajetan* <note>Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> here, while interpreting the opinion of Saint Thomas, denies that any right favors Christians to drive them from their seats and possessions. For as *Saint Thomas* says in the *Second Part of the Second Part, Question 10, Article 10*: *Faith does not take away nature, but perfects it.* And thus, it takes away from no one the possessions which mortals obtain by the <term>law of nations</term> <note>Original: "iure gentium." This refers to the customary laws shared by all civilized peoples, including the right to own property and govern themselves.</note>. This is primarily because the species of "negative infidelity"—that is, the state of those who have heard nothing of the Christian name—is neither a sin nor worthy of any punishment. On the contrary, he says that we do not read that the children of Israel ever declared war on any infidels solely because they were infidels. Regarding this point, Cajetan is poorly understood and criticized by some. For first, he does not deny that it was lawful for them to war against infidels on account of idolatry by God's command; he only denies that they were warred upon *solely* because they were infidels—that is, "negatively," meaning only because they lacked the faith—as opposed to being warred upon for idolatry. Furthermore, if he is speaking of the war waged against the possessors of the Promised Land, he can also be understood soundly. For I see some scholars "clashing swords" <note>Original: "digladiari," a metaphor for a sharp intellectual dispute.</note> over whether God ordered those nations to be driven from their seats because of their own crimes and the impiety of their idolatry, or rather solely to fulfill the promise He had made to Abraham and his seed to hand that region over to them. Yet, beyond any doubt, it is more certain than certain that both were the cause.

<column-break/>

For in that instance, one must consider both the expulsion of the nations and the introduction of the divine people. Indeed, the most just cause of the expulsion was their own crimes; but the cause of the introduction was the promise made to the people. But while God could have extinguished all the idolaters of the whole world by the same right, He nonetheless singularly expelled those ones from there so that He might plant His own people there. Therefore, perhaps He commanded that war not only because of idolatry, but so that God might fulfill His promise. And I believe this is the legitimate sense of those words in *Deuteronomy 9, where both causes are joined:* *Because those (namely the nations) acted impiously, they were destroyed as you entered: and that the Lord might fulfill His word which He promised with an oath to your fathers.* ¶ But the point of the question—whether it is lawful for us to attack in war those infidels of the third order who attempt nothing against us—does not consist in this: that the impiety of idolatry and the monstrosity of their other crimes are worthy of death. For this cannot be denied by anyone, since the Christian commonwealth most deservedly punishes those same crimes with death. Therefore, those who contend over this point torture themselves in vain. Nevertheless, since (as we said in Book 3) two things are required for a right judgment—namely, both a just cause in the crime and a legitimate power in the judge—the whole dispute depends on this: whether we are their legitimate judges and the punishers of their crimes. For just because God, the Lord of the whole world, has at any time punished whatever crimes He willed, to argue that we can do the same to all infidels is just like arguing that because a king can root out all evildoers in his entire kingdom, any one of the nobles who has jurisdiction under him can likewise enter the territory of another to carry out that duty. Therefore, it must be demonstrated from another source—if it be true—that we possess such power. However, as we said in the preceding book under the title "On Dominion," we have decided that for a good reason we should refrain from this dispute in this work. If perhaps by divine favor it is permitted to us to publish a small book *On the Method of Promulgating the Gospel*, this dispute will be completed there in all its parts to the best of our ability.

<summary>Soto argues that Christians cannot justly seize the property of non-hostile non-believers who have never heard the Gospel, as faith does not abolish natural property rights (ius gentium). He emphasizes that while crimes like idolatry are inherently punishable, the central legal issue is whether Christian princes have the specific jurisdiction to act as judges over foreign peoples.</summary>

### ARTICLE VI.
*Whether robbery is more serious than theft.*

<note>In scholastic legal thought, "theft" (furtum) refers to taking property in secret, while "robbery" (rapina) refers to taking property by force or violence.</note>

Since we have discussed theft and robbery in the present question, and have shown them to be two distinct types, it is appropriate at the conclusion of this dispute to ask which of these vices excels the other in gravity. It is argued that theft is worse: first, because beyond robbery it adds fraud and deceit, which in themselves increase the degree of sin; and also because shame and fear arise from the baseness of the act. Men are more ashamed of theft than of robbery; therefore, theft is more wicked. ¶ Furthermore, a crime is more iniquitous the more people it harms; yet theft causes harm to more people—namely, not only to the great lords, but also to the commoners and people of every class. Violence and robbery, however, are only inflicted upon the powerful who are able to resist. Therefore, theft is more serious than robbery. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that the laws punish bandits and robbers more severely than they do thieves.

**I**t is responded to the question with a single and very easy conclusion: Robbery is a more serious sin than theft. This conclusion is clearly evident from what has already been said. For it was stated that these two meet in this one definition: both are the taking of another’s property against the owner's will. The difference is that theft removes the owner's will through ignorance <note>original: "per ignorantiam" — meaning the owner is unaware the act is happening</note>, whereas robbery does so through violence. Now, violence is more directly opposed to the will than ignorance is. For violence fights in "open war" <note>original: "aperto Marte"</note> against the act of refusing, while ignorance makes the act involuntary simply through the absence of choice. For he who is ignorant does not "will" the loss, but he who resists "wills" the opposite. For this reason, robbery is worse. There is also the reason of the injury, which is more heaped up in robbery. For a thief shows a kind of respect for the owner—whom he does not dare to attack openly out of fear, but only secretly—whereas a robber thinks much less of him, since he attacks him without fear. Therefore, the robber harms him not only in his goods, but also in his honor through ignominy <note>Public disgrace or dishonor.</note>. For this same reason, an insult is worse than backbiting (as we shall say below). Indeed, a third reason is added: the robber inflicts injury not only upon external goods and honor,

<column-break/>

but also offers a danger to life. For the robber and the bandit use arms to kill anyone who resists. The thief, however, is always pale with dread and fear. For this reason, the common laws themselves, which grant thieves their lives, adjudge bandits entirely to death—so much so that they do not even allow the refuge of sacred sanctuary to protect them. <note>original: "perfugium ad sacrun" — the medieval right of a criminal to seek safety from the law within a church.</note> ¶ And through these points, the solutions to the arguments become clear. For even if there is some fraud in theft, the audacity and injury of robbery are nonetheless worse. ¶ To the second argument, it is responded that among worldly people, audacity is commonly regarded as a sign of courage; and so it happens that even while it is displayed in the perpetration of crimes, men are less ashamed of it. Yet, in crimes, fear (such as a thief feels) is actually an argument for lesser guilt. ¶ To the third, it is finally responded that although harm is usually inflicted on more people through theft, more serious harms are inflicted through violence.

# QUESTION FOUR,
## On the injustice of a judge.
### ARTICLE I.
*Whether it is lawful for a judge to judge someone who is not subject to him.*

The next type of injustice after those committed by deed (whether against a person or against property) is that which is committed by words. Of this kind, the most iniquitous is that which is customary in legal judgments: namely, the fault of judges, as well as of witnesses and the other ministers of justice. For there are five persons involved: the Judge, the accuser, the defendant, the witness, and the advocate. These five demand five questions. But among these, the crimes of the Judge are considered the most serious. Four things are necessary in a judge: the power of judging <note>Jurisdiction.</note>, truth, proper form, and the force of execution. These will be explained in four articles. The first vice, then, is if he should usurp the faculty of judging which he does not possess. Therefore, to examine this in this first article, it is asked whether anyone can judge a person who is not subject to him. And it is argued on the affirmative side: Christ...

# Book Five, Question IV.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Christ, being indeed the King of Kings and Lord of lords, was subject to no creature; and yet he underwent the judgment of Pilate. Pilate is not typically rebuked for this on the grounds that he judged someone not subject to him, but rather because he condemned an innocent man. Therefore, it seems someone may exercise jurisdiction over a foreign citizen. ¶ Second: Daniel (as his history in chapter 13 relates) condemned those elders who were false witnesses to a crime, yet he is not recorded as having been a judge; therefore, jurisdiction can be exercised without formal authority. ¶ Third: Laws often grant a judge the power of punishing based on the nature of the crime for those who, although they are not his subjects, nevertheless commit a transgression within the limits of his legal territory <note>original: "fori," referring to the 'forum' or specific legal jurisdiction</note>. Therefore, judging someone who is not a subject of the judge is not always unlawful. ¶ On the contrary is Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> commenting on that passage in Deuteronomy 23: "If you enter the standing grain," etc., where he says: "No one may put the sickle of judgment into a matter which appears to be committed to another."

<margin>Second.</margin>

<margin>Third.</margin>

<margin>Gregory.</margin>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
**T**o this question, although it might seem to require more extensive treatment given the nature of the arguments, two conclusions are sufficient. The first is: It is lawful for no one to judge anyone except the person who is subject to him, either simply <note>meaning by birth or residency</note> or by the circumstances of the specific case.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is proven. The sentence of a judge is like a certain particular law applied to a specific individual case. Now, a law (as shown above) must have coercive force: therefore, a sentence must as well. Otherwise, it would be frustrated and of no efficacy. However, no one can have this force except a prince, or the commonwealth and its ministers, to whom the citizens are subject as parts are to the whole. Therefore, each person can only legitimately judge one who is subject to him, insofar as he acts in the place of the commonwealth. For the same kind of practical wisdom necessary for making laws—namely, the authoritative kind—is also necessary for declaring the law <note>original: "ius dicatur"</note> according to those laws. Indeed, no coercive force would exist in laws unless it persisted in their application. From this, those legal principles flowed: "a sentence passed by one who is not the proper judge does not hold" (from the decretals on judges), and "one declaring the law outside his territory is not obeyed with impunity" (from the laws on constitutions). Hence, a judge is the same as one who "declares the law" <note>original: "ius dicens"</note>, and "jurisdiction" refers to both the power and the territory included within it. Nor does Paul command us to be subject except to "higher powers": that is, to those who are placed over us in rank and authority. For just as the celestial spheres do not influence higher substances, but rather the bodies that are subject to them in place, so too a man cannot

<column-break/>

govern anyone with laws and judgments except those subject to him. For this reason (as we said above), man as a "civil animal" lives in society.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: It happens in four ways that one person is subject to another. First, in an ordinary way, such as those subject to one who possesses power in his own right—as all Christians are subject to the Pope, and in secular matters, the whole kingdom to the king. In the second way, because one holds delegated power: such as a province being subject to a proconsul, or a city to a governor. In the third way, because someone voluntarily submits himself to the judgment of another: such as one who chooses an arbitrator <note>an independent person appointed to settle a dispute</note>, or one who prefers to undergo a trial that he could have otherwise contested. And fourth, if someone commits a crime in a foreign territory or "district" (as they say), or enters a foreign jurisdiction by some other path.

¶ Through these points, the objections are easily dissolved.

<margin>To the first argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
To the first, Saint Thomas Aquinas answers nothing else than that Christ submitted himself to Pilate by his own will to be judged, following the example of those who choose an arbitrator to whose judgment they are bound to obey under a set penalty.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
There is, however, some ambiguity in this example. For if the comparison is weighed strictly, it seems St. Thomas might have felt that Christ constituted Pilate as his judge by conferring on him a new power which he did not possess ordinarily—just as one might appoint a private person as a mediator over oneself. But this is false. For Pilate had received that power from Caesar, and therefore from God himself, by that reasoning shown in Book 4, Question 4: that the civil commonwealth is derived from God through the law of nature and the law of nations. And the Redeemer signified this in John 19, saying, "You would have no power against me at all unless it were given to you from above." From this, an argument is drawn against those who say that civil power descends from the Pope as if from the Vicar of Christ. For indeed, he does not say, "Unless it were given to you by *me*," but "from *above*." For Christ, as we said in the previous book, did not assume a temporal kingdom, but the use of temporal things that were necessary for his kingdom of heaven.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
Therefore, Saint Thomas only means that by the reason of being King of the kingdom of heaven, and likewise King of Kings and Lord of lords, he was exempt from all human judgment. In this exemption, he certainly left his Vicar, the Supreme Pontiff, and subsequently the lower priests, according to that passage in Matthew 17: "the sons are free." And therefore, although he could have contested Pilate's judgment, he nevertheless subjected himself to it by his own free will for the sake of our salvation, to be driven to his death.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
From this, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note> concludes that Pilate did not sin by "usurpation of judgment" <note>taking a jurisdiction he didn't have</note>.

<summary>This page explores the limits of judicial jurisdiction, arguing that a judge only has the right to rule over those who are naturally, legally, or voluntarily subject to him. It specifically addresses the theological problem of Christ being judged by Pilate, concluding that Christ submitted voluntarily rather than being naturally subject to Roman secular power.</summary>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right

... (for that he sinned by condemning an innocent man cannot be doubted), yet I would not so easily draw that conclusion. However, if Augustus was the legitimate king of the Jews, Pilate did not sin on those grounds: because Christ willed to be regarded as one of the Jews. But if he [Augustus] was a tyrant, Pilate failed in the same way by judging Christ as he did by judging the Jews: for our Redeemer did not grant him any other special faculty. Nor did St. Thomas intend to compare him in this regard to one who chooses an arbitrator. For an arbitrator receives power from the one who confers it, having lacked it before. Christ, however, did nothing other than freely suffer whatever was done to him. ¶ From this example of Christ, it follows that the Pope—His vicar, who is similarly exempt—can nonetheless submit himself to the judgment of another. This is true not only in the court of penance <note>original: "foro pœnitentiæ," referring to the internal sacramental confession</note> (which is a settled matter) but also in a judicial court. This was done by Pope Leo IV who, as we read in the canon *Nos si* (2. q. 7), submitted himself to the judgment of Emperor Louis <note>Louis II, Holy Roman Emperor</note> regarding certain matters to be judged so that he might justify himself.

<margin>*Corollary.*</margin>
<margin>*First doubt.*</margin>
¶ However, a twofold doubt arises concerning this matter. First, that it would follow that he could generally be compelled by the sentence of another in any causes whatsoever, even that of anathema <note>excommunication</note>: for the same reasoning seems to apply to all. Yet the Doctors, in their commentaries on the *Four Books of Sentences*, consistently deny this consequence: as seen in St. Thomas (distinction 19, question 1, article 3), Richard <note>Richard of Middleton</note> (distinction 18, article 5), and Petrus de Palude (question 2).

<margin>*St. Thomas. Richard. Petrus de Palude.*</margin>
<margin>*Final doubt.*</margin>
The second doubt concerns the manner of subjection. I mean to say, it seems he could so submit himself to another as to constitute that person as his superior or equal. But that this is false is shown by the fact that, since he is the Vicar of Christ, he does not have the power to place another in that same position. The logic is proven thus: Either his free subjection passes into necessity—so that he cannot withdraw from the one to whom he has once submitted while the trial lasts—and then it becomes clear that the one to whom he submitted is his superior, as his power does not depend on the Pope. Or, if the subjection is not necessary, it is useless.

<margin>*To the first doubt.*</margin>
¶ To the first of these, the logic is answered by striking down the consequence. For it does not follow that whatever he can do in some things, he can do in all. Rather, the rule is that whatever faculty he can exercise over himself in the external court <note>original: "foro exteriori," the public legal jurisdiction of the Church</note>, he is able to commit to another. For example, if perhaps a dispute is contested between himself and another—specifically where one seeks a debt from him, or he from another—or if there is an appeal from some sentence he himself brought forth, as if from an unjust

<column-break/>

grievance: just as he can then sit as judge over those causes himself, so he can also commit them to another and submit himself. And this he did in the aforementioned canon *Nos si*. However, he cannot excommunicate himself, nor suspend himself, nor properly punish himself; and therefore, he cannot appoint a judge for himself who may excommunicate, suspend, or punish him, but only one who may command him to make restitution or to revoke a sentence.

<margin>*To the second doubt.*</margin>
¶ Similarly, the logic of the second argument is struck down. For he cannot constitute someone as his superior or equal. Therefore, since there are two types of necessity—one of justice, and the other simply of coercion—his subjection can become "necessary" in the first way, but not the second. He can, I say, fortify and establish his subjection with a penalty—much like one who chooses a trustee—and he is bound to undergo the sentence, even in the court of God. Thus, it would be a mortal sin not to stand by his word, and he would be obligated to pay the penalty; therefore, the subjection is not in vain. Yet, by the necessity of coercion—such that the power of the judge would not depend on his own—he can subject himself to no one. Indeed, as often as he might wish to retract the sentence of the other and revoke that person’s power, even if he did so wrongly, the act would hold legal weight.

<margin>*Argument 1.*</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, a great argument exists that the Pope can submit himself to another, not only in minor causes, but even so that an anathema may be proceeded with against him, even unto deposition. For let us suppose from the chapter *Si Papa* (distinction 40) that when he is defiled by the stain of heresy, he can be convened and deposed by a Council. And since he should by no means be deposed unless he is heard, he could be compelled under the censure of anathema to appear. Suppose, then, that he suffers from a heavy infamy of heresy, such that a Council is just now about to judge that matter. Reason seems to persuade that he could delegate the judgment to circumspect and remarkably grave men. For it is argued thus: He can already then by right be made a defendant and be deposed once the cause is known, and this cannot be done without great expense to the bishops; therefore, to avoid that crowd of trials, he can commit the business to those who may settle the matter more expeditiously.

<margin>*Argument 2.*</margin>
Second, it is argued: Once a trial is contested in a council, both the council and the Pope himself can delegate judges to carry out the matter; why, then, can he not commit this separately?

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
¶ It is answered that the Pope can by no means do this. Truly, that power of coercing the Pontiff at that time is not in his own hands—since he cannot exercise coercive force over himself—but only in the hands of the Council; and therefore it is not in

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>

This is because the law strictly forbids them from being dragged into a secular court <term>secular forum; the civil legal system as opposed to the Church's courts</term>, to the point that they are even stripped of the power to renounce their own right to this immunity, as is clear in the decretals <note>original: "extra, de foro comp. c. si diligenti," referring to the Decretals of Gregory IX</note>.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether a judge may rule against the Truth<-
->which he knows for certain, when the<-
->contrary is legally proven.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter P with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
After the authority of the judge, the second requirement is the truth of the judgment. Therefore, we ask in the second place whether a judge is permitted to judge against the truth which he knows for certain, when the opposite is legally proven.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
And the argument is made for the negative side. For we read in Deuteronomy 17: "You shall come to the priest of the Levite race, and to the judge who is there at that time: and you shall seek from them the truth of the judgment." However, it often happens that an innocent person, whose innocence is clearly known to the judge, is brought before his tri-

<column-break/>

bunal by false testimony; therefore, the judge should not abandon the truth because of such testimony.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued that a man ought to imitate divine judgment in his own; but divine judgment is always according to the truth. For the justice of God's judgment will be revealed (as Paul says in Romans 2) because He will "render to every man according to his works." And of Christ it is said in Isaiah 11: "He shall not judge according to the sight of the eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of the ears: but he shall judge the poor in justice, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth." Therefore, a judge is not permitted to be led away from the truth by false testimonies.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: Testimonies are necessary for the purpose of making the truth established; but when a matter is manifest, there is no need for testimonies, according to that saying of Paul in 1 Timothy 5: "Some men's sins are manifest, going before them to judgment." Therefore, when a matter is clearly discovered by the judge, he has no need for the testimony of others.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, it is argued: A judge who condemns an innocent person acts against his conscience; and conscience is nothing other than knowledge <term>scientia</term> applied to an action. Therefore, he acts against conscience, which is undoubtedly always a sin; thus, it is by no means permitted.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the authority of Augustine in his commentary on the Psalms: "A good judge does nothing by his own will, but pronounces according to the laws and the rights."

<image-desc>Large ornamental capital Q at the start of the paragraph.</image-desc>
This question is debated among the doctors of both Law and Theology with great ambiguity. And while it is disputable on both sides, it is of the highest importance that it be understood. We have proposed the question in the form asked by St. Thomas: namely, whether it is lawful for a judge to judge against the truth he knows for certain because of contrary testimony. However, the title includes two parts.

<margin>Twofold sense of the question.</margin>
The first is: when he knows evidently that a person held in chains is guilty, yet it is not legally proven—or rather, perhaps the person is cleared by legal testimony—can he condemn him? St. Thomas does not ask this, because

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
there has never been any doubt about it. Indeed, it is beyond controversy that this is not lawful: because the external court <term>forum exterius; the public legal system</term> does not extend to hidden crimes. Crimes are considered "hidden" by law if they are not legally established according to the rules of law. The personal knowledge of a judge is not regarded by law as sufficient testimony, as held in the chapter *Si sacerdos* on the office of the ordinary judge. For by both natural and divine law, "in the mouth of two or three

<meta>This page continues the legal and ethical inquiry into judicial power, moving from the jurisdiction of the clergy to the moral obligations of a judge when faced with a conflict between legal evidence and personal knowledge of the truth.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,

<margin>The legitimate sense of the proposed conclusion.</margin>The legitimate sense of the phrase "on the word of two or three witnesses let every word be established" <note>original: "trium stat omne verbum," a reference to Deuteronomy 19:15 and Matthew 18:16</note> is well-known. However, there is a contrary sense to consider: when it is clearly evident to a judge that a defendant—who has been legally proven guilty—is actually innocent, is it permissible for the judge to condemn him? And although we are only asking if it is permissible, we must also investigate whether he is sometimes *obligated* to do so. Furthermore, to proceed in a clearer order, we will first lay out those points that are universally agreed upon, so as to narrow the matter down to its most difficult core. The answer will consist of three conclusions.

<margin>First instruction.</margin> ¶ It is first assumed here, based on what was said earlier, that a judge does not act by private authority, but by public authority while he is judging. From this, it follows that he must be informed not by his own private judgment, but by common and public information. To this is added a second instruction: <margin>Second.</margin> namely, that the judge utilizes two types of knowledge: universal knowledge of the law, and particular knowledge of the facts. This knowledge of facts must be sought through the ordinary route of testimony. For every judicial question has two parts: first, "did he do it?" and second, "what is the law regarding it?"

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> ¶ Here is the first conclusion: a judge is bound to follow the universal knowledge of the law so sacredly that he cannot listen to his own private judgment if it is contrary to it, nor can he admit any evidence to the contrary. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> And the reason is this: he is not the judge of the laws, but their guardian. It is not his place to judge whether a law is good, but what it commands. Therefore, if either the accuser or the defendant tries to prove that a law is not just, they are not to be heard. Truly, even in the "court of conscience" <term>forum conscientiae; the internal moral judgment of an individual before God</term>, once a law has been promulgated by the prince's edict, no one can safely transgress it by claiming it is unjust, because no one is its judge—unless, perhaps, it displays an intolerable and most manifest iniquity.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion: in a particular matter of fact, although knowledge must be sought from the testimony of witnesses and documents, the judge may nonetheless assist himself with his own wit and prudence—specifically in cross-examining both the documents and the witnesses. And he ought to do this most especially when it is clear to him that an innocent person is being crushed by the falsehood of slanders. <margin>Persuasion for the conclusion.</margin> Natural reason itself, which favors innocence, urges this conclusion. For this reason, it can very rarely happen in practice that a judge is entirely forced to sentence an innocent man to death when his innocence is evident to the judge. For in such a case, the judge will know not only that the witnesses are false, but also by what paths their falsehood can be detected. Because of this, he will be able to interrogate them more insistently and scrutinize more distinctly the hour, and

<column-break/>

the place, and the circumstances. He should use that same prudence by which Daniel detected the iniquity of the elders to reveal the innocence of Susanna. <note>A reference to the biblical story where Daniel cross-examined two elders separately to prove they were lying about Susanna's adultery.</note> Furthermore, if we are to listen to Cajetan <margin>Cajetan.</margin> <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note>, the judge ought then to swear before the people that the man is innocent—for instance, if the judge himself had seen the man at another location at that same hour. No injury is done to the witnesses in that case. On the contrary, since they themselves are being injurious, their injury is refuted. And even if they were perhaps acting in good faith, no injury is done to them while the innocence of a wretched man is protected. However, it would not be permitted to betray a hidden guilty person.

I would add a third point: that the judge ought then, if he sees it would be helpful, to temporarily set aside the persona of the judge and act as a witness before a superior. Indeed, if it could be done without scandal and with the best possible concealment, it would even be permissible for him to secretly leave the prison doors open so the innocent man could take to his feet and escape. Therefore (as I was saying), extreme necessity can hardly ever arise where one is forced to put an innocent man to death. Regarding the remaining two remedies and refuges—namely, whether the judge is bound to refer the innocent man to a superior or to resign his office—we shall speak shortly.

¶ Therefore, to come down to the specific point of what should happen if such a necessity *did* occur, authors are divided into different opinions, which number three. The first opinion <margin>First opinion.</margin> is at one extreme and is entirely contrary to St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note>. It holds that in no case—neither in a civil nor a criminal cause—is it permissible for a judge to condemn someone whom he clearly knows to be innocent, no matter how legitimately he is proven guilty. For short of such certainty, no one doubts that the public judgment must be followed. I believe this opinion took its rise and origin from Hugo <margin>Hugo.</margin> <note>Hugo of Pisa, a 12th-century canonist.</note> on the law *Praetor* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. de iuris. omni. iudi." referring to the Digest of Justinian, Book 2, Title 1.</note>. However, this same opinion was embraced by Calderinus and Panormitanus <margin>Calderinus, Panormitanus, Summa Angelica, Nicolaus de Lyra.</margin> in the chapter *Pastoralis* on the office of delegates; and by the *Summa Angelica* <note>A famous handbook for confessors by Angelus de Clavasio.</note> under the word "to judge," question 7; and by Nicolaus de Lyra on Exodus 23.

The second opinion uses a distinction: <margin>Second opinion.</margin> namely, that in a criminal case, whether it involves the death penalty or any mutilation, the judge cannot condemn the innocent person according to the things alleged and proven. However, it is otherwise in civil cases—for example, when the dispute is about money or the possession of other things. This opinion is falsely attributed to Calderinus and Panormitanus, who were more certainly of the first opinion; but it belonged to a certain Rodolphus <margin>Rodolphus.</margin> whom Angelus cites in the place mentioned above. Imola and other legal consultants <margin>Johannes de Imola.</margin> subscribed to this view on the law *A divo Pio* in the Digest regarding judged matters; as did the *Summa Rosella* <margin>Summa Rosella, Supplement.</margin> and the *Supplement*. And this is the middle-ground opinion that pleased Adrian <margin>Adrian VI.</margin> <note>Pope Adrian VI (reigned 1522–1523).</note> in his *Quodlibeta*, question 6, article 3. But I am surprised that he asserts this to be the opinion of the theologians.

### Book Five, Question 4.

Since, however, there is no one among the ancient writers who does not undoubtedly hold with Saint Thomas; indeed, any other view holds the least probability among all.

<margin>The third opinion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the third opinion lies at the other extreme, according to which we establish the third conclusion. A judge, even when driven into the greatest of straits, must in every case—whether criminal or civil—pronounce a sentence according to what is alleged and proven, even if it is against the truth known to himself. This, I say, is the opinion of *Saint Thomas in the Second Part of the Second Part, question 67, article 2, and previously in question 64, article 3, at the third point*, where he provides an example in a capital case: namely, that an innocent person is sooner to be sentenced to death than public testimony is to be disregarded. This same view was held by *Alexander of Hales, a most weighty Doctor, in part 3, question 40, member 6, article 2; and Richard [of Middleton], article 3, question 26; and the distinguished doctor Peter of Tarentaise [Pope Innocent V].* It was also the opinion among the legal experts, such as *Bartolus on the law "Illicitas" in the Digest regarding the office of the governor; and Johannes Andreae in his Novellae on the title concerning allegations*, where he recites the opinion of *Saint Thomas* and asserts his agreement with it. It was also the judgment of *Petrus de Palude and Sylvester [Prierias] under the entry "Judge," part 2, section 5.* After citing many authors, he admits this to be the opinion of all the ancient theologians and interpreters of both civil and canon law—against which *Adrian [Pope Adrian VI]* argues. Truly, the laws consistently and plainly support this [third] opinion and its reasoning.

<margin>
Alexander of Hales.
Richard.
Peter of Tarentaise.
Bartolus.
Johannes Andreae.
Saint Thomas.
Petrus de Palude.
Sylvester.
</margin>

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ First, *Augustine*, already cited above, affirms this, stating that a good judge does nothing by his own whim, but pronounces judgment according to the laws and the rights. *Ambrose* says exactly the same thing in his commentary on the *Psalm "Blessed are the undefiled,"* and it is recorded in the *Decrees, case 3, question 7, canon "Judge," and case 11, question 3, canon "With great care."* *Gregory* also says this, and in the *Digest, on the office of the governor, law "Illicitas," section "The truth,"* the governor is commanded to follow that which is appropriate for him to follow based on the reliability of those things which shall be proven. Therefore, the laws consider it an abomination for a judge to rule except according to what is alleged and proven.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
<margin>Gregory.</margin>

<margin>A quibble.</margin>
¶ But perhaps someone might say that these cited laws define nothing other than that a judge must speak the law according to the laws and the rights; they do not necessarily mean he must pronounce sentence according to what is alleged and proven. Rather, they command that he follow the knowledge of the law; and furthermore, the law itself (as seen in *Exodus 23*) commands that the innocent and the righteous should not be condemned. However, this quibble is easily refuted. For it is the same thing to judge according to the laws as it is to judge according to what is alleged and proven. The laws most holily command this: that no one be condemned by prejudice—that is, in an unexamined case—but rather through a case examined by legitimate witnesses.

<margin>Calderinus.</margin>
But there is a clever gloss by *Calderinus* on the words of the cited law, *Illicitas*. There, the governor is commanded to follow the reliability of those things which shall be proven. He says

<column-break/>

truly that the judge is only advised to follow what is alleged and proven when those things are true. But he should answer us: by what path must a judge recognize that the things proven are true, except through the oaths of suitable witnesses? For if he were left free afterward to deny that those things are true, the testimonies would be in vain. Much better, therefore, is the gloss on that word in *Chapter 1, on the office of the ordinary judge,* by which bishops are advised to judge according to what the Canons decree; which gloss plainly concludes from this that a judge must judge according to what is alleged and proven. This is further confirmed by the divine teaching in *Deuteronomy 17*, where, after the warning that "on the mouth of two or three witnesses he who is to be killed shall die," it is added that the judges should follow the truth in judgment. Therefore, judges are taught there to follow that truth—not the one they know personally, but the one they hunt for from the mouths of witnesses.

¶ Nevertheless, so that the authorities may be clarified by logic, the argument is made by the first reason, which is the foundation of all.

<margin>The first reason.</margin>
No one has the right to condemn anyone by private authority, but only insofar as he performs a public function. Now, for a judgment, knowledge of both the law and the fact is required. Therefore, he must use both in a public capacity, not a private one. Just as in the knowledge of the law he must not follow his own opinion (even if he considers it to be certain knowledge) but must listen to the laws, so too in the knowledge of the fact he cannot follow his own private knowledge, but is bound to stand by the public reliability of witnesses, which the laws approve.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued: a judge can condemn no one by his own private knowledge, as was said above, no matter how clearly he knows the person to be guilty. Therefore, he cannot acquit anyone either. Even the proponents of the contrary opinion admit this. If, therefore, he cannot acquit the innocent man [in the eyes of the law], but must keep him in perpetual chains—and perpetual chains are equated with death—it is surely denied for no good reason that he cannot proceed against him by the law, having "washed his hands of his blood" <note>A reference to the ritual of declaring oneself innocent of a death sentence.</note>.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you object: therefore Pilate was innocent, who judged Christ according to what was alleged.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
There is surely no logical consequence there. Because the innocence of Christ was so evident—not only to him, but publicly to everyone—and the falsehood of the testimonies was so immediately open, that their wickedness could not be hidden even from Pilate himself; rather, he could easily have convicted them of falsehood. Hence, when he said, *"I am innocent of the blood of this Just man: see to it yourselves,"* he confessed not only the innocence of Christ but also the wickedness of the testimonies. Yet he sentenced Him to death (as is discovered from the Gospel) because—

...of Caesar, who loathed even the very name of "king"; and Christ was accused of making himself a king. Indeed, it was that same fear—that the Romans would come and take away the Jewish nation—which sharpened their hatred to the point of prosecuting him as a criminal. <margin>Third reason</margin> ¶ Thirdly, it is argued from the purpose of public authority. Public trials are established for the tranquility and quiet state of the republic, and in such a way that no path is left open for a judge to deviate from the truth whenever he pleases. If he were not bound to judge according to the allegations <note>original: "secundùm allegata," a legal term meaning based on the evidence and testimonies formally presented in court</note>, the peace of the republic would be immediately disturbed. For since the people cannot judge hidden things, when they see that public proofs are not being upheld, they could not help but cry out against the judge. This is especially true when the dispute concerns an atrocious crime, such as the betrayal of a city or something similar. Furthermore, a path would always be left for a judge to excuse himself from the execution of justice by claiming that a contrary truth was known to him. In short, it is necessary that a judge who administers the law in the eyes of the citizens persuades the people of his sentence, at least to the extent that it is shown to have been brought forth according to the laws; he could not do this unless he judged according to the allegations. <margin>Fourth reason.</margin> ¶ Fourthly, if (for the sake of example) it were certain that one of two men—say, Peter or Paul—had sown heresy, but it was hidden which of them had done it, and Peter, truly guilty, confessed his heretical depravity sacramentally in the ear of the judge <note>This refers to a private confession of sins to a priest, which is under the "seal of confession" and cannot be revealed</note>, and afterward Paul, who was innocent, was brought forward for that crime—whose innocence was certainly known to that same inquisitor—then the inquisitor would surely be held in a state of double-edged perplexity. For if he could not condemn Paul, he would reveal the secret of the confession, because Peter’s crime would thereby be discovered. <margin>The evasion of some.</margin> ¶ There are those, however, who slip away from all these points by responding that a judge, in a case where he clearly knows an innocent man is being accused by legitimate witnesses, ought to refer the case to a superior. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> Saint Thomas advises this in *Question 64, Article 6, in the response to the third objection*. There is no doubt that this remedy is lawful, for an inferior judge may refer any case to a superior. And I admit, furthermore, that when a distinguished person is accused of some infamous crime, a pious judge ought to escape through that detour after all other attempted remedies have failed. Nevertheless, I do not see that this is necessary. <margin>First reason.</margin> For first, the inferior judge has legitimate authority to terminate the case according to the allegations. Furthermore, that remedy

<column-break/>

is very weak—indeed, it is useless—because since the superior does not know the innocence of the accused, he could not acquit him based on the testimony of the inferior judge, but would be bound to stand by the sworn word of the other witnesses. And therefore, referring the man to a superior would be the same as offering him up for execution. Wherefore, if it were not lawful to kill him, it follows that he should not hand him over to a superior either, but should instead free him. <margin>Second reason.</margin> ¶ Furthermore, the question is raised again regarding the supreme judge himself, before whom the wretched man is brought, whom he knows to be innocent; yet he is accused of a most grave crime, so much so that he cannot grant him his life without great scandal. But truly, a supreme judge has many more remedies. For he could deter the witnesses more forcefully, and he could devise other ways to snatch the innocent man from such great danger—especially since (as we shall see in Article 4) he can grant life even to one condemned to death. <margin>Another subterfuge.</margin> ¶ Another subterfuge is the claim that the judge ought then to resign his office. Indeed, others say he is bound to suffer the loss of all his goods sooner than kill the man. This, however, is surely much more improbable than what we were just discussing: <margin>Reply.</margin> both because that remedy is useless, and especially because no one is bound to ward off a loss to a brother at such a massive inconvenience to himself, when he himself did not cause the harm. For it is hard to believe that a man who lives by his office should have to suffer such a great loss. Especially since, if he cannot hand him over to punishment, he ought rather to suffer death himself than pronounce a sentence of death upon the man—which is a belief too rigid to hold. <margin>Sylvester did not fully grasp the mind of St. Thomas.</margin> Hence it happens that our Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note>, although he seemed to defend the opinion of Saint Thomas, did not do so in the best faith. He says, I say, that a judge is bound to kill an innocent person when he can neither refer him to a superior nor resign his office. For Saint Thomas never said this; and in that case, our opinion would surely be null, because since anyone can resign his office, this remedy would always be at hand.

Let us first dissolve those which Saint Thomas brings forward with his solutions. ¶ Regarding the first authority from Deuteronomy, by which a judge is commanded to judge the truth, it has already been answered that "truth" there is considered to be that which consists in the mouth of two or three witnesses. <margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ And to the second it is replied that...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether a judge, acting in an official capacity, must follow the evidence presented in court even if he knows privately that the accused is innocent. Soto is defending the position of St. Thomas Aquinas against several objections, including those raised by Pope Adrian VI.</meta>

### Book Five, Question IV. ###

Ee 4

that God, who requires no external testimony because His infinite wisdom knows all things most deeply, and likewise Christ insofar as He is a man, judge most rightly according to their own knowledge. However, it is different for human judges, who are bound to rely on public testimonies "begged" from others; for otherwise,
<margin>To the third [reason].</margin>
no faith would be placed in such judges. ¶ To the third argument, it is answered that when a matter is manifest—not only to the judge but publicly—there is no need for witnesses. It is different when it has become known to the judge alone.
<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, there are those who respond that it is not absurd for a public person to act against their conscience, though it would be different if they were a private citizen. However, these thinkers are not well-versed in the schools of the Theologians. To act against conscience is intrinsically evil, because it is to do that which the person acting believes to be evil. Therefore, it is denied that the judge acts against conscience. For he does not act against conscience who merely acts against <term>speculative knowledge</term><note>Speculative knowledge refers to the judge's private awareness of the "raw" truth (e.g., "I saw he didn't do it"), whereas practical knowledge refers to his duty to apply the law based on the evidence available to the court.</note>: rather, he acts against conscience who acts against <term>practical knowledge</term>. The judge, I say, acts against that [speculative] knowledge—this man is innocent—yet not against the [practical] knowledge that he must not be killed. On the contrary, he rightly judges that the man must be executed because of the fit testimonies. If, however, a judge held a settled opinion contrary to ours, and consequently believed that an innocent person should under no circumstances be condemned, he could by no means deliver him to death against such a conscience. For here we define only this truth: that the innocent man in such a case is to be condemned; but that no one is permitted to act against their conscience is another truth entirely.
<margin>First argument against the stated conclusion. The solution.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, other arguments are gathered: namely the fifth, from that passage in Exodus 23: *The innocent and the just you shall not kill* <note>original: "Insontem & iustū non occides"</note>, where Nicolaus <note>Likely the medieval commentator Nicholas of Lyra</note> denies the opinion of Saint Thomas. To this, however, one responds that the command was given simply to private persons; but for public powers, a man should not be considered "innocent" whom public testimonies make "guilty" <note>original: "sontem," the opposite of "insontem" (innocent)</note>. For this reason, when a judge devotes his effort to his public duty, because he does not then intend to kill an innocent person but rather performs the duty of his office—whatever the outcome may be—he in no way sins, but acts diligently. He is like one who, in the defense of a blameless protection <note>original: "tutamine inculpatæ tutelæ," a legal term for legitimate self-defense</note>, kills an aggressor. ¶ And by this, the argument of others is solved, who argue that this is against <term>natural law</term>. For those who falsely accuse violate natural law, if they do so knowingly (though they might do it in good faith). But the judge would rather transgress that same law if he did not perform the duty of his office, which was established by the law of nature for the sake of the common good.

<column-break/>

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ These arguments are common to the first and second opinions. There is a second argument which Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), who was a prominent theologian before becoming Pope</note> particularly uses to advocate for his "middle way." No mortal is the master of human life, but God alone; therefore, it is lawful for no one to destroy the innocent. It is different, he says, regarding temporal goods, of which man is the master. For the people could, he says, consent that whenever any innocent person is legitimately accused in a civil case—where they ought to be fined precisely in external goods—that innocent person would consent to the penalty because of the allegations and proofs.
<margin>Adrian's opinion is most inconsistent.</margin>
This opinion, however, is the most inconsistent of all, nor is it propped up by any support. For what he says—that no one has a right over their own life or limbs—only proves that no one can kill themselves or another by private authority (except when repelling force with force). It is different for a public person; therefore, in such a case, public and fit testimonies grant the judge the right to kill the innocent.
<margin>Reasoning against Adrian.</margin>
¶ Adrian is quickly refuted. If an innocent person could not be condemned in a criminal case, surely they could not be in a civil one either. Because just as a judge has no power to deprive a man of life except for a crime, so neither has he power over external goods. From where did Adrian fish out that "consent of the people"? Especially since (as we are often accustomed to say) there could be such a vast heap of goods that it would equal the life of a private man. Therefore, the argument truly has no sting or weight against this opinion of Saint Thomas, which many have most deservedly embraced, except that which is drawn from piety. For the soul seems to dread driving an innocent person to death. Yet this only persuades us that the greatest possible diligence and care should be applied to his defense; it does not mean that the laws or public tranquility should be abandoned for his sake. For every human law, however just, is nothing other than a **sieve for cleaning wheat**; it cannot distinguish between the just and the unjust so exactly that some grains do not occasionally fall through with the chaff.
¶ However, one must not overlook this argument, which could deceive some.
<margin>Another argument against the conclusion.</margin>
The argument is this: where there is a dispute regarding the condemnation of some proposition noted for heresy, and many Doctors, being deceived, should condemn it, but the truth of it is evident to the Pope or the presiding Bishop, he could by no means subscribe to the opinion of the others, but must constantly maintain his own truth. Therefore, similarly, a judge cannot act against the truth known to himself...

<margin>Response.</margin>
to listen to the proofs of witnesses. It is answered that there is no similarity between these things. For it is in no way permitted to deny the truth; however, a judge, while sentencing an innocent person to death <note>based on the legal evidence provided in court</note>, asserts nothing false. For the sake of the whole world, he should not affirm that the person is at fault; but by his act, he declares that the person is to be condemned—and that is true, because the legal testimonies offer the person up to death <note>meaning the legal reality created by the evidence justifies the sentence, even if the judge knows the factual reality is different</note>.

### ARTICLE III. ###

->Whether a Judge may judge anyone without an accuser.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' featuring a figure in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>

THE THIRD thing required for the rectitude of a judge is the form of the trial. Regarding this, it is asked whether a judge may judge any defendant without an accuser. And it is argued on the affirmative side, both by the <margin>First argument.</margin> example of God and of the saints: God punishes wrongdoers with no prior accusation; our justice is derived from His; therefore, this is also permitted to us.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly, the same is shown in the story of Daniel, as his history relates in chapter 13, where he was both accuser and judge at the same time.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Thirdly, it is argued: An accuser is necessary for this purpose—to bring the crime to the ears of the judge. However, it can reach his notice by another way; therefore, an accusation is not always necessary.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
To the contrary is the opinion of Ambrose on the Apostle’s sentence regarding the fornicator in 1 Corinthians 5, where he says: “It is not the part of a judge to condemn without an accuser,” because the Lord did not cast out Judas, even though he was a thief, because he was not accused.

<margin>Concluding response.</margin>
The question is very brief and contained in this single conclusion: In criminal cases, a judge cannot condemn anyone in judgment unless they have been accused. The reason is that since a judge is the interpreter of justice—to whom, according to Aristotle in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, people run as if to a <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> <term>living justice</term><note>original: "animatum iustum"</note>—and human justice is not directed toward oneself but toward another, it follows that a judge must sit to judge between two parties: namely, the prosecutor or accuser and the defendant. This is supported by the authority of Acts 25, where Festus says: “It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man before he who is accused has his accusers present and receives the opportunity to defend himself to clear away the crimes of which he is accused.”

<margin>Argument</margin>
However, an argument immediately arises against the form of this conclusion, which seems too narrow and strict. It is

<column-break/>

argued, I say, to the contrary: The logic of criminal cases and civil cases is the same; why then was it strictly said "in criminal cases," as if an accuser were not at all necessary in civil cases? We answer that we have followed the form of Saint Thomas. He himself, if <margin>Cajetan.</margin> Cajetan is to be believed, placed the example in criminal cases because in those, the presence of the offender is required; and therefore the necessity of an accusation is more evidently clear there. But <margin>The true solution.</margin> yet this explanation is not sufficient; for he should have stated the conclusion as broadly as it applied. Therefore, Saint Thomas’s reason was that although in every trial two persons are necessary besides the judge, in a civil case—where the punishment of a delinquent is not sought, but rather the restitution of property—it was very clear that a trial could not be entered into without a party seeking their property. Such a person is not called an "accuser," but a <term>plaintiff</term><note>original: "actor"</note>. And therefore the question was specifically raised regarding an accuser, about whom it might be doubted whether he was necessary, because a judge seems able to punish crimes by virtue of his office.

Furthermore, it is argued against the conclusion: Natural law <margin>Argument 2.</margin> does not forbid public power from extinguishing a dangerous man without waiting for an accusation. For both a head of a household and a superior of monks can punish their family without that form of trial; therefore, no human law should have prohibited it.

It is answered that although natural law does not <margin>Response.</margin> expressly prohibit it, it is nevertheless solemnly prohibited by both types of human law <note>Canon Law and Civil/Roman Law</note>: as in the *Decretals*, on accusations, the chapter "If legitimate"; and the law "Illicit acts" cited above in the *Digest*, on the office of the governor; and in the *Digest*, on duties and honors, the law "By rescript": "If someone does not have an accuser, he ought not to be barred from honors." And other Roman laws which Festus alluded to in the passage cited from the Acts of the Apostles. Christ seemed to allude to these laws in John 8: "Woman, has no one condemned you? Neither do I condemn you." And it is highly consistent with natural law. For the peace and quiet of the commonwealth is sufficiently preserved if those who have been brought to judgment by accusation or public outcry are punished in the sight of the people. For if the judge acted as both accuser and punisher at the same time, a path would be paved for false charges <note>original: "calumniis"</note>. Therefore, the judge must be a third party, an arbiter between two other persons. Wherefore Aristotle, in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 4, says that he is a <margin>Aristotle.</margin> mediator. But a head of a household, who does not use coercive force nor can he strike with a capital sentence <note>the death penalty</note>, does not need this ceremony of accusation. The same applies to a prelate of monks in offenses of lesser importance, which he ought to punish as a father.

<summary>This page discusses the legal necessity of having a formal accuser (prosecutor) present before a judge can pass sentence, arguing that a judge must remain a neutral mediator between two parties to prevent abuse of power. Soto clarifies that while a judge acts as "living justice," procedural law requires a separate accuser in criminal cases and a plaintiff in civil cases to ensure a fair trial.</summary>
