441 **Book Five, Question IV.**

And he holds this right by the concession of the popes, by whose authority monastic institutions are granted their stability. Indeed, even outside of religious orders, in minor matters there is no need for a strict form of accusation: as is held in the law *levia* <note>original: "l. leuia. ff. de accu." — a reference to the Digest of Roman Law regarding "light" or minor crimes</note>, where minor matters are ordered to be heard and discussed plainly. However, grave crimes which cannot be punished without the offender's infamy <term>infamy: a legal status involving the loss of certain civil rights and reputation</term>—namely, where imprisonment is necessary—cannot be punished even within monastic cloisters unless a formal accusation has preceded the trial.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The arguments are therefore answered as follows. For the examples of God and the saints that were raised to the contrary do not change the position. God indeed has no need for an accuser, because He both knows all things and, by His absolute power and supreme equity, does not allow even the smallest fault to go unpunished. Nevertheless, He punishes nothing without an "accuser" <note>Soto is arguing that even God follows a form of "prosecution," albeit an internal or symbolic one</note>. For He created our reason to be so hostile to fault that conscience itself constantly accuses the criminal before His divine <margin>Paul.</margin> tribunal: as the teacher Paul says in Romans 2. Furthermore, the deed itself—which, although it may be most hidden from men, is most open to Him—stands as an accuser before His sight. Hence in Genesis 3, as if Adam's transgression had brought him to his own tribunal, God called him into judgment saying, "Adam, where are you?" and in chapter 4, "The voice of your brother Abel's blood cries out to me from the ground." And in chapter 18, regarding the vengeance upon Sodom: "I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry which has come to me." Indeed, the form of the final judgment seems likely to involve an accusation: as held in Matthew 12, "The men of Nineveh will rise in the day of judgment with this generation and condemn it. The Queen of the South, etc." ¶ And by the same reasoning, because Daniel acted by God's authority and impulse, he was able to make those same elders defendants by accusing them, and to hand them over to death once they were condemned. ¶ To the third argument <margin>To the third.</margin> it is answered that, besides a human being (whose proper duty is the task of accusing), four other causes exist, any of which claims for itself the place of an accuser. The first is a manifest crime, which they call "notorious": for example, where someone commits a fault in the sight of the people or the judge with lawful witnesses. For then no other accuser is to be waited for, according to that saying of Paul in 1 Corinthians 5: "Some men's sins are manifest, going before them to judgment." Hence the gloss of <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine on the passage cited from Genesis 4 regarding Abel's blood: And it is stated in the Decretals <note>original: "extrà, de accu." — referring to the "Extra" or Decretals of Gregory IX</note>, the evidence of a committed crime does not need the cry of an accuser.

<column-break/>

The same is held in the Canon Law <note>original: "2. q. 1. can. manifesta"</note>. The second cause is infamy, or evidence, or a clamorous report. For these take the place of an accuser in a certain way. Not indeed that they are a sufficient cause to immediately drag a defendant to punishment, but they open the way for an inquiry once the matter has been explored and discussed: according to the form of the chapters *qualiter et quando* and *Inquisitionis* <note>procedural headings in Canon Law regarding how and when an investigation should begin</note>. The third cause is when someone is reported to a judge by a legal denunciation that aims at punishment: such as is done for inquisitors of heretical depravity. Then also the process moves by way of inquiry to the knowledge of the case and the punishment of the crime. For that denunciation differs from a formal accusation only in this: that he who denounces is not bound to prove the charge; otherwise, no one would dare to denounce. Finally, the fourth cause is when someone, after a preliminary "brotherly correction," denounces a brother to a prelate <note>a high-ranking church official</note> as to a father, in the Gospel manner. For then, if the person denounced listens to the warning, the prelate is not permitted to proceed to punishment and infamy; rather, he must stop there once the corrected brother has appeared reformed. For that is the goal of that process. But if he remains rebellious, then the rebellion takes the place of an accuser so that the prelate can proceed against him by law, as will be more clearly shown below. For this is not the place to examine these matters more minutely.

### ARTICLE IV.
#### Whether it is free for a judge to relax the penalty of the law.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a sun-like floral motif within a square frame.</image-desc>
The fourth thing required in a judge pertains to the execution of judgment. And therefore it remains to see whether it is lawful for a judge to relax a penalty. The argument is made from the affirmative side. James in chapter 2 <margin>First argument.</margin> warned us that judgment without mercy remains for him who has not shown mercy; therefore, it is not only permitted for a judge to relax a penalty mercifully, but it is also his duty. ¶ Secondly, this is confirmed <margin>Second.</margin> by the example of God, who (as held in Ezekiel 18) does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live. ¶ Thirdly: <margin>Third.</margin> That which benefits one person but harms no one can be justly provided by anyone; therefore, at least where the person who suffered the injury forgives the offense, the judge will also be able to remit the punishment. ¶ On the contrary are the testimonies of the law. For we read in Deuteronomy 13 regarding idolatry: "Let not your eye spare him—"

### F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,

<note>original: "Ius tuum vt miserearis & occultes eum: sed statim interficies eum." — This is a reference to Deuteronomy 13:8-9, regarding the treatment of those who entice others to idolatry.</note> Your right is to have mercy and hide him: but you shall immediately kill him. And concerning a murderer, chapter 9: He shall die, and you shall not have mercy on him.

<margin>A distinction.</margin>
To this question, which is quite easy, an answer is given through two conclusions, based on a distinction. For the reasoning regarding a supreme judge—namely, a prince who holds the highest power of command—is far different from the reasoning regarding an inferior judge, who acts merely as his minister, appointed only to execute the sanctions of the laws.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, let the first conclusion be: Before the injured party forgives the injury, no judge, whether he be supreme or inferior, can remit the penalty.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven: for a judge is bound to hand over a criminal to punishment on two accounts. First, because he must decide the case between the criminal and the accuser. Second, because he is a minister of the **commonwealth**, who is the avenger of injuries done against it, acting not by private but by public power. For he who inflicts an injury on a citizen subsequently strikes at the commonwealth itself. Therefore, a double obstacle prevents a judge from being able to absolve a defendant from guilt: one on the part of the accuser, and the other on the part of the commonwealth. For this reason, as long as the one who has been affected by the injury persists in the accusation, it is not free for the judge to keep the defendant unharmed. This is because, as the guardian of justice, he is bound to return to each person their own right when they seek it; and if he were to do the contrary, he would sin just as much as one who is "merciful with another's property" <note>A legal maxim suggesting that one cannot be "charitable" by giving away what belongs to someone else—in this case, the victim's right to justice.</note>, and he would subsequently be bound to make restitution for both the injury and the loss. Hence, in the *Ethics*, Book 5, 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
chapter 5, Aristotle says: When men see that injuries are not compensated to them through inflicted punishments, they consider themselves to be living in slavery.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: After the accuser has desisted, being satisfied, it is within the discretion of the supreme judge to relax or commute the penalty of the law; however, such discretion is not granted to an inferior judge.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
The latter part of this point is clear from the fact that a mode of action is prescribed for an inferior judge by his superior; and therefore he is so bound by the laws that he cannot step outside their prescriptions. Hence, regarding that passage in John 19, "You would have no power over me," 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine says: God had given such power to Pilate that he was under Caesar, so that it was not entirely free for him to absolve the accused. The first part of the conclusion, however, gains its truth from the fact that a prince is not only the guardian of the laws, but their **dispenser** <term>dispenser: an administrator who has the authority to grant exemptions (dispensations) from the letter of the law for the sake of equity or the public good</term>. I do not say he is "absolute" in the sense that he could dispense and scatter them at his whim, like his own cloak; but never-

<column-break/>

theless, he can dispense with the laws when it seems fitting or expedient for the public good. From this it follows that, even if the accuser desists and begs for pardon for the person they were accusing, the prince is not immediately obligated to forgive the penalty; rather, it is within his discretion to inflict it. Indeed, he ought to weigh the merits of the defendant. The person could be so wicked that he ought to be condemned to punishment; if the prince did not do so, he would be unjust to the commonwealth—for instance, when the man is a professional assassin, a robber, or someone devoted to crime. It is otherwise when a man has committed a single crime through human frailty.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
But could a defendant who is uniquely useful to the commonwealth be granted his life even if the accuser protests?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered that this is permitted only very rarely; nevertheless, it can happen in practice that it would befit the prince (as is held in *Decretum*, Case 2, Question 7, chapter "si quem poenituerit" <note>A reference to Canon Law regarding the abolition of charges</note>) to abolish the accusation and compel the accuser to be content with another satisfaction determined by the judgment of wise men, so that a person might be preserved for waging war or for other remarkably useful duties.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, to the first argument, it is answered that in private persons, an excess in forgiving injuries can very rarely—indeed, hardly ever—occur, so strictly did Christ commend to us the love of our enemies. To public magistrates, however, because they are the patrons and protectors of justice, a line is prescribed for inclining toward mercy. They ought, indeed, by their nature to be clement, and not to search out causes or weave technicalities for the purpose of slaughtering men. Indeed, as 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle also acknowledged in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, and as is found among the rules of law, a judge ought to be more inclined toward lessening and mitigating punishments, provided that the reasoning of justice and the law allows it. For to leap beyond that is not clemency, but a **public disaster**. Indeed, let those who, under the pretext of piety, try too hard to snatch evildoers from the hands of judges not think they are performing an outstanding work of piety; for they often inflict violence upon justice. Nor does the example of Christ, praying to the Father for pardon for his crucifiers, have a place here: for that pertained to the forgiveness of the **fault** <term>fault (culpa): the moral sin or guilt, as opposed to the "poena" or legal penalty</term>.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ And an answer is likewise given to the second argument: since God is the one against whom sin is primarily and chiefly committed, He can remit the fault and the penalty as it pleases Him. Although where He says, "I do not desire the death of a sinner," He understands that as referring to eternal death; and for that reason He adds, "but rather that he be converted and live," namely-

<meta>The catchword "cet" indicates the next page begins with "cetera" or a similar word continuing the thought on divine life.</meta>

<summary>Soto argues that while private individuals should always be merciful, judges must uphold justice for the sake of the commonwealth, though sovereign princes have the unique authority to grant pardons when it serves the public good.</summary>

# QUESTION FIVE,
# on the justice of the accuser.
## St. Thomas, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 68. <note>This refers to the *Summa Theologiae* by Thomas Aquinas, the standard authority for this text.</note>
## ARTICLE I.
### Whether anyone is bound to accuse another.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with floral patterns.</image-desc>THE SECOND person in a trial is the plaintiff or accuser: for unless the one who is harmful were brought into court by another, he would never come of his own accord. In the accuser, four things
<margin>Four things to be considered in an accuser.</margin> must be considered: namely, the obligation, the form, the justice, and the penalty if he accuses unjustly; concerning which four articles are therefore constructed. First, then, it is asked whether anyone is bound to accuse
<margin>First argument.</margin> someone. And it is argued on the negative side. First, because in Matthew 6 we are commanded to forgive our debtors their debts. And in Romans 12: *Do not
<margin>Second.</margin> defend yourselves*—that is, do not avenge yourselves, most dearly beloved—*but give place to wrath.* <note>original: "Nó vos defendentes... sed date locũ iræ."</note> ¶ Second: To bring a friend into judgment undermines the loyalty of friends;
<margin>Third.</margin> therefore, it is by no means lawful. ¶ Third: if accusation were a precept of virtue, no one would be exempt from it; yet many are barred from making an accusation, as is widely evident in Question 2, Case 7, concerning the excommunicated
<margin>Fourth.</margin> and the infamous; therefore, it is not a precept. ¶ Fourth: If there were such a precept, we should rather pay that duty to prelates <note>In this context, "prelate" refers to a high-ranking church official or superior.</note> and friends; but in the same case (8, q. 4), subjects are forbidden, except
<margin>Council of Toledo.</margin> in certain cases, from accusing their prelates. And furthermore, clerics are forbidden from being accused by laymen and from accusing them, especially in a case of blood <note>A "case of blood" refers to a trial involving the death penalty or physical mutilation.</note>, as is clear from the Fourth Council of Toledo, Question 23, Case 8, in the canons *his à quibus* and *clericis*, and frequently elsewhere; therefore, it is not a
<margin>Fifth.</margin> precept. ¶ Fifth: An accuser is bound to

<column-break/>

prove the crime; otherwise, he would undergo the penalty of retaliation <term>lex talionis|The legal principle that a person who makes an accusation they cannot prove must suffer the same penalty the accused would have faced.</term>. No one, however, is compelled to undergo such great danger; therefore, no one should be compelled to accuse. ¶ On the contrary is that passage from Leviticus 5: *If a soul sins, and someone hears the voice of one swearing, and is a witness because he himself saw it or is aware of it: unless he makes it known, he shall bear his iniquity.*

¶ We made this present question the fifth in our *Relection* <note>A "Relectio" was a formal public lecture or academic review common in Spanish universities.</note> on hiding and revealing secrets, where we disputed it with great precision. Nevertheless, we cannot help but bring some points here, lest the present treatise appear interrupted by this gap. Therefore, the question is answered, with a distinction provided first, by
<margin>A distinction.</margin> two conclusions. For there is a difference between fraternal denunciation and judicial accusation, which is taken from the perspective of the goal. For denunciation tends toward this: that the rebuked brother may be corrected and amended. For which reason (as we were saying), once that goal is obtained, one must not proceed further. But an accusation is entered into for this: that the guilty party may be punished, and this especially for the public good, so that the peace of the commonwealth may be preserved, and its honor not be defiled.
<margin>What fraternal denunciation is.</margin> Hence, fraternal denunciation is the reporting of a crime to a prelate, as if to a father, for the sake of correction.
<margin>What accusation is.</margin> But accusation is the reporting of a crime to a judge, as if to a public person, for the sake of vengeance <note>Here "vengeance" or *vindicatio* implies legal retribution or justice, not personal spite.</note>. ¶ The first conclusion, therefore, is:
<margin>First conclusion.</margin> Where someone knows a crime results in the ruin of the commonwealth, which he is able to prove with suitable witnesses, he is bound to accuse the guilty party.
<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> It is proven. The punishments for crimes that occur in this world are not to be sought for their own sake, as if they were revenges out of hatred and the destruction of the wicked—for punishments of that kind will be in hell, when the time of full retribution arrives—but they are like medicines to be procured, either for the one who is being punished or for the public good. Namely, so that through fear of them, men may be kept in their duty, lest they disturb the common good. Whoever, however, is constrained to assist the common good, as a part to the whole, when he sees it either infected by contagion or corrupted by crimes—and this indeed cannot happen except through the public power, to which crimes are brought by accusation—therefore, everyone in such a
<margin>A double condition when one is bound to accuse.</margin> case is bound to accuse the destructive person. Therefore, two conditions must coincide so that the obligation to accuse arises: namely, that the crime exists against the public good, and that it can be proven. ¶ And from this follows the later...

Soto concludes that an individual is bound to accuse a criminal when the crime harms the commonwealth and can be legally proven.</summary>

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin> ...the prior conclusion. Concerning a sin that neither leads to the ruin of the commonwealth nor can be proven by suitable witnesses, no one is bound by natural law to accuse. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> The first part of the conclusion is proven thus: Since everyone is the master of their own goods, including their reputation and honor (as was shown in Book 4, Question 2), they can waive those rights, both to be obedient to the word of Christ—who so greatly encouraged us to love our enemies—and also to make the most of one's time. <note>original: "redimendum tempus," a reference to Ephesians 5:16, suggesting one should focus on spiritual matters rather than legal disputes.</note> And in this case, the unique law is understood: *That no one be forced to sue or accuse against their will.* <note>original: "C. vt nemo inuit. agere, vel accusa. cog." This refers to a specific title in the Code of Justinian (Codex 3.7).</note> This is also the expressed <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> opinion of St. Thomas [Aquinas] in the *Summa Theologiae* (Second Part of the Second Part), not only in Question 68 where he treats this, but also in Question 73, Article 3, where he says <margin>St. Thomas's reason.</margin> it is within everyone’s discretion to suffer damage to their own reputation, unless this leads to danger for others. St. Thomas proves the second part of the conclusion because no one is bound to do what they cannot accomplish; and therefore, since proof is necessary in an accusation, one who cannot provide proof is not forced to accuse—especially so that they do not create a risk for themselves of either retaliation <term>talion: the principle of "an eye for an eye," where an accuser who fails to prove a crime might suffer the same penalty they sought for the accused</term> or other damage if they fail in the proof. I said "by natural law," lest we descend into another dispute: whether heirs of a murdered person are bound by civil law to accuse the murderer (according to the opinion of Bartolus on the law *In eum* in the Digest regarding accusations) lest they lose their right of inheritance; however, the law of the "Divine Brothers" in the same section, and the cited Code law "that no one is forced," seem to feel the opposite. <margin>Argument against the first conclusion.</margin> ¶ But so that the first conclusion may be more clearly unfolded, an argument is made against it: There is no sin that does not bring public harm—namely, either scandal, a bad example, or some influence over a companion. Therefore, if the conclusion is true, it carries no exception: regarding any sin for which a penalty is established, everyone must, if they can prove it, bring the offender to judgment. This argument is convincing to many. <margin>Solution.</margin> Nevertheless, there is a need for discretion. For not all sins are judged to be such a detriment to the commonwealth that they must necessarily be reported, accused, or investigated as such. Rather, only those whose immediate object is the common good—which is attacked and disturbed by them—fall into this category. Indeed, the rest, which are committed against a private good, are considered private; for the type of act is judged by its object. Examples: stealing a neighbor's goods is a private crime, as is killing a private individual. However, plundering the public treasury, like the crime of high treason <note>original: "læsæ maiestatis"</note>, are those things which lead to public ruin.

<column-break/>

In the same way, a harmful lie by which a fellow citizen is defrauded is a private sin. But heresy, by which the common religion is shaken, is a primary public crime. For even if crimes committed against individual private parts of the commonwealth affect the state in some way, they are not therefore to be considered public. However, highwaymen who beset the royal roads and Assassins are classified among public criminals. <margin>Second argument on the same point.</margin> ¶ The second argument is as follows: When someone has learned of such public crimes, it is sufficient if they report them; therefore, a formal accusation is not necessary. This is especially true because if one reports, one is not bound to prove the case, unlike one who formally accuses. Therefore, to be freed from that danger of failing in the proof, one seems to have satisfied the obligation by reporting. <margin>The *Summa Angelica*.</margin> ¶ Because of this argument, the *Summa Angelica* <note>A famous 15th-century handbook for confessors by Angelus Carletus.</note> holds against St. Thomas that no one is bound to accuse; for this opinion, he cites Bartolus on the law *In eum*. Here, however, it must be noted that reporting <margin>Twofold reporting.</margin>—as it pertains to the present matter—is twofold (although the Doctors of Canon Law distinguish more types beyond accusation). We have explained these in detail elsewhere. One is "fraternal" and "evangelical" reporting, which we just said refers to the correction of a brother. But the other is "judicial" reporting, which also has the public good as its goal; this therefore proceeds even to punishment, such as the reports made to Inquisitors. A servant who cannot formally accuse his master can report him; and a subject can report an inferior prelate to a superior. This is almost an accusation, differing only in this: that the reporter is not held to prove it, but the judge is then held to investigate. And perhaps St. Thomas includes this under the name of "accusation" here. Even so, where a crime is very harmful and contagious, one who could produce witnesses would also be bound to accuse and prove the crime, so as to relieve the judge of the labor of investigating a matter of such great importance. Therefore, whatever the civil law may say, there is no doubt that in a public cause, everyone is bound in conscience to accuse. Bartolus is only speaking of private causes. <margin>Doubt.</margin> ¶ The third doubt is whether, just as a brotherly warning is required before evangelical reporting, it is also required before a formal accusation. An argument is made for <margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin> the affirmative: In the Gospel, no exception is made for accusation or reporting; but it is simply commanded that a secret warning [should precede]...

<summary>Soto distinguishes between private crimes (like theft) and public crimes (like treason or heresy), arguing that while private wrongs can be forgiven by the victim, public crimes must be reported or accused to protect the commonwealth. He also clarifies the technical difference between "reporting" a crime to a judge and "accusing" someone, which carries the burden of proof.</summary>
<keywords>natural law, public good, private vs public crimes, burden of proof, treason, heresy, judicial reporting, fraternal correction, St. Thomas Aquinas, Bartolus de Saxoferrato</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into the obligation of a private citizen to act as an accuser. It specifically addresses whether one must first give a private warning (admonition) to the sinner before bringing a formal charge in court.</meta>

### Book Five, Question 5. 445

[The text begins by discussing whether] a warning should precede [an accusation]. On the contrary, however, a distinction is made in the legal chapter *qualiter & quando* <note>Latin: "c. qualiter & quando. de accusa." This refers to a chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding the procedure for accusations.</note> between a report <term>denuntiatio; a formal report of a crime to an authority meant to trigger an investigation rather than a personal lawsuit</term> and an accusation, using these words: "Just as a warning should precede a report, so a formal written charge must precede an accusation." In this legal text, no warning is required before an accusation. Therefore, 
<margin>Durandus.</margin>
Durandus <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a prominent medieval canonist.</note> says in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 19, Question 4) that in the internal forum of conscience a warning is required, but not in the external forum of the law. And Saint
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thomas [Aquinas], in the same distinction (Question 2, Article 3), recounts both opinions.
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
And although Sylvester [Prierias] <note>A 15th-century theologian famous for his manual for confessors.</note> under the word "Accusation" (§ 3) thinks he holds the affirmative view [that a warning is needed], he actually seems to more clearly hold the negative view: namely, that it is not required. And therefore
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Aquinas.</note> says (in his commentary on the *Summa*, 2. 2. question 33, article 7) that when an accusation is merely permitted but not commanded, it is not necessary for a secret warning to precede it; but when it is commanded by law, then a warning is not necessary either.

<margin>Solution to the proposed doubt.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these views, reason clarifies the matter such that there is no need for more citations, but rather for distinctions. The first distinction is: when an accusation is the duty of someone regarding their own private property or injury, no warning is required, neither in the court of law nor in the court of conscience. The reason is: because the aim of such an accuser is not primarily to correct their brother; therefore, a warning would be useless and vain. For even if the offender is corrected, the person who was injured can still pursue their legal rights. In this case, the opinion of Cajetan clearly fails: for this person is not bound to accuse, and yet they can do so without a prior warning. However, when the crime is "pestilential" to the commonwealth (in the manner recently explained), then a distinction must be made. Truly, if the one who finds out is absolutely certain that through their private warning the brother will be so reformed that the public harm will be entirely laid to rest and cease, then a warning is necessary. This is required not only by the law of charity but also by justice: because that "pestilent" sinner still possesses his own honor; therefore, if the public evil can be sufficiently countered without damaging his reputation, he should not be publicly exposed. For accusation is (as we said) medicinal; and therefore, if such a great loss of reputation can be avoided, it must be guarded against. But if one is not entirely certain that their warning will be effective, or if there is danger in delay, one must hasten to the accusation immediately. Hence, if there were a creeping betrayal of the city, or a plot for the death of the king, or above all the crime of heresy—especially among those preaching such doctrines—the command is to fly to the judges at once: because no one should think they can

<column-break/>

counter such enormous dangers in any other way. Indeed, even if suitable witnesses were not available for proof, one must hasten to make a judicial report <note>Latin: "denuntiationem iudicialem."</note>. This is the express opinion of Saint Thomas 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
(2. 2. q. 33. art. 7), where he says that in such cases one must proceed immediately to a report so that harms of this kind may be prevented. "Unless," he says, "someone firmly believes that they could immediately prevent such evils through a secret warning."

<margin>The Rule.</margin>
¶ From this, a rule is to be taken for General Inquisitions <note>Referring to the formal judicial inquiries into heresy and other crimes against the faith common in Soto's era.</note> when an edict commands that everyone report hidden crimes. If the sins are entirely corrected and finished, of whatever kind they may be, no one is bound to report or accuse them; rather, one is only bound to be a witness if their testimony is legally requested in a particular case. If, however, they are not corrected, then they are either private (such as concubinage or other things that do not have the public good as their object), and these are only to be reported fraternally for the correction of the brother. But if they lead to public ruin—such as treason, heresy, or if someone, perhaps not out of weakness but by design and as a sort of public enemy, solicits members of the commonwealth toward evil to corrupt the state—and that evil could not be countered otherwise, they must be reported by judicial report; indeed, they must be accused if the matter can be proven. Likewise, if danger threatens a third party. Although in these cases the necessity of accusing does not arise so frequently, because crimes of this sort can more often be prevented by the way of fraternal correction.

¶ Here we should examine the "fiscals" <note>Latin: "fiscalibus." These were government officials or prosecutors representing the state's financial and legal interests.</note> in criminal cases. Indeed, that prosecutors of the treasury <note>Latin: "fisci procuratores."</note> are appointed is just, so that they may take care of the public treasury. Likewise, it is just that they exist as accusers of crimes tending toward the ruin of the public good (as has been explained), since everyone is bound to uncover those. But that these "fiscals" act as investigators of private crimes—I believe neither St. Thomas nor the older saints would have approved of this. For to demand punishment and vengeance for such private sins belongs only to the private individuals who were struck by the injury. But since custom has established this practice, it is not for us to judge it.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, the second conclusion responds. For those testimonies prove that for private persons, it is a counsel of the Gospel to forgive their private injuries.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument concerning the loyalty of friends, the response is that friends are to be cherished "even unto the altars" <note>Latin: "vsq; ad aras." A proverb meaning one should be loyal to a friend only as far as religion and the law allow.</note>;

<summary>Soto discusses whether a private warning must precede a formal accusation, concluding that for public dangers like treason or heresy, immediate reporting is mandatory to protect the commonwealth. He also questions the expansion of state "fiscal" prosecutors into the investigation of private moral failings, which he believes should remain the concern of the injured parties.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...[one is bound to] protect [the common good]: and therefore where a matter concerns the common good, this must be preferred over those [individuals]. Nor is the loyalty of friendship violated by this, even if a promise to keep a secret preceded it—unless it is the sacrosanct secret of sacramental confession, which is not permitted to be revealed even for the sake of the whole world.

<margin>To the third [argument].</margin>
¶ To the third argument, it is responded that infamous and excommunicated persons (as held in the cited Question 7) are barred from making an accusation. This is not for their own benefit—since to accuse where and when it is appropriate is a virtue—but they are restricted from that duty as a punishment. This is because an accusation requires the authority <note>original: "autoritatem"; referring to the legal standing or moral weight of the person speaking</note> of the accuser, which that class of people does not possess. Furthermore, in the Digest <note>original: "ff."; a standard abbreviation for the *Pandects* or *Digest* of Roman Civil Law</note> under the title "on accusations," in the law "those who accuse" <note>original: "l. qui accusare"</note>, others are prohibited from accusing for many other reasons: namely by reason of sex, age,
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
condition, etc. ¶ But there is a doubt whether, at least when a crime is ruinous to the republic, those who are legally barred may be admitted
<margin>Response.</margin>
to make an accusation. The response is that they are not to be admitted even then. However, they can and should make the dangers known through a judicial report <term>denuntiatio; a formal notification to a judge that does not carry the same legal risks or personal involvement as a formal accusation</term>, as Cajetan
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
is the authority in his commentary on [Aquinas's Summa] Part 2-2, Question 68, Article 1.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ And likewise, it is responded to the fourth argument. For by the same cause and question, and by the same law cited in the Digest, children, subordinates, and servants are prohibited from accusing their superiors. However, Saint
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thomas [Aquinas] glosses this in the same question, saying that they can nonetheless accuse them out of the effect of charity, and especially in a case involving the common good. This is because they are not restrained as a punishment, as others are, but for the sake of propriety <note>original: "honestatem"</note>, because an accusation carries with it a certain air of hatred, which is a disgrace when directed against superiors.

<margin>How clerics may accuse.</margin>
¶ Regarding clerics, however, the response is that in a case of blood <note>A "blood case" refers to a trial involving capital punishment or physical mutilation.</note>, as those laws hold, they can by no means be accusers. They can, however, report crimes, protesting that they are not revealing such criminals for the purpose of seeking a "blood vengeance" <term>poena sanguinis; the death penalty</term>, but either to head off a public evil or to recover their own goods. For with this declaration, it is lawful for them to bring such crimes to court: not only those which are against the public good, such as the impiety of heresy and treason <term>laesae maiestatis; "injured majesty," or high treason against the state or ruler</term>, but even those by which a third party or they themselves are wronged or suffer loss, as is clear in the chapter *Praelatis* in the sixth book of the Decretals <note>original: "cap. Praelatis. de homicidi. voluntat. lib. 6."</note>.

<margin>To the last.</margin>
¶ To the last point regarding the "punishment of like for like" <term>poena talionis; the principle of an eye for an eye, where a false accuser suffers the penalty they sought for the defendant</term>, a more convenient place for responding will be given below in Article 4.

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE II.

-> Whether it is necessary for an accusation <-
-> to be presented in writing. <-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
AFTER the obligation of accusing, the question is asked concerning the form of the accusation: whether it must be presented in writing. And it is argued on the negative side. Writing is necessary only when we either speak of past events—lest our memory slip away—or when we speak to those who are absent, whom our words do not reach. But an accusation happens in the present time, and with the defendant himself present. For as it says in Question 2, Case 8, in the canon "of accusers" <note>original: "2. q. 8. can. accusatorū."</note>: No one can be accused while absent.
<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
Therefore, writing is not necessary. ¶ Secondly, a crime of another is revealed no less through a report <term>denuntiatio</term> than through an accusation; but in a report, no formal written brief <term>libellus</term> is necessary; therefore, neither is it necessary in an accusation.

¶ On the contrary is Augustine in the same cited canon (2. q. 8), where he says: Let the persons of accusers never be
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
received without a writing; nor should it be permitted for anyone to accuse if the one they wish to accuse is absent.

---

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
This question is very easy, to which a single affirmative conclusion is given in response. The form of an accusation is that it be made in writing. This is a conclusion of law, not only of Canon Law in the place cited (and in the same cause and question in the canons "whoever" and "crime"), but also of Civil Law in the Digest, on accusations, in the law "if to anyone" <note>original: "ff. de accusa. l. si cui."</note>. And although natural law <term>ius naturae</term> does not explicitly command this, a natural reason is nevertheless drawn from it.

<margin>Natural reason for the conclusion.</margin>
For the judge is (as was said above) a middle party established between two parties—namely, the accuser and the defendant—who must examine the case about which he is to deliver a sentence. Since, therefore, on the one hand, memory is slippery and cannot preserve all words for a long time, and on the other hand, it is necessary that those same words be retained until the final sentence, the aid of
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
writing is necessary. Add to this that since the accuser becomes liable to punishment—formerly the "punishment of like for like" <term>talio</term>, and even now to no light penalty—if he should be convicted of false accusation <term>calumnia</term>, it is worthwhile to sign the accusation so that he cannot later deny it.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
To these points, since defenses, exceptions, and even proofs must be applied to the accusation, it is expedient that the accusation occupy the head of the brief <term>libelli caput</term>. However, as is held in the law "Light matters" <note>original: "l. Leuia. ff. de accusati."</note> in the Digest, in minor cases one should proceed plainly without these kinds of ceremonies.

<meta>This page continues the legal analysis of how an accusation must be presented. It transitions from the formal requirement of written documentation to the moral qualities required of an accuser, specifically focusing on the vice of injustice in legal proceedings.</meta>

...formal ceremonies. Furthermore, in notorious cases, in which (as we said above) an accuser is not expected, a written document is likewise not required.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that a written record of the accusation is necessary not because it concerns past events, but so that it may be preserved safely for the future. And therefore, it is no obstacle that the accusation is made in the presence of the defendant; for both the defendant and the accuser ought to be present. Hence, in the same Case and Question of the Canon Law, in the canon *Per scripta* <note>original: "can. per scripta"; Canon law reference regarding written evidence</note>, Pope Stephen commands that no one’s accusation should be accepted through writing. This does not mean it is not to be offered in writing (as has been said), but that it must not be sent in writing by an *absent* accuser; rather, he must appear in person. Moreover, the rule that an absent defendant should not be accused is not to be understood so strictly that it is illegal to present an accusation to a judge in his absence; rather, it means he is not to be condemned by a sentence before he is heard in person. This is especially true in a criminal case, and most of all in a capital one, as is cautioned by the law *Absentem* in the Code <note>original: "C. de accusa."; referring to the Codex of Justinian regarding accusations</note>. If, however, he refuses to appear after being summoned by a public herald, a sentence can indeed be passed against him as a rebel; but if he is later captured, he ought to be heard before the sentence is carried out.

<margin>To the second [argument].</margin>
¶ The second solution is easily gathered from what has been said. For in a "fraternal evangelical denunciation" <note>Referring to the process in Matthew 18:15 of private correction before public legal action</note>, because one is not proceeding toward punishment, but both the judge and the one reporting are looking only to the salvation of the brother without the loss of his reputation, no writing is necessary. It is otherwise in a judicial denunciation. And this difference between a denunciation and an accusation is noted in the chapter *Super his* under the title "on accusations."

## ARTICLE III.

->*Whether an accusation is rendered unjust by these three things: calumny, prevarication, and tergiversation.*<-

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
The third thing required in an accuser is justice. Regarding this, it is asked whether justice is corrupted by these three vices: calumny, prevarication <note>In this legal context, "prevarication" refers to collusion or betraying one's duty to the court</note>, and tergiversation <note>meaning the desertion or abandonment of a case</note>. And it is argued from the negative side: Calumny (as held in Case 2, Question 3, the canon *Si quem pœnituerit*) is "knowingly intending false crimes." However, it happens that someone may bring

<column-break/>

a calumny against another out of ignorance, though a lightness of mind does not entirely excuse them; therefore, either that must be judged as calumny against the canon, or there is a fourth vice by which the justice of the accuser is defiled.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Second: To prevaricate (as is added in the same place) is "to hide true crimes." In this, however, there is not always underlying iniquity, because no one is bound to reveal all crimes, neither their own nor their neighbor's.

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
¶ Third: To "tergiversate" is to desist from an accusation altogether. But this is not always joined with injury; indeed, at the beginning of the same chapter it is prescribed that if one repents of having accused someone of what he cannot prove, if he comes to an agreement with the innocent accused, they may mutually release one another.

¶ To the contrary, however, is the same text, where it is held that the recklessness of accusers is detected in three ways: for they either calumniate, or prevaricate, or tergiversate.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with a single conclusion: It happens that an accusation is corrupted by the three named vices. This conclusion is based not only on the text of Canon Law cited, but also on Civil Law <note>original: "iuris ciuilis"; Roman Law</note> in the Digest, regarding the *Senatusconsultum Turpilianum* <note>A Roman law concerning the punishment of dishonest accusers</note>, or regarding abolitions, in the law *Accusatorum*. From this, the canon *Quem pœnituerit* took the exact same words. Moreover, the number of these vices is gathered as follows: Since an accusation is directed toward the common good, yet in such a way that a just punishment for the crime is achieved, an accuser can "limp on either foot" <note>original: "vtroque pede claudicare"; a metaphor for failing in one of two directions</note>. That is, either by favoring the defendant, or by favoring the republic or the injured party too much. He leans toward the republic <note>meaning he is overly zealous or malicious in prosecution</note> when he thrusts a false crime upon the defendant. And this is to calumniate. For calumny is the crafty harassment of a person through fraud. Nor is he only a calumniator who imposes a false crime, but also he who brings to court a hidden crime that cannot be proven by law. For in law, whatever cannot be made known by suitable witnesses or instruments is reputed as false. Secondly, the accuser can conversely be injurious to the republic when he is the cause for a person who has offended the public good not being restrained. And this happens in two ways. In one way, by constructing a fraud against the republic: namely, by leaning in favor of the defendant. And this is to prevaricate. For to "prevaricate" <note>original: "varicari"</note> is the same as to "bend" or "straddle." This prevarication happens in two ways: in one way by concealing all the crimes which he is bound to reveal for the benefit of the republic, and so...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral obligations of an accuser in a criminal trial. # F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

by neglecting proofs; and in the other way by admitting false excuses and exceptions. Therefore, prevarication <term>praeuaricatio: in this context, a betrayal of one's duty through a secret agreement with the opposing party</term> is called by another name, "collusion": as if then the accuser and the defendant together deceive the state or the injured party. On which account this vice is accustomed to fall in practice not only upon the accuser, but also upon the advocate, and other ministers, and even upon the judge. In the second way, it happens that he favors the accused, entirely and in general (as the law says) by desisting from the accusation. And that is called tergiversation <term>tergiversatio: from the Latin 'tergum' (back) and 'uersare' (to turn); the act of abandoning a cause or stalling</term>, as if the accuser turns his back on the case.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that the imposition of a crime is not judged by law as calumny <term>calumnia: a false and malicious accusation</term> unless it is done with zeal and on purpose. Nevertheless, no one ought to come forward as an accuser unless he has first been made certain of the crime, and also has certain and ready proof. And therefore, he who leaps into accusing lightly and rashly is not immune from fault. However, he ought not to be punished as a calumniator with the penalty of talion <note>original: "talione"; the principle of 'retaliation' where the punishment matches the intended harm</note> or another sharp punishment, but with another lighter penalty. Unless perhaps he was moved by a just error; for then he is worthy of none. All these things, however, must be weighed and estimated by the prudence of the judge.

<margin>To the second [argument].</margin>
To the second it is replied that no one ought to detect his own crimes unless he is legitimately made a defendant and interrogated by a legitimate judge. Nor truly should he detect another's except in a case where he is bound to denounce or accuse. But when he accuses for the public good, then he is bound to detect all things which contribute to the matter. Therefore, if by prayer or price <note>original: "prece vel pretio"; that is, through entreaty or bribery</note> or another cause he colludes with the defendant, he is a prevaricator.

<margin>To the third [argument].</margin>
<margin>Three ways to tergiversate without fault.</margin>
Similarly, to the third it is replied that to tergiversate is not always a crime, but only then when the accuser is bound to persist in the accusation. Therefore, it can happen in three ways that one tergiversates without fault. First, when someone has accused in his own private cause. For then, just as he freely signed the accusation, so he can desert it when he pleases. Second, when he has accused in a public cause, yet lightly; for then as often as he fears he will fail in proof, he can agree with the defendant and desist from the accusation. And this is the case of the said chapter "If anyone should repent" <note>original: "cap. fi quem poenituerit"; a reference to Canon law regarding those who withdraw an accusation</note>. Third, by the authority of the prince, who, on account of the illustrious dignity of the person and the utility of the state, can both reject the accusation at the beginning and abolish it during the process; as is subjoined in the same chapter.

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether an accuser who has failed in<-
->proof is bound by the penalty of talion.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring floral motifs inside a square woodcut border.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
The fourth thing that remains to be disputed regarding the accuser is whether, failing in proof, he is bound by the penalty of talion. And it is argued from the negative side. It happens sometimes that someone comes forward to accuse another of a false crime through a just error; for which reason Pope Fabian <note>original: "Fabianus Papa. 2. q. 3. can. Si quis iratus."; Pope Fabian, active in the 3rd century; reference to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of Church laws</note> grants pardon: therefore, not every calumniator is worthy of the penalty of talion.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second: If such a punishment is just, it is justly inflicted for this reason: that the accuser intends a loss through injury to another. Therefore, either this is because of the injury brought upon the defendant, and then the prince cannot remit it; or because of that which is inflicted on the state, and then the defendant cannot remit it. But both can remit it; therefore, the injury for which such a punishment is established cannot be designated.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Third: For one fault, no one should be punished with a double penalty, according to that saying of Nahum 1 <note>original: "Naum. 1. Non iudicabit Deus bis in idipsum"; biblical reference to Nahum 1:9, "God will not judge twice on the same thing"</note>. But calumniators are held as infamous <term>infames: a legal status involving the loss of reputation and certain civil rights</term> by law; as is clear in the second question, third canon, "If anyone regarding." Therefore, they ought not to undergo another punishment.

<margin>Damasus.</margin>
But to the contrary is the decree of Damasus <note>original: "Damasus... 2. q. 3."; refers to Pope Damasus I</note>: A calumniator, if he fails in proof, receives talion. And another nearby [decree] of Adrian <margin>Pope Adrian.</margin>: He who has not proved what he charged, let him suffer the penalty which he himself [sought to] inflict.

<margin>From where "talio" draws its origin.</margin>
For the solution of the question, it must be noted that talion <term>talio: retaliation</term> is so called from "such as" <note>original: "talio à tale dictum est"; an etymological explanation linking the word to "talis," meaning "such as the injury was"</note>: namely, that each person should suffer such a thing as he was attempting against another contrary to right. This is what Aristotle in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, chapter 5, calls <margin>Aristotle.</margin> "suffering in return" <term>repaffum: the Greek term 'antipeponthos' or reciprocal justice</term>, according to that saying of Rhadamanthus <note>original: "Rhadamanthi"; in Greek mythology, a judge of the underworld known for strict justice</note>:

> If he should suffer the very things he did,
> the judgment would be right.

<margin>Affirmative conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, an affirmative conclusion is established. It is just that he who through accusation has led someone into the danger of a heavy punishment should himself bear a similar one. This conclusion is not only from the cited places of Canon law, but also of Civil law: as is clear in the Digest regarding the Turpilian Decree <note>original: "ff. ad sena. conf. Turpil."; reference to the Senatus Consultum Turpilianum in the Roman Digest, which punished those who abandoned or faked accusations</note>. Since, therefore, the laws adjudge the one failing in proof to the penalty of talion, they show that not only he who imposes a false crime, but also he who reveals a hidden one that cannot be proved, is subject to the same <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> punishment. The natural reason is this: The accuser is established as the party adverse to the defendant, striving...

### BOOK FIVE, QUESTION VI.

...tending to drive him to punishment: the judge sits in the middle between both as the protector of justice. But it appears that the equality of justice requires that the danger which someone creates for another through injury should fall back upon himself: therefore the penalty of talion <note>The "lex talionis" or law of retaliation: an eye for an eye, where the punishment corresponds to the injury.</note> is just. 

<margin>Confirmation.</margin> 
The same conclusion is confirmed. For in the ancient law, which was most just, the same penalty stands written: namely Exodus 21: *An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.* And Deuteronomy 19: *When, searching most diligently, they find that a false witness has spoken a lie against his brother, they shall do to him as he thought to do to his brother.* However, it is not inferred from here, as some think, that this penalty is now purely of divine law: for that was not a moral law from the law of nature, but only a judicial law, which therefore entirely ceased. Not that Christ peculiarly abolished that law in Matthew 5—for there he only referred to the old law, advising us instead that we should not avenge ourselves, but forgive injuries to our enemies—but rather that the entire old law ceased. Except that the moral precepts, which were of the law of nature, were confirmed by the evangelical law. The ceremonial ones indeed ceased so that, like signs now false, they cannot be instituted again. The judicial ones indeed can, if it be deemed just, be established repeatedly. 

At the same time, the law of talion was always considered grim and harsh, but it was established because of the "hardness of that people" <note>A common theological reference to the Israelites being governed by strict law due to their perceived stubbornness.</note> and their inclination to weave false accusations. For if you consult natural reason, it is enough that he who kills should be killed. But he who *procured* a killing is not immediately guilty of such a great crime, except by the highest rigor of the law. Especially because then men would be deterred far too much from the duty of accusing. And therefore (as held in the *Institutes on Injuries*, paragraph: penalty) that punishment has now almost passed away through disuse. It is retained, however, to some extent in well-ordered provinces: especially regarding a witness who deliberately speaks false testimony in a capital case. And that most of all when, because of him, an innocent person is killed. Even though wicked informers ought to be punished with sharp punishment even outside such a case.

<margin>To the first argument. Aristotle.</margin> 
To the first argument, therefore, Aristotle responds in the cited place, Book 5 of the *Ethics*: that "suffering in return" [reciprocation], which we call talion, is not always demanded by justice, since it differs greatly whether someone does something voluntarily or involuntarily. For a spontaneous wrongdoer is worthy of punishment, but he who harms involuntarily is worthy of pardon. And therefore, he who, through blameless ignorance, makes a defendant of someone...

<column-break/>

...whom he thinks to be in crime, is not held by law as a "calumniator" <term>calumniator: a person who brings a false, malicious accusation in bad faith</term>, as we said above; and thus he is not worthy of the talion. 

<margin>To the second.</margin> 
¶ To the second, it is replied that the calumniator is injurious both to the defendant and to the state. Whence in Deuteronomy 19, both were commanded: namely first, that he who had spoken false testimony against a brother should suffer what he thought to make his brother suffer—namely, because of the injury done to him. Secondly, that such people should be removed from the midst of the people, so that those hearing might have fear. Wherein the injury inflicted upon the state was hinted at. From which it follows that as long as the accused has not remitted [forgiven] the penalty of talion, the prince cannot remit it, as was said in the previous question. But after he has forgiven it, then it will remain in the judgment of the prince to relax it. 

<margin>To the third.</margin> 
¶ To the third, it is replied that the accuser incurs the penalty of talion by reason of the harm he intended for his neighbor, but infamy <term>infamia: a legal status involving the loss of reputation and certain civil rights</term> because of the fault. And therefore, to remit the infamy belongs to the prince. If it be ecclesiastical, it belongs to the Pope, as Gratian says in the Decree, Case 2, question 3, canon *Euthemium*. There he responds to those words of Pope Gelasius: "Although we can save souls through penance, yet we cannot abolish infamy," saying that this is understood regarding infamy inflicted by a civil judge, which does not pertain to the Pope. Although perhaps the sense is clearer regarding "infamy of fact." For no one can delete that stain which is annexed to a shameful deed, since there is no power over the past.

->F. D. Soto, *On Justice and Law*,<-

concerning repentance, distinction 1, the canon "sometimes someone." <note>Latin: *de pœnitẽtia, d.1.can.quis aliqñ*. A reference to Gratian’s *Decretum*, the foundational collection of canon law.</note> I do not tell you to betray yourself in public, nor to accuse yourself before others. For it should be read thus: "not to accuse," rather than "to excuse," as the corrupted text has it. However, he who would disclose the truth of his own crime would be betraying himself; therefore, it is permitted for him to hide his crime.
<margin>Second [Argument].</margin>
¶ Second. An <term>officious lie</term> <note>A "lie of necessity" or "helpful lie" (Latin: *mendacium officiosum*) told to help someone without intending to harm another.</note>—namely, when someone lies to benefit another without harming anyone—is not a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A grave sin that, in Catholic theology, severs the soul's relationship with God.</note>. But he who lies to protect himself from death lies "officiously"; therefore, this is permitted without mortal harm.
<margin>Third [Argument].</margin>
¶ Third, no sin is mortal unless it is against <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the theological virtue of love for God and neighbor.</note>. He who uses a lie to guard himself against death acts neither against the love of God nor against his neighbor; rather, he acts according to the charity with which he loves himself. Therefore, it is not a lethal offense. ¶ To the contrary is that passage from Joshua 7, where that leader said to Achan: *My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel, and confess, and tell me what you have done; do not hide it.* Furthermore, everyone is bound to give glory to God, according to 1 Corinthians 10: *Do all things for the glory of God.*

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
This question is answered with three conclusions. First: whoever is **legitimately questioned regarding his own crime is bound, under the guilt of mortal sin, to make his crime known**, even if he must be led to his death by virtue of that same confession. When I say "legitimately," I mean by a legitimate judge and according to the proper form of the law.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason for this conclusion is manifest. For the virtue of justice is necessary for salvation; therefore, whoever is bound under the guilt of mortal offense is held to preserve it. Justice, however, compels a subject to obey a superior, according to the word of Paul: *Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.* <note>Romans 13:1.</note> Indeed, a superior often has the right to command a subject to disclose his own crime; therefore, the subject is then constrained to obey. That a judge sometimes has this right is clear: for no one—especially in a capital sentence, or indeed any other according to the common order—ought to be condemned based on any evidence or <term>infamy</term> <note>A legal status of "ill repute" or public notoriety that could trigger a trial.</note> unless he has confessed. At the very least, an appeal is granted to one who is condemned otherwise, as in the law *observare* <note>A reference to the Code of Justinian.</note> regarding those whose appeals are not received. Unless there is a sufficient number of witnesses by whom he is convicted, and that only by way of accusation. This same point is cautioned in Canon Law (2. quaest. 1. canon *nos in quenquam* and canon *iudex*). Therefore, unless the accused could be compelled to confess, the path to finishing

<column-break/>

judgments would be too narrow. And this conclusion is to be understood even when someone is questioned without an oath; for although perjury adds the impiety of sacrilege to a lie, a simple lie regarding a grave matter against the bond of obedience is nevertheless a mortal crime by its very nature.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: **When, however, someone is not legitimately questioned, even if he has been put under oath—for instance, either by one who is not his judge, or against the sanctions of the canons and laws—he is not bound to confess his crime.** Indeed, a similar thing must be affirmed regarding witnesses in the crime of another. This conclusion is clear because whoever has the right to defend himself and his property is not compelled to the contrary by law. But when one is questioned outside the causes and order of the law, he is compelled by no law; therefore, he is by no means convicted of betraying himself.
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: **To no one, whether he is questioned by right or by injury, is it permitted to lie**; because a lie is by its nature so evil and iniquitous that for no reason can he who utters it be free from fault. Nevertheless, when one is questioned unjustly and without an oath, that lie might not be a mortal sin, because it is not "pernicious" <note>A "pernicious lie" (Latin: *mendacium perniciosum*) is one intended to cause harm.</note> but "officious." It is otherwise, however, if it becomes perjury. Here, however, the second and third conclusions require that we provide the skill and <term>prudence</term> <note>In scholastic terms, "prudence" often refers to the use of "mental reservation" or careful wording to avoid lying while not revealing the truth.</note> by which one who is unjustly interrogated might then protect himself and escape without a lie. We shall answer this more conveniently in the following article, after we have inspected the causes by which an accused person is compelled to reveal the truth.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that Chrysostom is speaking in the case of the second conclusion, or when no one is questioning the accused. For when he is questioned by the order and merit of the law, he does not betray himself, but rather his notoriety, the witnesses, or the accuser betray him, whom it is not permitted to resist.
<margin>To the second [argument].</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that for someone to lie to avoid death, whether for himself or another, is not mortal if it is done without harm to another; however, when someone is asked by law and covers his fault with a lie, he commits an injury both to the judge to whom he owes obedience and to the accuser and the injured party.
<margin>To the third [argument].</margin>
¶ And it is similarly responded to the third. For it is denied that such a crime is not against charity. For it harms both the judge and the plaintiff; and thus it opposes the love of God, who commands us to obey our elders. For no one violates the virtue of justice without also violating charity, both toward God and neighbor. Whence, upon that Psalm: *Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses...* <note>Psalm 141:4 (Vulgate 140:4).</note>

<header>Book Five, Question VI.</header>

<margin>The Gloss.</margin>
...excuses in sins: the <term>Gloss</term> <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval commentary on the Bible or Law.</note> says, "This is the habit of the shameless, that when they are caught, they excuse themselves through other falsehoods."

<margin>Gregory.</margin>
And Gregory in Book 21 of the *Moralia* on Job 31: "If I have hidden my sin like a man": It is a common vice of the human race to commit a sin by falling; to hide the committed sin by denying it; and to multiply the convicted sin by defending it. <note>Original Latin: *Vsitatum humani generis vitium eſt...* Pope Gregory the Great (6th century) was a foundational moral authority for Soto.</note>

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ Here you ask whether a lie in court, when one is bound to confess the truth, is universally a <term>mortal crime</term> <note>A serious sin that causes the loss of divine grace.</note>: or whether, through the lightness of the matter, it can become <term>venial</term> <note>A lesser sin that does not sever one's relationship with God.</note>, just as it happens outside of court.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan responds in his commentary on the *Summa Theologiae* (II-II, q. 69, art. 2): Every lie told in court, even in the most trivial matter, is mortal. His reason is this: because such a liar does violence to the judgment, which, being founded on a lie, subsequently becomes false. Therefore, just as <term>perjury</term> <note>Lying under oath.</note> is by no means venial due to the smallness of the matter, but is always mortal, so too is a lie in court. Nor is this limited only to the court of sacramental confession, but also in the "external forum" (civil or ecclesiastical courts).

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ But in truth, neither Cajetan’s conclusion (with all due respect to his outstanding authority) presents the truth, nor does his reasoning show probability. Rather, I would believe without a doubt that a venial sin can occur even there. For first, St. Thomas [Aquinas] himself suggests this in the same II-II, q. 70, art. 4, where he says that to violate justice by lying is mortal "in its kind" <note>Latin: *in ſuo genere*. In Scholasticism, this means the act is grave by its nature, but specific circumstances might lessen the guilt.</note>: here he suggests it can be venial. Likewise, in matters of faith, charity, and religion, the insignificance of the matter can lessen the sin so that it is venial: why then not in court? Furthermore, a venial lie can occur there through a lack of full deliberation; why then not from smallness of matter? Add to this that otherwise every other tiny defect in court would be mortal: such as if someone kept silent about a matter of tiny importance. And finally, it is argued: venial sins are not necessary for confession; therefore, to deny them there is not a mortal crime. It is granted, then, that a venial lie is worse in court than outside it; yet it does not follow that every such lie is mortal.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether it is lawful for the accused to defend himself through <term>calumny</term>.<-
<note>Latin: *calumnia*. In this context, it refers to using legal tricks, false accusations against others, or malicious maneuvers to avoid conviction.</note>

Since it is not lawful for a suffering defendant, even when not legitimately interrogated, to deny the truth, nor to lie when requested beyond the law, it follows that we see whether in either of those

<column-break/>

cases it is lawful for him to defend himself through trickery. And the argument is made for the affirmative side.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
According to civil laws, it is lawful for one who has been reported for a capital crime to "transact"—that is, to make a pact with the accuser and bribe him to stop: as seen in the Code [of Justinian] regarding transactions, and more expressly in the Digest regarding the property of those who commit suicide before sentencing. Therefore, it is not unlawful to use trickery.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second. An accuser who colludes with the defendant to subvert justice is punished with the penalty established by the laws, as was seen in the previous question; but no penalty is decreed for the accused, even if he acts with tricks against the accuser and deceives him; therefore, it is not unjust. To the contrary is canon law, which commands that both the accused and the accuser be bound by the <term>oath of calumny</term> <note>Latin: *iuramentum calumniae*. A standard legal oath where parties swore they were acting in good faith and not using false evidence.</note> at the start of the lawsuit; where civil laws on the same matter are also cited. The oath of calumny, as the name implies, means that neither the accuser nor the accused will use tricks or false claims.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is very grave: which we analyzed in our said *Relection* [Academic Lecture] in the sixth place through all its details, as I believe. But we cannot (as we said above) leave this place empty of this dispute. We will respond here with seven conclusions. The first is that well-known one we established in the previous article: even if it is lawful for no one to deny the truth with a lie, it is nevertheless sometimes lawful to hide it with prudence.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
For (as was just said) no one is bound to reveal the truth unless compelled by law; therefore, outside of such a case, anyone can guard a secret, especially their own. But the point and knot of the matter is hidden there, so that we may know when a judge, who is legitimate, can legitimately question a subject about their own crime, even under oath.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ To explain this, the Second Conclusion is established. There are three differences of cases in which a judge can lawfully question a defendant, in which the defendant is then bound to answer the truth: namely, if his <term>infamy</term> <note>Latin: *infamia*. Public notoriety or loss of reputation due to a crime.</note> regarding some crime has preceded, or some express signs [evidence] have appeared, or "half-full" proof was present.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
The conclusion is from St. Thomas, II-II, q. 69, art. 2. And although he does not provide a reason, he nevertheless clearly gathers it from the previous definition. Namely, that a judge cannot condemn anyone without an accuser or one filling his role. These three things, however, take the place of an express accuser so that the defendant can be legitimately questioned.
