Book Five, Question VII.

# QUESTION SEVEN,
## On the injustice of the witness.
### ARTICLE 1.
### Whether a person is sometimes bound to give testimony.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a seated figure of a scholar or judge wearing a cap and robes, sitting at a desk and writing in a book.</image-desc>
The person of the witness occupies the fourth place in a judgment: regarding whom four things must be examined: namely, the obligation, sufficiency, rejection, and fault of witnesses. It is asked, therefore, first, whether someone is sometimes bound to give testimony. And it is argued on the negative side.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
Fraudulence is permitted to no one, because individual malice is inherent in it. He who reveals a secret crime, especially one entrusted to his faith, is unfaithful and fraudulent, according to Proverbs 11: "He who walks fraudulently reveals secrets; but he who is faithful conceals the matter entrusted by a friend" <note>original: "Qui ambulat fraudulenter, reuelat arcana: qui autem fidelis est, celat amici commissum"</note>. Therefore, it is not permitted to anyone to reveal such secrets; far less is anyone bound to do so.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If testifying were a virtue, it would especially befit priests and clerics due to their greater authority. For more steadfast faith is owed to those who handle sacred things. And yet, clerics are prohibited from being witnesses in cases of blood <note>A "cause of blood" refers to a capital case where the penalty is death or mutilation; canon law often forbid clergy from participating in such judgments.</note>. Therefore, testifying does not seem to be a virtue.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ To the contrary is Augustine, where he says: "He who hides the truth and he who brings forth a lie are both guilty. The former because he does not want to reveal it, the latter because he desires to harm." <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational authority for medieval legal and moral thought.</note>

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
The response to the question is contained in four conclusions. For a distinction must be made between him from whom testimony is required and him who is not required.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion is: Whoever is summoned as a witness by a legitimate judge according to the form of the law is bound to give testimony.

<margin>Support for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is evident because this is a duty of obedience; and every subject is bound to obey their superiors when they command just things.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: One who is questioned about secret crimes, concerning which neither ill-repute <note>original: "infamia," referring to a person's public legal standing or a prior public rumor that justifies a legal inquiry.</note> has preceded, nor any other legal cause from those named above, is not bound to give testimony.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This is likewise manifest: because everyone is bound to look out for the good name of their neighbor

<column-break/>

by concealing their crimes, unless they have been legally compelled. Therefore, the same rules are to be observed by the witness as were prescribed for the accused. However, when either no one questions you, or he who is not your judge questions you, another distinction must be observed. Indeed, if your testimony is necessary to free a person from either an unjust death, or from false infamy, or from an unfair loss: then the third conclusion must be heard.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Everyone is bound by their testimony to free their neighbor from such dangers unjustly imposed.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
It is proven: because by the mandate of charity <term>charity: in this theological context, 'caritas' refers to the moral obligation to act for the well-being of others</term>, everyone is bound to prevent harm to their neighbor. An example is readily available in almsgiving, which everyone is bound to offer to one who is suffering severely. For this is also a certain kind—and indeed a principal kind—of almsgiving. Wherefore, not only is a person bound when asked and requested by their neighbor, but even if they have not been required at all, everyone is bound of their own accord to see to it that they deliver their testimony where it can be of benefit. For so the Psalmist admonishes us: "Rescue the poor; and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner." And the Wise Man in Proverbs 28: "Deliver those who are being led to death."

<margin>Paul.</margin>
And in Romans 1: "They are worthy of death, not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those doing them."

<margin>Gloss.</margin>
Where the gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> says: "to consent is to be silent when you could refute." And for the same reason, when you could testify. Wherefore this conclusion has a much more obvious truth in revealing crimes which tend toward the destruction of the commonwealth. For if then everyone is bound to be an accuser, it is much more just to be a witness.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Fourth conclusion: Outside the case of necessity for freeing a wretched person from injury or the commonwealth from danger, for the sake of condemning the accused alone, no one is bound to offer themselves as a witness of their own accord, unless legally compelled according to the order of law.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proven: because concealing the truth then is not a cause of either public or private loss. Therefore, neither the reason of justice nor of charity then compels any private citizen to reveal the secret that they hold in their heart.

<margin>Argument against the first conclusion.</margin>
¶ But indeed, it is necessary to weigh these conclusions more exactly, as they are simply asserted following the order of Saint Thomas. For an argument immediately arises against the first conclusion: that if a witness summoned by a judge were bound to give testimony, it would follow that it would by no means be permitted for him to hide himself so as not to be summoned. Furthermore, if he were to use any trickery so as not to give true testimony, he would be bound to restore the loss which either the plaintiff or the defendant might receive, to whom his testimony was beneficial. This inference is evident because...

<summary>This page discusses the moral and legal obligations of witnesses, concluding that while individuals must testify when summoned by a judge or to save someone from injustice, they are generally permitted to keep secrets if no legal or charitable necessity exists.</summary>
<keywords>witnesses, testimony, legal ethics, secrets, charity, Augustine, Saint Thomas Aquinas, judicial summons, infamia, obligation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the moral and legal obligations of witnesses, specifically focusing on whether failing to testify creates a debt of restitution to the injured party.</meta>

<page-num>466</page-num>
<header>Fray Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*,</header>
<columns>2</columns>
<page-type>text</page-type>

<margin>
First argument for the opposing side.
</margin>
...to then bear witness is an act of justice: and when justice is harmed, it demands restitution. But if you are convinced by this argument, it immediately follows that anyone who—contrary to the tenor of the third conclusion—fails to come to the aid of a victim of injury or loss with their testimony, even if not called by a judge, would be bound by that same reasoning to make amends through restitution. The logic is clear: for while Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose work Soto is commenting upon.</note> cites the testimony of Paul: *Not only those who act, but also those who consent to those acting* <note>original: "Non solùm qui agunt, sed etiam qui conſentiunt facientibus"</note>, he is of the opinion that the witness then consents to the neighbor's loss. However, that this should not be granted is argued as follows. First, no one is bound by the law of charity to rescue a neighbor from calamity unless they are pressed by extreme or grave necessity: therefore, although someone may need my testimony where loss of money or reputation is at stake, unless there is an extreme or grave danger of death, I am not bound to offer my service unless I am compelled by a judge.

<margin>
Argument 2.
</margin>
¶ Second: indeed, no one is compelled by that same law of charity to provide help in such extreme or grave dangers if it results in their own detriment.

<margin>
Argument 3.
</margin>
¶ Third: even if in such cases someone, being negligent of the duty of charity, does not fulfill their office, they do not immediately become liable for restitution. Therefore, the third conclusion is not as true as it sounds on the surface.

<margin>
The legitimate sense of the first and third conclusions.
</margin>
¶ These arguments have been brought forward so that the distinction between the first and third conclusions may be made clear. For indeed, while both are true, the first is true by the law of justice, but the third by the debt of charity alone. Through this distinction, other points become known. For someone who withdraws themselves through fraud and deceit so that they are not called as a witness by a judge—if the testimony were so necessary to the neighbor that the entire case would be endangered—then that person would both sin gravely and be bound to make restitution. In such a case, that person would have caused loss to another contrary to justice. And they would sin much more gravely, and be bound more strictly to restitution, if they gave false testimony from which the condemnation of another followed.

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>
¶ Therefore, to the first argument against this third conclusion, it is replied that although someone who is not summoned by a judge does not owe their testimony by the law of justice, but rather through the duty of charity, there is nonetheless a difference between this and other forms of almsgiving. In other cases, unless there is extreme and grave necessity, no one is forced to give what is their own; however, when another needs your testimony, they have a certain right to it, because everyone is given a commandment regarding their neighbor. And therefore,

<column-break/>

if you can provide it without any detriment at all, even if the other person does not undergo danger of life, but rather of reputation or money, you are bound by the love of charity. Just as if you held some document upon which their right and case depended, you would be bound to produce it. And another singular bond is added: there is a different rationale for necessity when someone suffers through injury or some accidental disaster than if they suffered through mere poverty. For indeed, when a neighbor lacks a house, I am not bound to give them one; but when their house is burning, even if they are wealthy, I am bound to extinguish the fire if I can do so without harm to myself.

<margin>
To the second argument.
</margin>
¶ To the second argument, however, we concede its conclusion: namely, that no one is compelled to perform such a duty of charity at the cost of their own grave danger or detriment; indeed, not even with the detriment of those close to them. For example, if there were a lawsuit against my father, I would not be bound to come forward as a witness against him of my own accord. Just as if my own parent were to attack an innocent person with a drawn sword, whom I could not defend except by killing that same parent, I am not bound to do so.

<margin>
To the third argument.
</margin>
And likewise, to the third, it is replied that where only the service and gift of charity is omitted, no obligation of restitution arises.

<margin>
Augustine.
</margin>
¶ Furthermore, from the fourth conclusion, some difficulty arises. For it appears that even outside the case of liberating an innocent person, everyone who has not yet been summoned by a judge is compelled by right to offer themselves as a witness for the condemnation of a guilty person: specifically, when they have been lawfully accused. Nor is the solution of Saint Thomas likely to be true, where he says that even if danger threatens the accuser, the witness ought not to care about this. For when an accuser is constrained to accuse, it seems the witness is immediately compelled to testify; otherwise, the condition of the accuser would be unjust: namely, that they would be bound to immerse themselves in a case where they would fail in the proof. It is replied that Saint Thomas is speaking precisely of cases where the accuser was not bound to accuse. And therefore he adds: *because they cast themselves into this danger voluntarily* <note>original: "quia ipse in hoc periculum ſponte ſe iniecit"</note>. For then no one is bound to favor them, as they would be for a defendant suffering injury against their will. And in this case, that saying of Augustine regarding the word of Abraham in Genesis 12—*Say that you are my sister*—holds true: *It is permitted to hide the truth, but not to tell a lie* <note>original: "Veritatem celare licet, non mendacium dicere"</note>. (22. q. 2. can. *Nè quis*). However, when there is an obligation to accuse, as in crimes destructive to the public good, then everyone is bound to offer themselves as a witness even if not called.

<summary>This page explores the moral distinction between legal justice and the duty of charity regarding witnesses. It argues that while one may not always be legally forced to testify, failing to do so out of malice or when a neighbor is in dire need (like a house on fire) is a moral failing, though restitution is primarily required when justice—rather than just charity—is violated.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral analysis of the duty to testify. It transitions from discussing when a witness is obligated to speak (even regarding secrets) to the specific requirements for how many witnesses are needed to establish a fact in court.</meta>

# Book Five, Question VII.

<sig>Gg 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: ...ness, who</meta>

<margin>To the first main argument.</margin> To the first argument, then, the response is that we must distinguish between different levels of secrets (as was discussed in the previous question). Regarding the seal of sacramental confession <note>The "seal" refers to the absolute duty of a priest not to reveal anything heard during the sacrament of Penance.</note>, there can be no reason—nor can one even be imagined—for it to be disclosed, unless there were an express revelation from God. In such a case, the cited proverb holds true: to reveal it would be a sacrilegious fraud and a breach of faith. I specify *sacramental* confession because the common habit of revealing secrets to others "under the seal of confession"—even if one kneels, makes the sign of the cross, and recites the *Confiteor* <note>The "I Confess" prayer.</note>—does not bind one to the sacramental seal unless a full and formal confession of all sins is made. Instead, it binds only to a "secular seal" (an ordinary secret). Therefore, when such secrets are legally required by a judge, they can and must be revealed, despite any oath of secrecy. For example, if these secrets are harmful to the commonwealth, they ought to be brought to the judge’s ears immediately by way of accusation. This also applies if they involve grave danger to a third person that cannot be otherwise avoided, or if you are summoned as a witness. However, outside of such cases, everyone is bound to keep a secret; otherwise, one would violate natural law <note>The inherent moral principles believed to be common to all humans.</note>, which would be a mortal sin, or a venial fault in trivial matters. Therefore, outside the cases just named, in a doubtful matter, one should lean toward keeping a neighbor's secret rather than betraying it. For instance, if a judge asks only whether you *know* something, and you have only heard it but not seen it, you can say "I do not know," because we do not truly "know" what we merely hear. But if you are justly asked whether you *heard* it, you are compelled to admit it. Likewise, if you saw a murder committed, even with other witnesses present, and you are questioned by way of an inquiry <note>A specific legal procedure where a judge investigates a crime without a formal accuser.</note>, you are not bound to answer unless there is already a public reputation of the crime or existing evidence. However, if the trial proceeds by way of formal accusation, even if you are the only witness, you are bound to give testimony once brought forward. As for the defendant, he cannot be justly interrogated without a prior oath from a suitable witness.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin> Regarding the second point, enough has already been said above. In the first question of this book, we gave the reason why clerics <note>Members of the clergy.</note> cannot be judges in criminal cases: namely, so that those who handle sacred things are not stained by the blood of slaughter. For the same reason, in Question 5, we said it is forbidden for them to act as accusers in such cases, and consequently, we now say it is also forbidden for them to testify in them.

---

### ARTICLE III.

->*Whether the testimony of two or three witnesses suffices in a trial.*<-

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape with figures and buildings.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin> We follow in the second place with the sufficiency of testimony: whether two or three witnesses are enough. The argument is made from the negative side. For testimony to create belief, it must be in agreement; however, it often happens that two or three witnesses disagree on some point. Therefore, such testimony is not legitimate.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second: in several types of cases, three witnesses are not enough. For in the signing of wills, civil law <note>The legal system derived from Roman law.</note> requires seven witnesses, as is clear in the *Institutes* regarding testaments, the final paragraph, and in the *Codex* under the same title, the law *Hac consultissima*. In other cases, the same caution is observed.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third: against persons of high rank, and especially those of the Roman Church, a group of three witnesses is not sufficient. For we read in the law <note>original: "2. q. 5. ca. Praesul"</note> that a Prelate <note>A high-ranking bishop or abbot.</note> may not be condemned except with seventy-two witnesses, which was the number of Christ's disciples. A Cardinal Priest may not be deposed except with sixty-four witnesses; a Cardinal Deacon of the city of Rome may not be condemned except with twenty-seven. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, lector, or porter <note>The "minor orders" of the clergy.</note> requires no fewer than seven. This is found in the text of Pope Sylvester in a General Council. Yet in the case of such churchmen, whose crimes are less to be tolerated, the testimony of *fewer* people should be required; therefore, by even stronger logic, three are not sufficient for others.

<margin>Paul.</margin> ¶ On the contrary is that passage from Deuteronomy 17: *By the mouth of two or three witnesses shall he that is to die be put to death.* And in chapter 19: *In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.* Christ cited and approved this in Matthew 18, and Paul did the same in 1 Corinthians 13.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> THE question is answered with a single conclusion: The testimony of two people, provided they are trustworthy, is sufficient in a trial, and three are sufficient for greater certainty.

<margin>The conclusion is supported.</margin> This conclusion is asserted by a threefold law: namely, Natural, Divine, and Human. Regarding Divine law, the testimonies have already been cited. Furthermore, in John 8, Christ argued by the same logic that his testimony—which was simultaneously his own and his Father's—was worthy of belief.

<margin>Augustine</margin> In that passage, Augustine says that in this number of witnesses, the Trinity is commended according to a mystery, in which there is the eternal firmness of truth. Human law is also clear in the Canon law <note>original: "2. q. 5. ca. quod verò"</note> and in the *Decretals* regarding witnesses. It is also proven by natural reason. Certainty (as Aristotle writes in the first book of the *Ethics*) is not to be sought in the same way in every subject. Therefore, in human acts, which...

<meta>This page continues a legal and moral discussion regarding the requirements for witness testimony in a court of law. It specifically addresses why multiple witnesses are required for a conviction and how a judge should handle discrepancies in their stories. # Francisco de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

...knowledge regarding earthly and passing matters, which are the subject of legal trials, does not require the same absolute certainty found in the **demonstrable sciences** <note>Aristotelian "demonstrable sciences," like mathematics, provide absolute proof. Law, dealing with human actions, relies on "moral certainty"—what is most likely true.</note>. Rather, it is sufficient to reach a level of truth that holds in most cases and rarely fails. It is more probable, and closer to the truth, that something asserted by many is true rather than something asserted by only one. For this reason, when many witnesses are brought against a single defendant who denies the charge, it is consistent with reason to stand by their testimony rather than the defendant's denial.

Now, a "multitude" is comprised of three parts: the beginning, the middle, and the end, which form a line. Likewise, it is defined by length, width, and depth, which define a **physical body**. <margin>Aristotle</margin> This is why Aristotle says at the beginning of the first book of *On the Heavens* that "the total" and "the all" are first applied to things in groups of three. For two things, we only say "both." Two witnesses, combined with the accuser <note>original: *actor*</note>, make three. However, so that the testimony might be absolute and perfect even without the accuser (to whom the law does not grant total trust in his own case), a third witness is added. This is why Ecclesiastes 4 says: *A triple cord is difficult to break.* Therefore, when the law says "by the mouth of two or three," the first part signifies necessity and sufficiency, while the latter signifies a more abundant completeness.

<margin>Objection.</margin> If you object and ask why one person's affirmation should not be enough against one person's denial, <margin>Solution.</margin> the answer is that since the defendant is the "possessor" of his own life and goods, and the condition of the possessor is legally stronger <note>This refers to the legal principle *in pari delicto melior est conditio possidentis*—possession is a strong legal standing that requires more than a single person's word to overturn.</note>, the affirmation of a single accuser is not considered enough to strip him of that possession, even if supported by one other witness.

But does not the authority of one person sometimes outweigh the testimony of many? It must be admitted that, as is often said, laws do not consider what happens rarely, but what happens most often. To be sure, the testimony of one person of exceptional authority, such as the Emperor, is judged sufficient (as held in the law *Omnium* in the Code regarding wills). Conversely, the affirmation of many is not always reliable. As we read in 1 Kings 21, Naboth was condemned by the false testimony of many. So too was the most innocent Christ.

<margin>Argument.</margin> An argument emerges from this conclusion against human law: Human laws cannot take away from natural law, and much less from divine law. Since the rule that three witnesses are sufficient is a matter of natural and divine law (as just stated), human laws should not be able to weaken the testimony of three by requiring five witnesses for an open will, or seven for a closed one, or even more in other cases. <margin>Solution.</margin> The answer is that natural and divine law do not

<column-break/>

establish the testimony of three so rigidly that more cannot be required for a specific reason. Indeed, were it not for the excessive growth of human malice, the testimony of two or three would be more than enough. However, because the faith and justice of mortals has been corrupted, that same natural law suggests that stronger evidence should be required—especially in the wills of the deceased, who can no longer speak to confirm their own wishes after death.

<margin>Regarding the first argument.</margin> To the first argument, then, the response is that "singular" witnesses <term>singular witnesses: witnesses who testify to separate incidents or different facts rather than the same specific event</term> do not create legal proof in court; only "co-witnesses" do. They are called "singular" when each testifies to a separate act on its own. 

However, regarding their disagreement, one must distinguish along with <margin>St. Thomas</margin> St. Thomas Aquinas. If they disagree on the **substance of the act**—for instance, if one says the defendant struck a blow with his hand, but the other says he used a club—or if they disagree on the place or time, which are the immediate circumstances of the action (such as one saying it happened in the morning or at home, but the other saying it was in the evening or in a field), then the testimony is either rejected or judged insufficient for a sentence. They appear to be "singular" witnesses, meaning they are talking about different acts. This is especially true if they assert these things as certain. If one says he does not remember, his testimony is not as easily discarded.

<margin>The Rule of Saint Thomas.</margin> Nevertheless, there is a rule that Saint Thomas wisely established: namely, that if the accuser’s witnesses and the defendant’s witnesses disagree, then—all other things being equal—the judge must side with the defendant. Since the condition of the "possessor" is better, the judge should be more inclined to acquit than to condemn. 

If, however, the witnesses for the same side disagree with each other, or if the witnesses for both sides disagree amongst themselves, the judge must weigh which side to believe based on several factors: the number of witnesses, their dignity, or the "favor of the cause" (for example, if the case involves someone's liberty). 

A witness who contradicts himself is rejected with even greater justice, especially when questioned about what he saw and knows. However, a witness asked about his opinion or a general rumor is not necessarily rejected just because he wavers based on different things he has seen or heard. Furthermore, when they disagree on minor circumstances that add little weight to the substance of the case, the testimony is not invalidated—for example, if one says the event happened at three o'clock and another says four o'clock, or that the weather was cloudy...

<summary>This page discusses the legal requirement for multiple witnesses (usually two or three) to establish "moral certainty" in court, arguing that while this is a baseline of natural law, human laws may require more witnesses to prevent fraud, particularly in wills. It also provides guidelines from Thomas Aquinas on how judges should handle conflicting witness testimony, emphasizing the preference for the defendant in uncertain cases.</summary>

<margin>Chrysostom, Augustine</margin>
...whether it was cloudy or somewhat clear; or whether a house was painted or otherwise. These are circumstances to which people do not usually pay close attention. On the contrary (as Chrysostom and Augustine wisely noted in their work *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*), a certain amount of disagreement among historians actually grants them a more solid credibility than if they agreed down to the smallest detail. For in the latter case, they might appear to have conspired by design and agreement to forge a story. Furthermore (and I note this alongside <margin>Cajetan</margin> Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534) was a major Italian theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>), I would gladly note for the present that even if witnesses are "singular" <note>A "singular" witness is one who testifies to a unique event that no one else saw, rather than corroborating the same event as others.</note> regarding multiple identical acts committed by the same person, they do not make for weak evidence. This is especially true in religious orders, where there ought to be a sincere and plain knowledge of crimes; for example, if one witness testifies that a person committed one theft, and another testifies that the same person committed a different theft. In such a case, although by the strictness of the law they might not be fully believed, in religious communities they could be taken as "indications" <note>Legal "indications" or "clues" (indicia) were not full proof but allowed a judge to investigate further.</note> so that one might proceed to an inquiry and to the questioning of the accused himself, even using some form of light torture. It is different, however, in secular courts, where one proceeds to more bitter punishments. ¶ <margin>To the second argument.</margin> Regarding the second argument, the reason has already been given as to why more abundant testimony is required in certain cases. ¶ <margin>To the third argument. St. Thomas.</margin> To the third argument, St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> responds that the cited chapter is understood to refer to bishops and the other specific ministers of the Roman Church. For three reasons, such a massive abundance of witnesses is expected before their condemnation. First, because they ought to shine with holiness and, consequently, authority, so that more faith is placed in them than in many witnesses. Second, because since they are the judges of the universal Church, they incur envy among many due to the execution of justice; therefore, false testimony could easily be brought against them. The present times are proof of how many blasphemies heretics have spat out against the Roman Curia <note>This likely refers to the Protestant Reformation's criticisms of the Papacy.</note>. The third cause is that much of the Roman Church’s authority would be lost by their condemnation, which would be more dangerous than tolerating some of their evils, provided they do not cause a public scandal.

# ARTICLE III.

## *Whether anyone’s testimony should be rejected without any fault on their part.*

<column-break/>

<margin>First argument.</margin>
THIRDLY, we must speak regarding the fitness of witnesses. Specifically, we must ask whether anyone’s testimony should be rejected without any fault of their own. The argument is made from the negative side: In those matters that are necessary for the common good, and consequently must be provided as a necessity for salvation, no one should be rejected except on account of a fault or crime. To bear witness is a duty of this kind; therefore, no one should be rejected from that office unless they are marked by some wickedness. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second: the rejection of a witness is either decreed as a punishment for them, or it happens because they are not trusted. Now, no one is worthy of punishment except for a fault, nor is anyone unworthy of trust for any other reason: because everyone is presumed to be good until their own malice betrays them. Therefore, a witness is in no way to be refused except on account of a fault. ¶ On the contrary is the canon *Si Testes* (4. q. 3.), where several sorts of men are rejected from bearing witness without any fault of their own.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
To the question, it is responded with this affirmative conclusion, citing the chapter *Consona*: By right and merit, men are rejected from the duty of testifying for other causes as well as for fault. This conclusion, besides being clear by <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> human law, is also clear by natural reason. Truly, since the certainty of human testimony (as was just said) is not entirely infallible but is open to many deceptions, it is reasonable that any testimony that weakens the credibility of the evidence should be refused. Now, fault primarily weakens this credibility, which is why infidels and infamous persons are not admitted as witnesses. Furthermore, those who have been guilty of a public crime are also excluded. Beyond fault, however, there are other defects that weaken the probability of testimony: such as a lack of reason, for which reason children and the insane <note>original: *amentes*</note> are refused, as well as women, except in certain cases <note>In historical legal contexts, women's testimony was often restricted or required specific conditions to be met.</note>. Second, there are causes that stand in the way of full liberty, such as enemies, friends, and even members of the same household. Third, there is the condition of the humble, such as the poor, who might be corrupted for the sake of relieving their hunger. Furthermore, there are the lowly, such as slaves. Finally, these sorts of defects are enumerated very broadly in the cited canon: namely, by reason of sex, age, crime, condition, and other similar causes. <margin>Question.</margin> ¶ Regarding this conclusion—not so much out of doubt but as a point of instruction—it remains to be asked whether, when such a defect is hidden in a witness, it is permissible for a litigant to bring it into the public eye so that the testimony against them might be...

...weaken or completely shatter it. And as it is most certain that it is by no means permissible to charge a witness with a false crime, not even for the sake of preserving the entire commonwealth. For if it is not lawful to lie even to be helpful <note>original: "mentiri officiosè" – an "officious lie" is one told to help someone rather than harm them.</note>, how much less is it lawful to lie harmfully? Therefore, the practice now frequent in courts is most unjust and should not be tolerated in a well-ordered state: namely, when advocates charge witnesses with shameful acts they do not even suspect them of, saying they are using their right to alleviate their own harassment. Yet that custom contains more diabolical wickedness <term>than legal right</term> <note>original: "quam iuris"</note>. We admit that those legal pleaders and procurators have very little authority in this matter, for they are most deservedly considered the greatest liars in these things; nonetheless, a witness rarely emerges from there without injury to his honor and reputation. And so, besides the injury they arrogantly inflict on private persons, they also harm the commonwealth; for by that reasoning, honest men are deterred from being witnesses. And sometimes they are legitimately excused, even when requested by a judge, because no one is bound to provide his service at such great risk to his honor and reputation. Therefore, those "taxers" <note>original: "taxatores" – those who formally challenge or "tax" the credibility of a witness.</note> (as they call them) of witnesses ought to be punished if they fail in their proof.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But regarding a true crime that is nevertheless hidden, there remains a reason for doubt. For he who reveals a hidden crime (as was said in the preceding book, Question 5), even if in the second degree, is nonetheless considered a defamer by law, just like one who imposes a false charge.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is answered that by its nature it is not a sin to reveal a hidden crime of a witness for which he is legally rejected. For after the law grants that right, it is lawful for anyone to use that same benefit of the law. However, many conditions are required so that detecting such crimes is not contrary to charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the Christian duty of love and care for one's neighbor.</note>. First, it is required that the revelation be necessary to win the lawsuit. Therefore, if the crime is not among those for which testimony is legally rejected, it is a sin to make it public. Next, one must weigh the foulness of detecting the crime against the harm that might occur if it were not detected. For if in a case of small importance you were to reveal a massive crime of a witness, because of which he might face the danger of death or live thereafter in infamy, you would certainly gravely wound charity. Thirdly and especially, it must be considered whether the witness involved himself through his own fault or of his own accord; for then his crime could more justly be used against him to stop his mouth. When, however, he gives testimony not only without his own fault but because he was compelled,

<column-break/>

it would be dangerous to defame him—especially when it is done not so much out of necessity as for revenge. Fourthly, finally, it must be considered whether, although he may be wicked in other respects, he nevertheless gives his testimony honestly and candidly. For if it were clear that it was false, it would be much more just to silence his impudent mouth, even with his infamy.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The **a**rguments of the question are very easy. For to the first, it is answered that those testimonies are entirely necessary to the commonwealth which have a good weight of authority; which weight is indeed diminished by other defects even without fault. And therefore, those who have such defects are rejected.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And through this, the solution to the second argument is clear. For not every rejection of witnesses is a punishment inflicted for a fault; rather, it is sometimes a precaution. To the other part, it is answered that where the matter does not result in harm to another, everyone is presumed good as long as he is not proven bad. When, however, the matter involves a third person, no injury is done to anyone while a necessary precaution is applied.

## ARTICLE IV.
### *Whether false testimony is always a mortal sin.*

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral patterns and a central circular motif.</image-desc>
How much fault is considered in a witness if he is false? Regarding this, it is asked whether it is always a mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a grave violation of God's law that destroys the divine life in the soul.</note>. And it is argued on the negative side. First, thus: Sometimes a witness says false testimony not out of desire but through ignorance of the fact; ignorance, however, excuses one from a mortal stain; therefore, false testimony is not always a mortal sin.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: A lie that benefits someone but harms no one, and which is therefore called "obliging" <note>original: "officiosum" – a white lie or a lie of convenience.</note>, is not mortal. But false testimony is often of this kind: for example, when a witness strives by that falsehood to free someone from death or from injury, whether from a judge or from other witnesses. Therefore, this kind of testimony will not be a lethal crime.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: An oath is required from a witness so that he may fear to sin mortally by perjuring himself; however, this would not be necessary if false testimony were always a mortal sin in itself. It is a sign, therefore, that without an oath it is sometimes [not mortal].

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal ethics from Book V, Question VII, specifically addressing whether false testimony is always a mortal sin (a grave moral failure that separates one from God). It builds on the previous page's distinction between different types of lies.</meta>

->F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law<-

...it can happen that it becomes a venial <note>A "venial" sin is a minor offense that does not break one's relationship with God, as opposed to a "mortal" sin.</note> sin. ¶ On the contrary is that passage from Proverbs 19: *A false witness shall not go unpunished.* Since this refers to punishment before God, it denotes a mortal fault.

## This question is resolved by three conclusions, according to the three levels of wrongdoing that usually occur in false testimony.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
For it is considered according to the sacrilege of perjury, the injustice of the judgment, and the falsehood of the statement itself. ¶ This is the first conclusion: Every perjury <note>original: "periurium" – swearing a false oath using God's name.</note>, whether in a court of law or outside of it, no matter how small the matter may be, is a mortal sin. Nor can it be lightened for any reason to become venial: because to bring God as a witness to any falsehood is a sacrilegious impiety.

<margin>Second conclusion. St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: To lie in a court of law, thereby violating justice—even without an oath—is by its very nature a mortal sin. These are the words of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the foundational theologian for Soto’s work.</note>, by which he suggests the opinion we established in the preceding question against Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan, a major commentator on Aquinas.</note>: namely, that a lie in court can be a venial sin. For this reason, he added the phrase "by its nature" <note>original: "genere suo"</note>, because in a specific individual case <note>original: "in individuo"</note>, it can be venial.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is evident from the fact that the noble virtue of justice is necessary for salvation; therefore, whoever transgresses it turns away from the charity in which salvation consists. For this reason, the commandment of the Decalogue in Exodus 20 is established in this form: *Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor.* For false testimony in favor of a neighbor is not a mortal sin; nor is it so when it is spoken to prevent that same neighbor from doing an injury. This is because such a lie is not *against* him; rather, that which is said *against* him exists so that his rights might be taken away.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: A lie, if it has no other stain than that of falsehood, is not by its nature a mortal sin. This is clear: because it is neither against religion <note>Meaning it is not a false oath involving God.</note> nor against justice; and therefore, by its nature, it does not expel charity from the soul. Therefore, let the difference between these conclusions be held in memory: Every perjury, not only in general but in every specific instance, is mortal. A lie without an oath, if it is harmful <note>original: "perniciosum"</note>, is mortal by its nature, but can become venial in certain cases. However, a "jocose" lie <note>A lie told in jest or for fun.</note> and an "officious" lie <note>A lie told to be helpful or perform a service.</note> are not mortal by their nature, though they can grow to that level due to circumstances.

<margin>Question. Solution.</margin>
But if you ask which is more serious: any perjury committed outside of court, or a harmful lie told without an oath inside a court? The answer is that, based on the object of the sin,

<column-break/>

perjury is more serious, as it opposes religion, whereas a lie opposes justice. Nevertheless, in specific instances, the circumstances must be weighed; through these, the malice of a simple harmful lie can exceed that of a particular perjury.

<margin>To the first argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
To the first argument, then, St. Thomas responds: First, that no one in a court of law ought to testify by asserting something unless he has certain knowledge of it through vigilant consideration; but what he holds as a doubt, he ought to bring forward as a doubt. Nevertheless, if after prudent vigilance he holds it as certain, and subsequently asserts what is false, he is not held guilty of a lie: because he did not go against his own mind, which is what the word "lie" implies. For this reason, even if he affirms it under oath, he is not a perjurer.

<margin>Cajetan's Corollary.</margin>
¶ From this response, Cajetan gathers that such a witness does not undergo any obligation of restitution <term>restitution</term> <note>The legal and moral obligation to give back what was taken or to compensate for damages.</note>. For (as was said in the preceding book), restitution arises either by reason of the taking or by reason of the thing taken. However, such a witness does not become a debtor of restitution by reason of the taking, in which there was no fault. Nor is he liable by reason of the thing taken, because since the witness is not acting in his own cause, that which the other person loses does not accrue to him. But this corollary is true with these qualifications: First, that no negligence, lightheadedness, or rashness in believing preceded it; for then the witness is certainly held liable in part according to the proportion of his negligence. Then, he who is false through no fault of his own, although he is not bound to make restitution from his own substance, is nevertheless bound to retract his statement if that path can be of use, so that the person who suffered the loss may recover what was lost—especially when it concerns the life or reputation of another. Indeed, although by law a witness is not permitted to retract testimony except immediately and without delay (as is clear in the section *on witnesses*, chapter *moreover* <note>A reference to Canon Law.</note>), nonetheless, because (as the gloss <note>A marginal commentary on legal texts.</note> there says) even after an interval of time the strength of the prior testimony is weakened by a retraction—especially when the witness is of good reputation, regarding whom there is no suspicion that he lied on purpose—he ought to change his testimony after any amount of elapsed time, provided he understands that he can in some way repair the reputation and honor of the other person.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, the response is that an "officious" lie is so far from being mortal by its nature that it does not even become so in a court of law. Therefore, when an innocent person is accused by the false charges of witnesses...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal ethics from Book V, Question VII, focusing on the moral obligations of defendants and witnesses when faced with an unjust legal system. It then transitions to Question VIII regarding the duties of advocates (lawyers).</meta>

->F. D. Soto, *On Justice and Law*<-

...is harassed or oppressed by the injustice of a judge, to speak something against the truth so that he may be rescued from an unjust judgment through that path is not a mortal sin, provided that no oath is involved. The reason is (as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says) that an unjust judgment is not a true judgment; therefore, nothing is committed there against justice. However, when he says universally that an unjust judgment is not a judgment, he is not speaking in the manner or style of legal doctors, but in the language of moral philosophers, who consider anything that is flawed or vicious to be "nothing" or "null." For those prudent in the law do not consider every unjust sentence to be void. Among lawyers, a sentence is null for two reasons: either because it comes from someone who is not a judge, or because it contains an error that is both intolerable and manifest. 

Nonetheless, even if it is not legally null, it happens to be unjust for three reasons, as Gratian <note>A 12th-century jurist and the father of Canon Law</note> notes in the canon *Episocpus* 11, question 3. Namely: either from the intent <note>original: "ex animo"</note>, as when a judge proceeds out of hatred (though this alone does not void a sentence unless other inequity is present); or from the procedure <note>original: "ex ordine"</note>, specifically when the necessary order of law is not observed; or from the cause <note>original: "ex causa"</note>, namely when a sentence is pronounced against the truth of the facts or the law. And this last one is the essential injustice, for the others are accidental. What we say about the sentence, which is the end of the trial, must also be judged regarding the trial itself. 

But truly, although a sentence may be unjust in this way, it is not (as we began to say) immediately considered null unless the error is both intolerable and clearly visible. Therefore, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> <margin>Gregory.</margin> advises in the same cause and question, saying: *The sentence of a pastor, whether just or unjust, is to be feared.* This is because when an error is not manifest, it is not for the defendant to judge it. Therefore, carefully weigh two words: *sentence* and *pastor*. By the first, he means it is not an intolerable error; and by the second, that it comes from a true judge. All these things are understood in the judicial forum. For in the forum of conscience <note>The internal "court" of one's own moral standing before God, rather than a public court</note>, whoever knows beyond all doubt that a sentence is wicked—that is, against the truth—may choose not to obey it, provided he does so without causing a scandal. And this is why Saint Thomas considers every wicked judgment to be null. 

¶ To the third argument, <margin>To the third argument.</margin> the response is easy: witnesses are bound by an oath so that they may be struck by a greater fear. For it is a more serious thing to betray the religion of God than to wound human justice.

To hide a talent is a fault, as is understood from the punishment that the servant suffered; therefore, providing legal defense is a commandment.

### Book Five, Question VIII.

Just as we discussed whether a witness is bound to testify, it is also worthwhile to know whether an advocate, by the duty of mercy, is bound to go to the aid of the wretched with his support. Since providing legal defense <term>patrocinari</term> for the poor for free is a type of almsgiving <term>eleemosyna</term>, the response must be the same as for other works of mercy, about which

<margin>
Saint Thomas.
Responsive conclusion.
</margin>
Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* 2-2, Question 32.</note> disputed. There is, therefore, one conclusion that suffices for the question: An advocate is not always bound to provide his legal defense for the poor for free; he is bound only when it is not readily apparent how they can otherwise be helped.

<margin>
Proof.
</margin>
The conclusion is proven as follows. The command <term>preceptum</term> of mercy, as we were just saying, is "affirmative" <note>An affirmative precept is a commandment to do something (like "honor your father"), which applies at specific times, unlike a "negative" precept (like "do not kill"), which applies at all times.</note>; it does not, therefore, obligate at every moment, but only when the misery of the person in need requires it. Therefore, when it is obvious that the poor person can be assisted in another way, the command does not constrain you, but counsel <note>A "counsel of perfection" is an act that is spiritually beneficial but not strictly required for salvation.</note> advises you. This is primarily because no one is bound to the impossible, and no one can bring aid to everyone—though it is a counsel to anticipate others by doing good while you can. However, when assistance through another path is not readily available, it is then

<margin>
Augustine.
</margin>
considered an "extreme necessity," and thus you are bound. Hence, Augustine says in the beginning of *On Christian Doctrine*:
> Since you cannot benefit everyone, you must especially look out for those who, by the opportunities of place and time or any other circumstances, are more closely joined to you, as if by a kind of lot. <note>original: "Cum omnibus... prodesse non possis, his tibi potissimum consulendum est qui pro locorum & temporum vel quarumlibet rerum opportunitatibus constrictiùs tibi tanquam quadam forte iunguntur."</note>

There he gives the reason why we are not bound to everyone: namely, because we cannot be. Presently, he defines the affirmative command by its specific qualities so that it becomes obligatory. First, by reason of place: because you are not bound to go searching for people to benefit, but to be present with help for those who come across you; according to that cited passage in Exodus 23: "If you come across your neighbor's ox or donkey wandering, lead it back." Second, he adds the reason of time: because you are not bound to provide for the future legal cases of the poor, but to help them in the present; according to 1 John 3: "He who sees his brother in need and closes his bowels of compassion, etc." Furthermore, Augustine adds "or any other circumstances," because since a man is not sufficient for everyone, he ought to give help more quickly to those who are joined to him by some necessity; according to 1 Timothy 5: "If anyone does not have care for his own, and especially those of his household, he has denied the faith."

<margin>
Two requirements for the command of charity.
</margin>
Two things are therefore required for the command of charity: first, that these circumstances align; second, that a more ready way of assistance is not apparent.

<column-break/>

And what is affirmed regarding the advocate must likewise be judged regarding the physician, and similarly regarding others who can relieve hardships through the duty of mercy and assist the needs of the wretched, whether they be public or private.

<margin>
The first doubt.
</margin>
¶ However, a first doubt arises concerning these matters: how this excuse from the command should be understood—when it appears obvious how a need can be assisted by another. Is it enough to excuse you that there are others who, seeing the necessity, are better able than you and are bound by a tighter bond? For the common people think this way; you may hear them everywhere excusing themselves in this manner: "There is someone else who can and should do better; why then should I be bound?"

<margin>
Response.
</margin>
The response is that these physical abilities and natural obligations of others do not excuse the rest who can help unless an actual deed follows. For what does it benefit a wretched man that many *could* and *should* help, if no one actually runs to him? Therefore, these words—"if it appears assistance can be provided otherwise"—must be understood as a "proximate fitness for the work": namely, that you believe that, in truth and without your help, assistance will be provided immediately by others. Otherwise, if you do not act, the fault of others will not excuse yours.

<margin>
The second doubt.
</margin>
¶ But then a second doubt remains here. It seems that Saint Thomas did not sufficiently settle the matter: he speaks, I say, of "extreme necessity," but says nothing of "grave necessity." And yet the doubt is whether, short of extreme necessity, an advocate is bound to defend a poor person in grave necessity, or a physician to treat a sick person.

<margin>
Cajetan.
</margin>
And indeed, Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, a 16th-century commentator on Aquinas.</note> currently judges that only "extreme necessity" carries with it a command obligating under mortal sin. For he distinguishes three degrees: First, extreme necessity, which must be assisted under the guilt of mortal sin. Second, grave necessity short of extreme: he says not meeting this is a venial sin. Third, to assist in lighter matters is a counsel, but to omit them is no sin at all.

<margin>
Cajetan forgetting himself.
</margin>
It is surprising, however, how Cajetan could have forgotten himself; for in his commentary on the *Summa* 2-2, question 32, article 5, rightly interpreting Saint Thomas, he confessed two cases where the command of almsgiving falls under mortal sin: namely, "extreme necessity" regarding necessities of life, and "grave necessity" regarding superfluous goods. In confirmation of this, he later composed a treatise on almsgiving, where he asserted that same opinion—that the necessity of granting aid is required. For John <note>The Apostle, in his First Epistle.</note> speaks not only of extreme, but of urgent necessity. "He who sees," he says, "his brother in need, and shuts his bowels, etc." For the "bowels" which alone...

## ARTICLE II.

->**Whether some people are rightly barred from the office of advocacy.**<-

<column-break/>

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Following this, we inquire into the quality and dignity of advocates: whether some are to be driven away from this office as **unfit**. The argument for the negative side is: no one should be barred from works of mercy.
<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second: Different causes are not incongruously assigned to the same effect. However, being dedicated to sacred things and being defiled by sins are contraries; therefore, it is incongruous that **infamous** persons <note>In Roman and Canon law, "infames" were people who had lost their legal standing due to crime or certain "dishonorable" professions</note> are barred from this office on one hand, and **clerics** on the other.
<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Third: Everyone is bound to love his neighbor as himself. No one is restrained from defending his own cause; therefore, no one should be restrained from protecting the cause of his neighbor.
<margin>In the contrary.</margin>
¶ To the contrary is the fact that infamous and excommunicated persons are rejected from this office, as is clear in Book 3, Question 7, canon *infames*. Also, monks are barred, except by permission of their Prelate in pious causes (Book 16, Question 1, canon *monachi*).

In response to the question, based on a distinction, two conclusions are provided.
<margin>Distinction.</margin>
For a person can be rejected from a duty in two ways: either because of **incapacity** <term>impotentiam</term> or because of **unsuitability** <term>indecentiam</term>. But they differ: incapacity simply excludes a person, whereas unsuitability does not always do so, because necessity can make what was unsuitable become suitable.
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, the first conclusion: He who lacks the capacity for advocacy can by no means act as a patron, whether that capacity is lacking in the **internal sense**—such as the insane, who do not have sound judgment, and minors, who do not have full and solid judgment—or in the **external sense**, such as the deaf or the mute. For a speaker first requires a mind that is not only sound but also built for judging; and secondly, since causes are conducted in an external forum, he needs the instruments to express his thoughts.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: There is a double quality which, if present in an advocate, makes the advocacy unsuitable unless necessity is present. The first is **excellence of dignity**. The second is some **deprivation or defect**. Regarding excellence of dignity, it makes it unsuitable for priests, and especially monks, to be involved in the courtroom. For those who are handed over to sacred ministries and devoted to prayer and contemplation, it is least becoming for them to be brought down to secular causes. These causes are both a hindrance to them so that they cannot attend to spiritual things, and they diminish and overshadow their authority, preventing them from being held in the honor appropriate to their condition and status.

### ARTICLE III.
#### Whether it is a crime for an advocate to defend an unjust cause.

<note>Decorative initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, likely a jurist or philosopher, in a square frame with floral ornamentation.</note>
After the dignity of the advocate, we must consider the proper form of advocacy: namely, whether it is lawful to defend an unjust cause. Indeed, arguments for the 
<margin>First argument.</margin>
affirmative side are not lacking. For just as the glory of the medical art shines most brightly when a doctor heals desperate diseases, so an advocate is usually most praised when he defends weak causes. ¶ Second: If 
<margin>Second.</margin>
he were required to abandon a cause because of its injustice, advocates would not be punished for losing cases. But they are punished as **prevaricators** <term>prevaricatores</term> <note>a legal term for a lawyer who colludes with the opposing side or betrays their client</note> when they help the opposing side, as is clear in the decree *Si quem poenituerit* (2. q. 3). Therefore, it is lawful to defend a cause once undertaken, even against justice. ¶ Third, it appears that a 
<margin>Third.</margin>
greater fault is committed when a just cause is defended unjustly—for instance, when false witnesses are produced or false laws are cited—than when an unjust cause is defended by the **royal road** <note>original: "via regia"; meaning a straightforward, standard, or legitimate legal path</note>. It is lawful for an advocate to use cleverness and tactics, just as it is for a soldier to fight from ambush; therefore, to protect an unjust cause is not entirely a sin. ¶ On the contrary, however, is that rebuke in 2 Chronicles 19: "You give help to the ungodly, and therefore you deserved the wrath of the Lord."

The question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: An advocate who 
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
knowingly and intentionally defends an unjust cause both commits a mortal sin against justice and is likewise bound to **restitution** <note>the legal and moral obligation to pay back or restore what was lost by the victim of the injustice</note>. This is proven: 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
Whoever cooperates in an evil act is guilty of the same iniquity as the one who does it, according to the 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
words of Paul in Romans 1: "They are worthy of death, not only [those who do these things, but also those who consent to them]."

### 476 F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...not only those who commit the act, but also those who consent to those doing it: now, the advocate, through both counsel and support, cooperates with the one who wages an unjust lawsuit. Indeed, he is the one who "nourishes" the litigation; therefore, he sins mortally. And subsequently, since the sin is committed against justice—namely, to the harm of the opposing party—he is bound to **restitution** <note>Restitution is the legal and moral obligation to restore something to its rightful owner or to compensate for a loss caused by one's actions.</note>.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The latter conclusion: He who defends an unjust cause through **ignorance** <note>original: "per ignorantiam"</note> may be excused by reason of that ignorance, both from the fault of the sin and from the obligation to make restitution. This conclusion is clear across all subject matters.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ However, an occasion for doubt arises from the first conclusion regarding a **doubtful cause** <note>A "doubtful cause" refers to a legal case where the right of the matter is not immediately clear or where the law could be interpreted in multiple ways.</note>. Specifically, whether an advocate may take up and subsequently defend a case that, in his own judgment, is uncertain. Indeed, if the doubt hangs in a balance, the answer is readily affirmative: for the duty of a legal expert is nothing else than to apply the meanings of the laws in good faith to one side or the other. In fact, all lawsuits depend on the fact that the matter is in doubt, either in law or in fact. But the most significant reason for doubting is whether an advocate, even if he understands that the opposing side has the **stronger legal weight** <note>original: "maiorem habere iuris energiam"; literally "greater energy of law," meaning a more compelling legal argument.</note>, can still defend the side that has the lesser probability.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
For it appears that this is not permitted, because it seems to be nothing other than an iniquity to incline and draw the judge toward that side, contrary to the judgment he ought to pronounce.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
¶ The answer is nevertheless given with a distinction. When it is a case involving death, or "blood," or where someone's honor is at stake: then to advocate for the accuser, unless the accusation flourishes with at least as much probability as the defense, would certainly be a great crime. This is because **the condition of the possessor is better** <note>original: "melior est conditio possidentis"; a legal maxim meaning that the burden of proof lies on the challenger, and the one currently "holding" their life, honor, or property is in the stronger position.</note>, especially in favor of honor and life. The same is nearly true when a defendant is at risk of being driven out of the possession of all their goods. Indeed, in these cases—most especially in a capital case—unless the defendant is considered most dangerous, it would be a pious act to take up their defense, even if their cause has the lesser probability, provided no room is opened for fraud. In cases of lesser importance, although a weaker and more feeble cause can hardly be defended without risk, nevertheless, if we speak according to the **rigor of conscience** <note>Refers to the strict moral requirement as opposed to mere legal technicality.</note>, there is no reason why it should be entirely condemned. This is provided that the patron first takes care to warn his client that justice seems to smile more upon the other party than upon him; and second, that he uses no falsehood whatsoever—such as alleging fabricated laws or interpreting them falsely. He should always use those things that support his case, while remaining

<column-break/>

silent about the arguments that work for the opposing side.

<margin>To the argument.</margin>
And to the argument to the contrary, it is answered that it is lawful for anyone to test and pursue their right without force or fraud. Therefore, since the duty of the patron is to favor his client, he does no injury to anyone if he makes the merits of his own case known. Let the other party see to it themselves which patron they entrust their case to; and let the judge also see to it that he stands **square** <note>original: "quadratus stet"; an architectural metaphor meaning the judge should remain balanced and impartial, not leaning one way or the other.</note>, so that he does not tilt toward the weaker side. Nevertheless, as I was saying, the defense of such cases is not without the risk of "adulterating" the laws.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, then, the response is that the reasoning for a doctor and an advocate is different. For a doctor who undertakes to treat a desperate illness causes injury to no one—neither to a third party nor to the sick person, if he himself consents. However, an advocate who fights for one side in a way that defeats the other, though he may deserve praise for his skill, is nevertheless unjust in his will.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ The second argument concerns the person who takes up a case in good faith, but after the **joinder of issue** <term>contestata litem</term> <note>The formal start of a trial after both sides have stated their positions.</note> understands it to be unjust; this is a point of ambiguity regarding withdrawal.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
For **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the highly influential theologian whose "Summa Theologiae" Soto is often commenting upon.</note> answers that he ought not to betray the case so as to help the other side by revealing the secrets of an unjust cause; for he would then be a **prevaricator** <term>praeuaricator</term> <note>In Roman law, a lawyer who colludes with the opposing side or betrays his client's trust.</note>, according to the chapter *If anyone should repent* [2. q. 3.], which we have already explained. Instead, he ought to abandon the case discreetly.

<margin>Reasoning regarding Thomas's position.</margin>
¶ But truly, this solution offers an opportunity to argue against it. For if someone were advocating for an accuser against a person in a capital case, and during the course of the case he came to know evidently that the person was innocent, he would be bound to betray the cause to free them from death. Indeed, he should act as a witness to their innocence and cross over to defend their case. For innocence possesses such a great right that even a judge—as we said above—to whom this was known, would be bound to the same, let alone an advocate.

<margin>The mind of St. Thomas.</margin>
Therefore, the conclusion of this argument is granted. Nor does Saint Thomas speak except regarding the common order and style of law. Furthermore, if the case were a most grave one, which was estimated to be only slightly less than death—for instance, if it were a question of a very famous reputation and honor, or the status of some illustrious person—I would judge the same according to my understanding. I say this under the censure of others: provided that the advocate knows it not by doubt, but by most certain knowledge. And furthermore, provided he could do it without scandal, and after a **fraternal admonition** <note>A private warning intended to correct a person's wrongdoing before taking public action.</note> by which he would threaten the accuser unless he desisted. And by giving...

# ARTICLE IV

## Whether it is lawful for an advocate to provide legal representation for a fee.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' at the beginning of "Sequitur", depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or legal official, at a desk within a room that features architectural details and a window opening onto a landscape.</image-desc>

<margin>The first argument for the negative side.</margin>
It follows, finally, to discuss the advocate's <term>stipend</term> <note>original: "stipendio"; here referring to the professional fee or payment for services</note>, and whether it is lawful. For an argument is made for the negative side. Works of mercy are not to be performed for the sake of human reward; according to that passage in Luke 14: "When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends or your wealthy neighbors, lest they perhaps invite you in return." Providing legal defense, however, as we said in Article 1, is a work of mercy: therefore, it should be bestowed for free. This is especially true because it is a spiritual work, and it is not lawful to trade spiritual things for a valuation of temporal goods.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued that a judge—because he is a necessary person in a trial—is not allowed to receive anything from either of the litigating parties, as Augustine says in his writing *Against Macedonius*.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
And this is cited in the Decretals <note>original: "14. q. 5. can. non sanè"; a reference to Gratian’s Decree, a collection of canon law</note>. An advocate is also a necessary person; therefore, the same is not allowed for him. On the contrary, Augustine says in the same place that an advocate lawfully sells "just patronage" <note>original: "iustum patrocinium"; meaning legitimate legal protection or representation</note>, and a legal expert sells "true advice."

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with two conclusions. The first: It is lawful for an advocate to value his representation at a price. This is easily gathered from what was said above. For

<margin>The reason for the conclusion.</margin>
those things which are a man's own property, and which he does not owe to another out of justice, he can sell without injury: because no one is bound to give away his own things for free. Now, the knowledge of the legal expert, and the skill and prudence of the advocate, are their own proper goods, just as the knowledge of a doctor or a teacher of any other faculty is theirs. Nor is he always bound to provide these to others by the rigor of justice; therefore, he will be able to value them at a price and offer them for sale.

<margin>The final conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: If any of these men, through wickedness, should extort anything beyond measure, he 

<column-break/>

sins mortally <note>A "mortal sin" in this context refers to a grave offense that destroys the virtue of justice and requires restitution for spiritual reconciliation.</note>; and this is a sin against justice. The conclusion is evident,

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
firstly, by the authority of Augustine in the same place: where he says that things extorted from these people through "immoderate wickedness" are usually reclaimed; but those given through "tolerable custom" are not usually reclaimed. And the reason, then, is ready at hand: for duties of this kind are to be valued at a price; but in those things which are paid for by a price, an excess of price works an injustice. Indeed, the civil law applauds this reason. <note>original: "C. depostul. l. si qui"; a reference to the Codex of Justinian regarding legal petitions.</note>

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
Regarding the first conclusion, however, you may perhaps doubt how the price of such representation is to be estimated: whether it consists in a fixed, indivisible point, or rather permits a range so that anyone can bargain for as much as he wants. For it is argued that it is lawful for anyone to ask for as much as he can manage to express: since in truth the knowledge of a man is like a pearl, which is valued by no certain price, but according to the will of the contracting parties. Indeed, it is more precious than any pearl, according to that passage in Proverbs 16: "Possess wisdom, because it is better than gold."

<margin>The solution.</margin>
It is nevertheless answered that the price of advocates, just like that of other things, is twofold (as we shall say in Book 6): namely, both "legal" and "natural." By "legal," I mean that which is taxed by law: for it has been customary for the wages of the works of the ministers of justice—namely, both scribes and advocates, and others—to be taxed by law, so that for such a writing or such a service, a certain price is paid to them. Concerning these prices, certainly, it cannot be doubted that it is a sin of injustice to receive anything more by agreement; and he who receives more is bound to <term>restitution</term>. This holds if the law is currently received by custom and has not been abolished with the prince's consent. Since, as was said in Book 1, laws bind the conscience, and especially those which are passed for a just cause regarding the valuation of things. And it is indeed most just to establish wages by public law for providing representation and delivering legal responses. Otherwise, since on one side shame may overwhelm the litigants if they contribute too little, while on the other side the greed for winning goads them on, the fees cannot help but be immoderate. By this reasoning, it happens by common usage that lawsuits are "nourished" <note>A common legal metaphor meaning to prolong litigation for profit.</note>: and whichever side wins, the greater portion of the wealth nonetheless falls to the lawyers. But truly, when wages are not 

<margin>A scruple.</margin>
established by law—because they cannot all be conveniently set—then there remains a reason for doubting whether a legal consultant can demand as much as he can...

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of legal fees, concluding that while advocates may lawfully charge for their expertise and labor, extorting excessive fees is a mortal sin against justice. It distinguishes between "legal prices" set by statute and "natural prices" determined by the market, emphasizing that legal fees should be regulated to prevent lawyers from exploiting their clients' desperation.</summary>
