<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 477 regarding the ethics of legal fees. In the previous section, the author began addressing whether it is lawful for an advocate to charge for their services, specifically responding to the argument that legal defense is a work of mercy and should therefore be free.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

it is permitted to demand payment. For then the argument we made above regarding precious things—which are worth as much as they can be sold for—seems to apply.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ It is answered that this is nevertheless not permitted. For among things, as we will say in Book 6 of this same work, some are not strictly necessary for human use; therefore, although they may be valued at as much as they can be sold for, this does not result in the ruin of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "reipublicæ"; the state or community</note>. But others are entirely necessary for human use, such as grain, wine, wool, etc., which cannot be sold without injustice except at a <term>just price</term> <note>a central concept in Scholastic economics where a price must reflect the true value and needs of the community</note>, according to the conditions of the times and places. And legal duties are of this kind. 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Wherefore, **Augustine** says most excellently that things extorted through immoderate greed are usually reclaimed. For greed, if it means nothing more than the insistence of seeking payment, does not contain injustice; but it does when it is immoderate, that is, excessive with respect to the just price. And this is how our latter conclusion is to be understood.

¶ Therefore, neither a scribe nor an advocate can demand as much as they please. Indeed, they cannot even receive it. For even if those higher prices seem to be given freely, they are never truly given except with a coerced will. I admit that the labors which students exhaust themselves in to acquire legal expertise must be weighed, as well as the expenses they incur, and above all their talent and knowledge; but this must be done with moderation, having considered the quality and quantity of the case, and the financial ability of the litigants. Nor should their excuses be listened to. For they say they cannot otherwise maintain their **status**, yet their status and condition are not to be judged by their own estimation, as they usurp for themselves such arrogant displays of pomp. If scribes strive to show off nobility in their food and clothing, and advocates an illustrious status, they ought not to sustain those splendors at the expense of the wretched.

<margin>An advocate cannot contract for a share of the litigation.</margin>
¶ One thing, however, is strictly provided for by law: that an advocate may not contract for a <term>quota litis</term> <note>original: "quota litis"; a contingency fee where the lawyer takes a percentage of the amount won in court</note>, such as for half, or a third, or two-thirds, etc., as held in the Code *de postulan.* law *si qui*, and there **Bartolus**, and law *litem* in the Code *de procura.* and law *sumptus* in the Digest *de pact*. And there was an excellent reason for the law: for in that way, frauds and tricks would be introduced, which the advocate would devise in order to win. Indeed, for the same reason—whatever some of the **Glossators** <note>medieval legal commentators who added "glosses" or notes to the margins of law books</note> may mutter to the contrary—it is not permitted to contract for a certain fixed amount on the condition of victory, which would be like an **honorarium**. For the exact same opportunity for wicked fraud would then be offered. But it is only permitted to 

<column-break/>

contract absolutely for a certain amount, regardless of which side the case turns out for.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
TO the first argument, therefore, it has already been answered often. A man ought not to do everything he can out of mercy; but the Gospel only reminds us of this, that for those things which we perform out of mercy, we should expect a reward from God alone. Therefore, when the cause of a poor person compels you to patronize him, you ought to do it solely out of a divine perspective. However, as we said above, we are not always bound to such works; rather, a man may sell his patronage. For even if knowledge is a spiritual thing by reason of its subject, it is not of that kind of spiritual thing which we received for free and owe for free; rather, it was acquired by our own sweat and vigils, as will be made clearer in Book 9 under the title *on Simony*.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ The second argument seeks a distinction between a judge, a witness, and an advocate. For since each of these ought to defend the truth entirely—the advocate just as much as the others—there appears to be no reason why it is more lawful for him than for the others to receive a fee for defending the truth. 

<margin>The distinction between the judge, the witness, and the advocate regarding receiving payment for the protection of truth.</margin>
There is, however, a distinction: the proper end of the judge and the witness is justice and truth in common, without respect to the plaintiff or the defendant; and for that reason, neither of them is allowed to receive anything for telling the truth. The goal of the advocate, however, is not justice simply, but the justice of his client, whose cause he protects with all his strength, neglecting the other; and therefore, not only for labor (as some think), but for the patronage itself and the defense of truth, he can receive a fee—just as a **Doctor** <note>a teacher or scholar</note> may for teaching the truth which he elucidates. Nevertheless, a difference remains between the judge and the witness: the judge cannot perceive anything from the litigants not only for pronouncing the truth (because the truth is common to both), but neither is he allowed to do so for his labor and study; instead, the commonwealth ought to provide for him as a public person. This is not because it is prohibited by the law of nature—indeed, if there were no fear that he might lean toward one side or the other, corrupted by the sight of payment, the law of nature does not prohibit him from receiving something from the litigants—but because of such fear, it is provided by civil law that he be sustained by the public treasury. But a witness, because he is not entirely a public person but is summoned by the party whose interest is at stake, although he can receive nothing for telling the truth <margin>alt. because</margin> (since he owes it to whichever party to bring it forth sincerely), nevertheless, for his labor...

<summary>This page discusses the ethical limitations on legal fees, arguing that while advocates can be paid for their expertise and labor, they must not overcharge or use their fees to fund a lavish lifestyle. It specifically prohibits contingency fees ("quota litis") to prevent fraud and distinguishes the advocate's right to payment from the duties of judges and witnesses.</summary>

## QUESTION Nine, on insult.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, Second Part of the Second Part, question 72.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether insult consists in words.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring a landscape scene with figures and floral patterns.</image-desc>Having dispatched with those verbal injuries which usually happen in legal judgments, we must proceed to those injurious words which come into use outside of court. It is asked first, therefore, concerning <term>contumelia</term> <note>Latin: "contumelia"; an affront, insult, or verbal assault intended to strip someone of their honor</note>, whether it consists in words.
<margin>First argument.</margin>
For the argument is made for the negative side. "Contumelia" is a name for harm: yet no harm seems to be inflicted by a word, but rather a person or their honor is harmed by deeds: therefore, insult occurs not in words, but in deeds.
<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second, the dishonoring that is done with words has its own peculiar name, such as "vituperation" or "reproach": these, however, seem to differ from an insult: therefore, an insult does not consist in words.
¶ On the contrary is the fact that only a word is perceived by hearing: yet insult pertains to the ears, according to that passage in Jeremiah 20: "I heard insults on every side": therefore, insult is in words.

<margin>The difference between insult and detraction.</margin>
There are five capital species of verbal injuries outside of the courtroom: namely, insult, <term>detraction</term> <note>original: "detractio"; the act of lowering someone's reputation by revealing true but hidden faults</note>, whispering <note>original: "susurrus"; gossiping to sow discord between friends</note>, derision, and cursing. Now, insult and detraction differ primarily in themselves based on their object: for an insult is an injury committed against the honor of another, while detraction is the damaging of their reputation (<term>fama</term>). For honor and reputation differ in this way: honor is the reverence shown to someone because of some excellence and especially because of their virtue. Reputation, however, as is held in the <term>Gloss</term> <note>The standard medieval commentary on Canon Law</note> on the chapter "Vestra," regarding

<column-break/>

the cohabitation of clerics and women, is the status of unharmed dignity, proven by one's life and morals. Or, if we speak with the theologians and philosophers, it is that clear knowledge which others have of us. Thus, there can be honor without reputation, and vice-versa. For reverence is sometimes shown to a nobleman on account of the excellence of his blood, even though a sinister opinion is held regarding his morals. And conversely, private men are often found lurking in corners, bereft of honors, of whose lives a clear and positive opinion is nevertheless held. ¶ This distinction having been laid out, the question is answered with two conclusions.
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first: Insult, properly speaking, consists in words.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
The proof. Insult, as we were just saying, is the same as dishonoring, the opposite of the reverence that is usually shown as honor. Now, honor is taken away from someone in two ways. In one way, we might say, mediately: for instance, while that which was the cause of the honor is removed. For he who steals the substance of a wealthy man—for the sake of which alone honor was held for him—darkens his honor. Just as one who takes away the knowledge of a wise man by an injury to the brain; for from that point they begin to be held in lower esteem. Wherefore, that honor alone is true which is owed to virtue: because it depends on no external cause except God. Such dishonorings, however, do not constitute a specific type of their own, but are referred to other injuries: such as theft, homicide, and the rest. But in the second way, honor is taken away from someone directly and properly. And this happens when someone brings something to another's notice that is detrimental to their honor. For just as honor is owed to excellence, so the notice of some foulness is the cause of dishonor; and in this, the essence of insult properly consists. To bring something to the notice of another, however, belongs to the nature of a sign; and since, according to
<margin>Augustine</margin>
**Augustine** in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*, words have obtained the primary role of signifying among men—for they are, according to
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
**Aristotle** in the first book of *On Interpretation*, the indicators of those concepts which are in the soul—it follows that the essence of insult is properly found in words. Hence,
<margin>Isidore.</margin>
**Isidore of Seville** says in his *Etymologies*: "He is called contumelious who is swift and 'swells' with words of injury." For there is an allusion in the words "swells" (<term>tumet</term>) and "insult" (<term>contumelia</term>).
<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The final conclusion. By an extension of the name, insult is also located in deeds, insofar as they have the nature of signifying.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is clear: because, as **Augustine** teaches in that same place, it is also fitting for things themselves to be signs of other things. Wherefore, one can also point out another's fault through deeds.

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on legal fees and begins an investigation into "contumelia" (insult), defining it as a verbal injury against a person's honor and distinguishing it from detraction, which targets one's reputation.</summary>
<keywords>insult, honor, reputation, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine, Aristotle, Isidore of Seville, verbal injury, detraction, justice</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of insults (contumelia) from the previous page, where the author began exploring whether an insult must necessarily consist of spoken words or if it can also be conveyed through actions or gestures.</meta>

F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,
<meta>image quality: good; catchword: uitando (to be avoided)</meta>

to reveal. Whence, regarding that passage in Romans 1: "Slanderers, proud men, etc.," the <margin>Gloss.</margin> <term>Gloss</term> <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria" was the standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> says that insulting people are those who, through words and deeds, inflict affronts and shameful treatment. From this, it follows that no action, insofar as it is a mere physical event, has the character of an insult; rather, it is an insult insofar as it has the power of signifying something. For when someone breaks down another's doors with the intent to steal, he is not an "insulter," but a thief. However, if he attempts this to cause shame and contempt for the master of the house, he becomes an insulter. By that action, he signifies that he considers the master to be worth nothing. Similarly, if someone strikes a <term>stableman</term> <note>Latin: "agasonem"; a low-ranking servant or groom.</note> with a club, not with the intent of dishonoring him but merely to strike him, he is not an insulter in the same way as if he were to beat a nobleman—not to cause pain, but to strip away his honor. By the same reasoning, one who solicits his neighbor's wife for the sake of lust is not <term>formally</term> <note>In scholastic logic, "formally" refers to the essential intent or defining characteristic of an act.</note> an insulter toward his neighbor, unless he were to attempt it specifically to harm the husband's honor. In that case, he strives to use that shameful act to mark the man as worthless. Indeed, as far as the matter of an insult is concerned, it is not always required that the vice being exposed be a sin (though this type of insult is more significant). It is enough that it be a defect of one's lineage, or some other sickness of mind or body, or anything contrary to the excellence for which men are held in honor. For example, if you maliciously point out that a man is of low birth, or a coward, etc. Nor is it required for you to be an insulter that you defame a man by revealing a hidden vice; for even if you call a man who is a public adulterer, or one who is <term>one-eyed</term> <note>Latin: "coclitum"; a person with only one eye.</note>, or of lowly birth by those names, you inflict an insult upon him—and a greater one if you falsely attribute such things to him. Besides these types of deeds, there are others that are insulting in themselves because they contain nothing else but a signifies: such as showing one's nose or thumb between two fingers <note>A gesture similar to "the fig," often considered obscene or a sign of contempt in the Mediterranean world.</note>, or a tongue between the teeth. For these signs, as it is said, represented a most foul vice to the Romans.

<margin>Inquiry.</margin> ¶ This description of insult offers an opportunity to ask whether such acts must be done in the presence of the other person. For it appears that this is necessary.
<margin>Reasoning for the other side.</margin> For insult and <term>detraction</term> <note>Latin: "detractio"; backbiting or slander done behind someone's back.</note> differ in this: the former carries force and contempt with it, while the latter leans toward fraud and deceit. Therefore, the former is done openly in someone's presence, just as the latter is done secretly in their absence.
<margin>Solution.</margin> ¶ The response is that insult differs from detraction in the same way we distinguished earlier between robbery and theft. For insult, because it signifies contempt and is opposed

<column-break/>

to the reverence that is shown in one's presence, is by its very nature inflicted in person. Or, if it is done in one's absence, it is not because the insulter wishes to hide it like a slanderer; rather, he tosses the words about in the person's absence specifically so that they might reach that person's notice. For this reason, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> deliberately said that an insult occurs when someone brings something against another’s honor to the notice of that person and others: that is, when his intention is to hurl such a reproach to the person's face.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> TO the first argument, it is responded that words, insofar as they are a natural sound, hurt no one—unless perhaps someone has very sensitive ears. But insofar as they exist as signs, they confer honor if they are honorable, and take it away if they are shameful. This is because honor arises from the excellence that exists in the knowledge of men. Actions, however, insofar as they are actions, have their own species of vices (as we have said); but insofar as they are signs, they are considered as words.

<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third argument, it is responded by that distinction usually made between insult, <term>reviling</term> <note>Latin: "convitium"; a loud or public verbal attack.</note>, and <term>upbraiding</term> <note>Latin: "improperium"; a reproach or taunt.</note>.
<margin>The gap between insult, reviling, and upbraiding.</margin> ¶ For those who over-observe the similarity of letters with Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), known for his "Etymologies."</note> contend that <term>contumelia</term> is derived from <term>contumeo</term> ("to swell against"); for an insulting person is "swelling" and puffed up with a turgid soul.
<margin>Isidore.</margin> Although, as Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD).</note> wishes in the <margin>Ulpian.</margin> Digest, book on injuries, law 1, it is more correctly said to come from <term>contemnendo</term> ("despising"). Therefore, in its primary meaning, it only signifies the bitterness of a statement against another's honor. However, by the adaptation of usage among theologians, it signifies that specific type by which a mortal sin is charged against another—such as that he is a heretic, or a thief, etc. "Reviling" (*convitium*), however, is more broadly defined: it is a curse by which any evil you wish—whether of fault or punishment—is charged against another.
<margin>Cicero.</margin> Whence Cicero says in *Pro Caelio*: "A curse has no purpose besides insult; if it is thrown about petulantly, it is called reviling; if wittily, it is called urbanity (wit)."
<margin>Labeo.</margin> ¶ Moreover, what Labeo says in Ulpian, in the Digest on injuries, the law *Item apud Labeonem*: namely, that *convitium* (reviling) sounds just like *convocium* (a "con-shouting")—as if the voices of many are coming together to hurl curses as one. Just as we read in 2 Kings 2 <note>Now usually cited as 4 Kings in the Vulgate, or 2 Kings in modern Bibles.</note> concerning the shouting of the boys against Elisha, crying out: "Go up, baldhead!" Perhaps this does not pertain much to the matter. For the prefix "con" in this name does not signify a gathering of many so much as intensity, just as in the word "conficio" (to complete). And I would believe it is composed from "vitium" (fault); for to revile (*convitiari*) is nothing other than to splatter another with faults. Unless it is said to be from "inviting together" [to avoid]...

It uses Roman legal definitions and theological distinctions to categorize various forms of verbal abuse and the importance of intent.</summary>

### Book Five, Question IX.

<margin>Lorenzo Valla.</margin> ...to be avoided: as Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457) was a famous Italian humanist and philologist.</note> says in book 6. For we avoid the company of the one we tear apart with insults, as if driving him away from us out of contempt. However, these matters pertain to the grammarians. In Ecclesiasticus 20, it says: "He will give little, and upbraid <note>Original: "improperabit." This refers to the act of "throwing back" a favor in someone's face.</note> much." And according to the <margin>Terence.</margin> Comic Poet: "This reminding of yours is like a reproach for an unremembered benefit." <note>A quote from Terence’s play *Andria*. It suggests that reminding someone of a favor you did for them is essentially an insult because it implies they are ungrateful.</note> Nevertheless, in common usage, these terms are used interchangeably.

<margin>A small question.</margin> ¶ A small scholastic question might perhaps present itself to the reader here: whether all these modes of insults and others are of the same <term>species</term> <note>In scholastic logic, "species" refers to the specific category or essence of a sin, which determines how it must be confessed.</note>, or whether they differ in species just as the shames that one casts upon another differ. I would believe, along with <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas de Vio Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>, that they are all of the same species. For an insult is a "most specific species," as it has one single object—honor—which it takes away from one who suffers it involuntarily through force. For a single species is constituted by a single formal reason of the object. Nonetheless, the gravity of an insult can increase so much that its specific nature must necessarily be explained in confession. For example, if you call someone a "heretic" or a "traitor," or something similar, that specific detail must be explained in confession.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether an insult, and generally a reproach, is by its nature a mortal sin.<-

Since an insult consists in words, as has been said, which do not seem by their nature to have such an enormous capacity for injury, it is rightly asked whether it is a <term>mortal fault</term> <note>A "mortal" or "deadly" sin is one that, in Catholic theology, destroys the relationship with God, as opposed to "venial" or lesser sins.</note> by its nature, just as homicide, theft, and adultery are. <margin>First argument.</margin> The argument is made from the negative side. No mortal crime can be an office of virtue; but to reproach someone is an act of the virtue of <term>eutrapelia</term> <note>From the Greek *eutrapelia* (εὐτραπελία), which Aristotle defines as "well-bred insolence" or "witty playfulness"—the virtue of being a good conversationalist.</note>, to which, according to the <margin>The Philosopher</margin> <note>Aristotle.</note> in the 4th book of the *Ethics*, it belongs to reproach well; therefore, an insult is not a <margin>Second.</margin> mortal sin. ¶ Second, it is argued: Perfect men do not commit mortal sins, yet they sometimes use reproaches and insults, as is clear with <margin>Paul.</margin> Paul in Galatians 3: "O foolish Galatians!" Indeed, even Christ in the last chapter of Luke said: "O fools, and slow of heart to believe!" <margin>Third.</margin> Therefore, an insult is not a sin. ¶ Third: although that which is venial by its nature and object can become mortal through its end or circumstance (as when a lie becomes harmful), conversely, that which is mortal by its nature and object cannot become venial through intention. For it carries its object with it: in whatever way or for whatever purpose you steal, you sin mortally. If, therefore, an insult were a mortal sin by its nature, it could never fall from that rank; but this is clearly false, for no one has ever considered a light reproach or a slip of the tongue to be a mortal sin.

<column-break/>

<margin>Fourth.</margin> ¶ Fourth: Every mortal sin is either a <term>capital sin</term> <note>One of the "Seven Deadly Sins," like Pride or Anger.</note> or the offspring of some capital sin. An insult is not a capital sin, as is clear in itself; nor is it the sprout of a capital crime. For <margin>Gregory.</margin> Gregory in the 31st book of the *Morals* says it is the author of great anger. Yet this seems to be false, for it is rather born of pride, according to Proverbs 10: "Where pride is, there is insult." Or it is reduced to folly, according to another passage in Proverbs 20: "All fools are embroiled in insults." ¶ To the contrary is the fact that nothing merits eternal punishment unless it is a mortal crime; but one who reproaches is worthy of the punishment of hell, according to that passage in Matthew 5: "Whoever shall say to his brother, 'Thou fool,' shall be in danger of hell fire."

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The question is answered with three very easy conclusions. The first is: An insult, by its nature, is a mortal sin; and it is more atrocious than theft or robbery. However, <margin>The gap between sins of deed and sins of word.</margin> here a distinction must be noted between sins that consist in deeds and those that are placed in words. For in the former sins, the category is weighed by the object alone; but in words, it is only weighed by the intention joined to them. Therefore, "by its nature" here does not signify only what arises from the object (as in theft and homicide), but also from the intention. And the reason is that since words do not offend by the physical thing itself, as deeds do, but by their significance—and significance arises from the intention of expressing something—it is not formally judged an insult unless it proceeds from a mind intending to reproach, or from gross ignorance and negligence in attending to what you say. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> The conclusion is thus proven: That sin is mortal which is against <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the theological virtue of love for God and neighbor.</note>; but charity is taken away by any sin through which peace and friendship are disturbed; such is the nature of an insult; therefore it is a mortal sin. This last premise is proven: Honor is a more excellent human good than external things, according to the saying: "A good name is better than great riches." <note>Proverbs 22:1.</note> And since honor is placed in...

<meta>This page continues the discussion by Domingo de Soto (1494–1560) on the moral gravity of insults. The previous page established the definition of an insult as an act of contempt. Here, he compares the loss of honor to the loss of property and categorizes the different levels of sin involved in verbal abuse.</meta>

### Book Five, Question IX.

Because of the supreme excellence of virtue, mortals rightly value honor more than other external goods. Indeed, refined men use all those other goods as means to acquire honors, and they even spend those goods to maintain them. Therefore, an insult is, by its very nature, a more serious sin than theft or robbery. For men prefer to be deprived of other goods than to be held in contempt—although the quantity of a theft could be so great that it exceeds the gravity of an individual insult.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: The tossing about of a taunt or a reproach that is done without the specific intent to insult must be judged sometimes by the intention of the speaker, sometimes by the magnitude of the matter, and sometimes by the lack of caution that ought to have been applied. Hence, it can exist in a threefold degree: namely, it can sometimes be a virtue, sometimes a venial <note>A "venial" sin is a minor offense that does not break one's relationship with God, unlike a "mortal" sin.</note> fault, and occasionally a mortal sin.

<margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven. When either a father, a prelate, or an elder uses some reproach in correcting an inferior, if he uses moderation, he is performing his duty. However, when someone vomits out a grave taunt out of wrath, it is a mortal sin. But where there is some lack of caution, it is usually a venial sin. This often happens among simple women and people of the lowest class who sprinkle each other with taunts as they "come to the mouth" <note>Original: "in buccam veniunt." This refers to speaking impulsively or saying whatever pops into one's head.</note>, to which very little credit is usually given. But truly, since men have always been so tenacious regarding their honor, everyone—even prelates—should most carefully abstain from taunts, which embitter human souls more painfully than physical wounds. Furthermore, they usually contribute very little to correction. These conclusions are very easy; there is no need for us to dwell on them further.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: An insult, by its own nature, is born from anger, as Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a foundational doctor of the Church.</note> says in the place cited. It is not that pride or hatred, by which someone despises another, is not sometimes sufficient to cause an insult; rather, it is that a vice is judged to take its origin from where it most frequently arises. Insult most often arises from anger because it has the greatest connection to the goal of anger. For the goal of anger is vengeance and revenge, and there is no more immediate compensation or stronger way to take revenge than an insult. For he who is not powerful enough to avenge himself with a deed, or does not dare to do so, immediately leaps into insults—as the temperament of women bears witness. For by the fact that someone tramples another with words, he satisfies his own soul to some extent.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
To the first argument, it is responded that taunting, according to Aristotle in the fourth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 8, belongs to the virtue of "wittiness" <note>Original: "eutrapelia." This is the Aristotelian virtue of pleasantness in conversation or "well-turned" wit.</note> insofar as it is contained within the limits of moderate jesting—namely, when the charm of refinement is present in the taunt. This follows the phrase of Cicero cited above: "If a slur is tossed about too boldly, it is a taunt; if it is done more facetiously, it is called wit." Therefore, those court jesters should by no means be permitted to use scoffs that bring more bitterness than wit. For laughter should be provoked in such a way that bile is not stirred up.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that just as it is permissible to use lashes for the sake of discipline, so too one may use moderate words which, by their sharpness, may afflict the mind of the delinquent with some pain.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
But truly, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430).</note> warns in his book *On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount*, these types of bitter rebukes are rarely to be employed.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ In the solution to the third argument, the mind must be applied to understanding that word which Saint Thomas treated in the *Prima Secundae*, question 88, article 2. There he taught that a "jocose lie," which by its nature is venial, can become mortal because of its purpose—such as if it is directed toward adultery or the infamy of another. However, a sin that is mortal by its nature, which is committed by an act like theft, remains mortal regardless of the purpose to which it is directed, even if it is done to give alms.

<margin>The intention of Saint Thomas.</margin>
Therefore, the opinion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s scholastic method.</note> is that while the intention of an end can drag a venial sin into the mortal category, it cannot extenuate a mortal sin down to a venial one. Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that what is mortal by its nature can become venial either from the "lightness of the matter" or from "stealth" <note>Original: "surreptione," referring to a lack of full deliberate consent or a sudden impulse.</note>. But an insult, as has already been said, since it is committed through "signification" (which proceeds from intention), although it is mortal by its nature, can nonetheless become venial because of the intention itself. Indeed, sometimes it may even have the merit of virtue.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, it has already been satisfied by the third conclusion. For an insult is a "daughter of anger," not of pride. For a sin that is born from another ought to be ordered toward the same end; but an insult is not ordered toward self-exaltation, which is the goal of pride. Nonetheless, pride disposes one toward insult, for he who is puffed up easily despises others; and therefore the Wise Man <note>Solomon, traditionally credited with the Book of Proverbs.</note> says: "Where there is pride, there is insult." And again, because the fury of insult clouds the reason, he adds, saying: "Fools are mingled with insults."

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that honor is a person's most precious external possession, making insults more naturally grave than theft. However, he clarifies that the morality of a taunt depends heavily on the speaker's intent and status, noting that even "wittiness" can be a virtue if it avoids true malice.</summary>

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether everyone ought to endure insults with equanimity.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
After having discussed the nature of the insult itself, it follows that we should discuss how it ought to be endured. There is an argument that enduring it is not a virtue. For one who suffers the taunts and reproaches of a slanderer fosters that person's audacity and insolence; this is truly not the duty of virtue.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued that everyone is bound to love themselves more than another, and thus to value their own honor more than another's. No one, however, ought to allow the honor and reputation of a friend to be disparaged in their presence, according to Proverbs 26: "He who imposes silence on a fool mitigates rages." <note>This is a paraphrase of the Latin Vulgate for Proverbs 26:10, suggesting that stopping a fool's speech prevents further harm.</note> Therefore, no one should have to endure their own reproaches.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Third, no one is permitted to take private revenge. However, he who with a level mind endures the "foam" of an insulting person is actually taking revenge on them, insofar as he professes to despise the attacker. This follows the words of John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note> on Matthew: "If you wish to be avenged, be silent; and you have dealt him a fatal blow." Therefore, such silence is not permitted. ¶ On the contrary is the Psalm: "Those who sought evils against me spoke vanities." And it adds: "But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute man not opening his mouth." <note>Psalm 38:13-14 in the modern numbering.</note>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To this question, the answer is given in two very widely accepted conclusions. The first: Everyone is bound to have a mind prepared to endure insults wherever it may be expedient; however, they are not <margin>Proof.</margin> always bound to endure them in practice. Both parts of this conclusion are proven. Patience is necessary both in actions done against us and in evil words spoken against us. However, in things done against us, patience is only strictly necessary in the "preparation of the soul." <margin>Augustine</margin> This follows the exposition of Augustine on Matthew 5: "If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other." Since this "preparation of the soul" is commanded as an affirmative precept, <note>In theology, an "affirmative precept" is a command to do something good (like "honor your parents"). These are always true in principle but do not require the action at every single moment of the day, unlike "negative precepts" (like "do not kill"), which apply constantly.</note> it does not obligate us at all times, but only for that moment when reason demands it. Therefore, we must have a prepared mind, yet we are not always bound in reality to endure insults in silence. We are taught this by the example of the Redeemer himself. For he asked for a reason from the one striking him, saying in John 18: "Why do you strike me?"—which bore the appearance of a certain rebuke.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: Sometimes it is necessary to repel an insult that has been offered. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> This is proven on two main grounds. First, for the good of the person who is being

<column-break/>

insulting: namely, so that the insolence of their swelling pride may be repressed, and they do not become accustomed to such injuries. This is according to the cited passage of Proverbs 26, and according to another in the same place: "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself." Second, it is for the good of others, both those present and those absent, who sometimes tend to hold a person in lower esteem when they are affected by insults; consequently, such a person's teaching and advice would be less profitable to them. Hence, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> in his 9th homily on Ezekiel says: "Those whose lives are set as an example for imitation ought, if they can, to quiet the words of detractors; lest those who could have heard their preaching fail to listen, and thus, remaining in wicked habits, they despise living well." ¶ Here, first of all, I think it should be noted regarding the teaching of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text.</note> that which we judged to be true in the previous book (Question 6): namely, that it is permitted for anyone, at least as a private <margin>Any private person can waive the injury to their reputation.</margin> individual, to waive the injury to their reputation caused by a slanderer. For if we are not bound to resist those who blacken our honor with insults, there is no reason why we should always be bound to maintain the brilliance of our reputation by any other way than by devoting ourselves to the duties of virtue. ¶ However, this formal part of the first conclusion—namely, that we are bound to have minds prepared to endure insults when reason dictates—requires some explanation. And first it is asked: <margin>Question.</margin> Is there a command to always have the will, that is, an actual purpose, to endure future injuries for the sake of place and time? For "preparation" seems to signify such an act. <margin>Answer.</margin> It is answered that this is not necessary. For affirmative precepts do not obligate us to external works at every moment, nor do they obligate us to internal acts at every moment. Rather, it is enough not to have a contrary purpose, and to have purposed in general to keep the commandments; for this specific purpose is included by virtue of that general one. And it must be noted that this kind of preparation is not only necessary for not avenging injuries through private authority (for it is most certain that this is permitted to no one, as was said above), but also for not resisting where resistance cannot be made without grave scandal and immense harm, and where the logic of faith and the public good demand endurance. Therefore, he who carries in his mind the intent to avenge himself for any insult whatsoever, and to oppose anyone without discernment, is in a state of perdition. Yet, outside of those cases, anyone can both resist privately with the moderation of virtue and seek redress through public power and the order of law. <margin>Hesitation.</margin> ¶ You ask, however, whether outside of cases of necessity, while...

<margin>Solution.</margin>
For the Wise Man <note>A reference to Solomon, the traditional author of Proverbs.</note> advises both things at once: namely, that we should not answer a fool according to his folly, lest we be made like him; and again, that we should answer him, lest he seem wise to himself. <note>original: "nè respondeamus stulto iuxta stultitiā suā, nè efficiamur ei similes: & rursus vt respondeamus ei nè videatur sibi sapiens." See Proverbs 26:4-5.</note> Therefore, it must be weighed by the <term>plumb line of prudence</term> <note>A metaphor for careful, precise moral judgment.</note> when it is appropriate to respond to someone insulting us, and when it is not at all. For one must respond to him when the reason of <term>fraternal correction</term> <note>The practice of correcting a neighbor's sin out of love for their soul.</note> shows it to be fitting; for then it is a precept of charity to calm his mind and to warn him of his own fury and folly. Yet, we must apply a greater care to ourselves: namely, lest the fury of the other person excite our own, and so that we, who ought to restrain another, do not instead irritate them further by burning with a similar impulse. We ought, therefore, to warn him gently by showing that he is agitated without cause or reason. This follows the example of Christ, who only said: "Why do you strike me?" <note>John 18:23.</note>—that is, you had no cause for striking. But when insults are hurled against the honor of the faith and religion, then in turn it is a matter of religious duty to use a sharper rebuke against them.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
For it is to this that we refer when Paul called the Galatians "senseless" <note>Galatians 3:1.</note> and when Christ called some "fools" and others a "wicked and perverse generation." <note>Matthew 17:17.</note> However, public persons—even for the sake of their own personal honor, as has been said—ought to resist insults, since their honor is necessary for the commonwealth. Private persons, though not bound to do so, nevertheless may. ¶ However, there remains one

<margin>The final doubt.</margin>
final doubt: whether, when it is lawful to resist, it is then permissible to throw back one insult in exchange for the one received. If someone calls me a thief, I call him an assassin. If he notes my lineage, I note his character and habits. It is answered

<margin>Solution.</margin>
firstly, that it is never lawful to charge another with a false crime; for that would be a lie, and a destructive one at that. Furthermore, it is not lawful to throw back a crime or any defect, whether hidden or public, by way of revenge against the insulter, but only by way of defense in repelling force. That is, it is not lawful to charge him with a crime that is irrelevant to undermining his authority; but only that which is strictly necessary for that purpose. For example, if I say he is a lying man and, to confirm this, I expose some of his lies, so that the trust in what he is falsely accusing me of may be broken. If, however, he calls me a concubinary <note>Someone living in an unsanctified sexual union.</note>, it is not lawful for me to call him a thief—just as there is no right to strike back at one who strikes you.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, then, it has already been answered that it is lawful to suppress the audacity of the insulter with mild words, lest he seem wise to himself; yet not with bitter ones, lest we be made like him. ¶ To the second, it is said that when

<margin>To the second.</margin>
we respond to someone who hurls insults at another, we do not seem to do so out of an excessive love of ourselves, but out of charity—both for the one insulting and for the one suffering the insults—and therefore to do so is always a duty. When, however, we repel insults against ourselves, we do not then seem to be practicing charity as much as we seem to succumb to our own pride and irritate our anger. Therefore, in that case, the advice is more often to remain silent. ¶ Finally, to the third, it is answered that if

<margin>To the third.</margin>
someone hearing insults were to remain silent out of craftiness—specifically with the intent to provoke the other to anger by treating them with contempt—it would be a sin of revenge. But if he remains silent to look after himself and in obedience to virtue, even if he knows the other will be more severely agitated by it, it ought to be of no concern to him. And this is what Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century church father.</note> says, following the counsel of the Wise Man in Ecclesiasticus 18: "Do not argue with a talkative man, and do not pile wood upon his fire." <note>This citation actually refers to Sirach 8:3.</note>

### ARTICLE I.
-> Whether detraction is the blackening of another's reputation through secret words. <-

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'P' depicting a figure (likely a scholar or saint) seated at a desk with an open book, surrounded by architectural motifs.</image-desc>

Following the "insult" by which honor is disparaged, we turn to "detraction," <note>In scholastic theology, detraction is the sin of revealing a person's real but hidden faults to others without a valid reason, thereby harming their reputation.</note> by which reputation is taken away. And first, concerning its essence, it is asked whether it is the blackening of another's reputation

<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
through secret words. For it is argued from the negative side: "Hidden" and "manifest" are circumstances that do not constitute the moral species of an act. In a definition, however, only that which pertains to the species ought to be placed. Therefore, there is no reason why the distinction of secrecy should be placed in the definition of detraction. ¶ Second, it is argued: Reputation is a public and well-known notice. Therefore, it is not blackened by

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
that which is secret. For which reason, detraction that is done through secret words is not [a blackening] of reputation...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into injuries committed through speech. Having previously discussed insults (contumely) which are delivered to a person's face, the author now transitions to "detraction," which occurs behind a person's back.</meta>

# Book Five, Question X.
### Page 485

<margin>Third.</margin> ...contrary to reputation. ¶ Thirdly, detraction is the same as subtraction or taking away from a whole. However, it happens that a reputation is blackened without any truth being subtracted, but rather by making secret crimes public. Therefore, detraction is not the same thing as the blackening of a reputation. ¶ To the contrary is that passage from Ecclesiasticus 10: *If a serpent bites in silence, he who detracts in secret is no better.* <note>original: "Si mordeat serpens in silētio, nihil eo minus habet qui occultè detrahit." See Sirach 10:11.</note> Therefore, to secretly bite another’s reputation is to commit detraction against them.

<margin>Single conclusion.</margin> To this question, a single conclusion suffices, which clearly follows from the previous question. <term>Detraction</term> <note>From the Latin *detractio*, meaning to take away or pull down; a form of backbiting or slander.</note> is the secret blackening of another’s reputation. This conclusion has already been demonstrated from the preceding arguments.

<margin>Proof.</margin> Indeed, just as it is common to harm someone by a deed in two ways—as we showed regarding theft and robbery—namely, either by manifest force or by a deceitful injury, so it also happens by word. For one person harms another openly through <term>contumely</term> <note>From the Latin *contumelia*, referring to a manifest insult or scornful treatment intended to dishonor someone to their face.</note>, but another harms secretly through detraction. He who attacks another with manifest words in his presence shows that he holds him in low esteem; therefore, as we said, he openly wounds his honor. For this reason, we said that contumely is contrary to honor. But truly, he who mutters against someone in corners while they are absent shows not so much that he despises him, but that he fears him. On that account, he does not plot against the man’s honor, but against his reputation—that is, against the good opinion held of him by others—which he either clouds or extinguishes by spreading a contrary opinion. Therefore, detraction is nothing other than the blackening of another’s reputation through secret words. From this, the differences previously established between contumely and detraction become clear: both as to the method (the former is manifest, while the latter is secret) and as to the object (the former is contrary to honor, the latter to reputation).

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> There is no reason to linger here any further, but the solution to the first argument should be noted. For contumely and detraction differ by a specific difference, not only by reason of their material objects (honor and reputation), as many of the disciples of Saint Thomas <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas.</note> believe, but by the formal reason of how they affect the victim's will. It is just as we said regarding theft and robbery. For even though both the robber and the thief take what belongs to another, in theft, a man suffers an involuntary loss through ignorance <note>because he does not know it is happening</note>; in robbery, however, he suffers through force. According to Aristotle, these are different causes of involuntary action. In the same way, he who suffers a loss of honor through a received insult suffers involuntarily through force; but he who receives damage to his reputation through detraction suffers involuntarily 

<column-break/>

through ignorance. Therefore, the response to the argument is that although "secret" and "manifest" do not change the species of an act in an absolute sense (as is clear in one who lies either secretly or openly), yet when the reason for the act being involuntary is changed by these factors, the species of the sin is changed accordingly. ¶ To the second argument, he responds that the detractor is said to speak ill "secretly," not in an absolute sense, but specifically hidden from the one being defamed—in contrast to the person who insults to one's face. Nevertheless, he speaks in front of others, from whom he takes away the good opinion they held of the person. Thus, the difference between detraction and contumely does not consist in whether it is done before many or few people, but in whether it is done in the presence of the one being harmed or behind his back. <margin>To the second.</margin>

<margin>To the third.</margin>
<margin>Eight ways the splendor of reputation is diminished.</margin> ¶ Finally, to the third argument, it is responded that detraction is not named in respect to truth—as if something of the truth were being subtracted—but in respect to the reputation, which is always diminished. This happens in eight ways: four directly and four indirectly. 

Directly, in the first way, when a falsehood is imposed. And this is the worst of all. Secondly, when someone exaggerates another’s fault with his words; this is a pestilential style, common to babblers and those who speak ill. Thirdly, when a secret is revealed. Those who infect the commonwealth with this plague are people who, out of a greed for sharing news, know not how to contain any secret, but like a leaky vessel, pour everything out. Fourthly, when someone strives to show that a good deed proceeded from a bad intention. For although this also pertains to rash judgment, nothing prevents one sin from belonging to two species of malice. Thus, when someone does this to blacken another’s reputation, he is a defamer; for he suggests that he knows the man's intentions are depraved, and thus the man's good reputation is obscured.

Indirectly, he is also a defamer who either denies another’s good qualities or, out of envy, remains silent where he ought to speak. For when a good conversation starts about someone in my presence, whom it is established I know very well, and I remain silent, my silence is a kind of judgment that he is not worthy of such great praise<gloss>*</gloss>: which is a type of infamy. <margin>worthy <gloss>*</gloss></margin> And thirdly, this also happens when someone diminishes another’s merits. And finally, fourthly, when someone maliciously praises another; this craftiness is by no means the lowest form of defamation. Hence Favorinus <note>A Roman philosopher known for his learning and oratory.</note> says in Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of *Attic Nights*.</note>: "It is more shameful to praise sparingly and coldly than to disparage obsessively and gravely." For he who speaks ill, the more bitterly he does it, the more he is considered an unjust enemy, and thus he earns less credit. But he who praises in an unrefined and meager way seems to strip the person of their reputation through the very cause itself...

<sig>Hh 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: itself</meta>

It outlines eight specific direct and indirect ways a reputation can be damaged, including lying, revealing secrets, and "faint praise."</summary>

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether detraction is by its very nature a mortal sin.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar or cleric seated at a desk and reading a book.</image-desc>
**J**ust as with an insult, so he asks concerning detraction, whether it is by its very nature a mortal crime. It is argued from the negative side: To reveal another’s sin which is hidden, either through brotherly correction or through an accusation, is detraction; for by this, another’s reputation is blackened. And yet that is a duty; therefore, detraction is not by its very nature a sin.
<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly: no vice which is common to the whole human race should be considered mortal. For from mortal sin, especially among Christians, there are many who abstain; but <term>venial sins</term> <note>Minor, pardonable sins that do not destroy the state of grace.</note> are those which no one can claim not to have without lying. However, the whole human race is endangered specifically by this vice, 
<margin>Gloss.</margin>
as the <term>gloss</term> <note>A standard marginal commentary on the Bible or Law.</note> has it on that passage of Proverbs 24: *Do not meddle with detractors.* <note>original: "Cum detractoribus non commiscearis." See Proverbs 24:21.</note> 
<margin>Third argument.</margin>
Therefore, it is not by its nature mortal. ¶ Thirdly: 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine, in his sermon on the fire of purgatory, numbers it among the smaller sins when we speak evil with all ease and rashness; therefore detraction 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
is nothing but a venial sin. ¶ To the contrary, however, is what Paul says in Romans 1, where he groups detractors and those hateful to God together; the cause of which the gloss adds: lest detraction, because it consists in words, be thought a light thing.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
**T**o the question, it is answered with four conclusions. First: Detraction is by its very nature a mortal sin. It is proven by presupposing the same 

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

noting that we declared regarding insults: namely, that since detraction is a sin in words, which harm only by their meaning, it is perfected not by the object alone but by the intention of signifying harm. Therefore, he is properly called a detractor who, out of intention or the grossest negligence, spreads a rumor about an absent person and obscures his reputation. And one is said to do something by intention not only when he directly proposes it in his mind, but also when he notices what he is saying and nevertheless blabs the word without a legitimate cause. This being supposed, the conclusion is proven, as similar points are customarily demonstrated. That vice is against <term>charity</term> <note>The theological virtue of love for God and neighbor.</note> and is therefore mortal, by which a neighbor is harmed in a matter of great moment; for peace is disturbed. Such a thing is detraction, by which reputation is clouded—which is rightly held at a higher price than external goods. This is according to Ecclesiasticus 41: *Have a care for your good name, for this shall continue with you more than a thousand great and precious treasures.* <note>original: "Curam habe de bono nomine..." See Sirach 41:15.</note> ¶ Second conclusion. When someone 
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
proffers some words, even if they are derogatory to a reputation, yet he does not intend that, but something else, that speech is not considered detraction properly in itself—or as they say, "formally"—but as if by accident. This conclusion follows from the preceding one. For since the intention of signifying harm is native to detraction, where that is absent, the form of detraction is missing. ¶ Third conclusion. In 
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
such a case where an iniquitous intention is not present—if that speech is made with a good soul and stout-hearted zeal, and cautiously where it is appropriate—it is a virtue. If, however, it slips from the mouth out of levity of mind or a lust for talking, and is done for some unnecessary cause, it is for the most part a venial sin. Unless, perhaps, the word is so bitter that by its own reasoning it brings mortal guilt with it. For then prudent caution is so required that any negligence in speaking, unless it be a sudden impulse, is a mortal crime. And this is especially so, says 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas, in those things which pertain to the honesty of life. As if someone should mark another for heresy or any other crime, 
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
especially of the flesh; which even though they are, as Gregory says, of lesser guilt, <margin>Cajetan's superfluous dispute.</margin> they are of greater infamy. ¶ Therefore, the dispute of <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> seems superfluous as to what the pronoun "this" refers to in the text of St. Thomas, where he says: *This, from the very nature of the words, has the character of a mortal sin.* <note>original: "Hoc ex ipso genere verborum habere rationem peccati mortalis."</note> Namely, whether it refers to the act of saying words against the honesty of another, or to the assertion itself: so that the sense is that as often as someone asserts a mortal sin about another, the assertion itself is a sin.

<summary>This page argues that detraction—backbiting intended to harm someone's reputation—is a grave 'mortal' sin because reputation is more valuable than material wealth. However, it notes that if the harm is unintended or spoken out of a sense of duty or zeal, the severity of the sin is reduced unless the accusation (like heresy) is extremely damaging.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 486 regarding the moral weight of detraction—damaging someone’s reputation behind their back. Soto is specifically weighing the opinions of Great Doctors of the Church like Thomas Aquinas, Cajetan, and Duns Scotus on whether certain types of gossip or the revealing of secrets constitute a mortal sin requiring "restitution" (making amends to the victim).</meta>

**Question 10 of the Fifth Book**

<margin>The meaning of Saint Thomas.</margin>
...is a mortal sin, because that which he asserts about another is mortal. It is clear that this is the primary meaning of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential theologian whose "Summa Theologiae" Soto is commenting upon.</note>; for he does not mean that every time I affirm that another has sinned mortally, I likewise commit a mortal sin. For when that is not uttered with such an intention, he had already said it is not mortal. But he means to say that when the word spoken by me is excessively grave, the utterance itself is mortal by its very nature, even if it is not done with that intention, due to a lack of circumspection <note>original: "incircunspectionem"; a failure to consider the consequences or the weight of one's words.</note>.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The fourth conclusion.** Whoever has unjustly taken away the reputation of another is bound to make restitution to them, in that order and manner which were very broadly explained in Book 4, Question 6. ¶ Many things would have had to be said here if they had not been treated by us in that same book and question. Nevertheless, because the commentators on the divine Thomas are accustomed to noting several things here, it is worthwhile to recall a few.

<margin>Cajetan’s opinion.</margin>
For Lord Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Aquinas.</note> does not presently consider it to be mortal infamy when someone secretly reveals the hidden crime of another to a single prudent man, with whom it will be as well-concealed as if it were told to a wall. This I certainly cannot approve of at all, with all due respect to him.

<margin>Refuting the previous opinion.</margin>
Indeed, I would rather my crime be known to three or four common people than to one very weighty and serious man. For while on one hand a more immediate danger looms that it will be spread abroad by the former than by the latter, on the other hand, I value being in good standing with that one most serious man more than with many others of lesser authority. Therefore, <term>infamy</term> <note>original: "infamia"; the loss of standing or the stain on one's character.</note> is not only to be understood here in the rigor of the law when it is among many people, but also according to the nature of the thing itself. Wherefore, those people act most wickedly and harmfully who—unless there is an urgent cause for correcting a brother—reveal the hidden crime of another to even one man, however prudent he may be. For even if he keeps it hidden in his own breast, the other person nonetheless suffers a great loss of honor and reputation in that man's eyes.

<margin>Another saying of Cajetan in which he agrees with Scotus.</margin>
¶ However, regarding that which the same Cajetan adds—namely, that to recount the sin of another from which they contract no infamy is not "to defame"—we have already similarly confessed that there. For example, if you recount the love affairs of young men, about which they themselves boast.

<margin>Reasoning against Cajetan.</margin>
But as for that in which he subsequently agrees with Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Franciscan philosopher and rival school of thought to the Thomists.</note>—namely, that he who sows rumors not assertively, but relatively, by saying that he "heard" this or that, should not be considered a defamer—I certainly could not agree. Rather, as we have already said there, this is a type of defaming. For those who had not heard it otherwise cannot help but conceive a new sinister opinion of their neighbor. By which reasoning, as we noted there,

<column-break/>

in that way "reputation acquires strength as it goes" <note>original: "fama vires acqrit eũdo"; a famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid describing how rumors grow larger and more powerful as they spread.</note>.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ What we only touched upon there in passing remains to be examined more closely here: namely, whether it is lawful to defame someone in another place where they enjoy a good name, if they have already been defamed in one place.

<margin>Cajetan's opinion.</margin>
For Cajetan, in his sixteenth work, response nine, asserts this.

<margin>Adrian.</margin>
Adrian <note>Pope Hadrian VI (1459–1523), who wrote on moral theology before becoming Pope.</note>, however, in his eleventh "Quotlibet," question one, denies it.

<margin>Cajetan's reasoning.</margin>
And indeed, the reason is that he who is deprived of the right to a reputation suffers no injury from one who reveals the same crime elsewhere, on account of which he lost his reputation. It would be otherwise if another crime, which is hidden, were revealed.

<margin>Adrian's reasoning.</margin>
Adrian’s reasoning, however, is the opposite: namely, that although someone may suffer from infamy in one place, they may have it unimpaired elsewhere; therefore, an injury is done to them while they are stripped of it.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And Adrian’s opinion is confirmed: Although someone may be infected with a public vice, whether pertaining to morals or to nature, no one is allowed to spit that in their face; therefore, it will be even less lawful to disseminate here that for which they were defamed elsewhere.

<margin>First distinction.</margin>
¶ This disagreement, however, is to be reconciled through distinctions. For a person can have contracted the stain of infamy in two ways: namely, either condemned by public authority and judgment, or privately through the neighborhood or the city.

<margin>Second division.</margin>
Again, one can offend in two ways by defaming another: namely, either against <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitatem"; the theological virtue of selfless love for one's neighbor.</note> or against justice.

<margin>Solution of the proposed conclusion.</margin>
With these things established, when someone has been stripped of their honor and reputation in the first way (by public judgment), it is no injustice to defame them everywhere regarding that same crime.

<margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin>
And the reason is: because that person was rightfully fined their reputation by public proclamation as a punishment, and thus the power of making that crime known was granted to everyone. Therefore, he who defames a man in this way is bound to no restitution. Nevertheless, it is a sin against charity; indeed, it could even be a mortal sin to strip bare the shameful things of such condemned men again—especially when they have amended their ways and have recovered a good name elsewhere. For a good reputation is of the greatest help to men toward virtue; when it is lost, they are disheartened. Yet, such a crime of defaming does not obligate one to restitution. And the legal text supports this: "He who [defamed] a guilty person" <note>original: "l. eum qui nocentem. ff. de iniur."; a reference to the Roman Digest, Book 47, Title 10, Law 18, which suggests that revealing the truth about a criminal isn't always a legal injury.</note>, where it is held that he who defamed a guilty person is not to be condemned for that matter as a point of fairness and equity. When, however, someone has lost their reputation in the second way, outside the order of law in one place, he who sprinkles the same infamy on them elsewhere acts not only against charity, but against justice; and he is bound to restitution in whatever way it can be done. Since that loss was not made by right...

<summary>Soto debates the morality of gossip, arguing that revealing a secret sin even to one "wise man" is harmful and that spreading a person's past crimes in a new place where they are respected is an act of injustice unless the crime was a matter of public legal record.</summary>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law ###

->Page 488<-

...a private person. For on account of rumors, even if they are privately known to be true, no one loses their right to their own honor and reputation if they change their place of residence; rather, the crime is considered secret in that new location.
<margin>Regarding the arguments of Cajetan and Adrian.</margin>
Therefore, consider this as a response to the argument of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> and the earlier response of Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), who wrote extensively on moral theology before his papacy.</note>. Regarding the latter point, it is answered that the logic of an "affront" <term>contumelia; a direct insult to someone's face</term> is different from that of "detraction" <term>detractio; speaking ill of someone behind their back</term>. For by way of an affront, it is in no way permitted to reproach another with their crime or a natural defect, even if that defect is natural.
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ After this follows another doubt: whether it is permitted to defame someone who has acquired a reputation in the commonwealth through craftiness and false, feigned virtues—whether those virtues be moral or intellectual.
<margin>Reason for the doubt.</margin>
For it appears to be a duty of virtue to do so, since such impostors lead the commonwealth astray. Regarding this doubt, although
<margin>Adrian.</margin>
Adrian, in the place cited, answers absolutely that it is permitted, one must nevertheless respond with a certain moderation and
<margin>Resolution of the immediate doubt.</margin>
distinction. For when such sycophants pose a danger to the commonwealth through their deceptions, then it is not only permitted but expedient to uncover their crimes and fallacies; for example, if someone falsely claimed to be an excellent doctor or a theologian who would be "pestiferous" <note>original: "pestiferi"; meaning someone whose teachings or practices are as harmful as a plague</note> to the people. In that case, the people must be taught the truth. However, if they are simple women who present a display of holiness in public so that they may live on alms, even if they are infected by some secret crime that is in no way harmful to the commonwealth and they otherwise live innocently, there is no reason why they ought to be defamed.
<margin>A doubt regarding historians.</margin>
¶ Concerning historians, one might rightly doubt whether it is permitted for them to hand down the crimes of men to perpetual memory. To this, one must respond with a "grain of salt" <note>original: "cum grano salis"; a classic idiom suggesting caution and nuance.</note>. First, when they do not recount infamous and shameful sins, but rather wars, homicides, and other things which are not a disgrace to illustrious men, they are not to be condemned. Furthermore, although they may recount some shameful things that are not entirely secret, this should not be turned into a vice for them, but rather attributed to their duty. For they ought to narrate with the best faith those things which pertain to the matter at hand. Nevertheless, when they mark someone with a vice moved by envy or some other depraved affection, they are not free from sin. This is especially true when they burn a mark into a certain lineage or family tree that will remain in perpetual memory.
<margin>Another doubt regarding astrologers.</margin>
¶ Finally, regarding astrologers, who often impose false vices upon men—such as thefts and other shameful acts—there is no doubt they should not be tolerated. For besides the fact that the greatest part of what they claim to know is the smallest part of what they are actually ignorant of (wherefore they employ infinite lies), such great faith should not be attributed to the stars, nor should it be permitted to investigate crimes by that path.

<column-break/>

Indeed, it is stated in the law *item apud Labeonem*, in the section *si quis astrologus* <note>A reference to Roman Law, specifically the Digest, involving the jurist Labeo.</note>, that if an astrologer, upon being consulted, says that someone is a thief who was not, an action for "injury" <term>iniuria; a legal claim for damages to one's person or reputation</term> cannot be brought against him. However, it is added that he can be held by the constitutions—that is, he can be condemned by municipal laws. Therefore, in the Code *concerning sorcerers*, in the law *nemo* <note>A reference to the Codex Justinianus, Book 9, Title 18, which forbade consulting soothsayers.</note>, it is cautioned that no one should consult a "haruspex" <term>aruspicem; a priest who predicted the future from animal entrails</term> or a "mathematician" <term>mathematicum; here meaning an astrologer or fortune-teller</term>. Furthermore, these people should be driven to the "extreme crosses" <note>original: "vltimas cruces"; a metaphor for the severest punishments or capital punishment</note>, not only as impostors but as public defamers.
<margin>A question worth knowing.</margin>
¶ A very famous and necessary question to know is whether it is the same or a greater crime for someone to defame themselves than to defame another. We have indeed treated this in our *Relection on the Reason for Concealing and Uncovering Secrets*, and we placed it earlier in this work in Book 4, Question 2, and again in Question 6, in this very place,
<margin>Cajetan's opinion.</margin>
since it is its proper place. And indeed, Cajetan, here and in his *Summa* under the word "detraction," holds the affirmative view without doubt, bringing forward four propositions.
<margin>Cajetan's first proposition.</margin>
The first is: Whoever defames themselves commits a sin that is "mortal by its nature" <term>genere suo mortale; a serious sin that breaks one's relationship with God</term>, and it is graver than if they had harmed another's reputation.
<margin>Second.</margin>
Second: That sin is committed not only against charity but against justice, because it is against the Church and the commonwealth, to whom
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
our reputation belongs, as Saint Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Doctor of the Church.</note> seems to say in 11, Question 3, canon *non sunt audiendi*.
<margin>Third.</margin>
Third: No one is excused from this kind of sin, even if they do it out of fear of death.
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
Fourth: Whoever defames themselves is bound to make "restitution" <term>restitutio; the act of restoring something lost or stolen, in this case, a reputation</term>.
<margin>Cajetan's foundation.</margin>
The foundation of this opinion is that he judges a man's reputation in the same way as his life: just as we do not have "ownership" <term>dominium; the legal right to use and dispose of property</term> over our lives, so we do not have it over our reputation.
¶ But although I am not unaware that this opinion is commonly thought to be true, its foundation still always lacks a demonstration, because it is nowhere proved. For even if we are admonished by the "Wise Man" <note>A traditional reference to King Solomon or the author of the Book of Ecclesiastes/Proverbs.</note> to have care for a good name, it by no means follows from this that we are not the owners of our own reputation.
<margin>Cajetan's foundation is false.</margin>
For we are also bound to have some care for external goods, yet we nonetheless enjoy ownership over them. Therefore, so that we may satisfy the present dispute with a path and order, we judge the contrary foundation to be true: namely, that every person has ownership of their own reputation. I believe I have demonstrated this in the preceding Question 2, as far as moral matter allows. From this foundation, we later elicited in Question 6 that it is in the judgment of any private person to waive the restitution of their own reputation.
<margin>The author's first assertion.</margin>
Therefore, with these points shown there and assumed here, let the first assertion for the present be this: For a man to defame himself without cause is a sin; however, it is neither against justice nor is it mortal by its nature.

<summary>Soto argues that while historians can report famous crimes and the state can punish lying astrologers, individuals generally "own" their own reputations. He disagrees with Cajetan, asserting that while defaming oneself is a sin, it is not a mortal sin of injustice.</summary>
