<meta>This page continues Dominic de Soto’s investigation into the ethics of reputation (fama). On the previous page, he discussed whether it is a sin to reveal the secret sins of others. Now, he turns the lens inward: is it a sin for a person to damage their own reputation? He weighs the requirements of "charity" (love for oneself) against "justice" (obligations to the community), ultimately arguing that while we should value our name, we have the right to "spend" our reputation to avoid greater evils like physical torture.</meta>

### Book Five, Question Ten ###

->Page 489<-

<margin>Proof of the previous assertion.</margin>
...such a thing. For it is clear that this is a sin, because it goes against charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the theological virtue of love for God and oneself.</note>. Indeed, we are bound to love ourselves and our own goods: and reputation is a good belonging to us. This is why we are commanded by the Wise Man <note>A traditional reference to Solomon; here referring to Proverbs 22:1 or Ecclesiasticus 41:12: "A good name is more desirable than great riches."</note> to have a care for a good name, because it is more precious than much wealth. Therefore, he who defames himself without cause is a prodigal <term>prodigal; a person who wastefully spends their resources</term> of his own reputation, and such wastefulness is indeed a sin. 

However, it is clear that this is not a sin against justice. For it would only be so if we were not the masters of our own reputation; some argue that just as our life belongs to the commonwealth, so does our reputation, and by wasting it we do the community an injury. But in the place cited, we have shown at length that this is false, and we have dissolved the contrary arguments. We conclude that we have the same ownership <term>dominium; legal right or mastery</term> over our honor and reputation as we do over our external goods. Consequently, a person who is wasteful with his own reputation inflicts an injury on no one; nor is he bound to any restitution, since no one is bound to make restitution to himself. 

From this it follows again that, in its general nature, this is not a mortal sin <note>A "mortal sin" is considered a grave offense that severs the soul's relationship with God, as opposed to a minor "venial" sin.</note>. Thus we have said it is not against justice, but rather "outside" the bounds of charity, because we are not bound by the precept of charity to love these goods so intensely that neglecting them would constitute a mortal fault. 

Indeed, as we were saying in that other place among other points, Christ our Redeemer did not instruct us to place such a high value on honors and reputation—namely, seeking the "first seats at the table" and the splendor of honors. Rather, we are warned to endure infamy patiently, as 
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> excellently teaches in his ninth homily on Ezekiel. And 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Paul thought it a small thing to be judged by any human court <note>original: "ab humano die"; a Latinism for "human judgment day," referring to 1 Corinthians 4:3.</note>. And 
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
Ambrose—if his history is true—introduced women into his house so that he might use that infamy to avoid being made a bishop. And 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine and 
<margin>Anselm.</margin>
Anselm made their own sins known through their writings. And 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note>, in the fourth article of the present question, says in the first response that it is within anyone's discretion to suffer the loss of their own reputation. And 
<margin>Adrian.</margin>
Adrian confirmed this more broadly in the fourth question on the restitution of reputation and in his eleventh Quodlibet. These things would certainly not be true unless we held ownership over our reputation in a different way than we do over our lives. 

Abundant discussion of this can be found in the places cited. However, I would say that it is not a mortal sin in its general nature. For a man who, under oath, falsely charged himself with a crime would be guilty of perjury. And a prelate <note>A high-ranking church official like a bishop.</note> whose reputation is bound up with the governance of his subjects would act against justice by defaming himself—just as a man with a family to feed or who sees the poor suffering greatly would sin if he threw his goods into the river. Furthermore, someone who charged themselves with heresy or another most heinous crime, even without an oath, could sin mortally on account of the remarkable disgrace involved. But in truth, outside of such cases, those lies would be nothing more than "officious lies" <note>An "officious" or "helpful" lie is one told for a good purpose, traditionally considered a minor sin.</note>. Therefore, there is no reason to judge that someone who defames himself commits a more serious sin—indeed, not even as serious a sin—as one who defames another, since the latter is against justice while the former is not at all.

<column-break/>

And as for Augustine, we have already responded in that place that he only intends for our reputation to belong to the commonwealth in the same way our external goods do: namely, that when the community is in need, we are bound to serve it through our good name, just as we are bound to preserve our money for its use. But just as we are not bound to save money for every future necessity of the commonwealth, neither are we bound to save our reputation. 

Regarding his other saying in *The City of God* (Book 1, Chapter 20)—namely, that by the commandment "Thou shalt not bear false witness," we are also commanded not to defame ourselves—we respond that this is true regarding the force of charity, but not regarding the force of justice. For he who obscures his own name acts "outside" the charity by which he ought to love himself; yet he does not act "against" justice, as does the man who gnaws away at another’s name. And that phrase, "Have a care for a good name," we have said is an admonition to procure a good name through the cultivation of virtues.

<margin>Second assertion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, from these points, to move toward our present subject, let us gather this second assertion: When someone is interrogated in a legal proceeding contrary to the law regarding his own most secret crime, although he is not legally bound to answer, nevertheless, if he reveals it—thereby defaming himself—to escape the pressure of the rack <term>eculeus; a wooden torture frame or "horse" used to stretch the body</term>, not only is it not a sin for him, but it can even be a duty of virtue. 

This conclusion is an appendix to the previous ones. 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
For since everyone is the master of his own reputation, he may incur its loss for a cause, just as he may with other temporal goods. Therefore, just as it is lawful for a wretched man in such a case to redeem his liberation from those torments with his own money, so too may he do so by the confession of his crime, through which he suffers the loss of his reputation. 

<margin>Another reason for the same.</margin>
Secondly, this is proven thus: A pile of coins can be so great that it equals the value of a common man's reputation, just as a weight of silver can be so great that it outweighs gold—which surely no one of sound mind can deny. Since, therefore, it is permitted for anyone in that case to escape such torture by the loss of a large sum of money, it follows that he may also do so by the loss of his reputation. 

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Thirdly, the same thing is argued: If someone were subjected to the rack contrary to the law to reveal another's crime which he had received under the seal of secrecy—we are not speaking of the seal of the sacrament of confession, for which a priest is bound to endure the most cruel death before revealing it, but of other secular secrets—he would by no means be bound to endure such grave torments before he disclosed it. This is especially true if it were not a secret of the King or the commonwealth, or one extorted from another by injury, upon the revelation of which a life might depend. Therefore, by a stronger logic <note>original: "a fortiori"</note>, no one is bound to endure such sharp torture to conceal his own private crime. 

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ However, if he were interrogated regarding a *false* crime, there is a greater doubt as to whether it would be a mortal sin for him to charge himself with it without an oath...

<sig>Hh 5</sig>
<meta>Catchword: ...to charge (nere:)</meta>

# Book Five, Question Ten #

->Page 490<-

<header>F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law</header>

...to persist: for no one doubts that perjury <term>periurium; the act of swearing a false oath</term> is a mortal sin. Nor indeed is it doubted that even without an oath, lying would be a venial <term>venial; a "pardonable" or minor sin that does not fully sever one's relationship with God</term> sin; and it is so certain that one should rather succumb to death than admit to it <note>Soto is following the strict Augustinian view that one may never tell a lie, even to save a life.</note>. But the doubt is whether that lie, told without an oath, would be "pernicious" <note>original: *perniciosum*; meaning a lie told with the intent to harm or one that causes grave damage</note>, and consequently a mortal sin. And truly, if what has been said is true, I do not see why it would be pernicious, nor why it would require restitution: since that self-defamer, if he is a private person, does no injury to anyone by lying; since he takes away the reputation of himself alone. For we are speaking of that private man whose crime which he would charge against himself would not be heresy, or another crime of the most serious enormity or foulness. Otherwise, on account of the dignity of the person, or the enormity of the disgrace, it would be a mortal sin.

<margin>Argument against the aforesaid.</margin>
¶ An argument exists, however, against this opinion: when from such a confession of a crime a danger of death would follow by which that defendant would be condemned. For then it seems not to be permitted to lie, because we are bound to preserve life above all other things.

<margin>The first solution.</margin>
To this, however, it is responded in several ways. First, for up to this point we have said nothing about the danger to life, but only about the loss of reputation. Next, that confession so extorted is not one to which faith should be given, so that on account of it the defendant is sentenced to death: indeed, nor should it properly be taken as a cause for disgrace <note>original: *infamia*; a legal status of dishonor</note>: as is clear in the legal codes <note>original reference: 15. q. 6. can. si quandoq; from the Decretum of Gratian</note>.

<margin>The second.</margin>
Then, even if the danger of death is imminent, a man is not bound to preserve his life with such great torture, but can permit a shorter death for himself, so that he may escape one so bitter.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that where reason demands denouncing someone either fraternally or legally, it is not "disgrace" to reveal the hidden crime of a delinquent.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, however, it is responded that that gloss <note>A 'gloss' is a traditional scholarly commentary on a legal or biblical text.</note> does not brand the whole human race with the mark of this vice in the degree of a mortal sin. For first it adds "almost," and then it is understood as trivial murmurings, which are accustomed to spread among the common people without being mortal: which 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine (cited in the third argument) considers smaller sins. 
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
Jerome, in his letter to Celantia, noted the reason for the universality of this disease: where he says, "There are very few who renounce this vice; and rarely will you find those who wish to present their own life as blameworthy so that they do not willingly blame another's. And so great a lust for this evil has invaded the minds of men, that even those who have withdrawn far from other vices nevertheless fall into this one, as if into the devil's final snare."

### ARTICLE III.

->*Whether detraction is more serious than all sins committed against one's neighbor.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' decorated with foliage patterns.</image-desc>It is asked in the third place concerning the gravity of detraction <term>detractio; the sin of "backbiting" or revealing a person's secret faults to damage their reputation</term>: since it seems to be the greatest of all crimes committed against one's neighbor. 
<margin>First argument.</margin>
For a gloss says upon that Psalm, "In return for my love, they slandered me": those who detract from Christ in his members <note>The "members of Christ" refers to fellow Christians; the argument is that slandering a Christian is an attack on Christ himself.</note> do more harm, because they kill the souls of those who will believe the slander, than those who killed his flesh which was soon to rise again. From which it seems to follow that detraction is as much more serious than homicide as the life of the soul surpasses that of the body: since therefore homicide is more serious than all other things by which a neighbor is offended, it follows that detraction is simply the most serious of all. 

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second. Detraction seems to be more serious than insult <note>original: *contumelia*; an insult spoken directly to someone's face</note>, because a man repels an insult more easily than a hidden detraction which he does not know about. Moreover, insult is more serious than adultery: for through adultery two are joined in one flesh for sinning; but the insulting person separates those who were joined in love: insofar as he offers an occasion to others to hate the one whom he affects with insults. Therefore, detraction is worse than adultery: which nevertheless holds great weight among the sins by which a neighbor is harmed. 

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: insult arises 
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
from anger, as we brought forth from Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> in the preceding article; but detraction arises from envy, as the same Saint says in the same place in Book 31 of the *Moralia*. But envy is a more serious sin than anger: therefore detraction is also more serious than insult. 

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourth. A sin is more serious by as much as it induces a more harmful effect: but detraction induces the most pestilential effect among all sins: namely, the blinding of the mind, from which root all things sprout. 
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
For Gregory says (Question 11, Case 3): "What else do detractors do but blow into the dust, and stir up the earth into their own eyes? And the more detraction they blow out, the less they see from there." Therefore, detraction is the most serious among those things committed against one's neighbor. 

¶ To the contrary is the fact that it is more wicked to sin by deed than by word: but homicide and adultery are sins in deed; whereas in detraction one sins within words.

<meta>This page continues Dominic de Soto’s exploration of "detraction" (slander or backbiting). On the previous page, he discussed the moral weight of lying about oneself. # Book Five, Question Ten #

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Furthermore, this crime <note>Referring to "detraction" or slander</note> can rightly be suspected of being the most serious of all, so multi-faceted and plague-like is it to the commonwealth. Nevertheless, the question is answered with three conclusions. **First:** Among all sins that mortals commit against one another, homicide <note>original: *homicidium*</note> is the worst. We always exclude here those sins which have God as their object, such as infidelity, despair, hatred of God, blasphemy, perjury, and similar acts.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
The conclusion is proven. The primary and formal reason <term>formal reason; the defining characteristic that gives an act its specific moral nature</term>, as they say, why any sin committed against a neighbor is considered wicked is based on the harm inflicted. For the worse the harm, the more it is opposed to charity. Harm is considered worse in proportion to the greatness of the "good" that it takes away. Now, the greatest good that one can take from another is physical life. Therefore, homicide is the worst. This final premise is proven: human "goods" exist in a three-fold hierarchy. First is the good of the soul; next to it is the good of the body; and third is that which consists of external things. Although the good of the soul is the most excellent of all, no one can take it from another against their will, though they may provide the occasion for it <note>Soto means that while you can tempt someone to sin, you cannot force their soul to lose God's grace; only the person's own consent can do that</note>. For the good of the soul is the grace by which it lives, which is taken away only by consent to mortal sin, and no one can force another into such consent. Therefore, although leading another into sin carries a greater objective gravity than if you killed them, because such induction is not coercion, you do not sin as enormously as if you killed them with a temporal death. This is the reason we used in Book 4, Question 6 against those who thought it was graver to "kill" a neighbor's soul by occasioning sin than to remove the soul from the body. There remain, therefore, two kinds of goods that one can take from another against their will by force or fraud. Of these, the good of the body—namely life—is more excellent than external goods, because life is the foundation of all else. It follows, then, that the crime of homicide is, by its very nature, the most atrocious of all those committed against a neighbor.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
**Second conclusion:** Detraction <note>original: *detractio*; slandering someone behind their back</note>, according to its kind, is a greater sin than theft, but less than homicide and adultery.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This is clear from what has been said: since reputation <note>original: *fama*</note> is a more excellent good than external substance <note>meaning property or money</note>; but it is lower than life, which is taken by homicide, and lower than that which is harmed in future

<sig>Q</sig>

<column-break/>

offspring through adultery. For, generally speaking, a son born of an uncertain parent cannot be properly raised. From this, it follows—by the same reasoning we established in Question 3 against Marcus de Magistris—that simple fornication is a graver fault than theft. Secondly, it follows that insult <term>contumelia; an external, face-to-face dishonoring of someone</term> is even worse than theft, for it is a form of detraction made more bitter by violence and contempt.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion:** Notwithstanding these things which belong to these acts by their very nature, the gravity of a sin can be accidentally increased or diminished by other factors. For he who deliberately perpetrates an evil sins more gravely than one who admits to it out of weakness or ignorance. By this reasoning, sins contained within words are considered lighter (all else being equal) because they are "spit out" by the speed of the tongue or fall lightly from the mouth. For this reason, we asserted a little earlier that sins consisting of deeds are graver than verbal ones. This is understood when you compare the nature of the word with the nature of the deed. For on the part of the "object" <note>the thing being acted upon</note>, it was specifically asserted in the second conclusion that detraction (by which reputation is clouded) is graver than theft (by which external goods are snatched). These things must always be understood "in species" <term>in species; referring to the general category or type of sin</term>; for in an individual case, a theft can be worse than detraction, and detraction can be worse than homicide—for instance, if one slanders God or His faith, which pertains to blasphemy.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The first argument is answered by this last point. For those who slandered Christ by murmuring against His faith, and thus prevented those who were going to believe from receiving it, were blasphemers against His divinity. And thus, they sinned in some measure more enormously than those who deprived His flesh of life for a time. For He assumed that life for the sake of confirming the faith.

<margin>To the second argument. Solution of Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ In solving the second argument, Saint Thomas defines insult <note>original: *contumelia*</note> as being worse than detraction; although it can be more easily repelled, it involves greater contempt and violence, just as robbery <note>original: *rapina*</note> is worse than theft <note>original: *furtum*</note>.

<margin>The solution of some.</margin>
¶ Against this, however, someone might be tempted to argue: "Reputation is a more excellent good than honor; therefore detraction is worse than insult because it is more harmful." You may find those who, not knowing how to resolve this argument according to the mind of Thomas, deny that reputation is a more excellent good than honor. Indeed, when they hear Thomas asserting that insult is worse, they infer that honor pre-exists reputation.

<margin>Rejection of the previous solution.</margin>
Yet, in reality, the truth stands to the contrary. For the proper and formal objects of insult and detraction, as we said above, are not honor and reputation; rather, they involve the nature of the "involuntary" <note>meaning how much the victim's will is violated</note>. And from this, it is gathered that insult is...

He argues that detraction is generally worse than theft because a person's reputation is more valuable than their physical property.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dominic de Soto’s scholastic analysis of "detraction" (slander or backbiting). Having established that homicide is the greatest sin against a neighbor because it takes away life, he now compares the gravity of damaging someone's reputation (*fama*) versus insulting them to their face (*contumelia*).</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice & Right #

...more bitter: namely, because through it one suffers an involuntary act by force, whereas through detraction <note>original: *detractionem*; the act of speaking ill of someone behind their back</note> one suffers only through ignorance. However, this decision is in no way inconsistent with the fact that reputation is a more cumulative and illustrious good than honor. For a good estimation of one's probity <note>integrity or moral uprightness</note> held by the people is more precious than honor—that is, the reverence which is often shown deceitfully and craftily, and not always because of virtue, but sometimes because of other minor goods. For this reason, the Wise Man <note>Refers to Solomon, traditional author of the Wisdom books</note> ascribed three preeminent qualities not to honor, but to a good name (by which "reputation" is understood). First, regarding its price: that a good name is better than many riches (Proverbs 22). Second, regarding its sweetness and wide reach: that it is more precious than ointments which delight with their scent (Ecclesiastes 7). And third, regarding its duration in time: that it lasts longer than a thousand precious and great treasures (Ecclesiastes 41).

<margin>Instruction.</margin>
¶ But this must also be noted again: although because of the contempt involved, contumely <note>original: *contumelia*; a public or face-to-face insult</note> is, by its nature and object, worse than detraction, nevertheless the practice of detraction teems with a thousand troubles and plagues. 

<margin>The harms of detraction</margin>
First, it obscures the glory of virtues, which is a representation of the celestial. Next, it is more easily committed and infects more people than contumely. For since it happens in secret, it creeps in with impunity—everywhere and whenever an occasion for speaking arises—whereas contumely is not so much in use because of fear. Furthermore, detractors fight from ambush, and for that reason, they are most difficult to guard against. This is especially true when they are double-tongued and double-faced: namely, those who soothe you to your face and enchant your ears, but secretly bite you behind your back. No kind of betrayal can be more pestilential in a commonwealth than this. For since no one guards against such men, but all securely lay open their hearts to them, they suck the blood of some only to vomit it into the ears of others. Hence Ecclesiasticus 28: "The whisperer and the double-tongued shall be cursed." 

¶ Added to this is that detractors do not only destroy their own souls, but they also bring the same spiritual death to all those among whom they sow their taunts; insofar as they generate hatred toward the one they slander, they subsequently violate and darken the public peace and friendship, which is the bond by which the commonwealth shines most brilliantly. Moreover, detractors are uniquely called "homicides" <note>murderers</note>, as I believe Clement says in a certain epistle (referred to regarding penance, distinction 1, canon *homicidium*), because they strive to strip and bare the soul of the one

<column-break/>

whose reputation they blacken of the virtues by which he spiritually lives. And perhaps the word in 1 John 3 refers to the same thing: "He who hates his brother is a murderer." 

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, it is granted that contumely, as was said in the previous article, is born of anger: because one seized by anger—as Aristotle is the author in Book 2 of the *Rhetoric*—desires manifest revenge, 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
which he more easily achieves through contumely. And therefore detraction, because it does not tend toward such manifest revenge, is not the daughter of anger, but of envy. For the detractor, because he wastes away with malice, strives to defile the brightness of others' virtues. It does not follow, however, that if envy is worse than anger, its daughter <note>In scholastic theology, "daughters" of a vice are the specific sins that flow from a root capital vice</note> must be worse than the daughter of anger. For these lineages of vices are judged by the reason of their "turning toward" the same end: namely, that to which both the daughter and the mother are ordered. But the malignancy and gravity are considered on the part of the "turning away" <term>aversion; the act of turning away from God or charity</term>. And because it is a more distant turning away from charity to inflict an involuntary harm through force than through fraud, contumely is worse. 

¶ Nonetheless, detraction is also defiled by this stain among others: that it is born of envy, which is the most sordid vice, insofar as it is diametrically opposed to charity. For charity, as 

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Paul says, is not envious, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, and does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth—all the opposites of which are contained in envy. For envy has this most enormous quality among all vices, and the most repugnant to the nature of things: that it rejoices over evil (which is to be abhorred) but grieves over good—and especially over the virtues of others, which are most of all to be venerated with love. This is a diabolical disposition. Therefore, there is no one who can avoid envy, since all are bound to strive for the heights of virtue; and the higher anyone is raised, the greater the envy he excites in the malicious. Let detractors, therefore, recognize themselves as the offspring of this hydra. 

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fourth argument, it is likewise granted that it is the nature of detraction to blind the mind. For since everyone, as the Wise Man says in Proverbs 15, rejoices in the judgment of his own mouth, he who proceeds to detract begins to love his own words, to feel ill toward the good, and subsequently to hold the upright in hatred; by this path, the mind is blinded. Yet, since this same effect is also common to other vices, such as gluttony, lust, and others, it is not thereby proven that detraction is the worst of all.

<summary>Soto compares detraction (slander) and contumely (insult), concluding that while insult is a "harder" sin because of its violent nature, detraction is more insidious and "diabolical" because it springs from envy and destroys social trust in secret.</summary>

### ARTICLE IV.

#### Whether one who hears and tolerates a detractor commits a mortal sin.

Due to the destructive nature of detraction <note>original: *detractionis*; the act of revealing a neighbor's hidden faults to damage their reputation</note>, it remains at last to be asked whether those who listen to detractors commit a mortal sin <note>a grave sin that severs one's relationship with God</note> unless they silence their mouths.
<margin>First argument.</margin>
An argument is made to the contrary: No one is bound more to another than to himself. However, it is considered praise-worthy for anyone to endure their own detractors, according to the words of 
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> cited above in his 9th homily on Ezekiel: "Just as we should not, by our own effort, incite the tongues of detractors, so we should endure them with equanimity when they are incited by their own malice, so that our merit may increase." Therefore, it is not a sin 
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
not to oppose the detractors of others. ¶ Secondly, in Ecclesiasticus 4 <note>also known as the Wisdom of Sirach</note>, we are commanded not to contradict the word of truth in any way. It often happens that the one who detracts does not depart from the truth; therefore, in such cases, it is not a virtue to contradict him.
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, no one should prohibit that which results in the benefit of others. Detraction frequently turns out to the advantage of those being slandered. As Pope Pius says in the Decretals (6. q. 1. can. *Oues*): "Sometimes," he says, "detraction rouses one toward the good, so that those whom domestic flattery or the favor of others had raised up high, detraction 
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
may humble." Therefore, it is not a duty to repress detractors. ¶ To the contrary is Jerome, where he says: "Take care that you do not have 'itching' tongues or ears, so as to either detract others or listen to others detracting."

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
In response to the question, three conclusions are given. First: Whoever either induces another to detract, or delights in the detraction out of hatred, sins no less than the detractor; indeed, sometimes
<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
somewhat more. The conclusion is proven from Romans 1: "They are worthy of death, not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those doing them." For such consent happens in two ways. In one way, directly: when someone either induces another to sin or is pleased by it. Truly, whoever consents in this way becomes entirely a participant in the crime. Indeed, if he induces it, he sins more severely, as there is more fault in the mover than in the moved. Furthermore, if he rejoices, he may perhaps sin even more severely if he possesses a greater store of hatred than is in the detractor. And 
<margin>Bernard.</margin>
concerning these people, we understand the word of Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux</note> near the end 

<column-break/>

of his second book *On Consideration*: "To detract or to listen to a detractor—which of these is more damnable, I could not easily say." In the second way, someone is said to consent indirectly: namely, because he does not resist. This happens in two ways. For he who does not resist is either bound to resist by his own specific duty and public office, or he is a private person upon whom it does not fall as a matter of office.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let the second conclusion be this: For a private person not to repel the detraction of others is a sin, yet much less than that of the detractor; this is, indeed, most often a venial sin <note>a lesser sin that does not fully break the bond with God</note>. ¶ Third conclusion:
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Sometimes, failing to resist a detractor can be a mortal sin. First, in a public person—for instance, in one who has authority over the detractor. Second, because of a danger that the listener sees looming from the detraction. And third, if someone shrinks from opposing the detractor solely out of human fear. These are the conclusions of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>. And both are confirmed by a single reason. For it has already
<margin>Both conclusions are supported.</margin>
been shown several times above that for someone to be the indirect cause of any evil, it is not enough that they *could* avoid it, but it is further required that they are *bound* to do so. Now, a person is bound either out of justice or merely out of charity <note>love for neighbor</note>. A private person is not bound by the rigor of justice to prevent the neighbor's evil, but only out of charity if they can do so without personal detriment. Therefore, it is not inherently contrary to charity to fail to deliver a neighbor from such damage to their reputation; yet, one is hardly excused from a venial sin, as asserted in the second conclusion. For wherever detraction arises, one can easily meet the detractor with politeness and gentleness; thus, if one does not do so, they are considered to entirely neglect their neighbor’s reputation. However, if that detractor were so puffed up and intractable that danger loomed from him, the listener would be excused even from venial sin. But this happens very rarely. Add to this that someone might be excused by shame alone—as when the one detracting is very illustrious, and the listener is his servant or another lowly person who does not dare to mutter a word. However, a Prelate <note>an official with authority, like a bishop or superior</note> is bound primarily by justice, and therefore he is bound, far beyond any fear or shame, to rebuke his subordinates for detraction if it is of any significance; the omission of which is, for that reason, a mortal sin. I say a Prelate *of the detractors*; for the Prelate of those *being slandered* is not bound by such justice to protect them, because the Prelate's duty is to ensure his subjects do not sin. Although he is also bound, in a certain way, by the bond of charity.

to protect the honor of subjects. Furthermore, when a private person sees that a danger of death or a disturbance of the state is imminent due to detraction <note>original: *detractione*; the act of revealing a neighbor's hidden faults to damage their reputation</note>, they are bound to intervene, even at some personal disadvantage. However, human fear would only rise to the level of a mortal sin when someone prefers the loss of temporal goods over charity. But one is not to be judged as committing a sin whenever they cease to prevent harm to a neighbor out of human fear—as stated in the second conclusion—but rather when their resistance would be absolutely necessary by commandment, such as if faith or religion were being slandered.

<margin>A most beneficial lesson</margin>
¶ From these points, let us finally gather this most beneficial lesson: that we may understand how greatly necessary it is for the peace and health of the state, and especially for the Christian family, to confront detractors everywhere. This, as I was saying, is something everyone can easily accomplish according to their own rank. And when one cannot do so, it will be the duty of a prudent person to leave the conversation, so that by that means he may cover the detractor 

<margin>Jerome</margin>
with shame. Hence Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, a 4th-century scholar and Church Father</note>, in his 14th epistle to Celantia, excellently rebukes both those who detract and, no less, those who do not oppose them, according to that verse of the Psalm: "Whosoever secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued" <note>original: *Detrahentem secretò proximo suo, hunc persequebar*; Psalm 101:5 (Vulgate 100:5)</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ To the first argument, therefore, the response is that the insults <note>original: *maledicta*</note> which are hurled in the presence of the one being insulted are not "detractions" but "affronts" <note>original: *contumeliæ*; direct insults to the face, as opposed to gossip behind the back</note>; and therefore it pertains to the virtue of humility to bear them. However, when they crawl into other ears, they take on the nature of detraction. And then, as St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says (whom we have often cited above), it is within a person's own judgment to suffer the loss of their own reputation, unless it results in danger to others. But while someone gnaws at the reputation of an absent person in our presence, it is not within our discretion to spare the slanderer, because we are not the masters of another person’s reputation. Therefore, it is counted as a vice in us if we do not resist when we easily can. For if in Deuteronomy 22 it was commanded that no one should neglect to lift up a neighbor's fallen donkey, it is a much more serious matter not to protect a neighbor’s reputation when it is in peril.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, the response is that even if the detractor speaks the truth, he is not to be contradicted in the facts, but his words must nevertheless be repressed so that he does not aggravate the wounds of another; or at least, by a furrowed brow, it should be shown to him that his speech displeases us. For as we read in Proverbs 25: "The north wind dissipates the rain, and a sad face dissipates a 

<column-break/>

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
detracting tongue." ¶ To the third, finally, it is responded that the utility and benefit which comes from detraction does not proceed from the intention of the detractor, but from the grace of God who softens the heart of the other person. Therefore, the detractor must be opposed just like robbers and thieves, even though from such inconveniences, the merit of patience often increases for those who have suffered them.

# Book Five: Question XI.

...than it is in whispering. ¶ On the contrary, however, is that which is written in Ecclesiasticus 5: "A very bad mark is upon the double-tongued; but for the whisperer there is hatred, and enmity, and insult." <note>original: "Denotatio pessima super bilinguem: susurratori autē odium, & inimicitia, & contumelia"; Ecclesiasticus 5:17 in the Vulgate.</note> In this passage, worse effects are attributed to whispering than to detraction.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The question is answered with two conclusions. First: although whispering <term>susurratio; the act of spreading rumors specifically to destroy a friendship</term> agrees with detraction in both its form and its matter, it differs in its end <note>original: *fine*; the goal or purpose of the act</note>. For both the whisperer and the detractor speak evil against their neighbor, and do so secretly and in their absence; for this reason, both differ from insult <note>original: *contumelia*; which is done to someone's face</note>. And by this reasoning, both words are sometimes used interchangeably by the Doctors of the Church. Hence, regarding that passage of Ecclesiasticus 5, "You shall not be called a whisperer," the Gloss <margin>Gloss.</margin> <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible</note> says, "that is, a detractor." Nevertheless, if you consult the etymology of the words, "detraction" is the same, as we said above, as the withdrawal and diminishing of reputation. "Whispering," however, only denotes secret, and thus vicious, speech. And for that reason, perhaps by an accommodation of common usage, it signifies that back-biting by which one strives not so much to detract from a reputation, but to dissolve friendships: and therefore it differs in its end. Wherefore, even if both the whisperer and the detractor speak evil in general about another, yet specifically, the detractor scatters those things which are truly evils of fault—namely, those by which a reputation is stained. The whisperer, however, considers it enough to bring forth those things which can tear the listener's mind away from the friendship of another, even if the thing spoken is actually good, provided it either appears evil or is displeasing to the listener. For instance, if one whispers to a spendthrift about his friend that he is stingy with money; or murmurs to a cheerful and relaxed person that his friend is too composed and modest.

<margin>Proof of the above conclusion.</margin> This distinction is first evident from the gloss on that passage in Romans 1: "whisperers, detractors," which says that whisperers sow discord among friends, while detractors deny or diminish the good qualities of others. And Proverbs 26: "When the whisperer is removed, quarrels cease." And Ecclesiasticus 28: "A sinful man (and the discourse here is about the whisperer and the double-tongued) will trouble friends and bring enmity into the midst of those at peace." Although we also attributed this effect to the detractor above, and Jerome <margin>A small doubt.</margin> attributed the same to him in his letter to Celantia. But if you ask us whether—since there are many types of friendship according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in Book 9 of the *Ethics*—namely, one founded on the honorable good,

<column-break/>

and another on the useful, and another on the pleasant—there are also diverse species of whispering. <margin>Solution.</margin> The answer is negative. For the whisperer only strives to break apart friendships in general. However, while he strives to reach another target through that path, then his whispering can contract diverse stains of malice. For example, if someone whispers against another into the ears of a prince in order to obtain his honor, he is ambitious or greedy; and if he whispers about a husband to a wife, so that once friendship is removed between them, he may enjoy her embrace, he will be an adulterer. But these matters are outside the present scope. <margin>Final conclusion.</margin> The second conclusion: Whispering, by its very nature, is a more serious sin than detraction, and even than insult. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> For indeed, as was said above, we determine the gravity of a sin by the fact that it inflicts greater harm; and the harm is judged greater where the good taken away is more precious. But friendship is a more precious good than reputation and honor; therefore, whispering—the disturber of peace—is worse than detraction and insult. This last premise is proved both by the authority of Ecclesiasticus 6: "Nothing can be compared to a faithful friend," and by reason. For good reputation and honor are useful for this: that one may win the friendship of many; and thus, by the logical rule <note>original: *regulam posterioristicam*; referring to Aristotle's *Posterior Analytics*, where the end is greater than the means</note>, friendship is more excellent than <unclear>reputation</unclear>. Add that after the virtues, for the sake of attaining happiness, as Aristotle says <margin>Aristotle.</margin> in Book 8 of the *Ethics*, nothing is more helpful than an abundance of friends. Truly, since not only are all things common among friends, but all are to some extent <unclear>one person</unclear> <note>referring to the classical idea that a friend is "another self"</note>. Wherefore, to him who has an abundance of legitimate friends, nothing can be lacking in life.

<margin>Objection.</margin> But it is still argued to the contrary. A detractor, as was said above, also dissolves friendships just as a whisperer does; therefore, they do not differ in their goal. <margin>Solution.</margin> The response is that although friendships are sometimes overturned through detraction, that is not the goal of the detractor, but only to defile the reputation, which then paves the way to enmities. The immediate goal of the whisperer, however, is to stir up those same enmities, and therefore it is more foul. ¶ Regarding this conclusion, two smaller doubts present themselves. The first is about this comparison in which friendship is preferred to reputation and honor. <margin>First doubt.</margin> For reputation appears more precious from the fact that it is more widely extended: for there are more people to whom a studious man is known than those to whom he is a friend. Also, because it is closer to virtue. For he who excels in morals immediately comes into the notice of others, even if not so easily into...

<summary>De Soto distinguishes "whispering" (tale-bearing) from "detraction" (slander), arguing that while both involve secret speech against others, whispering is a graver sin because it directly targets friendship—a more valuable social and moral good than mere reputation.</summary>

...ly into friendship: because not all are lovers of virtue. ¶ To this, it is first answered that neither reputation, nor honor, nor even friendship are virtues; and thus they are not even the spiritual goods in which true happiness consists. However, they are related to virtue. Whence <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle says in the 8th book of the *Ethics*: "Friendship is not a virtue, but is close to virtue." <note>original: "Amicitia non est virtus, sed virtuti proxima"</note> There, he speaks of that friendship which truly enjoys this name—namely, that which proceeds from an honest good, which is to say, from virtue. For friendship entered into for the sake of utility or pleasure is only friendship in a qualified sense <term>secundum quid; in a limited or relative way rather than absolutely</term>, just as the goods themselves upon which it rests are limited. And because friendship is not born from virtue except through the knowledge of it (in which reputation consists), it follows that friendship is more excellent than reputation, as its end or goal. For the knowledge of virtue would be in vain unless it enticed men to the love of the studious person. And therefore, in heavenly blessedness, that mutual knowledge of the blessed pertains to their happiness because it glues them all together with the same love.

<margin>
Friendship is superior to reputation.
</margin>
¶ Whence, regarding the first argument to the contrary, it is denied that reputation extends more broadly than friendship. For as many as have knowledge of a man's integrity and the excellence of his virtues love him, unless they themselves are of corrupt character. <margin>To the argument made.</margin> And likewise, regarding the second argument, it is denied that reputation is closer to virtue than friendship. Indeed, friendship is more closely related to it; <margin>Regarding reputation.</margin> wherefore, just as virtue depends not at all on fortune, so having friends is born from virtue rather than from the recklessness of fortune.

<margin>
Final doubt.
</margin>
¶ The second minor doubt concerns the gravity of the sin of whispering <term>susurratio; specifically, gossip intended to break up a friendship</term>. <margin>Response.</margin> To this, it is easily answered that although it is a mortal crime in its genus <note>meaning it is inherently a serious sin</note> because of the gravity of the harm, it can nevertheless be a venial sin <note>a lesser, pardonable sin</note> due to the lightness of the matter. As to whether it can ever happen without any fault: <margin>A point of difficulty.</margin> It is first answered that whispering to break up a ruinous friendship—provided it is done without defamation—is a virtue, even if some of a person's natural defects are mentioned. For instance, if to move a man away from a mistress <note>original: "amica"</note> you say she is deformed and dull, etc. But truly, to dissociate friends whose friendship is founded on virtue and honesty can never be without sin, and indeed a mortal one if you strive to make enemies out of friends. For if you only strive to remove constant familiarity, it can be a venial sin. ¶ Whether indeed someone can dissolve the friendship of others, not with the intention that they should be enemies, but as a means so that, after the other is expelled, he might slip himself into

<column-break/>

the friendship of another: for instance, because a prelate or a prince will not admit this man to such great familiarity unless the other is excluded.

<margin>
Solution.
</margin>
It is first answered that this is in no way permitted if it involves defaming the other. However, by relating some of his natural defects that are public, perhaps there is no sin, because everyone may, without force or fraud, procure for himself a benefit of which he is worthy. <margin>Objection.</margin> ¶ But if you argue that this is true only if the other is not repelled from his right: <margin>Resolution.</margin> It is answered that when that right belongs to him by justice, it would be a crime to despoil a man of such a right. But when he is retained in the friendship of another as a free gift, no injury is done to him.

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it has already been answered that the whisperer is called a detractor according to that general reasoning by which he speaks ill of another; however, he differs in his goal, as has been said. Regarding that passage in Leviticus 19, it is answered that a "slanderer" <note>original: "criminatorem"</note>, as the name implies, differs both from a whisperer and from a detractor. For he is one who, contrary to justice, either falsely charges, or denounces, or exaggerates and reproaches the crimes of others—although the detractor and the whisperer sometimes do this as well. Regarding the other passage in Ecclesiasticus 28, we concede that the whisperer is sometimes "double-tongued" <note>original: "bilinguem"</note>; for to each of two friends, he says what is displeasing about the other. Thus, he says one thing to one and subsequently another thing to the other. Yet the detractor may also be double-tongued for a different reason, as we said above: because he says one thing in someone's absence and another in their presence.

<margin>
To the second argument.
</margin>
¶ To the second, it is answered that although the detractor always speaks of what is evil, and the whisperer does not always do so (but rather what *appears* evil to the other), whispering is nonetheless worse. This is because the gravity of sins is not weighed by the material object, but by the end and the effect, which is worse in the whisperer.

<margin>
To the third argument.
</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third, it is answered that he who detracts from a man is judged to detract from the law for this reason: that he acts against the law of love for one's neighbor. Wherefore, the whisperer, as an extinguisher of friendships, offends God more severely because he more harmfully transgresses the same law of love—for, as held in 1 John 3, God is love. Wherefore Proverbs 6 says: "There are six things which the Lord hates, and the seventh" (as if the worst of all) "his soul detests." And that seventh is he who sows discord among brothers.

# Book Five, Question XI.
## ARTICLE II.

#### Whether mockery is a special sin distinct from those preceding it, and whether it is a mortal sin.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
After these matters, it remains to see regarding mockery <note>original: "derisio"</note> what kind of sin it is and how great. First, it is argued that it does not differ from contumely <note>An "insult" or "affront" that attacks a person's honor to their face.</note>; for scoffing <note>original: "subsannatio," a physical gesture of mockery like wrinkling the nose or sneering.</note> seems to be the same as mockery, and both fall into the category of contumely. This is discovered both from the matter and from the harm inflicted. For no one is mocked except regarding something shameful; if this is thrown in their face, it is contumely; if it is done in secret, it is detraction <note>Spreading true but harmful information behind someone's back.</note> or scoffing. Likewise, the harm brought about through mockery is either against honor (and then it is contumely), or against reputation (and then it will be detraction), or against friendship (and then it will be whispering).

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
<margin>Regarding the question being debated.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is argued that mockery is not a mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a grave offense that separates the soul from God, whereas a "venial sin" is a lesser offense.</note>: because since mockery is done in play or jest—as it often happens among friends—it does not seem to be contrary to charity. Add to this that even mockery directed against God does not always appear to be mortal. For whoever relapses into a sin from which they had risen by the grace of God is a mocker of Him, even if that sin is venial; <margin>Isidore.</margin> according to that saying of Isidore: "He is a mocker and not a penitent who still does that which he repents of." <note>original: "Irrisor est & non pœnitens qui adhuc agit quod pœnitet"</note> And yet, not everyone who relapses into a venial sin is guilty of a mortal sin. Likewise, a hypocrite <margin>Gregory.</margin> is a mocker of God; according to Gregory: "By the ostrich is signified the hypocrite, who mocks the horse and the rider, that is, God." <note>A reference to Gregory the Great’s commentary on Job 39:18.</note> And yet, not every relapse or hypocrisy is a mortal sin.

¶ On the contrary is the fact that mockery is done in jest, whereas the others are done in earnest; and therefore this sin differs from those. And in Proverbs 3, it is read that "God mocks the mockers"; but for God to mock is to punish eternally, as the Psalmist testifies: "He who dwells in heaven shall laugh at them." <note>original: "Qui habitat in cœlis irridebit eos" (Psalm 2:4).</note> From this it is gathered that mockery is, by its nature, a mortal sin.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
To the question, he responds with three very simple conclusions. The first is: the sin of mockery is distinguished from the others named above. This is proven. Sins committed by words are judged by intention, as was said above; therefore, a different

<column-break/>

intention constitutes different species among them. Just as the insulter intends to derogate honor, the detractor to diminish reputation, and the whisperer to extinguish friendship; so the mocker intends to pour out confusion and shame <note>original: "erubescentiam & pudorem"</note> upon another. This end is distinct from the others; therefore, it is separated as a distinct species. It differs further, as we were saying, because the others are in earnest, but mockery covers its taunts <note>original: "scommata"</note> under the form of a joke; hence it is called "play." For this reason, mockery very frequently consists of irony: as if you were to call a deformed man beautiful, or one of the lowest birth "noble," or a tongue-tied man "eloquent and elegant."

<margin>Instruction.</margin>
¶ To understand the subsequent conclusions, it must be considered beforehand that since mockery is only about some vice—whether moral or natural—one must wisely discern whether that evil is great and grave in itself, or small. For if it is great in itself, it is not by its nature the subject of mockery; rather, mentioning it is considered by its nature a serious reproach. Therefore, if it is brought forth in laughter and jest, this is because it is related as if it were a small thing. Thus, a vice is brought forth in laughter and play as if it were trivial in two ways: namely, either as small and slight in itself, or in respect to the person who is held in low esteem.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Proof.</margin>
¶ Let the second conclusion be: To expose another's sin or natural defect to mockery as a small thing is not, by its nature, a mortal sin, but a venial one, if the other is made ashamed by it in some way; for the matter can be of such little weight that it is no sin at all. The conclusion is manifest in itself, since every sin can become venial by reason of the lightness of the matter. I say "by its nature" because if someone mocks another for a vice that is not particularly great in itself, yet knows the other will take the mockery very heavily, he commits a sin against charity. For example, if someone were to say to the face of a highly honorable and religious man, without witnesses, that he had spoken to a girl—thereby causing him to flush with great shame—he would certainly not escape the stain of mortal guilt.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: If some vice is spat in a man's face under laughter and jest as if it were small—not because it is thought small in itself (since it is judged absolutely great), but in respect to the person to whom it is objectified, who is held as base and therefore the marking of such a vice is considered as nothing—it is a mortal sin; and it is more serious...

<summary>This page defines mockery (derisio) as a distinct sin of the tongue, characterized by the intention to cause shame rather than merely damage reputation or friendship. It distinguishes between lighthearted joking (venial) and mockery that targets someone's dignity or status with contempt (mortal).</summary>

<meta>Continuing the discussion from the previous page, Dominicus de Soto is now evaluating the gravity of "mockery" (derisio). Having defined it, he moves to prove that mockery is a serious sin, often more severe than a direct insult, because of the profound contempt it expresses.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>The conclusion is argued afterward in all its parts.</margin>
...more serious than a direct insult <note>original: "contumelia"</note>, and it is all the more enormous depending on the greater reverence that was owed to the person being mocked. Each part of this is proven: for it is the sin of contumely to cast a great vice into another’s face; this, as we said above, brings mortal guilt. However, the fact that it is delivered through irony or under the guise of laughter does not, in truth, diminish the guilt; rather, it increases it, because by such mockery the person is marked as so worthless that it is not considered a matter of great weight to thrust such a vice upon them. Just as it is considered a matter of nothing to label children, foolish men, and others of lowly lot with the names of similar vices.

For this increases the element of contempt; therefore, the crime is more serious than if such vices were cast at them seriously through a direct insult. ¶ Hence the third part of the conclusion becomes clear: that the more the person was worthy of greater reverence, the more the biting jests <note>original: "scommata"</note> of such mockery constitute a more serious guilt.

<margin>The first degree of mockery.</margin>
Wherefore, when such mockeries are vomited out against God, or against faith and religion, they exist as the most enormous crimes of blasphemy. Hence Isaiah 37: *Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed, and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice?* And it is added, *Against the Holy One of Israel.*

<margin>The second degree.</margin>
After this, the mockery of parents holds the second place. Hence Proverbs 30: *The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth the labor of his mother, let the ravens of the brooks pick it out, and the young eagles eat it.*

<margin>The third.</margin>
Then, in the third place, is held the derision of the righteous <note>original: "iustorum," the just or upright people</note>; for since honor is the reward of virtue, to mock a just man is to inflict injury upon the virtues themselves and, in a certain way, upon God. Indeed, this can sometimes exceed even the mockery of parents because of a man's distinguished holiness. And against these mockers it is read in Job 12: *The simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn.* This kind of derision is indeed harmful and pestilential, for by it men are drawn back from the exercise of virtues out of shame <note>original: "pudor"</note>. Hence Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, a foundational theologian for Soto</note> says: *Those who see good things arising in the actions of others soon pluck them out with the hand of pestilential reproach.*

<margin>Gregory.</margin>
<margin>A doubt <note>original: "scrupulus"</note>.</margin>
¶ Concerning this third conclusion (for regarding the others there is no doubt), an argument raises a doubt: that since a direct insult <note>contumelia</note> exists against honor, while mockery is against shame <note>verecundia</note>, and honor is a more excellent good than shame, it seems that a direct insult is a more serious crime than mockery.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
It is nonetheless answered that the gravity of vices is not always taken from the same source from which their species are distinguished:

<column-break/>

for mockery is distinguished from a direct insult by a different end, namely, that which produces embarrassment and shame. However, its gravity is weighed by the greater contempt which is in the mocker than in the insulter. For we said by that reasoning that an insult <note>contumelia</note> is worse than detraction <note>gossip/slander</note>, even though the reputation which is harmed by detraction is a more precious gift than honor. Add to this that mockery always has an insult joined to it; for by it a person's vice is reproached in the presence of the one mocked, but in a singular way. Furthermore, that the mockery of God, or faith, or religion, or of any virtue whatever is most harmful is evident from this: that many people of otherwise proven virtue—precisely because they have conquered other monsters of vice—because they are called hypocrites by the "children of this world," and thus because they live excellently they are mocked, they become ashamed in public to devote themselves to distinguished virtues. For this reason, Christ took care to providently warn his family. First in Matthew 5, where he proposed a singular degree of blessedness to those whom men would curse for this reason: that they held the world in derision, and the world's wisdom was reckoned as folly, and they lived as fools in the eyes of worldly people. And Matthew 10: *He who shall confess me,* he said, *before men, I will confess him before my Father who is in heaven.* And more clearly in Luke 9: *He that shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of man shall be ashamed, when he shall come in his majesty, and that of his Father, and of the holy angels.*

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
TO the first argument, therefore, it is replied that although scoffing <note>original: "subsannatio"</note> and mockery <note>irrisio</note> agree in the purpose of causing shame, they differ in their mode: because mockery is done by word alone, and by loud laughter <note>original: "cachinnis"</note>, and especially by the biting jests of irony; but scoffing is done by other gestures, such as a twisted or wrinkled nose: as the gloss <note>A standard medieval commentary</note> has it on that verse of Psalm 2: *He that dwelleth in heaven shall laugh at them.* Or by protruding lips, or other signs shown by the limbs or objects by which a man’s vice is noted. Such a difference does not vary the species <note>The category of the sin</note>, because all those gestures serve in the place of words. Yet both differ from a direct insult just as shame differs from dishonor. For shame is, as Damascene <note>John of Damascus</note> says, the fear of dishonor.

<margin>To the other part of the same argument.</margin>
¶ To the other part of the same argument it is replied that although mockery is not made except regarding something shameful—for which reason it agrees in matter with direct insult and detraction—

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

...the manner of a cause, either as an efficient or moving cause: namely, by which someone else is moved to act. And this same thing primarily and properly belongs to God by excellence, who by his word alone created all things; according to that verse in the Psalms: *He spoke, and they were made.* <note>original: "Dixit, & facta sunt" — Psalm 33:9 / 148:5</note> Therefore, for God to bless is the same as to impart good, and to curse is the same as to inflict evil. Secondly, however, after God, it also belongs to men in their own degree and order, specifically to those who by command move their subjects to execute something; the words of the **imperative mood** were established to express this impulse. Finally, in a third way, "to speak" is a certain expression of an impulse desiring that which is expressed by the word; the word of the **optative mood** <note>The "optative mood" is a grammatical form used to express wishes or hopes.</note> serves this impulse. And this mode is what is commonly and properly called "cursing" or "blessing"—that is, the calling down of good or evil. From this, it follows that speaking in these last two ways, and willing that which is said, follow one another according to goodness and malice: namely, that whatever goodness or malice lies hidden in the will 

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
of the speaker, the same is brought forth in the speech. ¶ These things having been established, let this be the **first conclusion**: To command that evil be done to another, and to desire or call down evil insofar as it is evil for them—namely, as if intending it for its own sake—is by its nature a mortal sin. This conclusion is manifest. For to either inflict or desire evil for another 

<margin>Second.</margin>
is openly repugnant to charity. ¶ **Second conclusion**: To command, desire, or call down evil in such a way that it takes on the character of a good is permissible and sometimes a 

<margin>Proof.</margin>
necessary duty. **It is proven**: Sometimes the evil of a particular person is conceived as a means to attaining a good. For although evil in itself is not a necessary means to a good end, through the malice of men it can happen that it becomes conducive to it. In such a case, just as the will for that end is good, so also are the commanding and the calling down of that means, even if it is an inconvenience to the person. Therefore, such an impulse is not properly a "curse" in itself, but only accidentally: because then one does not intend evil for its own sake, but good—just as the death inflicted by one who was defending himself 

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
is justified. ¶ **Third conclusion**: This kind of command or calling down of evil can take on the character of a good in two ways. In one way, because it has the character of **justice**, just as God and subsequently a human judge lawfully curse a wrongdoer by sentencing him to punishment; just as Holy Church herself, when she strikes rebels with anathema <note>An "anathema" is a formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note>, curses by right and merit. And for this reason, the prophets also often curse, calling down evil upon sinners, conforming themselves to the divine will; as in that verse: *Let the proud be confounded:* <note>original: "Cōfundantur superbi"</note>

<column-break/>

*because they have done iniquity unjustly against me.* <note>Psalm 119:78 (Vulgate 118)</note> And the whole of Psalm 108: *Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand.* And Psalm 100: *In the morning I put to death all the sinners of the land, that I might scatter all workers of iniquity from the city of the Lord.* <note>In modern Bibles, these are Psalms 109 and 101.</note> Although such imprecations sometimes have the force of prophetic pronouncements. In the second way, it happens that one calls down evil upon another under the character of **utility**: by which reason it is certainly permissible to call down some sickness or other calamity upon one who is corrupt in morals, so that, being wholesomely chastened, he may rise again more cautiously. ¶ Regarding these 

<margin>Guideline.</margin>
conclusions, therefore, that same thing must be recalled which we noted above regarding other injuries of words: namely, that to judge the guilt of a curse, the purpose of the mind must be weighed. Therefore, when parents curse their children, having no internal desire for evil, it is never a mortal sin; although the habit is certainly a very bad one and is peculiar to people of the lowest class. Nor does it contribute anything toward correction, except that the very impulse of cursing often stirs anger into hatred and changes the mind, so that they eventually desire whatever evils they call down. Finally, the naming of the Devil, calling him upon the one being cursed, can hardly be excused from mortal sin. For it is a kind of **blasphemy** and a **scandal** to call down eternal death upon someone. Nor indeed is the fact that the curser regrets the speech after vomiting it out an indication that consent (and thus guilt) did not precede it; rather, it is merely a sign that the impulse emanated not so much from habit as from passion. Lighter curses, however, are for the most part venial sins. But as we said in the previous article regarding whispering <note>original: "susurratione" — the sin of backbiting or gossiping to destroy friendships.</note>, the sin draws its species from the object of the curse. For he who commands or calls down murder is considered a murderer; and he who commands theft, a thief; but not necessarily he who merely wishes that someone be despoiled of his money by another. ¶ This distinction, however, should be noted between a curse in the form of a command and one that is a wish. For he who curses another in the tone of a wish, if he has no evil intention and gives no scandal, commits no fault; but he who **commands** that an evil be done, even if he has no sinister intention but does it feignedly, can incautiously cause harm; and thus commit as much sin as there was cause...

He warns that while casual cursing by parents may not always be a mortal sin, it is a dangerous habit that can lead to genuine hatred.</summary>

# Book Five, Question XII.

negligence of speech. For instance, if someone commands their servants to terrify another with naked swords, from which some injury or inconvenience follows. But since we have mentioned scandal <note>original: "scandali" — in Catholic theology, a "scandal" is an action or word that provides a "stumbling block," leading another person into sin or spiritual harm</note>, it is most often judged by the status of the person speaking the curse. For a prelate or any person of heavy influence can hardly wish ill upon their subordinates without causing a scandal. Furthermore, it is not permitted for children to curse their parents, or inferiors their superiors, even in jest. This would be not only a scandal but a type of insult; so great is the reverence owed to them.

<margin>Argument against the third conclusion</margin>
¶ Against the third conclusion, an argument exists that a private person may not wish evil upon someone as a medium for achieving a good. Since no one is seen as being able to wish for another that which they are not permitted to do: and no private person is permitted to cause harm to one of corrupt character so that they might be amended; therefore, it is not permitted to wish it upon them either.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered by rejecting the first premise. For although I am not permitted to inflict evil on another, because I am not a minister of justice, it is nevertheless permitted for me to wish—by the permission of God, who holds supreme power, or by public authority—that evil should befall them, so that by this lash of punishment they might come to their senses <term>resipiscentia: the act of returning to one's right mind or repenting</term>. Truly, we may wish temporal evil upon a vicious person not only for a spiritual good, but also to guard against a worse temporal evil. Indeed, we can wish some temporal inconvenience upon a squanderer of their own goods, lest they waste them away in gambling and games. We can even wish death upon someone, although it may be clear to us that they are entering the path of perdition, so that the evils facing our commonwealth might be avoided, and peace and tranquility might be attained. For anyone can pray for the death and all the calamities of the Turk <note>original: "Turcæ" — the Ottoman Turks were seen as the primary external threat to 16th-century Europe</note>, so that we might be delivered from his tyranny. Indeed, even against Christian enemies who persecute us unjustly, when no other way lies open, it is permitted to wish for the same thing.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>

<margin>To the final argument.</margin>
¶ To that which was brought forward in the final argument, it is answered that Balaam <note>A biblical prophet in Numbers 22-24 who was hired to curse the Israelites but found he could only speak blessings</note> rightly refused to curse the people of Israel, because it was clear to him that God was blessing that same people. However, the matter is different regarding sinners whose faults—though we cannot look into their hearts—we weigh by external signs and evidence; and therefore we may call down curses upon them for their own benefit.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether it is also permitted to curse an irrational creature.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure or swan within a rectangular floral frame.</image-desc>
Since the previous article defined those curses which are hurled at men, a second article is joined regarding the irrational creature.

<margin>Argument for the negative side.</margin>
It is argued that it is not permitted to curse such a creature. For a curse is permitted either as a punishment or to correct a fault. An irrational creature, however, is capable of neither fault nor punishment. Indeed, there is nothing in an irrational creature except nature, which is the handiwork of God and is moved by His instinct and impulse. Therefore, he who curses it splashes an injury back upon God.

¶ To the contrary is that the Lord, as is told in Matthew 20 <note>This likely refers to Matthew 21:18-22, the cursing of the barren fig tree</note>, cursed the fig tree. And Job cursed the day of his birth, as his history has it in chapter 3.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with four conclusions. The first, which is the foundation of the others: Blessing and cursing can properly be cast only upon a rational or intellectual creature.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proven thus: Blessing and cursing are appropriate only for that thing to which good and evil pertaining to happiness or unhappiness can happen. That, however, belongs only to a spiritual creature or a man. For brute animals, which do not have mastery over their own actions—as we demonstrate in Book 4, Question 1—are neither capable of happiness or justice in the proper sense, nor of unhappiness and injury. For happiness consists in the attainment of the ultimate end which a creature intends through its actions. Irrational and inanimate creatures, however, neither recognize ends, nor do they...
