<meta>This page continues the investigation into the moral nature of cursing. Having discussed curses directed at humans, Soto now explores whether it is permissible to curse "irrational" things—animals, plants, and even inanimate objects or moments in time.</meta>

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Objection.</margin>
...they are related to something else, and therefore they do not possess a right <note>original: "ius" — a legal or moral claim</note> to anything by themselves; rather, whatever they are, they belong to man. ¶ However, a greater doubt arises from the previous premise. For although neither good nor evil pertaining to their own happiness happens to irrational creatures <note>animals and plants</note>, they nonetheless go hungry, fall ill, and die. We can indeed wish these evils upon them, and thus curse them.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this, however, it is truly responded that the good or evil things we call for through blessing or cursing are not of the purely natural kind—the sort that happens to wood and stones through God's general movement—but those which, under the special providence of God, relate to human happiness. This is what the "optative" mode <note>expressing a wish or desire</note> of prayer signifies.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ From here, then, we step toward the second conclusion. Blessing and cursing irrational creatures happens in relation to man, for whose sake they were created; thus, the curse or blessing of these things reflects back upon the person themselves.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The proof is that their good and evil relate to our own happiness or misery. This relationship is considered in three main ways. First, by way of support, insofar as we use their service and help. Therefore, one who curses the fields with sterility would do an injustice to the people for whom the fields bear fruit; and one who wishes death upon herds or flocks wishes that loss upon the owner. For this reason, sterility and livestock plagues often occur as punishment for our sins. In this way, the Lord cursed the earth in Genesis 3, saying, "Cursed is the ground because of your work," so that man might pay the penalty for his fault by seeking food through the sweat of his brow. Conversely, in Deuteronomy 28, He blessed it, saying, "Blessed shall be your barns," and immediately after cursed it, saying, "Cursed shall be your barn." Second, an irrational creature serves man by way of significance. In this way, the Lord cursed the fig tree as a sign of the sterility of Judea. Third, the same irrational creature relates to us by way of "containing" us, such as time and place. In this way, Job cursed the day of his birth. He did not do so by wishing evil upon men—as someone does who desires harsh weather to the detriment of crops (for such a person would sin, whereas we read in Job 1 that in all these things he did not sin). And in chapter 2, God warned Satan not to touch Job's soul. Rather, he cursed that day out of love

<column-break/>

for the human race, and most of all for God. Specifically, he did so because of the original sin <note>original: "culpam originalem"</note> contracted at his conception, and because of the calamities and miseries that grow from it for the human race. To this category we also assign David’s curse in 2 Samuel 1 <note>original: "2. Reg. 1" — in older Bibles, the books of Samuel were often called 1 and 2 Kings</note>, where he wished evil upon the mountains of Gilboa—the place where the slaughter of Saul and the people occurred.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion. To curse irrational things, or even demons (as we said above), insofar as they are God's creatures, is blasphemy.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Finally, the fourth: To curse these same things considered in themselves is idle and vain, and frequently illicit. This conclusion is clearly gathered from the first.

¶ From these points, any sensible person will know how far it is permissible to curse storms, rust <note>crop blight or rot</note>, locusts, and other such portents.

<margin>Superstition of the peasants.</margin>
For let us be far from such mockery of sacred things as is said to happen among some peasants: namely, that locusts and grubs are summoned to court, assigned a patron and a prosecutor (so it is said), and after the legal case is contested on both sides, they are finally driven out by a sentence of excommunication <note>original: "anathematis"</note>. What thing could be more worthy of ridicule among Christians than to treat such pests, worms, and birds—which act purely by natural instinct—as if they were serious legal parties?

<margin>By what path occurring calamities should be met.</margin>
Therefore, what is permitted in such calamities is only this: that we implore divine help against demons through legitimate exorcisms. These demons are often permitted by God to infest us with such invasions and whirlwinds as punishment for our sins. In this way, it is also permitted to bless the boundaries of fields. Although this is not strictly necessary, it is enough to pray to God for the prosperity of the harvests. Blessing bells has a religious pretext, just as chalices are blessed, though I would not deny that sometimes a bit of superstition can get mixed in with these things.

¶ Therefore, the solutions to the arguments are clear through what has been said.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the moral nature of cursing (malediction). Having previously discussed whether cursing irrational objects is permissible, Soto now compares the gravity of cursing a person to the sin of detraction (damaging someone's reputation).</meta>

# Book Five, Question XII.

...first, because doing evil is worse than speaking evil; and yet, not everyone who does evil commits a mortal sin. On the other hand, that cursing is a graver sin than detraction <margin>Argument 2.</margin> appears first from this: that a curse is a type of blasphemy, as held in the gloss upon that passage in the Epistle of Jude: "When Michael the Archangel, disputing with the devil, contended about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy." <note>original: "iudicium inferre blasphemiæ"</note> Now, blasphemy is a graver sin than detraction. Add to this that one who curses is the cause of evil by his command; however, he who detracts only signifies the evil that already exists. It is worse to be the cause than to be the sign. ¶ On the contrary side of both parts is the fact that nothing excludes one from the kingdom of heaven except mortal sin; yet cursing excludes one, according to 1 Corinthians 6: "Neither cursers, nor the greedy, shall possess the kingdom of God." <note>original: "Neque maledici, neque rapaces regnum Dei possidebunt"</note> That it does not equal the gravity of detraction is established by the fact that cursing can sometimes be licit; detraction, however, never is.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> To the question, it is responded with four conclusions. First: cursing, according to its kind, is a mortal sin. We are speaking in this context of that cursing which is done with the intention of causing evil; for that which is done with a good purpose is not brought into the question <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> of sin. The conclusion is proven: To command evil to be inflicted on another, just as to desire to imprecate <note>To "imprecate" is to invoke or call down a curse.</note> it, is by its nature contrary to charity, the character of which is to wish good things for those we love. This vice, therefore, kills the soul of the one cursing. It follows that the sin is graver to the extent that we are bound to love the person more dearly, or to the extent that the evil we wish upon them is more ruinous and harmful. Hence Leviticus 20: "He who curses his father or mother shall surely be put <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> to death." <note>original: "morte moriatur"</note> ¶ Second conclusion: It can nonetheless happen that cursing is a venial sin, either because of the slightness of the evil we imprecate, or because of a lack of deliberation—namely, that the word slips from the mouth out of a light impulse, or in play, or perhaps by surprise. For the meaning of words, and thus the blame, must be weighed primarily by the intent of the heart. <margin>Corollary</margin> ¶ From these points, what we said in Article 3 becomes clearer: namely, that the sin of cursing is of multiple species. It is to be judged in the same way as hatred; hence, if a curse is made in a general way, with no specific evil explained—as if one were to say, "May you be cursed by God"—then a general crime of malediction is committed.

<column-break/>

Then a general crime of malediction is committed; but if, as we were saying, you have heartily imprecated death upon another, you have committed homicide in your mind. <margin>Third conclusion.</margin> ¶ Third conclusion: Malediction which expresses a simple desire is, by its nature, a lesser fault than detraction. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> This is proven from what was said above. First, the detractor—just like the insulter—scatters or throws the "evil of fault" <note>original: "malum culpæ" — the moral stain of sin or guilt</note> against another. However, he who is a simple curser wishes upon the other only the "evil of punishment," <note>original: "malum pœnæ" — physical suffering or loss as a consequence of sin</note> such as death, or various calamities, or perhaps a fault under the reasoning of punishment. But a fault is a graver and more harmful evil than a punishment. Therefore, for this reason, detraction—and consequently the other sins of the tongue—are graver than a curse. <margin>Confirmation.</margin> Second, this is confirmed by the manner of utterance. For detraction, insult, and derision are the proclamation and assertion of evil; but a simple curse (for we are not speaking now of a command) is nothing but a desire. But a proclamation and assertion are worse than a desire; for the one desiring is not immediately the cause of evil through his desire, just as he who proclaims is the cause of infamy. Thus, detraction is worse than a simple curse. Nevertheless, the internal desire for evil is infected by the malice of its object. <margin>Chrysostom.</margin> Hence Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> says on Matthew: "When you have said, 'curse him, and overturn his house, and make all things perish,' you differ in nothing from a murderer." <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> ¶ Fourth conclusion: A curse which is made by way of a command, since it has the nature of a cause, can be graver than detraction—provided it inflicts a more massive injury than the blackening of one's reputation. It will be lighter, however, when the damage given through it is lighter. These things must be understood according to what belongs to the nature of these vices in themselves; for other accidents can be considered by which the aforesaid vices either increase or decrease. <margin>Scruple.</margin> ¶ One scruple <note>A "scruple" in scholastic writing is a small remaining doubt or technical difficulty to be resolved.</note> remains, however, regarding the third conclusion, which stated that simple cursing is a lighter fault than detraction because it is not a cause of evil. For it is argued to the contrary: the curses of parents upon children are often effective, and for this reason they are to be greatly feared. For God sometimes grants imprecations of this kind, and most especially those of the saints—as we read of Elijah in 2 Kings 1, that because of his curse, fire falling from heaven devoured first one, and then another captain of fifty. And of Elisha...

<summary>This page analyzes the moral weight of cursing (malediction) compared to detraction, concluding that while cursing is generally a mortal sin when intended to harm, it is often a lesser sin than detraction because detraction attacks a person's moral character directly.</summary>

## Soto of Segovia, Theologian, of the Order

# BOOK SIX.
### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'E' depicting a figure in a landscape, possibly a scholar, gesturing with one hand.</image-desc>

<margin>Subject of the following books.</margin>
We have finally arrived at that part of the intended work for which we primarily began to contemplate this project. This "forest," I say, of usury, contracts, exchanges, and simony <term>simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred things, such as church offices or sacraments</term> was what most strongly moved our mind to undertake such a massive labor. For we see the current times so saturated with such portents of injustice and greed that hardly any hope remains for us to persuade others of the truth. Nevertheless, we will apply our efforts to the best of our ability, with the help of God’s divinity; it will be His task to touch the hearts of those concerned, so that they may be moved toward truthful conduct—for whose sake, according to Aristotle in the second book of the *Ethics*, <margin>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 2</margin> the entire study of moral philosophy is established. Therefore, to keep our sequence of discussion consistent, we divided the treatment of commutative injustice <term>commutative injustice: unfairness in private dealings and exchanges between individuals, as opposed to distributive justice handled by the state</term> at the beginning of the previous book as follows (which is the division from Aristotle’s *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 2): in the preceding book, we would speak of injustice arising from involuntary and violent seizures; in this book and the one following, however, we would then explain the other branch of injustice, which involves those pacts and agreements that men enter into of their own free will. Therefore, we have specifically dedicated this Sixth Book to usury <term>usury: in this period, the practice of charging any interest at all on a loan of money, which was strictly regulated by the Church</term> and contracts, which hold a prominent place under the title of Justice and Law. And indeed, Saint

<column-break/>

Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose work Soto is expanding upon.</note> discussed only two principal questions on this matter: one concerning buying, and the other concerning usury; in these, the entire subject of contracts is virtually contained. <margin>The Foundation</margin> Truly (which must be noted as the basis of the entire treatise), every injustice in any contract is reduced to one of two heads. Either a price is demanded for a thing that is not worthy of any civil price: and this, in temporal matters, is reduced to usury <note>original: "usuram." Charging for the use of money itself.</note>, and in spiritual matters, to simony. Or, a thing that is indeed estimable by price is handed over for an unjust price—either through excess or received through deficiency—and this is reduced to the injustice of buying and selling. But because he [Aquinas] decided to treat only the two aforementioned questions, and those very briefly, he placed the one on buying before the one on usury in order, because buying seems a more honorable contract. However, for us, who have established a more open and detailed treatise on every kind of buying and the nature of other contracts, it is worthwhile to follow a different order. For since the entire injustice of contracts must be measured and weighed against the form of usury, it was necessary to explain its nature immediately at the beginning, lest this question later interrupt the thread of our discussion of contracts. Furthermore, a good reason for this order is not lacking: namely, that it begins with the greater iniquity. For it is more unjust to seek a price from a source where none is owed than to extort an unjust price from a source where a just one is owed.

<summary>In this preface to Book Six, Domingo de Soto introduces his detailed study of economic contracts and usury, arguing that usury is the most fundamental form of injustice in voluntary exchanges. He explains his departure from Thomas Aquinas's organizational structure, choosing to address usury first because he considers it a more severe moral violation than unfair pricing in sales.</summary>

# QUESTION ONE, On Usury.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 78.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether usurious lending is, by its nature, a mortal sin.<-

<margin>
First argument.
</margin>
To descend to the matter itself, we first ask whether usurious lending is, by its nature, a mortal sin. The argument for the negative side is made as follows. First, by the example of Christ, who is the standard for our morals. In Luke 19, he himself affirms that he demands usury <note>The Latin text cites the Parable of the Ten Minas (Luke 19:23), where the master asks why the servant did not put the money in the bank so it could be collected with interest/usury.</note>.

<margin>
Second argument.
</margin>
¶ Second, the divine law given to the ancient fathers—which David in Psalm 18 calls "immaculate" because it prohibited sins—nevertheless permitted usury. For we read in Deuteronomy 23: "You shall not lend to your brother at usury, but to a foreigner." Indeed, in chapter 28 of the same book, he proposed this to those mortals as a reward: "You shall lend to many nations, and you yourself shall receive interest from no one." Therefore, lending at usury is licit.

<margin>
Third argument.
</margin>
¶ Third, even human laws, through which justice is established among men, permit usury, as is evident throughout the titles "On Usury" in the Digest and the Code <note>These refer to the *Corpus Iuris Civilis*, the foundational body of Roman law</note>. Therefore, these practices are licit.

¶ On the contrary is the precept of Exodus 22: "If you lend money to my people, to the poor man who lives with you, you shall not press him like a debt collector, nor shall you oppress him with usury." And David, among those who shall dwell in the tabernacle of God, includes the one "who has not given his money at usury."

<margin>
Multiple meanings of usury.
</margin>
<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>
At the very beginning of the question regarding the name "usury," as is our custom, let us first note that for the Latins it is not named as if it were "the use of bronze" (*usus aeris*), as those imagine who superstitiously scrutinize the collision of syllables. Rather, if you look at its primary meaning, it is exactly the same as "use." Thus Cicero, against Verres: "Why did you grant the pirates the usury of light for so long?" <note>original: *Cur piratis lucis usuram tam diuturnam dedisti?*</note> Therefore, the "usury of light" is the same as the "use of light," namely, life. Soon after, the same name descended to signify that which grows from the use of any thing, as if it were its fruit. Likewise, in the book *On Old Age*: "The earth never returns what it has received without usury," where "usury"

<column-break/>

<margin>
Cicero.
</margin>
is the name given to the fruit of seeds. And in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 1: "Nature gave the usury of life just like money, with no fixed day." Therefore, "usury" (*usura*) is derived from "use" (*usus*), just as "offspring-breeding" (*fetura*) comes from "offspring" (*fetus*), and "culture" (*cultura*) from "cultivation" (*cultus*). For this reason, according to these meanings, it is not the name of a vice. However, in a third way, it was eventually adapted by custom and usage to signify specifically that which grows from the principal through the use of money or any consumable thing. Perhaps the reason for this adaptation is that the name itself might denote the perversity of the thing through antithesis: namely, that since the use of such things (which is consumed by the very act of using) is sterile in itself, it is nevertheless treated as if it were fruitful. Therefore, according to this meaning, "usury" is used as the name of a crime. Furthermore, usury is also called <term>foenus</term> (interest), as Aristotle notes in the *Politics*, Book 1, Chapter 7.

<margin>
Aristotle.
</margin>
And this is an allusion to the Greek etymology. For what we call usury, the Greeks call <term>tokos</term> <note>original Greek: <term>τόκον</term></note>, from the word meaning "to give birth" <note>original Greek: <term>ἀπὸ τοῦ τίκτω</term></note>. Just as animals give birth to offspring similar to themselves, so too does money beget money. For which reason, says the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, this mode of acquisition is most especially against nature. For money is not fertile, like the earth or a flock, such that it might give birth. It is therefore called <term>foenus</term> in Latin, as if it were a <term>fetus</term> (offspring).

<margin>
What is the difference between usury and interest.
</margin>
However, among legal scholars there is such a distinction that the name "usury" is broader, and to speak dialectically, it is a superior category to <term>foenus</term>. Specifically, <term>foenus</term> is used only for usury in the strict sense: namely, for that which grows unjustly from a loan alone. Usury, however, is taken more extensively for any increase from any contract, even when it is licit. For example, if you sold something on credit, and because the debtor was in delay <term>mora: a legal term for a failure to pay a debt on time</term>, something was added to your payment by reason of "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: the profit a creditor misses out on because their money was tied up in a late debt</term>, that addition is indeed "usurious" (in the broad sense of "use"), but it is not "interest-bearing" (*foenebris*) in the sinful sense. For so says the legal expert in the law *cum quidam*, section *si pupillo* in the Digest's title on usury: "Usuries are not inflicted for the sake of the gain of those seeking them (that is, the legitimate ones), but because of the delay of those not paying." Likewise, while someone litigates over an inheritance or some thing, or even over money, if he wins, the court awards him, along with the principal, whatever has grown from its use; and that is called usury. But nevertheless, where there is no question about this specific legal point, the use of the terms "interest" and "usury" is promiscuous. We, therefore, as common usage holds—not only among theologians but also in the state—take the name only for the illicit usury of a loan. So much so that where something is paid either as a penalty or by reason of delay or otherwise justly, the contract is not considered usurious. ¶ Moreover, what we call usury, and the Greeks call "birth," the Hebrews call "a bite" <note>Hebrew: *Neshek*</note>. Whence in Deuteronomy...

<summary>This page introduces the moral and legal debate over usury, exploring its etymology in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. Soto distinguishes between "usury" as a general term for the use of something and its specific, sinful meaning as an unnatural "breeding" of money from a loan.</summary>

# Question I of the Sixth Book.

<margin>St. John Chrysostom.</margin>
In Deuteronomy 23, where we read, "You shall not lend to your brother at interest," the Hebrews have it as: "You shall not inflict a bite upon your brother," or, "You shall not bite your brother with interest." <note>The Hebrew word for usury is *neshek*, which literally means "a bite."</note> For just as a dog tears at the entrails of a carcass with its teeth, so the usurer tears apart the substance of his debtor. This is certainly what St. John Chrysostom alluded to regarding that passage in Matthew 5 (as we noted there), "and to him who wants to borrow," etc. He says that the money of a usurer is like the bite of an Asp. For one struck by an Asp goes to sleep as if delighted, and dies through the sweetness of that slumber; this is because the poison then spreads secretly through all the limbs. In the same way, one who accepts a loan under usury feels a benefit for a time; but the usury runs through all his resources and turns everything into debt. These are the words of that Divine man. Therefore, if you have considered these things thoughtfully,

<margin>Usury only takes place in contracts of a loan.</margin>
usury does not occur except in the contract of a loan <note>original: *mutuum*; specifically a loan of consumable goods where ownership is transferred</note>, and in other things where the nature of use is present. And since a loan has no place except in things that are consumed by their use, usury is concerned only with these. For example: I sold you my property at an expected price, and I demand an additional payment because I must wait for you. Because this contract is treated just as if I had immediately loaned you that same price for a time, it is usurious. ¶ Rather, this

<margin>The Rule.</margin>
rule, which is incapable of failing, must be placed at the head of these contracts: to weigh whether any given contract is usurious, one must investigate whether it involves some element of a loan for which a price is being paid. For then it is entirely usurious; otherwise, not at all. And for this reason, in the title of the question, we have considered "usurious contract or action" and "usurious loan" as the same thing. ¶ Furthermore, labor is spent in vain by those who sweat over searching for a definition of usury, and (unless I am mistaken) never finding a perfect one. For it is

<margin>Usury in two ways.</margin>
taken in two ways. In one way, it is for the action—that is, for the lending with a pact to receive something beyond the principal <note>original: *sors*</note>. For this is how it seems to be used in the Council of Agde (Question 3, Canon "Usura"), where it says: "Usury is where more is required than what is given." In another way, it is taken for the price which increases beyond the principal by the estimation of use. As St. Ambrose says in the same section: "Whatever is added to the principal is usury." And this is certainly the meaning of the original name. For the conventional action is more correctly called a "usurious loan" or the "sin of usury" rather than "usury" itself—just as a "tonsure" is what remains after the act of "shaving." Thus, usury is the object of the sin. Therefore, the lender is said to lend at usury and to receive usury;

<column-break/>

the borrower, however, is said to receive a loan at usury and to pay usury. ¶ Usury is, therefore (if you desire a precise and concise definition, as it ought to be), the price for the use of a loaned thing.

<margin>The definition of usury.</margin>
By saying "the price of use," it excludes contracts of sale, where the price is paid not just for the use, but for the thing itself. By saying "of a loaned thing," it is removed from the definition of a contract of *emphyteusis* <note>A long-term lease of land</note> or a rental, in which the thing is not "loaned" in the sense of a transfer of ownership. Furthermore, the name "price" designates a preceding agreement in the lending, or at least that the receipt is made by reason of the loan. For this reason, I have chosen this word more carefully than "profit." For we construct this definition of usury strictly for "cursed interest" <note>original: *fœnore*</note>. And therefore, where something increases beyond the principal justly—either by reason of "lost profit" <note>original: *lucrum cessans*</note>, "emerging loss" <note>original: *damnum emergens*</note>, or as a penalty—it is indeed called "usury" in an extended sense of the word, yet it is not the *sin* of usury of which we treat here; for that, although it is a profit, is nevertheless not a "price," since it does not spring from a loan agreement. Nor indeed, if the borrower gives something back to the lender out of gratitude or honor, is it usury; for where there is no pact, there is no price. Likewise, if you provide gold or silver money (as St. Thomas says in the solution to the sixth point) for another use that is accidental to it—for instance, for display or for use as ornament—and you receive a price for that, it is not usury. This is because the price does not come from a loan (since ownership is not transferred there) but from the hiring out of the money. In the same way, the contract of partnership <note>original: *societas*</note> is excluded from the nature of usury; for he who puts in the principal does not lend it, because he does not hand over ownership. Furthermore, if that which you receive was otherwise owed to you, even if you receive it from a loan agreement (namely, while you lend to your debtor so that he may pay the debt), it is not usury, because it is not a price for the use of the loaned thing, but the recovery of your own property. ¶ In the present context, the "principal" <note>original: *sors*</note> is the

<margin>What is the principal?</margin>
loaned substance itself which belongs to you and which the law grants to you. And I believe the name was drawn from the contract of partnership and applied to all general cases. For there, everyone puts his own "lot" <note>original: *sortem*</note>, that is, his portion, into the pile; whence they are all called "partners" <note>original: *consortes*</note>, that is, those sharing their lots together. In Greek it is called *archaion* <note>original: ἀρχαῖον</note>, which means "the original," and *kephalaion* <note>original: κεφάλαιον</note>, which means "the capital"; which names are also in use among the Latins. ¶ From this clear definition is gathered the reason for the distinction between

<margin>The difference between mental and external usury.</margin>
external and mental usury. For they differ not only as the interior and exterior act of the same object, but because external usury implies a pact...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the definition of usury, moving from the etymology of the word "bite" to the legal and moral distinctions between "mental" usury (intention) and "external" usury (formal agreements). # F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

tacit or expressed: however, mental usury (which must be considered carefully) is committed without any intervening agreement. Therefore, set before your eyes these three things: the loan <note>original: "mutuum"; a loan of goods consumed by use</note>, the price or profit, and the agreement. Wherever an agreement intervenes, it is usury in deed—that is, "external" usury; otherwise, not at all. Yet, for an expressed agreement in the court of God, neither writing nor witnesses are required. Even when you explain your will without witnesses—namely, "I lend to you so that you pay me back so much above the principal"—it is an expressed agreement. If, however, you do not state it in such a form, but suggest your will by nods or gestures, it is considered a tacit agreement. For instance, if you say: "Look, I lend to you; but you know the custom; I have no means to live. You are usually grateful to others," or something similar. For although it may not be a civil agreement such that you can legally compel the borrower, there is nevertheless an obligation, and therefore it is external usury. 

However, hope combined with intention is sufficient to constitute mental usury without any formal agreement. For example, if you lend to me hoping and intending that, by reason of the loan, I will provide you something, it is mental usury: just as the intention to kill a man is considered homicide <note>In Catholic moral theology, the internal intent to commit a sin is often treated with the same gravity as the act itself</note>. This is because the object—namely, to receive profit by reason of a loan—is the object of usury. Therefore, do not be deceived by distinguishing external and internal usury in such a way that the former requires an expressed agreement while the latter requires a tacit one; for even a tacit agreement creates external usury. But when I say "hope," it is understood that this hope is the cause and intention for lending—meaning you would not have lent unless some profit came to you by reason of the loan. For if you lend to me out of benevolence, even if there arises in you a hope of repayment which I am going to make to you freely out of friendship, no mental usury is born from that: because to receive based on that reasoning is not real usury. But concerning these things, the discourse will return in the next article.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
Having laid these points about the name of usury, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first: Usurious lending—that is, to receive a price for the use of a loaned thing by agreement—is by its nature a mortal sin, contrary to <term>commutative justice</term> <note>Commutative justice governs the fairness of exchanges between individuals, requiring that what is given and what is received are of equal value.</note>. Indeed, this conclusion is confessed by everyone; yet, there is some controversy over which law provides its foundation.

<margin>The opinion of some. Ancharano.</margin>
For there are those (a view attributed to Pietro d'Ancharano <note>A famous 14th-century Italian jurist</note> in one of his disputed questions) who deny that usury is prohibited by the law of nature; instead, they say it is only contrary to divine law. And for that reason, perhaps the same author

<column-break/>

held that treating usury does not pertain to theologians, but to jurists—because he perceived that weighing the law of nature was the task of theologians. But it cannot be denied that it is a matter of divine law, of which theologians are the interpreters. Therefore, answering regarding external law and deciding on the punishments of moneylenders is left to the legal experts; but to explain the nature of usuries from their own principles belongs to theologians. 

¶ To return from this detour, however: this opinion, that usury is not contrary to natural law, is not only plainly false, but it even places the truth of the conclusion (that usury is a sin) in danger. 

<margin>The first reason against the previous opinion.</margin>
If, I say, you remove natural law, you leave a very weak foundation for the stability of the conclusion. For although usury was blamed and cursed in many places in the ancient law <note>The Old Testament</note>, nevertheless, since it was also permitted there to the Jews to practice it with foreigners, those precepts must be strengthened from elsewhere, lest a suspicion arise that it is in some way lawful and just. 

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Furthermore (and this presses the matter forcefully), that entire law, as Paul teaches in Hebrews 7, was fulfilled through Christ and subsequently abolished. Therefore, absolutely no precept of the Old Law retains any force in the "law of grace" <note>the New Testament era</note>, except those which are part of natural law, or were commanded again by Christ. For in this sense, as we are often accustomed to say, it must be understood that the moral precepts remained: namely, because they were sustained by the force of natural law, and likewise confirmed in the Gospel. Therefore, anyone who denies that this crime is against natural law weakens the precepts of the ancient law on this matter. 

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
¶ However, the passage of the Gospel in Luke 6—"Give loans, hoping for nothing therefrom"—which is most commonly cited for this very purpose, certainly does not have the strength that is commonly thought. For this reason, St. Thomas [Aquinas], the most eagle-eyed observer of sacred meanings, 

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
not only did not use that passage to assert the conclusion, but even raised a fourth argument against the same from it. For he recognized that it is not a prohibition of usury, but a "counsel" <note>In theology, a 'counsel' is a recommendation for higher perfection, whereas a 'precept' is a mandatory command.</note> of lending without hope of human compensation. And therefore he argued that since lending while hoping for nothing therefrom is strictly a counsel of Christ, it is not a mandatory command to receive nothing from a loan. Although he did not leave the argument unanswered. And in truth, the Gospel is most evident. For there Christ commends the love which we owe not only to friends, but also to enemies. And he warns that we should not perform benefits of charity for the sake of human favor and the gratitude which men repay, but looking only to the divine reward. And therefore he says, if you do good...

He also critiques common interpretations of Luke 6:35, suggesting it is a spiritual counsel rather than a simple legal prohibition of interest.</summary>

Having previously defined usury as a sin of intent (mental) or agreement (external), he now addresses specific scriptural passages—primarily from the Gospel of Luke—and legal arguments from the Church Fathers and Aristotle to determine if usury is a violation of natural law or simply a religious prohibition.</meta>

### Book Six, Question I.

...if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? For even sinners lend to sinners, so that they may receive back equal things. <note>Original: "æqualia." Soto argues that if Jesus were talking about usury (interest), he wouldn't use the word "equal," because usury implies receiving back more than the original amount.</note> If he were speaking of usury, he would not have said "equal things": because it is not the custom for usurious profit to be equal to the principal; rather, he said "equal things," that is, a similar amount of goods, returned freely. It is the same point that he adds: "But love your enemies, do good and lend, hoping for nothing in return": that is, no favor from men, but from God. Wherefore he adds: "And your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High." 

Therefore, it is a foolish <term>gloss<note>A "gloss" is a traditional marginal or interlinear commentary used by medieval scholars to interpret scripture or law.</note></term> to say that the first part of the sentence is a "counsel" <note>An optional good deed that brings extra merit.</note> while the latter part is a "precept" <note>A mandatory command or law.</note>. Nor did Saint Thomas Aquinas, in his first solution to that fourth argument, intend that meaning of the second part to be found in the Gospel when he said that "to lend" is a counsel, but "not to seek profit therefrom" is a precept; rather, he meant that it is a law of justice not to expect profit. Therefore, he immediately adds the legitimate meaning: namely, that no mention is made there of the hope for usurious profit, but rather of any hope placed in man. For no prohibition of the injustice of usury is decreed there; instead, it is a commendation of the mercy of the loan, which ought to be shown toward neighbors for the sake of God alone.

<margin>First objection.</margin>
¶ But you may ask: how, then, does Pope Alexander III say in the Council of the Lateran (in the chapter *Super eo* regarding usury) that the crime of usury is "detested by the pages of both Testaments" <note>Referring to the Old and New Testaments of the Bible.</note>?

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
The response is that in the Old Testament, the testimonies are plain; in the New Testament, however, that prohibition of the Decalogue, "Thou shalt not steal," abundantly forbids it.

<margin>Second objection.</margin>
But you say again: Pope Urban III (in the chapter *Consuluit* under the same title) cites this same passage, "Lend, hoping for nothing in return," to confirm the prohibition of usury.

<margin>Urban III.</margin>
<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that a Pope, whenever he cites testimonies of the Sacred Page in a certain sense, does not always intend to "canonize" that specific sense as an article of faith; rather, he sometimes cites it according to the opinion of the Doctors. Furthermore, that evangelical sentence provides strength to the argument by a "logic of the greater" <note>Original: "a maiori." If a smaller thing is true, then a larger, related thing must also be true.</note>. Specifically, if Christ counseled that we should not even hope for a *free* gift from men (which they could lawfully give back), it follows all the more strongly that one must not expect a price 

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
for the use of the thing, which justice forbids. ¶ The conclusion is therefore drawn from the very "guts" of natural law in this way. There are two differences among things. Some are those whose use is the very consumption of the things themselves: such as food and drink. For that 

<column-break/>

<margin>Note.</margin>
reason, in these cases, the "use" cannot be calculated separately from the thing itself. And one should note the words of Saint Thomas to repel the trickery of certain people. Indeed, they argue for the contrary: since the use of a thing is an action or a "passion" of it, while the thing itself is a substance, they differ by nature, just as things in two different categories. To these people, the answer is that St. Thomas makes no mention of a distinction regarding the nature of the things. Therefore, he was cautious and did not say, "the use does not differ from the thing"; rather, he said it "is not to be calculated separately"—namely, with a distinct price—insofar as it pertains to human use. 

And this is the reason why, in such things, <term>ownership<note>Original: "dominium." In legal terms, this is the right to possess and dispose of property.</note></term> is transferred through a loan <term>mutuum<note>A "mutuum" is a specific type of loan involving "consumable" goods (like grain or money) where the borrower consumes the specific items and returns an equal amount of the same kind later.</note></term>. For if you do not transfer ownership, you grant no proper use of bread, which is to be eaten. And for this reason, as held in the *Institutes* regarding <term>usufruct<note>The legal right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it.</note></term> (at the section "constituitur") and in the *Digest* (regarding the usufruct of those things which are consumed by use, law 2), when the usufruct of such things is bequeathed, the ownership of the things themselves is also bequeathed. Except that the recipient is held to provide security for restoring the value later, so that it serves as a kind of image of a loan. 

But there are other things whose use is distinguished from the things themselves: such as land, a house, a horse, clothing, etc. For we can use these while keeping their substance intact. (Even though clothing wears out through long use, it is by its own nature consumable, like all mixed things.) And therefore, the use of such things can be rented while the ownership is retained. And vice versa, ownership can be transferred while the use is retained. 

Things of the first order, then, are those given in a loan; and thus the reason for the conclusion is drawn out in this form: Whether the same thing is sold twice, or that which is of no value in itself is sold, in both ways one sins against the natural reason of <term>commutative justice<note>The branch of justice governing fair exchange between individuals, requiring that one receives exactly what they give.</note></term>. But to transfer the ownership of such [consumable] things so that another charge is added to the price of the thing for its "use" is either to sell the same body twice, or to sell the "use"—which has no price apart from the thing—for a new price. Therefore, usurious lending is a sin against nature. 

Now, among such things, money is considered most of all; for 

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
as Aristotle states in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, it was invented for the purpose of exchanging things. And through this, the argument that is customarily made is solved: "The lender, for that benefit, is worthy of the borrower returning something equal; therefore he can include that in the agreement." But in truth, for the benefit of lending (as St. Thomas says in his solution to the fifth argument), in terms of justice, he does not owe me more than I give: and one hundred gold coins that I lend to you are worth nothing more than one hundred. Therefore, if I demand more, I am in a way selling the thing for more than is just.

<summary>Soto argues that usury is a violation of natural law because charging for the 'use' of consumable goods (like money or food) is the same as selling the same item twice, as the use cannot be separated from the item itself.</summary>

...just. Since the use of a thing is worth no more than the thing itself when that thing is consumed by its very use. Out of honesty, you owe me a benefit, but it must be given freely. And therefore, to legally bind you to pay for it—if that benefit is measurable in money—is an act of injustice. But if you were to argue more pressingly: <note>Original: "Scienti, & volenti non fit iniuria."</note> "No injury is done to one who knows and is willing"; the borrower binds himself of his own accord; therefore, usury bears no resemblance to theft or robbery. Saint Thomas Aquinas responds to this seventh point by saying that the borrower does not entangle himself in that bond of his own free will, but is instead driven by necessity—just as someone might be compelled by necessity to buy a thing for more than its fair price. But what if someone seeks a loan not out of necessity, but for pleasure? The answer is that "necessity" is to be understood in this way: that however the loan is sought, it cannot be obtained unless interest is paid. ¶ From this conclusion, it follows that usurious wickedness—as we have said above—is prohibited by that commandment of the Decalogue: *Thou shalt not steal.* Whence Ambrose says (14. q. 4.): "If anyone accepts interest, he commits robbery: he shall not live." Indeed, Augustine, in the very next canon, compares it to homicide. For he says, "Is he any more cruel who steals or snatches something from a rich man, than he who slaughters a poor man with interest?" For to eat away at the substance of the needy is to slaughter them. 

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
And at the end of the second book of *On Duties*, Cicero introduces Cato, who, when asked what it was to lend at interest <note>Original: "fœnerari."</note>, responded: "To kill a man." Therefore, the testimonies of the Old Law are most frequent—such as in Exodus 22, Leviticus 25, Deuteronomy 23, Ezekiel 18, and various Psalms—in which this plague and destruction of human society is repeatedly condemned; these are explanations of this natural law. It is to such an extent that when the royal Psalmist decided to emphasize the benefits that the Messiah would provide for us, he placed usuries and iniquities together as things from which He would deliver us. For he says, "He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity." ¶ If, finally, you should doubt to what degree it is certain that usurious exchange is a sin: the answer is that it is a matter of Catholic faith. Consequently, the denial of this truth would be heresy, as it was condemned in the decree *Clementina vnica, de usuris*.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion is an appendix to the first: The profit from usury is subject to <term>restitution<note>The legal and moral obligation to return stolen or ill-gotten gains to their rightful owner.</note></term>, even if the borrower does not demand it; for the moneylender does not acquire ownership of it in the slightest.

It remains, therefore, to resolve the three arguments raised at the beginning of the question; for the other four have already been resolved by Saint Thomas in the preceding sections.

<column-break/>

Now, in the first argument, there is no ambiguity. 
<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
For Christ transferred the name of usury from secular matters to spiritual ones. And therefore, the use of the word is metaphorical. There is indeed a great deal of similarity, but also much dissimilarity. For God lends us spiritual gifts <note>Original: "charismata."</note> because he gives them freely and without any price on our part; yet he wills that we cultivate them through our use and duties—just like seeds cast into us—through his favor and heavenly dew, so that we may bring forth multiplied fruits, in the manner of the earth. And because this results in His glory, He calls these His "usury"; nevertheless, the benefit of the rewards and the heap of increase falls to us, as if we were making our own interest. There is, however, this difference: that temporal money is consumed by use (and thus usury becomes vicious), whereas spiritual gifts grow by use; for that reason, their "usury" is commended by God.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ in the second argument, a solution is sought for that difficulty: whether usury was permitted in the Old Law to the extent that it was free from guilt before God, or whether it was merely permitted with impunity as far as the human court was concerned. For Saint 

<margin>St. Thomas. Alexander of Hales.</margin>
Thomas (Question 78, Article 1) and Alexander of Hales (Part 3, Question 36, Member 4) and other authors of this rank hold this latter 

<margin>Conradus.</margin>
opinion. Conradus, however, in Question 24, although he reports both as probable, prefers the former to the other. And some of the 

<margin>Usury was never lawful.</margin>

Furthermore, not only is the opinion of Saint Thomas most certain—and therefore by its own right and merit received by the common consensus of the Doctors—but the other opinion is barely sustainable. ¶ And first, their way of speaking, by which they say God "dispensed" <note>An official exemption from a law.</note> with them, is false and inept. In truth, the vice of usury (as we were just demonstrating) is against the natural law; specifically, it forbids taking a price for a thing that has no value in itself, such as the use of money considered separately from the money itself. But natural precepts are not dispensable even by God Himself, as we have shown in Book 2, Question 3. For that which nature forbids is as intrinsically evil as it is for a man to be rational. The contrary of which is certainly not feasible. And for the same reason, that which nature forbids cannot be made lawful. And those who say the contrary think so because they are ignorant of either what a natural precept is, or what it means to dispense. Therefore, those who contend to support that side ought not to call it a dispensation. And least of all against one who proves, with such a well-equipped phalanx of arguments, that usury is...

### Question I of the Sixth Book

...against natural law. ¶ But to make the matter clear, it is necessary to recall that usury was permitted to that nation <note>The Israelites</note> not with loose license, but in a specific way: namely, that they should not lend at interest to their neighbors, but only to foreigners. For thus it says in Deuteronomy 23: 
> You shall not lend to your brother at usury, neither money, nor grain, nor any other thing: but to the stranger. To your brother, however, you shall lend what he needs without interest. 

Furthermore, he was called a "brother" who was of the same people, as is clear from Exodus 22: 
> If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not press them as a debt collector, nor shall you oppress them with usury. 

<margin>The assertion of some.</margin> These men argue, therefore, that because God had granted the land of the Gentiles to the Jews, He consequently permitted them to take usury from those same people as if from enemies, whose goods had come into their own right. Just as, they say, Caesar could grant his army the right to despoil enemies under the appearance of usury. 
<margin>Ambrose.</margin> And they cite a text from Ambrose (14, q. 4, canon *Ab illo*), where he says: 
> From him demand usury, whom you rightly desire to harm. Against whom arms are justly carried, from him usury is lawfully taken. <note>original: "Ab illo exige vsurā, cui meritò nocere desideras. Cui iure inferuntur arma, huic legitimè auferunt̄ vsuræ." Ambrose’s point was that usury is a weapon of war used to destroy an enemy.</note>

But first, even if we were to grant them this, that 
<margin>God did not grant a dispensation for usury.</margin> would by no means have been a "dispensation" <note>A legal exception to a moral law</note>, but rather a gift from God, who is the universal Lord of all things. Just as He gave them the vessels of the Egyptians, He did not grant a dispensation for theft, but either delivered the goods to them as their Lord, or—as is more probable—adjudged the goods to them as a judge, paying them the wages for the labors and works with which they had served Pharaoh. Similarly, when I give my own property to a friend, I am by no means granting a dispensation for theft. Nor does a king grant a dispensation when he transfers ownership through the law of prescription. For to "dispense" in usury would mean that someone could lawfully receive a price for the use of money without the other person (who has the power to give) freely giving it. 

<margin>The second assertion of Conrad is rejected. First argument.</margin> ¶ But indeed, putting aside the dispute over the name, we must not believe that God conceded those usuries of foreigners to the Jews in such a way as to make them the owners of them. First, because He permitted them the exact same species of usury regarding the Gentiles that He forbade regarding neighbors. However, when He forbade them from lending at interest to their brothers, He prohibited that which is forbidden by natural law; therefore, He permitted that same vicious and iniquitous practice regarding the nations. Conrad <note>Likely Conrad Summenhart, a 15th-century German theologian who wrote extensively on economic contracts.</note> responds that although it was the same in genus <note>the general category</note>, it was not the same in species <note>the specific type</note>. 

<margin>First argument.</margin> But surely, if it were not the same in species, it would not be usury in genus either, but would be a true gift from God; and therefore they would be receiving nothing except what was already theirs. And yet, it is absurd to admit such excessive homonymy and equivocation <note>Using the same word to mean two entirely different things</note> in the same word of Scripture. For it says: 
<margin>Second [argument].</margin> "You shall not lend at interest to your brother, but to the stranger." ¶ Second—and I marvel that these men have not noticed this—the land of the Gentiles given to the Jews 

<column-break/>

consisted only of both banks of the Jordan, which extended one hundred and sixty miles in length and sixty in width; yet the permission of usury 
expanded much more widely. For they accepted usury with impunity from any of the Gentiles who, arriving from the most remote provinces, entered into commerce with them. Add to this that in the same chapter of Deuteronomy 23, God commanded them not to abhor the Edomite or the Egyptian; and yet they could accept usury from them with impunity. Therefore, that permission was not based on the rationale of hostility. 

<margin>Third reason.</margin> ¶ And the third argument is that surely, to steal the substance of enemies through such tricks would not be a good example among Christians, nor would any well-instituted republic permit frauds of this kind. Therefore, it is not credible that God conceded this to them for that reason. Otherwise, He would have equally indulged them to plunder their goods by whatever way possible. 

<margin>Fourth reason to the contrary.</margin> ¶ Also, fourth: the Prophets of God, where they explained natural law (which all are bound to keep), absolutely condemned usury. As in Ezekiel 18, where that justice was numbered among others: 
> If a man has not lent at usury. 

And below: 
> He who gives at usury and takes back more, shall he live? 

And when David says: 
> He shall redeem their souls from usury and iniquity, <note>Psalm 72:14. In modern bibles, this is often translated as "oppression" or "fraud."</note>

certainly he did not mean those usuries which they extorted from their brothers, because they took none; but rather those which they were allowed to wring from strangers. 

<margin>The last [reason].</margin> ¶ Finally, it is apparent that God did not give them the goods of the Gentiles through that "image of theft," both because those who did not know the true God would have attributed it to iniquity, and because if the Jews were receiving it as their own, they would have scraped it together without limit or measure; and thus they would have frightened the Gentiles away from their company. Therefore, nothing else is credible than that it was a sin for the Hebrews to snatch usury even from Gentiles, except up to a certain limit and line, which they would not have prescribed for themselves if they had thought they were receiving what was already theirs. 

<margin>Eusebius.</margin> ¶ There is also the fact that Eusebius, in Book 8 of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 2, where he narrates the precepts of the Mosaic law, reports that usury was absolutely illicit for them, in these words: 
> Do not take up what you did not lay down; do not touch what belongs to another; do not lend at interest. 

<margin>Josephus.</margin> And Josephus, most learned in the law, in Book 4 of the *Antiquities*, also reports the precept absolutely, saying: 
> Indeed, it was allowed to none of the Hebrews to lend at interest, neither food nor drink, etc. 

In support of this opinion, Conrad also cites a certain Rabbi, an interpreter of the law. A sign of this is that while the prohibition of usury is frequently repeated in the law, that permission to lend at interest to strangers is read nowhere except in one single place, Deuteronomy 23. ¶ Therefore, that permission must be understood as having been granted to the Jews for the exact same reason that...

civil law now allows the same to Christians. Namely, that it might be done with impunity <note>Without legal punishment, though still considered a sin in the eyes of the Church.</note> to avoid greater evils: specifically, highway robbery, because they <note>the people of that time</note> were most devoted to avarice. In the same way, prostitutes are permitted to avoid adulteries. For with a similar figure of speech, it was foretold in the same chapter: *There shall be no harlot from the daughters of Israel, nor a whoremonger.* It is as if He had said, "I permit this among the nations with impunity." For this reason, Saint Thomas [Aquinas], in his first point, says that by the word, "You shall not lend at usury to your brother," natural law is denoted: namely, that since all mortals are brothers by the "glue of nature," usury should be accepted from no one. The other part, however, is a permission. Here, I would not think to hide the false accusations of certain men who impose upon Saint Thomas the idea that by the name "brother" in that place he understood all men. For he clearly saw the distinction between a brother and a foreigner; <margin>The mind of St. Thomas.</margin> but he understands that although by the name "brother" those who were of the people <note>the Israelites</note> were specifically understood, nevertheless, because in the widest meaning of the word (as <margin>Augustine</margin> Augustine is the authority in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 30) all men are brothers and neighbors, it is hinted there that the natural prohibition of usury extends to all men. ¶ But neither should this be passed over in silence: that there are those who wish to attach another sense to that concession "to the foreigner," namely that there is no permission at all, but rather a prohibition. As if He had said: "To your brother you shall not lend at usury. But if anyone were to be considered a foreigner by you, he would be one to be crushed by usury. However, you ought to regard no mortal in such a way." They say that the canon of Ambrose cited above (14. q. 4) <margin>The cited passage from Ambrose is explained.</margin> is to be read in this way: *Demand usury from him whom you rightly desire to harm.* It is as if he says, according to the <term>gloss|an interpretive commentary written in the margins of legal or biblical texts</term> added there: just as you ought to harm no one, so you ought to seek usury from no one. Therefore, from the word added in the same place—*To him against whom arms are justly carried, usury is legitimately taken*—it should not be inferred, as common opinion suggests, that it is lawful to snatch usury from enemies. For in truth, as we were saying a little earlier, such a custom carries no mark of honesty, nor should this stain be branded upon that Saint <note>Ambrose</note>, as if he were advising this. Rather, he wished to skin alive <note>figuratively: to expose the cruelty of</note> the most unjust nature of usury. And therefore he adds: *He fights without steel, who demands usury; he avenges himself on his enemy without a sword, who has been a usurious collector from his foe.* It is therefore not a license, but counsel; since no one ought to avenge himself on an enemy, neither should he afflict him with usury. For he was not speaking with kings, who alone are permitted to declare wars, but generally with private citizens, to whom the advice

<column-break/>

is that they should forgive injuries to their brothers. Therefore, as far as Ambrose is concerned, it seems to me by far most probable that he presented this mind to us. But that this same sense could be accommodated to the text of Deuteronomy 23 would be new, and, I believe, forced; but the sense is that which we have already explained. ¶ Moreover, regarding what is objected in the same book of Deuteronomy, chapter 28: *You shall lend to many nations, and you yourself shall receive a loan from none*—this pertains to nothing. For they cannot do so, since they are against nature and against divine commands (as in the chapter *Super eo* "On Usury"). Instead, they are like prostitution, [permitted] to prevent robberies. Because the avarice of mortals, just like lust, cannot be entirely extinguished by human laws. <margin>Human laws permit usury.</margin> ¶ Moreover, the permission of usuries is clear throughout the entire title "On Usury" in Book 22 of the <term>Digest|the 'ff' symbol refers to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Civil Law</term> and in the <term>Code|The Codex of Justinian</term> under the same title, especially the law *Eos*. There, a limit is prescribed for the quantity of usuries, the highest of which is the <term>centesima|the "hundredth," or 1% per month (12% per year)</term>. For the laws call this the maximum, as in the law *Qui sine* (Digest, "On matters conducted"). The same is called the "most heavy." Mention is also made of this in the canon *Si quis* (14. q. 4). Then there were the <term>bes centesimae|eight-twelfths of the 1% monthly rate</term>, the <term>triens|one-third of the 1% monthly rate</term>, etc. Concerning these, <margin>Bartolus.</margin> Bartolus <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, the most influential medieval jurist.</note> composed a diffuse treatise on the law *Si haeres* (at the law *Falcidiam*), where in the section *Item*, the *trientes* usuries are named. In that treatise, he gathers many opinions. For many of the interpreters of the law, hallucinating, multiplied many <term>glosses|comments</term> on this matter. ¶ For the understanding of this, it must be noted that it was the custom of the Romans to pay usuries on the <term>Calends|the first day</term> of each month. <meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of usury laws. Having previously discussed the biblical distinction between "brothers" and "strangers," he now moves into a technical analysis of how Roman civil law calculated interest rates and how modern practices have surpassed ancient limits.</meta>

### Question I of the Sixth Book.

<margin>Guillaume Budé.</margin>
...I had given a hundred gold pieces: you owed me one each month. <term>Guillaume Budé</term> <note>A famous French humanist and jurist (1467–1540) who wrote "On the As," a definitive study of ancient Roman coinage and measures.</note> in the first book of *On the As*, thinks the name "hundredth" <note>original: "centesima"</note> comes from the fact that in a hundred months they returned double the principal: but it is much more significantly derived from the aliquot part <note>A portion that is contained an exact number of times in the whole.</note> paid each month. Therefore, twelve out of a hundred were accrued each year, to use the language of merchants. And this was considered so heavy that it was not permitted except in <term>maritime loans</term> <note>original: "traiectitijs mercibus." These were high-risk loans where the lender assumed the risk of the sea voyage; if the ship sank, the debt was canceled.</note>: that is, when someone lent money to a sea merchant so that the lender himself underwent the risk of the capital. From this "hundredth" rate, the others were named, namely: the eight-twelfths-hundredth, the third-hundredth, <margin>The "As" is the name for any whole unit.</margin> the nine-twelfths, etc. For every whole is rightly called an <term>As</term>, which is divided into twelve <term>unciae</term> <note>literally "ounces," representing 1/12th of the whole.</note>. Hence a *triens* is a third part, namely four ounces; a *semis* is a half, etc. And thus someone is said to be appointed heir to the *as* (the whole), to the *semis* (the half), or to the *bes* (the two-thirds part, namely eight ounces). And <margin>The nine-twelfths. The third-part usury.</margin> the *dodrans* is nine. Wherefore the "third-part usury" <note>original: "triens vsura"</note> is not (as some think) a third part of the principal, nor is the "fourth-part" a quarter: otherwise the quarter would be far greater than the hundredth, even though the same law considers the hundredth to be the maximum. Rather, the *triens* is a third part of the hundredth: as if for a hundred gold pieces, a third of one gold piece was paid each month. And a similar proportion applies to the rest. ¶ One must therefore consider how much more licentious the madness of usury has become in these times. For not only is twelve out of a hundred per year considered too little, but neither fourteen nor sixteen per single trade fair <note>original: "nundinas." Large seasonal markets where international trade and banking settlements occurred.</note> are held to be enough. Furthermore, the <margin>Compound usury was once prohibited with the greatest rigor.</margin> "usury of usury" <note>Compound interest.</note> was prohibited with the greatest rigor, as seen in the Digest *on usuries*, the law *Placuit*, and the Code under the same title, the law *Ut nullo*. For the law states: "That in no way shall usury of usury be exacted from a debtor." "Usury of usury" refers to what is now most common in practice: You took a loan of a thousand, for which you owe a hundred in interest. You do not pay on the fixed day; therefore, those first interests give birth to others—namely, so that for that hundred, you pay an additional ten. This is surely something that the civil laws never permitted. And yet this plague has now crept in to such an extent that whoever rebukes it as a crime is held up as a laughingstock. <margin>A doubt.</margin> ¶ But a remaining doubt arises from these points: how far does the permission of civil law extend? Does it only mean that no penalty is decreed for the usurer, just as prostitution is permitted? Or does it go so far that a person harmed by usury is denied a legal action in court to reclaim it, just as is said of a buyer who <margin>A buyer who is deceived by less than half the just price.</margin> is deceived by less than half the just price?

<column-break/>

Or perhaps it goes even further, so that one who had promised usury could be compelled in court to pay it. Indeed, the permission can be understood in these three degrees. To enter into this, <margin>The solution.</margin> one must remember the distinction proposed between lawful and unlawful usury. For lawful usuries—namely those paid because of a delay in payment, or by reason of a "loss emerging" or "profit ceasing" <note>Two standard legal exceptions: "damnum emergens" (direct loss) and "lucrum cessans" (opportunity cost).</note> against the owner's will—are not only permitted by law, but he who is in delay is compelled to pay them. And the laws commanding usury to be paid must be understood as referring to these: such as the first law of the Code *on usuries*. If, following an interrogation, the promise of usury is proven to have been rightly made, it is owed by right. "Rightly made" means for a just cause and in the proper manner of a formal agreement <note>original: "stipulationis modo"</note>. However, concerning unjust usuries, which were called *foenus*, I believe they were never so permitted that those who promised them were compelled to pay. On this point, the third law of the same title should be noted, which says: "Although usury on loaned money cannot be sought through the bond of a formal agreement..." Behold, usurious interests could not be sought in court; nevertheless, because of a pact, they were paid just as is done now. But whether someone who paid could reclaim it in court is a matter of doubt. For it follows immediately in the same law: "Nevertheless, those paid by agreement of a pact are neither reclaimed as if not owed, nor are they to be credited toward the principal." Behold, they were not reclaimed. But whatever was the custom among the ancients, certainly a law would not be just that denied an action to one wishing to reclaim them. ¶ Let us say, therefore, that the civil laws could rightly and properly permit usury with impunity—meaning that while a thief is punished, the usurer is immune from that punishment. But to compel a borrower to pay usury is something no law ever permitted, nor could it. Moreover, it would be unjust to deny the one who pays a legal action to reclaim it. For the reasoning is not the same as in the case of one deceived by less than half the price. For since that fraud (as we said above) is not always easily established, a doorway would be opened to the plague of litigation if a legal action were granted. But in usury, the injustice is most obvious. Likewise, to hinder someone wishing to reclaim it would be against <margin><meta>handwritten mark like a crossed slash</meta></margin> Canon Law, which grants reclamation to the one harmed by usury. Indeed, in the *Clementinae*, the single chapter *on usuries*, any rulers, judges, or officials who act as an impediment to those wishing to reclaim the usuries they have paid are struck with the sentence of excommunication. ¶ Through these points, therefore, another doubt is easily dissolved: whether secular princes who permit usury are condemned by Canon Law. This question indeed "tortures" <note>Causes great difficulty or debate among scholars.</note> many, judging...

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>Civil law does not oppose canon law regarding the contract of usury.</margin>
...thinking that canon law stands in the way of civil law in this matter. In truth, however, it is no obstacle at all. For if civil law asserted that usury were lawful in the **court of God** <note>original: "foro Dei" — this refers to the "internal forum" or the court of conscience and divine judgment, as opposed to a human courtroom.</note>, it would be heresy, as condemned in the *Clementines* <note>The *Clementinae* were a collection of papal decrees issued by Pope Clement V in the early 14th century.</note>. Yet it does not assert this. Likewise, if it compelled usury to be paid, or prohibited the recovery of interest already paid, it would be intolerable, because it would contradict that same Clementine decree. Therefore, it is well stated by the commentary of **Bartolus** <note>Bartolus of Saxoferrato (1313–1357), perhaps the most influential jurist of the Middle Ages.</note> on the law *All Peoples* <note>original: "l. cunctos populos" — the famous opening law of the Code of Justinian which established Catholic Christianity as the official religion of the Empire.</note> (in the Code under the title "On the Highest Trinity") that by civil law, usury cannot be sought *as usury*, but rather as **interest** <note>original: "interesse"</note> by reason of **delay** <note>original: "mora" — a legal term meaning that if a debtor is late in paying, the lender can charge a fee for the loss incurred by the wait, which was distinct from charging interest on the loan itself.</note>. Indeed, there is no contradiction in the fact that secular princes do not strike usurers with their own punishments, while canon law punishes them with its own. For princes, as we said in Book I, only avenge those things that disrupt the peace and quiet of the republic, especially through force. The Pope and the ecclesiastical prelates, however, being more attentive to their duty, look to the care of consciences. And therefore, it is no wonder if they notice and punish usurers more sharply than secular princes do.

¶ Canon law, then, both tears usurers apart with many reproaches and heaps numerous punishments upon them. **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a prominent theologian and legal expert.</note> counts these up to eleven under the entry "usury," item 9.
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
<margin>The punishments of usurers fixed by canon law.</margin>
The first is **infamy** <note>original: "infamia" — a legal status where a person loses their good name and certain legal rights, such as the ability to testify in court or hold office.</note>, as is clear in the canon *Infamous* (13, question 7 and 6, question 1). Indeed, they say usurers are infamous even by civil law. However, in the law *The Wicked* <note>original: "l. improbum"</note> (in the Code under "On those who are branded with infamy"), they are not pronounced infamous unless they are demanding interest-on-interest, which we said above the civil law itself forbids. And that is called **wicked interest**. Three other punishments are established in the chapter *Because in all things* regarding usury: namely, that manifest usurers are not to be admitted to the **communion of the altar**. Some understand this so strictly as to mean they should not be admitted even to hear the sacred rites. However, because punishments should not be expanded beyond their definition, and because a sentence of excommunication is not actually carried out against them there, we should only listen according to the sound of the words: namely, that they are not to be admitted to receive the most holy Eucharist, because they are public sinners. Likewise, they are not to be granted ecclesiastical burial. Finally, no priest should receive their offerings, because they are considered plunder. And whoever does receive them is suspended from his duties. As for the rest of the punishments, anyone who wishes may seek them in the place cited.

¶ From these points it finally becomes clear how superfluous was the labor that **Baldus** and **Bartolus** 
<margin>Baldus.</margin>
<margin>Bartolus.</margin>
expended on the law *All Peoples* (in the Code under "On the Highest Trinity"), and how far from the mark they responded to that question concerning the Catholic Emperor **Justinian**. Specifically, they asked how these two things could hang together: that by the same law he commanded all peoples

<column-break/>

subject to him to live in the religion which Saint Peter the Apostle had delivered to the Romans, and yet he permitted usuries, which the Catholic faith teaches are illicit and which the Church forbids. To this, **Baldus** responds that he commanded the faith of the Trinity to be held, but not with respect to other articles that are required for the salvation of the soul.
<margin>Baldus's erroneous response.</margin>
Truly, this solution was not worthy of Baldus. For the Emperor commands all to live in the religion of the Roman Church, which includes not only the faith of the Trinity, but the whole of it, and along with it, moral conduct. The response, therefore, is the one we have already declared: namely, that the Imperial permission of usury in no way opposes the faith, because it does not claim that it is lawful in the **court of God**. That would indeed be manifest heresy. But the fact that usurers are not subject to civil punishments is not against the faith—just as it is not against the faith that prostitutes are not subjected to any legal execution.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether any benefit can be sought by reason of a loan.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a figure seated in an armchair or throne, gesturing with one hand, set against a background with foliage.</image-desc>
SINCE it has been established that nothing can be brought into a contract by reason of a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum" — a specific type of loan of "fungible" goods (like money or grain) where the borrower is expected to return the exact same amount and quality.</note>, it remains to be explained whether any **benefit** <note>original: "commoditas"</note> can be sought. And the argument is made from the affirmative side.
<margin>First argument.</margin>
The comparison seems to be the same between "given for given" and "loaned for loaned." But for money given, it is lawful by contract to receive the same or its value; therefore, for the benefit of lending, it is lawful to expect an equal duty in return. Namely, that the borrower should be bound to lend back to the lender.

¶ Secondly, he argues: If a son-in-law receives a **pledge** <note>original: "pignus"</note> for a loan that is fruitful, such as a garden or an estate, 
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
he can use its fruits until he is satisfied regarding the dowry, as is clear in the chapter *Healthfully* regarding usury. Therefore, it is lawful to receive something by reason of a loan.

¶ To the contrary is what is written in Ezekiel 18 among those things required for a man’s justice: "if he has not taken usury and **overabundance**." Where, by the name of overabundance, every thing is included that can be valued in money. There is also the word of **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan.</note> in the chapter *Most people*: "Whatever is added to the principal is usury." 
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
And **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> in the canon *He thinks*: "To receive all little gifts of whatever kind is usury."
<margin>Jerome.</margin>

TO the present question, a response is given in three conclusions according to the mind of **St. Thomas**. <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note>
