# Book Six, Question I.

<column-break/>

<margin>*The first conclusion.*</margin>
...[it is forbidden]. First: It is not permitted to receive or expect anything from a loan agreement <note>original: "pacto mutui"</note> whose price is estimated in money. This conclusion is clear: because 
<margin>*Aristotle*</margin>
according to the **Philosopher** <note>A standard title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 4 of the *Ethics*: Everything whose value we measure by money is to be considered money. Therefore, since it is not permitted to lend for a price, it follows that nothing estimable in money may be received by reason of the loan.

<margin>*The second conclusion.*</margin>
¶ The second conclusion. To receive something that is not part of a formal or implied agreement, but is repaid freely to the lender, carries no stain of usury. This is proven: because the benefit of lending not only does not turn away friendship, but actually fosters and strengthens it. Therefore, nothing prevents a lender from being able to receive any gift by which friends are accustomed to repay the favors of friends.

<margin>*The third conclusion.*</margin>
¶ The third conclusion. No law prevents it from being lawful for a lender to seek or demand, by reason of a loan, things that are not valued by a monetary price: such as the friendship and 
<margin>*Three things which make a loan usurious.*</margin>
goodwill of the borrower. ¶ From these conclusions, the judgment of the present question is summarized. For three requirements are needed for a loan to be infected with the stain of usury. First, that what is sought be estimable in money. Second, that it be expected by reason of the loan, and not for some other debt or by another path. And third, that it be brought into a pact <note>A formal agreement or contract.</note>, whether expressed or implied. This is to be understood so that the act of lending is an external usury. For even if a pact does not intervene during the lending itself, if the reception of a gift later happens specifically because of the loan, it is a usurious reception. Therefore, **mental usury**, as we have said, consists of intending in the mind to receive profit by reason of the loan. By these criteria, any prudent person may judge all cases. ¶ Against the third conclusion, however—where it was said that it is permitted to demand for a loan that which is not estimated in money—a sophisticated argument immediately arises: that it would be permitted to demand a priesthood from a bishop by the obligation of a loan, since spiritual things are not to be estimated by price. The response, however, is that the conclusion speaks of those things which, in human society, pertain to grace and politeness: namely, things that do not fall under a legal obligation but are usually given for free. Spiritual things, on the other hand, are not estimated in money for a different reason: namely, that they are not the property of those who confer them, but are entrusted to them by God as His goods to be dispensed freely. For that reason, in matters of this kind, it is a crime <note>This refers to simony, the sin of buying or selling sacred things or church offices.</note> to both give and receive for a price. ¶ But because **St. Thomas** says that goodwill and friendship are not

<column-break/>

estimable in money, it is argued to the contrary. 
<margin>*Argument*</margin>
According to human estimation, a man would value the friendship of good men more than any sum of money. Indeed, he would even buy it for a price; therefore, it is estimable in money. 
<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
The response is that it is not considered "estimable in money" because it is less valuable than money, but because by its nature, it is neither bought nor sold. For it consists in the **will**, which cannot be forced. You can indeed, by providing money, soften the heart of an enemy so that he loves you; but you can by no means "buy" it like a loaf of bread. For this reason, not only is it lawful to lend with the view of forming a friendship, but one may even include signs of friendship in the contract—for true love itself is impossible to contract. For example, [one might agree] that the borrower will not harm you, or will show himself affable and polite to you, and so on. ¶ What, 
<margin>*A Scruple.*</margin>
however, if you seek to creep into the friendship of someone through a loan who can grant you either a priesthood or a magistracy <note>A high-ranking government office.</note>? Suppose he is a King or a Bishop. 
<margin>*Solution. Mental Usury.*</margin>
Some say that when the purpose does not stop at friendship but proceeds further toward profit, it is mental usury. However, we have already touched upon a rule regarding this above, which we now repeat for confirmation: namely, that **mental usury** <term>mental usury: the internal sin of intending to profit from a loan, even if the written contract appears legal and interest-free.</term> must be weighed by the object of the intention, not by whether the intention was primary or secondary. That is, if by a loan you intend to entice the borrower to grant you something *by reason of the loan*, you commit usury in the mind, even if that perhaps was not your main intention. But if you intend only to bind him in friendship so that later, not because of the loan but because of goodwill, he grants you something of which you are worthy, there is no mental usury. This is true even if that was your primary intention: for example, making a friend so that later, being well-disposed toward you, he might give you something freely and liberally. Thus, the whole matter depends on whether you hope to have it by reason of the loan or by reason of friendship. If, however, you are unworthy of the office you hope for, that is a different kind of wickedness. This is the opinion of **St. Thomas** in question 13 *On Evil* <note>original: "de malo"</note>, which 
<margin>*St. Thomas. Cajetan.*</margin>
**Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a famous cardinal and commentator on Aquinas.</note> followed in *Quodlibet* 1, question 3. The conclusion is clear from examples. When you know a very just bishop, whom you know confers priesthoods for no other respect than justice, it is lawful for you to serve him to seek his goodwill, so that later he may confer a benefit on you for which you are worthy, freely and not because of the services rendered. For you are certain that he will not give it because of the services, nor will you receive it for them. Likewise, if you are worthy of a magistracy but are hated by the King, you can appease him with gifts to insinuate yourself into his friendship and the list <note>original: "albo" — referring to the *album*, the official list or register of names.</note>...

<summary>Domingo de Soto defines usury as the intent to profit from a loan and distinguishes it from the lawful pursuit of friendship or goodwill. He explains that while money cannot be charged for a loan, a lender may hope for non-monetary benefits like social standing or favor, provided the intent is rooted in mutual goodwill rather than a strict trade for the loan itself.</summary>

<page-num>516</page-num>
<header>Brother Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,</header>

...enroll you on his list <note>original: "albo te adscribat"; likely referring to a list of friends or a social register</note>; why then should you not also be able to "fish" for his goodwill using borrowed gold? This holds even if you would not otherwise lend except so that his friendship might be profitable to you. In short, since the object of external and mental usury <term>mental usury: the internal intention or desire to profit from a loan, even if no formal agreement is made</term> is the same, the external act is the most reliable rule for judging the internal state. To receive something by reason of a loan is usury in practice; therefore, to propose that in one's mind is usury in the mind. But to receive something by reason of friendship is not real usury; therefore, to desire that is not mental usury. I know indeed it can be answered that although simply desiring it is not a sin, nevertheless procuring that friendship through a loan is not free of fault. Yet since the object of the intention is lawful, I do not see what fault might be hidden here. However, it must be admitted that since it is a very subtle thing to discern when the intention is to receive by reason of friendship or by reason of a loan, such an intention is always suspect. But where a prudent man discerns the difference, no fault lies beneath.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ But can I not, through a loan, join myself in the benefit of friendship with someone to whom I am a debtor, so that he might forgive my debt? For example, if someone calls me into a lawsuit over some matter, can I enter into a treaty with him by lending money, with a settled pact that he withdraws from the lawsuit?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is that if I truly owe that thing, I cannot include it in a pact. But if I am being harassed through false accusations <note>original: "per calumniam"</note>, I can indeed redeem my harassment by means of a loan agreement.

<margin>Argument against the solution.</margin>
¶ There exists, however, an argument against the first part. If I have injured someone, either by harming his honor or his reputation, even if he could by right demand monetary restitution from me, I can nonetheless bind him to me with the bond of lending.

<margin>It is permitted to seek [pardon] for an injury by reason of a loan.</margin>
Response: It has already been asserted that it is lawful for me to arrange things so that he pardons me by reason of the friendship created through the loan. However, whether it is lawful to make a formal pact for this is a slightly more difficult matter to weigh; yet I think I am correct to concede that as well, at least before I have been condemned to pay a fine. For although honor and reputation can be valued in money, they are by their nature usually pardoned through the law of friendship. Therefore, that pact is nothing other than a treaty of friendship. Sylvester [Prieras] <note>A significant 16th-century theologian often cited by Soto.</note> supports us on the word "usury," part 1, section 11.

¶ You may perhaps ask, and not without cause, whether that friendship which is of a shameful use can be included in a pact. Namely, whether a lustful young man could agree on a loan with a woman in exchange for shameful compliance. The reason for doubting is that this appears to be nothing other than friendship. The answer is that to procure friendship through a loan, so that later, overcome by love, she might consent, is not

<column-break/>

the vice of usury. However, to obligate her [by pact] is not at all excused from that same vice, because that obligation is estimable in money. ¶ Behold these things which are not estimable in money. By contrary reasoning, nothing worthy of a monetary price can be established in a loan pact: thus it is not permitted to you to lend to a king by agreement so that he might exempt you from the payment of taxes, or through a signed privilege so that you might become a nobleman, whether for a time or permanently—unless perhaps it were clearly the case that these taxes were being exacted through injustice and tyranny. For then, because I do not owe those things, I receive nothing [extra] by reason of the loan, but I vindicate myself by defending what is mine from injury. By the same reasoning, I cannot obligate a prince by reason of a loan, as St. Thomas [Aquinas] says in Work 21, to confer on me a magistracy or any other thing. Nor can I lend a hundred on the condition that the borrower extorts those funds (or part of them) at his own expense from those debtors of mine from whom they were difficult to collect. Nor, if I have grain ten miles away from here, can I lend it on the condition that you transport it from there or consume it there, but you pay me back here; for in this I burden you with the cost of transport. Nor indeed can you receive any service of the "hand or the tongue" <note>original: "à manu vel à lingua"; meaning physical labor or professional advocacy/speech.</note>. That is, that another might stand as your advocate in a cause, or be your secretary. Indeed, one may not even enter into a pact that the borrower performs alms or other works of mercy. These things, I say, are not permitted to be put into a pact, nor to be expected by reason of profit. It is otherwise if the other person repays the favor freely. Nor [can you require] that the borrower sings for you, or dances, or manages your business, or prays to the prince for you. Unless the things were so small that a price is not usually paid for them.

¶ And for the same reason, a merchant cannot, without the mark of usury, lend under the condition that the borrower must take the whole loan or part of it in merchandise, even if the merchant sells it at a fair price—provided that the borrower does not actually need the goods but is forced to buy them by reason of the loan. This is because that obligation to buy is estimable in money. Indeed, profit comes to the merchant from this: for even if the goods are worth the price, he sells a larger quantity than he would have otherwise sold.

<margin>The notable fraud of merchants.</margin>
¶ From this, the most wicked fraud of merchants is revealed: those who lend to a king who is in need for his soldiers' pay, on the condition that the soldiers receive so much in goods and so much in money. For this is a triple or quadruple form of depravity. First, because although the merchants think the goods are worth that much, the reality is otherwise, because the rarity of buyers decreases the price;

<summary>Soto distinguishes between using a loan to foster legitimate friendship (which is permissible) and using it to extort services or goods that have monetary value (which is usury). He specifically condemns merchants who force borrowers to accept goods as part of a loan, labeling it a "wicked fraud."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral and legal complexities of usury, specifically focusing on how indirect benefits or "cloaked" contracts can hide usurious intent. It follows a discussion on military pay and the exploitation of soldiers through credit.</meta>

<page-num>517</page-num>
<header>Book Six, Question I.</header>

...and if [the distributors] did not sell it off among the soldiers, they would not so quickly find buyers to whom they could sell it at that price. The second injustice is that because they sell on credit, they sell at a higher price. And while they scrape together a profit by claiming "ceasing profit" <term>lucrum cessans: a legal concept where a lender claims compensation for the profit they could have made if the money hadn't been lent</term> from the king, they nonetheless sell the same "time" twice. And thirdly, since the wretched soldiers do not actually need such merchandise, they are immediately forced to resell it at the lowest possible price. To put it briefly: for every ten thousand that the king pays out, the soldiers barely get hold of six thousand.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ But you ask whether you can, by reason of a loan, bind a borrower to cultivate your field at a fair price, or frequent your mill, or oven, or tavern. Indeed, there are those who claim this is permitted, such as the *Summa Angelica* <note>A famous dictionary of moral theology by Angelus de Clavasio, died 1495</note>, and Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI, a significant theologian</note> in the question on usury, and those whom Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a Dominican theologian</note> mentions under the word "usury," part 1, section 7. Their reasoning is that since a borrower of this kind suffers no loss, no "price" (interest) is being extorted.

<margin>Summa Angelica. Adrianus. Syluester.</margin>
However, the opposing side argues that such a civil obligation has a value estimable in money. For there is no doubt that the loss of one's freedom of choice is, by its very nature, worthy of a price.

<margin>Solution to the proposed doubt.</margin>
Others, indeed, think that no usury is committed if you give a loan to be repaid at the term when the borrower stops coming to your mill or serving you in another way at a fair price. But in truth, it falls back into the same trap. It is therefore a "cloaking of usury" <note>original: "vfuræ palliatio"; a common legal term for disguised interest</note>. This is unless, perhaps, it is a contract of buying and selling; for nothing forbids you from binding a man for a set price to come to your mill for so many years, or for his whole life—even adding a penalty so that if he fails to do so, he must pay you a certain fine.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From this, it is clearly gathered that the lords of estates are stained with the filth of usury when they lend money or grain to tenant farmers on the condition that they lease their lands and estates at an increased price. Nor are they excused by saying that the use of the estates is worth that much; rather, it is because they cannot find tenants under any other condition that they offer the loan. For if they cannot find them, it is a sign that the lease is not worth that much. Therefore, only when you could find someone else willing to lease at that price would it be safe for you to then lend to a poor man so that he might lease it at the same price; otherwise, not at all. ¶ Furthermore, there are those who recognize no "use" <note>likely referring to interest or benefit</note> in this agreement: "Bind yourself to harvest my crops in the summer at the current market price, so that I may pay you part of the price now." For here, no reason for a loan appears, but rather a reason for payment. Yet, I would not dare to admit this. For that anti-

<column-break/>

cipated payment is a kind of loan of money to be repaid through the labor of another. Therefore, the obligation is made by reason of a loan.

<margin>Argument to the contrary.</margin>
¶ But you argue to the contrary: so long as the borrower receives a fair price for his labor, no restitution seems to be owed to him. Joannes Andreae <note>A 14th-century expert in canon law</note> responds, as Adrian reports in that same place, that the restitution should be given to the poor. However, no reason commands this. For restitution does not fall to the rights of the poor except where the creditor cannot be found, or where he is condemned to lose the money, as in the case of simony <note>the buying or selling of church offices or spiritual things</note>. Rather, he must be restored however much that obligation was worth.

<margin>The legitimate solution.</margin>
From this it follows that if, in order to bind the tenant farmer, a slightly higher price were set for him, or if he were given a discount on the mill-fee to come to the mill, there would be no usury. Likewise, if the landlord were also bound to hire him; for then, because one is bound, the other is also bound, and it is not by the power of an anticipated payment. ¶ And these are the points regarding the first condition of usury, which is that what is received must be estimable in money. The second condition is that it be received "by reason of the loan." Therefore, if a borrower is already my debtor in another way, I can bind him more strictly through a loan agreement so that, along with the borrowed money, he also pays me the other debt he owes. For example, if I lent him ten without witnesses, which he could deny in court, I can lend him another ten on the condition that he signs a formal bond <term>syngrapha: a signed written contract or promissory note</term> before a notary for the whole twenty. For although that obligation is estimable in money, he already owed it to me. By the same logic, it is excluded from the definition of usury if I receive something either by reason of "ceasing profit," or as a gift, or in some other way.

<margin>The second condition of a usurious contract.</margin>
<margin>A famous question. <insert>concerning the hope / let it be / let it be done / must be restored</insert></margin>
¶ At the end of this section, however, it remains to be explained in what form a loan should be repaid so that justice is observed without the crime of usury being committed by either party. For lending has a place only in those things (as was said above, and as is held in the law *mutuum* <note>referring to a specific section of the Roman Digest on loans</note>) which are consumed by use. If, therefore, I lend you ten bushels of grain at a time when it is sold cheaply: must you owe me the same measure I gave you at the time of repayment, when it might be more expensive, or only the price it was valued at when I gave it to you? And vice versa: if it was selling for more when I handed it over, do you later owe me exactly the same measure, or the price at which I would have sold it? The same applies to wine, oil, honey, and similar things. Sylvester treats this under the word "usury," part 1, sections 16 and 17, as do many others, whom in truth I do not see hitting the mark exactly. The response to these matters...

<margin>The solution.</margin>

<summary>Soto examines "cloaked usury," where lenders hide interest behind labor contracts or tied services like using a specific mill. He concludes that any obligation with monetary value attached to a loan constitutes usury unless the borrower is compensated or the obligation is mutual.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Vitoria’s or Domingo de Soto’s (as indicated by the header) exploration of the ethics of lending and contracts. The previous page discussed how merchants and officials might exploit soldiers or use indirect obligations to mask usurious loans. This page moves into the technical distinction between a sale and a loan, particularly concerning fluctuating market prices of commodities and currency.</meta>

<page-num>518</page-num>
<header>F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,</header>

...be clear in its distinctions. First, a loan must be distinguished from a sale. For instance, when you have provided ten measures <term>modios: a Roman unit of dry volume, often translated as bushels</term> of grain during the winter, one must see whether you sold it to me at the price it was then going for, or whether you truly lent it. If you had sold it, I do not owe you grain, but the price. Therefore, if at that time individual measures were worth one ducat, I owe you ten ducats, regardless of the price at which grain is sold later. And thus, if it was agreed between us that I should pay back the same price of the grain, and afterwards a measure is worth only half a ducat, I owe you twenty measures. The matter is clear. However, if it was nothing but a loan, then I am the debtor not of the price, but precisely of ten measures to you, regardless of the coin for which it is sold later. For example, if I received grain in the month of January to be paid back in the same month of the following year, I am bound to measure back to you those same ten measures of the same quality: so that, naturally, the grain is of the same goodness. Nor does it matter whether the market price <note>original: "annona"</note> was far higher when you gave it to me, or much lower. And the judgment is the same for wine and other things consumed by use. For by reason of a loan, I do not owe you the price, but the physical goods in the same species and quality. For this reason, if when I pay you a measure is worth only half a ducat, I satisfy you with five ducats' worth: even though when I borrowed from you, ten measures were bought for ten ducats. But indeed, if you measured out old grain to me, obliging me to measure back new grain to you, it is a usurious loan. For you are seeking grain of a better quality than what you delivered to me. Nor does it matter whether the new grain is sold more cheaply.

<margin>Renovators (Hoarders)</margin>
And for this reason, those storers of grain who long for high prices are branded with the name of "renovators." For they lend grain that is slightly sour and close to spoiling so that new grain may be returned to them. And consider the same in the case of oil and wine and other things: as when you lend sour wine so that sweeter wine may be returned to you. This doctrine, because it is the twin of reason, is also found in civil law: as is evident in the Digest, "On things credited" <note>original: "ff. de rebus cre." referring to the Pandects of Roman Law, specifically Digest 12.1</note>, throughout, and especially in the law regarding wine.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ You ask, however, what if a certain day was not designated for paying back the loan; is it then lawful for the lender not to seek repayment when he sees it being sold cheaply, but to wait for a time when it is at the highest price, so that the grain doubles or triples in value?

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
It is answered that from the nature of the thing, no image of injustice is produced. However, it would be a more evident sign of greed than of charity. I say it is not injustice unless the lender takes pains to ensure that the

<column-break/>

other does not pay before then: for then injustice occurs. Otherwise, it is imputed to the borrower if he did not look out for himself by paying when it would have been to his advantage. But indeed, when a pact is entered into so that payment is not made before a certain time, when conjectures suggest it will be valued at an increased price, it is a usurious contract.

<margin>Objection against the stated views.</margin>
¶ Against this opinion, however, an argument is taken from the valuation of currencies. It would follow, I say, from these things which have been said, that it would be lawful for me to lend you a hundred ducats when they are valued at a lesser amount of silver or copper: and later, while the King’s decree <term>pragmatica: a royal edict or ordinance</term> increases the value of gold pieces, to receive the same weight of gold.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
Sylvester, in the entry on "usury," part 1, section 14, records the Doctors of Law saying that if it is probably doubted whether it might be worth more or less at the time of payment, then the same gold coinage is to be restored. But in truth, either a fallacy blinds me or it blinds them.

<margin>Distinction between the value of money and other things.</margin>
For there stands, if I am not mistaken, a very clear gap between the value of money and the value of other things consumed by use. For while the price of—for example—grain, or wine, or oil increases, the thing itself remains unchanged in itself. And therefore, the same measure must be restored which was received in the loan, in the manner already explained.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
When, however, the value of money increases, the nature of the money itself—insofar as it is money, which is to say the measure of things—increases just as if the measure of grain were increased: as if, for instance, a bushel <term>modius</term> were made larger. And therefore, if when you borrowed a ducat from me it was worth only eleven royals <note>original: "regalia"</note>, and afterwards its valuation was increased to twelve: you do not owe a whole ducat, but eleven silver royals. Exactly as if I were to lend you ten urns of grain while an urn was filled by only twelve small measures, and afterwards it was increased by law so that it holds thirteen small measures, you owe me nothing but the urns which yield precisely twelve.

<margin>Moderation of the above assertion.</margin>
Nevertheless, what we say about the variation of the value of money at different times in the same province would fail if the money were transferred from one province to another. A ducat, for example, in Spain, which is more abundant in gold, is weighed for less silver than in England, where there is a greater supply of silver. Because of this, eleven silver royals are worth more here than there. Concerning this, therefore, the dispute must be put off until the next book, where we must discuss exchanges.

It remains, therefore, that I respond to the arguments which only we two proposed. For the first one of Saint Thomas regarding "ceasing profit" <term>lucrum cessante: the profit a lender loses out on by not having their money available</term> immediately...

<meta>The catchword "statim" (immediately) at the bottom right indicates the first word of the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page distinguishes between a loan (returning the same quantity/quality) and a sale (returning the price), and addresses the ethics of hoarding commodities or exploiting currency fluctuations. Soto argues that if the legal value of money changes, the borrower should repay the original value, not the nominal face value, comparing money to a physical measure like a bushel.</summary>

### Book Six. Question I.

must be explained clearly in the very next section.
Regarding the second point, it is almost the same as what was argued in the fifth place of the preceding section, and which we left resolved there. It is of this nature: A borrower is bound out of a sense of honor <note>original: "ex honestate"</note> to compensate a benefit received; therefore, he can be legally <term>civilly: meaning bound by civil law or enforceable contracts</term> obligated to that benefit by reason of the loan. However, this conclusion has already been denied above. For the law of justice is satisfied by that repayment in which as much is returned to you as you lent; but other obligations of honor must remain free, just as you lent freely.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Therefore, regarding the fourth point, which we made first—namely, whether it is permitted by reason of a loan to bind a borrower to lend in return—Angelus <note>Angelus de Clavasio (1411–1495), a Franciscan theologian and author of a famous manual for confessors</note> responds affirmatively. His reasoning is the same as that brought forward a little earlier: namely, that in such a contract, no loss is given to the borrower. But indeed, we have already shown in that same place that this reasoning is deceptive. For although the benefit of lending is a duty of liberality and mercy, nevertheless the obligation itself is something that can be valued in money <note>original: "aestimabilis pecunia"</note>. Because of this, Saint Thomas, with great insight, denies that it is permitted.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ But is it permitted to lend on this condition: that in the present moment you lend me another thing? For example, I lend you grain so that you may lend me wine? Indeed, from the words of Saint Thomas, it seems this permission can be gathered where he says: it is permitted for someone who is lending to receive some other loan at the same time; however, it is not permitted to bind the person to make a loan in the future. Yet, a difference can hardly be found: for if I cannot bind you to lend tomorrow, how can I bind you to lend immediately? Nor is the response solid if you say that lending in the present is not valuable in money; for even if this were true, the obligation itself is still valuable.

<margin>Solution. Saint Thomas.</margin>
It is responded, therefore, that Saint Thomas does not say that a legal obligation can intervene in the present—namely, that you would not grant a loan to someone asking you unless you bound them legally to lend back immediately. Rather, he assumes, as is the case, that loans in the present are made freely <note>original: "gratuitò"</note>. As in: you lend to me, and I lend to you. And therefore, he says simply that it is permitted to receive a loan.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
¶ For this reason, that appendix of Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), known as Cajetan, a major commentator on Aquinas</note> pleases me in this place: namely, that it is permitted for a guarantor <term>fideiussori: a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt</term> to receive a price in order to act as a guarantor. Since that obligation by which he binds himself to pay in your name can be valued in money, and is consequently salable. But if you object to the contrary: acting as a guarantor is a certain species of a loan; yet if a guarantor were to lend money to a friend, he could not receive a price; therefore, neither can he receive one for acting as a guarantor. This premise, however, is de-

<column-break/>

-nied. For it is one thing to act as a guarantor for you, and another to lend to you. From this it is further inferred that someone, in order to bind himself to be ready to lend to citizens whenever they have need, could accept a salary from the state; for this is not for the loan itself, but for the obligation. And finally, it is gathered from these points that I am not permitted to tie you with the knot of a loan so that you must act as a guarantor for me.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
The fifth argument of Saint Thomas introduces the matter of the contract of partnership <term>societatis: a partnership or company where risks and profits are shared</term>, about which we shall discuss a long question below.

¶ Therefore, regarding the text which we placed in the second spot concerning the use and fruits of a pledge <term>pignoris: collateral or property held as security for a debt</term>, it is answered plainly: when a pledge is productive <note>original: "fructuosum," literally "fruit-bearing," like a field or an orchard</note>, its fruits must be counted toward the principal <term>sortem: the principal amount of the loan, as opposed to interest</term>. Otherwise, those same fruits would be received as a price for the loan, from which the stain of usury would be contracted. This is a caution of both laws <note>meaning both Canon Law of the Church and Civil/Roman Law</note>, as found in the section on usury, chapters 1 and 2, and the Code on the Distraint of Pledges, law 1.

<margin>The first difficulty regarding the fruits of a pledge.</margin>
¶ However, a double difficulty arises from this same law. The first arises from the chapter *Conquestus* on usury, where after it is commanded that the fruits of a pledge be applied to the principal, it is added: "Unless the land itself is a fief <term>feudo: land held from a lord in exchange for service</term> of your monastery." Namely, that if the Church has granted some lands as a fief or in a long-term lease <term>emphyteusin: a type of perpetual or long-term lease of land</term> to someone, and later the holder of that fief pledges those same lands to the same Church, the Church can receive the fruits without counting them toward the principal of the borrowed money. The same is held in the section on fiefs, chapter 1. And yet, this appears to be the crime of manifest usury. There are some, therefore, who think this cannot be defended in any other way than that it was permitted for the benefit of the Church. Nevertheless, this solution is not satisfactory. For the custom and practice of the Church is rather not to exact usury; nor could it do so licitly, as is clear in the chapter *Fraternitas*. And therefore, no other reason can be given than that

<margin>Solution.</margin>
this is the natural condition of fiefs: that whenever they return to the true lord, they return

<margin>The condition of fiefs.</margin>

It is true, however, that it appears close to equity that if the fief-holder, because he made the land better, collected more fruits than he paid in dues, that excess should always go to him, even if he had pledged it. Nevertheless, because he is relieved of that burden of cultivating the land thereafter and making it better, he is also deprived of that excess.

# Sixth Book, Question I.

either one is bound either to pay the dowry or to support her according to her status and condition: for a husband is bound by the law of marriage to support her until he pays her full dowry to her; which ought to be reserved for her heirs as much as is possible. 
<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ However, a doubt occurs to me at present, not at all irrelevant to the matter: whether someone could endow a daughter in no other way than by lending money to the son-in-law: such as if someone were to lend ten thousand ducats <note>A gold coin used as a standard currency in Europe at the time.</note> to a merchant under a contract and obligation that he would marry his daughter. 
<margin>Reason for hesitating.</margin>
For it appears that this is lawful. First, because anyone could (as we were saying) marry a woman without a dowry: therefore, he can do so for the sake of a loan. Likewise, because taking a wife seems to be a work of friendship: for every most prudent man ought to join to himself in marriage one whom he would hold honorably dear; and to ask for friendship in exchange for a loan is not usury, as was said above. Furthermore, if that man were diligent and skilled in business, he would value ten thousand lent 
<margin>Response.</margin>
more than one thousand given. It is responded, nonetheless, that it is not lawful. For while you obligate another to marry by the bond of a loan, since that obligation is estimable at a heavy price of money, you are paying back the use of the lent money (considered separately) into the price of that obligation: namely, in place of the thousand ducats which he would have received as a dowry. Nor does it matter whether he 
<margin>To the arguments made.</margin>
values the loan more or less. And to the other point, it is responded that although through friendship he could marry a wife for free, yet in this case he does not do it for free, but for the use of the money at an estimated price. From these things, it follows as a consequence that Kings or magnates can in no way enjoy the use of cities or villages which they receive as a pledge for a loan beyond the principal <term>principal: the original amount lent, referred to in Latin as the "sors"</term>: nor can they be excused by any reasoning from the iniquity of usury. The remedy, however, is that they should not receive them except as things purchased with a contract of repurchase <note>original: "pactum retrouendendi" — a legal loophole where a loan is disguised as a sale that the original owner can later "buy back."</note>. For then the fruits belong to the buyers. ¶ This, however, should nonetheless not be kept silent. You pledge, for example, a sterile field which was of no use to you: because it was neither fruit-bearing nor greening, nor did you think to cultivate it; but another, to whom you pledged it, cultivates it so that he may at least gather vegetables from it; perhaps he is not to be condemned for not applying it to the principal: since while you suffer no loss, the industry of another ought not to be counted toward the principal—just as if a depositary gains from the use of your money, he owes you nothing. These things, however, must be weighed prudently. For if the profit 

<column-break/>

was of any significance: suppose that the field was not actually sterile, but was not being cultivated due to the owner's neglect, and afterwards it became fruitful through cultivation; I believe the fruits must be counted toward the payment of the principal.

### ARTICLE III.

-> *Whether by reason of emergent loss or* <-
-> *ceasing profit, it is lawful for a lender to* <-
-> *receive anything beyond the principal.* <-

IN the contract of lending, frequent account is taken of emergent loss <term>emergent loss: Latin "damnum emergens," referring to an actual financial loss a lender suffers because they lent the money</term> and ceasing profit <term>ceasing profit: Latin "lucrum cessans," referring to the profit a lender misses out on because their money was tied up in a loan</term>. And therefore it is asked whether, by reason of these things, it is lawful for a lender to receive anything above the principal. 
<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
¶ And it is argued for the negative side. If this were lawful, it would follow that there would be no vice of usury in including such profit in a contract: however, the consequence is false; because since lending is a work of charity, it ought to be done for free: and therefore, while anyone of his own accord lends his money, he ought immediately to detach it from profit for free. Otherwise, let him not lend, since he is not forced. 
<margin>Argument 2. St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued from the word of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential theologian whose "Summa Theologiae" Soto is commenting upon.</note>, question 78, article 2. That which someone does not yet have, he cannot sell: the lender does not have the profit; indeed, it is open to many dangers by which it can be hindered: therefore, he cannot value anything certain for it in a contract. 
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: if a merchant could immediately agree with a borrower concerning ceasing profit, a very wide path would be opened for cloaking usury. Therefore, it is not permitted to grant such a license. 
¶ To the contrary, however, is the fact that no one is bound to inconvenience himself for a benefit provided to another: and it often happens that for the sake of a loan, both a loss occurs to someone and profit ceases: therefore, he can then lawfully keep himself safe and unharmed.

THE question is both controversial among the doctors and dangerous among merchants. It has, however, something certain and discovered, and another part that is doubtful. Therefore, for its understanding, the significance of the terms must be known beforehand. For "emergent loss" is the detriment which the lender suffers solely because of the lending: such as if he was preparing to repair ruinous buildings, or to buy grain in the summer for the whole year: and being moved by the prayers of a friend...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ethics of lending and usury from the previous page. Having established that charging interest for the sake of profit alone is generally forbidden, Domingo de Soto now begins to define the specific legal and moral exceptions where a lender may be compensated for losses incurred due to the loan.</meta>

->F. D. Soto, *On Justice and Right*<-

from honest people, the money borrowed from him, because he himself perhaps has a more serious need, he pulls it back: and if the lender then warns him of his own loss: if afterwards his house collapses without any other negligence on his part, or he is forced to buy grain later at a higher price, or to take out money through interest <note>original: "vsuras"</note> to pay his other debts, that is called <term>emergent loss<note>original: "damnum emergens" — an actual, tangible loss or expense incurred by the lender because they lack the funds they lent out.</note></term>.

<margin>What is lost profit.</margin>
Truly, <term>lost profit<note>original: "lucrum cessans" — profit that a person would have reasonably made if they had kept their money for investment or trade instead of lending it.</note></term> occurs if a merchant lends money that was set aside for business, perhaps even overcome by pleas; or, to speak of what is beyond doubt, if the money is extorted from an unwilling person, or is not paid at the appointed time, the profit which he could have increased ceases.

¶ The question is therefore answered with five conclusions, starting from those that are most certain.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First: when an unwilling lender—that is, against his will—either suffers an emergent loss or a lost profit, he can justly and without any danger of usury demand compensation for it.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Remember that profit only "ceases" in this sense when the money was dedicated to the merchant's business. And the reason is most obvious: because when someone is unwilling, they suffer force, and thus an injury similar to robbery. And to this pertains the law *Cum quidam* in the Digest <note>A reference to the *Digest* of Roman Law, section "on interest" (de usuris).</note>, where the Legal Consultant says: "interest is not imposed for the profit of those seeking it, but because of the delay of those not paying" <note>original: "vsuræ non propter lucrum petentium, sed propter moram non soluentiū infliguntur"</note>. And in the first law of the same section, it is held that if a partner converts common money to his own uses, he is bound to provide interest to his partner. And in the Code <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, another primary source of Roman Law.</note> under the same title, the law *Usuras* states that a buyer who is delayed in payment is compelled to pay interest to the seller on top of the price.

Therefore, this conclusion cannot be called into doubt.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ But whether it could be lawfully agreed between both parties right from the start, that if you do not pay on the appointed day, you will thereafter be bound to pay a certain amount of interest?

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
It is responded first of all that, in the name of a penalty, it can undoubtedly be done. For since the borrower is bound to pay on time, the lender is already deprived of his coins against his will from that moment. And therefore, by the rigor of a just fine, he can compel him, just as a judge would compel him. But whether the same is allowed by reason of lost profit, even if there is a slightly greater doubt, it is nevertheless not to be denied that it is permitted; provided, however, that it is not done in fraud to cover up usury. Specifically, if the lender is truly a merchant living by trade. For he can lend in good faith up to a certain day, and have warned the borrower from that point forward that it is not his intention to continue the loan, but that thereafter he is being kept from his business against his will.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion. If anyone has money committed to trade, and is in any way forced against his will to lend it, he can justly claim back beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note> not only the emergent loss, but also the lost profit. I say "unwilling": because either some force is applied to him, or a fraud is laid. Examples: as if someone should threaten a merchant with death or some other disadvantage unless he lends to him; or if a vassal should prudently and seriously fear that unless he gave a loan to his lord, he would be harassed by him and suffer troubles. For this is a certain species of violence. Or if perhaps a King, with war pressing in, should need to borrow money from merchants: by which reason he could certainly compel them, and they would be bound to obey. In these and that kind of occurrences, I say it is clear that the lender can keep himself free from loss despite such compulsions. And indeed, Canon Law supports this assertion, in the sections on "guarantors" <note>Latin: "extra, de fideiuss. cap. peruenit. & cap. constitutus"</note>, by which it is ordered that if a guarantor pays in the name of the one for whom he stood surety, and incurred another expense or accepted a loss, then he for whose sake he paid should restore him to his right and return him entirely unharmed and immune from every loss.

<column-break/>

¶ However, to get down to the matter, the heart of the question lies where the lender suffers no form of force or fraud, but lends of his own accord when asked. Concerning this, therefore, the third conclusion is applied, of a little less certainty than the ones above.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
He who lends when asked can include a foreseen and defined emergent loss in the contract of the loan. That is, if he fears the ruin of his house, or a high price of grain which he is now prevented from buying, or if he is forced afterwards to pay interest for a debt in which he remains so that he might lend.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
This is the conclusion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 78, article 2.</note>, and it is similar to another which he had asserted in the preceding question concerning a seller, who can add to the price of a thing the loss which he incurs by selling. And for that reason, it is proven by similar logic. For the loss which such a lender suffers concerns his own interest: which he is not bound to accept for the sake of the loan: and therefore he can bargain for his own indemnity. However, we have deliberately moderated the conclusion just as we said regarding selling. Namely, that he lends when asked and warns the borrower. For if he lends voluntarily and silently, the loss must be imputed to himself; since if the other person knew the matter, he might perhaps not want to accept the loan under that condition. And from this it follows that if the loss was not foreseen, nor feared, but after perhaps...

unexpectedly occurs, the borrower is not held liable for it: since he did not intend to return anything except a simple <term>loan<note>original: "mutuum" — a loan of consumable goods like money where the exact same thing is not returned, but an equivalent amount.</note></term>. And by this, let what we have said about being "requested" be understood: for we have signified nothing else than that the borrower, knowing and being prudent, as if wanting to borrow a thing useful to himself from another, is willing to do so even with that loss to the lender. For if it were not for his benefit, he would by no means accept it. Thus it happens that even if one who is about to suffer a loss offers the condition to another out of charity as a friend, he does not thereby become ineligible to receive compensation for the <term>emergent loss<note>original: "damnum emergens" — an actual loss or expense the lender incurs because they lack the money.</note></term>. I say this because being requested or offering, as we are about to say, does nothing in itself to create or remove the character of <term>usury<note>original: "vsuræ" — in this context, any payment required above the principal of a loan.</note></term>.

<margin>Difficulty of the question.</margin>
Up to this point, all things are clear. ¶ Therefore, the entire weight of the question leans toward this: whether <term>lost profit<note>original: "lucrum cessans" — profit the lender would have made if they had invested the money instead of lending it.</note></term> can likewise be received beyond the principal from the same act of lending. For the examination of this, it is worthwhile to set forth this distinction:

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
Money can be considered in two ways: in one way, absolutely according to its common use. And regarding this, everyone agrees that it is not lawful for anyone to receive anything beyond the principal by reason of a loan. The example of this matter is widely evident among all those who are not occupied in business. For this is the use which is not to be calculated separately. In the other way, money is considered as it is subject to the industry of business:

<margin>Opinion of Conrad.</margin>
namely, because the owner has it set aside for trade. And regarding this money, <term>Conradus<note>Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on economic ethics.</note></term> and many later writers say that a merchant can immediately bargain so that the lost profit is added to the principal for himself, even if he is not unwilling, but is requested to lend.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, I establish for myself this fourth conclusion: That lost profit can be included in a contract in this way is not so certain as the patrons of this assertion think; rather, it is both less probable and exposed to very many dangers of usury. And indeed, that it is not so entirely certain is proved by many reasons.

<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
First, you will find no law, whether canon or civil, which permits this: which is certainly not the weakest argument. For since there are so many existing laws that command usury to be paid by reason of <term>delay<note>original: "moræ" — a legal term for a failure to pay on time, which often allowed for interest as a penalty.</note></term>—namely, while the lender or any creditor lacks his property against his will—if this spontaneous contract for lost profit were so clearly licit, a law would not have been lacking to suggest it.

<margin>Second reason. St. Thomas.</margin>
Next, if you consult the ancient doctors, <term>Saint Thomas<note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for Soto’s school of thought.</note></term> denies it, deliberately distinguishing between emergent loss and lost profit. Namely, that it is permitted to put the former in an agreement, but the latter not at all. To this

<column-break/>

opinion is added <term>Scotus<note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian.</note></term> in the 4th book of Sentences, distinction 15, question 2; and <term>Durandus<note>Durand of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334).</note></term> in the 3rd book of Sentences, distinction 37, question 2; and among the illustrious jurists, <term>Innocentius<note>Pope Innocent IV (r. 1243–1254), a major canonist.</note></term> on the chapter *Naviganti* regarding usury. Indeed, among the ancient and grave doctors of either law or theology, you will find no one who asserts it in explicit words, except by reason of delay or some other fault of the debtor. Those, however, who affirm it are Conrad, a recent author, in question 30—and even he surrounds it with fear and trembling with seven conditions. Afterward, <term>Sylvester<note>Sylvester Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523).</note></term> under the word "usury," part 1, paragraph 19, and <term>Cajetan<note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Aquinas.</note></term> in his commentary on St. Thomas 2-2, question 78, and in his *Summa*, defend the same affirmatively. And <term>Hadrian<note>Pope Adrian VI (r. 1522–1523), who was a theologian at Leuven before becoming Pope.</note></term> in his question on usury, although he admits (to use his own word) that it is the "opinion of the moderns."

<margin>The most powerful reason for the preceding conclusion.</margin>
¶ But if we proceed by reason, there is one most powerful reason which fights strongly in my mind against this opinion. "Lost profit" (*lucrum cessans*), as the name sounds, is a man being restrained from profit. No one, however, is restrained unless his will is impeded. Truly, according to the teacher <term>Aristotle<note>Referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 3.</note></term>, only force, fear, or ignorance makes a thing involuntary. Therefore, where none of these intervenes, profit is not properly judged to "cease."

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Certainly, it is a thing difficult to believe: that if a merchant who has money set aside for trade offers it as a loan, he cannot receive compensation for lost profit; and yet, through this alone—that another asks for that same loan from him with the slightest word—he could include that same profit in the contract: since he acts no less spontaneously when requested than if he had approached the other first.

<margin>First argument of the contrary opinion.</margin>
¶ And yet, by this reasoning, the arguments of others are undermined. For first, there is a clear distinction between emergent loss and lost profit: for the former does not depend on industry, but is a mere passive suffering, from which anyone can therefore keep himself unharmed. The latter, however, depends on industry, and if someone voluntarily withdraws his money from it, there is no reason why he should be considered "impeded."

¶ They argue furthermore: after a delay, it is permitted to receive lost profit; but money set aside for trade was of just as much utility before that delay; therefore, the same profit could be sought without ignorance. But you see that this argument "dances outside the chorus" <note>An idiom meaning the argument is irrelevant or misses the point.</note>.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
For we do not deny that that money is worth as much before as after the delay; but nevertheless, it is not "impeded" before the delay as it is afterward. For that injury which occurs after the delay moves the will of the unwilling merchant away from his business: and therefore profit is owed to him. But when he lends spontaneously, he is not properly impeded. And this difference was best perceived by St. Thomas, specifically in the second part of the second part, question 62, article 4, in the solution to the second point,

<margin>Solution</margin>therefore, the same applies to a merchant who lends. For the consequence is denied. Rather, the contrary is proved by this. If indeed you hinder him by force or fraud, you are indeed bound: but if, led by your prayers alone, he wishes to cease his work out of love for you, you owe him nothing. And we say a similar thing in the present case. If, however, he ceases for a price by an agreement made, you bring forward no example relevant to the purpose. And yet, deception lurks in the ignorance of this distinction. For the labors of a hired worker are by their nature let-able for a price and contractable: money, however, is not. For if it is worth anything more, it does not have this from itself, but only from the industry of the possessor joined to it; and for that reason, when he lends of his own accord, he freely strips it of such value. ¶ Wherefore, it is not similar to the case of one who is hindered from attaining a benefit, to whom restitution is owed. For that man does not attain it against his will. Nor, again, is the reasoning equal regarding instruments. For 
<margin>Argument 3</margin>they argue: A craftsman can lease the instruments of his art for a price: but money is also the instrument of the merchant for profit: therefore he 
<margin>Solution</margin>can lease them. For there is a very wide gap: because the use of instruments, since they are not consumed by use, is worthy of a price on its own, just like the use of a horse and a house; which are therefore let-able. But the use of money by itself is not let-able for that use by which it is consumed, but the entire value is born from your industry, which therefore you cannot receive except when you are hindered; and you are only hindered when you cease against your will. For Aristotle calls riches "instruments of happiness" by themselves—namely, so that the virtue of liberality may have a use—but not because they are like the instruments of other arts. ¶ And likewise the dissimilarity regarding a sown field will be evident. For 
<margin>Argument 4</margin>they argue, furthermore, that just as a bushel of grain by itself is worth no more than a bushel, but a sown and budding bushel is estimated to be worth more because of its potential; and therefore not only when it is destroyed by 

<column-break/>

someone through force, but also by agreement it can be sold for as much as it is worth with that potential: so indeed a merchant, they say, can lend money with that potential. Furthermore, however, from a sale 
<margin>Solution</margin>to a <term>loan<note>original: "mutuum" — specifically a loan of goods that are consumed by use, like grain or money.</note></term>, no solid consequence is made. For a salable thing by its own nature is worth a price: a loan, however, ought to be made for free. For—to say this repeatedly—the industry of the merchant is not hindered except when his will is opposed either by force or by fraud. Wherefore, the argument concerning the "cast of a net"—which is declared in the law <note>A reference to the Roman law *Digest* 18.1.8.1, which discusses the "sale of a hope," such as buying the catch of a fisherman before he pulls the net.</note> to be salable in hope—does not pertain to the present purpose. For that thing is salable by itself. This would only conclude that after a merchant has already bought goods, which he has sent to the market, he could sell the profit which is in hope. For it is then like a sown field; and therefore that profit is salable. When, however, you have bought nothing, but lend of your own accord, you have nothing that you may sell. And much less to the point is the argument made concerning a son-in-law receiving the fruits of a pledge beyond the principal; since it has already been proved that he receives those not by reason of lost profit, but on account of marriage expenses. ¶ Besides these, there are other arguments by which it is openly taught how much danger is fueled by that opinion. For 
<margin>The opinion of Conrad carries no small danger.</margin>Conrad and his other supporters surround it with many necessary conditions, as they say, so that the contract may be freed from the dangers of usury. The chief of these is that the merchant ought rather to seek and desire to increase his money by trade than by a loan. For by this they think his will is hindered. For if he prefers to lend, they admit he is not hindered, and thus it is not lawful to receive lost profit. But how weak this condition is, is openly shown. It is no sin to desire that which is lawful in the nature of things; nor does such a desire vitiate a contract. But a merchant having money prepared for business is allowed to receive lost profit for the mere fact that he is requested; therefore he is allowed to desire that someone approach him as a petitioner, so that in that way he may be hindered from trade. If he had so determined within himself: "Unless someone seeks a loan from me, I am unwilling to commit my money to trade," the vice of usury would be plain, because he does not have the money exposed to risk. But while he firmly determines to trade, unless someone seeks a loan from him, I truly do not know, according to the opinion of those men, why the desire that someone seek a loan so that he may receive profit should fuel the vice of usury. And...

He warns that allowing compensation for missed opportunities in voluntary loans risks encouraging usury.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "lost profit" (lucrum cessans) as a justification for charging interest. Soto is specifically analyzing whether a lender can contractually demand compensation for profits they might have made if they hadn't lent the money, even before a delay in repayment occurs.</meta>

<page-num>525</page-num>
<header>Book Six, Question 1.</header>

And so it follows that by the mere fact that the lender is asked for a loan, he is not properly hindered from his own profit; for one is allowed to hope for such a thing. But if this were true, see how wide a path would be spread for usury! For to say that the lender ought to lend because he is overcome by charity, so that he might then be able to receive profit, is a fiction. Indeed, charity does nothing to remove the nature of <term>usury<note>The practice of charging interest on a loan, which was heavily restricted or forbidden by Church law during this period unless specific "titles" like lost profit could be proven.</note></term>. Add to this that there would then be no need for him to wait to be asked; for it would be a greater charity if, knowing a friend was in need, he offered him the money as a loan, even with a contract for <term>lost profit<note>original: "lucri cessantis" — the profit a lender misses out on by not investing their capital elsewhere.</note></term>. For while there is a fear of <term>emerging loss<note>original: "damni emergentis" — a direct financial loss or expense incurred by the lender specifically because they made the loan.</note></term>, it is certainly permitted for one who has money to offer it to a friend, so that if it is in his interest, he may receive the loan back despite such a risk. ¶ Another of their conditions is that labor, expenses, and risks should be deducted from the total sum of the lost profit. However, even this condition, if their opinion were true, is not solid. It is clear that expenses ought to be deducted, because they remain with the merchant. But the same reasoning does not apply to labors and risks. Suppose I am, for example, a merchant living by this trade; you ask me for my money as a loan. <margin>Argument against the recited opinion.</margin> It is argued, therefore, that if I were permitted to receive lost profit even now, I could also receive as much as I would have earned if I had applied my own efforts. For I am ready to expend my labor, and I prefer to make ten in profit by working than eight without labor. I am also willing to undergo risks. If, therefore, these men think that mere prayers are an impediment to my will (so that profit is said to "cease"), surely since I am hindered from my labors and risks, I can demand the whole amount. Indeed, if you hindered a hired worker from putting his labor into a vineyard, you owe him the full penny without any deduction for his labor; for he would have preferred the full penny by working rather than a reduced one by sitting idle. Behold the reasons that have always held me in doubt regarding this matter. And I confess, I would prefer to hold this opinion. But I would consider it enough to leave my reasons to the judgment of others; though I would wish to have patrons who would help me drive away these masked monsters of usury. For this image of "lost profit" has, for many years now, opened up this gap and abyss of usury. <margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin> ¶ Nevertheless, because I do not presume so much as to be the first to utterly reject that opinion, let our fifth conclusion be this: It is not entirely lacking in probability that lost profit can be brought into a contract from the moment of the loan, provided that it truly "ceases" and is not done as a fraud for usury. For it is to be judged as truly ceasing at that point, not

<column-break/>

because you *could* have committed the money to trade, but when you had in fact already firmly decided to put it to use, and specifically that same money which you are now lending. For if you have twenty thousand and you have not decided to commit more than ten thousand to commerce, you cannot seek lost profit from a loan of the others, even though you *could* have traded with those as well. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> The reason for this conclusion that has any probability is this: that after that money has been devoted to your industry, it is valued at so much; and since the other person, knowing this and being wise, wishes to receive it with that burden, it seems you can contract for that price. And then <term>Saint Thomas<note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s theological and legal framework.</note></term> is to be interpreted as saying that it is not permitted to receive the "entire" amount that would have resulted in the actual outcome—because that is not yet certain, and much less how much it could have grown—since this has less certainty; but only as much as it is "in habit," that is, in hope, according to a likely and prudent conjecture. Although, if our reasons have persuaded someone to the other opinion, he will defend himself with excellent judgment by saying that profit never "ceases" properly except in one who is unwilling. And therefore, the arguments proposed at the head of the question will be dissolved by him whose interest it is.

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether whatever profit usurious money has produced is subject to restitution.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a landscape or architectural scene inside the letter frame.</image-desc>
AFTER these things follows the discourse on the restitution of usury. And because no one can doubt that it must be restored, it is further asked whether whatever profit usurious money has produced is subject to restitution. And it is argued on the affirmative side, according to Paul in Romans 11: <margin>First argument.</margin> "If the root be holy, so are the branches." Therefore, by the opposite sense: if the root is infected—as is usurious money—so are the branches (that is, its profits), and they must be restored accordingly. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly: If a moneylender buys some property with usurious money, it must be sold, as is ordered in the Decretals, <note>original: "extrā, de vsur. cap. cùm tu." — Refers to the "Extra" or Decretals of Gregory IX, a major collection of Canon Law.</note> so that the usurious money may be restored from its price. Therefore, by equal reasoning, the profit of that same money ought to be returned to the owner. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Thirdly: A moneylender has no more right to the profit obtained by usurious money than to the money itself; but he acquires no ownership of that money; therefore, he acquires no ownership of the profit, and consequently is bound by the same law to refund it to the owner. ¶ On the contrary is this reason: That which a man has acquired through his own proper industry, with no law forbidding it, he legitimately possesses...

-> F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law <-

...will trust: however, it can happen that a usurer acquires through his own effort <note>original: "industria"</note> what the law does not forbid him to possess: therefore, he is not bound to restore that.

As I stated at the beginning of this question, no one doubts the necessity of the restoration of <term>usury<note>The practice of charging interest on a loan, which was considered a sin against justice in Catholic social teaching of this era.</note></term>; it is accepted as a certain fact. Nevertheless, because the reasoning behind it involves some doubt, this must also be answered. The response will consist of three conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ First: whatever was received as a price by reason of a loan through usury remains subject to restitution. This conclusion was already inferred above in Article 1: namely, from the fact that usury is a sin of <term>commutative injustice<note>A violation of the justice that governs exchanges between individuals, requiring that what is given and what is received be of equal value.</note></term>. This is because in such a case, either money is sold twice, or its use is sold once—which, on its own, is worth no price.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Regarding the profit that subsequently grows from the money or other usurious property, a distinction must be made following <term>St. Thomas Aquinas<note>The influential 13th-century theologian whose "Summa Theologiae" forms the basis of Soto's arguments.</note></term>. For, as has been said, some things are such that their use consists of their consumption—such as grain, money, and so on—while other things are such that their use is not their consumption, like a plot of land, a house, and similar things.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the second conclusion is this: when things that are consumed by use are extorted through usury—such as money, grain, wine, etc.—then the moneylender is not bound to restore anything except the exact amount he received, along with any damages the other party suffered, and any profit that the other party missed out on. However, the fruits <note>profits or yields</note> which he accumulated through those same things by his own effort are free from the obligation of restitution. Suppose you extorted a thousand gold coins from a borrower through usury, to which you later added a hundred through your own business efforts: you owe him only the thousand, plus any damages he incurred because of you, and any profit he missed. The same applies if you seized a hundred casks of wine and multiplied your wealth by selling them. I say you owe only the hundred casks. The reason is manifest: no one owes another more than the damage he caused him. Therefore, he who only stole a thousand owes only that single amount; for what grew through his own effort did not belong to the other person. We must say the same thing below regarding a buyer, who is not forced to buy his own advantage, but rather the seller's loss. And exactly the same applies to a <term>depositary<note>Someone entrusted with the safekeeping of another person's property.</note></term>, who, if he profits by using someone else's deposited money, owes nothing but the original deposit.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: If the moneylender received a "fruit-bearing" thing through usury, he is bound to restore that same thing along with its fruits. For example, if he received a field, he owes not only the field itself but all the crops it produced. And if he received a house, from the leasing of which he acquired ten

<column-break/>

coins, he owes those same coins along with the house. <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> And the reasoning of St. Thomas is that ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> of those things which the moneylender acquired through usury does not pass to him, but remains with the lender. For this reason, the things bear fruit not for the moneylender, but for the other person. The same was said regarding a pledge <note>collateral</note>.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you might argue: Did not the ownership of the usurious money likewise remain with the one who provided it? Why then is the profit from that money not owed to him, just as the fruits of other things are?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is that there is a very clear distinction: those things that are consumed by use are "sterile" by themselves; they do not give birth to fruit. Therefore, although they belong to another, the resulting profit is entirely due to the effort of the person trading with them. Those things, however, which bear fruit by their own nature, bear fruit for their owner.

<margin>Replica.</margin>
What if you argue: If the moneylender were to buy a field with that usurious money, he is bound to restore the field with its fruits? Since he bought it with another's money, it seems to be the same as if he had extorted that field from him through usury; therefore, by the same reasoning, he is bound to restore the profit from that usurious money. The premise is denied. Rather, the fruits of that purchased field belong to the moneylender who bought it, as they are owed to his own effort. Nor is he bound to restore anything but the money; just as if a depositary were to buy a piece of land with someone else's money, he owes nothing but the money.

<margin>A grave question.</margin>
¶ However, so that the understanding of these conclusions—and especially the first—may become clearer, that old question must be examined: whether ownership is transferred through a usurious exchange.

<margin>Opinion of the Gloss.</margin>
For it was the opinion of the <term>Gloss<note>The "Ordinary Gloss," a standard collection of marginal commentaries on Canon Law.</note></term> on that text of Ambrose, "If anyone [charges] usury" (14, question 4), which asserted this. <margin>Scotus.</margin> ¶ Duns Scotus agrees with this (in book 4, distinction 15, question 2, article 3), as does <margin>Adrianus.</margin> Peter of Palude in the same place, and Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI</note> in the question on usury, who says it is the common opinion of the Canon lawyers. <margin>Henry.</margin> And he cites Henry of Ghent in the same opinion (in *Quodlibet* 4, question 27). Indeed, even St. Thomas is cited (in book 4, distinction 15, question 2, article 4). However, St. Thomas does not say there anything except that "some people say this."

<margin>Reason for the previous opinion.</margin>
And the reason for this opinion is that everyone has the free power to give away what is his own; but the borrower gives freely; therefore, he transfers ownership.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
But if you respond, as was said in Article 1, that the gift is not entirely free because it is made by one compelled by necessity, this does not stand in the way: <margin>Replica.</margin> both because one could take a loan at interest without necessity, and also because fear removes the "voluntary" nature of an act much more effectively—and yet, despite fear, ownership is transferred, as is evident in both types of law <note>Civil and Canon Law</note>. Specifically, in the chapter *Abbas* (on things done through force or fear) and the law *Metum* (in the same section). Although a claim for recovery <note>original: "repetitio"</note> is granted...
