<meta>This page continues the legal and theological debate regarding the restitution of usury. The previous page established that charging interest on a loan is a sin against commutative justice. Now, Soto addresses a technical legal question: when a borrower pays usurious interest, does the "ownership" (dominium) of that money actually transfer to the lender? If it does not transfer, the lender is holding someone else's property; if it does, the obligation to return it stems from a different legal principle.</meta>

### Book Six, Question I

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
...and whether such contracts ought to be revoked as void. Furthermore, a marriage contract holds firm even if fear is present, provided it is not the kind of fear that would break a steadfast man. This aligns with the opinion of **Aristotle** in the third book of the *Ethics* regarding a merchant at sea: who, out of fear, throws his goods overboard. In that case, although there is an element of the involuntary mixed in, the casting away is nonetheless "simply spontaneous" <note>Aristotle argues that actions done under duress, like saving a ship by jettisoning cargo, are "mixed" but ultimately voluntary because the person chooses the action in that moment.</note>. Likewise, a borrower does not give money to a usurer as if it were a deposit, or a pledge, nor through a lease—contracts by which ownership is not transferred. Rather, he truly gives it as a loan; therefore, he transfers ownership. Furthermore, if ownership were not transferred, it would follow that every contract the usurer subsequently made with that money would be void—just as if a thief made them with stolen money. Therefore, whoever sold bread, wine, or any other thing to a usurer would be bound to restore the price to the true owner.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these arguments, the negative opinion is beyond doubt. **St. Thomas Aquinas** expressly holds this opinion here in the final words of the article: where he says that the "fruits" <note>In legal terms, "fruits" refers to the profit or offspring produced by property, such as crops from a field or interest from capital.</note> of a thing extorted through usury must be restored because the one who gave them remains the owner of that same thing. It would be nothing other than a quibble to say that while ownership is not transferred for things not consumed by use, it is nevertheless transferred for money. Indeed, the reasoning is the same in both cases. Therefore, St. Thomas, in his solution to the third point, asserts the same regarding money. Because of this, **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI, who was a respected theologian before his papacy.</note> should not have cited him in support of his own opinion, nor indeed should all the legal doctors. For one of them, **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prieras, a prominent 16th-century theologian.</note>, under the word *usury*, section six, says that the opinion of St. Thomas is commonly held by the doctors. But it is their habit to rarely agree even on this: which opinion is "common." And therefore, that word of his—"all"—should deter us very little.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
<margin>Alexander.</margin>
<margin>William of Auxerre.</margin>
<margin>Richard.</margin>
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
¶ Moreover, all the ancient fathers embraced the opinion of St. Thomas: such as **Alexander of Hales** (Part 3, Question 66, Member 4), **William of Auxerre** (Part 3, Treatise 21, Question 1), and **Richard of Middleton** (In Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 4, Article 5). And **Cajetan**, in his first set of *Quodlibets*, made this his third question.

<margin>The first reason in favor of the upcoming assertion.</margin>
But so that the reasons for this opinion may shine forth, it must be presupposed that the "mere delivery" <note>original: "nuda traditio"</note> of a thing is not a certain sign of the transfer of ownership. For so it is held in the *Digest* <note>The "ff" refers to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law.</note> regarding the acquisition of ownership of things, in the law "Never mere" <note>original: "l. Nunquam nuda." A reference to the principle that delivery alone doesn't transfer property without a valid legal cause like a sale or gift.</note>. For delivery transfers ownership only if a sale or a "just cause" has preceded it, on account of which the delivery would follow. This being presupposed, the argument is as follows: If ownership were transferred by a usurious payment, this would happen either by the rigor of the law or by the decision of the giver's will. For there is no other way of

<column-break/>

transferring it. But it is not transferred by law, since every law forbids such a contract. As for the will of the giver, it has already been said that it is not established simply because he voluntarily delivered the money. For we presuppose that he does not give it by reason of friendship or purely as a gift—for that is outside the scope of this discussion—but by reason of a contract of a loan. This contract, however, does not indicate a transfer of ownership, insofar as the *use* of the money is being "bought," which is worth no price on its own. Therefore, there is no convincing argument that the will of the giver is to transfer ownership. Since, therefore, no one is presumed to give a gift unless it is established by clear evidence, it follows that no transmission of ownership occurs there. This is especially true because in deliveries of this kind, which do not have "full will," the very least amount of alienation that can be imagined is what should be believed to have occurred.

<margin>A Scruple.</margin>
<margin>The Solution.</margin>
¶ If you ask, then, why the borrower gives the money, since (as argued above) he gives it neither as a deposit nor as a pledge: the answer is that he gives it because otherwise he cannot "extort" the loan from the lender. And if you press further—saying that he therefore deceives the man—the conclusion is denied. On the contrary, the usurer deceives himself. For once he accepts what he ought not, he himself must see to how he receives it: for that delivery has no specific name other than "usurious giving." There is a similar example of one who, in a shipwreck, throws his goods into the sea. He does not, by that act, abdicate his ownership of them. Therefore, if they are later thrown onto dry land by the force of the waves, they are still his by right.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ Second, and more forcefully: everyone (even those on the opposing side) confesses that if a usurer extorts a field instead of usury, he is bound to restore that same field with its "fruits," as St. Thomas says. No other cause for this can be given than that of St. Thomas: namely, that its ownership always remains with the one who gave it. For if the farm truly belonged to the usurer, even if he had extorted it unjustly, it would produce fruit for him; he would be bound to restore nothing more than the farm itself. But if you say they are owed by reason of "delay" <note>original: "ratione morae." A legal term for damages resulting from a delay in fulfilling an obligation.</note> because the other person is hindered, then it would follow that if the borrower had no intention of farming the field, no fruits would be owed to him—which is false.

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it is argued thirdly: since all laws cry out against receiving usury, the usurer should be denied legal rights as much as possible. If ownership were granted to him, the restitution would be put at risk. For if that "gift" were valid, the usurer could in some way equivocate, denying that he is bound by the bond of restitution, at least until the other party asks for it.

<margin>The fourth reason.</margin>
¶ To these things, moreover, a fourth point is added: that laws are accustomed to [governing] the transfer of ownership...

### F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law,

...hinders the transfer in gifts made for a shameful or injurious cause: such as if you give to an assassin to kill a man, or to corrupt a judge, or for a simoniacal <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling sacred things, like church offices or sacraments.</note> transaction. In these cases, the thing itself is not "saleable." Since the use of loaned money has no price of its own, it is a sign that the laws prohibiting that contract also prevent the transfer of ownership. The borrower, moreover, who gives money not out of friendship but by reason of the loan, never intends to give it in any way other than what the laws permit. Perhaps the reasoning of **William of Auxerre** <note>original: "Altissiodorensis"</note> points to this, as he proves from this that a borrower cannot "gift" the money by reason of such a convention: because it is prohibited by God—specifically, by the natural and divine laws that condemn the contract.

<margin>The author's final argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, I have devised an argument for myself. If the usurer were the owner of the usurious money, it would follow that if he had other older creditors to whom he owed money (not through usury), and he later contracted a debt through usury, and had no other assets except that usurious money, he would be obliged to pay the older creditors first. For if those assets truly belong to him, a truly older debt must be preferred. Yet, no one concedes this. Therefore, the reason why restitution must be made to the victims of usury first is none other than that the usurer does not acquire ownership of that money.

<margin>To the first argument of the opposing party.</margin>
¶ Therefore, regarding the first argument to the contrary, it is granted that this is the reason why ownership is not transferred: because there is no free gift, but rather a payment for the use of loaned money, which is worth nothing. Nor does it matter (as was said above in Article 1) whether the borrower asks for it compelled by dire necessity or follows his own mind; for it is enough that after he decides to seek the loan, he is compelled to give [interest], because he cannot obtain it otherwise. We respond the same way regarding a payment made through fear. For since it is not spontaneous, there is no reason why ownership should pass to the other. Nor do the laws intend the contrary; indeed, they clearly teach this very thing when they establish that such "gifts" are not merely to be revoked, but are to be declared void from the start. We admit, of course, that if you swear to give something to a thief out of fear, you are bound by the nature of the oath; yet, when you hand it over, you by no means

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
transfer ownership.

¶ But what if the borrower, at the usurer's demand, says that he is handing over his money

<margin>The solution.</margin>
along with the ownership? The answer is that if he does not give it out of pure friendship, but for the sake of the loan, no matter what he says or swears, he is not understood to transfer ownership, because the laws prohibit it. It is otherwise in marriage, where if the fear is not the kind that 

<column-break/>

would affect a steadfast man <note>original: "constantem virum"; a legal standard referring to a person of reasonable courage and firmness.</note>, the consent becomes legitimate, because regardless of such fear, no one ought to hand themselves over and bind themselves in such a "blind knot."

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ The second argument has been resolved. But the third—namely, whether the usurer can alienate <note>To "alienate" in a legal sense means to transfer the ownership of property to another.</note> things acquired through usury with such force that those contracts are valid—will be treated more conveniently a little further down.

<margin>To the first principal argument.</margin>
¶ Through these points, the arguments proposed at the head of the question are answered. Regarding the authority of **Paul**, it must be said that the quality of the root, whether good or bad, overflows into the branches because the root has the nature of an efficient cause. Usurious money, however, is nothing but the mere "matter" for one's industry <note>Soto distinguishes between the money itself (which is tainted) and the "industry" or work the usurer does to make that money grow through other business.</note>; and therefore, although the money itself is subject to restitution, its profit is not.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ And by a similar logic, the second argument is answered. For possessions bought with usurious money belong to the buyer, and they bear fruit for him; however, they are encumbered by the debts of usury. Therefore, in the legal chapter *Cum sit*, they are ordered to be sold if the usurer is otherwise unable to pay.

¶ From this, it follows that the *Gloss* <note>The "Gloss" refers to the standard medieval legal commentary written in the margins of Canon Law.</note> on that same chapter did not understand the text. For it deduces from there that things bought with usurious money must be restored; yet the text did not say this, but rather that they are to be sold. This matters greatly. For since those possessions are in the ownership of the usurer, if they are worth more than the usurious money was, that excess—as **St. Thomas Aquinas** teaches here—belongs not to the person from whom he extorted the money, but to the usurer who bought it. Unless, perhaps, something is owed to the victim by reason of "emergent loss" or "ceasing gain" <note>Terms from medieval economics: *damnum emergens* (direct loss) and *lucrum cessans* (lost opportunity for profit).</note>. Likewise, if the possessions themselves had to be restored, their fruits would also have to be refunded with them, which is false. Therefore, there is a vast difference between things being "obligated to debts" and things being "subject to restitution."

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ And from this, the response to the third argument is clear, which argued that the usurer has no more right to the thing purchased than to the money itself. For that is false: since by reason of his industry <note>His work or investment.</note>, he has a right to the thing which he did not have to the money.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ And through these points, another question is dissolved: namely, whether all the assets of a usurer are subject to restitution. For on the same chapter, *Cum tu*, some affirm this (as **Panormitanus** <note>original: "Niccolò de' Tudeschi," a famous canon lawyer.</note> reports), while others deny it.

those things that were extorted through usury remain obligated; but the rest, which were legitimately acquired, are not, because no law, they say, commands it. But **St. Thomas**, in 

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s discussion on the legal status of property held by usurers. This page extends that logic to the assets bought with such money and how obligations for restitution pass to heirs or third-party buyers.</meta>

### Sixth Book, Question 1.

<margin>
The threefold goods of a usurer.
</margin>
...those things which were bought with usurious money; indeed, he affirms that all such things are bound by obligation. Therefore, a distinction must be made. First, the assets of a usurer are of three types. Specifically: those acquired as the actual price of usury; those bought with usurious money; and besides these, any other things he possesses 
<margin>
Distinction.
</margin>
through legitimate inheritance or any other lawful means. Furthermore, an obligation is either personal—namely, that which descends from the person onto their possessions—or "real," which binds a 
<margin>
Solution to the previous question.
</margin>
person by reason of the thing itself. <note>In legal terms, a "real obligation" (obligatio realis) follows the physical object, while a "personal obligation" follows the individual's legal identity.</note> Therefore, things of the first order—for instance, those not consumed by use, which were taken as usury or by theft—remain subject to a real obligation for restitution. This is because the very same items must be returned, since the fixed ownership remains with the original owner. Consequently, this obligation travels wherever the thing itself goes. Indeed, whether they are sold, given away, or possessed by right of inheritance, the person possessing those same things is obligated to restore them to the true owner by reason of the object received.

However, there are other things, whether bought with usurious money or legitimately acquired by the usurer—for example, his ancestral estates. These are not subject to restitution by a real obligation, but by a personal one. For a moneylender who collects usurious copper <note>original: "æs," referring to money or currency</note> through usury becomes liable for restitution, and by reason of his person, so does everything he possesses. There is a very wide difference here: this personal obligation does not pass with the things in the same way a real obligation does, but only to those who succeed the person in their legal standing. For example: if a usurer sells his ancestral estate while he still has other assets with which he could restore the usury, but later falls into poverty and cannot pay, the buyers are free from the duty of restitution. This is because the assets they bought truly belonged to the moneylender. 

On the other hand, if the deceased left some assets—whether those acquired through usury or something else legitimate—even if he lost the entire usurious substance, the heirs are bound to pay the father’s usury by reason of the obligation; not a real one, to be sure, but a personal one, because they succeed to the place of the deceased.

¶ From these points, we can now move toward the contracts of a moneylender, to examine which are valid and which are not—a matter that was sought in a certain previous argument. Indeed, if a usurer does not acquire ownership, it seems to follow that he cannot in any way alienate <note>To "alienate" in a legal sense means to transfer ownership to another person.</note> usurious goods through any contract. To this, we first respond using the distinction laid out above. Specifically, things consumable by use that were received as the price of a usurious loan can in no way be alienated by the usurer; for such a transfer would be void, 
<margin>note †</margin>
since they never came into his legal right. Regarding other things, 

<column-break/>

however—for instance, those consumed by use—the reasoning is different. Truly, if the usurer has other assets with which to make restitution, then even if he has transferred those usurious assets, the contract of transfer holds—whether it is made freely as a gift or under a burdensome bond—because it is not necessary that the exact same items be restored. 

But if he has nothing at all except what he scraped together through usury—or even if the things he has are not usurious but legitimate goods, yet they do not exceed the sum of his debts—then the almost universal answer of the Doctors <note>Refers to the "Doctors of the Church" or established legal and theological authorities.</note> is that all his contracts are void. This is because all those goods are bound by debt: either by a real obligation, if they are of the first kind, or by a personal one, if they are of the latter, because the person is bound to make restitution.

<margin>
Moderation of the common opinion.
</margin>
¶ However, I do not believe I can sufficiently approve such a universal opinion without a certain moderation. For if a contract is made freely—
<margin>A gift.</margin>
for example, a donation—it is clear that it is not valid, since that gift is then exempt from the usury debts. But if it is "onerous" <note>An "onerous" contract is one where both parties give and receive something of value, like a sale.</note>, then I would make a distinction: for if the usurer receives nothing through that contract which he might pay to his debtors, I admit it would similarly be void—such as if he were to provide a dowry for his daughter, because he does not have enough left for himself to pay what he owes justly. The same must be judged if he pays wages to servants, or even if he buys food, which is certain to be consumed by him. See, then, how much danger there is in entering into contracts of this kind with usurers and others who are believed to possess no assets other than those acquired illicitly. 

<margin>
A sale made by a usurer is valid according to natural law.
</margin>
Nevertheless, if he sells something, provided it is not done in fraud, I believe the contract is firm according to natural law, and the buyer is in no way bound in conscience to restitution. For even though the seller sold the thing, he received the price; therefore, he has no less in his assets than before, and he can pay the usury debts from that price just as he could from the thing itself. Therefore, to void a contract, one must look to whether the usurer’s substance becomes less through that contract than what suffices to pay his debts. 

Our reasoning is made clear in this way: suppose a usurer has no more money than his debt; if I then sell him my land, the contract is firm, because he has as much in property as he had in coins. If, therefore, I were to buy back that same land for the same money, why should the contract not be solid for the same reason? Civil law perhaps will rescind it because it presumes fraud, but nevertheless, once that is set aside, there is no reason for the conscience to be troubled. 

<margin>
Regarding the heirs of moneylenders.
</margin>
¶ From here, there is an easy transition to the heirs of moneylenders. For to them derives not only the real obligation, but also the personal obligation of the deceased. I say this is true not only while in the inheritance...

<sig>Ll 5</sig>

<summary>Soto explains the legal difference between "real" obligations (which follow stolen or usurious property) and "personal" obligations (which follow the usurer and his heirs). He argues that while contracts made by a bankrupt usurer are generally void, a fair sale might be valid under natural law if it doesn't decrease the usurer's ability to pay back his victims.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s legal and theological analysis of usury. Having previously established that usurers have a "real obligation" to return stolen property and a "personal obligation" to settle debts, Soto now examines how these debts pass to heirs and introduces the concept of "mental usury"—the internal desire for profit without an explicit contract.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...the same things remain in their original state which were acquired as the price of usury, they are bound to return those same things to their owners because of the "real obligation" <note>A "real obligation" (obligatio realis) is a legal bond that stays with a specific physical object regardless of who possesses it.</note> which travels with the items. However, even if none of those things remain, but the deceased left other legitimate goods from which debts may be paid, the heirs are bound to restore whatever he owed because of the "personal obligation," since they are substituted in his place. I say they are bound in conscience if the goods equal the sum of the debts. Otherwise, it is sufficient if they restore the entire inheritance. In the external forum <note>The "external forum" refers to public law courts, whereas the "internal forum" or "forum of conscience" refers to the soul’s standing before God.</note>, however, if they accept the inheritance, they would be compelled to pay the total—unless perhaps they had declared themselves heirs only to specifically recorded assets.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ There remains now a final reason for doubt: whether each individual heir is bound for the whole amount <note>original: "in solidum"</note>, or only for their proportional share <note>original: "pro quota assis"</note>. For there are diverse opinions among the Doctors of Law regarding this. And

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a prominent Dominican theologian.</note> judges under the entry "Usury," section 6, paragraph 10, that he has sufficiently answered: according to the opinion which holds that all of a usurer's goods are bound by the debts of usury, every single heir is bound for the whole amount. If, however, they are not so bound, each is held for their share. But this distinction contributes little to the matter. For, as was shown above, all the usurer’s goods remain bound, whether by a real or personal obligation. And

<margin>The proposed doubt is resolved.</margin>
therefore it should rather be judged thus: those specific things which were the price of usury, by whichever heir they are possessed, must be returned to the owner. In that case, the other co-heirs are bound to reimburse that heir in proportion to their own portions. If, however, there are other goods, I judge that no one is held except for their proportional share: such that one who was heir to a half-share <note>original: "ex semisse"</note> is held for half the usury, and one who was heir to a third-part <note>original: "ex triente"</note>

<margin>Reason for the stated assertion.</margin>
for a third, and the others similarly for each of their portions. And the reason is this: because a personal obligation does not pass to heirs except by reason of the inheritance; for that reason, the obligation is distributed according to each person's portion of the inheritance. And I hold this even if those goods were bought with usurious money. And so much for the restitution of those things

<margin>Another question.</margin>
which are acquired through "real" usury <note>Visible, contractual usury.</note>. ¶ It remains, however, to answer regarding "mental" usury, whether it binds one to restitution, as Urban III defined in the chapter *Consuluit* in the section on usury. And first, let us suppose what was established from the

<margin>The first foundation.</margin>
previous discussions: that mental usury occurs when, even with no preceding pact, something is hoped to be received by reason of a loan. For when it is hoped for solely by reason of benevolence, the contagion of usury is never contracted, whether that be the principal intention or otherwise. For this has already been 

<column-break/>

shown above, not only by the testimony of Saint Thomas but by clear reason. Secondly, it must be

<margin>The second [foundation].</margin>
supposed that mental usury, although it is always a sin of the heart, never binds one to restitution unless the receipt of usury actually follows. Indeed, even if a pact is made and the lender wickedly strives to squeeze out usury, unless he actually receives it, no obligation of restitution arises, because nothing is owed except to God as satisfaction for the fault. Therefore, the chapter *Consuluit*, where restitution of mental usury is ordered, must be understood in this way. ¶ But the understanding of that same text is not yet sufficiently clear. For there are some who judge that mental usury binds no one to the bond of restitution unless he has insinuated his 

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
wicked mind to the other person. Indeed, Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note> in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 2, Article 2, seems to feel this way. For he says that the intent, without any verbal pact or other equivalent sign showing the debtor that the lender would not lend without hope of gain, does not cause the recipient to hold what belongs to another without a pact; and therefore he is not bound to restitution. And

<margin>Richard.</margin>
Richard <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302), another major Franciscan theologian.</note> appears to be of the same opinion in the same distinction, article 5, question 5: for instance, if a usurer, as is held in the same chapter "The Parable of the Oath," refuses to return the promissory note <note>original: "chirographum debiti"</note> until something beyond the principal is paid to him.

<margin>Scotus's motive: Gregory.</margin>
And Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great.</note> seems to support Scotus in the *Register*. It is also found in 1, q. 2, chapter *Sicut*, where he says: the offering of the borrower brings no stain of fault if it did not proceed from the petition of the one seeking it. Furthermore, this opinion, as it

<margin>Scotus's opinion has no probability.</margin>
stands among authors, holds no probability. For those who insinuate the wickedness of their purpose are not to be judged "mental" but "real" usurers. Since, although they do not enter into an express pact, they nevertheless insinuate it tacitly. For this reason, in the said chapter *Consuluit*, the mental usurer is separated from the one who signifies his mind in that way. Likewise, the reason is manifest

<margin>Argument against Scotus.</margin>
that even without such a sign, usury binds one to restitution: for although you hide your greedy mind, yet while you know the other person gives to you by reason of the loan, then you clearly understand that his giving is not a free donation, but is done for that which is not worthy of a price; and accordingly, you retain what belongs to another against the owner's will. ¶ So that this matter may be clearly open, it must be noted that the receipt of something by a lender from a borrower can happen in four ways. First: if the lender intends to receive it by reason of benevolence, and receives it in the same way; for then it is clear that no usury is forged...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into "mental usury"—where a person lends money hoping for a gift or gain without an explicit contract—and examines the legal obligation to return such gains (restitution) based on the intent of both the lender and the borrower. It references major medieval legal authorities like Hostiensis and Panormitanus.</meta>

### Book Six, Question I.

...there is no sin: it is so far from any restitution being required. Second. If he intends to receive something because of the loan <note>original: "causa mutui"</note>, and in truth receives it so: and this, although no pact intervenes, nor any sign of intention, is beyond controversy a sin liable for restitution: both for the reason just given: and because it is the express determination of the aforementioned chapter "Consuluit" <note>A famous decree by Pope Alexander III in the Decretals (X 5.19.10) regarding the intention to commit usury.</note>.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
However, one doubt strikes me regarding the words of the chapter. For it contains these words: "If he would not otherwise have been about to lend." From which words everyone concludes that a secondary intention of usury does not bind one to restitution, but only the primary and principal intention. Namely, if you would not lend except for the sake of such hope and intention: for if you would lend even without that, they say this is permitted: because this is, as they say, having a "sinister eye" toward profit. Nevertheless, I truly cannot understand this. Indeed, although you would lend without such hope, so that this is not your principal intention, yet afterward while you receive it, you know the other gives it to you by reason of the loan—truly you are not permitted to receive it. Rather, it would be a sin entangling you in the bond of restitution: because you receive what is neither yours, nor what he gives for free.

<margin>The cited text is explained.</margin>
Therefore, I do not otherwise perceive the "secondary intention" of the chapter, excusing one from restitution, except when I do not lend in any way so that I may receive something by reason of the loan: but rather for free: although a thought creeps in that the borrower will bestow something extra upon me: which, however, I am certain not to receive unless he has conferred it freely. Otherwise, even if it were a secondary intention of receiving by reason of the loan, it would be a crime of the heart. ¶ In a third way, profit can happen thus: that the moneylender <term>fœnerator</term> <note>A "fœnerator" is a professional usurer or someone who lends specifically for interest.</note> does not think he is receiving beyond the principal by reason of the loan, but perhaps by reason of goodwill: nevertheless, the other gives it because of the loan. And then perhaps someone might judge that no obligation of restitution emerges: because that intention was no sin. Nevertheless, this opinion must be distinguished and moderated: for as long as that man believed he received it by reason of goodwill, he is free from both fault and restitution. However, as soon as he finds out the borrower did not give it except by reason of the loan, he is bound under the guilt of mortal sin to return it. And the reason is, that he then recognizes it was not a free gift. But truly, because the obligation is not born by reason of the acceptance, but by reason of the thing accepted, he is not bound to restore it unless he still possesses it, or has been made richer by it. Thus, if he consumed anything in good faith, thinking it was his own, he does not owe it. ¶ The fourth

<meta>catchword: The fourth</meta>

<column-break/>

way it can happen is that the lender had a corrupt intention, but nevertheless the other did not bestow it except freely out of liberality. And regarding this branch, there are diverse opinions. For Hostiensis and Panormitanus <note>Two of the most influential medieval canonists: Henry of Segusio (Hostiensis) and Nicolaus de Tudeschis (Panormitanus).</note> on the chapter "Consuluit" regarding usury, and the Gloss on the final chapter regarding simony, and Johannes Andreas in his *Mercuriales* on the rule "Pactum," affirm that an obligation of restitution arises from this. And their reason is that since that intention is a sin, it vitiates the reception, and accordingly, whatever is received is entangled in the debt of restitution. And they mean this even when it is established that the other gave it out of goodwill. For they say that restitution is then not to be made to him, since he gave it for free: but to the poor by reason of the sin. Nevertheless, in this opinion, there is absolutely no probability: for the matter is clear. Regarding the sin, I say, primarily of the thought, there is no doubt.

<margin>Hostiensis. Panormitanus. The Gloss.</margin>
<margin>Reasoning for the aforementioned opinion.</margin>
<margin>The author's judgment.</margin>
Second, neither should this be doubted: that as long as the lender has the consciousness that the other gave by reason of the loan, he is bound to restitution: not indeed simply, but by reason of an erring conscience <note>An "erring conscience" is when a person believes they are doing something wrong (like stealing), even if the act itself is technically legal.</note>: because he thinks he is retaining what belongs to another. And thus far the aforementioned authors speak correctly. However, that he is bound from the reality of the matter <note>original: "à parte rei"</note> is false. And therefore, where it is established that the other did not give by reason of the loan, but gratuitously, although he received it with a most depraved intention, he is entangled in no knot of restitution. And this is manifestly proven.

<margin>Reason for the statement.</margin>
The obligation of restitution arises from no other cause than from damage given to another: for the name itself reveals this. For to "restitute" is to restore another into his own right: but when the borrower confers something out of mere goodwill, he receives no damage, nor is he driven from his right: therefore the other owes him nothing. For the profit which the moneylender acquired does not induce restitution: otherwise, you would be obligated to return whatever was given to you as a gift.

<margin>Another reason for the same.</margin>
Then it is argued: while I snatch my own property from another, which I think is his, even if I then commit theft in my heart, yet if it afterward becomes known to me that the thing is mine, I am bound by no guilt of restitution. Indeed, even if it had been his own, if he afterward made it known to me that he had given it to me as a gift, I would certainly be released from the yoke of restitution: and there is the same reason in the present case. Therefore, nothing was owed to that borrower. If, however, nothing is owed to him, much less to the poor. For restitution, as was already said above, does not fall into the right of the poor, unless either when a wealth of creditors cannot be had, or when the giving itself...

<meta>catchword: itself</meta>

<summary>Soto analyzes "mental usury," arguing that restitution is only required when someone is actually deprived of their rights; if a borrower gives a gift freely, the lender may sin in their heart by desiring profit, but they do not owe legal restitution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "mental usury" and the legal requirements for restitution. It specifically addresses the conflict between laws governing usury (interest on loans) and simony (the sale of church offices), and concludes by examining the liability of agents, judges, and middlemen who facilitate usurious contracts.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right.

[the act] itself is condemned by law, as in the case of **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred things or church offices.</note>: however, that benevolent giving is in no way prohibited. To say, however, that a bad intention deserves that penalty—namely, that the usurer must distribute alms to the needy—is certainly supported by no foundation.

<margin>A Corollary.</margin>
¶ Therefore, conclude from these points that the mere reception [of a gift] by reason of a loan <note>original: "ratione mutui"</note>, and all such reception universally—whether the intention was primary or accidental—obliges one to restitution. Therefore, when **Gregory** <note>likely referring to Pope Gregory IX or a decree in the Decretals</note> said that the borrower's offering does not bring the stain of guilt if it did not proceed from the usurer's request, he meant that it does not stain the usurer with a flaw if he neither asks for it nor knows that it is being repaid to him as a price because of the loan. For when he knowingly and intentionally receives it for that reason, it falls back to the same as if he had asked for it.

<margin>On the argument of Scotus.</margin>
And thus anyone who undertakes his defense must interpret **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval philosopher and theologian.</note> in this way.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, a final doubt here must not be ignored, as it twists the minds of many. For the aforementioned chapter *Consuluit* (on usury) and the chapter *Mandato* (which is the final one, on simony) seem to fight against each other. For this chapter, as has been explained, binds the "mental usurer" <note>Someone who intends to profit from a loan even without a contract.</note> to the bond of restitution. But that chapter on simony says that a **simoniacal affection** <note>The inward desire to buy a church office.</note>, where no contract has intervened, is washed away by penance alone, nor does it obligate one to resign the **benefice** <note>term: "beneficium" — a church office that provides an income</note> which was received with such an affection. And yet, whatever constitutes usury in temporal matters constitutes simony in spiritual matters. Indeed, the crime of simony is more grave.

<margin>Adrian’s solution.</margin>
¶ **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (r. 1522–1523), who was also a noted theologian.</note>, in that question on usury, established this distinction: that since the restitution of a simoniacal price must be made to the Church, the Pope can remit it; it is otherwise, however, with usury [which is owed to a person].

<margin>Adrian’s solution is not quite fitting.</margin>
However, this solution is entirely void: because the Pope there makes no relaxation of a debt; rather, having been asked about the law, he simply answers. He teaches, therefore, that no resignation is necessary.

<margin>The response of others.</margin>
Others say that the chapter *Consuluit* speaks regarding the **conscience**, by which everyone is bound to restore usury; but the chapter *Mandato* speaks only in the **exterior forum** <note>term: "exterior forum" — the public legal system of the Church, as opposed to the "internal forum" of private confession and conscience</note>: namely, that a "mental simoniac" is not compelled in a court to resign his benefice.

<margin>The previous solution is refuted.</margin>
But truly, even this is not satisfying. For even if he is not compelled in a human tribunal, he ought nonetheless to resign in his own conscience; and yet the Pope there settles the consciences through penance alone. **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> and many others comment on various interpretations in that chapter.

<margin>The true solution.</margin>
I judge, however, that the conflict they argue over does not exist. For that chapter *Mandato* perhaps intends nothing else than this: that if someone offered services or gifts to a bishop

<column-break/>

with the intention that, in view and by intervention of those things, he might obtain the priesthood, but later discovers that the office was granted to him not by reason of the gifts, his past guilt is deleted by penance alone. He is not, however, bound to resign: because in truth the granting of the office was not simoniacal. If, however, it were established that the granting was done because of the gifts, perhaps resignation would be necessary. Concerning this, however, we shall examine it in its proper place in Book 9.

<margin>A final doubt.</margin>
¶ After all this, it remains to speak regarding the **cooperators** of usurers, whether they themselves are bound to restore by reason of the reception [of the profit], even if none of the usury remained with them. Such are the usurer’s agents and ministers. But the rule was established at the very beginning of the question.

<margin>The Rule.</margin>
¶ Whoever is truly the **cause** of someone harming another through usury is bound to full restitution. For it is a rule of law that he who provides the cause of damage is seen to have caused the damage himself. And the reasoning is the same for those who participate with a thief. For since, according to **Paul** in Romans 1, not only those who do these things, but those who consent to those doing them are worthy of death, it is much more just for those who are actually the cause.

<margin>Who may be called the cause of usurious depravity.</margin>
Now, those especially are considered the cause who compel borrowers to pay usury—such as if **Princes** should fall into this error, and subsequently **Judges**, even while they dare to do so by the Prince’s command; for such laws would have manifest injustice. And likewise **lawyers**, and likewise all who participate in such a judgment, would be held to restitution. In the same way, **brokers** and **middlemen** <note>original: "proxenetę & intercursores"</note> who seek out borrowers and arrange the usurious contracts between them and the moneylenders. For these are most truly the causes. Likewise **advisors**, as if someone were to persuade a son or friend to enter such a way of life; he would certainly be bound to restore just as if he had favored a bandit with his counsel. I say this because of certain people who think that cooperating with usurers in lending does not cast the snare of restitution, but is merely cooperating in the receiving of profit. For certainly, if profit follows from the loan, the reasoning for both is the same. However, to advise a borrower to *pay* usury is neither a fault nor does it obligate one to restitution: because paying usury is not forbidden in itself.

<margin>What should be thought of the ministers of usurers.</margin>
¶ Concerning **ministers**, however, it is not easy to judge. For those they call **agents** and **factors**, to whom usurers commit their business and who give their money out for interest, are absolutely bound by reason of the reception. All these things are understood if the usurers do not restore the money themselves and are capable of paying. Although, while the usurer [restores] nothing...

### Book Six, Question I.

nothing came to the use of these [administrators], the advice is that they should do their best to see that the **usurers** <note>Those who lend money at interest, which was considered a sin in medieval church law.</note> make restitution. If they do not succeed, I think it is a case for meeting with the creditors to earnestly plead for a remission of the debts or at least a part of them. For then there is a place for mercy especially, if they sinned out of some ignorance. ¶ But since the talk has turned to ignorance, it must be noted that if such administrators happen to be held by an ignorance that completely clears them of all fault, they would not afterwards be bound by the bond of **restitution** <note>The legal and moral obligation to return ill-gotten gains.</note>. For since the obligation of restitution arises only by reason of the taking, or of the thing taken, if the taking involved no fault and the thing does not remain with the administrator, all obligation ceases. Nevertheless, the crime is so blatant that ignorance can hardly excuse anyone entirely. Except perhaps in some cases where the opinions of the weightier **Doctors** <note>High-ranking theological and legal scholars whose opinions carried the weight of law.</note> differ. In such cases, one whose conscience does not prick him to the contrary may listen to Doctors who possess good authority.

<margin>What about servants carrying the money of moneylenders.</margin>
<margin>What about scribes.</margin>
¶ Besides those named, there are other administrators who are not properly considered the "cause" [of the usury]: such as servants who carry and guard the money. For example, a borrower was about to pay interest; the moneylender sends a servant to ask for it and hands it to another to keep; these are not properly the cause, nor would they be bound to restitute. Indeed, I believe the same for **amanuenses** <note>Scribes or secretaries who write what is dictated or copy manuscripts.</note> who enter the accounts of "given and received" into the ledgers. For these men merely serve the memory.

<margin>What about the notary.</margin>
But truly, regarding the public scribe <note>original: "publico scriba"</note> whose instrument provides legal proof, there is a slightly greater reason for doubt. For he confirms by public trust a pact which is the true cause of the usury. And therefore, the most soul-saving advice would be not to sign such pacts. Indeed, if by the power of that document another person were later condemned, the **notary** <note>original: "tabellio"</note> would not be immune from the debt of restitution. Although, since such usurious lawsuits are not admitted into the [secular] court, the danger is not so imminent from that quarter. Unless the notary, knowing the fraud, were to sign the usurious instrument with a hidden wickedness. For instance, if the loan was for a thousand **ducats** <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe.</note> and a hundred in interest, and he attested that the borrower had received eleven hundred as the loan. Then indeed he is guilty of making restitution. ¶ The remaining points that can be applied here regarding restitution are not specific to this kind of restitution, but are common to others. For the usurer is held liable for the damages which the borrower suffered because of the usurious payments. Likewise, there can be a **compensation** <note>An offsetting of debts.</note> of usury.

<column-break/>

As in, if I received from you the same amount of interest which you had extorted from me through a similar injustice, neither remains the debtor of the other. Indeed, in the chapter *Quia frustra* (on usury), he who paid interest is not permitted to seek it back before he himself pays back what he received. To this, if neither the presence of the creditor nor his heirs can be had, restitution must be made to the poor: as **Alexander** <note>Likely Pope Alexander III, a major contributor to Canon Law.</note> established in distinction 3, chapter *Cum tu* (on usury).

## ARTICLE V.

## Whether it is lawful to receive money as a loan under Usury.

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
-> <image-desc>Ornamental initial 'C' containing two hybrid creatures facing each other.</image-desc> <-
**C**onceding that to give a loan at interest is a sin, and the borrower seems to provide the cause for that same evil, it is rightfully asked whether it is lawful to receive money as a loan under usury. For it is argued on the negative side. By the same law, the **Apostle** in Romans 1 condemns those who consent to evildoers as well as those who do the evil themselves; but he who accepts a loan under usury not only consents to the usurious crime, but also provides the occasion, and thereby gives **scandal** <note>In a theological sense, "scandal" is an act that leads another person into sin.</note>: therefore, he sins in every respect.

<margin>The second [argument].</margin>
¶ Secondly. If necessity were to excuse the taking in this kind [of transaction], it would follow that it could also excuse someone placing their own money in a deposit with a usurer. For the necessity could be equal: yet this is in no way excused from crime: for it would be the same as committing a sword to a madman, or a virgin to a lewd man: therefore, it is also not lawful to take up a loan under the bond of interest.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the **Philosopher** <note>Standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> in the 5th book of the *Ethics*, where he teaches that to suffer an injustice is not a crime, but to commit one is: the lender, however, inflicts injustice on the one seeking the loan if he "bites" <note>original: "morsicat" - a common pun on 'neshek', the Hebrew word for usury meaning 'a bite'.</note> him with interest; the other, however, merely suffers it.

---

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Second [conclusion].</margin>
<margin>Reason for both conclusions.</margin>
-> <image-desc>Ornamental initial 'A' with stylized floral patterns.</image-desc> <-
**A**s to the question, it is answered with two conclusions. The first is: No one is permitted to induce one who is not prepared to lend at interest to do so. ¶ The second: It is lawful to borrow under interest from one who is already prepared to lend at interest. Both conclusions are proved at once by a two-part reasoning. No one is permitted to induce anyone to evil. For the primary kind of cooperating in evil is to move and incite someone toward it: since therefore to practice usury is evil, you cannot cast anyone into such a purpose which he did not already have himself. But yet...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral implications of usury, specifically moving into Question 1, Article 5: whether a borrower may lawfully accept a loan from a usurer when they know the lender will commit the sin of charging interest.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

nevertheless, to use the sin of another for a good purpose involves nothing absurd. For even God is accustomed to this. For He uses our sins for good, as <margin>Augustine, *Enchiridion*.</margin> **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western Christianity.</note> clearly teaches in his *Enchiridion*. The same author, writing to **Publicola** <note>A Roman official who asked Augustine about the morality of using oaths sworn to false gods.</note>, says: "He who uses the oath of one who swears by false gods—not for an evil purpose, but for a good one—does not associate himself with the sin of the one who swore by demons, but rather with his good deed of keeping his word. However, if he were to lead him to swear by false gods, he would indeed sin." **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto’s work.</note> adds the example from Jeremiah chapter 41, of the ten men who, in order to ransom their lives from **Ishmael** <note>Ishmael son of Nethaniah, who had assassinated the governor of Judah; the men offered him hidden stores of food to spare them.</note> who wanted to kill them, offered him their treasures. Therefore, just as when someone falls among thieves, although they suffer a wrong from those who wish to slaughter them, they are not being **prodigal** <note>Meaning wasteful or reckless with money.</note> by offering gold to ransom their life; so too must we judge the person who, to provide for their own necessity, accepts a loan subject to interest. <margin>Doubt 1.</margin> ¶ Here, however, certain doubts arise that should by no means be bypassed. The first is whether it is a sin to take a loan from a usurer without any necessity at all. For Saint Thomas seems to affirm this, as he only excuses the taking of such a loan when it is done to relieve one's own necessity or that of another. But this is very easily resolved. <margin>Solution.</margin> Indeed, he who is led by no necessity—or at least no just necessity—to borrow at interest from one who is ready to lend, commits no other sin than that of prodigality, which by its nature is not a **mortal sin** <note>A "deadly" sin that separates the soul from God's grace, as opposed to a venial or minor sin.</note>. For anyone can squander their own property without committing a mortal sin. Nevertheless, from the circumstances, it can become mortal: for instance, if he has a family to support and children for whom he must provide in the future, or if he were a **prelate** <note>A high-ranking church official, such as a bishop.</note> who would cause a scandal. <margin>Inquiry.</margin> But if you ask: what kind of necessity must be pressing to entirely wipe away the fault? <margin>Solution.</margin> The answer is that the necessity does not have to be extremely grave; it is enough that it meets the **decency of one's status** <note>The social expectation that a person lives according to their rank or class.</note> and the dignity of the person. For example, if nobles borrow at interest for the equipment of a **tournament** or to celebrate similar festivities, it is not a sin. Indeed, if they did it for mere pleasure, it would only be a **venial sin** <note>A lesser, pardonable sin.</note>. Although even in this class of nobles it might happen to be mortal: for example, when by this means they contract a massive debt to the very great detriment of their children. Moreover, I believe they sin gravely because they provide the "fuel" for usury and are the cause for all types of commerce to be abandoned and turned into the pursuit of usury. <margin>Scruple.</margin> ¶ Whether it is truly lawful to take a loan at

<column-break/>

interest to conduct trade or to enter into other lawful business dealings? It is said that Saint Thomas answered a Florentine merchant that it was a sin; however, it is not a mortal sin by its nature. <margin>Solution.</margin> Indeed, perhaps sometimes it is no sin at all. For when a person has no other way to establish a livelihood, I do not see why they could not seek an interest-bearing loan to provide for themselves and their family through that trade. However, one thing must not be kept silent at present, which is daily leading toward the ruin of the **commonwealth**. For you may see a huge crowd of men who, having no assets of their own, seek to avoid the **mechanical arts** <note>Manual labor or trades like smithing and weaving, which were often seen as lower status than merchant work.</note>; having found the opportunity through the easy terms of moneylenders, they scrape together loans under usury which they put into business. And suddenly emerging as merchants, they establish a more refined lifestyle. By this reasoning and luxury, they soon betray their own poverty, and having broken faith with their creditors, they cry out that they are unable to pay. These men should certainly be kept away as if they were a public plague, and should be regarded as public robbers. <margin>Doubt.</margin> ¶ This specific reasoning regarding using another's sin for good calls us to a more general investigation: namely, whether it is equally lawful in other matters. And the answer is given through this rule: <margin>Solution.</margin> Whenever that which is requested can be done justly, and is requested for a good reason, even though you know the other person will act wrongly, you are permitted to use your right. An example is the present case: when you ask for a loan from a usurer, you are only asking for that which he himself could provide to you without interest. Therefore, if he charges you interest for the benefit, the fault is his, not yours. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Similarly, in the example from Augustine: when you demand from an **infidel** <note>A non-Christian, in this context specifically referring to someone who does not believe in the "true God."</note> the sworn faith of a treaty they have entered into, they could lawfully provide that oath by the true God; if, however, they swear by false gods, it is attributed to their own impiety. Nevertheless, if that which you demand to be performed by the other cannot be done justly, your request is wicked. For example, if you asked a friend to steal so that he might provide for your expenses, or to wound your enemy so that your injury might be avenged. However, I do not believe this rule is of such universal truth that it does not suffer an exception even without violence. For he who seeks shameful consent from a wretched **prostitute** for a set price is to be condemned for no other crime than simple fornication; for he is not considered to be "moving" that kind of woman to sin, since she is already most ready for such gain. It would be otherwise if he were soliciting a virtuous woman. <margin>Grave Doubt.</margin> ¶ From here, let us take a step to examine another doubt, which is more serious: 

<summary>Soto discusses whether a borrower sins by taking a loan from a usurer. He concludes that while it is generally permitted to use another's sin (charging interest) for a good end (meeting personal necessity or maintaining social status), it becomes a sin if it leads to reckless debt or encourages the destructive culture of usury.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on using the sins of others for a good purpose. Having established that one may borrow at interest for a necessary cause, the author now transitions to the broader moral dilemma of whether one can advise someone to commit a smaller sin to prevent them from committing a much larger one.</meta>

### Question 1 of the Sixth Book

The question is: **Whether it is permissible to advise a lesser evil in order to avoid a greater one.** Just as it is permissible to seek a loan under usury—thereby using another person's sin for a good purpose—so too, would it be proper to dissuade someone from murder (which is good) by persuading them to take a milder form of revenge? <margin>Cajetan.</margin> **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> seems to deny this here, although we affirmed it in passing while discussing the third chapter of Romans. Therefore, we have decided to examine the matter more closely here.

<margin>First argument.</margin> From the negative side, the primary argument seems to be the statement of **Paul** <note>The Apostle Paul, specifically referencing Romans 3:8.</note> in the place cited: "Evil things are not to be done so that good things may come from them." <note>original: "Non sunt facienda mala, vt inde eueniant bona."</note> Since the person giving advice is a cause of the thing they advise, it follows that the one who advises a lesser evil is considered to be doing that evil. And since avoiding a greater evil is a species of "good"—as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose *Nicomachean Ethics* was the foundation of medieval moral philosophy.</note> asserts in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, chapter 1—it appears to follow that advising a lesser evil to avoid a worse one is the same as "doing evil so that good may come."

<margin>Second argument.</margin> Furthermore, it is not permissible for a person to do any evil themselves to avoid a worse one; <margin>Confirmation.</margin> therefore, it is not permissible for you to advise them to do it. This is confirmed: if it were lawful for you to offer such advice to another, it would not be unlawful for you to take that same path yourself. Thus, it would be lawful for you to do evil to avoid a worse evil, which is absurd.

<margin>Third argument.</margin> Moreover, to advise a lesser evil is to lead someone toward evil. But <margin>Thomas.</margin> **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for this text.</note> generally denies that it is lawful to lead another into evil; therefore, such advice is wicked.

<margin>Last argument.</margin> Finally, according to the established rule, it is not permissible to ask someone for something that they cannot lawfully provide. But no one can lawfully commit even a lesser evil; therefore, it is not lawful to ask this of anyone.

<margin>Solution.</margin> ¶ Notwithstanding these points, I believe the teaching is not only just but true and soul-saving, provided the matter is considered with careful perspective. Indeed, because this is a moral issue, the case must be narrowed to these specific constraints: the person to whom you give such advice must be absolutely determined and most certain to commit the graver crime. It must be a situation where, having left no stone unturned, there remains no other way to turn their hardened mind from that purpose except by gently leaning them toward something else where they might "vent their venom." <note>The author uses the metaphor "virus evomat" to describe the release of a person's malicious intent.</note>

Indeed, even if you believed by certain clues that your friend was going to commit adultery tomorrow—which he has not yet decided to do—it would still be a sin to persuade him to commit simple fornication <note>Sexual intercourse between unmarried people, considered a "lesser" sin than adultery in this legal-moral hierarchy.</note> now to quench his passion. Nor, if he had a corrupted nature toward his own sex, would it be lawful to persuade him to have relations with women to uproot that habit. <column-break/> For to prevent a planned evil, or to restrain a corrupt habit, it is not permissible to incline a person toward other vices. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> For there is a rule of Aristotle in the second book of the *Ethics*, chapter 9: that he who errs toward one extreme should be leaned toward the other; but this must remain within the line of virtue. Therefore, it is not permissible to advise a lesser evil except to uproot a mind that is currently fixed in evil with a firm purpose.

Suppose, then, a man is absolutely determined to slaughter another and is prepared for the deed; you have omitted no reasoning to dissuade him. ¶ Regarding the advice you might give him then—to vent his venom with a milder injury—it is <margin>First reason for the preceding assertion.</margin> argued as follows: That advice has a good object and a good end without any sinister circumstance; therefore, it is good. There is no doubt about the end, since it is to avoid homicide. But the same is proved regarding the object. For the object is not—as the opponents falsely think—simply that milder harm (such as a beating with a club, or a slap, or something similar); rather, the object is this conditional: "If you are certain to do one or the other—namely to kill or to wound lightly—do this one sooner." This object is good and consistent with reason. For as the rule of the *Topics* <note>Aristotle’s work on logic and dialectic.</note> holds: "Of two evils, the lesser is to be chosen." This holds true universally, even in sins of fault, as <margin>Gregory.</margin> **Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a foundational doctor of the Church.</note> clearly teaches in the 13th *Distinction*, in the canon *Nervi*. Therefore, since the person advising the lesser of two evils does nothing other than urge that choice, they commit no evil, but advise something good.

<margin>Objection.</margin> But you argue: at the very least, it is not lawful to advise that lesser evil "absolutely" (without conditions). <margin>Solution.</margin> We must distinguish the word "absolutely." If you mean outside of such a case, it is granted. However, in a case where the person is most certain to commit a graver evil—which you cannot persuade him not to do—even if you do not express the comparison but simply advise the lesser, the comparison is always understood: namely, "if you are going to do the other."

<margin>Second reason.</margin> Secondly, this is also clarified: if that advice were evil, it would be primarily because through it another is induced to sin. But that this is false is proved: No one induces another to do that which the other is already most determined to do. That man is already determined to do either this evil or that; therefore, the advisor does not "induce" him to do evil, but to do the *lesser* evil. Therefore, the logic does not follow: "I move him away from the worse by inclining him toward the lesser; therefore, I induce him to evil." On the contrary, in such a case, to induce him to the lesser evil is to induce him toward the good. ¶ Thirdly...

The author concludes it is lawful as a "lesser of two evils" strategy, provided the person is already determined to act and cannot be stopped otherwise.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the debate on whether it is permissible to counsel someone to commit a lesser sin to prevent them from committing a much graver one. Soto is currently critiquing the view of Thomas Cajetan, arguing that the distinction between "proposing a choice" and "giving advice" is logically thin.</meta>

...is argued against **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian.</note>. For he admits that in such a case, it is permissible to propose to that person the "matter" of a lesser evil. It follows from this that it must also be permissible to explain that same matter to him: for instance, that he could wound his enemy more mildly, and in that way satisfy his anger and his honor, while looking out for his own interests and avoiding greater dangers. This is similar to how **Lot** <note>A biblical figure from the Book of Genesis.</note> offered his daughters to the wicked inhabitants of **Sodom** <note>The biblical city of Sodom, whose inhabitants demanded to "know" Lot's angelic guests.</note> so that he might prevent the abuse of his guests. This "proposing of the matter" (to use his term) is clearly a form of advice and persuasion. After all, how can you advise someone on something other than by explaining the reasons that might move them? Indeed, this is also a form of "inducing" them to act.

Therefore, it is a mere fiction—and one that contributes very little to moral behavior—to grant that it is permissible to propose the matter of a lesser evil, yet deny the permission to advise it. For this reason, Lot did not merely "expose" his daughters, but said, "do to them as you please" <note>original: "abutimini illis." Genesis 19:8.</note>. To say that this was only "permission" goes against the structure of the words, which appears to be more than just advice. Consequently, later in his *Summa*, under the word "tyranny," Cajetan plainly admits that it is permissible to advise a lesser evil to avoid a greater one. Thus, either he thought he was not contradicting himself (since in the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*, which Cajetan famously commented upon.</note> in the present article he never denied the permissibility of *advising* a lesser evil, but rather the permissibility of *inducing* one), or perhaps he devised some distinction between "advising" and "inducing" that I simply do not grasp.

<margin>Adrian.</margin> Or perhaps he corrected his opinion. And **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), who was also a noted theologian.</note> in his first *Quodlibet*, question 2, embraces our view. But setting aside authors of this sort who speak simply without full dispute and examination,

<margin>Augustine</margin> there exists the opinion of **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> in his book of *Questions on Exodus*, and he records it in the canon titled "If what is more true" <note>original: "si quod verius," referencing Canon Law (Decretum Gratiani, 33. q. 2).</note>. Speaking of the spouse of an adulteress, he says: "If he is going to do what is not allowed—for instance, either to kill his wife or divorce her—let him commit adultery rather than commit homicide" <note>original: "Si facturus est quod non licet, puta vel vxorem occidere, vel dimittere, iam faciat adulterium, & nõ faciat homicidium."</note>. This is also the expressed

<margin>Chrysostom.</margin> opinion of **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> in his 27th Homily to the People: where he warns that one who is accustomed to swearing oaths should be advised to swear by his own head, so that he does not swear by God. And from the cited Gregorian chapter,

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> the core of the matter is gathered. ¶ Hence, regarding the first of the arguments to the contrary: while it is granted that evil things may not be done so that good results may follow, it is denied that it follows from this that it is illegal to advise a lesser evil. For such an advisor, as has been said, although they are a cause of the lesser evil, is not for that reason a cause of *evil* itself. To suggest otherwise is a most fallacious inference. Rather, they are the cause of a *good choice*: since to turn someone who is fixed on a more wicked purpose toward something milder is truly a good

<column-break/>

act. And the response to the second argument is the same. For it does not follow that because it is not permissible for the other person to do the lesser evil, it is therefore not permissible for me to advise it. For that person, since they have it in their power to do neither, is guilty if they do either one. But for me, because I do not have the ability to move them away from both, it is just to divert them from the more serious sin by advising the lesser one. And from this it follows that I cannot take similar advice for myself: for it is always in my power, when two sins are presented, to avoid both.

<margin>To the remaining arguments.</margin> And as for the other arguments, it has already been shown that advising a lesser evil is not inducing someone to evil, but rather to good. And thus, such a counselor does not ask for what the other person cannot justly provide: for in an absolute sense, they only ask that the person does not commit the more serious evil. For that reason, it is the other person's fault if they refuse to comply except by falling into the other evil. A similar case is seeking a loan under usury.

<margin>Corollary.</margin> ¶ From these points, therefore, conclude that it is permissible for no one to commit even the smallest **venial sin** <note>In Catholic theology, a "venial" sin is a lesser sin that does not result in a complete break with God's grace, as opposed to a "mortal" sin.</note> to avoid a most monstrous evil in another person. For it is a contradiction in terms for something to be "evil" and yet "permissible." Nor is it permissible to advise this to a third party. For this reason, while a tyrant threatens me with death, I ought rather to permit the homicide than to tell a lie. Nor, to avoid the most serious adultery in a young man, would it be permissible for me to induce him toward another woman who is unmarried, so that by knowing her, he might turn away from adultery.

<margin>Whether Lot sinned by offering his daughters.</margin> ¶ But regarding **Lot**, it cannot yet be clearly established from what has been said whether his deed should be excused. Furthermore, **Ambrose** <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD), Bishop of Milan.</note> seems to hold his zeal as excused. And **Peter** in his second Epistle calls him "just." Yet it does not follow from this that he did not sin in that one particular act. Indeed, it is even probable that he did sin. Nonetheless, if you weigh the deed by its own nature, it was certainly in no way permissible, unless you excuse it through ignorance. For it was not a prudent piece of advice, but an indecent thing. The reason is that since the care of his daughters was incumbent upon him, and he was held by paternal right to guard their modesty, he should not have blocked a worse evil by that route. For it has already been said that not even the smallest sin is permitted to you to avoid a very serious one in another. It would be different if, in advising them, he had said: "there are women in the city to whom you can offer your lust." For this reason, the excuse that **Cajetan** 
<margin>Cajetan.</margin> 
weaves for him here—saying that he only "exposed the matter" of a lesser evil—appears to me to be deficient in two ways...

# Book Six. Question I.

<margin>Augustine: How Lot is to be excused.</margin>
...acting. First, because it truly was an induction <note>An "induction" in this context refers to a person being led or persuaded to perform an act.</note>. For he said, "use them as you please" <note>original: "Abutimini enim eis." Genesis 19:8.</note>. Secondly, because that exposure of his own daughters did not befit him. Therefore, the *Gloss* on that passage of Genesis 19—which belongs to **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Western theologian.</note> and is cited in the Canon Law <note>Referencing the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Church laws, specifically Distinction 14.</note>—does not attribute what Lot did to a deliberate plan, but to a "perturbation of the mind." This distress partially mitigated his fault. However, whether he was entirely excused must be weighed according to the knowledge that the people of that age were held to have.

<margin>To the first principal argument.</margin>
It remains, then, to respond at last to the arguments of the negative side regarding the principal question. Indeed, the solution to the first is clear enough from what has been said above. It is denied that he who receives a loan under usury consents to the usurer's sin; he is far from offering the usurer the cause or occasion for sinning. Since the usurer is already prepared to act, the one asking for the loan does not "move" him to sin, just as we were saying regarding the one who advises a lesser evil. Rather, it is the usurer himself who creates the scandal; it would be different if the usurer were not already prepared to do it.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
The response to the second argument is the same as what was said earlier regarding those who enter into commerce with usurers. If a usurer were believed to have no other worldly substance than that acquired through usury, it would certainly be forbidden for anyone to deposit their money with him. For it would then be as if your purpose were for your money to be put out at interest as well—and such a purpose is wicked. But if he possesses more abundant funds, you may, with a sound mind, deposit your money with him for safekeeping.
