## ARTICLE VI.
### Whether the Mount of Piety is usurious.

<margin>What is a Mount of Piety?</margin>
At this point, I have decided to introduce an article regarding the **Mount of Piety** <term>Mons Pietatis: A charitable institution, often run by the Church, that provided low-interest loans to the poor to protect them from exploitative moneylenders.</term>, which seems to incur the stain of usury under the form of a loan. For a "Mount of Piety" is said to be a gathered heap of money destined to relieve the miseries of the poor through loans. However, it operates under the rule that every borrower contributes a small amount of money each month—not, as they say, by reason of the loan itself, but as a "stipend" for the officials appointed to guard and inspect the **pledges** <note>Collateral or items left as security for a loan.</note> and to keep the accounts of what is given and received. Since there is "piety" (charity) in the loan, the question is whether it is infected with the stain of usury because of that collected stipend.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
And it is argued from the negative side: if any usurious iniquity were committed here, it would primarily be because the borrowers pay something beyond the **principal** <note>original: "fortem." The original amount of money lent, excluding interest.</note>.

<column-break/>

But they do not do this by reason of the loan, but rather to support the officials necessary for the business. Therefore, the perversity of usury is far removed from this. The "minor premise" is proved: it is fair that this treasury be kept intact by those who have an interest in it. It is the poor who have an interest; for the wealthy man who donated the money does not care what happens to it after he has already devoted it to such a work of mercy. Nor does it matter to the state, as nothing accrues to it from the fund. Therefore, the burden of guarding the fund falls solely on the poor, for whose benefit it was deposited. However, it could not be kept safe unless loans were made under the security of pledges, and thus with officials added to the business to guard the pledges, sell them after a delay, and keep a faithful account of each item. Therefore, it is the duty of the poor to sustain such officials with their own contributions (*symbols*); thus, all usury is avoided there.

->¶ On the contrary is the fact that they must pay a certain amount every month, and consequently pay more the longer the payment of the loan is delayed. Because this is done to make the loaned money safe—a precaution that certainly serves the business of the lender—it has a certain "appearance" of usury.<-

<margin>The establishment of the Mount of Piety. Pius II. Lateran Council. Cajetan.</margin>
This institution of the Mount of Piety arose in Italy a hundred years ago. For **Pius II** <note>Enea Silvio Piccolomini, Pope from 1458–1464.</note> is recorded as its first approver. Later, it was accepted again at the **Lateran Council** <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517).</note> under **Leo X**; a Bull of approval for it certainly exists. But as **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and Cardinal.</note>—a Cardinal of the same holy Church who was present at that Council—records in a unique treatise on this matter, not all the chapters (rules) of the Mount were approved by that Bull. Rather, they were approved only insofar as they were not contrary to the sacred canons. Thus, no injury is done to the Apostolic See if the reasoning of the Mount is debated. This is especially true because the Pope and the Council, in whom resides the supreme authority to establish both articles of faith and laws of behavior, do not care to "put their sickle" <note>An idiom meaning to interfere or define authoritatively.</note> into defining philosophical disputes as if they were matters of faith—disputes which are drawn not from Sacred Scripture, but from bare philosophy. Such a dispute is the one undertaken to examine which contract is usurious and which is free from this crime. For this is not gathered from Sacred Scripture, from which the Holy See draws its truths, but from the very nature of things. Finally, it is one thing to prohibit usury under these or other censures—which involves not only moral philosophy, but...

<meta>This page continues the transition from general moral dilemmas to a specific economic and legal investigation into the "Mount of Piety" (Mons Pietatis) and whether the administrative fees charged by these charitable institutions constitute the sin of usury.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

As gathered from Holy Scripture, the Apostolic office is distinct; it is one thing to exercise that office, and quite another to examine which contracts are usurious, a task which allows for judgment based solely on the nature of things. And so, although in that same Bull <note>Refers to the Papal Bull *Inter multiplices* (1515) issued by Pope Leo X, which approved the Mounts of Piety.</note> a sentence of excommunication is pronounced against those who preach or dispute to the contrary, it must nevertheless be understood with this clause: namely, if they should attack those chapters which are not contrary to the sacred canons. Otherwise, **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), known as Cajetan, was a leading theologian and cardinal who initially opposed the administrative fees of the Mounts of Piety.</note> would have been condemned; yet when he published a small work in the time of **Pope Leo** in which he did not approve of the Mount, he was not in the least bit rebuked. Therefore, with this declaration we make—that we in no way wish to go against the decrees of the council, insofar as they have been received (since not all the acts of that Lateran Council <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517).</note> were received), or the Holy See, but rather to obey them most holily—I consider it worthwhile to explain the reasons that seem to oppose the Mount, and afterwards to submit how that same Apostolic Bull is to be interpreted.

<margin>The custom of piety.</margin>
¶ Therefore, a **Mount of Piety** <note>A *Mons Pietatis* was a charitable pawnbroker run by the Church to provide low-interest loans to the poor as an alternative to predatory moneylenders.</note> can be established in many ways. First, if someone who possesses the goods of this world, moved by compassion, grants a sum of gold to some city or state—not simply by transferring ownership to it, but by dedicating it to this use of lending. Secondly, if the state either sets aside money for such use from the public treasury or compiles it through the contributions of citizens. For as far as the present matter is concerned, it makes no difference. Nor does it matter whether it is a weight of gold, a supply of grain, or other consumable things.

<margin>Chapters of the Mount of Piety.</margin>
The "chapters" (rules) of the Mount are, first, that money or grain should not be given as a loan except for a fixed time—for example, a year. Otherwise, it would not serve the common good, but would be entirely occupied by a few. Again, it is not fitting for the Mount to dispense funds without the security of collateral <note>original: "pignoratitia cautione."</note>. Otherwise, since the borrowers must be poor, it would very often happen that they would be unable to pay; through such dissipation, the Mount would shortly vanish into nothing. For this reason, collateral is not to be kept beyond the pre-set time, but must be immediately put up for auction <note>original: "sub hasta," literally "under the spear," a Roman term for a public sale.</note> so that the fund may be replenished.

<margin>The root of the present dispute.</margin>
¶ Having established these points, the root of this dispute is essentially one, yet understood in different ways it produces different opinions. The root, I say, is this: that he whose interest it is to keep that capital sum of money safe ought to support the administrators at his own expense. However, there are

<column-break/>

those who think it is in the interest of the poor; and therefore they judge that the contribution made by them—insofar as it is necessary for nourishing the administrators—is immune from the vice of usury. But others, among whom is **Cajetan**, think this is not in the interest of the borrowers, but of the lender; whose burden it therefore ought to be to support his own administrators. And thus, they say that whatever he receives beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem," the original loan amount.</note> is extorted by reason of the loan, or by reason of the delayed payment.

<margin>Conclusion and truth of the question.</margin>
¶ And our conclusion leans toward this opinion. I judge, I say, that such a method of the Mount can in no way be cleansed from the filth of usury. And so that the truth of this opinion may become known, let us first of all use this example, which I believe to be the rule for all.

<margin>The first reason for the conclusion.</margin>
They are argued against in this way: If any wealthy and merciful man, listening to the Gospel, had decided to lend to anyone asking of him—but only upon receiving collateral, and only up to a certain time according to the laws of the Mount of Piety—he could by no means receive anything beyond the principal. Therefore, neither can that which they call the "Community of the Mount" do so lawfully. Let us first demonstrate the premise, so that we may descend from there to the inference. If a lender of this sort receives collateral, he does this not for the benefit of the borrower, but for his own, so that he may make the repayment of his money secure for himself. Therefore, that the same collateral be guarded is in his interest, not the borrower’s. For the borrower would prefer to keep it himself. But because the lender is unwilling to trust him with his money otherwise, he receives the collateral; and thus, by reason of that same acceptance, he becomes the debtor responsible for returning the collateral. And he is responsible for this not merely as a "depositary" <note>A *depositarius* is someone holding an item for someone else's benefit; usually, they are only liable for gross negligence.</note>. For a depositary, because he receives the deposit to be kept not for his own benefit but for the benefit of the depositor, is not held liable simply by reason of acceptance, as was said in Book 4 under the title of "Restitution." For that reason, if the deposit is lost without his own serious fault, he is not bound to restore it. But he who receives collateral is bound by reason of the acceptance; and therefore, even if he loses it through a lesser fault, he is nonetheless held by the snare of restitution. I should say "lesser fault," because if it perishes through no fault of his own, he remains free. For in this place, **Cajetan** appears to be in error, having placed such a gap between collateral and a deposit that he thinks the one who receives collateral is just as bound to restore it by reason of acceptance as if he had received it as a loan or by theft; and thus even if the collateral perishes without any fault of his own, he always remains tied by the rope of restitution. Yet there is a very wide difference. For he who receives a loan acquires ownership of it...

The argument relies heavily on Roman contract law concerning ownership (dominium) and the nature of loans (mutuum).</meta>

# Book Six, Question I.

acquires. Therefore, in whatever way it is lost, it is lost to himself <note>The author is discussing the "risk of loss" (periculum rei). In legal terms, if an object is destroyed through no one's fault, the owner suffers the loss.</note>. However, the **ownership** of a **pledge** <term>pignus: an item given as security for a loan</term> remains with the debtor, just as the ownership of a deposit remains with the depositor. Wherefore, it is lost to the same debtor, as is clear in the express law, *pignus*, under the action of pledge <note>original: "l. pignus. de pigno. actio." A reference to the Digest of Justinian, the foundation of Roman Law.</note>. This holds unless it is lost through some fault of the creditor, as is gathered from the law *quæsitum*, in the Digest on the sale of pledges. For our purpose, therefore, it is enough that the duty of **custody** of the pledge falls upon the creditor.

<margin>*Objection.*</margin>
¶ But if you argue: The benefit of lending yields to the utility of those who receive the loan; and the borrower is bound to keep himself unharmed; therefore, he can do this at the expense of others.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
The fallacy of this argument has already been exposed above. For the benefit of a loan <term>mutuum: a loan of fungible goods like money, to be returned in kind</term> must be granted for free; and therefore, he who lends must accept the burdens that are annexed to lending, namely, to keep the pledge and return it. Otherwise, let him not lend. This is indeed true where the pledge is of such a nature that it might be eaten by moths, such as a garment; or perish for another reason, such as if it is a very precious thing and consequently very dangerous to guard: the lender ought to warn the borrower with a protestation that it perishes at his own risk. But if he wishes the pledge to be cared for, let it be done at his own expense. It is indeed accidental that a pledge is of such a nature. And by the same reasoning, if a lender refuses to trust his money before the borrower binds himself by a public instrument <note>A legal document or contract drafted by a notary.</note>, that document must certainly be prepared by a notary at the expense of that same borrower.

<margin>*Second reason against the Mount of Piety.*</margin>
For the lender asks for nothing but faith <note>original: "fidem," implying credit or trust.</note>, which the other is bound to exhibit at his own loss. And from here a new argument against the Mount is taken. Namely, that which is accidental and peculiar to certain pledges ought not to be turned into a law, such that every borrower should pay a fee by reason of guarding every pledge. Furthermore, what is considered to be of the particular owner regarding the loaned money, it is certain must also be thought regarding that which the state holds ownership of: namely, that it is the state's care to keep it safely.

<margin>*Objection of the opponents.*</margin>
¶ But nevertheless, you argue: Let it be so while the Mount has a certain owner; but it is otherwise in a Mount of Piety. For the reason is far different. Therefore, the inference made above is null. For a fund of this kind has no proper owner besides the borrowers; for the rich man who contributed it abdicated his ownership of it. Therefore, it no longer concerns him to guard it. Nor indeed is the state, or as they say, the community, bound to keep the same Mount, since it

<column-break/>

obtains no benefit from it; nor indeed does it have ownership of it. Suppose, for example, that the Mount was not gathered from the subsidies of the citizens, nor from the public treasury, but was given by a rich man for those uses, who committed the mere administration to the state or to certain persons. Since, therefore, there is no other owner, it follows that the custody of the same treasury falls upon the borrowers.

<margin>*Solution to the preceding objection.*</margin>
Behold the argument of the contrary opinion: it seduces its patrons, unless a contrary reason proves us false. It is proven, therefore, that this money falls back into the same condition of lacking another owner as if it had a certain one. For that money then exposed for lending does not belong to the poor who receive the loan. For it is most obvious that it never came into their ownership, nor is it going to come by that reasoning; rather, they are merely borrowers just as if that money had another owner. Therefore, it no longer pertains to them to guard it than if it belonged either to a private person or to the state.

<margin>*Another argument for the same.*</margin>
From this head, therefore, an argument is taken. The borrowers are not bound to guard it; therefore, the judgment regarding that fee which they then pay beyond the principal is exactly the same as it would be if the same money belonged to a private person. But it has already been shown that in that case it is not lawful to extort that fee; therefore, neither is it lawful where a naked administration exists within the state.

<margin>*Question.*</margin>
¶ But you ask, who then is bound to guard it?

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
It is answered: If it has no other owner, it guards itself. And so no remedy remains but that the expenses be subtracted from the capital of the same fund. But you argue more closely:

<margin>*Reply.*</margin>
Would it not eventually be exhausted?

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
I confess it frankly. And this is what deceived the supporters of the other opinion. From which it follows that whoever thinks to erect such a Mount from his own substance, if he wishes it to be perpetual, must establish stipends by which it may be sustained, or obligate the state to sustain the Mount; otherwise, the Mount will consume itself by lending.

<margin>*Another objection.*</margin>
¶ But on the contrary: That Mount will then perish only to the ruin of the miserable people who were borrowing from it; therefore, it was in their interest to keep it at their own expense.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
The consequence is denied. For by similar reasoning, you would prove that it falls upon the poor to keep the riches of a merciful man at their own expense, who is accustomed to be a defense to them with loaned money. For the labors of his ministers are considered to be done in favor of the poor because

The author concludes that such funds will naturally deplete over time unless sustained by further donations or the state, rather than by fees taken from the poor.</summary>

### Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right.

they themselves receive the benefits of the loan, and that for this reason they are obligated to support the ministers through that contribution, it has already been shown how fallacious that argument is. For by the same reasoning, you could defend many other forms of **usury** <term>usury: the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was strictly regulated or forbidden by Church law</term>. Indeed, as many as are forced by poverty to receive a loan under interest enjoy a favorable benefit. Therefore, to say it again: since a loan <term>mutuum: a loan of fungible goods, like money, where the same value is returned</term> must be granted for free, one should not weigh whose favor the ministers' labors serve based on the fact that receiving a loan is a benefit to the poor. Rather, assuming the loan is made, one must observe whose interest it is to keep the money safe. However, when a borrower is late in paying, it is clear that the **pledges** <term>pignora: items left as collateral</term> must be sold at his own expense and loss.

<margin>Confirmation of the above reasons.</margin>
Our opinion is confirmed by the examples of certain cities in Italy—namely Milan, Brescia, and others, as Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian of the era.</note> reports and as we have heard there—in which the administrators of the Mount are supported by a public salary.

<margin>The final argument.</margin>
¶ However, one argument remains that seems to support the opposite opinion. For even if nothing can be received beyond the principal for the benefit of the loan itself, nevertheless, the **obligation to lend**, as we asserted above, is worthy of a price. I say that someone can receive a salary so that he is obligated to lend; since that "Mount" is bound by such a bond, something is lawfully required from the borrowers for that obligation.

<margin>The response.</margin>
The response is that in this case, no vice of usury appears, provided that the fee is very small and charged solely for this reason—and provided nothing is charged for the care of the pledges, for the written accounts of debits and credits, or for other work of that kind.

<margin>To the principal argument.</margin>
**And** through these points, the response to the argument raised at the beginning of the question is clear. I say it is denied that such contributions are not made by reason of the loan, unless they are made perhaps only for this reason which we just added. And likewise, the Council's Bull <note>original: "Bulla Concilij." Likely referring to the decree of the Fifth Lateran Council (1515) which approved the Mounts of Piety.</note> permits three solutions. The first is (to say it with due obedience and reverence) that not all the acts of that council have been received into common practice and usage. For that decree of the Ninth Session, which was among the most important—namely, that those not performing the Divine Office should return the fruits of their priesthood proportionally and be deprived of their benefices after six months—it is not yet clearly known if it has been observed in practice. 

<column-break/>

Although, because it is so close to divine law, I do not dare to advise entirely against it. The second solution is the one we gave above: namely, that excommunication is not handed down except with the moderation that dispute should be restrained against the chapters, insofar as they are not contrary to sacred canons and natural reason. For a "matter of faith" <note>original: "articulus fidei"</note> was not simply established there.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ But you ask: Would it not be conducive to the Church if all cases being fought over—whether they are usurious or not—were defined by the authority of the Church? For this appears necessary for the salvation of souls.

<margin>The resolution.</margin>
The response is that it is not at all expedient for them to define such things as if they were matters of faith, if they are such that they ought only to be weighed by mere philosophy. This is because the Holy Spirit does not care for the Church except to explain Sacred Scripture and to enact necessary laws. And when there are probable opinions among grave Doctors, whichever one you follow, you have a safe conscience. It is different regarding the immortality of the soul and similar truths, which, although they are disputed among philosophers, are nonetheless held in sacred writings or gathered from them. Finally, the third solution is that the payment which the Bull approves in the Mount of Piety is only that which is paid by reason of the **obligation to lend**; and this, it says, goes toward the support of the ministers.

<margin>Other types of "Mounts" which display a more obvious wickedness.</margin>
¶ However, other types of Mounts which I see in use betray their vice far more openly. For it is customary, especially among the country folk, to gather a supply of grain which is distributed as a loan to the needy without a pledge, and without other business that would require the labor of ministers. Nevertheless, they are burdened with a tax such that at harvest time they must pay back an extra twelfth part of the measure—namely, one *modiolus* for every *seneca* <note>Units of dry measure for grain; the "modiolus" is a small peck and the "seneca" (likely a local variation of *senina* or *sextarius*) is the base unit.</note>. I truly do not see how this can be defended, unless all the townspeople indiscriminately both received the loan and paid that as a sort of free and voluntary tax per person. For if it is not collected from everyone, but only from those who need the loan, it is clearly extorted by reason of the loan.

# SECOND QUESTION:
# On the general nature
# of the contract of buying
# and selling.

## ARTICLE I.
## Whether the contract of buying and sell-
## ing is necessary for the commonwealth.

We established above two main headings by which human contracts are corrupted. Namely, either selling that which has no price <note>original: "nullius est pretij"</note>, or selling that which is precious for more than its just value. Regarding the first vice, under the name of **usury**, we disputed in the preceding question; it follows, therefore, that we should proceed with the discussion regarding the latter. This discussion is inscribed under the heading of **contracts**. And since the contract of buying and selling is the foremost of all and a guide to the others, this second question is established concerning the general nature of such a contract—and thus the first article asks whether it is necessary for the commonwealth.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
The argument for the negative side is as follows: The more simply and sincerely human life were conducted, the more quietly and happily it would be lived. But if there were only the exchange of goods—that is, if things were not sold for money but were exchanged for other things—the life of mortals would be more peaceful and calmer from the tumults which the turbulence of trade brings with it. Therefore, the contract of buying and selling should be removed from the human commonwealth.

<margin>Second argument. Aristotle. Pliny.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Many ages passed without the use of coins, as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose works on ethics and politics were foundational for medieval law.</note> testifies in the 5th book of the *Ethics* and the 1st book of the *Politics*, chapter 6. And **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> says in Book 33, chapter 3, that Servius, the King of the Romans, was the first to stamp bronze with the mark of cattle—from which it is called **money** <term>pecunia: derived from 'pecus' (cattle), reflecting ancient trade before coinage</term>—and afterwards silver was stamped in the year 585 of the City, and gold long after. And in Book 7, chapter 56, he says that Father Bacchus instituted buying and selling. Yet in those ancient ages, life was led more happily, and more safely from frauds and anxieties than we are permitted to live now through these trades. Therefore, this contract is pernicious; far from being necessary.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ To the contrary is the same **Aristotle** in the place cited: where he says that the necessity of human life was the

<column-break/>

inventor of money <note>original: "nummi"</note>, which was to be as a measure and rule of the equity of things. This is also what the **Jurist** <note>Referring to the Roman legal scholar Ulpian.</note> expressly reported in the first law of the Digest, *On contracting a sale*.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, so that we may begin the question from the genus itself, let our first conclusion be: **A contract is an action between two people from which an obligation arises on both sides.** For so **Ulpian** <note>A prominent Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD).</note> says in the law *Labeo*: "A contract is an obligation on both sides" <note>original: "Contractus est vltro citroque obligatio"</note>. This is what the Greeks call **synallagma** <note>original: "συναλλαγμα"</note>, which means "a thing completed." Namely, when I have done something for your sake, and you for mine, having given and received faith on both sides, we have completed the matter and hold it as settled. Wherefore that statement "a contract is an obligation" is not (so to speak) an identical statement, but a causal one, showing the sense which we explained in our conclusion. Because we bargain at a fixed price that I will deliver the goods to you and you will deliver the same price to me, a mutual obligation emerges from the sale.

<margin>In a strict sense, no pact is called a contract.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, it follows from this that in a strict sense, no pact is called a **contract** unless an obligation arises from both sides. Such are: "I give, so that you give"; "I do, so that you do"; "I give, so that you do"; "I do, so that you give." These four are enumerated in the law *Naturalis* in the Digest. Just as in marriage, and in sale, exchange, and other things of that kind. For every contract, if you weigh the matter by its own name, is an **act of justice**, binding both parties together. However, others loosen the name more broadly to include those actions from which a bond arises on only one side, such as a gift <note>donation</note> or a simple promise.

<margin>Baldus. Sylvester. Conradus.</margin>
And therefore **Baldus** <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous jurist.</note>, whom **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Mazzolini (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian.</note> cites under the word "contract," and whom **Conrad** <note>Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian.</note> follows in Question 16, distinguishes the name of "contract" such that it is taken *properly* when the obligation arises from both sides, *improperly* for that which arises from only one side, and *most improperly* when it arises from neither. But in truth, these abusive uses of the term should be driven away from common usage. For this is to alienate names from their native meaning; since neither a gift nor a simple promise pertains to **justice**, but they are acts of **liberality**.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Whence Aristotle says in the 4th book of the *Topics*: "A gift is a giving that cannot be taken back." But a **loan** <term>mutuatio: a loan for use where the equivalent is returned</term>, although Conrad and Sylvester feel otherwise in the same place, does not depart at all from the proper nature of a contract: both because it is a giving so that it may be returned, and because if you promised to lend with faith given, you are bound to give, and the other to return. However, as for those who wish to call it a contract even where there is no force of obligation, but rather...

Mm 3

->### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,###<-

the relaxation of an obligation, they rightly admit that it is—to use their own term—most "improper." An example is found in **formal release** <note>original: "acceptilatione"; a verbal contract in Roman law by which a creditor discharges a debtor without payment</note>: for instance, when a debtor asks a creditor if he holds as "received" whatever is owed to him, and the creditor responds that he does. For this is a payment or remission of a debt arising from a previous contract, rather than a contract itself. ¶ Furthermore, authors multiply the species of contracts more numerously than the art of logic permits. <margin>Scotus.</margin> For **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian.</note> in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 2, distinguishes eight species, and <margin>Gerson.</margin> **Gerson** <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), Chancellor of the University of Paris.</note> in his treatise *On Contracts* lists just as many, though with little difference. <margin>Antoninus.</margin> **Antoninus** <note>Saint Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), a Dominican famous for his work on moral theology and economics.</note> indeed, in Part 3, Title 8, Chapter 2, lists twelve. But <margin>Conradus.</margin> **Conradus** <note>Conradus Summenhart (c. 1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts.</note>—such is his ingenuity—drags the division into thirty species. These, however, are not truly species, but rather an enumeration of things about which contracts can be made. Such material divisions, since they are not contained by the art of the subject, extend toward infinity. ¶ <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> Let our second conclusion therefore be: There are seven species of contracts: namely, **buying**, **exchange**, **lending for consumption**, **ground-lease**, **lending for use**, **mutual lending for use**, and **leasing**. Nevertheless, the first is somewhat reduced to the second, and the sixth to the seventh. For we set aside here the contract of **marriage**, which is a mutual handing over of persons; we are only considering the others which are celebrated regarding external goods, which is the subject of the present treatise. <margin>Sufficiency of the aforementioned division.</margin> Among these, you will find only three orders. Since three things can be considered in such goods—namely, **ownership**, **right of fruit** <note>original: "usumfructum"; usufruct, the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property without destroying it</note>, and **use**—one order consists of contracts by which ownership is transferred; another by which the right of fruit is granted; and a third by which bare use is granted. Therefore, where ownership of a thing is transferred: if it is done for free without any obligation of return, <margin>Donation.</margin> it is a simple **donation**, which is therefore not counted under the name of "contract." To this may be added a free legacy, where there is no debt of justice. If, however, the transfer is not free, three species of contracts emerge: namely, <margin>Exchange.</margin> **exchange**, **selling**, and **lending for consumption**. Exchange <note>original: "cambium"</note> is where a thing is exchanged for a thing: such as bread for wine, honey for oil, leather for cloth, etc. (Though there is a far different reasoning regarding the exchange of coins, as we shall see below). <margin>Buying.</margin> Buying <note>original: "emptio"</note> occurs where ownership is transferred for an estimated price. <margin>Lending for consumption.</margin> But **lending for consumption** <note>original: "mutuatio"; a loan of fungible goods like money or grain where the borrower returns an equivalent amount, not the exact same items</note> is where ownership is transferred so that the same thing or an equal amount is returned. This occurs in things consumed by use, and most especially in coinage. If, however, the right of fruit is transferred while ownership is retained, and not for free but for a price, a third <margin>Ground-lease.</margin> contract is made: this is **emphyteusis** <note>A long-term or perpetual lease of land for a yearly rent, often involving the duty to improve the land</note> or a census-payment. As when you hand over a plot of land to another for an annual payment, either for a time or in perpetuity.

<column-break/>

Although when it is done in perpetuity, the tenant <note>original: "emphyteuta"</note> is said to have **useful ownership**, he does not have **direct ownership** <note>Soto is using feudal legal distinctions between the person who works/enjoys the land (useful ownership) and the ultimate lord/owner (direct ownership)</note>, because it always depends on the true owner if the tenant should fall into a breach of contract. And it is called *emphyteusis*, which means "improvement" <note>original: "melioratio"</note>; for this reason, such a contract was invented in ancient times so that sterile fields, which the owner could not cultivate, might be tilled by the diligence of another. When, however, mere **use** is transferred, then three other species arise. For if you grant the use of a thing for free, so that only the substance itself is restored to you, it is **lending for use** <note>original: "commodatio"; unlike a "mutuatio," the borrower must return the exact same item, like a specific horse</note>. This differs in name from lending for consumption because a *commodatum* is returned in the same specific form: such as a horse, a garment, etc. But a *mutuatio* is returned in either that form or another. For a lender is satisfied with gold even if silver is restored to him. <margin>Distinction between lending for consumption and lending for use.</margin> In reality, they differ in species because in a *mutuatio* ownership is transferred, whereas in a *commodatio* it is not. <margin>Mutual lending for use.</margin> If, however, you grant use not for free but for the use of another thing, that is **mutual lending for use** <note>original: "permutata accommodatio"</note>: as if you lend your horse to another so that he may lend you his mule. <margin>Leasing. Hiring.</margin> If you grant use not for another use but for a price, that is **leasing** <note>original: "locatio"</note>, to which **hiring** <note>original: "conductio"</note> corresponds, whether you lease a house, a horse, or your own labor. See, therefore, how just as exchange is reduced to buying, so mutual lending is reduced to leasing. For exchange (as held in Law 1, *On Contracting Purchases*) is only distinguished from selling in that the price is not separated from the thing, as in a sale, but each thing is considered the price of the other. In the same way, in mutual lending, the use of one thing is the price of the use of the other thing; and because of this, it is a type of leasing. Therefore, neither of these species has peculiar difficulties beyond those in the others to which they are reduced. It would have been enough, then, to number five species, except that for the sake of explanation two others were added. For **selling** is not separated as a distinct species from **buying** by any color of probability; they are, in fact, nothing other than two correlative parts of the same <margin>Corollary.</margin> contract, just like leasing and hiring. ¶ From this, it follows that neither **deposit** nor **pledging**—in which neither ownership nor use is transferred—are contracts in themselves. <margin>What a deposit is.</margin> For a **deposit** <note>original: "depositio"</note> is the placement of a thing with another for the sake of custody alone. Therefore, it is nothing but a type of trust. <margin>What a pledge is.</margin> A **pledge** <note>original: "impignoratio"</note> is the temporary placement of some thing with another to secure the obligation of a contract. For that reason...

### Book Six, Question II. ###

<margin>
Suretyship cannot be called a contract.
</margin>

...tion <note>original: "tione"; likely "stipulatione" or a similar suffix from the previous page</note> it is called a contract, because it is a confirmation of a contracting act, such as a loan or a sale. Indeed, **suretyship** <note>original: "fideiussio"; a legal arrangement where a person takes responsibility for another's debt</note> is not a contract in itself between the guarantor and the person for whom he stands surety, since an obligation arises only on the part of the one acting as guarantor; for the other person owes him nothing if a friend has provided the guarantee for free. But such a guarantee is called a contract by law because it provides the strength of a contract between the debtor (for whom the guarantee is made) and the creditor (to whom it is promised). The same must be said of a **stipulation** <note>original: "stipulatione"; a formal verbal agreement in Roman law</note> if it is taken as a guarantee. If, however, it is taken as a simple commission, it is no contract at all. Yet, as the law more frequently employs the term for that action where someone, having been asked, binds a pledge, then if the other party promises some condition, it is a most true contract, because an obligation is born on both sides. But if the other party is bound to nothing, then—because only the stipulator is bound—even though it is called a contract by law, it is reduced instead to a gift. Behold, they call these species of contracts "named" <note>original: "nominatos"</note> because each obtains its own name. Although "unnamed" <note>original: "innominati"</note> contracts are numerous, they are nevertheless reduced to these types. For all are comprised under those four species established above: **I give that you may give** <note>original: "do, ut des"; one of the four classes of innominate contracts in Roman law, alongside "I give that you may do," "I do that you may give," and "I do that you may do."</note>, etc.

<margin>
Third conclusion. Aristotle.
</margin>

¶ The third conclusion: **Buying and selling** <note>original: "Emptio & venditio"</note> are the contracts most necessary for the republic. This is the conclusion of **Aristotle** <note>Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose *Politics* and *Ethics* form the basis of medieval economic thought.</note> and the legal experts in the places cited in the argument following the question. For in the first ages of the human race, there was only the **exchange of things** <note>original: "rerum cambium"; barter</note>. However, custom and use showed that it was almost impossible for human life to be conducted by that method. For while a shoemaker might need a house, he would have need of a massive pile of shoes to exchange for it—shoes which the master of the house perhaps did not need, requiring instead other things that the shoemaker lacked. And while you, being rich in grain, might need another man's wine, perhaps that other man did not need your grain. Therefore, Aristotle in the *Politics*, Book 1, Chapter 6, calls those nations "barbarous" among whom, even then, the exchange of things persisted without the 
<margin>
The use of coinage.
</margin>
use of **coinage** <note>original: "numismatis"</note> (about which more will be said in the following book). Coinage was therefore marked for this use: namely, that it might be a standard for valuing things, and also a vessel and **guarantor** <note>original: "fideiussor"</note> in the name of the republic, so that whenever you offer it, they may give you the things you need. 
<margin>
The genuine sense of the sacred passage.
</margin>
And I judge this to be the genuine sense of that passage in **Ecclesiastes 10**: *All things obey money.* <note>original: "Pecuniae obediunt omnia"; from Ecclesiastes 10:19. Soto interprets this to mean that money contains the virtual value of all goods.</note> For money, in its power, is all things. For he who possesses money has all things that are for sale. By this reasoning, therefore, buying and selling had their origin in barter. For this reason, since in that earlier contract the thing was not distinguished from the price, it was called "exchange" on both sides. In this current contract, however, the delivery of goods is the "sale," while the receiving of them, once the price has been paid, is the 

<column-break/>

"purchase." Wherefore, **purchase** <note>original: "emptio"</note> is the end or goal of **selling** <note>original: "venditionis"</note>, because this contract is ordained so that everyone may provide for their own necessities. Therefore, as if from the more worthy part, it is called the contract of purchase.
<margin>
Definitions of buying.
</margin>
¶ From these points, a concise definition of selling and buying is elicited, in the establishing of which many have worn themselves out without gathering anything exact. For **selling** is the **dispersal** <note>original: "distractio"; literally "pulling apart," here meaning the alienation of property</note> of a thing for a price; **buying**, however, is the **acquisition** <note>original: "contractio"</note> of a thing for a price. For these are the words of the law, by which is generally signified the transfer of **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> of a thing that is not to be returned, as in the Code, *On the Rescinding of a Sale*, Law 2: *If you or your father dispersed a thing of greater value.* <note>original: "Rem maioris pretij si tu aut pater tuus distraxisti"; a reference to the Roman legal principle of "laesio enormis," protecting against selling items for less than half their value.</note> By this word, the distinction is noted between this contract and **emphyteusis** <note>original: "emphyteusin"; a long-term or perpetual lease of land</note> and **renting** <note>original: "locationem"</note>, in which not ownership, but the use or the "fruit of use" is transferred. Likewise, by that same wording, this contract is distinguished from **usurious lending**. For although the ownership of money is transferred there for a price, nevertheless, since that same money is returnable, it is not properly "dispersed." The phrase "for a price," moreover, separates this same contract from **barter** <note>original: "cambio"</note>, by which a thing is exchanged for a thing.
<margin>
Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>
¶ Through the understanding of these points, the responses to the arguments to the contrary are clear. For the human race progressed from the imperfect to the perfect. And so in the beginning, while it was unrefined, unpolished, and entangled in fewer necessities, it was sufficient for itself through the exchange of things. But later, establishing a more cultured, refined, and adorned life, it found it necessary to devise new methods of commerce, among which the use of trade was most well-advised—even though human greed depraves everything.

### ARTICLE II. ###

->**Whether trade is licit.**<-

Although the simple buying and selling by which each person provides for his own family has been shown to be necessary for the republic, it is not immediately clear whether **trade** <note>original: "negotiationem"; business or commerce for the sake of profit</note> is licit—that is, to buy so that you may resell. Although this question is disputed in summary by **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). The reference is to the *Summa Theologiae*, II-II, q. 77, art. 4.</note> in Article 4, Question 77, it nevertheless seems more fitting to place it here in the order we have established, where it must be discussed somewhat more extensively. It is asked, therefore, whether trade is licit. And it is argued from the negative side: buying and selling were shown to be necessary because not everyone abounds in everything, and therefore it is necessary for each person to buy what he lacks by selling that in which he abounds. Wherefore, purchase 
<margin>
First argument.
</margin>
(as has been said) is the end of selling. Trade, however, is contrary to the nature of this kind of purchase. For a trader does not sell so that he may buy what he lacks, but...

He argues that while barter was the original form of commerce, the invention of money was a necessary advancement for civilization, though trade for profit remains morally complex.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right #

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
...he buys perversely in order to resell: therefore, trade is not permitted. For this reason, Aristotle, in Book 1 of the *Politics*, chapter 6, calls the purchase of things necessary for life—and the sale thereof—"natural contracts" <note>original: "contractus naturales"</note> because of the nature of such a purchase. However, he calls commercial purchases "against nature" <note>original: "contra naturam"</note>, insofar as their end is not the sufficiency of life, but rather profit.

<margin>The Second Argument from Aristotle</margin>
¶ And from this is taken the second argument which the same Philosopher adds in that place. That art which has no predefined or fixed limit is not permitted. But the art of money-changing and profit-seeking—which is the nature of merchants—prescribes no limit to its goal, but rather heaps profit upon profit; therefore, it is wicked.

<margin>The Third Argument</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued that trade is the reason why the prices of things increase: both because goods are reduced to a small number of sellers (which is a cause of high prices) and also because the merchant sells for more than he bought. Therefore, if everyone flocked to the original sellers, they would buy for less. This is what experience teaches everywhere in the use of things; therefore, as something harmful to the state, trade should be forbidden.

<margin>The Fourth Argument</margin>
¶ Fourthly: Moral actions must be judged based on what happens most frequently. Most often, trade is full of frauds, tricks, and deceits; therefore, by its very nature, it is depraved and should be removed from our midst. For this reason, trade has the worst reputation, both in the Holy Scriptures and among the holy Doctors of the Church. Thus David 
<margin>(According to the Septuagint)</margin>
in Psalm 70 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 71:15.</note> says: "Because I have not known trade <note>original: "negotiationem"; some translations read "learning" or "literature" here, but Soto follows the version used in canon law</note>, I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember Your justice alone." It is as if the justice of merchants is not the justice of God. And 

<margin>Chrysostom</margin>
Chrysostom, commenting on that story of Christ in Matthew where He cast the buyers and sellers out of the temple—and this is recorded in Distinction 88, the canon *Ejiciens*—said: "It signifies that a merchant can never please God. Therefore, no Christian ought to be a merchant; or if he wishes to be one, let him be cast out of the church." This is because the Prophet said: "Because I have not known trade, I will enter into the powers of the Lord."

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
And for this reason, it is forbidden to clerics <note>Members of the clergy.</note>, as is clear throughout that entire Distinction <note>A division within Gratian's *Decretum*, the standard textbook of medieval Canon Law.</note>.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
¶ On the contrary is the opinion of Augustine in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, which is recorded in the same Distinction, the canon *Fornicari*. There he says: "It is never permitted for men to commit fornication, but to trade is sometimes permitted and sometimes not permitted: it is permitted for laypeople, but not for priests."

<margin>The Foundation</margin>
For the decision of this question, it must be noted that "business" <note>original: "negotium"</note> is the opposite of "leisure" <note>original: "otio"</note>. It is effectively the same as "without leisure" <note>Soto is using an etymological play on words: *neg-otium* (not leisure).</note>. Hence it is taken to mean labor and occupation, just as we speak of "forensic business" or "domestic business," etc. But more specifically, "to trade" means to practice commerce.

<column-break/>

And this is perhaps a certain *antonomasia* <note>A figure of speech where a descriptive phrase replaces a proper name, or a general term is used for a specific one.</note>, because this art is so entangled with worries that it is most alien to leisure. Therefore, to trade is to buy so that you may resell. 

<margin>What trade is</margin>
Hence, merchants are called "co-buyers" <note>original: "coemptores"</note> because they buy from all places at once, and they are called "traders" <note>original: "mercatores"</note> because, in common usage, "to trade" <note>original: "mercari"</note> is not simply to buy, but to buy for the sake of profit in reselling. Furthermore, they are called "agents" <note>original: "institores"; specifically shopkeepers or those who manage a business for another</note> because, as Ulpian <note>A famous 3rd-century Roman jurist.</note> says, they "press upon" <note>original: "instent"</note> their business. Hence Proverbs 31: "She is made like a merchant ship."

<margin>Two types of trade</margin>
¶ Two types of trade are distinguished: namely, one where a thing is bought so that it may be resold after being changed by industry. But this (as held in the same chapter *Ejiciens*) is not "naked trade" <note>Pure commerce without adding value.</note>, but is to be counted among the other mechanical arts. For just as a craftsman weaves cloth from wool or fashions a sword from iron, so (to give an example) he who is industrious in caring for birds or horses, if he buys a raw animal to sell it as a better-trained one, is judged not so much to be practicing trade as an art. For he who shears cloth, or buys worn-out clothes to sell them after they are repaired, provides something further through his art. Therefore, "pure trade" <note>original: "negotiatio mera"</note>, which we are discussing at present, is that by which someone buys something to make a profit by selling it without changing it in any way.

<margin>First conclusion</margin>
¶ The question is therefore answered with five conclusions. First: Trade is neither good in itself (that is, intrinsically, like the virtue of charity) nor bad in itself (like a lie), but is "indifferent" <note>A technical term in ethics meaning an action that is morally neutral until intent and circumstances are added.</note>. It is like eating, which can be done well or poorly depending on the quality of the end and the circumstances. This conclusion is evident from the quoted words of Augustine. For he says it is not like fornication, but is something that is sometimes permitted and sometimes not.

<margin>Second conclusion</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: If you consider the end of trade in itself—which is nothing other than to make a profit—it carries a certain baseness. This is the conclusion of St. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 77, article 4), which he proves by the second argument taken from Aristotle above. For "making a profit" in itself names nothing necessary or honorable. But if profit is directed toward another purpose, it can be sought lawfully.

<margin>Third conclusion</margin>
¶ And therefore the third conclusion is added: Trade is simply necessary for the state. For not every province abounds in all the things it needs; rather, according to the variety of climates, one land overflows with crops and crafts that another lacks. And conversely, one is rich in things for which another suffers a shortage. Neither could every individual who is in need make such long journeys to bring back the small items they require, nor indeed can all those who have plenty practice the transportation necessary to carry those goods elsewhere...

# Question III of the Sixth Book #

...therefore, those who take care to transport supplies of goods from place to place so they can sell them in smaller quantities <note>original: "minutiùs," referring to retail or small-scale selling</note> to individuals are necessary. And what we say regarding location must also be considered regarding time. For it often happens that at one time there is an abundance of things, but at another, a scarcity; yet a poor man cannot always preserve his own produce. Therefore, unless there were those who bought goods to store them for another time, the **commonwealth** <note>original: "res publica"</note> could not be kept safe and sound. Indeed, while merchandise is being unloaded either in a seaport or in a city, buyers are necessary to preserve that supply for the future, because individuals cannot 
<margin>Question.</margin> 
provide for themselves for the future. But you ask: Would it not be more prudent if the state hired its own officials to undertake this duty? 
<margin>Response.</margin> 
In truth, the state could not conveniently manage so many types of merchandise in this way. Therefore, it considers it more advisable to permit this art among others, and even to encourage it. ¶ And from this follows 
<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> 
the **fourth conclusion**, which St. Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> asks in the said article 4: *It is lawful to sell goods for more than they were bought for the sake of trade.* This is by reason of expenses, labor, locations, and times; for the value of a thing increases according to whether it is improved, or moved to a different place or time. However, I will not easily concede what some assert: namely, that it is lawful for a merchant to sell for more in the same place and time than any other person simply because of the "office" or status he holds. For the **justice of the price** <note>original: "pretij iustitia"</note> has no respect for persons, but is weighed absolutely in itself. Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus, a Franciscan theologian</note> says in Book 4, distinction 15, question 2, that merchants should only earn as much profit as the state would decree for them as a salary. This rule is neither to be despised, nor can it be followed to the letter. But we shall discuss the price of things in the very next article. 
<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin> 
¶ **Fifth conclusion.** The art of trade becomes illicit both due to many circumstances and because it is open to many frauds; furthermore, it is frequently involved in many dangers. First, it becomes illicit by its **object**, for instance, if you buy something that is by its nature unsellable, such as a Sacrament or a priesthood—which, since they are received freely, must be given freely—or something prohibited by law from being sold (about which you may read in the Code under "things which cannot be sold"). Second, by reason of the **person**, such as priests who are forbidden by law from trading, as is clear throughout distinction 88; or by reason of the persons with whom one trades. For it is not permitted for Christians to carry arms to the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims</note> or to infidels, as is clear in the decretals regarding Jews, in the chapter "Ita quorundam" and those following.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, trade becomes indecent by reason of **time**. For example, if it were practiced on a Sunday or another exceptionally solemn feast day, as held in chapter 1 regarding holidays; or in a **sacred place**. For this reason, Christ cast out the buyers and sellers from the temple. These circumstances of time and place would constitute a mortal sin if they caused scandal, but otherwise, not necessarily. Or, if the divine office were hindered in a church, which Christ noted by saying: "Because my house is a house of prayer." For this reason, in the chapter "Decet" regarding the immunity of churches in Book 6, the types of trade especially prohibited in churches are the noise of **fairs** <note>original: "nundinarum"</note> and any kind of marketplace tumult. Outside of these cases, it would not be a mortal sin. For to conduct business in a church by talking, without the display of merchandise, is not a great sin unless it is during the time of the sacred rites or a sermon, although it does not lack indecency. ¶ Regarding other circumstances which do not uniquely corrupt trade but creep into all arts—such as lies and frauds—this must be specifically noted: that commerce, by some spirit of its own <note>original: "nescio quo suo genio"</note>, generates above all other arts and offices 
<margin>An inextinguishable thirst for singular profit.</margin> 
an **inextinguishable thirst for profit**. For farmers and craftsmen living by their trades are content; but merchants, both because they always have money at hand and because this art is very much open to the outcomes of fortune, gape most greedily for profit. In this, they are surely very similar to gamblers. This greed indeed absorbs their minds, nourishes lies, and weaves deceits. And for this reason, St. Thomas says in the same place, in the solution to the third argument, that this art has the "appearance of evil" <note>original: "speciem mali"</note> and is therefore forbidden to clerics. ¶ Furthermore, there is in this matter 
<margin>Another inconvenience.</margin> 
another plague: because trade is practiced without great labor or sweat, and is held in higher honor than the mechanical arts, idle men and those desirous of honor, abandoning other crafts, plunge themselves into this abyss. And they do so not to transport goods from place to place, or to save things for a future time, or to improve them; but for the sake of mere gain, they buy up all salable things so that they may immediately squeeze out a profit. Because of them, since they do not permit a free market, prices are increased. For that reason, they should be driven out and banished from the state and forced into other arts that lack workers. We are speaking of those who forestall citizens ready to buy privately. For those are not to be condemned who, after individuals have bought what is necessary for themselves, purchase the surplus to keep for a time. Nor indeed those who publicly...

...they are prepared to buy those things which the poor are forced by necessity to sell—such as clothing, books, and so on—when they can find no other buyers. However, those who buy up the grain supply <note>original: "annonam," referring to the yearly harvest or grain provisions</note> so that they may resell it in the future, although they are sometimes useful as custodians of necessary goods, are much more often a plague <note>original: "pestiferi"</note>. This is because they cause prices to increase immoderately; therefore, unless necessity demands otherwise, such a market is most rightfully forbidden.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**T**hrough these points, therefore, the arguments made above are very easily resolved. To the first, it is denied that trade fights against the nature of necessary buying; rather, it is its servant. Indeed, through the service of merchants, goods are held as if in a pantry <note>original: "penu," a storehouse for food</note>, laid out for each person in need.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ However, that form of trade which has mere profit as its end—because it makes the soul insatiable—is not only unnecessary but profoundly destructive. Nevertheless, this thirst for gain creeps into the hearts of all mortals. And by this, the second argument is answered.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, we concede that it is necessary for the prices of things to increase in this way <note>due to the merchant's costs</note>; however, on the other hand, even greater losses would occur if every individual had to make long journeys to seek out what is missing in their own city.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, Augustine responds in his commentary on Psalm 70 (which is also cited in Decree 88, canon <margin>Augustine.</margin> "Quoniam") that the vices of merchants are the fault of the people, not the profession. For if trade were to be banished from the commonwealth because of their frauds, by that same reasoning we would have to outlaw farmers and all craftsmen and laborers alike, and drive them from the city. For even a farmer sometimes lies to sell his grain, and a craftsman lies to increase his price. That merchants have a bad reputation in the Sacred Scriptures is explained in the same section by <margin>Cassiodorus</margin> Cassiodorus (canon "Quid est"). He says those merchants are considered abominable who, giving no thought to God's justice, pollute their merchandise through an immoderate greed for money, burdening it more with perjuries <note>false oaths used to trick buyers</note> than with prices. Nevertheless, we cannot deny, as I declared a little while ago, that this art is threatened by much more danger from deceit and fraud than others. Hence Ecclesiasticus 26 <note>also known as the Wisdom of Sirach</note>: "Two things have appeared difficult and dangerous to me. A merchant is hardly freed from negligence, and a huckster <note>original: "caupo," a small-scale trader or innkeeper</note> shall not be justified from the sins of the lips." And in the following chapter: "As a stake is driven into the middle of a joint of stones, so shall sin be squeezed between selling and buying."

<column-break/>

Wherefore in Proverbs 20, the Wise Man says generally: "It is bad, it is bad, says every buyer; but when he has gone his way, then he boasts."

## ARTICLE III.
### Whether the prices of things should be fixed by the judgment of merchants.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' containing a depiction of a seated scholar at a desk, surrounded by books.</image-desc>

**S**ince the first foundation of justice in buying and selling is the price, we must ask in the third place whether it should be fixed by the estimation of the merchants. And the argument is made for the affirmative side. First: <margin>First argument.</margin> It is an axiom among legal experts and a celebrated rule that "a thing is worth as much as it can be sold for" <note>original: "Tantum valet res, quantum vendi potest"</note>; which they note in the law regarding prices in the Falcidian law <note>The Lex Falcidia was a Roman law regarding inheritance and the valuation of estates</note>, and elsewhere often. Therefore, as long as fraud and deceit are absent, it should be the merchants' choice to set the prices for their goods.

¶ Second: In every art, the experts in that field should be believed, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> teaches in the third book of his *Politics*, chapter 7; <margin>Argum. 2.</margin> <margin>Aristotle.</margin> and as the legal expert says in the law *in rem data*, every man is the moderator and arbiter of his own property. Merchants are the experts of merchandise; therefore, it should be left to their judgment to set prices.

¶ Third: Everyone has dominion over their own things, and consequently, free power over them; <margin>Argum. 3.</margin> therefore, anyone can ask for and receive as much price for his property as he can manage to extract. This is found to be the common practice regarding gems and precious objects.

¶ On the contrary, however, stands the law "Pretia" <note>Prices</note> cited regarding the Falcidian law, whose words are: "The prices of things are determined not by the affection or utility of individuals, but commonly"; that is, they are fixed by common estimation.

**T**his question is answered with four conclusions. First: The prices of things <margin>First conclusion.</margin> are not to be valued according to their natural essence, but insofar as they serve human uses. The natural reason for this conclusion is <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> that since the world and what is contained in it were made for man, things are worth as much in civil estimation as they serve humanity. Wherefore Aristotle in the fifth book of his *Ethics*, chapter 5, <margin>Aristotle.</margin> says that "need" <note>original: "indigentia," referring to the demand or scarcity of a good</note> is the cause and measure of human exchange. For if no one needed the property or labor of another, all exchange of human things would cease; therefore, we must measure the prices of things by need.

<meta>catchword: Living things (Viuentia)</meta>

<summary>Soto defends the necessity of merchants despite the moral risks of the profession, then begins a discussion on price theory, arguing that the value of a good is determined by human utility and common estimation rather than its inherent nature.</summary>

### Question II of the Sixth Book

Living things are by their very nature more excellent than those devoid of life; nevertheless, as Saint Augustine says (in Book 11, Chapter 16 of *The City of God*), a man would rather have grain in his house than mice. It is common for a house to be sold for more than a horse, and sometimes a horse for more than a servant—even though, regarding the nature of man, nothing in the realm of physical bodies can be compared to him in value. Furthermore, when we speak of "need" <note>original: "indigentia"</note>, we also include the "ornament of the state" <note>original: "ornatum reipublicæ," referring to things that enhance public life beyond mere survival</note>, so that we may encompass everything which can be of use to humans for pleasure and splendor as well as for the necessities of life.

<margin>The second conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The second conclusion.** To discover the just price of a thing, one must draw from many reasons, which fall into a threefold order. First, one must consider the necessity of the item, then its abundance or scarcity; second, the labor, care, industry, and dangers involved in the business. Furthermore, one must consider whether the goods have changed for the better or worse, the frequency of buyers and sellers, and other matters of this kind which any prudent man can observe.

<margin>The third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The third conclusion.** Since the just price of things is twofold—namely, one being legal <note>original: "legitimum"</note> and the other natural—the legal just price consists in an "indivisible point" <note>original: "in indivisibili," meaning it is fixed and cannot vary</note>, whereas the natural or "arbitrary" price does not; rather, it exists within a "divisible range" <note>original: "in latitudine divisibili," meaning there is a high, middle, and low end of fairness</note>. The legal just price is that which is established by the law of the prince; the arbitrary or natural price runs when it has not been established by law. This distinction comes from Aristotle in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, Chapter 7, concerning natural and legal justice.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
¶ To understand this conclusion, it must be noted that estimating those merits and causes for establishing the prices of things belongs primarily to the state <note>original: "rem publicam"</note> and its governors. They ought to weigh all the factors mentioned above and set specific prices for each type of merchandise. But because this is impossible in all cases, it is left to the estimation of the buyers and sellers. We call this the "natural price" because it follows the nature of things as they are adapted for use. Therefore, where the price is set by law—for instance, if a measure <note>original: "modius," a Roman dry measure similar to a peck or bushel</note> of grain or wine, or an ell <note>original: "ulna," a unit of length for fabric</note> of cloth is sold for ten—then the addition of even a single small coin <note>original: "oboli," a tiny fraction of currency</note> is not permitted. It is a mortal sin if a notable excess is added, requiring restitution; and if the excess is very small, it will be a venial sin. This is why we say the price consists in an indivisible point. This is what Aristotle means in the cited passage: that "legal justice" is that which matters nothing before it is established, but matters once it has been set. However, a price not set by law is not indivisible, but has a "latitude" or range of justice, of which one

<column-break/>

<margin>Rigid, pious, and moderate price. Both eleven and nine. But the reason for this is that human prudence, by which the price is estimated through consideration of the aforementioned factors, cannot hit the mark exactly like a pinpoint, but only through a certain judgment. Just as Aristotle says in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, Chapter 6, concerning virtue, it consists in a mean as defined by a prudent man himself. And thus, as long as the state—in which such authority resides—does not indicate a specific point, justice remains more relaxed, having a range of price.</margin>
extreme is called "rigid," the other "pious," and the middle "moderate." Thus, a thing which is sold justly for ten is also sold justly for eleven or for nine. But the reason for this is that human prudence, by which the price is estimated through consideration of the aforementioned factors, cannot hit the mark exactly like a pinpoint, but only through a certain judgment <note>original: "arbitramento," a discretionary assessment</note>. Just as Aristotle says in Book 2 of the *Ethics*, Chapter 6, concerning virtue, it consists in a mean <note>the balanced "middle way"</note> as defined by a prudent man himself. And thus, as long as the state—in which such authority resides—does not indicate a specific point, justice remains more relaxed, having a range of price.

<margin>The first deduction.</margin>
¶ From which it follows, first, that it is permitted to sell a thing more dearly when the money is lent <note>on credit</note> than when it is paid in cash; more to an enemy than to a friend; and finally, more to a rich man than to a poor one.

<margin>The second.</margin>
¶ It follows, secondly, regarding the sense of that law "In causæ" in the *Digest* <note>original: "ff. de minor.," referring to the Pandects or Digest of Roman Law</note> where Pomponius states that it is "naturally permitted for contracting parties to deceive one another" (similar to the law "item si pretio" in the *Digest* on hiring). This does not mean (as Conrad and others think) that this "deception" occurs within the range of the just price; for within those boundaries, no deception takes place, nor is there any need for forgiveness of the debt (as the aforementioned doctors suggest), since the entire range is just. Rather (as will be explained in the next question), it refers to cases within half of the just price. Therefore he says "naturally," because the human mind is greedy for profit. Thus, "permitted" there does not mean "without fault," but "without punishment" in a human court.

<margin>The third collection.</margin>
¶ It follows, thirdly, that it would be much safer—if it were possible—both for the consciences of merchants and for the common good, if the prices of all things were made clear by law. Hence, in the *Digest* regarding the office of the Prefect of the City, among the other cares of the Prefect is counted the duty to set just prices for goods. For this reason, since it cannot be maintained for everything, prices should be taxed <note>fixed by authority</note> as much as possible. For indeed, merchants—especially because, as was said above, they thirstily gape after profits—are not only deceived by their own blindness, but even deliberately and craftily deceive out of their own avarice. For this reason, when the price is not fixed by law, one must not stand by the whim of any merchant, but by the judgment of prudent men and those who are cultivators of equity.

<margin>A fallacious rule in taxing labor and prices.</margin>
For it is a most fallacious rule if someone always wants to sell for as much as he bought it, plus the cost of his labor and risks, with an added profit. Indeed, if a merchant, ignorant of the craft and business, bought for more than was just, or if adverse fortune blew against him—because, for instance, an unexpected abundance of goods arose...

<summary>This page defines the "just price" of goods, distinguishing between those fixed by law (legal price) and those determined by the market (natural price), which exists within a range of fairness. Soto argues that while the state should ideally set all prices to prevent merchant avarice, it is practically impossible, necessitating the use of "prudent judgment."</summary>
