<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "natural" just price, focusing on how market fluctuations and external circumstances—rather than the merchant's personal costs—dictate the moral price of goods.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right [Iustitia & Iure]

...even if a merchant has acted diligently, he cannot justly extort the expenses he incurred if the market has fallen. Conversely, if another merchant is more industrious or more fortunate—perhaps he managed to buy for less, or "Fortune smiled upon him" <note>original: "fautrix arrisit fortuna"</note> (meaning an unexpected scarcity occurred later)—he can certainly sell for a higher price. This remains true even if he sells on the same day and in the same place, and even if the goods themselves have not improved in quality. Since the art of business is largely subject to the accidental outcomes of events, merchants must both endure the risks of misfortune at their own expense and wait for favorable fortune. We speak here with Christians regarding "Fortune" as meaning an event that was unexpected to us. 

This is the sense of the law regarding prices in the *Digest* <note>original: "l. pretia. ff. ad legem Falcidiam," referring to Roman civil law on inheritance and valuation</note>. There, it is held that the prices of things do not depend on the affection or utility of individuals, but are determined "commonly." This means they are not set according to the private estimation of one person, but according to common prudence. A similar phrase in the fourth law of the same title alludes to this, stating that a thing is not to be valued at a "formal price"—that is, a price formed by the specific parties to a contract—but according to its present state, namely, the price currently running in the common market <term>common market: original "communi foro," the public marketplace where prices are set by general demand</term>. For the value of a thing should not be judged according to a future time when the thing does not yet exist, but according to the present moment in which it does. 

Consider these examples: There is a shortage of grain in Spain. A Sicilian merchant, hearing this, sails to us with a ship loaded with grain. When he arrives, however, either because a more merciful heaven has breathed upon us <note>i.e., a good harvest occurred</note> or because we have received a supply of grain from elsewhere, the price has greatly decreased. He cannot, therefore, sell it for as much as the goods cost him. Indeed, if he were to sell it at a higher price on credit for future payment simply to keep himself from loss, he would not be free from sin, nor would he be exempt from the duty of restitution.

<margin>A deception frequently used by merchants at fairs.</margin>
By this, another deception is uncovered which is commonly used at fairs <term>fairs: original "nundinis," large seasonal markets that were the centers of international trade</term>. At the beginning, when there is a larger crowd of buyers, goods are sold for more; at the end, for the opposite reason, the price decreases. Merchants then think that because they waited for a time, they can licitly sell for as much as the goods were worth at the beginning, even though they could not extort that same price for ready money. They are deceived to their own spiritual peril.

<margin>The fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Finally, for a clearer understanding of these matters, the **fourth conclusion** must be noted. An abundance of buyers increases the prices of goods, while a scarcity decreases them. Conversely, an abundance of sellers decreases the price, while a rarity of sellers makes it grow. Indeed, where goods flow in, the number of sellers is larger and the number of buyers is smaller.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
¶ From this you can derive an answer if you have wondered whether the reason for selling and the manner of selling

<column-break/>

vary the price. In itself, the reason for selling or buying has no effect on the matter. Whether you sell because you are compelled by necessity, or because you have an abundance of things and despise them; likewise, whether you buy out of necessity or for pleasure, the price is not varied by these factors. 

However, because a seller's necessity might cause him to put his goods up for public auction <note>original: "sub hasta," literally "under the spear," the Roman sign for a public sale or auction</note>, it happens that since there are fewer buyers at that moment, the price of things becomes cheap—just as in war, the plunder is sold for a tiny coin once victory is achieved. Conversely, when public merchants wait for buyers, because more buyers emerge for that method of selling, the value of the goods increases. For the same reason, at the start of fairs, things are usually sold for much more than at the end.

<margin>The iniquity of monopolies.</margin>
¶ This conclusion clearly shows the iniquity of monopolies. This occurs, for instance, when someone buys a privilege from a prince to be the sole seller; or when two or three, getting ahead of the rest of the merchants, buy up a heap of goods so that everyone is forced to flock to them; or when they swear an oath among themselves that none of them will sell for less than a certain price. In these cases, the price increases due to the rarity of sellers. 

By the same logic, although it does not happen as frequently, monopolies of buyers—intended to diminish prices—would be no less iniquitous. For example, if in a port where a very valuable ship has docked, those who could afford to buy it promised one another not to buy except at a certain low price; or if at an auction I were to turn others away so they would not bid, so that I might buy for less. This would certainly be a sin that would not be forgiven before restitution was made.

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
And this is what Cicero says in his book *On Duties* <note>original: "lib. de Officijs"</note>: A seller shall not appoint a "shill" <note>original: "licitatorem," someone who bids just to drive up the price</note>, nor shall a buyer appoint someone to bid against himself. However, when sellers form a monopoly, then buyers may justly use a contrary prudence, as if "repelling force with force" <note>original: "vim vi repellentes"</note>: namely, they may agree among themselves that no one will buy except at a certain price.

<margin>Regarding the first argument.</margin>
It remains, then, to respond to the arguments. First of all, regarding that rule: *A thing is worth as much as it can be sold for.* It is obvious that this does not have as vast a meaning as the words sound. Otherwise, it would be licit to sell for more than half the true price—indeed, even double or triple. If you moderate the rule so that it means "as much as it can be sold for *lawfully and justly*"—since we can only truly "do" what we can do legally—then you would make the rule useless, as it would be "begging the question" <note>original: "principiū petens"</note>. For if someone asks how much they can sell for, and you answer, "As much as justice allows," you have answered nothing.

<summary>Soto explains that the "just price" is determined by the collective market value (supply and demand) rather than an individual's costs or motivations. He also condemns monopolies and price-fixing as sinful practices that require financial restitution.</summary>

<keywords>just price, market value, monopoly, Roman law, Cicero, ethics of trade, restitution, supply and demand, auctions, fairs</keywords>

# Book Six, Question 3

...that which he himself did not know. The meaning, therefore, is that a thing is worth as much as it can be sold for, provided that force, fraud, and deceit are excluded <note>original: "seclusa vi, fraude, & dolo"</note>—for these remove the voluntary nature of the buyer's consent. And although the answer might seem to fall back on the same point as if I had said "justly," it is not quite the same. Indeed, if you were to ask what a human is and I responded, "a human," I would teach you nothing. But if I respond that a human is a "rational animal," although it refers to the same thing, I am not begging the question because I am explaining the definition.
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
To the second argument, the response is that an expert in a craft should be believed when he is not infected by an affection for his own property. Everyone is an arbiter in their own affairs as long as it does not concern anyone else; however, he who sells is not dealing with his own private property, but rather a matter common to both himself and the buyer. Therefore, he is not a legitimate arbiter in the price.
<margin>A distinction.</margin>
¶ Since mention was made of gems and precious things in the third argument, a distinction must be made between types of merchandise. For some things are not at all necessary for the republic; these, anyone can sell for as much as a knowledgeable and prudent buyer is willing to give. Of this kind are precious horses, gems, hawks, and the like. These serve for the ornament, decorum, and splendor of the nobility; therefore, it is part of the magnificence of the great lords to value such things highly. Other things, however, are necessary to the republic, such as those pertaining to food, clothing, and other uses of that kind. In these, even if no fraud or deceit has crept in, it is still a form of force if you sell them for as much as you can possibly extort.

### QUESTION THREE,
### On the injustice committed in buying and selling.

->Saint Thomas [Aquinas], Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, question 77.<-

### ARTICLE I.
### Whether one can lawfully sell a thing for more than it is worth.

<margin>The injustice that creeps into this contract.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' showing a figure (perhaps a scholar or cleric) seated at a desk or lectern, surrounded by ornate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
HAVING ALREADY laid out three articles in the previous question—namely, the necessity of buying and trading, and the price of things—there follows the third question concerning the injustice that creeps into this contract. However, right at the start, I will not silently pass over a point where the reader might perhaps feel doubt regarding Saint Thomas.

<column-break/>

For in the distribution of the 
<margin>Doubt regarding the words of Saint Thomas.</margin>
question, he immediately asserts that only two questions are to be treated: buying and usury. This is because, regarding other voluntary exchanges <term>voluntary exchanges: original "voluntarias commutationes," contracts where both parties agree to the trade</term>, no injustice is found that cannot be reduced to robbery or theft. In these words, there is a twofold doubt. First, that by the same reasoning, he could have omitted these two as well: for the fraudulent nature of buying and usury is a type of theft. But if he says these two are "voluntary" exchanges, then a second doubt emerges: why does he not treat leasing, stipulations, and other contracts by the same reasoning? To these doubts, it is answered together that the consideration of 
<margin>The solution.</margin>
Saint Thomas was both knowing and prudent. For the injustice of buying and usury differs from robbery and theft because they are not done simply against the will of the owner, but with his spontaneous involvement—that is, the owner transferring his things to another. Therefore, although the owner may be unwilling regarding the unfairness of the price, it is still a contract, which a theft is not. And although the same reasoning applies to leasing, its injustice—and that of all other contracts—must be weighed and measured according to the standard of these two. For all injustices in voluntary exchanges are reduced to these two heads: either you sell something for a price when it is worth nothing (which is generally reduced to usury), or you transfer your property or its use for a price that is either higher or lower than the just value. This is to be judged by the rules of buying and selling. ¶ The first article, then, is whether one may lawfully sell a thing for more than it is worth. These words imply the question of whether one may conversely buy it for less. And it is argued from the affirmative side.
<margin>First argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
What is "just" in exchanges has been established by civil law; however, the same law permits those contracting with each other to deceive one another <note>original: "permittit contrahentibus inuicem se decipere," referring to a famous principle in Roman law allowing for hard bargaining as long as it doesn't reach "enormous loss"</note>, as found in the Code and the Digest. Therefore, it is permitted to resell for more and buy for less than a thing is worth.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, a common desire of all people seems to proceed from nature, and consequently is free of fault. But to buy cheap and sell dear—as that Mime said in Augustine's *On the Trinity* <note>original: "vili autem emere & magno vendere," referring to a story where a stage actor claimed to know everyone's secret desire: to buy low and sell high</note>—is a common desire of mortals. The Wise Man agrees with this in Proverbs 20, where he says: "It is bad, it is bad, says every buyer; but when he has gone away, then he boasts." Therefore, selling above the just price and buying below it is lawful.
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued: The law of
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
friendship, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the *Ethics*, Book 9, is that a compensation for a useful thing should be made according to its utility...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the ethics of commerce, specifically addressing whether a seller can charge more than a thing's objective value based on the buyer's need or the seller's loss. It transitions from general definitions to the specific four conclusions of Thomas Aquinas on the "just price."</meta>

550 F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

...be done than what the one who received the benefit achieved. However, it happens that a buyer may receive a more abundant benefit from the purchased item than the item itself was worth—for example, if he buys a horse by which he escapes a danger from enemies. Therefore, it will then be permissible for the seller to value that thing more highly. ¶ To the contrary is that saving admonition of the Redeemer: *Whatever you wish that men should do to you, do also to them* <note>Matthew 7:12; original: "Quæcunq; vultis vt faciant vobis homines, hæc & vos facite illis."</note>. From which it follows that since no one wants a thing to be sold to himself more dearly than is just, no one ought to sell it more dearly to another.

Lest we subvert our established order, which is to place the opinion of Saint Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was the primary theological authority for Soto and the School of Salamanca.</note> before our own everywhere, we respond to the question with four of his conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Proof. Paul.</margin>
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
The first conclusion is this: To use fraud and deceit <note>original: "fraude vti & dolo"</note> so that a thing is either sold for more or bought for less is a crime—just as it is in every kind of contract—and is in its very nature a mortal sin. First, this is evident by the authority of the Apostle Paul in 1 Thessalonians 4, where he warns that no one should circumvent his brother in business: *for the Lord is the avenger,* he says, *concerning all these things.* And Cicero says in *On Duties* <note>original: "Cicero de Offic." Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman whose ethical writings were heavily integrated into Christian moral philosophy.</note>: "Therefore, all lying must be removed from the contracting of business: the seller shall not appoint a shill <note>term: licitatorem (a fake bidder used to drive up the price)</note> to bid against the buyer, nor the buyer one to bid against himself." For indeed, where fraud is present, voluntary consent is absent; and consequently, an injustice is committed that is contrary to charity.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: If you consider buying and selling according to their bare nature, it is in no way permitted to sell a thing for more than it is worth or to buy it for less.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is most evident. For this type of contract was introduced for the common good and for equal advantage. That which is so established ought not to burden either of the parties, but must be carried out according to the equality of justice. Now, the measure and, as it were, the scale of the balances is the price, for the use of which money (as we said above) was invented. Therefore, to increase or decrease the <term>just price</term> <note>The "iustum pretium" was a central economic concept arguing that goods have an objective value based on community estimation rather than just what the market will bear.</note> is a sin of injustice, and consequently mortal in its nature.

¶ Nevertheless, a sale can be considered according to its "accidents"—namely, insofar as the salable item results either in a loss for the seller or a utility for the buyer.
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
With this presupposed, the third conclusion is applied: It is lawful to include in the price of a thing the loss <note>original: "damnum"</note> which the seller accepted, so that the thing is valued not only for what it was in itself, but also for what it was worth to the seller. For example, if my plot of land by itself was worth only ten, but it is worth twelve to me because I consider it most convenient to build a house there, I can both ask for and receive that very price from you.

<column-break/>

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
And the reason is plain: because everyone can sell the whole of what is his own; and in such a case, not only the thing but also its benefit <note>original: "emolumentum"</note> belongs to the seller.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But if, to the contrary, you argue thus: After the owner of the thing prefers of his own accord to sell it rather than to keep the benefit of the thing, he ought to blame himself, and not demand more than he confers upon the buyer. And especially because if the buyer had known the thing was not worth that much by itself, he perhaps would not have bought it.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that the argument proves that this is by no means permitted unless the seller discloses the matter to the buyer and warns the man so that he may see whether it is expedient for him to buy under that condition. For when a buyer, knowing and being prudent—either because he himself suffers such a great or even greater necessity for the thing, or because he wishes to satisfy his own mind—strives to buy the thing with that burden, the seller justly sells for as much as it was worth to himself; otherwise, not at all.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The fourth conclusion: The benefit <note>original: "commodum"</note> that accrues to the buyer, if the seller receives no loss therefrom, is not permitted to be included in the price.
<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is proved by the contrary reason: since a seller cannot sell except what was his own. Now, the benefit of the buyer was not the seller's property; rather, the buyer's own necessity or his skill is the cause of it. For example, if someone buys a horse which is necessary for war, not for the seller but for himself; or another thing by which, through the use of his own skill, he can make a more abundant profit than the seller would have made. Otherwise, if the utility of the buyer were added to the price, it would be lawful for pharmacists <note>original: "pharmacopolis"</note> to sell medicines for as much as the health of the sick person is worth. It is a matter of courtesy, however, that such a buyer should return thanks <note>original: "grates"</note> to the seller. And by this, the third argument taken from Aristotle is solved. For in <term>commutative justice</term> <note>The justice governing exchange between individuals, aiming for exact arithmetic equality.</note>, only the equality of things is weighed; but in a "useful friendship," it is the utility that is weighed, which is repaid through a grateful gift.

<margin>The false rule of Mair.</margin>
See how false and deceptive is the rule of John Mair <note>John Mair (c. 1467–1550) was a prominent Scottish philosopher and historian whose views Soto often contested.</note> in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 29, where he asserts that whatever is owed according to natural equity can be included in a pact. For then it would be lawful to oblige a borrower not only to repay the loan (as Mair himself admits), but to buy from the lender's workshop and grind in his mills; and likewise to oblige a buyer to increase the price on account of his own benefit.

<margin>Question. Sylvester.</margin>
¶ Here, however, the attentive reader might ask concerning this conclusion whether, conversely, a hardship which the buyer suffers is a legitimate cause for some of the price to be deducted. Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian known for his "Summa Sylvestrina."</note> indeed responds in the affirmative under the word "buying" <note>original: "verb. emptio"</note>, section 7. "If someone," he says, "having no need of your services but overcome by your pleas..."

<summary>This page discusses the morality of pricing in trade, arguing that while a seller may charge more to compensate for their own personal loss, they cannot ethically increase a price based solely on the buyer's urgent need or potential profit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 550 regarding the "just price" in commerce. Having established that fraud is a sin, the author now examines legal thresholds of "deception" in contracts and whether the law’s tolerance of certain price fluctuations implies moral permission in the court of conscience.</meta>

### Question III of the Sixth Book

...because you are poor, he employs you; he will be able to purchase your labor for less than if he had asked you himself. Nevertheless, the cause of this is certainly not a loss to the buyer, but rather (as we said in the preceding article) the seller’s abundance causes the price to decrease. And therefore, when you seek a buyer for your property or an employer for your labor, you and your goods are valued at less.

<margin>Argument</margin>
¶ Indeed, another more apparent argument can be made against the same conclusion. For it would follow from that conclusion that even when someone makes a profit using another’s money which they hold on deposit, they would not be bound to refund that profit, or even a part of it, to the owner.

<margin>Response</margin>
The conclusion is plainly granted. Nor can the depositor make a pact with the depositary for a share of the profit without the crime of usury <note>Usury was the prohibited practice of charging interest on a loan. Here, Soto distinguishes between a simple deposit and a risky partnership.</note>, unless he enters into a partnership with the risk of the principal <note>original: "periculo sortis"</note>, about which we shall speak below. Nevertheless, that same depositor can and should, out of honesty and courtesy, be grateful to the other, even in material terms. Nor does the fault of usury underlie this. If you deposit your money with a grateful merchant whom you hope will be beneficial to you, he is not judged a usurer if, in that hope, he is grateful to you with a gift so that you might again entrust your gold to his keeping.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ The first of the arguments at the head of the question requires a solution to that doubt: namely, by what means is "deception" <note>In a legal sense, "deception" here refers to an imbalance in the exchange, not necessarily malicious lying.</note> permitted by law in buying and selling. Indeed, in the previous article, we explained the sense of that law, *In causae. 2. §. idem Pompo. ff. de mino.* <note>A reference to the Digest of Roman Law regarding contracts made by minors.</note>, where it is held that it is naturally permitted for contracting parties to "deceive" one another. A similar law harmonizes with this: *Item si pretio. ff. locati.* This is by no means understood to be within the latitude of the just price, because in that case, there is no deception. It is therefore understood to be within half of the just price. For not only the civil laws just cited—and Law 2 of the Code *on rescinding a sale* and the law *If by will* under the same title—but even the canon laws <note>The laws of the Catholic Church.</note> permit this, as is clear in the chapters *Since the beloved* and *Since the cause* under the title *on buying and selling.*

<margin>What it means to sell beyond half the just price.</margin>
¶ As for selling "beyond half of the just price," there are those who—as Conrad <note>Conradus Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts.</note> reports in Question 57—think this means selling for more than double the value. But they can defend this with no probability; for the name itself explains it. It means selling for more than one and a half times the value. For example, a thing that is worth ten has a latitude of justice between nine and eleven; but to sell it for sixteen is to sell beyond half of the true value. Likewise, to buy for less than half is to buy for four, since five is the middle part. For thus does that cited law, *A thing of greater value* in the Code, state: the price is seen to be less

<meta>catchword: is seen</meta>

<column-break/>

if not even half of the true price has been paid.

<margin>Question</margin>
¶ The question, therefore, is whether the law permits this as something morally licit. Regarding this, there are three opinions.

<margin>First opinion of Durandus.</margin>
<margin>Conrad.</margin>
<margin>Antoninus.</margin>
The first is that of Durandus of the Order of Friars Minor <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Scholastic theologian.</note>, whom Conrad also cites in Question 57, and whom Antoninus <note>St. Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), an authority on moral theology and economics.</note> rebukes in part 2, title 1, chapter 16. He holds that it is permissible for a seller in the court of God <note>original: "foro Dei"; referring to the internal moral conscience as opposed to human courts.</note> to demand a price greater than what is just, even if the excess is immoderate, provided it is not beyond half.

<margin>First argument for Durandus.</margin>
And one could argue in favor of this opinion thus: Human law binds in the court of conscience; therefore, it can condemn the buyer to that excess as a penalty for imprudence, just as it does in the case of prescription <note>Legal "prescription" refers to gaining ownership of something simply because a certain amount of time has passed.</note>.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second: A just sentence binds in the court of conscience unless it proceeds from a false presumption; but if a buyer brings a seller to judgment over this matter, the seller will be acquitted; therefore, his conscience remains safe.

<margin>Sentence of Gerson.</margin>
¶ Next to this is the opinion of Gerson <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), Chancellor of the University of Paris.</note> in his treatise *On Contracts* and in his *Flowers*, where he says that a deceiver of this kind certainly sins, and even mortally so if the excess is notable, yet he is not bound to make restitution. In the treatise *On Contracts*, he says this somewhat hesitantly, but in the *Flowers*, he asserts the same more boldly.

<margin>Gerson's reason.</margin>
And his reason is: because no injury is done to one who knows and is willing <note>original: "scienti & volenti non fit iniuria"; a fundamental legal maxim.</note>.

<margin>Third opinion of St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ However, the third opinion is that of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> in the present location, 2.2. And although Gerson says there is no agreement among theologians on this, certainly in Book 4 of the *Sentences*, Question 15, all are of this mind by common consent. But perhaps someone might cite Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308).</note> to the contrary, who in Question 2 says that it is a matter between the contracting parties that they do not always intend to yield to each other something of "indivisible justice," so that a certain donation accompanies every contract. Perhaps his follower Durandus was led astray by these words.

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
But in truth, Scotus means nothing else than that in going slightly above or below an indivisible price, the contracting parties intend to yield to each other—but only within the latitude of the just price, where we said above that no yielding or donation is necessary. For later in Article 3, he says that in cases of fraud, there is no voluntary donation.

<margin>The opinion of St. Thomas is urged.</margin>
¶ Therefore, that neither canon nor civil laws wish to permit "deception" within half of the just price as something valid in the court of God is clear primarily from that natural and divine precept cited above: "Do not do to others what you do not wish to be done to you." For no one would want to be cheated by craftiness. This contract of buying and selling was invented (as we were saying) for the common good; therefore, neither party ought to be burdened by the other.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
And this is the natural demonstration: No human law can override natural precepts...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into the "just price" of goods. Soto is specifically addressing whether human laws—which often only allow a contract to be overturned if the price is off by more than half (the principle of "laesio enormis")—absolve a person of the moral duty to pay a fair price in smaller amounts.</meta>

->. Friar Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*,<-

[...the] law can derogate <note>To derogate is to partially repeal or take away the authority of a law.</note>: because commands of this kind (as is clear in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>) are not dispensable: at the very least, no one doubts they are indispensable by human law, and even less can they be abolished. Furthermore, preserving justice in exchanges is a natural precept, and indeed a divine one: because natural precepts are derived from the eternal law. Therefore, it cannot be abolished by any human law. Moreover, the minor premise is as well known as the major: since the object of justice is to create equality in things. And for that reason, <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle, in Book 5 of the *Ethics*, teaches that the whole virtue of commutative justice <note>Commutative justice governs the fairness of individual exchanges, like buying and selling, ensuring both parties receive equal value.</note> is concerned with this: establishing equality between persons; namely, that I should return to you as much as I received from you, and that you should not extort more from me. Therefore, to receive beyond the range of the just price is manifestly repugnant to the natural reason of justice. <margin>Second reason</margin> ¶ Second. Fraud (as we have often said) is opposed to what is voluntary; but in such a case there is an inequitable fraud: therefore the buyer, unwillingly, gives more than half, and thus the seller commits a kind of theft. And furthermore, it is against the precept of <margin>Paul</margin> Paul, in the first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4: *That no one circumvent his brother in business*; where all fraudulent dealing is condemned. <margin>Third reason</margin> ¶ Third. If it were permitted to deceive up to half of the just price, it would equally be permitted to defraud in measure: as if you sold ten bushels of grain, it would be permitted for you, having received the full price for all of them, to craftily deliver only six. This is clear: because it falls back into the same error. But this is most inequitable, and the assertion is most absurd, going against that passage in Deuteronomy 25: *You shall not have in your bag diverse weights, a greater and a smaller: nor shall there be in your house a greater and a smaller measure.* <margin>Corollary against Gerson</margin> <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a famous French theologian who Soto often engages with.</note> ¶ From these things it follows that a deceiver of this kind is bound to restitution. This is most certain: because the sin of injustice (as we repeatedly say) by its very nature obligates one to restitution <note>Restitution is the act of giving back what was taken or making up the difference to restore fairness.</note>: according to that chapter *si culpa* in the section *de iniuriis et damno* <note>A reference to Canon Law (the law of the Church) regarding injuries and damages.</note>: *If a loss is given or an injury inflicted through your fault, you ought by right to make satisfaction regarding these things.* <margin>Argument 4</margin> ¶ And from this is taken the fourth argument against that opinion of Durandus <note>Guillaume Durand, a medieval jurist and theologian.</note>, and (if there are any, as is reported) the doctors of law who patronize him. If the deception were to exceed half of the just price, the obligation to restore would emerge from it: which they cannot deny. Then, either the entire excess beyond the just price would have to be restored, or only that which is beyond the just price plus a half. They cannot say this second thing. Indeed, even the civil law rescinds a contract unless the entire excess is restored to the buyer: as is expressly held in the aforementioned law 2 of the Code *on the rescinding 

<column-break/>

of a sale.* <note>Soto is referring to the Roman Code of Justinian, specifically the law regarding "laesio enormis" (enormous loss).</note> If, however, the entire excess must be restored then, it follows that in a deception of less than half, that part must also be restored. For it is a marvelous thing to say that if I bought a thing from you worth ten for sixteen, you are bound to restore six to me; but while I bought it for fourteen, you owe me nothing. Wherefore one should wonder much more at Gerson than at the first opinion: for after he acknowledged that a deception of this kind is a crime, how could he be ignorant that it is a prevarication <note>A violation or turning away from duty.</note> of justice? For it is natural to justice to ensnare the delinquent in the bond of restitution. Nor is it clearly understood what he meant by alleging that rule of law: *To one who knows and is willing, no injury is done.* <note>original: "Scienti & volenti non fit iniuria." A common legal maxim suggesting that if someone consents to a deal knowing the facts, they can't later claim they were harmed.</note> For even if the buyer buys knowingly and willingly, the just value is nevertheless hidden from him: and he is subsequently seduced, thinking the thing is worth as much as the seller asks. <margin>Objection</margin> ¶ But those men say (as we argued on their behalf) that human law could free the seller from restitution by transferring ownership to him, just as in prescription. <note>Prescription, or "adverse possession," is a legal rule where someone can gain ownership of property simply by holding it for a long time without challenge.</note> <margin>Solution</margin> Certainly, it could not do so justly: because there is not a sufficient cause. For in prescription, the reason of peace and the avoidance of lawsuits persuades that the prince, who is the guardian of peace, should deprive the negligent who leave their property for a long time: because after the passage of a long time, many deceptions would arise. In a contract of sale, however, not everyone can know the prices of things. And therefore, for those who buy in good faith, there is no reason why they should be penalized by that excess because of the merchant's iniquity. This is especially so because in prescription the possessor possesses in good faith: and therefore it would be inequitable for him to be disturbed after the delay of so long a time. But the fraudulent merchant deceives in bad faith: for that reason, no reasoning allows him to report a profit from his own iniquity, especially that which is extorted from an innocent person. ¶ Therefore, to bring the matter to a conclusion, the power of human laws in this part is twofold: One, that it does not give a legal action in court to one harmed below the half-price threshold. The other, that it does not permit the contract to be rescinded: as is held in the cited law, *Si voluntate*, in the Code *on rescinding*, etc. <margin>Scruple</margin> ¶ But indeed you ask, why then is a legal action not granted in such a case? <margin>Response</margin> It is answered that the legislators did this most deliberately. For those mortals did not value these temporal goods so much that they would allow such a whirlwind of litigation for their sake as we see now: contrary to the teaching of Christ, who admonishes us that to redeem time, we should let go of our cloak to the one who asks for our tunic. For that reason, in prescription where there was a greater cause for the sake of consulting [the public peace...]

# Question III of the Sixth Book.

<margin>2 }</margin>
...for the sake of preserving peace, ownership is awarded to the possessor; however, in cases of deception <note>The term used here is *deceptio*, referring to price gouging or underpaying.</note> below half <note>original: "citra dimidium." This refers to the legal principle of *laesio enormis*, where a contract could only be legally overturned if the price was off by more than 50% of the true value.</note> of the just price, legal action is denied to the petitioner. This is because such deception below half of the just price can only be perceived with difficulty and uncertainty; therefore, allowing lawsuits for every small discrepancy would give birth to many forms of fraud. Nevertheless, the matter is referred to the court of God <note>original: "forum Dei," meaning the realm of conscience and divine judgment rather than human civil courts.</note>. And let this response suffice for the second argument made above. For indeed, the judge's acquittal in such a case is not sacramental <note>That is, being found "not guilty" in a human court does not mean one is absolved of the sin in the eyes of the Church.</note>. <margin>Objection.</margin> ¶ But perhaps an opponent might allege that axiom: "He who sins by the authority of the law, does not sin." This suggests that if the law permits it, it isn't a sin; but rather, one only sins when acting *against* the law. As Augustine says against Pelicianus (23. q. 4. canon *Qui peccat*) and as is found in the law of Gracchus regarding the Julian law on adultery. <margin>Solution. }</margin> This citation, however, is deceptive. For that axiom is understood to apply to **commanding law** <note>original: "lege iussoria," laws that tell you what you MUST do.</note>; it is different, however, regarding **permissive law** <note>original: "permissoria," laws that simply choose not to punish an act.</note>. I say that he who does what the law *commands* does not sin; but it is different for him who does what human law merely permits to go unpunished. For divine law does not permit everything that human law does. Otherwise, prostitutes would not be sinning, because they are permitted by [human] law. <margin>Chrysostom.</margin> Whence Chrysostom says (as held in 33. q. 1. canon *hac ratione*): "What we permit," he says, "we do not command, but rather we allow it because we cannot fully prohibit the evil wills of men." And in the Digest <note>A collection of Roman legal writings.</note> regarding the rules of law: "Always in conjunctions" (for so the law begins), "one must consider not only what is **lawful**, but also what is **honorable**" <note>original: "non solùm quod licet considerandum est, sed & quod honestum sit." This is a famous legal maxim: just because you *can* do something legally doesn't mean it is the right thing to do.</note>. Here the gloss <note>An interpretive commentary on a legal text.</note> provides an example for our proposal. For even if it is lawful, it says, for parties to a contract to deceive one another [within limits], it is nevertheless not fitting for a good man. Therefore, no doubt remains that such tricksters and deceivers, whether the seller or the buyer, are bound to make restitution even if they are not asked to do so. <margin>Innocentius</margin> ¶ And if you should object against us using the distinguished doctor Innocent <note>Pope Innocent IV, a major canon lawyer.</note>—who says in general that when a contract holds by law, the party who causes harm is not bound to make restitution until the harmed party seeks it—this in no way fights against us. This is because he understands that to apply to contracts in which the law does not forbid the transfer of ownership. <margin>Innocent's Meaning.</margin> By this reasoning, a winner is not bound to restore profit from gambling unless it is demanded; however, in the present case, the transfer of ownership [of the excess money] is prohibited by both natural and divine law. Therefore, the same excellent author teaches in a specific case regarding usury that laws permitting deception below half of the just price are to be understood as the **law of the court** <note>original: "iure fori," civil law.</note> but not the **law of heaven** <note>original: "iure poli," divine or moral law.</note>. Panormitanus says the same; <margin>Panormitanus.</margin> and <margin>Baldus.</margin> Baldus states this excellently, where, citing that singular gloss on the rule "Always," he says such fraudulent contracts

<column-break/>

are not licit in the court of conscience, but that the souls of merchants are placed in danger. Although elsewhere he may seem to vary, indeed, those who do not examine the inner causes of things cannot be consistent with themselves. Nevertheless, all the jurists of the most distinguished name subscribe to this same opinion. <margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, Augustine himself responds there, saying that the Mime <note>An actor or performer. Augustine famously told a story of a mime who claimed he could tell the audience what was in all their hearts: "You want to buy cheap and sell dear."</note> spoke truly when he said that selling dear and buying cheap is a vice of nature, and the **broad way** <note>A reference to Matthew 7:13, the path to destruction.</note> through which (as Christ testifies) the common multitude walks. Against this, however, anyone can strive for justice to resist it. And he adds the example of a certain man who, when a seller asked a very low price for a book, paid the just price instead. ¶ To the third argument, however, a response has already been given above.

### ARTICLE II.

-> Whether a defect in the item sold makes the <-
-> sale illicit in such a way that it is <-
-> necessary to always disclose it. <-

<note>The decorated initial 'P' begins the text below.</note>

After we have seen to the substance of the sale, which consists of the **just price**, it follows that we explore its conditions. Unless one looks very closely, the second and third articles of Saint Thomas [Aquinas], Question 77, would hardly seem to differ. For in the second article, he asks whether a sale is rendered unjust because of a defect in the item sold. After he responded to this question affirmatively, he added that if anyone knowingly commits fraud in a sale, it renders the sale illicit, and he is bound to make restitution. In the third article, he nevertheless proceeds to ask whether a seller is bound to state the defect of the thing sold—which he might seem to have already decided in the affirmative in the second. But in truth, the distinction is this: selling a defective item sometimes happens at the same price as if it were whole and sound. And it is in this sense that the second article proceeds. Or it happens at a price that reflects only what it is worth with the defect. And it is to this that the third article is applied: namely, whether—after the item is sold for no more than it is justly worth—it is lawful for the seller to remain silent about the defect. But truly, these small questions are so closely related <note>original: "germanitate connexæ," literally "connected by brotherhood."</note> that perhaps they may be more conveniently clarified together in the same article. It is asked, therefore, whether a defect in merchandise renders a sale illicit in such a way that it is always necessary to disclose it. And it is argued on the negative side...

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "gatiua," completing the word "negatiua" (negative) for the next page.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the ethics of commerce, specifically focusing on the moral and legal obligations regarding defective goods. Having previously discussed the "just price," Soto now turns to whether a seller is required to disclose flaws in their merchandise.</meta>

# Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>First argument.</margin>
...[deri]gative. There are three ways in which a piece of merchandise can be found lacking: in its substance, its quantity, or its quality. However, a defect in substance—which is the most harmful of all—is not a reason to always void a contract. For instance, consider someone who sells alchemical silver or gold <note>original: "argentum, aut aurum, alchemicum." In the 16th century, "alchemical" metals were base metals treated to look like precious ones; Soto is debating if they are "real" if they function the same way.</note> as the true metal. For, as the masters of that art say, it serves almost the same human uses, such as for engraving vessels or minting coins. Therefore, much less should a sale be rendered illicit because of other defects in quality or quantity.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly, where a buyer is not forced to buy, the knowledge of the thing is subject to their own judgment, and therefore the deception is to be blamed on them. Thus, as long as the seller does not lie, they are not bound to "teach" the buyer. Otherwise, the seller would be marked by that kind of foolishness recorded by Cicero in *On Duties*, where he says: "What is so absurd as if, by the master’s order, a crier should proclaim: 'I am selling a plague-ridden house'?"
<margin>Cicero.</margin>

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Added to this is a third point: the only reason that might compel someone to reveal a flaw is so that the price might be lowered. Yet a seller is not always bound to disclose the reasons why a thing might be valued at less. For a merchant who has foreknowledge of a coming surplus of goods may lawfully, while remaining silent, sell his own stock at the current price. Therefore, for the same reason, he is not bound to reveal other defects.

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
To the contrary is Ambrose in his book *On Duties*, where he says: "The rule of justice is clear: it becomes a good man not to deviate from the truth, nor to inflict unjust loss on anyone, nor to attach any deceit to his property." And again in the same place: "In contracts, the defects of those things being sold are ordered to be brought forward; and unless the seller has made them known, even if the property has passed to the buyer, the contracts are voided by an action for fraud."

---

Since we have divided the question into two senses—namely, whether it is permissible to sell a defective thing as if it were intact at the same price, and whether, while selling it at a price not exceeding its value, it is permissible to remain silent about its defect—the first sense will be answered with three conclusions, and the second with another three.

<margin>Three things to consider in a saleable item.</margin>
In a saleable item (as we said in the first argument), three things are to be considered: namely, the substance, the quantity, and the quality.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion is this: A defect in merchandise, whether in substance, quantity, or quality, renders a contract illicit if it is sold at the price of a true, whole, and solid thing.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This conclusion is too obvious to require many witnesses. For justice is then violated, and it is therefore by its very nature a mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a grave offense that destroys the relationship with God, as opposed to a "venial" or minor sin.</note>, unless the smallness of the matter makes it venial. Indeed, against the person who acts in this way

<column-break/>

regarding substance, it is proclaimed in Isaiah, chapter 1: "Your silver has turned to dross; your wine is mixed with water." Regarding the measure of quality, an admonition is given in Deuteronomy 25: "You shall not have in your bag diverse weights, a greater and a lesser; nor shall there be in your house a greater and a lesser bushel." And a little later: "For the Lord abhors him who does these things, and turns away from all injustice." Here, the nature of a mortal sin is expressed. The same applies to quality—for instance, if someone sells a diseased beast of burden as if it were healthy and strong. Furthermore, there are protective laws regarding all these matters. For by the law "In sales" <note>original: "In venditionibus. ff. de contrahend. empt." A reference to the Digest of Roman Law (denoted by "ff").</note>, a contract is rescinded if one substance or body, as they say, is sold for another: for example, if you sell me one farm or slave, but deliver another. Laws also abound concerning measures and the qualities of goods.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion follows from the first: A seller who, knowing a defect in a thing, fraudulently conceals it from the buyer, sins against justice. However, one who makes a contract while ignorant of the defect, although he is free from fault, is nevertheless bound—as soon as the defect is discovered—to undo the contract. Otherwise, he is bound by the cord of restitution <note>This means he is morally obligated to pay back the difference or refund the money to clear his conscience.</note>. The matter is clear and accessible even to those with "bleary eyes" <note>A Latin idiom meaning something is obvious to everyone.</note>. Yet, one is considered to "conceal" who uses such verbal craftiness that the flaw is left hidden. For example, those brokers who, when selling a defective horse, describe it with every possible trait so that they may hide the true defect in the heap of words.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
The third conclusion: A similar judgment applies to the buyer. For it often happens that a seller, ignorant of the substance, quality, or quantity of his own property, sells the item to a buyer who knows the truth. Such a buyer likewise sins and is bound by the same obligation of restitution if he buys the thing for less than it is worth.

And these are the points regarding the first sense. In the second sense, however, there is a need for distinctions.

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
For a defect is either hidden or manifest. And when it is hidden, it either results in loss or danger to the buyer, or it does not.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
Let the fourth conclusion be this: When a defect in merchandise is hidden, by which either loss is given to the buyer or danger is created, it is a crime for the seller to conceal it; and he is bound to restitution.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason for this conclusion is as follows: Although no one is compelled by the law of justice to provide counsel or help to another to rescue them from dangers and losses—except when it is incumbent upon them by their own duty and office, or when the other person is in extreme distress—nevertheless, on the occasion of danger or loss to another...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s discussion on the ethics of the marketplace. Having previously addressed whether a seller is bound to disclose every minor flaw, he now explores the specific conditions under which silence becomes a sin of "manifest injustice" or a "mortal sin," drawing on the views of St. Thomas Aquinas and debating with later scholars like Conrad Summenhart.</meta>

# Question I & II of the Sixth Book

it is not lawful to give such a thing to another. A seller, by the very fact that he offers for sale a thing affected by some defect, provides an occasion for loss and danger which an unknowing buyer might incur. It is a loss <note>original: "damnum"</note> indeed if the thing is sold for more than it is worth due to the defect; it is a danger <note>original: "periculum"</note> if, because of that same defect, the use of the thing is either useless or perhaps even harmful. For example, if you sell a maimed horse as if it were healthy to a soldier who later cannot use it in battle; or if you were to sell a house threatening to collapse, or pestilent food. Therefore, such concealment is a fraud of manifest injustice, and is consequently a mortal sin <note>original: "mortale," referring to a serious sin that severs one's relationship with God</note> by its very nature, and subjects the person to the obligation of restitution <note>The legal and moral requirement to return ill-gotten gains or compensate for damages.</note>.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Fifth conclusion.** If the seller takes care to avoid causing loss—for instance, by not selling the thing for more than it is worth with the defect, and by not exposing the buyer to any danger—and if the thing remains useful to the buyer in proportion to the price, he is compelled by no law to reveal the defect. St. Thomas does not state this conclusion in this exact form regarding hidden defects, but it is clearly gathered from the preceding points.

<margin>The Proof.</margin>
The reasoning is this: a seller is bound to warn the buyer only insofar as he might be the cause of loss or danger. But in this case, he is the cause of neither; therefore, he may look out for his own interests by remaining silent about the flaw. For if the buyer happened to know, he might refuse to buy even at a just price.

<margin>Sixth conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Sixth conclusion.** When a defect is manifest—for example, a horse is one-eyed, or lame in one part, or a house has visible holes—there is no necessity to announce it more evidently, because unless the buyer is blind, he can see it for himself. Therefore, if he buys it, he is presumed to buy it knowingly. Thus, to speak briefly: if the defect is known, there is no necessity to divulge it; if, however, it is hidden and dangerous, the sale is illicit no matter how much you lower the price, unless you warn the buyer. But if it is not dangerous, and you measure the price according to the quality of the defect, you are not bound to reveal it. Nevertheless, to sell it for more is an iniquity because of the loss inflicted. ¶ Around each of these conclusions, however, smaller doubts arise.

<margin>Conrad does not entirely approve of the previous conclusions.</margin>
First, Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart (c. 1455–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on economic ethics.</note> in Question 54 does not fully approve of these conclusions of St. Thomas, even though he admits they are the same as those of Gerson <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a prominent French scholar.</note> in his *Moral Rules*. For he says this requires a moderation which he establishes as a rule: If, while the defect is hidden, the seller knows by probable conjecture that the buyer would buy the thing regardless even if he discovered the defect, then the seller lawfully sells it at a fair price while keeping the defect silent. If, however, he conjectures that the buyer would not purchase it, he conceals the defect unjustly. And this is the same opinion as

<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
Panormitanus <note>original: "Panor." refers to Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> in the chapter *Iniustum* regarding the exchange of things, whom

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), author of the *Summa Sylvestrina*, a handbook for confessors.</note> seems to follow under the word "buying," section 20. And the reasoning

<column-break/>

of those authors is that as long as the other person would not have been a buyer,

<margin>The reasoning of Conrad and others.</margin>
he contracts involuntarily <note>The idea is that if the buyer wouldn't have agreed if they knew the truth, their "consent" isn't fully free or voluntary.</note>, and consequently suffers an injury. Indeed, for the same reason, they add that even when a defect is manifest, if the buyer does not notice it, the seller is bound to warn him. And almost all the younger scholars follow this opinion. ¶ But nonetheless, this rule of theirs, although very well established among them, does not have a foundation in reason. For even if the seller knew the other person would buy, perhaps that person would not want to buy it for as much as the thing is worth; and thus, even while he is known to be a buyer, he is nonetheless involuntary and unwilling regarding the price. And yet they themselves admit that the seller can nonetheless sell at a fair price by keeping the defect silent, lest the other person diminish the price. And they are forced by reason to admit this: for a seller is not bound to give an occasion for the wearing down of his own just price. If in such a case he is permitted to hide the defect, surely it is equally permitted even if he knew the other would not be a buyer, because he is using his own right.

<margin>To Conrad's argument.</margin>
We therefore deny that there is any consequence that if the buyer’s ignorance is the cause of his buying involuntarily, the seller becomes injurious to him. For no one, while using his own right, gives another a cause of loss. Wherefore, as Diogenes said in Cicero’s third book of *On Duties* <note>original: "Ciceronem lib. 3. Officiorum."</note>, it is one thing to hide, and another to keep silent. You hide when you do not reveal what you are bound to disclose; you are silent when you are not compelled by right to speak. Just as if some third party knowing the defect did not warn the buyer, he would not fall into fault—especially if he knew neither loss nor danger was being created for him—so too the seller is not in fault, because he preserves his own right. However, we do admit this: if the seller knew that the thing would be entirely useless to the buyer, he cannot keep the defect silent. For example, if I sell a slightly lame horse to a noble youth who is accustomed to riding in haste, even though I sell it at a just price, I nonetheless act unjustly. But if I sell it to an elderly physician who desires a horse that walks gently, I certainly inflict no injury upon him. And therefore we have set down three conditions: namely, that danger and loss are avoided, and the thing is of use to the buyer. Add to this that if the buyer is believed to be going to sell the thing to another after it is bought, and because he is ignorant of the defect he will ask as much as it would go for without the defect, then the first seller is bound to make the buyer aware, lest he deceive the other. And in this way, harmony can be reached between Diogenes and Antipater, whom Cicero mentions there. For the former did not at all constrain the seller to uncover the defect of the merchandise, while the latter, on the contrary, thought he should. What then might be...

<sig>Nn 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: concerning the law</meta>

<summary>De Soto argues that sellers must disclose hidden defects that cause financial loss or physical danger, but may remain silent about minor flaws if the price is fair and the item remains useful to the specific buyer. He critiques later scholars like Conrad Summenhart, maintaining that a seller is not obligated to provide information that would unfairly lower their own just price.</summary>

# F. Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

Regarding civil law in the public courts <note>original: "foro exteriori"</note>, we defer to the legal experts, whose business it is to know when both the goods should be returned to the seller and the money to the buyer on account of a defect in the contract. But nevertheless, by the law of nature, the conclusion of St. Thomas is most true. But then most especially, when a defect is obvious, who can doubt that if the buyer does not notice it, he himself must be considered the cause of his own error?

<margin>Argument</margin>
¶ But yet those critics of St. Thomas could have raised another argument against him, by which they might inject a sharper doubt. For indeed, if this opinion of his is true, it would be equally lawful not only regarding the quality of the thing, but also in the quantity of the measure and in the substance itself. Indeed, let us bring forward as an example a merchant who has grain, or types of wine, which are truly worth more than he can sell them for in the public market; and add the example of those things which are sold either by number or by weight. It would follow that if a just bushel <note>original: "modius," a Roman unit of dry measure roughly equivalent to 8 or 9 liters</note>, for example, is worth two gold pieces, but there is no one who will give that price—and let us grant that an injustice is being done to him, either because of a monopoly of buyers or because an unfair city governor oppresses him with this burden—he could, I say, then sell for less, but nonetheless by shortening the measure. In this way, the quantity he delivers most justly equals the price he receives.

Indeed, the same would be permitted in the substance itself. Suppose someone has for sale excellent wine, a jar of which is most justly worth ten; but yet if the people did not believe it was Rhenish <note>Wine from the Rhine region, highly valued in the Renaissance</note>, they would not give such a price. It would follow by the same consequence that he could—even if it is not from that vineyard—sell it for ten by remaining silent. Add that by the same reasoning, one could also dilute wine with water. For if there were such a great scarcity of wine that a jar stood at two gold pieces, for which reason no one would buy, why could the innkeeper not mix it with water, selling the jar for twenty silver pieces, which in truth, with that water, is worth only that much? And yet there is an error in the substance, as St. Thomas says, according to that passage in Isaiah 1: *Your wine is mixed with water.* <note>Isaiah 1:22</note> Certainly, the conclusions of these arguments are gathered with great logical force from the sayings of St. Thomas; for as far as moral use is concerned, it is the same to remain silent about a defect in the quality of a thing as in its quantity and substance. Especially when the substance is not so different that it does not serve in the same way. Just as if you think my silk is from Granada and my cloth from Segovia <note>Granada and Segovia were famous for high-quality textiles; De Soto uses them as benchmarks for luxury goods</note>, when it is actually of a lesser brand; yet I sell it for what it is worth, and it is useful to you in proportion to the price.

<margin>First assertion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, so that we may not leave these points unanswered: First of all, these arguments do not apply where the price is

<column-break/>

legally fixed, namely established by law: because then there can be no private judgment against the law. But if they do apply, it is where the price does not consist in a fixed, indivisible point.

<margin>Second assertion.</margin>
Second, we do not wish to offer an occasion for weaving frauds to innkeepers and others, whether tavern-keepers or buyers of another kind; for they are most unfair judges of their own affairs, surely valuing their own wares highly.

<margin>Third assertion.</margin>
And therefore I add thirdly that the magistrates of the commonwealth ought not to attend to the weight of these arguments, but should act by law against those who violate the public trust either in measure or in substance.

<margin>Solution of the proposed argument.</margin>
Nevertheless, in the court of conscience <note>original: "foro conscientiae"</note>, standing alone on natural law, for a man who is otherwise sincere and candid—if those three conditions concur, namely that risk and loss are avoided, and the merchandise is useful to the buyer according to the ratio of the price—there would be no reason why he should be condemned for those aforementioned concealments. For natural laws regarding the fairness of measure and the substance of a thing are understood to apply either when a thing is sold for more than is just, or when the things are not suitable for the same uses.

¶ However, it is established of itself that it is not permitted to cover a defect by lying. Therefore, if the buyer asks about the quality of the thing, the seller is bound to disclose the truth; but if he does not ask and receives no loss, let him blame himself. Although perhaps a seller’s lie in such cases—if justice is maintained in some aforementioned way—is not "pernicious" <note>In moral theology, a "pernicious lie" is one that causes harm, as opposed to an "officious lie" told to help someone or a "jocose lie" told for fun</note>. It would be otherwise, however, if the buyer had no need for such a quality of the thing. As if, perhaps, for some medicine he needed the strongest wine, and diluted wine was sold to him. And therefore among pharmacists <note>original: "pharmacopōlas"</note> such an exchange of things would be wicked.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ These matters having been dispatched, there remains a no less significant doubt regarding the third conclusion: by which it was said that by a similar reasoning of justice, the buyer is also involved. Namely, he is bound by the same law to warn the seller if he sells a thing for less than it is worth.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
St. Augustine relates an example of this in book 13 of *The City of God*.

<margin>First reason for doubting.</margin>
For a reason to the contrary appears. Indeed, it does not seem that a buyer is as strictly bound by reason of the contract to instruct the seller, as the seller is conversely bound to instruct the buyer. For he who exposes his wares by inviting buyers offers them an occasion for error unless he warns them; but the buyer offers no occasion to the seller. This is clear from examples. Someone offers for sale a precious little stone, which he thinks is either glass or something of less value than a gem. He happens upon a lapidary <note>A specialist in gems and precious stones</note> skilled in that matter, who indeed knows the price of the little gem. Can he not silently buy it for as much as the other asks, even though it is far less than the just price? The same applies if you offer a piece of jewelry to a goldsmith and a body of metal which you do not know to be the purest gold...

<summary>De Soto debates whether sellers can morally justify "short-weighting" or diluting goods if the market price is unfairly low, concluding that while conscience might be clear under strict conditions, the state must punish such acts to maintain public trust. He also begins an inquiry into whether expert buyers (like jewelers) are obligated to tell sellers if they are underpricing their goods.</summary>

### Question III of the Sixth Book

...finest gold; yet he [the buyer] knows it. For we are proceeding with the case of sellers who do not bring these things forward, asking to be taught the value of the object. Otherwise, there is no doubt that buyers are bound to teach them; but we are speaking of those who in no way suspect what lies hidden in the object: because perhaps the object did not cost them more.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ And a second reason is applied which more urgently persuades us of this. If someone knows, either by skill or by some other means, that a gold mine <note>original: "aurifodinam"</note> is hidden on your land, or another vein, whether of Jasper or another precious stone, he can approach you to buy the land and, keeping the mystery silent, buy it. For this is often known to happen in practice. Indeed, Christ our Redeemer, as we said in the previous book, question 3, seems to recount the same thing as lawful and legal in Matthew 13, where he says: "The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field," etc. That is, the lord of the field conceals the secret until, having sold everything he possesses, he buys it so that the entire treasure belongs to him; as we discussed at length in the cited place. Therefore, a buyer is by no means compelled by law to disclose the value of the object to the seller.

<margin>Response.</margin>
¶ To these very points, it is nonetheless responded that the reasoning for land is different from that for other things. For the price of land is weighed based on its surface alone; for its nature is to bear fruit. Because of this, he who buys land is no more bound to disclose what is hidden in its bowels than if he were someone else who did not intend to buy it. Other things, however, are weighed according to what they are; and therefore, when someone sells you one thing for another, first of all, if he asks you, you are bound to reveal the truth. But furthermore, even if not asked, if you were that person who did not wish to buy, you would nonetheless be bound by the bond of charity to warn your brother in a matter of such importance, since the warning costs you nothing. Indeed, if you feared a grave loss for your neighbor, it would be a mortal sin not to teach him according to the rules of charity, which we explained in the previous book in the question on witnesses. But truly, when you decide to buy, the law of justice also enters in. For since he, being ignorant of the object, sells his property to you for less than is just, he parts with it at that price involuntarily, and therefore you are held under the guilt of sin and the obligation of restitution to inform him of the truth. ¶ Although in the same category, the offense would be more serious in a seller; because when he offers an object, he is more strictly forbidden to deceive.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
It remains, therefore, to gather responses from the conclusions of the arguments to the contrary. The solution to the first, then, is specific to gold and brass <note>original: "aurichalco" — orichalcum, a golden-colored alloy</note>, in that the latter can never reach the purity and preciousness of the former; nor its dignity and all its uses.

<column-break/>

Especially because no art can provide the nature of gold, which contributes to the health of bodies. And therefore the cited law, "In sales," <note>original: "In venditionibus"</note> forbids that [brass] to be sold as the real thing. But whether true gold could be produced through Alchemy, he leaves to the judgment of Saint Thomas. And therefore he adds that if by chance that should happen, it would not be unlawful to sell it as true; provided you understand that the effects which artificial gold cannot provide are revealed. For nothing forbids, according to Augustine in Book 3 *On the Trinity*, that by the art of demons using natural causes, the true effects of nature may be produced.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that even if a buyer buys of his own accord, it is nonetheless incumbent upon the seller to disclose the object to that extent, so far as it causes neither loss nor danger. Not indeed through a public crier, which Cicero mocks, but nonetheless privately between himself and the buyer. Otherwise, his judgment of the thing does not allow him enough, which he cannot know except through the seller's account. It is different when defects are manifest.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third, it is responded that the same reasoning does not exist for a defect in goods and for goods that are about to arrive. For the value of an object is estimated according to what it is in the present: and therefore it decreases through a defect in the object. By which reasoning, it must certainly be disclosed. But goods that are to come later in no way make the valuation of the present object cheaper. And therefore the seller is not bound to reveal what is expected in the future.

<margin>History of Thales of Miletus, from Aristotle Politics Book 1, chapter 7, and others.</margin>
There is the story of Thales of Miletus, which Aristotle recounts in *Politics*, Book 1, chapter 7. For when that philosopher was reproached that philosophy made its pupils poor, and he himself had foreseen a wealth of olives through Astrology <note>The term here refers to what we would now call astronomy or meteorology</note>, having collected a small amount of money, he bought on credit in winter, in a general way, all the oil that anyone was going to collect, and gave deposits; afterwards, however, when both a very huge supply came forth, and because he alone was the seller, he made a very large amount of money. Clearly showing that it is easy for philosophers to grow rich: but yet it is the part of a wise man to hold riches in contempt. Something similar is read concerning Joseph in Genesis 41, who, having been divinely taught of the coming seven years of abundance, which were to be followed by the barrenness of others, by buying cheaply first and selling dearly later, enriched Pharaoh.

<margin>Cicero's example.</margin>
There is, furthermore, the example from Cicero's third book *On Duties* <note>original: "De Officiis"</note> concerning the Alexandrian merchant: whether, when he had brought a quantity of grain to Rhodes which was suffering from a high cost of food, knowing that other merchants [were on their way]...

<summary>De Soto discusses whether buyers and sellers must reveal hidden information, such as buried treasure or future market changes, concluding that while land is valued by its surface, justice and charity require the disclosure of hidden defects or true substance in other goods.</summary>
