...events to follow, would he be bound to forewarn the citizens? Or could he, in silence, sell at the price then current? For Antipater <note>Antipater of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher</note> said he should; but Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Babylon</note> denied it. We, for the present, embrace his opinion along with St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whom Soto is commenting upon</note>; yet so tempered that it would be an act of "accumulated virtue" <note>An act of exceptional charity beyond strict legal obligation</note> if that seller were to subtract something from the price. ¶ Regarding the fourth article of St. Thomas’s 77th question, after those things we discussed in the previous question regarding negation, nothing remains for us to say.

# QUESTION FOUR,
## On Buying on Credit.

### ARTICLE I.
#### Whether it is lawful to sell a thing at a higher price when payment is deferred than when paid in cash.

<margin>First argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a dog and foliate patterns.</image-desc>
After the general laws of buying and selling, we ask in particular whether it is lawful to sell a thing at a higher price by reason of credit <note>original: "ratione crediti pretij"; i.e., charging more because the buyer pays later</note>. And the argument is made for the affirmative side. The just price of a thing ought to be estimated according to the judgment of prudent men and according to the common market; however, twelve coins to be paid in the future are worth no more than ten coins present today. Therefore, a thing which can be sold for ten in cash can justly be sold for twelve on credit.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly: A seller is permitted to keep himself "unharmed" <note>original: "indemnem"; to avoid financial loss</note>. For this reason, St. Thomas (2.2. question 77, article 1) did not hesitate to assert that a seller may add to the price for a loss he suffers. Furthermore, from a delayed payment of the price, the seller undergoes many disadvantages: first, that of "lost profit" <note>term: <term>lucrum cessans</term> (profit that ceases because the money was not available to invest elsewhere)</note>; second, the danger to the principal itself, which perhaps will never be paid to him; and third, the danger of costs and expenses which he might incur before he recovers the price. These fears of danger are estimable in the price; therefore, he can sell at an increased price for the sake of these things.

By the same token, the opposite argument runs

<column-break/>

concerning the buyer, who by reason of advance payment <note>original: "anticipatæ folutionis"</note> seems by right able to buy at a lower price. For advance payment is valued more highly than the same payment when delayed, and the buyer undergoes similar risks before he gains possession of the goods.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Thirdly and finally, it is argued: There are some goods necessary for the commonwealth which cannot be sold unless the price is deferred <note>original: "expectato pretio"</note>, which is to be made from the goods themselves. Therefore, the just price of these is not what is paid in the present, but what is to be paid in the future. Conversely, there are other goods which cannot be sold except with advance payment. Therefore, the just price will not be what they are worth when the goods are delivered, but what is paid at the advanced time. An example of the first point is clear in maritime goods, which cannot be brought in except in great quantities. Indeed, since the entire load of a ship (if you consider common occurrences) cannot be sold all at once for cash, but one must wait for the time when the buyers are able to retail the same goods in smaller parts, the just price will be that which is promised for the future, even though it is higher than what would be paid immediately. An example of the second point is offered in the wool trade. For since, as happens for the most part, shepherds cannot afford the feed for their flocks unless the price of the wool is advanced to them, it appears that the just price is that which is advanced, even though it is less than what the wool is worth when delivered.

¶ On the contrary is the fact that the price—as we said in the second question, and as is held in the fourth law of the *Lex Falcidia* <note>original: "l. in lege quarta, ad leg. Falcid."; a Roman law regarding the valuation of estates</note>—must be estimated according to the truth of the matter: that is, according to the present price. These are the words of the law. And the same is gathered from the subsequent law, *Pretia* <note>original: "l. Pretia"; likely referring to Digest 35.2.63 regarding market prices</note>.

<margin>Negative conclusion.</margin>
The solution to the present question is open, as it is clearly gathered from what has gone before. I respond, I say, with a single negative conclusion: In no way is it lawful to sell a thing at a higher price by reason of credit and extended payment than it is worth in the present. "Higher," that is, beyond the "latitude" of the just price <note>The "latitude" refers to the range between the lowest and highest fair market price</note>. For within that range, it has already been said above that the price can be lawfully increased.

<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The argument recently suggested proves the conclusion first: because it is neither lawful to sell a thing for more than it is worth, nor is it worth more than the price currently running in the present. And the natural reason is that the price of any thing follows its existence, so that it is valued at as much as it is worth when...

<summary>Domingo de Soto examines whether it is morally and legally permissible to charge a higher price when a buyer pays on credit rather than in cash. He concludes that while some argue credit justifies a higher price due to risk or lost profit, the "just price" must fundamentally be based on the current market value at the time of the transaction.</summary>

# BOOK SIX, QUESTION IV.

...exists: for then it is of use to men.
<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
¶ Secondly, this is made clear by the rule established in the first question: namely, that to determine whether a contract is usurious, one must examine if it involves any element of a loan <note>original: "mutui"; a loan of fungible goods intended for consumption, the basis of usury theory</note> for which a price is received. You will indeed find this in sales of this kind. For it is exactly the same to sell a thing worth ten for twelve on credit, as it would be if you gave the buyer ten in cash as a loan at an interest of two <note>i.e., charging 20% interest</note>. This is the proof of St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, 2a 2ae, question 78, article 2, response to the 7th objection</note>. From this it follows, as we said in Question 2, that a seller cannot use the pretext that the goods cost him a certain amount, nor that he cannot recover his expenses unless he sells on credit. This is because business of this kind is subject to fortuitous events. Therefore, at the conclusion of market fairs, the prices of goods decrease; a merchant cannot sell on credit for the same price he would have sold for in cash during the height of the buyers' excitement, because the item is then valued at less. This same conclusion applies equally to buyers: namely, it is not lawful for them to buy more cheaply by reason of early payment. For the "legitimate price" is that at which goods are valued at the time they are delivered. Therefore, if they buy for less, the contract is reduced to a usurious loan: namely, that they are lending money to the sellers to be paid back with an increase in goods.

<margin>Response to the first argument</margin>
But because there can be no doubt regarding the conclusion, let us proceed to the resolution of the arguments. The first is of very slight weight. For it is denied that twelve coins to be paid in the future are worth no more, in themselves, than ten present ones; indeed, twelve "absent" <note>future or distant</note> coins are worth the same as present ones. And although accidentally <note>in the sense of an "accidental" rather than "essential" quality</note> ten coins might be increased to twelve by a merchant through his industry, the price of the thing does not grow from this, as its value is estimated according to its nature at ten.

<margin>Richard of Middleton. Cajetan.</margin>
<margin>The author's solution.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other part, namely "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: a legal concept where a person is compensated for the profit they could have made if their money hadn't been tied up</term>, Richard and Cajetan, and those who approve of their opinion, judge it just as they do a loan. Namely, that it is lawful for a merchant to increase the price because of lost profit. For the reasoning is the same for both. I, however, can only with great difficulty be drawn to this opinion, led surely by the argument that profit does not "cease" for one who is not forced to sell, and no one is forced to sell without force or fraud.

<column-break/>

<margin>Response to Panormitanus</margin>
He who sells only because he is asked, sells voluntarily. Therefore, neither Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer</note> in the chapter "Ad nostram" regarding buying and selling, nor any of the ancients approves of this exception. Instead, they simply find all those guilty of usury who sell for more on credit than they would for cash. And Antoninus <note>St. Antoninus of Florence</note> in the second part, title 1, chapter 8, § 2, fearlessly denies that it is lawful to demand a higher price by reason of lost profit. And in truth, through this heading of "lost profit," usury would become more frequent in trade than in direct loans. Therefore, although I do not yet dare to refute this opinion with absolute certainty, but remain in my "fear" <note>theological doubt</note> as expressed above, nevertheless the arguments for the contrary opinion are not as weighty as its patrons believe. Therefore, regarding the authority of St. Thomas which Richard cites as a parallel, we respond the same as above: namely, that "emergent loss" <term>damnum emergens: actual loss or damage suffered by the seller, which is legally compensable</term> which the seller suffers is one thing, and is thus "sellable" <note>compensable in the price</note>; but "lost profit" is another, which in truth does not cease except when one is unwilling.

<margin>Juan de Medina</margin>
¶ The opinion of Medina is much more improbable, and I am quite surprised that some "moderns" <note>Neotericos; refers to contemporary 16th-century scholars</note> defend it: namely, that by reason of the risk <note>periculi</note> to which a seller exposes his goods while he trusts the price to time <note>i.e., waits for payment</note>, he has the right to sell at a higher price. Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart</note>, in the cited 59th question where he discusses this matter, refuses to grant this; yet the younger Medina, in Question 38 on Restitution, imitating I know not whom, boldly affirms it. But since usury—by the testimony even of the pagan Aristotle—is so hateful and pernicious, no one should offer occasions for it unless the clearest reason demands it. Furthermore, in this opinion, no reason, not even a probable one, exists.

<margin>First reason against the aforementioned opinion</margin>
First of all, Conrad argues to the contrary that there is almost no sale for future payment that is not subject to some risk. Therefore, it would always be lawful to receive something beyond the principal. But the opposing authors will defend themselves by saying they do not hold this for just any risk, but only where it is "legitimate." Namely, when the debtor is either poor, or fraudulent, or for any other reason untrustworthy; then, they say, the seller can sell the "fear of risk" for a price.

<margin>Second argument for the same</margin>
¶ His second argument is not of much greater efficacy. He argues that then not only the capital, but also that "price of fear" is itself at risk. Therefore, by reason of that, it would be lawful to receive another price. But...

<sig>Nn 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: nevertheless</meta>

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that selling goods at a higher price on credit is generally a form of usury, refuting modern opinions that justify price increases based on "lost profit" or "risk of non-payment." He maintains that unless a seller is forced to sell or suffers an actual direct loss, they cannot charge more for the mere delay of payment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of usury in credit transactions. Having established on the previous page that selling goods at a higher price simply because the buyer is paying later is generally usurious, he now moves to refute specific counter-arguments—particularly the idea that a seller can charge extra to compensate for the "risk" or "fear" of not being paid.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice & Right, Page 560

<margin>
The author's first reason.
</margin>
...nevertheless, the adversaries would respond that by the expectation of that increase to be received beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"; the "principal" or "capital" amount of a loan or debt</note>, all fear is compensated. ¶ Therefore, the opinion is more urgently refuted in another way. In the first place, the merchant does not sell against his will. If, therefore, he sees that his goods cannot be safely sold, let him not sell on credit, or let him accept some other security. Why, then, should he be allowed to sell that fear?

<margin>
Second reason.
</margin>
Secondly, it is argued: That seller—or suppose he is a lender—suffers no "emerging loss" <note>original: "damnum emergens"; a legal term for an actual loss incurred by the creditor because of the loan</note>, nor does he suffer a "loss of profit" <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; profit a creditor misses out on because their money is tied up</note>, nor any outlay or expense in receiving the price. For we assume all these factors are absent, since we are debating about fear alone: by what right, then, can that fear be sold for a price? But you say: because it is estimable by a price. I admit that: for a man would prefer to suffer the loss of some money than to be distressed by such anxiety. Yet it does not follow from this that it is saleable for that reason: both because the seller plunges himself into it of his own accord, and especially because the buyer is not bound to relieve him of such fear in any way other than by paying the price of the merchandise; therefore, when he pays, he satisfies the debt. 

The force of the argument is further clarified: if at the beginning no mention of fear had been made, yet the seller had been vehemently tormented by fear on account of the danger; later, when the buyer pays, the seller could receive nothing beyond the principal by reason of that past fear and danger. Therefore, he cannot include it in the contract at the beginning either. Indeed, if such an opinion were true, the condition of the seller—suppose, for instance, he were naturally greedy and therefore prone to fear—would be a legitimate reason for receiving a higher price.

<margin>
The first argument.
</margin>
¶ Let us therefore weigh the arguments by which these opponents dare to offer these "handles" for usury. The first is this: a <term>fideiussor</term> <note>a guarantor or surety who takes on the legal obligation to pay if the debtor fails</note> (as was said above) can receive a price for the obligation by which he is bound to pay another's debt. Therefore, it should be lawful for a seller to bargain with the buyer in these words: "Give to me what you would have given to a guarantor, and I will undergo the risk myself." For no reason for a distinction appears. Indeed, even a guarantor seems, in effect, to be lending to the debtor when he pays on his behalf. 

<margin>
The solution.
</margin>
The answer is that there is a very wide discrepancy. A guarantor does not receive a price for the fact that he lends (since it may happen that he never actually has to pay for the debtor), but because he is *obligated* to pay; he can sell that obligation. But a lender truly lends, which he is bound to do for free <note>In Catholic social teaching of this era, a "mutuum" or loan of fungible goods like money had to be free of charge unless there was a specific "extrinsic title" to justify interest</note>. I wonder that these opponents are not mindful of their own positions. For since they admit that it is lawful to receive a price for the *obligation* of lending, but not for the loan itself,

<column-break/>

they ought to perceive by a similar interval that a guarantor can receive a price for the obligation of paying or lending, but a lender cannot receive a price for the loan. This is true even though both are involved in the same danger. 

<margin>
Argument 2.
</margin>
¶ And in the same way, their second argument is struck back—the one concerning a person who, through a <term>contract of insurance</term> <note>original: "contractum assecurationis"</note>, takes upon himself the risk of another's goods. This person lends nothing; rather, for the obligation of paying for the goods if they perish, he receives a price. This is similar to a person who, through a <term>contract of partnership</term> <note>original: "contractum societatis"</note>, exposes his money to risk; he does not receive profit because of the risk itself, but because of the business negotiation. 

<margin>
Response.
</margin>
In this case, he does not lend his money, but exposes it to trade, and therefore he receives the profit from it. Therefore, no argument can be drawn from these cases to justify a lender charging a price. A lender, by the very act of lending, must transfer ownership to the other party for free, with only the obligation that he receives back just as much as he gave. This is strongly confirmed by this fact: a lender is not obligated to *lose* his money in the same way an insurer is, or as a partner is if the goods perish. The borrower is always obligated to pay back the debt regardless of what happens to the money. Therefore, such risk is not worth any other price than that the borrower simply repays the loan.

<margin>
Argument 3.
</margin>
¶ They argue thirdly: a person who leases his horse to a man and fears that the man might exhaust the horse with excessive work, or perhaps kill it in some other way, could agree on a price so that if the horse were endangered, the loss would fall on him [the owner]. Therefore, they argue the same should apply to lent money. 

<margin>
Solution.
</margin>
But you see how there is no similarity here. In the <term>leasing</term> <note>original: "locatione"</note> of a horse, ownership is not transferred; therefore, the true owner can bargain regarding the risk of his own property. But he who sells or lends transfers ownership to the other person. Since the borrower is bound to pay the whole amount back, he should not be burdened with an additional price just because of the creditor's fear.

<margin>
Another question.
</margin>
¶ It remains to answer whether it is lawful for a seller, by reason of expenses which he probably fears he will incur before he receives the price, to include something beyond the principal in the contract. The cited author grants this permission in two ways: first, that it is lawful to make an agreement between the parties regarding "conjectural expenses." Secondly, that he can receive something by reason of the anxiety he will suffer from the fear of litigation and labor. This second point, however, has now been sufficiently refuted. Fear and danger alone, without actual labor or financial loss, grant no right to receive anything in return.

<summary>
Domingo de Soto refutes the idea that a lender or seller on credit can charge extra to compensate for the "fear" of financial risk. He distinguishes lending from insurance, partnerships, and leasing, arguing that since ownership of money transfers to the borrower, the lender cannot charge for risks that do not involve actual expenses or lost profits.
</summary>

### Book Six, Question IV.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
But as far as the matter of expenses is concerned, there is no doubt that whatever a creditor spends in recovering a debt, he can demand from the debtor. However, it is much safer, when you fear a man's craftiness and dishonesty, to neither lend him anything nor sell to him on credit; or, when you do lend, to wait for the term of payment, so that it may perhaps be done without any expense. For prior agreements regarding expenses hardly escape the suspicion of <term>usury</term> <note>original: "usuræ"; the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender</note>. Nonetheless, when expenses are feared based on good conjectures and without any fraud—namely, when your debtor is far from your city or location—there is no injustice in entering into a pact with him regarding expenses and labor, and receiving a fixed price, even if he is not going to incur any expenses afterward. For even if you were to spend more, you could not receive more than what was confirmed by the agreement. ¶ Regarding the matter of the third argument, opinions also vary among the Doctors. For on one hand, it represents a usurious <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutuatio"; specifically a "mutuum," a loan of fungible goods like money where the same amount must be returned</note>, but on the other hand, it appears to be a just purchase. And because the case is confusing, a decision is necessary. Therefore, having looked into it more closely, I

<margin>Solution to the third argument.</margin>
think we must respond by making a distinction. For when a debt is subject to no danger at all, but is expected to be paid most certainly without any expense or labor, it would by no means be lawful to buy such a debt for less, even if one had to wait a long time. This would indeed be not only a cloaked usury, but an exposed usurious loan. Since receiving more than you give by reason of the delay of time is usury. Nor does it matter that twelve units a year from now are more convenient for the creditor selling the <term>legal action</term> <note>original: "actionem"; the legal right to sue for or collect a debt</note> than ten units now. I say this would not clear the buyer, because it is certainly not a purchase, but a loan. When, however, the payment is in danger, I have no doubt that it would be lawful to buy it for a cheaper price than the whole debt is worth. For example, when a royal salary is owed to a soldier, and the creditor fears he will receive either not all of it, or not without great trouble and annoyance, or not without expenses, anyone can buy such a debt from him for less. Anyone, I say, without force or fraud. For if someone is the king's treasurer and redeems for less what he ought to pay, that would be a form of coercion. The example of our assertion is if a debtor has fallen into poverty or has fled, etc. In that case, there is no rationale for a loan, neither in form nor in substance; rather, it is the purchase of that "action," which in truth is not worth as much as some think (i.e., the full amount of money owed). Indeed, it is like buying a standing crop or buying a legal action that depends on a lawsuit. Which is buy-

<column-break/>

ing a thing in hope. ¶ However, the argument that might be thought to work from the opposite side is that

<margin>Reply against the solution.</margin>
it would then seem the debtor himself could lawfully redeem his own debt for a lower price. For if it is lawful for another, why should it not be lawful for himself? But that it is not lawful for him is clear from the fact that he who does not pay as much as he owes does not preserve the equity of justice. Therefore, it is responded:

<margin>Response.</margin>
the argument does not hold by any similarity. For the debtor, by reason of the preceding contract, owes the entire sum; but a third party, because he owed nothing, can justly buy that "action" for what it is worth. ¶ But from here arises

<margin>Another argument.</margin>
an argument against what was just decided by us. The argument is this: Twelve units under risk are not worth more than ten certain units, since that action is justly bought for ten. Therefore, he who could sell a thing for ten coins in cash could sell the same on credit for twelve, provided a probable danger of non-payment is imminent. It is responded that it is one thing

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
to buy a thing that is subject to risk, and another thing to lend or sell on credit under risk. For he who lends or sells on credit, since he suffers no force or fraud, can receive nothing by reason of the postponed payment; he should either take security or not lend with risk. Therefore, if he wishes to undergo that risk for free, let him blame himself. ¶ Finally, the fourth capital argument certainly held me in much doubt for a long time. For according to the universal and royal rule, the just price of things is that which is paid promptly upon receiving the goods. Nevertheless, I do not think I can

<margin>Solution to the fourth argument.</margin>
deny that in such a case a legitimate exception to the rule is made, so that the just price is only what is expected in the future. For goods that are brought from abroad, and especially those transported through maritime dangers, cannot be brought in such a large quantity that they can be sold all at once for cash. I would say "cannot," if you consider those things that happen most frequently. According to which consideration the laws must be judged. For this reason, those who load ships with such goods must of necessity buy some of them on credit. Because of this, they are allowed to hope to sell them to other merchants in the port at that same price which is to be made from selling them piece by piece. However, by this concession, we do not intend to provide an opening for merchants who sell goods in the cities, since the whole reason excusing the contract is necessity.

F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

the freedom of selling and buying such a large supply of merchandise that it cannot be sold for counted cash; and for that reason, it is sold to those who are going to collect the price from it later. Outside of this necessity, however, things must be valued at their present price. Therefore, private merchants in the markets should see to how they buy; furthermore, they must understand that they cannot resell except at the present price. For no excuse can be made from the fact that buying citizens do not always have cash on hand. For this would be to force them, out of necessity, to buy at usurious rates.

<margin>On the advance payment for wool.</margin>
¶ It is no wonder that even the most prudent person might doubt the second part of the fourth argument. For indeed, the wool market, which involves advance payment, bears the appearance of <term>usury</term> <note>original: "usurarum"; the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender</note>, since the goods are bought at a lower price for that reason. Yet, I do not judge such purchases to be entirely usurious, provided fraud is absent. Namely, as long as the payment is not advanced except for two or three months—when the payment for pasturage is usually made—or at most within the same year in which the wool is to be received. For if payment is advanced into another year, so that you buy at a much lower price due to the long delay, it is manifest usury. The reason that compels me to this opinion is that the merchandise itself, by its nature, requires this. Namely, because the owners of such numerous flocks cannot bear the expense of feeding them unless they secure immediate support for themselves from the wool that is being grown. Added to this is the fact that the form of this kind of market has already become so prevalent through custom and usage that even the shepherds, upon whom the burden of the lower price falls, refuse to sell otherwise.

<margin>On marine fishing.</margin>
¶ And perhaps the same advance price is permitted in marine fishing: not only because of the expenses of poor fishermen, but also because the fishing trade could not be maintained unless buyers were very ready to receive the catch bought beforehand. However, an example is not drawn from this for other smaller things, such as allowing one to buy grain at a lower price from a farmer with advanced money. For it is accidental that a farmer is in such poverty that he cannot bear those small expenses; for which reason he is forced to seek a loan at usury. And the judgment is the same for other things of this kind: namely, when the necessity of the person is the cause of selling at an improper time. For in the wool trade, there is not so much an accidental necessity of persons as there is a native necessity of the thing itself.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether it is lawful to sell a thing more dearly on credit than at the present price, when the owner of the thing was not then intending to sell it.<-

<image-desc>Large ornamental drop cap 'T' depicting two figures, possibly merchants or scholars, seated at a desk or table, consulting books or ledgers.</image-desc> Although the general rule is what we established in the previous article, it remains nonetheless to explore whether it admits any exception: specifically, when goods were not to be sold until a time when they were expected to be worth more, whether it is lawful to sell them more dearly on credit than for present money.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
And it is argued on the negative side from the rule established above: namely, that the price of a thing must be valued according to its present value, as held in Law 4 of the <term>Falcidian Law</term> <note>original: "ad l. falcid."; a Roman law regarding the valuation of estates and legacies</note>.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If it were lawful to sell more dearly then, it would be permitted primarily by reason of <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucri cessantis"; a legal concept where a party is compensated for the profit they failed to make</note>, which is hoped for from the increase in price. However, it has been said according to the opinion more approved by us that no one properly experiences "lost profit" except one who suffers force or fraud. Therefore, he who sells of his own accord cannot sue for lost profit, and thus cannot sell more dearly for that reason.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: If it were lawful to sell more dearly for that reason, it would follow conversely that it would be lawful to buy a thing with an agreement that it be kept whole until it was either valued higher or bore fruit. For example, it would be lawful to buy sheep before they gave birth with the agreement that the seller would guard them at his own risk until they produced their offspring, cheese, and wool. The consequence is proved: For if the seller can make certain from now the future price at which things will be worth later, by the same right the buyer will also be able to make certain the fruits of the purchased thing which he buys. Yet the consequence is false. For by law, things do not perish except for the owner <note>original: "res lege non pereunt nisi domino"; a legal principle meaning the owner bears the risk of loss</note>. Hence, as soon as someone acquires ownership of things, they are at his own risk, as gathered from the laws "Incendium" and "Pignus" in the <term>Code of Justinian</term> <note>original: "C. si cert. petat. &. l. pignus. C. de pignora. actio."</note>.

¶ On the contrary is the chapter *Naviganti* regarding usury.

<margin>Chapter *Naviganti* and chapter *In civitate* regarding usury.</margin>
This article requires an understanding of the said chapter *Naviganti* and the chapter *In civitate* concerning usury. And indeed, in the chapter *Naviganti*, there are three parts. In the first, the contract of usury is condemned, by which someone lends money to one sailing or going to the markets, undergoing the risk of the principal, so that something beyond the principal is repaid—

# Book Six. Question IV.

...be repaid: indeed, this condemnation requires an interpretation to reveal its true 
<margin>Doubt regarding the first part of the chapter *Naviganti*.</margin>
meaning. For as we shall decide in Question 6 in the article on partnerships, a person commits no usury who puts his money into a partnership hoping for profit, because he takes on the risk of the capital. This is not by reason of a loan, but because he is trading with his own money. Furthermore, someone who entrusts his money to a navigator at his own risk does not strictly provide a loan, since if the money is lost, it is lost to him. Therefore, it seems that such a contract is undeservedly condemned. ¶ The response is that it is condemned because, since a loan should be provided for free, it is usury to refuse a loan unless the borrower is also forced into an insurance or partnership contract. If you argue the opposite—that someone who is not bound to lend can refuse to do so in order to make other contracts profitable for himself—the answer is that this is true. However, by the nature of a loan, one cannot compel another who perhaps had no need for insurance. For perhaps there was no imminent danger there, but it was merely feigned. This is evident from that provision regarding "one sailing or going to the fairs." For those going to fairs are under no danger, and thus perhaps the discussion concerned a voyage that was free of all danger. But more on this later. 
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ To the present question, then, the response is given in two conclusions. The first is: It is lawful to purchase merchandise at a lower price by paying in advance than it would sell for in the current market, provided there is a reasonable expectation that it will be worth more or less at the time it is to be delivered. For example, if someone buys wheat in winter which he will not receive until the harvest, even if a bushel sells for four <term>shillings</term> <note>original: "solidis"; a common unit of currency</note> at the time of the contract, it can justly be bought for three if it is believed it will be worth about that much in the summer. This is the second case mentioned in the said chapter *Naviganti*. 
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ The reason is that since things are produced for use, that which does not yet come into use for a purchase should not be valued at the present price, but at the price it will be worth when it is delivered to him. 
<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you might argue that this reason only proves it is lawful to buy now at an *indefinite* price, using words such as: "I buy from you so many bushels of wheat at the price it will be valued at the time of harvest." However, to fix a certain price now has the appearance of usury, for it might be worth much more; and yet the chapter *Naviganti* speaks of a fixed price. 
<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that when a thing is in a state of uncertainty, it can be defined by prudence and likewise by agreement. Therefore, the justice of this contract is not founded on the advance payment—otherwise, it would taste of usury—but on the conjectural estimation of a doubtful thing. From which it follows that

<column-break/>

even if the payment were not advanced, if the contract were still finalized so that an obligation resulted for both parties, it would be fair and honest. Just as if someone, by giving a deposit and fixing a price, indefinitely bought however much oil or wine was expected to be produced (as Aristotle related concerning <term>Thales</term> <note>Thales of Miletus, who famously bought up all the olive presses in advance of a bumper crop to prove philosophers could be rich if they chose</note>, which we mentioned above), he would commit no usury, even if much more were produced than hoped for; nor would the seller be bound to make restitution, even if the whole crop perished. 
<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The final conclusion: Someone who was not planning to sell his goods until the time when the price is expected to increase may sell them for more than they are worth at the time of the sale, provided he deducts expenses, labor, and risks—and in the event that, as noted above, he sells because he was asked to. For instance, if someone intended to keep his grain until the month of May, he may sell it around <term>Christmas</term> <note>original: "Natalem Domini"</note> for a higher price than it is then worth. For this is the third case of the same chapter *Naviganti*. And the reason for the conclusion is a sibling to the one above: 
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
because the price then should not be estimated according to the present, but according to the time when he was going to sell his goods. Otherwise, he would suffer an "emerging loss" <note>A legal concept where a person loses potential profit they would have otherwise made</note>, from which, as was said above, a seller can rightfully keep himself unharmed. Therefore, not only can he sell indefinitely at the price the goods will be worth in the month of May, but a certain price can be defined and established. For a doubtful thing can, as we were just saying, be determined through prudence. ¶ There is no reason, however, as in the previous case, to ask whether it is lawful to sell more dearly for cash on hand. For anyone who would buy in such a way would be in more need of a mind than of money. Who, indeed, would buy for counted cash a thing more dearly than he could buy it elsewhere more cheaply? Nevertheless, if the seller does not deceive the buyer, and the buyer wishes to give as much as the seller would have sold it for in the future, it is not usury by its nature. ¶ But there remains a significant doubt regarding the chapter *In ciuitate*. 
<margin>Argument.</margin>
It is argued, I say, that it is not only permitted for one who was going to keep the goods to sell more expensively, but also for one who was *not* going to keep them, provided he sells on credit. For indeed, the chapter *In ciuitate* makes no mention of that condition—whether the seller was going to keep the goods or not. Instead, it responds absolutely that whether it is pepper or cinnamon which sells for five pounds in ready money, it can be sold for six without sin, provided it is believed it will be worth more or less at the time of payment. <margin>Cajetan's solution.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of commercial ethics and usury, specifically analyzing the views of Cardinal Cajetan regarding whether a seller can charge a higher price when payment is delayed (selling on credit). # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law.

...can be considered in two ways. First, on its own as an action separated from the purchase: for example, if the contract of sale is not considered simply as such, but as having a loan <note>original: "mutuum"; a formal loan where the same amount must be returned</note> attached to it. Thus, the sale is completed and settled now, but because payment is waited for, something extra is extorted by reason of a tacit loan. And this, he says, is illicit and usurious. In the second way, the same delayed payment can be considered not on its own, but as part of the sale itself, which was not yet completed, but only begun and pending in the future. And then, he says, to receive something above the present price—if the goods are expected to be worth more later—is not usury. This is because the sale is deemed to be perfected only when the payment is made. For this reason, he says it is foolish to explain the chapter *In Civitate* <note>original: "cap. in ciuitate"; a decree of Pope Alexander III regarding credit sales</note> by using the other chapter, *Naviganti* <note>original: "Nauiganti"; a decree of Pope Gregory IX on seafaring risks and usury</note>, since they are two different cases.

¶ However, against this opinion is the argument that this Cajetan distinction <note>referring to the influential theologian Cardinal Cajetan</note> is too obscure to be easily understood. For a contract, as cited above from the law of Labeo <note>a famous Roman jurist</note> in the Digest regarding the meaning of words, is an obligation on both sides. Therefore, a contract of purchase is settled and perfected at the moment the seller either delivers or is obligated to deliver the goods, and the buyer either pays or is obligated to pay the price. It follows that the expectation of payment does nothing to prevent the contract from being perfect. Therefore, based on that chapter, nothing beyond the present price can be received.

<margin>Reasoning in the Law.</margin>

¶ Second. The form of a sale made on credit is always the same: namely, "I sell you this thing at such a price to be paid at such a time." Therefore, no reason for a distinction remains to say that sometimes the contract is "begun and not perfected," while at other times it is "perfected and including a loan." In fact, it always includes a loan—that is, the expectation of payment.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>

¶ Third. If the seller was not going to keep the goods anyway, it does not matter to him how much they will be worth later, and thus no "emergent loss" <term>damnum emergens: actual loss incurred by the seller</term> arises for him, nor does "lost profit" <term>lucrum cessans: profit that would have been made if the deal hadn't happened</term> occur. Therefore, by reason of that, he can receive nothing except the price currently running in the present.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>

¶ Because of this, the much safer solution is that the chapter *Naviganti* is a gloss <note>an explanatory commentary</note> on the chapter *In Civitate*. Namely, that it is never lawful to sell more dearly on credit, except when the goods were intended to be kept. For although the chapter *Naviganti* was issued by Gregory IX and the chapter *In Civitate* by Alexander III, Gregory nonetheless explained Alexander's intent.

<margin>The safer solution.</margin>

Nonetheless, Cajetan's opinion is not immediately improbable, especially if the sale is made at an indefinite price. Indeed, if someone who has an abundance of grain at the time of the Nativity <note>Christmas</note> is asked to sell on credit, even though he was not going to keep it, he can refuse the sale. He can instead give it as if it were a loan of ten measures to be received back in the month of May, or the price for which it will then be sold.

<margin>Cajetan's opinion is not immediately improbable.</margin>

<column-break/>

However, if it is treated like a loan, he cannot compel the buyer to pay in the month of May and not before. And for this reason, the contract is said to be "imperfect," because the price is not fixed but is pending in the future. But whether a doubtful price can be fixed at a higher valuation than what currently runs in the present market, I would not dare to grant to one who was not going to keep the goods. And therefore, one is well-warned in the same chapter that although the contract may not be usury by its form—because it has the appearance of a sale—nonetheless, the contract is suspicious and should therefore be forbidden to the common people.

The first argument has therefore already been resolved. For the rule teaching that the "just price" is what runs in the present market assumes that the goods are delivered to the buyer then. For otherwise, they should not be valued except at the time they come into the buyer's use.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>

¶ The second argument, however, fights more strongly: namely, when it asks by what reasoning one who was going to keep the goods can sell them at a higher price. For if it is by reason of "lost profit," we have already judged above that it is more probable that profit does not "cease" unless the seller is unwilling. Therefore, we can respond first that he can receive it by reason of "emergent loss." Indeed, even a voluntary seller can include this in the agreement when he sells for the convenience of the buyer, as was decided above.

<margin>To the second.</margin>

If, however, you do not rest satisfied with this answer because it looks like "lost profit," it is answered secondly and more clearly that "lost profit" occurs in two ways. In one way, when a thing is delivered to another, it is not worth more in itself, but only by reason of the industry of trading; such is the case with money. And in that case, I judged that he who voluntarily alienates it from himself by lending cannot receive profit, because he is not strictly "hindered," as was explained above.

Secondly, it happens that the thing itself which is delivered is going to be worth more—not only by reason of industry, but by its own nature and in itself. Therefore, even if a person sells such a thing of his own accord, if he does so because he was asked, he can sell it for more because of that expected value; however, the expenses and labors must be deducted from that, as has been said.

¶ By the third argument, doubt is removed regarding a certain common contract of purchase that is not safe enough. For there are those who, refusing to lend to poor peasants, weave a thousand frauds. First, the livestock...

...buy from them things they do not have; and they fictitiously lease the same back to them. Namely, they hand over twenty gold pieces <note>original: "aureos"</note> to a farmer, as if it were the price of oxen he does not have, obliging him to keep them safe as if they were leased, and to pay a monthly price for that lease. For this is usury. Indeed, when at the end of the year those same twenty gold pieces are returned—as if they were the "preserved oxen"—the price of the said lease is added on top.

Second, there is the one who buys, for example, a thousand sheep in autumn, obliging the sellers to keep them safe until May. This means they perish at the sellers' risk. After the buyer receives all the offspring, he resells the same sheep back to the same sellers at the same price. Many injustices lie hidden in this contract. First, if the farmers are obligated to buy them back at the same price, it is manifest usury. For since they are bound to measure back the same amount of money, it is a loan <note>original: "mutuum"; a formal loan of fungible goods where the same amount must be returned</note>; to which is added the value of the lambs, cheese, and wool. Furthermore, to obligate them to keep the flock unharmed is a "cloaking" of usury. For if the buyer were the true owner, the flock ought to be at his risk. If the sellers take on this risk, they should be paid a just amount of money based on the degree of risk; yet they receive nothing for the risk or the guarding, except perhaps a very small payment. Therefore, the logic of the argument is denied: namely, that if a seller who was going to keep the goods can keep himself immune from loss, a buyer could also constrain a seller to keep the goods safe; for as soon as he buys them, they should perish at his own risk.

# QUESTION FIVE
## On Annuities.
### ARTICLE I.
#### Whether the buying and selling of annuities is usurious.

In the final question regarding buying and selling, which occupies the fifth place in this book, we inquire about annuities <note>original: "censibus"; a financial arrangement where a lump sum is exchanged for a regular annual income, often secured by land or property</note>: a contract which has become extremely common in the state. The first article, then, is whether this type of contract for buying and selling annuities is usurious. The argument for the affirmative side is as follows:

<column-break/>

<margin>First argument. Aristotle.</margin>
Money <note>original: "numisma"</note>, as stated above, is not something to be sold, but rather something to be loaned; and he who sells its use separately is a usurer. For as we cited from the 5th book of Aristotle's *Politics*, chapter 6, money was only invented to be the price of things, not to be sold itself. However, he who buys an annuity buys money that is to increase for him beyond the principal <note>original: "sortem"</note>; therefore, he is a usurer. The secondary premise is proven: He who gives, for example, a thousand ducats <note>a high-value gold coin</note> so that he may receive a certain amount of money every month or year, buys nothing else but that money which grows for him beyond the principal. For if he receives a hundred every year, in ten years he recovers the exact principal. Therefore, if the annuity is redeemed, he doubles it; if it is not redeemed, whatever he receives beyond that is accumulated onto the principal.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued: This type of contract is a "cloak and shield" for all kinds of usury; therefore, it ought to be banished far from the state. The preceding point is proven: Whoever refuses to lend for free uses this trick to buy up redeemable annuities while keeping his capital safe—which is exactly the same as if he were lending at interest <note>original: "sub foenore"</note>.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Third, it is argued: If annuities could be established upon a thing or the fruits of things, they could equally be established upon a person, even one who lacks property. For just as things are fruitful, so a person "bears fruit" through their labor. However, the consequence of this seems to be condemned in the second chapter of the title *On Pledges* <note>original: "de pigno."; referring to a title in Canon Law</note>, where it is held that a free man is not held liable for debt if property is lacking.

¶ On the contrary is the argument that annual returns on immovable property are legally judged as property, as is clear from the *Clementines* <note>a collection of Canon Law</note>, in the chapter *Exivit*, under the title *On the Meaning of Words*. Now, immovable property can be justly bought and sold.

<margin>Livy. Tullus.</margin>
The present question is perhaps disputed with more opinions among the Doctors than the subject requires. For it is straightforward. Therefore, to begin the matter from the name itself: *Census* <note>annuity/tax</note>, as we said in Book 3 under the title *On Tributes*, is derived from *censendo* <note>assessing or judging</note>. This is because, as held in the law *Forma* in the *Pandects* <note>the Digest of Roman Law</note>, under the title *On Censuses*, the resources of citizens must be assessed so that each may pay tribute according to his means. From this, however, a second meaning was derived: that it specifically signifies the tribute or tax demanded per head <note>a poll tax</note>, namely when a prince wants the heads of persons to be enrolled in a catalog so that the extent of his empire may be known to him. Regarding this, Christ was asked whether it was lawful to give the *census* <note>tribute</note> to Caesar. For such pride David was punished, namely because he numbered the people, as read in the Second Book of Kings, chapter 24. Thirdly, *census* is also used to refer to one's means, substance, and the valuation of one's patrimony. For Livy reports in Book 1 that Servius Tullius <note>the sixth king of Rome</note>...

### Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>The two-fold establishment of an annuity.</margin>
Tullus, the King of the Romans, first established the "census" <note>original: "census"; here referring to the Roman tax assessment or registration of citizens</note> of the citizens. However, in our current context, the term **annuity** <note>original: "census"</note> is understood as nothing other than a pension which someone establishes upon their assets or their person. Or, to speak more significantly, it is the right to receive a pension either in produce, in money, or in some other useful thing. ¶ It must, nonetheless, be noted secondly that an annuity is established in two ways. One way is **reserved**; the other way is **consigned**.

A **reserved annuity** <note>original: "census reseruatiuus"</note> is when someone transfers their property to another, but reserves for themselves the right to receive a certain portion every year. Concerning this, there exists a law <note>original: "lex fin. C. de rer. permut."</note> where anyone is permitted to give a thousand units to another, while reserving for themselves either an annual or monthly annuity. This type of annuity is mentioned in the commentary on the chapter *Constitutus*. For in that same chapter, a certain abbot is condemned who owed a pension and had not paid it for many years. He is condemned, I say, not so that he would lose the use of the estate for which he owed the pension, but so that he would pay the pension itself.

And yet, if it had been a **long-term lease** <term>emphyteusis: a type of contract where a person gains the use of land belonging to another in exchange for a yearly rent and a promise to improve it</term>, he would have had to be stripped of the estate itself. Therefore, the commentary rightly says that a long-term lease differs from an annuity in this way: when someone gives their estate to another in a long-term lease, they do not transfer the "direct ownership" <note>original: "dominium directum"</note>, but only the "useful ownership" <note>original: "vtile"</note>; thus, if the pension is not paid, the estate returns to the owner. But when someone gives their goods to another under an **annuitized pension**, because they transfer the full ownership of the thing to the other person, no matter how long that person stops paying the pension, they do not lose the right to the estate, but they still owe the pension. This, therefore, is called a reserved annuity. However, no further mention of it will be made at present, because it is not so much in common use.

The other type is the **consigned annuity** <note>original: "census consignatiuus"</note>: as when someone, while retaining their goods and the use of them, "consigns" or assigns to another a certain pension, which they are obligated to pay every month or year.

<margin>Various divisions of the annuity according to Conrad.</margin>
Conrad <note>referring to Conrad Summenhart, a 15th-century German theologian</note>, in his usual manner, divides this annuity into many categories in Question 71. Regarding the foundation upon which it is established, one is **real** (instituted upon a thing/property) and the other is **personal** (constituted upon a person). Next, regarding the thing that is received, one is **fruit-bearing** (when grain or other produce is received) and the other is **pecuniary** (when money is received). This latter type is the more frequent. Again, one is **certain** (when the produce or money is fixed) and another is **uncertain** (when it is defined only by a quota, such as receiving a third or another portion of the fruits).

<column-break/>

Furthermore, one is **perpetual** and the other is **temporary**. Moreover, one is for a fixed number of years, and another is for an uncertain time, such as for a whole life—which he calls a **life annuity** <note>original: "vitalitium"</note>. And finally, one is **redeemable** and the other is **irredeemable**. Regarding almost every one of these, specific doubts are raised, though some are of little importance.

¶ Therefore, the question is answered with four conclusions.

**First conclusion.** Anyone can establish a real and fruit-bearing annuity upon their own goods, provided they are "free" <note>referring to property not legally tied up in debts or family trusts</note>. I say this to exclude those goods which are bound by the link of **entailment** <term>maioratus: a legal arrangement where property is passed down to the eldest son and cannot be sold or broken up</term>. This conclusion is generally very well received, and there is no one who doubts it. For it is quite manifest that anyone can give away or sell their goods for free, or alienate them through any other contract. Therefore, they may likewise give away either a certain quota of their fruits or a certain part, binding themselves to pay the same, either for a set time or certainly in perpetuity. This, however, is what it means to establish—or consign—an annuity.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But there is a doubt: just as it can be established under the form of a gift, is it also permitted through a **contract of sale**?

Indeed, among the theologians, Henry of Ghent <note>original: "Henri. quolib. 1. q. 39."</note> (citing others in support of his opinion) and among the jurists:

<margin>Henry's solution.</margin>
<margin>Innocent.</margin>
<margin>Johannes Andreae.</margin>
<margin>Salicetus.</margin>
<margin>Gregory of Rimini.</margin>

Innocent IV, Johannes Andreae, and Salicetus (who cites Gregory of Rimini for his cause) speak on this. Distinguishing between types, they say that anyone can buy **old annual revenues**—that is, those which had already been established previously, whether upon things or a person. However, no one can rightfully buy such revenues in a way that establishes them *at that moment*. 

For example: anyone can freely establish an annuity upon their goods or their person to give as a gift to another; and after it is established, a third party can buy it from that recipient. In the same way, anyone can buy royal taxes <note>original: "tributa regia"</note> which have been established upon citizens; this is called the "purchase of rights." Nevertheless, for me to buy from you an annuity which you are *just now* establishing upon yourself or your goods is considered **wicked** <note>original: "iniquum"; often implying it is a hidden form of usury</note>.

<margin>The reasoning for the previous opinion.</margin>
The reason, they say, is that in a sale, the **price** and the **merchandise** must be distinct. When an annuity is already established, it has the character of merchandise; if it is not yet established, there is no merchandise, but rather money is being bought with money <note>a classic definition of usury in Scholastic thought</note>. Hence, Johannes Andreae says he does not know how to excuse such a contract. ¶ Nevertheless, saving the authority of the Doctors who...

### Book Six, Question V.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Hostiensis.</margin>
<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
...are rightly considered outstanding, no one should doubt that just as an annuity <note>original: "census"</note> can be established by way of a donation, so too can it be established by way of a purchase. And here we reach the **second conclusion**: which all others—both theologians and legal scholars (such as Hostiensis <note>Henry of Segusio, a famous 13th-century canon lawyer</note> and the rest) writing on the same chapter *In Civitate*—confess without fear. For since every free person can sell their own goods, it follows clearly that they can also sell the fruits of those goods or a portion of them, binding themselves to pay either a quota of those fruits or a fixed part. In this way, they sell to another the legal right to demand those same fruits from them.

<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
Secondly: if one can give such a right as a gift for free, why could they not give it to a son-in-law as a dowry, or even to anyone else, either in exchange for service or for a price?

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
Thirdly, this is confirmed thus: anyone can be compelled by the order and law of a superior to pay a portion of their fruits annually (as is evident in the collection of tithes and taxes); therefore, one can voluntarily bind oneself to the same payment for a set price.

<margin>Fourth [reason].</margin>
Fourthly: anyone can (as we have very recently shown through both civil and canon law) donate their property to another and then sell it while reserving an annuity for themselves; therefore, conversely, they can sell an annuity while retaining ownership of the property.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
For this reason, as Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras, a 16th-century theologian</note> says under the word *Usura* (2, § 12), the contrary opinion is mistaken because it fails to distinguish the "merchandise" from the "price" here. For just as when previously established revenues are bought, it is that right which is purchased; so too, when the right is being established now, that very right itself takes on the nature of merchandise.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
<margin>Proof 1.</margin>
<margin>Ancharano.</margin>
¶ But because there is considered to be a somewhat greater doubt regarding monetary annuities, a **third conclusion** is applied: anyone may also lawfully establish a monetary annuity <note>original: "pecuniarium censum"</note> based on their resources, not only in the form of a donation but also as a sale. This is easily gathered from the above points, and it is the assertion of Conrad (Question 75). Indeed, if an annuity based on produce <note>original: "fructuarius census"</note> can be established, and produce can be valued in money, no reason forbids a monetary one from being established as well. Nor is there a loan <term>mutuum: a loan of a fungible item where the same amount must be returned, often the basis for usury charges</term> underlying this contract, as Ancharano (cited there by Sylvester) thinks; rather, it is a true sale. This is because the price is not handed over to the seller with a pact to return it, but is given perpetually.

<margin>Second [proof].</margin>
Secondly, anyone can bind themselves for free to an annual payment of money, handing over to another the right to claim it; therefore, they can sell such a right for money.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
Thirdly, an annuity can be assigned to a house whose "fruit" is nothing but money <note>i.e., rental income</note>; therefore, that same annuity can be fixed in money. In truth, regarding a **real annuity** <note>an annuity tied to a "res" or physical thing</note>—whether it consists of produce and fields or is monetary—the matter is too clear to require further proofs. Besides these reasons, there are also civil and canon laws

<column-break/>

approving contracts of this kind. There is the *Authenticum* (Under the heading: *Those who bind themselves...*), where curators of minors are advised to purchase annual revenues for them. And in our kingdom, there exists the 68th Law of Toro <note>a set of Spanish laws promulgated in 1505</note> permitting it. Above all, there are two *Extravagantes* <note>papal decrees circulating outside the main official collections</note> under the common title *On Purchase and Sale*. The first was issued by Martin V in the year 1423; the second by Callixtus III in the year 1455. These Supreme Pontiffs, when asked about this type of law, decreed that such contracts are licit. Nor do these laws distinguish between produce-based and monetary annuities.

<margin>Martin V.</margin>
<margin>Callixtus III.</margin>
<margin>Doubt concerning personal annuities.</margin>
<margin>Johannes de Lignano.</margin>
<margin>Abbas.</margin>
<margin>Summa Angelica.</margin>
<margin>St. Antoninus.</margin>
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
¶ However, a more serious doubt arises here concerning **personal annuities** <note>annuities tied to a person's labor or person rather than to a piece of real estate</note>. Indeed, many of the Doctors who admit that "real" annuities are legitimate deny this regarding "personal" ones. These include Johannes de Lignano, Abbas <note>Panormitanus, a famous canonist</note> in his 5th disputation, the *Summa Angelica*, St. Antoninus (Part 2, Title 1, Chapter 8), and Sylvester, who leans toward the same view in the place cited. Sylvester says that when an annuity is established upon a house that is only rented for five units, an annuity cannot be established for a greater amount. Therefore, all these authors say that an annuity cannot be established except upon a thing whose fruits are worth at least as much as the annuity itself.

<margin>Foundation of the past opinion.</margin>
We can suggest this as the foundation for this opinion: since a buyer becomes the owner of the thing purchased, they must undergo the risk <term>periculum: the legal principle of who bears the loss if a thing is destroyed</term>, as is clear in the law. If, however, the annuity were established upon a person, the buyer would face no risk. For even if the person's possessions were destroyed, the seller would always remain bound. Therefore, it would be an unjust condition if the seller were always in danger of loss while the buyer faced none.

<margin>Second argument for the same.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If an annuity could remain fixed to a person, it could be established in the same way upon all their resources combined with the person bound, so that even if all their goods perished, the bound person himself would survive. Such a contract does not appear to be a sale, but rather a loan secured by a pledge. This is because the ownership of the goods does not pass to the buyer; rather, they serve as a pledge, since the person is nonetheless held liable even if the goods are extinguished. But if it is a loan, receiving an annuity on top of it is usury.

<margin>Last reason.</margin>
¶ Finally, this opinion seems to be favored by the chapter cited above, *On Pledges*, where it is held that a free man is not held liable for a debt if his property is gone. It is also favored especially by the aforementioned constitutions of Martin and Callixtus, which state that annuities are to be established upon goods—namely houses, estates, etc.

However, it introduces a significant debate on whether these annuities must be tied to specific physical property (real annuities) or if they can be tied to a person (personal annuities).</summary>

# Friar Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*.

It is further stated that even if the possessions themselves which are bound <note>The Latin *obligatis* refers to property used as collateral or the source of the annuity.</note> are seized or destroyed, the sellers should not be held liable.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, a **fourth conclusion** is added: Anyone can justly purchase a personal annuity <note>original: *personalem censum*</note>; namely, one which the seller has established upon their own person.

<margin>Conrad. Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This conclusion belongs to the same Conrad <note>Conrad Summenhart, a 15th-century German theologian who wrote extensively on economic ethics.</note> in his 74th question, which he repeats in the 75th. In my judgment, it is proven by sufficiently firm reasons. A person can bind themselves for free—even if they lack temporal goods—to a monthly or annual payment of money, graciously conferring on another the right to demand it. The same right can be conferred on a son-in-law for a daughter's dowry. Therefore, one can also sell that same right to another. For as was said above, the buyer in this case does not provide a loan <note>original: *mutuat*</note>, since they do not retain the right to demand the principal back; rather, they use that money to buy the right, which takes on the nature of a commodity.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Secondly: anyone can bind themselves to pay a certain amount of money annually to a hired laborer for their work; why, then, can that same obligation not be valued in money and subsequently sold?

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
Thirdly: a personal annuity can be established by the law of a prince. This is clear from Nehemiah 10:32, where the Hebrews established upon themselves a third of a shekel as a yearly personal tax. For this reason, it is now the custom in some churches to demand personal tithes, which are mentioned in the chapter *Apostolicae* (under the heading "On Tithes" <note>A reference to the Decretals of Gregory IX, a core text of Canon Law.</note>), and tithes are paid on business dealings, as seen in the same source in the chapter *Pastoralis*. And, as we said above, a prince can demand taxes not only from resources but from a census of heads <note>A poll tax or capitation tax.</note>; likewise, a person can be forced to pay an annual tribute by reason of a crime. Therefore, anyone can voluntarily sell such a right over themselves.

<margin>Fourth [reason].</margin>
Furthermore, anyone is free by right to sell the obligation of their labors. Specifically, one may be bound to serve with their body; therefore, by equal right, one is able to sell a personal annuity. Why not? A free man can be bound not only by other civil contracts, but can even sell himself into servitude—as was shown in Book 4—and his son. He can establish an annuity upon his slave just as he can upon his other possessions; why, then, can he not sell a monetary right upon himself?

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
¶ And (what gives strength to all these points): every real annuity <note>An annuity tied to land or "real" property.</note> has a personal obligation annexed to it. Therefore, even when the things themselves perish, the obligation survives in the person, and thus a personal annuity can be established. The premise is proven first: the form of the contract always holds that the seller binds himself and his goods. Indeed, inanimate things are only said to be bound through

<column-break/>

a metaphor; it is the owner who is bound and compelled by a judgment. Furthermore, and most importantly, through a contract of this kind, neither the ownership of the thing is transferred, nor are the fruits sold, but rather the *right to demand* them. Therefore, those goods upon which the annuity is established do not so much have the nature of the thing sold as they do the nature of a pledge or mortgage <note>original: *pignoris atq; hypothecæ*</note> by which the seller’s good faith is secured; this is according to the tenor of the law, *fundus* (Digest, on annual legacies <note>original: *fundus. ff. de ann. legatis.*</note>). This very point is proven because if the fruits were sold in that contract, it would follow that the buyer, not the seller, would undergo the risk of their loss. Therefore, in a year when the fruits perish, they would not be owed to the buyer, but would be lost to him; yet this is false and contrary to universal practice. By this reasoning and practice, it is shown that he who buys an annuity does not buy the fruits, but the right to demand them; for the seller remains subject to the risk of the fruits as if they were his own property. For things bound to an annuity are like a pledge: if the pledge disappears, the creditor’s right of action is not thereby extinguished, as noted in the law *servuo* (Code, on pledges <note>original: *l. seruo. C. de pigno.*</note>). This is further confirmed by the fact that otherwise, monetary annuities could not be bought without designated fruits being assigned, the contrary of which was proven above.

<margin>First corollary.</margin>
¶ From this conclusion, it follows first: real annuities can be established not only upon specific and designated goods, but also upon indefinite and uncertain ones; namely, upon whatever the seller either possesses or will possess, because the obligation is resolved in the person.

<margin>Second [corollary].</margin>
¶ It follows secondly: an annuity can be instituted even upon a thing whose fruits do not equal the annuity. Finally, in such purchases, there is no usury. Nor, indeed, is there any injustice, provided the price is just, which is what must be attended to. Look closely, I say, at whether that right to receive such a great payment is bought for a just price. For then, if the thing upon which it is established is not safe, or does not yield so much fruit, the risk falls upon the buyer. How a just price should be estimated will be made clear in the next article. For this reason, the Bishop of Modena <note>original: *Metynensis*</note> is hardly consistent with himself; for although he had previously asserted the opposite of this corollary, he later affirmed personal annuities. For if the person remains bound, even if the land does not supply a just fruit, an action against the person remains.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you argue: when a thing does not produce enough fruit to pay the annuity, then the annuity is not "safe"; therefore, a suspicion of usury creeps in. This consequence is denied.

# Book Six, Question Five.

<margin>Solution.</margin> Indeed, injustice arises more quickly on the part of the seller than on the part of the buyer. For the buyer purchases an annuity <note>original: "census" — a financial arrangement where one pays a lump sum for the right to an annual income.</note> at their own risk when the underlying property is unreliable; but the seller is the one who ought not to sell unless it is based on something secure.

<margin>Response to the first argument.</margin> It remains, therefore, to respond to the arguments to the contrary, starting with those we raised at the beginning of the question. To the first, the response is: perhaps a dispute arises over the name—specifically, whether in these types of contracts "money" is being bought. Although, strictly speaking, nothing is bought except the right to demand a payment <note>original: "pensionem" — here meaning an annual return on investment.</note>; even if the value of that right is no higher than the payment itself. For this reason, in our mother tongue [Spanish], annuities established upon royal taxes are called "rights" <note>original: "iura"; likely referring to the Spanish "juros," which were state-backed annuities.</note>. They are said, I say, to be "rights" that are bought and sold. But whatever money might be purchased to be paid annually, it would be nothing other than the purchase of immovable goods, as is held in the cited *Clementine* decree *Exiuit*. Nor should the contract be considered usurious because the payments exceed the principal over the course of time; for it differs diametrically from a loan. This is the root of justice in this kind of contract: he who provides a loan binds the borrower to restore the same sum of money to him in full; but he who buys an annuity does not. Instead, he gives the money as a permanent price. Therefore, nothing prevents the "fruits" [returns] from exceeding the price over the course of time, just as in other purchases. And by this, the second argument is resolved. For no wickedness of usury is hidden in this type of contract. ¶ Furthermore, the remaining points by which the personal annuity was discouraged are solved with equal ease. For it is granted to the first premise that the buyer undergoes no risk. Indeed, even if the annuity were established upon a physical thing, the buyer would face no risk—either to the thing itself or its fruits—because ownership <note>original: "dominium"</note> does not pass to him. Rather, it is the seller who, having received the price, remains under that risk as the owner of the goods. Nevertheless, the buyer is subject to this danger: that even if the property perishes, he can never force the seller to redeem the annuity. Similarly, in a personal annuity, this risk hangs over him: that the seller, reduced to poverty, might be unable to pay the annuity. ¶ And <margin>To the second.</margin> regarding the second argument, the logical consequence is granted: and therefore we admit that while someone sells an annuity upon their goods, while the person nevertheless remains bound, those goods take on the form and image of a pledge <term>pledge (pignus): a physical object or property given as security for a debt</term> and a mortgage <term>mortgage (hypotheca): a legal claim on property as security without the lender taking possession</term>.

<column-break/>

However, in the second chapter concerning pledges, it is only advised that a free person cannot be made into a pledge for a debt like a slave, as is clear from the law *Qui filios* [in the Code of Justinian]. Yet it does not follow from this that a person cannot be bound by the bond of an annuity, just as they are by other contracts. ¶ <margin>Argument.</margin> Now, the argument that I construct more strongly against myself regarding the personal annuity is this: establishing an annuity on a thing that is consumed by its use is not lawful, but usurious. A personal annuity is of this kind; therefore, it is unjust. The premise is proven: if I were to hand over a thousand gold coins to you and burden you so that you paid me a certain amount every year for their use, I would be committing usury because I would be selling the "use" of money separately [from the money itself]. The minor premise is clear: for he who buys an annuity on a person seems to do the same thing: namely, paying a certain return for the use of that money. However, both premises of this argument are <margin>Solution.</margin> denied. First, I say that establishing an annuity on the use of money is not usury, unless it is done with the principal <note>original: "capitali"</note> remaining intact—for example, with an obligation to restore the price—for then it would be a loan. But if I were to grant you a thousand ducats forever, nothing forbids me from receiving a payment for their use. And this is clear. First, because I can give them with an agreement made that you buy a productive farm with them; if you do not buy it, the fault will be yours. And this is exactly what <margin>Baldus.</margin> Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a famous Italian legal scholar.</note> says in his commentary on fiefs. Furthermore, this has the force of a contract of partnership <note>original: "societatis"</note>. Secondly, the other premise is also false. For a personal annuity is not established upon the use of money, but is the right of seeking and receiving such a payment from a person. ¶ Nor indeed do the *Extravagantes* <note>original: "Extrauagantes" — papal decrees not included in the main official collections of Canon Law.</note> of Martin [V] and Callixtus [III] oppose our fourth conclusion in any way. But it is first necessary to advise that when you look at the *Summary of Councils*, which our reverend <margin>Miranda.</margin> Miranda <note>Bartolomé de Carranza y Miranda, a Dominican theologian and contemporary of Soto.</note> compiled (not without personal praise), you will see six conditions appended after the said *Extravagantes* were reduced into one form. You should not understand these as being necessities found in the *Extravagantes* themselves or as having papal authority. Rather, the author himself, by his own excellent judgment, gathered them as if they were necessary. The first of those conditions is that the annuity returns must be assigned to specific things, such as a house or a field, which...
