# Book Six, Question Five

...which alone remain obligated for the payment of those same annuities. By this condition, personal annuities <note>A "personal annuity" was one secured by the person's assets generally, rather than a specific piece of real estate.</note> are rejected. However, that condition is by no means gathered from the *Extravagantes* <note>The "Extravagantes" were collections of papal decrees that "wandered" outside the primary organized bodies of canon law.</note>. For the Bull <note>A "Bull" is an official papal decree, named for the lead seal (bulla) attached to it.</note> contains this only in the narrative proposed to the Pope: that the things being obligated should be clearly identified. Yet afterward, in the formal approval, it does not exclude the possibility that they can be established upon a person. Indeed, mention is made there only of real annuities (those tied to property), which the Bull approves; however, it makes no mention of personal ones, which it does not subsequently condemn.

<margin>Second</margin> ¶ The second condition of the same author—namely, that the annuities be bought at a just price, and that the entire price be paid immediately at the time of the contract—is true regarding the first part. This is not because the contract would become usurious if the price were not just (since a salable right is being bought), but because it would be an act of injustice, just as when any item of value is sold for more or less than it is worth. But as for the second part—that the price must be paid in full immediately—it holds no probability. For although this is also mentioned in the narrative portion of the Bull, it is not established as a necessary rule in the final approval. For what forbids the seller of an annuity from being able to credit part of the price to the buyer, just as in any other contract? 

Nor is the fifth condition gathered from the same Bull: namely, that if the property upon which the annuity was established should perish, the buyer cannot thereafter be compelled to pay the annuity. For the clause of the Bull only cautions that sellers should not be compelled to *redeem* <note>To "redeem" an annuity meant to buy back the right to the annual payment, effectively ending the contract.</note> the annuity if the goods are lost. It does not, however, prohibit them from being compelled to pay the annual pension <note>original: "pensionem" — the recurring annual payment.</note>. Indeed, if the debtors were to be freed from the debt of the pension once the property was destroyed, the Popes would surely have explained this. Therefore, since they were silent on this matter, they implied that personal annuities are also licit. Perhaps they were not in common use in those regions at that time because they are not quite as safe for the buyers, and therefore the Popes were not petitioned concerning them. ¶ And through these arguments, it is also shown that the sixth condition is not necessary, as was said above: namely, that it is necessary for an annuity to be established upon a fruitful thing <note>Property that produces income, like a farm or a rental house.</note>, and that the payment should not exceed the value of those fruits.

### ARTICLE II.

#### Whether annuities, both temporary and perpetual, are licit.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling vine or acanthus leaf patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>
IT WAS SUFFICIENT to have decided the question in general terms, were it not for certain particular doubts regarding both temporary and perpetual annuities. It is asked, therefore, whether both types are licit. 

Regarding perpetual ones, the argument is made on the negative side: If they were licit, it would follow that not only the seller, but also his successors, would remain perpetually "entangled by the same cord" of payment. Such a consequence seems unjust, especially after the property upon which the annuity was established has perished.
<margin>First argument.</margin>

¶ Second, an argument is made against the conditions by which this perpetuity is usually secured. Namely, that the seller is bound to maintain the estates upon which the annuity is established; that he cannot sell them without the permission of the annuity-holder; and if he does sell with permission, a tenth or twentieth part of the sale price nonetheless goes to the holder. 

<margin>Second.</margin>
<margin>Third.</margin>
Third, that unless he pays at the appointed times, he is deprived of the very property upon which the annuity was assigned. Fourth, that even if the things themselves disappear, the person nonetheless remains obligated. They add guarantors and six hundred other protections, which do not seem "married to equity" <note>original: "æquitatis marita" — a legal phrase meaning consistent with fairness.</note>.

¶ Third, an argument is made against temporary annuities. If they were licit, it would follow that they could not be bought for less than the total sum of all the future pensions. For example, if you buy a ten-year annuity of ten gold pieces per year, you would not be able to buy it for less than one hundred. Otherwise, whatever you received beyond your initial investment would be added to the principal (interest); and yet the common practice is the opposite.
<margin>Fourth.</margin>

¶ Fourth, it is argued: if it were permitted to buy temporary annuities, it would likewise be permitted to buy them for an uncertain time—such as "life annuities" [*vitalitios*] which last for the duration of the buyer’s life. But this appears unjust for two reasons: first, because since God alone knows the length of a life, it would often happen that the contract lasts much longer than the seller expected, causing grave loss; and second, because charity would be endangered, as the seller might be tempted to hope for the buyer's death.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Ratio of the conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with two conclusions. The first: Not only are perpetual annuities licitly bought, but there is actually less suspicion of usury in them than in temporary ones. This conclusion is evident from what has been said: such a contract is a pure act of buying and selling, just as if you were buying estates or other things to leave as a hereditary right to your descendants. From this, it follows that annuities of this kind can never be purely personal, but must be "real" and tied to "immovable" property <note>Real estate or land, as opposed to "movable" goods like furniture or cash.</note>.

# Book Six, Question Five

<margin>Latter conclusion.</margin>
For all other things decay as time collapses. For this reason, the *Clementina* <note>The *Clementinae* were a collection of canon laws published by Pope Clement V in the early 14th century.</note> cited above, *Exivi* <note>original: "Exiuit [de paradiso]"; a famous decree regarding Franciscan poverty and property rights.</note>, states that annual returns are classified by law as immovable property. They bear even less of a resemblance to **usury** <note>The practice of charging unethical or illegal interest on a loan.</note> because the price is never to be returned to the buyer. ¶ **Latter conclusion.** By equal right, it is permissible to buy temporal annuities for a certain time—such as for a decade or any other term—or for an uncertain time, such as "secular" annuities for the life of the buyer or his children. This conclusion is well-known. This is because here, too, the merchandise is distinguished from the price; the merchandise is the right to seek a payment. Therefore, unless there is inequity in the price (which we will discuss shortly), no such stain of usury infects the contract. For just as anyone can grant their land to another in **emphyteusis** <note>A type of long-term lease where the tenant improves the land and pays a regular rent, holding most rights of ownership.</note> for their lifetime while retaining a payment, so conversely can they sell a payment for life while retaining the property itself. Likewise, any individual can lease another's estate for life to live off its fruits; why, then, can they not also buy the right over that same estate to receive a set amount of money? Add to this that the *Clementina* *De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis* <note>original: "1. de rebus ecclesiæ nõ alien."; a law regarding the non-alienation of church property.</note> permits this very thing regarding church goods. Namely, that when necessity presses, a prelate can alienate church possessions for his lifetime; therefore, a buyer can also buy annual returns for his own life.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
In these conclusions, therefore, there is no ambiguity except those points suggested by the arguments. The first of these is: whether every obligation of a **perpetual annuity** descends perpetually to the heirs. For when an annuity is established upon buildings, or mills, or similar things, reason seems to suggest that if such a thing is destroyed, the obligation should no longer burden the heirs; and yet it was said above that the obligation of the thing is transferred to the person, and therefore, even if the thing is destroyed, the person is nonetheless similarly held bound. If that were true, the same obligation ought to remain with the heirs. Some consider this absurd. However, this is answered by the following distinction: When a perpetual annuity is established upon "uncertain goods"—that is, upon whatever a man possesses or will possess—then the obligation passes to the heirs, whether they succeed to the goods the seller then had, or (if those are destroyed) to other goods; for all those things are liable for the same payment. Therefore, the heirs should look out for themselves when they accept the inheritance. For he who sold the annuity could bind all his present and future goods with that bond. But when an annuity is established upon a specific, designated thing that is not entirely permanent—such as buildings—and no

<column-break/>

other **mortgage** <note>original: "hypotheca"; a legal security or pledge of property.</note> secures the contract, the annuity is not considered entirely perpetual, but only lasts as long as the thing endures and the person who sold it survives. For that personal obligation does not pass to the heirs except by reason of that specific designated thing.

<margin>The price of annuities.</margin>
¶ Regarding the price of perpetual annuities, we can say nothing else except that not only the quantity of the annuity must be valued, but also the stability and firmness of the things upon which it is established. For this reason, rights over castles, perpetual pastures, and estates are of a higher price. By this reasoning, a single price cannot be established for everything by law. Rather, the just price is that which is sold publicly without force or fraud. Nonetheless, it can happen that the urgent necessity of the poor compels them to buy at a lower-than-just price. Therefore, it does not appear that one redeemable coin is bought at a just price for ten—as has now begun to be practiced. Although where the custom has become prevalent, I would not entirely condemn it. ¶ It was, however, most advisable for **grain annuities** <note>Annuities paid in grain or based on the value of grain.</note> to be regulated by law. Namely, so that they would not be paid in grain, but at an estimated price, one for fourteen. For example, you bought a grain annuity for one hundred and forty gold coins. The law therefore commands that since the price of grain varies widely, it should not be paid to you daily, except for the amount of grain valued at ten gold coins.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second point, which inquires about the other conditions usually added to these contracts, this is asserted most firmly right at the start: no stain of usury is contracted by them. For usury, as has often been said, only arises from the point where a thing is bought which is not salable. Nonetheless, justice can be violated by these conditions through an inequity of price and the excessive oppression of the seller. First of all, the condition that the seller cannot alienate those goods upon which the annuity is established without the permission of the annuity holder is not an unjust condition. For otherwise, it might happen that the property passes to another owner who might not be as secure a debtor.

<margin>That the annuity holder receives part of the price because he grants the power to sell is unjust.</margin>
But that the annuity holder, while granting such permission, should be able to receive a portion of the sale price, displays no equity to my ears. For although in *emphyteusis* the one who receives the payment enjoys that right because he retains the direct ownership of the thing, nonetheless, that an annuity holder (who has no ownership of the thing) should receive something for the mere permission he grants to sell, is certainly not consistent with reason. But if it is permitted by the particular law of a kingdom, I dare not speak against it.

<margin>Another unjust convention usually applied to these annuities.</margin>
Likewise, reason certainly demands that to secure an annuity of ten gold coins, the seller be compelled to mortgage sufficient goods. However, that he must so bind his goods (even when they are very extensive) for greater caution that he can neither sell them, nor pledge them, nor dispose of them in any way,

This is approved in Law 68 of Toro <note>The Laws of Toro (1505) were a set of Spanish laws clarifying the application of Roman and Visigothic law; Law 68 specifically dealt with the loss of property due to unpaid debts.</note>. <margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ In the third argument, a doubt is removed concerning the price of temporal **annuities** <note>A "census" or annuity was a contract where one party paid a lump sum in exchange for an annual income, often secured by land.</note>.
<margin>Richard's opinion.</margin> For **Richard of Middleton** <note>original: "Richard. q. 80"; referring to the 13th-century Franciscan theologian's work on the Sentences.</note>, in question 80, holds that a temporal and monetary annuity for a certain time can be bought for a lower price than the total sum of the payments. He says that one could buy an annuity of ten per year for ten years for ninety gold pieces. The reason, he says, is that ninety pieces now are valued as much as one hundred paid out over ten years. However, this reason is invalid unless it is a true purchase. For it fails in the case of a **loan** <note>original: "mutuo"; a "mutuum" was a loan of consumable goods like money where the exact same amount must be returned, and charging interest was considered usury.</note>: since it is not permitted for you to lend ninety so that you may receive one hundred in that manner. Therefore, since the author himself fears this type of purchase might be reduced to a loan, he adds that the contract is licit when the buyer would prefer not to buy rather than buy, but buys at the request of the seller. I say he adds this tempering factor: judging that it is not licit to receive those ten pieces beyond the principal except by reason of **foregone gain** <note>original: "cessantis lucri"; a legal justification for interest where the lender is compensated for profits they could have made elsewhere.</note>, which he had previously said was entirely licit when the person would have preferred not to lend the money. But in truth, since this "foregone gain"—as we have frequently said above—is suspect when someone lends voluntarily, and especially so in the present cases: for he who buys an annuity does not think of himself as lending; and for that reason, he buys not only when asked, but also when he is the one asking. I cannot deny that this type of contract for buying monetary annuities for a fixed time carries a suspicion of usury if the price is less than the total annuity. Nor are they frequent in practice, nor should they be, unless there is some underlying doubt about receiving more or less. I say it would be licit to buy for ninety gold pieces a possession lasting ten years which would produce fruits of ten gold pieces every year; and it would likewise be licit to buy similar "fruit-bearing" annuities. For since the fruits are in doubt, the nature of a purchase is truly recognized; it is not corrupted simply because the fruits, over the passage of time, will exceed the price. But when, for ninety ducats, you buy not a possession but the right to demand one hundred in money, which involves no doubt (for let us assume that neither expenses,

<column-break/>

nor labors, nor any danger exists), then truly it can hardly be distinguished from a loan. It is exactly as if you gave ninety now with the obligation that after ten years one hundred should be returned to you all at once: where usury is plain. For whether they are paid in parts or all at once at the end seems to bring no difference. Therefore, I would not dare to approve without fear that monetary annuities for a fixed time can be bought,
<margin>How annuities are licit.</margin> unless for exactly the same price as the total sum of all the payments: so that it takes the form of a loan. If anyone, however, distinguishes in his own judgment between a payment of one hundred made at the end of ten years and one made annually, let him see to it himself. Nevertheless, discourse will return to this ambiguity in the next article. But regarding annuities
<margin>On life annuities.</margin> of an uncertain time—suppose for a lifetime, or until you enter into your paternal inheritance, and similar cases—there can be no doubt that they are licit. For since there is doubt as to how long you will live, or how long your parent will, and consequently how much fruit the buyer will receive, the nature of a purchase and sale is manifest.

->Whether the purchase of annuities with a<-

FINALLY, the last doubt, which is among the most important regarding these types of contracts, concerns the **redemption clause** <note>original: "pacto retrovendendi"; a "pact of resale" which allowed the seller to buy back the right to the annuity, effectively ending the contract.</note>: whether it is licit. Otherwise, the buyer would be burdened compared to the seller. But this is not licit for the buyer: for if the seller were bound to return the price to him, it would be considered a loan, and thereafter it would be usury for the buyer to receive anything beyond the capital.

<margin>Second.</margin> ¶ Second, it is argued: if a covenant of this kind were legitimate, it would follow that similar additions would also be legitimate, such as that the seller cannot redeem the annuity before a certain time, and that he cannot redeem it piecemeal by parts, but only the whole at once. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Question V in Book Six of Soto's treatise, focusing on the moral and legal distinctions between usury and injustice in the context of annuities (census). # Question V of the Sixth Book

...remain perpetual. All these grievances seem both unjust in themselves and contrary to the decrees of the aforementioned Extravagants <note>The "Extravagantes" were collections of Canon Law; here referring specifically to decrees by Popes Martin V and Calixtus III that regulated annuities to prevent them from becoming usurious loans.</note> of Martin and Calixtus. On the contrary, however, it seems that usury is committed in none of them. Therefore, unless the contract is stained by some other injustice, there is no reason it should be rejected.

<margin>A twofold wickedness in annuities.</margin>
For the decision of this question, first of all, that distinction is necessary in these types of contracts which we mentioned above: namely, that a twofold wickedness must be distinguished in them: that of **usury** and that of **injustice**. For, as was said above, where a thing is sold that is worth nothing in itself, it is usury; but where a saleable thing is sold at an unfair price, injustice is committed without it being usury.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
With this foundation laid, the question is answered with four conclusions. The first is: It is by no means lawful to buy an annuity with a pact of resale <note>original: "pacto retrouēmendi"; a clause allowing or forcing the buy-back of the contract.</note>—for example, by obligating the seller to redeem the same at the same price, or a lesser one—unless the buyer receives nothing more than he gave, once the fruits are calculated into the principal. Indeed, every such contract is clearly usurious. This is a condition of the Extravagants of Martin and Calixtus; even if it were not contained there, it is manifest in itself. For truly, wherever money or any consumable thing is handed over with a pact to receive the same again or its value, plus something beyond the principal, there usury is either open or hidden. Therefore, when you buy for a thousand ducats an annuity that pays you fifty annually, and you force the seller to buy it back from you, you make your capital safe; because of this, you are in reality lending it and receiving the fruits of the thing beyond the principal. This, therefore, is the root of usury in such contracts. `<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>` I would say "with a pact of receiving beyond the principal": since nothing forbids you from buying a thing, agreeing with the seller that if it displeases you within a certain term, the contract is rescinded: provided that you count the fruits received toward the principal. The law of the kingdom also sanctioned this same conclusion.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: It is lawful to buy an annuity with a pact of resale, and no stain of usury underlies it there: namely, when the buyer is obligated to resell it if the seller wishes to redeem his property; so that the choice is placed not in the buyer, but in the seller. Therefore, unless injustice is present from elsewhere, there will be no iniquity in such a contract. This is also a condition of the same Extravagants of Martin and Calixtus, which natural reason itself makes clear. Where-

<column-break/>

fore, by this pact, **redeemable** and **irredeemable** annuities are distinguished. From which it follows that all perpetual ones are irredeemable, but not the reverse. For even if they are not redeemable, they can be sold only for a time, as was said above.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is proved. If any reason for usury were present here, it would be chiefly because the nature of a <term>mutuum</term> <note>A "mutuum" is a specific type of loan in Roman law involving goods consumed by use (like money), which must be returned in the same kind and quality, and was strictly interest-free under Church law.</note> would creep in. But truly, since the buyer does not reserve for himself the right of forcing the seller to restore the price, it is no loan, but a true sale. Moreover, it is clear that such a sale can also be free from other injustice; for such injustice would be committed either because of a burden on the seller—and this is not so, since that condition of liberty comes from his own property—or because of a constraint on the buyer, and this is least of all, since that task is relieved by a reduction in price. For example, ten perpetual florins are worth two hundred ducats; but because of that bond of reselling, the price is diminished, so that they are bought for no more than one hundred and forty florins. Therefore, since that obligation by which the buyer is forced to resell is valued at the whole remainder, no iniquity remains.

<margin>Second reason for the conclusion.</margin>
A second reason proves this. In a contract of sale, the buyer can voluntarily undertake any other burden if a reduction in price is made. For instance, that he may not open windows in the purchased house, or that he may not sell to certain persons, and similar things; he can therefore also undergo this yoke of reselling of his own accord. This is a conclusion which is also considered just by civil law, as is clear in the law *si fundum* <note>Code of Justinian, Book 4, Title 54, Law 2.</note>, on pacts between buyers and sellers. And the chapter *ad nostram* <note>Decretals of Gregory IX, Book 3, Title 17, Chapter 5.</note>, on sales, also suggests it is just if the price is just. For that reason, a similar contract is considered usurious there because he who had bought a redeemable annuity had paid such a low price that it was considered a loan instead.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
But if someone should object with an argument from **Leviticus 25**, where it was commanded that if the seller should later redeem the thing sold, the fruits received should be counted toward the principal.

<margin>Response.</margin>
It is responded that that law was a judicial law <note>original: "legalem"; referring to the specific civil laws of the Old Testament as opposed to eternal moral laws.</note> like the other: so that in the **Year of Jubilee** <note>In ancient Hebrew law, the Jubilee occurred every 50th year, when debts were forgiven and land returned to its original owners.</note> all things sold would return to their sellers. For God had provided that, so that by way of sale the estates of the land of promise should not be accumulated among a few, with others left in poverty; and therefore those laws have ceased.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
The third conclusion: It is also lawful, and does not have the flavor of usury, to buy annuities with a pact of resale: once a time is established—both that before which the seller does not have the faculty of redeeming, and that within which, if it is not redeemed, no further faculty of redeeming remains, but the annuity remains perpetual. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Book Six, Question Five, regarding the legality and moral implications of annuities (census). Specifically, it examines whether restrictions on the seller's right to buy back (redeem) the annuity constitute usury according to the papal decrees (the Extravagants) of Martin V and Calixtus III.</meta>

# Dominic de Soto, on Justice and Right.

...this conclusion is what seems to be condemned by the same cited author according to the same *Extravagants* <note>The "Extravagants" refers to a collection of Canon Law; here specifically the decrees of Popes Martin V and Calixtus III which regulated financial contracts.</note> of Martin and Calixtus. This, however, is to get stuck in the same difficulty: namely, to infer a negative from an affirmative. For the description of the proposal contains the idea that as often as it pleases the seller to redeem it, the ability should be available. But although the Pope agreed to the proposal, he did not thereby judge that such a condition was necessary to avoid usury. Indeed, that condition was proposed to him precisely because it seemed to present a stronger appearance of a loan, and subsequently of usury, if the seller were free from the annuity whenever he wished to return the money. For, as we said above, the less freedom there is for the seller to redeem, the greater is the nature of a "purchase" in the contract, and subsequently the less suspicion of usury. For this reason, a perpetual annuity bears less resemblance to usury than a temporary one does.

<margin>Both parts of the conclusion are supported.</margin>
Therefore, both parts of the conclusion are proven by manifest reason. One can buy a perpetual annuity where the seller's ability to redeem is entirely taken away; therefore, that ability can be granted to him for whatever time is agreed upon between him and the buyer.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And this is confirmed. That burden which the buyer imposes on himself—to sell it back again as often as it pleases the other—is estimable in money; and therefore he buys it for less than if he were buying it in perpetuity. However, that he should bind the seller so that he cannot buy it back before a certain time contains no other evil than that the burden on the same buyer is lightened; and thus the annuity should be valued at more then than if full liberty were left to the seller. Therefore, if the price is increased to a just level on account of this matter, there is no usury. Indeed, even if the price were less than just, it would not be usury, although it would be an injustice that "tastes" of usury, as is held in the cited chapter, *Per vestras*. By the same reasoning, an annuity can also be purchased where the power of redemption is granted precisely up to a predetermined time.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The fourth conclusion. It is lawful and removed from the nature of usury to buy these types of redeemable annuities with the condition attached that they be redeemed not piecemeal and in parts, but all at once. Nor does it stand in the way that it is proposed in the text of the said *Extravagants* that it should be at the seller's discretion whenever he wishes to redeem the whole or parts. For it is answered in the same way: that although this is permitted, nevertheless other options are not excluded in that permission. Indeed, reason shows it should not have been excluded. For if a pact of this kind vitiated the contract, it would be primarily because it caused it not to be a contract of purchase and

<column-break/>

sale: however, it does not do this. For if, without that condition, it was a true purchase because the price was given in perpetuity without an obligation of restitution (for the true nature of a purchase consists in this), the fact that such a condition is added does not stop it from being a purchase. There could indeed be injustice: because it is by no means to be denied that such a condition lightens the buyer's obligation to sell back, and for that reason the annuity becomes worthy of a higher price; but nonetheless, no appearance of usury is presented there. For if an annuity can be perpetual, why will it not be a true purchase if the buyer is unwilling to bind himself more heavily than to reselling the whole?

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ Add to this that if the contrary opinion were true, it would follow as a consequence that no condition could be attached to any certain part; rather, if I bought seventy in annuity for a thousand ducats, the seller could redeem every single ducat as often as he wished—which in truth would be a grave inconvenience to the buyer. For the buyer could have used that money to buy a farm with which he might be supported, with the farm always remaining secure. But if he received the price in such tiny portions, he could not do that. ¶ Furthermore, it is accidental and thus beside the point that the seller cannot redeem the whole at once. For if I bought an annuity of only one ducat, who could not redeem the whole at once? And if the seller is rich, even if the annuity is quite large, he will be able to redeem it all; however, whether he is poor or the annuity is larger does not change the nature of the contract. ¶ Indeed, as I was saying, injustice can be committed due to a deficiency in price: for on account of conditions of this kind which tend toward the burden of the seller and the relief of the buyer, the valuation of the annuity ought to be higher. Nevertheless, regarding this, I judge that one should abide by the custom of the province, provided there is no violence or fraud.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the first argument, therefore, it is answered that in the first two conclusions a distinction was assigned between the buyer and the seller. For if the power remained with the buyer so that whenever *he* wished, the seller was bound to return the price, the nature of a loan would be manifest there, and thus whatever the seller had received in the annuity would be usurious. But because the liberty of redeeming remains with the seller alone, it does not take away the nature of a purchase: because he himself might never redeem it.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, the answer is likewise given that in the two remaining conclusions, these same conditions are declared lawful.

<summary>Soto argues that restricting a seller's right to buy back an annuity (either by time or by requiring a lump-sum payment) does not make the contract usurious. He distinguishes between usury (which involves the nature of the contract as a loan) and injustice (which involves an unfair price).</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of annuities to the moral and legal framework of partnerships (societas). It follows Question 5, which concluded the analysis of "census" contracts, and now addresses how two parties—one providing capital and the other labor—can licitly share profits without falling into the sin of usury.</meta>

# QUESTION SIX, on the Partnership Contract.

### ARTICLE I.
*Whether the partnership contract is lawful.*

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure at a desk, likely a scholar or merchant, surrounded by a floral frame.</image-desc>
After the contract of buying and selling follows another, which is frequently used: the contract of partnership. It is argued, however, that it is not lawful. If it were lawful, it would follow that two people could legally enter a partnership where one exposes all his money to risk, while the other risks nothing but his labor. For as it is held in the *Institutes* on partnerships, in the section "On that one" <note>original: "Institut. de societat. §. de illa"</note>, the labor of some is so valuable that it is just for them to be admitted into a partnership on better terms. Yet the consequence appears false: first, because it seems unfair for one to undergo the risk of a thousand or ten thousand ducats <note>A gold coin used in trade across Europe.</note>, while the other undergoes none, yet still receives a portion of the profit; second, because if it should happen that no profit accrues, it also appears unjust that the one who contributed the money loses nothing of his principal, yet the other loses all of his labor.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued that if such a partnership were legitimate, it would follow that the distribution of profit should be done such that a much larger share would go to the one who provided the money than to the one who provided only labor, in proportion to how much greater the value of that money is than the other’s labor. This consequence, however, is false. For if ten thousand ducats are compared with the labor and diligence of one man, almost all the profit should go to the one who provided the money, since he preserves his entire capital <term>capitale</term> <note>The original principal amount invested.</note>, while the other has suffered the loss of his labor. ¶ On the contrary is the chapter *Through yours* <note>original: "c. per vestras"</note> regarding donations between husband and wife, where Pope Innocent III approves of the partnership contract.

<margin>Who are called partners.</margin>
Here, first of all, before asserting any conclusions, it must be noted that from the name itself, those are considered "partners" <note>original: "socios"</note> who come together in a single

<column-break/>

business venture, so that each person, whether by their money, their labor, or their expenses, becomes a sharer in the profit. Indeed, as we said above, the term "principal" <term>sors</term> <note>Literally "lot" or "fate," referring here to the capital sum.</note> is derived from this contract: namely, because individuals contribute their portions to a common fund, and these portions are called the "capital" or "shares."

<margin>A twofold kind of partnership.</margin>
Second, it should be noted that there are two kinds of partnership. One is when many merchants pile together a single heap of their money and have common servants. Thus, the money, the labor, and the expenses are all shared. This kind of partnership is very frequent among famous merchants—namely, those of Burgos, Genoa, Bruges, and London, and others. In this case, there is no reason for doubt. For whoever trades with his own money undergoes its risk, and to them falls the account of expenses in proportion to each person's share, as well as the distribution of profit. ¶ But the second kind is where one person provides the money and the other provides industry and labor; as is found in the law "Partnership" <note>original: "l. societatem"</note> in the Digest under the title "For a partner" <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>; or where one provides industry along with some portion of money. Regarding such contracts, there is a specific question. Perhaps there is an honest man who does not have the skill for trading but has money—either from a dowry or otherwise acquired—which he places with a merchant so that a portion of the profit may be paid to him in proportion. Regarding this, it is asked whether it is lawful. We have divided this question into two articles. The first is: where the one who provides the money undergoes the risk of it. The second: whether it is also lawful if the capital, or some part of it, is guaranteed safe.

<margin>Alternative reading: regarding capital.</margin>
¶ And indeed, the first part is very easily resolved by a single and indubitable conclusion. If the one who provides the money undergoes the risk of it, the contract is lawful; nor does it smell of any scent of usury <term>vsura</term> <note>The practice of charging interest on a loan, which was considered a sin in Canon law.</note>.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
This conclusion is found first in Canon Law in the cited chapter *Through yours* <note>original: "per vestras"</note>; and then in Civil Law throughout the *Institutes* on partnerships, and in the Code and the Digest regarding partners. These laws are gathered from the nature of the matter. For since trade is lawful, it does not matter whether you trade with your money yourself or whether you entrust it to another who enters into business in your name, provided that the money remains under your ownership. He who puts his money into a partnership does not transfer ownership of it but retains it for himself, provided that he undergoes the risk of it. Therefore, he can lawfully receive the profit that falls to him for that share of money.

<margin>How the distribution ought to be made.</margin>
¶ However, as to how the distribution of profit should then be made...

<summary>This page introduces the ethics of partnership contracts (societas), defining a partner as one who shares in risk and profit. Soto argues that as long as the investor bears the risk of losing their capital, the contract is not usurious and is legally sound in both Church and Civil law.</summary>

# Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Distribution of profit in a partnership contract when one provides money and another labor.</margin>
...to the second argument asked, it should be defined thus: First, a total pool <note>original: "cumulus"</note> must be made of all the stakes <note>original: "fortium"</note>, with each one valued so that it is clear what portion each represents of the whole pool. Here one must be careful lest anyone, as happens to some, be deceived by thinking that the entire value of the money one provides should be counted as a single stake. For example, if Peter provides industry and labor, and another provides two thousand ducats <note>A standard gold coin of the era.</note>, the entire value of the ducats should not be treated as the stake. For in that case, it could hardly ever happen that labor would be valued as highly as the money, yet the cited text of the *Institutes* <note>A foundational Roman law textbook.</note> holds the opposite: namely, that work is sometimes more precious than money. This is confirmed by the fact that the total value of the money should not be used to calculate profit, because the person who provides money in this way does not spend it or give it to the other—since it is to be returned to him later—but only exposes it to risk. Therefore, only the risk to that money should be valued. For if Peter’s work, labors, and industry are worth one hundred, perhaps the risk of two thousand ducats is not valued higher; for if you made a contract of insurance <term>assecurationis</term> <note>Soto uses the logic of modern insurance premiums to value financial risk.</note> with another, he would insure those two thousand for that price of one hundred. Thus, an equal portion of the profit falls to each. This is the case in the law *si non fuerint* in the Digest <note>original: "ff. pro socio"</note>, where it is held that there can be shared profit even if only one person undergoes the risk—for instance, if the other person sails or undertakes other labors. Indeed, there can even be three partners: one providing money, another providing "industry" (the prudence by which business is governed), and the third providing physical labor. In such a case, each must be valued individually. By this reasoning, the deception of those who think someone can put a thousand into a partnership on the condition that they bear only one-fifth of the risk and receive one-fifth of the profit is uncovered. For since the other person undergoes the risk of the other four parts, by that reason he deserves the other four parts of the profit, and thus the first would receive nothing for his industry. In the same way, if the person providing industry also provided some money at the same time, he ought to receive from the profit as much as his labor and industry are worth, and additionally as much as the risk of his gold is weighed. This is the case through which that cited paragraph in the *Institutes* on partnerships should be understood, where it is established that one of the partners can receive two parts of the profit while bearing only one third of the loss. Mucius <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola, a famous Roman jurist.</note> used to condemn this because of the unfairness that appears at first glance, but the opinion of Servius Sulpicius <note>Another renowned Roman jurist whose view became law.</note> prevailed: that this is lawful. For instance, if, 

<column-break/>

for example, Peter provided two hundred ducats, but Paul provided only one hundred, yet Paul also provided industry and labor valued at three hundred. This might happen because the business is one where there is little risk to the money but a great deal of industry is necessary, or where the tasks and labors are great, such as in seafaring. In that case, the pool is worth six hundred, of which Paul provides four hundred; therefore, he should receive two-thirds of the profit, and Peter one-third, because he provided two hundred. Regarding loss, however, Paul only undergoes the risk of one hundred, while Peter undergoes the risk of two hundred. The case in the law *societas* in the Code <note>original: "C. de soci."</note> alludes to this same point. One must judge in a similar way regarding other partnerships, such as when someone buys sheep or herds with his money, and another pastures and cares for them with his industry. If the one who bought the sheep bears the risk as owner of his property, the value of that risk must be compared with the value of the other’s industry and labor. For if you make it so that the shepherd bears the risk, we have already said above that this is a usurious loan <term>usurarium mutuum</term> <note>A loan where the lender takes no risk but demands profit, which was considered a sin.</note>, since the capital stays safe for the owner of the sheep. Likewise, if you give money to an artisan so that he may practice his craft at your risk, the risk of your money must be compared with his work and labor, and the profit divided on that basis. But might you not be able to sell him leather,
<margin>Doubt.</margin>
or wool, or other material, so that after the industry of his craft has produced money, he pays you a higher price than the wool or leather would be sold for if cash were present? For this contract is in use in many places, and is therefore thought lawful because it results in the benefit and convenience of the artisan. The answer is that it is
<margin>Response.</margin>
nonetheless entirely illicit, even if it is useful to the artisan who lives off that borrowed value. For it is a manifest loan <note>original: "manifestum mutuum"</note>: namely, where a thing is sold for more because the money is credited. To the first 
<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
argument, therefore, there are those who respond that where no profit has accrued, the one who provided labor ought not to lose it, but something should be given to him from the capital. Nevertheless, the answer is that just as if a loss of capital occurs, the one who provided it must lose it all, so vice-versa, if the capital remains safe but no profit accrues, it all belongs to the one who provided the capital, and the other must lose his labor. For this was the bond of the agreement: that one would undergo the risk of the capital, and the other the risk of the labor. To the 
<margin>To the second.</margin>
second argument, it has been openly stated: namely, how the distribution of profit should be made—not by valuing the total money, but by its risk.

# Book Six, Question VI. 577

<margin>First argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
### ARTICLE II.
### Whether it is lawful to invest money in a partnership while keeping the capital safe.

Regarding a contract of partnership <term>societas</term> <note>A "societas" was a formal business partnership where partners shared both profits and risks.</note> where the partnership is legitimate, no doubt exists. However, a doubt remains whether it should also be permitted while keeping the capital safe <note>This refers to a "guaranteed" investment where the investor's initial sum is protected from loss.</note>. For the affirmative side, it is argued first from the cited chapter *Per vestras* regarding donations between husband and wife, where a husband is permitted to place dowry money with a merchant so that he may live off its profit; this cannot happen unless the capital is safe, since a dowry—as stated above—must remain intact.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued: one who places a large sum of money in a partnership can bargain with the partners so that he does not undergo the total risk himself, but they take a portion; therefore, by the same reasoning, they can agree among themselves that the others undergo the risk while he only contributes the money.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: one who invests money in a partnership can enter into a contract of insurance <term>assecurationis</term> with a third party who takes the risk upon himself. Therefore, he can enter into that same contract with a partner, who faces the risk in the same way, while the one who contributed the money is kept whole. Thus, this is lawful. ¶ To the contrary, however, is the cited law *Societatem* in the Code, *Pro socio*, where a partnership is approved in which one contributes money and the other labor; however, it seems to be rejected when one undergoes neither the risk of the money nor of the labor.

Although this question is controversial among the doctors <note>The "doctors" refers to established academic authorities in law and theology.</note>, it contains very little ambiguity; therefore, it is answered with a single conclusion.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
Such a contract is in no way lawful where someone invests money in such a way that he exposes himself to no risk, but the other party is bound to keep him harmless <note>original: "indemnem"</note> regardless of what happens.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason is manifest: because this is not a partnership, but truly a loan <term>mutuum</term> <note>In Roman and Canon law, a "mutuum" was a loan of fungible goods where ownership transferred to the borrower; charging certain interest on it was considered usury.</note>. By the very fact that another undergoes the risk of your money, he is made the owner of that money. For he is truly the owner who bears the loss if the thing is destroyed; and therefore, whatever the lender receives beyond the capital, he is guilty of usury. And from this, it follows that there is no partnership. For he truly contributes nothing, since the money is no longer his in principle. In short, he who exposes neither labor nor money to risk does not trade rightly. For that is true trade <note>original: "negotiatio"</note> where the merchant's own money is exposed to the business.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, there are those who respond by granting that in the said chapter, a husband is indulged so that he may place a dowry with a merchant with the capital safe, so that he may support the burdens of marriage from its profit—just as we showed above that a son-in-law is permitted to take the fruits of a pledge beyond the principal. They say the same regarding the goods of a ward. However, this assertion is as improbable as it is most harmful; since receiving usury is against natural and divine law <note>original: "contra ius naturæ & diuinum"</note>, it is by no reason dispensable, as is expressly held in the chapter *Super eo* regarding usury, not even for redeeming a life. Nor is it similar to a pledge, the fruits of which the father-in-law is judged by law to grant while he does not pay the dowry. That chapter, therefore, only declares how a husband can live from the fruits of a dowry: namely, if he places it with a reliable merchant under the common law of partnership—meaning that the capital is exposed to risk.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, we grant that someone can contribute, for example, ten thousand ducats to a partnership on the condition that he does not undergo the risk except for six or eight thousand. However, in that case, he cannot receive from the profit except precisely that part which corresponds to the money for which he himself undergoes the risk; for the remainder is judged to be a loan to the partners, since they receive it at their own risk. And thus, that part of the profit which arises from his risk belongs to him, while the rest belongs to those who submitted themselves to the danger.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
<margin>John Mair.</margin>
<margin>Accursius.</margin>
<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
¶ The third argument is where the greatest difficulty lies; John Mair <note>A Scottish philosopher and theologian (1467–1550) known for his work on logic and economics.</note> treats it at excessive length in Book 4, distinction 15, questions 48 and 49. And indeed, Accursius <note>A 13th-century Italian jurist famous for his "Great Gloss" on Roman law.</note> and Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading expert in Canon Law.</note> undoubtedly, and rightly, hold that a contract of partnership is in no way lawful where the capital is safe, for in truth it is merely a loan. Nor is the argument by which Mair argues to the contrary of any weight. For he argues from the fact that one partner contributes money and the other undergoes the risk, that it is not sufficiently gathered that the same money is judged to be a loan. For in the contracts of a loan-for-use <term>commodatio</term> and hiring <term>locatio</term>, the weakness of the argument appears. For one can lend his horse to another or some item of furniture on the condition that the borrower or hirer takes the risk upon himself; and nonetheless, it is not a "mutuum" loan. Why, then, is it different with money? This argument, however, as I was saying, is of no weight: because if in such contracts you hand over the thing at a fixed price to another for whatever use, the contract is surely one of sale...

<summary>This page argues against the "guaranteed capital" partnership, asserting that if an investor takes no risk, the contract is actually a usurious loan rather than a legitimate business partnership. Soto refutes arguments from John Mair and others who tried to justify such risk-free investments through analogies to insurance or equipment rental.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological debate over the "triple contract." Soto is responding to arguments by John Major and Cardinal Cajetan regarding whether a merchant can guarantee both the principal and a fixed profit to an investor without it becoming the sin of usury.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law,

...price of the credit: since money has a fixed price—namely, that the exact same amount be restored—the other party becomes the owner, and he can dispose of the money however he pleases as if it were his own, provided he restores it with profit. It is, therefore, truly a <term>mutuum</term> <note>original: "mutuum"; a specific type of loan where ownership of the thing (like money or grain) passes to the borrower, who must return an equal amount later. In Soto's time, charging interest on a "mutuum" was considered usury.</note>.

<margin>Hostiensis. Ioan. Andr.</margin> ¶ For this reason, the moderating views of <note>Henry of Segusio (d. 1271), a famous expert in church law.</note> Hostiensis and Joannes Andreae <note>A renowned 14th-century canon lawyer.</note>, who are cited there by the same doctor, do not suffice for the matter. For they say that the contract is lawful, keeping the capital safe, on the condition that if it is lost through business dealings, the merchant is bound to restore it, but not if it is lost by a chance accident. And indeed, <note>John Major (1467–1550), a Scottish philosopher and theologian.</note> Major approves of the first part but rejects the latter; for he says that the capital can be kept safe in such a way that even if it is lost through adverse fortune, the merchant is bound to pay it back. Nevertheless, without a doubt, in whichever way it is lost, the contract will not be lawful if the capital is to be restored in an equal amount.

<margin>Major's Argument.</margin> ¶ Therefore, the same author shows that the said contract is lawful by this reasoning, which in his judgment is manifest. For example, let us speak thus: Peter can place a thousand gold coins with Paul the merchant, which he can make safe through a contract of insurance <term>assecurationis</term> celebrated with John for the price of, for example, fifty ducats. Then he can "insure" the profit with Titius, as they say; namely, so that Titius gives Peter himself one hundred for the profit. By this reasoning, he has his capital safe and fifty in profit. If, therefore, he can contract in these ways with diverse persons, what forbids him from doing all these things at once with the same person? "I give you a thousand in partnership <term>societate</term>, from which you take fifty for insurance (let us suppose the risk is very small), and you will give me one hundred or eighty for profit." Here, he therefore has his capital safe, and nonetheless receives something beyond the principal.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin> <note>Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian who wrote influential commentaries on Thomas Aquinas.</note> Cajetan, in his work 16, response to question 11, partly rejects the contract and partly approves it. He says, I mean, that if those contracts are made all at once with the same person, they are not lawful: for instance, "I enter into a partnership with you on the condition that we also agree between us on both the price of insurance and the quantity of profit." For then it is a "cloaked" loan <note>original: "palliatum mutuum"; a legal fiction used to hide an interest-bearing loan behind the appearance of a legitimate business partnership.</note>. But, he says, if they are made successively—so that the one who provides the money does not then obligate the other to those same contracts, but after the money has been put forth under the common law of partnership, the merchant partner wishes to make those same contracts—there is no reason why it should be condemned. A distinction of this kind pleased the same author regarding pensions <note>original: "pensionibus"; annual payments often linked to land or offices.</note>: namely,

<column-break/>

that a pension cannot be established with a pact of redemption <note>The right to buy back the source of the pension to end the debt.</note>, but yet, he says, it is not unlawful if done successively.

¶ But truly, such is the smallness of my wit <note>A common scholarly humility trope; Soto is about to strongly disagree with Cajetan.</note> that I cannot see anything else in these contracts than a usurious loan, whether they are done successively or simultaneously.

<margin>The rejection [of the distinction] he seems to relate. For indeed when [it occurs] distinction. For Cajetan's.</margin> Nor does this distinction seem to me to be at all relevant to the matter. For indeed, when they are done simultaneously, it is clearly a loan. For by the very fact that Peter gives the money to Paul, and they agree between them on the profit, and that the capital is kept safe for Peter by the same Paul, then, as I was saying just now, Paul can dispose of that money as if it were his own—for example, to buy estates, to provide a dowry for his daughter, etc. Therefore, he truly becomes the owner of the money. But where ownership of money is transferred in such a form, it is truly a loan, and thus whatever is received afterwards beyond the principal has the iniquity of usury.

¶ From this, it follows that the cited doctor's argument is a most powerful fallacy, since he argues from "many" to "one."

<margin>Solution to the argument made.</margin> For when I hand over my money to one person and bargain with another for insurance, I am not truly lending to either. For the one to whom I hand it is not bound to restore it to me (and thus I do not transfer ownership to him), and the other who is bound to restore it does not receive my money. But when both [roles] concur in the same person—namely, that the very same man to whom I hand the money is obligated to me for its restoration—from those two things arises the nature of a loan. I can indeed agree with him on the quantity of profit, because by this I do not transfer ownership; I cannot, however, simultaneously agree on keeping the capital safe.

<margin>Corollary.</margin> ¶ From this again, it is clearly gathered that exactly the same vice is committed even if the same contract is made with the same person successively. For even if a month ago, or at any other time, I legitimately contracted a partnership with someone by counting out my money to him at my own risk, whenever I bargain with that same person for safe capital, I effectively transfer the ownership to him, and thus I make a loan. This would not happen if I celebrated that same contract of insurance with a third party.

¶ Through these things that have been said, a judgment can be made regarding a certain contract that is very frequently used elsewhere, and at that time in Rome. Peter has an office, whether he is a scribe or serves the palace in some other way; it happens that he needs cash. He reaches an agreement with a merchant or anyone else who gives him a hundred gold ducats, for which Peter...

# Book Six, Question VII.

In his official capacity, he signs for ten or twelve years; however, with this condition: if within a six-month period that merchant who paid the money departs from this light <note>original: "ab hac luce demigrauerit"; a poetic way of saying the person dies</note>, he suffers the loss of his capital, and Peter is not held to restore it to his heirs. If, however, he remains alive after six months, he protests to the debtor that he no longer wishes to remain in the partnership, and therefore warns him that unless he pays immediately, he will thereafter pay the same established interest <note>original: "vsuras"</note> by reason of delay <term>mora</term> <note>original: "mora"; a legal term for a "default" or "delay" in payment that justifies interest as compensation rather than profit.</note>. This is, I say, a contract they call a partnership <term>societas</term>; but truly its justice is not entirely clear. For first, it cannot be reduced to the logic of a purchased annuity <term>empti census</term> <note>original: "empti census"; a common 16th-century contract where one "bought" a right to annual income from a property to avoid usury laws.</note>: because then he who provided the money would have to deprive himself of its ownership forever, so that neither the other party nor his heirs would be bound to redeem the annuity forever, but it would be at their discretion if they wished to do so. And yet, that is not how it happens. On the contrary, it is in the power of the provider to reclaim his capital; indeed, he truly does reclaim it. Therefore, they only call such contracts a "partnership." For they imagine that if someone has a profitable office—worth, for example, a thousand—the fruits of which amount to a hundred, a merchant who provides a hundred enters into a partnership with him. That is, he puts forward a tenth part of the price so that he may also receive a tenth of the fruit. But truly, this seems to differ from the law of partnership, because he does not undergo the risk of the capital in the way usually done in partnerships: namely, by exposing himself to the risk of the capital being lost in trade; instead, he only faces the risk of whether he dies before six months are up.

Therefore, to open our opinion on this matter—if it is worth anything—as far as that six-month period is concerned, the contract appears just. For that risk which the one contributing the hundred underwent (namely, that if he died then, he would lose it) is estimable in money. And so, just as is customary in games of chance and other fortuitous events, it seems just that six gold pieces are received for that risk of a hundred. However, the fact that after the lapse of six months, twelve pieces are received every year by reason of delay, seems to savor of fraud. This is both because that delay was foreseen from the beginning, and thus seems to have been granted as a fraudulent loan; and especially because, by reason of delay, nothing can be received above the capital except for emerging loss <term>damnum emergens</term> <note>actual financial loss caused by the delay</note>, but certainly not for ceasing profit <term>lucrum cessans</term> <note>profit the lender could have made elsewhere</note>—unless such money had been exposed to lawful trade. Wherefore, if the matter were so, the contract is perhaps lawful; otherwise, not at all. Indeed, I would hardly

<column-break/>

dare to approve a contract of this kind, unless it were under the form of a purchased annuity, or a plain partnership: namely, where the money would be exposed to the risk of the business.

## QUESTION SEVEN, on the Contract of Insurance.

### SINGLE ARTICLE.

-> Whether the contract of insurance is lawful. <-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The final contract is named insurance <term>assecuratio</term>. For although the word has not been granted Latinity by those skilled in the language <note>The word "assecuratio" was Medieval Latin/Law Latin, not Classical Latin.</note>, it is nevertheless accepted in use by legal commentators to mean "placing in the care of a protector." Now, that this kind of contract is not lawful appears decreed in the chapter *Naviganti* regarding usury. <note>A famous decree by Pope Gregory IX which was often interpreted as forbidding taking profit for the risk of a sea voyage.</note>

<margin>Second argument and reason.</margin>
Second, reason also seems to prove this: for he who takes a risk upon himself for a price—for example, the risk of a loaded ship—neither buys anything nor commits anything to a partnership; rather, he gains money without any business transaction. Therefore, he receives something for nothing, which has the appearance of usury.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
Third, it is added that if this contract were lawful, an opportunity would be offered to reckless men, so that even if they had absolutely nothing in assets, they could present themselves as insurers; since they do not have to offer any money at present, this would be ruinous to the commonwealth.

On the contrary, there is the accepted custom, approved by both theologians and jurists alike.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
The question is easily answered with an affirmative conclusion. An insurance contract, if done according to law and custom, is lawful.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This conclusion is proved by the object. For anything that can be estimated by a price, anyone can receive payment; but to place a thing in safety which is exposed to dangers is estimable by a price; therefore, anyone can redeem that for a price, and likewise he who undergoes that danger can receive the same price. And this is especially because...

because each party submits himself to danger: namely, the shipowner by paying the price <note>The "price" here refers to the insurance premium.</note> if the ship remains safe, and the other party by paying for the goods if they should perish. <margin>Second reason.</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is argued from **necessity**. A contract of this kind is of no small necessity to the commonwealth; therefore, since it is stained by no vice in its objective, it is good. The premise is evident from the fact that it is a necessary support for trade. Indeed, many merchants would fear to load ships with goods at such great risk; yet, when they set aside a large weight of gold for a small price, they dare to undertake trade of this sort, which is indeed necessary for the commonwealth. <margin>Third reason.</margin> ¶ Added to this, thirdly, is that it is permitted for someone acting as a guarantor <term>fideiussor</term> <note>A "fideiussor" is someone who legally guarantees the debt of another.</note> for another—whom it is not entirely safe to assume will be able to pay—to receive something in exchange for the risk of payment to which he exposes himself. A very similar thing <margin>Final reason.</margin> occurs in insurance. ¶ Furthermore, by way of a stake <term>vadiatio</term> <note>original: "vadiatio"; a form of betting or wagering where money is deposited based on an uncertain outcome.</note> (which some call a wager), it is permitted to expose money to uncertain outcomes so that the depositors might gain something from that risk, just as we said regarding honest games; likewise, whether it will rain tomorrow or not, etc. Therefore, in a similar way, it is permitted to expose, for example, a thousand ducats to risk with the hope of gaining fifty or sixty.

¶ There are indeed those who think a man is "stupid" who, for the hope of gaining a hundred or a thousand, undergoes the risk of a merchant’s ship worth perhaps twenty or thirty thousand. To these, however, we respond that we are not debating the price; it can indeed be just or unjust—let the contracting parties see to that themselves. But in truth, there is no "stupidity" nor mark of madness in undertaking such risks at the current price, since the dangers are not so evident that the insurers cannot hope for a good outcome. And although sometimes there is a loss, at other times profit increases—especially since prudent men do not cast the die with such great danger <note>Meaning wise people don't take on risks they can't handle.</note>. Conversely, where no danger was imminent at all, he who made an insurance contract for his goods would be lacking his mind. <margin>Vices that can occur in the insurance contract.</margin> ¶ However, several small doubts arise here. First of all, the trickery and impostures that can occur in other contracts must not be admitted here. For if someone who has no assets says he is undertaking the risk of a ship—with the hope that if it is safe, he will have the fee, but if it perishes, he will hide himself or declare bankruptcy—he is most unjust, since in truth he exposes himself to no risk; and thus he demands the fee 

<column-break/>

contrary to justice. And conversely, if the master of the ship directs the prow to another, less reliable port than the one expressed in the contract, the other party is not bound by the agreement. For all these things ought to be clear in the contract. <margin>A doubt.</margin> ¶ But it is a doubt whether a contract is also licit if someone wishes to sail with an empty ship, yet wants to insure it as if it were loaded. "I will give you a thousand so that you pay me back twenty thousand if my ship is submerged." For it appears not to be a legitimate contract on the part of the sailor, because he will not have as much care in preserving a ship which, being empty, is only worth a thousand, as he would if it were loaded. <margin>Response.</margin> The response is that if the sailor deceives the other—perhaps because they are not in the port—by saying his ship is full of goods of such value when he has none, the contract would certainly not be valid. This is because the other party, if he knew the truth, would not enter into it, fearing the sailor would not take great care to preserve the ship. Indeed, fraud would be feared: namely, that he might deliberately allow it to be submerged to gain twenty thousand. If, however, the insurer did this knowingly and prudently, he suffers no injury; for it would then be a type of wager or stake: "if the ship escapes safely, you give me this much; if not, I give you that much." In the same way, others to whom the safety or sinking of the ship does not pertain could make a deposit: "if it arrives safely at the port, I will give you a hundred; if not, you will give me a thousand." ¶ In a similar way, insurance can be made at the fairs <term>nundinae</term> <note>Major international trade fairs where financial settlements and insurance often took place.</note>: "grant me this much, and I make it secure to you that you will gain this much." <margin>Another doubt.</margin> ¶ This, however, generates another doubt: namely, whether the same contract is licit in other matters besides merchandise. For there are some whom <margin>Sylvester.</margin> Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a prominent theologian whose "Summa Sylvestrina" was a standard reference for moral theology.</note> cited under the word *Business*, section 4, who deny that anyone can insure another’s life. For there would be a danger that the party who has an interest might wish for the other's death. But in truth, we are speaking here of the justice of contracts, and thus of their nature—whether they are usurious; a vice against charity of this sort does not change the nature of the contract. Therefore, they always remain licit in their objective. Indeed, they are sometimes of use to the commonwealth. A son under paternal authority <term>filius familias</term> asks me for a loan; if he dies prematurely before his parent, he will not pay me. But if he survives him, my coins are safe. In that case, I will rightly dread lending him anything

# BOOK SEVEN
# On Justice and Right.

## QUESTION ONE,
## On Exchange in General.

### ARTICLE I.
### Whether the art of Money-changing is lawful.

<image-desc>Decorative initial C at the beginning of the text, featuring ornate floral scrollwork within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

THE discussion of exchanges <term>cambiorum</term> <note>original: "cambiorum"; in this context, the term refers to the professional business of banking and currency exchange</note> belongs to the treatise on usury; indeed, a good part of it was settled in that very place. Therefore, what remains to be addressed must necessarily be very brief. However, we have decided to give this small fragment—though it is much shorter than a proper volume—the title of a "Book" because of its great fame and importance. For this subject is as necessary to understand as it is profoundly obscure in its own right, and it has become further entangled by the new and daily inventions of merchants, and subsequently clouded by the many differing opinions of learned men. For this reason, I have been shamelessly and frequently hounded by the requests of many to expose the rot and poison of this plague, which spreads more and more every day within the commonwealth. I will therefore attempt to do so to the best of my natural ability. May God suggest to us what truth contains. ¶ Therefore, at the entrance of this book, we first inquire regarding the art of money-changing <term>ars campsoria</term> <note>original: "ars campsoria"; the professional practice of a "campsor" or money-changer</note>, whether it is lawful. Arguments are made for the negative side.

<margin>First argument for the negative side. Aristotle.</margin>
The art of money-changing is "nummularia" <note>The Greek term *kapelike*, referring to retail trade or money-brokering for profit's sake</note>: specifically, the exchange and increase of coins. This, however, Aristotle condemns in the *Politics* (Book 1, chapters 6 and 7) as being against nature. This is because in the exchange of coins, there is no inherent natural benefit, such as there is in the exchange of food, clothing, and other things necessary for life.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is added that the end of this art, as we were saying in the previous book, is the pursuit of wealth which proceeds unto infinity; yet temporal desires ought to have a limit. For this reason, it is a plague to the commonwealth, as experience itself testifies. This is why Christ overturned the tables of the money-changers.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, through this it is clear—as we said above—that it is

<column-break/>

against nature that, through this art, it most often happens that sterile money becomes more fruitful than the land itself; and from this, money-changers <term>campsores</term> <note>Bankers or exchange dealers</note> draw hatred upon themselves among men. Furthermore, there is the fact that these men are almost always sedentary: namely, they live in idleness, and yet they scrape together more profit than others who are active and sweating from the labor of their own hands. This is especially true because they subject their money to no risk, as happens in other forms of business. ¶ On the contrary, however, stands the fact that this art is in some way useful to the commonwealth for the exchanging and transferring of currencies. 

First of all, the name "exchange" <term>cambium</term> is Latin.
<margin>What is Exchange.</margin>
For to "exchange" <term>cambire</term> is the same as to trade one thing for another. But we must, with Aristotle in the place cited (and as we partially noted in the previous book), now more clearly recall that three 
<margin>A three-fold form of permutations.</margin>
forms of exchange have grown up in order over the course of time. For men first began to exchange the things themselves: for instance, a vineyard for a house, wine for grain, a garment for a shoe, etc. This kind of exchange is, from its very origins, native to the sincerity of nature. However, it was ultimately insufficient because not all things can be carried to different places to be exchanged, nor can they be preserved for long periods of time. Therefore, a second type of exchange followed: namely, money <term>nummus</term> was invented to be the price of things, and to be exchanged for the things themselves. This method of exchanging comes very close to the first and serves it entirely. Therefore, this was further sufficient for the sufficiency of life. But indeed, once money was invented, human sagacity—aroused by greed—gave birth to a third generation of exchanges: namely, that one would exchange money for money. This exchange first took its origin from the fact that it was necessary to trade gold and more precious currency for smaller denominations. Then, it followed because in one region gold was valued at a higher amount of silver than in another; and merchants would sell the same gold for more there than they had bought it for elsewhere. And from that point, human industry more skillfully enriched this same art. Therefore, this...
