### [Page 583]
### BOOK SEVEN, QUESTION I

Therefore, by this reasoning, the general name "exchange" <term>cambium</term> <note>original: "cambium"; derived from the bartering of physical goods</note>, which had its origin in the bartering of goods, was eventually adapted—as its use became more frequent—to the exchange of money, which is less "natural." For this reason, exchange is not the same as the "money-handling art" <term>ars nummularia</term> <note>original: "ars nummularia"; the professional business or craft of managing money</note> itself. For the "art" signifies the industry of trading, while "exchange" refers to the actual action of commuting it. There are those who, unable to understand the name "exchange" in any other way than as a trade between different things, say that "exchange" cannot properly be understood except between currencies of either a different metal or a different mark. However, the logic of exchange by no means requires this condition; indeed, in exchange "by reason of location" <note>This refers to bills of exchange where money is paid in one city to be received in another, a central topic of early modern banking</note>, as will be clear below, the same coins are properly exchanged for one another because of the difference in place. ¶ These things having been established, it might perhaps seem to someone that, based on the arguments made, one should simply respond in the negative: namely, that this kind of art is not lawful. Most people, however, respond to the contrary—that it is not only lawful, but also useful.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
I would believe, however, that the response should be made with the following conclusion: The art of exchange, which Aristotle calls the "money-handling art," if it is considered purely in itself according to the sound of the words, has a bad reputation; nevertheless, it does not possess such inherent malice that it cannot be made lawful through a good end and proper circumstances. ¶ For in our third book, we distinguished four types of actions. One is good by its very nature, such as a work of virtue; another is indifferent, such as walking; another is so intrinsically evil that it can never be done lawfully, such as lying. But there is a fourth kind which, considered purely in itself, "sounds bad," yet there is nothing to prevent it from being done lawfully given certain circumstances: such as a priest holding multiple church offices <note>original: "sacerdotia"; ecclesiastical benefices or positions</note> at once. And if I judge correctly, the art of exchange belongs to this fourth category. For the name of the "money-handling art," as Aristotle teaches in the place cited, carries two absurdities in its meaning. First, by reason of its subject matter: because beyond the primary use of money, which is to be the price of things, one money is exchanged for another. Second, by reason of its end: because such an exchange is not done for the immediate provision of life's necessities, but for profit, which creates an infinite thirst for desiring more. And thus, considered so nakedly, it sounds bad. Added to this same art are the same kinds of inconveniences and dangers—and subsequently frauds and other evils—which we showed were attached to trade in the second question of the previous book; indeed, this art is exposed to even more opportunities for sinning. For other types of trade—

<column-break/>

—which consist of buying and selling, have more of the character of natural commerce. This is because in those cases, things necessary for life are exchanged, and they require more industry, diligence, and labor; furthermore, the capital is subjected to more risks. By these reasons, those trades are made honorable. In this art of money-changing, however, none of those elements are present. Furthermore, it holds a greater lure for fishing for the goods of others; moreover, since extravagant men who wish to serve their own pleasures find a ready path through money-changers to quickly boil away their estates. And since the vices of this art are to be treated throughout the course of this book, enough has been said of them for now.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
¶ But indeed, the second part of the conclusion is nonetheless proven thus: This very same art can bring some benefits to the commonwealth; therefore, if it is purged of those vices and directed toward an honest end, it will be lawful, and even useful. The premise is evident from the fact that it is sometimes necessary for citizens to exchange more precious currency for cheaper coins, as will be made clear in what follows. Moreover, that it can be washed of those stains with which it is soiled is clear: for a money-changer can desire an honest profit, provided it is not without moderation. ¶ Nor is the exchange of coins, which seems to oppose their original institution, entirely contrary to their nature.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For just as in other things, Aristotle (in the *Politics*, Book 1, Chapter 6 <note>In modern editions, this is Book 1, Chapter 9</note>) recognized a double use, so it is also permitted in money. For there is a double use for a shoe, a garment, and other utensils: one is the primary use for the sake of which it was invented. Just as the use of a shoe is for wearing, and a garment for clothing, and a horse for riding, etc. The other use is buying and selling. Although the first of these is the "proper" use, the second is not "repugnant" to it. For the sale of a shoe is ordered toward that primary use. In the same way, therefore, even if the proper use and end of coins is the valuation of things and exchange for them, nevertheless their exchange for one another is not entirely absurd, if it is permitted insofar as it is necessary for the commonwealth. In short, if there were any danger of a "usurious loan" <term>mutuum</term> <note>original: "mutui"; a loan of fungible goods where the same amount must be returned, often associated with hidden interest/usury</note> underlying this kind of exchange, it would be mostly on the part of the money-changer; for it is not feared from the other party who wishes to transfer money to another place. Most of the time, however—indeed, always—the broker <term>campsor</term> receives the money before he pays it back, in which case every image of a loan is wiped away. ¶ And through these points, the response to the argument posed at the beginning of the question becomes clear.

<summary>This page analyzes the moral status of money-changing, arguing that while it may appear "unnatural" or prone to greed, it is a lawful profession when it serves the public good and is conducted with moderation. Soto uses Aristotle’s theory of "double use" to justify why exchanging money for money (rather than just for goods) is acceptable in a functioning economy.</summary>

### ARTICLE II.
#### Whether there are multiple types of exchange.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Regarding exchange in general—the subject of the current question—it remains to explore the different types of exchange. For it is argued that there are not several species. After all, "exchange" <term>cambium</term> sounds like nothing other than a "permutation of things." Because the matter (that is, the things being swapped) might be of different types, the actions themselves do not change species. For example, it is the same species of art to make a garment out of either silk or <margin>Argument 2.</margin> cloth. ¶ Secondly, they do not vary simply because an exchange is made by reason of place, or by reason of time, or by reason of the currency, since in all these instances the same currency is being exchanged. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the most widely accepted usage—not only of the common people, but also of scholars—who distinguish between various species of exchange.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To this question, we respond with five conclusions. First: If the things themselves are considered strictly as objects, then exchange is not a genus consisting of multiple species. The argument just made certainly demonstrated this conclusion. For it is the same action to exchange wine for oil, gold for a house, or silver for gold (or for another metal), whether the coins are stamped or are a mass of raw metal. Actions change their species based on their object, not their material. For instance, the art of sculpture is the same whether the carving is done in wood or in stone. And in the realm of morality, the theft of gold and the theft of clothes are the same species of theft. Therefore, as we have said, "theft" is a very specific category, differing from "robbery" <note>Soto is distinguishing between "furtum" (theft by stealth) and "rapina" (robbery by force).</note> only by the nature of the involuntary element in the object: because one is done through fraud and the other through force. Indeed, the species does not change even regarding the logic of justice or injustice. For if we take the three types of exchange mentioned in the previous article as an example, the logic of justice and injustice is the same whether exchanging wine for oil, money for grain, or a gold coin for a silver one. The equality maintained in all these things follows the same logic of "commutative justice" <term>iustitia commutativa</term> <note>Commutative justice is the principle of fairness in private dealings, requiring that what is given and what is received are of equal value.</note>; while inequality follows the same logic of injustice. Therefore, speaking physically, there are not different "genera" or species of exchange; but in Latin they are called different genera because of the different materials, and furthermore, because of their different

<column-break/>

adaptation to civil use. ¶ Second conclusion. If money is considered not as a natural object, but <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> insofar as it is a coin—and thus exists as the legal price of things—the exchange of things for money is a contract that differs civilly in species from the first or third type of exchange. We assigned the reason for this in the previous book. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> For this exchange is specifically a contract of "buying and selling" <term>emptio et venditio</term>, as held in the law <note>original: "l. 2. de contrahen. empti."; a reference to the Code of Justinian regarding the formation of sales contracts</note>, because in that case the price is distinguished from the object; whereas in exchanges of other types, one thing is the price of the other. ¶ Third conclusion. The third type of exchange, which is an action of the "money-handling art" <margin>Third conclusion.</margin>, is also a distinct species civilly and in the realm of morality from the first type of exchange. For in the first type, there is nothing but a simple exchange of things of equal value, naturally instituted for the provision and sufficiency of life. Here, however, it is not natural things being traded, but legal coins; and that is done not for food or clothing, but for profit. Therefore, I am not sure if this is a proper species of "business" <term>negotiatio</term>, since business involves buying a thing to resell it (which does not sound like an evil thing); but here, as we said, it is not a "proper purchase" where the price is distinguished from the object. It is nevertheless called business because it is a permutation of coins for the sake of pure profit. ¶ From these points it follows that exchange <margin>Difference between exchange and other contracts.</margin> (the subject of this present treatise) differs in logic from other contracts. For it has already been shown not to be a "purchase." Nor is it "renting" or "lending," since in exchange ownership is transferred, which does not happen in those cases. But neither is it a "simple loan" <term>mutuum</term>, because ownership is not transferred simply (meaning that the simple principal is to be restored), but rather with profit, and interest, or a price. ¶ Fourth conclusion. Several species are named <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> of the exchanges we are discussing. Whether these are truly species—as philosophers speak of species, whether natural or moral—or whether they are named by the common usage of merchants and legal courts, matters very little to the present business. ¶ Therefore, since in the realm of morality the first consideration is directed toward what is just or unjust, the first <margin>First division of exchange.</margin> division of exchanges for our purposes is into "real" and "dry." You will hardly find the logic of these names explained among authors. And yet "real" exchange, so called from "the thing" <term>res</term> <margin>Real exchange.</margin>, is the same as an "exchange in fact": that is, one made with a legitimate logic of commuting—whether by reason of different currencies, or by reason of place, or whatever else may be legitimate, as will become clear in the process. "Dry" exchange <term>cambium siccum</term> <margin>Dry exchange.</margin> <note>"Dry exchange" was a financial fiction used to bypass laws against usury (charging interest). It looked like a currency exchange between two cities, but no money actually moved; it was effectively a high-interest loan.</note>, however, is the same as an exchange which is not actually an exchange...

<summary>Soto categorizes the types of money exchange, distinguishing them from simple barter and sales. He introduces the critical moral distinction between "real" exchange and "dry" exchange, the latter being a potentially usurious financial fiction.</summary>

...exchange, but a feigned one and a cloak for usury: which is therefore opposed to the real exchange. It is called feigned, that is, sterile and lacking the moisture to bear fruit. Not because the banker <note>original: campsori; a specialized money-changer or medieval banker</note> does not gain a profit from it, but because, as we said in the previous book, it is against the nature of things for money to "give birth" <note>An Aristotelian concept that money is "barren" and should not produce more money through interest</note>. It is also called "dry": because it is a pure and bare usurious loan, which possesses nothing of a legitimate contract. Wherefore these two types of exchange, although they deal with the same natural matter—namely, money—yet in the realm of morality they are entirely contrary and differ in species along a diametrical line, just as the just and the unjust. Beneath both of these members, many species are subdivided, or you might call them modes of exchange.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, let the fifth conclusion be this: All forms and modes of exchange, including both the illicit and the licit, are conveniently reduced to three heads: some of which possess manifest injustice, others manifest justice. But there are others that can be called into doubt. For the exchange of money only occurs because of some diversity: namely, either of the coins themselves, or of places, or of times. No other variety is found except in substance, or in place, or in time. However, since the diversity of money can be the cause of exchange in two ways—either because more precious coins are exchanged for cheaper ones for human use, or because in truth one is sold for another by reason of a higher valuation due to a difference in place or time—let us reduce the types of exchange to four heads. Henceforth, we shall not dispute philosophically whether these are genera, species, or modes; rather, in the Latin custom, we will use these names interchangeably.

<margin>Small exchange.</margin>
¶ The first type of exchange is that which they call "small" <note>original: minutum</note>: this is when gold money is exchanged for silver or copper, or vice versa. It takes its name from the fact that smaller coins are exchanged for more precious ones, or vice versa.

<margin>Exchange by letters.</margin>
The second type is by reason of place: as when someone who needs money elsewhere but has it here, pays it here so that it may be assigned to him elsewhere. This is usually called "exchange by letters" <note>original: cambium per literas; this refers to the 'bill of exchange,' a precursor to the modern check</note>, to distinguish it from the former, which can be called "manual exchange." For that first type is done with money counted out by hand on both sides in person. In this type, however, the person who receives the money delivers letters, on the faith of which payment is made elsewhere. And these two types, if no fraud is mixed in, are real exchanges and therefore clearly just. Th-

<column-break/>

-ird type is by reason of time: as if someone should receive money now which he must restore with interest on a certain day by reason of the time waited. This is "manifestly dry exchange" <note>original: cambium siccum; a loan disguised as an exchange to bypass anti-usury laws</note>, and therefore wicked: of which we spoke abundantly in the preceding book. Therefore, these two roots must be placed before the eyes of those beginning a discussion of exchanges, in order to distinguish between the justice and injustice of exchanges.

<margin>A beautiful lesson for discerning the justice and injustice of exchanges.</margin>
For where an exchange occurs precisely by reason of place—that is, for the sole purpose of transmitting money—the exchange is real and legitimate. However, where any reason of "time waited" <note>original: ratione expectati temporis</note> has inserted itself, it is "dry" and usurious. It is also customary to distinguish

<margin>Pure exchange.</margin>
"pure" exchange from "impure." Some call "small exchange" pure, where nothing else is mixed in. "Impure exchange" is where something else is mixed in, either by reason of place or by reason of time; and subsequently they admit that an exchange can be impure yet nonetheless legitimate.
<margin>impure.</margin>
But truly, since "impure" sounds like something bad, it will be more significantly called "pure" for every real exchange, whether small or by reason of place; and "impure" for that in which some injustice is mixed, whether by reason of time or any other iniquity. The fourth type of exchange is by reason of the currency itself: I do not mean that they are exchanged piece by piece, but because in truth the money of one place is exchanged for the money of another place according to the different estimated prices of both locations. And the dispute over exchanges is chiefly concerned with these types; for since they are mostly used by merchants and bankers, they give birth to very many "reefs" <note>original: scopulos; a metaphor for moral hazards or difficult legal traps</note> that bloodily wound human consciences. They keep confessors perplexed and render the scholars both obscure and varied, as can be seen in Cajetan's singular work on exchanges, and in Silvester under the word "Usury," section 4, and in many others. Would that the same character not be branded upon us! For Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> wrote nothing on this matter professionally. For that treatise on usury (as we said above in Opusculum 73) bears no trace of Saint Thomas, and much less does Chapter 13, where a brief discussion of exchanges occurs.
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
<margin>Silvester.</margin>
¶ Therefore, regarding the principal argument placed at the front of the question, the first conclusion has responded.

F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

# SECOND QUESTION,
-> Regarding petty exchange. <-

### SINGLE ARTICLE.
-> Whether petty exchange is licit. <-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative large initial 'Q' showing a figure seated in a classical or outdoor setting with building elements in the background.</image-desc> Although it has been asserted in passing that petty exchange <note>original: "minutum cambium"; this refers to "manual exchange," the simple act of changing a large coin for smaller denominations or swapping different types of local currency for a small fee</note> is licit, it remains necessary to demonstrate this with clearer and more certain reasons, beginning from the fundamentals. For it is argued that it is not licit: Coins are struck with a public mark for this purpose—that they might serve as a just and legitimate price for things. However, a price that is "legitimate" (that is, established by law) consists in an "indivisible point," as we showed in the previous book <note>The "indivisible point" refers to a fixed legal value that does not allow for a range of negotiation; if the law says a coin is worth ten, it is exactly ten</note>. If, therefore—to use an example—a ducat is valued by law at eleven reals, it cannot be exchanged for a greater amount of silver.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, if this were permitted, it would follow that it would be licit for any private person, and even for any buyer in purchases and sales, to buy more cheaply simply because they pay in gold coin. Conversely, if a seller, while giving back the remaining change after receiving gold, could take a fee for providing smaller coins that are more convenient for use (just as a banker does), it would follow that such a concession would open the way to overturning the established valuation of money. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the accepted custom, which is condemned by neither the "exterior forum" (civil law) nor the "interior forum" (the court of conscience).

<margin>Foundation.</margin>
To understand not only the present question but also all subsequent ones, it must be noted that since money is struck from metal, it is held in value for a twofold reason: namely, both as a physical object and as a struck coin. For the fact that it has a public seal impressed upon it does not change the value of the metal. Rather, that seal is like a sign engraved on other measures and weights by public authority to serve as a testimony to the value of the currency. Thus, if a certain province abounds more in gold than in silver, gold is valued there at less silver than in another province that might be richer in 

<column-break/>

silver than in gold. And the same applies to copper and bronze. For the scarcity of gold and silver could be so great, and the abundance of other metals so high, that the estimation of the former would depend much more on the gold and silver than in another region overflowing with those metals. Furthermore, this same reasoning is held in the minting of coins: for among us, a ducat is valued at eleven silver reals because, according to the supply of both metals available to us, that is the legal valuation. But in Italy, it is valued at twelve Carlini, and elsewhere at more or less. From this it follows that even if the money were not struck with a seal, the same weight would be held as the price of things. Indeed, as Aristotle says in the place cited, before money was struck with a seal, it was valued by weight; but the State <note>original: "respublica"</note> testifies to the value of the metal by that mark.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>A twofold consideration of coinage.</margin>
¶ There are, therefore, two ways in which one may exchange one coin for another: one, if it is considered under the aspect of its metal; and the other, under the aspect of its status as currency. Therefore, the question is answered with three conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first is this: To exchange different coins according to the nature of the metal—even if a small amount is received above the value of the struck coin—has no appearance of evil. For example, if someone needs gold either for gilding, for preparing a medicine, for an ornament, or for other uses for which it has a natural utility, one can sell him a ducat of the finest gold for more than its value as a coin, provided that the increase is only small.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
This is the conclusion of Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> in his entry on "usury," part 4, section 3, and of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major commentator on Aquinas</note> in his small work; and it appears manifest. Because, just as one could then sell raw gold to a person in need, so too can one sell that which has been struck with a mark.

<margin>Argument of Metinensis.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, there are those who do not grant this conclusion so freely; among these is Johannes Metinensis <note>Juan de Medina, a Spanish theologian who wrote on contracts</note>, who does not accept it in his treatise on exchanges. His argument is that when the King mints money, he estimates the value of the gold with regard to all its uses—just as when he sets a price on grain by a "Pragmatic" <note>term: Pragmatica; a royal decree or ordinance having the force of law</note>. Therefore, just as after such a law it is not permitted to sell grain for even a penny more, so it is not permitted for struck gold.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that money is not "taxed" (priced) except under the aspect of its use as a price—even though it also possesses the quality of metal value. Therefore, nothing stands in the way of an exchange of gold for silver being made at a slightly higher price because of the conveniences of the metal. Indeed, a coin could be so beautiful that it is valued like a gemstone. Therefore, it is not like grain, which has no other nature or use than that of being grain.

<summary>This page discusses the morality of "petty exchange" (money-changing), arguing that it is licit to charge a small fee for swapping coins because money has a dual value as both legal tender and a physical commodity (metal). Soto refutes the idea that royal price-fixing on currency applies to its use as a raw material, distinguishing it from essential goods like grain.</summary>

It then transitions to Question 3, which begins the investigation into "exchange by reason of place"—essentially the early modern system of bills of exchange and international banking.</meta>

<header>Question III of the Seventh Book</header>

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion is this: It is likewise lawful to exchange coins simply as coins, with a small price granted by one party to the other. This is evident in "petty exchange" <note>original: "cambio minuto"; the manual swapping of one type of coin for another, such as silver for gold</note>, which we previously called manual exchange: namely, when a money-changer gives gold in exchange for small silver coins, or vice versa.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> This is proven by the fact that this type of exchange in no way opposes the law regarding the legal valuation of coins. For that valuation only applies to coins insofar as they are the "price" of goods <note>That is, the price of bread or cloth is fixed, but here the coin itself is being treated as the object of the trade</note>. Petty exchange is permitted because it is not a matter of buying or selling a product, but a trade for the sake of human utility. For perhaps there is a poor man who spends money in small amounts, for which he offers gold so that he may have small change for his family expenses; or perhaps there is a rich man who needs silver to have vessels crafted. Conversely, there is another who needs to transport a large sum of money, or who intends to store away a treasure; so that such a great weight of silver or copper is not a burden to him, he exchanges it for a small amount of gold. Since, therefore, it is a service and a benefit to the community to have various currencies ready—which cannot be collected, stored, and provided without expense and labor—a public person who devotes his work to this duty may receive a just price. Indeed, it is not only for these uses: perhaps you have coins worn down by age that barely show their mark and are not easily accepted by merchants; to exchange those for other whole coins, it is fair that you pay an additional price. However, this price must be both small and established by common use, so that the path to fraud is closed.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin> ¶ Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note>, however, in his treatise, grants this power only to professional money-changers, because they are public ministers of the state; therefore, he says it is not lawful among private persons. Yet, I do not see why it should not also be lawful privately. For if that exchange is valuable by its very nature, why should it not be permitted to anyone? If it were not worth a price, it certainly would not be permitted to the money-changers either. For, as must be shown more clearly below, before expenses and labor are deemed worthy of a price, the matter must be judged based on its object—whether it is lawful or not. This much is true, however: if I owe twelve reals, I cannot satisfy that debt by paying one gold ducat simply because I prefer to pay in gold; the same applies to prices. Nonetheless, if someone freely and without force or fraud sells their property, nothing

<column-break/>

prevents them from voluntarily selling it for a lower price in gold than they would for silver or copper. In such a case, the other party can justly buy for less by offering pure and excellent gold. So much for this kind of exchange according to the law of nature.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin> ¶ The third conclusion: The state and the Prince can forbid such petty exchanges among private persons. This was very prudently provided for by law some time ago in Spain: both to prevent the injustice that immediately creeps in from price increases, and especially to prevent gold currency from being transported to foreign kingdoms—which truly does not happen without grave harm to the commonwealth. Therefore, if such a law is received, it binds the conscience under the guilt of mortal sin; and anyone who exchanges gold currency for another above the legal valuation of stamped gold would be liable for restitution.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> ¶ To the first argument, therefore, it has already been answered that although in petty exchange coins are exchanged as money, they are not exchanged as the "price" of things, but for other uses ordered toward those very purchases and sales.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, it has likewise been answered that this type of exchange is lawful even for private persons, provided that the door to fraud is not opened in buying and selling, and that it is not forbidden by civil law.

# QUESTION THREE,
## Regarding exchange by reason of place and by reason of time.

### ARTICLE I.
#### Whether exchange by reason of place is licit.

<margin>First argument.</margin> argued, as is customary, from the negative side. In every exchange, an equality of justice is required; however, coins have their own either native or...

assigned value: therefore, wherever it exists, they ought to be exchanged at equality; and thus, a price cannot be received by reason of location.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: In this type of exchange <note>original: "cambijs"</note>, the nature of a loan <note>term: "mutuum" - a loan of fungible goods where the exact same type and quality must be returned</note> lies hidden. For one person receives ownership of money in one place so that he may restore the same in another, just as it is received at one time to be restored at another. However, by reason of time, nothing may be received <note>This refers to the prohibition against usury, or charging interest solely for the passage of time</note>; therefore, neither may it be received by reason of place. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that this exchange serves the purpose of transferring money from one place to another, which is of use to the commonwealth.

<margin>Double sense of the question.</margin>
The title of this question presents two meanings to the ears. One is whether, when the same currency is valued at unequal rates in different places, it is lawful to count it out here so that the same may be restored where it is worth more. This sense is reserved for the following dispute, for the entire mechanism of exchanges is based on understanding this. The other sense is simpler: whether it is fair to receive a price by reason of the transportation or transmission of currency from one place to another. This is what we said above is called "exchange by letters" <note>term: "cambium per literas" - the use of bills of exchange to move money without physically carrying gold</note>, to which we respond with a single affirmation.

<margin>Responsive conclusion. Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
¶ I say it is lawful to receive a price by reason of such transmission. The conclusion is plain: since it is often profitable to transport merchandise and other types of things to various places, so it is also profitable to transfer money—both to settle other business and especially to purchase goods that must be carried from one province to another. Since, therefore, this task is necessary and estimable in money, anyone is permitted to receive a wage for it.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued: If there were any iniquity in this matter, it would be chiefly because it has the appearance of a loan. But in truth, it is not a loan; for he who provides money here to receive it elsewhere does not simply transfer ownership so that it may be restored at another time, but in another place. Therefore, the expectation of time is accidental to this contract: namely, because letters cannot become known in another place so that the money may be presented except over time. The time, I say, which does not vitiate this kind of exchange, and is thus considered accidental, is that which is necessary for the transmission of the written documents <note>original: "chirographa"</note>. For if a longer time intervenes, that exchange becomes impure: that is, mixed with the expectation of time, and consequently

<column-break/>

smelling of usury. Wherefore, to explain the legitimate reason for this kind of exchange, the time of payment is usually set for immediately upon the letters being seen and read. This will be more fully illuminated in what follows. ¶ And the same conclusion is proven thirdly.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
A driver or a sailor could receive a price for transporting money just as they do for the carriage of other things. He who gives here to receive elsewhere does the same thing: he transfers money from one place to another. Just as he who receives here to return it elsewhere transfers it from here to there; therefore, this can be valued at a price. Added to this is the fact that the transfer of money, especially from one kingdom to another, is subject to many dangers, both of wars and of robbers, and also of sinking if it is committed to the sea and the winds. Indeed, it is also because it is very often forbidden for coined money to be taken out of a kingdom. For these reasons, it is most expedient that there be money-changers <note>term: "campsores" - international bankers or exchange specialists</note> who have money in different provinces or who possess strong credit—and as they say, "trust"—so that they may transmit money by letters without the physical transportation of gold and copper. If this is necessary, then a stipend is justly established for this business: whether the money-changer counts out money to you here which you are to return to him in Rome or Bruges, or you count it out to him so that he may return it to you in Bruges or Rome. For in the former way, he transfers your money to you from elsewhere to here; in the latter, from here to elsewhere. From this, what we said above becomes known: that it is not of the intrinsic nature of exchange to be done in different currencies. For it can be done in the same ones.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But although the conclusion appears to be of the most certain truth, perhaps you doubt whether, if someone in Medina <note>Medina del Campo, a major financial center in 16th-century Spain</note> (to use an example) counts out money to another to receive it in Rome or Bruges, it is expedient for him to transport his own funds there. Therefore, should the price be paid to the transmitter himself, or is it lawful to receive a price for that exchange? For it appears not to be lawful at all: because he undergoes neither labor nor danger, but rather has looked after his own affairs and himself.

<margin>Response.</margin>
It is responded that it is nonetheless lawful: because by counting out money to another in Medina to be counted out to himself in Bruges, he transfers his own funds from Bruges to Medina. Therefore, although it might be expedient for Peter to transmit his money from Medina to Bruges, and for Paul to bring his from there to Medina, each of them—namely, the one who is anticipated by the other—can receive a price from the one who does the anticipating.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This response is proven. For in all these things which...

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that "exchange by letters" (international banking via bills of exchange) is a morally lawful service. He justifies charging a fee for this because it provides a necessary public service, avoids the risks of physical transport (robbers, shipwreck, war), and is distinct from usurious loans since the fee is for the "reason of place" rather than the "reason of time."</summary>

# Book Seven. Question III. 589 #

In those matters which must be said regarding exchanges <note>original: "cambijs"</note>, one's eye must always be held toward the object of the contract itself: namely, whether it is a thing which, first, does not involve malice, and second, is estimable by a price. For then, it can generally be done for a price.

<margin>First corollary.</margin>
¶ From this it follows that labor and all other such things are "accidents" <note>In scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that does not change the essential nature of a thing.</note>, which do not vary the nature of the thing regarding the stain of usury. I say it is accidental whether I perform my duties with labor or without labor, or with my own convenience or inconvenience; whether I have the money paid out elsewhere, or merely have credit with someone who answers for me: provided, however, that I do that for you which is estimable in money.

<margin>Second corollary.</margin>
For in these matters, industry <note>skill or diligence</note> is of great value. It follows, then, that this exchange is permitted by the law of nature not only to those who might be appointed to this duty by the commonwealth, but also to any private individuals, unless it were perhaps forbidden by civil law. This is evident from the fact that the thing itself is, by its nature, licit and estimable by a price. Indeed, there are no persons specifically deputed by the commonwealth for this, but it is the custom for all sorts of merchants to exchange in this manner.

<margin>Instruction.</margin>
¶ However, regarding what pertains most to the present matter, there is need for a warning: where the transmission of money is not a reality but is feigned, it is a craftiness; it is not even "cloaked" usury, but certainly a shameful one. For example: some illustrious man is in need of coins in Spain. He meets a merchant who might help him with borrowed gold; the merchant refuses, yet offers that the man may repay him in Flanders. Therefore, merchants and money-changers <note>term: "campsores"</note> who do not have a great care for their own salvation think this is acceptable. For those who are of a fearful conscience do not contaminate themselves with impostures of this kind. I say they think contracts of this sort are not illicit. They say, "I, who provide the money here to be received in Flanders, intend to transport it from there to here; therefore, I receive a price for that." Yet, in truth, that nobleman neither has any money in Flanders, nor does he dream of bringing it here, but rather seeks to provide for his necessity here. Nevertheless, the money-changers say it is no concern of theirs, nor is it their duty to know whether others have money or not. Yet they can coat these exchanges with no veneer at all to prevent them from being manifestly usurious. Since the foundation of the justice of this contract which we are treating at present is nothing other than that a transmission of money truly takes place: otherwise, it is an open loan <note>term: "mutuum" - a simple loan where no interest may be charged</note>, and thus whatever is perceived beyond the principal is extorted by reason of time. Another shield with which they protect

<column-break/>

themselves is even more iniquitous, as they think they can deceive the all-knowing God with that fiction. For they ask those who receive the money for letters to Flanders; the recipients indeed provide them and direct them to the very ministers of those same money-changers, as if those ministers held the money of the noblemen. Those ministers, acting as their factors, afterwards send the debt back to Medina <note>original: "Metinam" - referring to Medina del Campo, the great Spanish trade fair city</note> under a new interest charge. Yet, in truth, such concocted missions and remissions serve no purpose except to wait for time, and likewise to increase the interest to suck dry the substance of the debtors. And in truth, if this were not usury, it would be lawful even for any private persons who practice no trade and have no money elsewhere to contract in the same way. "I do not want to lend to you, but yet I will count out money to you here so that you may repay me in Flanders at such a price." Men should be satisfied, therefore, with being deceivers of men, lest they also be deceivers of God. Add to this that the transmission of money ought not to be to just any nearby place: as if it were feigned to be transmitted from Medina to another Medina or to Toledo. For a transfer that takes place within the kingdom is not worthy of a price, but is a cloaking of the time waited for. Of which more will be said more extensively below.

<margin>*To the first argument.*</margin>
¶ To the first argument, therefore, it is answered that in this type of exchange, the equity of justice is in no way violated; for the same money, or an equal amount to that received, is returned, but with the price of the transfer added.

<margin>*To the second argument.*</margin>
¶ To the second, it has already been answered that it is not strictly a loan; rather, it has more of the form of a deposit. For that person places his money here with this man, so that he may carry it as far as another place.

->*Whether a price for exchange is lawful by reason of time.*<-

<margin>*First argument.*</margin>
The argument is made, therefore, on the affirmative side. It was said in the previous book that it is lawful to receive a reward for the obligation of lending; for that obligation is estimable in money. But exchange by reason of time

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law #

it is nothing other than a certain kind of loan <note>original: "mutui"</note> which appears to bring benefit to the merchants themselves; and thus, it is licit to receive a price for that public service.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, money changers <note>original: "campsores"</note> undertake many labors and incur expenses; and above all these things, profit also ceases for them <note>This refers to *lucrum cessans*, or "lost profit"—the potential earnings a lender gives up by not using the money for their own trade.</note> which they could have acquired by exercising trade with that money. Therefore, for these reasons, taking into account the time during which they lack their money, they seem able to receive something. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the definition of natural law which we showed in the previous book: namely, that to receive anything for the use of money beyond its substance is usury.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
The response, as I was just saying, must be most accepted by everyone on the negative side. Therefore, a single conclusion may suffice here: Exchange <note>original: "Cambium"</note> by reason of time can in no way be licit. This is because it has the manifest character of a loan, the price of which therefore carries the open inequity of usury. For this reason, it is surprising that doctors of otherwise high reputation do not condemn exchanges of this kind because of the reasons we brought forward in the argument: namely, because of labors, expenses, and lost profit. Truly, for labors and expenses spent on some function to be deemed worthy of reward, one must first see whether the function and business itself is, by its nature and object, a duty of justice. For otherwise, neither labors nor expenses are worthy of any retribution—rather, they deserve punishment. Otherwise, we would have every usurer excused. For which of them does not put labor and expense into practicing their craft? Indeed, do not public robbers themselves perform wicked works in carrying out their robberies? Therefore, since a loan <note>original: "mutuum"</note> is condemned by the indispensable law of nature and divine law, if money changers receive something from a loan by reason of time, they can pretend no labors or expenses for themselves for which they may receive a reward. ¶ But they say the art is necessary for the commonwealth, and for that reason it is licit. Behold another fallacy: one must first weigh from the nature of the thing whether the business is licit before it is asserted to be necessary. For what is not licit by its nature can be necessary for no just end. Therefore, it is a perverse inference when, because a thing is judged necessary by some, it is inferred to be licit.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ But regarding the pretext of lost pro-

<column-break/>

-fit that they employ, it is much less effective at masking their usury. For first of all, if what we argued in the previous book (not without great probability) holds truth: he who voluntarily—that is, without force or fraud—alienates his money from his own industry, cannot contract for lost profit before there is a delay in repayment. But even if we were to subscribe to the contrary opinion, nonetheless no cause for lost profit can be imagined in the case of money changers. For it is confessed by all that no one is allowed to demand lost profit except one who has money exposed to trade, from which trade he withdraws it at the request of another. Money changers, however, do not have their money exposed to any other trade, but rather devoted to that duty of exchanging; therefore, they are hindered from no licit trade. For even if they say they could make a profit through another form of trading, all the doctors who are patrons of "lost profit" will reclaim in agreement. They say, indeed, that the mere potential is not enough to seek lost profit, but it is required that the

<margin>A Scruple.</margin>
money be already destined for trade. But you say: not only money changers who have dedicated their money solely to the banking art <note>original: "arti nummularie"</note>, but other merchants occupied in licit trades perform exchanges; they, therefore, can take lost profit into account.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that it is not at all permitted for them either. For merchants of that kind do not exchange their money to be received elsewhere unless it is the money remaining to them after they have bought their goods. Indeed, there are those who have money destined for trade, and other money for entering into exchanges. Add to this that the same merchant who pays out money to another in Medina <note>original: "Metinae"; referring to the famous trade fairs of Medina del Campo.</note> to be received in Flanders <note>original: "Flandria"</note>, also receives money from another to be paid in the same place, as it seems to be to his advantage. Since, therefore, these exchanges are a business in themselves, according to no opinion can any account be held of lost profit. And this is what I beg the reader to keep attentively in view here at the threshold, so that we may legitimately enter the dispute over exchanges. ¶ Through these points, therefore, the arguments made above remain diluted.

<summary>Soto argues that charging fees for currency exchange based on the passage of time is a form of usury, rejecting the excuses of "labor" or "lost profit" (lucrum cessans). He contends that for a fee to be just, the underlying activity must be moral, famously comparing the "hard work" of a usurer to that of a common robber.</summary>

# FOURTH QUESTION,
## On the fee for paying in cash.

### SOLE ARTICLE.

->Whether it is lawful for a money changer to receive some reward for paying in cash the money deposited in his bank.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap P featuring elaborate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
Following this, it follows that we must examine the most accepted custom by which a money changer <note>original: "campsori"</note> is permitted to receive a certain price for counting out money <note>original: "pecuniam numeret"; this refers to paying out in physical coin rather than transferring credit.</note>.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
There is an argument on the negative side: counting out money is the proper duty of the debtor. For counting out money appears to be nothing other than paying it; therefore, just as no one is allowed to receive anything because they pay a debt, neither should it be allowed to receive something for counting out the owed money.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
This is further confirmed by the fact that, surely, no other citizen besides money changers would be allowed to receive this as a price. For any citizen who owes money to another, no matter how large the sum, can demand nothing for counting out the money. Since when he counts it, he is looking after his own interest. For if he does not want to count it, let him entrust that task to the creditor. ¶ To the contrary is the fact that this is permitted by the law of princes.

After we have established the foundations in the previous questions, upon which the machine of this dispute rests, it is necessary for those entering the field and the "abyss" of exchanges to uncover their roots and veins. For except for merchants, we are few—even among scholars—who understand the actual facts of the matter. For this reason, we cannot help but stumble regarding the law itself.

<margin>The first root from which the art of money changing takes its origin.</margin>
Therefore, it must be noted at the outset that the first root for devising the art of money changing <note>original: "artis numulariæ"</note> was that high-ranking merchants who trade with large sums of money cannot carry money in a purse to the fairs <note>original: "nundinas"; these were massive seasonal international trading events.</note>, or keep it present in a chest. It would be a massive burden and impediment to transport it to such diverse and distant places. Instead, they transact everything with handwritten notes <note>original: "chirographis"; these functioned as bills of exchange or promissory notes.</note>. Because of this, money changers were introduced who respond to these

<column-break/>

sorts of notes: namely, those in whose exchange <note>original: "cambio"; here meaning their bank or place of business.</note> merchants deposit their money. Secondly, it should be noted that payments of these kinds of notes are usually made only at the fairs, and especially at those fairs which are famous for such payments—where, specifically, there are set times for payments, as will be shown below. For this reason, a merchant who buys goods before the fair, to be paid at those times, is considered to pay in present money. For example: while a merchant buys goods, the price of which he deposits by his note with a money changer to be paid at the next fair, he is not considered to be buying on credit, but with present money. But again, it should be known that when creditors, who have sold their goods on the faith of the money changer, present the notes to him, they receive that debt in two ways. One way is without physical money. The money changer, I say, recognizes the note and remains obligated to pay that sum to whomever that same creditor assigns it with his own note. And in this way, all things are handled by notes, which they call "credits." If, however, such creditors have need of counted money <note>original: "numerata pecunia"; hard cash.</note>, they are bound to pay the money changer five for every thousand <note>original: "quinque in singula milliaria"; a 0.5% fee.</note>. We are asking, therefore, whether this is lawful. For there are those who think the reason for the justice of this is that they are counting the money. But in truth, the argument raised above strongly opposes this view. For since it is in the interest of the debtor to count out what is owed, he is allowed to perceive nothing for that labor. And thus Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading theologian.</note>, in the cited booklet, asserts this without doubt.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
¶ But besides this argument, there are other manifest proofs that they do not receive that price for the business and labor of counting, but because the money is paid in cash, which is valued more highly. First, because the creditor would certainly rather count it himself than pay those five. Second, because he who, conversely, pays the money changer receives nothing for counting it. And third, especially, because when there is a shortage of physical money at the fairs, the price for counting it increases so that it may be paid in cash. So much so that sometimes ten, and perhaps thirty, are paid for every thousand. Therefore, the price is not paid for the act of counting, but in truth because present money is valued more highly. Nor does the reason seem to satisfy that this is received as a stipend for safekeeping, because the money changer is the guardian of the money. For if that money is his own, the duty of guarding it falls on him.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, the response is given with an affirmative conclusion.

That such a price can be received lawfully. Not indeed, I believe, for those reasons already refuted, but because since money changers <note>original: "campsores"</note> are like the depositories and guarantors <note>original: "fideiussores"</note> for merchants, due to the necessity already explained, this type of stipend <note>original: "stipendij"</note> is deemed established for them for the sake of this duty and service: so that as often as they pay out cash, they receive those five-thousandths <note>original: "quinq; milliaria"; a standard small commission of 0.5% for handling physical currency.</note>.

<margin>Deduction.</margin>
¶ From this it follows, therefore, that they can receive nothing beyond what is permitted to them by law. For it is considered a public stipend only insofar as it is permitted by public law or the custom of upright men. But if they receive more due to a shortage of counted money, or for another cause, it is surely usury: since they extort a price for the payment of what they truly owe. For once they are established as guarantors for merchants, they are bound by that law to pay, or they must withdraw from that duty and office.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ And by this argument, consider the response to the contrary given. For they do not receive that price as payers of money which they simply owe, but as payers of that which they owe as guarantors, and as a public stipend for that necessary service. Hence it follows that this is not allowed for private persons. ¶ Furthermore, the practice of these men involves, as it is said, that if any merchant deposits cash in an exchange <note>original: "cambio"</note>, the changer may respond with greater favor toward him. I have counted out ten thousand to the changer; I will have credit with him for twelve, and perhaps for fifteen: because for a changer to have cash is a good profit. Nor indeed does any vice appear in this agreement. For to act as a guarantor for another is a service that can be valued in money, and thus the changer can do the same for the benefit he receives from such a deposit.

# FIFTH QUESTION,
## On the exchange of coins by reason of their diverse valuation in different places or times.

->ARTICVLVS I.<-

### Whether it is permitted to exchange money of one region for money of another where it is worth more.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'Q' featuring a circular landscape scene showing a town with towers, framed by intricate floral and scrolled ornamentation.</image-desc>
TO introduce ourselves to the common types of exchanges, it is asked whether the pursuit <note>original: "ambitio"</note> of money from different regions, which under the same weight <note>original: "podere"</note> and number are of different values, is lawful.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
And it is argued from the affirmative side. He who gives one ducat for another of the same gold and the same weight performs a legitimate loan <note>original: "mutuum"; a type of loan where the same kind and quality of a fungible item is returned.</note>. For he asks nothing to be restored to him except that which he confers; therefore, it is lawful just as if you were to loan grain to be returned to you in the same measure, even if at the time of payment it sells for more.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly: If I loan you ten ducats which you are to restore to me after a year has passed, although at the time of payment the price of a ducat has been increased by law, I can receive from you the same number of ducats: therefore, in a similar way, if gold is valued more in another place, I can receive the same weight. ¶ On the contrary is the fact that justice does not allow you to receive more than you delivered, unless it is a price for some lawful thing: if therefore you have conferred a ducat here worth eleven silver reals <note>original: "regalia argentea"</note>, the debtor is not bound to restore one worth twelve.

<margin>Sense of the question.</margin>
AT the very beginning of the subject of exchanges, which are founded upon the swapping of currencies by reason of different value—in which the whole ambiguity of exchanges is centered—it must be noted first that different methods of exchanging must not be mixed together. For now, we are not disputing whether it is lawful to demand a price for the transport of money to another place; for that has already been established. Rather, we only ask whether, setting that reason aside, it is lawful to exchange currency worth less here for the same currency valued more elsewhere. Secondly, it should be noted that it can happen in four ways that one currency is worth more in one place or at one time (to speak of both together) than in another. First, by reason of the grade of gold or silver: namely, that in England, for example, it is purer and of a higher grade, or in Portugal, than in France. Just as in truth, English silver is most precious. In the second way, because gold is rarer in one region than in another: or vice versa, silver or another metal from which coins are struck is more abundant. In the third way, because the prince, when it benefits the state, increases the price of the same currency: for which reason at one...

...valued more at one time than in another. And in a fourth way, because in a general sense there is a greater abundance of money in one place than in another, and thus it is valued less there; whereas where there is a greater scarcity, it is valued more highly. In the present article, we intend to speak of the first three ways; we shall speak of the fourth in the following section, where the nature of <term>exchange</term> <note>original: "cambiorum"; the system of international financial transfers through bills of exchange.</note> is primarily to be explained. Therefore, the present question is answered with three conclusions.

<margin>*First conclusion.*</margin>
**First:** To exchange money of lesser value—that is, of an inferior grade of gold or silver—for another of a superior grade, unless a compensatory payment intervenes, is a manifest injustice. This is evident first if it occurs in the same city: for example, if you were to exchange *crowns* <note>original: "coronas"; a gold coin of lower purity.</note>, which are an inferior gold, for the gold of *ducats* or *Castellanos* <note>original: "Castellanorum"; high-purity Spanish gold coins.</note> of the same weight, which are far purer. For it is the same as if you were to exchange wheat, wine, bronze, or copper for another type that was better by its nature. The same applies, therefore, if someone were to count out a thousand French crowns in Paris so that as many pure ducats would be paid back to him in Spain. The matter is plain if the difference is of any significance. For to exchange a Spanish ducat for a Hungarian one—which, although it is more precious, is valued by the same weight of silver among us—holds no injustice.

<margin>*Second conclusion.*</margin>
¶ **The second conclusion.** To exchange money of lesser value so that you receive exactly the same weight, even when its value has been increased by law, carries the appearance of usurious iniquity. We established this conclusion in the first question of the preceding book, but we have decided to repeat it here so that we might bring together all the reasons for the variations in money. This conclusion is understood to stand against the 
<margin>*Sylvester.*</margin>
opinion of <term>Sylvester</term> <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), an influential Dominican theologian.</note> in the entry "Usury," section 14, whether that increase in value was foreseen or unexpected. Indeed, when I lend you ten ducats, each of which is valued at eleven silver <term>reales</term> <note>original: "regalibus argenteis"; the standard Spanish silver coin.</note>: if afterwards they are mandated by public law to be worth twelve, you owe me no more than one hundred and ten silver reales. And so it is the same if in another province where you are to pay me, the valuation of the money is higher. Nor is it the same, as we said there, regarding money as it is with other things. For while the value of grain increases, the thing itself remains exactly the same, which by its nature has only a single use: and therefore, however many <term>bushels</term> <note>original: "modios"; a dry measure.</note> I lent you, you owe me just as many, even if they are worth more. But when the value of money is increased, although it does not change the nature of the metal, it changes the nature of the money insofar as it is the measure of things. It is as if our <term>fanega</term> <note>original: "faneça"; a Spanish unit of dry volume.</note>, which is filled by twelve 

<column-break/>

small bushels, were increased so that it held thirteen: for if I lent it to you when it held only twelve, you owe me only another of the same quantity. We have, I believe, sufficiently confirmed the conclusion there.

<margin>*Third conclusion.*</margin>
¶ **The third conclusion.** To exchange money in one province so that the same amount is paid back in another where, due to the rarity of the metal, it is valued more than where it was counted out, is not permitted by law, but is usury. For example, a gold ducat is worth eleven silver reales among us, and among the Italians, thirteen *Carlini* <note>original: "Carlinos"; a silver coin used in Naples and Rome.</note>, which are the equivalent of our reales; or let us suppose for the sake of argument that this is the custom. It is by no means permitted to count out a hundred ducats here, whether as a loan or an exchange, to be paid in Rome at the valuation of thirteen Carlini; unless perhaps that increase goes toward the cost of transporting the money; indeed, we are saying nothing of that for now. The matter is clear: because it is just as if you wanted to receive one thousand two hundred in Rome for the one thousand one hundred reales you provide here. I would say this if the Carlino were of exactly the same value among them as the real is among us; for perhaps it is not of the same value. And therefore, it is perhaps the same to receive twelve Carlini as it is to receive eleven reales. For this reason, it might perhaps be permitted to exchange a ducat worth three hundred and seventy-five <term>maravedis</term> <note>original: "dupondia"; small copper coins used as units of account in Spain.</note> in Spain so that four hundred and forty <term>Tournois</term> <note>original: "Turonuli"; coins of Tours, France.</note> were returned in France. For the French Tournois is not of the same value as the Spanish maravedi.

¶ Against this conclusion, nonetheless, two arguments arise, by which the way to subsequent matters is opened in no obscure manner. The first is: 
<margin>*First argument.*</margin>
One could, for example, lend a hundred bushels of wheat in Sicily to be restored under the same measure in Spain, where grain is valued more highly; therefore, by the same law, one can lend a hundred ducats to be paid where they are worth more. 
<margin>*Second.*</margin>
**Secondly**, it is argued: one can carry his own gold money from a region where it is valued less to one where it is held more highly, and exchange it there at the price it currently goes for, just as one can buy goods for less in one region and sell them for more in another. Therefore, by the same reasoning, I can lend a hundred ducats to someone in Spain to be restored where they are of increased value.

<margin>*To the first argument.*</margin>
¶ To the first of these arguments, the premise is distinguished: for that contract of grain can have both the nature of a loan and the nature of an exchange. The difference between them is that a loan is made based on the time in which payment is expected. Because he who...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law

...borrowed from another, he lacks the thing in the present; however, in **exchange** <note>original: "cambium"; the financial practice of swapping currencies or transferring funds across distances.</note>, this is only by reason of the location. Peter truly has grain in Sicily, and Paul has some in Spain; an exchange of one for the other is made between them. Therefore, where there is a **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"; a simple loan where the exact same value must be returned without interest.</note>, if it is not known how much it will be worth in Spain at the time of payment, the contract is lawful. If, however, the loan were made under the condition that it be paid back when grain is more expensive in Spain, it would be unjust and **usurious** <note>Charging interest on a loan was considered a sin and a crime in the 16th century; Soto is looking for hidden interest in these contracts.</note>, as was said in the previous book. Therefore, an exchange of two things existing in different places—whether they be grain or any other goods—is by no means permitted if they are valued more in one place than in the other. For then the unfairness of the injustice is clear. And the same must be judged concerning the exchange of money.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
Finally, regarding the latter argument, it is granted that everyone is free by the nature of the thing (unless forbidden by civil law) to transport their money to another place where it is valued more highly, and to sell it there at the current local valuation. Likewise, anyone can entrust their gold to another to be returned to them elsewhere. For this does not have the character of an exchange. Since in a loan—and in a certain way, as has been said, in an exchange—the **ownership** <note>original: "dominium"</note> is transferred, and therefore nothing can be received except a thing of the same value.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
From these points, it follows that since at the **fairs** <note>original: "nundinis"; large international trade gatherings where prices and exchange rates were set by merchants.</note> among merchants (as we shall describe more fully below) the **crown** <note>original: "scutum"; literally a shield, referring to the "escudo" or "écu" coin.</note> often varies with an increase or decrease in value, one must beware of **usuries** that lie hidden in loans for this reason. If someone, for example (to use the speech of other nations), lends one hundred **ducats** to another at the price current in the city’s civil market—where, for example, a ducat is valued at twenty-eight **grossi** <note>Small silver coins.</note>—so that they are paid back at the price taxed for merchants at the Lyon fairs—where it is almost certain that the ducat will be worth thirty grossi—this is manifest usury. This is true whether the loan is made in gold or in silver. For the lender is then going to receive two grossi beyond the principal for every crown. And conversely, if at the fairs someone lends one thousand two hundred silver **reales** <note>original: "regalia"; Spanish silver coins.</note>, but counts them in gold ducats at an evaluation of twelve silver reales (at which price they circulate among merchants), he thus counts out only two hundred ducats. If, however, he does this on the condition that he receives one thousand two hundred reales where, by local custom, a ducat is valued at only eleven silver pieces, he commits usury. For since he gave only one hundred ducats, he wishes to receive one hundred reales more than that. And it should be noted that in this there lies a hidden

<column-break/>

fallacy: that while the value of the ducat or crown rises or falls among merchants, it is not because of the scarcity of gold (of which our third conclusion spoke). Rather, that coin in the market always has its valuation in silver and copper; and so, among the merchants, he who has given one gold piece will receive nothing except, for example, eleven silver reales. But they devise those names of crowns and ducats which they value at a higher or lower price. And therefore, he who lends a gold crown valued at the price of the fairs values it at more silver when he lends it than when he receives it. For merchants have no regard for the gold or silver itself, as will immediately become clearer.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
And from this is gathered the response to the first argument raised at the beginning of the question. For when you lend ten ducats, whether in gold or in silver, nothing more is owed to you than money of the same value.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
And likewise, the premise of the second argument was shown to be false by the second conclusion. For I cannot receive anything back when the value of gold money increases except that value at which it was appraised when I lent or exchanged it.

---

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether the exchange of currencies is licit when they are of unequal value in different places because of the abundance or scarcity of the entire kind of money.<-

IT REMAINS here to dispute the fourth way in which the value of money varies. Suppose, for example, that in **Flanders** (perhaps because of the wars being waged there) or in **Rome**, there is a much tighter scarcity of coined money than in **Spain**. By this reasoning, a ducat is valued more highly there than among us. Is it lawful, for this reason, to receive more in Spain for the crowns that are paid out there? For it appears that in the previous article, the question was settled on the negative side.

<margin>Argument for the negative side.</margin>
Truly, since it was denied in the third conclusion that it is lawful to exchange gold money where it is worth less, to be restored where it is valued more because of the scarcity of gold, by that same reasoning it will not be permitted to receive a greater amount of money where, because of the abundance of money, it is valued at less than where the money had been contributed. In the contrary view is the fact that the abundance of things diminishes their price; by which reasoning it is permitted for one **bushel** <note>original: "modio"; a unit of dry volume for grain.</note>

# Book Seven, Question 5

...of grain where it is valued at twice as much, to receive two where it is sold for half as much. Thus it will be in the case of currencies.

<margin>The practice of merchants.</margin>
We have finally reached the point where the nature of the **exchanges** <note>original: "cambiorum"; the financial system of moving funds between currencies or locations.</note> used by merchants must be explained. Indeed, if I am not mistaken, I have never read this understood among authors until now. Whether I have hit the mark, let others be the judges. Therefore, after the foundations laid in the previous sections, the actual practice of merchants must now be placed before the eyes of those who wish to understand the customs of such exchanges. For it has been said that the payments of **promissory notes** <note>original: "chirographorum"; written agreements to pay a debt, often used as early checks or bills of exchange.</note> by which merchants conduct their business are celebrated at **trade fairs** <note>original: "nundinis"; periodic markets that were the heart of international finance.</note> at stated times; these payments are regarded as if they were made in ready cash at the time the goods were sold. Let us therefore provide examples from our own country which are very similar to those practiced in other provinces, whether in Venice, Genoa, Lyon, or London.

There are four fixed fairs in our lands, to which four others correspond in Flanders. The first are held at **Medina del Campo** <note>original: "Metina Campensis"; a major commercial center in Castile.</note> around the month of May: where the **exchange tables** <note>original: "camporum mensae"; the physical benches where bankers sat.</note> are set out for payment, or, in their own idiom, "**exchanges are opened**," on the 15th of July, and payments last until the 10th of August. To these correspond others in Flanders around the month of September, where exchanges are opened for making payments on the 10th of November, and payments last throughout that month. 

The second fairs are held at **Medina de Rioseco** <note>original: "Metina Riui Sicci"</note>: where exchanges begin on the 15th of September and end on the 10th of October. To these correspond others in Flanders celebrated around Christmas: in which exchanges begin on the 10th of February and last through the whole month. 

The third are held among us at the same Medina del Campo in the month of October, whose exchanges last from December until the beginning of January. To which correspond the **Resurrection fairs** <note>Easter fairs</note> in Flanders: in which exchanges begin on the 10th of May and last the whole month. 

The fourth fairs are held among us in **Villalón**, whose exchanges take place from Mid-Lent until Easter: to which correspond the June fairs in Flanders, whose exchanges last almost the whole month of August. Therefore, the practice of these exchanges is this: that three months after the money is received in Medina, it is restored in Flanders. For the **exchanger** <note>original: "campfor"; a banker or money-changer.</note> who, at the May fairs of Medina, 

<column-break/>

counts out money at the beginning of August, will receive it in Flanders during the September fairs, where payments, as we said, are made throughout the month of November. And he who counts out money at Medina de Rioseco at the beginning of October receives the same in Flanders in the Christmas fairs, namely in the month of February. A similar logic should be applied to the others. For they say that this interval of time is necessary so that the promissory notes can conveniently arrive there and the money be prepared.

Once this practice is understood, here is the crucial point of exchanges. When Flanders suffers from a **shortage of coins** <note>original: "nummorum penuria"</note>, whether because of wars or any other cause, he who wishes to transmit his money from here to there among merchants pays a price. But he who, conversely, counts out money in Flanders to be restored to him in Medina, not only pays nothing, but even gains more than the one who paid in Spain to receive it in Flanders. 

For example: At this present time, when because of continuous wars the **Emperor** <note>original: "Caesar"; referring to Charles V.</note> needs many funds in Flanders, there is a great scarcity of money there. Therefore, a smaller amount of money there is considered worth as much as a larger amount here. Just as where there is a scarcity of grain, one measure would sell for as much as two would sell elsewhere. (In the following question, Article 1, we will discuss the causes for increasing the price of exchanges). For this reason, a merchant who gives another 410 of our small coins—which we call **maravedís** <note>original: "dupondia"; Soto equates them to Italian "quatrini" and French "turonos" (tournois).</note>—in Medina, receives no more than 360 in Flanders. Thus, for the transmission, he loses fifty: although, as we said above, this is not a loss in value, but a gain in utility. But he who conversely counts out 300 in Flanders receives 375 in Spain. Thus he gains more in sending money back here than he had paid while transmitting it from here to there. A nearly identical situation currently occurs between Spain and Rome, where the lack of money is tighter than usual.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
Through these points, let us note in passing, it is clear that such exchanges were not understood by the **Doctors** <note>Scholastic theologians and legal experts.</note>; and therefore they disagree in various opinions. For **Cajetan** <note>Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>, in his little work, chapter 7, devises this foundation for exchange: that money absent in a location is held to be worth less than if it were present in that location. And **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523).</note> applauds the same under the entry "**usury**," point 4. For that which is distant in place, they say, is subject to more dangers; therefore, a smaller amount which is safer can justly be exchanged for a larger amount which is less safe. And indeed, if this were truly the case—

He begins to challenge the traditional view that these price differences are merely compensation for the risk of transporting money.</summary>
