### Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Law

...if risks were truly present, I would not deny it. For we admitted above that a debt owed by someone from whom recovery is difficult—either due to their poverty or their lack of credit—can be sold for less than its face value. Nor are goods committed to the "insane waves" of the sea valued as highly as if they were safely in port. However, among merchants, there are no such risks, or scarcely any. For the merchant who receives money in Medina <note>original: "Metina"; referring to Medina del Campo, the premier financial hub of 16th-century Spain.</note> to be paid in Flanders is considered as trustworthy as if he held the money in Spain. Therefore, to grant them this license <note>The freedom to charge a fee for the exchange.</note> is to indulge them more than they even ask. Furthermore, if risk were the basis for these exchanges, then the person who pays out money now in Medina to receive it later in Flanders ought to buy that Flemish currency for less: that is, a larger amount should be restored to him in Flanders to compensate for his risk. Yet, in practice, he receives much less there.

<margin>Refutation of the previous opinion.</margin>

¶ Others, therefore, think that the reason the justice of this exchange is established is that gold is valued more highly in Flanders. They say this is only permitted if the exchange involves different currencies—for example, silver for gold or copper. But as we said above, this is merely stated without proof. For exchanges based on location do not necessarily need to be conducted in different currencies. Our third conclusion in the previous article spoke of this type of exchange. Indeed, as we were just saying, among merchants no account is taken of whether the money is gold, silver, or copper. Suppose there were no gold or silver at all, but only these same tiny copper coins. Of those who now provide 410 units in Medina, they receive only 360 in Flanders. Conversely, he who provides 300 there receives 375 here. Since the profit is greater when money is first paid in Flanders to be returned in Spain than the loss incurred if paid in Medina to be returned in Bruges, one of the most profitable businesses is to "store" money in Flanders—that is, to send it from us to there—primarily so that it can then be sent back here. For a profit of 25 **farthings** <note>original: "dupondiorum"; literally a Roman coin, here used to denote a small unit of profit or interest.</note> is made on every **ducat** <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe.</note>. Although it appears to be a loss for the person who pays more in Medina than he later receives in Flanders, in reality, it is not a loss, but often a profit.

¶ Finally, one must know that the more abundant money is in Medina, the more cheaply it is exchanged: that is, the person who pays out money to be repaid to him in Flanders

<column-break/>

pays a higher price because people needing money in Medina are rarer. And the scarcer money is, the less he pays, because there are more people wanting to receive money in Medina so they can settle debts in Flanders.

¶ The present question, therefore, is whether these exchanges are licit. In addition to the argument made at the beginning of the question, it is argued in this way:

<margin>First argument.</margin>
If this exchange were real and licit, it would be so primarily either because it was a **manual exchange** <note>original: "diminutum cambium"; a simple hand-to-hand swap of one currency for another, like at an airport counter today.</note> or because of the location—namely, because money is moved from one person to another. But there is no evidence of manual exchange here. For the more valuable currency is not exchanged for a cheaper one; rather, pennies are exchanged for pennies. Nor is the entire basis for it found in the location; for if that were the case, just as a price is paid for the transfer from Spain (where money is more plentiful) to Flanders, so too a price would be paid for the transfer from Flanders to Spain. However, as shown in practice, this does not happen; instead, a profit is made. Add to this that the person who provides money in Flanders to be returned to him in Spain does not do so because he needs to move his money here (for perhaps he had moved it there from here originally), but for the sake of profit.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: this type of exchange presents a clear appearance of **usury** <note>original: "vsuræ"; the sin of charging interest on a loan, which was strictly prohibited by the Church.</note>. For the one who pays out money in Medina, for example, to be restored to him in Flanders, transfers absolute ownership of it to the other, who spends it there just as if it were a simple **loan** <note>original: "mutuum"; a contract where the lender expects only the exact amount back.</note>. And (what makes the matter more probable) the one who receives it does not seem to do so to move the money he has in Flanders to Medina—for perhaps he has none there—but because he needs it in Medina. To wait for the payment, it is "colored" or disguised by saying it will be paid in Flanders. Furthermore, if someone in Spain truly lent money to another which the borrower was to pay back in Flanders (perhaps because both were traveling there), it would not lose the nature of a loan simply because it was to be paid in a different place.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
¶ And this reasoning is confirmed. For an exchange based on location to be licit, no delay of time should necessarily intervene. For example, I have money present here, and you also have money present in Rome; I measure it out to you here so that you may measure it back to me in Rome. Thus, if it were possible for me to be in Rome today, you would repay me there today; but time is required only because a messenger cannot fly there. However, in these merchant exchanges, the factor of time is considered. For if the person who receives in Medina today had to pay in Flanders tomorrow...

He highlights how merchants manipulate the abundance and scarcity of money at trade fairs to generate profit through time-delayed repayments.</summary>

### Book Seven, Question V

...dria, or within a week: if a messenger were to fly on steady relay horses <note>original: "succussarijs equis"; referring to the postal relay system used by merchants to move bills of exchange quickly.</note>, the one receiving the money would, in truth, either not receive it at all, or only at a lower price. Since this is indeed the case, it is a sign that the expectation of a three-month period is the cause of the profit in these types of exchanges.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, a fresh argument is also drawn from the notable point established above. For if the prices of exchanges vary according to the abundance or scarcity of money present at the trade fairs, it is an indication that these same exchanges have the nature of a <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutui"; a "mutuum" was a specific type of loan in Roman and Canon law that was strictly required to be interest-free.</note>. Indeed, if a larger amount of money remains for the merchants after their other business is completed, they provide it more easily and lose more; but if there is a greater shortage, they provide it with more difficulty and for a greater profit. ¶ But if we deny that this is a loan, we seem to fall back into the position of granting (as some believe) that this is the buying and selling of money: so that money in Spain, where there is a greater supply, is valued at a lower price, while similar money in Flanders is valued higher. This would be like the olives that grow here with us, but not there. By this reasoning, money that is in Medina <note>Medina del Campo, the primary financial center of 16th-century Spain.</note> is sold for the price of money that is in Flanders. And vice versa. However, since money is itself the *price* of things, it cannot be sold for another price. ¶ These points certainly make the matter doubtful. Indeed, to those who look only at the surface, they will rightly demonstrate that it is an unjust practice. Nevertheless, as far as I can gather according to my understanding, the matter is otherwise.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, the question is answered with this conclusion: it is lawful to exchange money from one place to another, taking into account the abundance in one place and the scarcity in the other. That is to say, so that a larger sum paid where there is abundance might result in a smaller sum received where there is a scarcity: provided that no consideration of time is involved beyond what is necessary to transport the <term>written notes</term> <note>original: "chirographa"; the physical bills of exchange or promissory notes.</note> (for which, as will be seen below, the price cannot be increased), and that all types of fraud and deceit are absent. In truth, unless my reasoning fails me, this—as far as I can gather—is the foundation of the exchanges that are celebrated in common use in our time.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The proof of this conclusion, in my view, is this: The law of justice requires that there be an equal valuation of what is given and what is received. Now, for example, four hundred small coins where money is affluent are not held to be worth more than three hundred and fifty where there is a struggle with a scarcity of money. Therefore, to pay four hundred there so that you may receive three hundred and fifty here is not a violation of justice. Nor is it a violation, vice versa, to give three hundred and

<column-break/>

fifty here, so that four hundred may be returned to you there. An example is offered in oil, as we were just saying, of which there is an abundance here; or in wine, which is carried from us to that place. For one hundred casks are not valued more highly with us—indeed, they are valued less—than sixty or seventy in Flanders. Therefore, just as one can exchange a larger measure of these types of liquids here for a smaller measure to be paid in Flanders, so can it be done with money. And vice versa: just as one can exchange fewer yards of linen in Medina for a larger amount to be paid in Flanders, because linen is dearer here; so a merchant in Flanders can now exchange a smaller amount of money for a larger amount to be returned in Spain.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
¶ And the conclusion is further confirmed by this: if someone wished to exchange money simply by reason of location—for instance, to send his money from Spain to Rome—but because of wars or other very present dangers, no other path was open except by exchanging this [money] for that; and if Rome were heavily pressed by a shortage of coins, it would be lawful to receive a smaller amount there, because it is held to be worth as much as the somewhat larger amount here. Therefore, no iniquity appears in this exchange. If this is lawful, it matters not whether someone does it occasionally and outside of custom, or as a professional duty. For that which is just by its nature, anyone may practice intentionally.

<margin>Argument against the conclusion.</margin>
¶ Against this conclusion, nonetheless, this argument immediately presents itself: shifting the argument from place to time. I say it would follow by the same reasoning that it would be lawful for anyone now in Flanders to pay his fellow citizen, for example, ten <term>Scuta</term> <note>original: "Scuta"; gold or silver crown coins.</note> (each of which is valued at three hundred small coins, whether in gold or in pence, for it matters not), on the condition that when there was an abundance of money as great as there is in Spain or greater, he would receive for each scutum three hundred and seventy-five pence, which he now receives in Spain. For if this is allowed because of the abundance in Spain, why will it not be allowed when there is such an abundance in Flanders?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is that this which appears to be a similarity is not one: because to transfer the ownership of money now so that it may be restored at a designated time later cannot be anything other than a loan; and by reason of a loan, no price can be extorted. But when consideration is given to the diversity not of time, but of place, it is not a loan, but an exchange of two present things whose value is now equal.

<margin>Regulations of the stated conclusion.</margin>
¶ From these points, therefore, the regulations and temperaments of the conclusion are easily gathered, by which its truth must be circumscribed.

He compares the fluctuating value of money in different regions to the trade of commodities like oil, wine, and linen.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "just price" of currency exchange (cambium). In the previous section, the author argued that if the price of an exchange fluctuates based on the length of time allowed for repayment, it is likely a "disguised loan" rather than a legitimate trade. # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right

...First, we have said that we must take care that the consideration of time does not creep in here, which would make the judgment one of a <term>disguised loan</term> <note>original: "palliati mutui"; a common legal term for a transaction that looks like a sale or exchange but is secretly a loan intended to bypass laws against usury.</note>.

<margin>Rule.</margin>
Regarding the understanding of this matter, I believe this rule should be established. Nothing more can be received by virtue of this kind of exchange than if two things existing in the present were being traded. That is to say, a person who pays out money in Flanders cannot receive more in Spain (as far as the nature of the currency is concerned) than if it were possible for him to receive it in Spain at the very same moment he provides the money in Flanders. For example: if the man measuring out the money in Flanders were certain that on that same day his agent would receive it in Medina <note>original: "Metinae"; referring to Medina del Campo, the site of the great Spanish trade fairs.</note>—because they had previously agreed to this through letters and messengers—and if, by reason of the stated conclusion, he receives more than he gave, he cannot receive one penny <note>original: "obolum"; a small Greek coin, used here metaphorically for any tiny amount.</note> more in value, whether the payment is to be made after one month, three, or ten. I believe it is absolutely necessary to firmly establish this rule here. For if it is as true as I believe it to be, it is an infallible indicator of the justice of these types of exchanges. We have, however, qualified the conclusion by saying "as far as the nature of the currency is concerned," because the "present time" at which the value of money in another distant place must be estimated cannot be judged in the same way as other goods, as we shall explain in the next article.

<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, the truth of this becomes very clear from what has been said. For the foundation of the justice of these exchanges—and indeed the reason why the nature of a <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutui"; specifically a "mutuum," which in Catholic theology was a loan of a "fungible" item that had to be returned in kind without interest.</note> is not hidden here—is that a larger amount of money is exchanged for a smaller one, or vice versa. This is because in one place, the smaller amount is valued as much as the larger amount is in the other. Therefore, the ratio of the value of these currencies must refer to the same point in time, and their exchange must be judged as if the things were present. Thus, no consideration of time can intervene that would either increase the price of one or decrease the price of the other. And since we have supported this conclusion with the comparison to other things, let us use them as an example in this explanation. It is indeed permitted for me, while in Spain where grain is sold for more, to exchange two bushels for three in Sicily, which I know are valued at the same price as the two in Spain. However, this ambition is not permitted except for the same time: namely, because you have grain in Sicily and I have it in Spain. Therefore, from that moment in which I give you mine in Spain, that which you had in Sicily has become mine.

<column-break/>

For if you have no grain there now, but you expect to have some, and because I wait for you, you give me three for two, it is clearly a <term>usurious loan</term>. To the point, then: if the person who receives in Flanders pays you back after three months more than he would pay if he returned it in Spain on the same day you gave it in Flanders, it is manifest that this is not a sincere exchange of thing-for-thing. Rather, that additional amount is added because you wait for him during that time while he secures the money which he did not have ready; and thus, it is by reason of a loan hidden therein.

<margin>The merchants' quibble is rejected.</margin>
¶ And through this, the flaw in that reasoning which merchants offer in their defense will be revealed. For they admit that one reason why they wait a full three months is so that the one who receives the money in one place can prepare and perhaps secure the funds for payment. This, I say, is a manifest sign of a loan. For in order for an exchange to be simple, it is required (as we frequently repeat) that both things exist; and thus, that the one who receives it has the money ready at hand. Therefore, if he does not have it in the present, it becomes clear that he is increasing the price of the exchange in return for the wait while he goes looking for the funds.

¶ But the merchant says: "A <term>bill of exchange</term> <note>original: "chirographum"; literally a handwritten note or promissory note used by merchants to move credit between cities.</note> is not a bird that can suddenly fly away; and thus, time is required." We admit this, as we admitted above. However, since that time serves no purpose other than the necessity of making the exchange known, no price can be extorted by reason of it. And this is the point that must be meditated upon most carefully. For if an exchange is thing-for-thing, it must be reduced to the same point in time; therefore, nothing can be received for the time it takes to notify the other party. Consequently, when we said that the time necessary for transmitting the bills of exchange must be allowed, it must not be understood in such a way that it can be factored into the price received—for then, truly, it would be received for the expectation of that time—but rather we meant that this necessary time is not, as some believe, a sign of usury.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But the one who defends the merchants' side says again: "If the person who sends money elsewhere entrusted it to a courier to be carried, he would grant a delay of time to that courier, and then he would pay a price for that time."

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The answer is that more than one fallacy lies hidden in this argument. First, the one who argues this way mixes together different types of exchanges at the same time—something we warned must be avoided at the very start of this question. For now, we are not disputing the "exchange by reason of place," which is done solely for the sake of transmitting money...

<summary>In this page, Dominicus de Soto argues that for a currency exchange to be morally just and not usurious, it must be treated as a simultaneous trade of values, regardless of the time it takes for a physical bill of exchange to travel between cities like Flanders and Spain.</summary>

# Book Seven, Question 5

...money that you need elsewhere: but regarding the exchange of money of one place for the money of another, on account of the variety of abundance and scarcity. For he who gives money in Flanders to be received in Spain loses nothing, as we have said, but rather gains. Likewise, he who entrusts money to a courier <note>original: "cursori"</note> does not transfer the ownership of the money to him, as happens in currency exchanges. And thus, no logic of a <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutui"; a "mutuum" is a specific type of loan where the exact same thing is not returned, but its equivalent in value, often associated with usury concerns.</note> can be hidden there. As far as the matter is concerned, the price is not established for him based on time, but for his labor. Therefore, exchanging money which is in Medina <note>original: "Metinae"; referring to Medina del Campo, the primary financial center of 16th-century Spain.</note> for that which is valued in Flanders ought not to be judged by the same norm as a mere transfer by a courier. This is especially true because the prices do not match. For a courier might transport four thousand <term>ducats</term> <note>original: "ducatorum"; high-value gold coins used throughout Europe.</note> from Spain to Flanders for a price of one hundred; and yet, a person who first receives money in Flanders to repay it in Spain pays a fifth part of the total, and even more.

<margin>Argument</margin>
¶ But perhaps some banker <note>original: "capsorum"; literally "keepers of the money-chests."</note> might argue as follows: "While wars or other obstacles prevent money from being physically transferred, the price of that transfer ought to be much higher. Therefore, I can charge a fee above the standard rate at which one currency is traded for another." For since both types of exchange are lawful in their own right, there is no 
<margin>Response.</margin>
injustice if one is added to the other. To this it is answered—and in my judgment this response is especially to be noted—that if the exchange we are currently discussing is lawful (namely, that money from one place is exchanged for money of another), then even when no wars are in the way, this is the most direct and ready way of transferring currency. Therefore, it is most unjust to add another price on top of the profit from this kind of exchange by claiming a fee for "transfer from place to place." One or the other must be chosen; or, if any price is added for the second reason, it must be 
<margin>1. First corollary.</margin>
extremely small. ¶ From this it follows that since merchants only take account of the first kind of exchange (the trading of currency), it would be unjust if an exchange were made with a citizen who is neither a merchant nor a trader and a new price was added for the transfer. I believe, therefore, that our conclusion is most certain: namely, that from the exchange we are currently discussing, nothing more can be received than if the money were provided on the same day in one place and received in the other—or perhaps some very tiny amount more. 
<margin>2. Second [corollary].</margin>
¶ Finally, we should note at the end of this whole question that the fairness of this difference is not yet clear. Namely, that when

<column-break/>

the person who first takes money in Medina and returns it later in Flanders gains only fifty, the person who does the opposite—at the same time and with the same valuation of money, providing it first in Flanders to receive it in Spain—gains seventy-five. Indeed, the reason the first exchange is lawful is that the three hundred and sixty which the person who receives in Medina later returns in Flanders is valued as much as the four hundred and ten they had received; and vice versa. Therefore, there is no reason why someone who provides three hundred and sixty first in Flanders should later receive more than four hundred and ten in Medina. For the value is the same. Therefore, it should make no difference whether one first receives money in Medina to pay it in Flanders, or first counts it out in Flanders to receive it later in Medina.

# It remains, therefore, to provide responses to the arguments, insofar as they seem to work against our assertion.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the first argument opposed at the start of the question: the logic is different when the price of gold increases (or the valuation of silver or copper decreases) solely because of the rarity of gold, compared to when the entire money supply is valued higher or lower because of its 
<margin>To the second.</margin>
general abundance or scarcity. In the first case, someone who provides a ducat in Spain, for example, provides no more than eleven silver <term>reales</term> <note>original: "regalia"; the standard Spanish silver coin of the period.</note>. It is the same whether they provide it in gold or in silver. But the person who receives it in Rome 
<margin>To the third.</margin>
receives thirteen *reales* there according to the Roman valuation. This is not because thirteen *reales* are not 
<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
worth more there than eleven are here, but because gold is valued more dearly. It is as if someone exchanged wheat worth eleven 
<margin>To the fifth.</margin>
for other wheat worth thirteen. However, when there is a greater abundance of money of all kinds in one province than in another, thirteen 
<margin>To the sixth.</margin>
*reales* are not valued higher where there is a great abundance of money than eleven are in a place where there is a scarcity. Therefore, a person can give eleven in Flanders in any currency—whether gold ducats, silver, or copper coins—to receive thirteen in Spain. 
<margin>To the other.</margin>
¶ To the first of those points we added just before the conclusion, enough has already been answered: the justice of this kind of exchange of "currency for currency" is not based on it being a <term>loan exchange</term> <note>original: "cambium mutuum"</note> or a simple transport fee, but rather on the difference in the value of money in different places.

<summary>Soto argues that currency exchange prices should be based on the local market value of money rather than the time taken to repay, warning that adding extra fees for "transportation" can often hide illegal usury. He uses a mathematical comparison of exchange rates between Flanders and Medina del Campo to show how value fluctuates based on local abundance and scarcity.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

Therefore, a contract is not changed simply because it is made out of a need to move money for business rather than for profit, just as occurs with other types of merchandise.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second point, it is denied that this is a <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutuum"; in Roman and Canon law, a "mutuum" is a loan of fungible goods (like money) where the same value must be returned, but charging interest on it was generally considered usury.</note>, as has been explained. This exchange is not performed—nor should it be—so that a fee is demanded based on the length of time. Rather, it is an exchange of two sums of present money. For this reason, we freely admit that the person who exchanges the money transfers the ownership of his money to the other party, so that they may spend it on whatever use they please. However, it does not follow from this, as some <term>modern writers</term> <note>original: "neoterici"; referring to contemporary legal and theological innovators.</note> think, that it is a loan. Even in an exchange (<term>cambio</term>), ownership is transferred, just as when you swap any of your goods for others. Nor does it matter, as the same author thinks, whether the money is to be returned in a currency of a different metal or the same.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other point I raised there—namely, that it sometimes happens that the person receiving money in <term>Medina</term> <note>original: "Metinae"; Medina del Campo, a major financial and trade fair center in 16th-century Spain.</note> has no money in Flanders—it has already been said that in such a case, if he is not actually going to pay in Flanders, it is entirely a disguised loan (<term>palliatium mutuum</term>). This is because it is not an exchange of "thing for thing," but rather a price paid for a delay granted for repayment.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ To the other point, it is also answered that receiving money here and paying in Flanders does not remove the character of a loan if it is done based on time. However, if it is done because of the difference in value, it is not a loan, but an exchange. ¶ Moreover, regarding the confirmation, enough has been answered by agreeing with its conclusion: namely, that it is not permitted to receive more through this exchange than the amount the money given in one place would be worth in the other on that same day.

<margin>To the fifth.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other point about the increase and decrease of exchange rates, we shall speak of it immediately in the next article.

<margin>To the last.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the last point, it is denied that money is being bought or sold under this cover of exchange. Neither sum acts as the "price" for the other; rather, it is a pure swap of things.

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether the prices of exchanges can vary among money-changers.<-

<image-desc>Decorative ornamental drop cap 'I' (translated from the Latin 'S' for 'Subsequitur') featuring a figure in a classical or religious setting, possibly a scholar or saint, amidst floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc> It follows that we should ask about the variation in the price of exchanges, and whether it is licit. For it is argued that among merchants, such prices cannot vary. For since money is not a salable good, its

<column-break/>

price cannot be changed in any way like other merchandise, unless it is by the law of a prince increasing or decreasing its value. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the very famous use of exchanges which, until now, has not been customarily condemned.

This question is extremely necessary for the clarity of the previous one. Since it has been established that the currencies of different places are justly exchanged due to their different valuations, it is worth knowing whether the prices can justly vary among merchants at the fairs (<term>nundinis</term> <note>original: "nundinis"; large regional markets where international debts were settled and currency rates were set.</note>). Therefore, this question is answered with two conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First: Circumstances can arise where, provided fraud and deceit are excluded, the prices of exchanges may justly vary. This conclusion follows clearly from the previous article.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Indeed, if it is not the scarcity of gold or silver, but of money in general that causes a smaller amount to be valued as much as a larger amount where money is abundant, then it follows that if at the fairs—for example, in Medina—there is a shortage of coined money (perhaps because the King has seized the money, or due to some other disaster), yet it is still necessary for the trade and other business of the republic to transfer money by exchange from Spain to Flanders and vice versa, the person paying it in Medina can receive it on better terms in Flanders. Conversely, if money is more abundant in Medina, the one receiving it there can also receive it on better terms. And this is the most common way for exchange rates to increase or decrease: where no consideration is given to the weight of gold or silver.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
¶ <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534) was a prominent Dominican theologian who wrote extensively on economic ethics.</note> Cajetan, however, in his small work on exchanges, describes another type of increase and decrease; I do not know if it is real or imagined. This occurs when a merchant in Milan receives money with a pact to repay a "Mark" of gold in Lyon at a lower price than it will be worth. For example, if we say someone receives a thousand silver <term>reales</term> <note>original: "regalia"; Spanish silver coins.</note> to repay one hundred <term>ducats</term>, which are actually worth one thousand one hundred reales. Cajetan does not condemn this exchange; indeed, he thinks it is a sale of gold at a lower price due to necessity, because the merchant would rather lose a hundred silver reales than stop another business deal where he will earn more profit. I, however, do not believe this kind of exchange is in use; nor, if it were, would I dare to approve it. For (as we have often said), among merchants there is no distinction between gold and silver, nor do they increase the value of a <term>crown</term> <note>original: "scuti"; the gold scudo or crown coin.</note>...

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that currency exchange is a legitimate "swap" rather than a loan, provided the fee is based on the currency's regional value rather than the passage of time. He explains that market fluctuations at trade fairs (like Medina del Campo) are justly driven by the local scarcity or abundance of cash.</summary>

### Book Seven, Question 5.

<margin>Sylvester</margin>
...of a scudo or a ducat <note>original: "scuti vel ducati"; these were common gold coins in early modern Europe.</note> based on the value of the gold, as the King does when he increases the legal price of gold. Instead, they use those names—scudo or ducat—as we mentioned above. And perhaps this is what Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian and author of a famous manual for confessors.</note> meant by the word "usury" (Chapter 4, Section 6), where he says that merchants do not use money in the same way as the common people. Furthermore, if it were handled in that usual way, it should certainly be considered usury. For that is not a sale of gold, but the restitution of a <term>loan</term> <note>original: "mutui"; a loan of fungible goods like money where charging interest was forbidden by Church law.</note> with usury. Indeed, it makes no difference to the one who provided the money earlier whether he receives payment in gold or in another currency, provided he extorts a higher amount as a fee for the delay. ¶ However, I would say that this is licit, provided that frauds and deceits are excluded—which, in truth, very frequently creep in when the value of money is being increased. For those who set aside all religious scruples for the sake of profit from these exchanges practice <term>monopolies</term> <note>Soto uses "monopolia" to describe market cornering or collusion among a few powerful actors.</note> just as they do with other goods. For two or three people will form a confederacy and scrape together all the available money. That is, at the beginning of the trade fairs, they receive money from everyone to be paid back partly in Flanders, partly in Lyon, or London, or Genoa, and so forth. Consequently, those who later have need of entering into these exchanges—specifically needing ready cash in **Medina** <note>original: "Metina"; referring to Medina del Campo, Spain’s premier financial center.</note>—find no other <term>Exchange</term> <note>original: "Bursa"; the financial market or meeting place of merchants.</note> open except that of the monopoly; they are thus forced to accept it at whatever price those merchants please. This is a most harmful plague and should not be tolerated in any way.

<margin>Causes by which the price of exchanges can be legitimately increased.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, the primary reason for doubting this conclusion concerns the causes by which the price of exchanges can legitimately vary. And indeed, it is very well established—and ought to be a most settled principle—that the scarcity and abundance of money can be legitimately considered as a cause. This scarcity and plenty can be of two kinds: namely, absolute and relative. By absolute, I mean (as said above) if the King were to collect money from everywhere because of wars or any other massive expenditures, or if it were truly tighter due to some other calamity. Conversely, if it were flowing in abundance due to some prosperity. Regarding this, there can be no doubt that it is a legitimate cause. But there is another kind about which the prudent must deservedly hesitate. Namely: whether the frequency or fewness of those in need—and thus of those seeking money in the form of an exchange—increases or decreases

<margin>Cajetan. The writer from Medina.</margin>
the prices of exchanges. Indeed, Cajetan <note>Cardinal Cajetan (Thomas de Vio), a major 16th-century commentator on Thomas Aquinas and economic theorist.</note> in his *Opuscula* (Chapter 7) does not fear to assert this. The writer from Medina also subscribes to this; regarding him, I would note in passing that he seems to contradict himself for no reason. For he grants

<column-break/>

that the price of exchanges varies according to the number of recipients, and yet he denies that the abundance or lack of money can be considered a legitimate cause for those same prices to vary. This is despite the fact that the number of recipients increases or decreases the price for that very reason: when there are many people, money is considered scarcer in relation to them; but when there are more [funds available], it is considered more plentiful, just as with other merchandise. ¶ Furthermore, this cause for varying the price is doubtful. First, because comparing money with other merchandise in this way is not entirely legitimate. For money is not a <term>saleable good</term> <note>In Scholastic thought, money was a "consumptible" medium of exchange, not a commodity to be sold for profit in itself.</note>, and therefore it does not seem it should be valued by price in the manner of other goods. Second (which must be observed with careful consideration), if you grant this license to the <term>money-changers</term> <note>original: "campsoribus"; the bankers or merchants who operated the exchange tables.</note>, you open the door to frauds. For they are accustomed to "closing their purses" <note>Stopping all lending or exchange activity to create artificial scarcity.</note> at the start of the trade fairs, waiting to see at what price the exchanges will run. And when they see a favorable market, they bring that money out for exchange; otherwise, they keep it back. And although at first glance no iniquity reveals itself there—since anyone can either keep or dispose of his own property at his own judgment as it suits his affairs—nevertheless, if the matter is inspected more closely, that very action is the cause of increasing the price of exchanges. For the reason there are more people seeking exchanges is that money is scarcer; but it is scarcer because it has been hidden—indeed, hidden for the very purpose of increasing the prices. And in truth, if the valuation of exchanges is to be varied according to the rule of other prices, as the merchants want, they must be subject to the same law that the state usually observes for other goods. For when many people lock up their granaries, causing a high price for provisions, they are compelled to open them and sell at a legitimate price. Indeed, even if they were not compelled, it would be a sin; because since these things are necessary for the state, their owners cannot afflict the people with a common injury in that manner. If, therefore, the merchants admit that exchanges are so necessary, they truly seem to "cut their own throats with their own blade" <note>A metaphor meaning they are trapped by their own logic.</note> when they hide their money. This is especially true because it can hardly happen without some appearance of a monopoly. For if they did not agree among themselves to lock their purses, one or perhaps another would open an exchange. ¶ Truly, this matter is not yet sufficiently proven to me; nevertheless, I find myself leaning toward this side, which is the final conclusion.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>

<summary>Soto argues that while currency exchange rates can legitimately fluctuate based on supply and demand, merchants often create artificial scarcity through collusion and monopolies at trade fairs. He challenges the idea that money should be treated as a saleable commodity like grain, warning that "closing the purses" to drive up rates is a sinful injury to the public good.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

<margin>Proof.</margin>
An abundant supply of people seeking bills of exchange <note>original: "accipientium"; those receiving money now to be paid back elsewhere later.</note> can be a reason for increasing exchange prices, provided that all cunning and craftiness are avoided, just as a scarcity of seekers is a cause for decreasing them. This conclusion is supported by several points. First, because exchanging the money of one place for the money of another has been shown to be not only licit but even necessary for commerce. Next, because the scarcity of coins in one region is the reason why a smaller amount of money there is valued as highly as a larger amount elsewhere. Since, therefore, a larger number of people receiving exchanges causes a smaller supply of money to be available than when seekers are fewer, it is concluded that the price can be increased for this reason as well. But truly, there are so many tricks and deceits that will immediately insinuate themselves into this reasoning to raise prices, that the conclusion should be admitted into practice only with fear and dread. For this is a matter that rests not so much on <margin><unclear>conscience and knowledge</unclear></margin> theoretical knowledge as it does on practical wisdom and prudence; and therefore, this kind of practice should be deferred to the judgment of the most upright people. ¶ In response to the argument we proposed at the top of the <margin>To the first argument.</margin> question: although money is not "salable" <note>in the sense of being a commodity like grain or cloth</note> and thus cannot be valued by its own price, yet because it is exchangeable and commutable, it can be valued as more or less when it is exchanged for money of another location. ¶ To the other point <margin>To the second.</margin> that we added regarding frauds, we can respond nothing else than what we have already said: it must be left to the judgment of a god-fearing conscience. For even if it is not simply to be condemned for someone to keep his money—just like any other goods—for a time so that he can distribute it more conveniently and profitably, it can nonetheless hardly be done, as we said, without fraud.

### ARTICLE IV.

->*Whether exchange involving an uncertain amount of payment is licit.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial E featuring a landscape with a bridge and buildings.</image-desc>
From the previous article, a new question arises here: namely, whether present and certain money can be exchanged for future money whose value is uncertain. For example, if someone pays another one hundred <term>ducats</term> <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe; its value fluctuated relative to local silver currencies.</note> on the condition that repayment be made according to the valuation of the exchanges at the next <margin>Argument.</margin> <term>fairs</term> <note>original: "nundinarum"; these were periodic international trade gatherings in cities like Medina del Campo, Lyons, or London where debts were settled and exchange rates set.</note>—whether those of Medina, Lyons, or London; for it matters little. And it appears

<column-break/>

from this that it is not licit, because the scales of justice are exposed to danger: either less is returned than was contributed, or (which happens much more frequently in practice) more. For if either happens, justice will be violated. ¶ On the contrary, however, since it is licit to commit money to an ambiguous outcome—as is clear in gambling and in lots—there is no reason why it should not be licit in the form of exchange.

The question is answered with two conclusions. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> The first: if all fraud and deceit are far removed, it possesses in itself no character of <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of charging interest on a loan, which was strictly regulated by the Church.</note> for someone in Milan, Paris, or elsewhere to provide money to another—namely a hundred or a thousand ducats, whether in gold or silver (for it has already been said many times that it makes no difference)—to be paid back at the price of the exchanges of the first upcoming fairs.
This is also the admission of Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> in his <margin>Cajetan.</margin> short work on exchanges: provided that fraud is far away. Namely, first, that there is an equal doubt as to whether the ducat will be valued at more or less. Second, that the one who provides the money is not the one who will work to manipulate the value of the money. And the reason is plain: indeed, it can be licit under the form of a loan. It is like a deposit, which they call <term>vadiatio</term> <note>A wager or a pledge involving risk.</note>: that is, exposing money to the risk of a future event, as we also said regarding insurance. "Take a hundred on this condition: and if the prices of the exchanges increase, you will pay me more; but if they decrease, you pay less, or the same." For both parties are subject to the same <term>alea</term> <note>original: "alea"; literally "the roll of the dice," referring to the element of risk or chance in a contract.</note>. ¶ Indeed, Cajetan <margin>Cajetan.</margin> in the sixth chapter of his work adds something else, which I do not know can be safely affirmed or sufficiently taught. Namely, that this can happen in two ways: In one way, by leaving the restitution to uncertainty, as asserted in our conclusion; but in the other way, by a pact where that which is in doubt is fixed at a certain quantity. For example: I lend you a hundred ducats now, worth, let us say, one thousand silver <term>reals</term> <note>A Spanish silver coin.</note>; however, it is doubted whether at the fairs they will be worth a thousand or perhaps one thousand two hundred. He says it can be agreed between us that you return one thousand one hundred to me, which is the middle point of that excess over the capital. ¶ I truly do not think I see the equity of this contract; indeed, I would believe it is not at all licit. For first, our asserted conclusion is not true unless tempered by its own moderation: namely, that there is an equal doubt...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s ethical analysis of currency exchange (cambium). On the previous page, he discussed how supply and demand affect the "price" of money. Here, he examines the specific morality of "future" exchanges where the value of currency might change between the time the contract is made and when it is paid at a distant trade fair.</meta>

# Question V of the Seventh Book

...whether it will be worth more or less: following the instruction of the chapter *In civitate*, concerning usury <note>original: "In ciuitate. de vsuris"; a reference to a specific section of Canon Law dealing with interest and loans</note>. For example, if a hundred ducats are currently worth a thousand silver coins, and there is an equal doubt whether the value at the market will be estimated at eleven hundred or nine hundred, then the risk <note>original: "alea"; literally "the die," referring to the speculative risk or "gamble" inherent in the contract</note> is equal. However, if it is certain that they will be worth either what they are worth now or more, but not less—as in the case described by Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian and commentator on economic morality</note>—it is absolutely not permitted. For we have said that such an exchange has the nature of a deposit, or what they call "radiation" <note>original: "radiationis"; a technical term for a specific type of financial settlement or speculative arrangement</note>, or a game, in which the outcome must hang equally for both parties. 

<margin>*Second.*</margin> Likewise, this second case clearly involves a loan with profit. For if it is an exchange, only equal things can be exchanged for one another, just as if I were to lend you grain now. Therefore, it is not similar to other goods according to the tenor of the chapter *Naviganti* <note>A famous papal decree concerning maritime loans and the "price of risk"</note>: that he who is to keep goods can sell them for more if they were going to be worth more at the time they were to be sold by the owner. This is because money can by no means be sold, but only exchanged. Therefore, if a profit is fixed, it is a loan that takes the form of usury. For instance, if I were to lend you grain now, and because it is believed it will be worth more, I were to bind you by that bond so that you would restore eleven measures to me for every ten. 

<margin>*Instruction*</margin> ¶ From these things we gather this instruction: that even according to the tenor of our second conclusion (though it is true in its own kind), it is not safe to make these types of exchanges for an uncertain payment. For there is always a snake hidden there <note>original: "abditur anguis"; a classical idiom for a hidden danger or deception</note>, because very rarely—indeed, we might say never—when these exchanges are made, is a lower price feared; rather, it is always certain that it will increase. They are made for no other reason than to personify <note>original: "personandas"; to mask or give a false face to</note> usury. For a person in need approaches a merchant or a money-changer <note>term: "campforem" (money-changer); a specialist in currency exchange, usually operating at a bank or table during a trade fair</note> to borrow money; the latter does not refuse, provided it is repaid at the current price later at the market, because he is certain of profit. 

<margin>*To the arguments made.*</margin> ¶ Therefore, the conclusion of the argument presented at the beginning of the question is granted. Namely, that according to what happens most often, the exchange is not licit because justice is exposed to danger. However, the argument to the contrary proves only this: that if an equal doubt could occur—that the future price might be less than it is worth while the exchange is made, just as it might be more—then it would be licit.

## ARTICLE V.

-> Whether an exchange of this kind, which is made by skipping and passing over the first markets into other subsequent ones, is licit. <-

<image-desc>A large historiated initial "I" featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or theologian, gesturing toward a radiant sun—a symbol of divine truth or clarity—in the upper corner.</image-desc>

In this final article, it remains to conclude the business of the entire practice of money-changers, so that it may be related more clearly and examined more brilliantly. 

<margin>*First argument.*</margin> It is argued that it should be permitted to celebrate such exchanges in this way: that because they are made for the third or fourth markets, the price can be increased. Indeed, if this condition were to invalidate the exchange—especially because something is received by reason of delayed payment—this does not happen here; therefore it is licit. The second premise is proved because that price, as the money-changers claim for themselves, is not received by reason of time, but because exchanges made for a longer time are less profitable for the one providing the exchange. For if I have paid you money in Medina <note>Medina del Campo in Spain, one of the most important centers for international trade fairs in the 16th century</note>, and you do not pay me back in Flanders <note>The Low Countries, a major commercial hub for Spanish trade</note> on time, I am prevented from sending it back here opportunely with a profit, and thus for that loss which I incur, I can receive more profit from you. 

<margin>*Second.*</margin> The second reason for demanding a higher price when payment is postponed is, as they say, that when exchanges are "looser"—that is, more time is granted for payment—there are more people who will receive them; whereas where they are "stricter" [shorter-term], they are much rarer. Since there are more people to receive them, the prices of the exchanges are rightly increased, just as with other goods. 

<margin>*Third.*</margin> Third: because the more time the provider of the exchange grants the debtor for payment, the less trouble he causes him in preparing the money elsewhere, since he can prepare it more easily over a longer time. For this reason, the addition made to the price is not unjust. 

¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that in these types of exchanges, the price is clearly increased by reason of time, which is a sign of a usurious loan.

In the practice of money-changers among honest men and those of circumspect virtue, an exchange in which (to use their phrasing) the markets "leap over" has always had a bad reputation. This occurs when, the nearest markets having been skipped and passed over, the payment is postponed until the third or fourth markets. Nevertheless, among them there is doubt concerning certain markets which they consider necessary to skip and pass over, and they even think...

<margin>Basis.</margin>
Therefore, we must recall the dates of the trade fairs <note>original: "nundinarum"; these were massive, scheduled seasonal markets where international debts were settled</note> which we mentioned in the second article. For we said that from the Medina fairs <note>original: "Metinensibus"; referring to Medina del Campo in Spain, a major financial hub</note> in May—that is, from the end of July—it is the custom to exchange for the Flanders fairs in September: that is, for the month of November, with the June fairs skipped over. The payments for the June fairs are made throughout the month of August; because the payments in Medina are finished by the tenth day of that same month, the handwritten notes <note>original: "chirographa"; these were the physical bills of exchange or promissory notes</note> cannot be conveniently transmitted within the same month. Likewise, in the next fairs of Río Seco <note>original: "Riui Sicci"; another major Spanish fair location</note>, the payments of which are finished in the month of October, no exchange is made for the Flanders fairs of September (the payments of which last through all of November), because that time is not considered sufficient to transmit the notes. Instead, an exchange is made for the Nativity fairs, the payments of which are made in February. And finally, from the October fairs, whose payments are made in December, most exchange for the Resurrection fairs celebrated at Bergen <note>original: "Bergis"; referring to Bergen op Zoom in the Netherlands, a key market for the English cloth trade</note>, the payments of which occur in May. And regarding this, there is a greater doubt. For in the middle of Lent, certain exchange payments are also made in Flanders, even if there are no trade fairs; it appears, therefore, that an exchange could have been conveniently made in the month of December for that time. Nevertheless, merchants offer this excuse for themselves: that the time is not long enough, and especially because there are no fairs held then in which debtors could raise the cash <note>original: "æs"; literally "bronze" or "copper," but used generally for money or currency</note> to pay; and therefore, the payment is stretched out until the month of May. They say, therefore, that since a three-month period is necessary to send the notes, it is nothing other than equity <note>original: "equitas"</note> to receive some price on account of that time which is granted to the other person so that they may pay more conveniently. And they apply the reasons which we have just narrated.
<margin>Decree of the Parisians.</margin>
And the opportunity for this opinion was chiefly provided by a decree of certain Parisians in the year of our Lord 1517. Responding to three questions from merchants, they granted them the license in the third response to receive a price by reason of time, on account of lost profit <note>original: "lucrum cessans"; a legal concept allowing compensation if a lender misses out on other certain profits because their money is lent out</note>, labors, and industry. And they even added that if the payment is deferred to other fairs with a fair skipped in between, then the longer the time is, the more can be received. The leaders <note>original: "Coryphæ"; a term for the heads or protagonists of a group</note> of that business were two brothers, the Coronelli <note>Luis and Antonio Coronel, Spanish theologians who taught at the University of Paris</note>, our fellow citizens—men, to be sure, of no regrettable' erudition and fame—but nevertheless in this matter, even by the confession of the merchants themselves, they missed the mark. Saving

<column-break/>

their authority, I would say they wandered from the truth, both regarding the facts and subsequently regarding the law, and not without causing a "sore" on the consciences of the merchants.
<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, the question is answered with this conclusion, which certainly seems impossible to doubt for anyone who has examined the matter attentively: Not only is it in no way permitted to receive a price because of the skipping and omitting of trade fairs, but indeed, if the matter is weighed by the condition of time itself, it is not even permitted on account of that time that stands between the exchange and the next fairs. This conclusion is drawn from what was said above; indeed, it was expressly demonstrated in the second article. However, for the sake of greater clarification and confirmation, it is resumed here. Namely, so that we may show that the exchangers <note>original: "campsores"; the bankers or money-changers</note> fight against themselves with their own arguments. For they say that a price is not received for that three-month period that runs between the Spanish fairs and the Flanders ones, but because the notes cannot be sent any sooner. For it is not necessary to have fixed horses by which they might fly; indeed, in time of war, it cannot be done. We, however, certainly admit that time is necessary for that task. Nevertheless, that time ought not to serve this purpose (as we have said): so that the one who
<margin>First proof.</margin>
receives the money can pay conveniently. For if he does not have it at present, it happens that he pays a price for the "waiting"; but if he does have it, the time serves rather the one who contributed the money. For it is in his interest to recover the money, and therefore to send the notes; wherefore he can receive nothing by reason of that time. Therefore, to say that because a gap of time is necessary for sending the instruments of the contract, it is permitted for the exchange to be made more expensive, involves a contradiction. Indeed, in whatever way something is paid on account of that time, it signifies a loan <note>original: "mutuum"; a gratuitous loan of fungible goods</note>, and therefore usury. Take the example of other things. If I were to exchange my grain, or wine, or anything
<margin>Second.</margin>
else with your similar goods, which you have elsewhere of exactly the same value as mine, yet I added that because time is required for the contract to become known to your ministers who should restore mine, you should pay me some price—this would surely be unjust usury, unless I received only that very small expense which I incurred in sending the letters. But they still persist in their defense, saying: "We admit that the one who receives an exchange in Flanders does not have the money ready in Medina, but waits for the fairs, by selling his wares which he sends there to be collected..." <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the final word "collecturum" means "about to collect" or "going to gather."</note>

And by this reasoning, the exchanges which are deferred from Medina to those fairs become more expensive. For then, present money is not exchanged for present money, but for that which is hoped to be increased in the future. Besides, more is always received simply by reason of the longer delay. Therefore, all these are usurious exchanges. And this reasoning is confirmed: because if that account of future value could be held in exchanges, the same reasoning could be applied to exchanges between nearby places in the same kingdom, or even in the same place. One could, I say, count out money in the May fairs at Medina to be restored there in the October fairs, and the same with a profit, because it is hoped the price will then be increased; yet this would be most patent usury, as we shall show by repeating the next question. Wherefore, the intercalation <note>The practice of inserting extra time or delay between payment periods.</note> of payments for Mid-Lent cannot but be suspect.
<margin>The legitimate method of exchange.</margin> ¶ Therefore, I seem to see no other legitimate method of exchanging than if the value of the money in the present or in the nearest fairs is estimated without fraud or deceit, based on the preceding fairs of that place to which the exchange is made and on present conjectures; and the payment of the exchange is established according to that. For I judge this to be exchanging present money for present money. And especially when it is exchanged to Rome and to whatever place where trade fairs are not expected. From which it follows that an exchange after a fair has passed is never presumed to happen without the fraud of usury. But if you say, perhaps by the time the payment is to be made things will have changed: the answer is that you ought to undergo such risks. For this is the condition and lot of merchants <note>original: "negotiatorum conditio & fors"</note>. Indeed, if you wish to place your money in such total safety, it is no longer business, but truly a loan <note>original: "mutuatio"; a loan of fungible goods where the lender cannot profit solely from the act of lending.</note>: for the sake of which you cannot legally receive a price.

For it is precisely for this reason that one who receives a loan at usury pays more according to how much more time is granted to him.

# QUESTION SIX,
On the remaining types of exchanges.

## ARTICLE I.

### Whether exchanges between nearby places in the same kingdom are licit.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure seated at a desk or table within a room, looking out a window.</image-desc>
Having emerged, then, from the denser thickets <note>Soto repeatedly uses the metaphor of "thickets of thorns" (spineta) to describe the legal and moral complexity of currency exchange.</note> of exchanges, let us propose in this final question the remaining matters which are easier to decide. And first, it is argued that it is licit to receive a price for an exchange between <margin>First argument.</margin> two places in the same kingdom. For the distance of the place is accidental to this business, and thus, although the justice of the price might be violated if it is not appraised according to the distance, usury cannot be committed; since transferring money from one place to another can also be valued at a price. <margin>Second [argument].</margin> ¶ Secondly: because since it has been said that the money of one place can be exchanged for a greater amount in another when it is valued higher there, the same thing can be done in the trade fairs of the same kingdom. The question is answered with three conclusions. The first of those reasons we were just making demonstrates <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> this conclusion. But truly, not more than that small amount for which it could be sent via a courier—unless perhaps a real and not feigned danger of bandits or some other kind of risk loomed over the journey. For then it would be just for the price to be somewhat more substantial. ¶ However, these prices are of such tiny importance that they are considered as nothing among bankers <term>campsores: money-changers or professional bankers who operated at the fairs</term>. Wherefore, the second conclusion is applied. For exchanges to be paid within the kingdom, <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> no price can be received in equity. I am speaking of those prices of such great value as are customary among bankers. <margin>Proof.</margin> The proof: because those transactions are not made for the sake of transferring money. For neither is labor necessary for that purpose, nor is there industry or diligence due to the dangers of the roads, which would be worthy of any price. And therefore it is manifest...

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion.** Bills of exchange that are in reality to be repaid in the same place—or at a very short distance within the same province—even if they are feigned to be for the fairs of other kingdoms, can in no way be cleansed of the stain of usury. Rather, they hold the first place among those which are properly called **"dry exchanges"** <term>cambium siccum: a fraudulent transaction where a loan is disguised as a foreign currency exchange, but no money ever actually leaves the local area</term>. For this reason, those exchanges which are made, for example, in Milan by way of Genoa, Venice, or Bruges; or in Medina <note>Medina del Campo in Spain, a major site for international trade fairs</note> by way of Lyon or Flanders: if the person receiving the money in Milan or Medina does not actually have money in those distant places, nor hopes to have it there to make the payment, but instead needs the money where he receives it and intends to pay it back there—no matter what the bankers <term>campsores: professional money-changers or private bankers</term> may pretend—these are "shameless exchanges." We have already noted this above under the title regarding exchange based on location. For these are the fictions and cloaks with which bankers "skin" <note>original: "deglubunt," literally to peel or flay</note> the assets of the nobility. They know well that when citizens who do not practice trade request exchanges from them, those citizens have no coins in Flanders; nonetheless, the bankers force them to direct letters to the bankers' own servants to "return" the exchange. They proceed therefore to impose not only upon men, as we said there, but even upon God Himself. But they say, "It does not matter to me whether he is going to pay me elsewhere or not."

<margin>Sylvester</margin>
Furthermore, Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> responds to these people in the word "Usura," section 4, paragraph 9: that when the banker knows or presumes this, he is plunged into the vice of usury. This is because he knows well that he is receiving no price except for the time of the loan. It is just like a man who buys "fictitious oxen" from a peasant—oxen which the peasant does not even own—and then "leases" those same oxen back to the peasant so that the peasant might support himself and pay a fee for their labor. And so that the poison of this usury might be more clearly exposed: suppose any citizen who is *not* a banker were to give his money to another through that same cleverness, to be restored to him in a larger amount—would he not be held as a manifest usurer? Why then should bankers not be held the same? These exchanges are made much more shamelessly from Medina to Villalon, or to another fair in Medina; it amounts to the same thing in essence, even if they are named as going through Flanders or Lyon. For, as we were saying, if the payment is to be made at the Spanish fairs, it comes to the same result. Therefore, regarding those exchanges made in Italy within the same province—namely Milan by way of Florence or Genoa—I do not know how they can be "masked" so that they do not appear usurious, since the price is clearly increased not because of the location, but because of the time.

<column-break/>

Therefore, the first argument has now been answered. To the second argument, it is replied (as we were saying above) that within the same province, an exchange of "present money for present money" at a different estimated value cannot occur in the same way it does between different provinces and kingdoms. For in different provinces, the variety arises from the fact that in one place there is a struggle with a scarcity of money, while another enjoys an abundance. In the same kingdom, however, this difference cannot be had unless one takes into account different times: as if there were a greater supply now and a scarcity feared at future fairs. To exchange under this hope would be usury based on time, as was explained in the previous question.

<margin>To the first argument. To the second.</margin>

---

### ARTICLE II.
#### Whether exchanges are licit which, although they are made for the first fairs distant in time and place, yet become more expensive the further away they are.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
FINALLY, the last scruple regarding exchanges is whether an exchange can be made more expensive the further away the next fairs of another location are. And it is argued on the affirmative side: to exchange for the first fairs, no matter how far distant in time, is not usury, as was declared above. If these exchanges are made outside the kingdom, a larger amount of money can be exchanged for a smaller one (and vice versa), as has also been defined. Since the further away the fairs are in time, the more people there are who seek money from exchanges, nothing prevents the exchange from being made more expensive. After all, a more abundant number of recipients increases the price of exchanges, provided it does not sprout from a corrupt root. ¶ On the contrary: this increase seems to arise from the fact that the payment is waited for longer, which is evidence of usury.

WE have added this article chiefly because of those exchanges which are customary among our people—namely, because of the exchanges celebrated between the Castilians and the Portuguese. Indeed, if an exchange is made for the fairs of the same province, it has already been sufficiently said that it is not licit to receive more simply because the fairs are further away. For in that case, only the consideration of time is held. But when the exchange is made outside the province, then there is a doubt, because...

### Book Seven, Question VI

<margin>The proposed question is explained.</margin>
¶ Either the differing value of money in another location, or the transfer of funds, seems to justify an **exchange** <term>cambium: a transaction where money is paid in one place to be received in another, usually in a different currency</term>; provided the trade fairs are distant in time. Therefore, our practice of exchanging with Portugal is as follows: since they do not have **trade fairs** <term>nundinae: massive international markets held at specific times of the year where bankers and merchants settled their accounts</term> like those mentioned in Rome, exchange is only made for a certain period of time. However, it is done differently from us to them than the other way around. For the scarcity of money experienced in Medina <note>Medina del Campo, the primary financial center of 16th-century Spain</note> must be paid in Lisbon <note>original: "Olyfsippo"</note> after a full month. And since there—as was said of Flanders at this time—there is not a great abundance of money, it is valued more highly there than among us. Because of this, a person who has counted out a thousand in Medina, although he might receive a little less in Lisbon, still receives just as much in value, similar to what we said of the man who counts out money in Medina to receive it in Flanders. Even if he receives the same amount in form, he receives more in value. Therefore, in our language, this exchange is called **at par** <note>original: "ad par"</note>; that is, exactly the same amount is received as was given, even though that "equal" amount is worth more by the standards of Portugal. Merchants may say this profit is lawful by reason of the transfer of money. However, in the "remission" <note>sending money back</note> from there to us, **a more venomous snake lies hidden** <note>original: "venenosior latet anguis," a Virgil-inspired idiom for a hidden danger or deception</note>. For money is sent back to coincide with our first trade fairs. But the more distant they are, the higher the fee demanded, and a grace period of four months is usually granted.

¶ Now, the bankers <term>campsores: professional money-changers or private bankers</term> claim they do not receive that extra amount because of the *time*, but because at that time there are more people seeking to receive exchanges. And indeed,
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian</note> in his famous short work, chapter 7, openly favors this cause of the bankers. He warns that it must be carefully noted that it is not a sufficient sign of an unjust contract to give less for an exchange when a long time lies between now and the fair, and more when the fair is near. That is, that a banker who pays out first gives less when the fairs are distant, and more when they are near, so that he receives the same money: in other words, to profit more because of the longer delay in time. For that is how his obscure writing must be explained. For perhaps, he says, this custom could have been introduced because, over a longer time, there are fewer bankers acting as sellers and more people seeking to receive exchanges. But truly, unless I am gravely deceived, I cannot help but marvel that a man of such great learning offered this indulgence to the bankers. ¶ To this question, then, we respond with two conclusions specifically adapted to exchanges

Therefore, since—as is the custom—far more is received, such exchanges are not without fault.

In neither of these can **time** be taken into account; only the labor of transporting it and the current valuation of both places. But the logic shines more brightly here, and the path for cloaking **usury** <note>charging interest on a loan, which was prohibited by Church law</note> is more firmly blocked, because here there is no refuge in "the trade fairs." Fairs do not happen in Portugal such that one must wait to see how much the money will be worth then. Furthermore, the fact that manifest usury accompanies the sending of money from there to us is made clear by this: the greater the interval of time until the fair, the more the exchanges are valued. And as for the argument we mentioned, and likewise for Cajetan’s opinion, let us respond: it is manifest that the larger multitude of people seeking exchanges arises from no other source than that longer delays are granted for payment. Therefore, to increase prices for that reason is manifest iniquity. It would be different if, as we said in the preceding question, the same number of recipients increased for some other reason. ¶ Furthermore, the face of usury is also uncovered by the fact that the bankers of Medina force the recipients of the exchange to pay in the first month, so that afterwards there is a longer distance of time until the next fair, allowing the money to be sent back more profitably. ¶ But perhaps the bankers ask how they shall exchange?
