¶ Indeed, I am well aware that many more types of exchanges are multiplied by others, which we have deliberately left out: both because they are so obscure that they can in no way inform the reader, and also because I believe I have delivered all the foundations in summary, through which any very observant person can judge individual cases. For I confess that unless someone is of moderate intelligence, has observed the matter with attentive consideration, and has furthermore been instructed by the **money-changers** <term>campsoribus: professional bankers or dealers in currency</term> themselves, they cannot answer regarding the many ambiguities that occur in this art. For the calamity of wars, which the sins of citizens are accustomed to bring upon the state, is usually the primary reason why kings scrape together money from everywhere—and especially from the famous trade fairs—by way of exchanges. And for this reason, a crowd of exchanges is often permitted, even beyond what the law allows. But it would be much more well-advised if, in such a calamity, the King allowed such exchanges to be made only with himself; but forbade them to others: for since there is not an equal necessity in others as there is in him, it ought not to follow that if they are done with the king, they ought to be done with others. Nonetheless, those which are **disguised usuries** <note>original: "personatae usurae"; contracts designed to hide a loan at interest under the guise of a different transaction</note> are not made lawful even when done with the king.

<margin>On the ministers of exchanges.</margin>
CONCERNING the ministers of exchanges, judgment can be made through those things said in the previous book regarding the servants of usurers: although in celebrating exchanges, certain new things remain to be noted about them. For it is a matter of doubt whether he who receives an exchange in the name of others does so safely. <margin>Doubt.</margin> For example: there are very wealthy merchants who assist the king with money, and not without immense **usury** <term>fœnore: interest or profit from a loan, often considered a sin in this period</term>: but they say that as his ministers, they collect exchange money from many places which they contribute to him: and therefore they are clean of every stain of usury, if they receive from him whatever usuries they pay out. <margin>Solution.</margin> ¶ Here, however, many things must be considered. For receiving in the name of the king happens in two ways: or rather, it happens in only one way in truth, but they feign another. I say that he properly receives an exchange in the name of the king, or another nobleman, or merchant, who as his ser-

<column-break/>

vant carries it out: for instance, because he is his steward, or secretary, etc. Thus he himself does not become the debtor for the exchange he receives, nor does he afterward grant it to the king as his own: rather, it is the king who receives it through him. And such a minister commits no usury, but receives on behalf of the master at interest: which is done lawfully in cases of pressing necessity. But there is another who, although he is feigned to be a minister of the king, is not so in reality: namely, a merchant or money-changer who receives at interest from elsewhere so that he may grant it to the king under the same or greater interest. For example: Peter receives from Paul and from John, etc., and gives to the king: therefore the king does not exchange with Paul or John, but with Peter, who becomes the owner of the money. This man, therefore, becomes a "disguised" minister of the king, since he performs the office of a money-changer: and therefore to receive at interest is a sin for him: not only because he does so without his own personal necessity, but because he receives for an illicit use; and likewise to grant those things to the king under usury is for him another new sin of usury. This becomes even clearer from another of their practices. For they say that by the same reasoning they can seek out money from elsewhere under interest to give to the king, they can also give their own property. They do this, therefore, not in the name of another, but in their own name. Wherefore, regarding these men, if they make usurious exchanges, they are truly usurers without any doubt. <margin>On exchange brokers.</margin> ¶ Concerning the **brokers** <term>proxenetis: middlemen or agents who negotiate prices between parties</term> of exchanges—that is, those running between parties and setting the prices for exchanges—I do not doubt that they are ministers of usury to such an extent that they are rolled into the same vice: although those who are **factors** <term>factores: business agents or managers acting on behalf of a merchant</term> for money-changers and make exchanges in their name are worse. ¶ Concerning these factors, therefore, who make exchanges in the name of others, there is great reason for doubting when and how they are held to **restitution** <term>restitutio: the moral and legal requirement to return ill-gotten gains to the rightful owner</term>. To which, therefore, at the conclusion of this dispute, it is worthwhile to respond according to our understanding. And indeed, if they knowingly and prudently make usurious exchanges, they are undoubtedly held to restitution: and this by reason of the acceptance, which is a sin for them, even while they have acquired no profit for themselves. If, however, they do so ignorantly and in good faith: believing the exchanges to be lawful, to the extent that (if it can happen) they are free from all fault, it is clear they are not held by reason of the acceptance: however, they seem to be held by reason of the thing accepted, when they later learn of the inequity of the exchanges. At the very least, they are held without a doubt when some profit remains with them. If, however, absolutely no profit has come to them, they are held in the first place to very diligently see to it that those in whose name they made the exchanges make restitution. <margin>Doubt.</margin> ¶ If, however, they cannot achieve this, then

### Question VI of the Seventh Book

<margin>
The first argument from the negative side.
</margin>
...at that point, it is most deservedly doubted whether these same agents are bound to make **restitution** <term>restitutio: the act of restoring something to its rightful owner or making amends for a loss</term>. Nor is this doubt easily solved. Indeed, an argument can be built—showing they are in no way bound—from those foundations which we established in Book 4 under the title of Restitution.

For the bond of restitution arises from no other source than one of two heads: namely, either by reason of the *taking* of the thing, or by reason of the *thing received*. However, a person who committed no fault at all in the act of taking is not bound by reason of the taking, except in a **loan** <term>mutuum: a loan of money or goods that are consumed by use, requiring the return of an equivalent amount</term> and similar cases where they promised to return it. This is evident in both branches of law <note>meaning both Roman Civil Law and Church Canon Law</note>: for the entire **Aquilian Law** <term>Lex Aquilia: a Roman law that provided compensation to owners of property injured by another's fault</term>, which was written concerning injury and damage caused, gives no legal action to anyone except against the person who was at fault. Furthermore, in the Canon Law regarding injury and damage caused, the canon *Si Culpa* <note>Latin: "If by fault"</note> does not say "if it was caused by your case," but "if the damage was given by your **fault**." Hence, neither in practice nor in the external courts of judgment is anyone condemned for damage or injury unless they were at fault, at least in the slightest degree. To this is added what we said above: that if someone receives a 
<margin>
Argument 2.
</margin>

<column-break/>

portion of stolen goods as a gift from a thief, which they then consume without becoming any wealthier because of it, they are in no way bound to pay it back. Therefore, these **agents** <term>factores: business representatives or middle-men acting on behalf of a merchant</term> are not bound by reason of the taking, nor does it appear they are bound by reason of the thing received, since no profit at all reached them. These arguments would certainly prove the negative side, were it not for the fact that **ignorance of the law** never, or hardly ever, provides a full excuse, unless the person is uneducated or the law is extremely hidden and complex. However, the practice of **currency exchanges** <term>cambium: the business of trading different currencies, often used as a cover for usury (charging interest)</term> has such a bad reputation publicly that no one can shield themselves with the excuse of ignorance, unless they consult experts in good faith—and indeed, the most learned men of high reputation. For everyone cries out that this is a most dangerous art. Therefore, I would not dare to excuse these men entirely, at least not from the whole debt. But if they are able to pay, they are bound to meet with the creditors and reach a settlement with them, so that they pay something, while something else is forgiven them.
<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>

# BOOK EIGHT
## On Justice and Law.
### QUESTION ONE,
#### On the substance of a vow.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 88.<-

### ARTICLE 1.
#### Whether a Vow is possible regarding something to which we were not bound by the force of a commandment.

<image-desc>A large, square decorative woodcut initial 'H' containing a scene of a person, possibly a scholar or saint, seated in a landscape.</image-desc>
HITHERTO we have spoken of justice and injustice, and their **subjective parts** <term>subjective parts: the specific types or species that fall directly under a general category</term>—that is, the specific kinds of virtues that fall under this general category of justice. From this point forward, we shall speak of its **potential parts** <term>potential parts: annexed virtues that share some characteristics with a main virtue but lack its full technical definition</term>. A "potential part" refers to a virtue which, while not a direct species of justice because it does not align with it in every respect, is nevertheless reduced to it as if to a head category because of something they both share. For example: the absolute definition of justice encompasses three things. First, it exists between **one person and another**; second, it concerns a **debt**; and third, it establishes **equality** between what is paid and what is owed. Now, **liberality** <note>original: "liberalitas"; the virtue of being generous with one's wealth</note>, although it does not concern a strict legal debt, is nonetheless directed toward another person upon whom a benefit is conferred. For this reason, although it is not a species of justice, it is reduced to it as a potential part. However, the virtue of **religion**, which exists between us and God, does indeed concern the debt of reverence and service which we owe Him. Yet, because we cannot render an **equal** return to God—as He is our Creator—as Aristotle notes in the 5th book of the *Ethics* <margin>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 5</margin>, it falls short of the true definition of justice. Therefore, it is reduced to justice, even though the nature of its object <note>God</note> is far more excellent than that of human justice. Regarding liberality and mercy, and others of that kind which are more distant from justice, we have decided to treat nothing in the present work. Instead, we shall treat **religion**. Nor shall we speak of all its

<column-break/>

parts, for that would cause the work to grow to an immense size. We shall speak only of those things which have a closer affinity with justice: namely, the **vow**, since fulfilling it pertains to **faith** <note>original: "fidem"; here meaning "keeping one's word" or "fidelity"</note>, which is the foundation of justice; and regarding **tithes** and **simony** <term>simony: the act of buying or selling sacred things, such as church offices or sacraments</term>, which (except for the difference in subject matter) is very similar to usury and is a sacrilegious species of injustice; and finally, regarding those things which people in turn owe—especially bishops, both to the people and to the churches—both in **alms** and in **residency** <note>the legal and moral requirement for a bishop to live in his assigned diocese</note>. ¶ This present eighth book, therefore, will be occupied with a discourse on the vow. Nor should it be held against us as a fault that we do not follow the order of Saint Thomas in every way. For not only is the treatise on tithes related to the dispute over Simony (which follows the discourse on the vow), but also because the consideration of a **voluntary promise** <note>the vow</note> precedes the consideration of the obligation to pay what is owed. In this eighth book, we have decided to deal with the vow by which something is promised to God voluntarily, and in the following book, with the offerings and tithes that are owed to Him. ¶ And for that reason, we propose this article immediately at the front: **Whether a vow is possible regarding something which we did not previously owe by force of a commandment.** For if there is nothing that is not already owed to God by the force of a commandment, the religious practice of vowing is useless. And the argument is made from the negative side: We can
<margin>The first argument.</margin>
present nothing to God that is not already owed by us through the requirement of the commandment to "love Him above all things." Therefore, it is vain to vow anything. The premise is proved: we are bound to love Him with our whole heart, with our whole mind, and with all our strength <note>original: "ex toto corde, ex tota mente, & ex totis viribus"</note>; therefore, there is nothing that we do not owe Him by virtue of this greatest commandment. ¶ Second: He created us from nothing, and by His mercy He feeds and sustains us; therefore, whatever we are, and indeed whatever we are able to do, we owe to Him. In fact, as even the Philosopher
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle himself acknowledged in the 5th book of the *Physics* <note>The text cites the *Physics*, though this point on "repaying God" is a famous theme from his *Ethics*</note>, we can repay Him nothing equal for the benefits we have received; therefore, we can promise Him nothing that is not otherwise already owed. ¶ On the contrary side, however, all of Holy Scripture cries out, as in Deuteronomy 23: *When you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay in fulfilling it*; and Psalm 75: *Make vows and fulfill them to the Lord your God.*

<summary>This page introduces Book 8, transitioning from commercial justice to the "potential parts" of justice, specifically the virtue of religion. It begins an inquiry into the nature of vows, debating whether a person can truly vow to do something "extra" for God when humans technically owe God everything by virtue of creation and the commandment of love.</summary>

#### Book Eight, Question 1. 613

This minor question, although unusual for the Schoolmen <term>Schoolmen: the Scholastic philosophers and theologians of the medieval and early modern universities</term>, which we touched upon superficially at the end of the second book, we have placed at the very entrance of this entire discussion of ours, so that we might confront the Lutherans who contend that this religion of taking vows is futile and fabricated. Regarding this matter, we brought them to judgment in Book 3, *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 2.

<margin>Luther.</margin>
Luther, I say, in his condemned work *On Monastic Vows*, strives to demolish this ecclesiastical custom: because, he says, it is a thing without the authority or example of Scripture, and a mere and ruinous human invention. Listen to the monk [Luther], with what force he vomits out against his own institution: and later the Lutherans took care to confirm this in their dogmas. For

<margin>Wycliffe.</margin>
Luther was a faithful and shameless reviver of all the heresies of Wycliffe. He indeed had attempted this effort before. Against

<margin>Thomas Walden.</margin>
whom the most celebrated Thomas Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), a prominent English Carmelite who wrote against Wycliffe</note>, in volume 5 of *On Sacramentals*, title 9, chapters 83 and 84, discussed this matter most learnedly and richly. But to omit others, the reason and origin of this error, as we explained in the place cited,

<margin>The twin source from which Luther drew his past error.</margin>
Luther derived from two sources. The first was that he thought by the commandment to love God above all things, we are bound to offer Him all works and duties we can perform: as we said in the first argument. Whence he immediately inferred, not only that there is no work which is not by its nature a commandment, but that mortals in this life can in no way sufficiently fulfill that commandment. Therefore, he says that anyone, however just, fails in all works, as he asserts in Articles 31 and 32 to Leo <note>A reference to Luther's response to the Papal Bull *Exsurge Domine* issued by Pope Leo X</note>. Since he thought this "mode of love" <note>original: "dilectionis modum"</note> was included in every commandment—and since we cannot apply this mode in proportion to the commandment—we fail in every work. Yet, he says, it is the mercy of God that He does not impute this same omission to us. From this, they infer for themselves that there is no "work of supererogation" <term>supererogation: works done beyond what is required by God's commandments, such as the voluntary poverty of a monk</term> which could be the specific matter of a vow. The other foul source of these men was that the works of the just must be done most freely: whereas a vow introduces necessity and consequently hinders freedom. But the error of this second head will be shown in the following question. We have, however, already fought against the first in the place cited. Truly, we

<margin>The Author in the book *On Nature and Grace*. Reasoning.</margin>
showed how they persist in that blasphemy: that God binds us to the impossible. This refutation, however, is not relevant to the present. But we have mentioned this error for this reason,

<column-break/>

so that we might reveal the root from which they derive those blasphemies against us: namely, that we distinguish "counsels" from "commandments," while they believe all things are included in commandments. Likewise, that we think there are some works of supererogation through which men, and we monks especially, boast of making "satisfaction" <note>original: "satisfacere"; the performance of penance to repair the harm caused by sin</note>—not only for our own sins, but for the sins of others—regarding which works of supererogation we issue vows. Yet this heresy was condemned against the Pelagians <term>Pelagians: followers of Pelagius who believed humans could achieve salvation through their own efforts without divine grace</term>, as Augustine relates in his

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
letter to Paulinus. There, among their ten errors, he identifies the fifth as the claim that baptized wealthy people were bound to renounce all their riches.

<margin>Catholic Conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the question is answered with a Catholic conclusion. Beyond the works of the commandments, there remain other non-obligatory works which it is just to vow, and this is a celebrated duty of religion. This conclusion is established both by frequent testimonies of both Testaments and also by the most abundant examples of the saints, and consequently by inescapable reason. For we have already begun to cite the oracles of the Old Law from Deuteronomy

<margin>First proof.</margin>
23, and from Psalm 75. There also exists the law in Numbers 6: "A man or woman, when they have made a vow to be sanctified, and wish to consecrate themselves to the Lord, shall abstain from wine and everything that can inebriate." <note>Numbers 6:2-3</note>. And Ecclesiastes 5: "If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it." <note>Eccl 5:3</note>. And Proverbs 20: "It is

<margin><insert>remove the first [rashly]</insert></margin>
ruin for a man to vow holy things <note>original: "denotare sanctos"; a common Vulgate reading meaning to rashly dedicate things to God</note> and after the vows to retract." <note>Proverbs 20:25</note>. Nor do they protect themselves sufficiently from these arrows with that shield—that the Old Law has long been antiquated with its commandments—for these things are not found among the ceremonial or judicial laws which have been abolished, but clearly among the moral laws which endure by the law of nature. Indeed, so that the blindness of these men may be more openly perceived, the custom of the Gentiles is a most abundant testimony that this religion of vowing is founded on the very law of nature. Truly, it was always a solemn custom everywhere on earth to name vows to their temples both in times of trouble and for joyful victories. Whence Livy says in Book 1: "Tullus, in a time of peril, vowed twelve Salii <term>Salii: a college of Roman priests dedicated to Mars</term>, and shrines to Pallor and Panic." And the Psalmist foresaw the Gospel law when he said: "Immolate to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High." <note>Psalm 49:14 in the Vulgate, 50:14 in modern Bibles</note>. For the "sacrifice of praise" is our most holy banquet [the Eucharist], to which he joined the paying of vows.

<margin>Second proof.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, the examples of the fathers endure forever so that we may imitate them. Of Jacob, it is read in Genesis 28 that he vowed a vow to God. And of Hannah, the mother of Samuel, in 1 Samuel 1. And to remain silent about the rest, from that passage in Luke 1. Because...

# Friar Dominicus Soto, On Justice and Right

...“since I know not a man.” <note>original: *quoniam virum non cognofco*; Luke 1:34</note> From this, it is clearly gathered
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
that the most holy Virgin had taken a vow, as Augustine asserts in his book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*; this is also cited in the Canon Law <note>27. q. 2. can. *fufficiat*</note>. And in the New Law, we read of Paul in Acts 18 that he had his head shorn at Cenchreae because he had taken a vow. Furthermore, in the Gospel of Matthew 19, it is evident that the institution of vows was most approved by Christ. For He says, first, that there are eunuchs who have made themselves such—that is, by their own will without the bond of law—for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. And lest this be thought a commandment, as the Lutherans might imagine, He adds: “Let him who can accept it, accept it.” <note>original: *Qui potest capere capiat*</note> Following this example, Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7: “Concerning virgins, I have no commandment, but I give counsel.” Next follows the story of the young man who, questioning Christ on what he should do to have eternal life, received the answer that he should keep the commandments. To him, who said in turn that he had kept them all from his youth, Christ replied: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all you have and give to the poor, and follow me.” Here, Christ clearly distinguished the state of perfection from the matter of the commandments. For He said first: “If you wish to enter into life,” as if speaking of a necessary thing. Therefore, as read in Mark 10, after the young man replied that he had kept all these, Christ, looking upon him, loved him. From this, it follows
<margin>Jerome. Origen.</margin>
that he had not lied, although Jerome and Origen seem to suggest the contrary. For this reason, the Lord, desiring to move him toward a more abundant fruit, showed him the summit of perfection, which stands out in the "counsels" <term>counsels: voluntary recommendations for spiritual perfection, such as poverty or celibacy, as opposed to "precepts" or mandatory laws</term> after the foundation of the commandments. Whereupon Peter, speaking in the name of all the Apostles, immediately adds: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” Regarding this
<margin>Augustine</margin>
passage, Augustine says in Book 17 of *The City of God*, chapter 4: “The most powerful had vowed this vow,” according to that verse in 1 Samuel 2: “Giving a vow to the one who vows.” It is certain, therefore, that the Apostles consecrated themselves to the service of Christ by a vow. However, it is not necessary to discuss these matters more fully in this present place; they will return to mind in Question 5 under the title *On the Vow of Religion*. But it was expedient to reveal the reason immediately in the entrance of this book as to why the subject of vowing lies open to many things outside the commandments, which are not owed by law.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ The reason for this conclusion, drawn from a principle contrary to that which the Lutherans rely upon, is this: There exist many works to which no commandment compels us, and many other things from which the prohibition of the law does not restrain us; therefore, by a vow, we can both bind ourselves to the former and restrain ourselves from the latter. This premise is proven:

<column-break/>

God, in His supreme providence when issuing the laws by which He would compel us, did not look only to what we owed Him by the benefit of creation, and what He could demand from us by His absolute authority. Rather, since He disposes all things "sweetly" according to each person’s condition, He looked precisely to what all mortals were capable of performing according to our weak nature. For the law ought to bind all equally, and especially to that which was necessary both for His worship and for our mutual charity. This, however, is not whatever any single individual might be able to achieve with all his strength, but specifically those things contained in the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note> and those which are attached to them as if implied therein. Therefore, all other things are placed in our liberty, whether we wish to do them or not.
<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
¶ And this is more clearly confirmed. God, the author of nature, has enacted nothing for us beyond the decrees of the Sacraments other than what nature itself would have commanded. But nature does not bind all people so that each person must do as much as they possibly can; therefore, neither does God. Otherwise, He would not bind all equally by His laws, since not everyone is equally capable. It is, therefore, nothing less than insanity to think of God as those men [the Lutherans] preach. Let us conclude, then, that many things are arbitrary and free for us outside the line of the commandments, which may serve as the matter for our vows. Add to this that the matter of vows—as will be clear a little further down—consists not only of works of "counsel" but also of "precepts." But thus far we have spoken of that specific matter which becomes owed only by the obligation of a vow.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**T**o the first argument to the contrary, then, we deny that all works which any person can perform are folded into that greatest commandment of love. Rather, it is enough to love God with all one’s mind, soul, and strength in such a way that we admit nothing contrary to that love; which, indeed, we can fulfill in this life through the favor and help of God. For as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>
<margin>D. Thomas.</margin>
teaches in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 44, article 6, this commandment can be fulfilled in two ways. In one way, perfectly: namely, when one arrives at the end which God intends, which is surely that man joins himself to Him in every way by love, so that he can neither sin venially <term>venial sin: a lesser, pardonable sin that does not break one's relationship with God</term> nor admit any other love. And this will happen in the homeland <note>Heaven</note> when, according to the word of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15, “God will be all in all.” Hence Augustine says in the book *On the Perfection of Justice*: “That commandment will be fulfilled by that
<margin>Augustine</margin>
fullness of charity in the homeland: You shall love the Lord your God with all...”

He refutes the Lutheran claim that the commandment to love God with all one's strength makes all possible good works mandatory, arguing that perfect love is only achieved in heaven.</summary>

...with all your heart. But in another way it is fulfilled imperfectly: namely, when even if one does not reach the goal, one does not depart from the rule that leads there. And in this way it is fulfilled in this life <note>original: *in via*; literally "on the way," referring to the earthly journey toward heaven</note>. Wherefore this fulfillment is not called imperfect because it is not sufficient to avoid fault, but because through it we do not attain the end. Whence the same Augustine in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 26, distinguishes between the militant life <note>The Church on earth</note> and the triumphant life <note>The Church in heaven</note> thus: that for the justice of this life, which is prescribed by that commandment of love, it is enough not to sin. "Nor," he says, "is it to be counted as a fault that there cannot yet be such love of God here as there will be when He is seen by us."
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
To the second argument, however, it is replied that although whatever we are, we are the handiwork of God, yet not everything we do is owed to Him by virtue of a commandment; for He has measured His laws according to the weakness of our nature.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether a Vow is perfected in the purpose of the will alone.<-

Having supposed that a vow is possible because of free matter <note>Soto refers to actions that are not already mandatory by divine law, such as specific fasts or pilgrimages</note> which remains outside the obligation of the commandments, we ask about its substance, which becomes known through its definition. But according to the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> order, the first investigation is concerning the genus <note>The general category</note>, and thereafter the form of the definition; the second is concerning the matter. The first is explored in this article, and the second in the following one. Since it is very well established that a vow is a human action, it is asked of which power it is an act: namely, whether it is a purpose of the will, or rather a promise of the intellect. And it is argued that it is a purpose.
<margin>First argument.</margin>
For the definition of a vow accepted by many is that it is the conception of a good purpose, strengthened by the deliberation of the mind, by which someone binds themselves to God to do or not do something. But a firm purpose of this kind is perfected by the movement of the will alone; therefore, a vow consists in such a purpose.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Secondly, the word itself shows the thing. For "vow" <note>original: *votum*</note> is named from "will" <note>original: *voluntas*</note>; for each person is said to do by their own vow what they do by will. Since, therefore, a promise is nothing but a work of reason, it follows that a vow consists in the will.
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Thirdly, a vow is perfected there from whence the obligation arises; for this is the 

<column-break/>

genuine power of a vow. But obligation arises from the purpose alone without any promise; therefore, a vow is completed there. The minor premise is proved: By the fact that someone puts their hand to the plow, they are bound to the work, according to that saying of Luke 9: "No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God." Namely, because he breaks the obligation. But by the fact that someone proposes a work, they put their hand to the plow; therefore, the obligation is made there, and thus the vow.
¶ On the contrary is that of Ecclesiastes 5: "If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to pay it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him." Where what was first named a "vow" is immediately called a "promise"; in which, therefore, its substance is placed.

---

<margin>First meaning of 'vow'.</margin>
For the clarification of the question, this must first be noted about the name, which is celebrated among the Latins, and that it has a double meaning. For there is the noun of that verb which is "to vow" <note>original: *vouere*</note>; this is to promise—not to just anyone, but to God or the saints. For to promise, to pledge, and to guarantee are common words for promises made either to God or to men; but "to vow" signifies precisely that which is made to God. For a vow is, as will be clear in what follows, a promise of religion, and a virtue by which we serve God alone and His saints. Whence Cicero to Atticus:
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
"I think myself bound by a greater religion than anyone ever was by any vow." Wherefore, to "pronounce vows" <note>original: *vota nuncupare*</note> is to promise aloud to the gods and to designate something for a happy outcome of affairs.
<margin>Second meaning.</margin>
But because we greatly desire that which we ask from God through vows—that is, through offered promises—it has come about through usage that the desire itself is called a vow. Whence we are said to be "masters of our vow" <note>original: *voti compotes*; meaning one has attained what they wished for</note> and we rejoice that things "succeed according to our vow" <note>original: *pro voto*</note> when we attain our desires. And "to make vows" is the same as to wish, to long for, and to pray. Here, however, the name is not used in this latter sense, but in the former; so that to vow is to send forth vows, and as it is said in Latin, "to undertake vows" <note>original: *vota suscipere*</note>; that is, to promise something holily to God.
¶ Having established these things, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first is:
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Three things are necessarily required for a vow. First, indeed, the deliberation of reason. Second, the purpose of the will. But thirdly, the promise in which the reason <note>the formal essence</note> of the vow is perfected.
<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is proved: A vow brings with it an obligation to do or avoid something. But an obligation that arises from one's own will (for it is otherwise with those that arise from law) is made by way of a promise; therefore...

<summary>This page explores the theological and linguistic definition of a vow, debating whether it is primarily an act of the will (a purpose) or an act of the intellect (a promise). Soto concludes that a vow requires deliberation, purpose, and a formal promise to God to be complete.</summary>
<keywords>vow, voluntas, obligation, promise, St. Augustine, Cicero, religious law, deliberation</keywords>

--- Page 620 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition and essential components of a vow. On the previous page, the author began defining a vow as a promise made to God, and he is now explaining how this promise is essentially an act of the mind and reason, rather than just words spoken aloud.</meta>

...a promise is no vow. The secondary point is proven thus. A man binds himself to another in no other way than by ordering himself toward that person and offering that to which he is bound: but "order" is a work of reason. Therefore, just as by commanding (which is an act of the virtue of **prudence**) a man orders and disposes what should be done by his servant, and by entreating <note>asking or praying</note> orders what should be done for him by a superior, so by promising he orders what he himself disposes to do for others. And thus the obligation, and subsequently the vow, consists in this act of reason. Now, a promise proceeds from a purpose of doing something; but as for a purpose, since it is an act of the deliberate will, a deliberation of the reason must come before it. Therefore, these three acts—deliberation, purpose, and promise—are necessary in order for a vow. Add to this that since an obligation emerges from a promise, it must be made known to the one to whom it is made. However, there is this gap between men and God: because another's mind does not become known to us except through words or external gestures, a man cannot promise anything to another man except by voice or signs. Whence it says in Proverbs 6: *You are ensnared by the words of your mouth.* But to God, to whom the innermost parts of hearts lie open—according to that passage in 1 Samuel 16: *Men see those things that appear, but God looks at the heart*—a promise can be made through the speech of the mind alone. From this it follows that if you look at the essence and necessity of a vow, it is completed in the intellect without any spoken voice.

<margin>The final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion. Two other things are sometimes added to a vow, which are accidental to it <note>meaning they are not required for the vow to be valid, but are often present</note>. Nevertheless, they pertain to its more expressive firmness. For instance, the external pronunciation of the mouth: according to that Psalm: *I will pay you my vows which my lips have uttered.* These words are not necessary with respect to God, but with respect to ourselves; just like vocal prayer, they serve to awaken our souls and rouse the eyes of the mind toward God. Secondly, the testimony of others is also often called upon, so that not only the fear of God but also human shame may make us firmer, lest we break the faith of our vow.

<margin>The Master of the Sentences.</margin>
To which the "Master of the Sentences" <note>Peter Lombard, whose *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages</note> perhaps alluded in Book 4, Distinction 38, where he says that a vow is a certain "testification of a spontaneous promise," which ought to be made to God and concerning those things that belong to God. Although he perhaps also speaks of internal testification, by which a man witnesses to himself that he is a debtor to God. ¶ But truly, although these things are clear, they nevertheless require a little more light.

<margin>A teaching from Aristotle.</margin>
In the first place, regarding the three acts of the prior conclusion, it must be recalled from the *Philosopher* <note>Aristotle</note> in the *Ethics*, Book 6, chapters 9 and 10, that there are three acts of prudence: namely, to take counsel, to judge (or pass sentence), and thirdly, to com-

<column-break/>

mand. For, once we have an intention toward a goal that proceeds from moral virtue—for example, "one must live temperately"—the will uses the intellect to deliberate about the means. This involves comparing the difficulties found in the religious life with those found in marriage; and that comparison of means is "counsel." Once the means are found, a judgment is made through *synesis* <note>original: *syneſin*; Greek for "good sense" or "insight"</note>, which is the approval of the better and more convenient means. Therefore, when "deliberation" is mentioned, both are included: the counsel and the judgment. And this is the proper foundation of a vow.

<margin>A question about the maturity of deliberation.</margin>
¶ However, it remains to investigate how much "maturity" this kind of deliberation must have. Must everything be deliberated upon through counsel before a vow binds—specifically things whose ignorance might have restrained the man from vowing? For this appears to be the opinion of certain legal experts, among whose group Richard

<margin>Richard of Middleton.</margin>
of Middleton seems to be, in Book 4, Distinction 38, Article 1. There he says that where there is not "full deliberation," even if it is "half-full," no

<margin>Richard's motive.</margin>
binding of a vow arises from it. And the argument for this opinion is: A vow, since it is named from the "will" <note>votum / voluntas</note>, ought to be spontaneous and voluntary; but ignorance takes away the voluntary nature of an act. Therefore, where all things are not fully weighed, there is not full freedom, and thus no vow.

<margin>Another reason for the same.</margin>
Secondly: These vows are broken just as easily as they are made; therefore they are dangerous and cannot turn out well. Thus, it is safer to consider them void. For this reason, there are those who say (as reported by Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, a Dominican theologian</note> under the word "vow," section 2, paragraph 13) that a person who is angry or "well-drunk" <note>original: *bene potatus*; intoxicated</note> who vows or swears to enter a religious order is not bound; because what is done in the heat of anger ought to be treated as if it were not done. ¶ Despite these points, I believe we should agree with Pierre de la Palud in Book 4, Distinction 38, Question 1, and with Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note> on the present article: that "full deliberation" is required for a vow. However, "fullness" of deliberation can be understood in two ways. In one way, it is opposed to "surreption"—that is, to a sudden movement, whether it be purely natural (which is called "first-first," where there is no capacity for fault or merit) or "second-first" <note>Scholastic technical terms for degrees of involuntary or semi-conscious impulses</note> in which there can only be a venial <note>minor</note> sin. Such fullness of deliberation *is* necessary for a vow. In another way, "full deliberation" is that in which nothing that *could* have been deliberated is omitted; this is certainly *not* necessary.

<margin>Proof of the recent opinion.</margin>
The first part is proven: A vow must not only be spontaneous, but so deliberated that it binds under the penalty of mortal sin <note>a grave sin that separates the soul from God</note>. But a "first-first" movement is in no way voluntary; and a "second-first" movement, which is without full attention, [is not sufficient...]

<summary>Soto explains that the essence of a vow is an internal act of reason and will made before God, though spoken words and witnesses help human resolve. He debates the level of deliberation required for a vow to be valid, concluding that while a person must be conscious and intentional, they do not need to have considered every possible detail or consequence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the mental requirements for a valid vow. On the previous page, the author established that a vow is essentially an act of reason and intellect. Now, he addresses the specific degree of deliberation required—whether a "sudden" vow made in a moment of crisis carries the same weight as one made after long reflection.</meta>

### Eighth Book, Question I.

<margin>First proof for the other side.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
<margin>Third.</margin>
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
...cannot be a mortal sin <note>A grave sin that separates a soul from God’s grace.</note>: therefore, such an act of the will does not suffice for the obligation of a vow, since a vow binds a person under the penalty of mortal sin. This "full deliberation" consists in a person knowing by their own judgment what they are doing. This is confirmed: a vow is not broken by a sudden impulse where there can only be a venial sin <note>A lesser, pardonable sin that does not break one's relationship with God.</note>; therefore, it is not established by such an impulse either. However, the latter part is proven by a contrary reason. For the bond of a vow, it is enough that it be a spontaneous work; but prior deliberation is sufficient for this—namely, judging what you are doing—therefore, a subsequent or long-term deliberation is not required. Secondly, this is confirmed: such a promise made to a human being would be binding—for example, if by that same judgment you promised money or pledged yourself to a wife—therefore, it also binds in respect to God. For God is not more lenient in demanding promises than a human being is. Thirdly, that prior deliberation is sufficient for merit <note>A good deed deserving of spiritual reward.</note> and for mortal sin; therefore, it is sufficient for the obligation of a vow. Indeed, if someone placed in sudden danger of death should undertake a vow for a good thing, they earn merit, and this is only through the virtue of religion; therefore, such an undertaking of a vow is truly a vow. Likewise, if it were for an illicit thing, it would be a lethal crime; therefore, while the subject matter is proper, the obligation of the vow emerges under the threat of mortal guilt. Fourthly, if a member of a religious order, using that same judgment and deliberation (which is the opposite of a "surreptitious" or unintended impulse), were to act against their vow, they would be violating and breaking it; therefore, the same level of deliberation is sufficient to confirm a vow.

<margin>The deceptive rule of the *Summa Angelica*.</margin>
¶ Let us conclude, then, that if someone—driven by anger, or heat, or fear of death—were to emit a vow that took away the judgment of reason, they would not be bound. However, where that light of reason persists, which can create either merit or a mortal offense, the vow is binding. For that reason, the Rule found in the *Angelus* <note>original: "apud Angelum"; referring to the *Summa Angelica*, a famous 15th-century handbook for confessors by Angelus Carletus de Clavasio.</note> under the word "vow" for weighing whether a sudden vow was valid is deceptive. It suggests that if, once the distress of the danger has passed, the one who vowed regrets the deed—or, as he says, is "ill-content"—it is a sign the vow does not hold. I say this rule fails gravely. For even if you deliberate for a long time, you can still grow weary of the deed after it is done.

¶ Furthermore, this conclusion is supported by canonical authority, such as in the chapter "Sic Nos" <note>original: "cap. sic nobis. de regula"</note> regarding the Rule, where a cleric who vowed to enter a religious order while suffering from excessive illness is compelled to receive the habit. And in the 17th Question, 4th Canon, "Sunt qui opes," even those who bestowed perpetual wealth upon the Church by a tumultuous impulse of the mind rather than by judgment are rebuked for the levity of their vow—and nevertheless

<column-break/>

<margin>An adjustment of the aforementioned opinion. Panormitanus.</margin>
they are held as sacrilegious if they revoke those gifts. ¶ However, I would add this temperament <note>A moderating qualification or adjustment.</note> to this opinion: that such vows, undertaken with sudden deliberation, bring with them a just cause for a dispensation <note>An official release from a legal or religious obligation.</note>. This is what Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as "The Sicilian" (Panormitanus).</note> learnedly advised regarding the chapter "Veniens" on vows and the redemption of vows. Indeed, that very chapter clearly teaches this. Yet, I would not overlook this warning: where you name a vow to God so that He might rescue you from present danger—whether at sea, in bed, or elsewhere—if you are afterwards safe, you surely act wickedly and unfaithfully by procuring a dispensation. For although sudden deliberation may allow it, the cause of the vowing and the benefit received convict you of ingratitude.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Therefore, in response to the first of the arguments to the contrary: when someone knows what they are doing by the judgment of reason, it sufficiently clears away the ignorance that would remove the "voluntary" nature of the act, even if they do not consider everything that could possibly be considered. The solution is confirmed by this: the labors and difficulties present in a religious life are never sufficiently perceived without experience. Therefore, if every single thing had to be weighed, no simple vow to enter a religious order would be binding without prior experience of the life.

<margin>A scruple.</margin>
<margin>The solution.</margin>
¶ But you might ask: what if someone deceived you, asserting that in such a religious order the choice of foods is not restricted, nor are there fasts, or anything else difficult—which, if you had known beforehand, you would never have vowed? When you vow having been so seduced, are you subject to the yoke? The answer is that if the deception concerns things you could not bear, the vow is not binding, because it is a grave injury. The sign of this is the "year of probation" <note>A trial period, like a novitiate, before permanent vows are taken.</note>, in which the law intends for you to weigh the gravity of the matter. But if the deception concerns other, more minor things, you are nonetheless bound. In the same way, if someone deceived a peasant, saying that Jerusalem could be reached without sailing, or that Rome was not far away when it is very far, and for that reason he vowed a pilgrimage, the vow would not hold. It would be otherwise if the person merely claimed the beauty of the roads was greater than it truly is. Here it might seem to some that one should speak immediately of fear and force, which remove the voluntary nature; however, since the discussion here is only about deliberation (by which ignorance is avoided), it will be more convenient to treat fear in the following question under the title of the obligation of a vow.

¶ There follows, then, the second act, which is the "purpose of the will." For no one can doubt that this is necessary for a vow. Since...

It also examines how deception regarding the difficulty of a task (like joining a monastery) can invalidate a vow if the deception involves something the person cannot physically or mentally bear.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law.

<columns>

...outside an act of the will there can be no voluntary promise, and thus no obligatory vow. Therefore, after deliberation, which occurs in the intellect, a **purpose** <note>Latin: *propositum*; the internal resolve to act.</note> is necessary in the will: that is, the choice and consent by which the will proposes to act according to the judgment of the deliberation.

<margin>*Argument*</margin>
¶ However, it is argued that this purpose is not necessary, but that a promise alone suffices. For when someone promises or swears anything to either God or a human being, even if they do not **propose** to keep the promise, they are still bound; since by the very nature of a promise, the faith of the promiser remains restricted.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
It is answered that a promise happens in three different ways. **One way** is when someone proposes both to make the promise and also to keep the promise. Regarding this, there is no doubt whatsoever that it is obligatory. In this case, the deliberation, the purpose, and the promise all concern the work itself: namely, when you have deliberated upon, purposed, and promised the work. Regarding this, Saint Thomas says: *A promise proceeds from the purpose of doing.*

Another way is through the opposite extreme: namely, when someone intends neither to do what they promise, nor even to promise what they say, but rather to trifle or to deceive. Therefore, regarding this case, there is no doubt; it is certain that such a promise does not bind before God, because a promise is a sign of a purpose and an intention—and when it lacks these, it is empty.

Nevertheless, in the **external forum** <note>Latin: *foro exteriori*; the public legal sphere of the Church or State, as opposed to the "internal forum" of a person's conscience before God.</note>, whether Ecclesiastical or Civil, and whether the promise is made to God or man, the person so vowing or promising is compelled to keep their word, because the Church does not judge internal matters. Otherwise, if everyone who claimed they had no purpose of binding themselves had to be heard, the commonwealth would immediately go to ruin. For everyone would contend that they were not a monk, or that they had not contracted a marriage. Therefore, it is required that whoever thinks to use this as an excuse before a judge's tribunal must prove it legitimately.

<margin>*Question.*</margin>
¶ But is a person who has uttered such a vow in words only, or who has contracted a marriage, bound to obey the sentence of the court?

<margin>*Cajetan’s Solution.*</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> answers here that the person is bound by reason of the Church and the risk of **scandal** <note>In a theological sense, "scandal" refers to an action that leads others into sin or confusion about the truth.</note>. However, this opinion must be taken with a grain of salt. For if that which is commanded cannot be done lawfully—furthermore, because it is intrinsically evil—that person ought to suffer death rather than obey. For example, if someone after a secret marriage <note>A "clandestine" marriage performed without public witnesses.</note> contracted a second marriage publicly: even if they are compelled in the external

<column-break/>

forum to fulfill their marital debt, they cannot obey. For they would be a fornicator. If, however, the act can be done lawfully—such as a "fake" monk being forced to live in a convent and wear the habit—then he is bound to comply when he cannot escape without causing scandal. For if he could steal away and take himself to another province where, because he was not known, he could live exempt from the sentence without scandal, he would not be bound to submit to a sentence founded on a false presumption.

¶ **Thirdly**, in a middle way between these, someone can utter a vow intending to truly promise, yet not intending to keep the promise; or intending to swear, but not to keep the oath. This can indeed happen in the **military orders** <note>Latin: *militaribus religionibus*; such as the Knights Templar or Hospitallers, where men took religious vows but lived as soldiers.</note>, and in others where such vows are usually celebrated more for the sake of obtaining temporal goods than for religion. And regarding this vow, one might doubt in some way whether it is obligatory. For it seems to be the case that a purpose of *doing* did not precede it; and yet Saint Thomas says that an obligatory promise proceeds from the purpose of *doing*.

<margin>*He who vows with the intention of promising, but not of standing by it, remains truly bound. St. Thomas. Doubt. Solution.*</margin>
It is answered, nonetheless, that in this case there is a true obligation of the vow. For a promise, by its nature, gives birth to an obligation. Therefore, if it is "human"—that is, willed—it binds. Thus it follows that someone promising in this way sins gravely, because they do not propose to do that to which they are bound. It is similar for one who intends to swear an oath. He remains bound. Nor does Saint Thomas deny this. For he is only speaking of the **regular way** of vowing.

But what if someone proposes and intends to promise, or to swear, but nevertheless does not intend to **bind** himself? It would appear then that no obligation arises, since the obligation was not willed. Yet it is answered nonetheless that the obligation arises because it is a **natural effect** of the promise. And therefore it is sufficient that the *cause* was willed. For you cannot throw a noose over yourself without being ensnared.

<margin>*Question.*</margin>
¶ Next follows the discussion of the **promise** in which it was said the vow is perfected. Regarding this, it is asked whether a promise is necessary after the "purpose" for the obligation of the vow to exist.

<margin>*The opinion of the Jurisconsults.*</margin>
There are some among the **jurisconsults** <note>Legal scholars and experts in Canon or Civil law.</note> who, commenting on the chapter *Consulti* regarding monks, affirm that the purpose alone suffices without a promise, at least when the act has already begun. As when someone, with the purpose of remaining in religious life, puts on the habit: for that is the case in that chapter where whoever it was is commanded to be a member of the order. And it is argued in favor of this opinion, that...

</columns>

<summary>This page analyzes the internal mental state required for a vow to be binding, distinguishing between the internal "purpose" of the heart and the external "promise." Soto concludes that while God judges the heart, the law must hold people to their spoken words to prevent social and ecclesiastical chaos, using the "ensnaring noose" as a metaphor for how legal obligations naturally follow a voluntary promise.</summary>

# Question I of Book Eight

<margin>First argument for the previous opinion.</margin>
To clarify the nature of what is proposed: a purpose <note>Latin: *propositum*; a firm intention or internal resolve.</note> to do something is to have the mind applied to the work. Moreover, applying the mind appears to be the same thing as an obligation. Secondly:

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
A purpose to act is an affirmation about the future—"I shall do it." Therefore, one who does not act after forming such a purpose lies, since they make their own proposition false. Now, a lie in a grave matter is a mortal sin <note>A "mortal sin" is considered a serious offense in Catholic theology that separates the soul from God's grace.</note>; therefore, one who purposes to enter a religious order, go on a pilgrimage, or something similar, sins mortally if they do not do it, and is thus obligated to do it. This obligation is sufficient to constitute a vow.

<margin>Purpose is not enough for a vow.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, the answer is that a purpose is not sufficient for a vow; rather, a promise is necessary.

<margin>Proof 1.</margin>
First, this is clear from the most widely accepted definition of a vow. As cited from Ecclesiastes 5 <note>Ecclesiastes 5:4: "When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it."</note>, a vow is a promise. And the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1164), whose *Sentences* was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> says that a vow is the testimony of a spontaneous promise. Hence, to "name" or "declare" vows is to pledge something to God.

<margin>Second [Proof].</margin>
This is also confirmed by reason. A vow only exists in relation to another. However, the ordering of one person toward another, as Saint Thomas says, occurs only through the faculty of reason by which a person subjects and devotes themselves to another. Therefore, it is accomplished only through reason—just as commanding and praying are.

<margin>Third [Proof].</margin>
Thirdly, to touch upon the point precisely, a vow is that in which one’s "faith" <note>Latin: *fides*; here meaning "word of honor" or "fidelity."</note> is bound. As Cicero says in the first book of *On Duties*:

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
...faith is the foundation of justice. Faith, as both he and Augustine say, exists because "what is said is done" <note>Latin: *fides autem... est quia fit quod dicitur*. This is a classic medieval etymology of *fides* (faith/fidelity) as coming from *fiant* (let it be done) and *dicta* (what was said).</note>. Therefore, a vow has no force unless that which is to be done is spoken. To speak, however, is an act of the intellect. Therefore, the obligation consists in the promise, and not before then.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And this opinion is confirmed by the chapter *Literaturam* regarding vows and the redemption of vows <note>A reference to Canon Law, specifically the Decretals of Gregory IX.</note>. There, a certain man who, while sick, had said, "I shall not delay," purposing in his mind to enter a religious order, was absolved from the vow because he did not actually *promise*. These words are expressed in the chapter *Si bona* (17, question 1): it is one thing to conceive a purpose in the heart and even announce it with the mouth, and another to make oneself guilty of a vow through a subsequent obligation.

<margin>Gregory.</margin>
For this reason, Gregory there absolved the man who had the purpose without the promise. In Civil Law, too, an obligation arises from a formal pledge <note>Latin: *pollicitatio*; a unilateral promise made to a state or deity.</note>, as found in the Digest, *on pledges of service*.

<margin>Distinction between purpose and promise.</margin>
Hence, to solve the contrary argument, one must note the difference between a purpose and a promise. Because a purpose exists in the will, it is neither an affirmation nor a speech; rather, it is a consensus or a will that is expressed through 

<column-break/>

a simple affirmation of the intellect regarding the future—namely, "I shall do." This simple assertion does not carry the meaning "I promise to do," but is a simple affirmation of what someone is currently carrying in their mind. Therefore, it is not a lie, because to lie is "to go against one's mind" <note>Latin: *mentiri est contra mentem ire*; a standard medieval definition of lying.</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Regarding the form of the argument, then, it is denied that if someone who previously purposed something does not later do it, they are lying—even though they cause the original proposition to have been false. This is because they were able to change their purpose. Thus, although they said something false, they neither lied when they uttered it (because they then said what they intended to do), nor when they later acted to the contrary (because they were not bound not to change their purpose). A subsequent promise, however, so fixes the purpose and binds the soul to another that one cannot change it without a breach of faith and justice. Therefore, a promise is necessary. Nor is the contrary gathered from the chapter *Consulti sane*, which merely ordains that he who purposed to serve God by entering a religious order should persevere, either in the habit he took up or in another more relaxed one. For Innocent <note>Pope Innocent III.</note> speaks there in the customary way about a purpose strengthened by a promise.

¶ Finally, the last argument remains. A promise belongs to that part of "prudence" where command and petition reside, as we learned above from the words of Saint Thomas. However, the command and order of prudence precede "election" <note>Latin: *electio*; the act of choosing or deciding after deliberation.</note>, as Saint Thomas seems to feel.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
*Summa Theologica* II-II, question 47, article 8. Election, however, seems to be the same as the purpose of the will; therefore, the promise does not follow, but precedes the purpose.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note>, making a distinction here, responds: namely, that the "command" <note>Latin: *imperium*; the mental act of directing oneself or others to action.</note> by which one commands oneself precedes election. For after the deliberation of the intellect, it commands the will through prudence so that the will may choose. However, the command by which one commands others follows election, as do petition and promise.

<margin>Rejection of Cajetan's solution.</margin>
¶ But on the contrary, as I believe, stands the opinion of both Aristotle and Saint Thomas, and consequently the truth: namely, that the "command," whether regarding another or regarding the commander himself, always follows election. Indeed, immediately after deliberation, election follows. But after election, the work does not follow unless prudence, acting as the commander, applies the will to the task. For a command is not "Choose," but "Do." And so Saint Thomas says there that it consists in the application of things counseled and judged toward the act of working.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the definition of a vow, specifically clarifying that while a vow begins as an internal purpose, it only becomes a formal vow when it is expressed as a promise. # F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

Similarly, a promise follows from a purpose. ¶ From these points, if you wished to derive a definition of a vow that encompasses all types—the vain as well as the solid, the unjust as well as the legitimate—it would be enough to say that a vow is a promise made to God. However, that definition which applies only to a legitimate vow will be more conveniently established in the next article. ¶ Regarding the words of Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for this work.</note> while proving the prior conclusion, the reader may perhaps doubt whether a simple promise is binding, and whether an obligation arises among humans by a sole act of the intellect. But these matters will be more conveniently disputed in the following question when dealing with the obligation of a vow; furthermore, Saint Thomas touches upon this specifically elsewhere.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, then, it has already been denied that the conception of a purpose is sufficient without a promise. Therefore, those who say that a vow is the conception of a purpose strengthened by the soul’s deliberation mean "strengthened by a promise."

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, the answer is that a vow <note>Latin: *votum*.</note> is not named after the "will" <note>Latin: *voluntas*.</note> because it is an act of the will, but because it is born from the will’s purpose.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ And likewise to the third, it is denied that one is said to "put his hand to the plow" <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note> by a mere purpose alone. For to put one's hand is to move the soul toward the work, which does not happen except through a promise. Therefore, Christ says of the one who *promises* that if he looks back, he is not fit for the kingdom of heaven.

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether a Vow Must Always Concern a Greater Good.<-

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
In the preceding article, the genus and form of a vow were determined; it follows, therefore, to explore its "matter" <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "matter" refers to the specific subject or substance of an act.</note>. Specifically, whether it must always concern a "greater good," which they call a work of supererogation <note>Supererogation refers to performing more than what is strictly required by duty or command.</note>—namely, an obligation that does not fall under a command. And the argument is made for the negative side. Baptism, as the *Gloss* <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> says regarding that Psalm—"Make vows and fulfill them" <note>Psalm 76:11 (or 75:12 in the Vulgate): *Vovete et reddite*.</note>—is a vow; and yet it is a work of command. And Jacob is read in Genesis 28 to have vowed to the Lord that

<column-break/>

He would be a God to him; which is nonetheless a necessity for salvation. Therefore, a vow does not always concern a work of supererogation.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: Jephthah, as read in Judges 11, being bound by a vow, killed his daughter; whom Paul nevertheless numbers among the other saints in Romans 11 <note>Soto likely means Hebrews 11:32, where Jephthah is listed among the heroes of faith. The text cites Romans 11.</note>. <margin>Paul.</margin> And yet that act was not only not a "better" good, but was not even a "good" thing at all.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third, sometimes vows are emitted which result in harm to the person, such as when someone entangles themselves in a vow to afflict themselves with fasts and vigils that excessively drain their life. And sometimes they concern indifferent or useless things, such as when someone promises not to wash or comb their hair, or to set out on a journey on certain days. These are not "greater goods"; therefore, a "greater good" is not necessary for the obligation of a vow.

<margin>On the contrary.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is that passage in Deuteronomy 23: "If you refrain from vowing, you will be without sin." Here, the matter of a vow is designated as that which is not a command.

To this question, so that we may follow the order of Saint Thomas, we respond with five conclusions. For since a vow is clothed in many qualities, its matter must be weighed according to them. Therefore, among those things that can be thought of as subject to the virtue of vowing, some have a manifest reason why they cannot be offered to God as a vow; others, by contrast, have a manifest reason why their matter becomes licit; but there are others about which there is doubt. All of these generally fall into five categories. In the first grade are placed those things that are either adverse and contrary to God, or at least dissonant and hateful to Him—namely, sins, whether mortal or venial.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Regarding these, the first conclusion is established: No vow can be lawfully made concerning any illicit thing—for example, neither concerning murder, nor even the slightest lie.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is proved by the nature of a vow, which is a promise made to God. A promise concerns a thing which one intends to do for the sake of another; for this differs from a threat (which is its opposite) in that a threat concerns something injurious or harmful to the other. To promise another that you will kill him, or harm him in any way, is rather a threat. A promise, therefore, is only of a benefit. Sins, however, result in injury to God; therefore, he who would vow to kill or steal would be threatening God rather than promising Him.

<summary>This page discusses whether a vow must always be about a "greater good" (something beyond what is strictly commanded by God) and establishes that a vow cannot legally involve any sinful or illicit act.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into Article III: What constitutes the proper "matter" or subject of a vow. The author, Domingo de Soto, is systematically evaluating what kinds of actions can or cannot be the basis of a binding promise to God.</meta>

### Book Eight: Question I

Why such a vow <note>Referring to the previous page's discussion on vowing to do something sinful.</note> would not be binding. Indeed, to utter such a vow would be a sin, and to fulfill it later would be a greater crime.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Close to this is the second conclusion. **Regarding an indifferent matter**—namely, one that brings no benefit nor divine honor—**no religious vow can be made.** For example, if someone were to vow not to cut their nails on the Sabbath, or not to set out on a journey on a Tuesday.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is proved thus: since a vow ought to be made for the grace and honor of God, it is not proper to make one regarding something hateful to Him (which would be wicked), nor regarding something that is not acceptable to Him. Indeed, since such a thing does not result in glory for God, it is vain; furthermore, it is even superstitious when some divine power is believed to reside in those specific actions. ¶ Now, among those things which are neither contrary to God nor discordant with Him, some are either impossible or necessary, while others are contingent and placed within our own power.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Regarding the former category, the third conclusion is established: **A vow cannot be made concerning a thing that is either necessary or impossible.** For a person would be foolish who vowed either that they would die, or that they would never die. The first is necessary, while the second is impossible. It is the same as one who would vow either never to fly, or

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
that they would fly eventually. The reason for this conclusion is that a vow must not only be made of one’s own will, but must also proceed from **prudence** <note>Latin: *prudentia*; in scholastic thought, this is the virtue of making right decisions.</note>. Impossible and necessary things do not fall under our will; therefore, they cannot fall under the obligation of a vow. ¶ Of those things which are in our power and not opposed to God, some are necessary for salvation—namely, all works of the **precepts** <note>The Commandments and laws of the Church.</note>—while others are not. When you hear "necessary," extend the name also to those things whose opposites hinder us from the path of salvation. Thus, you should include not only the precepts that are strictly such—namely, those binding under the guilt of mortal sin—but also those which bind under venial sin.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Concerning these, the fourth conclusion is presented: **An act of precept, insofar as it is a necessity, is not the matter of a vow; however, it is so insofar as it is within our will.** For the matter

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
of a vow is that which becomes "due" by reason of the vow itself. Therefore, insofar as a work is already "due" by the obligation of the law, it does not fall under a vow, because its status as a debt does not depend on our will, but on the necessity of the law. But in truth, because the necessity of a precept is not "absolute necessity" (like that in the third conclusion, such as dying or not flying), but rather something we voluntarily fulfill

<column-break/>

or transgress, for this reason it can fall under a vow. This is not so that we are bound to something we were not previously held to, but so that we are bound by a **double obligation** to that which we were already held to. I say, for example, you were bound by the precept of temperance not to commit fornication, the transgression of which was only the vice of lust; but if you added a vow of the same thing, you are then additionally bound by the virtue of **religion** <note>In this context, the virtue of "religion" refers to the specific justice owed to God; breaking this vow adds the sin of sacrilege to the sin of lust.</note>. ¶ Finally, regarding those things which are neither necessary for the end goal nor indifferent, but are nevertheless conducive and expedient—such as the **counsels** <note>The "Evangelical Counsels" of poverty, chastity, and obedience, which are seen as going beyond the basic requirements of the law.</note>—the fifth conclusion is applied.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
**The works of counsel are the proper and particular matter of a vow.** For all the conditions and qualities of a legitimate vow converge in such works. First, the quality of a vow is that it is not about something opposed to God (for which reason we excluded sins); second, that it is not about a vain thing (for which reason we drove away indifferent things); and third, that it be done prudently (for which reason we rejected the impossible and the necessary). Therefore, the first kind of vow is wicked, the second is vain, and the third is foolish. Although works of the precepts are in some way the matter of a vow, they are not entirely so, because their obligation does not simply depend on us, but on the necessity of the law. However, in the works of the counsels, everything aligns. They are, above all, most pleasing to God and established within our power; and their obligation depends not on the necessity of the law, but on our pure will. ¶ These things having been established in this manner, it is worthwhile to weigh them more closely and to aim our gaze more keenly. And indeed, concerning the first conclusion, this remains to be meditated upon: that he who vows a sin to God threatens His majesty, which is a most enormous **blasphemy**. For truly, since whatever is a sin is done against His law and will, vowing to kill a man or to steal is the same as if you were threatening that same evil against God Himself. See, therefore, how great a perversion is here! Namely, that since a vow is an act of religion by which the most pleasing services are to be dedicated to Him, you contaminate religion to such an extent that you turn service into the audacity of a threat. From this it follows that since a vow is made to God and pertains to the **First Commandment** of the **Decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, there is more absurdity in vowing an illicit thing to God than in threatening a man with injury under an oath. For the violation of an oath is against the second commandment. And from these same points it follows again, that to vow the matter of a mortal sin to God is universally a sin...

<summary>Soto categorizes what can be the subject of a vow, concluding that while precepts can be vowed to create a double obligation, the "proper" matter of a vow is the "counsels" (voluntary acts of virtue) because they are entirely voluntary and pleasing to God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the "matter" of a vow—specifically, whether a vow can be made concerning minor sins or trivial, indifferent actions. He continues to apply Scholastic logic to determine the spiritual weight of these promises.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,
