mortal sin. Even if it were not done with the purpose of fulfilling the vow, provided the intention to vow is present: because the object in itself is mortal. <note>Soto is arguing that if the thing promised is a serious sin, the act of vowing it is a serious sin, regardless of the person's follow-through.</note>
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ You ask, however, whether making a vow to commit a venial fault <note>A "venial" fault is a minor sin that does not fully separate a person from God's grace, as opposed to a "mortal" or deadly sin.</note>—for instance, lying in jest or speaking idly—is always a mortal sin.
<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
And it is argued from the affirmative side: Anyone who promises God something they are bound not to do seems to inflict a grave injury upon Him. And this is strengthened more urgently: A vow, as we were just saying, is a greater bond when made to God than an oath made to a human. Yet an oath to commit a venial fault seems to be a mortal sin, since whoever swears is bound to make that oath false <note>original: "falsum." In legal theology, if you swear to do something minorly bad, you are obligated to break that oath to avoid the sin, which makes the oath "false."</note>; therefore, the same should apply to a vow.
<margin>The solution.</margin>
Nevertheless, the answer is that a vow concerning a venial matter is only a venial sin, because fulfilling it is only a venial sin.
<margin>To the argument.</margin>
Therefore, the person does not expose themselves to the danger of mortal sin. Hence, regarding the first reason, it is denied that promising God what you are bound not to do under pain of venial sin is a mortal sin for you. But regarding the oath mentioned in the second reason, in our little book *On Oaths*, chapter 9, we asserted it is only venial when it concerns a venial matter, for the same reason: namely, because fulfilling it is only venial. However, it is no wonder if someone thinks it is mortal. The reason can be built thus: Every false oath is a mortal sin, no matter how trivial the matter; therefore, making an oath which, after you have uttered it, you are bound to make false—even if you are only bound under venial sin—seems to be mortal based on the object, since the object of the obligation is the falsehood of the oath. Hence, whoever wishes to hold this opinion will deny the logical consequence drawn from an oath to a vow. For although a vow is a greater bond, its transgression can nevertheless be a venial offense by reason of the matter. The falsehood of an oath, however, is mortal in every individual instance; and falsehood arises from the fact that one swears to do what they are bound not to do. Nevertheless, it is always easier to maintain that such an oath is only venial: because to act against such an oath is no sin, and thus not a lie. For to act against an oath that is not binding is in no way illicit. For example, if you swear not to hear Mass on Easter Sunday, but later you hear it. But the whole fault is committed while you are swearing, because you swear to do what you are bound to make false. And therefore, for that reason, the whole fault must be weighed by the object—not indeed of the obligation, but of the oath.

<column-break/>

The object of the oath is venial, therefore even not fulfilling the oath itself is only venial.
<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second conclusion about indifferent matters, a doubt emerges because there are many indifferent things about which a vow can be made. For it is indifferent whether one walks through a street or crosses the threshold of a house, and yet there are sometimes salvific vows by which a person restrains themselves from such acts.
<margin>The response.</margin>
To this, it is very easily answered that indifferent things, insofar as they are indifferent—that is, persisting in their indifference—ought not to be dedicated to God or the saints by a vow. And in this sense, the conclusion is understood. If, however, after weighing some reason or end, they become relevant to the good, then a vow concerning them is nothing other than an act of religion. I say "by some reason or end" so that no one thinks that just because any thing is vowed, it immediately shifts from being irrelevant to relevant by reason of the vow. For example: vowing to trim one's nails, or not to trim them, is illicit; because even after the vow, the matter remains indifferent—namely, fruitful for nothing. And by the same reasoning, if without any other purpose you vowed not to walk through a street or not to enter a house. But if those acts offer you an occasion for sinning—for instance, to look at a woman or another enemy—then they become relevant to the matter and, consequently, the material for a vow. By the same reasoning, a simple woman vowing not to bake bread on the Sabbath in honor of the Virgin, yet not abstaining from other works, emits a vain vow; because while you are taking up other tasks, it matters nothing to the Blessed Virgin whether you take up these or those. If, however, you vow to abstain from all servile work <note>Historically, "servile work" refers to physical labor forbidden on holy days.</note>, it is a legitimate vow. There are, however, some things which are neither entirely approved nor disapproved. For instance, if someone vowed to wear white on the Sabbath in memory of the virginity of the Mother of God <note>original: "Deiparae," the God-bearer.</note>, it would not be entirely vain. Therefore, the end or cause which makes the work relevant must be considered.
<margin>A fine deduction.</margin>
¶ From these things it follows that when a vow is made regarding such things, it does not bind except as long as that end serves and the cause lasts which made the vow legitimate. For when that cause ceases, since the work returns to its own indifference, it ceases to be the matter of a vow, and thus the obligation ceases. You vowed not to tread upon a neighbor’s threshold because of a danger lurking within; when that danger ceases, the vow no longer holds you. This is proved because a vow binds no more than if it were a law. But a law ceases when its cause and end entirely cease; therefore, a vow ceases likewise. ¶ Finally, instructed by these lessons,

<summary>Soto explains that vows regarding minor sins or indifferent actions (like walking a certain path) only carry moral weight if they serve a higher spiritual purpose or help avoid temptation; if the underlying reason for such a vow disappears, the obligation also ends.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s discussion on the "matter" of vows. He is now transitioning from the discussion of minor sins to "indifferent" actions—things that are neither inherently good nor bad—and whether such things can be the subject of a binding promise to God.</meta>

### Question 1 of the Eighth Book

Anyone can judge for themselves concerning vows that are commonly made about such indifferent things <note>In Scholastic theology, "indifferent" things are actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden, such as choosing what to eat or whom to talk to.</note>. Perhaps you were speaking with someone, and in the conversation something unpleasant happened, because of which you vowed never to enter into speech with them again. Or perhaps you were playing a game, and therefore you vowed never to play with that person again, or not to play cards, or not to play in such a house. If these things are no occasion of evil for you, and no cause exists for them to serve a good purpose, then such vows do not hold in any way. Rather, making the vow was a sin of vanity. But if speaking with such a person is an occasion of evil for you, the vow holds—just as if you vow not to gamble because of the loss you inflict on your property, or because of other dangers. Nor can there be any doubt about these things that would wound a person's conscience in any way. Instead, without any dispensation <note>A "dispensation" is an official release from a religious vow or law granted by a Church authority.</note>, someone who has made vows of this kind regarding indifferent things can act against them; it is enough for them to repent of the vow.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But regarding an oath <note>Soto distinguishes between a "vow" (made to God) and an "oath" (calling God as a witness to a promise).</note>, because of the reverence due to it and because every perjury is a mortal sin, someone might hesitate in their mind. Indeed, if that which is extorted by fear of death must be fulfilled—as when someone, struck by fear of death in a forest, makes a promise to robbers, as the Doctors of the Church believe—it seems that reason would more strictly persuade us that an oath concerning even an indifferent thing must be kept; otherwise, it would become false.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
Nevertheless, the answer is that a promissory oath of such things, contributing to nothing for any cause or end, obligates no more than a vow does. For such an oath is nothing other than a confirmation of a promise and a vow. And therefore, if the vow does not obligate, it follows that neither does the oath. You swore that you would never speak with such a man again, or never again cross a threshold where you happened to stub your foot, or other similar things that are of no benefit. You did indeed sin when you swore against the second commandment <note>"Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain."</note>; nonetheless, the oath in no way becomes obligatory. Therefore, acting against it without a dispensation is no sin, and thus it is not even a lie; because, as was said above, the entire malice of such oaths is committed while they are being made. You swore not to hear Mass on a feast day: to do the opposite, because it is not an evil, does not then become a lie, even though you make the oath to have been false. And that it is not obligatory is clear: for just as if you promised it to a man, he would consider your promise as nothing, so too does God. Therefore, in Ecclesiastes 5, both kinds of 

<column-break/>

promises are said to displease God: namely, the unfaithful and the foolish. But where there is a doubt whether a thing might be useful in some way, then it would be the part of a God-fearing soul to procure a dispensation. Nor is it the same as an extorted oath when it falls upon matter that is of some benefit; for paying promised money to a robber is a useful thing <note>Meaning it serves the purpose of civil peace or personal safety.</note>, and thus by its nature is the matter of an oath. Therefore, although it is extorted, it must be fulfilled out of reverence for the divine name. But vain matter is not the subject of an oath, and therefore it is not capable of creating an obligation. ¶ Concerning the third conclusion, there is no reason for doubt, but 

<margin>A point of scruple.</margin>
concerning the fourth, we must explore what truth it contains. For there is an argument that the matter of the commandments <note>The "matter of the commandments" refers to things already required by law, like "thou shalt not kill."</note> should not be the matter of a vow. For since a vow is a "work of counsel" <note>An "evangelical counsel" is a spiritual practice that goes beyond the basic requirements of the law, such as voluntary poverty or celibacy.</note>, and the matter should correspond to the form, it seems to follow that its matter should likewise be discretionary and belonging to the counsels; and therefore, where the law already holds us obligated, a vow becomes vain. Indeed, it is in some way ungrateful to God. For he who vows to do what God otherwise commands seems to attribute greater force to his own will than to God who commands. Likewise, to add a vow to a commandment is judged to proceed from a weakness of soul; namely, that a person is so destitute of strength that they cannot fulfill what God commands without it. Furthermore, it provokes the demon to attack them more fiercely with temptations.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
¶ It is answered, nonetheless, that the matter of the commandments can also be the matter of vows. And the 

<margin>The first reason of Saint Thomas.</margin>
reason of Saint Thomas <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas.</note> is that obedience is not simply necessary but depends on our will. Therefore, we can bind ourselves to such works with a tighter bond. For no repugnance exists between the two obligations. 

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
Second, this is proven by the solemn usage of the Church. For those vowing the religious life <note>Entering a monastery or convent.</note> are bound by a new knot to abstain from adultery and fornication, from which they were already prohibited by divine law. And this is required of clerics when they are initiated into the major holy orders. 

<margin>The third.</margin>
Third, it is lawful and holy to further bind yourself by an oath to that which you were held by law—as when you receive a loan, or a deposit, or another legal contract; therefore, in a similar way, you can confirm the same faith by a vow. 

<margin>The fourth reason.</margin>
Fourth, although we are bound by law not to kill, not to steal, etc., punishments are nonetheless decreed for wrongdoers, so that the fear of punishment may restrain those whom the honesty of virtue does not suffice to move. Therefore, there is no repugnance in adding the second obligation of a vow to the obligation of the law.

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s analysis of the "matter" of vows—specifically, whether one can make a binding vow to perform an action that is already required by law or commandment, such as vowing not to steal or to keep the Sabbath.</meta>

->**Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,**<-

There are those who, as if disputing over a name, say that this kind of promising is not properly a "vow," for the reason that the subject matter is not properly suited for it <note>In theology, the "matter" of a vow usually refers to a "greater good" that is voluntary, rather than something already mandatory.</note>. Nevertheless, they argue that someone who promises in this way would sin in two ways if they did not fulfill the promise: namely, against the law and against the promise. But truly, there is no reason to deny that it is properly a vow, since it is a true promise made to God. And it is confirmed that it must be acknowledged as such. For someone who transgresses such a vow, as we were saying above, truly sins against the virtue of religion; yet they would not sin in this way unless they were truly acting against a vow. For if the substance of religion (which is the general category) is contained in this observance, it follows that the substance of the vow (which exists as a specific type of religion) is also contained. Therefore, anyone can emit a vow concerning the subject matter of individual commandments.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Hence, in response to the first argument to the contrary, although making a vow is a "work of counsel" <note>A "work of counsel" refers to the Evangelical Counsels—poverty, chastity, and obedience—which are considered higher goods recommended by Christ but not strictly commanded for all Christians.</note>, it is not required that the matter itself be exclusive to counsel. For it can be a matter of counsel to bind ourselves more strictly to that which we were already held to by law. If you should perhaps bring against us the words of Saint Thomas from his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 38, Question 1), where he says that vows of this kind are called such "broadly" but not "properly," the response is this: "broadly" is not used to mean "incorrectly," but rather "commonly," just as the Master <note>The "Master" refers to Peter Lombard, the author of the *Sentences*, the standard medieval theology textbook.</note> speaks there. For he does not deny that they have the proper nature of a vow; but because the matter is common to both vows and precepts—to which all people are generally bound—he says such matter is not "proper," that is, not unique to a vow. Therefore, he is speaking more precisely here. This distinction of matter is drawn from the words of Saint Augustine (Question 17, Case 1), where he says: "There are certain things which we owe even if we do not vow them, and certain things which we do not owe unless we have vowed them."

<margin>To the second.</margin>
Nor in this do we attribute more to our own will than to God's; rather, we bind our will to divine religion so that we may more firmly fulfill what He commands us. And although in this we profess our own weakness, we nevertheless strengthen it. And while it is true that demons may assault us more fiercely because of it, divine aid is also sent to us more abundantly. ¶ However, to speak the truth, these vows to perform commanded works should never, or hardly ever, be undertaken or advised, because they do not often turn out well. Therefore, they should either not be made, or they should be voided or easily dispensed <note>A "dispensation" is a formal release from a religious obligation granted by an authority like a bishop.</note>, except when the person is prudent and constant,

<column-break/>

yet inclined toward some particular thing which is an occasion of grave evil or scandal for them. In such a case, with vigilant care applied, a vow can help avoid that evil. ¶ Furthermore, the question arises whether a vow "never to sin venially" <note>A "venial" sin is a lesser sin that does not result in a complete break with God's grace, as opposed to a "mortal" or deadly sin.</note> is the product of a sane mind. To this it is answered that a vow of this kind is insane and does not bind in any way, because it concerns a thing that is impossible for human beings. For "if we say," as John the Apostle says, "that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves." However, to vow never to sin mortally is not evil in its nature, because that is possible through the grace of God. Yet I would not entirely advise even this, because the matter is very difficult, both in the doing and especially in the knowing—chiefly regarding sins of the heart. For a "scruple" <note>A "scruple" is an unfounded fear or nagging doubt that one has committed a sin.</note> often pricks the conscience as to whether one has consented to a mortal fault; a vow, however, ought to be about a certain thing and about a work whose transgression is clearly visible. But to vow to beware of specific sins is permitted: such as not to commit fornication, not to tell a joke-lie, and the like.

<margin>A small question.</margin>
¶ You ask, moreover, whether if someone were to emit a vow never to sin, they would be held by reason of the vow to avoid at least those sins which they were able to avoid, such as "jocose" (humorous) lies. For reason suggests this: since he who promised to give ten, if he cannot give all, is nevertheless held to contribute what he can. And he who promised to fast through Advent, if he cannot do the whole, is nonetheless held to fast as much as he can.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
It is answered, however, that such a vow binds to nothing, because it is foolish. ¶ Nevertheless, let the decision on this final point be set aside: whether the transgression of any such vow is a mortal sin—for instance, if someone vowed not to tell a joke-lie. The reason supporting the affirmative side is that then lying would be a violation of religion, which by its nature is a mortal sin. The solution to this depends on the following article, where it will be disputed whether a transgression of a vow can become a venial sin due to the "lightness of the matter." It is there that this will be examined.

<margin>The first doubt.</margin>
¶ From the fifth conclusion, although it is most certain, much graver doubts emerge. First, whether it is lawful to vow for an evil end. For example, if someone (as we were just saying) were to profess the religion of the Military Order of the Crusaders for the sake of the wealth of the prebends <note>A "prebend" was a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or monastery granted to a member of the clergy as a stipend.</note>; or if someone—which happens very frequently—became a priest not for the holiness of the state, but for the sake of the benefices <note>A "benefice" is a church office that provides a living or income.</note>, desiring to be enriched more than to offer sacrifice.

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
For it appears that the vow is not lawful, and therefore not binding.

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that one can validly vow to keep God's existing commandments, though he warns that vowing never to sin is often "insane" or "foolish" due to human frailty. He also begins to explore whether vows made for selfish or corrupt motives, such as seeking church wealth, are spiritually binding.</summary>

### Question I of the Eighth Book

...tory. For a bad end <note>The "end" refers to the goal or intention behind an action.</note> corrupts the object: and concerning a bad object (as was stated in the first conclusion), a vow is unjust. ¶ Although Cajetan discusses this doubt learnedly in this passage, it nevertheless requires a more accurate examination. Indeed, it is necessary to use a manifold distinction at this present time. In such vows of a "better good," I say that a threefold relationship can occur regarding a bad 
<margin>Distinction.</margin>
end. For either the object of the vow itself can be directed toward a bad end, or the application of the mind toward vowing, or the vow itself. For example: if someone were to make this offering in their mind: "I vow to give alms for the sake of vain glory": then the small word "for" can govern and, as they say, determine either the verb "to give" or the verb "I vow." And indeed, in the first way, the object of the vow itself—which is "to give"—is directed toward a bad end, by which the giving itself is contaminated and depraved. And the 
<margin>Cajetan’s first assertion.</margin>
first assertion is concerning this sense: that a vow of this kind is null; instead, it is among those which are condemned by the first conclusion. For to give for the sake of vain glory is a bad object, and it will be much more unjust to vow to do something for the sake of a mortal sin, such as if you vow to go to church to solicit a girl. For the "going" itself is then evil, which is the object of the vow. An example of the second: as if someone, intending to obtain a lucrative priesthood for which he is not worthy, should become a priest, where a vow of chastity or a precept is implicit (about which we are not disputing now). Or when a nobleman puts on the habit of a military religious order <note>Likely referring to orders such as the Knights of Malta or Santiago.</note> with such a mindset. Here, the object of the vow is not directed toward evil. For if he says here, "I vow to be a priest for the sake of fishing for a benefice" <note>A "benefice" was a church office that provided an income.</note>: the preposition "for" does not modify the thing itself which is "being a priest," but this act which is "I vow." For having been made a priest or a soldier, he does not perform the works of his religion—suppose, he neither prays, nor celebrates Mass, nor obeys—for the sake of a bad end, as does the one who gives alms for vain glory: but he only made his profession for a bad end. And concerning this understanding, the 
<margin>Second [assertion].</margin>
reason is that its object is a lawful and good thing, namely to be a soldier or a priest: surely to serve as a soldier, to pray, to sacrifice: things which indeed are not directed toward a sinister end. In the same way, if someone were to profess religion, led by a perverse end: furthermore, so that he might later be able to steal the property of the convent. For he does not direct the object of the vow—suppose, vigils, prayers, and acts of obedience—toward evil, but the end of vowing was bad. Therefore the vow, because it concerns a good object, is solid and 

<column-break/>

firm. However, for a clearer understanding of the matter, it is argued: just as giving alms for the sake of vain glory is a sin, and going to church with a corrupt end is a sin, so also is making a vow for a bad end. Therefore, just as a vow of the first kind is evil because it concerns a bad object, so also a vow of the second kind is evil because it has a bad end. But if both are evil, it results that neither should hold. For the solution to the argument, this must be especially noted in the present matter, which could greatly deceive a less attentive reader. Namely, that it is not universally true that every illicit and bad vow becomes void; nor has this been asserted by us, but only this: that every vow concerning a *bad object* is void and empty. We concede, therefore, that one vowing the priesthood or religious life for a bad end certainly sins by vowing; nevertheless, because the vow has a good object (for even if the vow is directed toward a bad end, the object is not directed toward the same), the vow holds. Therefore, the final logical consequence is denied—"a vow made for a bad end is bad, therefore it does not bind"—as if it had a bad object: since a thing devoted to God is good, even if dedicated for a bad end. ¶ However, in the third way, a little more 
<margin>Third [assertion].</margin>

<margin><gloss>perhaps read as "gift" [munus]</gloss></margin>
a talent of gold if he should obtain victory. Here the object of the vow—suppose, to give a weight of gold—is good in itself: yet the end of the vow—suppose, to obtain an unjust victory—is bad. Concerning these vows, therefore, it must be distinguished in this manner. If such a vow is made so that God might grant a victory of that kind, it is not an act of <term>religion</term> <note>In this context, "religion" refers to the virtue of giving God his due honor.</note>; indeed, it is entirely contrary to religion, because he who vows in this way makes God the author of evil: for which foulness, which he strikes against God, he promises him a gift. Because of this, the vow is null, but it is a grave sin of impiety and blasphemy. And thus it is far more wicked than if it were a vow concerning an illicit thing. For it is much more enormous to make God the author of evil than to vow a different thing to him. In the same way, if someone were to vow gifts to God so that He might make him successful in a desired adultery or homicide. Wherefore, it makes no difference whether you make the vow before you begin the act, or after you have obtained your desires. For even if, after an achieved victory or a committed adultery, you vow something to God on that account—because He made you master of your desire, or an unjust victor—the vow does not hold: because it is defiled by the same plague of impiety. Nor if you were to vow it in thanksgiving: because it is not pleasing to God to hear thanks for that. Nor indeed does it matter if you emit such a vow without expressing that God should patronize you in your

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s discussion on the validity of vows, specifically addressing those made under bad conditions or involving the "evangelical counsels."</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Law

...will be bound, but purely conditionally, in this manner: "If I obtain this victory, or if I achieve my desire, I will perform this alms-giving." Since no one vows under such a pure condition unless they are calling upon God as the patron and supporter of their crime. To imagine any other case would be to invent an unusual circumstance. Therefore, these vows are all absurd and of no force.

<margin>Objection.</margin> ¶ But if you argue against this: similar stipulations made to men are held by natural law. For what one promises to a harlot, he is bound to pay; therefore, they should also be valid in respect to God.

<margin>Refutation.</margin> The consequence is denied: because a man can obtain a shameful service from another man, for which he must owe a reward; but from God, no one receives that which is absurd, nor ought he to repay Him anything for it. Therefore, the vow will not hold, even if someone ignorantly thinks such vows are lawful; for by the nature of the matter, they are impious and blasphemous. ¶ But truly, because in an evil thing there can be some good within which God can be invoked as the author without impiety, these vows can be made holily in a second way. Namely, if a king, having embarked on a wicked war, vows something for the safety of his army, the vow holds. Just as if someone entering into a duel promised something if he escaped safe; because to ascribe these outcomes to God is nothing but virtue. Therefore, such an end does not vitiate the vow. It is otherwise if he vows for this: that he may wickedly kill his enemy. For although the Almighty is the cause of all entities—such as the pleasure which is in a crime and similar things—He is in no way the cause of the sin. In the same way, if someone vows if he receives a child from adultery. For although God is not the cause of the adultery, the conception and birth of the offspring is natural and ascribed to God. Nor is it the same concerning a victory: since that very thing which is to win unjustly is a crime <note>original: "piaculum"</note>. By similar law, if a usurer or a gambler <note>Soto refers here to those who gain money through unethical means.</note> vows a vow for the profit gained, that indeed holds: according to the word of Christ: *Make for yourselves friends of the Mammon of iniquity.* Yet this is understood with the moderation that he does not fulfill the vow out of debt which he cannot otherwise repay. For it would then happen that he would be dispensing alms from robbery.

<margin>Penal vows.</margin> ¶ Finally, by a stronger reason, a vow will hold where you have uttered it to punish an evil, or by which you may be more cautiously restrained from it. As if you uttered a vow of this kind: "If I commit such a crime, I will perform such alms, or a pilgrimage, or I will bid farewell to the world as a religious." For vows of this kind are, as it were, works of pen-

<column-break/>

-tence, acting as a punishment for a committed iniquity, or a prohibition of one to be committed; and thus, the condition being met, they hold. Concerning which we shall speak more precisely below.

<margin>Second doubt.</margin> ¶ The second doubt concerning the same conclusion exists regarding works which are of the <term>counsels</term> <note>The "evangelical counsels" are spiritual suggestions in the New Testament, like poverty, chastity, and obedience, which are seen as paths to perfection rather than mandatory laws.</note>, being either directly contrary or hindrances. These are divided into three orders. For some are altogether contrary: concerning which it is responded that it is in no way permitted to utter a vow.

<margin>Response.</margin> For it is not permitted to vow not to enter religious life <note>Meaning life in a monastery or convent.</note>. For although no one is bound to enter, it ought to be free for everyone and always unimpaired. Therefore, a contrary vow does not bind; and thus it is unjust, not only as something vain, but also as being concerning a thing hateful to God: since His counsels are exceedingly pleasing to Him.

<margin>Objection.</margin> ¶ But you argue: Not all works which are counsels in themselves are a counsel for all men to do: and therefore he who is certain that he is not fit for religious life, or for a pilgrimage, can vow not to do it.

<margin>Solution.</margin> It is responded that such a vow cannot be excused from fault. For he who is incapable of doing it vows in vain not to do it: and he who in any way hopes he might be able is unjust while he restrains himself by a vow. ¶ For the same reason, it is permitted to no one to vow or swear that he will never fast, or go on pilgrimage, or lend money or act as a guarantor, or never bestow any other offices of mercy upon the unworthy: since to do these things is often a counsel. Lest we condemn the many who are accustomed to this, we understand this when doing those things would be a counsel. For to give a loan to everyone and to be a guarantor for everyone is not a counsel. Therefore, he who would vow thus: "I will not lend to everyone indiscriminately," would vow nothing evil; but he who would say, "To no one, nor in any case." ¶ From these things it follows as a consequence that it is not a lawful vow "not to vow": since to vow in general is a counsel. But because it is not always a counsel for everyone, it is permitted to make a vow not to vow, except before such a person or with such circumstances. Nevertheless, if notwithstanding that you do vow, although you sin, the vow nevertheless holds by divine and natural law, which you were not able to derogate. Let us conclude, therefore, that it is permitted to no one to make vows or oaths of this kind: since, having been made, they do not hold. For God, as David witnesses, disposes "ascensions" in our hearts: not "descensions" <note>A reference to Psalm 84:5, interpreting spiritual life as a climb toward God.</note>. Wherefore the religious practice of vowing is by its own nature and character established for the purpose of moving men toward the sublime, not for pulling them back.

<summary>Domingo de Soto examines the validity of conditional and "penal" vows, arguing that while a vow cannot be made to facilitate a crime, one may vow to perform a good act as penance for a sin. He also establishes that one cannot vow to refrain from "evangelical counsels" (like joining a religious order), as vows are intended for spiritual progress rather than limitation.</summary>

# Book Eight, Question I.

<margin>The second level of works that can be included under a vow.</margin>
¶ The second level of works consists of those which, although they are not incompatible with greater goods, are duties in themselves; vows of these and the fulfillment of such vows do not prevent one from ascending to more sublime states. Therefore, vows of this kind are solid and binding. For example, if someone binds themselves by a vow to the service of the poor in a hospital, even if they say, "I shall remain here forever," I say this vow is binding. Nevertheless, this does not prevent that person from entering religious life <note>original: "religiosus fieri"; in this context, "religious life" refers to joining a formal monastic or mendicant order</note> if they wish, without any need for a dispensation.

<margin>The third level.</margin>
¶ In the third category are placed those things which, although they are not formally contrary to religious life, are by their very nature obstacles to it, such as the marriage bond. For someone who has once consummated a marriage cannot migrate to religious life while the spouse is still living.

<margin>A Doubt regarding the first argument.</margin>
It is therefore turned into a doubt whether it is lawful to issue a vow to enter into marriage. It is argued that this is permitted, since the object is good and lawful for virtue, and anyone, before making a vow of religious life, is free to choose whichever way of living they prefer.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
Likewise, it is lawful for anyone to swear an oath to celebrate their nuptials, and by that oath they are subsequently bound; therefore, anyone should also be able to issue a vow for the same thing.

<margin>The Response.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, it is responded that vows of this kind are not lawful in their nature and object, insofar as they offer to God something that is not acceptable to Him. I do not say this solely because they impede a greater good—for both contracting and consummating a marriage impede religious life—but because through the vow you offer what does not please God, insofar as you offer an impediment to His counsel <note>A reference to the "Evangelical Counsels" of poverty, chastity, and obedience, which were seen as higher paths than the common life</note>. Thus, you may place an obstacle to religious life by contracting marriage, but you cannot dedicate that obstacle to God by a vow. For although no one is forced by law to make a vow, everyone is nevertheless compelled not to close off the path to the Holy Spirit by creating an impossibility, until such time as you change and fix your state of life, should He perhaps deign to breathe His inspiration upon you.

¶ But you might say it is at least lawful to issue a vow of marital companionship without the consummation of the union, since that is no impediment to religious life. The response is that one who simply issues a vow of marriage is, by the nature of the matter, bound to consummate it; otherwise, the marriage would be hollow and deceptive. For this reason, when it is issued absolutely, it is always illicit. If, however, it could happen that someone vowed a marriage such as existed between the Virgin and Joseph—namely, with a second vow of perpetual virginity added by both parties—it would be nothing other than a religious duty.

<margin>Argument against the previous definition.</margin>
¶ Against this decision, however, it is argued: regarding marriage,

<column-break/>

we can meditate in two ways. In one way, as it is a duty of procreation <note>original: "ingenerationis officium"</note> and a certain state and way of life. And in this way, we undoubtedly admit that no one is allowed to bind themselves to it by a vow; because it is a lower state that impedes a higher one, and thus it is an abuse of the vow, which should always be for a more fruitful purpose, or at least one that does not hinder it. But in the second way, it is considered as a remedy <note>term: "remedium" — a theological concept where marriage is seen as a legitimate outlet to prevent the sin of lust</note> to restrain unlawful lust. And in this way, it is argued that such a vow is lawful. For to oppose the allurements of the flesh is just and holy, and marital intercourse is even a permitted duty for this purpose; therefore, there is no absurdity in such a vow.

<margin>Cajetan's solution.</margin>
Because of this argument, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note>, in the present article, intrepidly asserts that it is lawful in such a case and for such a cause to issue a vow of marriage. And he brings against himself an argument from Saint Thomas in the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 31), which many adhere to, asserting that it is not lawful to use a spouse solely to avoid fornication. For that would be an abuse of the marriage bed, which is granted only for duty <note>i.e., procreation</note>. But Cajetan nevertheless responds that he recognizes nothing absurd in such use that would prevent it from being the object of a vow. However, whatever may be the case regarding the use—even granted that the sole cause of avoiding fornication were lawful—it does not follow that it is permitted to issue such a vow. For the reason why it is not permitted is not only that the object itself is not good, but that it is an impediment to a greater good. And I marvel that Cajetan did not see this. For it is free and lawful for anyone to enter marriage, and indeed it is sometimes a counsel; because as Paul says, it is better and more advisable to marry than to burn. And yet the reason why it is not permitted to issue a vow is that as long as someone does not contract marriage, they ought to remain free, so that if the Holy Spirit breathes upon them more favorably, they may change their mind.

<margin>The first reason against Cajetan.</margin>
And the reason Cajetan gives is shown to be fallacious: for otherwise it would follow that it would be lawful to vow marriage insofar as it is a duty, since that is a good thing. If, therefore, it is not permitted because it is an impediment to religious life, for the same reason it will not be permitted as it is a remedy for another evil.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And it is confirmed that, notwithstanding such a vow, the one vowing could change their purpose and pass over to religious life; therefore, the vow is vain and even illicit. And for this reason, I cannot help but disagree with Cajetan on this matter.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Wherefore, the first argument made above has already been answered: that even if the marriage bond is a good and lawful object, yet this only concludes that...

<summary>This page discusses whether it is lawful to vow to marry. De Soto argues that such a vow is illicit because it preemptively blocks the higher calling of the Holy Spirit to religious life, even disagreeing with Cardinal Cajetan's view on marriage as a remedy for lust.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
Anyone can enter into such an agreement <note>original: "illud inire"; referring to a promise of marriage</note>, yet they cannot truly emit a binding vow for it. This is because such a vow would be vain; despite the vow, that person would still be permitted to profess a religious life <note>original: "religionem profiteri"; in this era, "religion" specifically refers to joining a monastic or mendicant order under the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience</note>. ¶ And likewise, in response to the second point, it is held that although it is lawful to swear an oath to a future marriage, the person swearing is nonetheless permitted to take up the monastic habit regardless of that oath. Nor are they bound to fulfill that oath unless they choose not to become a member of a religious order or a priest, which is an even better state of life. This is because these conditions—the freedom to pursue a higher spiritual calling—are always understood by the law to be implicit exceptions.

<margin>Another Doubt.</margin>
¶ There remains one final doubt: namely, how much weight is contained in vows of this kind that are made against the <term>counsels</term> <note>The "evangelical counsels" are the voluntary practices of poverty, chastity, and obedience that go beyond what is required for salvation.</note>. For it seems such a vow never reaches the level of a mortal sin, because it binds no one, and therefore it is not an impediment to any "more excellent fruit"—just as we said regarding the man who devoted himself to a hospital by vow.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The response is that three things are weighed in these matters. The first is the object and the intent itself. Since performing works of mercy, such as giving alms and similar counsels, sometimes reaches the threshold of a command—for one is indeed bound to give alms at certain times—if someone were to vow with the intent never to give alms, they would clearly sin mortally, because they would be proposing to act against a divine command. Secondly, one considers in such vows the resistance to the divine will; by this reasoning, someone vows to God as if it were pleasing that which is actually unpleasing to Him. Anyone who did this knowingly and deliberately would undoubtedly sin mortally, for it would be a manifest abuse of the nature of a vow. However, one acting out of ignorance might be excused. Nevertheless, if these vows are considered solely as impediments to a greater good, they possess no other malice than that of vanity, because in truth they do not bind. Therefore, they do not seem to be mortal sins by their nature unless they were made out of a hatred for religious life; in that case, they would be impious.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ If you should argue that such a vow has no weight at all, any more than if you vowed to serve in a hospital: that comparison is denied. For when the object of a vow does not stand in the way of a greater good even while it is being carried out, the vow carries no fault. But truly, although a vow of marriage does not impede a higher good before the marriage is consummated, the fact that the consummation itself *does* impede the higher life makes the initial vow flawed.

<margin>Reply.</margin>
And if you argue that it is lawful to swear to a future marriage because an exception is always understood (unless the one swearing vows to enter religious life), then by the same logic it should be lawful to vow marriage. The response is that when a promise is made to a human being, even under oath, the law understands an exception for a divine counsel. But because a vow is made to God, it is illicit to promise Him something contrary to His own counsels, unless you were to openly

<column-break/>

state the exception—namely, "I vow marriage to God, unless He Himself disposes something more healthfully for me."

<margin>It is lawful to vow for the sake of temporal goods.</margin>
¶ Truly, no one can doubt whether a vow is lawful when it is emitted for the sake of temporal goods <note>Temporal goods refer to worldly benefits like health, safety, or children, as opposed to eternal spiritual rewards.</note>. For instance, if someone vows something on the condition that God grants them a prosperous journey, as Jacob did in Genesis 28; or if He grants a husband, or children, or victory. Even though some of the heretics <note>likely referring to Protestant Reformers who criticized the practice of "bargaining" with God via vows</note> mock us, saying this is to buy and trade with God, it is actually nothing other than a profession that all things come to us from Him. For this reason, the Church prays for these types of goods, because they are useful to us for reaching eternal life. Therefore, if a vow is made under a condition—suppose, "if this or that happens to me"—then it does not create an obligation until the condition is fulfilled. It is otherwise if the vow is made absolutely; for then, even if your intention is to obtain that temporal thing, you are bound to fulfill the vow even if you do not obtain it.

¶ From these points, at the conclusion of this question which we have established concerning the substance of a vow, anyone can hunt for the definition which the Doctors <note>Refers to the Scholastic theologians, specifically commenting on Book 4, Distinction 38 of Peter Lombard's "Sentences."</note> have established in various ways. For a definition ought to contain both the genus and the differences in a summary, which explains both the form and the matter of the thing.
<margin>Definition of a Vow.</margin>
A vow, therefore, is a promise of a deliberate will, made to God, concerning those things which belong to God. The genus is a promise proceeding from deliberation and purpose. By saying "made to God" (where it is understood to include the saints), it is separated from a promise made to humans, and is categorized as an act of religion. "Concerning those things which belong to God" is added to explain the matter of the counsels, which is the proper and peculiar subject of a vow, although it may be extended to matters of command.

<margin>Regarding the first argument. St. Thomas.</margin>
**TO** the first argument to the contrary, St. Thomas seems to respond that a vow is indeed made in baptism, even though that is not a work of <term>supererogation</term> <note>Supererogation refers to doing more than what duty or the law requires.</note> but of necessity.

<margin>A vow is not emitted in baptism.</margin>
It is called a vow, he says, because it is done voluntarily, just as when someone vows to do something that is already a command. The Master of the Sentences calls this baptismal vow a "common vow." ¶ However, as Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas.</note> rightly discusses here, it is not properly a "vow" in the sense of something added to a command; and this is proved by many reasons.
<margin>The first reason for the previous assertion.</margin>
First, a Christian who transgresses the precepts of Christianity commits a single sin, not a double sin; this is a clear sign that we are bound there only by law, with no additional vow superimposed. Furthermore, it is evident from the words spoken there. For the person is questioned...
<margin>The second.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of vows from Book 8, Question 1. Having previously addressed whether one can vow to enter marriage (a state of life) despite the "higher" calling of the religious life, the text now examines the specific nature of baptismal promises, the famous biblical vow of Jephthah, and the limits of vows involving physical penance.</meta>

### Book Eight, Question I.

Does the catechumen <note>A person receiving instruction in the Christian faith in preparation for baptism.</note> renounce Satan, and does he wish to be baptized, and does he believe? And he responds: "I renounce, I will, and I believe." <note>original: "Abrenuntio, volo, & credo."</note> However, those words are only a profession of the law and the Christian religion, and the assumption of a new status; these are certainly not signs of a new vow.

<margin>The last point.</margin>
And finally, this is confirmed because to be baptized is a commandment of necessary obligation; however, to make a vow is a free and voluntary act of <term>counsel</term> <note>In Catholic theology, a "precept" is a requirement for all, while a "counsel" is a voluntary path to higher perfection, such as a vow of poverty.</note>. But there is no need for more obligations. For no one has ever thought that baptism is a "vow" in such a way that it becomes a new obligation added to the obligation of the commandment. It is just as when priests or monks profess their statutes by a knot of binding chastity (which is already in the commandment), they add a new obligation through a vow. But this is called a "common vow," because Christianity is a kind of religion to which all men are bound; and therefore, in baptism, all profess the same religion, essentially enlisting their names into such a military service.

¶ Regarding Jacob, however, when he vowed to God that He would be his God, it must be said either that he bound himself more religiously by a vow to that which he was already held by law, or certainly that he vowed a new worship of counsel. Whence he adds: "Of all that you give to me, I will pay tithes to you."

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second point regarding Jephthah, it is answered—following Jerome—that he was foolish in vowing, because he lacked discretion, and impious in fulfilling it. For as Saint Thomas says, there are some things which are not only good by their nature, but also in every event—such as works of virtue. Others, however, are not only bad in their nature, but also in every case—namely those which are evil by their kind. Therefore, anyone can safely and absolutely vow the former, but the latter by no means. But there are others besides which, even if they are good by their nature and thus the legitimate matter of a vow, can nevertheless turn out to have a disastrous outcome; and such was that which Jephthah vowed. Note here that this work was not "indifferent" <note>An "indifferent" act is one that is neither inherently good nor evil, like picking up a straw.</note> (for indifferent things have already been excluded above from the matter of a vow); rather, it was good by its nature—namely, to offer a sacrifice to God. Nevertheless, because the matter of the sacrifice was not predetermined by him, but he said, "whoever first comes out of the doors of my house, I will offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord," the vow lacked prudent discretion. And similar are "indiscreet vows" when they are uttered under a mark of universality. For instance: "I vow to hand over to a poor person whatever he shall ask of me." For perhaps he will ask you for a sword to commit a murder,

<column-break/>

or something else which it is not fitting to grant. For this reason, vows of this kind do not bind at all in those events which are not lawful by natural law.

<margin>Jephthah was impious in fulfilling the vow.</margin>
And for this reason, Jephthah was impious in fulfilling the vow. Since it was understood by its own nature to refer to a beast, or a herd, and to other animals accustomed to being offered in sacrifice. Nor does it seem that any ignorance can be excused, because he drove not just a human being against the law of nature, but even his own daughter, to a cruel death. Therefore, as for what is prefaced in his history—namely, "The Holy Spirit came upon Jephthah"—this is to be referred neither to the making of the vow nor to its fulfillment, but to the fact that, animated by divine zeal, he attacked the Ammonites, the enemies of God. And although Paul commemorates him among the just of the Old Law, it does not follow from this that he committed no sin. For he also lists Samson and David, who it is well known sometimes fell, both because they were just at other times and because of their remarkable victories.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third point, it is answered that neither a vow of the mortification of the body, nor any other whatsoever, holds, except insofar as it is a work of virtue. Therefore, when they stray beyond the line of prudence, they cease to bind.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Wherefore Paul, in Romans 12, warns his students to present their bodies as a holy sacrifice, living, and pleasing to God. And only then does he add: "Let your service be reasonable." <note>original: "Rationabile sit obsequium vestrum."</note> But truly, because men (as Saint Thomas says) judge themselves too indulgently in those things that pertain to themselves, it is more advisable, when a doubt about this matter arises, to submit to the judgment of a superior.

<margin>A Scruple</margin>
¶ But you ask: what shall be the judgment of a "crossed line" in vows of this kind? <note>A "scruple" is a small doubt or nagging concern about whether one has sinned or broken a rule.</note>

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The answer is that it is nothing else than when the law of nature cries out against it. I do not say that where the law of nature does not command such fasts and harshness of works, such vows are not lawful (otherwise even Lent would not be lawful); but when that which you do is contrary to the law of nature—namely, when the affliction turns into homicide—then the obligation of the vow is abolished.

¶ Regarding the other part of the argument—namely, regarding vows of "indifferent" things—it has already been answered that they have no weight. Wherefore they are sometimes ridiculous and the follies of simple women. Indeed, sometimes they are to be cursed, namely when they are like sorceries, and superstitious ravings or sacrileges.

<summary>This page analyzes the binding nature of different types of vows, concluding that baptismal promises are not "new" vows but professions of faith, and that vows (like Jephthah's) are invalid if they lack discretion or violate the natural law.</summary>

The previous page concluded that baptismal promises are a "common vow" or profession of faith rather than a new voluntary obligation added to the commandments. Here, Soto begins Question 2 to determine if every vow is strictly obligatory under penalty of sin.</meta>

Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,

# QUESTION TWO, Concerning the Strength and Virtue of a Vow.

->Saint Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica II-II, question 88, article 3.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether every vow binds one to its observance.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or theologian, at a writing desk with books.</image-desc>

Having established the substance of a vow, it follows to investigate its strength and virtue. First, we ask about its binding power: specifically, whether every vow is obligatory.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
The argument is first made for the negative side. A vow, as we have said, is a promise made to God. However, a simple promise made to men does not bind. In civil law, not everyone who makes a promise is compelled to pay it. Furthermore, since God has no need of our goods, He is not considered a more demanding collector of promises than a human being is. Therefore, a vow does not always bind.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued that if a vow were obligatory, it would follow that no amount of fear could excuse the person vowing from breaking that vow. Just as it is not permissible to violate any law of God because of fear, so too one could not undertake any vow that one does not fulfill in the best of faith. However, the consequence is false because a vow must be spontaneous and voluntary; yet, according to Aristotle, fear stands in the way of the will. <note>In Aristotelian ethics, actions done out of fear are considered "mixed," neither fully voluntary nor fully involuntary.</note>

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
¶ Third, no one is bound to the impossible. It often happens in practice that someone who has vowed something cannot fulfill the vow—either because it depends on someone else (for example, if a man vows to enter a religious order but the monks refuse to admit him) or if a woman who had vowed virginity subsequently loses it through a lapse, or when someone who had vowed money is reduced to beggary. Therefore, a vow does not always bind.

<margin>Fourth [argument].</margin>
¶ Furthermore, fourth: If every vow bound the vower with a knot of fulfillment, it would follow that every vow must be fulfilled immediately; for what you owe, you are compelled to pay at once. However, it is not necessary to fulfill every vow immediately—for instance, when it was issued under a certain condition. Therefore, not every vow binds.

<margin>Fifth [argument].</margin>
¶ Fifth, it is argued that if every vow were binding, it would follow both that someone could bind a subordinate (such as a father binding a son) and also that someone who could not fulfill it personally would be held to do so through another person; both of which seem absurd.

¶ On the contrary is that passage from Ecclesiastes 5:
> Whatever you have vowed, render it. <note>original: "Quodcunque voueris redde."</note>

And it is much better not to vow than not to perform what was promised after the vow. For it is one thing to not take a piece of advice <note>Referring to a "counsel" or voluntary spiritual path.</note>, but it is another to violate justice.

<column-break/>

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Proof.</margin>
The solution to the question is easy and clear, consisting of a single conclusion: A vow, by its very nature and object, binds under the penalty of mortal crime and sacrilege. It is proven: Natural reason convinces us that the faith of a promise must be kept. From this, as Cicero says in Book 1 of *On Duties* <note>original: "1. de Off."</note>—from which Augustine also took his point in Letter 19 to Jerome:

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
<margin>Augustinus.</margin>
"Faith" <note>original: "Fides"</note>, he says, signifies by its two syllables that "what is said should be done" <note>original: "vt fiat quod dicitur." A common but historically inaccurate etymology where "Fi-des" is linked to "Fi-at" (let it be done) and "Dic-tum" (said).</note>. If men are held to one another by this law, they are held far more strictly to God: both by reason of His lordship, which He has over us by right of creation, and also by reason of the benefits with which He heaps upon us daily. From these things, the tightest bond of fidelity is born, by which men are held to pay their promises to God. Hence the Wise Man says that an unfaithful promise is most displeasing to God. From this it follows that a vow binds under the guilt of mortal sin. For although vowing is a work of "counsel" <note>A voluntary act of devotion not required for salvation.</note>, nevertheless, paying it is an act of justice, which cannot be violated without an injury to charity <note>In this context, "charity" refers to the love of God that sustains the life of the soul.</note>, as justice is most necessary among men. Whatever opposes charity, through which the soul lives, is a mortal sin.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ And second, the guilt is increased by reason of wounded religion. <gloss>Proof.</gloss> A promise made to men binds by the bond of justice; however, that which is made to God binds further by reason of religion <note>Here, "religion" is used in the sense of the moral virtue that renders to God the honor and worship due to Him.</note>. Therefore, to vow to God is an act of religion, and thus to pay it is an act of justice distinguished by religion. Therefore, on both counts, a vow binds by its nature under mortal guilt.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ No ambiguity remains in the conclusion, but there is this one thing—which is universal to all commands—that we can investigate regarding the vow: whether, by reason of the lightness of the matter, it can happen that the transgression of a vow is only a venial <note>A minor sin that does not destroy the relationship with God.</note> fault.

<margin>Another [opinion] here on the vow.</margin>
For it seems from the negative side that a vow is a stricter bond than an oath, and thus displays greater sanctity. Yet a false oath never becomes venial by reason of the matter, but in every individual instance is mortal.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
On the other hand, since it is common to every precept...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence "praecepto..." as indicated by the catchword "cepto" at the bottom. The next page will likely address how "light matter" (small issues) might affect the severity of breaking a vow.</meta>

<summary>This page argues that all valid vows are morally binding under the penalty of mortal sin because they are acts of justice and religious devotion toward God. Soto refutes arguments that vows are non-binding, grounding his reasoning in natural law, the etymology of "faith," and the biblical command to fulfill promises to the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>vows, obligation, mortal sin, justice, virtue of religion, Cicero, Saint Augustine, Saint Thomas Aquinas, sacrilege, fidelity</keywords>

--- Page 635 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Question 2, Article 1, regarding whether every vow is strictly binding under the threat of mortal sin. The previous page established the basic arguments for and against the binding power of vows. Here, Soto explores the distinction between mortal and venial sins in the context of breaking a vow, using the "gravity of the matter" as a primary criterion.</meta>

# Question II of Book Eight.

<margin>The previous assertion suggests this.</margin>
Since it appears that something can become a venial <note>A "venial" sin is a minor offense that does not completely break one's relationship with God, whereas a "mortal" sin is a grave offense that leads to spiritual death.</note> sin by way of a precept, it is evident that the same applies here. And so, I believe it must be indubitably confessed. And lest anyone perhaps shrink from believing this because of the sanctity of religion, I prove it to myself thus: A vow is a certain law that flows from a person's will—a law which one sets for oneself. Therefore, it ought not to bind otherwise than if it were a law established by the Church or by God Himself. Indeed, the necessity of a law seems more urgent than that of a vow. Yet a law, even if it binds under the guilt of mortal sin by its nature <note>original: "genere suo"</note>, nevertheless relaxes its rigor by reason of the lightness of the matter, so that its transgression is only venial. For stealing is mortal by its nature, but nevertheless, stealing a single penny <note>original: "obolum," a small coin of negligible value</note> is only a venial sin. Therefore, by equal reasoning, if I vow not to steal, then snatching one penny will only be a venial sin. If you should say that the loftiness of religion does not permit this, I certainly do not see it, since it is in no way repugnant to the precepts of faith and charity.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Second: the transgression of a vow, when there is not full deliberation, can thereby become venial;
<margin>Third.</margin>
therefore, it can also be so by reason of the matter. ¶ Third: If someone has vowed to recite the Rosary daily, they would not sin mortally because they omit one or two "Hail Marys" <note>original: "Ave"</note>, because neither ecclesiastical law nor even divine law binds us with such rigor to complete set psalms. ¶ Therefore, the conclusion is not doubtful when a tiny part of what you had vowed is skipped over.

<margin>Another doubt.</margin>
But a doubt remains when the whole thing you vowed is a light matter. For example, if you promised to give a penny to a poor person, or to say only one "Our Father" <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>, whether the omission of these is mortal. The affirmative side argues that since you omit the whole thing, you break your word. Nevertheless, I
<margin>Solution.</margin>
think such an omission is only venial. For while the matter is light, it makes no difference whether it is the whole object of the vow or a part. Wherefore, if you have made a vow to say one Creed <note>original: "Credo"</note> every day, even if you omit it every day, you never sin mortally. It is otherwise if perhaps you promised by vow to give a penny to the poor every day. In that case, although the omission of one payment or two is not mortal, you are nevertheless bound tomorrow for what you do not give today. Therefore, when the sum of the debt has grown large, the fault becomes mortal.

¶ Through these points, we respond to what we touched upon above. Namely, that if someone vows to avoid one venial sin, then committing that sin will be a double venial fault, because in these matters forbidden by law, a person does not intend to bind himself except in the manner of a law. Whence, if the law does not bind

<column-break/>

except under the guilt of venial sin, it seems the one vowing does not bind himself otherwise. Indeed (as you ought to consider more carefully here), it is not within the choice of the one vowing to bind himself under either mortal or venial guilt; rather, the quality of the fault must be weighed from the quantity and the necessity of the object.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ However, there is an argument against this. It may be that gambling, for example, ten or twenty ducats <note>Gold coins used as currency across Europe</note> before a vow is made is only venial, because prodigality <note>Wasteful spending</note> is by its nature only venial; and yet, after a vow is made, it becomes a mortal sacrilege.
<margin>Response.</margin>
It is responded that we do not deny that what was previously venial sometimes becomes mortal through a vow. For what was not evil—suppose, not giving alms—would be mortal once a vow is made. Indeed, perhaps gambling that money would be a virtue before the vow, and a mortal sin after the vow. But I say that one must look to the quantity. Whence, after you have established "not gambling" as a virtue in the category of religion and justice (where it was not before), the quantity of the object must be weighed; and as long as that quantity is grave, it will be mortal.

The difficulty of the question, therefore, does not lie in the question itself, but consists entirely in the solution of the arguments. In the first part, indeed, the
<margin>The question touched upon in the first argument.</margin>
doubt mentioned above is introduced: namely, whether a simple promise made to a person is obligatory. And when you hear "simple promise," understand it as that which is neither by reason of some preceding debt, nor confirmed by an oath, but when someone of their own accord promises anything to a friend with a simple word. And indeed, there is no one who doubts that in such a promise there is always some obligation, because at the very least it is an assertion, such that if you do not fulfill the thing, you have lied. Every lie is a transgression, at least a venial one; but the doubt is whether by its nature it binds under mortal guilt. And indeed, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas</note>, in the second part of the second part [of the Summa], both in question 88 and more
<margin>Cajetan's opinion.</margin>
clearly in question 113, recognizes no other force of obligation in a simple promise than this one just mentioned. He thinks, I say, that the obligation of a promise pertains to no other virtue than to that which is moral truth—namely, speaking the truth. For that reason, he says that not fulfilling it is, by its nature, nothing other than a lie. Therefore, from the object itself, it is not mortal unless it becomes harmful from elsewhere—as if you vowed something that mattered much to another, such as bringing help to a friend against an enemy, or marrying his daughter, which you then did not fulfill. ¶ But
<margin>A simple promise generally...</margin>
indeed, the truth seems to stand to the contrary. For...

# Friar Domingo Soto, on Justice and Right,

<margin>A promise binds under mortal sin by its nature.</margin>
<margin>Proof.</margin>
Indeed, a simple promise binds, by its very nature, under the guilt of mortal sin, unless it is rendered venial <note>A "venial" sin is a minor spiritual offense, whereas a "mortal" sin is a grave violation that severs one's relationship with God.</note> due to the lightness of the matter. The reasoning for this holds a root contrary to that of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534) was a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas with whom Soto often engaged in dialogue.</note>. For truly, making a promise does not simply pertain to the virtue of truth-telling, but is reduced to **commutative justice** <note>Commutative justice governs the fairness of exchanges and promises between individuals.</note>. For it is not merely asserting what is true in any way, but rather binding one’s word to another.
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
Wherefore, as Cicero says in Book 1 of *On Duties* <note>original: "De Officiis"</note>, this "good faith" <note>original: "fides"</note> not only pertains to justice but is the very foundation of justice itself, upon which all human agreements and pacts rely. From this, therefore, it is argued: A sin which by its nature opposes charity is mortal; failing to fulfill a promise is such a thing, since it is the subversion of justice, which is the bond of human society. It is therefore by its nature a mortal sin, insofar as a great harm is inflicted upon one's neighbor who
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
placed his trust in the promisor. Furthermore, a promise made to God binds under the guilt of mortal sin, not only insofar as it is an act of religious worship, but also insofar as it is a duty of justice; therefore, the same applies to a promise made to a man, because in this respect, they are of the same kind.
<margin>Final reason.</margin>
To these points, it is the estimation of all nations to curse a violator of faith as a wicked man; and the public voice is the voice of nature; therefore, it binds under the guilt of mortal sin. Hence, what Solomon says—that an unfaithful promise is displeasing to God, which denotes a mortal fault—is extended to every promise, even that which is made to a human being.
<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But if you should object to the word of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto’s work.</note>, who says here that a promise binds only according to "decency" <note>original: "honestatem"</note>, where he seems to exclude the obligation of justice (for "decency" is usually used for that which is not strictly necessary for justice):
<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is responded that he does not accept "decency" so as to exclude justice, but rather to exclude the **civil forum** <note>The "civil forum" refers to human law courts, as opposed to the "internal forum" of the soul or God's judgment.</note>. He does not, I say, deny that it is an obligation of justice, but he suggests that as far as the civil tribunal is concerned, a simple promise is not sufficient unless it is confirmed by an oath, a writing, or witnesses. Indeed, even regarding the decency of justice in the forum of God, conditions can occur that remove the force of the obligation. For instance, if what I promised you later becomes useless or harmful to you—such as if I promised you a sword which I later see you wish to misuse. Or if it becomes impossible or ruinous for the promisor—as if I promised money which I later cannot return due to misfortune. Or if you have shown me signs of ingratitude.
<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ Against this obligation of a promise,

<column-break/>

the custom of wills <note>original: "testamentorum ritus"</note> seems to stand. For as long as the testator lives, he can freely change all bequests, nor is he considered bound to fulfill them; and yet a bequest is seen as a kind of promise. It is responded, however, that bequests are not properly promises that have any firmness until the death of the testator, by which (as Paul says) a testament is confirmed. Wherefore all things are to be referred to that final moment.
¶ In addition to these things, it should be recalled from the previous sections that a simple assertion of the future is not always a promise. For if you say "I will do it," you are only expressing what you have in your intention; you are not thereafter bound unless you utter it in the sense of "I promise to do it"—as when someone asks something of you and you reply, "I will do it." Otherwise, as we have already said above, you are able to change your mind.
<margin>Another difficulty.</margin>
¶ It is a somewhat more difficult question whether a promise which you make to a person in your mind alone is binding. For Saint Thomas in Article 1 seemed to deny this, saying that a promise made by a man to a man cannot be made except through words. Reasoning also supports this. For an obligation 
<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
is between two people; but a man does not speak to a man except through words or outward signs; therefore he is not able to bind himself to another otherwise. Perhaps this is a problem if we stay strictly within the mere law of nature and conscience. For in the external forum, it is manifest that a mental obligation—indeed, not even every obligation made to an absent person—is binding. But in conscience, perhaps one can argue for either side. And although it happens very rarely in practice, it is nonetheless necessary to know, if it should occur, whether
<margin>The other side, which is closest to reason, is persuaded by the following arguments.</margin>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
the conscience of the promisor remains bound. And that it *is* obligatory, there are indeed arguments not to be regretted. First: Words are signs of concepts; if therefore a word binds, it is only from the force of the concept. And since a mental promise is truly a speech, it cannot—if not fulfilled—lack a lie <note>original: "mendacium"</note>, which is by its intrinsic nature a fault. Next: when you have only deliberated on a matter in your mind and intended to do it,
<margin>Second.</margin>
you are not yet bound; therefore, if you add to this by speaking in your mind, "I promise such money to such a needy friend," you have added some degree of obligation to what preceded.
<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third: If you had confirmed such a promise in your mind with an oath, you would remain bound to fulfill it; and yet a promissory oath does not bind except by virtue of the preceding promise; therefore the promise was binding. Fourth: if afterward
<margin>Fourth.</margin>
you had conceived no other promise in your mind, but later notified that friend of the one you had made...
