# Book Eight, Question II.

<margin>Fifth.</margin>
...saying: "I promise you nothing now, but nevertheless yesterday at my house I pledged this to you: see if you consider the promise accepted." In that case, you would seem to be bound, therefore, by the virtue of the prior promise. **Fifth.** If you promise something by word to a deaf person who hears nothing, or similarly if you say in the presence of one person, "I promise this to such-and-and-such an absent friend," the promise seems to hold in conscience, whatever the case may be in the civil court. Therefore, even if it is made in the mind, it is
<margin>Objection.</margin>
a promise in absence. ¶ But if you argue to the contrary: A promise depends on the acceptance of the other; therefore, before he knows of it, it does not hold. I indeed
<margin>Solutio.</margin>
confess this: but nevertheless, what we contend is nothing other than that he who has promised to another in his mind is bound to signify it to him; and if the other wishes to accept it, he is bound to fulfill it. However, when a promise is mutual—for example, "I give that you may give" or "I do that you may do," as is the case with matrimonial consent—then a mental promise is not sufficient unless it is externally evident to both parties. By the same logic, no other contract would hold—such as buying or selling—unless consent were externally signified. Regarding a simple promise, however, several arguments seem to persuade by probability; but perhaps it is more probable that a promise made only in the mind does not bind. For before the other person knows of it, it can be rescinded and changed, as I remember saying in Book 4, in the question on the transfer of ownership. This is because, since it is natural for humans to signify their thoughts with words or signs, no obligation seems to result before the promise is signified. ¶ In the second argument, the issue of fear <note>original: "metus"</note> is touched upon. For it is most firmly established that a vow must be voluntary. Ignorance, force, and fear stand in the way of the will, as Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BC) discusses the voluntary nature of actions in Book 3 of his *Nicomachean Ethics*, a foundation for later medieval legal theory.</note> is the authority in Book 3 of the *Ethics*. Regarding ignorance, enough has been said in the first argument. Concerning fear, it remains to respond in the present circumstances in this manner. First, it is confessed that fear prevents a vow from binding for the reason already stated: because it takes away the
<margin>Twofold fear.</margin>
voluntary nature. But truly, since fear is manifold, a doubt remains whether every fear has the same power of hindrance. For it is solemn practice to make vows in danger of death, which it would indeed be a crime not to fulfill afterward. Therefore, two types of fear are distinguished: one struck from without <note>original: "forinfecùs incussus," also known as extrinsic fear—fear caused by an external human agent.</note>, and the other arising from within <note>original: "ab intrinseco," or intrinsic fear—fear arising from natural circumstances like illness or storms.</note>. And indeed, imminent fear from without prevents a vow from binding unless it is later freely ratified and made firm; but that which is from within does not take away the obligation. This distinction is most widely accepted, not only by theologians but also by jurists,
<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
as is clear in Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), nicknamed "Panormitanus," was one of the most famous canon lawyers of the Middle Ages.</note> in the chapter *Sicut*, 2, regarding the rule. Indeed, both of these conclusions are sanctions of Canon Law. The first—

<column-break/>

<margin>Explanation of the above assertion.</margin>
—is indeed found in the chapter *Relatum*, concerning those things which are done through force or fear, where a woman who had uttered a vow of religion <note>A "vow of religion" usually refers to a commitment to enter a monastery or convent.</note> out of fear of her husband is absolved. The second is found in the same cited chapter *Sicut*, regarding the rule, where a cleric who had vowed to become a monk due to excessive illness is compelled to be a monk. ¶ But it must be carefully weighed what is considered fear from an external source that provides an excuse in these circumstances. For it is not enough that it be struck by an external thing; for a vow uttered in a shipwreck out of fear of the turbulent sea holds. Nor is it required to be struck by a human; for one who, cast into chains or dragged to a hanging, utters a vow, remains bound, although the fear is from a human. Rather, it is required that it be struck through **injustice** <note>original: "iniuriam." This implies a moral or legal wrong committed by the person inducing the fear.</note>. Yet even that is not enough; for if a Turk holds you captive and you make a vow to God or the divine Virgin to snatch you from there, it truly holds. Similarly, if you make a vow when attacked by an enemy in conflict so that you might escape unharmed. It is required, therefore, that it be struck by a person through injustice intending to extort such a vow. For example, if he says: "I will kill you unless you vow." Wherefore, the reason for this distinction is drawn from the fact that fear arising from within is offered by God, who does injury to no one; but that which is brought by a human is born from injustice. But although it perhaps comes to the same thing, the genuine reason is that a vow made through fear from without is not voluntary like the other. For he who vows when struck by external fear in no way considers what he vows as pleasing; and therefore he does not accept it of his own accord, but only to defend himself from the enemy. When, however, the fear is from within, because no battle with an enemy exists, he considers it pleasing to vow so that he may merit divine protection, by which he may be freed from danger. And therefore it is voluntary in a different way than before. Moreover, an example from human affairs shows that this holds. For while lying gravely ill, you promise a large reward to a doctor out of fear of death if you survive; thus the vow holds because you choose that means to be saved. Much better, then, will a vow uttered to God hold. ¶ Nonetheless, several arguments are raised against this truth. The first is: An
<margin>First argument against these statements. Canon: "If by swearing," etc., Question 6, where they are absolved. Solution.</margin>
oath extorted through fear, even the kind that would affect a steadfast man, binds absolutely. But a vow, by its nature, because it is made to God, binds with greater rigor than an oath. Therefore, a similar vow binds. The consequence is denied. For even if a vow, because it is made to God...

### Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Perhaps read as: of the one vowing.</margin>
...binds one to God more strictly than an oath made to a human being; nevertheless, an oath has a different nature of obligation than a vow. For the obligation of a vow depends solely and purely on the will of the <insert>one vowing</insert>: and therefore, fear directed at that same will, by removing the voluntary nature of the act, removes the obligation. However, the bond of an oath results and depends not from the will of the one swearing, but from the very nature of an oath. For there is a reverence due to the divine name such that what you swear, you must never allow to be false, in whatever manner you swear it, provided you are of sound mind.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 3; see also the chapter *Maiores* under the title "On Baptism".</margin>
The second argument is: Is a consensus expressed externally through fear truly a consensus? For Aristotle says in Book 3 of the *Ethics* that he who casts his goods into the waves during a shipwreck "simply" wills it, although "conditionally" <note>original: "simpliciter vult, licèt conditionaliter nollet"</note> he would not want to. Therefore, a vow is "simply" voluntary, and thus it holds. There is no shortage of legal experts who give their support to this argument: namely, confessing that if the one vowing gave consent—by whatever fear they were compelled—it holds in conscience before God. It is otherwise, however, in the ecclesiastical court.

<margin>The solution of Panormitanus.</margin>
<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
This is the opinion of Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as "Panormitanus" because he was the Archbishop of Palermo.</note> in the chapter *Cum locum* regarding betrothals, which is supported by Silvester <note>Silvester Mazzolini da Prierio, an influential theologian.</note> under the word "fear," section 8. Whence, regarding that cited chapter on things done through force or fear, they respond that the Pope absolved that woman who had vowed out of fear, assuming she had not given true consent. By a similar reasoning, the Church absolves those who legitimately prove they were in fear; for if it were established that they had truly consented, the Church would certainly not absolve them.

<margin>Refutation of Panormitanus’s solution.</margin>
But truly, with all due respect to these grave Doctors, they argue poorly. Indeed, even if the accused admits that they gave consent, if they nevertheless prove the fear with legitimate witnesses, it is the custom that they be absolved. This is proved by a similar example in marriage: whenever it is celebrated under a fear that would affect a "constant man," <note term="constant man">original: "constantem virum." A legal standard referring to a person of firm and reasonable character, not easily swayed by trifles.</note> it is held as void in the court of the Church. This is clear from the chapters *Cum locum* and *Veniens* regarding betrothals, and Question 5 of Case 33, in the canon *Notificasti*. And the reason is that, since the obligation of a vow has its origin only in the choice of the one vowing, it is natural that while that will is compelled by necessity, the vow is not legitimate—especially because a vow is a "work of counsel," <note term="work of counsel">A "work of counsel" (opus consilii) refers to a virtuous act that is encouraged but not strictly commanded by divine law, such as a vow of poverty.</note> to which fear and force are repugnant.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
From this it follows that the same fear which prevents a vow from binding at the time it is uttered also washes away the guilt of transgressing that same vow by way of excuse. For example: if you vowed to fast on the Sabbath, or

<column-break/>

not to gamble, or to give alms, and afterward a fear of death is struck into you to make you do the opposite: then by doing the opposite you are excused, unless a tyrant threatened you with it in contempt of religion. For the same cause that acts as an obstacle to a promise so that it does not bind also brings with it an excuse for the transgression. Furthermore, this is proved by the reasoning established above: namely, that a vow does not bind except in the manner of a law. However, ecclesiastical law does not compel one to fast with such rigor that it would strive to drive us to death for its observation, unless an infidel tyrant threatened us with it specifically in contempt of the law.

<margin>A grave doubt.</margin>
But a graver and more intricate doubt at present is whether what has been said—namely, that fear inflicted from the outside through injury prevents the obligation of a vow—should be understood universally regarding all fear, whether it be grave or light. And first, there is a universal consensus among all that any fear falling upon a "constant man" removes that quality of "the voluntary" which is necessary for binding. But it is not yet sufficiently discovered among everyone just who should be considered a "constant man" upon whom such fear falls.

<margin>Opinion of the Lawyers.</margin>
For there is a common opinion of certain lawyers, and indeed of theologians, which at first glance carries the appearance of truth: namely, that fear falling upon a constant man is that to which a constant man does not succumb so as to do what he ought not. However, this definition is both false and appears to "beg the question." <note term="beg the question">petitio principii: a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note>

<margin>First reason against the previous opinion.</margin>
For it would follow from this that no fear, no matter how much it was of the most atrocious death, for which a man would transgress natural and divine law, should be considered to "fall upon a constant man." This is because whoever is driven by any fear to transgress such a law is not a "constant man." For the principle of virtue binds us to suffer death rather than to steal, or lie, or do anything similar which is intrinsically evil. And yet, surely the fear of death by its very nature "falls upon a constant man," as the matter is self-evident, since of all terrifying things, death is the most terrifying.

<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
And that the same definition begs the question is clear from this: when the question was whether some fear removed the obligation of a marriage or a vow because it was "falling upon a constant man," a loophole would easily open for someone to say that such fear did not fall upon a constant man simply because he did what he ought not have done because of that fear. Therefore, the very word itself teaches us the legitimate description of such fear. For that fear is...

<meta>The catchword "le est" suggests the next page continues "Metus enim ille est..." (For that fear is...)</meta>

Soto refutes circular legal definitions of a "constant man," arguing that even virtuous people naturally fear death, which can excuse them from religious obligations not strictly commanded by divine law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how fear affects the validity of religious vows, specifically defining the legal and theological standard of "fear that would affect a steadfast man" to determine when a person is truly excused from their promises.</meta>

### Book Eight, Question II.

<margin>What constitutes fear that would affect a steadfast man.</margin>
"Fear that falls upon a steadfast man" <note>original: "metus cadens in constantem virum," a standard in Roman and Canon law referring to a level of pressure that would compel even a person of average courage</note> is that which the very nature of a steadfast man allows him to experience. That is to say, it is a fear that a man can feel without losing his reputation for fortitude, as it is not contradictory to be both steadfast and afraid; indeed, one part of courage is to fear when it is appropriate to do so. However, it must be particularly noted that no fear—no matter how great or how much it might affect even the most steadfast man—excuses one from the sin of breaking divine or natural laws. For instance, if a threat of death is made against a young woman to force her to submit to sexual assault, that fear is truly "falling upon a steadfast person," for even the bravest woman would fear it. Nevertheless, if she were to consent to the act because of that fear, she would not be acting with steadfastness. On the other hand, if because of that same fear a person were to break an ecclesiastical fast or fail to hear Mass on a feast day, they would not be considered inconstant. This is because such laws of the Church do not bind with such severity that we must always choose death over their violation. Therefore, simply because someone succumbs to fear does not mean the fear itself ceases to be "falling upon a steadfast man"; in such cases, the fear provides an excuse so that the one succumbing does not act against what they are truly obligated to do.

<margin>Solution to the proposed doubt.</margin>
It is this type of fear, then, that removes the obligation of a vow.

<margin>A point of doubt.</margin>
¶ However, the reader’s curiosity will not be satisfied here; perhaps they will ask further: how is fear to be weighed so it can be recognized as "falling upon a steadfast man"? Specifically, does this fear consist of a single, indivisible standard that is the same for everyone?

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
To this it is answered that there are three main headings from which such a judgment must be drawn. First, regarding the **object** of the fear: for fear of death—which is the most terrible of all temporal evils—is certainly judged to fall upon a steadfast man. Under the name of "death," we also include exile and life imprisonment. Indeed, we include even significant infamy <note>loss of reputation or legal standing</note>, which men usually dread no less than death itself. Second, it is weighed regarding the **manner** in which the fear is inflicted. For if a woman, or a child, or an unarmed man were to threaten you with death, that fear would not be judged to "fall upon a steadfast man." But thirdly (and this must be carefully considered here), it is weighed regarding the **subject** <note>the person experiencing the fear</note>. For the rightful steadfastness of men does not consist of a single point, but has its own range or "latitude." Not everyone can, or must, possess the strength of a Theseus or a Hercules. Nevertheless, there is a line beyond which there would be no

<column-break/>

steadfastness at all. Therefore, a fear that is compatible with the degree of steadfastness found within that range is considered "falling upon a steadfast man." Consequently, a fear that might excuse a woman, or an old man whose "heat of the blood" has already failed him, would not excuse another man. Thus, by the word "man," we understand a strength of soul relative to each person's condition. From this it follows that if a girl enters a religious order because of fear of her parents—a fear that is terrible relative to her condition, especially if they treat her harshly with words and deeds unless she allows herself to be thrust into a monastery—certainly a vow uttered with such consent would not hold. Let parents therefore take counsel for themselves and their children, so that they might relax such harshness in forcing them. To conclude the matter, "light fear"—that is, fear weaker than that which falls upon a steadfast man—neither hinders the obligation of a vow nor excuses its transgression.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you argue that even these sorts of vows are not entirely spontaneous, since they are made by reason of fear:

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered that "light fear" in spiritual matters, such as in vows and marriage, is not even considered under the name of "fear." Regarding civil law and the courts, we dispute nothing here; rather, we refer the reader to the laws and judicial rulings to see which fear voids a contract and which does not.

<margin>Subject of the third argument.</margin>
The third argument, which holds the second place in the writings of Saint Thomas Aquinas, opens up several subjects for discussion. The first concerns those for whom it is impossible to fulfill a vow: whether because they are in such a state of impossibility through no fault of their own, or because they have blocked their own path to keeping the promise. The first part relates to one who has vowed to enter a religious order, but the monks refuse to let him join. Concerning this, Saint Thomas judges that a distinction must be made. Either the person’s intention was to vow a religious life in a general and primary sense (though they later chose a specific house out of personal devotion), or their primary purpose was to bind themselves only to *this* specific order or *this* specific place. In the first case, they are bound to seek entry into that monastery with good faith and diligence. If they are not admitted there, they are bound to go to another; and finally, if access to that specific order is not open to them, they are bound to try another and then another, so that it is not their own fault that they do not take up the habit. But if the intention of vowing was only for a specific house or a specific order, then if they are rejected or excluded, they are not bound to go to another; but

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>St. Thomas clarifies this.</margin> ...is free from the vow. ¶ In these cases, first of all, the object of the vow must be carefully weighed. Suppose you vowed to enter the religious life <note>term: "religious life" (Latin: *religio*). In this context, it refers specifically to joining a monastic or mendicant order, such as the Dominicans or Franciscans, rather than "religion" in the broad modern sense.</note> in general. Because you did not specify this or that order in the object of your vow, then even if you are more inclined toward one than another, you are not more obligated to that one than to any other. If, however, you specified not just the general state of religious life but this specific order in the object of your vow, you ought to approach that one first, and if rejected from there, seek others. Therefore, if your vow was to enter this particular house—perhaps one where study flourishes—and you suffer a rejection from the monks, you are by no means bound to investigate another, even of the same order and even if it is of better observance. Nor should anyone cause you any spiritual anxiety <note>original: "scrupulum," a "scruple" or nagging doubt of conscience</note> to the contrary, because your vow was not issued with any other religious intent than for this specific convent. Therefore, even if the same religious rule flourishes in another house, it is nothing to you. By the same logic, if you vowed to enter a specific order—namely ours <note>the Dominicans</note>, or that of St. Francis, or another specifically—you are indeed bound to visit several convents, and if you are not admitted, you are not bound to another order. If, however, you vowed to enter the religious life in general, then <margin>A doubt.</margin> you are bound to try others. ¶ But there is a doubt as to whether you are bound to travel to every convent and every religious order. It appears so; for after you have issued a vow that depends on all of them, you ought to investigate all of those upon whom your vow depends. On the contrary, it is argued that you would then have to travel the whole world, which would be a most burdensome task. Likewise, if you were not received into well-established convents, you might have to enter one where religious discipline has collapsed, which would not be safe for your salvation. <margin>The answer.</margin> Therefore, the first answer is that everyone must first consult their own intention and what it was: for if it was only to commit oneself to those orders that were surrounding and known to them, they are not bound to travel beyond them. Furthermore, even if someone did not so restrict their intention but vowed to enter religious life absolutely, they are not bound to travel through all regions. For neither have the French ever traveled to us for this reason, nor any of our people to them. Otherwise, you would even have to wander as far as Greece and the Islands for the same reason. Truly, the law of nature itself wisely teaches that vows of this kind are to be fulfilled within our own kingdom and language. For who would make a vow if they were bound to visit unknown nations because of it? But if you <margin>A concern.</margin> inquire more insistently whether you are at least compelled to visit every

<column-break/>

convent in your own region, it appears that reason at least demands this, since the vow depends on all of them. <margin>The solution.</margin> The answer is that the obligation does not extend so widely. For when you devote yourself to a certain religious order, you are only bound to approach it in good faith. However, this "approaching the whole" is not to be understood in a metaphysical or logical sense—that every single convent must be visited—but in a moral sense. For a person is said to have investigated the whole order who has gone around a good part of it: namely, if they visit five or a few more convents. For it is possible to judge the rest from a few. ¶ From what <margin>A deduction.</margin> has been said, it clearly follows that anyone who has some impediment to religious life—which they either did not consider when they made the vow, or which they incurred after the vow, whether without fault or through their own fault—is made free from the obligation of such a vow. For no one is legally compelled to do the impossible. For instance, if you specifically vowed to enter that order where converts from other faiths <note>original: "neophyti," neophytes, often referring to those of Jewish or Muslim descent in Soto's Spain</note> are not admitted, as soon as you find this out, you are not bound to enter that one nor any other. The same applies if you suffer from a permanent illness or are subject to another permanent impediment for which the laws reject you; you are safe in your conscience, and you do not need any dispensation. It is otherwise if the impediments are only temporary: for example, if you are suffering from a quartan fever <note>a form of malaria where the fever recurs every four days</note>, you are bound to fulfill the vow once it passes. Here, a theological axiom mentioned by St. Thomas (in the fourth book, distinction 38, article 3) must be committed to memory: namely, whatever would have prevented the making of a vow if it were present, also removes the obligation once the vow has been made. However, lest this deceive anyone, it must be referred to the obligation of the vow, not to the hindrance of the will of the person vowing. For example: that illness which, if it were present while you were vowing, would have prevented the obligation, also removes that same obligation if it arrives after the vow. Nevertheless, even if after issuing the vow you experience some difficulty which, had you known it beforehand, would have stopped you from vowing, the obligation of the vow does not cease for that reason. Otherwise, all marriages would be dissolved, and all the cloisters of the religious would be emptied. ¶ What if you are rejected because you do not know grammar <note>in this period, "grammar" specifically meant the ability to read and write Latin</note>, or you do not know some other duty required to be received among the lay brothers <note>original: "professos laicos," members of the order who were not ordained priests but performed manual labor and service</note>? Are you bound to learn grammar or another trade? To this, one should not answer simply, but with discretion. For indeed, when someone has issued a vow of religious life, intending it for an order that is initiated into holy orders, yet believed in good faith that it was not required to know Latin...

### Question II of Book Eight

...if it is later required of him, he does not truly appear obligated to learn Latin <note>term: "Grammar" (Latin: *Grammatica*). In this era, this specifically referred to the study of Latin, which was the essential language for Church liturgy, law, and scholarship.</note>: nor is he held to enter the rank of the lay brothers <note>term: "lay brothers" (Latin: *laici*). These were members of a religious order who focused on manual labor and service rather than the priesthood or the chanting of the Divine Office.</note>: because his ignorance seems to excuse the man. Likewise, if he vowed the religious life of the lay brothers, he is not held to learn any difficult trade, because he thought it was not necessary. However, when someone vows religious life under common law <note>original: "communi lege," referring to the standard rules and requirements governing religious orders</note>, then I believe he is held to learn Latin—provided he has the capacity—because he knew it was necessary; otherwise, he is held to enter so that he may be assigned to the rank of the lay brothers.

<margin>An excellent doubt</margin>
¶ However, an excellent doubt remains: whether someone who has suffered a rejection or has been excluded from a religious order is held to keep the rule of that order as much as possible, and to fulfill the religious duties. I said "suffered a rejection" or "excluded." For a "rejected" person is one who is not admitted; an "excluded" person is one who, due to being incorrigible <note>meaning someone who refuses to correct their bad behavior</note>, is stripped of the habit and cast out. The judgment for each is not the same. Therefore, let us first dispute the former case. And we are speaking of one who sought in good faith to profess the religious life, but was simply unable to do so.

<margin>First argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
Regarding him, it is argued for the affirmative side—namely, that he remains nonetheless bound to what he is able to do. A girl who has made a vow of virginity, if she later loses that flower through her own fault, must nonetheless observe perpetual continence <note>original: "continentiam," refraining from sexual activity</note>, as Saint Thomas and the Doctors <note>the "Doctors" refers to established, authoritative theologians of the Church</note> consistently assert here. In the vow of religious life, just as in the vow of virginity, chastity is included; therefore, one who vows religious life, even if he is rejected, is held to observe perpetual continence, and thus cannot even seek his marital debt <note>term: "marital debt" (Latin: *debitum*). This refers to the obligation of spouses to provide sexual intimacy to one another within a marriage; a person bound by a vow of chastity would be forbidden from this.</note>.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second. If someone vows to give ten to the poor, or to endure the fasts of Advent, but cannot pay the whole amount, he is held to do what he can. Therefore, the law is the same for those who have vowed religious life.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third. While one solemnly confirms a vow, he is held to all the offices and duties established in that same religious life. A simple vow, however, has as its object a solemn vow; for he who vows simply is held at the lawful time to establish the vow with solemnity. Therefore, he is equally held to perform and fulfill those same religious duties as far as he is able.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
¶ Fourth. Added to this are the texts concerning the conversion of married persons: the canon *Quidam* and the canon *Placet*, in which the same opinion is defined. For the case of the first chapter is that a certain man entered religious life against his wife's will, and subsequently, upon her...

<column-break/>

...seeking him, he was recalled to the secular world <note>the "secular world" refers to life outside the monastery or cloister</note>. After the death of that same wife, he intended to move on to a second marriage. However, Alexander III <note>Pope Alexander III (reigned 1159–1181), an important figure in the development of Canon Law.</note>, having been consulted on the matter, although he did not force him back into the cloisters of the religious life, nonetheless forbade him from taking a second wife. The same is decided in the second chapter regarding a woman who, thinking her husband had died, entered a monastery. When she was later removed from there by her spouse and then later widowed, she attempted to marry a second time, and yet she was forbidden.

<margin>Solution to the previous doubt.</margin>
¶ Notwithstanding these points, it is answered under a distinction: that if the person who vowed religious life explicitly stated "continence" in his intention, he is held to observe it while remaining in the secular world. If, however, he vowed nothing else but religious life, to which he is not received, he is free to the extent that he is not held to perform anything of the religious life in the secular world.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is proved. If such a person were held either to chastity or to another religious duty, it would be either by virtue of that same vow, or because having suffered a rejection, entry becomes impossible for him. It is neither of these; therefore [he is not bound]. The minor premise <note>note: "minor premise" refers to the second part of a logical syllogism.</note> is proved. For if he were held by reason of the vow, that obligation would begin immediately from the time it was issued; however, experience shows this to be most false. For who would assert that one who has taken a simple vow of the Carthusians <note>term: "Carthusians" (Latin: *Carthusienses*). A Catholic religious order of enclosed monastics known for their extreme austerity, silence, and total abstinence from meat.</note> is immediately bound both to recite the Psalms and to abstain from meat? That he should be held by reason of the rejection is much more improbable. For that rejection was not within his power. Therefore, it did not entangle him in a new bond; thus, he is in no way held to fulfill any religious duty in the secular world.

<margin>Second proof.</margin>
¶ Second, this is argued so that the legitimate cause may be made clear. No one is obligated by virtue of a vow except to that which is its proper object. The object proposed by the one who simply vowed religious life was only the religious life itself. Therefore, he is held only to that; and if he cannot fulfill it, he becomes immune from the vow. But perhaps you rise up with an opposite view:

<margin>Objection.</margin>
He who is obligated to something is simultaneously obligated to that which follows from it. Since the institutes of religious life follow from the religious life itself, he who vowed religious life simply, vowed everything else by virtue of that.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
This argument is not only not contrary, but actually favors our opinion. For he who promises to take up a certain state of life does not obligate himself to the laws of that state until he actually takes up that state: because he is not...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...does not express in his vow an obligation to the specific laws of that state. Since, therefore, "religion" <note>term: "religion" (Latin: *religio*). In this legal context, "religion" refers specifically to the state of living under a religious rule in a monastery or order, rather than general belief.</note> is a certain state, although you have promised to take it up, you are not bound by its laws until you actually assume it. Indeed, those laws do not bind anyone except those who profess that state, as they are the ones who have expressly obligated themselves to them. An example is found in Christianity. For all mortals are bound to accept Christianity; and yet, until they profess it through baptism, they are not bound by the laws of our sacraments, nor to other laws peculiar to us that are not of natural law. The example of one who has made a vow to take holy orders pertains to the same point: for he is not bound to recite the ecclesiastical psalms <note>original: "psalmos recitare"; referring to the Divine Office, the daily cycle of prayers required of clergy</note> before he is initiated into the sacred rites, and thus he is not bound to observe chastity except insofar as it is prohibited by divine law. The same, therefore, applies to one who has made a simple vow of religion. He can not only render the marital debt to his spouse, but also seek it for himself in turn.

<margin>To the arguments made to the contrary.</margin>
¶ And by this, the argument previously raised is resolved. For the following logic does not hold: "A solemn vow obligates one to the specific statutes of a religious order, and that is the object of a simple vow; therefore, a simple vow also obligates one to the same." For a solemn vow is "completive," as they say: namely, it is the profession of a state by which each person expressly says they vow obedience, chastity, and poverty; and the laws bind those who have professed. A simple vow, however, only obligates you to take up the state. And the response is the same regarding those canons cited above concerning the conversion of married persons. For those individuals had issued solemn vows by explicitly promising chastity; and therefore, insofar as they could obligate themselves without their spouse's consent, they were bound. They were able to obligate themselves never to seek the use of marriage; and for that reason, they were prohibited from passing on to a second marriage. But because the vow did not hold regarding other matters, they were not called back into the religious life after their spouses died.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other argument—namely, concerning the person who vowed the "whole": where if the whole is not valid, he must pay the "part"—no example is brought to the matter, since he who vowed the whole, formally vowed the part.

<margin>To the first</margin>
But regarding the woman who dedicated her virginity to God, a distinction must be made. For one can vow virginity in two ways. One way is looking properly at the thing itself, so that her intention was only to abstain from the "first Venus" <note>original: "prima Venere"; a classical euphemism for the first act of sexual intercourse</note>; for this is what usually happens. In that case, once that virginity is lost, she is no longer bound to chastity, because her purpose was entirely centered on 

<column-break/>

preserving the physical integrity of the flesh. If, however, she issued a vow of virginity simply and without any qualification, then even if she has been deflowered, she is nonetheless bound to chastity. This is because such a vow is simply negative: that is, "not to know a man." Therefore, every time she experiences one, she violates the vow. For that reason, no example can be drawn from this for the man who vowed to enter a religious order.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ If you should ask here in passing whether a woman who vowed "not to marry" is thereafter held to a vow of chastity—so that every time she commits fornication she sins doubly—it would seem so, because a woman does not marry so that she may live chastely.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that, nonetheless, a vow of this kind by its very nature does not obligate one to chastity unless something else is expressed. For the subject matter of chastity is twofold. One is that which is opposed to lust. This is the common matter of both commandment and vow, and it is what a person who professes a religious order obligates themselves to. The other is a matter of "supererogation" <note>term: "supererogation" (Latin: *supererogationis*). This refers to performing more than what is strictly required by duty or commandment; doing an "extra" good deed.</note>, which is properly the subject of a vow: namely, to abstain from the marriage bed. And she who only vows "not to marry" obligates herself only to this: that is, not to place an obstacle (marriage) in the way of her religious life. Therefore, if she commits fornication, she sins by a simple disgrace <note>meaning she has committed the sin of fornication, but has not additionally broken a religious vow of chastity</note>.

<margin>Scruple.</margin>
¶ What if she vowed not to marry with the purpose of being able to act as a prostitute more freely?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that this vow is in no way obligatory, because it concerns an evil thing. For the object, which is "not to marry," is then directed toward an evil end, and thus it is corrupted. For that reason, she transgresses the vow neither by marrying nor by committing fornication. ¶ Thus far, we have discussed the person who, through no fault of their own, encounters an impossibility in fulfilling a vow.

<margin>Another question.</margin>
It follows, then, that we should speak of the person who made fulfillment impossible by his own will. Namely, whether someone who married a wife after making a simple vow of religion is bound to observe chastity as much as he can: for instance, by not demanding the marital debt <note>term: "marital debt" (Latin: *debitum*). In medieval theology, this referred to the obligation of spouses to provide sexual intimacy to one another upon request.</note>.

<margin>Reason for the affirmative side</margin>
For this reasoning seems to persuade us: No one should benefit from their own fault, nor should their own deceit protect them. Such a man, by his own fault, closed the way to fulfilling his vow, and likewise joined a wife to himself in fraud of that vow; therefore, he remains bound as much as he can be. And the legal experts embrace this opinion for this reason.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
Thus Sylvester <note>note: Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), an influential Dominican theologian and canon lawyer.</note>, under the word "vow" (*votum*), 2. §. 1., along with other authors of "Summas," says that such a person is hindered from completing the vow because he is bound to render the debt; as if it were an established fact that he cannot seek it.

<margin>Solution to the question.</margin>
Nevertheless, the contrary opinion—namely, that he can also seek it—

### Book Eight, Question II.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
...this opinion should be embraced, which Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Italian theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> rightly established in this place: since the reasoning just provided applies with equal force to both cases, whether one has made it impossible to fulfill a vow of religion through fault or without fault. For as we have previously stated, that person was only bound to take up that state which was the direct object of his vow. Since the statutes of a religious order only bind those who have "professed" <note>term: "professed" (Latin: *professus*). In canon law, this refers to someone who has taken their final, formal vows after a period of testing.</note>, he is not bound to them until he has expressly professed them. This is further confirmed as follows: the religious life consists of three vows: namely, obedience, poverty, and chastity. However, one who makes a "simple vow" <note>A promise made to God that is recognized by the Church but does not have the same legal finality as a "solemn" vow taken during formal entry into an order.</note> does not specify these, as does one who vows solemnly. Therefore, he is not yet bound to them. For who would listen to you if you asserted that someone who vowed to join the Order of Saint Francis, but later became bound by marriage, is required to renounce ownership and possession of goods? Or that he is bound to the fasts and other duties of obedience which he could perform while living in the secular world? If, therefore, he is not bound to the other two, it follows that he is not bound to the vow of chastity either.

<margin>A second doubt.</margin>
¶ From this definition, another doubt arises: namely, whether someone who vowed not only to enter a religious order but also to persevere in it until death—though without a solemn ceremony—and nonetheless voluntarily entangled himself in the "knot of marriage" <note>original: "matrimonij se nodo implicuit"</note>, is bound to anything more than the person who only vowed to enter. And

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
the reason for doubting is that this person formally vowed to strengthen his vow with solemnity; therefore, it appears he is bound to whatever chastity is possible for him: namely, that he is not permitted to request the "marital debt" <note>term: "marital debt". A traditional theological term for the right of spouses to sexual intimacy within marriage; the argument here is whether a person who made a vow can still initiate such intimacy.</note> from his spouse.

¶ Cajetan spends many words on this matter which, in my judgment, are unnecessary. For I confess I do not perceive what new obligation a "vow of perseverance" adds to a "vow of religion." A simple vow of religion can be made in three forms. First, that one vows only to enter: not with the intention of staying or professing solemnly, but of leaving immediately. I consider this to be "vain" <note>meaningless or legally void</note>, as Paludanus <note>Pierre de la Palu (c. 1275–1342), a French theologian and expert in canon law.</note> says. Second, that perseverance and solemn profession are included in the object of the vow. And third, that one simply vows religion. I believe the second form adds no extra binding force to the third. For he who vows religion absolutely, sends forth that vow according to both divine and human laws. Now, the divine law

<margin>The solution.</margin>
is that he should vow with the intention of truly becoming a religious; and thus, that he should persevere until

<column-break/>

death. However, ecclesiastical laws grant a "time of probation" <note>The novitiate, a trial period before a person commits for life.</note>, so that if he learns through good-faith experience that the religious life does not suit him, he need not take up what he cannot bear. Therefore, even if you add "to persevere" to your vow three or four times, it is always understood: *unless experience during the time of probation teaches you otherwise.* Thus, after such a vow is made, whether you are not admitted to profession through no fault of your own, or you contract a marriage of your own will, you remain no more strictly bound in the secular world than if you had made a simple vow of religion.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
And the response to the contrary argument is that although you vowed to persevere or to profess the religious life, you only bind yourself to profess according to the laws. Therefore, until you have professed, you are bound neither to chastity nor to the other statutes.

<margin>Doubt concerning one excluded from a monastery for being incorrigible.</margin>
¶ Finally, there remains a doubt to discuss regarding someone who, after a solemn vow, is expelled from the monastery as "incorrigible" <note>term: "incorrigible" (Latin: *incorrigibilis*). In this context, someone whose behavior is so disruptive or sinful that the monastery determines they cannot be reformed.</note>: whether he remains safe in his conscience after being forcibly expelled and cast out. The answer is that

<margin>The solution.</margin>
as long as it is his own fault that he is not received back, he is not safe, but is bound to amend himself and return to the right path; for since he was excluded by his own fault, he will remain in spiritual danger as long as he persists in it. If, however, after correcting his life, he is not admitted back to the cloisters, he remains safe in the secular world. If you ask whether he is bound to keep his religious vows while in the world, the answer is: He remains released from the vow of obedience, since the prelate has rejected it; and consequently, from the vow of poverty, since the community does not support him. Likewise, he is released from performing the Divine Office (unless he is in Holy Orders <note>original: "nisi fuerit in sacris"; i.e., if he was ordained as a priest or deacon, he still has clerical duties even if expelled from a monastery.</note>) and from fasts and other things attached to the religious life; for he did not make an express vow of those things, nor was he bound to them except by reason of the religious life from which he is expelled. Nevertheless, he is not exempt from the vow of chastity, because he made that vow expressly, and a prelate cannot free him from it. ¶ What if, before putting on the habit, he had vowed religion in general? Once excluded from *this* specific order, is he bound to move to another after he has reformed? In truth, reason seems to compel this. For just as someone who is not admitted here is bound to explore another religious order, so too does he seem bound who is expelled after profession. I would lean toward this view. Although, perhaps it could be said that through the solemn vow of *this* specific religion, that simple general vow ceased to exist; and therefore, if he is not received back here later, he is entirely free. Nevertheless, the first opinion seems more probable to me.

# Frater Dominicus de Soto, On Justice and Law #

<margin>To the fourth point. Saint Thomas.</margin>
In the solution to the fourth point, the doubt regarding the time for fulfilling a vow is removed. To this, Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text.</note> replies only that he who proposed to bind himself so as to fulfill it without any delay is bound immediately; however, he who proposed it for a certain time or under a certain condition is bound at that time. Nevertheless, if you desire a more exact answer, take it thus.

<margin>Regarding the time when a vow is to be rendered.</margin>
One can issue a vow in three ways: namely, by establishing a time, by assuming a condition, or simply without any addition. And indeed, the first category must be further distinguished. For if you vowed to do something at a certain time, and did so in view of that time—that is, out of devotion to it (such as when you vowed to fast on the eve of Corpus Christi or during Advent)—you are bound at that time under penalty of mortal sin. But if you did not fulfill it then, you are not bound to make up the fast at another time, because your intention was inclined toward that specific time. In that case, the vow is to be judged in the same way as a law that specifically commands the Lenten fast. If, however, the addition of that time was not because of an attachment to it, but so that you might set a deadline for the principal vow, then you are indeed bound at that time; but nonetheless, once that time has passed, the obligation is not abolished, and you are still bound at another time. For example, if you vowed to enter a religious order within a year, it will be counted as a fault against you unless you render what was promised to the Lord your God within that year; and nonetheless, once that year has passed, you are still bound to take up that same religious life. The matter is clear.

<margin>Conditional vow.</margin>
¶ A conditional vow, however, is made not in one way but in two. For one is sincerely conditional, while the other is penal. It is conditional whenever a person is inclined toward a thing, but because an impediment stands in the way or the means are not available, they vow under a condition. For instance, if you vow to enter a religious order after the death of your mother, who was an impediment to you; or to go on a pilgrimage after the death of your father when you have sufficient funds; or if God grants you such a benefit, to provide a dowry for an orphan.

<margin>Penal vow.</margin>
A penal vow, however, is when you were not inclined toward such a thing, nor was it in your heart; indeed, because it is loathsome and hateful to you, you drive yourself toward that cross <note>original: "in illam crucem" — a metaphor for a difficult or unwanted burden.</note> by a vow if you should happen to sin in some matter. For example, when you vow that if you gamble, or if you commit adultery, you will enter a religious order. For although this has the form of a conditional vow, it is nonetheless penal, since it is not directly a vow of religious life, but a vow of not gambling or not committing adultery.

<column-break/>

For you added the penalty so that you might either be careful or, after the fact, punish yourself. For this reason, there is one very well-established difference between these vows, and likewise one clear point of agreement, but one controversy remains. Regarding the difference, I say that for a purely conditional vow—if the vow is for religious life or another of the three matters reserved to the Supreme Pontiff <note>Certain serious vows were "reserved," meaning only the Pope or a high council could grant a release (dispensation) from them.</note>—it cannot be dispensed except by the Pope himself or by a Council. In a penal vow, however, a Bishop can dispense it. The reason is that in the former, the thing to which the vow is directly directed is the religious life; however, a penal vow is not directed straight, as we said before, except toward that immediate object, which is not gambling or not committing adultery. Therefore, he who can grant a dispensation for those matters also has power over a penalty applied indirectly, even if it concerns the religious life. The point of agreement is that both are binding once the condition is met; nor is this disputed in any way. What remains under judgment, therefore, is whether a penal vow, once the condition is met, can only receive dispensation from the Supreme Pontiff, just like the other conditional vow. Regarding this, we shall speak in Question 4, under the title of dispensation, Article 3. For it seems to be indispensable <note>term: "indispensable" (Latin: *indispensabile*). In this legal context, it means a vow that cannot be set aside or "dispensed" by a lower authority.</note> in the same way, since the obligation of religious life has already arisen by virtue of the vow.

<margin>To the fifth principal point.</margin>
¶ The fifth point is easily answered. First, no one can bind another by his own vow—neither a son, nor a servant, nor any other subject—since a vow is an act of religion by which someone offers his own will to God. Therefore, if you vowed to offer your son to a certain temple, you are bound to bring him; but he is only bound to obey you out of filial obedience, and in no way by the force of the religious vow. Furthermore, he who cannot fulfill a vow by himself, if it is a personal vow, is in no way bound to perform it through another. This is both because the condition of possibility is always understood in a vow, and because a personal vow is made for one's own mortification or affliction of the body, or to stir up devotion, as is clear in a vow of fasting or pilgrimage. No one achieves these things through another. It is different if the vow is not purely personal: for example, if you vowed one person for the support of the war for Jerusalem <note>A reference to the Crusades or defensive wars in the Holy Land.</note> and you cannot go, you ought to send another. Again, if you vowed to build a monastery or provide a dowry for a virgin, which you did not pay during your life, your heir is bound if you leave him property, as 

<margin>Paludanus.</margin>
Paludanus <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a French theologian and canon lawyer.</note> says in Book 4, Distinction 38, Question 3. Supporting this is Law 2 of the Digest regarding promises <note>Latin: *ff. de pollicita.* refers to the *Digest* of Roman Law, specifically the section on *pollicitatio* (informal promises to a city or deity).</note>.

# Book Eight. Question II. #

### ARTICLE II. ###
#### Whether it is useful and expedient to make a vow. ####

<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
After discussing the power of a vow to bind a person, we must next address its utility: namely, whether it brings us any benefit. The argument begins from the negative side. It is not expedient for anyone to deprive themselves of their greatest good, which is liberty. It is through liberty that we humans surpass all other living creatures; for this reason, it is more precious than any amount of gold. Yet, through the necessity imposed by a vow, a person is stripped of this liberty. Therefore, making a vow is not expedient.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ Second. It is not wise for anyone to expose themselves to dangers. However, a person who makes a vow is exposed to a danger from which they were previously free. Hence Augustine, in his letter to Armentarius and Paulinus, says: <note>original: "Quia iam vouisti, iã te obstrinxisti..."</note> "Because you have now vowed, you have already bound yourself. It is no longer permitted for you to do otherwise. You will not be the same if you do not do what you vowed as you would have remained had you vowed no such thing. You would have been of lesser status then, but not worse. Now, however, you would be all the more wretched (God forbid) if you break faith with God, just as you would be more blessed if you fulfill it."

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ Third, it is argued from the counsel of Paul in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 4, that we should be imitators of him, just as he is an imitator of Christ. Yet we nowhere read that Christ made any vow, nor any of the Apostles. Therefore, there is no benefit in making vows.
¶ On the contrary, however, is that Psalm: <note>original: "Vouete & reddite Domino Deo vestro."</note> "Make vows and perform them to the Lord your God" <note>Psalm 76:11.</note>.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Proof.</margin>
To this question, a single and most certain conclusion is given in response: Making a vow is indeed useful—not, however, to God, but to us. This is proven as follows. A promise is made to a human for a different reason than to God. We promise something to a human because it is useful to them not only to receive the benefit, but also to be promised it. For just as they are helped by the gift itself, they are also made more certain of a future benefit by the promise, which generates hope in them—a hope they value as much as another benefit. Therefore, thanks are given not only to the one who grants the gift, but also to the one who promises it. But since no advantage accrues to God from what we give Him—because He has no need of our goods—it is likewise not useful to Him that we promise Him anything. He knows more clearly than we do what we are going to provide. However, both the act and the promise are useful to *us*. By giving Him something, we increase our own rewards; if nothing else, our glory is extended. Hence Augustine says in the same letter: <note>original: "Benignus exactor est, & non egenus..."</note> "He is a kind debt-collector, and not a needy one;

<margin>Augustine</margin>

<column-break/>

He is not one who grows because of what is paid back, but one who makes those who pay grow in Himself. For what is paid to Him is added to the one who pays." Furthermore, because we promise Him something, this gain accrues to us: we fix and strengthen our will toward the good, so that we cannot rightfully change our minds. Therefore, making a vow is for the sake of the matter—not His sake, indeed, but ours.

<margin>Corollary of the conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ The corollary of this conclusion is that it is a healthy thing to advise others to make vows. However, both the conclusion and the corollary are understood in a general sense and regarding the object of the vow; for specifically, it is not always advantageous for every individual. This does not descend from the nature and quality of the vow itself, but from the weakness and defect of the persons—namely, because they are not sufficiently constant to overcome the difficulty of the vow.

<margin>Luther.</margin>
Therefore, among Catholics, this matter is so evident that no battle remains for us except with the heretics. There is, then, that first argument made above, by which heretics—as most recently Luther in his impious book *On Monastic Vows*—contend that making a vow is pernicious; so far is it from being useful. These are the words of Luther in that same book. And a little later, he says: "A vow of chastity, and of the whole monastic life, if it is pious, must necessarily involve the freedom

<margin>Luther’s motive.</margin>
to abandon it again." This heresy can be disguised using the words of Christ: <note>original: "Qui potest capere capiat."</note> "He who can take it, let him take it" <note>Matthew 19:12.</note>, and "If you wish to be perfect." And from that saying of Paul: "I have no command of the Lord, but I give my counsel." And the reason, he says, is this: because we deprive ourselves of the liberty by which the righteous ought to serve God, and not like slaves. For this reason, he titled another wicked book *On the Babylonian Captivity*, for that is what he calls the traditions of the Church.

<margin>The solution of Saint Thomas.</margin>
Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 88, a. 4.</note> responds, therefore, that just as being unable to sin does not diminish liberty, neither does the necessity of a will strengthened toward the good—which is the necessity created by a vow.

<margin>A clear solution of Saint Thomas is provided.</margin>
¶ For a clearer understanding of this, it must be noted that there are two kinds of necessity in acting. One is natural necessity, such as is found in brute animals and inanimate things. This entirely removes the possibility of praise and merit. The other is the necessity of obligation. This does not remove merit; it increases it. Otherwise, God would have unwisely bound us by laws to our own destruction. If you desire the deepest reason for this matter, you may weigh it by the purpose of liberty. For although our liberty is natural to us, nonetheless, God, the very author of nature, created us and the angels free so that through our works...

Soto utilizes Thomas Aquinas and Augustine to show that the "necessity" created by a vow does not destroy human freedom but rather perfects it.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law #

our [works] might be worthy of praise and merit before Him. For natural works, as we were just saying, cannot be merits. For this reason, He created our freedom so that, while we are able to do evil, by doing good we might merit eternal life. If He had bestowed this upon us without any merits of our own or of Christ, it would have lacked that secondary flower of glory, which is to merit what you possess. For it is more excellent to merit what you do not have than to have what you do not merit. Therefore, when our freedom is fixed upon the good so that it does not sin, it loses nothing of its liberty, because it is fixed upon that for which it was created. For this reason, neither the will of the Apostles, confirmed in the good, lost any liberty; much less the blessed in heaven; and least of all Christ. Although He had the freedom to choose either way, He did not have it for that which is evil in a "composite sense" <note>A technical logical term meaning "considering all factors together." Soto means Christ remained free even though He was morally incapable of sinning.</note>.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence Augustine says in that same letter: "Happy is the necessity that compels us toward better things." <note>original: "Felix necessitas est quae in meliora compellit."</note> From this, those authorities cited above—which show that Christ left his family free for "works of counsel" <term>works of supererogation; acts like poverty or celibacy that go beyond the basic commandments</term>—are wrongly understood by the heretics <note>Soto is likely referring to Protestant reformers like Luther or Calvin, who criticized monastic vows.</note>, as if He prohibited us from consecrating ourselves to those works by a vow. The legitimate meaning is that He did not wish to bind us to them by command. However, for one who wishes to bind themselves to them by a vow, this very counsel is most healthy. Otherwise, there would be no stable "monastic state" if anyone were allowed to leave at their whim; but this is exactly what they [the heretics] are attempting to bring about.

<margin>A difficulty in the words of Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ However, perhaps a certain "scruple" <note>A small doubt or difficulty</note> will be raised in your mind by the words of Saint Thomas [Aquinas], in which he compares the necessity of a vow to that [necessity] of being unable to sin; even though a vow concerns a work of supererogation, the contrary of which is not a sin.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
It is responded, however, that he did not intend those words to affirm that a vow is a fixed state of not sinning; rather, he used a similarity: just as the stability of not sinning in the Apostles and the blessed does not diminish liberty, so neither does the firmness of performing a work of counsel, which is a greater good.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, the response is made through a distinction. For there are two types of danger: one which arises from the deed itself, to which it is certainly not wise to expose yourself—as when someone commits themselves to a bridge threatening to collapse, or throws themselves between the horns of a wild bull. But the other is a danger not arising from the deed, but from human frailty and weakness. And for a person to offer themselves to this for the sake of a better good is not only not always rash, but sometimes

<column-break/>

expedient: just as one mounts a horse to complete a journey more quickly, even though because of your own sluggishness you might fall from it. Likewise, it is not rash to commit yourself to dangers that usually happen by chance. For the Wise Man says in Ecclesiastes 11:

> He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap.

The danger of a vow is not of the first kind, but of the second; that is, something a constant and strenuous man can overcome.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Hence, in that same letter, Augustine says: "Do not repent having vowed; indeed, rejoice that what was once permitted to you to your own detriment is now no longer permitted." <note>original: "Non te vouisse poeniteat..."</note>

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, the response is that it was not fitting for Christ to make a vow for any reason: both because He was God, and because as a man He possessed the most constant will in the good, existing as a "comprehensor" <term>one who already possesses the full vision of God</term>. Hence that verse in the Psalm, "I will pay my vows in the sight of those who fear him," is understood not of His own person, but of His body, which is the Church. The Apostles, however, took vows of poverty and the rest, as gathered from Matthew 19, where Peter says: "Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what then shall there be for us?" Concerning which, see more extensively in questions 3 and 6.

### ARTICLE III. ###

-> Whether a Vow is an act of "latria" or religion. <-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'C' depicting a figure seated at a desk or pulpit, dressed in academic or clerical robes, representing a teacher or doctor of the Church.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
Since in this question the discussion turns to the virtue of a vow, it is asked to which virtue this duty belongs. And it is argued first that it is the work of no special virtue. For every work of any virtue, as was said above, can be the matter of a vow; and it seems to belong to the same virtue both to promise and to do. Therefore, it belongs to any virtue to vow its own work, and thus it is not a special virtue.

<margin>Argument 2. Cicero.</margin>
¶ Second. That virtue alone is "religion" (as Cicero [Tully] is the authority in *On Duties*) by which we offer worship and ceremony to God. But he who vows does not yet offer anything to God, but only promises; therefore, it is not an act of religion.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third. Religious worship is to be exhibited to God alone, to whom "latria" <term>the supreme worship reserved for God alone</term> is owed. But a vow is made not only to God, but also to the saints, and even to prelates to whom those about to profess religion promise obedience. Therefore, a vow is not an act of religion.

¶ To the contrary is that passage from Isaiah 19:

> They shall worship Him with sacrifices and offerings, and they shall make vows to the Lord and fulfill them.

Where "worshipping," which belongs to religion, is explained through that which is "vowing."

<meta>The previous page discussed how human freedom is perfected, rather than diminished, when it is directed toward the good through vows, using the examples of Christ and the Apostles. This page continues the scholastic investigation into the nature of vows, specifically asking which virtue "owns" the act of making a vow.</meta>

### Book Eight, Question II. ###

<margin>The Foundation.</margin>
To understand this question, it must be noted that any virtuous act can be viewed in two ways. Namely, it can be *elicited* <term>Latin: *elicitus*; an act produced directly and immediately by a specific virtue</term> or *commanded* <term>Latin: *imperatus*; an act motivated by one virtue but carried out through the power of another</term>. An act is *elicited* by the virtue that has that act as its formal object. In this way, believing is the elicited act of faith, and returning what belongs to another is the elicited act of justice. This is similar to the powers of the senses: vision is elicited by the sense of sight because it is the sensation of color. On the other hand, an act is *commanded* by a virtue when it is produced through the command of that virtue moving another for the sake of its own end. For example, fasting—which is said to belong to the virtue of temperance—is *commanded* by charity when a person is moved to fast not only because it is an act of temperance, but for the love of God. The same logic applies to vices: when someone steals for the sake of committing adultery, the theft—which is elicited by the vice of injustice—is commanded by the vice of lust. Therefore, when we ask to which virtue a specific duty belongs, we are not investigating which virtue *commanded* it (for many could command it), but rather which virtue *elicited* it. This is exactly what we are inquiring about regarding a vow. To this, we respond with a single conclusion.

<margin>Responsive Conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
**Making a vow is an elicited act of the virtue of religion, as a form of divine worship.** This is proven as follows: A vow is a certain ordering and offering of the things a person promises for the service and worship of God. This is the very meaning of promising to God. Furthermore, to order and offer any work for the worship of God is an act of the virtue of religion; therefore, the act of vowing belongs to that same virtue. The second part of this argument is demonstrated thus: The work of any virtue can be offered to God as a sacrifice—such as fasting, the giving of alms, or any act of either courage or temperance. However, this kind of ordering and offering is not attributed to the specific *commanded* virtues from which those acts are elicited, but to the *commanding* virtue, which is religion. Therefore, vowing is an elicited act of religion.

<margin>A minor doubt.</margin>
¶ However, a minor doubt might arise for you from these points. Since ordering and directing something toward God belongs not only to the virtue of religion but also—and primarily—to charity (love for God), one might argue that vowing should be considered an act of charity rather than religion.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The response is that our conclusion is not drawn simply from the fact that vowing is an "ordering and directing" of something to God, but specifically because it is "offering" something to God for His reverence and worship. Thus, the first difference is that charity refers works to God as an *end* <note>The "end" refers to the ultimate goal or purpose.</note>. We fast, pray, and so on *for* God; here, the preposition designates the goal.

<column-break/>

But we vow these same works *to* God; here, we do not describe God as the "end," but as the recipient to whom something is offered. Therefore, God is placed as the *object* of religion, just as He is the object of faith. The second distinction is that charity regards God as its object as the "beloved"—that is, the one for whom we wish all good and no evil. Religion, however, regards God as the one whom we revere and obey, offering ourselves and our possessions to Him through worship. A vow, therefore, is not only ordered toward God, but specifically toward His reverence and worship.

<margin>Regarding the first argument.</margin>
The first argument, therefore, makes the truth of the conclusion clearer. For the response is that although the *matter* of the vow—such as fasting or maintaining celibacy—consists of elicited acts of other virtues, the *vow itself* is never elicited by anything except religion. Occasionally, however, it happens that not only the vow but the devoted acts themselves are elicited by religion: for instance, when you vow to pray or to offer a sacrifice. This is because praying is itself an act of religion. Thus, sometimes a vow is an act of religion solely by its "form" (because the promise itself is elicited by religion), while at other times it is so by both "form and matter" (namely, when the very acts promised are elicited by the same virtue).

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ A reason for doubting arises here: whether there is any transgression of a vow that includes two distinct faults—one against the specific virtue from which it is elicited, and another against religion, through which it is offered to God. For example: if you have vowed to fast, do you, by failing to fast, sin both against temperance and against religion? Likewise, if you vowed to God to obey a superior, do you violate both the virtue of obedience (which falls under justice) and the religion of the vow?

<margin>Argument.</margin>
There is an argument that it is a double sin. This is because, as we said before, a vow is a kind of particular law that the one vowing prescribes for himself. Whatever a law commands, it establishes within some genre of virtue; for example, when a law commands fasting during Lent, it establishes that act within the genre of abstinence. Just as divine law, commanding spouses not to defraud one another, establishes that practice within the genre of continence, so too someone vowing to fast establishes that act within that same genre of virtue. And, additionally, it is within the genre of religion; therefore, its transgression would be a double crime.

¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that by common judgment, such an act is considered only a single sin against the vow.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
¶ To this it is answered that the transgression...
