<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 643 regarding the nature of vows. The previous text established that a vow is an act of the virtue of religion (the virtue concerning worship) because it is an offering made to God. Here, the author examines whether breaking a vow constitutes one sin or two, and explores the theological nuance of vowing to saints versus vowing to God.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law, #

the violation of a vow is, by its very nature, a single sin. However, it should be noted that the act which one vows—the "matter" underlying the vow—can be established as a virtue in two ways: either by another law (whether divine, natural, or human) or solely by the vow itself. If it is the first way, the sin is doubled; but if it is the second, it is only a single sin. For example: if you have vowed to honor your parents, or to go to confession, or to fast during <term>Lent<note>Original: *Quadragesimam*; the forty-day period of fasting before Easter.</note></term>, you commit a double sin if you transgress. This is because, even without the vow, these were already duties of specific virtues. However, suppose you vowed to fast on the <term>Eve of Corpus Christi<note>Original: *vigilia corporis Christi*; a feast day honoring the Real Presence of the Eucharist.</note></term>. I admit you have categorized that act under the virtue of abstinence, but since it is only a duty because of the vow, breaking the fast is only a single sin. In the same way, if you promise a dowry to a girl, you are already bound by human faith <note>Meaning a standard social or legal contract between people.</note>. If you then confirm that same promise with a religious vow, then breaking that faith will be a double sin: specifically, a sin against both human justice and against the virtue of religion. But if you vowed to God alone to give alms, and you do not do it, you sin only against the vow. From this it follows that for a member of a religious order, it is a single crime to disobey a superior: for although that act is categorized as obedience, it is only so because of the vow. For you do not vow obedience to the prelate himself, but to God—vowing that you will be obedient to the prelate.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, the response is that although the person who vows has not yet "given" (if "giving" refers to the fulfillment of the promise), they nevertheless give in a causal sense. By binding themselves, they create an obligation that contains the promised thing through the power of that commitment. Furthermore, they truly give their mind and their will, which they hand over <note>Original: *mancipat*; a legal term for a formal transfer of property, implying total surrender.</note> to God.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The third argument asks whether a vow made to saints or prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> belongs to the virtue of religion, given that the virtue of religion has God alone as its object. Indeed, no one doubts the fact itself, but the underlying method is hidden.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Now, <term>Saint Thomas Aquinas<note>Soto is referencing the *Summa Theologiae* of Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational authority for this type of scholastic theology.</note></term> makes no distinction between a vow made to prelates and one made to saints. He considers both to be promises made to humans, which pertains only to human faith. However, he says both can be the "matter" of a vow insofar as we offer to God the very thing we promise to the person or the Saint. Therefore, a vow we make to the Blessed Virgin (to use the highest example among the saints) is only a vow because we offer to God what we promise to her: specifically, promising Him that we will do this or that in honor of the Virgin. It is as if I vowed to God

<column-break/>

that I would give a dowry to a girl or show honor to another person. ¶ However, it is not surprising if some consider this teaching of Saint Thomas to be not necessarily false, but perhaps "short" or incomplete. For the practice of vowing to saints suggests another reason. When someone vows a pilgrimage to the Virgin, or Saint Peter, or Saint James, they do not formally vow to God that such honor be shown to the Saint. I say they do not vow it in the same way a monk does when he says to a Superior: "I vow to God that I will be obedient to you." Rather, they say, "I vow to the Virgin," and "I vow to Peter." Indeed, members of religious orders join the saints together with God, saying: "I promise obedience to God, and the Blessed Virgin, and Blessed Dominic (or Francis)." Let us say, then, that saints are regarded in two ways. First, as humans or angels who are pure creatures. In this sense, Saint Thomas’s opinion is true: a promise made to them is not a "vow" unless it is offered to God. But in the second way, they are considered insofar as God is in them—not merely through grace as He is in those still on the journey of life, but through glory, as those who participate in His own present divinity by reason of their state. And thus, vowing to the saints is vowing to God, who is in them. However, Saint Thomas perhaps bypassed this method not by accident, but because just as praying to saints is not the same as praying to God (the reasoning is different), so too the reasoning for vowing to saints is different than vowing to God. Nevertheless, where there is agreement on the Catholic meaning, a dispute over the name is useless.

### ARTICLE IV. ###
### Whether it is more praiseworthy and meritorious to do something out of a vow than without one. ###

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a seated human figure in a landscape or architectural setting.</image-desc>
Since it was defined in the second article that vowing is useful, and in the third that it is an act of the virtue of religion, the most fitting question follows: is a work performed under a vow of greater praise and merit than if it were done without a vow? It would seem from the previous points that this follows.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Nevertheless, the negative side is argued using the authority of Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390–455), a Christian writer and disciple of Augustine.</note> in Book 2 of *The Contemplative Life*, where he says: "We ought to abstain and fast in such a way that we do not subject ourselves to the necessity of fasting; lest we no longer act out of devotion, but perform a voluntary thing against our will." A vow, however, subjects us to necessity. Therefore, it is more excellent to work without a vow.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, it is argued from the words of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> in 2 Corinthians 9.

### Book Eight, Question II ###

<margin>2 Corinthians 9</margin> "Each one as he has purposed in his heart, not out of sadness or necessity. For God loves a cheerful giver." <note>original: "Unusquisq; prout destinauit in corde suo, non ex tristitia aut ex necessitate. Hilarem enim datorem diligit Deus."</note> However, a vow, as often happens in practice, generates sadness; and this is because of necessity. For as <margin>Aristotle</margin> testifies in book 5 of the *Metaphysics*, text 6, and book 1 of the *Rhetoric*, chapter 11: necessity brings about sadness because it pressures the will. Therefore, a work done without a vow is more excellent.
<margin>Argument 3</margin> ¶ Third: a vow is necessary for this purpose—that the will may be firmed in what it promises. However, it cannot be firmed more immovably than while it is performing the act itself. Therefore, it is better to act without a vow, for the thing is firmer when it is being done than when it is merely being promised.
¶ On the contrary is that Davidic admonition: "Vow, and pay your vows." <note>Psalm 76:11</note> The solemn interpretation of this is that vowing pertains to <term>counsel<note>In Catholic theology, a "counsel" is a recommendation for a higher spiritual path, as opposed to a "precept" or commandment which is mandatory for all.</note></term>. Moreover, counsel, as we have stated before, concerns a "better good." Therefore, it is better to work from a vow than without a vow.

The title of this section asks two questions regarding the deliberate work of a vow: namely, whether it is more praiseworthy when it is a morally good act performed outside of <term>grace<note>Refers to the state of a person's soul; "outside of grace" usually means being in a state of mortal sin, though the act itself may still be "morally good."</note></term>, and whether it is more meritorious when performed in <term>charity<note>The theological virtue of love for God; acting "in charity" means the act earns spiritual merit.</note></term>. <margin>St. Thomas</margin> St. Thomas Aquinas responds with a single affirmative conclusion, which <margin>Conclusion</margin> he corroborates with three reasons. The conclusion is: An act performed out of a vow is attributed greater praise and merit than one offered without it.
<margin>First reason for the question</margin> This is proven first from the object of the virtue. For an act of a nobler virtue is of higher praise as well as merit. Therefore, the act of an inferior virtue becomes more excellent when it is commanded by a superior one—just as if you were to act temperately for the sake of charity. Now, the virtue of <term>latria<note>From the Greek 'latreia,' meaning the highest form of worship or service reserved for God alone.</note></term>, into which we have placed the act of vowing, is the most excellent of virtues, as it is centered on the worship of God. Therefore, an act commanded by that virtue through a vow is more excellent than one done without a vow. <margin>Augustine</margin> Hence Augustine, in his book *On Virginity*, says: "Virginity itself is honored not because it is virginity, but because it is dedicated to God; it is nourished and preserved by the continence of piety."
<margin>Second reason</margin> Secondly, this is confirmed again by the nature of the thing that is offered. For he who performs a work without a vow offers only the act to God; but he who works from a vow offers not only the act, but the power itself. For he assigns and delivers up his will and freedom to Him, so that thereafter he cannot rightfully do otherwise. This is just as one who would bestow a fruit-bearing tree upon another, as <margin>Anselm</margin> argues in book 1 of *On Similitudes*, would give more than one who gave only the fruits. By this same reasoning, for those who make promises, individual acts of grace are owed, in addition to those acts performed while they are bestowing them.
Thirdly, this is also confirmed by 

<column-break/>

the manner of acting. Truly, through a vow, the will is fixed and asserted in the good. To do something out of a greater stability and constancy of soul is more praiseworthy. Hence the <margin>Aristotle</margin> Philosopher in book 2 of the *Ethics* considers no duty to be worthy of the name of virtue until it proceeds from a firmed <term>habit<note>In Aristotelian ethics, a "habit" is a stable disposition of character achieved through repeated action.</note></term>.
¶ However, before descending to the solutions of the arguments, it remains to explain the conclusion. For it is not doubted by any Catholic, yet it is often misunderstood and falls into abuse. Therefore, it is argued to the contrary: If it were <margin>Argument</margin> true, it would follow that monks, in performing any duty of obedience, should always demand and wait for a written command from their superior. Specifically, this would be so that the work might be of greater merit due to the greater energy of the vow, just as the transgression would be a worse fault. For many religious do this, whom we proceed to advise here: because you obey with swiftness from the opposite side, you show a more illustrious obedience. He acts more promptly who does not wait for an urgent command but is listening to a simple order.
It is answered, therefore, under a <margin>Solution</margin> distinction. When a matter is difficult and likewise doubtful—such as sailing to the Indies, or taking on the burden of government, or something similar—the counsel is that the monk should not undertake such provinces by his own judgment without a command, but should wait for the mandate of the prefect. When, however, the matter is not ambiguous, then it is either vain or certainly a fault to wait for a compelling command. For if you are ready to act, but you require a compulsory command only for the sake of increasing the merit of the duty for yourself, it is vain. For by the virtue of the vow of obedience, promptness is more meritorious. A command is not given except to the rebellious or to those hanging in doubt. If, however, you truly refuse to act unless forced by a command, then the merit not only fails to grow, but is diminished to such an extent that it is sometimes turned into a fault. Therefore, the conclusion is not to be understood in that way, but rather that all works which you do from a vow, even without a new command, are of greater merit and praise than if you did them without the necessity of the vow; and indeed of greater merit than if you waited for the compulsion of a command.
<margin>To the first argument</margin> Therefore, to the first argument taken from the opinion of <term>Prosper<note>Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390 – c. 455 AD), a Christian writer and disciple of St. Augustine.</note></term>, it is answered that the "necessity of coercion"—as when someone works unwillingly—takes away the voluntary nature of the act and thus diminishes praise and merit. Indeed, sometimes it removes it entirely. And it was of that necessity that Prosper spoke...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right, #

<margin>Objection.</margin> Prosper said: "Lest we no longer do a voluntary thing as devotees, but as those acting against their will." <note>St. Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390–455), a theologian and disciple of Augustine. He is warning that obligation might turn a willing act into a chore.</note> Yet the necessity of a vow, by which it asserts the will more deeply toward the good, actually increases devotion. ¶ But perhaps you argue more urgently, as the heretics <note>Soto likely refers to Protestant Reformers who argued that monastic vows were a form of spiritual bondage that destroyed Christian liberty.</note> believe: He who acts without a vow possesses freedom in individual actions, such that he can stop without violating the law; but he who is ensnared by a vow, even if he vowed freely, nevertheless lacks that freedom in individual subsequent actions. Therefore, he who is not bound by a vow acts more freely; and freedom increases praise and merit; therefore, the conclusion is false. 

One who looks at the matter superficially might perhaps respond by conceding the major premise—that there is greater freedom in the one who acts without a vow, because it is always within his power not to act. But he would say, on the other hand—specifically for the reasons brought to the conclusion—that merit grows more abundantly in the one who has made a vow. 

<margin>Solution.</margin> Nevertheless, this is not the legitimate solution. Rather, the truth is that there is greater freedom in the one who has vowed. For indeed, he who shrinks from vowing does not vow because he does not possess such free mastery over himself as <margin>perhaps read: "freedom."</margin> the one who vows. 

Hence, just as freedom would be more illustrious in a man (to persist in Anselm's example) <note>St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109). The "tree and fruit" analogy is a classic defense of religious life: giving the tree is more total than giving the fruit.</note> who would give not only the fruit of the tree every year, but the entire tree at once, than in him who would give only the fruits; so it is a more excellent and more magnificent freedom to dedicate to God not only your works, but your very will itself once and for all. Wherefore the freedom of that first act is diffused, as if from a root, to the individual works, so that they are of a more precious freedom than if they were done without a vow. 

<margin>To the second argument.</margin> ¶ To the second argument, taken from that saying of Paul, *Not out of sadness or necessity*, Saint Thomas responds with three distinctions. 

<margin>The solution of Saint Thomas.</margin> <margin>Aristotle. Paul.</margin> First, that there is a necessity of coercion which, since it is contrary to the will, produces sadness; it is about this that Aristotle speaks. And it is already conceded that this is not good. Paul likewise condemns this same thing. 

Second, that the necessity of a vow in those who are well-disposed does not generate sadness, but plainly joy, for the opposite reason: namely, because they have their will fixed upon the good. 

<margin>Augustine</margin> Hence Augustine, in the same cited letter to Armentarius, says: "Do not repent," he says, "that you have vowed; rather, rejoice now that what would have been permitted to your detriment is no longer permitted to you." <note>original: "Non te, inquit, vouisse pœniteat: imò gaude iam tibi id non licere quod cum tuo detrimento licuisset."</note> And indeed, regarding these two assertions, no doubt remains. 

But he says thirdly, that even if sometimes a work of a vow, considered in itself, is rendered sad and involuntary after the vow, so long as the will to fulfill it remains unshaken, it is not 

<column-break/>

only not evil, but it is more meritorious than if it were done without a vow; because it proceeds from <term>religion<note>In scholastic theology, "religion" is the specific virtue of offering due worship and service to God. Soto argues this virtue is "higher" than mere self-discipline like fasting.</note></term>, which is a more powerful virtue than abstinence; by which (for example) we say that work is elicited—say, fasting. 

¶ However, this teaching is not without ambiguity. <margin>Ambiguity arising from the solution of Saint Thomas.</margin> And therefore it must be investigated whether regret over a vow is sometimes a fault; and of what kind it is in its genus—whether venial or mortal. 

For on one side, it seems to be the same to regret a vow as if you were unwilling to vow before the vow; and this "unwillingness," since it does not concern a matter necessary for salvation, is not evil. For the object of both acts is the same: "I do not want to vow," and "I wish I had not vowed." 

But on the other side is the argument that regret for a good thing is evil, since regret ought to be only for what is evil; however, to have vowed is good; therefore, regret for it is evil. And so it is usually attributed to vice. 

<margin>Cajetan's response.</margin> Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), known as Cajetan, a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>, in his response, lays out a threefold distinction. For he says anyone can regret either the *vow* (that is, the promise); or *having vowed* (for instance, having applied the mind to vowing); or thirdly, the good works which he did because of the vow. 

To regret the vow, he says, is to grieve over the promise; for he who so grieves, he says, does not keep the promise. But to regret *having vowed* is to regret that he subjected himself to the vow, yet he does not therefore change his mind. 

<margin>Cajetan's distinction is exploded.</margin> But although the difference between changing and not changing one's purpose is clear, there is no such difference between the words themselves: "regretting the vow" and "regretting having vowed." For in Latin, they are certainly the same thing. Indeed, if you understand "regretting the vow" in the abstract—that is, not as a vow made by you—this regret is impossible. For no one can regret anything except his own deed. But if you use it in the concrete sense, then to regret the vow is exactly the same as to regret that you vowed. Just as to regret a sin is the same as to regret that you sinned. 

Therefore, the distinction should not be taken from the "vow" and "having vowed," but from the verb itself, "to regret" (*pœnitere*), which is of ambiguous meaning. 

<margin>Immediate solution to the ambiguity.</margin> For "to regret the vow" or "having vowed" is understood in one way as retracting the purpose. For he is said to "regret a deed" who changes his mind. And of this meaning, there is no discussion at present. For it is beyond controversy that this is, in its genus, a lethal sin, as has been said—both against justice and also against religion. 

But in the second way, and more commonly, "to regret" is understood as "to wish one had not done it." And regarding this is the present doubt. To which it is answered that this kind of regret, although considered absolutely it sounds like something evil, [continues...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the psychological and moral implications of vowing. Having argued that vows increase merit by binding the will to a good purpose, the author now addresses the specific problem of "regret" (poenitentia) — when a person who has made a vow later feels sorrow or wishes they had not done so.</meta>

### Question II (Continued) ###

...nevertheless, as long as the intention of performing the act remains firm, the act can be clean of any stain of guilt based on the surrounding circumstances. I say it "sounds" like something bad—just as "to kill" sounds bad. Because to have vowed is a good thing, yet just as a judge or one repelling force does not sin in killing, so too it is not always a sin for one to regret having vowed. This is especially true when the matter of the vow is a difficult and lifelong thing, and the one who took the vow feels the difficulty through experience—a difficulty which, had he known it beforehand, he would not have made the vow. Therefore, just as it is no vice to be unwilling to vow at the beginning, so too it is no vice to be unwilling to have vowed once the vow is sent forth. This happens not so much from a weakness of spirit as from the very nature of the object encountered. 

Thus, in response to the argument made above, the regret for a good thing—when that thing is not absolutely necessary—is not evil in itself. Regarding this, Saint Thomas <note>original: "S. Tho."; referring to Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the dominant theologian of the Middle Ages.</note> says that it is more excellent to do something from a vow with such sorrow than to do it without a vow. The truth of this is evident from the fact that vowing is useful and healthy for this very reason: so that the soul may be strengthened by the obligation, lest the difficulty and sorrow of the task later deter us from the work. Instead, having overcome all impediments, we persist in our purpose. I would add, however, that although such regret is not reproachable in itself, it can incline one toward vice by reason of danger. For he who admits frequent sorrows of this kind regarding a vow begins to be weakened, until he might abandon his purpose. Therefore, when someone feels their purpose faltering, they cannot avoid a venial sin <note>A "venial" sin is a lesser offense that does not fully break one's relationship with God, as opposed to a "mortal" or deadly sin.</note> unless they reject such regret. However, as long as there is no consent to breaking the faith of the vow, you need not fear a mortal sin. 

On the other hand, when vows are not perpetual nor concerning difficult matters, but about smaller things, then regretting having vowed—while the intention to fulfill it remains—is not only not a fault, but it is rarely a danger. This is because the one who vowed can change their purpose for the better. For instance, if you vowed a pilgrimage or to recite lengthy Psalms, and this becomes an obstacle to you—either for your studies, the benefit of the state, or other works of mercy—there is no danger in regretting the vow. Nevertheless, it would be a sin to change the purpose without a dispensation <note>A legal release from an ecclesiastical obligation or vow.</note>.

<margin>
What kind of crime regret of a vow is in monks.
</margin>
The third part of this discussion concerns when someone, after they have performed the works of the vow (for instance, living a life in a religious order), regrets having lived under such an institute. We must make a distinction here. Either he regrets that past life assuming the vow was valid—that is, he regrets having paid the works he owed by reason of the vow—and this is clearly a mortal crime. For 

<column-break/>

since he would have sinned mortally if he had not performed them, it follows that this kind of regret concerns a matter necessary for salvation, and is thus mortally wicked. 

However, if the regret is directed at the fact that you *vowed* it, not caring whether you lacked those spiritual fruits, it falls into the second category treated just above: it is not a mortal sin by its nature, though it may have a bit more gravity. For after you have produced the fruits, you cannot regret them without some fault—unless the vows were concerning a light and temporal matter. In that case, there is no absurdity in regretting that you did not spend that time in other, more convenient affairs.

<margin>
To the third argument.
</margin>
Finally, in response to the third argument: although someone may have a firm will while they are actually performing a duty in the present, they do not necessarily have it for the future in the same way as one who vows. This is especially true if one vows to perform the same works continually.

Among the virtues of the vow, the highest is in the **solemn vow** <note>In canon law, a "solemn" vow is a public, official commitment recognized by the Church that carries greater legal weight than a "simple" or private vow—for example, a solemn vow of poverty or chastity could legally invalidate a subsequent marriage.</note>: as it is the kind that not only hinders marriage but dissolves it. For this reason, the most important distinction among vows is recognized as being between the *simple* and the *solemn*. It is argued from the negative side:

<margin>

</margin>
A vow, as we have said before, is made to God, who knows the secrets of hearts; but solemnity consists in an external ceremony, which takes place in the sight of men. Therefore, such solemnity is not necessary for a vow, but accidental, so that it might bring a new bond by divine law.

<margin>
Argument 2.
</margin>

This is because the substance of a genus is shared by all its species. However, there are many things outside of the reception of orders and religious profession—such as pilgrimages, fasts, etc.—which are not usually strengthened by solemnity. Therefore, such solemnity does not belong to the substance of the vow.

a vow of religion and of sacred order <note>The "sacred orders" refer to the ranks of the clergy, such as subdeacon, deacon, and priest.</note> made in secret: therefore, solemnity is not a necessity for a vow to exist.
¶ Fourthly and finally, a specific argument is made against the vow of clerics. If a solemn vow were inherently attached to sacred orders, it could happen in practice that a person—before the legitimate age of puberty, or even before the proper use of reason—could be bound by the cord of perpetual chastity. No reason seems to allow for this. The consequence follows because, since the sacrament of Order imprints a "character" <note>An indelible spiritual mark on the soul.</note> regardless of when it is conferred, it is received. This absurdity is avoided in a vow of religion, as it cannot be made solemnly before the fourteenth year. ¶ On the contrary is the fact that only vows of this kind [solemn] both impede a marriage from being contracted and dissolve one already contracted: a power which belongs to the solemn vow alone.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To this question, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> responds with two conclusions. The first is: the solemnity of a vow is considered according to something spiritual; namely, according to a blessing or consecration, which is applied based on the institution of the
<margin>Proof.</margin>
Apostles. The proof: the solemnity of a thing ought to be measured and accommodated to its nature and condition. This is evident in physical matters: the solemnity of a wedding consists in the preparation of guests; the solemnity of a new knighthood consists in the preparation of horses and the gathering of soldiers—as can be seen especially in Germany when someone is created an Elector, and in other kingdoms when one is made a dubbed knight. However, since a vow is made to God, it is a spiritual thing; therefore, its solemnity must likewise be spiritual, such as a certain blessing. This is customary in religious orders and in consecration, as when someone is initiated into sacred orders. This religious practice had its origin in the time of the Apostles, as is clear from Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian theologian whose writings were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>. For he mentions the rite of sacred orders in the second chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and concerning monks in the sixth chapter.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: a vow becomes solemn both in the profession of a certain rule and in the
<margin>Proof.</margin>
reception of major orders. The proof: solemnity is not usually applied except when someone is handed over to something through the reception of a new status. For the solemnity of a marriage is not celebrated unless both spouses hand themselves over to each other and profess the matrimonial state, which ought to be publicly known. By the reception of a sacred order—for instance, the subdiaconate—a man devotes himself to divine ministry,

<column-break/>

assuming a firm clerical status. Similarly, in the profession of a certain rule: when, through the renunciation of the world and his own will, someone assumes a state of perfection; therefore, the vow then becomes solemn. ¶ At this point, first of all, the Doctors of both Law and Theology pile up innumerable divisions of vows, as can be seen particularly in Palude <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and jurist.</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, distinction 38, question 2), where he multiplies them up to twelve. Even the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, author of the standard medieval theology textbook.</note>
<margin>Multiple divisions of the vow.</margin>
posits some. One is a **personal vow**, such as chastity; another is a **real vow**, such as almsgiving; and another is **mixed**, such as a pilgrimage, where expenses are necessary. Likewise, one is **temporal** (for a certain time) and another **perpetual**. Also, one is **common**, as when the matter is common to both a commandment and a vow—the Master gives the example of baptism—and another is **proper**, concerning a work of supererogation <note>An act that goes beyond what is required by duty or law.</note>, which is the proper matter of a vow. These and other such divisions, however, contribute little to the present matter. But that division which separates the vow into **simple** and **solemn** is sufficient for us, for their bonds and obligations differ greatly.

¶ Again, one must note the difference between a
<margin>Difference between a simple and solemn vow regarding their effect.</margin>
simple and a solemn vow if judged by their effect: a simple vow hinders a marriage that is to be contracted, but does not dissolve one already contracted. I say it "hinders" because it is a mortal sin to celebrate a marriage covenant after making a simple vow of religion; nevertheless, the marriage holds. A solemn vow, however, not only stands in the way of a marriage being contracted but also dissolves a contract already made. This is not because it is a "dissolution" in the strict sense (since the marriage was never valid), but it is said to "dissolve" because it renders the persons legally incapable of contracting. This distinction is found in the decree of Pope Boniface VIII <note>Pope from 1294 to 1303, known for his contributions to Canon Law.</note> (found in the *Sext*, book 6, under "On vows and their redemption," the only chapter). Thirdly, it must be further supposed that a solemn vow takes place in only two subject matters: namely, in the profession of religion and in the reception of a sacred order, such as the diaconate, as the same Pope defines in that place. This does not mean this definition was first established there; for Saint Thomas preceded Boniface VIII by twenty years, yet he mentions it as an ancient practice. ¶ With these things
<margin>Question.</margin>
supposed, the dispute turns on what exactly makes a vow solemn—that is, what gives it the power to dissolve a marriage: whether this is a matter of **merely positive law** <note>Human-made laws, such as those of the Church or State.</note> or indeed of **divine law**. It is of no small importance which side is true. For if it is...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether a "solemn" vow (a formal, public commitment) can be waived or dispensed by the Pope. ### Question II of the Eighth Book ###

<margin>Cajetan. The first opinion.</margin>
By divine law, a solemn vow cannot be dispensed by the Pope; however, it is a different matter if the vow is based on positive law <note>Positive law refers to laws established by human or ecclesiastical authority rather than inherent divine or natural law.</note>. Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> therefore recounts three opinions on this matter. The first opinion is that the solemnity of a vow consists either in a blessing—such as occurs in a religious order—or in a consecration, which is used in the receiving of holy orders. However, this opinion is refuted by many arguments. <margin>First argument against the first opinion.</margin> First, because a "tacit profession"—that is, when a year of probation passes with the novice’s consent—is in effect a solemn vow, and yet it occurs without any formal blessing. <margin>Second argument.</margin> Second, because in some religious orders, such as our own <note>The author, Francisco de Soto, was a Dominican; he refers here to the Dominican practice.</note>, the person making the profession is not blessed, but rather the scapular <note>A garment worn over the shoulders as part of a religious habit.</note> is blessed; and this happens after the person has made their profession into the hands of the superior. Therefore, that blessing is neither part of the essence of the vow nor a requirement for it. <margin>Third argument.</margin> Third, neither a blessing nor a consecration is sufficient on its own. For the priests of the Greeks are consecrated, and yet they are not bound by a solemn vow of chastity; the Church could likewise decree the same for our own priests. Therefore, if the Church’s statute were removed, anyone being initiated into sacred orders could (as some believe) profess a religious life by making a simple vow of chastity, or even no vow at all. <margin>The mind of Saint Thomas.</margin> ¶ Before we proceed further, I wish to advise the reader that this opinion was never held by Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>; indeed, I believe no one who understood him correctly has embraced it. For Saint Thomas, in his earlier conclusion (which must be considered carefully), does not claim that the substance of a solemn vow consists in a blessing or consecration. Instead, he precisely says that the solemnity of a vow is "attended to according to" the blessing and consecration. Thus, he only means to say that the solemnity of the blessing is used as a sign of the vow: just as the solemnity of a wedding is not the essence of a marriage, but is its public testimony. Therefore, he does not mean that the ceremony is strictly the essence, but he is merely explaining the ritual that actually flourishes in the Church now. However, the reasoning is different regarding the reception of holy orders. For by the very fact that a subdeacon receives orders, he simultaneously receives the vow. <margin>Second opinion.</margin> ¶ The second opinion is that the solemnity of a vow consists in the "handing over" of the person. Thus, the substance of a solemn vow differs from a simple one in this: a simple vow is merely a promise to give something in the future, whereas a solemn vow is the actual delivery of the person, whether it was promised beforehand or not. And although Cajetan rejects this opinion, I nevertheless judge it to be the truest one. It is expressly the opinion of Saint Thomas in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 38, Question 1, Article 3) and even more explicitly in this passage. And so that it might shine more brightly by comparison to the other—

<column-break/>

<margin>Cajetan's third opinion.</margin>
—the third opinion, which Cajetan embraces, is that the solemnity of a vow consists in this: that by the authority of the Church, it has been established that through such a vow, a person becomes legally "incapable" of marriage. This is not unique to Cajetan, but is also the view of <margin>Scotus.</margin> Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan theologian.</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences*. The proofs <margin>First argument for the opinion of Cajetan and Scotus.</margin> offered by Cajetan are these. First, that the Church could decree that anyone who vowed celibacy before three witnesses would be making a solemn vow, just like one who receives sacred orders or professes into a religious order. This is a sign that the whole matter depends on the judgment of the Church. <margin>Second argument.</margin> Second, that conversely, even if someone were to profess the three vows <note>Poverty, chastity, and obedience.</note> with every possible solemnity in a religious order not approved by the Apostolic See <note>The Papacy</note>, a solemn vow would not result, solely due to the lack of ecclesiastical authority. Furthermore, there are the words of the Pope in the cited passage (from the *Book of Sext*, chapter on vows), namely: "the solemnity of a vow was invented solely by the constitution of the Church." <margin>Argument of Saint Thomas against the previous opinion.</margin> ¶ However, Saint Thomas rejects this opinion in the cited passage of his commentary using this argument: If a solemn vow made a religious person incapable of marriage only by the statute of the Church, and this were not a matter of divine law, it would follow that the Church could decree the opposite. Namely, that the Church could dispense someone from that solemn vow of chastity—which, however, is false, as we shall dispute later. <margin>Cajetan's metaphysical solution.</margin> Cajetan responds here with I know not what sort of "metaphysics": namely, that although neither the vow on its own (without the Church’s statute) is enough to void a marriage, nor the legal command on its own, nevertheless both together are sufficient. ¶ However, this solution limps in two ways. First, if a person is not made "incapable" of marriage by the vow (on the grounds of handing oneself over) nor by the legal command, it cannot be understood at all how they are made so by the two combined; for this remains to be explained. <margin>Argument against Cajetan.</margin> And it is argued thus: It is clear that even if the Pope commands a layperson, even under the penalty of automatic excommunication, not to marry (for instance, because another person is claiming them in his court), nevertheless, if that person is not already bound to another marriage and contracts one against the Pope’s command, the marriage "holds" (is valid), even though he sins. This is because commanding someone not to contract a marriage is not the same as making them legally incapable of it. Therefore, if the vow (as a handing over of the person) does not make them incapable of marriage, the additional legal command will not accomplish it either. <margin>Second argument.</margin> Furthermore, he does not really answer Saint Thomas. For if only the statute of the Church is the cause for why a religious vow makes a person incapable of marriage, the same Church can make it so that—

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s scholastic analysis of religious vows. Specifically, it examines the distinction between a "simple" vow (a promise) and a "solemn" vow (a total legal handing over of oneself), and whether the Church's power to dispense such vows derives from human law or divine law.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law, #

true religion exists without that legal inability; for once the statute is removed, the vow remains by itself a **simple vow**. Likewise, he would be able to dispense such a solemn vow after it has been issued. Indeed, he [Cajetan] does not answer this directly, but it is a consequence of his conclusion. And so finally, as we shall see later, he concedes that the Pope can dispense a solemn vow. For that opinion is the natural sprout of this root. ¶ Therefore, if the opinion of Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), whose *Summa Theologiae* is the foundation for this commentary.</note> regarding the indispensability of the solemn vow is to be upheld—as I believe it should be, as the most ancient confession of the doctors—then we must judge the solemn vow in this way: we should say its substance consists in this, that it is a <term>tradition</term> <note>From the Latin *traditio*, meaning a "handing over" or "delivery" of property or oneself into the legal possession of another.</note>, whereas a **simple vow** is merely a **promise**. He [Thomas] holds this opinion expressly both in his commentary on the *Fourth Book of Sentences* and here. By using the likeness of marriage, he says that just as in marriage a "solemnity" occurs because each spouse is totally enslaved to the marital reality, so through the receiving of holy orders a man is enslaved to the divine ministry, and through the renunciation of the world and his own will, he assumes the state of perfection. From this distinction another is born: namely, that a simple vow can be made to God alone without any of His ministers, but a solemn vow cannot be made except through His minister. And the reason is that a promise, since it is not a "giving," does not require a solemn reception; rather, because you promise to God, only your own faith remains bound. However, a "handing over" (*traditio*) does not happen unless the one who is being handed over 
<margin>Objection.</margin> is solemnly received. ¶ But you say: God will also receive you if you give yourself to Him. Here is where the point stands. 
<margin>Solution.</margin> Since a man handing himself over by changing his state and renouncing his own will is a matter of the greatest importance, it ought not to be done without judgment and examination. This judgment is not to be committed to the one who vows, but to the Church, which must explore whether he who prepares to hand himself over is fit and suitable for that state. Because of this, the Church receives no one into religion <note>Meaning a religious order or monastic life.</note> before a time of probation. Nor indeed does she admit one to holy orders without examination, as is clear in the titles regarding the age and quality of those to be ordained. And so, the substance of a **solemn vow** consists in this: that a man hands himself over to God through that person by whom he is received in the name of God. For then he abdicates from himself the right of passing to another state. That ecclesiastical mode of receiving, which is the "solemnity" of the vow, belongs to <term>positive law</term> <note>Human-made law or Church decrees, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>. For example, if someone according to ancient laws sold himself to another, by that very law of nations he would be that person’s slave; yet the king could decree by civil law that no one is permitted to sell himself except with such a 

<column-break/>

solemn ceremony; otherwise, the "handing over" would not hold. And this is what Boniface says in the stated chapter <note>Referring to Pope Boniface VIII in the *Liber Sextus* of Canon Law.</note>: namely, that the solemnity of a vow was invented solely by the constitution of the Church. For he does not say that the *substance* of a solemn vow—for instance, that he who hands himself over cannot contract marriage—is an invention of the Church; rather, he says that the *mode* of handing over is a decree of the Church's constitution. In short, to 
<margin>To Cajetan’s motive.</margin> respond to the aforementioned objection, it can be certain to no one that they are received by God through a solemn vow except through the judgment of the Church. And this is what Saint Thomas says in the stated *Distinction 4, Article 2, Question 3*: namely, that a vow is never solemn, no matter how much one professes, unless the order of positive law is observed. And for that reason—namely, because in other vows, such as pilgrimages and fasts, no "handing over" occurs, nor a change of state—they cannot be made solemn. Likewise, this applies to a religious order that has not been approved by the Church for this effect. 
<margin>Doubt.</margin> ¶ But you ask: from what place in Scripture is it inferred that a solemn vow, by divine law, voids a marriage? 
<margin>Response.</margin> It is answered that this is concluded by this <term>syllogism</term> <note>A logical argument consisting of a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion.</note>: Whoever hands himself over to another, enslaving his will to him, becomes by natural and divine law incapable of another state; he who vows solemnly hands himself over, abdicating from himself the right of taking a wife and possessing property, etc.; therefore, he becomes incapable of marriage. The major premise is of natural and divine law, which is evident: for if you have handed over the ownership of your property to another, you can in no way snatch it back again without committing theft. It is otherwise if you merely *promised* it; for then, since you have not yet alienated the ownership from yourself, reasons can arise (as was said above) why you might not give it. Therefore, in the same way, if you have handed *yourself* over, natural and divine law forbids you from committing a "theft of yourself." It is clear that the minor premise regarding religious life is of divine law: because religion must be a state of following Christ, according to that word: *If you wish to be perfect, go and sell [what you have], etc., and follow me* <note>Matthew 19:21.</note>. For unless you accept this institute by way of a "state," it is not firm; but a state is not made firm through a promise (such as a simple vow), but through a "handing over" (*traditio*). Therefore, both premises are of divine law, and so is the conclusion. ¶ Distinguish, therefore, between the "solemnity" and the "solemn vow." For the "solemnity"—that is, the ceremony—is not of divine law, but of ecclesiastical law. Nevertheless, that a solemn vow voids a marriage is of divine law, because it is a "handing over."

<summary>Soto argues that a solemn vow is more than a promise; it is a "traditio" (handing over) of one's self and will to God via the Church. While the specific ceremonies are human law, the resulting inability to marry is a matter of divine and natural law because one cannot "steal" back the self they have already legally given away.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholastic debate regarding the nature of solemn versus simple religious vows. The author is specifically refuting the positions of Duns Scotus and Thomas Cajetan, arguing that a solemn vow is not merely a human legal construct but a "delivery" of the self to God that carries divine legal weight.</meta>

### Question II of the Eighth Book ###

<margin>
Another argument against Scotus.
</margin>

¶ And although I may seem to be bothersomely persistent, the point is further confirmed against Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan theologian.</note> and Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Dominican commentator on Aquinas.</note>. For it would follow from their opinion that the Pope could grant a dispensation for a ratified but non-consummated marriage <note>original: "matrimonio rato non consummato"; a marriage that is legally valid but has not yet been physically completed through intercourse.</note>. It is proved thus: A solemn vow dissolves such a marriage; and the entire force of a solemn vow (as they claim) is a decree of the Pope, which is <term>positive law</term> <note>Human-made law, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>. Therefore, by the same authority, he would be able to dissolve that marriage through a simple dispensation without such a vow. Behold the argument of Cajetan, which indeed follows logically from his own opinion; and thus, defeated by his own logic, he conceded the conclusion. But truly, if I may speak with all due respect to such a grave author, that conclusion is so absurd and should be admitted in no age, that before he conceded it, he ought to have moved his mind away from that reasoning regarding the solemn vow which we are refuting here. We therefore deny the minor premise: namely, that a solemn vow dissolves a ratified marriage by virtue of an Ecclesiastical statute; rather, it is dissolved by divine law. This is because it is a change from an inferior state to a superior one. For this reason, although consent establishes the state of marriage, it is nevertheless permitted from that point—so long as it is not consummated—to rise to a better harvest <note>A metaphor for entering the higher spiritual "state" of religious life.</note>. However, once the union is consummated, because by its nature it is for the procreation of offspring, it prohibits that ascent because of the injury that would be done to the child who must be raised. See then, this is what the solemn vow consists of.

<margin>
Scotus’s first argument.
</margin>

¶ Against this conclusion, however, the first argument is that of Scotus, who in the place cited says that this opinion is the weakest of all. A man, he says, has <term>dominion</term> <note>original: "dominium"; the legal right of ownership or control.</note> over himself through his own will; therefore, by that same will alone he can transfer it. Now, through a simple vow which he makes to God alone, he binds his will; therefore, through that simple vow, he confers his ownership to God just as much as through a solemn vow. In this, therefore, there can be no distinction.

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>

It is responded, however, that this is to deny the most manifest nature of promising and giving. Truly, he who promises to give money or a horse to a friend does not thereby renounce his ownership of it. For if he later gave it to another, the gift would hold, as it proceeded from the true owner. Otherwise, you would have to say that whoever owes something to another would no longer be the owner of it—an assertion that would be against all law and courtroom practice. We grant, therefore, that a man can transfer ownership through his will; however, not through a mere promise, but through a <term>delivery</term> <note>original: "dationem"; the physical or legal handing over of a thing.</note>.

<margin>
Cajetan’s argument.
</margin>

¶ Secondly, Cajetan argues: If the Church decreed that if anyone made a vow before three witnesses, that vow would dissolve a future marriage, then that vow would be "solemn" without any official reception by the Church.

<column-break/>

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>

We respond with two points: first, that such an act would then constitute a "reception" by the Pope; for in whatever way he himself established it to be solemn, he would be judged to be receiving the vow. Second, we add that the Holy Spirit will never permit the Church to accept the "handing over" of a human being through a vow without first applying judgment and examination. Otherwise, it would lead to the destruction of religious orders and the priesthood. But in fact, once the year of probation has passed, the Church receives the unspoken profession through its own decree. And conversely, when the Church does not approve of a religious order, then no matter how much the three vows are expressed, it is not a solemn vow, because the Church does not receive it.

<margin>
Argument 3: Dionysius.
</margin>

¶ Thirdly, it is argued: Near the age of the Apostles, as can be seen in Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century author then believed to be a direct disciple of St. Paul.</note> in the sixth chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, orders of monks were flourishing, strengthened (as it is believed) by the solemnity of vows; and yet they were not as they are now. For later, Anthony and Benedict instituted this form of religious life by the authority of the Church.

<margin>
The Response.
</margin>

The response is that if they uttered solemn vows, they did so by the authority of the Church and perhaps into the hands of bishops. From the most holy Virgin Mary, however, no argument can be drawn against us; for if she made a solemn vow, it was by a unique revelation from God. Whether the vow of chastity is so intrinsic to the religious life that not even the Church could make it a "true religion" without it must be debated in Question 5. For there, and in Question 6, we must return to explain the solemn vow, regarding both religious life and the priesthood.

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>

TO the first of the primary arguments, then, it is responded: that the solemnity of a vow, though it happens in the eyes of men, nonetheless belongs to God insofar as a man’s will is received through His ministers. In this act, the man transfers his right to God and renounces his own power and judgment to change his state. For this reason, it is granted that a simple vow binds one before God just as much as a solemn one, in that the transgression of either is a mortal sin. But nonetheless, each binds in its own order. For the simple vow binds like a promise; the transgression of which is therefore a failure to return what you promised. But a solemn vow binds like a <term>delivery</term> <note>original: "traditio"; the legal concept of passing possession to another.</note>; and for that reason, he who transgresses it sins by taking away what he delivered, or by abusing a will that has been enslaved to God. From this, it follows that the transgression of a solemn vow is more serious than that of a simple one.

<margin>
Objection.
</margin>

¶ But if you argue that a solemn vow is just as much a promise as a simple one...

Soto argues against Scotus and Cajetan, asserting that a solemn vow uniquely dissolves a non-consummated marriage because it changes the person's fundamental legal and spiritual state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Dominic de Soto’s exploration of religious vows. In the previous section, he argued against Scotus and Cajetan, asserting that a solemn vow is not merely a legal distinction made by the Church but a fundamental change in a person's status—a "delivery" of the self to God rather than a mere promise. This page addresses specific objections and the complex issue of whether these obligations can be forced upon those below the age of reason.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right ###

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>
In a similar way, one who professes a vow says: "I promise obedience to God and that I will be obedient to you." The response is that there is a difference: the person who makes a solemn vow, although they promise obedience regarding the execution of religious duties, nonetheless promises it by handing over, assigning, and transferring <note>original: "mancipando"; a legal term for transferring property or ownership</note> themselves, their will, and their entire right to God. A simple vow, however, is not a delivery of the will, but a promise by which one is obligated to deliver it and to change one's state later.

<margin>
A question debated by Cajetan.
</margin>
¶ Through these points, the question treated here by Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian.</note> will be decided: whether the distinction between a simple and a solemn vow is a specific one <note>meaning a difference in kind/category, not just degree</note>, and likewise whether a transgression of each is a different species of sin. He answers with a distinction. Namely, that if the distinction is considered from the perspective of the subject <note>the person making the vow</note>, they differ in species: this is because someone who has made a simple vow is not legally disqualified from contracting marriage, unlike one who has vowed solemnly. He supports this by citing Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Scholastic thought.</note> in the first book *On the Soul*, who asserts that a human eye differs in species from a lion’s eye because the souls themselves differ in that way. However, Cajetan says that if the difference is considered from the perspective of the object, then they do not differ in species—just as a human eye and a lion's eye do not differ for that reason, since they share the same formal object and perceive through the same means. For he says the same power of binding exists in both, although it is greater in the solemn vow while remaining within the same species.

<margin>
Cajetan's definition is refuted.
</margin>
And certainly, if the entire difference consisted only in the state of the Church <note>meaning, if it were only a matter of Church law</note>, he would have had to speak this way. However, by holding that one is a promise and the other is a delivery, they undoubtedly differ in species based on the formal reason of the object. This is how it is judged in legal practice: for a promise is one type of action, and the transfer of ownership <note>original: "transactio dominij"</note> is quite another.

<margin>
St. Thomas.
</margin>
And thus St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> says in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4) that they differ like vegetative and sensitive life <note>the difference between the life of a plant and the life of an animal</note>: they differ because of their object. Nevertheless, these distinctions matter little to moral conduct, provided you are certain that a graver sin is committed against a solemn vow than against a simple one.

<margin>
To the second argument.
</margin>
¶ To the second argument, an answer has already been given: since the vows of other works <note>vows other than the standard religious vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience</note> do not cause a change of state, there is no reason for them to be made solemnly. And finally, to the third, it is answered that the distinction between public and secret is one thing, while the distinction between solemn and simple (or private) is another. A vow does not become solemn simply because it is made in public; rather, it is solemn because it is made according to the statute of the Church that receives the person vowing. If that statute is observed, a vow can become solemn even if made in a corner <note>meaning, in private</note>.

<margin>
To the fourth argument.
</margin>
¶ Finally, it remains to answer the fourth argument, where the difficulty is greater. In the first place, it cannot be doubted that even if Holy Orders are received before the use of reason, they imprint a "character" <note>an indelible spiritual mark on the soul</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>
St. Thomas. Richard.
</margin>
and are thus truly received. This is what St. Thomas (in Book 4, distinction 25, question 2) and Richard <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302), a Franciscan theologian.</note> and the other theologians admit. This is because for the reception of a sacrament that imprints a character—such as Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders—no act is required from the recipient. Thus, a specific age is not required for the necessity of the sacrament itself. It is otherwise regarding the necessity of the precept <note>church law/rules</note>: subdeacons cannot be created before their eighteenth year, nor can priests be anointed before their twenty-fifth, under the guilt of mortal sin and the penalty of suspension. Therefore, those who think the sacrament of Orders cannot be received at any age whatsoever are rejected, as St. Thomas says there, because their assertion is supported by neither reason nor authority.

¶ This being established, the conclusion inferred by the fourth argument seems quite clear: namely, that someone can be bound by a vow of chastity before the legitimate use of reason. This is no more absurd than the obligation of marriage. For a girl whose "precociousness supplies for her age" <note>original: "malitia supplet aetatem"; a legal maxim meaning that if a child understands the nature of the act, they can be held responsible even if they are below the legal age</note>, even if she marries before twelve, is held by the bond of marriage, as is clear in the chapter *De illis* regarding the betrothal of minors. Therefore, even if someone is initiated into sacred orders through consent extorted by fear (the kind of fear that might affect a steadfast man), they are still bound by that same vow of chastity. This is according to the more favorable opinion, as Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), author of a famous manual for confessors.</note> well says under the word "Order," section 4; unless perhaps he was already joined to a wife in marriage, from whom he cannot abstain without her consent. This is proved by an argument taken from the chapter regarding the Jews (distinction 45), where those who were believed to have been baptized against their will by Sisebut <note>Visigoth King of Hispania (r. 612–621) who forced many Jews to convert.</note> were nonetheless compelled to keep the faith because they had been marked with the character. Yet, for those who refuse, it is a heavier burden to be obligated to the entire Christian religion than to a single vow of chastity.

<margin>
Sylvester.
</margin>

¶ But truly, I believe a distinction must be made regarding a cleric ordained before the proper age. If he had the use of reason—suppose he had reached his tenth or twelfth year, or perhaps his eighth—and was initiated freely, he must be compelled to keep the vow. If, however, he had no use of reason at all, but was ordained without knowing what was happening to him: it is certainly most agreeable to reason that he be given an option. Namely, that if he wishes to remain in the function of his order, he must abstain; if not, he may marry, though he is suspended from all official duties.

It also examines the difficult legal case of children or those coerced into Holy Orders, debating whether the indelible spiritual "character" of the sacrament forces a lifelong vow of chastity upon them.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion by Dominic de Soto on the nature of religious vows. Having previously established that a solemn vow constitutes a total "handing over" of oneself to God, he now turns to the practical legal question of who has the legal and moral capacity to make such a promise, specifically focusing on those who are under the authority of another person, such as children, spouses, or members of religious orders.</meta>

# Book Eight, Question III.
<sig>Tt 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: man-</meta>

## QUESTION THREE,
## Concerning those who have the capacity to make vows.

->Saint Thomas [Aquinas], Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part, question 88, article 8.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether those who are subject to the power of another are able to make vows.*<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
After examining the substance and virtue of the vow, it follows that we must investigate its subject: namely, who are the people who possess the capacity and the free judgment <note>original: "arbitrium"</note> for making a vow. And first, regarding those who are under the power of another, it is argued that they *can* make vows. For a lesser bond is overcome by a greater one: however, the obligation by which a person is subject to a man is less than that by which they are obligated to God. Therefore, the prior [human] obligation cannot be an impediment to the latter [divine] one.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second. Children who live under paternal care and have not been emancipated <note>original: "mancipati"; a Roman legal term for being released from a father's legal control</note> from it, have the judgment to profess "religion" <note>In this context, "religion" refers specifically to entering a religious order as a monk or nun</note> without the will of their parents. Therefore, nothing prevents those subject to another's power from the virtue of making a vow.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third. A greater capacity is required for doing something than for promising it. However, those in religious orders can perform certain works of religion without the permission of their superiors, such as reciting the Psalms, or mortifying themselves through fasting <note>original: "inedia"</note> and other afflictions. Therefore, subjection in no way takes away the capacity for making a vow.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourth: Anyone who attempts that which they are prohibited by law from doing commits a fault. However, subjects do not sin by making a vow, since it is nowhere found to be prohibited. Therefore, it seems they are able by right to make vows. ¶ On the contrary stands that passage in Numbers 30: "If a woman in her father’s house, and still in her girlhood, vows anything... she shall not be held liable for the vow, unless her father consents." <note>Numbers 30:3-5</note> And the same is added regarding a woman who has a husband. This is cited in the Decretals, Case 33, question 5, in the chapters *manifestum* and *noluit*. From these, it is gathered by equal reasoning that no others who are subject to another’s power are able to bind themselves by a vow without the judgment of their superior.

<column-break/>

<margin>Concluding response.</margin>
There are two conditions of men who do not possess full capacity for making a vow: namely, subjects, who have handed over their will to others; and children, who by their age are not yet sufficiently illuminated by the light of reason. We must speak of the former in this article, and of the latter in the following one. To the question, therefore, a single conclusion is given, and it is a negative one: No one who is under the power of another is able to undertake any vow regarding those matters in which they are subject to that person, such that it becomes solid and firm without the superior’s consent.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is clear. Indeed, a vow, as is evident from the sections above, is a promise made to God. But God, who is the author of natural laws, does not wish for the property of another to be snatched away to be given to Himself. For this reason, He does not find pleasing those alms which are made from stolen goods. But he who is under the power of another is not his own master <note>original: "sui iuris"</note>. Therefore, he can vow nothing to God that he owes to his master or superior, but he is entirely dependent upon that person's power. It follows, then, that such a vow is not valid without consent, but can be invalidated by the superior. ¶ First of all, because this question—both this article and the following one—are established regarding the "irritation" <note>The legal term for annulling or voiding a vow</note> of vows, let us assume that by the name "irritation," it is understood that the vow is null, and is considered as void as if nothing had ever happened. How this differs from dispensation, commutation, and redemption will be more conveniently explained in the next question, which follows concerning dispensation.

<margin>A point of doubt.</margin>
¶ The first cause for doubt here is regarding the foundation of the authority of prelates <note>High-ranking church officials or superiors</note> to invalidate the vows of their subjects: specifically, whether that authority belongs to them only by human law, or also by divine and natural law.

<margin>Reason for the doubt.</margin>
The reason for the doubt is that the passage cited from Numbers 30 only speaks of a woman who is under the care of a parent, or under the power of a husband, as Augustine explains there.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
And it is cited in Case 33, question 5, chapter *noluit*. However, it does not appear by what reasoning a general rule for all subjects can be established from that. For the subjection of a wife and children is natural; but the subjection of those in religious orders, although it is divine, nevertheless does not seem to extend beyond the observance of the three vows [poverty, chastity, and obedience] and their own constitutions. This is especially true because, since religious members profess a state which is a way toward perfection, they do not seem to be barred by divine law from being masters of their own judgment in promoting themselves more urgently toward better fruit through new vows. # F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

that mandate <note>original: "mandatū"</note> appears to be among the legal requirements which were extinguished by the presence of the Gospel.
¶ There are, therefore, those who believe that the capacity for a monk to make a vow without the consent of his superiors was taken away only by human law: namely, by that chapter, *monacho* [a monk], 20. q. 4. But truly, since that decree has no authority other than that of Basil as its author and Gratian as the collector of the decrees, it cannot have the force of law, which only a Council or the Pope can enact. For this reason, unless that authority rested upon divine or natural law, it would not be sufficiently established. <margin>Response.</margin> It is responded, therefore, that this prohibition regarding monks flows from divine and natural law. For by the very fact that someone professes "religion" <note>In this era, "professing religion" specifically meant taking the formal vows of a monk, friar, or nun</note>, he is assigned through obedience to the judgment of the prelate; and thus, by natural law, he cannot move his will from that state without injury to the prelate. Therefore, not only can a prelate dispense a subject from a vow in his capacity as a spiritual superior by virtue of his jurisdiction, but he can also—as a master of their will, much like a secular father—nullify <note>original: "irritare"; a technical legal term meaning to make void or invalid</note> those same vows.
<margin>A doubt.</margin> ¶ You may ask, however, whether this faculty of nullifying is the same in all prelates who possess the authority of dispensing. For it seems that the affirmative side is true: since dispensation, being a duty of a spiritual function, requires greater power than <margin>Solution.</margin> nullification. It is responded, nevertheless, that the matter is not quite so. For Bishops can dispense, but they can by no means nullify: because they are not the absolute masters of the liberty of their subjects, but only their judges. Indeed, not even the Supreme Pontiff <note>original: "Pont. Max."; the Pope</note> can nullify the vows of secular persons; it is otherwise for the "religious" <note>members of religious orders</note>, of whom he is not only the judge, but also their particular prelate. For he is like a general minister or master of every order, and like a Provincial, and like a Prior. Wherefore, in this case, the rule also fails which says that "if a bishop is able to do that which is greater, he should likewise be able to do that which is less": because these powers are not of the same kind. Therefore, those who have the faculty of nullifying vows, besides the prelates of the religious, are—by natural law—parents and guardians of both sexes, and the masters of servants who are bondslaves. For a head of a household <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note> does not exercise the same authority over his domestic servants, as he does not have ownership of their wills. ¶ Regarding the use of this power—namely, whether a superior can nullify any vows whatsoever at his pleasure without any cause at all—it is debated. <margin>Archdeacon. Sylvester. Palud.</margin> For the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous medieval canonist</note>, whom Sylvester <note>Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio</note> cites and imitates under the word "vow" [votum], 3., and Paludanus <note>Pierre de la Palud</note> in 4. d. 38. q. 4., believe the power of nullifying to be so much more absolute

<column-break/>

than that of dispensing, that they believe a nullification can be done without any cause at all, even though a dispensation cannot. <margin>Reason for the aforementioned opinion</margin> And the reason, they say, is that a dispensation is not made because the vow was invalid, and therefore it requires a cause; but nullification happens because the vow was not valid without the superior’s consent, and therefore they think it is within the mere judgment of the superior to nullify it without another cause: just as he who vows was able not to vow without any cause. <margin>Moderation of the opinion.</margin> But truly, this opinion must be tempered with moderation: for although there is a distinction in that a nullification made without an intervening cause is valid (which is certainly not so easily granted in the case of a dispensation), nevertheless, a prelate nullifying a vow without any reason at all would surely not be free from at least venial fault. For since nullification is in some way an act of jurisdiction, he ought to use judgment and foresight before he nullifies: so that he may weigh whether it is more useful and proper to deny the faculty or to grant it. Therefore, there is not such absolute liberty in a superior to nullify after a subject has proposed and desired to vow, as there is in a subject before he asks for the faculty from the superior. ¶ Having set forth these matters regarding the power of nullifying, a second <margin>Second Doubt.</margin> doubt follows immediately concerning that qualification in the conclusion, namely: *In those things in which he is subject to another.* Specifically, let us examine in which things a monk is subject to a superior. For it appears that no exception was necessary. Since, as was just said, he has simply consecrated his entire will to the prelate as the vicar of God. For the understanding of this, it must be noted <margin>Fourfold works.</margin> that the works of monks are fourfold. For the first kind consists of those things which are comprised by the solemn vow, such as the three essential vows <note>Poverty, chastity, and obedience</note> and the specific statutes of the order. And in these, without a doubt, the monk is subject to the prelate. It appears, nonetheless, that he can add a vow to these vows so firmly that the prelate cannot nullify it: as if he should vow never to taste meat in our order <note>Soto was a Dominican</note>, and never to break silence at forbidden times and places; since it was permitted to emit a solemn vow regarding those things, it seems he can also bind himself more strictly to observe them. <margin>First assertion.</margin> It is responded, nevertheless, that the prelate can also nullify these vows; indeed, he ought to: because this doubling of bonds upon the same matter is hardly ever done prudently. Moreover, the power is evident from the fact that since the superior is able to dispense for a cause regarding all constitutions and statutes of the rule (except for the three essential vows), he can restrain the judgment of his subjects so that they do not create new vows concerning these statutes.

<summary>Soto argues that a religious superior's power to nullify (irritare) a monk's vows is rooted in natural law and the vow of obedience, distinguishing this from a bishop's more limited power of dispensation. He concludes that while a superior can technically nullify vows without cause, doing so without careful moral judgment is a venial sin.</summary>
