### Question III of the Eighth Book

->Tt 4<-

For even in those matters over which he can grant a dispensation—making what was illicit into something licit by his authority—the superior can sometimes command an action for a just cause. For instance, he may order a subordinate to break a period of silence or a religious fast; consequently, he has the power to cancel the vows related to these matters.

<margin>Second category.</margin> ¶ In the second category are "free works," which are neither commanded by law nor bound by a prior vow, such as praying more or adding new fasts. In these matters, a superior cannot compel a subordinate against their will, according to the saying of Bernard: "A Prelate should not increase my vow without my consent." <note>original: "Votum meum non augeat Prælatus sine mea volūtate." Refers to St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century monastic reformer.</note> Nevertheless, in a case of necessity, he might occasionally command prayers or perhaps a fast, though that is not our current concern. However, he can impede such works whenever he pleases; and thus, these are the specific works whose vows a Prelate can most properly nullify.

<margin>Third category.</margin> ¶ The third category of works consists of those that entirely exceed the Prelate’s authority, such as transferring to a stricter religious order. <note>original: "transitus ad arctiorem religionem." In canon law, moving to a more rigorous monastery was often permitted even without a superior's permission, as it was seen as seeking a higher spiritual path.</note> Because this concerns the departure of the subordinate from that prelate's obedience, it is not included under that obedience. Thus, as Cajetan rightly says, a vow that a monk makes to make such a transfer cannot be nullified by the Prelate. <margin>Cajetan.</margin> Therefore, you should consider this kind of work excepted by that phrase in the conclusion: "in those things in which he is subject to another." Yet, I would not easily believe that a vow to transfer to a higher religious order entirely escapes the Prelate's authority, as the same author seems to suggest. I believe it only escapes regarding *nullification*; indeed, I think the same Prelate can grant a dispensation regarding that same vow. We will discuss the distinction between these two powers in the third article of the following question. <margin>Fourth assertion.</margin>

<margin>Cajetan.</margin> ¶ The fourth category of works includes those necessary for salvation, such as keeping the commandments of the law. This applies not only to the laws themselves but also to matters pertaining to the fervor of charity, the contrary of which would be venial sins. Cajetan argues that a vow regarding these cannot be nullified by a superior—for example, if a monk vows to God not to steal or not to lie. His reasoning is that this matter is not subject to the prelate, since the prelate cannot grant a dispensation for these things as he can for monastic rules. He says, nonetheless, that the prelate can commute such a vow in the name of God. Therefore, he considers this also to be an exception in the conclusion. However, I would not readily agree with him on this matter. For even if the *necessity* of fulfilling these duties is not under the prelate's power to dispense, I do not see why that *new obligation* by which a subordinate intends to bind himself of his own accord cannot be

<column-break/>

nullified by the prelate. For regarding voluntary acts, the master of the subordinates' wills is the superior.

<margin>The third doubt.</margin> ¶ A third doubt then arises concerning the same conclusion, specifically regarding the phrase: "a vow of a matter in which a subordinate is subject to a superior is not firm without his consent." The doubt is whether the subordinate's vow holds *until* the superior's consent is given, or whether it is void by the very fact it was made. The point of the debate is whether, since a superior's condition is always implied in a subordinate’s vow, it should be understood affirmatively (valid *if* he consents) or merely negatively (valid *unless* he dissents). In the former case, the vow is nothing before consent; in the latter, it is valid until it is made void. Indeed, Richard <margin>Richard.</margin> <note>Richard of Mediavilla, a 13th-century Franciscan theologian.</note> in his commentary on the 4th book of the Sentences, distinction 38, article 4, followed by many "Summists," <note>Authors of "Summas," or manuals for confessors and canon lawyers.</note> distinguishes between the vows of those in religious orders and those of other subordinates, such as a son in a household or a wife. Regarding those in religious orders, they assert a general and absolute conclusion: that they are so inhibited by their solemn vow from making new vows that whatever they do of any kind without the express consent of the superior is void and empty by that very fact. Therefore, not only is breaking such a vow not a sin, but making it is somewhat harmful, for to vow in vain is a fault. Indeed, Richard and his followers believe this was the opinion of St. Thomas [Aquinas], because of the final words in his solution to the third and fourth arguments, where he says a religious person's vow is not firm unless it pleases the superior or he does not refuse it. He also cites the canon *Monacho* (20. q. 4) in support of this. He adds two reasons for this. The first <margin>Richard's first reason.</margin> is that since the burden of religious life is very heavy, it is neither fitting nor permitted to load the vow of profession with new burdens, lest the religious person succumb to the weight. The second reason <margin>Second reason.</margin> is that since the religious vow is of such height that it extinguishes all preceding vows by commuting them into itself, it follows that subsequent vows are also nullified by its power. However, concerning a son or a wife, he does not deny that they can make some vows regarding things not prohibited to them.

<margin>The contrary opinion of Silvester.</margin> ¶ Against this opinion, as Silvester <note>Silvestre de Prieras, a 16th-century theologian.</note> rightly says under the word "vow" (3. §. 3), St. Thomas does not actually support it, nor does it align with the truth. <margin>Peter de Palude, Innocent.</margin> Therefore, Peter de Palude and Innocent [IV], cited there by the same Silvester, frankly admit that those in religious orders who vow something that does not impede the prelate's obedience are bound by the vow, unless they fulfill it before it is nullified by the prelate. And the reason is quite clear. <margin>Reason for the opinion.</margin> For if other subordinates, without the interference of their superiors...

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
the same faculty should be denied to those in religious life. ¶ Secondly, it is argued against his reasoning: despite the burden of religious life, a member of an order can add further vows once they have obtained the prelate's <note>The "prelate" is the high-ranking superior of a religious house or order.</note> permission. Therefore, nothing prevents them from undertaking a vow on their own initiative regarding a matter not prohibited to them, provided they are prepared never to be absent from the duties of obedience for the sake of the vow, and to cease whenever the superior is displeased by the vow. Moreover, the chapter "On the Monk" <note>original: "Capitulū monacho." A reference to a specific section of canon law or monastic rule.</note> does not oppose us at all; in fact, it supports us. Indeed, Basil does not say there that a monk’s vow is null without the Abbot’s consent, but rather that it must be broken—which implies that it was valid before being broken. However, even that warning should not be heard with such rigor as to mean that whatever a religious person vows must be broken immediately; rather, only that which is heavy or troublesome either to the individual or to the prelate should be broken. ¶ Let us then descend to the sense of Saint Thomas, who seems to feel that a vow made before the prelate’s consent is in no way obligatory. For both in his conclusion and in his solution to the third and fourth points, he says that it is "not yet firm," which seems to suggest it is not obligatory. 
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), was a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> explains the meaning of this word with a learned distinction. For the matter of a vow in respect to a religious person can be of two kinds. One is prohibited: either in general—such as a vow of pilgrimage being prohibited by the decree of the constitutions that no one should leave the monastery grounds <note>original: "monasterij septa." The enclosure or cloister.</note>—or in particular, such as if a prelate for a good cause forbade anyone from making a vow regarding a specific thing. The other kind is matter that is not forbidden: such as praying during free hours, studying, fasting, and so on. According to this distinction, the doubt is answered: when a vow is made regarding matter of the first kind (prohibited), an affirmative condition must be understood—namely, "if the prelate ratifies it." But if the matter is of the second type (free), then a negative condition is understood—namely, "unless the prelate nullifies it." And the reason for this difference is that a vow must be made regarding a licit <note>Licit: legally or morally permitted.</note> thing. When the matter is prohibited, it is not licit unless a dispensation <note>A "dispensation" is an official exemption from a law or rule given by an authority.</note> is granted for it; therefore, whoever makes such a vow is not bound until the prelate's consent is added. Nevertheless, when the matter is not prohibited, it is suitable for a vow. And so, a religious person making a vow to pray, fast, or not to lie, is by that very fact bound

<column-break/>

until the prefect <note>A "prefect" or "prelate" refers to the religious superior.</note> nullifies the vow. For this reason, perhaps, Saint Thomas says in his fourth solution that a "due condition" is understood in the vows of religious persons—namely, "if it pleases their superiors," whether they resist or not. Thus, the first part refers to prohibited matter, and the second to free matter. Therefore, when he says a vow without the prelate's consent is "not firm," if it is a vow of the first kind, he means it is not valid; but if it is of the second kind, he clearly means that even if it is valid, it is not so solid that its nullification does not always depend on the will of the prefect. ¶ Regarding both parts, however, some doubt remains, which is worth answering. <margin>A doubt.</margin> Concerning the first, I say there is a doubt that a vow regarding an illicit thing is by that very fact null—indeed, it is a sin; therefore, a vow by a religious person regarding a prohibited thing is not even valid under a condition; indeed, it is a sin. <margin>Solution.</margin> The answer is given by a distinction of the premise. For when a thing is prohibited because it is evil in itself, then the vow is wicked; but when it is only evil because it is prohibited, it can be the matter of a vow under the condition of a dispensation. <margin>A fine point.</margin> You ask whether someone so vowing is bound to report it to the prelate? For it seems that since they are not bound by the vow, they are not bound to report it. <margin>Solution.</margin> The answer is that they are bound to do so, lest the vow be in vain, as it cannot be fulfilled without his permission. But we shall see this more clearly in a moment. 
<margin>Another doubt.</margin> ¶ There is also a doubt regarding the second part: whether a religious person who has vowed "free matter" (for instance, to pray or fast) is bound to hide the matter from the Prelate so that he does not nullify the vow; or, on the contrary, whether it is licit for them to reveal it to him so that he might make it void. For it seems this latter option would be a "fraud against the vow." <note>Essentially, finding a loophole to get out of the promise.</note> <margin>Response.</margin> The answer is that it is licit to reveal it. For in this, one is using their own right. In fact, if the vow is heavy, they can reveal their distress and burden to him so that he may nullify it. Nor is any injury done to the vow, since it is the duty of superiors to correct the rashness of their subordinates. Nonetheless, when a vow is not bitter, it is healthier to pay it willingly. <margin>Hesitation.</margin> ¶ But again, a doubt arises regarding the first part: whether a religious person who made a vow regarding a prohibited thing satisfies it by asking their prefect for the faculty to do the work without explicitly mentioning the vow. For it appears this is enough. For since the consent of the superior is required for this—that he, as the master of the matter, should permit it—by the same reasoning we said that when one makes a vow regarding non-inhibited matter, it holds immediately; it follows that if he himself inhibits the work (for instance, "you shall not go on pilgrimage"), that is enough to nullify the vow. Cajetan heaps up much unnecessary metaphysics here; for the matter is

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether a superior (prelate) has the authority to annul or invalidate a vow made by a subordinate, specifically focusing on members of religious orders and the parallels found in marriage law.</meta>

# Question III of the Eighth Book.

...it is clearer than requiring so many words.

<margin>*The first assertion.*</margin>
First of all, this is most certain: if a prelate, unaware of a vow, merely prohibits the work associated with it, the vow does not thereby become void. For taking away the material of a vow for a time is not the same as annulling the vow itself. Furthermore, since annulment is a legal action that requires knowledge of the matter, the prelate must know of the vow in order to strike it down. From this, the consequence is clear: the subordinate is bound to reveal the vow to the superior before they are in default of it. This is why in Numbers 30 <note>The biblical book of Numbers, chapter 30, outlines the laws concerning vows made by daughters and wives, and the rights of fathers and husbands to uphold or void them.</note>, the father’s knowledge of his daughter’s vow is required so that he may either consent or dissent.

<margin>*Objection.*</margin>
¶ But if you argue to the contrary: A married woman who has made a simple vow of chastity <note>A "simple vow" is a public or private promise made to God, whereas a "solemn vow" usually involves a permanent change in legal status, such as entering a religious order.</note> is not bound to disclose it to her spouse; she may lawfully choose not to request the marital debt <note>original: "debitum"; refers to the "conjugal debt," the traditional theological term for the obligation of spouses to be sexually available to one another.</note>, provided she pays it when asked. Therefore, a subordinate may likewise remain silent.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
The response is that the argument fails because there is no true similarity: because by the very fact that a woman is joined to a man in marriage, she has lost the power to vow not to "pay the debt," even conditionally. Therefore, her vow is understood only as a vow not to *request* it, which she can do without her husband’s knowledge—just as a member of a religious order might fulfill a vow of prayer secretly from their prelate. However, when a vow is made concerning a prohibited matter under a condition, the one vowing is bound to make it known to the dispenser of the law; otherwise, they would be vowing in vain, which would turn into a mockery of God.

<margin>*Question.*</margin>
¶ A greater occasion for doubt is asked: after a member of a religious order has undertaken a vow regarding some matter with the permission of the prelate, does the power to annul it nevertheless remain with that same superior?

<margin>*Richard.*</margin>
It would seem that no such power remains. This was the opinion of Richard <note>Richard of Middleton (c. 1249–1302), a Franciscan theologian and philosopher known for his commentaries on the Sentences.</note> in the passage cited: indeed, he even doubts whether the superior can grant a dispensation at that point, saying one must instead fly to the Pope. For since nothing more is required for the firmness of a subordinate’s vow than the prelate’s consent, it follows that once it has been confirmed by that consent, no further power of annulment remains to the superior.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
Nevertheless, the response is that it remains within the prefect’s <note>A general term for a superior or governor in a religious or administrative context.</note> judgment to annul it even then. The reason is this: even after a vow is emitted, the religious person remains simply a subordinate; and thus, the prelate is not robbed of his authority. Indeed, add to this that sometimes, even if a good cause initially granted the permission, the superior can nonetheless rightly and properly revoke what he once ratified if circumstances change <note>original: "mutatis rebus"</note>.

<margin>*Augustine.*</margin>
This teaching is supported by Augustine in his commentary on Numbers (cited in the Decree of Gratian, Case 33, Question 5, Canon "He did not wish") <note>Reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a foundational collection of Canon Law. The canon "noluit" discusses paternal and marital authority over vows.</note>, where he teaches that a vow which a girl had firmly undertaken with her father’s permission can later be rendered void by her husband. Add to this that even if the superior annuls the vow without any cause, although he may sin in doing so, the vow is nonetheless voided.

<column-break/>

This assertion is further supported by the same Augustine in the same Case and Question, Canon "It is manifest," where he says expressly that if a wife makes a vow by her husband’s authority, and he later annuls it (not without fault of his own), the wife is nonetheless bound to obey. Indeed, the sacred text itself contains this very point. That a husband—and likewise a prelate—sins by revoking it without cause is attested not only there by Augustine, but by the text of Numbers 30 itself. There it says that even when a husband seemed to ignore it at first but later contradicted it, the wife shall not be held guilty of the vow, but the husband himself shall bear her iniquity. The reason is that although a superior has the power to annul an inferior’s vow, it is not so absolute (as we said above) that he shouldn't do so with reason and judgment. And therefore, once he has granted permission, he ought not to revoke it without cause.

¶ This opinion regarding members of religious orders is clearly confirmed by a similar example taken from a married woman. Truly, if a wife, even with her husband’s prior permission, vows some gift to a particular Saint, as long as it is not yet paid, it is always in the husband’s judgment to retract the statement. If he retracts it, although he may be at fault, she cannot help but obey.

<margin>*Ambrose.*</margin>
This is the express opinion of Ambrose in his book *On Paradise* (cited in Canon "Nor that," Case 33, Question 5, as Gratian infers there). The reason is that the granting of permission is not an absolute transfer of ownership of that thing to the wife, but only the right to offer it to the sacred. Therefore, until the thing itself is handed over, it always depends on the superior, should he wish to revoke it. Nor is your logic valid if you argue: "The superior sins by retracting his word; therefore the subordinate is not at all bound to obey him." That inference, I say, is null: for it is not for the subordinate to examine the commands of elders in matters that are not evil in themselves but depend on their own judgment—it would be otherwise if they commanded something inherently illicit, such as stealing or lying.

<margin>*Another question. Cajetan.*</margin>
¶ But just as it was asked above concerning monks, so it remains to be asked concerning a wife in respect to her husband: whether a husband can annul all of a wife's vows universally. Indeed, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a powerful Dominican cardinal and philosopher known for his defense of Thomism.</note> would in a similar way except a vow not to sin—for example, a vow not to lie—because in that matter the wife does not seem to be a subordinate.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
But I would believe that he can annul even that. For although she is not a subject regarding the necessity of the law, she is nonetheless a subject regarding a voluntary obligation. Therefore, with no exception, a husband can annul all of his wife's vows; and if there were any that he could not annul...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of whether a superior—specifically a husband in the context of marriage—has the authority to annul or invalidate a vow made by a subordinate, comparing the husband's authority to that of a religious prelate.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law.

...it is most well-known that dispensing <note>To "dispense" a vow is to formally release someone from their promise to God, a power usually reserved for the Church hierarchy.</note> is not at all possible for [a layman]: because, as we shall see in the next question, that is the specific property of a spiritual prelate.
<margin>A scruple.</margin>
¶ However, conversely, whether a wife can also void a husband’s vow is called into doubt. For on one hand, it appears she has no such faculty. For as it is written, she shall be under the power of her husband, and not the other way around.
<margin>Response. Paul.</margin>
The response is that since they are equals in the faith of the marriage bed <note>original: "fide coniugalis tori"; refers to the mutual obligation of sexual fidelity and availability.</note>, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 7: because the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife does; just as the wife does not have power over hers, but the husband does. Neither can make a simple vow of chastity without the other’s permission. Indeed, notwithstanding such a vow, each is bound to pay the debt to the other: as Gratian <note>Gratian was a 12th-century jurist who compiled the "Decretum," the foundation of medieval Canon Law.</note> rightly concluded in the canon *Manifestum*, case 33, question 5.
¶ But whether either one can make a vow of **not asking** for the debt is a greater reason for doubt. For in this, so far as the faith of the bed is concerned, one does no injury to the other. Nevertheless, that a husband can void such a vow made by his wife should not be in doubt—not because it is against the faith of the marriage bed, but because she is truly a subject. And so Augustine expressly says in the same chapter, *Manifestum*.
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
However, whether the wife can conversely void a similar vow of her husband is a more hidden doubt. For she cannot do so on the grounds that it is against the faith [of the bed], since he remains ready to pay the debt when asked. Nor can she do so by reason of subjection, since a husband is not the wife’s subject. It is answered, first, that such a vow is very burdensome to a wife and almost contrary to marital faith. For since women, out of modesty, hardly dare to ask for the debt, if the husband were prohibited from asking, it would result in a "fraud of marriage" <note>An act that undermines the essential purpose or fairness of the marital contract.</note>. Therefore, one would not be far from the mark in saying such a vow does not hold without the wife's consent. At the very least, it is certain that it ought to be abolished through a dispensation by a Bishop to remove all scruples.
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ You may perhaps ask whether, outside of this matter, a husband has absolute power to make vows without consulting his wife. It appears this is the truth, since he is not subject to the wife. But on the other hand, an argument nonetheless exists that in those things which pertain to the common family of both, he cannot. For instance, if he were to vow a long pilgrimage through which the conjugal office would be defrauded of its fruit, or if he were to vow a large sum of money which is necessary for the maintenance of the wife and children. Surely it is not entirely lacking in probability that he cannot do this, since it turns toward the ruin of the wife.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this it is nonethe-

<column-break/>

-less answered that the faculty of voiding vows is simply not to be granted to the wife in respect to the husband, especially in the distribution of goods. For even if he wishes to squander goods against her protest, although he does wrong, the act nonetheless holds, since he is the absolute administrator of them; and thus such a vow is not under the wife’s power. Nevertheless, if the vow were to fall into the vice of prodigality or injustice, by that very fact it would have no binding force, and thus would need no formal voiding. The same must be said of absence. For a husband can travel abroad without "fraud of marriage," and thus can take a vow if the cause requires it; nor is he subject to the wife in this. However, if there were no legitimate cause, it would likewise not hold, and it would be a sin to make the vow.
<margin>A grave doubt.</margin>
¶ But the most significant doubt here, and one not easily solved, is whether, after both spouses have taken a vow of chastity by mutual consent, the husband can revoke the permission he gave to his wife and thus void her vow—and by the same right, whether a wife who perhaps regrets the deed can retract the permission she gave to her husband and demand the debt from him. Gratian’s opinion in the same canon *Manifestum* is negative. For after each has renounced their right, each becomes free from the other.
<margin>Gratian’s opinion.</margin>
<margin>Argument for the other side.</margin>
¶ However, the argument that makes the matter doubtful is of this sort: After a husband has given his wife the faculty of vowing continence—namely, not to ask for the debt—he can revoke it, as has just been confirmed not only by the authority of Saint Augustine, but also by Holy Scripture and reason. Now, because he granted a fuller permission (namely, that she neither ask nor pay), this does not prevent him from being able to retract both for the same reason. Therefore, a husband at least can annul such a vow of his wife. And since the spouse is equal to the husband in this right, she also seems able to retract the granted faculty. Additionally, it can happen that both may find themselves in danger from the allurements of the flesh, and so it would be more prudent to return to the use of marriage according to the warning of Paul in 1 Corinthians 7.
<margin>Paul.</margin>
But if you say that because both made the vow by mutual consent, both are deprived of the power of revoking it, the reason for this is truly not so evident. For if a husband is able to revoke a faculty he gave his wife when the wife did not grant him the same in return, it does not appear why the husband should be deprived of his faculty just because the wife granted the same to him. Truly, the argument seems to make the matter doubtful. Nevertheless, we can answer that since in that office they are equals...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological discussion regarding the power of a superior—such as a husband, father, or master—to annul the vows of those under their authority. Specifically, it concludes the discussion on mutual marital vows and addresses whether a voided vow can "revive" once the subordinate gains independence.</meta>

### Book Eight, Question III.

<margin>The Solution.</margin> When spouses mutually and reciprocally consent <note>original: "vicario mutuoq; cõsensu"</note> to make a vow, it constitutes a specific type of mutual contract: "I do so that you may do" <note>original: "facio ut facias"; a standard legal formula for reciprocal obligations.</note>. That is to say, "I renounce my right so that you may renounce yours." Therefore, because the wife renounces her right to demand the **marriage debt** <note>The "marriage debt" refers to the medieval legal and moral obligation for spouses to provide sexual intimacy to one another upon request.</note> from her husband, the husband is deprived not only of the right to seek it but also of the power to revoke the act. For this reason, the vow of both parties is judged to be an absolute vow of chastity.

<margin>A final doubt.</margin> ¶ Another doubt follows after these: whether a vow once annulled by a superior "comes back to life" <note>original: "reuiuiscat"</note> if the person later leaves that superior’s care and servitude. On this point, there are those who distinguish that an annulled vow of a minor <note>original: "impuberis"; a child who has not yet reached the age of legal puberty (12 for girls, 14 for boys).</note> does not revive. However, if the person was already an adult when they made it—namely, if they had exceeded their fourteenth year—even if it is annulled, they say the person is bound once they are emancipated <note>Legal "emancipation" in this context refers to being freed from the "patria potestas" or the legal power of the father.</note>. (For if it is a "real" vow involving property, as we said above, it can be annulled until the twenty-fifth year). 

<margin>Innocent</margin> In support of this opinion, **Innocent** <note>Pope Innocent IV (1195–1254), a major canon lawyer.</note> is usually cited regarding the chapter *Scripturae* in the section on vows. Yet, he says nothing more than that minors making vows, or those under the care of parents, are bound to fulfill them when they have been emancipated. Since he does not explicitly state this applies even if the vows were quashed, 

<margin>The opinion of Paludanus.</margin> he should not be believed to hold that view. But **Paludanus** <note>Peter de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a Dominican theologian.</note>, although he is ambiguous, seems to agree with this in Book 4, Distinction 38. Nevertheless, with all due respect to that author’s reputation, the contrary opinion should undoubtedly be embraced, which **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), author of the "Summa Sylvestrina," a popular handbook for confessors.</note> holds under the entry "Vow." Specifically, that in general, any vow—whether of a wife, a son, a servant, or a religious subordinate—once annulled, retains no further power by which it could be binding at any time, unless it is made anew.

<margin>The aforementioned opinion is rejected.</margin> For there exists a rule of law that an obligation once extinguished cannot be restored <note>original: "obligatio semel extincta instaurari non potest"</note>, found in the Code under "On the Remission of a Pledge." 

<margin>Panormitanus.</margin> And **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading expert in Canon Law.</note> more readily favors this opinion in his commentary on the same chapter *Scripturae*. Indeed, the texts of the chapters *Quidam* and *Placet* regarding the conversion of spouses confirm this. There it is held that when a spouse enters religious life, insofar as the move was quashed by the protest of the other spouse, the vow no longer binds even after the death of that spouse. ¶ However, a more difficult reason for doubt arises when a wife, for example, emits a vow to be carried out only if she outlives her husband. The same applies to a son making a vow while under a parent's care to be fulfilled after his emancipation, and likewise a servant under the condition that he is 

<column-break/>

granted his freedom. The question is whether superiors can also annul these kinds of vows. For the negative side seems to be confirmed by the fact that such vows are made for a time when the vower’s freedom is not constrained under another's power. Furthermore, such a vow by a wife in no way harms the husband at that time. To this, one could respond in three ways. First, by a distinction: some such vows are burdensome and inconvenient to the superior, while others result only in a burden to the vower. Those of the first kind cannot be annulled by the superior if they are made for a time after he has passed away—such as if a wife vows to enter a religious order or keep chastity after his death—because these carry no inconvenience, except that they might seem to stand in the way of marital duties while the husband is still alive. If, however, they are burdensome to the vower, and thus the annulment works for their benefit, then it seems the husband or father can annul them; for instance, if they vowed a long pilgrimage or great expenses. Others, however, respond more scrupulously that vows issued in that manner of either kind cannot be annulled, and they subsequently advise recurring to a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A formal release from a vow granted by a church authority.</note>.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin> **Sylvester**, however, under the entry "Religion," holds the contrary: namely, that any vow which anyone emits while under the power of another can be annulled while that power lasts. For example, if a boy in his thirteenth year vows to enter a religious order in his fifteenth year; and similarly, if before his twenty-fifth year he vows something to be carried out after that age. The father can annul those immediately: namely, the "personal" vow before the fourteenth year and the "real" vow before the twenty-fifth, as is to be seen in the next article. And truly, this opinion is not to be feared. For it appears safe because, since the will of a subordinate at that time is simply bound to the superior’s judgment, under whatever condition he vowed it, it can then be annulled. Add to this that the reason for this power inherent in the superior is founded on the care for the subordinate's welfare, because the subordinate's will is not presumed to be illuminated by the proper light of reason enough to make a vow. Therefore, even if he adds the condition of fulfilling it after he is free, the same reasoning demands that he weigh it by the superior's judgment at the time he is making the choice. Thus, it is in the superior's power to annul it at the time the vow is issued—especially since there is no vow that does not result in some burden upon the vower themselves.

<summary>This page discusses whether vows made by subordinates (wives, children, or servants) remain valid or "revive" after they gain independence if a superior had previously annulled them. The author concludes that once a superior voids a vow, it is legally extinguished and does not automatically bind the person later in life.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the first article of Question III, regarding the power of parents and religious superiors to annul the vows of those under their authority. # F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law

Therefore, the distinction made in the first response seems superfluous. ¶ However, there is much greater perplexity and doubt regarding whether a father can annul a vow after a son has passed the age of parental power, if the vow was never annulled while the son was still under that power; but this will be more fittingly resolved in the next article.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
It remains at last to respond to the arguments posed at the beginning of the question. The response to the first has already been explained above. For although an obligation made to God is greater than one made to men, God nevertheless does not wish anything to be offered to Him unless it is under the **dominion** <note>original: "dominio"; meaning the right of ownership or legal control.</note> of the person offering it. For the obedience owed to parents is also a divine obligation, as is the obedience which subordinates owe to their **prelates** <note>A "prelate" here refers to a high-ranking religious superior, such as an abbot or bishop.</note>; therefore, God does not find it pleasing when subordinates vow anything against the will of such superiors.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that after children have reached the years of **puberty**—namely, when a male has exceeded his fourteenth year and a female her twelfth—they are **of their own right** <note>original: "sui sunt iuris"; a legal term meaning they have the capacity to manage their own persons and make certain binding legal decisions.</note> regarding matters that pertain to their own person, provided they are not servants or slaves. This includes the right to profess a religious life or to contract marriages. However, they remain under the care of their parents regarding the disposal of property. Therefore, a **real vow** <note>original: "reale votum"; a vow involving "res" (things or property), such as promising to give money or land to the church.</note> made before their twenty-fifth year can be annulled by a superior, as will be seen in the next article. A servant, however, because he is in the power of a master, is never able to bind himself to a religious order, nor to a pilgrimage, nor to anything else through which he would be withdrawn from his master’s service, as the Doctors note in the chapter *Scripturae* in the section on vows and the redemption of vows.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, Saint Thomas responds that although it is more significant to act than to promise—and thus those in religious orders can do many things without consulting their superiors—they nevertheless cannot firmly vow anything without their consent. And the reason, he says, is because there is no time exempted in which a prelate could not occupy the subordinate with some duty. However, **Conrad** <note>Likely referring to Conradus Koellin, a 16th-century commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> does not approve of this reason in the passage cited.

<margin>Conrad's objection.</margin>
For he argues that this does not prove a subordinate cannot vow certain things that a prelate cannot forbid: such as not lying, not speaking ill, etc.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
But in truth, Saint Thomas does not intend to introduce that as the sole, adequate reason. For in the context of the question, he had given the reason why a subordinate cannot vow without consulting a prelate: namely, because he has a will

<column-break/>

bound to the judgment of that superior. He explains this same point at the beginning of the response: specifically, that a religious subordinate is subject to the prelate regarding his actions according to the profession of the **Rule** <note>The "Rule" refers to the specific code of conduct for a religious order, such as the Rule of St. Benedict.</note>. The other subjoined reason is only a particular one, regarding those works for which the prelate can command the opposite. For since he has the power of commanding at any time, the subordinate's will must be free to obey; and therefore, he cannot vow to the contrary. But this reason does not prove the case as clearly regarding these kinds of works as the one narrated before. For one could argue, saying that although a prelate has the power to occupy a subordinate at any moment in time, it does not follow from this that he can annul the subordinate's vows; rather, it only means that, notwithstanding the vow, the subordinate must obey him when he commands the opposite. Nevertheless, the vow would remain firm, obliging the subordinate to act according to it as long as the prelate does not command a contrary work. Thus, the prelate's authority would extend to sometimes hindering the execution of a vow, but not to annulling the vow itself. However, it is nonetheless a fitting reason that if he can hinder the execution as often as he pleases, he can also remove the vow, which to some extent seems to stand in the way of free obedience.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the fourth, it is responded that although a subordinate's vow made without the prelate's consent is not entirely firm, nonetheless, because it can be put into execution with his permission, the subordinate does not sin by vowing—whether they be a person in a religious order, a wife, or a son. From this word, it is gathered that a vow is immediately obligatory if it concerns a matter that is not prohibited, even though it is **pendent** <note>A legal term meaning the obligation is "hanging" or conditional upon the approval of another.</note> upon the prelate. It is otherwise if the matter is prohibited. But even then, it is not a sin to vow if it is done under the condition "if it pleases the prelate," just as one might vow something else with the condition "unless he refuses."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question III from Book Eight, focusing on the legal and moral capacity of minors to take religious vows. # Book Eight, Question III

...whether they are to be bound by the religious practice of vowing. <margin>First argument.</margin> For a vow to be binding, deliberation is required; since this cannot occur without the light of reason, it does not apply to the insane and the mad, who are likewise excluded from the religious practice of vowing. In children, however, either no ray of reason shines at all, or it is more faint and meager than is necessary for them to be able to deliberate; therefore, whatever they vow is void. <margin>Second argument.</margin> ¶ Second, it is argued: that which can be done rightly cannot be rendered void by another. However, a religious vow taken by a boy or girl before the years of puberty can be retracted by parents, and likewise by a guardian, as provided in the legal decree <note>original: "20. q. 2. cano. puella"; referring to the Decretum Gratiani, a foundational collection of Canon Law.</note> "Puella." Therefore, it seems such children cannot rightly vow before those same legitimate years. <margin>Third argument.</margin> ¶ Third: a year of probation is permitted to those entering religious life so that they may weigh with mature counsel what their shoulders are able to bear. This mature weighing is not suitable for children; therefore, they cannot legitimately vow. ¶ On the contrary is that same cited decree, "Puella," where it is advised that a girl's vow is valid unless it is revoked by the parents within a year; this is evidence that it was previously done rightly. For that which is not done rightly, even if it is not revoked, never becomes solid for that reason.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
# Regarding the question, the response is given in four conclusions.
The first is: If a boy or girl before the years of puberty does not possess enough light of reason to be able to deliberate, they cannot bind themselves by any vow. Before proving this conclusion, however, it is necessary to recall from the previous sections that one type of vow is **simple**, and the other is truly **solemn**. <note>A "simple" vow is a private promise to God; a "solemn" vow is a formal, public commitment recognized by the Church that changes one's legal status, such as becoming a monk or nun.</note> Their difference is that the solemn vow is confirmed by the authority of the Church alone, because it is made solid in a blessing or consecration according to ecclesiastical decrees, in the manner explained above. A simple vow, however, has no efficacy other than that which arises from the deliberation of the person vowing, by which they intend to obligate themselves. This deliberation is weakened for two reasons, as has been said, so that it lacks strength: one way is from a defect of reason, as was said regarding the mad and insane while they are held in their paroxysm <note>A "paroxysm" here refers to a period of active madness or a fit.</note>; the other way is because they have a will tied to the judgment of another. From the first part, therefore, our conclusion follows: that if a child does not yet enjoy the use of reason, they can by no means bind themselves by a vow. <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second conclusion: If a child enjoys the gift of reason before the years of puberty, they can indeed, as far

<column-break/>

as is in their power, obligate themselves by a vow; but it nonetheless depends on the judgment of the parents, or whoever has care of the child, so that it can be voided by them. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> This conclusion is proven. For children before the legitimate age are hindered in both of the aforementioned ways: namely, both because of a defect of reason and because of the bond by which their will is under the yoke of their parents. But because—even if not frequently, yet sometimes—it happens that a premature light of reason shines upon some before the usual age, and they become from that point **capable of discernment** <note>original: "doli capaces"; a legal term meaning old enough to understand the nature of their actions or to be capable of deceit/intent.</note>, they then become fit to issue vows rightly as far as is in their power. Nevertheless, the other impediment remains: namely, the dependence on another's will, by whose judgment they can be overruled.
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin> ¶ Third conclusion: No one, no matter how capable of discernment they may be, can take a **solemn vow** before the years of puberty. This conclusion needs no proof other than the authority of the Church, for that is the sole cause of this assertion; the Church has prescribed the fourteenth year for males and the twelfth for females. <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> ¶ Finally, the fourth conclusion: After the years of puberty, anyone can bind themselves most firmly by a religious vow, no less solemn than simple, even if the parents protest. <margin>Three age limits.</margin> ¶ Here, first of all, three age limits must be distinguished: namely, **infancy**, which lasts through the first seven years. During this time, infants are considered to act under no guidance of reason, and thus their vows are considered as nothing. The first conclusion alludes to this time. Next follows **childhood**, which for males extends until the fourteenth year, when puberty arrives. At that age, children can be capable of discernment, but the power of parents to void their vows still lasts, even if they are personal vows, such as a religious one—as held in the chapter "Non solùm" regarding the rules <note>original: "de regul. lib. 6"; referring to the Liber Sextus of the Decretals.</note>. For females, however, the twelfth year is prescribed, from which puberty begins for them—as held in the cited decree "Puella" (20. q. 2). But this refers to "real" <note>In legal terms, "real" refers to "res" or property/material goods.</note> vows, namely those by which things or expenses are vowed. Then follows the third age, namely **adolescence**, which is called puberty; at this time, adolescents are under the care of parents so that they cannot dispense of their goods without their authority, as held throughout the legal title regarding minors under 25 years <note>original: "ff. toto titul. de minor. 25. annis"; referring to the Roman Civil Law Digest.</note>. <margin>A question.</margin> ¶ From this, perhaps a questioner might not irrelevantly interrupt: why is a shorter time before puberty prescribed for girls than for males? For since women are of "lighter judgment" and prudence, reason seemed to demand the opposite: namely, that a longer time...

It establishes that while children with reason can take simple vows, these can be annulled by parents, and solemn vows are strictly prohibited until the onset of puberty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological examination of when a minor’s vow becomes binding. It follows the previous discussion on the stages of childhood and focuses on the distinction between personal commitments (like fasting) and material commitments (like donating property).</meta>

### F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The question is raised as to why a period for consultation should be established. Perhaps it may be answered that the reason is that the use of reason hastens more quickly in women; for just as fruits of a loftier nature ripen more slowly, so it is with humans. <note>This reflects a common 16th-century Aristotelian view that "nobler" organisms take longer to reach maturity.</note> However, the legitimate reason was that more excellent prudence is required in a man, who is meant to preside over his wife, than in women, upon whom the governance of the household does not weigh so heavily. For a greater wisdom is required for governing than for obeying.

<margin>First instruction.</margin>
¶ At this point, a warning is necessary: when it is said that a child who lacks the use of reason before puberty cannot make a vow, this should not be understood as applying only to those under the age of seven. For even a girl in her eleventh year, or a boy in his thirteenth, who lacks that use of reason, is prohibited for the same reason. Conversely, according to the tenor of the second conclusion, if a child were to have that same use of reason before the age of seven—which must be weighed by the judgment of prudent men—they could bind themselves by a vow, unless the parents refused. Therefore, those age limits are designated according to the "presumption of law"; <term>presumption of law (praesumptio iuris)</term> <note>A legal assumption that stands as true unless proven otherwise.</note> thus, when a matter is in doubt, judgment must be drawn from those limits.

<margin>Second instruction.</margin>
¶ But it must furthermore be noted here that when someone has uttered a vow before the legitimate age of puberty—even if it is a religious vow—and it was neither later invalidated nor confirmed again at the legitimate age: then, for that person to be judged guilty of a vow according to their conscience, any old opinion is not enough to say they had the use of reason when they vowed. Rather, it is required that the matter be so certain and established that no doubt, or only the slightest doubt, remains among prudent men to the contrary. I have appended this warning here, according to my understanding, because it is commonly thought that while a matter is in doubt, judgment should be rendered in favor of the vow—namely, that it is binding. I would believe exactly the opposite: for since such a child is presumed by law not to have had the use of reason, they should not be forced to the contrary unless reason clearly proves it. Indeed, the condition of the one in possession is better; <note>original: "melior est possidentis conditio," a legal maxim meaning that in a tie, the status quo or the current "possessor" of liberty wins.</note> and for a person to remain free is considered remaining in their own possession. Indeed, I have always judged that this favors the vow, and especially the religious life: since the matter is of such grave importance, no one ought to be thrust into it unless compelled by reason. And this is confirmed: because no one is bound by ecclesiastical laws—such as those regarding the sacraments or fasting—before that legitimate age; therefore, there is no reason why they should be bound by a vow, which depends on their mere will, unless it is clearly evident that they are capable of deceit. <note>original: "doli capacem," a legal term for being old enough to be held responsible for one's actions or intentions.</note> ¶ From these age limits thus arranged:

<column-break/>

<margin>Difference and similarity between a personal and real vow.</margin>
one gathers both the similarities and the differences between a personal vow and a "real" vow. <term>Personal vow</term> <note>A promise concerning one's own actions, like praying or fasting.</note> A personal vow is that which pertains to the person: such as a vow of religious life, prayer, or fasting. A <term>real vow</term> <note>From the Latin "res" (thing/property); a promise to give money or goods.</note> is that which pertains to things: for instance, where expenditures are required. Both, therefore, agree in this: that neither can be uttered before the use of reason; yet once reason is present, both are "simple" vows. However, a "solemn" religious vow <note>A permanent, legally binding commitment to a religious order.</note> cannot be made until after the fourteenth year. Again, they agree that before the years of puberty—namely, before the fourteenth year for a boy and the twelfth for a girl—either can be invalidated by parents or guardians, even if it is a religious vow; once invalidated, no obligation from it ever rises again. They differ, however, in that a personal vow cannot be invalidated after the fourteenth year. The reason is: because the youth already has the use of reason to bind their own person. A real vow, however, can be invalidated until the twenty-fifth year. <note>The age of full legal majority in Civil Law, required for managing property.</note>

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding the first of these parts, someone might perhaps doubt whether this should be understood regarding *every* personal vow. Namely, if a boy in his fifteenth year vows a fast or daily prayer, whether this can be invalidated in any way, just as if it were a religious vow.

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
For there is an argument for the affirmative based on equal reasoning: since the canons do not prohibit the invalidation of any vow except the religious vow, which seems to have been done in its favor. Nor does St. Thomas speak of any other vow in his fourth book.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Likewise, if a wife uttered similar personal vows, they could be invalidated by her husband, and similarly a prelate could invalidate every vow of a subordinate. But a father has as much power over a son as a husband over a wife; therefore, a father has the power to cancel these in a son who has not yet reached his twenty-fifth year. To the contrary is the fact that the reason which proves a religious vow cannot be invalidated at that age is that there is already full use of reason; which same reason proves the same thing concerning any other personal vow.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
Therefore, I do not easily believe that the exception was made solely in favor of the religious life; rather, it is a declaration of natural law. And therefore, since that which is more difficult to observe and requires greater deliberation (the religious life) is forbidden from being invalidated, it appears to follow that lesser vows are even less capable of being invalidated. Therefore, I would more freely answer the question in the negative: namely, that no personal vow of a son who has entered puberty can be invalidated by the father. For the Doctors of Law offer the same judgment concerning every personal vow. Nor is the case of a wife similar: for she is not prohibited from vowing because of a defect of reason, but because of her subjection to her husband,

### Question III of the Eighth Book

who can void his every vow: just as a prelate can void every vow of a subordinate. A son, however, after reaching puberty, is not so much subject to his father regarding the use of his liberty, but only in the management of his goods. And therefore, in such a case, no other remedy is available than that of a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A legal release from a religious obligation granted by an ecclesiastical authority.</note>. If anyone should judge otherwise, let him devise a more proven reason.

<margin>Argument against the third conclusion</margin>
¶ Next, an argument is made against the third conclusion, which denied that a <term>solemn vow</term> <note>A formal, public vow (usually of poverty, chastity, and obedience) recognized by the Church as creating a permanent change in legal status, such as becoming a monk or nun.</note> is valid before the age of fourteen. It is argued as follows: The marriage of those who are <term>capable of guile</term> <note>Latin: *doli capaces*. A legal term referring to children old enough to understand the difference between right and wrong, usually between ages 7 and 14.</note> holds firm, as we are taught in the chapter "Concerning those" in the section on the betrothal of minors. Therefore, a vow ought also to be valid, especially since it should be favored with greater privileges than marriage. Add to this that even Holy Orders—as we said in the preceding question—holds firm if someone is initiated into them before the legitimate time. A vow of chastity is certainly annexed to these Orders; therefore, there is no reason why a solemn vow should not be valid. Nor is it enough to answer that "it so pleased the Church," for since the Church is guided by the Holy Spirit, it establishes nothing rashly. We seek, therefore, the reason for a decree of this kind.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
¶ The response is that the sacraments are not subject to the judgment of the Church in such a way that they may be changed according to their essence. Therefore, where competent matter exists, the Church cannot void those sacraments. Hence, since a man and a woman freely consenting can join themselves in marriage by the law of nature, it happens that if "maturity makes up for age"—that is, if not only the light of reason shines in both, but also the woman is fit for a man and he himself is able to consummate the marriage—the Church could not void such a marriage after the sacrament is perfected there. The reason regarding the sacrament of Holy Orders is similar and equal. However, because entering "religion" <note>The "religious life" or state of being a monk, nun, or friar.</note> is not a sacrament, the same Church can void a solemn vow of religion; and thus it most wisely judged such a vow to be voided before the fourteenth year.

<margin>A Scruple.</margin>
¶ But if you ask again whether such a religious vow should at least be considered a <term>simple vow</term> <note>A private or less formal vow that binds the conscience but does not have the same public legal standing as a solemn vow.</note>, it appears that it should. For since the Church denies only the "solemnity," it seems the person remains bound as far as they were able—namely, by a simple vow. A similar case is found in the chapters "A certain person" and "It pleases," regarding the conversion of spouses. For a spouse who has been dragged away from the religious life because the other spouse protested, although they are considered absolved from the solemn vow, they nevertheless remain bound so that, upon the death of the other, they may not pass to a second marriage; for they are obligated not to seek the "fleshly debt" <note>A traditional term for the right of spouses to sexual intimacy within marriage.</note>.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, notwithstanding the similarity of the argument, which has some weight, I would believe that in the present case the matter stands differently:

<column-break/>

namely, if someone made a solemn vow before the fourteenth year, having never made another simple vow either before or after, they are bound by no cord, not even that of a simple vow. This is because that vow is held as void by the Church, as stated in the chapter "Not only" in Book 6 of the Decretals. Nor is it similar to the case of the spouse. For in the solemn vow of a spouse, two parts are included: not to pay the debt, and not to ask for it. Therefore, although their will is hindered by the other spouse (under whose power they sit) in respect to the former, the power of binding themselves in respect to the latter nevertheless remains to the survivor. However, the one who vows solemnly before the proper age is not hindered because they have a will bound to another, but because of a defect of age. Therefore, when a solemn vow of religion is simply voided, there is no reason why it should retain the force of a simple one.

<margin>The final doubt.</margin>
¶ Finally, there is the last doubt which we touched upon in the section above: namely, if a father does not void the vow of a son while he is under his power, is it still open to him to void that same vow after the son has been emancipated? For example: A boy in his thirteenth year made a simple vow of religion, which the father did not void before the fourteenth year, and which the son himself did not later confirm. In his fifteenth year, the son regrets the vow. Does the power then persist in the father to cancel it? For it is certain that if the son had vowed *at that time* (age 15), the father could not void it. Similarly, if a "real vow" <note>A vow concerning property or land, rather than a personal action like fasting.</note> is made by a son before his twenty-fifth year, can it be voided by the father after the son is emancipated when that same time has elapsed?

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
Truly, the matter is doubtful. However, I would incline more favorably toward the negative side. For even if at the time the vow was made the father could void it, that same power does not persist except until the time predefined by law. Therefore, if he does not exercise it within that time, he is not able to execute it afterward. And this is confirmed by a similarity: For if a slave, while under the dominion of another, made a vow which the master never voided, the master cannot later recur to void it once the slave is a freedman. Nor would the voiding hold.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ To the first argument, therefore, it is responded that it only concludes that children to whom the use of reason has not yet dawned can by no means make a vow; as the first conclusion asserted.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, the first premise is denied. For truly, although it is in the power of a father to render the vows of his children void, nothing nevertheless hinders...

### QUESTION FOUR
### On the dispensation and commutation of a vow.

->Saint Thomas, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 83, Article 10.<- <note>In many modern editions of Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologica*, the discussion on vows is found in Question 88; Question 83 typically deals with prayer.</note>

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether a dispensation can be granted for a Vow.*<-

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
After discussing the <term>voiding</term> <note>original: *irritationem*; the legal act of declaring a vow null and void from the beginning because the person lacked the standing to make it.</note> of vows made by those who cannot firmly vow, there follows the question of the <term>dispensation</term> <note>A formal release from the obligation of a valid vow, granted by a religious superior.</note> of those vows which are firm. It is argued, according to custom, that no dispensation can occur in such vows. It is a lesser thing to <term>commute</term> <note>To change the requirement of a vow to a different, usually equivalent, act of piety.</note> a vow than to be dispensed from it; yet a vow cannot be commuted, as is suggested by those words in Leviticus 27: "An animal that can be sacrificed to the Lord, if anyone vows it, shall be holy and cannot be changed: neither a better for a worse, nor a worse for a better." Therefore, much less can a vow be dispensed.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, in matters belonging to natural or divine law, no human can grant a dispensation, and much less in the precepts of the "first table" <note>The first part of the Ten Commandments, which concern a person's direct relationship and duties toward God.</note> which pertain to the love of God—which, according to Paul, is the end of all commandments. To actually fulfill a vow once it has been uttered is a matter of <term>divine law</term> <note>Laws believed to come directly from God's revelation, rather than human legislation.</note> pertaining to religion; therefore, no dispensation can apply to it. 

¶ Thirdly, it is added that the fulfillment of a vow pertains to the faith and loyalty which is firmly owed to God once it has been pledged to Him. To dispense from this seems absurd; therefore, it is not permitted. 

¶ On the contrary, there stands an argument of greater strength: that which proceeds from a collective will holding public authority is stronger than that which flows from the will of a single person. But in a law which is established by the common

<column-break/>

consent of the commonwealth, a dispensation can be granted (as was shown in Book 1); therefore, it can also be granted for a vow, which is confirmed solely by the personal choice of the one vowing.

To understand the present question, we must recall the distinction we set forth in the last question of Book 1 between <term>dispensing</term>, <term>voiding</term>, <term>abrogating</term>, and <term>interpreting</term>; and add to these, regarding vows, <term>commuting</term> and <term>redeeming</term>. 

<margin>The voiding of a vow.</margin>
For to <term>void</term> a vow—whether you consider it in law or in a vow—is to render it empty by removing the underlying matter. We provided an example of this regarding law in that section, and we produced many examples regarding vows in the question immediately preceding this one. 

<margin>Commutation.</margin>
To <term>commute</term>, as the name implies, is to change one thing into another; such as if a vow of pilgrimage is changed into a fast. 

<margin>Redemption.</margin>
And <term>redeeming</term> is the same thing, except that <term>redemption</term> implies a change into money or something of monetary value; for example, when a vow of pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint James <note>The Way of St. James, or Santiago de Compostela.</note> is changed into gold to be offered to that same temple. 

<margin>Abrogation.</margin>
<term>Abrogation</term>, however, has no place except in law, when the law itself ceases because the reason for the law has ended. But <term>interpretation</term> and <term>equity</term> <note>original: *epieikeia*; the principle of interpreting the law according to the spirit of fairness rather than the strict letter.</note> have a place in vows just as they do in law; this occurs when it is declared that the law or the vow does not hold in a specific case, as we shall see shortly. A <term>dispensation</term> in law is an exception of a person from a universal obligation (as we said there); such as when someone is excused by privilege from fasting during Lent. A dispensation of a vow, however, since it only binds a single person, cannot be defined so easily: it is the removal of the vow because the cause for which it was made no longer seems appropriate. 

¶ So that these matters may shine more clearly, let us descend to the response to the question, which is contained in this conclusion. 

<margin>The responsive conclusion.</margin>
Any <term>simple vow</term> <note>A vow made without the full legal formalities of a religious order, yet still spiritually binding.</note> is subject to the power of the Church, both so that it may be dispensed and so that it may be commuted into something else. 

<margin>The proof.</margin>
The conclusion is proved: the dispensation of a vow must be weighed in the same way as the dispensation of a law. To "dispense," according to the sound of the word, is the same as applying common things to individual persons according to the rank and order of each—much like a <term>steward</term> <note>original: *oeconomus*; a household manager.</note> does in a family. Through this, the dispensation of law becomes clear. For since a law (as shown extensively in Book 1) is not established except with consideration for the common good and those things that happen most frequently, it may happen that the law fails in some specific case or person. Therefore, it is necessary for the one who carries public authority to discern in such a case...

### Question IV, Article I

In the same way, we must judge concerning a vow. For one who makes a vow establishes a kind of law for themselves, regarding that which they judged to be good for them and, above all, pleasing to God. However, it can happen that as circumstances change, that which was once good for them becomes either simply bad, or inconvenient, or an obstacle to a more fruitful result—which is contrary to the very purpose of a vow.

For this reason, it is expedient that the power of judging resides with the person who holds spiritual jurisdiction, to determine whether it is better that the vow not be kept or that it be <term>commuted</term> <note>original: *commutandum*; to exchange one religious obligation for another equivalent or better one</note> into something more moderate. Now, the former action is called <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: *dispensatio*; a total release from the obligation of a vow</note>, which requires greater authority; the latter is called commutation, which can be done more easily. Hence, the reason why this kind of authority was necessary in the church is explained by <term>Innocent III</term> <note>Pope Innocent III (reigned 1198–1216), a major figure in the development of Canon Law.</note> in the chapter *Dispensationes*. There, he wisely says that dispensations sometimes compel us to relax something from the required rigor, much like sailors who, when a storm presses upon them, jettison some cargo so that the rest may remain safe.

¶ For the present, Saint Thomas reports only three causes for a just dispensation: namely, if the matter of the vow is bad, or useless, or an obstacle to a greater good. In the third article, however, all the reasons for dispensing will be explained more fully. For now, it was enough to provide an example.

<margin>The difference between dispensation and the rest.</margin>
¶ Regarding this conclusion, nothing else remains to be noted except to make clear the distinction between those five or six terms that have been mentioned. First, the difference between <term>dispensation</term> and <term>commutation</term> is clear. For through dispensation, the bond of the vow is entirely untied and removed; but in commutation, it is not. For by the very same bond by which you were compelled, for example, to go on a pilgrimage, you are subsequently bound to the prayer into which the vow was commuted. Therefore, you are not bound to that prayer by virtue of the command of the one who commuted it (since he commands nothing, but only changes the requirement), nor do you undertake a new vow; rather, the power of the first vow remains in the second matter. And thus, it is the same religious duty to keep it in the second matter as it was in the first.

<margin>How much difference there is between dispensation and voiding.</margin>
¶ Next, the difference between dispensation and <term>voiding</term> <note>original: *irritationem*; also known as "invalidation."</note> is not obscure. For voiding is the removal of the matter, and thus of the obligation of a vow that was not yet firm, but was hanging upon the will of the person doing the voiding. For this reason, it pertains not only to spiritual power, but a father and a husband can do the same. Dispensation, however, is the untying and removal of a bond that was firm; therefore, this function pertains to spi-

<column-break/>

ritual power. Nor can it be done without cause and judgment, by which it is judged that the cause for vowing is now useless. This is not necessary for voiding.

¶ However, the gap between dispensation and <term>equity</term> <note>original: *epieikeiam*; from the Greek *epieikeia*, meaning a fair or merciful interpretation of the law that looks to the spirit rather than the literal letter.</note> or interpretation is not so clear. For he who dispenses seems to do nothing other than interpret and declare that the vow does not bind in that specific case. To this, we responded in Book 1 when we were discussing the dispensation of law. For the interpretation of a vow, like that of a law, requires that its fulfillment be contrary to natural reason. For a dispensation, however, it is enough that the reason for the law or vow fails for such a person. From this, it follows that interpretation requires no authority from a <term>prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note> for that specific point, as we declared there, if recourse to him is not possible.

Take an example: You vowed not to eat meat, yet you have fallen into a situation where, unless you eat it, you will perish. Then, because the situation has become contrary to natural law, you yourself can eat it by your own private authority, notwithstanding the vow. You are not, however, thereby released from the bond of the vow; for surely, once that necessity has passed, you are bound to keep it.

But perhaps fasting harms you in some way, or is an obstacle to you so that you cannot apply yourself so attentively to the study of letters; you cannot, therefore, act against the vow through equity. Instead, it can only be a cause for why a prelate might dispense you, and remove the obligation of the vow either for a time or forever. Therefore, dispensation is not an interpretation that the vow does not hold; rather, it removes the vow even if it would otherwise hold. Thus, it has some similarity to the <term>abrogation</term> <note>The total repeal or cancellation of a law.</note> of a law, which is done by the authority of a prince when the cause ceases. Although more is required for a dispensation: namely, that the matter of the vow be, as we said, either useless, or bad, or an obstacle to a better good.

Beyond all these, there is also the <term>cessation</term> of a vow, which needs no dispensation. We mentioned this in Question 1: namely, if you vowed never to enter a certain house, and the cause was the danger that threatened you there; when that cause entirely ceases, the vow also ceases. For not entering a house is a trivial thing, and thus an unworthy matter for a vow.

<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to return to the conclusion: it is very well established that it was appropriate for the prelates of the church to exercise the same authority over a vow as they do over a law. For since the prudence of the one vowing is not always so great that a vow is made with mature delibera-
