# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

undertake the obligation with proper consideration. Furthermore, because human affairs are constantly changing, it is very often consistent with reason that what someone has vowed should be reconsidered. And since through a vow one’s faith is pledged to God, and a private individual cannot be a suitable judge in their own case, reason itself—arising from nature—taught that he who acts in God’s place <note>The Pope or authorized prelates acting as Christ's vicars on Earth.</note> should exercise such judgment and arbitration. For this reason, Christ left this authority to his Church. However, the entire difficulty of this matter lies in the causes by which a <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: *dispensatio*; a formal release from a religious obligation or vow.</note> is justified, which will be discussed in Article 3.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, the response is that the same distinction established in the Old Law <note>The laws of the Old Testament.</note> between animals offered at the Temple appears between a **solemn vow** and a **simple vow**. For an animal that was fit for sacrifice was considered from that moment as being dedicated to divine worship; for this reason, it could not be redeemed for a price. Similarly, as we are about to say, a dispensation does not apply to a **solemn vow**, by which a person has surrendered themselves to divine worship. However, an animal that could not be sanctified through sacrifice was ordered to be redeemed; and similarly, a dispensation can now be granted by the Church for a **simple vow**.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, the response is that although a human cannot grant a dispensation for matters of natural or divine law, a person is nonetheless bound to obey the commands of their superiors just as much as they are bound to fulfill a vow. For this, too, is natural and divine law. Therefore, although fulfilling a vow is a matter of natural and divine law, when a superior grants a dispensation, nothing is done *against* the vow itself; rather, the vow is removed because it is judged that it ought not to bind in such a case. Just as when a prince grants a dispensation from a human law, it is not done so that the subject may disobey the law—which would be against divine right—but so that the law itself, as it was, ceases to apply in this specific case. Therefore, a prelate dispensing a vow does not dispense with divine or natural law; for he would only be doing that if he judged a contrary act to be lawful while the vow still remained in place. But if this seems like a <term>circular argument</term> <note>original: *petitio principii*; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note> to you, you might argue thus:

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Divine and natural law cannot be removed by man; fulfilling a vow is divine law; therefore, that law cannot be removed, and thus neither can its obligation.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The response is that the one dispensing does not remove the divine law—which dictates that as long as a vow remains firm, it must be kept—but rather removes the obligation which arose from the mere will 

<column-break/>

of the person making the vow. For the fact that a man is bound by a vow is gathered from two premises: namely, because he vowed, and because the law requires that a vow be fulfilled. The one dispensing does not remove this second part, but the first: that is, the obligation insofar as it emerged from that person's will, which, as we said above, is in a sense a human law.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ And in the same way, the response to the third argument is that whoever does not fulfill a vow which a superior deems inconvenient breaks no faith with God; rather, they are obeying His vicar.

### ARTICLE II.

->*Whether a dispensation can be granted for a solemn vow of continence in a religious order.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a seated figure in robes, possibly a scholar or clergyman, holding a book within a circular medallion flanked by ornate scrollwork.</image-desc>
Although the Church has the power, as has been said, to grant dispensations for vows just as it does for its own laws, it remains to be explored whether this same power extends even to the singular privilege of the **solemn vow**.

<margin>First argument for the affirmative.</margin>
The argument is made for the affirmative side. One of the reasons mentioned above for dispensing a vow is if it becomes an obstacle to a "more precious good." But this can be found even in a solemn vow of <term>continence</term> <note>original: *continentiae*; here referring specifically to the vow of celibacy taken by monks, nuns, or priests.</note>. For the common good, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC), whose Ethics and Politics heavily influenced medieval legal thought.</note> testifies, is more divine than the private good of any individual. It is possible for the common good to be endangered by the vow of continence of a specific person—for instance, if the perpetual succession of a kingdom could be preserved through the marriage of someone who had solemnly vowed continence, thereby ensuring public peace for a distressed state. Therefore, it would be a religious duty to dispense with such a vow.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second: <term>Latria</term> <note>original: *Latria*; the highest form of worship or religious devotion, reserved for God alone.</note> is a nobler virtue than chastity. But a vow of worship (such as offering a specific sacrifice) can be dispensed for a just cause; therefore, the same should apply to a solemn vow of chastity.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third: Just as a vow of abstinence can present a danger to the life of the one who vowed, so too can a solemn vow of continence. But the cause of saving a life is a lawful reason for a dispensation of the former; therefore, it is also for the latter.

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
¶ Fourth: Under a solemn religious vow, not only chastity but also poverty and obedience are included. A dispensation for these latter two can be legitimate and just; therefore, the same applies to chastity.

# Book Eight, Question IV.

it is clear when someone is promoted from the monastic state to the office of a bishop: for then he is both exempt from the obedience of his monastic profession and is permitted to live in wealth. ¶ On the contrary, however, is that passage from Ecclesiasticus 26: *No weight of gold is worthy of a continent soul* <note>original: "Omnis ponderatio non est digna animae continentis"</note>; that is, there is nothing that can compensate for the state of continence <note>The vow of celibacy or refraining from sexual relations.</note>. To this agrees the chapter *Cui* regarding the state of monks, the final words of which are: "The renunciation of private property, as well as the keeping of chastity, is so closely joined to the monastic rule that not even the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> can grant a dispensation against it."

<margin>Three things to be considered in the vow of continence</margin>
St. Thomas [Aquinas] responds to the question by refuting three opinions, explaining his own through five conclusions. To understand the matter, one must first know that three things are to be considered in the vow of continence: namely, the **matter** [the substance of the vow], its **perpetuity** [lifelong duration], and its **solemnity** [the formal, public ritual]. Three opinions—specifically the first two and the fourth—agree on the same negative conclusion: namely, that the Church can in no way grant a dispensation <note>A formal release from a religious obligation.</note> for a solemn vow of continence; however, they disagree on the reason.

<margin>William of Auxerre and the Gloss</margin>
The first opinion, which belongs to the ancient William of Auxerre <note>A 13th-century theologian.</note> and the *Gloss* <note>Standard legal commentary on Church law.</note> on the chapter "Since [at the monastery]" regarding the state of monks and the chapter on vows and their redemption, reduces the cause to the **matter**. The authors of this view say that such a solemn vow is indispensable because the excellence of the virtue of continence accepts no equal compensation, as the cited Church authority suggests. They assign the reason that through continence, a man both triumphs over his "domestic enemy"—namely, the flesh, which is more troublesome than the devil or the world—and represents the nature of the angels, being likened to Christ according to the purity of soul 
<margin>A very pressing immediate reason. Paul.</margin>
and body. This reason is not entirely pressing: for the good of the soul, such as contemplation and prayer, is more excellent and makes us more closely conformed to God than the goods of the body. This is also attested by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 7, where he considers continence a means for fostering contemplation, which is its end. For he says that an unmarried woman thinks of the things of the Lord; and therefore he advises spouses to separate from the common bed for a time so they may devote themselves to prayer. And yet, a dispensation can be granted for a vow of contemplation and prayer.

<margin>The reason of Albert the Great</margin>
¶ For this reason, others, including Albert the Great <note>Teacher of Thomas Aquinas and a major philosopher-scientist of the Middle Ages.</note> in his fourth book, derive the reason for this same conclusion from the **perpetuity** of the vow. They say that this vow is not subject to dispensation because it cannot be set aside except by doing what is entirely contrary to it; and that which is contrary to the vow 
<margin>Albert's reason is refuted</margin>
is repugnant to its perpetuity. However, this reason has no force: for even a vow

<column-break/>

to abstain perpetually from eating meat cannot be set aside except by eating meat, and yet a dispensation can be granted for that. ¶ Therefore, a third opinion differs in its judgment on the conclusion: for it asserts that a solemn vow of continence *can* be dispensed for the sake of the common utility of the state, as was argued above. Nevertheless, despite these arguments, St. Thomas 
<margin>The first proposition of Saint Thomas</margin>
responds with four preliminary propositions, from which he gathers a fifth as his main conclusion. The first proposition is: No prelate of the Church, including both the highest and the lowest, can bring it about that someone who has made a solemn vow should cease to be that which they were consecrated or blessed to be: namely, that a priest should not be a priest, or a "religious" <note>Someone who has taken formal vows in a religious order, like a monk or nun.</note> should not be a religious. 

<margin>The Proof</margin>
This is proven from the last chapter of Leviticus: *That which has once been sanctified to the Lord cannot be changed to other uses*, because it is already dedicated to God. The Church cannot remove the sanctification of what is once holy, even in inanimate things: for it cannot make it so that a consecrated chalice, or a temple, or an altar, is no longer consecrated. Much less, then, can a human being once consecrated or dedicated to God cease to be consecrated; and thus the Church cannot lead them away from that use to which they were consecrated or blessed and apply them to other uses. The solemnity of the vow consists in the consecration and blessing of the one vowing; it follows, therefore, as our assertion: namely, that it cannot happen that one who is once a priest or a religious ceases to be such. This remains true even though a priest can be suspended from the function and execution of his orders. But because this is more certain regarding a priest due to the "sacramental character" <note>An indelible spiritual mark believed to be left on the soul by certain sacraments.</note>, some Lawyers [Jurists] denied this regarding a "religious," saying one could cease to be a religious. But St. Thomas says they said this out of ignorance. ¶ With this first proposition established, in order to descend to the vow of continence, it remains to investigate whether the vow of continence is essentially attached to that office for which the consecration or blessing occurs through the solemn vow. For if it is so, then by the same reasoning that one who is consecrated cannot be "un-consecrated," it would follow that no dispensation can be made regarding such a vow of continence. If, however, continence is not indivisibly attached to such an office, a dispensation can be granted so that such a consecrated or blessed person is released from the vow of continence. The matter is very clear. ¶ Therefore,
<margin>The second proposition</margin>
the second proposition is added: The obligation of continence is not **essentially** attached to Holy Orders, but is so by the statute of the Church, as we have already established above. This is evident because it is not...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law,

it is [not] <note>The context of the previous page and the following argument implies "not," as he is distinguishing between the essence of the priesthood and the monastic rule.</note> of the essence of a priest to observe chastity: since even the Greeks are permitted by the Latin Church to remain in the bond of marriage <note>A reference to the Eastern Rite priests who are permitted to be married, unlike the Latin Rite.</note>.

<margin>Third proposition.</margin>
¶ From this, therefore, the third proposition follows immediately. It seems the Church can grant a dispensation in the vow of continence <term>continence: the practice of abstaining from sexual relations</term> which is solemnly undertaken through the reception of Holy Orders. This is evident because there is no inherent conflict between being a priest and not being continent.

<margin>Fourth proposition. The proof.</margin>
¶ Fourth proposition: The duty of continence is essential to the religious state <note>In this context, "religious state" refers specifically to monks, friars, and nuns who live under a rule.</note>. This is proven: a person through the religious state utterly renounces the world, handing himself over entirely to the service of God; therefore, by 그 vow, he cuts off from himself whatever can be an obstacle to such service. The greatest obstacle is the "burden of marriage," as it imposes on a man the necessity of caring for a family, according to that saying of the Apostle [Paul]:

<margin>Paul.</margin>
in 1 Corinthians 7: *He who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided* <note>original: "Qui cum uxore est solicitus est quae sunt mundi, quomodò placeat uxori: & diuisus est"</note>. Therefore, the duty of chastity is essential to the religious vow. This is also confirmed by the name itself. For a "monk" <note>from the Greek 'monachos'</note> is so named from "unity" or "solitude": namely, because he lives alone and applies himself to the sole business of God, and is not divided toward a wife or other worldly matters.

<margin>Concluding response.</margin>
¶ From these points, finally, a fifth principal conclusion is drawn, which answers the question. In the vow of continence which is made solemn by the profession of religion <note>monastic profession</note>, the Church cannot grant a dispensation. The cited *Decretal* <note>A papal decree forming part of canon law.</note> adds the reason: namely, that the guardianship of chastity is annexed to the monastic rule. ¶ Regarding the third proposition, which pertains to the priestly vow, St. Thomas [Aquinas] has no doubt that continence is separable from it.

<margin>A scruple.</margin>
But perhaps a beginner might feel a "scruple" <note>A small doubt or hesitation</note> here: whether the vow of chastity which priests undertake in the manner established by the Church is to be understood as chastity opposed only to marriage, or truly that which opposes all sexual union, whether within marriage or in fornication. This matters much: for if it is only understood in the first way, then the fornication of a priest would only be a simple sin; but if in the second way, it would also be a breach of a vow. It appears, however, that it is only understood in the first way—namely, that they only vow not to take wives—for this is what seems sufficient for their state.

<margin>The response.</margin>
Nevertheless, the response is that it must be understood simply as chastity, just as it is in the religious vow. For every purity befits those who are devoted to their function in consecrating the venerable sacrament [the Eucharist]. For this reason, the Church annexed that vow to Holy Orders. Therefore, those who commit fornication are stained by a double fault <note>The sin of the act itself, and the sacrilege of breaking a vow.</note>.

<margin>A question.</margin>
¶ But someone might ask how the Pope can grant a dispensation for a vow of this kind: namely, whether he can do so before it is made—by abolishing the current law so that those who henceforth wish to be initiated

<column-break/>

into sacred orders would not be liable to the vow of chastity—or whether he can also do so with those who have already made the solemn vow. For it appears that this second way is not permitted: namely, that those who have made a solemn vow should be allowed to take wives.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
The response is that he can do it in both ways, since a vow of this kind has no other force than that which comes from the Church’s statute; for by the nature of the thing itself, the vow of continence is not inherently annexed to Holy Orders. We shall say something similar in Question 6 regarding the military religious orders.

¶ Concerning the principal conclusion, however, there are many who depart from the opinion of St. Thomas, holding that the Church can grant a dispensation for the solemn vow of continence for religious [monks] just as it can for the vow of priests. These include Henry of Ghent (*Quodlibet* 5, q. 25 & 26), Richard of Middleton (on Book 4, distinction 38, article 9), and Durandus (on the same distinction, question 2).

<margin>
Opinion of Henry.
Richard.
Durandus.
Paludanus.
Cajetan.
</margin>
And from our own order, Petrus de Palude (question 4). Indeed, even St. Thomas himself at one time did not reject the contrary opinion, as is clear in his commentary on Book 4, distinction 38, question 1, article 4. Nay, what I cannot help but marvel at is that Cajetan, at present, not only asserts the contrary opinion but also claims that the opinion of St. Thomas here regarding the impossibility of dispensation is not his absolute view, but merely "opiniative" <note>An opinion held for the sake of argument or based on current legal interpretation rather than a fixed theological truth.</note>; because, he says, Thomas drew that sense from the *Decretal*, which Cajetan himself does not judge to be the correct legal interpretation. He contends the same in his minor works (question 12 of his first *Quodlibet*). ¶ Therefore, for the examination of the present question, it must be carefully noted how St. Thomas, from the first and fourth propositions, concludes that a dispensation cannot be granted for the solemn vow of continence in religion, which is the principal conclusion. Specifically: the Church cannot make it so that one who has once been blessed into the religious state ceases to be a "religious" <note>a monk/nun</note>. Just as it cannot be brought about that one who is consecrated as a priest ceases to be a priest. Perpetual continence is part of the intrinsic reason and essence of the religious state; therefore, a dispensation cannot be granted for it. Those who attack this opinion, however, attempt to demolish both premises. Indeed, not only outsiders, but even Cajetan here does not approve of the first premise:

<margin>Cajetan strives to demolish the reasoning of St. Thomas.</margin>
because he does not judge the "religious" person in the same way as a cleric in Holy Orders. This is because an "indelible character" <note>A permanent spiritual mark on the soul.</note> is imprinted through Holy Orders, which makes it impossible for one who was once a priest to cease being one, even if he is "degraded" <note>Stripped of his office and rights.</note>. In the religious state, however, no character is imprinted, but only a blessing is applied. Therefore, although it cannot be made that a religious was never blessed, nothing prevents such a religious, for a legitimate cause, from being "distracted" to other uses: for example, that a dispensation be granted so that he may move from celibacy to marriage.

# Question IV of Book Eight

Just as a consecrated chalice can, through a dispensation, be taken up for other uses; for even the priest of the old law reached out the sacred showbread <note>original: "sacros propositionis panes" - the twelve loaves placed in the Jewish Temple, usually reserved only for priests.</note> to David to alleviate the hunger of his men. All these things he [Cajetan] borrowed from Palude <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and legal expert.</note>. ¶ From which he then asserts that St. Thomas did not cite the Decretal <term>Decretal: a papal decree that forms part of Canon Law</term>, *Cum ad monasterium*, in its legitimate sense. For there it is only held that one cannot remain in a religious order without a vow of chastity; but one cannot conclude from this, he says, that one cannot be extracted from a religious order. Indeed, he says that if the author [St. Thomas] had seen that the Supreme Pontiffs had interpreted the same Decretal in this way, he undoubtedly would not have taken on the burden of defending that Decretal with this opinion. Certainly, since the Roman Pontiff has dispensed from a solemn vow multiple times: as with the King of Aragon, mentioned by Peter de Palude in Book 4, distinction 38; and Pope Celestine dispensed the nun Constance, daughter of King Roger, so that, leaving the monastery after her profession, she might marry King Henry VI, as the histories relate. ¶ But other Thomists, in order to defend St. Thomas, invent some kind of "indelible quality" imprinted on the religious through the blessing—which is a ridiculous fiction. ¶ Therefore, what Cajetan judgments regarding St. Thomas—namely, that if he had understood the sense of the Decretal, he would not have persisted in this opinion—I myself would judge the same regarding him: namely, that if they had wished to penetrate the mind of St. Thomas, they would not have departed from him so easily. For the force of St. Thomas's reasoning to prove that a religious cannot become a non-religious did not rely on his blessing as if on its primary root,

<margin>Explanation of St. Thomas's reasoning.</margin>

but on legitimate *traditio* <term>traditio: the legal act of handing over or delivery of property or oneself into the power of another</term>: because, clearly, while they solemnly profess, they have given and handed themselves over into the possession of another—that is, into the power of another—namely, because they dedicate themselves to a religious order just as if someone were to hand themselves over as a slave to a master, as we declared in the final article of Question 2. But because that handing over is celebrated under the form of a blessing, he uses the blessing as if it were a sign of the handing over. For in our order [the Dominicans], profession is made before the blessing. Whence in Book 4, distinction 38, question 1, article 2, he expressly says that a solemn vow is then made when someone presentially hands himself over to God, enslaving himself to divine precepts, either in Holy Orders or in religious profession. And in Article 3, while solving the third argument of the last short question, he says that for this reason a marriage is dissolved by a solemn vow—which does not happen by a simple vow—because a solemn vow involves the actual delivery of one's own body. ¶ But this reason is certainly not as weak as Cajetan and others judge; for if what is in a man's lordship and possession cannot be justly torn from him by human power, nor indeed a spouse from the other spouse, it becomes much more probable that he who has already enslaved himself to God in this service,

<column-break/>

cannot be removed from there. This reason was held in such high regard in the time of St. Thomas that, beyond his innate and most customary urbanity and modesty, he did not fear to say that those who felt a religious could become a non-religious said so out of ignorance. For St. Matthew used this very argument against that king who wished to marry the nun Iphigenia; since she was the spouse of the Heavenly King, he thought it a crime to permit it, even though he offered half the kingdom to her. Cajetan was unable to respond to this authority except by denying the history. ¶ And the foundation of the reason is what we declared in Question 2, in the article on the solemn vow: namely, that although the ceremony of the solemnity of the vow is a human institution, its obligation is nevertheless divine and natural law: namely, that he who in reality has already enslaved himself perpetually to another cannot be torn away from there without injury. That religious life is a perpetual handing over is clear from that Gospel passage: *Go and sell all that you have, and follow me*—namely, with perpetual firmness of soul. Therefore, those who patronize the contrary opinion are deceived in this, unless we are mistaken: because the ceremony of profession is of ecclesiastical law, they infer from this that the bond is not of divine law. But if that were true, a dispensation could certainly be granted over a solemn vow as easily as over a simple vow—which is, however, absurd. For which reason, Altisiodorensis <note>William of Auxerre (d. 1231).</note>, Albert the Great,

<margin>Altisiodorensis, Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure.</margin>

Alexander of Hales in the third part, and also Bonaventure in Book 4 at the end of distinction 38, and others of this class, have always held this as most established. For this reason, St. Thomas changed the opinion which he seemed to wink at in Book 4, after inspecting the matter more clearly in the *Summa*; and he embraced the contrary view most affirmatively, whatever Cajetan might have said. ¶ And there is to me, indeed, an argument by no means weak in confirmation of his opinion: for if a religious could become a non-religious through dispensation, there would be no firm reason why

<margin>A most firm reason for the opinion of St. Thomas.</margin>

through religious profession an unconsummated marriage should be dissolved. For suppose a husband makes a religious profession before copulation, and the wife joins herself in marriage to another; then if that man could become a non-religious, he could pass to another marriage, since the first had been dissolved. Whence it would happen in practice that after a valid marriage *de praesenti* <note>original: "de præsenti" - a marriage established by present consent, even before physical union.</note>, it would be permitted for the man to have another wife, and for the wife another husband. I have brought these things forward in corroboration of the first premise: namely, that a religious cannot become a secular. ¶ From these things it follows that St. Thomas did not cite the Decretal *Cum ad monasterium* for the purpose Cajetan thinks—namely, to confirm that a religious cannot become a non-religious—for he saw well that this was not defined there. But having established this from elsewhere, he cited it to assert the other premise: namely...

### F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

namely, that perpetual continence is so essentially linked to the religious life that not even through the Church can it happen that there is a true "religion" <note>In this context, "religion" refers to a formal religious order or the state of being a monk or nun.</note> without a vow of continence. And indeed, it is surprising that Cajetan, in his commentary on St. Thomas, did not perceive this. ¶ But in truth, regarding the second premise, there are those who deny it: specifically those who think that continence is not so deeply innate to the religious life that a true religious order could not exist without it. Indeed, although Cajetan seems to affirm and defend something else here, yet in those words of his on Question 88, Article 7—where he says that it is only by a statute of the Church that a religious person is disqualified from marriage—he seems to feel the same as Duns Scotus. However, concerning this matter, a singular discussion awaits us in the following Question, Article 3, where we will dispute regarding the military religious orders <note>Such as the Knights Templar or the Knights of Malta, who were both soldiers and monks.</note> and whether they are true religious orders, since soldiers of that kind may contract marriages. In the meantime, however, let the decree of Innocent III already cited be sufficient for us: where he says that it cannot even be granted by the Supreme Pontiff that there be a true monkhood without a vow of chastity.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Through these arguments, therefore, the opposing opinions are dissolved. For the comparison they bring from the priesthood to the religious life is invalid: namely, that if the Pope can dispense with the continence of a priest, he can do so with a monk. For chastity is not inseparable from the priestly office as it is from the religious life.

<margin>Reply.</margin>
But they argue further in this way: that which would have been a legitimate cause to prevent a vow from being made in the first place is also a cause to undo it once done. If a great danger to the state were imminent unless a specific free man contracted a marriage, he ought to choose that rather than the religious life; therefore, if the same necessity falls upon him after he has become a religious, he should then also be released.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The first premise of that argument is denied. Let those who use this "Achilles" <note>original: "Achille" - a common term in Renaissance logic for a "strong" or "invincible" argument.</note> answer me: If the safety of the entire state depended on a man who already has a legitimate wife taking another, ought he to dismiss the one he has to join himself to another? They will certainly say no. And yet, if the matter were undecided—that is, if he were free—he ought to join himself to the woman who would contribute to the public safety. Therefore, we respond similarly regarding the religious person: for he is bound by a much stronger bond.

<margin>Another reason of Palude.</margin>
¶ Again, Palude <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a famous theologian and legal expert.</note> argues that in every vow, the authority of the Pope is implicitly understood as an exception, should he wish to dispense it. And others add another reason to the same effect: namely, that a man is in no way able to exempt himself from natural law. Therefore, regardless of any vow, if natural law presents a case of necessity, one must obey it; and thus a religious person must be dispensed entirely.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
But that teaching is denied. On the contrary, just as a man can so commit himself to another through marriage that he cannot be separated even by the Pope, so he can also hand himself over to the religious life through a vow. Therefore, it is false that in a solemn vow that 

<column-break/>

exception is implicitly understood. ¶ The remaining arguments of those men are of no weight at all, except for one which, although it is rightly held in high regard, does not compel us as much as they think. And it is that which Cajetan here considers inescapable: namely, that the Supreme Pontiffs mentioned above are read to have dispensed with religious people so that they might exchange their religious life for marriage.

<margin>To another of their arguments.</margin>
To this, however, it can first be answered that those historical stories—at least the one about the King of Aragon—are not entirely certain. For it does not appear in the Chronicles of that kingdom, nor indeed in the sacred canon, but is cited by Palude. Secondly, as Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), Master of the Sacred Palace and early opponent of Martin Luther.</note> records in the word "vow" (item 4), there are those who assert that the famous King of Aragon had not yet made his profession <note term="profession">The formal act of entering a religious order by making permanent vows.</note>. They claim the same thing regarding the nun Constance. Or perhaps they alleged that they had not made their solemn vows entirely of their own free will—which happens very frequently. Furthermore, the same Sylvester, Master of the Sacred Palace, does not fear to say that the Popes do many other things that are neither according to law nor without scandal. But in truth, there is no need to resort to this. Rather, since this matter was long ago a subject of differing opinions, the Pope in granting the dispensation followed that opinion which he judged probable. It does not follow from this that he decreed that opinion as an article of faith. For the acts of the Popes do not constitute articles of faith. I am surprised that others, and especially Cajetan, did not notice this. Therefore, if Celestine dispensed Constance, there is no doubt that this was very well known to St. Thomas, for he lived shortly after him. And nevertheless, there was no reason why he should fear to prove the contrary opinion. Nor in this did he condemn the Pope, since the Pope had judged his own opinion to be probable. Therefore, if St. Thomas had been Pope, he would never have granted the dispensation, nor could he have done so without fault, unless he had changed his opinion.

<margin>Cajetan’s affirmation.</margin>
¶ Come now, let us consider what Cajetan thought. For he says that since Innocent III, the author of that Decretal *Cum ad monasterium*, succeeded immediately after Celestine III (who had dispensed Constance), it is not likely that he would have condemned the act of his predecessor.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
I, however, gather that St. Thomas felt differently, as he wrote shortly after: namely, that Innocent issued that canon for the very reason that he held a different opinion than Celestine had. This he could do for the reason already stated, without injury to him. For Celestine had not made a canon as if it were a matter of faith. And therefore, St. Thomas embraced the canon of Innocent rather than following the act of Celestine.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>

### Question IV of the Eighth Book

...should be understood as referring only to a **simple vow**: for a solemn vow, just like marriage, is indissoluble. For this reason, he allows no cause for granting a dispensation. Whence Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian whose *Summa Theologiae* is the basis for this commentary.</note> says most excellently that the dangers of human affairs must be met through those same human affairs, and not by profaning divine things for human uses. Therefore, since religious <note>Those who have taken vows in a religious order, such as monks or nuns.</note> are entirely dead to the world, they are not to be recalled from that state for any cause or outcome. See how firmly Saint Thomas held this opinion, against which Cajetan <note>Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Aquinas who often debated the limits of Papal power.</note> felt otherwise.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that it only proves that just as a dispensation can be granted for a vow of prayer or sacrifice—which are more excellent objects—so it can be granted for a **simple vow** of continence, whether temporary or perpetual. However, when it is made **solemnly**, it is considered indispensable not merely because of the dignity of the object of chastity, but, as we repeatedly say, because of the tradition and <term>mancipation</term> <note>original: "mancipationem" — a legal term for a formal transfer of ownership; here, it refers to the person "handing themselves over" as a gift to God.</note> of the will: for the sake of which the work of chastity becomes a higher virtue, namely, one of religion and <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latriæ" — the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note>.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is responded that there is a wide distinction between abstinence <note>Refraining from food.</note> and continence <note>Refraining from sexual activity.</note>. For food is, by its nature, a means for the preservation of the individual’s life; however, sexual intercourse is only for the preservation of the species. Because of this, where continence leads to a manifest and most immediate danger to life, even without a dispensation—as we said above—it does not bind. Rather, through <term>epieikeia</term> <note>original: "epieikeiam" — a Greek term for "equity" or a higher sense of justice that looks at the spirit of the law rather than the letter.</note>, the one who had taken the vow may break it. Likewise, where the matter is doubtful, there is room for a dispensation. For in such cases, continence ceases to be the "matter" or subject of the vow. However, where sexual intercourse is considered "medicinal" for the health of the individual, it does not cease to be the matter of the vow simply because it was not naturally ordained for individual life; and thus, while the vow is solemn, it cannot be removed through a dispensation. Instead, such danger must be relieved through other medicines or through abstinence.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, finally, Saint Thomas responds that a monk, when he is decorated with the <term>episcopal infula</term> <note>original: "episcopali infula" — refers to the miter or the office of a Bishop.</note>, is no more absolved from the vow of poverty than from that of continence: because he ought to hold nothing as his own property, but should act as a distributor of the common goods of the Church. Similarly, he is not freed from the vow of obedience; for the fact that he does not obey the superiors of his religious order happens because he has no superior other than the Pope—just as a General Master of an order, though he obeys no one within the order, is not considered exempt from the vow.

<margin>To the other argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding that word from **Ecclesiasticus** <note>Sirach 26:15: "No price is worthy of a continent soul."</note> cited against the question, insofar as it seems to support the first

<column-break/>

opinion rejected above, it remains to be answered. For it seems there that continence is considered indispensable because of its preciousness; but if that were true, not even a **simple vow** could be dispensed. It is answered, therefore, that the text only teaches that neither the fruitfulness of the flesh nor any bodily good is to be compared to continence, which is a good of the soul. But nonetheless, if the vow is simple, a dispensation can be granted.

<margin>Ambiguity in the writing of Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ However, what Saint Thomas affirms in this place regarding a monk who is a bishop certainly does not lack difficulty. For first, he leaves it ambiguous whether he intended there to be no distinction between a monk-bishop and those taken from the secular world in terms of poverty; or whether he judged that only the monk is forbidden from having private property, while it is permitted for the others. For if he asserted this specifically about monks, it seems to contradict custom and practice. Since a monk created as a bishop becomes the master of the tithes and revenues destined for his function just as if he had been taken from the secular world. However, if he intended that no bishop should have any ownership of his revenues, but only their distribution, the matter would be much harder to believe: which we shall treat in Book 9, and discuss more closely according to our ability in Book 10. For I would believe that since episcopal fruits are the stipends <note>Salaries or support.</note> of the bishops, they have ownership of them; although by the law of mercy they are bound to pour out more generous alms than secular people, as they are the fathers of the poor. Otherwise, if they did not have ownership, whatever they spent on superfluities they would be usurping against justice, and would be bound to make restitution—an opinion which would be most harsh. But because this article will have its own proper place there, we must pause for now.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
Perhaps, however, Saint Thomas did not wish to distinguish between a bishop taken from the secular world and one taken from a religious order regarding episcopal revenues, but regarding other private possessions. For he concedes in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, Question 85, Article 6, that a secular bishop can have private property, which he denies to a religious bishop. But perhaps the vow of poverty is not as indispensable in a religious person as the vow of chastity. For after they are created bishops, a dispensation is sometimes granted to them in this regard. And it is known that those who are taken into the <insert>service of the</insert> First Apostolic See <note>The Roman Curia or the Papal court.</note> possess private property, even though they are not absolved from the vow of chastity attached to their religious state.

<vocab>
- Votum simplex: Simple vow, a private promise to God.
- Votum solenne: Solemn vow, a public legal commitment that changes one's status in the Church.
- Continentia: Continence, the act of refraining from sexual relations.
- Epieikeia: Equity, the principle that the law may be set aside in extreme cases to serve a higher justice.
- Latria: Worship and service due to God alone.
- Proprium: Private property or personal ownership.
</vocab>

F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law.

## ARTICLE III.
### Whether the authority of a prelate is required for the commutation or dispensation of a vow.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
Since it has been seen that the authority for commuting <note>Commutation refers to replacing one promised act with another of equal or greater value.</note> and dispensing <note>Dispensation is the formal release from the obligation of a vow.</note> vows exists in the Church, it remains to be seen whether this power resides solely with the prelates <note>A "prelate" is a high-ranking church official, such as a bishop or an abbot.</note>. It is argued from the negative side: Every free person is able to enter a religious order without the permission of a prelate. However, by the **solemn vow** of a religious order, one is absolved from whatever vows were made while living in the world—as stated in the chapter "Scripturae" in the Decretals, under the heading "On Vows." Therefore, the absolution of vows occurs without the authority of a prelate.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Secondly: The dispensation of a vow seems to consist in this—that it is decreed by the judgment of a superior that the vow is not to be observed. But if a prelate should decree this wrongly, the subject does not immediately seem to be absolved from the vow, because no one has the power to grant a dispensation against the divine precept of fulfilling a promise. Therefore, the authority of the prelate is not sufficient. Indeed, it does not even seem to be required. For if someone entangled in a vow rightly judges that in such an event the vow should not be kept, they immediately become free; for a vow does not bind in a case where it would be an evil to keep it. Thus, the authority of a prelate is not necessary for this task.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: If the power to dispense a vow belonged to superiors, then it would belong to all of them. However, not all superiors have the faculty to dispense every kind of vow. Therefore, this is not a power of prelates simply by virtue of being prelates.

¶ On the contrary stands the fact that a vow binds just as a law does. But for the dispensation of a law, the authority of a superior is necessary; therefore, it is also necessary for the dispensation of a vow.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
In the present article, although the question is only about the authority to dispense and commute, we must likewise respond regarding the legitimate *cause* for dispensing. Therefore, it is worthwhile to answer with two conclusions. The first is: **The authority of a superior is necessary to dispense a vow.** For—if I may mention this briefly for the sake of beginners—we are not speaking here about absolution from the *transgression* of a vow. Even if you have fallen into a sin of the flesh after vowing chastity, your parish priest is able to absolve you of the sin. But regarding the *dispensation* (the release from the future obligation), the conclusion is proven: A vow, as we showed in the previous sections, is a promise made to God concerning something that is acceptable and pleasing to Him. But what is acceptable 

<column-break/>

and pleasing to God depends upon His judgment, and thus upon the judgment of the superior who acts in His place <note>original: "vices eius fungitur" — performs His duties or acts as His representative.</note> in the Church. Therefore, it pertains to that superior to dispense vows, according to that passage in 2 Corinthians 2: "For if I have forgiven anything... I have done it for your sakes in the person of Christ." <note>2 Corinthians 2:10.</note>

<margin>Final conclusion. Proof.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: **A cause is required for the dispensation of a vow, and likewise for a commutation that results in a lesser good.** This is proven first by the authority just cited. For where Paul says, "in the person of Christ," he designates **authority**; but where he adds, "for your sakes," he indicates the **legitimate cause** for dispensing. This cause must indeed be directed toward the good of the Church; otherwise, it does not result in the honor of Christ. We have already demonstrated this above at the end of the second book regarding the dispensation of law: since a law is only established for the public good, it follows that it cannot be lawfully dispensed except for the sake of that same good. Regarding a vow, the reasoning is not much different. For after someone has bound their faith to God, His vicar <note>A representative or deputy; here referring to the prelate acting for Christ.</note> ought not to remit the promise unless it is for the good of the Church, over which Christ placed him. Otherwise, he would not be a faithful steward, but an unjust squanderer <note>original: "dissipator iniquus" — a wordplay on "dispensator" (steward/dispenser) and "dissipator" (one who scatters or wastes).</note>.

¶ Regarding the first conclusion, a distinction must first be recalled which we established above between those who can **annul** <note>original: "irritare" — to make void or invalid.</note> vows and those whose duty it is solely to **dispense**. For the former function (annulment) does not require ecclesiastical power; thus it is appropriate for parents, husbands, and masters. The latter (dispensation), however, belongs to prelates alone. Prelates, however, do not have the power to annul in the same way, unless they are the superiors of religious orders, since both faculties belong to them.

<margin>Doubt</margin>
¶ But regarding **commutation**, we must investigate whether it can be done privately without the authority of a superior. For Silvester <note>Silvester Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian.</note>, under the word "vow" (*votum*), question 4, section 7, leans toward the negative side, asserting that not even a commutation into a *better* thing can be done without the authority of a prelate.

<margin>Opinion of Silvester. Silvester is refuted.</margin>
However, this opinion is hardly supported by the truth, as his evidence is not firm.

<margin>The true solution.</margin>
A distinction must therefore be made. Either a **simple vow** is changed into something that is clearly better, or into something about which there is some doubt. If it is clear that the commutation is being made into a better thing, then the authority of a superior is not required, as Cajetan <note>Cardinal Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> rightly judges here.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
For both reasons and witnesses support this truth. It is an assertion, as in the chapter "Pervenit" (2) in the Decretals, under "On Oaths," that one does not break a purpose or a promise who commutes it into something better. And in the chapter cited,

-> ### Book Eight, Question IV. <-

<margin>Reason for the previous assertion.</margin>
As cited in the text "Scripturae" <note>original: "scripturæ. *de voto*." A reference to a specific chapter in the Decretals, the collection of Church law.</note> regarding vows, the reason that vows made while living in the world are considered extinguished by a **solemn religious vow** <note>A "solemn vow" is a formal, public commitment to the religious life (monasticism), which the Church considers more binding and transformative than private promises.</note> is that everything is changed for the better. This change is indeed made by the private authority of the person who dedicates themselves to religion. But the logical reason is no less effective: since the obligation of a vow is strictly that you should return what you have promised, when you pay back that which is established as being both better and equally acceptable and pleasing to the creditor, your payment is made more fully. Therefore, since it is certain that God—who is the assessor of things with an ineffable and infallible judgment—considers things more pleasing and acceptable the better they are, there is no doubt that someone who changes a vow for the better pays Him more abundantly, and thus requires no authority from a superior. 

Consider an example to confirm this point. If someone, for instance, vows a wax candle to God, or a sheep, or an ox, and in their place bestows a silver chalice upon the church, who would doubt that the vow has been satisfied? The sacristan and the guardian of the church would be acting unwisely and unfaithfully if they rejected such a payment. Nor does civil law stand in the way of this truth. For in the law "Mutuum" <note>original: "*l. mutuum. ff. si certum petatur.*" A reference to the Digest of Justinian regarding loans and specific claims.</note>, it is only held that one thing cannot be paid for another against the creditor's will because, among men, what is objectively "better" is not always more acceptable to a creditor—either because it is not as useful to him, or not as pleasing, or for some other reason. This cannot happen in respect to God. On the contrary, while it is clear to us that a thing is better, it is clear that He holds it more acceptable, and thus He always consents to such a payment, according to the Institutes <note>original: "*Institutio. titu. quibus modis tollitur obligatio.*" A section of the fundamental Roman law textbook regarding the ending of obligations.</note>: "With the creditor consenting, one thing can be paid for another." 

Add to this that perhaps, if it could be certain that a thing was of equal value in God's eyes, a commutation <note>The substitution of one promised act for another.</note> could be made without consulting a superior. However, this would not be as safe, because whenever quality is at issue, the judgment of another is required. For if a commutation is made by the sole will of the debtor, it seems to demand an even greater payment to be valid. Furthermore, not only can a **simple vow** be changed for the better by private authority, but even a **solemn religious vow** can be changed for a stricter and thus higher one, as is permitted in the chapter "Licet" regarding regulars <note>Members of religious orders living under a rule (regula).</note>. Yet it cannot be changed into a different kind of vow, just as it cannot be dispensed.

¶ But when there is doubt whether a change is being made for a better or a lesser good—specifically where it is not absolutely certain that the new work is more excellent—the authority of a prelate is always necessary. For this reason, a private person cannot change a simple vow of chastity, because nothing in the realm of vows is

<column-break/>

judged to be better. Nor can a vow of pilgrimage to Jerusalem be changed privately; for since these are reserved to the Pope alone, no one else can commute them. Indeed, neither a vow of abstinence nor other personal vows are safely changed without a decree from a superior. This is chiefly because whenever a vow is changed to something easier, it has something of a dispensation <note>A formal relaxation of the law or obligation.</note> mixed in, seeing as the bond of obligation is being loosened.

¶ Now, which ranks of prelates have the faculty to grant dispensations must be determined from canon law. First of all, all bishops <note>original: "Antistites."</note>, unless they have been prohibited by the Supreme Pontiff, could—by their own ordinary office—dispense from every vow within their own diocese, just as the Pope can in the whole of Christendom. However, because more important matters of faith should be referred to the highest head of the Church and Vicar of Christ (as advised in the section on baptism and its effects), five types of vows are reserved to him by law. These are: the vow of entering religion, the vow of perpetual chastity, and the vows of pilgrimage to Jerusalem, Rome, and Compostela <note>The shrine of St. James in Spain, a major medieval pilgrimage site.</note>. 

Although the vows for Rome and Compostela are reserved to the Roman Curia only by custom, by law only the Jerusalem vow is excepted, as is clear in the chapters "Quod super his" and "Ex multa." Indeed, since the reason for the reservation given there is that such a vow is undertaken for the aid of the Holy Land, Panormitanus <margin>Panormitanus</margin> <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> noted that only the vow undertaken for that reason is reserved to the Pope. Therefore, he says, if it is made out of devotion and not for aid, a bishop could dispense it. However, custom holds otherwise, and must therefore be followed. Consequently, a bishop's dispensation would not be valid.

¶ Beyond these reserved cases, every bishop can dispense from any simple vow of his own parishioners. This power in an archbishop, however, does not extend to the dioceses of his suffragans <note>Bishops who are subordinate to an archbishop within a province.</note>, because the ordinary care of souls does not fall to him except in his own diocese, though an appeal may be made to him in legal cases.

¶ Likewise, abbots and superiors of religious orders—not only the Generals and Provincials, but also the Conventuals <note>Local heads of specific monasteries or convents.</note>—possess the same authority of dispensing. In this regard, they are like the ordinary bishops of those subject to them. However, this same power does not extend to the vows of laypeople who may be subject to them, unless by a special privilege. And it is a general rule that the power of dispensing is the same everywhere as the power of commuting; for as <margin>General rule.</margin> **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says, the power of dispensing is greater.

...dispensing as much as commuting. However, the distinction made by <margin>Panormitanus.</margin> **Panormitanus** <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading authority on Church law often called "the Panormitan" because he was the Archbishop of Palermo.</note> regarding the chapter titled *Proposuit* <note>original: "capitulum, Proposuit. de concessione præbendæ." A reference to a specific section of the Decretals, the codified law of the Catholic Church.</note>—namely, that a Papal dispensation is an absolute release from the entire obligation, while a bishop does not strictly commute vows but merely relaxes them—has no foundation in either law or reason. For in that chapter, the faculty of dispensing is granted to the Pope in such a way that it is not forbidden to bishops. In contrast, **parish curates**, because they lack jurisdiction, lack this same authority to dispense. Nor do **archdeacons** exercise this same power. ¶ However, the law books must be consulted on these specific points. ¶ From this, the <margin>First corollary.</margin> following conclusion is reached: a bishop can dispense a vow of **chastity** that is temporary rather than perpetual. For since he can, by his ordinary power, remove all vows for a just cause, prohibitions and exceptions must be interpreted strictly as they are written. Therefore, because only the vow of *perpetual* chastity is excepted from a bishop's power, it follows that *temporary* vows are left to their discretion. ¶ It <margin>Second.</margin> follows immediately that the superiors of religious orders can also dispense the vows of their subjects regarding a transfer to a **higher religion** <note>The "higher religion" refers to a more rigorous or austere religious order (e.g., moving from the Franciscans to the Carthusians).</note>; although, as we said in the previous question, they cannot annul them. There is a wide gap here: to annul is to coerce the will of another, whereas to dispense is simply to grant the spontaneous petition of a subordinate. A Prelate cannot forbid a subordinate who wishes to cross over to a "happier harvest" <note>A metaphorical way of describing a more spiritually rewarding or stricter religious life.</note>. But if that person wishes to remain under the Prelate's obedience, they can be dispensed from such a vow by that same Prelate. This is because it is not a "simple vow of religion" (which is reserved for the Pope), but rather a vow to transfer from one order to another; and such exceptions, as I was just saying, must be interpreted narrowly. ¶ However, we have reserved one <margin>Doubt.</margin> doubt for the second question in this section: regarding **penal vows** of religion and the pilgrimage to Jerusalem—whether these are reserved for the Pope just as if they were absolute. For example, you have vowed to guard against a certain sin or anything else that was troublesome to you, adding the warning that if you did it again, you would take up the monastic life or go to Jerusalem. This kind of vow is extremely common among **inconstant young people**, and it is done with the greatest contempt and trivialization of God. This is because there is no one who actually fulfills it. Therefore, those who make such vows should be sharply rebuked by their confessors with the most severe rigor of punishment. The doubt, then, is whether after you have committed that evil (as always happens), the dispensation is 

<column-break/>

reserved for the Pope. Indeed, the arguments for the negative side contend that such a vow is not strictly conditional, like this one: "If my father dies, I will become a monk." For in that second case, the heart of the person is set on religion, and thus their intention is directed toward it. Therefore, once the condition is met, the vow becomes firm. But someone who threatens themselves with entering religion as a punishment is not affected by a love for religion, nor is the intention of the vow directed there; rather, it is directed toward the avoidance of that evil—for instance, to restrain themselves from gambling or adultery. Therefore, it is beyond doubt that before that evil is committed, one can be dispensed by the bishop or by any prelate who has authority over that direct vow. This reasoning, then, makes it probable that even after the evil is committed, it remains dispensable by that same prelate without the Pope, since it is not a "direct" vow of religion. <margin>Solution.</margin> Yet, until now, I have never been able to fully persuade myself of this. For even if it is not a direct vow of religion, once the condition has been met, an obligation to religion is born and confirmed by the force of the vow. And so, I am altogether afraid to assert anything other than that it is **reserved for the Supreme Pontiff**. Nevertheless, I would admit that not as great a cause is required for its dispensation as if the vow had been absolute. <margin>On the causes for dispensing and commuting vows.</margin> ¶ Regarding the causes for subsequently dispensing and commuting vows, the distinction must be carefully weighed. For through **dispensation**, the bond of the vow is entirely dissolved and its subject matter is removed. Therefore, the "good" which is the cause for the dispensation must compensate for both aspects: it must be greater than the matter of the vow itself, and greater than the bond which pertained to the virtue of religion and worship. **Commutation** of a vow, however, does not dissolve the bond, and therefore nothing more is needed than that the new matter be better, if it is a pure commutation. Behold the rules usually established for these cases. However, they are both obscure and deceptive, and of little use in practice unless they are explained more accurately. Therefore, to explain this, the causes for dispensing a vow must be recounted. Earlier, in Article 1, we reported three causes from the mind of **St. Thomas**, namely: if the vow is bad, or useless, or an impediment to a greater good. Here, however, he says such a cause ought to result in the "good of the Church" and consequently in the "honor of Christ." These are not new causes, but rather the goal and explanation of the others. <margin>Cajetan's doubt.</margin> ¶ There is, then, a doubt moved here by **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas and a cardinal.</note>: whether a cause that obstructs the execution of the vow is always required for its dispensation. It seems...

### Question IV of the Eighth Book

For **Saint Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for this text.</note> seems to affirm this in his solution to the second objection, where he says that if a prelate dispenses a simple vow of religion when no apparent cause stands in the way, the dispensation is not valid. On the other hand, it seems that a commutation <note>Commutation refers to "swapping" one religious obligation for another of equal or greater value, rather than simply canceling it.</note> is permitted even if no cause stands in the way; and yet, the same judgment seems to apply to both. Likewise, a vow is sometimes dispensed even if it could be fulfilled, for the sake of some public benefit. ¶ To clarify these matters, then, the following instructions are provided.

<margin>First instruction.</margin>
First, for the dispensation of a vow, an obstructing cause is necessary. Here it must be noted that a cause can obstruct in three ways: namely, from the nature of the matter of the vow, from the person making the vow, or by reason of the common good. Regarding the matter: First, if it is illicit. In that case, its wickedness stands in the way. If indeed it is useless, that very uselessness also hinders it in some way. For a vain work is not pleasing to God. And in these cases, it is not necessary that the cause for dispensing be a greater good than the bond of the vow considered absolutely; rather, it must be better than the bond of *such* a vow—one that is evil or useless—which is consequently of very little value. Therefore, it can be changed into something of small importance or abolished altogether. Second, an impediment can arise from the person making the vow: for example, their infirmity or weakness, because of which they cannot conveniently fulfill it. And even then, in a commutation, that weakness must be weighed so that the change is made more leniently and mercifully. Indeed, the weakness can be so great that the obligation must be dissolved entirely. But thirdly, an obstacle can exist regarding the common good. For instance, if you vowed a fast that is an impediment to your studying or preaching; for all such goods contribute to the common good. And then the rule holds true: that the good obstructing the vow, for the sake of which the dispensation is made, must be judged more precious than the matter and the bond of the vow itself. Similarly, if you have vowed a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, but it is more useful to the Church that you serve her in another way. Or if you have bound yourself to religious life by a simple vow, but it contributes to the common peace of the state <note>original: "reipublicæ"</note> that you marry. In such cases, a dispensation is lawfully made because the common good stands in the way of your vow's execution. However, if it only benefited your own particular good, that same dispensation would by no means be permitted. ¶ From these points, it follows that for a commutation—which is a pure commutation, that is, one made for something better—no obstructing cause whatsoever is required; it is enough that it leads more

<column-break/>

effectively toward the goal. An example exists in the chapter *Regarding these matters* <note>original: "c. Quod super his. de voto." A reference to the Decretals of Pope Gregory IX regarding the commutation of vows.</note> concerning vows, where women’s vows to visit the Holy Land are permitted to be changed into almsgiving. This is not because anything stood in the way of the vow's execution, but because women's money contributes more to the aid of the Holy Land than their physical presence. However, when a commutation is made into a *lesser* good, an obstructing cause is always required. This is because such a commutation includes a dispensation—namely, a certain relaxation of the vow. ¶ From this, let the faithful and prudent administrator gather that while a vow's impediment is sufficiently met through commutation, he should use that remedy rather than dispensation. Otherwise, he would be unfaithful; for every dispensation made without necessity is not without fault, nor does the guilt of the one dispensing excuse the petitioner from being entangled in the same. Although, the guilt is greater in the one who grants the dispensation.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ At this point, perhaps the diligent reader may inquire: which is to be dispensed with greater difficulty, a law or a vow? For arguments exist for both sides. Since a law is established for the common good and binds all citizens, it appears it should be more sacredly guarded than a vow. On the contrary, because a vow is made to God and thus pertains to the virtue of religion, it seems to require a greater cause for dispensing.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
We can hardly answer this with a single certain rule. Therefore, there may be some law which is more destructive to violate by dispensation than it is to remove a particular vow. Conversely, there may be a vow whose dispensation constitutes a greater offense against religion. The legitimate causes for dispensing are commended at length in the first part, question 7 <note>original: "1. q. 7. ... can. requiritis" (Gratian's Decretum).</note> in the canon *You ask*, and the gloss there, and the canon *Necessary*, and the following one. For time, utility, the person, and the quality of the matter must be weighed. ¶ Now, as to whether that cause for dispensing should be admitted as legitimate and suitable—namely, that it is heavy and troublesome for the one bound by the vow to fulfill it—we have already responded at the end of the first book: when the trouble and difficulty arise from the thing itself (because the task is arduous and beyond one's strength), then it offers a legitimate cause for dispensing. However, when it proceeds from a corrupt affection or a sickness of the person making the vow <note>Referring to spiritual "sickness" like sloth or lack of devotion.</note>, it is certainly not a legitimate cause. For since you made the vow for this very purpose—to heal your sickness and your evil habit—to bring forward that same habit as a cause to be released from the vow is not to maintain the sincerity of faith. ¶ After these things, regarding the privileges granted in the Crusade diplomas <note>original: "diplomatibus Cruciatæ." These were formal documents or "Bulls of the Crusade" granting spiritual benefits and powers to commute vows to those who contributed to the defense of Christendom.</note> for the dispensation of vows, this must be noted: they are not equally...

### Book Eight, Question IV.

[...however,] by the judgment of the one making the vow, because he himself does not act in God's place. Unless, perhaps, in a case where the matter of the vow was clearly unlawful, and no timely recourse to a superior was available. For then, as has been said, there would be room for *epieikeia* <term>epieikeia: a Greek term for "equity," referring to the sensible interpretation of a law in specific cases where following the literal letter of the law would be unjust or harmful</term>.

<margin>
First doubt regarding the assertions of St. Thomas.
</margin>
¶ Regarding these assertions of Saint Thomas, several reasons for doubt arise. The first concerns the logical inference of his argument: "A prelate cannot prohibit the duties of virtues; therefore, he cannot dispense them at his own whim." Indeed, either by the name of "virtue" he means the subject matter of the vow, or the act of vowing itself. If the former, the meaning would be: "A prelate cannot restrain subjects from fasting, praying, or going on pilgrimages, etc.; therefore, he cannot at his whim remove the bond of such works." This reasoning would fail in two ways. First, because the inference has no force: for even if a monastic superior could not prevent someone from freely praying or fasting, he could nevertheless prevent the vow. Just as a husband, though he might act unjustly by preventing his wife from praying, could nonetheless void her vow. Similarly, then, a bishop, though he might not stand in the way of a subject freely exercising works of virtue, could nonetheless remove the bond at his whim, so that the subject would not be bound by a new cord. Second, the premise of that same inference is false. For a prelate in a religious order can sometimes prohibit the work of one virtue for the sake of another: for instance, so that a monk does not remain idle, but serves the sick; or so he does not fast, but studies. However, if by "virtue" he means the act of vowing itself, even then the argument will not be solid, which is this: "He cannot command sins, therefore he cannot prohibit vows from being made, nor remove those already made at his whim." For the weakness of this conclusion is evident in the case of a religious prelate or a parent regarding a child: who cannot command them to sin, yet can nonetheless cancel their vows.

<margin>
The Solution.
</margin>
¶ To understand these matters, it must be noted that there is one kind of reason for a superior who has dominion over the will of a subject—such as a husband, a father, a master, or a monastic prelate—and another for the prelates of the people (such as bishops), who do not have that kind of dominion, but only spiritual jurisdiction. Saint Thomas is not speaking here of the first order of superiors, whose role it is to void vows; for he had already settled that matter in articles 8 and 9. Rather, he is speaking of prelates only insofar as they are prelates and spiritual judges, who therefore possess the faculty not of *voiding* vows, but of *dispensing* them. And regarding these, he proceeds to establish

<column-break/>

that since they are not the masters of their subjects' wills, the subjects' vows do not depend on the prelates' will. Consequently, in such vows, the authority of the Bishop <note>original: "Antistitis"; a high-ranking cleric or bishop</note> is not understood as an implied exception, as if the vows were conditional on whether they pleased the bishop or the Pope—unlike the vow of a child, a wife, or a monk. This teaching is manifest in itself; and therefore Paludanus <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent French theologian and jurist</note> and others who hold the contrary have, in this matter, been blindly deluded. For Popes are not the masters of their subjects, nor of their wills. Therefore, just as marriages and other contracts of citizens are firm and solid without consulting the bishops, so too are their vows. This firmness of the vow being granted, the reasoning of Saint Thomas proceeds excellently in both senses we recently challenged. In the first sense: just as a bishop cannot prohibit works of virtue—such as fasting, praying, entering a religious order, etc.—so he cannot prohibit them from vowing those same works absolutely, since he is not the master of their will. Therefore, the argument we made concerning the parent and the wife does not apply. Likewise, in the second sense—taking "virtue" to mean the vow itself—the argument also proceeds: namely, that just as a bishop or Pope cannot command sins for their subjects, neither can they at will hinder works of virtue, such as vows (which are firm and solid without the superior's consent), nor can they break their knots and bonds. And I judge this second interpretation to be the legitimate mind of Saint Thomas.

<margin>
Second Doubt.
</margin>
¶ But a doubt remains regarding the meaning of the conclusion where he says that when a prelate dispenses without at least some apparent cause, such a dispensation does not excuse one from fault. This statement gives rise to a triple understanding. First, that the prelate granting the dispensation is not excused from fault; and there is no doubt that this is true, for he sins either against prudence or against the "faith of dispensing" <note>the duty to manage the Church's spiritual treasures faithfully</note>. Second, that the subject procuring the dispensation is not without fault, which is also certain. For he who procures an unjust thing is guilty of harm. But there can be a third sense: that even after the dispensation, the subject is not excused from that specific fault, as if the dispensation does not hold. And concerning this sense, a doubt may arise for someone; for after the dispensation has been granted, the subject seems to be absolved. But in truth, Saint Thomas seems to have asserted all three senses: for he says that just as a prelate cannot command sins, so neither [can he...]

The response is that he calls those vows "perpetual" there which, when they are uttered absolutely, have perpetuity annexed to them by their very nature: such as the vow of religion and chastity. For whoever vows chastity absolutely, understands it as perpetual. But a vow of fasting and prayer, unless the condition of perpetuity is expressed, does not bring that about from its own nature. And therefore, even if they are made in perpetuity, they can be dispensed by inferior prelates.

This conclusion is established both by the testimony of Christ cited above—"On these two commandments depend all the law and the prophets"—and also follows directly from the previous point. <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> For if charity itself is our perfection, it follows that from the observance of its precepts this same perfection and our salvation depend, according to the word of Christ: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." Although not in the same degree. For the essence of our perfection is situated in the love of God; however, according to this, it is also in the love of neighbor. Indeed, the second degree of charity belongs to the same perfection for the reason that love of neighbor is nothing other than a certain love of God, according to 1 John 4: "If anyone says 'I love God' and hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother whom he sees..."
