<margin>Third conclusion. Proof.</margin>
¶ **The third conclusion.** These precepts of charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the theological virtue of selfless, supernatural love for God and neighbor.</note> prescribe no specific limit <note>original: "modum," often translated as "measure" or "mode."</note> for our loving. This is proved because precepts must be measured according to their own end: we are therefore commanded by these precepts to love God and neighbor in the way that each is worthy of being loved.
<margin>Bernard.</margin>
The "mode" of loving God, as Saint Bernard of Clairvaux says, is to love without any mode or measure. Therefore, His precept sets no limit—that is, it does not say he must be loved by us to this or that specific degree, or that some should love Him one way and others another—but rather the command to love is absolute. Nor is there a lack of examples for this provided to us by nature itself.
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
For as Aristotle acutely observed in Book 1 of his *Politics*, there is a difference between the "end" (the goal) and the "means" (the tools) such that the end, being good in itself, is loved without limit or boundary. No one, for instance, sets a limit on how much health they want for themselves; because the greater the health, the better it is, it is desired without limit. Medicines, however, because they derive their entire goodness from the end (health), are not "better" simply by being larger or more numerous. For that reason, they are desired by the sick person and applied by the physician not infinitely, but according to a specific weight and measure. God, therefore, because He is the supreme "end" of all things, is commanded to be loved without limit. This is the meaning of those words: *You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.* As for our neighbor, although he is not to be loved entirely without limit—since a limit is prescribed: *And your neighbor as yourself*—nevertheless even that limit carries a certain reflection of infinity. For men also, in a way, love themselves without limit; indeed, when they truly love themselves, they ought to desire that eternal happiness for themselves without any measure, and the same for others. Our perfection, therefore, essentially consists in those mandates by which we are commanded to love God and neighbor without limit.
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Hence Saint Augustine says in his book *On the Perfection of Justice*: "Why then," he asks, "should this perfection not be commanded of us, even if one might not fully possess it in this life?" He means that most perfect degree of love which admits of not even a venial <note>A "venial" offense is a minor sin that does not break the relationship with God, as opposed to a "mortal" sin.</note> offense.

<margin>Argument</margin>
¶ There exists, however, an argument against this conclusion. If the perfection of the Christian life consists in these precepts of charity—by which we are commanded to love God and neighbor without limit—and since all mortals are bound by these same precepts, then everyone would be forced to live at the very peak of perfection,

<column-break/>

and thus no one could be free from fault. It would be impious to concede this, as it is contrary to divine kindness.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this it is responded: the mandate of charity being set "without limit" is not to be understood as obliging every person to actually reach the absolute summit of charity, but rather so that every person may understand the goal toward which they ought to strive in their loving. Therefore, to avoid the sin of transgression, it is enough that a person commits nothing contrary to charity and its precepts; this will appear more clearly in the response to the second point.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The fourth conclusion.** All other precepts—both those expressed in the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> and all those reduced to their underlying logic—as well as all the <term>counsels</term> <note>The "evangelical counsels" are voluntary practices like poverty, chastity, and obedience, as opposed to "precepts" which are mandatory laws.</note> are directed toward attaining this very perfection of charity. Consequently, our perfection consists in them as if in instruments, though in a different way for precepts than for counsels. Precepts serve charity by removing impediments that are directly contrary to it, such as: *Thou shalt not steal*, *Thou shalt not commit adultery*, and others which bind under the threat of mortal sin; or those which cool the fire of love, such as venial sins. The counsels, however, as stated above, cut away those things which, even if they are lawful and not entirely hostile to charity, are nonetheless obstacles to those progressing toward the summit—such as the possession of property and marriage, which create innumerable worldly distractions for mortals.

¶ Therefore, let those who petulantly bark against the institutes of the monks be gone! For we do not, as they falsely charge us, place perfection in the exercise of these counsels in such a way that we believe the substance and essence of perfection lives in them alone. Nor do we prefer these counsels to the precepts, as if we thought them equally necessary. Rather, we profess that the monastic state <note>original: "monachatum"</note> regards perfection just as a steep shortcut is a faster way to reach a destination. It is "steep," I say, for beginners; for those who are advanced, it is the smoothest path. And here perhaps is the true sense of that word of Christ in Matthew 5: *He who does these least commandments and so teaches men, shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.*
<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
This meaning did not escape Saint John Chrysostom, and it has been more fully explained by us elsewhere. For there, Christ appears to call the "least commandments" those counsels by which he was instituting the Apostolic order; nevertheless, he asserted that those who observe them would be called "great" in the kingdom of heaven. From this, some contradiction seems to arise: for if they are the least...

# Book Eight. Question Five.

...[how] are they, and how do those who practice them become great? Or if they make them great, how can they be called the "least"? The answer, therefore, is that counsels are considered "least" because they are not necessary for salvation in the same way as the precepts. The precepts are consequently considered "greatest," for it is upon them that our salvation depends. However, those who perform these counsels will be called "great" for this reason: they not only observe the necessary precepts but also those things which, although lawful <note>That is, things like marriage or owning property which are permitted to Christians generally.</note>, could nonetheless stand in the way of their striving toward the perfection of charity by a shorter path. See how perfection is not established in the counsels themselves; rather, the perfection of both the counsels and the precepts is situated in charity. Regarding both of these orders, 
<margin>*Augustine*</margin> 
Augustine says in his *Enchiridion* <note>original: "Enchiridio August." The *Enchiridion* is Augustine's handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love.</note>: "Whatever God mandates, of which one is *Thou shalt not commit adultery*; and whatever is not commanded but advised by special counsel, of which one is *It is good for a man not to touch a woman*: these are then done rightly when they are referred to the love of God, both in this world and in the future." And a certain Abbot 
*Moses*, as one reads in the *Conferences of the Fathers* <note>original: "Collationibus Patrum," a famous work by John Cassian recording the wisdom of Egyptian desert monks.</note>, says: "Fasts, vigils, meditation on the scriptures, nakedness, and the deprivation of all resources are not perfection, but the instruments of perfection; for the end of our discipline does not consist in them, but through them one arrives at the end." 
<margin>*Fifth conclusion.*</margin>
¶ **The fifth conclusion.** The observation of the counsels is a support for obtaining a higher degree of charity, not only for other reasons but also because they provide a safeguard, so that the precepts may be kept more excellently and safely. I would not say that the counsels have that alone as their end. Indeed, a vow of chastity is not directed toward the goal of merely avoiding adultery or fornication. Nor is a vow of poverty directed toward avoiding theft. In fact, most people who take these vows are already free from those crimes. However, it may happen that someone undertakes such vows for that very reason. But it is nonetheless certain that the exercise of the counsels exists as a shield for the precepts. For he who has chosen poverty from his soul is further removed from committing theft; and he who has bound himself by a vow of chastity is even more withdrawn from adulteries. And he who has said farewell to the pomps of the world is safer from killings and other injuries inflicted on others. ¶ For this reason, I believe that prophecy of Isaiah 26 is brought to this meaning without any distortion. Where the prophet, speaking of the city of strength to which the Savior is compared, says: *A wall and a bulwark shall be set within it.* For what are we to understand by the name of 

<column-break/>

"walls" except the precepts of the law, by which our salvation is hedged around and protected? The "bulwark" <term>antemurale: a secondary, outer defensive wall or rampart</term> then—and, if we may call it so, the *pomoerium* <note>original: "pomœrium," the sacred open space just inside or outside the city walls of Rome.</note> of the law—is quite aptly the exercise of the counsels, with which our Savior fortified the Gospel law. Behold how monks do not place perfection in their own institutes. But to use the words of Augustine in *On the Morals of the Church*, where he speaks of their life: charity is especially guarded among them if they are legitimate; virtue is adapted to charity, speech to charity, dress to charity, and countenance to charity. 
<margin>*Sixth conclusion.*</margin>
¶ **The sixth conclusion.** The religious vow consists of poverty, chastity, and 
<margin>*Reason for the conclusion.*</margin>
obedience. The reason for this is that "religion" <note>In this context, "religion" refers specifically to the "religious life" or monastic state.</note> is situated in this, as has been said: that you desert the world so that, following Christ, you may progress through the degrees of charity. 
<margin>*Paul.*</margin>
That word of Paul in Galatians 6 pertains to this: *Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.* For he wished those who were to embrace the Apostolic institute to leave the world behind them in such a way that they would not only hand it over entirely to oblivion, but also take diligent care that the world, in turn, would forget them. And thus each should be as alienated from the other as if they were two corpses. However, this abdication of the world happens in no other way than if we leave those things by which the world holds us. These things, as 
<margin>*Aristotle.*</margin>
Aristotle is the author in Book 1 of the *Ethics*, are three kinds of goods: namely external goods, goods of the body, and goods of the soul. Concerning these, John says in his first Epistle: *Everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life.* Therefore, lest these goods—by their excess—either drive out charity or dampen its fervor, they are limited by the lines and norms of the precepts. Therefore, he who keeps the precepts can lawfully use those goods, for he does not step outside the boundaries of justice. Yet, because even then the possession of worldly goods cannot fail to create many dangers for the nourishing of charity, Christ added the "salvific counsels"; so that with those impediments entirely cast out, we might follow our cross more unencumbered. For that the possession of worldly goods is dangerous even to those who obey the precepts, Christ divinely explained in Luke 18, in that parable of the threefold malignant earth <note>The Parable of the Sower, where thorns represent worldly cares.</note>. For that which is cast as the sowing of the word in the earth designates the precepts of the law received by human minds. But either the pride of life of those who walk along the way—that is, in all the world’s honors—

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

...gape after [worldly things], or the dryness of heart in those who, dripping with the desires of the flesh, wither in spiritual matters, or the anxiety of those who are entangled by "thorny" riches; all these either expose that same life-giving seed to demons, or dry it out for lack of dew, or finally suffocate it through the greed for things. For this reason, Christ our law-giver—when he ascended the mountain as recounted in Matthew 5, from where the world might hear him—did not open the mouth of a man or an angel, but opened *his own mouth* to lay down laws for the world. Immediately, like the best of architects, he began from the very end <note>That is, the goal or purpose</note> of the laws, namely from happiness [beatitude]. "Blessed," he said, "are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek; blessed are those who mourn." Here, 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

he outlined the three vows of monks. For in a three-fold way, as Aristotle the author states in Book 1 of his *Ethics*, the "wise men" of this world were wandering in error regarding supreme happiness. Some placed it in riches, others in honors, and still others in pleasures. The Redeemer, therefore, blunts their drunken madness with a three-fold sentence. Since the whole world of mortals was dying to know where the happiness—which everyone desires—was located, he went out to meet the common desire of all with his very first word. "You desire," he said, "to know the happiness toward which every law leads: Blessed, therefore, are the poor in spirit," which means those who are so voluntarily. It is as if he were to say: "An immoderate abundance of things is so far from making men happy that justice consists rather in their moderate use, and happiness in their utter neglect and rejection." Next, "blessed are the meek," namely those who are not satisfied with a just moderation of honors, but rather, binding themselves by a higher obedience, flee from the tumult of honors. "Blessed are those who mourn," which means it is not those submerged in pleasures who are happy, but those who enjoy them according to the law's prescription are the just; while those who have repudiated them even to the point of "filth" <note>original: "ad lutum," meaning treating worldly pleasures as worthless as mud</note> are the blessed. And so that what we said a little earlier may become clear—namely, that the exercise of the "counsels" greatly assists in the excellent guarding of the "commandments"—he adds: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice," and "blessed are the merciful." For those who bind themselves by the vows of the counsels do not think it enough to keep the precepts of justice and mercy in any old way, but rather do so most thirstily. And since both the counsels and the precepts lead to the summit and perfection of charity (as has been said), by which hearts are cleansed—and the purity of hearts purifies and sharpens the mind's eye to see God, in which vision happiness consists—he adds: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." And since in that total 

<column-break/>

satisfaction and tranquility of desires it is established that we be named and be children of God (according to the word of John), he finally concludes: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God." ¶ But if you desire to see this three-fold 

<margin>The number of vows derived from the Sacred Scriptures.</margin>

vow of the counsels—which is established in this one place—dispersed throughout the Gospel, you will find it in various places. For poverty is the first in order and use; as Ambrose 

<margin>Ambrose</margin>

noted in his commentary on Luke. For just as the resources of things are the instruments of all vices, so their rejection is the mother and nurse of all virtues. Concerning this, there exists a most distinguished and full teaching of Christ in Matthew 19, where he instructs the young man who was thirsting for eternal life step by step. For first, he advised him on what was necessary: "If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments." Soon, when the young man responded that he had kept those from his youth, Christ added: "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and follow me." For selling what you have, if you consider it plainly, is not the counsel itself; rather, it is distributing it to the poor. But because perfection does not consist in any one of the counsels, but rather in the fact that you become a follower of Christ and thus a cultivator of charity, he adds: "And follow me." ¶ I confess that Jerome 

<margin>Jerome & Origen</margin>

and Origen lean toward the idea that the young man was not actually keeping the commandments. An argument for this is taken from what follows: "It is impossible for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven." From this, the Lutherans <note>The Protestant reformers, who generally rejected the distinction between mandatory "precepts" and voluntary "counsels" of perfection.</note> conclude that no "perfection" is designated there except that which is situated in the cultivation of the commandments. However, once the matter is considered more deeply, the opinion of the other Fathers is to be preferred. Namely, that the young man answered truly when he said he had kept them from his youth, even if he had not done so very fervently. For Mark relates that Christ "looking at him, loved him"; he would not have done this unless he understood the young man to be speaking the truth. Add to this that if Christ had known he was lying, he would have either indicated it to him or would not have added "If you wish to be perfect" as if it were a higher grade above the cultivation of the commandments. In short, since he had first said with such a distinction of words, "If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments," and then, "If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have" (which in truth is not necessary for entering life), he undoubtedly added voluntary "counsels" to the necessity of the "commandments." This is certainly a safer and shorter way to perfection. Peter, clearly understanding this, immediately asked in the name of everyone: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?" From these words, as we shall see in the following question, we are taught that the Apostles took a vow, which the religious <note>i.e., members of religious orders like monks or friars</note> now perform following their example.

### Question V of the Eighth Book

When the young man refused the advice <note original: "consilium">The "counsels" or advice Christ gives, which are optional paths to perfection, distinct from the mandatory commandments.</note>, Christ added that it is indeed difficult for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven. This was an exaggeration of the dangers that threaten those who possess wealth. For if that young man—who had kept the commandments in some way and had approached Christ (whom he confessed as Teacher) with such eagerness to learn the way to the kingdom—rejected Christ’s advice before he would reject his possessions, what can be hoped for from others? ¶ Observe, therefore, how the vow of poverty is not perfection itself, but a means to perfection, which is situated in the service of Christ and the fire of charity. The same must be judged regarding the vow of chastity. For another word of the same Redeemer in the same chapter denotes this: *There are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.* <note original: "Sunt eunuchi qui se castrauerunt propter regnum caelorum">Matthew 19:12. In this context, it refers to those who choose celibacy for spiritual reasons.</note> <margin>Paul.</margin> And Paul teaches the same in 1 Corinthians 7: *He who is without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord: how he may please God. And the unmarried woman and the virgin think on the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in both body and spirit.* In these passages, perfection is placed not in chastity itself, but in charity. Likewise, the vow of obedience is easily drawn from the word of Christ in Luke 9: *If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.* For since human nature, which excels all other living creatures, is deeply characterized by the freedom through which it was made in the image of God, for a man to "deny himself" is the same as submitting his own liberty to the judgment of another by the bond of a vow. Yet perfection is not fixed even in this, unless you "follow Christ," wherein charity is located. <margin>Seventh conclusion.</margin> ¶ I would deliberately add a seventh conclusion here. The renunciation of the world in the manner explained not only exists in divine law established by Christ our lawgiver, but is drawn from the very "bowels" of natural law. <note>Natural law refers to the moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> Thus, Christ’s preaching was a declaration of the natural law. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> This is proven. Christ, who was the author of nature (as we have frequently said above), neither destroyed nor changed it, but by his law he both declared it and, where nature was lacking, perfected it. Since he advised us to renounce the world, that very principle must have been latent in the law of nature, <margin>Argument 2.</margin> even if it was not known to everyone. ¶ Second, it is argued for the same point: It was most fitting that when God became man and came into this world to live with us, he should enter into that way of life which was best according to the nature he himself had created. He chose that life which is placed in the exercise of the counsels, namely

<column-break/>

poverty, and the very peak of chastity. As for the obedience annexed to the vow of chastity, since he was the head of the church, he could perform it for no one except his parent <note>Referring to God the Father.</note>. Therefore, this is the best life by its very nature. <margin>Solution.</margin> ¶ But perhaps someone might respond: "He did not choose this condition of life because it is the best according to nature, but because it was a more efficient path for us toward eternal life; it was fitting that he should instruct us not only with words but by his own example." It was indeed appropriate that he began to do what he was going to teach in words. However, this quibble does not break the strength of the argument. Rather, it confirms it. <margin>Reply.</margin> For if this life was more efficient for us, it is a sign that it is efficient by the very nature of things; otherwise, he would have instructed us differently. Since he would not change the nature of things, he taught us its truth. ¶ And this is finally demonstrated by legitimate reason and cause: That state of life is naturally best which is more fit and efficient for attaining eternal happiness. It is clearly gathered from the nature of things that such a state consists in the renunciation of the world. For it has already been shown that temporal goods and the trappings of wives and family toss and entangle human souls, preventing them from being carried toward spiritual things by their own natural impulse. <margin>Objection.</margin> ¶ But what if someone were to challenge us, saying that these temporal goods were created by God's authority for the sake of the human race and granted to us for our use? Therefore, the legitimate use of them should come closer to perfection than their total rejection. <margin>Solution.</margin> The answer is that the argument would hold true if the human race had remained in that state in which God created it <note>The state of innocence before the Fall of Man.</note>. In that case, no danger would threaten us from such goods; rather, they would serve us in inflaming divine love. In such a state, neither chastity nor poverty would be a task of virtue. However, after the fall of our race, those things which were healthy for us became harmful. It is not that the things themselves changed their natures, but that we depraved our own nature. Just as wine is useful to the healthy but harmful to the sick, and fasting—which harms strong and healthy men—is a remedy for those suffering from a fever. <margin>Eighth conclusion.</margin> ¶ Finally, the eighth and last conclusion is made. For the state of perfection (as it has been explained to consist in the counsels), it is neither sufficient nor required that it be legitimately kept in actual practice; rather, this state consists in being stabilized by the perpetual obligation of a solemn vow. This conclusion is against the same Lutheran heresy—

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s defense of religious vows. ### Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>
Luther’s error.
</margin>
...thus, in the same cited book *On Monastic Vows*, he <note>Martin Luther</note> permits the vows of religion, yet in such a way that they are not perpetual. And so that you may recognize the man by his own words, he says: "Monks should vow: I vow obedience, chastity, and poverty, according to the rule of Saint Augustine until death, freely." That is to say: so that whenever it seems good to me, I may be able to change my mind. See the drunken conflict of his words: <note original: "temulentam verborum pugnantiam">A sharp rhetorical jab; Soto suggests Luther’s logic is as unstable as a drunkard.</note> *until death*, yet *so that I may be able to change*. For if it is until death, how can it be changed? For a bond that is broken before death is not firm "until death."

<margin>
The first argument against Luther.
</margin>
¶ Therefore, this conclusion depends on two points. The first is whether anyone can legitimately and properly make such a vow perpetual. The second is whether a perpetual vow is necessary for the <term>state of perfection</term> <note>In Catholic theology, the "state of perfection" refers to a stable, public way of life (like monasticism) dedicated to pursuing spiritual excellence.</note>. Indeed, no one unless they are mentally blind can deny the first part. For truly, since a human can bind themselves in civil contracts forever, why should they not be able to hand themselves over to God eternally? Why should that which was previously whole and free for them to do, not pass thereafter into a bond of command through a given pledge? I say that anyone can sell their property forever; they can also bind their freedom to a spouse in a marriage covenant, so that an indissoluble bond remains from then on. Moreover, even according to civil laws, someone can sell themselves as a slave to another forever; and thus in many other ways, one can so pledge their faith to another forever that no path back to freedom lies open without fault.

Why then does anything stand in the way of someone offering themselves as a servant to God—to whom "to serve is to reign"—and confirming that with a most holy and indissoluble bond? Add to this that even priests properly bind themselves to the ministry of sacred things by an irrevocable covenant.

<margin>
The second argument.
</margin>
¶ Add further that by the same reasoning these men deny that anyone can legitimately and fittingly bind themselves forever, they are forced to deny that it can be done for any certain and predefined time, however small. For if a man can bind himself for a year, he can do so for two, and for ten, and perpetually. But if he cannot do so for a year, it follows he cannot do so for a month, nor a day, nor an hour. This is to deny the entire nature of a vow. In short, these men recognize no obligation in a vow. Therefore, one ought not to respond further to their frenzy, lest we seem like them, contrary to the teaching of the wise man.

¶ It remains for us to show whether the exercise of the counsels <note>The voluntary practices of poverty, chastity, and obedience.</note> without a perpetual vow deserves the name of a "state."

<column-break/>

This is elucidated as follows: "state" <note original: "status">Soto is playing on the etymology of the word, which implies standing firm or a stable condition.</note> is indicated by its very name to be the same as a condition of freedom or servitude. For instance, we speak of the "marital state" because of the bond of faith between spouses (which is a kind of servitude), and the "state of a single woman" because of her freedom. However, a spiritual state—whether of servitude or freedom—requires not only an internal obligation which is open to God, but also an external solemnity in the sight of the Church. For we are not speaking here of the state of grace or sin, which is judged only in the court of God, but of those states and orders by which the beauty of the Church is joined together; she who sits as a queen at the right hand of the bridegroom, "clothed in variety." <note>A reference to Psalm 45:9, often used to describe the various ranks and vocations within the Church.</note> An example is clear in civil matters. For a person is not in the "state of slaves" simply because they serve another (for anyone can freely serve another), but because they solemnly hand themselves over as a slave. Nor is one established in the "state of freedom" simply because they snatch themselves away from servitude in any way they can (for they might be a runaway), but because they are granted freedom by a public instrument. In exactly the same way, even if someone were to profit in the exercise of the counsels without a solemn vow, and even reach that level of charity and merit before God which many religious have not yet attained, nevertheless, no one possesses the "state of perfection" without a perpetual bond. And vice versa: although a religious person might not have progressed in charity according to the reason and dignity of their institute, they are nonetheless in the state of perfection by reason of their solemn vow. Because of this, where all else is equal, the same work of a religious person is of more abundant merit before God, as was said in Question 2.

<margin>
Confirmation against Luther.
</margin>
¶ This same conclusion of ours is confirmed against these heretics. For unless religion consisted of a perpetual vow, many Evangelical testimonies would have no legitimate meaning. For that saying in Luke 9: *No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God*—although it holds truth for the Christian religion in general—the saints apply it specifically to the monastic life. So too with that saying in Luke 17: <note>The text mistakenly says Luke 7.</note> *Remember Lot’s wife.* And yet, if it were permitted without fault to go backward from the monastery into the world, nothing of the right to the kingdom of God would be lost by that reasoning. And that passage cited above from Leviticus 27: *Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it be man or animal, shall not be sold nor can it be redeemed, but it shall be the holy of holies*—this is not inaptly applied to priests and monks, as we saw above. But why do we even dispute with these men? Unless the institutes of religion were strengthened by a solemn vow, what would the cloisters of the religious be, other than a mockery of men? Namely...

<summary>De Soto argues against Luther's view that monastic vows should be revocable, asserting that a "state of perfection" legally and spiritually requires a permanent, public commitment. He compares the stability of religious vows to civil contracts like marriage or even voluntary servitude to illustrate that a life-long bond is both possible and necessary for the Church's structure.</summary>

### Book Eight
### Question 5
#### Page 685

...namely full today, empty tomorrow. And he who today wears the cowl, tomorrow would be a married laborer. ¶ It remains, however, to resolve the final argument against what has been said.
<margin>Argument.</margin>
That among <term>cenobites</term> <note>Monks who live in a community, as opposed to hermits.</note> three orders of men must be distinguished no less than among the secular: namely, the beginners, the progressing, and the perfect; therefore, not all are in a state of perfection. To this, indeed, a response is given through what we were just saying regarding the final conclusion.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
For although the premise is true, the conclusion is nonetheless void. For they are said to be in a "state of perfection" not because of their progress toward the summit, but because of their **vow**. Although all monks ought to be filled with shame who do not strive toward that goal which they profess by their habit and ceremonies. ¶ Therefore, he who denies that the state of monks, thus explained, is one of perfection, is injurious to every law: natural, divine, and human. For there has never been any age of the world in which there were not some people set apart from the rest of the population by their way of life, who displayed some specimen of religion. Indeed, at the very beginning of the rising world, among other mortals, it is read in Genesis 5 that Enoch uniquely "walked with God"; for which reason he is not recorded as being taken by death, but as "not appearing." And among the Philosophers, the school of the Pythagoreans and the followers of Diogenes led a life secret from the common assembly: namely, by abstaining from those secular enjoyments which are cast aside by monastic vows. And in Rome there were holy women who consecrated themselves to the goddess Vesta by a vow of virginity. And in Jeremiah 35, the Rechabites are commemorated, whose religious profession was to drink no wine, nor build houses, nor sow seed, nor plant vineyards. And concerning Elijah and other Prophets,
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Paul reports in Hebrews 11 that they "wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins: being in want, distressed, afflicted: of whom the world was not worthy: wandering in solitudes, in mountains, in dens, and in caves of the earth." And, as we reported on the third chapter of Matthew from Josephus's 18th book of *Antiquities*,
<margin>Josephus.</margin>
before the coming of Christ, there lived in the desert of Judea a college of Essenes, segregated from the rest of the people in small cells: namely, abstaining from marriage and using the most sparing food—finally, by the same institution by which the Christian <term>Anchorites</term> <note>Hermits or religious recluses.</note> live with miraculous holiness. Among whom it is said John the Baptist was nourished. ¶ And when we happen upon this divine man, who, looking upon him, would dare to snarl against religious orders? For this Precursor of the Lord, holy before he was

<column-break/>

born, did not attempt to preach that the kingdom of heaven was approaching in any other way than as one removed from human company; and by the dread of his clothing and diet, he warned us more significantly than by word of that life of the penitent, which the founders of monks have busied themselves to imitate according to their strength. Moreover, concerning the Apostles, the narrowness of space does not allow me to say how they received the first seeds from their master and laid the first foundations of the cenobitic life. Others have done so, among whom Thomas Walden,
<margin>Thomas Walden.</margin>
<note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), an English Carmelite who wrote extensively against the Wycliffite and Lollard movements.</note> in the 2nd and 5th volumes of his work *On Sacramentals* against Wycliffe, has most richly expanded this argument. For my part, however, the intention was only to clarify the matter summarily in the scholastic style.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**TO the first argument**, therefore, it is responded that the name "religion" in its common and vulgar meaning encompasses all mortals, and especially Christians, insofar as they worship God through the duties of virtues according to the precepts of the law. But truly, <term>by antonomasia</term> <note>A rhetorical term meaning a title used as a proper name, or "by excellence."</note> it is attributed to those who, beyond the cultivation of the precepts, take up the state of the counsels. Whether "religion" is said to come from *binding again* <note original: "religando"></note>, as Augustine says in *On True Religion*—namely, because beyond the bond of the precepts, they bind themselves more tightly—
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
or whether, as seemed right to
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
Cicero in the 2nd book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, the religious are so called from *re-reading* or *re-tracing* <note original: "relegando"></note>, as those who retract and, as it were, re-read all things pertaining to the worship of God. Priests, however, are called by this same name—namely "priests" <note original: "sacerdotum"></note>, which we shall speak of again in the following book—through a similar *antonomasia*: because among Christians who, in their own way, sacrifice themselves and their possessions to God, priests properly offer sacrifices. Therefore, the ancient Fathers were not afraid to call the religion of monks "perfect," as can be seen in Walden, volume 5, chapter 83. ¶ To the second argument,
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
Augustine responded excellently in the book *On the Perfection of Justice* that the perfection of charity is commanded to us in this life absolutely and universally; so much so that under that general precept, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," the love of the Fatherland <note>Meaning Heaven, the true homeland of the soul.</note> is also encompassed. Indeed, just as in hell one never ceases from the hatred of God (which is a sin even there, though it is not a demerit for greater punishment), so also in the Fatherland, where one never ceases from the love of God, the mandate of love is obeyed: even if the merit of glory is not increased. ¶ From this assertion of Augustine, however, Luther elicited that 
<margin>Luther's pestiferous dogma.</margin>
delirious dogma of his: "That no one in this life is able to fulfill the commandment of love." From

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

...from which he again inferred that since we are bound to perform every single work according to the standard of the same mandate, we sin in every work of every virtue. For such was the nature of that man’s <note>Referring to Martin Luther.</note> intellect, that he would say contradictory things everywhere. He could not, being blind, see how he could say that God obliges us to the impossible; which, according to the 
<margin>Jerome</margin> 
opinion of Jerome, is an impious assertion, as we have demonstrated at great length in Book 3, *On Nature and Grace*, Chapter 4. Therefore, Augustine clearly explains himself there, where he distinguishes a twofold perfection of <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitas"; in this context, the supreme love for God and neighbor.</note>: namely, that of the **way** and that of the **homeland**. For by the charity of the **way**, we strive toward that which belongs to the **homeland** <note>The "way" (*via*) refers to our earthly life as pilgrims, while the "homeland" (*patria*) refers to heaven.</note>. Wherefore, the perfection of this life of ours is to run straight toward the prize, as Paul says. The perfection of the homeland, however, is to rest in God Himself. And thus, in this life, we fulfill the precept as travelers, so that "with all your heart" means to conceive nothing in the mind's assent that is contrary to charity. But in the homeland, as those who have attained the goal, "with all your heart" means to love so continually that we never relax any of the fervor of love, even through the smallest negligence. Indeed, not only can the fulfillment of the mandate of charity exist in this life (which, for beginners, involves some struggle with fear), but also **perfect charity**, which, according to John, casts out fear. For as he himself says in the First Canonical Epistle, Chapter 2: "He who keeps His word, truly in him the charity of God is perfected." And Christ admonishes us to be perfect, even as His Father is. 
<margin>Paul</margin> 
And Paul in 2 Corinthians 13 says: "Finally, brothers, rejoice, be perfect." In short, to satisfy the Lutherans, not only Augustine but also Paul, in Philippians 3, clearly distinguished both degrees of perfection—namely, of the way and of the homeland. For he says first: "Not that I have already attained, or am already perfect," referring to the perfection of those who triumph in heaven. "But I follow after, if I may somehow lay hold." Therefore, the perfection of the way is to "follow after"; regarding which he immediately adds: "Let us, therefore, as many as are perfect, be of this mind." Thus, in 1 Corinthians 13, he was speaking of the perfection of the homeland, through which those things that belong to the "way" of faith will be emptied away. James, however, understands that even the perfect on the "way" offend in many <term>venial</term> <note>Minor or pardonable sins that do not destroy the relationship with God.</note> ways, which are not contrary to charity.
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the other point regarding Colossians 3, it has already been conceded that perfection indeed consists in charity. However, it exists in the <term>counsels</term> <note>The "evangelical counsels" of poverty, chastity, and obedience.</note> as if in instruments. To the third argument, satisfaction has been given through the second conclusion: namely, that in those two mandates, as if in the things that preserve them, the same perfection is situated.

## ARTICLE II.

### Whether poverty even to the point of begging belongs to the perfection of monastic life.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap "P" containing a woodcut scene of figures in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
AFTER we have spoken in general about the perfection of the communal religious institution, is it not fitting that I should apply some discussion to each of the three vows? And first, it is asked concerning **poverty**, whether it is fitting even to the point of <term>mendicancy</term> <note>The practice of begging for alms as a religious discipline.</note>. For the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 8 seems to set a limit on the almsgiving of Christians. "If the will is ready," he says, "it is accepted according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. For it is not intended that others should be eased and you burdened, but as a matter of equality." Here he encourages the followers of Christ to give alms in such a way that he simultaneously warns them not to weigh themselves down with the trouble of poverty.
<margin>Gloss</margin>
And the <term>gloss</term> <note>A standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> upon that passage in 1 Timothy 6—"Having food and wherewithal to be covered"—says that these temporal things are not to be cast away.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, he who exposes himself to the danger of impatience is in fault; but he who drives himself into begging undergoes such a danger: therefore, that is not a virtue. The second premise is proved by many testimonies. For the Wise Man says in Proverbs 30: "Give me neither begging nor riches; give me only the necessaries of life, lest perhaps being compelled by want, I should steal and forswear the name of my God." And in Ecclesiasticus 27: "Through poverty many have sinned."
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
And the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in the 4th book of *Ethics* says: "The corruption of riches seems to be a certain ruin of the man himself, since man lives by riches."
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, virtue—as stated in the 2nd book of *Ethics*—consists in the **mean**, but begging is an extreme. Especially because riches are instruments of happiness, as the Philosopher is the author in the 1st book of *Ethics*, with whom Ecclesiasticus in chapter 31 agrees. Therefore, begging is an adversary rather than a nurse of perfection.
<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourthly: let it be granted that it is a counsel to cast away all personal property entirely; yet it does not immediately follow from this that one is permitted to beg. Instead, monks are then bound to work with their hands, just as Paul in 1 Corinthians 4 testifies that he did; and in Acts 20, he says: "These hands have ministered to those things which were necessary for me." And in 2 Thessalonians 3: "If any man will not work, neither let him eat."

### Book Eight. Question V.

<margin>Argument 5.</margin>
¶ Fifthly, if all these other things were to cease, it would be more conducive to the quiet of monks to possess at least something in common, rather than wandering about among secular people seeking a living. ¶ Finally, there is the fact that bishops are of a higher rank and kind than <term>cenobites</term> <note>monks who live in a community</note>: yet <term>mendicancy</term> <note>the practice of begging for a living</note> does not suit their state of perfection. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the word of Christ in Matthew 5: *Blessed are the poor in spirit*: where the Greek text has, *Blessed are the beggars*. <note>The Greek word "ptochos" used in the Gospel of Matthew literally translates to a beggar or someone who is destitute, rather than just "poor."</note>

Although it was asserted in the previous sections that poverty serves the perfection of **charity**, it remains to be known at what level it should be embraced. For you may find two kinds of poverty among practitioners of religion: for some are fourfold, whose original institution was **mendicancy**, that is, so that nothing is possessed either privately by any monk, nor in common by the whole monastery: but they lived on daily alms, whether offered to them or sought and requested. As to which of these two modes of poverty is to be preferred to the other, there is no lack of those who debate it. Indeed, there have not been lacking heretics who would refute both. 

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ The response is therefore given in three conclusions. **First.** All-encompassing mendicancy—namely, that nothing be possessed either privately or in common—if considered in its own nature, has more dignity and merit before God than possession in common. 

<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The first reason for this conclusion proceeds from the nature of things, as was said above: for the institution of the monastic religion is to embrace that discipline through which one may more expeditiously ascend to the perfection of **charity**. But the first thing that baits the fascinated souls of men toward the love of itself is the possession of things. For since all things obey money, he who loves it desires all things through it; and he who casts it away easily cuts off from himself all worldly affections, in a certain manner. 

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Hence **Augustine** says in his *Book of Eighty-Three Questions*: "The nourishment of charity is the lessening of desire; perfection is no desire." It would therefore be safer never to have fixed one's love in this slippery nature of things. Yet, according to him, there is another step: to tear the soul away from things even while they are possessed; which is by far more difficult. 

Wherefore the same **Augustine** says to Paulinus and Therasia: "Earthly things," he says, "are loved more tightly when acquired than when merely desired." For that reason, that young man in the Gospel departed sad because he had great riches. For it is one thing to be unwilling to incorporate things which are lacking, and another to tear away what is already incorporated. Those

<column-break/>

things are rejected like strangers, but these are cut off like limbs. Not without thought, therefore, did our Lawgiver <note>Referring to Christ.</note> begin his law-bearing sermon from there: *Blessed are the poor in spirit.* For this reason, even if no other praise were found in holy poverty, this would be the most excellent: that the first word with which God opened his mouth when about to give the law to the world was to place happiness in poverty itself. 

<margin>Mendicancy is commended in the sacred scriptures.</margin>
¶ That this poverty, even unto mendicancy and nakedness, is commendable for the students of Christ, **Paul** magnificently emphasizes in his second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 8: *For you know,* he says, *the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might be rich.* If therefore, as we said above, He performed no duty which was not honorable by the nature of the thing, it is a counsel for the rich that, distributing their goods to the poor, they should become destitute so that they may enjoy celestial riches. 

¶ There is also the example of the same Savior, who is read to have possessed nothing except what was provided to him for the day and for his family. Hence in Matthew 8, He says: *The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.* There is also His institution in Matthew 19: *Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.* See how He strips of all things the one who desires to be perfect. Wherefore, to the Apostles, whom He wished to be the light of the world and the salt of the earth, He said: *Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts.*

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ But indeed, because of the quibble of the fourth argument, a second conclusion is subjoined. **Religious who have renounced their own property are not bound to seek a living by the labor of their hands, but can most justly beg.** 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
This is the conclusion about which **St. Augustine** wrote a whole volume titled *On the Work of Monks*; 

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
which **St. Thomas** subsequently elucidated most richly and eloquently against the enemies of religious orders in his *Opusculum 19, chapter 5*. 

<margin>Gloss.</margin>
For the **Gloss** on the fifth chapter of Exodus graphically compares those heretics who drive monks into manual labor with Pharaoh, who rebuked Moses and Aaron, saying: *Why do you distract the people from their works? Go to your burdens.* 

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is therefore proved by natural law, the law of nations, and especially by divine law. The end of spiritual goods is more excellent than temporal ones: but in a republic, soldiers and knights, and even judges who are for the conduct of wars, or... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the next page.</note>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Those who are appointed to protect justice, or finally to administer the state, are supported by the common stipends of the people. Paul, in Romans 13, considers this just even by divine law: *For this reason,* he says, *you pay taxes: for they are God's ministers.* <note>original: "Ministri enim Dei sunt." Soto is arguing that just as civil servants are paid via taxes, spiritual "servants" deserve support.</note> However, the religious who live the monastic life serve the state through their spiritual function, which is much more necessary to the state than the administration of temporal affairs. Therefore, it is nothing other than the law of nature, the law of nations, and divine law that they should be supported by the alms of the people. For those who devote themselves to the ministry of the word are worthy of their reward; for the sake of their studies, they must be exempt from manual labor. Regarding these men, Paul in 1 Corinthians 9 gathers several examples taken from nature to conclude that those who sow spiritual things have the right to reap temporal things. *For so,* he says, *the Lord ordained that those who preach the Gospel should live from the Gospel.* Here, the <term>Gloss</term> <note>The "Ordinary Gloss" was a standard collection of medieval biblical commentaries used by scholars like Soto.</note> says: God reasonably arranged this for preachers so that they might be more free to preach. Indeed, Christ himself explained this in Matthew 10. For he sent his disciples out to preach without a purse for the reason that *the laborer is worthy of his food.* And even when they have not taken up this specific duty <note>the duty of preaching</note>—which is nevertheless the formal mission of the <term>mendicant orders</term> <note>Religious orders like the Dominicans and Franciscans who relied on alms.</note>—they are still occupied with hearing sacramental confessions. Indeed, even if these duties cease, because they solemnly perform the appointed Psalms and pour out constant prayers for the people, and above all else, they devote themselves to the study of sacred things and divine contemplation, they have a divine and natural right to live on the support of the people. Hence, Augustine says in the work cited: *If they are Evangelists,* he says, *they have the power to live at the expense of the faithful; if they are ministers of the altar, they do not merely claim this power, but plainly demand it for themselves.* Furthermore, the Apostle himself in the place cited does not restrict the matter to a specific office, but says in general: *Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat what is of the temple? And those who serve at the altar share in the altar?* Thus it happens that those who strive to entangle monastic religious in the anxieties of manual labor are following the opinion of Martha, who tried to pull her sister away from sitting at the feet of Christ enjoying contemplation so that she might help her. Christ himself refuted this opinion, saying: *Furthermore, one thing is necessary.* <note>Referencing the story of Mary and Martha in Luke 10:42; Mary represents the contemplative life, Martha the active life.</note> Because of this, 
<margin>Gloss.</margin>
the <term>Gloss</term> rightly attributes that passage of Matthew 6—*Look at the birds of the air, they do not labor, etc.*—to the saints who are free for contemplation. They have been carried so far upward from the world that, doing nothing and laboring at nothing on earth, they dwell in heaven through contemplation alone. Rightly, there-

<column-break/>

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
-fore, Jerome in his prologue to Job rebukes those who would prefer monks to weave baskets from reeds or fold palm leaves so that they might eat bread in the sweat of their brow, rather than, according to the Savior's sentence, working for the *food of the divine which does not perish.* <note>original: "cibum... qui non perit" (John 6:27).</note> Finally, it is added that <term>mendicancy</term> <note>the act of begging for alms</note> contributes in no small measure to humility; for this reason, praise is given to <term>Saint Alexius</term> <note>A 5th-century saint who abandoned his wealthy family to live as a beggar.</note> and other saints because they renounced splendid wealth to live on begged alms. It is therefore an act of impiety to attack holy mendicancy, and it is a duty of extraordinary charity to nourish monastic mendicants. ¶ **Third conclusion.** 
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Although mendicancy of every kind is to be preferred in its own nature, it can nonetheless—by reason of the goal and other circumstances of time and place—be more beneficial to possess in common those things necessary for the monks' livelihood. This is a conclusion gathered from Saint Thomas 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Aquinas, in the *Summa Theologiae* 2.2, Question 188, Article 7. First of all, such possession does not detract from the perfection of religion, as is clear from the <term>canon</term> <note>church law</note> *Expedit* (12, q. 1) and from what was said above. For we have shown that perfection is not situated in poverty, but in **charity**. Since, therefore, poverty only consists in that 
<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
reason of cutting off the love and anxiety for things, that species of poverty is more excellent in each religious order which contributes more aptly to its goal. For just as a tool or a medicine is not better because it is larger, but because it is more suited to its end, so it must be judged regarding poverty. Hence, if an order is instituted for works of contemplation and preaching—a task which requires deep mental quiet—and times exist when the people do not easily help the poverty of the religious, it not only does not contradict perfection to have something in common, but it actually contributes to it. For that wandering about by monks which is necessary to seek a living does not allow for the leisure that is worthwhile for exercising such spiritual duties. ¶ Secondly, from the same harshness of the times, 
<margin>Second reason.</margin>
another advantage for such possession in common can arise. Specifically, that after charity has grown cold, mendicants become a nuisance and a burden to the people. By this reasoning, religion begins to be cheapened in their eyes. Moreover, excessive destitution might force the beggars to handle some business with secular people, and sometimes to extort a living through certain dishonesties, which overshadows their religious institutes.

<summary>Soto defends the right of monks to be supported by the public as "spiritual workers" while arguing that, when public charity fails, holding property in common is a practical and holy necessity to protect the order's spiritual mission.</summary>

# Book Eight. Question V. 689

<margin>Third point.</margin>
¶ Add to this that when religious orders were first established in that sincere state of begging, many factors supported their founding which we have seen fading for some time now. For first, they were content with the greatest scarcity of food and the lowliest of clothing. Thus, the alms which now scarcely suffice for twenty religious were then enough for more than a hundred. This is because the nature of the body has become weaker, and spiritual strength has slackened. For we read in the history of our holy father Dominic <note>Saint Dominic (1170–1221), founder of the Dominican Order, to which the author, Soto, belonged.</note> that he once rebuked the steward for providing a **pittance** <note>original: "pitanciam." In a monastic context, a pittance was an extra portion of food, such as eggs or fish, added to the basic vegetarian diet.</note> to the community more often than was proper. This is proof that the use of eggs or fish was indeed very rare for the brothers, but they lived on legumes. Furthermore, the charity of the people was then more abundant and more sincere. And—what we monks cannot admit without shame—our life then possessed a splendor different from what it has now, which served to attract the hearts of the common people.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But you say: The possession of things cannot fail to preoccupy the minds of those who possess them, both regarding their cultivation and their increase.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
We certainly admit this. Nevertheless, we must weigh which anxiety more bitterly tortures and distracts the mind: searching daily for necessities, or caring for what is possessed in common. For the anxiety of possessions, except for one or two people who manage them, either does not touch the rest at all or touches them only very slightly; however, the daily anxiety of finding food occupies many. If we wish to take an example from Christ our teacher, although, as has been said, he chose a life of poverty, he nonetheless reserved alms offered to him for the day. For he had money bags entrusted to Judas. For in John 4, it says that the disciples went into the city to buy food. And in John 13, Judas was ordered to buy those things which were needed for the feast day. However, he did not allow anything to be kept except small and temporary coins. For this reason, the disciples lacked the money to buy bread to satisfy the crowd. And so that those things which were kept only for food and for the support of the poor would not be turned to secular uses, he did not wish for the tax to be paid from them, but sent Peter to the fish to bring him the **didrachma** <note>original: "didrachma." A Greek silver coin worth two drachmas, used for the Temple tax. See Matthew 17:24-27.</note> from its mouth. And sometimes, due to poverty, he sent those same disciples to gather ears of grain.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Let it be far from me, then, to bark against every form of begging, especially since I have illustrated its merits above. For there were formerly some whom Saint Thomas persists in refuting in his *Opusculum* 18, chapter 14, who rejected poverty unless necessities were held in

<column-break/>

common. To agree with them, I consider an error. Indeed, those who sincerely and purely observe supreme mendicancy are to be looked up to and embraced. Yet these things have been said both so that the cause of those possessing things in common may be defended, and so that I may have all those who beg warned about how much scarcity they ought to be content with. For this reason, as Christ asserted, God feeds the birds of the air—to which the religious are certainly compared—and clothes the lilies of the field; for the former are content with the simplest food, and the latter with the simplest clothing. Furthermore, then, Saint Benedict <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), the father of Western monasticism.</note>, studying the quiet of those contemplating on high, deliberately accepted possessions offered to him, and other founders of religious orders did so thereafter. But nonetheless, the human mind, which knows not how to hold the middle ground, increased their wealth to such an extent that it cast down that most famous order not a little from its high standing. Therefore, in our order [the Dominicans], it has not been permitted to hold possessions until now except for the sake of study; but there are many monasteries in which life is lived in the ancient state of begging. Would that God might sustain us, as much as this is especially necessary for the Christian family in this age.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that in that passage Paul in no way condemns a person if they wish to distribute everything they have to the poor, but he is indulging human weakness. For those who take up this arduous counsel are very rare. And therefore he says he compels no one to consult the miseries of others in such a way that they deprive themselves of necessities. And the cited **Gloss** <note>A standard medieval biblical commentary.</note> on Timothy pertains to the same point: namely, that temporal things are not to be entirely cast away.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is replied that he who voluntarily abandons temporal goods for the sake of Christ exposes himself to no danger, neither temporal nor spiritual. I say "spiritual" because what a person does of their own will for a good cause brings no danger of regret or sadness; that only happens when someone is stripped of their goods against their will. On the contrary, a more present danger looms from the possession of riches, according to that passage in 1 Timothy, the last chapter: *Those who wish to become rich fall into the snare of the devil.* Nor are they truly subjected to bodily danger. For as the Psalmist says: *The rich have felt want and hunger, but those seeking the Lord shall not be diminished of any good.* For He who forbids us to be anxious for tomorrow takes care of us. Solomon, however, sensing his own temperament, did not dare to commit himself to extreme poverty; and for that reason, he asked for a middle-way of life. For even if, as we said above, of wealth...

# Fray Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law,

Though abundance may be harmful to a man of corrupt nature, there are few who can endure extreme need. Just as with the sick, even if they see that wine is harmful to them, they nonetheless cannot always restrain themselves from taking a small taste. For this reason, many have fallen into sin because of poverty. Furthermore, Solomon was a king; for this reason, he could not live without wealth. <margin>To the third point.</margin> ¶ To the third argument, the response is that the "mean" of virtue, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, specifically in Book 2 of the *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> in the second book of the *Ethics*, is to be determined not by quantity, but by reason. Therefore, whatever is done according to the prescription of reason does not deviate from that mean. Reason teaches that one should leave behind temporal goods so as to follow Christ more readily. For even Socrates, as Saint Jerome <margin>Jerome.</margin> says in his letter to Paulinus, was taught by the light of nature to cast away a weight of gold so that he might devote himself more freely to contemplation. <margin>To the fourth. Saint Thomas.</margin> ¶ To the fourth argument, Saint Thomas responds in the *Summa Theologiae* (2.2.q.187.art.3) <gloss>that</gloss> manual labor—a term which encompasses all human duties, <margin>Manual labor is useful for four things.</margin> whether performed with the hands, feet, or tongue, because the hand is the most excellent of the organs—is useful for four things. First, to seek a livelihood. Thus, the first man was commanded to eat his bread in the sweat of his brow; and in the Psalm it says, "For you shall eat the labors of your hands." Second, it is convenient for avoiding idleness, which is the cause of many evils. Hence the Book of Sirach <note>Soto cites this as "Ecclesiastes" or "Ecclesia," referring to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 33:28.</note> says: "Send your servant to work, lest he be idle: for idleness has taught much malice." Third, it is directed toward restraining concupiscence <term>concupiscence: the disordered desire for worldly or carnal pleasures</term>, insofar as the body is worn down by labor. Thus, in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 6: "In labors, in watchings, in fasting, in chastity." Fourth, labor is fruitful for the distribution of alms. Hence, in Ephesians 4: "He who stole, let him steal no longer; but rather let him labor, working with his hands what is good, that he may have something to give to him who is in need." Therefore, through these four categories, a response is given to all those passages where Paul seems either to command or commend manual labor. For that cited passage in the second letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 3—"If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat"—is nothing but a natural admonition: namely, that he who has no other source of livelihood should seek his food by his hands, so that he may carefully avoid theft and illicit business. In this very sense, we cited the letter to the Ephesians just now. However, this truth does not prevent the religious who are occupied with divine matters from having the right to live on alms. For the Apostle teaches this very thing in the same passage. For after he said that he did not eat anyone’s bread for free,

<column-break/>

but worked in labor and fatigue so as not to be a burden to any of them, he adds: "Not as if we did not have the power, but so that we might give ourselves as a model for you to imitate." Therefore, that passage in the first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4—"Work with your hands, as we commanded you"—is not a general commandment that involves even monks, as the attackers of religious life claim; rather, it only involves those who cannot otherwise live without scandal. This is clear from the following words: "that you may walk honestly toward those who are outside." Religious, however, can receive and request charity without scandal. ¶ There is also the second utility of bodily labor, and subsequently the third: namely, the avoidance of idleness and the affliction of the body. This is not a commandment except when those same troubles cannot be met in any other way. Monks, however, avoid idleness and subdue the body through other salutary exercises. Finally, the fourth point: namely, distributing alms, is not a required virtue in the religious, as they have already given everything away at once. This is unless there is a case of extreme necessity among the poor, in which event they would be bound to labor with their hands just like laypeople. These are roughly the points made by Saint Thomas in the place cited. <margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ Finally, to the fifth argument, a response has been given in the third conclusion.

### Question V of the Eighth Book

<margin>Fourthly.</margin>
...a vow of this kind is not part of the intrinsic nature of the religious life <note>Latin: *religionis*. In this context, "religion" refers specifically to the "religious life" or "consecrated life" of monks, friars, and nuns.</note>. ¶ Fourthly and finally, it is argued: All perfection of the Christian life began to be practiced by the Apostles according to Christ's example. But the Apostles do not seem to have observed continence, for we read in Matthew 8 that Peter, the Vicar of Christ, had a mother-in-law; therefore, chastity is not part of the intrinsic nature of the religious life. ¶ On the contrary stands the wording of the chapter cited above, *Cum ad monasterium* (regarding the state of monks), at the end of which it is stated: "The renunciation of property, as well as the preservation of chastity, is so annexed to the monastic rule that even the Supreme Pontiff cannot grant a dispensation against it."

<margin>The twofold sense of the question.</margin>
This question has two senses. The first is whether, in truth, the vow of chastity is currently annexed to the religious life, and most fittingly so. The affirmative conclusion to this is a definition of the Church against heretics, as found in the chapter *Quod votum* (regarding vows) in Book 6. For there was Jovinian <note>Jovinian (died c. 405) was an opponent of Christian asceticism who argued that virgins, widows, and married women, once baptized, had equal merit.</note>, who made marriage equal to celibacy; he was condemned for this heresy just as Vigilantius was for another, namely, for equating riches with poverty. The second sense, however, is whether—since the "solemnity" of the vow (that is, the ceremony of profession) is a matter of ecclesiastical law, as is reported there—the annexation of chastity to the religious life is likewise a matter of ecclesiastical law. If so, the Church could make it possible for the religious life to remain a "true" religious life without chastity. Or, on the other hand, is it a matter of divine law, such that the substance of the religious life cannot be established by the Church without chastity? ¶ But since our only intention is to debate this second sense with fellow Catholics (because the first sense is orthodox and thus doubted by none but heretics), the answer is given in a single conclusion, offered under a degree of probability that seems to me to be the highest.

<margin>The responsive conclusion.</margin>
Chastity is so annexed to the religious life that it cannot be brought about by any human dispensation that the religious life could truly exist according to its name without chastity. Therefore, we are not debating here whether the Pope has the power to dispense from the solemn vow of religion—that is, whether he can release a professed person from their religious order, a matter sufficiently discussed in the preceding question. Rather, we deny only this for the present, under the judgment of more learned men: that a person truly persisting as an evangelical monk could remain in marriage and its use. And indeed, this is the conclusion <margin>St. Thomas. Scotus.</margin> of Saint Thomas, as we saw in Question 4. It appears, however, that Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (1266–1308), a major Scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> denies it in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, distinction 38). There, he feels the only reason a solemn vow of religion voids a marriage is because the Church, in

<column-break/>

whose hands the person making the vow has placed themselves, has rendered that person illegitimate for marriage. <margin>Cajetan.</margin> Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> uses similar words in his commentary on the *Summa* (2-2, Question 88, Article 7), as we have seen in Question 3. From this, it seems to be inferred that it lies within the power of the Church to allow religious to retain their religious state alongside marriage, just as a priest retains his holy orders. Nevertheless, our <margin>First proof of the conclusion.</margin> contrary conclusion seems clearly asserted by Pope Innocent III in the cited chapter, *Cum ad monasterium*. Truly, he there implies that chastity is annexed to the religious life by divine law. And he proves that <margin>Second proof.</margin> this is so by reason. The word "Religion" in its very name signifies nothing else than what Christ taught the evangelical young man: "If you wish to be perfect, go and sell [what you have], etc., and follow me." And what Peter subsequently added: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you," etc. But one who has once bound himself in the knot of marriage may be called so by name, but in reality, he has not left all things; indeed, he has not even left the world. Therefore, he is not a true evangelical religious. This middle proposition is proven by the reasoning of Saint Thomas (2-2, Question 186, Article 4). For the <margin>The affairs of a wife conflict diametrically with the religious life.</margin> state of marriage, from two sides, conflicts diametrically with the religious life. First, it pushes against contemplation and the meditation on divine things, to which a religious, according to his very name, ought to be diligently devoted. It resists, I say, because of the "vehemence of pleasure" that arises from Venus <note>A common classical metaphor for sexual activity.</note>; by the frequent practice of which, concupiscence <note>Unordered desire or lust.</note> is increased, as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle warns in the third book of the *Ethics*. Whence Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin> says in the first book of the *Soliloquies*: "I feel," he says, "that nothing more effectively casts down the manly mind from its height than the blandishments of a woman, and that contact of bodies without which a wife cannot be had." ¶ Nor is the natural reason for this very hidden. For since contemplation is nourished by the most subtle and pure spirits, and that carnal and brutal use consumes a multitude of spirits and violently draws the blood away from the heart (the gathering of which is necessary for the attention of the mind), it follows that the same use effects a dullness of the mind. For this very reason, Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 advised spouses to separate from the bed during a time of prayer. ¶ On the other "horn," the married state struggles against the religious life because of the administration and anxiety of household affairs. Whence Paul says in the same place: "He who is without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but he who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife; and he is divided." Here, if you attend more meditatively, he has expressed the face of the religious life to the life, and placed it in direct opposition...

<summary>Soto argues that chastity is an essential, divinely-mandated requirement for the religious life, asserting that the distractions of marriage and physical pleasure are fundamentally incompatible with a monk's duty of contemplation.</summary>
