<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Therefore, monks—that is, the "solitary" <note>Latin: *monachi*, from the Greek *monachos* meaning "single" or "solitary."</note>—derive their name primarily from the fact that they live apart from the companionship of marriage. ¶ Second, this is explained more clearly: The other two vows, namely poverty and obedience, are so dependent upon the vow of chastity that if you remove the latter, you immediately undermine the others. Indeed, the "baggage" of marriage <note>Latin: *matrimonialis sarcina*</note> utterly rejects a vow of legitimate poverty. For how can a man support a wife, children, and the household that comes with them while living in poverty? This is especially true because he must not only provide for his children for the present but must look toward the future, seeking possessions and rights of primogeniture <term>primogeniture: the right of the firstborn son to inherit the entire family estate</term> to leave to them. Add to this that a married man cannot be free for that legitimate obedience of which Christ said, "Follow me." For this reason, Paul specifically desired the followers of Christ to remain as he was: without a wife. Therefore, if the Church were to separate the vow of chastity from religious orders, it would fundamentally destroy the very evangelical sincerity of those orders. Therefore, to speak according to the Church's judgment, such a separation is certainly not feasible.

¶ From this, we can gather the distinguishing mark by which we judge whether any "religion" <note>In this context, *religio* refers to a specific religious order or the state of being a monk/nun.</note> is truly and absolutely called a "religion." The sole criterion is whether it intrinsically includes the power to annul a marriage already contracted—or rather, a marriage *attempted*. No religious order possesses this power except by the authority of the Church, which establishes the "solemnity" of the vow <term>solemn vow: a formal, public vow recognized by the Church that creates a legal barrier to marriage, rendering any attempted marriage invalid</term>, as found in the cited chapter of the Book of Six.

¶ For this reason, the religious of the Third Order of Saint Francis, and of our own order <note>Soto was a Dominican, referring here to the Dominican Third Order</note>, do not take a solemn vow, even though they may say quite expressly and repeatedly that they make three vows. I say this regarding the ancient law; however, Pope Sixtus IV has since declared through his Bull <term>Bull: a formal proclamation or decree issued by a Pope</term> that brothers of this kind do make a solemn vow. Later, other Supreme Pontiffs decreed the same regarding certain of our holy women of that same order, whom we call *Beatas* <note>Latin: *Beatas*, referring to "Blessed women" or Beguines who lived a semi-monastic life</note>, who live in enclosure. However, those who do not observe enclosure are not subject to that same Bull. Much less are those hermits who, in our time, live scattered throughout the mountains. For even if they promise obedience to a bishop, they only intend it for the time they wish to remain there. Indeed, it is not even part of the nature of their institute that they take a simple vow of chastity, although they should not be admitted without it.

Regarding the first of the main arguments, he concedes that the solemnity of the vow, as 

<column-break/>

contained in the cited chapter of the Book of Six, is established by the Church. It is the Church that institutes and approves this or that religious order, from which the legal impediment to marriage follows. But in the very next question, the conclusion is denied that would suggest the connection between chastity and the religious vow is not a matter of divine law <note>Latin: *ius divinum*</note>. For it is within the power of the Church to decide that *this* or *that* group counts as a "religion"; however, once a "religion" is established, it is a matter of divine law that it has chastity annexed to it, according to the command: "Go and sell all that you have, and follow me." For no one can hold the state of following Christ via the "counsels" <term>Evangelical Counsels: the three recommendations of Christ—poverty, chastity, and obedience—for those seeking perfection</term> unless he is free from a wife; and this arises from the very inner nature of the thing.

¶ Regarding the second point, it is answered that the priestly order <note>Latin: *sacerdotalem ordinem*</note> is in no way a "religion" in the monastic sense. Otherwise, the cited Canon and the Doctors of the Church would not have explained the solemn vow under two distinct forms, saying it consists both in the reception of Holy Orders and in the profession of a religious order. From this, it follows that there is a difference between the priesthood and the religious life, as Saint Thomas teaches in the cited passage (article 11): the vow of chastity is not part of the intrinsic nature of the priesthood in the same way it is for the religious life. Indeed, the priestly ministry can be preserved without that same vow. For this reason, a man being initiated into Holy Orders does not expressly say "I vow," as a monk does. Therefore, it is not an explicit vow, but an implicit one, added during the reception of orders. I say it is a vow *only* of chastity. For he does not make the other vows of the religious life even implicitly. He does not vow poverty or obedience, though he becomes a subject of his bishop—even if the bishop is absent—rather than a subject of the one who ordained him.

<margin>Second corollary.</margin>

It follows secondly that the Roman Church could remove this same vow while keeping the essence of the priesthood intact. Therefore, the argument used to prove that a religious order could exist without such a vow is denied.

That is, it is only by a statute of the Church that priests are rendered "illegitimate" and "unfit" for contracting marriage.

# Question V of the Eighth Book

...of them: as we were arguing a little earlier. <margin>Solution.</margin> We respond, however, that it is not merely a precept [a command], but a statute that makes them incapable of marriage, just like close relatives. It stands, therefore, in a middle ground between a simple command and a solemn religious vow. For this reason, the Church could remove this vow from priests, just as it could remove the prohibition against marrying within the fourth degree [of kinship]. Whether this would be permitted, however, will be debated in the question immediately following this one.

¶ From this it follows that a ratified but not consummated marriage <term>ratified but not consummated: a marriage that has been legally and sacramentally entered into but where the couple has not yet had sexual intercourse</term> is not dissolved by the reception of holy orders, whereas it would be dissolved by making a religious profession [becoming a monk]. <margin>Cajetan.</margin> Cardinal Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> admits this in his first *Quodlibet*, question 12. The reason is that a priest is not simply rendered incapable of contracting another marriage in the same way a monk is, because a priest can be granted a dispensation [permission to marry].

<margin>Paludanus's opinion.</margin> ¶ While this is true, I do not know what Paludanus <note>Petrus Paludanus (c. 1275–1342), a Dominican theologian.</note> intended in his commentary on the *Sentences* [Book 4, distinction 38, question 3], where he says that if a man enters holy orders after a ratified but not consummated marriage, and the wife remaining in the secular world makes a simple vow, she is rendered incapable of a second marriage even after the man's death. <margin>Refutation of Paludanus.</margin> First of all, that reception of orders is not licit because it does not dissolve the marriage. Second, there is no appearance of reason why the wife's simple vow would become a solemn one in such a case, as he believes. Therefore, if she marries another after her husband dies, although she sins against her simple vow, the marriage nonetheless holds—which he denies.

<margin>A serious doubt concerning military orders.</margin> ¶ The third argument concerns military orders, which presents the most significant point of ambiguity here. For these "cross-bearing" knights <note>original: *cruciferi*</note> are commonly held to be "religious" [in the monastic sense]: for they make three vows. Nevertheless, they are joined to wives by the bond of marriage. Thus, both states—the religious life and marriage—can coexist. This can be supported by the reasoning deduced from the sections above. For the reason we showed earlier that marriage conflicts with religious life was that it was a hindrance to contemplation and prayer; however, the "religion" of soldiers does not have this as its goal, but rather military service, where no contemplation is necessary. 

<margin>Solution to the proposed question.</margin> Nevertheless, for the reasons cited above, I have never been able to be persuaded that such "religions" [orders] are simply and strictly "religious" orders. The reason is that they do not observe chastity—for they serve marital matters just like other laypeople, seeking the same honors and procuring the same wealth for their offspring. This is worlds apart from the religious institute. Furthermore, they profess neither poverty nor obedience, except in name 

<column-break/>

only. I am not, of course, speaking of the "cross-bearing" priests who live within the walls of monasteries. For there is no doubt regarding their legitimate religious status. I am speaking instead of the "commendatory" knights <term>commendatory: knights who held land or titles (commanderies) from the order but often lived in the world as nobles</term>. For what kind of poverty is it, I ask, merely to report their assets to a master—assets which, if he took even a penny from them, they would protest just like any other nobles of the kingdom? Their obedience, meanwhile, consists of hearing no command from a superior for almost their entire lives, except when their assemblies are held.

¶ But they say: "This is our religion [our rule], and we are bound to nothing else." To this we respond in two ways. First, we deny this if we look at their original founding. For at that time, they lived in a kind of enclosure; they performed duties of obedience much more frequently; and they had a far different standard of poverty. But over time, their orders have so decayed that they have now cast off the sincere nature of religious life. Therefore, secondly, we say that if their life is no stricter than this, it is not the "evangelical" life, which consists in the exercise of the [evangelical] counsels <note>The evangelical counsels are the three vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.</note>. Furthermore, if our order or that of Saint Francis (God forbid) were to collapse to the point where no more poverty, chastity, or obedience flourished, it would cease to be a "religion." I do not mean that wherever statutes are not observed, an order immediately ceases to be a religion—for perhaps through the neglect or fault of superiors, things considered bad go unpunished. But if a religious order were to sink to the point where no greater obedience, poverty, or chastity was required than among these kinds of knights, it would not be the evangelical religion of the counsels. 

And lest I seem to be the first to assert this opinion, you will find the same in Saint Thomas <margin>Saint Thomas.</margin> in the place cited (Summa Theologica, II-II, question 186, article 4). He argues in his third point that continence [chastity] is not required for the perfection of religious life, because there are some "religious" who have wives. He responds that those modes of living, where there is marital use, are not religions "simply and absolutely speaking," but only "in a certain respect" <note>original: *secundum quid*</note>—namely, insofar as they participate in some things belonging to the religious state. Thus says Saint Thomas. 

<margin>Limitation of the above assertion.</margin> ¶ From these military orders, therefore, I would rightly except the Knights of Saint John <note>Also known as the Knights Hospitaller, now the Knights of Malta.</note>; who indeed, according to their rule, maintain a community and a form of obedience, and do not contract marriages. Therefore, there is no reason why they should not be considered "religious."

<margin>Objection.</margin> ¶ But if you argue against the above assertion: if these knights [contract] a marriage bond without a papal privilege...

<margin>A two-part question long and much debated in Spain.</margin>
This question was two-fold. First: was it expedient to grant a dispensation <note>a "dispensation" is a formal exemption from a church law or vow</note> so that knights of this type <note>Soto is likely referring to the Spanish military orders like the Knights of Santiago or Calatrava</note> could take wives for themselves? Second: was it permissible to grant a dispensation even to those who had already uttered their vows solemnly? This second part was much more troublesome. 

<margin>Solution to the first part.</margin>
Regarding the first part, according to my own understanding, I have always judged such a dispensation to be expedient. If I considered such military orders to be "true" religious orders in the strict monastic sense, I would deem it impossible. However, the advantage of the dispensation is this: that chastity in an institution of that kind is—to speak in a human manner—not possible to preserve. For they live sumptuously and splendidly, having female servants at home and maintaining constant social interaction with courtly women abroad; they spend their time contemplating tournaments and other military exercises. By what reason, then, should they be bound by a vow of chastity? 

<margin>Solution to the second question.</margin>
For almost the same reason, the second question was solved in the affirmative. For since their vow is not a legitimate religious vow <note>in the sense of the "solemn" vows taken by a monk</note>, but a statute of the Pope that hinders marriage, a dispensation is not impossible if a legitimate cause exists, as was recently said regarding the vow of priests.

<margin>Regarding the fourth [argument].</margin>
¶ Regarding the fourth argument, which was asked concerning the Apostles—whether they took a vow of chastity—it will be more conveniently answered in the next question.

## ARTICLE IV.
### Whether the vow of obedience is of the essence of the religious state.

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
FINALLY, the third member of monastic profession is obedience. So that we may commend it in all its parts, it is argued in the usual fashion that it is not necessary. For those services most please God which are done from freedom, not from necessity, according to that passage in 2 Corinthians 9: *not from sadness or from necessity.* However, those things which are done out of a vow of obedience bring sadness along with necessity; 

<column-break/>

therefore, it is not an evangelical counsel <term>evangelical counsel: a recommendation by Jesus for those seeking spiritual perfection, rather than a command for all Christians</term> to vow obedience.

<margin>The second [argument].</margin>
Secondly: since God created man free, it is not prudent for him to abdicate his own freedom, except where God has commanded him to obey. In the Gospel, however, no such command for vowing obedience exists. For that which Paul commands in 

<margin>Paul, Hebrews 13.</margin>
Hebrews 13, saying: *Obey your leaders and submit to them,* pertains to all Christians. ¶ To this is added, thirdly, that Christ—as the same Apostle says in 

<margin>Third [argument], Romans 8.</margin>
Romans 8—has freed us from the law of sin and death, and by consequently earning us the adoption of sons, has gifted us with perfect liberty. From this, it appears to follow that Christian perfection consists in the highest freedom; and thus, the vow of obedience is not an evangelical counsel. ¶ To the contrary is the fact that perfection, as was said above, is achieved by following and imitating Christ. That which is chiefly commended in Him, as is clear in Philippians 2, is obedience. For *He was made obedient even unto death, because of which God also exalted Him,* etc.

OF THE THREE vows by which monastic life is constituted, the most powerful is obedience. For the renunciation of possessions and the vow of chastity are ordered toward this end: that we may be able to obey with the freest and most indissoluble service. Thus it happens that poverty, as we said above, is first in execution, but obedience is first in intention. Yet, while obedience is the most excellent of all duties, so—

<margin>Luther.</margin>
such is the nature of heretics—it was most cursed by Luther. Whence, in his book *On Monastic Vows* and in another *On Christian Freedom*, he attacks monastic obedience with every possible insult. For he says it stands in diametric opposition to Gospel liberty—inasmuch as all human mandates, and whatever can be observed in external ceremonies, were abolished by that same Gospel liberty. ¶ Nevertheless, despite the refusal of Luther and his master Wycliffe, the conclusion stands solid in its own truth, 

<margin>Conclusion and response.</margin>
unshaken by any wind of the heretics. The state of those in religious life, which is an evangelical counsel, requires obedience above all, which must be offered by a vow to a specific superior in the name of God. 

<margin>The reason for the conclusion. Part 2-2, Question 186, Article 5.</margin>
And the reason is manifest. For if perfection consists in following Christ while leaving all things behind, it is necessary, as Saint Thomas says in Part 2-2, Question 186, Article 5, to choose some superior who may direct the one vowing in the name of Christ, even by command (if necessary), so that he may fulfill what he promised to Christ.

He then begins a defense of the vow of obedience as the most essential of the three monastic vows, countering arguments by Martin Luther and John Wycliffe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's examination of the religious state, moving from the specific case of military orders to a broader theological defense of the vow of obedience. He specifically targets the "Lutheran error" regarding Christian liberty and the necessity of human hierarchy.</meta>

### Question V of the Eighth Book

<margin>Two roots of the Lutheran error.</margin>
...should fulfill it in good faith. ¶ But behold, here are the two roots of the Lutheran error. The first is that he does not admit that a vow undertaken voluntarily in a state of necessity passes into a command <note>original: "necessitate transire præcepti"; meaning once a vow is made freely, it becomes a binding law for that person</note>. For once this is granted, it is necessary that he who solemnly vows obedience be subject to someone by whom he may be lawfully compelled if the need arises. His second ignorance is that he thinks it is enough to obey Christ while neglecting any human authority. But he does not see how we humans cannot be governed by Christ, who is in heaven, except through other humans. For we lack a present leader who can act in God’s stead toward us in a human manner. ¶ But perhaps someone says: "Bishops and other ordinary prelates <note>A "prelate" is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot, who has jurisdiction</note> are enough." This, however, is denied. Indeed, through this, the clarity of this truth shines forth more brightly. For ordinary prelates are nothing but guardians of the laws, which is why they can compel no one except according to divine and human laws. Therefore, since vows are undertaken concerning **works of supererogation** <note>original: "operibus supererogatis"; these are "extra credit" pious acts not strictly required for salvation but performed for greater perfection</note>, it is necessary that he who vows must offer obedience either to the bishop individually (as was perhaps the custom in the primitive church) or to a specific superior (which is now considered more beneficial). This is so that he may be guided and compelled toward that which he is bound by his vow, even above those things commanded by the laws. Christ demonstrated this with the word cited above: *If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.* For to "deny oneself" is to deny one's own will, through which a man is a man. In truth, unless you hand over your will to another by a binding vow so that it is no longer in your power to reclaim it for yourself, this cannot be done.

<margin>The argument against Luther.</margin>
¶ Why then do we oppose Luther? For by that liberty of his, which he calls "evangelical," he intends to remove not only the superiors of monasteries but also all secular and ecclesiastical princes. For he proceeded to teach later that we have been liberated by Christ in such a way that He exempted us from all human power, so that we might serve Him alone. This kind of liberty should rather be called "Satanic" and—what is the same thing—"Lutheran." For if you remove from the commonwealth the hierarchical orders and all the acts of obedience which we perform for men at God’s command, and if you reserve all punishment of evildoers until the final Day of Judgment, then human morals—indeed, all things human—must immediately perish. For how many more people are there who cultivate virtues out of fear of punishment than out of love for honor? And besides this reasoning, which demonstrates the matter abundantly, the whole of Gospel scripture cries out against Luther’s impudence with open testimony. For elsewhere you hear: *Let every soul be subject to the higher powers.* Elsewhere: *Be subject to your superiors, even the harsh ones.* And Christ says: *He who hears you, hears me.* Indeed, the same Redeemer wished us to be so obedient to the word of our elders that he diligently warned us that even if those who sit upon the chair of Moses (that is, all our superiors) do things that we should not imitate, we should nevertheless fulfill what they command us without hesitation. However, it is unnecessary to dwell longer on this well-known argument.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, let it be responded to the first argument that the **necessity of coercion** <term>necessitas coactionis: being forced to do something against one's will</term>, which makes an act involuntary, does indeed produce sadness and excludes the possibility of praise and merit. However, that necessity which arises from a vow freely emitted for the sake of God, first of all, does not bring sadness. Furthermore, even if it occasionally gives birth to it, it nevertheless does not diminish merit, for the original liberty of vowing remains present in all the resulting virtuous actions.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that the liberty in which man was created by his own nature ought to serve us in this: that we may serve our Creator. Therefore, to dedicate that liberty to His service is not against nature, but is most especially according to nature.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third, it is responded that from the fact that Christ liberated us from the **law of sin**, it does not follow that Christian perfection consists in exemption from all obedience. Rather, it consists entirely in our being free from the shackles of sins. Since we are so dangerously compliant with our own minds and lovers of our own will, it contributes greatly to asserting that same liberty to submit our will to the steering of another. For if "to serve God is to reign," the more people we obey in His name, the more perfectly we reign. For we then more safely dominate the allurements and assaults of the flesh, and thus we reflect the **Heavenly Jerusalem**; where, just as those blessed ones are most firmly confirmed by a certain necessity so that they cannot sin, they likewise enjoy the highest liberty.

<summary>Soto defends the vow of religious obedience against Martin Luther, arguing that true Christian liberty is found in submitting one's will to human superiors as representatives of God, rather than in total independence.</summary>

# QUESTION SIX
## On the vow and continence of Priests.

### ARTICLE I.

#### Whether the vow of priestly continence was appropriate and necessary for the dignity and stability of the church.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'I' depicting a landscape with a large leafy tree in the foreground and clouds in the sky.</image-desc>Finally, at the end of this book, in which we have disputed concerning vows to the best of our ability, we have decided to add this final question regarding the continence <note>The state of abstaining from sexual relations</note> of priests. Specifically, this concerns the vow which, according to the institution of the Western Church, they implicitly undertake when they are initiated into holy orders. For indeed, among the various efforts of the Lutherans by which they strive to utterly demolish the Church of God, one is this: they contend with all their might to drive celibacy away from the clergy. For this reason, when I was acting on behalf of the Emperor in Germany and we were treating with them to establish peace, they persisted in holding stubbornly to this point: that priests should not only not be forbidden from the company of a wife, but rather should be compelled to marry. They consider it so impossible for a human being to live without the "use of Venus" <note>original: "Veneris vsu"; a classical euphemism for sexual intercourse</note>. If this were once granted to them, it could not happen otherwise than that this same concession would crawl through all of Christianity and root out and subvert the holy Church. For this reason, I would have left this treatise on vows incomplete if I had not added this question to it. 

Regarding this matter, as with any other, according to "the Philosopher" <note>A standard reference to Aristotle</note> in the *Posterior Analytics*, three things could be asked: namely, *if* it is, *what* it is, and *why* it is. As for *what* it is—namely, in what the priestly vow consists—we showed in the previous question: establishing it to be a vow that is not explicit but implicit; neither is it annexed to orders by its intrinsic nature (like the vow of a religious order), but rather it is a statute of the Church that renders a marriage void. Therefore, two articles remain here. The first is concerning the appropriateness of this ecclesiastical institution. For in moral matters, to ask "if it is" and "why it is" is the same thing. For that which is not appropriate to exist is superfluous. The second article is

<column-break/>

how ancient it is: namely, whether it was in use immediately from the very beginnings of the nascent Church.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
¶ The first question is argued in the negative. And first, indeed, by bringing forward things "new and old" to color the error. For first, the example of Christ our Lawgiver fights on the negative side: for he chose apostles who were not celibate, but certainly married: such as Peter, whose mother-in-law is mentioned in the Gospel; and Andrew and the others, who it is thought were joined to wives. Indeed, it is said that he called only one, John, whom he chose as a virgin, away from the very midst of the marriage chamber.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Soon, the teachings of the disciples agree with the example of the master. For Paul says in 1 Timothy 3: "A bishop must be the husband of one wife, having children who are subject in all chastity." And in Titus 1: "If anyone is without crime, the husband of one wife," etc., you should appoint him as a priest, just as I directed you.

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
¶ In the third place is the example of the priests of the Old Law, who were a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as prefiguring something in the New Testament</note> of our own. For it is well known that Aaron and thereafter the offspring of the Levites constituted their own tribe, and thus lived in the bond of marriage; as is also read in Luke 1 concerning Zachariah, the progenitor of John the Baptist. The Greek priests have their own institutions modeled after these: namely, they serve in the administration of sacred things by turns, and nevertheless attend to the affairs of a wife. Add to this, if we wish to argue by figures, that Noah’s Ark (as Peter says in his first Epistle) was a figure of the Church saving us from the flood of sins. Priests preside over that Church; however, no celibates entered that ark, but rather eight souls joined in marriage. Therefore, there is no reason why the institution of marriage should be forbidden to priests.

<margin>Fourth [argument].</margin>
¶ Fourth, it is argued by reason. Marriages were instituted at the very beginning of the world as a duty exceedingly necessary for the human race. Therefore, when they are forbidden with such religious strictness to priests, who hold the primary place in the family of Christ, it seems—saving the Church's honor—to detract from marriages against divine and natural permission, alongside Marcion and Manichaeus, whom the Apostle noted for their error in 1 Corinthians 4 <note>Likely referring to 1 Timothy 4</note>, because they were going to prohibit marrying.

<margin>Fifth [argument].</margin>
¶ Fifth, it is argued directly to the point: The vow of chastity is a thing very difficult to observe. For provident Nature so deliberately looked out for the propagation of the species that she instilled in all living creatures a most vehement and scarcely escapable appetite for that same duty. This rabid appetite, after nature was corrupted, among all species...

<meta>catchword: species</meta>

He presents several common counter-arguments, including the marriage of the Apostles and Old Testament priests, which he intends to refute.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on clerical celibacy, moving from the theoretical difficulties of the vow to a historical overview of those who opposed it, specifically focusing on the lineages of what the author considers "heretical" thought from Jovinian to Luther.</meta>

...the sight <note>original: "species"; referring to the visual appearance of beauty or womanhood</note> burns the human heart far more ardently. Furthermore, the priestly office is so necessary to the church that the Christian family cannot possibly exist without it. Indeed, such a great number of people are necessary for performing this duty that a portion of the population—only slightly less than a tenth or a twelfth—is devoted to it. Therefore, it is no wonder if it seems more than justly rigid and forced to drive such a vast number of people into so difficult a religious observance. For truly, while the monastic life is a holy institution, it is not strictly necessary for the administration of the sacraments and sacrifices; nor is it so numerous. Therefore, there is no harshness if those who wish to be assigned to monastic vows are permitted to do so freely. However, to compel such a huge multitude of priests with the same rigor might not seem particularly well-advised to some.

<margin>Sixth point.</margin>
¶ Sixthly: as we were saying, the vow of chastity is so difficult that it seems it should only be permitted to those who are enclosed and surrounded by cloister walls. For this reason, monks hide themselves away in monasteries. Priests, however, have their own homes, and they cannot live comfortably enough without female servants <note>original: "ancillis"</note>, nor without the turmoil of the secular world. Therefore, it does not appear to be a mark of prudence to permit a vow of chastity in the face of such great danger; thus, it is not appropriate.

<margin>Seventh point.</margin>
¶ Seventhly, the outcomes themselves teach us this. For there are very frequent keepers of concubines and those who lie in wait for the beds of others. For this reason, they are hated by the people and do an injustice to the sacraments they handle. It would therefore seem better for both matters to be consulted if each man had his own wife, so that they would defile themselves with no outrage. For the further they are kept from the use of the flesh, the more foully they are stained.

¶ On the contrary is the solemn and laudable custom of the Western Church according to the decrees of the Popes, such as the very ancient Calixtus (Decree 27, distinction, canon *Presbyteris*) and Siricius (Decree 82, distinction, canon *Plurimos*), and many others.

There are two branches of this pestiferous heresy that barks against the continence of priests: the first is that which grants them the license to contract marriages; the second is that which even compels them to do so. Among the moderns, there are those who make Luther the first parent of this; for Jovinian, they say, although he equated marriage with virginity, did not go so far as to reproach priests for lacking wives.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Indeed, as Augustine relates in his book *On Heresies* (chapter 82), Jovinian himself abstained from marriage—not for the sake of merit, but to avoid the troubles of having a wife.

<column-break/>

<margin>Jovinian was the first of all to teach that marriage is permitted to priests.</margin>
But notwithstanding the opinion of these people, it cannot be doubted in the first place that Jovinian was the first author of the "concession"—that is, that it should be lawful for priests to be husbands—since he recognized no extraordinary merit in celibacy. Indeed, he declared such open war on every kind of modesty that he impudently attempted to drag virginity down from its position, even as it fled to the Virgin Mother of God as if to a sacred fortress.

But Luther was not the first author of the other, even more impudent branch: namely, that priests should not only be permitted but even compelled to join themselves to spouses. For Vigilantius, a disciple of Jovinian, succeeded him; he fell into such impudent insanity that he would not permit anyone to be initiated into holy orders before they had taken a wife. Whence Jerome, in his second letter against him to Riparius, says: "O, the wickedness! He is said to have bishops as partners in his crime—if indeed they are to be called bishops—who do not ordain deacons unless they have first married wives, trusting no celibate person’s modesty."

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
There were also, I believe, the Nicolaitans <note>An early Christian sect mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often associated by medieval writers with clerical marriage or sexual license</note> who were authors of the same heresy, whose immodesty Augustine mentions in his book *On the Catalog of Heretics* (chapter 5). From these, a certain Greek named Nicetas derived the custom of the Greeks, as we shall see in the following article; for even they do not ordain priests unless they are first joined to wives. This heresy, which had long been dormant and buried, that arch-heretic Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320–1384), an English theologian whose critiques of the Church prefigured the Reformation</note> took care to call back into the light, as Thomas Walden faithfully relates in his second volume *On the Sacraments* (chapter 128); he took care to crush this heresy in the subsequent chapters.

<margin>Luther.</margin>
From these "patriarchs" of his, therefore, Luther drew this contagion, so that he not only disapproved of the continence of priests but condemned it with the monstrous insolence that was native to him. Whence in that book of his, repeatedly condemned, *On the Abrogation of Private Mass* <note>original: "De abroganda Missa priuata"</note>, discussing that commandment "Thou shalt not commit adultery," he vomited out these diabolical words: "Satan never rages so through the Pope as he does in the handling of chastity and lust. First, although he does not prohibit chastity by word, and teaches how to play the scout <note>gloss: likely a mistranslation or euphemism for 'scortari' (to frequent prostitutes) used in the source</note>, yet he compels prostitution by his intolerable and most ruinous decree on the celibacy of his entire priesthood, which is so widespread; since the grace of chastity is so rare and narrow." And he adds: "since they can neither abstain nor ought they to, it is a Satanic madness and more than sacrilegious to keep them from wives." See how far the temper of this beast was unbridled in its insults. And so, this dogma was impressed so deeply in the hearts of his followers...

# Brother Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
...impressed upon them, so that there is no power that can eradicate it from them. Truly, this error has not only occupied the minds of heretics, but has even crept into the ranks of Catholics. For among the most illustrious interpreters of Canon Law was **Panormitanus** <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canonist known as "Panormitanus" because he was the Archbishop of Palermo.</note>, who nevertheless, in his commentary on the chapter *Since once... concerning married clerics* <note>original: "cap. cùm olim. de clericis coniugatis"</note>, judged that it would be in the best interest of the Church if priests who were unwilling to remain continent were granted the faculty to take wives. He argued this because, as he said, they are daily defiled by illicit intercourse, and the Church ought to act like a "good physician": who, when he sees that a medicine is doing more harm than good, removes it.

<margin>Catholic Conclusion.</margin>
¶ Against this error, therefore, a Catholic conclusion is established: The continence of priests is not only fitting, but so necessary to the Church of Christ that without it, the Church can neither preserve its beauty <note>original: "decorem"</note> nor retain the legitimate image of Christ. And since the following article reminds us that the antiquity of this decree must be corroborated both by ecclesiastical testimonies and sacred oracles, for the present—as the title requires—we must only employ the reasons by which it may be shown how fitting and necessary it has been. For we can contemplate eight or nine points from which reasons of this kind may be deduced.

<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ First, so that we may begin our proofs with the example of Christ, just as we did with the objections. Priests, in the likeness of Christ, are joined to the Church in a spiritual marriage. Christ, however—a virgin born of a virgin—joined to himself the Church as a single, white, and immaculate dove. **Paul** was the author who taught that the marriage of our first parents bore the sacrament <note>or "sign"</note> of this; for which reason it was added there: *For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave to his wife.* This is, therefore, the unique wife for whose sake priests ought rightly to leave not only father and mother, but also carnal wives. For if the Church is a chaste virgin—to speak with **Paul in 2 Corinthians 11**—betrothed to Christ, it is also fitting for his priests to be chaste bridegrooms. Otherwise, their spiritual marriage would not maintain its sincerity.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second, that which supports this holy institution is the purity <note>original: "mundities"</note> that is necessary for the function of priests, especially in performing the most holy Sacrament of the Altar. Indeed, as the Church has always deemed it most becoming that the ministers of that Sacrament—where the most innocent Lamb is sacrificed—should not be contaminated by any shedding of blood (so much so that even those who administer secular justice become "irregular" for receiving holy or-

<column-break/>

-ders), so, and with much greater justice, was it fitting that they should not be polluted by the use of the flesh and commerce with women. For after the marital embrace began to be the conveyor of original sin, by which our race is infected, it subsequently contracted such filthiness <note>original: "foeditatem"</note> that it cannot fail to make men feel shame. From this, the "shameful parts" <note>original: "pudenda membra"; referring to the genitalia</note> inherited their name. Therefore, since carnal things are directly opposed to spiritual things, no use of the flesh is so adverse to spiritual brilliance as this sordid use. This is so much the case that even a holy place is polluted by the emission of semen, just as it is by the shedding of blood. Nor was a "figure" <note>A "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament person or event seen as a symbolic preview of a New Testament reality.</note> of this religious practice lacking in antiquity. For we read in **1 Kings 21** <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 21.</note> that when **David**, fleeing from the face of **Saul**, came to **Abimelech** the Le-

<margin>A most clear figure of the previous conclusion.</margin>
-vitical priest and asked him for loaves of bread to refresh himself and his men, the priest replied: "I have no ordinary bread at hand, but only holy bread"—namely, that which had been placed on the table of the sanctuary for the use of the priests. "If the young men are clean, especially from women, let them eat." Nor indeed were they permitted to eat until **David** assured him, saying: "Truly, we have been kept from women since yesterday and the day before, and the vessels of the young men were clean." If, therefore, it was a crime to eat that bread—in which nothing of divinity lay hidden other than that it was a sacrament (that is, a figure) of the most holy bread which descended from heaven—unless by those who were clean from their wives, how much more justly does that same brilliance befit those who handle the very reality of the Sacrament? That is, those who daily eat the body of God under the appearance of bread?

<margin>Second figure.</margin>
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
¶ There is also another figure: that it was not permitted to eat the legal lamb except with "loins girt." Explaining this in his **22nd Homily on the Gospels**, **Gregory** says that the delight of the flesh resides in the loins; and for that reason, it was signified there that those who eat the Passover ought to subdue their pleasures and restrain the flesh from luxury. Therefore, since evangelical priests daily sacrifice the immaculate Lamb, it is right and most becoming to their office that they should shine with perpetual abstinence from the flesh.

<margin>Third shadow of the same truth.</margin>
<margin>Bede.</margin>
¶ Add also a third and specific "shadow" <note>Another term for a symbolic preview.</note> of this matter in the priests of the Old Law. For we read in **Exodus 28**: "Furthermore, you shall prepare linen tunics for the sons of Aaron." And further down: "You shall make linen breeches to cover the flesh of their shame from the loins even to the thighs." Interpreting this, the **Venerable Bede** says in **Book 3 of On the Tabernacle** that those breeches properly designated chastity, which prohibits the appetite for marital copulation; without which, he says, no one can either receive the priesthood or be consecrated for the ministry of the altar—that is, unless he has either remained a virgin or has dissolved the bonds of union after having taken a wife. But truly, just as ecclesiastical matters are connected like a golden chain, so when one is broken...

# Book Eight. Question VI.

...if the knot is broken, everything is dissolved. For this reason, the Church requires this holiness from its priests because it firmly believes that the true body of Christ is handled by them. Since the Lutherans <note>Followers of Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation, who rejected clerical celibacy.</note> deny the sacramental truth of that same body, it is no wonder they do not desire the same purity <note>original: "candorem"</note> from their own ministers.

<margin>Third reason</margin>
¶ The third basis for this fitness is taken from the highest peak of meditation and prayer to which priests are dedicated. For they must give themselves entirely to reading and re-reading the Holy Scriptures, so that like clouds flying on high, they may provide the people with life-giving rain. However, the use of a wife not only defiles the body but also weighs down and clouds the mind, rendering it most unfit for the contemplation of heavenly things. Hence the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> in 1 Corinthians 7, where he warns spouses not to defraud one another of their conjugal duty, nonetheless makes an exception, saying: *Unless perhaps by consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer,* <note>1 Cor 7:5</note> clearly teaching how great a hindrance that duty is to the elevation of the mind toward God. Since priests are consecrated to constant meditation and prayer for themselves and the people, they ought to be perpetually estranged from that duty, and thus from that covenant. On this point, even if it is permissible to seek testimony from the pagans, the Peripatetic <margin>Theophrastus.</margin> **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle.</note> wrote wisely in his book on marriage that the studies of philosophy are hindered by marriage, and that no one can serve both books and a wife equally. And to return to the priests, <margin>Origenes.</margin> **Origen** <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> in Homily 23 on the Book of Numbers, explaining the same passage of Paul, concludes thus: "From which it seems to me that it belongs to him alone to offer the perpetual sacrifice (speaking further of priests) who has devoted himself to unceasing and perpetual chastity." And **Ambrose** <margin>Ambrose.</margin> on the third chapter of 1 Timothy says: "For if," he says, "laypeople are commanded to abstain for a time for the sake of prayer, how much more is it required for Levites or priests, who must pray day and night for the people committed to them?" And **Jerome** <margin>Jerome. Epiphanius.</margin> in Book 1 against Jovinian, repeating almost the same words (which both seem to have taken from **Epiphanius**, Volume 1, Book 2, in the *Heresy of the Cathars* <note>original: "hæresi Catharorum," referring to a work by Epiphanius of Salamis</note>), adds: "If priests must always pray, they must therefore always avoid marriage." Indeed, an example of this was not lacking in the priests of the Old Law. For this reason, as instituted by David in 1 Chronicles 14 <note>The text cites 1 Paralipom. 14, but the division of priestly courses is found in chapter 24.</note> and mentioned in Luke 1, they served in the temple by turns:

<column-break/>

and during that time, shut within the temple, they abstained from the company of their wives. Specifically, since they professed that their prayers ascended before God like the incense burned at the altar, they simultaneously confessed that they could not pour them out purely unless they were separated from their wives. From this, <margin>Beda.</margin> **Bede** <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 672–735 AD), an English monk and historian.</note> in his commentary on the same passage, draws the lesson that our priests—who are commanded to serve the altar not by turns but always—must be devoted to perpetual chastity.

<margin>Quarta ratio.</margin>
¶ Then, the fourth source of this same institution is that Gospel priests, who (as Paul warns in Colossians 1) fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, must continually mourn the sins of the people and produce the perpetual fruits of penance. For this reason, as read in Hosea 4, they "eat the sins"—that is, the offerings for sins—of the people. Nothing, however, is more diametrically opposed to mourning than sexual pleasure <note>original: "venerea voluptas"</note>, which, by exhaling all the spirits, transforms the soul into flesh. On account of this, it was said of man before the flood: *My spirit shall not remain in man, because he is flesh.* <note>Genesis 6:3</note> Thus, if the sorrows of fasting are appropriate for penitents (as read in Jonah 3), and if wine, strong drink, and everything that could intoxicate was forbidden to those who in ancient times offered themselves to the worship of the temple, then Venus <note>Refers to lust or sexual activity, named after the Roman goddess of love.</note> is much more appropriately forbidden to Gospel priests, for she intoxicates more violently than wine.

<margin>Quinta ratio.</margin>
¶ Add a fifth reason: unless one is a most impudent heretic, no one can deny that celibacy is an outstanding virtue. Priests, above all, should preach and commend this virtue to the people, encouraging widows and others who are continent toward chastity. But how can he be an exhorter of widowhood, virginity, or chastity who himself lives under the law of marriage?

<margin>Sexta.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, this holy institution had its origin in a sixth root: namely, the care that priests are bound to have for the people. For they are bound to uphold the protection of the poor, widows, and orphans, and to distribute their goods among the needy. Nothing more forcefully opposes the fulfillment of this duty than the care of a household, where there is a wife and the offspring of children. Hence <margin>Paulus.</margin> **Paul** in 1 Corinthians 7 says: "I want you to be without anxiety. He who is without a wife is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But he who is with a wife is anxious about how he may please his wife, and he is divided." <note>1 Cor 7:32–34</note> At this passage, <margin>Ambrosius.</margin> **Ambrose** says: "Once cut off... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>"

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

[The mind], he says, is trained to merit God through the worry over marital matters <note>original: "solicitudine rei vxoriæ"</note>, which alone in this world is heavier than all others. Thus, he concludes: among all worldly worries, marital matters are the most troublesome and most occupied with the anxieties of business. For all other things serve this end—not only so that those present burdens may be sustained, but so that perpetual succession <note>The raising and providing for heirs.</note> may be provided for. Indeed, it was for this reason that Jovinian himself—a hater of modesty <note>Jovinian (died c. 405 AD) was a monk who argued against the superiority of virginity over marriage; he was declared a heretic by St. Augustine and St. Jerome.</note>, as Saint Augustine reports in his book *On Heresies*, chapter 82—did not wish to commit himself to marriage; not because he valued the merit of celibacy, but to guard himself against such a heavy bundle of troubles. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Therefore, for a man who is bound to a wife, no liberty remains; yet such liberty is most necessary for the function of priests.

<margin>Seventh reason.</margin>
¶ The seventh point for persuading one of this ecclesiastical sanction is taken from the authority with which priests in the Church of Christ ought to shine for the ministry of the sacraments, and from the honor due to them, according to that verse from Ecclesiasticus 7: *Honor God, and honor the priests.* This is to be understood especially of our priests, who touch not only divine things but God himself in the sacrament <note>Refers to the Real Presence in the Eucharist.</note>. For this authority arises for them primarily because they are in an eminent place—that is, set apart from the flock of the common people. If, however, they were husbands, they would be involved in the midst of the common people; wherefore neither eminent honor nor reverence would be held for them. Indeed, it would be a shame to adore the mysteries of the divine body and blood in the hands of a married man; and there would be a fear of entrusting the confession of sins to those whose wives would always be present. For between a husband and a wife, nothing is kept secret. But truly the Lutherans, as I said above, because they deny all these sacraments, it is no wonder if they pay no veneration to their own priests. 

<margin>Eighth.</margin>
¶ The eighth point—and one not to be held as inferior in this institution—concerns both the provision of priestly sustenance and the peace and tranquility that would be disturbed by the granting of wives. Indeed, if priests were hedged in by a crowd of wives and offspring, then their priesthoods and prebends <note>term: <term>prebends</term>: The portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note> would not suffice for them. For they would have to be supported honorably. In the old law, the Levites <note>The tribe of Israel dedicated to the service of the Temple.</note>, who were a twelfth part of the people, found the tithes sufficient because they received them in full. Furthermore, there were not as many men necessary for the ministry of a single temple then as there are now for such a vast multitude of churches. From this, it would follow that priests would have to be craftsmen and farmers—as the Levites perhaps were, and as the Lutherans wish for and have their own priests. Anyone can consider for himself how much contempt their order would fall into among us if this were the case.

<column-break/>

Moreover, if wives were attached to priests, they would concentrate all their worry and vigilance on passing their priesthoods on to their sons as if by hereditary right. We see a lesson in this from the ambition of those priests who [unlawfully] have sons today. For if those for whom it is a crime and a shame to enrich their sons with prebends still busy themselves with it so much, how much more freely and boldly would they do it if it were an honor, not a shame, to abound in a long line of children? 

<margin>Last reason.</margin>
¶ To this is finally added that if priests were married, then only magnates—such as Dukes, Counts, and other secular princes—would be chosen for bishoprics, and other secular nobles for the rich benefices. Because of this, everything would be full of lawsuits, discords, and wars, and all ecclesiastical matters would be totally confused. These are the things I am accustomed to meditate on regarding this matter.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
### To the first argument on the contrary, 
therefore, it is answered that Christ chose Apostles from marriage because at that time the religious practice of celibacy was not established in counsel or use as it is now. However, to teach that once the Law had passed (to paraphrase the apostolic words in Hebrews 7 <note>Hebrews 7:12: "For when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed also."</note>), the manner of priests was to be changed at the same time, he called them to celibacy, and even John from the midst of marriage to virginity. 

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
Although, as Jerome is the authority in his first book *Against Jovinian*, it is certain only of Peter that he had a wife, while it is not so established regarding the others. Yet, even if that were admitted as extra information, it ought not to be doubted—as Jerome says in the same place—that they made vows of chastity with the consent of their wives. This is gathered from those words of Peter in Matthew 19: *Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall there be for us?* For he alluded to what he had heard from the mouth of Christ spoken to the young man: *If you wish to be perfect, go and sell... and follow me,* which is where the institutes of religious life are founded. 

<margin>To the second.</margin>
To the second argument, which was brought from the words of Paul, it will be more conveniently answered in the next article. 

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third regarding the ancient [Old Testament] priests, as it pertains to the present matter, it is answered that their condition differed most widely from ours. First, because they did not handle the truth of the sacraments—through which Christ is now offered and the grace of the Holy Spirit is conferred—but they handled entirely the shadows of these things <note>A common Scholastic distinction: Old Testament rituals were "shadows" or "types" of the "truth" found in New Testament sacraments.</note>. Therefore, such great cleanliness was not required of them. Nonetheless, through the frequent washings they performed, they signified the purity <note>original: "candorem"</note> which ought to shine in our priests...

### Book Eight, Question VI. 701

[They] prefigured these things. Furthermore, as we read in Leviticus 21, the high priest was to marry a virgin, and not a widow, or a divorced woman, or a dishonored woman. And when they served in the temple, as has been said, they abstained from their wives, which was a mark of <term>candor</term> <note>In this context, "candor" refers to ritual and moral purity or "shining" integrity.</note>. On this point, <margin>Ambrose on 1 Timothy 3.</margin> Ambrose says that it was permitted for the priests of old to make use of their wives because they had much time of leisure away from their ministry. For there was a multitude of priests so that they could serve in turns; but now, priests must be constantly engaged in ministry.

To these points, we add that the <term>counsel of celibacy</term> <note>The "evangelical counsel" of voluntary chastity encouraged by Jesus in the Gospels.</note> had not yet been put forward at that time. Add to this that the <term>Levitical order</term> <note>The priesthood of the Old Testament, which was inherited through the Tribe of Levi.</note> constituted its own twelfth tribe—a sign of the coming Apostolic number. Because of this, it was necessary for them to produce offspring through the duty of marriage. To our priests, however, only a <term>spiritual generation</term> <note>The concept of "birthing" new Christians through baptism and the Word rather than biological children.</note> has been committed: namely, to nurse, cherish, and nourish souls reborn in Christ through their word, ministry, and devotion. This is what Arator excellently declared in his poem, in which he wove together the Acts of the Apostles with these verses:

> Now the nourishing faith of the Church commands its 
> Bishops to be chaste without end: and she seeks 
> Carefully in every tribe for those she may rightly approve; 
> This succession shall not be one of blood, 
> But of merit.

Wherefore the Greeks, by imitating the institution of the Levites, would have acted much more wisely if they had listened to the Latin Christian sanctions. But we must return to them later. <margin>To the fourth.</margin> ¶ To the fourth argument, Jerome responds extensively against Jovinian, stating that the Church, by preferring celibacy, in no way condemns marriage. Rather, she teaches that just as marriage is necessary for propagating the human race, so celibacy befits the ministers of the sacraments. Just so, she does not condemn the ministers of justice <note>Civil judges or executioners.</note>, even though she bars her own priests from that bloody duty. This is a common argument and has been sufficiently enriched by the Church Fathers. <margin>To the fifth.</margin> ¶ The fifth argument is that which touches on the point along with the subsequent ones. For we admit that the vow of chastity is not easy to observe, and the order of priests, necessary to the church, is very <margin>To the sixth.</margin> numerous. And (as was alleged in the sixth argument) we acknowledge, moreover, that in private houses such a vow cannot be kept as safely as in the cloisters of monks. Nor do we indeed <margin>To the seventh.</margin> deny, as the seventh argument warned,

<column-break/>

that there are frequent cases of concubines and adulterers among the clergy. But nevertheless, we give a multifaceted response to these things. <margin>The first solution.</margin> First: the statutes of a Commonwealth, and especially of the Church, must be judged by their goal, even if it is not possible to prevent every inconvenience. Therefore, since that "candor" of both mind and body is becoming to priests for the most holy ministry of the altar, it was fitting to institute them in this way—notwithstanding the assaults of the flesh, which human frailty must necessarily endure in any state of life. Otherwise, even the divine law, which forbids all lust, would be "unjust." For there are countless people polluted by a slip of the flesh, and very many adulterers. Should the laws prohibiting these things therefore be deleted? <margin>The second.</margin> ¶ Second: No one is compelled to the priesthood. Indeed, if you consult the sacred canons, no one is even admitted except by mature judgment: namely, one who is of legitimate age, so that he can deliberately see for himself what his shoulders can bear. Furthermore, he must shine with the integrity of his morals and with the light of knowledge and <margin>Alexander.</margin> science, as can be seen among many other sanctions in [the decrees of] Alexander III, under the whole title concerning the age, quality, and order of those to be preferred. <margin>Paul.</margin> For this reason, Paul says to Timothy that it is necessary for a bishop, and indeed a priest, to have a good testimony from those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. And he saw to it that the same disciple was warned not to lay hands on anyone hastily; and he taught Titus with what great virtues one who was to be assumed into the priesthood ought to shine. <margin>The third.</margin> ¶ Third, we respond that human nature is not so weak and slippery that, with vigilant care and caution applied, it cannot protect itself from the incursions of the flesh through the grace of God. <margin>The Synod of Nicaea.</margin> For this reason, the holy Synod of Nicaea, as can be seen in its third canon, drove away every "extrinsic" woman <note>original: "extraneam mulierem"; women other than close relatives who lived with clergy, often called *subintroductae*.</note> from the roofs of priests; and after they were driven out, <margin>Pope Siricius.</margin> the decree of Siricius wished for the same (which is in Distinction 81, the canon "Feminas"): namely, that only a mother, or sister, or aunt might dwell with them. However, as Jerome wisely noted on the third chapter of Jeremiah, since the heretics dwell in the "North" <note>A common biblical and patristic metaphor for the source of evil and spiritual coldness.</note>—from whence all evil is spread—once the heat of faith is lost, they are unable to hear that word of the Apostle: *Be fervent in spirit.* Hence, surrendering themselves to pleasures, being enemies of chastity, they cannot but be foes of modesty and defamers of nature, asserting that men cannot...

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

...except to live as slaves to women. Although we cannot deny that the number of priests currently permitted in the Church is greater than is right; and it admits plebeians and men of the lowest class into this order without selection; and that such a practice has cast the order into the lowly place where it now lies.

<margin>Fourth solution.</margin>
In the fourth place, we add to our response that the marital duty—even if, according to the Pauline warning and the confession of the Fathers, it is a certain remedy for well-born men to calm the unbridled flesh—nevertheless, for the lascivious and obscene, it is so far from being a remedy that it is even a ruinous danger. Listen to Paul in 1 Corinthians 7: "If you take a wife," he says, "you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned; yet such will have tribulations of the flesh." These <term>tribulations</term> <note>St. Paul uses this term to describe the worldly distractions and anxieties that come with domestic life.</note> are not only to be referred to the troubles of the family, but also to those same allurements of the flesh which they thought to meet through that marital license. For fleeing the enemy, they fall into hostile battles; they wish to extinguish the fire, and they stir up the fire.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Whence Augustine, in the book *On the Singular Life of Clerics* <note>original: *de singul. cleric.*</note>, says: "Husbands and wives, carrying out their marriages daily, do not satisfy themselves." Thus he spoke. Let no one believe, therefore, that by obeying carnal pleasure, he is opposing it; rather, it must be fled from entirely. Add that marital use, both by its own nature, brings about satiety, and then—at the devil's prompting—nausea and a desire for another's bed. Wherefore, while these heretical priests <note>Soto refers to the Protestant Reformers of his time who advocated for ending clerical celibacy.</note> wish to make husbands continent, they instead produce adulterers. It was not right, therefore, to look back at Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as "The Sicilian" or Panormitanus, who suggested that the Church might allow clerical marriage to prevent scandals.</note>, that the expositor of the sacred canons should deem it a "salubrious medicine" that the flesh should be foully indulged against the spirit. For Paul did not wish us to be so instructed when he said: "I wish you all to be as I am myself." Certainly, Saint Thomas [Aquinas], in the present question, Article 11, more holily wished the <term>prelates</term> <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> of the church to be warned: namely, that dangers of human affairs should be met through human things, but not by converting divine things to human use. This is especially true because other remedies are more present for healing the disease of the "tickling flesh" than by exciting its itch through obedience to it. If only the Church would more vigilantly restore these same remedies in the order of priests and demand they follow the sacred canons. Namely, that they should be strong in the doctrine of the sacred writings, use a frugal table, abstain from secular matters,

<column-break/>

both luxuries and commerce, and finally devote themselves to prayer. For by these institutions, the corruption of the clergy would be provided for much more effectively than by drowning them in matrimonial impediments.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether priestly continence began from the very cradle of the Church.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' containing a woodcut illustration of a haloed saint or scholar seated in a landscape, holding an open book.</image-desc>
Secondly, it remains to speak of the antiquity of this institution. And in our custom, [to argue] that it did not arise from the very beginnings of the Church, [the opposition] argues in the same place cited above, so that it may be explained more precisely.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
First, the Apostle [Paul] warned bishops that they should be "the husband of one wife"; therefore, this custom did not draw its origin from that century.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
Second, there exists a canon of the sixth Synod of Constantinople <note>Commonly known as the Council in Trullo (692 AD), which allowed Eastern Orthodox priests to remain married if they were wed before ordination.</note>, which was held under Pope Agatho in the time of Constantine IV, in the Year of Salvation 673, and is cited in <term>Distinction 31</term> <note>A division within the *Decretum Gratiani*, the standard collection of medieval canon law.</note>, canon *Quoniam*. The canon is: "Whoever is found diligent in subdiaconal, diaconal, or priestly ordination, these are in no way prohibited from ascending to such a rank because of cohabitation with their wife. Nor should they be forced at the time of their ordination to profess that they must abstain from familiarity with a legal wife."

<margin>Third [argument].</margin>
Third, it is argued by the authority attributed to Augustine in Book 15 of *The City of God* and cited by <term>Gratian</term> <note>The 12th-century monk who compiled the foundational textbook of canon law.</note> in canon *Cum igitur*, 35, question 1. His words are: "The Church, after the apostolic institutions, added certain counsels of perfection, such as concerning the continence of the ministers of the church; therefore, this was not a precept of necessity, but a counsel of honor."

<margin>Calixtus.</margin>
But the decree of Calixtus I <note>Pope from approximately 218 to 222 AD.</note> teaches us the contrary, which is found in Distinction 27, canon *Presbyteris*, where he says: "We utterly forbid priests, deacons, subdeacons, and monks to have concubines or to contract marriage; we judge that marriages already contracted by such persons must be dissolved, according to the definition of the sacred canons." Now, Calixtus sat [as Pope] around the year of Redemption 218; since he himself cites "older canons," it is proof that the matter is very ancient.

<meta>This page continues the discussion in Book Eight, Question VI, regarding clerical celibacy. ### Book Eight, Question VI.

In the age of the Apostles, it was permitted for those who were already bound by the bonds of marriage to be initiated into the sacred orders. This requires no other evidence than that of Paul, which I have already cited twice, in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, where he says that a bishop must be "the husband of one wife" <note>original: "unius uxoris virum"</note>. We cannot evade those passages by claiming he meant those who had been married but were now widowers. For the context of Paul’s writing clearly demonstrates that he referred to those who remained in marriage: first, because "husband of one wife" sounds exactly like "one having a wife"; and second, because among the other virtues of a bishop, Paul includes that he should "rule his own house well." But there is no reason to dwell on proving this. For if that were not Paul's meaning, the laws of the Church would never have subsequently permitted married men to become priests—yet they do permit it, as seen in the canon "Since" <note>original: "quoniam"</note> cited above in Distinction 31, and the canon "If anyone" <note>original: "si quis"</note> in Distinction 32, as well as the custom of the Greeks themselves. Therefore, what Jerome says in his exposition of that passage—namely, "He does not say 'one who marries,' but 'one who has had one wife'" <note>original: "Non dicit qui unam ducat, sed qui unam habuerit"</note>—is not to be understood as meaning the man did not have a wife at that time, but rather that he had not previously married another. He taught this for the sake of the sacrament of Christ, who betrothed the Church as His only bride.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The reason for the assertion in this conclusion is that, since the Eastern Church at that time suffered from a shortage of ministers and celibacy had not yet been heard of with such religious strictness, the Church was compelled to recruit from the ranks of married men. They took philosophers, elders, and others who excelled in wisdom, to whom they could temporarily entrust their ministries and functions until the maturing Church could establish a holier standard for itself.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion. It is a most widely accepted rule that it has never been permitted for priests, after they have been dedicated to the sacred ministry, to involve themselves in the business of marriage. This is a conclusion affirmed by, among others, the very famous 

<margin>Waldensis.</margin>
Waldensis <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), a prominent English Carmelite theologian known for his defense of traditional doctrines.</note>, a most vigilant searcher of antiquity, in Volume 2 (on the Sacraments), chapter 129, and Volume 5 (on Sacramentals), chapter 66. 

<margin>Josse Clichtove.</margin>
And Josse Clichtove <note>A Flemish theologian and humanist (1472–1543) who wrote extensively on the priesthood.</note>, an author not to be disregarded, says in his book *On the Continence of Priests*, chapter 4, that this was the opinion of the most approved authors, in which all the holy Fathers agree with one consensus. We cite these authors because, since this is a negative historical conclusion, it earns its credibility primarily from the fact that if the contrary had ever been the custom or habit, its history would not be missing; yet no such history exists. Furthermore, this same conclusion is clearly 

<column-break/>

gathered from the canons just cited, both of which are from the Sixth Synod of Constantinople <note>Also known as the Council in Trullo (692 AD), which established specific disciplines for the Eastern Church.</note>. For in the canon "Since," in which priests are allowed to remain in marriage, mention is only made of marriages contracted *before* undertaking sacred orders. And the canon "If anyone" (Distinction 32) states: "If any of those who enter the clergy wish to be joined to a woman by the law of marriage, let them do this before the ordination of the subdiaconate." From this, the opposite sense is inferred: that it is not permitted afterward.

<margin>Council of Neocaesarea.</margin>
And in the Council of Neocaesarea <note>A regional council held around 315 AD.</note>, which is recorded in Distinction 28: "If a priest takes a wife, he must be deposed from his order." However, so that we may report everything with total integrity, 

<margin>Pope Stephen.</margin>
there are the words of Pope Stephen in the canon "Otherwise" <note>original: "aliter"</note> in the same Distinction 31, which seem to make the matter doubtful. For he says that the priests, deacons, and subdeacons of the Greeks "are joined in marriage" <note>original: "matrimonio copulantur"</note>. 

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Because of these words, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a powerful Dominican theologian and cardinal.</note>, in Question 12 of his first *Quodlibeta*, boldly says that it was once permitted even for priests to be joined in marriage after undertaking orders. To be sure, he considered the gloss on that same chapter to be foolish; for where the text says "they are joined," the gloss explains it as "they use the marriage they joined." Furthermore, he ought not to have abandoned the universal confession of the Doctors because of that text, which is excellently founded on the laws just cited and is corroborated by the best reasoning, and is confirmed by the custom of the Greeks, as it is reported. For in Latin, the passive verb signifies not only a present action but also a past state. There is therefore no violence in saying "they are joined," meaning "they remain joined"; so that the sense is not that it was permitted for them to be joined in a *new* marriage, but to live as those *already* joined, as held in the chapter "When once" <note>original: "cum olim"</note> regarding the marriage of clerics. Nevertheless, I confess it cannot be denied that formerly deacons and subdeacons were permitted to fly to marriage even after sacred orders, provided they

protested this at the reception of orders, as is found in the text of the Synod of Ancyra, Distinction 28, canon "Deacons." However, they were not admitted to the priesthood unless they had confessed chastity with a purpose of conversion; these are the words of the 4th Council of Arles, which is recorded in the same Distinction, canon "Furthermore."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Book Eight, Question VI, concerning the history and legality of clerical celibacy.
