# F. D. Soto, on Justice & Law,

I say, for this reason, those who were free from wives <note>original: "vxoribus soluti" — referring to widowers or those never married</note> and sought sacred orders were compelled, if they wished to be made priests, to take a vow of chastity, as is the case now. Although, due to the scarcity of candidates at that time, as we said before, married men were admitted even without such a vow, as held in the cited text "Since" in Distinction 31 <note>This refers to Gratian's Decretum, a foundational collection of canon law</note>.

Therefore, these conclusions are accepted without controversy by all Catholics. Nor does anyone deny the second conclusion except for the Jovinianists, the Wycliffites, and finally the Lutherans <note>Groups who historically challenged the Church's teachings on celibacy and monasticism</note>.

<margin>The opinion of Clichtove.</margin>
But indeed, what some of the orthodox affirm—among whom is Clichtove <note>Josse Clichtove (1472–1543), a prominent Flemish theologian</note> in the previously cited book, chapter 13—namely, that the vow of priestly continence is indispensable and cannot be relaxed by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff so that one who is once a priest may marry, can hardly be considered probable.

<margin>The first reason against the preceding opinion.</margin>
For if they mean this regarding the period before the vow is even made, such that the Pope cannot repeal the church's decree, it is plainly false. For the Greeks, who according to the decrees of the Sixth Synod <note>The Council of Trullo (692 AD), which allowed Eastern priests to remain married</note> are both priests and husbands, are truly and legitimately priests. Therefore, there is no doubt that the Church could decree the same for Westerners, as Saint Thomas Aquinas confesses in the *Summa Theologiae* (Secunda Secundae, Question 88, Article 11): because chastity is not intrinsically linked to the priesthood as it is to the religious life <note>original: "religioni" — here meaning the state of being a monk or friar who takes solemn vows</note>. The aforementioned authors, failing to notice this, apply arguments that properly apply to the religious life to the priesthood. Therefore, the Church could likewise decree that after receiving orders, men might turn to marriage and remain simultaneously in the priesthood; for all of this pertains to ecclesiastical law <term>ius ecclesiasticum: laws created by the Church hierarchy rather than being divinely mandated in scripture</term>, since no law—neither natural nor divine—forbids it. If, however, they mean their opinion regarding a solemn vow already taken, such that a dispensation cannot be granted to the priests currently in the Western Church, they speak with a bit more probability; yet they still do not sufficiently prove what they set out to demonstrate. For since that church decree does not belong to the inner essence of the priesthood, no reason necessarily compels us to deny that the Pope can dispense even on this matter—although, as shown in the previous article, it would be a most disastrous calamity for ecclesiastical affairs.

But this is the point toward which our present dispute hastens: whether from the very birth of the Church the custom grew that those received from marriage into the priesthood were not admitted until, with their wives' consent, they vowed perpetual chastity. For it is of no small importance to know this to convict these

<column-break/>

heretics. And there exists on both sides a combative line of arguments that have held me almost always in perplexity.

<margin>The third conclusion.</margin>
I would affirm here, however, with a probability that seems very great to me, a third conclusion: namely, that around the times of the Apostles, the use of marriage was forbidden to all priests, even though the custom was later corrupted. For this argument stands on my side:

<margin>Argument for the conclusion.</margin>
The Gospel priesthood was never held to be less excellent than the Levitical one <note>The priesthood of the Old Testament</note>. Now, those ancient priests, when they served in the temple, abstained from the company of their wives so they might worthily eat the bread of presence <note>original: "panes propositionis" — the sacred bread kept in the Tabernacle</note>, as was shown in the preceding article. How, then, can it be believed that the divine Apostles and their disciples would allow the Living Bread that descended from heaven <note>The Eucharist</note> to be handled by the hands of those who had risen from their wife's side that very day? Add to this: if this consideration persuaded posterity—namely, the Western Church—to bar priests from conjugal commerce, what necessity could there have been to excuse those primitive fathers from providing the same? But you say: there was then a scarcity of men to whom the priestly office could be entrusted. I admit it, certainly; but the frequency of churches was not then so great that, while the blood of Christ was still warm <note>A phrase used to describe the era immediately following Christ's sacrifice, characterized by extreme piety</note>, men of advanced age, endowed with learning and integrity, could not be found who would profess that chastity with the consent of their wives.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And it is confirmed: If the Greeks, who do not follow the Latin decree in this matter, never dare to visit their wives when they minister in the temple, is this not testimony that from the very cradle of the Church something more sacred was in the custom?

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
The second argument, and one that urges me vehemently, is one I have thought out for myself from the previous conclusions. For it is most established for all that from the very cradle of the Church, married men were indeed admitted to the priesthood, but priests were restrained from taking wives. Now, this distinction could have arisen for no other reason than that neither group was permitted to indulge in matrimonial use. Otherwise, if those who were in marriage could use their wives, what would prevent priests from likewise entering into marriages? For if we admit that married men were forbidden the use of their wives, the reason becomes clear why...

He contends that the holiness of the Eucharist requires greater purity than the Old Testament priesthood, justifying the requirement for continence.</summary>

### Book Eight, Question VI.

Why was the contracting of marriage forbidden after entering the priesthood? Clearly, it was because they vowed chastity, just like others who were already joined to wives. Add to this that such a disparity—where some might enjoy the embrace of a wife while others could not—could not fail to disfigure the decorum of the Church.

<margin>Epiphanius</margin>
<margin>Jerome</margin>
<margin>Ambrose</margin>
Truly, even if no assertion from an author existed, reason would vehemently compel me toward this opinion; nevertheless, there exist testimonies from the holy fathers which, when weighed more carefully, reveal the truth of the matter. First among these is the authority of the very ancient Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a Church Father known for his defense of orthodoxy</note>, who was highly esteemed in the praises of Jerome and Augustine. His words, found in Volume 1, Book 2, regarding the heresy of the Cathari, are: "In truth, the holy preaching of God, since the coming of Christ, does not accept those into the priesthood who, after the death of their first wife, have joined in a second marriage, because of the excellent honor and dignity of the priesthood. And the holy Church of God certainly observes this with sincerity. But it also does not accept a man of one wife who is still fathering children; it only accepts the man who has restrained himself from his one wife or lived in widowhood as a deacon, priest, bishop, or subdeacon; especially where the ecclesiastical canons are followed in their purity." And he adds: "But you will say to me that in certain places, priests, deacons, and subdeacons are still fathering children. But this is not according to the canon, but according to the minds of men, which have grown weak over time, and because of the great number [of people], when a ministry could not be found." He gathers these and other points subsequently to confirm that it was never lawful for priests to use their wives, even if they were married, except where the purity of the canons was not preserved due to lust. And in Volume 2, Book 3, near the end, where he writes on ecclesiastical discipline, he expressly says that none are to be admitted to the priesthood except those who are either virgins, or observe continence from their own wives, or maintain widowhood after a single marriage. 

The testimony of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), the translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> supports the same point, where he says: "What shall the Eastern Churches do? What shall those of Egypt and the Apostolic See do? They who receive as clergy either virgins or the continent; or if they have had wives, they cease to be husbands." Behold, in the time of Epiphanius, the Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, and Jerome, who lived his life in the East, although priests supported their wives, they nevertheless abstained from sexual relations with them. 

Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan</note> agrees with this in his exposition on the first letter to Timothy regarding the words, *The husband of one wife*. There he says: "If any have governed their children well, etc., they can become worthy of the priesthood." And further

<column-break/>

<margin>Haymo</margin>
<margin>Bede</margin>
<margin>The Council of Carthage</margin>
down: "From then on, they must restrain themselves from use of a woman." And Haymo <note>Haymo of Halberstadt (d. 853), a Carolingian author</note> says in the same place: "Husband of one wife means that he is not twice-married; afterwards, however, he ought to abstain entirely." And the previously cited Venerable Bede <note>The English monk and scholar (c. 672–735)</note>, in Book 3 *On the Tabernacle*, asserts that at that time it was lawful for no one to be created a priest unless he had either remained a virgin or had dissolved the bonds of union after contracting a marriage. 

Finally, let the words of the Council of Carthage <note>A series of influential church councils held in North Africa in the 4th and 5th centuries</note> be added, which are recorded in Distinction 32, the canon *Placuit* <note>Part of the "Decretum Gratiani," the collection of Church law</note>. Specifically: "It has pleased us that bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons, according to previous institutes, should also abstain from their wives." And then the words of Pope Leo <note>Pope Leo I (r. 440–461)</note> in the very next canon: "If anyone from among the married desires to ascend to the subdiaconate, he cannot do so without the consent of his wife, so that from a carnal marriage it may henceforth become a spiritual marriage; no one forcing them. Nor is the wife permitted afterward to be joined to that same husband of hers carnally, nor to marry anyone else during his life or after his death." This was because the wife was also required to make a perpetual vow of chastity. And this council calls these "previous constitutions"—namely, as I judge, those closest to the age of the Apostles. 

Indeed, even the canon of the Sixth Synod <note>The Council of Trullo (692 AD), which established different rules for the Eastern Church</note>, the canon *Quoniam* in Distinction 31, which the Greeks use for their defense, plainly teaches this: where it says that clergy are not forced to profess chastity at the time of their ordination, it says that in the primitive church they were so compelled. Behold the things that make the conclusion for me exceedingly probable—indeed, certain: and furthermore, the Church would never have striven so hard afterward to bind priests to a vow of chastity unless it had been taught this by the holy Apostles themselves.

<margin>The first argument of Clichtove against the aforementioned opinion.</margin>
<margin>The solution.</margin>
Nevertheless, it must not be denied that there are arguments of no small weight against this opinion, by which some, such as Clichtove <note>Josse Clichtove, a Flemish theologian who argued that clerical celibacy was an unchangeable divine law</note>, think the contrary is established. The first is the passage from Paul cited in the previous article and the present one: *It is necessary for a bishop to be the husband of one wife*. This is used as an objection against us differently by heretics than by Catholics. The heretics use it in the sense that it is necessary to marry a wife before one is initiated into sacred orders. But this so clashes with Paul's words that it needs no other blade to strike it down. 

However, it is opposed by Catholics in a different and milder sense: namely, to infer from it that it was lawful then to share the marriage bed with wives. Both, however, are sufficiently excluded by the testimonies of those saints whom we recently brought forward to confirm the previous conclusion.

This appears even more clearly in his decree to Titus: where he says, "just, holy, continent" <note>Titus 1:8</note>. It is as if he had said: living with a spouse just as if with a sister. For who would call him "continent" who devotes his efforts to the business of a wife? Add to this that the blessed John was the bishop of Ephesus: yet he was chosen as a virgin by the Lord, and remained a virgin forever. Indeed, you may find numerous other holy fathers testifying that priestly continence was observed in the time of the Apostles.

But in truth, without such contempt, they abstained from the common bed by mutual consent. 

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>

The sense of the words—not to repeat everything—is that when the synod was preparing to decree that priests should not sleep with the wives they had married before consecration, Paphnutius <note>original: "Panutius". Paphnutius the Confessor was a famous Egyptian monk at the Council of Nicaea (325 AD)</note>, although he himself was inexperienced in marriage, persuaded the fathers not to impose such a law, asserting it to be a grave occasion for fornication. This opinion was upheld: and thus it was placed not as a necessity, but in the will of each individual. 

<margin>First response.</margin>
To this history, it is first answered that it is not recorded among the acts of the Council, but stands only on the authority of Cassiodorus. Indeed, it is a wonder if this were true, for in the third canon of the same council, where priests are forbidden to have a "strange woman" staying with them—unless perhaps it were a mother, sister, grandmother, or aunt—no mention of a wife was made among those excepted. But nevertheless, so that we do not reject the authority of history, a second response must be applied: namely, that only what we added in our conclusion is proven: that after the age of the Apostles, the observance of the sacred canons was overlooked due to the corrupted morals of priests, as we cited from Epiphanius. And because the Nicene synod was then thinking of recalling the priesthood to its ancient form, Paphnutius advised that it was better to turn a blind eye on account of the corrupt age, just as the Church does now with the Germans. And the same answer must be given to the canon of the Council of Gangra <note>An early regional council (c. 340 AD) that addressed extreme asceticism</note>, "If anyone discerns," in the same 28th Distinction, where it is ordered that priests who are unwilling to abstain are not for that reason to be barred from sacred rites.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>

And it is added "according to the definition of the sacred canons": where it is taught that it was already canonical before then. Now, Calixtus preceded the Nicene synod by a hundred years. ### Book Eight, Question VI.

<margin>Siricius.</margin>
This was confirmed by Pope Siricius (who is mistakenly thought by some to have been its first founder) in the year 388. His decree survives in the *Decretum Gratiani* <note>The "Decretum Gratiani" was the standard textbook of medieval Canon Law.</note> at Distinction 82, the canon beginning *Plurimos* <note>original: "can. Plurimos"</note>. 

<margin>Innocent I.</margin>
Later, in the year 408, Pope Innocent I stabilized the same sanction by his own decree in a letter to Exuperius, which is cited in the same Distinction under the canon *Proposuisti*. To these are added two canons on the same subject by Saint Gregory the Great: *Nullum* (Distinction 28) and *Ante triennium* (Distinction 31), in which he holily forbids anyone from being ordained as a subdeacon <note>The subdiaconate was the first of the "Major Orders" in the Western Church requiring a vow of celibacy.</note> unless they first profess a vow of perpetual chastity. There exist very many other testimonies on this matter, but it would be laborious and tiresome to gather them all here. This concludes our discussion on the institution of the Latin priests.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
Therefore, to move from here to the practice of the Greeks, the fifth and final conclusion of this article is: the Greeks not only rejected the Roman institution, but they embraced a practice for which they can find no permission whatsoever from either the Apostles or the Councils; indeed, it is entirely repugnant to all Church antiquity. For they do not merely initiate those into holy orders who are already bound to a wife, but they actually admit no one to that same order unless, upon being asked, he replies that he is married. In this, they follow the error of Vigilantius <note>Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who opposed clerical celibacy and the veneration of relics; Jerome wrote a famous polemic against him.</note> to the letter. Jerome, in his letter to Riparius—cited by us at the start of this question—laments this very thing: namely, that they would appoint no one as a priest unless they were not living in continence. ¶ So that these matters may be clearly revealed, let us begin with the canon *Quoniam* (Distinction 31), which we brought forward in our second argument in favor of the Greeks. This canon is found among the decrees of the Sixth Synod of Constantinople <note>Also known as the Trullan Council or the Quinisext Council (692 AD), which established many of the distinct laws of the Eastern Orthodox Church.</note>. If this decree possessed the synodal authority of the Church—as Gratian and those who judge it at face value believe—it would fight vehemently against our third conclusion. It would also offer a great defense to heretics who prefer the Greek institution to the Roman one and argue that it should be adopted by the Latins. Therefore, we have deemed it highly worthwhile not to let this pass without a critical examination <note>original: "absque censura"</note>: namely, so that we may weigh how much this Greek custom opposes the sacred institutions of the Apostles. It is necessary first to note the words of the canon which follow: "Since we have learned that it has been handed down in the order of the Roman canon that those who are ordained as deacons or priests must confess that they will no longer have intercourse with their wives; we, following the ancient canon of Apostolic diligence and the 

<column-break/>

constitutions of holy men, will that legal marriages shall remain in force from now on: in no way dissolving the unions with their wives, or depriving them of their mutual familiarity at the appropriate time." And further down: "Neither shall they be forced to profess chastity at the time of their profession, [namely] that they must abstain from familiarity with a legal wife. Likewise, it is necessary that those who minister at the altar, during the time of the offering of the sacred mysteries, be continent in all things: so that they may obtain from God what they simply ask for." ¶ Gratian says that all these things are to be understood as applying to the Eastern priests. However, he should not have let the matter pass without a sharper critique. Since it was not too much trouble to hear all the words of the canon, let it not be tedious to weigh each point to see how much strength it has: for if they are looked at more deeply, they clearly prove themselves to be false. Indeed, others before us have not hesitated to affirm that this same canon is profane, full of insolence and impudence, and published by those who were open enemies of the chastity of Roman priests. First among these was Albertus Pighius, a man of 

<margin>Albertus Pighius.</margin>
exceptional skill and erudition in defending the Roman Church. He attempted to undermine the authority of that Synod with no small arguments: specifically, that it undeservedly condemned Pope Honorius <note>Pope Honorius I (d. 638) was posthumously condemned by the Sixth Ecumenical Council in a controversy over the "One Will" of Christ (Monothelitism).</note> for the same heresy for which it had condemned Sergius. It also pronounced the person of Origen <note>An early Christian theologian whose works were condemned centuries after his death.</note> to be a heretic, who, although he fell into some errors, is not truly considered to have been stubborn in his zeal against the Church. For my part, I do 

<margin>The critique of Pighius is rejected.</margin>
not support Pighius entirely, nor did I intend merely to oppose him here, as this is not the place for it. Nevertheless, even those who wrote apologies for that same Synod against him—one of whom was Francisco 

<margin>Francisco Torres.</margin>
Torres <note>Also known as Turrianus (c. 1509–1584), a Spanish Jesuit and theologian.</note>—cannot deny that Canon 13 is not only apocryphal <note>Meaning of doubtful authority or not genuinely from the Council it claims.</note> but also highly corrupt. For the words I just quoted are from that very canon. First of all, it is well known that canons of this kind were not published in that Sixth Synod, but rather—as Tarasius reports in the 4th act of the Seventh Synod—they were published by bishops who returned there five years later; or, as is more likely and can be gathered from Canon 3 of that same Sixth Synod, twenty-seven years after it ended. Therefore, although Pope Adrian later accepted the Sixth Synod insofar as it did not oppose Roman institutions, he is not considered to have given Catholic authority to these specific canons, since they were not even published in the Council itself.

[...they] were published, nor were they under a Roman legate. Furthermore, that the said canon possesses not only so much authority, but indeed no authority at all, is evident from its very appearance. For first of all, what kind of majesty would a Council have if, in the presence of a Roman legate, the presiding officer had sat and, after a Roman decree had been recited, immediately substituted a contrary judgment from that region? By saying: *Following the ancient canon of Apostolic diligence* <note>original: "Antiquum nos sequentes canonem Apostolicæ diligentiæ"</note>. For who is that canon? Or where does it exist? As for the claim in the gloss <note>A "gloss" is a marginal or interlinear commentary on a legal text.</note> that it refers to the word of Paul, *lest spouses defraud one another* <note>original: "nè coniuges se inuicem defraudent"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 7:5</note>, this by no means fits the text. Indeed, it adds, *and the constitutions of holy men* <note>original: "constitutiones sanctorum virorum"</note>: where the Council indicates the second Council of Carthage is being denoted, which is cited in Distinction 31, in the canon *Episcopos*, and in canon 84, *cùm in præterito*, and subsequently the fifth Council. But who would believe that any holy synod would prefer a provincial Council over an ecumenical Roman one?

<margin>
The previous assertion is strengthened.
</margin>
¶ But what clearly reveals the falsehood of that same canon is that no Council of Carthage decreed as is reported in that canon, but rather the complete opposite. For the second canon of the Second Council expressly commands—which was the opinion of Aurelius—that all prelates, priests, and levites <note>In this context, "levites" refers to deacons.</note> must be continent in all things, even regarding their wives, so that they may simply obtain what they ask from God. These are the express words. Therefore, this canon cited that one wrongly, adding that they should be continent *at the time of the offering* <note>The text Soto is critiquing claimed priests only had to abstain from sex when they were scheduled to perform the liturgy.</note>. For Paul had commanded this to all people, even laymen. But see how those

<margin>
A corrupted fragment of the fifth Council of Carthage.
</margin>
imposters corrupted the fifth Council of Carthage: Canon 3 of which, according to the letter, reads as follows: *When it was reported concerning the continence of certain clerics, even toward their own wives, it pleased the bishops, priests, and deacons, according to their own institutes, to also abstain from their wives.* The subdiaconate was omitted, which perhaps at that time was not considered a sacred order. However, regarding the phrase *according to their own institutes* <note>original: "secundùm propria instituta"</note>—which is understood literally according to the law appropriate to the priestly order, which from the Apostles until then was that no married man was initiated into sacred things unless he took a vow of chastity—they themselves prevaricated, saying: *When the time of sacrifice was imminent.* And for that reason, they added that their own priests should not be forced to profess chastity at the time of ordination, nor to abstain from their wives. This we have well noted above, as a testimony that such was the ancient custom of the church. See, therefore, how one is not permitted to 

<column-break/>

adore as an oracle whatever has been recorded among the decrees by Gratian <note>Johannes Gratian, the 12th-century compiler of the "Decretum," the foundational text of Canon Law.</note>, as is the custom of the Canonists. Rather, either he himself or his glossators ought to have consulted the histories at their roots, so that they might extract the marrow of the matters. But even if we were to grant freely that the same canon is legitimate, it nevertheless does not contain the rule that priests are not to be admitted to that office unless they were first married—as the custom of the Greeks holds—but only this: that they are not forced to vow chastity. To this accords another canon of the same synod which is cited in Distinction 32, the words of which are: *If any of those who approach the clergy wish to be joined to a woman by nuptial right, let him do this before the ordination of the subdiaconate.* And the subsequent canon of the fourth Council of Carthage: *Lectors, when they come to the years of puberty, shall be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.*

Heresy of the Nicolaitans.
</margin>
<margin>
Augustine
</margin>
¶ Deservedly, therefore, it is believed by many (as the same Torres <note>Francisco Torres, also known as Turrianus, a Spanish Jesuit and scholar.</note> says) that the Greeks contracted this custom from the Nicolaitan heretics. For their father, Nicholas—as the already cited Augustine says in his catalogue of heretics—since he had a very beautiful wife, who had likewise come under his suspicion of unchastity, and because he could not sufficiently drive suitors away from his house, persuaded his disciples to the common use of wives. These disciples indeed later corrupted many things into that error. Among these, they deceitfully substituted the seventeenth canon into the sixth book of the *Apostolic Constitutions* of Clement. A certain Greek author named Nicetas Pectoratus <note>An 11th-century monk and polemicist who defended Greek customs against the Latins.</note> later defended this canon and persuaded the Greeks of it. ### Question VI of the Eighth Book

...the text of Innocent III <note>Pope Innocent III (reigned 1198–1216) was one of the most influential popes of the Middle Ages, shaping much of canon law.</note> in the chapter *Cùm olim* concerning married clergy must be understood: namely, that on account of the "hardness" <note>original: "duritiam"; likely referring to the stubbornness or cultural persistence of the Greeks</note> of the Greeks, it was permitted to their priests not to take a vow of chastity; however, this does not mean they are compelled to be married. Therefore, to return to our Lutherans <note>The followers of Martin Luther and the burgeoning Protestant Reformation, whom Soto, a Catholic theologian, views as heretical.</note> from whom we departed, they can in no way protect themselves using the Greek custom.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
From these points, the arguments raised at the beginning of the question remain resolved. For the heretics summon the first argument from Paul, understanding those words, *A bishop must be the husband of one wife* <note>original: "Oportet episcopum esse vnius vxoris virum"; from 1 Timothy 3:2</note>, as if it were a command by which priests are forced to enter into marriages. But we have already shown above how differently the saints interpret this same word. For it was merely a prohibition against "digamists" <note>men who had married twice, usually after the death of a first wife</note> being accepted into the priesthood, and furthermore, due to the scarcity of priests, a permission that even married men might be initiated. But, as we have shown, this was granted only on the condition that, with the wife’s consent, a vow of chastity was made beforehand. ¶ With similar wickedness and misrepresentation, they interpret the fifth Apostolic Canon—which states that priests or deacons should not cast out their wives under the pretext of religion—as if it were a command that they must use them [sexually]; this is contrary to what we explained above. ¶ Likewise, by cutting short the words of a certain letter said to be from Clement <note>referring to the Pseudo-Clementines, writings once attributed to Pope Clement I</note>, they twist them to suit their own lust. For the words of the letter are: *Let such men be chosen for the offices of the Lord as ministers of the altar who knew their wives before their ordinations.* Regarding this, consider the absurdity: they claim 

<column-break/>

this is a command and a prohibition, so that no one may be initiated into holy orders before a marriage has been consummated. Others, to avoid this absurdity, 
<margin>Correction of another canon.</margin>
read it in the negative: *who did not know* <note>original: "non nouerint"</note>; yet it should only be read in the affirmative. However, it should not be read in a truncated way, but as "if they were not willing to remain continent forever." That is, if they were not virgins or continent men, but married, they may be received into the priesthood on the condition that they "knew" <note>a biblical euphemism for sexual relations</note> their wives only up until that time. It is as if he were saying: from then on, however, let them abstain from them, as we demonstrated in the third conclusion. ¶ Regarding the second 
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
argument, concerning the chapter *Quoniam*, it has already been sufficiently resolved. As for the third, which relies on the authority 
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
attributed to Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential 5th-century North African bishop and theologian.</note>—namely, where he appears to say that the continence of priests was added by the Church after the Apostolic institutions—it in no way fights against our third conclusion. This is partly because those are not actually the words of Augustine. Because the beginning of that chapter, *Cùm agitur*, is his, the "half-learned" <note>original: "scioli"</note> read the whole thing as if it were by Augustine, even though it belongs to Gratian <note>Gratian was the 12th-century compiler of the *Decretum*, the foundational collection of Canon Law. Soto is pointing out a common scholarly error where Gratian's commentary was mistaken for the ancient source he was quoting.</note>. Furthermore, Gratian says only that the continence of priests is a work of "counsel" <note>In Catholic theology, a "counsel" is a recommended spiritual practice, while a "precept" is a binding law.</note>: because it is a counsel that they become priests; but once they have been ordained, it then becomes a "precept" for them. However, as for his claim that it was added after the institutions of the Apostles—if he means that in the time of the Apostles it was not yet the custom—the authorities of the saints and the reasons brought forward for that same third conclusion contradict him, and they are therefore to be valued more highly.

Header: Friar Dominicus Soto, on Justice and Law

# BOOK NINE
## On Justice and Law.

### PREFACE.

In the previous book, where we entered into the subject of religion, we discussed vows: namely, regarding those things which a person promises to God of their own free will, and likewise concerning the priests who are devoted to performing divine sacrifices. It follows, therefore, according to the order set forth in that same place, that we should speak of those things which mortals are constrained by the bond of religion to give back to the same Greatest God: such as offerings and tithes, which are the substance and sustenance of priests; and subsequently concerning the vice of simony <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred things, such as church offices or sacraments.</note>, by which the entrances to the same holy church are often polluted. We cannot begin the treatment of offerings and tithes more aptly and subsequently more beautifully from any other place than from their root and foundation: namely, from sacrifices, which not only Christians but all mortals are bound to offer continually to their God. For sacrifice is the highest of offerings, to which all the others are referred. Therefore, we have deemed it worthwhile to prefix two questions regarding sacrifices: one in general, and the other in particular.

# FIRST QUESTION,
## On Sacrifice in General.

->St. Thomas, Summa Theologiae, Second Part of the Second Part, question 85.<-

### ARTICLE I.
->Whether sacrificing to God belongs to the law<-
->of nature.<-

<margin>First argument from the negative side.</margin>
THE FIRST article of the question concerning sacrifice is, therefore, whether the offering of sacrifices belongs to natural law. For it is argued in the negative. Those things which belong to natural law are common to all mortals; but

<column-break/>

offering sacrifices to God was not always common and uniform among all mortals. For Abel is read to have offered from his flock, but Cain from the fruits of the earth. Yet Melchizedek, as related in Genesis 14, offered bread and wine; others, however, offered other animals: therefore the offering of sacrifices does not belong to natural law. ¶ Second.
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
It is not permitted to believe that righteous men bypassed those things which the law of nature teaches; yet it is nowhere read of Adam that he offered a sacrifice, nor indeed of Isaac: although Wisdom itself <note>Referring to the Book of Wisdom in the Bible, which Soto treats as an authority.</note> in chapter 10 testifies concerning that same first parent that she [Wisdom] "led him out from his sin"; where the offering of a sacrifice would seem especially appropriate. ¶ Third.
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Sacrifices, as Augustine is the authority in *The City of God*, book 10, are offered as a kind of "signifying"; however, to signify—which fits words first (as the same author states in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2) and then things—is established by human pleasure <note>i.e., by human convention or choice rather than biological necessity.</note>: therefore sacrifices did not flow from the law of nature, but from human law. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that in every age there has always been some form of sacrificing among all mortals; and what all mortals have been taught, they learned with nature as their teacher.

SINCE the matter is evident in itself—that sacrifices, whether to [pagan] gods or the true God, have been most celebrated in custom and use among mortals since the very beginning of the world—it would have been superfluous to ask whether they existed. But the first question is established regarding their source and origin: namely, whether it is a human invention, or rather a teaching of nature. Where first of all it must not be overlooked that, just as the thing itself was always most solemn to the Latins, so too is the name most accepted by them. For sacrifice <term>sacrificium: "the making of a sacred thing"</term> is the same as the "making of a sacred thing" <note>original: "factio sacri"</note>; and to sacrifice <term>sacrificare: "to do sacred things"</term> is the same as "to do sacred things" <note>original: "sacra facere"</note>. Wherefore, as St. Thomas knowingly noted in article 3 of the present question, sacrifice is not exactly the same as an offering. For whatever is offered in the Church is called an offering <term>oblatio</term>, even if nothing is done to the thing itself—such as when coins, or bread, or other things are offered. However, a sacrifice does not occur unless something is performed upon the things themselves offered to God. Such as

<meta>Following the introduction to Book 9, Dominicus de Soto begins the first question regarding the nature of sacrifice. Having established that he will cover offerings, tithes, and the priesthood, he now seeks to prove that sacrifice is not merely a religious tradition, but a fundamental requirement of natural law for all human societies.</meta>

[page 711]
# Question I of Book Nine.

What animal sacrifices were to the ancients, the blessing, breaking, and consuming of the holy bread is to us; for this is what it means "to perform sacred rites." <note>original: "sacra facere." Soto is connecting the Latin word for sacrifice with the liturgical actions of the Mass.</note> Therefore, among the pagan nations, besides the priests who offered sacrifices, there were "sacrificers" who carried out those duties.
<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> Sacrifice is, therefore, the specific duty of the priesthood. ¶ To the question, then, we respond with a single conclusion: The offering of sacrifices is not only a matter of divine and human law, but it is also among those things established within the law of nature. <term>Law of nature (ius naturae)</term> <note>Universal moral principles that can be discovered through human reason alone, independent of specific religious revelation.</note>
<margin>Proof.</margin> This is proven as follows. Natural reason itself, acting as a teacher through the things a person experiences within themselves, clearly teaches that man is subject to some higher power. For the miseries, hardships, and calamities by which he is incessantly afflicted remind him that help must be brought to him from elsewhere—that is, from above. Thus, he feels that someone exists on high whose help he needs; and whatever that may be, all men hold it to be God. Furthermore, from the very nature of things, he learns that these earthly <note>original: "sublunaria," referring to the world below the moon.</note> things are subject to the same place because they receive the influence of the heavens; and by the same reasoning, the earth is subject to the other elements, as it is aided by their dew and air. Consequently, man learns that he owes subjection and honor to God, by whose help he lives. However, the mode of expression suitable for a sensory human being is that he should not only offer the reverence he owes to God internally in his soul, but also exhibit the same externally through sensible signs. Therefore, taught and warned by this natural reason, all mortals—by whatever reasoning they have known God—offer sacrifices to Him as a sign of due reverence and subjection. Just as among us humans it is the duty of subjects to offer gifts to their lords as an acknowledgment of their lordship, so too do we understand this very act under the name of "sacrifice" in the present context. Our conclusion follows logically: namely, that the offering of sacrifices belongs to the law of nature. And one should note the persuasion of this conclusion: it proceeds not only regarding the internal sacrifice offered in the mind, but also the external one. For although the true worship of God (who is the inspector of spirits and hearts) consists primarily within the heart—according to Psalm 50: *A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit*—which both Christ himself testifies in John 4, saying, *The hour is coming and is now here when true worshippers will worship in spirit and truth*, and also <margin>Paul.</margin> the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 14: *I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind*—nevertheless, since we are bodily beings, we ought to worship Him with both parts of our humanity.
<margin>Corollary.</margin> ¶ From these points, it is certainly gathered that as far as God’s knowledge is concerned, an external sa-

<column-break/>

crifice is not necessary, nor indeed is vocal prayer, as is the case among men, to whom the hearts of others are known only through external signs. Nor is external worship praised except insofar as it is referred to internal worship. However, it is not for that reason to be lightly esteemed. For it serves both to stir up and to testify to the affection of the mind. Therefore, it does not lack its own outstanding merit. For through these things which overflow from the soul, we pay what is owed to God according to our nature. Therefore, it was holily instituted that divine matters should be celebrated publicly and with renown in temples. ¶ Now, someone might argue against the reasoning of the conclusion as follows: Natural reason, although it warns us of our defects, does not teach us that help comes to us from a higher principle than natural causes. For if you consult only natural light, natural philosophers have taught that as far as the body is concerned, we are provided for by nature through the celestial spheres; as far as the mind's knowledge is concerned, through intellectual light; but as far as our emotions are concerned, through our own free will.
<margin>Solution.</margin> The response is that when natural reason is purged of all clouds, it clearly shows that these natural aids are not sufficient for us to heal all the miseries we suffer in body and soul; and thus, at least in a general way, it points to another superior cause which men hold to be God. Even if some nations are found so barbarous that they recognize only the heavens or other lower protections, they still pay divine honors—and subsequently sacrifices—to the sun or some other creature. ¶ The conclusion, therefore, is so well known by the light of natural reason that there has never been a nation that did not worship God, possess priests, and offer sacrifices. For I am accustomed to think of these two pairs upon which every republic has always stood: namely, sacrifice and priesthood; the law and the governor. For the goal which the founder of a republic usually sets before the eyes of the citizens first was God, whom the people should venerate and from whom they should seek aid. Soon after, they instituted sacrifices by which He would be worshipped. Then they established laws consistent with that same religion, and subsequently magistrates, in whose hands the custody of the laws would be placed. For this is how Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> records that the famous Numa, the second King of the Romans, established the republic. Hence <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle, in the last chapter of the 6th book of the *Ethics*, <note>Soto likely refers to the *Politics* here, where Aristotle discusses the essential roles in a city-state, though he cites the *Ethics*.</note> counts among the magistrates without whom a republic cannot stand the priests who perform the public rites.

<summary>Soto argues that offering sacrifice is a requirement of natural law because humans instinctively recognize their dependence on a higher power. He explains that while God primarily seeks internal devotion, humans need external rituals and public priesthoods to express this reverence and maintain a stable society.</summary>

Here, he addresses specific objections and moves to the second article: whether sacrifice belongs to God alone.</meta>

[page 712]
# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right, ARTICLE II.

...must be dedicated to the duties of sacrifice; those who preside over these are called both "kings of the sacred rites" and "Supreme Pontiffs." <note>original: "reges sacrorum... Pontifices Maximi." Soto is referencing how ancient Roman and Greek societies combined political and religious leadership.</note> He repeats this in Book 7, chapter 8, where he places priests in the first rank of magistrates. And in the *Ethics*, Book 8, chapter 9, alluding to the reasoning of our conclusion, he says that ancient sacrifices were traditionally performed after the gathering of the harvest. ¶ Furthermore, if you examine both our own histories and secular ones, you will see that from the very beginning of the world, Abel, Noah, and Melchizedek offered oblations and sacrifices under the law of nature. And even before the written Law <note>The Mosaic Law or Torah.</note> was given, Abraham and Jacob did the same. Additionally, in sacred history (Genesis 47), there is a record of the Egyptian priests, who were distinguished by royal privileges.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is responded that the offering of sacrifices, if considered in a general sense, has always been common to all nations. However, the fact that they used these specific rites or those ones was a matter of human constitutions, based on the specific knowledge of God that each nation attained. For it was by this reasoning that we said in the previous and second books that human laws are derived from the law of nature—specifically, through the "determination" of a general principle into specific forms. <term>Determination (determinatio)</term> <note>A legal concept where a general natural principle (e.g., "crimes must be punished") is given a specific shape by human law (e.g., "the punishment for theft is a fine").</note> For it is a law of nature that wrongdoers should be punished; but that they should be punished in this way or that way is enacted by human law according to the character of each nation. The same applies to worship and sacrifices.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ And by this, the third argument is answered: namely, that it is natural for man to signify his inner concepts; but doing so with these particular words or signs is according to the pleasure and custom of each nation.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second, the response is that there should be no doubt that Adam and Isaac, just like the other righteous men, offered sacrifice—especially since Adam’s own fault was known to him, as was Isaac’s original fault. According to Gregory, <note>Pope Gregory the Great.</note> among the ancient fathers, this fault was remitted through the offering of sacrifices. However, it was not necessary for every single instance to be recorded in sacred history. And perhaps this was intentional. For since sin began in Adam, he is not named as an offerer of a sanctifying victim; instead, his sons Abel and Cain are named, in whom the disparity of sacrifices—which has always existed between those pleasing and displeasing to God—was noted. As for the sacrifice that Isaac might have offered, there is perhaps no record in the scriptures because he himself was offered as a sacrifice by his father, serving as a "prognostic" <note>A prophetic type or foreshadowing.</note> of the victim Christ, who was the peak and root of all things.

<column-break/>

### Whether sacrifice should be offered to God alone.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a figure kneeling in prayer or contemplation before a simplified altar or landscape.</image-desc>SINCE we have already said that sacrifices are owed by us to God, whose help we need, 
<margin>First argument.</margin>
it is argued that he is not the only one to whom we should offer sacrifice. Holy men, according to the word of Peter in the Second Epistle, are made "sharers of the divine nature." Furthermore, angels are called "sons of God," as is clear in Job 1. Therefore, it is fitting to offer sacred rites to both.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: Greater honor is owed to them than to earthly princes; but men grant honors and offer gifts to princes; therefore, it is lawful for sacrifices to be made to the saints. This is especially true since the Church builds shrines, temples, and altars to them.
¶ On the contrary is that verse from Exodus 22: "Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be put to death, except to the Lord alone."

<margin>Negative conclusion.</margin>
**TO** this question, we respond with a simple negative conclusion. It is lawful for no one except the one Supreme God to immolate sacrifices.

<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Beyond the cited testimony, the conclusion is proven by a threefold reasoning. The first is easily gathered from what was said above. For it was stated that exterior sacrifice must be offered as a testimony of that interior sacrifice which is in the soul. Exterior religion serves this purpose above all: the soul dedicates itself as a sacrifice to the one in whom it recognizes its protection and help to be situated. That one is God alone; therefore, sacrifices are owed to Him alone. This final premise is proven thus: Man, like every other thing besides God, recognizes that he emanates from some principle and tends toward some ultimate end, which is his supreme happiness. God alone is both this principle and, consequently, this end. Thus, from Him as from the first fountain, we have received whatever we possess, and we are aided toward that end for which we strive. To Him alone, therefore, is it lawful to pour out sacrifices.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Added to this is a second reason: it is only lawful to sacrifice to the one to whom it is lawful to run with our prayers and petitions as the one upon whom we and our salvation—of both body and soul—depend. By this reasoning, we pray to God alone to have mercy on us and bring us help.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
¶ A third reason is found in the example we see among men. For to the King, the supreme head of the state, those honors are dedicated which it would be a crime of lèse-majesté to grant to another, inferior person. <term>Lèse-majesté (laesae maiestatis)</term> <note>A "crime against majesty" or treason; specifically, treating someone else as if they held the supreme power of the monarch.</note> For he must possess such excellence above all citizens that he...

<summary>Dominicus de Soto argues that while the impulse to sacrifice is a universal law of nature, the specific forms it takes are determined by human culture. He concludes that sacrifice is a unique act of worship reserved exclusively for God, as it acknowledges Him as the ultimate source and end of human existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of sacrifice. On the previous page, Soto argued that sacrifice is a natural obligation for humans. Here, he defines sacrifice as an act of worship reserved exclusively for God (latria) and addresses why God, who needs nothing, requires these external signs.</meta>

# Book Nine, Question I.

...to make anyone equal to Him cannot be done without injury to His majesty.

<margin>Paul</margin>
¶ This conclusion therefore teaches us that to sacrifice is an office of the worship of <term>latria</term> <note>original: "cultus latriæ." From the Greek *latreia*, this refers to the highest form of worship and absolute submission that is owed to God alone.</note>, which is the service and subjection owed to God alone. St. Paul took great care to remind us of this in Romans 1, where he rebuked the most impudent idolatry of the Gentiles. He detested their altars, their groves, and their subsequently wicked sacrifices; though these honors were due by right to the immortal God alone, they bestowed them upon lowly creatures.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Furthermore, this is the conclusion of St. Augustine in Book 10 of *The City of God*. In chapter 4 and those following, he explains this brilliantly, where he introduces the reasoning of St. Thomas Aquinas. For God does not demand our sacrifices because He has any need of them. As David testifies, God has no need of our goods; rather, He demands them for the sake of their meaning. First, so that through external things we may express the true sacrifices of the heart. Hence, he says, "a visible sacrifice is a sacrament—that is, a sacred sign—of an invisible sacrifice." <note>original: "sacrificium visibile, inuisibilis sacrificij sacramentum est." Augustine argues that the outward ritual is only meaningful as a symbol of the inward devotion.</note> Internal sacrifices must be protestations by which we profess that He is the one upon whom our salvation, the sum of all things, and ultimately our highest happiness depends. Therefore, when we sin, confessing with the Prophet that we have sinned against Him alone, we bruise and humble our hearts, and we offer up our prayers to Him like the sweetest incense. The sacrifices offered under the Old Law, involving victims and incense, were certainly signs of this internal sacrifice.

<margin>Psalm 50</margin>
Here, that holy father [Augustine] excellently interprets that verse of the penitent David:
> If you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it; but you will not be delighted by burnt offerings. The sacrifice for God is a broken spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise. <note>This is Psalm 51:16-17 in modern English Bibles, though Soto refers to it as Psalm 50 following the Vulgate numbering.</note>

For the prophet warns us that God does not want sacrifices for the reasons the common people think He does—namely, that He takes pleasure in the slaughter of cattle or that He needs those animals for food. He strikes down these insane thoughts in another Psalm, saying:
> If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world is mine, and the fullness thereof. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? 

It is as if He were saying: "I cannot be hungry; and therefore I have no need of your bulls and goats for food. Nor, if I could be hungry, would I need your nourishment, for the world is mine and everything in it."

He does not, therefore, want sacrifices for that reason. But because He does not entirely reject or despise them, but holds them pleasing as signs of a spiritual sacrifice, he adds: "The sacrifice for God is a broken 

<column-break/>

spirit," etc.

<margin>The reason for ancient sacrifices</margin>
Through these points, the reason for the ancient sacrifices is illuminated—specifically the immolation of animals, the <term>scapegoat</term> <note>original: "emissio hirci." This refers to the ritual of the Day of Atonement where a goat was sent into the wilderness bearing the sins of the people (Leviticus 16).</note>, and the rest. The reason, I say, was that they were not offered as simple things in themselves, but as signs.

<margin>The first doubt</margin>
¶ However, two remaining doubts arise from these points. The first concerns the most holy Sacrifice of the Altar <note>The Eucharist or the Mass.</note>, which in truth is not offered by us merely as a sign, but as a thing of inestimable price. Indeed, we offer God Himself to God as the price for our debts, as we shall discuss in the next question.

<margin>The solution</margin>
To this, it is responded that the nature of this immense <term>host</term> <note>original: "hostiæ." From the Latin for "victim" or "sacrifice."</note> is far different from the others; for it is a commemoration of the price of human redemption. Nevertheless, it is no less a sign of our servitude, by which we profess that our entire race had fallen through transgression against God and was saved by His benefit, and thus called back into His grace by such an expiation. But more on this shortly.

<margin>The second doubt</margin>
¶ The second doubt is that the customs of Christians seem to contradict the present conclusion. For it is our custom to offer gifts to the Virgin Mother of God and to other saints, and to have designated places where, out of devotion, we offer ourselves and our goods to various saints. This is even done under the form of sacrifice, for we burn incense to the saints, light candles, and do other things that bear the image of sacrifice. The responses to the arguments will dissolve this doubt.

<margin>To the first argument</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is responded that although the name of "divinity" is communicated to angels and saints through the grace of God—according to the scripture, *I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High*—this refers to those adopted into the order of sons. However, this is not divinity by nature or equality with God. Therefore, it is not right to bestow divine honors on anyone besides Him, and thus one must not perform sacrifices to them for the reason already stated.

<margin>To the second argument</margin>
¶ From this follows the solution to the second argument: namely, that although greater things may be offered to human princes than those which were anciently offered to God (excepting the Sacrifice of the Altar), the value of a sacrifice is not judged by the material thing being offered, but by the significance of worship and subjection. And therefore, just as that obedience and veneration by which humans are subjected to God can be paid to no one but Him, neither can any ceremony of sacrifice.

<margin>To the third argument</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third argument it is responded that from this confession of truth, it by no means follows that not only heretics,

...others also believe, who do not wish to be judged by that name, that no image of idolatry is cloaked by this religion because we offer gifts to the divine [saints]: for in the first place, those are not sacrifices, but mere offerings. For it is lawful to offer the true sacrifice of the altar to God alone. 

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence, Augustine says in Book 8 of *The City of God*: "We do not establish priestly temples for the martyrs, because they themselves are not our God, but their God is our God." For this reason, the priest does not say, "I offer sacrifice to you, Peter or Paul," but we say to God, "Accept the offering which we offer to You" <note>original: "Accipe oblationem quam tibi offerimus." This is a standard part of the Roman Canon of the Mass.</note>. Moreover, the memory of the saints is made in the Mass, both because we give thanks to God for their victories, and because we appoint them as our advocates and intercessors before that same God of ours. Furthermore, even the simple small gifts we offer to the saints are directed toward the praise and honor of God; for He loves to be praised in His saints, insofar as they are His children already received into their eternal inheritance. Just as you honor a king by honoring his servants. In short, just as we honor the saints with the adoration of <term>dulia</term> <note>From the Greek *douleia* (service); in theology, this refers to the veneration given to saints and angels, as distinct from the worship due to God.</note> alone, and not <term>latria</term> <note>Worship and absolute submission owed to God alone.</note>, and we knock by prayer, not so that they might have mercy on us [as God does], but so that they might pray for us: in the same interval, we make offerings to them, not sacrifices.

<margin>It is permitted to ask for and provide alms in honor of the Virgin and the saints.</margin>
¶ Hence it happens that those err absurdly who deny that it is permitted to either ask for or provide alms in honor of the Virgin and the saints. For the first is nothing other than the virtue of gratitude, if we confer alms out of love for the saints themselves because they are our intercessors with God, so that we may repay their office of charity with an equal one. And besides, the alms which we pay in honor of a saint, just as has been said of other offerings, redound to the honor of God.

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether the offering of sacrifices is an act of a special virtue.<-

After seeing to the substance, object, and end of sacrifice, it is asked how widely it extends. First, in this article, as much as pertains to acts: namely, whether all works of all virtues are sacrifices. And following in the next article, as much as pertains to persons who are obligated to sacrifices: whether all mortals are obligated to this. It is asked, therefore, whether offering sacrifices

<column-break/>

belongs to a special virtue. For the argument is made in the negative. First, from Paul. 

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Indeed, he admonishes us in Romans 12: "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God," etc. And in the last chapter of Hebrews: "Do not forget beneficence and communion; for with such sacrifices is God won over." <note>original: "hostijs promeretur Deus." Soto is using the Vulgate translation of these verses.</note> But to present the members of the body as a sacrifice pertains to the disposition of the body, the mortification of which is done through many virtues: namely, through abstinence and fasting, through the continence of chastity, and through fortitude in martyrdom. And likewise beneficence, which is a duty of charity, is exercised through mercy and through liberality: therefore, to sacrifice is not the office of a singular virtue, but of all virtues.

<margin>Argument 2. Augustine</margin>
¶ To this is added, secondly, Augustine in Book 10 of *The City of God*: where he says every work that is done so that we may cling to God in holy society is a true sacrifice. 

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Add thirdly that everything which is offered to God is considered a sacrifice. But we offer to Him both devotion and prayer with the mind, and also physical things: such as tithes, first-fruits, and burnt offerings, etc., which are duties of various virtues.

¶ On the contrary is the fact that singular precepts are not given except concerning the acts of a singular virtue: and in Leviticus, singular precepts are placed concerning sacrifices.

<margin>The error of the Lutherans.</margin>
It is now more important to know the truth of this question on account of the Lutherans than it was in times past. For they deny, no less obstinately than impudently, that there is any singular sacrifice of the Christian family belonging to a certain virtue and worship: but they say all duties of the virtues are nothing other than certain sacrifices. And thus in Christianity they recognize no singular order of priests, but they say all Christians of both sexes are priests indiscriminately, according to the word of Peter in his first Canonical epistle, calling everyone a "royal priesthood." <note>1 Peter 2:9. This is the doctrine of the "Priesthood of all Believers" championed by Martin Luther.</note> And accordingly, they deny that the most holy sacrament of the altar is a sacrifice. Concerning the refutation of this error, our next question, which follows, is established here.

¶ So that this article may be the foundation for that same question, the response to the present question is given in three conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First: The offering of sacrifices, according to its own proper definition, is an act of a special virtue: namely, of Religion. It obtains its praise from the fact that it is done for divine reverence. For in this, as was said in Book 2, the proper definition of religion consists.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second: All duties of all virtues are sacrifices in a "participative" sense...

# Book Nine, Question I.

<margin>The reason for both conclusions.</margin>
...participatively and from the outside, insofar as they are directed toward divine honor and worship through the virtue of religion, they are certain kinds of sacrifices. Both conclusions are made clear by an example. Individual virtues receive their specific identity from their own proper objects: for example, courage is one thing, and justice is another, and so on for the rest. However, when they are directed toward God through charity, they participate in a certain quality of charity; yet charity still has its own proper object and act, which is to love God for the sake of His goodness, and subsequently to love one's neighbor for that same reason. Similarly, among the vices, theft is a sin in itself; however, when it is committed for the sake of adultery, it contracts the stain of that same vice, as <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Aristotle is the authority in the 5th book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, in a like manner, the proper object of religion is the excellence of God and His omnipotence in helping us, which we testify to through sacrifices and offerings: signifying that we are subject to Him, and that as our Lord, such honors are His due. For this reason, we establish our hearts as altars for Him, upon which, through penance, we offer Him the blood-stained victims of our sins <note>original: "cruentas peccatorum victimas." A metaphor for the "killing" of one's own sins through the pain of repentance.</note>; through courage, we consecrate ourselves to Him by martyrdom for His truth; through the fervor of charity, we burn incense to Him; and likewise, through mercy, we help the poor for His love; and through temperance, we mortify our bodies. When, I say, we direct all these things toward the worship and honor of God through the virtue of religion, they participate in the nature of sacrifices. And in this way, we must understand Augustine in the cited book of *The City of God*, chapter 4, where he gathers several of these examples. And that passage from the end of Hosea: "We will render the calves of our lips" <note>original: "Reddemus vitulos labiorum nostrorum." Hosea 14:2, meaning praise offered instead of animal sacrifice.</note>. And in the last chapter of Hebrews: "Through Him (that is, Christ) let us offer a sacrifice of praise always to God," that is, celebrating His name with the fruits of our lips. ¶ <margin>Third conclusion.</margin> **Third conclusion.** Nevertheless, there are certain actions and duties that have no praise from any other source except that they are performed for the sake of signifying divine reverence. And these are most properly called "sacrifices." For example: giving alms, or acting temperately and courageously, would be virtues in themselves even if they were not made sacrifices through the virtue of religion. However, that ancient slaughter of animals, the sprinkling of blood, and the burning of fat—if you remove the reason for their symbolic meaning—would have no quality of virtue in themselves. And therefore, these are called sacrifices in a specific sense, as if deserving no other praise than that of religion. <margin>To the arguments made.</margin> ¶ The arguments brought to the contrary are therefore dissolved through

<column-break/>

these three conclusions. For they prove that the duties of other virtues are not sacrifices internally and by their own nature, but externally because of their relationship to the reverence of God. Nevertheless, despite this, the task of sacrificing is the duty of the specific virtue of religion.

### ARTICLE IV.
### Whether all mortals are bound to offer sacrifices to God.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'P' with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>
After seeing how the virtue of sacrificing governs the other virtues, as if directing them toward its own end, it remains to see how far it extends to all mortals. It is argued <margin>First argument.</margin> nonetheless from the negative side. Priests <term>sacerdotes</term> <note>Literally "givers of sacred things."</note> derive their name from the fact that they are assigned to offer sacrifices, but not everyone is a priest; therefore, the task of sacrificing does not fall upon everyone. ¶ <margin>Argument 2.</margin> **Secondly:** To sacrifice is characteristic of the people acting specifically under the Law of God. For as the Apostle says in Romans 3: <margin>Paul.</margin> "Whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are under the Law." The Old Law was where the people were first instructed to sacrifice to the true God, as is clear throughout the book of Leviticus; therefore, the gentiles, who live by the law of nature alone, are bound to no sacrifices. ¶ To the contrary is the fact that to revere and venerate God with sacrifices is a matter of the law of nature; however, the whole of mankind is bound to those things which are of the law of nature.

---

The question is answered with four conclusions under a distinction. For there is <margin>Two kinds of sacrifice.</margin> a two-fold kind of sacrifice: one is internal, which is immolated in the mind; the other is external, which is performed outwardly. And this external kind is again two-fold, as said above: one which is so specifically a sacrifice that it has no praise from any other source; the other which is indeed a duty of virtue in itself, though it becomes a sacrifice when directed toward the reverence of God—such as all the duties of the virtues. ¶ There is, therefore, <margin>First conclusion.</margin> a **first conclusion:** Not only the ancients under the Written Law <note>The Law of Moses.</note> and Christians under the Law of Grace, but the whole of mankind is bound by the law of nature to the internal sacrifice of the mind. For there exists no living person who, insofar as they are a creature of God and created for Him as their supreme end, is not bound to [direct] that...

He concludes that all humans, regardless of their specific religious law, are bound by nature to offer the "internal sacrifice" of the mind to God.</summary>

...to exhibit within that reverence which is owed to the first principle of things and the supreme end. <note>The "first principle" refers to God as the origin of all existence, and the "supreme end" refers to God as the ultimate goal of human life.</note>

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Second conclusion.** Regarding those sacrifices which take on the virtue of religion through their meaning alone, only those who live under the written law of God are bound to them: as the ancient Fathers <note>The "Fathers" here likely refers to the Old Testament Patriarchs.</note> were bound to their specific number of sacrifices, while we are bound to our unique one.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
For that passage of Paul cited in Romans 3 proves this, for that law only bound its own subjects, just as our law binds us.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion.** Nevertheless, those living by natural law alone <note>The "law of nature" refers to moral truths discoverable by human reason without the need for divine revelation.</note>, in whatever age they have lived or will live, are always bound by the same law to offer some sacrifice. By this act, according to the legitimate knowledge they are bound to have of the one First Cause, they may profess themselves to be subject to Him and owe Him divine honors. Through the profession of this sacrifice under the law of nature, the stain of original sin would be washed away for them. This conclusion is manifest: since by the very fact that one knows the one first parent of all things, he ought to understand that he is subject to Him, and thus is bound to worship Him not only in mind but also in body. This is especially true because God never left the human race destitute of a remedy for washing away original fault, unless a blindness of mind prevented some mortals from perceiving it.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Fourth conclusion.** Regarding sacrifices which are so called "from the outside"—that is, all works of the virtues—everyone is bound to offer these to God, either by what is called "actual" or "virtual" relation. For everyone is bound to resolve to serve the one First Cause and the supreme end of all things by turning away from evil and following good; and consequently to offer all their duties and services to the same one to whom all good things must be acknowledged as received. However, this is not the place to dispute these matters from higher principles; they are mentioned by us here only so that, by organizing the text of Saint Thomas <note>Refers to St. Thomas Aquinas, the medieval theologian upon whose work Soto is commenting.</note> into conclusions, we might pave the way for the next question, which concerns our own particular sacrifice. ¶ And by these points, the initial argument is answered. For insofar as humans refer the duties of all virtues to God, Peter the Apostle called all Christians "priests"; yet the name fits those more properly who perform actual sacrifices—that is, who carry out those ceremonies in which divine worship consists.

<margin>To the arguments made.</margin>
¶ The arguments from the beginning of the question prove this much: that not every individual mortal offers sacrifices in the strict sense; and therefore they do not

<column-break/>

stand in the way of the definition of the present question. Namely, it is established that by the law of nature, every commonwealth was bound—through its own priests whom it ought to appoint to this duty—to offer some kind of sacrifice to God, the Best and Greatest.

### SECOND QUESTION: On the ineffable sacrifice of the altar in particular.

#### ARTICLE I.

##### Whether the most holy Sacrament of the altar is truly a sacrifice.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'C' containing a figure in a landscape, possibly a prophet or scholar pointing towards the text.</image-desc>Since it has been sufficiently demonstrated that the rite of sacrifice belongs to religion by natural law, it follows that we should descend to the ineffable victim <note>original: "hostiam." In a liturgical context, this is the "Host" of the Eucharist.</note> of the Christians. We ask first: is there any particular sacrifice belonging to the Christian family, and is that sacrifice the most holy sacrament of the altar?

<margin>First argument.</margin>
For Paul seems to oppose such a confession in Hebrews 10. Comparing Christ, our supreme priest, with the ancient priests who frequently offered a multitude of victims daily, he says: "But this man [Christ], offering one victim for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God." and immediately following: "For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified." And consequently: "For those of us who sin willfully after receiving knowledge of the truth, there is no longer left a victim for sins." By these assertions, he seems to testify that there was only one true victim, which Christ offered on the cross; and thus the sacrament of the altar is not a sacrifice. Otherwise, there would exist not one, but many victims left by Christ for us when we sin.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Add secondly that since this ceremony of the altar is nothing other than a memory of that passion of Christ, as His command demonstrates: "Do this in memory of me"...
