### Book Nine, Question II

->Zz 3<-

It seems to be a boldness not only of speech but of rashness to call that a sacrifice; for a memory of a thing is not a new event, but a representation of an old one. Indeed, while we festively celebrate the memory of the Nativity <note>The birth of Christ/Christmas.</note> or the Resurrection, we do not consider that Christ is then being born or rising again. Therefore, neither while we offer Him on the altar is it permissible to imagine that He is then being crucified or dying; rather, we bring to memory the manner in which He once offered Himself.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ To this, thirdly: Christ did not offer Himself under the appearances of bread and wine; therefore, our sacrament is not a sacrifice, but a memory of a sacrifice.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Furthermore, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western Christianity.</note> says in *The City of God*, Book 10, Chapter 20, and *On the Trinity*, Book 4: "In the immolation of Christ, the priest offering and the offering itself are the same," which is not the case in the practice of the Mass.

¶ To the contrary is the solemn confession of the Church in the venerable Canon <note>The "Canon of the Mass" is the central, ancient prayer of the Eucharist, which Soto notes is "older than memory."</note>, which is older than any memory. For before the consecration of the venerable sacrament, the Holy Church maintains that she offers to the divine majesty "holy, unblemished sacrifices"; and immediately after the consecration, she protests that she offers to the same divinity a "pure victim, a holy victim, a spotless victim: the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of eternal salvation." <note>original: "hostiam puram, hostiam sanctam, hostiam immaculatam: panem sanctum vitæ æternæ, & calicem salutis æternæ."</note>

The most holy sacrament of the altar is so clear in our religion and confession of faith as being a sacrifice, that unless such great power were divinely permitted to the devil for the purpose of driving men mad, no Christian could be so foolish as to ever

<margin>Wycliffe.</margin>
deny it. Nevertheless, that Englishman Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English theologian and forerunner to the Reformation who questioned the Real Presence in the Eucharist.</note>, seized by a Satanic fury when he strove to abolish all ecclesiastical rites and sacraments, also attempted to demolish this one, which is full of divine majesty—both insofar as it is a sacrament and insofar as it is a sacrifice. Concerning this article, the

<margin>Waldenfis.</margin>
venerable Netter of Walden <note>Thomas Netter (c. 1375–1430), also known as Waldenfis, was an English Carmelite who wrote "Doctrinale Antiquitatum Fidei Ecclesiae Catholicae" against Wycliffe.</note> disputed excellently against him in his second book on the sacraments; and specifically on this point of whether it is a sacrifice, in chapters 31 and 32. Afterward, however, Luther—who swore diabolically to all of Wycliffe's words—denied that the same sacrament is a sacrifice.

<margin>Lutherus.</margin>
On this matter, he published a poisonous little book to which he gave the title, *On the Abrogation of the Private Mass*. <note>original: "De abroganda Missa priuata." Written by Martin Luther in 1521.</note> In this work, after he seemed to himself to have demonstrated the matter with the empty reasons we just reported, he attacked us with bitter taunts, saying that we who call the sacrament of the altar a sacrifice are stained by

<column-break/>

idolatrous impiety. Indeed, with the same word, he says we deny that Christ died only once. For he says that Christ willed His own death to be the unique sacrifice. He then infers that there is no specific sacrifice in the Church of Christ, but that all Christian works—namely alms, prayers, offerings, and the duties of the other virtues—are our sacrifices. And since a priest <term>sacerdos</term> <note>The Latin word "sacerdos" (priest) is etymologically linked to "sacra faciens" (one who performs sacred rites/sacrifices).</note> is so called from the act of immolating a sacrifice, he subverts the entire ecclesiastical hierarchy by the same reasoning, denying that there are distinct ranks of bishops, priests, and laity. Instead, he says that as many as are Christians are priests, according to that passage in the first epistle of Peter, chapter 2: "But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, etc." Because of this, he claims anyone can offer their own sacrifice and minister the sacraments, even that of the altar.

¶ Against this most absurd heresy, I will not say merely that two conclusions are established, but rather they are shown to have been legitimately established by the Church. The first:

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The adorable sacrament of the altar is not only a sacrament, like the others, but is undoubtedly a victim and a sacrifice; and it is the unique one for the followers of Christ.

<margin>First proof.</margin>
The conclusion is proven, first of all, by natural law. For as we said in the previous question, there was never any republic of mortals which, according to the estimation it had of God or the gods, did not institute specific sacrifices so that it might be distinguished from another republic by that ritual above all. For this reason, there were certain sacrifices for the Athenians, others for the Spartans, and others for the Romans. So much so, that it was everywhere and always confessed by those four <note>Referring to the four groups or perhaps four pillars of society mentioned next.</note> that a republic consists of these things: sacrifice, priesthood, laws, and a governor. Since we, therefore, by the grace of God, are marked by such high knowledge of the true God, it is not only impious but even barbaric to doubt that there is a specific sacrifice for us in which our religion consists. Unless we confess this one of the altar, nothing remains among Christians that has the proper nature of a sacrifice. For indeed, other offerings—namely tithes and first-fruits—and in short, the rest of the works of virtue (as we said in the preceding question) are not sacrifices according to their own proper species, but by an extrinsic relationship: because through the virtue of religion, they are directed to the honor of God. But as for a sacrifice by which we properly worship God as a sign of subjection, if you take away this one of the altar, nothing remains.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Next, the second reason is taken from the law of Moses...

Having previously addressed the argument that the Mass is merely a "memory" of Christ's death, Soto now argues that the Christian religion requires a specific, ongoing sacrifice to be superior to the Old Law and to maintain its internal hierarchy.</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right,

...argument. For that law <note>The "Old Law" of the Hebrew Bible.</note> commanded a most numerous offering of sacrifices and victims, through which it both commended its own subjection to God and prefigured our own law. Therefore, unless you wish to place that law above ours in dignity, it is necessary that those who profess the Gospel have a specific sacrifice: and if we are to repeat it again and again, there is none properly so called except that of the altar.

<margin>Luther's Evasion.</margin>
¶ But indeed, Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the German theologian and central figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> responds that all these things prove there is some Gospel sacrifice; however, he says, this was nothing other than that which Christ offered once upon the altar of the cross.

<margin>Reply.</margin>
Yet this response in no way satisfies our reasoning. For truly a sacrifice, which is specific to a religion, ought to endure as long as the religion itself persists; however, that sacrifice of Christ in its own proper form <note>Meaning his physical death on Calvary.</note> is not repeated. For as Paul says, *Christ having died once, since he rises from the dead, now dies no more: Death shall no longer have dominion over him.* <note>A reference to Romans 6:9.</note> It was therefore necessary for a sacrifice to be instituted which the Christian religion might offer daily to its God, both for other benefits received from Him, and especially for that remarkable benefit of redemption. Otherwise, as we were saying, our law would be inferior and more obscure in this regard, not only than the Old Law, but even than the Law of Nature <note>The "Law of Nature" refers to the inherent sense of religious obligation and sacrifice found in all human cultures before formal revelation.</note>.

<margin>Third reason</margin>
¶ The third argument follows: Christ—as both the Psalmist prophesied and Paul interpreted—was a priest *according to the order of Melchizedek* <note>Melchizedek was a mysterious king and priest in Genesis 14 who offered bread and wine; he is viewed in Christian theology as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ's priesthood.</note>, who offered bread and wine. Since, therefore, on the cross he did not immolate these physical forms, but his own proper body in dying, it is the greatest proof that this which we—who are his members—offer daily under those same species <note>The appearances of bread and wine.</note>, is our legitimate sacrifice. For this reason, he called himself the *bread descending from heaven*. Moreover, as a sign of this, besides the Paschal Lamb (which the ancient fathers immolated once a year according to the command of the law in Exodus 12 as a figure of Christ's passion), they were also commanded in Numbers 28 to offer two unblemished lambs daily in the temple as a holocaust: namely, so that we might be taught that not only what Christ offered <note>on the cross</note>, but also what we offer daily, is a legitimate sacrifice.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
¶ In the fourth place, it is argued: Whoever, as we said a little earlier, denies that there is any specific sacrifice proper to our religion, must likewise altogether deny a specific order of priests and bishops—as Luther did. If this order were removed, the most beautiful

<column-break/>

ornament and beauty of the Church is confounded and thrown into disorder; how unbecoming this is to Christ's providence, there is no one (even one lacking in wit) who does not clearly see.

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
For since—as that most ancient and divine Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential early Christian philosopher who wrote on the "hierarchies" of angels and the church.</note> testifies in his book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*—the assembly of those in triumph <note>The saints in heaven.</note> is most beautifully arranged in hierarchies of angels, why, I ask, should the holy Church Militant <note>The Church on earth.</note>—which by prophetic testimony sits like a queen at the right hand of Christ clothed in variety—not be distinguished by a similar arrangement of orders and distinction of functions, as the same Dionysius most excellently gathered in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*?

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
The force of this reasoning is increased by the example of a civil commonwealth: which, since it ascends through distinct magistrates all the way to the king, stands as testimony that unless the Church were so arranged, it would not reflect the providence of Him who instituted it. Indeed, since God willed the world itself to consist of such a manifold variety of heavens, elements, and things, why would he have deprived his own Church of that same similar beauty?

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
Add to this that the Old Law—the shadow of the Gospel—was divinely instituted with distinct orders of priests and Levites, over whom a High Priest presided. If He honored the "shadow" with such dignity, why would he have dishonored the "truth" itself <note>The Gospel/Christianity.</note> with promiscuous confusion?

<margin>Last.</margin>
Since, in short, the gentiles <note>The non-Christian, pagan nations of antiquity.</note> had their own specific priests for their religion, why should these men deny that a specific rank and order of priests exists in ours, which alone is legitimate?

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Furthermore, there is the analogy of Paul in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 12, where he declares that just as the human body is joined together, so also is the Church by various members. Whence in Ephesians 4: *He gave some as Apostles, some as Prophets, others as Evangelists, others as pastors and Teachers: for the perfecting of the saints in the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.* Therefore, since it is clearly established that there is a singular order of priests in the church, it follows that there is also a specific sacrifice, which is their duty. Let us conclude, therefore, <gloss>that</gloss> just as all Christians are called priests by a general name according to Peter the Apostle because they offer the duties of virtues (which are called sacrifices in an external and common sense), so by antonomasia <note>A figure of speech where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name.</note>, those should be called priests by their proper office who immolate a singular and proper sacrifice.

¶ In addition to these reasons, there are the decrees of the most holy Church: namely, the most ancient in the first...

<summary>Soto argues that the Christian religion must have a unique daily sacrifice (the Mass) to fulfill the "order of Melchizedek" and to justify the existence of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, which reflects the divine order found in heaven and nature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s theological defense of the Eucharist. Having established that a religion requires a visible sacrifice to endure, he now turns to historical Church authorities—the Council of Nicaea, Pope Innocent III, and the Church Fathers—to prove that the Mass is not merely a symbolic memorial, but a "true sacrifice" where Christ is both the priest and the victim.</meta>

### Question II of the Ninth Book

<margin>*The Council of Nicaea.*</margin>
...decrees of the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church.</note>, as found in distinction 93, chapter *pervenit*. Its words are: "Neither rule nor custom has handed down that those who do not have the power of offering the sacrifice <note>Referring here to deacons.</note> should hand over the body of Christ to those who do offer it <note>Referring to priests.</note>."

<margin>*Innocent III.*</margin>
And Innocent III, in the Lateran Council <note>The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), which defined the doctrine of transubstantiation.</note>, as held in the chapter *firmiter* on the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith, says: "There is one universal church of the faithful, outside of which no one at all will be saved: in which the same Jesus Christ is both priest and sacrifice." <note>original: "Una est fidelium universalis ecclesia... in qua idem ipse sacerdos est & sacrificium Iesus Christus."</note> And lest you think this is only an allusion to his death, it is added: "Whose body and blood are truly contained in the sacrament of the altar under the species <note><term>Species</term>: the outward appearances of bread and wine (color, taste, texture) that remain after the substance has changed.</note> of bread and wine." This is as if to say: That sacrifice which he once offered in the form of flesh, we offer daily under the appearances of bread and wine.

<margin>*To the first argument.*</margin>
Therefore, to the first argument taken from Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, it is responded that the Apostle there is speaking entirely of the victim which Christ offered on the altar of the cross—namely, his own body dying in the form of flesh. This was indeed a unique event, and in an infinite way sufficient for the forgiveness of all sins. For this reason, it neither should nor can be repeated. Nevertheless, with this truth standing firm, that which we offer daily is also truly a sacrifice, insofar as it was instituted by Christ as a memorial of that same sacrifice.

<margin>*Ambrose.*</margin>
Hence Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> says on that same passage: "The victim was offered once, powerful enough for eternal salvation. What then of us? Do we not offer every single day? But we do so in remembrance of his death; and it is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because Christ was offered once. This sacrifice is the model of that one: it is the very same thing always. Therefore, this is the same sacrifice. Just as that which is offered everywhere is one body, and not many bodies." <note>original: "Hoc autem sacrificium exemplum est illius: idipsum semper idipsum: proinde hoc idem est sacrificium."</note> See how the sacrament is truly a sacrifice, and the same one that Christ offered.

¶ But from this arises the force of the second argument. This sacrament has nothing else to make it a sacrifice except that it is a commemoration of that one; however, a memory is not the real thing itself—otherwise, the memory of a birth would be a birth. If you say, as Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), whose writings shaped much of Western Christian thought.</note> says in his work *To Simplician*, that images are customarily called by the names of the things themselves;

<margin>*Augustine*</margin>
<margin>*St. Thomas.*</margin>
and that St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary philosopher and theologian of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.</note> cited this for this purpose in the Third Part, Question 83, Article 1; this certainly contributes little to the matter. First, because for images to be called by the names of things is not the same as being the things themselves; and yet we

<column-break/>

profess our sacrament to be a *true* sacrifice. Second, because by that same reasoning, Christ could be considered sacrificed in the victims of the Old Law <note>The animal sacrifices of the Hebrew Bible.</note> under a figure, according to that passage in Apocalypse 13 <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>: "Whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb, who was slain from the beginning of the world."

But if you say our offering is considered a sacrifice because through it we are made participants in the passion of Christ (as St. Thomas adds in the same place), even this does not seem to satisfy the requirement; for every sacrament has that same effect. The Lutheran heretics <note>Followers of Martin Luther, who denied that the Mass was a "propitiatory sacrifice."</note> therefore seem to have found no small opportunity

<margin>*To the second argument.*</margin>
to deny that our sacrament is truly a sacrifice, and to assert that it is only a commemorative sign of that passion, like a theatrical representation <note>original: "instar comicae repraesentationis"</note>.

¶ It is responded, nevertheless, that the root of this understanding is the Church’s true confession: that the body of Christ is <unclear>truly</unclear> contained under these species of bread and wine, and that Christ consecrated these same things at the Last Supper. For if this Catholic truth is denied, it follows plainly that the mystery of the altar is not a sacrifice, but a bare memorial sign. Therefore, the Lutherans gathered the latter from the former; but once the Catholic confession is assumed, the matter becomes immediately clear. For the sacrament of the Eucharist is a victim and a sacrifice because we offer that same identical body and the same blood which Christ offered on the cross.

Thus, there is no similarity with the feast of the Nativity or the Resurrection; for in those cases, we do not have Christ present so that he might then be offered as one being born or rising again. Nor, in performing this sacred rite, do we profess that he is dying then—for our profession would then be false. But because we offer the very crucified body and the shed blood in memory of the passion, we sacrifice truly and properly without any fiction.

<margin>*To the third argument.*</margin>
¶ And from this, the solution to the third argument is gathered. For we distinguish that Christ did not offer himself under the species of bread and wine on the wood of the cross, but he did so at the Supper when he instituted our sacrifice, offering himself just as we do now. As for the word of Augustine—that in Christ’s immolation <note>sacrifice</note> the priest and the sacrifice are the same—it is responded that because the priest performs the sacrifice in the name of Christ and acts in his place (though not as properly as when Christ offered himself), it is not unfittingly granted that in our immolation, the priest and the sacrifice are the same.

He reconciles the "once-for-all" sacrifice of the Cross with the daily Mass by explaining that the priest acts in Christ's person to offer the same victim in a different form.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s examination of the Eucharist as a sacrifice. Following the establishment of the Mass as a true sacrifice, Soto now addresses a practical and theological debate: whether the spiritual benefits of a single Mass are "diluted" when offered for multiple people simultaneously.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

# ARTICLE II.

### *Whether the sacrifice of the altar, when offered for many, profits each person toward satisfaction just as much as if it were offered for only one.*

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
Since the previous article defined the most holy Eucharist as being both a sacrament and a sacrifice, the matter itself requires us to explore how it is "satisfactory" <note>In this context, "satisfactory" refers to <term>Satisfaction</term>: the payment of a debt of temporal punishment due to sin, which remains even after the guilt has been forgiven.</note>. It appears, in fact, that the sacrifice profits each individual toward satisfaction no less when offered for many than if it were offered precisely for one. First, because since in this sacrifice—as has been stated—the true body and blood of Christ are offered, it seems to be of infinite value, just like the things themselves which are offered. This is especially true because it is a memorial, as stated, of the Passion of Christ, which was of infinite value in terms of its sufficiency. Moreover, infinite value is not diminished in individuals simply because it is applied to many; therefore, the affirmative side of the question is true.

<margin>Argument 2. Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ Second, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Dominican theologians like Soto.</note> seems to support the same opinion in the third part of the *Summa*, question 79, article 5. There he says that although this offering, by its own magnitude, suffices to satisfy for every punishment, it is nevertheless "satisfactory" for both those offering it and those for whom it is offered according to the magnitude of their devotion, and not for the entire punishment. In this passage, he seems to designate the magnitude of value as infinite, but he considers it limited according to the amount of devotion in the recipients. Now, the devotion of one person does not hinder the devotion of another; therefore, the fruit for each individual is not diminished by the number of those for whom it is offered. This is like those who stand in the sight of the sun: each individual receives no less heat simply because the sun shines upon many others.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third, an argument is made from the rite of the Church. For the priest offers in the name of the Church for the Pope, for the King, and for those present—in short, for the living and the dead. And yet, it does not seem right to say that the more people for whom it is offered, the less it profits each individual. For as Jerome says regarding consecration (distinction 5, canon *non mediocriter*): "When a Psalm or a Mass is said for all souls, it is received no less than if it were said for any one of them individually." <note>original: "Cùm pro cunctis animabus Psalmus vel Missa dicitur, nihilo minùs q̃ si pro vno quodlibet ipsorũ diceretur, accipitur."</note>

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, although the Passion of Christ was of infinite value in terms of its sufficiency, nevertheless, in terms of its effi-

<column-break/>

-cacy <note>Scholastic theologians distinguish between <term>Sufficiency</term> (the infinite potential value of Christ's act) and <term>Efficacy</term> (the actual effect applied to a person).</note>, it is applied through individual sacraments according to a certain and limited degree. This also applies to the sacrament of the altar; and when a finite thing is distributed among many, each receives less.

<margin>Scotus.</margin>
The present question is famous among theologians, and it is not as easy to explain as it is useful to know. For Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Franciscan theologian who often disagreed with the Dominican Thomist school.</note> in *Quodlibet* 20 leans toward the negative side: namely, that a Mass offered for many does not profit each person as much as if it were offered uniquely for one.

<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
And Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian and papal official.</note>, under the word "Mass" (section 9), cites many jurists in favor of the same opinion, among whom Paludanus <note>Pierre de la Palu (c. 1277–1342), a French theologian and jurist.</note> should be counted, as he appears to agree with them in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, distinction 45, question 2). <margin>Paludanus.</margin> However, Sylvester himself takes a middle path: namely, that if the priest offers with a general offering for a multitude, then it does not profit each person as much. But if he refers his intention specifically to each individual one by one, no less satisfaction reaches each individual.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note>, however, in his commentary on the *Summa* (2a 2ae, q. 79, art. 5) and most extensively in his *Quodlibet* 1, question 18, maintains the absolutely affirmative response: namely, that it profits each individual just as much if it is offered for many—even for an infinite number—as if it were offered precisely for one. He also believes this to be the opinion of Saint Thomas. Nor are there lacking those who embrace this same opinion with great favor. But to confess my own ignorance, I have always judged this opinion not only to be false, but contrary to the most ancient use of the Church. Moreover (to abstain from a harsher word), it is hardly conducive to encouraging the common people to give alms <note>A reference to "stipends" given to priests to celebrate a Mass for a specific intention.</note> for the celebration of Masses, as will be made clear below.

<margin>Three things to be considered in the mystery of the altar.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to respond to the question, it must be assumed from what has been said previously that three things are considered in this sacrifice: namely, the sacrament, the sacrifice, and the prayers that are poured out to God. The third of these is not of the essence of either the sacrament or the sacrifice. For the consecration of the sacrament consists in those words alone: *This is my body*, and, *This is the chalice of my blood*, etc.; while its use is in the receiving of it. To both of these, the nature of sacrifice adds the "offering." The Church, however, deliberately added prayers and praises of the saints, as can be seen in the Canon <note>The <term>Canon of the Mass</term>: the central, fixed prayer of the Eucharistic liturgy.</note>. Indeed, the nature of the sacrament is not relevant to the present point, for it profits only those who receive it, to whom it confers grace and sweetness as the nourishment of spiritual life, and thus excites greater devotion. But as a sacrifice, which is the subject of the present question, it profits not only those receiving it, but also those offering it and those for whom it is offered.

<summary>Soto debates whether the spiritual value of a Mass is divided when offered for many people, contrasting the views of Aquinas and Cajetan (who argue it is not diminished) against Scotus (who argues it is). Soto expresses skepticism toward the idea of infinite "dilutable" merit, noting it might discourage individual Mass stipends.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s examination of the Eucharist as a sacrifice. In the preceding section, he established the Mass as a true sacrifice; here, he addresses the "value" of that sacrifice—specifically, whether its power to satisfy the debt of punishment for sin is infinite or finite.</meta>

# Question II of the Ninth Book.

<insert>It is beneficial</insert>
[The sacrifice] is offered <unclear/>. Nor indeed is only the priest considered the one offering, but also those present and those giving alms, as will be shown below. I say it is beneficial to them for **satisfaction** <note>In this context, "satisfaction" refers to the payment of the "temporal punishment" due to sin, which remains even after the guilt has been forgiven.</note> for sins: namely, for the remission of the punishments of those crimes whose guilt has been wiped away. ¶ Having established these three points, the question is answered. And since the sole foundation of Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Catholic theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> is that this sacrament is of infinite value:
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Let the first conclusion be this: The things contained in this sacrament—namely, the body and blood of Christ—are of infinite value in themselves; for they are the body and blood of God, through which, as far as **sufficiency** <note>Theological term for the theoretical power of Christ's merit to save everyone, as opposed to "efficiency," which is its actual application.</note> is concerned, He satisfied for the sins of the whole world.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: The sacrifice which is performed by the priest, as Christ's minister, is not of infinite value. For this must first be noted here: namely, that by this name "sacrifice," we do not mean precisely the body and blood of Christ in isolation, but these things insofar as they are being offered. Indeed, while they are kept in the pyx <note>A small container used to hold the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>, they are a sacrament, but they are not a sacrifice; they are a sacrifice only when they are celebrated by the priest through consecration, offering, and consumption. Therefore, the term "sacrifice" encompasses the action of the priest in its meaning.
<margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is thus proven. The "quantity" or value of a sacrifice, since it implies the offering of a thing, must be weighed not only from the perspective of the thing offered, but also from the dignity and intention of the one offering. For the sacrifice of Christ which He offered on the cross was of infinite value not solely by reason of the thing offered, but because the one offering was God Himself, and was therefore infinitely pleasing to the Father. However, priests, who are ministers of Christ, do not possess that power, nor has it been divinely granted to them. Truly, to equate the priest’s sacrifice in value to Christ’s offering is not in harmony with the apostolic words we cited earlier from the 10th chapter of Hebrews; for there it says that by *one offering* he perfected forever those who are sanctified. Because of this, that offering neither can nor ought to be repeated further. He would not have asserted this truly about our sacrifice, even though it is a commemoration of that one.
<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
¶ Second, to make this matter clearer, it is argued: The infinite value of Christ’s satisfaction is only estimated in terms of its sufficiency. But in terms of its **efficacy** <note>The actual effect or application of grace to a person.</note>, it does not work through the sacraments except in a finite way. Therefore, although the sacraments are instruments of that same Passion, it grants them to be causes of grace only according to a finite degree and a certain measure. This is evident in Baptism and the others, by the "work performed" <note>original: *ex opere operato*. A theological term meaning the sacrament works by the power of the rite itself, provided no obstacle is placed in the way, rather than by the merit of the priest or recipient.</note>, as they say; namely, by the power of the sacrament. This is also common to the sacrament of the Eucharist:

<column-break/>

for although it truly contains the body and blood, by its institution it confers only a limited measure of grace. Since, therefore, the same sacrament—insofar as it is a sacrifice—effects satisfaction just as the other sacraments confer grace by the power of the "work" itself, it clearly follows that by its own nature as a "work"—that is, by the institution of Christ, who arranged to work through the instruments of His Passion only in a finite way—it is not of infinite value for the purpose of satisfaction, but certainly of finite value.
¶ But here is the crossroads
<margin>Cajetan’s hallucination.</margin>
where Cajetan turns away from us and, as I believe, from the truth: namely, that he attributes no power to this sacrifice from the "work performed" (*ex opere operato*), but considers the entire measure of satisfaction to be determined solely by the degree of devotion, either of those offering or of those for whom it is offered. In truth, Saint Thomas, whom he thinks he is following, neither held this opinion nor could he have held it. For since the Eucharist is an instrument of Christ's Passion not only as a sacrament but also as a sacrifice, it is manifest that in both respects a certain and limited degree of satisfaction corresponds to the power of the work, or what they call the *opus operatum*.
<margin>Third reason.</margin>
¶ Third, for greater explanation, it is argued: All sacraments are perfected chiefly through the intention of the one conferring them. Therefore, the Eucharist, even insofar as it is a victim, becomes a sacrifice through the minister of Christ and the Church, and thus through his intention; namely, because the minister intends to offer it according to the intention of the Church. From this it follows again that, setting aside any particular devotion, a certain degree of satisfaction corresponds to the sacrifice offered through the intention of the minister. And this is the point in which the truth of the opinion we defend consists, if it is true. This point is confirmed by the fact that even if the priest and all the bystanders who offer were in a state of sin—even those for whom it is specifically offered—it would nonetheless be a true sacrament, and likewise a sacrifice, and equally satisfactory. Indeed, if that fruit did not benefit them, it would be stored in the **treasury of the Church** <note>The "Treasury of Merit" or "Treasury of the Church" consists of the infinite merits of Christ and the surplus merits of the saints, which the Church can dispense to others.</note>.
<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But perhaps some disciple of Saint Thomas might argue against this, noting that the same Holy Doctor, in the place cited (Part 3, Question 79, Article 5), seems to measure the total satisfaction by the amount of devotion.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
I respond that this is how Cajetan understood him and where he drew his opinion; however, Saint Thomas did not mean this. For he only says...

<summary>This page argues that while Christ's presence in the Eucharist is of infinite value, the Mass as a sacrifice performed by a human priest has a finite "satisfactory" value determined by divine institution (ex opere operato) rather than just the participants' devotion. Soto critiques Cardinal Cajetan's view that the benefit of the Mass depends entirely on the level of personal devotion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s discussion on the "value" of the Mass as a sacrifice. He is currently rebutting the idea held by some (like Cajetan) that the Mass has an infinite effect in every instance. He argues that while Christ’s merit is infinite, the ritual application of it—the "efficiency"—is finite and regulated by the Church and the devotion of the participants.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

...[that in the] offering, the disposition of the one offering is considered more than the quantity of the offering: so that he does not deny that the priestly offering of the sacrifice itself has its own value in its own right—and that same value is fixed at its own degree, just as Christ arranged in the other sacraments. This is clear from the very same example that Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), whom Soto follows closely.</note> brought forward concerning the widow who put two small copper coins into the treasury <note>original: "duo ænea minuta in gazophylacium miſit"; see Mark 12:42.</note>. For although her merit was increased because of her disposition and her poverty, nonetheless those coins offered by anyone had some value in themselves.

But in truth, perhaps this fact—that the value of this sacrifice increases from the devotion of the one offering or receiving it—is not unique to it, but common to all sacraments. Perhaps, I say, that degree of grace which corresponds to the sacramental power in baptism receives an increase from the devotion of the recipient, if he is an adult. For the benefits of grace are conferred, in this respect, like the works of nature: for instance, more abundantly to the one who is more aptly prepared. Indeed, there are even those who say it increases also from the holiness of the minister, although this second point does not seem as probable to me. But it is much better established that the value of the sacrifice increases from devotion rather than the value of the sacraments, by reason of the offering which is the act of the one offering; for in the other sacraments, nothing is offered. And this is what Saint Thomas signifies.

<margin>The value of the sacrifice does not increase according to the proportion of the devotion of those offering.</margin>
¶ From these things, for the clarification of the matter, it follows that the value of the sacrifice does not increase entirely according to the proportion of the devotion of those offering; for that degree which corresponds to the sacrament always remains the same. Take an example in baptism: Grace (for instance) from the **work performed** <term>opus operato: a theological term meaning the sacrament's efficacy comes from the act itself, provided it is done correctly, rather than the personal holiness of the priest</term> is of one degree, with which a small child is indeed imbued before the use of reason. If, therefore, two adults receive the sacrament, and one has double the devotion and merit of the other, the baptismal grace is not immediately doubled; this is because the whole cause is not doubled, since the same sacrament is conferred on both. By a similar reasoning, even if one priest consecrates with double the devotion of another, the **satisfaction** <note>payment for the debt of punishment due to sin</note> that proceeds from the sacrament will not be doubled for him; because the sacrament itself is not doubled, nor is its efficacy which it has from Christ’s arrangement—which indeed is much greater than what is added from devotions—though more will fall to the one who offers it better.

<margin>Another passage of St. Thomas is explained, which seems to support Cajetan.</margin>
¶ To these things I would further add another word of Saint Thomas, where he says that the offering of the sacrifice, from its quantity, is sufficient for all punishment (namely of the one offering or the one for whom it is offered); this does not signify that it is of itself of infi-

<column-break/>

nite value. For this also applies to baptism, and indeed even to the sacrament of penance of itself, insofar as it is an instrument of Christ's passion. For to him who would rise with the best contrition, all punishment would be forgiven. Therefore, Saint Thomas never felt that this sacrifice was of infinite value except in Christ. But wherever he or another has called it infinite, he understands it precisely regarding the thing offered <note>i.e., the Body and Blood of Christ</note>. Yet the sacrifice includes the action of the priest in its meaning, as has been said, with which Christ concurs—as has been said—only in a finite measure and manner.

¶ Therefore, to conclude summarily, this sacrifice is not called a memorial of that Christ because, while the priest consecrates, Christ is then considered to satisfy infinitely as for **sufficiency** <note>the theoretical capacity of Christ's sacrifice to save all</note> (as He once did), but because as for **efficiency** <note>the actual application of that merit to an individual</note> He works in a finite manner through the same body and blood as in the other sacraments, both for satisfaction and for grace. For so that you may clearly understand: our sacrifice is not Christ's passion, but its application.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion by which the question is answered: The ineffable sacrifice of the Mass, when it is offered for many, profits individuals less for satisfaction. This conclusion is a corollary and appendix to the one above; for when a finite thing is divided among many, a smaller portion falls to each one. But furthermore, this same conclusion is both declared and confirmed by the assertion of Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, Cardinal Cajetan, a contemporary of Soto who argued for the Mass's infinite value.</note> himself.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
For he admits that if the one who offers the sacrifice—namely either the priest, or a bystander, or one paying an alms—has such great devotion that one degree of satisfaction in the sacrifice corresponds to it, and he imparts the same to two people, it does not result for the individuals except for a half of that degree; and if to three, for a third part; and so on. By the same similarity, we argue in two ways. First: that which he says about devotion is to be understood by a far more efficacious reason regarding the intention of the priest. For even if all bystanders and those who contribute alms are considered to offer, yet the priest who performs the divine matter as the minister of the church differs far more. For he alone consecrates, and offers in the words of the church, and consumes. Wherefore, to his particular function and consumption by which the victim is perfected, there corresponds a certain and limited degree of satisfaction from the **work performed**, as they say—as has been shown through the analogy of the other sacraments—even if the priest consecrates in mortal sin without any value of devotion. Wherefore, di-

<summary>Soto argues that while Christ’s sacrifice on the Cross is infinite in its sufficiency, the Mass—as its ritual application—is finite in its efficiency. Consequently, if a single Mass is offered for multiple people, the "satisfaction" (remission of punishment) received by each individual is proportionately less.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto’s critique of Thomas Cajetan’s view on the "value" of the Mass. Soto argues that the spiritual fruit of a single Mass is finite and cannot be infinitely distributed among many people without diminishing the portion for each, especially when alms or stipends are involved.</meta>

### Question II of the Ninth Book

...as Thomas [Aquinas] says in his commentary on the 4th book of the Sentences, distinction 45, question 2, article 1, speaking about the Mass of an evil priest: it is certain that it benefits those for whom it is offered, by reason of the subject, because the **work performed** <term>opus operatum: the objective spiritual benefit of a sacrament that does not depend on the personal holiness of the priest</term> itself—namely the sacrifice of the altar, just like the other sacraments—benefits even when offered by an evil minister. And this is the essential level of the sacrament; for that which is added from the devotion of others who are offering is accidental, whether it be greater or lesser. And so, it is this essential benefit which the person providing the **alms** <note>original: "eleemosynam"; here referring to a Mass stipend or donation</note> desires to be applied to himself. From this it follows that the more people it is distributed among, the less there is for each individual.

<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Add another argument for the same matter that is by no means weak. The priest, as a minister of the church, if he consecrates legitimately, ought to bring not only intention but also devotion, according to the words of the **Canon** <note>The central, traditional prayer of the Roman Catholic Mass.</note>: **Whose faith is known to You and whose devotion is noted.** <note>original: "Quorum tibi fides cognita est & nota deuotio"</note> Therefore, the person who contributes his alms so that the sacrifice may be offered for him, asks by right of justice that the priest offer for him not only with intention, but with devotion—especially according to **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian and cardinal of the Dominican Order.</note> himself. For since it would be unthinkable for anything else to be of the intrinsic nature of the sacrifice, and since he places the whole offering in the devotion, it follows that the priest becomes a debtor of that devotion. However, according to the same author, the more people devotion is applied to, the less it benefits each individual; therefore, our conclusion follows clearly. But this argument "against the man" [Cajetan] proceeds from his own assertions. For in truth, the action necessary for the sacrifice is the offering with intention, which is found even in a priest while he consecrates in a state of sin. Therefore, by the rigor of justice, he satisfies the one who provided the alms even without devotion—although certainly it is a new fault unless he has offered it out of devotion, for which he received the alms.

<margin>Sylvester's Argument.</margin>
However, **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), an influential Dominican theologian and opponent of Luther.</note> makes one argument by which he thinks the opposite is concluded, which nevertheless fights on our side. For he argues thus: the more people there are offering the sacrifice, the more it is increased; therefore, no one is defrauded of their fruit through the partnership of others. Otherwise, it would be more advisable to attend a sacrifice where fewer people were present. And he adds an example in baptism: for even if many were baptized with one sacrament, each would receive no less grace.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
But in truth, he does not see that baptism is multiplied according to the number of those who are baptized; for if I were to baptize four or ten with one sprinkling, there would be as many sacraments of baptism as there were baptized persons. But the sacrifice is not multiplied because of the multi-

<column-break/>

-plication of the offerers, but is only one because of the single offering and intention of the priest, which is of the essence of the sacrifice. And therefore, although it may be true that the more people who offer, the sacrifice is in a certain way increased extensively (for every single person obtains his own satisfaction), nevertheless that value does not grow internally in the sacrament in the same proportion as the multitude of the offerers is greater. Therefore, that distinction of the same Sylvester regarding an offering being **specifically designated** or **general** <note>original: "sigillata aut confusa"</note> does not help him so much; for even if it is distributed through specifically designated offerings, smaller portions will fall to each individual.

<margin>The most powerful argument against Cajetan's opinion.</margin>
The most powerful argument, however, for which the contrary opinion should be rejected, is that if it were true, it would be lawful for a priest to receive **stipends** <term>pitantias: small charitable donations or "pittances" given for a specific religious service</term> (as he calls them) from two or three people for one sacrifice—indeed, from thirty or three hundred. For if the sacrifice then benefits each individual as much as if it were offered for one, it defrauds no one of their fruit, and thus does no injury to anyone. This indeed appears so unsuitable to grant that no one has dared to grant it yet. In fact, **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), the "Subtle Doctor."</note> and **Palude** <note>Peter de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a Dominican theologian.</note> in the place cited entirely deny it, although the latter submits some excusatory cases. Furthermore, not even Sylvester admits it. Therefore, Cajetan should not have passed over this argument disingenuously and silently; because if anyone responds that it is not permitted because of **scandal** <note>A term for an action that might lead others into sin or confusion about the faith.</note>, at the very least, a priest could do it secretly without scandal. Likewise, the scandal arises from the falsehood of that opinion; for if it were true and the common people could be persuaded of it, it would give no scandal.

<margin>This opinion is prohibited.</margin>
And therefore, in **our Order** <note>The Dominican Order (Order of Preachers), to which Soto belonged.</note>, it has been holily cautioned that no one should receive alms from many for the same Mass based on the confidence of that opinion. Indeed, he who cannot remove his assent from that same opinion nonetheless cannot receive such numerous stipends; for since that is neither an article of faith nor proven science, but an obscure opinion, no one should expose himself to the danger of injustice on its persuasion by receiving multiple payments for one Mass. Indeed, another argument that he himself brings against himself fights not weakly: namely, that a priest could satisfy the one to whom he owes ten [Masses] through one Mass, at least if he brought as much devotion there as ten scattered ones would have. But for now, we define nothing regarding the alms to be received for the solemnities of Masses—as to what quantity and number they can be received—since that doctrine pertains to the next question, which is about offerings.

Above these...

He rejects Cajetan's view, noting that the Dominican Order prohibits taking multiple stipends for one Mass to avoid injustice and scandal.</summary>

Soto is arguing against the idea that the Mass has an infinite value that can be applied to an unlimited number of people without diminishing the benefit to each individual. ### Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

->**Fourth reason for the conclusion.**<-
<margin>Fourth reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Neither should this next reason be overlooked, which concerns the prayers of the sacrifice; for the same author also denies this point. The reasoning is as follows: Whoever requests that a Mass be offered for themselves by giving **alms** <note>original: "eleemosyna"; here referring to a Mass stipend</note> justly desires that not only the **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the spiritual "payment" or compensation for the temporal punishment of sin</term> of the sacrifice be applied to them by merit of their gift, but also the prayers of the Church established by the Church. For the sacrifice satisfies a debt by way of payment, but prayer benefits by way of **impetration** <term>impetratio: the act of obtaining a favor or mercy from God through petition</term> of pardon. Therefore, both of these must be applied specifically to the one offering the alms. However, a single prayer that is not multiplied or repeated benefits individuals less if it is poured out for many people; the very custom of Christians and the teaching of the Church demonstrate this truth to us. First, in the **Canon** <note>The central, fixed prayer of the Mass.</note> itself, it is not without reason that after the offering for the Church in general, specific mention is added for the Pope, and so on. Likewise, when some calamity strikes, we pray specifically for its removal—whether it threatens the Church or a specific friend. For even though God can grant many things as easily as any single benefit, He is nevertheless more moved (to speak in our human way) when He sees someone specifically focused on a matter upon which they dwell in prayer, provided it is a just request. Therefore, since those prayers established by the Church in the Mass are not multiplied, it happens that while the sacrifice is performed for many, it helps each individual less than if it were offered singularly for one.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you object to us using the opinion of **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Church Father.</note> (found in Question 1, Case 8), where he seems to feel the opposite when he says that individuals rejoice all the more in prayer the more it is poured out for many;

<margin>Solution of St. Thomas.</margin>
To this, **Saint Thomas [Aquinas]** <note>The dominant theologian of the Middle Ages (1225–1274 AD), whom Soto follows closely.</note> responds in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, distinction 45, question 2, article 2), while speaking of **suffrages** <term>suffragia: intercessory prayers or good works performed for the benefit of others, especially the deceased</term>. He says that although the value of suffrages (among which he counts prayer), insofar as they proceed from **charity** <note>original: "charitate"; the supernatural love of God and neighbor</note> through which the members of the Church are united, becomes in a certain way greater—because it more excellently represents that same unity and thus generates greater joy in each person—nevertheless, if it is considered by way of "satisfaction" which one person applies to another, the same value is divided among those to whom it is applied. And he confesses this at length in the solution to the third point regarding prayer.

<margin>Final reason.</margin>
Finally, there is this reason: pious followers of the faith want particular Masses to be offered for them, either proper to certain mysteries of Christ or the feast days of saints, because of the singular affection they have and the assistance they participate in from them.

<column-break/>

For this reason, a priest could by no means celebrate a single Mass for each of these individuals at once. Finally, there remains to be answered a word from **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> cited by us above in the third argument (concerning consecration, distinction 5, the canon "Not slightly"). Specifically, he says: "When a Psalm or Mass is said for all souls, it is received as nothing less than if it were said for any single one." **Sylvester** <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian.</note> and others interpret this in various ways. But first of all, it supports our view primarily because he compares a Psalm with a Mass, saying that both offered for many are worth as much as if offered for one. For it is very well known that a Psalm is not of infinite value; therefore, he does not imply that the Mass—for the reason that it is of infinite price—is no less profitable to individuals when offered for many. Therefore, two **glosses** <term>glossata: explanatory notes or interpretations of a text</term> are applied to that text. The first is that it refers to the merit of the one offering: namely, that he who offers it for many merits no less than he who offers it for one. The second (which on the surface seems to fit the preceding words) is that a single Psalm offered for many with attention and ardor of soul benefits each individual as much as one said for a single person in a shorter time. But truly, the text embraces these interpretations poorly. I think it should be resolved in the same way we recently stated according to Saint Thomas: namely, that if the offering is estimated from the root of charity uniting the members of the Church, it benefits individuals no less if it is offered for many—that is, the merit of the offerer's charity helps each person equally because it is not diminished by extension. However, if it is considered in the sense of satisfaction and the payment of a debt applied to such persons, it does not benefit as much as if it were applied to individuals alone. For Jerome would hardly deny that if you recited this Psalm for one person, then again for another, and again for a third, it would benefit each more than if you said it once for all three.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The first argument of those things objected to at the beginning is solved there: where we said that although the things contained in this sacrifice are of infinite value, nevertheless, the sacrifice—since it includes the priestly action through which Christ works only in a finite way and by a certain measure—is finite. Therefore, it is not called a memorial of Christ’s passion because it is of equal power, but because the same thing is offered here as was offered there.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
And likewise, regarding the second point gathered from the words of Saint Thomas, similarly...

<summary>Soto argues that the intercessory and "satisfactory" benefits of a Mass are finite and divided among recipients, meaning a single Mass offered for many people provides less spiritual benefit to each individual than a Mass offered for one. He reconciles this with Church Fathers like Jerome and Augustine by distinguishing between the merit of charity (which is shared) and the merit of satisfaction (which is partitioned).</summary>

### Question II of the Ninth Book

...we have sufficiently satisfied this point: since we have shown that we in no way denied that the sacrifice has, of itself, a certain and finite value. This value does not always exert its power if an obstacle exists in the recipient; nevertheless, one must also weigh the **devotions** <term>devotio: the internal piety, faith, and intentionality of the person participating</term> of those offering, according to which the sacrifice's benefit increases. However, it does not increase in total proportion to those devotions, as has been explained.

<margin>*A Doubt.*</margin>
¶ Regarding this devotion, a doubt remains: should we estimate the devotion not only of those performing and offering the sacrifice, but also of those for whom it is offered? For the holy
<margin>*St. Thomas.*</margin>
**Thomas [Aquinas]**, in the place cited earlier, speaks only of the affection of the one offering, which he illustrates with the example of the widow in the Gospel <note>referring to the "widow's mite" (Mark 12:41–44), where the spirit of the giver mattered more than the amount</note>. And in his *Commentary on the 4th Book of Sentences* (distinction 12, question 2, article 2), he says this sacrifice removes punishment in whole or in part, according to the measure of the punishment due and the devotion with which the sacrament is offered. Nevertheless, in the same work (part 3, question 79), he seems to immediately add that it provides **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the "payment" or compensation for the temporal punishment of sin</term> to those for whom it is offered according to the quantity of *their* devotion. He repeats this same point in article 7, in the solution to the second point, and again in his *Sentences* (book 4, dist. 43, q. 2, art. 1). Arguments exist on both sides: for the argument that the devotion of the recipients must be weighed is that, just as in nature—for example, fire—the more suitable the material it finds, the more effectively it produces its form; and in a state, more abundant benefits are conferred upon the more worthy. Thus, the intention of Christ, and subsequently of His Church, seems to be that this sacrifice should confer its effects more kindly upon those who are better prepared.

<margin>*Augustine.*</margin>
For this reason, **Augustine** says to Renatus: <note>original: "Quis offerat corpus Christi nisi pro eis qui sunt membra Christi?"</note> "Who should offer the body of Christ except for those who are members of Christ?" Nevertheless, an argument for the negative side stands: when someone privately applies equal fasts or equal alms as satisfaction for two friends who are unequal in their goodness, it profits them both equally. From this, it seems a reasonable conclusion that while the sacrifice—which by its own nature is equal—is offered for many, even if they are of unequal virtue, it nonetheless confers its benefit upon them equally.

<margin>*Those who are present at the sacrifice, as well as those who pay alms for it, are to be considered offerers.*</margin>
¶ For the understanding of these matters, it must first be noted that "those offering" are considered to be not only the priest who performs the divine rite, but also all those standing by and those who pay **alms** <note>Mass stipends</note> for the Mass, or in any way favor the celebration of the Mass—though, as we have said, the priest is the offerer in a far more excellent and proper sense.

<margin>*Solution to the proposed doubt.*</margin>
And regarding these people, there is no doubt that their devotion is a cause for receiving greater fruits. Indeed, since they are truly "offerers," 

<column-break/>

the very value of the sacrifice is extensively increased. And perhaps where Saint Thomas says that the devotion of those for whom the Mass is offered increases the fruit of the sacrifice, he means the devotion of those who *commission* the Mass to be celebrated. Since they bring an actual devotion, they are, as it were, "offerers." For this reason, regarding those standing around, it is specifically held in the **Canon** <note>The central prayer of the Mass</note>: "Whose faith and devotion are known to You" <note>original: "Quorum tibi fides cognita est & nota devotio"</note>; as if they are actually affected toward the sacrament. And so God, to whom their devotions are known, grants to each according to their measure. 

There are others, however, who never had an actual devotion toward this individual sacrifice being celebrated today in this Basilica: such as children before the use of reason, and other faithful Christians who never thought of this. Nevertheless, the Church offers for them, as we shall soon discuss. These are not called "offerers" except perhaps in a very general way by habit, insofar as they are members of the body of the Church which offers. Regarding these, therefore, there would be no further absurdity in judging that all receive equal portions of the sacrifice, even if they flourish in unequal levels of **charity** <term>caritas: the theological virtue of love for God and neighbor</term>. For since they have neither acted nor thought anything at all regarding this specific individual sacrifice, it appears that nothing falls to them except the bare portion which comes to them **by the work performed** <term>ex opere operato: the concept that sacraments are effective by the very fact of being performed, regardless of the merit of the person</term>; just as is certain regarding the grace of baptism, which is conferred on infants before the use of reason. However, let those who feel otherwise follow their own judgment. Therefore, the arguments made on both sides are left to the judgment of those choosing how to resolve them.

¶ The third argument, however, is the greatest of all those that support the opposite opinion. For the Church offers for many: first in common for the peace and governance of the Church, according to the words of the Canon: "For your holy catholic Church, which may You deign to pacify," etc. <note>original: "Pro ecclesia tua sancta catholica, quam pacificare, &c."</note> Next, it offers for the Pope, for the Bishop, for the King, and for those standing by, who offer for themselves and their own. Nor are prayers alone offered for them, but also the very satisfaction of the sacrament; for it is added: "For the redemption of their souls" <note>original: "Pro redemptione animarum suarum"</note>. Then, it is offered for the souls detained in the fire of **Purgatory**. Since the Church offers the sacrifice for so many, it is not likely that less satisfaction reaches each individual as a result. Otherwise, barely a tiny particle would reach anyone. If you say the Church offers for many in such a way that individuals nonetheless obtain the benefit, but a priest does otherwise in individual applications, the reason for this distinction is lacking.

<summary>This page discusses whether the spiritual benefits (satisfaction) of a Mass depend on the personal devotion of the recipient or the offerer. Soto concludes that while the devotion of those commissioning or attending the Mass matters, those who cannot participate (like infants or the general faithful) still receive a baseline benefit through the "work performed" (ex opere operato).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's investigation into the distribution of the "satisfaction" or spiritual merit generated by the Mass. Having established that the sacrifice has a finite value, he now explains how that value is divided between the universal Church, the specific intentions of the priest, and different classes of people (infants, sinners, non-believers, and the deceased).</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ It is responded, therefore, that in this respect the Church is in no way distinguished from the priest; for he, as the minister of that same Church, performs and offers the sacred rite. However, it should be gathered from what was said above that the Sacrifice of the Mass, considered purely in itself—that is, as it describes the action of the priest with his intention of doing what Christ instituted—corresponds *ex opere operato* <term>ex opere operato: "from the work performed," meaning the grace is provided by the rite itself rather than the priest's personal holiness</term> to a certain quantity of **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the spiritual "payment" or compensation for the temporal punishment of sin</term>, just as other sacraments provide grace. For the sake of example, let us say the value is ten units, for I believe it to be ample. This value is indeed applied according to the institution of the Church. The Church itself, therefore, distributes a certain portion of that value to those who are named in the **Canon** <note>the central, unchanging prayer of the Mass</note>, even if she does not name the specific amount; the other portion she leaves to the particular intention of the priest, to be applied according to his own specific obligation. From that portion belonging to the Church, one small part proceeds to the entire **mystical body** <note>the collective community of all Christians</note at once, another to the Pope, another to the Bishop, another to the King, and so on. And although only a tiny amount may fall to each individual in any single sacrifice, nevertheless, according to the vast number of sacrifices offered daily throughout the entire Church, a most rich treasury is accumulated. This is in addition to the fact that the specific mention of individuals in the prayers confers much upon them. Therefore, the portion left to the priest, just like the other portion belonging to the Church, the more people it is applied to, the less is sufficient for each. And if he applies it for himself, he always has the right to do so. Whether, however, he can receive multiple alms (donations) for one Mass by another reasoning, whether he be a parish priest or a wandering priest, will be seen immediately in the next question.

<margin>The general offering of the Church extends to faithful infants.</margin>
¶ But because we have begun to speak of those for whom the sacrifice is offered, under the name of the Church to which the offering is primarily directed, even infants dipped in the sacred font <note>meaning baptized</note> before the use of reason are included. For even if the offering is not necessary for the satisfaction of punishment (of which they owe none), it nevertheless pertains to the comfort of the living and to representing the mystical body of Christ and His redemption, which has flowed down even to them. Nevertheless, although wicked and criminal Christians are also contained within that same generality of the Church, none who lack **charity** <note>here meaning "state of grace" or love for God</note> become participants in that same sacrifice insofar as it is "satisfactory," for satisfaction presupposes the remission of the guilt of sin.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence, Augustine says to Renatus: "Who would offer the body of Christ except for those who are members of Christ?" <note>original: "Quis offerat corpus Christi nisi pro eis qui sunt membra Christi?"</note> Here he is certainly speaking of living members. Nothing, however, prevents prayers from being made therein for those who are not heretics nor legally

<column-break/>

<margin>It would be an error to establish a Chaplaincy for non-believers.</margin>
excommunicated. For that reason, it would be an error to establish a Chaplaincy or Masses for non-believers <note>original: "infidelibus"</note>; such a case was brought to me to respond to. For to establish a Mass is to establish that the sacrifice be offered for them, and thus that its satisfaction be applied to them—which would be a violation of divine law. Nothing, however, forbids establishing that prayer be poured out during the Mass for their conversion.

¶ Regarding the excommunicated and heretics, one cannot pray for them if they are truly excommunicated. However, on Good Friday, by a dispensation of the Church which excommunicated them, prayer is offered for heretics.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ The sacrifice is also offered, as we have said, for those deceased who are assigned to the place of the fire of Purgatory. This is not because they are understood to be under the name of the "Church" <note>the Church Militant on earth</note>, since they are not contained within its earthly fold and jurisdiction, but perhaps they are designated by that word of the Canon along with the souls of the living, where it reads: "For the redemption of their souls" <note>original: "Pro redemptione animarum suarum"</note>. Indeed, where it is held that those standing around offer for their own, their deceased relatives are also included. Whatever the case with that specific word, they are later expressed in the "second Memento" <note>a specific prayer for the dead in the Latin Mass</note>, where prayer is poured out for those "who have slept with the sign of faith in the sleep of peace." For even if it is said by way of petition—"We pray that You grant indulgence"—it is nonetheless understood as God accepting the satisfaction of this sacrifice. Hence, Augustine says in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*: "Not small," he says, "is the authority of the universal Church which shines in this custom, so that in the prayers of the priest, which are poured out to the Lord God at His altar, the commendation of the dead also has its place."

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
This custom, as Damascene relates in a certain sermon on the suffrages of the dead, flowed down from the Apostles. For he says that the disciples of the Savior and the holy Apostles decreed that a memory be made in the awesome and life-giving mysteries for those who have fallen asleep in faith. Dionysius also relates this in the final chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy*.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
<margin>Gratian.</margin>
<margin>Cajetan's Solution.</margin>
¶ But lest we leave anything related to the question untouched, one last doubt remains regarding the understanding of the words of Augustine in that same book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, and in the *Enchiridion*, which Gratian cited in the *Decretum* (13, question 2). For he says that both the sacrifice of the altar and other suffrages offered for the deceased benefit only those who, while they lived, merited that such things could benefit them. **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> alone offers a reason for doubting this in his *Opuscula* of twenty-one questions...

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

...of the questions, Question 5. There, he [Cajetan] narrows this general saying of Augustine specifically so that he judges that neither sacrifices, **suffrages** <term>suffragia: prayers, acts of charity, or indulgences offered on behalf of the deceased</term>, nor **indulgences** <term>indulgentia: the remission of temporal punishment for sin</term> benefit any of the deceased existing in purgatory unless, in this life, they held a devotion toward the keys of the Church and indulgences, or a concern for making **satisfaction** <term>satisfactio: the "payment" or penance required to balance the scales of divine justice</term> for sins, or a zeal for offering suffrages for the dead, or something similar. He says that at the very least, special sacrifices offered specifically for them do not help them. Yet truly, although it wearies me to go against a man so most learned and most worthy of my respect throughout this whole question, nevertheless, because this view—if it is believed—contributes nothing to the piety of those who are benefactors to the deceased, I did not think I should remain silent here.
<margin>First reason against Cajetan.</margin>
For indeed, since this is gathered neither from the Gospel nor from any decree of the Church—but rather the contrary—certainly since the Church offers indiscriminately for all who are in **charity** <term>charitas: the state of being in God's grace and love</term> and confers indulgences, it was not so easy to assert something to the prejudice of those who have fallen asleep piously in Christ. For the offering of the **Canon** <note>original: "Canonis enim oblation," referring to the central prayer of the Mass</note> excludes no one, but says generally: *Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.* And immediately after: *To these, and to all who rest in Christ.* But if all people become participants in this sacrifice, there is no reason why private suffrages should not also assist everyone.
<margin>Second [reason].</margin>
¶ Secondly: Whoever is in charity, by that very fact that they are a friend of God, just as they can make satisfaction for themselves, so also they have the right that any of the just may apply whatever satisfaction they wish to them. Wherefore, Augustine asserted above that the sacrifice is offered for all the members of Christ, namely the living.
<margin>Solution of the doubt.</margin>
<margin>The Master of the Sentences.</margin>
Hence, regarding what he [Augustine] says in the cited passages—namely, that suffrages benefit those deceased who, while they lived, "merited that they might be able to benefit them"—he himself clearly explains it immediately: as can be seen in the **Master** <note>original: "Magistrum," referring to Peter Lombard, the standard medieval theology textbook author</note> in Book 4, Distinction 45. Indeed, he teaches that all those have "merited" this who died in faith working through charity, and thus in the communion of the body and blood of Christ. Therefore, although someone may have had no particular affection for indulgences or the deceased, nor diligence in making satisfaction, if they nevertheless departed in the charity of God, there is no reason why "avenging and conquering justice," as Cajetan puts it, should stand in the way of our being able to bring them help through sacrifices, suffrages, and indulgences.
<margin>Final reason.</margin>
¶ And to conclude the matter with a final reason—

<column-break/>

—Christ the Lord effectively applies his own sacrifice, namely his Passion, to all those endowed with faith working through charity; therefore, both the offering of the altar, and likewise whatever suffrage—whether common or special—pleases Him, is applied to them. Therefore, that distinction of Cajetan's—that a deceased person being capable of receiving another's satisfaction applied to them pertains not to essential **merit** <term>meritum: the spiritual "credit" earned by a good act</term> but to an accidental one (supposing the deceased was affected toward those things mentioned above)—shows no roots of a foundation.

## QUESTION THREE, On offerings and firstfruits.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Part 2-2, Question 86.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether humans are bound to make offerings by the necessity of a commandment.*<-

After the discourse on the most holy sacrifice, which holds the summit of all the offerings of the Christian family, it remains for us to add mention in this question of **offerings** <term>oblationes: gifts given to the Church, often during the liturgy</term> and **firstfruits** <term>primitiae: the first portion of the harvest dedicated to God</term>; and in the following question, of **tithes** <term>decimae: the tenth part of one's income given to the Church</term>, which are supplied for the celebration of that same sacrifice. First, therefore, it is asked regarding offerings, whether they are of the necessity of a commandment.
<margin>First argument.</margin>
For it is argued in the negative. The offerings of the Old Law were numbered among the **ceremonial precepts** <note>laws regarding religious rituals rather than moral behavior</note>; for in Exodus 23, they are applied to the mode and form of celebrating ceremonial festivals: *You shall not appear before me empty-handed.* Truly, all ceremonial things ceased through the Gospel; therefore, we Christians are not compelled to make offerings. This is what Christ seems to designate in Matthew 5, saying: *If you offer your gift before the altar*; as if he left it to the judgment of those offering.
<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Whoever owes any right to the Church, if they do not pay, they can be compelled to it by the withdrawal of the sacraments; however, it would be harsh to deny the sacraments of the Church to one refusing to pay an offering; according to the canon...
