### Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right, Book I

...that canon of the Sixth Synod: <note>original: "Nullus qui sacram communionem dispensat, à percipiēte gratiam aliquid exigat: sin verò egerit, deponatur." This refers to the Quinisext Council (692 AD), which forbid charging for the Eucharist.</note> "No one who dispenses holy communion should demand anything from the recipient of grace; if he does so, let him be deposed." Therefore, no one is bound to make offerings by the force of a **precept** <term>preceptum: a formal command or rule intended as a binding legal requirement</term>. 

¶ On the contrary, <margin>*Gregory VII*</margin> there is the statement of Gregory VII: <note>Pope Gregory VII (r. 1073–1085), a reformer who asserted papal authority and ecclesiastical discipline.</note> "Every Christian should take care to offer something to God at the solemnity of Masses, and to call to mind what God said through Moses: 'You shall not appear before my sight empty.'"

<margin>*What the name "oblation" signifies.*</margin> In the introduction to the present question, the meaning of the name must be noted. Indeed, the word **oblation** <term>oblatio: an offering; from 'offerre,' to bring before</term> encompasses in its meaning all actions by which any thing is presented for divine worship. Thus it happens that "oblation" is a broader and more extensive term than "**sacrifice**." For whatever is a sacrifice is considered an oblation, but the reverse is not always true. For when something is offered that is intended to remain whole—that is, something not consumed in the sacrifice itself, nor subject to a specific ceremony, but offered to the Church for its building or its ministers—it is indeed an oblation. This is the case if you offer coins or wax candles, or perhaps bread or wine at a funeral, or even a landed estate. 

A sacrifice, however, as we have said, is nothing other than the offering of a thing that is **immolated** <term>immolatio: the ritual act of killing or transforming an offering, such as burning incense or the consecration of the Eucharist</term>, like animals in the past, or now the sacrifice of the altar. Regarding **firstfruits** <term>primitiæ: the first portion of a harvest offered to God</term> and **tithes** <term>decimæ: the "tenth part" of one's income or produce given to support the Church</term>, we shall say in their proper place how they differ from these. Hence Exodus 29 says: "You shall offer the whole ram as a burnt offering upon the altar." And it follows: "It is an oblation to the Lord, a most sweet odor of the victim of God." And Leviticus 2 says: "When a soul offers an oblation of sacrifice to God, his oblation shall be at the same time."

¶ <margin>*First conclusion.*</margin> With these things understood, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: Oblation, in its natural meaning, designates a voluntary presentation; for "to offer" is to give some gift of one's own accord. It follows that the act in itself, if considered simply, is a work of **supererogation** <term>supererogatio: performing more than is required by duty or law</term> pertaining to the worship of religion; by which, as we said above, we profess obedience and subjection to God. Hence Exodus 25: "Speak to the children of Israel that they may take firstfruits for me; from every man who offers voluntarily, you shall receive them."

¶ <margin>*Second conclusion.*</margin> The second conclusion: Oblations can fall under a precept for a fourfold reason. First, from a preceding agreement: as when the Church grants a piece of land to a citizen while retaining a pension to be paid at fixed times. This type of pact takes on the nature of a **census** <term>census: a periodic payment or ground rent attached to land</term>. Second, because of a preceding deputation: because the thing is owed by a gift, a promise, or a legacy in a will. Third—and this approaches the matter more closely—because of the necessity of the Church: namely, if the ministers could not be nourished and sustained from any other source. Fourth, because of custom, which passes into law: namely, if it is customary for this or that to be offered on certain solemn festivals. Although sometimes in these last two cases, the quantity of the offering is left to the liberty of the one vowing it.

¶ Regarding the second conclusion (since the first is very clear), there are several, albeit small, notes to be made. Having set aside the first type of obligation as less relevant (since it is like a ground rent), regarding the second there exists <margin>*First teaching.*</margin> the text in Distinction 13, Canon 2, "Those who [withhold] offerings," and the two following canons. By these, those whose duty it is are compelled under the threat of **anathema** <term>anathema: a formal curse or excommunication by the Church</term> to pay out the offerings of the deceased, whether donated or bequeathed, easily and without delay. For these are clearly debts. And generally concerning all oblations, there is the canon "Besides this" (Dist. 32) and the canon "We have decreed" (Dist. 16, Q. 1), which threaten the same punishment for those withholding oblations owed to the church.

The third reason for obligation should be noted, as it is especially legitimate. For since the Christian religion is situated in the reception of the sacraments and the offering of sacrifice—to which the whole of Christendom is bound by natural and divine law, as it is both most holy and most strict—it follows that <margin>*The people are bound by the law of nature to nourish the ministers of the church and build the temple.*</margin> every people is bound by law, under the guilt of criminal impiety, both to build a temple according to their means and to nourish the ministers and contribute what is necessary for worship. Therefore, where tithes are not paid, and where no other provision has been made for such expenses, the people are bound to supply those same expenses from their own substance. If they refuse, they can be compelled through ecclesiastical censures and even, if necessary, by the judgment of the secular power. 

This is a well-established point <margin>*Paul.*</margin> in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 9, where he teaches that ministers of the altar have more right to receive temporal support than a soldier has to his pay, or the planter of a vineyard to its fruit, or the shepherd of a flock to its milk; for indeed the Lord ordained that he who serves the altar should live from the altar.

¶ <margin>*Doubt.*</margin> A doubt then arises from that cited text of Gregory, "Every Christian": namely, whether one is bound to the solemnity of Masses...

</margin>
¶ If you should ask for some sign by which such customs may be recognized, perhaps this is not so deceptive: where **tithes** <term>decimae: a tenth part of agricultural produce or income paid as a tax for the support of the church</term> are not in use, and no other just salaries are established for the ministers, there the most common offerings are judged to be mandatory. Likewise, it is a command if the custom of the people is older than all memory to offer certain gifts to the church on fixed solemnities, either for the building's maintenance or for other expenses. But truly, where the payment of tithes is observed according to custom and is sufficient for the ministers, daily offerings—whether offered on weekdays or on festivals, however significant—should not be considered subject to the obligation of a command. Nor can it be pleaded with any color of truth to the contrary that legitimate pastors usurp all the fruits of the tithes for themselves, "flaying the flock," and leave to the miserable "mercenaries" <note>Referring to substitute priests or vicars hired at low wages</note> those small daily gifts offered at the steps of the altar. For since the pastors are fattened by the tithes, it is incumbent upon them first to serve in person; then, if they are permitted to be absent from duty—whether justly or unjustly—they must substitute vicars for themselves with a just salary. For this reason, this matter was excellently

I say "daily" according to human fragility; for although he may stop for one or two days, either because he does not feel himself fit or for the sake of relaxing his mind, he is not thereby placed in guilt.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether offerings are owed to priests alone.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure in a landscape, possibly a scholar or saint.</image-desc>
<margin>The first argument.</margin> After the obligation of offerings, it follows that we should speak of those to whom they are owed. For it appears they should not be granted to priests alone. For that which is most important in offerings is what is designated for the sacrifices of the victims; but the "victims" <note>here referring to the fruits of the sacrifice or the offerings themselves</note> are ascribed to the poor, according to that passage in the last chapter of Hebrews: *Do not forget kindness and sharing: for with such victims <note>original: "hostijs," often translated as sacrifices</note> God is well pleased* [Hebrews 13:16]: therefore offerings are also to be bestowed upon <margin>Second.</margin> the poor. ¶ Secondly: In many parishes, monks receive a portion of the offerings; yet, according to Jerome, the care of clerics is one thing and that of monks is another: therefore, offerings should not only be distributed to <margin>Third.</margin> priests. ¶ Thirdly: Even laypeople purchase offerings, namely bread and wine, from the priests for their own use; therefore the use of them is not permitted to <margin>Damasus.</margin> priests alone. ¶ On the contrary is the canon of Pope Damasus <note>Damasus I, Pope from 366–384 AD</note>, in the 10th Question, 1st Causa. It is only permitted for priests who are seen to serve the Lord daily to eat and drink the offerings which are offered within the holy church: because in the Old Testament the Lord forbade the holy breads to be eaten by the sons of Israel, except only Aaron and his sons: as is clear in 1 Samuel 21 <note>original: "1. Reg. 21," using the Vulgate numbering where 1 Kings is 1 Samuel</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> To the question, it is responded with two conclusions. One is: The <term>dispensation</term> <note>The management and distribution</note> of all offerings which are presented to God by the people belongs to the priests. <margin>Proof.</margin> It is proved. An offering, by its nature, is nothing other than a thing dedicated to God for religious worship: for our discourse is about sacred offerings, not secular ones. Between men and God, the priest is established as a <term>sequester</term> <note>A mediator or middleman</note>, and in his rank is a mediator according to Christ: as is read of Moses in Deuteronomy 5. For it is his duty both to teach the people the divine dogmas revealed through God, and also to administer to the same people the sacraments instituted by Him in His name. And conversely, it is his function on the part of the people to stand before God: namely, to pour out their prayers before Him, to offer sacrifices to Him, and to present gifts, offerings, and favors: according to that word of the Apostle in Hebrews 5: *Every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in those things which pertain to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.* Therefore, the use, administration, and distribution of all the gifts which the people decide to dedicate to God belongs to those same priests. <margin>A doubt.</margin> ¶ But if a reason for doubting creeps in by example—that the Christian family dedicates many things to the churches, not for the priests, but for the construction of temples and the decoration of utensils, which therefore ought not to be for the use of priests— <margin>Solution.</margin> it is responded that we have deliberately not asserted that all offerings have passed into their ownership so that they can consume everything for their own personal use: but rather that the distribution of them is their responsibility. <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> ¶ Wherefore another conclusion is added. Priests can use those things which are offered for divine worship in three ways. First, for the construction and repair of churches and the preparation of items which pertain to divine worship. Second, for their own proper livelihood: since, as Paul cited above says: *He who serves the altar ought to live from the altar* [1 Corinthians 9:13]. Third, for the support of the poor, whom it is fitting to be fed and sustained by ecclesiastical goods. This conclusion is well-known. For whatever is presented to God, since He Himself does not need our goods, is useful for only two things: namely, either for the buildings or ornaments of temples, or for the nourishment of priests. But whatever remains over, they ought to distribute to the poor. Except that in ancient times, as the following sections will demonstrate, some things were also accustomed to be given to the chur—

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether it is permissible to make offerings from all<-
->things that are lawfully possessed.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental drop cap 'S' featuring a figure, likely a saint or scholar, set within a detailed rectangular frame with floral and decorative patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>Reasoning from the negative side.</margin>
It follows in the third place, after speaking of the dispensers of offerings, to speak also of their substance. For not everything that a person possesses seems to be suitable material for an offering. For a prostitute lawfully possesses what she earns through shameful means, as is clear in the law <note>original: "l. idem ob stuprum. ff. de condicti. ob turpem cau." referring to the Digest of Roman law regarding recovery of property for immoral causes.</note>; and yet it is read in Deuteronomy 23: *You shall not bring the hire of a prostitute into the house of the Lord your God.* And immediately in the same place it is forbidden

<column-break/>

for the price of a dog to be offered, even though that animal is lawfully sold. ¶ And in Malachi 1: *If you offer the lame and the weak, is it not evil?* Therefore, not everything that is lawfully possessed is likewise lawfully offered. ¶ On the contrary, however, is that saying from Proverbs 3: *Honor the Lord your God from your substance.* By this one word, everything that is possessed is included.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To the question, it is responded with three conclusions. First: Regarding those things which are acquired and possessed unjustly, no offering is lawfully made to God. 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proven: Since an offering is a virtue of religion, it ought not to be a violation of justice. For that same virtue is under the commandment of God; and just as Aristotle says that all truths harmonize, so do all other things harmonize with every divine mandate. Moreover, all things acquired unjustly are subject to the law of justice, and thus to <term>restitution</term> <note>The legal and moral obligation to return stolen or unfairly gained goods to their rightful owner.</note> commanded by God; therefore, they cannot be dedicated to that same God. 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine, in his book *On the Words of the Lord*, brings a beautiful example of this matter. *If you should plunder some weak person,* he says, *and from his spoils you gave something to some judge who would judge in your favor, the power of justice is so great that it would displease even you. Your God is not such a one; and you ought not to be so either.* Thus he spoke, where he skillfully explained the reason for the matter. For an offering is made to propitiate and appease God, who is the judge of all virtues and the guardian of laws. Since, therefore, He is certain to condemn you unless you restore whatever you owe, it is a kind of divine insult if you strive to appease Him with the very thing for which He is certain to condemn you. Whence also in Ecclesiasticus 34: *The offering of him who sacrifices from what is wrongful is defiled.*

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion: As far as the nature of the thing itself is concerned, a lawful offering can be made from any thing that is justly possessed. 
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
It is evident: for a person is truly the master or legitimate possessor of such things, and therefore has legitimate use of them, with God Himself providing them. Everyone can, and indeed ought to, with the moderation of prudence, pay back to Him a part of those things which they have received from Him; according to that saying in the last chapter of 1 Chronicles: *What we have received from your hand, we return to you.*

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion: From the circumstances surrounding a thing, an offering can be defiled, even of those things which are lawfully possessed. This is proven: because for the excellence of a work, it is not enough for it to be good in its kind unless the surrounding circumstances are likewise honorable. It can happen that an offering made in such a way becomes evil.

<summary>This page discusses the ethical requirements for religious offerings, concluding that while priests and bishops manage church resources, offerings must come from justly acquired property. Soto emphasizes that God cannot be appeased by gifts stolen from others, as this violates the divine law of justice and the duty of restitution.</summary>

# Book Nine, Question III.

...evils. And first, for the observers of the ancient law <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note>, for whom all things happened in figures <note>In traditional theology, "figures" are Old Testament events or laws seen as symbolic precursors to New Testament truths.</note>, there were many legal restrictions. This was either because of their symbolic meaning, or because that which was considered impure or shameful to that commonwealth was not permitted to be offered. This reasoning for prohibition has indeed ceased under our law; for as Paul says in Titus, chapter 1:

<margin>Paul.</margin>
> Every creature of God is considered clean. <note>original: "Omnis creatura Dei reputatur munda."</note>

Nevertheless, other troubles can affect our offerings: either because that which is lawfully possessed is owed through mercy to another rather than being offered in the temple; or because of scandal; or because of contempt; or for some other reason. For Christ rebukes the Pharisees in Matthew, chapter 5, who argued that the people should be persuaded to neglect helping their parents rather than fail to make offerings. And a prostitute, when she offers shameful gain, causes a scandal; and <unclear>whoever</unclear> offers to God what he holds in contempt, despises God himself.

<margin>Argument</margin>
¶ However, against the first part of this third conclusion—where it was said that things are sometimes owed to parents or the needy rather than being offered to the temple—it is argued that, in general, it is more beneficial and more suited to divine worship to bestow our goods for the preparing and celebrating of sacrifices than for the support of the needy. For it appears to be commonly judged so, because through sacrifice we actually draw nearer to God. Yet, the poverty of the miserable sometimes cries out against this common opinion.

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
¶ To this, it is answered by making a distinction. A work of virtue is estimated for its perfection based on two things among others. First, from its object, from which it receives its specific nature. Second, from necessity, which charity always strives to assist. Therefore, if we look at the first reason, sacred offerings, and likewise sacrifices, far surpass other alms. For religion—as Saint Thomas <note>Diuus Thomas: Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text's theological arguments.</note> is the author in the Second Part of the Second Part, Question 81—is a more sublime virtue because it has the reverence of God as its object. It is higher not only than mercy, but also than all moral virtues, insofar as those are concerned only with our neighbors. And to this belongs the word of Christ in Matthew, chapter 21 <note>The author likely means Matthew 26, which contains the story of the anointing at Bethany.</note>, where he defended the duty and the cause of Mary Magdalene, who had anointed him with the expense of a most precious ointment, against the indignant disciples. Truly, they valued the work of mercy more. For he taught that the work performed in reverence to the person of God himself was to be preferred because of its religious nature. And therefore,

<column-break/>

he did not condemn mercy toward the poor; indeed, he commended it greatly, saying:
> The poor you will always have with you. <note>original: "Pauperes semper habebitis vobiscum."</note>

However, he declared that the world would never again have that opportunity for almsgiving to be joined to such a high degree of religion. And therefore he said,
> But me you will not always have. <note>original: "Me autem non semper habebitis."</note>

Moreover, it was an act of religion both to confess the majesty and immortality of his divinity with that precious and incorruptible ointment, and also to prefigure the incorruption of his humanity. For it was written:
> You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption. <note>original: "Non dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem."</note>

And perhaps the heavenly Redeemer declared this with that word:
> She has done this for my burial. <note>original: "Ad sepeliendum me fecit."</note>

That is: "She testifies that I, truly dead, am to be buried, such that as if with a prophetic spirit she has foretold my singular manner of burial, where my body will not turn to ashes by the common law of nature." Add to this that among such duties of religion, the most significant and desirable is the sacrament where nothing less than God himself is sacrificed.

¶ Nevertheless, this is most true—and I wish that, as it is most certain, it were also most thoroughly persuaded to the Christian family—that the weight of necessity (from which virtue, and especially the increase of mercy, takes its strength) can bring it about that it is more conducive to the worship of God, and thus more desirable, to bring aid to the miserable than to make offerings and sacrifices. And the reason is that sacrifices, as has been said, are celebrated and offered not for the benefit of God (who does not need our goods) but only for his glory and to arouse our devotion. But truly, God has such care for the poor that he often values their benefit more for the sake of his charity, and subsequently his glory, than other sacrifices. And this is especially true after the same God, though he was rich, as Paul says, became poor for our sake, and made our miseries and hardships his own to such an extent that on that terrible day, in the presence of the whole gathering of angels and men, he will not be afraid to confess that he himself was hungry among us, and naked, and a beggar; and finally, that whatever we did for one of the least of those in need, we did as if to him in his own person. Hence, in Matthew 9, he rebukes the Pharisees, and not without indignation, because they had not understood the prophetic oracle. For he said, "Go and learn what this means:
> I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." <note>original: "Misericordiam volo, & non sacrificium."</note>

...sacrifice. For thus it was written in Hosea 6:6, to which the Prophet added: *And the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.* <note>original: "Et sapientiam Dei plus quàm holocausta." The Latin "sapientia" here translates the Hebrew "da'at," meaning knowledge or acknowledgement of God.</note> ¶ For this reason, after Paul—in his Epistle to the Hebrews, who were so devoted to the frequent performance of sacrifices—had spent nearly the whole letter commending the singular sacrifice of Christ our High Priest (whose presence abolished all those ancient rites), he finally added a concluding note to the Epistle. He did this so that they would not conclude that mercy toward the poor should ever be dismissed because of that sacrifice, ensuring they were especially mindful of beneficence. *Let the charity of brotherhood,* he says, *remain in you, and do not forget hospitality; for by this some have entertained angels unawares.* And further down: *Do not forget beneficence and sharing; for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.* <note>A reference to Hebrews 13:1-2 and 13:16.</note>

<margin>The Solution.</margin> To the contrary argument, therefore, it is replied that nothing prevents a virtue which is lower in its own kind from sometimes being more precious due to necessity. ¶ I have emphasized these points at such length because there are those who falsely believe that all their goods—especially when they depart from this light <note>A common idiom for dying.</note>—should be spent on a vast number of Masses and on Chaplaincies <term>endowments for priests to celebrate Mass for the deceased</term>. For even if these were exceedingly necessary in the early Church, and should be provided where they are currently lacking, yet where divine worship is already sufficiently celebrated, it would be much more advisable to relieve the calamities of the needy. For in the Gospel, Christ took care to warn us of this mercy far more frequently than he told us to convert our alms into sacrifices. For although the prayer and satisfaction of the sacrifice <note>The Mass</note> is most acceptable, yet alms, which are the chief duty of charity, and the prayers of the poor are, by Christ's own testimony, very effective in receiving us into the eternal tabernacles. <note>Referring to the Parable of the Unjust Steward in Luke 16:9.</note>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that in the Old Law, offering the "wages of a prostitute" was prohibited because of impurity; a reason which has ceased in the New Law. However, it would still be a scandal to receive such an offering, because the priests would seem to be conniving at the shameful conduct of harlots.

<margin>Josephus.</margin> Regarding the "price of a dog," Josephus in Book 2 <note>Referring to *Antiquities of the Jews*.</note>—as we mentioned when treating legal matters—interprets the law to mean that the labor of dogs, just as with asses and horses for breeding, was accustomed to be redeemed with a price for the impregnation of female 

<column-break/>

dogs. Therefore, that price was also rejected from offerings because of its shameful filth. This interpretation gains probability from the fact that the "wages of a prostitute" and the "price of a dog" are placed together <note>In Deuteronomy 23:18.</note>. However, another interpretation is used by the Doctors <term>Scholastic theologians</term>: that while the firstborn of a "clean" animal was to be kept in the temple so that it could not be redeemed, the firstborn of an "unclean" animal was redeemed with a price. A dog, however, was considered so abject that it was not worth the five shekels <note>original: "quinque siclis"</note> with which such animals were usually redeemed; and therefore, they say, dogs were killed outside the temple. Furthermore, this exposition is consistent with neither reason nor the text. For if it was useful for nothing because of its worthlessness, why would it need to be presented at the temple at all? Wherefore it is better to say that it was simply prohibited from being offered, both because of the animal's lowliness and also because perhaps, as Saint Thomas says, it was used by the Gentiles for sacrificing to idols. That reason, therefore, has ceased in the Gospel.

<margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ To the third argument, it is replied that a blind animal, or one otherwise maimed or weak, was unfit for offering. First, because the offering had to be unblemished. Second, because it would be an act of contempt and a disgrace. Furthermore, by reason of a vow, which must be paid to God with the very best. Therefore, the offering of Cain was not as acceptable to God as that of Abel. These reasons indeed retain their force in our law. For anyone who would offer sour wine or moldy flour for the celebration of the divine rite would act wickedly; for those things are not suitable for performing the sacrifice. And whoever would dedicate to the temple vessels or garments that had served the filthiest uses, so that sacred vestments and vessels might be fashioned from them, would be judged a despiser of those same sacred things. And whoever would devote an animal to God by a vow, and then pay with one that is lame or blind or of the cheapest price for some other reason—or pay tithes from the worst grain and new wine—would certainly not be keeping his faith purely toward God, to whom he is bound.

### ARTICLE IV.
## Whether men are bound to pay first-fruits.

<meta>Catchword: Between</meta>

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that while religious sacrifice is a high virtue, the necessity of helping the poor (mercy) often takes precedence. He also clarifies that while Old Testament prohibitions on "unclean" offerings (like the price of a dog) have technically ceased, the principle of offering one's best to God remains a moral requirement in Christianity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the virtue of religion and the types of offerings made to God. Having previously addressed whether mercy takes precedence over sacrifice, the author now turns to the specific legal and moral status of "firstfruits" (the first of the harvest) compared to "tithes" (the tenth part).</meta>

# Book Nine, Question III.
->Aaa 4<-
<meta>catchword: ctiore</meta>

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
Among the various types of offerings, **firstfruits** <term>primitiae; the first portion of agricultural produce or livestock offered to God</term> are numbered. We therefore inquire whether they are owed by the force of a commandment. For there is contrary testimony cited above from Exodus 25:2, where the Lord says to Moses that firstfruits should be accepted from any man who offers them voluntarily. Furthermore, in Exodus 13, when the law of the firstborn (which were legally considered firstfruits) was given, it is added: *It shall be as a sign in your hand.* <note>original: "Erit quasi signum in manu tua"</note> The word "sign" designates **ceremonial matters** <note>In traditional theology, "ceremonial laws" were specific to the Old Testament and were believed to have ceased with the coming of Christ, unlike "moral laws" (like the Ten Commandments) which remain binding.</note> which have ceased in our Law; therefore, just as we are not bound to offer our firstborn, neither are we bound to offer the firstfruits of other things.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
Second: in ancient times, firstfruits were returned to God so that the people might repay Him with thanks for the singular benefits received from Him. For it is held in Deuteronomy 26:2-3: *You shall take of all your fruits and the firstfruits... and you shall go to the priest who shall be in those days, and say to him: I profess this day before the Lord your God, that I have entered into the land for which He swore to our fathers that He would give it to us.* Therefore, neither foreign nations nor we ourselves are bound to provide them.

<margin>The third argument.</margin>
Third: If the law of firstfruits were compulsory, then a prescribed and assessed quantity of payment ought to have been established, just as it is with **tithes** <term>decimae; a tenth part of one's income or produce given to the church</term>. But in neither Testament is such a law of assessment found; therefore, they are not included under any commandment.

**On the contrary**, however, is the canon of Pope Gregory VII, *Decimas* (16, q. 7), whose words are: "It is fitting that we more appropriately receive from all the people the tithes and **firstfruits**, which we decree to be the right of the priests, and which the faithful offer at the Lord's command."

<margin>The fourfold difference between firstfruits and other offerings.</margin>
Firstfruits hold a unique place in the category of offerings. Indeed, they differ from the general nature of the rest in four ways, which **Saint Thomas Aquinas** <note>A hugely influential 13th-century theologian and philosopher whose work "Summa Theologica" is the basis for much of this legal reasoning.</note> distinguished here. First, they differ in their **material** according to the sound of the word. Namely, they were offered from the "firsts" and the "choicest beginnings" of things. Though there are some who understand by the name "firstfruits" not the "first" things, but the "best" things—just as it is recorded of **Abel** <note>The son of Adam and Eve who offered the best of his flock to God in Genesis 4.</note> that he offered from the fatness of his flock. However, the text of Numbers 18 suggests both. For that which is first is considered the best. Hence, in the same place: *All the marrow of the oil, and of the wine, and of the corn: whatever firstfruits they offer, I have given to you*—namely, to **Aaron** <note>The first High Priest and brother of Moses; his descendants were the priestly class.</note>. And it adds: *All the firstfruits of the produce which the ground brings forth and are carried to the Lord,*

<column-break/>

*shall fall to your use.* Second, they differ from the others by reason of their **cause**, because they were returned to God for a special reason: namely, so that men might recognize the divine benefit and profess that whatever they receive from the fruits of the earth comes to them through God as the author. To Him, therefore, according to the word cited in the last chapter of 1 Chronicles, they ought to return what they have received from His hand. Third, they differed in their **manner**, because they were offered with a specific ceremony. For we read in Deuteronomy 26, after the words cited above regarding those offering firstfruits: *The priest, taking the basket (which is the basket of firstfruits from the hand of him who brings the firstfruits), shall set it before the altar of the Lord.* And further down, after commemorating God's benefits, the words of the offerer are added: *Therefore now I offer the firstfruits of the corn of the land which the Lord has given me,* etc.

Fourth and finally, they differ on the part of **those for whose use they were provided**. For since they were repaid to God for a benefit—between whom (as we have said) and the people the priest is the mediator—they fell singularly to his use. This is in contrast to **tithes**, which pertained to the entire tribe of Levi <note>The Levites were the larger tribe responsible for religious duties, while only the descendants of Aaron were priests; tithes supported the whole tribe, but firstfruits were specifically for the priests.</note>. Hence, in the cited passage of Numbers 18, God says to Aaron: *All the firstfruits of the sanctuary which the children of Israel offer to the Lord, I have given to you, and to your sons and daughters, by a perpetual right.* And it is added: *But to the children of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel for a possession, for the ministry which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant.*

Having established these points, the question is answered with two conclusions.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
First: Firstfruits are owed to God and His ministers by the commandment of both **natural** and **written law**; and consequently by **pontifical law** <term>canon law; the laws of the Church</term>, derived from that same ancient divine law. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> The conclusion is proven by the reason already hinted at. The **law of nature** <term>ius naturae; moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason</term> has taught us such gratitude that we should return thanks to benefactors. God, however, is the first author of all natural benefits; therefore, we owe Him the first payments. This is not just out of decency, but as a commandment, argued as follows: By the law of nature, we are compelled to profess God as our author and the author of our possessions, since *in Him we live, move, and have our being.* <note>A quote from Acts 17:28.</note> For if we are strictly compelled to assist our parents, from whom we received life (as the fourth commandment of the Decalogue warns us), from those things we possess for our sustenance when they are in need, then by a far stricter...

<summary>This page analyzes the religious and legal nature of "firstfruits," distinguishing them from tithes by their purpose, ceremony, and recipients (priests versus the tribe of Levi). It concludes that giving the first and best of one's harvest to God's ministers is a requirement of natural law rooted in gratitude to the Creator.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the religious obligation to offer firstfruits to God. Having established that even the ancients recognized this duty, Domingo de Soto now distinguishes between natural law and human custom regarding the specific quantities and recipients of these offerings.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

with even greater right we owe God this same recognition: not indeed because of any need on His part, for He can have none, but for our own benefit and His glory. Nature has so instructed the whole of mankind in this reasoning that it was well known to all pagans in every age (as we were saying above). For this reason, we did not specifically ask here whether Christians, but whether human beings—namely all mortals—are bound to pay firstfruits. Therefore, the response extends to all of them. <margin>Pliny.</margin> Hence the Romans, as Pliny relates in their history (Book 18, Chapter 2), would taste nothing of the earth's produce before the priests had offered the **firstfruits** <term>primitiae; the first portion of the harvest</term> of the new grain and wine. ¶ But perhaps someone will meet us here with an objection: that this reasoning is not <margin>Objection against the previous reasoning.</margin> specific enough to conclude a debt of firstfruits, but only proves that we are bound by the law of religion to offer sacrifices to God, as was said above. By these sacrifices, we profess Him to be our creator. Firstfruits, however, are far removed from sacrifices, since they are simple offerings. <margin>Solution.</margin> It is answered, however, that natural reason persuades us toward sacrifices in one way, and toward other offerings—specifically firstfruits—in another. For to God, insofar as He is God (that is, the supreme good in Himself), we owe divine honors and thus obedience. For this reason, we are bound to perform divine service and to sacrifice to Him. But furthermore, because He supplies us with the fruits of the earth daily, we conclude it pertains to His honor to offer back a portion of those things He gives us, and especially the first of those things. By these, we profess that He is the first and supreme author, by whose will the circuit of the sun and the <margin>Final conclusion.</margin> clemency of the air produce these things for us in abundance. ¶ **Second conclusion.** Although the law of nature, expressed of old in divine law, reminds us of this kind of offering of firstfruits, nevertheless the qualities and circumstances—namely, the persons to whom they must be handed over, the material (that is, whether they must be from the very first fruits), and even the quantity—are determined for us by human laws and the use and custom of the homeland. For formerly, firstfruits fell specifically to the priests, while **tithes** <term>decimae; a tenth part of produce or income</term> went to the Levites. Now, however, tithes belong to the priests, whereas firstfruits are mostly assigned to the **sacristans** <term>officials in charge of the sacred vessels and vestments</term> and the keepers of the sacred items. In some churches, however, they are assigned to the **fabric fund** <note>original: "fabricae sumptus"; funds dedicated to the maintenance and construction of the church building</note>, and sometimes to the priests themselves. Nor indeed is it so strictly required that they be paid from the very first fruits

<column-break/>

collected. Nor is it required from garden herbs or legumes, but only from grain. For all those things were legal requirements for the ancient fathers, by which we are now not at all bound. For God enjoined that law of tithes and firstfruits upon His people in that age with such high commendation that, as we read in Exodus 34, He commanded the **Feast of Weeks** <note>original: "hebdomadarum solennitatem"; also known as Shavuot or Pentecost</note> to be celebrated with the firstfruits of the wheat harvest—a practice which is not in use among us. ¶ Regarding the quantity of firstfruits, we read nothing written in either the Old or the New Testament, except for that passage in Ezekiel 45: *These are the firstfruits you shall take: the sixth part of an Ephah from a Kor of wheat, and the sixth part of an Ephah from a Kor of barley. Also the measure of oil, a Bath from every Kor.* <note>original: "Haec sunt primitiae quas tolletis: sextam partem Ephi de coro frumenti... Mensura quoque olei Batus de quolibet coro."</note> Upon these words, Jerome declares that this pertains to tithes; <margin>Jerome.</margin> for an **Ephah** <term>a dry measure</term> was the tenth part of a **Kor** <term>a large unit of volume</term>, <margin>An Ephah is the tenth part of a Kor: so is a Bath in liquids.</margin> just as a **Bath** was for liquids. Indeed, that Kor contained thirty **modii** <note>A Roman unit of dry measure, roughly two gallons</note>. The same holy Doctor adds these words, which are cited in the section "On Tithes," Chapter 1: "But in truth, the firstfruits which they offered from the crops were not defined by a specific name, but were left to the discretion of the givers." We have also received a tradition of the Hebrews, not commanded by law but established by the judgment of the teachers: that those who gave the most gave a sixtieth part to the priests; those who gave the least were permitted to offer whatever they wished between a fortieth and a sixtieth. These things were in the Old Law. In the New Law, however, no quota is designated. But in Spain, if a harvest of more than ten *modii* comes to anyone, he pays one—even if the harvest grows to a thousand or ten thousand. And in other places, the payment is even smaller. In this matter, the most deference is given to custom. Indeed, where tithes are fully sufficient for the entire worship of the churches, unless custom dictates otherwise, there would be no reason why firstfruits should be demanded by legal obligation; for since we said natural law commands firstfruits to be paid, tithes would then sufficiently fulfill that requirement. <margin>To the first argument.</margin> To the authority cited above from Exodus 25, he responds that by the name "firstfruits" there—as the text plainly teaches—were understood the offerings which the people were advised to make for the crafting of the temple ornaments; namely, that each person should contribute gold, or silver, or hyacinth-colored cloth, or purple, and other precious furnishings of that kind for making the vessels and vestments of the temple. Moreover, in Exodus 13, the offerings of the firstborn were "signs," that is...

->**Question Four of the Ninth Book**<-

St. Thomas does not deny that these are called ceremonies, but he responds as we did in the first article regarding offerings in general. Namely, that it is not permitted to restore those specific ceremonies of the holy Christian Church from the ancient law which were "figures of things to come" <note>original: "figurae futurorum"; these are rituals that foreshadowed Christ</note>: for the reason that they would now be false. On the other hand, ceremonies that were used simply in recognition of God's benefits may still be instituted by us, since the same reasoning for them remains valid.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it is answered that the people of old owed **firstfruits** <term>primitiae; the first portion of a harvest offered to God</term> to God not only because of the fruits which the earth brings forth by God's kindness, but also because of the lands themselves which had been both promised and given to them by His favor. Therefore, this second cause does not survive among us, but the first one does. Nevertheless, since God also created the world itself for our sake and subsequently gave it into our possession—according to that verse of the Psalm: *The earth he has given to the children of men* <note>Psalm 115:16</note>—firstfruits are still owed to Him for this reason as well.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ The third argument has already been resolved where we said that the quantity of firstfruits is not prescribed by law. Since they fall under the category of "offerings," people ought at least to set something aside of their own free will.

# QUESTION FOUR,
## On Tithes.
### St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae 2.2, Question 87.
## ARTICLE I.
## Whether men are bound to give tithes by necessity of precept.

<margin>The first reason from the negative side.</margin>
**P**ollowing the discussion on offerings comes the discourse on **tithes** <term>decimae; a tenth part of produce or income consecrated to religious use</term>. It appears that not all men are bound by the necessity of a command to pay them. For that commandment appears in Leviticus 27, where it is read: *All the tithes of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, are the Lord's.* And further down: *Of all the tithes of oxen, and sheep, and goats, that pass under the shepherd's rod, every tenth that cometh shall be sanctified to the Lord.* However, this commandment cannot be categorized among

<column-break/>

moral laws because the moral law is commanded by nature; yet nature does not command a tenth part any more than an eleventh or a ninth part. If, however, it was a ceremonial or judicial law, it has already been sufficiently shown in Book 2 how those laws have been rendered obsolete.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
¶ Second. We are only bound to accept those laws under a "precept" <note>a binding religious rule or command</note> which Christ or His Apostles enjoined upon us, according to the final chapter of Matthew: *Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you.* And Paul in Acts 20 <note>The text says 21, but refers to Acts 20:27</note>: *I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.* But no obligation regarding tithes is read among the teachings of Christ or the Apostles. For what the Lord mentions regarding tithes in Matthew 23 <note>The text says 20</note>—*Woe to you who tithe mint, and rue, etc.: these things you ought to have done*—is considered to refer to the time of the former law. This is according to <margin>Hilary.</margin> Hilary of Poitiers in his commentary on Matthew: "That tithing of herbs, which was useful as a **prefiguration** <term>an event or ritual that symbolically foreshadows a future reality</term>, ought not to have been omitted." Therefore, in the time of Grace, the yoke of tithes has been loosed from us.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third. In the time of Grace, only those things from the Old Law are left to us which nature commands. Therefore, we are not bound to more than the Gentiles were before that Law. In those ages, tithes were not presented by command, but by vow. For we read of Jacob in Genesis 28 that he made a vow to God, saying: *If God will be with me, and keep me in the way that I go, etc., of all that thou shalt give me I will offer tithes to thee.* Therefore, we should not be more strictly bound to tithes than he was.

<margin>The fourth reason.</margin>
¶ Fourth. Under that law of the ancients, a triple tithe was paid. The first indeed was given to the tribe of Levi, regarding which (as we said in the last article) it is read in Numbers 18: *The Levites shall be content with the offering of tithes, which I have separated for their uses and necessities.* The second tithes are those referred to in Deuteronomy 14: *Thou shalt separate the tenth part of all thy fruits that come forth of the earth year by year, and thou shalt eat it in the sight of thy God in the place which God shall choose.* And finally, the third tithes, which follow immediately in the same place: *The third year thou shalt separate another tithe of all things that grow at that time, and shalt lay it up within thy gates; and the Levite shall come, who hath no other part nor possession with thee, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, and they shall eat and be filled.* However, the Law of Grace has absolved us from the second and third tithes; therefore, in the same way, from...

**F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,**

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
...those of the first kind. ¶ Fifthly: whatever is commanded without a specific determination of time places the negligent person in fault unless it is paid at a suitable time. Therefore, if the necessity to pay tithes urged those who profess the Gospel, it would consequently follow that in lands where this payment is not the custom, they would be guilty of a criminal offense—not only those failing to pay, but also the ministers of the church who look the other way. This is not a conclusion that should be easily granted.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the testimony of Augustine in the 16th question, 1st canon, titled "Tithes," where he says: tithes are required as a debt, and those who refuse to give them are invading the property of others.

<margin>The distinction between tithes and other offerings.</margin>
In the entryway of this question, one must immediately weigh the distinction between tithes and other offerings. They differ, in fact, according to every type of cause. First, regarding the purpose by which the others are judged: other offerings are dedicated to God for His honor "immediately" <note>original: "immediatè"; in Scholastic philosophy, this means without an intervening step or secondary purpose</note>, to speak with the scholastics, even though they then redound to the use of the ministers—since they receive them in His name, as was explained regarding sacrifices (the ceremony of which worships the Divine Majesty) and firstfruits (which are paid back to Him for the fruits received). But tithes, as **St. Thomas** says here, were specifically instituted as the **stipend** <term>stipendium; a regular payment or salary for services rendered</term> of the ministers. We have shown this more than sufficiently in Book 3, under the title "On the Acceptance of Persons." For thus it is held in **Numbers 18**:

> To the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession for the ministry by which they serve me in the Tabernacle of the Covenant.

And below, regarding the same tithes:

> It is the price for the ministry by which you serve in the Tabernacle of Witness.

And in **Malachi 3**:

> Bring all the tithes into my storehouse, that there may be food in my house.

And for the same reason, under the Law of Grace, they are paid to priests for their service at the altar and the administration of the sacraments, according to the word of Christ in **Luke 10**:

> The worker is worthy of his hire <note>original: "Dignus est operarius mercede sua"</note>.

And that often-cited verse from **1 Corinthians 9**:

> No one ever served as a soldier at his own expense.

<margin>Innocent</margin>
Which Pope Innocent III cites toward the same opinion in the *Decretals*, in the chapter "Since according to the Apostle." And this—which we have indicated more than enough in the place cited—is the greatest foundation for those things which must not only be said here, but also repeated in the following book. From this follows the second difference regarding the "matter": namely, that while other offerings are not necessary from all 

<column-break/>

things, tithes are paid from everything produced either at home or in the field according to strict law. And finally, a third difference is taken from the "form": for while other offerings are offered voluntarily (or at least as to the amount), tithes are owed by the rigor of a precept, and specifically under that quota which the name itself implies <note>The word "tithe" literally means a "tenth part"</note>.

¶ Having briefly noted these points, the question is answered with four conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First: the payment of tithes is owed by a precept of law that is partly divine and natural, and partly human. For it is a **natural precept** <term>ius naturale; a moral law derived from human nature and reason</term> that the ministers of the church be supported at the people's expense in a general sense; thus, it was included among the "moral" precepts in the Old Law. However, that a "tenth" part of the fruits should be set aside for those expenses was at that time a "judicial" law, and thus in our law, it is a "pontifical" <note>meaning established by the Pope or Church authority</note> law. Both parts are very evident, provided you recall that distinction between moral and judicial precepts which we elucidated extensively in Book 2. For a "moral" precept is whatever is drawn from the principles of nature like the conclusion of a logical syllogism—such as "You shall not kill," derived from the general rule "Do not do to others what you would not have done to you." But a **judicial precept** <term>ius iudiciale; specific applications of general laws that can be determined by a ruler's discretion</term> is one which descends from the universal to the specific by a certain choice; for instance, if you decide that because "something must be offered to God" (the universal), you should specifically offer a two-year-old heifer or some other animal.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
This distinction being assumed, the conclusion is easily clear. Indeed, the first part was sufficiently demonstrated by us in the preceding question under the title "On the Poverty of the Religious." For whoever administers and serves the commonwealth in a necessary matter has a right to receive—and even to demand—a stipend from that same commonwealth. Moreover, the administration of divine worship is necessary to the commonwealth; indeed, much more so than that of secular magistrates. Therefore, the commonwealth owes a stipend to such ministers, and this much more justly than those which are conferred upon princes and soldiers; for by divine order, temporal things serve spiritual things. Therefore, God by the highest right instituted churches and their ministers; for their support, as the Lord of all things, He could command the people to give whatever portion of their goods He Himself deemed just. This same natural right is taught by **Paul in 1 Corinthians 9**. The other part of the conclusion, however, is no less clear. For the law of nature only commands the support of ministers according to their number and dignity. But truly, what the tax on the people ought to be must be established by the judgment and prudence of the commonwealth according to the quality of the matter.

<summary>Soto argues that while the general support of clergy is a requirement of natural law, the specific requirement of a "tenth" (tithe) is a matter of human or ecclesiastical law. He distinguishes tithes from voluntary offerings by noting that tithes are specifically intended as a salary for the spiritual services provided by ministers.</summary>

### Book Nine, Question IV.

...while leaving it behind. However, God, who governed that ancient people <note>The Israelites</note> with peculiar care, set apart one of the twelve tribes for the administration of divine worship. Because of this, that tribe could not devote itself to agriculture, and therefore was not to possess its own portion in the Promised Land. To ensure they received no less than the others—and indeed a little more, as a mark of honor—from the fruits of the earth, God commanded a tenth part from each of the remaining tribes for the support of these **Levites**, as is clear in Leviticus 23 and frequently elsewhere. Because of this, even if the payment was perhaps not made perfectly, that tribe received a bit more than the rest. For out of the 110 parts that the eleven tribes gathered into their barns each year, they gave eleven to the Levites; thus, each of the other tribes retained only nine parts for themselves.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From this, it follows that the precept concerning the specific quota was, as **St. Thomas Aquinas** says, **judicial** <note>In Scholastic law, "judicial" precepts were those governing the civil and social equity of the Israelites, which could be adapted by later governments, unlike "moral" laws which never change</note>, like many other laws for maintaining equity and decorum among the people. Nevertheless, as a consequence, it also signified something for the future, just as almost all their deeds did, according to 1 Corinthians 10: *All these things happened to them in figure.* For the tenth part is a symbol of perfection, since the number ten is the highest limit of the fingers' counting, encompassing all others. By this quota, that people protested that their law and status were not yet perfect, but that its completion depended upon Christ. But truly, although for this reason that precept agreed in some way with the **ceremonial** laws, it was not of the same kind, because it was not established primarily for the sake of signifying something.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Second conclusion.** There was a difference between the ceremonial and judicial precepts of the law, as we demonstrated near the end of the second book and repeated just a moment ago: ceremonial laws <note>Laws regarding religious rituals, like animal sacrifice</note> are not permitted to be integrated after the Gospel. Judicial laws, however, although they have been entirely invalidated regarding the force of that ancient Law, can nonetheless be restored in some parts for Christians. For example, the **law of retaliation** <note>Lex talionis: the principle of "an eye for an eye"</note> or the rule that one who steals a sheep must return fourfold, can be instituted by a prince through modern law.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Third conclusion.** The determination of tithes to this specific quota is a matter of **ecclesiastical and pontifical law** <note>Law created by the Church and the Pope</note>, which was instituted through prudent considerations. That the Church could establish this is beyond doubt, since it was not of that ceremonial class which prefigured something of the New Law; rather, it was judicial, and related to divine worship—which among us remains even more

<column-break/>

excellently. But as to why the Church ought to have commanded that same quota:

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is proven both on the part of the people and on the part of the priests. On the part of the people: because a person of the Gospel excels the ancient person in dignity and is endowed with a more abundant justice, according to Matthew 5: *Unless your justice abounds more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.* On the part of the priests: because they are of a far more excellent dignity than the ancients, handling a more sublime sacrament, as the Apostle showed in 2 Corinthians 3. Therefore, the general concept of tithes has its origin in **natural law**, but the specific type has been rightly sanctioned by the Church through human law. ¶ **Fourth conclusion.** This quota of tithes can be instituted as greater or smaller according to the judgment of the Church, based on the quality and opportunity of times, places, and persons. This conclusion is an appendix to the one above.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding the corollary of the first conclusion, which asserted that tithes belong to the judicial order, someone might perhaps feel uncertain. Firstly, because since they pertain to divine worship, they seem rather to be a ceremony. Secondly and primarily, because of the chapter *Tua nobis* concerning tithes, where **Pope Innocent III** says that God commanded them to be paid to Himself as a sign of His universal lordship; from which it follows that they belong to the religion of worship.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ To this, however, one may easily respond through what has already been said. For tithes are not offered immediately to God like a sacrifice; rather, they are paid to ministers as wages, just as taxes are paid to princes. Therefore, the tithes themselves are not the worship, but the stipends for the ministers who are deputized for worship, according to the cited word of Malachi: *that there may be food in my house.* For this reason, the Prophet immediately adds that because the tithes were not being paid, God withheld the rain and oppressed the people with hunger. But because God instituted the churches, the sacraments, and their ministers to whom He assigned these stipends, the Pope says they are presented to God as a sign of His universal lordship. Our solution is confirmed because the quota was established for our church ministers, just as for the ancient ones, to maintain equality among the people and to ensure the humanity of the common folk and the honor owed to priests—which is an indication that it exists within the judicial order.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Another argument is taken from the same canon: namely, that not only tithes in their general substance, but also the specific quotas, are a matter of **divine law**. For the Pope was speaking there about the integrity of tithes; but we shall speak of this shortly in the solution to the final argument, where I will speak again...

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's investigation into the legal nature of tithes. Having previously established that the specific "tenth" is a judicial rather than moral law, he now addresses whether the Church has the authority to change this amount and responds to critics—specifically Cardinal Cajetan—who argue that the tithe is primarily a fund for the poor rather than the property of the clergy.</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Law

We shall repeat our statement that the specific quota <note>The "quota" refers to the specific 10% amount of the tithe</note> is not required by divine law. Indeed, the Old Law <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament</note> no longer binds us, and nothing is written concerning such a quota in the New Sacred Word <note>The New Testament</note>. Instead, there exist ecclesiastical and papal constitutions modeled after the ancient laws, as is clear throughout the entire title on tithes <note>original: "de decimis"</note> in Canon Law and elsewhere frequently. Nevertheless, these same holy decrees bind us under the guilt of mortal sin; thus, unless custom excuses the fault, it would be a sacrilege not to pay that same quota.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
From these points, it is inferred—as we stated in the fourth conclusion—that this same quota can be varied, and by the dispensation of the Pope, it can be both reduced and abolished. This remains true as long as that which belongs to natural law remains intact and preserved: namely, that from some source, the ministers of the churches should have sufficient food and other supports for life according to their dignity and office. For no custom or dispensation can violate this principle.

<margin>A serious doubt.</margin>
Having explained these evident matters, the third conclusion presents us with a primary doubt, one most worthy of explanation. For if this quota—as is well known—is commanded neither by the Gospel law nor any divine law, it seems the Church has demanded too much from the Christian family for its administrators. In doing so, it seems to have preserved neither the equity of the ancient law nor the humanity that the New Law should have adopted. For if the tenth was assigned to the temple ministers among the Hebrew people, there was a reason for it: the **Levites** <note>The tribe of Israel designated as priests and temple workers</note> were one-twelfth of the people. Therefore, even if they received eleven tenths, it was not an enormous excess, since each of the remaining tribes retained nine parts. This was especially justified because they had wives and families to support. However, the Christian clergy of pastors—to whom alone (if we believe **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas</note>) tithes are owed for their ministry—is perhaps not a tenth part of the people; perhaps they are only a fiftieth. Therefore, that they should receive as many tenths from the remaining forty-nine, while each of those others is left with only nine, seems to be supported by no equity. This is especially true because they ought to have neither wives nor offspring. Furthermore, Christians are even commanded to pay personal tithes <note>Tithes on labor or income, rather than just on the fruits of the land</note>, which were not in use in ancient times.

From these points, it follows that neither of the reasons with which **St. Thomas** supported the third conclusion is solid. For even if the Christian people ought to surpass the Hebrews in justice, it is not necessary to abound in this to the point of pouring out more than what is just upon their priests. And although priests are to be honored more than those of old, they need not be honored with such a massive heap of stipends.

<column-break/>

<margin>Cajetan's solution.</margin>
These are the reasons by which others, and especially Cajetan in this passage, are convinced. They find no other justice in the quota of tithes than that it is paid to the clergy not for themselves alone, but for the poor, to whom they are bound to distribute the fruits of the church. Indeed, if these authors merely meant that ecclesiastics are bound by a far stricter and holier bond of mercy to be charitable to the poor than laity are, the assertion would be most certain. However, they contend that tithes are not paid to them entirely as owners, but are entrusted to them as administrators, a part of which they are bound by the rigor of justice to return to the needy. Indeed, Cajetan says they are bound by as great an obligation as that by which the tithes are owed to them. Thus, it follows for these authors that those who do otherwise are liable for restitution. Truly, this does not possess such great probability that the contrary is not far more probable; indeed, if I am not mistaken, the contrary is true by certain reason, as will be established in the following book. We are preparing an extensive dispute on this matter there, and for that reason, we must refrain from it for the present. But because this is the primary argument with which our adversaries strive to support their opinion, it is worthwhile to respond to them on this point now.

<margin>Solution to the proposed doubt.</margin>
First, then, let us affirm the contrary foundation if possible: namely, that the tenth part under this quota does not exceed a just stipend for the ministries of the church, even if the whole is awarded to them as true owners.

<margin>Reason for the first assertion above.</margin>
And this is proven by a reason contrary to the one the adversaries use: The just number of clergy who are necessary for divine worship in the Law of Grace <note>The Christian era</note> is not so much smaller than the rest of the people that they receive the tenth unjustly. Indeed, perhaps they are a twelfth part of the people, just as the Levitical tribe once was, or at most a fifteenth, or much less than a twentieth. This is proven as follows: In the Old Law, there was only one single temple to which all twelve tribes flocked for sacred rites, and that only four times a year, for there were only that many principal solemnities. In our Church, however, there are scarcely a hundred houses that do not have their own temple, which is served daily by all the priests (for the ancients served in weekly shifts). If, therefore, a twelfth part of the people was enrolled for the service of precisely *one* temple, what miracle is it if an equal part is now enslaved to the administration of such a multitude of temples? Since the calculation of means must be measured by the end...

<summary>Soto debates whether the 10% tithe is excessive for the Christian clergy compared to the ancient Levites, ultimately arguing that the high number of Christian churches justifies the expense, while disagreeing with Cajetan's view that tithes belong to the poor.</summary>

# Book Nine, Question IV.

...is taken. But Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), was a prominent Italian Dominican theologian and cardinal.</note> says that tithes are owed only to those clerics who have the "care of souls" <note>term: "cura animarum" (care of souls); the spiritual responsibility for a specific group of laypeople, such as a parish.</note>. Truly, I do not know what foundation he could have had for such an assertion, for he brought forward none. Indeed, if such a numerous multitude of singers and other ministers—as we read in the books of Chronicles—was assigned to that ancient Temple which housed nothing but the Ark of the Covenant, why should a larger number of priests beyond just the parish ministers not be dedicated to our temples, in which the Body of Christ is adored and worshipped? And should tithes not be contributed to them so that, according to the word of Malachi, they may have "food in the house of God"?

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
Furthermore, let us add to this that our priests are of much higher dignity than those of old. Among them, there ought to be a very large number of prelates, and likewise Canons <note>term: "Canons"; clergy members who are part of a cathedral or collegiate church, often living according to a specific rule or "canon."</note>, who are necessary for the church to shine forth in splendor, and who have a need for assistants and households. For if someone should object to us that everyone ought to live in poverty, certainly no one would reject this opinion if it were possible for such a great number of clerics as is necessary to shine with decent holiness; for then, even without other adornment, they would be held in high esteem by the people. But because that cannot be done, it is necessary to make allowances for the human condition.

Not everyone can be like Saint Martin or Saint Nicholas <note>Saint Martin of Tours and Saint Nicholas were famous for their extreme asceticism and legendary charity.</note>. Therefore, it is necessary to honor priests with households and authority so that the people do not despise them, but rather respect them as leading members of the commonwealth. For this reason, it is not unbecoming if bishops live like other great lords, canons like other nobles, and priests like other citizens. Indeed, there is clear evidence for this: in those provinces where priests are oppressed by excessive poverty, they become vile in the sight of the people; and from there, the sacraments and holy things tend toward a state where they are held in contempt. Therefore, to take up another argument, it is not fitting for our priests, given the dignity of the sacraments, to be craftsmen or to practice manual labor, which was permitted for the Levites <note>The Levites were the tribe of Israel designated for religious duties, though they were sometimes allowed certain forms of manual work.</note>. Let us conclude, then, that if it is fitting for the ecclesiastical order to be so large and distinguished, and if we consider all its ranks with their households, it constitutes no less than a twelfth part—or as they used to say, a fifteenth—of the population.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
Furthermore, our priests must be free for the study of literature <note>In this context, "literature" refers to theology, law, and the liberal arts.</note>, and must expend their inheritance on this pursuit. Thus, people could not be found who would undertake such great expenses and spend so much of their life and labor without some proposed reward. For those who would do this solely out of

<column-break/>

love for religion would be very rare indeed. Therefore, the Church had to consider human nature and indulge its weakness. I confess frankly that ecclesiastical offices <note>original: "sacerdotia"</note> are most unfairly distributed. Thus, some have an abundance and overflow with pomp and luxury—not without scandal—while others are hungry. Nevertheless, if distributions were made according to the rule of divine law, based on the quality and dignity of the persons, it would be clearly established that the ecclesiastical decree concerning the ten-percent quota is not superfluous, but most equitable. It was for this reason that in the early Church, where the faith was more sincerely practiced, many enriched the churches from their own substance.

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
Added to this is the fact that tithes are not paid so exactly everywhere, and in many places they are quite meager; many monasteries and hospitals were founded upon the income from them. Beyond this, when some calamity strikes the Church, larger expenditures are necessary; for which reason a good portion of the tithes has already been granted to kings. All these things, therefore, the Church foresaw with maturity when it decreed the tithes.

Therefore, to justify this law, there is no need to resort to the argument that clerics are bound by justice to distribute their goods as alms. For this reason, Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian.</note>, with great deliberation, did not mention this reason when proving his third conclusion; he only mentioned that our people ought to be more just than those of old, and our priests of greater dignity. However, because the law of mercy binds clerics more strictly, the same Holy Doctor adds two or three times in this question that tithes are given to priests so that they may be more lavishly kind to the poor.

<margin>The last reason.</margin>
And to place the strongest argument for our position at the end, it is finally argued: The quota of tithes is nothing other than a moderation and specification of natural law. Natural law commands tithes only for this: that they serve as food and stipend for the ministers of the Church. Therefore, the quota was established precisely for this purpose according to the rigor of justice, not for the use of the poor. For even Cajetan himself concedes in the present discussion that tithes are owed to ministers only for their livelihood according to natural law; but the law of almsgiving, he says, is the reason they are given more abundantly to those same priests on behalf of the poor. But truly, I do not see why the people should be forced to entrust the alms for the poor to the priests. Concerning this, however, we shall speak below in the cited place. Therefore, no one should have worried about that devised proportion—that the clergy is not even a fiftieth
