# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right,

...a part of the people fall into this opinion: that clerics are bound by justice, under penalty of restitution <note>Restitution is the moral obligation to return something taken or kept unfairly; Soto is debating if priests "steal" from the poor if they don't give away their extra income.</note>, to bestow their stipends upon the poor. For a matter of such great importance certainly ought not to be affirmed without an express decree of the Church. I would say the proportion [they have] devised is imaginary; for to sum everything up, if you consult experience (upon which moral science relies), there is no city or notable town where you will not find many more wealthy people than there are priests. It is therefore a fiction to say that they themselves have fifty-nine tenths, while individuals in the rest of the population have [only] nine.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Therefore, the first argument has been sufficiently discussed and diluted. 
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
To the second, it is answered that the precept of tithes, in that part which is natural and moral, was designated there by Christ where, in Luke 10, He says that "the laborer is worthy of his hire" <note>original: "dignum esse operarium mercede sua"</note>. It was more fully emphasized by the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 9, where he established through many natural and civil examples that "he who serves the altar should live by the altar" <note>original: "qui altario seruit de altario viuat"</note>. But as for the specific amount <note>term: "quota"; the fixed portion or percentage, in this case, the one-tenth portion.</note>, it was committed to the judgment and decision of the Church.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
To the third, it is answered that before the time of the Old Law, from Adam onward, the same mandate always flourished insofar as it is natural. For there were always priests in any well-ordered republic, who are said to have been the firstborn. But truly, because they were not decreed in a certain number, each republic established the specific amount at its own discretion, or provided for its priests from elsewhere. Moreover, Abraham—as read in Genesis 14—offered tithes to Melchizedek by prophetic instinct; Melchizedek, as Paul witnesses, prefigured our priesthood. And perhaps by the same spirit, Jacob vowed those same tithes not to specific priests, but to God.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
To the fourth, it is answered that since sacrifices were repeated so frequently among those ancient people [the Israelites], they found it necessary to reserve "second tithes" for the offering of sacrifices, in addition to the tithes to be paid to the Levites. These are not commanded for us, for whom those animal sacrifices have now ceased. Truly, the third kind of tithes, which were to be divided with the poor, is increased in the New Law by the mandate of mercy, by which Christ repeatedly warned us to be generous toward the poor. For He says in Luke 11: "What remains, give as alms" <note>original: "Quod superest, date eleemosynam."</note>. Moreover, Saint Thomas [Aquinas] adds that the tithes given to the ministers of the Church ought to be dispensed by those same ministers for the use of the poor. That he did not understand this as a precept of justice, but of mercy,

<column-break/>

is evident from the fact that he joined this with the other precept of almsgiving.

<margin>A question touched upon by the last argument.</margin>
Finally, by the last argument, that doubt is touched upon: whether the law of tithes can be abolished through disuse. This depends on another question: whether tithes are by divine law <note>term: "ius divinum" (divine law); laws believed to come directly from God, which humans cannot change.</note>. And indeed, some 
<margin>The opinion of the Jurists.</margin>
interpreters of Canon Law <note>term: "Canon Law"; the internal legal system and regulations of the Catholic Church.</note>, commenting on the chapter *In Aliquibus* regarding tithes, judge them to be entirely of divine law, even regarding the specific amount. For after it is said there that tithes are to be paid in full, it is added: "because they are owed by divine law, or by the approved custom of the place." And in the chapter *Paroecianos* under the same title, it is read that tithes were instituted not by man, but by the Lord Himself; and in the chapter *Tua Nobis* cited above, and the chapter *Revertimini* elsewhere regarding tithes, the same seems to be suggested. And although the sayings of other doctors could be explained away <gloss>original: "glossari"</gloss> as referring to tithes in their substance [rather than amount], 
<margin>Hostiensis.</margin>
Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canonist known as "Hostiensis."</note> in his *Summa*, under the title "On Tithes," section 7, expressly maintains that even the specific amount is of divine law. He says both that the precept of the amount was moral, and that the law has not entirely ceased, emphasizing this with many authorities and even mocking Raymond <note>Raymond of Peñafort (c. 1175–1275), a Dominican friar and famous legal scholar.</note> and the theologians who think otherwise. But truly, this is not a matter that can [reasonably] come into controversy, since it is very clear that the amount of the tithe in the Old Law was a judicial precept, not a moral one. This Hostiensis would never have denied if it had been within his faculty to know the reason for the distinction between a moral precept and a judicial one.

<margin>The previous opinion is rejected.</margin>
For a moral precept (as has often been said) is a conclusion of natural principles. While from these it may be drawn that the ministers of the Church must be supported (which pertains to the kind and substance of tithes), nevertheless, no law of nature commands that this or that specific portion of the fruits be contributed, but only that as much be given as suffices for them. But the explanation <note>gloss</note> that he strives to attach to the words of Paul in Hebrews 7 must be noted. Paul says: "The priesthood being changed, it is necessary that a change of the law also be made" <note>original: "Transacto sacerdotio necesse est vt legis translatio fiat."</note>. The meaning of this is that the law expired with Christ, and thus those legal ceremonies ceased. But he [Hostiensis] responds that it does not have that meaning, because, he says, it must in no way be conceded that the law has entirely ceased. Rather, he says the sense is that the right of the Levites to seek tithes has passed to the Gospel priests. See how much more wisely those who do not profess Theology would act if they kept their pens away from the interpretation of Holy Scripture, and did not treat divine or natural law, which is for them another man’s harvest. For it ceased...

He critiques legal scholars like Hostiensis for overstepping into theology and failing to distinguish between eternal moral principles and historical Jewish laws.</summary>

# Book Nine, Question IV.

...for that law has indeed ceased entirely, as we most broadly demonstrated in Book 2; except for that which either the law of nature retained or the Church ordained. Therefore, it is most certain that this specific portion <term>quota; the fixed amount of one-tenth</term> is not from divine law. But if any words are found among the Decretals and sacred Canons by which tithes are attributed to divine law, they must be understood either regarding their substance <note>The "substance" refers to the core moral duty to support the clergy, which is considered a divine and natural requirement.</note>, or if the discussion concerns the specific amount, it must be interpreted so that it is from divine law *by way of example*—that is, established after the pattern of the ancient law of the Old Testament.

<margin>The solution of St. Thomas to the main question.</margin>
Therefore, as to whether the obligation of tithes can be abolished through disuse <note>original: "desuetudinem"; the legal principle where a law loses its force because it is no longer practiced</note>, St. Thomas [Aquinas] seems to deny this entirely for the present. For he responds that in Italy, and in those lands where tithes are not paid, the inhabitants are cleared from fault for this reason alone: that the ministers of the Church are deemed to grant them an indulgence by not demanding them; just as Paul testifies he did in 1 Corinthians 9. For there, after he demonstrated that he had the power to seek sustenance from his followers, he adds that he "did not use that same power," lest he should give any offense to the Gospel of Christ.

However, this response of St. Thomas is not altogether clear. For its understanding, therefore, one must distinguish regarding the disuse of tithes. For it is weighed either as to the specific portion, or in its entirety. And in the former way, perhaps one might judge that disuse alone suffices so that they are not owed, because the portion is only from positive <note>Human-made or ecclesiastical law, rather than natural or divine law.</note> law. And accordingly, one would think St. Thomas understands this as a cessation of the obligation in its entirety. But truly, both are false. The first indeed, not certainly because of the reasoning of Hostiensis <note>Henry of Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a famous expert in Canon Law</note> and others who say the portion is of divine law, but because although it is of pontifical <note>Papal or Church-made</note> law, nonetheless, because that law is both so powerful in equity and also established in the likeness of the ancient divine law, no disuse is deemed to prevail against it so as to prevent the Church from using its right where necessary—unless it has consented and turned a blind eye.

<margin>The view of St. Thomas.</margin>
And this is the mind of St. Thomas. For by the name of "tithes," he understands the specific portion. And in the same way, his *Quodlibeta* 2, Article 8, is to be understood, where he responds in the same manner. And it is confirmed that he speaks of the specific portion, for the disuse of tithes in their entirety can in no way be permitted by the Church. Since, as has already been shown, it exists as a natural right and a moral precept—and a most strict divine one—that there be churches where divine matters are celebrated and sacraments dispensed and administered, and thus priests and ministers be nourished at the people's expense. Therefore, concerning this whole matter, the Church does not have the authority to grant a dispensation...

<column-break/>

...nor will it ever be permitted by the Holy Spirit to do so. This is clearly shown by practice itself: since neither in any corner of Italy nor anywhere else among nations is a place of Christians found where there are not priests, for whom there are either fixed annual revenues or stipends provided by the people.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
But truly, against the first part of the solution, there exists an argument which, as Augustine says in the 16th [book], Question 1, in the canon "Tithes," the payment of tithes is the "tribute of needy souls."
<margin>Augustine</margin>
And those who refuse to give them, he says, "invade the property of others," and "the poor, having perished by hunger because of that penury, are killed by those who do not pay." Therefore, it seems the Church cannot overlook the matter against the rights of the poor. But if it is said that it permits this to avoid scandal, it follows that it does not do so freely;
<margin>To the argument.</margin>
therefore, those not paying seem least of all to be excused from fault. To the first part of the argument, it is answered that the right of the poor is not one of strict justice, but of mercy—not only in those paying tithes, but also in the clerics themselves. And therefore, the Church can overlook extorting those same alms by that method. To the second part, however, it is answered that even if it permits this to avoid scandal—and lest, as Paul says, an "impediment be given to the Gospel"—nonetheless the subjects are excused; because the Church does this laudably, putting temporal things after spiritual ones. But where a people might become hardened by stubbornness of mind so that they would not wish to obey the Church when it asks, then it would not be free from fault. If, however, some nation wished to give their names to Christianity <note>i.e., to convert to the faith</note> on the condition that they would in no way be burdened by the tax of tithes, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading theologian of the Dominican order.</note> responds that the Church can and ought to receive that same condition. Provided that if it is understood regarding the specific portion, it is true. Nevertheless, so that they would be bound in no way to nourish the ministers of the Church, certainly the Church could not allow it, unless it provided from elsewhere that by which they might live; for otherwise that condition would be contrary to natural and divine law in a matter which is of the greatest importance among Christians.

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<columns>
<column-break/>

<margin>Argument 2.</margin> Furthermore, in that place <note>Referring to the biblical law codes</note>, no commandment is read concerning personal tithes: namely, those things which a person acquires by their own industry and business, such as trade, military service, and the like. Therefore, no tithes are owed on these. ¶ Second, regarding ill-gotten gains (as was said above), no offering can be made; therefore, no payment of tithes can be made either. For since offerings are more closely related to divine worship, they should rather be made from all things.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third, in the last chapter of Leviticus where the law of tithes is written, it is commanded only concerning the fruits of the earth and the produce of trees and concerning animals that pass under the shepherd's staff; therefore, tithes are not owed on the smaller herbs produced by garden cultivation.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin> ¶ Fourth, no one can pay except what is in their own power; but not all fruits harvested from estates remain in the owner’s power. For some are paid by the tenant farmers to the lords of the lands; some as wages to servants; some even to princes as taxes. And often some perish either by theft or by some other way; therefore, nothing is owed from those. ¶ On the contrary is the example of the law in Genesis 28 regarding Jacob, who said: *Of all that you give to me, I will offer a tenth to you.* <note>original: "Cunctorum quae dederis mihi decimas offeram tibi."</note> Moreover, all things that a person possesses are given to them by God; therefore, tithes are owed on all things.

<margin>Negative conclusion.</margin> To the question, it is answered with a single conclusion: tithes are owed on all things, both from the produce of the land and from those parts acquired by the labor of persons, if you weigh the pure law and custom does not stand in the way.

<margin>Proof.</margin> This is proven. The judgment of any matter must be taken from its own proper causes and roots. Now, the native root of tithes is that, according to the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 9, a right belongs to those sowing spiritual things to reap material things. <note>original: "carnalia," literally "carnal things," referring to physical or worldly goods.</note> *If we,* he says, *sow spiritual things, it is no wonder if we reap your material things.* For this is the foundation of the ecclesiastical institution. Moreover, all things that a person possesses are included under the term "material things"; therefore, tithes must be paid on all things. ¶ Indeed, the present conclusion is established in many places of canon law, such as the chapter *Tua nobis* on tithes, and the chapter *Revertimini* (16, question 1). But it is more expressly stated in the canon *Decimae*, which is by Augustine, where he says that tithes are to be paid from business, from military service, from craftsmanship, and finally from all things. Pope Celestine says the same in the chapter *Non est* in the Extra <note>The *Decretals of Gregory IX*, a collection of canon law.</note>, regarding tithes, where it is held that they are even owed from hunting. And the chapter *Pervenit* includes fishing and

<column-break/>

mills, etc., and the chapter *Nuntios* even adds bees.

<margin>Other tithes: Real tithes.</margin> For this reason, a famous distinction of tithes is customary: into "real" (or "predial") and "personal." "Real" tithes are those owed from things: for instance, from the fruits of estates which the earth produces by its own nature through the mercy of the sun and air. "Personal" tithes, however, are those paid from the works and business of persons carried out without the help of the land.

<margin>Objection against the reasoning of St. Thomas.</margin> ¶ Whatever truth the conclusion may contain, the reasoning of St. Thomas [Aquinas] does not seem to carry great force here. For he infers a universal from a particular: namely, that if the right belongs to clerics to reap material things, then stipends are owed to them from *all* material things.

<margin>Solution.</margin> It is answered, first, that Saint Thomas brought forward this reason rather to declare and defend ecclesiastical law than to demonstrate its absolute necessity. Second, since the law of nature (as has been said) supplies the right to clerics to reap temporal things in exchange for spiritual ones, the reasoning does not lean so heavily toward some temporal things that it cannot be understood of almost all of them. For what is usually brought against this—that tithes are more justly owed from the fruits of the field than from crafts, because God as the author of nature creates those fruits, while crafts and other businesses pertain to human industry—although it carries a certain probability, it does not carry necessity. This is because industry is also employed in agriculture, and God’s natural cooperation is not lacking in business. This is especially true because the obligation of tithes, if you look at what has been said, is not founded on that natural benefit from God, but rather on the fact that the people are bound to sustain the ministers of the Church from whom they receive the sacraments. And therefore, because there are very many who do not practice agriculture but another art, and these are equally participants in the sacraments, there is no reason why they should be exempted from the collection of the ecclesiastical tribute. Therefore, the word of Paul, by which he names "material things," seems to present a universal sense to the ears.

<margin>Doubt.</margin> ¶ Notwithstanding these things, someone might inquire whether disuse <note>original: "desuetudo"; the legal principle where a law loses its force through lack of practice.</note> could be a legitimate cause of prescription regarding personal tithes, so that they need not be paid.

<margin>The opinion of Hostiensis.</margin> Someone might inquire, I say, because of Hostiensis in his *Summa* <note>Henry of Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canonist known as Hostiensis.</note> in the place cited, and other interpreters of the law on the chapter *In aliquibus* regarding tithes. These authors distinguish between decimal <note>meaning land-based or "real"</note> and personal tithes in such a way that they believe a prescription <note>a legal claim based on long-term custom</note> can grow against the latter, but not against the former.

<margin>Foundation of the above opinion.</margin> Their foundation is that the former are from divine law, but the latter are not at all; since in the cited place of the last chapter of Leviticus, nothing is commanded except

</columns>

### Book Nine, Question IV.

...unless tithes are declared only on the crops, the fruits of trees, and animals. But enough has already been fought against those opponents regarding this matter. For that ancient law, which was judicial in nature, has already expired as far as the force of that specific law is concerned; therefore, one should not dwell so much on the distinction between these types of income. Nor does Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential theologian whose "Summa Theologiae" Soto is commenting upon.</note> distinguish between them regarding this type of <term>prescription</term> <note>A legal principle where a right is gained or lost through the passage of time or long-standing custom.</note>.

<margin>The author’s solution.</margin>
Therefore, as we were saying at the end of the last article, whether you consider them <term>predial tithes</term> <note>Tithes derived from the land and its products (from the Latin "praedium," meaning estate or farm).</note> or <term>personal tithes</term> <note>Tithes derived from an individual's labor, such as wages or business profits.</note>, no amount of disuse or prescription can at any time prevail against the Church to prevent it from commanding taxes—whether from estates or from persons—sufficient to honorably support the ministers of the Church, provided no other path is open for their maintenance. Furthermore, it cannot be ignored that temples must be built and ministers assigned to them. However, it must be admitted that there is a distinction: tithes are more justly and readily demanded from the produce of the earth than from trades and businesses, because those fruits are more natural. For this reason, if enough support is available from the land, one can claim a prescription against personal tithes; that is, unless a custom of paying them is already in force, it is not right that they be demanded.

<margin>Tithes should not be demanded from servants or farmhands unless a custom for this exists.</margin>
For this reason, regarding the practice of demanding tithes from servants out of their wages: unless a custom older than all memory compels it, there is no apparent equity in it. And there is even less reason to demand them from the servants of farmers, whose wages are paid from a pile of grain that has already been tithed; this is gathered from Saint Thomas in his solution to the fourth point. For the opinion of Saint Augustine—that tithes should be paid from business and military service—perhaps retains its force in places where the land tithes are not particularly rich or abundant. This is why in Spain there is no custom of paying tithes from the profits of tradesmen and businesses.

¶ Whether a farmer can take out his labor costs and expenses, or at least his seeds, from the pile of grain before tithing is a question I see no reason to doubt; nor does reason allow custom to prevail in this matter. Indeed, it is so certain that this is not permitted, as is cautioned in the legal chapters *Non est*, *Tua nobis*, and *Pastoralis* <note>These are specific chapters in the "Decretals of Gregory IX," a primary source of medieval Canon Law.</note>. For at present, we must imagine a certain kind of partnership between man and God. Man provides his seeds, labor, and expenses, and he exposes them to risk, trusting in God. Therefore, since God by His kindness confers a heaped-up harvest, it is enough if the man, for his risk, keeps nine parts for himself and returns the tenth to God.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**T**o the first argument, therefore, the response is as follows: The reason personal tithes were not demanded among the ancient people <note>The Israelites of the Old Testament.</note> was that each of the eleven tribes had their own portions of estates, the tithes of which were sufficient for the tribe of Levi, which lacked a portion. This was especially true because the Levites were not barred from other trades and secular businesses; therefore, it would have been unfair to scrape tithes from similar trades practiced by others. However, it is different in the Christian family, as has been said: not everyone possesses land from which to pay tithes, and clerics must not involve themselves in worldly business, as Paul warns in 2 Timothy 2.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ **T**o the second argument, the response is that "ill-gotten" gains fall into two categories. There are some whose acquisition is unjust and injurious, such as theft, robbery, and likewise usury <note>The practice of charging interest on loans, which was heavily restricted by the Church.</note>. And because these must be restored in full to their true owners, they cannot be tithed. It is different, however, for the fruits of trees bought with usurious money; for those, as shown in Book 6, are not subject to restitution, nor are the profits made from that same usurious money. Others are called "ill-gotten" not because the acquisition is injurious or unjust, but because they are obtained through a shameful cause. Examples include the earnings of prostitutes, stage actors, and others of that kind. And of these, says Saint Thomas, tithes are owed. He was speaking, however, according to the custom of his own time and region, where Augustine’s opinion was fully in use. Yet now, so far as I have heard, such an observance of tithes persists nowhere.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ **T**o the third argument, the response is that since tithes were once paid as the portion of the Levites, they ought to have been demanded honorably and without pettiness. Regarding pettiness, Aristotle <margin>Aristotle.</margin> writes in Book 4 of the *Ethics* (in the chapter on liberality) that it is the mark of a petty man to be an exactor of the smallest things; thus it was not fitting for the Levites to demand tithes from tiny garden herbs. But the Pharisees, who sought a splendor of justice beyond the rest of the people, paid tithes even on those. Nor did the Redeemer scold them for tithing mint, dill, and rue, but rather because they valued those things more than the greater commandments. Indeed, he commended it to some extent when he added: *These things you ought to have done, without neglecting the others* <note>original: "Haec oportet facere, sed alia non omittere." Matthew 23:23.</note>. In that passage, he attributed such tithing not so much to a command as to a counsel. Under the Law of the Gospel, however, immemorial custom must be observed. Indeed, where tithes of crops and wine might be meagerly produced, tithes on gardens could be demanded anew...

<summary>Soto argues that while land-based tithes are more "natural," personal tithes on wages and business depend on local custom and the Church's need. He maintains that farmers cannot deduct expenses before tithing, viewing the harvest as a partnership between human labor and divine providence.</summary>

Having established that tithes are a moral and legal necessity for supporting the Church, he now addresses specific cases of loss, the priority of tithe payments over taxes, and whether the right to collect tithes belongs exclusively to the clergy.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...is true, as found in the Decretals, <note>Original: "extrā, de decimis," referring to the *Decretales*, a collection of papal laws outside the original Decree of Gratian.</note> in the chapter "They are not required." This applies especially to those gardens from which gardeners make their living by selling vegetables. For tithes are not to be required from small private gardens, nor from the most insignificant greens, as noted in the chapter "From manifold." <note>Original: "ex multiplici."</note>

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the fourth argument, it is replied that if the farmer's grain is stolen before the tithing has occurred, then he does not owe the tithes, unless the theft happened through his own culpable negligence. I certainly judge the same if either the standing crops or a heap of grain already threshed is destroyed by some flood on the threshing floor. <note>Original: "area," the open space where grain was separated from stalks.</note> For if he left it on the threshing floor for a long time through his own serious fault, he would certainly not be immune from the debt of tithes. It is otherwise if he were free from blame; for as long as the grain is in the open air, the priests also share in the risk. But after it has been stored in the barns, the owner is then the debtor for the tithes, regardless of what ruin or disaster causes it to perish. Furthermore, it is clear that anyone who sells grain or wine that has not been tithed is held liable for paying the tithe. Indeed, even the buyer, if they knew this, is nonetheless obligated to the Church until the seller makes restitution.

<margin>A Point of Instruction.</margin>
¶ Moreover, it must be noted that since tithes are paid from things obtained through divine favor, they are subject to neither wages nor tribute. Because of this, the farmer can deduct neither the wages of his servants nor the King's tax <note>Original: "regis tributū."</note> from the heap before he pays the tithe of the whole. And I judge that Saint Thomas, <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> under the name of "tribute," also includes the rent <note>Original: "pensionem."</note> which a tenant farmer pays to the owner of someone else's land. Therefore, if you look at the rigor of the law, the farmer who cultivates the land—whether it is his own or someone else's that he has rented for cultivation—is held to the full amount of the tithes, unless it has been otherwise agreed between the same tenant and the landowner. Therefore, if the owner does not pay, the Church can sue the tenant.

¶ From this, we gathered above that a hired laborer who receives wages from already-tithed money owes no other tithe from it. And likewise, it appears the same must be concluded regarding the landowner from the income which the tenant pays him after the tithing has been done.

### ARTICLE III.
### Whether tithes are owed only to clerics.

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
Following the subject matter of tithes, we now turn to the persons to whom they are owed by right and custom. You might argue that they are not owed to clerics, even though the opposite is gathered from what was said above. Tithes were assigned to the ancient Levites, as has already been frequently cited from

<column-break/>

Numbers 18, because they lacked a share of the promised land. In our Christian family, however, clerics sometimes have patrimonies, and they receive offerings and firstfruits in addition to tithes; therefore, tithes seem to be superfluous for them.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: if tithes were owed to clerics by right, there would frequently follow a perplexity in paying them. For it can happen by custom that an inhabitant of one parish <note>Original: "parœciæ."</note> cultivates the fields of another, or has fields in another parish which he leases to be cultivated by a resident of that parish. It also happens that a shepherd might graze his flock in the pastures of one diocese or parish for part of the year, and partly in the pastures of another; or perhaps he himself stays in one, but has his sheepfold in another. Therefore, such men would be perplexed as to which church they should owe tithes.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third: custom frequently holds that secular laypeople possess tithes as a fief, <note>Original: "in feudū." This refers to the historical practice where lay lords were granted the right to collect tithes by the Church or Crown.</note> and they are even conferred upon some monks; therefore, they are not owed to clerics alone.

¶ On the contrary is the fact that, as read in Numbers 18, they were adjudged to the Levites alone, whom the clerics succeed in our time.

<margin>Two things to be considered regarding tithes.</margin>
Having set forth a distinction, the question is answered with two conclusions. For there are two things to consider in tithes: namely, the right of demanding them, and the things themselves.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion, therefore, is: The right of demanding tithes belongs to clerics alone by their own merit.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
It is proved: A spiritual right suits only clerics, as they are the administrators of spiritual things. But this right is spiritual, according to that saying of Paul: "If we sow spiritual things, it is no wonder if we reap your carnal things." <note>1 Corinthians 9:11.</note> Therefore, this right is proper to clerics.

<margin>The final conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: Regarding the things themselves which come to the clerics by this right, nothing forbids them from passing into the right of laypeople by their concession.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
It is proved: because things of this sort, such as grain and wine, are not spiritual.

¶ Here, first of all, the careful reader must discern between the *right of demanding* and the *things themselves*. Otherwise, you might be deceived. Indeed, the holder of a fief—and even kings and princes to whom a portion of tithes has been granted—not only possess the tithes, but they seem to have the right of demanding them. And so, since they are secular themselves, they seem to have a spiritual right. However, this fallacy is dissolved if you understand the "right of demanding" in this context as the faculty of demanding tithes from parishioners as a proper stipend for a spiritual office. For this right exists in the Church alone and its ministers who dispense spiritual things. A fief-holder, however, demands those same tithes only in the name of the same Church. And likewise, the King and the secular Prince do so by the privilege and concession of the same Church.

Soto also clarifies that while the spiritual right to collect tithes belongs only to the clergy, the physical goods may be collected by lay authorities through specific Church concessions.</summary>

# Book Nine, Question IV.

of the church. And to hold such a privilege is not to possess the right of seeking <note>Latin: *ius petendi*</note> for one's own spiritual office, but rather to enjoy the fruits of things: either because they redeemed those things from the church, or because they performed some other service for it—whether by battling infidels or some other similar act, in respect of which they were deservedly granted such a reward.

<margin>Cajetan's assertion.</margin>
¶ Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major Italian theologian and contemporary of Soto.</note>, persisting in his current opinion which we reported previously—namely, that tithes are owed only to clerics who carry the care of souls—says that for this right of seeking, two things must be present simultaneously: the ministry of the altar (specifically the administration of the sacraments) and additionally the "sowing of spiritual things" (that is, the preaching of the Gospel), both of which should be the personal duty of the individual.

<margin>Cajetan is refuted.</margin>
For this reason, he argues that other clerics serving the altar in different ways, as well as monks—to whom preaching belongs only accidentally and not as their own specific duty—do not enjoy this same right as their own. But in truth, we have already stated above that tithes are owed not only because of the administration of sacraments, but also because of other services to the altar: such as singing, as is the case with canons, and assisting in the most holy sacrifice of the altar, which is the duty of deacons; this too is a spiritual work. Indeed, even among the Levites of old, tithes were conferred because of the ministry of the temple, even though there was nothing strictly "spiritual" in the modern sense either in them or in the priests of that time. Although it must be fully admitted that the duty of those with the care of souls <note>Latin: *curatorum*, referring to parish priests or those with a *cura animarum*</note> holds the pinnacle of spiritual effects, and for that reason tithes are primarily owed to them, nonetheless canons, archdeacons, and others of that kind must not be denied a share in the same right according to their rank and order. However, "mercenary" priests who are not attached to any particular church, just like monks, do not enjoy this same right except by special privilege.

<margin>A rule for discerning which prebends are spiritual and which are not.</margin>
¶ From this teaching and the distinction between the "right of seeking" and the possession of the goods themselves acquired by that right, a rule must be drawn to determine which priesthoods and ecclesiastical prebends <note>A *prebend* is the portion of a church's income granted to a cleric as a stipend.</note> are spiritual. This is the fundamental basis for the discussion on simony <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred things or church offices.</note>, which we will enter in the next question. For a prebend that is attached to a spiritual duty is considered spiritual. A spiritual duty is not only the administration of sacraments and the care of souls, but also several other duties of the church. I wonder who could assert the contrary. Otherwise, canonries and other diverse priesthoods established for the service of churches would not be spiritual, and therefore would not be the subject of simony—which would be an error to concede.

<column-break/>

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> responds that tithes were not given to the Levites so that they might give alms from them more than the rest of the people; for another kind of tithe was decreed for that act of piety. In the New Law, however, tithes are contributed not only for the livelihood of clerics, but also for the abundance of alms for the needy. Therefore, although clerics may have other possessions besides tithes—whether ancestral patrimony or things conferred on the church by the kindness and piety of the people, which the Levites did not have—the payment of tithes is not thereby made redundant. Whether Saint Thomas's claim regarding the alms of clerics belongs to the "rigor of justice" (so that those who are negligent are held to restitution) or rather to a particular duty of mercy, will be examined in the next book. In the meantime, however, I do not think he is speaking of the rigor of justice, but of the mercy to which our clerics are obligated more than the Levites, since they do not support the burdens of a wife, and thus more remains for them.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is replied that "personal tithes" are owed to the church of which one is a parishioner, as held in the Decretals <note>Original: *extrā, de deci. cap. Ad Apostolicæ*</note>. "Predial tithes" <note>Tithes based on the produce of the land (praedia).</note>, however, if you consider the nature of things simply, seem to be owed to the same church where the lands lie. Nevertheless, the Church prefers to refer to custom, as is clear in the same chapter and the chapter "Since they are men." Therefore, if a farmer lives in one parish but cultivates the lands of another, it is commanded that the established custom be observed. For both churches can allege their right: one because it dispenses the sacraments to the person, the other because the lands lie in its territory. For this reason, in many places, the tithes are usually divided.

¶ In the same way, if a noble citizen who lives in a city parish owns estates in some fort or village which he leases out for cultivation, reason seems to require—and indeed usage mostly holds—that the tithes be divided. However, where a prescribed custom commands otherwise, it must be followed. Saint Thomas responds the same regarding a shepherd who has his flock in one parish during the spring and in another during the winter: namely, that he should pay to each church proportionally. However, in some places it is the custom that the tithing occurs where the "increase" of the flock is taken—that is, where they are either sheared or where they give birth. But Saint Thomas seems to feel the opposite here, saying that because the fruits of the flock come from the pastures, the tithing should be done where the pastures are rather than where the sheepfold is located. All these things are to be noted...

...must be noted, not for the sake of uprooting long-standing customs, but to know who ought to be chosen according to reason in cases where a clear custom does not prevail. <margin>To the third argument.</margin> ¶ Finally, in response to the third argument, it is stated that just as clerics <note>A general term for any ordained minister in the Church.</note> may sell or in any way distribute things acquired under the name of "tithes," they may also grant laypeople the power to receive tithes that are to be given in the future. This may be done either by reserving a tax for the church or for the support of the poor—just as tithes are attached to hospitals and monasteries by papal privilege. ¶ Furthermore, as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note> says, the care of souls <note>Latin: *cura animarum*; the spiritual responsibility for a specific group of people, such as a parish.</note> is often joined to certain religious orders, and thus tithes are decreed to them. On this matter, however, there are persuasive arguments on both sides: namely, whether it is appropriate for priesthoods involving the care of souls to be annexed <note>The legal process of joining a parish's income and governance to a monastery.</note> to monasteries. On one hand, it seems that monks are able to watch over the flock more skillfully and vigilantly. On the other hand, it seems closer to the Gospel for a proper parish priest to reside in his own parish, to live among his subjects, and finally to help them with counsel, resources, and the abundance of alms. This is difficult when monks can only administer the matter through a vicar <note>A substitute or deputy priest.</note>. <margin>It is not appropriate for priesthoods with the care of souls to be annexed to monasteries.</margin> And certainly, this latter reasoning has always prevailed with me. I pass over the antiquity of the Benedictines and Cistercians <note>Two of the oldest and most influential monastic orders in Europe.</note>, against whom one should not "bark" <note>Latin: *oblatrandum*; to speak out or criticize harshly.</note>; nevertheless, in this age, I could hardly support the making of such annexations.

### ARTICLE IV.
->Whether even the clerics themselves are bound to pay tithes.<-
---

After discussing the substance and matter of tithes, and recognizing those to whom they are owed, it follows finally that we should see which mortals ought to pay them. <margin>The first argument.</margin> And first, it is argued that the clerics themselves are debtors of tithes. It is common law <note>In this context, *Ius commune* refers to the universal Canon Law of the Church.</note> that a parish church should perceive tithes from all estates lying within its territory. However, it often happens that clerics also have possessions, either in their own parish or perhaps in another. Similarly, the patrimony <note>Inherited property or church-owned land.</note> of one church might be situated in the territory of another. Therefore, in such cases, the clerics—and indeed the church itself—

<column-break/>

seem to owe tithes. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second, it is argued: The "religious" <note>Members of monastic orders (monks, friars) as opposed to "secular" priests who live in the world.</note> are numbered among the clerics; and yet they owe tithes by reason of their estates to the churches in whose territory they are located, as is clear in the chapters *Dilecti* and *Licet* regarding tithes. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third: In Numbers 18 <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Numbers.</note>, the Levites are commanded to pay "tithes of tithes" to the High Priest; therefore, by the same reasoning, clerics—succeeding the Levites—owe the same to the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note>. <margin>Argument 4.</margin> ¶ Fourth: Tithes are paid not only, as has been said, for the support of clerics, but also for the relief of the poor. Therefore, if clerics were exempt from the payment of tithes, the poor would be equally affected. But this is false; therefore, the former is not true either. ¶ To the contrary, however, is the second chapter on tithes, where Pope Paschal says: "It is a new kind of extortion that clerics should demand tithes from clerics."

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin> The question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: Clerics, insofar as they are clerics—that is, regarding the tithes they receive for their spiritual office, and regarding the church lands from whose fruits they live by clerical right—are bound to pay no tithes. <margin>The second conclusion.</margin> ¶ The other conclusion: Clerics, not insofar as they are clerics, but by reason of possessing secular lands through secular right—whether by inheritance, purchase, or any other way—are debtors of tithes: namely, from the fruits that come to them from those lands. <margin>Both conclusions are urged.</margin> Both conclusions are proven together. The foundation and reason for giving something and receiving it can by no means be the same. For it is against nature for the principle of acting and the principle of being acted upon to be the same. Indeed, fire, insofar as it is heat-giving, cannot be heated; but clerics, because of their spiritual function, have the right of receiving tithes and likewise the fruits of the estates which the church possesses. Therefore, by that same reasoning, they owe nothing back in tithes. But truly, nothing prevents different principles from existing in the same person—one for acting, the other for being acted upon. Just as water, insofar as it is cold, cools things down; but insofar as it is material, it is heated. In the same way, therefore, in a cleric—notwithstanding the spiritual principle of receiving tithes— <margin>rely</margin> there can be found <gloss>perhaps, temporal</gloss> a secular possession from which he ought to pay them. ¶ These conclusions are most widely accepted in law. Therefore, nothing remains to be doubted concerning them, except that some privileges exist granted to certain groups against the tenor of the second conclusion. For to the Cistercians and the Hospitalers <note>The Knights Hospitaller, a medieval Catholic military order.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on who is required to pay tithes. Having addressed whether the clergy themselves are exempt when they farm their own lands, Soto now moves to a broader jurisdictional question: does the Church's right to collect tithes extend to those who are not part of the Christian faith, such as Jews or Muslims living in Christian territories or abroad?</meta>

# Book Nine: Question IV.
### Page 749

...to the **Knights Hospitaller** <note>A medieval Catholic military order dedicated to caring for the sick and protecting pilgrims.</note>, Pope Alexander III granted that they should not pay tithes on the estates they possessed, however they acquired them, provided they cultivated them with their own hands. Pope Adrian granted the same, as is evident in the chapter *Ex parte* in the section on tithes; this was understood to apply even if they cultivated the land through their own servants. Therefore, no others—whether clerics or monks—are exempt; they must pay tithes even if they till their own fields, unless they are exempted by a similar specific privilege. Furthermore, when they lease those same lands to tenant farmers, there is even less doubt that they are debtors of such tithes, as is held in the chapter *Licet* and the following one, *Ad audientiam*. Nevertheless, regarding these matters, local custom should also be consulted.

<margin>The Question.</margin>
¶ Now, since we are speaking here of the persons who are held to the payment of tithes, the question is asked whether not only Christians, but also **unbelievers** <note>Latin: *infideles*; in this context, anyone not baptized into the Christian faith, such as Jews, Muslims, or pagans.</note>, are bound to pay ecclesiastical tithes. I say "ecclesiastical," because according to natural law, any republic enlightened by a true knowledge of God would be bound to sacrifice to that same God in its own way and to establish magistrates for that duty—but that is a different matter. Indeed, they were so bound, as can be gathered from what was said previously.

<margin>The opinion of Panormitanus.</margin>
We investigate this question because of several legal experts, and most notably because of **Panormitanus** <note>Nicola de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), an exceptionally influential expert in Canon Law.</note>, who decided the question affirmatively in his commentary on the chapter *De terris* in the section on tithes. For in the aforementioned chapter, Jews are ordered to pay tithes on the lands they cultivate; and in the chapter *Quanto* in the section on usury, they are likewise compelled to pay tithes on houses and possessions which were subject to that burden before they came into their ownership. From these points, Panormitanus, following Odoardus, infers that all unbelievers, wherever in the world they may live, could be legally compelled to pay tithes if it were possible to enforce it. And he means not only **predial tithes** <note>Tithes calculated based on the produce of the land.</note> but also **personal tithes** <note>Tithes calculated based on an individual's personal income or labor.</note>. At the very least, he says, a Jew is bound to pay what a Christian living in his place would have paid. Otherwise, he argues, the Church would be defrauded. He even says that when they convert to Christianity, they can be forced to pay the tithes they refused to pay while they were unbelievers.

<margin>The opinion of Panormitanus is supported by no probability.</margin>
<margin>Argument against Panormitanus.</margin>
¶ But in truth, whether you consult the texts, or divine law, or natural reason, this opinion is supported by no probability—if I may say so with all due respect to such a great Doctor of the Church. First, regarding divine law, there is no doubt: not only because, as we have often said, the old law regarding the "tenth" was **judicial** <note>Refers to the civil/legal codes of ancient Israel which Christians believed were fulfilled and superseded by the Gospel.</note> and has now become obsolete, but also if we persist in looking at natural and moral law. For tithes were

<column-break/>

ordered in ancient times solely for the salary of the ministers of the Temple, and among us for the same reason: for the nourishment of the clerical order serving the Church. Therefore, if there were no Church, there would be no reason to demand them. Since, then, unbelievers are not within the bosom of the Church, nor do the priests dispense any spiritual thing to them, no right exists for the priests—on the authority of **Paul** <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 9:11, "If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much if we reap a material harvest from you?"</note>—to seek material things from them.

<margin>The solution of Panormitanus.</margin>
But Panormitanus says: they are nevertheless bound to receive the sacraments and to give their names to Christianity. Behold how such men treat divine law!

<margin>Reply.</margin>
Indeed, although the whole of humanity is bound to embrace the faith, nevertheless, until a person actually professes it, they are not bound by our laws, nor are they bound to obey our prelates. This is according to the word of Paul: "What have I to do with those who are outside?" <note>original: "De his qui foris sunt nihil ad nos"; referencing 1 Corinthians 5:12.</note> Just as someone who has made a vow to join a religious order is strictly bound to become a monk, yet until he has actually made his profession, he is not bound by the specific commands of that religious rule. For who among those who know divine law would dare to assert that the **Turks** <note>A common 16th-century term for Muslims, particularly those of the Ottoman Empire.</note> sin because they do not confess using our sacrament, do not taste the Eucharist, or do not observe our feasts and fasts?

<margin>The deception of Panormitanus.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, that saying cited above seduces the authors of this opinion; it is found in the chapters *Tua nobis* and *Cum non sit* regarding tithes: namely, that God reserved tithes for Himself as a sign of His universal lordship. From this, they conclude that every mortal owes them, since He is the Lord of all. But truly, if that word carried such a meaning, the Popes themselves or the Church would have handed that same meaning down to us somewhere; yet they have never done so. And indeed, by that same logic, it would be concluded that all mortals in the past owed tithes to the **Levites** <note>The tribe of Israel designated as priests and ministers in the Old Testament.</note>. This would be an absurd concession. Therefore, the legitimate sense is that as a sign of His universal lordship, God wished to be worshiped with sacrifices by every republic at all times, and consequently that priests be sustained. But because the specific moderation of that sustenance by a "tenth" was appropriate for the Levites of the Mosaic people, He commanded that people by a judicial precept to pay a tenth of their fruits to them. The Church, in imitation of that precept, commanded the same to its own subjects for the sake of its own priests. Therefore, this command does not include those who have never embraced the faith. Neither the chapter *De terris* nor the chapter *Quanto* acts against this in any way. For there, the discussion is specifically about Jews who live among Christians and hold possessions which...

<summary>Soto argues against the view that non-Christians (unbelievers) are bound by Church law to pay tithes. He asserts that while the Church may collect tithes from Jews living in Christian lands to prevent the Church from losing revenue on previously tithable land, the obligation of tithes does not extend to the global population of non-believers who are "outside" the Church's jurisdiction.</summary>

And although this discourse might also be extended to those lands which were never held by Christians—though I do not easily believe this—there is perhaps another reason regarding the Jews, who are permitted to live among us only on the condition that they do not defraud the Church of its territory <note>The argument here is that if a Jew buys land that previously paid tithes to a Christian church, they must continue paying so the Church does not lose its income.</note>. However, regarding unbelievers possessing lands that were never under our dominion before they professed the faith, if they were compelled to pay tithes, I have no doubt that the ancient Fathers skilled in sacred matters would have considered it most foreign to the Gospel. Therefore, under this pretext of title, I do not see how tithes can be demanded from those to whom the faith is preached. Whether, by reason of the preaching, some tribute can be demanded from them for the maintenance of the preachers, let those whose duty it is to know this see to it. For I, as I said elsewhere, have decided to say nothing of the **islanders of the West** <note>original: "occidentalibus insulanis"; Soto is referring to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas and the debates surrounding Spanish colonial rights.</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To return to the matter at hand, the first argument raised at the beginning of the question had two parts. The first concerned the goods of clerics which they possess by **secular title** <note>Private property owned by a clergyman as an individual, rather than property held by his church office.</note>. To this, **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the primary authority for Soto.</note> responds according to the tenor of the second conclusion: that they are bound to pay tithes from the fruits of such land, even if they are clerics of that same church.

<margin>Argument</margin>
However, some raise an argument against this decision from the cited chapter *Novum genus* <note>original: "A new kind"; a heading in Canon Law.</note> regarding tithes, where it is stated that those clerics who receive tithes from the clerics of spiritual ministries owe the same to them. Since, therefore, clerics do not receive ministries from other clerics of the same church, but all together administer to the people, there is no reason why one should owe tithes to another.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To this it is replied that the word is not exclusive. It is asserted, I say, that clerics (and perhaps, as the **gloss** <note>A standard legal commentary written in the margins of law books.</note> has it, this is understood of married clerics) are liable for the payment of tithes because they receive the sacraments. Yet it is not excluded that for another reason—namely, because of the lands they possess individually—even higher clerics should owe them. Whence, as St. Thomas says: It is one thing to have something as one's own, by reason of which tithes are owed; it is another to hold common ecclesiastical property, by reason of which they are not owed. Besides this solution, there is another: that clerics of the same parish sometimes receive the sacraments from others besides the **Parish Priest** <term>Curatus: the cleric with the "care of souls" in a specific district</term> (who only receives them from his vicar); nevertheless, he owes tithes from his personal

<column-break/>

estates. ¶ The latter part of the same argument touched upon the church itself, which perhaps has estates in another parish. St. Thomas responds to this in a different way than to the first part:

<margin>The solution of Saint Thomas.</margin>
namely, that such a church owes no tithes from its possessions. The reason is that by the very fact that the estate belongs to a church, it becomes **ecclesiastical**: that is, dedicated to a spiritual duty or the church building itself.

<margin>Reply.</margin>
¶ But if someone should object that by this law it could happen that a certain church might be stripped of absolutely all its tithes—for instance, if the parishioners donated their goods to foreign churches:

<margin>The solution of Cajetan.</margin>
The response of **Lord Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian.</note> is pleasing: that this law must be tempered and moderated so that the matter does not turn to such great detriment of the church. Therefore, in that case, the estates should pass with their burden of tithes. An example exists in the chapter *Suggestum* on tithes. For when a certain order was granted the privilege of not paying tithes, and subsequently such an addition of estates was made to them that other parishes suffered great loss, it was ordered that an agreement be made on this matter. Therefore, in such a case, clerics would pay tithes to clerics accidentally—that is, by reason of the estates. Nor would the chapter *Novum genus* stand in the way, for that is understood to mean that clerics should not demand tithes from clerics *insofar as* they are clerics.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second, it is answered that those religious <note>Members of religious orders, such as monks or friars.</note> to whom the care of souls is enjoined have the right of receiving tithes, but not for that reason an obligation of paying them. Others, however, by **common law**, owe **predial tithes** <term>Tithes on the produce of the land, such as grain or fruit</term> unless they are exempt by any privilege, as was cited above from the chapter *Ex parte*.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is answered that since in the Old Testament the **Levites** (to whom tithes were decreed) lived under the obedience of the priests, and only the **firstfruits** came to the priests, it was a fitting command of God that they pay a **tenth of the tithes** to the High Priest. By which same reasoning, the **Supreme Pontiff** [the Pope], when a just and urgent necessity arises, is able to demand a tenth of the tithes from the clergy. Indeed, would that a universal and perpetual one were imposed on the whole clergy—provided that by that means every other way and method of devising other laws and inventing other arts of sustaining the **Apostolic See** <note>The Papacy in Rome.</note> were forever closed; for by these, the ecclesiastical laws cannot but be most dangerously battered <note>Soto is suggesting that a direct tax on the clergy would be better than the "inventive" and potentially corrupt financial schemes the Papacy sometimes used to raise money.</note>.

¶ Finally, to the fourth it is answered that although tithes are granted to clerics also for the support of the poor,

### QUESTION FIVE,
## On the Sin of Simony
### in general.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 100.<-

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether Simony is the deliberate will of buying and selling something spiritual, or something annexed to the spiritual.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' depicting a landscape with classical architecture and trees.</image-desc> THE THIRD PART of this present book, which we promised after the treatise on sacrifices and the other on offerings, firstfruits, and tithes, is about Simony: concerning which St. Thomas disputes in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 100. Therefore, the first question of this treatise, which holds the fifth place here, is established concerning simony in general: the first article of which investigates the definition: namely, whether simony is the deliberate will of buying or selling something spiritual or annexed to the spiritual. And it is argued from the negative side. First, regarding the name. This vice consists as much in the selling as in the buying of spiritual things. However, Simon <note>Referring to Simon Magus, the sorcerer in Acts 8.</note>, as can be seen in Acts 8 <note>original: "Actuum. 18." — likely a printer's error for Acts 8.</note>, did not wish to sell anything, but only to buy the Holy Spirit: therefore, the name is not quite fittingly derived from Simon. It would be more fittingly derived from Balaam: who, as read in Numbers 22, hired out his services to the Moabites so that he might curse the people through a gift of God. Peter, in his second canonical letter, chapter 2, makes him guilty of this crime. And again, the apostle Jude. Or from Gehazi <note>original: "Iesi"</note>, who as read in 4 Kings 5 <note>2 Kings 5 in modern Bibles.</note>, sold the gift of health to Naaman for a price. Therefore, they ought to be called Balaamites or Gehazites <note>original: "Iesitæ"</note>, of whose name Gehazi mention is made for this purpose in the Canon Law <note>original: "1. q. 1. can. qui studet"</note>. Indeed, even Judas committed a more monstrous sacrilege by selling Christ, the author of all spiritual gifts, than Simon Magus did. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second. There are many spiritual goods that can be sold without the stain of simony: such as advice, as held in the canon *Non licet*. 11. q.

<column-break/>

3. and likewise the arts and natural sciences: therefore, that is not a legitimate definition. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third. Simony, as read from the register of Gregory in the canon *eos* (1. q. 1.), is a heresy. For he says the impious heresy of Macedonius is more tolerable than that of the Simoniacs. For the former, by deliberating, confess the Holy Spirit to be a creature and a servant of God the Father and the Son; but the latter actually make the same Holy Spirit their own servant. For every master sells what he has if he wishes, whether it be a servant or something from what he possesses. However, heresy is not in the will but in the intellect: therefore [it cannot be defined as a 'will']. ¶ On the contrary are the words of the canon *qui studet* (1. q. 1.): "He who strives <note>original: "studet"</note> to purchase the gift of God for a price can by no means remain in or be recalled to holy orders." From the word "strives," indeed, "deliberate will" <note>original: "studiosa voluntas"</note> is derived.

->To the question, a response is given in three conclusions: the first regarding the name, the second regarding the matter:<-

from which the third concludes regarding the definition of simony. <margin>First conclusion.</margin> ¶ The first, therefore, is this. The name of this vice could not be derived from any more significant source than from that Simon Magus with whom Peter had a contention. <margin>First reason.</margin> First, because Balaam and Gehazi belong to the history of the Old Testament, whose sacraments did not confer grace like ours, and thus were not spiritual to such a degree. <margin>Second reason.</margin> Second, because they only sold "graces freely given" <note>term: "gratis datas" — refers to charismatic gifts like healing or prophecy given for the benefit of others rather than for the recipient's personal salvation.</note>, such as the gift of health and of warding off enemies through a curse, which the Moabites sought from Balaam; but Simon wanted to buy nothing less than the Holy Spirit himself. Not indeed in his own person—for such a thought would be most insane—but his gift: as held in the canon *Salvator* (1. q. 3.); namely, his "sanctifying grace" <note>term: "gratu facientem" — refers to grace that makes the soul pleasing to God and justifies the person.</note> which holds the peak of spiritual gifts by its essence. <margin>Third reason.</margin> Third, to respond to the first argument: those others only sold, buying nothing; but Simon aimed to buy the Holy Spirit so that he might sell it. For thus the history goes: When Simon had seen that the Holy Spirit was given through the imposition of the Apostles' hands (for it was then given visibly), he offered them money, saying: "Give me also this power, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit": namely, for a price by which he could recover the offered money with interest: as held in the same canon *Salvator*. Judas, however, although he sold Christ the author of spiritual grace—of whom Gregory makes mention for this purpose in the same canon *qui studet*—nevertheless, because he did not sell him as a gift useful to the buyers, but rather as one to be destroyed by death, the name of this sacrilege was not drawn from him, but from Simon...

### F. D. Soto, On Justice & Law

...liberately to buy and sell the Holy Spirit, to whom all divine gifts are attributed, and the same from the Apostles, the founders of the Church under Christ; which Church is specifically stained by this crime. Therefore, just as arts are accustomed to take their names from their first inventors, so too is simony named after him <margin>Second conclusion.</margin> who first devised it. ¶ **The second conclusion.** Spiritual things are the proper matter of simony, but <margin>The word "spirit" is used in many ways.</margin> not of every kind. Here it must be observed that "spirit" is the same as the "breath" of living things, which live by breathing in and out; from there, by similarity, it signifies any blast of wind. But because wind and spirit are invisible, and to the senses incorporeal, the name was transferred to signify all things that lack bodies: such as God, angels, and the soul: and likewise spiritual accidents. Therefore, there are those who presently distinguish two kinds of spiritual things: one of those derived from a created spirit, and the other of those that flow from the uncreated spirit <note>The "uncreated spirit" refers to God/The Holy Spirit.</note>. But truly, because even natural things flow from the uncreated spirit—in which, as will soon be clear, the nature of simony <margin>A double kind of spiritual things.</margin> is not established—it is more fitting to the matter to distinguish one kind of spiritual thing as natural: such as the intellect, acquired sciences, and virtues; and the other as supernatural: such as grace freely given <note>term: "gratia gratis data" — spiritual gifts given for the benefit of others, like prophecy or healing.</note> as well as sanctifying grace <note>term: "gratia gratum faciens" — grace that makes a person pleasing to God.</note>, the sacraments, and the priesthoods annexed to them. Therefore, many of the Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to authoritative theologians and scholars of the Church.</note> believe that all spiritual things, both of the first and second kind, are the matter of simony. Consequently, these Doctors assert that to sell sciences and arts is the vice of simony. <margin>The opinions of Altisiodorensis, Alexander of Hales, the Gloss, Sylvester, and St. Thomas.</margin> Of this opinion were William of Auxerre <note>original: "Altisiodoren."</note> in Book 3, tract 21; and his contemporary Alexander of Hales in Part 2, question 185, member 3; and it is the Gloss <note>The "Ordinary Gloss" was the standard medieval commentary on Canon Law.</note> on chapter *non licet*, 11, question 3; and almost all the doctors of Canon Law, as can be seen in Sylvester Prieras under the word "Doctor" and the word "Simony," section 10. Furthermore, St. Thomas also held this in his commentary on the *Sentences*, book 4, distinction 25, question 3, article 2. <margin>The foundation of the first opinion.</margin> And the proof of William of Auxerre, who offered this latter opinion, was first the authority of Proverbs 23: *Do not sell wisdom, and teaching, and understanding.* Second, because as Augustine teaches in his book *On the Teacher*, it is the Holy Spirit who teaches men sciences internally, even natural ones. Therefore, he who sells them profanes the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Nonetheless, the contrary opinion can be believed to be true without fear: namely, that it is permitted to sell natural sciences. Not indeed in themselves, like bread or cloth, for that would be a foolish thing to say. Since it is in no one's power to transfer their own science into another like a physical thing. In which sense one must read Proverbs 17: *What does it profit a fool to have money, when he cannot buy wisdom?*

<column-break/>

But we are speaking of the sale of teaching: that is, that it is permitted to teach for a price, just as it is to give counsel, etc. In the first place, this is an opinion that does not lack authors: <margin>The opinion of Durandus, Paludanus, Adrian, Armachanus, and Richard.</margin> among whom are Durandus in book 4, distinction 25, question 3; Paludanus in the same, question 5; Adrian <note>Likely Pope Adrian VI.</note> in *Quodlibet* 9; and from the older writers, Richard FitzRalph of Armagh <note>original: "Armacha."</note> in book 10, chapter 8; and Richard of Middleton in book 4, distinction 25. Indeed, even St. Thomas in the *Summa* II-II, question 100, article 3, in response to the third objection, does not shrink from this same opinion, as we shall see below in that same place. But even if it had no patron, reason patronizes it enough: for we are speaking of natural <margin>The first reason for the second opinion.</margin> sciences. First, therefore, he argues: the nature of the vice of simony must be tracked from the Gospel. Truly, as in Matthew 10, where Christ bestowed the gifts of grace upon the Apostles to be communicated to the people: *Heal the sick,* He said, *raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons: freely you have received, freely give.* Here He mentions nothing of natural things. Likewise, in John 2, by casting the buyers and sellers out of the temple, He only signified that the sale and exchange of sacred things is sacrilege. And in Acts 8, in the case of Simon, that first of the Simoniacs, nothing is condemned except that he wished to buy the Holy Spirit and His graces. For this is called there "the gift of God." Since, therefore, no mention of natural goods was made anywhere, there is no reason that their sale <margin>The second reason.</margin> should be marked by the stain of simony. ¶ Second, he argues by reason: If it were not permitted to sell natural sciences and arts, chiefly because they are gifts of the Holy Spirit, yet they are not gifts through a "special influence" <note>A technical term for direct supernatural intervention.</note> of which Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 10 <note>The text says 10, but the famous passage on gifts is 1 Corinthians 12.</note>, but through "general concurrence" <note>God's standard way of upholding the natural order.</note>. Therefore, such a sale ought not to be condemned on this ground. Otherwise, it would not be lawful to sell any other natural goods, neither grain, nor wine, nor oil. Likewise, it would follow that it would not be permitted to teach mechanical arts or the art of writing for a price; which would be an absurd thing to grant. ¶ And by this, the argument of <margin>To the argument of Altisiodorensis.</margin> William of Auxerre is answered. For although the Holy Spirit teaches all truth, He teaches supernatural truths (such as the mysteries of Scripture) in one way—about which Christ specifically meant when He said, *He will teach you all things*—and He teaches natural truths in another way. And certainly, to sell these is not simony, because they are not given to those who have them for free so that they may be communicated for free to those who do not have them. <margin>The third reason.</margin> ¶ Third, it is argued: If it were not permitted to sell sciences of this kind, it would follow that it would not be permitted to receive a price for the labor by which a teacher exhausts himself in teaching. For when a thing is truly spiritual, such as the administration of a sacrament, it is not permitted to receive anything even for the labor. For it would be the same to receive a price for the labor of baptizing or administering holy orders as it is to receive it for the work itself, which is the administration of the sacrament. Labor...

Soto concludes that while supernatural gifts must be given freely, teaching natural subjects for a fee is lawful because it compensates the teacher's labor and involves natural rather than strictly sacramental "gifts."</summary>
