### Ninth Book, Question V.
Bbb 5
<meta>catchword: God</meta>

...for it does not distinguish labor from the work. How it may be lawful for ministers of sacred things to receive sustenance <note>original: "alimoniã" (alimony/nourishment)</note> will be made clear below. ¶ And lastly, when a temporal thing is annexed to a spiritual one, it is not lawful to accept a higher price for that thing than it would be worth without the spiritual element. I say, for instance, it is not lawful to sell a chalice or sacred vestments for more than if they were not consecrated. However, as is manifest, it is lawful to sell one kind of knowledge at a higher price than another, even if less labor was spent upon it. Indeed, one and the same Doctor, because he is more learned, even if he has incurred fewer expenses and exhausted less labor, can lease his services for teaching at a higher price. Therefore, even if he could pour his knowledge into another without any labor, like a breath of air, he could still receive a price for it. ¶ That passage in Proverbs 23 <note>Proverbs 23:23: "Buy the truth and do not sell wisdom."</note> in no way fights against us. On the contrary, what is held there is: *buy the truth: and do not sell wisdom.* It is as if he had said it is of such great price that he who does not have it ought to buy it, and he who has it should never sell it—that is, should never be deprived of it. And that gloss on the chapter *Non licet* <note>A reference to Canon Law</note> contradicts the text, as it is asserted there that an advocate can sell his counsel and a patron his protection. Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> held the same in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 71, where he seems to have revoked the opinion he asserted in the fourth book <note>The *Sentences*</note> when following Alexander <note>Alexander of Hales</note>. Therefore, it is irrelevant to resort to the labors exhausted in teaching as the sole justification for payment.

<margin>The final reason.</margin>

<margin>A specific question regarding Theology.</margin>
¶ But truly, there is a particular doubt regarding **Theology**. This is because it seems spiritual in the first sense <note>Referencing the previous page's definition of supernatural spiritual things</note>. For through the gift of the Holy Spirit the Scriptures are opened, which are the principles of Theology.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is not simony to lecture on this science to scholars for a price from the chair, even if it is done without any labor or expense, for these things are accidental.

<margin>The reason for the assertion.</margin>
And the reason is that, although faith and the revelation of mysteries belong to the Lord God, the *science* of Theology is nevertheless acquired by human sweat. Therefore, what Hostiensis <note>Henry of Segusio, a famous 13th-century canon lawyer</note> says regarding the chapter *Nonnullis* concerning teachers—namely, that a Theologian having a public salary is not permitted to receive anything for an extraordinary lecture, otherwise he commits simony—is stated without weight and without any reason. For what, I ask, does it matter whether you receive a public salary or a particular fee for a particular lecture?

<margin>An evangelical preacher is not permitted to receive a price by agreement for the duty of preaching.</margin>
However, it is true that it is in no way lawful for a preacher teaching theology from the pulpit to receive a price for preaching by agreement without simony. And the reason for the distinction is this: because Theology only instructs the intellect, just like any other science; but preaching is done in itself for the salvation of souls

<column-break/>

and for moving minds upward. And therefore it pertains to the gift of prophecy, which Paul counts among others in 1 Corinthians 12. However, it is lawful for a preacher to receive the support of sustenance just like other ministers of the church.

¶ Let us therefore conclude that "spiritual" in the definition of simony is not understood as a natural gift, but as a supernatural one—that is, for grace and the sacraments, and other gifts of the Holy Spirit which advance us toward eternal happiness. Moreover, that phrase "or annexed to a spiritual thing" signifies those things which do not have the name in themselves, but acquire it through their order toward spiritual things. Examples include priesthoods <note>term: "sacerdotia" — the office or status of a priest</note> and prebends <note>term: "præbendæ" — the portion of cathedral revenues granted to a canon</note>, which are the stipends of priests; and the right of patronage <note>term: "ius patronatus" — the right to nominate a candidate for a church office</note>, and other rights of electing ecclesiastical persons.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From these things it follows (which confirms the asserted opinion more evidently) that to give something spiritual in exchange for instruction in any science, however much it may be Theology, is simony. For example, if a bishop confers orders or a benefice upon a Doctor so that he may teach him. For he then confers a spiritual thing for instruction, which is estimable in money.

<margin>Another question.</margin>
¶ Through these points, another dispute is settled which Doctors are accustomed to contest: whether simony can occur outside the Church among infidels <note>non-Christians</note>.

<margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin>
For on the affirmative side, the argument exists that among them there is a priesthood by which, according to their own judgment, they worship God; therefore, if they sell it, it is simony. On the negative side, another argument no less weak is offered: that among them there is nothing properly spiritual. Durandus and Paludanus <note>Scholastic commentators</note> answer that they do not truly commit simony, but only according to their own estimation. Nonetheless, one must respond more carefully with a distinction. Indeed, before the coming of Christ, it is beyond doubt that among the fathers of the Old Testament, simony could truly be committed. For there was then the true gift of prophecy, which if it were sold, would have been simony, as is clear from the words of Jerome cited in the canon *Nunquam*, question 1.

<margin>Jerome</margin>
Likewise, their priesthood, although no grace was then conferred through it, was nevertheless a spiritual gift pertaining to divine worship. Therefore, Jeroboam in 3 Kings 13 <note>1 Kings 13 in modern bibles</note> is accused of creating priests for a price. Indeed, there was a priesthood even by the law of nature, such as that in Melchizedek; and certainly it was legitimate for that age; if he had conferred it for a price, simony would have emerged. For in its own way, whatever God and nature have ordained in any state of mortals for the salvation of souls is considered spiritual.

<summary>This page discusses whether charging for theological instruction constitutes simony, concluding that it is lawful as it is an acquired human science, unlike preaching which is a supernatural gift. It also explores whether simony can exist outside the Christian faith, noting that even under natural law and in the Old Testament, the sale of priesthoods was considered a spiritual violation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological investigation into simony—the sin of buying or selling sacred things. The previous page discussed whether charging for the labor of teaching or for consecrated materials (like chalices) constitutes simony. Here, Soto defines where simony resides within the human soul (the will) and how it relates to other sins like heresy and greed.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>Solution to the question.</margin>
...ordained the worship of God. However, after the Christian redemption, nothing remains outside the Church that is legitimately spiritual—unless, perhaps, there are those who suffer from an "invincible ignorance" <note>A theological term for ignorance that a person cannot overcome by their own efforts, and for which they are not held morally responsible.</note> of our law. For that same ignorance excuses them if they only use natural rites. Therefore, outside the Church, simony can no longer exist, except according to human estimation.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion is finally the one we promised regarding the definition. The nature of simony is properly expressed by the definition we set out earlier. This is proven as follows:

<margin>The Proof.</margin>
That definition explains the "object" from which a vice or virtue receives its specific character, and equally explains its "subject" and its "manner." Therefore, it is a good definition. Concerning the object, the matter is already clear. But the "subject" of justice—and likewise of injustice and all its parts—is the **will**. This is what Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> wisely taught in the *Summa Theologica* (Part 1 of the 2nd Part, Question 56), following Aristotle. For there is a difference between those virtues that organize a man in relation to himself and those that dispose him in relation to another. Since the will is naturally inclined and determined toward its own personal good, it requires no virtue regarding that good except for those virtues found in the "powers" <note>Refers to the lower faculties of the soul like the appetites.</note> which are disturbed by affections and passions. Indeed, if there were no passion in either the "irascible" or "concupiscible" appetites <note>The "irascible" appetite deals with obstacles and anger; the "concupiscible" deals with basic desires like hunger or sex.</note>, the will would have no difficulty obeying reason. For this reason, **temperance** is located in the concupiscible appetite, and **fortitude** in the irascible; by these, such diseases and turbulent affections are calmed, as Aristotle testifies in the second book of the *Ethics*. However, since a man’s will is not naturally so affected and inclined toward the good of another, it follows that even if he suffers no sensory affections, he still requires virtues to fulfill the duties owed to his neighbors.

<margin>The argument of Scotus.</margin>
¶ But there is a contrary argument found in Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note> in Book 3, Distinction 33: that power which is the seat of virtue and vice is the one whose action completes the basis for praise and blame, or merit and demerit. This power is the **will**, since it is by the choice <note>original: "electione"</note> of the will that both virtue and sin are completed. Therefore, the will is the subject of all virtues.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
However, along with Aristotle, we deny his first premise. This opinion is not held by Saint Thomas alone, but is most clearly stated by Aristotle in the second book of the *Ethics*. Virtue, therefore, is not in that power which makes the choice—otherwise, **faith** would be in the will, since its merit consists in the will's assent—but it must rather exist in that power in which the entire difficulty of choosing well resides. And cer-

<column-break/>

tainly, once the affections of the sensory appetite are pacified, the choice of the will is made most freely; for this reason, virtue is called an "elective habit" <note>A habit or disposition involving choice.</note>. To the point then: since justice is a virtue regarding another, it follows that it resides in the will, as Aristotle teaches in the fifth book of the *Ethics*; and so do religion and similar virtues. Since simony is a vice of both injustice and a sin against religion, it follows that it is in the will. Because of this, the definition uses the phrase "studious will" <note>original: "studiosa voluntas." In this context, it refers to a deliberate, focused, or purposeful intent rather than just "studying" in the academic sense.</note>.

<margin>Objection. Response.</margin>
¶ Now, if you argue that **greed** is the cause of simony—insofar as greed stands in the way of the duties of justice—and greed is located in the concupiscible appetite, the response is: we do not deny that there are other vices by which simony is commanded, but the act itself is "elicited" <note>Drawn out or performed directly.</note> by that which is in the will.

<margin>Second argument. Solution.</margin>
¶ There is another argument against the use of the word "studious." For since to sin "studiously" is the same as to sin out of malice, and such a sin would be against the Holy Spirit, it would follow that all simony is a sin against the Holy Spirit—which no one has ever granted. The response is that "studious" does not mean "out of malice," but rather "deliberately"—meaning it is not excused by ignorance. Rather, it is done knowingly, whether out of malice or out of passion.

<margin>Panormitanus, Hostiensis, Richard.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous canon lawyer.</note>, following Hostiensis on the chapter *Nemo*, adds to the definition that the "buying" must follow in actual deed. Richard <note>Richard of Middleton.</note> says the same, following the gloss on the chapter *Qui studet*, which says "with effect." However, this would be to restrict the name to "external" simony alone, when it is equally common to "internal" simony. For as will be shown below, the sin of simony is committed internally, even creating an obligation for restitution. Therefore, it is more prudent to say "studious will" without any further addition.

¶ "The Subtle Doctor" <note>Duns Scotus</note>, by the words "buying and selling," understands all usurious contracts: such as the exchange and bartering of prebends <note>A portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church, granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note> without the authority of the Pope, and other services that are considered as a price.

From these points, the first and second main arguments have been satisfied.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
To the third argument, which argued from the words of Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> that simony is a heresy and thus exists in the intellect, Saint Thomas gives two responses. First, that although a simoniac is not strictly a heretic—since he can fall into this vice out of greed without an error of the intellect—nonetheless, by his very act and deed, he seems to profess that the dominion of the Holy Spirit belongs to men, which is a heretical error. And this response...

<summary>This page defines simony as a sin residing in the will (the "studious will") rather than the sensory appetites or the intellect. Soto argues against Duns Scotus and others, asserting that simony can occur through internal intent alone, even if no physical transaction takes place.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of simony. Having previously defined what simony is, the author now addresses why it is considered a specific type of sin and whether it constitutes a "mortal sin"—a grave offense that severs one's relationship with God.</meta>

# Book Nine, Question V. 755

Gratian <note>The 12th-century author of the *Decretum*, the foundational collection of Canon Law.</note> embraced this response in the canon *Ventum* (1. question 1). Secondly, as if this did not sufficiently satisfy him, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says that Simon Magus—besides wanting to buy the Holy Spirit—was also a heretic in that he believed the world was not created by God. Nevertheless, simoniacs would not be called heretics for this reason alone, yet they are frequently branded with that iron in the law. And so, perhaps it must be said that Simon wanted to buy the Holy Spirit because he believed it was for sale and could be given by the Apostles for a price. This is clearly shown by the apostolic response: *May your money perish with you, because you thought the gift of God*—that is, you believed it—*could be possessed with money.* It is from this heresy, as if from its own source, that the vice itself derived its name.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether the vice of simony is, by its very nature, a mortal sin.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'S' depicting a scholar or monk seated at a desk with an open book, writing.</image-desc>Once the definition of simony is established, we ask about its quality: whether it is a mortal crime. The argument is made from the negative side. Among all created spiritual things, the Kingdom of Heaven holds the summit, as all other things are directed toward it; yet the Kingdom itself is "saleable." <margin>Gregory.</margin> Hence Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> says: "The Kingdom of Heaven is worth as much as you have." Therefore, it is not simony to wish to buy something spiritual. <margin>Second.</margin> ¶ Second: If simony were by its nature a sin, it would follow that even the Pope, if he were to sell spiritual things, would be stained by the same vice. However, it is said that he cannot be a simoniac because "the Prince is not bound by his own laws" <note>original: *Princeps non ligatur suis legibus*. A famous legal maxim from Roman Law (Digest 1.3.31) often debated in the context of papal authority.</note>. Therefore, it is not by its nature a mortal sin. <margin>Third.</margin> ¶ Third: To exchange spiritual things—namely, to barter one for another, such as a chalice for an altar; or even a sacrament for a sacrament, as when a priest refuses to hear another priest's confession unless that priest hears his in turn; or if a student of the faith refuses to baptize another unless they agree to baptize each other—does not appear to be simony. Therefore, neither is selling spiritual things. ¶ On the contrary side are the sacred canons. For it is held in the Register of Gregory, which Paschal II <note>Pope from 1099–1118</note> cites (1. q. 3): "Let no member of the faithful be ignorant that to buy or sell an altar, or tithes, or the Holy Spirit, is the simoniacal heresy." And it is called a "heresy" to emphasize its 

<column-break/>

gravity. And in the chapter *Sicut* regarding simony: "The simoniacal plague, by its magnitude, overcomes all other diseases." And in the next chapter: "So great is the stain of this crime that even servants against masters, and any criminal persons, are admitted to bring the accusation."

---

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
To the question, it is answered with a single conclusion, which is the most widely accepted by everyone: **Simony is, by its nature, a mortal crime.** <margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin> This is proven. To buy or sell that which is saleable for no price is, by its nature, a mortal crime, as we said under the title on <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of charging interest on loans, which was historically seen as an injustice similar to simony.</note>. For since it is contrary to justice—a virtue most necessary for the commonwealth—it follows that it is also contrary to <term>charity</term> <note>In this theological sense, 'charity' refers to the supernatural love between God and humanity.</note>, which is what constitutes the nature of a mortal sin. However, the <margin>alt: viciousness</margin> religious nature of the crime increases in simony by reason of contaminated religion. The "minor premise" is proven from three points. First, from the nature of the object. For things that are spiritual (in the way explained above) can be valued by no earthly price, because they are supernatural; between these and earthly things, there is no proportion. Hence, regarding Divine Wisdom, Proverbs 3 asserts: *She is more precious than all riches, and all things that are desired cannot be compared to her.* Peter, observing this, said to that Magus: *May your money perish with you, because you thought the gift of God could be possessed*—that is, appraised—*with money.* <margin>Second.</margin> ¶ Second, the same is proven from the fact that even if spiritual things were saleable in themselves, they could by no means be sold by the leaders of the Church. For no one justly sells a thing unless he is its owner. If a steward were to sell the master’s property without his order, he would be unjust. The leaders of the Church, however, do not have ownership of spiritual things but are mere <term>stewards</term> <note>original: *dispensatores*. Meaning those who manage or distribute goods that belong to another, in this case, God.</note>, according to Paul’s confession in 1 Corinthians 4: *Thus let a man regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.* <margin>Third reason.</margin> Third, the same is confirmed by the origin from which spiritual things come to us. For that which is granted freely by God—not for the private convenience of the one to whom it is given, but for the public good of the whole Church—no one can justly sell. It is not his own, but belongs to those to whom he "sells" it; and such are the spiritual gifts of God. Christ took care to warn the Apostles of this in Matthew 10, where he says: *Freely you have received, freely give.* And he denoted this by that word in Luke 12: *Who do you think is the faithful and wise steward?* "Faithful," evidently, so that what he received freely,

<meta>The catchword "pit" at the bottom of the page indicates the next page begins with "accépit" (he received).</meta>

<summary>This page argues that simony—the buying or selling of spiritual things—is a mortal sin because spiritual gifts are supernatural, priceless, and belong solely to God. Church leaders are described not as owners of these gifts, but as stewards who must distribute them freely as they were received.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of simony. Having previously discussed its definition and status as a mortal sin, Soto now moves to the legal foundations of its prohibition, specifically whether it is forbidden by Natural, Divine, or merely Human (Positive) law.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right, 756

...bestows [what he has received] for free. And he should be prudent: that is, one who discerns the merits of persons with an observant judgment, so that he may dispense all things according to each person's worthiness. It follows from these points that simony is a sin, not only against justice, but also—by reason of its matter, which is spiritual—against religion. For this reason, it is specifically called sacrilege, for it is an injury to sacred things. First of all, concerning this conclusion and its reasoning, we must investigate by which law simony is prohibited: whether by divine law only, or also by natural law.

<margin>Simony is prohibited by both natural and divine law.</margin>
The answer to this doubt is straightforward: the simony of supernatural spiritual gifts is prohibited by both natural and divine law. Indeed, the divine law is manifest in both testaments. For in Matthew 10, after listing gifts of this kind, Christ adds: "Freely you have received, freely give." And in John 2, as a symbolic act, he cast out those buying and selling doves from the temple with a whip; for the dove signifies the Holy Spirit and his gifts. The same is evident in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 8) in the story of what happened to Peter regarding Simon <note>Simon Magus, the magician who tried to buy the power to bestow the Holy Spirit, giving his name to the sin of "simony."</note>. And in Numbers 22, the same is noted in the story of Balaam, whom both Peter and Jude, in their canonical letters, rebuke as one selling the gift of God—even though, after being divinely warned, he did not do what the Moabites wanted. And Jeroboam (1 Kings 13 <note>Original: 3. Reg. 13. In the Latin Vulgate tradition, 1 and 2 Kings are titled 3 and 4 Kings.</note>) became guilty because he appointed priests for money—although they were not truly priests, but followers of Baal. And in 2 Kings 5, Gehazi is also brought to shame because he received something in exchange for the gift of healing. Whether it is also against the law of nature is doubted because spiritual things, which are its subject matter, are supernatural things to which the natural law does not seem to reach. For by this reasoning, the commands regarding the sacraments are not natural, but above nature.

<margin>The first reason to persuade that simony is prohibited by natural law.</margin>
Nevertheless, the contrary must be asserted. This is proved first because all divine law expressed in the Gospel—besides that part pertaining to the sacraments of faith—contains nothing except what is necessary by natural law. This is the one reason why it is called the "law of liberty," as we noted in Book 2, the final question, article 1. Since, therefore, the prohibition of simony does not pertain to the [ritual form of] sacraments, it follows that in the Gospel it is prohibited only as something natural.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
Secondly, the reasons by which the perversity of simony is demonstrated confirm this. For even if spiritual goods are supernatural, nevertheless, because by their nature they are not for sale, and the leaders of the church

<column-break/>

are not their masters—but rather received them freely and ought to give them freely—the law of nature itself cries out against their sale.

<margin>The third reason.</margin>
And thirdly, unless it were prohibited by the law of nature, Balaam would not have sinned by selling, nor the King of the Moabites by buying; for they were Gentiles, who were held only to the natural law. Indeed, by the same reasoning, Simon Magus would not have sinned; since he was a neophyte <note>A new convert to the faith.</note> in Christianity, unless the law of nature had condemned his daring attempt, he could have been excused by ignorance of the Gospel mandate. Therefore, regarding the argument to the contrary, the logical consequence is denied. The subject matter of simony may be such by divine law, yet that does not mean it is not against the law of nature. One must reflect on the fallacy of that consequence. For from wherever a thing becomes spiritual, it follows thereafter that it is not for sale; and the law of nature forbids putting up for sale that which is not saleable.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
A somewhat weightier reason for doubt exists: whether there is any simony that is contrary neither to divine law nor natural law, but only because it is forbidden by human law.

<margin>The Gloss.</margin>
The "Gloss" <note>The standard legal commentary on the Decretals of the Popes.</note> offers us this reason for doubt in the chapter *Ex parte* (1. *de officio delegati*), which distinguishes between simony prohibited because it is evil—such as that which is so by Gospel law—and another which is not evil except because it is prohibited by positive law <note>Positive law refers to man-made laws enacted by an authority, such as the Church or the State.</note>. This distinction is common among the Doctors of Canon Law, as can be seen in Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a theologian and legal expert.</note> under the word *simonia*, section 4.

<margin>Durandus.</margin>
Indeed, it is also common among many theologians. However, Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a philosopher and theologian known for his independent thinking.</note>, in Book 4, distinction 25, question 5, refutes this distinction with two reasons, admitting no simony against merely positive [human] law.

<margin>The first reason of Durandus.</margin>
The first is this: regarding that which is not evil in itself but only because it is prohibited, one does not happen to sin except by the sin of disobedience. For example, when a superior commands you to do something otherwise indifferent, if you do not obey, you become nothing other than disobedient. If, therefore, there is only a human prohibition against selling this or that, it will be disobedience not to obey, but not simony.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
His second reason is that simony is a spiritual sale; however, the Church cannot change the nature of things so as to make something spiritual that was not so before, for this belongs to divine law alone.

Nevertheless, one must judge by a middle way between these opinions.

<margin>The Church can make something spiritual that was not so before.</margin>
First, against the second reason of Durandus, it is certain that the Church can make something spiritual that was not so by divine law. This is evident in the consecration of a church, and of an altar, and in the blessings of chalices, corporals <note>The sacred linen cloth used during the Mass.</note>, and vestments. For these things by divine law...

<summary>Soto argues that simony is prohibited by both divine and natural law, using biblical examples like Balaam and Simon Magus to show that even those outside the Church are bound by its rules. He also begins to debate whether human law can create new categories of simony by designating physical objects as "spiritual" through consecration.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 756 regarding whether simony—the sin of buying or selling spiritual things—is prohibited by divine law, natural law, or positive law (laws established by human or church authority). The text concludes a point about consecrated objects and moves into specific assertions about the nature of their sale.</meta>

### Book Nine, Question V.

...by divine law they are not spiritual. For regarding the essence of the matter, the consecration of Christ’s body and blood could take place even if the vessels and ornaments were not themselves consecrated or blessed.

<margin>Second assertion.</margin>
¶ **Second assertion.** Nevertheless, the sale and purchase of these items is simony against divine and natural law if they are sold for more than the object is worth by reason of its consecration.

<margin>Reason for the assertion.</margin>
For both laws <note>Natural and divine law.</note> forbid that which is not for sale to be sold for a price. Therefore, since that status is spiritual—even if it was made spiritual through positive law—its sale is nonetheless contrary to divine and natural law. This is confirmed because whoever sells the blessing of a chalice or holy water is certainly selling that which is given freely for the public good. Thus, simony of this kind is prohibited by divine law.

<margin>Second reason for the same point.</margin>
Secondly, it is argued for the same point: the minor orders <note>Lower ranks of the clergy, such as porters, lectors, exorcists, and acolytes.</note> are not established by divine law. Indeed, even the diaconate <note>The office of deacon.</note> was not formerly considered a "sacred order," as is clear from the words of Innocent III in the chapter *A multis* <note>original: "A multis. de ætat. & qualita. & ordin. præfi." — a reference to canon law regarding age and quality of those to be ordained.</note>. Rather, they exist by purely positive law. Yet, to sell these is the sin of simony prohibited by divine law. Therefore, although a thing may become sacred through positive law, its sale is nonetheless against divine law. This is just as we recently stated that the following logic is fallacious: "Spiritual things are by divine law; therefore, selling them is not against the law of nature."

¶ From this it follows that those Doctors <note>Theologians and legal scholars.</note> who use such consecrated things as examples of simony according to purely positive law are reasoning falsely. They infer this because the "matter" (the physical object) is established by positive law. We said much the same above regarding the "solemnity of a vow," which is a matter of positive law; yet the resulting obligation to perpetual chastity is a matter of divine law.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But you may press the question: is there any simony that pertains purely to positive law?

<margin>The resolution.</margin>
The answer is that there is. First, where an office attached to the church is sold which is not spiritual in itself. This is clear from the chapter *Salvator* cited above <note>original: "cap. Saluator. 1. quæstio. 3."</note>, where Urban <note>Pope Urban II.</note> forbids the sale of the office of church steward, sacristan, or protector, citing the Council of Chalcedon. Selling these offices is not against divine or natural law, since the persons or things are not sacred in themselves. Nor does the church make them sacred in the same way as temples, vessels, or persons (such as priests dedicated to the consecration of the Eucharist); rather, they are merely

<column-break/>

appointed as guardians of sacred things.

<margin>The prohibition of exchanging prebends without the authority of a superior is not purely positive law, but a sign of divine law.</margin>
¶ Those who bring up the exchange of prebends <note><term>prebend</term>: a portion of Anglican or Catholic cathedral revenues granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> provide another example of this same simony. For it is forbidden in the chapter *Quaesitu* <note>original: "c. quæsitu. de rerū perm." — regarding the permutation/exchange of church property.</note> for prebends to be exchanged by agreement without the bishop's permission. However, this prohibition is not purely positive law, but a sign of divine law. For anyone who attempted to exchange prebends privately would achieve nothing. Anyone can renounce his own priesthood, but he must do so into the hands of a prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, like a bishop.</note>. No one has the legal power to install another in the right of a prebend except the Pope and the bishop, or the prelates whose duty it is to confer priesthoods. What the Pope commands there is that no one should make a contract for exchange, because this tastes of the stain of simony. However, if it is done under the condition "provided the Pope consents," there is no guilt. If that condition is omitted, simony results. Therefore, if the condition were contrary to divine law—for instance, if the agreement was to pay extra money or another price for a greater prebend—then the simony would be against divine law, for such an exchange would involve the "purchase" of a prebend.

<margin>Moderation of the above assertion.</margin>
If, however, it were only contrary to positive law—such as an agreement to pay a pension without the Pope's grant—then the simony would be against positive law. Indeed, to exchange sacred and spiritual things is not against divine law, especially if they are such only by positive law; for example, if a chalice is swapped for a chalice, or for a sacred vestment. In fact, this is true even in things that are spiritual by divine law: for instance, if a priest refuses to hear the confession of another priest unless the other hears his own. Although Richard <note>Likely Richard of Middleton, a medieval theologian.</note> thinks otherwise (as we will discuss shortly), since prebends are not "so spiritual," an agreement to exchange them is not against divine law. Secondly, this is confirmed: if it were against divine law, the Pope could in no way grant a dispensation for it; yet the Pope does permit such exchanges with established pensions. Furthermore, if this kind of sale were forbidden by divine law just as the sale of sacraments is, it would not be permitted to contract for it even with the condition "if the Pope consents," because that is certainly not allowed with sacraments. Yet such a contract for prebends with that condition is not condemned. To conclude the matter: such exchange is not forbidden in the Gospel, which speaks only of the gifts of the Holy Spirit: "Freely you have received, freely give." Therefore, such a contract is not against divine law. Nevertheless, it is a species of simony according to positive law.

->Therefore<-

<summary>This page examines whether the sale of consecrated items or church offices constitutes simony under divine, natural, or positive law. Soto argues that while the objects themselves are made sacred by human law, selling them for profit violates divine law, though certain administrative exchanges (like prebends) may only fall under positive law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether simony—the buying or selling of spiritual things—is a violation of divine law or merely human (ecclesiastical) law. Soto is specifically addressing arguments made by earlier theologians like Durandus regarding the nature of Church prohibitions.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

Wherefore, the first argument of Durandus <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), an influential medieval jurist and theologian.</note> is answered in two ways. First, we deny his assertion that whenever a thing is prohibited that is not otherwise evil, the transgression is no other sin than disobedience. On the contrary, when the Church enjoined Lenten abstinence, it established that fast as an act of the virtue of abstinence; therefore, not only would he sin against obedience who breaks the fast out of contempt for authority, but also he would sin against the virtue of abstinence who does so out of gluttony rather than contempt. In a similar way, the Church has the power to define a certain act as falling under the vice of simony <note>simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred things, named after Simon Magus from the Book of Acts.</note>. Second, it is responded that the Church has not defined the selling of the office of Sacristan, or making a contract to exchange priesthoods contrary to ecclesiastical law, as strictly simony in the same sense as selling the priesthood itself; rather, it is called "simony" because it is punished with the same penalties as simony.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Through these points, the solution to the arguments becomes easy. To the first, it is responded that the "kingdom of heaven" is described as being "for sale"—not if you use the word "sale" in its proper sense, but through a metaphor, just as it is said to "suffer violence." That it is not literally salable is first evident from the fact that, since it is supernatural, it cannot be valued by any price. Hence Paul says in Romans 8:
> The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us. <note>original: "Non sunt condignę passiones huius temporis ad futuram gloriam..."</note>

And he speaks of the works of the children of God through grace, signifying that our works, judged by their own merits, are not the "price" of the kingdom of heaven, but only insofar as they proceed from grace. What is given freely (*gratis*) is not sold. Furthermore, nothing is added to God by our services, for He does not need our goods. Hence Isaiah 52 says:
> You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money. <note>original: "Gratis vænundati estis, & sine argento redimemini."</note>

However, "buying" is used as a metaphor, according to the words of the same Prophet in chapter 55, where Wisdom herself says:
> All you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you who have no money, hasten and buy; come, buy without money and without any exchange milk and honey; <note>original: "Sitientes venite ad aquas..."</note>

this refers to the sweetness of the celestial kingdom. The metaphor consists in this: that the kingdom of heaven is proposed to the works of the righteous man as a reward, as is clear in the Parable of the workers hired for the vineyard for a set daily wage, and in the words of the Psalm: "I have inclined my heart to perform your justifications because of the retribution." <note>retribution: here used in the sense of a just reward or recompense.</note>

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second argument: although there is a dispute among the interpreters of Canon Law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership.</note> as to whether the Pope can

<column-break/>

commit simony, the response becomes clear through what has already been said.
<margin>The Pope can commit simony.</margin>
Indeed, regarding simony which is defined as such by divine and natural law, there can be no controversy that he can commit it. If, I say, he were to administer the sacraments for a price, or dispense any other gift of the Holy Spirit for money, no one could doubt that he would be a simoniac. He would, in fact, be acting against divine law, over which he himself has no power to grant exemptions. Nor is he the owner of such gifts, but merely their distributor. Indeed, he would sin all the more gravely and cause greater scandal because of the eminent position he holds in the church. Hence Peter, the first Vicar of Christ, most vigilantly guarded himself against this crime when dealing with Simon. Furthermore, if he were to consecrate temples, vessels, or sacred vestments for a price—even though such a ritual is established by positive law <note>positive law: laws created by human authorities, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>—it would still be simony because selling them is against divine law. In the same way, if he were to sell priesthoods or prebends <note>prebend: a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman.</note>, he would be a simoniac, as he is only their distributor and by no means their owner. 

However, if you allow that selling the office of a sacristan or a church steward is not simony except by positive law (because these are not strictly sacred persons), the Pope could bestow those for a price without sin, provided it caused no scandal, because he has the power to grant exemptions from his own laws. By the same reasoning, he cannot incur the legal penalties decreed against simoniacs. Even if he were to sell priesthoods, he would not be excommunicated or suspended, since he is the sovereign and is not subject to the coercive force of his own laws.

<margin>¶ But a Doubt.</margin>
¶ But there remains here a doubt: whether, if he sold a priesthood to someone, he should be considered by that very act to be exempting the buyer from the legal penalties, so that the buyer would not be excommunicated nor required to give up the prebend. For some, such as 
<margin>Paludanus</margin>
Paludanus <note>Pierre de la Palud (1275–1342), a French theologian and archbishop.</note>, affirm this; but others, including
<margin>Adrian</margin>
Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), who was a respected theologian before his papacy.</note>, deny it. Truly, this is a matter that leaves me undecided. On the negative side is the 
<margin>Argument from the negative side.</margin>
argument of Joannes Andreas <note>Giovanni d'Andrea (1270–1348), an expert in Canon Law.</note>: that if a bishop were to forbid a certain game to the clergy under penalty of excommunication, even if he later encouraged one of them to play, he would not be considered to have granted an exemption from the law unless he stated so explicitly; for he might have forgotten the law or be leading the man into evil. Again, although one might offer the "kiss of peace" to an excommunicated person, it does not mean he has been absolved. ¶ On the affirmative side is the argument that the Pope should not be thought to sin so significantly as to...

It also examines the legal status of the Pope, concluding he can commit the sin of simony under divine law, even if he is exempt from the human penalties of Canon Law.</summary>

<header>Book Nine, Question VI.</header>

<margin>The Pope selling a benefice to someone is considered to be granting a dispensation for simony.</margin>
...he might think of selling to a priest something that the priest can neither buy nor keep without facing excommunication <note>Excommunication: a censure that excludes a person from the sacramental life of the Church.</note>, and therefore not without guilt. Furthermore, regarding this ambiguity, I would choose this side over the other. For perhaps even a bishop who induces a subordinate to do something prohibited by his own law is believed to be granting a dispensation <note>Dispensation: an exemption from a church law in a particular case.</note>, just as if he were commanding it—whatever Ioannes Andreas <note>Ioannes Andreas (c. 1270–1348) was a celebrated Italian canonist, often called the "fountain and doctor of canon law."</note> may think.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
Next, whatever truth this may hold, when the Pope sells a prebend <note>prebend: a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church, granted to a clergyman (canon) as a stipend.</note>, since he is the one who grants it, he seems entirely capable of making the recipient fit to receive it. ¶ To the third point, finally, it is responded—following Saint Thomas Aquinas—that under the name of "purchase," any exchange of a spiritual thing for a temporal one is included. Therefore, just as buying a prebend with coins is simony, so too is exchanging a secular estate for it. Indeed (as we said above), a prebend cannot even be exchanged for another prebend without the Pope's permission without it being simony. However, as has been explained, this would not be simony except by positive law <note>positive law: man-made laws (here, Church law) as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>. Therefore, to exchange other sacred things is not simony, because it is not prohibited by such law—provided that only the value of the physical object is considered, and nothing is paid for the consecration. I say a chalice can be exchanged for a chalice. Indeed, it can be sold for as much as the material and workmanship would be valued at without the consecration; and it may even be leased to another church.

<margin>Lawful exchange of sacraments.</margin>
¶ Regarding the sacraments, however, Conradus <note>Conrad Summenhart (1450–1502), a German theologian who wrote extensively on contracts and simony.</note> in his 4th book, distinction 25, article 3, denies that one can be exchanged for another. For although it is not, he says, as illicit as simply selling them, there is nonetheless some appearance of a sale: because one is then considered the price of the other. But truly, I do not see what of a sale or a price is mixed in if reciprocal services are brought into an agreement: "I will baptize you if you baptize me," or, "if you are willing to hear my confession, I will hear yours in turn." And, "I will pray for you if you in turn repay me with a similar benefit."

# QUESTION SIX
## On the matter of simony.
### ARTICLE I.
*Whether it is ever lawful to either give or receive money for the sacraments.*

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Large ornate woodcut initial 'C' containing a circular medallion with a figure holding a dish or paten.</image-desc>
<margin>The first argument.</margin>
Having established the definition and the sinful nature of simony, it follows that we should dispute its subject matter in order. And first, concerning the sacraments, it is argued that it is sometimes lawful to redeem them with a price. Baptism is the gateway to the sacraments; and yet, when a wicked priest refuses to baptize a child who is just about to die without a price, and the father has neither the hands nor the tongue to wash the child himself <note>The "tongue" refers to the ability to speak the formula of baptism correctly.</note>, it would seem the father acts more wisely if he offers money to the priest than if he allowed the soul of his offspring to go to ruin. Therefore, it is lawful to purchase a sacrament.

<margin>The second.</margin>
¶ Second. The Eucharist is the greatest of the sacraments, yet for its consecration and offering, it is lawful to offer money, and for the priest to receive what is offered. Therefore, it should be more easily granted that other sacraments can be redeemed with a price.

<margin>The third.</margin>
¶ Third. Penance is a sacrament of necessity that requires absolution from excommunication beforehand; but it is customary for judges to receive money for absolution from excommunication. Therefore, this is not sacrilege.

<margin>The fourth.</margin>
¶ Fourth. Custom is the reason that what was previously a crime can be done lawfully. By this reasoning, Augustine says that having several wives was not a crime when it was the custom. Now, a custom prevails among some that for the consecration of bishops, the blessing of abbots, and the anointing of priests, something may be given and received for the chrism and the oil <note>chrism: a mixture of oil and balsam used in several sacraments.</note>. Therefore, that is lawful.

<margin>The fifth.</margin>
¶ Fifth. Everyone has the right to buy off their own harassment; but it often happens in practice that someone is unjustly barred from a bishopric or another priesthood. Therefore, it will be lawful for such a harassed person to rescue themselves from that injustice with money.

<margin>The sixth.</margin>
¶ Sixth. Marriage is a certain sacrament, but money is given for marriage—namely, the wife's dowry. Therefore, it is lawful both to give and to receive a price for a sacrament.

---

¶ The contrary view is advised by that canon of the 8th Synod <note>Original: "Qui per pecuniam consecrauerit..."</note>: *He who has consecrated for money, or has been consecrated by another [for money], shall be alienated from the priesthood.*

Already above, a distinction was made between spiritual things that are the matter of simony and other types of spiritual things. For those spiritual things which are natural, and are not given to us for free so that we may bestow them, are not subject to the vice of simony; but those spiritual gifts (*charismata*) which are given by gift...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of simony—the sin of buying or selling sacred things. Having previously discussed the Pope’s role, Soto now categorizes different types of "spiritual things" and determines which can and cannot be associated with a price or a contract for labor.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Fourfold difference of spiritual things.</margin>
...we receive as a gift from the divine, which in some way pertain to grace. These are divided into a fourfold difference. First, some are **spiritual by their essence**: such as grace, which is the very spiritual life of the soul; and charity, which is the habit <note>habit: in medieval philosophy, a stable disposition or quality that allows a person to act well.</note> by which we perform the duties and works of life. It can in no way be questioned whether these can be sold or bought; for they are gifts of God to such an extent that it would be madness to think anyone could transfer them to another, whether by gift or for a price. In the second rank are **spiritual things that precede these as a proximate cause**. Such are the sacraments, which, as instruments of Christ’s passion, are the effective causes of grace. In the third degree of spiritual things are the **acts of charisms**, which are called "graces freely given" <note>original: "gratis datae." These are spiritual gifts meant for the benefit of others, such as prophecy.</note>: such as the gifts of prophecy and tongues, to which we can also add prayer and religion. Finally, in the fourth place come **spiritual things by annexation**: such as priesthoods and prebends <note>prebend: a portion of church revenues granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note>, which serve the spiritual function. Therefore, putting aside the first category, the individual articles here must examine each of the other three.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, in this first part—which stands as the second article in the works of Saint Thomas Aquinas—the sacraments are addressed with two conclusions. The first: To receive money for the spiritual grace of the sacraments is the sacrilegious crime of simony <note>simony: the sin of buying or selling sacred things, named after Simon Magus from the Book of Acts.</note>; it is so contrary to natural and divine law that it cannot be excused by any custom. Indeed, no such rights can be prejudiced. And certainly, by the name of "money," according to the teaching of the Philosopher <note>The Philosopher: Aristotle. Soto is referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book 3.</note> in the third book of the *Ethics*, whatever is valued by coin is understood.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The proof of the conclusion is most manifest. For the sacraments of the New Law <note>New Law: the era of Christianity and the Gospel, as opposed to the Old Law of the Hebrew Bible.</note> are spiritual to the highest degree, since they exist as the cause of grace and spiritual life. This power was not present in those ancient Mosaic rites. Grace, however, as the name itself suggests, is conferred upon us freely <note>original: "gratis." Soto is making a wordplay on "gratia" (grace) and "gratis" (free).</note>; otherwise, according to the author Paul, it would not be grace. Therefore, no mortal can receive a price for its bestowal. For besides the fact that it would most unjustly violate the law of nature—selling that which is neither one's own nor estimable by any price—it would be most impiously injurious toward God. Furthermore, it would be to think of selling what the Most High alone confers by His own kindness. And this is the height of simony, from which it also drew its name. For as we said above, this gift of the Holy Spirit was to be conferred, which that evil Simon thought to buy. To this is added
<column-break/>
the canon of Leo, *Gratia* (Causa 1, Question 1), and many other sections of the same Decree.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: It is no vice of simony, nor indeed any sin at all, for ministers of the church to receive stipends and food from the people for their own sustenance. The first conclusion is so clear that it leaves us no doubt. The second, however, has been demonstrated time and again above from the words of Paul in 1 Corinthians 9, to which is also added 1 Timothy 5: *Let the priests who rule well be held worthy of double honor.* Here the Augustinian gloss <note>gloss: a traditional commentary or explanation of a text.</note> says: "Let them receive sustenance for their necessity from the people, and the reward for their distribution from the Lord." Therefore, priests possess a very great right to be supported—not just in any manner, but decently according to their dignity.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ What remains to be doubted here, then, is this: whether for those things annexed to the sacraments—namely for the use of vessels, for the material, and especially for the **labor itself**—a price can be received, and that by agreement. For it appears that no agreement can intervene that is not simoniacal, as Saint Thomas seems to assert in Article 3, in response to the second argument. On the contrary, however, is the custom permitted by the Church. For it allows a priest to agree on a stipend to serve a chaplaincy—for instance, being bound to celebrate Mass in a certain place three times a week or daily. To this custom, reason also supports <note>original: "fragatur," likely a misprint for "suffragatur" (supports).</note> it, as Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, known as Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> says here. Since if it is permitted to desire a stipend for sustenance (as was asserted in the second conclusion), nothing forbids it from being procured and brought into an agreement. For it is the *matter* that makes a contract simoniacal. Therefore, since the matter is the same without an agreement as it is with an agreement—namely, temporal sustenance—it follows that if it is permitted without an agreement to hope for and receive what is necessary for life, without which spiritual things cannot be ministered, it is no vice to agree on a price.

<margin>Adrian. William of Auxerre.</margin>
¶ This matter is greatly controversial among the Doctors, especially those of Canon Law <note>Canon Law: the internal religious law governing the Catholic Church.</note>. The authors of the *Summae* speak of it variously under the word *simonia*. Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a theologian before becoming Pope.</note>, in his ninth *Quodlibet*, along with the ancient theologian William of Auxerre, cites many legal experts in favor of the affirmative opinion: namely, that it is lawful to agree on a price for the **labor of administering the sacraments**, according to the apostolic doctrine cited above. The last canon of Causa 1, Question 2, seems to harmonize with this, where it is asserted that clerics can receive stipends earned by just labors. Indeed, even the Gospel says, where Christ speaks: *The laborer is worthy of his hire.*

<summary>Domingo de Soto categorizes spiritual things and argues that while grace and the sacraments themselves can never be sold, it is lawful and necessary for clergy to receive a stipend for their sustenance and labor through a formal agreement.</summary>

### Book Nine, Question VI.

<margin>Durandus.</margin>
...his own: And it is the common opinion of Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334) was a Dominican theologian known for his independent and often "modernist" views.</note> in Book 4, distinction 25, question 1, who entirely refuses the idea that anything can be received for the labor of administering a sacrament.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
And Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534) was a leading Catholic theologian and cardinal, famous for his commentaries on Thomas Aquinas.</note>, both here and in his *Summary* under the word "simony," and in the 9th question of his first *Quodlibets*, learnedly discusses many points regarding the settlement of this dispute—provided the matter is gathered a little more clearly and concisely.

<margin>Distinction.</margin>
Therefore, for the understanding of the matter, a three-part distinction is pleasing: between the **price of spiritual things**, a **stipend for support**, and a **wage for hired labor**. Indeed, regarding the first part, no one is in doubt: it is so clear that a price cannot be received for a spiritual thing or something annexed to it, as was explained above, for the reason that such things are not sellable for a price. Truly, the distinction between the other two parts is not as difficult to understand as it appears at first glance. For a **wage** <note>original: "merces"</note> is made equal to the work, about which it says in Matthew 20: "Give the laborers their hire." A **stipend for support** <note>original: "stipendium sustentationis"</note>, however, although it eventually refers to the works of the ministers, nevertheless directly pertains only to the necessary maintenance of the minister. We can illustrate this distinction regarding these two parts with this example: If some craftsman, whose works were worthy of a great price, were to agree with a certain master in this way: "Give me food, and I will devote all my labors to you, however much they might be worth," then the labors would not be valued, but only the necessary support. Conversely, when a wealthy craftsman asks for as much as the workmanship is worth for a statue or other structure, he does not value the necessity of his food, but the value of the work. For this reason, Augustine, whom I recently cited, sharply distinguished by saying: "Let them receive the support of necessity from the people; but the wage of stewardship—that is, the equal value of the work—from the Lord." Therefore, there is no doubt that clerics can receive a stipend for support. And they can do this in two ways. First, by the public authority of the Church, which has taxed the quota of tithes. And likewise by the constitutions of bishops, who surely can determine how much stipend he is worthy of who is bound to such service of the church.

<margin>Clerics can receive a stipend for support.</margin>
The second way is by private liberty. For even a priest himself who is in need of food, when he is hired for the service of a chaplaincy or a vicarship, can bargain for a stipend for support according to the arrangement of the place and time. However, I would not approve of this with the same ease as Cajetan

<column-break/>

asserts: namely, that when a stipend for support has been decreed by the authority of a superior, a priest can receive it whether he be poor or wealthy. For a wealthy priest can undertake the same priesthood with no less right than a needy one. But when such a stipend is not established by law, but is to be established by private agreement, then he says a poor man can bargain for it, but a rich man not at all. Because since support is supplied to him from elsewhere, it is a sign that he makes the agreement not for support, but for the wage of his labors. However, I say I would not easily approve of this rigor of judgment. For if, from the nature of the thing, such a moderation of support is necessary for the support of a minister bound to such a function, then from the nature of the thing no simony emerges; and thus it is not created by the quality <note>In this context, "quality" refers to the social or financial status of the priest.</note> of the priest. For God alone is the searcher of intentions. Moreover, that such a stipend is permitted for the sake of support was sufficiently demonstrated above by natural and divine law, and that the priestly order ought to be decently supported. But whether it is permitted to receive something also as a wage for labor—which was the third part of the distinction—this is what is doubted and disputed among the doctors. Although the doubt is not as great as many authors think. Indeed, through a distinction, all are so reconciled that they cannot disagree. For some labors and works are **antecedent** to the sacrament, and thus incidental to it; while others are **concomitant**, or rather, of its very substance.

<margin>A priest can hire out antecedent labors, but not subsequent ones.</margin>
Therefore, the former can be hired out for a fixed price. But the latter not at all. It is, for example, the case that a sick person for whom a priest must be summoned from a distance to hear his confession, or celebrate Mass, or perform a divine service. Surely the priest can demand a price for the labor of the journey. Different is the labor and operation intrinsic to the sacrament: such as the celebration of the Mass, or the work of baptizing, or any other application of a sacrament. And for these labors and works, it is manifest that no price can be received. But concerning these, Augustine says: "Let him receive the wage of stewardship from the Lord." For it would be just as if it were received for the grace of the sacrament. For the act of baptizing and baptism are regarded as the same, just as the Mass and the celebration of the Mass; just as he who builds a house receives the same price for the house and for its construction. Nor can he receive two: one for the thing, another for

<sig>Ccc</sig>

<summary>Soto distinguishes between the forbidden sale of spiritual things and the lawful receipt of a stipend for a priest's living expenses. He argues that while priests cannot charge for the "intrinsic" labor of a sacrament (like the act of baptizing), they may charge for "antecedent" labor, such as the travel required to reach a remote location.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between a "wage" for work and a "stipend" for support, specifically addressing whether a priest can contract for the obligation of service without committing simony.</meta>

F. D. Soto, on Justice & Right,

<margin>A priest is permitted to contract for a wage for the obligation of celebrating.</margin>
...but truly for the work. ¶ However, while it is argued that nothing of a wage can be received for functions of this kind, it is not denied that something can be received for the **obligation** <note>original: "obligatio"; Soto distinguishes between paying for the spiritual act itself and paying for the priest's commitment to be present and available.</note> of performing them. Just as you cannot demand any price for the service of lending, yet it is not illicit to receive something for the obligation of lending. I say it is permitted for a priest, when he is hired for the service of a parish, to enter into an agreement for a stipend for the obligation of celebrating on specific days and for assisting in hearing confessions. This assertion is supported by the chapter *Significatum* in the section on prebends <note>A "prebend" is a portion of Anglican or Catholic cathedral revenues formerly granted to a canon or member of the chapter as a stipend.</note>. ¶ Through these points, everyone will easily judge concerning the use of vessels and the matter of the sacraments. For it would be a sin to demand any reward for the use of the chalice or the corporal cloths from the one who consecrates; for that use is part of the intrinsic nature of performing the sacrament. Although, as we have said, one church may sell or lease a chalice to another. For that leasing is accidental, occurring far before the sacrament itself. In the same way, if there were no oil in a city, one church could sell consecrated oil for as much as if it were not consecrated. Indeed, one could buy **chrism** <note>original: "chrisma"; a mixture of oil and balsam consecrated by a bishop and used in various sacraments.</note> in one place and sell it in another. For all those contracts are similar to the actions we recently said precede the sacrament accidentally. This is true unless it is done to the injury and contempt of the sacred thing, such as if the consecration itself were sold. However, just as neither the action itself (which belongs to the essence of the sacrament) nor the labor annexed to it can be sold, neither can the use of the material of the sacrament which pertains to its substance. That is: just as neither a bishop for the labor of confirming, nor a priest for the labor and work of anointing the sick, can receive a wage; so neither can they receive anything for the use of the Chrism or the oil consumed there. And what has been said regarding the actions of the sacraments must likewise be understood regarding **sacramentals** <note>original: "sacramentalibus"; sacred signs or actions, such as blessings or exorcisms, that resemble sacraments but do not confer grace in the same way.</note>. For a priest cannot receive any reward as a wage for exorcisms and catechisms, or for the blessings of those getting married. Therefore, regarding the final canon in the 1st Question, 2nd [of the Decree of Gratian], the answer is that it speaks of stipends for support, as do the words of Christ. Which is why Luke says, "The laborer is worthy of his hire," or Matthew, "of his food." ¶ From these things, finally, it is gathered how

<column-break/>

absurd a custom it is, and how sacrilegiously simoniacal, to demand money or some gift for the conferring of [holy] orders. This practice was introduced by **titular bishops** <note>original: "titulares episcopos"; bishops who possess the title of a former diocese that no longer exists, often serving as assistants to local bishops.</note>; for since the proper and legitimate bishops are either not in residence, or—which is shameful—do not deign to celebrate the orders themselves, they summon titular bishops for this duty. And what is more absurd, they do not pay them a sufficient stipend to prevent them from all extortion. It is therefore unjust to compel those being ordained to offer not only candles, but even money. Indeed, I believe that nothing can be demanded even for letters of testimony.

<margin>To the first argument. The solution of St. Thomas.</margin>
To the first main argument, then, Saint Thomas [Aquinas] responds in such a way that, surveying all remedies, he never concedes that it is lawful to offer a wage for a sacramental action. For he says that if the person to be baptized has not yet reached the use of reason, and a sacrilegious priest refuses to dispense baptism without a price, it is to be considered as if no priest were present. Thus, just as in a case of extreme necessity where anyone is a minister, the child should be baptized by anyone else rather than giving assent to the priest's sacrilege. Although the water, which is a physical element, may be bought from him. If, however, the person is an adult and no one else is present from whom he may receive the sacrament, he should rather depart from this life without the sacrament than buy baptism. For then the **baptism of the spirit** <note>original: "baptisma flaminis"; often called "baptism of desire," where the intent to receive the sacrament suffices for salvation in emergencies.</note> will be enough for his salvation.

<margin>A Doubt</margin>
¶ But truly, this does not resolve the matter in the most extreme straits. For let us suppose a wicked priest in the presence of a small child and only the parent, who is himself unable and unfit to baptize, and the priest expresses his corrupt intent: namely, that he will by no means administer the sacrament unless a price is paid to him for the sacramental function itself. Is it then lawful for the father to offer such a price to him? For no weak reason seems to persuade it. For as we were saying a little before, it is permitted for anyone to **redeem their own harassment** <note>original: "vexationem redimere"; a legal and moral concept where one pays an extortionist not to buy a right, but to stop the extortioner's illegal interference.</note>. That parent, acting in the place of the child, suffers a great injury, and the child an even graver one—since divine, natural, and human law all support the child's right that the wicked sacrilegious man be bound to baptize him. The father can therefore redeem that harassment with a price. An example for us is the one who seeks a loan at interest in a time of necessity; which...

He condemns the practice of charging fees for ordinations and discusses Thomas Aquinas's view on whether a parent may pay an extortionist priest to baptize a child in an emergency.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on simony and the ethics of payments related to sacred duties, specifically focusing on whether one may pay a priest to perform a necessary sacrament like baptism when the priest is unjustly obstructing it.</meta>

### Question VI of the Ninth Book.
Ccc 2

...can truly do so without fault. Indeed, reason seems to support this view far more effectively. For since all laws are directed toward the salvation of souls, and no other remedy is available to a wretched infant, that obstruction <note>original: "vexatio"; referring to a priest's unjust refusal or delay in performing a duty unless paid.</note> ought to be repelled by a price rather than allowing the infant to be forever excluded from the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, since Saint Thomas has not thoroughly examined the reason for this doubt until now, it remains for us to respond to it.

<margin>The solution of Paludanus.</margin>
And indeed, Paludanus <note>Petrus de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a prominent Dominican theologian and canonist.</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 5), considers it entirely sacrilegious, even in such a case, to buy a sacrament with a price to redeem an obstruction. And perhaps he asserted this because of Saint Thomas, who in the same Book 4, Question 2, deems that view more probable.

<margin>Alexander of Hales. Richard.</margin>
This was also the opinion of Alexander of Hales <note>A 13th-century Franciscan theologian known as the "Irrefragable Doctor."</note> before him (Part 2, Question 189, Member 3) and of Richard of Middleton <note>Richardus de Mediavilla (c. 1249–1302), another influential Franciscan scholar.</note> (Book 4, Distinction 52, Article 3). Paludanus adds a reason: he says that redeeming an obstruction can happen in two ways. One way is from a person who can cause harm but cannot provide a benefit; the other is from someone who can both harm and benefit. He says the redemption of the first kind of obstruction is licit, but the latter is not at all. His examples are: a bishop-elect may buy off the obstruction of those who disturb his possession and confirmation, but he may not pay the one who is actually confirming him. The reason for the difference is that in the first case, no suspicion arises that he wants to buy the bishopric, since those people cannot grant it. In the latter case, however, he is tainted by that very suspicion. And therefore, since a priest is able to provide the benefit by baptizing, Paludanus says the obstruction cannot be bought off from him. Hear, however, a witty commentary <note>original: "lepidam glossam"; a clever or pointed marginal note in canon law collections.</note> on the chapter *Baptizandis* (Question 1, Chapter 1). After saying that a price can by no means be paid for baptism in such a case, it adds: "I would, however, rather give the money than let the child die thus; and rightly so, even though I ought not to do it."

<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
Consider this: if he "ought not" to do it, how could he "do rightly"? Therefore, Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> on the chapter *Cum in ecclesiae* regarding simony, and others whom Richard cites in the place mentioned, distinguish between an infant and an adult. They properly concede that the person caring for a small child ought to buy off the obstruction with a price due to extreme necessity; however, this does not apply to an adult, who can be saved through the baptism of the spirit <note>original: "baptismus flaminis"; the "baptism of fire/wind," refers to the Catholic doctrine that a person's intense desire for baptism and love for God can provide the grace of the sacrament if water baptism is impossible.</note>.

<margin>Solution to the proposed doubt.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> subscribes to their opinion, and rightly so, in my view. For that a small child suffers

<column-break/>

extreme necessity should come into no one's doubt. Indeed, to say that the intention of the person wishing to baptize suffices for the child, and that God supplies the place of baptism, is not only rash and supported by no reason, but is even deserving of a worse name. For since no one can merit grace for another without the act of the one who is to receive it, no intention for baptism is considered "baptism of the spirit" except the specific intention of the one who desires to be baptized. And the law is: no one is saved without the baptism of blood <note>Martyrdom.</note>, or of the spirit <note>Desire.</note>, or of the river <note>Water baptism.</note>. Since, therefore, the priest in our case is bound by such strict law to baptize this child, and the child consequently suffers such a notable injury, that obstruction is licitly bought off with a price. Nor is it similar to the case of a bishop-elect regarding the one who confirms him, because such a great necessity does not press upon him to be confirmed, nor is the other party compelled by a similar law to confirm him. Wherefore, in our case, the father of the boy does not pay the money for the purpose of buying the benefit of the sacrament, but to repel an injury.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
But so that the matter may be made more clear, a more urgent argument is raised. Suppose that person, whether a priest or some infidel, is so perverse that he will not baptize the child until the father swears solemnly to grant a price, not to redeem the obstruction, but to buy the sacrament itself and the sacramental grace: would it then be licit? It appears not to be licit, for then the one providing the price seems to be doing the same thing that Simon Magus attempted <note>Simon Magus tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit from the Apostles, the origin of the term "simony."</note>.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan here does not seem to agree that it would be licit to give for the sacrament; and in Question 9 of his first *Quodlibetal*, he seems to deny this more openly. Furthermore, he considers it as intrinsically evil to buy a spiritual thing as it is to sell it.

<margin>Argument against Cajetan.</margin>
But truly, in my judgment, those things are not consistent with each other. For if buying a sacrament were, like lying, intrinsically evil, it would not become licit even to redeem an obstruction. Because providing a price to redeem an obstruction is essentially buying the sacrament as a means to repel an injury; for even if the ultimate intention is not directed at the purchase of the sacrament, it is nonetheless accepted as the means used to avoid the obstruction. Just as one who, to redeem an obstruction, would buy a favorable sentence from an unjust judge. And this reasoning is confirmed: because no matter how much that man compels me to swear that...

<summary>This page discusses the moral dilemma of whether a parent can pay a priest to baptize an infant in danger of death if the priest unjustly demands money, concluding that it is permissible to pay to remove the obstruction for the sake of the child's salvation.</summary>
