# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>The author’s solution.</margin>
...I provide money for the sacrament, nonetheless my supreme intention remains intact: that I am doing this to redeem an obstruction <note>Latin: *vexatio*; the unjust hindrance or refusal by a priest to perform a spiritual duty.</note>. Because of this, there is no falsehood in the oath. Therefore, unless my own ignorance deceives me, this opinion regarding the redemption of an obstruction cannot be defended in any other way than through a distinction between the buying and the selling of a sacrament. Thus, if selling a sacrament—or any spiritual thing—is entirely and intrinsically evil, so much so that it cannot be done lawfully for the sake of redeeming an obstruction nor for any other imaginable cause, one must nevertheless say that offering a price for it is not so intrinsically evil that extreme necessity would not permit it. A similar example of this is found in the exchange of a loan for interest <note>Latin: *fœnore*; usury.</note>, which is intrinsically evil for the one receiving the interest, yet the one paying it can be excused by necessity.

<margin>Regarding the argument made.</margin>
¶ Nor can any argument be brought against this from the case of Simon Magus <note>A biblical figure (Acts 8) who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit, giving his name to the sin of "simony."</note>, who is condemned for the attempted purchase of grace. For he wished to buy it specifically so that he might have the power of reselling it. By this reasoning, he inflicted a most foul injury upon grace. However, one who offers a price for a sacrament for the reason just stated does not do so with that intention, but out of veneration for the commandment of baptism and a supreme estimation of grace, without which he believes no one can be saved. In short, just as it would not be lawful to give a price for a sacrament outside of extreme necessity, so does extreme necessity make it lawful.

<margin>Limitation of the previous solution.</margin>
I would affirm all these things, however, only so long as the one who intends to sell the baptism does not do so out of contempt for religion. For if it were a heretic or a tyrant who, in mockery of religion, wished to persuade someone toward the depravity of simony, and demanded that price as a sort of confession of that falsehood, it would in no way be lawful to comply by giving the price. For that would be to deny the faith. It is otherwise if he seeks it not for that reason, but either out of greed or by leading the other into what he himself considers an evil.

<margin>Another argument.</margin>
¶ From these points, a judgment regarding an adult is easily reached. For if you argue that an adult who desires to be baptized has just as much right to be baptized by another as an infant does, and subsequently suffers the same injury, and therefore can redeem the same obstruction, it is denied that the cases are at all similar.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
Because in the simony of spiritual things, much greater caution must be applied than in the usury of temporal things. For in usury, a grave necessity liberates one from the fault of receiving. But in spiritual matters, because of their ex-

<column-break/>

cellence, only extreme necessity excuses, lest the one offering the price appear to consent to the other’s simony, and thus become a participant in it. An adult, however, does not labor under extreme necessity <note>Soto likely refers to the "baptism of desire," where an adult's sincere intent to be baptized can suffice for salvation if the physical sacrament is impossible to obtain.</note>.

<margin>A reply.</margin>
Nor is it truly pressing if you argue that perhaps that person has only attrition <note>Imperfect contrition or sorrow for sin based on fear of punishment.</note>, which could become contrition <note>Perfect sorrow for sin based on the love of God.</note> through the act of baptism.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
For it is his own fault if, while he sees that the other person is unwilling to baptize except sacrilegiously, he does not sufficiently turn his own mind toward God with His help. Be careful, however, if you are wise, that no suspicion touches you from these things which have been said: that it is lawful for anyone, however worthy, to offer anything temporal to electors or to a Bishop so that he may be elected, even to "redeem an obstruction." For that would be open simony, as will be clear in the next question.

<margin>To the second principal point.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> responds well that a priest does not receive a price or a wage for the labor of the Sacrifice of the Mass—which would indeed be simoniacal—but rather alms for his sustenance. One must look back at that distinction fixed earlier between sustenance and a wage for the labor of the work.

<margin>A scruple.</margin>
¶ But is it then lawful to bargain over the amount of alms for sustenance? For it appears not to be lawful, because a suspicion would arise from it that the priest is valuing a divine thing at a price.

<margin>Response.</margin>
The response is that if we weigh the matter purely according to its nature, it does not seem to be illicit for a priest to be unwilling to celebrate Mass except where sustenance is provided, and to explain this to the person who asks for the divine rite to be performed for them. By this same reasoning, we granted above that a priest could receive two "pitances" <note>Small portions of food or allowances.</note> for performing one sacred rite. Nevertheless, to contend over the quantity can hardly be done without scandal, for the reason already given.

¶ Therefore, there remains at present a warning about a certain practice beginning to creep in, which I believe the ancient fathers, had they known of it, would have strongly discouraged and cursed. For it is said that in some churches, the alms to be offered for a Mass are so taxed by the bishops that they forbid priests, under the penalty of excommunication <note>Latin: *anathematis*; anathema.</note>, from accepting the task for a lesser amount. And if someone in a will has bequeathed alms for a certain number of Masses, and the taxed alms for each is higher, they compel the heirs and executors of the wills under that same penalty to increase those alms. Truly, I do not know how this can be done without scandal and without a violation of the law. I confess indeed that a bishop can and ought to urgently admonish the people that for their...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on simony and the ethics of financial transactions related to spiritual offices. The previous page established that while selling a sacrament is intrinsically evil, paying to "redeem an obstruction"—that is, paying to remove an unjust hindrance to a spiritual right—may be excusable in cases of necessity. This page applies that logic to Mass stipends, legal penalties, and the election of church officials.</meta>

### Book Nine, Question VI.
Ccc 3

...according to each person’s ability and according to the conditions of the times, they might increase the **alms for the Mass** <note>Latin: *eleemosyna Missæ*; the stipend given to a priest for celebrating a Mass.</note> so that the priest might be able to sustain himself. However, to constrain the people by law, and to bar the parish priests so that they cannot celebrate for a lower price, is diametrically opposed to the nature of alms, which ought to be free. Otherwise, it takes on the appearance of a **price or a wage** for the celebration of the sacrifice. Note the words of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theologian of the Catholic Church.</note> in the present question, article 3, while solving the second argument: "Such an ordinance," he says, "would be illicit." If you argue that a Bishop has the power to tax a stipend for sustenance, a distinction must be made. Indeed, I admit he can do this for an obligation by which a priest binds himself to a chaplaincy or to service for a time, or in perpetuity. However, to set a tax for a **single Mass**, which is not an obligation but a simple action—"I give so that you may celebrate" <note>original: *Do ut celebres*</note>—and to do so under such a penalty that less cannot be given or received: I truly do not see law there, but **scandal**.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third argument, it is answered that in absolution from excommunication, money is not paid as a price for a sacred thing, but as a **penalty for a crime**.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fourth argument, it is answered that where an ancient custom has grown that something be returned for such hierarchical acts, it is to be believed that this was introduced as a **stipend for sustenance**. For that reason, it would not be a sin to receive it. However, where it is paid as a price for the action, it is made lawful by no custom, as held in the chapter *Cùm in ecclesiæ* regarding **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling spiritual things or church offices.</note>, where it is forbidden to receive anything for all such actions. For since simony is a vice against nature, no custom has force to the contrary. Therefore, in such behaviors, the **appearance of evil** must be carefully avoided, according to the word of the Apostle in 1 Thessalonians: *Abstain from every appearance of evil.*

<margin>To the fifth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fifth argument, Saint Thomas answers that before someone acquires a legal right to a bishopric, or to any other priesthood or dignity through election or provision, it is a crime of simony to use money to drive away the obstacles of opponents. For in this way, a man would be paving a path for himself to **purchase a spiritual thing**. But after a right has been acquired by someone, it is permitted to remove **unjust impediments** through money—namely, if some were standing in the way so that the elect could not reach the one confirming them, or were not admitted into possession. However, I understand the former part in such a way that just as...

<column-break/>

<margin>It is permitted to use money to redeem an obstruction from one who strives to hinder an election by force.</margin>
...we said in the fourth book regarding those who hinder the attainment of a **benefice** <note>A church office that provides an income.</note>, you should excuse those who use force. For if someone, even before an election, were to thrust you into prison so you could not seek the dignity, or imprisoned any of the electors so they would not elect you, you could then use money to **redeem that injury**. It is otherwise if they sought to exclude you through ambition, flattery, or what they call **subornation** <note>Bribery or illicit persuasion.</note>. Nor, as we said above, could you use money to "soften" a confirmer who refused to confirm you; this is because, as we said above, they have the power not only to hinder but to benefit. Therefore, that gift would show the appearance of a **purchase**. This is not found in the case of another who was merely hindering you. And perhaps it is not permitted to redeem an obstruction even from the one who is to put you into possession: for **possession** is something spiritual, which you would seem to be purchasing. Although, regarding possession, the matter is not as certain as it is regarding confirmation.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ Around these matters, however, a doubt arises that must not be silenced: Whether, to prevent an **unjust election** which is harmful and ruinous to the Church, it is permitted to offer money.

<margin>Cajetan's assertion.</margin>
**Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note>, in that ninth question of his first *Quodlibet*, does not fear to assert that in the election of the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>The Pope.</note>, if it clearly appears that the election is leaning toward an unworthy person who would be a plague to the Church, it is permitted to prevent such an election by offering a price; for this would be **redeeming the Church from an obstruction**. But yet, he says, this is not permitted for the sake of electing a good man. And indeed, I think the first part of his opinion should be agreed with to such an extent that I believe even the latter part should be tempered. For truly, it is as great a ruin and atrocious distress to the Church if a worthy man is *not* elected as if an unworthy man *is* elected—since there is no middle ground between these. Therefore, where there are only two between whom the election wavers, one of whom is worthy and the other unworthy, if it were permitted to repel the unworthy one with a price, it would certainly be permitted to turn the election toward the worthy one; because the rejection of one would be the election of the other. For I judge, as I said above, that although selling such spiritual things is entirely and intrinsically evil, **redeeming** them is not so evil that extreme necessity cannot make it lawful. Wherefore, where there are many worthy candidates, it would by no means be permitted to seek the election of one through a price. Indeed, even if some were more worthy than others, it would not be permitted to do this in favor of the most worthy...

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of money in the Church, distinguishing between "redeeming an obstruction" (paying to remove an unjust hindrance to a right) and simony (buying a spiritual office). It concludes that while Mass stipends and legal penalties are acceptable for sustenance or punishment, using money to influence elections is generally forbidden unless it is to prevent an "unworthy" person from harming the Church in a case of extreme necessity.</summary>

...for where a worthy person is expected to be elected, no extreme necessity of electing another arises; and it is only such necessity that wipes away the stain of **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling spiritual things, named after Simon Magus from the Book of Acts.</note> from these kinds of gifts.

<margin>To the sixth point.</margin> Finally, in responding to the sixth point, **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto's commentary.</note> rebukes certain people who claim it is lawful to receive money for marriage as if it were not a **sacrament** <note>A visible sign of inward grace; the Church counts seven, including marriage.</note> that bestows grace. This was the opinion of Bernard in the *Apparatus* regarding the chapter *Cum in ecclesia* on simony. There he says that although it is not lawful to receive money for the blessing of the newlyweds, it is not illicit for the marriage itself. His reasoning was that even if it is a sacrament, it does not confer grace. 

<margin>The Master of the Sentences.</margin> Some suspected that the **Master of the Sentences** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose book "The Sentences" was the standard theology textbook for centuries.</note> held this view, because in Book 4, Distinction 26, he does not explain this sacrament as anything other than a "remedy" established for human weakness. 

<margin>Durandus.</margin> Even **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a philosopher known for его independent and often controversial views.</note> did not fear to wink at this same opinion in his commentary on that same distinction. It is, however, an error that is more than just false, as almost all Doctors of theology conclude in that passage. Therefore, the **dowry** money of a wife is provided for the marriage, not insofar as it is a sacrament and an instrumental cause of grace, but insofar as it is a "duty of nature"—the burdens of which certainly cannot be met without expenses.

### ARTICLE 11.

->Whether it is lawful to give and receive money for spiritual actions.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin> <note>The decorative 'C' in the original shows a man in a landscape, a common motif in Renaissance printing.</note> CONSEQUENTLY, we argue regarding another order of spiritual things: specifically, whether it is right to both give and receive money for spiritual actions. The use of prophecy is a spiritual act, yet in ancient times something was offered for it, as we read in 1 Samuel 9 regarding Saul, and 1 Kings 13 regarding Josiah; therefore, it is not 

<margin>Second argument.</margin> illicit. ¶ Secondly: Prayer, preaching, and even divine praises are among the foremost spiritual actions. But to obtain the support of prayer, it is lawful to win over just men—especially those in need—with the kindness of gifts, according to the passage in Luke 16: "Make friends for yourselves with the **mammon of iniquity**" <note>A biblical phrase referring to worldly wealth or dishonest gain used for a good purpose.</note>. Furthermore, temporal goods are owed to the ministers of the Word—such as preachers who sow spiritual things—according to the Apostle’s decree 

<column-break/>

in 1 Corinthians 9. Moreover, for those who celebrate divine praises and Psalms, and those performing ecclesiastical rites like processions and funeral rites for the dead, certain **stipends** <note>Latin: *stipendia*; fixed payments or offerings for religious service.</note> are decreed, and sometimes even annual incomes. Therefore, there is no iniquity in receiving fixed rewards for spiritual actions of this kind. 

<margin>Third argument.</margin> ¶ Thirdly: Knowledge is a spiritual thing, since it is a faculty for teaching, much like a prelate's power for correction or his duty of administration. Yet there is nothing absurd about receiving a fee for the use of knowledge; for a Teacher, a lawyer, and a physician are permitted to lease and sell their labor for a price. Therefore, a prelate may likewise receive a price for his spiritual function. 

<margin>Fourth argument.</margin> ¶ Fourthly and finally, it is argued: Religious life is a state of spiritual perfection, and yet in monasteries—especially those of nuns—virgins are usually not admitted to the order unless they bring dowries with them. Therefore, it is lawful to both give and receive something for such acts. 

<margin>The Council of Toledo.</margin> ¶ To the contrary, however, stands a canon of the **Eleventh Council of Toledo** <note>A regional Church council held in Spain in 675 AD.</note> (found in 1. q. 1.), which begins: "Whatever is granted for the consolation of invisible grace must never be sold for gain or any rewards whatever, as the Lord says: 'What you have received freely, give freely.'" But these spiritual things just reviewed are granted through invisible grace; therefore, it is a sin to dispense them for a price.

After the sacraments, through which **sanctifying grace** <note>Latin: *gratia gratum faciens*; the grace that makes a soul pleasing to God and heals it from sin.</note> is conferred, another level of spirituality is held (as we said above) by those actions which pertain to **freely given graces** <note>Latin: *gratias gratis datas*; charismatic gifts like prophecy or healing, intended for the benefit of others rather than the holiness of the possessor.</note>. These clearly either proceed from that same sanctifying grace or prepare the soul to receive it. Regarding these, we respond with the same two conclusions used for the sacraments. 

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The first is: It is not only lawful, but necessary, that those who administer spiritual gifts through these actions be sustained by the people. This has already been more than sufficiently demonstrated above, both by natural reason and by the testimony of **Paul** <margin>Paul.</margin> in 1 Corinthians 9, where he says: "Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who... does not drink the milk of the flock?" 

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin> ¶ The second: To sell or buy that which is spiritual in such acts is **simoniacal sacrilege**. This is evident, and no other reasoning is needed than what was said

He concludes that while selling spiritual grace is sacrilege, providing for the physical needs of those performing spiritual duties is a requirement of natural and divine law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of simony, moving from the definition of the sin to the practicalities of Church life. ### Book Nine, Question VI.

...the understanding of the preceding points requires proof. In these matters, **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the central authority for this text.</note> says that first of all, one must beware lest the intention of buying or selling spiritual things occupy the mind. The clearest sign of this intent is if a priest demands a fee so strictly that the spiritual gifts themselves are withheld from those who are unwilling or unable to offer it. However, after the service has been freely provided, he states that the established and customary offerings can be lawfully required from those who are able to pay but refuse, provided it is done by the authority of a superior.

<margin>A serious doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding these conclusions, a somewhat greater reason for doubt arises: whether it is lawful to receive a price for the *labors* attached to such duties, more so than for the administration of the **sacraments** <note>Holy rites like Baptism or the Eucharist.</note>.

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
For in these cases, the labors and efforts seem to be somewhat distinct from the spiritual acts themselves: such as singing, whether with voices or the organ and other instruments; going in procession to lead a funeral; or celebrating other funeral rites there which are not strictly necessary for a simple burial. Likewise, the work of studying for a sermon, giving counsel, visiting subjects, and investigating their legal cases—all these labors seem capable of being hired out for a wage. For this reason, you may find several authors who allow that a price may be received for such labors based on the nature of the work, provided it does not outwardly look like an evil deed. However, this opinion is not cautious enough. For contracts in these matters are not only bad because they are prohibited by the Church, but because they are evil by their very nature, and are therefore prohibited.

<margin>The difference between the administration of sacraments and other spiritual actions.</margin>
¶ Therefore, first of all, assuming that three-fold distinction made above—between the "price" of spiritual things (which is never allowed), the "sustenance" of the clergy, and the "wages" for work—one must note the difference between the administration of the sacraments and other spiritual actions. Specifically, in a sacramental function, it is impossible to avoid the appearance of **simony** <note>original: "simonia"; the sin of buying or selling sacred things.</note> if one institutes other fees or offerings beyond the **tithes** <note>The traditional tenth of income given to the Church.</note> or those revenues established for sustenance. But for other "second-order" actions, other fees are usually established that take the form of a wage: such as for funeral rites, for singers, and even for preachers, processions, and other things of that kind. And the reason for this difference is that such actions 

<column-break/>

are not so necessarily attached to the spiritual act. For instance, such great pomp at a funeral is not necessary for the burial itself, nor are musical singers necessary for the celebration of the Divine service. Therefore, in these kinds of actions where something temporal is usually mixed in, a careful distinction is needed. For when that temporal element is not necessary for the spiritual one, no appearance of simony occurs if it is done for a wage by contract.

<margin>Solution to the immediate doubt.</margin>
For this reason, singers and organists can hire out their services without any **scruple** <note>A feeling of doubt or hesitation regarding the morality of an action.</note>. That office is an accessory to spiritual things. To this category, **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> and several others add the work of lawyers and doctors—though we shall deal with them shortly in the solution to the third point. But when the thing primarily sought is spiritual, it is not lawful to receive anything as a wage for it: such as for the Divine Psalms themselves, for necessary prayers, and for the necessary rites of burial.

¶ Nevertheless, to guide the consciences of the unlearned, these matters must be weighed according to the rules set down above. For we have said, following Saint Thomas, that offerings established for these actions must not be demanded so rigorously that the spiritual services are withheld from those who do not pay. For example: if a **parish priest** <note>original: "Plebanus"</note> refused to bury the dead unless the customary fees were paid first, he would cause scandal and show the appearance of simony, because burial is a necessity. If, however, some people want the funeral cared for with great pomp and to bury their dead with a grand display, the pastor is not bound to perform that for free; and therefore, he can lawfully demand the customary fees. But because even these things touch upon the spiritual order in their own way, one must avoid scandal—at least until after the office of burial is completed, as Saint Thomas warns here.

<margin>Sacrilegious extortions by clerics.</margin>
¶ At this point, we feel it necessary to warn how scandalous and sacrilegious are the extortions of the **secular clergy** <note>Priests who serve in a parish, as opposed to "regular" clergy who live in a monastery.</note> against the rights of **monks** and the liberty of Christians. For you will find dioceses where the clergy refuse to lead a person who chose burial in a monastery to that place with pomp; to the point that they sometimes will not carry a cross or sing psalms. Christian religion truly abhors this. For since everyone is free to choose a place of burial for their own devotion wherever they prefer, the will of the deceased should not be restricted by such extortions.

<sig>Ccc 4</sig>

<summary>Soto distinguishes between essential spiritual acts (which must be free) and non-essential "pomp" or music (for which a wage may be charged). He also condemns parish priests who extort fees or obstruct those who wish to be buried in monasteries.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,

<margin>A final doubt.</margin>
¶ A final, common doubt remains here concerning canons and other clerics who gather in the church for the **canonical hours** <note>The set of daily prayers—such as Matins, Vespers, and None—that clergy are required to recite.</note> solely for the sake of the stipend: whether they contract the vice of simony.

<margin>St. Thomas’s solution.</margin>
¶ To this, **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> responds in his *Quodlibets* (8, question 6, article 11): that if the stipend is the ultimate goal of the intention for celebrating the divine office, simony is committed. This is because the stipend then takes on the nature of a price, for which it is not lawful to sell a spiritual thing like the divine office. However, if the principal intention is nothing other than divine worship, and the temporal fruit is merely accessory—necessary for one's sustenance—it is not simony. ¶ Yet, unless this solution is soundly understood, it will prick human consciences with anxieties. For Saint Thomas seems here to condemn as simoniacs all those who proceed to the church with a view toward the **monetary distributions** <note>Small payments or "per diems" given to clergy for their actual presence at a service.</note>, who otherwise would by no means go. This is indeed hard to believe. Likewise, as we argued above regarding the reception of girls for the monastic veil, the necessity of household needs is irrelevant; something that would not otherwise be simony should not be marked with that vice just because of one's financial status. For simony consists entirely in a spiritual thing being sold, whether by a poor man or a rich one. Therefore, the same intent that would make a wealthy man a simoniac would also make a poor man one; and whatever would excuse the poor man would excuse the wealthy one—at least from simony, whatever might be said of his greed.

<margin>The author’s solution.</margin>
¶ The resolution, therefore, is that going to the church at a time when a cleric is not otherwise bound to go, solely for the sake of the distributions—such that he would not go otherwise—is not "true" simony, unless he intended to receive a price for the spiritual thing in the manner explained above. Nevertheless, that cleric would sin gravely against his order and institution if he never or rarely visited the church except for that reason, and if he did not have a general, principal purpose of frequenting the church for the sake of divine worship—for whose sake alone the rights to **prebends** <note>A portion of the cathedral's revenues granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> were instituted. Indeed, one who directs worship toward a temporal reward as if it were the ultimate end would have a perverse and sacrilegious intention against the legitimate order of things, which is that "the benefice exists for the sake of the office" <note>original: "beneficium sit propter officium" — a legal maxim meaning Church income is given only to support the performance of spiritual duties.</note>.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, then, it is responded that just as we do for sacred things, the ancients used to offer voluntary gifts to the good Prophets, as **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> noted in his commentary on Micah. This is also seen in the history of **Damian** <note>Likely referring to Saint Peter Damian or the stories of the "unmercenary" physicians Cosmas and Damian.</note>,

<column-break/>

who accepted small voluntary gifts for the gift of health almost against his will. However, to *demand* them is a crime, as is clear from the case of **Gehazi** <note>A biblical figure who secretly took money from the cured Naaman against the prophet Elisha's wishes (2 Kings 5).</note>, whom Elisha sharply rebuked for the price he requested from Naaman for the gift of healing.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ The second argument had three parts. Regarding the first part concerning alms given to the poor for their intercessions and the support of their prayers: the response is that these are not lawful if given as a *price* for such support (which is truly a spiritual thing), but they are given for the nourishment of the poor themselves. Whether it is lawful to bargain for a wage for the "work" of praying (in the third manner, as if for hired labor), someone might perhaps hesitate, since it is permitted for musical singers. But in truth, I would not dare to affirm this. There is a great difference. For music (as we said) is not strictly necessary for the celebration of the sacred rites. In prayer, however, the labor and effort are not distinguished from the spiritual gift itself. Indeed, the labor is the very spiritual office itself.

¶ Regarding **preachers**, it ought not to be called into doubt whether they can receive a price for the function itself: that would be open simony, as we just said regarding prayer. Nor is it similar to academic knowledge, which can be sold. For in knowledge, even in Theology acquired through human effort, nothing is valued except a mere temporal aid—namely, to direct, instruct, and enlighten the intellect. But the gift of preaching is not only to enlighten the intellect, but to do so according to the gift of the Holy Spirit, and thus to purge hearts according to His grace, to lift up minds, and to consolidate and perfect them in divine love. It is about these Teachers that the Apostolic word in Ephesians 4 is understood: *And he gave some, apostles; and some, pastors and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.* And in Romans 10: *How shall they preach, except they be sent?*

<margin>The function of preaching cannot be sold for a price on two grounds.</margin>
Therefore, the function of preaching cannot be sold for a price on two grounds: namely, because it is a spiritual thing, and because it is a divine delegation. This office is therefore included in the number of those spiritual things of which Christ said: *Freely you have received, freely give* <note>Matthew 10:8.</note>. Whence the **Gloss** <note>Standard medieval biblical commentary.</note> on 1 Timothy 5 regarding "the elders who rule well" says: It is a matter of necessity to receive that by which one lives; it is a matter of charity to provide it; yet the Gospel is not for sale so that one might preach for these things. Therefore, as we recently said regarding prayer, a preacher cannot hire out for a wage the very labor of preaching and the effort he spends in delivering the word, because that labor itself is a spiritual thing. He can only [receive] an honest maintenance...

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that while clergy should not attend services solely for attendance fees, doing so is not technically simony unless they view the payment as a "price" for the sacred act. He further clarifies that preaching cannot be sold for a wage because it is a direct spiritual gift and a divine commission, though preachers may accept support for their living expenses.</summary>

# Question VI of the Ninth Book

...to receive sustenance, both for the food necessary to support the labor of study, and for the expense of books. Nor does one contract the **taint of simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling spiritual things or church offices, named after Simon Magus from the New Testament.</note> if, when preaching is not strictly necessary, he prefers to sow the Word where he is better supported. Indeed, even if he refuses to preach where he does not expect to be provided with food, he commits no fault. However, scandal must always be avoided, especially by monks.

¶ The third part concerned the praises of the **divine offices** <note>The daily cycle of prayers and psalms recited by clergy.</note>, both for the living and the deceased: of which enough has been said. For a "price" is never lawful, but rather stipends for sustenance; and also other rights (as we have explained) as if a wage for labors which are not entirely necessary but pertain to ceremony. But the words of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whom Soto follows closely.</note> are nonetheless to be noted: namely, that it is not lawful to make a pact, nor to have the intention of receiving a purchase price. Hence, he says, that "negative" law would be illicit which stated that a funeral procession should by no means occur without a certain price; for by this, the possibility of such a ceremony being performed for free would be precluded. And thus it would have the appearance of an **exaction** <note>A forced or illegal demand for payment, often viewed as extortion in a religious context.</note>: which indeed, as we have said, would be much more absurd in the celebration of **Masses**. However, an "affirmative and conditional" law would not have the same absurdity. For example, if someone offers such an alms, let such a ceremony, which is not necessary, be provided for him. For a law of this kind would have the appearance of a **gratuitous retribution** <note>A gift given freely in return for another gift, rather than a commercial transaction.</note>.

<margin>Regarding the third argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the third argument, because it compared the hierarchical functions of **prelates** <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots.</note> with the knowledge of doctors and the counsel of advocates: the response is given through a distinction, since the reasoning is different. For prelates and other ecclesiastical superiors are obliged to administer their provinces by virtue of the power committed to them and by reason of the stipend established for their very sustenance. Therefore, those who receive anything beyond this for the use of that same power would be understood not so much to receive it for labors they owe for free, but rather to be selling the use of **spiritual grace**. Hence Saint Thomas concludes that it is not lawful for them to receive anything for any **dispensation** <note>A formal exemption from a church law, such as a marriage rule or a fast.</note>; neither for the fact that they commit their duties to others, nor for correction, nor for the fact that they do not correct someone. By the name of "dispensation," you should understand not only the relaxation of a law as the word commonly sounds, but also every spiritual administration. Therefore, to receive a price so that a subject may be granted a dispensation

<column-break/>

from the law is manifest simony: for to grant a dispensation for a cause pertains to spiritual governance, which is done through the grace of the **Holy Spirit**. For it belongs to the office of the pastor, of whom Paul says: *And He appointed others as pastors*; and therefore it ought to be done freely, just as correction and instruction. If, however, it is done without cause, it is iniquitous, and far worse because it is sold for a price. Nor indeed is there any pastor so mindless, from the least to the greatest, who does not understand this. But they paint those exactions made in dispensations with I know not what other color. For they call them **compositions** <note>original: "compositiones" – legal settlements or payments made to commute a penalty or obligation.</note>, and as it were, "commutations of the law": so that he who is exempt from the burden of a law or vow may undergo another—let them see to it themselves. But truly, to bargain for a price with a subject so that he is not corrected would be a more heinous crime: for instance, when a license is given to him to sin with impunity.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ Saint Thomas adds, however, that it is lawful for prelates to receive fixed **procurations** <note>original: "procurationes" – the provision of necessities (food and lodging) for a bishop and his retinue during an official visit.</note> while they visit their subjects. Not indeed as a price for correction—which is undoubtedly a spiritual thing—but as a due stipend. In this word, I observe two things for myself.

<margin>Stipends for visitations; those visiting in person do not have suitable sustenance from elsewhere.</margin>
First, that in truth the stipends for visitations are judged lawful because prelates ought to visit their flocks in person, so that they might "know the face of their cattle" and hear their voice, according to the word of Christ: 
> I am the Good Shepherd, and I know my sheep, and mine know me. <note>original: "Ego sum Pastor bonus, & cognosco oues meas, & cognoscunt me meæ." John 10:14.</note>

<margin>Those visiting in person, visit</margin>
For to send others who merely scrape together the payment was worthy of no reward. The second thing I would observe here is that, since stipends of this kind were established for the sake of sustenance, they seem able to be exacted with a very pure conscience precisely where **bishoprics** are not excessively wealthy; for where **tithes** <note>The tenth of produce or income given to the church.</note> abound, it is certainly not so safe.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
¶ Regarding the second part of the argument, which pertained to **knowledge** <note>original: "scientia" – scientific or scholarly knowledge.</note>, Saint Thomas gives a two-part response. For he says that one who has not undertaken an office by reason of which it is incumbent upon him to teach others can lawfully receive a price for his teaching: not as if he were selling truth or knowledge, but as if hiring out his labors. But for one upon whom that duty is incumbent by office, if he were to receive any price, he would be understood, he says, to be selling the truth: and therefore he would sin gravely. This passage of Saint Thomas will perhaps seem to some to stand against us: for in the preceding question, contrary to what many believe, we were striving to show that acquired sciences and arts can lawfully be taught for a price. For he says it is not lawful for him to receive...

# 770 F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

<margin>The mind of Saint Thomas is explained.</margin>
...a price for truth or knowledge, but acts as if hiring out his own labors. Yet, in truth, his view favors us rather than being contrary. First, he does not consider the doctrine of truth to be an entirely spiritual matter; otherwise, it would not even be lawful to hire out one's labor for it (as was said regarding sacraments, preaching, and prayers), but only to receive sustenance. Nevertheless, even a very wealthy teacher is permitted to hire out his labor for a just price. Furthermore, where the knowledge is more excellent, and the teacher more skilled and clear, those labors may be valued more dearly. Likewise, although it is not permitted to receive any price for telling the truth (as we said in Book 5, Question 8 regarding witnesses)—because since lying is a sin, no one is permitted to do anything but speak or teach the truth—nonetheless, for extracting that same truth from its principles, and subsequently discussing, elucidating, reading, and re-reading it, there is no doubt that it is lawful to receive a price. Indeed (as we said above), even if it could be done without any labor, it would be lawful to sell it. Just as if someone were to teach another to write or paint: because that is not the "spiritual" thing of which we speak—namely, that which we "received for free, so that we might give for free" <note>A reference to Matthew 10:8, often cited in debates about simony.</note>—but is spiritual only by reason of its subject matter. In fact, not even **Theology** <term>Theology: Here refers to the academic study of God and scripture as practiced in universities, rather than divine revelation itself.</term> is spiritual in this sense: for although the faith of the scriptures is a gift given freely, and the knowledge infused into the Apostles for preaching was also free (and thus it would have been a sin for them to sell it), nevertheless, the theology we learn in schools is acquired through human effort. The same must be judged regarding the counsel of **advocates** <note>Lawyers or legal representatives.</note>: where certainly no spirituality is violated, even if a very wealthy man provides counsel for a price in conducting cases. Indeed, even if he extorts a price from the poor, he commits no **simony** <term>Simony: The sin of buying or selling sacred things, named after Simon Magus.</term>, though he violates the precept of mercy. It is otherwise with **fraternal correction** <note>The practice of privately correcting a neighbor's sin out of charity.</note> and counsel given to relieve the sorrow of an afflicted person; for such duties, which are directed toward the salvation of the soul, are indeed spiritual and therefore must be bestowed for free. ¶ Regarding the second point of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note>, namely that he who is bound by office to teach cannot receive a price:

<margin>Hostiensis.</margin>
**Hostiensis** <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a famous expert in Canon Law.</note>, commenting on the chapter *Quia nonnullis* <note>Latin: "Because some"; a specific chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding masters and students.</note> concerning teachers, extends this to mean that no one who teaches for a public salary is permitted to demand any other private reward. However, this is stated without proof. For nothing prevents someone who is only bound to give one lecture from receiving a price for another. But what Saint Thomas says, he immediately demonstrates by example according to the tenor of the said chapter *Quia nonnullis*: namely, that where the church has a **canonry** <note>An office in a cathedral or collegiate church that provides a fixed income.</note> or a certain stipend decreed

<column-break/>

for a **chair** <note>A "cathedra" or professorship.</note>, the one who holds it is obliged to teach the poor for free. Nevertheless, one who acts to the contrary is not thereby marked with the stain of simony; however, someone who demands a price for the license he grants a teacher to lecture is ordered to be deprived of his **ecclesiastical benefit** <term>Ecclesiastical benefit (beneficium): A church office (like being a rector or canon) that comes with an income or property attached to it.</term>.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fourth argument, concerning entry into **religion** <note>Meaning entry into a religious order or monastery.</note>, there is a three-part response. First, it is established that for entry—that is, for the **profession of vows**—it is in no way lawful to demand or offer a price. Furthermore, the practice of the religious life is a spiritual thing, to which a prelate must therefore receive those who are willing freely and with gratitude, seeing as it is an established divine benefit. The texts in the **Canon Law** <note>Soto cites "Quam pio" and chapters from the sections "de regularibus" and "de simonia" in the Corpus Iuris Canonici.</note> declare this. Therefore, the spirituality through which simony is observed in entering religion is not to be judged by the fact that some religious live off tithes and ecclesiastical goods (for tithes can be applied to secular titles, for instance to kings or dukes for the defense of the church; besides the fact that there are religious who enjoy no such tithes or spiritual offerings). Rather, the reason for the spirituality consists in this: that the profession itself and the religious life are an institution of Christ, so that those willing to follow Him may be admitted for free.

¶ The second assertion is that where a monastery is poor <note>Latin: "tenue," meaning thin or meager in resources.</note> and insufficient to support such a large number, it is no simony to receive something for food and clothing. We can place a similar example in **matrimony**. For regarding marriage insofar as it is a **sacrament**, a husband can receive nothing from his wife; yet he may accept a dowry to sustain the burdens of the marriage. From this, a third consequence follows: that it is not simony if a woman is received more willingly among **nuns** <note>Latin: "moniales."</note> because she, out of her own devotion, has bestowed generous alms upon the monastery. Just as, conversely, it is lawful for nuns, by bestowing temporal benefits, to entice secular women to devotion so that they might take up the nun's habit—provided they cannot give a "price" to purchase such a religious institution.

<margin>The first doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second conclusion, small doubts arise. First, whether it is simoniacal to demand a price when the monastery is wealthy enough to support the persons being received.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
For there is an argument for the affirmative side: since such an exaction is just for no other reason than the sustenance of the nuns, where that is available from elsewhere, it appears that a price for entry into religion...

# Question VII of the Ninth Book.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
...of religion to be demanded. This argument indeed compels almost all the doctors of Canon Law—as can be seen in the works of Sylvester, under the entry for **simony**, section 15 <note>Reference to Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio, known as Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), a prominent Dominican theologian and canonist.</note>—toward the same affirmative conclusion. Nevertheless, the answer is that the wealth of a monastery has absolutely no bearing on making an act simony in a rich house that was not simony in a poor one. The reason is quite clear: simony takes its character from its object—namely, because a spiritual thing is being sold, such as the religious profession itself and the place within the order. If, however, care is taken that money is received only for sustenance, even if the monastery does not strictly need that support, it may indeed be the sin of avarice, but it is not simony. But this much must be admitted: in such a case, simony is *presumed*. For if the means of sustenance are already abundant, it is presumed that the money is being received as a price for entry, as Sylvester rightly proves in that passage.

¶ For this reason, very wealthy monasteries that refuse to receive the poor without a price—and a large one at that—certainly cannot do so without causing scandal. This is especially true when they appear to receive money not for maintenance, but for other reasons: namely, because a girl is not of sufficiently "noble blood," or is marked by some other infamy or physical deformity. To value such things by a price for admission to a convent can hardly be cleansed of the stain of simony; and this is especially true if the community demands higher prices simply to make its own grandeur and magnificence more illustrious.

# QUESTION SEVEN,
## On Simony in the Acquisition of Priesthoods and Dignities.

<margin>Saint Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica II-II, Question 100, Article 4.</margin>

# ARTICLE I.
## Whether it is lawful to receive a price for priesthoods and other prebends attached to spiritual things.

AFTER DISCUSSING spiritual matters—namely the sacraments and other spiritual actions—it follows that we should examine the nature of **simony** <term>Simony: The sin of buying or selling sacred things or ecclesiastical offices, named after Simon Magus from the Book of Acts.</term> regarding priesthoods, **prebends** <term>Prebend: A portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon or member of the chapter as a stipend.</term>, and the dignities which

<column-break/>

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
are devoted to those same functions. For it appears that the trade of these offices is not defiled by any stain of simony. If buying or selling these were simoniacal specifically because they are joined to spiritual actions, then by that logic it would be unlawful to sell any temporal thing at all. Since all temporal things in the world were created for the sake of spiritual things, everything would be considered "annexed" to the spiritual.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: sacred vessels and consecrated vestments are numbered among those things connected to the spiritual. However, it is lawful to sell a chalice or sacred vestments to meet the needs of the Church. Therefore, it should also be lawful for the Supreme Pontiff, when the Church is pressed by grave necessity, to grant a bishopric or any other priesthood for a price, provided it is granted to a worthy person.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third, it is argued: Among things annexed to the spiritual are listed the right of burial, the **right of patronage** <term>Right of Patronage (ius patronatus): The right of a person (a patron) to nominate a candidate for a vacant ecclesiastical benefice or office.</term>, and, according to the ancients, even the right of primogeniture (birthright), because at that time the priestly right was joined to it. But Abraham bought from Ephron a double cave for a burial place, as is recorded in Genesis 23; and Jacob bought the right of primogeniture from his brother for a miserable dish of lentils, as is read in chapter 25 of the same book. Furthermore, the right of patronage passes along with a sold property and is granted as a fief. Likewise, tithes have been granted to certain kings and soldiers, from whom they can in turn be redeemed. Finally, prelates retain for a time the fruits of the prebends they bestow on others—as the Pope does with half of the **annates** <term>Annates: The first year's revenue of an ecclesiastical benefice, paid as a tax to the papal treasury.</term>—even if those prebends are annexed to spiritual things. Therefore, the trade of priesthoods does not fall into the vice of simony.

¶ On the contrary, however, stands the canon of the Supreme Pontiff Paschal <note>original: "canon Paschalis Pontificis summi." Likely referring to Paschal II.</note> in the Second Part of the Decretum, Question 3, the chapter beginning "If anyone should object." His words are: "Whoever sells one of them, without which the other cannot be obtained, leaves neither unsold. Therefore, let no one buy a church, or a prebend, or anything ecclesiastical, as it is something without which a spiritual action cannot proceed." So it is stated there.

<margin>A distinction.</margin>
The question is answered with two conclusions, after first establishing a distinction. For it happens in two ways that something temporal is annexed to the spiritual. In one way, as that which depends on the spiritual: such as holding ecclesiastical priesthoods, which is joined to the clerical office. Concerning this type of annexation, the first conclusion is established.

### [Book IX, Question VII, Continued]

# F. Domingo de Soto, on Justice and Right

<margin>
First conclusion.
</margin>
That which is connected to spiritual things in this way is by no means saleable for a price. Indeed, such a sale would be simoniacal <note>Simony is the act of buying or selling spiritual things, named after Simon Magus from the Acts of the Apostles.</note>. The reason is clear according to the tenor of the cited canon. For since a temporal thing of this kind does not pass to another without the spiritual thing, when the temporal is sold, the spiritual is sold along with it. ¶ In another way, a temporal thing is joined to spiritual things insofar as they are ordered toward those spiritual things: such as the **right of patronage** <note>original: "ius patronatus"; the right of a layperson or institution to nominate a candidate for a church office.</note>: since its duty is to present clerics for ecclesiastical priesthoods. It also includes the vessels and vestments destined for sacred use, concerning which the following conclusion is applied.

<margin>
Final conclusion.
</margin>
It is not simony to sell those things which are referred to spiritual things in this way, provided they are not sold insofar as they are sacred, but insofar as they are physical objects.

<margin>
Proof.
</margin>
This is proved by the opposite case: for since these temporal things do not presuppose anything spiritual, they can pass into the ownership of another who possesses no spiritual status: as when a layman buys a villa to which a right of patronage is annexed. And if a chalice is melted down into a mass of silver and loses its form, it can pass into the ownership of another, who can fashion a secular vessel from that same mass.

<margin>
A Doubt.
</margin>
¶ Regarding the first conclusion, a doubt emerges, both because its reasoning is somewhat obscure and because it does not seem sufficiently solid. Therefore, for a clearer explanation, it is asked by what law the buying and selling of **prebends** <note>A prebend is a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church, granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note> is forbidden as simoniacal: whether by ecclesiastical law alone, or indeed by divine law. For although in Question 5 regarding simony in general we debated a similar question—where it was decided that the sale of sacramental actions is simony by divine law—nonetheless, concerning the trade of prebends and dignities, it is not so well established. It appears indeed that simony of this kind is forbidden only by human and papal law: for these priesthoods are nothing other than the fruits of **tithes**, which are purely temporal things. Therefore, notwithstanding that they are annexed to spiritualities, they can be separated from that spirituality and sold, just as the material of a chalice is saleable, provided the consecration itself is not sold. Furthermore, even if the substance of tithes is dedicated to spiritual functions by divine law, the specific amount (the "quota") is nonetheless established by human law, as shown above. Therefore, if a priesthood is worth a hundred units, the Pope could sell the right to half and leave the other half to the Church.
¶ Regarding this question, the interpreters of canon law are divided into various opinions, which—

<column-break/>

**Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>, in his *Quodlibets* <note>A collection of "quodlibetal" questions—theological debates on any topic proposed.</note>, book 1, question 9, reduces them to three. The first is the most extreme: that simony of this kind is entirely a matter of human law. This originated from a gloss on the chapter *Ex parte*, "On the office of the delegate," which Antonius de Butrio and the Cardinal <note>Francesco Zabarella (1360–1417), an influential canonist known as "the Cardinal."</note> approve in chapter 1, "On simony."

<margin>
Cajetan.
First opinion.
The Gloss.
Antonius de Butrio.
The Cardinal.
Second opinion.
</margin>
The second opinion is the other extreme: that all such simony is prohibited by divine law, which **St. Thomas [Aquinas]** seems to teach here. The third is that of **Panormitanus** <note>Nicola de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer.</note> in the same chapter 1, "On simony," and again in his *Repetitio* on the chapter *Extirpandae*, "On prebends." There he says that the sale of a prebend to which the administration of orders or the exercise of the **keys** <note>The "power of the keys" refers to the authority of the Church to forgive sins or exercise jurisdiction.</note> is annexed is simony by divine law, because the thing to which it is annexed is spiritual by that same law. However, the sale of a prebend which is not devoted to such sacred orders is only simony by **positive law** <note>Human-made law, such as church canons or civil statutes, as opposed to divine or natural law.</note>, such as those destined for the administration of hospitals. Cajetan differs from this third opinion of Panormitanus only in this: he says not only does a prebend annexed to the exercise of a sacred order or the "keys" involve simony by divine law if sold, but also any prebend annexed to any clerical status below sacred orders—for instance, the **first tonsure** <note>The ritual cutting of a candidate's hair, marking their entry into the clergy before they receive higher orders.</note> or minor orders. His reason is that the clerical state itself is of divine law, since every clerical office consists in spiritual acts, even the first tonsure.

<margin>
St. Thomas.
Third opinion of Panormitanus.
</margin>
¶ I judge, however, that each of these opinions needs to be weighed on its own merits. First, regarding Cajetan’s claim that every clerical state up to the first tonsure is of divine law: this is not very probable, and the contrary is more likely. Indeed, it is certain to many (as debated in Book 4 of the *Sentences*) that these are not of the essence of the priesthood. But nevertheless, it does not follow from this that Panormitanus is correct in saying that no sale of a prebend (unless devoted to major orders or the keys) is simoniacal by divine law. Rather, I would believe with Cajetan that it is sufficient for the prebend to be annexed to a simple clerical state. I do not agree with his specific reason, but rather because although minor orders are sacred by positive law, selling the right of a prebend assigned to them is against the **law of nature**, and thus divine law. This is like what was said above regarding the chalice and the altar: although these things are sacred by positive [human] law, they cannot be sold for a higher price because of their consecration without it being simony against divine law. The first opinion, that of the cited gloss, has no force to the contrary.

<margin>
Not all clerical states up to the first tonsure are of divine law.
Cajetan's opinion is proved.
</margin>

### Book Nine, Question VII.

...holds: for in that chapter no mention is made of simony, but it only states that if a certain Archdeacon wished to renounce his **prebend** <note>A prebend is a portion of a cathedral or collegiate church's revenues used as a stipend for a canon.</note>, it should be given to a specific person. From this, the **gloss** <note>A "gloss" is a marginal or interlinear commentary on legal or scriptural texts, often treated as authoritative.</note> infers that if he renounced it in favor of another, when he otherwise would not have renounced it, it would be simony according to
<margin>The double error of the gloss.</margin>
**positive law** <note>original: "iure positiuo"; law established by human authority, such as the Pope or a Council, rather than natural or divine law.</note>. In this gloss, there is a double error. First, it asserts something false: indeed, provided it is done with the consent of the Pope, it is not simony, for such is the universal custom. Second, to infer from this that the sale of a prebend is simony only by positive law has no appearance of truth—though not even this is actually contained in the gloss.
<margin>The foundation of the previous conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to declare the force of the reasoning behind this previous conclusion, let us get to its heart: its foundation is that prebends and priesthoods are established from the fruits of **tithes** <note>original: "decimarum"; a tenth part of agricultural produce or income paid to support the church.</note>. Moreover, tithes are commanded by divine and natural law for no other reason than to be the stipends and nourishment for clerics in exchange for their spiritual functions. For this reason, to confer a prebend upon someone is not merely to confer the fruits of it—for fruits of that kind could be sold to a layman—but to confer the **right to tithes**. This right is certainly Ecclesiastical, and therefore spiritual, since by its very institution tithes are required because of an Ecclesiastical office. And this is the meaning of the cited Papal canon: namely, that when a prebend is sold, the spiritual thing itself is sold—that is, the clerical right itself.
<margin>An objection.</margin>
¶ Now, if an opponent were to challenge us thus: at the very least, for one who is already a priest, it should not be simony to buy a priesthood. This is because he does not acquire the holy orders to which the prebend is attached, as he already possesses them. And let us suppose it is a prebend that does not have the "care of souls" <note>An office without "care of souls" (sinecura) did not require the priest to perform pastoral duties like confession or baptism for a specific parish.</note>, lest you say he is then acquiring that spirituality. Likewise, a prebend is sometimes granted by dispensation to a boy before he is ordained; therefore, nothing spiritual passes with it, and thus it
<margin>The solution.</margin>
can be sold. The answer (as has been said) is that the very right of seeking tithes is spiritual. Therefore, whether the person to whom it is conferred is already a cleric or is to become one, a spiritual thing is
<margin>A scruple.</margin>
always being sold. ¶ But what about the land attached to a prebend? For that land is not part of the tithes.
<margin>The solution.</margin>
The answer is that it cannot be sold along with that Ecclesiastical title, such that the buyer could receive those same fruits by clerical right. It can, however, be separated from that sacred title and sold, just as the material of a chalice can be sold once the
<margin>Regarding the first argument.</margin>
consecration is removed. ¶ Hence, the first of the previous arguments had no strength; for to buy a

<column-break/>

prebend is not only to buy the fruits, but the spiritual right.
<margin>Regarding the second argument.</margin>
As for the latter argument regarding the "quota" or amount of tithes—which seems to be established by Ecclesiastical law alone—the answer is (and this solution should be noted): that a Papal decree of this kind is not in itself something distinct from divine law (which commands the substance of tithes), but is the determination and moderation of it. Just as Ecclesiastical precepts regarding the celebration of this or that feast, or regarding annual confession, are nothing other than determinations of divine law. Therefore, not only is it simony against divine law to sell the right to tithes in its entirety with the clerical title, but also to sell it as a specific amount. ¶ However, we do not deny that some simony exists by positive law: namely, that which is not forbidden because it is evil, but is "evil because it is forbidden" <note>A classic legal distinction: "malum in se" (evil in itself) vs "malum prohibitum" (evil because prohibited by law).</note>, as the same gloss holds. For example, when a prebend is not attached to a clerical duty, but to other offices, such as service in hospitals, or to churchwardens <note>original: "sacrorum edituis"; those in charge of sacred vessels and the building.</note>, or a church steward. As we declared in Question 5, Article 4, these kinds of duties and offices are not properly spiritual; rather, their sale is inhibited solely by Papal law.
¶ Concerning those prebends which they call **Préstamos** <note>original: "Præstameras"; a type of Spanish ecclesiastical benefice, often granted to students or secular officials, which Soto is arguing must still be treated as spiritual.</note>, I hear some hesitate as to whether they are purely spiritual. Yet there is no reason to bring this into dispute, since they are not like pensions which are conferred without a title. Indeed, they have a true title. And since that title is not secular, it follows that it is clerical, and therefore spiritual.
<margin>The prebends called Préstamos are spiritual and carry the obligation to recite the Divine Office.</margin>
For what they say—that these are withdrawn from the common pile of tithes solely for the sake of study—has no foundation in law, nor is the truth of this clear; it is merely devised by some. Therefore, in a doubtful matter, one must stand by the common law of tithes: namely, that a title of this kind is spiritual. For this reason, I cannot doubt that such a title obliges the holder to the performance of the **Divine Office** <note>The daily cycle of prayers (psalms, lessons, hymns) required of clergy.</note>; and thus, its purchase and sale undoubtedly gives rise to simony. It is otherwise for other secular titles, such as those that secular princes and kings have toward tithes, as will be clear in the following article.
¶ Finally, at the end of this question, it must be committed to memory that simony only sprouts up when something is conferred as if it were a price. For as **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> rightly says in his *Summary* under the word "simony," there are many reasons and ways a temporal thing is customarily given back when a spiritual thing is received—namely, by way of the sustenance of Ecclesiastical ministers, which we said above is necessary.

<summary>Soto argues that selling church offices (prebends) or the right to collect tithes is simony by divine law, not just human law, because these funds are intrinsically tied to spiritual duties. He distinguishes these from secular administrative roles in the church where simony is only a matter of human legislation.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

...matter, or by way of a generous honor to return or earn **grace** <note>original: "gratiam"; here meaning a favor or a state of goodwill rather than divine grace</note>: or perhaps as if by law due to a praiseworthy custom: and by other means besides, no one commits **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred or spiritual things, named after Simon Magus from the Book of Acts.</note>, unless something is paid back by way of a price. Nor, conversely, is the one who confers something spiritual a simoniac if he expects some retribution by any of these other methods. Indeed, even if he demands what is owed to him from a praiseworthy and established custom before he confers the spiritual gift—in order to avoid a lawsuit which he fears he would later have to pursue to recover it—he
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
contracts no stain of simony. ¶ Finally, let there be a final **doubt** <note>original: "dubitatio"; a standard scholastic method of posing a counter-argument for investigation.</note>: whether it is at least permitted to give a temporal gift for a **prebend** <note>An income-generating office in a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> in order to "redeem vexation" <note>To pay someone to stop harassing or blocking one's legal rights.</note>. For it is argued on the affirmative side from a previous decision, in which it was asserted that it is not simony to offer a price to redeem the harassment regarding the baptism of a small child who is just about to breathe his last. Since a **sacrament** <note>A religious rite regarded as an outward sign of inward grace, such as baptism.</note> has a greater degree of spirituality than a prebend, it seems that it should also be permitted for the office itself.
<margin>The solution.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is answered with a distinction: "redeeming vexation" can happen in two ways. In one way, as we said, when someone hinders you by force or fraud from seeking a prebend: as if someone were to detain you by force so that you could not go to compete for a **canonry** <note>The office or "stall" of a canon in a cathedral.</note>; or if you feared someone would spread false rumors about you to block your election. It is permitted to redeem this with a price, since anyone who is fit for the office has such a "sought right." In another way, if someone thought they excelled other candidates in dignity, and therefore thought they suffered an injury to their honor from the electors if they were not chosen, and for that reason offered a price to the electors or another intermediary. This is undoubtedly not permitted: for even if everyone has the right to seek the office, they do not have an equal right to be elected. Rather, this must remain in the free will of the electors. Therefore, let every wise man beware of using this "cloak" as a pretext; for it would be a true spiritual purchase. It is otherwise, however, regarding baptism in extreme necessity, in which case the child has a right to be baptized because of the necessity of the sacrament. Truly, no one has such an "acquired right" in respect to a prebend. Furthermore, no one is not deceived when judging their own fitness. Nor would it be permitted to promise a pension upon a future prebend, even if he declared it was with the consent of the Pope: for all of this would be to buy a spiritual thing with a temporal one. It is different in cases of **permutations** <note>The legal exchange of one ecclesiastical office for another.</note> or resignations.

<column-break/>

For I can indeed allow a pension upon a benefit which you resign in my favor: as will be clear in the immediately following article.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
The dilution of the first main argument appears somewhat obscure in **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for scholastic theologians like Soto.</note>; for he grants that all temporal possessions can be attached to spiritual things as their end. For just as the body was created for the sake of the soul, so temporal things were created for the sake of the spiritual. He concludes from this that they can be sold, but not in terms of the order they have toward spiritual things. This is to say: just as any layperson can sell his goods because he does not sell them insofar as they refer to spiritual things, but insofar as they are taken for human use; so also priests can sell the fruits of their **tithes** <note>The tenth of produce or income given to the church.</note>. However, to sell the "order" to spiritual things—namely, the right to receive tithes insofar as they are assigned to a clerical function—is simony. ¶ In the same way, it is
<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
answered to the second: that sacred vessels, insofar as they are material things, can be sold; but the **consecration** <note>The act of making a thing holy or dedicated to God.</note> itself, by no means. If, however, they are sold for profane uses for the necessity of the Church or the poor: then they ought to be either broken or melted down, so that they cease to be sacred. But if one Church sells to another for sacred use, it can indeed be done without breaking them, provided that nothing is received for the consecration. And the same applies to vestments. For by tearing them they can lose their "form" and then be sold, even for secular uses. ¶ Truly, the third argument
<margin>To the third argument.</margin>

consequently the mark of simony. ¶ But truly, since there was not...
