### Book Nine, Question VII.

<margin>The reason for doubting.</margin>
Since the consecration of temples then was not such as it is now, the doubt remains whether among us it is **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred or spiritual things.</note> to sell plots in a cemetery for burying the dead. Indeed, it appears to be prohibited by law in the chapters *Abolendæ* (on burials) and *Qui in Ecclesia* (on simony). This is confirmed by reason: for the right to bury the dead pertains to religion. If, therefore, for that reason it was a crime for the pagans to sell graves, it will be so for us by an even greater reason, as we are the ones who consecrate or bless cemeteries. Indeed, it appears to be simony by divine and natural law, for by that same law, religion is a virtue.

<margin>The Response.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, it is answered through this distinction: Just as the office of burying the dead, regarding that which is a matter of necessity, cannot be sold without the stain of simony (as was established above for the reason just given), so also to demand a price for a necessary place in the cemetery would be simony. For instance, if the clergy were unwilling to bury a dead person in any sacred place unless something were paid for the ground: for surely the reasoning is the same for the office of burial as it is for the necessary soil, since it is a Christian practice that corpses be stored in a cemetery. And this is what **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> says was simoniacal even among the pagans. But in truth, if someone desires a more honorable place in the Church as a matter of non-necessary **pomp** <note>Used here to mean outward display or status.</note>, it is not entirely to be condemned as simony if something is demanded for that place for the building-fund of the Church—just as we said above regarding superfluous displays.

<margin>The opinion of Hostiensis is refuted.</margin>
Hence, where such a custom flourishes and has now been accepted as law, a designated sum of money can be requested without **scandal** <note>An action that leads others into sin or diminishes the reputation of the Church.</note>. For this reason, the opinion of **Hostiensis** <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a famous expert in Canon Law.</note> on the chapter *Audivimus* (on simony), which denies that a pact of this kind is permitted, is not necessary. Because in truth, if nothing is received for the consecration or blessing of the place, but the land is sold just like the material of a **chalice** <note>The cup used in the Eucharist; the metal itself has a market value separate from its sacred use.</note>, nothing spiritual is sold there, but rather a human and temporal honor—provided that scandal is avoided. Just as places in the Church have been accustomed to be designated for certain lineages as a matter of honor for sitting. Although it cannot be denied that these titles of honor, when too greatly desired in sacred places, possess an ugly vanity.

¶ To the cited chapters, however, it is answered that they prohibit nothing other than that which is of the necessity of burial being sold—namely, by a forced agreement so that one who has not bought the land may not be buried.

<margin>Jacob, by buying the birthright from</margin>
¶ Regarding the history of **Jacob** <note>The biblical patriarch who purchased his brother's birthright for a bowl of stew (Genesis 25).</note>, it is answered that he by no means committed simony, because it had been divinely granted to him

<column-break/>

<margin>Esau, did not commit simony.</margin>
the right of **birthright** <note>The status of the firstborn, which included a double inheritance and, in the patriarchal age, the role of family priest.</note>, and even of the priesthood, according to that passage in Malachi 2: "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated." But **Esau**, from whom this same mystery was hidden, sinned by selling it, according to the Apostle in Hebrews 12: "Lest there be any fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright."

<margin>The first objection.</margin>
¶ However, this response does not remove every doubt from the reader. For first, it is not established that such a mystery, which was covered from Esau, was open to Jacob.

<margin>The second.</margin>
Furthermore, even if it had been known to him, he is not thereby cleared of fault: both because of the inhumanity of refusing to offer a dish to his needy brother, and because he induced Esau to sin, since Esau was not (in the manner of a victim of **usury** <note>Lending money at interest, often considered exploitative in this period.</note>) ready to sell. Indeed, since by the law of nature Esau possessed the birthright in good faith, he was in no way harassing Jacob; therefore, it is not a legitimate excuse to say that Jacob was "redeeming his own harassment."

<margin>To the first objection.</margin>
¶ To the first of these, it is answered that it is gathered from the sacred text that the mystery had become known to **Rebecca** <note>Jacob and Esau's mother, who received a prophecy that the elder son would serve the younger.</note>, either by her husband or by another divine means. Otherwise, she would never have persuaded her younger son of it, saying: "Let this curse be upon me, my son." By which reasoning Jacob also understood the same thing. And therefore, he used his own right. For in saying "Sell to me," he meant the same as "Give what is mine." Nor was he bound to reveal the mystery to his brother, because then Esau would not have yielded to his brotherly persuasion. Wherefore, although Esau himself was not prepared to sell, Jacob is not for that reason judged to have induced him; for he who uses his own right induces no one. Therefore, since the other possessed what belonged to someone else, Jacob is rightly said to have been harassed by him, since no other way was open to him to recover what was his own, and thus Jacob redeemed his harassment. Besides the fact that Esau was moved not by necessity but by gluttony for the **lentils** <note>Referring to the "mess of pottage" or stew for which Esau traded his birthright.</note>; by which reasoning Jacob is defended from the charge of inhumanity.

<margin>Selling the right of patronage is simony.</margin>
¶ Regarding the **right of patronage** <note>term: The privilege of a lay person to nominate a candidate for a church office (like a parish priest).</note>, as is clear in the same title elsewhere, it is to be judged just like a spiritual matter: so much so that it is simony to sell it by itself for a price. But it passes along with the villa or castle to which it is attached. Wherefore, he who sells a villa can by no means demand a higher price on account of the right of patronage.

<margin>The fruits of tithes can be sold.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other branch concerning **tithes** <note>term: A portion (usually 10%) of agricultural produce or income given to the church.</note>, it must first be noted that two things are considered in them: namely, the fruits and the proceeds, which are purely temporal things. And therefore, as has been said, they can be sold, as is evident in the case of **tax collectors** <note>original: "publicanis"; agents who contracted the right to collect taxes or tithes for a fixed fee.</note> who purchase those same fruits for a set price. And this is what Saint Thomas says the Pope granted to secular lords and princes.

# BOOK IV. Domingo de Soto, on Justice and Law

## By what reasoning the "thirds" were granted to our King as a subsidy for wars against the infidels.

Secondly, it must be noted that we have considered the spiritual right of requesting them <note>Referring to the "thirds" (tertiæ), a portion of the tithes traditionally granted by the Papacy to the Spanish Crown for the Reconquista and subsequent defense of the faith.</note>; and that this cannot be granted to laypeople, because it is a priestly right.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
¶ Against this, however, there is an argument that the King and any secular persons who hold tithes of this kind—such as those who possess the goods of the **Templars** <note>The Knights Templar, a military order whose properties were often redistributed to the crown or other orders after their dissolution.</note>—have the same right to request them as the clerics themselves. For the King takes the "thirds" from the common heap of tithes, and other lords take the whole tithes just as bishops do. Indeed, it is they who assign the designated portion to their own parish.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
One can respond to this in two ways. First, that they receive them in the name of the **Pope**. Second, more fittingly to the matter, that when the Pope adjudicates a portion of the tithes to princes, he establishes them under a secular title—for instance, for the sake of defending the Church. And therefore, princes indeed have the right of requesting them, but not a spiritual right (which **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian.</note> alone denies can be granted to laypeople), but rather a secular right, which they themselves can sell to others and distribute or alienate just like other secular goods.

<margin>Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ Finally, regarding the last part of the response, the solution of Saint Thomas must be weighed: namely, that if the Pope, before the conferring of **benefices** <note>A church office that provides an income or "fruit" to its holder.</note>, has ordained that a portion be taken away for his own just maintenance or for other pious uses, he can rightly do so. But note the word "ordained"—that is, established by a common and equitable law for a just cause. For certainly, if he did this at his whim without a law, it would be suspicious. And by this reasoning, the law accepted in **Spain** and established in several other provinces dictates that from the "annates"—that is, from the time when one obtains a priesthood—he must pay half the fruits of that year. And he could, if necessity pressed (as we said above), retain for himself "tithes of tithes," provided that by that reasoning all other exactions and compositions were extinguished. But this must be especially noted, which Saint Thomas adds: "if indeed," he says, "he who confers a benefice requires something to be presented to him from the fruits of that benefice beyond the previously established law, it is the same as if he were demanding a gift from him; and therefore, it is not free from the vice of **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred or spiritual things.</note>."

<margin>To whom.</margin>
I strictly observe this opinion for the confirmation of our own, which we declared in Book 3 regarding **pensions**. For just as the Pope cannot enjoin pensions for himself, so neither can he for others, except as a stipend for office and service, whether spiritual or secular, which

<column-break/>

is beneficial to the Church.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But if anyone to the contrary argues thus: Whatever can be conferred upon another by the Pope's grant, he is able to apply to himself, since he himself is the dispenser of the goods of the Church. Moreover, one who is exchanging or resigning a position can, by the Pope's authority, retain a pension for himself; therefore, the Pope can also adjudicate the same for himself. The response is that a fallacy lies hidden in the argument: for although a pension may be granted to one exchanging or resigning by the authority of the **Pontiff**, the cause is not the same for the Pontiff himself to retain it. Since he himself is not the "master" of the **prebend** <note>An endowment for a church official, usually attached to a cathedral.</note> like the one who exchanges or resigns, but only the dispenser; he must therefore interpose his authority for a just cause.

---

### ARTICLE II.

-> Whether the exchange of prebends can be done without simony. <-

The exchange <note>original: "permutatio"</note> of prebends is akin to the sale of them; and therefore it is asked whether it can be done without simony. For an argument is made from the negative side.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
First, from the **Gloss** <note>A standard marginal commentary on canon law.</note> cited above, in the chapter *ex parte* 1, "on the office of the delegate," where it is held that if anyone resigns a priesthood for the sake of another, not being otherwise about to resign, simony is committed against human law. Since, therefore, all exchanges are made by that pact, they savor of simony.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: if exchanges of this kind were permitted by law, it would follow that it would be lawful—when a smaller prebend is exchanged for a fatter one—to retain a pension on the fatter one equal to the amount by which it exceeds the other. That this is false is shown thus: it would then equally follow that if one position had no **fruits** <note>Incomes or revenues produced by a church office.</note> but only a personal title, while the other abounded in fruits, an exchange could be made by paying an amount of money equal to the value of those riches. For what is permitted for a part, there is no reason to forbid for the whole; and yet this contract clearly seems to be the purchase of a prebend.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly and most importantly, it is argued: If such exchanges were in harmony with the law, it would follow that pensions of this kind could be valued and redeemed with counted money—just as an annual pension of 10 **ducats** <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe.</note> might be redeemed with 80 or 100 in cash. If this conclusion is true, it opens the door to selling priesthoods.

¶ To the contrary is the chapter...

### Book Nine, Question VII.

The chapter <note>original: "cap. quæsitum"</note> regarding the **exchange of things** <note>original: "de rerum permut." (De rerum permutatione)</note> states that exchanges involving a pact are forbidden only when done without the bishop's license. However, the bishop is granted the faculty to perform them, which certainly would not be granted if such an exchange were inherently **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling sacred or spiritual things, named after Simon Magus from the New Testament.</note>.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Regarding the question, a response is given in three conclusions following the number of arguments. **The First Conclusion:** The resignation of a **prebend** <note>A portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman (canon) as a stipend.</note> into the hands of a legitimate **Bishop** <note>original: "Antistitis"</note> in favor of another designated person, and not otherwise, carries no reason of simony—neither by divine law nor human law—provided no other pact intervenes, whether it is done by way of exchange or by way of simple renunciation. We asserted this conclusion above against the cited **gloss** <note>An explanatory note or commentary on a legal text.</note>. If you were to interpret the gloss as meaning this applies when the renunciation or exchange happens without the license of the Pope or Prelate, it would then be pointless, as we said in Question 5. For since no one can give up a prebend except into the hands of the prelate (whose role it is to confer **benefices** <note>An ecclesiastical office that provides a living or income.</note>) nor can a person adjudge it to another by private authority, such an act would not be simony—unless perhaps in the mind—because it would have no effect. However, it is clearly evident that renouncing with that condition is not simony; for since the task of conferring priesthoods falls to the prelate, he is forbidden by no law from allowing it to be placed at his discretion, should he wish to confer it upon Peter. If he does not wish to do so, the one who legally possesses it simply does not renounce it.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The Second Conclusion:** To exchange prebends with a pact is simony, unless the pact includes the phrase "with the consent of the **Pope**" <note>original: "Pontificis"</note>. For example, if two men agree on an exchange, and the one with the smaller prebend promises a **pension** <note>An annual payment carved out of the church office's income.</note> to the other, but they only report a simple exchange to the Pope and he does not grant that same pension, it is the most blatant simony—and yet, it is very frequent among the unlearned <note>original: "idiotas"</note>. Likewise, it is simony if someone renounces not by way of exchange, but simply in favor of another, without revealing to the Prelate the pact for a pension that intervened between them. This, however, is simony by **positive law** <note>Laws created by human authority (like the Church), as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>; for exchanging prebends while retaining a pension is not prohibited by divine law, but by papal law, as is clear in the chapter *Ad quæstiones* regarding the exchange of things. But it cannot be done without the consent of the prelate, as is clear there and in the cited chapter *Quæsitum*. Therefore, as long as the Pope does not grant that pension, it is regarded as the "price" of the exchange. Accordingly, I would truly believe that such a conferral of office is not valid, even if it is done by a Pope who is ignorant of the secret pact.

<column-break/>

For if a pact has intervened against divine law—namely, that someone pays money for such a resignation—then not even the Pope could grant a dispensation without fault for the resignation to be done in such a manner. Therefore, anyone who obtained a prebend in that way would become **unfit** <note>original: "inhabilis"</note> to possess it, unless afterward, the pact having been treated as if it never existed, the Pope (who alone has the power) rendered him suitable and capable again.

<margin>No prelate lower than the Pope is able to establish pensions.</margin>
Add to this that, as is the Roman custom, no prelate lower than the Pope has the power to establish pensions, neither in exchanges nor in simple renunciations. However, that pacts for such pensions can be made in exchanges with the assent of the Pope is expressly held in the cited chapter *Ad quæstiones*.

<margin>In the exchange of prebends, no account should be taken of their dignities.</margin>
¶ There is, however, an excess that must be avoided in a Christian manner. For I hear that in exchanges of this kind, people estimate not only the quantity of the fruits <note>The income or produce generated by the land or office.</note> but also the honor and **dignity** <note>High-ranking offices like archdeacon or dean.</note> of the priesthood itself. For instance, when an **archdeaconry** or a **deanery** of a famous church is exchanged for a simple prebend, even if the incomes are equal, an additional pension is demanded for the sake of the "dignity." I do not see how this can be done, since dignity is a spiritual thing. In the aforementioned chapter, it is expressly cautioned that the exchange of dignities should not be mixed with the compensation of fruits; rather, a priesthood should be exchanged simply for a priesthood, and a dignity for a dignity, without any repayment of money. Separately, the poorer fruits may be compensated to reach the equality of the richer ones.

<margin>It is unjust to establish all the fruits as a pension for priesthoods that have an annexed service.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, I do not know who could approve of establishing all the fruits as a pension, especially in priesthoods that have an annexed service, and most of all in those with the **cure of souls** <note>original: "curatis" (parish priests responsible for the spiritual care of a congregation).</note>. This is not only because it is provided by law that a pension should not exceed a third part of the fruits, but because it opposes divine and natural law that anyone should be bound to service without any stipend. Therefore, I consider it a lesser absurdity for someone to retain two priesthoods with the care of souls than for him to leave one while retaining all its fruits. For he who has two can visit both alternately and distribute alms to his parishioners; but he who plunders a benefice of its fruits causes the one who holds the title to be unable to care for souls or give alms. For since he is forced to seek his living elsewhere, how can he attend to his duty?

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ Regarding the third part of the question, which was touched upon in the third argument—namely, concerning the **redemption of pensions**—doctors of law hold varying opinions. For **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and cardinal.</note>, in his *Opuscula* of 16 responses...

# Brother Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Major.</margin> Question 10 generally affirms that perpetual pensions can be redeemed with a sum of money; however, other more recent authors, including John Major <note>John Major (1467–1550) was a highly influential Scottish philosopher and theologian known for his works on logic and ethics.</note> in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 25, Question 5), deny this entirely. This variety of opinions arises from a difference in their underlying principles. For Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a leading Catholic theologian and cardinal, famous for his commentaries on Thomas Aquinas.</note> believes that a pension is purely temporal in nature, referring only to the "fruits" <note>In canon law, "fruits" refers to the income or produce generated by a church office or property.</note> or income. <margin>Third conclusion.</margin> Others, however, believe the right to a pension is clerical and therefore spiritual. ¶ Between these opinions, a third conclusion is established: Pensions assigned to spiritual functions can by no means be redeemed for a price. It is otherwise for those granted under a secular title. <margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin> Each part of this conclusion requires not so much a proof as an example. Indeed, if you look at the ancient custom of pensions, they were never granted unless they were attached to spiritual functions. It was not enough, for example, for a bishop to visit and govern an entire diocese; he would summon an assistant to help him, to whom he would assign a certain pension from his own income. Such pensions, where they are still in custom today, can neither be sold nor redeemed. They have the character of **prebends** <term>A prebend is a portion of a cathedral's or monastery's revenue granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</term> which are attached to spiritual matters. And perhaps the same judgment should be rendered regarding a pension given to an elderly or well-deserving bishop or priest because of his exhausted labors, if he wishes to resign his priesthood because his strength fails him for service. For in Book 3, we judged this type of pension to be legitimate; such a pension seems attached to a clerical right. But there are other pensions which, as we have said, are applied to secular titles—for instance, those given to princes or soldiers. There is no doubt that these can be redeemed, since, as has been said, they can be sold. If a pension is established for a soldier over a bishopric, the bishop can redeem it. But there are others that involve some doubt, namely those that intervene in exchanges or simple resignations: "I resign my **benefice** <term>A permanent church appointment for which property and income are provided in respect of pastoral duties.</term> in your favor, provided a certain pension is retained." This type of pension seems to be purely temporal; for as we said in Book 3, such a pensioner is bound to no ecclesiastical office, nor does he hold a title, but only the right to claim income from the possessor. Regarding these, Cajetan says that if you perform both acts in a single contract—that is, you establish a pension of ten ducats to be redeemed for eighty—the contract is **simoniacal** <note>original: "simoniacus"; relating to simony, the forbidden practice of buying or selling spiritual things or church offices.</note>. If, however, you wish to redeem it separately after the pension has been established,

<column-break/>

no law stands in your way. <margin>The chapter "Ad quaestiones" is explained.</margin> ¶ And first, regarding exchanges, the cited chapter *Ad quaestiones* from the section on the "exchange of things" <note>original: "Ad quæstiones. de rerum permutatione."</note> could mislead a careless reader. For there, no mention is made of a pension; it only states that when the income of prebends is unequal, a quantity of money can be paid back to the one who had the greater share. Here it appears that a total sum of present money can be counted out, and consequently, a pension can be established and redeemed in a single contract. Indeed, even without naming it a "pension," if yours is worth one hundred and mine ninety, and I pay you ten for yours, or perhaps eighty all at once, the contract seems to be approved there. This certainly must not be granted; otherwise, it would be legal to even buy a prebend. For example, if I held no prebend, I could buy yours, which is worth ten, for eighty ducats. The text must therefore be understood as referring to a quantity of money that has the nature of an annual pension. But that it can be redeemed seems to be gathered from said text. For it is held and ordered that the simple exchange of prebends be done separately, and afterward the incomes are balanced. Therefore, that pension seems to be given without clerical right, and for that reason, perhaps it can be redeemed. However, I frankly confess that I cannot perceive Lord Cajetan's distinction between two separate contracts and one single one. For if I can redeem an established pension because it is a matter without an ecclesiastical title, I do not know why—when it is established and thereby extracted from that same ecclesiastical title—one cannot bargain for the redemption at the same time. But lest we grant so much license, it must be said that such a contract carries a strong suspicion of buying and selling. Therefore, it cannot help but cause scandal. Regarding other pensions currently in use—namely those granted at will without any title—let those who think them lawful answer for them. For I, as I said in the third book, cannot "swallow" <note>original: "deuorare"; he means he cannot accept or tolerate the legal logic.</note> that right: that a pension can be placed unless for some ecclesiastical or secular title, or for an exchange, or while a doubt in a lawsuit is being settled. Otherwise, I say, it cannot be. <margin>To the arguments made.</margin> ¶ Through these points, the arguments proposed at the start of the question remain resolved, except for the second one, which we added for the sake of Cajetan. For he concedes that in exchanges, compensation for the excess of a larger prebend is lawful, provided the other party has some income; he remains stuck...

### ARTICLE III.

### Whether it is lawful to confer spiritual things in exchange for a gift, whether of the tongue or of any other service.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'Q' containing a woodcut illustration of a seated figure in academic or clerical robes within a study or interior setting, framed by ornamental patterns.</image-desc> ALTHOUGH it has been established that spiritual things are not to be valued by price, it appears nonetheless they can be conferred in exchange for other gifts. Indeed, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a foundational authority in canon law.</note> says in the 
<margin>First argument.</margin>
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
Register: It is right that those serving the needs of the Church should enjoy ecclesiastical remuneration. But to serve the needs of the Church is a "gift of service" <note>original: "munus ab obsequio"</note>: therefore, ecclesiastical priesthoods are lawfully repaid for a gift of this kind. ¶ Second. It is just as 
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
sordid and carnal to confer a benefice out of regard for kinship as it would be if it were given for a received gift or service: yet the former does not appear so sordid as to be simoniacal: 
<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
therefore, neither is the latter. ¶ Third. What is granted because of prayers seems to be done freely <note>original: "gratis"</note>, and is likewise foreign to simony; for simony is constituted 
<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
by sale and purchase alone. ¶ Fourth. Hypocrites perform spiritual works outwardly so that they may hunt for human praise through the "gift of the tongue" <note>original: "munus linguae"; this refers to using flattery or seeking verbal approval to gain an advantage</note>: yet such hypocrisy is not attributed to simony: therefore, a gift of the tongue does not produce simony. ¶ To the contrary is the word of Pope Urban, in the canon *Salvator* (1.q.3): Whoever bestows or acquires Church property—not for what it was instituted, but for private gain through a gift of the tongue, or service, or money—is a simoniac.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To the question, we respond with two conclusions. First: Simony is committed just as much if a spiritual thing is bestowed for some temporal gift or service—whether already performed or to be performed—as if one were to grant it for money, 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
whether paid or promised. The proof is clear: because all things that can be valued by money are included under the name of "money." It is manifest, however, that services of this kind, which are directed toward some personal advantage, can be weighed by a price: for 

<column-break/>

even servant laborers are hired for a coin. ¶ 
<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
The final conclusion: Just as simony is contracted by receiving money or any other gift, so it is also through a "gift of the tongue." For example: if a bishop, bent by prayers to secure some temporal utility, should confer a priesthood with the intention of gaining favor from which some benefit might come to him by reason of that bestowal. It is proved by the same reasoning, because this also is estimable by money. ¶ Regarding these conclusions, after those things which were decided concerning usury, 
<margin>Bestowing a priesthood for even a shameful gift is simony.</margin>
hardly anything remains to be noted: for simony in spiritual matters is almost exactly what usury is in temporal matters. Therefore, just as giving a loan in exchange for some gift is usury, so also bestowing a priesthood for the same gift is simony. Nor does it truly matter whether the gift is otherwise honorable in its nature or not. For if someone, on account of a shameful intimacy with a woman, should pay out a priesthood to her brother or someone else as if for a price, it would be simony: and he who received it would be bound to resign it. It is otherwise if he conferred it freely out of friendship, even if that friendship were shamefully contracted. Add that even if the one who receives the priesthood does not know, but another has offered a price for him, simony emerges: as is clear in the chapter *Nobis* concerning simony. Therefore, as soon as he finds out, he is bound to renounce the priesthood: because the bestowal was void. 
<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ You ask, then, by the same reasoning, if someone who seeks a prebend <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> gives a gift not to the bishop, but to other intermediaries who might procure it for him, whether such a case is simony such that he is bound to leave the prebend. On one hand, it appears the reasoning is not equal. For if the bishop receives no price, nor prayers estimable by money (as will be declared in the solution to the third argument), he surely confers it freely, and consequently the bestowal holds. On the other hand, 
<margin>Solution.</margin>
it appears the reasoning is the same: for as we shall explain in the following question, by divine and natural law, not only is the giving of spiritual things for a price prohibited, but also the receiving. In the present case, although the bishop confers it freely according to his own mind, the other nonetheless does not receive it freely, but for a price. And this second reason is of such weight to me that I would more willingly assent to it than the first. If any other small doubts emerge from this, they are touched upon by the arguments proposed.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first, therefore, it is responded that the opinion of Gregory pertains only to this: That if a cleric should perform an honorable service for either the church or a prelate, leading to the benefit of the church or another spiritual business, by that...

# Ninth Book: Question VII.

...they truly are not. Soon, because they cannot help but cause scandal. Then, because they do no small injury and arrogance toward others who are worthy, and perhaps more worthy. Indeed, they offer them an occasion for discouragement: lest, when they are deprived of favor and reward, they become slower to the study of letters and to the exercise of the pursuit of integrity. Wherefore, Micah, in his third chapter, well deplores among other iniquities of the ancient priests and judges, <note>original: "qui aedificarent Sion in sanguinibus, & Hierusalem in iniquitate"; Micah 3:10</note> that they "build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity."

<margin>To the third argument. The first assertion of St. Thomas.</margin>
To the third argument, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian whose "Summa Theologiae" is the basis for this discussion</note> responded with several points: specifically three. The first is that whoever, in the granting of a priesthood, primarily intends a "gift of the tongue"—that is, for example, to hunt for praise and likewise human favor, or prayers, or those things by which human favor is acquired, or by which contrary envy or hatred is avoided—contracts the stain of simony <note>the illegal and sinful act of selling or trading spiritual things for temporal gain</note>.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if someone should argue to the contrary: He who gives because of praise, or because he is overcome by prayers, gives freely; therefore, he incurs no legal penalties. Let him weigh the words carefully. For St. Thomas does not attribute the intention of praise simply to simony, even if it is the primary intention, nor the cause of prayers; but rather when through these things some temporal advantage estimable by a price is sought: as if a bishop confers a priesthood on a king’s servant, or is led by his prayers, so that the servant might extol him with praises before the king, using this as a hook to "fish out" a wealthier Church <note>meaning to get promoted to a more lucrative diocese</note>. Indeed, it is not simony even then, unless that gain is primarily intended; the evidence of this is when the office is given to an unworthy person. For since then the primary intention is not the fitness of the person, it is proved to be for temporal advantage. Therefore, the crime of simony is then added to the crimes of injustice and unfaithfulness. Furthermore, the one receiving the prebend <note>a church office that provides an income</note> is bound to relinquish it, unless the provision is made whole again. However, when a prelate only simply desires praise, or through prayers desires friendship and grace, then there is no simony. Indeed, when one confers an office on a worthy person, chiefly because of their dignity, even if a "sinister eye" <note>an secondary, selfish motive</note> looks not only to human praise and favor but even to temporal advantage and profit, he is not infected by simony. If you consult Innocent <note>Pope Innocent III, referring to his legal decrees</note> on the chapter *Tua* regarding age and quality of orders, he teaches similar things in his own manner. Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, a major 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note> also agrees with him in his *Summa*, under the word "simony."

<margin>Second.</margin>
The second assertion, therefore, is that as long as prayers are offered on behalf of a worthy person, then the granting is not simoniacal by its nature; since a legitimate cause for both praying and granting underlies it. It is 

<column-break/>

nevertheless possible for "mental simony" <note>a hidden, internal intention to trade spiritual things for gain, even if no money is exchanged</note> to creep in there if the granting is not done because of the person's dignity, but chiefly because of favor and an advantage estimable by a price, as has been said.

<margin>But a Doubt.</margin>
But because we have fallen into a discussion about prayers and favor, another doubt occupies us: Whether a granting extorted by fear is simoniacal, such that he who has received such a benefit is bound to resign it. For the aforementioned Cantor of Paris <note>Peter the Chanter</note>, as reported by the same William of Auxerre <note>original: "Altisiodorensi"; a medieval theologian</note>, holds this. <margin>Auxerre</margin> Since fear, he says, is redeemable by money. <margin>Solution.</margin> But truly, it is answered in the same way as concerning blood-relationship and friendship: namely, that although to confer an office on an unworthy person out of fear is a mortal sin in its nature; and even some fault for a worthy person, because the granting is not done for a legitimate end; nevertheless, neither is simony. For to give because of fear is not to give for a price. For even if someone gave a price to dispel fear, the one who fears nevertheless receives nothing. Indeed, the law does not condemn conferring sacraments because of fear; as if someone were to hear a confession out of fear. Nor would such a bishop commonly be held as simoniacal. Nevertheless, when that fear is incited in a way that is estimable by a price—as just explained—then it would be simony: for example, if a king or his courtier threatened a bishop that unless he conferred a priesthood on such a person, he would fall out of royal favor and would not ascend to another see <note>meaning he wouldn't be promoted to a better bishopric</note>. For he who confers a priesthood out of such fear would be doing so to "hunt" for an episcopacy; and thus he would be a simoniac. It is otherwise if fear were incited in him of losing his life, or the temporal goods which he already possesses: for then the one fearing has no regard for profit.

But since it has been said that to confer an office on an unworthy person because of fear is a mortal sin by its nature—not indeed of simony, but of injustice and unfaithfulness.

<margin>Scruple.</margin>
A final scruple remains: Whether any fear excuses such a fault. <margin>Response.</margin> It is answered, however, that there is no excusing fear in such a matter: for since both divine and natural law forbid it, and it is thus an intrinsically evil act, one must rather succumb to the sword than perpetrate it.

<margin>Third assertion.</margin>
The third saying of Saint Thomas is: For anyone to ask for himself to obtain a priesthood to which the "care of souls" <note>the responsibility for the spiritual life of a parish or congregation</note> is joined, is presumptuous, and therefore he is rendered unworthy by his own prayers; and thus he who prays for an unworthy person sins. If, however, the priesthood is without such care, and he himself is in need of life's sustenance, <margin>Reason for the assertion.</margin> he can seek it without simony. The reason for the first part is...

But regarding restitution, it must be observed that it is one thing to offer anything to another under a **condition**: that is, "I give if you are such as you appear." It is another thing to give **absolutely**: even if the motive is that quality which appears. However, one must not doubt that the appointments to priesthoods and ecclesiastical dignities are made **absolutely**, and entirely without any condition: just like the administration of the **sacraments**. Otherwise, nothing in the church would be firm or solid. Therefore, whoever thought to dispense these offices otherwise would not be doing what the church intends. Hence it happens that even if the one who is admitted to the Church has "sold" a flawed holiness with that intention, the appointment would nevertheless hold. And whoever, after obtaining a dignity or any priesthood, contaminates their life with corrupt morals, they nevertheless truly possess it, nor are they bound to the restitution of the fruits <note>Income or benefits derived from the office.</note>.
<margin>He who extorts alms by simulated poverty is not bound to restitution.</margin>
¶ Through these points, therefore, judgment should be made almost similarly concerning **alms**. For truly, if someone bestows alms upon either a **hypocrite** or a rich man disguised as a poor man, if they did so under such a condition—"if you are truly what you appear"—it is certain that ownership does not transfer if that condition is not met. But in truth, they are not deemed to be conferred by that pact, but are given **absolutely**: although the motive is false: and therefore it must truly be believed that ownership of them is transferred, even if they are conferred upon hypocrites and false poor people. Moreover, that they are given absolutely appears from the fact that men bestow alms for the sake of God. Indeed, in a certain way, to **Christ** himself in the poor. For "whatever you did," He says, "to one of these my least, you did to me." And therefore, such an exact inquiry into the dignity of the person should not be made when offering a gift.
<margin>Confirmation of the previous statement.</margin>
And it is confirmed: for as **Adrian** <note>Likely referring to Pope Hadrian VI, known for his work on canon law and ethics.</note> himself concedes, when the **final cause** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the ultimate purpose or "that for the sake of which" something is done.</note> is true, even though 

<column-break/>

<margin>1st assertion.</margin>
the motive is false, the transfer of ownership is not hindered: as is evident in other matters. For if someone hires a servant whom they think is good, although they are not such, they nonetheless acquire ownership of the wages: provided they serve, which was the final cause: even if they do not serve as well as the master thought. The final cause of **alms**, however, is the charity of God, who "makes his sun rise over the good and the bad": therefore, although the motive is false—namely, the worthiness of the person—ownership is not hindered. Otherwise, whatever kind of lie a poor person might tell, they would be subjected to the yoke of restitution.
<margin>Another reason for the same.</margin>
And finally, it is argued from another assertion of theirs: If the hypocrite and the lying poor man are bound to restore, it is asked to whom the restitution should be made.
<margin>Solution of Alexander.</margin>
**Alexander** <note>Alexander of Hales, a 13th-century theologian.</note> responds that it should not be made to those who offered the alms: since they alienated the ownership from themselves for God’s sake; but it must be made to the state or to other poor people to whom they might perhaps have been given.
<margin>Reply.</margin>
But it is argued against this. If those who bestowed alms abdicated ownership from themselves, it follows that they transferred it to those to whom they gave it: for they did not transfer it to God except in those to whom they gave it for His sake. Furthermore, therefore, that opinion is not necessary.
<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you urge us again: Those offering alms did not do so spontaneously and voluntarily: since ignorance was the cause, which according to **Aristotle** <note>Greek philosopher whose "Ethics" defines voluntary and involuntary actions.</note> makes an act involuntary.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
Wherefore **Saint Thomas** says a hypocrite "steals" praises by theft. An involuntary donation, however, is not valid. The first premise is denied: for not all ignorance makes an act involuntary when the most powerful cause of the work is not ignored. For all know that **mercy** is an office of **charity**, which does not require such a great exploration of the merits of the person: since even if the poor person is not worthy, no loss of merit occurs. And therefore, although that same worthiness is unknown, the mercy is nonetheless spontaneous.
<margin>Limitation of the above statement.</margin>
I would assert this in daily alms: for if a notorious impostor were to feign an extraordinary holiness or necessity to squeeze out a heavy weight of money, I would believe such a wicked person is bound to restitution: for then that huge alms should not be deemed spontaneous, but extorted by fraud. ¶ Therefore, the arguments to the contrary remain resolved. For it is conceded that such a hypocrite is a deceiver, and in a certain way has scraped together alms by a false title: but it is nonetheless denied, for the reasons stated, that they did not acquire ownership: because voluntarily—

# QUESTION EIGHT,
## Concerning the restitution for Simony and the punishment of the Simoniac.
### ARTICLE I.
*Whether whatever is either given or received through simony is subject to restitution.*

<margin>First argument.</margin>
FINALLY, the last question regarding **simony** <note>The sin of buying or selling ecclesiastical preferments or spiritual benefits, named after Simon Magus from the New Testament.</note> must explore **restitution** <note>The act of restoring something to its proper owner or state.</note> and the remaining penalties. For it appears that it is not strictly necessary that whoever possesses a **prebend** <note>A portion of church revenue granted to a member of the clergy.</note> or dignity through simony must relinquish it. Indeed, there are certain spiritual things which, once obtained, cannot be cast away: such as the **characters** <note>An indelible spiritual mark believed to be imprinted on the soul by certain sacraments, such as Baptism or Holy Orders.</note> which are impressed through sacramental consecrations. Therefore, even if these are acquired simoniacally, they are not to be restored.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly. It happens that a bishop is promoted simoniacally, whose subsequent punishment is **suspension** <note>A legal prohibition preventing a cleric from exercising their orders or office.</note>; and yet he might command a subordinate under **anathema** <note>A formal curse or excommunication by a pope or council of the Church.</note> to receive orders from him, and the subordinate would therefore seem obliged to obey. Yet no one ought to receive a thing from one who does not have the power of conferring it; therefore, the bishop is not suspended from that episcopal power by the debt of simony.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Thirdly. No one should be punished for a crime that was committed without their knowledge or will, since punishment is due only to a voluntary crime. It sometimes happens that someone receives something spiritual while others procure it for them in secret; therefore, there is no reason that the person should be deprived of the appointment made for them.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ Fourthly. No one should report a profit from their own fault. However, it usually happens that if a simoniac resigned what he thus acquired, it would fall back to those who were participants in the simony: such as when a **prelate** <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note> or

<column-break/>

the entire college to whom restitution must be made consented to the simony. Therefore, in such an event, no restitution should be made.

<margin>Argument 5.</margin>
¶ Fifthly. When someone is admitted to the solemn vow of religion through simony, they cannot release themselves from that same vow. Therefore, they are absolved from the restitution of what they obtained through simony.

<margin>Argument 6.</margin>
¶ Sixthly. An external punishment in this world ought not to be inflicted for an inward movement of the heart, which is open to God alone. Yet simony occurs not only outwardly in action but also inwardly in the heart; by which reasoning, as was shown above, it is defined by the will. Therefore, simony of this kind is subject to no restitution.

<margin>Argument 7.</margin>
¶ Seventhly, it is argued: It is a much greater thing to be promoted to higher things than to remain in those already received. Sometimes a **dispensation** <note>An exemption from a rule or usual requirement.</note> is granted regarding simony so that people may be raised to more sublime offices; therefore, they should not always be deprived of the things they have received.

¶ To the contrary is that opinion of the **canon** <note>A rule or law enacted by a church council.</note>, "If any bishop" <note>original: "Si quis episcopus." 1. q. 1.</note>: "He who is ordained—let no one profit from an ordination or promotion which is made through trade; but let him be an alien to the dignity or the responsibility which he acquired through simony."

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with a single conclusion: Whatever is acquired through simony, whether by a monetary price or by another gift of equal value, is subject to restitution. That is to say, neither can the one who buys a spiritual thing retain it, nor can the one who sold it retain the price.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is proven. No one can retain that which they acquired against the will of the Lord: as if a steward were to sell off his master's property, neither could he retain the price, nor could the buyers retain the items. But the Lord, whose stewards are the heads of the Churches, cautioned by law that spiritual things, which were bestowed upon them freely for the common good, should not be distributed for a price; according to that passage in Matthew 10: "Freely you have received, freely give." Therefore, if spiritual things are dispensed for a price, neither the seller can retain the price nor the buyer the spiritual thing.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Regarding this conclusion and its proof, which belongs to **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, the highly influential medieval theologian.</note>, the first doubt is by what law it holds the force of truth: whether by divine and natural law, or only by papal law. For regarding this, no doubt exists. The entire **canon law** <note>The body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority for the government of a Christian organization.</note> proclaims it: as is clear from the cited canon, "If any bishop," where he who buys a dignity through simony is ordered to be an alien to it; and the canon "A priest" <note>original: "presbyterum."</note> in the same cause and question: he who obtains a Church through money is ordered to be deprived of it. And vice versa, in the chapter "On this" <note>original: "de hoc"</note> concerning simony: Kings who have accepted a price to consent to an election are to restore the same price

<meta>catchword: restore</meta>

<summary>This page explores whether goods or offices obtained through simony (the buying/selling of spiritual things) must be returned. Soto argues that according to both Scripture and Canon Law, neither the spiritual office nor the money paid for it may be kept by the parties involved.</summary>

# Book Nine, Question VIII.

<margin>Martin V</margin>
...they are compelled to restore. And in the *Extravagantes* <note>A collection of papal decrees that circulated "outside" the main official codifications of Canon Law at the time.</note> of Martin V, which appears among the acts of the Council of Constance, Session 43, it is decreed that elections, requests, and any simoniacal provisions are null by the law itself (*ipso iure*). From this, it follows that neither 
<margin>Paul II</margin>
prebends <note>An income-bearing position within a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> nor the price paid for them can be retained. This is also what Paul II intended to be most firmly established in his decree *Cum detestabile*. Besides the fact that such simoniacal prelates are perpetually driven to eternal damnation, and, being excommunicated, they are suspended from the duties of their order: as is clear in that same place, and in the canons *Si quis dator* and *Si quis episcopus* (1. q. 3). Indeed, all mediators, go-betweens, and agents are likewise excommunicated. Whether, however, both forms of restitution—namely of the prebend as well as the price—are commanded by 
<margin>He who sells a priesthood is bound by divine and natural law to restore the price.</margin>
natural law, and consequently divine law, is a matter of debate. And indeed, that he who has sold a priesthood is bound to restore the price is clearly gathered from natural and divine law. For since a spiritual thing is not by its nature salable, but is commanded to be given for free—as is clear from the word of Christ recently cited <note>referring to Matthew 10:8: "Freely you have received, freely give."</note>—it is obvious that it is received wickedly, just as was shown above regarding money from usury <note>The practice of charging interest on loans, which was historically considered a sin of injustice.</note>. However, regarding whether he who received a prebend or any spiritual thing for a price is bound by divine or natural law to relinquish it, no reasoning seems to be entirely convincing. For to persist with the example used in our conclusion, a steward can alienate his master’s property against his will in two ways. In one way, because the master in no way commanded it; and then, by the law of nature, the one to whom these things are handed over does not acquire ownership. In the other way, because the master commanded that they be given for free: for example, that grain be distributed to the poor. And then, even if the steward, selling it to the poor, is bound to return the price, nevertheless the poor who were going to receive it for free, even if they pay some price, are in no way bound to restore the things themselves. In the same way, the Lord commanded His stewards to distribute spiritual things freely; therefore, those who were suitable, even if they bought them, are not bound to restore what they bought by divine or natural law, but rather by reason of ecclesiastical law which voids such provisions. This is confirmed by the example of usury. For although he who gives at usury is obliged to restore it, he who pays usury for a loan is not bound to do so. By these reasons, it might perhaps seem probable to some that it is not 
<margin>One buying spiritual things</margin>
founded in divine and natural law that a buyer of spiritual things is bound to resign them. But in truth, the matter is otherwise: for

<column-break/>

<margin>holds to these studies</margin>
primarily, Saint Thomas and the Doctors of the Church, based on that divine law—*Freely you have received, freely give*—
<margin>to resign by divine law.</margin>
infer that spiritual things purchased must be resigned. Indeed, not only the Doctors, but the laws themselves say so. 
<margin>Reason for the assertion</margin>
It is demonstrated, therefore, that the restitution not only of the price but also of the spiritual things themselves draws its foundation from divine law, though in a slightly different way. Not only to sell a spiritual thing, but to buy it, is simony; therefore, its restitution is founded in the law of nature. The premise is proved: a spiritual thing is the pure grace of God. But grace ceases to be grace not only because it is not given freely, but because it is not received freely; as Pope Leo rightly noted in the chapter *Gratia* (1. q. 1), where he says: "Grace, if it is not given or received freely, is not grace." And Urban in the chapter *Salvator* (1. q. 3) says: "He who sells or buys the gifts of God, which are received freely so that they may be given freely, for his own gain, thinks with Simon [Magus] <note>A figure from the New Testament (Acts 8) who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit from the Apostles.</note> that the gift of God can be possessed with money." Indeed, Simon sinned against the grace of the Holy Spirit, and thus against divine law, in this: that he first wanted to *buy* a spiritual thing, even though he later intended to sell that same grace. Not only is the buying of grace contrary to divine law, but it is also against the very nature of things; for grace ought to be possessed not for a price, but freely. Thus, even if Christ only said, "Freely you have received, freely give," in saying "freely give," He understood that all ought to receive freely. Hence, he who buys brings no less injury upon Him than he who sells. For God wills that His grace be owed to Him alone; and he who buys professes that he receives it not from God Himself, but from the seller. Therefore, not only selling but also buying, because it is against divine grace, is a sin—as we said above—against the virtue of religion. And in this, simony differs from usury. For usury is only prohibited for the good of one’s neighbor: namely, to avoid the injustice of a price being received for that which is not salable. Therefore, usury is an injustice only on the part of the receiver, and not on the part of the giver. In simony, however, both sides sin against religion and against God's justice; since He not only commanded His stewards to give those things freely, but forbade everyone from receiving them in any other way than freely, so that by that reasoning they might confess that they receive them from God alone. And through this, the solutions to those arguments we were just making are clear. Therefore, if buying spiritual things is simony, against divine and natural law—namely, against the nature of grace—then the restitution of spiritual [offices] is established there as well.

<summary>This page argues that simony—the buying or selling of spiritual offices—is a violation of divine and natural law because grace, by definition, must be both given and received freely. It establishes that both the buyer and seller are obligated to make restitution, as the act of purchasing a church position treats a gift of God as a commodity controlled by men.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral foundations of simony, specifically addressing whether the sale of a church office is invalid under natural and divine law. It builds upon the previous page's assertion that spiritual things cannot be sold for a price.</meta>

...foundation of spiritual things. I would say the foundation has been laid: because for now we have only established that both buying and selling are simony by natural and divine law. However, whether the same law prevents the transfer of both the prebend <note>A "prebend" is a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> and the ownership of the price—so that restitution itself is required by divine law, just as in the case of usury—will be clarified in the response to the sixth argument during the commentary on the chapter *Mandato* regarding simony.

<margin>The distinction of simony.</margin>
¶ Following this, for a deeper understanding of the conclusion, we must recall the famous distinction between real and mental simony, just as we do with usury. Real simony is that which is done by a pact <note>original: "pacto"</note>, whether express or tacit (that is, signaled by nods or gestures). However, unless the execution of the pact actually follows—meaning, if the agreed price is not paid—then the seller is bound to no restitution in conscience, as we also said regarding the usurer, since he has received nothing. Whether, however, the one who receives the prebend is bound to resign it will be examined shortly. Mental simony, on the other hand, is the internal purpose and intention of giving or receiving something spiritual for something temporal. To understand this, one should refer back to what we said in Book 6 regarding mental usury. For that rule—whether the price is intended principally or less principally—is slippery and deceptive; rather, the mind must be weighed by its object, in the philosophical manner.

<margin>That should be considered mental simony whose object is real simony.</margin>
Namely, let that be precisely considered mental simony whose object is real simony: specifically, the intention of giving or receiving a spiritual thing for a temporal price. Hence, if someone serves a bishop out of his own liberality to win his friendship, and is certain that he will neither receive anything nor will the bishop bestow anything for the service, but hopes that, having become a friend, the bishop might perhaps give it for free (of which he is worthy), there is no mental simony. This is because the object itself—namely, giving by reason of friendship—is not real simony. Nor is it simony if he thinks of giving something by a liberal and honorable gift, as if returning thanks, or as something owed by a laudable custom. Nor, conversely, if the bishop intends to receive it in such a manner.

<margin>The triple species of simony</margin>
¶ Now, Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Italian philosopher, theologian, and cardinal.</note> in his *Summa* gathers three species of simony. The first consists in the intention alone without any action: namely, when someone has decreed in his mind to sell or buy a spiritual thing. It is most certain that this is not subject to the penalties of the law, since the Church does not judge internal matters. The second is that of which the Doctors speak, when someone offers gifts outwardly with a wicked but hidden intention. Specifically, when he con-

<column-break/>

-ceals the intention with which he does it. And when a prelate, even with a corrupt intention which he hides, confers a spiritual thing. The third, he says, is when a pact intervenes, but it is not carried out. In fact, before the collation <note>The formal act of presenting a clergyman to a benefice or office.</note> takes place, both sides desist from the previous agreement. This, however, should not be called mental simony so much as "imperfect real simony." Because of this, although it is a grave sin, no one incurs the penalties of the law.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ A doubt arises here that must not be ignored: whether, just as mental simony occurs without real simony, real simony can conversely occur without mental. For example, suppose there is some deceiver and impostor who promises a price to the bishop for a priesthood, and confirms it with a legal instrument, yet without any intention of fulfilling it. It appears then that simony arises on one side: since if this had become known to the Church, he would be driven by the penalties of the law and stripped of his priesthood.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
On the other hand, there seems to be no simony, since an external operation must be weighed by the intention from which it takes its character. It must be said, therefore, that in truth it is not simony; nor in the court of conscience <note>The "forum of conscience" refers to the internal moral judgment of an individual before God, as opposed to a legal court.</note> is the one gifted the prebend bound to leave it, as Cajetan says in Question 10 of his first *Quodlibet*. Nevertheless, the Church, having become certain of the fact, would condemn him by legitimate presumption, because it judges based on external things.

<margin>All real simony binds one to restitution where the price has been paid.</margin>
¶ Finally, having premised these points, the conclusion commanding restitution primarily embraces all real simony where the price has truly been paid. But where a pact preceded but the price did not follow, it has already been said that the seller is bound to nothing except repentance for the crime.

<margin>A further doubt.</margin>
Whether, however, the buyer is bound to resign the priesthood must be distinguished. For if, before the collation, he explains that he will not give the price, there is no doubt that the collation, if it happens, holds; nor is there need for a dispensation to make him fit to receive it. And this true saying, which we just mentioned, must be understood according to this truth: that if the pact is not carried out, he does not incur the penalties of the law. But if the collation happens under such a pact, it should not be doubted in the least that the collation is null. We affirm this so assertively because I see that some are deceived about this. And primarily, this was the assertion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note> in the preceding article: for he deliberately expressed that if someone gives a spiritual thing for some temporal service performed or to be performed, it is simony. And the reason is manifest: for there is an express buying and selling. For he who sells on credit...

Therefore, simony is already present from that moment, regardless of what follows: namely, whether the price is eventually paid or not. Otherwise, usury could never be committed under a mere promise, which is false. Nor does it matter whether the pact was celebrated in writing and with legal solemnity, or by word alone between two people without witnesses: as long as you pledge your faith, promising that you will give something for a prebend <note>A "prebend" is a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note>. <margin>
When the preceding pact is dissolved before the grant of the spiritual thing, restitution of the received price must be made to the one who paid.
Cajetan.

And indeed, when the preceding pact is dissolved before the grant of the spiritual thing, even if the price has been paid, there is no doubt that restitution must be made to the same person who bestowed the price. For, as we were just saying, because of that simony, no one is yet guilty of the legal penalties. This is the confession of Cajetan in his *Summa*. But if the simony has been put into execution—namely, the grant of both the price and the prebend has been made—then there is doubt. For everyone seems to agree on this, including Saint Thomas in his solution to the fourth point, that restitution of the price must be made either to the church in which the simony was committed, or to the poor. For Augustine, as held in chapter *Non sane*, question 14, case 5, adjudges the restitution of ill-gotten gains to the poor. Yet in the chapter *de hoc* and the chapter *audivimus* concerning simony, we read that such simoniacal prices were ordered to be restored to the churches. The Emperor Caesar <note>Referring to Justinian I and his legal code.</note> expressly commanded the same in the *Authentica* <note>original: "Authentica de sanctissimis episcop." — a collection of Justinian's legal decrees regarding bishops.</note> concerning the most holy bishops. However, if the matter is inspected more deeply, a distinction 

<margin>
A simoniac after condemnation must restore to the church or the poor; otherwise to the one who gave.
Reason for the proximate assertion.
</margin>

must be made. For after condemnation, it is beyond controversy that restitution must be made to the church or the poor, because he who gave on account of a crime is fined the money he gave, and he who received it does not acquire ownership. Nevertheless, while the crime has not been brought to court, but remains hidden in the forum of conscience <note>The "forum of conscience" refers to internal moral judgment and confession, as opposed to a public legal trial.</note>, I cannot persuade myself of anything other than that restitution of the price must be made to the very person who gave it. And the reason is that a penal law, as we argued in Book 1, does not bind a defendant before 

<column-break/>

condemnation so that he himself is held to be the executor of his own punishment or fine. Since, therefore, the buyer of that prebend comes to be fined his own price on account of the crime, it happens that before condemnation for the crime, he has not lost either ownership or possession, as we declared in that place. And accordingly, since ownership has not been transferred to the receiver, it follows that it must be restored to its owner. Nor does it matter whether the transfer of ownership is hindered by divine and natural law, or by ecclesiastical law alone. For perhaps someone might presently devise an argument that the transfer of the price is not prohibited by divine or natural law; for although our Lord commanded that spiritual things be conferred freely, nevertheless, because a prebend is a thing estimable in money, even though selling it is a sin, ownership of the price is nonetheless acquired by natural law, just as that of the prebend is. But because the Church annulled such contracts—as is clear from the laws cited above, proclaiming them to be void—it could, by that very fact, apply the price to the poor. However, a device of this kind errs in two ways, as I believe. First, because I think that by divine and natural law, ownership of the price is not transmitted. For since God commanded to give freely, the price is given for a thing that is not sellable—whatever may be said of the granting of the prebend. Secondly, even if such an annulment of the contract had its origin solely from a statute of the Church, the same Holy Church could not drive a simoniacal buyer into a penalty without the case being heard, until he was condemned for the crime. From these things, therefore, it follows that he who received such a price, just like a usurer, must restore it without any delay and without waiting for any judge's sentence, as something belonging to another, of which he does not have ownership—provided that he takes caution lest later, when the treasury finds out, he be forced to pay it a second time. Although the right of recovery is not legally permitted to the one who gave it, since once the matter is known, he will be fined that price. 

<margin>
Restitution of the prebend.
</margin>

¶ Regarding the restitution of the prebend, however, the reasoning is far different. For if the grant has been made, it cannot be restored immediately to the previous possessor. For while the prelate, according to his own judgment, granted it to Peter, he simply took it away from Paul. Therefore, neither is its owner: namely, not Paul, because it was taken from him; nor Peter, because by reason of simony he was made unfit to receive it. Wherefore, it cannot be restored to Paul otherwise than by a resignation made into the judgment of the prelate who might return it to him; yet with a prior dispensation regarding the irregularity <note>In canon law, an "irregularity" is a canonical impediment that prevents a person from receiving or exercising Holy Orders.</note> contracted through simony.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
TO the first argument, therefore, the Divine Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note> responds with several points. First, that even if someone is initiated into a sacred order simoniacally, they receive the "character" <note>original: "characterem" — the permanent spiritual mark believed to be imprinted on the soul by sacraments like Baptism or Ordination.</note> because of the efficacy of the sacrament, yet they are not infused with sacramental grace because the sin of simony acts as a barrier. Second, he adds that such a person is suspended from exercising that order because they have, in a sense, stolen the "character" through theft against the will of the Lord. Here we must recall what was said before: that not only giving, but also receiving a spiritual thing for a price, is the crime of simony. Third, he adds that the suspension of the order extends so far that not only are the suspended forbidden from performing the duties of the order, but it is also not permitted for others to communicate with them in such performance, whether the crime was public or secret. Therefore, while someone receives the priestly order for a price—however secret it may be, that is, not yet brought into the public courts—he can neither celebrate Mass, nor can others who know of it participate in his celebration. Fourth, he adds that such a simoniac cannot sue to recover the price paid. I understand this as applying to the public court, as I said very recently; for privately, before a condemnation, the price must be restored to the person by an arbitrator. Fifth and finally, he concludes that a simoniac—whether he committed simony by conferring an order, or by giving or receiving a prebend, or acting as a mediator—if the crime is public (for example, in a judicial court), is suspended by law both in regard to himself and in regard to others. If, however, the crime is secret, then he is only suspended in regard to himself. A difference must be noted here: in the conferring of "benefices" <note>Church offices with revenue.</note>, when the crime is secret, neither the giver nor the receiver is suspended in regard to others, but only in regard to themselves. However, in the conferring of "orders" <note>The sacrament of Ordination.</note>, although the one conferring them is freed by the same law (that is, in a secret crime he is only suspended in regard to himself), the one receiving them is suspended in both ways, even if the crime is secret.

<column-break/>

This is an ancient opinion, which Panormitanus <note>original: "Panormita." — Niccolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a leading expert in canon law.</note> confirms in his commentary on the chapter *Tanta* concerning simony. And <margin>Reason for the assertion.</margin> I believe the reason is that since the very root of the reception was infected, the laws intended to bar him from execution, and also to bar any others who privately knew of it, even if the crime was secret (that is, not brought into public judgment). However, regarding the giver, if he was legitimately ordained, they considered it sufficient that he himself abstain, while others would not be bound to avoid him unless he was publicly condemned. Concerning these suspensions, there are laws in the *Extravagant* <note>A term for papal decrees that "wandered" outside the main early collections of canon law.</note> of Martin V cited above, <margin>Martin V.</margin> *Sacro*, which is from the Council of Constance, and in the *Extravagant* *Damnabile* of the same Martin and of <margin>Eugenius.</margin> Eugenius IV, and in another, *Cùm detestabile*. However, those things recounted here regarding the communication of others with simoniacs must be referred to the age of the Divine Thomas; for afterward, to provide for those with anxious consciences, it was decreed in the <margin>Council of Constance.</margin> Council of Constance <note>An ecumenical council held from 1414 to 1418.</note> that no one is bound to avoid an excommunicated person unless they are named specifically, or are a public striker of clerics. It is not enough that they be named by the general name of the crime—for instance, "simoniac" or "heretic"—but it is required that they be expressed by their own name. Otherwise, delicate consciences would not be sufficiently helped. Therefore, since every excommunication brings suspension with it, it happens that even from those suspended, before they are named by a public sentence, legitimate subjects may receive the sacraments, even absolution. Indeed, if a subject is seeking his right, the parish priest can administer the sacrament to him without fault, because this whole rule was granted in favor of the subject. This is provided, however, that the priest does not celebrate the Mass himself, which a sinner cannot do without a monstrous crime of sacrilege. ¶ To <margin>To the second.</margin> the second argument, it is answered in a similar way: that no one should receive orders from a bishop promoted through simony, not only because of the command but also because of excommunication, unless a dispensation is granted. This, however, must be understood in the same way I just mentioned: for Thomas was speaking according to the laws of his own age. For now, unless such a bishop is specifically named as excommunicated, a subject may, according to the said decree, request the sacraments from him if it is necessary. # Book Nine, Question 8.
