However, from the communion of a bishop who is a simoniac in a way other than through his own promotion, unless the crime were legally made public, no one was bound to abstain according to the ancient laws.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is answered that there are two ways a person is held to restitution, just as was said regarding a usurer and a thief. One way is **by reason of the taking**: that is, when he sinned in the act of receiving. The other way is **by reason of the thing received**: namely, when he possesses something that is not his own. Therefore, when someone knowingly and prudently, of his own accord, has received either holy orders or the <term>prebends</term> <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note> attached to those orders, he is held by reason of the taking. For this reason, not only is he deprived of what he received—namely, the exercise of the office and the <term>benefice</term> <note>A "benefice" is a permanent church appointment for which property and income are provided in respect of spiritual duties.</note> along with the <term>fruits</term> <note>The "fruits" refer to the income, produce, or financial profits generated by the church office.</note> already collected—but he is also held to restore other fruits which he perhaps did not collect, but which a legitimate possessor could have collected. This is because he caused the loss of all these through his wrongdoing. However, the expenses made for the sake of producing those fruits are to be deducted, as well as any expenses he legitimately made for the benefit of the church, as he was bound to do. When, however, someone is promoted through simony without his knowledge or will, then he is held only by reason of the thing received. Therefore, as soon as he finds out, he ought to be suspended from the exercise of the order; but nevertheless, he must restore only those fruits by which he was made richer. He is not held to restore those which he consumed for his own uses in good faith. If, however, the person who offered money in his name did so through fraud and trickery so that the recipient might later be stripped of his position, then unless the recipient himself consented, he is by no means to be despoiled.

<margin>To the fourth.</margin>
¶ To the fourth, Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian whom Soto is commenting upon.</note> responds that both the money or possession (that is, what was spent on the prelate) as well as the fruits perceived simoniacally are to be restored to the church, even if the prelate or someone of the <term>college</term> <note>A "college" here refers to the governing body or assembly of a religious institution, such as a chapter of canons.</note> consented to the simony. If, however, the whole college was infected by the same contract, then by the authority of the prelate, restitution must be made either to another church or to the poor. And indeed, what he asserts concerning the fruits is true to the letter according to ancient laws; yet, the current Roman custom is that they fall to the Pope to sustain his apostolic expenses. Therefore, a <term>composition</term> <note>A legal settlement or financial arrangement made to resolve a canonical penalty.</note> can be made with him regarding them, and a remission obtained from him. However, regarding what he adds about the "price of simony," I think it must be understood in the way we explained above: Namely, after someone has been condemned for the crime:

<margin>To the fifth: The Lateran Council.</margin>
¶ In the solution to the fifth, Saint Thomas relates a decree of the <term>Lateran Council</term> <note>The Fourth Lateran Council (1215), one of the most important councils of the Middle Ages.</note> under Pope Innocent III, which was celebrated near his own time and is referred to in the chapter "Since" concerning simony. There, those who are received into religious profession simoniacally—unless it was for the sake of sustenance (as explained above)—are not indeed freed from the obligation of their solemn vow, because they were unable to be; but nevertheless, they are expelled from their monastery and sentenced to undergo perpetual penance under a stricter rule. That which follows, however, does not pertain to the present times, but to those who were offenders before such a decree: namely, those who were only compelled to stay in other convents of the same order.

<margin>To the sixth.</margin>
**F**inally, the sixth argument, which at present brings far more ambiguity, is applied to exploring the nature of **mental simony**: whether it binds one to restitution when it does not break out into an external act. And indeed, if someone who received a prebend gave nothing in return, then the granter, even if he had hoped for a price from an agreement, is bound to nothing: just as we said concerning a usurer.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
But there is a doubt about him who received a prebend if, without an agreement, he believed himself to receive it through simony—namely, either because he thinks the granter conferred it because he was enticed by the hope of a price, or because he had sent gifts with a wicked intention, which the prelate had received with no healthier intent. Then, I say, it is a doubt and not a small annoyance whether he is bound to resign the prebend, and likewise whether the prelate must restore whatever he had received. For if you consult the laws on usury, when a usurer conceives in his mind that what is offered to him by another beyond the principal is offered not freely, but by reason of the loan, he is held to restitution. However, there exists a text to the contrary, as it appears to many, expressed in the chapter *Mandato* <note>original: "cap. mādato." — a specific legal citation within canon law.</note>, which is the last under the title of simony. There it is held that when it so happens between two people that one receives something spiritual—namely, a place in a monastery—and the other (the community) receives something temporal, yet with a corrupt heart on both sides—namely because each believed in himself that it was conferred simoniacally, or perhaps each was giving with that same intention—as long as no external agreement intervened and no expression of the corrupt mind, neither is bound to restitution, as most think. Instead, it is enough for both through penance alone

...repentance to satisfy his creator. This chapter, therefore, insofar as it seems to hold a different view than what has been defined regarding usury, creates a great deal of work for the <term>Doctors</term> <note>The "Doctors" refers to the established "Doctors of the Church" or authoritative legal scholars whose opinions shaped Canon Law.</note> to explain.

<margin>Hostiensis's solution.</margin>
Wherefore **Hostiensis** <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a preeminent canonist.</note>, distinguishing on the same chapter, says that those things acquired through simony against divine law are necessary to be restored; but those acquired through simony of <term>positive law</term> <note>Positive law refers to man-made laws (civil or ecclesiastical) rather than natural or divine law.</note>—that is, a wrong because it is prohibited—are free from restitution. Of these latter cases, he says, the Pope was speaking in that passage.

<margin>Henry of Ghent.</margin>
**Henry of Ghent** <note>A famous 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> agrees in *Quodlibet* 6, question 26, saying that in the said chapter, the discourse is held not regarding one who had contributed money for entry into a religious order, but regarding those monks who had bought honorable positions, for example, proximity to the Abbot.

<margin>The previous solution is rejected.</margin>
However, if you look into the legitimate meaning, "a place in a monastery" is used as a synonym for admission to the religious life. Therefore, there is no doubt that the discourse there concerns simony against divine law. Wherefore, mention of the resignation of spiritual things is immediately subjoined.

<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
Therefore, **Panormitanus** <note>Nicolò de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canonist known as "The Abbot."</note>, believing there that no kind of "mental simony" <note>Simony committed in the mind/intent without an explicit verbal or written contract.</note> obliges one to restitution—even if a gift is both given and received with a sinister intention—devises this distinction between usury and simony: that in hatred of usurers, the restitution of "mental usury" was ordered, specifically so that the crime would not be covered up by that cloak; but the restitution of simony was not so ordered. Yet, in truth, simony ought to produce greater indignation than usury, being as it is more virulent.

<margin>Another solution by the same Panormitanus.</margin>
He adds, therefore, a second point: that perhaps the said chapter is to be understood as applying when the principal intention is not simoniacal.

<margin>Objection against the solution</margin>
But nonetheless, even this solution is not valid: because in usury, as we have declared in its proper place, by whatever intention something is received beyond the principal for the use of money, it is usury.

<margin>John Andreas.</margin>
¶ **John Andreas** <note>Giovanni d'Andrea (c. 1270–1348), an expert in Canon Law.</note>, on the said chapter, brings forward another distinction of less probability: namely, that in usury only the mind of the usurer is depraved, as he is the one demanding something beyond the principal, but not the mind of the one paying. Therefore, restitution is ordered to be made to the payer. In simony, however, the minds of both parties are corrupt. For it is forbidden both to buy and to sell a spiritual thing; and therefore, all other things being equal, the condition of the possessor is better, so that both are permitted to keep what they received. Besides, he says, charity is more severely wounded by usury.

<margin>Interpretation of John Andreas is refuted.</margin>
But yet, that this contrived interpretation is poorly suited to the matter is evident from the fact that a depraved mind ought to benefit no one. Why, then, should a simoniac be much less likely to

<column-break/>

acquire <term>dominium</term> <note>Ownership or legal property rights.</note> than a usurer? For otherwise, even if a formal pact had intervened, both would be able to acquire ownership.

<margin>Cajetan's solution</margin>
¶ **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian of the Dominican order.</note>, therefore, proceeds by a far different path. He says, I say, that simony is different from usury: for he who pays usury, he says, gives unwillingly. Therefore, he by no means acquires ownership. In simony, however, both give voluntarily; for since a <term>prebend</term> <note>A stipend or portion of church revenue.</note> is by its own nature valuable (as it seems to him) for a price, he who receives it willingly pays the price. Therefore, unless the Church prohibited the transfer of ownership, the giving would hold on both sides; and because the Church does not prevent it unless a pact is involved, both emerge as owners.

<margin>The reasoning of "unwilling" and that of Cajetan.</margin>
But neither does this solution satisfy a hesitant mind: for a simoniac seems just as "unwilling" to provide the price as he who accepts usury; indeed, he would prefer to receive the thing for free, as the other was bound by divine law to provide it. Finally, there are innumerable other expositions of this text, which is an indication of its great obscurity.

<margin>Opinion of the author.</margin>
¶ Therefore, so that I may proceed to explain the matter as clearly as I possibly can, the whole doubt depends on what we have placed here from the preceding parts to be unknotted: namely, whether the restitution of both the simoniacal price and the spiritual thing is of divine and natural law. And first of all, let this be most confessed: that on both sides simony is committed against divine law—that is, on the part of the buyer as well as the part of the seller. By this reasoning, as we have explained above, simony differs from usury: because not only the seller, but also the buyer, opposes the nature of the grace of spiritual things, which ought not only to be given for free, but also received as a gift of God. Secondly, this also is most certain: that restitution on both sides in simony is thus far of divine law, because it is founded in such a divine prohibition of selling and buying. But this is what I find disputed by no one—though it ought to be examined by all interpreters of this chapter—namely: whether by divine law the transfer of both the spiritual thing received for a price and the ownership of that same price is hindered. For if by divine law a simoniac becomes incapable of receiving, then the Church could in no way bring it about that a "mental simoniac" (for instance, one believing something was given to him as a price) could acquire ownership. If, however, the transfer of that same ownership is hindered by ecclesiastical law alone, the Church could indeed hinder it when a pact intervenes, but permit it where no pact exists.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
And indeed, Cajetan has entered upon this second path. For he judges that although...

### Question 8 of the Ninth Book

<margin>First reason in Cajetan.</margin> Although spiritual matters are commanded to be given and received freely, they are nonetheless valuable by their very nature. Therefore, someone who pays a price for them of their own accord, while certainly sinning against the divine prohibition, nevertheless transfers the <term>dominium</term> <note>Dominium refers to the legal right of ownership or property rights.</note> of that payment, except in cases where the Church has blocked such a transfer. I admit that this perspective makes the literal meaning of the text quite clear. 

On the other hand, however, I will strive to argue—though I am not sure I can fully persuade—that the transfer of ownership, at least regarding the price paid, is blocked by divine law; for there is not as strong a consensus regarding the spiritual thing purchased. Let us begin with the divine prohibition itself, where Christ says: **"Freely you have received, freely give"** <note>original: "Gratis accepistis, gratis date" from Matthew 10:8.</note>. By this, He intended to remove every right to receive anything in exchange for the spiritual. If He left no right to receive, it follows that the one receiving the price in no way becomes the owner, as God forbids it; for surely, no one can be established as the owner of a thing except by some right.

<margin>Second reason.</margin> Secondly: One who gives a loan is bound to restore the interest precisely because he ought to lend freely. A <term>prelate</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note> is bound by the same divine law to confer spiritual things; therefore, by that same law, he is rendered incapable of becoming the owner of any payment received for them. Now, if you say a usurer is bound to restore not for that reason, but because he sells the use of money separately (which has no value in itself), the same argument applies to a spiritual matter. For everyone admits that a spiritual thing is not a commodity that can be valued in money. 

If you respond that it is valuable by its nature—at least where a priesthood yields financial fruit—it is nonetheless proven that these are not for sale. For when someone accepts a public salary to administer a magistracy on the condition that he administers it freely, if he receives anything beyond the set price, he does not become the owner but is bound to make restitution. Ecclesiastical prelates are of this kind: therefore, if any of them receives anything for conferring spiritual things, they are bound by divine law to return it. This is especially true since neither the Pope nor any bishop is the "owner" of spiritual things, but merely the <term>dispenser</term> <note>A steward or administrator who manages property on behalf of the true owner, in this case, God.</note> of his Lord’s goods, who commanded everyone to do this freely.

<margin>Third reason.</margin> Therefore, they acquire ownership of the price neither as owners nor as dispensers. Furthermore, there is a very pressing argument: if the transfer of ownership in simony were prohibited only by pontifical law, it would follow that if someone demanded payment for administering the sacraments (other than holy orders), they would truly acquire legal ownership. For in pontifical law, such a transfer is only read as prohibited (as Saint Thomas says in the present article) regarding the conferring of orders, benefits, and entry into a religious life—in which cases

<column-break/>

contracts are considered null and void, as was said above. Truly, therefore, it is highly probable that in this sense also, restitution was commanded in simony by divine law.

<margin>That it must be restored by divine law according to Henry of Ghent, FitzRalph, and Adrian.</margin> This is something the ancients always believed: such as **Henry of Ghent** in *Quodlibet* 6, question 26, and **Richard FitzRalph** <note>The Latin text calls him "Armachanus," referring to the Archbishop of Armagh.</note> in Book 10, chapter 23. **Adrian** <note>Adrian of Utrecht, later Pope Adrian VI.</note> also adheres to them in *Quodlibet* 9, article 3. Indeed, **Saint Thomas** seems to feel the same way here; since he derives the obligation of restitution in simony from no other source than the word of Christ: **"Freely you have received, freely give."** Although 

<margin>Cajetan, Sylvester, Panormitanus.</margin> **Cajetan** here and in his *Summa* (under the entry "Simony"), and **Sylvester** in section 2, and **Panormitanus** (cited above), follow the contrary opinion.

I would say, however, that there is not as much certainty regarding the simoniacal acquisition of the spiritual thing itself being void by divine law. Firstly, because although the one giving the price sins against the nature of grace, yet while he gives it of his own accord, he does not seem to be rendered incapable of receiving the spiritual office. Secondly, and most importantly, because if it were void by divine law, the Pope could in no way grant a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A formal exemption from a law or requirement.</note> for it. Yet there is a common consensus that if the Pope simoniacally confers a <term>benefice</term> <note>An ecclesiastical office that provides a living or income.</note> on someone, although both parties act wickedly, the appointment still holds—as will be debated in the next article.

Holding, therefore—as I judge to be by far more certain—that restitution in simony is commanded by divine law, it remains to respond to the cited chapter, which is not easy. Passing over other solutions, there are two that can be considered of some importance. One is that although someone offered something to a prelate as a price,

<margin>First interpretation of the aforementioned chapter.</margin> yet without an express agreement, ownership did not transfer to him. However, because restitution is not to be made to the giver, but to the Church, the Pope was able to grant that money to the same prelate and thus free him from the bond of debt. But this does not seem at all 

<margin>Reasoning against the previous solution.</margin> probable to me: that the Church can condemn anyone to a penalty before a conviction for the crime. Therefore, the Church could not deprive the one who gave the price of his rights as long as his crime remained hidden. For this reason, **Adrian** rightly says in the 

<margin>Adrian.</margin> place cited (*Quodlibet* 9) that the Pope cannot remit the restitution which must be made to the party who gave the payment, but only that which must be made to the Church. Although even this can be applied to the text with some probability: for those "mental simoniacs" <note>Those who committed simony in intent or thought without a formal contract.</note> among the monks were revealing their own crime when they sought a dispensation. Therefore, the Church could already fine those who had given the price and grant it to the Church, and thus...

### [Page 792]
#### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...so far as to waive restitution for the one who was in possession. Nevertheless, for this reason, this solution does not entirely fit the text, because in that passage the Pope does not appear to confer any benefit of <term>indulgence</term> <note>In this legal context, an indulgence refers to a formal grant of leniency or a waiver of a legal obligation, rather than the more common religious sense of remission of temporal punishment for sin.</note>; rather, he seems to respond exactly as the law requires.

<margin>Second solution which the author approves.</margin>
¶ There is, therefore, another solution from Adrian <note>Adrian of Utrecht, later Pope Adrian VI, a significant theologian and contemporary of Soto.</note> in the place cited, which, if looked at closely, will—in my judgment—be very pleasing. Indeed, the Pope there in no way decrees that in cases of mental simony the resignation of spiritual offices or the restitution of temporal goods is unnecessary; on the contrary, he teaches the opposite. However, a reading that poorly places the periods and commas generates an error. For commonly, after the narrative of the case, the response is divided into two parts: specifically, after the word "extended," a <term>rubric</term> <note>A rubric is a title or heading in a legal text, traditionally written in red ink, which summarizes the following section.</note> is inserted. From there, it is read as a new clause: "And regarding the resignation of spiritual and temporal things which [were acquired] by no pact but by a preceding affection of the soul: in which case it suffices for the delinquents to satisfy their Creator through penance alone: they are not held liable for simony of this kind." Thus, this last phrase is referred back to what preceded it: namely, that they are not held to the resignation of temporal and spiritual things. 

This is certainly not what the Pope—who was Gregory IX—appears to have intended. For Gregory I <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note>, as is clear in the canon *Si quis neque* <note>original: "Si quis neque" meaning "If anyone neither," a reference to a specific chapter in the Decretals.</note>, seems to have established the opposite: where he warns that whoever has accepted an ecclesiastical dignity through a "fraudulent little gift" is bound to resign it under pain of damnation. A "fraudulent little gift" clearly signifies that which a fraudulent mind assumes without an express pact; for where a formal agreement intervenes, it is not fraud, but open iniquity. Therefore, it is not credible that Gregory IX wished to teach the contrary.

<margin>How the cited text ought to be read.</margin>
¶ Therefore, so that the text may be read correctly, the specific case of the chapter must be presented first. Certain individuals, having given a price with a depraved intention but without a pact, were received into a religious order; and perhaps they had given some <term>prebend</term> <note>A portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman.</note> to the monastery, and furthermore some temporal gift. Afterward, being moved by remorse, they sent to Rome so that a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A formal exemption from the rigors of the law granted by the Church.</note> might be made for them. The Pope indeed sent a mandate that it should be done. However, their Abbot later doubted the extent of the mandate regarding two points: namely, whether the faculty extended to Abbots so that he himself could dispense with them; and likewise, whether it extended even to dispensing with resignations, so that they would not happen on either side—specifically, so that the community would not be bound to resign, but could retain everything that the monks had contributed. He responds, therefore, to both.

<column-break/>

The Pope responds affirmatively, saying: "Our mandate having been received, so that regarding the monks who, through simony, by giving something (namely a gift both temporal and spiritual) have obtained a place in the monastery according to the constitution of the General Council" (namely the Council of Constance <note>A 15th-century ecumenical council that addressed the Western Schism and issues of Church reform.</note>, as found in the chapter *Quoniam* reported a little earlier in the same title) "and so forth." The response follows: "Responding briefly to your consultation, we say that the Apostolic mandate (that is, the faculty of dispensing) is extended to Abbots (so that they themselves may have the power to dispense) and to the resignations of spiritual and temporal things." 

Thus, the word "extended" is carried into what follows: but the interlaced rubric obscured the matter and subsequently perverted the reading, so that it was understood that they were "not held to resignations." You ought, therefore, to read it thus: "It is extended to Abbots so that they themselves may dispense, and it is extended to resignations, both temporal and spiritual, provided that no pact intervened: namely, so that the Abbot may dispense, lest the resignation of both temporal and spiritual things, which would otherwise be necessary, should occur." He adds: "which are acquired in such a way on both sides": meaning that it is dispensed so that neither the monastery must restore what it had received, nor must the monks be forced to leave; which otherwise, according to the tenor of the said Council, they were bound to do, and to move to another monastery. 

The Pope therefore says that in that case—that is, once the dispensation is made—it suffices for the delinquents to satisfy their Creator through "penance alone." The word "alone," therefore, does not exclude the fact that by the nature of simony, both the resignation of spiritual things and the restitution of temporal things would have had to be made. On the contrary, since he says the mandate of dispensing is extended to this, he openly teaches that a dispensation was necessary regarding these things. Rather, it excludes those things ordered in the said Council: specifically, that the monks should not exit the monastery, but stay in their place with penance alone. Certainly, to me, this response seems more than sufficient to explain the force of the chapter; and thus, since the common opinion—that mental simony does not bind one to restitution—is founded on this single chapter, there is no reason to put faith in it.

<margin>Objection from St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ But St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic theologian.</note> remains to be answered: since he says in the present solution that it is enough for a person guilty of mental simony to repent for their evil intention.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
To him, it is responded that he does not speak of mental simony in the way the common opinion understands the said chapter *Mandato*; otherwise, since it was already extant among the Pontifical decrees then, he would have cited it.

[set.] But he calls a "mental simoniac" one who intends to give or receive a price for a spiritual thing, even if they do not actually give it. Let us therefore summarize our view. If a prelate has received something for the <term>collation</term> <note>Collation is the formal legal act by which a bishop or other authority confers a church office or "benefice" upon a person.</note> of a spiritual thing, even without an express agreement, believing that it was given to him as a price, he certainly acquires no more ownership over it than a usurer does. Thus, he is bound to restore it to the one who gave it. However, if he later discovers it was not given as a price, he may keep it. Yet, if at the time he confers a <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office, like being a priest or bishop, that comes with a guaranteed income or property.</note> he knows that gifts were paid to him as a price, the collation does not hold. If, however, when he conferred it, he did not believe it was given as a price, the collation is valid on his part; but if he later learns it was given as a price, he is bound to restore it, and the collation is considered invalid due to the legal "inability" of the buyer. Indeed, until I or the experts of the Church teach me otherwise, I cannot persuade myself of anything else.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether the Supreme Pontiff can grant a dispensation regarding the penalties for simony.<-

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
Lastly, it is asked whether the penalties for simony are <term>dispensable</term> <note>A "dispensation" is a formal legal waiver where a superior authority (like the Pope) allows a person to be exempt from a specific law or penalty.</note> by the popes. It is argued in the negative: whatever the Pope can do for the whole Christian family, any bishop can do in his own diocese; but none of them are able to dispense from penalties of this kind; therefore, neither can the Pope.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
Second: One of the most significant penalties, as we discussed in the previous article, is the resignation of spiritual offices and the restitution of temporal goods. No mortal seems able to grant a dispensation for this, since such restitution appears to be commanded by divine law.

<margin>The third argument.</margin>
Thirdly: If such a power existed in the Pope, it would open a wide path to the "pit of simony." For the Pope could then dispense for himself, so that he might sell priesthoods whenever he wished, and the conferring of those offices would nonetheless remain valid.

¶ On the contrary is the text in the chapter *Mandato* (recently explained) regarding simony, where the Pope granted the power to dispense in cases of simony. This is confirmed by very famous practice.

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with two conclusions. First: The penalties decreed for the vice of simony are four or five in number. The first—if it can truly be called a penalty—is the resignation of spiritual offices and the restitution of temporal goods. This

<column-break/>

<margin>Proof.</margin>
is clear from the chapters cited above, *Si quis episcopus* and the chapter *Presbyterum* [1. q. 1.], as well as the chapters *De hoc* and *Audivimus* concerning simony. It is also found in the <term>Extravagantes</term> <note>Decrees or "Letters" from Popes that were circulated outside the main organized collections of Canon Law at the time.</note> of Martin, Eugenius, and Paul II, specifically in *Cum detestabile*. According to these, a simoniacal contract is considered null and void—whether that declaration is a matter of divine law, as I believe, or an ecclesiastical decree. Where a contract is null, a bond of restitution immediately arises from it. For this reason, it should not strictly be considered a "penalty," but rather a natural obligation for each person to give back what belongs to another. Therefore, no legal sentence needs to be waited for (as we said above).

The second penalty is Papal excommunication, as is clear from those same *Extravagantes* and the canon *Reperiuntur* [1. q. 1.]. This is incurred *ipso facto* (by the very fact of the act) through the sentence of the law itself and its inherent warning (as we explained in Book 1).

The third is suspension from the function of the orders that are received through simony, as is clear in the same chapter *Si quis episcopus* and *Reperiuntur*, and in the same *Extravagantes* of Martin and Eugenius. Furthermore, the penalty of excommunication is common even to the "middlemen," as is clear there. Thus, those who provide the means for others to contract simoniacally are excommunicated by the very fact.

<margin>Under the old law, whoever was a witness to simony with certain knowledge was bound to reveal it under penalty of anathema.</margin>
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
Indeed, all who were witnesses to simony with certain knowledge were bound under the old law to reveal it under penalty of <term>anathema</term> <note>The most severe form of excommunication, involving a formal curse and exclusion from the Christian community.</note>; they could not be absolved before they revealed it, as read in the *Extravagant* of Martin. However, as Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prierias, an influential 16th-century Dominican theologian and canonist.</note> noted under the word "Simony" (§ 19), this was understood only for those who were present in the Roman Curia. In fact, he says that even that moderated law has no force now, as it has been abolished through disuse. Furthermore, the penalty of <term>irregularity</term> <note>A legal status that prevents a man from being ordained or performing the duties of a priest or bishop.</note> is not expressly named under this term in the law, nor in the *Extravagant* *Cum detestabile*, where all penalties are listed.

Nevertheless, the suspension from office of one who simoniacally received or conferred orders is a type of irregularity. Moreover, since all simoniacs are excommunicated, if they later celebrate [Mass], they become irregular by the common law of excommunication. Indeed, even if they do not celebrate, as long as they are excommunicated, they cannot be promoted to other orders, which is another form of irregularity. For this reason, Saint Thomas [Aquinas] in Article 6, in his response to the seventh point, judges that the greatest dispensation that can be made with a simoniac is that he may attain higher orders in the same church; there he denotes that simoniacs are irregular.

Finally, the last penalty is <term>infamy</term> <note>A legal status where a person loses their good name and certain civil or religious rights.</note>, as held in [15. q. 3.] in the canon *Sane* and in the chapter *Inquisitio*...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral inquiry into simony—the illicit sale of sacred things. Having previously established that simony is a grave sin against divine law, the author now examines the limits of the Pope's authority to grant "dispensations" (legal exceptions or pardons) for those who have committed this crime.</meta>

<margin>
The final conclusion.
The reason for the conclusion.
</margin>
...inquiries. ¶ **The final conclusion:** The Supreme Pontiff alone has the power to grant a dispensation to one who has been tainted by the stain of simony. The first part of this is clear because, since he possesses the fullest power to remit sins, it follows that he is able to remit any of their penalties for a just cause; otherwise, the Christian family would be left without a remedy. Furthermore, all penalties that are truly punishments—with the single exception of <term>restitution</term> <note>Returning the ill-gotten gains to their rightful place.</note>—are decreed by ecclesiastical law, over which the Pope himself exercises the fullest authority. However, the latter part of this conclusion is not as certain; indeed, Saint Thomas [Aquinas], in the place cited just above (Article 6, Question 6), thinks otherwise. He says that the Pope alone can dispense with someone who has knowingly obtained a <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office that provides an income.</note> through simony. But in other cases, he believes even a bishop can do so. Indeed, by his <term>ordinary power</term> <note>The standard legal authority inherent in the office of a bishop.</note>, a bishop is able to absolve someone from any crime committed, unless the Pope restrains that power by reserving the case for himself. Therefore, as the common opinion of the Doctors holds (which Sylvester [Prieras] records under the word *dispensatio*, section 14), a bishop cannot dispense against a canon of the Pope or a Council. Since all penalties for simony have been established by the decrees of Councils or Supreme Pontiffs, it is now the custom that only the Pope or a Council may dispense. At least in the case of simony regarding Holy Orders or a conferred benefice acquired knowingly, there is no doubt that this is reserved to the Pope alone, as is held in the <term>Extravagant</term> <note>A type of papal decree that "wandered" outside the standard legal collections of the time.</note> *Cum detestabile* of Paul II. The same must be judged regarding entry into religious life, as is clear in the said chapter *Mandato*, where it is established that the Pope alone was consulted on this matter. Furthermore, Martin V, in his own Extravagant, strikes down even the simoniacal reception into a monastery with the blade of <term>anathema</term> <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church.</note>; therefore, absolution for this belongs to the Pope alone. However, if something is given or received simoniacally in the receiving or administering of other sacraments, Saint Thomas believes the bishop can dispense.

<margin>
Excommunication of every simoniac is reserved to the Pope under the new law.
</margin>
Nevertheless, the more recent decree, *Cum detestabile*, strikes every single act of simony with an excommunication reserved to the Pope alone. For it says that whoever commits simony in any way—by giving or receiving, or by acting as mediators or procurers—shall incur the sentence of excommunication, from which they cannot be absolved except by the Roman Pontiff, except at the point of death. Since, therefore, it says "in any way," I would not dare to set any simoniac's conscience at rest until he has approached the Supreme Pontiff or his vicar. ¶ There are, however, levels of dispensation formerly used regarding simony,

<column-break/>

<margin>
Four levels of dispensation regarding simony.
</margin>
four in number, which Saint Thomas recounts in the same Article 6. For there was the Small, the Great, the Greater, and the Greatest dispensation. The **Small** was so that a simoniac might be admitted to communion with the laity. The **Great** was so that, after penance, he might remain in his <term>order</term> <note>His rank as a member of the clergy, such as a priest or deacon.</note> but in a different church. The **Greater** was so that he might remain in the same church, but only in the <term>minor orders</term> <note>Lower ranks of the clergy, like acolytes or lectors, who were not yet priests.</note>. But the **Greatest** was so that he might remain in the same church and even be promoted to <term>major orders</term> <note>The higher ranks: subdeacon, deacon, and priest.</note>; yet never to the dignity of a prefecture. For this was never granted in the past. Indeed, as the same Holy Doctor says there, not a word was heard regarding dispensation until restitution had been made of both temporal and spiritual goods. In the present day, however, dispensations for all these things are easily granted.

<margin>
To the first argument.
</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, he responds: Whatever bishops can do by their ordinary right, the Pope has nonetheless rightly summoned such dispensations and absolutions to himself out of a hatred for simony. This was done so that if all diocesan bishops were to exercise the same power, the jaws of simony might not open wider due to the ease of obtaining a dispensation.

<margin>
To the second.
</margin>
¶ To the second, it is responded that a dispensation regarding simony can be considered in two ways. One way is **after the fact**; the other is **so that it may be done**. And indeed, after the fact, there is no controversy that the Pope can dispense regarding all penalties and restore the simoniac to his former honor and place. To that extent, he can dispose of not only the fruits [income] but also the price of the simony at his own discretion. For once the crime has been brought to his court, restitution is not to be made to the one who gave the bribe, but to whomever the Pope designates. In the latter way, however, the Pope can by no means dispense so that someone may buy a spiritual thing for a price; such buying and selling would remain a sacrilegious and monstrous crime, since it is forbidden by divine and natural law—whether he dared to dispense for another or for himself. Indeed, whenever he might sell spiritual things for a price, both he and the buyer would be entangled in the same execrable vice of simony. He can, however, dispense from excommunication, infamy, and other ecclesiastical penalties, so that a simoniacal contract might be celebrated without the guilt of those specific punishments.

<margin>
A doubt.
</margin>
¶ **But a doubt** remains regarding restitution: specifically, if he himself, or another receiving the price, were to confer a spiritual gift, would the dispensation be valid to the extent that the conferring of the office would hold, and the price would remain free from the obligation of restitution? In truth, I do not know if the ancient fathers...

It details the four historical levels of such pardons and clarifies that while the Pope can remit legal punishments after the fact, he cannot authorize the act of buying or selling spiritual things because it violates divine law.</summary>

### Book Nine, Question VIII.

<margin>Solution.</margin> ...they would confess this. For Saint Thomas [Aquinas] does not allow a dispensation except on the condition that the spiritual offices have first been resigned and the temporal goods restored. Although it could be said that he was only speaking of a legitimate dispensation <note>A dispensation granted for a just cause, rather than one obtained through corruption.</note>. Therefore, it must be said that if the opinion is true—that by divine law a simoniac is ineligible to receive a <term>prebend</term> <note>A portion of cathedral or collegiate church revenues.</note>—it is not within the Pope’s power to make that appointment valid. And thus, whoever believes the premise must necessarily confess the conclusion. And I admit, if common opinion did not cry out against it, I would speak thus. Nevertheless, let us admit—as we suggested above while hesitating—that such an appointment, though bought with a price and therefore wicked, is not so hindered by divine law that it cannot hold; however, that Pope who would commit such a crime would be remarkably wicked (if I may say so without impiety). But if he were to sell it, I have no doubt that he would always be bound to restore the price; since (as has often been said) the transfer of ownership of such a thing is null by divine law. ¶

<margin>To the third.</margin> From here, a step is taken toward the solution of the third argument. For it must be conceded that the power to grant a dispensation in this way—so that a simoniacal appointment to the priesthood remains firm—is by its very nature a cliff-edge leading to the abyss of simony. However, we must trust in God that he will never, or only very rarely, allow his Vicar [the Pope] to fall into such an absurd sacrilege. ¶

<margin>Doubt.</margin> Whether, by the very fact that a Pope grants himself a dispensation to sell a priesthood, he likewise grants a dispensation to the buyer to receive it—I do not mean regarding the guilt (since he cannot do that), but so that the buyer might be the true possessor:

<margin>Solution.</margin> we have already left an affirmative answer in Question 5, following Paludanus <note>original: "Palud." Referring to Peter de Palude (c. 1275–1342), a French theologian and canonist.</note> con-

<column-break/>

<margin>Cajetan.</margin> -trary to Adrian <note>original: "Adrian." Referring to Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), known for his strict moral stance.</note>. Cajetan <note>original: "Caietan." Referring to Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note>, however, first opposes this same opinion here, though later he seems to support it. For the true reason he constructs against it is not of primary importance. For he argues that since the Pope's act of selling is not an explicit dispensation, it should not be presumed unless right reason

<margin>Cajetan's Reason.</margin> persuades one of it. Indeed, reason rather suggests the opposite: because from such a presumption it would follow that everyone everywhere would approach the Pontiff to buy priesthoods, and nothing could be more destructive than that. Therefore, he says, even if there is wickedness in the Pope who sells, it would be worse if he were presumed to dispense while selling:

<margin>Solution.</margin> because it would double the sin. It is answered, however, that right reason rather suggests that the same dispensation should always be presumed; for if he were to sell without a presumed dispensation, his crime would be doubled even worse. For he would not only attempt to sell a priesthood, but he would also employ an even more wicked fraud: namely, that while receiving the price, he would be conferring nothing; since unless he rendered the buyer immune from excommunication and made him legally capable, the appointment would not hold. Nor does the path to simony become more open in this way. Furthermore, if a dispensation were not presumed by the very act, a Pontiff who wished to be wicked would sell just as easily—and expressly dispense at the same time—as he would sell without a dispensation. Finally, and most importantly, even though such a power exists in the Pope, since its use is so detestable, one should not fear so badly of him that such an occasion would cause a rush of priests to him for the purpose of selling priesthoods.

# BOOK TEN
->On Justice and Law.<-

<margin>Summary of the book.</margin>
### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring two figures in classical robes within an architectural frame.</image-desc>WE promised that this tenth book—which serves as the conclusion to our intended work—would address the order of Bishops, and specifically their residency within their own dioceses. For after we completed, in the first seven books, all the types of justice and injustice that fall directly under that category, it was our intent to weave into the subsequent three books the subject of religion, which is closely linked to justice itself. In this way, we believe we have dealt as best we can with the entire business of justice and law, which is the title we gave to this work. Therefore, we thought we could apply a "finishing touch" <note>original: "colophonem"</note> to the work in no more useful, beautiful, or fitting way than by turning our final efforts toward the dignity and function of the Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials, specifically bishops.</note>. In them, the sacred pillar of justice ought to shine most prominently above everyone else who is counted within the Christian religion.

<margin>Division of the book.</margin>
We have therefore divided the present book into five members and questions. In the first of these, the dignity and nature of their office is clarified, as well as the law by which it was established. In the second, we discuss the process of entering into an episcopal province. In the third, we discuss their residency. In the fourth, we discuss the reason and manner in which they are required to spend and distribute church revenues. And finally, in the fifth, we discuss the Divine Office <note>The daily cycle of prayers and psalms recited by the clergy.</note>, through the performance of which the clergy earn those same fruits of the church.

## QUESTION ONE,
### on the episcopal office and the law by which it was established.

#### ARTICLE I.

##### Whether the dignity of a bishop was necessary in the church above that of a priest.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a figure seated at a writing desk with books and a crucifix.</image-desc>THE beginning of our dispute must be taken from this point: that we weigh the reason for the episcopal "pinnacle" <note>original: "culminis," referring to the high status or peak of authority.</note>. For it appears that, besides the dignity of a priest, the episcopal dignity was not at all necessary for the church.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
Indeed, the dignity and power of ministers is weighed by their function. However, the function of a priest is the consecration and distribution of the most holy body of Christ, and no sacred act can be greater than that.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second: If one wishes to refer to symbolic figures, the priest carries the image of Christ in the church, insofar as He offered Himself for us on the altar of the cross. But no one higher than Christ can be imagined in the church—since He is its head—and therefore no representation can be more sublime. Thus, no power is more excellent than the priestly power.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ Third, to allude to the title of this question, even if that higher rank were possible, it was not necessary. This is because all ecclesiastical duties could be administered by individual priests. Access to them would actually be more convenient, as any parishioners could very easily run to their own local priest <note>original: "Plebanum," a parish priest.</note> to have their cases settled.

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
¶ On the contrary, however, is the tradition of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian mystic then believed to be an associate of St. Paul.</note>, writing in the age of the Apostles. In the 5th chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, he prefers the "Pontifical" <note>The rank of a Bishop.</note> dignity to the priestly one, saying that it is the role of priests to purify and illuminate the people, but it is the role of the bishops to do these same things and, above them, to "perfect" the work.

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
AT the very entry of the present treatise, we must place before our eyes the rank of the bishops, as well as their institution and function. Regarding this—to weigh the name first—we read in Jerome (who was skilled in Greek), in his epistle to Evagrius, which is cited in Canon 93, that bishops are called "superintendents."

<margin>What the word "bishop" sounds like in Latin.</margin>
For *Episkopōn* <note>original: "Ἐπισκοπῶν"</note> is the same as "superintending."

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine says the same thing regarding the epistle to Timothy (cited in Question 8, Canon 1), concerning those who seek the office of bishop. Although the word is Greek, it explains the intensity and attention of the mind, making it the same as "to look into,"

# Question I of the Tenth Book

...to watch [over them], and to remain vigilant with the full sharpness of the mind and the skill of the soul; so that to be a bishop is the same as standing on a perpetual watchtower <note>original: "specula"; a common metaphor for the bishop's office as an overseer.</note> and to watch over and look out for one's flock without weariness. Wherefore, as we begin to focus our eyes on the obligation of residency from this point forward, let no one deceive themselves with a narrow interpretation of Jerome and Augustine: namely, by thinking that a bishop is called a "superintendent" <note>The Latin *superintendens* is a literal translation of the Greek *episkopos*.</note> because, while priests are simply called "intendants," it is enough for a bishop to be "over" them—that is, to oversee their morals alone—and to entrust the rest of the flock to the priests. This would surely be a most harmful fallacy. For that prefix "super" [over/above] does not only signify that; it signifies a more thorough care and a more vigilant skill, which he owes not only to the priests but also to the entire flock. This care is far greater than that which simple Parish Priests <term>Plebani: local clergy who serve the common people or "plebs"</term> ought to have. For how else would the word of Christ contain the truth, by which he commends the Good Shepherd for the fact that he knows his own sheep by face and voice, and is known by them in return?

<margin>The duty of a Bishop is the same as that of a shepherd.</margin>
¶ Therefore, from the name itself, the proper and natural office and duty of the bishop is discovered. For he is nothing other than a shepherd; Christ most wisely observed this metaphor and analogy throughout the entire Gospel. Indeed, if the matter is looked at closely, it is perhaps not just a metaphor, but a literal property: for the education of the mind and the instruction of morals is truly the food <note>original: "pabulum"</note> of the soul. Since there were many other ranks of rulers and subjects, Christ did not wish to be called a King or a General (though he could have been), nor a Judge or a Consul; instead, he chose to be called a Shepherd, which most truly represented what he was: namely, the one who brought the reality and the name down from heaven. For since it is "noon" in that place where holy minds rest in ineffable leisure and enjoy the food of divinity—a noon which the bride in the *Song of Songs* pleaded to have shown to her—God himself, as a shepherd, professes to have descended to us, leaving behind the other ninety-nine sheep to seek the hundredth which was lost. For this reason, it was sung that he would come as a shepherd: *Isaiah 40: "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd."* Because of this, the Angels brought the first news of his birth to shepherds who were keeping watch over their flock. And immediately after, he solemnly likened himself to the Good Shepherd, who would not hesitate to even lay down his life for his flock. Remaining, therefore, in this same image of the thing, he did not substitute a vicar for himself in any other dignity than that he should be a shepherd of his sheep.

> For he said: **"Feed my sheep."**

By which word the episcopal office is most significantly expressed. Not only because

<column-break/>

all the benefits that Bishops owe to their people, as well as the harms they cause them through greed, or sluggishness, or cruelty, have a genuine similarity to the things found in shepherds and herdsmen (as the following very broad discussion will declare more clearly), but also because pastoral leisure, more than all other public activities, most deeply reflects that supreme peace and tranquility which Christ established to teach the world. For although the names of Kings and Generals designate magistrates who are just in their own duty,

<margin>The name of Shepherd expresses the function of the bishop much more correctly than others. Homer, Book 1 of the *Iliad*.</margin>
so much so that Homer asserted that a King is also a "shepherd of the people," nevertheless they cannot help but be frequently disturbed by wars. If, however, you call him a Consul or another kind of judge, it is necessary that they be overwhelmed by lawsuits. But the office of a Shepherd is furthest removed from all tumult; it is most sweet because of the innocence, silence, and simplicity of the sheep. And thus, it displays both that silence by which Christ wanted his family to be pulled away from earthly things to be free for the business of heaven, and also that sincere and most silent obedience which Christ wanted his sheep to show to his ministers without any back-talking.

<margin>Concluding response.</margin>
¶ Therefore, lest we proceed beyond our aim and forget our usual custom, the question is answered with a single affirmative conclusion: It was necessary for bishops to be established from among the priests, who would excel the others in dignity, authority, and function.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven: There are two natural powers belonging to the priestly dignity. The first and most important is the power of consecrating and administering the body and blood of Christ, to which all ecclesiastical religion is directed. The other power serves the first by preparing and adapting the people so that they may receive that most holy Synaxis <term>Synaxis: a Greek term for the Eucharistic gathering or assembly</term> according to the dignity of the matter; namely, by cleansing the people from sins, illuminating them with doctrine, and thus governing them. And indeed, as far as the first is concerned, a priest—by the very fact that he has been initiated into that sacred order—no longer depends on anyone else; by the very character of Christ, he is fully powerful in that duty, so that whenever he attempts to consecrate, he truly performs the sacrament. For this, therefore, he has no need of a superior. But as far as the second is concerned, it was most fitting and most in harmony with natural law that among the priests in a whole diocese there should be one who would govern the whole, and upon whom priestly jurisdiction would depend; so that, for example, priests could not rashly absolve any random person they meet from their sins. This pertains to the power of preparing...

He concludes that the episcopal office is necessary for the orderly governance and spiritual preparation of the faithful within a diocese.</summary>

### [F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right, Page 798]

...of governing the people, except through the jurisdiction distributed among them by the bishop. Therefore, the bishop is superior to priests, though not in the consecration of the body and blood <note>original: "consecratione corporis & sanguinis"; referring to the Eucharist or Mass</note>, yet certainly in jurisdiction. 
<margin>A fitting reason.</margin>
That this is consistent with natural reason is evident. First, if you look to the celestial things above, among those blessed minds there are distinct orders and hierarchies: namely, so that the lower may be illuminated by the higher. Among these are the angels, archangels, principalities, and so forth. Furthermore, God—who is the first cause of all things—produces and generates sublunary things <term>sublunary: things on Earth, literally "below the moon"</term> through the sublime spheres of the heavens and the stars. Likewise, in civil polities, orders of magistrates are also necessary: so that the common people are subject to judges, and the judges are subject to princes and kings. 
<margin>The conclusion is clarified.</margin>
But behold the root from which this reasoning springs. For the government of the people, great prudence, wisdom, and moral integrity are required, as well as the authority to compel those who wander back onto the path. These qualities cannot be found in such a vast multitude of priests; it was therefore necessary to set a bishop over both the people and the clergy themselves, who would be to them like the sun for illumination and like a standard <note>original: "norma"</note> for guidance. From this, consider how great a peak of dignity and holiness is necessary for a bishop. But another place below awaits for this discussion. If, moreover, one wishes to seek a particular example from the Old Law <note>The Old Testament/Mosaic Law</note>, you will see those same distinct ranks there. For although the entire tribe of Levi was dedicated to divine worship—as the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard, a primary medieval theological authority</note> noted in Book 4, Distinction 24—only Aaron and his sons were priests. Yet even they were not all equal: the father was the High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex"</note>, who alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies once a year, while his sons were simple priests. For this reason, Aaron was clothed in different ornaments (just as bishops are now) and was consecrated with a different anointing than the others, as read in Leviticus 8. Mention is made of this in the consecration of a bishop through that verse of the Psalm: *Like the ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron’s beard: that went down to the skirts of his garment.* <note>Psalm 133:2</note> For so great was the pouring out of the oil that it flowed down to the very bottom.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first of the main arguments, therefore, it is replied that although no function can be greater than the priestly one in consecrating the most holy species <note>the bread and wine</note>, nonetheless

<column-break/>

the episcopal dignity is superior regarding the other faculty of preparing the people. For the priest depends on the bishop for jurisdiction in the absolution of sins. 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
This is the solution of Saint Thomas [Aquinas] in Book 4 of the *Sentences*, Dist. 24, Q. 3, Art. 3. There, he does not seem to grant simply that the episcopal rank is higher than the priestly one, but only in terms of jurisdiction. 
<margin>Scotus. Durandus.</margin>
However, [Duns] Scotus in the same distinction, Art. 2, and Durandus [of Saint-Pourçain] in the same place, Q. 5, as well as others, proceed to grant simply that the episcopal order is inherently more dignified, because it includes the priestly faculty of consecrating the body [of Christ]. For as cautioned in the chapter *Ex Literis* regarding the excesses of prelates, no one can be consecrated as a bishop before he is a priest. Furthermore, it adds both the superior faculty of jurisdiction and the power to confer orders, and to consecrate and bless churches, vessels, and ecclesiastical vestments. Yet this matters little, and it comes to the same thing. For if you consider the bare dignity of consecrating, there is none greater in the bishop. Therefore, that which the bishop has over the priest is not more excellent than the priestly dignity itself. But since that same episcopal splendor presupposes the priestly one, its entire fullness is greater than its part. 
<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, it is replied that since Christ was the head of the Church, he was likewise the model of all ecclesiastical duties, just as God is the model of all natural things. Whence, as the Master of the Sentences says in the place just cited, all teachers of the Church—namely, each in his own order—represent Christ according to the various things He did; yet those represent Him more perfectly who reflect Him according to a higher quality. Priests, therefore, represent Him according to a specific and personal act by which He offered Himself on the cross for us. Bishops, however, represent Him not only in this (insofar as they are priests), but insofar as they are bishops, also according to the fact that He was the Head and the founder of the Church. Thus, they also consecrate the priests themselves and all ministers (which Christ did), and they bless all other ecclesiastical preparations which He instituted; and from the fullness of the Holy Spirit, they confirm the baptized.

### ARTICLE II.

->Whether the episcopacy is, by its nature, an order distinct from the simple priesthood.<-

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues for the superiority of bishops over priests based on jurisdiction, natural and celestial hierarchies, and Old Testament precedents like Aaron. He navigates scholastic debates between Aquinas, Scotus, and Durandus regarding whether this superiority is merely legal or inherent to their spiritual "order."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the status of the bishopric. The previous page established that while bishops and priests share the same power to consecrate the Eucharist, the bishop possesses a superior authority of jurisdiction and governance over the clergy and the faithful.</meta>

# Book Ten: Question I

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
It is not enough to know that a bishop performs a more excellent office than a simple priest; rather, one must examine whether they differ by the very nature of the thing <note>original: "ex rei natura"</note>. For it appears that the office is not an order distinct from the priesthood by its nature. Indeed, Jerome says in his letter to Evagrius (cited above) and again in his commentary on the Letter to Titus—which is recorded in Decree 95, canon "Olim"—that a bishop was once the same thing as a presbyter <term>presbyter: a priest or elder</term>. He confirms this with many sacred testimonies. For Paul says in the greeting of his Letter to the Philippians: *Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons.* Here he calls the presbyters "bishops," for there were not multiple bishops in a single church. For this reason, he groups bishops and deacons together. And in Acts 20: *Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops.* And to Titus, after he says he left him in Crete for the purpose of appointing presbyters throughout the cities, he adds: *For it is necessary that a bishop be without crime.* And Peter, who was a bishop, says in his first letter: *I, a fellow-elder, beseech the elders.* Therefore, the episcopal dignity does not differ from the priestly dignity by its own nature or institution.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If a bishop were distinct in order from a priest, such an order would be a true sacrament, and thus it would differ just as the sacramental character <note>An indelible spiritual mark imprinted on the soul</note> of a priest differs from that of a deacon. That this is false is evident from the fact that there would then be more than the seven traditional orders.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is the authority of Augustine in his letter to Jerome, which is cited in Question 2, canon 7, "Quanquam." There he says that according to titles of honor, it had already become the established use that the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate.

<margin>A distinction.</margin>
To understand the present question, it must first be noted that a bishop can be understood to excel other priests in dignity in two ways. In one way, within the same category: namely, within the line of the priesthood. In another way, as if he were in a higher category. For example, a priest differs from a deacon in a different category because there is a distinct sacramental character and a distinct consecration. However, an archdeacon differs from deacons, and archpriests from priests, within the same category: namely, because they elect one who may preside over them. Nor does it matter whether the Pope appoints one over them or they appoint one for themselves.

<margin>Jerome's opinion.</margin>
Jerome, therefore, seems to think that the bishop was once higher than presbyters only in this second way—that is, within the same category—namely, that it was established as a remedy for schism that one should be placed over the others from among the number of presbyters. He was, therefore, nothing but a "great presbyter." For a presbyter is nothing other than an elder, to be venerated and cherished for his age.

<column-break/>

<margin>The name "order" is used in two ways.</margin>
¶ Therefore, lest I proceed through synonyms and ambiguities, the name "order" is used in two ways. In one way, according to the breadth of its meaning, by which in the purest Latin it signifies every rank and dignity. For we speak of the order of senators, and of doctors, and of leaders. Hence Cicero very often calls the rank of consuls one order, and that of tribunes another, and so forth.

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
In the second way, through solemn usage, Christian theologians have adapted the name to signify one of the seven sacraments: such as the priestly order, the diaconate, etc.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Having supposed this, the question is answered with two conclusions. The first is: According to the first meaning, the episcopal power has always been by its nature a singular order: that is, a rank and dignity more sublime than the priestly one.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
This conclusion has its first foundation of all in the authority of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian then believed to be a direct disciple of St. Paul</note>, who lived in the age of the Apostles and enjoyed Paul as his teacher. For in the place cited above, in *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 5, he clearly and extensively distinguishes between bishops and other priests by the nature of the thing. For he says that "pontiffs" <term>pontiff: here used to mean a Bishop</term> participate fully in priestly perfection, as if the rest do not possess full perfection. And he adds: *Therefore, the order of Pontiffs is more sacred; it is the first of the divine orders of contemplation, and the same is both the highest and the last; for in it every distinction of our priesthood is perfected and fulfilled.* Just as we see the whole Hierarchy terminate in Jesus, so each function terminates in its own divine Pontiff. See how he sets the Pontiff before the rest of the clergy as a representative of Christ. He is, therefore, of a more restricted category. And more clearly he adds, according to another translation: *But to this man, beyond the other orders, the divine law has distributed more divine sacrifices in his operation.* These, however, are the perfecting images of divine power: completing all divine symbols and all sacred arrangements. For neither shall a priest perform sacred baptism without the most divine ointment <note>Chrism oil</note>, nor shall he even be a priest unless he has obtained that office from the pontiffs. See how broadly and eloquently he explains the difference between a bishop and a priest, and that by divine law: since no priest is ordained without a bishop.

<summary>This page explores whether the office of bishop is naturally distinct from that of a priest, weighing St. Jerome's view of original equality against the hierarchical distinctions asserted by Dionysius the Areopagite. The author concludes that, at least in terms of rank and dignity, the bishopric is a distinct and superior order established by divine law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the episcopal office, moving from the historical equivalence of bishops and priests to the specific theological reasons why the episcopacy is considered a distinct degree of dignity and power, while debating its status as a sacrament.</meta>

### Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

...nor can he use chrism <note>original: "chrismate"; holy oil used in anointing</note> unless it is prepared by a bishop, nor can he use garments or vessels unless they have been consecrated or blessed by the bishop himself: this is in addition to the higher jurisdiction he holds. Finally, he says this is sanctioned by divine law. For as we shall see in Article 4, the episcopacy was instituted by divine law: although the preparation of the chrism and other such ceremonies are believed to have been instituted by the tradition of the Apostles.

<margin>Another reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ From these words of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian theologian</note>, the following reasoning is gathered: That must be considered a distinct order—that is, a rank and dignity in the church—which possesses some proper and peculiar spiritual function ordained toward the sacrament of the Eucharist. Such is the episcopal rank: for, as has been said, it belongs to the bishop to consecrate priests and other ministers, and finally both the chrisms and the temples, and so also to confirm the people. Simple priests cannot perform these things; therefore, by its very nature, it is an order and rank distinct from the priestly one.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
¶ And this reasoning is confirmed: for such an order, rank, and power is recognized by its own solemnity. A bishop, besides the priestly anointing, is more solemnly anointed and consecrated, as if receiving a new power in the administration of sacred things. For while priests are only anointed on the hands for the purpose of consecrating the sacrament, the bishop’s head is anointed, just like Aaron’s was: to denote that he is the head of his church, just like Christ—as Dionysius recently said. The exception is that Christ is head not only over men, but also over angels and the entire creation.

<margin>Third reason.</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued that the assembly of bishops is a state of perfection far higher than that of monks. For they solemnly profess not to be taught, but to teach perfection: therefore, it is an order in itself. The example of the ancient law <note>The Old Testament or Mosaic Law</note> is also added: for the dignity of Aaron was higher by divine law than that of the rest of the priests. In short, the episcopal dignity is not established in a higher rank solely by reason of jurisdiction, nor for that reason did it require a difference in garments or anointing; rather, it is established by reason of spiritual functions. On this account, a bishop can exercise jurisdiction before his consecration, even though he does not yet possess the episcopal order, as is held in the chapter cited above from the letter *On the Excesses of Prelates*.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ Regarding the other meaning of "order," there is a controversy among the Doctors <term>Doctors: learned theologians of the Church</term> as to whether the episcopacy is an order—that is, a sacrament. Durandus believes the affirmative side in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 24, Question 5). And in the same Distinction, Scotus says this is the opinion of the Canonists <note>Experts in Church law</note>. Against them, a later conclusion is established. The episcopacy

<column-break/>

is not an "order" that is numbered among the seven sacraments. This is the opinion of Hugh <note>Hugh of Saint Victor</note>, a most weighty author, who after numbering the seven sacraments up to the priesthood, adds: "This order has different levels of dignity, such as the episcopal, etc." The Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard</note> follows the same in Distinction 24, as does Saint Thomas and the rest of his interpreters. And it is proven by reason. A bishop receives no new character <term>character: a permanent spiritual mark believed to be imprinted on the soul by certain sacraments</term> in relation to the consecrating of the body and blood of Christ. Therefore, since every sacrament of "order" is referred to this goal, the episcopacy is not a sacrament of order. The premise is proven: for if he were to receive such a character, it would be either lesser or greater than the priestly one. It is not lesser, for all functions of such characters (as seen in the deacon and subdeacon) are administrative in the consecration of the most holy sacrament. But a bishop, by his native nature, does not administer to the sacrament in this way. Nor can there be a character more excellent than the priestly one regarding this same matter. For the consecration of the sacrament—which any priest can do—is the peak and summit to which all other sacraments are referred.

<margin>Second reason of Saint Thomas.</margin>
¶ Saint Thomas provides a second argument in the place cited. The nature of a sacrament is that it does not depend on a preceding one for its necessity; however, the episcopacy depends on the priesthood. For as was said before, the consecration of a bishop would not be valid if he were not already a priest.

<margin>Scotus's solution.</margin>
In Distinction 24, Scotus eludes this argument rather than refuting it.

<margin>Refutation.</margin>
He says that from the fact that the episcopacy requires the priesthood, one should take it as an argument for its perfection. But this is irrelevant. For we are not disputing perfection here; rather, we are showing from the nature of the sacrament that it is not a sacrament, because otherwise, even without a prior priesthood, the consecration of a bishop would be valid—just as the consecration of a priest imprints its character even if he were not a deacon, as is read in the decree (Distinction 52, canon *Solicitudo* and *De clerico per saltum ordinato*).

<margin>Last reason.</margin>
Added to this is the rite of the church: the sacraments of order are conferred on the Sabbath <note>Saturday</note>, but the bishop, as a legitimate spouse of the church, is consecrated on the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note>.

<margin>Alexander. Bonaventure.</margin>
Therefore, this opinion is not only that of Saint Thomas, but of Alexander <note>Alexander of Hales</note> and Bonaventure, and the common opinion of all.

<margin>Argument of Scotus.</margin>
However, Scotus says in the cited place that the Canonists hold the contrary because of this argument: that unless the episcopacy were an order, it could be fundamentally taken away; for then nothing remains of it other than jurisdiction...

<summary>This page explores whether the episcopacy is a distinct sacramental "order" or a higher dignity within the priesthood. Soto concludes that while it is a distinct rank with unique spiritual powers (like ordaining), it is not one of the seven sacraments because it does not add a new spiritual "character" relative to the Eucharist.</summary>
