<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the office of a bishop (the episcopacy) constitutes a distinct "sacrament" or "order" compared to the priesthood, or if it is simply a higher level of authority (jurisdiction) and dignity.</meta>

# Book Ten: Question I

...anyone can be deprived of jurisdiction; indeed, a bishop is deprived of his church because of the crime of heresy and other reasons. And indeed, Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a highly influential Franciscan philosopher and theologian.</note> seems bound by this reasoning. For he agrees to grant that if the episcopacy is not a sacrament, nothing remains in it but removable jurisdiction.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
But truly, there is no necessary consequence in this. On the contrary, although a sacramental character <term>character: an indelible spiritual mark believed to be imprinted on the soul by certain sacraments</term> is not imprinted, nevertheless a certain priestly fitness and an indelible faculty are applied, which cannot be removed even by a bishop, as Bonaventure says in the place cited. Therefore, if a deposed bishop is restored again to his order, he has no need to be consecrated a second time.
<margin>Durandus.</margin>
But Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a Dominican theologian known for his independent and often controversial views.</note> also, in the same distinction, question 5, denies our conclusion by another path. He concedes, I say, that the episcopacy is a sacrament—not indeed one distinct from the priesthood, but the priesthood itself in its perfected state. Thus, he says, a simple priest, although he possesses the priestly character in a basic sense, it is not yet entirely complete and perfect. He adds an example: just as the consecrations of the body and blood <note>The bread and wine of the Eucharist.</note> constitute one perfect sacrament, so too do the consecration of a priest and the consecration of a bishop. Therefore, he subsequently confesses that the episcopacy imprints the character of a perfect and complete priesthood.
<margin>Argument of Durandus.</margin>
The argument by which he convinced himself of this is that the episcopal dignity is ordered toward the sacrament of the Eucharist equally, or rather more perfectly, than the diaconate or subdiaconate, since the bishop himself institutes those ministers. From this, he concludes it is a more perfect sacrament.
<margin>Solution to the argument.</margin>
Responding both to him and his reasoning, we frankly admit that the episcopal dignity adds perfection to the priesthood, which it presupposes and includes; but that perfection is not of the essence of the priesthood, but rather accidental and accessory to it. Therefore, it does not constitute a true sacrament together with it, nor is it an integral part of it. Nor is it easy for the mind to grasp that two separate priestly characters are imprinted—one on a simple priest, the other on a bishop. Therefore, his reasoning does not follow. One might say: "The episcopacy is ordered toward the true body of Christ, therefore it is a sacrament." But it is further required that it be a power pertaining most closely to that act: namely, that its function be either the celebration of the Mass or its administration, as is the case with the diaconate and subdiaconate. But the function of a bishop is not of that kind; rather, it is to institute and prepare the ministers.
<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you argue back: a bishop, insofar as he is a bishop,

<column-break/>

confers certain sacraments, for instance, Holy Orders, which he could not do insofar as he is only a priest. Therefore, his own power is a sacrament, since power over one sacrament constitutes another sacrament.
<margin>Solution.</margin>
The consequence is denied. It only concludes that the episcopal power presupposes the priestly sacrament. For unless he were a priest, he would be unable to confer orders. Furthermore, William of Auxerre <note>original: "Altissiodorensis"; a 13th-century theologian.</note>
<margin>Opinion of William of Auxerre.</margin>
not only leans in the same direction as Durandus, but going further, says that the office of an archbishop is also a sacrament distinct from that of a bishop; he must therefore be brought into the discussion in the following article. ¶ Through these conclusions, therefore, the laws and the assertions of the saints that seem to vary are reconciled. For whenever you read of someone being "ordained" a bishop, you should not understand it in the same strict sense as when priests are ordained. This applies also to what Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose works were foundational for medieval law and theology.</note> says in the 21st distinction of the canon *cleros*: namely, that the order of bishops is fourfold. But nevertheless, as we asserted in the previous conclusion, there is no reason why you should hesitate to call it truly an "order." Although others, to remove ambiguity, call it not an "order" but a "dignity"; such as Hugh of Saint Victor 
<margin>Hugh.</margin>
in his work *On the Sacraments* cited above. And the Master of the Sentences <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1160), whose *Sentences* was the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>
<margin>Master of the Sentences.</margin>
in Book 4, distinction 24, says that outside the count of the seven sacraments, "There are also certain other names, not of orders, but of dignities, such as 'bishop'."

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that perhaps Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), a Church Father known for his views on the original equality of priests and bishops.</note> was influenced by the opinion that a bishop and a priest were the same thing by divine law alone, and that it was only by human decision that one of the priests was placed over the others. For besides the cited testimonies, he adds that at Alexandria, from the time of Mark the Evangelist until Heraclas and Dionysius, the priests always named as "bishop" one elected from among themselves and placed in a higher rank. He adds an example: just as deacons elect an archdeacon. However, I do not fully understand Jerome here, since he adds that a bishop can confer orders while a simple priest cannot; here he suggests a distinction based on the nature of the office, unless he wishes this only to be a matter of the church's legal arrangement, as he says at the end of the same cited chapter *olim* <note>original: "cap. olim"; referring to a specific chapter in the Canon Law.</note>. These words, as Durandus says, are worthy of great wonder. For he says that bishops are greater than priests more by custom than by the truth of the Lord's own arrangement, and that they ought to rule the church in common. Yet, since the above-cited Dionysius, already in the time of the Apostles...

Soto argues against Durandus and William of Auxerre, maintaining that the episcopacy adds accidental "perfection" and jurisdiction rather than a new sacramental character.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ecclesiastical hierarchy, specifically whether the distinction between a bishop and a priest is rooted in divine law, and begins a new inquiry into the hierarchical differences among bishops themselves, including archbishops and the Pope.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right.

<margin>Augustine</margin> ...argued by divine law that a bishop is distinguished from a simple priest. Indeed, Augustine says in his book *On Heresies* that the Arians <note>Arianism was a 4th-century theological movement; here, Soto refers to their view on church structure rather than their more famous views on the nature of Christ.</note> were infected by the error of saying that priests ought to be distinguished from a bishop by no difference at all. However, the words of Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), who famously suggested that in the early church, "priest" and "bishop" were largely the same office.</note> should not be branded with such an infamous mark; for he himself acknowledges a difference both in the conferring of orders and in the eminence of the position, regardless of the law by which it was established. Yet, in this matter, we ought to listen more readily to Augustine and the other holy fathers, because that real difference traces its origin back to divine institution through the apostles. To those sacred passages
<margin>Jerome</margin> that Jerome brings forward, the response is that they only conclude that in the past, the names "bishop" and "priest" were used interchangeably: so that a bishop might be called a priest, just as a priest might be called a bishop. Thus, it was a name common to both to signify two
<margin>To the second argument.</margin> different dignities. ¶ To the second argument, enough and more than enough was satisfied by the second conclusion. For we concede that the episcopacy is an "order" according to the broadness of its meaning. But we deny that it is a sacrament.

### ARTICLE III.

*Whether bishops differ among themselves in the same way that they themselves differ from simple priests.*

<margin>First argument.</margin> **A**FTER it has been seen that the episcopal dignity differs from the priestly dignity by its very institution, the next thing to explore is whether bishops similarly differ among themselves. For it appears to be so: for it falls to an archbishop by his own proper office to consecrate a bishop, which seems not to be competent for a simple bishop except by commission; as is clear in the chapter *Quod sedem* concerning the office of the ordinary judge. For this reason, he also uses the pallium <term>pallium: a circular band of white wool worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and communion with the Pope</term>, which is not granted to a bishop; therefore, they differ in species. ¶ Secondly: The Pope at
<margin>Argument 2.</margin> least is more excellent in the species of his dignity than the others: since he is the successor of Peter, to whom Christ uniquely committed the entire flock. Wherefore he is also uniquely consecrated as Pope (even if he was already a bishop elsewhere), and he uses a singular Tiara <term>tiara: a triple crown worn by the Pope, representing his multifaceted authority</term>. For this reason, in Distinction 21, Pelagius <note>Pope Pelagius II (reigned 579–590), though the quote is often attributed in canon law to indicate the divine origin of the Papacy.</note> says that the Roman Church was not preferred to other churches by synodical decrees, but obtained the primacy by the Evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior. ¶ But on the contrary, in those things which pertain to the consecration of the body and

<column-break/>

blood <note>The bread and wine of the Eucharist.</note>, one bishop can do nothing that every individual bishop cannot do: as is clear in the conferring of orders and in their mutual consecration; for one consecrates another. Indeed, Hostiensis <note>Henricus de Segusio (c. 1200–1271), a famous expert in church law known as "Hostiensis" because he was the Bishop of Ostia.</note> consecrates the Pope, and yet if he were of an inferior power, he would be unable to do so; according to that passage in Hebrews 7: <note>original: "Sine vlla contradictione quod minus est à meliore benedicitur."</note> "Beyond all contradiction, that which is less is blessed by the better."

**T**wo parts of this question are suggested. The first concerns episcopal offices and functions. And the second concerns their distinction: since the knowledge of the latter depends on the understanding of the former. Therefore, the question is answered with two conclusions.
<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The first is: All functions that pertain to the office of a perfect pastor are peculiar and proper to a bishop. For it has already been shown above in Article 1 that the genuine task of a bishop is the office of a pastor; in testimony of which, while he is being consecrated, the pastoral staff <note>The crozier or shepherd's crook.</note> is handed to him. Indeed, he is designated as a pastor before he becomes the "spouse" of the Church by the ring. Therefore, all functions that are adapted to feeding the flock are parts and qualities of the episcopal dignity, insofar as it is common to all. ¶ But you may say, are not also the parish priests
<margin>A scruple.</margin> the pastors of their own parochial churches? They are indeed. However, they are not
<margin>Solution.</margin> in every respect absolute and perfect. Wherefore, all the collective duties of pastors do not fall upon everyone by reason of their dignity, but only certain ones. To understand this, it must first be noted that the
<margin>The office of a pastor.</margin> office of a pastor is to provide life to the flock, and to nourish, heal, and sustain the same. Now, functions of this kind are reduced to three types and orders. For first, this is done most especially through the administration of all the sacraments. For we are reborn through Baptism: then, having been confirmed, we are nourished by the Eucharist: and through Penance we are healed, etc. Therefore, those sacraments which are entirely necessary and fitting for this kind of life fall upon any parish priest to administer. Such are baptism, the Eucharist, penance, and sacred anointing; and furthermore, to bless spouses. Nevertheless, the ordaining of ministers falls to the bishop: and furthermore, for a more abundant supply of the Holy Spirit, to confirm the people. Therefore, in the administration of the sacraments, the pastoral office first begins to be more rich and perfect in a bishop than in a parish priest. Both because priests cannot confer all things, and also because those things which they can confer, they do so by juris- <meta>catchword: juris-</meta>

<summary>Soto concludes that the office of bishop is a distinct "order" established by divine authority, even if the names were once used interchangeably with priests. He then begins examining hierarchical ranks among bishops, noting that while all bishops share the same fundamental sacramental power, higher offices like archbishops and the Pope possess more complete pastoral authority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, specifically detailing the duties of the pastoral office and how the roles of parish priests and bishops differ in teaching, governance, and their status as successors to the Apostles.</meta>

# Question I of the Tenth Book

...possess by jurisdiction granted by the bishop.

<margin>It belongs to the pastoral office to teach the people.</margin>
¶ The second duty belonging to the same pastoral office is to teach the faith to the people. There are two degrees of this function. One is to explain those articles which are necessary for salvation. This specifically falls to the parish priests who have the care of souls. Wherefore, if there is great negligence in this duty, it is certainly a mortal sin for them. For they are bound to teach the people the Articles of Faith and the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>. Indeed, they must also teach the Lord’s Prayer: specifically those things which penitents must be asked if they know. For every Christian ought to know what they must believe, what they must do, and what they must ask of God. The other degree is to reveal the higher mysteries of the faith by explaining the Holy Scripture, and to imbue and instruct the flock in the uprightness of morals. This properly belongs to the office of the bishop. It is for this reason that during his consecration, when the Book of the Gospels is handed to him, it is said as a command: "Go and preach to the people of God" <note>original: "Vade & prædica populo Dei"</note>.

<margin>Governance and correction belong to the pastor.</margin>
¶ The third thing that pertains to the duty of a pastor is governance and correction; for in this way the life of the flock is preserved. It is clear how this faculty is full and complete in any bishop, unless it is restricted by the Pope. In a parish priest, however, there is none, or it is of the thinnest sort. He can command the people to hear the holy rites and receive the sacraments at the appointed times. However, whether he can compel them by excommunication or other punishment in the external court <note>The "external forum" refers to the church's legal and public jurisdiction, as opposed to the "internal forum" of private confession.</note>, we shall discuss a little further below.

<margin>Dionysius is explained.</margin>
¶ Through these points, one must grasp the understanding of the doctrine of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose writings on "Celestial" and "Ecclesiastical" hierarchies were foundational for medieval church structure.</note> cited above, who distinguishes three hierarchical actions—that is, actions of the sacred leadership—namely: to purge, to illuminate, and to perfect. He says the first belongs to the deacon, the second to the priests, and the third to the bishops. For to purge is to separate the pure from the impure, as wheat is separated by a sieve and flour by a sifter. For the deacon would examine those coming to baptism to see if they wished to forsake their former life and abjure their errors; thus he separated those worthy of baptism from the others. The priest, however, by instructing them in the catechism of the faith, would dip them in the sacred font; there, through "grace-making grace" <note>Sanctifying grace</note>, he would illuminate them. But the bishop confirmed them; that is, he perfected them through grace. Furthermore, through their preaching of what they had drawn from Holy Scripture, the bishops would more fully inflame them with divine love, in which Christian perfection consists.

<margin>Parish priests are truly pastors.</margin>
It should not be denied, therefore, that parish priests truly hold the care of souls, for which they will also have to give an exact

<column-break/>

account to God, and they are truly pastors. Nevertheless, the perfect and absolute name of "pastor" belongs only to bishops, as they are reminded by the very nature of their title.

<margin>Only bishops succeeded the Apostles.</margin>
¶ Through these points, it also becomes clear how all bishops—and only bishops—are those who properly succeeded to the place of the Apostles and perform their roles. This is held in the canon *In Novo*, distinction 21, and the canon *Ecclesiæ Principes*, distinction 35. This is supported by the authority of Augustine in the canon *Quorum Vices*, distinction 58, who says: "Instead of your fathers, sons are born to you." The Apostles were sent as fathers; instead of the Apostles, bishops were born as sons.

<margin>Three things in which the order of the Apostles consists.</margin>
To understand this, however, it must be noted that there are three duties in which the reality and order of the Apostles consist:
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
as Saint Thomas [Aquinas] noted regarding that word of Paul in 1 Corinthians 12: *God has placed some in the church first as apostles.* Namely: the authority to govern the faithful people; the faculty to teach the faith and Christian morals; and thirdly, the power to perform miracles for the confirmation of doctrine, according to Luke 9: *Jesus, having called the twelve Apostles together, gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases, and he sent them to preach the kingdom of God.* By this last word, it is understood that they should govern those who received the word, according to Luke 10: *He who hears you, hears me; and he who rejects you, rejects me.* And indeed, as far as the first duty is concerned, bishops have been substituted in their place. Nevertheless, each of the Apostles had power over the whole world of Christians, whereas bishops have power only in their own dioceses—except for the Pope alone, who, as the substitute for Peter, retains universal jurisdiction. Regarding the second power, which is to preach the faith, degrees must be distinguished. For the Apostles were so powerful in that virtue that (as Peter says in his second canonical letter), possessing the most firm prophetic word, whatever they preached was a matter of faith simply because they asserted it. Since they were the instruments through which the Holy Spirit spoke, they had no need to think about how or what they should say. This degree of power did not remain in the Church after the Apostles and Evangelists. The Pope and a Council can indeed explain articles of faith, but only those which are implicit in Holy Scripture or held most firmly by word of mouth from the tradition of the Apostles—namely, by using the foundation of Christ and subsequently of the Apostles. But the Apostles [acted] without the searching of Scripture, moved by the Holy Spirit...

It also explains the three hierarchical functions of purging, illuminating, and perfecting as they relate to deacons, priests, and bishops.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, specifically comparing the authorities of bishops and parish priests, their origins in the New Testament, and their varying degrees of jurisdiction.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

...were moved. Truly, in individual bishops, that same faculty which exists in the Pope and the Council does not reside; rather, they possess only the faculty of preaching, interpreting, amplifying, and persuading regarding those things which Christ taught through himself and through the Apostles.

<margin>The power to perform miracles is not present in the Church in the same way it was among the apostles.</margin>
¶ The third faculty, that of performing miracles, is not present in the Church now in the same way it existed among the Apostles: because the necessity is not entirely the same. Nevertheless, where the reason of faith required it today, God would not have his hand closed. Observe the difference between the pastoral function of a bishop and that of parish priests. And therefore, as read in the chapter *In Novo* <note>In the New [Testament]</note> cited above, just as bishops succeeded the Apostles (whom Christ is read to have chosen in Luke 9), so the rest who succeeded as parish priests represent the seventy-two disciples: whom Christ appointed to assist the bishops because the harvest was great, as read in Luke 10—namely, so that they might be auxiliary ministers. Therefore, by common law, it is the duty of bishops to institute priests in parish churches, as read in the chapter *Sicut*, Question 7 of Case 16.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ But you ask: does the duty of preaching also belong to them, along with some image of jurisdiction?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered, first regarding preaching, that it is certain that nothing further is required of them by necessity of office than to teach the Christian doctrine necessary for the people, as we were saying. However, whether it is a beneficial counsel to enjoin them with the duty of preaching was brought before the public council at the Council of Trent <note>A major 16th-century ecumenical council that shaped the Catholic Counter-Reformation</note>. At first glance, it appeared so to some of the Fathers; but there was one who humbly prayed that the opinion be more carefully weighed, after which the decree was postponed. For indeed, while it is proper and life-giving for those parish priests who are true theologians to bestow this service upon their people, it is most pestilential to commit it to those ignorant of theology. For the Church now lies in such a miserable state that in committing the care of souls, hardly any account is taken of dignity—except for the fact that parish priests do not even manage their own churches, but do so through vicars who barely know Latin, whom they hire for the lowest possible price. Add to this that in some provinces I have surveyed, those who are parish priests, although they have not even "greeted theology from the threshold" <note>An idiom meaning they have no education in the subject</note>, nevertheless, swelling with a bit of Latin and perhaps Greek, they think they can preach successfully. And these are the ones who spread most pestilential errors. It is therefore healthier for the people to lack such sermons than to be infected by them.

<margin>In a priest</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>no coercive power exists regarding the judicial court if viewed from bare authority.</margin>
Regarding the second part of the question, it is answered that in a priest, according to his own proper authority, no coercive power exists regarding the judicial court. This is seen most especially in excommunication, which is a punishment attached to the pastoral staff <note>A symbol of a bishop's authority</note>. To excommunicate by one's own authority belongs solely to the episcopal office, as held in Case 24, Question 3, Canon *Corripiantur*, and in the works of Saint Thomas Aquinas in his commentary on the *Sentences* (Book 4, Distinction 18, Question 2). However, that same Holy Doctor excepts theft and robbery, for which he says it is granted by law that a parish priest may excommunicate. Yet, that grant is no longer in use today. Nevertheless, it remains a sin of disobedience not to obey a priest in those things which we said above he can rightfully command: namely, that the people celebrate ecclesiastical feasts, receive the sacraments at the appointed times, and learn church doctrine. But unless contempt is present, there is no new mortal sin beyond the transgression of the ecclesiastical precept itself. Many more things could be added here regarding the duties and functions of bishops, which are very useful to know, but we have decided to reserve them for the third question, where they will be more conveniently discussed while treating the obligation of bishops to reside in their own churches.

<margin>Final conclusion.</margin>
¶ The final conclusion: Episcopal dignities—whether you mention an archbishop, a patriarch, or even the Supreme Pontiff himself—are not different in species <note>Theological category</note>, but differ only in the scope of their jurisdiction, some being superior or inferior to others. For Isidore says, as cited above from the canon *Cleros* (Distinction 21), that the order of bishops is fourfold: namely, Patriarchs, Archbishops, Metropolitans, and Bishops. A Patriarch is the highest of fathers and a prince; an Archbishop is a prince of bishops. For <term>archos</term> <note>original: ἀρχός</note> in Greek is the same as "prince." A Metropolitan is one who has jurisdiction circumscribed to certain cities; a Bishop is one who rules a single cathedral church. Now, there is no Metropolitan who is subordinate to an Archbishop; rather, they themselves are the Metropolitans. Patriarchs, however, such as those of Alexandria, Jerusalem, and Constantinople, each have several archbishops under them. Indeed, even the Roman Pontiff was formerly called a Patriarch. Regarding these dignities, William of Auxerre <note>original: Altisiodoren[sis]</note> says in his fourth book on Orders—at least regarding the episcopal and archiepiscopal ranks, for he does not mention the others—that they are truly sacraments and distinct from one another. For as argued in the first place, since a bishop ordains priests and other ministers...

# Question I of the Tenth Book

...ordains and consecrates, just as an archbishop has the duty of ordaining a bishop by his own office. Bishops, however, do so only by commission. Nevertheless, the conclusion we asserted must be beyond doubt. First, regarding the claim that episcopal dignity is a sacrament, this has already been sufficiently refuted above. Furthermore, it was proven that these orders of bishops do not differ from one another in kind, but are of the same genus and species.

<margin>Proof of the asserted conclusion.</margin>
For whatever an archbishop and a Patriarch can do, a bishop can also do in his own diocese—even consecrating bishops and the Pope. And although they perhaps do this by commission, this happens because of a lack of jurisdiction, not from a lack of episcopal dignity. In the same way, due only to a similar lack of jurisdiction, a priest cannot absolve anyone, even though by the power of his <term>character</term> <note>original: "virtute characteris"; in theology, an indelible spiritual mark on the soul.</note> he could do so for anyone indiscriminately. And through this, the argument remains resolved.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Regarding the second argument concerning the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note>, it is likewise denied that he excels others subject to him in the species of his dignity. But as for the universality of his jurisdiction, all laws grant him primacy. For regarding dignity, even the Bishop of Ostia is accustomed to consecrate him. Nor is there anything spiritual related to the consecration of Christ’s body that the Pope can perform which a simple bishop cannot also perform regarding his own dignity, unless he is restrained by the Pope by reason of jurisdiction. Therefore, the Supreme Pontiff relates to other bishops (regarding episcopal dignity) just as Peter related to the Apostles; he was their head insofar as they represented the Church, yet they were equals insofar as they were Apostles, as is held in the canon *In novo* <note>In the New [Testament]</note> cited above, Distinction 21. Truly, they were not ordained as bishops by him, but were appointed by Christ. Therefore, bishops excel priests by a higher kind of dignity, while the Pope excels bishops within that same kind; yet, as the Vicar of Christ, he is the head of all. Hence it was uniquely said to him first: "I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" <note>original: "Tibi dabo claues regni cœlorū"; Matthew 16:19</note>, although later in John 21 they were given to all; and it was said to him specifically: "Feed my sheep" <note>original: "Pasce oves meas"; John 21:17</note>, although in him it was said to all bishops, who were to be distributed throughout the world through him by reason of jurisdiction. For it was most fitting that Christ should commit his power to one head so that the entire Christian <term>polity</term> <note>The organized structure of the Church as a community.</note> might present an image of a spiritual kingdom, which is the best of all forms of government.

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE IV.
->*Whether the institution of episcopal dignity is by divine law.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring two figures within a framed decorative border.</image-desc>
<margin>First argument.</margin>
After these things, so that this whole question may finally be resolved, it is asked whether bishops were instituted by divine law. For it appears the matter is otherwise. First, because we do not read that Christ instituted anyone as a bishop except the Apostles; rather, the Apostles themselves instituted them by their own authority, as is clear regarding Timothy and Titus, whom Paul appointed. Therefore, bishops should likewise not be considered created by divine law, but by the Pope through <term>positive law</term> <note>Laws established by human authority rather than nature or God.</note>, in whom we have said the supreme jurisdiction of the Church resides.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, this is confirmed by the very act of Christ substituting Peter for himself. For he commanded him uniquely, saying: "Feed my sheep." As if he had said: "I entrust the summit of this matter to you; you yourself dispose of it according to your judgment." Therefore, the institution of bishops belongs not to Christ, but to Peter and his successor. Whence that voice of his in his first canon <note>1 Peter 5:2</note>, chapter 5: "Feed the flock which is among you," appears to be not a divine but a human precept—namely, Peter's.

<margin>Paul, Acts 20.</margin>
¶ To the contrary is that statement of Paul in Acts 20: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to rule the church of God, which he acquired with his own blood."

We have already established above that from the age of the Apostles, episcopal dignity has been separate from the priesthood by its own dignity and duties. However, for the clarification of the present matter, it is deliberated most carefully by what law it was instituted. For since it belongs to the Pope to choose bishops, their institution seems to be his. It is of such great importance to know this for the sake of persuading them to <term>residence</term> <note>The requirement for a bishop to live in his diocese to serve his people.</note> that the primary arguments must be sought from there. And those who persist in caviling and eluding the reasons by which that most healthy and divine law of residence is supported, protect themselves with no other "bronze shield" than by saying that bishops are made not by God immediately, but by the Pontiff.

<margin>Catharinus’s foundation for denying residence.</margin>
For a certain person <note>Likely referring to Ambrogio Catarino Politi, a contemporary theologian who argued that episcopal residency was a human, not divine, law.</note> armed himself thus in defense of bishops (as he himself judged)—namely, to free them from the divine law of residency, as will appear more fully and clearly in Question 3. For he says that just as a bishop is bound by divine law to reside...

# 806 | Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Law*

...bound to reside, since no one is made a bishop immediately by God, but by the Pope: for it is his role to divide dioceses and particular flocks, and to assign the care of them. He adds many other points of that kind which we shall discuss further in that place.

¶ Here, therefore, following our custom, two conclusions must be asserted and strengthened, as they are to be the basis and foundation of this entire dispute. For one can imagine two ways in which particular bishoprics—namely, those lower than the supreme office <note>The Papacy</note>—might not be of divine right. One way is to claim that the dignity itself was not instituted by God himself, like the sacraments are, but by the Pope, just as Lenten abstinence, the observation of particular feast days, and annual confession are. The second way is to claim that their election, which is done through the Pope, is not divine—that is, not by divine right. Both of these claims are openly false.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ Let this be the first conclusion: The episcopal order—that is, the rank and dignity—is an entirely divine institution, which Christ established with his own mouth. This has already been sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding sections. For Christ himself chose the Apostles, to which office the episcopal dignity was attached—namely, the duty of feeding the Christian flock. Moreover, he did not institute that dignity for a limited time (apart from the prophetic spirit with which he imbued them), but so that it would endure perpetually in the Church. Therefore, the episcopal dignity and rank, as it continues now in the Church, is the very institution of Christ. The second premise of this argument can be doubted by no one, since Christ founded the Church to endure forever, needing the perpetual support of feeding and the help of governance. In every province, the standard of faith and morals had to be perpetually clarified; therefore, he did not institute this dignity for a time, but for eternity.

<margin>Second reason</margin>
To this is added, secondly, the testimony of Paul in Ephesians 4: *And he gave some as Apostles, some as Prophets, others as Evangelists, others as Pastors and Teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all meet in the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God.* By the name of "Pastors," bishops are chiefly understood, as has been said. Therefore, they are necessary for the building up of the body of Christ, and thus they were instituted by Christ to last as long as the Church itself.

<margin>Third reason</margin>
¶ Thirdly: The Gospel priesthood is more excellent than the Mosaic one, and even more necessary. But that earlier priesthood, divided into the high priest and priests, was divinely instituted for the whole

<column-break/>

duration of the Law. Therefore, our priesthood, in which bishops are placed above priests, was instituted by Christ until the end of the world. Paul testifies to this in Hebrews, saying: *When the priesthood is changed, it is necessary that a change of the law also takes place.* <note>original: "Translatio sacerdotio, necesse est vt legis translatio fiat"</note>. The only difference is that under that old law, only one people and one synagogue existed, so only one high priest was needed; but for the Gospel Church, which lies open across the entire world, many are required.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, this is also evident by reason. Christ was the sole founder of the Church. Where Paul says that no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus, he designates not only Christ's person, but also his laws and <term>polity</term> <note>The organized structure and government of the Church.</note>. Hence, Christ said to Peter: *Upon this rock I will build my church.* For the foundation of the church, it was necessary not only to teach faith in things hoped for (which was the goal we must strive for) and to establish laws leading there, but also to institute magistrates who would govern the church according to those same laws. These are none other than the bishops, who, according to the word of Augustine, were born to us as sons in place of our fathers the Apostles. Therefore, the episcopal function is an institution of Christ; otherwise, he would not have founded the church firmly enough.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
¶ Fifthly: Christ himself personally instituted the Sacraments and those things necessary for them, and likewise the ministers of the sacraments, which is why he himself ordained the priests. But bishops alone, in their own right, have the power to administer certain sacraments: namely, <term>Orders</term> <note>The ordination of clergy</note> and Confirmation. There is therefore no doubt that Christ instituted not only the Papacy, but also the episcopal dignity which extends broadly to all prelates.

<margin>Sixth reason.</margin>
¶ Sixthly: The episcopal dignity, as we have shown in the preceding sections, is of the same kind in all bishops. For they differ among themselves only in the breadth of their jurisdiction. Therefore, insofar as it is common to both the Pope and the other bishops, it was instituted by the same author, Christ.

<margin>Seventh reason.</margin>
<margin>Paul.</margin>
¶ Seventhly: The episcopal dignity is numbered among the <term>charismata</term> <note>original: "charismata"; spiritual gifts or graces granted by God for the benefit of others.</note> with which Christ endowed his spouse, the Church. Of these, Paul surely says in 1 Corinthians 12: *There are varieties of graces, but the same spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of works, but it is the same God who works all things in all.* Therefore, the episcopal dignity is a gift of God, given to the church through him, according to the word of Paul...

<summary>In this passage, Domingo de Soto argues that the office of the bishop is a divine institution established directly by Christ, rather than a secondary administrative rank created by the Pope. He uses scriptural evidence from Saint Paul and logical comparisons to the Mosaic Law to prove that bishops are essential, perpetual "magistrates" necessary for the Church's survival.</summary>

# 807 | Book Ten, Question I.

<margin>Final reason.</margin>
> 1 Timothy 4: "Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the eldership." <note>original: "Noli negligere gratiam quæ in te est: quæ data est per prophetiam, cum impositione manuum presbyteri."</note>

¶ Finally, this is confirmed. When the Pope elects or confirms a bishop, he no more institutes the episcopal dignity than the Papacy is instituted when he himself is elected; rather, a specific person is simply applied to that existing dignity. 

<margin>Pope Pius.</margin>
Furthermore, Pope Pius <note>Likely referring to a decretal attributed to an early Pope Pius in the Canon Law</note> testifies to this truth in the canon *Oves* (Case 6, Question 1), saying that God chose bishops to be eyes for Himself. Therefore, it is more certain than certainty itself—and if one may speak this way of matters of faith, clearer than light—that Christ instituted the episcopal dignity that now flourishes in the Church. For who would believe that such a distinguished magistracy was placed at the arbitrary will of the Pope, so that he himself might create it? All theologians hold this in the 4th book, distinction 24, as do all interpreters of canon law, who hold this to be most confessed. By this same reasoning, Paul teaches that we should consider bishops not as ministers of man, but as Apostles of God, and likewise their successors, and finally as priests. For he says: "Thus let a man consider us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." When the Pope creates bishops or bishops ordain priests, they do nothing else but dispense the mysteries of God as ministers of Christ. ¶ We have thought it necessary to assert this conclusion at such length, not because anyone should be believed to doubt it, but so that through it, the falsehood of the assertions of those we cited above may become more clearly known. Among these is Catharinus <note>Ambrogio Catarino Politi (1484–1553), a Dominican theologian known for his original and sometimes controversial views at the Council of Trent.</note>, who says that episcopal functions and their obligations to reside in their dioceses belong only to <term>pontifical law</term> <note>human laws made by the Pope, rather than God</note> because it is the Pope who elects them and assigns them to their individual churches. The following conclusion is asserted as the opposite of that view for the present.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The election of bishops, and indeed the obligation to perform their duties, is of <term>divine law</term> <note>Ius divinum: laws or rights originating directly from God.</note>. However, there are some who, though this conclusion is true, do not sufficiently derive it from its proper principles.

<margin>Torrensis.</margin>
Among these is that Torrensis <note>Francisco de Torres (c. 1509–1584), a Spanish Jesuit theologian.</note>, an author not to be regretted, whom we cited above in Book 8. Indeed, such authors insert more than the truth allows. They think, I say, that the elections of bishops are of divine law for the reason that they are performed by the Pope in his capacity as a minister of the Church. This cause is certainly not firm enough to support the conclusion, nor does the example they provide have universal effectiveness. For they say that just as baptism, because it is performed by a minister of God in His name, is of divine law, so too is the election of a bishop 

<column-break/>

which the Pope performs. But those who defend the opposite view could weaken this reasoning in this way: Christ committed to the Pope and the Council not only the administration of those things which He Himself had instituted, but also granted the faculty of establishing new laws and rites. Therefore, the observation of Lent and of many feast days are purely of <term>positive law</term> <note>man-made law</note>, namely pontifical law. And the same is usually and rightly judged regarding the consecration of churches and altar ornaments. Therefore, this deduction is invalid if applied universally: "The Pope does this or that as God’s minister, therefore it is of divine law." This is only true if you add to the premise that he does those things as an institution of God Himself, or something God explained to the Apostles so they could pass it on to the Church by word of mouth. For this reason, we laid down the first conclusion as the foundation for this second one. ¶ However, our conclusion must first be explained by us.

<margin>The election of bishops can be understood in two ways as being of divine law.</margin>
That the elections of bishops are of divine law is understood in two ways. In one way, in general: that bishops are applied to individual churches according to ecclesiastical division. In another way: that this man, Peter or Paul, is applied to this or that specific church. In this second sense, it is well known that the election of this specific person is not of divine law in the same way that the election of Matthias and subsequently Paul was—just as the election of the other Apostles was made by God—but is from the human judgment of the electors or the Pope. Therefore, the truth of the conclusion must be understood in the first sense. This is easily gathered from the preceding argument as follows:

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
When a minister of God dispenses what God Himself instituted by His command, the action is to be considered of divine law. But when the Pope confirms and consecrates a bishop and assigns a church to someone, he carries out what Christ instituted in general and what He commanded him to do; therefore, it must be considered of divine law. The latter premise was sufficiently demonstrated in the previous conclusion. The former is made clear in the administration of the sacraments. For baptism, sacramental absolution, and similar things, although they are performed immediately by the ministers of the church (as they say), are nonetheless of divine law because Christ instituted them and commanded them to be so done and dispensed in His name. And this is what Paul took care to warn about in the first epistle to the Corinthians, where he rebukes those different slogans: "I am of Paul, I am of Apollo," etc. "Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" and below in chapter 3: "What then is Apollo? What indeed is Paul? They are his ministers..."

<summary>Soto argues that the office and election of bishops are based on divine law (instituted by Christ) rather than just papal administrative law. He distinguishes between the general requirement for bishops, which is divine, and the specific selection of an individual for a city, which involves human judgment.</summary>

...of him whom you have believed: and to each as the Lord has given. I planted, Apollos watered: but God gave the growth. <note>Original Latin: "Igo plantaui, Apollo rigauit: sed Deus incrementum dedit." A reference to 1 Corinthians 3:6, illustrating that human ministers perform the work, but the spiritual result comes from God.</note> Therefore, God dispenses grace through the ministers of the sacraments. And it must be judged entirely the same regarding the elections of bishops; in the same way, Paul taught us to speak. For in the places cited above, he says: Christ placed some as Apostles, others as pastors and teachers, etc. And elsewhere: "Take heed to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you." <note>Acts 20:28</note> And when, in Exodus 28, God commanded Moses, saying: "Bring Aaron and his sons near to you, so that he may serve me in the priesthood": <note>Exodus 28:1</note> simply because that application was made through a minister of God, does it then follow that it was not divine? Is it not also a true assertion regarding bishops who are created by the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> that they are "servants whom the Lord has appointed over his family"? <note>Matthew 24:45</note> Look at the words of the consecrator. For among other blessings, he says, speaking to God: "Let him be a faithful and prudent servant, not whom I or the Pope, but whom **You, O Lord, constitute over your family**: so that he may give them food in due season, and present every man perfect." For this is the episcopal function: both to teach and to persuade toward perfection. Therefore, it is a seductive argument to say: "The elections of bishops and the distributions of churches are done by the Pope; therefore, it is not by divine law." For indeed, since Christ was not to remain with us forever to govern us by an external function as he did while he lived among mortals, but sent the Holy Spirit to us for this purpose—to assist the Church only by an inward motion of the mind—it could not happen otherwise than that he should commit those things he had instituted to ministers, who would represent him in the external forum <term>external forum: the public, legal, and administrative jurisdiction of the Church, as opposed to the "internal forum" of private conscience</term> and judgment in his name. Whence Paul ordained Timothy and Titus not simply, but through an external ceremony: namely, through the laying on of hands. 
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
Jerome noted this in his commentaries on Isaiah, saying that ordination is perfected not only by prayers, but by the laying on of hands, lest a silent prayer of the voice ordain clerics without them knowing it. ¶ Add to this that what those opponents say—that such elections are made "immediately" by the Pope—suffers from equivocation. <note>Equivocation: using a term in different ways to create a misleading argument.</note> Rather, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, that cause is called "immediate" which is the first of all: just as immediate principles are those into 
<margin>God acts immediately</margin> 
which the final resolution is made. Therefore, it is God who immediately makes these elections through

<column-break/>

his ministers. But nevertheless, let a secondary cause be called "immediate" because nothing mediates between it and the effect. Just as when someone moves a stone with a 
<margin>elections of bishops.</margin>
stick, the stick is said to "immediately" touch the stone: for even in this way, the expression is permitted among philosophers. However, the inference is foolish: "Whatever the Pope does immediately, he therefore excludes from divine law." That is to say, in cases where God, who instituted it and commanded it to be done, confers the spiritual gifts and powers as the primary author—as happens to a bishop who is elected and consecrated. But another reasoning must be consulted to explore whether that which the Pope does is of human law: namely, as I said above, whether it is an ecclesiastical institution through power handed down by God to institute new things, both laws and ceremonies. ¶ And so that we may finally refute the adversaries 
<margin>Another reason for the same.</margin>
by their own confession, it is asked: When a bishop, by the Pope's commission, elects and consecrates another, is that election and consecration considered to belong to the Pope, or to that bishop who acts in his place? Surely they will not deny that it belongs rather to the delegating Pope, by whose authority it is done, than to the delegate. In the same way, therefore, it must be said that when the Pope elects or consecrates, that election is of divine law. This is corroborated by this final testimony. For if the dignity of a bishop were an effect of the Pope, he could certainly deprive him of it; as he can when he deposes him, stripping him of ecclesiastical jurisdiction. And yet, whatever the Pope might attempt after consecration, he cannot take away that dignity—just as if it were a sacramental character. <note>Character: an indelible spiritual mark placed on the soul by certain sacraments (Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Orders) that can never be removed.</note> ¶ But perhaps there is no lack of someone who would argue against us from our own confession in this way: "Although election in general is of divine law, nonetheless this specific election of this person is not done except by human will; therefore, this is sufficient for elections to be called simply matters of positive law." This is confirmed by the fact that just as many reign (as God complains through the Prophet) and not through Him; so in Jeremiah 23, he laments that pastors tear apart the flock of their pasture; and in the Gospel, that they enter not through the door, but like thieves and robbers from elsewhere. These are chosen not by the divine will, but by human will, and thus not by divine law, but by human. ¶ To this it is answered: the law <term>ius: the underlying right or legal principle</term> is one thing, and the use of the law is another. For the law is the faculty and precept of doing that which God himself instituted. Which is therefore divine. But the use is the exercise which consists in the act: and this is left to the prudence...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 808, where Soto argues that although the Pope or other ministers perform the physical act of choosing a bishop, the authority of the office is essentially derived from God. He is refuting the "adversaries" (likely those who argue the episcopacy is purely a delegated papal office) by showing that the sacramental and legal roots are divine.</meta>

# Book Ten, Question I.

...the prudence and judgment of those who choose and confirm. Therefore, episcopal power, unless it happens through an "erring key" <note>An "erring key" (*clavis errans*) refers to a legal or procedural error in the exercise of ecclesiastical authority.</note> against the laws—for instance, if someone who is irregular <term>irregular: a person barred from holy orders due to specific canonical impediments, such as certain crimes or physical defects</term> is chosen—is always conferred by divine law. But whether a good or bad person is chosen depends on human action and practice: from which a bad election can proceed against God’s will. And in this matter, where our adversaries think we are deceived, they themselves are mistaken. They think, I say, that we are led astray because we conclude that since the episcopate is of divine law, episcopal elections are made by that same law. But this is not our fallacy, but theirs: because from the fact that the exercise of the law is by human choice and judgment, they infer that elections are merely of human law. Let them hear, I pray, Pope Leo in his sermon on his assumption. 
> The favor, he says, of heavenly grace produces the Prelate. <note>Original Latin: "Dignatio cœlestis gratiæ gignit Antistitem." From Leo the Great, Sermon 2.</note>

And Ambrose, in his *Pastoral*, against those who confer orders for a price:
> Who, he says, gives episcopal grace? God or man? 

And he responds: 
> Without doubt, God: but nonetheless, God gives it through man. Man imposes hands, God bestows grace. The Bishop initiates the order, and God grants the dignity. 

If man performs nothing more in the order than the service entrusted to him, why do they deny the whole to God, who bestows the order itself upon you? Thus Ambrose writes. Therefore, the election is made by divine law. But lest we seem to dispute over a name, we say that whatever power the electing Pope confers, he confers by divine law and in God's name; and therefore, whatever he then commands the bishop is to be considered commanded by divine law. For example, when the consecrator says: 
> Receive the Gospel, and preach to the people committed to you. <note>Original Latin: "Accipe Euangelium, & prędica populo tibi cõmiſſo."</note>

Those authors opposed to us say that this voice is not immediately God’s, but the Pope’s. Therefore, they say, the ordained bishop is bound to execute it at the Pope's whim: so that if the Pope wishes that he does not reside <note>Reside in his diocese</note>, or if he does not care that the episcopal duty is performed rightly, it is to be imputed to the Pope, not to the bishop. 
<margin>Conclusion.</margin>
And at this point, the status of the dispute consists. But who could bear to hear this? Who, I say, could in any way doubt that this voice is to be held just as if Christ had uttered it with his own mouth? Since he himself instituted it, and by his command, it is uttered by the mouth of his instrument. Therefore, the bishop ought to listen to God speaking it: and subsequently, he must believe it is commanded of him by divine law. For let us step back a little earlier in the consecration. When the consecrator says: 
> Receive the staff of the pastoral office, so that in correcting vices you may be piously severe, maintaining judgment without anger, etc. <note>Original Latin: "Accipe baculum pastoralis officij ut in corrigendis vitijs piè sęuias, iudicium sine ira teneas..."</note>

In whose name are those things uttered? Is it not God’s? Is it not he himself who, through his minister, confers that power and the gift of grace 

<column-break/>

which he himself instituted? See how very clearly the subsequent prayer, poured out to God, explains this. For he who consecrates adds: 
> Creator and consecrator of the human race, giver of spiritual grace, bestower of eternal salvation: You, Lord, send forth your blessing upon this ring, so that whoever walks distinguished by this sign of the most holy faith, may profit unto eternal salvation through the power of heavenly defense. <note>Original Latin: "Creator & cõſecrator humani generis, dator gratiæ ſpiritualis..." From the rite of episcopal consecration.</note>

And as if God has already nodded in agreement to the prayer: 
> Receive the ring: namely, the seal of faith, so that adorned with untainted faith, you may preserve the spouse of God—that is, the holy Church—without blemish. 

It is God, therefore, in whose name the election and the donation of power take place. This becomes better known from that word in Numbers 11. For God commanded Moses, saying: 
> Gather for me seventy men of the elders of Israel, etc., and I will take of your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you, and you are not burdened alone. <note>Numbers 11:16-17</note>

In truth, that institution was divine. Moreover, when he says, "I will take of your spirit," it is not to be heard as if the gift conferred on Moses was to be shortened, but that from the same spirit with which he had gifted him, he would also gift his helpers. Therefore, the same kind of grace is conferred on all bishops. Whence the consecrator says: 
> Be appeased, O Lord, by our supplications: and having inclined the horn of priestly grace upon this your servant, pour into him the power of your blessing. <note>Original Latin: "Propitiare, inquit, Domine ſupplicationibus noſtris..."</note>

¶ From these things, therefore, it is clearly consequent that a bishop binds his faith not to the Pope, but to God himself. Therefore, once the election is made, he is to return an account of the souls committed to him not to the Pope, but to Him. Behold where the truth stands apart from the opinion of those whom we have deemed necessary to refute here, and where we have decided to lead the present question: Namely, that the election which is made by the Pope is to that extent of divine law, so that he who takes on the person of a bishop is bound by its bond both to reside in his church and to exhibit and perform the other duties that lie upon his pastoral dignity. And so, from here we must take the beginning of the third question concerning their residency.

**TO** the first argument, therefore, of those which were proposed at the front of the question, it is responded: that even if Christ is not read to have instituted anyone as bishop except the Apostles, when he sent them to preach (for the episcopal function was annexed to that); and uniquely Peter under the name of pastor: nonetheless, since that same...

He uses the language of the consecration rite and biblical precedents to prove that the Holy Spirit, not just the human minister, confers the office.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the divine origin of episcopal authority (the office of a bishop). Soto is concluding his response to arguments regarding how Christ's command to Peter applies to all bishops, before transitioning to a new question regarding whether it is appropriate for a person to actually want to become a bishop.</meta>

**Header: Friar Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law**

...established authority, as has been said, to remain forever, by that very act He spoke to all future bishops in the person of the Apostles, and specifically in Peter. Therefore, what He said to Peter, "Feed my sheep" <note>original: "Pasce oues meas," from John 21:17</note>: He intended to be said to all who were to be created bishops through him; namely, so that by the very fact that someone was created a bishop, he would understand that same command was given to him by God.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
To the second argument, it is responded that "Feed" was said specifically to Peter because, as far as the fullness of jurisdiction is concerned, He constituted Peter specifically as the head. Therefore, just as the keys of the kingdom of heaven were uniquely permitted to him in Matthew 16—which He later gave to all the Apostles in John 20 <note>The text cites John 9, but this is likely an error in the original or OCR for John 20:23</note>—and indeed to all priests of their rank in the forum of conscience: so He acknowledged that what He said to Peter, "Feed," was said to all. Furthermore, regarding those other words of the same Peter, "Feed the flock of the Lord which is among you" <note>original: "Pascite qui in vobis est gregẽ Dñi," from 1 Peter 5:2</note>: we deny in a Catholic and most firm manner that this voice is primarily Peter's own. Rather, he gave that admonition in the name of God. Indeed, I cannot wonder enough at those who think the opposite: namely, that the voice was brought forth by Peter just as if a bishop were commanding his subjects, or a prelate his monks, regarding some other matter that was his own regulation or precept. For it is plain and clear that he spoke as a divine instrument, just as Paul did when he said: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you" <note>Acts 20:28</note>. For he deliberately said, "Feed the flock of the Lord." For if they are the Lord's sheep, whose pastors are they if not the Lord's? And by whose command are they bound to feed them, if not the Lord's? Hence Jerome, in his *Letter to Nepotian* (which is cited in Distinction 95, Canon *Esto*), says that Peter spoke those things according to the Lord's command.

# QUESTION TWO, On desiring, entering, and conferring the episcopacy.

## Saint Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* 2-2, Question 185.

## ARTICLE I.

## Whether it is lawful to desire the office of bishop.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' illustrating a scholar or saint seated at a desk with books and writing implements.</image-desc>
HAVING ESTABLISHED what the episcopal dignity is and by what law it was instituted, it follows in the order of things to weave in a discussion concerning the desire for it, the choice of it, and its

<column-break/>

conferral. And lest we take away the honor we have hitherto shown to Saint Thomas—namely, that where he speaks, we interpret his mind—we must explain his 185th Question of the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of the *Summa Theologiae*</note>.

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
For it is argued that to desire and strive for the episcopal duty is not only lawful, but even praiseworthy. For first of all, Paul says in 1 Timothy 3: "Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work." But the desire for a good work is worthy of praise; therefore, it is also praiseworthy to hope for the office of bishop.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Second: The status of bishops is more excellent and eminent than the religious life of monks <term>monachatus: the state of being a monk or living under religious vows</term>. But to seek the monastic life is a matter of piety and religious duty; therefore, it is even more desirable to long for the office of bishop.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
Third: In Proverbs 11 <note>The text says Proverbs 10, but the quote is from Proverbs 11:26</note> it is read: "He who hides grain shall be cursed among the people, but a blessing shall be upon the head of those who sell it." But he who excels in life and knowledge, and is thus suitable for the episcopal duty, seems to "hide spiritual grain" if he withdraws himself from that same duty. If he submits himself to it, he can healthily dispense that same spiritual grain. Therefore, to reject the same duty should be considered a vice, while to desire it should be attributed as a virtue.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
Fourth: The examples or teachings of the Saints are proposed to us for imitation, according to Romans 15: "Whatever things were written, were written for our instruction." But we read in Isaiah 6 that the same prophet offered himself for the duty of preaching when he said: "Here am I: send me." Therefore, such an act is worthy of no reproach, but rather of reward.

On the contrary is that word of Augustine in Book 19 of *The City of God*: "A higher position, without which a people cannot be ruled, even if it is administered as is fitting, is nonetheless sought after indecently."

### REGARDING the question, so that we may gather the text of Saint Thomas into conclusions in our usual manner, after posing a three-part division, we respond with five conclusions. For there are three things to consider in the episcopal duty.

<margin>Three things to be considered in the episcopal duty.</margin>
The first, which is the head and end of all, is the episcopal operation and function, through which the common salvation of the people is consulted; this is what Christ designated with those words in the last chapter of John: "Feed my sheep." The second is the high rank and eminence of order to which a bishop is raised, according to Matthew 24 <note>OCR says 25</note>: "A faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has set over his household." Finally, the third...

### Book Ten, Question II.

...finally, in that same office, as a consequence and something annexed to it, honor, reverence, and an abundant supply of temporal revenues are observed, according to that saying of the Apostle in 1 Timothy 5: "The priests who rule well are worthy of double honor" <note>original: "Qui bene psunt presbyteri, duplici honore digni sunt," from 1 Timothy 5:17</note>—namely, both before God and before men.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, with this distinction laid down, the first conclusion (starting from the last point) is this: To seek the <term>episcopacy</term><note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note> out of a desire for and an affection for temporal goods is a manifest crime of ambitious greed. For since temporal goods are nothing but supports and sustainment established for the purpose of administration, to seek these same temporal things with one's primary intention is a perverted desire. Our Redeemer rebuked the Pharisees for this very crime in Matthew 23, where He said: "They love the first places at feasts, and the first chairs in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace, and to be called 'Rabbi' by men." <note>original: "Amāt primos accubitus in cœnis..." from Matthew 23:6-7</note>

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion concerns the second part of the distinction. To long for the episcopacy by reason of its loftiness and eminence is no less criminal. For the height of such a rank is a consequence of the function of the work; therefore, when that height is sought first, the desire is backwards. Hence our same Savior, in Matthew 20, attributed this to reproach when He said: "You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them; but it shall not be so among you: but whoever is greater among you, let him be as a minister." <note>original: "Scitis quia principes gentium dominantur eorum..." from Matthew 20:25-26</note>

<margin>Chrysostom</margin>
On this point, <term>Chrysostom</term><note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> says that through this, it is shown to be a pagan thing to desire primacy, and thus he turns their feverish souls away by comparison with the pagans.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion. For one who is considered worthy to desire the function of the episcopacy for the salvation of souls is a diligent duty, and is to be commended with extraordinary praise. For this is what Paul praises: since the affection is weighed by its object, and that work is, in itself, a duty of <term>charity</term><note>In this context, "caritas" refers to the theological virtue of selfless, divine love for others.</note>.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The fourth conclusion. To seek after this kind of episcopal work even for the sake of looking after the benefit of one's neighbors—because the loftiness of the rank is joined to it—seems presumptuous, and is therefore to be greatly feared, except where manifest necessity demands it.

<margin>Gregory</margin>
Hence <term>Gregory</term><note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604) in his "Book of Pastoral Rule."</note>, in the first part of his *Pastoral Care*, chapter 8, says: "At that time, it was laudable to seek the episcopacy, when through it there was no doubt that one would reach the most severe punishments." By these words, he knowingly explained that the work is good in itself, provided it does not have the peak of loftiness attached to it. For this reason, in those times, there were few who desired to have that burden imposed upon them: namely, only those who were divinely stirred to it by the zeal of charity.

<column-break/>

In that same way, Gregory, in chapter 7, commends the zeal of Isaiah offering himself <note>A reference to Isaiah 6:8, "Here am I; send me."</note>.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The fifth conclusion. Nonetheless, someone can, without that presumption, desire to be worthy of the episcopacy and to worthily administer that province, whether he has already been distinguished by the <term>infula</term><note>A Roman sacrificial bandage, here used metaphorically for the bishop's miter or the dignity of the office.</note> or before he is assumed into that office; provided that the desire is directed not toward the loftiness and primacy, but toward the service of God itself and the benefit of the flock. This conclusion is an appendix to the third. Hence, Chrysostom on Matthew says: "To desire a good work is indeed good; but to lust after primacy is the vanity of man. For primacy desires one who flees from it, and it shrinks from one who desires it."

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ Although these assertions are true, they still require a little more light. And first, there is a doubt regarding the first two conclusions: exactly how much fault is in that immoderate affection when someone desires either temporal revenues or human honors above the episcopal function itself—specifically, whether it is by its nature a <term>mortal sin</term><note>A grave sin that, according to Catholic theology, destroys the relationship with God.</note>. For it appears to be so, because it is a perverted affection toward sacred things. But nonetheless, an argument fights from the other side: that since those things are the just rewards of that office, to be moved by an affection for them to choose the episcopacy (as long as the man is prepared to administer it rightly and properly) seems to be either no fault or a very small one. For since "honor nourishes the arts," as the saying goes, such rewards seem to have been deliberately proposed so that men, attracted to study, might become worthy of entering into such dignities.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ It is responded that desiring the episcopacy on account of temporal goods can happen in two ways. In one way, so that this perversion of order is the object of the desire. In this case, the word "on account of" designates that temporal goods are the *end* (the goal) of the episcopacy. As when you say, "I seek the episcopacy for the sake of temporal goods," the affection of seeking is carried into that inverted order—namely, the episcopacy for the sake of temporal good. And in truth, this is by its nature a mortal sin, because the order of things divinely implanted in them is perverted. For the proper order is that the episcopacy be sought for the sake of its legitimate function, while temporal supports are for sustenance, so that the enjoined burden can be rightly administered.

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
Indeed, <term>St. Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Soto's scholastic theology.</note> intended to teach this immediately in the head of the question, saying that the principal and final thing in the episcopacy is the episcopal operation, through which one intends the utility of neighbors. Therefore, it is responded to the argument just made: First...

Soto concludes that seeking the office primarily for money or power is a mortal sin as it perverts the divine order of the ministry.</summary>
