### Book Ten, Question II, Page 812

...firstly, because even if such a man intends in his mind to administer the bishopric rightly, he is nonetheless exposed to the most imminent danger of making his primary concern the fleecing of the flock, the procuring of honor and pride, and the neglecting of the care of souls. For as the order of priorities is in the object of one’s desire, such is the order to be feared in the actual work. Furthermore, even if no such danger were imminent, the desire would be corrupted by its own perverse object. Secondly, however, it happens that a <term>episcopacy</term><note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note> is desired by reason of the temporal things annexed to it: not that this reason is established as the final goal of the bishopric being sought, but that it was the first motive for moving the desire. And an affection of this kind does not appear to be <term>mortal</term><note>A grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note> in its own nature, since a perverse order among things is not established by it. For temporal goods can move a man to desire a bishopric, even if the episcopal function itself is not directed toward that end. Indeed, the love of temporal things can move a man to love God for His own sake, and thus also the bishopric—just as the fear of hell can move someone to love God Himself for His own sake. Nonetheless, because the things desired do not move the appetite in the same order that they hold among themselves, a desire of this kind is not without fault—at least a <term>venial</term><note>A lesser sin that does not result in complete separation from God.</note> one. But although these things can be explained in the schools after a fashion, they are nonetheless distinguished with difficulty in actual feeling and practice. For he who is first moved by a temporal reward would so easily pervert the order of priorities that it cannot be discerned whether he desires the bishopric for the sake of such rewards; and thus he is in danger of mortal sin. Therefore, another rule must be consulted: namely, that he who is certain that no crime will be committed in the administration of the church for the sake of temporal goods, but that he will serve his office according to the laws, even if he is moved by a desire for temporal things, is outside the fear of mortal sin. But truly, such things rarely hold together.

<margin>The second ambiguity.</margin>
¶ The second ambiguity lies in the distinction between these two conclusions: for they seem to coincide into the same thing. For although desiring temporal goods pertains to greed, and desiring the loftiness of dignity pertains to <term>presumption</term><note>The sin of overstepping one's bounds or assuming a status one does not deserve.</note>, nonetheless, desiring honors—which was applied to the first conclusion—also seems to pertain to presumption, which is mentioned

<column-break/>

in the second.

<margin>The response.</margin>
It is responded, however, that the desire for honor, which is **ambition**, is different from the desire for loftiness, which is **presumption**. For height of rank and honor relate to each other as cause and effect. Indeed, honor is the effect and subsequently the testimony of excellence. Therefore, ambition—as Saint Thomas says in the <term>Secunda Secundae</term><note>The second part of the second part of Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologica*.</note>, Question 131 <note>The Latin text says "q. 31," likely an OCR error or printer's typo for 131, which is Aquinas's section on Ambition.</note>—is an inordinate desire for honor: for instance, either when someone desires the testimony of an excellence which he does not have, or does not desire it for the benefit of others; for honor is to be desired not for itself, but as a benefit for others. Presumption, however, is an immoderate hope: namely, the longing for some dignity or place which exceeds the strength of the one desiring it. These vices are indeed distinct in the desire for a bishopric.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ These things having been thus explained, however, someone could rise up against them: namely, that to desire such goods for themselves is not a sin. Since—to begin with greed—there are two species of it, as Saint Thomas teaches in Question 118 of the same work. One, namely, which is opposed to justice: specifically when someone wickedly desires the things of another, which is indeed mortal by its very nature. The other, however, is that which is opposed to **liberality**: specifically when someone desires temporal goods too much; which is certainly not a sin, except insofar as it brings the danger of desiring something against charity. Moreover, someone can long for temporal goods annexed to spiritual ones, while yet holding a firm purpose of dispensing those same temporal goods rightly. By the same reasoning, someone can recognize in himself the dignity of virtue and knowledge, in testimony of whose excellence he can rightly desire honor, and thus he will be able to foresee his own strength, so that he may desire the loftiness of the place without presumption.

<margin>The solution.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, these arguments are solved by the things stated above, except that they clarify the same matter more brightly. For the height of a place, by its own nature, is not to be desired for its own sake, but so that one, "raised up upon a lampstand, may shine for all who are in the house." <note>A reference to Matthew 5:15.</note> And one must think in the same way concerning secular magistrates. For truly, high offices are instituted for this purpose. He, therefore, who longs for such a place for this end, commits nothing evil in the nature of the thing—except on account of the danger, as the fourth conclusion declared. But he who desires a bishopric for the sake of its loftiness, by that very fact declares himself unworthy: since he has a perverse affection, and thus desires it beyond his own strength, which is presumption. One should think similarly concerning honor: which is not to be sought except as a testimony of virtue, so that you may benefit others. And likewise concerning the temporal goods annexed to a spiritual matter, which ought not to be desired except for sustenance, so that you may perform the office for the benefit of others. ¶ Concerning the third conclusion, no reason for doubting can appear, so clear is it that the desire for consulting and being free for the salvation of souls is licit. But truly, the fourth is to be considered meditatively, where Sir Thomas says that this very thing seems presumptuous on account of the annexed loftiness of rank—unless a manifest necessity should exist. For who [does] not...

### Question II of the Tenth Book

...it does not seem to condemn such a desire entirely, yet he says it appears <term>presumptuous</term><note>The sin of overconfidence in one’s own spiritual state or abilities.</note>. It follows from these conclusions, therefore, that the desire for a <term>prelacy</term><note>A high-ranking office in the Church, such as that of a bishop or abbot.</note>, if it is not directed toward the salvation of souls, is by its very nature a sin—either mortal or venial, as has been explained. However, when directed toward such salvation, it neither possesses innate malice by its nature, nor is it truly good in itself; for if it were good in itself, it would require no circumstance to excuse it. If, however, it were evil in itself, no cause could render it excused. Therefore, because of the annexed danger, it is evil unless a cause demands otherwise; but when a cause demands it, it becomes permissible. Just as if someone were to throw themselves into a rapid river or any other dangerous place without cause, they would commit a sin; yet a cause could sometimes wash away the fault. Indeed, <term>Saint Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for this work.</note> acknowledges no cause other than necessity—not the necessity of the person themselves, but the common necessity of the Church. 

<margin>Objection.</margin> But if someone should rebut him, saying that another cause could occur besides that one: for instance, if someone knows himself to be sober, chaste, learned, and finally, irreproachable—the kind of bishop <margin>1 Timothy 3.</margin> Paul depicts in 1 Timothy, chapter 3. Such a man seems to contract no fault if he should desire the <term>episcopacy</term><note>The office of a bishop.</note> for the sake of the salvation of souls, even while the necessity of the Church is not pressing. 

To this it is responded that Saint Thomas deliberately remained silent about this cause because no one <margin>Solution.</margin> ought to believe this of himself unless he has been divinely touched, as he says in the solution to the fourth argument. This is clear from the example of <margin>Isaiah 6.</margin> Isaiah; for as is related in his 6th chapter, the angel first touched his mouth to cleanse him of all iniquity before he said: "Here am I: send me." <note>Original Latin: "Ecce ego: mitte me."</note> And of <margin>1 Samuel 3.</margin> Samuel it is read in 1 Kings, chapter 3 <note>In the Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>, that he was divinely awakened from sleep to speak the word of the Lord in Israel. And for the other Prophets, it was similarly arranged by a holy divine power. And in the book of the <margin>Gregory.</margin> *Dialogues* concerning the monk Equitius, <term>Gregory</term><note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> relates that he felt his tongue was touched by God so that thereafter he was unable to restrain himself from long-lasting speeches. These things, however, are supernatural and occur very rarely; they are not to be reduced to a general rule of doctrine. Add to this that such divine providence never happens except in a time of necessity. Therefore, to summarize the reason why the desire for the <margin>Whence the desire for the episcopate is rendered wicked or suspected of presumption.</margin> episcopacy is either always wicked or suspected of presumption: first, its sublimity must be placed before our eyes. For it is a state not just of any perfection—like that of the religious <note>Referring to monks or members of religious orders.</note>

<column-break/>

who are learning perfection—but one which requires that very peak of perfection so that he may teach the same to his flock. Truly, since they are, as has been said, the successors of the Apostles, they are the guardians of souls which Christ redeemed with his own blood. For that reason, they must be equipped with both eminence of knowledge and of life, so that (as Paul says of Christ) they may be able to present their Church to God on the day of judgment without wrinkle or stain; for the fulfillment of which duty they must even desire death, if it should be necessary. 

With this goal set before one's eyes, if anyone desires this office for the sake of temporal goods, it has already been said how perverse an affection he has. If, however, he desires it for the sake of the salvation of souls, then he either feels himself worthy and fit, or otherwise. If he does not judge himself fit, he is wicked—that is, entangled in the crime of injustice. But if he judges himself to be fit, he can hardly be free from the fear of presumption; for scarcely anyone can, without fault, ascribe to himself as much dignity as this office demands. However, when it is evident that the Church is suffering from a lack of men who can serve her according to the dignity of the matter, then he who clearly sees himself as fit for that same province, although he wishes for it for the salvation of souls, may be excused by that same necessity. Therefore, if it is a sin to desire the episcopacy in one's mind, how much more deformed is it to procure and solicit it by action? Furthermore, it is a matter of great shame that these kinds of leadership roles are sought, procured, and campaigned for so licentiously and with such a <term>shameless brow</term><note>A Latin idiom (perfricata fronte) meaning "with a bold or hardened face," implying a total lack of modesty.</note>.

***

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> To the first argument, therefore, a solution is gathered from what has been said, which comes to be explained in two ways. First, that in that passage the Apostle wished to define a *legitimate* desire for the episcopacy; as if he said, he who rightly and correctly desires the episcopacy desires nothing but a "good work," which is to devote his labors to the salvation of souls. This was asserted as permissible and <margin>Augustine.</margin> praiseworthy in the third conclusion. Whence Augustine says in book 19 of *The City of God*: the Apostle there wished to explain what the episcopacy is. For it is a name of work, not of honor. For *skopein* <note>Original Greek: Σκοπεῖν</note> means to watch over or to intend; and thus *episcopus* is the same as "superintendent," about which we have already spoken above. Therefore, as he had said a little before, it is not the honor and power of the episcopacy that should be loved (which are vain in themselves), but the work. <margin>Another interpretation of Paul’s passage.</margin>
¶ Secondly, however, the same Apostolic word [from Paul] should be interpreted a bit differently and perhaps more purely: that it be understood as a warning, which strikes fear into those desiring this office. It is as if he had said: "He who desires the office of bishop should watch himself, and look forward with prudence to what he is actually desiring." For he desires a work that is not merely good, but so excellent that there is scarcely anyone sufficient to fulfill it. The words that follow clearly support this sense. For he adds: *A bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent,* etc. Regarding this, <term>Gregory</term><note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose *Pastoral Rule* was the standard manual for bishops.</note> says in the same place, praising it: "He immediately turns that which he praised—the desire for a good work—into a cause for fear." Therefore, <term>Saint Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> prudently joins a fourth conclusion to the third.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
¶ The second argument is likewise resolved by what was said above. Indeed, we said that the state of <term>prelates</term><note>High-ranking church officials like bishops.</note> is different from the state of perfection of monks. For <term>religious</term><note>Those living under monastic vows.</note> profess perfection only as disciples and followers; but bishops profess it as teachers, as if they have already attained it. For Christ did not ask the young man whom he invited to the religious life whether he was perfect, but whether he *wished* to be perfect. However, He did not appoint Peter as the pastor of His flock until He had asked him three times whether he loved Him more than the others—that is, whether he was more perfect than the rest. From this, <term>Dionysius</term><note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian who wrote extensively on church hierarchies.</note> concludes that perfection belongs to the bishop actively, as one who makes others perfect, but to the monk passively, as one being made perfect. To wish to be made perfect is not presumptuous, as wishing to make others perfect is, nor is it exposed to the same danger. Add, moreover, that a monk submits himself to others to lay hold of spiritual things.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
According to <term>Augustine</term><note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430), influential Church Father.</note> in *The City of God*, book 19, this is praiseworthy for anyone; for he says that no one is prohibited from the study of knowing the truth, which is a "praiseworthy leisure." But he who takes on the persona of a bishop chooses to have others subject to himself. The Apostle discourages everyone from this desire in Hebrews 5, where he says: *Neither does anyone take this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God.* And <term>Chrysostom</term><note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), Archbishop of Constantinople and famous preacher.</note>, commenting on Matthew, says: "To long for the primacy of the church is neither just nor useful. For what wise man wants to subject himself to such slavery and danger as to give an account for the entire church? Except perhaps one who does not fear the judgment of God, abusing the ecclesiastical primacy in a secular way—namely, so that he may turn himself into a man of the world."

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
¶ To the third, Saint Thomas also responds excellently: that the distribution of "grain" <note>A metaphor for spiritual teaching and the Word of God.</note> 

<column-break/>

should not be done at anyone's personal whim, but first by divine dispensation, and then by the command and order of superiors, according to that passage in 1 Corinthians 4: *So let a man regard us as ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.* And in Romans 10: *How shall they preach unless they are sent?* Therefore, he who is not burdened by his own duty, nor has had it enjoined upon him by a superior, is not considered to be "hiding the grain." Rather, it is the one who either neglects the office he has assumed or stubbornly refuses to receive it. Thus, Augustine says in *The City of God*, book 19: "The love of truth seeks a holy leisure; the necessity of charity undertakes a righteous business. If no one imposes this burden, one should be free to perceive and contemplate the truth. But if it is imposed, it must be undertaken because of the necessity of charity."

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, the fourth has already been answered above. For the examples of the Saints teach us nothing more than that no one should thrust themselves into the bishopric before they are called by God, unless they have been divinely purified for it, as can be seen in the example of Isaiah.

### ARTICLE II.

#### Whether it is permissible to entirely refuse a commanded bishopric.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
<margin>Gregory.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q depicting a figure seated in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>SINCE it is possible to deviate from the line of virtue toward either extreme, and it has been seen how much sin or danger lies in the desire for the bishopric, it follows that we should see whether sin can occur in its refusal. Therefore, no one can safely accept unless perhaps they know it divinely.

### Book Ten, Question II.

accepts the <term>episcopate</term><note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note>, he sins mortally by that very fact. Nevertheless, if he is otherwise suitable and refuses to cleanse his stains in order to obey, <term>Saint Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a foundational theologian for this period.</note> also warns that he sins in this: since he says he is bound to remove the sin. But this certainly requires a bit more careful meditation. First, it should not be understood as a new sin distinct from disobedience; rather, he means that he who refuses to obey so that he may persist in sin has no legitimate excuse to be cleansed of the crime of disobedience.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
This question, however, can immediately move the mind of the reader: Whether, if the man who is chosen is corrupted by a plague of affections—even if hidden—such that he cannot quiet the turbulence of his conscience, but prudently fears he will be repeatedly overcome by them, even if he proposes in some way to leave his sin, is he bound to obey the elector? For reason appears to prove this, since he has an impediment of the first kind: namely, one that he himself can cast off.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
In truth, this is an ambiguous matter. But since "possibility" in this context is to be used not dialectically but according to the rules of prudence and, as they say, morally: even for that which is very difficult, he who feels he cannot tame the wildness of his affections would certainly not be bound to obey. Indeed, it would be a transgression before God to expose himself to such a great risk. It is otherwise, however, if he considers himself unsuitable in terms of knowledge or other qualities—which are evident to others—out of his own modesty. For if a prudent and upright <term>prelate</term><note>A high-ranking church official with authority over others.</note> recognizes these things, the judgment must be deferred to him, and thus one must comply.

<margin>A Question.</margin>
But you ask: who exactly is to be considered the prelate who must be listened to out of necessity in this matter? Is it only the Pope, the confirmer of a bishop's election, or also the bishop in the conferring of the priesthood, or even the electors? It seems that only the Bishops <note>original: "Antistites"</note> are such; for electors are not Prelates. Indeed, there are now Kings who present candidates in the place of electors.

<margin>The Response.</margin>
It is answered that, as far as the rigor of the law is concerned, only the prelate who duly holds <term>jurisdiction</term><note>The legal power or authority to command and judge.</note> imposes the necessity so that you cannot retract his orders without the crime of disobedience; indeed, only then when he has commanded it by virtue of obedience. Nevertheless, when the electors are upright men who conduct the election with holy zeal, there is no need for the elected person to behave with difficulty. Indeed, it is more advisable to accept the election, provided that a member of a religious order does not do so unless the permission of his prelate has first been granted, since his rule of life so requires.

<column-break/>

Truly, in fleeing such honors, everyone ought to be circumspect: for they are accustomed, like the <term>Scythians</term><note>Ancient nomadic warriors known for the "Parthian shot," firing arrows backward while retreating.</note> fleeing, to wound their own people in the back with danger. I say that the despisers of these dignities are often seized by a worse snatching of pride than if they had accepted them with fear. Add to this that even if refusing these heights could be an act of heroic virtue, a faithful and prudent servant can nevertheless perform very frequent duties in the administration of the church which are simultaneously of much more cumulative commendation before God than a single act of humility. Therefore, for men of proven life, prudence and modesty must be exhibited in embracing magistracies in such a way that no less caution is applied in refusing them. This is especially true when there is a lack of worthy leaders, and thus the Church of Christ has need of the service of good men, as <term>Augustine</term><note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430), whose writings often balanced the desire for peace with the duty of service.</note>, whom we cited a little earlier, warned us.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
<margin>The Council of Nicaea.</margin>
To the third, it is answered: Since the episcopate is not simply a <term>necessity for salvation</term><note>original: "de necessitate salutis"</note>, like the sacraments and the duties of the virtues, but only when the reason of obedience demands it, it implies no inherent iniquity for someone to hinder himself from taking it by a vow or other obstacle. Just as transitioning to a second marriage is not illicit simply because it stands in the way of taking orders: provided that the vow never to accept the episcopate has a restricted intention, meaning that as far as it lies within him, he will neither procure nor accept it. For if he proposed to obey no prelate concerning that matter, it would be a transgression, and such a vow would not be binding to that extent. As for what was brought up regarding <term>Blessed Mark</term><note>Tradition holds that Saint Mark the Evangelist cut off his thumb to make himself ineligible for the priesthood under Jewish law, which required physical perfection.</note>, if the matter was so—for <term>Jerome</term><note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), known for his Latin translation of the Bible.</note> does not fully affirm it, but says, "it is said"—it must be confessed that he did it by divine revelation. For to mutilate a limb of oneself for such an end would be a sin, as is made known from the <term>Council of Nicaea</term><note>The first ecumenical council in 325 AD; its first canon forbade self-mutilation as a disqualification for the clergy.</note> in the canon "If anyone" <note>original: "si quis. d. 55"</note>.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>

For it is a case that happens very frequently: namely, that someone in the administration of a magistracy is not going to do everything he ought, and yet among all who could be, he is the least bad, and most useful to the state. It appears, therefore, that to desire this is not licit. For to wish something for someone which...

<margin>The Solution.</margin>

To this, the following is nonetheless answered. First, that no one is permitted to undertake a public office with such great danger; nor indeed to remain in it if they cannot cast off their fear. For "what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his own soul?" <note>A reference to Matthew 16:26.</note> Indeed, it is diametrically opposed to the love of God to place one’s own spiritual health after the health of the entire world.

Second, it is asserted: it is not only lawful, but indeed a laudable desire, that he should be the <term>Leader</term><note>The original Latin is *Antistes*, a term for a high-ranking prelate or bishop.</note> who is most suitable for the church, or at least the least inconvenient, regardless of how much fear is held for his personal safety. I do not say that you can advise him to accept it—for he would then accept or retain it wickedly—but that it is lawful for you to desire this for another: and even to procure it. Therefore, however much another might be joined to you by friendship or other close ties, you ought to wish for this. And the reason is most manifest: 

<margin>Reason for the assertion.</margin>

because the universal good is more excellent than the particular good; and thus, with one’s own self excepted, it is more to be desired than the spiritual good of any friend. And this very point is confirmed: for if you were an elector, you would be bound to choose him; for it is the duty of the one chosen to examine what is expedient for himself.

### ARTICLE III.

->*Whether it is necessary that he who is chosen for the episcopate be better than the others.*<-

After considering the desire for the <term>episcopate</term><note>The office of a bishop.</note> and the temperate obedience of the one chosen, it follows to explore regarding the electors and those who confirm the choice, whether they are always bound to choose the one who is better than 

<margin>First argument.</margin>

all the others. For it appears that Christ taught us this by his action. For he did not place Peter over his Church until he had examined him with a triple questioning as to whether he loved Him more than the others. However, <term>charity</term><note>In this context, *charitas* refers to the theological virtue of supernatural love for God.</note> alone makes one "better" in the absolute sense: therefore, no one should ever be chosen unless they are the better person.

<margin>Second.</margin>

Second: Pope <term>Symmachus</term><note>Symmachus (Pope from 498–514); this refers to a decree found in Canon Law.</note> says (1. q. 1) that he who is more prominent in dignity must be considered the most vile unless he also excels in knowledge and holiness. But whoever excels in knowledge and holiness is considered better in an absolute sense: therefore, no one is to be chosen unless they surpass the 

<column-break/>

others in the integrity of their character.

<margin>Third.</margin>

Third: In every kind of thing, the lesser are governed by the greater, just as corporal things are governed by spiritual things, and the lower by the higher; as <term>Saint Augustine</term><note>The influential Church Father (354–430 AD).</note> is the authority in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*. But a bishop is chosen for the governance of others, therefore he ought to be better than the others.

On the contrary is the text of the <term>Decretal</term><note>A papal letter forming part of Canon Law.</note>, *On Elections*, in the chapter "Scriptum," which says that it is enough to choose a "good" man, and it is not necessary to choose the "better" man.

ALTHOUGH we have discussed this question very extensively in the third book regarding all church magistrates, nevertheless, because it is specifically inserted here by <term>Saint Thomas</term><note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> regarding bishops, the order of topics compels us to repeat it. The summary of Saint Thomas's response, based on a 

<margin>Distinction.</margin>

distinction, is contained in two conclusions. For in the election to the episcopate, he says, one thing must be weighed on the part of the electors, and another on the part of the one elected. There is therefore 

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>

the first conclusion: No one is bound to choose the "better" man, if you use the name "better" according to its proper meaning; but rather him who is more expedient and fit for the pastoral duty. For no one is "good" in an absolute sense except by charity alone. For, as we have said elsewhere, one can be a good craftsman without moral virtue; but only moral virtue makes a man good in an absolute sense. Hence, since charity is the "form" <note>In scholastic philosophy, the "form" is the essential characteristic that makes a thing what it is.</note> of all virtues, it is by charity that men are called and are "good" in the eyes of God: and the more one is advanced in it, the better he is.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>

The conclusion is thus proved. The election of a person to the episcopal see must be weighed by his function, as that is the "end" <note>The purpose or goal.</note> for which the person is chosen, and the goodness of the means is judged by the end. For we have shown very extensively in the cited Book 3, Question 1, that the tithes and stipends of the churches were not instituted as a reward for the quality and goodness of the person. For that reward awaits us with God in heaven; rather, they were instituted so that the churches might be rightly administered; according to that passage in 1 Corinthians 14: "Seek that you may excel for the building up of the church." Hence, it says <note>Referring to 1 Timothy 5:17.</note> that not those who are "good" presbyters, but those who "rule well," are worthy of double honor. To undertake and perform such services, not only integrity of character and charity (which makes one "better" in the absolute sense) are necessary, but also other virtues, both intellectual and natural: such as knowledge, prudence, effectiveness, and gravity. Therefore, it is not necessary to choose the better man in the absolute sense, but the one who is more expedient for the governance of the church.

<summary>This page explores whether a candidate for bishop must be the holiest person available (the "better" man) or simply the most effective leader (the "fit" man). Soto concludes that while holiness is vital, the practical requirements of governing the Church mean that electors should prioritize suitability and administrative competence.</summary>

### Book Ten, Question II

Wherefore **Jerome** says: "Some," he says, "do not seek to choose those as columns in the church whom they know would benefit the churches more, but those whom they themselves love more." <note>original: "Hierony. Quidam, inquit, non quærunt eos in ecclesia columnas eligere quos plus cognoscãt eccle∫ijs magis prode∫∫e, ∫ed quos plus ip∫i amant." Jerome is criticizing appointments based on personal friendship rather than merit.</note> So far his words. This indeed pertains to <term>partiality</term><note>The original Latin is *acceptionem personarum*, often translated as "respect of persons," meaning showing favoritism or bias regardless of merit.</note>. Wherefore, concerning that passage in James 2: "My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord of glory with partiality."

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
**Augustine** says: "If this is applied to ecclesiastical honors, it must not be considered a light sin."

<margin>The latter conclusion.</margin>
**The latter conclusion.** He who is elevated to the seat is not bound to consider himself better than the others. For such a thought would drive a man toward pride and presumption; rather, it is enough if he does not recognize in himself some crime through which it would be a' wicked thing for him to occupy the seat. Therefore, even though **Peter** was asked by way of comparison whether he loved more than the others, he nevertheless responded only simply: "Lord, you know that I love you."

All these matters we have elucidated so widely and extensively in Book 3, Question 6, through ten conclusions, that we can add nothing more relevant now; but it shall be enough not to have passed over the text of **Saint Thomas** for his sake.

<margin>An elector is bound by the duty of office to explore and weigh the merits of those to be elected, and to give the better one to the church.</margin>
Two or three things must be perceived by the mind in the fabric of his words. First, that since the very word "election" designates a comparison among many—where one is chosen while the others are set aside—the elector is reminded by the name itself that it is not enough for him to find someone suitable to elect, but he ought to weigh and ponder the merits of many so that he may grant the more outstanding one to the church: not only taking into account the integrity of his life, but of the other things which are expedient for public function. Nevertheless, in the place cited, we took care to advise that the first foundation of suitability must be integrity <note>The Latin *probitas* implies both moral uprightness and proven honesty.</note>. For no other qualities can make a man who is wicked suitable to be elected. Wherefore **Paul** requires it as necessary in a bishop that he be held in sufficient testimony "without crime." Which name indeed refers not to a lighter fault, but to a mortal one.

<margin>Three things required in a bishop besides charity.</margin>
Furthermore, the things required in a bishop besides <term>charity</term><note>In this theological context, charity (*charitas*) refers to the supernatural love of God and neighbor.</note> are reduced to the three things which **Saint Thomas** reports here: which are to instruct the people in faith and morals, to defend them from the dangers of heretics and others who pervert morals, and finally to govern peacefully. For the goal of governance is the peace of minds and bodies. For by this reason, the sons of God retain their name. For, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

<margin>Objection.</margin>
Regarding that noteworthy word by which **Saint Thomas** says that divine mysteries, and even

<column-break/>

salaries <note>Original: *stipendia*. While this can mean military pay, in a church context it refers to the financial support or "living" attached to a church office.</note>, are not given to men as a reward for their charity and integrity, someone might doubt this: because both natural reason and ecclesiastical laws seem to cry out against it; for they wish that clerics who have deserved well of the church be remunerated by it.

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
It is responded, however, that the said sentence needs no interpretation. For as it stands, it is true. For he does not deny that those who are of upright life are worthy of church <term>prebends</term><note>A *prebend* is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend.</note> and dignities, but only that which we demonstrated not lightly in the cited place of Book 3: namely, that the priesthoods and their salaries were not instituted for the remuneration of the good, but only for the service of the churches. For if this were not necessary in the Christian family, certainly, neither would tithes have been commanded, nor salaries established. Therefore, if these are to be granted to the worthy, that is not the supreme cause—that they are owed to their own goodness—but that the elector must provide a suitable minister to the church in proportion to his salary.

If you please, revisit the remaining matters in the cited place of Book 3. For we took care to demonstrate there that, although regarding the rigor of the <term>external forum</term><note>The *forum exterior* refers to the public legal system of the Church (Canon Law).</note> and the bond of restitution it is enough to elect a worthy person, nevertheless, regarding the <term>heavenly forum</term><note>Original: *forum poli*, literally "the forum of the pole/heavens." It refers to the court of God and one's conscience.</note>, it is necessary to elect the *more* worthy. If this is necessary in all priesthoods, and especially in those having the care of souls, how much more is it necessary in the appointment of bishops: seeing as by their administration the entire spiritual salvation of the Christian republic is endangered. And likewise, the very blood of Christ—which not only through their iniquity and fraud, but through their ignorance, laziness, and sluggishness can be frustrated—and very often is accustomed to be deprived of the fruit of its redemption. Let those, therefore, upon whom this duty falls, see to themselves how much they ought to skillfully survey with their eyes the merits of those whom they substitute for the Apostles themselves, who were chosen by God. And they ought especially to beware of those who <term>ambitiously seek</term><note>The Latin *ambiunt* refers to political-style campaigning or craving for office, which was a canonical offense.</note> honors of this kind. For they are not to be considered shepherds of the sheep, who long to pour out their blood for them; but wolves who, thirsting for their blood, think nothing of extinguishing their souls.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, **Saint Thomas** responds that since the other qualities of **Peter** suitable for the governance of the church were very well known to Christ, He specifically examined him on the greatness of his love for this reason: that where other conditions are present, this one ought to be judged...

But it is chiefly because **Christ** instituted bishops as pastors to fatten their flock with the food of the doctrine He Himself taught, and to imbue them with the morals He Himself instituted; they were not primarily instituted as Doctors of the laws which men added later, or as judges of lawsuits. This is especially true since the canons are derived from the fountain of Theology. This is what his two-horned miter signifies. For as is clear in his consecration, the head of a bishop is armed with horns—not of **"both laws"** <note>original: "vtriusque iuris"; referring to the common degree in Civil and Canon Law.</note>, but of **"both Testaments"** <note>The Old and New Testaments.</note>—so that he may appear terrible, not to those opposing each other in court, but to the adversaries of truth. ¶ <margin>To the third.</margin> To the third point, it is responded that there is a difference between the rule of natural things and governance in spiritual matters, which pertain to supernatural grace. In natural things, by the very fact that a thing is simply higher, it is by its own nature more fit for ruling: as the heavens are more fit than the elements, and the other elements more than the earth. But in the gifts of grace, which, as **Paul** says in the first [letter] to the Corinthians, the Holy Spirit divides as He wills, nothing prevents one who is simply lower

<column-break/>

according to charity from being better equipped for governing through an abundance of graces and gifts. And ecclesiastical governance belongs to this order of grace. Indeed, not only this, but even civil government. Therefore, not only in choosing civil magistrates, as **Aristotle** says in Book 3 of the *Politics*, <margin>Aristotle.</margin> must one attend to the integrity of the man insofar as he is a private person (which is what charity does), but also to whether he is a **good citizen**. Therefore, other qualities of kings and judges also belong in their own degree to the "divisions of graces" <note>A reference to the *gratiae gratis datae*—spiritual gifts given for the benefit of others, such as the gift of administration.</note>.

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether it is permitted for a bishop to leave his episcopal care to join a religious order.<-

<note>Decorative drop cap P</note> **AFTER** the qualities of those who are to be elected and the obligation of the electors, it follows to dispute whether the status of bishops is so firm that, after a bishop has assumed it, he cannot leave it. <margin>First argument.</margin> For it is argued that it is not permitted for him: primarily with a view toward entering a **religious order** <note>original: "religionem"; in this context, "religion" refers to a monastic or mendicant order (the "state of perfection").</note>. But this is not permitted, because to look back from perfection toward what is less perfect is damnable, according to the sentence of the Lord in Luke 9: "No one putting his hand to the plow and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God." However, the status of bishops is higher than the institute of monks, as we were saying a little while ago; therefore, just as a return from the monkhood to the world is wicked, so is it from the episcopal office to the cloister of a religious order. ¶ **Secondly.** <margin>Second.</margin> The order of grace is more fitting than the order of nature. However, according to nature, nothing is moved by contrary motions: just as a stone, which naturally descends, cannot naturally ascend. But according to the order of grace, the ascent from monkhood to the episcopacy is permitted; therefore, the contrary descent is illicit. ¶ **Thirdly.** <margin>Third.</margin> Nothing in the works of grace ought to be idle. But he who is once consecrated as a bishop perpetually retains the power of conferring orders and performing other things of that kind. If someone were to abandon the pastoral care, this power would remain idle; therefore, it is by no means permitted. ¶ **On the contrary** is the fact that no one can be compelled to do that which is illicit. But he who seeks a resignation from pastoral care is thereafter compelled to it if he hesitates to resign, as is clear in the chapter *Quidam* regarding renunciation; therefore, it is not illicit for a bishop to depart from his bishopric.

->### Question II of Book Ten<-

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The question is answered with four conclusions. The first, which serves as the foundation for the others, is: A bishop is obligated to retain his pastoral care and endure its struggles for as long as there remains any hope that he can be of benefit to the people.
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
This is proven as follows: The episcopal state consists in a person committing themselves to caring for the salvation of their neighbors out of divine love. Christ clearly taught this when he chose Peter. For he did not first ask, "Do you love the flock more than these?" but rather, "Do you love me?" <note>Referring to John 21:15–17. The author argues that love for God is the necessary prerequisite for the grueling work of leadership.</note> No love is sufficient to undergo the labors and persist in the vigilance and concern necessary for the episcopal function unless it is derived from divine love. Therefore, a bishop binds his faith not only to the church or the people, but to God Himself, so that he may govern his flock as a faithful and prudent steward.
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Indeed, this obligation is a type of vow, as **Saint Thomas Aquinas** states at the end of the question. The questions asked by the consecrator during the bishop's ordination allude to this: "Do you wish to teach the people, both by words and examples, those things which you understand from the divine scriptures?" "Do you wish to exhibit faith and obedience to the Blessed Apostle Peter and his successors?" Thus, although no new vow of chastity is emitted beyond the priestly one, nor any other solemn vow upon which the Pope cannot dispense, a vow of obedience is nonetheless made that is dispensable only by the Supreme Pontiff. If it is a vow, as Saint Thomas says, it is made not only to the Pope but to God Himself. And so, as the conclusion asserts, the bishop remains bound by a perpetual bond to his church, which he weds to himself through the "ring of faith." <note>The ring given to a bishop at his consecration symbolizes his "marriage" to his diocese, implying a lifelong commitment.</note> Therefore, it would be a "divorce" if he did not remain with her perpetually.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion: He cannot leave that same church for the sake of the "sweetness of contemplation," <note>Referring to the "contemplative life" (prayer and study) as opposed to the "active life" of administration.</note> nor to avoid any discomfort, nor to pursue his own personal advantage.
<margin>The proof.</margin>
This is proven: for **Paul**, whom we cited above in Philippians 1, was as if caught between two choices and unsure which to pick; although he judged that to "be dissolved and be with Christ" was far better, yet seeing that it was necessary to remain in the flesh for the sake of his brothers, he added: "And trusting in this, I know that I shall remain." And Christ says in John 10: "The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep." If you look closely at these meditations, you will see with what energy all advantages and disadvantages that might personally affect the bishop are excluded. For if Paul did not judge that even the eternal enjoyment of happiness—

<column-break/>

which, even for a brief moment, unspeakably surpasses everything that can be desired—was a just cause to abandon his brothers in their necessity by leaving his protection and office, what possible personal convenience could be imagined to excuse a bishop? And if Christ warns the shepherd to expose his very life for the flock, what remaining loss is there, for the sake of avoiding which the flock might be deserted?
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
The third conclusion: Nevertheless, certain impediments can occur because of which a bishop may step down from the episcopate.
<margin>Innocent III</margin>
**Innocent III** <note>Pope Innocent III (r. 1198–1216), a major figure in the development of Canon Law.</note> enumerates these in the chapter *Nisi cum pridem* regarding resignations. <note>original: "de renuntia." referring to the Decretals of Gregory IX.</note> But these impediments must be weighed in respect to the function of the office, which cannot be carried out properly. For example, there may be a spiritual defect in the person, or a physical one: namely a crime, such as **simony**, <note>The buying or selling of ecclesiastical offices or spiritual things.</note> or homicide, or heresy, or any other reason for which a bishop ought to be deposed; or through which he incurs "infamy." <note>A legal term for the loss of one's reputation and standing, which barred a person from exercising authority.</note> Once stained by this, even if he has performed penance, he lacks the authority to rule, because his status causes more harm than good. Indeed, if he is able to clear his name of infamy, he is bound to do so under pain of mortal sin if he wishes to persist in his dignity. For by the same law that he is bound to right administration, he is also bound to remove obstacles when he can, even if he incurred the infamy through no fault of his own. However, when he is unable to wash away the stains of infamy, if he was infected by them through no fault of his, he is not bound to resign the bishopric. But if he truly gave cause for that infamy, and it is so dark that it truly hinders his function, he is certainly bound to step down from the prelacy. And the same applies if he is seditious or scandalous. 
<margin>Paul.</margin>
As the **Apostle** says in 1 Corinthians 8: "If I scandalize my brother, I will never eat meat." This applies provided it is "given" scandal, not merely "taken" scandal. For those who take scandal lightly <note>Meaning those who are offended without a just cause or out of malice.</note> are to be left alone, as Christ says, like "the blind leading the blind." Or, there may be a defect in knowledge and prudence. Let no one persuade himself that if he is entirely unworthy of the priesthood, he can have a clear conscience simply because it was granted to him by a legitimate judge in a way that the appointment holds. On the contrary, just as accepting it is a sin—especially if it involves the care of souls—so retaining it day by day is a more absurd crime, and ascending to another church is a much more wicked one. Hence in Hosea 4, the Lord says: "Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not perform the office of priesthood for me." If, however, he is irregular... <note>The text cuts off as it moves to the next page.</note>

If an irregularity existed at the time he was admitted to the priesthood, there is no doubt that the appointment was void. If, however, he incurred it after he obtained the office, it has already been stated that he cannot perform the duties of the dignity without a <term>dispensation<note>A formal exemption from a church law or requirement granted by a superior authority.</note></term>. ¶ If, however, the impediment is physical—such as extreme old age or illness—resignation from the church is not strictly necessary; instead, the advice might be to remain while retaining some means of support. But at the very least, according to the ancient laws, a worthy person should be joined to him as an assistant. Yet, there might be such great authority in an old man that it would be more prudent for him to persist in the magistracy and govern by his "shadow" rather than committing the task to another. This is according to the same title on renunciation, the canon *Literas*, as stated by <note>original: "Innocẽ." refers to Pope Innocent III, a major figure in the development of Canon Law.</note> Innocent. ¶ Finally, regarding the subjects (the laity), there can be a certain failure, though not just any failure. For just because the people are somewhat stubborn, they should not be immediately rejected out of despair; rather, one must trust in divine protection. But it is permissible to leave them—even if no obligation arises to do so—when there are no honest people among the wicked, and the labor is entirely fruitless and therefore superfluous. For often, due to the failure of the people, the preaching of the <term>prelate<note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note></term> becomes ineffective, according to that passage in Ezekiel 3: <note>The OCR says Ezekiel 5, but the quote is from 3:26.</note> *I will make your tongue cleave to the roof of your mouth,* because the Lord is exasperated. Wherefore, in the second of his Dialogues, <margin>Gregory.</margin> Gregory says: The wicked are to be borne with equanimity only where some good people are found who may be helped. But where fruit from the good is entirely lacking, laboring among the wicked sometimes becomes superfluous. Hence it often happens in the souls of the perfect that when they see their labor is without fruit, they migrate to another place to labor with fruit; as Paul said: *Behold, we turn to the Gentiles, because you have made yourselves unworthy of the word of God.* <margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin> ¶ **Fourth conclusion.** No matter how many just causes there may be for resigning, the resignation cannot be made without the authority of a superior: for example, the Pope, if a bishop wishes to resign, since he alone possesses the power (as Saint Thomas says) to dispense from that <term>vow<note>The 'vow' refers to the bishop's lifelong commitment to his diocese, discussed on the previous page.</note></term>. A parish priest, however, may resign with the permission of the bishop. This is the opinion of the same Innocent in the final words of the same chapter, where he says: *Even if you have wings with which you strive to fly away into solitude, they are so strictly bound by the ties of the commandments that you do not have free flight without our permission.* Indeed, it is not even permitted for a bishop to move to a <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> religious order without the Pope's faculty, as is clear in the chapter *Licet* regarding rules. And the reason is that just as no one should be admitted to the church 

<column-break/>

without the judgment of a superior, so too it is not permitted for anyone to abandon it without his judgment. But finally, one must consider the caution in the chapter *Quidam* cited above: that if someone seeks a resignation and then draws back, he must be compelled to proceed. For some were, and still are, accustomed to renounce a poorer bishopric, or one otherwise less convenient for them, so that they might "fish for" a richer one. And therefore, when they see themselves frustrated by their own tricks, they draw back. It is only right, then, that they be compelled to resign and be removed from the church.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin> To the first argument, then, the response is: Since the perfection of a monk consists in seeking his own salvation, while the perfection of a bishop is more excellent because he must apply himself to the salvation of his neighbors, it follows that as long as he can be useful to the church, he must zealously devote his efforts to that same duty. Because of this, if he were to move to a religious order at that time, he would be judged to be "retreating"—namely, that while he was obligated to procure not only his own but also his subjects' benefit, he sought only to attend to his own. Hence <margin>Innocent.</margin> Innocent says in the cited chapter: *It is more easily permitted for a monk to ascend to the prelacy than for a prelate to descend to the monkhood.* Nevertheless, when he is already useless to the church, or perhaps even harmful, the advice is that he should retreat into a monastery so that he may more healthily consult his own conscience. <margin>To the second.</margin> ¶ To the second, the response is based on the same foundation: that a man should never, through any impediment, overlook the care of his own salvation, which pertains to the state of religious life. He can, however, be hindered from the business of another's salvation. And therefore a monk can indeed ascend to the bishopric where no danger is prepared for his own salvation. And likewise, a bishop—where he is prevented from applying himself to the salvation of others without detriment to his own—may betake himself within the cloisters of a monastery. But when the impediment ceases, he can return again to his previous institution; unless perhaps he was deprived of the bishopric because of some crime and thrust into a monastery to perform the fruits of penance. This is how that decree in 7, question 2 is understood: *The holy Synod commands that whoever descends from the pontifical dignity to the life of monks and penance shall by no means rise again to the pontificate.* <margin>To the third.</margin> ¶ Finally, to the third, the response is that just as in natural things, infirmity causes a power to remain deprived of its use,

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the physical and spiritual impediments that might prevent a bishop from fulfilling his duties. It transitions into a major new section (Question 3) concerning the controversial and heavily debated topic of whether bishops are required by divine law to live within their own dioceses, a central issue during the Council of Trent.</meta>

# Question Three: On the Residence of Bishops

## Article I

->*Whether bishops are bound by divine law to reside in their dioceses.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' depicting a scholar or cleric in robes seated at a writing desk within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc>
In the third place in this book, we promised to address this distinguished question concerning the residence of Bishops and priests who hold the care of souls.

<margin>First argument for the negative side.</margin>
It appears that this is not ordained by divine law. For that which is considered "divine law" is primarily what is read in the Gospel or in either Testament as a divine precept—such as the precept of baptism: "He who believes and is baptized shall be saved"—or what is clearly gathered from those sources. However, a precept of residency of this kind is not found there; therefore, it is not a sanction of divine law.

<margin>Second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly: The keys of the kingdom of heaven were committed to Peter alone, and to him alone it was said that he should feed the entire flock of Christ. Therefore, the highest authority in this matter was committed to him alone, and consequently, the manner of "feeding" the flock. But residency pertains to the manner of feeding; and thus, it is not a matter of divine law.

<margin>Third argument.</margin>
¶ Thirdly: Timothy, the bishop of Ephesus, was frequently urged by the command of Paul to travel through other churches and to be absent from his own for a long time; therefore, residency is not a matter of divine law.

¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that bishops are "pastors" <note>The word "pastor" literally means shepherd; Soto is emphasizing the personal care required of a shepherd for his sheep.</note>, according to that Gospel saying: "Feed my sheep." Now, feeding a flock is a personal duty that requires the presence of the person; therefore, by that same Gospel law, they are bound to reside in their own churches.

The iniquity of the times has made this question famous. Indeed, the affirmative side—if one considers only the name of "pastor"—sets the truth so clearly before one's eyes that it almost refuses to be called into question at all. 

<column-break/>

For this reason, among the ancient writers, you will see this duty mentioned everywhere, but it was hardly ever debated. But since ecclesiastical morals have fallen so miserably from that flowering state of the ancients, they have brought this same truth back into question to such an extent that it is now not easy to persuade people of it.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
And yet <term>Cajetan<note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), known as Cajetan, was a leading philosopher and theologian of the Dominican order.</note></term>, in his commentary on this place (specifically, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 185), settles the matter briefly as a settled fact.

<margin>Bartholomew Miranda.</margin>
However, at the time of the <term>Council of Trent<note>A major ecumenical council (1545–1563) that addressed church reform and challenged Protestant doctrines.</note></term>, the excellent brother Bartholomew Miranda <note>Bartholomew Carranza de Miranda (1503–1576), a Dominican who became Archbishop of Toledo.</note>—who was very closely joined to me then by the bond of our religious order and our companionship there—supported this same question with numerous testimonies from the sacred texts and with many reasons. He did this so richly and eloquently, as is typical of his talent and skill, that he could have spared others the labor;

<margin>Catharinus.</margin>
unless the Reverend <term>Catharinus<note>Lancelot Politi (1484–1553), known as Ambrogio Catarino, was a Dominican theologian and Bishop of Minori known for his many theological disputes.</note></term>, the Bishop of Minori, had come forward to contradict him. I do not mean to say he denied that prelates are bound to reside; but he persisted in asserting that they are obligated to it by human law—that is, by papal law—but not by either natural or divine law. From this, he went on to infer that the care of making them reside rests on the Pope alone, and that they themselves are not bound except as the Pope has disposed. I, however, do not wish to engage in a legal battle with the man. For he is a man who is otherwise religious, but of a very sharp mind for contradiction. I previously had a controversy with him concerning the certainty of grace, and later in my Commentaries on Paul regarding predestination. Concerning which matter, as I have heard (for I have never read it), he sprinkled me with many of those figures of scoffing that are innate and natural to him. In truth, if he would sweat as much over confirming his own assertions as he usually does on hurling these kinds of insults, he would have celebrated his name more happily. But he thinks his words should be listened to simply as oracles. And while he finds it hard to bear that everyone wants to be a master, he himself does not fear to come forward as the master of everyone. But I have determined—since it is neither theological nor Christian—not to return evil for evil. And I find it harder to bear that a bishop should vomit such things about anyone than that someone should vomit them about me. Especially since he did not spit out such evils against me that I would need much long-suffering to bear. Therefore, I only strive to clarify the matter according to my own small talent, not to contend with the man.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, so that we may begin with some common ground, let us set forth a first conclusion most widely accepted by all professors of learning. It is most certain that the Prelates of churches, and indeed all pastors of souls down to the <term>parish priests<note>original: "parœcios," referring to local clergy in charge of a specific parish.</note></term>, are bound to reside among their flocks. But what has turned into a question is the nature of the law compelling this: is it merely human, or indeed [divine?]

<summary>Soto introduces the debate on whether bishops are required by divine law to live in their dioceses, framing it against the backdrop of the Council of Trent and his personal disagreements with Bishop Catharinus. He concludes that all pastors are certainly bound to reside with their flocks, though the legal source of this obligation remains debated.</summary>

<margin>The stated conclusion is urged.</margin>
Indeed, it is both divine and natural law. For what person of sound mind would call into question whether a doorkeeper, to whom the rights of closing and opening have been committed, ought to remain at the door? Or whether the one upon whom the steering of a ship is incumbent should sit at the helm? Or whether a leader in war, while it is being waged, or a soldier in the battle line, ought to be present? Indeed, not only do human laws refuse to allow this to be questioned regarding bishops, but it is certain that both divine and natural law would count it as madness in us that we even attempt to debate it. For if God—as our opponents themselves admit, because they cannot deny it—instituted the episcopal dignity, which extends widely throughout the Church, did He not also institute the office of feeding <note>original: "officium pascendi"</note> itself? Moreover, does not <term>natural law</term> <note>ius naturale: Universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> openly proclaim that "feeding" requires a personal presence? Therefore, even if we were to grant them that elections are made only by human law, they would never obtain from that the idea that the Pope could change the fact that the office of a pastor is, by divine law, to feed the flock by oneself, and consequently to reside there. But lest the impulse of speaking carry us into the heart of the dispute without the light of orderly arrangement and economy, and having assumed our first fundamental conclusion, what is being called into question is: upon what law does this obligation of residing rest? And the first article concerns divine law. Now, a treater of sacred matters—as <margin>Augustine.</margin> Augustine is the authority in his first book *On Christian Doctrine*—listening to the instruction of the master of the house, ought to bring forth from the treasury of scripture first the new, then the old. For this reason, we have made a specific title here: concerning <term>divine law</term> <note>ius divinum: Law believed to come directly from God's revelation, such as the Bible.</note>, both evangelical and ancient. From this, the foundation of the present matter must first be sought; then in the next article, from natural law; and in the third, from human law. Although these types of law are so mutually deserved and so vicariously illustrative of each other that sacred testimonies might seem weaker unless they are immediately explained and confirmed by natural reason and law; and therefore, it will often be necessary to fetch arguments mixed from every type of law. ¶ For a perceptive understanding of these things, it is necessary to remember from books 1 and 3 that, first, law is divided into natural and <term>positive law</term> <note>ius positivum: Man-made law, or law specifically "posed" or decreed by an authority.</note>; then positive law is divided into divine and human. For natural law is that which nature itself has taught us. Positive law, however, is that which has the force of law either from the agreement of men or from the command of a prince. And because the highest prince is God, it follows that positive law is divided into divine and human. Consequently, it is not at all contradictory for something to be of 

<column-break/>

natural law and divine law at the same time. This is evident in the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments.</note>, which, even if God had not written it, nature itself would have taught us. But nevertheless, because it was expressed in the writing of God, it is also considered to be of divine law. Hence, divine law is distinguished into natural and positive. Positive divine law is that which God taught us beyond or above the knowledge of nature, such as the commands regarding the sacraments. And we speak of this kind of divine law in this article: namely, that which is written on the sacred page. This can happen in two ways: either that which is written in express words—such as, *He who believes and is baptized shall be saved* [Mark 16:16], and, *Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained* [John 20:23]—or that which is clearly gathered from the express words of scripture. And indeed, no one affirms that it is expressed under this specific phrasing in the Gospel "that bishops should reside," because it is nowhere read. But nevertheless, we contend to persuade you that this is asserted in the same Holy Bibles in equivalent words having exactly the same meaning. ¶ Let this, therefore, be the second conclusion.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin> **The obligation of Prelates to reside, and of all pastors of parish churches, is of divine law.** And especially, since we act as interpreters of <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> St. Thomas, this is his own conclusion on the present question, which we have thought should be explained here in Article 5. There, from the testimony of Christ that a good pastor is bound to lay down his life for his sheep, he infers that it is not permitted for a prelate to depart from his church for any temporal danger. Moreover, we shall dispute the matter of that article in Question 4: namely, whether there are any causes that might make such a departure excusable. In the meantime, the present conclusion must be demonstrated more affirmatively. Now, the beginning of the demonstration is usually taken from the office of the pastor; however, it must be sought from a deeper source. For a Bishop is not the one for <margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin> whom the church was established, but he is rather instituted for the sake of the church. God indeed made the world for the sake of man: namely, that it might be a support for his life; but man was not made for the world's sake, but was created as its master. And secular fathers of families enlarge their houses with riches for the sake of their successors. Therefore, in such families, persons are not built for the sake of houses, but houses for the sake of persons. In public affairs, however, things stand in a different way. For a kingdom was not made for the sake of the king, but the king for the sake of 

<summary>Soto argues that a bishop's duty to reside in his diocese is a matter of both natural and divine law, using analogies of doorkeepers and captains to show that an office inherently requires the presence of the office-holder. He defines the distinctions between natural, divine, and positive law, asserting that even if the word 'residency' isn't in the Gospel, the obligation is clearly implied by the pastoral duty to 'feed the flock.'</summary>

### Book Ten, Question III. ###

<margin>A twofold distinction between the civil and ecclesiastical commonwealth.</margin>
...for the sake of the kingdom. And in this, as we said in Book 1, a king differs from a tyrant, because the former uses everything for the public good, while the latter abuses the kingdom for his own sake. This is much more certain in the case of bishops. For Christ, who for our sake as men descended from heaven, founded churches for his own sake and for their sake, [appointing] both other pastors and especially bishops. Except that there is a twofold distinction between the civil and ecclesiastical <term>commonwealth</term> <note>republicam: Referring here to the organized body of the state and the church respectively.</note>. One distinction arises from the nature of the "end" (the goal), from which the other is derived regarding the manner of administering. For the immediate end of the civil commonwealth, as we noted in earlier sections, is its peaceful and tranquil state, even if it is subsequently referred to the super-celestial state. However, the immediate end of the ecclesiastical commonwealth is eternal happiness, to which Christ, the founder of the Church, seeks and strives in every way to lead us through his ministers. The other distinction is that secular princes, in their mode of governing, have the appearance of lords <note>original: "effigiem habent dominorum"</note>; bishops, however, are permitted to display no appearance but that of ministers and entirely of those who serve. For the "princes of the Gentiles," says Matthew 20, "lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them. It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you, let him be your minister; and whoever would be first among you, shall be your servant. Just as the Son of Man came not to be ministered to, but to minister, and to give his life as a ransom for many." Whence
<margin>Augustine</margin>
Augustine, in his 7th Homily on Isaiah: "Those who are called to the episcopate are not called to a principate [rule], but to the service of the entire Church." Behold, therefore, the foundation of the episcopal institution, which is most firmly established as being of <term>evangelical law</term> <note>iure evangelicum: Law derived from the teachings of the Gospels rather than human legislation.</note>: namely, that just as a servant is whatever he is for his master, so a
<margin>The episcopal dignity is not instituted except for the sake of the office.</margin>
bishop, whatever he is, becomes the Church's. ¶ From this it follows that the episcopal dignity was not instituted except for the sake of the office. For the duty of the pastoral dignity is to feed [the flock]. To commend this truth most deeply, dignity in the Sacred Scripture is never designated except by the name of office <note>officium: Meaning duty, service, or function.</note>. For to begin demonstrating this conclusion from that first passage, which is John 21 <note>The text cites John 20, but the quote "Feed my sheep" occurs in John 21:17.</note>, "Feed my sheep," by which the episcopal dignity is most clearly declared, Christ does not say, "Be a prelate or a bishop." Nay, not even "be a shepherd"; for shepherds can also be sluggish and sleep while the flock is present. But "feed": that is, teach, instruct, and thus govern by my example my

<column-break/>

sheep. And when he sent the apostles out to preach, he did not say: "The harvest indeed is great, but those who are learned in harvesting are few," but rather "laborers" <note>operarii</note>; namely, those who exercise power through practice. For it matters nothing with what doctrine or faculty priests are endowed, unless they perform their duty. Therefore God sent not those who *could* work, but those who *would* work. For similarly God had instituted Aaron in Leviticus 28 <note>likely referring to the consecration of priests described in Exodus 28</note>: "Bring near to me," he said, "Aaron and his sons." He did not say "so that they may be priests to me," but "that they may perform the priesthood for me." And as we noted above in Paul: "He who desires the episcopate," he says, "desires a good work." That is, if his desire is legitimate, it must be referred not to the dignity, but to the work. Wherefore he immediately added: "A bishop must be a teacher." By this name is designated not a habit or faculty and dignity, but the use; that is, it is necessary that he teach. Hence Augustine, cited above to Paulinus and referenced in Decree 8, question 1, canon *Qui episcopatum* <note>A reference to the Decretum Gratiani, the foundational collection of Canon Law</note>: "The Apostle," he says, "wished to explain what the episcopate is: because it is a name of work, not of honor." And Jerome to Honoratus: "He who desires the episcopate desires a work: that is, not dignity or luxuries, but work and labor." ¶ From this second point, as we descend by degrees, a third is gathered: namely,
<margin>Corollary</margin>
that <term>tithes</term> <note>decimae: A tenth of produce given to support the church.</note> and firstfruits, as we demonstrated extensively in Book 3 and repeat very often, were not commanded among this people so that they might be rewards for the excellence of men, as if because they are either good or learned. But rather for this purpose: that they might preside well over the churches, as Paul says, and serve them. For it will not trouble me to repeat most insistently that which pertains most deeply to the matter: that if this ecclesiastical service had not been necessary for Christians, no account would have been taken by Christ of the persons who are suitable, as far as the imposition of tithes is concerned. Therefore, let neither the most noble, nor the most learned, nor the most holy think that ecclesiastical stipends are owed to them by any reason, nor that they were instituted for their sake; but precisely because the Lord has need of these persons for the service of the churches. See again (lest I be tedious) those things which we brought forward in Book 3, question 6, article 2, for the demonstration of this. For in Numbers 18, God is read to have instituted tithes for no other reason than for the ministry by which the Levites and especially the priests served the Tabernacle. And when Christ sent out the apostles, he wished them to be harvesters who are worthy of their reward for their work. And Paul, in 1 Corinthians 9, gathers all natural
<margin>Paul</margin>

<summary>De Soto argues that the office of a bishop is fundamentally a role of labor and service (officium) rather than a position of honor or worldly status. He concludes that ecclesiastical income, such as tithes, is a wage for active ministry rather than a reward for personal merit or noble birth.</summary>
