<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s argument regarding the residency of bishops. Having established that a bishop’s office is defined as a "work" or "labor" rather than a mere title of honor, he now moves to prove that this labor requires the bishop to be physically present with his flock—a concept known as "divine law" residency.</meta>

->## F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right, ##<-

...the Church deems them worthy of ecclesiastical reward not simply because they are good people, but because they rule well. And if you consult the <term>Canon Law</term> <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church authority.</note>, 
<margin>Innocent III</margin> 
Innocent III, in the chapter *Cum secundum apostolum* (Regarding Prebends), using the same sacred oracles, established exactly the same principle: that ecclesiastical stipends and even dignities are conferred solely for the sake of the "work." Finally, in the final chapter (Regarding Rescripts), it is asserted that a <term>benefice</term> <note>An ecclesiastical office that guaranteed an income to the holder.</note> is not given except for the sake of the office. These are common points, but in these present times, they must be repeated even to the point of nausea.

<margin>Reasoning for the conclusion.</margin> 
From these points, therefore, our conclusion is gathered by that inference which we hinted at a little earlier. Christ instituted pastors for no other reason than for the sake of the churches—that is, for their service and administration. He willed that their specific duty be to "feed" the flock. And it is only as a reward and stipend for this labor that <term>tithes</term> <note>A tenth part of agricultural produce or personal income set apart as a tax for the support of the church.</note> were commanded from the people. Therefore, as far as the nature of the thing and divine institution are concerned, it is incumbent upon them to feed the flock by themselves. However, this cannot be done without personal presence. Therefore, residency is of <term>divine law</term> <note>Ius divinum: Law that comes directly from God, which even a Pope cannot override.</note>; for by whatever law one is obligated to an end, one is also obligated to the means without which that end cannot be conveniently reached.

<margin>Solution.</margin> 
The first premise no one denies, but our adversaries attempt to reject the first consequence. 
<margin>Response.</margin> 
For they say that because the Pope creates bishops, it is therefore his responsibility to arrange whether they should feed the flock themselves or through others. But that this quibble carries no color of probability is clearly gathered from what was said above. For first, it has already been sufficiently established that the creation of a bishop, although it happens through the Pope, is nonetheless done by divine law. Indeed, since it is an institution of God, it is commanded to be done through him, just like the administration of the sacraments. But lest a dispute over a name trouble us, let it be that the Pope "immediately" (as they say) performs the election; does it then follow that the Pope can change the very nature of the dignity which God instituted and declared by its own specific meaning? From where, I ask, does the consequence follow for two things so disparate? When the Pope elects and consecrates a bishop, can he make him *not* a pastor, any more than when he ordains a priest he can make him *not* a priest? Can he, I say, make it so that the function of a bishop is not to administer the sacraments of orders, to teach the people, to instruct them in morals, and—as his very name suggests—to watch over the flock? Who could even say such a thing? For all these things are annexed to the episcopal office by divine law; indeed, they are the very substance of the dignity by that same law. Truly, if God's institution has the same force as the nature

<column-break/>

instituted by Him, it is clear that just as one who sows a mulberry tree cannot make it so that a plum tree or any other tree sprouts from it except a mulberry, so too he who makes a bishop cannot make it so that his divinely instituted nature is not to "feed" the flock by himself. For we are not currently disputing whether, for some cause, he can justly arrange that the bishop does not feed by himself but through another—for that dispute awaits us elsewhere. Rather, we are establishing only the nature of the thing: teaching that just as one who 
<margin>The conclusion is further illustrated.</margin> 
builds a bench or a chest cannot make it so that it lacks the shape of a bench or a chest; or he who makes a shoe cannot make a thing that does not have the form of a foot; so he who makes a bishop (which is a thing divinely instituted) cannot make it so that, by the same law by which it was instituted, the bishop lacks the duty and the subsequent obligation of feeding the flock by himself and, consequently, of residing there—whatever might later happen from outside circumstances.

Indeed, lest the <term>homonymy</term> <note>A word that sounds the same but has different meanings.</note> and ambiguity of the word "pastor" cause us trouble from now on, one must understand that a bishop is a pastor according to the proper 
<margin>A bishop is a pastor according to the proper definition.</margin> 
meaning of the name, and not according to that abusive sense by which the owners of flocks are called pastors. For it is common to call those who own sheep and cattle "pastors" because their wealth and property consist of livestock. For example, when the sons of Jacob were asked by Pharaoh what their work was, they replied: "We are shepherds" <note>original: "Pastores sumus"</note>—meaning, this is our possession of riches. And such people exercise no care of the sheepfold themselves, except through their servants; instead, they live delicately and softly, enjoying only the fleece, the cheese, and the offspring. But bishops are not instituted as pastors of Christ's flock in this way, but entirely as ministers who are bound to endure the vigils of the flocks, to lead the flock through the meadows of Holy Scripture, to give them drink from its fountains, to anoint their scabs with oil, to ward off the wolf from them, and to guard against whatever could harm them in any way.

<margin>Solution to a silent objection.</margin> 
For there is no reason for anyone to object to this holy truth by saying that it was said to Peter alone, "Feed [my sheep]." For in this word, there is something unique said to Peter, and another thing general to all prelates. It was unique, I say, in that he, as the universal pastor, should feed the universal flock in his own grade and order—not indeed by being present to all churches, but by enlightening and instructing everyone with his constitutions and his judgments on faith and morals, and by assigning worthy ministers to every church. But the episcopal function was explained generally, being established in the apostles and in the Pope himself through the very institution of the Church by Christ: namely, that as soon as each one was created...

<summary>De Soto argues that the office of a bishop is a divinely instituted role that requires personal residency, comparing a bishop to a working shepherd rather than a wealthy livestock owner. He contends that even the Pope cannot change the fundamental nature of the bishop's duty to personally "feed" his flock.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s argument on the divine origin of the bishop’s duty. He is refuting the idea that the obligation to reside with the flock is merely a human law or a papal decree, arguing instead that it is a direct command from Christ, passed through the example of Peter to all bishops.</meta>

### Book Ten, Question III. 827 ###

...ordered by Christ himself, he should think to feed his own special flock in a similar way. Indeed, Augustine says in chapter 13 of his *Book on Pastors* <note>original: "lib. de pasto." Referring to *De Pastoribus*, a sermon on Ezekiel 34.</note> that for this reason Christ commanded Peter individually what was common to all: to commend unity. "For there were many apostles," he says, "and it is said to one: Feed my sheep." Thus far Augustine. It is as if he had said: In one man He gave power to all. In one man He expressed the general form of ruling for all, and thus in one man He commanded the same thing to all. And Ambrose says in his *Pastoral Care*: "The stewardship of the divine words has been entrusted to us, and we have undertaken to nourish the flock of Christ." By "divine words," he is alluding to those words spoken to Peter. And further down: "The Lord repeated a third time, 'Feed my sheep.' Not only did the blessed Peter then receive those sheep and that flock, but he received them with us: and we all received them with him." The Lord commanded Peter to feed the sheep, through whom the power and authority of feeding flows from God to all the rest. Thus says Ambrose.

¶ From these points it follows that it is a perverse and slanderous interpretation to think that the voice of the consecrator saying, "Go, preach to the people committed to you," is understood as if it belongs to the Pope alone. For he acts as the instrument of God, and thus it is an expression and, as it were, a repetition of the word of Christ himself: "Feed my sheep." Paul clearly alludes to this in Acts 20, saying: "Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops," etc. For the <term>gloss</term> <note>A standard commentary or explanation of a text, often found in the margins of legal or biblical manuscripts.</note> of our adversaries is of no value, in which they say he said "the Holy Spirit placed you" only because the Church is governed by His nod according to <term>positive law</term> <note>Human-made laws, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>. For in 1 Corinthians 7, Paul distinguishes between those things which God commanded and those which he himself commanded: and here he designates the proper action and command of God. For he does not say that he himself placed them, but that God did.

¶ But in order that the matter may become even clearer, it is necessary to explain the office of the spiritual pastor a little more fully. For we have already left it stated above that the duty is to take the most diligent care for the life of the spiritual sheep. This care is indeed threefold: namely, that the bishop generates and nourishes the people in spiritual life through the **sacraments**, fosters them through **preaching**, and governs them with **prudence**. Saint Thomas expressed these under other names: namely, to institute, to defend, and to govern. Under the name of sacraments, certain <term>sacramentals</term> <note>Sacred signs (like blessings or objects) that resemble the sacraments but do not confer grace in the same way.</note> are also understood, which Pope Leo recounts in the <term>canon</term> *Quamvis*, distinction 68. For upon them rests the consecration of priests, deacons, and other ministers of the altar, and of virgins. Then the establishment of the altar, and the blessing

<column-break/>

and anointing, and even of all the vessels and vestments belonging to that same altar, and finally, confirming the baptized with <term>chrism</term> <note>A consecrated oil used in the administration of certain sacraments and ecclesiastical functions.</note>. But the most proper task of all is to preach: that is, not only from the pulpit, but specifically to interpret the sacred oracles and to give answers concerning ambiguities. Whence, regarding that passage of Paul to the Ephesians 4: "Some pastors and teachers," Jerome noted that he deliberately did not say "some pastors and *others* teachers," as he had said "some apostles and *others* prophets": but "some pastors and teachers": namely, because in the church, he who is a pastor is the same as a teacher. And Augustine, in Letter 58, responds to Paulinus who was asking how pastors differ from teachers: namely, that they differ by no distinction: which he confirms by that same apostolic word.

<margin>Gregory.</margin>
¶ Finally, the third part of this same office is governance, to which the care of the poor, widows, and orphans is joined in no small measure. Both Gregory in the first book of his *Pastoral Rule* and other holy fathers assert that these are explained more expressly by the prophet Ezekiel <margin>The first passage of the Old Testament used for the conclusion.</margin> in chapter 34, where the Lord says: "Son of man, prophesy about the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not the flocks fed by the shepherds? You ate the milk, and you clothed yourselves with the wool." By these two things, all things which pertain to food and clothing are designated. These things the people supply to the bishops for their sustenance. But to designate their luxury, it is added: "That which was fat, you killed": where the greatest iniquity of the shepherd is suggested. For since his office is to fatten the flock with the richness of doctrine and morals: they instead care to grow fat on the people's substance. "And my flock you did not feed." But he proceeds to explain what it is to feed, saying: "That which was weak, you did not strengthen: that which was sick, you did not heal: that which was broken, you did not bind: that which was cast away, you did not bring back: and that which was lost, you did not seek."

<margin>The oracles of the ancient law do not have the same force for the present matter.</margin>
¶ Here, however, it must be noted first of all that the oracles of the Ancient Law do not have exactly the same <term>energy</term> <note>Referring to the legal or spiritual force and applicability of a text.</note> for the present matter as the testimonies of the New. For our priesthood exists as far different and therefore more sublime than that which they performed. For since their sacraments conferred no justifying grace (we say nothing of that which was conferred under the sign of circumcision), nor did they have the <term>power of the keys</term> <note>The authority to forgive or retain sins, which the Catholic Church teaches was given by Christ to the Apostles.</note> for the remission of sins, nor did they thereafter carry the care of souls as our priests do; what...

# Book Ten, Question III. 828 #

...is a most certain foundation that our prelates are bound to reside. Arguments for our proposition are sought from there. First, by reason of the **figure** <note>original: "figurae" - a theological term for a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a reality in the New Testament</note>, in which, as Paul says, all things happened to them: namely, that the ancient priesthood was a foreshadowing of our own. Then also by way of example: for if it was attributed to them as such a great vice that they did not take care of the flock, and they were compelled to be perpetually on watch in the temple. For we read the command in Numbers 18 to Aaron and his sons and the Levites: "Keep watch in the custody of the sanctuary." It is much more effectively proved that our pastors, as guardians of souls, must always be present to look after the flock. However, to return to the present passage of Ezekiel, not only are the priests denoted there by the name of "pastors," but all judges and governors of the people. Although even at that time, the scepter of government
<margin>The cited passage is examined.</margin>
was in the hands of the priests. ¶ Skillfully, therefore, the Prophet delineates the duty of the pastor with that five-fold discourse, at least regarding those things which must be healed in the flock. For the Christian flock is accustomed to be endangered by five troubles. The first is in **faith**, which is the foundation of the entire Christian life: for without faith it is impossible to please God. But the first detriment to faith is languor and weakness: namely, when a person wavers and vacillates because of the greatness of the things to be believed.
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Wherefore Paul in Romans 4 attributes praise to Abraham because he was not weakened in faith. And in Romans 14: "Accept the one who is weak in faith," (that is) sustain him so that he does not fall. This, therefore, is the first function of the <term>Prelate</term> <note>original: "Antistitis" - a high-ranking priest or bishop</note>, who is the teacher of faith: namely, to remove the scruples of faith from the minds of the flock by explaining doubts: and thereafter by affirming and consolidating their spirits so that they may, as Paul says, lead the intellect captive into the obedience of faith. **Sickness**, however, pertains to morals, when someone is infected with corrupt affections. For, just as the intellect is weakened by the scruples of faith, so also the appetite is sickened by the tumult of the affections. Wherefore, just as the former must be consolidated by the light of doctrine, so this latter must be healed by salutary warnings. **Fracture** <note>original: "Confractio" - a breaking or literal fracture, here used metaphorically for social division</note>, truly, pertains to discord among brothers: namely, when the people disagree among themselves either through various opinions or through lawsuits and quarrels. For then they must be bound together by the bond of peace and unity, and glued together by friendship. For from these fractures, unless they are gathered in time, heresies are accustomed to swell up. The present times teach us by 

<column-break/>

example that this most frequently happens through the foolishness and inertia of the prelates, and especially by their absence from their churches. Wherefore, that which follows, **the cast out** <note>original: "abiectum" - something thrown away or rejected</note>, refers to manifest heresy and apostasy. For the dissension of the people is the nursery of heresies, through which one exits the church; and the care of the prelate extends even to the medicine for this: so that, as Paul teaches, he must strive with at least one or two warnings to lead those who were cast out back into the church. Finally, he concludes: "And that which had perished you did not seek," following the example of Him who had come from heaven to seek that which was lost. Now, a man perishes through any mortal sin, but remarkably through obstinacy. Yet one must not utterly despair even of such a person, but rather every way of seeking him should be attempted. Furthermore, these effects are received and credited to the grace of God and His singular favor. Nevertheless, because He Himself supplies such grace to us through the ministry of priests, it happens that because of their negligence, the people are deprived of that same grace. This is something God clearly warns about in the same place, saying: "And my sheep were scattered because there was no pastor: and they became food for all the beasts of the field," that is, they were overwhelmed by all vices and trampled by every error. For which cause He immediately threatens the pastors: "I will require the flock from their hands." For by this same reasoning,
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Paul says in the last chapter of Hebrews that those set in authority must watch over the flock as those who are to give an account for their souls. Furthermore, unless these duties and offices of the bishop were so buried in oblivion, there would be no one, I believe, who could even hesitate whether bishops are bound by **divine law** <note>original: "iure divino"</note> to perform these things in person, and likewise to reside in their dioceses. For they must perform these things not only by public preaching, if they know their institution well, but by private visitations, exhortations, recreations, counsels, and even consolations. Indeed, not only by word, but also by example, and finally by helping in deed: namely, by defending the causes of the needy even in business, and by assisting with alms. Behold the office of the priest in the part where he must guard against harms to the flock. ¶ But truly, in the part where he is bound to promote the flock toward perfection, his function stands out even higher. It is for this reason that Christ, in the person of their predecessors, calls them the
<margin>Pastors of the church are the light of the world.</margin>
**light of the world**. See with what bounty He imparts His own names to them: so that if they do not persist in their office, He may shame them more severely on the day of judgment. Indeed, as we said above, 
<margin>Pope Pius.</margin>
Pope Pius, in the canon *Oves* <note>original: "cano. oues. 6. q. 1." - a reference to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of canon law</note>, calls them the eyes of God...

### Book Ten, Question III. ###

<margin>The pastor of the church is a city set upon a hill.</margin>
...he says that he instituted them. Whether they are the ones through whom God Himself provides for His flock, or those through whom the people receive divine things, He also calls them a **city set upon a hill** <note>original: "civitatem supra montem positam"; a reference to Matthew 5:14</note>. This is because they must not only shine with the light of doctrine from the lampstand, but also by a prominent example of life in the sight of the people; and like the **salt of the earth**, they must
<margin>The same as the salt of the earth.</margin>
season the morals of others. Consider whether those who are absent are able to perform such duties as is fitting. Indeed, to embrace everything at once, bishops ought to be in such a height of perfection that they do not merely learn perfection, but—as they are admonished in their own consecration—they must teach it entirely. What perfection should they ultimately teach? That as ministers of Christ, they should so purge, so promote, and so adorn His church that they may offer it to God the Father without blemish, as becomes the bride of Christ. Behold the first Gospel passage: **Feed my sheep** <note>original: "Pasce oves meas"; John 21:17</note>.
<margin>A second passage for the conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second passage from which the truth of the present conclusion is drawn is found in John 10, where Christ commends the nature of the good shepherd with this emphatic phrasing: **I am the good shepherd. A good shepherd gives his life for his sheep: but the hireling flees.** I cannot understand with what face anyone could mock this passage by saying it should not be understood generally of the whole body of pastors, on the grounds that Christ asserted it particularly (as they say) about Himself.
<margin>The interpretation of certain people is refuted.</margin>
For there is no need to call upon the holy interpreters who reject this sense <note>the sense that it only applies to Christ</note>. It is always better to elucidate Holy Scripture from its own words whenever possible. Consider therefore the context of the words: **I am the good shepherd.** Behold the assertion. But He did not think it enough to simply assert it; He proceeded to demonstrate it. And how did He demonstrate it? Because **a good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.** He did not, therefore, assert this uniquely and strictly of Himself; otherwise, He would have proven what He said by the very same thing—namely: "I am the good shepherd because I myself, the good shepherd, lay down my life for my sheep." Through that proving proposition, He instead revealed the nature, character, and substance of a good shepherd by a definition. He did this so that one might conclude: "He who gives his life for his sheep is a good shepherd; I give my life for my sheep; therefore, I am the good shepherd." He thus established a general rule by which a good shepherd is distinguished from those who are not good. Hence, Gregory says in a homily: "He added the form of His goodness for us to imitate, saying: **The good shepherd**

<column-break/>

**lays down his life for his sheep.**" He did what He advised; He showed what He commanded, etc. And Augustine, in his fifth sermon on the words of the Lord:
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
"The good shepherd is Christ. What of Peter? Was he not a good shepherd? For he also laid down his life for his sheep. What of Paul? What of the other Apostles?" Therefore, if you look closely at the words, Christ did not only wish to show Himself as an example before our eyes for us to imitate, according to that passage in John: **In this we have known the charity of God, because He laid down His life for us all: and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.** <note>1 John 3:16</note> And as Augustine says to Honoratus: when persecution is imminent, a bishop cannot flee, because by the example of the Lord, a good shepherd is bound to lay down his life for his sheep. For though adversaries might quibble, saying that even if Christ said this uniquely of Himself, He nevertheless set an example of Himself to be imitated, we further affirm that He established a rule and definition by which He proved Himself to be a good shepherd. Even if it were impossible for Him to have kept it, all prelates would still be bound by divine and natural law to keep it.
<margin>The previous reason is further strengthened.</margin>
¶ Come now, let us strengthen the same point from the following words. For He adds: **But the hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees.** I ask you, how did He use the name of "hireling" there? Was it specifically for one person? Truly, it was only in a general sense; therefore, He had used the term "good shepherd" in the same way. Otherwise, He would not have set the hireling in direct opposition to it. He explained the nature of both by their opposition. Unless you would prefer to admit the absurdity that He explained the nature of the bad shepherd, but not the good one. Nor was He content to state this simply, but He subjoined the natural cause: **For the hireling**, He says, **flees because he is a hireling, whose own the sheep are not.** Therefore, the care of the sheep does not belong to him, because they are not his own. Inasmuch as they were not entrusted to him by Christ, it follows that he does not love them—certainly not with that love which He required of Peter when He asked if Peter loved Him more than the others. ¶ But furthermore, the most pressing argument that our Lord and Redeemer stated this not only of Himself, but as a necessity for all who are legitimate bishops, is that all the Saints and Doctors conclude from this passage (as we shall see in Article 4) that a bishop is bound to expose his life before he departs from his flock when necessity threatens them. Since they themselves...

He refutes those who claim these mandates are specific only to Christ, citing Gregory the Great and Augustine to support the obligation of episcopal residence.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law #

...opponents would surely not dare to deny this, and from there they ought to conclude that residency is a matter of divine law. This is inferred so clearly from this passage that, otherwise, the Church would not constrain them to reside at such great risk. But we shall deal with that more precisely there.

¶ I would wish to stand firm here, if I had the faculty to persuade according to the dignity of the matter, and to ask the most venerable bishops to consider whether Christ could have opened the matter more significantly, or more vehemently discouraged them from trusting their flocks to hirelings <note>original: "mercenariis"</note>. For how can they love souls even to the shedding of blood if they do not hold them as their own? And unless they hold them so dear in the Lord, how can they legitimately look after them? For hirelings think they have done enough when, in proportion to the salary <note>original: "stipendij"</note> they receive, they put in a few hours for the hearing of lawsuits.

¶ Christ continues to further reveal the nature of the good shepherd. **I am**, he says, **the good shepherd: and I know my sheep, and mine know me** <note>John 10:14</note>. Therefore, let there be no room left for turning away, as if one might say Christ is speaking specifically only of himself. On the contrary, he introduces the same demonstration: namely, that because it is the character, faith, and care of a good shepherd that he and the sheep know each other mutually by face and voice, then he, in whom these qualities meet, is the good shepherd.

<margin>Theophylactus</margin> On this point, Theophylactus <note>A 12th-century Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator known for his accessible explanations of the Gospels.</note> says: *In this place, I recognize the difference between a shepherd and a hireling. For the hireling indeed does not know the sheep; this happens because he does not visit them often, etc. For he who has not betrothed the church to himself through the love of God cannot take great delight in the sight and familiarity of it.* Furthermore, he will not provide the duties of a shepherd to the flock unless he knows the face and the bleating <note>original: "balatū"</note> of each sheep, so that—not through a report or through another person, but from the countenance, gesture, and voice—he may detect the disease of the soul. Nor, in turn, can the flock love him enough, and thus both imitate his example and listen to his commands, unless they know him by his face and speech. Wherefore, what those men say—that Christ is affirming this strictly of himself—is proven false by the fact that he perhaps alluded to that proverb of Solomon which he himself had long ago uttered through Solomon's mouth, both because of the ancient shepherds and as a figure of our own. For he says 

<margin>Proverbs 27</margin> in Proverbs 27: **Be diligent to know the face of your cattle, and consider your flocks: for you shall not have power forever: but a crown shall be given to you from generation to generation** <note>Proverbs 27:23-24</note>. Where the Hebrew text has: *In knowing you shall know*—or evidently recognize—*the face of your flock*; and, as it is said,

<column-break/>

**face to face, and set your heart to the flocks.** In this context, some people—not very appropriately to the matter—imagine that in the word "set" <note>original: "appone"</note> an allusion is made to that saying of Christ: **The good shepherd sets down** (or lays down) **his life.** For besides the fact that the Gospel word <note>Greek: *tithesin*</note> means nothing other than "gives," there is a manifest difference in the things described. For Solomon’s word refers to the internal care and solicitude which a shepherd ought to have toward the flock: namely, that he should most intently have his heart attentive to the necessity of individual sheep. But Christ’s voice refers to the testimony of love: namely, that if necessary, he should face death for its sake. For if the care of a brute herd demands that mutual recognition, how much more the zeal which must be spent toward the Christian family—especially since there are as many kinds of diseases as there are subjects. For one needs consolation, another counsel, another rebuke, and finally another needs the assistance of alms.

<margin>Confirmation</margin> Wherefore, right at the beginning of the same chapter of John, where Christ was preparing to say that he is the door of the sheep: **He who does not enter by the door,** he says, **but by another way, is a thief and a robber: but he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the gatekeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice: and he calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out: and when he has let out his own sheep, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.** See how the law of the good shepherd consists not only in this—that one attains the dignity according to the laws of Christ—but also that he administers the same by his example: namely, by knowing the individual sheep by name, and by going before them by the example of his life, which they themselves may follow. How those who are absent can provide and accomplish this, they themselves must see. From which it follows: **But a stranger they do not follow, but flee from him: because they do not know the voice of strangers.** By the name "strangers" <note>original: "alieni"</note> he judges not only those who have entered illegitimately, but even those who administer the matter illegitimately: namely, both hirelings and those who do not observe the things he had mentioned before. And indeed the Apostles did not know what he was saying to them—namely, the mystery of his faith, through which alone all who were to possess true pastures would enter—because there is no other name under the sun in which men can be saved. But for us, who already know that for certain through the same faith, another thing remains to be held with most constant faith: namely, that those who are instituted as shepherds by him must fulfill their office after his likeness. Hence Pope Damasus, in his golden fourth epistle, where he speaks of the removal of the country-bishops <note>original: "chorepiſcopis"; these were rural bishops who had limited authority and were often the subject of jurisdictional disputes in the early church.</note> 

<margin>Damasus</margin>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's theological and legal argument that bishops are required by divine law to reside personally within their dioceses. He is currently refuting the argument that a bishop can fulfill his duties through a deputy or "vicar."</meta>

...has discussed richly, and by this testimony of Christ he vehemently attacks those bishops who entrust their people to be educated by others; since Christ asserts that the good shepherd lays down his life for his fold, while the hireling <note>original: "mercenarium"; referring to someone who works only for pay rather than out of duty or love</note> abandons the sheep when the wolf approaches. But concerning this letter, more will be said in the next article.

<margin>Objection of the adversaries.</margin>
¶ Let the adversaries, therefore, hold their position and argue to the contrary as follows: Whatever a man does through his representatives, he is deemed to perform by himself; therefore, when a bishop delegates a vicar for his church, he is not bound to reside, but satisfies his obligation through his substitute.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
Let such arguers see what answers follow them.

<margin>To the first point</margin>
First of all, as we said above, we are not disputing here whether some cause might intervene for which a bishop might be granted a dispensation to be absent—about which we must speak again in Article 4—but we are establishing the nature of the matter and those things commanded to a bishop by divine law. First, therefore, if we look at the facts, absent bishops do not substitute a vicar for all their duties, but only one who sits to hear lawsuits—which, in truth, is not the most important duty. And furthermore, they appoint a visitor to fly around the diocese; yet these things cannot be done conveniently in their absence, nor can anything else to which they are chiefly bound. For the most powerful part of a spiritual shepherd—as the Fourth Council of Carthage <note>A series of councils held in North Africa; the Fourth (c. 398) focused heavily on the discipline and lifestyle of the clergy.</note> advises in brief words—is this: he upon whom a far greater care of souls than of temporal things is incumbent should strive to settle disputes that can be defined without the noise of courtrooms, and should take care to pacify and extinguish them, so that he may redeem the time according to Christ's command, which the sheep may then spend in Christian exercises. This indeed no one can accomplish without the authority, gravity, and love with which a bishop is bound to follow his flock—and thus not without his presence.

<margin>Visitations cannot be done by anyone other than the bishop himself.</margin>
Likewise, long experience testifies that visitations cannot be carried out purely and justly by anyone other than the bishop himself. For crimes are not to be healed by a fine of money or excommunication alone, but surely by the word—now gentle, now sharp—and finally by applying other remedies, for which visitors feel no concern because they are hirelings. Add to this that almsgiving, which holds such a high place among episcopal works (for a bishop, as Paul says, must be hospitable), cannot be done effectively except by the leaders being present. For the sight of a poor man and the cry of the needy, moving the inner heart, may either draw out an alms...

<column-break/>

...or at least some other consolation by which he might lighten his misery. For those points we were just discussing regarding the word of Christ look to this: namely, how much it matters to recognize the face of the flock by sight and to hear their voice.

<margin>Another objection.</margin>
But you say: what if the bishop correctly dispenses all these things and others through another? For it can happen that others are more effective preachers than the bishop himself, and others more learned and fit for other duties; when he has supplied these, has he not fulfilled his office so that he might live away from his church?

<margin>First response.</margin>
The first response to this is that it is impossible.

<margin>Second response.</margin>
The second, which is especially to be noted, is that the vicars of bishops are not appointed as if they were to be the future prelates, but as helpers to the prelates. And therefore their residence is not excused by this. For vicars ought to be like limbs in a body, while the bishop himself is like the soul. For Christ did not send them as managers of workers, but as workers.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
And Paul does not say that it is necessary for a bishop to be a substitute for a teacher, but to *be* a teacher; and in the second letter to Timothy, chapter 2, he says: "Carefully study to present yourself approved unto God, a workman who need not be ashamed <note>original: "operarium inconfusibilem"</note>, rightly handling the words of truth." Here he covers that prelate in shame who is not a workman. And elsewhere he warns that he who does not work should not eat. In short, those who place the office of bishops in having good subordinate ministers do not see how they take away all the laws of the election of bishops and pastors. For what need is there to apply such great care and vigilance to choosing the most worthy candidate, as all the laws cry out for, if it is enough for a bishop to delegate other ministers to his church? Therefore, if those laws were established for a certain reason, it is clearly gathered that personal industry is chosen in a bishop, and thus he is bound to fulfill his duties by residing in person. Therefore, there is no reason for them to throw Valerius in our faces, who substituted Augustine for himself <note>Valerius, the Bishop of Hippo, famously sought Augustine as a co-bishop because he felt his own preaching in Latin was insufficient.</note>. For he did that when his age was already weighing him down and his strength did not suffice. Indeed, even then he is not to be believed to have ceased so much that he did not perform what he could. On the contrary, an argument is taken from this for how necessary the presence of the person is. For this reason the Apostle Peter, as Theodoret reports in his book on the 70 disciples, and the ancient Epiphanius in Volume 2, chapter 26—namely because it was necessary for him as an Apostle to wander through other churches—appointed a bishop of Rome for himself; not one who would be Pope, but one who would be a helping vicar to him.

<margin>To the argument made.</margin>
¶ To their argument, therefore, it is responded that...

### F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

->**Page 832**<-

...for although anyone is free to dispose of his own private goods as he pleases through a servant—in which case what one does through another, he is deemed to do himself—the matter stands quite differently in public administrations. For public magistrates, and especially those for whom just stipends have been decreed because of their personal function, are not administered according to justice through deputies. For who is created a consul, or a praetor, or a general, so that he may administer the matter through another? On the contrary, 
<margin>
A beautiful reason.
</margin>
even in private matters, who has hired a household manager, a cupbearer, or even a cook—or what is even more to the point—a ship captain or certainly a driver, who does not require the service of that specific person? Now, if other magistrates have this nature of residency, who does not see that the office of a bishop—which is for looking after souls, whom God both created for His own fellowship and redeemed at the cost of His own life—holds the first place under this law? Hence Paul says in 2 Corinthians 9: "Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel: necessity is laid upon me." <note>original: "Væ mihi si non euangelizauero: necessitas mihi incumbit." </margin>
the adversaries strive to avoid this blow. For they say it was necessary for the apostles to preach by themselves because their personal industry was specifically chosen. Bishops, however, did not succeed them in the apostleship, but in the episcopacy. Yet, even if we admit that the obligation to preach was more urgent in the apostles because of the doctrine revealed to them, nevertheless, who could deny that in bishops, 
<margin>
He refutes the nearest solution.
</margin>
personal industry is also chosen, insofar as they succeeded them in the episcopacy? Nor should their other invention be admitted: namely, that the apostles were commanded to preach only to infidels, but bishops only to their subjects. On the contrary, Paul often preached to converts, which certainly he had to do for their confirmation. Nor is it said to a bishop, as they claim, "Go, preach to the people of God," but rather, "to the people committed to you," which does not prevent him from being able and obligated to preach to infidels at times. 
<margin>
Another quibble.
</margin>
¶ Another of their quibbles is that although it was said to the Pope, "Feed my sheep," <note>original: "Pasce oues meas"</note> it is not therefore concluded that he is bound to reside in all churches; and thus it is not concluded of individual bishops that they are bound to reside in their own. But who does not clearly see that this quibbling is worthy of a worse name? For the Pope is commanded to feed them by himself, and thus to reside in his own church, which is designated as the Roman one, or wherever it seems expedient. However, because of the gathering of the world there, it is fitting that he should not

<column-break/>

wander through others, but should assign his own bishops to each, as God commanded him: who, by that same divine law, should be held 
<margin>
Paul.
</margin>
to reside in their own dioceses. Hence Paul says to the Thessalonians, Chapter 5: "We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord, and he warns you to hold them in the highest regard in love because of their work." <note>original: "Rogamus, inquit, vos fratres vt noueritis eos qui laborant inter vos..." 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13.</note> Therefore, it is not on account of their dignity, but on account of the work which those residing perform personally. ¶ Finally, another of their subtleties is not worthy of a response. For they argue that since the Pope can move a bishop from his diocese and assign him to another, it follows that the "marriage" of a bishop with this church is not by divine law, and thus neither is residency. For the weakness of this logical consequence has already been shown above: namely, that although the Pope can exchange bishops, he cannot change their nature and functions, which are annexed to the dignity by divine law. ¶ But you ask, can a bishop not 
<margin>
A doubt?
</margin>
dispense many things through ministers? For it appears he can: such as conferring orders and confirming; blessing temples and ornaments, and so on. Likewise, there are many episcopal duties which are performed only at fixed times and even then rarely: such as preparing the chrism <note>Consecrated oil used in sacraments.</note> and initiating the sacred rites; which therefore do not require constant residency. 
<margin>
Solution.
</margin>
The answer is that degrees must be distinguished among episcopal duties. For there are some things which, although they might not be done as decorously, are nevertheless not so absurd to perform through substitutes. Such are the preparation of chrism and the consecration of temples and ornaments. I say there is in these, when they are done through titular bishops, <term>titular bishops</term> <note>Bishops who hold the title of a defunct diocese and often serve as assistants to resident bishops.</note> a certain lack of decorum, because they are not celebrated with as much gravity as they ought to be. Furthermore, it provides an excuse for introducing titular bishops. Nevertheless, these are not the duties that most urgently require the residency of the bishop; but rather the others mentioned above, which demand constant presence and diligent care. Indeed, <insert>as we have already said,</insert> the reason bishops have forgotten the obligation of residing is that they do not think other burdens are incumbent upon them than hearing lawsuits and conferring orders once a year. For if they recognized themselves to be the light for the ignorant, the rule for the delinquent, the refuge for the afflicted, and the support and protection for the needy (as they truly are), there would be no need for great labor to make them thoroughly persuaded of the law of residency. We pass over many other testimonies of the scriptures here, thinking it sufficient to have brought forward those of the greatest importance. And we pass over many subtleties of the adversaries in silence, to which it would be more troublesome than useful to respond. ¶ Moreover, what we have asserted concerning the bishop 
<margin>
Parish pastors are also included.
</margin>
must also be understood concerning all parish pastors. For indeed, since the cited testimonies mean the same thing, they are bound to reside.

<summary>De Soto argues that the duty of residency for bishops and parish priests is a personal obligation under divine law that cannot be delegated to substitutes, just as certain secular roles require the specific person hired to perform them. He refutes various legalistic "quibbles" used by his opponents to justify absenteeism.</summary>

# Question III of the Tenth Book.

...although they urge bishops much more effectively.

¶ At the summit of all that has been said, although this may be quite evident in itself, it will not be a useless reminder: namely, that the obligation of residency is commanded in such a way that residency is not the ultimate goal of the command. For you may see prelates indeed residing in their churches, but behaving so negligently and sluggishly in the administration of the Word, in governing, in consoling the afflicted, and in aiding the poor, that it makes no difference whether they are absent or present. Residency is necessary for the sake of these duties; if they are not performed, residency becomes useless—indeed, it sometimes becomes the reason why a bishop is held in greater shame and contempt by his own people.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, it is replied that there was no necessity for those formal words—that bishops are bound to reside—to be expressed in the Gospel. Surely they are gathered most evidently from the episcopal function itself, which was divinely instituted. Even according to our adversaries, this is sufficient for residency to be a matter of <term>Divine Law</term> <note>original: "de iure diuino" — law believed to be derived directly from God's revelation.</note>. For Christ sent the Apostles and the seventy-two disciples <note>The 72 disciples mentioned in Luke 10:1 are traditionally viewed as the predecessors of the priesthood, just as the Apostles are the predecessors of bishops.</note> as workers to preach, whom the bishops and parish priests have succeeded. And where He commands all bishops, in the person of Peter, to "feed my sheep" <note>original: "pasce oues meas" — John 21:17</note>; and where He teaches that a good shepherd is one who knows his sheep by name; and where Paul says a bishop must be a teacher and hospitable; and where he admonishes Timothy to show himself a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth; and where he warns the prelates to attend to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit placed them as bishops to rule the Church of God—in these and other places of that kind, He commanded the residency of shepherds more clearly than light, so that it would be foolish to require more explicit words.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, enough has already been answered: although Christ committed the supreme jurisdiction of the Church singularly to Peter and his successors when He said "Feed my sheep," and likewise the power of choosing shepherds, He did not leave the *manner* of feeding to their own whim so that they could change it. For it is not within the Pope’s discretion to make it so that a bishop is not a teacher, is not hospitable, or is not a watchman over the flock—duties for which residency is an essential requirement.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third argument, it is replied that if Timothy and other bishops perhaps traveled away from their churches by Paul’s command, this was nevertheless done because of the necessity of the universal Church, and thus by an interpretation of that same divine and natural law. For it is not contradictory for residency to be a matter of Divine Law and yet cases can occur in which it is not only lawful but highly expedient for a bishop to depart from his church for a time.

### ARTICLE II.

#### Whether the residency of bishops is founded on natural law.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' with classical motifs.</image-desc>
**S**ince it has been shown that the residency of bishops is a matter of Divine Law, it follows that we should see whether the <term>Natural Law</term> <note>original: "ius naturæ" — a body of unchanging moral principles seen as a basis for all human conduct.</note> also supplies its own reasons for the same truth. For the argument is first made from the negative side.

<margin>First argument</margin>
First: The Gospel episcopacy is a supernatural order. Since the very foundation of the Church was instituted by Christ beyond the scope of nature, the residency of bishops is therefore not founded in natural law.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second: If residency of this kind were commanded by natural law, it could in no way be dispensed with. For as we declared in Book 2 regarding the Decalogue, a thing is indispensable for the reason that it has an individual bond of obligation from nature; and yet, as will appear in Chapter 4, such a necessity can arise that a bishop may legitimately become absent from his church.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third and finally, it is argued: Let us acknowledge a command regarding residency. However, the nature of <term>affirmative commands</term> <note>Commands that tell you what *to* do, rather than what *not* to do.</note> is that they do not bind (as they say) <term>at all times and for every moment</term> <note>original: "pro semper" — a legal term meaning an obligation that must be fulfilled continuously without any interruption.</note>. Therefore, a constant and continuous residency is not necessary.

¶ On the contrary is the fact that since the law of nature is inscribed in our minds by God as the author, it greatly serves to explain the laws of faith proceeding from that same God. For divine laws exist as the perfecters of natural ones.

<margin>Concluding response.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' with floral patterns.</image-desc>
**I**t has already been said above that natural law is what nature has taught us. Thus, it is not at all contradictory that what is sanctioned by divine law is also strengthened, to some extent, by natural law. Therefore, the question is answered with this affirmative conclusion: The obligation of residency is most closely related to natural law. Indeed, although the institution of bishops was made by divine law, its suitability is nevertheless made known through natural reasons, as was said above. Furthermore, the manner of episcopal administration is elucidated by these same reasons, which we have suggested in the preceding sections to such an extent that this...

### Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Law

...it is nothing other than a more explicit repetition.

<margin>First reason</margin>
The first argument, therefore, is taken from the nature of the office. Indeed, since the office of a pastor, as has been said, is to provide for the spiritual salvation of souls, this function is twofold: namely, in respect to the flock that is sick and failing, so that it may be helped and healed; or in respect to the healthy flock, so that it may be lead toward perfection. Furthermore, a deficiency can occur both in terms of the intellect and in terms of the emotions. Therefore, the pastor is a light against ignorance. For He says, "You are the light of the world" <note>Matthew 5:14</note>. Now, nature teaches that light cannot shine unless it is present. For those who wander from the path, the pastor is a city set upon a mountain, and by looking at the star of his life, the people ought to walk in the right path; however, he cannot be in the sight of the people unless he resides among them. Truly, for seasoning corrupt emotions, he is the salt, who must demonstrate the flavor of virtue through his works. Finally, for the sick, he is the physician. For Christ called Himself such when He said: "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick" <note>Matthew 9:12</note>. 

Consider, then, I ask you: if a King were to choose a most distinguished physician and pay him a just salary according to his means, could the King endure it if the physician served him through another substitute when his physical life was at risk? If, therefore, in a bodily physician, the personal diligence of the individual is sought and desired, who would deny that this is so much more just in a spiritual physician, as spiritual life surpasses temporal life? Finally, a bishop is, as we said above, a charioteer, a pilot, a leader, and a faithful servant and steward of the mysteries of God. And yet, if you look at the civil commonwealth, who among mortals would allow these duties to be performed by proxies? Why, then, would God allow it? In truth, the <term>natural law</term> <note>original: "naturæ ius" — the moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> openly cries out against it. There are also guards and watchmen to keep away enemies, and they cannot be absent. Regarding the flock, even if it were healthy and safe from enemies, the highest duty of the bishop—as we have already said above and as is held in his consecration—is to lead the people to perfection (as is read of John the Baptist in Luke 1): so that the church may be without spot or wrinkle, and thus worthy to appear in the sight of God. To achieve these things, natural reason clearly demonstrates that diligence, and indeed the presence of the person, is required.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ The second basis for demonstrating the same thing naturally is taken from the stipend <note>the financial support or salary provided to a member of the clergy.</note>. As was sufficiently proven above, this is paid not for scientific knowledge, or uprightness of character, or nobility, or episcopal dignity, but for the presidency and the function itself—and indeed for the exercise, the work, and the service. As the divine admonition in Numbers 18 holds, and as the 

<column-break/>

<margin>Paul.</margin>
Apostle teaches in 1 Corinthians 9. For where a stipend is paid for work, natural reason immediately demonstrates that it is not enough to appoint a <term>vicar</term> <note>original: "vicarium" — a substitute or deputy acting in place of the official office-holder.</note>, even if you substitute someone worthier than yourself. For that person is like an assistant, who does not excuse the bishop from performing what he is able to do while present. 

<margin>Third reason</margin>
¶ But the third basis is taken from the harms which the absence of bishops generates and brings forth. The greatest of these—and one that pastors must dread unless they are utterly devoid of all feeling—is that because of their negligence, many souls very frequently perish in perpetual death. If these pastors were diligent according to their obligation, those souls would enjoy eternal happiness. Revisit that prophecy cited above, Ezekiel 34. For after God says, "Woe to the shepherds of Israel," and recounts their negligence in strengthening the weak, etc., He adds: "And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd: and they became food for all the beasts of the field." Behold: "because there was no shepherd." Not that there was *none* at all (otherwise He would not have said, "Woe to the shepherds of Israel"), but that none was legitimately fulfilling his care. And therefore He adds: "And I will require my sheep at the hands of my shepherds." 

<margin>A profitable and healthy meditation for the Ecclesiastical pastor to keep in mind constantly.</margin>
I would wish Christ's pastors to be attentive to this. If a King saw his most beloved children slaughtered due to the negligence of their tutor and guardian, who could endure the King’s wrath? When God, therefore (which happens often, and more often, and most often indeed), sees Himself deprived of the company of souls because of the carelessness of pastors—souls whom He had created to enjoy His own glory, and for whose sake He sent down His own Son to die for them—and when He sees those same souls slaughtered forever in the abyss of hell, what kinds of punishments, I ask, would He not demand from those unfaithful and so remarkably sacrilegious pastors? 

Indeed, God is accustomed to be indignant not only against the wicked pastors themselves, but because of their wickedness, His indignation flows out upon the people. For thus it is read in Numbers 18: "Keep watch in the custody of the sanctuary and in the ministry of the altar, lest my indignation arise upon the children of Israel." This is not because the people are punished eternally for someone else's fault, but because there is never a lack of a vast number of delinquents among the people who ought to be sustained by the prayers of the prelates; when these prelates cease their work, God is indignant with the people for their own crimes. Or it is because when the bishops are absent, they cease to lift their hands to heaven with prayers alongside Moses, and...

### Book Ten, Question III.

...and thus to those neglecting the care of the people, the flock is easily laid low by their own hostile desires, and the pastor becomes worthy of God’s indignation. Since, therefore, from the absence of the pastor, such an immediate danger of negligence in governing the flock stands out, natural reason most clearly demonstrates how much those present ought to keep watch. ¶ Soon, besides the detriment to the flock, the same absence of prelates has given birth to another indecency in the Christian republic. For since, regarding personal residency, the law compels each church to be bound to its own bishop, where they are persuaded that it is permissible for them to be absent, it is not considered an inconvenience for one person to hold several churches, receiving the fruits of all of them at once. This was prohibited in the Lateran Council <note>Referring to the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215, which targeted the abuse of "pluralism"—holding multiple paid church offices at once.</note>: as is evident in the chapter *Quia nonnulli* regarding rules, and in question 21, canon 1, *Clericos*.

<margin>The Lateran Council</margin>
And then immediately the custom of titular bishops <term>Titular Bishops: Men consecrated as bishops of defunct or distant dioceses who served as substitutes for wealthy prelates who did not wish to perform their own duties.</term> was thrust into the Church: through whom—as experience itself testifies—the orders and other episcopal sacraments are performed. For from there it flowed out that spiritual matters of this kind are sold, and indeed handled so despicably that they are held in contempt in the sight of the Christian people. ¶ Fourthly, it is added that since bishops are appointed by God as cultivators of souls, and sent as harvesters of spiritual fruits, they themselves ought to carry their own sheaves into the sight of the Lord: which in truth those who govern through others do not do at all. And they themselves ought to return to God the interest on their talent which they should accumulate by themselves, and as legitimate pastors, following the example of that heavenly one who appointed them, carry their sheep on their own shoulders and handle them with their own hands. For thus Isaiah had prophesied of Him in chapter 40: *He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and shall lift them up in his bosom: he shall carry the young ones himself.* <note>Isaiah 40:11</note>

<margin>Fourth power: for demonstrating the previous conclusion.</margin>
For by these and other examples of this kind, Pope Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I (r. 366–384), who sought to centralize papal authority and reform the clergy.</note>, as can be seen in that previously cited Epistle 4, took holy care to drive out <note>original: *explodere*, literally to hiss off the stage or reject with disapproval</note> the country-bishops <term>Chorepiscopi: "Country-bishops" in the early church who assisted city bishops but whose lack of full authority led to disputes about the validity of their actions.</term>: who indeed did not differ very much from these titular bishops, as is explained in distinction 68, the canon *Ecclesiis*, and the two following. And the most powerful cause for driving them out and extinguishing them was that the legitimate bishops committed their flocks to them to be fed so that they themselves might grow sluggish in leisure: like—as that holy Pontiff says—harlots: who, as soon as they give birth, hand over their infants to other nurses to be raised, so that they may more quickly fulfill their own lust. For thus do these pitiable bishops do while they entrust the people committed to them to vicars to be raised...

<margin>Pope Damasus</margin>
<margin>Bishops who are absent from the flock are like harlots.</margin>

<column-break/>

...so that they themselves may more freely gape after secular cares. Perceive, therefore, how natural reason persuades that those who are betrothed to the Church should produce offspring through the blood of Christ by themselves and nurse them with their own breasts. For the bride, as we read in the chapter of the Song of Songs, gave her breasts to the bridegroom; and the same were fragrant above the best perfumed wines. These things, surely, when they are without use in a bishop, are dried up by God the avenger. But oh, the calamity of the times! For forgetfulness of the obligation of residing has obscured the necessity of all these things. For who now behaves as a bridegroom of his church, and as a father of his subjects? Paul, indeed, among his episcopal labors and the anxiety for the Churches, commemorates this especially in 1 Corinthians 9: that he became a Jew to the Jews, and a Gentile to the Gentiles, and weak to the weak, and finally adapted himself to the feelings of all, so that he might win all for Christ. And in the second letter to the same Corinthians: *Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I burn not?* <note>2 Corinthians 11:29</note> But now in this time, this degree of charity has so vanished from use that the sower of weeds <note>A reference to the Devil, from the Parable of the Tares in Matthew 13.</note> has nowhere sown worse scandals than between bishops and their cathedral chapters. This is what many of the bishops use as a pretext to excuse their absence. Nevertheless, they should first strive greatly to win over the canons with fatherly hearts; but if they were unable to achieve this, they should not for that reason depart from the diocese. For the sake of the fault of a few, the whole flock should not be abandoned. On the contrary, it should be so vigilantly cared for and cultivated that the leaders of the clergy, overcome by shame, would offer their bound hands to them.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
<margin>Paul.</margin>
**A**ND through these things, the answer to the arguments proposed at the head of the question is considered given to us. For the solution to the first is both that episcopal dignity is not so supernatural that it is not related to natural reason, and also that even if it were supernatural, once that is granted, then natural reason greatly illuminates the manner in which it must be administered. The response to the second argument will be clear in Article 4: where it will be established that even natural and divine law sometimes offer causes for which it is permissible for bishops to leave their dioceses. ¶ Finally, it is answered to the third that affirmative precepts <note>Affirmative precepts (commands to do something) differ from negative precepts (commands NOT to do something). Negative ones bind at every second; affirmative ones bind only at the appropriate time and place.</note> do not bind "for always" because they bind according to place and time and with other circumstances: for which reason a bishop is not bound to always be preaching or ordaining, etc.

Francisco de Soto, *On Justice and Right*,

Yet because many of a bishop's duties have no fixed time, but the necessity for them arises very frequently and unexpectedly, he is bound to remain always in his diocese, except in cases where divine and natural law itself grants him leave to be absent.

### ARTICLE III.

->Whether Bishops are bound to reside by human law, that is, by papal law.<-

<margin>First argument.</margin>
ALTHOUGH after establishing divine and natural law it does not matter much to know about human law, it nevertheless helps toward achieving a total victory. Arguments are nonetheless made, as is the custom, from both sides. For either the obligation of residency binds by divine law, or it does not: if it binds by divine law, then Ecclesiastical law was superfluous, because a human bond cannot be more urgent than a divine one; if it does not, then it seems the church has commanded it more rigidly than is just. For since the matter is so grave—as the prelates themselves believe—the church ought not to have made divine law even more burdensome.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If residency is a matter of divine law, then the papal commands concerning it cannot be anything but declarations of that same law, and thus it cannot be said to be a matter of human law. ¶ On the contrary stands the entire title "On the non-residence of clergy," specifically the chapters *Quia* and *Relatum* and the others, where those who are absent from their parish churches are punished with excommunication <note>original: "anathemate"</note> and other penalties.

<margin>The responsive conclusion.</margin>
SO that finally no escape remains, and it is clear to pastors beyond all controversy that they are strictly bound to reside, this final conclusion is applied in this third article: The residency of bishops, and likewise of priests who hold the care of souls, is ordained by human law—that is, ecclesiastical law—and established under penalty of mortal sin.

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
This conclusion, however, is not to be understood in the same way as the laws for yearly confession, Lenten abstinence, or the observance of specific feasts and ceremonies. For although those are considered to have been instituted since the age of the Apostles, they were not instituted immediately by Christ himself, but by the church through the power granted to it by Him to make laws. The Ecclesiastical command of residency, however, is an explanation of divine institution. For Saint Paul distinguishes in 1 Corinthians 7 between these

<column-break/>

two things, where he says: "To those who are joined in marriage I command, not I, but the Lord." For to the rest he says, "I say, not the Lord." <note>Soto is citing 1 Corinthians 7:10-12 to show that some rules come directly from God, while others come from Church authority.</note> There is therefore a difference: things that are of human law, even if they are established through power handed down divinely, would have no force of obligation unless they were commanded by the church. But those things that are of divine law would have bound even if the church had decreed nothing concerning them. The obligation by which prelates and pastors are forced to reside is of this second kind: since, as we were saying, it is divine law. It is said, however, to be of human law because that same divine law is explained and reinforced by Ecclesiastical sanctions. Indeed, it is commanded by those same sanctions to such an extent that even those who, out of perverse obstinacy, refuse to acknowledge the divine law, are nevertheless forced to admit the papal law. For none of the doctors of either Theology or canon law has ever hesitated about this; only the pastors, whose duty it is to know and confess this, deny it by their very actions. For they travel away from their churches—not indeed safe, but carefree—as if they were free by every law. Yet it ought to be most acknowledged without any controversy that even if they were bound to reside by papal law alone (which law is undoubtedly clear and firm), they could not, without a dispensation—and that requested and obtained for a legitimate cause—prolong a notable absence outside their dioceses.

<margin>First proof of the conclusion.</margin>
¶ The conclusion is therefore strengthened by many testimonies of law. For first, as we were saying earlier in the title "On non-resident clergy," in the chapter *Quia nonnulli* of the Lateran Council, it was ordained that an ecclesiastical ministry should by no means be committed except to a person who is able to reside in the place and exercise the care of the church by himself. For which reason it is most strictly forbidden there that anyone should hold two parishes in which he cannot reside by himself, nor receive their fruits. And in chapter 32 of the same Council the same prohibition is repeated: namely, that whoever holds a parish church should serve it not through a vicar <term>Vicar: A substitute priest hired to perform the duties of a high-ranking cleric who lived elsewhere.</term>, but by himself, unless perhaps it is annexed to a prebend or a dignity of the parish church. Concerning this exception, we will return to the discussion immediately in the next chapter.

<margin>Alexander III.</margin>
And subsequently Pope Alexander III confirms the same in the chapter *Relatum* under the same title.

<margin>Celestine.</margin>
Likewise Pope Celestine in the chapter *Ex parte*, and Innocent in the chapter *Qualiter*, and in two others following. And in the Council of Antioch, chapter 21, a bishop is most strictly forbidden from leaving his diocese. And in the Council of Sardica, canon 14, it is prohibited...

Soto cites various councils and popes to prove that personal residency is a requirement for holding a church office and cannot be legally bypassed without formal dispensation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's legal and theological argument for the residency of bishops. Having already discussed the requirements of divine and natural law, he now surveys Church history and "human law"—the canons of various councils and the decrees of popes—to show that the Church has always demanded that a pastor stay with his flock.</meta>

# Question III of the Tenth Book.

<margin>Council of Agde. Council of Sardica.</margin>
...it is ordered that a bishop should not stay in a foreign province for more than three Sundays. The same is held in the Council of Agde, which is cited in Case 7, Question 1, Canon "If anyone" <note>Original: "si quis." Legal citations in this period often refer to the first word of the specific canon or law.</note> and Canon 9. And in the two following canons of the same Council of Sardica, the access of bishops to the courts of princes is prohibited. Truly, these are things that cannot happen without the envy and reproach of men. To such an extent is this forbidden that if just causes arise—namely for the protection of the poor, widows, or orphans—he should then send a deacon so that he himself may remain among his own flock. The same is held in the 
<margin>Sixth Synod.</margin>
Sixth Synod <note>Also known as the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681 AD).</note>, chapters 18 and 80. And in the Roman Council under Sylvester and Constantine, Canon 17, this same access to the court is most strictly forbidden. For the court <note>Original: "curia."</note>, it says, is named after "blood" <note>Original: "à cruore." This is an ancient etymological pun; the author is suggesting that secular courts are places of violence or worldly "blood" compared to the spiritual sanctuary of the church.</note>, because it is the sacrifice of idols. 
<margin>Roman Council.</margin>
<margin>Council of Chalcedon.</margin>
And in the Council of Chalcedon, Canon 17, which is cited in Distinction 92: If any bishop has received the episcopate through the laying on of hands, and being appointed to lead the people, neglects to undergo the ministry, and does not comply by returning to the church committed to him: it is necessary that he be deprived of communion until, having been compelled, he takes up the office. This penalty is proof of a massive crime. And in Case 21, Question 1, Canon "Cleric," for the sake of residency it is forbidden for anyone to be counted in two churches. This is confirmed by divine testimony: because, of course, "no one can serve two masters" <note>A reference to Matthew 6:24.</note>. 
<margin>Eighth Synod.</margin>
And in the 8th Synod, Canon 19, it is forbidden for any of the archbishops or metropolitans to leave their own church to go to others under the pretext of a visitation. 
<margin>Fifth Council of Carthage.</margin>
And in the 5th Council of Carthage, which is cited in Case 7, Question 1, Canon "It pleased," it is held that no one has the power, having left the principal chair <note>The cathedral city.</note>, to betake himself to some church established in the diocese, or to neglect the care and attendance of his own chair by remaining longer than is proper on his own private property. 
<margin>Pope Nicholas.</margin>
And in the same case and question, in the Canon "You Inquire," Pope Nicholas says that it is just as contrary to natural law for a bishop to desert the church during a persecution as if a sailor were to abandon ship amidst the raging waves. And in Case 10, Question 1, Canon "We have decreed," bishops are ordered to visit their diocese annually. Indeed, in Distinction 82, Canon "Bishops," they are ordered to be in the church at least on the Lord's Day. Finally, there are more laws than can be cited. And to finally conclude the matter, the same truth was at last sanctioned by the most recent decree in the Council of Trent, Session 6, by which it was defined that no bishops, shining with whatever rank or dignity (so that even Cardinals are included), are excused 

<column-break/>

from personal episcopal residence in their churches, unless they have legitimate impediments—namely, those proven by natural law itself. Concerning these, we shall speak in the very next article. ¶ In addition to canon law, there is also the imperial law. First, in the *Authenticum* <note>A collection of Justinian's legal "Novels" or new laws.</note>, "How bishops ought to be," etc., Collection 1, Section "And this," at the verse "And that," where it is read: "and we also define this, that none of the God-beloved bishops should dare to be absent from his church for more than a whole year, unless this be done by Imperial command." And this is more broadly provided for in the *Authenticum* concerning holy bishops, Collection 9, Section "We interdict," where it most strictly forbids them to leave their own churches except with the consent of the patriarchs or the metropolitan. 
<margin>Council of Antioch.</margin>
For a similar sanction is held in the Council of Antioch, Canon 11. It is permitted, however, that they may remain for a year at the Emperor's court <note>Original: "curia Caesarea."</note>. But concerning this, we will speak in the next article.
<margin>Damasus. Augustine. Gregory Nazianzen. Chrysostom. Gregory. Ambrose. Jerome.</margin>
¶ If, after the councils, it does not weary one to hear the holy fathers on this matter, see Damasus in the cited letter concerning the requirement of rural bishops <note>Original: "chorepiscopis."</note>; and Augustine in his book *On Pastors*; and Gregory Nazianzen in his oration *On the Episcopal State*; and Chrysostom in his book *On the Priesthood*. And Gregory and Ambrose in their *Pastoral* works. But most extensively Jerome in his 2nd letter to Oceanus, on that passage of Paul to Titus: "A bishop must be without crime." Where he discusses many things regarding the proposal, concluding that it is not enough for bishops to be innocent, unless they are also dogs that bark. For those who are absent cannot bark. 
<margin>Bernard.</margin>
Whence Bernard in Sermon 77 on the *Song of Songs*:
> "He who leaves his sheep," he says, "in the pasture without a guardian is a shepherd not of the sheep, but of the wolves." 

And in the same place, he eloquently heaps up many brilliant arguments against the negligence of pastors who, he says, truly desire to be successors of the Apostles but not their imitators; for they are not as vigilant in care as they are eager in running toward the bishop's chair. And in the cited book *On Pastors*, 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Augustine, Chapter 10, teaches that bishops who do not labor in the preaching of the word ought not to receive the fruits <note>Income or tithes.</note> from the sheep; for Paul says:
> "If I preach the Gospel, I have a reward," namely, both with God and with men.

By which he implies: "If I do not preach the Gospel, I am not worthy of a reward." 
<margin>Origen.</margin>
And Origen, in his 7th homily on Joshua, reproves those who cease to be with the sheep by the example of Christ the Shepherd, who, leaving ninety-nine sheep in heaven, came to seek the one that had perished. But I am becoming tedious; for it is entirely impossible to follow everything written by the fathers on this argument, and it is of little use to pluck a few fruits in such a frustrated manner.
