<margin>Bernard.</margin>
...therefore with Bernard concerning the endurance of persecution, chapter 31, regarding that passage: *The hireling saw the wolf coming, and fled* <note>original: "Mercenarius vidit lupum venientem, & fugit." A reference to the Gospel of John 10:12.</note>: Would that today, whoever are not shepherds, would at least show themselves as hirelings to the flock, and not as wolves! Would that they themselves would not do harm! Would that they would not flee when no one is pursuing! Would that they would not expose the flock until they see the wolf coming! ¶ Let those, therefore, be silent who say that this question is a new one. For it was, as appears from the cited places, most ancient, and especially from the letters of Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), a prominent Church Father known for his defense against Arianism.</note> which we proceed to append in the next article. Ancient, I say: not because it was a matter of doubt among the upright, but because those who acted to the contrary were rebuked.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument previously proposed from the negative side, it is responded that although it is divine law by which residency of this kind is enjoined, it was nonetheless not superfluous—on the contrary, it was a matter of great public utility—for it to be explained by ecclesiastical constitutions, so that no one could pretend ignorance of it. Furthermore, even if divine law did not stand out in the sacred scriptures, the very nature of the pastoral office would admonish the Church to prescribe it most strictly. Nor, truly, is a precept of this kind so rigid as either greed and ambition, or luxury and sluggishness, falsely suggest to the minds of bishops. For besides the fact that the richness of temporal fruits <note>original: "fructuum temporalium pinguedo" — referring to the material wealth and tithes associated with a bishopric.</note> is worthy of that labor, the charity of Christ, who entrusted his flocks to them, ought primarily to sweeten the task for them. For what is sweeter to anyone than to be mentioned in his own home as the bridegroom with the bride, and the father with his children?

<margin>To the last argument.</margin>
¶ To the latter argument, it has already been answered how this is called "human law." For it is by no means to be understood by way of exclusion, as if it were not also divine or natural law, but rather that it is an explanation of these.

### ARTICLE IV.

#### Whether any cause can emerge for which it is lawful for a bishop to be absent from the flock committed to him.

->St. Thomas Aquinas, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 185, Article 5.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'I' depicting a landscape with two figures, possibly representing a teacher and a student or a religious scene.</image-desc>
At the conclusion of the present dispute, we must return to the exposition of Saint Thomas, namely to the fifth article of the same 185th question, where he debates whether any cause can intercede

<column-break/>

<margin>First argument.</margin>
on account of which it is lawful for a bishop to desert the flock committed to him. For an argument is taken from the negative side: first from that passage of John 10, already explained above, where Christ says the good shepherd gives his life for his sheep, but the hireling, seeing the wolf coming, leaves the flock and flees. <margin>Gregory.</margin> In his homily on this, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), influential for his "Pastoral Rule."</note> says: "The wolf comes upon the sheep when any unjust man or plunderer oppresses the faithful and the humble." If, therefore, a bishop, when the persecution of a tyrant looms, should deprive the flock of his protection, he shall be reckoned a hireling and not a shepherd. <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Second. In Proverbs, chapter 6, it is read thus: *My son, if you have pledged yourself for your friend, you have fastened your hand to a stranger.* And it adds: *run about, make haste, stir up your friend.* <margin>Gregory.</margin> Which same Gregory in his *Pastoral Care*, explaining it for our purpose, says: "To pledge for a friend is to receive another's soul into the danger of one's own way of life." But he who is placed before others as an example for living is admonished not only that he himself should be watchful, but also that he should rouse his friend. However, he cannot do this unless he is physically present with the flock; therefore, in a time of persecution, it is not lawful for any of the shepherds to withdraw himself. <margin>Argument 3.</margin> ¶ Third. It pertains to the perfection of the episcopal state to take care of souls. But it is not lawful for anyone who has professed a state of perfection to desert those things which pertain to perfection because of any danger; therefore, since a bishop professes a state of perfection, he can in no way turn his back, even when placed in danger of death, when his office is required. ¶ To the contrary is that command of Christ in Matthew 10 to the Apostles: *If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.*

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
To this question Saint Thomas responds with two conclusions. The first: It is in no way lawful for a bishop or any of the shepherds to withdraw himself personally when the salvation of his subjects requires his presence, neither on account of any temporal advantage, nor on account of any imminent danger. <margin>Proof.</margin> The conclusion is proved. The obligation of any person must be weighed from the end <note>The "end" here refers to the "final cause" or ultimate goal in Aristotelian-Thomistic philosophy.</note> of that same obligation (which is the nature of every means). But the end of the episcopal office, and thus of the bishop's obligation, is the spiritual salvation of the people. Therefore, when that requires his presence, no danger shall excuse him from being bound to be present. This is confirmed by the testimony of Christ: for if he is bound to lay down his life for the sheep...

He then begins a new discussion on whether a bishop may ever be absent, citing St. Thomas Aquinas and St. Gregory the Great to argue that a shepherd must remain with his flock even in the face of death or persecution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's legal and theological defense of the "residency" of bishops—the requirement that a bishop live within his diocese. Having established that this duty is rooted in divine law, he now addresses the extreme scenario: whether a bishop is required to stay even if it means facing certain death.</meta>

### Question III of the Tenth Book

...is held to be, as the Philosopher <note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle (384–322 BC).</note> says, the most terrible of all terrible things: yet no minor danger, nor even any temporal advantage, will excuse the fault of abandoning one's post. This is because nature more easily allows for the avoidance of physical harm than the seeking of mere comforts.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
**Second conclusion.** When a legitimate pastor can sufficiently provide for and consult the safety of his people through someone else, then it will not be a sin for him to withdraw from his church for a time, even to avoid personal danger to himself. In fact, when doing so is in the interest of the church, it is expedient that he should do so.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
The conclusion is gathered from the points above: for in that case, the withdrawal in no way goes against the ultimate purpose of his obligation <note>The "purpose" (finis) of a bishop's office is the salvation of his flock; if that is secured by a deputy, the bishop's physical presence is not strictly required during a moment of personal peril.</note>.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Hence, in his letter to Honoratus, Augustine says: "Let the servants of Christ flee from city to city when any one of them is specifically sought by persecutors; provided that the church is not deserted by others who are not so sought. However, when the danger is common to all, those who need others must not be deserted by those whom they need."

<margin>Nicholas.</margin>
The same point is made by the previously cited Nicholas <note>Pope Nicholas I (r. 858–867 AD), whose decrees became part of Canon Law.</note> in Question 7, Canon 1, *Sciscitaris*. There, he does not deny that it is sometimes permissible for a prelate to avoid a tyrant by flight. Nevertheless, when the people need his presence, he sins just as much, says Nicholas, as a sailor who deserts a ship in danger. Indeed, he sins all the more enormously because spiritual safety is more excellent than physical safety. ¶ At this point, first of all, we must consider the opinion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note>, which is drawn from the very heart of the Gospel.

<margin>The Doubt.</margin>
But to make the matter clearer, the question is asked: whether the faith that a bishop has pledged to his church—and indeed to his God—obliges him to reside there even to the point of suffering death.

<margin>Reason for hesitating.</margin>
To those with only a little knowledge <note>original: "sciolis", referring to "smatterers" or those with superficial learning.</note>, this will appear hard to believe at first glance. An obligation to undergo death—which is the greatest fear for mortals—should not be asserted unless a divine command regarding this is clearly established. And yet, when Christ says that the "good shepherd gives his life for his sheep," He seems to signify a counsel <note>In theology, a "counsel" is a recommendation for higher perfection, whereas a "precept" is a mandatory command.</note> rather than a mandatory precept. For the phrase "Good Shepherd" does not seem to imply necessity, but rather an act beyond the call of duty. Furthermore, martyrdom is only necessary when the faith is in danger and demands a confession of itself. To oblige bishops to martyrdom when no such danger to the faith is imminent appears reckless.

<margin>The bishop is bound to undergo the risk of his own life in-</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, one must undoubtedly hold the affirmative side, which Saint Thomas expressly affirms here in his first conclusion. He states that a bishop is not permitted, on account of any imminent personal danger,

<column-break/>

<margin>the face of necessity to provide for the flock.</margin>
to desert his church in a time of necessity. He confirms this by the testimony of Christ, which he understands in a "preceptory" or mandatory sense: specifically, that no one is a "good shepherd"—possessing the goodness necessary to retain the grace and friendship of God—unless, whenever a case of necessity occurs, he remains present to favor and help his flock with the risk of his life, even unto death.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
And Augustine, cited above in the letter to Honoratus, asserts this forcefully, saying that when persecution is imminent, a bishop cannot flee, but must follow the example of Christ and lay down his life for his sheep.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
For the word "cannot" signifies the necessity of a command. Hence, Saint Thomas in his *Summa Theologiae* (II-II, q. 26, art. 5, in response to the third argument), where he says that the necessity of charity does not *always* oblige a man to offer his life for a friend, makes an exception for the case where a person is bound to provide for another's salvation: alluding especially to the office of a bishop.

<margin>The Argument</margin>
¶ From this truth, which no one has ever been able to doubt, an excellent argument is drawn that residency is a matter of divine law. For if it were only a matter of positive law <note>Human-made laws, such as those passed by the Church or a state, as opposed to "divine law" revealed by God.</note>, then since papal commands (such as the Lenten fast or the observance of feast days, as we wrote in Book I) are not accustomed to oblige one under the danger of death, you could not easily persuade anyone that a bishop is bound to reside in his diocese at the risk of his life. This is especially true because, as seen above, the aforementioned authors judge the word of Christ to be spoken properly of Himself; and yet, if you deny that those words have the force of a command, you leave no basis from which to infer that a bishop is bound to lay down his life for his flock in a time of necessity. Yet this is the general confession of everyone.

<margin>To the argument made.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to the contrary argument, the response is that a command of this kind should not be considered "atrocious" or harsh. On the contrary, since all the temporal safety of the world is a means to promote spiritual safety—and this is so certain that God Himself laid down His temporal life, the most excellent of physical things, for our salvation—natural and divine order demanded that those who were to be pastors of souls should be bound by the same rule. Nor should anyone previously be chosen for that office until he was found fit to fulfill it in the highest good faith. Indeed, even a king is bound to lay down his life for his republic. Therefore, just as it is martyrdom to face death when the confession of faith demands it, so it is when the reason of justice demands the same. John the Baptist left us a lesson in this, who offered his head for the defense of justice <note>John the Baptist was executed by Herod for speaking out against Herod's unlawful marriage—a matter of moral justice rather than a direct denial of a creed.</note>. ¶ From this, it is easy to...

<summary>This page argues that a bishop's duty to remain with his flock (residency) is a divine command that holds even in the face of death, unless the flock's safety is already guaranteed by a deputy. Soto links this duty to the example of Christ and the sacrifice of John the Baptist, arguing that spiritual salvation outweighs physical life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's legal and theological defense of the "residency" of bishops—the requirement that a bishop live within his diocese. Having established that this duty is rooted in divine law, he now addresses the extreme scenario: whether a bishop is required to stay even if it means facing certain death.</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right

<margin>Legitimate causes for which a bishop is permitted to be absent from his flock must be weighed not in respect to himself, but to the church.</margin>
We now descend to the explanation of the second conclusion: for from what has been said, it is gathered that all causes for which a prelate <note>A "prelate" refers to a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note> can legitimately depart from his church must by no means be considered in respect to his own person. This is because his very life ought to belong to the flock; rather, such causes must be judged only in respect to the good of the church to which he has pledged his faith. Therefore, even if Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and cardinal.</note> currently groups these causes into three types—namely: **Necessity of impediment**, the **quality of the business**, and the **condition of the person**—they must all nonetheless be referred back to the benefit of the church. 

<margin>The first cause justifying absence.</margin> 
Now, as for an impediment, one type arises from within and another from without. From within, for example, is the poor health of the bishop, by reason of which he must change his soil and air. It is clear that even this must be weighed in respect to the church. For if at that time the church were pressed by the necessity of the Bishop's presence, he ought rather to succumb to death than to leave, according to the law of the "good shepherd" prescribed by Christ. However, when the church is not so severely afflicted, it turns to its advantage that the bishop consults his own health so that he may be able to serve it more effectively later. Truly, natural law grants that he may set aside small amounts of time, not only for the sake of health, but also for refreshing the mind and visiting his relatives, which he may spend on these or other business of that kind. For an obligation of this sort is not to be understood as if he ought to be bound in prisons or shackles.

In the same way, we must judge if an impediment attacks from the outside: as when a tyrant is hostile to the church. For if he rages not specifically out of hatred for the prelate, but against the church itself, then the prelate must persist even unto death. The examples of Augustine in his letter to Honoratus, cited above, applaud this necessity. So too do the words of the Lord in Sermon 5 regarding Peter and Paul and the other holy martyrs who, following the example of Christ, succumbed to the swords of tyrants for their churches. But if the tyrant is hostile to the church because of a particular envy toward the prelate, then it is in the interest of the same church that he withdraw himself from there for a time, as Augustine says in the same place, lest the subjects be forced to flee. We have examples of this in John the Evangelist, who withdrew at the prayers of his church as was expedient, and in Thomas of Canterbury <note>Thomas Becket (c. 1118–1170), who famously fled to France during his conflict with King Henry II before returning to face martyrdom.</note>. Yet afterwards, when there was need, they returned to those same sees even at the risk of their lives. 

<margin>The second cause.</margin> 
The **quality of business** must similarly be weighed in respect to the same church, so that a legitimate excuse for

<column-break/>

absence may be sought from it. For there is a threefold particular relationship of the church to be observed. I say we consider the general utility of the Church of Salamanca <note>De Soto was a professor at the University of Salamanca; he uses his local diocese as a primary example.</note> in regard to its individual ministries, such as preaching, visiting, etc., as a whole relates to its individual members. Then, in its order toward the universal Roman Church, as a member relates to the head or to the whole body. Finally, in its order toward other churches, as one member relates to the rest of the same body. All these necessities can provide a bishop with just causes for withdrawing from his church, even by divine and natural law.

Therefore, when a particular church is established in some calamity, then because of the first relationship (the whole to its parts), its bishop can cease from other duties and offices and go to the Royal or Roman court to protect his church; and this is by divine and natural law. Since he owes it not only other particular duties but this one especially—provided that he cannot accomplish it through others. 

If, however, the necessity of the **Universal Church** demands the absence of the bishop, no one doubts that he is compelled to depart by divine and natural law. For just as individual members, by natural order, expose themselves to protect the safety of the head, so also particular churches are bound to offer themselves, and thus their bishops, for the common good.

<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
The note of Lord Cajetan is very pleasing here, not only for its <margin>It is lawful for a pastor to be absent for the sake of the universal Church's flock.</margin> teaching but also because of his dignity, as he was a Roman Cardinal. He says indeed that judgment must be applied here to discern whether the personal labor and industry of the bishop is necessary to the universal church. For if it is not necessary, his absence is not excused. 

<margin>To send to another communal or provincial synod.</margin> 
For example: when an Ecumenical Council or a provincial synod is announced, it is most certain that bishops ought to travel there by divine law. For a Council is a gathering of churches, and the bishop comes in the name of the church. In the same way, if outside of a council it is expedient for the Pope—on account of the distinguished learning or singular authority of a person—to summon some bishop whose counsel he may take for the common good, it will indeed be permitted to call him away from his see for a time. 

But truly, if the Pope wishes to use him as a secretary or singer because he writes or sings elegantly, or if he wants him to be an auditor of the Camera or the Rota <note>The Apostolic Camera handled financial matters, and the Rota is the highest appellate tribunal of the Catholic Church. De Soto argues these are administrative roles that do not require a bishop's specific sacramental character.</note>, since it is not necessary for this to be performed by a bishop—indeed, there is an abundance of people at hand to perform such duties—it is certainly not a legitimate excuse before God.

<summary>De Soto argues that a bishop may only leave his diocese if the absence benefits the Church, such as for health, escaping personal persecution, or attending a General Council. He critiques the practice of bishops leaving their flocks to serve in administrative or courtly roles that could be filled by others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's argument that the residency of bishops is a matter of divine law. He is currently addressing whether the Pope has the authority to grant dispensations that allow bishops to live away from their assigned dioceses.</meta>

# Question III of the Tenth Book

An excuse before God. This is especially true if residency, as the matter truly stands, is necessary by divine law. For from this it is certain that the Pope cannot grant a dispensation unless he is interpreting that same natural and divine law—which, in truth, excuses no one except in a case of true and legitimate necessity. Such necessity by no means occurs in cases similar to these.

<margin>The fallacy of the jurists.</margin>

¶ Indeed, I am well aware that some legal experts will come to meet us here, saying that those who reside in Rome are considered to be residing in their own churches; for they argue that "he who resides in the head, resides in the member." <note>The "head" refers to Rome as the center of the Church, while the "member" refers to the individual diocese.</note> However, that this is a mere fiction is something that even Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major theologian of the era.</note>—who was not ignorant of the law—does not fear to affirm, nor is it anything but obvious to anyone skilled in law or theology. For since it is divine law that a bishop be dedicated to each individual diocese—and this, as has been demonstrated, is for the sake of the particular care and vigilance which is necessary for that church—it is clearly concluded that residing in Rome is not only *not* residing in Salamanca <note>The author uses Salamanca, a major Spanish university city, as his example.</note>, but it does not even excuse the absence of the non-resident, unless a legitimate necessity demands it. For this reason, some bishoprics in Germany, which I have seen, were established such that the bishop receives no other fruits <note>Income or revenues from church lands.</note> besides food and the most honorable sustenance for his household in all necessities while he is present; but to the absent bishop, nothing is given.

<margin>That Cardinals are forbidden from becoming bishops.</margin>

¶ Through these points, one must certainly judge the most Reverend Cardinal-bishops: for they ought to be judged by their own law. For it was not in vain that it was provided by a law of the Sacred Senate <note>The College of Cardinals.</note> itself that bishops should not be elevated to that distinguished dignity. This was surely because they judged that the residency of bishops is by divine law; therefore, it did not admit a dispensation unless by another interpretation of that same law—for instance, the gravity of a necessity. Indeed, this law is held so sacred by the Supreme Pontiff that he cannot bring himself to dispense with it in any way. And yet, a chosen Cardinal is often given a "commendation" <note>The practice of *in commendam*, where a benefice was given "in trust" to avoid certain legal restrictions of a full title.</note> without the title of the church. This, as I was saying in Book 3—if it is permitted for a humble monk, yet a Christian, to speak on a Christian matter—presents an open evasion of the law. As if one to whom a church is commended were not bound by the same strict law to reside there as if he were a legitimate bishop! The title of the church is taken away from the Cardinal solely because he cannot reside there, and yet they do not fear to commend that very same church to him. I pray this is not an attempt to deceive God! Furthermore, he who consults divine law will first judge this most justly: that no bishop should be created a Cardinal. But

<column-break/>

truly, if the contrary is done, the fault is much smaller—indeed perhaps none at all—if, by remaining in his own church, he never visits Rome, rather than staying in the Roman Court and deserting his church. If someone had a diocese very close to Rome,
<margin>A limitation of the previous assertion.</margin>
which he could visit frequently, and if he were of such excellence in doctrine and authority that it would greatly benefit the good of the Church for him to be present in the Sacred Senate, perhaps he could defend his cause. For by this reasoning, as they say, the six bishoprics surrounding Rome are permitted to be held by Cardinals. Outside of these cases, however, let them see to it themselves; for it is not permitted for us to place these men in heaven, except insofar as the Lord of Heaven himself has allowed.

<margin>Innocent III.</margin>

¶ Finally, the decree of Innocent III in the chapter *Bonae memoriae, 1. de postulatione praelatorum* greatly supports this opinion. There, he refused to present a Cardinal as the Archbishop of Ravenna because he was necessary to the Roman Church. From this it follows that, except in such a case—namely, on account of the excellence of both the authority and the integrity of the person, and on account of the church's proximity—the opinion of Panormitanus <note>Nicola de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as "The Sicilian" (Panormitanus).</note> on that same chapter is not to be heard: namely, that a Bishopric and a Cardinalate are compatible dignities. For this reason, in the most recent Council of Trent (as we
<margin>The Council of Trent.</margin>
mentioned above), where it was decreed that no bishops are excused from personal residence, it was added: *By whatever rank or dignity they may shine.*

¶ Beyond these things, the necessity of even one particular church can, by the law of charity, persuade the bishop of another to come to its aid, provided he can do so without detriment to his own people. For we are all, as Paul says, members of the same body; and thus, when individuals lack the help of others, they can and ought to help one another mutually, so that what is written in the Creed regarding the "Communion of Saints" may be expressed in action. This is especially true when a more prominent member requests the help of an inferior one. And for this cause, Paul sometimes ordered Titus and Timothy and other disciples to depart from their own churches, on account of the scarcity of similar men available to the church at that time, and because of the necessity of promulgating the faith.

<margin>The argument of the adversaries.</margin>

¶ Through these points, one answers the arguments of the adversaries, which are fictional rather than legitimate. For they occasionally argue that it is necessary for bishops to go to a Council, or to carry out other orders of the Pope, and that the disciples of the Apostles wandered away from their churches. But these things
<margin>The solution.</margin>
in no way oppose the conclusion: since residency was certainly instituted for the salvation of the church. Therefore...

He critiquies the practice of Cardinals holding distant bishoprics and cites the Council of Trent's recent reinforcement of residency requirements.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Francisco de Soto's argument regarding the residency of bishops. Having established that residency is generally required by divine law, he is now examining specific exceptions and whether the Pope has the authority to grant dispensations for absence.</meta>

### Francisco de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

...so that the same purpose may be served, natural and divine law themselves not only permit but command such exceptions. By the same reasoning, a bishop may travel to lands of non-believers for a time, or go as an ambassador to arrange peace, or to perform some other task of this kind necessary for the Church. It would be otherwise if the embassy concerned a purely worldly matter that could be settled by someone else. In that case, it would be an abuse of the episcopal dignity to the detriment of the Church, since it is forbidden that one "soldiering for God" <note>original: "Deo militans" — a common metaphor for clergy based on 2 Timothy 2:4</note> should involve himself in secular business.

<margin>The third type of causes for which a bishop may withdraw from his church.</margin>
¶ Finally, the third type of causes for which a bishop may sometimes withdraw from his church concerns the condition of the person, combined with the circumstances of the time and the quality of the churches. For instance, if there were a scarcity of people to whom churches could be entrusted, and a person existed who was exceptionally fit, and the nearby churches were such that the alternating visits of such a prelate would be more fruitful than the permanent residency of another. In such a case, the titles of two churches could be committed to a single person, as is clear in the canon *Illud* (21, q. 1), where the Archbishop of Tarragona <note>A major see in Spain.</note> was permitted to also be the Bishop of Huesca <note>The text says "Fundenfis," likely referring to Fondi or a similar see, but the legal precedent cited usually involves Spanish sees in Soto's context.</note>. However, this is accidental and happens very rarely in practice. Beyond this, the law allows that when a parish is annexed to a higher dignity, the one residing in the higher church may serve the parish through a vicar, as held in the Lateran Council (canon 32, cited above). However, he is commanded to have a fit and permanent <term>vicar</term> <note>A substitute or representative who performs the duties of the office.</note> canonically instituted; and by the word "permanent," it seems to be designated that he should be as one having the care of souls.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ At the end of these present exceptions, someone might perhaps ask whether the Pope can grant a <term>dispensation</term> <note>A formal exemption from a law or obligation.</note> regarding this law beyond these causes. However, the solution is easily accessible, as it is clearly gathered from what was said above. For he who holds the opinion that this residency is only a matter of human law will subsequently answer that the Pope can dispense from this just as he can from ecclesiastical fasting or any other law of that kind. Thus, he could not only interpret the law—namely, that it does not extend to such a case—but truly remove the obligation of a specific individual. But he who confesses that the law here is divine and natural <note>original: "ius diuinum & naturale"</note>—which is not only more probable but certainly more certain—will subsequently answer that the Pope cannot grant a dispensation, but rather interprets the divine and natural law: namely, by declaring that such a case is exempted by that very same divine law.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But if someone argues to the contrary: Fulfilling a simple vow is also a matter of divine law, yet the

<column-break/>

Pope can grant a dispensation for it; therefore, he can likewise dissolve the bond of residency. <margin>Solution.</margin> The comparison is denied. For although the fulfillment of a vow (while the vow remains) is a matter of divine law—and the Pope cannot permit the opposite—nevertheless, because the obligation of a vow arises from the specific will of the person making the vow, the Pope can dispense from it: namely, so that the vow made is considered as if it had not been made. However, divine law commands the bishop to reside. Therefore, as long as he remains a bishop, he cannot be released from that same bond of residency by any papal dispensation. See how much it matters to speak in one way or the other! Nevertheless, even if you persist in that hardly probable opinion that residency is only of human law, the Pope still does not have the power to dispense at his whim, but only when a legitimate cause requires it. Nor can the person who received the dispensation safely use it otherwise.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ Following this teaching, someone might perhaps doubt whether, by reason of the civil administration of the state, a bishop can lawfully live at the royal court or elsewhere. And it is argued on the affirmative side. <margin>Reason for the doubt.</margin> First, by the authority of the law in the *Authentics* cited above, *How bishops...* and *Regarding holy bishops*, it is permitted that they may stay at the court for a year, and longer by the Emperor's permission. And this is evident by reason: because the more common a good is, the more excellent it is. Now, administering the state of the kingdom is more universal than sitting at the helm of a single church—as, for example, if a bishop becomes a viceroy or a president of the court. For it is more likely that such offices will be administered with holier faith, justice, and more vigilant care by a bishop than by secular administrators. And beyond these, if he becomes a general protector of the faith against heretical depravity; for no one can be more conveniently or fittingly placed in charge of such a province than an ecclesiastical prelate, because of the illustrious ecclesiastical authority required for that same duty.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ To this, however, one must respond with a careful distinction. That a bishop may perform a royal embassy to another prince for the sake of arranging peace or for another cause that is not feigned but truly honorable—likewise, that he may become an Inquisitor <note>A formal investigator into matters of religious orthodoxy.</note> of heretical depravity—surely no law opposes this; indeed, equity itself supports it. But that they should stay for a cycle of years, enslaved to civil offices and administrations—both the laws cited above reclaim this in agreement, and the reason of the high office and the faith by which they enslaved themselves to their churches, and moreover the justice of the salary they have received, can in no way endure it. <margin>The responses can be persuaded.</margin> For first, such administrations...

<summary>Soto discusses the legal and moral exceptions to a bishop's duty to reside in his diocese, arguing that while the Pope can interpret exceptions for missions or peace-making, he cannot simply abolish the divine duty of residency. He also addresses whether bishops should serve in secular government roles, concluding that while temporary religious or diplomatic missions are acceptable, long-term civil service is a violation of their sacred office.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the residency of bishops, focusing specifically on why bishops should not be distracted by secular or political duties, even when such duties seem beneficial to the state.</meta>

### Question III of the Tenth Book

<margin>Paul.</margin>
It is not only unnecessary for these duties to be carried out by bishops, but it is also not fitting for their status. For in the first place, secular men can carry them out excellently, whereas bishops cannot do so with sufficient dignity. Since Paul admonished Timothy that "no one soldiering for God should entangle himself in secular affairs," <note>original: "neminem qui Deo militat implicari debere negotijs sæcularibus" — 2 Timothy 2:4. This was a foundation for the legal separation of clergy from worldly business.</note> who, I ask, would consider it right for a bishop—who is devoted to such a holy, spiritual office—to waste all his time listening to secular discords and lawsuits? This is time that should truly be spent either in the deep silence of contemplation or in teaching and raising his own sheep.
<margin>Nicholas.</margin>
Pope Nicholas once summoned certain bishops to Rome who were residing at the court of Emperor Charles. When the Emperor made the excuse that they were keeping watch against maritime pirates and therefore could not go, the Pope replied (as is seen in Question 8, Causa 23) that this was clearly very reprehensible. For since it belongs to the soldiers of Christ to serve Christ, he said, secular soldiers ought to serve the world.

¶ The most powerful reason that cries out against this abuse, however, is that even if such duties were performed better and more wholesomely by bishops than by others, this is nonetheless not the "talent" which God committed to them to increase. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25.</note> It is not what He commanded them to do, nor is it that for which they receive such ample payments from tithes, nor that for which He will demand an accounting from them. For what do individual churches owe to the civil state that they should pay back such a great abundance of tithes for a service that bishops bestow not on the church, but on the world? Or how will they answer when Christ, on the Day of Judgment, demands an account for the blood He shed, with which He redeemed the souls He entrusted to them to be saved? Will they respond that they were busy with other affairs not committed to them by Him? Let them consider this: if a king asked his general for an account of an army that was poorly led, and the general responded that he had been busy with the affairs of the royal court, how would that answer be received?
<margin>Paul.</margin>
If those who compete in a secular struggle "abstain from all things," as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9, so that they may give themselves entirely to their duty, consider how much more those who soldier so notably for Christ ought to withdraw themselves from all other things so they may be fully present for such a great task. And if those in the Gospel who were invited to the wedding were spoken of poorly because they declined the feast to buy villas or yokes of oxen, how much worse do you think the prelates will be heard by God? These are the ones sent to call people to the feast—indeed, according to Christ, they are the bridegrooms themselves who are to celebrate the wedding with the Church—if they surrender themselves to other

<column-break/>

business, by which that care for the Church is either defrauded or neglected? To King Uzziah, as we read in 2 Chronicles 26, it was attributed as a disgrace and a sacrilege that he attempted to burn <term>incense</term> <note>A ritual act of prayer and sacrifice reserved for the priesthood.</note> on the altar to the Lord. The priests, rebuking him, said: "It is not your office, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord, but the office of the priests." But by the same token, it is much more justly a matter of reproach for priests, and especially bishops, that they desert their own office of "burning incense" to offer it instead to the world. For the spirit which God breathes into them when they are consecrated is not meant for that, but rather so they may beget and nourish spiritual children. Listen to Moses in Numbers 11, and how much meaningful language he uses to emphasize the similar cares God commits to the shepherds of souls. "Why," he asks, "have you laid the weight of all this people upon me? Did I conceive all this multitude, or did I give them birth, that you should say to me: Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse is accustomed to carry a little infant, and carry them into the land for which you swore to their fathers?" Truly, Christ requires much greater care and skill from Prelates to be spent on the souls He himself begot with His own blood, for which He specifically provides His spirit and favor. Therefore, it is added immediately thereafter: "Gather for me seventy men... and I will take of your spirit and give it to them, so that they may support the burden of the people with you." Some believe that Moses' spirit was diminished then, but perhaps, as I said above, that is not the meaning. Since it was not a fault for him to ask for helpers, he did not deserve a punishment. Rather, the sense is perhaps: "I will take," that is, I will take the same *kind* of spirit and pour it into them.
<margin>Paul.</margin>
For, as Paul says, there are diverse graces and gifts of the spirit, which God distributes to His own according to the necessity of the offices He commits to them. For this reason, in the consecration of bishops, God is asked to pour the "priestly oil" <note>The sacred chrism used in the ordination of a bishop.</note> upon the one being consecrated. We mention these things so that bishops may understand that no other grace, favor, or spirit is imparted to them by God than that which is necessary for ruling their church. But it is human appetites and efforts that submerge them in other secular business, letting the ship sink which God entrusted to them to steer as pilots (as Clement says in a certain letter).

<margin>From the time that bishops began to be created by kings rather than by chapters, the church has suffered.</margin>
¶ Truly, it cannot be denied that this plague, which strips the churches of the presence of their pastors, has crept in more widely since the time bishops ceased to be elected by their <term>chapters</term> <note>The college of clergy (canons) attached to a cathedral who traditionally held the right to elect their bishop.</note> and began to be created in royal courts or in Rome.

<summary>Soto argues that bishops must avoid secular and political duties because their "spirit" and "talent" are specifically consecrated for the care of souls, not worldly administration. He traces the decline of pastoral residency to the shift from local clerical elections to political appointments by kings and the Roman court.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s argument against bishops residing at royal courts. He argues that neglecting their dioceses leads to a loss of authority and the spiritual ruin of the people, citing the contemporary religious upheavals in Germany and England as proof.</meta>

# Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Right*

<margin>...the loss of residency.</margin>
...or be created by royal decree. Indeed, it is not that I murmur entirely against the permissions granted to princes. For human malice has now reached the point where, if the power of election remained solely with the cathedral chapters <note>The "chapter" is the college of clerics (canons) who traditionally advised a bishop and, in the Middle Ages, often elected him.</note>, everything would be full of discord and torn apart by bloody dissensions. Nevertheless, because human nature is such that no remedy can be applied to affairs without bringing some disadvantage with it, it is from this practice that the courts—both the Roman court and, especially, the royal courts—began to be crowded with bishops. These bishops, neglecting their poorer "spouses" <note>A common metaphor: a bishop is considered "married" to his diocese.</note>, are always gasping to commit "adultery" with wealthier ones. This evil is not new. For this very reason, as Jerome reports in his cited letter to Oceanus, a precaution was taken in the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church.</note> that these "ascensions" of bishops and exchanges of churches should not be permitted.

¶ Furthermore, to hurry now at last toward the end of this question: because of both the absence of such bishops from their own churches and their frequency in the royal courts, the common people began to despise their dignity. I say that they began <margin>The disadvantages that come to bishops from frequenting royal courts.</margin> to be shown little reverence by the secular laity and even less obedience by the clergy; moreover, much of their judicial power was taken away by civil courts and forums. For, as <margin>Athanasius.</margin> Athanasius says regarding the final chapter of Hebrews: just as it is necessary for the people to show themselves obedient to those presiding over them, so too it is necessary for the priest to care for the souls of others and to spend sleepless nights.

¶ It is, therefore, a most just vengeance that those who neglect their own place should gradually fall away from it. This was the retribution against priests prophesied by Malachi in chapter 2, where he says:
> And now, O priests, this commandment is for you: If you will not hear, and if you will not lay it to heart, to give glory to my name, says the Lord of hosts, I will send poverty upon you, and I will curse your blessings. Behold, I will cast down your arm <note>The "arm" symbolizes strength or authority.</note> and I will scatter upon your face the innards of your solemnities.

And further on:
> I have made you contemptible and humble before all the people, because you have not kept my ways.

These curses must be weighed: *I will send poverty upon you*, that is, I will withdraw from you the light of doctrine and the favor of grace by which you were accustomed to bear rich fruit among the people. *And I will curse your blessings.* Perhaps this is the same thing. For the blessings of priests are the fruits which the people gather through their doctrine and favor. Therefore, to curse their blessings is to cause them to bear malignant fruit. Although, even if this is referred to the sacraments, it is in a

<column-break/>

certain way true. For even if the fruits of the sacraments cannot be evil in themselves, nevertheless, when they are dispensed by the ignorant and the greedy, they often do not "hold." Specifically, because of irregularity, they do not truly confer the orders they attempt to grant, and they frequently absolve from sins those whom they cannot <note>Referring to legal "irregularities" in canon law that could render certain official acts of a bishop or priest invalid if they lack proper jurisdiction or standing.</note>. This happens very often because of the absence of the prelates. Add to this that "to curse" can also sound like "I will permit them to be cursed." We have experienced, to our own misfortune, that this has happened by a lamentable custom in Germany and England <margin>The root and origin of the slaughter in Germany and England produced in our century.</margin> and other regions. For because of the laziness and most ruinous neglect of the bishops and other pastors, everything is full of heretics who curse all the sacraments and defile them with blasphemies. Hence follows:
> And behold, I will cast down your arm, which is the strength of your dignity and the staff of your governance. And finally, I will scatter upon your face the innards of your solemnities.

Another translation uses a more impudent but more significant word for "innards": *dung* <note>original: "steris" — Soto is noting that the Hebrew/Vulgate text of Malachi 2:3 refers to spreading the "dung" or refuse of sacrificial animals on the faces of the priests.</note>. This is an allusion to the Mosaic sacrifices in which animals were slaughtered. For now, among the heretics, our sacraments have begun to stink so much that the faces of the priests are thought to be filthy with dung. There is a similar passage in another Prophet, namely Zechariah 11:
> O shepherd and idol, you will abandon the flock.

He truly expresses to the life the nature and character of the shepherd who abandons the flock. For such a man is nothing other than an "idol" of a shepherd: namely, presenting only an image and the persona of a shepherd, like a carved stone, yet lacking the reality itself. *A sword upon his arm*: that is, upon the power of his governance; *and upon his right eye*: namely, upon right sense and judgment. For after their lust forces them to desert the helm of the church, it immediately begins to persuade them that they are not bound by that obligation which the wise men teach—which is to pluck out their right eye. Would that He who came as Light into the world would so illuminate and inflame all those whom He has raised upon the candlestick of His church, so that they might both clearly know the laws of their duty and exhibit them in their conduct with the fire of charity!

¶ Therefore, the arguments proposed at the head of the question—since they campaigned for the idea that it is in no way permissible for a bishop to depart from his diocese—are very easily solved. For to the first <margin>To the first argument.</margin> it is replied that not everyone who removes himself from his church for a time is "fleeing like a hireling..." <note>A reference to John 10:12–13; the text cuts off here with the catchword "vt mer-" (ut mercenarius).</note>

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that bishops who abandon their dioceses for royal courts lose their spiritual authority and public respect, leading to the rise of heresy as seen in the Reformation in Germany and England.</summary>

# Book Ten, Question III.

<margin>Gregory.</margin> He is judged to be a "hireling" <note>original: "mercenarius." In the Gospel of John 10:12-13, the hireling is the one who flees when the wolf comes because he cares only for his pay, not for the sheep.</note> who acts solely for his own private convenience, placing his own bodily comfort ahead of the spiritual salvation of the people. This follows the words of St. Gregory in that same homily: *He cannot stand in the face of danger for the sheep who, in the very fact that he presides over the sheep, does not love the sheep but seeks earthly gain. Therefore, he trembles to set himself against danger, lest he lose that which he loves.* Therefore, he who avoids danger to himself through his departure—provided it is without harm to the flock—is not a <margin>To the second argument.</margin> hireling. ¶ Likewise, in response to the second argument from Proverbs 6, it is said that he who pledges his faith to another, if he is lawfully hindered, serves sufficiently <margin>To the third argument.</margin> through another. ¶ Finally, to the third, it is answered that since a bishop is in a higher state of perfection than a monk <note>In Catholic theology, the "state of perfection" refers to a life dedicated to spiritual growth; bishops are considered to be in the "state of perfection to be exercised" (serving others), while monks are in the "state of perfection to be acquired."</note>, as long as he is hindered from the exercise of that function, he is not bound to commit himself to a religious order.

Even though we have completed this dispute according to our ability—and perhaps more at length than was right—it will not be shameful to append fragments of certain letters of St. Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD) was the Patriarch of Alexandria and a fierce defender of orthodoxy against Arianism.</note>, which others before us have both translated and taken care to attach to the present question. For they are indeed most worthy for all bishops to have deeply impressed upon their hearts. Whoever is not too lazy to read them will certainly not regret having done so; and he who is already worn out by boredom and refuses to read will not be burdened by having them written here. Indeed, let it be clear how ancient this question has been, and how the most holy Fathers considered the affirmative truth of it to be most sacred, and how necessary they believed the residency of bishops to be for the salvation of souls and the endurance of Christianity. For even back then, a custom had crept in that bishops would frequent the Imperial city of Constantinople, <margin>The first letter of Athanasius to the Bishop of Crete, intended to strengthen the practice of residency.</margin> where Athanasius was patriarch. ¶ He wrote the first letter to the Bishop of Crete, who, while he was absent from his church, proposed to travel there. Athanasius commends this proposal with the highest praise and reasons:

> "For, my dearest brother and fellow-minister," he says, "grace and peace to you from God. That plan and will of yours, which has reached my ears, seemed to belong to a strong and manly soul, one looking only upward, truly and lawfully striving, and responding to his own name and calling. It is not the soul of a hireling or one who flees—not only if he sees a wolf, but even if he sees a fox—whereby he creates loss for the flock of Christ, the Prince of Pastors, and prepares infinite torments for his own soul."

Take note of the emphasis of these words. And it follows:

<column-break/>

For why did this man—namely, he who does not remain in his own diocese—not rather prefer to live a private life, if he intended to succumb and to feed himself rather than the sheep for whom Christ shed his blood? How did it not come into the mind of this man that he who does the work of the Lord negligently is struck with a curse? Although he pretends to do the work in name, in his soul resides that which is written of the fool: "he said in his heart, there is no God." For they do not place God before them who dare to do these things in his sight. Listen: they "do not place God" because they deny him by their deeds. God grant that we may not be of their number and rank, but may he enroll us among the faithful stewards and kindly grant that we may be ready for the Prince of Pastors to fulfill what is necessary, and that we may lay down our lives for his sheep, who demonstrated this both by example and ordained it by edict. Thus, he recognized the precept in the words of Christ in John 10. And a few things being interposed, he says:

> "Wherefore, it is not safe for true pastors not to be vigilant, and not to survey all things on every side, and not only to seek the wandering sheep, but to be even more solicitous for those that do not wander, being terrified by the darkness of these times, which have been brought upon us by the just permission and judgment of God: namely, because we do not live as becomes him who called us. But oh, the loss of our souls! Oh, the great punishments to be inflicted upon us for our lusts and disordered wills, which have fathered this evil! This evil, I say: that the holy people should be dispersed and scattered through all the fields and mountains by the fault of absent pastors!"

Therefore, all good pastors, whoever are worthy of this name, ought to do this (that is, reside in their own dioceses), so that he who ceases to do so shall not cease without punishment. For if every pastor were to stay in the diocese that fell to him for even two days, one might see by experience through many sins and losses that these things would not happen among the people. For it seems just as much for a flock to be away from its shepherd as for a blind man to lack a guide. Truly, the sheep increase and are in safety when true pastors preside—not those who only drink the milk and are covered by the wool, and with all zeal and art feed themselves and not the sheep. These and many other things of this kind are in that letter. <margin>His second letter sent to the Bishop of Sardinia.</margin> ¶ He sent a second letter of the same sort to the Bishop of Sardinia: where, immediately after the prologue, he begins thus: "I know that you are not ignorant of what has been decreed by the holy Apostles concerning the constitution of ecclesiastical affairs. Of which one is, that every pastor, within his own borders..."

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law

...stays within the boundaries for the sake of peace and charity, of which Jesus is the closest bond that cannot be broken. You know, moreover, that it might appear what kind of men we should be, to whom that great High Priest Christ—marking out for us the true shepherd—defined the duty of a shepherd: namely, through mutual charity toward Him. He alludes to that saying, *Do you love me more than these?* <note>original: "Diligis me plus his?" from John 21:15, where Jesus restores Peter.</note>. Furthermore, you are not unaware of the prayer of the excellent shepherd, who is to know his souls clearly—that is, face to face; concerning which it is written in Proverbs that a good shepherd ought to know his flock by face <note>Proverbs 27:23: "Be diligent to know the state of thy flocks." To know someone "by face" implies a personal, intimate knowledge of the individuals in one's care.</note>. And further on: You have also understood who the hireling <note>original: "mercenarius"</note> is and of what sort, about whom I am ashamed both to speak and to remain silent; since the state of the times and of affairs itself sufficiently shows and proves it. Regarding him, if I listen attentively to the prophets when they rail against shepherds like me in these words: *The shepherds feed themselves, not the sheep* <note>Ezekiel 34:2</note>. And that: *O shepherds who destroy the sheep of the pasture!* <note>Jeremiah 23:1</note>. Likewise, *the priests have hidden the law of the Lord, and have violated my law, and have profaned my holy things* <note>Ezekiel 22:26</note>. Also that saying, *to be clothed with the wool of the sheep, and to slaughter that which is fat, to drink the milk* <note>Ezekiel 34:3</note>. Hearing these things attentively, I say, what should I do, lest I fear those who rebuke me and set clearly before my eyes what sort of man I am? If anyone who does not look upon that final fire thinks these are fables, to me they are certainly not fables, but everything seems so horrible that they exceed horror itself and consume the very marrow. Yet we do not care to do what is in our power, lest on account of some of these vices and crimes, bound by the tightest chains, we be afflicted with eternal punishments. But what follows immediately after is worthy of note. For he says that although it was established from the beginning that a synod <note>A regional meeting of church leaders.</note> should be held twice every year, it later seemed more convenient to hold it once, so that the sheep might not be easily invaded by wolves on account of the frequent absence of the shepherds. See how much care those Fathers had for residency <note>original: "residentia"</note>, that for its sake they abstained from celebrating a synod. And it follows, appropriately suited to the customs of our times, against those bishops who, having deserted their flocks, were spending time in the court of Constantinople; concerning whom he says: Finally, they preferred to indulge the flesh, content with a brief pleasure, rather than to labor with the people of God, having despised the divine laws which prohibit being away from the flock with impunity for even a little while. Listen: by divine law, that residency was so commanded that it is not permitted to be away from the flock with impunity even for a little while. And he adds: And unless, as the Apostle says, the enemy...

<column-break/>

...should see, speaking the truth, I could say something truly: What, I ask, does it profit those bishops and shepherds to stay in the city, unless (to omit other things) they might move some patriarchs <note>High-ranking bishops in the Eastern Church.</note> and elect others, lest if the same man remains patriarch for a long time, all ecclesiastical matters might be settled: which noble deed those men have been accustomed to do since the time we took possession of Constantinople. Which indeed, along with the remaining evils, is not ambiguous or uncertain but increases the wrath of God toward us. For it is certain that shepherds who neglect the flock will not depart unpunished and unavenged; yet perhaps it does not seem so to those who voluntarily draw a veil over themselves, lest they behold the refined truth of the Gospel. These are his words.

<margin>His third letter.</margin>
¶ And in another third letter to the bishop of Apamea <note>Apamea was a major city in Roman Syria and a significant center of early Christianity.</note>, among other things, he warns him thus: As a true bishop ought, you should reside holily at the holy altar, of which you must partake, just as the Lord pronounced, *The worker is worthy of his hire* <note>Luke 10:7</note>. For which reason it must not be thought that you are permitted to be away for a long time for any reason: but rather you must act so that you can go quickly to that church which is assigned to you and commended to your charge.

<margin>Fourth letter.</margin>
¶ But in another to the same man, which is the fourth, he heaps up words of even greater emphasis. For he says: Truly, I think that he to whom the flock of Christ is committed, if he knows the dignity of the office, is wicked if he does not strive and apply himself to it even unto blood <note>original: "vsq; ad sanguinem," a common idiom meaning to the point of death or extreme sacrifice.</note>; unless perhaps you were ignorant that it was God who said, *Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.* But alas for me, now shepherds no longer feed the sheep, but they feed upon the sheep as if they were bread! Now those horrible evils of shepherds, which the prophet Ezekiel describes, have crept in with the greatest license! If such and so grave things seem so to you, come, best of men, be content with your diocese, remain in it, see that you are with your sheep, so that you are joined to them even unto blood—those whom divine providence now guards in the thickets, among figs and roses, and on the mountains. For it is not, as is most certain, by your pastoral rod and staff that they are in the green pastures of peace and the goods of the heavenly Jerusalem. For you know it has been confirmed by canons <note>Church laws.</note> and laws that those who have been absent from their diocese for more than six months, unless a grave illness holds them back, should lose their priesthood and their flock. But a new and wicked plan has been devised here by the men of our age: namely, you send someone who knows how to milk the flock, while you yourselves stay in the city of Constantinople to look after your prefectures...

<sig>Hhh 4</sig>

...civil prefectures, signatures, and untimely ordinations; add even bulls and decrees. These are our times. And as if you will go unpunished, you withdraw so far from the diocese committed to you, and you commit other tasks of this sort to whomever you please. It would have been better if all the bishops from everywhere were gathered into one place, and each one's diocese were marked out with a measuring line of distribution <note>original: "funiculo diſtributionis," a biblical metaphor for determining boundaries or inheritance</note>, and thus your part were assigned to you by the patriarch, or you were removed by the patriarch.

<margin>Fragment of another letter directed to the Emperor.</note>

¶ Besides these, he adds other letters on the same matter, which I will pass over lest I become tedious. But he also commemorates many things to the Emperor, who allowed bishops to stay in Constantinople and did not compel them to depart to their own churches; among these he says: "If you were to commit sheep to a shepherd, and then you saw them abandoned while he indulged and served his own rest and his own desires, tell me, I ask, would you leave that shepherd unpunished? We do not allow sheep and cattle to be neglected with impunity, and shall we allow the shepherds of souls to feed themselves with impunity, and not the sheep? What excuse, I ask, shall we offer before God? Would that this were not a reproach to us: *All seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.*" <note>original: "Omnes quærunt quæ ſua ſunt, non quæ Ieſu Chriſti," from Philippians 2:21.</note>

¶ Then he adds another on the same matter to the same person in this tenor: "If it is true what is usually said—that he who deprives the flock of a shepherd creates danger for both—surely a heavy punishment awaits him who keeps the shepherd away from the sheepfold. And he who is a shepherd ought to endure labors for the flock of Christ, even to the point of shedding blood, rather than abandoning them; except when it is necessary to be absent for a short time at a synod held each year to conduct necessary business. Once these are concluded, he must return quickly, if he believes he will give an account to Christ, the High Shepherd, and if he is worthy of the name of shepherd. Unless, perhaps, he is called away by the Emperor or the patriarch for a necessity pertaining to the benefit of souls, and is to return immediately. But if it should seem otherwise to the bishops or the Emperor, or if anything should happen differently, I will by no means follow it, nor assent in any way. For God will not take account of our excuses and desires, but will demand accounts concerning truth, justice, and divine laws and statutes."

¶ And finally, in another shorter letter, he writes: "Remember the Scripture that commands that men should be saddened rather than God. But as for you, Emperor, why should it seem a heavy thing to ordain justice, temperance, and mercy for your people? From this you would report no disadvantage, but rather win the mercy of God through good works."

<column-break/>

"What is more just than if every bishop were commanded, whether he likes it or not, to return to his diocese? Are they not bound to pay this debt? And is it not sanctioned by canon law?" I see that I have drawn out this matter more extensively than perhaps anyone will think necessary; however, I do not regret the length.

# QUESTION FOUR
## Concerning the bond and the manner in which bishops and priests are bound to dispense their goods.

### ARTICLE I.

->Whether it is lawful for a bishop to possess anything as his own.<-

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'Q' depicting a seated cleric or scholar within an ornate architectural and foliate frame.</image-desc>
WE have proposed the FOURTH question of the present book concerning the bond and the manner in which priests—and especially parish priests, and most particularly bishops—are bound to dispense ecclesiastical goods. This question has kept me in doubt for so long and so much that I would have preferred to listen to others who might teach me sufficiently, rather than explain my own opinion. Nevertheless, I will bring forward those things I have meditated upon regarding this matter; let others be the judges. For it is an abstruse and perplexed matter, supported on both sides by its own reasons and testimonies. Furthermore, it is a subject very necessary to know. 

The first article, therefore—so that we do not depart from the order of Saint Thomas—is whether it is lawful for a bishop to possess anything as his own.

<margin>First argument.</margin> There is indeed the oracle of Christ in Matthew, chapter 19: *If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all you have and give to the poor, and come and follow me.* <note>Matthew 19:21.</note> Here, voluntary poverty is taught as being required for perfection. Bishops, however, profess a state of perfection; therefore, they can no more justly possess property of their own than monks can.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly, bishops (as has been sufficiently proven above, and as the gloss on Luke 10 holds) take the place of the Apostles. But Christ forbade the Apostles the ownership of things in Matthew 10: *Do not possess gold, nor silver—* <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "argentum" (silver) from Matthew 10:9.</note>

He then begins Question IV, investigating whether bishops and priests have the right to personal property or are bound to dispense their wealth to the poor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the legal and moral status of bishops, specifically transitioning from their duty of residence to the question of whether they may rightfully own private property (dominium) or if they are bound to a state of apostolic poverty.</meta>

# Francisco de Soto, On Justice and Right #

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
<margin>Jerome?</margin>
...gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts <note>original: "zonis vestris," referring to Matthew 10:9</note>. Peter confessed obedience to this in Matthew 19: "Behold, we have left all things and followed you." Therefore, bishops can have no ownership of property. ¶ Thirdly: "Clergy" in Greek, as Jerome is the authority in his letter to Nepotian (cited in Decree 12, question 1, canon *Cleros*), is the same as "lot" or "portion" in Latin. Hence, clerics are so named either because they are the Lord’s portion, or because the Lord is their portion. However, he whose possession is the Lord ought to possess nothing outside of Him. For if he has gold, if he has silver, if he has property, or various household goods, the Lord does not deign to become his portion alongside these other participants. These are Jerome's words; therefore, it seems bishops are forbidden from the ownership of things.

<margin>The Council of Agde.</margin>
¶ On the contrary is the canon *Episcopi* from the Council of Agde <note>A church council held in Gaul in 506 AD</note>, in the same cause and question. There it is held that bishops may leave to their heirs, if they wish, their own property, whether acquired or whatever they possess of their own.

<margin>Two types of goods which a bishop possesses.</margin>
The title of the present question is general, as it does not distinguish between ecclesiastical goods and others which a bishop can obtain by natural and civil law. For there are two types of goods which a bishop possesses: namely, those that fall to him by law, whether by inheritance, gift, or any other secular means; and other goods which are ecclesiastical. Regarding those of the first type, there is no ambiguity that he may possess them properly and privately; but regarding the latter, the entire dispute of the matter will arise. In this first article, therefore, it is only disputed whether the status of bishops is a state of poverty, just like that of monks, such that they cannot possess anything of their own.

<margin>Concluding response.</margin>
Because of this, the answer is clear and very easy to resolve, contained in a single conclusion: Although bishops profess a state of perfection, they are not, however, like monks, obligated to live without private property. This conclusion, I say, is plain and most consistent, because it affirms nothing in particular regarding ecclesiastical goods. Thus, the truth can be drawn from the fact that by the right of secular acquisition, the ownership of things can belong to bishops. But indeed, this has been asserted by us generally, following Saint Thomas. For I think—as anyone can clearly note in the solution to the second point, and will become clearer in the following article—that he also felt this was true regarding ecclesiastical goods, specifically for that portion which falls to them by reason of their stipend.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
It is proved, therefore, according to this general sense. To those things which are of **supererogation** <term>supererogation: performing more than what is required by duty or command</term>, no one is bound unless he specifically binds himself to it by a vow.

<column-break/>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
For Augustine says in his letter to Paulinus and Armentarius: "Because you have already vowed, you have already bound yourself; and it is not permitted for you to do otherwise. Before you were liable to the vow, you were free to be of a lower rank." To live without property is a work of supererogation; truly, it is not contained under the bond of a command, but under the choice of counsel <note>i.e., the "evangelical counsels" of perfection</note>, as is clear in Matthew 19. For after the necessity of the commandments ("If you wish to enter into life"), there was added that he who wishes to be perfect should leave all he has to follow Christ. It is manifest, however, that bishops do not entangle themselves in a vow of this kind, because it is not necessary for the pastoral office. It is enough that they love Christ exceedingly. Therefore, according to the laws of his dignity, a bishop is not barred from exercising ownership of property.

<margin>Instruction</margin>
¶ Here no reason for doubt emerges, but this alone must be committed to memory: since a bishop does not take a vow of religion <note>i.e., the formal vows of a monastic order</note>, it follows that he makes no special vow of chastity beyond that which is joined to the priesthood, nor a vow of poverty. He only promises obedience to the Pope and his faith to this Church, from which bond he cannot be dissolved except by the authority of the Pope himself. And therefore, insofar as anyone is a bishop, it is not repugnant <note>inconsistent or contradictory</note> for him to possess property, not only by hereditary or any other civil law, but not even by ecclesiastical law. For it is not repugnant to his dignity to receive a just stipend according to the nature of his function, of which he would be the true owner, just as the priests and Levites once were. Whether such ecclesiastical ownership is prohibited to them for another reason—namely, so that he may have no portion of the tithes that come to him—must be examined in the next and subsequent article. For now, let it be sufficiently established that holding the episcopal dignity is not a state of poverty, and thus it is not repugnant for a bishop to have ownership of the things he possesses.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
To the first argument, therefore, that proposition is denied: that poverty is generally and absolutely necessary for the nature of perfection or the state of perfection. Rather, it is only necessary for the particular state of perfection of those in religious orders <note>monks and friars</note>. That it is not necessary for perfection was already sufficiently established above in Book 8, where we showed that the essence of perfection consists in the abundance of charity, to which anyone in any state...

<vocab>Cleros, supererogation, dominium, stipend, state of perfection, evangelical counsels</vocab>

<summary>Domingo de Soto argues that unlike monks, bishops are not bound by a vow of poverty and may legally and morally own private property, distinguishing between secular inheritance and ecclesiastical stipends. He concludes that while the episcopal office is a "state of perfection," this perfection is defined by charity and pastoral duty rather than the renunciation of all goods.</summary>
