<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether bishops are required to live in a state of absolute poverty like the religious orders (monks and friars), or if they may legally and morally own property.</meta>

### Question IV of the Tenth Book ###

<margin>Gregory the Great.</margin>
...one can proceed in their spiritual state. However, poverty is necessary for the state of the "religious" <note>In this context, "religious" refers specifically to members of monastic or mendicant orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans, who take a vow of poverty.</note> for the reason that they profess to "be perfected" (that is, to learn and acquire perfection); for such a lifestyle, the possession of property is a burden and an obstacle. Bishops, however, do not profess to "be perfected," but rather to "perfect others" <note>The author distinguishes between the *learning* stage of the monk and the *active leadership* stage of the bishop.</note>. Therefore, they ought to have their roots so firmly planted in charity that they cannot be uprooted by any wind—namely, neither by the love of the riches they possess, nor by any other human affection. This is illustrated by an example from the life of Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604)</note>, where a response from a divine oracle is related regarding a hermit: it was said that the hermit loved his cat more than Gregory loved his own riches. Consequently, it was not said to the young man in the Gospel, "If you are perfect," or "If you wish to be a perfecter," but rather, "If you wish to become perfect, go and sell all you have," etc. <note>Matthew 19:21</note>. Yet, when Peter was installed as pastor, no poverty was demanded of him, but rather the very height of charity.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
¶ To the second argument, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> applies three modes of responding. One is from Jerome, which is a mystical interpretation: that under the names of "gold and silver," which were forbidden, preachers are actually prohibited from relying on the wisdom and eloquence of this world.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Another response is from Augustine in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: namely, that the command "Do not possess gold," etc., does not have the force of a command <term>precept|A binding rule or law</term>, but rather of a permission. It is as if He had said: "There is no need for you to carry gold and silver, for you are permitted to accept food as workers." Hence He adds: "The worker is worthy of his hire." For the fact that Paul, as recorded in 1 Corinthians 9, sometimes chose not to use the support offered to him, was a "work of supererogation" <note>original: "supererogationis" — an act going above and beyond what is strictly required by duty.</note>.

<margin>Chrysostom.</margin>
But the third response is from Chrysostom: that the prohibition was specifically made to the disciples while they were being sent to preach to the Jews. This was done partly so that the Jewish people might be more easily attracted to them, and partly so that the disciples themselves might have a firmer confidence that divine aid would not fail them.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
From this, it follows that neither they nor their successors are obligated to preach the Gospel without their own means of support. Therefore Paul, as he mentions of himself in 2 Corinthians 11, "robbed" <note>original: "mendicabat," literally begged or took stipends from</note> other churches for support so that he could preach to the Corinthians for free; he therefore rightfully possessed those things sent to him from elsewhere. Furthermore, Saint Thomas confirms this solution—namely, that a bishop can possess his own property—by noting that it would be foolish to suggest that those holy bishops Athanasius, Ambrose, and Augustine had transgressed a command of holiness of this kind.

<margin>A Scruple.</margin>
¶ However, two points regarding this solution should not be ignored. One is that the solution does not appear entirely true, nor does it fully satisfy the argument. For it would appear

<column-break/>

to deny that the apostles truly professed poverty, which is known to be false based on the authority cited by Aquinas himself: "Behold, we have left all things" <note>Matthew 19:27</note>. Therefore, the response does not satisfy the very authority assumed in the argument.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ To this, it is responded that Saint Thomas is not disputing here whether the apostles took the three vows <note>The vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience</note> as models for future religious orders—which Saint Thomas does indeed concede in Book 2, Question 88, Article 4. Rather, he is only discussing them now insofar as they were apostles and bishops, for poverty does not essentially belong to that specific state or office.

<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
¶ A second point must be especially noted here which the author seems to affirm: indeed, he plainly affirms that a bishop can have ownership <term>dominium|The legal right of full ownership and control</term> not only of things acquired by other legal means, but also of the ecclesiastical stipend assigned to his function. For the argument was that bishops, as bishops (that is, preachers of the Word), ought to be poor. The response is a negation of that. Since poverty consists in the denial of ownership, and since he denies they must be poor because they can possess the stipends of their office, he concedes to them the "dominium" of those things, which is the opposite of poverty. But this will be discussed more closely in Article 3.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ So that the third solution may be fully understood, it must be noted that God is called the "portion" of the cleric, not to imply a relationship to another part possessed by the cleric, but just as one heir possesses a portion of an inheritance which is his entire substance. It is called a "portion" in respect to the other part which goes to another heir. For example: a cleric ought to be content with God, whom he possesses, so that he possesses nothing else alongside Him—not that he cannot possess reputation, honor, health, or some temporal goods, but that he possesses everything else according to God's will. Thus, his devotion toward God should in no way be diminished by the care of other things. To do otherwise would be, according to Jerome, to possess something outside of God. For he who possesses God in this way has God as his "portion"—that is, his entire possession in respect to the rest of the universe, which he leaves for others to possess.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the financial obligations of bishops, specifically addressing whether they are morally required to give all surplus wealth to the poor or if they have legal ownership of their property.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right #

<meta>catchword: in such</meta>

<margin>First argument. Ambrose.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative initial 'N' showing a scholar or saintly figure kneeling in prayer within a lush, fenced garden, representing a life of contemplation and spiritual labor.</image-desc>Lest we break the thread of Saint Thomas's <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto.</note> argument, the second question is whether a bishop sins mortally <note>A "mortal sin" is a grave offense that, in Catholic theology, leads to the loss of divine grace unless confessed.</note> if he does not distribute the church property he manages to the poor. It appears that Saint Ambrose <note>Ambrose (c. 339–397), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> defines it as such while explaining the passage in Luke 12 regarding the rich man whose land brought forth a bountiful harvest. Indeed, he says: "Let no one call what is common their own; whatever is held beyond what is sufficient for one's needs is obtained by violence." And a little later: "It is no less a crime to take from one who possesses than it is to deny those in need when you are able and have an abundance. To take the property of another by force is a criminal offense." Therefore, bishops who do not pour out what remains to them upon the poor commit a mortal transgression.

<margin>Second [argument].</margin>
¶ Second, regarding that passage in Isaiah 3, "The plunder of the poor is in your house," Saint Jerome <note>Jerome (c. 347–420), known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> says in a commentary that church property is the property of the poor. The same is found in the letter to Damasus (Canon 16, question 1, "Since..."), which has now been accepted as a common proverb: whoever either usurps for himself what belongs to another, or spends it on other uses, sins mortally and is bound to make restitution <note>Restitutio: the legal and moral obligation to give back stolen or misused goods to their rightful owner.</note>. Therefore, since the property of bishops is church property, it follows that if they retain what is redundant for themselves, or give it to their relatives, they appear to be bound to make restitution.

<margin>Third [argument]. Jerome.</margin>
¶ Third, it is much more permissible for priests to take from the resources of the church what is necessary for themselves than to increase their surplus. Indeed, Jerome says in a letter to Damasus (recorded in 1, question 2) that those clerics are fittingly supported by church stipends whose parents' and relatives' property is insufficient to support them; however, those who can be supported by their parents' goods and their own wealth commit and incur sacrilege if they take what belongs to the poor. These are his words. Hence the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 5: "If any faithful woman has widows, let her assist them, and let the church not be burdened, so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows." Therefore, it is much more certain that bishops sin mortally when they do not pour out upon the poor the wealth that overflows from the church's goods.

¶ On the contrary is the practice of certain bishops who do not distribute all that remains to the poor, but rather spend it—laudably, it seems—on increasing the revenues of the church.

IT IS worthwhile at the beginning of our dispute to distribute the text of Saint Thomas into conclusions, which for the sake of clarity we shall establish as seven in number. We must persist...

<column-break/>

...however, in that distinction between a bishop's private property—which he possesses properly, for instance by inheritance or other civil right—and church property. Therefore, the first conclusion is:

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
Bishops have true ownership of their own property, that is, what they possess by secular right. This has already been sufficiently confirmed above in Article 1, based on the fact that the state of a bishop is not a profession of poverty <note>Unlike monks or friars, bishops do not take a formal vow of poverty that strips them of legal ownership of personal property.</note>. Thus, by the condition and nature of the things themselves, they are not bound by the law of justice to distribute those goods to the poor or others, but they may both retain them and give them away as they please.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ Second conclusion. Although they may sin in the distribution of these goods just as secular citizens do—namely, either through greed by retaining them against the duty of charity, or by wasting them unworthily—they are nevertheless not obligated to make restitution to anyone. For, as we have often said in Book 4, where justice is not violated, no obligation of restitution arises.

<margin>Third conclusion. Augustine.</margin>
¶ Third conclusion. Bishops are the stewards or managers <note>original: "procuratores"</note> of church property. This is evident from the words of Saint Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430), influential theologian and philosopher.</note> to Count Boniface, which are recorded in 2, question 1, the last canon: "If we possess privately what suffices for us, those church goods are not ours, but belong to those for whom we act as managers; let us not claim ownership for ourselves through damnable usurpation." Hence it follows that those goods must be managed with the highest good faith, according to 1 Corinthians 4: "Here it is required among stewards that one be found faithful." This is understood regarding goods held in common, as the following points will declare.

<margin>Fourth conclusion. Pope Simplicius.</margin>
¶ And therefore, regarding their distribution, the fourth conclusion is added. Church goods of this kind are to be spent not only for the use of the poor, but also for divine worship and for supplying the needs of the ministers, according to the tenor of the decree of Pope Simplicius <note>Pope from 468 to 483.</note> in 12, question 2, who says: "Of the revenues of the church or the offerings of the faithful, let one portion be set aside for the bishops alone. Two portions should be administered by the priest for the church buildings <note>original: "fabricis"</note> and for the distribution to the poor, under the risk of his rank; the final portion should be divided among the clergy according to the merits of each."

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Fifth conclusion. Where the goods intended for the bishop's use are distinct from the other three portions assigned to the poor, the ministers, and worship: if the bishop retains anything from these three portions, there is no doubt that he sins mortally against the good faith of his stewardship and is bound to make restitution. This conclusion is made known through the law of commutative justice <note>Commutative justice governs the fairness of exchange and the return of what is owed to another.</note>; for in such...

# Question 4 of the Tenth Book #

<meta>catchword: &</meta>

in such a case he truly commits a theft of another’s property.

<margin>Sixth conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Sixth conclusion.** Regarding those things which are specifically set aside for the bishop’s own use, the same reasoning seems to apply as with one's own personal goods: namely, that he indeed sins through immoderate attachment and use if he retains an excessive amount for himself and does not help others, as the debt of charity <note>In scholastic theology, a "debt of charity" is a moral obligation to help others, distinct from a "debt of justice" which is a legal requirement to return what is owed.</note> requires.

<margin>Correction of the text of Saint Thomas.</margin>
The printed editions that lack this final phrase—*as the debt of charity requires* <note>original: "Sicut requirit debitum charitatis." Soto is acting as a textual critic here, correcting errors in the published versions of Aquinas's works.</note>—must be corrected. In fact, I am strongly of the opinion that the statement "he is not bound to restitution" is also missing. He had said the opposite in the previous conclusion; here, however, he says: *The same reasoning seems to apply as with personal goods,* the wasteful consumption of which does not demand restitution.

<margin>Seventh conclusion.</margin>
¶ **Seventh conclusion.** If, however, the aforementioned goods are not distinct <note>That is, if the bishop's personal allowance and the church's general funds are all in one pot.</note>, their distribution is committed to the bishop's good faith. In many editions, the entire phrase *If, however, the aforementioned goods are not [distinct]* is missing; in those versions, one reads *distinctly does not help*, which makes the text unintelligible. ¶ Regarding these indistinct goods, the explanation of the conclusion is applied: namely, that if the distribution is slightly deficient or slightly excessive, this can happen without a loss of good faith. Indeed, a man cannot always hold the exact point of virtue so perfectly that, due to the human condition, he does not lean toward one extreme or the other. If, however, there is a great excess, then it can neither be hidden nor excused from mortal sin; for then good faith is violated, and likewise distributive justice <note>Distributive justice concerns the fair allocation of resources among members of a community.</note>. Hence, three stains of the unfaithful servant are noted in Matthew 24, where it is read: *If that evil servant shall say in his heart, "My Lord delays his coming"*—which pertains to contempt for divine judgment; *and shall begin to strike his fellow servants*—which pertains to pride; *and shall eat and drink with drunkards*—which pertains to luxury, for the sake of which a distribution is made in bad faith. *The lord of that servant shall come on a day when he does not hope, and shall divide him*—that is, separate him from the society of the good—*and shall place his portion with the hypocrites*—namely, in hell. Behold the text of Saint Thomas, which it was useful to place before our eyes at the start of this disputation. It must be further unraveled in the following article, where, among other things, the arguments proposed from Ambrose and Jerome at the head of the question will be resolved.

<column-break/>

### ARTICLE III. ###

->**Whether bishops and other priests have true and legitimate ownership of the ecclesiastical fruits that fall to them as their portion.**<-

---

HAVING LAID DOWN the opinion of Saint Thomas, we shall subsequently move through individual points regarding his articles, which are general. And first, concerning the former article in which it was disputed in general whether bishops can have ownership of things, it is asked specifically regarding the sixth conclusion: whether they, as well as the rest of the priests, have true and legitimate ownership (*dominium*) <note>The Latin term *dominium* implies full legal right and control over property, including the right to give it away or sell it.</note> of those ecclesiastical fruits <note>In this context, "fruits" refers to the income, produce, or revenue generated by church lands or offices.</note> which fall to them as their portion. For there are innumerable authorities that seem to argue for the negative side. First among these is Holy Scripture. For even if the state of clerics <note>A "cleric" is any member of the clergy (priests, deacons, etc.), as opposed to "monks" (religious orders), who take a formal vow of poverty.</note> does not have a vow of poverty attached to it in the same way as monks, it seems that nothing of what is administered to them for their clerical function belongs to them, except for food and clothing; according to the word of the Lord, *The worker is worthy of his food* [Matthew 10:10], and the word of Paul in 1 Timothy 6: *Having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content*; like the oxen, as he says elsewhere, treading out the grain. Therefore, the apostles were sent to preach without a pouch, commanded not to possess gold or money. And for that reason, in the preceding book under the title of "Simony" <note>Simony is the sin of buying or selling sacred things or church offices.</note>, we showed that nothing is owed to clerics, nor can they themselves perceive anything from the people for the administration of the sacraments and other spiritual functions by any other right than the right of sustenance. ¶ Second, there is also the very numerous crowd of testimonies from the Holy Fathers. For besides the passages of Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine recently cited, the most grave Prosper <note>Prosper of Aquitaine (c. 390–455), a Christian writer and disciple of Augustine.</note> says in Question 1, Canon *Expedit*, that the resources of the church are not private property but are possessed in common. And in the Council of Agde <note>A regional church council held in Gaul in 506 AD.</note>, as recorded there in the Canon *Episcopi*, it is held that whatever comes from the provision of the church—whether from fields, fruits, or offerings—all must be kept as the right of the church. And Pope Urban says in the same place, in the Canon *Res*, that the property of the church should be held not as one’s own, but as common; and not for uses other than those aforementioned—namely, for the support of the poor and the ministers...

For this reason, the same must be judged regarding priests if they do not distribute those goods. There are many such passages from the Saints. And Jerome, writing to Damasus—referenced in Chapter *Quoniam*, 16, q. 1—says that clerics who abound in secular goods cannot receive the support intended for the poor.

¶ On the contrary, however, stands the text in the single chapter of *On Non-Resident Clerics*, where it is held that those who do not participate in the divine offices—unless relieved by illness, or a just and reasonable necessity, or an evident benefit to the church—are not the owners of the daily distributions; nor do they make them their own, but are bound to the <term>restitution</term> <note>The legal obligation to return stolen or misappropriated goods.</note> of what they have so received. From this, the opposite sense is gathered: that those who *are* resident acquire true <term>dominium</term> <note>Absolute ownership or right of control under the law.</note> over those same distributions, and by the same reasoning, over other ecclesiastical fruits.

This present question, as I said at the beginning, is exceedingly ambiguous. Indeed, since the testimonies of the Saints seem to define it differently at the first sound of their words than deeper reason seems to permit. Let us, therefore, set aside the secular goods of bishops and priests...

<column-break/>

...about which, as concluded in the previous article, no one is in doubt; for everyone agrees they are possessed by priests by private ownership. But regarding ecclesiastical goods, three opinions are debated, as is often the case.

<margin>The first opinion: Alexander of Hales, Richard.</margin>
One is that of Alexander of Hales, a most weighty author (Part 3, Question 36, Member 5, Article 2), and Richard of Middleton (in Book 4, Distinction 45, Article 3, Question 1), who expressly say that clerics have only the *use* of ecclesiastical revenues, and not the *ownership*.

<margin>The Archdeacon</margin>
And the doctors of Canon Law have almost entirely embraced this; for instance, the Archdeacon <note>Guido de Baysio, a famous 13th-century canonist.</note> on the chapter *Statutum*, section *Assessorem*, where he says it is heretical in law to claim that a cleric acquires for himself true ownership of the fruits of a prebend <note>A portion of church revenue granted to a member of the clergy.</note> or a church.

<margin>Panormitanus, Dominicus, Thomas Walden.</margin>
To this is added Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a leading expert in ecclesiastical law.</note> in the chapter *Cum esses* on testaments, and Dominicus de Sancto Geminiano in the chapter *Praesenti*. And, someone who should not be considered least among them, Thomas Walden supports the same opinion in Volume 1, Book 4, Chapter 42, and the four following. There, by many testimonies of the Fathers, he seems to himself to prove most constantly that no ownership of ecclesiastical goods resides with the clerics.

<margin>The second opinion: St. Thomas.</margin>
Nevertheless, the second opinion is the one held here by Saint Thomas: namely, that regarding that portion which is specifically assigned to the bishop, he seems to be the owner in the same way as he is of other goods he possesses in a secular manner, as is clear in the sixth conclusion. It is otherwise if all the goods of the church were held in common and their distribution merely entrusted to him, as is clear in the third and seventh conclusions. And Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI, who was also a significant theologian.</note> embraces the same opinion in his work on the matter of restitution.

<margin>The third opinion: Cajetan.</margin>
The third is that of Cajetan in this present place, which he also suggested above, as we saw in the previous book under the title *On Tithes*. For he partly holds with Saint Thomas—namely, that bishops are regularly the owners of their portion after the distribution of goods into four parts <note>Historically, church income was often split four ways: for the bishop, the clergy, the poor, and the building maintenance.</note> has been made. However, he devised this exception: that when the portion falling to them is notably abundant, they are then bound to return two parts of that same portion to the poor and the church fabric. And although he does not expressly state whether they are bound by the law of charity or of justice, he nevertheless seems to feel they are bound by the rigor of justice, just as they were before the goods were divided. From which it follows, according to him, that they are by no means truly owners of that portion, just as they were not owners of the whole pile before.

<margin>Proof of the opinion of St. Thomas.</margin>
¶ But in truth, the second opinion has always been so persuasive to me, according to my own meager judgment, that as long as the Church does not define the contrary...

<margin>Four types of temporal goods enjoyed by the clergy.</margin>
¶ Therefore, for a full understanding of the matter, it is necessary to note two things immediately at the outset. One concerns the various types of Church property, and the other concerns its various states. For these points clarify the matter immensely. Regarding the first, there are four types of temporal goods <note>Physical or worldly assets like money, land, or food, as opposed to spiritual goods.</note> which the clergy enjoy, or which were formerly stored in the ecclesiastical storehouse. The first were those which the Christian faithful contributed in common in the early days of the Church, so that both the clergy and the poor might be supported from them. Regarding this rite, it is written in the fourth chapter of the **Acts of the Apostles** that there was no one needy among them. For as many as had possessions of fields or houses sold them and brought the price of what they sold and laid it before the feet of the Apostles. It was then divided to each person as there was need. And although that institution had its origin in Jerusalem, the custom nevertheless grew in Christianity that Christians would contribute at least a part of their goods into the assembly of the clergy for the same purpose; they did not sell their possessions but let them remain in the 

<margin>Pope Melchiades.</margin>
Church. For Pope Melchiades says in the canon *Futuram* (Case 12, Question 1) that since the Apostles foresaw the future Church among the gentiles, they did not acquire estates in Judea, but only the price of them to support the nations. But indeed, as the Church grew, all people—as is most evident regarding the Emperor Constantine—contributed not only the prices but also the possessions themselves to the Church. 

<margin>Urban.</margin>
And Urban, in the very next canon, says: "The high priests, seeing that it could be of more use if they handed over the inheritances and fields which they used to sell to the churches presided over by bishops, because they could provide more and more elegant things for the faithful living a common life from their income—both for present and future times—than from the sale price alone, they began to hand over the estates and fields they used to sell to the mother churches and live off their income." Thus he spoke. For perhaps at that time the exact payment of tithes <note>The practice of giving a tenth of one's income to the Church.</note> had not yet become common throughout the whole Church, but the

<column-break/>

Other goods are those which later began to be offered to the Church: not only for the support of the building <note>original: "fabricæ." This refers to the physical maintenance and construction of the church structure.</note> or the poor, but as a stipend for some perpetual chaplaincy. Indeed, perhaps precisely for this burden alone: which in collegiate churches are now called **anniversaries**, the foundations of which exist, and in which no mention is made of any burden for either the building or the poor, but only for the perpetual celebration of a memorial mass. Added to these are those goods designated for episcopal sees, namely castles and vassals, of which there will be discussion in Article 5. The third kind of ecclesiastical goods consists of daily pitances <note>Small food allowances or additional gifts for clergy.</note> and offerings, either for the celebration of sacred rites or those made at the foot of the altar. The fourth and most formal kind is the quota of tithes added to the right of the clergy, as is held in the canon *Decimas* (Case 16, Question 1) and in many other places there, and in the *Decretals* under the title "On Tithes" throughout.

# F. D. Soto, On Justice & Right #

...number, that communal life could scarcely be endured. Hence, in the time of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential theologian who championed communal living for his clergy.</note>, the matter was already in dispute and before a judge as to whether priests ought to be ordained unless they were willing to live in common. For as was defined in the first article, their office does not necessarily require it. Certainly, it does not have a vow of poverty attached to it, nor indeed a vow of obedience that one could not fulfill to a bishop while living in his own house. <margin>Augustine.</margin> Whence the same Augustine, as cited in the same Cause 12, question 1, canon "Certè," confesses that he had decided to ordain no cleric except one who wished to remain with him; or if he wished to withdraw from that purpose, he would take away his clerical status. "But behold," he says, "in the sight of God and yours, I change my plan. Those who wish to have something of their own, for whom God and his Church are not enough, let them remain where they wish and where they can; I do not take away their clerical status. I do not wish to have hypocrites," etc. However, when the clergy did not lead a common life with their head <note>Their superior or bishop.</note>, the bishops began to distribute those common goods unfaithfully.

<margin>The division of Church goods was made in the year of our Lord 470.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the Popes, seeing that communal life could not be maintained, having made a partition of the Church’s goods into four portions, assigned each to specific uses. Namely, one to the Bishop, another to the rest of the clergy, a third to the fabric <note>The physical maintenance and needs of the church building.</note> and necessity of the church, and finally a fourth to the poor. This began to happen around the year of our Lord 470, specifically on the borders of the times of Jerome and Augustine. For then sat Pope Simplicius, to whom belongs that canon regarding revenues (12, q. 2), where this division is found. And after twenty years sat Gelasius, to whom belong the canons "Vobis enim" and "Quatuor," by which the same division is confirmed. And later, nearly in the year 600, sat Gregory, to whom belong the canons "Cognovimus" and "Mos," by which the same partition is recounted. I have noted these times so that the opinions of Augustine and Jerome extant on this matter may be understood as referring to that time when they lived in common and all things were under the bishop’s administration.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
¶ With these things considered beforehand, the question is answered with three conclusions. The first is: If there now exist anywhere goods of that kind which the Christian people offered for the support of the poor, it is certain that neither those goods nor their fruits <note>The income or profit generated by the assets.</note> can be entirely usurped by the bishop or the clergy, but by the law of justice they ought to be distributed. If they are not distributed, he who neglects the distribution is bound to restitution. For in the fourth book, we declared, according to the word of Saint

<column-break/>

Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, Secunda Secundae, Question 62, Article 1.</note>, that he who neglects a distribution out of duty immediately becomes guilty of restitution by the law of commutative justice <note>A type of justice governing the balance of exchange between individuals; if you take or keep what belongs to another, you must pay it back.</note>. The same, and indeed more certainly, must be asserted regarding goods that are dedicated to hospitals. And this is one true sense of the fifth conclusion of Saint Thomas. Therefore, if any of these goods are found to have been usurped by a bishop and applied to his own see, there can be no doubt that he is bound to restore them along with their fruits. This judgment, however, goes beyond the limits of the present business. For where the contrary justice is not established, he who possesses in good faith is free from all restitution. Although there is some suspicion that castles, villages, and other possessions of the churches were perhaps granted to the church with some respect for the poor.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion pertains more to the matter: Estates, castles, and all possessions, whether annexed to the episcopal see, a canonical college, or any other ecclesiastical prebend <note>A portion of the church's income granted to a member of the clergy as a stipend.</note>, do not pass into the absolute ownership of the bishop or the priest possessing the prebend; rather, they are only the administrators of those same possessions. <margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin> The conclusion is proved because they can neither sell nor alienate <note>To transfer ownership to someone else.</note> them except with the consent of the bishop and the chapter <note>The governing body of a cathedral or collegiate church.</note>, and those who have an interest—indeed, often only with the approaching consent of the Roman See—and that for the good and the permanence of the Church. This is the sense of the canon of Boniface (12, q. 2): "Let no one be permitted to be ignorant that everything consecrated to the Lord shall be the Holy of Holies to the Lord, and belongs to the right of the priests; because of which everyone who takes it away, wastes it, or invades it from the Lord or the Church shall be inexcusable." And in Cause 12, question 1, canon "Expedit," Prosper says that the resources of the Church are not private but common. Whence in the same cause and question, canon "Multi," and Cause 16, question 1, canon "Possessiones," and throughout the whole question, and in the Decretals <note>The collection of Papal decrees forming part of Canon Law.</note> regarding not alienating church property, their alienation is most strictly guarded against. <margin>Explanation of the next conclusion.</margin> This conclusion is understood regarding any goods whatsoever possessed by the church, whether by reason of an anniversary chaplaincy <note>A fund set up to pay for an annual mass for a deceased person.</note> or any other clerical service. The matter is very clear, and in one sense, the third conclusion of Saint Thomas comes to be understood from these. For regarding the first two, nothing remains to be disputed.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ The third conclusion: Of the fruits arising from possessions which are annexed to the church by reason of some clerical service—namely, an anniversary or chaplaincy—the clerics are truly the owners, each for his own portion; just as they are of the daily pittances <note>Small stipends or allowances for food and basic needs.</note> which are given to them for Masses or...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological investigation into how Church property is owned. Here, the author examines whether individual clerics and bishops truly "own" the property and alms they receive.</meta>

### Book Ten, Question IV. ###

<margin>First reason for the first conclusion.</margin>
...or offered during other divine services. And this will be one sense of the sixth conclusion of Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this text's legal arguments.</note>. I do not know who can deny this conclusion. Indeed, if the poor acquire <term>ownership</term> <note>Latin: *dominium*. In this context, it refers to the legal right to possess and use property as one’s own.</note> of the alms bestowed upon them, there is no reason to doubt that the same happens for alms given to priests, making them the owners. This is especially true because, as has been said, they have taken no vow of poverty. For ownership, as we said in Book 4, is transferred by no title more justly than by the free will of the giver. But he who gives alms for the celebration of a Mass or for the funeral rites of the dead confers them most freely in exchange for that spiritual service; therefore, he establishes the cleric in true ownership. Nor does it matter in any way whether such alms are temporal and daily, or indeed perpetual—namely, the fruits of lands and possessions that are handed over to the clergy for such services without any consideration for the poor or the construction of the church.

<margin>Second reason</margin>
¶ Likewise, the stipends given to civil magistrates for their labors—such as judges and governors, and even indeed to kings and other lords—truly pass into their own ownership. Therefore, the same applies to those things bestowed upon clerics for their services and duties, since they serve the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>Latin: *respublica*. The author views the Church's spiritual work as a vital public service to society.</note> in a much more precious way. 

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But if you argue that spiritual things are not for sale, it has already been answered 

<margin>Solution.</margin>
in the preceding sections that clerics can receive stipends for their own support, and perceive the rights established for them for funeral rites and other offices, and thus acquire ownership of them.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ From these points, a fourth conclusion regarding bishops is gathered. If it is established that the castles and lands they hold (which we will discuss in Article 5) were not awarded to them under the condition that they feed the poor, but absolutely to uphold the honor and authority of their <term>see</term> <note>The "see" refers to the bishop's official seat or jurisdiction.</note>, then even if the donors believed those same bishops would be charitable to the poor, they are nonetheless the true and legitimate owners of the fruits of those same possessions. They do not act against the rigor of justice, however they may spend them. And in this sense, that same sixth conclusion of Saint Thomas is verified.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
And it is proven: because if such possessions were given to them as a gift without any condition or bond of burden—except that they remain in the perpetual possession of those succeeding to the see—there is no reason of justice that prohibits them from being the owners of the annual fruits. ¶ Certainly, I do not know who could object to these things with any firm reason.

<column-break/>

Regarding <term>tithes</term> <note>A "tithe" (decima) was a tenth of one's produce or income given to support the Church.</note>, however, the time periods must be distinguished. For concerning the time when they were held in common, and wherever they are held in that manner today, the Fifth Conclusion is established. 

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
At that time, the bishop did not have such full ownership that he was not bound to distribute a portion to the poor, just as he gave a portion to his clergy and another to the church building. This was the seventh conclusion of the divine Thomas. Nevertheless, it is not without ambiguity whether the entire ownership of tithes was then in the hands of the clergy, or a part was in the hands of the poor. That is: did the poor have as equal a right to their portion as true owners as the clergy did to theirs? Or rather, was the entire ownership with the clergy, though with the burden that they were bound to give a portion to the poor, either by the law of mercy or even by justice? And as far as I can gather, the common opinion tends to hold the first view. This is both because such a great abundance of fruits is not deemed to be assigned to the clergy alone, and because the division that was made later seems to testify that a portion always belonged to the poor. But in truth, upon closer inspection, 

<margin>Ownership of tithes before their partition belongs solely to the clergy.</margin>
the second view is not only much more credible but, as I judge, most certain: namely, that ownership was held only by the clergy.

<margin>First reason for the nearby assertion.</margin>
And the first reason for this is gathered from the previous book. The purpose of tithes was none other than the service of the churches and the administration of the sacred rites and sacraments. For if this were removed—that is, if there were no churches—certainly no tithes would be commanded from the people. 

<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
And that same reason is confirmed by the fact that tithes are demanded from the people of the Gospel for the same reason they were from the Mosaic people. In that case, as is clear from Numbers 18 <note>Referring to the Old Testament book of Numbers, chapter 18, which outlines the support for the Levites and Priests.</note>, they were paid only to the Levites and priests, and for no other reason than for the ministry of the temple. And the Church's quota of tithes was taxed after the likeness of that law: namely, because the ministers of our Church are more excellent than the ancient ones, as Saint Thomas says in 2.2. question 77, article 1 <note>original: "2.2.q.77. artic. 1." The author likely refers to the *Summa Theologiae*, though usually tithes are discussed in question 87.</note>, where he assigns no reason concerning the poor. From this, therefore, it is clearly gathered that the ownership of tithes was even then with the clergy. Unless you say they had no owner except God—which is certainly false, because they are conferred to no one but clerics and for their service. 

<margin>Second reason</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued toward the same point. The right to demand tithes, as is the confession of all, is an ecclesiastical right; therefore, it exists in the hands of priests alone, and not in the hands of the poor. Indeed, as we said above, not even the poor themselves, however destitute, are excused from the payment of tithes. Therefore, no [ownership was] ever...

<summary>This page argues that clergy and bishops hold true legal ownership (dominium) over alms and stipends given for their service, comparing their right to that of civil magistrates. It further asserts that tithes historically belonged to the clergy for the purpose of maintaining divine worship, rather than being legally owned by the poor.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right #
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

...ownership of tithes belonged to the poor.

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
¶ A third invincible argument is added here: If the intention of the Church at that time had been to grant the poor a share in the **ownership** <term>dominium: the legal right to possess, use, and dispose of property</term> of tithes, then surely not only would their specific quota have been marked out for them, but their payment would not have been entrusted to the bishop. On the contrary, the people would have been commanded that each individual should set aside a portion of their tithes to be distributed to the poor. This was the case in the Old Law <note>The laws found in the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament.</note>, as we saw in the previous book, where everyone set aside tithes for strangers. For what need was there to entrust to the bishop that which truly belonged to the poor—namely, that of which they themselves were the owners—so that he might pay it back to them? Did not the Holy Spirit, by whose will the Church was ruled, well know that there would be not so many bishops who would be faithful stewards? Why then would the property of another be entrusted to them?

<margin>Last reason.</margin>
¶ Finally, it is added that the nature of alms is different from that of tithes. For alms, as the word "alms" <note>original: *eleemosyna*, derived from the Greek for "mercy" or "pity."</note> testifies, is entirely based on mercy; whereas the payment of tithes is demanded by justice itself.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From these points, it follows as a consequence that the ownership of tithes has always remained with the clergy, just as in the Old Law it remained with the Levites <note>The priestly tribe of Israel who received tithes because they held no land of their own.</note>. For since our priests are not hindered by any other vow of poverty, nor do they perform lesser labors—indeed, they perform much greater ones if they serve vigilantly—there is no reason why they should not become the owners of their stipends just as the Levites did. However, since the clergy were not very numerous at that time and, living in community, were content with little, it was most equitable that they should support the poor according to their means; and therefore the bishop was bound to make that distribution.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ But the mind is not yet settled as to whether he is bound by law to this distribution: is it by **justice** or by **mercy**?

<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
On one hand, the term "distribution" seems to suggest a law of justice. On the other hand, if ownership remained with the clergy, it does not appear by what justice the goods were owed to the poor, but only by mercy—which usually binds one even under the guilt of mortal sin. Indeed, the law of justice only has a place when you either possess the property of another (as seen in theft) or you received it under the faith that you would return it (as seen in a loan). Neither of these seems to apply in the present case.

<margin>Response.</margin>
It is answered, therefore, that the root of that distribution proceeded from mercy, not from a debt of justice. It is of no small importance to know this, as will become clear in what follows. But nevertheless, because giving alms from what is **superfluous** <term>superfluo: what remains after one’s reasonable needs and status are met</term> is also a precept of mercy, as 

<column-break/>

Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, Second Part of the Second Part (2. 2.), Question 32.</note> is the authority, 
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
and because the quota of tithes at that time appeared to be in surplus for the colleges of clerics, it is believed that a precept was added—as the sacred canons <note>Church laws.</note> seem to teach—that the distribution should be made in that manner, even though no specific quota was designated for the poor at that time. But because the precept was always contained within the limits of mercy, I strongly suspect, and would willingly believe, that the omission of that same distribution at that time did not bind one to **restitution** <term>restitutio: the legal and moral obligation to give back property that was wrongfully taken or withheld</term>. And lest I seem to be the first to assert this, not only does Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a theologian who taught Soto.</note> seem to support it, but also Saint Thomas suggests it to me here. 

<margin>Adrian.</margin>
For when Adrian asserted in his fifth conclusion that where goods are distinct and their own portions have been adjudged to each, if a bishop steals for himself what belongs to another's portion, he not only sins mortally but is bound to restitution. However, in the explanation of the seventh conclusion, which speaks of where goods are *not* distinct, he first says that a small defect does not create guilt; secondly, although he attributes a larger defect to mortal sin, he adds not a single word regarding restitution. Indeed, even if Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas.</note> for some reason turns elsewhere, I would certainly believe that he deliberately remained silent about restitution because, where goods are indistinct, he recognized only a precept of mercy, and not of justice. This is different from where a certain portion has been adjudged to hospitals, or for the building of a church, or otherwise specifically for the poor.

<margin>Sixth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The sixth conclusion, toward which the present discussion was hurrying, is finally established. After the division of ecclesiastical fruits has been made, the bishop is truly the owner of the portion which fell to him; nor does he owe any of it to the poor or to anyone else by any bond of justice. I would not affirm this conclusion with the intent that I believe they are bound to give less in alms than those who hold the opposite opinion, as will be clear in the following article. Rather, I affirm it so that I may discern, to the best of my ability, a legitimate right from that which is not a legitimate right. This must be asserted against two opinions that differ significantly. First, against the first of those cited, Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Hales (c. 1185–1245).</note> and certain jurists, who consider it heretical in law to say that any ownership of ecclesiastical fruits remains with the clergy. Second, against the third opinion of Cajetan, who, moderating the opinion of Saint Thomas, excepts the case where the abundance of tithes is exuberant. And first, that this was the opinion of Saint Thomas is most clearly established from his sixth conclusion, which...

<summary>This page argues that clergy and bishops have true legal ownership (dominium) of tithes and church income, rather than merely acting as trustees for the poor. Soto concludes that the obligation to give to the poor is a moral duty of mercy (charity) rather than a legal debt of justice requiring restitution.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological debate regarding whether bishops possess true ownership of the portions of church revenue assigned to them, or if they are merely stewards for the poor. The previous page argued that the poor do not have a legal right of ownership over tithes, framing the distribution as an act of justice or mercy rather than a transfer of title.</meta>

### Question IV of the Tenth Book ###

...which is almost the same as this opinion of ours; indeed, where he <note>Likely referring to St. Thomas Aquinas</note> says: "Concerning those things which are specifically assigned for the bishop’s use, the same reasoning seems to apply as for his private goods, as we have declared in that place." And as we noted in Article 6, in the solution to the third point, when it was argued that bishops ought to be poor by vow—at least regarding the salaries for their functions—he denied this, and accordingly granted that they have **proper ownership** <term>dominium: the legal right to possess, use, and dispose of property as one's own</term>, which is the opposite of a vow of poverty. Indeed, it is not the authority of St. Thomas alone, although his authority by itself might be enough to persuade one of this opinion.

<margin>First reason against the earlier opinion denying bishops ownership of their portion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, it is first argued against the first opinion (which denies all such ownership) from the very division of the law. For the division of ecclesiastical fruits <note>original: *fructus*; refers to the income or revenue produced by church lands and tithes</note> into four parts can be understood as nothing else than the awarding of ownership to each respective party. Therefore, just as the rest of the clergy has ownership of their share, and the **fabric** <term>fabrica: the fund or assets dedicated to the maintenance and repair of the church building</term> has its share, and the poor have theirs (where it is designated), so too the bishop shall have ownership of his own share. Indeed, no distinction can be devised between them. But the premise is proven: specifically because the Church, as we were saying, found through experience and custom that bishops were breaking faith in the distribution of funds, it took away from them the power of arbitrary distribution. Therefore, so that they would not take more than was just, a portion was assigned to them for their living; and thus it was committed to their own ownership, just as each portion was committed to the others.

<margin>The Gloss.</margin>
The **Gloss** <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, the standard medieval commentary on Canon Law</note> holds this view on the chapter *Duo sunt*, case 12, question 1. And the chapter *Pervenit* (under "on sureties") is relevant here, where it is commanded that the creditors of a cleric be satisfied from the fruits of his benefice; if they were not the owners of those fruits, this would not be commanded.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If ownership of his portion were not ascribed to the bishop through that division, but he were instead bound to distribute it just as he was bound to distribute the whole before, the division would surely be useless. Since, therefore, it was not made in vain, but so that each person’s portion might be certain, it is clearly gathered that the ownership of his lot was applied to him just as the ownership of their lots was applied to the others. Hence, in the cited chapter *Vobis enim* (case 12, question 2), the bishop’s portion is explained in the same words as that of the others. For

<margin>Gelasius.</margin>
**Gelasius** <note>Pope Gelasius I, who established the fourfold division of church revenue in the 5th century</note> says: "Let the prelate take one of the four portions for himself, distribute another to the clergy according to his judgment and choice, a third to the poor, and a fourth to the fabric." What, then, does "let him take for himself" mean, other than that it becomes his? Just as the other portions belong to the others. Hence, later in the course of time, it happened that the distribution was taken away from the bishop entirely, but the fabric takes its part from the general heap, and the clergy takes theirs.

<margin>Third [reason].</margin>
¶ Thirdly, it is argued: In the creation of all magistrates of the commonwealth,

<column-break/>

the rule is always held that just salaries should be distinguished for them, of which they subsequently become the owners. Since, therefore, the office of bishop is surely the most excellent and most necessary among all offices, both civil and ecclesiastical, its condition would be most unjust if a salary were not decreed to the bishop by the same right, of which he would truly be the owner. Nor does it stand in the way that he is the "father of the poor." For this relationship adds an obligation to him (as we will explain in the next article) to be more beneficent and merciful toward the poor from his own substance than secular wealthy men are. For even the wealthy of this world, as Paul says, are bound to be beneficent toward the poor—yet from their own property. Indeed, if we wish to persist in the analogy, a father is also truly the owner of all that he grants to his sons.

<margin>Fourth reason for the same.</margin>
¶ Fourthly, and most forcefully, it is argued: If the opinion of those who entirely deny bishops ownership of ecclesiastical fruits is true, it follows (which they themselves freely admit) that no certain part has been assigned to them, but they are only permitted to live off the fruits according to the requirements of their status. However, whatever remains, they must—by the rigor of justice—bestow upon the needy as if upon the true owners. But this consequence is surely incredible. For suppose that the fourth part of the fruits attributed to a bishop is worth ten thousand ducats. I ask: can he spend the whole sum on his own uses? You grant it, perhaps, where it is necessary for the requirements of his status; but if not, he cannot, except for what is necessary for him. However, it is proven that this solution cannot stand. First, you do not establish a certain rule by which the "decency of status" ought to be judged. For if the rule is the size and majesty of the church, that is certainly not certain; for some churches tend to be of great authority and have a very numerous population, yet are not so rich in temporal revenues, while others of much less authority are far wealthier. Therefore, there is no reason why a bishop who is wealthier cannot maintain a larger household and make greater expenditures. For who could deny that the bishops of Spain can maintain a more splendid household than those of Italy? Seeing as they have churches twice or thrice ten times more opulent. But if the "decency of status" ought to be estimated according to the amount of revenue, that too is surely not a reliable enough rule; for, conversely, a church could be of such small authority that it would not require more in a bishop, even if he were wealthier. But even if this were admitted, nothing certain can be held...

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological investigation into whether bishops and clergy possess full legal ownership (dominium) over the church revenues assigned to them, or if they are merely stewards who must distribute any surplus to the poor as a matter of strict justice. Soto is currently arguing that fixed portions are necessary to prevent legal uncertainty and moral anxiety.</meta>

-># F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law #<-

...size. For who is to measure the expenses that a bishop is permitted to make? Indeed, if you say that this must be left to the judgment of a "prudent and good man," there is a great variety of opinions even among the good and prudent. For example, regarding the **Bishop of Salamanca**, perhaps one prudent person will judge it sufficient for him to spend four thousand **ducats** <note>The ducat was a gold coin used throughout Europe; 4,000 ducats would be a very substantial sum for a Renaissance bishop’s household.</note>; another might grant him six thousand, and another eight. To which of these opinions, then, should the bishop adhere?

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
¶ Moreover—and this is a more evident argument—let us grant that, according to all prudent men, he is allowed to consume eight thousand. If he possesses twelve thousand, it is enough that he pours out four thousand upon the beggars. But perhaps he wishes to live more sparingly and spend only six thousand. In that case, is he bound by **justice** to give those remaining two thousand to the poor? If you answer in the negative, you are already conceding that he has full ownership of the eight thousand ducats deemed necessary for his status. Thus, if he wishes to "cheat his own genius" <note>original: "fraudare genium suum"; a classical idiom meaning to deny oneself pleasures or to live more frugally than one’s means allow</note>, he may spend that remaining portion at his own pleasure, either on his relatives or on other lawful uses, provided there is no scandal. This is exactly what we are striving to prove.

¶ If, however, you answer that as long as he only consumes six thousand, he owes the remaining two to the poor by justice, you must proceed by the same logic to affirm that if he does not wish to spend more than four thousand (being very frugal) out of the eight thousand he could lawfully use, he immediately owes the remaining four to the poor. And if he only wants to spend two, he owes the remaining six. From this it follows that a bishop, in respect to his own goods, would be nothing more than a **guest sitting at another man’s table**, who is only allowed to eat as much as he pleases but may take nothing more away. Truly, I do not know who would concede this as a matter of the rigor of justice. For we are not currently speaking of the duty of **mercy** <note>Soto distinguishes between "Justice" (legal obligation) and "Mercy/Charity" (moral/religious obligation). He argues that while a bishop should be charitable, the law does not strip him of ownership if he is frugal.</note>. Furthermore, if the Church had intended this when it divided the goods into four parts, it would not have displayed that prudence which we are certain it possessed by the instinct of the Holy Spirit; for it would have left the law of justice—which ought to be most firmly established—in a state of ambiguity, namely, dependent on human judgment, which is highly variable.

<margin>Objection of the adversaries.</margin>
¶ But here is the "Achilles" <note>An "Achilles argument" refers to a speaker's strongest or most "unbeatable" point.</note> of our adversaries: The Christian people are bound to nothing more regarding priests than to nourish and sustain them; therefore, provision should only be made for them to take what is necessary, while they should return the rest to the poor.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ But this inference is most fallacious. For even if nothing more is owed to them than sustenance, the principle of prudence required that a **fixed stipend** be designated for them at the

<column-break/>

judgment of the Church for that same sustenance. Furthermore, they should be the **true owners** of this stipend, so that it is neither left to them to take as much as they please, nor, on the other hand, should a restless conscience strike them with fear as to whether they are taking more than is appropriate. This is how matters are handled in a civil republic. Nothing more is owed to public magistrates—namely, senators and judges, or even kings—than sustenance in proportion to the service they render to the state; and yet, fixed and prescribed stipends are decreed for each. Otherwise, it would not be good governance.

<margin>Fifth reason.</margin>
¶ Fifth, it is argued: if all ownership of ecclesiastical fruits is taken away from bishops, by the same reasoning it ought to be taken from the rest of the priests and all the clergy. Surely no one dares to say this. Indeed, **Cajetan** <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Dominican theologian and contemporary of Soto.</note> admits here that the rest of the priests have true ownership and are not bound by justice to distribute their goods. Yet it is clear that the reasoning is the same: there is no reason why a bishop should be in a lowlier or worse condition than the rest of the parish priests and others of various dignities. This is especially true since their "fourth" has been assigned to them just as the others have been assigned theirs.

¶ Likewise, I can hardly grasp the opinion of these opponents. For they say that bishops are not owners of their portion, yet they claim it is enough if they give a fourth part to the poor. What happens, then, in places where the poor already have their own specific fourth share? Indeed, if they do not have it, why is that fourth not cut from the whole pile before the division is made, rather than being taken solely from the bishop's portion? Additionally, they are effectively making him the owner of the other three parts.

<margin>An escape-route for the adversaries.</margin>
¶ But they say: "Perhaps the bishops are believed to have applied the portion of the poor to themselves." But this is not established by any certain reasoning. On the contrary (and I do not believe this is without reason), since that fourth part for the poor did not have its foundation in the justice of **tithes** <term>decimae: a tenth part of agricultural produce or income set aside for the church</term> as we said above, but only in mercy—seeing as the total heap of tithes was considered to be in surplus—it was perhaps changed into other ecclesiastical **benefices**, and thus it disappeared. For this is a primary point to be observed for their understanding: that feeding the poor from tithes is not a matter of divine or natural law, but purely **ecclesiastical positive law** <note>Human-made laws enacted by the Church, which can be changed, unlike natural or divine laws.</note>, and one of mercy; because of this, the Church can vary it. For the poor, by natural and divine law, must be sustained through other means besides tithes. To this conjecture is added the fact that, besides the shares for the bishop, the building maintenance, and the clergy, we see many other portions cut from the heap of tithes; such as the priesthoods which are called **prestimonies** <term>praestimonia: a fund or endowment used to support a priest, often without the obligation of "cure of souls" or local residence</term>. These often constitute a much larger part than what falls to the bishop. For it has frequently been the custom for a third part of the entire heap to be such; of which benefices there remains no memory...

<summary>Soto argues that bishops must have legal ownership (dominium) of their assigned revenue portions to avoid moral uncertainty and ensure stable governance. He contends that supporting the poor via a specific "fourth" of tithes is a flexible church rule of mercy, not a fixed natural law that strips clergy of their property rights.</summary>

# Book Ten, Question IV. #

...memory of why these were established by reason: but it is usually suspected (for there is no certain conjecture) that they were intended for the support of poor students. Indeed, it is not read that these men were bound to do anything else in the church. From this, the conjecture is that the portion for the poor was taken from there. Rather, perhaps even if those **prebends** <note>A prebend was a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church, used as a stipend for a member of the clergy (a canon).</note> were established under the pretext of study, it is not without suspicion that they had no other root than that, as ecclesiastical revenues grew, human ambition panted after them and overcame the **Apostolic See** <note>The Vatican/Papacy.</note> with persistence, so as to cut those prebends from the "trunk" of the **tithes**. Furthermore, now in Spain and other provinces, a good portion is set aside for the kings. Therefore, there is no reason why the whole burden of feeding the poor, as far as the rigor of justice is concerned, should now be thrown upon the bishops. Although they are not to be exonerated from that most sweet and peculiar burden of mercy.

<margin>The last argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, the last argument, which concludes the matter against the opposing opinion, is formed against the **restitution** <note>Restitution is the legal and moral obligation to return something to its rightful owner if it has been taken or withheld unjustly.</note> to which they say bishops are bound if they do not restore whatever remains to them to the poor. For those who say that by the rigor of justice it is owed to the poor as to true owners, are consequently forced to say that those who do otherwise are bound to restitution. However, that this consequence is ineptly and (if I may say so with your kind permission) vainly granted, is argued. Let it be, for example, as we were saying, that the **bishopric of Salamanca** is worth ten thousand **ducats** <note>A significant gold coin; 10,000 ducats was an enormous sum.</note> for the fourth part which perhaps falls to him, of which six thousand are necessary for his support according to his dignity. And suppose that he has withheld from the poor the remaining four thousand that he owed them in the present year, and wasted them on other private uses: then in the following year, from where will he restitute? For he needs six thousand for his support, and the other remaining four thousand belong to the poor: therefore, he has nothing from which to restitute. In short, if whatever overflows for a bishop annually above what is necessary belongs to the poor by the law of justice, from where, I ask, will the bishop restitute what he once took from the poor? Unless perhaps he has other family property: or unless you say he ought to "cheat his own genius" <note>original: "fraudantem genium"; a classical idiom meaning to live more miserably/frugally than one's status requires</note> by cutting from his necessary portion what he owes to the poor: which is not worthy of being granted. Therefore, this opinion seems in no way consistent with reason. ¶ From these things, another question is resolved: namely, whether those to whom the bishop has wrongly given his goods, whether they be relatives or other strangers, are bound to restitution.

<column-break/>

For those who do not make the bishop the owner certainly affirm this: unless they received those things as poor people. However, if bishops are truly owners, as has been proven, although they sin mortally against the precept of mercy by stinginess and excessive parsimony in almsgiving, and waste their goods otherwise, even on bad uses, they truly transfer ownership.

<margin>A bishop is not at all bound to restitute the goods of his portion; nor are those to whom they were granted.</margin>
Wherefore those who receive them are not at all bound to restitution. And **Adrian** <note>Pope Adrian VI (r. 1522–1523), formerly a professor at Louvain and a colleague of Soto’s circle.</note> felt the same before us. And an example is clear. For when someone, neglecting to help someone established in extreme necessity, wastefully bestowed what he was bound to provide him upon another rich person, neither he nor the one who receives it becomes in any way guilty of restitution. ¶ There remains, therefore, to be examined the opinion of **Cajetan** <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a prominent Dominican theologian and commentator on Aquinas.</note> which we said above holds a middle ground. For he uses this distinction: namely, that while episcopal revenues are either thin and only sufficient for the bishop, or moderate so that they are not very abundant, he is not bound by justice to distribute them. But he says it must then be judged concerning these and the prebends of other clergy which are deputed for their support. 

<margin>Cajetan's opinion.</margin>
And so far he seems to hold with **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note>: namely, that the bishops are truly owners of those goods just as of others that are their own. But when such fruits greatly overflow above what is necessary for them, they are bound, he says, to divide even the quota that falls to them into three parts, of which one should be given to the **fabric** <note>The "fabric" refers to the fund for the maintenance and construction of the church building.</note> and another to the poor; for the clergy already have their own. His proof is twofold. First, that it cannot enter the mind of a wise person that such great fruits were assigned to a bishop for his own support: and therefore the fabric and the poor, he says, are not to be cheated of their quota.

<margin>Cajetan's first reason.</margin>
Afterward, the superior reason is that which he touched on in the *Summa Theologiae* (22. q. 77. ar. 1), where he judged that the tenth part of the fruits far exceeds that proportion by which the clergy stand in relation to the Christian people: since they are scarcely a fortieth part of it. But truly, this opinion of Cajetan’s he could not elicit from Saint Thomas; for he, in the sixth conclusion, says simply that regarding those things which are assigned for the bishop's use, the same reasoning seems to apply as for private goods.

<margin>Antoninus.</margin>
And **Saint Antoninus** <note>Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), a Dominican archbishop and famous moral theologian.</note> (Part 3, Title 20, Chapter 8) felt the same simply. Indeed, this opinion of Cajetan is new, having no author besides himself. Since everyone else falls into one of the two extre-

He also critiques Cajetan’s "middle ground" opinion as being a novel departure from the views of Thomas Aquinas and Antoninus of Florence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the refutation of opposing views regarding the bishop's ownership of ecclesiastical revenues. Soto is specifically addressing the nuances of Cardinal Cajetan's position, which attempts to find a middle ground between total ownership and no ownership.</meta>

...simply persist in extremes: namely, either that bishops have no ownership at all, or that they enjoy ownership of their portion in an absolute sense. Furthermore, Cajetan introduces various elements into this opinion. <margin>The first argument against Cajetan.</margin> For first, merely because a bishop's revenues are very abundant, he seems to conclude that the bishop is bound to distribute them to the **fabric** <note>The "fabric" (fabrica) refers to the fund or endowment dedicated to the maintenance and repair of the church building itself.</note> and the poor. However, in the reasoning by which he proves this, he turns in another direction: namely, that the fabric and the poor are not to be defrauded of their parts, clearly implying that the fabric and the poor then had no parts. 

To argue clearly against him, then, let us ask how he understands the bishop's revenues to be "too abundant." For either he means that the bishop's share is greater than a quarter—specifically because the fabric and the poor have no portion, as his reasoning implies—and in that case, the reason compelling him to look after both the fabric and the poor is not that his revenues are overly abundant, but because it is presumed he has unjustly applied the portions of the fabric and the poor to himself. Yet a certain conclusion cannot always be drawn from that. For perhaps the portion for the poor, as we said above, was changed into another **benefice** <note>A church office that provided an income to the holder.</note>; or perhaps the **canons** <note>Clergy members belonging to the staff of a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> snatched it for themselves; or perhaps the fabric and the poor were provided for in another way. 

This, however, is accidental to the point at hand. If, on the other hand, he understands such revenues to be overly abundant not by reason of the division—namely, that he has a larger share than he ought—but because the church itself is "fat" (wealthy), and therefore the bishop's portion grows just as the other portions do; then no reason persuades us that the bishop should be burdened more than the rest of the clergy to provide for the fabric or the poor from his portion by the rigor of justice. For that which is accidental does not change the substance of justice. Moreover, that revenues might be more bountiful in one year and leaner in another, or that one church is wealthier or poorer than another: this could indeed increase or decrease the force of the precept of mercy (if there is more or less surplus), but not by reason of justice. For the Church did not make the division dependent on future variation, but gave the bishop a fourth absolutely, whatever the future outcome might be. Therefore, where the **tithes** <note>The "tithe" (decima) was a ten-percent tax on agricultural produce paid to the church.</note> are wealthier, the bishopric is also wealthier, and the bishop requires more according to his status. Therefore, to respond to Cajetan's prior reasoning, we deny that this cannot be grasped by a wise mind.

<margin>The second argument.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it is argued: If such an overflow of revenues changed the nature of justice, it would follow that even if the poor had their own portion

<column-break/>

and the fabric had its own, the bishop would nonetheless be bound by justice to contribute to them from his own portion. Indeed, if after he had once contributed to them, that which remained was still overflowing, the same law of justice would compel him to give again. Thus, one would fall back into the first opinion, which denies all ownership to the bishop and asserts that whatever remains to him is owed to the poor by justice. Therefore, that middle opinion of Cajetan can certainly be sustained with more difficulty than the first.

¶ Regarding Cajetan's second argument—persisting in the claim that the quota of tithes is excessive compared to the proportion the clergy has to the rest of the people—this has been answered partly in Book 9 under the title *On Tithes*, and partly just now. For I would wish those who hold this opinion to consider that when, among that so numerous a people who constituted a righteous kingdom, there was only one Temple in which neither the **Sacraments** conferring grace were administered, nor the Body and Blood of God adored, and yet a twelfth part of the nation was dedicated to its service, and a tenth part of the fruits was assigned not as relief for the poor, but freely as their stipend; why in our most holy religion—in which there are so many countless temples, and in which God is worshiped so much more excellently—will it be considered an "excess" if there are so many bishops, and they live with such dignity and authority, and so large a clergy is nourished? This clergy is needed not only for administering the Sacraments and the care of souls, but also to serve the churches by their presence and chanting. Take away that majesty of priests in cathedrals and other churches, and those chants which cannot be harmonized without a number of priests, and perceive in your mind what place the Christian religion would hold. 

If such a religious apparatus is necessary, then surely the quota of tithes is not superfluous. This is especially true since, as I was saying just now, such large portions have already been cut away from them for secular titles. I confess, as I said there, that there are the greatest abuses both in the ordination of priests and in the provision of priesthoods and prebends. Nevertheless, if these things were done according to the dignity of the matter and according to divine laws, and the ministers themselves faithfully held their places and were merciful to the poor, there would be no remaining occasion for grumbling against the amount of tithes and certain riches of the churches. ¶ Through these points, the question is also resolved which was once posed to me. For many ecclesiastical goods have been transformed into secular titles, as is evident from the royal "thirds" <note>original: "regijs tertijs"; refers to the *tercias reales*, a portion of the tithe in Spain claimed by the crown.</note>. Indeed, the entire tithes of some churches...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether the revenues of a bishop are legally owed to the poor or if the bishop possesses true ownership of his portion.
