# Question IV of the Tenth Book

<margin>Ecclesiastical goods transferred to a secular title are in no way liable to the poor.</margin>
...as is evident from the property of the Knights Templar and many others which were adjudicated to illustrious lords and are possessed by seculars through the right of succession. It can therefore be doubted whether those goods, by way of justice, are liable to the poor for their portion. But the answer is negative. For the entire right that the poor have to tithes <term>decimas: a tenth part of agricultural produce or income given to the church</term> is positive and ecclesiastical law, over which the Pope can dispense; and therefore, when for some reason he assigns ecclesiastical goods under a secular title, he leaves them free of that obligation.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
<margin>A twofold mode of avarice according to the holy doctors.</margin>
**F**or the solution of the arguments: namely, the authorities of the saints which, I confess, seem to show great force at first glance, it must first be noted that since avarice—as we have said elsewhere—is of two kinds, one being the opposite of justice (which is properly called theft and robbery), and the other being the opposite of liberality, the holy fathers are fond of using a certain *hyperbole*. They use the name of "robbery" <note>original: "rapina"</note> to denote avarice when it is opposed to the liberality and mercy that ought to be exercised toward the poor. They do this because, in cases of necessity, all things are considered common in terms of their use. This applies not only to the clergy but even to the secular people. However, they deservedly lash the clergy more sharply for this, and especially the bishops, as will be seen in the next article, because they are more strictly bound by the precept of almsgiving. Therefore, this kind of "robbery" does not carry with it the bond of restitution <note>Restitution is the legal and moral obligation to return stolen goods; Soto is arguing that failing to give alms is a sin against charity, but not necessarily a legal theft requiring formal "restitution" in the same way.</note>. Likewise, it must be noted that many sayings are found among the holy fathers concerning the state of the clergy living in common, which do not fit the time after the division of property was made; and many other things are merely counsels, even though they are exaggerated with emphasis so that they take the form of commands. ¶ Through these points, then, the arguments are dissolved. For if we begin with the authority of Ambrose, cited at the beginning of the preceding article, and in *distinction 47, canon "Sicut hi,"* which elucidates the matter greatly, where he says: *"Let no one call their own what is common,"* it is manifest that he is not speaking properly about clerics or bishops, but generally, as Saint Thomas says, about the entire Christian family. For he says to every avaricious person: *"Why do you call 'own' those things which you did not bring into this world?"* Thus he adds to everyone: *"Let no one call their own what is common; whatever is held beyond what suffices for one's expenses is obtained by violence."* Jerome says something similar, as reported in *canon 42, "hospitalem."* He says: *"He is convicted of seizing the things of others who is proved to retain more than is necessary."* It was

<column-break/>

indeed the idiom of those saints to consider whatever was superfluous as common, in terms of its use. ¶ Wherefore, that which was cited in the second argument of the same article from the same Jerome on that passage of Isaiah: *"The robbery of the poor is in your house,"* namely, that ecclesiastical goods belong to the poor, he would have said almost the same regarding seculars. For the word of the Prophet is understood to apply to all who withdraw alms when they ought to distribute them. However, there is another gloss which Saint Thomas <margin>*St. Thomas.*</margin> suggests: namely, that under the name of "the poor," not only secular poor people are included, but also the clergy themselves. Thus, just as when the bishops lived in common with their people they could take what was necessary for themselves, so when the division was made—of which Jerome was not speaking—the bishop acquires ownership of his portion, just as the rest of the clergy do of their own shares. ¶ Similarly, we must respond to those objections we raised at the beginning of the present article. To the first, it is replied that the word of the Lord, *"The laborer is worthy of his hire,"* or *"his food,"* does not prevent the bishop from being able to acquire ownership of that portion which is taxed <note>In this context, "taxed" (taxatur) means legally assessed or allocated by church authority.</note> by the judgment of the Church for his sustenance. Moreover, the word of Paul, that *"having food and wherewithal to be covered, let us be content,"* is understood not only of clerics, but universally of all people, including seculars. For he is speaking there against the rich of this world. To the other point, that the Apostles were sent without a pouch, a response has already been given above. ¶ To the second, namely to the authority <margin>To the second.</margin> of Prosper, in *canon "expedit," 12, question 1,* namely, that the resources of the church are not private property but are possessed in common: to this and similar canons of the same case and question, it is replied that this is understood regarding the possessions themselves, which, as has been said, may neither be sold nor alienated except for the good of the church. But if it is understood regarding the fruits <note>In legal terms, "fruits" (fructibus) refers to the income, produce, or profit generated by an asset.</note>, as the *canon "episcopi"* seems to speak—namely, that whatever comes from the provision of the church, whether from fields, or from fruits, or from offerings, all are to be preserved by the right of the church—this must be referred to the time when the clergy lived in common. The canons *"res"* and *"episcopos"* also speak of this. ¶ Regarding <margin>To Augustine.</margin> the saying of Augustine to Count Boniface, cited in *12, question 1, final chapter*: certainly, even if he applies it to ecclesiastics, he feels it pertains almost equally to seculars. For in that letter, he introduces the precepts of mercy...

<summary>Soto explains that while Church Fathers like Jerome and Ambrose used strong language calling wealth "robbery," they were often using moral hyperbole to encourage charity. He argues that once church property was legally divided into portions, bishops gained true ownership of their specific share, distinct from the portion designated for the poor.</summary>

**D. Soto, on Justice & Law**

...commandment, by which individuals who possess their own property ought to make it common in terms of its use. But because he was speaking there against the Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian group in North Africa that clashed with St. Augustine over the purity of the church and the validity of sacraments.</note> who were complaining about being fined of their goods, he says that if they wish to return to the church, all things shall become common to them, even those things which the church possesses privately. Furthermore, what he himself says in the canon on tithes (16. quest. 1) <note>A reference to Gratian’s *Decretum*, the foundational collection of canon law.</note>—namely, that he who does not pay tithes kills the poor—must be referred to the time when life was lived in community. For at that time, both secular poor people and the clergy were sustained by tithes. ¶ The final authority of Jerome to Damasus, which is cited in 16. q. 1. c. *quoniam*, creates a singular problem for legal scholars: whether not only bishops, but other clerics who abound in paternal wealth or goods acquired by other civil rights, may live off ecclesiastical goods. Indeed, Jerome says there that clerics who overflow with secular goods cannot be fed by the goods of the poor. Rather, they commit sacrilege, and through such abuse "eat and drink judgment" upon themselves <note>original: "iudicium manducare & bibere"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 11:29 regarding the unworthy reception of the Eucharist.</note>. A similar sentiment is found in the canons *clericos* and *pastor ecclesiae* (1. q. 2). This is also the fourth doubt in Panormitanus <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer known as Panormitanus because he was the Archbishop of Palermo.</note> in the small book of his questions.

<margin>
Panormitanus.
</margin>

But truly, the question was not worthy of such a long dispute, since the universal practice of the Church has decided it in the affirmative. Moreover, both reason and the canons confirm the same opinion. Indeed, since ecclesiastical prebends <term>prebend: a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a cleric as a stipend</term> are like stipends for ecclesiastical functions, nothing prevents clerics—even if they are able to lead their lives from other sources—from being fed, as Paul says, like the "oxen treading out the grain on the floor" (1 Corinthians 9:9). Hence, in 1. q. 2, from the Council of Agde <note>A local church council held in Gaul in 506 AD.</note>, the canon *clerici* holds without exception that all clerics who serve the church faithfully and vigilantly should receive the stipends due for their holy labors, according to the word of the Apostle: "If he sows spiritual things, it is no great thing if he reaps temporal things" (1 Corinthians 9:11). And the law permits a priest to leave his private property to his heirs if he wishes, and to "live off the Gospel." Indeed, such is the practice. Therefore, bishops ought to record those things which belong to their personal patrimony, as is held in the canons *manifesta* and *sint manifestae* (12. q. 1), where it is permitted that they may leave such things to their kinsmen and relatives if they wish. Added to this is the division made in the chapter *quatuor* regarding revenues, where a fourth part is awarded to the bishop without distinction.

<margin>
Clerics having a suitable living from elsewhere can live off ecclesiastical goods.
</margin>

<margin>
Council of Agde.
</margin>

<margin>
A twofold solution to the citations.
</margin>

¶ Therefore, these cited canons are satisfied by two solutions, though Panormitanus gathers many more.

<margin>
St. Thomas.
</margin>

The first is the one St. Thomas provides in Article 7: namely, that those sayings of Jerome are understood to refer to the extreme necessity of the poor. For since even secular people are then bound to give whatever they can, it is much more just that bishops, abounding in patrimony, should impart ecclesiastical goods to the poor. The other solution is perhaps the one gathered from the said chapter *sacerdos* (1. q. 2) and from the chapter *illi autem* (12. q. 1): namely, that Jerome was speaking about that state of the Church when clerics, living in community, gathered all their goods into one pile. For they were given the option to either leave the goods they had to their parents and relatives and lead their lives from the fruits of the church with the rest of the poor, or, if they preferred, to retain their own goods which would suffice for them—but they would then spare the expense of those things which were possessed in common.

### ARTICLE IV.

->Whether bishops are bound by a singular law, more so than secular rich people, to the aid of alms.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial P containing a landscape illustration with architectural elements.</image-desc>

After having seen to the ownership of ecclesiastical fruits, the fourth article follows concerning the law of alms by which bishops are bound. For it is argued that the clergy are not more strictly bound than seculars; for if they are just as truly the owners of their fruits as seculars are of theirs, there seems to remain no reason that would constrain them more strictly than seculars.

<margin>
First argument.
</margin>

¶ Second: The duty of mercy does not obligate except from what is superfluous, outside of extreme necessity. However, there are many wealthy seculars who have more abundant goods and more that is superfluous to their status than bishops; therefore, bishops are not universally bound by a more rigorous law of alms.

<margin>
Second.
</margin>

¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that bishops are peculiarly the "fathers of the poor." Hence Jerome says to Nepotian, as recorded in 12. quest. 2: "It is the glory of a bishop to provide for the wealth of the poor; it is the shame of a priest to strive for his own riches."

<margin>
Jerome.
</margin>

Hitherto we have spoken concerning the rigor of justice, according to which, as far as we can grasp, we could not judge otherwise than that bishops are the owners of their portion. For on account of no work of mercy must the truth of justice be either denied or hidden; but nonetheless...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Question III regarding the property rights of the clergy. Having established that clerics can possess private property, Soto now moves to Question IV to define the specific moral and legal obligations bishops have toward the poor, distinguishing between the "law of justice" and the "law of mercy."</meta>

# Question IV of the Tenth Book

->As I was saying there, it was not our intention in confirming the truth of this matter to elevate the consciences of bishops and priests to such a degree that they become more malicious or harder of heart toward the poor. Indeed, to express my own judgment on this matter, I would bind them far more urgently—if such authority were granted to me—than many others I have seen who follow the opposing opinion. I have met many who hold that bishops are not "owners" but that whatever overflows from their needs belongs to the poor by right of justice; nonetheless, these same people assert it is enough if they bestow a sixth or a fourth part upon the needy. Indeed, you may hear some who think a prelate possessing a hundred thousand ducats <note>The ducat was a high-value gold coin; 100,000 was an enormous sum, equivalent to the revenue of the wealthiest sees like Toledo.</note> has satisfied his duty if he gives six or ten thousand. This is something I shall certainly never be persuaded of.<-

<margin>The first conclusion.</margin>
The question is therefore answered with three conclusions. The first is inferred from the previous article.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Neither a bishop nor any priest is bound to almsgiving from the portion that falls to him by the law of justice in such a way that, if he omits any, he is held to restitution <term>restitution: the legal and moral obligation to return or compensate for what was unjustly taken or withheld</term>. For if it is true that through the celebrated division of the Church, absolute ownership of their portion was adjudged to them, they are held to almsgiving from that portion by no other law than they are from other goods: as we noted in our sixth conclusion, which we also showed was the opinion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for Soto’s school of thought.</note>. An exception, however, must always be made for cases where there is a strong suspicion that the bishop has applied to himself goods assigned to the "fabric" <note>The "fabric" refers to the fund for the physical maintenance and construction of the church building.</note>, to hospitals, or to the poor by some other means. In such a case, it is certain that he is held to restitution by the law of justice. Outside of such cases, however, they are free from that specific form and bond of distribution which they were bound by while living in community; and thus, they are constrained by no precept of justice.

<margin>The second conclusion.</margin>
The second conclusion. By the mandate of mercy, by which all people are compelled to give alms (as Saint Thomas writes in *Secunda Secundae*, question 32, and as most weighty theologians agree), bishops are bound most strictly of all Christians, and consequently of all mortals. This conclusion is proven on many grounds.

<margin>The first reason for the conclusion.</margin>
First, as I was just saying, because bishops are held to protect widows with favor and help, to be like fathers to orphans, and finally to be a singular defense and refuge for all beggars and the destitute. Indeed, since the cultivation of virtues and the subsequent salvation of souls are frequently endangered by the lack of temporal things—the reason why Solomon feared both an abundance of riches and extreme want <note>original: "rerum inopiam metuebat"; a reference to Proverbs 30:8-9.</note>—and since bishops are the shepherds of souls, they are held not only to feed and advance the flock by word and example, but also to bring assistance to the needy in actual fact. For the respectability of widows and the modesty of virgins are violently buffeted by the lack of household means; and those suffering from hunger are exposed to the dangers of stealing, perjury, deception, and many other such misfortunes. 

<column-break/>

Bishops must watchfully look out for these dangers and provide for them according to their individual means.

<margin>The second reason.</margin>
Secondly, there is the fact that although the division of church goods—whereby each was assigned his own portion—was made because of the declining life of the clergy, bishops nonetheless ought not to strip off that "ancient beauty" of the Church which shone forth in the support of the poor. This was the time when the Apostles, through the ministry of deacons, so diligently took care of widows, orphans, and the indigent. Nor should they entirely erase from memory the fact that ecclesiastical fruits are spiritual, and are spent for the sake of divine worship and specifically in honor of Christ, who so dearly took to heart the commending of the poor to his family, and especially to the shepherds to whom he confidently entrusted that family.

<margin>Third.</margin>
Thirdly, there is the fact that the very source of the precept of mercy—namely, the redundancy and superfluity of things—is, or ought to be, much greater in bishops than in secular people, all other things being equal. For first, they ought to live more frugally, and with much less pomp than the rich of this world. For the splendor and luxury of banquets are not permitted to them, nor other domestic displays. For, as Jerome says, it is right for them to live from the altar, not to live in luxury <note>original: "de altario illis viuere fas est, non luxuriari"; a common medieval legal maxim derived from St. Jerome.</note>. Furthermore, since they lack wives, they are spared the extraordinary expense by which husbands are burdened. And so, since they have no offspring for whom they must establish entails <term>majoricatus: the legal practice of primogeniture, keeping an estate intact for the eldest son</term> or otherwise provide for in perpetuity, they ought to have no other children than the poor; nor should they provide for their kinsmen in any other way than they do for the poor. For a shepherd should not bestow goods on those for whom their own means suffice: as is held in the canon *pastor ecclesiae* (12. question 1).

<margin>Moderation of the previous assertion.</margin>
Although this last point is taught, it must not be understood with the utmost rigor, but must be seasoned with "a grain of salt," that is, with natural equity. For where scandal can be avoided, it should not be considered a total vice if a bishop who is in charge of a wealthy church brings his previously destitute kinsmen to a certain moderate standard of living...

<summary>Domingo Soto argues that while bishops legally own their share of church revenues and aren't strictly required by law to give a specific percentage to the poor, they are morally bound by the "mandate of mercy" to be the most charitable of all people. He emphasizes that because clergy live frugally and have no families to support, their surplus wealth belongs spiritually to the poor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question IV regarding the obligations of bishops toward the poor. Soto is currently addressing whether a bishop can use his ecclesiastical income to provide for his relatives or successors without committing a sin or causing scandal.</meta>

### F. D. Soto, On Justice & Law,

...honorable status: not only for his own lifetime, but for his successors in perpetuity. I do not say this so that he may create wealthy rights of primogeniture <note>The legal right of the eldest son to inherit the entire estate; here, Soto warns against using Church funds to establish dynastic wealth</note>, but so that they might be able to change their status to some extent, so as to lead their lives thereafter without necessity. For if someone who has twenty thousand or more—indeed, even one who has ten or fifteen thousand ducats <note>A gold coin of high value; ten thousand ducats was a massive fortune in the 16th century</note>—expends a fourth part on the poor and for pious uses, he will certainly be judged by everyone to have satisfied his debt. And if he dispenses a third for such uses, nothing more will be desired from him, as far as the matter pertains to avoiding fault. Since, therefore, he can lawfully consume the remainder on his own uses without any scandal, why shall it not be permitted to him to take just a little every year from the remaining expenses so that he can leave an honorable and perpetual support to some relative? But I confess that scandal must always be carefully avoided. This will certainly be avoided when the subjects see the Prelate pouring out ample alms according to his means, and cutting what he gives to his relative out of his own personal expenses; and truly, not enriching him to such an extent that he raises him from a very humble status to an illustrious one. I have said this, therefore, not because I wish to indulge the proud and ambitious, but so that I may not deny what the truth of the matter offers me.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ **The third conclusion.** This precept of almsgiving by which bishops are bound cannot be estimated universally according to a fourth or fifth, or some other larger or smaller portion; rather, it must be estimated according to the judgment of prudent men, having weighed both the quantity of the revenues and the indigence of the poor, as well as the calamity of the times.

<margin>The conclusion is explained.</margin>
The conclusion will become clear to all who have scrutinized the reasoning behind the precept of mercy. For it is intended that alms be given from what is "superfluous" <term>superfluous: in scholastic theology, the "superfluum" is income that remains after one's necessary living expenses and the requirements of one's social station are met</term>; however, the "superfluous" must be estimated with respect to the status of both the possessor and the needy. For example: there are Italian bishops who, since they do not have tithes <note>The "decima" or tenth of agricultural produce traditionally given to the church</note>, scarcely have enough to live on. Therefore, no scruple, or a very small one, should be cast upon them if they do not give alms. Indeed, besides those, there are also some who, although they enjoy tithes, their revenues are so thin and meager that if they return a sixth or even a smaller part to the poor, they should be judged to have done enough. However, those who have two or three thousand ducats, and more, certainly ought not to think

<column-break/>

that they have abundantly fulfilled the precept unless they distribute either a fifth or at least a sixth part. Furthermore, those whose incomes exceed twenty or thirty thousand ought certainly to bestow a larger portion. These things are said by way of example; for, as I was saying, the calamity of the times and the number of the poor can increase the rigor of the precept. Moreover, what has been said concerning bishops should be understood in its own degree concerning the rest of the priests: and especially concerning those upon whom the care of souls is incumbent; and even concerning the monasteries of religious orders where revenues are redundant.

¶ Therefore, bishops ought not to quiet their consciences more securely if they are negligent in bestowing alms simply because they are not bound by the bond of justice to restitution; thinking they will do enough if, at the point of death, they wash away such faults through the sacrament of penance. For since even the precept of mercy, of which we spoke before, binds under the penalty of mortal sin, they ought to be sufficiently terrified by that to keep their faith to God unimpaired. Furthermore, although the law of justice does not bind them to restitution, their confessors—both during their life and at the point of death—ought certainly to impose the most generous alms as a form of sacramental satisfaction upon those they know to have been negligent toward the poor, so that the matter ends up almost the same as if they were bound to restitution by the law of justice.

<margin>The manner of almsgiving most pleasing to Christ.</margin>
¶ Now, the manner of almsgiving most pleasing to Christ is that the rich be kind to the poor who are present. Indeed, I would not deny that where hospitals have not been built, it is laudable for a bishop to devote himself to their construction, and even to repair the ruins of churches. Nevertheless, to spend on enlarging and adorning buildings so that his name might be celebrated forever—funds which could have succored the present poor lest they perish of hunger—is not only vain, but truly ruinous and most ungrateful to Christ. For when He says, *You will always have the poor with you* <note>original: "Pauperes semper habebitis vobiscum," quoting Matthew 26:11</note>, He presents this as a warning to our ears so that the care of those poor who are with us might weigh upon us; for God will provide for future wretches through future merciful people.

¶ And from these points, the solution to the arguments proposed at the head of the question is gathered. For to the first, the answer is that although bishops are no more bound by the law of justice than secular rich men, they are nonetheless held by a stricter bond of mercy.

<summary>Soto argues that bishops must give alms based on their total wealth and the local level of poverty rather than a fixed percentage. He emphasizes that while neglecting the poor may not legally require "restitution," it remains a mortal sin, and funds should be used for the immediate needs of the living poor rather than grand architectural projects.</summary>

<header>Question IV of the Tenth Book</header>

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
Regarding the second argument, the response is that although it can happen that a layman, due to an excessive abundance of riches, might be more urgently bound to give alms than a bishop; nevertheless, all other things being equal, bishops are more strictly and vehemently bound by reason of their status. <note>original: "exuberantia vrgentiùs ad eleemosynas obligetur... ratione sui status pressiùs." Soto argues that while a very rich layperson has a moral duty to give, a bishop’s very identity is tied to being a steward of the poor.</note>

### ARTICLE V.

*Whether it is fitting for the ecclesiastical state to have, among other possessions, castles, vassals, and civil jurisdiction.*

<image-desc>Large decorative initial letter Q featuring ornate vine and foliage patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>

SINCE in Article 3, among other ecclesiastical goods, we mentioned towns, it would not be out of place to apply this fifth article to this kind of possession. For it appears to be least fitting for ecclesiastical Prelates and other dignitaries to possess castles and towns, or to have vassals to be governed by civil jurisdiction. <term>Civil jurisdiction</term> <note>The legal authority to preside over non-religious matters, such as criminal trials, taxes, and property disputes.</note>

<margin>The first argument.</margin>
First, because the ecclesiastical state is spiritual, and thus entirely dedicated to the service of Christ; the civil state, however, is entirely secular and placed in temporal matters, where a great deal of iniquity is mixed in. Therefore, they seem to differ as much as light and darkness.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
For Paul says in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 6: "What participation has justice with iniquity? Or what society has light with darkness? Or what agreement has Christ with Belial?" <note>original: "Quæ participatio iustitiæ cū iniquitate?" Paul’s rhetorical questions were frequently used to argue for the separation of sacred and worldly duties.</note>

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second, the ecclesiastical order is placed chiefly in withdrawal and the silence of contemplation; the civil order, however, is exposed to lawsuits, frauds, and other such whirlwinds of business, by which it is necessary that the minds of Prelates be frequently disturbed from their own quiet. This is especially so because "causes of blood" <note>original: "causæ sanguinis." These are legal cases involving the death penalty or physical mutilation; canon law strictly forbade clergy from participating in judgments that shed blood.</note> are conducted in that court, from which every cleric is prohibited lest he stain himself with blood; therefore, it is not fitting for them to preside over such turbulent matters, but rather to set them all aside.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ The third argument is taken from the ancient custom of the Old Law. For no portion of possessions was assigned to the Levites, but only the support of tithes. <note>The Levites were the priestly tribe of Israel who, according to the Bible, did not receive an inheritance of land like the other tribes, but lived off the offerings of the people.</note>

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
¶ But a fourth argument is also applied from the example of Christ. For, as we said in Book 4 under the title of "On Lordship," and as we demonstrated more extensively upon the first chapter of Matthew, He himself accepted no secular kingdom of this world, but was only the King of the kingdom of heaven. Regarding temporal things, He was content with precisely that power—insofar as He was man—that was directed

<column-break/>

toward the end of redemption, so that when there was need for any temporal things for that same end, He might use them. This is what He indicated there, where He said: "My kingdom is not of this world." And in Luke chapter 12, when asked to judge between a man and his brother, He responded: "Who appointed me a judge or a divider over you?" And often elsewhere: therefore, civil jurisdiction does not befit His ministers either.

<margin>Argument 5.</margin>
¶ Fifth: This kind of jurisdiction and secular power over vassals drives bishops toward proud disdain and worldly excellence, which are diametrically opposed to the humility and modesty in which Christ instructed them, according to His admonition in Matthew 20: "You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them: and those who are greater exercise power over them. It shall not be so among you: but whoever wishes to become greater among you, let him be your minister: and whoever wishes to be first among you, shall be your servant: just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve." Therefore, it is not honorable for ecclesiastical dignitaries, but rather highly dishonorable to shine with such secular jurisdictions; and it seems much less fitting for religious monasteries, through whose entrance the world is renounced and all secular pomps are left behind.

<margin>Argument 6.</margin>
¶ Sixth and finally, it is argued: Those citizens ought to be committed to leaders in civil and criminal cases by whom they may be more decently governed. However, secular people cannot be duly and rightly governed in such cases by ecclesiastics. This is both because it does not befit them to be steeped in civil laws, and especially because they do not carry the authority to be a terror to subjects, which is very necessary for restraining human audacity. Indeed, it seems they would preside over civil matters so precariously that subjects, despising them, would hand over their cases to the royal courts. For this reason, Paul warns us in the letter to Timothy that no one soldiering for God should entangle himself in secular business.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
And Christ was content with "two swords" <note>The "Two Swords" theory argued that God gave two types of power—spiritual and temporal—to the world, but they should be held by different hands to ensure peace and order.</note> which should be distinct: and just as in heaven, so also on earth He willed there to be two lights: namely, the sacred authority of the Pontiffs, and the royal power: as is held in Decree 96, canon *Duo*. Therefore, it is not expedient for civil jurisdiction to be mixed with ecclesiastical.

<margin>Sylvester. Constantine.</margin>
¶ To the contrary is the use of Christians, most approved from the age of Sylvester and Constantine <note>A reference to Pope Sylvester I and Emperor Constantine the Great; the Church traditionally claimed its land and power originated from Constantine's grants to Sylvester.</note> by the most holy fathers and orthodox Emperors and kings, through which it is established that not only the primary see of the Church, but also other lower sees, were endowed in this way—

<sig>Iii 5</sig>
<meta>catchword: were endowed—</meta>

<summary>Soto begins exploring whether the Church should hold secular power and land, presenting six arguments against the practice based on Christ's humility, the separation of spiritual and worldly duties, and the prohibition of clerics judging "causes of blood."</summary>
<keywords>civil jurisdiction, ecclesiastical state, two swords, Constantine, Sylvester, Levites, causes of blood, temporal power, poverty, humility</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Article V of Question IV, which asks whether the Church should possess secular power and feudal territories. The previous page established that while the Church is primarily a spiritual institution, it does indeed possess towns and jurisdictions. This page explores the historical and theological justifications for these temporal holdings.</meta>

<page-num>866</page-num>
<header>F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,</header>

...adorned with endowments: in which very many vassals are held, subject not only to bishops, but even to the abbots of monasteries.

<margin>Two parts of the question.</margin>
We have decided to attach this question here, not only because the present treatment required it, but because it is being debated in these very days. There are, however, two parts to this same question. First, whether it is fitting for the decorum of the church to exercise this kind of civil authority. Second, whether, on account of some emerging necessity of the ecclesiastical or civil republic, it is expedient to sell these same castles and vassals to secular persons. Regarding the second part, I have decided not to involve myself much in the discussion: for since it is a matter pertaining to the Supreme Pontiff and the Emperor, it is not my place to answer unless asked.

<margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to the first part of the question, a single affirmative conclusion is given in our usual manner. It was consistent with ecclesiastical authority to be distinguished among other endowments of temporal things with this as well: namely, to have under its own dominion castles—indeed even cities—with the power of <term>both swords</term> <note>The "Doctrine of the Two Swords" refers to the medieval belief that God gave two types of power: the spiritual sword (held by the Church) and the temporal sword (held by the State).</note>.

<margin>The proof.</margin>
This conclusion is most strongly proved by the fact that the most Christian Emperors, in the time of the most holy Popes, honored the church with such endowments. In the first place, Constantine the Great, that greatest worshipper and supporter of the Christian religion, among other privileges with which he enriched the church, also increased it with this authority, so that he granted Rome along with other cities to the Apostolic See <note>original: "Romam cum alijs vrbibus Apostolicę sedi donauerit." This refers to the "Donation of Constantine," a document later proven to be a forgery, though Soto accepts it here as historical fact.</note>. And later Theodosius in the time of Ambrose, and many other Catholic Emperors thereafter, enriched the church with donations of that kind; which they certainly would not have offered, nor would those holy bishops have accepted, unless it were considered a holy thing. To this is added that, as the Annals of our own land <note>Refers to the histories of Spain.</note> hand down, the Christian kings of the Spains, when they were driving the <term>Moors</term> <note>A term used by European Christians to refer to the Muslim populations of the Iberian Peninsula and North Africa.</note> out of the province through wars, offered to the church—in exchange for the victories granted to them—the same castles and wealth which they snatched from the hands of the enemy. They did this not only by enlarging episcopal sees in that manner, but also by founding and enriching monasteries of both sexes. Therefore, what those lovers of Christ did ought to be defended by every reason rather than condemned by any pact.

<margin>The reason why Christian Princes formerly [endowed] the church...</margin>
¶ Therefore, the reason which those founders of churches kept in their minds was this: that since all temporal things were created for the sake of spiritual things and for their service, and since men (such is our nature) are most greatly moved by the splendor of such things—for our knowledge, as nature teaches, begins from the senses—they judged it worthwhile not only to establish the church with holy laws, but also to equip and support it with a wealth of resources. In this way, by representing majesty to the Christian people, the church would be held in greater value and veneration. For the same reason, so that noble and illustrious men might be initiated into the sacred rites to be the mainstay of the church, the laws permit that they may hold two <term>benefices</term> <note>A church office, such as a parish or bishopric, that provides an income to the holder.</note>; as is held in the chapter *de multa* regarding prebends.

<column-break/>

<margin>...so that they enriched so many with wealth.</margin>
¶ Indeed, I am not unaware that someone could immediately hurl arguments against this opinion. First, against the aforementioned assertion, from the example of the Apostles and the ancient prelates, who drove away such pomp on account of their excessive humility.

<margin>The second [objection].</margin>
Second, from absurdity: for it has been discovered by use and experience that these kinds of secular possessions of bishops have brought many disadvantages: namely, not only wars and the need for their defense, but even the disturbances of heresies and the assaults of rebellions. For against the church of Germany and of England, this is even placed as a cause of the disturbed state of affairs: that neither the secular princes could bear the power of the bishops with an easy mind, nor the common people the riches of the monasteries. Indeed, we see that the religious orders themselves are most greatly undermined by the fact that they abound even in moderate riches.

<margin>To the first objection.</margin>
¶ To the first, however, it is answered, as I said in Book 9 under the title *On Tithes*, that if all bishops and prelates of the church were like Peter, or like Augustine, or Martin, or Nicholas—so that they could win favor and reverence from the Christian people by their own holiness—perhaps there would be no need for the church to be supported by temporal aids of this kind. But nevertheless, because it is not possible for such a great multitude of bishops and priests as is necessary for the church to be so outstanding in religion, it was advised in another way, so that the reputation of the church might be preserved: and that there might be those who, in some measure, are encouraged toward the cultivation of virtues and letters by respect for these things.

<margin>To the second [objection].</margin>
¶ To the second, however, we respond, as we are often accustomed to do, that no reason or prudence can so providently heal human morals that the iniquity of the times does not corrupt everything. For it cannot be denied that the riches of the churches stir up many dangers for spiritual matters; but perhaps poverty would create greater ones—unless (which is impossible) the priests and all the people were holy.

Soto argues that such wealth is necessary to maintain the Church's majesty and respect among common people, despite the risks of corruption or secular conflict.</summary>

Relying on this confidence, ancient kings committed such jurisdictions to them: namely, because they surely hoped that they would treat their subjects as fathers treat sons. Therefore, citizens thought themselves to be faring excellently when they were subject to the jurisdiction of the church. And in truth—if I may say so without causing offense <note>original: "ut absit invidia verbo"</note>—unless the ecclesiastical lord is very corrupt, we have learned by experience that subjects of the clergy are oppressed by much smaller exactions <note>Taxes or forced payments.</note> than those of secular lords. <page-num>868</page-num>
<header>F. D. Soto, on Justice and Law,</header>

One must say that anyone who claims ecclesiastical possessions were either given to the Church against divine law or are not entirely consistent with reason and religion is in error. This will become clearer through the solutions to the arguments.

¶ If these things are true, as the case stands, one must pay close attention and apply Christian considerations before ecclesiastical sees and sacred colleges are uprooted from such possessions. For nothing should be muttered against kings, for it is not believable that they would seek anything from the Apostolic See <note>The office of the Pope</note> that carries even a hint of wrongdoing unless they were constrained by extreme necessity; nor against the Supreme Pontiff, for it is unthinkable that he would grant anything except by mature counsel. Nevertheless, the matter is of such great importance that it should not be decided until many considerations have first been taken into account. We admit, indeed, that disastrous times can create such dangers for the Christian commonwealth that subsidies must be sought even from ecclesiastical revenues by Apostolic authority to repel them. But before these kinds of church endowments are distributed among laypeople, it must first be investigated with the utmost good faith whether the cause is truly necessary. Then, one must watchfully consider whether the church is in any way tarnished or suffers any loss of honor; for if that is the case, all temporal things must be set aside—especially in these times when heretics strive by words and deeds to strip the church of its endowments and thus obscure it through poverty. For if the actions of Catholics align with the attempts of heretics, we will seem to approve of their dogmas. Next, it must also be carefully considered whether the Royal Majesty and the civil commonwealth derive a greater benefit from it; for if what is taken from the churches were to accrue to the king or the commonwealth, the reasoning for such a sale might gain some strength. However, since these possessions are transferred to other secular lords, it must be seen whether this is more advantageous to the king. Especially since those prices refunded to the churches are subtracted from royal possessions, but it is the great lords <note>original: "magnates"</note> who grow fat by that reasoning. Third, it must also be weighed out of charity whether such sales are in the interest of the subjects: namely, whether it is believable that they will be treated with as much benevolence and charity by secular owners as they are supported by the churches. And fourth, it must be weighed with no less counsel

<column-break/>

that while the Pope is the father of the churches and kings are their patrons, although they can request subsidies from the clergy, this will only be lawful when secular taxes <note>original: "tributa"</note> are not sufficient. For those who are exempt from the exaction of taxes, whether by reason of blood or other privileges, must be kept immune above all others. Beyond all this, when it becomes necessary to turn to the clergy, such a subsidy ought to be demanded from all with an even scale. Hence, if those who have vassals are burdened more than others for that reason, no equity can support it; for since vassals are valued at no small price, the law of justice does not seem to permit tearing them away from their lords without a fair price being paid for them, but rather by a precise compensation of revenues. In short, the holy canons <note>Church laws</note> must be consulted, which, as we said above, forbid such alienations in every way. For <margin>Boniface.</margin> Boniface says in Case 12, Question 2: "Let no one be permitted to be ignorant that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether it be a man, an animal, a field, or whatever has once been consecrated—is the holy of holies to the Lord." And therefore, he who seizes or invades it is inexcusable: namely, because it is consecrated not only to men, but to God himself. For this reason, <margin>Gregory.</margin> Gregory, in the following chapter, wishes that person to be subject to excommunication who possesses any such thing even by the king's grant. And <margin>Nicholas.</margin> Pope Nicholas most holily provided the same in the canon *Concerning property* <note>original: "de rebus"</note> in the same case and question: namely, that if things once contributed and dedicated to God are later invaded and plundered under the pretext of princes, the possessor shall be restrained by the punishment of excommunication until they make amends. There is no doubt that the most holy Pope and every most just king will meditate long and hard on these things before stripping the church of such ancient and holy rights; fearing, among other vengeances of God, this one as well: that God might permit them to be uprooted from their own positions. For if kings of old considered these the vows of their victories—so that they might both return thanks to God and hold in gratitude the ecclesiastical order that poured out prayers for them—it is to be feared that if churches are deprived of that same honor and possession of property, the prayers of private individuals will grow cold, and the victories of kings will not be so frequent.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**T**O the first argument, therefore, it is responded that although the ecclesiastical order is spiritual, and in this respect distinct from the civil and temporal commonwealth: nevertheless, no contradiction arises therefrom...

<page-num>869</page-num>
<header>Book Ten, Question 5.</header>

[...no difficulty] emerges to prevent an ecclesiastical prelate <note>a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</note> from presiding over citizens in a civil manner. For the virtue of justice is not so distant from spiritual matters that it does not receive strength and splendor from them. Nor does the passage from Paul cited here apply; it refers to the interaction of the faithful with unbelievers. For he says, "Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has justice with lawlessness?" <note>original: "Nolite iugum ducere cū infidelibus. Quæ enim participatio iustitiæ cum iniquitate?" - 2 Corinthians 6:14</note> from which he concludes, "Or what part does a believer have with an unbeliever?"

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
¶ Similarly, it is answered to the second point that although the episcopal dignity <note>the office of a bishop</note> should be dedicated as much as possible to contemplation, a bishop can nonetheless appoint men of proven life and learning to hear secular cases, who may frequently report back to him. For a bishop must play the part of both Mary and Martha <note>In the Gospel of Luke, Mary represents the life of prayer and contemplation, while Martha represents the life of active service; a bishop is expected to balance both.</note>. He can accomplish this without having to pronounce a sentence of blood <note>a death sentence</note> himself.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
¶ To the third, it is answered that a different reasoning is recognized between our law and the Mosaic law <note>The religious laws of the Old Testament</note>. Indeed, when God gave that land to the people, He wanted the tribe of Levi—so that they might be entirely dedicated to the temple—to be relieved from the business of agriculture; for this reason, no portion of land was assigned to them. In our law, however, besides tithes, Christians can donate their own goods to the church. And regarding jurisdiction, priests were not forbidden from holding it. Indeed, the governance of the people remained in the hands of priests for a long time: because that priesthood did not have that level of spirituality attached to it which ours does.

<margin>To the fourth argument.</margin>
¶ The fourth argument, taken from the example of Christ, carries greater weight: namely, that He did not accept a civil kingdom of the world. Nonetheless, it is answered that only this much is gathered from it: that spiritual power does not consist in the civil administration of a republic. However, it is not subsequently forbidden for ecclesiastical prelates to have such jurisdictions attached to their seats of authority.

<margin>To the fifth argument.</margin>
¶ To the fifth, it is answered that although a precipice toward pride may lie open to some extent for those with such power, the matter must be judged by its own nature. For the nature and condition of those who hold ecclesiastical dignity, as we said above, is a state of perfection. And therefore they ought to possess all these fleeting and slippery secular things in such a way that they can overcome all the dangers sprouting from them.

<margin>To the confirmation.</margin>
¶ Regarding what is added about the monasteries of religious orders, to which such pomp appears less fitting, it is answered first that monastic orders,

<column-break/>

which are not allowed to leave their enclosures to beg, must abound in greater wealth, lest poverty disturb them from their quiet contemplation. For those religious institutions have always been extremely useful to the church; if they maintain their proper decorum, they are to be nurtured with the greatest favor. And among other reasons why towns with jurisdiction were offered to them, it is believed to have been so that they could collect their revenues more easily and quietly. Truly, it is not contrary to their purpose to govern suitable ministers as vassals <note>individuals who held land and owed service to a lord—in this case, the monastery</note>. Many laws speak on this matter.

<margin>To the sixth argument.</margin>
¶ Finally, responding to the sixth and last point, which seems to press the matter more strictly, we admit that churchmen are by no means able to rule and govern their vassals except by royal favor. For if the king, in whom the supreme power resides, does not favor the jurisdictions inferior to his own, they must all collapse. But if this argument had any weight, it would prove with equal force that it is not even fitting for bishops to have ecclesiastical jurisdictions: because unless they are supported by royal authority, it would be better for them to be removed. However, if the king were to cherish the tribunals of the churchmen—whether civil or ecclesiastical—just like all others, as if they were his own and granted by his predecessors, the churchmen would govern their subjects with no less decency and authority than secular lords. For in both orders, there are those who administer their offices well and those who do so poorly.

## QUESTION FIVE,
## On the Obligatory Office of the Clergy.

### ARTICLE I.

->*Whether among the duties of those who are initiated into sacred orders, a particular one to which all are generally bound is to recite the prescribed Psalms at set hours.*<- <note>This refers to the "Divine Office" or "Liturgy of the Hours," the daily cycle of prayer required of clergy.</note>

### F. Domingo de Soto, On Justice and Law

...we grant. For it appears that the clergy, nor those who are in holy orders, are least of all held to fulfill the fixed hours. 
<margin>First argument.</margin> 
Truly, since the payment of the canonical hours is deemed too heavy a yoke, it does not appear that it should be lawfully imposed by the church upon the entire clergy: unless one had first read such an institution by Christ or the Apostles in the sacred pages; which, however, is found nowhere therein. Indeed, Christ, in Matthew 6, taught us no other prayer than the **Our Father** <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>. Therefore, clerics are not held to pay the Canonical hours.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin> 
¶ Secondly, it is argued: Prayer serves this purpose, that the mind may be raised to God, and that we may open our desires to God, which He may fill by the bounty of His mercy. For this, however, there is no need for a voice, since our hearts are open to God. Therefore, there is no need for vocal prayer. But it is enough, as Christ taught in John 4, to worship God in spirit and truth. And as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 14: To pray with the spirit, and to pray also with the mind.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin> 
¶ Thirdly: Clerics, at least those upon whom the care of souls is incumbent <note>referring to parish priests or bishops with pastoral duties</note>, are instituted for this duty especially: that they may administer the sacraments to the people, feed them with the word and doctrine, and govern and moderate them with prudence. Therefore, at least for them, there is no reason why they should be obliged to fulfill other Psalms.

<margin>Council of Agde.</margin> 
¶ To the contrary is the text of the Council of Agde <note>A church council held in 506 AD in Gaul</note>, regarding the celebration of Masses, the chapter "Presbyter," where all priests are commanded that, having completed the morning matinal office, they should fulfill the task of their service, namely: Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, and Vespers. And finally, afterward, Compline is added: so that according to the word of the Prophet, "Seven times a day let us say praises to God" <note>A reference to Psalm 119:164: "Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous laws."</note>.

->**The title of the question is made clear.**<-

Since there are many services and duties by which the clergy earn their stipends—such as administering sacraments, preaching, visiting, judging, and others of that kind—concerning those, as they present no difficulty to the present matter but require other places in which they may be discussed, I do not intend to speak at present. For it would be a work drawn out into immensity. But I speak only of the payment of the Psalms, which they call the **Canonical Hours** <term>Canonical Hours: the specific times of day set aside for the "Divine Office," a structured sequence of prayers and readings required of those in holy orders</term>. This obligation indeed encompasses the entire clergy acting in holy orders. By the omission of which, the ownership of ecclesiastical revenues is lost, in a manner to be explained below, concerning which it was disputed in the preceding question. The affirmative truth of this question must be asserted both against heretics and discussed for the sake of Catholics.

<column-break/>

Never, indeed, from the beginnings of the nascent Church, have heretics been-lacking who have shaken this sacrosanct institution and contended to demolish it. Indeed, there was a very ancient heresy with which the **Pelagians** <note>Followers of Pelagius (c. 354–418 AD), who emphasized human effort over divine grace</note> were infected, as **Augustine** reports in his book *On Heresies*, chapter 88; they destroyed ecclesiastical prayers. Indeed, they denied all necessity of praying, but thought it sufficient to lead a good life: because they did not refer the grace they received to God, but attributed it to their own strengths. 

<margin>Wycliffe. Thomas Walden.</margin>
And **Wycliffe** <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), an English reformer who challenged many Catholic doctrines</note> maintained the same heresy, as **Thomas Walden** <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1370–1430), a leading opponent of Wycliffe</note> reports in the beginning of the fifth volume on sacramentals, saying that a good life is enough. Moreover, the first who cast the seed of that heresy into the world was that famous **Nimrod**, of whom it is reported in Genesis 10. For concerning him and his followers, it is read in Ecclesiasticus 16: "The ancient giants did not seek pardon for their sins, who were destroyed, trusting in their own strength." 

<margin>Josephus.</margin>
Concerning this Nimrod, **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian</note> also says thus in Book 1 of his *Antiquities*: "Since he was more audacious and strongest of hand, he persuaded his people not to ascribe to God that happiness came to men through Him, but that this was provided to them by their own virtue." For since the force of prayer relies on the fact that nothing of good can come to us except from God, those who deny the necessity of divine help can acknowledge no religion in prayer. 

¶ But indeed, it is not the present purpose to dispute concerning prayer in general, insofar as it is a common name for private, solemn, and public prayers. For this belongs to another place. I speak only of those public prayers which the Church commands the clergy to fulfill. For he who denies the religion of praying to God is not worthy to be numbered among rational creatures. For he is ignorant not only of human nature, which is utterly dependent upon God, but also takes away from the divine its own glory; indeed, he contends that God Himself is removed from things. 

<margin>The first virtue of prayer.</margin>
For the first and supreme virtue of prayer is not to be estimated with respect to us: namely, that through it we pray for and obtain all good things for ourselves, both temporary and eternal; but with respect to God: namely, that through it we confess and profess that the perennial fountain of all good exists in God: as He who is the substance of all goodness, upon whose nod all things depend which exist outside of Himself. For he who approaches to pray to God ought to establish this confession as the first head of prayer. Which indeed is the greatest of all things that can be most pleasing to God.

### Book Ten: Question V.

...by which the greatest benevolence is sought from Him. Hence, the reason He so strongly demands that we ask something of Him, and that Christ so thirstily desires that we request whatever we need in His name, is not so much for our own benefit as for His own glory. For this reason, in John 16, He complains somewhat, saying: *Until now you have asked for nothing in my name: ask and you shall receive.* <note>John 16:24</note> It is as if He were saying, "You have not yet granted me that glory which is owed to me by everyone as the true God."

<margin>A good life cannot exist without prayer.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the response to the Pelagians <note>A group following the teachings of Pelagius, who emphasized human effort over divine grace</note> and the Wycliffites <note>Followers of John Wycliffe, a 14th-century English reformer</note> is that not only is a good life without prayer insufficient, but it cannot even exist. For a good life that is pleasing to God proceeds supernaturally from His grace and favor alone, which we indeed obtain through prayer. But because these men deny that such supernatural help is necessary, relying instead on their own strength, they remain ignorant of the power of prayer and trust in their own merits. Regarding these men, I would say that by denying prayer, they either completely remove divine Providence from the world or believe that everything happens by necessity; therefore, they are not worthy of being drawn into any dispute.

<margin>Twofold prayer.</margin>
¶ Returning then to the present matter, since prayer is twofold: one is private, to which everyone is bound by that precept, *Ask and you shall receive*; and the other is public, which is performed by the ministers of the Church. Our present inquiry does not concern the former, but specifically this latter type.

<margin>Wycliffe’s motive for abolishing public prayer.</margin>
As Thomas Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden, an English theologian who wrote against Wycliffe</note> reports in the same place, Wycliffe rejected this public prayer because he held it as a most holy foundation (as we indicated in the first argument, which is his) that absolutely nothing should be permitted among ecclesiastical ceremonies that is not explicitly expressed in the Sacred Scriptures <note>original: "sacra pagina"</note>. This foundation was held by the Lollards before him, and much earlier by the Arians, and now it is even held by the Lutherans. For they call everything else the "traditions of the Pharisees." On this account, they say that the precise words of consecration constitute the entire Mass; the rest they call additions: namely, that the vestments, the readings, and the prayers are human inventions. Consequently, they have utterly rooted out the Canonical Hours from their churches. Therefore, they say, "Granted, let prayer be good as a part of a good life; nevertheless, the time and manner of praying ought to be left to each person’s liberty."

<margin>Aeneas Silvius.</margin>
Aeneas Silvius <note>Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, who later became Pope Pius II</note>, in his book on the origin of the Bohemians, attributes this heresy to the older Waldensians, who said that time was wasted in singing the ca-

<column-break/>

-nonical hours in vain.

¶ These matters having been reviewed, the Catholic truth is established by five conclusions: both regarding the substance of the matter, and also regarding the number of prayers and the fixed hours.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The first conclusion: It was exceedingly fitting for the beauty <note>original: "decoro"</note> of the Church, and most necessary for the salvation of the Christian people, to institute a clergy whose specific duty—beyond the administration of the sacraments—would be to offer Psalms to God daily in the name of the whole people.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
For natural reason is manifest. Truly, since among all the duties and functions of a republic, religion and divine worship hold the highest place—the chief part of which is to extol God with praises and to appease Him for us with prayers—it ought to have been persuaded with most holy equity among Christians that, just as soldiers are dedicated to military service, and judges to the courts, and other ministers to their respective functions, so also clerics are appointed. This is so that they might not only sanctify the people with sacraments and move them forward by doctrine and example, but also that they might incessantly offer praises to God and pour forth prayers as mediators between God and the people. This is for the benefit of those who, being occupied with other arts, trades, duties, and business in the public name, cannot do so continually. Clerics, who carry out the ministry of channeling grace to the people through the sacraments, should in turn return thanks to Him in the name of the people, asking for the subsidies they need, and most especially for the remission of sins. For this reason, as it says in Hosea chapter 4, *The priests eat the sins of the people*: that is, they live on the alms of the people which are offered for the remission of sins.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
Added to this is a second reason: because the celebration of such praises and prayers ought to be performed with a specific language, art, and skill that the common people cannot possess, it is necessary that there be designated persons who, as in other arts, are learned in performing them.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second conclusion: It was not only most fitting for specific persons to be destined for this duty, but also for fixed times and hours to be set in which such Psalms and praises are celebrated. For this, several reasons exist.

<margin>First reason.</margin>
The first is that when specific moments of time are not fixed for any business, there can be neither order nor any subsequent continuity. For such is our nature: that where we are not constrained by a time that reminds us to do a thing, our freedom immediately loosens into a habit of postponing business, by which means custom easily perishes.

<summary>Domingo de Soto defends the necessity of public prayer and the Canonical Hours against reformers like Wycliffe and Luther. He argues that the clergy serve as essential mediators who praise God and seek grace on behalf of the busy laity at specific, ordered times.</summary>

...it passes. Therefore, he who has decided to endure perpetually needs to fix times.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ Second, he [Paul] took care that we were warned of this in the letter to the Thessalonians, where he says: *For this reason we also give thanks to God without ceasing.* <note>original: "sine intermissione"</note> And more expressly in chapter 5: *Pray without ceasing.* <note>1 Thessalonians 5:17</note> For this prohibition of "ceasing" cannot be understood so absolutely that we give no time to rest or sleep; rather, "without ceasing" is understood as not skipping any hour appointed for that purpose. Since individuals among the common people cannot maintain the same order while being called away by other cares, it was necessary to entrust this same care of praying without ceasing to a specific order of men <note>referring to the clergy and monastics</note>.

<margin>Third reason</margin>
¶ Third. This is evident because, as the Wise Man <note>Referring to Solomon in the book of Ecclesiastes 3:1</note> says, *all things have their time*, and each thing its own proper place; this certainly applies most especially to prayer. Since prayer demands the deepest silence among all tasks, not all times have the same suitability for praying. The tranquility of the night especially invites prayer, for which reason David said: *At midnight I rose to give thanks to you.* <note>Psalm 119:62</note> Thus it happens that the morning hours are more suitable for prayer the closer they are to the dawn, and the afternoon hours are more suitable the closer they approach the night.

<margin>Fourth reason.</margin>
¶ Fourth and finally, this is most strongly confirmed because the people ought to gather for the celebration of these same praises. Unless there were set times at which they could come for the same worship, they could not all gather at once; nor would they know how they should arrange their household business so as not to be an impediment to the religious duty of prayer.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ From these points follows the third conclusion: namely, that it is also fitting for there to be set places where this offering of praises and Psalms may take place. This is partly because, since worship is a most sacred thing, that place ought to be consecrated, as well as the vessels, vestments, and other ornaments by which a representation of the Majesty being adored may be made. It is also because prayer ought to be performed in common; for where there are *one, two, or three gathered in the name of Christ*, He promised that He Himself would be present there. Unless a place is designated, prayer cannot be performed conveniently.

<margin>Wycliffe. Walden.</margin>
We have added this third conclusion because the "brutish" Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320–1384), an English theologian whose critiques of the Church prefigured the Reformation</note>, as Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1370–1430), a prominent opponent of Wycliffe's teachings</note> reports in volume 5 *On Sacred Matters*, title 17, chapter 43, detested temples.

<margin>Proof of the conclusion.</margin>
Even if histories, both sacred and profane, did not defeat him, he should still be convinced by the fact that since other public acts have their designated places—such as the <term>forum</term> <note>the public square or marketplace used for judicial trials</note> for judging, the senate for 

<column-break/>

conferring counsel, and schools for teaching, and even theaters for watching games—there remained no reason for him to deny the religious nature of temples, in which the people, gathered as one, might adore their God.

<margin>Wycliffe's argument.</margin>
¶ But look at his argument. In the state of innocence <note>the state of humanity before the Fall of Adam and Eve</note> there would have been no temples, just as there were no clothes, as the nakedness of our first parents before sin testifies. Christ, however, wished to call us back to that state; therefore, such buildings are not fitting for our state.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
¶ See how "brutish" the man's <term>syllogism</term> <note>a form of logical reasoning</note> is. First, although in that state the harshness of the weather would have brought no necessity for coverings, perhaps for the sake of beauty and the exercise of the arts, some structures would have been built. But even if temples had not been built, those mortals would nonetheless have worshipped God; and so, as is more than believable, they would have come together as one to adore and praise God. Therefore, according to the state of our nature <note>i.e., our fallen state</note>, temples are necessary for us to practice the same religion. But we will speak more broadly of such proofs shortly.

<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ The fourth conclusion, regarding the most specific matter. Just as it was fitting for persons, temples, and other ornaments to be defined and prescribed, so also was it necessary for the same worship that the Psalms, orations, and prayers be established.

<margin>Proof 1.</margin>
It is proved: because it was necessary for such worship of praise to be predefined with the greatest doctrine and prudence; this sort of erudition cannot exist in every individual. Therefore, it was necessary for it to be devised by the leaders of the Church—indeed, by the whole assembly over which the Holy Spirit presides—and established by law, just as it is necessary for other laws to be instituted not by individual citizens, but by the whole republic.

<margin>Proof 2.</margin>
¶ Second: because as in the rest of worship, so especially in the giving of thanks and praise, and in orations and prayers, it was necessary for the whole Christian people to represent unity, so that for this greatest reason we might profess *one faith, one baptism, and one God*, as Paul says. <note>Ephesians 4:5</note> This concord and unity could not be preserved unless the body and substance of the Psalms were established by law, to be observed by all Christians. I say "body and substance": because it is not at all inconsistent—indeed, it is most fitting—that various provinces vary somewhat in the performance of the Hours; so that the Church, just as the Wise Man depicted her, might represent a queen standing at the right hand of the bridegroom, *clothed in variety*. <note>Psalm 45:9/44:10</note>

¶ These things regarding public prayers, as far as they pertain to the persons and other circumstances of time,

He specifically refutes Wycliffe's rejection of church buildings, arguing that while they might not have been needed in Eden, they are essential for human unity and devotion in our current state.</summary>

### Question V of the Tenth Book

<margin>First reason against the cited heretics.</margin>
[The arguments regarding...] time, place, and manner, having been briefly affirmed, before we descend to the fifth conclusion regarding the sevenfold number of the hours <note>This refers to the "Canonical Hours," the seven times a day—such as Matins and Vespers—that clergy and monks are required to pray.</note>, it is worthwhile to strengthen and fortify our position with the firm defense and rampart of antiquity. For all these things are corroborated and established by natural law, by the divine law of both Testaments, and subsequently by human law. For first of all, nature itself—which is God's handiwork—taught all mortals living by its law alone (however wickedly and impiously they might have thought regarding the variety of gods) that regardless of which gods they worshiped, priests were necessary, as were groves, temples, and designated altars, where they might practice their religion at fixed hours and with established ceremonies. A good part of this was to sing psalms in their own manner and to pour out prayers to God, both in war and in any other business or affairs, so that they might win His favor and return thanks to Him.

<margin>Valerius Maximus.</margin>
Both other writers and Valerius Maximus <note>A 1st-century Roman historian whose works were popular in the Renaissance for their examples of ancient virtues and customs.</note> (Book 1, Chapter 1) record these rites, where he says: "Our ancestors took care that fixed and solemn ceremonies were explained by the knowledge of the High Priests, so that by ancient institution, attention might be given to divine matters; namely, when something was to be commended by prayer, or asked for by a vow, or fulfilled by a thanksgiving." Not only does secular history attest to this, but sacred history does as well; for it records not only that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob built altars to the Lord before the written law, but also that Melchizedek <note>A mysterious priest-king mentioned in Genesis; he is seen as a "type" or precursor to Christ's priesthood.</note> performed a different kind of priesthood—about whom there is no doubt that he had fixed hours and ceremonies for praising God.

<margin>Second reason.</margin>
¶ But lest we linger too long in reviewing secular examples, the custom of the Old Law should abundantly shut every mouth of the heretics. Furthermore, God commanded the Tabernacle to be built with such careful attention, even while those mortals were wandering and camping through the desert. And soon after they took possession of the Promised Land, he ordered a most magnificent Temple which would shine with all sorts of gold and a variety of gems. Then, he commanded the High Priest to be distinguished by the ornament of his robes, along with other priests and a very great multitude of Levites, as read in Exodus 26 and following; these men were indeed dedicated not only to the duty of sacrifice, but also to that of prayer.

<margin>The heretics' evasion. The reply.</margin>
¶ But they say that all those things were ceremonial, and thus have ceased. We admit, indeed, that what was ceremonial has passed out of use, but nevertheless, 

<column-break/>

since worshiping God with hymns, praises, and prayers is established in natural law, this not only ought not to be abolished, but should be retained with even greater religious devotion under the Law of the Gospel, just as the reality <note>original: "veritas" (truth/reality)</note> required it more essentially than the shadow <note>original: "vmbra" (the Old Testament "shadows" or precursors).</note>. For all things happened to them as a figure <note>A "figure" is a symbolic event in the Old Testament that points toward a Christian truth.</note> of the divine truth of the body and blood of Christ, which is contained, adored, and worshiped under the Sacrament in our temples.

<margin>The heretics turn away from temples.</margin>
¶ In order to descend from these points to our Gospel Law, let us begin with the religion of temples, which—since they are places of public prayer—do not please the heretics. 

<margin>First reason against past error.</margin>
Nevertheless, Christ himself testified how much they pleased Him, not only by being frequently brought to the temple as a small child, and by going up there very often for feast days when he was a man, but also by driving out the merchants from there with the lash of a whip, reproaching them because they made his Father's house a house of business (John 2). And in Luke it is expressed more clearly: *My house is a house of prayer.* For the house of the Father and His own house are the same, because the Trinity is worshiped in it with the same religion of prayer. For He himself revealed how pleasing it was to God to dwell in temples (2 Kings 7), where he says, as if complaining: *For I have not dwelt in a house from the day that I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt even to this day, but I walked in a tabernacle and in a tent through all the places I passed with all the children of Israel.* With what face, then, can the heretics deny the houses of prayer which God once valued so highly, and which the same God, Christ, wanted to be consecrated to this duty and removed from all business? Indeed, it is believed without a doubt that He himself had established prayers which he used. For he was accustomed, as held in Luke 6, to spend the night in the prayer of God. And in Matthew 26, it is recorded that *after saying a hymn*, he went out to the temple to pray. By these words, a certain designated hymn is indicated which he used in thanksgiving. And in Luke 18, he says: *It is necessary to pray always and not to fail.* This, as we said above regarding that other passage of Paul's, *Pray without ceasing*, cannot be understood except as referring to prayers which are said at fixed hours. And in 1 Corinthians 11, the same Apostle says that every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head, but a woman with it uncovered. 

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
Where, according to Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church.</note> and other interpreters, even at that time in the days of the Apostles, it was the custom for Christians to confess the faith with prescribed words—the Symbol <note>The "Symbol" refers to the Apostles' Creed or a similar statement of faith.</note> of which they themselves established (for he calls this "prophesying")—and also with certain prayers...

<summary>Dominicus Soto argues that organized prayer at specific times and in consecrated buildings is a requirement of natural law and divine tradition. He uses the examples of Christ's reverence for the Temple and Apostolic customs to refute heretical claims that such external ceremonies are obsolete.</summary>
