# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

<margin>Confirmation.</margin> to pray. And this is clearly confirmed from that passage in Luke 11, where the Apostles—as if asking for something difficult and not accessible to everyone—petitioned the Lord with one voice, saying: *Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.* And He added: *Thus, then, you shall pray: Our Father, etc.* <note>original: "Domine doce nos orare sicut docuit Ioan. discipulos suos... Sic autem vos orabitis: Pater noster, &c."</note>

It cannot, therefore, be denied that in the time of the Apostles there were certain established prayers.

<margin>The testimony of the heretics.</margin> ¶ But the heretics <note>Soto refers here to Protestant Reformers who argued that only the Lord's Prayer was necessary or divinely commanded, rejecting the elaborate Catholic liturgy.</note> say: "There was no prayer except that which Christ taught, the *Our Father*." This is surely false. For Paul designates certain others in the first [Epistle] to Timothy, chapter 2, where he says: *I desire therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men and for kings, etc.* <note>original: "Obsecro igitur primùm omnium fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus & pro regibus. &c."</note> Two things are designated there. First, that there were different modes of praying already established at that time. Second, that this duty was especially incumbent upon the clergy.

<margin>Chrysostom.</margin> Whence Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence.</note> says on that same passage: *What is this? First of all, this is in the daily worship, and the priests first know this: how prayers are made through each and every day, both in the evening and in the morning.*

<margin>Isidore.</margin> And Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and bishop who compiled much of the knowledge of the ancient world for the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 1 of *On Offices*, chapter 8, says: *Christ the Lord both taught and established that we should entreat the Lord with prayers.* For when the Apostles, not knowing how to pray, asked of Christ, saying, *teach us to pray*—that is, compose prayers for us—Christ immediately taught them. From that point, the custom of the church was brought forth: namely, to use prayers modeled after those which Christ instituted, which the Greeks first began to compose. Therefore, by these words of Isidore, the clever argument of the heretics is dissolved—namely, the claim that no other prayer should be used except that which Christ uttered. For it was by no means the intention of Christ to restrict the people so precisely to that one prayer that it would be in no way lawful to use another. Rather, He proposed that model to the Church so that whatever prayers or supplications and praises it might institute, they should be reduced to one of those parts. For this reason, the psalmody of praise is referred to the phrase, *Hallowed be thy name*; while petitions for grace and the remission of sins are referred to, *Thy kingdom come, etc.* It was appropriate, therefore, for Christ to institute a prayer necessary for all the people, but He committed the rest to be instituted by the Church after its likeness.

¶ Since this public manner of praying—as I was saying above—had to be performed through doctrine and skill, it required certain persons upon whom this duty would fall, such as the clergy. Whence the same Apostle in the first [Epistle] to the Corinthians, chapter 14, says: *When you come together* (namely, for public prayers), *each one of you has a psalm, has a doctrine, has a revelation, etc.* <note>original: "Cùm conuenitis... unusquisq; vestrûm psalmum habet, doctrinam habet, apocalypsim habet. &c."</note> As if he were saying: a different task is incumbent upon each person; namely, that some should intone the psalms, others should teach, and another—the preacher—should interpret the "apocalypsim," that is, the revelation. Whence he adds: *if any speak in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most by three*—that is, let those who publicly perform the hours do so in order, number, and turn. But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the Church, and speak to himself—that is, he who does not have the duty of speaking or singing should listen to others and pray to God in silence. Behold, regarding the four conclusions prefixed at the head of the chapter, how they all draw their foundations from antiquity, even from the time of the Apostles: namely, that there were persons decreed for praying, as well as psalms, temples, and certain prayers.

¶ Concerning the times and the hours of the day established for praying—which is the chief point of the present dispute—the fifth conclusion is finally applied. <margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin> The sevenfold number of the Canonical Hours <note>The fixed cycle of daily prayer in the Catholic Church, consisting of specific prayers said at specific times.</note>, as it is a most ancient institution of the Church, is likewise most congruent and becoming: namely, that after the night office of Matins, the daytime hours are six in number: specifically, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline.

And first, that the night office took its origin from the age of the Apostles, <margin>Jerome.</margin> Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> testifies regarding that passage in Matthew 25: *At midnight a cry was made.* For he says that since the tradition of the Jews was that the Messiah would come at midnight—similar to the time in Egypt when the Passover was celebrated and the exterminator came—the Apostolic tradition likewise remained, so that on the day of the Easter vigils it was not permitted to dismiss the people before the middle of the night, as they awaited the coming of Christ. Whence the Psalmist also said: *At midnight I rose to praise thee because of the judgments of thy justification.* So says Jerome.

But since we have come upon this verse of the Psalm, there are many others of this sort by which the office of nightly praise is commended. For the same Psalmist says elsewhere: *I will wash my bed every night.* And elsewhere: *It is good to give praise to the Lord, and to sing to thy name, O most High: To show forth thy mercy in the morning, and thy truth by night.* And elsewhere: *I remembered thy name, O Lord, in the night.* And

He introduces the seven Canonical Hours, justifying the practice of midnight prayer (Matins) through both biblical prophecy and the writings of St. Jerome.</summary>

### Book Ten, Question V.

And in the hour of **Compline**, <note>The final prayer service of the day in the Christian liturgy.</note> we sing: *In the nights lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the Lord.* <note>original: "In noctibus extollite manus vestras in sancta, & benedicite Domino." This is from Psalm 134:2.</note> Therefore, the custom of night prayer did not only take its origin from the Apostles, but from the oracles of the Prophets. ¶ Furthermore, Christ our teacher taught us this same custom through his own actions. For he was "spending the whole night in prayer," as is reported in **Luke 6**. And, as held in **Matthew 26**, he went out to the Mount of Olives at midnight to pray: where, rebuking the disciples because they could not "watch one hour" with him, he was betrayed by Judas and captured by the Jews. These mysteries should certainly keep the Christian people occupied in night prayers.

<margin>Objection of the Wycliffites condemning the night office.</margin>
¶ Therefore, since the **Wycliffites** <note>Followers of John Wycliffe (c. 1320s–1384), a precursor to the Reformation who criticized many Catholic traditions.</note>—as Thomas Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), a Carmelite theologian who wrote extensively against Wycliffite teachings.</note> reports in the same chapter 25—criticize these night psalms, arguing that since God granted us the night for rest, we make the Christian religion burdensome by consuming it with vigils: to crush their blasphemy, we respond:

<margin>First solution.</margin>
First, that very nightly quiet, as we said above, naturally invites one to contemplation and thus to prayer, because when the senses cease from their use, the mind is more peaceful within.

<margin>Second.</margin>
Second, both the oracles of the Prophets and the example of Christ admonish us toward this same practice.

<margin>Third.</margin>
¶ But thirdly—and this should be considered of primary importance—the ancient fathers held this to be holy because in the primitive church the nightly incursions of demons were most hostile; against these, they therefore instituted night vigils equipped with prayers.

<margin>Isidore.</margin>
As **Isidore** <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and bishop whose works served as an encyclopedia for the Middle Ages.</note> excellently relates in his book *On Offices*, chapter 19: Just as soldiers in an army or sailors on a ship arrange four nightly stations, which they call "watches" <note>term: "vigilias" — Latin for "watches," referring to the military shifts of the Roman guard.</note>—each lasting three hours. For the three hours from sunset, when drowsiness compels men to lie down, they call the "first watch"; the next three until midnight they call the "second"; from midnight they immediately call the "third"; and then until daybreak, the "fourth." In these, while others sleep, those on guard keep watch.

<margin>The reason for singing the office in the primitive church.</margin>
After this fashion, in the early church—namely from the age of the Apostles—the clergy were divided into three parts: one part sang the first "nocturn" of three psalms during the first watch; another sang the second in the second watch; and another sang the third in the third watch, so that they might profess the Trinity in each watch as well as in all of them together. Finally, at daybreak in the fourth watch, they all gathered together to harmonize the **Lauds**. <note>The morning prayer service, literally meaning "Praises."</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Whence **Augustine**, in his 14th sermon *On the Words of the Lord*, says: "The Lord came to visit his disciples who were troubled on the sea during the fourth watch of the night." The fourth watch of the night is the last part of the night: one watch has three hours, and through this, the night has four watches. ¶ And lest the heretics think such vigils were an invention of the holy fathers, let them see that they had their foundation in the very words of Christ: as can be seen in **Luke 12**, where the second and third watches are named, and more expressly in **Mark 13**: "Watch," he says, "for you do not know when the Lord comes: in the evening (that is, the first watch), or at midnight, or at cock-crow (that is, the second or third), or in the morning (that is, the hour of Lauds); lest when he comes, he finds you suddenly sleeping. What I say to you, I say to all: Watch." Instructed and taught by these words, the Church organized its stations and vigils.

<margin>Valerianus.</margin>
Whence **Valerianus** <note>Likely Valerian of Cimiez (d. c. 460), a bishop known for his homilies.</note> says in his first book *On Matins*: "We divide the vigils into three-hour night shifts, so that we may preach the three watches not only in word but in deed, about which the Lord says: 'Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, shall find watching,' etc."

<margin>Vigilantius.</margin>
Regarding this matter, when the heretic **Vigilantius** <note>A 4th-century priest who opposed monasticism and the veneration of relics.</note> was the author of that treachery—claiming that the night should be granted to rest and sleep and not spent in prayers—on that occasion,

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
**Jerome**, as can be seen in his letter to Riparius, gave him a distorted name, calling him **Dormitantius** <note>note: "Dormitantius" is a pun on Jerome's part, changing "Vigilantius" (The Wakeful One) into "The Sleepy One" from the Latin *dormitare* (to slumber).</note> instead of Vigilantius. Indeed, he says: "That you say he execrates vigils, he does this even against his own name, so that Vigilantius wants to 'slumber' (*dormitare*), and does not hear the Savior saying: 'Could you not watch one hour with me?'" For this reason, in the very next letter, he calls him Dormitantius. Whence the same Jerome says to the virgin Eustochium: "One must rise to pray twice or thrice in the night." But truly, because later, as the clergy increased, human frailty could not bear such a heavy burden, that rotation ceased, and all three nocturns began to be sung together with Lauds by the whole clergy at once. This occurs on feast days; for on ordinary days only one is sung, as is also done during the Easter season. And although some chose the first watch and others the third, most churches and religious orders established midnight as the time more suitable for prayer, according to the testimony of David. <note>Psalm 119:62: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee..."</note>

<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
For as **Ambrose** <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397), the influential Bishop of Milan.</note> is the authority in his commentary on Psalm 118, he did not say "at midnight" without deliberation. At that time...

For then the allurements of the flesh burn, food is cooked, and drink is digested. <note>Soto uses the physiological theories of his time—suggesting that digestion and bodily heat during the night can stir up physical temptations—to explain why the night is a spiritually dangerous time that requires the protection of prayer.</note> On this occasion, the tempter strikes the flesh with many trials and occupies the mind. This is what he [Walden] says. From this, between the stroke of midnight and the cock-crow, the heat of Peter's faith grew cold, and moved by the warmth of a temporal fire, he denied Christ. <note>A reference to Peter warming himself by a fire in the courtyard of the High Priest while Jesus was being interrogated (Luke 22:55–60).</note> Wherefore, the relaxation of this time should not be so easily sought or granted. <margin>Testimony for the daytime hours drawn from Sacred Scripture.</margin>
¶ Regarding the daytime hours, there are also testimonies and reasons of no less power. In the first place, three hours—namely the **Third**, **Sixth**, and **Ninth**—were most famous for praying even during the lives of the Apostles themselves. For there exists the record in **Acts 1**, how after the Lord’s ascension the Apostles were in Jerusalem, persevering with one mind in prayer; nor is there any doubt that this was in solemn prayer, which was celebrated by everyone together, just as it is now in the choir. <note>The "choir" refers to the area of a church near the altar where the clergy or monks gather to sing the Divine Office.</note> For "with one mind" designates not only a unity of hearts, but also a harmony of voices. And finally, at the **Third Hour**, as read in chapter 2, the Holy Spirit appeared to them, the inflamer of tongues and hearts. For this reason, it should not be doubted that they were saying the destined psalms at that hour. Because of this, the Church then uses that hymn: *Come, Holy Spirit...* <note>original: "Nunc Sancte nobis Spiritus." This is the traditional hymn for the hour of Terce, commemorating the descent of the Spirit at Pentecost.</note> Concerning the **Sixth**, we read in **Acts 10**, specifically where Peter is reported to have gone up to the upper parts [of the house] to pray around the sixth hour. But mention of the **Ninth** is also made in **Acts 3**, for it is held that Peter and John went up into the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer. Indeed, that these same hours were celebrated by the custom and use of the Hebrews, beyond the conjecture which is very strong, authors are not lacking who affirm it.

<margin>Cyprian.</margin>
For **Cyprian**, <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and influential theologian.</note> at the end of his book *On the Lord's Prayer*, says: "In celebrating prayers, we find that the three youths, strong in faith and victors in captivity, observed with Daniel the third, sixth, and ninth hours." He alludes then to that passage in **Daniel 3**, <note>Soto cites Daniel 2, but the account of the "three youths" in the fiery furnace is found in Daniel 3.</note> that those three praised, glorified, and blessed God as if from one mouth. And he alludes most especially to **Daniel 6**, where it is reported that he [Daniel] bent his knees three times a day toward Jerusalem, and adored and confessed before the Lord his God, just as he had been accustomed to do before. For there was a custom among the prophets to sing together at fixed and stated hours. Whence in **1 Samuel** <note>original: "Primi Regum" (1 Kings). In the Latin Vulgate used by Soto, 1 and 2 Samuel were titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>

<column-break/>

**10**, Samuel says to Saul: "When you have entered the city there, you will meet a flock of Prophets descending from the high place, and before them a psaltery, and a timbrel, and a pipe, and a harp, and they themselves prophesying"—that is, singing psalms with a prophetic spirit. "And the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them." Whence it became a proverb: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" Furthermore, Cyprian adds there that the mystery of the Trinity was prefigured in those three hours, which was to be manifested in the final times.

<margin>The number of daytime hours founded in the Old Testament.</margin>
**Isidore**, <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), a scholar whose works helped preserve classical knowledge for the Middle Ages.</note> in book 1 of *On Offices*, chapter 19, founds this same number of hours—namely the third, sixth, and ninth—in that same book of Daniel. Therefore, in that age of the Apostles, no mention is found except of those three hours before noon, with **Prime** <note>The "First Hour," roughly 6:00 AM, the first of the little daytime offices.</note> being omitted.

<margin>Isidore. Jerome. Cassian. Isidore.</margin>
Wherefore **Jerome**, <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the priest and scholar famous for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> upon that same passage of **Daniel 6**, says: "Ecclesiastical tradition understands these three hours, namely the third, sixth, and ninth." Thus he says. For I conjecture that at that time when people rose three times for the night psalms and the Lauds <note>The "Praises," a major prayer service held at daybreak.</note> were sung at dawn, another hour until the third was considered superfluous. Whence the same Jerome, speaking to Eustochium about the hours divided for praying, says: "There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and also the dawn and the evening." Here, by the name of **dawn**, he perhaps understands Lauds. And to proceed with conjectures, **Cassian** <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD), who brought the monastic traditions of the East to the Western Church.</note> in book 3 of *Institutes of the Monks*, chapter 4 (which Isidore mentions in book 1 of *Offices*, chapter 23), says: "It should be known that this morning [service] which is observed in the Western regions especially, was first instituted as a canonical function in our time and in our monastery." Therefore, perhaps he calls "morning" what we call **Prime**. To this also the word of Cyprian in the place cited seems to refer: namely, "But for us, most beloved brothers, besides the hours observed of old for praying, the intervals and sacraments have now increased: for one must also pray in the morning so that the resurrection of the Lord may be celebrated at the morning hour." Therefore, he calls the third, sixth, and ninth the "ancient hours," to which he adds the first.

<margin>On the division and start of the hours.</margin>
¶ And yet, these hours are to be understood through the division of the **artificial day**, <note>In the medieval and ancient world, an "artificial day" was the time from sunrise to sunset divided into 12 equal hours. Because the length of daylight changes with the seasons, a "seasonal hour" in summer was longer than one in winter.</note> so that at any time of the year the first hour begins at sunrise. Moreover, the Third finishes at the third hour of the day, and the Sixth also from the same sunrise. For thus are those hours in **Matthew 20** to be understood: namely, that the father of the family went out early in the morning to hire laborers, and then at the third hour and the sixth hour. ¶ Concerning **Vespers** <note>The evening prayer service.</note> and **Compline**, <note>The final prayer service before sleep.</note> St. Jerome says in the place cited that there is no one who does not know them; remaining... <meta>Catchword "res" is for the Latin "restant" (remain).</meta>

### Question V of the Tenth Book

...as if the matter were of the greatest antiquity and most widely accepted by all Christians.
<margin>Concerning Compline.</margin>
<margin>Ambrose.</margin>
¶ Indeed, regarding **Compline** <note>The final prayer service of the day, traditionally said before retiring for the night.</note>, Ambrose says in the place cited that the memory of birds comes to his mind, which are accustomed to soothe themselves when they go to sleep. Just as they are accustomed to restore this at the rising and setting of the sun, so that at the passing or the onset of night and day, they might return just praises to their Creator. From this, we ought to take a great incentive for exciting our own devotion.

<margin>Three reasons why the seven Canonical hours were instituted in the Church.</margin>
¶ Therefore, let us gather what we have mentioned in various places and apply them collectively to confirm our conclusion. This sevenfold canonical number was instituted by the Holy Spirit and is most holy for the Christian family for three reasons. The first, and literally the most powerful, is so that, according to Christ’s command and Paul’s warning, an unceasing and uninterrupted memory of God might persist in us—praise, thanksgiving, and finally, prayer and the seeking of favor. For since in a natural day there are six intervals of three hours each, and since we have fixed psalms in each, we persist in prayer in a perpetual circle. Furthermore, we profess the **Trinity**, which is the confession of our faith, in every three-hour interval; for by the same logic, we distribute both psalms and prayers by that same number.

<margin>The Gloss.</margin>
Secondly <note>The text says "thirdly," but follows the second point regarding the Trinity.</note>, the mysteries are added, both other mysteries and specifically those of Christ; these the **Gloss** <note>A standard medieval commentary on law or scripture.</note> collects regarding the chapter *Presbyter* on the celebration of Masses. This is indeed from the Council of Agde, celebrated during the papacy of Zosimus, around the year of our Lord 420. <note>The Council of Agde actually occurred in 506 AD; Soto may be following a different chronological tradition or citing a specific collection's dating.</note> There, all the aforementioned hours, both of the day and of the night, are ordered to be performed. One must be careful of the deception, as heretics attempt to blaspheme, that these were then instituted for the first time. For we have brought forward the earlier testimonies so that we might trace them back to antiquity and the time of the Apostles. Therefore, they are confirmed there as an ancient practice.

The **mysteries**, however, are these: there are seven days of the week in which the world was created; seven gifts of the Holy Spirit by which it is recreated; seven ages of the world in which it shall endure; and even seven petitions of the Lord's Prayer by which we ask for those same gifts. Furthermore, Christ was captured at the hour of **Matins** and suffered through the remaining hours of the day. Hence the verses:

> These are the seven things for which we sing at the hours:
> **Matins** binds Christ, who purges our crimes:
> **Prime** fills Him with spit, the **Third** hour gives the cause of death:
> **Sext** binds Him to the cross, the **Ninth** pierces His side in two.
> **Vespers** takes Him down, **Compline** replaces Him in the tomb.

<column-break/>

Therefore, from all these things that have been said, it is gathered that there are seven Canonical hours, according to that verse of the Psalm: *Seven times a day I have spoken your praise.* <note>Psalm 119:164.</note> For in that place, "day" is understood as the natural day, so as to include the night. Therefore, those who separate **Matins** from **Lauds** and count them as eight are not to be listened to.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
TO the first argument objected above by **Wycliffe** <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320–1384), an English theologian whose critiques of the Church prefigured the Reformation.</note>, we deny that the weight of the canonical hours is burdensome to such an extent that we affirm it to be most sweet. Regarding his insinuation that it is not within the Church’s power to decree anything not expressed in one of the two Testaments, we respond with several points. First, that is a heretical foundation, belonging to that beast which John wrote he saw in Revelation 3 <note>Soto likely intends Revelation 13:11, which describes the beast with two horns like a lamb.</note>, which, though it seemed a lamb bearing horns on its forehead, was nevertheless a dragon.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
Upon this passage, **Augustine** says in his 11th Sermon that the heretical church is signified there: which, like the Lamb of Christ, displays two horns on its forehead—that is, the two Testaments—yet tears the Catholic Church with the bite of a dragon. So says he. For the Catholic Church has Apostolic power from Christ by which it can establish laws, which it either draws from the sacred page or deems necessary for the adornment of Christians. This is just like the Apostles, who spread their garments over those beasts of burden so that Christ, about to enter Jerusalem, might ride more softly.

Indeed, **Jerome** says on the same passage that the Apostolic garment can be understood either as the doctrine of virtues or the publication of the scriptures: just like the variety of ecclesiastical dogmas, with which, unless the soul has been instructed, it does not deserve to have the Lord as its rider.

<margin>Anselm.</margin>
And **Anselm** says: See how the Apostles placed their garments upon the beast, but the rest of the Judean crowd placed theirs under the beast's feet; because we are instructed and adorned by the mandates of the Apostles, but we trample the mandates of the old law when we reject carnal observations and circumcisions. Add to this that the Church, being taught not only inwardly by the Holy Spirit but also enlightened by the living voice of the Apostles and Christ, has embraced the religious practice of these hours.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
To the second argument, it is answered that in private prayers there is no need for the voice, but it is enough to pray with the mind, except to stir up devotion. But when Christ and Paul say (according to him) that one must pray with the spirit and the mind, they teach nothing else than that the voice of the one praying and singing psalms should not be...

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
...like the chirping of birds: but full of mind and spirit. ¶ The third argument will be more fully resolved in the third article, where it will be shown that the duty of clerics initiated into sacred orders—even if they have the care of souls—is to perform the requirement of the hours.

### ARTICLE II.

*Whether it is fitting and proper that the Canonical Hours, consisting of Psalms and Hymns, should be sung in a loud chant.*

After discussing the substance and institution of the Canonical Hours <note>The set cycle of daily prayers performed by the clergy</note>, it follows now to explore whether they should be performed with songs and hymns. <margin>Wycliffe. Walden.</margin> For the same Wycliffe <note>John Wycliffe (c. 1320–1384), an English theologian whose critiques of the Church prefigured the Reformation</note>, as Thomas Walden <note>Thomas Netter of Walden (c. 1375–1430), an English Carmelite who wrote extensively against Wycliffe's teachings</note> reports in volume 5, chapter 16, mocked Catholics for this, saying they cried out praises and prayers to God in a loud chant. The Lutherans have revived this heresy, laughing at us as if we were ridiculous for making a noise to God with our voices in the temples. <margin>First argument.</margin> Their argument is that God is not deaf or sleeping, such that He needs our shouts to be awakened. Therefore they call us "Baalites," that is, like the priests of Baal: whom Elijah mocked, as recorded in 1 Kings 18, urging them to cry out louder, adding: "For perhaps your God is talking with another, or is at an inn, or on a journey, or surely he is asleep, so that he must be awakened." And when I was among them <note>Soto likely refers to his time at the Council of Trent or other diplomatic missions where he encountered Protestant reformers</note>, they sometimes challenged me on this same matter: "If you were speaking with the Emperor, would you do so by singing, or would you ask for something from him with the loudest voices and musical artifice? Would you not be ridiculous? Why then do you not fear to do before God what you would not dare before the Emperor?" <margin>Argument 2.</margin> ¶ Secondly, it is argued by the example of that matron, the mother of Samuel <note>Hannah, from the Old Testament</note>, who, as reported at the beginning of 1 Samuel, prayed with pressed lips so silently that she appeared to be drunk. This example is very celebrated among the saints as a model for those who pray. Hence an author says in his 13th homily on the "perfect man": We can understand the mouth of the body as the door of the house, so that we do not pray to God with a loud voice, but with silent desire. For he says that many evils arise from loud prayer, especially these three: First, that the one praying with a loud voice does not believe God is everywhere and hears secrets. Second, that he commits the mysteries of his secret petitions—which perhaps should not be known

<column-break/>

by anyone except God—to be heard by the ears of both the good and the evil. Third and finally, that the one praying loudly does not allow another standing near him to pray. This is what experience testifies: for while there is singing in the Church, those standing by cannot pray, as the voices carry away their senses. Finally, it is added that because the music is like that which secular people use in their festivals, they seem to profane sacred things. <margin>Final argument.</margin> ¶ On the contrary, however, is that word of David in Psalm 149: "Sing to the Lord a new song." And again: "Let them praise his name in the choir." To this is added the Fourth Council of Toledo, concerning consecration, distinction 1, whose words are: "Concerning the singing of hymns, we have the example of both the Savior and the Apostles." <margin>Council of Toledo.</margin>

Since these innovators and disturbers of ecclesiastical affairs strive so much to drive out church chants from the Christian assembly, as I just mentioned, we would not have done justice to the present matter unless we added this article. Concerning this, Saint Thomas [Aquinas] touched upon it somewhat in the *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 91. To which the response is given in a single and most widely accepted conclusion of the Church. <margin>Responsive conclusion.</margin> Ecclesiastical chants, by which the Canonical Hours are solemnly celebrated, are established in the church for the best reason, and they are also most ancient. ¶ And so that testimonies may become clear through reasons, we must take our beginning from the reasons themselves. But it should be noted first of all that the Canonical Hours, in which the religion of worshipping God consists, contain three types of relationships between us and God. The first is divine praise, which we owe to Him for His own sake as the highest good. For this reason, we owe that confession <note>original: "confessio," here meaning an acknowledgment of God's nature</note>: because He is supremely and infinitely good, just, and merciful, and so all-powerful, all-knowing; and whatever good exists in things, His immense essence contains it. Therefore we sing Hymns and the praises of the Psalms to Him. The second reason for these same hours is so that we may ask from Him whatever is necessary for our life and salvation, both temporal and spiritual: confessing that we are His own creatures, and that no good can happen to us except from Him. Finally, the third duty which we perform for Him by praying is the giving of thanks for benefits received. ¶ This being established, the conclusion is demonstrated by several reasons. <margin>First reason for the conclusion.</margin> First of all, chant is so far from being incompatible with the nature of praise that it is most fitting to it.

# Question V of the Tenth Book

For if we consult the natural talent of humanity, heroic poems had their origin in the desire to sing the praises and deeds of heroes in sonorous meter. As the poet of the *Aeneid* <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> signifies at the very beginning when he says: *I sing of arms and the man.* <note>original: "Arma virumque cano"</note> For this reason, Aristotle in Book 8 of his *Politics* (chapter 5) and Boethius in the prologue to his *Music* greatly commend music as a thing 
<margin>The second reason.</margin> that contributes much to the emotions and dispositions of the soul. ¶ Indeed, to add a second argument, harmony in singing such praises is so natural that even the Author of Nature Himself is said to be sung to in the same way in the heavens. For this reason, in Revelation 4, John reports of the "holy animals" <note>The four living creatures surrounding the throne of God</note> that they had no rest day or night, saying: *Holy, Holy, Holy.* From this, the Church in the Preface of the Mass exhorts itself so that—just as the powers of the heavens and the heights of heaven, the Cherubim and Seraphim also, do not cease to cry out in shared exultation—it might sing along with them. Therefore, it also supplicates God to command that its own voices be admitted along with theirs, saying: *Holy, Holy,* etc. For this reason, there are those who rightly claim that God is praised in the heavenly realms with real voices, though they be supernatural ones. And the angels brought testimony of this matter from above to the earth: when the Lord was born, they not only shone upon the shepherds with the splendor of divine glory, but also sounded out in song: *Glory to God in the highest.* Hence, 
<margin>Gregory.</margin> toward the end of his second book on the Epiphany, Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604)</note> says: "Worship with the shepherds, sing the hymn with the Angels, lead the dance with the Archangels. Let this be a common solemnity for us, shared between those on earth and those in heaven." With what impudence of mouth, then, can the heretics <note>Referring to the Reformers like Wycliffe and Luther</note> deny these proclamations of praise? For this reason, the Church Militant <note>The Church on earth, still struggling against sin and trial</note>—namely, so that it may reflect the fellowship it has entered with the Church Triumphant <note>The Church in heaven, victorious and at rest</note>—divides the clergy into two choirs to sound out praises with alternating voices. One side stands while the other sits: specifically, so that the one who stands represents the battle-line of the "militant," while the one who sits represents the rest of the "triumphant." Thus, since each responds to the other, both—namely the angelic and the human choir—venerate the same God in 
<margin>The third reason</margin> most beautiful concord. ¶ The third argument, after the nature of mortals and the condition of the immortals, is taken from the Old Law. For David, being inspired by the same divine power, composed the psalter and the lyre, with which he was accustomed to sing the divine mysteries. For he said, *Your justifications were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage.* <note>Psalm 119:54</note> By this rite, he not only communicated to God whatever 

<column-break/>

he carried in his soul, but also used it to drive away the besieging demons, as is clear in 1 Samuel 16. <note>In the original Latin text, this is cited as 1 Kings 16, following the Vulgate numbering.</note> Surely he was admonishing the future Church to put the insulting demons to flight with the harmony of the Psalms. For this reason, as we read in 1 Chronicles 23, he appointed four thousand singers in the house of God, singing to the Lord with the instruments he had made for music. And for that reason, in Psalm 148 and the two following it, he admonishes the saints of God in every way to sound out praises to God with hymns, songs, and every musical instrument. Furthermore, in confirmation of this matter, there are those most famous spiritual songs which the holy Prophets and Fathers of that Law are read to have sung at the dictation of the Holy Spirit, and which the Church now sings throughout the week: such as the songs of Moses, Anna, Deborah, Isaiah, Hezekiah, and the other Prophets. ¶ Nor 
<margin>The fourth reason.</margin> is there any reason for anyone to protest that those songs were suited to that Temple and not to ours; for since that Temple was a "figure" <note>A prophetic preview or symbol</note> of our own, they are much more fitting for us. Hence, as a fourth argument, when Christ entered Jerusalem—where His entry into our Church was signified—He was received by a harmony of children playing psalms and singing, *Hosanna to the Son of David.* And when the Jews grumbled and interrupted the Lord, asking Him to order them to be silent, He replied: *If these keep silent, the stones will cry out.* Therefore, if the Canonical Hours are considered insofar as they are divine praises, it is most fitting that they be performed with songs. ¶ Moreover, if they are offered as acts of thanksgiving, song is no less fitting for them. That this was 
<margin>The fifth reason.</margin> the custom and practice of Christ Himself is testified to by the fifth argument: Matthew chapter 26, where in recounting the Last Supper it says: *And when a hymn had been said, they went out to the Mount of Olives.* From this, it is gathered that Christ performed acts of thanksgiving with His followers by singing. For as Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636)</note> says in Book 6 of his *Etymologies* (chapter 34): 
<margin>Isidore.</margin> hymns are the songs of those praising God. Therefore, he says, if it is praise but not of God, it is not a hymn; and if it is praise and of God but is not sung, it is not a hymn. Regarding this matter, Augustine,

...should sound to the reader of the psalm, so that he was closer to one reciting than to one singing <note>original: "vicinior esset quàm canenti"</note>, he adds: "Yet when I remember my tears which I shed at the songs of your Church in the early days of my recovered faith, and now I myself am moved, not by the singing, but by the things which are sung with a clear voice and most fitting modulation, I again acknowledge the great utility of this institution." <note>Quoting Augustine's *Confessions*, Book 10, Chapter 33.</note> Thus I fluctuate between the danger of pleasure and the experience of healthfulness, and I am more inclined—though not offering an unretractable opinion—to approve the custom of singing in the church, so that through the delights of the ears, the weaker mind may rise into an affection of piety.

<margin>The author's second reason.</margin>
¶ Indeed, I apply another reason for myself for extolling such songs. For they are also powerful for magnifying the love of God toward us. For who would not love his God even for this: that He instituted a duty of religion so necessary, but which from another side could bring some bit of trouble, with His holy power, so that such melody would be offered by us that it might both lighten the labor and refresh and soothe the soul? Add to this that such spiritual songs show Him to be more merciful toward us. For if He allows us to bring our crimes—by which we offend His justice and which ought rather to be mourned and lamented with all sorrow—to His ears with harmonious song, how could we not believe Him to have the most open heart <note>original: "visceribus," literally "bowels" or "innards," a common metaphor for deep compassion or mercy.</note> toward us, and to be most ready to indulge us? > After he rejected the secular sweetness of melody which tends to weaken human souls, a little further down he adds: "Therefore, if it is a pleasure to hear songs and poems, let it be pleasant to sing and hear the praises of God."

For those who condemn these ceremonies of singing, I would wish them to be present in Catholic churches, in which the harmony is sung with antiquity and religious modesty, and afterward that they might visit the temples of heretics <note>Likely referring to the more austere Protestant groups of the 16th century who removed music or simplified it drastically.</note>, where the silence represents nothing other than the corpses of churches, so that in that gap of difference they might judge concerning both.

that might offend pious ears, as has been the custom in some places during the Nativity of the Lord <note>Christmas.</note> and on other feast days. Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into Latin.</note> records and reproves such things in Distinction 92, the canon "Singing." <note>A reference to Canon Law (Gratian's Decretum).</note> Although this must be weighed according to the nature of the people. <margin>To the first argument.</margin>
**TO** the first argument, therefore, it is responded that either the heretics are blasphemous regarding this by comparing church singers with the priests of Baal. For Elijah did not mock them because they sang, but because they worshipped stones, and marbles, and dead men, and finally demons in that manner, whom they thought had to be aroused to hear by shouting. But those who sing to arouse the joy of the soul and devotion, or to return that honor to God, are worthy of praise, not blame. Just like the Jerusalemites acclaiming "Save us!" <note>original: "Hosanna."</note> to Christ. And the children in the furnace, like angels, singing hymns. Therefore, no other comparison which they bring from human majesty to the divine has any relevance to the matter. For it is not fitting to pour out prayers by singing before human princes because they are not to be worshipped as gods; although the praises of heroes, as we said above, are accustomed to be sung in their presence.

<margin>To the second.</margin>

The matter is otherwise concerning solemn ceremonies which are done in the public name. Nor is there anything absurd if, while it is being sung in the choir, the people listen if they cannot pray.

<margin>To the last.</margin>
To the last word it is responded that secular music is not permitted in churches; but church music is not profane.

### ARTICLE III.

*Whether all those who have been initiated into holy orders, as well as those who hold the title of an ecclesiastical priesthood, are bound to say the Hours.*

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'I' featuring two figures in a landscape setting.</image-desc>In the first article, it was shown how, for the sake of praying solemnly, it was necessary for four things to be established: namely, the persons, the substance of the prayers, the places, and the times. To these, from the very nature of the matter, a fifth is understood to be added, namely intention and attention. Therefore, regarding the first point—the persons—we shall speak in this article; regarding the remaining points, we shall speak in those that follow.

But it is argued that not all who are initiated into holy orders are bound to the divine office by that argument which we touched upon above. <margin>First argument.</margin> In the church, the duties of the clergy are distributed: for some are assigned to the care of souls, while others are assigned either to preaching or to other business pertaining to the affairs of the church. Therefore, there is no reason why those who are thus hindered by other duties should be bound to the canonical hours. 

¶ In the same way, it is argued secondly <margin>Second.</margin> that not even all those holding ecclesiastical priesthoods <note>Soto uses "sacerdotia" here to refer generally to ecclesiastical benefices or offices.</note> are bound to pay the hours: partly because benefices are instituted for diverse duties—such as *praestimonia* <term>praestimonia: funds or lands set aside to support a cleric, often specifically for their education</term> which, as it is said, were established for the sake of study—and partly also because, by the same reasoning, those who are being tested in a religious order before their profession would be bound to perform the canonical office, since they are supported by those fruits which the people bestow upon the religious for the sake of such spiritual duties. This, however, is not consistent with reason. 

¶ Finally, it is argued thirdly: <margin>Third.</margin> If such clerics were bound to say the hours, it would be primarily by divine law, upon which the religious observance of the canonical hours was shown above to be founded. But if this is true, it seems to follow that the Pope cannot grant a dispensation regarding them; however, custom and usage hold the contrary. 

¶ On the other hand, there is the chapter *Presbyter* in the section "On the Celebration of Masses" <note>original: "cap. Presbyter. de celebratione Missarum," a reference to Canon Law</note>, by which all priests are bound to the divine office. In that text, the name "priest," according to the gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria" was the standard commentary on Canon Law.</note>, is extended to all clerics, following the tenor of the chapter *Si quisquā* in the section "On the Cohabitation of Clerics and Women."

Regarding this question, some things are established among the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to established academic and theological authorities.</note>, while others can hardly 

<column-break/>

be defined with certain reason. Two causes, I say, are held as certain, each of which by itself <margin>From which things the obligation to perform the canonical hours arises.</margin> binds one to the task of the canonical hours: namely, holy orders and an ecclesiastical benefice <note>A "benefice" is a church office that provides an income.</note>. 

¶ Therefore, the question is answered with two conclusions. 

First conclusion: <margin>First conclusion.</margin> Every cleric in holy orders—namely, a subdeacon and those superior to him—is bound to perform the day and night office. This is the conclusion held by the gloss, <margin>The Gloss. Panormitanus.</margin> and it is embraced by Panormitanus <note>Niccolò de' Tudeschi, a famous 15th-century canon lawyer.</note> and the other Doctors of canon law of chief renown, regarding the said chapter *Presbyter* on the celebration of Masses. It is also the opinion of Saint Thomas <margin>St. Thomas.</margin> in *Quodlibeta* 6, article 8, and the unanimous view of the theologians. 

For although in the said chapter—which, as we said above, is from the Council of Agde—mention is made only of the priest, nevertheless, <margin>Innocent</margin> Innocent III, in the chapter *Dolentes*, also expresses this for minor clerics. And in Distinction 92, in the final chapter, the priest, deacon, and any cleric are more expressly bound to the daily office. 

The reason, however—which <margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin> is the best interpreter of the law—emerges from this: that he who is initiated into holy orders is assigned to the singular worship of God and is established in that state which was instituted for divine praises. This is according to Isaiah 43: "Everyone who invokes my name, I have created him for my praise." <note>original: "Omnem illum qui inuocat nomen meū, in laudem meam creaui illum."</note> However, the order and manner of these praises, as we said above, has been sanctioned by the law of the church. Therefore, by the very fact that someone is received into the order of clerics, he is bound by such a bond. 

For this reason, I greatly desire all clerics to be most fully persuaded of this: that whatever business weighs upon them, whether the study of literature, or the duty of governing or reading, or even preaching, they should hold it as most fixed never to interrupt any canonical hour. They should know for certain that this is their own genuine duty, and thus to be preferred above all others. This is especially true because the time dedicated to fixed prayers—no matter what other business it is cut from—is never a hindrance (God so disposing) to that business being well dispatched. 

¶ Regarding clerics, however, who are established in minor orders and who enjoy no ecclesiastical prebend <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a stipend.</note>, although <margin>Clerics established in minor orders are bound to no canonical hours.</margin> Panormitanus in the place cited leans toward the other side, it must be believed without doubt that they are bound to no canonical hours. Nor is his reason of any weight—namely, that as the very name "cleric" sounds, they are "taken into the lot of the Lord." <margin>Panormitanus.</margin> <note>original: "assumuntur in sortem domini." This refers to the etymology of "cleric," from the Greek *kleros*, meaning "lot" or "inheritance."</note> For they are not so "taken" as to firmly change their state; for as long as they are free to join themselves in marriage, they do not change their state.

<summary>Soto establishes that all clergy in Major Orders (subdeacons and above) or those holding a benefice are legally and morally bound to recite the Divine Office, regardless of other duties like preaching or study. He argues that minor clerics not holding a benefice are exempt because they have not yet made an irrevocable change in their legal state (such as the ability to marry).</summary>

<margin>Paludanus. <note>original: "Pierre de la Palud," a 14th-century French theologian and canonist.</note></margin>
...They argue this because the function of those minor orders is completed solely in the preparation of the temple and the sacred vessels; such an order does not have an immediate connection to the Sacrament of the Eucharist, as do the offices of deacon and subdeacon. There is no law or custom that imposes such a religious scruple, nor can a bishop mandate this obligation.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
**Second conclusion.** Whoever holds an ecclesiastical benefice <term>benefice: an official church position or "living" that provides an income to the holder</term> or a prebend <term>prebend: a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church</term> under a clerical title, is bound under the guilt of mortal sin to the full office of the canonical hours. This conclusion is to be understood with the same precision as the previous one. Therefore, just as a holy order binds a person even without a benefice, so too does a benefice bind a person even without a holy order.

<margin>Proof of the first conclusion <note>referring to the second conclusion above.</note></margin>
Regarding this conclusion, I have not seen an express text of law; however, it is noted in the final chapter of Distinction 92, whose words state that a priest, or deacon, or any cleric assigned to a church, is bound to the daily office. In that text, the word "assigned" is understood to mean by the title of some benefice, so as to distinguish them from the previous members mentioned—the priest and deacon. The final chapter of *On Rescripts* in the Sixth Book <note>original: "lib. 6," referring to the *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law</note> also supports this: "A benefice is not given except for an office." For the specific and proper office of a cleric, as we said above, is the weight of the canonical hours. This is also supported by the chapter *Since according to the Apostle* regarding prebends, where it is decreed that all clerics are chosen for a burden, and thus should not be kept from their reward. Consequently, it is ordered that no one should be ordained without a title of either a benefice or an inheritance; or if it happens otherwise, the bishop must provide him with a living. Since, therefore, the reward is owed because of the burden, and the proper burden of a cleric is to say the office, it follows that this obligation arises from any prebend whatsoever. For this reason, we have moderated the conclusion such that such a prebend is possessed under a clerical title:

<margin>Moderation of the conclusion.</margin>
for those who receive tithes through a secular title, such as kings and knights, or a preacher or lecturer, are not bound to pay the debt of these hours.

<margin>Those who possess *praestimonial* priesthoods are bound to the divine office.</margin>
For this reason, I would not dare to excuse those who possess *praestimonial* priesthoods <term>praestimonia: funds or lands set aside for the support of a cleric, often specifically for students</term> from performing the divine office, though others may feel differently. This is because that title is clerical, not secular. For their claim—that these were instituted only for the sake of

<column-break/>

study—does not carry enough legal authority to exempt them from such a duty. Therefore, in the chapter *Since* regarding the granting of prebends in the Sixth Book, *praestimonia* are numbered among other ecclesiastical titles.

<margin>The opinion of Laurentius is rejected.</margin>
<margin>Sylvester.</margin>
<margin>Panormitanus.</margin>
<margin>Johannes Andreae.</margin>
Consequently, the opinion of Laurentius is not upheld, as Sylvester rightly says under the word "hour," section 3. Laurentius claimed that clerics in minor orders who hold benefices and serve through others could be excused from the divine office. Rather, Panormitanus <note>Nicola de Tudeschis, a famous 15th-century canonist.</note> says in the place cited that since paying the hours is a personal duty, they are always bound to it. And although Johannes Andreae <note>A renowned 14th-century canonist.</note> says in his *Novellae* that he would gladly see the church free such beneficed clerics in minor orders (who do not have the care of souls) for the sake of their studies, so that they would only recite the Office of the Virgin, this would certainly not be healthy advice. This is because ecclesiastical stipends are paid, as we said, primarily for these offices.

<margin>A pensioner alone is not bound to the hours.</margin>
However, regarding those who only have pensions, because they have no ecclesiastical title but merely a right to seek payment from the one who holds the title, we have already said many times that they are by no means bound to the canonical hours.

<margin>Doubt.</margin>
¶ A doubt remains, however, when a prebend is extremely meager. For there are some who affirm this conclusion to such an extent that even when the benefice is so tiny that it does not suffice even for leading a wretched life, they nevertheless judge it to bind. Indeed, even if one has the mere title without any fruits <note>Revenue or income produced by the benefice.</note>, they do not excuse him from fault if he omits the canonical hours. Sylvester follows this in his entry for "hour," section 3.

<margin>Sylvester's solution.</margin>
<margin>Sylvester’s solution is refuted.</margin>
So do some of the most recent theologians. But truly, I would subscribe much more willingly to the contrary opinion. For since a cleric below the rank of subdeacon is bound to the divine office for no other reason than his stipend, when the benefice is so small that it is considered almost nothing, there is no reason why it should induce such an obligation. Nor does the objection of those who say the fault is to be imputed to the one who accepted it prevail; for an extremely tiny benefice, by its very nature, does not bind. Therefore, he who receives it is not bound. I would call it "extremely tiny" if it is regarded as almost nothing: namely, if in these times it did not reach a sum of at least eight ducats. For if it is richer, even if it does not suffice for a living, if it can still be a good part of the support for a poor cleric, he is not entirely excused from possessing it. On this matter, therefore, the wisdom of the learned must be consulted.

<margin>He who only has the title of a benefice without fruits.</margin>
¶ In the same way, one should judge regarding the man who holds either a litigious title (as Paludanus says) or a mere title of a prebend without the fruits, and that by the grant of the Pope, those same fruits...

# Question 5 of the Tenth Book

<margin>Jerome.</margin>
and it is referenced in Decree 16, question 1: <note>original: "Alia est inquit causa monachi, alia clerici: illi de altario viuūt &c."</note> "The case of a monk," he says, "is one thing, and that of a cleric is another; those [clerics] live from the altar, etc." And to the monk Rusticus: "Live so in the monastery that you may deserve to be a cleric; when the people elect you as a cleric, perform those things which belong to a cleric." Therefore, the order of the religious differs from the clerical order in this: that clerics are assigned to the service of churches, while the religious are assigned to nothing but contemplation. This distinction is supported by the divine
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
Thomas [Aquinas] in the *Summa Theologiae*, Second Part of the Second Part, in the final question, article 8, in the response to the second objection. The second reason, which is the most famous among all, namely that they live on alms <note>original: "eleemosynis"</note> which are distributed to them by the common people for the sake of divine worship, seems to have no greater weight of force.
<margin>The second reason is also ineffective.</margin>
For tithes <term>tithes: a tenth of one's income paid to the church</term> are the proper reward of those serving the churches; other alms do not have that burden attached to them. Furthermore, monasteries that live from tithes are rare. Besides, such tithes could be awarded to them, just as to other hospitals for the poor, without such a burden. And those who live without tithes, though they receive alms, receive them just as other poor people do. And even if they are bound to pray for their benefactors, they are not for that reason bound to perform the canonical office. ¶ Moreover,
<margin>Argument.</margin>
an argument occurs to me that is most troublesome of all. If a religious person assigned to the choir <note>Members of an order specifically tasked with singing the liturgy in the church choir.</note> who is not yet in sacred orders were bound to the office, he could not be exempt from that burden without a dispensation from the Pope. And yet, if in the same religious order he becomes a lay brother (whom we call "converts" <note>original: "Conuersos"; lay brothers who performed manual labor rather than liturgical duties.</note>), he will no longer be bound to the canonical office. Such a change requires no Papal dispensation, but can be done solely by the assent of the prelate. It will perhaps seem strange to anyone that a prelate alone could free a monk from the obligation of performing the office to which he was bound. For if you say that someone who holds a church benefit <note>original: "beneficium"</note> is similarly bound, but is freed from that obligation if he leaves it, you offer no similarity to our case: for that obligation existed only because of the payment. The obligation of a monk, however, ought to exist by reason of his status, which he cannot leave. Therefore, he who is removed from the choir to become a lay brother does not change his religious status. If, therefore, the lay brother is not bound, it appears that neither is the one assigned to the choir, unless he is in sacred orders. A similar argument, or rather a stronger one, is made concerning nuns who, being removed from the choir, become lay sisters. ¶ If you were to argue against us in turn that at least such

<column-break/>

religious are bound by the bond of their rule, we do not dispute this. For they will then be bound, at least in our order, not to guilt [mortal sin], but to penalty: as we are about to say regarding lay religious. The question, however, concerns a precept such as exists for subdeacons and above. ¶ Notwithstanding these things, although it cannot be denied that if you consider only the force of reason, they move one greatly; yet it must not be denied that the most celebrated and laudable custom, approved by the unanimous consent of the ancient
<margin>The solution of the proposed conclusion.</margin>
fathers, has the force of a precept: namely, that no religious person dedicated to the choir is exempt from such an obligation to perform the divine office. Indeed, one must not stand upon mere custom here, but the law itself must be recognized. ¶ It is argued, therefore, in confirmation of the present opinion: All and each
<margin>The following assertion persuades [us].</margin>
monastic community of whatever spiritual order, who are approved by the Church under the logic of a solemn vow, are bound to celebrate the divine office in common. Therefore, as many as are assigned to that same duty are bound to pay the same office that they would have sung publicly in the choir whenever they are absent from it. Truly, no one could, nor would anyone dare to deny the premise: for when the Church instituted religious orders according to the Gospel—those, namely, which she admitted for the sake of spiritual matters—she devoted them to divine praises. Since that is the chief duty of contemplation, if, where it is possible, through the prelate's negligence such an office
<margin>A prelate's negligence regarding the performance of the divine office in common is a mortal sin.</margin>
were not performed in common, it would be a mortal crime for him without doubt. I speak of the ancient orders: for if another mode of religious life were admitted without this kind of obligation, it would certainly hardly deserve the name of "religion," as it would lack the greatest splendor of religious life. Someone might perhaps deny the logical consequence of the argument, thinking it sufficient that those in sacred orders perform such an office, while the rest do so only while they are present in the choir. Yet the consequence has the greatest probability because the entire religious order is devoted to that same duty. Thus, just as a cleric is bound to the office by reason of his order, so too a religious person assigned to the choir is bound by reason of his religious status. Therefore, St. Thomas, in the place recently cited (2.2, final question, in the solution
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
to the second objection), whatever Cajetan may think, exempts only the lay monks from the office of the clerics. ¶ If this holds true for religious men, it must also be judged so for nuns. Namely, that they are bound to the divine office in common where possible; but if not, then privately.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
¶ Therefore, in response to the first argument, it is said that although the state of monks is dedicated to contemplation, that contemplation consists most especially in the fulfillment of the Divine Office <note>The Divine Office, or canonical hours, refers to the structured cycle of daily prayers, psalms, and readings performed by clergy and religious orders.</note>. At the very least, that is the most powerful effect of contemplation.

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ As for the other argument, which I confess is difficult, the response is that a person is obligated to perform the hours of their status by reason of being assigned to the choir; however, in whatever way one is removed from it, they become free from that bond. For the Apostolic See <note>The central authority of the Catholic Church, the Papacy.</note> granted the superiors of religious orders this power of liberation during the founding of those orders. Even if these reasons could not be fully resolved, custom should nonetheless prevail, which is considered to have the force of a command among all the fathers of religious orders. Furthermore, if this permission were granted—that religious, and especially nuns, were not held to the Divine Office—there would be no spiritual exercise left for them to spend their time on according to the purpose of their institution. In truth, I confess for myself that I sense some kind of error creeping in whenever the thought enters my mind to deny that such an illustrious custom has the force of a command.

<margin>Paludanus.</margin>
<margin>Sylvester. Non-professed monks are not bound to the divine office, contrary to Paludanus, Augustinus de Anchona, and Antoninus. Sylvester.</margin>
¶ As for those who have not yet professed their vows, although Petrus de Palude <note>Peter of the Palatinate (c. 1275–1342), a Dominican theologian.</note> in the cited place (Book 4, distinction 15, question 5) thinks they are bound on two counts—namely, that they are supported by alms and that they enjoy the privileges of the religious—this assertion is not based on any law, as Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian known for his "Summa Sylvestrina."</note> rightly says in the cited place; thus, there is no reason to accept it. Indeed, since they possess neither the religious nor the clerical status, no cause remains to bind them.

<margin>Similarly, regarding lay religious brothers, Augustinus de Anchona—whom the Blessed Antoninus cites and seems to follow in Part 3, Title 13, Chapter 4—judged that they are held to their prescribed divine office under the guilt of mortal sin. However, others guess better at the matter, and Sylvester embraces their opinion there: namely, that they are not so bound, since they are not dedicated to the Divine Office.</margin>
<margin>The author's judgment on lay monks.</margin>
Therefore, if a superior of a religious order should enjoin that lay order to pray, it will have no other force of command than what is expressed in that specific religion. Thus, in our order <note>The Dominican Order (Order of Preachers).</note>, that bond will not obligate one to a fault <note>Meaning it is not a "sin" in the legalistic sense.</note>, except where contempt has crept in, but rather to a penalty at the discretion of the superior.

<margin>To the first main argument.</margin>
To the first main argument, then, the response is that however other clerical duties may be distributed,

<column-break/>

the burden of the canonical hours is common to all. And likewise, it is responded to the second argument that whatever priesthood someone possesses under a clerical title, even a "prestimonial" one <term>prestimonial: a type of ecclesiastical endowment or income traditionally given to support a cleric without a formal "benefice" or parish assignment</term>, they are bound to fulfill the office, as was shown regarding the second conclusion. And regarding non-professed religious, it has already been declared that they are not bound.

<margin>To the third.</margin>
¶ Finally, to the third argument, in which a question was asked about dispensation from this bond: the response is that this obligation is partly of divine law and partly of positive law <note>In theology, "Divine Law" is seen as unchanging and from God, while "Positive Law" refers to rules established by human church authorities.</note>. For in general, that all clerics in holy orders are bound to fulfill some divine office is of divine law, over which the Pope cannot dispense. However, that this or that specific prayer is said is a matter of ecclesiastical positive law—as will immediately be clear in the next article—over which the Pope can therefore dispense when a legitimate reason requires it.

### ARTICLE IV.
### *Whether some order and manner is necessary for fulfilling the Divine Office.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial P featuring a dense floral and leaf pattern inside a square frame.</image-desc>
After seeing who those people are who are bound to say the Divine Office, there follow three other circumstances: namely, what, when, and where; for the manner of it must be addressed in the subsequent article. And it is argued that as far as substance is concerned, no specific office is determined; for, as held in the canon:
<margin>First argument.</margin>
"in die" under Consecration, distinction 5, different churches and religious orders sing different things. And in the canon "placuit," distinction 12, it is forbidden for the customs of monasteries to be mixed with those of secular churches; therefore, nothing certain has been established that must necessarily be sung by all.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Second. Nor are the times necessary: because the order is not of the essence, as is almost the common practice of clerics; and the chapter "presbyter" regarding the celebration of Masses suggests this, commanding that a rural priest fulfill the burden of the other hours immediately after the morning office, before he visits the sick and goes out into the countryside. Therefore, the temporal order of the hours is not necessary. Indeed, neither is the circumstance of the place, because wherever someone performs the office, even outside a church, they fulfill the command.

¶ On the contrary, however, are the canons "de his" and "placuit" in the 12th distinction, where it is commanded that the same order of chanting according to the metropolitan church <note>The principal church of an ecclesiastical province, usually the seat of an Archbishop.</note> should be held by everyone.

### Question V of the Tenth Book

And in the cited chapter *Dolentes* <note>original: "Dolentes"; a chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX concerning the celebration of Masses, emphasizing the need for focused prayer</note>, devotion and attention are commanded.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
We proposed five things to be disputed in the previous article regarding the canonical hours: namely, who is bound, to what, when, where, and how. Since the first was settled there, and the fifth requires a special article, it remains for us to answer the present question according to the numbering of others with three conclusions. The first, regarding the substance of the prayers, is: Those things which are established to be sung or recited in the canonical hours are not exactly the same in all churches and religious orders. The root of this conclusion is what we touched upon in the last article: namely, that although the payment of the divine office is commanded by divine and natural law, nonetheless, what they should say—this or that—is pontifical law <note>Human-made church law as opposed to immutable divine law</note>. Therefore, these things vary according to the different seasons of the year, different provinces, and the temperaments of men.

<margin>Gregory VII</margin>
Hence, in the canon *In die*, regarding consecration, distinction 5, Gregory VII <note>Pope from 1073 to 1085, a major reformer of the medieval church</note> says that in the Easter season, only three psalms and as many readings are sung. The cause of this is understood to be twofold or threefold: namely, to refresh the spirits after the labor of Lent, and to signify both the days in which Christ remained in the tomb and the joy of the Resurrection. On other feasts, however, nine psalms are sung with the same number of readings; but on ordinary days, three readings are sufficient. Yet the "black monks" <note>The Benedictines, named for the color of their habits</note> sing twelve psalms, and others eighteen; still others are content with three psalms throughout the entire circle of the year. As the Pope says in that place, they are proven to do this not from the rule of the holy fathers, but out of weariness and negligence. Thus, in the chapter *Novit*, distinction 12, the same Pope warns Augustine of the English <note>St. Augustine of Canterbury, sent to convert Anglo-Saxon England</note> that he should strive to collect from many churches those things by which he might more healthfully institute that new church.

<margin>Canon law regarding the hours of chanting.</margin>
¶ But truly, even if churches vary somewhat, that law must nonetheless be observed which is established in the same distinction, in the canons *De his* and *Placuit*: namely, that there be one manner of chanting according to the custom of the metropolitan church, and in religious orders according to the statutes of each. And although it is the opinion of some that anyone may follow the use of the Roman Church, I would not easily believe that this is free for individual persons without the authority of the Pope. For what Augustine of the English is warned of in the cited chapter *Novit*—to consult the custom of the Roman Church—is understood to be for the purpose of sanctioning the laws of that new church,

<margin>Individual persons are not free to follow the Roman use</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>reciting the hours without the authority of a superior.</margin>
not, however, so that each person might take the same license privately. Therefore, although I would not dare to completely contradict the opinion of Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note>, who says in his *Summa* that it is not a mortal sin to discharge the office of the saints on a day when it should be of the ferial day <note>A standard weekday office without a specific saint's feast</note>, nor to discharge it according to the Roman rite when it should be according to the monastic institution; nevertheless, it is not entirely without fault. Nor should the reins be so loosely released in such a matter. Rather, Bishops and the prefects of religious orders ought to completely restrain such audacity: namely, lest any of the clerics or religious discharge the office privately in a different way than they would in the choir.

<margin>The guidance of the Directory has no legal foundation.</margin>
For that guidance in the *Directory* <note>A guide for reciting the office</note>, which claims that one who is ordained to the title of a patrimony <note>Ordained based on private family wealth rather than a church appointment</note> can discharge whichever divine office he pleases, has no foundation in law. For the obligation of praying does not arise solely from a benefice <note>An ecclesiastical office providing income</note>, but from clerical status. Therefore, everyone is bound to be subject to their mother church in this as well, unless they have obtained a priesthood in another church; for then they ought to sing, and indeed pray, according to the custom of that place. And if one holds a benefice in several churches, he ought to follow the one he is more bound to serve. ¶ I confess, indeed, that the excessive length of the psalms and the most troublesome repetition of some prayers often deter the subjects of certain churches from discharging the office in that manner, and thus are the cause for them seeking a more concise Breviary <note>The book containing the Divine Office</note>. For this, as we said in Book 1, legislators ought to foresee above all else: lest they pass those laws which the passage of time might corrode because of their intolerability. For men who are more pious than they are prudent think they are consulting the matter well if they pile psalms upon psalms and prayers upon prayers by law; yet they instead offer the occasion for such institutions of prayer to perish more quickly. It was once most holily instituted that the office should depend very frequently on the season; by which reasoning the entire Psalter recurred weekly. However, the suffrages for the living and the dead, prayers, and litanies were later increased so much that they have now moved toward devising very short feasts of saints. This is to the point that not even in Lent or for three days is the office of the most holy season celebrated; which surely, especially among the religious, is not fitting by reason of study. In our order <note>The Dominicans (Order of Preachers)</note>, however, moderation <note>original: "mediocritati"; here meaning a balanced middle path</note> was always so provided for that the office of the season is most frequent for us through use. ¶ Through these things, if they are true, one can weigh...
