# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>Critique of the Roman Breviary.</margin>
Everyone can weigh the observations we began to make in Book 1 regarding the most recent Roman Breviary <note>The "Breviary" is the book containing the hymns, psalms, and readings for the daily cycle of prayer. Soto is likely referring to the reformed Breviary of Pope Quiñones (1535), which was controversial for its brevity.</note>. First, the purpose of praying is not to learn the Psalms or to study the Sacred Scriptures—as is suggested there—but to speak praises to God and to pour out prayers. For this reason, one should not look down upon the responsories, antiphons, hymns, and other songs which were established not only by such a long line of Holy Fathers with great meditation and consultation regarding the requirements of each season, but were even brought down from heaven by the angelic choir. Indeed, if (as we said in the same place) the antiquity of civil law is worthy of such honor that it should not be changed except out of the most urgent necessity, it should be permitted much less in the laws and institutions of sacred things, with which the people have been imbued from of old.

<margin>A pretext.</margin>
¶ But they say that this Breviary was not devised to be sung publicly in churches, but so that each person might fulfill their daily portion of the hours privately. This pretext, however, is surely the cause of many inconveniences.

<margin>The preceding argument is refuted.</margin>
For first, since the assembly of clerics is made up of all individuals, if they once become accustomed to that private mode of praying, they will easily admit it into public use. This has already been attempted in a certain church in Spain. This was heard at the Council of Trent <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the major 16th-century ecumenical council that addressed the challenges of the Protestant Reformation and reformed Catholic practice.</note> not without sorrow and scandal; for when the people did not hear the accustomed services during Lent and Holy Week, they could not help but be disturbed by intense sadness and scandal. And even if this danger did not exist, it has already become so accepted by the custom of church canons to fulfill the hours at home via that Breviary, that they sit mute in the choir—and would that they were as attentive as the laity! They are too forgetful that they receive stipends <note>Payments made to clergy for their service.</note> not just to be present and merely be a number, but truly to sing the psalms. For the law says, "A benefice is not given except for the sake of the duty" <note>original: "beneficium... non datur nisi propter officium"; a fundamental legal principle of the Church stating that the income from a church position is tied to the performance of its spiritual tasks.</note>. On the contrary, matters have reached the point that they disdain to sing and think it a slight to their majesty; instead, they delegate it to chaplains of a lower class. See how unmindful they are of their duty: I myself was asked by one of them whether they satisfy the debt of performing the hours if they do not perform them at home, but by singing in the choir. Truly, hearing this, I was moved on one hand to laughter and on the other to sadness. Observe, therefore, how much care must be taken so that no one fulfills the divine office privately in any other way than it is fulfilled in the choir. Furthermore, as Gregory says in the day cited above, to sing only three psalms (which that Breviary has) 

<column-break/>

arises from negligence and a weariness of the divine office, and is against the most holy and ancient custom of the Church regarding the three "nocturns" <note>Nocturns are divisions of the night-time prayer service (Matins). Traditional services had more psalms than the reformed versions Soto is criticizing.</note> which we demonstrated in the first article. Now, therefore, especially at this time when heretics <note>Referring to Protestant reformers who were simplifying or abolishing traditional liturgical forms.</note> are striving to drive the most holy institution of prayer from the Church, it should be asserted with all care and vigilance, and if it falters in any part, it should be restored.

<margin>Controversy regarding the Office of the Blessed Virgin.</margin>
¶ Regarding the Office of the Blessed Virgin <note>Often called the "Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary," a shorter cycle of prayers in her honor.</note>, there is likewise a controversy among the Doctors as to whether it is also a commanded obligation, because no law exists regarding this matter, but only custom. Indeed, if you consult history, the practice is not ancient, but perhaps from three hundred years ago. For before the times of Bernard and the institution of the Mendicant orders <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux (12th century) and orders like the Dominicans and Franciscans (Mendicants) were key in spreading devotion to Mary.</note>, such great devotion to the Virgin had not become widespread. Therefore, if one may proceed by conjectures, this custom did not begin as having the force of a command (otherwise it would be read somewhere), but out of piety and devotion, of which the most holy Virgin was most worthy. And some evidence of this is that in the institution of our order <note>Soto was a Dominican; the "Order of Preachers."</note>, it was commanded that the brothers, rising in the dormitory, should fulfill the night office of the Virgin by reciting it; if this were an ecclesiastical command, it would be ordered to be fulfilled in the choir.

<margin>The Office of the Virgin is owed by command.</margin>
But truly, regarding the course of the Office of the Blessed Virgin, the custom of the time has so prevailed that no doctor or holy father would dare to deny that it has the force of a command. Therefore, it ought not to be driven out entirely from ecclesiastical custom, although the cited Breviary has dissolved that kind of bond. For now the clergy possess ecclesiastical priesthoods as if by secular right: namely, because they either inherit them from predecessors as successors, or acquire them by their own cleverness and the spending of money, so that they hardly think they are bound to the office. Instead, putting it behind all other business, they take care daily to make it lighter.

<margin>St. Thomas on the Office of the Dead.</margin>
¶ Regarding the Office of the Dead <note>Prayers specifically for the souls in Purgatory.</note>, the same must be thought: although this custom, as Saint Thomas suggests in *Quodlibet* 6, article 8 <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas's "Quodlibetal Questions," a collection of his academic debates.</note>, was introduced more by reason of the "prebends" <note>The portion of church revenues granted to a cleric.</note> which the clerics possess than by reason of the order itself. For it is manifest that all clerics in holy orders are bound to the Office of Souls on the day after the Feast of All Saints, since it is proper to that day; but as for the other office, which is performed in different ways daily or weekly according to the customs of various churches, it appears that only those who live off tithes are bound: namely, the beneficiaries <note>Clergy who hold a "benefice" or paid church office.</note>, as Saint Thomas seems to judge there, even those who are in schools.

He also explores whether supplemental devotions like the Office of the Virgin Mary have become legally mandatory through long-standing custom.</summary>

### Question V of the Tenth Book

And therefore, in religious orders, individual clerics are bound according to their own statutes, as I reckon, under the penalty of mortal sin <note>A "mortal sin" is considered a grave offense that separates the soul from God's grace, as opposed to a "venial" or lesser sin.</note> to discharge that duty. However, for secular clerics who hold no ecclesiastical <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office that provides an income or living.</note>, it is not as certain that they are compelled by law to such a burden; nevertheless, since they are already consecrated to sacred things, they seem to be bound by the custom of the church to which they are subject.

<margin>On the litanies added to the night office</margin>
¶ Finally, regarding the litanies that are added to the night office <note>Matins and Lauds, usually prayed in the early morning or late night.</note> on ferial days <note>Non-feast days.</note>, I think those who judge that such a custom does not have the force of a command are correct. For they do not have the form of being part of the Divine Office itself, but are certain prayers addressed to the saints, offered by those who have already fulfilled their duty to God. And perhaps they had their origin among the religious orders because of the "satisfactory scourgings" <note>original: "satisfactoria flagella." This refers to the practice of ritual self-flagellation or physical penance common in medieval monastic life.</note> with which they were then whipped. Therefore, it is now decreed in our Order <note>Soto was a Dominican friar.</note> that only the choir should say the Litanies; those who pray privately, however, are released from saying them.

¶ Next follows the time and order of the hours
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
**Second conclusion.** Although in a communal setting it is so necessary for the Office to be performed at the hours established by the Church that its omission is a mortal sin, nevertheless, to change the times and order in private, while it may involve some fault, is not a mortal sin.

<margin>Proof of the first part of the conclusion.</margin>
The first part of the conclusion is established by the fact that—as shown in Article 1—the Church established the hours for public praises for the most holy reasons, and especially so that the people would know at what time they ought to gather in the church. Therefore, if that order were interrupted, the Church would suffer a very grave offense. The magnitude of the fault is estimated from the gravity of the object; therefore, it would be mortal. Hence, in the <term>Clementines</term> <note>A collection of canon laws promulgated by Pope Clement V.</note>, book 1, "On the celebration of Masses," the council says: "We are moved by grave disturbance that, through the negligence of some rectors, etc." From this it follows that a crime of this sort should be charged to the superiors, and to those upon whom the public care rests to ensure that the Divine Office is performed in common. Hence, to signify how much this matters, the council adds: "We decree that those to whom it pertains, etc." and further: "that in cathedral, regular, and collegial churches, the psalms be sung devoutly at the due hours."

<margin>The second part of the conclusion is urged.</margin>
¶ The second part of the conclusion is indeed proven. For the fact that the time and order are changed by private persons, since it does not happen in the sight of the people, does not carry so much absurdity that it induces a lethal stain of sin. On the contrary, although

<column-break/>

when it is done without cause, it is at least not free from venial fault, yet sometimes it brings no fault at all. For he who, I say, passes over the established hour without any cause, undoubtedly sins at least venially. For what I am not afraid to emphasize over and over again: since this is the cleric's proper duty, he ought to prefer it before all other business—namely, that when it is sung in the choir, he himself should discharge the office, so that he may be seen to pray with the others. This is especially true because if you once pass over the legitimate hour, the danger is imminent that, by putting the matter off until night, you will discharge your debt unworthily by mumbling rather than by praying—which is foul. Therefore, as is noted in the chapter *Presbyter* <note>original: "c. presbyter." A reference to a specific section of Canon Law.</note> "On the celebration of the Mass," it is better for him who fears an impediment to perform the hours early rather than late.

<margin>The famous assertion of the Summists is explained.</margin>
Therefore, when you read in some <term>Summist</term> <note>Authors of "Summæ," which were encyclopedic handbooks of moral theology for confessors.</note> that the order of the hours is not a matter of command, temper that with two qualifications: namely, as it applies to those who pray privately; and further, that it does not bind them under mortal guilt. Nevertheless, if someone—whether through fault or without it—omits to say, for example, Prime or Terce, or even the night office when he ought to have, if a time later occurs when he can attend the choir, it is more advisable that he discharge the later hours there first, and afterwards the earlier ones privately, rather than being absent from the choir just to maintain the chronological order.

¶ Furthermore, concerning the order of the Mass among the other hours, 
<margin>Veruecensis. Sylvester.</margin>

Sylvester says the same thing, claiming that all the Summists hold this. And 
<margin>Antoninus. Hostiensis. It is not a mortal sin to celebrate Mass before the Matin office has been completed.</margin>

However, this is said without any legal basis or support of reason. Nor is custom to be thought in any way to involve such a command. For the sacrifice of the Mass is not numbered among the <term>canonical hours</term> <note>The seven times of daily prayer: Matins/Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline.</note>, since there are only seven; but by itself, from ancient times, it had its own stated times—at least the "High Mass," which they call the Greater Mass: namely, on feast days after Terce <note>Around 9:00 AM.</note> (according to "On Consecration," distinction 1, canon *Nocte*), and on ferial days after Sext <note>Noon.</note> (as in the canon *Solent*), and on fast days after None <note>Around 3:00 PM.</note>. Concerning private Masses, however, nothing is cautioned, except that—unless by privilege—they should not be celebrated after midday nor before dawn, except on the night of the Nativity of the Lord (Christmas). If, therefore, it is not a mortal sin to discharge the night office at the sixth or ninth hour of the day, I do not know from where it is inferred that [to celebrate...]

to celebrate Mass before [the Office] is a mortal sin: since the offices are distinct, and one does not have a necessary order in relation to the other. Perhaps due to custom, it would be a venial <note>A minor, forgivable sin.</note> fault, where it could be done conveniently, if the night office <note>The prayers of Matins and Lauds, typically said in the middle of the night or early morning.</note> were not finished first; for to anticipate the order for some cause is no fault: as if for him who has not yet said Matins, a cause for celebrating [Mass] is pressing: because either a superior commanded it, or someone offers an alms that he say it immediately. Indeed, truly if someone, because of some illness, had a legitimate excuse for not performing the divine office, I do not see why he could not perform the sacred rite of the Mass: although he neither said nor was going to say the remaining hours.

<margin>It is better to be present in the choir for Prime after celebrating Mass than to perform it before Mass.</margin>
¶ Regarding <term>Prime</term> <note>The first of the "Little Hours" of the Divine Office, traditionally prayed at daybreak.</note> however, no scruple <note>A doubt or hesitation based on moral or legal grounds.</note> remains. For those who are ordered in a convent to say the dawn Mass and the rest before Prime, they will do better to attend the choir for Prime after the celebration of Mass, rather than performing it before Mass: unless you wish to obligate them to say the same thing twice: which would be ridiculous. Therefore, the legitimate order is that you perform the divine office at its proper hours: but a private mass when it shall be more expedient. Although it is fitting that if you celebrate after Prime, you should perform it first.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
¶ After this, concerning the place where the hours are to be said, a third conclusion is established almost like the one above. The hours indeed, in common and solemnly, are to be celebrated in the church by precept <note>A formal command or rule.</note>: but privately they can be said anywhere.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
The first part is similarly known as above: for temples are constructed and destined for this, so that the hours may be celebrated there just like the solemnities of Masses. Wherefore in the *Clementines* <note>A collection of canon laws promulgated by Pope Clement V.</note> in the chapter *on the celebration of Masses*, the hours are ordered to be sung in churches. Nothing however prevents the same offices from being sung in the halls of princes, and elsewhere by privilege. Although Mass indeed should not be permitted at home. But about this elsewhere. Privately indeed there is no fault, anywhere, provided the place is not so indecent, in performing the hours.

<margin>Innocent, Hostiensis, Sylvester.</margin>
Although <term>Innocent</term> <note>Pope Innocent IV, a major medieval canonist.</note> and <term>Hostiensis</term> <note>Henricus de Segusio, an influential 13th-century canon lawyer.</note>, whom <term>Sylvester</term> <note>Sylvester Prierias, a prominent theologian and contemporary of Soto.</note> cites under the word *hour*, section 3, judge that a cleric with a <term>benefice</term> <note>A church office that provides an income or living.</note> is bound each day to say or hear the hours in the church, unless excused by a just impediment: otherwise if he says them in his chamber, they say he does not render what is owed. But in truth this is so rigid that it is not to be held. Yet nevertheless, Innocent's opinion holds true to this extent, that he who enjoys an ecclesiastical stipend, which is supplied to him because of the office, ought not to de-

<column-break/>

vise and feign causes for absence, so that he defrauds the church of his service to which he is bound, by whose sustenance he lives. Otherwise he would commit an injustice: indeed he could be so clearly unjust in this part that he would be bound to restitution <note>The legal and moral obligation to pay back what was taken or withheld.</note>.

<margin>Divine prayers</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, even those who privately perform the divine office canonically <note>In accordance with the rules of the Church.</note> ought to take care that, if not in the church, they have at least an honest place at home, an oratory <note>A small private chapel or room for prayer.</note> destined for their performance as they are able, where they can offer so excellent an office of religion to God attentively and devoutly. For to perform that in the marketplace or in the streets in the manner of other secular business, besides that an impediment to attention is thrown in the way, it does not have that honesty which the matter demands for its dignity. Add that in indecent places, such as where profane things are done and during drinking, and while yielding to nature <note>original: "dum naturæ ceditur" — a common Latin euphemism for using the latrine.</note>, it cannot be without fault. Wherefore it is much more fitting to delay the time of praying than to pray in those places or times.

¶ Therefore, the arguments set forth at the beginning of the question remain resolved.

### ARTICLE V.

->Whether attention is required to perform the divine office canonically.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' containing a miniature illustration of a religious figure or saint gesturing towards the heavens.</image-desc>THE FIFTH thing finally to be meditated upon concerning prayer is the mode of praying: which is placed in the devotion and attention to be applied.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
It is argued therefore that attention of this kind is necessary throughout the whole office. For it is necessary, says the Redeemer in John 4: since God is spirit, those who adore him must do so in spirit and in truth: wherefore prayer is called the ascent of the intellect into God; but where there is no attention, neither is the spirit present by which one can ascend into God: therefore it [attention] is always necessary.

<margin>Second.</margin>
¶ Secondly it is argued: For prayer, since it exists as an act of religion, it is necessary that it be free from every stain of sin: but he who would pray something to God without attention would appear to mock him rather than honor him.

<margin>Basil.</margin>
Of which an example <term>Basil</term> <note>St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> in the book *On the Perfect Life*, chapter two, draws from a human prince. For attention, he says, is needed above all by one who prays: for if you stand before a prince,

<meta>This page continues Soto’s discussion on the mental state required for the "Divine Office" (the set of daily prayers performed by clergy). # Book Ten, Question V.

...[by] behaving quite negligently, hardly listening, hardly responding, and hardly looking at them: but by turning your eyes elsewhere, you will not only fail to please that person, but you will provoke them to anger. How much more so before God, who knows your conscience intimately <note>original: "intus & in cute," literally "inside and under the skin."</note>, and who immediately detects if you waver in any way.
<margin>Third point. Innocent</margin>
¶ Thirdly, the commandment of <term>Innocent III</term> <note>Pope Innocent III (r. 1198–1216), a major figure in the development of Canon Law.</note> in the chapter *Dolentes* regarding the celebration of the Mass agrees with this, where he strictly commands by virtue of obedience that we celebrate the divine office as studiously as God grants us, and likewise with devotion. ¶ On the contrary, however, is the fact that what is not within a person's power is by no means imputed to them as a fault. To keep the mind so fixed that it does not wander is not always possible for us; indeed, for this reason David said lamenting, "My heart has forsaken me."

The most powerful consideration of prayer concerns devotion and attention, which are partly necessary for it and partly its greatest ornament. And as it is a most precious thing, it is likewise both very difficult and subsequently very rare. For such is the nature of all things that are most excellent. We have framed this article concerning attention in prayer in general, following the same course that <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian whose *Summa Theologiae* Soto is here commenting upon.</note> treated in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 83, article 13, so that we may descend from there to the attention
<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
<margin>Something is necessary in two ways.</margin>
necessary for the <term>canonical hours</term> <note>The specific prayers (like Matins, Vespers) that clergy are required to recite at set times of the day.</note>. Therefore, to set forth his mind, he says that something is necessary in two ways, as the "Philosopher" <note>Aristotle.</note> is the author in the 5th book of his *Metaphysics*. In one way, it is that through which one reaches an end better and more decently: just as a horse is for completing a journey. And in the other way, simply [necessary]: namely, that without which a thing cannot reach its end; like food for life. In the same way, the necessity of attention is judged in two ways: One, that it should persevere as long as the prayer lasts; and the other, that when someone prepares themselves to pray, they attend to what they are setting out to do. ¶ With these things established, the question is answered with seven conclusions: five looking at the nature of prayer universally, and two pertaining properly to the canonical hours.
<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
First: Attention in the first way—that is, through the whole prayer—is "necessary" for it, if "necessary" is used in that first sense. For it is the most splendid ornament and glory of prayer to attend to every single word,

<column-break/>

[considering] who you are, what you are saying, and with whom you are speaking. ¶ If, however, you take the name of necessity in the second way—that is, as simply necessary—then a threefold effect must be considered in prayer. The first is that the act be morally good (if done without grace) and the same act be <term>meritorious</term> <note>An act that deserves a spiritual reward from God.</note> (if it proceeds from grace). And regarding this, the second conclusion is established.
<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
In order for the act to be morally good, and even a merit before God, it is not simply necessary that attention assist the entire prayer: but it is enough that the person who approaches to pray realizes what work they are beginning; for then the force of that attention lasts by virtue through the whole, so as to make that act a human one. ¶ The second effect of prayer is <term>impetration</term> <note>The act of obtaining something through petition or request.</note>. And regarding this, the third conclusion is established in a similar way. Attention that accompanies the whole prayer is not simply necessary for this effect; rather,
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
if someone attends at the beginning to what they are seeking, they will be able to obtain it. ¶ Finally, the third effect of prayer—and the most important—is a certain spiritual refreshment of the mind and a most sweet recreation which drops down from the conversation entered into with God. And regarding this, the fourth conclusion is applied. To achieve this kind of
<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
effect, attention that is the inseparable companion of the whole prayer is simply necessary. For attention is the co-existing cause of this effect: because as soon as attention ceases, the effect also vanishes. And the reason is that
<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
this kind of mental refreshment consists not in a habit, but in the *act* of spiritual life: Therefore, unless it is present through attention, it cannot exist. Whence Paul says in 1 Corinthians 14: "If I pray in a tongue (meaning alone), my mind is without fruit." ¶ The
<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
fifth conclusion is explanatory of attention. There is a triple attention that can be applied to vocal prayer. First, that each person attends only to the words, so as not to err in the pronunciation. Second, by which one attends to the sense of the words. Third, by which one attends to the end of the prayer: namely, to God and to the thing for which one prays; which is indeed the most necessary. And even <term>unlearned</term> <note>original: "idiotæ," meaning laypeople or those without formal education in Latin or theology.</note> people can have this. Indeed, even the learned can be so fixed upon God through this that they forget other things. These are the words of Saint Thomas, which are general to all vocal attention, namely both the spontaneous prayer of the people and the canonical prayer of the clergy. ¶ However, before we descend to that which is necessary for the canonical hours, let these things be unfolded more explicitly. It must be noted that the question of attention has a place in vocal prayer: for in mental
<margin>First lesson.</margin>
prayer, since the attention itself is the very prayer itself, it is vain to ask whether it is required there...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the internal state of the person praying. Having previously discussed the necessity of the Divine Office, he now distinguishes between "attention" (mental focus) and "devotion" (willful dedication), outlining three levels of spiritual focus that lead the soul toward God.</meta>

...attention is required. For it is a contradiction to pray with the mind and not pay attention: for as soon as the mind begins to wander, it stops praying. Indeed, for this reason mental prayer is often more desirable, because when the mind is not poured out into words, it is more freely available to drink in the divine mysteries. Therefore, only vocal prayer can lack attention: namely, while the thoughts of others drift away, the tongue gives out sound without the mind.

<margin>Second point.</margin>
¶ Secondly, it should be noted that attention and devotion—especially as the common people use the word "devotion"—are different things. For the common people think that devotion is what we called the refreshment and recreation of the mind in the fourth conclusion; yet in Latin, the word sounds different to the ears. For "to devote" <note>original: "deuouere"</note> is to promise something solemnly. Hence devotion (as <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the foundational theologian for Soto’s Dominican order.</note> says in the *Summa* II-II, question 82) is a certain inclination and application of the soul to the service of another: namely, when someone is most prepared and prompt to serve God or a saint. For in this way someone is said to be "devoted" to the most holy Virgin. Indeed, when someone has destined themselves to death for some cause, they are said to have "devoted" their soul. But "to attend" means nothing other than to have the mind present to what is being said: namely, so that what the tongue sounds out externally, the mind speaks simultaneously by conceiving it internally. And, as <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> says: let that be turned over in the heart which is brought forth in the mouth. Hence, in that passage Paul calls the mind the "soul" of the words. Those things without a soul, he says, are things giving a voice, like a flute or a harp, etc. For he who prays without attention is like the blast of a trumpet. And therefore he adds further down: "I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 14:15.</note>

<margin>Devotion and attention are distinct things.</margin>
Devotion and attention are therefore distinct things. For it is possible for someone to have a soul destined for God’s service who nevertheless is not attentive with the mind while praying: and perhaps vice versa. Although devotion, by its own nature, is the cause of attention. For he who takes care to have his soul present for divine services will also have it attentive in prayer. But since from that presence and attention of the mind there drips—as we said—a certain spiritual sweetness by which the soul is refreshed and recreated, the common people call *this* devotion: even though it is rather the effect and fruit of devotion and attention.

<margin>Corollary.</margin>
¶ From this it follows that the last of those three types of attention is the most fruitful. For the first—namely, attention to the pronunciation of the words—is the lowest grade of attention: which cannot be had

<column-break/>

except by one who knows the language. And for this reason, all clerics should at least be proficient in Latin; otherwise, they will not be able to utter the words correctly and appropriately. But the second grade—namely, attending to the meaning—does not suit all who know Latin, except those skilled in theology. But the third [grade] is familiar to spiritual people, even if they are uneducated <note>original: "idiotæ," referring here to the "laity" or those without formal academic training in Latin and theology.</note>. For these people, who are not experts in other mysteries, attend while they pray both to the divine majesty with whom they speak, and to their own smallness as they speak—and furthermore, to the necessity of those things they request.

<margin>The supreme goal of praying.</margin>
¶ The supreme goal of praying ought to be to "deify" the heart and mind as much as can possibly be done. Therefore, if it were possible, it would always be better to attend to the Deity itself. ¶ But if one attends to other saints or to the holy Virgin, the mind should not fix its step there as if that were the final goal—an error the unlearned commoners very often make—but it should be taken as a means through which one may ascend to the divinity, as much as God grants.

<margin>The nature of prayer.</margin>
¶ Therefore prayer is described by the saints as an ascent of the mind, not to the saints nor to other supreme substances, but to God himself. Indeed, although meditation on the passion of Christ and his other mysteries of humanity while praying is holy counsel, the mind must not stop there as if at the end, but use it as a means, which is the highest of all means toward the love of divine things. The Church reminds us of this most thoughtfully in the preface for the Nativity. For through the mystery of the Word made flesh, it says, "a new light of your brightness has shone upon the eyes of our mind: so that while we recognize God visibly, we may be snatched up through him into the love of invisible things." <note>Soto is quoting the "Preface of the Nativity" from the Roman Missal.</note>

<margin>Second corollary.</margin>
¶ From this it follows again that attending to what you ask for, if it is a temporal thing, although it is permissible to some extent, is not without danger—lest you direct the divine majesty toward that end <note>The danger is in treating God as a tool for worldly gain rather than the ultimate end of prayer.</note>. And therefore one must not linger there too long. Indeed, since among those things we must earnestly request from God, eternal glory—and subsequently the grace and virtues by which we are advanced toward it—hold the peak and summit, yet even in these the end of prayer is not to be established. For although it is most healthy to ask for them because God himself is their object, nevertheless the summit of intention must be directed toward God himself and his glory, by which he himself is blessed. That is to say, we should desire to enjoy the sight of him not so much for our own good (which pertains to the love of desire) as for...

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s legal and theological analysis of prayer. In the previous section, he distinguished between "attention" (mental presence) and "devotion" (willful dedication). He now moves to his sixth and seventh conclusions, arguing that attention is not merely a suggestion but a formal requirement (a "precept") for those reciting the Divine Office, while tempering this strictness by distinguishing between intentional and accidental distractions.</meta>

### Tenth Book, Question V.

...refer our own self, which is the love of benevolence, namely: not so much to the fact that our will is fulfilled, as to the fact that His will is fulfilled, by which He wished to pour out His own proper happiness into us. For this reason, in each of the <term>Canonical Hours</term> <note>The set of prayers, such as Matins or Vespers, recited at specific times by clergy and religious orders.</note> as they begin, immediately after the petition for divine help, the *Gloria Patri* [Glory be to the Father] etc. is sung at the very start, as if it were the goal to which the entire prayer is directed. However, it is better to discuss this more extensively in another place.

<margin>Sixth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Therefore, returning to the proposal at hand, we establish the **sixth conclusion**. Attention is a requirement of the precept, not only for clerics <note>original: "clericis"</note> who are canonically singing and praying—binding them under the guilt of <term>mortal sin</term> <note>In Catholic theology, a grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note>—but also, in their own way, for laypeople

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
when they pour out spontaneous prayers. The reason for both parts arises from the very nature of the thing: for since praying is an act of virtue—and indeed not just any virtue, but the virtue of <term>religion</term>—it is necessary that it be done when, where, and most importantly *how* it ought to be. These are the "ornaments of circumstances" with which every virtue is clothed, according to **The Philosopher** <note>A standard reference to Aristotle (384–322 BC).</note>. Moreover, no mode is more natural to the essence of prayer than attention. Furthermore, as far as the matter pertains to the <term>Canonical Hours</term>, the conclusion

<margin>Innocent.</margin>
is specifically proved from the words of <term>Innocent</term> <note>Pope Innocent III (r. 1198–1216) at the Fourth Lateran Council.</note> in the General Council, in the chapter *Dolentes* regarding the celebration of Masses, where he says: "We strictly command in virtue of obedience that they [namely, the clerics] celebrate the divine office, both nocturnal and diurnal, as much as God grants them, both studiously and devoutly." For those words, *strictly in virtue of obedience*, most clearly show the force of a precept, binding under the guilt of mortal sin. Nor is there any appearance of truth in the kind of quibbling that claims the precept there is not imposed upon the *manner* of praying attentively and devoutly, but only upon the *substance*, so that the divine office is performed in its entirety.

I say it has no appearance of truth: for since that precept had already existed in the Church for a long time (as has been said), no question had arisen in the Council concerning it; but because the manner of reciting was gradually falling into ruin, care was taken to restore it under a formal command.

¶ However, that addition, *as much as God grants them*, might at first glance offer an excuse for saying that the manner of attention was left to the judgment of the one praying. Nevertheless, the matter is not so: rather, its sense is that no one is bound to apply the *highest* possible attention and devotion; but they must nevertheless prepare themselves (in a manner to be explained immediately) so that it does not

<column-break/>

depend on them if God does not flow in with devotion and the refreshment of the soul.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
¶ But if you argue against this opinion on the grounds that the Church ought not to judge internal acts of the soul—since it cannot know them—

<margin>Solution.</margin>
it is answered that although internal acts, if viewed in isolation, do not fall under the judgment of the Church, they can nonetheless be commanded as the "root" or "circumstance" of external acts. For when the Church ordained annual confession, it subsequently commanded that you think about your sins in your mind and recall them to memory. Indeed, in the *Clementines* <note>A collection of canon law promulgated by Pope Clement V in the 14th century.</note> (chapter *Multorum* regarding heretics), the Church strikes with excommunication those who investigate heretics—or fail to investigate them—out of hatred or love; they will not incur this unless they transgress because of such internal affections. Therefore, the Church could similarly command attention, which is innate to the nature and condition of prayer.

<margin>Seventh conclusion.</margin>
¶ But lest anyone be too terrified by the rigor of the mandate, the **seventh conclusion** is applied. The precept of attention in performing the divine office canonically includes two things: namely, that at the beginning of the prayer, everyone should attend to what they are setting out to do. Furthermore, that they should not deliberately and "from a profession" <note>original: "ex professo," meaning intentionally or as a matter of course.</note> interrupt such attention while praying: that is, they should do nothing purposefully and meditatedly by which they perceive the mind is distracted from its prior attention. Indeed, regarding the first part, it is enough that it be done by the power of some preceding intention and habit. For example, if someone, when the signal for the hours is given, goes to the choir out of custom, or privately begins to recite by doing what they are accustomed to do, they satisfy the precept through that act.

<margin>St. Thomas.</margin>
**Saint Thomas** explains the second part in the cited article, in the third solution. For he says: "If anyone wanders in mind during prayer on purpose, this is a sin, and it hinders the fruit of prayer." He says it is a *sin*, which denotes a precept. And he says one loses the *fruit* of prayer—namely, not only the refreshment of the soul (which we said above does not last unless the attention lasts), but also the merit and the obtaining of the request <note>original: "impetrationem"</note>: because one is moved away from attention by study.

<margin>Augustine.</margin>
And in this sense, he says, we must understand that statement of **Augustine** in his *Rule*: "When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let that be turned over in the heart which is uttered by the mouth." But a wandering of the mind that happens "outside of the purpose" <note>original: "praeter propositum," meaning unintentionally.</note> does not take away the fruit of prayer. Understand this to mean the merit and the obtaining of the request, as we explained above: for the soul...

<margin>Basil.</margin>
...for my own refreshment does not come to me unless you are attending to the matter at hand. Hence <term>Basil</term> <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), one of the Greek Church Fathers, who wrote extensively on monastic life.</note> says in the cited passage concerning the perfect life: "If," he says, "you are weakened by sin and cannot pray with a fixed mind, restrain yourself as much as you can, and God will forgive you; for it is not out of negligence, but out of frailty that you cannot stand before God as you ought." This is his view. Here, note that to permit the mind to wander out of gross negligence 
<margin>What the fear of wandering is.</margin>
amounts to the same thing as if you were doing it intentionally. ¶ For "wandering of the mind" occurs when one's thoughts, turned away from the intended purpose, roam about without any goal. Indeed, the cause of this is manifold. The first is that which Basil indicates, namely
<margin>Multiple causes of the aforementioned wandering.</margin>
the weakening and lethargy of the mind which we have contracted from <term>original sin</term> <note>The theological concept that humanity inherited a flawed nature from the first humans, leading to a loss of self-control.</note>, through which we lost the "bridle" of original justice. For just as one who is not firm in the knee cannot walk steadily, so too our mind cannot adhere firmly to a proposed meditation. And just as the sun, while it shines upon rippling water, cannot fix its rays solidly there, but they seem to waver; so it is with the divine rays in our minds. Furthermore, there are the wicked habits of our own crimes and the deep-seated worldly custom of thinking. For just as a corrupt bodily fluid, once it begins to flow, always runs persistently in that direction, so too is our slippery thought process. Added to all this is the assault of demons, who are most hostile to us in prayer, where we converse so familiarly with God. Therefore, we should neither wonder that we cannot hold our mind in prayer, nor should we despair; rather, as with a matter that is as difficult as it is precious, we must strive with all diligence so that we are present in spirit while praying. First, by imploring divine favor against the demons. For the Church has instructed us in this method, beginning the start of the chanting with: *Lord, open my lips* <note>original: "Domine labia mea aperies"</note> and *O God, come to my assistance* <note>original: "Deus in adiutorium meum intende"</note>. Then, by moving our thinking mind away from other things as much as lies within us, and by accustoming it to divine matters. ¶ To return to the point,
<margin>Whenever someone does not intentionally move their mind from attention, they do not omit the precept of praying.</margin>
whenever someone does not move their mind from attention with dedicated effort, they do not omit the precept of praying. However, to provide clarity for those with <term>timid consciences</term> <note>Refers to people who are overly anxious about committing sins (scrupulosity).</note>, no one should be judged as distracted by profession [intentionally] unless these things concur: namely, that while he is weighing the hours [reciting the prayers], he is occupied with another business which by its very nature is opposed to 

<column-break/>

the attention of prayer. Such as if someone, for example, were then to read, or write, or paint, or do something of that kind which requires attention. Therefore, if while one prays, he washes his hands, or dresses himself, or does something else that does not demand so much mental focus, although he may act wrongly against the dignity of prayer and perhaps commit a <term>venial sin</term> <note>A lesser sin that does not result in a complete break with God's grace.</note>, he does not, however, act mortally against the precept. I said "perhaps venially," because it is not always a sin. Indeed, in our Order, it is commanded of us that upon rising we say the <term>Office of the Virgin</term> <note>A shorter cycle of prayers dedicated to Mary, separate from the main Divine Office.</note>; and as the ancient arrangement of the Dormitory indicates, the brothers would begin it while dressing: namely, so that the wicked phantasms [imaginations] that usually occur upon waking might be driven away. Furthermore, it is required that he who does or thinks something foreign to the attention of prayer should notice that through this he is slipping away from that same attention. Therefore, even if he thinks of other things of his own accord and voluntarily (as <term>Cajetan</term> <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a major Catholic theologian and commentator on Thomas Aquinas.</note> rightly says 
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
in his *Summa*), until he perceives that he is being distracted, he is always considered to be wandering inadvertently, and thus he is excused from the omission of the precept regarding attention; and so he fulfills the mandate of praying. Nevertheless, one should not be complacent, both because of the dignity of prayer and because of the danger that venial fault frequently creeps in. ¶ Beyond this, add that not every time a mortal sin is committed through omission of attention is the necessity of <term>restitution</term> <note>The legal/moral obligation to "make up" the missed prayer or return money (stipends) received for saying it.</note> incurred, as we are about to say in the next article. However, the obligation to repeat the same hour emerges. But if you argue against this last 
<margin>Objection.</margin>
statement as follows: "He who enters a church to hear Mass on a feast day, yet with a soul mortally corrupted [in a state of sin], fulfills the precept if he hears the Mass; therefore, he who utters the substance of the psalms, even if he does so with a wandering mind knowingly and prudently, satisfies the debt in the same way." The consequence is denied: because the precept of hearing Mass only obliges one to hear it in such a way that it is a human act; which it can be, even if another sinister purpose is simultaneously present. However, to discharge the Divine Office obliges that it be done attentively. Therefore, if attention is removed, the precept is not fulfilled. However, the aforementioned argument does prove that if someone prays attentively, even though he does so while having <term>vainglory</term> attached to it—or even though he simultaneously has some other mortal purpose—he will satisfy the precept as far as the substance is concerned.

<summary>Domingo de Soto discusses the causes of mental distraction during prayer, such as original sin and demonic interference, and concludes that only intentional distraction involving a conflicting task (like writing or painting) constitutes a mortal sin.</summary>

# Book Ten, Question V.

...so that he is not bound to repeat the office. Let these things be said for the peace of consciences; nevertheless, no one ought to be content to pray in such a manner. Rather, as we were saying just recently, care and diligence must be applied so that attention may persevere throughout the entire prayer, and the mind may be refreshed more and more.

<margin>Laypeople praying are also bound to attention in their own way.</margin>
¶ But truly, since by the nature of our conclusion we have also touched upon laypeople praying freely, it must be noted that they too are bound to attention in their own way. First, because at times a precept of prayer occurs for them as well, as we noted on chapters 6 and 7 of Matthew regarding that word of Christ: *Ask, and it shall be given to you* <note>original: "Petite, & dabitur vobis." A reference to the Sermon on the Mount.</note>. Although, since this is an affirmative command, it does not bind at every moment, but for a specific time and place—a matter not to be discussed here. Hence, when someone falls into a time of fulfilling such a precept, they are bound to attention just as much as a cleric. For this reason, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for Scholastic theologians like Soto.</note> in the place recently cited says generally that for the mind to wander by design during prayer is a sin.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
¶ But indeed, there is a doubt whether, while someone prays freely and of their own accord, they are also bound to attend with their mind. For it appears they are not bound at all; for if I am in no way obligated to pray at this time, no fault appears if I wish to pray according to my own whim, even by intentionally turning my mind elsewhere. For example: when a craftsman or a hired laborer sings secular songs while working with his hands, why should he not also be able to pray then, even if he has his entire attention fixed on his manual labor by dedicated effort?

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered that there is no logical connection in saying: "I am not bound to pray, therefore, however I pray, I am not bound to attend." For although it may be permitted for me sometimes to be vacant from the work of religion, nevertheless, while I am doing it, I am bound by the very nature of the virtue to do it properly. This is just as happens in leisure activities. For, although I am not bound to work, nevertheless while I work, I am bound to do it for some honest end; otherwise, there is some degree of fault. Likewise, therefore, while I pray, I am bound to pray according to the dignity of the matter, lest I be held as a despiser and a mocker before God. I should say "while I pray," for if someone, whatever business he is doing, wishes to recite Psalms to avoid other thoughts, there is no reason it should be seen as a vice; because that is not chosen by way of a formal prayer, but rather as a "leash" for the mind.

<margin>A hesitation.</margin>
¶ But you ask: will it therefore be a mortal sin <note>A serious sin that severs one's relationship with God, as opposed to a venial or minor sin.</note> to either neglect or remove attention from prayer while one prays without a precept, just as if a cleric were to do so during the <term>canonical hours</term> <note>The set of daily prayers (the Divine Office) that clergy and monastics are legally required to recite.</note>? For it appears to be so, because, as we were just saying, the di-

<column-break/>

-gnity of prayer requires attention.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It is answered that, nevertheless, one does not sin in the same way. For where a precept of praying intervenes, attention is commanded by that same precept. However, where one prays freely and without obligation, it is only a <term>venial sin</term> <note>A lesser, pardonable sin that does not break one's state of grace.</note> to pray indecently; therefore, distraction, even if deliberate, will never be mortal unless contempt is present.

The arguments, therefore, which were proposed at the head of the question, do not proceed from the necessity of a precept; otherwise, they would be effective, as was asserted in the sixth conclusion and declared in the seventh. But they were directed toward proving that attention is necessary through the whole prayer—which, in truth, they do not prove.

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
And therefore, to the first, it is answered that he prays "in spirit and truth" <note>A reference to John 4:24.</note> who, by the instinct of the Holy Spirit and according to divine and ecclesiastical decree, applies himself to prayer, even if afterward the mind wanders elsewhere due to the sluggishness of the soul. And the same suffices so that the prayer may be an "ascent of the mind to God."

<margin>To the second.</margin>
¶ To the second, it was sufficiently answered during the explanation of the seventh conclusion: namely, that not everyone who wanders in mind while praying provokes God, but only he who does so either by design or by gross negligence. To the authority of the chapter *Dolentes* <note>A specific chapter in Canon Law (Decretals of Gregory IX) concerning the conduct of the clergy.</note>, its conclusion is granted: namely, that there is a precept of attention, but not one which must necessarily accompany the entire prayer.

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law,

<margin>Boniface.</margin> ...within a year he must become a priest so that he is able to reside in the church; if he fails to do so, he is deprived of his prebend <note>A prebend is a portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon as a salary.</note> without any prior warning. To this, Boniface <note>Pope Boniface VIII (r. 1294–1303), referring here to his contributions to Canon Law in the *Liber Sextus*.</note> added in the chapter *Commissa* under the same title, that if he does not have the intention of being promoted to the priesthood, he is bound to the restitution of the fruits <note>original: "fructuum." In this context, "fruits" refers to the financial income or revenues generated by a church office.</note>.

<margin>Second.</margin> ¶ Second. In the Lateran Council under Leo the Tenth <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517).</note>, in the 9th session, it was decreed that whoever does not canonically perform the Divine Office is bound to restitute the perceived fruits in proportion to the neglect. If he persists in this same negligence for more than half a year, he is to be deprived of the benefice, since it was given for the sake of the office.

<margin>Third.</margin> ¶ Third. Not only he who does not perform the canonical hours, but even he who is of corrupt morals, seems to be obligated to restitution. Indeed, since the people offer ecclesiastical fruits to the clergy as a price for their sins and as vows before God—as held in the 12th Question, 1st Canon, *Videntes*—for this reason, as read in Hosea 4 and cited in the 1st Question, 1st Canon, the priests themselves are said to "eat the sins of the people." Those who are intercessors for others before God are bound to live an upright life with a pure mind. Therefore, if they live otherwise, they are bound to restitution, according to the tenor of the title *On the condition of a cause given but not followed* <note>original: "de condiction. caus. dat. & non sequuta." A reference to a specific legal action in Roman Law (Digest 12.4) regarding things given for a purpose that was not fulfilled.</note>. ¶ On the contrary, it is argued that neither stipends nor tithes are granted under the condition that if a paid servant fails in any act, he is bound to restitution. For no one, such is human fragility, can serve so blamelessly. Furthermore, as we discussed in Book 1, he who incurs a penalty is not bound to pay it before condemnation.

<margin>Four heads of the present controversy.</margin> There are four heads about which there can be controversy at present, regarding whether clerics are bound to the restitution of either the prebend or the fruits, which are designated in the order of the arguments. First, when he who possesses the priesthood does not carry in his soul the intention to become a priest or cleric. Second, when he has not received the aforementioned orders in time. Third, when he does not perform the office of the canonical hours. And fourth, when he does not live an honest life as becomes a cleric. For we are not dealing here with simony, or homicide, or other crimes for which either an "irregularity" <note>A legal impediment in Canon Law that prevents someone from receiving or exercising Holy Orders.</note> is contracted for obtaining a benefice, or a penalty of deprivation is incurred. Discussions of those matters belong to other, different places. But

<column-break/>

here we only discuss those things which are necessary for clerics to earn the fruits of tithes and other stipends. ¶ To the question, therefore, despite the number mentioned above, it is answered with six conclusions.

<margin>First conclusion.</margin> The first is the express assertion of the aforementioned chapter *Commissa* regarding elections, in Book 6. He who holds a parish church, not intending to be promoted to the priesthood, is bound to the restitution of the perceived fruits. I say "parish" because it has the "care of souls" <note>original: "curam animarum." The pastoral responsibility for the spiritual welfare of a congregation.</note> annexed to it; it is otherwise for a collegiate church, as the gloss <note>The "Glossa Ordinaria," the standard commentary on Canon Law.</note> holds there. And the reason is: because, as provided in the cited chapter *Licet* under the same title, such a cleric is bound to reside in his church and to serve the church by himself; which he cannot do before he becomes a priest. Wherefore, a bishop is included under the same law. And although the text speaks of the *reception* of the office, by equal reasoning it is understood to apply to its *retention*. Just as, I say, if while you take up a parish you do not think of being promoted to the priesthood, you are compelled to restitute the fruits as long as you have not changed your mind: so, although you may have had a sound purpose when you took it up, if you later change it, deciding you will not be a priest, from that point in time you are bound to restitute the fruits. Thus, at whatever time you do not intend to take up the priesthood, you do not make the fruits of that time your own; for the reasoning for reception and retention is equal, as is expertly noted in the gloss there. ¶ And note, **"Not intending":** by which word is also included he who is of a doubting mind; for he who hesitates does not "intend." Wherefore, if someone who takes up a parish has not yet decided on his life, but is of a hanging mind—as if, should things turn out more happily another way, he would renounce the clerical habit—certainly he does not receive the fruits with a safe conscience. If, however, he should have the intention of taking up the priesthood, yet under a condition—unless by the death of his firstborn brother the paternal inheritance should fall to him, or some other secular prosperity should succeed—there might be someone who says he can perceive those same ecclesiastical fruits, because a conditional intention is, in a way, an intention. But I would not judge even this kind of conscience to be healthy: since when the text says, "Not intending," it requires an absolute intention. And reason also supports this: for he who absolutely perceives the fruits ought to have an absolute intention. Otherwise, as the text says, he receives them fraudulently. Indeed, that parenthesis in the text (unless he was promoted after his will was changed) is not to be understood so craftily as to mean that when he was promoted to the priesthood after changing his will, he could [keep the] fruits...

Soto emphasizes that church revenues are tied to the performance of a specific office and the maintenance of an upright life.</summary>

It specifically examines the moral and legal consequences when a cleric fails to progress to the priesthood or fulfill their duties.</meta>

### Tenth Book, Question 5.

...to recover the income of that time in which he did not have the intention of entering the priesthood; but when he has resolved to be promoted, from that moment he makes those revenues his own.

<margin>Question.</margin>
¶ You ask, however, whether in making this kind of restitution one must wait for a judge's condemnation, or whether the restitution must be carried out without waiting for any formal sentence.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
It appears that a sentence should be awaited, because that law seems to be penal <note>A penal law is one that imposes a punishment for a crime; usually, such punishments require a trial and a judge's verdict.</note>. Nevertheless, the answer is that there is no need for a judge's formal inquiry. By the very fact that someone does not intend to take up the priesthood, they do not make the income their own, because that law is not penal. Rather, the granting of a parish priesthood—even if it is done unconditionally—is nevertheless granted with the obligation that the one to whom it is given must become a priest; otherwise, they do not acquire ownership of the income. In this case, the title from the *Digest* cited above applies, concerning "conditions given but not followed" <note>original: "de cond. cau. data & nõ sequu." This refers to a principle in Roman Law where if you receive something based on a specific future condition that you then fail to meet, you must return it.</note>.

¶ But it should be further noted that even if he did not intend to be promoted—indeed, even if he intended to involve himself in marriage—he does not lose the legal title to the prebend <note>A "prebend" is the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a clergyman as a stipend.</note> according to the strict rigor of the text. Rather, whenever he wishes to become a priest, he is able to retain the same prebend without a new appointment. Furthermore, however, someone who possesses a parish church with a firm mind of never taking up priestly orders is not to be judged free from sin, beyond the fact that (as the text says) he does not make the income his own. Indeed, I would believe it to be a mortal sin unless he leaves the office, since he occupies a church which he does not intend to serve. This certainly cannot be done without the deadly loss of souls, the care of which is attached to that very prebend.

¶ Regarding other benefices <note>A "benefice" is a permanent Church appointment, typically including property and income.</note> which are outside the care of souls, even if they have a service attached to them, nothing has been decreed. Therefore, it should not be rashly asserted that an obligation to restore the income arises if they are possessed without a clerical intention. For "odious laws" <note>original: "odiosa iura." A legal maxim suggesting that laws which impose burdens or penalties should be interpreted strictly and not expanded to other cases.</note>, as the Rule of Law holds, are to be restricted rather than expanded. But truly, I do not think a person is clean of mortal sin who holds a benefice to which clerical service is attached, unless he has the intention of taking up—if not the priesthood—at least that order which is necessary for such service. Or, if no order is required, at least the intention to live in the manner of the clergy is necessary. For it would be most absurd for someone to retain a canonry or other such benefice assigned to ecclesiastical service with the intention of flying off to marriage or living secularly.

<column-break/>

Indeed, not even "prestimonia" <note>A "prestimonium" was a fund or property set aside to support a cleric, often outside the formal structure of a parish or cathedral.</note>, 
<margin>What about prestimonia.</margin>
as they are called, are possessed without guilt with such a secular mind and habit; since, as we have often said before, this kind of title is clerical.

<margin>What about pensions.</margin>
¶ Regarding pensions, however, the reasoning is different; for these are granted without an ecclesiastical title. Although, unless they are granted for some service to the church, it is not without absurdity. For there are those who, while they hold priesthoods, change their minds and resign them while retaining the pensions—which married men then keep, using them to support a wife, children, and secular pride. This is so inconsistent with the ecclesiastical institution that I do not see why the Church tolerates it.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
¶ The second heading of restitution which we established was when a parish cleric does not take up the priesthood within a year. Regarding this, in the said chapter *Licet* under "On Elections" in the *Sixth Book* <note>Referring to the *Liber Sextus*, a collection of Canon Law.</note>, there exists a conclusion which shall be our second one here: He who holds the title of a parish church and is not promoted to the priesthood within a year is deprived of that same prebend, even without any prior warning. This is to be understood similarly to the preceding: namely, that there is no need for another sentence of deprivation, because that law is not penal, but conventional <note>A "conventional" law here means it acts like a contract; if you don't fulfill your side of the bargain, the deal is automatically void.</note>.

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Indeed, since the care of souls should be entrusted to no one unless he is a priest who can immediately administer his province, the Church has held it sacred to grant no one such prebends except with that agreement—which, if not observed, means he is deprived by that very fact.

<margin>Objection.</margin>
But if you argue: "Once the provision is made, he is truly and absolutely the master of the prebend; therefore, unless he is heard [in court], he is not to be stripped of it."

<margin>Solution.</margin>
The logic is denied: because a grant of this kind is always, in a way, dependent on the future. Just as if you were to grant your money to someone under a certain obligation and pact; by the very fact that he does not stand by the pact, he is bound to return it to you.

<margin>Limitation of Boniface to the previous conclusion.</margin>
However, Pope Boniface later moderated that canon in the chapter *Cum ex eo* under the same title, so that the bishop may dispense <note>A "dispensation" is a formal exemption from a church law.</note> with such clerics for up to seven years, specifically for the sake of study, so that he might later be a more fruitful priest for the church. Now, however, dispensations are granted for any reason whatsoever. Regarding this conclusion, therefore, there is no reason to linger.

¶ The third heading of restitution of ecclesiastical income arises from the omission of performing the Divine Office of the Hours <note>The "Divine Office" or "Liturgy of the Hours" refers to the official set of daily prayers (Psalms, hymns, readings) that clergy are required to recite at specific times.</note>, in which several doubts are folded together.

<margin>Doubt <image-desc>small floral/leaf ornament</image-desc></margin>
And the first is: whether he who does not perform the Divine Office is bound to restitution, and by what

<meta>This page continues Domingo de Soto’s exploration of the moral obligations attached to ecclesiastical income. Having previously discussed the requirement for a cleric to intend to become a priest, he now examines the specific duty of reciting the "Divine Office"—the daily cycle of prayers—and whether failing to do so requires the cleric to pay back the income they received.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Law

<margin>First argument.</margin>
...law. And beginning with natural and divine law, it appears at first that one is not held to restitution: because in the chapter *Presbyter* concerning the celebration of the Mass, and in others cited above up to the Lateran Council under Leo X, there is no mention of restitution; rather, it is only commanded that the divine office be performed. If, however, restitution were a matter of divine law, it would not have been passed over by the church in such a long silence, but would have been explained in express words. For the fact that it was foreseen that one must pray does not sufficiently express that those who do otherwise are bound to restitution. 
<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
Likewise, benefices <note>A 'benefice' was a church office, such as a rector or canon, that provided the holder with a living or income.</note> are granted to clerics not only for the sake of the daily hours of prayer, but also for other duties. However, if someone neglects those other duties—for example, if a parish priest is negligent in his care of souls—he is not therefore bound to restitution by divine law. ¶ Nevertheless, 
<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
notwithstanding these points, he establishes a third conclusion: Anyone who holds an ecclesiastical stipend under a clerical title—namely from tithes or similar offerings—is bound to some restitution unless they perform the divine office. 
<margin>Proof.</margin>
This is evident: because although such stipends are not fixed in amount by divine law, they were nonetheless instituted by both divine and natural law as wages for ecclesiastical functions. However, the most proper duty of a cleric, as we said above, is to perform the divine office at certain hours. This is why, in the Lateran Council, it is alleged for this purpose that "the benefice is given because of the office" <note>original: "beneficiũ datur propter officium". This is a famous legal maxim: the income is for the work.</note>. Therefore, he who does not perform the duty is subjected to the yoke of restitution by that same law, because he has sinned not just in any way, but against justice. I would not say that if he fails to perform the office in this or that specific way he is bound to such and such a specific restitution—for all these details are matters of positive <note>Human-made or ecclesiastical law, as opposed to natural law.</note> law—but rather that every cleric is bound to the duty of prayer under the penalty of some restitution. 
<margin>Confirmation.</margin>
¶ Moreover, in confirmation of this conclusion, it is not credible that before the most recent Lateran Council the custom of the church was anything other than that he who did not say the divine office was held to some restitution; otherwise, the aforementioned Council would not have suddenly brought forth such a significant precept. And yet, as we were saying, express mention of restitution is not found in the law before this. Therefore, the precept of prayer itself was interpreted according to natural and divine law under the penalty of some restitution.
<margin>Fourth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, a fourth conclusion is added: Not every defect in performing the divine office—indeed, not even every defect that constitutes a mortal sin—obliges one to restitution. For instance, if you pronounce words incorrectly, or if, out of lazy negligence and drowsiness, you 

<column-break/>

muddle some verses. This is proven because to do otherwise would be to ensnare consciences too much, since the falling and slippery life of man can hardly be passed without such negligences. Indeed, even if you skip the office of Matins <note>The prayers said after midnight or at dawn.</note> or another hour, whether out of culpable forgetfulness or deliberate intent—which is perhaps always a mortal sin—or even if you neglect to pray for an entire day—which is certainly lethal—you are not therefore held to restitution by the strictness of the law. For first of all, he who is bound by the law of prayer not by reason of a benefice (since he has none), but by reason of his holy orders, has nothing to restore. However, even for one who is obligated by reason of a benefice—even though it was granted to him because of the office—the portions of the stipend ought not to correspond so minutely to each of the canonical hours that the omission of any one hour obliges the restitution of that portion. For service is not required so exactly even in civil households, nor did the Holy Spirit, by whose nod the church is ruled, wish to cast such anxieties upon His ministers. From which follows a 
<margin>Corollary.</margin>
corollary: if while you pray, you deliberately move your attention and meditation away from the task, although it may be a mortal crime (as we said above), you would not be bound to restitution, since you would not be so bound even if you omitted the office entirely. ¶ But 
<margin>Doubt.</margin>
a doubt remains concerning those who neglect to pray canonically for a longer period of time, especially if they hold ecclesiastical prebends <note>A 'prebend' was the specific portion of the cathedral's or church's revenues assigned to a cleric.</note>. 
<margin>Reason for doubting.</margin>
And the reason for doubting is offered to us by the cited ninth session of the Lateran Council, the words of which are: 
<margin>Lateran Council.</margin>
> **We decree and ordain that anyone holding a benefice, with or without the care of souls, who—after six months from obtaining the benefice—has not said the divine office (unless there is a legitimate impediment), shall not make the fruits of his benefice his own in proportion to the omission of the office and the time; rather, he is bound to distribute them as unjustly perceived income toward the construction of the churches of such benefices, or as alms to the poor. If, however, he continues contumaciously in similar negligence beyond the said time, he shall be deprived of the benefice itself after a legitimate warning has been given,**

since the benefice is given because of the office. Let it be understood that he "omits the office" (to the extent that he can be deprived of the benefice) who, over a period of fifteen days, has failed to say it at least twice. These are the words of the Council. However, in this decree, as the sequence of words stands, it may seem to some to be partly too relaxed and partly too restrictive. 
<margin>Examining the words of the Lateran Council.</margin>
For it is a too great relaxation that a cleric is not compelled by some penalty to say the office until after six months from obtaining the benefice.

<summary>This page discusses the moral obligation of clergy to return income (restitution) if they fail to pray the Divine Office. While Soto argues that skipping a single prayer out of negligence doesn't require a refund, he cites the Lateran Council's decree that long-term neglect (over six months) requires the income to be given to the poor or church repairs.</summary>
