<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral and legal obligations of clerics who receive income (benefices) but fail to perform their primary duty: the recitation of the Divine Office. Soto is specifically critiquing the strictness of the Fifth Lateran Council's decrees on this matter.</meta>

# Question V of the Tenth Book

it is. Furthermore, the idea that someone who stops praying for only one or two days should be held to pay back a proportional amount <note>original: "pro rata"</note> seems excessively rigid. Moreover, what is more pressing is that the words of the Council, as they stand, are not sufficiently intelligible. For it is first stated that anyone who has not prayed within six months of obtaining a benefice <note>A 'benefice' was a church office, such as a rector or canon, that provided the holder with a guaranteed income from church lands or tithes.</note> must restore the income proportionally. But then it adds: *If, however, beyond the said time, he remains stubbornly in similar negligence*, etc. These words do not fit well with the previous ones; for these last words, "in similar negligence," clearly denote that the negligence of the first six months obliged him to restitution; since after those months, the severity of compulsion is applied through the threat of being deprived of the benefice.

<margin>The Council just cited is explained.</margin>
¶ I conjecture, therefore—indeed, I would certainly believe—that the word of the Council is not "after" <note>original: "post"</note>, but "throughout" <note>original: "per"</note>. That is to say, the meaning is that whoever does not say the office *throughout* six months from obtaining the benefice, or during any part of them, is only held to proportional restitution. Once the six-month period has passed, however, if after a warning he does not pray twice within fifteen days, he should be deprived of the benefice. Thus, the first six months are not given as a grace period during which a cleric who does not pray is subject to no penalty—for that would be contrary to all reason—but rather, it is a period during which he is not yet *deprived* of his office. In this way, the words are intelligible; otherwise, they are not. ¶ It is gathered from this Council, then, that any omission of the hours <note>The 'hours' refer to the Canonical Hours, the specific times of day (like Matins or Vespers) when the Divine Office must be recited.</note> from the moment someone holds a benefice obliges him to restitution. Indeed, if you look at the rigor of the words, even if he omits only a single hour, he would be compelled to pay it back. Furthermore, this strictness of judgment seems to be "too much law" <note>This is a reference to the legal maxim "summum ius, summa iniuria"—extreme law is extreme injustice.</note>. This is especially true because, although the primary duty of a cleric is the cycle of hours, a benefice is nonetheless granted for other duties as well; therefore, reason does not demand that restitution be made down to such minute details. Neither does divine law compel this, nor is it to be believed that the synod uttered its words with such narrow rigor.

<margin>The Lateran Council has not been received by custom and usage regarding the proportional restitution of the fruits of a benefice for the omission of the divine office.</margin>
¶ Therefore, to summarize the matter: the council—at least this chapter—has not yet been fully received into practice and custom, as far as I know. For that Synod was excessively long, and some things (while respecting the supreme authority owed to councils) I do not know are entirely necessary regarding the rigor of this session—specifically, whether those omitting one or two days are obliged to restitution. Truly, neither is the other part in use anywhere (that I have heard)—namely, that he who has not paid the divine office beyond six months should be punished with the deprivation of his benefice.

<column-break/>

Neither has that warning, which is ordered to be given there, become customary. For he is not deprived "by the very fact" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note>, as we said above concerning those who do not intend in their hearts to be promoted to the priesthood, or are not promoted within a year. But, if the council were strictly observed, he would have to be deprived.

<margin>The author's advice regarding the previous doubt.</margin>
¶ Therefore, the advice I would gather for myself from these points is not to cast a scruple of restitution upon anyone for one or two days, even though it is a mortal sin. At the very least, I would believe those who enjoy the relaxations of the "Crusade Bull" <term>Bulla Cruciata <gloss>A papal decree granting various spiritual privileges and indulgences, originally to supporters of the Crusades, later more generally available.</gloss></term>—which contains absolution for poorly performed hours—to be safe enough, even if they have committed such small negligences. When, however, the omission of prayer proceeds further, then a settlement <note>original: "compositio"</note> with the Supreme Pontiff or his legate would have a place. I say this out of respect for the authority of the Council. For standing by divine law alone, it could be settled with the bishop. Truly, such restitutions—if you consult divine and natural law, or even ancient papal law—should be adjudicated to the construction of churches or spent on pious uses. For since the income from tithes are the proper property of the churches themselves, the ministers who do not serve them would owe restitution to those very churches. Indeed, the same Lateran Council orders this to be paid to the same churches or the poor. Nevertheless, in this day and age, as we have said elsewhere, the Supreme Pontiffs consider these funds necessary for their own uses, and therefore one bargains with them concerning restitution.

<margin>The final doubt.</margin>
¶ Finally, the last doubt pertaining to this remains concerning those who are bound to serve in churches, but do not serve sufficiently for the dignity of their office: specifically, concerning canons who, in entering the choir and leaving it, observe the appointed signal exactly to the point <note>meaning they arrive at the last second and leave the moment it is over.</note>—that is, they neither enter before nor remain after. Are they likewise held to restitution? For Peter of Palude <margin>Peter of Palude</margin> <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian and canon lawyer.</note> in Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 5, lashes the consciences of these men, saying that if they spend the rest of their time on the business of the church, it is well; but he who is absent voluntarily, idly and without good cause, is not safe, even if the statute or custom of the church excuses him. This is because such a statute would be irrational; and therefore it applies to those living together: because those who bequeathed their goods to churches under such a bond are not deemed to have subjected them to the statutes of the canons, unless they are reasonable.

<margin>Fifth conclusion.</margin>
¶ Nevertheless, against such a scruple, a fifth conclusion is submitted: Where there is no manifest perversity in a statute, whoever is in the choir according to the tenor of the institutions of his church...

<summary>Soto argues that while clerics are morally bound to recite the Divine Office, the Fifth Lateran Council's strict penalties for missing a few days are not followed in practice. He suggests that while missing prayers is a sin, proportional financial restitution is only necessary for significant omissions and can be settled via papal dispensations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion regarding the income of clerics, specifically addressing whether personal sin or moral failings require them to return church funds. It then transitions into a new article concerning the obligations of monks who have been elevated to the rank of bishop.</meta>

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

...serving the church in good faith and conscience gathers the fruits <note>original: "fructus"; refers to the income or produce derived from church-owned lands or offices</note>; nor is he bound to any restitution. This conclusion is clear in itself: for after the whole community <note>original: "collegium"; likely referring to a cathedral chapter or monastic body</note> has established a law through custom and usage, unless it clearly shows wickedness and corruption, no member of that same society is bound to debate the logic of the law any further, but will satisfy his obligation by keeping it.

<margin>Fourth point regarding the restitution of church goods. Adrian.</margin>
¶ Finally, a fourth and last point regarding the restitution of church goods is established by some, as we said above, concerning whether a cleric’s morals and life are not what they should be. Adrian <note>Pope Adrian VI (1459–1523), a strict reformer and theologian</note> seems to embrace this opinion in the question cited above regarding restitution: where he says that a cleric living a dissolute life and continually provoking God with wicked morals, or neglecting his required duty, is bound to restore whatever he has spent from the church's income. We placed the argument for this above in the third place at the start of the question.

<margin>Alexander of Hales.</margin>
However, this opinion might only be held by certain jurists who philosophize out of holy zeal rather than reasoned logic. For Alexander of Hales <note>A famous 13th-century Franciscan theologian</note> (Part 3, Question 36), to whom Adrian attributes that view, only speaks of one who does not serve the church: of whom he says that, just as a hired farmer who does not work is not worthy of his wage, neither are clerics who do not serve.

<margin>Sixth conclusion against the cited opinion.</margin>
¶ Against that opinion, therefore, a sixth conclusion is subjoined. Although clerics, by reason of their status, ought to shine in their morals among the laity—and all the more excellently the higher the dignity they are honored with—nevertheless, corruption of life alone does not oblige them to restitution: for his stipends are by no means granted to him under such a condition, but rather so that he may serve the church. Indeed, even kings and any public magistrates are bound to excel in the integrity of their morals; yet who would say they receive their salaries under such a contract?

<margin>Reason for the conclusion.</margin>
Add to this that if there were any probability in such an opinion, it would cast a snare <note>original: "laqueum"; a trap for the soul</note> upon men's consciences: for in such a great multitude of clerics, there are countless numbers who daily fall into mortal sin. Furthermore, as the facts clearly demonstrate, the Church—by prescribing punishments for crimes like simony <note>the buying or selling of church offices</note>, homicide, and others of that kind for which clerics are stripped of their prebends <note>a portion of the cathedral's income</note>—manifestly reveals its intent: that it does not intend to deprive anyone of their priesthood for any of the other sins.

¶ From what has been said, therefore, the answer to the question is gathered, which is neither entirely affirmative nor entirely negative, but a middle ground. Therefore, regarding the first argument composed from the chapters "It is permitted" and "Since" in the sixth book <note>original: "capitulis licet. & quoniam. libr. 6."</note>, we have 

<column-break/>

granted its conclusions, which were our first and second. But regarding the third argument, we denied in the sixth conclusion what it contended to prove. And thus, satisfaction has been given to those same arguments.

### ARTICLE VII.

->Whether members of religious orders made bishops are<-
->bound to their monastic observances.<-

->St. Thomas, Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 185, Article 8.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' set in a square border with a floral design.</image-desc>
BECAUSE in the previous questions we began to treat St. Thomas’s 185th question on the status of bishops, but the meditation on the canonical hours <note>The daily cycle of prayers</note> which the other question on clerics' goods offered us compelled us to divert for a little while (though not without reason), we thought it worthwhile to return to the last article of that same question, which we had set aside. We do this so that this tenth book, which was primarily instituted for the sake of bishops, may conclude with a consideration of monks who shine with episcopal dignity.

<margin>First argument.</margin>
¶ It is argued, therefore, that members of religious orders <term>religious: people bound by monastic vows</term> promoted to be bishops are not bound to their monastic observances. For it is held in the canon "It is decreed" (18, Question 1) that a canonical election absolves a monk from the yoke of the rule of monastic profession, and sacred ordination makes a bishop out of a monk. But monastic observances are contained under the yoke of the monastic institution; therefore, those who are created bishops are exempted from them.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
¶ Second. He who is raised from a lower to a higher grade seems to be absolved from the bonds of the lower, because a man cannot be burdened with so many packs. Just as those who profess the monastic life are released from all the vows by which they were bound in the secular world, and the episcopal status is higher than the monastic; therefore, a member of a religious order promoted to that level is freed from all canonical institutions.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
¶ Third. The most unbreakable bonds of monks are obedience and poverty. But a bishop is made exempt from the obedience of his former superiors. And that he is also untied from the other cord of poverty appears to be the opinion of the aforementioned canon, where it says that a monk created a bishop can legitimately enter into his father’s inheritance. Add to this that they are even permitted to make wills; therefore, they are also freed from other observances.

¶ To the contrary, it seems...

### Book Ten. Question V.

...on the canon of Innocent <note>original: "cano Innocentij"; referring to a decree by Pope Innocent I regarding monastic discipline</note> concerning monks (16. q. 1), which says: "Concerning monks who, after living a long time in monasteries, later reach the ranks of the clergy, we decree that they ought not to depart from their prior purpose." <note>original: "De monachis qui diu immorãtes in monasterijs posteà ad clericatus ordines peruenerint, statuimus nõ debere eos à priori proposito discedere."</note>

<margin>First conclusion.</margin>
The opinion of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary authority for this theological tradition</note> regarding this question is contained in three conclusions. First: A monk who has attained an episcopal seat is held to those religious observances which cannot be a hindrance to his duties as a bishop, and indeed may even be a help. Of this kind are **chastity**, **poverty**, and even the **religious habit** (the monk's clothing), which serves as a sign of that same obligation.

<margin>Second conclusion.</margin>
Second conclusion: If there are any regular observances <note>rules of a specific religious order</note> that could pose an obstacle to the administration of a bishop's duties, the religious person is exempted from their yoke by virtue of the episcopate. Such things include solitude, silence, and severe fasts or vigils which, by weakening the body, could render the bishop unfit for his duties.

<margin>Reason for both conclusions.</margin>
He demonstrates both of these conclusions together by this reasoning: Since both states—that is, the religious state <note>living as a monk or friar</note> and the state of bishops—are "states of perfection," they differ in this: the religious state paves the way to perfection as a form of discipleship, whereas the state of bishops is like a mastery of perfection. Now, the preparation for a certain form does not cease when that form is perfected, except insofar as it becomes an impediment. For example, a student’s reading and meditation should not cease when he becomes a teacher; indeed, he ought to do these more intensely. However, he should no longer merely listen, but teach, because the former would hinder the latter. In the same way, those religious observances that do not hinder the episcopal function do not cease for a monk-bishop, but those that do hinder it certainly do.

<margin>Third conclusion.</margin>
Third conclusion: Regarding other observances from which he is not absolved, such a bishop can sometimes use a dispensation through his own authority, just as he could have done in the religious life through the authority of a prelate.

<margin>Three types of works in a religious person.</margin>
These are the points of Saint Thomas, which sometimes require further explanation. First of all, following the number of conclusions, he denotes three types of works in a religious person that must be considered when they are assumed into the order of bishops. Some, naturally, do not hinder but contribute: such as **chastity**, **poverty**, and **obedience**. He does not abandon obedience, but changes its direction: so that he who once obeyed the superior of a religious order, 

<column-break/>

afterwards obeys the Pope. Some things, however, are clearly incompatible: such as solitude, silence, and immoderate fasting. Others are of a middle kind, which do not always hinder, but sometimes do: for example, if you consider the remaining moderate fasts, or wearing wool against the skin, and sleeping in one's habit. Therefore, regarding the first type, he says the monk-bishop is bound; regarding the second, he is absolved by the law itself. But in the remaining matters, although he is not entirely absolved from them, he can nevertheless dispense with them as it proves expedient.

Regarding each of these, some doubt arises. For the first category includes the triple vow: namely, **chastity**, **obedience**, and **poverty**. Regarding the first, there is no doubt that the monk remains bound to it, not only by the law governing priests, but also by the law of his religious order. Therefore, although the Church could dispense other bishops regarding continence (as we explained in Book 8), it cannot do so with monk-bishops. Nor is there any ambiguity regarding the second (obedience). For just as when a religious person is chosen as the General Master or Minister of an order, they remain subject to the Pope alone despite their vow of obedience, so it happens to a monk when he becomes a bishop: I say he does not desert obedience, but changes it.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
However, regarding the **vow of poverty**, there remains a real doubt that is not easy to solve. First, Saint Thomas, in this part of the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*</note>, both in Question 88, article 4, and here, most clearly defends the position that a monk made bishop is in no way absolved from the vow of poverty. For in the first conclusion, he uses continence and poverty as examples. And in his reply to the third argument, he says a religious bishop cannot have personal property. The reason appears plain: for, as was said in Book 8, the vow of religion is "indispensable" <note>cannot be set aside by any human power</note> because it includes these three vows.

<margin>An argument to the contrary.</margin>
On the other hand, there is the argument we hinted at there, which will demonstrate its force more clearly here. In a bishop, as stated above, two types of goods are considered: namely, secular and ecclesiastical. Setting aside secular goods for now, we argue regarding ecclesiastical ones. Other bishops taken from the secular clergy <note>priests who are not monks</note> have ownership of their portion after the division of church funds has been made, as we confirmed in many ways in Question 4. Therefore, since bishops summoned from religious orders are awarded their portion for exactly the same reason and in the same way as others chosen from the rest of the clergy, they should have ownership of that portion just like the others. I confess, for my part, that I do not know how to answer this argument, since I do not see how either of the premises can be denied.

<summary>This page discusses the legal and spiritual obligations of monks who become bishops, concluding that they remain bound to vows like chastity and poverty while being excused from monastic rules that would interfere with their active duties, such as silence and extreme fasting.</summary>

# F. D. Soto, on Justice and Right,

<margin>The Solution.</margin>
...I cannot deny. For it cannot be doubted that all are made bishops in the same manner. Indeed, St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> does not assign a different kind of poverty regarding these ecclesiastical goods to religious bishops than he does to the rest. In fact, in the sixth article of the present question, where he establishes that a bishop is not bound to poverty, he responds to the argument that the Apostles were poor by saying that a bishop is not held to that same level of poverty. He confirms this with the examples of Athanasius, Ambrose, and Augustine, who were both monks and bishops at once. There, he clearly shows that monk-bishops possess church property just like other secular bishops. Since the same Holy Doctor <note>A title for St. Thomas Aquinas</note> said in the very next article (the seventh) that regarding things designated for the bishop’s use, the reasoning seems to be the same as for private property, he certainly does not deny this to monk-bishops. But because he always kept his eye on that time when the clergy lived in common, he says simply that a monk made bishop is not released from his vow of poverty. Therefore, it should be said—under the judgment of those more expert—that just as a monk’s **obedience** is changed when he becomes a bishop so that he is subject only to the Pope, so too is his **poverty** changed. Thus, a portion of the tithes and other episcopal goods are granted to him just as they are to other bishops. This is, of course, so that he may support himself and, by a special command of mercy—which binds religious bishops more than others—be a source of aid to the poor. ¶ Regarding the other kind of goods, namely **secular goods** <note>private wealth or family inheritance</note>, there can be no doubt that even the vow of poverty is changed for him to some extent. This is clear from the canon *Statutum* (18. q. 1), where a monk who could not be a paternal heir while in the monastery is declared fit to enter into that same inheritance, which he can certainly enjoy for the rest of his life. The reason given is that his canonical election releases him from the "yoke of the rule" of monastic religion, and his sacred ordination has transformed him from a monk into a bishop. Furthermore, if you consult the custom that is now most widely accepted, the Pope sometimes grants dispensations to monk-bishops so that they may buy secular property, which they may afterwards leave to whomever they
<margin>The vow of poverty.</margin>
wish. If this custom is indeed legitimate, it certainly shows that the vow of poverty is not as indispensable as the vows of **continence** <note>chastity</note> or **obedience**. ¶ Regarding the second class of observances—namely those from which a monk is freed by the very fact that he becomes a
<margin>Cajetan.</margin>
bishop—Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a major commentator on Aquinas</note> noted here that this includes not only those things that clearly

<column-break/>

oppose the episcopal function, such as silence and solitude, but also those that are discordant with such a dignity or are unsuitable for it. This is easy to grant, but I do not know if the examples he adds are truly suitable. For he says that the bishop is freed from the ceremonies of having a companion of his order, drinking while seated, using two hands, the blessing, and similar things. Yet, although it may perhaps be so because these are matters of small importance, it is not for the reason he brings forward: namely, that such things are unbecoming of a bishop. Quite the contrary;
<margin>Cajetan's reasoning is not approved.</margin>
since such a bishop ought not to take off the religious habit unless he becomes the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, these types of monastic ceremonies do not so much disgrace him as they decorate his habit. In Italy, where monks are appointed to any poor bishopric, they either cast off the habit entirely or cover it with another shape; they set aside all monastic ceremonies with it because the Italians do not deign to see bishops in a monk's habit—a "plague" <note>Soto uses the word 'pestis' to describe this trend of devaluing the monastic habit</note> which has now crept into other nations. Cajetan took his judgment from there. However, he did not do so for himself, as even as a Cardinal he always lived most religiously in his monastic habit. Therefore, if a religious bishop joins to himself a companion of his order who thrives in authority, and uses whatever ceremonies of his religion and the <term>idiom</term> <note>the specific manner of speaking or behavior</note> of his order, it is so far from being indecent that those who do the opposite offend the eyes of prudent secular people. ¶ Regarding the third order of ceremonies, from which Saint Thomas says a religious person is not freed (even though he can dispense himself from them): such as not using linen <note>wearing wool instead</note>, keeping the regular fasts of the order, or (if he is of our order <note>the Dominicans</note> or the Carthusians) abstaining from eating meat,
<margin>A doubt.</margin>
there is a doubt. This is the primary question at present: by what bond are religious bishops held to these observances? That is, whether by a **legal debt** or only a **moral** one. For a legal debt is when someone is bound by a law through **coercive force**, such that whoever acts against it is subject to the penalties of the law. A moral bond, however, is when someone is bound only by the **directive force** <note>the inner guidance or spirit</note> of the law, but is not subject to penalties. An example is a Prince, who is not bound by coercive force but by directive force. St. Thomas seems to feel here that a monk is bound by both forces of the law, saying that in these matters he can only dispense with himself; by which he seems to imply that he is bound just as he was when he was in the cloister. ¶ Nevertheless, the opinion of Cajetan pleases me,
<margin>The solution.</margin>
which he set forth for the present case...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on whether a monk or friar (a "religious") who is elevated to the rank of bishop remains bound by the rules of his former monastic order. The previous page established that while certain vows like chastity remain, the "coercive" or legal power of the monastic order over the individual is removed once they become a bishop, as they are then subject only to the Pope.</meta>

### Book Ten, Question V.

...but he expressed this more clearly in a specific short work he titled on this matter: namely, in the *Little Book of Twenty-One Questions*, question 19. The opinion, indeed, is that he is not held by the debt of the law <note>original: "ex debito legis"</note>, but by moral honesty. This is because it is signified in the cited chapter *Statutum* <note>A specific decree in Canon Law</note> by these words: "He is absolved from the yoke of the monastic rule, and from a monk he becomes a bishop." For the word "yoke" designates a coercive force. Likewise, since he is exempt from the subjection of the superiors of his order—because he can in no way be punished except by the Pope—it is proof that he is not subject to the penalties of the monastic statutes. However, it is clear that he is bound by moral debt and decency: for after a man has professed the monastic life, which is a discipline of perfection, it is fitting that, having been made a master of perfection <note>i.e., a Bishop</note>, he should keep that same discipline. For although he is not bound by coercive force, he should keep it freely. Just as a student, although made a teacher, is freed from the fear of the rod and other compulsions by which he was driven to study, he ought nonetheless to devote himself to those same studies of his own accord. Nor is the example taken from the natural world unfitting: for as long as heat in wood prepares it for the form of fire, it is held by a certain coercive force of the agent; but when the substantial form of fire arrives, the heat becomes natural, and thus remains in the fire of its own accord.

<margin>First corollary.</margin>
From this it follows that the moral debt for a religious bishop—because he was taken from a religious order—is greater than that of a secular bishop <note>A priest who was never a monk</note>.

<margin>Second corollary.</margin>
It follows nonetheless, secondly, that a religious made bishop—even if he was bound under penalty of mortal sin to specific fasts on Fridays by a particular rule of his order (as is said to be the case in the Order of Saint Francis <note>The Franciscans</note>)—once made bishop, he may eat meat and break the fast on Christmas Day if it falls on a Friday. Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> currently says the opposite, but in his short work he more wisely changed his opinion. For in the chapter *Explicari*, where that privilege is granted to all Christians, none are excepted unless they are bound to fast by a specific vow or by regular observance. And this is understood as the legal debt of regular observance, which does not remain in a bishop except as a moral one. Nor did he make a specific vow of abstinence, except by vowing the religious life in general. Therefore, St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> is to be understood as meaning that a monk-bishop is not absolved from the said observances as far as the moral debt is concerned.

<margin>Argument.</margin>
But on the contrary: if that is so, then he is not bound to chastity either under the guilt of a moral crime, because a moral debt does not seem to bind under such guilt.

<column-break/>

The consequence is denied: because he made the vow of chastity expressly and specifically. By virtue of this, even if the coercive force of monastic observance ceases, the vow still binds. But he did not formally vow the other things (like specific fasts) except by vowing the religious life as a whole, the legal force of which ceases in him. It is true, however, that he does not remain subject to the penalties decreed in the religious order for those who break the three essential vows <note>Poverty, chastity, and obedience</note>.

¶ But does that moral debt bind a bishop from the Order of Saint Francis more than one from our order <note>The Dominican Order, to which the author, Soto, belonged</note>? This is asked because a Franciscan is bound to certain rules under penalty of mortal sin, while we Dominicans are bound to none <note>Dominican rules were generally considered to bind "under penalty of the rule" rather than "under mortal sin"</note>. And a prince, although not bound by coercive force, is perhaps nonetheless bound by some of his own laws under the guilt of mortal sin. The response is that if this opinion is true, the bishops of Saint Francis are no more bound than ours, because they are equally absolved from the legal debt. There is a difference here regarding a prince: for although he is not coerced, as long as a law lasts, if it pertains to him, he is bound by it.

¶ Religious, however, just as they ought to be much more hesitant in accepting bishoprics than secular priests, so they ought to be far more vigilant in administering them. For those who have hidden themselves in cloisters, saying farewell to the world, ought not—like Lot’s wife—to look back toward secular splendors. For besides offending God, they are a scandal to the lay people, and are consequently held in contempt and mockery; unless it is publicly clear both that they were dragged from their cloisters against their will, and that they serve the churches with all fear of God, while abstaining from other pomps which are not necessary for the dignity of their office.

---

<margin>To the first argument.</margin>
Thus the first argument at the beginning of the question regarding the canon *Statutum* has now been solved by this explanation.

<margin>To the second argument.</margin>
St. Thomas responds to the second argument that vows made in the world are not dissolved by religious profession simply because one ascends from a lower to a higher state, but because those vows are like a "particular" thing compared to a "universal" one: for example, like one who offered a part of himself to God compared to one who offers himself entirely. The part is included in the whole, and therefore, when the whole arrives, the part becomes superfluous. But the ascent from the religious life to the office of bishop is like moving from a preparation <note>original: "dispositione"</note> to perfection. Now, the preparation does not cease when perfection arrives. Understand this, as we said, regarding the moral debt, just as the heat that prepares the wood for fire remains within the fire.

<margin>To the third argument.</margin>
To the third argument, as far as it concerns obedience...

# F. D. Soto, On Justice and Right,

It has already been answered that [the vow] is not abandoned, but transformed: and the same applies regarding the vow of poverty.
<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
There remains, nevertheless, a doubt that Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority for Soto</note> suggests there regarding that chapter *Statutum* <note>original: "cap. statutum," a reference to a specific decree in Canon Law</note> concerning the paternal inheritance that a monk-turned-bishop acquires: to whom does it fall after his death, to the monastery or to the episcopal church? Indeed, the words of the chapter are obscure: for they explain nothing else except that what the monk had acquired [previously], he should leave to the monastery; but what he acquired after being made a bishop, he should restore to the altar at which he was consecrated.
<margin>The Solution.</margin>
The sense of these words, therefore, is what common usage declares: namely, that what he had acquired while still in the secular world, he leaves to the monastery; but what he added after being made bishop, he leaves to his episcopal church. However, regarding the goods of those religious who become titular bishops <note>Bishops who hold the title of a defunct diocese but do not oversee a physical territory</note>: because they do not have a see, even if things were acquired by them during their time as a bishop, these goods fall to their monasteries. 
Furthermore, it is manifest that they cannot make a will <note>original: "testamenta," legal testaments for the distribution of property</note> without a dispensation from the Pope. 
<margin>A religious bishop cannot make a will without permission.</margin>
And then Saint Thomas says, if a bishop is a member of a religious order, he is not granted the ability to make a will as if the property were his own, but because the Pope expands his power of distributing

<column-break/>

his goods, so that the same power lasts even after death.
But truly, after he is so freely granted this dispensation <gloss>permission</gloss> as are other bishops, it matters little how it is actually done. 

<margin>Epilogue.</margin> 
Behold the Work of ten Books which we promised concerning *Justice and Right*: and we have divided it into seventy-three Questions, and two hundred seventy-one Articles. Through various and slippery, and through arduous and difficult types of matters, with the divine breath <note>The Holy Spirit</note> breathing upon us, it has been led to the desired port in the Year of Christian Salvation One Thousand Five Hundred Fifty-four. 

In this work, if anything has been missed or mistaken by us through our lack of skill and ignorance, or certainly through negligence and drowsiness (for I am certain, through God’s mercy, that I have by no means failed through a lack of study), may the God of mercies himself forgive it. If, however, we have provided anything that might be of use to the Christian family, it must be credited to God alone: to Whom be praise and perennial glory through infinite ages of ages. 
Amen.

# Index of Books

**Fourth [Article]**, Whether **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), whose *Etymologies* served as a standard reference for law and definitions in the Middle Ages.</note> and those who follow him divide civil laws and human law appropriately. page 44.

## ¶ Book Three.

**Third [Part]**, On Law, insofar as it is the object of Justice: and on the substance of this virtue and its related parts, up to distributive justice: It boasts six Questions. page 191.

**QUESTION One, On Law:** possesses four articles. page same.
**First**, Whether law <note>original: "ius". This can mean "right" or "law" in a legal and moral sense.</note> is the object of justice. ibid.
**Second**, Whether the division of law into natural law and positive law <note>"Positive law" refers to laws specifically enacted by human or divine authority, as opposed to law inherent in nature.</note> is appropriate to the category, or not. page 194.

<column-break/>

**Third**, Whether the law of nations <note>original: "ius gentium". This refers to the common laws shared by all human civilizations, distinct from local "civil law."</note> is the same as natural law. page 196.
**Fourth**, Whether paternal right and masterly right <note>The specific rights and duties governing the relationship between a father and his children, or a master and his servants.</note> are distinguished from political justice and from each other by any reason. page 198.
**QUESTION Two, On justice:** encompasses eight articles. page 200.
**First**, Whether the definition of justice was rightly established by legal experts. page same.
**Second**, Whether justice is a virtue that directs the one who has it toward another. page 202.
**Third**, Whether justice is a virtue. page 203.
**Fourth**, Whether justice is in the will. page 204.
**Fifth**, Whether justice is a general virtue. page 206.
**Sextus**, Whether justice has a particular matter, or whether it concerns the passions and matters of others. page 209.
**Seventh**, Whether the "mean" of justice <note>In Aristotelian ethics, a virtue is the "mean" or balance between two extremes; justice is unique because its "mean" is often a literal equal distribution of things.</note> is the mean of the thing: and its act is to give to each their own right. page 212.
**Eighth**, Whether justice is the most eminent among the moral virtues, or not. page 214.
**QUESTION Three, On injustice:** is dispatched in only three articles. page 220.
**First**, Whether injustice is a special vice. page same.
**Second**, Whether whoever does an unjust thing is immediately judged to be unjust, or not. page 221.
**Third**, Whether someone can suffer injustice willingly. page 223.
**QUESTION Four, On judgment:** claims six articles for itself. page 225.
**First**, Whether judgment is an act of justice, or not. page same.
**Second**, Whether judging is lawful, or not. page 226.
**Third**, Whether rash judgment, for example proceeding from suspicion, is lawful. page 229.
**Fourth**, Whether doubts should be interpreted in the better part <note>A legal and moral principle suggesting that if a person's intent is unclear, one should assume the best of them.</note>. page 234.
**Fifth**, Whether judgment should always be according to written laws, or not. page 236.
**Sextus**, Whether a usurped judgment <note>A judgment made by someone who does not have the legal authority to do so.</note> is always perverse. page 239.
**QUESTION Five, On the division of Justice:** requires four articles. page 240.
**First**, Whether particular justice is rightly divided into distributive and commutative. <note>Distributive justice concerns how a community shares goods; commutative justice concerns fair dealing in private business and exchange.</note> ibid.
**Second**, Whether the mean of distributive and commutative justice is the same, or not. page 243.
**Third**, Whether the matter of distributive and commutative justice is the same. page 245.

*First, Whether a vow is possible regarding something to which we were not bound by the force of a command. same page.*
*Second, Whether a vow is perfected solely by the intent of the will. page 615.*
*Third, Whether a vow must always be made concerning a greater good. page 620.*
### QUESTION Two, On the force and virtue of a vow: requires five Articles. page 630.

<column-break/>

*First, Whether every vow obliges one to its observation. same page.*
*Second, Whether it is useful and expedient to make a vow. page 641.*
*Third, Whether a vow is an act of worship <note>original: "latriæ," the highest form of worship reserved for God alone</note> or religion. page 642.*
*Fourth, Whether it is more praiseworthy and meritorious to do something by vow than without it. page 644.*
*Fifth, Whether a vow becomes solemn through the reception of holy orders and through religious profession. page 647.*
### QUESTION Three, On those who have the capacity to make a vow: consists of two Articles. page 653.
*First, Whether those who are subject to the power of another <note>such as children, servants, or monks under an abbot</note> can make a vow. same page.*
*The other, Whether children can bind themselves by a religious vow. page 660.*
### QUESTION Four, On the dispensation and commutation of a vow: contains three Articles. page 664.
*First, Whether a dispensation <note>a formal release from an obligation</note> can be made in a vow. same page.*
*Second, Whether a dispensation can be made regarding a solemn vow of religious continence. page 666.*
*Third, Whether the authority of a prelate is required for the commutation <note>original: "commutationem," the substitution of one religious obligation for another equivalent one</note> or dispensation of a vow. page 672.*
### QUESTION Five, On the religious vow in particular: occupies four Articles. page 678.
*First, Whether a religious vow pertains to the state of perfection. same page.*
*Second, Whether poverty, even unto beggary, belongs to the perfection of monastic life. page 686.*
*Third, Whether the vow of chastity is part of the intrinsic nature of religion or not? page 690.*
*Fourth, Whether the vow of obedience is of the essence of religion. page 694.*
### QUESTION Six, on the vow and continence of priests: completed in only two Articles. page 696.
*The former, Whether the priestly vow of continence was fitting and necessary for the dignity and stability of the Church. same page.*
*The latter, Whether priestly continence began from the very cradle of the Church <note>original: "incunabulis," literally "swaddling clothes," referring to the earliest period of Church history</note> or not? page 702.*

## ¶ Book Nine.

**NINE, On Tithes and Simony: enriched by eight Questions. page 710.**

*QUESTION One, On sacrifice in general: enjoys four Articles. same page.*
*First, Whether sacrificing to God is part of the law of nature. in the same place.*
*Second, Whether sacrifice should be offered to God alone. page 712.*
*Third, Whether the offering of sacrifices is an act of a special virtue. page 714.*
*Fourth, Whether all mortals are bound to offer sacrifices to God. page 715.*

*QUESTION Two, On the ineffable sacrifice of the altar <note>original: "sacrificio altaris," referring to the Eucharist or Holy Mass</note> in particular: has one and then another Article. page 716.*
*One, Whether the most holy sacrament of the altar is truly a sacrifice. same page.*
*The Other, Whether the sacrifice of the altar offered for many profits individuals for satisfaction just as much as if it were offered for only one. page 720.*

*QUESTION Three, On offerings and firstfruits <note>original: "primitiÿs," the first portion of a harvest dedicated to God</note>: contains four Articles. page 727.*
*First, Whether men are bound to make offerings by the necessity of a commandment. same page.*
*Second, Whether offerings are owed to priests alone. page 731.*
*Third, Whether it is lawful to make offerings from all things that are lawfully possessed. page 732.*
*Fourth, Whether men are bound to the payment of tithes <term>Tithes: a tenth part of income or produce paid to support the church</term>. page 735.*

*QUESTION Four, On tithes: completed by the fourth Article. page 737.*
*First, Whether men are bound to give tithes by the necessity of a commandment. same page.*
*Second, Whether Christians are bound to pay tithes on all things. page 743.*
*Third, Whether tithes are owed to clerics <note>the ordained clergy</note> alone. page 746.*
*Fourth, Whether even the clerics themselves are bound to pay tithes, or not? page 748.*

*QUESTION Five, On the sin of Simony <term>Simony: the act of buying or selling sacred things, such as sacraments or church offices</term> in general: consists of only two Articles. page 751.*
*One, Whether Simony is a deliberate will to buy and sell something spiritual, or something attached to the spiritual. same page.*
*The Other, Whether the vice of Simony is, by its very nature, a mortal sin. page 755.*

*QUESTION Six, On the matter of Simony: has obtained two Articles. page 759.*

<column-break/>

*First, Whether it is ever lawful to either give or receive money for the Sacraments. same page.*
*The Other, Whether it is lawful to give and receive money for spiritual actions. page 766.*

*QUESTION Seven, On Simony, in the pursuit of priesthoods and dignities. has attained three Articles. page 771.*
*First, Whether it is lawful to receive a price for priesthoods and other prebends <term>Prebends: a portion of church revenues granted to a clergyman as a stipend</term> which are attached to spiritual matters. same page.*
*Second, Whether an exchange of prebends can be done without Simony. page 776.*
*Third, Whether it is lawful to bestow spiritual things in exchange for a gift, whether it be of the tongue <note>original: "à lingua," meaning praise or flattery</note> or from any other service. page 779.*

*QUESTION Eight, On the restitution for Simony and the punishment of the Simoniac <note>one who commits simony</note>: has been allotted two Articles. page 784.*
*One, Whether whatever is either given or received through Simony is subject to restitution. same page.*
*The Other, Whether the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> is able to grant a dispensation regarding the penalties of simony. page 793.*

## ¶ Book Ten.

**TEN, finally and lastly, on the state, order, and residence of Prelates, and on the Canonical Hours: completed in five Questions. page 796.**

*QUESTION One, On the Episcopal institute <note>the office of a Bishop</note>, and the law by which it was instituted: contained in four Articles. same page.*
*First, Whether the episcopal dignity was necessary in the Church above the priestly dignity. in the same place.*
*Second, Whether the episcopate is an order distinct by its nature from a simple priest. page 799.*
*Third, Do bishops differ among themselves just as they differ from simple priests? page 802.*
*Fourth, Whether the institution of the episcopal dignity is by Divine Right <term>Divine Right: law established by God's will rather than human or ecclesiastical legislation</term>. page 805.*

*First, Whether it is lawful to desire a Bishopric, or not. same page.*

*Third, Whether it is necessary that he who is elevated to the Episcopate be better than others. page 818.*

**QUESTION Three, on the residency of bishops: requires four Articles. page 823.**
*First, Whether bishops are bound to reside in their dioceses. page 823 (same).*

*First, Whether a bishop is permitted to possess anything of his own, or not. page 847 (same).*
*Second, Whether bishops sin mortally if they do not bestow the church goods they manage upon the poor. page 850.*

Cattle-rustling <term>Abigeatus: the Roman law term for the specialized crime of stealing livestock from a herd.</term>, the theft of a scattered herd. 417.b.
¶ Abraham was chosen not by his own merit, but by the mercy of God, so that Christ might take His origin from him. 90.b.
It is more probable that Abraham and Sarah were siblings than cousins <note>original: "fratrueles"</note>. 120. a.
¶ The renunciation of the world exists not only by divine law established through Christ, but is drawn from the very vitals of natural law. 683.a.
¶ What abrogation is: and whether it differs from dispensation and invalidation <note>original: "irritatione"</note>. 79.a.
¶ "Respect of persons" <term>Acceptio personarum: the unfair favoring of one person over another in a legal or social context, often translated as "partiality."</term> is a term granted Latinity by sacred interpreters; it is also called regard for persons. 250.a.
Respect of persons is a crime of injustice in which, during the distribution of goods or honors, consideration is given not to causes relevant to the matter, but to the person; for this reason, it is by its nature a mortal crime. Ibid., b.
Respect of persons is not simply the act of considering the quality of a person which increases their merit or crime. 251.a.
Respect of persons in spiritual matters is, by its nature, more serious than in temporal matters. 253. b.
Respect of persons presents an obvious crime when a worthy person is passed over and an unworthy person is chosen. 254.b.
When the crime of respect of persons occurs because a magistracy is conferred upon an unworthy person, it obligates the offender to make restitution to the people. 267.a.
Respect of persons is often committed in the delivery of judgments. 272.a.
No one is bound to pay the penalty for unjust partiality before a formal condemnation. 351.b.

One can be a cause of partiality <note>original: "Acceptionis causa"</note> in nine ways. 373.a.
The acceptance of a thing is considered in three ways and happens in two manners: namely, directly and indirectly. Ibid., b.
¶ In an evil action, the nature of the evil is considered differently from the nature of the fault. 370.a.
¶ A zealous act <note>original: "Actus studiosus"</note> is judged to belong to a virtue in two ways. 643.a.
Who is bound to accuse, and when. 443.b. and 444.a. & b.
¶ It is always forbidden for the excommunicated and the infamous to accuse, although they are bound to denounce a crime when it is ruinous to the republic. 446.a.
Subjects are forbidden from accusing their superiors, as are clerics in cases involving bloodshed <note>original: "causa sanguinis," referring to capital cases where a life is at stake.</note>. Ibid.
The required form of an accusation is that it be made in writing. Ibid., b.
An accusation is corrupted by three vices, namely: calumny, collusion <term>Praevaricatio: a legal term for when an accuser or advocate colludes with the opposition or betrays their own side.</term>, and evasion <note>original: "tergiversatione"</note>. 447. b.
One who has no accuser ought not to be barred from honors. 440. b.
An obvious crime does not require an accuser. 441.a.
Infamy, evidence, and clamorous report <note>original: "insinuatio"</note> take the place of a formal accuser. Ibid., b.
There is no need for an accuser where a legal denunciation is present, just as there is none in the case of "fraternal correction" <note>A Christian practice of private admonition before seeking public or legal remedy.</note>. Ibid.
¶ Adam was prince by that right as the first parent, and thus was lord of the whole world. 298.a.
By the transgression of Adam, we all incur the penalty of death. 19.b.
¶ No warning <note>original: "Admonitio"</note> is required when it is incumbent upon someone to accuse regarding their own property. 445.a.

...[fruits] do not equal the annuity. 568. b.
One buying a **real annuity** <note>original: "Censum realem"; a financial contract where a person pays a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment secured by real property</note> does not buy the fruits of the pledged thing, but the right to demand the annuity. Ibid.
Anyone can justly buy a **personal annuity** <note>original: "Censum personalem"</note>, which the seller establishes upon their own person. 568. a.
The Papal Decrees of Martin V and Calixtus III <note>original: "Extrauagantes Martin. & Calix."; specifically referring to the *Extravagantes* or supplemental canon laws regarding finances</note> do not condemn personal annuities or those established on uncertain goods, even those that do not bear fruit. 569. b.
Anyone can also establish **monetary annuities** <note>original: "Census pecuniarium"</note> upon their own assets, not only in the form of a gift, but also as a sale. 567. a.
An annuity can be established upon the use of money. Ibid. b.
Temporary monetary annuities for a fixed time, where the payment is of greater value than the price paid, are suspect and should be rejected <note>This refers to the concern that such contracts might be a cover for usury</note>. 572. a. b.
**Perpetual annuities** are not only lawfully purchased, but there is less suspicion of usury in them than in temporary ones. 570. b.
The obligation of a perpetual annuity pertains to the heirs when the annuity was established on uncertain and undefined goods; but if it was assigned to a specific thing, it lasts only as long as that thing remains; if it is destroyed, the heirs are no longer bound. 571. a.
Temporary annuities are lawfully purchased. 571. a.
A **life annuity** <note>original: "Census vitalitius"</note> is lawful. 572. b.
**Redeemable annuities** are lawfully purchased, provided the condition is added that it be redeemed not in portions and parts, but all at once. 574. a.
It is by no means right to buy an annuity with a **buyback agreement** <note>original: "pacto retroemendi"</note>: for example, by obligating the seller to buy back the same at the same or a lower price. 573. a.
To buy an annuity with an agreement to sell back <note>original: "pacto retrouendendi"</note> is lawful. Ibid.
Buying an annuity with a sell-back agreement at a set time—both before which the seller has no power to redeem, and after which if not redeemed, no further power to redeem is granted and the annuity remains perpetual—is lawful. Ibid. b.
What price for an annuity is called just. Ibid.
Many conditions render an annuity unjust. Ibid.

## Knowledge

## Of Exchanges
Some are voluntary, others involuntary. 246. a.
The name "exchange" <note>original: "Commutationis"</note> does not imply a simple giving or receiving, but giving so that they may receive, and receiving so that they may return. 246. a.
A voluntary exchange implies a certain spontaneous and voluntary action on the part of both the giver and the receiver. 246. a.
An involuntary exchange supposes an involuntary action on the part of the victim as much as the taker. 246. a.
Involuntary exchanges are divided into those which are done secretly and without the owner's knowledge through fraud, and those which are done manifestly through violence. 246. b.
Voluntary exchanges are also divided into their own constituent parts. 246. b.

## Compensation
Which must be made for a life taken away. 337. b.
Compensation for reputation can be excellently made. 346. a.

## Common things
Things ought to be common regarding their use through the kindness of mercy and liberality. 297. b.
There can be a threefold community of things. Ibid. a.

## Loan
In what way a **loan for use** and a **loan for consumption** are distinguished. 370. a. <note>original: "Commodatum & mutuum"; *commodatum* is a loan of a specific item to be returned, while *mutuum* is a loan of fungible goods like money or grain to be replaced by an equal amount</note>.

## Of the Council
Explanation of the Council of the Apostles in Acts 15. Ibid. a.

## Conclusion
A practical conclusion is less certain the closer it is to singular [specific] cases. 35. b.

## For one condemned
It is permitted for one condemned to death to flee and free himself from impediments. 462. a. & b.
It is not permitted to provide tools for one justly condemned to death so that he may free himself from chains and flee. Ibid. b.
One justly condemned to perish by hunger can abstain from foods offered to him against the will of the judge. 464. a.
It is not permitted for one justly and legally condemned by a legitimate judge to defend himself. 461. a.
It is lawful for one unjustly condemned to resist the judge, provided that no scandal would be given from which a grave disturbance might be feared. Ibid. a.
One condemned by legitimate testimony, but nevertheless without any cause because he is innocent, is bound to obey the judge's sentence if he cannot defend himself without inflicting wounds. Ibid. b.

## Of those having confessed
Let those having confessed their own crime not be interrogated regarding the consciences of others, except in the crime of high treason and heresy. 455. a.

In a legal sentence for a penalty that does not involve death or bodily harm, the defendant himself is bound to execute the sentence even if he is condemned to take action. 66. a.

A Judge makes use of a twofold knowledge: both a universal knowledge of law and a particular knowledge of fact. In the same place.

A Judge is bound to follow the universal knowledge of law so holistically that he cannot even consult his own private judgment if it is contrary. In the same place.

A Judge in a particular fact can assist himself with his own talent and prudence in examining documents and witnesses, which he is especially bound to do when an innocent person known to him is accused. In the same place.

A Judge is bound to condemn an innocent person [who is] proven guilty <note>A difficult concept in medieval law: the judge must act as a public official based on public evidence, not as a private person based on private knowledge.</note>. 341. a.

A Judge must, in every cause, pronounce sentence according to the allegations and proofs, even against the truth evidently known to himself. 437. a.

A Judge who condemns an innocent person known to himself, but proven guilty by suitable testimony, does not act against conscience. 439. a.

In criminal matters, a Judge cannot condemn anyone in a trial unless they have been accused. 440. a.

No Judge, whether supreme or lowest, can remit a penalty before the injured party forgives the injury. 442. a.

It is within the discretion of the supreme judge, but not within the discretion of an inferior one, to relax the penalty of the law after the accuser has ceased the accusation. In the same place.

A supreme Judge can sometimes abolish an accusation even if the accuser protests. In the same place. b.

Four things are necessary in a Judge: namely,

<column-break/>

the power of judging, truth, reputation, and the force of execution. 432. b.

A Judge cannot condemn one whom he evidently knows to be guilty when the defendant is not proven [guilty] by legitimate testimony. 435. b.

The personal knowledge of a Judge is not considered sufficient testimony. In the same place.

**The Judicature** <note>original: "Iudicatus," likely referring to the office of judging or those holding judicial rank.</note> or the places of those who are on the king's councils; it is illicit and scandalous to see them <note>This likely refers to the secrecy of royal council deliberations.</note>. 270. b.

¶ It is not lawful to judge anyone except one who is subject to the judge, either simply or in such a case. 433. a.

In a judicial court, it happens in four ways that one person is subject to another. In the same place. b.

Pilate sinned in judging Christ. 434. a.

By divine **Judgment**, [they] are not to be abandoned because of many offenses. 454. b.

Judgment is the greatest act of one's own justice. 225. b.

The name of "Judgment" first signifies the right definition of just things; then the right definition of other virtues concerning their own objects. In the same place.

A right Judgment requires two virtues: both that which sets forth the judgment, and that which disposes the power of the judge toward the rectitude of the judgment. In the same place.

The particular judgment of a diligent person is only required in the remaining virtues; however, in matters of justice, the judgment of a superior is also necessary. 226. a.

It must be observed by **Judgment** whether such an evil is one that another would take more bitterly to hear about himself than if it were a mortal sin. In the same place.

That a Judgment may be right, it requires three things: namely, that it proceed from the authority of the judge, from an affection for justice, and from the rectitude of prudence. 226. b.

Each of the judges subverts the substance of judgment if he takes away anything from the right of one party to give it to another. 227. a.

A judgment usurped without the authority of a presiding officer [is void]; without the substance of justice, it is iniquitous; without prudence and the order of law, it is suspicious; if, however, it is from levity and not legitimate proof, it is called rash. In the same place.

A defect in the individual conditions of judgment by its nature constitutes a mortal sin. In the same place.

A judgment delivered from a bad affection is a sin according to that affection. In the same place. b.

...from the object. 229. b.
There are four degrees of rash judgment. 230. a.

Rash judgment is the same as that which is deliberately conceived without a legitimate cause. 230. a.

A certain judgment in speculative <note>theoretical or academic</note> matters requires this one thing: that it have absolutely no mixture of ambiguity; in moral matters, however, a little is considered as nothing. 232. a.

Our law was contained in the Old Law, not in actual form, but in its power <note>original: "virtute," meaning potentially or through its underlying moral power</note>. Ibidem. b.
The law of divorce <note>original: "Lex repudij"</note> did not command one to divorce his wife, but permitted it; and the New Law corrected this so it would have no place except regarding the marriage bed. Ibidem. 181.a.
The ancient law was more burdensome than the new, if the difficulty is weighed from the perspective of the object. Ibidem.
Beyond natural law, the Gospel Law commanded nothing except the sacraments. Ibidem.
Our law is in a certain way more burdensome than the old, if you consider the difficulty of the manner of acting; especially for those who are not imbued with virtuous habits. Ibidem.

<column-break/>

The Law of Christ contains only three things: moral precepts, sacraments, and counsels. 182.a.
The Gospel Law differs from the Old by twelve distinctions. 182.b. & 183.a.
In external works, the Gospel Law laid the seven sacraments as foundations. 183.b.
The majesty of the Gospel Law did not teach that other ceremonies should be instituted through it, except those necessary for administering the sacraments. 184.a.
The Gospel Law is called by James <note>the Apostle James in the New Testament</note> the "law of perfect liberty" for a threefold reason. 185.a.
The Gospel Law perfectly shapes all human conduct, both inwardly and deeply <note>original: "incutè," meaning "under the skin" or profoundly</note>. 186.a.
The Gospel Law proceeds in a wonderful order to instruct people regarding internal and external acts. Ibidem.
The Gospel Law corrected some judicial precepts, but it did not correct the ceremonial ones at all; rather, it discarded <note>original: "ablegauit"</note> them. 187.a.
The New Law not only explained natural counsels but also recently added others. 188.b.
At what point in time the New Law began to be binding. 16.a.b. 160.a. 163.b.
Four distinct laws found in Paul <note>the Apostle Paul</note>. 10.a.
**Human law** <note>original: "Lex humana"</note> does not flourish with the same certainty as speculative conclusions. 39.a.
It is better for the law to rule than for a man; and this is urged for excellent reasons. 39. b.a.
Every law established by humans, if it is right, is derived from natural law. 40.a.
The derivation of human law from natural law, by way of conclusion, is more an explanation of a natural principle than a new precept of virtue. 41.a.
The qualities of human law handed down by Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville, a 7th-century scholar whose definitions of law were foundational for the Middle Ages</note> are explained. 42.a.b. 43.a.
A multitude of laws is harmful <note>original: "vitiosa," meaning full of vice or defects</note>. 43.a.
Law ought to be plain and free from obscurity, lest, like a mousetrap, it catch the ignorant. 43.b.
How law and custom differ. 43.b.
Why law is compared to a "Lesbian rule." <note>original: "regulæ Lesbiæ." This refers to a flexible lead ruler used by ancient builders on the island of Lesbos that could bend to the shape of stone; it is a metaphor for a law that can be adapted to specific circumstances (equity).</note> 44.a.
Law ought to be established for the common good. 46.b.
The fourfold division of human law. 44.a.
Law does not look at things that happen rarely, but at those which happen frequently. 46.b.
Human law especially punishes those crimes that are adverse to the tranquility of the state. 48.a.

->Alphabetical Index.<-

### Index Alphabeticus.

**Human law** commands every act of virtue, though not every individual one. 48. b. 49. a.
**Law** does not command the habit <note>the internal disposition or character trait</note> but the act. 49. b.
**Human law** conducts itself differently regarding the commanding of virtues and the prohibition of vices. 49. b.
**Human law**, whether it be civil or canon: provided it is just in its force, it has the power to bind the consciences of subjects. 50. b.
The justice of a **law** is to be weighed based on all its causes. 50. b.
An unjust **human law** does not bind in conscience. 50. b.
**Although laws** that only oppose the human good do not bind in conscience, they must sometimes nevertheless be obeyed for the sake of avoiding scandal <note>in this context, "scandal" means leading others into spiritual error or social disorder</note>; it is otherwise if they are repugnant to the divine good. 51. a.
**Human law** is able to compel its observance even at the cost of one's own life <note>original: "capitis detrimento," literally "detriment of the head," referring here to the risk of death or capital punishment</note>. 54. b.
It is permissible for **human law** to be changed at times. 73. b.
**Human laws** command acts of justice alone by their primary intention; however, concerning the rest of the virtues, only insofar as they relate to justice. 104. b.
The rectitude <note>straightness or correctness</note> of **human law** is not of the same nature as physical rectitude found in bodily quantities. 75. b.
The distinction between **laws and arts** regarding their variation. 75.
If a **law** were to decree that no future custom would have force against it, it would be annulled by no custom. 77. a.
**As long as the reason** for a law remains, a custom cannot prevail against it. 78. a.
**Regarding human law**, the one upon whom governance rests has the power of granting dispensations <note>exemptions from the law for specific cases</note>. 78. b.
**Canon law** and ecclesiastical law bind under the guilt of mortal sin <note>original: "reatu mortalis noxae"</note>, which assertion of faith is sufficiently strengthened against certain heresiarchs <note>leaders of heretical movements</note>; however, concerning civil law, there is not equal certainty of faith. 51. b. 52. a.
**Ecclesiastical law**, as well as civil law, binds men; and not only insofar as they are interpreters of divine law—as Gerson <note>Jean Gerson, a famous 15th-century theologian and reformer</note> devised—but insofar as they are human laws. 52. b. 53. a. b.
**Ecclesiastical law** does not bind at the risk of death, unless contempt for the law or injury to the faith intervenes. 55. a.
**In those laws which** concern the Church most greatly, neither the Pope nor a council can grant a dispensation so as to change them immediately. 75. a.

<column-break/>

What **civil laws** decree regarding the children of clerics and those in religious orders, 311. b., and regarding the illegitimate <note>original: "nothis"</note> children of laypeople. 310. b.
**Laws do not prohibit** the transfer of ownership in games <note>referring to gambling or wagering</note>. 315. a. see, game.
Every **obligation of laws** is with God as its author. 329. b.
**Tax laws** <note>original: "leges vectigalium"</note> bind in conscience. 352. a.
All **penal laws** bind to guilt <note>meaning they create a moral obligation, not just a legal one</note>, unless the contrary is expressed, whether they are mixed or purely penal. This is against Henry <note>likely Henry of Ghent, a 13th-century philosopher who argued some laws only bind to the penalty, not to the sin</note>. 56. a. 57. a.
The **penal laws** of the Old Law against thieves and adulterers <note>original: "mechos"</note>, Exodus 22 and Leviticus 20, bound to guilt; similarly also now in canon law. 58. a.
**Penal laws**, by reason of saying "by the fact itself" <note>original: "ipso facto"</note> or "by the law itself" <note>original: "ipso iure"</note> or something similar, do not bind to punishment before a sentence is handed down by a judge, such that the defendant is held to offer it himself. 60. b.
When a **law** decrees a punishment "by the fact itself," there is no need for a sentence to be passed upon the punishment, but rather upon the crime. 62. b.
The **penal laws** of colleges bind to punishment before condemnation if their founder sanctioned such laws under this form. 67. a. b.
The **penal laws** of the Academy of Salamanca <note>a major center of Spanish legal and theological thought</note> passed against those who take precedence or seek office <note>original: "prefatores & ambitores"</note> do not bind before condemnation; unless someone, when legally interrogated, wickedly denies the truth. 67. b.
**Laws of prescription** <note>the legal acquisition of property or rights through the passage of time</note> are not purely penal. 68. a.
A **law** is most unjust which commands that one condemned to corporal punishment should carry it out himself. 464. b.
**Liberty** is not diminished by the obligation of a vow. 636. a.
In what **Christian liberty** consists. 695. b.
**Litanies** which are used in the night office on non-feast days <note>original: "profestis diebus"</note> do not have the force of a command by custom. 889. a.
**Lot**, by offering his daughters, did a shameful thing; and therefore he sinned, unless perhaps ignorance might excuse him. 536. b.
**Lot** did not fail by the sin of incest because he was drunk. 407. b.
**Lucretia** <note>the legendary Roman woman whose suicide followed her rape by the king's son</note> failed by killing herself. 395. b.
The desire for **profit**, if it keeps itself within the bounds of deceit or fraud, is not a mortal sin. 314. b.

### Price
The **Price** of a thing is not to be valued according to its own nature, but inasfar as it comes into human use. 546. b.
The **Price** of a thing, for it to be just, is weighed from many factors. 547. a.
A **Just Price** is twofold: natural and legal. ibid.
A **Natural Price** is threefold: rigid, pious, and moderate. <note>Scholastic economics often defined the "pious" price as the lowest fair price and "rigid" as the highest.</note> ibid. b.
The **Price** of all things, if it were possible, ought to be fixed by law. ibid. b.
A **Price** is not called "just" by anyone's whim, but according to the estimation of prudent men. ibid.
A **Price** often becomes unjust if the seller considers his own expenses for the thing sold during the sale. ibid.
The **Price** of gems and other things which are not necessary for the commonwealth will be as much as a knowing and prudent buyer is willing to give. 549. a.
An abundance of buyers increases the **Prices** of things, while a rarity decreases them. 548. a. 551. a.

The distinction between a **solemn vow** and a **simple vow** <note>In canon law, a solemn vow is a public, perpetual commitment recognized by the Church as absolute, such as those taken by monks; a simple vow is often private or temporary.</note> is a specific one. 652. a.

A vow that a religious person has made regarding a "free matter" <note>A matter not already governed by their monastic rule.</note> can be revealed to the prelate; and if it is burdensome, they may disclose their distress and grievance so that he may void it. 656. b.
A religious person is bound to reveal a vow they made regarding a forbidden thing to the prelate before they fall into delay. 657. a.
A vow made by a religious person with the permission of the prelate can nevertheless be voided by that same prelate. Ibid.
A husband can void all the **vows of his wife**. 657. b.
Whether a vow made by a husband not to seek the **marital debt** <note>original: "debitum"; the traditional term for the right of spouses to physical intimacy.</note> holds without the consent of the wife. 658. a.
A vow of chastity made by both spouses by mutual consent cannot be voided by them again; rather, the vow of each is considered an absolute vow of chastity. 659. a.
Any vow, whether of a wife, a son, or a religious person, once voided, retains no power thereafter by which it might bind at any time, unless it is made again. 659. a.
Whether superiors can void vows made by a wife to be fulfilled if she outlives her husband; and the same regarding a son who makes a vow while under a parent's care to be fulfilled after his emancipation; and likewise a servant under the condition that he is granted freedom. 659. b.

<column-break/>

No boy or girl can bind themselves with any vow before the years of puberty, unless they are endowed with the light of reason so that they can deliberate. 661. a.
No one, no matter how capable of discernment, can take a **solemn vow** before the years of puberty. 661. b.
Anyone can bind themselves most firmly with a solemn or simple vow of religion after the years of puberty, even if their parents object. Ibid.
The difference and similarity between a personal vow and a real vow <note>A personal vow involves an action by the person; a 'real' vow (from 'res') involves a physical thing or property.</note>. 662. b.
To hinder oneself by a vow from accepting a **bishopric** involves no wickedness in itself. 817. b.
A vow made by a son while he was under his father's power, and not then voided by the father, cannot be voided by the father after the son is emancipated. 663. b.
Any simple vow is subject to the power of the Church, both so that she may dispense it and so that she may **commute** <note>To change one obligation for another, usually of equal or greater spiritual value.</note> it into another thing. 664. b.
The dispensation of a vow does not remove divine law, but it removes the obligation that arose from the mere will of the person making the vow. 666. a.
A vow made upon receiving **holy orders** can be dispensed by the Pope before it is made—namely, by repealing the current law—and after it is made with those who have already taken a solemn vow. 668. b.
No dispensation applies to a **solemn vow of religion**. 699. a. & b.
The authority of a superior is necessary to dispense a vow. 672. a.
A cause is required for the dispensation of a vow, and likewise for a commutation into a lesser good. Ibid. b.
The authority of a superior is not required for the commutation of a vow into a better thing, when it is manifest that the new act is better. Ibid. Indeed, perhaps not even for a change into an equal thing. 676. b.
Vows made while "in the world" <note>original: "in seculo"; meaning secular life as opposed to life in a monastery.</note> are considered extinguished by a solemn vow of religion, because all things are changed for the better. 673. a. & 676. b.
A solemn vow of religion can be changed into another higher religious vow by one's own authority, but not into another kind of vow. Ibid.
Every bishop can dispense from any simple vow of his parishioners. However, this power in an **Archbishop** does not extend to the dioceses subordinate to him. The same [power] exists in Abbots and [superiors] of religious...

**Vow, Vows, Chastity, Dispensation, Religion, Bishop, Pope, Marriage, Parents, Sons, Servants, Authority**
