# Alphabetical Index.

The authority of any prefects of regions to dispense from the vows of their subjects. 673. b.
The faculty for dispensing a vow is the same everywhere for the purpose of commutation <note>Commutation refers to the legal practice of substituting one religious obligation for another of equal or greater value.</note>. 673. b.
Vows of subjects regarding moving to a higher religious order can be dispensed by their own prelates. 674. a.
The dispensation of a "penal vow" of religion <note>A vow taken as a form of self-imposed penance for a sin.</note> and of the pilgrimage to Jerusalem is reserved to the Supreme Pontiff. Ibid. b.
A cause is necessary for the dispensation of a vow; however, if the change is for something better, no opposing cause is required at all. It is enough that it leads more toward the spiritual goal. 675. a.
A vow cannot be dispensed or commuted by the privilege of a Crusade Bull <note>original: "cruciatæ bullæ"; specific papal decrees granting indulgences and legal privileges to those supporting the Crusades.</note> unless it was made before the bull was received. 676. a.
To dispense a simple vow of religion or perpetual chastity has not yet been granted by any Crusade diploma. Ibid. a.
The vow of priests is dispensable by the Church. 704. a. & 692. b.
The vow of religion consists of poverty, chastity, and obedience. 631. b.
Christ outlined the three [vows] of monks in Matthew 5. 636. a.
The manner of vowing which Luther <note>Martin Luther, whose views on monastic vows were a central point of conflict during the Reformation.</note> established. 684. a.
Transgression of a vow is, by its nature, a mortal sin and a sacrilege. 630. b.
A simple vow of religion made after a marriage contract does not carry any further obligation. 638. b.
Penance for a vow can be a sin, and how it is not a sin. 347. a.
**Acquisition by Prescription** <note>original: "Usucapio"; a legal concept where ownership of property is gained through long-term possession.</note>: in what amount of time it occurs. 323. a.
**Usury**: its manifold definitions. 506. a. & 507. a.
Usury is committed in many ways. 516. b.
Usury differs from lending at interest <note>original: "foenore"; in Roman law, 'foenus' was the legal rate of interest, while 'usura' often carried a more negative moral connotation.</note>. 506. b.
Usury is the same as "offspring" and "a bite." Ibid. b <note>This refers to the etymology of the Hebrew word for usury, 'neshek', which literally means 'a bite', and the Greek 'tokos', which means 'offspring' or 'birth', as money is unnaturally "breeding" more money.</note>.
Usury only has a place in a contract of exchange and in others where the nature of a loan is present. 507. a.
Usury is the price of the use of a loaned thing. 507. b.
It is not usury if it is the price received for money leased for show or decoration <note>Such as renting coins to a banker to display in a window to suggest wealth, where the actual money is not spent.</note>. 507. b.
How internal and external usury are distinguished. 507. b. & 516. a.
External usury exists wherever an express agreement intervenes. 508. a.

<column-break/>

Usury is a mortal sin, contrary to commutative justice <note>Justice regarding the equivalence of exchange between individuals.</note>. 508. a. & to hold the opposite is manifest heresy. 510. a.
It is dangerous to assert that usury is not prohibited by natural law. 508. b. This is shown by many arguments. 510. b. & 511. a. Thus, God has never dispensed from usury, nor is it even possible to do so. Ibid.
The crime of usury is detested by the pages of both Testaments [Old and New]. 509. a. & 510. a.
Usury was permitted to the Jews in a certain way, but not as something lawful; nor was ownership of usurious profit ever granted to them by God. 511. a.
The best explanation of that passage: "You shall not lend at interest to your brother." 512. a.
Usury is permitted by civil law just as prostitutes are <note>Meaning it is legally "tolerated" to prevent greater evils, though still considered morally wrong by the Church.</note>. 512. b. & in what way it is permitted. 513. b. Civil law does not actually oppose canon law by permitting usury. 514. a.
"Usury of usuries" <note>Compound interest.</note> was formerly prohibited with the greatest rigor. 513. a.
To receive or expect anything based on a contract is usury; however, to receive something not by the bond of an agreement, but as a gratuitous repayment to the lender, incurs no stain of usury, just as seeking and demanding friendship and goodwill from a loan does not. 515. a.
He commits usury who, by reason of a loan, includes in the agreement that the borrower must drop a legitimate lawsuit. 516. a.
He is entangled in the vice of usury who, by reason of a loan, demands shameful embraces; but it is otherwise for one who seeks friendship, such as when a woman, overcome by love, acquiesces to a shameful thing. Ibid.
He incurs the stain of usury who forces a borrower to receive either the whole loan or part of it in goods, even if the goods do not exceed a fair price. This is common with merchants lending to the king, resulting in great loss to the soldiers. Ibid.
He commits usury who, by reason of a loan, obligates the borrower to buy, grind, or work, even at a fair price. 517. a.
In a loan, to include in the agreement that which is otherwise justly owed is not usury. Ibid. b.
Whether it is usury to obligate a borrower to lend [in return] by reason of a loan. 519. a.
Whether usury is committed by selling at a higher price when credit is extended. 558. b. & 564. a. See **selling** and **seller**.
He commits usury who does not count the fruits of a pledge <note>If someone gives a field as collateral (a pledge), the lender must subtract the harvest's value from the debt owed.</note> toward the total.

# Alphabetical Index.

...it does not count unless it is a pledge of a fief, or handed over for a dowry to a son-in-law or a widow. 519. b. & 520. b.
**Usury** has the flavor of binding a loan by reason of the loan itself for the purpose of taking a wife. 521. a.
**Usury** by reason of "lost profit" <note>original: "lucri cessantis"; a legal concept where a lender claims compensation for the profit they could have made if their money hadn't been tied up in a loan.</note>. See: profit.
**Usury** is involved in the "mount of piety" <note>original: "mons pietatis"; a charitable institution, often run by the Church, that provided low-interest loans to the poor to prevent them from falling victim to predatory moneylenders.</note>. 538. b.
**Usurious** payment—whether it transfers ownership—an excellent discussion. 526. b.
It is not conducive for all doubts regarding **usuries** to be defined by the Church. 540. b.

### Mental Usury
How it differs from external [usury]. 507. b. & 516. a.
An excellent discussion on mental usury <note>Mental usury refers to the internal sin of intending to profit from a loan, even if no interest is explicitly charged in the contract.</note>. 530. a.
**Mental usury**: how it differs from mental simony <note>simonia: the sin of buying or selling sacred things, such as church offices or sacraments.</note>. 532. a.
Restitution for **mental usury**: how and when it is necessary. 530. a. & 531. a.

### Restitution of Usury
It must necessarily be made even if no one asks for it. 510. & 526. a.
Restitution of **usury** is only necessary when something is received specifically by reason of the loan. 522. a.
If things that are consumed by use <note>Such as food or money itself.</note> are extorted through usury, the money-lender gives satisfaction by restoring only as much as he received, along with damages and profit; if it is withheld from another, the fruits [profits] accumulated through those same things by his own industry are free from restitution. 522. a. b. & 528. b. Otherwise, however, in the case of the fruits of a house or an estate extorted through usury. Same place.
Regarding the restitution of usury, not only the usurer, but also the judges who compel the payment of usury, the lawyers who advise it, certain officials, etc., are also held liable if the money-lender does not make restitution. 532. b. On this, see: loan, and lost profit.

### The Usurer
He does not acquire ownership of those things he has scraped together through usury. 527. a. And if the borrower asserts he wishes to transfer the ownership itself, provided he gives it by reason of the loan. 528. a.
The **usurer** becomes the owner of a possession which he bought with usurious money; as a result, he is not bound to restore the things themselves; however, they remain

<column-break/>

liable for the debt. 528. b.
How the goods of a **usurer** are subject to restitution. Same place.
The goods of a **usurer** fall into three different categories. 529. a.
By natural law, all contracts of a **usurer** are valid through which he does not become less capable of paying back the usury. 529. b.
One receiving usurious money or anything else from a usurer through purchase or any other contract is safe in conscience, provided the usurer does not thereby become unable to pay [restitution]. Same place.
To what the heirs of a **usurer** are bound. Same place.
A **usurer** can receive profit from a borrower in many ways. 530. b.
A **usurer** receiving money from a borrower beyond the principal, with whatever evil intent—if the borrower did not give it by reason of the loan—is not bound to restore it, unless perhaps out of an erroneous conscience. 531. a.
To what the accomplices and officials of a **usurer** are bound. 532. a.
It is not permitted to induce a usurer who is not ready to lend under usury, but it is permitted to receive a loan under usury from one who is ready. 533. b. & 534. b.
A **usurer** who binds a borrower, by reason of a loan, to enter into a contract of partnership or insurance, commits usury. 563. a.
Canon law <note>original: "ius canonicum"; the body of laws and regulations made by Church authority.</note> both attacks **usurers** with many reproaches and piles on several punishments. 514. a.

### Use
Whether "use" is distinguished from "ownership" in things consumed by use is debated at length. 281. b.
The **use** of edible things and utensils is distinguished in a certain way from ownership. 282. b.
The **use** of things is twofold: of law and of fact. 282. a.
It is not permitted to receive anything for the use of a vessel or a sacred chalice, although the Church may lease or sell the item itself. 762. a.
To **use** one's own right happens in two ways. 359. a.
